Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: The organocatalytic cascade deprotection/intramolecular aza‑Michael reaction of substrate 5 gave only modest yields and poor enantioselectivity (13 % ee) even when 1 equiv of the chiral phosphoric acid (CPA) I was used; higher loadings did not improve the outcome.
Solution_Description: Replacing the expensive CPA I with cheap l‑(+)-tartaric acid (acid II) afforded quantitative conversion of the cascade (yield ≈ 100 %) although the ee remained low; this change demonstrated that a simple, inexpensive acid can drive the reaction to completion, eliminating the low‑yield problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acceptable yields were obtained only when at least 1 equiv of I was used. Some enantioselection (13 % ee) was observed… the cheap l-(+)-tartaric acid II furnished the desired product in a quantitative yield, even if with low ee.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: The original process isolated the target enantiomer by supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), which was judged too expensive for commercial‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A fractional‑crystallization resolution using a diastereomeric salt of the racemate with 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid was developed, removing the need for SFC and providing a scalable, cost‑effective purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “Supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) was originally used… estimated too expensive for commercial‑scale production… the chiral resolution… via fractional crystallization allowed to produce (S)‑4 in high enantiomeric purity and good yield.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: Screening of chiral acids/solvents showed that most salt combinations either remained fully soluble or precipitated as near‑racemic mixtures, giving low enantiomeric excess and poor isolation.
Solution_Description: The combination of 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid with acetone (or acetonitrile) gave significant ee (84.9 % and 64.3 %). The optimized crystallization used a 9:1 acetone/water mixture (10 mL g⁻¹), an equimolar amount of resolving agent, and cooling to –15 °C to induce selective precipitation of the desired diastereomer, delivering >99 % ee on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the presence of 2,3‑dibenzoyl‑d‑tartaric acid in acetone or acetonitrile, encouraging chiral purities of 84.91 and 64.30 % … The best results were obtained using 10 mL of acetone/water mixture (9/1 v/v) per gram … isolating the salt at −15/–20 °C … a single crystallization … gave the target with an enantiomer excess higher than 99.0 %.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: Initial racemization attempts led to degradation products when run for extended periods or at high dilution, and the process required an excessively long reaction time to reach completion.
Solution_Description: A robust racemization protocol was established using 0.1 M NaOH (1.8 equiv) in 75 % ethanol (10 vol) at reflux (72 °C) for 8 h, which completed racemization without detectable degradation and could be applied at 164 g and 18.8 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “With NaOH (0.1 M) as the base and 75 % ethanol as the solvent (10 volumes)… the racemization goes to completion in 8 h at reflux temperature (72 °C). Under these conditions formation of degradation products was minimized.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: After chiral resolution, a substantial amount of the undesired (R)‑enantiomer remained in the mother liquor, representing waste and lowering the overall material efficiency.
Solution_Description: An RRR (resolution–racemization–recycle) strategy was implemented: the recovered (R)‑4 was racemized under the optimized conditions and fed back into the resolution step, raising the overall isolated yield of (S)‑4 to 72 % (scale 1) and 71 % (scale 2).
Supporting_Evidence: “The chiral resolution combined with the recovery of the partially resolved (R)‑4 and its racemization constitutes an efficient integrated RRR process… overall yield… 72.8 % for the trial at 164 g scale … 71.3 % for the scale‑up to 18.8 kg.”

Paper Title: Reiterative Chiral Resolution/Racemization/Recycle (RRR Synthesis) for an Effective and Scalable Process for the Enantioselective Synthesis of a Dual IDO1/TDO2 Inhibitor Imidazoisoindole Derivative
Problem_Description: During the crystallization step, heating the suspension above 58 °C caused complete dissolution of the precipitate, preventing solid formation.
Solution_Description: The temperature profile was carefully controlled: heating to 75 °C externally while keeping the internal temperature ≤ 58 °C, followed by a controlled cooling ramp to –15 °C and a 16 h hold, ensuring selective precipitation of the diastereomeric salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction mixture was heated to +75 °C (external temperature; the internal temperature should not exceed 58 °C to avoid complete dissolution of the precipitate)… then cooled from +75 to −15 °C… and left at −15 °C for 16 h.”

Paper Title: Process Development Overcomes a Challenging Pd-Catalyzed C–N Coupling for the Synthesis of RORc Inhibitor

Solution_Description: A high‑throughput screen identified XantPhos‑Pd‑G2 as the optimal precatalyst. Catalyst loading was stepped down to 5 mol % (then to 1 mol % with KOAc additive). K₃PO₄ (anhydrous) was retained as base, dioxane chosen as solvent, reaction concentration increased, and reaction time adjusted (up to 48 h at low loading). The KOAc (up to 20 mol %) restored turnover at 1 mol % Pd, giving >85 % crude HPLC purity and reduced catalyst cost.

Paper Title: Process Development Overcomes a Challenging Pd-Catalyzed C–N Coupling for the Synthesis of RORc Inhibitor

Solution_Description: The free base was converted to the tosylate salt by direct addition of p‑TsOH·H₂O in dioxane, then the crude salt was resuspended in MEK, basified with aqueous NaHCO₃ to regenerate the free base, and finally treated with the solid‑supported metal scavenger MP‑TMT, reducing Pd to 15 ppm. Crystallization from MEK gave the desired polymorph with <2 % epimer impurity and >98 % HPLC purity.

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original discovery route required a copper cocatalyst in the Sonogashira step, which introduced environmentally unfriendly reagents, made copper removal from the product difficult, generated alkyne homocoupling side‑products and demanded strict exclusion of oxygen.
Solution_Description: The copper was eliminated by switching to a copper‑free Sonogashira/Cacchi sequence catalyzed by Pd(OAc)₂/BINAP, providing a cleaner, safer process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of a copper salt as a cocatalyst … has several drawbacks, including the application of environmentally unfriendly reagents, the difficulty of removing the copper species from the products, the formation of undesirable alkyne homocoupling side products, and the necessity of strict exclusion of oxygen.”

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Product 5 showed very poor solubility, forcing the use of a labor‑intensive reversed‑phase chromatography for isolation and making scale‑up unattractive.
Solution_Description: The poor solubility was exploited: after aqueous quench the mixture formed a filterable slurry; the cake was triturated with EtOAc (to strip the side‑product 8) then with CH₂Cl₂ (to remove BINAP/Pd) and finally crystallised from ethanol, giving a chromatography‑free route.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because of the formation of a significant amount of side product 8 and the poor solubility of product 5, its isolation and purification … would depend upon a tedious reversed‑phase chromatographic purification… Quenching the reaction mixture … resulted in the formation of a filterable slurry… Tritration of the filter cake with EtOAc completely removed 8… further trituration with CH₂Cl₂ removed significant amounts of BINAP and the Pd complex… Crystallization from ethanol … gave the pure product.”

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Using Pd(OAc)₂ with PPh₃ or X‑Phos as the ligand gave only traces of the desired product 5 and a complex mixture of side‑products (hydroamidation product 8, homocoupling, etc.).
Solution_Description: A systematic ligand screen identified BINAP as a superior ligand, delivering a clean reaction profile and high conversion to the alkyne intermediate 3.
Supporting_Evidence: “Use of Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %) with either PPh₃ (20 mol %) or X‑Phos (20 mol %) … resulted in a complex mixture, with only trace amounts of the desired product 5 detectable.”

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Elevated temperatures accelerated the formation of the hydro‑amidation side‑product 8, decreasing the isolated yield of the target.
Solution_Description: The temperature was carefully controlled (80–83 °C for the Sonogashira step and 90 °C for the Cacchi step) to minimise side‑product formation while maintaining acceptable reaction rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was completed in 3 h at 90 °C with a 95:5 ratio of product 3 to side product 8… controlling the temperature plays a significant role in limiting the formation of 8.”

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Even after the one‑pot sequence, product isolation required removal of residual BINAP, Pd species and the side‑product 8 without chromatography.
Solution_Description: A step‑wise work‑up using water quench, filtration, EtOAc trituration (to remove 8), CH₂Cl₂ trituration (to strip catalyst residues), and final ethanol crystallisation gave product 5 of >99.6 % HPLC purity with <10 ppm Pd.
Supporting_Evidence: “Quenching … resulted in a filterable slurry… Tritration of the filter cake with EtOAc completely removed 8… Further trituration with CH₂Cl₂ removed significant amounts of BINAP and the Pd complex… Crystallization from ethanol … gave the pure product.”

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: A limited supply of high‑quality racemic BINAP constrained large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The enantiomeric (S)-BINAP was employed for the kilogram‑scale batches, rescuing the process despite the shortage of racemic material.

Paper Title: A Practical Synthesis of the TGFβRI Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Multiple reaction steps required isolation of intermediates, which would have necessitated repeated chromatographic purifications on scale.
Solution_Description: The sequence was telescoped in a single pot: after the copper‑free Sonogashira step the crude alkyne 3 was directly subjected to the Cacchi reaction without isolation, eliminating intermediate work‑ups.
Supporting_Evidence: “A chromatography‑free one‑pot synthesis of 5 via sequential Sonogashira and Cacchi reactions …”

Problem_Description: HPA, the key donor substrate for transketolase, is unstable in water above 25 °C and is traditionally prepared from toxic bromopyruvic acid, giving only moderate yields.  In addition, the presence of formaldehyde (a product of the DTA step) inhibits DAAO and transketolase, and the reaction suffers from pH drift, temperature‑induced degradation of formaldehyde, and overall low conversion when substrates are used at higher concentrations.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the chemical HPA synthesis with an enzymatic, in‑situ generation of HPA from d‑serine using D‑amino‑acid‑oxidase (DAAO).  The cascade was split into a first DTA step (performed separately) followed by simultaneous addition of DAAO and transketolase (order‑and‑rate‑of‑addition).  The process runs at 30 °C (temperature‑optimization) with continuous pH control using KOH, and the intermediate d‑serine is precipitated with methanol and filtered (new‑purification‑procedure) before feeding it into the second step, thus telescoping the three reactions without intermediate isolation (telescope‑directly).
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The main problems with the TK‑catalyzed reaction ... are on one hand the synthesis of HPA, which is commonly obtained from toxic bromopyruvic acid ... and on the other hand its instability in water at temperatures above 25 °C" (Section Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthetic Process for Broflanilide
Problem_Description: The previously reported routes (R1, R2, R3) gave poor overall yields (2.5 % for R1 and 19.6–20.3 % for R2/R3).  R1 required a low‑temperature (‑70 °C) LDA condensation and silica‑gel chromatography; R2 used sodium hydride for bromination, which is hazardous on scale; R3 generated an imide side‑product and employed highly toxic dimethyl‑sulfate for N‑methylation, leading to safety concerns and decomposition of the acid‑chloride intermediate.
Solution_Description: A completely redesigned synthetic sequence was introduced: condensation of 2‑fluoro‑3‑nitrobenzoic acid with aniline in xylene (avoiding LDA), Pd/C‑catalyzed nitro reduction, paraformaldehyde/5 % Pt‑C N‑methylation, acyl‑chloride amidation, and NaBr‑NaClO bromination.  The new route eliminates hazardous reagents, avoids imide formation, and reduces the number of isolations to six steps, giving an overall isolated yield of 60.3 % for broflanilide.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Route R1 successfully provided 1 in a 2.5 % overall yield… however, key intermediate 7 needed to be prepared in the presence of lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) at a low temperature (‑70 °C), and this synthesis required purifications with silica gel chromatography.", "In route R2, the bromination… required the hazardous reagent sodium hydride, which is not always easy to handle on a large scale.", "In route R3… highly toxic dimethyl sulfate (DMS) was employed in the N‑methylation reaction.", "The alternative route… condensation of 2‑fluoro‑3‑nitrobenzoic acid (2) and unbrominated aniline (3) in dichloroethane (EDC) smoothly formed nitroamide 16 (83 % yield). This method avoided the harsh reaction conditions required for the condensation in route R1 and showed no imide generation, providing an ideal path for the development of an alternative route.", "Using paraformaldehyde and Pt/C for N‑methylation and NaBr‑NaClO for bromination increased the industrial suitability of this route.", "The new route… overall yield was 60.3 %."]

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthetic Process for Broflanilide
Problem_Description: The initial condensation of 2‑fluoro‑3‑nitrobenzoic acid with aniline was incomplete after 24 h at reflux in EDC, requiring a much longer reaction time.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was raised to the reflux temperature of toluene (110 °C) and later to 100 °C in xylene, which completed the condensation in 5 h with >96 % isolated yield.

Under the optimal conditions, the reaction was completed after 5 h."]

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthetic Process for Broflanilide
Problem_Description: During the bromination step, the target product showed very low solubility in toluene, which required a large amount of solvent to keep the product in solution and complicated the work‑up.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane (DCM) was selected as the bromination solvent; it gave high conversion (96 % yield) and avoided the precipitation issue.  The final product was also recrystallized from 98 % aqueous methanol, a solvent that dissolves the product at elevated temperature but allows clean crystallization on cooling.

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthetic Process for Broflanilide

Problem_Description: The original “neat” procedure (no added solvent) required dosing DCTDA into morpholine at 95‑110 °C. The sulfone → sulfoxide → SNAr sequence eliminated the DIBAL reduction and the Heck step (new route). Reaction stoichiometry was tuned (e.g., reducing SOCl₂ from 3.1 → 3.0 eq) to suppress chloro impurity formation. Longer SNAr times were mitigated by improved agitation, temperature control (80 °C) and avoidance of agglomerates (mass‑transfer optimisation). Paper Title: Reductive Amination Bicarbonate Quench: Gas-Evolving Waste Stream Near-Miss Investigation
Problem_Description: Slow reaction of boric acid with excess potassium bicarbonate in the quenched aqueous waste generates carbon‑dioxide over days, causing internal pressure buildup and deformation of the steel waste drum.
Solution_Description: Acidify the aqueous waste stream prior to drumming (lower pH eliminates the boric‑acid/ bicarbonate reaction, preventing CO₂ generation).
Supporting_Evidence: The bulging drum likely contained carbon‑dioxide gas only and no appreciable hydrogen gas. The gas evolution could be a result of boric acid slowly reacting with excess KHCO₃ to generate CO₂ after the drum was bunged. After a period of 2 days, an increase in the internal pressure of ~10 psig was observed. A mixture of boric acid and aqueous potassium bicarbonate, after ~48 h, showed an internal pressure increase of ~9 psig. This side reaction to slowly generate carbon‑dioxide in stored waste drums was unforeseen. A process change was recommended to include acidification of aqueous waste streams prior to drumming, storage, and removal from site. To avoid a potential hazard of this type, waste streams from reductive amination processes quenched with bicarbonate should be acidified prior to storage.

Paper Title: Reductive Amination Bicarbonate Quench: Gas-Evolving Waste Stream Near-Miss Investigation

Solution_Description: Charge STAB in three aliquots and hold the reaction overnight (~17 h) to allow safe decomposition of excess STAB, attenuating heat and gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: An overall moderate exotherm of ~133 kJ/mol was observed. Low‑level hydrogen gas evolution was observed during the hold period due to the slow reaction of excess STAB with residual water. The total hydrogen gas output observed represented 88 % of the theoretical amount. STAB was charged in three aliquots to attenuate heat and gas output and the reaction mixture was held overnight (∼17 h).

Paper Title: Reductive Amination Bicarbonate Quench: Gas-Evolving Waste Stream Near-Miss Investigation
Problem_Description: Reducing the post‑STAB hold from overnight to 60 min (to meet a two‑shift schedule) increased the amount of hydrogen gas evolved during the subsequent bicarbonate quench, raising safety risk.
Solution_Description: Restore a longer hold (overnight) or otherwise adjust the timing/order of the quench to keep hydrogen evolution minimal.
Supporting_Evidence: The shortened hold period was necessary to reduce the overall cycle time, thereby accommodating a two‑shift operation. Following the shortened hold period post STAB addition, the preponderance of hydrogen gas evolved during the bicarbonate addition. Reaction mixture was held for 60 min (vs. overnight) ... resulting in increased hydrogen gas evolution.

Paper Title: Reductive Amination Bicarbonate Quench: Gas-Evolving Waste Stream Near-Miss Investigation

Solution_Description: Reduce the amount of bicarbonate to the stoichiometric minimum or replace it with an alternative quench (e.g., carbonate, organic base, or water) that does not leave excess base capable of reacting later.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction mixture was quenched with methanol (1.5 vol) and aqueous KHCO₃ (15 wt %, 3.5 equiv). It was hypothesized that the gas evolution could be a result of boric acid slowly reacting with excess KHCO₃ to generate CO₂ after the drum was bunged. Other options considered were the use of self‑venting waste drums and further process development to eliminate the excess of bicarbonate used.

Paper Title: Reductive Amination Bicarbonate Quench: Gas-Evolving Waste Stream Near-Miss Investigation

Supporting_Evidence: The drummed, aqueous waste stream from a reductive amination process generated unexpected internal pressure, resulting in significant deformation of a mild steel drum during temporary storage. Other options considered were the use of self‑venting waste drums and further process development to eliminate the excess of bicarbonate used.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: The first‑generation route required multiple column‑chromatography purifications, especially after the Suzuki coupling (2 + 3 → 4) and after the Sonogashira coupling, which made the process labor‑intensive and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: A four‑step synthesis of the boronate 3 was developed from inexpensive benzoic‑acid derivative 10 that required **no column chromatography**, and the Suzuki product 4 was purified by a simple aqueous acidic wash after treatment with N,N‑dimethyl‑ethylenediamine, eliminating the need for chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “the requirement of multiple column chromatography purifications”, “a challenging purification following the Suzuki cross‑coupling (2 + 3 → 4)”, “The four‑step sequence did not require any column chromatography and was later used for the multikilogram synthesis of boronate 3”, “the crude reaction mixture ... was then treated with N,N‑dimethyl ethylenediamine… the resulting adduct was removed by aqueous acidic washing.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: Boronate 3 (the pinacolboronate used in the Suzuki step) was expensive and of limited commercial availability, inflating the cost of the multikilogram synthesis.
Solution_Description: The authors synthesized boronate 3 from cheap, readily available benzoic‑acid‑derived 10 via amide → nitrile → Miyaura borylation, removing the dependence on a costly commercial boronate and reducing overall material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “the high cost of boronate 3… we sought to synthesize it from readily available and low‑priced starting materials”, “benzoic acid derivative 10… was converted to benzamide 11… then to nitrile 12… finally the desired boronate 3 was obtained using Miyaura borylation… did not require any column chromatography and was later used for the multikilogram synthesis of boronate 3.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: The Sonogashira coupling of 4 to give 5 showed poor reproducibility on scale, and the Suzuki coupling suffered from formation of a second coupling by‑product (13) because of the low solubility of 2 relative to product 4.
Solution_Description: For the Suzuki reaction, the crude mixture was treated with N,N‑dimethyl‑ethylenediamine to selectively quench unreacted 2, and the product was isolated after simple aqueous work‑up; for the Sonogashira step, the authors switched from TMS‑acetylene to the more stable TIPS‑acetylene, which eliminated partial deprotection and provided a robust, reproducible coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: “poor reproducibility of the Sonogashira coupling (4 → 5)”, “propensity of product 4 to undergo a second Suzuki coupling, resulting in the formation of by‑product 13… partly because poor solubility of 2…”, “switching to TIPS‑acetylene led to stable 14, which was isolated via recrystallization”, “The crude reaction mixture containing by‑product 13 … was then treated with N,N‑dimethyl ethylenediamine… the more electrophilic 2 reacted preferentially… and the resulting adduct was removed by aqueous acidic washing.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: The use of TBAF (a corrosive fluoride source) for TIPS deprotection and the isolation/purification of the azide intermediate 9 posed safety hazards at large scale.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a buffered, catalytic TIPS‑deprotection using only 10 mol % TBAF with water or n‑Bu₄NOH/K₂HPO₄, avoiding excess fluoride; the azide 9 was generated **in situ** and directly used in the CuAAC step, eliminating the need to isolate a potentially explosive azide.
Supporting_Evidence: “use of a corrosive fluoride reagent in the silyl‑ether cleavage (5 → 6)”, “We were interested to find that removal of the TIPS group could be achieved by using only 10 mol % TBAF and water as an additive… Tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (20 mol %) and K₂HPO₄ buffer were found to be optimum…”, “To alleviate the safety concern associated with isolation of large quantities of azide 9, it was generated in situ and used directly in the subsequent CuAAC reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: The azidation/CuAAC sequence suffered from phase‑separation and impurity formation when performed in non‑homogeneous media, complicating work‑up and purification.
Solution_Description: THF was chosen as the reaction solvent for both the azide formation and CuAAC steps, giving a **homogeneous mixture** that facilitated large‑scale manufacturing and allowed simple precipitation and silica/charcoal treatment to afford the final product with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “development of this successful protocol was enabled using tetrahydrofuran (THF) as a reaction solvent, which was found to be efficient in both azidation and CuAAC reactions… THF gave a homogeneous reaction mixture, which is preferred for large‑scale manufacturing.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: The Suzuki coupling in the first‑generation route gave only 28 % isolated yield of 4 and required chromatographic removal of by‑product 13, limiting overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: In the second‑generation synthesis, the pyrimidine core was built **de novo** via condensation of guanidine with β‑keto ester 20, a regiospecific route that avoided the problematic Suzuki step, gave 50 % higher yield of 4 and required **no column chromatography**.
Supporting_Evidence: “the requirement of multiple column chromatography purifications… poor yield of the Suzuki coupling…”, “we developed a de novo approach, in which the pyrimidine ring was constructed through condensation of guanidine with β‑keto ester 20… unlike the previous method, the new approach is regiospecific and eliminates problematic by‑product 13, allowing easy isolation of 21 in excellent yield without chromatographic purification… This second‑generation route offers 50 % higher yield of 4 and eliminates two palladium‑catalyzed steps.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Practical Synthesis of AB928, a Dual A
Problem_Description: Intermediate 6 tended to dimerize to a Michael‑addition product 15 under the basic conditions used for TIPS deprotection, leading to impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Buffered deprotection (TBAF with acetic acid, or catalytic TBAF with water and n‑Bu₄NOH/K₂HPO₄) suppressed the formation of dimer 15 by maintaining a controlled pH and avoiding strong base excess, delivering clean 6 in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “susceptibility of 6 toward dimerization to form putative 15 through Michael addition under the basic reaction conditions… formation of 15 was completely inhibited when TIPS deprotection was carried out using TBAF and acetic acid as a buffer… a longer reaction time was required… removal of the TIPS group could be achieved by using only 10 mol % TBAF and water as an additive… Tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (20 mol %) and K₂HPO₄ buffer were found to be optimum.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Traditional decarboxylative bromination requires stoichiometric amounts of toxic heavy‑metal reagents (Ag, Hg, Tl, Pb) and large excesses of Br₂, which pose safety hazards, waste‑disposal problems, and high cost on scale.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free/Br₂‑free protocol was developed using inexpensive, stable KBr as the bromine source and commercially available (diacetoxyiodo)‑benzene, eliminating hazardous metals and reducing reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
“However, it traditionally requires a stoichiometric amount of precious metal or toxic metal reagent, such as Ag, Hg, Tl, or Pb, as well as multiple equivalents of Br₂, which may present a waste disposal problem if the reaction is performed on a large scale.”
“... using commercially available (diacetoxyiodo)‑benzene and potassium bromide, one of the most stable and cheapest bromine sources in nature.”
“The present method features a metal‑free/Br₂‑free system, mild reaction conditions, …”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Initial screening gave only 42 % conversion of cyclopropanecarboxylic acid to the bromide, indicating low yield under the first set of conditions.
Solution_Description: Increasing the equivalents of (diacetoxyiodo)‑benzene and KBr (1.5 eq 1 / 1.7 eq KBr) raised the isolated yield to 71–80 %, while maintaining the same reaction time (17–22 h).
Supporting_Evidence:
“The reaction of 1.0 equiv of 1 and 1.1 equiv of KBr … provided 42 % conversion of cyclopropanecarboxylic acid … into cyclopropyl bromide (3).”
“The use of small excess amounts of 1 and KBr resulted in higher conversion of 3 (entries 5 and 6).”
“Entry 5 (1.5/1.7) gave 71 % yield; Entry 6 (1.5/1.7) gave 80 % yield.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Replacing KBr with Bu₄NBr to avoid a heterogeneous system gave a dramatically reduced yield (5 %), showing that the bromide source must be well‑mixed and soluble.
Solution_Description: The reaction was reverted to using solid KBr, which dissolves sufficiently in the chosen solvents and provides a homogeneous reaction mixture, restoring high yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The chemical yield of 3 was drastically decreased to 5 % when we used Bu₄NBr as the Br⁻ source in order to avoid a heterogeneous system (entry 3).”
“... 1.0 equiv of 1 and 1.1 equiv of KBr in CH₂Cl₂ at room temperature … gave substantially higher yields.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Acetonitrile and ethyl acetate proved inferior solvents, delivering low conversion, likely due to poor solubility of the hypervalent iodine reagent and/or the substrate.
Solution_Description: Switching to dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂) or trifluorotoluene (PhCF₃) dramatically improved reaction efficiency, giving the best yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Examination of several solvents showed CH₂Cl₂ or PhCF₃ (entry 4) to be greatly superior to acetonitrile or ethyl acetate.”
“Table 1 … entry 4 … 45 % yield with PhCF₃.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Addition of one equivalent of water almost completely shut down the reaction, indicating extreme moisture sensitivity that could lead to reagent decomposition.
Solution_Description: Reactions are performed under dry conditions (no added water) and using anhydrous reagents; the process tolerates air but excludes moisture to maintain activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
“While no decrease in the yield of 3 was observed when the reaction was conducted under air in an open vessel, addition of 1 equiv of water almost shut down the reaction.”
“Reactions were performed … at room temperature under air …”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: No product formation was observed in the dark, demonstrating that the reaction is light‑dependent and would be inconsistent without controlled illumination.
Solution_Description: The reaction is carried out under weak fluorescent ceiling light or, for higher efficiency, under a blue‑LED (λ = 455 nm) source, ensuring reliable radical initiation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“No reaction occurred in the dark (entry 7).”
“… irradiation with blue LED light (λₘₐₓ = 455 nm) promoted the reaction (entry 8).”
“The mixture was stirred … in the presence of usual laboratory illumination with a standard ceiling fluorescent light fitting.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: The hypervalent iodine reagent PhIF₂ can etch glassware in the presence of moisture, posing a safety risk on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Large‑scale reactions using PhIF₂ are performed in Teflon/PFA apparatus to avoid glass corrosion and exposure to moisture.
Supporting_Evidence: “CAUTION: PhIF₂ may etch glassware in the presence of moisture, so large‑scale operation should be carried out in Teflon/PFA apparatus.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: The commercial hypervalent iodine reagent (diacetoxyiodo)‑benzene can be relatively expensive for gram‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: The difluoro‑iodobenzene reagent (35) was prepared via the cost‑effective Gilmour method, providing a cheaper alternative that also gave higher reactivity for certain substrates.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Use of (difluoroiodo)‑benzene (35) instead of 1 improved the system dramatically in some cases, probably because of its facile ligand exchange ability.”
“For larger‑scale reactions, we found that 35 separately synthesized by means of the more cost‑effective Gilmour method was applicable without a significant decrease in yield.”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Some carboxylic acids showed poor solubility in PhCF₃, limiting substrate scope.
Solution_Description: For such substrates the solvent was switched to CH₂Cl₂, which provided sufficient solubility and maintained high yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
“In the case of acids with poor solubility in PhCF₃, CH₂Cl₂ was used as the solvent.”
“... CH₂Cl₂ or PhCF₃ (entry 4) to be greatly superior …”

Paper Title: Decarboxylative Bromination of Sterically Hindered Carboxylic Acids with Hypervalent Iodine(III) Reagents
Problem_Description: Radical scavenger 9,10‑dihydroanthracene completely suppressed product formation, indicating that inadvertent addition of scavengers would abort the reaction.
Solution_Description: The protocol expressly avoids the presence of radical scavengers and maintains a reductant‑free environment to preserve the radical chain mechanism.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of the radical scavenger 9,10‑dihydroanthracene shut down the reaction (entry 9), supporting the free radical mechanism.”

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Previously reported batch syntheses of p‑mentha‑2,8‑dien‑1‑ol (1) gave overall isolated yields lower than 20 % and poor stereo‑/regio‑selectivity, making the intermediate difficult to obtain on a useful scale.
Solution_Description: The authors moved the photo‑oxygenation to a home‑made continuous‑flow micro‑chip reactor (tube‑in‑tube gas‑transfer module) and employed a CH₃CN : CH₂Cl₂ (3 : 1) solvent mixture, which together provided a high surface‑to‑volume ratio, improved photon transfer and better O₂ solubility, delivering quantitative conversion (>99 %) and a 48 % selectivity for 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the approaches already described present overall yields lower than 20%, as well as low stereo‑ and regio‑selectivity.” (Intro, p. 2) ; “…the key intermediate 1 was obtained with quantitative conversion (>99 %) and moderate selectivity (48 %) after 2 h, using meso‑tetraphenyl‑porphyrin (TPP) as a sensitizer and CH₃CN:CH₂Cl₂ as a solvent mixture.” (Results, p. 4) ; “Continuous‑flow reactors have a high surface/volume ratio that improves photon transfer and increases the homogeneity of radiation through the reactor.” (Intro, p. 3)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Batch photo‑oxidations required large excesses of the photosensitizer (up to 0.4 mol %) and long irradiation times (≈2 h) to reach acceptable conversions, increasing material cost and reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: In the flow system the sensitizer loading was lowered to 0.1 mM (≈0.01 mol %), and the intensified photon flux in the micro‑reactor allowed full conversion within minutes, dramatically cutting reagent cost and reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the use of large amounts of sensitizer, and results in non‑quantitative conversions of the substrate.” (Intro, p. 3) ; “…using a low concentration of TPP (0.1 mM) and requiring 20 min for total conversion.” (Abstract) ; “…with a low concentration of TPP (0.1 mM)… 20 min for total conversion.” (Results, p. 4)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Hydroperoxide products generated during the photo‑oxygenation are thermally unstable and decompose under the high‑temperature conditions of GC‑MS analysis, hindering accurate conversion measurements.
Solution_Description: Before GC analysis the reaction mixture was treated with a stoichiometric amount of triphenylphosphine (Ph₃P) to reduce the hydroperoxides to the corresponding alcohols, stabilising the analytes for reliable quantification.
Supporting_Evidence: “…due to the thermal instability of hydroperoxide products in GC analysis, the reaction mixture was reduced using a Ph₃P solution.” (Results, p. 4) ; “The reaction mixture was then reduced using Ph₃P (1 equiv) in dichloromethane (5 mL).” (Experimental, General Procedures for Batch Reactions)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Insufficient dissolution of O₂ in the reaction medium limited the singlet‑oxygen concentration, reducing conversion rates in batch experiments.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system of CH₃CN : CH₂Cl₂ (3 : 1) was adopted to raise O₂ solubility, and a tube‑in‑tube membrane reactor was employed to continuously saturate the liquid phase with O₂ at 100 psi, ensuring a homogeneous gas‑liquid mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “To improve the oxygen solubility, mixtures of dichloro‑methane–acetonitrile (CH₃CN:CH₂Cl₂) were also tested.” (Results, p. 4) ; “…a tube‑in‑tube reactor was employed as a gas‑transfer module, affording the reaction medium saturated in O₂ as well as a homogeneous system.” (Results, p. 5) ; “These studies were initiated using a 1000 μL microchip reactor… pumping a solution… and a white LED… to perform the photo‑oxidation without the need for a using a mass flow controller and increasing the gas mixing, a tube‑in‑tube reactor was employed as a gas‑transfer module.” (Results, p. 5)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: The conversion of limonene did not increase proportionally with longer residence times in flow; beyond ~7.5 min the conversion plateaued, leading to inefficient use of reactor volume.
Solution_Description: Systematic residence‑time screening identified optimal short residence times (2–5 min) that maximised productivity (up to 1.6 μmol·min⁻¹ with white LEDs, 2.9 μmol·min⁻¹ with blue LEDs) while maintaining high conversion, thereby reducing unnecessary reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “A nonlinear dependence of conversion and residence time was observed… no significant differences… at residence times greater than 7.5 min.” (Results, p. 6) ; Table 1 and Table 2 showing productivity peaks at 2–5 min residence times (Entries 1–2) (Tables 1‑2) ; “high productivity values were obtained in up to 5 min of reaction time (1.6 μmol·min⁻¹).” (Results, p. 6)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Using a white LED as the light source yielded modest conversion and productivity compared with the same power blue LED, indicating sub‑optimal photon absorption.
Solution_Description: The light source was switched from a white LED (6500 K) to a blue LED (100 W), matching the absorption maximum of TPP and doubling both conversion and productivity (up to 2.9 μmol·min⁻¹ at 2 min residence).
Supporting_Evidence: “To our delight, an important improvement of the chemical rate could be obtained by simply changing the light source to blue LEDs. Compared with the white LED lamp, both conversion and productivity values increased by 2 times…” (Results, p. 7) ; “…examining the match of the visible absorption spectrum of TPP… we decided to test how the use of blue LEDs (100 W) would improve the productivity…” (Results, p. 7)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: At high substrate concentrations (400 mM) the conversion was low at short residence times, limiting productivity despite the desire for higher throughput.
Solution_Description: By extending residence times and maintaining the low sensitizer loading (0.1 mM), the authors achieved quantitative conversion even at 400 mM limonene, attaining up to 491.6 μmol·min⁻¹ productivity while using ~30‑fold less TPP than literature values.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 3 entries 6–10 show gradual increase in conversion and productivity with longer residence times at 400 mM; “total conversions were achieved for the higher concentration of 2 using up to 20 times lower content of TPP compared with initial parameters.” (Results, p. 8) ; “…lower conversion and productivity were achieved for a concentration of 400 mM and with the same residence time. Nevertheless, with reaction times above 5 min, higher conversions and productivities could be observed.” (Results, p. 8)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Selectivity toward the desired allylic alcohol 1 was only moderate (≈48 %) under standard conditions, limiting the amount of usable product per batch.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to –20 °C using a double‑wall jacketed glass reactor, which shifted the product distribution toward the target compound, achieving up to 66 % selectivity while maintaining high productivity (580.8 μmol·min⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: “…temperature‑controlled home‑made photoreactor… at –20 °C… the decrease of the reaction temperature shifted the selectivity toward the desired compound by up to 66 %.” (Results, p. 9) ; Table 5 entries 1–3 show increased selectivity (55 % → 66 %) with low temperature (Results, p. 9) ; “the reaction progressed slowly and required longer irradiation times to give quantitative conversion values… although under these reaction conditions low conversion values were obtained, the decrease of the reaction temperature shifted the selectivity toward the desired compound by up to 66 %.” (Results, p. 9)

Paper Title: Process Intensification for Obtaining a Cannabidiol Intermediate by Photo-oxygenation of Limonene under Continuous-Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Scaling the process from the 1 mL microchip to gram‑scale required a larger reactor volume while preserving conversion, photon distribution, and avoiding sensitizer precipitation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 30 mL PFA coil (Setup 3) was constructed and irradiated with higher‑power blue LEDs (124 W). The same tube‑in‑tube O₂ saturation strategy was retained, delivering quantitative conversion and a productivity of up to 491.6 μmol·min⁻¹ without any sensitizer precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “These reactions were performed by using a PFA coil… irradiated by blue LEDs (124 W)… achieving productivity values of up to 491.6 μmol·min⁻¹.” (Results, p. 9) ; “It should be noted that, even with an increase of 30 times the volume of photoreactor, setup 3 delivers the desired product with quantitative conversion, showing the efficiency of the LED arrangement to homogeneously irradiate the reaction. Furthermore, no precipitation of sensitizer was observed in any tested conditions.” (Results, p. 9)

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: Recovery of rhodium from the homogeneous batch process is poor (≈70 % recovery) and requires incineration of large volumes of organic solvent, generating hazardous waste and making the metal expensive to recycle.
Solution_Description: Immobilize rhodium(II) on a polymeric support and run the cyclization in a packed‑bed fixed‑column reactor, allowing direct catalyst removal and incineration of a solid support instead of solvent‑borne metal waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “One drawback to large‑scale implementation of this chemistry as a traditional batch reaction with a homogeneous catalyst is the difficulty recovering valuable rhodium… recovery is typically about 70 % and requires incineration of vast quantities of organic solvent.”; “We were therefore attracted to the idea of immobilizing rhodium‑(II) on a polymeric support in a fixed‑bed reactor to facilitate recovery.”; “The solid support can be incinerated directly… higher metal recovery: >90 % for the flow process versus ∼70 % for the batch process.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: In the flow cyclization, feeding ZnBr₂ together with substrate caused rapid rhodium leaching from the resin, deactivating the catalyst and lowering conversion.

Supporting_Evidence: “When ZnBr₂ was included in the feed solution… rapid leaching of rhodium from the resin occurred, effectively deactivating it.”; “…allowed targeting of residence times measured in minutes… this in turn enabled the addition of ZnBr₂ in MeOAc solution after the cyclization was complete rather than feeding it into the reactor along with 2, mitigating leaching.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: The cyclization reaction is gas‑liquid‑solid; uncontrolled temperature rise (ΔH = 96.4 kJ mol⁻¹) and pressure drop in a tall packed column risk reactor blockage and safety issues.
Solution_Description: Select a reaction temperature window of 45–51 °C (below the boiling point of methyl acetate) to balance reaction rate with heat removal, and limit column height to 320–600 mm to keep pressure drop ≤0.15 MPa.
Supporting_Evidence: “According to calorimetry results, the exothermic heat of the reaction is 96.4 kJ mol⁻¹… we selected the reaction temperature range of 45–51 °C.”; “When the height of the reaction column is over 320 mm, the pressure reaches 0.15 MPa… a sharp increase… leading to blocking. Therefore, the optimal height… was designed as 320–600 mm.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: In the phosphorylation stage, poor mixing in the plug‑flow reactor gave only 91 % solution yield at 10 min residence time, with Reynolds numbers in the laminar‑to‑turbulent transition.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Install a static mixer upstream of the PFR to promote rapid, uniform mixing; this allowed reduction of residence time to 5 min while achieving >95 % yield even at turbulent flow (Re ≈ 13 800).
Supporting_Evidence: “Mixing can be an issue in PFRs… the highest solution yield of the product was 91 % at 10 min… with a Reynolds number of <4300.”; “Therefore, a static mixer was introduced… the residence time was reduced to 5 min and gave a solution yield of >95 % with the well‑mixed process.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: Longer residence times (13–20 min) in the cyclization column caused a decline in product yield from ~96 % down to 84 %, decreasing throughput.
Solution_Description: Optimize residence time to 7–12 min (with temperature 44–51 °C) which gives >97 % area% of product, balancing conversion speed with minimal side‑reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the continuous reaction was carried out… the area % of the product at 45 °C was only 85.5 % when the residence time was 5 min. When the residence time was in the range of 7–12 min, the yield of the products increased to approximately 97 %… a longer residence time has an adverse influence on the yield… decreases from 96 % to 84.3 % for residence times of 13–20 min.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: Suspension polymerization of the resin produced a broad bead‑size distribution, leading to high pressure drops in the packed column and potential safety hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adjust the organic‑solvent‑to‑water mass ratio during polymerization (Table 2) to obtain a narrower bead size distribution while keeping polymer loading constant, thereby reducing pressure drop and improving column flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “Suspension polymerization performed in this manner often leads to a broad bead size distribution… disadvantageous for use in packed columns because it leads to high pressure drops.”; “An examination of the effect of the organic solvent mass ratio on the particle size distribution was therefore performed (Table 2). Similar particle size distributions and metal loadings were obtained across the ranges investigated, indicating that the polymerization process tolerated variation without a substantial impact on the performance of the resulting resin.”

Paper Title: Semicontinuous Process for GMP Manufacture of a Carbapenem Intermediate via Carbene Insertion Using an Immobilized Rhodium Catalyst
Problem_Description: Early catalyst formulations (7a, 7b, 7e, 7f, 7g) showed rapid activity loss after one or few runs due to leaching or poor polymer properties, leading to lower yields and inconsistent performance.
Solution_Description: Select catalyst 7d (derived from monomer 4c and cross‑linker 5c) which exhibits excellent swelling (4.5 mL g⁻¹), low Rh leaching (≈1 % / run), and can be reused six times with unchanged activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Catalysts prepared from monomer and cross‑linker with an ester linkage… catalyst 7a provided the insertion product in 79 % yield… both 7a and 7b could be used only once because of attenuating activity… catalyst 7d, which could be used six times without appreciable activity loss, with the Rh leaching dropping to 0.99 % per run.”; “We attribute the performance of catalyst 7d to its excellent swelling characteristics (4.5 mL/g in MeOAc at room temperature).”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: When the optimized small‑scale reaction (magnetic stir bar, 50 mg) was transferred to a 5 g scale in a round‑bottom flask with an overhead stirrer, conversion dropped to ~21 % and a large amount of unreacted starting material remained. The poor conversion was traced to insufficient attrition and suspension of the manganese dust; the overhead stirrer did not grind the particles as effectively as the magnetic stir bar.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team added chlorotriethylsilane (TESCl) (0.5 equiv) as a functional additive to chemically activate the manganese surface, and delivered it in five 0.1‑equiv portionwise additions while keeping the reaction temperature ≤ 40 °C. This avoided the need for mechanical grinding and provided reliable activation of the manganese. In parallel, they increased the agitation speed (≥ 500 rpm for PBT agitator, 80 rpm for anchor agitator) based on Dynochem modelling to ensure solid suspension, and employed a slow, controlled addition protocol to manage the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the reaction proceeded only to ∼21% conversion… we attributed the superior performance on the smaller scale to a possible grinding effect of the magnetic stir bar on the manganese.”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: Anhydrous NiCl₂ showed very low solubility in DMF, which limited its effectiveness as a catalyst despite comparable activity to the hydrated form.
Solution_Description: NiCl₂·DME was selected as the catalyst precursor because its coordinated DME ligand improves solubility in DMF, allowing higher catalytic turnover.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The low solubility of anhydrous NiCl₂ in DMF favored the use of NiCl₂·DME for further optimization.”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: Using zinc as the terminal reductant increased the formation of the protodehalogenated side‑product (compound 11), thereby lowering the isolated yield of the desired cross‑coupled product.
Solution_Description: Replacing zinc with manganese dust and adding TESCl as a silicon‑based activator suppressed the protodehalogenation pathway, improving product conversion and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of zinc as the terminal reductant led to higher levels of the protodehalogenated product 11.”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: Addition of HCl as a Mn‑activating agent caused rapid gas evolution and frothing, which would pose a handling risk and operational difficulty at multikilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The researchers substituted HCl with chlorotriethylsilane (TESCl), which provided comparable activation without frothing or gas evolution, thereby improving safety on scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The addition of HCl led to ca. 75% product formation… significant gas evolution and frothing were observed… would present a scale‑up challenge.”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: Calorimetry revealed the reductive coupling is thermally accumulative with an adiabatic temperature rise of 92 °C; addition of TESCl produced a sharp spike in heat flow accounting for 18 % of the total heat released, creating a potential runaway hazard.
Solution_Description: TESCl was added portionwise with strict temperature control (maintaining ≤ 40 °C) to dampen the exotherm, and the overall reaction temperature was kept low throughout the 16‑hour run to stay within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction was found to be thermally accumulative with an adiabatic temperature rise of 92 °C… the addition of TESCl… led to an immediate spike in heat flow accounting for 18 % of the total heat evolved.”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: In a 2 L lab reactor equipped with an anchor agitator, the manganese particles settled at lower agitation rates (≤ 380 rpm), leading to incomplete conversion (13 % unreacted starting material).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Supporting_Evidence: • “While Dynochem calculations predicted a Zwietering N_JS of 311 rpm for the 2 L reactor with an anchor agitator, attempts to lower the agitation rate to 380 rpm led to incomplete reactions (13% unreacted 1).”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: Scale‑up to 600 L pilot‑plant reactor using an anchor agitator required a very low agitation speed (≈ 80 rpm) to avoid vortexing, yet still needed sufficient solid suspension; initially, insufficient mixing would have caused low conversion.

Solution_Description: Using a combination of tip‑speed and power‑per‑mass scaling criteria, an operating speed of 80 rpm was selected—well below the agitator’s maximum but enough to keep manganese suspended, delivering > 98 % conversion on a 7 kg batch.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Under these conditions, a 7 kg batch carried out in the 600 L Hastelloy reactor at an agitation rate of 80 rpm proceeded to completion (1.3% of 1 remaining).”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of an Ni(II)-Catalyzed Reductive Cross-Coupling of Substituted 2‑Chloropyridine and Ethyl 3‑Chloropropanoate
Problem_Description: After reaction, the crude mixture contained insoluble manganese residues and trace dimer impurity (compound 10) that required removal to achieve API‑grade purity.

Supporting_Evidence: • “The mixture was filtered through Celite to remove the insoluble manganese residues… Norite charcoal treatment was performed for 16 h… to effectively purge dimer impurity 10 and also to reduce the residual metal content in the isolated product.”

Problem_Description: An explosion risk exists when performing aerobic oxidations with the MC (Co‑Mn‑Br) catalyst in conventional batch reactors because the reaction is highly exothermic and involves a flammable oxygen/organic gas mixture.

Supporting_Evidence: “However, there is an explosion risk when aerobic oxidations are performed in batch reactors with MC catalysts.”; “Many of the safety and process challenges involved in performing gas–liquid aerobic oxidations in batch reactors can be overcome by employing continuous flow microchannel reactor technology…”; “chip‑based reactors offer good heat transfer capacity due to their exceedingly high surface‑to‑volume ratios…"

Problem_Description: When conversion of o‑chlorotoluene (OCT) becomes too high, the desired o‑chlorobenzaldehyde (OCBD) is further oxidised to o‑chlorobenzoic acid (OCBA), lowering the selectivity and overall yield of OCBD.

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: The aryllithium intermediate (3) is highly unstable at the temperatures required for batch processing and forms a solid precipitate that fouls reactors, leading to blockages and loss of material.

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: THIQ 6 is isolated as a thick oil that cannot be crystallized, making isolation and impurity removal difficult.

Supporting_Evidence: “THIQ 6 was isolated as a thick oil and could not be crystallized. This problem was quickly solved when a small screen of acids identified multiple crystalline salts; we chose to proceed with a tosylate salt (13), which could be isolated in good yield and provided significant improvement in d.r. from the crude mixture of isomers.”

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: Heck coupling followed by hydrogenolysis of the benzyl ether is slow; prolonged hydrogenolysis erodes the diastereomeric ratio and the piperidine moiety poisons the Pd catalyst.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was reordered: the benzyl ether was removed early using BCl₃ (in DCM) before Heck coupling, eliminating the slow hydrogenolysis step and avoiding catalyst poisoning.
Supporting_Evidence: “In practice, the olefin was easily reduced, but the cleavage of the benzyl ether was slow… erosion of the d.r. was observed with prolonged hydrogenolysis… It was proposed that a redox cycle was operative with Pd effectively oxidizing the benzylic center and then reducing it… Addition of acid improved the rate of the hydrogenolysis… As a result, the benzyl ether would be removed prior to side‑chain introduction… BCl₃ was used for deprotection and gave clean conversion.”

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: Isolation of the tosylate salt (13) showed variable yields and purity during technology transfer, leading to inconsistent material quality.

(59:1 vs 15:1).”

Problem_Description: Large‑scale use of n‑BuLi (in hexanes) presents safety concerns due to its pyrophoric nature and the exothermic lithiation step.

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: The deprotection of the benzyl ether using BCl₃ in various solvents exhibited gumming and incomplete conversion, limiting overall yield.

Paper Title: Development and Production of an Enantioselective Tetrahydroisoquinoline Synthesis Enabled by Continuous Cryogenic Lithium–Halogen Exchange
Problem_Description: The continuous cryogenic lithium‑halogen exchange required large cooling loads (dry‑ice/EtOH bath) and posed a risk of temperature excursions if cooling failed.

Paper Title: Synthesis of an Oxathiolane Drug Substance Intermediate Guided by Constraint-Driven Innovation

Paper Title: Ir/Ni Photoredox Dual Catalysis with Heterogeneous Base Enabled by an Oscillatory Plug Flow Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Large Na₂CO₃ particles (Sauter mean diameter ≈122 µm) settled in the peristaltic pump at low flow rates, leading to loss of slurry conveyance.
Solution_Description: Wet‑milling reduced the particle size to ≈14 µm, which kept the slurry stable even at very low flow rates, enabling accurate dosing.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reduction of the Na₂CO₃ particle size by wet milling decreased the Sauter mean diameter (…) from 122 to 14 µm… the resulting suspensions were maintained in the aspiration line even at very low flow rates.”

Paper Title: Ir/Ni Photoredox Dual Catalysis with Heterogeneous Base Enabled by an Oscillatory Plug Flow Photoreactor
Problem_Description: The original batch protocol showed low productivity (≈0.014 g h⁻¹) due to the long 6 h irradiation and sub‑optimal catalyst turnover.
Solution_Description: Increasing the reactor temperature to 50 °C accelerated the rate‑determining nickel step, and doubling the Ni loading to 1 mol % (with 2 mol % dtbbpy) further improved conversion and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The desired reaction proceeds faster at 50 °C without compromising the selectivity… To further optimize the thermal component of the catalytic cycle, the Ni loading was doubled to 1 mol %, while 2 mol % dtbbpy facilitated catalyst dissolution.”

Paper Title: Ir/Ni Photoredox Dual Catalysis with Heterogeneous Base Enabled by an Oscillatory Plug Flow Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Batch reactions used a 34 W Kessil blue LED and required 6 h, resulting in low space‑time yield and high energy per gram of product.
Solution_Description: Switching to 75 W 405 nm LEDs and shortening the residence time to 30 min increased productivity to 0.87 g h⁻¹ (STY = 62.1 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹) while delivering a higher photon flux per reactor volume.
Supporting_Evidence: “In this work, finally, 0.87 g/h was produced in an oscillatory plug flow reactor irradiated with quasi‑monochromatic 405 nm LEDs… the STY thus achieved amounts to 62.1 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹, a marked improvement compared with the state of the art.”

Paper Title: Seeking for Selectivity and Efficiency: New Approaches in the Synthesis of Raltegravir
Problem_Description: The hydrate form of intermediate 3 (the Cbz‑protected hydroxypyrimidinone) required a lengthy azeotropic dehydration step before it could be coupled with acyl chloride 5, adding extra time and cost to the process.
Solution_Description: The team generated a new anhydrous salt of intermediate 3 (compound 12) by performing the Cbz‑deprotection in the presence of methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) in a hydro‑alcoholic medium, then switching the solvent to 2‑propanol and isolating the salt as an anhydrous solid. This eliminated the azeotropic anhydration operation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The hydrate form of intermediate 3 that requires lengthy azeotropic anhydrification procedures before the following coupling …” (list item a).
