Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: The DIBAL‑H reduction of the diester is highly exothermic (ΔH = –319 kJ mol⁻¹, adiabatic temperature rise ≈ 119 K) and generates large amounts of over‑reduction impurities (3, 4, 5) when the reaction temperature cannot be kept sufficiently low.
Solution_Description: The process was moved from batch/semibatch to a continuous‑flow reactor.  Flow gives a much higher surface‑area‑to‑volume (SAV) ratio, enabling rapid heat removal and operation at lower temperatures (‑40 °C to ‑78 °C), which suppresses the exotherm and the formation of over‑reduction products.
Supporting_Evidence:
"the strongly exothermic nature of the reaction and the formation of high levels of impurities as a result of over‑reduction" (p. 1‑intro)  
"enthalpy of reaction of –319 kJ mol⁻¹, corresponding to an adiabatic temperature rise of 119 K" (p. 5‑calc)  
"By changing the reaction paradigm from batch to continuous flow, several advantages could be realized: greater control over reaction time; improved heat transfer and temperature control" (p. 8‑list)  
"continuous flow chemistry enabled operation at lower temperatures and better control of the reaction time" (abstract)  
"The rapid, highly exothermic, and temperature‑sensitive reaction was successfully scaled … using a flow reactor system" (conclusion)

Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: Early runs at low substrate concentration (≈ 3 wt %) gave poor conversion even with long residence times, and the original “caterpillar” micromixer generated high back‑pressure, limiting throughput and causing variable impurity levels.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The substrate concentration was increased to 14.3 wt % (≈ 0.9 M), which dramatically accelerated the reaction and allowed complete conversion at –40 °C.  At the same time the micromixer was replaced by a simple T‑mixer of appropriate inner diameter, providing adequate mixing with a far lower pressure drop.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Initial runs at low concentration showed poor conversion…" (p. 9‑table 1 discussion)  
"Increasing the concentration of compound 1 to 14.3 wt % in THF dramatically accelerated the reaction rate" (p. 9‑table 1 discussion)  
"the mixing device … was limited in its throughput because of significant back pressure… several sizes of simple T‑mixer were subsequently evaluated" (p. 11‑mixing)  
"mixing proved to be influential in terms of reaction purity, adequate mixing did not require specialized equipment" (p. 11‑mixing)  
"T‑mixers gave similar reaction outcomes as the caterpillar micromixer … with a much lower pressure drop" (p. 12‑table 3 footnote)

Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: Controlling the exotherm in batch required very slow, metered addition of DIBAL‑H (> 6 h for 18 kg scale), which gave the reaction ample time for the tetrahedral intermediate to collapse and for over‑reduction to occur.
Solution_Description: In flow the reaction time is set by the residence time (≈ 75 s) rather than by a prolonged addition.  The short residence time together with low reaction temperature (‑40 °C) prevents intermediate breakdown and limits over‑reduction.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Control of this vigorous exotherm was possible only by slow, metered addition of DIBAL‑H, which required long addition times (> 6 h at 18 kg scale)" (p. 5‑exotherm)  
"The formation of tetrahedral intermediate int‑1 … was relatively fast, on the order of 1–2 min … collapse … leads to impurity 3" (p. 4‑intermediate)  
"shortening the residence time to 75 s and using a bath temperature of –40 °C … yielded the most promising result" (p. 9‑opt)  
"continuous flow enabled operation at lower temperatures and better control of the reaction time" (abstract)  
"The rapid, highly exothermic, and temperature‑sensitive reaction was successfully scaled … using a flow reactor system" (conclusion)

Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: The original caterpillar split‑and‑recombine micromixer caused high back‑pressure and inconsistent product quality when flow rates were increased, making scale‑up difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A series of standard T‑mixers (inner diameters 0.254–3.18 mm) were tested; the smallest T‑mixers (≤ 0.254 mm) reproduced the high‑purity results of the micromixer while delivering much lower pressure drop, thus stabilising the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
"significant back pressure at higher flow rates, a known characteristic of this micromixer design" (p. 11‑mixing)  
"several sizes of simple T‑mixer were subsequently evaluated… At large inner diameters… both lower conversion and increased over‑reduction were observed… At small inner diameters, T‑mixers proved to give similar reaction outcomes" (p. 12‑table 3)  
"mixing proved to be influential in terms of reaction purity, adequate mixing did not require specialized equipment" (p. 12‑conclusion)  
"efficient mixing could be delivered with a much lower pressure drop by the use of a simple T‑mixer" (p. 12‑table 3 footnote)

Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: Triethylamine·HCl (≈ 5 mol % of the substrate stock) precipitated on cooling, fouling the precooling heat‑exchanger, the narrow mixing tubing, and raising system back‑pressure, which also partially quenched DIBAL‑H and lowered conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The DIBAL‑H feed rate was increased by ~5 % (≈ 0.075 equiv) to compensate for the quenching effect, and the lines were routinely flushed with water/THF between modules to clear fouling.
Supporting_Evidence:
"the stock solution contained approximately 5 mol % TEA·HCl… led to significant buildup… pressure drop increased from ≈ 12 psi to 30–35 psi" (p. 14‑fouling)  
"the presence of such quantities of TEA·HCl … led to lowered reaction conversion due to partial quenching of DIBAL‑H" (p. 14‑fouling)  
"the lowered conversion was counteracted by a slight increase in the flow rate of DIBAL‑H… an additional 0.075 equiv… to drive the reaction to completion" (p. 15‑adjust)  
"Between modules, flushing with room‑temperature water followed by THF was sufficient to clear the lines of the fouling" (p. 14‑flushing)

Paper Title: Selective DIBAL‑H Monoreduction of a Diester Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: From Benchtop to Kilo Lab
Problem_Description: When excess DIBAL‑H was used to ensure full conversion, the aqueous work‑up turned dark and opaque with insoluble particulates, which hindered impurity removal and raised safety concerns about handling the slurry.
Solution_Description: The crude product solution was passed through a pad of silica (vacuum filtration) to remove the discoloration and insoluble particles, delivering a clean stock solution suitable for downstream chemistry.
Supporting_Evidence:
"the aqueous workups … became exceedingly dark and opaque, with large amounts of insoluble particulates forming" (p. 15‑color)  
"we opted to upgrade the color and remove the insoluble particulates using a simple filtration through a pad of silica" (p. 15‑color)  
"Color removal was accomplished by vacuum distillation … and filtration through 700 g of silica … yielded <bold>2</bold> as a pale‑yellow crystalline solid" (lab‑scale experimental)  
"This also offered a modest purity upgrade… allowing successful use of the material in downstream chemistry" (p. 15‑color)

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: Control experiments without catalyst or without CO₂ circulation gave almost no formation of the desired cyclic carbonates, showing poor conversion of the epoxide.
Solution_Description: Adding the tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB) catalyst and using the circulating gas‑flow system (continuous CO₂ flow) enabled rapid formation of cyclic carbonates at ambient pressure.
Supporting_Evidence: “The control reaction without a catalyst and the one without circulation of CO₂ (0 L/min flow rate) did not lead to a significant formation of cyclic carbonate using BADGE as a model epoxide (Fig 2).”; “The catalyst TBAB leads to the formation of cyclic carbonate … in all tested solvents even at ambient pressure.”; “The designed circulating gas‑flow system … allows a safe, environmentally benign, and ultimately economical manufacture … the same reaction mixture … can be used for the ammonolysis by simply switching the CO₂ flow off and adding the amine.”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: When the gas‑flow was switched on, aerosol formation occurred for all solvents, causing transport of the solvent as a fine mist and potential loss of material.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The gas distributor was redesigned (cone‑shaped PTFE BOLA with 16 × 0.4 mm ports) and the solvent stream was back‑led to a second coil condenser, allowing controlled removal and recycling of the aerosolized solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Aerosol formation was observed for all solvents … the observation of transport of the solvent even below the boiling point.”; “The cone‑shaped PTFE gas distributor … was modified to have 16 ports … Back‑leading of the solvent that was collected in the second coil condenser … allows for homogeneous and continuous distribution of CO₂ within the solution or melt.”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: The choice of solvent strongly affected the reaction rate; acetone gave the slowest conversion while iBMK gave the fastest, leading to inconsistent yields across solvents.
Solution_Description: Switching to methyl isobutyl ketone (iBMK) as the reaction medium dramatically increased the conversion and reduced reaction time, especially when used together with TBAB.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the tested solvents, methyl isobutyl ketone (iBMK) resulted in the highest conversion within the shortest time, whereas acetone … resulted in the slowest reaction rate.”; “The catalyst TBAB leads to the formation of cyclic carbonate … in all tested solvents even at ambient pressure.”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: The epoxide EcHMEcHC displayed markedly lower conversion (30‑60 %) and evidence of side‑product formation, indicating limited reactivity and possible degradation under the reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: The authors suggest employing a more reactive catalyst, a different (more suitable) solvent, or higher temperature to improve conversion of the less‑reactive epoxide.
Supporting_Evidence: “EcHMEcHC … lower conversion and side products… conversion 30‑60 %.”; “A variation of the catalytic system (by, e.g., using a more reactive catalyst or a different solvent) might reduce the reaction time for less‑reactive epoxides like EcHMEcHC.”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: Aminolysis of the cyclic carbonates proceeded slowly, especially with 1,6‑diaminhexane, giving low yields after several days at room temperature.
Solution_Description: The amine is added directly to the reaction mixture after CO₂ flow is stopped, without isolating the carbonate, allowing a one‑pot conversion (telescoped process).
Supporting_Evidence: “We were able to observe a reaction by adding the amine directly in the reaction mixture both at reflux and at room temperature … The reaction rate was low and the yield was inadequate.”; “If the cyclic carbonates could be processed without, e.g., separation and/or recrystallization, then an advantage from economic and economical aspects can be achieved.”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: Unreacted epoxides showed poor storage stability, oxidizing/hydrolyzing in air within days, whereas the formed cyclic carbonates remained stable for at least two months.
Solution_Description: Converting epoxides to cyclic carbonates before storage prevents decomposition and improves safety handling.
Supporting_Evidence: “The storage stability of the epoxides toward air is much smaller than that of the cyclic carbonates. The FTIR epoxy signal vanished within a few days … the storage stability better under air for the cyclic carbonates (at least 2 months).”

Paper Title: Chemical Reaction of Carbon Dioxide with Bisepoxides for Synthesis of Organic Cyclic Dicarbonates at Ambient Pressure for Polyhydroxy Urethane Synthesis
Problem_Description: High‑pressure CO₂ reactors used in literature pose safety hazards and are expensive to construct and operate, limiting scalability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors developed a circulating gas‑flow system operating at ambient pressure with a modified PTFE distributor, providing a safer, more economical, and easily scalable platform.
Supporting_Evidence: “The safety and scalability of a reactor system working at ambient pressure are much better to control than those based on a high‑pressure‑based system.”; “The designed circulating gas‑flow system … allows a safe, environmentally benign, and ultimately economical manufacture … The circulating gas‑flow system with a modified PTFE distributor … allows for homogeneous and continuous distribution of CO₂ within the solution or melt.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: The traditional nitrile‑anion alkylation route to the esp ligand (2) requires the generation of LDA from n‑BuLi on‑scale, anhydrous solvents and inert atmosphere, leading to a high‑cost, pyrophoric, and operationally hazardous process.
Solution_Description: Replaced the nitrile‑anion strategy with an oxidative rearrangement of a 1,3‑diketone derived from bulk acetylacetone (13) under basic conditions, eliminating the need for n‑BuLi and allowing a milder, less costly, and safer synthesis of the esp ligand.
Supporting_Evidence: “The nitrile anion strategy seems to be responsible for the high cost of this ligand as it requires inert conditions, anhydrous solvents, and large amounts of n‑BuLi to generate LDA on‑scale.”; “We recognised that esp (2) could be synthesised via the oxidative rearrangement of 1,3‑diketones in basic media that our group has recently developed…”.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: Attempting the direct combination of esp (2) with RhCl₃·xH₂O (8) under the classic acidic, ethanol‑reduction conditions produced extensive formation of rhodium black (Rh⁰) even with a 10‑fold excess of ligand, indicating over‑reduction and loss of material.
Solution_Description: Introduced inorganic basic additives (e.g., Li₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, K₂CO₃) at ≥2 equiv and a minor amount of LiCl to control the reduction rate of Rh(III) to Rh(II), suppress over‑reduction, and improve isolated yield of Rh₂esp₂ (1) to up to 86 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “In our case, the direct reaction of esp (2) and RhCl₃·xH₂O (8) … results in extensive formation of rhodium black…”.; “A drastic improvement … when more than 2 equiv of base are added (entry 4)… Li₂CO₃ offers the best balance … and it facilitates the isolation of the pure 1.”; “The presence of LiCl is beneficial to enhance yield and robustness … likely forming a more stable tetrachlororhodate reservoir of rhodium(III).”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: Screening of bases showed that small quantities of NaOH were ineffective (entries 2‑3), and yields varied dramatically with different counter‑cations (entries 5‑11).
Solution_Description: Optimised the amount of base to 3.7 equiv and identified Li₂CO₃ (with LiCl) as the most efficient additive, giving consistent high yields (≥85 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Small quantities of base were unsuccessful (entries 2, 3)… addition of more than 2 equiv results in a drastic improvement (entry 4)”.; “Li₂CO₃ offers the best balance … (entry 12) … LiCl is beneficial … (entry 15)”.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: The oxidative rearrangement of the tetraketone intermediate (12) using LiOH/H₂O₂, previously effective for simple diketones, failed completely for 12, leading to quantitative retro‑Claisen deacylation.
Solution_Description: Switched the base from LiOH to NaOH, which suppressed retro‑Claisen deacylation and allowed clean double rearrangement to esp (2) in excellent yield; methanol was identified as the optimal solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Surprisingly, the oxidative rearrangement … using LiOH and H₂O₂ proved completely ineffective … quantitative retro‑Claisen deacylation … It was found that replacing the base by NaOH suppressed this process, obtaining the doubly rearranged esp ligand (2) in excellent yield (entry 2).”; “The reaction also occurred in a variety of solvents … but none proved superior to methanol.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: The first methylation of acetylacetone (13) with methyl iodide (14) required mitigation of methyl iodide volatility during scale‑up, which posed safety and handling challenges.
Solution_Description: Implemented an autoclave reactor and switched the reaction solvent to butanone (plus glyme for the second step) to safely contain the volatile methyl iodide and maintain a homogeneous mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “On‑scale, we found that an autoclave reactor and butanone were required to mitigate the volatility of methyl iodide in this reaction.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: The multistep synthesis of the tetraketone (12) involved sequential alkylations and required careful addition of reagents to avoid phase separation and ensure complete conversion.
Solution_Description: Developed a one‑pot telescoped procedure where after the initial methylation, glyme, K₂CO₃, and the m‑xylene dichloride (5b) were added directly to afford crude 12 without intermediate isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The tetraketone 12 was crystallised …; after the initial methylation was deemed complete, glyme, K₂CO₃, and m‑xylene dichloride (5b) were added to obtain the crude 12 in one pot.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: Scaling the final Rh₂esp₂ (1) preparation required controlled heating to reflux; abrupt temperature changes led to irreproducible results.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employed a controlled temperature ramp to reach reflux steadily in a simple reflux system under air, ensuring reproducible conversion and high isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “With large quantities of esp ligand in hand, we scaled up the synthesis … using technical ethanol under air. … a controlled ramp to steadily reach the reflux temperature … was important to obtain reproducible results.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: Traditional syntheses of Rh₂esp₂ required 90–120 equiv of the esp ligand, dramatically increasing material cost and waste.
Solution_Description: Optimised the protocol to use only 1.4 equiv of the esp ligand, reducing reagent excess by two orders of magnitude while maintaining high yield of Rh₂esp₂ (1).
Supporting_Evidence: “Only 1.4 equiv of the esp ligand is used, as opposed to the 90–120 equiv that was previously required … and the catalyst is obtained for the first time in a single step … decreasing two orders of magnitude the excess of carboxylate ligand required.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of Esp and Rhodium(II) Carboxylates from Acetylacetone and RhCl
Problem_Description: Synthesis of monocarboxylate Rh(II) catalysts with extremely hindered cyclopropanecarboxylate ligands gave low efficiencies, likely due to unfavorable binding kinetics.
Solution_Description: Acknowledged the limitation and suggested that alternative conditions or ligand designs may be required; no concrete modification was reported in the current study.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, low efficiencies are observed using this protocol with the most extremely hindered cyclopropanecarboxylate ligands, probably due to unfavorable binding kinetics.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Mono- and Diisocyanates in Flow from Renewable Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: The acyl azide intermediate generated during the Curtius rearrangement is highly energetic, unstable and potentially explosive, posing serious safety hazards on scale‑up.

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling
Problem_Description: Scaling‑up photochemical reactions is difficult because reaction‐related parameters (concentration, path length) and radiation‑related parameters (wavelength, intensity) are strongly coupled, leading to inconsistent conversions when moving from micro‑HTE plates to larger batch or flow reactors.
Solution_Description: A combined high‑throughput experimentation + computational modeling workflow was developed.  The model uses measured kinetic parameters (quantum yield, rate constant) together with optical data (irradiance, absorbance) to predict conversion for any reactor geometry, enabling the design of flow reactors with short light paths and low concentrations that give reproducible, high conversions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using light to drive a chemical transformation introduces challenges for ensuring the robust transferability of photochemical reactions across different platforms and scales.”; “Reaction kinetics is not only determined by the intrinsic reaction parameters… but also by radiation components… the impact of reaction‑related and radiation‑related parameters on the reaction rate is often coupled.”; “We demonstrate a modeling tool to predict the performance of a photochemical reaction as a function of the reactor geometry… concentration… irradiance… and residence time.”; “The model successfully predicts conversion… without the need for an intensive experimental optimization for each … enables a robust and efficient scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling
Problem_Description: High substrate concentration or large reaction depth (0.65 M, 1 cm path length) leads to poor light penetration, making the reaction light‑limited and giving < 30 % conversion after 4 h.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow photoreactor with a thin FEP tube (reaction depth ≤ 0.4 cm) and high‑intensity LEDs, thereby minimizing path length and ensuring uniform illumination, which restored full conversion at short residence times.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the 0.65–0.68 M starting material cases with a reaction depth of 1.0 cm, the conversion increases linearly and stays below 30 % after 4 h… indicates that the reaction is light limited.”; “Minimizing reaction depth ensures efficient light penetration without the need for overly diluting the reaction mixture and therefore reducing the residence time needed to achieve the desired conversion. Using such continuous flow photoreactors maximizes the productive volume of the reactor by ensuring sufficient illumination.”

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling
Problem_Description: The batch‑scale HTE plate required several hours of irradiation to reach high conversion, especially at high concentration, reducing throughput for process development.
Solution_Description: Higher‑intensity 415 nm LEDs (177 W m⁻²) were employed instead of lower‑intensity 365 nm LEDs (87 W m⁻²), providing more photons at the productive 380 nm band and cutting the required irradiation time roughly in half.
Supporting_Evidence: “The 415 nm LED photomat used in this study has significantly higher irradiance than the 365 nm LED (177 vs 87 W m⁻²) and hence can provide a greater number of photons that are capable of exciting the starting material at its excitation band of 380 nm.”; “We observed faster conversion when we use these higher intensity 415 nm LEDs.”

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling
Problem_Description: Direct spectral irradiance measurements for high‑intensity LEDs saturated the detector, preventing accurate intensity determination for scale‑up reactors.
Solution_Description: The kinetic data obtained from the HTE experiments were used as a chemical actinometer to back‑calculate the average irradiance of the LEDs, providing an approximate intensity when direct spectroscopic measurement was impossible.
Supporting_Evidence: “When we used a different light source, a Chanzon 410 nm LED, we were not able to directly measure the irradiation using spectrophotometry due to detector saturation … we used the kinetic data generated from the 415 nm Lumidox LED photomat studies as a chemical actinometry to determine the intensity of the Chanzon 410 nm LEDs.”

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling

Supporting_Evidence: “Applying chemical actinometry to large‑scale reactors is challenging due to the extensive material needs… Spectroscopic tools can allow estimation of irradiance with minimal time and material consumption.”

Paper Title: Predicting Performance of Photochemical Transformations for Scaling Up in Different Platforms by Combining High-Throughput Experimentation with Computational Modeling
Problem_Description: In the HTE plate the LEDs generated heat that raised the reaction temperature, causing a mismatch between model predictions and experimental conversion for the 0.3 cm path‑length experiments.

This high dilution…ensure that the process can be safely operated.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: Differential scanning calorimetry showed that 2‑chloro‑5‑iodopyrimidine (compound 9) undergoes a very strong exothermic decomposition (> ‑630 kJ kg⁻¹) above ≈ 275 °C, posing a thermal‑runaway risk if temperatures were to exceed the intended 60 °C.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was designed to keep the temperature far below the decomposition onset (operating at 60 °C), eliminating the need for additional safety measures for this intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “We first observed that 9 shows the onset of a very strong exothermic reaction… starting above ca. 275 °C… Nevertheless, considering the reaction conditions used… no specific measures needed…”. “The reaction can be run… at 60 °C for 2 h.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: Compound 10 (2‑hydrazinopyrimidine) exhibits an extremely strong exothermic decomposition (≈ ‑1111 kJ kg⁻¹) starting above ca. 155 °C, with a potential adiabatic temperature rise of ~ 741 °C, indicating a serious thermal hazard.
Solution_Description: The authors limited the reaction temperature to 60 °C, performed an iso‑DSC safety test at 110 °C (reaction + 50 °C) to verify a safe margin, and emphasized careful control of drying steps to avoid unintended heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulting product 10 was submitted to DSC analysis, which revealed an extremely strong exothermic reaction (≈ ‑1111 kJ kg⁻¹) starting above ca. 155 °C…”. “After ca. 460 min at 110 °C, a very weak heat release was detected… In light of these data, we concluded that the process… can be safely operated at the proposed temperature.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: Phenylacetylene (compound 13) displayed a violent exothermic decomposition (ΔH = ‑1921 kJ kg⁻¹) beginning at 115 °C, raising concerns for safe handling during the Sonogashira coupling.
Solution_Description: The coupling was performed at ambient temperature (room temperature), far below the decomposition onset, and the authors verified that the presence of palladium/copper catalysts did not lower the decomposition temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC analysis revealed its strong decomposition reaction starting at 115 °C… ΔH = ‑1921 kJ kg⁻¹”. “The dynamic SEDEX thermostability test of 13 in the presence of the palladium and copper catalysts showed no significant heat release up to 165 °C.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: The Sonogashira cross‑coupling to afford ynone 15 left trace amounts of palladium and copper in the crude product, which could be detrimental for downstream steps and increase material cost.
Solution_Description: A brief filtration through a small pad of silica gel was introduced after work‑up to remove residual metals before the next reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “A simple filtration on a small pad of silica gel was found to be important to remove traces of the metals that could be detrimental in the next steps.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: When the condensation of 10 and 15 was performed without 3 Å molecular sieves, yields dropped to the 60 % range, likely due to water generated during hydrazone formation shifting the equilibrium.
Solution_Description: 3 Å molecular sieves (1 g) were added to the reaction mixture to scavenge water, thereby driving the condensation forward and restoring yields to ≈ 90 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the absence of molecular sieves, the yields are in the 60 % range. The role of this desiccant is to trap the water equivalent produced during the formation of hydrazone … and thus to drive the equilibrium to the right.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of 7‑Azaindazole by a Diels–Alder Cascade and Associated Process Safety
Problem_Description: The final benzylation of 16 to give 17 produced a minor N2‑benzyl isomer (5 %); separation required chromatography, adding a purification step and solvent waste.
Solution_Description: Flash chromatography on silica gel (PE/EtOAc gradient) was employed to isolate the desired N1‑benzyl product, achieving an 84–85 % isolated yield of pure 17.
Supporting_Evidence: “The two compounds could be easily separated by chromatography on silica gel… 1‑benzyl… was obtained as a white solid (84 % yield).”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: Low solubility of the polymeric impurity (suspected maleic‑anhydride/ethylene polymer) caused precipitation and clogging in the flow reactor during extended operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to acetone as reaction solvent (improved solubility of reactants and reduced formation of insoluble impurity), adopt a crystallization protocol using toluene/MTBE that precipitates the polymeric impurity for filtration, replace the tee‑mixers with a mixing‑tank to avoid ethylene slugs, add active cooling and a convection fan to control temperature rise from LED heat, install automated mass‑flow control and nitrogen purge with LEL sensors to keep ethylene below its lower‑explosion limit, and use larger‑diameter FEP tubing and high‑power LED panels to maintain light penetration and throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The isolated impurity demonstrated poor solubility in the range of solvents evaluated and was deemed a clogging risk for extended continuous operation (ca. weeks).', 'A procedure was designed such that dissolution of cyclobutane 2 could be achieved in toluene … followed by a filtration operation to purge the undesired impurity.', 'The tee mixer was employed for the 500 g/day demonstration but replaced by a mixing tank … to eliminate ethylene slugs observed at the increased flow rates.', 'The solution temperature within the reaction module reached 52 °C due to the significant heat generated from the LED bank. For future runs, this was addressed by adjusting the flow rate of the cooling medium, relocating the thermocouple to improve accuracy, and including a convection fan within the module.', 'Dilution of excess ethylene below the lower explosion limit (LEL): A vapor/liquid separator is introduced at the outlet of the reaction and continuously purged with nitrogen … Inclusion of LEL sensors … interlocked to immediately stop the flow of both the ethylene and acetone solutions.', 'The production skid comprised three separate modules in series of FEP tubing (20.76 L irradiated volume, 10 mm o.d.) and 6 × 3 kW 365 nm LED panels.', 'A faulty back‑pressure regulator (BPR) impacted the ethylene stoichiometry and mean residence time, causing conversion fluctuations.', 'Cyclobutane 2 was isolated in 58 % yield with 97.2 % potency and 99.3 % purity by GC area % … the polymeric impurity accounts for the low potency of the isolated solids.']

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: The target cyclobutane product is highly soluble in acetone ( > 100 mg mL⁻¹ ), making direct antisolvent addition (cyclohexane or MTBE) impractical for crystallization and resulting in low isolated potency despite high GC purity.
Solution_Description: Develop a two‑step solvent‑exchange crystallization: first exchange acetone for toluene (good solubility for product, poor for impurity) then add MTBE to precipitate the product while filtering out the polymeric impurity; this improves recovery (80 % from crude) and overall isolated yield (73 %).
Supporting_Evidence: ['The high dilution of the photochemical process (33 volumes), coupled with the high solubility of cyclobutane 2 in acetone (>100 mg mL⁻¹), rendered the direct addition of cyclohexane or MTBE as an antisolvent impractical.', 'Of the solvents evaluated, toluene demonstrated high solubility for cyclobutane 2 and poor solubility for the impurity; therefore, a procedure was designed … followed by a filtration operation to purge the undesired impurity and limit losses of the desired product to 2–3 %.', 'The filtrate could be cooled to generate a slurry and filtered to isolate cyclobutane 2 as a white crystalline solid with 80 % recovery from the crude mixture and 73 % overall isolated yield.']

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: Manual control of ethylene flow caused slight variability in maleic anhydride concentration over a 51 h demo run, risking deviations from target conversion and potential safety hazards.
Solution_Description: Implement an automated mass‑flow controller for ethylene to maintain constant flow and stoichiometry, reducing conversion drift and improving process safety.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The slight variability observed for the maleic anhydride concentration over the 51 h run was attributed to the use of a manual control valve for ethylene flow. Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: Significant heat generated by the high‑power LED bank raised reactor temperature to 52 °C, posing a risk of overheating and potential decomposition.
Solution_Description: Adjust cooling‑medium flow rate, relocate temperature sensor for accurate monitoring, and install a convection fan to dissipate LED heat, maintaining reactor temperature near ambient (≈ 40 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: ['The solution temperature within the reaction module reached 52 °C due to the significant heat generated from the LED bank. For future runs, this was addressed by adjusting the flow rate of the cooling medium, relocating the thermocouple to improve accuracy, and including a convection fan within the module.', 'The average temperature and pressure readings for the duration of the full‑scale engineering run were 40 °C and 7 bar, respectively.']

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: Initial isolation protocol (distillation followed by solvent exchange) gave inconsistent purity and low potency (90–95 wt % despite high GC purity) because a white, poorly soluble polymeric impurity remained in the solid.

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: At increased flow rates, ethylene formed slugs when using a union‑tee mixer, causing conversion fluctuations and risk of clogging.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Supporting_Evidence: ['The tee mixer was employed for the 500 g/day demonstration but replaced by a mixing tank with a residence time of 30 min at production scale to eliminate ethylene slugs observed at the increased flow rates.', 'The mode of gas–liquid mixing was also evaluated … demonstrating that a union tee mixer and mixing tank provided comparable efficiencies.']

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Production-Scale Continuous [2 + 2] Photocycloaddition
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction required significantly larger LED panels and high‑power lighting, raising concerns about the cost and availability of suitable light sources for multi‑kilogram production.
Solution_Description: Utilize commercially available 365 nm surface‑mounted LED panels (3 kW each) and increase tubing diameter (10 mm o.d.) to achieve the required photon flux without excessive light‑source cost, while maintaining chemical compatibility with FEP tubing.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The production skid … comprised three separate modules in series of FEP tubing (20.76 L irradiated volume, 10 mm o.d.) and 6 × 3 kW 365 nm LED panels.', 'The impact of light‑source intensity demonstrated a nearly linear correlation … consistent with a photon‑limited process.']

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 1: CDI-Promoted Amide Bond Formation
Problem_Description: The process suffers from occasional partial or total blockage of the CDI slurry feed line, which reduces the effective CDI flow rate and can lower Boc‑d‑leucine conversion below the required >95 % target. This variability threatens product quality and may necessitate waste‑stream diversion.
Solution_Description: A control strategy was developed that (i) increases the CSTR‑1 and CSTR‑2 temperatures to boost reaction rates when a flow reduction is detected, (ii) adjusts the MeTHF diluent flow to compensate for changes in product concentration, and (iii) uses model‑based predictions to decide when a blockage can be tolerated and when the line must be cleared. These actions keep conversion >95 % even with up to a 40 % flow‑rate reduction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “One case study highlights the dynamics of flow blockage for a key reagent, N,N′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI), resulting from line clogging… the model demonstrated that the acceptance criteria for reaction conversion were met even with a flow rate reduction of 40 %.” (Abstract)
• “a partial or total blockage of the CDI feed slurry was identified as a possible failure scenario.” (Section 4.1)
• “The desired level of conversion (>95 %) is attained at flow rates as low as 60 % of the nominal set point.” (Fig. 9 caption)
• “…the temperatures of CSTR1 and CSTR2 serve as levers to increase the reaction conversion… can increase the conversion in the worst‑case scenario by 2 % through an increase of 10 °C.” (Section 4, Fig. 8 discussion)
• “The blockage was resolved within 22 min… material was continuously fed through the entire system.” (Section 4.2)

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 1: CDI-Promoted Amide Bond Formation
Problem_Description: Morpholine amide decomposes when the distillation temperature exceeds ~40 °C, limiting the operating window for the azeotropic water‑removal step and jeopardizing the downstream Grignard reaction that is water‑sensitive.
Solution_Description: The batch/semibatch distillation drum was replaced by a truly continuous packed‑bed distillation column. The column’s reflux ratio and reboiler duty are used to keep the top temperature below 40 °C while achieving the required water content (<0.25 wt %). Continuous operation also provides additional instrumentation for tighter temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The distillation temperature must be kept below 40 °C to avoid morpholine amide decomposition… target water content after distillation is ≤0.25 wt %.” (Section 3.1.3)
• “A truly continuous distillation column operation … can tolerate variations in product concentration and still process the solution to meet the desired specifications.” (Section 4.1)
• “The packed column operation … reflux ratio was used to control the concentration of morpholine amide… reboiler duty was used to control the maximum temperature in the column.” (Section 3.1.3)
• “The integrated distillation column unit operation was a key step in the updated process control strategy to achieve target end‑point product specifications.” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 1: CDI-Promoted Amide Bond Formation
Problem_Description: Variations in CDI flow rate cause fluctuations in the total stream throughput, leading to changes in morpholine amide concentration in the hold‑tank and consequently in the feed to the downstream distillation. This creates a potency drift (45–55 wt % target) and can affect water removal efficiency.
Solution_Description: A UPLC inline assay was proposed to measure morpholine amide concentration in the hold‑tank; the measured value is used to adjust the MeTHF diluent flow (concentration tuning) or to vary the feed rate to the distillation column (order‑and‑rate‑of‑addition) so that potency stays within spec. The continuous column’s flexible reflux/flow control also mitigates the impact of upstream concentration swings.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The impact of the morpholine amide stream flow rate (mmol/min) on the distillation operation… blockage… decreases total amount… resulting in higher concentration…” (Section 4.1)
• “The measurement from this UPLC can then be used to control the MeTHF flow rate to the hold tank to dilute the morpholine amide to its desired potency.” (Section 4.1)
• “An alternative approach is to replace the semibatch distillation drum operation with a truly continuous distillation column operation that can tolerate variations in product concentration.” (Section 4.1)
• “The hold tank composition prior to the distillation operation… the morpholine amide concentration in the hold tank increases… because the overall flow rate of MeTHF decreases.” (Section 4.1, Fig. 12 discussion)

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: The Grignard reaction is highly exothermic (304.1 kJ mol‑1 of 2‑BP) and the temperature in batch runs oscillates up to 4 °C above the set‑point, posing a safety risk and risking loss of control.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in continuous stirred‑tank reactors (CSTRs) with improved heat‑transfer (UA regression, temperature‐controller dynamics) and operated at controlled temperatures, allowing rapid removal of the exotherm while maintaining safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the heat of reaction … measured to be 304.1 kJ/mol of 2‑BP … results in temperature oscillations of up to 4 °C above the set point during the batch runs.”
 • “heat transfer within the reactor was modeled … the overall heat transfer coefficient (UA) and the process time for the temperature controller (τ) were regressed with the supplied temperature data.”
 • “CSTR performance can be maintained … the process was designed to be operated at ≥500 rpm, which is well above N_js.”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: Grignard reagents are extremely sensitive to air and moisture and the traditional Grignard initiation protocol is difficult to implement safely on an industrial scale, leading to variability in reagent formation.
Solution_Description: A Barbier‑type Grignard process was adopted, forming the Grignard reagent in situ in the presence of the alkenyl bromide (2‑BP) so that it is immediately consumed, reducing exposure to air/moisture and eliminating the need for a separate initiation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the sensitivity of Grignard reagents to air and water, which complicates storage and shipping.”
 • “the Grignard process described herein adopts … a Barbier reaction that forms the Grignard reagent in situ … such that the reagent is consumed upon its formation.”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: Solid magnesium has extremely low solubility in THF/MeTHF, making bulk diffusion an unlikely mechanism and risking mass‑transfer limitations in the heterogeneous reaction mixture.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reactor agitation speed was increased to ≥500 rpm (well above the just‑suspended speed of 350 rpm) to ensure the Mg particles remain suspended and mass transfer of 2‑BP to the Mg surface is not rate‑limiting; solid Mg is dosed portion‑wise to control concentration.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the extremely low solubility of solid Mg … makes bulk diffusion … unlikely.”
 • “the just‑suspended agitation speed (N_js) was determined to be 350 rpm, and the process was then designed to be operated at ≥500 rpm.”
 • “Reactions at various agitation levels (500 to 200 rpm…) … identified the just‑suspended speed …”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: Irregular magnesium dosing intervals and low magnesium equivalents cause high variability in morpholine amide conversion (range 94.3 %‑98.5 %) and can drop below the 95 % target.
Solution_Description: In silico studies were used to select a magnesium charging interval of 40 min and to maintain at least 12 equivalents of Mg, which minimizes conversion variability while simplifying operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The conversion of morpholine amide varied from 94.3 % to 98.5 % …”
 • “The inflection point for this variability is around 12 magnesium equivalents … operation at a minimum of 12 magnesium equivalents to achieve the 95 % conversion target.”
 • “A residence time of 40 min and a minimum of 12 equiv of Mg were recommended as operating parameters.”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: Operational disturbances in feed flow rates and concentrations (±10 % deviations) strongly affect morpholine amide conversion, sometimes dropping it below the required 95 % specification.
Solution_Description: The flow rate of 2‑BP was identified as a robust manipulated variable; increasing the 2‑BP flow rate compensates for negative disturbances and restores conversion, forming the basis of the control strategy.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “operational disturbances in the morpholine amide flow rate, morpholine amide concentration, 2‑BP flow rate, and 2‑BP concentration have a strong impact on the conversion.”
 • “the flow rate of 2‑BP was selected as a desirable manipulated variable to control the reaction conversion.”
 • Figure 13 shows conversion monotonically increasing with increased 2‑BP flow rate under worst‑case disturbances.

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 2: Enone Synthesis via a Barbier-Type Grignard Process
Problem_Description: After reaction, residual solvents (MeTHF, THF, MTBE) must be reduced to ≤0.5 wt % and the product solvent swapped to a mixture of acetonitrile and acetic acid for downstream epoxidation.
Solution_Description: A semibatch distillation drum was introduced, modeled with NRTL activity coefficients and fast mass‑transfer assumptions, to perform a two‑stage solvent swap and meet the stringent solvent‑level specifications.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The final unit operation, a distillation drum, serves to swap the enone solvent from MeTHF, THF, and MTBE to a combination of acetonitrile and acetic acid … ≤0.5 wt % each of MeTHF, THF, and MTBE.”
 • “The vapor–liquid equilibrium was modeled using temperature‑dependent NRTL … Fast mass transfer … the enone and any impurities were treated as non‑volatile species.”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: The epoxidation of enone 1 to give the (R,R)‑epoxy ketone 2 is strongly exothermic (ΔH ≈ –250 kJ mol⁻¹) with an adiabatic temperature rise of ~60 °C, creating safety and heat‑removal challenges at scale.
Solution_Description: A continuously‑stirred‑tank‑reactor (CSTR) platform was adopted; the hydrogen‑peroxide feed was split between two CSTRs to lower the instantaneous heat release, and temperature control loops (embedded model, heat‑transfer coefficient tuning) were implemented to keep reactor temperatures within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “A major challenge of this chemistry is its strongly exothermic nature, with a heat of reaction of almost −250 kJ mol⁻¹ and an adiabatic temperature rise (ART) of 60 °C.”
2. “The observation of gas evolution resulting from the disproportionation of H₂O₂ to form oxygen and water … prompted the use of a continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR) platform for this reaction sequence.”
3. “Splitting the H₂O₂ addition between two CSTRs is critical for reaching the desired conversion, as it reduces the exotherm and total H₂O₂ decomposition.”
4. “For temperature control, an embedded model was used to manipulate the temperature of the incoming heat transfer fluid.”
5. “Heat transfer coefficients for glass reactors were estimated to be 4.56 W K⁻¹ …”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: Hydrogen peroxide undergoes catalytic disproportionation on the Mn catalyst, generating O₂ gas and causing vigorous gas evolution and variability in concentration measurements, which hampers reaction characterization and poses safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The peroxide‑decomposition pathway (eq 3) was added to the kinetic model, and the amount of peroxide fed was increased (and split between CSTR 1 and CSTR 2) to compensate for the loss, thereby stabilizing conversion and reducing gas‑generation spikes.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Another challenge addressed in this work is the undesired competing disproportionation of hydrogen peroxide by the manganese catalyst.”
2. “The large exotherm associated with this reaction and vigorous O₂ evolution challenged the characterization of this reaction.”
3. “With these new data, the kinetic parameters for the reactions … were refit … to include eq 3.”
4. “The updated model … resulted in lower conversion of the desired reaction due to H₂O₂ decomposition.”
5. “An 80 % increase in the hydrogen peroxide flow rate sent to CSTR1 and a 100 % increase … are required to maintain the target‑level process specifications.”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: Gas evolution in CSTR 1 caused large fluctuations in the measured concentration of the reaction stream, making the data more variable than in downstream reactors.
Solution_Description: Using a CSTR configuration and increasing the peroxide feed (as a manipulated variable) mitigated the impact of gas bubbles on measurement precision and ensured consistent conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The gas evolution observed in CSTR1 challenged a quantitative assessment of the reaction stream and rendered the concentration measurements more variable than those obtained in CSTR2 and CSTR3.”

4. “Splitting the H₂O₂ addition between two CSTRs is critical for reaching the desired conversion, as it reduces the exotherm and total H₂O₂ decomposition.”
5. “The models were then integrated into an end‑to‑end flowsheet …”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: The (R,R)‑epoxy ketone has very low solubility in heptane, leading to experimental variability when measuring solubility data for the wash step.
Solution_Description: A van’t Hoff solubility correlation (eq 8) was fitted to temperature‑dependent solubility data (–5 °C to 25 °C) in heptane, providing a reliable model despite the low intrinsic solubility.
Supporting_Evidence:

2. “To determine the model parameters, a set of experiments with temperatures from –5 to 25 °C were conducted, and the model parameters can be found in Table 9.”

4. “The values of the parameters A, B, and C obtained by regression are given in Table 6.”
5. “The solubility data for the (R,R)‑epoxy ketone were observed to follow a van’t Hoff relationship …”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: Aggregates observed in the crystallizer produced a bimodal chord‑length distribution, complicating the kinetic model for crystal growth and nucleation.

Supporting_Evidence:

5. “Because of the significant size difference, it was possible to employ only the first peak …”

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: Partitioning of the (R,R)‑epoxy ketone, its (R,S) impurity, and water between the organic and aqueous phases depends on temperature, water fraction and acetonitrile fraction, creating uncertainty in impurity removal during liquid–liquid extraction.

Paper Title: A Virtual Plant for Integrated Continuous Manufacturing of a Carfilzomib Drug Substance Intermediate, Part 3: Manganese-Catalyzed Asymmetric Epoxidation, Crystallization, and Filtration
Problem_Description: Filtration of the crystallized product required accurate prediction of cake resistance and compressibility to ensure reliable operation under variable pressure.

Supporting_Evidence:

2. “A set of two experiments were designed and executed in which ΔP was varied from 12.6 to 25 psi and the mass of the filtrate over time was recorded …”

4. “Short filtration times were achieved, and no particle compression or breakage was observed.”
5. “The filtration device … uses two parallel batch filtration units … to allow for continuous production of the product solution.”

Paper Title: Short and Easily Scalable Synthesis of the Sex Pheromone of the Horse-Chestnut Leaf Miner (
Problem_Description: Previous literature routes to the pheromone required many steps (seven‑nine), gave overall yields as low as 12‑28 %, used expensive palladium catalysts and relied on volatile, highly reactive acetylide reagents (e.g., lithium acetylide) that are difficult and hazardous to handle on large scale.
Solution_Description: The authors devised a short six‑step convergent synthesis that uses an inexpensive iron catalyst (Fe(acac)₃) in a ligand‑ and additive‑free Kumada cross‑coupling, eliminating the need for costly Pd catalysts and hazardous alkyne reagents, thereby increasing overall yield to 40 % and reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “Several syntheses of 1 were reported… seven steps, 28 % yield… nine steps, 12 % yield… relied on… highly reactive or volatile alkyne sources… This hampers… high scales, making them unattractive for industrial eco‑friendly purposes.”; “Our strategy relies on… a cheap, eco‑friendly, and abundant transition metal such as iron as a catalyst of the key cross‑coupling step is an appealing alternative to the use of noble metals.”

Paper Title: Short and Easily Scalable Synthesis of the Sex Pheromone of the Horse-Chestnut Leaf Miner (
Problem_Description: The crude mixture of (E,Z)- and (E,E)-dienol phosphates (6a/6b) obtained after the t‑BuOK/diethyl chlorophosphate step could not be separated by silica‑gel chromatography on an industrial scale.
Solution_Description: A selective Diels–Alder reaction with maleic anhydride was employed to convert the minor (E,E) isomer (6b) into a cycloadduct, which after basic hydrolysis leaves pure (E,Z)-dienol phosphate (6a). This telescoped purification avoids chromatography and is easily scalable.
Supporting_Evidence: “Separation of the 6a/6b mixture by chromatography on silica gel is not easily carried out at high industrial scales.”; “(1 E,3 Z)-dienol phosphate 6a and the minor (1 E,3 E) isomer 6b were conveniently separated by treating the 6a/6b mixture with 1.0 equiv of maleic anhydride… leading to the corresponding cycloaddition product… basic hydrolysis… allowed easy purification of 6a…”

Paper Title: Short and Easily Scalable Synthesis of the Sex Pheromone of the Horse-Chestnut Leaf Miner (
Problem_Description: During the iron‑catalyzed Kumada cross‑coupling, the reaction mixture became highly viscous, making stirring difficult and requiring an overnight stir at 20 °C to achieve full conversion.
Solution_Description: The authors cooled the reaction to –5 °C before adding the Fe(acac)₃ catalyst and then added the dienol phosphate dropwise. After addition, the mixture was allowed to stir at 20 °C overnight, improving mass transfer and ensuring complete consumption of the Grignard reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction medium was cooled to −5 °C, and after the addition of Fe(acac)₃ (0.001 equiv), dienol phosphate 6a was added dropwise… The reaction mixture was then stirred at 20 °C overnight.”; “Because of the high viscosity of the bulk, the reaction medium was stirred overnight at 20 °C to ensure full consumption of 5.”

Paper Title: Short and Easily Scalable Synthesis of the Sex Pheromone of the Horse-Chestnut Leaf Miner (
Problem_Description: Typical iron‑catalyzed Kumada couplings in the literature require toxic co‑solvents/additives such as N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone (NMP) to achieve good yields, posing health and environmental hazards.
Solution_Description: The authors demonstrated that the cross‑coupling proceeds efficiently without any additional ligands or toxic additives (e.g., NMP), using only Fe(acac)₃ and the substrate‑derived ω‑alkoxide Grignard, thereby improving safety and reducing waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “It is worth noting that the alkyl–alkenyl Fe‑catalyzed Kumada cross‑coupling… remarkably proceeds without requiring additional ligands or any toxic additive such as N‑methylpyrrolidone (NMP), as usually required by classic procedures.”

Paper Title: Short and Easily Scalable Synthesis of the Sex Pheromone of the Horse-Chestnut Leaf Miner (
Problem_Description: Alkyl‑Fe(II) intermediates can undergo β‑hydride elimination, leading to loss of the Grignard reagent and lower coupling efficiency.
Solution_Description: Incorporation of an ω‑alkoxide group in the Grignard reagent stabilises the transient Fe‑alkyl species by chelating the metal and preventing β‑agostic interactions, thereby suppressing decomposition pathways and delivering high coupling yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “DFT calculations… suggest that ω‑alkoxide groups on iron‑ligated chains in transient organoiron(II) intermediates can enhance their stability and hamper their decomposition in off‑cycle β‑hydride elimination reactions.”; “The high yield obtained… suggests that the transient organoiron‑II intermediates… exhibit good kinetic stability toward β‑hydride elimination.”

Problem_Description: During batch mesylation of 2‑phenylethanol, precipitation of the ammonium chloride by‑product caused solid formation and reactor clogging, especially at higher concentrations.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow micro‑reactor and heated to 40 °C, which kept the ammonium chloride dissolved and prevented clogging. The flow system allowed operation at 0.3 M concentration without solid formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In batch reactions, precipitation of the ammonium chloride salt is typically observed. Consequently, only few examples of mesylation processes in continuous flow have been described.” (sec 2)

Problem_Description: Several alkyl mesylates (e.g., S5, S6) showed low solubility in the chosen reaction medium, leading to low conversion and reactor fouling.

Supporting_Evidence: “Whereas dichloromethane or ether could be used as solvents at a concentration of 0.1 M, only acetonitrile was suitable at higher concentration (0.3 M).” (sec 2)

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process

Solution_Description: A new scalable route was devised that started from commercially available 4‑bromo‑3‑fluoroanisole, employed regioselective lithiation and copper‑mediated alkylation, and used a telescoped, chromatography‑free sequence (one‑pot saponification, Boc‑deprotection/demethylation, and cyclization) to afford the key bromo‑benzofuran intermediate, eliminating the need for HPLC purification and raising the overall yield to 30 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The discovery route ... resulted in an overall yield of 2.5 %.", "...the tedious chromatographic purification and the low overall yield for these two steps rendered the discovery synthetic route unsuitable for scale‑up.", "To surmount these scale‑up issues, a modification of this route designed to avoid purification by chromatography was developed...", "The formation of the benzofuran ring ... a chromatography‑free, telescoped process was developed to generate the highly functionalized key bromo benzofuran 26."]

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: Attempted cyclization of intermediate 12 (approach A) to the bromo‑benzofuran 16a gave no detectable product and generated complex mixtures, indicating a failure of the key ring‑closing step.
Solution_Description: Approach A was abandoned; the research program switched to approach B, which relied on a regioselective lithiation/acylation sequence from 4‑bromo‑3‑fluoroanisole and ultimately succeeded in delivering the desired benzofuran core.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The cyclization of 12 to 16a employing the literature conditions proved problematic, with no detectable amounts of product 16a... Complex mixtures were observed, and approach A was therefore abandoned.", "Although approach A was not a viable option, we were particularly encouraged by the reaction profile associated with the regioselective lithiation and acylation of 11 to give 12. Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The early steps of approach B (formation of ester 14 and keto‑amide 20) required column chromatography on laboratory scale, which led to low isolated yields (42 % for 14, 53 % for 15, 72 % for 20) and was impractical for multigram production.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot telescoped process was introduced: after copper‑mediated alkylation, the crude ester 14 was directly saponified with aqueous NaOH, the resulting acid 21 was precipitated by acidification and filtered, thus avoiding chromatography; subsequent steps also proceeded without isolation, culminating in a chromatography‑free preparation of the benzofuran intermediate 26.
Supporting_Evidence: ["While the preliminary results from exploring approach B were successful, the tedious chromatographic purification of compounds 14 and 20, which resulted in low recovery and yields, presented a major problem for scale‑up attempts.", "Indeed, after the formation of ester 14, treatment of the reaction mixture with a solution of 2.5 N NaOH at 50–55 °C for 20 h led to the complete conversion of 14 to acid 21... Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The Suzuki coupling of bromo‑benzofuran 26 with the boronate 7 gave only 47 % conversion at 50 °C and required hot trituration with ethanol to remove residual palladium and achieve high purity (99.3 % HPLC, Pd = 48 ppm).
Solution_Description: Raising the reaction temperature to 83 °C completed the coupling within 2 h and afforded 85 % isolated yield; subsequent hot trituration with ethanol and crystallization removed palladium to acceptable levels and increased product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Using 1.2 equiv of 7 with Pd(PPh₃)₄ (2 mol%) as the catalyst ... the reaction proceeded at 50 °C to afford a 47 % conversion in 3 h. However, at 83 °C, the reaction was complete in just 2 h and afforded product 8 in an 85 % isolated yield.", "It is important to note that after precipitation of the crude product from the reaction mixture and filtration, hot trituration with EtOH followed by crystallization from EtOH was essential to improve the purity (up to 99.3 %) and to reduce the Pd content to 48 ppm."]

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of BMS-929075, an Allosteric, Palm Site Inhibitor of HCV NS5B Replicase, Involving the Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Benzofuran through a Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The final amide coupling using HATU left residual palladium in the product; direct precipitation from the reaction mixture gave a slurry that was difficult to filter efficiently.
Solution_Description: Addition of water to the HATU‑mediated coupling mixture generated a filterable slurry; the product was then isolated by hot filtration, EtOH recrystallization, and washing with cold EtOH, delivering API of 99.2 % HPLC purity and Pd = 10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...the mixture was stirred at rt for 3 h, and then H₂O (600 mL) was added over 10 min with stirring. The white suspension was stirred at rt for 1 h and filtered. The filter cake was washed with H₂O (3 × 100 mL)... The filter cake was dissolved in EtOH (750 mL) under gentle reflux, ... The suspension was gradually cooled to rt over a period of 2 h and then filtered. The filter cake was washed with cold EtOH (−20 °C, 50 mL) and dried... to give BMS‑929075 ... 99.2 % HPLC purity, Pd = 10 ppm."]

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: The peptide‑coupling step between 2‑amino‑5‑bromo‑2′‑fluorobenzophenone (1) and Boc‑d‑alanine using DCC gave only moderate conversion on multigram scale (≈58–62 % yield) and the basic conditions required for the subsequent 7‑membered 1,4‑diazepine ring caused racemisation of the chiral centre.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the DCC/DMAP protocol with an N‑carboxyanhydride (NCA) of d‑alanine.  Activation of the NCA with a catalytic amount of TFA reacted cleanly with the non‑basic amine 1, and neutralisation with triethylamine generated the imine without the need for strong base, giving 77 % isolated yield of the protected diazepine and >99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Investigations of peptide coupling reagents on a multigram scale resulted in moderate yields due to incomplete conversions.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: Earlier routes required column chromatography to isolate the intermediates because the products and by‑products had overlapping solubilities, which made scale‑up inefficient.
Solution_Description: A work‑up strategy that exploits divergent solubility of the intermediates in selected solvent mixtures (e.g., hexanes, ethyl‑acetate/heptane, MeOH/H₂O) was developed, allowing the crude material to be triturated and filtered without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Carefully designed workup procedures and divergent solubility of the synthesic intermediates in solvents and solvent combinations were utilized to eliminate the need for column chromatography.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: The formation of the imidazodiazepine ring (step 3) is highly exothermic; uncontrolled heat release at low temperature caused poor conversion and required excessive stirring.
Solution_Description: Reagents were added dropwise at –20 °C using a dry‑ice/isopropanol bath, maintaining the reaction temperature throughout the sequential additions of t‑BuOK, diethyl chlorophosphate, and ethyl isocyanate.  This controlled the heat evolution and gave full conversion in a single batch.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The third step … temperature‑controlled slow addition of reagents generated the imidazodiazepine at −20 °C.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: When DCC, EDCI, or other carbodiimide reagents were employed, the amide‑forming step consistently gave yields ≤ 60 %, even after increasing equivalents, changing temperature, or extending reaction time.
Solution_Description: Switching to a mixed carbonic‑anhydride activation (methyl chloroformate + N‑methylmorpholine) gave the best result (50 % yield) for the coupling of 1 with Boc‑d‑alanine, indicating that a more electrophilic acylating agent overcomes the low nucleophilicity of 1.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction using methyl chloroformate in the presence of N‑methylmorpholine gave the best yield for 2 with 50.0 %.” (Results and Discussion)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: Applying the previously published hydrolysis conditions (8 equiv NaOH in ethanol) on scale produced an insoluble, gel‑like MIDD0301 sodium salt that could not be isolated.
Solution_Description: The authors reduced NaOH to 4 equiv, lowered the temperature from 78 °C to 50 °C, and performed the work‑up in a 1 : 4 water/THF biphasic system.  This kept the mixture homogeneous, allowed full conversion in 4 h, and gave the free acid in 98 % yield after crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using our published hydrolysis conditions… an insoluble and gel‑like MIDD0301 sodium salt was observed. To overcome this problem, a 1:4 ratio of water and THF was employed… the initial 8 equiv of sodium hydroxide were reduced to 4 equiv and the reaction temperature lowered from 78 to 50 °C, achieving full conversion… the isolated yield was 98 %.” (Results and Discussion)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: Cyclisation of the protected intermediate 4 required up to 48 h for complete conversion; scaling from 60 mM to 116 mM introduced racemisation (ee fell to 53.9 %).
Solution_Description: Increasing the base loading to 1 equiv NaOH shortened the cyclisation to 12 h but gave a racemic product.  Heating the crude 4 in toluene at 60 °C for 4 h produced the desired product in 50 % yield with 99.2 % ee, eliminating the long, variable basic step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Longer reaction times were required for complete conversion of 4… scaling… led to racemization… To reduce the reaction time, one equiv of sodium hydroxide was used… Full conversion was achieved in 12 h, but a racemic product was obtained.” (Results and Discussion)

Paper Title: Improved Scale-up Synthesis and Purification of Clinical Asthma Candidate MIDD0301
Problem_Description: The synthesis of the N‑carboxyanhydride (6) generates CO₂, HCl, and residual phosgene, which are hazardous gases.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in a sealed reactor equipped with a dry‑ice / isopropanol bath and a methanolic scrubber system to trap CO₂, HCl, and phosgene, ensuring safe handling of volatile by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The formed CO₂, HCl, and residual phosgene were trapped by a methanolic scrubber system.” (Experimental Procedure)

Problem_Description: Using the T‑shaped (θ = 90°) micromixer at a low flow rate (Q = 1.625 mL min⁻¹, tᴿ = 220 ms) gave a 59 % conversion in the first run, but the same conditions produced widely differing conversions (31 %–71 %) and lower product selectivity in the following repeats, i.e. the reaction was not reproducible.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the total flow rate by more than five‑fold (Q ≈ 9 mL min⁻¹, tᴿ ≈ 40 ms) forced much faster mixing and a shorter residence time, which restored reproducibility and gave >98 % conversion with consistent selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The first assay gave a satisfactory result: 59 % conversion ... Unfortunately, these results were not reproducible.
