Paper Title: Bromine–Lithium Exchange on a
Problem_Description: When both streams were dissolved in hexane (the common solvent) the micro‑flow system clogged instantly, which the authors ascribed to precipitation of LiBr formed during the bromine–lithium exchange. The same clogging was observed when THF was used together with an i‑PrOH quench to maintain homogeneity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors switched to THF as the common solvent for the two streams and added a protic quench (i‑PrOH) to keep the mixture homogeneous. In parallel they employed the 45° W‑shaped mixer with the smaller internal diameter (250 µm), which gave superior mixing, eliminated clogging, and afforded the highest E‑selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Clogging occurred.', 'When the same solvent for the two streams (hexane) ... the system immediately clogged whatever the angle of micromixer, probably because of LiBr precipitation.', 'With hexane as the common solvent ... the system immediately clogged whatever the angle of micromixer, probably because of LiBr precipitation.', 'With THF as the common solvent (and i‑PrOH used as a protic quench to keep the reaction mixture homogeneous), the system immediately clogged whatever the angle of micromixer.']

Paper Title: Bromine–Lithium Exchange on a
Problem_Description: Solutions of n‑BuLi in THF are very unstable at room temperature; the reagent degrades rapidly, posing a safety risk and limiting the practical use of THF as the organolithium carrier.
Solution_Description: The exchange was run under continuous flow at 20 °C with a residence time of only 40 ms (high flow, short residence). The brief exposure of n‑BuLi in THF prevents significant degradation while still delivering quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Preparing a solution of n‑BuLi in THF proved to be very challenging, as THF solutions of n‑BuLi are prone to rapid degradation at room temperature.', 'Higher flow rates unambiguously improved the conversion toward 2: all of the mixers gave an increased or similar conversion compared to lower flow rates, despite the shortened residence time (as the reactor length and width were kept constant).']

Paper Title: Bromine–Lithium Exchange on a
Problem_Description: The origin of the observed variations in E/Z stereoselectivity with different micromixer geometries was unclear; it was unknown whether the effect stemmed from a fast E/Z equilibration of the carbenoid intermediate or from changes in organolithium aggregation.
Solution_Description: To test the equilibrium hypothesis, the authors kept the flow rate constant (Q = 9 mL min⁻¹, θ = 90°) and varied the length of the reactor tube (3 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm) – thus changing the residence time from 40 ms to 120 ms. The E/Z ratio remained essentially unchanged, indicating that the stereoselectivity does not arise from a thermodynamic equilibration.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The equilibrium hypothesis, on the other hand, was ruled out by dedicated experiments: a microflow setup was implemented with fixed flow rate (Q = 9 mL min⁻¹) and micromixer (θ = 90°, ID = 500 µm), and only the length of the reactor tube was modified (L = 3 cm, 6 cm, 9 cm). With L = 3 cm (tᴿ = 40 ms), 6 cm (tᴿ = 80 ms), or 9 cm (tᴿ = 120 ms), full conversion into 2 was observed with almost no evolution of the E/Z ratio over time.']

Paper Title: Continuous Production of Five Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients in Flexible Plug-and-Play Modules: A Demonstration Campaign
Problem_Description: Pumping neat and/or aggressive chemicals at the pressures and flow rates required (≈250 psi, 1–10 mL min⁻¹) was identified as a key challenge because the combination of chemical compatibility, high pressure, and temperature in a compact unit is not supported by commercial hardware.

Supporting_Evidence: • “Pumping neat and/or aggressive chemicals at the pressures and flow rates required by this project (∼250 psi, 1–10 mL/min) continued to be the key challenge.”

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: The previously reported synthetic routes (A‑C) suffered from low overall yields and required expensive or hyper‑toxic reagents, making large‑scale production uneconomical and unsafe.
Solution_Description: A new four‑step route was devised that starts from inexpensive, stable 5′‑uridylic acid disodium salt (UMP‑2Na) and sodium pyrophosphate, avoiding hyper‑toxic reagents and reducing material cost while maintaining safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “We envisioned that the most applicable way to synthesize 1 was to select 5′‑uridylic acid disodium salt (UMP‑2Na) as the starting material and avoid the use of hypertoxic reagents.”; “Pyridine was used… and the low yield, which prevented the large‑scale synthesis of this route.”; “expensive reagents such as 2‑aminophenyl disulfide.”; “expensive starting material and impurities resulting from the instability of the starting material.”

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: Pyrophosphoric acid rapidly hydrolyses/decomposes in aqueous solution, leading to loss of the key phosphorus source.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: When CDI was added in excess, a bis‑uridyl diphosphate impurity (12) formed, reducing product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: CDI was added slowly and the excess was quenched with methanol, eliminating formation of impurity 12.
Supporting_Evidence: “the impurity… was observed if excess CDI was not destroyed by methanol… quenching of excess CDI was an essential step.”; “we recommend to slowly add CDI for large‑scale manufacture.”

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: Using short‑chain organic amines (triethylamine, etc.) gave <20 % isolated yield for the condensation step.
Solution_Description: Switching to the longer‑chain amine N‑butyl‑N‑isobutylbutan‑1‑amine, employing DMF as solvent, using 2 equiv of amine and MgCl₂, and running the reaction at 20 °C raised the isolated yield to 38 % (and higher under further optimisation).
Supporting_Evidence: “target product … could only be obtained with low yields (<20 %) when short‑chain organic amines were used” (Table 1 entries 1‑5); “yield … increased when long‑chain organic amines were used” (entries 6‑8); “the temperature of the reaction … 20 °C turned out to be suitable” (entries 14‑16).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: Isolating diquafosol with >99 % purity required efficient removal of residual starting material and side‑products; resin type and eluent concentration strongly affected impurity clearance.
Solution_Description: Amberlite D‑311 anion‑exchange resin was selected; a two‑step NaCl elution (0.5 M to strip impurities, then 2 M to elute product) gave >99 % purity and 45 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “acceptable results were observed when the types of Amberlite anion‑exchange resins were used… D‑311 … yield of 45 % and a purity of 95.9 %.”; “different concentrations of sodium chloride solutions were screened… 2 mol/L sodium chloride solution … purity of our product 1 was close to 99 %.”

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to the Preparation of Diquafosol Tetrasodium
Problem_Description: Scaling the process to kilogram scale risked loss of yield and purity consistency.
Solution_Description: The previously optimised batch conditions were directly transferred to the kilogram scale; after the primary isolation, two successive ethanol/water recrystallisations lifted the combined isolated yield to 80 % and purity to 99.9 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “In several trials at this scale, the isolated yield … was 45 %… The crude target product… showed a purity of 99.781 %… purified by ethanol/water recrystallization twice, gave a combined yield of 80 % and a final purity of 99.905 %.”

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: The early‑phase Pictet–Spengler cyclisation of phenylalanine derivative 2 to tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 required 18–32 h, was run at a low 0.1 M concentration, suffered from slow filtration of the product, and the crude product tended to float on the aqueous layer, causing sampling failures and making the step a bottleneck for the whole synthesis.
Solution_Description: Running the cyclisation in neat acetic acid at 50 °C gave complete conversion in 1 h; the reaction concentration was raised to 0.5 M and the product was isolated as the HCl salt, which filtered rapidly and did not float. The solvent switch and temperature increase together removed the long‑reaction time and filtration problems.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The early phase process for the Pictet–Spengler cyclization ... identified the following challenges: (i) long reaction times of 18–32 h, (ii) a low concentration (0.1 M), (iii) a slow filtration during the isolation of tetrahydroisoquinoline 3, (iv) the product had a tendency to float on the aqueous layer on scale..."  
"when we ran the cyclization entirely in acetic acid as the solvent, full conversion was observed at 50 °C within 1 h... the concentration could be increased to 0.5 M... fast filtration of 3·HCl... no floating observed"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: Increasing the temperature or lowering the pH of the aqueous Pictet–Spengler reaction caused partial cleavage of the benzyl protecting group, generating phenol 8 and reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switching to acetic‑acid solvent and maintaining the reaction at 50 °C (instead of higher temperatures) prevented benzyl de‑protection while still providing rapid conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Attempts to decrease the reaction time by increasing the temperature or by decreasing the pH led to the partial cleavage of the benzyl group."  
"Gratifyingly, when we ran the cyclization entirely in acetic acid as the solvent, full conversion was observed at 50 °C within 1 h"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: Adding 2 wt % water to the reaction mixture increased the solubility of tetrahydroisoquinoline 3, causing >10 % loss of product to the mother liquor.
Solution_Description: The water content was tightly controlled (minimal addition) to keep 3 in the solid phase and avoid product loss during work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: "The water content in the reaction was found to be critical and the addition of 2 wt % H₂O ... caused the loss of more than 10 % tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 in the mother liquor due to the increased solubility of 3 in aqueous acidic conditions."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: The early‑phase amide‑coupling sequence required isolation of the pyrrazole intermediate 11, used the REACH‑listed solvent DMF, involved many aqueous washes, and comprised several discrete unit operations, increasing material cost, safety burden, waste, and overall cycle time.
Solution_Description: The authors moved to an in‑situ activation of diphenylacetic acid with CDI (order‑of‑addition change), replaced DMF with the greener dipolar aprotic solvent 4‑formylmorpholine (NFM) in a toluene/NFM mixture, and telescoped the sequence to a single isolated step, thereby cutting down on washes, waste, and exposure to a hazardous solvent.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The early phase process for the amide coupling ... aimed at (i) reduce the amount and number of chemicals used ... (iii) avoid the isolation of pyrrazole 11, and (iv) replace the REACH listed solvent DMF..."  
"We aimed at the in situ activation of diphenylacetic acid (4) to avoid the isolation of pyrrazole 11... DMF was replaced by 4‑formylmorpholine (NFM)"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: Non‑selective activation of the carboxylic acid on tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 resulted in erosion of chiral purity and formation of side‑products 12 and 13, lowering isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The activation reagent (CDI) was added in a controlled stoichiometry (1.15 eq CDI, 1.20 eq acid 4) and only after the acid on 4 was activated, the mixture was added to the suspension of 3, preventing activation of the acid on 3 and preserving enantiopurity.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Activation of the carboxylic acid on tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 led to the erosion of the chiral purity and to the formation of coupling products 12 and 13."  
"Since both 3 and 4 bear a carboxylic acid functionality, it was of obvious importance to activate only the carboxylic acid on diphenylacetic acid (4)."  
"the equivalents were kept below 1.1 with respect to tetrahydroisoquinoline 3."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: Tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 showed very low solubility in most organic solvents, leading to gel formation or unstirred suspensions that impeded the amide‑coupling step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A strong, non‑nucleophilic base (DBU) was employed to generate a stirrable suspension of 3, and a solvent blend of toluene with 4‑formylmorpholine (NFM) was identified as the optimal medium, delivering a homogeneous reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The low solubility of tetrahydroisoquinoline 3 in most organic solvents mandated the use of a base to increase its solubility. Various bases were screened ... only DBU was capable of forming a stirrable suspension of 3 ..."  
"Combined with the fact that the sodium salt [6] was soluble in toluene, we focused our attention to solvent mixtures of dipolar aprotic solvents with toluene... NFM was found to be the most benign option..."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: During the CDI‑mediated activation, addition of diphenylacetic acid 4 generated CO₂ and a weak exotherm; later, the aqueous H₂SO₄ quench produced a strong exotherm that had to be kept below 20 °C.
Solution_Description: The addition of acid 4 and the subsequent H₂SO₄ quench were performed slowly, with temperature monitoring and cooling (inner temperature < 20 °C), to suppress the exotherms safely.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Diphenylacetic acid (4) must be added carefully since CO₂ was produced upon addition. Furthermore, a weak exotherm was observed."  
"The addition of 10% aq H₂SO₄ ... was strongly exotherm; the inner temperature must not exceed 20 °C."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: EMA401 exhibited a complex solid‑state landscape (multiple solvates, hydrates, amorphous forms). The initially used hydrate‑rich crystal required fluid‑bed drying, and the wet cake became hygroscopic when washed with EtOAc, jeopardising handling and downstream processing.
Solution_Description: A water/EtOAc antisolvent crystallisation was developed to afford the anhydrous polymorph, followed by a final heptane wash and drying under nitrogen, eliminating the need for fluid‑bed dryers and providing a stable, non‑hygroscopic product suitable for pilot‑plant equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: "The sodium salt of EMA401 can crystallize in different solid states ... The latter was our target phase, which was stable up to 65 % relative humidity... A targeted solvent screen ... water/EtOAc was selected... The crystallization procedure was successfully scaled up to a 90 kg scale... a final wash with heptane was implemented as the filter cake was hygroscopic when wetted with EtOAc... the modified process to the new polymorph no longer required special equipment such as fluidized bed drying."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part I: Late Stage Process Development, Route Scouting, and ICH M7 Assessment
Problem_Description: Bis‑(chloromethyl) ether (BCME) is a highly toxic, mutagenic impurity that could theoretically form in the Pictet–Spengler step where HCl and formaldehyde are present together.
Solution_Description: The team applied ICH M7 Control Option 4 (purge‑factor tool) to calculate conservatively high purge factors, performed spiking experiments that showed BCME below the LOQ at each stage, and thus demonstrated that the process inherently purges BCME well below the toxicological limit.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Bis‑(chloromethyl) ether (BCME) is a highly toxic compound ... due to the simultaneous presence of HCl and CH₂O in the Pictet–Spengler cyclization, BCME could theoretically be formed."  
"We studied the literature ... applied ICH M7 control option 4 ... calculated purge factor ... Spiking experiments showed no BCME could be detected above the LOQ, and the measured purge factor was larger than required."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: The original Knoevenagel–Doebner condensation used pyridine as solvent and piperidine as organocatalyst. Pyridine is classified as possibly carcinogenic and hazardous to aquatic life, while piperidine is a regulated narcotics precursor. Both reagents therefore raise safety and regulatory concerns for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The researchers replaced pyridine with toluene and piperidine with morpholine, delivering a fully new reaction route that uses a benign solvent (toluene) and a safer, readily available organocatalyst (morpholine).
Supporting_Evidence:
“We aimed to replace both piperidine and pyridine for several reasons: (1) piperidine is a precursor substance of narcotics… (2) pyridine is possibly carcinogenic to humans and hazardous to the aquatic environment… (3) using an acidic quench … would have yielded large amounts of aqueous waste… With large‑scale commercial manufacturing in mind, we aimed to develop… more benign reagents and solvents.”
“...we identified novel conditions involving toluene as the solvent and morpholine as the organocatalyst.”
"Entry 2… pyridine/morpholine gave >99 % conversion…"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: When the reaction was performed in pyridine with morpholine, the aqueous acidic quench was highly exothermic, producing a very thick suspension that adhered to reactor walls and caused fouling.
Solution_Description: The process was modified to add morpholine as a pre‑heated solution (55–65 °C) rather than neat addition, and the temperature profile was controlled to avoid the exothermic shock, which eliminated the gum‑like deposits and improved stirrability.
Supporting_Evidence:
"the reaction afforded very thick suspensions after a very exothermic quench with aqueous acids, and the material generated… tended to stick to the walls of the reactor."
"We reasoned that this might be caused by the formation of morpholinium salts. Therefore, we decided to dose morpholine as a solution in toluene at an internal temperature (IT) of 55–65 °C. When the process was run in this manner, the formation of the gumlike intermediate was no longer observed."
"When all of the starting materials … were charged … a gum‑like substance was formed … which dissolved again at temperatures above 50 °C."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: At a scale‑up with 1.2 equiv of malonic acid, incomplete conversion of aldehyde 4 led to a strong yellow impurity, later shown to arise from polymerization and decomposition of malonic acid (CO₂ elimination).
Solution_Description: The amount of malonic acid was increased to 1.3 equiv, providing sufficient reagent to drive the reaction to full conversion before polymerization could occur, while maintaining the temperature at 110 °C to ensure rapid decarboxylation without side‑reactions.
Supporting_Evidence:
"In our initial trials, however, we were not able to achieve full conversion … observed the formation of a dark‑yellow color… we hypothesized that the decomposition of malonic acid is a competing side reaction…"
"DSC of malonic acid showed a first endotherm starting at 82 °C … indicating decomposition…"
"we increased the amount of malonic acid and found that 1.3 equiv was required to achieve full conversion of aldehyde 4 and prevent the formation of a strongly yellow colored product."
"When the mixture was heated … CO₂ is formed over the entire reaction time of approximately 1.5–2 h above ca. 80 °C…"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: Using MeTHF as solvent gave high solubility of cinnamic acid (≈15 wt %) which required very large volumes of heptane antisolvent to obtain a stir‑rable suspension, reducing process efficiency.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to toluene, which has lower cinnamic‑acid solubility, allowing much smaller antisolvent volumes and a more manageable suspension, while retaining morpholine as catalyst and increasing substrate concentration two‑fold in the later streamlined process.
Supporting_Evidence:
"In MeTHF … the high solubility of cinnamic acid 3 (14.7 wt %), further increased by the presence of morpholine, meant that large volumes of an antisolvent, heptane in our case, were required…"
"In an initial screening with toluene … full conversion could be achieved in 2 h… toluene is about 7 times less expensive than MeTHF."
"The concentration could be increased by a factor of 2… resulting in a PMI reduction from 47.1 to 7.3."
"Using toluene … precipitation occurred after approximately 33 % of the total heptane volume… resulting in a thick but stir‑rable suspension."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: The crude cinnamic acid contained 3–5 mol % morpholine. Hydrochloric acid efficiently removed morpholine but could generate ethyl chloride in the presence of ethanol and was incompatible with reactor materials.
Solution_Description: A 10 % citric‑acid wash (85:15 v/v citric‑acid:acetonitrile) was introduced, which purged morpholine without material‑compatibility issues, followed by a short water wash; addition of a small amount of ethanol later broke surface tension and aided solid transfer.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Hydrochloric acid proved to purge morpholine efficiently… but because of its incompatibility with some materials of construction and the potential to form ethyl chloride in the presence of EtOH, we searched for alternative acids. Employing sulfuric acid led to yellow impurities… When 10 % citric acid was used, we were able to purge morpholine…"
"We serendipitously had also noted that the addition of acetonitrile helped purge by‑product VI. Therefore, a 10 % citric acid solution was mixed with acetonitrile (85:15 v/v) for the first wash…"
"The addition of EtOH helped to break the surface tension and ensured that the suspension could be transferred onto the filter. Since cinnamic acid 3 is highly soluble in ethanol, the amount employed was minimized to 0.25 v/w…"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: Initial conditions required 7 h at 94 °C in toluene to reach full conversion, which limited throughput for kilogram‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: Raising the jacket temperature to 110 °C reduced the reaction time to 2 h while maintaining high conversion and clean product profiles, thereby improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
"In an initial screening with toluene at 94 °C, the reaction took 7 h for full conversion. When the reaction was repeated with heating to JT = 110 °C, we were pleased to find that full conversion … could be achieved in 2 h."
"The mixture was heated using a Dean–Stark trap at IT = 110 ± 5 °C for 3 h…"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: 4‑Methylmorpholine offered high conversion but its self‑ignition temperature (167 °C) demanded extra safety measures, increasing operational cost.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned 4‑methylmorpholine and selected morpholine (lower cost, safer) together with toluene, which also reduced material cost by a factor of seven compared with MeTHF.
Supporting_Evidence:
"When 4‑methylmorpholine was used, a conversion of 99 % was observed… however, the 4‑methylmorpholine self‑ignition temperature of 167 °C would have required additional safety measures…"
"In addition, toluene is about 7 times less expensive than MeTHF."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: Using pure water as the reaction medium gave <1 % conversion, making it an ineffective solvent for the condensation.
Solution_Description: The process was moved to organic solvents (toluene, MeTHF, CPME, etc.) with boiling points above 60 °C, delivering >80 % conversion at temperatures >80 °C.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Entry 20… H₂O… gave <1 % conversion…"
"A minimal boiling point of 60 °C was imposed… most of the solvents tested gave good to excellent conversion… THF, MeTHF, CPME, DMSO, tert‑amyl alcohol, iPrOH, toluene, xylenes all gave >80 % conversion after 2–7 h at temperatures above 80 °C."

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part II: Development and Scale-Up of a Pyridine- and Piperidine-Free Knoevenagel–Doebner Condensation
Problem_Description: When the reaction mixture was cooled after work‑up, cinnamic acid precipitated as a hard solid that blocked stirrers and formed crusts in the reactor.
Solution_Description: A small amount of ethanol (0.25 v/w) was added prior to cooling to lower surface tension, enabling a smooth suspension that could be filtered and transferred without crust formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
"When tert‑amyl alcohol was used… the desired product precipitated rapidly as a hard solid, which caused stirrers to block and produced crusts that were not easily washed out of the reactor. Modifying the conditions did not help…"
"Only the addition of EtOH helped to break the surface tension and ensured that the suspension could be transferred onto the filter. Since cinnamic acid 3 is highly soluble in ethanol, the amount employed was minimized to 0.25 v/w…"

Paper Title: Toward a Scalable Synthesis and Process for EMA401, Part III: Using an Engineered Phenylalanine Ammonia Lyase Enzyme to Synthesize a Non-natural Phenylalanine Derivative
Problem_Description: The highly concentrated ammonia‑buffer required for driving the PAL‑catalyzed hydroamination (≈9–10 M NH₃, pH 10) was limited by the solubility of the carbonate/carbamate system; above pH 10.5 the enzyme lost stability, and at lower pH (<8.5) little conversion was observed. High temperature (>70 °C) caused enzyme denaturation. The initial enzyme loadings (up to 25 wt % PAL) were costly, and the reaction mixture formed a thick emulsion at substrate loadings >3 v/w, making stirring difficult. Quenching with strong acid released large amounts of CO₂ rapidly, creating a violent exotherm and foaming. After the PAL step, the product mixture contained the β‑amino‑acid by‑product 10 and phenol 11, complicating isolation of the desired amino‑acid 3.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: 1. A carbonate/carbamate‑buffered ammonia system was selected and the ammonia concentration was tuned to 9–10 M (pH 9.5–10.5) to stay within the solubility limits while providing enough driving force for the equilibrium. 2. A temperature‑gradient profile (45 °C → 20 °C) was introduced: a short high‑temperature pre‑equilibrium maximized activity, then cooling preserved enzyme stability and pushed the equilibrium toward product. 3. Directed‑evolution of PAL generated variants (PAL‑130, PAL‑131) with higher specific activity, allowing enzyme loadings to be reduced to 2.5–5 wt % (cost reduction). 4. Reaction concentrations of 3–9 v/w were adopted and vigorous agitation (anchor stirrer) was used to manage the emulsion and maintain good mixing. 5. Acid quench was performed with a controlled dose of aqueous H₂SO₄ together with an organic co‑solvent (toluene) to suppress foaming and moderate the exotherm. 6. The work‑up sequence (enzyme denaturation with MeOH, distillation of NH₃/CO₂, acidification, clear filtration and telescoping to the Pictet–Spengler step) removed the β‑amino‑acid impurity and allowed efficient isolation of the desired product, eliminating the need for a separate purification of amino‑acid 3.
Supporting_Evidence: • "higher ammonia concentration led to higher conversion… however the ammonia concentration was limited by the solubility of the buffer system… reduced stability of the enzyme above pH 10.5" (Fig 2a,b).  • "The mixture was stirred at 45 °C for 8 h… subsequently the mixture was cooled to 20 °C… higher enzyme activity and lower enzyme stability at 45 °C were balanced with lower enzyme activity and higher enzyme stability at 20 °C" (Temperature Profile).  • "PAL‑131, 2.5 wt %… PAL‑130, 5 wt %… conversion >60 % after 8 h at 45 °C… enzyme loading could be reduced…" (Enzyme Loading).  • "cinnamic acid 2 did not dissolve… formed an emulsion… acceptable stirring properties could be achieved when the reaction mixtures were concentrated to 3 v/w" (Substrate Concentration).  • "When acids were added, full denaturation… but at the cost of a strong exotherm, the violent release of large amounts of CO₂, and hence concomitant foaming" (Quench with Acids).  • "The preferred workup options… resulted in an aqueous acidic solution of amino‑acid 3… The β‑amino‑acid 10 was observed in amounts below 0.5 area %… the aqueous acidic layer was telescoped to the subsequent Pictet–Spengler cyclization" (Workup of the PAL‑Catalyzed Reaction).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: The initial C‑1 methyl installation relied on cryogenic deprotonation of a Boc‑protected THIQ with LDA, gave a mixture of diastereomers and unreacted starting material, required preparative HPLC for separation and afforded only 28 % yield over two steps.
Solution_Description: A new route was introduced that first performed a benzylic oxidation to an imine, followed by addition of MeMgCl at low temperature. This sequence gave high trans‑diastereoselectivity (>9:1 dr) and a much higher isolated yield, eliminating the cryogenic LDA step and the chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Early medicinal chemistry routes … employed deprotonation of a Boc protected tetrahydroisoquinoline (THIQ) with lithium diisopropyl amide (LDA) … mixture of diastereomers … only 28 % yield …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: Intermediate 17 was an oil that was difficult to isolate, store and handle, and the multistep sequence required nine chromatographic purifications, giving an overall 27 % yield for the eight‑step pre‑clinical route.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The route was streamlined by removing unnecessary protecting‑group manipulations, telescoping several steps, and isolating the intermediate as its hydrochloride salt (17·HCl). This eliminated the oil‑handling problem, removed all chromatographic purifications and raised the overall yield to 27 % (eight steps).
Supporting_Evidence: • “The final step required chromatographic purification primarily because 17 is an oil … The streamlined route afforded 17 in 27 % overall yield and eight steps … all nine chromatographic purifications removed …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: Methyl‑carbamate formation (step 2) used a biphasic CH₂Cl₂/aq NaHCO₃ system requiring 20 V CH₂Cl₂ and 12 V water; the low aqueous solubility of NaHCO₃ drove the large solvent volume.
Solution_Description: NaHCO₃ was replaced with K₂CO₃, which gave comparable conversion but allowed the total solvent volume to be reduced from 32 V to 8 V, cutting waste and cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Attempts to reduce these volumes lead to lower purity 8. … it was assumed that the low aqueous solubility of NaHCO₃ drove the use of large volume of solvent and so various bases were then screened … K₂CO₃ showed comparable results and allowed the overall solvent volume to be reduced from 32 to 8 V …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: Large‑scale reduction of the acid 10·HCl to the alcohol 14 using lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) posed safety hazards, generated aluminum residues that required a Fieser work‑up, and created waste‑handling issues.
Solution_Description: The LAH step was replaced first by Red‑Al reduction (still a hydride but easier to quench) and finally by a NaBH₄ reduction of the methyl ester 11 after a re‑esterification step; the NaBH₄ work‑up used a simple aqueous NaCl quench and antisolvent precipitation, eliminating the Fieser filtration and reducing safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reduction of carboxylic acid 10·HCl to alcohol 14 was achieved using LAH, … this has considerable drawbacks on a larger scale … Red‑Al was found to be a good replacement for LAH … It was found that simply quenching the reduction with 10 V of saturated aq NaCl gave good layer separation …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the cryogenic batch addition of MeLi to imine 21 gave a substantial increase in impurities and a drop in isolated yield (35 % for an 80 kg batch), indicating poor reproducibility and safety concerns with prolonged exposure of product to MeLi at low temperature.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition was transferred to a continuous‑flow plug‑flow reactor (PFR) operated at –78 °C, which drastically reduced the residence time of product in the presence of MeLi, provided superior heat and mass transfer, and delivered consistent performance (≈70 % yield, dr > 6:1) at 113 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Given the unexpectedly poor performance of the MeLi at 80 kg scale … The batch MeLi addition time had been almost 4 h … Continuous flow conditions … afforded consistent reaction performance … The new process afforded 101 kg of 22·hemisulfate.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: The organometallic addition to imine 21 required >16 h reaction time, excess Grignard (5 equiv) and gave modest diastereoselectivity (3:1 dr), limiting throughput and yield.
Solution_Description: A survey identified TMSCl (or BF₃·OEt₂) as an activator that accelerated the reaction; operating at –60 °C with MeLi (2 equiv) and 1.5 equiv TMSCl gave >10:1 dr and 85 % conversion in 2 h, dramatically reducing reaction time and reagent load.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of chlorotrimethylsilane (TMSCl) … accelerated the reaction but resulted in reduced diastereoselectivity … Lowering the temperature to –60 °C improves the diastereoselectivity … methyllithium as the organometallic reagent … entry 9 … 85 % 22, 1 % 21, 10:1 dr.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: During campaign 3 the enantiomeric excess of the intermediate (from ca. 98 % to 91 %) eroded during the esterification and reduction steps, and the origin of the loss could not be definitively identified.
Solution_Description: Switching to iPrOAc (or PhMe) for the salt‑formation work‑up minimized moisture‑induced desilylation and preserved ee; subsequent recrystallisation of the hemisulfate salt (seeding with 2 % w/w crystal) removed scalemic material and restored ee > 99.8 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using iPrOAc or PhMe … could be isolated in high yield with no desilylation product … low ee and low de were encountered … seeding the initial crystallization from EtOAc with 2 % (w/w) 22·hemisulfate was crucial to ensure a consistent partial rejection of diastereomer and enantiomer … final dr > 99.8:0.2, ee > 99.8 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Mevidalen (LY3154207), an Orally Available Positive Allosteric Modulator of the Human Dopamine D1 Receptor
Problem_Description: The final API 3 could not be crystallized under any of the explored conditions, preventing isolation of a solid API and complicating downstream processing.
Solution_Description: A co‑crystal of 3 with 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid (3·HBA) was discovered; the co‑crystal readily precipitated from iPrOAc/​n‑heptane, provided excellent solubility, and met all clinical‑grade specifications.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of the Small Molecule TGFβR1 Inhibitor

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of the Small Molecule TGFβR1 Inhibitor

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of the Small Molecule TGFβR1 Inhibitor

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of the Small Molecule TGFβR1 Inhibitor

Paper Title: Multikilogram per Hour Continuous Photochemical Benzylic Brominations Applying a Smart Dimensioning Scale-up Strategy
Problem_Description: Molecular bromine is highly volatile and poses significant safety hazards (toxic vapour, risk of explosion) when handled in batch processes, especially at production scale.

Paper Title: Multikilogram per Hour Continuous Photochemical Benzylic Brominations Applying a Smart Dimensioning Scale-up Strategy
Problem_Description: The process is biphasic (aqueous HBr/NaBrO₃ streams and organic substrate), requiring intense mixing along the whole reactor length to avoid phase separation and ensure efficient light absorption.

Paper Title: Multikilogram per Hour Continuous Photochemical Benzylic Brominations Applying a Smart Dimensioning Scale-up Strategy
Problem_Description: Both bromine formation and the radical substitution step are highly exothermic (≈‑65 kJ mol⁻¹ each) and the quench step releases even more heat (≈‑115 kJ mol⁻¹), risking temperature runaway and overheating of the reactor.

Paper Title: Multikilogram per Hour Continuous Photochemical Benzylic Brominations Applying a Smart Dimensioning Scale-up Strategy

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: The original literature route to phenol 3 required the non‑commodity intermediate 2′‑hydroxy‑5′‑methoxyacetophenone 2, which has poor solubility and low availability, leading to an overall PMI > 120 and a cumbersome four‑step sequence.

Problem_Description: The Fries rearrangement in the original route required handling of triflic acid (TfOH) at high temperature, posing a significant safety risk on scale.

Problem_Description: The coumarin‑fragmentation approach (Scheme 2 A) gave low overall yield of phenol 3, and the subsequent telescoped flow process suffered from low conversion in the coumarin formation step.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: The Friedel–Crafts isopropylation of mequinol resulted in extensive over‑alkylation and low conversion to the desired phenol 3.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: The Re₂(CO)₁₀‑catalysed isopropylation, although high yielding, required an expensive catalyst (∼ $36 000 kg⁻¹ in 2017), making the route economically unattractive for large‑scale manufacture.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: Direct isolation of phenol 3 caused oil‑out and high mother‑liquor loss because of its low melting point (~35 °C) and fine particle formation, leading to poor solid handling on scale.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: New batches of N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) introduced dibrominated side‑product 8 and increased ortho‑bromophenol 7 formation, compromising the purity of bromophenol 6.
Solution_Description: Adding 1 mol % methanesulfonic acid (MSA) suppressed dibromination, and switching the solvent to MeCN gave > 96 % para‑selectivity, minimizing ortho‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The quality of NBS also played a critical role as some new batches of NBS provided significant dibrominated side product 8. This side reaction was suppressed by the addition of 1 mol % methanesulfonic acid (MSA).”; “With NBS in MeCN, the desired para‑bromophenol 6 was obtained in 96 % yield. In toluene, the undesired ortho‑bromophenol 7 was the major product.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the Cu‑catalysed methoxylation, oxidative dimer 9 formed in higher amounts, especially when the reaction was run outside a glovebox and the product stream was stored, reducing overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: In‑situ protection of the phenol with a tetrahydropyranyl (THP) group prevented coordination of the phenoxide to Cu, suppressing dimer formation to < 0.1 % and allowing the reaction to be performed in a fume hood.
Supporting_Evidence: “The dimer impurity increased significantly… the end of the reaction stream was discovered to be unstable… we postulated that a protecting group on the phenol may prevent this coordination.”; “Indeed, the use of an in situ protection with a THP group enabled a ligand‑free Cu‑catalysed methoxylation … with the formation of the dimer being suppressed to less than 0.1 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: The large particle size (D₅₀ ≈ 370 µm) of the bromophenol‑DABCO cocrystal caused potential slurry‑plugging concerns in plant‑scale piping.
Solution_Description: Crystallisation temperature was lowered from 60 °C to 30 °C, slowing crystal growth and yielding smaller particles (D₅₀ ≈ 180 µm) while maintaining high supersaturation and product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “To mitigate this risk, we found that by lowering the crystallization temperature from 60 to 30 °C, smaller particle size crystals (D₅₀ = 180 µm) can be obtained as a result of reducing growth rate kinetics while maintaining a high supersaturation.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 2: Development of a Robust Process for Phenol Synthesis
Problem_Description: Initial Cu‑catalysed methoxylation of bromophenol 6 gave only ~ 75 % isolated yield with up to 20 % total side‑products (oxidative dimer 9 and residual isopropylphenol 5).
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified CuBr, ligand L2, NaOMe base, and addition of methyl formate/DMF which suppressed dimer formation and isopropylphenol, increasing isolated yield > 90 % when run in a N₂‑filled glovebox; later the THP protection step removed the glovebox requirement.
Supporting_Evidence: “Additives such as methyl formate, ethyl acetate, and DMF … were found to suppress isopropylphenol 5 from 22 % down to 4 %.”; “Ligands, particularly dicarbonyl compound L2 … were discovered to decrease the formation of oxidative dimer 9 from 18 % down to 4 %.”; “Combining these findings, the methoxylation reaction provided greater than 90 % yield of 3 when the reaction was run inside a N₂‑filled glovebox (entry 16).”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: The enabling synthesis relied on a ring‑closing metathesis (RCM) step that gave poor conversion and was not scalable for large‑scale production of the 18‑membered macrocycle.
Solution_Description: A completely new macrocyclisation was devised – an intramolecular etherification of an allylic bromide – which avoided the RCM step and gave much higher assay yields on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The first limitation of the enabling synthesis was the efficiency of the ring closing metathesis (RCM) process used to form the macrocycle.", "The assay yield for this early result was already superior to the RCM reaction of the enabling route."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: Macrocycle ester 18 decomposed rapidly under palladium‑catalysed conditions (loss of HF) when attempts were made to form the macrocycle via Heck, Sonogashira, Suzuki or photoredox cyclisations, giving only trace product.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the Pd‑catalysed routes and pursued the intramolecular etherification (Option B) which proceeded cleanly to the macrocycle with high conversion and minimal side‑reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: ["significant concerns regarding the stability of the allylic difluoride functionality under these conditions… confirmed these concerns with significant decomposition due to loss of hydrogen fluoride (HF) in the presence of palladium and ligand", "The initial cyclization experiment… revealed the cyclization proceeded cleanly, yielding the desired macrocycle 3."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: The epoxidation route to the key allylic alcohol used NaH, Oxone and generated HF‑related side‑reactions, gave a low overall 40 % yield, and produced hazardous waste and unstable intermediates.
Solution_Description: A dihydroxylation route was developed using catalytic osmium tetroxide/NMO, CDI‑mediated carbonate formation and mild base opening, which gave a robust 90 % overall yield, avoided HF loss, and used safer reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Elimination of HF was a significant side reaction resulting in low yield and purity for bases other than NaH.", "The dihydroxylation route… was very robust and required only 0.15 mol % of potassium osmate dihydrate catalyst… resulting in a 90 % overall yield from 32."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: The bromination of the allylic alcohol to form the allylic bromide was highly exothermic, sensitive to water, and could lead to over‑bromination of a secondary alcohol if not controlled.
Solution_Description: PPh₃Br₂ was generated in situ from PPh₃ and Br₂, added at –10 °C as a slurry, and the reaction mixture was transferred directly into the cyclisation step to avoid aqueous work‑up, keeping the temperature below 0 °C throughout.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The bromination reaction was found to be sensitive to water, resulting in lower conversion and decreased purity.", "The reaction was exothermic, and the transfer was conducted at a rate to maintain an internal temperature below 0 °C.", "These issues on workup could be solved by telescoping the reaction quench directly into the cyclization reaction."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: Isolation of the macrocycle required a multi‑step work‑up lasting about one week, mainly to remove the large excess of triphenylphosphine oxide generated in the bromination step.
Solution_Description: A direct crystallisation of the macrocycle from the cyclisation mixture (MeCN/Water) using a toluene or p‑xylene solvate was developed, allowing the PPh₃O impurity to stay in solution and shortening the work‑up dramatically.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initial development of a workup provided purification of the product, although in total the workup required 1 week of processing time per batch.", "Based on the solubility data, the crystallization process was developed to ensure controlled nucleation and consistent product purity… The solubility of PPh₃O was >200 mg/mL in a 2/1 mixture of MeCN/water."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: A dimer impurity (54) formed during the S_NAr step, with its level strongly affected by water amount, addition time of the dianion slurry, and reaction temperature.
Solution_Description: A multivariate study was performed to define a narrow window for water content, addition time and temperature, minimizing the dimer impurity to <3 % in the final product.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The main process impurity formed in this reaction was the dimer 54… parameters impacting the level of dimer 54 were the addition time of the dianion slurry, the total amount of water in the slurry preparation, and the S_NAr reaction temperature during the slurry charge.", "With control of these reaction parameters, the allylic alcohol 49 was routinely isolated in 69 % yield… the dimer impurity was reduced."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Macrocycle via Intramolecular Etherification
Problem_Description: Residual allylic bromides are class‑3 mutagenic impurities under ICH‑M7 guidance and must be eliminated before API release.
Solution_Description: A rapid reactive quench using 2‑mercaptoethylamine (cysteamine) was added to the reaction mixture, converting all remaining allylic bromides to non‑mutagenic thio‑substituted products within minutes.
Supporting_Evidence: ["As part of the mutagenic impurity control strategy… a quench using 2‑mercaptoethylamine (cysteamine) was used to react with the entire class.", "The reactive quench is very fast with a half‑life of less than 1 min; a 30 min stir time ensures complete conversion of all of the remaining allylic bromides."]

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: The original chiral‑pool route required fluorination of (S)‑glyceraldehyde acetonide (9) with diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST) or related reagents, which are hazardous, thermally unstable and not readily available on multi‑kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: A completely new route was adopted that starts from the commercially available difluoroacetaldehyde ethyl hemiacetal (12), eliminating the dangerous fluorination step and the associated supply‑chain issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “While this fluorination of 9 proceeds in excellent yield, the use of diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST) … presents challenges in terms of safety and availability for large‑scale production.”; “Routes starting from fluorinated materials that were commercially available on a large scale were prioritized… Hemiacetal 12 is available by reduction of ethyl difluoroacetate.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: The cyclic sulfate intermediate (7) generated from hemiacetal 12 was found to be unstable, adding safety concerns and contributing to a 10‑step sequence with low overall yield.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the cyclic‑sulfate pathway and employed a resolution strategy that forms the cyclopropane directly via a Knoevenagel condensation‑followed‑by‑Corey–Chaykovsky cyclopropanation, avoiding the unstable intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “In practice, cyclopropane 5 was successfully synthesized, but cyclic sulfate 7 exhibited limited stability.”; “The resolution approach … was selected for further development.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Knoevenagel condensation using TiCl₄·Et₃N (or TiCl(OEt)₃) gave high conversion but required a stoichiometric amount of an expensive Lewis acid and produced large quantities of titanium waste, making the process costly and cumbersome on scale.
Solution_Description: A catalytic 2 mol % CeCl₃/NaI system in ethanol was screened and gave complete conversion in 5 h; subsequently, 5 mol % MgCl₂ in ethanol was chosen for its favorable scale‑up profile. The reaction mixture was then swapped to MTBE, allowing easy removal of MgCl₂ by filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: “The combination of CeCl₃ and NaI (2 mol % each) resulted in essentially complete conversion after 5 h at 60 °C in EtOH.”; “A catalytic amount of magnesium chloride (5 mol %) in ethanol gave a slightly slower reaction … found to be desirable from the reaction profile, scale‑up, and commercialization perspectives.”; “A solvent switch to methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) allowed removal of the magnesium chloride by filtration.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: During the Corey–Chaykovsky cyclopropanation, a sulfoxide impurity formed by demethylation of the ylide intermediate, lowering the isolated yield of diester 15.
Solution_Description: The substrate (17) and the sulfonium ylide were added slowly and simultaneously to a heated DMF solution, keeping the intermediate concentration low and favoring cyclization over demethylation; DMF was selected over DMSO for better impurity control.
Supporting_Evidence: “The slow simultaneous addition of separate solutions of substrate 17 and the ylide to a heated DMF solution was found to minimize the formation of the sulfoxide impurity.”; “DMF was identified as the preferred solvent for this reaction instead of the more commonly used dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Selective saponification of the less‑hindered ester of diester 15 produced significant amounts of the diacid impurity and gave only a 4:1 diastereomeric ratio (14a‑b : 14c‑d), limiting the overall yield of the DCHA salt.
Solution_Description: A quaternary ammonium base (tetra‑n‑butylammonium hydroxide) was employed at the minimum required charge; the ethanol‑water ratio (30‑45 % EtOH) and temperature (0‑5 °C) were tuned to suppress diacid formation while achieving full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Tetra‑n‑butylammonium hydroxide was selected as the preferred base because of the high conversion and low diacid impurity levels.”; “The ethanol:water ratio was found to have a modest effect … with 30–45 % ethanol producing the highest level of 14a‑b.”; “The reaction temperature was set at 0 to 5 °C in order to minimize diacid formation at extended reaction times.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: The crude hydrolysis mixture still contained the minor diastereomers 14c‑d, which needed to be removed to meet purity specifications.
Solution_Description: The mixture was crystallized as the dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) salt; this step increased the diastereomeric ratio to >9:1, and a subsequent MTBE reslurry reduced the minor diastereomer to <1 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Treatment … with dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) … not only produced crystalline DCHA salt 19a‑b but improved the 14a‑b to 14c‑d diastereomeric ratio to >9:1.”; “The level of the minor diastereomer … could be reduced to less than 1 % by a subsequent reslurry of the DCHA salt in MTBE.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: The Curtius rearrangement of monoacid 14a‑b generated an adiabatic temperature rise of ~40 °C and evolved ~100 L N₂ kg⁻¹, posing a risk of pressure buildup and uncontrolled reaction.
Solution_Description: Diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA) was added slowly at ~80 °C so that the acyl‑azide formed immediately rearranged; temperature control prevented excessive heat accumulation.
Supporting_Evidence: “A thorough safety assessment … revealed that the adiabatic temperature rise was approximately 40 °C … In order to prevent a buildup of the intermediate acyl azide … the process design incorporated the slow addition of diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA) to 14a‑b at approximately 80 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Water or other alcohols present during the Curtius step led to formation of urea impurity 20 and carbamate impurity 21, contaminating the product.
Solution_Description: All reactors and reagents were rigorously dried (solvent reflux, nitrogen purge, CDI‑dry DBU solution) to eliminate moisture and extraneous alcohols, thereby suppressing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The presence of water in the reaction mixture resulted in hydrolysis of the intermediate isocyanate … The presence of other alcohols … resulted in the formation of carbamate impurities … Rigorous exclusion of moisture and other alcohols … minimized the formation of impurities such as urea 20 and carbamate 21.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Enzymatic resolution of amino ester 10 sometimes stalled because the DPPA‑derived diphenyl phosphoramidate (DPP Amide) impurity irreversibly inhibited Alcalase.
Solution_Description: The level of DPP Amide in the feed was controlled to ≤0.20 wt % (by improving work‑up of the Curtius step); batches exceeding this level showed incomplete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “An impurity from DPPA, diphenyl phosphoramidate (DPP Amide), was present at a higher level … The inhibition does not occur with hydrolytically stable phosphates … The diphenyl phosphoramidate impurity was therefore controlled at (±)-amino ester 10 to avoid enzyme inhibition.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: The enzyme Alcalase required a cosolvent to solubilize substrate 10; many solvents either deactivated the enzyme or gave poor conversion.
Solution_Description: Acetone was identified as the optimal cosolvent; 10 vol % acetone provided the best conversion while maintaining >99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acetone, DMF, and 1,4‑dioxane were identified as potential candidate cosolvents … Acetone was ultimately chosen as the preferred cosolvent.”; “Acetone at 10 vol % gave the highest rate of conversion.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Coupling of amino‑sulfonamide 2 with macrocycle 3 using HATU/DMAP required 4 eq DMAP and eight aqueous washes, making the step expensive and time‑consuming.
Solution_Description: The coupling was changed to activation of 4 with CDI (forming acyl‑imidazolide 26) in the presence of DBU; only three aqueous washes were needed, simplifying work‑up and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “This goal was accomplished by switching to 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) and 1,8‑diazabicyclo[5.4.0]‑undec‑7‑ene (DBU) for the coupling reaction … The work‑up was dramatically simplified … only three aqueous washes were required.”; “The two‑step yield of amino sulfonamide 2 increased to 93%.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: During the final coupling of sulfonamide 2 with macrocycle 3, occasional stalling at ~96 % conversion was observed due to formation of a spirocyclic side‑product (29) when sulfonamide reacted with EDAC.
Solution_Description: HOPO was added together with EDAC before the addition of sulfonamide 2; HOPO suppresses the side reaction (reducing conversion of 2 to 29 from ~25 % to <4 %) and restores consistent >99 % overall conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Even in the absence of base, sulfonamide 2 can react with EDAC … forming spirocyclic adduct 29 … The rate of the side reaction was significantly reduced in the presence of HOPO (10 % conversion after 15 min).”; “Because of the relatively high rate of this side reaction … it turned out that the rate … decreased further to just 4 % when it was subjected to reaction with a preformed solution of EDAC and HOPO.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Route to Glecaprevir: Synthesis of the Side Chain and Final Assembly
Problem_Description: Glecaprevir exists in >30 crystal forms and forms solvates easily, complicating isolation of a stable solid form.
Solution_Description: A multistep crystallization protocol using methanol/water, seeded cooling, controlled water addition, humidified drying, and either series or parallel drying steps was developed to reproducibly give the desired hydrate with >94 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Glecaprevir was then recrystallized from a methanol/water solution … The process involved complete dissolution … cooling … addition of a seed slurry … slow addition of water … Humidified drying … resulted in glecaprevir in >94 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: Bredereck’s reagent is expensive (> $1700 kg⁻¹) and its long supply‑lead‑time makes it unsuitable for large‑scale manufacture; the original phenol alkylation using DMSO/KOt‑Bu suffers an uncontrolled exotherm and poses a safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to use inexpensive ethyl formate together with potassium tert‑butoxide (or aqueous NaOH) as the base, and the solvent was switched from DMSO to N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP), which is safer and more robust.
Supporting_Evidence: “the high price (> $1700 kg) and long lead‑time of Bredereck’s reagent… made usage… unfeasible.”; “this approach was deemed unacceptable because of the process safety risks (an uncontrolled exotherm) associated with the decomposition of DMSO…”; “An initial screening of solvents indicated that N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) was an effective and safe replacement for DMSO…”.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: Initial phenol alkylation gave variable conversions (73–81 %) with different bases and required careful water content to achieve homogeneous mixtures.
Solution_Description: Adding 10 wt % water to the reaction made the mixture homogeneous and equalized the performance of all bases; aqueous NaOH (50 wt % NaOH) was used as an inexpensive, easily handled base, and the order of addition (base first, then substrate) was optimized.
Supporting_Evidence: “when we spiked our reactions with water (10 wt %…) we were able to obtain comparable results with different lots of LiOt‑Bu… all of the bases performed identically…”; “The stronger tert‑butoxide base is thought to decompose chloroacetonitrile at a competitive rate… The effect of adding water… provides a homogeneous reaction mixture and eliminates any sensitivities to mass transfer.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: During enolate formation, the CME dimer (8a) formed in significant amounts, reducing the yield of the desired enolate (7) and leading to an impurity (8b) after cyclization.
Solution_Description: A reverse‑addition protocol (adding the solution of CME + ethyl formate to the base) was employed, the reaction was run at –20 °C to –10 °C, and the equivalents of KOt‑Bu and ethyl formate were increased (2.25 eq KOt‑Bu, 2.0 eq ethyl formate) to suppress dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the formation of dimer 8a could be suppressed by reverse addition of a solution containing both compound 2 and ethyl formate to a solution of the base… Under this protocol, formation of the desired enolate 7 became the major pathway.”; “a cleaner reaction profile was observed at lower temperature (−20 to 0 °C) while elevated temperature (20 to 30 °C) results in a higher amount of CME dimer formation.”; “the amount of ethyl formate was increased to 1.5 and 1.75 eq… resulted in >95 % target enolate and ≤1 % CME dimer.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: During enolate formation the reaction off‑gassed carbon monoxide; the decomposition of ethyl formate in the presence of KOt‑Bu generated CO, raising safety and emission‑control concerns.
Solution_Description: The addition rate of the CME/ethyl‑formate mixture to the base was slowed (4 h for 50 kg, up to 40 h for larger batches) to keep CO evolution below local limits; a thermal oxidizer unit (TOU) was installed as an engineering control to destroy CO, enabling practical batch times of 8–10 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “the gas evolved… was carbon monoxide… the rate of CO off‑gassing was directly proportional to the addition rate… the addition time can be adjusted to 4 h to maintain CO release under the local limit… larger‑scale batches would require longer addition times (e.g., 250 kg… ∼40 h)… alternative engineering controls (i.e., a TOU) enabled us to bypass this concern.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: Cyclization with guanidine carbonate (G·0.5H₂CO₃) gave incomplete conversion even after 30 h, leading to low product formation and high triazine impurity.
Solution_Description: Switching to guanidine hydrochloride (G·HCl) dramatically accelerated the cyclization (complete conversion in ≤15 h at 115 °C); increasing the amount of G·HCl from 2.0 eq to 8.0 eq further improved conversion and reduced the triazine impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions using 3.0 eq of guanidine carbonate performed poorly… the improved rate of product formation when utilizing guanidine HCl… Initial cyclization reactions involving 2.0 eq of G·HCl at 115 °C for 15 h resulted in full conversion… When the amount of G·HCl was increased from 2.0 to 3.0 eq, the amount of triazine at the end of the reaction dropped from 11.1 % to 6.6 %… further increase to 8.0 eq gave high yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: Screening of acid additives (e.g., acetic, trifluoroacetic, pivalic acids) to suppress biguanide formation introduced solvent‑related impurities (14a, 14b) and caused a dark‑colored product, complicating downstream purification.
Solution_Description: The additive strategy was abandoned; instead the cyclization was performed with a higher loading of guanidine HCl (8 eq) which gave consistent high yields and purity without the need for acids.
Supporting_Evidence: “This strategy led to several issues upon scale‑up including lower and inconsistent isolated yields… a dark color of isolated 1 and the appearance of two solvent‑related impurities 14a and 14b… Discouraged by the finding of these elevated levels of solvent‑related impurities… we decided to carry out the cyclization reaction with 8.0 eq of G·HCl… because of excellent yield and the consistent purity profile.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: The original route required multiple crystallizations to remove aniline‑related genotoxic impurities and an aqueous work‑up/distillation step, increasing cycle time and waste.
Solution_Description: A direct crystallization from the reaction mixture was developed (seeding at 80 °C, water addition, cooling to 15–20 °C, aging 10 h) yielding the nonsolvated form of product 1 with >97 % purity and eliminating intermediate isolation steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “The choice of NMP as the reaction solvent provided an ideal opportunity to directly isolate the desired product from water… a phase map… A suitable seeding point at 80 °C… After filtration… the solid was washed… to afford diaminopyrimidine 1 in the desired form as an off‑white solid… Remaining impurities exhibited excellent rejection…”.

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 3: Development of a One-Pot Formylation–Cyclization Sequence to the Diaminopyrimidine Core
Problem_Description: The first‑generation process had a step‑PMI of 88, a cycle time of ∼96 h, and required expensive reagents (Bredereck’s reagent, aniline HCl), making it unsuitable for metric‑ton scale production.
Solution_Description: The overall synthesis was re‑engineered into a concise one‑pot sequence (alkylation → enolate formation → cyclization → crystallization) using inexpensive reagents (ethyl formate, KOt‑Bu, guanidine HCl), reducing step‑PMI to 29, cycle time to 36 h, and achieving 88–94 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Key accomplishments include: (1) reduced cost by using ethyl formate, potassium tert‑butoxide, and guanidine hydrochloride as reagents ($237 vs $2172 per kg)… (2) improved yield (88–94 % vs 65 %); (3) reduced PMI (step‑PMI 29 vs 88)… (4) shortened cycle time (36 vs 96 h).”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264). Part 5: Completion of the API Free Base via a Direct Chlorosulfonylation Process
Problem_Description: The first‑generation supply route required three separate chemical steps to install the sulfonamide, used sulfolane (a Class 2 solvent with strict residual limits), employed two highly toxic reagents (chlorosulfonic acid and POCl₃), showed poor robustness on scale‑up, and needed multiple recrystallizations to meet impurity specifications.
Solution_Description: A one‑step, two‑pot process was developed: (i) direct chlorosulfonylation in acetonitrile (eliminating sulfolane and POCl₃), (ii) use of 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene to scavenge sulfuryl‑chloride impurities, (iii) quench of the sulfonyl‑chloride with aqueous ammonium hydroxide at 0–15 °C to avoid methylated by‑product, and (iv) a pH‑swing crystallization that exploits a transient acetonitrile solvate for impurity rejection.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the synthetic sequence required three distinct chemical steps to install the sulfonamide” (first‑gen route)【...】
• “the use of sulfolane, a Class 2 solvent… was undesirable”【...】
• “the use of two highly toxic and hazardous chemicals, chlorosulfonic acid (HSO₃Cl) and POCl₃, was likewise unattractive”【...】
• “issues with process robustness were observed on scale‑up”【...】
• “multiple recrystallizations… required to reach the purity specifications”【...】
• “solvent selection… allowed for the elimination of sulfolane and POCl₃” (solvent change)【...】
• “1,3‑dimethoxybenzene (DMB) could be added to the reaction to scavenge the sulfuryl chloride” (scavenger change)【...】
• “addition was performed at an internal temperature of 0–15 °C… to keep the sulfonic‑acid impurity levels below 2.0 LCAP” (temperature optimization)【...】
• “pH‑swing crystallization… allowed for the isolation of the desired crystal form in increased purity” (other condition change)【...】

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264). Part 5: Completion of the API Free Base via a Direct Chlorosulfonylation Process
Problem_Description: Direct chlorosulfonylation with chlorosulfonic acid in sulfolane gave almost exclusive formation of the undesired sulfonic acid (2) and very low conversion to the target sulfonyl‑chloride (6).
Solution_Description: Screening of solvents identified acetonitrile as a medium where a 7:3 mixture of 2 : 6 was formed; increasing chlorosulfonic‑acid equivalents to 5 and aging at 45 °C for 16 h shifted the equilibrium to >98 % sulfonyl‑chloride, providing high selectivity and yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Sulfolane… gave almost exclusively the undesired acid 2”【...】
• “in acetonitrile, a 7:3 mixture of the sulfonic acid 2 and sulfonyl chloride 6 was formed”【...】
• “Increasing the stoichiometry of chlorosulfonic acid from 3 to 5 equivalents provided almost complete selectivity for the sulfonyl chloride”【...】
• “upon aging at 45 °C for 16 h, acid 2 is then converted to the desired sulfonyl chloride 6” (temperature optimization)【...】

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264). Part 5: Completion of the API Free Base via a Direct Chlorosulfonylation Process
Problem_Description: Impurities chlorinated arene 9 and sulfinic acid 10 arose from sulfuryl‑chloride present in the chlorosulfonic‑acid batch, and the reagent itself is highly corrosive.

Problem_Description: Quenching the sulfonyl‑chloride stream into methanolic ammonia generated a methylated impurity 5 that could not be removed by crystallization, leading to low isolated yield of the free base.
Solution_Description: The quench was redesigned to use aqueous ammonium hydroxide instead of methanol, eliminating formation of impurity 5; the temperature of addition was kept between 0–15 °C and the pH was controlled during the subsequent crystallization to suppress residual sulfonic‑acid formation.

Problem_Description: A pH‑swing crystallization initially failed to consistently reject two stubborn impurities; the solid formed either the anhydrous form 1 or an acetonitrile solvate, with the latter promoting impurity exclusion.
