Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: Using the in‑situ generated Vilsmeier reagent (triphenylphosphine + Br₂) gave low isolated yield (81 %) of per‑brominated cyclodextrin because side‑products (triphenylphosphine oxide) formed and extensive washing was required to remove them.
Solution_Description: Replace the in‑situ preparation with the commercially available bromo‑Vilsmeier reagent 2. This eliminates the triphenylphosphine‑related side‑products and raises the isolated yield to 91 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although 1 could be isolated in a very good yield (81 %) … yield losses … could be due to the formation of triphenylphosphine‑related side products … These … could be avoided by the use of the commercially available bromo‑Vilsmeier reagent 2 … 1 was isolated in an improved 91 % yield.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: The traditional basic NaOEt/EtOH quench is highly exothermic, demanding slow addition, tight temperature control (70 → 0 °C cooling), and a specific pH endpoint; on a commercial scale this cooling is energy‑intensive and time‑consuming, and the exotherm poses safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Develop an acidic hydrolytic quench that adds only water (or aqueous acid) at controlled temperature (room‑temperature or 40 °C) instead of a strong base, removing the need for slow base addition and large temperature drops.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of the base is highly exothermic, requiring slow addition, careful temperature control, and a specific pH end point … cooling the reaction from 70 to 0 °C is energy‑intensive and time‑consuming … As an alternative, it was hypothesized that HBr … may be effective … addition of just water … at room temperature afforded 1 in 90 % yield after 11 h … optimized conditions gave 1 in 92 % yield after only 4 h at 40 °C.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: During the acidic quench, a background reaction between HBr, DMF and water generated dimethylammonium bromide (H₂NMe₂Br) and formic acid, inflating the measured equivalents of H₂NMe₂Br and obscuring the true number of Vilsmeier‑capped secondary alcohols (x).
Solution_Description: Use proton‑sponge (5) as a selective HBr scavenger that forms a sharp, quantifiable conjugate acid (6) for ¹H NMR titration, allowing accurate measurement and removal of HBr without reacting with intermediate 3.
Supporting_Evidence: “Proton sponge (5) was identified as a uniquely suitable candidate … both 5 and its conjugate acid 6 give sharp, discrete, and quantifiable peaks … An excess of 5 (28 equiv) was added … approximately 20 equiv of 6 was present, indicating 20 equiv of HBr … there was no reaction between 5 and 3.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: The bromo‑Vilsmeier reagent 2 slowly decomposes in DMF at 40 °C to amidinium 7 and CO, accounting for ~2.9 equiv of missing mass balance and generating additional HBr, which complicates stoichiometry and adds waste.
Solution_Description: Recognize the decomposition pathway and adjust reagent equivalents (≈19 equiv of 2) and reaction temperature (70 °C) to ensure complete conversion while accepting the inevitable formation of 7/CO, thereby maintaining overall mass balance.
Supporting_Evidence: “A solution of 2 in DMF at 40 °C … decomposes to amidinium 7 and CO … The fate of approximately 2.9 equiv of 2 remains elusive … on the basis of the HBr stoichiometry of 20 equiv, the remainder of 2 must decompose via a pathway that produces 1 equiv of HBr per equivalent of 2.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: Increasing the number of equivalents of reagent 2 beyond the optimum (e.g., 22 equiv at 60 °C) unexpectedly reduced the reaction rate, requiring longer times to reach completion.
Solution_Description: Employ a Design‑of‑Experiments (DoE) approach coupled with kinetic profiling to identify the optimal combination of equivalents and temperature (≈19 equiv of 2 at 70 °C) that yields high conversion within 6 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “Greater excesses of 2 actually reduced the reaction rate … especially pronounced for reactions at 60 °C … when the reaction temperature was increased from 60 to 70 °C using 22 equiv of 2, the reaction rate greatly improved … DOE … analysis … at the center of the contour plot, corresponding to the use of 19 equiv of 2 at 70 °C … to ensure product stability, time efficiency, and overall robustness.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: At high temperature and low equivalents of 2, the per‑brominated product 1 showed decomposition after ~1 h, especially when the number of Vilsmeier‑capped secondary alcohols (x) was insufficient.
Solution_Description: Select reaction conditions that maintain a sufficient average x (≈10) by using enough equivalents of 2 and a temperature of 70 °C, preventing over‑decomposition and ensuring product stability throughout the 6‑hour window.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions … using fewer equivalents of 2 … product decomposition occurred beyond 1 h … decomposition was exacerbated with increasing temperature … a critical number of Vilsmeier‑capped secondary alcohols, x, is required to ensure product stability … conditions … 19 equiv of 2 at 70 °C … ensure product stability.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: During kilogram‑scale bromination, the addition of 2 generated significant heat; to keep temperature below 20 °C the reagent had to be added in five portions, and volatile HBr released required a basic scrubber for safe handling.
Solution_Description: Implement portionwise addition of 2 combined with an overhead stirrer and a basic scrubber attached to the reactor, controlling the exotherm and safely neutralizing HBr fumes.
Supporting_Evidence: “On this scale 2 had to be charged in 10 portions to keep the reaction temperature below 20 °C. Additionally, a basic scrubber was required to neutralize any volatile hydrobromic acid released during the reaction.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: After the acidic quench, the mixture contains HBr, dimethylammonium bromide, and formic acid that must be removed to isolate the pure per‑halo cyclodextrin.
Solution_Description: Add excess water as an antisolvent to precipitate the product, then wash the solid with water to remove the acidic by‑products, yielding a white solid with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Isolation of the per‑(6‑deoxy‑6‑halo) CDs was accomplished simply by adding an excess of water (antisolvent) to the end‑of‑reaction solution to induce crystallization. The HBr, dimethylammonium bromide, and formic acid byproducts were conveniently removed by additional water washes.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Understanding of a Robust and Scalable Synthesis of Per(6-deoxy-6-halo)cyclodextrins, Versatile Intermediates for Cyclodextrin Modification
Problem_Description: The initial acidic quench at 0 °C with 100 equiv water gave <10 % yield even after >1 day, due to poor mixing and low temperature.
Solution_Description: Perform the aqueous acidic quench at room temperature (or 40 °C) with 100 equiv water, which dramatically increased conversion to 90 % in 11 h (or 4 h at 40 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: “These conditions afforded 1 in <10 % yield after more than 1 day … addition of water at room temperature afforded 1 in 90 % yield after 11 h … under the optimized conditions, 1 was formed in 92 % yield after only 4 h at 40 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: In the batch‑batch Step 3A, high equivalents of ethyl formate (EF) and potassium‑tert‑butoxide (KOt‑Bu) were needed because insufficient mixing or low EF concentration caused the cyanomethyl ether (CME) to dimerize to compound 4, consuming starting material and lowering isolated yield of the desired CME enolate (2).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The researchers moved the formylation step to continuous flow, where they could (i) premix CME and EF before contacting the base, (ii) tightly control temperature (‑20 °C to +45 °C) and residence time, and (iii) employ static mixers to improve mixing, which eliminated dimer formation and allowed the use of only 1.15 equiv EF and 1.3 equiv KOt‑Bu, restoring high conversion and yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “High levels of EF were needed to drive the complete conversion of the starting material CME to CME enolate (2). … using fewer than 1.5 equiv. of EF … led to dimerization of the starting material during the formylation step (Step 3A).”
• “Addition of the premixed solution of CME (3) and EF to the base solution gave the desired CME enolate (2) product in 98.5% yield.”
• “Performing the formylation in flow affords increased control over variables such as temperature and timing and can afford better control of stoichiometry through improved mixing.”
• “Temperature of the mixer yielded a similar increase in 4 … indicating that formation of the CME dimer (4) was localized at the point of impact of the two streams.”
• “Increasing flow rate … resulted in a decrease in the quantity of CME dimer (4) formed.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: The batch‑batch process generated large amounts of carbon monoxide (CO) from excess EF, creating an exothermic decomposition that posed safety and environmental hazards, especially when scaling to multihundred‑kilogram batches.
Solution_Description: By reducing EF to near‑stoichiometric levels (1.3 equiv) in the flow‑batch process and controlling the temperature profile, the amount of CO formed was cut by ~70 %, removing the exothermic CO‑producing side‑reaction and improving process safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The extra equivalent of EF used in the batch–batch process was ultimately converted to the toxic gas carbon monoxide … providing a significant driver to reduce the amount of this reagent used.”
• “Using less EF resulted in less carbon monoxide waste being generated.”
• “The flow‑batch process … allowed for more closely controlled stoichiometry and temperature … leading to an improvement in reaction performance.”
• “The number of equivalents of EF from 2.0 to 1.3 (a 35% reduction)… using less excess EF translated to 70% less carbon monoxide waste.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: With excess KOt‑Bu remaining after formylation, the basic environment promoted conversion of guanidine·HCl to biguanide, which then cyclized to triazine by‑product 5, decreasing the purity and overall yield of diaminopyrimidine (1).
Solution_Description: The flow‑batch protocol cut KOt‑Bu to 1.4 equiv and reduced G·HCl to 4.0 equiv, keeping residual alkoxide low enough to suppress biguanide formation, thereby eliminating triazine impurity and restoring high isolated yield (≈91 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Elevated levels of alkoxide have been shown to increase the amount of triazine byproduct (5) formed during the cyclization reaction.”
• “By performing the formylation in flow, with less EF and KOt‑Bu, a lower amount of alkoxide remained … the G·HCl charge was decreased from 8.0 to 3.0 equiv … without a concomitant increase in the amount of 5 formed.”
• “The number of equivalents of G·HCl … reduced from 8.0 to 4.0 (a 50% reduction).”
• “The final API production … 91% yield, 98.1% purity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, inadequate mixing in the flow reactors and occasional biphasic flow caused inconsistent conversion and occasional spikes in CME dimer (4) levels, leading to batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team introduced helical static mixers (21 mixing elements) in kilo‑lab and pilot‑plant reactors, increased flow rates, and selected larger‑volume Swagelok T‑unions to ensure monophasic flow and consistent mixing, which removed variability and kept dimer formation below 2 % LCAP across scales.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction … might be mixing sensitive. … an increase in the flow rate did result in a decrease in the quantity of CME dimer (4) formed.”
• “Removing the static mixer … CME dimer levels increased from ca. 2 % to 3 %.”
• “A minimum of 175 psi was required to eliminate biphasic flow … 250 psi would provide an adequate buffer.”
• “Increasing flow rates (as scale is increased) could yield further improvements to reaction performance.”
• “The modular design … allowed scaling up dimensionally while maintaining similar form factors, which helped keep performance comparable across scales.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: Pumps delivering KOt‑Bu suffered seal failure due to formation of insoluble potassium hydroxide (KOH) from moisture, causing over‑pressurization, pump damage, and operational downtime.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to oversized high‑performance HPLC pumps that operate at lower cycles per minute, and a dual 10‑µm filtration bank was installed upstream of the pumps to remove KOH, reducing seal wear and improving reliability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Pumping of the KOt‑Bu solution also proved challenging as moisture … resulted in the formation of insoluble potassium hydroxide. This potassium hydroxide accelerated the degradation of the pump seals.”
• “Filtering the base solution failed to adequately address this challenge. By using oversized high‑performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) pumps, the pistons could operate at fewer cycles per minute, which resulted in less wear and tear on the pump seals.”
• “Dual 10‑micron nominal filtration bank used for filtration of KOt‑Bu solution in the pilot plant scale reactor.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: High water content in the CME feed led to in‑reactor precipitation of potassium hydroxide, clogging the back‑pressure regulator (BPR) and risking over‑pressure events.
Solution_Description: A specification limiting CME water content to ≤ 500 ppm was instituted, Karl‑Fischer titration was added to the release procedure, and the BPR was upgraded to a larger‑pore‑size unit, eliminating clogging and maintaining safe pressure control.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “High levels of water in the CME (3) stream also yielded complications. … elevated water content … resulted in the formation of potassium hydroxide in the reactor, which led to clogging of the back‑pressure regulator.”
• “The holes in the back‑pressure regulator were identified as a point of constriction, and to prevent further issues, the back‑pressure regulator was upgraded to a unit with a larger pore size.”
• “A specification on the water content of the CME (3) stream was set (500 ppm) and the material release method was updated to include a Karl‑Fischer titration.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Part 4: Formylation–Cyclization as a Flow–Batch Process Leads to Significant Improvements in Process Mass Intensity (PMI) and CO Generated versus the Batch–Batch Process
Problem_Description: The original batch‑batch sequence required a 12 h cyclization heating step followed by multiple recrystallizations, extending overall batch time and reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: By moving the formylation to flow and retaining a batch cyclization, the overall process time was reduced to 7 h on production scale (vs ≈ 12 h for batch), while still achieving ≥ 91 % isolated yield, thereby increasing throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The final flow–batch process … run times on laboratory, kilo‑lab, pilot plant, and production scales were approximately 1, 2, 3, and 7 h, respectively.”
• “The batch cyclization was heated to 115 °C for 12 h in the original batch‑batch process.”
• “The flow‑batch process … led to a twofold increase in concentration … without sacrificing reaction performance.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: The initial trial of the patented nitration protocol (concentrated H₂SO₄ with KNO₃ or HNO₃) produced a heterogeneous, hard‑to‑stir mixture that delivered only trace amounts of the desired nitro product and generated a large exotherm.
Solution_Description: The amine was protected by acetylation with acetic anhydride to give the acetamide, thereby avoiding oxidation of the amino group and allowing a clean nitration of the protected substrate.
Supporting_Evidence: “These initial trials resulted in the formation of a heterogeneous mixture that was difficult to stir… the reaction mixture contained only trace amounts of the desired product… Major side products were detected, possibly caused by oxidation of the amino group.”; “we chose to acetylate 3 using acetic anhydride (Ac₂O) to afford acetamide 4 in order to avoid side reactions occurring at the amino functionality.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: Using AcOH/conc. HNO₃ for nitration generated a significant exotherm which raised safety concerns due to the highly exothermic and potentially explosive nature of nitration reactions.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a modular micro‑reactor (MMRS/FlowPlate) that provides excellent heat removal and precise temperature control, allowing the exotherm to be safely managed.
Supporting_Evidence: “We observed a significant exotherm during the initial batch microwave experiments, so we commenced flow experiments, which would provide better temperature control.”; “The system has been successfully demonstrated to withstand corrosive nitration mixtures because of its construction from Hastelloy C22… The heat generated from the exotherm could be far better controlled through the utilization of a continuous flow reactor.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: The aqueous HNO₃ nitration required a large excess of acid (30 equiv) which caused a strong exotherm, high salt waste and approached the corrosivity limit of the equipment at 80 °C.
Solution_Description: A water‑free nitration mixture of AcOH/fuming HNO₃ (100 % nitric acid) and fuming H₂SO₄ (oleum) was employed, reducing the amount of nitric acid needed while using fuming H₂SO₄ as a water scavenger and catalyst to enhance the rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “We concluded that under the identified conditions, the large excess of nitric acid would lead to exacerbated salt waste… Therefore, an alternative strategy was sought that used a more reactive nitration system and water‑free conditions.”; “We investigated … a water‑free nitration with acetic acid/fuming sulfuric acid (oleum)/fuming nitric acid as a mass‑transfer‑limited nitration regime.”; “To further reduce the amount of nitric acid used by employing an even more reactive nitration system… fuming H₂SO₄ … as a water scavenger and catalyst.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: Using 99 % fuming nitric acid led to decomposition of the starting material and formation of numerous oxidation/overnitration side products, some of which are potentially explosive or toxic.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to 40 °C and the substrate concentration was reduced to 0.5 M in AcOH to suppress decomposition and side‑product formation while maintaining acceptable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Decomposed starting material was observed even when only 1.0 equiv of nitric acid was used… The temperature was lowered in order to circumvent the formation of those potentially explosive or toxic side products.”; “When the temperature of the reaction feed was reduced to 40 °C, the product crystallized inside the flow reactor, making a dilution to 0.5 M substrate in AcOH necessary.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: At very low acid flow rates (e.g., 20 μL min⁻¹ HNO₃, 10 μL min⁻¹ H₂SO₄) small fluctuations of the syringe‑pump valves caused deviations in acid feed, which could lead to loss of selectivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 4 mL residence‑time loop downstream of the FlowPlate was installed to provide a longer residence time, smoothing out flow‑rate variations and ensuring complete mixing before the product left the reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: “We solved this issue through the installation of a residence time loop with a volume of 4 mL after the FlowPlate to enable a longer residence time in order to complete the reactor macromixing.”; “If there were a drop in either acid feed due to process deviation, then a drop in selectivity… would likely be observed.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: Combining excess Ac₂O with nitric acid in the telescoped acetylation‑nitration sequence could generate highly explosive acetyl nitrate.
Solution_Description: Ac₂O was added in slight excess (1.2 equiv) and used deliberately as a water scavenger; the feeds were mixed in a T‑piece at controlled temperature (20 °C) and the reaction stream was immediately quenched with cold 4 M NaOH, preventing any build‑up of acetyl nitrate.
Supporting_Evidence: “Ac₂O was used in excess, the formation of potentially explosive acetyl nitrate… could occur. We deemed this safety issue to be manageable because of the very small quantities that would be formed at any one time within the flow reactor.”; “The reaction stream was quenched by introducing the effluent into a stirred 4 M NaOH solution at 0 °C. … no exotherm was observed.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: Scaling the exothermic nitration to pilot‑scale required efficient heat removal and mixing to avoid temperature spikes and ensure uniform reaction throughout the larger reactor volume.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The laboratory FlowPlate (size 600) was scaled to an A5‑sized LL‑rhombus micromixer (11 mL) made of Hastelloy, operated with a pre‑heater and thermostat to keep the outlet temperature within +1 °C, thereby controlling the exotherm in a single plate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The laboratory procedure based on the smaller FlowPlate Lab of size 600 was then transferred to Lonza… The larger plates (A6 and A5) are individual Hastelloy‑made plates… The entire exotherm could be controlled within a single plate… highlighting the enhanced heat transfer capacities of this reactor technology.”

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of the Continuous Flow Acetylation and Nitration of 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxyaniline to Prepare a Key Building Block of Osimertinib
Problem_Description: During the de‑protection step the protected intermediate 5 precipitated upon mixing with aqueous HCl, making continuous‑flow processing infeasible.
Solution_Description: The de‑protection was performed in batch using dilute HCl at 76 °C, followed by liquid‑liquid extraction and recrystallization, providing a high‑yield, isolated product.
Supporting_Evidence: “Direct telescoping of the deprotection within a continuous flow environment was not attempted because the deprotection requires aqueous acid, which causes precipitation of the protected compound 5. Thus, we chose to perform the deprotection under batch conditions.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: Portion‑wise addition of NBS on multi‑hundred‑kilogram scale gave isolated yields of 68 % (vs 81 % in lab) and caused polymerized by‑products that precipitated during aqueous work‑up, making phase‑separation difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopted a slow, continuous addition of the NBS/AcOH slurry over 5 h to maintain a low, steady concentration of NBS (and thus Br₂) in solution, preventing periods where the active brominating species is absent, reducing polymer formation, simplifying extraction, and raising isolated yield to 75‑80 %.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction was initially performed via portion‑wise addition of NBS, resulting in 68 % isolated yield and polymer precipitation ("resulted in significantly lower isolated yields … and difficulties in phase separation due to precipitation of insoluble polymerized material").

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: NBS from different commercial suppliers contained variable Br₂/HBr content, leading to inconsistent bromination rates, higher dibromide formation and occasional failure to meet the in‑process control specifications.
Solution_Description: Using kinetic modelling the required NBS equivalents were minimized (1.31 eq predicted; 1.30 eq used) and a conservative target of 1.40 eq was set for manufacturing, ensuring robust conversion irrespective of supplier‑to‑supplier NBS activity.
Supporting_Evidence: "We observed differing levels of bromination using NBS from different suppliers … The source of this increased activity … variable quality of NBS …"; "Modeled optimization predicted 1.31 equiv … Experimental data demonstrated successful reaction completion using 1.30 equiv … NBS equivalents were conservatively reduced from 1.68 to 1.40 equiv."

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: The bromination is highly exothermic (ΔH₁ᵣ = 136 kJ mol⁻¹), raising safety concerns for scale‑up and making precise temperature control critical.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was held at 83 ± 2 °C and the NBS addition rate was engineered to feed the reaction slowly, limiting heat release per unit time and avoiding temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: "This procedure was adopted due to the exothermic nature of the reaction (ΔH₁ᵣ = 136 kJ mol⁻¹)."; "maintaining a reaction temperature of 83 °C"; "adoption of a simple procedural change ensured reliability and reproducibility during manufacturing."

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: During portion‑wise addition, long intervals without NBS caused accumulation of polymeric material that precipitated and interfered with aqueous extraction, complicating product isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous low‑rate addition kept the reaction mixture homogeneous and limited polymer formation, allowing clean phase separation after work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: "difficulties in phase separation during aqueous extraction due to precipitation of insoluble polymerized material"; "continuous addition … demonstrated the consistent presence of NBS in the solution phase"; "vast improvement in the absolute purity of the reaction mixture, with minimal impurity formation".

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: The reaction showed batch‑to‑batch variability in conversion when the reactor fill volume was low (<30 %), leading to inconsistent yields and polymer impurity formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the reactor fill volume to ≥48 % (or using continuous addition) minimized head‑space loss of Br₂ and reduced impurity formation, delivering more reproducible yields.
Supporting_Evidence: "reactor fill volume less than 30 % … leading to formation of polymerized material and low isolated yield"; "Using portionwise addition mode, increasing the fill volume from 17 % to 48 % resulted in a 50 % reduction in impurity formation"; "continuous addition … fill volume … had negligible effect on the final reaction mixture composition".

Paper Title: Kinetic Investigations To Enable Development of a Robust Radical Benzylic Bromination for Commercial Manufacturing of AMG 423 Dihydrochloride Hydrate
Problem_Description: The original portion‑wise protocol required ~21 h to reach completion, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Switching to a 5‑h continuous NBS addition reduced total reaction time to 8 h while meeting all specifications.
Supporting_Evidence: "The continuous addition model allowed accurate prediction … Maximal conversion … providing a significant reduction in reaction time (cf. 21 h using portion‑wise addition)"; "continuous addition of NBS could now be successfully conducted within the wide operating parameters desired for a manufacturing setting".

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264). Part 6: Development of an Improved Commercial Salt Formation Process
Problem_Description: The free‑base of gefapixant has very low solubility in most common solvents (e.g., 0.22 mg mL⁻¹ in IPA, 0.16 mg mL⁻¹ in water). Because the first‑generation process relied on a slurry‑to‑slurry conversion, the free‑base could not be fully dissolved, leading to incomplete reaction, residual free‑base (up to 10 wt % in product) and poor impurity rejection.
Solution_Description: The team replaced the slurry‑to‑slurry step with a homogeneous‑solution crystallization. By converting the free base to a highly soluble glycolate salt (≳100 mg mL⁻¹ in hot MeOH), the material could be completely dissolved, filtered (pure‑filtration step), and then subjected to a salt‑metathesis/crystallization that gave >90 % isolated yield of the citrate salt with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “As might be expected, gefapixant free base exhibited good solubility in certain polar aprotic solvents… However, the use of … DMF, DMSO, or NMP was ruled out… because of low solubility of the citrate salt and high‑boiling solvents.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: Uncontrolled, variable levels (0.11–1.22 %) of a 2′‑O‑methyl impurity were observed when scaling the alkylation of DAPR with 1‑bromo‑2‑methoxyethane (MOE‑Br). The impurity originates from trace methyl‑bromide present in the bulk MOE‑Br and from degradation of MOE‑Br during the reaction.
Solution_Description: A codistillation of MOE‑Br with MTBE (or with MTBE in the absence of DMSO) was implemented to strip out methyl‑bromide, reducing the 2′‑O‑Me impurity to <0.05 % on production scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “After failed attempts to bring the 2′‑O‑methyl impurity under control at the production scale… a simple codistillation of alkylbromide 4 and MTBE in DMSO was sufficient to reduce 2′‑O‑Me impurity formation to very low levels (<0.05 %).”; “we determined that carrying out the alkylbromide/MTBE distillation in the absence of DMSO resulted in reproducible control of the 2′‑O‑Me impurity.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: Significant formation of the 3′‑MOE regioisomer (critical impurity 8) and bis‑alkylated product (non‑critical impurity 10) during the 2′‑O‑alkylation of DAPR caused low overall yield and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: A DOE identified LiOH as the optimal base, a lower reaction volume (5 vol DMSO), 24 °C temperature, and single‑addition of base and alkyl bromide (2.15 eq each). These conditions minimized impurity 8, controlled impurity 10, and gave a higher, more consistent yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Analysis indicated that the maximum product was formed when the reaction was carried out under more dilute conditions (15 volumes of DMSO) using LiOH… The critical 3′‑MOE impurity 8 was affected by both the reaction volume and the type of base… The use of LiOH also favored lower levels of 3′‑MOE impurity 8 over those formed with KOH.”; “The optimal balance… was obtained using LiOH at 24 °C with the base and alkylbromide charged as single additions.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: Residual DMSO from the alkylation step inhibited crystallization of the deaminated product (MOE‑G) and could not be removed efficiently by biphasic extractions.
Solution_Description: A solid‑phase extraction using brominated polystyrene (SP‑207) resin was developed to bind the product, wash away DMSO with 10 % NaOAc, and release MOE‑DAPR with 80‑100 % MeOH, delivering a DMSO‑free aqueous solution for the enzymatic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempts at biphasic aqueous extractive removal of DMSO… showed an unfavorable partitioning… an alternative solid‑phase extraction was developed. The solid phase chosen was brominated polystyrene matrix SP‑207… Once DMSO is removed, the resin was rinsed… and the product was released… with a recovery of about 94 %.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: The enzymatic deamination step left residual 2′‑MOE‑DAPR and 3′‑MOE‑G impurities, limiting final purity and overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The process relied on the inherent selectivity of adenosine deaminase (which preferentially deaminates 2′‑MOE‑DAPR) combined with in‑situ crystallization of MOE‑G from the phosphate buffer, allowing filtration of pure product and removal of impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ADA enzyme selectively deaminates 2′‑MOE DAPR 5 over 3′‑MOE DAPR 8… 2′‑MOE G 6 crystallizes selectively from the sodium phosphate buffer… the crystallization allows for a simple workup by filtration… affording a material with a ∼180:1 ratio of 6 to 12 and residual 5 reduced to ∼0.15 %.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: The isobutyryl protection workup required a complex series of continuous extractions to separate product 7 from highly polar impurity 14, making the process cumbersome and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: By pushing the DMSO‑based alkylation farther to completion, impurity 14 was reduced, allowing a single batch extraction with 3 % MeOH in DCM, followed by brine washes and solvent‑swap to acetone and crystallization, simplifying the work‑up and improving yield (∼82 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Because the alkylation in DMSO can be pushed further… there is much less impurity 14… This allows for the continuous extraction to be replaced with a simpler batch extraction… The combined organic extract was washed with brine… The organic layer was azeotropically dried, concentrated … and swapped to acetone to crystallize the desired product 7 in ∼82 % yield.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: The final dimethoxytrityl (DMTr) protection step previously required silica gel chromatography and multiple extractions, which were not practical for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The chromatography step was eliminated; after methanol quench the reaction mixture was washed directly with aqueous NaHCO₃, then the product was precipitated and recrystallized from DCM/cyclohexane, giving crystalline MOE‑G PNS in ∼73 % yield without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “The methanol quench was maintained, but no concentration to a residue was employed. Rather, sodium bicarbonate washes were carried out… The column chromatography step was removed and replaced by precipitation and recrystallization from DCM/cyclohexane to afford crystalline MOE G PNS 1 in ∼73 % (w/w) yield.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Manufacture of 5′‑
Problem_Description: Codistillation of MOE‑Br with MTBE sometimes failed to control the 2′‑O‑Me impurity when applied to different nucleosides (e.g., adenosine), indicating inconsistent impurity removal.
Solution_Description: The codistillation was revised to be performed in the absence of DMSO, ensuring reproducible removal of methyl‑bromide across substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the same process was used in a subsequent campaign with a different nucleoside (adenosine), unexpectedly high levels of the corresponding 2′‑O‑Me impurity were generated… we therefore reexamined the codistillation conditions and determined that carrying out the alkylbromide/MTBE distillation in the absence of DMSO resulted in reproducible control of the 2′‑O‑Me impurity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Pentaerythritol (PE) and dipentaerythritol (DPE) are practically insoluble in most organic solvents and melt only at high temperature (PE ≈ 260 °C, DPE ≈ 220 °C), resulting in poor reactant dissolution and a very viscous or solid reaction medium.
Solution_Description: The researchers switched to sulfolane, a polar aprotic solvent in which PE shows moderate solubility (≈ 37 g L⁻¹ at 110 °C). By working at a PE/sulfolane ratio close to the solubility limit (≈ 2333 g L⁻¹) they obtained a suspended‑reactant system that allowed adequate mixing and improved DPE selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “PE is a white crystalline powder, mostly nonsoluble in usual organic solvents and melts at 260 °C.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Solvent‑free dimerisation produced a highly viscous, solid‑like mixture that was difficult to stir, leading to poor reproducibility and inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A polar solvent (sulfolane) was introduced, converting the system from a solid suspension to a slurry that could be mechanically stirred, which removed the viscosity problem and gave repeatable results.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Systems without solvent were usually very viscous and difficult to stir.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: During the acid‑catalysed reaction, oxonium‑oxetane intermediates rapidly polymerise, forming higher‑molecular‑weight oligomers (TPE, etc.) that consume DPE and lower its selectivity, especially after ~50 % PE conversion.
Solution_Description: The temperature was lowered to 175 °C, the acid loading reduced to 0.5 mol % H₂SO₄, and the reaction time shortened to 1 h, which limited side‑reaction pathways and maximised DPE selectivity (≈ 44 % at 48 % PE conversion).
Supporting_Evidence: • “After only 60 min, the conversion was 40 % and the DPE selectivity almost reached 52 %; then the DPE selectivity progressively decreased to 23 %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: The presence of water (either added deliberately or formed in‑situ) dramatically reduces PE conversion and DPE selectivity because water changes the solubility of PE and accelerates undesired side reactions.
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed with minimal water (no added water; only the small amount generated by the dehydration). Distillation of water during the reaction was used to keep its concentration low, which gave the highest DPE selectivity (56 % with 41 % PE conversion).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Best DPE selectivity (56 %) for best PE conversion (41 %) was obtained when sulfolane was used without water.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: When the optimized conditions from the autoclave were transferred to a glass batch reactor, PE conversion dropped from 47 % to 18 % and DPE yield fell from 20 % to 6 % because of temperature‑ramp delays and uncontrolled acid addition.
Solution_Description: The glass reactor was equipped with a three‑neck flask and a guard, the temperature was monitored directly in the medium, and the acid was added only after the system reached the setpoint (175 °C). This reduced the heating lag, improved mixing, and restored conversion and selectivity close to the autoclave values.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Performing the synthesis in the glass reactor reduced the PE conversion drastically from 47 to 18 %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: DPE, PE and oligomers have very similar solubilities, making it difficult to isolate DPE from the reaction mixture using simple filtration or washing.
Solution_Description: A two‑stage fractional crystallisation in water was developed (first crystallise oligomers, then DPE) which allowed 83 % of DPE to be recovered as a solid while keeping > 90 % of PE in the filtrate.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Recrystallization in water allowed separating DPE from PE… 83 wt % of DPE was solid and 93 wt % of PE was still in the filtrate.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Dipentaerythritol from Pentaerythritol under Acidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Even after the optimized crystallisation, 3 % of DPE was lost during the purification steps, lowering the isolated yield to 16 % (57 % based on GC).
Solution_Description: The isolation protocol was fine‑tuned (adjusting water volume, cooling time, and DPE seeding amount) to minimise product loss; the final isolated DPE yield was increased to 16 % with 72 % GC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “16 % isolated DPE yield was obtained (20.0 g DPE) with 72 % GC purity… 3 % of DPE yield was lost during the purification.”

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original bis‑alkylation step used a large excess of NaH in DMF, a reagent known to be explosively hazardous on scale and required expensive, stoichiometric dimethyl malonate (2).
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the NaH/DMF protocol with a mild K₂CO₃‑mediated reaction of Meldrum’s acid (7) and dibromoethane, using only 2.2 equiv of each reagent and avoiding NaH entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “use of excess NaH in DMF for alkylation, a well‑documented explosion hazard on scale” (Intro, lines …); “The use of this protocol avoided both the use of NaH and any cyclopropane byproduct formation” (Results, lines …); “Meldrum’s acid … with K₂CO₃ … delivered 8 … (70 % isolated yield, >500 g scale)” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: Isolation of intermediate 8 gave a yellow solid when only water washing was used, leading to lower yields in the subsequent step.
Solution_Description: An additional diethyl‑ether wash of the filtered cake was introduced, giving a white solid of 8 and improving the overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “Stirring with a glass rod to break the filter cake was necessary … Without the additional washing step, a yellow solid resulted, causing a lower yield in the ensuing step.” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: The batch electrochemical cyclization of 5 to 6 relied on expensive platinum anodes and raised safety concerns when scaling.
Solution_Description: Graphite anodes and stainless‑steel cathodes were substituted for the platinum/iron electrodes, maintaining high yields while drastically reducing cost and improving chemical inertness.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “Precious metals such as platinum would be cost‑prohibitive on scale … Graphite is a highly desirable alternative … delivering 6 in 95 % yield.” (Results, lines …); “Stainless steel … was selected … while maintaining high efficiency.” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: Scaling the batch electrochemical cyclization to the hundred‑gram level suffered from poor mass/heat transfer, uneven current distribution, low conversion, side reactions and associated safety hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A compact multilayer flow reactor with a large electrode surface‑to‑volume ratio, reduced inter‑electrode gap (2 cm, reducible to 0.2 cm), high‑flow magnetic circulation, and constant‑current operation was employed, providing efficient heat removal (temperature < 27 °C) and uniform current distribution.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “poor mass and heat transfer … uneven current and potential distribution … low conversion rate … safety issues” (Results, lines …); “a large working surface of the electrode … to both dissipate heat generated and reduce polarization effects” (Results, lines …); “the flow system tolerated higher current … resistance was low (6–8 V) and temperature <27 °C” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: In the batch electrochemical reaction, substrate diffusion between the electrodes was limited, contributing to low conversion and side‑product formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The substrate concentration was optimized to 100 g·L⁻¹ in the flow reactor and a high flow rate (≈95 L·h⁻¹, residence time 14 s) was applied to improve mass transport and maintain high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “The substrate concentration was also evaluated and optimized to 100 g L⁻¹ … affording yields comparable to that of the batch reaction.” (Results, lines …); “The pump was then turned on and kept at a flow rate of 95 L/h … the high flow rate can help dislodge evolving hydrogen gas … delivering a lower voltage, fewer side reactions, and higher efficiency.” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: Reduction of 6 to the tetraalcohol 9 with LiAlH₄ is pyrophoric and generates aluminum salts that complicate purification.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to Red‑Al (non‑pyrophoric, soluble in toluene) for the reduction, eliminating the safety hazard and simplifying work‑up, albeit still requiring removal of aluminum salts.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “Because of its pyrophoric and dangerous nature … the use of LiAlH₄ to reduce 6 … was avoided. Red aluminum was determined to be a suitable and safe reducing agent …” (Results, lines …); “the tetraalcohol … was contaminated with aluminum salts.” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: The crude tetraalcohol obtained after reduction contained aluminum salts, necessitating an extra purification step before nitration.
Solution_Description: Instead of isolating the pure tetraalcohol, the crude mixture was directly subjected to nitration, allowing the salts to be removed during the final work‑up and improving overall efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “This product was also contaminated with aluminum salts. Fortunately, this impure mixture could be subjected to nitration directly to afford tetranitrate 1 …” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclobutane Synthesis in Flow: Scale-Up of a Promising Melt-Castable Energetic Intermediate
Problem_Description: Platinum electrodes are expensive and would dominate the material cost for large‑scale electrochemical production.
Solution_Description: Graphite (an inexpensive carbon material) was adopted as the anode, delivering comparable yields (95 %) while drastically reducing electrode cost.
Supporting_Evidence: -> “Graphite was successfully tested as a replacement for the platinum anode, delivering 6 in 95 % yield.” (Results, lines …).

Paper Title: Efficient Processing of Reactions Involving Diazonium Salts: Meerwein Arylation in an Impinging-Jet Reactor
Problem_Description: In batch Meerwein arylation the overall yield is very low because the diazonium salts are highly unstable, the mixing is poor and the rapid exothermic nature of the diazotization/aryl‑addition steps leads to temperature spikes and local hot‑spots.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction is moved to an inverted impinging‑jet reactor (CIJR) that provides intense micromixing, rapid heat removal and a uniform temperature profile; an IR camera is used for real‑time temperature monitoring and the reactor is operated in an adiabatic mode to avoid external heating.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Both diazotization and Meerwein arylation reactions are fast and highly exothermic, and their relative rates can be manipulated by changing the reaction temperature and the catalyst concentration for the second step.",

 "Because the flowrates are high in the impinging‑jet reactor, a large amount of feed solution/starting material is required for optimization studies.",
 "The inverted impinging‑jet reactor (also known as submerged impinging‑jet reactor) will provide higher residence time compared to the conventional impinging‑jet reactor and gives rapid micromixing that minimizes side‑products.",
 "An IR camera was used to monitor the real‑time reactor temperature. The steady state of temperature was achieved at 90 s (3 times the residence time)."]

Problem_Description: Diazonium salts can decompose violently and generate nitrogen gas; in continuous flow they may cause clogging of reaction channels.

Problem_Description: The traditional batch process uses excess acetic acid as solvent; its close boiling point to water makes separation difficult, requiring azeotropic or extractive distillation, which adds large downstream processing cost.
Solution_Description: A solvent system free of acetic acid (acetone + methacrylic acid) is adopted, eliminating the need for azeotropic distillation and reducing material and separation costs.

Paper Title: Efficient Processing of Reactions Involving Diazonium Salts: Meerwein Arylation in an Impinging-Jet Reactor
Problem_Description: Using high catalyst loadings (5–10 mol % CuCl) promotes the Sandmeyer side‑reaction, reducing the isolated yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading is optimized to 3 mol % CuCl and the inlet temperature is set to 38.3 °C, which suppresses side‑reactions and gives the highest isolated yield (≈93 %).

Solution_Description: A T‑mixer was introduced upstream of the glass reactor chip to allow formation of the activated ester at 20 °C before heating, and reagent concentrations were reduced (0.277 M) to avoid precipitation. Mixing was optimized by employing a micro‑static mixer and temperature‑controlled inlet streams.
Supporting_Evidence: “Very low product formation was observed because of the formation of guanidino derivatives… We then changed the setup and employed a microstatic mixer … However, clogging due to the relatively low solubility of HATU … was observed” (p. 4). “We incorporated a T‑mixer … to allow for the formation of the activated ester before all of the reactants entered the glass reactor chip held at 50 °C using reagent concentrations of 0.277 M” (p. 4).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: Direct injection of the amine/acid/DIPEA stream and HATU stream without adequate mixing resulted in very low product formation and side‑product (guanidino) formation, indicating poor reaction control and variability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The order of addition was redesigned: the amine/acid/DIPEA solution and HATU solution were mixed in a T‑mixer at 20 °C to generate the activated ester before entering the heated reactor, improving conversion and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: “Very low product formation was observed because of the formation of guanidino derivatives… We hypothesized that this approach would allow for the formation of activated ester at 20 °C using 0.378 M solutions of the reagents” (p. 4). “After confirming the formation of intermediate 3 by (+) ESI‑MS … we decided to quickly identify the most favorable conditions using a 2² full‑factorial design” (p. 4).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: Intermediate 4 displayed poor solubility in EtOH (0.065 M) and in DMF at 20 °C, causing precipitation and pump stall during the telescoped flow synthesis.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The concentration of 4 was lowered to 0.065 M to stay below its solubility limit, and the compound was recrystallized from EtOH/EtOAc to improve its solubility. The flow configuration was adjusted (lower flow rates, use of coiled‑flow‑inverter (CFI) reactors in series) to avoid solid deposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions run at 0.075 M 4 caused deposition of solid in the syringe… Lowering the concentration of 4 to 0.065 M overcame this problem.” (p. 9). “We focused on 4 at 20 °C by recrystallizing it twice, first from EtOH and then from EtOAc. This treatment enabled a solubility increase to 0.0785 M (17.6 mg/mL in DMF).” (p. 7).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: Catalyst Pd(II) species decomposed at temperatures above 100 °C, leading to loss of activity, potential formation of homocoupling by‑products, and reactor clogging.
Solution_Description: Temperature was limited to ≤ 95 °C based on DoE findings, and PdCl₂(PPh₃)₂ at 1 % loading was selected as the most robust catalyst, providing > 90 % conversion without degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “We did not attempt to accelerate the reaction rate by increasing the temperature above 100 °C since this would lead to catalyst degradation as suggested by Figure 6… with subsequent reactor chip clogging.” (p. 7). “Entry 6: PdCl₂(PPh₃)₂, 95 °C, pyrrolidine, 85 % (79 % isolated) yield.” (Table 2).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: In the Sonogashira coupling, order of addition and catalyst choice strongly affected conversion; prolonged exposure of the catalyst and base at room temperature caused catalyst degradation and inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: A robotic liquid‑handling HTE campaign identified XPhos Pd G3 as the optimal catalyst and showed that adding base/catalyst after mixing the substrates prevented degradation. High‑pKa bases (piperidine, TMPH, TBAPF₆) were chosen to promote Cu‑acetylide formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Extended contact of the base and catalyst at room temperature… did not yield the desired product, likely as a result of catalyst degradation” (p. 5). “XPhos Pd G3 gave the greatest number of hits” (p. 5). “The most favorable bases were the ones with higher pKₐ values, such as piperidine, TMPH, and salts like K₂CO₃, TBAPF₆” (p. 6).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: Large‑scale telescoped flow synthesis required handling of 0.075 M 4, which precipitated during the run and stalled the pump after 8 h.
Solution_Description: The concentration of 4 was reduced to 0.065 M and the number of coiled‑flow‑inverter (CFI) reactors in series was tuned to provide an optimal residence time (4 h, two CFIs) that delivered 54 % overall isolated yield without precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions run at 0.075 M 4 caused deposition of solid … pump stalled … Lowering the concentration of 4 to 0.065 M overcame this problem.” (p. 9). “Overall yield of 54 % when lower flow rates and two CFI reactors in series were used (entry 4).” (Table 3).

Paper Title: Use of High-Throughput Tools for Telescoped Continuous Flow Synthesis of an Alkynylnaphthyridine Anticancer Agent, HSN608
Problem_Description: Isolation of amide‑coupled product 3 by column chromatography was tedious and low‑throughput.
Solution_Description: A precipitation work‑up was developed: addition of water to the reaction stream induced crystallisation of 3, which could be filtered to give 86 % isolated yield, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since isolation of the amide‑coupled product by column chromatography was tedious, we developed a precipitation method for reaction work‑up wherein addition of water at the end of the reaction produces a solid form of 3 that can be easily recovered by filtration in ∼86 % yield” (p. 5).

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: Mannich reaction of 3‑ethoxysalicylaldehyde (2) with methylpiperazine and ethanol gave 3.4 % HPLC area of an unknown impurity (entry 1, Table 1). The impurity persisted into the next step, lowering overall purity and yield.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent from ethanol (a nucleophilic solvent) to the more sterically hindered 2‑propanol reduced the impurity to 0.7 % HPLC area (entry 2, Table 1), providing a cleaner Mannich product (9) that could be telescoped without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the Mannich reaction … ethanol solvent … 3.4 % A % of an unknown impurity … When the more sterically hindered solvent 2‑propanol was used, the corresponding impurity was reduced to a very low level (0.7 % A %).”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: Alkylation of Mannich product 9 with tert‑butyl bromoacetate produced a quaternary ammonium over‑alkylated impurity (≈30 % A %), giving a low isolated yield of aldehyde 3 and requiring column chromatography for purification.
Solution_Description: Two strategies were employed: (1) addition of ZnBr₂ to complex the piperazine nitrogen, reducing the over‑alkylated impurity to 8 % A %; (2) replacement of the softer electrophile (tert‑butyl bromoacetate) with the harder tert‑butyl chloroacetate, which eliminated quaternary ammonium formation and raised the two‑step yield from 53 % to 79 %. The product was then purified by acidic aqueous extraction followed by basification and isopropyl‑acetate extraction, avoiding chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “We attempted to inhibit the N‑nucleophilicity by mixing the Lewis acid ZnBr₂ … yielded 3 with a reduced level of the overalkylated impurity (8 % A %). … we attempted to use the harder electrophile tert‑butyl chloroacetate … the quaternary ammonium did not form and the two‑step yield improved … these neutral impurities could be removed to the organic layer by extraction of the target 3 with an acidic aqueous solution. Subsequently, basification … and extraction … gave pure 3 in high quality (98.7 % A %).”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: The original Boc‑protection of amidine 4 used 1,4‑dioxane, a suspected carcinogen, and the subsequent amidation employed oxalyl chloride (producing CO) and 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE), both hazardous on large scale.
Solution_Description: 1,4‑Dioxane was replaced by THF for the Boc‑protection step, and oxalyl chloride was swapped for thionyl chloride while DCE was replaced by toluene for the amidation, eliminating the toxic reagents and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the Boc protection of 4, use of 1,4‑dioxane needed to be eliminated … THF was found to be a good alternative … oxalyl chloride … needed to be avoided. DCE is inappropriate for scale‑up … This problem was solved by replacing oxalyl chloride with thionyl chloride and DCE with toluene …”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: 5‑Chloro‑2‑nitrobenzoyl chloride, an intermediate for amide 10, showed exothermic decomposition at 170 °C (DSC), posing a severe safety risk during concentration.
Solution_Description: The concentration was performed at a temperature at least 100 °C below the decomposition point (≤70 °C) and the process was stopped at 2 vol % to prevent runaway decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “A previous report suggested that isolated 2‑nitrobenzoyl chloride decomposes violently … exothermic decomposition was observed at 170 °C … we concluded that 5‑chloro‑2‑nitrobenzoyl chloride could be safely concentrated in toluene solution by performing the concentration process at a minimum of 100 °C below the exothermic temperature and setting the concentration end point to 2 vol.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: Reductive amination of aniline 5 with aldehyde 3 suffered from poor reproducibility; water (by‑product) caused Boc‑deprotection to impurity 11 and cyclisation to cyclic aminals 14/15, requiring column chromatography.
Solution_Description: The order of addition was reversed: sodium triacetoxyborohydride was added to a slurry of aniline 5 in AcOH, then the aldehyde 3 was added. Using 3 equiv of reductant suppressed cyclic aminal formation (0.4 % 14) and gave 75.7 % A % of the desired product 11. Reducing the reductant to 1.5 equiv increased impurity formation, confirming the need for the higher stoichiometry. The reaction was kept at ≤0 °C (AcOH/i‑PrOAc solvent) to avoid decomposition of the boron‑complex intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “We predicted that addition of aldehyde 3 to the mixture of aniline 5 and reductant would induce immediate reduction … As a result, when 3 equiv of sodium triacetoxyborohydride … yielded the target 11 as the main product (75.7 % A %) while successfully suppressing the production of 14 (0.4 % A %). … When the reaction involved reducing the amount of reductant … the target 11 and 14 were obtained at 29.3 % A % and 52.9 % A % … The use of acetic acid/isopropyl acetate as the solvent enables the temperature to be lowered to <0 °C, and the decomposition of 17/18 can be suppressed.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: Isolation of aldehyde 3 after the Mannich‑alkylation sequence required column chromatography, which is impractical at scale.
Solution_Description: A simple acidic aqueous extraction of the crude mixture removed neutral impurities; basification of the aqueous layer followed by extraction with isopropyl acetate gave pure 3 (98.7 % A) without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “These neutral impurities could be removed to the organic layer by extraction of the target 3 with an acidic aqueous solution. Subsequently, basification of the aqueous extract and extraction of 3 with an organic solvent (isopropyl acetate) gave pure 3 in high quality (98.7 % A %).”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: Final deprotection of 11 to give the HCl salt yielded an amorphous solid (1·3HCl) with polymorphic impurities when alcohol was present, making isolation difficult without chromatography.
Solution_Description: Using excess aqueous HCl (no alcohol) suppressed solvent‑mediated substitution, and acetone was added as an antisolvent to crystallize the product as 1·4HCl·xH₂O. pH was tightly controlled at ≈5.5 during crystallization to avoid polymorph formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “We attempted to use an excess amount of hydrochloric acid without an alcohol solvent to suppress the solvent‑mediated substitution reaction … the side reaction was inhibited, and the subsequent addition of acetone as an antisolvent led to the formation of a crystalline rather than an amorphous solid … pH of the mixture was adjusted … to approximately 5.5 …”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: ASP5069 (1·HCl·2H₂O) is highly hygroscopic; drying could lead to loss of water and conversion to other hydrate forms, compromising product specification.
Solution_Description: The wet product was dried at 50 °C under vacuum at 7‑9 kPa for three days until loss‑on‑drying ≤1 %, delivering the dihydrate (2.1 ± 0.2 eq H₂O) with >98 % purity. Humidity‑controlled drying ensured consistent hydrate level.
Supporting_Evidence: “Drying was performed under a vacuum at 7–9 kPa until LOD was ≤1.0 % … to give ASP5069 … with 98.5 % A % purity … The hygroscopic profile … suggested that the target 2.1 ± 0.2 hydrate could be obtained by drying … at 50 °C under a vacuum.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Plasma Kallikrein Inhibitor ASP5069
Problem_Description: The Mannich reaction required 67 h at 80 °C, and subsequent aging steps added another 108 h, severely limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: By changing the solvent to 2‑propanol and optimizing work‑up, impurity levels were minimized, allowing telescoping of steps and eliminating the need for prolonged isolation procedures; while reaction times were not dramatically shortened, the overall process became more robust for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the more sterically hindered solvent 2‑propanol was used, the corresponding impurity was reduced … Because the purity of the resulting Mannich product 9 was sufficiently high without crystallization isolation, the reaction was telescoped to the next alkylation reaction.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: Pinacol boronic esters display very high solubility in many organic solvents, which makes crystallization‑based isolation difficult and non‑uniform across substrates.
Solution_Description: Switch to diethanolamine (DEA) boronic esters, which have intrinsically low solubility in low‑to‑moderately polar solvents, enabling a standard crystallization in MeTHF and avoiding chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “pinacol boronic esters present a challenge because they often display high solubility in a range of organic solvents, and thus, crystallization processes can be difficult to develop.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: Boronic acids exist in equilibrium with trimeric boroxines; the equilibrium position depends on water content and is hard to control, leading to unpredictable solubility, stability, and dosing.
Solution_Description: Use DEA boronic esters (DABO) that form a stable N→B dative bond, eliminating the boroxine equilibrium and providing consistent low‑solubility, air‑stable material across many substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Boronic acids are typically in equilibrium with a trimeric boroxine derivative, and controlling the position of the equilibrium, by controlling water content, is not trivial.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: Certain pinacol boronic esters (e.g., pyrazole‑derived) fail to crystallize during transesterification, likely because of unfavorable stereoelectronic effects that prevent sufficient shift toward the DEA ester.
Solution_Description: Employ a boronic acid or an acyclic diisopropylboronic ester as the starting material; the entropy‑driven equilibrium more readily favors DEA ester formation, restoring crystallization and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “several pinacol esters of pyrazoles did not crystallize as expected, most likely because of stereoelectronic effects.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: DEA is viscous and can oil out during large‑scale addition, making transfer and mixing problematic and raising operational safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Add a small amount of isopropanol (or charge DEA slowly) to reduce viscosity and aid transfer; isopropanol also acts as a co‑solvent to prevent oiling.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of isopropanol in the process is optional but should be added if oiling of the DEA in the reaction is evident. Alternatively, the oiling of DEA can be alleviated if it is charged slowly to the reaction.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: Traditional laboratory isolation (evaporation‑to‑dryness, chromatography) is slow, hazardous, and costly for multikilogram batches of organoboranes.
Solution_Description: Develop a simple, standard transesterification/crystallization sequence in MeTHF that can be telescoped directly from the crude borylation mixture, giving high‑purity crystalline DEA boronic esters in high yield without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The simple and standard process was successfully applied to numerous intermediates … to deliver high‑purity, crystalline DEA boronic esters.”

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: When DEA boronic esters are produced at kilogram scale, the reaction mixture can become viscous, impeding effective agitation and gas‑liquid mass transfer.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Intensify agitation (impeller design), consider batch‑to‑flow conversion, and adjust concentration to keep the mixture fluid while maintaining supersaturation for crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reactive crystallization was initiated instantaneously in most instances, and high‑purity crystalline DEA boronic esters were obtained in high yield via filtration.” (implies adequate mixing and rapid nucleation)

Paper Title: Diethanolamine Boronic Esters: Development of a Simple and Standard Process for Boronic Ester Synthesis
Problem_Description: Large‑scale isolation must avoid chromatography and evaporation‑to‑dryness due to safety, environmental, and operational concerns.
Solution_Description: Crystallize DEA boronic esters from moderately polar MeTHF (or alternative green solvents) and isolate by simple filtration, eliminating hazardous chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It is essential that the large‑scale isolation of solid intermediates proceeds via a crystallization or precipitation process and does not use typical laboratory methods such as evaporation‑to‑dryness or chromatography because these present safety and environmental concerns.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: Traditional cyclocondensation of 1,3‑diketones with methylhydrazine (Way A) gave poor regioselectivity, producing a mixture of inseparable 3‑ and 5‑CF₃‑pyrazole regioisomers; MeNHNH₂ is also inconvenient because both nucleophilic centers react similarly.
Solution_Description: Adopted Schlosser’s selective lithiation strategy on 4‑ethoxy‑1,1,1‑trifluoro‑3‑buten‑2‑one to access each isomer individually and introduced a scalable one‑step synthesis followed by fractional distillation (based on the measured boiling‑point‑vs‑pressure diagram) to isolate pure 1‑methyl‑3‑CF₃‑pyrazole (1a) and 1‑methyl‑5‑CF₃‑pyrazole (2a).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "the traditional method for the synthesis of diverse functionalized 3/5‑CF₃‑substituted pyrazoles … however, this approach is limited by … poor regioselectivity. Usually it gives a mixture of hardly separable regioisomers" (p. 2).
- "MeNHNH₂ is the most inconvenient partner … due to the similar activity of the two nucleophilic centers" (p. 2).
- "To solve all of the above‑mentioned problems … we drew our attention to the seminal paper of Schlosser … we describe our results of optimization and scale up the synthesis" (p. 3).
- "Based on the data obtained, the practical kilo‑scale synthesis of both individual regioisomers, including separation by distillation, was elaborated and optimized" (p. 4).
- "The boiling point vs pressure diagram was measured … the difference of the boiling points for the isomers was ca. 50 °C … very promising for the successful separation" (p. 5).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
