Therefore, the addition of excess of water to the reaction mixture leads to biphasic system formation, which could be easily separated. In this step, the impurities such as unreacted methylhydrazine hydrochloride and HCl formed are also eliminated" (p. 5).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: During flow lithiation of 1a, the original feed‑rate ratio (44 mL min⁻¹ pyrazole solution vs 6 mL min⁻¹ n‑BuLi) caused a mis‑balance, leading to unstable operation after 15–30 min, temperature drift and precipitation, reducing productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Two additional reactors were inserted: a 110 mL dilutor for the 2.5 M n‑BuLi solution and a 90 mL precooling loop for the 0.33 M pyrazole solution. This balanced the flow rates, prevented precipitation, and allowed stable operation for >8 h (productivity reduced by 38 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Due to the significant misbalance of the flow rates … the system worked stably only for 15–30 min. After this time, some problems with temperature control occurred as well as some precipitate formed" (p. 8).
- "We reduced the productivity … added a 110 mL reactor to dilute the 2.5 M n‑BuLi … and a 90 mL reactor for the precooling of the 0.33 M THF solution of pyrazole 1a… system was tested, and its behavior was stable during more than 8 h of the operation time" (p. 9).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The flow‑generated lithium intermediate 11x, when reacted with iPrOBPin at –50 °C, required only 5 min residence time, which was insufficient for complete conversion to the boronic ester, leading to low isolated yield (57 %).
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was collected and transferred to a batch reactor, then maintained at room temperature overnight before work‑up, allowing full conversion to the boronic ester (11d) with an improved isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: - "In the case of boronic ester derivative 11d, the reaction time 5 min at –50 °C was not sufficient for its completion. Therefore, in this case, the collected reaction mixture was additionally maintained in a batch reactor at room temperature overnight before product isolation. The yield … was 57 %" (p. 10).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The previously reported bromination of pyrazoles (Schlosser’s Br₂/Fe at 100 °C) is hazardous and requires handling of elemental bromine, limiting safe scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A milder protocol using NBS (1.3 equiv) in DMF at 60 °C for 10 h was introduced; it is safer, avoids elemental bromine, and affords high isolated yields (92 % for 12a, 83 % for 13a) on a 200 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "This developed procedure appears to be more convenient for the scale‑up compared to Schlosser’s one, where the Br₂/Fe system at 100 °C was utilized" (p. 13).
- "The bromination of 1.3 M solution of both pyrazoles in DMF by 1.3 equiv of NBS at 60 °C during 10 h was the optimal condition. … preparative yields … 92 and 83 %" (p. 13).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The original Br–Li exchange on 4‑bromo‑1‑methyl‑5‑CF₃‑pyrazole employed t‑BuLi in Et₂O, a combination that is unsafe and difficult to handle on large scale.
Solution_Description: The exchange was successfully performed using n‑BuLi in THF at –78 °C, which is more robust and safer for scale‑up; the organolithium intermediate 13x was generated on 50 g scale without precipitation problems.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The drawback of such an approach was the use of both t‑BuLi and Et₂O, which was not a convenient reagent/solvent combination for safe performance, especially on a large scale" (p. 14).
- "We found that selective Br–Li exchange could be achieved by n‑BuLi treatment in THF at –78 °C in a batch reactor" (p. 14).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: Direct ortho‑metalation (DoM) of 4‑bromo‑1‑methyl‑5‑CF₃‑pyrazole required temperatures below –85 °C; such low temperatures could not be transferred to flow, and at higher temperatures a ‘halogen‑dance’ side reaction occurred, reducing selectivity.
Solution_Description: DoM was performed in batch using LDA at –85 °C, followed by immediate trapping (dry ice for acid, iPrOBPin for boronic ester) and subsequent hydrogenative debromination when needed; the low‑temperature batch process gave clean product without halogen‑dance.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "It was found that the reaction proceeded cleanly but at the temperatures below –85 °C. The process requiring such low temperatures could not be successfully adapted to flow mode. … led to a significant formation of the isomeric side product due to the ‘halogen dance’ reaction" (p. 15).
- "The DoM generation of lithium derivative 15x was scaled up … at –85 °C. … the trapping … afforded the corresponding acid 15c in 66 % preparative yield. … the structure … proved the absence of the halogen dance reaction" (p. 16).

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Functionalized 1‑Methyl-3/5-(trifluoromethyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The Curtius‑type rearrangement of the pyrazolyl carboxylic acids releases a large amount of gas; uncontrolled evolution can be hazardous.
Solution_Description: DPPA was added dropwise at room temperature, then the mixture was heated very slowly to 100 °C over 2–3 h to control gas evolution; the reaction was monitored to keep the gas evolution stable and not too intense.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Caution! Take care of the intensity of gas evolution. It should be stable and not very intense" (p. 18).
- "DPPA … was slowly added dropwise … The reaction mixture was very slowly heated to 100 °C (during 2–3 h) … when the temperature reached 100 °C, the reaction mixture was maintained at this temperature for 1 additional hour" (p. 18).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: The catalytic Ru‑MACHO deuterogenation of ester 9 gave inconsistent deuterium incorporation and left a significant amount of unreacted starting material, making the process unreliable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the catalytic approach and reverted to a LiAlD₄ reduction (87 mol % relative to substrate), which provided quantitative conversion and ≥97 % D₂ incorporation on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “We were surprised to observe mixtures of products consistent with both under‑ and overincorporation of deuterium…”, “Variations to the optimized conditions were attempted, but we were unable to achieve consistently ≥97 % D₂ incorporation…”, “We ultimately chose to use LiAlD₄ for our scale‑up production. This allowed us to obtain the desired product 16 D in quantitative yield with ≥97 % D₂ incorporation (Table 1, entry 5).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: The first‑generation tosylation of alcohol 11 suffered from low conversion, formation of N‑tosylated and bis‑tosylated side‑products, required chromatography for isolation, and showed poor reproducibility on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A Brønsted‑acid‑promoted tosylation was developed using TsOH·H₂O (1.4 equiv) and Ts₂O (2.0 equiv) in MeCN, with a 10‑minute premix of alcohol 11 and TsOH before Ts₂O addition, followed by crystallization from NMP. This eliminated chromatography, gave >96 % conversion, and suppressed N‑tosylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Low yield of the tosylation and the requirement for chromatographic purification were clear opportunities for process improvement.”, “Initial experiments using TsCl … led to incomplete conversion and significant amounts of the N‑tosylated and bis‑tosylated impurities.”, “The use of Brønsted acid TsOH·H₂O completely shut down the unproductive N‑tosylation and bis‑tosylation pathways and provided clean conversion to the desired product.”, “It is essential to premix alcohol 11 and TsOH·H₂O for a minimum of 10 min before the addition of Ts₂O.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the SNAr coupling between deprotected piperidine salt 10 and bromide 8 showed poor reproducibility and low isolated yields, limiting the overall efficiency of the first‑generation route.
Solution_Description: A convergent, phosphoramidate‑directed annulation was introduced, coupling the α,β‑unsaturated amide 13 with 2‑aminobenzimidazole 5 (or its activated phosphoramidate derivative 21) to build the tricyclic core in a single step, bypassing the problematic SNAr step.
Supporting_Evidence: “We noted reproducibility issues during the scale‑up of the tosylation step and of the SNAr reaction between 10 and 8.”, “We proposed a more streamlined approach … a modified condensation/annulation reaction would assemble the entire carbon framework of the molecule in one step …”, “The key step of the route featured a novel and highly selective phosphoramidate‑directed annulation.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: During the phosphorylation of aminobenzimidazole 5, uncontrolled N‑phosphorylation led to mixtures of the desired exocyclic phosphoramidate 21 and the undesired N²‑phosphorylated product 22.
Solution_Description: Screening of bases identified N‑methylimidazole (NMI) as the optimal promoter, giving >99 % selectivity for 21. Adjusting base equivalents (1 mol % NMI) and using a stoichiometric amount of ClP(OEt)₂ ensured high conversion and clean product.
Supporting_Evidence: “The choice of a base in this reaction was critical… N‑methylimidazole provided 21 in the highest overall yield and selectivity (entry 1).”, “>99:1 ratio of 21 to 22 was obtained with NMI.”, “The reaction was performed with NMI (0.669 kg, 8.10 mol, 1.35 equiv) and ClP(OEt)₂ (1.41 kg, 8.15 mol, 1.35 equiv).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: The annulation of phosphoramidate 21 with acrylamide 19 in MeCN led to oiling‑out and heterogeneous mixtures, reducing assay yields and complicating isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 1:1 MeCN/2‑MeTHF co‑solvent system was adopted, providing a homogeneous slurry‑to‑slurry transformation and delivering >95 % assay yield with 98:2 isomeric selectivity. The addition of POCl₃ was performed at 0 °C with controlled rate, and the work‑up was performed via an inverse quench into aqueous K₂CO₃.
Supporting_Evidence: “Despite additional optimization, we observed oiling out when the reaction of 21 and 19 was conducted in MeCN.”, “A 1:1 mixture of MeCN/2‑MeTHF was optimal … providing product in 95 % assay yield and 98:2 isomeric selectivity while maintaining a homogeneous solution throughout the reaction.”, “An inverse quench of the reaction mixture into 25 wt % aqueous K₂CO₃ at 25 °C provided a safe and controlled workup protocol.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: Intermediate 24 decomposed during the initial solvent swap from the annulation mixture to EtOH, especially under neutral/basic conditions above 50 °C, leading to loss of material.
Solution_Description: The protocol was redesigned to perform the NaOEt‑mediated debenzoylation of 24 to alcohol 11 before any solvent exchange, thereby avoiding prolonged exposure of 24 to basic conditions and high temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: “We identified a decomposition liability for 24 during the first solvent swap to EtOH… after K₂CO₃ quench, 24 slowly decomposes at temperatures above 50 °C.”, “To minimize this liability, we redesigned the debenzoylation/isolation protocol to first accomplish the debenzoylation to 11 before performing the solvent swap.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a Stable Precursor for Positron Emission Tomography Imaging Agent
Problem_Description: The acetyl chloride addition for benzoylation of alcohol 16 generated a highly exothermic event, posing safety concerns during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Acetyl chloride was added slowly to a 0 °C solution of the substrate, and the temperature was carefully maintained below 5 °C throughout the addition to control the heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acetyl chloride (2.14 L) was charged slowly while maintaining the internal temperature <5 °C (caution: exothermic!).”, “The reaction mixture was stirred between 0 and 5 °C for 30 min.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Debenzylation and dehalogenation side‑reactions occur during catalytic nitro reduction of intermediate I, generating impurities that are very difficult to remove from the product.
Solution_Description: The Raney‑Ni catalyst was pre‑passivated with aqueous ammonia, which raises selectivity to >75 % and suppresses dehalogenation and debenzylation; the solvent was switched to dichloromethane (low‑polarity) where conversion remains >99 % and selectivity reaches 97.9 % with only trace by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The unpassivated catalyst gave only 6.2 % selectivity and produced dehalogenated and debenzylated impurities (Table 1).', 'Aqueous ammonia gave the best effect with the selectivity reaching over 75.8 % (Table 1).', 'Using the less‑polar solvent dichloromethane gave a conversion >99 % and a selectivity of 97.9 % with only 0.02 % 2‑aminopyridin‑3‑ol and 0.7 % azoxybenzene (sec 2.4).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: In batch catalytic hydrogenation the reaction mixture is flammable/explosive and the catalyst must be filtered from the product, which is dangerous and difficult on large scale.
Solution_Description: A packed‑bed continuous‑flow reactor was employed, immobilising the pre‑passivated Raney‑Ni within a stainless‑steel tube; the autoclave was replaced by a normal pressure vessel and high‑pressure nitrogen was eliminated, providing inherent safety and eliminating the need for downstream filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Catalytic hydrogenation was flammable and explosive, and the catalyst filtration was difficult and dangerous (Introduction).', 'The upgraded continuous‑flow system filled the catalyst up in the reaction tube, replaced the autoclave with a normal pressure vessel, and removed high‑pressure N₂, simplifying operation (sec 2.3, Fig. 2).', 'The packed‑bed continuous‑flow process has inherent safety, short reaction time and no post‑treatment (sec 2.9, Table 4).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Batch hydrogenation required >90 min reaction time and gave only 95–98 % isolated yield, limiting productivity for kilogram‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: Transition to continuous‑flow reduced the residence time to 4 s (total reaction time ≈ 6 s) while achieving >99.5 % conversion and >99.9 % selectivity, and the substrate concentration was increased 30‑fold (up to 120 g L⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: ['Batch reaction time >90 min and yield 95–98 % (Table 4).', 'Continuous‑flow with residence time 4 s gave conversion 96.3 % and selectivity 89.8 % (sec 2.3).', 'Optimised conditions (25 °C, DCM, 120 g L⁻¹, 30 psi, 6 s) gave conversion 99.9 % and selectivity 99.5 % (Conclusion).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The batch process consumed a large amount of Raney‑Ni catalyst (≈6 wt % of substrate), making the process economically unattractive.
Solution_Description: Immobilising a small amount of pre‑passivated Raney‑Ni in a packed‑bed reactor lowered catalyst consumption to 0.016 wt % while maintaining high conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Catalyst consumption (wt %) in batch: 5.99 % (Table 4).', 'Catalyst consumption (wt %) in continuous‑flow: 0.016 % (Table 4).', 'The packed‑bed reactor uses a small amount of pre‑passivated Raney‑Ni (sec 2.5).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: In the original continuous‑flow set‑up the catalyst was entrained in the product stream, causing it to flow to the collection vessel and requiring tedious filtration; the solid–liquid mixing and feeding device was also inconvenient.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reactor was redesigned so that the pre‑passivated catalyst was packed inside the reaction tube, eliminating catalyst carry‑over; a thermostat and pressure sensor were added to control temperature and pressure, improving mixing and flow stability.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Catalyst flows with the reaction mixture and filtration is tedious (sec 2.3).', 'The upgraded system filled the catalyst in the reaction tube, removed high‑pressure N₂ and added a thermostat (Fig. 2).', 'A pressure sensor was added to keep inlet pressure below 95 psi, preventing pressure spikes (sec 2.6, Fig. 5).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Increasing the reaction pressure above 30 psi caused catalyst crushing, loss of active surface area, and rapid pressure build‑up that could shut down the pump, posing safety risks.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The inlet pressure was limited to <95 psi and the outlet back‑pressure valve was set ≤30 psi; a pressure sensor was installed to monitor and control pressure, preserving catalyst integrity and ensuring safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Pressure in the plunger pump increased >600 psi, causing automatic shutdown and loss of conversion (sec 2.6).', 'High pressure crushed the catalyst and reduced active surface (sec 2.6).', 'A pressure sensor was added and optimum pressure set ≤30 psi (Fig. 5).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Using polar solvents (e.g., THF, ethanol) gave high conversion but poor selectivity (≤33 %), and the substrate showed poor solubility in alcohols at room temperature.
Solution_Description: Switching to a less‑polar solvent (dichloromethane) improved both solubility and chemoselectivity, delivering >99 % conversion and >97 % selectivity with minimal by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Methanol was not examined because of its poor solubility at room temperature (sec 2.4).', 'In THF conversion >99 % but selectivity only 32.9 % (sec 2.4).', 'Using DCM gave conversion >99 % and selectivity 97.9 % (sec 2.4).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Elevating the reaction temperature above 25 °C accelerated dehalogenation and debenzylation side‑reactions, lowering product selectivity.
Solution_Description: The temperature was optimized at 25 °C, which maximized conversion (99.9 %) and selectivity (97.9 %) while keeping side‑reactions to <1 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['When the temperature was higher than 25 °C, side reactions accelerated and selectivity declined (sec 2.5).', 'At 25 °C the conversion was 99.9 % and selectivity 97.9 % (Fig. 4).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Residence times shorter than 6 s resulted in incomplete hydrogenation (azoxybenzene 6.6 % at 2 s), while longer times promoted dehalogenation and debenzylation.
Solution_Description: A residence time of 6 s was selected as optimal, giving 99.9 % conversion and 99.5 % selectivity with negligible impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Residence time <6 s gave incomplete conversion and 6.6 % azoxybenzene (sec 2.8).', 'Residence time >6 s caused dehalogenation and debenzylation (sec 2.8).', '6 s residence gave 99.9 % conversion and 99.5 % selectivity (sec 2.8).']

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Crizotinib Intermediate via Highly Efficient Catalytic Hydrogenation in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: After multiple reuse cycles the Raney‑Ni catalyst showed physical destruction, pressure increase and a drop in conversion, indicating deactivation and the need for replacement.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was regenerated by washing between runs, restoring activity; the packed‑bed format also limited catalyst loss, extending its usable lifetime to ≈281 h (≈3 cycles).
Supporting_Evidence: ['Selectivity remained >99 % but conversion decreased with time, recoverable after washing (sec 2.9).', 'Physical form of the catalyst was destroyed after prolonged use (sec 2.9).', 'Catalyst life cycle reached nearly 281 h after three cycles (Table 3).']

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: Using inorganic Na₂CO₃ as the base in the micellar system gave extensive hydrolysis of the acyl chloride, resulting in only 17–20 % isolated amide and a significant amount of benzoic‑acid by‑product.
Solution_Description: Switching to the organic base DIPEA (3 equiv) raised the amide yield to 96 % with only 1 % hydrolysis, eliminating the decomposition pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
“When water‑soluble sodium carbonate was used as the base… afforded the hydrolysis byproduct 4aa in 17–20 % yield (entries 1–4).”
“DIPEA was used as the base… the desired product 3aa was obtained in 96 % yield with only a 1 % yield of 4aa (entry 6)."

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: A small amount of organic co‑solvent in the micellar mixture promoted hydrolysis of the acyl chloride, lowering the amide yield.
Solution_Description: Removing the co‑solvent and running the reaction in 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M aqueous solution alone restored full conversion (98 % isolated amide, no hydrolysis).
Supporting_Evidence: “It is important to note that the cosolvent was not essential, as the reaction performed well in 2 wt % aqueous TPGS‑750‑M alone, with a 98 % yield of the desired product 3aa and no hydrolysis observed (entry 7)."

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: In pure water without surfactant the reaction mixture formed a large, ball‑like agglomerate that stuck to the reactor wall or rode on the stirrer, making scale‑up impractical.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adding 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M surfactant generated a stable micellar suspension that was readily stirrable, eliminating the agglomeration problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “Removing TPGS‑750‑M … resulted in agglomeration of the material as a large ball‑like cluster … a clear no‑go within a process development organization … This phenomenon was reliably solved by the use of the surfactant, and a good and easily stirrable suspension was obtained.”

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: Conventional amide couplings often require chromatography or extensive extractions for product isolation, which are undesirable at scale.
Solution_Description: The micellar protocol allowed the product to be isolated by simple filtration (or a single isopropyl‑acetate extraction) without chromatography, delivering high‑purity material.
Supporting_Evidence: “The workup process was simplified by either direct filtration or extraction from the reaction mixture to give the desired products with high purity.”

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: When 2‑aminopyridine was coupled, the intended mono‑amide was not formed; instead incomplete conversion and undesired disubstituted amides were observed.
Solution_Description: Increasing the stoichiometry of the acyl chloride drove the reaction to the disubstituted amide, giving the desired product in good‑to‑excellent yield and removing the selectivity issue.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the amount of the corresponding acetyl chloride allowed us to exclusively form the disubstituted amides 6a–c in good to excellent yields.”

Paper Title: Simple Synthesis of Amides via Their Acid Chlorides in Aqueous TPGS-750‑M
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction to a 40 g batch required reliable agitation of the micellar suspension; traditional magnetic stirring was inadequate for larger reactors.
Solution_Description: A 1 L reactor equipped with mechanical overhead stirring was employed; after reaction completion the mixture was filtered and the aqueous TPGS‑750‑M phase was recycled up to four times, demonstrating robust large‑scale operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Under the developed conditions, benzoyl chloride was added to a suspension … After completion … the suspension was filtered, and the cake was collected… Further study showed that the filtrate can be recycled four times without loss of efficiency (>96 % for each cycle)."

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: 2‑Fluoroadenine is commercially scarce and contributes significantly to the API cost; the common impurity 2,6‑diaminopurine and the intrinsic low solubility of 2‑fluoroadenine prevent efficient purity‑upgrade by recrystallisation.
Solution_Description: A five‑step route from the inexpensive commodity guanine was devised, featuring a 9‑THP‑protected 2,6‑difluoropurine intermediate that crystallises cleanly. Direct isolation of the crystalline 9‑THP‑2‑fluoroadenine allows a high‑purity, high‑yield delivery of 2‑fluoroadenine.
Supporting_Evidence:
"2‑fluoroadenine … limited commercial availability and was a significant contributor to the API cost."
"The most common impurity present in commercial 3 is 2,6‑diaminopurine 4… The recrystallisation of neutral 3 offers minimal opportunity for purity upgrade, especially … due to their inherently poor solubilities and stabilities."
"low solubility of 3 … imposing particle size distribution (PSD) requirements"
"The route delivers 3 in five steps from the commodity chemical guanine via a novel 9‑THP‑2,6‑difluoropurine intermediate."
"9‑THP‑2‑fluoroadenine 12 is a crystalline intermediate found to offer a superior purity upgrade upon direct crystallisation and isolation"

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: The previously reported fluorination of a 6‑chloro‑2‑amino‑purine using concentrated HF/pyridine generates hazardous HF waste, requires isolation as an HF salt, and suffers from over‑fluorination at C‑6 that reduces overall yield.
Solution_Description: A benign nucleophilic fluorination was developed using inexpensive KF as the fluoride source together with trimethylamine (TMA) as a catalytic nucleophilic promoter, eliminating the need for HF and allowing the reaction to run at ambient temperature with high selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
"… this approach was developed into an operationally safe synthesis by our colleagues using flow chemistry. However, this route poses environmental and safety concerns for handling concentrated HF, the isolation of 3 as its HF salt, as well as quenching highly concentrated HF waste streams."
"… the use of HF in pyridine … over‑fluorination at C‑6 … compromises the yield significantly."
"Implementation of a nucleophilic catalyst to enable safe, benign fluorinations with potassium fluoride."
"The dual fluorination/amination proceeds … at ambient temperature!"

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: Direct amination of the 6‑chloro‑2‑fluoropurine with ammonia gave poor conversions and regio‑selectivity; elevated temperatures regenerated the C‑2‑amino group and produced over‑amination (2,6‑diaminopurine). Masked amines and hexamine also generated low‑level by‑product 4 and lacked a crystalline intermediate for purification.
Solution_Description: Hexamine was employed as an ammonia equivalent, providing >30:1 C‑6 regio‑selectivity. Masked amines (e.g., 2,4‑dimethoxybenzylamine) formed crystalline adducts that allowed facile removal of the minor C‑2 regio‑isomer by crystallisation, delivering the desired product in high isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Direct amination with ammonia was found to suffer from poor reactivities and regioselectivities."
"Elevated reaction temperatures led to regeneration of 6 … over‑amination to give 4."
"Hexamine is a readily available reagent widely used as an ammonia equivalent."
"Direct amination with hexamine in THF at room temperature provided >30:1 regioselectivity for C‑6 amination… still generated 4 at low levels (1–2 mol %)."
"Masked amines … minor undesired regioisomer … could be easily removed via crystallisation, and the desired C‑6‑regioisomer could be directly isolated."

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: Anhydrous tetramethylammonium fluoride (TMAF) needed for the dual fluorination is expensive, extremely hygroscopic, and difficult to source in anhydrous form; the tetrahydrate is inactive, creating handling and safety challenges on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Trimethylamine (TMA) gas was used as the catalytic promoter. It was introduced directly into the reactor via a mass‑flow controller (or pressure‑rated gas‑charging) into sealed vessels, avoiding the need for solid TMAF and simplifying handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
"… anhydrous tetramethylammonium fluoride (TMAF) … is expensive to source on manufacturing scale, and TMAF tetrahydrate is notoriously difficult to dehydrate. Anhydrous TMAF is also extremely hygroscopic…"
"The strong stench and low boiling point (3–7 °C) of TMA posed an initial practical challenge for handling and accurate charging…"
"Direct charging of TMA with the appropriate equipment was found to be the most reliable approach. On a developmental scale, a mass flow controller was suitable for charging TMA as a gas into pressure‑rated vessels."
"TMA is highly soluble in DMF … a gastight seal was necessary to avoid leaching TMA from the vessel over extended times…"

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: Dual fluorination performance was inconsistent; batches of KF with low specific surface area (SSA) stalled after the first fluorination, leading to impurity buildup and reaction failure, while high‑SSA KF performed well. Particle‑size distribution alone did not correlate with activity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: KF lots were screened and only those with SSA > 0.2 m² g⁻¹ were used. For low‑SSA KF, 18‑crown‑6 was added to increase the effective fluoride concentration at the solid–liquid interface, rescuing the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
"… the specific surface area (SSA) … lots of KF with SSA > 0.2 m² g⁻¹ were effective … lower SSA exhibited reaction failure."
"Intriguingly, it was found that lots of KF with low SSA could be rescued by additives such as 18‑crown‑6 ether to perform the dual fluorination."
"These observations suggested that … the additive is thought to potentially increase the concentration of solubilised fluoride …"

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Route to 2‑Fluoroadenine, The Key Unnatural Nucleobase of Islatravir
Problem_Description: Final 2‑fluoroadenine produced a very fine particle slurry in water, giving a thick, poorly filterable mixture that hindered isolation.
Solution_Description: A cosolvent (acetonitrile or ethanol) was introduced into the aqueous system to generate a homogeneous solution; controlled addition of water seeded crystallisation to afford either the hydrate or anhydrous form, enabling efficient filtration and isolation.

Solution_Description: The cyclization was switched to the bench‑stable 2‑chloro‑1,3‑bis(dimethylamino)‑trimethinium hexafluorophosphate salt (20‑PF₆). The reaction proceeded at 75 °C (well below the decomposition temperature of 18) and gave clean product without safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “DSC analysis of 3‑dimethylaminoacrolein (18) showed a major decomposition at 156 °C with release of 500 kJ kg⁻¹ energy.”
• “The compound could be sourced only in small quantities as a dark brown oil with low assay purity, and no reliable commercial sources for kilogram amounts could be established.”
• “We found 2‑chloro‑1,3‑bis(dimethylamino)‑trimethinium hexafluorophosphate … a suitable candidate … the cyclization already took place at 75 °C and was finished within 4 h.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Highly Polar Heterocyclic Aminocyclopropyl Building Block
Problem_Description: The hydrogenation of chloropyrimidine 21 required a catalyst capable of simultaneous Cbz deprotection and de‑chlorination without over‑reducing the pyrimidine ring; many catalysts gave high levels of the over‑reduced impurity 22, and the highly polar final product was difficult to isolate.
Solution_Description: A 20 % Pd(OH)₂/C Pearlman catalyst combined with 3 equiv NaOMe in MeOH at 1 bar H₂ gave >99 % conversion and kept impurity 22 below 1.2 % a/a. Optimization of base strength and equivalents proved crucial to suppress over‑reduction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The major challenges … were to find a catalyst that promoted the simultaneous Cbz deprotection and hydro‑dechlorination … while showing no activity toward over‑reducing the pyrimidine ring.”
• “The most efficient catalyst was found to be a Pearlman‑type 20 % Pd(OH)₂/C catalyst … using 3.0 equiv of NaOMe in MeOH … full conversion … while keeping impurity 22 below 1.5 % a/a.”
• Table 1 entries showing base effects and over‑reduction levels.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Highly Polar Heterocyclic Aminocyclopropyl Building Block
Problem_Description: Initial isolation of the final hydrochloride (1‑HCl) gave apparent yields >100 % due to residual NaCl, resulting in low w/w purity of the product.
Solution_Description: After hydrogenation, the mixture was acidified with 5 M HCl in iPrOH, then iPrOH (5 vol) was added to precipitate NaCl, which was removed by filtration together with the catalyst. The filtrate was solvent‑switched to THF and the product crystallized, giving 90–95 % isolated yield and >99 % a/a purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “It was found that the yield was constantly exceeding 100 % (110–120 %) and the isolated product had a low w/w purity. Ion chromatography analysis showed … high levels of NaCl (up to 20 % w/w).”
• “After complete conversion, the reaction mixture was quenched with 5 M HCl in iPrOH … followed by the addition of iPrOH (5 vol) to lower the solubility of NaCl and to remove it to a higher extent during filtration of the catalyst.”
• “The desired product was isolated after crystallization from THF as an off‑white solid in high yields (90–95 %) and with good HPLC (99 % a/a) and NMR assay purity (96–97 % w/w).”

Paper Title: Process Development of Sotagliflozin, a Dual Inhibitor of Sodium–Glucose Cotransporter-1/2 for the Treatment of Diabetes
Problem_Description: The first medicinal‑chemistry route required protection of l‑xylose, selective de‑protection, oxidation of a primary alcohol to aldehyde 3 and coupling with an aryl‑lithium reagent. The aryl‑lithium had to be prepared under cryogenic conditions and the aldehyde was unstable, giving poor diastereoselectivity (dr 9/1) and a low overall yield (≈12 %). Moreover, the use of corrosive HBr and hazardous bromine in later steps raised safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A hybrid process‑chemistry route was designed that starts from inexpensive l‑xylose, replaces the cryogenic aryl‑lithium with the corresponding aryl‑Grignard reagent, and eliminates the use of HBr and bromine. The new sequence is shorter (10 linear steps) and gives an overall yield of ≈40 % with improved safety and cost profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the initial medicinal chemistry synthetic route … required protection of l‑xylose … poor diastereoselectivity … oxidized to aldehyde 3 … cryogenic conditions required for preparing and handling aryl lithium … the use of corrosive HBr.”; “Using l‑xylose as the starting material … Substituting 4‑Li with the corresponding aryl Grignard reagent … to avoid cryogenic conditions.”

Paper Title: Toward the Scale-Up of a Bicyclic Homopiperazine via Schmidt Rearrangement and Photochemical Oxaziridine Rearrangement in Continuous-Flow
Problem_Description: Batch Schmidt rearrangement of bicyclic ketone 2a gave low overall isolated yields (10‑30 %) and poor selectivity for the desired lactam 3a (3a : 4a ratios close to 1 : 1), required long reaction times (2.5–4 h) and a lengthy (≈2 h) neutralisation of concentrated acid, and involved handling of hazardous hydrazoic acid generated in‑situ.
Solution_Description: Conversion to a continuous‑flow micro‑reactor using a MsOH‑DME / tetrabutylammonium azide (TBAA) system. The reactor was operated at 80 °C with controlled residence times (5–9 min) and a dilute (85 % wt) H₂SO₄/DME mixture to lower viscosity. Flow‑rate adjustments provided the required acid concentration while keeping the reaction volume small, thus improving safety, reducing reaction time and giving higher conversion (up to 40 % isolated lactam 3a) with comparable selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “Accurate control of the reaction time was challenging, as quenching the reaction required a lengthy (2 h) neutralisation of the concentrated acid solvent.”
• “We envisaged that the microreactor system using MsOH–DME in combination with tetrabutylammonium azide (TBAA) … could provide a practical way to overcome these issues.”
• “With a similar microreactor … under the optimized conditions (0.20 M ketone, 0.27 M TBAA, 67 % MsOH; t_R = 5 min, 80 °C), … gave a higher conversion …”
• “When concentrated acids were used, strong magnetic stirring was required to ensure efficient mixing.”
• “Increasing the acid concentration … significantly improved the reaction conversions and overall yields.”

Problem_Description: Generation of hydrazoic acid (HN₃) in batch reactors poses a severe safety risk because HN₃ is a toxic, volatile, explosive gas; large volumes of concentrated acid are also hazardous.

Solution_Description: The Schmidt step was performed in a sealed continuous‑flow micro‑reactor submerged in a water bath containing 5 % NaHCO₃; any leak would be immediately identified by gas evolution. The out‑flow was quenched into 2 M NaOH/ice, and the whole setup was operated behind a blast shield, limiting the amount of HN₃ present at any time and greatly improving the safety profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Hydrazoic acid is a toxic, volatile gas with explosive properties, and as such, its generation on scale in batch reactors must be carefully controlled.”
• “During operation, the micromixer and reactor were submerged in water baths containing 5 wt % NaHCO₃… any leak in the system could be quickly identified by the evolution of gas.”
• “Excess HN₃ in the outflow stream was neutralized upon collection into a vessel containing 2 M NaOH/ice (1:1), and operation of the microreactor was carried out behind a blast shield.”
• “Our reaction‑scale limit was set such that … the concentration within the laboratory could not reach predefined limits.”

Paper Title: Toward the Scale-Up of a Bicyclic Homopiperazine via Schmidt Rearrangement and Photochemical Oxaziridine Rearrangement in Continuous-Flow

Solution_Description: The authors turned to the photochemical oxaziridine rearrangement (Lattes–Aubé chemistry). Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: The Curtius‑type nitrene rearrangement required diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA).  ReactIR showed a buildup of acyl‑azide 4 before heating, which presented a significant safety risk on scale and generated degradative by‑products (carbamate 7, cyclobutenone 8, urea 9) leading to low isolated yields and limited batch size (~60 kg).
Solution_Description: The order of addition was changed – DPPA was added to a pre‑heated acid solution at 55 °C, eliminating the acyl‑azide buildup and improving safety.  In parallel the process was switched to a Lossen rearrangement (new route) that uses 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) instead of DPPA, removing the hazardous azide and giving clean conversion to the amine phosphate 17.  The solvent system was adjusted (2‑MeTHF/THF) to accommodate the new reagents and improve material handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Yield loss in this process occurred by known degradative pathways… including the formation of carbamate 7 and volatile cyclobutenone 8… and the subsequent reaction of 7 and 5 to form urea byproduct 9.”
• “ReactIR studies detected a buildup of 4 prior to heating… The most reproducible method for this reaction was to add DPPA to a pre‑heated solution of the acid at 55 °C, which showed little to no buildup of the acyl azide.”
• “Because of the significant safety risk associated with the potential buildup of 4, the batch size was limited on scale (∼60 kg of 3).”
• “The Lossen rearrangement… 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) emerged as effective at promoting the rearrangement while minimizing by‑product generation.”
• “Acidic hydrolysis was required to avoid urea formation, and a screen revealed that phosphoric acid was much more efficient than other mineral acids.”

Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: The sulfonylation of the amine phosphate 17 was problematic because the intermediate is poorly soluble in organic solvents, highly soluble in aqueous media and forms heterogeneous slurries with residual phosphate salts; use of propane‑1‑sulfonyl chloride (14) gave side‑reaction on the heterocyclic core and required very low temperatures that caused freezing of the aqueous phase, limiting scalability.
Solution_Description: A novel 1,2,4‑triazole sulfonylating reagent (21) was developed.  It is stable in aqueous/THF mixtures, reacts rapidly, and tolerates the phosphate salt, allowing the sulfonylation to be performed at ambient temperature without freezing.  The reaction is run as a biphasic THF‑water system; addition of the triazole reagent as a THF solution followed by water induces crystallisation of the API in 84 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Sulfonylation of amine 17 … poor solubility in organic solvents, high solubility in acidic or basic aqueous solutions, reactive heterocyclic core, and reaction heterogeneity due to complications with residual phosphate salts.”
• “The sulfonylation may be conducted in basic aqueous media using 14, but this also results in sulfonylation of the pyrrolopyridimine nitrogen … scalability was limited because of the risk of freezing of aqueous media at very low temperatures.”
• “1,2,4‑Triazole derivative 21 emerged as the lead sulfonylating agent on the basis of its excellent stability in aqueous systems, fast reaction kinetics, and an acceptable safety profile.”
• “After salt break of 17 in THF with NaOH, 21 could be added as a solution in THF. Addition of water resulted in crystallization of the product 1 in 84 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: The Hofmann rearrangement was explored as an alternative nitrene pathway but the I(III) oxidant was incompatible with the electron‑rich pyrrolopyrimidine, causing rapid oxidative degradation.  Moreover, protecting‑group strategies were required, which increased the process mass intensity and reagent cost.
Solution_Description: The Hofmann route was abandoned in favour of a Lossen rearrangement that proceeds without protecting‑group manipulations and uses less‑reactive dehydrative reagents (CDI).  This new route reduces PMI and cost, and avoids oxidative decomposition of the heterocycle.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Incompatibility of the I³⁺ oxidant with the electron‑rich pyrrolopyrimidine required prudent selection of reagents, protecting‑group strategies, and reaction conditions.”
• “Protection of the pyrrolo nitrogen was found to be critical … otherwise rapid oxidative degradation was observed.”
• “While this route was viable, we did not pursue this approach because of the increased process mass intensity resulting from the required use of protecting groups.”
• “The Lossen reaction requires less reactive reagents … would be more compatible with the unprotected pyrrolopyrimidine.”

Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: The target cis‑1,3‑diaminocyclobutane intermediate displayed pH‑dependent solubility, volatility and analytical difficulty, complicating isolation and scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A biocatalytic reductive amination using an engineered SpRedAm enzyme was employed on ketone 18 to give the cis‑amino ester 19 in 74 % yield with >99:1 d.r. after crystallisation as the succinate salt.  This enzymatic step provided a convergent, protecting‑group‑free route to the cyclobutane core, improving solubility handling and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Ketone 18 was screened for biocatalytic reductive amination. Several mutant libraries … resulted in a suitable enzyme that provided the desired cis‑amino ester 19 in 74 % yield with a >99:1 diastereomeric ratio after isolation as the succinate salt.”
• “The discovery route employed tosylated pyrrolopyrimidine 11 … While this worked well with amine 19, the tosyl protecting group was incompatible with the hydroxylamine required to generate the Lossen reaction precursor.”
• “Unprotected pyrrolopyrimidine 2 was competent for the SNAr reaction with an extended reaction time.”

Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: Alternative sulfonylating reagents (22, 23, 25) exhibited safety hazards (exothermic decomposition, potential reactor etching) and, for reagent 25, a high purchase price that would be prohibitive without a recycle strategy.
Solution_Description: A systematic screening eliminated unsafe or costly reagents, selecting triazole reagent 21 as the optimal sulfonyl transfer agent.  Its stability, lower cost and acceptable safety profile allowed scale‑up without the need for recycling expensive reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Combination of safety concerns and undesirable reactivity eliminated 22 and 23.”
• “Cost of purchasing large quantities of the reagent would necessitate developing a method to recover and recycle the reagent.”
• “1,2,4‑Triazole derivative 21 emerged as the lead sulfonylating agent on the basis of its excellent stability in aqueous systems, fast reaction kinetics, and an acceptable safety profile.”

Paper Title: Development of a Nitrene-Type Rearrangement for the Commercial Route of the JAK1 Inhibitor Abrocitinib
Problem_Description: Using propane‑1‑sulfonyl chloride (14) for sulfonylation required very low temperatures; at these temperatures the aqueous phase tended to freeze, creating a heterogeneous mixture that limited scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was raised to ambient conditions by employing the more stable triazole sulfonylating reagent 21 in a THF‑water biphasic system, avoiding freezing and improving mixing and heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The sulfonylation may be conducted in basic aqueous media using 14, but … scalability was limited because of the risk of freezing of aqueous media at very low temperatures.”
• “The sulfonylation may be conducted in basic aqueous media … This was more successful at low temperature, but the scalability was limited because of the risk of freezing …”
• “Addition of water resulted in crystallization of the product 1 in 84 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: The first‑generation cyclization using trifluoromethane‑sulfonic anhydride gave a 1:9 mixture of the desired amino‑1,3‑oxazine (3) and the undesired amino‑1,3‑thiazine (4).  The target oxazine had to be isolated by chromatographic separation, which is labour‑intensive and reduces overall material throughput.
Solution_Description: A new cyclization protocol employing trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) and DMSO was developed.  The reagents were added dropwise at low temperature (≤12 °C) and the reaction completed in the time of the addition, giving clean, selective formation of the oxazine with no detectable thiazine.  This avoids the chromatographic work‑up required previously.
Supporting_Evidence: “trifluoromethane sulfonic anhydride was used to cyclize thiourea 2, affording a 1:9 mixture of amino‑1,3‑oxazine 3 and amino‑1,3‑thiazine 4, respectively, which required chromatographic separation to isolate 3.”; “Armed with this finding, … the desired amino‑1,3‑oxazine (3) was formed cleanly and rapidly with no trace of the corresponding amino‑1,3‑thiazine (4).”; “TMSCl … was added dropwise at rate ∼1 mL min⁻¹, maintaining the internal temperature below 12 °C.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: The earlier laboratory route to the oxazine used cyanogen bromide, a highly toxic reagent that can release hydrogen cyanide, making it unsuitable for multihundred‑gram scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The toxic cyanogen bromide step was replaced by the TMSCl/DMSO protocol, which uses inexpensive, commercially‑available reagents and avoids the handling of cyanogen bromide, thereby greatly improving safety for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “the unprotected amino‑1,3‑oxazine was formed … using cyanogen bromide … was of concern for larger‑scale work because of its highly toxic nature and potential to liberate hydrogen cyanide.”; “it was possible to form the thiourea in situ … and the cyclization to be performed in a 2‑step, 1‑pot manner at >500 g scale … affording 3 in a 96 % yield.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: When the reaction was applied to a broader set of thioureas, some substrates did not reach full conversion and gave lower isolated yields, especially when only a single equivalent of HCl was employed, leading to incomplete reactions and formation of side‑products.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of hydrochloric acid (up to 10 equiv) and, where appropriate, adding TMSCl restored full conversion.  Adjusting the stoichiometry of the acid and silane reagents was sufficient to drive the reaction to completion for the problematic substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction did not reach full conversion… It was possible that the formation … was mediated by adventitious HCl… an increase in conversion was observed and increasing the number of equivalents of HCl rendered these reactions essentially complete, although several unidentified byproducts were formed.”; “Entry 3 … 10.0 equiv HCl gave 98:2 conversion.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: The cyclization failed completely when DMSO was omitted, indicating that the reaction mixture could not proceed in the chosen solvent system without a suitable co‑solvent to solubilise the reagents and intermediate.
Solution_Description: Inclusion of 1.2 equiv of DMSO was identified as essential; the solvent change provides the necessary solvation and phase behavior to allow the TMSCl‑mediated activation and subsequent cyclization to occur.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction was repeated using 2 equiv of HCl, but no DMSO. DMSO was found to be vital for the successful cyclization of the thiourea as without it the reaction failed to proceed showing only the presence of thiourea 27a.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: The original method required chromatographic purification of the oxazine, which is cumbersome and costly at large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A scalable work‑up was developed that uses aqueous quench, liquid‑liquid extraction, Celite filtration and a short silica gel flash column (or, where possible, direct filtration), minimizing chromatographic steps and simplifying product isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The precipitation of sulfur … the mixture was filtered through Celite, the organic layer was washed, extracted, and the residue was filtered … to afford a brown solid.”; “The reaction was fast … produced no observed exothermic events.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of highly exothermic reactions can pose safety hazards; the authors needed to ensure the new cyclization did not generate dangerous heat releases.
Solution_Description: TMSCl was added dropwise under a water/ice bath while keeping the internal temperature below 12 °C.  Small‑scale trials showed the reaction completed at the end of addition with no measurable exotherm, confirming safe scalability.
Supporting_Evidence: “TMSCl … was added dropwise at rate ∼1 mL min⁻¹, maintaining the internal temperature below 12 °C.”; “the reaction was fast, … produced no observed exothermic events.”

Paper Title: Efficient Method for the Synthesis of Amino-1,3-Oxazines from Thioureas
Problem_Description: The EDC·HCl cyclization method suffers from functional‑group incompatibility (e.g., carboxylic acids) that consumes the coupling agent and reduces product yield.
Solution_Description: The TMSCl/DMSO protocol tolerates a wide range of functional groups, as demonstrated by the robustness screening; thus it provides a complementary, more generally applicable route that avoids the reagent consumption issue observed with EDC·HCl.
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield using EDC·HCl conditions was dramatically reduced in the presence of 3‑phenyl propionic acid … activation of carboxylic acid by EDC was consuming the reagent.”; “the majority of the additives do not significantly affect the yield of the desired amino‑1,3‑oxazine 28a … both methods show a high level of functional‑group robustness.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow
Design of a Kilogram Scale, Plug Flow Photoreactor Enabled by High Power LEDs
Problem_Description: The first-generation kilogram‑scale photoreactor occupied ~1.2 m³ and suffered from low photon density, resulting in modest conversion and limited productivity. The long, narrow (3.18 mm ID) tubing (0.4 km total length) also restricted flow rates to ≤0.6 L min⁻¹ because of excessive pressure drop, making scale‑out impractical.
Solution_Description: The team replaced the bulky system with a compact 5.5‑gal aquarium reactor fitted with high‑power 100 W LED chips (440 nm, 6.29 W cm⁻²) mounted on an aluminum heat‑sink that incorporates a copper water‑cooled coil. This design drastically reduces the footprint while delivering much higher light intensity and controlled reactor temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "the original unit was approximately 1.2 m³, rendering it difficult to use in a numbering‑up strategy and leaving little room to increase the size of the reactor."; "low light density due to the light source"; "the long length of the reactor tubing (0.4 km)... limits its operation to flow rates below 0.6 L/min to avoid excessively high pressure drops."; "low light density"; "narrow tubing limits photon absorption without the use of an unnecessarily high loading of photocatalyst."

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Use of dichloromethane (DCM) throughout the early‑phase route posed a safety and analytical risk because DCM reacts with tertiary amines to form chloromethylammonium species that are difficult to quantify at low levels.
Solution_Description: The authors eliminated DCM from the process and replaced it with safer, non‑chlorinated solvents (toluene, EtOAc, MeCN, PhCH₃) while redesigning the purification strategy to rely on salt formation and crystallization rather than preparative chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Although it presents a critical analytical risk since it can react with tertiary amines to form chloromethylammoniums, which are challenging to quantitate at low levels in the absence of a UV chromophore.", "Therefore, as we set out to design a scalable synthetic route, we immediately made two choices. First, we would eliminate the use of DCM in all chemistry throughout the sequence.", "The chromatography‑free route developed to access 1 and 2 on kilogram scale… All DCM was removed from the process and all intermediates are now isolable, crystalline solids."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: The original routes relied heavily on preparative chromatography for isolation of intermediates and final cationic lipids, which is impractical at kilogram scale for excipient‑level production.
Solution_Description: A reverse‑development strategy was employed: physical‑property‑guided salt screening enabled isolation of every intermediate as a crystalline salt, removing the need for any chromatographic step.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A literature review demonstrates that preparative chromatography is the preferred method of purification, save for a few limited examples of isolations by precipitation.", "We wondered if we could employ a similar strategy throughout the synthesis and include salt formation steps in each isolation. This could provide access to crystalline intermediates and a more ‘traditional’ small‑molecule pharmaceutical process—one devoid of chromatography.", "All DCM was removed from the process and all intermediates are now isolable, crystalline solids."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Intermediate 9 (low‑melting solid) showed very poor solubility, making direct crystallization impossible.
Solution_Description: Salt screening identified the methanesulfonic acid (MSA) salt of the secondary amine 3, which crystallized readily. A 6:1 mixture of toluene (PhCH₃) and EtOAc provided optimal solubility and allowed efficient isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Solubility screening of the low‑melting solid 9 suggested that isolation by crystallization was not viable.", "Focus on the methanesulfonic and hydrochloric acid salts of 3 revealed several choices for the crystallization. … Testing MSA and HCl in the Boc deprotection of 9 revealed that MSA gave the best balance of reactivity and physical properties.", "Balancing reaction solvent choice against salt selectivity revealed that a 6:1 ratio of PhCH₃ and EtOAc would provide optimal results in terms of reactivity and isolation."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Phase‑transfer‑catalyzed acylation of diol 4 with myristoyl chloride generated emulsions that were difficult to stir and caused inconsistent yields on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction was switched to a single‑phase, Brønsted‑base‑promoted acylation using N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) in toluene, and the work‑up was changed to an acetic‑acid/NaCl wash, eliminating emulsion formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initial attempts to develop a phase transfer catalyzed acylation … showed excellent reactivity … however, despite extensive optimization of base, solvent, and phase transfer catalyst, mixing dependent formations of emulsions remained a significant risk.", "This strategy was abandoned in favor of a single‑phase, Brønsted base promoted acylation. Evaluation of solvents revealed toluene (PhCH₃) to be a good choice that would facilitate interface with the Boc deprotection and avoid a solvent swap.", "Switching from an HCl wash to an acetic acid wash containing sodium chloride solved issues related to emulsion formation during aqueous workup."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Rapid cooling of the 3‑MSA crystallization led to supersaturation buildup, causing uncontrolled nucleation and large variations in filtration flux (100‑4000 L·m⁻²·h⁻¹).
Solution_Description: A nonlinear cooling profile was implemented, where temperature segments with rapid solubility changes were traversed slowly (inverse to solubility), keeping supersaturation low and producing consistent powder properties with reduced cycle times.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Early experiments revealed that these powder property changes stemmed from supersaturation buildup during rapid cooling, ultimately inducing uncontrolled nucleation events.", "Maintaining low supersaturation was key to reproducing the desired performance during scale‑up. This could be achieved with a linear cool down … This operation, while simplest, is limited to only the initial, slowest cooling rate and therefore requires considerable time. Alternatively, the slurry could be cooled in a nonlinear fashion, where T segments with rapid S changes would be traversed over prolonged times … This mode of operation leads to low degrees of supersaturation throughout the crystallization, consistent powder properties across scales, and reduced cycle times."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: The final quaternary ammonium formation for lipid 1 required a large excess of bromoethanol, high temperature and prolonged reaction times (≥24 h) to reach full conversion.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified MeCN (and EtOAc/MeCN mixtures) that allowed the reaction to proceed efficiently with only 2.2 equiv of bromoethanol, reducing the temperature and overall reaction time while maintaining high yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The existing cooling crystallization from EtOAc performed well … however, the reaction conditions used a significant excess of bromoethanol to drive high conversions and, even then, full conversion required high temperatures and prolonged reaction times.", "A brief solvent screen targeting significantly lower amounts of bromoethanol… revealed that MeCN was a good option even when using as low as 2.2 equivalents of bromoethanol (entry 4).", "The overall solution volume was adjusted … 3:2 EtOAc:MeCN v‑v. The solution was heated to 70 °C for 24 h or until >97 % conversion was observed."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Impurity 14 formed in the synthesis of lipid 2 due to excess chloroacetyl chloride and the very low solubility of thiol 12 in EtOAc, leading to variable impurity levels (up to 4 % LCAP).
Solution_Description: DoE identified that increasing MeCN content and preparing thiol 12 as a 2 wt % water‑containing MeCN solution improved its solubility. A slow, reverse addition of the EtOAc solution of chloroacetyl chloride into the thiol solution suppressed impurity 14 formation. Final crystallization incorporating PhCH₃ (high impurity solubility) enabled >80 % purge.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The most obvious factor observed … was volume percent MeCN in EtOAc. Increasing the percentage of MeCN (Pct_MeCN) suppressed the formation of impurity 14.", "If the thiol 12 had poor solubility … its concentration would remain low … this could then favor the formation of impurity 14.", "To maximize the solubility of the thiol 12, we prepared it as a solution in MeCN containing 2 wt % water. … we performed a slow reverse addition of the EtOAc solution of 11 into the solution of the thiol in wet MeCN.", "PhCH₃ was included as a third solvent in the crystallization … impurity 14 has a relatively high solubility in PhCH₃ compared to 2‑oxalate, and crystallization in a mixture of EtOAc and PhCH₃ offered >80 % purge."]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Large‑scale distillation of TFA prior to crystallization of 3‑TFA posed safety and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: The route was redesigned to use the MSA salt of the secondary amine (3‑MSA) as the key intermediate, eliminating the need for TFA distillation and allowing direct crystallization from toluene/EtOAc.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The use of DCM as well as the need for distillation of significant quantities of TFA prior to crystallization of 3‑TFA were immediately identified as issues for scalability.", "Testing MSA and HCl … MSA gave the best balance of reactivity and physical properties.", "The MSA salt solvate … had better physical properties… the operation … required considerable time. Alternatively, … nonlinear cool down … led to low degrees of supersaturation …"]

Paper Title: Crystallizing Fats? Development of a Scalable, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of Cationic Lipids
Problem_Description: Impurity profiling using ELSD gave inconsistent results compared with CAD, leading to variability in impurity assessment.
Solution_Description: The analytical method was switched to a charged aerosol detector (CAD), which provided a wider linear range and more reproducible impurity quantification across instruments and labs.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initially, impurity analysis was performed using a high‑performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with an evaporative light scattering detector (ELSD). The results were slightly variable, from run to run, and there were few impurities detected. However, when the same samples were analyzed using a charged aerosol detector (CAD) additional impurities were seen.", "We hypothesized that differences in the ability of lipids to aerosolize and charge (CAD) versus aerosolize and dry to solid particles (ELSD) were responsible for the observed inconsistencies.", "The use of the CAD resulted in a more reproducible assessment of the amount of impurities in each sample and upon optimization; the method became applicable across multiple instruments and when transferred to additional analytical labs."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: The commercial 2‑fluorobenzyl bromide (2) contained up to 4 % of the 3‑fluoro isomer, which proved difficult to purge in downstream steps and caused variable impurity levels in the O‑alkylation product (4).
Solution_Description: A simple precipitation work‑up was introduced: after concentration the reaction mixture was treated with 2 % aqueous NaOH, filtered and washed with water to give the ether 4 in >99.4 % purity and ≤0.2 % 3‑fluoro impurity, eliminating the need for hexane and reducing the cycle time.
Supporting_Evidence:
The key issue for Step 1, O‑alkylation of 4‑bromophenol 3 using commercially available 2‑fluorobenzyl bromide 2, was the purity of 2. Commercial supplies of 2 contained no more than 0.1 % of the 4‑fluoro isomer, but up to 4 % of the 3‑fluoro isomer, and fate and purge studies demonstrated poor purge of the isomeric 3‑fluoro‑impurities in the downstream process.
A simple precipitation method was developed for the isolation of ether 4, which reduced the Step 1 cycle time, and avoided the use of hexane, which was used in the medicinal chemistry process.
The Step 1 reaction mixture filtrate was concentrated and the product precipitated by addition of 2 % aqueous NaOH. Filtration followed by washing of the filter cake with water afforded 4 in high yield and purity.
With these improvements, pilot‑plant‑scale batches were run, furnishing up to 58 kg of 4 in 91 % yield as a white solid of >99.4 % purity, with the level of the 3‑fluoro isomer below 0.2 %.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: During the Grignard addition (Step 2) significant benzyne‑derived impurities (10, 11) and a homocoupled impurity (12) were formed, giving modest isolated yields (∼53 %) and making downstream purge difficult.
Solution_Description: The addition order was switched to add the Grignard reagent to a –55 °C solution of the chiral pyrrolidinone ester (5) rather than the reverse, THF was retained as the solvent, and a ternary solvent system (ethyl acetate/IPA/hexane 2:2:6) was used for precipitation of the ketone 6, lowering the benzyne impurity 10 to <4 % and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
The major issues associated with the Grignard reagent generated from 4 relate to the formation of significant levels of impurities. Among the impurities are 10 and 11, which appear to be formed via Grignard addition to a benzyne impurity intermediate… The benzyne‑derived impurities 10 and 11 are difficult to purge at Step 2 and are carried through the route to related impurities in the final API step.
Addition of the Grignard reagent derived from 4 to a −55 °C solution of 5 was preferred to the reverse addition of 5 to the similarly cooled Grignard reagent.
The isolation procedure for ketone 6 was also evaluated. An extensive screening of solvents for precipitation and isolation resulted in identification of a ternary mixture of ethyl acetate/IPA/hexane 2:2:6. This solvent system provided the most effective purge of the major benzyne impurity 10 to below 4 %.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: The Boc‑deprotection (Step 3) employed TFA in dichloromethane, generating an emulsion during neutralisation and required up to 19 h of neutralisation with large volumes of hazardous solvents.
Solution_Description: Neutralisation was performed with aqueous KHCO₃ to pH 6‑7, eliminating the emulsion, and heptane replaced hexane as a safer antisolvent, reducing solvent hazards and simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
The Step 3 acid‑catalyzed removal of the Boc protecting group with TFA in dichloromethane (DCM) resulted in cyclization to the pyrrolidine imine 7… The remaining issues for pilot plant operation of Route 1 were the prolonged neutralization time (up to 19 h to maintain the vessel temperature below 10 °C and control effervescence) and the requirement of large volumes of TFA and DCM, which were undesirable from a safety and environmental perspective.
Neutralization with aqueous KHCO₃ to pH 6.0‑7.0 eliminated the emulsion and maintained the chemical yield above 80 %, while heptane performed well as an antisolvent.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the imine (Step 4) gave variable stereoselectivity (5‑10 % trans‑diastereomer 13) and formed hydrogenolysis by‑products (14, 15), reducing the effective yield of the desired stereoisomer.
Solution_Description: Screening of catalysts showed that 5 % Pt/C under 50‑60 psi H₂ in ethyl acetate/TFA gave high chemical yields (95‑97 %) though stereoselectivity remained marginal; later, the use of 5 % Pd/C type 487 in methanol in Route 2 achieved >30:1 cis/trans selectivity, substantially suppressing the trans impurity.
Supporting_Evidence:
Detailed evaluation of the Step 4 hydrogenation was conducted to increase its chemo‑ and stereoselectivity… The reduction of the imine was prone to high and variable levels (5‑10 %) of the (5S) trans‑diastereomer 13.
Replacing Pt/C with Pd/C resulted in much higher levels of the hydrogenolysis products 14 and 15… A selection of different grades of 5 % Pt/C was screened under standard conditions with only minor effects on the yield and level of trans‑isomer 13.
With 5 % Pd/C type 487 paste, a cis‑/trans‑selectivity of >30:1 was achieved in methanol in the Route 2 process, minimizing the level of trans‑isomer 34 formed.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: Overall Route 1 suffered from a low overall yield (~18 %), a high purification burden due to benzyne‑derived impurities, and variable API colour that required dye‑masking in the drug product.
Solution_Description: Route 2 was designed with a later introduction of the 2‑fluorobenzyl group, an O‑benzyl protecting group to avoid benzyne formation, and solvent/antisolvent changes (MTBE/heptane, EtOAc/heptane) that improved yields (∼40 %) and gave a white API without colour issues.
Supporting_Evidence: Route 1 … had several drawbacks that precluded its use for later‑stage development and commercialization… The yield of the Grignard addition reaction (Step 2) was poor… Benzyne‑derived impurities 10 and 11 … led to a high burden for purification in the later steps… The appearance of the final, isolated API was variable, with respect to colour… Route 2 was developed… The key advantage of the use of the benzyl protecting group was the ability … to reduce the benzyne‑derived impurities… The improved process eliminated the possibility of the formation of these impurities, substantially improved the stereoselectivity… and gave a pilot plant process with significantly enhanced yield and throughput.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: Step 5 of Route 1 used aqueous phosphoric acid (85 % aq) in MTBE, generating large volumes of inorganic salts and requiring long work‑up times, giving the free base as an oil with poor plant productivity.
Solution_Description: The deprotection was switched to p‑TsOH in methanol, allowing direct formation of the p‑TsOH salt of the intermediate (25) with higher yields (92 %), fewer salts, and a simpler work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
In Step 5 of the first campaign run using the Route 2 process, deprotection of the Boc group of 24 used aqueous phosphoric acid (85 % aq) in MTBE… the processing involved relatively large work‑up volumes, generated significant amounts of inorganic salts… and gave the free base as an oil after stripping to dryness, with poor plant volume productivity.
Studies of the best acid and solvent combination resulted in the selection of p‑TsOH in methanol as the procedure used for future campaigns.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 1: Development of Bulk Supply Routes to Enable Proof of Concept
Problem_Description: The final API HCl salt (1) formed an ethanol solvate that required prolonged drying and yielded a product with variable colour and particle size, necessitating colour‑masking and fine‑tuning of the drying process.
Solution_Description: An alternative salt‑formation process using IPA as antisolvent and a steeper temperature ramp with intensive agitation reduced drying time, increased bulk density, and produced a consistent particle‑size distribution, eliminating the need for colour masking.
Supporting_Evidence:
The final, isolated API was colored (yellow/brown), which required that the variability in colour of the API within the drug product be masked with a special dye coating.
An alternative process was therefore developed for campaigns 4 and 5 in which the free base 9 in IPA solution at 60–65 °C was treated with aqueous HCl and then cooled to 0–5 °C… This second process gave a product that dried more rapidly, with a higher bulk density and a d₅₀ measurement in the required range of 50–100 µm.
Following a reassessment of the PSD requirement, campaign 6 reverted to the process run in ethanol solvent, giving four batches with d₅₀ measurements in the 15–20 µm range. The drying times for these batches were significantly reduced by a steeper temperature ramp and more intensive agitation in the Nutsche filter dryer.

Paper Title: Design and Commercialization of an End-to-End Continuous Pharmaceutical Production Process: A Pilot Plant Case Study
Problem_Description: The secondary amine hydrochloride (reactant A) and the nitrile (reactant B) have limited solubility in the chosen solvent, leading to a turbid prereaction mixture and the introduction of suspended particulate matter (SPM) into the process.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
