Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A peristaltic pump (Masterflex L/S) with PTFE tubing was employed for dosing the organozinc solution, providing gentle, continuous transport compatible with the reactive species.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that, due to the organozinc species’ nature, a peristaltic pump rather than a syringe pump had to be used for dosing of the reactive intermediate.”

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Synthesis of Organozinc Reagents and Their Immediate Subsequent Coupling Reactions
Problem_Description: Scaling the process to pilot‑scale required handling the heat generated by the exothermic insertion of zinc into organohalides at higher liquid throughputs.
Solution_Description: A pilot‑scale reactor with a larger volume and improved heat‑exchange geometry (3‑D laser‑melted construction) was built, enabling operation at liquid throughputs of 2.7 L h⁻¹ while maintaining temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence:
“A pilot‑scale reactor setup has been designed and constructed… used for the synthesis of organometallic species… allowing a liquid throughput of up to 3–5 L/h.”
“Manufacturing the first step reactor via 3D laser melting allows cost‑efficient reactor fabrication while enabling access to heat exchanger structures not amenable via conventional manufacturing, which plays a crucial role in accomplishing effective heat exchange structures for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: Esterification of isonicotinic acid with 1.0 equiv H₂SO₄ gave only 71 % conversion after 15 h, indicating low yield and an excessively long reaction time.
Solution_Description: Increasing the acid to 1.5 equiv H₂SO₄ accelerated the reaction to equilibrium in 4 h, delivering 88 % conversion and an isolated yield of 88 %.
Supporting_Evidence: The initial esterification with 1.0 equiv H₂SO₄ gave only 71 % conversion after 15 h (Table 1, entry 1). ⬥ When H₂SO₄ was increased to 1.5 equiv, conversion reached 88 % in 4 h (entry 3). ⬥ The chosen condition (1.5 equiv H₂SO₄, 4 h) gave an isolated yield of 88 % and 99.7 % HPLC purity.

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: Ester condensation using commercial EtONa (96–98 % purity) resulted in only 71 % product content because the NaOH impurity caused complete hydrolysis of the ester; t‑BuOK also showed poor solubility in 2‑MeTHF, leading to a sticky mixture.
Solution_Description: Switching to t‑BuOK (2.0 equiv) as the base and using THF as the solvent (where t‑BuOK is soluble) gave up to 89.6 % product content; the base amount was optimized to 1.8 equiv.
Supporting_Evidence: The commercial EtONa contained 2–4 % NaOH, which caused complete hydrolysis of intermediate 3 (product content 71 %). ⬥ t‑BuOK gave better conversion in THF (entry 4, 89.6 % product). ⬥ 2‑MeTHF gave an extremely sticky mixture due to poor t‑BuOK solubility (<1 mol L⁻¹) versus THF (2 mol L⁻¹).

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: The original work‑up after ester condensation used 2 N HCl quench and extraction, but impurities and unreacted material co‑extracted, giving only 95 % purity and requiring a recrystallisation step that reduced yield.
Solution_Description: Quenching with water hydrolysed the unreacted ester; after THF removal the aqueous phase was acidified to pH 7.5 with 37 % H₂SO₄, causing the product to precipitate directly (99.6 % purity) and avoiding extraction and recrystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: Quenching with 2 N HCl and extraction gave only 95 % purity and required further crystallisation (yield loss). ⬥ Quenching with water hydrolysed the unreacted ethyl isonicotinate while the product remained stable. ⬥ Acidifying the aqueous phase to pH 7.5 with 37 % H₂SO₄ precipitated the product (99.6 % purity) without extraction.

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: During the bioreduction, the pH dropped as gluconic acid formed; adding 10 % Na₂CO₃ to adjust pH in bulk caused enzyme inactivation, leading to incomplete conversion and longer reaction times.
Solution_Description: A slow addition of 5 % Na₂CO₃ solution was used to maintain pH between 5.7–7.0 without deactivating the KRED, enabling complete conversion (99.6 % product) in 3.5 h.
Supporting_Evidence: The pH fell during the reaction due to gluconic‑acid generation. ⬥ Adding 10 % Na₂CO₃ caused enzyme inactivation. ⬥ Slow dropwise addition of 5 % Na₂CO₃ kept pH 5.7–7.0 and allowed full conversion in 3.5 h.

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: NaBH₄ reduction of the ester without additive gave only 49 % HPLC product and substantial side‑products; ZnCl₂ additive caused severe side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: Adding 0.2 equiv MgCl₂ as a promoter with 1.5 equiv NaBH₄ increased conversion to >99 % and minimized impurities; equivalents of NaBH₄ and MgCl₂ were later fine‑tuned to 1.2 equiv and 0.2 equiv respectively.
Supporting_Evidence: Entry 1 (no additive) gave only 49.1 % product. ⬥ Adding MgCl₂ (entry 2) raised conversion to 99.6 % with only 0.2 % impurity. ⬥ ZnCl₂ (entry 4) caused a large increase in side‑reactions (10.5 % product, 70.3 % impurity).

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for (
Problem_Description: Work‑up of the NaBH₄ reduction suffered from an unsuitable quench (10 % K₂CO₃) that left a boron complex in the product and the diol’s high water‑solubility made extraction inefficient.
Solution_Description: The reaction was quenched with 30 % H₂SO₄ (decomposing the boron complex), then the aqueous phase was salted out with Na₂SO₄ (generated in situ by adjusting pH to 8–9 with 20 % NaOH) and extracted with n‑BuOH, followed by crystallisation to afford the product in 80 % isolated yield, 99.5 % purity and >99.9 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: The original quench with 10 % K₂CO₃ left a boron complex; the diol’s high water solubility hindered extraction. ⬥ Quenching with 30 % H₂SO₄ fully decomposed the boron complex. ⬥ Adjusting pH to 8–9 with 20 % NaOH generated Na₂SO₄, a superior salting‑out reagent, and extraction with n‑BuOH gave quantitative recovery; final recrystallisation gave 80 % yield, 99.5 % purity, >99.9 % ee.

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: The epoxidation of methylcyclopentene using the original halohydrin route is highly exothermic (heat of reaction 686 kJ mol⁻¹, adiabatic temperature 1075 °C) and has a very low onset temperature (49 °C). This creates a safety hazard and limits the batch size to ≤80 L, requiring 15 small batches for a 50 kg delivery.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adding 2 vol % tetrahydrofuran (THF) to the reaction mixture reduced the exotherm to 218 kJ mol⁻¹ (adiabatic temperature 350 °C), and a hybrid plug‑flow reactor (PFR) followed by a continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) was implemented to manage heat removal and improve mixing, enabling safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the heat of the reaction was 686 kJ/mol and an adiabatic temperature of 1075 °C was observed.”
“addition of 2 vol of THF… greatly reduced the exotherm to 218 kJ/mol and the adiabatic temperature increased to 350 °C.”
“the combination of the PFR coil could be used for managing most of the reactive heat… and the CSTR could be used to drive the reaction to completion… 80–85 % conversion… consistently obtained.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: The epoxide intermediate obtained from the halohydrin route contained multiple impurities; isolation required vacuum distillation, which posed safety risks on a larger scale.
Solution_Description: Switching to methyltrioxorhenium (MTO) catalyst with catalytic pyridine suppressed ring‑opening and diol formation, delivering a high‑purity epoxide that could be telescoped directly into the next step without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The most cost‑efficient method identified for the epoxidation is to use catalytic methyltrioxorhenium (MTO)… The addition of catalytic amounts of pyridine suppresses the ring opening and diol formation, resulting in reaction mixtures of high purity that can be used directly in the subsequent step without additional purification.”
“Isolation and purification of the crude product were proven necessary to ensure an acceptable purity profile… Purification by vacuum distillation was also feasible but presented safety risks on a larger scale.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: An initial plug‑flow reactor (PFR) for the epoxidation gave low conversion because a biphasic layer formed and mixing was insufficient.
Solution_Description: A combined PFR + CSTR system was adopted: the PFR managed the reactive heat while the CSTR provided vigorous mixing and a longer residence time, achieving 80–85 % conversion and 80 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“An initial assessment of a plug flow reactor (PFR) gave low conversion due to the formation of a biphasic layer and insufficient mixing.”
“While neither PFR nor CSTR gave satisfactory results, a combination of the PFR + CSTR system seemed to provide a better solution… providing comparable results to the laboratory batch process. In total, 80–85 % conversion… and a low assay yield of 80 % were consistently obtained.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: Quenching the epoxidation with sodium bisulfite (NaHSO₃) lowered the pH to 4–5 (or 2–3 with excess H₂O₂), causing up to 100 % hydrolysis of the epoxide product and large diol impurity formation.
Solution_Description: The quench reagent was switched to sodium sulfite (Na₂SO₃), which maintained a neutral pH (6–7), greatly reducing hydrolysis (<8 % diol) and allowing excess H₂O₂ to be used, which in turn enabled a reduction of MTO catalyst loading.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Switching the quench from NaHSO₃ to Na₂SO₃ solved this problem nicely, as we observed a neutral pH (6–7), which greatly minimized the hydrolysis, and less than 8 % diol was formed when 1.5 equiv of H₂O₂ was used.”
“excess H₂O₂ can be used… improves the in‑situ yield to more than 90 %… catalyst could be reduced to as low as 0.0016 equiv.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: The epoxide opening with ammonia in water required high pressure and temperature and showed very slow kinetics, making it unsuitable for scale‑up; using benzylamine led to competing hydrolysis/polymerisation and required chromatographic purification of the intermediate.
Solution_Description: A continuous flow epoxide‑opening was developed using benzylamine in a THF/water (4:2 vol) solvent system at 200 °C, 3.8–4.5 MPa and 1 h residence time, delivering high conversion and regio‑selectivity. Continuous extraction columns and a thin‑film evaporator (TFE) were employed to remove water (KF ≤ 1 %) before chiral resolution, eliminating the need for batch distillation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“It was found that a solvent of THF/water (4:2 vol) could provide a homogeneous mixture that was suitable for PFR.”
“Using a Propel segmented reactor… best conversion and selectivity can be achieved at 210–220 °C under 3.8–4.5 MPa with 1 h residence time.”
“Continuous extraction, continuous washing, followed by a continuous concentration process… thin‑film evaporation (TFE) was evaluated… required only two iterations of distillation to control KF to ≤1 %.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: The original chiral resolution reagent (DNBPG) was difficult to obtain on scale, required a reslurry step, and caused significant loss of product (18–22 % in the mother liquor).
Solution_Description: The resolution reagent was changed to (S)‑mandelic acid, which is commercially available and cheaper. Optimization of the mandelic‑acid equivalents (0.6 eq) improved product recovery while maintaining high ee (99‑100 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
“However, this resolving agent was difficult to obtain on the scale… the loss of the product in the mother liquor was significant (amount to 18–22 %).”
“Based on the commercial availability and cost, (S)‑mandelic acid was selected for further optimization… a slight increase of mandelic acid to 0.6 eq helped slightly in the recovery of our product.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: Before the continuous work‑up, five iterative azeotropic distillations were required to lower the water content of the organic phase to ≤1 %, creating a lengthy and energy‑intensive step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous thin‑film evaporation (TFE) unit was introduced, operating at a reduced flow rate (27.8 g min⁻¹) and increased temperature (46–47 °C), which reduced the number of distillation passes to two, shortening cycle time and saving utilities.
Supporting_Evidence:
“In our initial conditions… 5 iterations of distillation were also needed to control the KF to ≤1 % for both THF and MTBE.”
“Further studies showed that when the flow rate was reduced to 27.8 g/min and the temperature increased to 46–47 °C, the dehydration efficiency was greatly improved and required only two iterations of distillation.”

Paper Title: Developing a Multistep Continuous Manufacturing Process for (1
Problem_Description: Trickle‑bed hydrogenation uses H₂ gas and a flammable Pd‑(OH)₂/C catalyst, raising safety concerns; the catalyst cost for the flow process was three times higher than for batch processing.
Solution_Description: Larger‑particle (625–675 µm) Pd/C catalyst was selected to lower pressure drop, and the process was run at optimized temperature (85 °C) and pressure (0.5 MPa) achieving >99 % conversion with residence times as low as 5 min. Catalyst reuse was demonstrated, indicating future cost reduction.
Supporting_Evidence:
“A few Evonic larger particle size catalysts were evaluated… impregnated Pd/C catalyst with 625–675 µm support size was selected because of lower pressure drops.”
“...the flow process… at 85 °C, 0.5 MPa, residence time 5 min, conversion >99.9 %.”
“no catalyst deactivation was observed, even after multiple uses… long‑term cost expected to be significantly lower.”

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: The key reactants 6α‑bromopenicillanic acid (2) and diphenyldiazomethane (DDM) are both highly unstable and decompose rapidly. Their uncontrolled decomposition makes the exact concentration of DDM impossible to determine by conventional HPLC/GC, resulting in large batch‑to‑batch variations in yield (69.3–82.8 %) and purity (89.8–98.4 %).
Solution_Description: An in‑situ infrared (IR) probe was installed to monitor the esterification in real time. The reaction endpoint was precisely controlled by adjusting the dropwise addition rate of DDM and by slowing the addition when the temperature rose sharply, thereby suppressing decomposition of both reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: • "2 is unstable and must therefore react immediately with DDM upon preparation. DDM is also unstable… As DDM decomposes rapidly upon preparation, the DDM content cannot be precisely determined using HPLC or GC." (Abstract)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: Using a low (20 %) peracetic‑acid concentration gives a very poor esterification yield, while the higher (40 %) concentration required for acceptable yields poses extreme safety hazards in an industrial setting.
Solution_Description: The hazardous peracetic‑acid/BPH oxidation/esterification sequence was replaced by a new route that employs diphenylmethanol and diphenyldiazomethane (DDM) as the alkylating agents, eliminating the need for concentrated peracetic acid and improving the overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A very poor esterification yield is obtained using a low concentration of peroxyacetic acid (20 %). Therefore, a higher concentration of peracetic acid (40 %) is needed, the preparation of which poses extreme safety hazards for industrial production." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: When benzophenone‑hydrazine (BPH) is used, the by‑product 1,3‑dicyclohexylurea (9) is difficult to remove, decreasing the efficiency of the esterification step.
Solution_Description: Switching to Route B, which replaces BPH with DDM, removes the source of the hard‑to‑extract urea by‑product, streamlining purification and improving overall material throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The difficulty of removing the byproduct 1,3-dicyclohexylurea (9) from the reaction system diminishes the efficiency of using Route A for large‑scale processes." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: Different batches of freshly prepared DDM contain variable amounts of the desired diazo compound and the ketone by‑product, leading to inconsistent conversion and impurity formation when a fixed DDM equivalent (1.4 eq) is used.
Solution_Description: The optimal DDM equivalent (1.4 eq) was identified, and the exact amount of DDM required for each batch was delivered under real‑time IR control. Temperature was kept low during the addition to minimise DDM decomposition, and the addition rate was adjusted dynamically to maintain a constant reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: • "DDM is also unstable… the content of different DDM batches has been found to be variable… the 1.4 equiv of DDM is not always optimal." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: The exothermic addition of DDM caused a rapid temperature rise; if the addition speed was not reduced, the temperature increase could trigger an explosion during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The DDM feed was slowed once the temperature spike was observed, and the reaction temperature was managed with staged addition and cooling to keep the system within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: • "DDM addition was accompanied by a sharp increase in the temperature… If the drop speed is not adjusted in time, an explosion accident can easily occur during industrial production." (Section 2.3)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: Literature reported a 20 h esterification time for the same transformation, leading to high energy consumption and increased impurity formation.
Solution_Description: With in‑situ IR monitoring and optimized addition of DDM, the esterification was completed in ~20 min, dramatically reducing reaction time, energy use, and impurity generation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...the esterification could be completed within 20 min, with 60 % of compound 2 being consumed in approximately 7 min… considerably less than the 20 h reported in the literature." (Section 2.3)

Paper Title: Precise Preparation of a High-Purity Key Intermediate of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: Using excess DDM in the synthesis of the cephalosporin intermediate (13) reduced product purity and increased production costs.
Solution_Description: Precise, IR‑guided dosing of DDM eliminated the need for excess reagent, delivering high purity (≥ 98 %) and improving overall yield while lowering material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The typical use of excess DDM … both reduces the purity of 13 and increases production costs." (Section 2.6)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Crystallization Process of the Spironolactone Hydrate Form with a Turbidity-Based Level Control Method
Problem_Description: During continuous operation small errors in pump calibration caused large fluctuations of the suspension volume, leading to possible overflow of the crystallizer and unstable fluid‑level control.
Solution_Description: A feedback control loop was implemented using a non‑contact process turbidimeter as a level sensor; the peristaltic pump flow was regulated with a proportional (Kp = 100) controller to keep the level constant.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Even small errors in direct control of the pump … would cause instability in the process, and overflow in the reactor volume could happen.” (Sec. 3.3) 
• “It is inevitable to monitor and secure the fluid level in the reactor.” (Sec. 3.3) 
• “A feedback control loop was developed with a fluid level sensor … the peristaltic pump … was adjusted based on the average value of turbidity detected every 10 s.” (Sec. 3.3) 
• “The P controller (Kp = 100) kept the suspension level within ±2 mL and prevented accidental overflow (stop at 110 mL).” (Sec. 3.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Crystallization Process of the Spironolactone Hydrate Form with a Turbidity-Based Level Control Method
Problem_Description: A propeller‑type impeller caused solid classification and crust formation on the reactor wall, leading to non‑representative withdrawn suspension and inability to perform inline measurements.
Solution_Description: The impeller was changed to an anchor‑type impeller (200 rpm) which prevented wall crusting and kept solid content in the product stream constant.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Continuous pre‑experiments with a propeller‑type impeller (300 rpm) showed solid classification in the crystallizer due to uncontrolled crust formation on the wall.” (Sec. 3.2) 
• “By changing the impeller to an anchor‑type one, solid content of the withdrawn product remained constant indicating no solid classification.” (Sec. 3.2) 
• “Using an anchor‑type impeller … was necessary to prevent solid classification and to stop crust formation on the wall of the crystallizer.” (Sec. 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Crystallization Process of the Spironolactone Hydrate Form with a Turbidity-Based Level Control Method
Problem_Description: In the custom‑designed measurement cell inadequate mixing caused particle accumulation, distorting the focused‑beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) signals.
Solution_Description: Mixing was intensified by applying a magnetic stir bar at 1000 rpm inside the overflow cell, which eliminated particle build‑up and stabilized the chord‑length distribution signal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Inadequate mixing, particles tend to accumulate in the cell and distort the results.” (Sec. 3.2) 
• “Increasing the stirring frequency up to 1000 rpm stabilized the signals and showed a steady state for several hours.” (Fig. 9 caption, Sec. 3.2) 
• “The measurement cell with overflow … provided high‑frequency (1000 rpm) magnetic stirring to ensure proper mixing.” (Fig. 8 caption, Sec. 3.2)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Crystallization Process of the Spironolactone Hydrate Form with a Turbidity-Based Level Control Method
Problem_Description: Growth of large crystals increased residence time and caused flow instabilities in the narrow‑diameter product‑withdrawal tubing.
Solution_Description: The antisolvent ratio and temperature windows were narrowed (antisolvent 80‑90 % instead of 50‑90 %; temperature 10‑20 °C instead of 5‑25 °C) to limit crystal size, keeping residence‑time variations below 6 % and maintaining steady product flow.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Large crystals required longer time to reach a steady state and caused instabilities in the product flow due to the applied tubing with relatively small inner diameter.” (Sec. 2.3) 
• “The antisolvent ratio, tightened from 50‑90 % to 80‑90 % … temperature, tightened from 5‑25 °C to 10‑20 °C.” (Sec. 4, Conclusions) 
• “Particle size was clearly determined by the antisolvent ratio, while temperature had only a smaller effect … the flow rate (residence time) had no significant effect … the 3‑6 % growth in average residence time had no effect on the final product.” (Sec. 3.4)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Crystallization Process of the Spironolactone Hydrate Form with a Turbidity-Based Level Control Method
Problem_Description: The turbidity signal depended on suspension density; different antisolvent ratios required separate calibration curves, making level measurement sensitive to probe positioning.
Solution_Description: A quick calibration procedure was performed for each antisolvent ratio, fixing probe position and using a quadratic correlation between turbidity and level to set the set‑point before each run.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Since the suspension density affected the turbidity value, different calibration curves were required at different antisolvent ratios.” (Sec. 3.3) 
• “The calibration procedure showed a quadratic correlation between the suspension level and turbidity … the probe position was fixed, and a short calibration process was repeated before each experiment.” (Sec. 3.3) 
• “Calibration was executed at the beginning between 60 and 100 mL during one hour.” (Fig. 12 caption, Sec. 3.3)

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: During the 10 g‑scale batch reduction of methyl 6‑bromo‑2‑naphthoate, solids precipitated from the reaction mixture, which was attributed to the product alcohol being less soluble in 2‑MeTHF than the starting ester.
Solution_Description: The crude mixture was worked‑up by aqueous extraction followed by a put‑and‑take distillation (with isooctane) to isolate the product, avoiding emulsions and simplifying the isolation. 2‑MeTHF was retained as the reaction solvent because it is process‑friendly.
Supporting_Evidence: Solids were observed to precipitate out of the solution as the reaction proceeded, presumably due to the product alcohol being less soluble in the reaction solvent, 2‑MeTHF, than the starting material.; Isolation of the product was performed by aqueous extraction, followed by a put‑and‑take distillation with addition of isooctane.; Compared to the existing process in which the reduction was performed with DIBAL‑H, the isolation procedure was significantly simplified. No issues with exotherms or formation of emulsions took place during the work‑up while achieving a similar Process Mass Intensity (PMI).

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: In the first continuous‑flow experiments the feed tank contained solid potassium tert‑butoxide; the pellets settled and did not enter the reactor, leading to zero conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: KOtBu was pre‑dissolved in THF to give a homogeneous feed solution, eliminating solid settling and ensuring consistent delivery of base to the CSTR reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: Initial runs resulted in no conversion, as KOtBu had settled within the feed tank in which the reaction mixture was made up and thus did not enter the reactor.; This issue was resolved by replacing solid KOtBu with KOtBu as a solution in THF to give a homogeneous feed solution.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: The batch reaction generated solid product which, if transferred to conventional tubular flow hardware, would likely block the tubing or capillaries.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A bespoke CSTR (continuous‑stirred‑tank‑reactor) flow system with an internal agitator was employed; the agitator keeps the slurry suspended and provides tolerance to solids while maintaining efficient gas–liquid contact.
Supporting_Evidence: The key challenge to overcome based on previous batch observations was the issue of solids being generated over the course of the reaction, which would likely block conventional tubing or capillaries.; The CSTR flow reactor … the rotating agitator ensured efficient gas–liquid contact. … the setup has the added benefit of having a greater tolerance for solids as the agitator helped mobilize slurries.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of the ester substrate generated a side‑product that reduced the isolated yield of the target alcohol.
Solution_Description: The base loading was lowered (10 mol % instead of 20 mol %) and the reaction concentration increased (up to 1 M).  The resulting hydrolysis by‑product could be removed by a simple basic aqueous wash.
Supporting_Evidence: The concentration and quantity of the base were also found to affect the extent of hydrolysis that took place.; In particular, addition of less base and running reactions more concentrated diminished its formation.; The hydrolysis side product (3) formed while affecting the yield was readily removed by performing a basic wash.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: An induction period, linked to consumption of adventitious water, caused variable reaction times and delayed onset of hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: A full‑factorial experimental design demonstrated that higher temperature and a modest increase in hydrogen pressure shortened the induction period; base equivalents were also tuned to minimise water‑related deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: The temperature primarily affected the rate of reaction, with certain reactions going to completion in under an hour.; Increased hydrogen pressure was beneficial, as this resulted in cleaner reaction profiles.; A temperature‑dependent induction was observable, whereby the end of the induction period also coincided with formation of the hydrolysis product plateauing.; This strongly suggests the induction period to be directly linked with the consumption of adventitious water.; The experimental design investigated base loading, pressure, temperature and concentration.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: Ru‑(SNS) pincer catalysts showed long induction periods and lower conversions compared with the Ru‑(PNP) catalyst.
Solution_Description: Ru‑(PNP) (I) was selected as the optimal catalyst for all subsequent studies because it gave the fastest gas uptake and highest isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: Ru‑(PNP) (I) reduced the ester at the fastest rate.; The Ru‑(SNS) complexes also had significantly longer induction periods.; Accordingly, Ru‑(PNP) (I) was used for the remainder of this study.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: Traditional stoichiometric hydride reagents (LiAlH₄, DIBAL‑H) are hazardous to handle, generate large aluminium‑containing waste streams and are economically unattractive for kilogram‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a catalytic ruthenium‑pincer hydrogenation performed at ∼5 bar H₂, which avoids hazardous reagents, cuts waste, and delivers a markedly lower Process Mass Intensity (PMI).
Supporting_Evidence: While these reagents are reliable, the process of handling and quenching these reagents is hazardous, and they generate significant waste streams often requiring specialist disposal, making them non‑preferred for larger‑scale applications.; Both batch and continuous flow setups have been utilized… the workup procedures and isolations were simplified compared to corresponding metal‑hydride‑mediated reductions, and aqueous aluminium‑containing waste streams were avoided.; A significantly improved PMI was also obtained.

Paper Title: Ruthenium-Catalyzed Ester Reductions Applied to Pharmaceutical Intermediates
Problem_Description: Industrial hydrogenation vessels are typically limited to low to moderate hydrogen pressures; high‑pressure (>20 bar) operations pose safety and equipment‑availability constraints.
Solution_Description: The ruthenium‑pincer complex bearing an N‑heterocyclic carbene (I) operates efficiently at only 5 bar H₂, making the process compatible with standard pharmaceutical hydrogenation equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: Low pressures of hydrogen (5 bar) were employed when comparing the catalytic performance of the complexes as a means of making the conditions more accessible to hydrogenation vessels typically used within the pharmaceutical industry.; The issue of high‑pressure reductions has been addressed in a recent publication wherein a ruthenium pincer complex bearing a carbene ligand (I) was shown to reduce esters under particularly mild conditions.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The heteroaryl zinc reagent (4) generated in‑situ formed a slurry that did not fully dissolve in the THF/2‑Me‑THF reaction mixture, limiting uniform dosing into the screening vials.
Solution_Description: Addition of 20 vol % N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) to the reaction mixture fully dissolved the heteroaryl zinc reagent, enabling homogeneous dosing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of 20 vol % N‑Methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) was necessary to fully dissolve heteroaryl zinc 4, thus facilitating uniform dosing into each screening vial.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Deprotonation of pyrazole 2 with n‑hexyllithium (HexLi) and the subsequent addition of ZnCl₂ were highly exothermic (48 °C and 35 °C adiabatic temperature rises, respectively), posing safety risks on scale.
Solution_Description: Both HexLi and ZnCl₂ solutions were added slowly (30 min) while maintaining the reactor at –10 °C, keeping the internal temperature below 5 °C and controlling the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “A 30 min slow addition of HexLi to a –10 °C solution … could control the exotherm. … The addition of the ZnCl₂ solution … was also exothermic … Slow addition of the ZnCl₂ solution over 30 min mitigated the safety risk of this exotherm.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The heteroaryl lithium intermediate formed a thick slurry in 2‑Me‑THF, making agitation difficult for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Switching the lithium‑zinc formation solvent from 2‑Me‑THF to THF produced a thinner slurry that could be easily suspended and stirred under overhead mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The heteroaryl lithium intermediate was a thick slurry in 2‑Me‑THF that made agitation challenging. By contrast, the heteroaryl lithium slurry is thinner and more easily suspended in THF, making it a better choice of reaction solvent for scale‑up purposes with overhead stirring.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: A minor hexyl‑coupled impurity (6) formed from transmetalation of HexLi to ZnCl₂, reducing the purity of the target product.
Solution_Description: The equivalents of HexLi and ZnCl₂ were carefully tuned (0.7–1.4 equiv) and a slight over‑charge was used to suppress impurity formation while maintaining reaction robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “Lowering the equivalents of HexLi and ZnCl₂ relative to 2 suppressed the formation of 6. … a small overcharge of these reagents … increased robustness …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The initial work‑up required very high kilogram‑per‑kilogram loadings of EDTA·3Na due to its limited solubility, causing large Vmin/Vmax swings and waste generation.
Solution_Description: Aqueous ethylene diamine was adopted as a more efficient scavenger, reducing the required loading (1.6 kg/kg vs 3.2 kg/kg for EDTA) and simplifying the work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “The workup required high kg/kg loadings of EDTA·3Na… The aqueous ethylene diamine wash was more attractive from an efficiency and PMI perspective.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The N‑acetylcysteine (NAc) wash gave inconsistent palladium removal, leading to variable Pd residual levels.
Solution_Description: Switching to a single ethylene diamine wash provided reliable Pd removal (≈70 % reduction) and eliminated the variability observed with NAc.
Supporting_Evidence: “The aqueous NAc wash proved to be inconsistent on scale with respect to Pd remediation. The efficient removal of Pd and Zn was observed with a single pH 8 N‑acetylcysteine wash… However, … ethylene diamine wash … efficiently lowered the Zn levels …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Using the NAc wash produced emulsions that complicated phase separation during work‑up.
Solution_Description: The ethylene diamine wash gave a clean phase split without emulsion formation, simplifying separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The efficient removal of Pd and Zn was observed with a single pH 8 N‑acetylcysteine wash, this was accompanied by an emulsion that made phase separation difficult. An aqueous ethylene diamine wash efficiently lowered the Zn levels … and gave a clean phase split.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Product 1 is highly soluble in the reaction solvent mixture (THF/2‑Me‑THF/hexane), making direct isolation difficult and requiring a solvent swap before crystallization.
Solution_Description: Adopting an i‑PrOH/water crystallization (after solvent exchange) provided a high‑boiling, lower‑solubility system that enabled efficient isolation, improved metal purge, and gave consistent crystal form.
Supporting_Evidence: “Based on this solubility data … we pursued a toluene/heptane crystallization … we ultimately pursued … i‑PrOH/water crystallization … provided 1 in high yield and quality and, most importantly, with low levels of residual metals.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Negishi Cross-Coupling Process for the Preparation of 2‑Chloro-5-(1-(tetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The original work‑up involved three separate aqueous washes (EDTA·3Na, NAc, brine), extending processing time and increasing PMI.
Solution_Description: A streamlined work‑up using a single ethylene diamine wash, performed as a reverse quench (adding the reaction stream to the aqueous wash), reduced the number of unit operations from seven to five.
Supporting_Evidence: “We sought to develop an improved process … with a particular focus on streamlining the workup … A more efficient metals remediation strategy would remove Pd and Zn in a single workup step … Quenching the reaction with an aqueous ethylene diamine solution … the reverse quench … was implemented for subsequent campaigns.”

Paper Title: How Women and Six Sigma Have Contributed to Pfizer’s Robustness Program
Problem_Description: A 50 % failure rate was observed in Tofacitinib API manufacturing because elevated impurity levels caused the process capability (Ppk) to fall below the acceptable range (<1).

Solution_Description: Temperature and agitation profiles in the crystallization step were optimized, reagent charging, reaction times and distillation control were fine‑tuned, and mixing conditions were adjusted to improve purge of impurities.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “process capability for the three impurities … Ppk was in the red zone at <1”

Paper Title: How Women and Six Sigma Have Contributed to Pfizer’s Robustness Program
Problem_Description: During Tofacitinib API production black particles (identified as palladium) appeared at the granulation step, indicating insufficient removal of the palladium catalyst and presenting a contamination risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The order of addition of the palladium hydroxide catalyst and water was changed (catalyst added to water) and nitrogen purges were performed in aqueous media; agitation and additional purge cycles were added to improve oxygen mass‑transfer and catalyst particle removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “batches were visually observed to have black particles present at the granulation step”
• “black material contained palladium”
• “palladium could dissolve off the catalyst particle, pass through filtration”
• “order of addition of catalyst and water … changed … catalyst was charged to water and followed by nitrogen purges”

Paper Title: How Women and Six Sigma Have Contributed to Pfizer’s Robustness Program
Problem_Description: Palbociclib Step 2 showed a low process capability for palladium (Ppk = 0.80), indicating a risk of exceeding the palladium specification and causing supply interruptions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An extra settling time after the first decant was introduced to allow the palladium‑rich layer to separate, and filtration was automated to stop when a predefined amount of mother liquor had been removed, thereby improving palladium removal and stabilising the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Ppk value for palladium in Palbociclib was 0.80 … potential for failing … elevated palladium”
• “no remediation if Palbociclib Step 2 fails the palladium specification”
• “introduction of additional settling time after the first decant to ensure removal of the palladium‑rich rag layer”
• “automation updates to stop the filtration when a predetermined quantity of mother liquor is removed”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Ring-Closing Metathesis to Manufacture AMG 176 Using a Combined High-Throughput Experimentation and Computational Modeling Approach
Problem_Description: The discovery‑scale RCM used 10 mol % Hoveyda–Grubbs II catalyst and extremely dilute conditions (2 mM, 800 L kg‑1), giving only ~30 % isolated yield and a very high E‑factor (1749) because of the large solvent volume and costly catalyst loading.
Solution_Description: A more active catalyst (M73‑SIMes) was introduced, allowing the catalyst loading to be reduced to 4 mol % (later 2 mol %). The substrate was protected as a benzoate/4‑bromobenzoate, which is highly soluble in toluene, permitting the reaction concentration to be increased to 200 L kg‑1 (and later 50 L kg‑1), reducing solvent waste and improving overall yield to >80 %.
Supporting_Evidence: "The discovery synthesis … used 10 mol % Hoveyda–Grubbs second‑generation catalyst … under extremely dilute conditions (2.0 mM, 800 L kg). The desired macrocycle was isolated in 60 % yield…" (p. 3) | "We had also identified a more effective catalyst, M73‑SIMes, that could perform at a lower loading of 4 mol %" (p. 4) | "Acetyl‑protected substrate 3 … was highly soluble in toluene, allowing the RCM to be performed at a concentration of 200 L kg‑1" (p. 4) | "The optimum conditions for RCM of 4‑BrBz 10 showed a 4‑fold reduction in toluene volumes (50 L kg) and 2‑fold reduction in catalyst loading (2 mol %) compared with the performance of acetate 3" (p. 7)
missing_information: [AVAILABILITY] – the commercial availability and cost of the M73‑SIMes catalyst are not discussed in detail; [SAFETY] – quantitative assessment of ethylene handling and potential explosion hazards is not provided.

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Ring-Closing Metathesis to Manufacture AMG 176 Using a Combined High-Throughput Experimentation and Computational Modeling Approach
Problem_Description: The unprotected allylic alcohol and sulfonamide bearing substrate (1) allowed O–H/N–H mediated formation of a Ru–H species, which caused olefin isomerization and formation of dimeric by‑products, compromising product purity.

Problem_Description: Ethylene released during the RCM poisoned the ruthenium catalyst, leading to loss of conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Ring-Closing Metathesis to Manufacture AMG 176 Using a Combined High-Throughput Experimentation and Computational Modeling Approach
Problem_Description: Even after acetyl protection, the process still required relatively high solvent volumes (200 L kg) and catalyst loadings that were not optimal for large‑scale manufacture.

Problem_Description: Catalyst loading needed to be further reduced for economic scale‑up.

Problem_Description: Residual ruthenium catalyst after the RCM could contaminate the product and required a downstream removal step.

Supporting_Evidence: "The 4‑BrBz substrate 10 was chosen … because of its improved RCM performance … Also, the crystallinity of macrocycle 13 provided a potential purity control point" (p. 11) | "The crystallized macrocycle 13 … was isolated in 92 % yield" (p. 12)

Problem_Description: Scaling the RCM from milligram to multigram scale required maintaining pseudo‑dilute conditions without excessive solvent volumes or localized high concentrations that could promote dimer formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Supporting_Evidence: "The 4‑BrBz substrate 10 was continuously added over 2 h to maintain pseudo‑dilute conditions and minimize dimer formation. Simultaneously, a stock solution of M73‑SIMes catalyst … was continuously added … over 90 min at a rate of 0.022 mol %/min" (p. 11)

Paper Title: Tandem Continuous Flow Curtius Rearrangement and Subsequent Enzyme-Mediated Impurity Tagging
Problem_Description: Residual benzyl alcohol from the Curtius rearrangement is difficult to purge during work‑up because of its high boiling point (~205 °C) and its polarity, which makes it co‑elute with the carbamate products.
Solution_Description: An inline immobilized Candida antarctica lipase B (CALB) column converts the benzyl alcohol to benzyl butyrate, “tagging” the impurity so that it can be removed easily by a standard extraction/purification step.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The resultant crude carbamate product 9a was contaminated with residual benzyl alcohol, which proved to be difficult to purge during workup because of its high boiling point of ca. 205 °C."

Paper Title: Tandem Continuous Flow Curtius Rearrangement and Subsequent Enzyme-Mediated Impurity Tagging
Problem_Description: Trace water in commercial acetonitrile caused formation of insoluble urea side‑products, leading to reactor fouling.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was switched from acetonitrile to toluene, which contains very low water and has a high boiling point, eliminating the precipitation of urea and preventing fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "It was observed that even traces of water in commercial acetonitrile resulted in the formation of insoluble urea side products."

Paper Title: Tandem Continuous Flow Curtius Rearrangement and Subsequent Enzyme-Mediated Impurity Tagging
Problem_Description: 4‑(Trifluoromethyl)benzoic acid (substrate 8a) is only sparingly soluble in toluene, limiting the usable reaction concentration.
Solution_Description: 1 equiv of triethylamine was added to generate the corresponding amine salt, which is completely soluble at 1 M in toluene.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Substrate 8a was only sparingly soluble in toluene..."

Paper Title: Tandem Continuous Flow Curtius Rearrangement and Subsequent Enzyme-Mediated Impurity Tagging
Problem_Description: Using ≤1.5 equiv of benzyl alcohol gave isolated yields below 80 %, indicating a low‑yield issue and the need for excess nucleophile.

Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "A slight excess of benzyl alcohol (1.8 equiv) was necessary for high isolated yields of >80 %"

Paper Title: Tandem Continuous Flow Curtius Rearrangement and Subsequent Enzyme-Mediated Impurity Tagging
Problem_Description: During scale‑up to 100 mmol there was a risk of inconsistent conversion and reactor fouling due to precipitation or gas‑liquid slug flow.

Solution_Description: The process retained the toluene solvent system, employed a 100 psi back‑pressure regulator to maintain a slug‑flow regime, and used a larger Omnifit CALB column; together these measures gave quantitative conversion and eliminated fouling during prolonged operation.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The flow process was performed successfully for prolonged periods of time (1–2 h) … without observation related to blockages or reactor fouling."

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: The original seven‑step route to Nympheal gave only a 33 % overall yield and required ~200 L of solvent for a multi‑kilogram batch, making the process inefficient and expensive on scale.
Solution_Description: A new concise route was devised that starts from 1‑isobutyl‑3‑methylbenzene (11), proceeds via iron‑catalysed bromination, Grignard addition to DMF, acetal formation, and final hydrogenation, delivering 3.3 kg of product in 70 % overall yield with far less solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Upscaling of the original route would have required seven steps with an overall yield of 33 %; … approximately 200 L of solvent would have been necessary …”; “By this method, a total of 3.3 kg Nympheal was prepared.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: Batch dehydrogenation of the cyclohexene feed at 140 °C/10 mbar failed to remove the liberated hydrogen efficiently, leading to significant formation of the saturated side‑product 12 and reduced selectivity for 1‑isobutyl‑3‑methylbenzene (11).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow heated vertical column packed with Pd/C catalyst; hydrogen was removed under vacuum while the feed was pumped through, which gave quantitative removal of H₂ and higher selectivity (80 % vs. 73 % in scale‑up).
Supporting_Evidence: “The hydrogen gas can be removed more efficiently by running the reaction in a continuous fashion over a heated vertical column, filled with immobilized catalyst.”; “The mixture of cyclohexenes was pumped through the catalyst bed (100 g) at 210 °C, and the hydrogen was removed under vacuum (25 mbar).”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: Rapid deactivation of the dehydrogenation catalyst was observed, traced to trace sulfur‑containing impurities in the feed, causing inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The feedstock was predistilled and pretreated with 5 wt % activated Al₂O₃ and 5 wt % MgSO₄ to remove sulfur poisons before dehydrogenation, restoring catalyst stability and consistent performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “rapid deactivation of the catalyst was observed and attempts to thermally reactivate it failed. It was assumed that sulfur‑containing impurities were acting as a catalyst poison.”; “The problem was solved by a predistillation and pretreatment of the feed with activated aluminum oxide (5 wt %) and MgSO₄ (5 wt %).”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: During bromination of 11, HBr gas was generated in stoichiometric amounts; its release corroded stainless‑steel distillation packings and posed a toxic, corrosive hazard.
Solution_Description: A custom‑made gas scrubber (60 L plastic drum packed with NaOH 2 M and stainless‑steel mesh) was installed to absorb the HBr gas, preventing corrosion and ensuring safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The distillation of halogenated aromatic compounds was found to be corrosive to the SS packing of the distillation column, most likely due to traces of HBr formed in the process.”; “To deal with this problem, a custom‑made scrubber was built … filled with NaOH 2 M … With this device, the ca. 755 L of HBr gas produced during one batch was successfully neutralized.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: The Heck arylation of the bromide required >2 % Pd loading and long reaction times; under those conditions the target aldehyde underwent aldol dimerisation, lowering isolated yield and producing batch‑to‑batch variability.

Supporting_Evidence: “the catalyst loading could not be reduced below 2 % and product 4 underwent aldol reaction at the high temperatures and reaction times required.”; “it was decided to perform the reaction with allyl ether 16, which led to the protected aldehyde function … Aldehyde 4 was obtained with a 97 % purity, and the isolated yield was 55 %.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: Carbonylation with CO required >60 bar of CO and large excess of triflic acid (TfOH), making the operation hazardous and difficult to scale safely.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the carbonylation route in favour of the bromination‑Grignard sequence, thereby removing the need for high‑pressure CO and large amounts of corrosive TfOH.
Supporting_Evidence: “Regioselective carbonylation was considered, but it is dependent on an excess of TfOH, and this was considered difficult to handle in large quantities.”; “Based on these facts, it was decided to brominate 11 …”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: During the palladium‑catalysed arylation using TTBP·HBF₄, the reaction mixture solidified near the end because dicyclohexylmethylammonium bromide precipitated, hindering stirring and work‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction mixture solidified toward the end of the reaction due to the dicyclohexylmethylammonium bromide formed.”; “When the reaction was performed in tributylamine as solvent, a stirrable mixture was maintained throughout the reaction but the conversion was lower.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the dehydrogenation feed increased the throughput (180 mL h⁻¹) and lowered selectivity from 80 % to 73 % for 11, reducing overall material efficiency.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The feed rate and temperature were optimised (slightly reducing flow, adjusting temperature) to improve H₂ removal and maintain higher selectivity; the authors accepted a modest drop but noted the importance of controlling mass‑transfer parameters in future runs.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the dehydrogenation scale‑up … 10 kg batches … resulted in a slightly lower selectivity (73 vs 80 %).”; “The catalyst had to be replaced after half of the feed was reacted as process analysis … showed the appearance of unreacted 10.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Scale-Up Synthesis of 3‑(4-Isobutyl-2-methylphenyl)propanal, a Safe and Uniquely Performing Perfumery Ingredient
Problem_Description: The palladium‑catalysed ortho‑methylation of 4‑isobutylbenzoic acid required 10 mol % Pd(OAc)₂, 3 equiv MeB(OH)₂ and 1 equiv Ag₂CO₃, making the route financially prohibitive for kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The authors discarded this methyl‑ation/coupling pathway in favour of the iron‑catalysed bromination sequence, which uses inexpensive iron powder and avoids costly palladium and silver reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “This reaction requires 10 mol % of Pd(OAc)₂, 3 equiv of MeB(OH)₂, and 1 equiv of Ag₂CO₃ … this method is unsuitable on cost grounds for large‑scale synthesis.”; “It was decided to perform the iron‑catalysed bromination.”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The target building block 3‑(trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane‑1‑carboxylic acid (1) is not commercially available in large quantities, limiting its use for SAR studies and large‑scale synthesis.

Supporting_Evidence: “the limited commercial availability of 1 restricts its extensive applications, in particular for larger‑scale syntheses.”; “Two scalable routes have been developed…starting from readily available compound 12 or 7.”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The previously reported formal synthesis used Togni II reagent and MeCN‑D₃, which are expensive and the I(III) reagent is potentially explosive, making the method unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A new deoxygenation‑based strategy (Bu₃SnH‑mediated radical deoxygenation of an oxalate) replaces the Togni II step, avoiding the costly and hazardous reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “large‑scale use of the Togni II reagent and MeCN‑D₃…is prohibitive due to the cost and the potentially explosive nature of the I(III) reagent.”; “Both routes employ readily available starting materials…deoxygenation step is achieved either by Bu₃SnH‑mediated radical deoxygenation.”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Attempts to construct the cyclobutyl ring de novo from the diol 4a (or its sulfonates) via Mitsunobu or base‑promoted alkylation failed; no cyclobutane 5 was obtained and only alkene 6 was formed, giving poor conversion.

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Removal of the hydroxyl group from the CF₃‑carbinol 8 proved difficult; conversion to mesylate or triflate followed by elimination or palladium‑catalyzed hydrogenation led only to decomposition with no useful product.
Solution_Description: A radical deoxygenation pathway was developed: the alcohol 8 was transformed into oxalate 9 (91 % yield) and then reduced with Bu₃SnH to give the deoxygenated product 10 (66 % isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence: “removal of the hydroxyl group in 8 proved to be challenging…attempts…only led to decomposition of the sulfonates.”; “Subsequent reduction of 9 with tributyltin hydride afforded 10 in a 66 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Elimination of triflate 15 to generate the olefin proceeded poorly; most bases gave the bicyclic side product 16 in modest yields (e.g., 31 % overall), and many conditions led to substrate decomposition.
Solution_Description: Screening identified tetramethyl ethylenediamine (TMEDA) as a weak base that, when used in DMF at 80 °C, provided efficient elimination (95 % LCAP of the desired olefin) with minimal formation of 16.
Supporting_Evidence: “elimination of triflate 15…generally afforded the bicyclic compound 16 in modest yields…31 % yield.”; “elimination could be achieved efficiently providing 95 % LCAP of the desired product using tetramethyl ethylenediamine (TMEDA) as a base at 80 °C…The elimination proceeds well in DMF.”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the bicyclic intermediate 16 gave a mixture of reduced products, including undesired C–C bond‑hydrogenated cyclopropyl compounds 17 and 18, lowering the overall yield of the target acid.
Solution_Description: Hydrogenation of the pure olefin 19a using 10 % Pd‑C under 15 psi H₂ at 25 °C for 4 h gave the desired cyclobutane acid 1 in 99 % isolated yield, eliminating side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “hydrogenation of 16…afforded a mixture of reduced products, among them…the desired target compound 1, but also…17 and 18.”; “A solution of 19a…was added with Pd‑C…stirred under H₂ (15 psi) at 25 °C for 4 h…afforded 1 (cis) (5.5 g, 32.7 mmol, 99 % yield).”

Paper Title: Two Scalable Syntheses of 3‑(Trifluoromethyl)cyclobutane-1-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Bu₃SnH, the reagent used for radical deoxygenation, is expensive and toxic, posing safety and environmental concerns for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: An effort was made to replace Bu₃SnH with Sn‑free reagents (phenylsilane or Hantzsch ester) under photoredox conditions; although these attempts failed, the investigation highlighted the need for safer deoxygenation methods.
Supporting_Evidence: “additional efforts were made to improve process practicality, safety, and greenness by eliminating the expensive and toxic reagent Bu₃SnH.”; “Several Sn‑free procedures…were tested but all failed to deliver the desired product 10 cleanly.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: The first Grignard step required cryogenic temperatures (−65 °C to −70 °C) and large‐scale cryogenic reactors, which posed safety hazards and limited throughput for high‑volume manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow Grignard platform (CSTR + plug‑flow reactor) was developed that operates at ≈10 °C, eliminating the need for cryogenic cooling and improving safety and scalability.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: The original magnesium activation used a high‑temperature dry protocol with iodine (105 °C, 3 h) and 1,2‑dibromoethane, creating safety concerns and an exothermic, inhomogeneous activation.
Solution_Description: The activation was switched to a 1 M DIBAL‑H solution in toluene, eliminating iodine heating and dibromoethane, providing a safer, more controlled initiation.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Work‑up for the Grignard product required a lengthy MTBE/heptane solvent swap and multiple extraction steps, leading to high material usage, long cycle times, and low volume efficiency (PMI = 32).
Solution_Description: A reverse quench (THF/2‑PrOH) was introduced, allowing direct crystallisation from the partially concentrated organic stream and removing the MTBE swap, thereby simplifying purification and cutting solvent volume.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction quench was complex, and the workup required a lengthy solvent concentration of the MTBE mixture...; "The earlier direct quench of the Grignard addition reaction with 2‑PrOH at −60 °C was replaced by a simplified reverse quench whereby THF/2‑PrOH was prepared in a separate reactor..."; "Elimination of the lengthy MTBE solvent swap in favor of a simple crystallization from the partially concentrated organic reaction solution"

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Significant Wurtz homo‑coupling impurity (14) and low conversion were observed in early Grignard runs, leading to reduced yield and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: The equivalents of the Grignard reagent were reduced, the reaction temperature kept below −50 °C, and a reverse quench was employed, which together suppressed the Wurtz impurity and restored consistent yields (~74 %).
Supporting_Evidence: The major process impurity ... was the Wurtz homo‑coupled impurity 14...; "low‑temperature conditions were used and reduced equivalents of the Grignard reagent 2b were implemented"; "The earlier direct quench ... was replaced by a simplified reverse quench..."; "Wurtz impurity 14 was not detected in 4"

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Alkylation of phenol 6 with bromide 7 required >50 h at 80 °C using heterogeneous K₂CO₃, and the one‑pot telescoped sequence showed inconsistent reaction times (6–17 h for alkylation, 12–20 h for amidation).
Solution_Description: A homogeneous 25 % NaOMe/MeOH base in DMF was adopted, enabling rapid alkylation (1–2 h) and telescoped amidation, reducing overall reaction time >50 % and eliminating heterogeneity.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction time for this step typically exceeded 50 h...; "The one‑pot process did not scale up consistently in terms of the reaction time for both the alkylation (6–17 h) and the amidation (12–20 h)"; "It was found that commercially available 25 % NaOMe in MeOH was a convenient and inexpensive reagent... the alkylation condition was developed using 1.06 equiv NaOMe/1.10 equiv 7 in DMF... reached completion in 1–2 h"

Paper Title: Synthesis of Vixotrigine, a Voltage- and Use-Dependent Sodium Channel Blocker. Part 2: Development of a Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Boc deprotection with p‑TsOH/MeOH generated a mutagenic methyl p‑toluenesulfonate impurity and required six extractions, increasing waste and cost.

Problem_Description: The original hydrogenation used 5 % Pd/C (7.5 wt %) and required long reaction times (≥5 h), leading to lower yields (≈87 %) and high catalyst cost.
Solution_Description: Pearlman’s 20 % Pd(OH)₂/C catalyst was introduced at 1–3 wt %, providing higher activity, shorter reaction time (2 h), and improved yield (92 %).

Problem_Description: HCl salt formation from ethanol produced a metastable solvate that shattered on drying, giving a wide particle‑size distribution (d₅₀ ≈ 15–20 µm) and poor flow, with batch‑to‑batch variability in fines content.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: The original manufacturing route relied on simulated moving‑bed (SMB) chromatography to separate the phosphorus diastereomers and on a benzyloxymethyl chloride (BOMCl) alkylation that was highly sensitive to electrophile quality. The diastereomer‑separation step contributed 36 % of production time and 20 % of total PMI, while the alkylation often required additional charges to reach full conversion. Moreover, the intermediates in the displacement step were prone to hydrolytic degradation, necessitating strictly anhydrous conditions.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route was designed that eliminated SMB by employing selective crystallization for diastereomer resolution and replaced the BOMCl alkylation with a benzyloxycarbonyl (Cbz) protecting group. The new route uses a telescoped five‑step sequence (silylation, Abramov reaction, Cbz protection, hydrolysis) performed in DCM/toluene, and the diastereomeric mixture is resolved by cooling crystallization from MTBE, CPME or toluene, drastically reducing cost, lead time and PMI.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The SMB accounts for 36 % of the production time and 20 % of the total PMI', 'The BOMCl alkylation step (step 1) turned out to be sensitive to the quality of the electrophile and often required additional charges to reach full conversion', 'The intermediates involved in the displacement reaction (step 2) were found to be highly susceptible to hydrolytic degradation, thus requiring strictly anhydrous conditions']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: Attempts to benzylate the phosphonamidate fragment 1 using standard alkylation conditions (hydride bases or Ag₂O) caused rapid decomposition of the substrate, preventing efficient synthesis of benzyl‑substituted analogues for crystallization studies.
Solution_Description: Acid‑catalyzed benzylation using trichloroacetimidates was employed, enabling the preparation of several crystalline benzyl analogues (27a–d) without degrading the phosphonamidate core.
Supporting_Evidence: ['However, such conditions resulted in the rapid decomposition of 1, and alternative benzylation conditions (benzylic bromide and organic/inorganic base) were equally unsuccessful', 'Acid‑catalyzed benzylation using trichloroacetimidates allowed for the preparation of several analogues']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: The deprotection of the benzylic chiral auxiliary by hydrogenolysis required very high palladium catalyst loadings (40–76 mol % each of Pd/C and Pd(OH)₂/C) and prolonged reaction times (up to 6 days), leading to low step efficiency and elevated material cost.
Solution_Description: Switching to the Cbz protecting group reduced the catalyst loading to 2 mol % each of Pd/C and Pd(OH)₂/C, shortened the hydrogenolysis to 6 h, and gave a cleaner reaction profile, improving overall yield and process economics.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Full conversion of 18 to 1 could only be achieved with a high loading of a mixture of Pd/C and Pd‑(OH)₂/C (76 mol % each), under 4 bar H₂ at 60 °C over 6 days', 'In comparison to the benzyl group deprotection in the previous route, the Cbz deprotection requires half the catalyst loading (0.05 vs 0.1 S, or 2 vs 4 mol %), proceeds in a much shorter reaction time (6 h vs ca. 3 days)']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: Selective crystallization of the benzylated analogue 27a from a near‑racemic mixture failed because the diastereomers formed a quasi‑racemic solid that did not enrich upon cooling, limiting the ability to isolate the desired diastereomer.
Solution_Description: Alternative benzylated analogues (e.g., 27c with a 9‑anthracenylmethyl group) were investigated. 27c displayed a slight thermodynamic preference for the desired diastereomer, and selective crystallization from solvent/antisolvent mixtures (e.g., EtOAc/heptane, iPrOH, THF) successfully enriched the product up to 99:1 dr, demonstrating a viable route for diastereomeric enrichment via crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: ['When crystallization was attempted starting from a 51:49 mixture, no enrichment was observed (entries 5–8)', 'The solids were nearly 50:50 mixtures of diastereomers and were identified by XRPD as a new solid form', 'Crystallization experiments ... showed improvement of the dr from 74:26 up to 98:2 (entries 1–4)']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: Hydrogenolysis of the 9‑anthracenylmethyl protected analogue 27c was problematic because the aromatic ring underwent competing reduction, yielding >40 % of a reduced by‑product (compound 29) and compromising the isolation of the target.
Solution_Description: The authors noted the limitation and deprioritized the 9‑anthracenylmethyl protecting group in favor of the Cbz strategy, effectively avoiding the decomposition pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: ['the 9‑anthracenylmethyl group cannot be removed easily under hydrogenolytic conditions due to the competing reduction of the 9,10‑ring, resulting in >40 % of compound 29']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: In the DYKAT approach using various O‑ and N‑substituted phosphonic dichlorides, the diastereoselectivity was highly dependent on the base and leaving group, with some conditions favoring the undesired R‑phosphorus diastereomer, leading to inconsistent yields and selectivity.
Solution_Description: A sequence using TsO‑phosphonic dichloride 23 and 3‑nitrophenol as a leaving group was established. After displacement with sodium phenolate, the desired S‑diastereomer 26 was obtained in 85:15 dr, providing a reliable method to obtain the target stereochemistry despite initial selectivity challenges.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The TsO‑phosphonic dichloride 23, combined with 24, yields excellent levels of selectivity (96:4 dr), yet favoring the undesired R‑diastereomer', 'the high R‑selectivity could be turned to our advantage by carrying out the displacement with 3‑nitrophenol (yielding 25), followed by treatment with sodium phenolate', 'Through this sequence, the desired S‑diastereomer 26 was obtained in 85:15 dr']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: The target phosphonamidate 1 and its R‑epimer 30 exhibit dramatically different solubilities; 30 is ~20‑50× more soluble than 1 in many solvents, making selective crystallization challenging without careful solvent selection.
Solution_Description: Solvent screening identified toluene, CPME, and MTBE as suitable for selective crystallization. Cooling a 50:50 1/30 mixture in MTBE (15 V) to –24 °C yielded pure 1 (100 % purity, 100 % dr), demonstrating that appropriate solvent choice enables efficient isolation of the desired diastereomer.
Supporting_Evidence: ['1 displays low solubility (<40 mg/g) in aromatic hydrocarbons, butyl esters, and ethers', '30 is approximately 20 times more soluble than 1 in ethers and 50 times more soluble in aromatic hydrocarbons', 'MTBE proved to be superior as it afforded 1 as a single diastereomer in high purity (entry 3)']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: The original hydrogenolysis step required multi‑day reaction times (up to 6 days) under high catalyst loadings, significantly extending the manufacturing timeline.
Solution_Description: The optimized hydrogenolysis using 10 % Pd/C at 3.5 bar H₂ and 60 °C completed in 6 h with only 2 mol % catalyst, drastically reducing reaction time and facilitating downstream crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Full conversion of 18 to 1 could only be achieved with a high loading ... over 6 days', 'In comparison to the benzyl group deprotection in the previous route, the Cbz deprotection requires half the catalyst loading ... proceeds in a much shorter reaction time (6 h vs ca. 3 days)']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part III): Evolution of the Synthetic Process to the Phosphonamidate Fragment
Problem_Description: The five‑step telescoped sequence for producing intermediate 35 suffered from variable impurity levels (phenol and triphenyl phosphite) in commercial diphenyl phosphite, impacting overall yield and material cost.
Solution_Description: A robust silylation/ Abramov protocol using BSTFA in DCM/toluene at 90 °C gave >99 % conversion to 31 and >99.9 % to 32, tolerating the impurities. Subsequent aqueous work‑up with potassium chloride and controlled hydrolysis minimized phenol loss, delivering 35 in 60–70 % overall yield (78 % corrected for diphenyl phosphite purity).
