Paper Title: pH-Dependent Degradation of T3P-Related Byproducts
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of API 5 the product batches sometimes displayed an unexpected PXRD peak (2θ ≈ 6.4°). The impurity responsible was identified as the disodium salt of phosphonate 2, which precipitated from the reaction/isolations despite being highly water‑soluble under most conditions. Its low solubility in the acetonitrile/water antisolvent caused it to co‑precipitate with the API, complicating isolation and purification.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was modified to (i) acidify the reaction mixture to pH 1, (ii) heat the mixture to 80 °C for 1–2 h to convert the sodium phosphonate 2 to the more water‑soluble propylphosphonic acid 3, and (iii) subsequently wash the crude API 5 with an acetonitrile/water mixture (1 : 4) to solubilize and remove the impurity. This combination of pH adjustment, elevated temperature, and a mixed‑solvent wash eliminated the PXRD impurity and restored product purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “PXRD analysis of the product after additional washing with water or acetonitrile/water mixtures revealed the absence of the peak at 2θ ≈ 6.4°, indicating that the impurity was soluble in water.”
• “The disodium salt of 2 was isolated … and matched the unidentified peak.”
• “Acidified to pH 1 and warmed to 80 °C … showed the anticipated shift … conversion of 2 to 3 … no change in the API (5) was observed by UPLC.”
• “Solubility data were collected for 2·2Na⁺ … >95 % solubility in 1:4 acetonitrile/water.”
• “Application of the conditions shown to degrade 2 were incorporated into the amidation reaction workup … acidified to pH 1 and warmed to 80 °C … further washing of 5 to remove 2 was carried out because of ease of implementation.”

Paper Title: pH-Dependent Degradation of T3P-Related Byproducts
Problem_Description: In the synthesis of the picolinamide ligand 6, phosphonate esters 9 and 10 formed as major by‑products (≈ 40 % area) under the basic T3P amidation conditions. Their high concentration interfered with product isolation, required additional distillation steps, and reduced overall isolated yield of the desired ligand.
Solution_Description: After the amidation, the reaction mixture was acidified to pH 1 with concentrated HCl and held (often at reflux) until the phosphonate esters were fully degraded to the target ligand 6. The pH was then readjusted to 5 to precipitate the product, which was isolated by filtration. Methanol was added during distillation to assist the degradation and to control the pH drop to 5–6 where precipitation occurred.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Phosphonate ester impurities 9 and 10 were observed and accounted for approximately 40 area % of the product distribution at reaction completion prior to quench.”
• “It was somewhat unexpected that phosphonate esters 9 and 10 were stable under strongly basic conditions and required reflux in methanol for degradation.”
• “Under standard conditions … the mixture was divided … pH adjusted to either 1, 3, 5, or 12 … phosphonate esters 9 and 10 rapidly degraded to form 6 at low pH, with lower rates at pH 3 and 5 and very little degradation at pH 12.”
• “Upon consumption of 7, the reaction mixture was acidified to pH 1 with concentrated HCl and held until 9 and 10 had fully converted to 6. Readjustment to pH 5 allowed for precipitation of the product and isolation.”

Paper Title: pH-Dependent Degradation of T3P-Related Byproducts
Problem_Description: The addition of T3P (50 wt % solution) to the amine/acid mixture can generate a rapid exotherm, especially at larger scale, and the reaction mixture can become heterogeneous if not properly managed, potentially leading to poor heat removal and uneven conversion.
Solution_Description: T3P was added dropwise (over 30 min) while maintaining the reaction temperature at 25 °C, and triethylamine was added in a controlled manner to keep the exotherm under control. This controlled addition prevented runaway temperature spikes and ensured a homogeneous reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “T3P‑mediated amidations are commonly conducted … sometimes at low temperature to control the exotherm that may occur upon addition of T3P.”
• “To the white suspension was added triethylamine (3.00 eq) in a controlled manner to maintain an exotherm at 25 °C.”
• “1‑Propanephosphonic acid cyclic anhydride … was added dropwise over 30 min while the temperature was maintained at 25 °C. During the addition, the reaction mixture became homogeneous.”

Paper Title: The Impact of Solvent Quality on the Heck Reaction: Detection of Hydroperoxide in 1‑Methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP)
Problem_Description: Hydroperoxide (NMP‑5‑OOH) formed in aged NMP oxidises the phosphine ligand (P(o‑tol)₃) to its oxide, deactivating the palladium catalyst and dramatically slowing or stopping the Heck reaction.
Solution_Description: Replace the contaminated NMP with a fresh bottle that contains no detectable NMP‑5‑OOH, thereby preventing ligand oxidation and restoring normal reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The old bottle of NMP used in the reaction was the root cause. Over time, NMP had reacted with O₂ in the air to form 5‑hydroperoxy‑1‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidinone (NMP‑5‑OOH)… which oxidized the P(o‑tol)₃ ligand to O‑P(o‑tol)₃ and ultimately slowed down the Heck reaction.", "When the NMP containing 0.46 mol % of the hydroperoxide was used, 15 % area of 1 still remained after 2 h, and the reaction could not reach the same level of completion (<0.2 % area) even after an extended reaction time."]

Paper Title: The Impact of Solvent Quality on the Heck Reaction: Detection of Hydroperoxide in 1‑Methyl-2-pyrrolidinone (NMP)
Problem_Description: Inconsistent reaction performance (slow or stalled Heck reactions) was observed despite rigorous N₂ purges and low O₂ levels, because the presence of NMP‑5‑OOH varied between solvent batches.
Solution_Description: Implement strict solvent‑quality control: store NMP under nitrogen, label bottles with opening date, discard opened bottles after ≤1 year, and perform ¹H‑NMR screening for hydroperoxide before each campaign.

Problem_Description: NMP is a peroxide‑forming solvent; if stored improperly it accumulates hazardous hydroperoxides, posing safety and compliance risks during large‑scale handling.

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: The original discovery route required a high palladium catalyst loading (4 mol % Pd) for the amination step, making palladium depletion problematic and driving up the material cost.
Solution_Description: The route was redesigned to a direct palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling of the pyrazole amide with the heteroaryl bromide, allowing the catalyst loading to be lowered to 0.5 mol % (and eventually 0.25 mol %).

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Intermediate heteroaromatic amine 4 triggered a mutagenic alert and was classified as a high‑hazard substance, requiring special equipment and protective measures.
Solution_Description: An amine‑free pathway was pursued, replacing the hazardous amine intermediate with a direct coupling of the pyrazole amide to avoid handling of the genotoxic compound.
Supporting_Evidence: “Intermediate heteroaromatic amine 4 triggered a mutagenic alert … and was classified as a substance of high hazard … isolation and handling … needed special equipment and personal protection.”; “We started to explore alternatives toward a more efficient amine‑free route … identified the palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling … as the most promising option.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Initial screening of reported catalytic systems (Pd₂dba₃/Xantphos in dioxane) gave extremely low conversion, and other ligand/solvent combinations (t‑BuXPhos, Me₄tBuXPhos in t‑BuOH) also performed poorly.
Solution_Description: t‑Butyl alcohol was identified as the optimal solvent for Pd₂dba₃/Xantphos, delivering full conversion and 98 % yield after 3 h at reflux; Xantphos was retained as the key ligand to suppress side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, we observed extremely low conversion. … On the other hand, the last‑generation Buchwald ligand AdBrettPhos … displayed reasonable conversion but very low selectivity.”; “Modification of the base and solvent … led to the identification of t‑butyl alcohol as the optimal solvent for the Pd₂dba₃/Xantphos combination. With K₂CO₃ as the base, full conversion and 98 % yield were obtained after 3 h at reflux.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: When the reaction was scaled 8‑fold, conversion dropped to 64 % after 3 h; the base particle size (K₂CO₃) was identified as a factor affecting kinetics, and batch‑to‑batch variation made grinding infeasible on large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Fine grinding of K₂CO₃ restored consistent conversions, but because grinding is impractical at scale, the team performed an extensive base/solvent screening (which ultimately left t‑BuOH as essential) and treated the issue as a mass‑transfer problem, opting for a robust protocol that does not rely on finely ground base.
Supporting_Evidence: “When we performed the reaction on an 8 times larger scale, … conversion plummet to 64 % after 3 h … Examination of the different reaction parameters pointed to the base particle size as a possible factor … Since the particle size is often batch‑ and supplier‑dependent … grinding is not feasible for large‑scale production, we were forced to find an alternative solution.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Using isopropanol as a solvent gave the desired coupling but caused 5–9 % transesterification to the isopropyl ester side product, complicating isolation.
Solution_Description: Switching to ethanol eliminated the transesterification side reaction; the product’s low solubility in ethanol was then exploited by concentration and simple filtration to isolate the product in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Full conversion and high selectivity were achieved … The major side reaction observed was transesterification to the isopropyl ester … Consequently, … we decided to try ethanol as a solvent. Pleasingly, the coupling was achieved … with no major side product detected … Because of the low solubility of the product in ethanol, simple volume concentration followed by filtration allowed the isolation of the product in 93–96 % yield.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: At the very low catalyst loading (0.13 mol % Pd), the reaction rate slowed, allowing competing side‑products to form and reducing isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Increasing the catalyst loading back to 0.25 mol % (or 0.5 mol % for more demanding substrates) restored rapid conversion and improved yields, albeit at a modest increase in metal use.
Supporting_Evidence: “With amide 8a the coupling … could be achieved with only 0.13 mol % Pd … However, the isolated yield … was lower … likely, as the coupling reaction rate slows down at lower catalyst loading, the formation of side‑products becomes competitive.”; “The catalyst loading could be reduced to 0.25 mol % without erosion of conversion and yield (entry 8).”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Imidazopyridine substrate 10a underwent ester hydrolysis during the reaction, eroding yield and creating an additional impurity.
Solution_Description: Doubling the catalyst loading (to 0.5 mol % Pd) shortened the reaction time to 3 h, minimizing hydrolysis and delivering the product in ~90 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Imidazopyridine 10a underwent hydrolysis of the ester functionality during the reaction, causing a slight erosion of the yield.”; “Importantly, doubling the catalyst loading shortened the reaction time to 3 h, and the product was isolated in 90 % yield with minimal hydrolysis observed.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Aryl bromide 11e (methyl‑substituted) showed very low reactivity (only 66 % conversion after 22 h) and gave a poor 15 % HPLC yield.
Solution_Description: The authors note that higher catalyst loadings and longer reaction times are required for such sluggish substrates; although not fully optimized, the strategy suggests increasing Pd loading and/or temperature to drive conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Replacing the aryl substituent with a methyl group dramatically suppressed the reactivity … only 66 % of 11e was converted after 22 h, and product 12e was observed in a poor 15 % HPLC yield. … This behavior is currently quite difficult to rationalize … catalyst poisoning cannot be excluded.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Screening of various phosphine ligands led to predominant hydrodehalogenation and C–O coupling side‑products, especially with primary/secondary alcohol solvents.
Solution_Description: Bulky, electron‑rich biaryl phosphines (e.g., Xantphos, AdBrettPhos) were found to suppress β‑hydride elimination and the undesired C–O coupling, restoring selective C–N coupling; ethanol as solvent further limited side‑reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “The bidentate ligand BINAP … led to … dehalogenation … The two Buchwald phosphines … suppressed the formation of the debromination side product almost completely and promoted the coupling with ethanol itself, giving rise to aryl ether 14 as the main product.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Pd₂dba₃ and Xantphos have limited solubility in alcoholic solvents, potentially affecting catalyst activation.
Solution_Description: The catalyst/ligand mixture was premixed in a minimal volume of THF before being added to the alcoholic reaction mixture, ensuring better dissolution and homogeneous catalysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “As Pd₂dba₃ and Xantphos are scarcely soluble in alcoholic solvents, we envisaged premixing them in a minimal volume of THF and then adding the resulting mixture to the reaction.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: The original three‑step synthesis required protecting‑group manipulations and generated waste, increasing overall process cost and making purification more labor‑intensive.
Solution_Description: The amide‑coupling route eliminated the need for the amine intermediate and protecting‑group steps, reducing material usage, waste, and simplifying work‑up (filtration and washing), thereby lowering cost and purification effort.
Supporting_Evidence: “The synthesis … was one step shorter.”; “The direct palladium‑catalyzed amidation displays an increased yield (85 % vs 65 %), improved atom economy (83 % vs 66 %), and higher mass efficiency (80 % vs 60 %). … avoids compounds 4 and N‑protecting group manipulations and requires 4 times less palladium directly impacting the overall process cost and purification effort.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling of Pyrazole Amides with Triazolo- and Imidazopyridine Bromides in Ethanol
Problem_Description: Handling of the high‑hazard amine 4 required exposure limits below 1 µg m⁻³, demanding special equipment and protective measures.
Solution_Description: By bypassing the isolated amine 4 altogether and using a direct C–N coupling of the pyrazole amide, the hazardous intermediate is never generated, eliminating the safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: “Intermediate heteroaromatic amine 4 triggered a mutagenic alert … and was classified as a substance of high hazard … meaning that the isolation and handling of the compound needed special equipment and personal protection … we started to explore alternatives toward a more efficient amine‑free route.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: The oxidative elimination generates large amounts of oxygen gas as Oxone decomposes, creating a fire‑ and explosion‑hazard, especially in the flammable MEK solvent.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A nitrogen sweep (200 L min⁻¹, up to 400 L min⁻¹) continuously dilutes the oxygen evolved; the head‑space O₂ concentration is monitored and limited to ≤8 % (later ≤6 %). Oxone and base are added over a minimum of 7 h to spread the exotherm and keep pH stable.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction generated a large amount of oxygen gas… a nitrogen sweep … coupled with constant monitoring of headspace oxygen concentration.”; “To mitigate the risk of combustion, large‑scale batches incorporated a nitrogen sweep… (200 L min⁻¹, sized to permit flow rates up to 400 L min⁻¹).”; “The process was amended to target a minimum addition time of 7 h… to accommodate the exotherm.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: Achieving full conversion required a very large excess of Oxone (up to 37 equiv), which inflated processing volumes (≈85 L kg⁻¹ reaction, ≈115 L kg⁻¹ after work‑up) and limited throughput.
Solution_Description: A “put‑and‑take” protocol was developed: only a portion of Oxone (and base) is added each cycle, the aqueous phase is removed, fresh MEK/buffer is replenished, and the cycle is repeated. This reduces the maximum reaction volume to ≈25 L kg⁻¹ while still delivering full conversion with only 15 equiv of Oxone.
Supporting_Evidence: “We envisioned a stepwise, ‘put and take’ protocol which would involve adding only a portion of the Oxone and hydroxide initially… the protocol also requires fresh MEK to be added with each cycle.”; “After accounting for the addition of base, the Vmax … is ca. 25 L kg⁻¹… only 15 equiv of Oxone to achieve full conversion.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: The substrate and product are hydrolytically unstable; pH drift outside the narrow 6.5‑7.5 window leads to rapid degradation (phosphanimine hydrolysis < pH 5, phosphonamidate cleavage > pH 8).
Solution_Description: Sodium hydroxide in a 0.5 M phosphate buffer (pH 7) was used to maintain neutral pH throughout the Oxone addition. Later an automated feedback pH‑control loop continuously adjusted hydroxide feed based on a real‑time probe reading, keeping the pH within the target range.
Supporting_Evidence: “Maintaining neutral pH is critical for stability of both substrate and product… a working pH range of 6.5–7.5 (target 7.0) was established.”; “Simultaneous addition of both solutions of Oxone and sodium hydroxide at a constant rate… continuously monitoring pH to confirm neutrality (6.5–7.5).”; “Feedback pH control … the addition of hydroxide is automatically and continuously modulated based on a real‑time reading of pH.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: During scale‑up inorganic sulfate salts precipitated, fouling the pH probe and causing a batch failure (complete hydrolysis after over‑charging base).
Solution_Description: Lithium hydroxide was substituted for sodium hydroxide; lithium sulfate is far more soluble, eliminating solid precipitation while preserving the needed basicity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The next batch failed due to precipitation of inorganic solids that blinded the pH probe… To resolve this issue … the electrode was placed … successful in the next batch.”; “Since lithium sulfate is significantly more soluble than either sodium or potassium sulfate, the reaction was evaluated using lithium hydroxide and exhibited a significant reduction in solid precipitation.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: When the Oxone solution was charged in ≤ 60 min, conversion dropped dramatically, demonstrating that rapid addition cannot sustain the required reaction rate.
Solution_Description: Oxone addition time was extended to at least 7 h (≈ 6 h for a 50 kg batch) to spread the exotherm, keep pH under control, and allow full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Poor conversion was observed when the Oxone solution was charged within 60 min.”; “The process was amended to target a minimum addition time of 7 h… This addition time also simplified pH control…”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: Oxone loses active oxygen rapidly in buffered aqueous media (≈ 70 % loss after 4 h, ≈ 95 % after 24 h), which forces the use of large excesses.
Solution_Description: Switching from fully miscible acetone to partially miscible methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) reduced water content in the organic phase, slowing Oxone degradation and allowing lower excess (still high, but improved).
Supporting_Evidence: “Solutions of Oxone in neutral phosphate buffer (pH 7) showed rapid loss of oxidant… > 70 % loss after 4 h.”; “The stability data prompted us to consider the use of methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) as the reaction solvent… reactions in MEK proceeded more cleanly… although significantly more Oxone was required….”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: At 185 g scale, the reaction gave only 31 % isolated yield because of substrate and product degradation in the aqueous phase.
Solution_Description: MEK was adopted as the organic solvent, sodium hydroxide (instead of bicarbonate) was used to provide stronger, more controllable base, and a phosphate buffer kept pH neutral, all of which together raised conversion (> 99 %) and isolated yields (up to 83 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “When the reaction was performed at 185 g scale, significant decomposition was observed and the desired product… was obtained in only 31 % isolated yield.”; “Compared to acetone… reactions in MEK proceeded more cleanly… the use of sodium hydroxide as the base allowed for more facile pH control and eliminated the vigorous off‑gassing… Successful 100 g scale with good purity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part II): Dynamic Control for Successful Scale-Up of an Oxygen-Releasing Elimination Reaction Mediated by Oxone
Problem_Description: Manual adjustment of hydroxide feed to maintain pH was labor‑intensive and prone to error, especially at larger scale.
Solution_Description: A Reaction Controller (J‑Kem) with a proportional‑only feedback loop was installed; the controller automatically modulated the peristaltic pump delivering lithium hydroxide according to the pH probe signal, eliminating manual intervention and improving robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “At laboratory scale, reactions were somewhat simplified by employing feedback pH control… The controller utilized proportional‑only control and was easy to tune in real‑time during processing; …no overshoot was observed.”

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: The original batch methylation of octacycle 1 gave inconsistent conversion (often <85 %) and required multiple charges of base and iodomethane to reach ≥97.5 % conversion, resulting in low isolated yield (≈52 %). Over‑methylation produced the impurity 3 (46‑Me‑397) which was difficult to purge.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Rapid, all‑at‑once addition of KHMDS (base) and MeI (methylating agent) within 5 s, together with stoichiometric water, gave complete conversion in a single charge. The reaction was translated to continuous flow (PFR for deprotonation, CSTR cascade for methylation) to ensure rapid base addition, precise stoichiometry, and short residence times, eliminating the need for multiple charges and reducing impurity 3 formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The methylation reaction typically did not reach greater than 85 % conversion with the initial charges of KHMDS and iodomethane… over‑methylation… impurity 3 … difficult to purge” (p. 2). 
• “Complete conversion was consistently achieved with a single charge of reagents when water was present… rapid base addition… within 5 s” (Table 1, p. 3). 
• “Rapid addition of base… necessary to achieve complete and consistent conversion” (Table 2, p. 4). 
• “A continuous process was developed… rapid base addition and short deprotonation residence time” (Abstract, p. 1). 
• “Proof‑of‑concept continuous flow ... >96 % conversion using appropriate reagent stoichiometries (3.2 eq KHMDS, 3.2 eq MeI, 1.4–1.6 eq water)” (Fig. 2, p. 5).

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: The reactive potassium di‑salt 1b formed after deprotonation aggregates over time, leading to particle growth (≈100 nm → 1 µm) and loss of reactivity; conversion drops to <5 % after prolonged aging.
Solution_Description: Keeping the KHMDS addition rapid (all at once) and limiting the aging time to ≤60 s prevents aggregation. Kinetic studies showed the deprotonation window must be ≤60 s, so the process uses a short‑residence‑time PFR for deprotonation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The vinyl carbon peak moved… after the addition of KHMDS… after extended aging… signals no longer detectable… suggesting aggregation” (Fig. 1, p. 4). 
• “DLS studies… particles grew to about 1 µm after 2 days of aging” (p. 4). 
• “Conversion decreased toward a minimum of 4 % as the reactive potassium di‑salt 1b solution was aged” (p. 4). 
• “Slow addition of KHMDS negatively impacted conversion (≈91 %)… rapid addition necessary” (Table 2, p. 4). 
• “Kinetic studies… deprotonation should be no more than 60 s due to deactivation of 1b via aggregation” (Fig. 4, p. 7).

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: During continuous operation, potassium iodide (KI) precipitated and clogged the static mixer and PFR tubing, causing pressure spikes and system shutdowns; the fine KI slurry also damaged Gore STA‑PURE pump tubing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The methylation step was moved from the PFR to a continuously‑stirred vessel (CSTR) which tolerates slurry transfer. Parallel static‑mixers/PFRs with switching valves were added for redundancy, and a methanol‑based solvent‑cleaning procedure (followed by THF flush) was integrated to remove KI deposits without dismantling equipment. Tubing material was upgraded to larger‑diameter PFA/PFL where needed.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The major by‑product… potassium iodide (KI)… observed to clog the tubing during extended runs” (p. 5). 
• “Performing the methylation in a CSTR was an effective solution to mitigate the constant clogging” (Fig. 3, p. 5). 
• “Clogging in the static mixer and PFR occurred… precipitate hypothesized to be KOH… pressure drops… cleaning with methanol…” (p. 9). 
• “Two parallel static mixer/PFR stages equipped with switching valves” (p. 9). 
• “Abrasive potassium iodide slurry damaged the Gore STA‑PURE PFL tubing … spare tubing was available and replaced” (p. 9).

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch inconsistencies in conversion and impurity levels were observed, making the process unreliable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Implementation of stoichiometric water (instead of azeotropic drying) stabilized the reaction, and rapid, simultaneous addition of base and MeI removed the need for additional charges, yielding consistent >99 % conversion and low impurity 3. Precise stoichiometry and an amine quench further standardized the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Batch‑to‑batch inconsistencies in reaction conversion and selectivity were experienced” (p. 2). 
• “Rapid base addition and the presence of stoichiometric water … critical to ensure consistent levels of reaction conversion” (Abstract). 
• “Complete conversion was consistently achieved … when water was present” (Table 1, p. 3). 
• “Rapid addition of base… necessary to achieve complete and consistent conversion” (Table 2, p. 4). 
• “Amine reaction quench … to consume excess iodomethane and prevent impurity 3 formation” (p. 5).

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: The original isolation required two crystallizations and a silica plug, resulting in a low overall isolated yield (≈52 %) and high impurity 3 (≈0.8 %).
Solution_Description: The downstream work‑up was streamlined: KI filtration, aqueous NaOH/NaCl washes, solvent exchange, and a single form‑setting crystallization from denatured ethanol/acetate. This reduced unit operations from 11 to 6 and increased overall yield to 76 % with >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Initial isolation… silica plug, and two crystallizations… low yield (52 %) and variable impurities” (p. 2). 
• “Optimized isolation consisted of a KI filtration, extractive washes, solvent exchange, and aqueous acetic acid/ethanol crystallization” (Sec 2.4, p. 11). 
• Table 4 shows yield improvement from 52 % (initial) to 76 % (GMP & second‑gen) and reduction of unit operations (11 → 6). 
• “The optimized process reduced the number of unit operations in the isolation to increase manufacturing efficiency” (p. 2).

Paper Title: Implementing Continuous Manufacturing for the Final Methylation Step in the AMG 397 Process to Deliver Key Quality Attributes
Problem_Description: During the 1 kg GMP run, pressure spikes and pump‑head failures occurred due to solid buildup and tubing erosion, extending the overall run time by ~30 % and risking equipment integrity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A cleaning‑on‑the‑fly protocol (methanol flush at 10 psi above baseline) was instituted, and spare tubing was kept on hand to replace damaged sections. The equipment design was revised to include pressure‑controlled switches and more robust tubing dimensions, minimizing downtime and preserving safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The system exhibited more frequent pressure spikes and required constant start, stop, and cleaning” (p. 9). 
• “Abrasive potassium iodide slurry damaged the Gore STA‑PURE PFL tubing … replaced when necessary” (p. 9). 
• “Methanol solvent flush… initiated by a system pressure increase, 10 psi above the 15 psi baseline, allowed intermittent cleaning without dismantling the equipment” (p. 9). 
• “The reaction run time was 30 % longer than expected, but the product quality was not compromised” (p. 9).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable and Sublimation-Free Route to MTAD
Problem_Description: The original literature‑based route started from dimethylurea (2) → nitrosylation gave the N‑nitroso compound 3, which is highly carcinogenic, and its thermolysis in boiling water released methyl isocyanate (a volatile toxic gas). Paper Title: Case-Based Thermal Safety Evaluation on a Pharmaceutical Process Using Dimethyl Sulfoxide as a Solvent
Problem_Description: During a SEDEX safety‑screening test the rupture disc of the autoclave burst when the oven temperature reached ≈182 °C.  The burst was accompanied by a rapid rise in sample temperature, pressure and a sulfide‑like odor, indicating an uncontrolled, highly exothermic, autocatalytic decomposition of DMSO that generated large amounts of gas.
Solution_Description: A reaction‑calorimetry (RC1) experiment was performed to map the heat‑flow of the desired hydroamination and the process was deliberately run at a lower temperature (75 °C) with a controlled heating profile and adequate reactor cooling.  The pilot‑plant reactor was equipped with a Hastelloy‑lined 1 L glass vessel, a downward impeller and a jacket capable of maintaining the temperature well below the DMSO decomposition region, thereby eliminating the runaway condition observed in the SEDEX autoclave.
Supporting_Evidence: “A rupture disc of the Parr autoclave … burst … as the oven temperature (T_O) arrived at around 182 °C … the curves of sample temperature (T_S), temperature difference (ΔT), and pressure increased dramatically, indicating that a highly exothermic reaction … was undergoing.”; “The RC1 results indicated that the main reaction was exothermic but at a moderate level … The maximum heat flow rate (9 W/kg) … could be generally controlled by the reactor cooling capacity in the plant.”; “The reaction was held at 75 °C for more than 4 h … the reaction temperature was decreased from the original 85 to 75 °C based on the identified thermal hazards of DMSO.”

Paper Title: Case-Based Thermal Safety Evaluation on a Pharmaceutical Process Using Dimethyl Sulfoxide as a Solvent
Problem_Description: The autocatalytic decomposition of DMSO is dramatically accelerated by several process components (CuCl, compound 1, compound 2).  DSC of mixtures showed peak heat‑flows up to 11 W g⁻¹, far larger than pure DMSO (1 W g⁻¹), indicating that trace contact with these substances can trigger a severe hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Prior to scale‑up a series of milligram‑scale DSC screenings of each individual material and of binary mixtures with DMSO were instituted.  The protocol mandates that DMSO never be pre‑mixed with accelerating species and that any potential foreign matter (e.g., stainless‑steel powder, rust) be rigorously excluded from the feed streams.  Process‑equipment cleaning and material‑hand‑off procedures were tightened to avoid inadvertent contact.
Supporting_Evidence: “Exothermic profiles of DMSO/substance mixtures are quite distinct … each individual exothermic peak has a higher value than that of pure DMSO, indicating that all of these substances can accelerate the decomposition of DMSO.”; “The mixture of DMSO with compound 1 has the lowest decomposition temperature at around 158 °C … The CuCl and compound 2 dramatically accelerated the decomposition of DMSO.”; “It is recommended to perform a milligram‑scale screening test first, such as DSC scan, to get a preliminary thermal behavior profile before conducting any gram‑scale test.”

Paper Title: Case-Based Thermal Safety Evaluation on a Pharmaceutical Process Using Dimethyl Sulfoxide as a Solvent

Solution_Description: Scale‑up was performed in a 1 L glass reactor equipped with a Hastelloy insert, a high‑speed impeller (400 rpm) and a well‑controlled cooling jacket, providing superior heat‑transfer compared with the SEDEX autoclave.  The heating rate was limited and the temperature set‑point was kept at 75 °C, far below the DMSO decomposition regime.
Supporting_Evidence: “The RC1 experiment … a 1 L glass reactor with Hastelloy inserts and a downward impeller stirrer.”; “The maximum heat flow rate (9 W/kg) … can be generally controlled by the reactor cooling capacity in the plant.”; “The reaction was heated from 25 to 75 °C … within 100 min … The reaction temperature was decreased from the original 85 to 75 °C based on the identified thermal hazards of DMSO.”

Paper Title: Case-Based Thermal Safety Evaluation on a Pharmaceutical Process Using Dimethyl Sulfoxide as a Solvent
Problem_Description: Process‑criticality assessment based on the solvent boiling point (189 °C) suggested a low‑risk class (Stoessel class 2).  However, the DMSO decomposition was found to initiate ≈50 °C below its boiling point, making the boiling point an ineffective safety barrier and introducing variability in risk assessment.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive thermal‑safety evaluation—including kinetic modeling (AKTS), determination of T_D24 and T_MTSR, and reassignment of the criticality class—was conducted.  The process temperature envelope was tightened (maximum jacket temperature limited to ≤ 150 °C) and the reactor design was upgraded to ensure that any inadvertent temperature excursions could be safely mitigated.
Supporting_Evidence: “The order of the four typical temperatures … lands in the criticality class 2 … However, the solvent decomposition in the reaction mixture has already been initiated below its boiling point. Therefore, the boiling point cannot be an intrinsic safety barrier any more.”; “Based on the kinetic parameters … T_D24 was found at 157 °C … the T_MTSR (106 °C) could be much longer than 24 h … if the mixture is heated under the maximum jacket temperature around 170 °C, the T_MR_ad can be less than 8 h, indicating a high possibility of thermal runaway.”; “The safety prediction of T_MR_ad gave a better explanation to the SEDEX burst case.”

Paper Title: Case-Based Thermal Safety Evaluation on a Pharmaceutical Process Using Dimethyl Sulfoxide as a Solvent
Problem_Description: Accurate prediction of the runaway potential required detailed kinetic parameters for the autocatalytic DMSO decomposition, which were not initially available for the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: Dynamic DSC experiments at multiple heating rates were performed on the post‑reaction mixture, and the data were fed into the AKTS software to obtain reliable kinetic models (isoconversional Friedmann analysis).  The validated model enabled calculation of T_D24, T_MTSR and T_MR_ad, providing quantitative safety metrics for scale‑up decisions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Five DSC tests were conducted under different heating rates … The fitting correlation coefficient R in AKTS kinetic modeling could be up to –0.98 … The simulation curves could almost reproduce the DSC experimental reaction rates.”; “Based on the kinetic parameters from AKTS, the T_MR_ad of the decomposition … was predicted … This supports that the decomposition runaway probability under a cooling failure scenario is low … However, if the mixture is heated … the T_MR_ad can be less than 8 h, indicating a high possibility of thermal runaway.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: Under the classical Minisci conditions the thiomethyl‑cyclopropyl substrate was oxidised to sulfoxide side‑products, reducing the amount of desired product.
Solution_Description: A more strongly reducing organophotoredox catalyst (3DPA2FBN) was introduced; its lower oxidative potential prevented oxidation of the sulfide and gave higher isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “...conversion of acid 2 to pyrimidine 3 using classical Minisci conditions… albeit with the accompanying formation of the sulfur oxidation products.”; “The product 3 is oxidised to sulfoxide 4 over extended time periods… could be controlled by identifying the optimal flow rate… In theory, the formation of sulfoxide 4 could be controlled by identifying the optimal flow rate…”; “When we compare solution yields at the shortest residence time of 4 min, … 3DPA2FBN gave a solution yield of 70 % … the change of catalyst also removed the unwanted over‑reaction sulfoxide product.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: Adding Brønsted or Lewis acids decreased conversion; a stronger acid gave lower HPLC response for product 3.
Solution_Description: The acid additive was omitted entirely; the reaction proceeded with higher yield in the additive‑free protocol.
Supporting_Evidence: “A variety of both Brønsted and Lewis acid additives resulted in the formation of 3, but surprisingly, we observed an inverse correlation between conversion to 3 … and increasing strength of the acid additive.”; “We therefore performed an experiment with no acid additive present and surprisingly found that the desired product was formed in higher yield than with any of the carboxylic acid additives present.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: During the flow reaction the solution darkened, attenuating light and causing the reaction rate to drop dramatically.
Solution_Description: Switching to the highly reducing 3DPA2FBN catalyst eliminated the need for DIPEA (which caused darkening) and restored a fast, consistent rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “We also observed very significant darkening of the reaction mixture… The solution darkening has the effect of reducing the number of photons that can reach the photocatalyst…”; “DIPEA has the ability to quench a photo‑excited catalyst, and although this appeared beneficial from a rate perspective, the resulting by‑products are likely to cause solution darkening.”; “The change of catalyst also removed the unwanted over‑reaction sulfoxide product.”; “When DIPEA was employed as an additive, a lower solution yield of 21 % was observed … more darkening of the reaction mixture was observed when DIPEA was employed as an additive.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: In batch the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law limited light penetration, requiring long residence times (≈50 min) for full conversion, which reduced throughput.
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a continuous‑flow photoreactor (FEP tubing) providing a short optical pathlength, enabling higher photon flux and shorter residence times while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because of the Beer–Lambert–Bouguer law, light penetration into the reaction solution is limited… For this reason, chemists have generally turned to flow reactor design to provide the required short pathlength for irradiation of the bulk of the solution… We were delighted to observe a 50 % solution yield… with a residence time of 50 min…”; “To render the current photo‑Minisci reaction viable… we investigated our highest yielding batch conditions … using a Vapourtec UV‑150 photochemical reactor… the use of malonic acid as an additive required a longer residence time of 100 min…”; “We initially evaluated our process in a photoflow reactor with 6 mm diameter FEP tubing… a 15 mL/min flow rate, giving a residence time of 13 min… When the process was performed at 6 mL/min to enable 33 min residence time, we observed an encouraging solution yield of 62 %.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: The reaction mixture contained DMSO, excess 2,4‑dichloropyrimidine, and the phthalimide by‑product, which were difficult to separate using conventional work‑up.
Solution_Description: An aqueous work‑up followed by heptane extraction, multiple water/DMSO washes, a solvent swap to propan‑2‑ol and crystallisation gave a scalable route to isolate product 3.
Supporting_Evidence: “We decided to trial an aqueous work‑up with an extraction into heptane. … >98 % of the product 3 was observed in the organic layer and >99 % of the phthalimide … resided in the aqueous layer. Also, almost all the DMSO was washed into the aqueous layer… The heptane solution was then switched to a propan‑2‑ol solution by performing a distillative solvent swap. Finally, the product 3 was crystallised from propan‑2‑ol using water as an antisolvent.”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: Achieving sufficient conversion required long residence times (≥50 min) in the flow reactor, limiting daily throughput.
Solution_Description: Increasing the internal diameter of the FEP tubing to 8 mm and adjusting the flow rate allowed a residence time of 33 min with higher solution yields, improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using the same reagent stoichiometry but switching to FEP tubing with 8 mm internal diameter and adjusting the flow rate accordingly to give an identical residence time of 33 min resulted in a very encouraging solution yield of 65 % (entry 3).”

Paper Title: Development and Proof of Concept for a Large-Scale Photoredox Additive-Free Minisci Reaction
Problem_Description: The initially screened photocatalysts included expensive transition‑metal complexes; cost considerations motivated selection of an organophotocatalyst.
Solution_Description: 4CzIPN, an inexpensive organic photocatalyst, was chosen for further optimisation based on cost and sustainability.
Supporting_Evidence: “The organophotoredox catalyst 4CzIPN was an attractive choice from a cost and sustainability perspective, so we decided to focus our initial reaction optimisation activities on this catalyst.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The Mitsunobu etherification step gave only 37 % isolated yield, generated large amounts of triphenylphosphine oxide waste, required column chromatography for purification and used toxic reagents (periodic acid, molybdenum hexacarbonyl) in earlier steps.
Solution_Description: The Mitsunobu step was replaced by a palladium‑catalyzed C–O cross‑coupling (new synthetic route). A rac‑BINAP/Pd(OAc)₂ catalyst system was identified as optimal, and the reaction was run in 1,4‑dioxane at 101 °C to give up to 95 % isolated yield of the ether.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Mitsunobu reaction ... was low‑yielding and required column chromatography. With the highest isolated yield being 37 % …”; “...the etherification could be performed reliably to give up to 95 % isolated yield of ether 9.”; “...rac‑BINAP was uniquely effective…”; “...the system we chose … palladium acetate, rac‑BINAP, potassium phosphate, and 1,4‑dioxane…”.

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The original route depended on cis‑aminocyclohexanol, which is expensive (≈ 730 €/100 g) and requires a troublesome synthesis, and it also used periodic acid and toxic molybdenum hexacarbonyl, posing safety concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: The process was changed to use the cheaper, readily available trans‑aminocyclohexanol (≈ 161 €/100 g), eliminating the need for periodic acid and molybdenum hexacarbonyl. The new route therefore reduced material cost and avoided hazardous reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Price difference between the two isomers … trans‑aminocyclohexanol = 160.90 €/100 g; cis‑aminocyclohexanol = 729.50 €/100 g.”; “...use of periodic acid and toxic molybdenum hexacarbonyl on a larger scale had to be avoided.”; “...use of the cheaper and more readily accessible trans‑amino alcohol 13 allowed us to bypass the use of periodic acid and toxic molybdenum hexacarbonyl.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Even after extensive optimization of the Mitsunobu reaction (different azodicarboxylates, slow addition of triphenylphosphine), the isolated yield remained low (max 37 %) and required tedious column chromatography to remove triphenylphosphine oxide.
Solution_Description: The optimal Mitsunobu protocol employed slow, portionwise addition of triphenylphosphine in toluene at 40 °C, and the resulting triphenylphosphine oxide was removed by crystallization from toluene and washes with DMSO and water, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Slow addition of triphenylphosphine suspended in toluene to the reaction mixture also proved to be beneficial.”; “Triphenylphosphine oxide could be reliably removed from the product using crystallization of the product from toluene and washes with DMSO and water, thus avoiding tedious column chromatography.”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Cross-Coupling as a Replacement for a Mitsunobu Reaction in the Development of an Androgen Receptor Antagonist

Paper Title: Scalable On-Demand Production of Purified Diazomethane Suitable for Sensitive Catalytic Reactions
Problem_Description: Purification of diazomethane is difficult; the harsh basic/oxidizing synthesis conditions require a work‑up, and traditional codistillation with diethyl ether needs remote explosion‑proof barriers that are not widely available.

Solution_Description: A dedicated tubular reactor extracts diazomethane directly into a nitrogen sweep gas; the gas stream is passed through a commercial hydrophilic membrane gas‑liquid separator (Zaiput SEP‑200) that isolates CH₂N₂ from the liquid reaction mixture, eliminating the need for codistillation or liquid–liquid extraction.

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: The first step gave a mixture of esters 3 and 4 that required a three‑step telescope lasting about a week in pilot‑plant scale, and the subsequent steps generated polymeric material that lowered intermediate purity and stalled the Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling, forcing recrystallisation and hot‑filtration of aryl chloride 11.
Solution_Description: Incorporation of three consecutive catalytic reactions – a palladium‑catalysed C–H functionalisation, an iridium‑catalysed borylation and a final C–N coupling – dramatically shortened the sequence and eliminated the need for the long telescoped ester‑formation steps.
Supporting_Evidence:

  - “polymeric material was produced in the synthesis of esters 3 and 4… resulting in low intermediate purity… forced us to rely on recrystallisation and hot filtration of aryl chloride 11 to ensure that stalling did not occur in the plant.”
  - “the synthesis of 4‑iodo‑6‑chloroindazole (5) required seven synthetic steps… over 60 % of the cost of materials for the route and to have a long production lead time.”
  - “Incorporation of three consecutive catalytic reactions, including a palladium‑catalyzed C–H functionalization and an iridium‑catalyzed borylation, significantly simplified and shortened the synthetic sequence.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: Polymeric impurities from the original oxazole‑ester synthesis persisted through the sequence, giving low isolated yields (≈55 %) after distillation because of degradation of the product and polymer‐induced fouling.

Supporting_Evidence:

  - “Distillation under high vacuum gave the product in 55 % yield with high purity on a 70 kg scale… the distilled product was free from the polymeric impurities that caused issues in the previous route.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: The legacy synthesis of 4‑iodo‑6‑chloroindazole (5) required seven steps, accounting for >60 % of the material cost and a long production lead time, making the overall route uneconomic and slow.
Solution_Description: A convergent approach using orthogonal C–H functionalisation of the 4‑ and 6‑positions of indazole allowed the key intermediate to be accessed from readily available 3‑halo‑2‑methylanilines, reducing step count, material cost and lead time.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “synthesis of 4‑iodo‑6‑chloroindazole (5) required seven synthetic steps, causing this intermediate to account for over 60 % of the cost of materials for the route and to have a long production lead time.”
  - “central to the development of an efficient synthesis of 13 is the application of methods for orthogonal functionalisation of the 4‑ and 6‑positions of indazole… Application of selective C–H functionalisation protocols would drastically simplify the starting materials.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: Coupling of oxazole ester 3 with 4‑bromoindazole failed in the absence of a protecting group because the free N‑H of the indazole inhibited the Pd‑catalysed C–H functionalisation.
Solution_Description: Robust N‑protecting groups (THP, PMB, N‑Me₂SO₂) were introduced on the indazole; these survived the basic conditions and allowed the desired C–H coupling to proceed in good isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “we attempted the coupling of 4‑bromoindazole with oxazole ester 3 under the same conditions; however, no reaction to give the desired product was observed.”
  - “coupling was inhibited in cases where the indazole protecting group was labile under the basic reaction conditions (Piv, Boc). When a more robust protecting group was used (THP, PMB, N¹‑Me₂SO₂), the desired product was formed readily and isolated in good yield.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: Using THP‑protected 4‑bromo‑6‑chloroindazole (31) gave a mixture of products from competitive addition into both the C‑Br and the C‑Cl bonds, complicating isolation and lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: The sequence was reordered so that the 6‑position was functionalised after the oxazole coupling, avoiding the competing C‑Br/C‑Cl insertions and delivering a single, clean product.
Supporting_Evidence:
