Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: Ir‑catalysed borylation of indazole 24 produced a mixture of mono‑ and diborylated products, including an undesired C‑B bond on the oxazole ring that could not be removed by treatment with acids or bases.
Solution_Description: Gentle heating of the diboronate mixture in methanol selectively cleaved the unwanted oxazole C‑B bond, affording the desired mono‑(pinacol boronate) 32 in high purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Treatment with a range of aqueous acids and bases… failed to selectively cleave the unwanted C‑B bond.”
  - “simply heating diboronate 35 gently in alcoholic solvents rapidly and selectively cleaved the oxazole C‑B bond, delivering highly pure mono‑(pinacol boronate) 32 after crystallisation.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: The Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling to close the carbon skeleton required palladium removal and generated large quantities of waste; a safe, scalable work‑up was needed.
Solution_Description: MIBK was selected as the reaction solvent because its solubility profile allowed reaction, work‑up and crystallisation in a single solvent; the aqueous N‑acetylcysteine wash efficiently extracted residual palladium, and azeotropic distillation of MIBK reduced product solubility to enable direct crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “MIBK was chosen as the solvent because the solubility profile enabled reaction, work‑up and crystallisation in a single solvent.”
  - “The reaction was worked up with basic aqueous N‑acetylcysteine to extract most of the residual palladium from the product, allowing facile control of the palladium content in the active pharmaceutical ingredient.”
  - “Distillation of the MIBK at atmospheric pressure azeotropically dried the solvent, which significantly reduced the solubility of 50, allowing direct crystallisation.”

Paper Title: Application of C–H Functionalization in the Development of a Concise and Convergent Route to the Phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitor Nemiralisib
Problem_Description: Reduction of the advanced intermediate 50 with DIBAL‑H required high dilution and generated large volumes of isobutane/isobutene on quench, posing a serious safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The reduction was redesigned using 10 % w/w LiAlH₄ in THF with AlCl₃ as a Lewis‑acid promoter; the reaction was quenched with EtOAc and then neutralised with triethanolamine/NaOH, which suppressed gas evolution and allowed removal of aluminum salts in the aqueous phase.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “the reduction typically did not reach completion… the high dilution required and large quantities of isobutane/isobutene produced upon quenching, which represented a significant safety concern.”
  - “optimal conditions were found to be the addition of lithium aluminium hydride (10 % w/w in THF) to a solution of the starting material 50 and aluminium chloride.”
  - “The reaction was carefully quenched with the addition of EtOAc to reduce gas production, followed by addition of triethanolamine and sodium hydroxide. The high ionic strength of the work‑up allowed the aluminium salts to be effectively removed in the aqueous phase.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: In the first‑generation route the reaction was stopped at 85 % conversion to avoid formation of the bis‑phosphorylated by‑product, wasting ~15 % of the penultimate material, giving only 45 % isolated yield after multiple crystallizations and a very labor‑intensive work‑up.
Solution_Description: Adoption of a dimethylaluminum chloride (Me₂AlCl)‑promoted phosphorylation gave >100:1 diastereoselectivity at phosphorus and >100:1 mono‑/bis‑phosphorylation selectivity, allowing the reaction to run to full conversion and raising isolated yield to 81 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction was stopped at 85 % conversion to avoid increased levels of bis‑phosphorylation, wasting 15 % of valuable penultimate and increasing the purification burden.”
• “The selectivity of mono‑ vs bisphosphorylation was low (∼6:1).”
• “A tedious workup procedure was applied … multiple crystallizations … 45 % overall yield and long cycle times.”
• “In the multikilogram synthesis … this methodology provided >100:1 diastereoselectivity … near doubling of the isolated yield from 45 % to 81 %.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: The initial optimized conditions used pyridine as solvent and required chromatographic purification, which were unsuitable for kilogram‑scale API production.
Solution_Description: A broad solvent screen identified THF (and later 2‑MeTHF, DMF) as providing nearly homogeneous solutions with clean reaction profiles, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the use of pyridine as a solvent and the required chromatography initially rendered the developed conditions unsuitable …”
• “Low conversion was observed in heptane… thick slurries were observed … due to the low solubility of the reactants and product … Nearly homogeneous solutions were observed in solvents such as THF, 2‑MeTHF, and DMF … THF (entry 11) chosen for further development as the reaction showed the cleanest overall profile.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Aluminum salts formed precipitates or emulsions under basic conditions, leading to significant product loss during aqueous work‑up and prolonged phase‑separation times because THF is partially miscible with water.
Solution_Description: A 25‑30 wt % aqueous tartaric‑acid solution was added to chelate the aluminum, giving rapid phase separation without emulsion; subsequent addition of isopropyl acetate further facilitated separation and reduced overall API loss to ~1 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Aluminum salts are prone to form precipitates or emulsions … rendering standard aqueous workup very challenging.”
• “substantial product loss attributable to entrainment of the API.”
• “a rapid phase split observed when an aqueous solution of the acid was added … it took several hours to achieve complete phase separation …”
• “addition of isopropyl acetate … minimized the overall API loss to approximately 1 %.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Me₂AlCl is pyrophoric and reacts violently with water, requiring special handling to prevent fires or exposure.
Solution_Description: The reagent was transferred from a sealed cylinder into a blow‑can containing heptane under nitrogen, then charged slowly to the THF reaction mixture at ≤0 °C, keeping the system inert throughout the addition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “due to its pyrophoric nature and water reactivity, it was necessary to implement additional procedural and engineering controls.”
• “transferring neat Me₂AlCl from a cylinder into a blow can … to reduce its interaction with air and moisture … allowed for an accurate mass measurement while keeping the entire system inert.”
• “the Me₂AlCl solution could then be charged slowly … under moderate pressure at 0 °C …”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Reaction in heptane gave very low conversion because the nucleoside substrate has extremely poor solubility in that solvent, and many polar or non‑polar solvents produced thick slurries.
Solution_Description: Screening identified THF (and related solvents) as providing high solubility and a homogeneous reaction mixture, thereby restoring conversion and enabling scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Low conversion was observed in heptane, likely due to the exceedingly low solubility of nucleoside 2 under these conditions.”
• “thick slurries were observed … due to the low solubility of the reactants and product … Nearly homogeneous solutions were observed in solvents such as THF, 2‑MeTHF, and DMF … THF (entry 11) chosen for further development.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: A cyclic phosphoramidate impurity (6) formed during the reaction (∼1.5 % LCAP) and, because of its very low solubility (0.9 mg mL⁻¹), could crystallize over the extended manufacturing cycle, threatening API purity.
Solution_Description: By limiting lutidine to ≤1.5 equiv, keeping the reaction temperature ≤35 °C, and restricting the aging time to 14–16 h, the impurity level was held at ≤0.6 % LCAP while maintaining >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “we observed a structurally related impurity in ∼1.5 LCAP … cyclic phosphoramidate 6 … solubility … only 0.9 mg mL⁻¹.”
• “impurity level increased linearly with the amount of lutidine … temperature … a moderate increase … from 1.7 % to 4.8 % at 45 °C.”
• “impurity level … could be controlled at 0.5–0.6 LCAP at temperatures not exceeding 35 °C for a period of 14–16 h … ∼95 % conversion and 92 % LCAP.”

Paper Title: Development and Implementation of an Aluminum-Promoted Phosphorylation in the Uprifosbuvir Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: On kilogram scale the crystallized product formed overly large crystals unsuitable for downstream processing.
Solution_Description: A wet‑milling step was introduced to reduce particle size to the required D₅₀ < 50 µm specification.
Supporting_Evidence: • “On the kilogram scale, we observed the growth of large crystals unsuitable for formulation studies … Fortunately, a wet milling process was developed to readily decrease the particle size to meet our D₅₀ < 50 µm specification.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Co-feed Process to Address Form and Physical Attribute Control of the Gefapixant (MK-7264) Citrate Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
Problem_Description: The citrate salt of gefapixant tends to form a methanol solvate that is kinetically stable, causing low yields (≈71 %) and unpredictable form conversion that can take 2–3.5 days, making batch‐scale control of the solid form difficult.
Solution_Description: A semicontinuous “co‑feed” process was created that keeps the reaction composition on the Form 1 region of the phase map by preparing a seed bed in the desired solvent composition and simultaneously feeding the free‑base solution and citric‑acid solution; a final excess IPA/citric‑acid charge raises the yield to ≈92 % while preserving thermodynamic form control.
Supporting_Evidence: The propensity of the citrate salt crystal to form solvates ("propensity of the citrate salt crystal to form solvates"), the methanol solvate can persist at up to 20 vol % IPA ("methanol solvate can hold in solvent systems as high as 20 vol % isopropyl alcohol"), turnover to Form 1 requires 2–3.5 days ("time required to completely turnover the methanolate to Form 1 was approximately 2–3.5 days"), primary nucleation is stochastic ("primary nucleation is a stochastic event"), new process keeps the system on the phase map ("new process enabled the system’s location on the phase map to remain constant"), simultaneous feeding of free base and citric‑acid solutions ("simultaneously charging the free base‑containing feed solution and the citric acid solution"), yield increase from 71 % to 92 % ("push the yield from ~71% to ~92%"), and thermodynamic form control is maintained ("desired thermodynamic form control was maintained").

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Co-feed Process to Address Form and Physical Attribute Control of the Gefapixant (MK-7264) Citrate Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
Problem_Description: The original wet‑milling strategy produced an overly narrow particle‑size distribution (17‑60 µm) and generated excessive fines, leading to slower filtration, sticking and picking during direct compression, and reduced overall yield.
Solution_Description: The target PSD was expanded to 10‑100 µm, allowing a broader, more robust size window; terminal wet‑milling was performed at half the seed‑bed tip speed for only five turnovers, which minimized fine generation while reliably meeting the final D₅₀ specification.
Supporting_Evidence: Two major issues with original milling ("end‑of‑milling target PSD range was unnecessarily low and conservatively narrow" and "significant generation of fines"), fines caused slower filtration and sticking/picking ("slower filtration rates... sticking and picking issues"), PSD range was widened to 10‑100 µm ("the end‑of‑milling target PSD range could indeed be expanded from 17 µm … to 10 µm ≤ D₅₀ ≤ 100 µm"), terminal wet‑milling at half tip speed with 5 turnovers ("terminal wet‑milling at half the tip speed… 5 turnovers… robustly deliver the correct API size").

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Co-feed Process to Address Form and Physical Attribute Control of the Gefapixant (MK-7264) Citrate Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
Problem_Description: Metered hot transfers of the glycolate solution suffered from inaccurate heat‑tape control, line heat loss causing solvent precipitation and plugging, and exposed heating coils that presented a burn hazard at larger scale.
Solution_Description: Custom temperature‑controlled glass syringes with integrated thermocouples were fabricated, and the transfer line was upgraded to a jacketed stainless‑steel pipe housing an inner cannula; a containment box was added around the heat‑wrapped pure‑pocket filter to eliminate the burn risk.
Supporting_Evidence: Heat‑tape feedback was inaccurate ("feedback control of the heat tape was not accurate enough"), line heat loss led to plugging ("uninsulated or nonheat‑traced transfer line… plugging of the line"), burn hazard from heat coils ("burn hazard presented by the exposed heat coils"), temperature‑controlled syringes with built‑in thermocouples were built ("temperature‑controlled glass syringes that had built‑in thermocouples"), stainless‑steel pipe with jacket service ("stainless steel pipe with jacket service capability"), containment box added ("containment box put around the heat‑wrapped pure pocket filter").

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Co-feed Process to Address Form and Physical Attribute Control of the Gefapixant (MK-7264) Citrate Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
Problem_Description: The purity of the free‑base feed varied from batch to batch, threatening impurity rejection performance and overall API quality.
Solution_Description: One‑factor‑at‑a‑time (OFAT) studies combined with impurity‑spiking experiments were used to demonstrate that the co‑feed process could reject key impurities to levels well below specifications, ensuring consistent API purity even with higher impurity loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: Need to handle purity variability ("new process had to be robust enough to handle purity variability in the free base crude product"), OFAT and impurity spiking experiments performed ("combination of one factor at a time (OFAT) experiments and impurity spiking experiments"), table showing impurity rejection ("Table 1… Rejection Capability of Key Impurities Using the Co‑feed Crystallization"), co‑feed process achieved comparable or better purity ("co‑feed process could achieve equivalent or better API purity compared to the batch process").

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Co-feed Process to Address Form and Physical Attribute Control of the Gefapixant (MK-7264) Citrate Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient
Problem_Description: Relying on slurry turnover to convert the methanol solvate to the desired Form 1 required 2–3.5 days, making the process impractically slow and sensitive to stochastic nucleation events.
Solution_Description: The co‑feed semicontinuous approach eliminates the need for long‑duration slurry turnover by maintaining the reaction composition in the thermodynamically stable region throughout crystallization, providing rapid and reliable form control.
Supporting_Evidence: Turnover time of 2–3.5 days ("time required to completely turnover the methanolate to Form 1 was approximately 2–3.5 days"), kinetic challenge of solvate ("kinetic challenges of the methanol solvate"), impracticality of slurry turnover ("it would not be a practical control strategy to rely on slurry turnover"), co‑feed maintains constant location on phase map ("new process enabled the system’s location on the phase map to remain constant"), rapid yield increase ("push the yield from ~71% to ~92%"), thermodynamic form control maintained ("desired thermodynamic form control was maintained").

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Air‑oxidation of the linear peptide precursor suffers from low solubility of both the precursor and the cyclic product in water, which forces the use of very dilute solutions (0.1–1 mM) and leads to large volumes of the hazardous solvent acetonitrile (CH₃CN).
Solution_Description: The oxidation was performed at 5.3 mM in a 2:1 H₂O/CH₃CN mixture, at pH 9.5, for 22 h. Raising the concentration (up to 10 × compared with classic dilute conditions) and adjusting pH reduced the required solvent volume and limited dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In particular, we focused our attention on the mild disulfide formation procedure based on the use of air, observing some drawbacks, such as the formation of unwanted oxidation by‑products, such as dimers, or the use of large volumes of an environmentally unfriendly solvent (CH₃CN).”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Strategy A uses the expensive building blocks Fmoc‑Cys(Mmt)‑OH and MPA(PyS), driving up raw‑material cost and contributing to low‑purity crude material because of costly side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: Strategy B replaces the costly MPA(PyS) with the inexpensive MPA dimer (3,3′‑dithiodipropionic acid, DTDPA). The same on‑resin disulfide formation is achieved with a cheaper reagent, lowering material cost while maintaining comparable yields.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The main disadvantage of Strategy A is the high cost of the building blocks Fmoc‑Cys(Mmt)‑OH and MPA(PyS).”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Strategy B uses N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) as the oxidant; excess NCS leads to unsafe instrument contamination, demanding intensive cleaning and increasing energy‑ and water‑consumption costs.
Solution_Description: Strategy D eliminates NCS by employing MPA (the native side‑chain thiol) as both reducing agent for StBu deprotection and oxidant for disulfide formation. MPA is inexpensive, non‑toxic, and already present in the target molecule, removing the safety and cost penalties of NCS.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of NCS reagent excess (data not shown)… requiring cleaning procedures that will increase energy and water costs, a prime concern for manufacturers.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Repeated washes with weak acid to remove the Mmt protecting group cause premature cleavage of peptide from the resin, giving variable and unacceptable loss of material.
Solution_Description: Strategy D replaces Mmt with the StBu protecting group on cysteine. StBu can be removed with MPA under mild basic conditions, avoiding acid washes and preserving resin‑bound peptide, thus improving yield and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Repeated washes with weakly acid solution to remove Mmt can cleave part of the peptide from the resin, leading to a variable, but unacceptable loss of yield.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: β‑Mercaptoethanol (βME) is highly toxic and difficult to clean from the microwave reactor, making it unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: MPA (40 equiv) is employed as a greener, inexpensive reducing agent for StBu deprotection. MPA is already part of the API, eliminating toxicity and cleaning issues while reducing raw‑material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “βME ... high toxicity and difficult cleaning procedures ... make its use not perfectly suitable for a kilogram‑scale production.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Using 2‑aminoethane‑1‑thiol (2‑MEA) for StBu reduction requires 16 h at room temperature and generates side‑products that complicate purification.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to MPA reduction (24 h at rt) performed directly in the microwave synthesizer, enabling a single‑reactor workflow and avoiding the side‑reaction observed with 2‑MEA.
Supporting_Evidence: • “10 % (v/v) 2‑aminoethane‑1‑thiol (2‑MEA) in DMF at r.t. allowed quantitative reduction in 16 h… side‑reaction involving the thiol functional group on Cys after StBu deprotection.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: A multi‑step, multi‑reactor process (linear synthesis → resin cleavage → off‑resin oxidation) requires several pieces of equipment, each of which must be qualified for cGMP, raising cost and safety exposure.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to the Liberty PRO microwave‑assisted solid‑phase synthesizer, allowing a fully automated single‑reactor workflow that eliminates the need for equipment transfers and reduces both cost and worker exposure.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Performing all steps in an automated instrument single reactor simplify the respect of cGMP compliances, cutting the financial and time costs related to multiple equipment qualification.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: A 4 : 1 H₂O/CH₃CN mixture (high water content) caused precipitate formation that stuck to the glass vessel, hampering reaction monitoring and cleaning after the oxidation step.
Solution_Description: Switching to a 2 : 1 H₂O/CH₃CN solvent system reduced precipitation, improved monitoring, and facilitated downstream cleaning.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In the higher water content mixture (4:1), a precipitate formation limited reaction monitoring and the putative side‑product aggregate, sticking to the glass vessel, affected postsynthesis cleaning procedures.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Scalable Fully Automated Solid-Phase Microwave-Assisted cGMP-Ready Process for the Preparation of Eptifibatide
Problem_Description: Traditional coupling reagents (HOBt, HBTU) are either explosive or require large amounts of base (DIPEA), increasing safety hazards and raw‑material cost.
Solution_Description: The DIC/Oxyma Pure coupling system was adopted. DIC/Oxyma is non‑explosive, safe, inexpensive, and does not require a base, simplifying the microwave‑assisted coupling step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The coupling system based on DIC/Oxyma, in addition to being safe and low cost, does not require the use of a base unlike the most popular onium coupling methods….”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: The original synthesis of arbaclofen placarbil (Scheme 1) required chromatography to separate the drug substance 6 from by‑product 2 because aqueous washes were ineffective, making the route unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A chromatography‑free second‑generation route (Scheme 2) was developed, eliminating the chromatography step and allowing scale‑up to 50 kg batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
“chromatography was the only method that could successfully separate desired product 6 … This limitation meant that the route … was not amenable to the large‑scale synthesis of drug substance 6.”
“... second, chromatography‑free route to the drug substance 6 … had been scaled up such that drug substance 6 could be manufactured in 50 kg batches.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: The chromatography‑free route gave an overall 30 % yield from R‑baclofen to drug substance 6, requiring 1.9 kg of R‑baclofen per kg of product – an inefficient and costly use of the expensive chiral building block.
Solution_Description: A new route was designed that introduces a kinetic resolution of the succinate ester intermediate, delivering the (S)‑enantiomer (compound 10) which reacts with R‑baclofen in high yield, reducing the required R‑baclofen to 0.7 kg kg⁻¹ of product.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The overall yield from R‑baclofen 5 to the drug substance 6 was 30 %… this would have equated to a saving of 24 000 kg of R‑baclofen per year.”
“... use of the (S)‑enantiomer of the succinate ester 8 … should give a high yield of drug substance 6.”
“... new route … required only 0.7 kg of R‑baclofen 5 per kg of drug substance 6 compared with 1.9 kg for the previous route.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: During enzymatic resolution of racemic thiocarbonate 3, background hydrolysis of the substrate and formation of side‑products (e.g., imine 21) reduced chiral purity and lowered isolated yields (≈36 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The pH was maintained at 7.5 using ammonium hydroxide (instead of KOH) and sub‑surface N₂ sparging was employed to remove volatile by‑products, which improved reaction rate and limited undesired hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The best hit … gave a chiral purity of 98.2% and losses because of background hydrolysis (47%)… The optimization … (1) increase … (2) minimize the background hydrolysis.”
“Control of pH … ammonium hydroxide … gave the best overall performance.”
“… sub‑surface sparging with N₂ was used … to remove volatile components.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: The addition of triethylamine to the reaction mixture after SO₂Cl₂ addition was highly exothermic, and uncontrolled temperature could cause decarboxylation and by‑product formation (compound 13).
Solution_Description: Triethylamine addition was performed at −20 °C with strict temperature control, and the addition sequence (SO₂Cl₂ → N‑hydroxysuccinimide → NEt₃) was rearranged to avoid premature heat release and decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
“NEt₃ addition was highly exothermic and promoted the conversion of chloroformate 12 … The temperature needed to be maintained at −20 °C to minimize decarboxylation and the formation of by‑product 13.”
“... NEt₃ was added while maintaining the temperature in the range –15 to –25 °C (exothermic addition, target = –20 °C).”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: Conversion of thiocarbonate 3 to succinate ester 8 using peracetic acid required a 12 h addition followed by a 12 h reaction, giving a maximum 56 % yield and poor space‑time efficiency.
Solution_Description: The peracetic‑acid step was replaced by a sulfuryl‑chloride mediated conversion (SO₂Cl₂) which achieved >80 % conversion in minutes, improving yield (65–70 % isolated) and drastically reducing batch time.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The peracetic acid solution needed to be added over approximately 12 h … the yield was never more than 56 % … A potential reason for the modest yield …”
“The complete consumption of thiocarbonate 3 was achieved using a minimum of 1.5 eq of SO₂Cl₂ at –18 °C … solution yields … >80 %, with the yields of the isolated product in the range 65–70 %.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: Sulfur‑containing by‑products generated a strong odor during work‑up of the SO₂Cl₂ step, creating a nuisance and potential safety issue.
Solution_Description: The work‑up solvent was switched from DCM to t‑BME, and the organic stream was passed through activated charcoal filters to adsorb odorous sulfur compounds.
Supporting_Evidence: “The workup solvent was changed from DCM to t‑BME … The organic layer was passed through a filter‑containing activated charcoal cartridges … The odor problem was overcome by passing a process stream through an activated charcoal filter unit.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: An unknown low‑level impurity (RRT = 0.75) appeared in the final drug substance 6, sometimes exceeding the specification limit (≤0.1 % w/w) and forcing a recrystallization step that reduced overall yield.
Solution_Description: A modified crystallization – reducing the amount of n‑heptane antisolvent and employing a seeded slurry – successfully lowered the impurity to <0.04 % w/w, albeit with a ~5 % yield loss, and the final product met specifications after a single recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The unknown RRT = 0.75 impurity … was above the specification limit … It was concluded that … the amount of n‑heptane antisolvent added to the crystallization was reduced … this modification did sufficiently reduce the level of the unknown impurity … at the expense of ca. 5 % of the yield.”
“The impurity … was controlled … the largest unspecified impurity in the isolated product was <0.04 % w/w.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: Stage 5 coupling of succinate ester 10 with R‑baclofen 5 formed a tri‑phasic mixture because R‑baclofen had very low solubility in t‑BME, leading to incomplete mixing at the start of the reaction.
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 45 °C and using a high‑t‑BME/ water ratio (3.37 vol t‑BME : 1.67 vol water) helped dissolve both components, resulting in a bi‑phasic system after reaction and a high (90–95 %) solution yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “R‑baclofen had poor solubility in t‑BME (<0.5 g/L) … This meant that at the start … it was a tri‑phasic mixture … however, by the end … it was a bi‑phasic mixture with all materials in solution … gave a solution yield of drug substance 6 in the range 90–95 %.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: The final drug substance 6 required removal of the n‑hexane solvent (Class 2) to meet ICH guidelines, prompting a need for a safer solvent system.
Solution_Description: n‑Hexane was replaced with a Class 3 solvent system (butanone / t‑BME for coupling, then butanone / n‑heptane for recrystallization), satisfying the ICH residual‑solvent limits while maintaining high recovery.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The focus … was to replace the ICH Class 2 solvent n‑hexane used in the final recrystallization with a Class 3 solvent.”
“The final process used butanone and heptane as antisolvent, achieving >90 % recovery and meeting impurity specifications.”

Paper Title: Process Development toward a Pro-Drug of
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch variability in impurity levels (e.g., unknown RRT = 0.75) was observed, likely due to inconsistent deliquoring of the filter cake during recrystallization.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Improved filter‑cake handling (using a smaller filter surface area) and tighter control of deliquoring were introduced to reduce variability in impurity carry‑over.
Supporting_Evidence: “A possible reason for the failure of one of the batches … was the poor deliquoring of the filter cake … the D90 of the undried filter cake was <20 µm. The addition of pure n‑heptane onto a poorly deliquored filter cake … may have caused more unknown impurity …”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: A new batch of the SEM‑protected amide 4 arrived tan, poorly soluble in THF and contained residual EtOAc; it failed the standard 3.0 equiv LiEt₃BH reduction, giving only 34 % HPLC conversion.
Solution_Description: The material was purified by silica‑gel chromatography and by precipitation from DCM with MTBE, which restored its color, removed EtOAc, improved solubility and raised HPLC purity to 96‑97 % (91 % recovery).
Supporting_Evidence: “a fresh batch of the starting material 4 showed immediate, unexpected differences… the new material was tan, challenging to solubilize in THF… NMR analysis of 4 revealed the presence of EtOAc… material failed an initial use test with 3.0 equiv of LiEt₃BH… only 34 area % conversion was observed by HPLC.”; “material could be improved in color, solubility, and HPLC purity by silica gel column chromatography which led to a 60 % recovery of material.”; “reprocessing the starting material 4 by solubilization in DCM, followed by precipitation with methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) allowed for the HPLC purity to increase from 92 to 96‑97 % a with 91 % recovery.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: The reduction step required nine equivalents of LiEt₃BH to achieve full conversion, which is costly and wasteful on scale.
Solution_Description: After re‑purifying 4, only 3.75 equiv of LiEt₃BH were needed to drive the reduction to completion, dramatically lowering reagent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: “adding more LiEt₃BH in 0.5–1.0 equiv portions (9.0 equiv total) would force the reaction to completion while maintaining acceptable product purity.”; “reprocessing only 3.75 equiv of reducing agent was needed for full conversion.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Quenching the LiEt₃BH reduction directly with water at –78 °C produced an icy, heterogeneous mixture and generated decomposition peaks adjacent to the product.
Solution_Description: The quench was redesigned: the reaction mixture was slowly diluted with DCM while keeping the internal temperature below –68 °C, then water was added slowly under the same temperature control, preventing ice formation and minimizing decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction was quenched directly with water at –78 °C… led to an icy, heterogeneous quench mixture… decomposition peaks observed were proximal to the product.”; “the reaction mixture was slowly diluted with DCM while keeping the internal reaction temperature below –68 °C… after dilution, the reaction could be slowly quenched with water, keeping the internal temperature below –68 °C.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: The SEM deprotection/elimination step used a thick silica‑gel slurry, gave variable reaction times (24 h–7 days) and produced emulsions during work‑up, making scale‑up difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A lean protocol was adopted: 10 g SiO₂ per gram hemiaminal 5 in EtOH/DCM/H₂O (32:12:4) gave complete conversion in 16 h; the work‑up was a simple filtration followed by dilute brine wash, eliminating emulsion formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the thick slurry posed scale‑up issues, the reaction was challenging to monitor, and… deprotection times varied from 24 h up to 7 days.”; “All attempts to lower the reaction volume… were met with emulsions in the workup… breaking the emulsion was challenging.”; “using 10 g of silica gel per gram hemiaminal 5 in EtOH/DCM/H₂O (32:12:4) led to complete conversion to bis‑imine 6 in 16 h… the workup involved a simple filtration followed by dilute brine wash at significantly lower solvent volumes.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Residual piperidine from the Fmoc deprotection carried into the final coupling, forming a piperidine‑maleimide by‑product that was hard to remove, reducing overall purity.
Solution_Description: Et₃N in DMF was used for Fmoc removal; the product was precipitated with Et₂O and filtered, which eliminated residual secondary amine and prevented by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “piperidine was not sufficiently purged during workup and it reacted in the subsequent coupling… piperidine‑coupled 6‑maleimidohexanoic acid by‑product could be observed… Et₂NH also gave by‑product 10.”; “Et₃N (72 mL, 0.64 M) was added… the product precipitated with Et₂O and filtered… residual Et₃N could not couple to 8 in the next step.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Free amine 7 showed poor solubility, requiring 10 % MeOH/DCM for the final peptide coupling; a methyl‑ester impurity 11 formed and was difficult to separate by chromatography.
Solution_Description: The coupling was run in 10 % MeOH/DCM with increased equivalents of EDCI·HCl and 6‑maleimidohexanoic acid; the crude mixture was precipitated into MTBE, which removed impurity 11 efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the poor solubility of starting material 7, this reaction was run with 10 % MeOH/DCM as a solvent rather than DCM alone.”; “During the toxicology lot purification… a methyl ester 11 (2.74 % a) was found… it could be removed by a final precipitation of linker drug 1 from 10 % MeOH/DCM with MTBE.”; “Additional equivalents of both reagents proved necessary to drive the reaction to >99 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Early Development, Scale-Up, and Reverse-Phase Purification of a Highly Potent Pyrrolobenzodiazepine Dimer, SG3259, for Use in Antibody–Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Reverse‑phase preparative HPLC gave rapid loss of purity in acidic mobile phases (0.1 % FA), column tailing, and a drop in recovery after several runs; impurity peaks grew and product degraded during long holds.
Solution_Description: The mobile‑phase modifier was changed to 100 mM ammonium acetate buffered to pH 4.0, elution was performed isocratically at 29 % MeCN, and fractions were quenched quickly and extracted with 10 % MeOH/DCM, giving a consistent 85‑94 % purity and improved recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “SG3259 suffers from poor solubility; acid‑, light‑, and oxygen‑sensitivity… crude sample left for 2 days in 1:1 MeCN/H₂O with 0.1 % formic acid degraded from 47 % to 29 % a.”; “Peak shape gradually broadened… column quality deteriorated… it was difficult to obtain >90 % purity.”; “ammonium acetate buffered to pH 4.0… isocratic elution 29 % MeCN/100 mM aq NH₄OAc (pH 4.0)… fractions were extracted with 10 % MeOH/DCM… final purity of 85.4 % a % (42 % recovery).”

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Fumaric acid (FA) has a very low solubility in the MeOH/DMC solvent system (≈5 % w/v at 90‑100 °C), which prevents preparing a homogeneous reaction mixture for the packed‑bed heterogeneous catalyst.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process uses a super‑heated coil reactor (90‑100 °C) to dissolve FA in MeOH/DMC, or a suspension‑to‑solution strategy with a peristaltic pump, ensuring a clear solution before entering the catalyst cartridge; the temperature is raised above the solvent reflux to increase FA solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: As FA is characterized by very low solubility in MeOH and in MeOH/DMC mixtures, there was the need of developing a suitable procedure to obtain a solution to be submitted to the reaction with heterogeneous catalyst.; Considering that FA solubility in a 1:3 mixture of MeOH/DMC is around 5% only at 90–100 °C, i.e., above reflux temperature.; The main limitation of this configuration is posed by the fact that it can be used only if the reaction mixture is a solution throughout the whole process.

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Traditional esterification uses mineral acids (H₂SO₄ or HCl) which generate toxic, potentially carcinogenic impurities such as dimethyl sulfate and methyl chloride, requiring special purification steps to meet ICH limits.
Solution_Description: Mineral acids were replaced by a silica‑supported propylsulfonic acid (SCX‑2) heterogeneous catalyst, eliminating the formation of carcinogenic by‑products and removing the need for downstream impurity‑removal purifications.
Supporting_Evidence: Use of mineral acids, usually sulfuric acid or hydrochloric acid, as catalyst in the presence of MeOH, with the possible formation of carcinogenic byproducts (e.g., dimethyl sulfate or methylchloride), that request specific purification.; It was possible to exclude the use of mineral acids as a catalyst, avoiding the formation of carcinogenic impurities.; The most common supports used in this field are polystyrene‑based resins bearing sulfonic groups; however, the use of such resins is usually not recommended… because of the possible presence of residual styrene monomer, a probable carcinogen.

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: The conventional batch esterification reaches equilibrium and requires long reaction times plus solvent distillation to drive conversion to completion, limiting throughput and overall yield.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow packed‑bed reactor with a water‑scavenging reagent (dimethyl carbonate, DMC) removes water in situ, allowing high conversion (>98 %) within 30 min residence time without the need for a separate distillation step.
Supporting_Evidence: Long cycle time, for reaction and distillation of part of the solvent.; The reaction reaches an equilibrium, and it is usually driven to complete conversion by distillation of most part of the solvent.; One of the most straightforward strategies to drive Fisher esterification to completion is the removal of water from the reaction mixture. … dimethylcarbonate (DMC) was selected as a cheap, nontoxic, and industrially available material, used as a reagent in methyl ester formation.

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Montmorillonite K10 showed negligible activity under the tested conditions, giving only ~4 % DMF, which is unsuitable for an industrial process.
Solution_Description: Screening identified silica‑supported SCX‑2 as the most efficient catalyst (≥98 % DMF at 110 °C in <6 h), which was then selected for all further development.
Supporting_Evidence: Montmorillonite K10 is not active under these conditions, whereas silica‑supported SCX‑2 is the most efficient catalyst, affording more than 98 % conversion to DMF at 110 °C in less than 6 h.; The screening experiments were performed in batch mode… The results clearly indicated that Montmorillonite K10 is not active under these conditions, whereas silica‑supported SCX‑2 is the most efficient catalyst.

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Using a peristaltic pump to feed a suspension of FA caused fluctuations in the amount of FA actually delivered, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was switched to a syringe pump delivering a pre‑made solution (two‑step configuration) which provides a stable flow rate and eliminates variability caused by solid suspension handling.
Supporting_Evidence: With the aim of reducing possible variability coming from the use of a suspension (using a peristaltic pump, the actual amount of FA pumped could change during the experiment, whereas a syringe pump can assure more stable flow rate).

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Potential catalyst deactivation over prolonged operation could reduce productivity and increase waste.
Solution_Description: Stability tests over 180 h (processing >44 g FA per gram of SCX‑2) showed constant DMF conversion and unchanged surface area/pore structure, confirming that the silica‑supported catalyst is robust under the chosen temperature and pressure.
Supporting_Evidence: The conversion to DMF was essentially constant for all of the experiment time, with no visible loss of activity.; Surface properties of fresh and used catalysts show no significant modifications after long reaction time at high temperature and pressure.; These observations are confirmed by SEM images… the morphology of the catalyst was not affected by the use.

Paper Title: Dimethyl Fumarate: Heterogeneous Catalysis for the Development of an Innovative Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: High catalyst loading can increase raw material cost, which is critical for a low‑price API like DMF.
Solution_Description: Design‑of‑experiment optimization identified a catalyst loading of 63 % (≈0.63 g SCX‑2 g⁻¹ mixture) as the best compromise, minimizing expensive catalyst use while maintaining >98 % DMF conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Catalyst loading … a good compromise to limit the amount of expensive material used in the process.; The optimal conditions … Catalyst loading L: 63% (level −0.5), a good compromise to limit the amount of expensive material used in the process.

Paper Title: Understanding and Controlling the Formation of an
Problem_Description: When the trityl‑protected intermediate was deprotected using an HCl/acetone system, an unknown N‑alkyl impurity (compound 10) appeared at up to 0.23 area % (well above the 0.10 % regulatory limit), giving inconsistent impurity levels between batches and reducing the overall product yield.
Solution_Description: A definitive screening design (DSD) was employed to identify the critical factors (water volume, HCl equivalents, and temperature). The optimal process was set to low HCl (2.5 eq), low temperature (25 °C) and a mid water volume (>0.95 mL), which suppressed impurity 10 to <0.1 % and restored quantitative de‑protection yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “an impurity of up to 0.23 area % was detected … in one batch of the product samples”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: Route A uses expensive 2‑acetyl‑4‑methoxyphenol and toxic ethyl bromoacetate/boron tribromide, leading to a low overall isolated yield of only 31 % and hazardous waste disposal issues.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a new three‑step one‑pot route that avoids the multistep isolation, uses cheaper, safer reagents, and gives isolated yields of 85–87 %, dramatically improving overall productivity and waste profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “Route A: using the expensive 2‑acetyl‑4‑methoxyphenol … and ethyl bromoacetate … the total yield of only 31 %.”; “The toxic and hazardous ethyl bromoacetate and boron tribromide brought difficulties in waste disposal.”; “Three‑step one‑pot synthesis… total yield of 89 %… dramatically enhanced the production efficiency through avoiding the tedious multistep isolation and purification operations.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: Route B requires a slow 12 h addition of p‑benzoquinone, followed by distillation of the enamine; reported overall yields vary widely (25–76 %), indicating poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: The process was telescoped into a single pot: the enamine, quinone addition, and deamination are performed sequentially without isolation, with optimized dropwise addition at 0 °C and shortened reaction times (10 min for enamine formation).
Supporting_Evidence: “Route B… slow addition over 12 h… The intermediate enamine needed to be purified by distillation. … total yields ranged from 25 to 76 %, indicating that the reaction process was difficult to control and repeat.”; “The feeding sequence influenced the yield… adding the mixture… in a dropwise manner to the solution of morpholine in an ice bath… presented the best yield.”; “In THF, the yield could reach over 99 % in 10 min at 0 °C.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: Residual morpholine after vacuum distillation remains in the reaction mixture, destabilising the enamine and suppressing conversion to the quinone adduct.
Solution_Description: Ti(OPr)4 (1 equiv) was introduced as a promoter; it consumes the excess morpholine and drives complete enamine formation (>99 % yield) when added together with propionaldehyde under ice‑bath conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “the excess morpholine … was incompletely removed via vacuum distillation, and the poor stability of the resulted enamine led to the low yield.”; “Using Ti(OPr)4 as an additive, the yield of enamine was up to 87 % without residual morpholine … when 1.0 equiv of Ti(OPr)4 was employed, enamine could be obtained in more than 99 % yield.”; “adding the mixture of propionaldehyde and Ti(OPr)4 in a dropwise manner to the solution of morpholine in an ice bath presented the best yield.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: Using 3 equiv of aldehyde eliminates morpholine but introduces ~20 % impurities, reducing the overall yield of the enamine.
Solution_Description: The optimal stoichiometry was found at 1 equiv of Ti(OPr)4 and 1 equiv of aldehyde (or slight excess) combined with a water‑adsorbent additive, delivering >99 % enamine yield without by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the use of 3.0 equivalents of aldehyde led to no residual morpholine, the product was accompanied by 20 % impurities.”; “4 Å molecular sieves … the increased amount of 4 Å MS did not improve the yield, which was leveled around 74 %.”; “When 1.0 equiv of Ti(OPr)4 was employed, enamine could be obtained in more than 99 % yield.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: CHCl₃, used in early trials, is toxic and gave lower conversions; safer solvents were needed for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: CH₂Cl₂ and THF were screened; THF was selected as the preferred solvent, affording >99 % yield in 10 min at 0 °C while eliminating the safety concerns of CHCl₃.
Supporting_Evidence: “Considering the toxic CHCl₃ and its limitation in the industry, several solvents … CH₂Cl₂ and THF were proved to be the appropriate solvents… THF gave yield over 99 % in 10 min at 0 °C.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: Higher temperatures or prolonged reaction times cause side‑product formation and degrade the enamine, dropping the isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The optimal condition was 0 °C for 10 min; any increase in temperature or time led to a marked decline in yield, so the reaction was kept cold and short.
Supporting_Evidence: “Elevated temperature or prolonged reaction time decreased the yield because of the formation of side products.”; “In THF, the yield could reach over 99 % in 10 min at 0 °C (entry 10).”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: When toluene or EtOAc were used in the deamination step, a biphasic mixture formed, severely limiting mass transfer and delivering only trace product.
Solution_Description: THF was chosen as the deamination solvent; 5 equiv of 2 M aqueous HCl (or 2 equiv) and 2 h reflux gave >95 % isolated yield, avoiding phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulted mixture was a two‑phase system when toluene or ethyl acetate was used … only a trace amount of the product was obtained because of the limited mass transfer.”; “THF … 5.0 equivalents amount of 2 M aqueous HCl … yielded 97 %.”; “a reaction time of 2 h was essential because shortening … decreased the yield.”

Paper Title: Three-Step One-Pot Process of 3‑Methyl-5-Benzofuranol from Amine, Aldehydes, and
Problem_Description: On kilogram scale, solvent consumption and waste generation could raise costs and environmental impact if solvent recovery is not efficient.
Solution_Description: The process was conducted at 1 M concentration in THF; >90 % of THF was recovered after reaction, cutting solvent cost and achieving a 52 % reduction in Process Mass Intensity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The recovery rate of solvent THF was still more than 90 %, which greatly reduced the cost of the solvent and the production of chemical wastes.”; “...represented a 52 % reduction in the Process Mass Intensity (PMI).”
