First, LiAlH₄ (2.5 eq) and TMSCl were added at –15 °C to activate the hydride, then 16 was added and the mixture warmed to 45–50 °C, delivering the β‑lactam reduction without cleavage. A second portion of LiAlH₄ completed the reduction of the remaining γ‑lactam at 50 °C. The protocol gave 96 % HPLC area for 3a and an isolated 86 % yield after crystallisation as the succinate salt. The use of TMSCl avoided the need for harsher reagents and simplified work‑up.

- "Reduction using DIBAL, Red‑Al, or LiAlH₄ … was also accompanied by β‑lactam fission (entries 2‑4)."
- "We found that reduction by chloroalanes generated by treatment of LiAlH₄ with AlCl₃ and TMSCl‑mediated LiAlH₄ reduction suppressed the β‑lactam fission and gave 3a in good yields (entries 5 and 6)."

Paper Title: Stereocontrolled Synthesis of Delgocitinib, a JAK Inhibitor for the Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis
Problem_Description: The original laboratory route to delgocitinib employed cryogenic temperatures, chromatography for purification, and expensive reagents (e.g., P₁‑t‑Bu‑tris‑(tetramethylene)), making the process unsuitable for large‑scale manufacture.

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Two-Step Process for Molnupiravir: Direct Hydroxamination of Cytidine Followed by Selective Esterification

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Two-Step Process for Molnupiravir: Direct Hydroxamination of Cytidine Followed by Selective Esterification

Paper Title: Integrating Continuous-Flow Electrochemistry and Photochemistry for the Synthesis of Acridinium Photocatalysts Via Site-Selective C–H Alkylation
Problem_Description: Working with acridinium salts in a micro‑flow system caused solid precipitation and channel blockage, especially when the neutral intermediate (3,10‑dihydroacridine 5) was formed.  Low solubility of this neutral species in the MeCN/H₂O mixture, as well as the use of other bases (Na₂CO₃, KOH, n‑Bu₄NOH, Et₃N) caused severe clogging.  Omission of pyridine gave a much lower isolated yield (46 %).  When the flow rate and current were increased simultaneously the yield dropped (68 % → 49 %).  The crude 3‑alkylated salts obtained after the first alkylation were difficult to isolate, making the downstream purification of 3,6‑disubstituted dyes problematic.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a MeCN/H₂O (5:1) solvent system to keep the salts dissolved and added pyridine together with the TEMPO electrocatalyst to control deprotonation and prevent precipitation.  They kept the current at 55–85 mA and did not increase it together with the flow rate, preserving high yields.  For the second alkylation they changed the base to Et₃N and used a MeCN/acetone/H₂O (5:6:1) solvent mixture, which prevented clogging.  The substrate concentration was halved while the flow rate was doubled, eliminating solid formation and allowing continuous operation.  A simple extractive work‑up after the first alkylation removed inorganic salts and pyridine, giving a cleaner crude that was easier to purify and improved overall yields of the dialkylated products.  Reaction time (charge passed) was optimized (e.g., 3.4 F mol⁻¹ → 5.3 F mol⁻¹) to achieve optimal conversion without over‑oxidation.

Supporting_Evidence: ["After extensive solvent screening, dichloromethane was found to be a suitable alternative, a change that provided several advantages, including most notably the compatibility with iodine and high solubility of 4 (>30 wt %).", "The replacement of molecular sieves with a soluble water scavenger; the slow addition of a solution of 4 to the reaction mixture containing iodine, 5, and dichloromethane; and the change to a buffered, inverse quench of the excess iodine and of the HI formed during the reaction.", "The exothermic nature of the quench limited the maximum rate of addition; implementation of an inverse quench largely mitigated this problem.", "Crystallization of 6a from MEK was developed, enabling isolation of 6a in high yield and typically with ~95 % AN purity."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The oxidative syn‑elimination of iodide 6 to fluoroalkene 7 required a very large reaction volume (Vmax > 115 L kg⁻¹), resulting in low throughput and a high process‑mass‑intensity (PMI ≈ 108).
Solution_Description: A “put‑and‑take” sequential addition protocol was introduced: Oxone and base were added in several portions with intermediate phase separations, limiting the total reaction volume to ≈25 L kg⁻¹ and reducing PMI dramatically while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["To address this shortcoming, an alternative mode of operation was developed, which involves repeated, sequential addition of portions of Oxone and a base to a solution of reactant 6a followed by phase separations to limit the overall process volume.", "This cycle was then iterated until full conversion was obtained, typically in three or four cycles.", "Effectively reduced the processing volume to a Vmax of approximately 25 L kg⁻¹ 6a."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The citrate salt form of the API (1a) was difficult to crystallise, yielded a solid that required two reslurriages for full crystallinity and gave a low overall yield (~40 %) from 7 to 1a.
Solution_Description: Two new solid forms were identified – the freebase (1) and the vanillate salt (1b). The vanillate form crystallises readily from EtOAc/toluene, delivering >95 % AN purity in a single crystallisation; the freebase shows improved chemical stability, eliminating the need for refrigerated storage.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The freebase form of 1 possesses excellent physical and physicochemical properties as well as improved chemical stability, but it was challenging to crystallize from crude streams of 1.", "The vanillate could be more readily crystallized from the crude stream of 1 and provided excellent impurity rejection.", "The route was amended to use the vanillate 1b as an intermediate purification and isolation point, and the freebase was selected as the final API form to replace the citrate 1a."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The process generated the des‑fluoro impurity 8 at levels > 2000 ppm in intermediate 1b, far above the required 100 ppm control limit for the API.
Solution_Description: A simulated moving‑bed chromatography (SMBC) process on EtOAc was developed, achieving < 5 ppm of impurity 8 in the final API with high overall purity (99.9 % AN) and acceptable recovery (≈ 95 %).
Supporting_Evidence: ["A control limit of 100 ppm was defined for des‑fluoro impurity 8 in the API... Simulated moving‑bed chromatography (SMBC) is a scalable chromatographic purification technique... Proof‑of‑concept studies... excellent removal of impurity 8 was achieved.", "The 10 kg batch performed as expected, providing 5.26 kg of API with less than 5 ppm of impurity 8 and 99.9 % AN total purity."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Although SMBC removed impurity 8 effectively, its per‑kg cost is a major driver of API price, requires specialized equipment that few CMO’s possess, and adds a 5–8 % loss due to the extra crystallisation/isolation step before the chromatography.
Solution_Description: A chromatography‑free control strategy was devised: a DOE on the iodoetherification reaction identified lower temperature, longer addition time of 4, and higher iodine charge as parameters that suppress formation of impurity 12 (the precursor of 8); combined with an iterative crystallisation of the API, impurity 8 could be reduced to the required level without SMBC, improving yield and reducing PMI.
Supporting_Evidence: ["While the throughput would be suitable... the cost of SMBC per kilogram of API was projected to be a major driver in the total cost per kilogram of finished API.", "Design of experiments (DOE) was used to characterize and further improve the iodoetherification reaction responsible for producing the progenitors of this des‑fluoro impurity and to reduce their formation in this step.", "Iterative recrystallisation of the API maintained the same ca. 50 % purge of 8 regardless of its starting level. This iter­ative recrystallisation could then yield API with levels of 8 below 100 ppm."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The aqueous quench after the iodoetherification generated a highly emulsified organic layer; filtration of the emulsion took > 24 h on multi‑kilogram scale and caused feed concentration loss for SMBC.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Molecular sieves were replaced with soluble BSA (water scavenger), and later magnesium sulfate was eliminated altogether by passing the organic layer through a cellulose depth filter (coalescer), which broke the emulsion and delivered an organic stream with < 0.5 % water, eliminating the long filtration step.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The beaded sieves pulverized to a fine powder, and removal of this powder from the product stream by filtration was tedious, in some cases requiring > 24 h of filtration time on multi‑kilogram scale.", "The replacement of molecular sieves with a soluble water scavenger; ...", "A more sustainable, long‑term solution to reduce the water content of the organic layer was found in the use of a cellulose depth filter acting as a liquid–liquid coalescer.", "The process greatly lowers the energy barrier for droplet‑droplet recombination, and so filtration of the emulsified organic layer through such a filter readily separated the emulsified water droplets."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The quench of excess iodine and the generated hydroiodic acid is highly exothermic; rapid addition caused temperature spikes, product degradation, and risk of over‑pressurisation.
Solution_Description: An inverse quench was implemented: the reaction mixture was added to a large, pre‑cooled aqueous sodium sulfite solution buffered with sodium bicarbonate, which both neutralises the generated acid and controls the temperature, allowing safe and rapid quenching.
Supporting_Evidence: ["To quench the reaction mixture, a large excess of sodium sulfite (serving as both a reductant and a base) was charged as quickly as possible to minimize the time to complete the neutralization.", "However, this arrangement was problematic on scale due to the exothermic nature of the quench limiting the maximum rate of addition.", "Implementation of an inverse quench in which the iodine‑containing stream is charged into a pot of aqueous sodium sulfite largely mitigated this problem since the exotherm and release of acid were now more controlled.", "A further modification of the workup to buffer the sodium sulfite quench solution with sodium bicarbonate provided rapid and complete neutralization of the acid as it is generated, greatly minimizing the observed hydrolytic degradation of 6 during the quench."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Pilot‑scale crystallisation of the vanillate salt 1b from EtOAc/toluene produced small, irregular particles that formed a compressible filter cake, leading to slow filtration, cake cracking and poor deliquoring, which reduced the overall two‑step yield to 55 %.
Solution_Description: The solvent system was changed to isopropanol, and vanillic acid was added as a single portion (instead of portionwise) to promote uniform particle growth; a small amount of MTBE was added before isolation to lower the viscosity of the mother liquor, resulting in faster filtration and higher recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Screening of alternative solvents for suitable solubility and any resulting differences in particle size or morphology revealed isopropanol as a promising alternative to the existing EtOAc/toluene solvent system.", "Counter to expectation, charging the vanillic acid as a single portion led to more uniform particle growth and ultimately to shorter filtration times.", "Addition of a small amount of MTBE prior to isolation was found to drastically reduce the viscosity of the solvent and afforded consistently fast filtrations without affecting the solubility of 1b or any impurities."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Rovafovir Etalafenamide (Part I): Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development, Scale-Up, and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Intermediate 6 is prone to hydrolytic degradation during work‑up and distillation when exposed to residual water, causing loss of material and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Water content of the organic layer was reduced from 2–4 % to < 0.5 % by using a low‑temperature phase separation and a cellulose depth filter; the process eliminated the need for magnesium sulfate drying and prevented hydrolytic degradation of 6.
Supporting_Evidence: ["As a stopgap measure, a cosolvent of isopropyl acetate was introduced to the workup, which easily broke this emulsion.", "A more sustainable, long‑term solution to reduce the water content of the organic layer was found in the use of a cellulose depth filter acting as a liquid–liquid coalescer.", "This modification significantly reduced the PMI, energy usage, and manufacturing time required per batch."]

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: The reductive‑amination step gave only moderate yields (≈60–70 %) and generated the impurity 3b (up to 11 % when NaBH₃CN was used).  The presence of this impurity complicated isolation of the desired intermediate 3a.
Solution_Description: The authors kept the original reagent ratio (1 : 2 : 3.9 vancomycin : 2 : Na(OAc)₃BH) and used Na(OAc)₃BH instead of NaBH₃CN, which lowered the formation of impurity 3b to trace levels.  They also cooled the reaction mixture below 5 °C before adding the reducing agent, controlling the addition rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “the percentage of impurity 3b increased from 4 to 11 % when the reducing reagent Na­(AcO)₃BH was changed to NaBH₃CN (entry 1 vs entry 3)”; “with the increasing equivalent of compound 2, the impurity 3b decreased to traceless amount and the yield of product 3a increased” (Table 2); “the reaction temperature should be cooled down to below 5 °C before the slow addition of Na­(AcO)₃BH to conduct the reductive amination.”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: The Mannich reaction showed a strong temperature dependence: at 45 °C the yield of SM‑V‑61 was only ~34 % with many side‑products, whereas lowering the temperature to –10 °C raised the yield to ~70 % and reduced impurities.
Solution_Description: The optimal condition was identified as –10 °C with 1.08 equiv of formaldehyde, which gave a 77.8 % isolated yield (entry 15).  Reducing the formaldehyde equivalents from 4 to 1.08 also prevented over‑alkylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “a high temperature will result in lower yield of SM‑V‑61, with a higher percentage of impurities (entries 7 and 8)”; “Yield of SM‑V‑61 increased from 34.1 to 69.9 % when the reaction temperature was decreased from 45 to –10 °C (entries 7 and 12).”; “The yield of SM‑V‑61 was affected significantly by the equivalent of formaldehyde… 1.08 equiv gave 77.8 % yield at –10 °C (entry 15).”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: When vancomycin hydrochloride and DIPEA were combined in DMF on the 30–40 g scale the mixture formed a suspension that did not dissolve until the temperature was raised to 55 °C.
Solution_Description: The mixture was heated to 55 °C while stirring until it became a clear solution before adding aldehyde 2; the subsequent steps were carried out at controlled temperatures (55 °C for Schiff‑base formation, then cooling before reduction).
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, the mixture was a suspension, which will become clear after heating the reaction mixture to 55 °C with continuous stirring.”; “the addition of compound 2 to the reaction mixture to form Schiff base was allowed and the reaction mixture was stirred at 55 °C for 2 h. However, the reaction temperature should be cooled down to below 5 °C before the slow addition of Na­(AcO)₃BH.”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: The original HPLC method used 0.1 % TFA (acidic mobile phase) which gave poor peak shapes and insufficient separation of SM‑V‑61 from its three secondary‑amine‑containing impurities.
Solution_Description: The analytical method was revised to use basic elution buffers (ammonia) on a C18 column, which improved peak shapes, separation degree, and baseline stability for both the impurity mixture and SM‑V‑61.
Supporting_Evidence: “Previously, SM‑V‑61 was analyzed and purified by the C18 column under acidic conditions, with 0.1 % TFA… we replaced the acidic elution buffers to basic ones with ammonia, looking forward to making better separations of impurities from SM‑V‑61.”; “all of the synthetic impurities exhibited good peak shapes and SM‑V‑61 was separated from the impurities in high resolution.”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: Scale‑up to 500–600 g in a 20 L reactor required reliable mixing; inadequate agitation could lead to uneven temperature distribution and inconsistent product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mechanical agitation was employed in the 20 L stainless‑steel reactor to ensure uniform mixing and temperature control; the same reaction sequence as the laboratory scale was followed, confirming robustness at larger scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “We magnified the preparation of SM‑V‑61 in a 20‑L reaction still and the reaction mixtures were stirred with mechanical agitation. The process of magnified synthesis was the same as that of the 30–40 g scale in the laboratory.”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: Isolation of the intermediate 3a after reductive amination required removal of excess vancomycin and reducing agent; traditional extraction gave low recovery.
Solution_Description: After completion, the reaction mixture was poured into large amounts of tert‑butyl ether, causing the product to precipitate; the solid was filtered and washed with water to afford crude 3a of high purity (48 g recovered).
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction mixture was poured into tert‑butyl ether to precipitate intermediate 3a, which was further washed with water to remove the remaining vancomycin and Na­(AcO)₃BH. HPLC analysis indicated the high purity of intermediate 3a (48 g crude product).”

Paper Title: Impurity Identification and Scale-Up of a Novel Glycopeptide Antibiotic
Problem_Description: During the Mannich step on the 30–40 g scale the isolated yield of SM‑V‑61 was only 60.33 % after purification, indicating material loss at larger scale.
Solution_Description: The authors kept the reactant concentrations (1 : 5 : 20 mol ratio of 3a : 4a : DIPEA) and employed the same temperature (–10 °C) and quench protocol (TFA, pH 3) as on the small scale, which allowed a comparable yield (≈54 % overall on 500–600 g scale).
Supporting_Evidence: “We treated 3a (48 g) and 5 equiv of galactose 4a in water and acetonitrile. The reaction temperature was strictly controlled under –10 °C… After purification, 33 g (60.33 %) of SM‑V‑61 was obtained.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: Batch synthesis of 3‑chloro‑4‑oxopentyl acetate suffers from massive work‑ups, limited heat and mass transfer, and reactions that take several days, giving low overall yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopt a fully continuous‑flow process using modular ceramic (Protrix) reactors and PTFE coil reactors, which provide superior heat and mass transfer, eliminate batch work‑ups and drastically shorten reaction times.
Supporting_Evidence:
“All of the processes mentioned above were operated in batch with massive unavoidable work‑ups, limited by poor heat and mass transfer. Some reactions took several days, which was time‑ and cost‑consuming.”
“After experimental screening tests in separated flow processes, a fully continuous flow synthesis … was successfully developed for the first time.”
“The fully continuous process ran smoothly for 12 h, generating approximately 19.1 g of the desired product…"

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: The decarboxylation/acylation step in the batch route required a stoichiometric amount of expensive acetic anhydride, increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: Eliminate the use of acetic anhydride by using excess acetic acid (4 equiv) and a cross‑mixer to achieve complete acylation, thereby reducing reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
“costly acetic anhydride for further acylation … is not required”
“...the optimum conditions … 4 equiv of acetic acid, cross‑mixer, 125 °C…”
“Therefore, we decided to simplify the synthesis route by eliminating the addition of acetic anhydride considering the high conversion obtained during the first decarboxylation/acylation step.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: Using a T‑mixer gave poor micromixing of the two‑phase streams, resulting in lower conversion, impurity formation and inconsistent product purity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Replace the T‑mixer with a symmetric cross‑mixer (PTFE, i.d. = 2.5 mm) to improve velocity and density distribution, leading to higher conversion and >96 % product purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The advantages of cross‑mixers over T‑mixers have been discussed … Therefore, a cross‑mixer … was employed to try to enhance the two‑phase liquid–liquid mixing.”
“...the cross‑mixer gave a better regulated velocity distribution … and a stable density distribution … resulting in 89–91 % yield with purity as high as 96.7 %.”
“Figure 9 … illustrates a significant increase in the acylation efficiency by using a cross‑mixer.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: Conventional batch routes required isolation, solvent exchange and vacuum distillation between steps, increasing processing time, waste, and exposing operators to toxic chlorine and corrosive acids.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Integrate an inline liquid‑liquid membrane extractor/separator to quench, extract and separate the product directly after acylation, eliminating intermediate work‑ups and reducing exposure to hazardous streams.
Supporting_Evidence:
“An inline extractor/separator consists of three PTFE plates … The reaction mixture and extraction solvent (DCM) entered the mixing channel … the organic layer … exited the extraction chamber.”
“The fully continuous flow synthesis … combined two steps of syntheses, flow neutralization and an inline extraction step without intermediate purification and solvent exchange.”
“The setup ... operated combining two steps of syntheses, flow neutralization and an inline extraction step.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: Chlorine gas (Cl₂) is highly toxic; its uncontrolled delivery could cause safety incidents and back‑flow into the system.
Solution_Description: Feed Cl₂ from a regulated cylinder through a mass‑flow controller, a surge bottle, and a drying bottle filled with concentrated H₂SO₄ to dry the gas and prevent back‑flow; calibrate the flow meter before each run.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Cl₂ gas from a regulated cylinder was fed into the Protrix reactor via a mass flow controller after passing through a surge bottle and a dried bottle filled with concentrated sulfuric acid, which were used to dry the chlorine gas and to prevent back flow influence.”
“The mass flow meter was calibrated every time before the reaction to ensure an accurate value for the Cl₂ gas content.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 3‑Chloro-4-oxopentyl Acetate: An Important Intermediate for Vitamin B1
Problem_Description: At the low total flow rates used (Re ≈ 3.6), the T‑mixer produced an uneven velocity profile and poor density distribution, limiting molecular diffusion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Perform CFD (ANSYS Fluent) simulations of both T‑ and cross‑mixers to evaluate micromixing performance and select the geometry that provides a more uniform flow field.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) was applied to simulate the mixing conditions in both the T‑mixer and cross‑mixer to obtain a better understanding of the micromixing process.”
“Figures 10a,c show the velocity profiles indicating a better regulated velocity distribution in a cross‑mixer than in a T‑mixer.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: The traditional nitration/reduction sequence uses nitro‑pyrazole precursors that are low‑molecular‑weight, nitrogen‑rich energetic intermediates with explosive properties, creating safety concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: Adopted an alternative copper‑catalyzed aryl‑amidation route that starts from commercially available bromide 4, avoiding the hazardous nitrated intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The nitrated precursors used in preparation of 1 raise safety concerns given the low molecular weight and high nitrogen content… While the risks associated with nitration reactions and high‑energy compounds can be appropriately managed on scale, avoiding these hazardous reagents is always preferable.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: Catalytic hydrogenation of nitro‑aryl intermediates requires precious‑metal (Pd/Pt) catalysts whose price has risen dramatically, increasing raw‑material cost.
Solution_Description: Switched to a copper‑catalyzed amidation using inexpensive CuI and a cheap diamine ligand (DMEDA, L2) that gave comparable performance while reducing catalyst expense.
Supporting_Evidence: “These reactions require specialized reactors and typically use precious metals such as palladium or platinum, the former of which has seen a significant cost increase… In contrast, stoichiometric reductions… use much less‑expensive reagents… the cost difference between these two ligands favored use of DMEDA (L2).”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: Suppliers of the target aminopyrazole displayed large colour variability; the free‑base 3 discoloured rapidly on storage and generated new impurities, indicating instability.
Solution_Description: The new route delivers the amide 10 directly (avoiding the unstable free‑base) and the subsequent acidic hydrolysis is performed under nitrogen‑purged conditions to keep oxygen out, limiting oxidative degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Despite the range of colors… the freebase 3 very rapidly discolors when stored neat… we observed simultaneous growth of new impurities… For these reasons, we explored the possibility of preparing target compound 1 via an alternative synthetic route… As with many other copper‑catalyzed couplings, the presence of oxygen was found to be detrimental, resulting in longer reaction times and incomplete conversion… sparging the reaction mixture and performing three purge cycles with nitrogen was sufficient for achieving consistent conversion.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: Product 10 showed very low solubility in toluene (<1 mg mL⁻¹), causing crusting of vessel walls and stir shafts, and leading to poor mass‑transfer and low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Switched the reaction solvent to tert‑amyl alcohol (t‑AmOH) where 10 is moderately soluble; used a 1.25 M reaction concentration (5 mL g⁻¹ t‑AmOH) to improve throughput, and developed a work‑up sequence (dilution with 1‑BuOH, filtration, activated‑carbon treatment, and antisolvent crystallisation with 2‑MeTHF/water) that efficiently isolates 10 despite its low solubility in many solvents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Toluene appeared promising … however, this resulted in significant crusting … due to the very low solubility of product 10 in toluene (<1 mg/mL)… ultimately, t‑AmOH gave a cleaner reaction profile and was chosen as the preferred solvent… Running the reaction using 5 mL/g of t‑AmOH … was found to be optimal to reduce reaction time and improve overall throughput… After full consumption of bromide 4, the reaction was cooled and diluted with 1‑BuOH to fully dissolve amide 10… Filtration removed the majority of the inorganic by‑products… circulated through an activated carbon cartridge… finally, after concentration of the solution, conditions were identified to crystallize amide 10.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: A bis‑arylated side‑product 11 formed in the coupling, lowering the assay yield of amide 10 and complicating purification.
Solution_Description: Increasing the equiv of acetamide (7) to 2.0 equiv reduced the level of impurity 11, and the subsequent crystallisation step efficiently purged residual 11, delivering an isolated yield of ~70 % for amide 10.
Supporting_Evidence: “The only significant impurity identified … was the bis‑coupled impurity 11… the stoichiometry of acetamide (7) used was found to be most effective at reducing the level of 11… Using 2.0 equiv as the optimal amount… Using these optimized conditions, the desired coupling reaction typically gave amide 10 in ~85 % assay yield… while bis‑coupled impurity 11 was found to purge very effectively during crystallisation and was never observed at >0.1 % in the isolated solids.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: Residual copper, inorganic salts (K₂CO₃, KHCO₃, KBr) and excess acetamide were difficult to remove due to competing solubility, risking metal‑related impurities in the final API.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a filtration step to discard insoluble inorganics, passed the filtrate through a large activated‑carbon cartridge to adsorb residual copper, and controlled the crystallisation solvent/water composition to purge excess acetamide, achieving <10 ppm copper in the final product.
Supporting_Evidence: “Filtration removed the majority of the inorganic by‑products… before the solution was circulated through an activated carbon cartridge… to improve the color, further remove inorganics to give better control over the ROI (typically <0.5 %), and ensure low levels of residual copper (typically NMT 10 ppm)… the ability to purge the excess acetamide ultimately became the deciding factor in selecting 2.0 equiv as the optimal amount.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: During acidic hydrolysis, residual acetamide hydrolyses to ammonium chloride, which does not purge well and could affect product purity and toxicology limits.
Solution_Description: Optimised the hydrolysis to use 1.2 equiv of 35–37 % HCl in 1‑BuOH at 80 °C, added a small controlled amount of water to accelerate the reaction and later removed water by azeotropic distillation, thereby minimizing residual acetamide and ammonium chloride formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Removal of the acetyl group in amide 10 was explored under acidic conditions using HCl… addition of water, even in small amounts, dramatically accelerated the reaction… 1.2 equiv of a 35–37 % HCl solution… the water present would help accelerate the reaction, but given the relatively small amount, it could be removed via azeotropic distillation prior to isolation… the high aqueous solubility of target compound 1 meant that water needed to be removed prior to isolation… the presence of high levels of residual acetamide (>10 %)… required additional HCl be added to achieve full conversion.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: During the final de‑acetylation step, overly dry reaction mixtures caused crusting of solids on the reactor walls, leading to lower recovery of the final HCl salt 1.
Solution_Description: Adjusted the water content of the 1‑BuOH reaction mixture to ~3 % w/w to keep a slight amount of water present, preventing crusting while still allowing efficient product crystallisation and high isolated yield (88 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Removing as much water as possible would result in maximum recovery … however, this also resulted in an increased likelihood for crusting of solids on the vessel walls and therefore opted to target a solution containing a small amount of water (∼3 % w/w) to help alleviate this problem.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: Potential formation of alkyl chloride impurities (e.g., 1‑chlorobutane) during HCl‑mediated hydrolysis could pose genotoxicity concerns.
Solution_Description: Monitored for alkyl chloride impurities and confirmed that 1‑chlorobutane was not detectable; process controls and analytical checks were implemented to ensure impurity levels remained below toxicological limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of HCl in the alcoholic solvent raises the possibility of alkyl chloride impurities that are a concern from a toxicology perspective… We have not observed detectable levels of 1‑chlorobutane in materials produced using this route, although it is worth considering this possibility as a part of an overall control strategy.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of an Aminopyrazole Building Block via Copper-Catalyzed Aryl Amidation
Problem_Description: The final solid product 1 sometimes turned pink/purple on storage, indicating colour change due to trace impurities, moisture or oxygen exposure.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented packaging under nitrogen and stored the material protected from moisture and oxygen; a reslurry in acetonitrile or an alcohol solvent was used to restore colour when needed.
Supporting_Evidence: “Samples of 1 were observed to be white during isolation, but upon storage would sometimes become light pink… protection from moisture and oxygen had the largest impact on preventing colour change… it could be dramatically improved using a simple reslurry in either acetonitrile or an alcohol solvent.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for a Novel Dual-Acting Serotonergic Antidepressant Vilazodone
Problem_Description: The original Merck route (Route 1) gave a very low overall isolated yield of only 3.5 % and generated many impurities; the similarity of impurity 3a/3b made product isolation difficult, reducing the overall yield.
Solution_Description: A redesigned synthetic sequence (Route 2) added two extra steps and changed reagents, raising the overall isolated yield to 48.2 % while still using the same 5‑cyanoindole starting material.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “the total yield is only 3.5%, and there are many impurities.” 2. “the difficulty of product purification… increases, and the total yield of the route reduces.” 3. “Route 2… the total yield of 48.2%.” 4. “This route overcomes the impurity problems in route 1.” 5. “The target compound vilazodone was synthesized… with a total yield of 48.2%.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for a Novel Dual-Acting Serotonergic Antidepressant Vilazodone
Problem_Description: Route 2 required p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride, which increased the process‑mass‑intensity (PMI) and overall material cost, making the route less attractive for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: A third synthetic design (Route 3) replaced the expensive sulfonyl chloride and the 5‑cyanoindole with low‑cost ε‑caprolactone as the commercial feedstock, providing a cheaper raw‑material basis (later optimized to Route 4 with a 56.2 % overall yield).

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling
Problem_Description: The original discovery route suffered from a very low overall isolated yield (≈12 % over seven steps). This was mainly caused by the Wittig reaction, which required equimolar triphenylphosphine (high cost, poor atom‑economy) and gave poor isolated yields, and by the intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation, which gave a messy work‑up, required chromatographic purification and showed slow phase separation. In addition, the free acid intermediate 5 displayed very low solubility (≈30 mL g⁻¹) leading to large reaction volumes and slow conversion, while the hydrogenation of the stilbene double bond generated the hydrodehalogenation side product 14 (dechlorinated impurity). The addition of Eaton’s reagent for the final ring closure was highly exothermic, causing a temperature spike during quench.
Solution_Description: A complete redesign of the early‑stage C–C bond formation replaced the Wittig step with a Buchwald‑catalyzed Heck coupling (new route).  The coupling uses a third‑generation Buchwald precatalyst (Pd G3 μ‑dimer) together with bench‑stable t‑Bu₃P·HBF₄, allowing Pd loadings as low as 0.1 mol % (catalyst optimisation and stoichiometry change).  The reaction solvent was switched from dioxane to greener, higher‑boiling solvents (DMF, EtOAc, MeCN) and, on multigram scale, to EtOAc without TBAC (solvent change, cost reduction).  Reaction temperature was kept at 80 – 100 °C for the Heck step and later reduced to 65 °C for the Eaton’s reagent cyclisation, with careful temperature control during quench (temperature optimisation, order‑of‑addition).  The free acid 5 was first esterified to methyl ester 11 to improve solubility before the Heck step (other condition change).  For the hydrogenation, mixed EtOAc/MeOH solvent systems and cooling below 20 °C were employed to suppress the hydrodehalogenation side reaction (solvent change, temperature optimisation).  Catalyst pre‑activation was eliminated; the ligand and Pd source are added directly to the degassed reaction mixture (order‑and‑rate‑of‑addition).  A precipitative work‑up (MeOH dilution followed by water addition) replaces chromatography for isolation of the Heck product 12 (new purification procedure) and the final intermediate 8 (concentration tuning to 0.67 M, reducing solvent waste).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem evidence: "Besides the fairly low overall yield of ca. 12 % over seven steps, the Wittig reaction ... required equimolar amounts of triphenylphosphine resulting in an unfavorable atom economy and delivering only poor yields."

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling
Problem_Description: The intramolecular Friedel–Crafts acylation step required a tedious work‑up with slow phase separation after aqueous quench and a chromatographic purification, making the step unsuitable for scale‑up and costly.
Solution_Description: The ring‑closure was redesigned by using Eaton’s reagent (a 70 % P₂O₅ solution in methanesulfonic acid) instead of the harsher polyphosphoric‑acid/sulfolane system, providing a homogeneous solution throughout the reaction and eliminating the problematic phase‑separation and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: "The workup of this reaction suffered from a slow phase separation after aqueous quench and the crude product required chromatographic purification resulting in a moderate yield of 58% for this step."

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling
Problem_Description: Free acid 5 showed very low solubility (≈30 mL g⁻¹), which forced the use of large solvent volumes and resulted in incomplete dissolution at the start of the reaction, slowing down the conversion.

Supporting_Evidence: "The main issue in this step was the low solubility of the free carboxylic acid (30 mL per gram 5) which resulted in large reaction volumes."

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling

Supporting_Evidence: "formation of the hydrodehalogenation side product 14 was observed as a competing reaction, especially at longer reaction times."

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling
Problem_Description: The initial Heck conditions used 1 mol % palladium and 10 mol % TBAC, which would be uneconomic on multigram scale.

Supporting_Evidence: "Gradually, we were able to reduce the necessary amount of palladium to a very low level of 0.1 mol %, and the concentration of TBAC from 10 to 1 mol %, which were considered to be acceptable parameters for the final scale‑up."

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling

Increasing the substrate concentration to 0.67 M also reduced solvent usage and facilitated precipitation.

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling
Problem_Description: Quenching the Eaton’s reagent cyclisation generated an exothermic hydrolysis, raising the temperature to 50‑60 °C and posing a safety issue.

Paper Title: Improved Multigram Route to a Tricyclic Key Intermediate for Dibenzosuberone-Based p38 Inhibitors via an Optimized Early-Stage Heck Coupling

Supporting_Evidence: "...the separate preactivation of the catalytic system … was not necessary for the gram‑scale reactions to proceed smoothly and completely. Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Synthesis and Workup of 1,5-Disubstituted Tetrazoles Enhanced by Real-Time Process Analytics

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: When the reactor was operated without rotation, a significant amount of the over‑oxidized product 3 formed, reducing the selectivity for the desired methoxylated product 2.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the rotation speed to 4000 rpm suppressed the formation of over‑oxidized product 3 and raised the selectivity for 2 to >97 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “With rotation of the central electrode, the yield and conversion increased substantially… rotation of the electrode is crucial for enhancing the selectivity of the reaction… at 4000 rpm the conversion is already high and the selectivity reaches 97 %.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Hydrogen gas generated at the cathode formed slugs in the outlet pipe, causing instability in the FTIR signal used for in‑line monitoring.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An off‑gassing column was installed downstream of the reactor to separate the gas from the liquid before the FTIR flow cell.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the H2 gas produced in the reaction, the solution contained slugs of gas in the pipes, which caused instability in the FTIR signals. Therefore, the liquid/gas mixture exiting the reactor was passed through an off‑gassing tube to allow the gas and liquid to separate.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Increasing the applied current above 6–8 A caused a temperature rise that approached the boiling point of the solvent, limiting further scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A cooling jacket (aluminum sleeve with a copper coil connected to a recirculating chiller) was fitted around the reactor to remove the heat generated at high currents.
Supporting_Evidence: “A temperature rise was observed as the current was increased up to 6–8 A, at which point the reactor could no longer maintain the desired current, presumably because the solvent inside the reactor began to boil… To circumvent this issue, the reactor was cooled using an aluminum sleeve with a coil of copper tubing… With the chiller set to 5 °C, the reactor is capable of achieving up to 18 A, and if the chiller is further cooled down to −20 °C, the reactor is capable of operating at a current of at least 30 A.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: An alternative carbon/polymer outer electrode performed worse than the graphite electrode, leading to lower conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: The outer electrode material was changed to graphite, which gave superior performance for the methoxylation reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “An alternative carbon/polymer outer electrode was tested, but the graphite anode performed better.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: When the annular gap between the electrodes was larger than 1 mm, conversion, yield and selectivity fell markedly, indicating insufficient mass‑transfer.
Solution_Description: The gap size was optimized (0.5–1 mm) to maximize vortex formation and maintain high conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “For all of the annular gap sizes, the conversion, yield, and selectivity are lower in the absence of rotation… The performance of the 1.5 and 2 mm gaps appeared to be inferior… the 0.5 mm gap size gives the highest value of the space‑time yield.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Prolonged use of the porous graphite electrode caused reactant leaching and the electrode to bind to the aluminum cooling jacket, indicating electrode degradation.
Solution_Description: Non‑porous electrode materials and improved sealing of the graphite surface are being investigated to prevent leaching and binding.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of porous graphite in the current reactor design can leach reactants to its outer surface after prolonged usage without cleaning. When the cooling jacket is fitted, this can lead to the graphite electrode binding to the aluminum jacket. We are currently investigating the use of nonporous electrode materials and other materials to seal the outer surface of the graphite.”

Paper Title: A Continuous-Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor: A Laboratory-Scale High-Throughput Flow Reactor with Enhanced Mixing for Scalable Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Scaling up required higher currents, but heat removal limited how far the current could be increased.
Solution_Description: The cooling jacket enabled operation at 30 A while keeping the electrode temperature below 40 °C, achieving >1 kg day⁻¹ productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The highest scaled productivity was achieved at 30 A… the reactor operated at 30 A with a stable voltage range of 11–13 V and a stable temperature of <40 °C for the extended duration.”

Paper Title: Effective Phosphorylation of 2,2′-Methylene-bis(4,6-di-
Problem_Description: The phosphorylation of 2,2′‑methylene‑bis(4,6‑di‑tert‑butyl) phenol generates insoluble triethylamine hydrochloride (3) that precipitates in the reaction mixture, causing channel clogging, pressure spikes and shutdown of continuous flow reactors. The solid is poorly soluble in the commonly used solvent toluene; alternative chlorinated solvents (CH₂Cl₂, DCE, CHCl₃) either only partially dissolve the salt or are too volatile/toxic for large‑scale use. In batch reactors the reaction requires slow, dropwise addition of POCl₃ over 30 min to avoid a violent exotherm, leading to long residence times and low productivity. The high temperature drop‑in in the reactor can also produce large amounts of HCl mist, a safety hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: 1) A continuous Coflore agitated cell reactor (ACR) based on the CSTR principle was employed; the reactor contains 10 cells with high‑shear spring‑like agitators that give violent vertical vibration (2‑9 Hz, 5 mm amplitude) and intense mixing, preventing solid sedimentation and allowing the slurry to flow without clogging. 2) The agitation provides effective mass‑ and heat‑transfer, mitigating the exotherm and keeping the reaction homogeneous; this is a classic example of a reactor‑platform change combined with mixing‑intensification. 3) Toluene was retained as the process solvent (to avoid the toxicity/volatility of alternative chlorinated solvents) while the ACR’s vigorous mixing allowed the precipitate to stay suspended, solving the solubility‑related clogging without changing solvent. 4) Reaction temperature was raised to 100 °C, which accelerates the phosphorylation rate, allowing the residence time to be reduced to 4 min while still achieving >95 % yield. 5) The equivalents of triethylamine (2.8 eq) and POCl₃ (1.1 eq) were optimized; too little base reduces pH and conversion, while too much consumes POCl₃ and lowers yield. 6) Separate feeds for the phenol/triethylamine solution and POCl₃ solution were found sufficient; a T‑mixer premixing step was unnecessary because the ACR’s high‑frequency shaking provides rapid and uniform mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem – Clogging: “the continuous Coflore agitated cell reactor (ACR) designed based on the continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) principle was proved capable of overcoming the severe channel clogging caused by the precipitation product triethylamine hydrochloride.”

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Many phenols and aldehydes are solids and have low solubility in super‑critical CO₂, making it difficult to pump them into the flow system without a co‑solvent.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent (initially MeOH, later EtOAc/HFIP) was added to the sc‑CO₂ stream to keep the substrates in solution and enable continuous feeding.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “since many of these compounds are solids, a cosolvent is required.” (sec 2.1) 
• “MeOH was initially chosen as the cosolvent to minimize the risk of precipitation of both the substrate and product in scCO₂.” (sec 2.2) 
• “EtOAc, a polar aprotic solvent, … is considered to be a greener solvent.” (sec 2.4) 
• “EtOAc with HFIP (2 eq.) gave the best yields.” (sec 2.5) 
• “The concentration of the starting phenol was 0.5 M … because of solubility issues … in EtOAc and HFIP.” (tbl 4 footnote b).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: At very high substrate concentrations (5 M) the mixture became viscous and caused blockages in the flow reactor, limiting productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The concentration was lowered to 1–3 M to keep the flow stable and prevent blockages while still achieving high conversion; sand‑filled static mixers and glass‑bead packed reactors were used to improve mixing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Increasing the concentration of the starting solution to 5 M MeOH caused blockages on prolonged running (>4 h).” (sec 2.2) 
• “Increasing the concentration of the starting material gave improved yields… 96 %.” (tbl 1, entry 4) 
• “The mixture is a ‘gas‑expanded liquid’ … CO₂ lowers viscosity, which will aid in penetration into the pores of the solid acid catalyst.” (sec 2.2) 
• “Static mixer 1 … loaded with sand to promote the mixing of CO₂ and O₂. … high‑pressure sapphire tube reactor … filled with glass beads to enhance mixing.” (Fig 1 caption).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: When MeOH was used as the co‑solvent in the second, acid‑catalysed step, its nucleophilicity led to polymerisation and blocked the cascade to trioxanes, giving low yields.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from MeOH to EtOAc, and 2 equiv of hexafluoro‑isopropanol (HFIP) were added as a less‑nucleophilic, stronger proton donor to suppress polymerisation and improve acidity of the solid catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The presence of an excess of MeOH, a nucleophilic solvent, appears to be detrimental to the acid‑catalyzed step, thus blocking the cascade.” (sec 2.4) 
• “No polymerization was observed and 69 % yield was obtained at 1.0 M … when EtOAc was used.” (tbl 3, entry 2) 
• “Higher yield … when tert‑butanol was used … but best yields … when using 2 equivalents of HFIP.” (tbl 3, entry 4) 
• “HFIP is a better proton donor … and the conjugate base … is less nucleophilic …” (sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Traditional batch methods for generating singlet oxygen either use solid oxidants (hard to scale safely) or molecular oxygen with reaction times up to 48 h, presenting safety and productivity concerns.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow photoreactor operated at 40 °C and 120 bar with sc‑CO₂ as solvent was developed, allowing rapid photogeneration of singlet oxygen and dramatically shortening reaction times.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Current methods employ either solid oxidants … or molecular oxygen, requiring long reaction times of up to 48 h.” (abstract) 
• “...continuous approach using a custom‑built high‑pressure sapphire photoreactor …” (abstract) 
• “Photo‑oxidation … using scCO₂ with MeOH (40 °C, 120 bar).” (sec 2.2) 
• “the reaction time was 26 min … good yields.” (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Peroxyquinol intermediates are highly reactive and potentially explosive, making their accumulation on scale a safety risk.
Solution_Description: The process was telescoped so that peroxyquinols are generated and consumed in the same flow stream without isolation, minimizing the amount of hazardous intermediate present at any time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...minimizing the quantity of potentially unstable peroxyquinols in the system at any one time.” (sec 2.1) 
• “The integrated two‑step flow synthesis … without the need for isolation of hazardous intermediates.” (abstract) 
• “telescoped process” (sec 2.1 title).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Efficient mixing of the peroxyquinol with aldehyde before contacting the solid acid catalyst was crucial; poor mixing led to decomposition of the peroxide and inconsistent yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Additional glass beads (1.5–2.0 mm) were packed below the Amberlyst‑15 catalyst to act as a premixer, improving contact and stabilising the intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “mixing reduces the decomposition of 2a when interacting with Amberlyst‑15 … an additional 0.85 g of glass beads (1.5–2.0 mm), filling the remaining volume of the reactor below Amberlyst‑15 to act as a premixer.” (sec 2.7) 
• “Efficient mixing … presumably because mixing reduces the decomposition of 2a.” (sec 2.7).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Traditional oxidants such as oxone or hypervalent iodine are stoichiometric, expensive, and generate waste, limiting economical scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Photochemical generation of singlet oxygen from gaseous O₂ in sc‑CO₂ eliminates the need for stoichiometric oxidants, using inexpensive, renewable gases and greener solvents (EtOAc, sc‑CO₂).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The use of ¹O₂ on scale would open up very economical routes … but all of this work involved batch reactions … safety grounds.” (sec 1) 
• “Our approach … uses a greener reagent (singlet oxygen, photogenerated from the renewable feedstock, gaseous O₂) and renewable solvents (supercritical CO₂ and EtOAc).” (conclusions).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Trioxanes Enabled by a Supercritical CO
Problem_Description: Halogenated solvents (e.g., dichloromethane) corrode stainless‑steel components of the high‑pressure apparatus, posing a safety and equipment‑failure risk.
Solution_Description: The reaction medium was switched to EtOAc, a polar aprotic and greener solvent compatible with the stainless‑steel reactor.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Previously reported examples … in dichloromethane. … the use of a halogenated solvent is not compatible with our approach particularly because of potential corrosion of the high‑pressure apparatus.” (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: The previously reported anodic oxidation of oxamic acids (Landais method) required a large excess of the alcohol nucleophile as the reaction solvent, a wasteful supporting electrolyte (0.1 equiv) and was carried out at very low current density, resulting in low productivity, high material cost and difficult product isolation.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a supporting‑electrolyte‑free electrolysis using collidine as a base in acetonitrile with cheap graphite electrodes. This new route eliminates the need for excess alcohol solvent and supporting electrolyte, allowing a one‑pot addition of a variety of nucleophiles and simplifying isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: The methodology is limited to the synthesis of simple carbamates…requires them to be stable toward anodic oxidation and used in a vast excess as the solvent. A wasteful supporting electrolyte is also needed (0.1 equiv)

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Supporting electrolyte (LiClO₄) was found detrimental to the reaction and adds unnecessary cost and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: The optimized protocol removes the supporting electrolyte entirely, running the oxidation in plain acetonitrile with collidine, thereby lowering material cost and eliminating the handling of hazardous salts.
Supporting_Evidence: The addition of a supporting electrolyte, such as LiClO₄, was shown to be detrimental (Table 1, entry 10).

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Oxamic acids bearing aryl substituents or low intrinsic conductivity gave very poor yields in batch because the solution could not sustain the required current.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Conversion of the batch process to a continuous‐flow electrochemical cell (C_gr/C_gr electrodes, adjustable inter‑electrode gap) increased conductivity, allowed higher current densities and gave the corresponding ureas in acceptable yields (84 % for 1o, low but observable yields for 1p‑1r).
Supporting_Evidence: Substrates that resulted in low conductivity were selected to be run under the optimized flow conditions… resulted in the clean formation of the corresponding ureas after reaction with propylamine (Scheme 3).

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Carbamate formation under the original conditions gave only 7 % yield at room temperature, and the reaction required 18 h to reach completion.
Solution_Description: Adding 10 mol % dibutyltin dilaurate (DBTDL) as a catalyst raised the yield to 63 % (room temperature) and 73 % at 60 °C, while the higher temperature shortened the reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: Using 10 mol % DBTDL gave 3aa in 63 % yield (Table 2, entry 7). Increasing the reaction temperature to 60 °C further increased the yield to 73 % (Table 2, entry 8).

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Attempts to replace acetonitrile with DMSO, DMF or CH₂Cl₂ led to phase‑separation, high viscosity and complex mixtures that were hard to purify.
Solution_Description: Acetonitrile was retained as the optimum solvent; the other solvents were discarded because they lowered the yield and complicated purification.
Supporting_Evidence: Attempts to replace acetonitrile (ACN) with other solvents… led to poor yields and complex mixtures of products that were challenging to separate.

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: When bulky secondary amines (e.g., di‑isopropylamine) were used, the isocyanate intermediate partially decomposed during work‑up, giving lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: By adjusting the addition order (post‑electrolysis addition of nucleophile) and performing the work‑up promptly at ambient temperature, the authors minimized decomposition and improved yields (58 % for 2ad).
Supporting_Evidence: Diisopropylamine afforded 2ad in a slightly decreased yield of 58 %, presumably due to its higher steric hindrance, leaving unreacted isocyanate, which degraded over time and during the workup.

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Collidine was used in excess (2.5 equiv) to generate the carboxylate; the exact role was unclear, raising concerns about material efficiency and safety of handling a tertiary amine at scale.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening showed that 2.5 equiv of collidine gave quantitative yields, while lower (1 equiv) or higher (10 equiv) loadings reduced conversion; the optimal stoichiometry balances cost and performance.
Supporting_Evidence: Both decreasing and increasing the amount of collidine led to a decrease in the urea yield (Table 1, entries 6–9).

Paper Title: Supporting-Electrolyte-Free Anodic Oxidation of Oxamic Acids into Isocyanates: An Expedient Way to Access Ureas, Carbamates, and Thiocarbamates
Problem_Description: Aryl amines failed to give the desired ureas, limiting the substrate scope for pharmaceutical applications.
Solution_Description: No satisfactory solution was found within this study; the authors noted the limitation and suggest future work to develop alternative conditions for aryl amines.
Supporting_Evidence: Unfortunately, this method does not seem to tolerate aryl amines as nucleophiles, as shown by the inability to prepare 2l.

Paper Title: Solid Form Selection and Process Development of KO-947 Drug Substances
Problem_Description: The free‑base of KO‑947 displayed strong dependence of solid form on the solvent system used in preparation (slurries, antisolvent precipitation, grinding). Different organic solvents produced different polymorphs (A‑K), creating a risk that the form could change during scale‑up washing, extraction or recrystallisation operations.
Solution_Description: A robust crystallisation route for the preferred free‑base form E was established by selecting a solvent system that consistently produced this form, employing seeding (≈5 % form E) and controlled cooling. This eliminated solvent‑induced form changes and gave reproducible batch‑to‑batch product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “KO‑947 free base polymorphism was highly dependent on the solvent system used in the preparation method… potentially leading to form changes” (Sec 2.1). 
• “Form E was recommended for further scaling up… a robust manufacturing process… to produce form E exclusively with consistent quality control.” (Sec 2.1). 
• “Seed of form E (≈5 %) was added and the solution was slowly cooled…” (Production Procedure).

Paper Title: Solid Form Selection and Process Development of KO-947 Drug Substances
Problem_Description: Mesylate salt of KO‑947 exhibited four crystal forms (I‑IV) with markedly different hygroscopicity and chemical stability. Form II (dihydrate) and Form I (hydrate) lost crystallinity quickly on drying and showed high degradation at 40 °C/75 % RH; the solid‑state behavior was inconsistent and hindered scale‑up.

Form VIII (acetone‑water solvate) was isolated, then acetone was removed by vacuum drying to generate metastable anhydrous Form X, which was re‑hydrated under a defined RH to give the stable Form IX. This route stabilized the polymorph and eliminated the unstable forms.

Paper Title: Solid Form Selection and Process Development of KO-947 Drug Substances
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the anhydrous mesylate Form III required mixed alcoholic solvents (MeOH/THF, EtOH/THF). After crystallisation, the solid was micronised, then vacuum‑dried at 60–70 °C to remove acetone and water, producing Form X, which was subsequently re‑hydrated to Form IX under controlled RH. Supporting_Evidence:

• “…particle size of form III crystal was rather small… rendering substantial manufacturing difficulties in solid filtration and transfer operations.” (Sec 2.2). 
• “…acetone/water (40:1 v/v)… dried … to generate form X … rehydrated … to afford form IX.” (Production Procedure).

Paper Title: Solid Form Selection and Process Development of KO-947 Drug Substances
Problem_Description: Form IX, although thermally stable, showed reversible water uptake/loss (5–7 % w/w). At RH > 40 % the crystal could convert to Form X and back, potentially affecting purity and storage stability.

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Implementation and
Problem_Description: During the high‑throughput campaign the work‑up filtration devices (FWU‑1 and FWU‑2) became progressively clogged by a gel‑like impurity that precipitated in the feed, causing a rapid decline in filtration rates and eventually preventing completion of the washing‑and‑product‑collection steps.

• “The module operated for another 5 h, where two more interruptions occurred, before it was decided to decrease the module’s throughput to allow more time for CIP.” (sec 5.2).

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Implementation and
Problem_Description: The pH of the crude stream fluctuated because the upstream synthesis delivered feed at pH ≈ 15 with variable composition. This caused spikes in the pH of the first precipitation vessel, leading to inconsistent solubility, variable supersaturation, and unstable yields during the work‑up precipitation.
Solution_Description: A feedback control loop was installed on the first MSMPR precipitation vessel (WMX‑1). A pH probe measured the instantaneous pH and automatically adjusted the rate of acetic‑acid addition to maintain the set‑point of 7.5, thus stabilising the precipitation environment.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The solubility of ciprofloxacin is highly sensitive to variations in solution pH… any fluctuations in flow rates … can lead to significant variations in the crude pH and in the amount of acid needed for neutralization.” (sec 4.2). 
• “A pH meter was installed to the first precipitation stage (WMX‑1), and its readings were used to control the amount of acid dispensed to the vessel.” (sec 4.2). 
• “The pressure‑driven transfer… is immediately met with a sharp increase in pH… which triggers the operation of the acid pump… until the pH has reached the set‑point value of 7.5.” (fig 9). 
• “Analysis of the precipitation filtrate… reveals a consistent mother‑liquid API concentration and purity, and the attainment of a constant state of control after 100 min of operation.” (sec 4.2).

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Implementation and
Problem_Description: During drying of the isolated ciprofloxacin HCl·hydrate the powder formed needle‑like crystals that aggregated into hard lumps, especially when the cake dry‑matter content fell below 70 wt %, which prevented effective mixing and risked dehydration of the hydrate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A two‑stage drying strategy was introduced: static drying with temperature control (inductive heater kept at 49‑50 °C) followed by an agitated delumping step (30 rpm, direction reversal every 30 s) that was triggered when the in‑situ heat‑duty dropped to 15–20 %, indicating a cake dry‑matter of 70–80 wt %. Real‑time heat‑duty monitoring allowed the transition to be timed precisely, avoiding over‑drying and limiting lump formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Ciprofloxacin is prone to the formation of lumps during the drying process, especially during agitated drying at dry matter contents below 70 wt %.” (sec 4.3). 
• “Two feedback control systems were implemented… the first controls the drying temperature… the second controls the transition between static drying and agitated drying through in‑situ measurements of the drying heat duty.” (sec 4.3). 
• “The heat duty for isothermal operation was tracked … a heat duty of 15–20 % corresponds to a cake dry matter content of 70–80 %.” (sec 4.3). 
• “The static drying step … once the heat duty drops … an agitation program is started, by which the impeller rotates at 30 rpm with direction switches every 30 s to promote bulk powder mixing.” (sec 4.3). 
• “Because the inductive heaters operate at a constant power, the heat supply recorded by the module is either 0 or 100 %… the drop in required heat duty can be used for tracking the dry matter content of the cake.” (sec 4.3).

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Implementation and
Problem_Description: In earlier PoD iterations the work‑up required a manually operated batch precipitation followed by offline filtration, which limited throughput, introduced long reaction times and made it difficult to consistently meet the 98–102 % USP purity specification.
Solution_Description: A continuous two‑stage mixed‑suspension‑mixed‑product‑removal (MSMPR) cascade was implemented. The precipitation agent (8 % acetic acid, 42 % water, 50 % acetonitrile) was continuously added to neutralise the basic crude to pH 7.5, exploiting ciprofloxacin’s low solubility in water while acetonitrile suppresses impurity precipitation. The process runs continuously, eliminating the batch step and enabling higher throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Ciprofloxacin ... is soluble in acidic and basic media but highly insoluble at neutral pH.” (sec 2.2). 
• “First, ciprofloxacin is precipitated from the basic crude … by neutralisation to a pH of 7.5. The precipitation agent … 8 % acetic acid, 42 % water, 50 % acetonitrile.” (sec 3.1). 
• “For these concentrations, the average volume of precipitation agent needed … is 0.58 mL/mL crude, although this value is prone to small variations from fluctuations in the crude pH.” (sec 3.1). 
• “In prior iterations … the work‑up steps had been conducted in the batch mode … In this iteration, the process was fully automated in the continuous mode.” (sec 5.4). 
• “These solvents were chosen … acetonitrile’s effectiveness in preventing the precipitation of critical impurities.” (sec 3.1).

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Implementation and
Problem_Description: Because the API throughput depended on the variable flow of crude solution, the API‑to‑solvent ratios in the downstream crystallisation and washing steps fluctuated, leading to inconsistent yields and occasional impurity carry‑over.
Solution_Description: In‑situ mass‑holdup sensors on the feed and product tanks (WMB‑1, DMB‑1) were used to control the API feed rate. The calibrated diaphragm pumps then delivered fixed solvent volumes based on the measured API mass, ensuring constant solvent‑to‑API ratios throughout the campaign.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The API throughput was monitored and controlled via in‑situ mass holdup measurements at the feed and product collection vessels.” (sec 6). 
• “To achieve a consistent solvent API/solvent ratio … feedback control was implemented for the API throughput … by means of in‑situ mass holdup measurements …” (sec 4). 
• “The feed tanks WMB‑1 … are located on top of scales. These tanks receive crude API solutions … This transfer is conducted continuously until their mass holdup reaches a target value, triggering the stop of the pumping operation.” (sec 4.1). 
• “The operating volume of both MSMPR vessels is fixed at 1600 mL … the transfer of feed and product … is achieved by pressure‑driven flow.” (sec 3.1). 
• “Because the solvent amounts … are controlled by calibrated pumps, consistent solvent ratios can be attained.” (sec 4).

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin
Problem_Description: The original DMA‑removal step used acetyl chloride 7, which left N,N‑dimethylacetamide in the stream and required acetonitrile, a solvent unsuitable for later steps because of solubility issues.

(1) adequate removal of DMA 6 ... (2) increasing the concentration of the reaction intermediate 5 ... Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin
Problem_Description: The base DBU used in the ring‑closure step decomposed under the reaction conditions, generating impurity 16 that reduced final product purity and posed safety concerns.

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin
Problem_Description: Use of NaOH in steps 4‑5 caused formation of an insoluble quinolone intermediate (14), leading to reactor blockages, pressure spikes and loss of conversion.

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin
Problem_Description: Long‑duration runs of steps 4‑5 suffered from tubing leaks, loosened fittings and pressure buildup caused by transient solids, leading to unplanned shutdowns and inconsistent operation.

Paper Title: On-Demand Continuous Manufacturing of Ciprofloxacin in Portable Plug-and-Play Factories: Development of a Highly Efficient Synthesis for Ciprofloxacin
Problem_Description: The high viscosity of TBAOH caused crystallization in the feed lines during start‑up, leading to line blockages and process interruptions.

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of a Bicyclic Amine Moiety Using an Enzymatic Amidation and Identification of a Novel Solid Form
