Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251. Part 1: Synthesis of the Cyclohexane Dicarboxylate Fragment
Problem_Description: Scaling the enol‑tosylate formation to 1 kg gave inconsistent yields; the original addition sequence (enolate into Ts₂O) was not reliable on larger scale.
Solution_Description: Reversing the addition order – adding the pre‑generated enolate solution to a cold solution of Ts₂O (below –5 °C) – produced clean conversion to the tosylates with reproducible yields at kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: "this approach worked well in the laboratory, but the reaction provided inconsistent yields at a 1 kg scale"; "problem was solved by simply modifying the addition sequence: addition of the enolate solution to a solution of Ts₂O in THF at below –5 °C (reverse addition) led to clean conversion to enol tosylates 5"

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251. Part 1: Synthesis of the Cyclohexane Dicarboxylate Fragment
Problem_Description: Crabtree‑catalysed hydrogenation of the phenyl esters 21 became sluggish on >100 g scale (up to 72 h) and left residual starting material and higher amounts of the all‑syn by‑product 23, threatening purity and yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the hydrogen pressure to 2.5 barg and raising the Crabtree catalyst loading to 14 mol % (entry 5) gave >99 % conversion with only 0.4 % residual 21 and 2.8 % 23. Scaling to a 300 L hydrogenator with higher k_La (>0.3 s⁻¹) further shortened reaction time and maintained impurity control.
Supporting_Evidence: "we examined the effect of hydrogen pressure (1, 2.5, and 5 barg) and catalyst loading (5, 10, and 14 mol %) … at 5 barg the reaction proceeded to completion … but higher all‑syn formation"; "at 14 mol % loading, the hydrogenation proceeded smoothly to >99 % conversion (∼0.4 area % 21 remaining), with excellent selectivity (2.8 area % 23)"; "the gas–liquid mass transfer coefficient (k_La) for the 2 L lab‑scale hydrogenators was measured to be <0.01 s⁻¹ … for the pilot plant hydrogenator … >0.3 s⁻¹ indicating better mass transfer on scale"

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251. Part 1: Synthesis of the Cyclohexane Dicarboxylate Fragment
Problem_Description: After Hydrogenation, residual Ir‑based Crabtree catalyst remained at ~11 000 ppm, which is problematic for product safety and downstream processing.
Solution_Description: The crude reaction mixture was treated with SiliaMetS Thiol to bind Ir species, followed by filtration and crystallisation from aqueous methanol, reducing Ir content to <400 ppm (and ultimately <10 ppm after the final TFA hydrolysis).
Supporting_Evidence: "the mixture was transferred … SiliaMetS Thiol (8.1 kg) … stirred for 2 h … filtration … the product was isolated … <400 ppm in isolated 22"; "hydrolysis of the t‑butyl ester … the all‑syn diastereomer 23 … was completely purged … and also reduced the residual Ir content to <10 ppm"

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251. Part 1: Synthesis of the Cyclohexane Dicarboxylate Fragment
Problem_Description: The first‑generation route produced many oil‑like intermediates that required chromatographic purification and lacked a chromophore for easy analytical monitoring.
Solution_Description: Introducing a phenyl ester at C4 created crystalline intermediates with a UV‑active chromophore, enabling HPLC analysis and simplifying purification by crystallisation rather than chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: "the absence of a chromophore … posed analytical challenges"; "we envisioned that the use of a phenyl ester at C4 would alleviate these concerns by imparting crystallinity to several of the intermediates, facilitating the use of HPLC analysis due to the presence of a chromophore"

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: The initial TiCl₄‑mediated condensation of 6‑iodotetralone (4) with 4‑fluorobenzenethiol (5) in the presence of HCl(g) gave poor selectivity (20‑30 % thioacetal 12) and was capricious; on larger scale the reaction was non‑reproducible, showing stalled conversions and higher impurity levels.
Solution_Description: Re‑ordered the addition: a premixed solution of Et₃N and thiol 5 was added slowly to the TiCl₄/4‑iodotetralone mixture at –5 to 0 °C, giving a 9:1 ratio of desired vinyl sulfide 6 to thioacetal 12 and improved reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The initial Discovery conditions for the formation of vinyl sulfide 6 involved condensation of 6‑iodotetralone 4 with 4‑fluorobenzenethiol 5 (1.2 equiv) in the presence of HCl (g). This reaction was capricious and routinely afforded ∼20–30 % of the thioacetal byproduct 12." (sec 2.1) 
- "It was gratifying to find that a change in the order of addition, i.e., slow addition of a premixed solution of Et₃N and 5 in THF to a mixture of 4 and TiCl₄ in THF at −5 to 0 °C, led to a much‑improved ratio (9:1) of 6:12." (sec 2.1) 
- "Under these conditions, the reaction proceeded to completion on scales up to 100 g with very low levels of other impurities... however, on larger scales, these conditions were not reproducible and resulted in either stalled reactions or higher levels of impurities, specifically disulfide 13." (sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: The Brønsted‑acid mediated protocol (p‑TsA/PPTS in refluxing toluene) required 60 h to consume the starting material and, when run in a constant‑volume distillation mode, consumed a prohibitive 70 L of fresh toluene per kg of substrate, making it unsustainable at scale.
Solution_Description: Adopted a Dean‑Stark‑type water‑removal system using toluene as solvent (9 L toluene kg⁻¹ of substrate). This enabled the reaction to reach completion within 24 h at laboratory scale and was successfully scaled to 50 kg in pilot plant, dramatically reducing solvent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "...sub‑stoichiometric amounts of p‑toluenesulfonic acid (p‑TsA; 0.4 equiv) and pyridinium p‑toluenesulfonate (PPTS; 0.6 equiv) in refluxing toluene led to ... 60 h ... a prohibitive 70 L of fresh toluene per kg of starting material 4 and hence would not be sustainable." (sec 2.1) 
- "We simultaneously explored Dean–Stark‑type conditions to effect the removal of water and were able to successfully demonstrate it on large scale... the reaction proceeded to completion within 24 h in the laboratory and was scaled up to a 50 kg scale in the pilot plant." (sec 2.1) 
- "Scheme 4… Dean‑Stark‑type water removal in toluene (9 L toluene kg⁻¹ of iodotetralone 4)." (fig 4)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Vinyl sulfide 6 was difficult to isolate by crystallization because of multiple impurities; however, the downstream oxidation product vinyl sulfone 7 crystallized well.
Solution_Description: The crude vinyl sulfide mixture from the condensation step was directly telescoped into the Oxone oxidation (aqueous Oxone in 2‑PrOH/2‑MeTHF) which gave quantitative conversion to vinyl sulfone 7, eliminating the need for isolation of 6.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The presence of multiple impurities precluded efficient isolation of vinyl sulfide 6 by crystallization. Meanwhile, vinyl sulfone 7 was found to possess better crystalline properties and therefore we sought to telescope the crude vinyl sulfide‑containing mixture into the subsequent oxidation step." (sec 2.1) 
- "treatment of the crude vinyl sulfide‑containing mixture from the condensation step with aqueous Oxone (5 equiv) in 2‑PrOH/2‑MeTHF (1:1) provided nearly quantitative conversion to vinyl sulfone 7." (sec 2.1) 
- "The two‑step condensation–oxidation sequence was scaled up in the plant to produce 190 kg of sulfone 7 in 50 % yield and 93 % purity." (sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Disulfide 13 formed by oxidation of thiol 5 when exposed to air, and reacted further to give ketone 14, leading to batch‑to‑batch variability and safety concerns from oxidative degradation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented multiple vacuum/N₂ purge cycles and extensive solvent degassing (sub‑surface N₂ sparging) to remove head‑space oxygen before charging reactants, limiting formation of disulfide 13 and ketone 14.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "We postulated that disulfide 13 was formed by oxidation of thiol 5 and that ketone 14 was formed by the reaction of vinyl sulfide 6 with disulfide 13... Exposure of a solution of thiol 5 in THF to air led to ca. 20 % of disulfide 13 within 2 h." (sec 2.1) 
- "Three vacuum/N₂ purge cycles were performed to remove headspace oxygen, and the solvent was degassed by subsurface sparging using nitrogen for 30 min." (sec 3.2) 
- "In hindsight, we rationalized that the relatively low reactor fill volumes in the scale‑up batches (20 %) presumably led to a higher level of oxygen in the headspace, which contributed to higher levels of disulfide 13 and ketone 14." (sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: The aza‑Michael adduct 8 readily underwent retro‑Michael reaction to regenerate vinyl sulfide 7, and mesylate 9 degraded to multiple impurities on storage, making isolation problematic.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture containing adduct 8 was immediately telescoped to the mesylation step without isolation; Ms₂O replaced MsCl to avoid chloro impurity, and the pH was maintained between 6‑9 by alternating portionwise addition of Et₃N and Ms₂O to preserve mesylate stability.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "intermediates 8 and 9 were unstable: adduct 8 was prone to a retro‑Michael reaction to regenerate 7, while mesylate 9 degraded to multiple impurities upon storage at ambient temperature." (sec 2.2) 
- "The reaction mixture containing ∼85 area % of adduct 8 was immediately telescoped to the mesylation step in the same solvent (THF)." (sec 2.2) 
- "We were able to successfully eliminate formation of the chloro impurity by switching to Ms₂O as the mesylating agent in THF (entry 3)." (sec 2.2) 
- "To maintain the apparent pH of the reaction mixture between 6 and 9… an alternating, portionwise addition of Et₃N (2.2 equiv in three portions) and Ms₂O (1.9 equiv in three portions)…" (sec 3.4)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Resolution of racemic (±)‑11 by supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) was not suitable for scale‑up due to equipment limitations and cost.
Solution_Description: Developed a classical resolution of the unprotected secondary amine (±)‑10 using (l)‑tartaric acid (LTA) in THF with controlled water content (20‑70 % v/v), achieving >96 % ee and eliminating the need for SFC.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Enantiomerically pure (R,R)‑11 was obtained by SFC separation of the racemic mixture, which was not well‑suited for scale‑up." (sec 1) 
- "We sought to circumvent this by attempting a classical resolution on the unprotected secondary amine (±)‑10. ... a simultaneous screen of resolving agents… suggested that (l)‑tartaric acid (LTA) in THF provided the highest yield and ee’s in the resolution of (±)‑10." (sec 2.2) 
- "The highest ee was obtained when salt formation and crystallization were carried out using ∼20–70 % water in THF (Fig 2)." (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: The Ullmann coupling of protected amine 11 with 2‑iodoheptafluoropropane (19) worked on small scale but gave <60 % conversion on >10 g scale, with low boiling point of 19 and sealed‑tube requirements, posing safety and scalability issues.
Solution_Description: Abandoned the Ullmann step and implemented a three‑step sequence: (i) one‑carbon homologation (carboxylation) of 11 to acid 23, (ii) bis‑trifluoromethylation of the acyl imidazole 25, and (iii) deoxofluorination of the resulting alcohol 27, providing a scalable route to the heptafluoro‑iso‑propyl side chain.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The initial Discovery conditions for the installation of the perfluoroalkyl side chain involved an Ullmann‑type coupling… while the reaction worked well on small scale, it proved capricious on >10 g scales, providing <60 % conversion… unsuitable for scale‑up." (sec 2.3) 
- "We explored a robust multistep approach involving a one‑carbon homologation–bis‑trifluoromethylation–deoxofluorination sequence to enable timely delivery of API (Scheme 9)." (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Metal‑halogen exchange of iodide 11 with i‑PrMgCl generated a highly exothermic CO₂ carboxylation; subsurface CO₂ sparging caused a 60 °C adiabatic temperature rise, posing safety risks.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Performed metalation at –40 to –30 °C, then cooled to –65 °C before CO₂ sparging; temperature was kept below –30 °C during sparging, and CO₂ was introduced via controlled pressurization cycles to mitigate the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Treatment of iodide … with i‑PrMgCl … at −40 to −30 °C; lower temperatures led to incomplete metalation, while higher temperatures led to significant degradation… subsurface sparging of CO₂ … resulted in an instantaneous spike in heat flow (329 W kg⁻¹) and an adiabatic temperature rise of ∼60 °C. To control this event, the reaction mixture … was further cooled to −65 °C…" (sec 2.3) 
- "The reaction proceeded smoothly at −40 to −30 °C; … CO₂ was sparged … while maintaining the temperature of the mass below −30 °C during scale‑up." (sec 2.3) 
- "Mild pressurization cycles… at <0.5 barg, below the pressure rating of the relief valve…" (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: The subsurface CO₂ sparging method required 2 h of continuous CO₂ flow for a 30 kg batch, leading to high solvent usage and operational cost.
Solution_Description: Developed a mild‑pressurization CO₂ method using three low‑pressure (0.16–0.24 barg) CO₂ cycles at –40 to –30 °C, which limited temperature spikes and reduced CO₂ consumption while maintaining yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "We sought to explore conditions that would obviate the need for extended continuous subsurface sparging of CO₂ (2 h for a 30 kg batch)." (sec 2.3) 
- "A simpler alternative mode of carboxylation under mild CO₂ pressures of <1 barg was examined… Multiple such repressurization cycles helped control the stoichiometry of CO₂ … and hence control the temperature spikes, which rendered the process inherently safer." (sec 2.3) 
- "The protocol circumvented the sharp temperature rise observed in the subsurface sparging protocol while furnishing carboxylic acid 23 in similar yield and purity and was demonstrated successfully in the pilot plant." (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Bis‑trifluoromethylation of acyl imidazole 25 using TMSCF₃ and TBAF (1 equiv) at 0 °C gave only 1.6 % of the desired alcohol 27, with substantial side‑product formation and gas evolution (fluoroform) due to moisture in TBAF.
Solution_Description: Reduced TBAF to 0.6 equiv, lowered the temperature to –20 °C (later –30 °C), increased TMSCF₃ to 10 equiv; under these conditions complete conversion to alcohol 27 was achieved with 82 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "addition of TBAF (1 M in THF; 1 equiv) … resulted in only 1.6 % of the desired alcohol 27… The addition of TBAF was accompanied by gas evolution (presumably fluoroform from decomposition of TMSCF₃)… we attributed this phenomenon … to the moisture present in TBAF (6–7 %)." (sec 2.3) 
- "Under these conditions, the conversion of acyl imidazole 25 improved significantly; however, the reaction stalled with the formation of ∼77 % of trifluoromethyl ketone 26. Ultimately, we were able to achieve complete reaction completion with 10 equiv of TMSCF₃ and by addition of 0.6 equiv of TBAF at –30 °C (entry 3)." (sec 2.3) 
- "This was scaled up to ∼15 kg scale, and the desired bis‑trifluoromethylated alcohol 27 was isolated in 82 % yield (>94.0 % purity)." (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Deoxofluorination with DAST required 48 h to reach completion and posed safety concerns due to the hazardous nature of DAST.
Solution_Description: Switched to XtalFluor‑E as fluorinating agent and added DBU (1.2 equiv) as an additive, achieving 98 % conversion in 21 h, improving safety and reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "DAST furnished the desired product 21, the reaction was slow, requiring 2 days to reach completion (entry 1). The safety concerns associated with DAST, as well as the slow reaction, prompted us to examine alternative deoxofluorinating agents… XtalFluor‑E provided ∼10 % conversion… Gratifyingly, the use of DBU (3 equiv, entry 5) led to ∼67 % conversion… after fine‑tuning, the reaction was improved to 98 % conversion using 1.2 equiv of DBU (entry 6)." (sec 2.3) 
- "The two‑step telescoped process was successfully carried out on a 22 kg scale… these operations were carried out in Hastelloy reactors after appropriate material compatibility studies." (sec 2.3) 
- Table 2 entries show entry 6: XtalFluor‑E (3 equiv) + DBU (1.2 equiv) → 98 % conversion.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: Fluoro‑alkylation and deoxofluorination steps used halide‑containing reagents that could corrode standard reactor materials.
Solution_Description: Performed the fluorination and deoxofluorination steps in Hastelloy reactors following material‑compatibility studies to prevent corrosion and ensure safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Due to the use of halide sources in the bis‑trifluoromethylation, fluorination, and deprotection steps, these operations were carried out in Hastelloy reactors after appropriate material compatibility studies." (sec 2.3) 
- The experimental sections for steps using XtalFluor‑E and deprotection note that reactions were performed in 2000 L Hastelloy reactors.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthetic Route to BMS-986251, Part 2: Synthesis of the Tricyclic Core and the API
Problem_Description: During hydrolysis of amide 28, SNAr substitution of fluorine by the 2‑propanol solvent formed impurity 29 (up to 0.25 % area) and transesterification impurity 30 (up to 0.45 % area) reduced purity.
Solution_Description: Controlled the pH of the citric‑acid work‑up to 6–7, which fully suppressed formation of impurity 30 and minimized SNAr product 29, allowing the API to be obtained with >99 % purity after recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The use of 2‑propanol led to formation of the SNAr product 29 (up to 0.25 area %)… Formation of 30 was completely avoided by controlling the pH of the reaction mass at 6–7 during the citric acid workup." (sec 2.4) 
- "The crude API after the citric acid workup was generally contaminated with 1.5–2.3 area % of phenol, which was removed to <100 ppm during the recrystallization step." (sec 2.4) 
- "Recrystallization … delivered the API 1 in 86 % overall yield… 99.30 % HPLC area % purity; 100 % de; 100 % assay." (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: During the batch lithiation‑addition step the reaction mixture gels rapidly after adding the isoxazolene (5) to the lithiothiazole (7). The gelling stops stirring, limits batch size (~9 kg in a 500 L reactor) and forces the reaction to be kept at –90 °C, giving only 57 % isolated yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A) Switch the solvent system to a toluene/THF mixture (2:1 v/v) that provides enough THF to complex BF₃·OEt₂ and break up the gel while retaining reactivity. B) Operate the addition at –75 °C to –70 °C (instead of –90 °C) to keep the mixture fluid. C) Move the reaction to a series of 5‑stage continuous stirred‑tank reactors (CSTRs) with gravity‑overflow transfer, which tolerate heterogeneous mixtures and give a high surface‑to‑volume ratio for efficient heat removal. D) Reduce the total solvent volume from 45 vol to 30 vol and adjust residence times (lithiation 6‑15 min, anion addition 20‑50 min) to keep the mixture fluid and shorten overall reaction time. E) Pre‑cool feed streams (–20 °C to –30 °C) before mixing to control the highly exothermic Li–Br exchange. F) Replace the traditional CO₂ quench and silica‑gel chromatography with an aqueous NH₄Cl quench followed by direct crystallisation of the methanesulfonic‑acid (MSA) salt of product 4, eliminating the need for chromatography. G) Telescope the crude MSA‑salt directly into the next step, avoiding yield loss from isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Gelling of the reaction mixture… within minutes… the stirring to stop… gelling would not occur if the reaction mixture was maintained at –90 °C… batch size was limited to ∼9 kg in a 500 L reactor” (list‑item 1). 
• “The solubility of dibromothiazole 6 in all solvents was rather poor at cryogenic temperatures… the gelling issue was closely related to the volumetric ratio of toluene and THF… at 2:1 (v/v) no gelling was observed” (sec 2.1.1, Table 1). 
• “The highly exothermic nature of the Li–Br exchange dictates the slow combination of n‑BuLi and 6 to control the reaction temperature… adiabatic temperature rise could be as high as 61.9 °C” (sec 2.1.3). 
• “The addition time was 12.7 h… prolonged Li‑Br exchange time is detrimental… impurity formation” (sec 2.1.3). 
• “Chromatographic isolation… was elusive… silica gel chromatography was utilized for product isolation” (list‑item 3). 
• “The formation of dilithiated species 8, 9 … gave rise to impurities 12‑15… when the reaction was carried out above the 10 g scale the UPLC profile started to become messy” (list‑item 2). 
• “The CSTR process … the contents … remained highly fluid… clogging was not observed” (sec 2.1.3, Fig 3). 
• “A salt screen led to discovery of a highly crystalline methanesulfonic acid salt of 4… allowed direct isolation of 97.7 % pure product from the ~80 % pure crude mixture” (sec 2.1.2, Table 2). 
• “The aqueous NH₄Cl quench… eliminated operational complexity for further scale up” (list‑item 3).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: 2,4‑Dibromothiazole (6) shows very poor solubility in all aprotic solvents, especially at cryogenic temperatures, which makes the lithium‑halogen exchange sluggish and leads to formation of dilithiated species (8, 9) that decompose to side‑products and lower the isolated yield of adduct 4.
Solution_Description: Increase the THF fraction in the solvent system (to 2 : 1 to 4 : 1 v/v) to improve solvation of 6 and to break up BF₃·OEt₂ complexes. Run the lithiation at –70 °C to –77 °C (instead of –90 °C) to maintain sufficient reagent reactivity while limiting over‑lithiation. Use a slight excess of n‑BuLi (1.1 equiv) to drive complete Li–Br exchange without generating high concentrations of dilithium species. These adjustments reduce impurity formation and raise the isolated yield from 57 % to >80 % on scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The extremely exothermic Li–Br exchange reaction, coupled with the poor solubility of 6 in all aprotic solvent systems studied, made it a challenge for scale up.” (list‑item 2). 
• “The solubility of dibromothiazole 6 in all solvents was rather poor at cryogenic temperatures… The gelling issue was closely related to the volumetric ratio of toluene and THF… at 2:1 the reaction was fluid.” (sec 2.1.1, Table 1). 
• “When the reaction was carried out above the 10 g scale the UPLC reaction profile started to become messy because the reaction time was prolonged… Elevating the reaction temperature above cryogenic conditions was known to be detrimental giving higher levels of both isomeric and other impurities.” (list‑item 2).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: The Li–Br exchange is highly exothermic (ΔT ≈ 60 °C adiabatic) and requires slow addition of n‑BuLi over many hours (≈ 12 h) in batch, creating safety hazards, poor temperature control and long process times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopt a continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor train (5 × 13 L CSTRs) with gravity overflow, allowing rapid heat removal (high surface‑to‑volume ratio) and eliminating the need for a 12 h addition. Pre‑cool feed streams (–20 °C → –30 °C) and control the addition rates of n‑BuLi and the isoxazolene so the exotherm is managed safely. This reduces the total lithiation + addition time to < 2 h while maintaining > 95 % conversion and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The highly exothermic nature of the Li–Br exchange dictates the slow combination of n‑BuLi and 6 to control the reaction temperature… adiabatic temperature rise could be as high as 61.9 °C.” (sec 2.1.3). 
• “On an early 9.0 kg scale batch reaction… the addition time was 12.7 h… prolonged Li‑Br exchange time is detrimental to the reaction due to the formation of impurities.” (sec 2.1.3). 
• “Continuous processes… high surface‑to‑volume ratio under flow conditions allows highly efficient heat transfer… safety hazards in handling exothermic reactions are minimized.” (sec 2.1.3). 
• “CSTR arrangements… the solution of 6… and n‑BuLi were independently pumped (pre‑cooled at −20 to −30 °C before mixing at CSTR) … the gravity overflow between reactors enabled mass transfer obviating any need for a mechanical pumping mechanism.” (sec 2.1.3).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: Isolation of product 4 required silica‑gel chromatography because direct crystallisation from the reaction mixture failed; the step was costly and difficult to scale, and the use of CO₂ quench added operational complexity.
Solution_Description: Develop a salt‑formation work‑up: add methanesulfonic acid (MSA) to the crude mixture in acetonitrile, which precipitates a crystalline MSA‑salt of 4. Filter, rinse, and break the salt with methanol/NaOH to give the free base. This eliminates chromatography, improves isolated yield (77 % free base, 99 % purity) and removes the need for CO₂ quench.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Direct crystallisation of the product from the reaction mixture was elusive… silica gel chromatography was utilized for product isolation.” (list‑item 3). 
• “A salt screen led to discovery of a highly crystalline methanesulfonic acid salt of 4… allowed direct isolation of 97.7 % pure product from the ~80 % pure crude mixture.” (sec 2.1.2, Table 2). 
• “In this improved product isolation protocol, carbon dioxide quenching was no longer required and a simple aqueous NH₄Cl solution quench was used instead….” (sec 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: The final deprotection of the benzamide group using SiliaMet‑Diamine (Si‑DIA) was highly chemoselective but the reagent is expensive, making the process cost‑prohibitive for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Replace Si‑DIA with inexpensive l‑lysine (5.5 equiv) as the nucleophile for benzamide cleavage. l‑Lysine’s water‑soluble by‑product (Bz‑lysine) can be removed by aqueous work‑up, dramatically lowering reagent cost while maintaining > 85 % yield and > 99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The use of Si‑DIA was not a long‑term option due to its relatively high cost… alternative methods were investigated.” (sec 2.3.2). 
• “Thus, l‑lysine, an inexpensive commodity chemical, fit the requirements perfectly; the Bz‑Lysine byproduct 27 is water‑soluble so it could be expediently rejected in the aqueous workup.” (sec 2.3.2). 
• “The reaction was carried out in n‑PrOH/water at reflux… product isolated in 86 % yield with 99.6 % UPLC purity.” (sec 2.3.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Second Generation β‑Amyloid-Cleaving Enzyme InhibitorImproving the Robustness of a Halogen-Metal Exchange Using Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: The amidation step to attach 5‑(difluoromethoxy)‑picolinic acid (3) required a labor‑intensive isolation by crystallisation after quench, adding time and complexity to the sequence.
Solution_Description: Implement a telescoped flow amidation using T₃P (or EDC/HOPO) directly after the previous step without isolation; the coupling proceeds in EtOAc at room temperature, followed by a simple aqueous HCl/isopropanol work‑up that crystallises the product directly. This shortens the step to a single operation and gives 95 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The coupling of hydropyranothiazine 2 with 5‑(difluoromethoxy)‑picolinic acid (3) … was straightforward… the product isolation was streamlined with the addition of aqueous HCl and isopropanol, which resulted in direct product crystallisation… isolated in 95 % yield.” (sec 2.3.1). 
• “The reaction was found readily adaptable to a continuous flow process… comparable yields and quality.” (sec 2.3.1).

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: When ethanol was used to solubilise intermediate 2 in the batch experiment, potassium bromide precipitated and blocked the micro‑reactor pipeline.  Without ethanol the intermediate was insoluble in the aqueous phase, adhered to the pipe wall and gave low conversion, eventually causing blockage of the line.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane was selected as the reaction solvent, forming a two‑phase system in sulfuric acid where intermediate 2 is soluble in the organic layer, preventing salt precipitation and allowing the same solvent to be used in the next step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The first step… uses ethanol to solubilize intermediate 2 in the batch experiment, but it will cause the precipitation of potassium bromide, which will block the pipeline in the microreactor.”; “When ethanol was not added… intermediate 2 was not soluble… results in low yield. When adhesion products… eventually result in blockage of the pipeline. Therefore, it is necessary to add a solvent to dissolve intermediate 2 without causing the precipitation of potassium bromide. Dichloromethane was chosen as the solvent… intermediate 2 was soluble in the organic phase.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: The preliminary semicontinuous experiment for step 1 gave only a 30 % isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Systematic variation of total flow rate, residence time, water amount (to control pH) and reaction temperature (5 °C) increased the yield to 88.2 % (comparable to the 90 % batch yield).
Supporting_Evidence: “The preliminary experiment yield was only 30 %, and then, the specific parameters of the reaction were optimized in detail.”; “When the total flow rate was 15 mL/min and the residence time was 2 min, the reaction yield can be greatly improved.”; “Finally, the reaction temperature was investigated and 5 °C was selected as the optimum reaction temperature.”; “After a series of optimizations… the reaction yield… reached 88.2 %.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: In step 2 the initial feeding strategy (all reagents introduced together) resulted in incomplete conversion of intermediate 2 regardless of changes in concentration, residence time, temperature, flow rate or pressure.
Solution_Description: The order of addition was altered: first mixing intermediate 2 with EDC and DMAP, then introducing diphenylmethanol. This new feeding order gave a dramatic increase in conversion and a final yield of 92.4 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “After experiments, intermediate 2 was not completely transformed regardless of changes… Afterward, the order of feeding was changed… the results were still not as expected… Finally, we designed the process… After changing the order of reactants again, the reaction results were much improved.”; “It was exciting to obtain excellent results with a yield of 92.4 % by the semicontinuous method.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: Increasing the temperature above 30 °C in step 2 caused a sharp decrease in yield, indicating thermal degradation of reactants.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature was kept between 10 °C and 30 °C (room temperature) and residence time was shortened to 1 min, which raised the yield to 98 % and avoided temperature‑induced decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the reaction temperature increased up to 60 °C, the yield decreased sharply because higher temperatures may have some impacts on the stability of the reactants.”; “When the temperature was between 10 and 30 °C, the reaction yield was relatively constant. Room temperature was chosen… without heating or cooling.”; Table 2 shows entry 3 (residence time 1 min) giving 98.2 % yield.

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: Peroxyacetic acid (40 % w/w) used as oxidant in the literature is highly hazardous and requires extensive safeguards in batch production.
Solution_Description: The oxidation was performed in a microreactor where the small inner diameter, high surface‑to‑volume ratio and excellent heat‑transfer dramatically reduce the risk associated with peroxyacetic acid, allowing its safe use in continuous flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “Peroxyacetic acid was initially selected… however, because of its accidents in the industry, the use of 40 % peroxyacetic acid was strictly restricted… Because of the small inner diameter of the pipe, larger contact area, high heat transfer efficiency, and continuous flow characteristics, the safety of peroxyacetic acid can be greatly improved. Here, peroxyacetic acid was chosen as the oxidant in the microreactor.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: Initial conditions for the oxidation step (step 3) gave sub‑optimal conversion.
Solution_Description: Residence time was set to 1 min and the peroxyacetic‑acid equiv. was increased to 1.2 equiv., which raised the yield to 96.8 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The residence time selected was 1 min, and 1.2 equiv of peroxyacetic acid would be better.”; Table 3 shows entry 9 (1 min, 1.2 equiv) giving 96.8 % yield.

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: Preparation, storage and transportation of bulk peroxyacetic acid pose explosion hazards.
Solution_Description: A continuous in‑situ synthesis of 20 % peroxyacetic acid was implemented in a microreactor (mixing H₂O₂ with acetic acid/H₂SO₄/EDTA), eliminating the need to handle large volumes of the dangerous peroxide outside the reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: “The danger of peroxyacetic acid was reduced in the microreactor, but its preparation, storage, and transportation had the same danger. If peroxyacetic acid could be prepared and used in situ in the microreactor, the abovementioned dangerous problems could be greatly reduced.”; Table 4 shows conditions giving ~20 % peroxyacetic acid in the microreactor.

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: When linking the four steps in a fully continuous flow line, the concentration of intermediate 2 after step 1 (0.84 M) did not match the required concentration for step 2 (0.23 M), causing potential accumulation and flow instability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Dilution of the intermediate 2 stream with additional CH₂Cl₂ to reach 0.23 M and simultaneous increase of flow rates in steps 2 and 3 were employed to maintain steady state and avoid blockages.
Supporting_Evidence: “The concentration of intermediate 2 was 0.84 mol/L after the first step, while the required concentration … was 0.23 mol/L… we decided to add some CH₂Cl₂… to maintain the concentration at 0.23 mol/L… It should increase the flow rates in the second and third steps… to avoid the accumulation of intermediate 2.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow in Tazobactam Synthesis
Problem_Description: In batch step 9 the deprotection required 55 °C for 4 h, which damaged the β‑lactam ring, lowering yield and purity.
Solution_Description: A semicontinuous flow protocol was used: 75 °C for 1 min residence, dramatically reducing the exposure time and preserving the β‑lactam, leading to an 85.6 % isolated yield and 99.85 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction temperature was 55 °C and the reaction time was 4 h in batch experiments… High temperatures and long reaction times may cause the β‑lactam ring to be destroyed… When the flow rate was 20 mL/min, the residence time was 1 min, and the reaction temperature was 75 °C, better yield and purity were obtained.”

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: The Fischer indole synthesis of the indole diester core gave a poor isolated yield (<30 %) because the electron‑withdrawing fluorine atom suppressed the required [3,3]‑sigmatropic shift, leading to many by‑products and necessitating a multistep purification of indole 8.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to an imine‑Heck reaction using Pd₂dba₃/P(t‑Bu)₃ as the catalyst system and cyclopentyl‑methyl‑ether (CPME) as the solvent, which afforded indole 8 in 84 % yield after crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "completion of the Fischer indole synthesis proceeded in poor yield (<30%) because of the formation of a series of byproducts and required a multistep purification of indole 8",
    "We hypothesized that the presence of the electron‑withdrawing fluorine atom served to render the necessary [3,3]-sigmatropic shift less favorable",
    "treatment of imine 12 with the combination of 2.5 mol % Pd₂dba₃, 10 mol % P(t‑Bu)₃·HBF₄, and dicyclohexylmethylamine (Cy₂NMe) as the base in CPME as the solvent at 100 °C afforded indole diester 8 in 84 % yield after crystallization"
  ]

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: Formation of the required imine 12 from electron‑deficient 2‑bromo‑6‑fluoroaniline (9b) and diethyl oxopimelate (10) gave <20 % conversion, and the acidic conditions needed for imine formation were incompatible with the basic conditions required for the subsequent Heck reaction.
Solution_Description: Imine 12 was generated in high yield by an acid‑catalyzed condensation of 9b with the readily formed diethyl ketal 13; ethanol was removed, leaving the imine in the reaction mixture, which was then directly subjected to the Heck reaction without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "formation of the imine proved to be extremely challenging; the reaction between electron‑deficient and hindered 2‑bromo‑6‑fluoroaniline (9b) and diethyl oxopimelate (10) proceeded in less than 20% conversion to imine 12",
    "imid 12 could be generated in high yield from the acid‑catalyzed reaction between aniline 9b and diethyl ketal 13, which was itself easily formed from ketone 10",
    "By removal of ethanol during this transformation, the resultant imine 12 was poised to undergo the desired imine‑Heck reaction without workup or purification"
  ]

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: The iridium‑catalyzed N–H insertion of ylide 15 to give ketone 7 showed highly variable assay yields (41–71 %) depending on temperature, solvent, concentration, and addition time, making scale‑up difficult.
Solution_Description: Optimal conditions were identified as DMF (5 vol) for the ylide, toluene (30 vol) for the Ir catalyst, a temperature of 100 °C and a 1 h addition of the ylide, which gave a consistent 64 % isolated yield of ketone 7 after crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "While more dilute conditions (entry 8) did lead to a slight increase in assay yield (AY), it was determined that this benefit was offset by the waste solvent generated and the need to remove that quantity of toluene",
    "Increasing the temperature led to a higher reaction rate (entry 3 vs entry 4 vs entry 6 vs entry 7), which enabled a concomitant decrease in the addition time of ylide 15",
    "The conditions ultimately applied are those captured in entry 7, and ketone 7 was obtained in 64% yield after crystallization"
  ]

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: Ketone 7 was unstable in the isopropanol/water mixture required for the ketoreductase (KRED) reduction, decomposing over 1 day and requiring 3 days to reach completion with low isolated yield of the mesylate.
Solution_Description: The mixture was degassed and run under an inert nitrogen atmosphere; the enzyme loading was increased to 12 wt % (relative to substrate) and the reaction time reduced to 16 h, delivering >99 % ee alcohol 6 in 98 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "The primary challenge with the biocatalytic conditions was the instability of the ketone toward the isopropanol/water solvent mixture",
    "Under the initial loading conditions explored, the reaction required 3 days to proceed to completion; for these conditions, only 78% of ketone 7 remained in the absence of enzyme after 1 day",
    "Degassing the reaction mixture improved the stability considerably, such that 93% ketone remained after 1 day",
    "the combination of degassing and running the reaction under inert conditions with an increase in the enzyme loading of Codexis P3H2 KRED to 12 wt % relative to the starting material allowed the third catalytic reaction in the sequence to achieve full conversion in 16 h in 98% assay yield"
  ]

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: In the Sonogashira coupling, mildly basic conditions gave the allene 16 as the major product, compromising selectivity for the desired terminal alkyne 4b.
Solution_Description: Using trimethylsilyl‑acetylene as the coupling partner, Pd(OAc)₂ with an electron‑rich phosphine (t‑Bu₃P or t‑BuXPhos) and Cy₂NMe base in methanol at 50 °C suppressed allene formation and gave >97 % conversion to TMS‑alkyne 4b, which was isolated in 89 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "Preliminary screening efforts for the Sonogashira reaction employed acetone‑protected acetylene for this transformation. Unfortunately, even under mildly basic conditions (e.g., using tertiary amine bases), the corresponding allene was formed as the major product",
    "When TMS‑acetylene was used as the coupling partner, >97% conversion to the desired terminal alkyne 4b was observed in the presence of Pd‑(OAc)₂, an electron‑rich phosphine ligand (t‑Bu₃P or t‑BuXPhos), and Cy₂NMe as the base in methanol at 50 °C",
    "Use of Cs₂CO₃ as the base led to near‑exclusive formation of the corresponding allene"
  ]

Paper Title: Harnessing the Power of Catalysis for the Synthesis of CRTH2 Antagonist MK-1029
Problem_Description: When all reagents for the ruthenium‑catalyzed azide‑alkyne cycloaddition (AAC) were combined at room temperature and then heated, a large exotherm caused uncontrolled reflux of the toluene solution, posing a safety risk.
Solution_Description: The Ru‑catalyst and alkyne were first heated to 70 °C; the azide solution in toluene was added slowly over 1 h, after which the temperature was raised to 90 °C for 10 h. This controlled addition eliminated the dangerous exotherm and gave the triazole 2 in 93 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
[
    "We observed that combining all of the reagents at room temperature followed by heating led to a significant exotherm and uncontrolled reflux of the toluene solution; this outcome failed to align with our safety group’s recommendation to maintain the reaction temperature at 90 °C or below",
    "To offset this potential for exotherm, a toluene solution of the Ru catalyst and alkyne 4a was heated to 70 °C, followed by addition of a concentrated solution of azide 3, also dissolved in toluene. The addition was conducted over 1 h, after which the temperature was increased to 90 °C for 10 h",
    "Through this catalytic process, triazole 2 was obtained in 93% assay yield"
  ]

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Microdetonations occurred when the tetrazole‑diazonium (DHT) intermediate accumulated or dried on reactor surfaces, causing violent decomposition of the explosive intermediate.
Solution_Description: The reaction pH was held ≥ 4.0 (typically 4.0‑5.5) by intermittent dosing of nitric acid, ensuring that nitrous acid (HONO) remained a minor species and that diazotization was rate‑limiting; the DHT intermediate was therefore consumed faster than it could accumulate, eliminating microdetonations.
Supporting_Evidence: – “microdetonations … due to the instability of DHT” (§1.1). “Performing the dose … at or above 4.0 completely eliminated the occurrence of microdetonations.” (§1.1). “Keeping the pH … high … ensured that the diazotization reaction was rate‑limiting and the nitro‑substitution was fast.” (§1.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Anhydrous 5‑aminotetrazole (5AT) has a solubility < 1.3 wt % in water at 20 °C, limiting the concentration of the feed stream and therefore lowering throughput and overall yield.
Solution_Description: 5AT was converted in‑situ to its sodium salt (Na‑5AT) by addition of one equivalent of NaOH, raising the solution pH to ~8 and increasing 5AT solubility to > 30 wt %, enabling highly concentrated feeds (up to 33 wt %).
Supporting_Evidence: – “Anhydrous 5AT was found to have a low solubility in water (<1.3 wt %) at 20 °C, necessitating a new method for the solubilization of 5AT.” (§1.2.1). “A stoichiometric amount of sodium hydroxide was added … to form the sodium salt … pH of this solution was ∼8.” (§1.2.1). “This salt formation increased the solubility of 5AT … allowing for generation of highly concentrated feed solutions up to 33 wt % 5AT.” (§1.2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Traditional routes required the precipitation, isolation, washing, and base‑elution of an acidic copper‑NT salt, a primary energetic solid that is hazardous to handle and difficult to scale, and also required removal of residual nitrite and 1‑H‑tetrazole impurities before DBX‑1 synthesis.
Solution_Description: A solid‑phase “catch‑and‑release” strategy using a strongly acidic cation‑exchange resin was introduced. The resin catalyticly stabilizes DHT, eliminates the need for copper‑salt precipitation, and permits direct aqueous processing; downstream purification is performed with ion‑exchange resins (copper‑modified) to remove nitrite and 1HTz.
Supporting_Evidence: – “Addition of cupric salts … required isolation of the acid copper salt of nitrotetrazolate … unsafe at large scale.” (Intro). “The use of ion‑exchange resins … avoided isolation of primary energetic solids … the stabilization is catalytic.” (§1.2.2). “After removal of nitrite and residual 1HTz with ion exchange resins, NaNT solutions were successfully used to generate high‑purity DBX‑1.” (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Micro‑reactor and tubular flow formats confined the evolving gases (N₂, NOx) and suffered from uncontrolled axial pH gradients, leading to uncertain residence times, poor reaction control, and long overall reaction times (several days) for some batch routes.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) was adopted, providing easy gas venting, excellent pH control, and uniform mixing. The CSTR allowed precise gravimetric dosing, inline filtration of resin, and periodic pump cycling to maintain liquid flow, shortening residence time to ~150 min while maintaining 88‑91 % yields.
Supporting_Evidence: – “Microreactors … confine the gaseous by‑products … leading to uncertainty in residence‑time distributions.” (Intro). “A CSTR design afforded several advantages … easily handle the generation of gaseous by‑products … excellent control of reaction pH.” (§1.3). “Residence time … 150 min … 93 % yield … matched the 91 % yield obtained in a comparable semibatch reaction.” (§1.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: In the cupric‑salt batch process, DHT decomposition on the copper salt decreased overall NaNT yield (≈ 75 %).
Solution_Description: Using 20 mol % sulfonic‑acid resin together with mineral acid (pH 4‑5) increased NT yield to 91 % versus 75 % without resin, indicating catalytic stabilization of DHT and better control of nitrite/acid balance.
Supporting_Evidence: – “higher yields of NaNT … 91 % and 75 % yields … with and without resin.” (Table 1). “The use of resins has the advantage … catalytic.” (§1.2.2). “pH between 4‑5 … ensured DHT formation rate‑limited.” (§1.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Residual 1‑H‑tetrazole (1HTz) impurity in NaNT solutions inhibits DBX‑1 formation; its removal is necessary but requires additional purification steps.
Solution_Description: Copper‑modified chelating ion‑exchange resins were employed to selectively extract 1HTz from NaNT solutions, achieving impurity levels below 16 ppm suitable for DBX‑1 synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence: – “NaNT solutions … required removal of excess nitrite ion … and the removal of 1HTz after synthesis.” (§1.4). “Pattison’s procedure … utilizes copper modified chelating resins to selectively extract 1HTz … tolerable concentration may be as low as 16 ppm.” (§1.4).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Continuous Process to Sodium Nitrotetrazolate via Solid Phase “Catch and Release”
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the micro‑reactor process showed a drop in yield (≈ 66 %) and poor control of residence time and pH, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Scaling the CSTR from 100 mL to 1000 mL preserved high yields (88‑91 %) and throughput (27.1 g h⁻¹), demonstrating that the CSTR platform mitigates the scale‑dependence observed in micro‑reactors.
Supporting_Evidence: – “Microreactor yields (66 %) … tubular reactor yields (73 %).” (§1.3). “10× scale up … 1000 mL CSTR … yield 88 % … less scale‑dependent.” (§1.3).

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free and Scalable Process for Synthesis of Novel MAP4K4 Inhibitor DMX-5804 and Its Glyco-Conjugates
Problem_Description: The original discovery route relied on a commercially unavailable boronate intermediate (2‑phenyl‑1,3,2‑dioxoborinone) and required a copper‑catalyzed Chan–Lam amination that gave only trace product even after 24 h.  When the authors substituted phenylboronic acid the reaction still gave only trace product after a 12‑day, room‑temperature run.  The subsequent microwave‑assisted Suzuki–Miyaura step caused severe charring and produced <5 % desired DMX‑5804, making the sequence irreproducible and unsafe.  All intermediates and the final product had to be purified by preparative HPLC, dramatically increasing cost and time.
Solution_Description: A completely new three‑step synthesis was designed that starts from inexpensive, readily available 2‑bromo‑1‑(4‑(2‑methoxyethoxy)phenyl)ethan‑1‑one.  The amination was performed with aniline, NaHCO₃ and DMF at 50 °C (metal‑free, inexpensive, high‑yielding).  The Knoevenagel condensation of the resulting ketone with malononitrile was optimized using KOH as the base, giving >95 % conversion.  The final cyclization to the pyrimidone was carried out by refluxing the nitrile in 95 % formic acid, affording DMX‑5804 in 80‑85 % isolated yield.  No column chromatography or HPLC was required; products were isolated by simple recrystallisation, shortening the overall process to 6–8 h and eliminating costly metal‑based reagents and hazardous microwave steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "we could not find any commercial source for 2‑phenyl‑1,3,2‑dioxoborinone"; "the reaction yielded only trace amounts… after 24 h"; "Arnold et al. reported the same reaction… 12 d at room temperature"; "microwave reaction… significant charring, desired compound in trace amounts (<5 %)"; "need of preparative HPLC for purification of intermediates and the final product"; "overall yield… 22 %".
Solution: "we identified substituted 2‑bromo‑1‑(4‑(2‑methoxyethoxy)phenyl)ethan‑1‑one as a suitable starting material… quantitative yields (90%)"; "KOH provided >95 % of 5… with 80–86 % isolated yield"; "refluxed in 95 % formic acid for 8–10 h… 80–85 % yield"; "did not require purification steps using column chromatography"; "the general scheme reported here takes 6–8 h to complete"; "eliminated the use of anhydrous solvents and the microwave‑assisted reaction step".

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free and Scalable Process for Synthesis of Novel MAP4K4 Inhibitor DMX-5804 and Its Glyco-Conjugates
Problem_Description: During attempts to install the O‑alkyl chain onto the phenolic pyrimidone (compound 6) with potassium carbonate in DMF, the reaction consumed the starting material but gave only 5–7 % DMX‑5804, while the undesired O‑alkylated isomer (7) was obtained in 88 % yield.  The poor conversion was attributed to the low solubility of the phenolic intermediate in dichloromethane and to competing O‑alkylation of the pyrimidone nitrogen.
Solution_Description: Switching to Lewis‑acid‐catalysed alkylation with BF₃·OEt₂ dramatically changed the regio‑selectivity.  Performing the reaction in neat BF₃·OEt₂ (no external solvent) or with an excess of methyl glycol as both solvent and reactant gave quantitative yields of DMX‑5804 and completely suppressed formation of the pyrimidone‑alkylated by‑product.  The increased acidity and the use of a highly polar medium improved solubility of the phenolic substrate and drove the desired C‑O bond formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "DMX‑5804 was obtained only in small amounts (5–7 %) whereas compound 7 was isolated as the major product (88 %)"; "DMX‑5804 was obtained only in small amounts… while the other regio‑isomer was the major product"; "its solubility in polar solvents was significantly better than that of DMX‑5804".
Solution: "we changed the reaction conditions to acidic by using boron trifluoride diethyl etherate… resulted in phenolic alkylation"; "hypothesizing that the relatively low separated yields … due to the insolubility … we decided to perform this reaction in neat conditions with BF₃·OEt₂… produced satisfactory yields of DMX‑5804"; "added an excess of methyl glycol as a solvent … to obtain quantitative yields of DMX‑5804 in good time".

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free and Scalable Process for Synthesis of Novel MAP4K4 Inhibitor DMX-5804 and Its Glyco-Conjugates
Problem_Description: The discovery synthesis employed palladium‑dppf catalyst and copper(II) acetate, both expensive and potentially hazardous on scale.  Additionally, the microwave‑assisted step required specialized equipment and generated charring, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The new route eliminates all transition‑metal catalysts, replaces the expensive boronate with inexpensive bromoketone, and removes the microwave step entirely.  Reactions are performed in common laboratory solvents (DMF, MeOH, formic acid) under conventional heating, greatly reducing material cost and safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "requirement of transition‑metal catalysts"; "high cost of boronate intermediate"; "microwave‑assisted reaction… charring"; "safety concerns in discarding metallic complexes".
Solution: "removal of transition metals from the process and reduced duration of reactions"; "low‑cost raw materials"; "microwave‑assisted reactions were removed"; "no need for anhydrous solvents".

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free and Scalable Process for Synthesis of Novel MAP4K4 Inhibitor DMX-5804 and Its Glyco-Conjugates
Problem_Description: Every intermediate and the final product in the original route required preparative reverse‑phase HPLC or column chromatography, which is time‑consuming, expensive, and not amenable to kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: All intermediates are isolated by simple recrystallisation from isopropanol, methanol/hexanes, or chloroform/ethanol mixtures.  The final API is obtained by crystallisation from a dichloromethane/ethanol (1:2) solvent system, providing >99.99 % purity without any chromatographic step.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "the discovery method generated DMX‑5804 in only a 22% yield"; "required purification by preparative HPLC"; "prep‑HPLC for intermediates and final product".
Solution: "the general scheme reported here takes 6–8 h to complete and also eliminates the use of anhydrous solvents and the microwave‑assisted reaction step"; "no column chromatography"; "crystallized products showed over 95% purity in each step"; "recrystallized from chloroform/methanol… to obtain DMX‑5804 as a white solid (80–85% yield)".

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: Fuming nitric acid (>90 % HNO₃) is a highly corrosive, toxic reagent that forms a sensitive high‑explosive mixture with most organics; many historic accidents have resulted from its use, especially near‑stoichiometric conditions.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive safety program based on reaction calorimetry (RC‑1, ARC) and accurate titration of the acid is implemented to define safe concentration, temperature, and stoichiometry limits before scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
● “In anywhere near stoichiometric composition, a homogeneous mixture of nitric acid and virtually any organic is a sensitive high explosive …”
● “>300 reports of serious chemical incidents involving nitric acid … accidents commonly stem from the small quantities of nitric acid required to produce a substantial explosion.”
● “As a highly corrosive and toxic reagent, nitric acid should be handled with extreme care …”
● “Reaction Calorimetry was used to accurately determine reaction progress … required for safe and scalable use of this nitration process.”
● “RC1 calorimetry … provides excellent insight.”

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: The nitration of substrate 1b at a 10 V (820 mM) concentration generates a maximal heat flow of ~226 W L⁻¹—a 5.5‑fold increase over substrate 1a—creating a serious risk of thermal runaway at larger scale.
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration is reduced (e.g., to 15 V, 547 mM) which lowers the maximal heat flow to ~44 W L⁻¹, keeping the exotherm within pilot‑plant cooling capacity.
Supporting_Evidence:
● “reaction of substrate 1b in 10 V (820 mM) resulted in a 5.5× maximal heat flow of ∼226 W/L.”
● “Simple dilution of the reaction concentration to 15 V (547 mM) demonstrated controlled reduction of this exotherm to ∼44 W/L.”
● “Both reactions had heat flows on the order of 15 W/L or less throughout the majority of the reaction time, which is well within the range of cooling capacity for a pilot plant reactor.”
● “These features highlight the necessity of determining a substrate‑dependent reaction concentration prior to scaling this process.”

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: The reaction rate and terminal exotherm are extremely sensitive to the amount of HNO₃; decreasing the charge from 1.30 equiv to 1.05 equiv doubles the reaction time (300 → 600 min) and reduces the temperature rise, while excess acid causes ΔT > 10 °C on 30 g scale.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry is optimized: sub‑stoichiometric HNO₃ (0.90 equiv) gives ~88 % conversion with no detectable terminal exotherm; careful selection of equivalents balances conversion and heat release.
Supporting_Evidence:
● “Decreasing HNO₃ equivalents from 1.30 to 1.05 doubles the reaction time from 300 to 600 min and reduces the ΔT_r – ΔT_j from ∼3 to ∼0 °C on 5 g scale.”
● “The exotherm observed using 1.30 equiv of HNO₃ on 5 g scale is a moderate and easily controllable ΔT ≈ 3 °C … this increases to ΔT > 10 °C using 30 g of substrate.”
● “The use of substoichiometric HNO₃ (0.90 equiv) … results in ∼88 % conversion and no detectable terminal exotherm.”
● “Proper evaluation of reaction exotherm and cooling capacity of equipment should be conducted prior to conducting this procedure on appreciable scale.”

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: Commercial fuming nitric‑acid batches labelled “>90 wt %” can differ appreciably (e.g., 91 % vs 97 %); this variability leads to inconsistent reagent charge and uncontrolled exotherms.
Solution_Description: Each batch is volumetrically titrated before use; the measured concentration is used to adjust the stoichiometric charge, ensuring reproducible kinetics and safe heat evolution.
Supporting_Evidence:
● “Two commercially sourced batches of HNO₃ … were determined by volumetric titration to be 91 % and 97 % … a volumetric charge of 1.1 equiv of 91 % HNO₃ is within 10 % of a volumetric charge of 1.3 equiv of 97 % HNO₃.”
● “Accurate determination of HNO₃ concentration allowed reproducible reaction kinetics and controlled final exotherm.”
● “The concentration of fuming nitric acid should be accurately determined by titration prior to conducting this process on any appreciable scale.”

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: During reaction completion excess HNO₃ decomposes to NOₓ gases; uncontrolled release can create over‑pressure and pose explosion/flammability hazards.
Solution_Description: The reactor is equipped with appropriate venting, nitrogen dilution, and quench capability to safely vent NOₓ while keeping the organic solvent below its lower‑explosive‑limit concentration.
Supporting_Evidence:
● “Emission of NOₓ gas should be considered for large scale reactions where adequate venting is likely to be necessary, as well as dilution of the off‑gassing with nitrogen to bring the DCE well below its lower explosive limit value.”
● “RC1 calorimetry with an ‘In‑Line’ gas flow meter was utilized to demonstrate emission of NOₓ gas occurs upon completion of the reaction.”
● “Release of excess HNO₃ as NOₓ gas … should be accounted for during equipment set‑up to include an appropriate vent and quench.”

Paper Title: Hazard Evaluation and Safety Considerations for Scale-Up of a Fuming Nitric Acid Mediated Nitration of Aryl Boronic Acids
Problem_Description: Nitro‑aromatic products are thermally unstable; distillation can approach decomposition onset, creating runaway or explosion risk.
Solution_Description: Thermal analysis (DSC) is performed on each product, and distillation is carried out under reduced pressure at temperatures well below the measured onset (the “100‑degree rule” for lab‑scale, tighter control for plant scale).
Supporting_Evidence:
● “When conducting distillation of nitroaromatics several safety considerations should be accounted for. The thermal stability of the compound should always be investigated with an appropriate calorimetric technique.”
● “Distillation temperatures should be kept well below the detected onset using reduced pressure.”
● “In the case of lab‑scale distillation we have found the 100‑degree rule to be sufficient; however, this may not work as well for larger plant reactors due to the time scale.”
● “We have used DSC for this, which can quickly give the approximate onset temperature of decomposition using only a few milligrams of material.”

Paper Title: Development of a Recycling Process for an Industrial-Scale Production of Tipifarnib
Problem_Description: The original tipifarnib synthesis has a low‑yielding chiral resolution step that discards ∼2/3 of the advanced intermediate as waste.  During the NaNO₂‑mediated racemization a new impurity (7) appeared and the use of NaNO₂ raised concerns about possible N‑nitrosamine (impurity 8) formation, creating a hard‑to‑purge impurity.  Impurity 7 could not be removed in subsequent steps and even became enriched.  In the NaNO₂‑free racemization, the reaction in pure water stalled because compounds 4 and 2 are poorly soluble, leading to a heterogeneous mixture that limits conversion.  The heterogeneity also caused mixing/viscosity problems that slowed the reaction.
Solution_Description: A recycling route based on racemization was devised to recover the waste stream and increase overall output (>60%).  The NaNO₂‑free route uses direct acid‑catalyzed cationization (water‑mediated racemization) instead of diazotization, eliminating NaNO₂ and its associated impurities.  MeCN or MEK were introduced as co‑solvents to create a homogeneous reaction phase, improve solubility, and accelerate the reaction; MEK was ultimately chosen for its superior impurity profile and class‑3 solvent status.  Adjusting the water‑to‑organic‑solvent ratio (e.g., 6 v MeCN + 1 v H₂O or 6 v MEK + 3 v H₂O) fine‑tuned conversion and impurity formation.  Refluxing the MEK/H₂O mixture (no added acid) provided robust, scalable conditions for kilogram‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "the main drawback is a low‑yielding chiral resolution step 2, where ∼2/3 of advanced intermediate 3 was disposed as waste" (Results section).
- "Current production of tipifarnib involves a late‑stage chiral resolution where the mother liquor containing ∼2/3 of the product is disposed of as waste" (Abstract).
- "a new impurity 7 was observed in small amounts… structural alert for potential mutagenicity…" (Results section).
- "concerns about potential N‑nitrosamine contamination" (Abstract & Results).
- "impurity 7 was inevitably present in the range of 0.1–1.1%" and "impurity 7 was not effectively purged, rather enriched through the steps" (Results).
- "both reactions stalled after 18 h, which we attributed to the heterogeneity of the reaction mixture due to the poor solubility of compounds 4 and 2 in pure water even at an elevated temperature" (Results, Table 1 discussion).
- "The large volume of acetone in the mother liquor was first reduced… biphasic solution…" (Results, mother‑liquor work‑up).

Solution:
- "We share the development of an industrial‑scale recycling process through racemization that returns the waste stream…" (Abstract & Conclusions).
- "it might be feasible to form intermediate 6 through direct acid‑catalyzed cationization, instead of NaNO₂‑mediated diazotization" (Results).
- "When enantiopure dibenzoyltartrate salt 4 was heated in pure water… 86 % conversion …" (Table 1, entry 1).
- "Among the four solvents investigated, MeCN and MEK afforded more rapid reaction and fewer impurities" (Results, Table 1).
- "MeCN demonstrated faster reaction rate, whereas MEK afforded an improved impurity profile" (Results, Table 3).
- "Impacts of water volume… increasing the water volume from 1 v to 3 v had a limited impact… MeCN demonstrated faster reaction rate, whereas MEK afforded an improved impurity profile" (Results, Table 2).
- "we selected the reflux condition in 6 v MEK and 3 v H₂O with no acid additive for further scale‑up" (Results).
- "the recycling process was seamlessly incorporated into the original production process" (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: The original discovery route produced the target amine as a racemic mixture, requiring chiral chromatography for resolution, which dramatically reduced overall yield. The route also employed a Stille cross‑coupling that required organotin reagents (toxic) and used PBr₃ together with chlorinated solvents, both of which raise safety and handling concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: A completely new retrosynthetic plan was adopted that avoided the Stille coupling, PBr₃ and chlorinated solvents. The new route uses a regioselective Heck coupling in water to make the key ketone, followed by an asymmetric Ru‑catalysed transfer‑hydrogenation and a stereospecific Mitsunobu reaction, delivering the drug substance as a single enantiomer without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The route is not stereoselective, and the target amine 6 is delivered as a racemic mixture…with an associated substantial reduction in overall yield.” (p. 2) 
• “The incorporation of the ketone moiety…required the use of a Stille cross‑coupling and the use of a vinyl stannane…Organotin reagents are known to possess toxicity issues and would not be amenable to future scale‑up.” (p. 2) 
• “Other issues included the use of PBr₃ and the application of environmentally unfriendly chlorinated solvents.” (p. 2) 
• “Considering all of the above issues, an alternative approach was sought…commences with a regioselective Heck coupling in water…followed by a ruthenium‑catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation, followed by a stereoselective Mitsunobu reaction….” (p. 10‑11)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: The initial Heck coupling of bromide 2 with vinyl ethers gave a mixture of the desired ketone 3 and the undesired β‑arylated enol ether 8 due to poor regio‑control of the π‑complexes, lowering material throughput and requiring extra purification.
Solution_Description: A cationic Heck protocol performed in aqueous medium (water as solvent, Pd(OAc)₂/1,3‑bis‑(diphenylphosphino)‑propane) was developed, which delivered the α‑aryl product (ketone 3) exclusively, eliminating the enol‑ether impurity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reaction with various vinyl ethers provided a mixture of the required ketone 3 and the undesired enol ether 8…poor regiocontrol in formation of the intermediate π complexes A and B.” (p. 3) 
• “A targeted screening of reaction conditions…led to the development of a process in water that delivered the required ketone exclusively.” (p. 4) 
• Scheme 5 shows “Successful Formation of Ketone 3 via a Modified Heck Reaction”.

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: During asymmetric transfer‑hydrogenation of ketone 3 the reaction mixture formed a slurry in EtOAc, THF, or 2‑MeTHF; the substrate and product remained insoluble and conversion stalled at 95 % (3‑5 % ketone left), despite excess reducing agent.
Solution_Description: A 1:1 THF/MeOH co‑solvent system was introduced, providing a homogeneous solution at 55 °C; the reaction went to complete conversion and gave >99 % ee of alcohol 7 with excellent isolated yield after crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In these solvents, the reaction mixture did not form a solution but remained as a slurry…the reaction did not proceed to completion (3–5 % unreacted ketone remaining)….” (p. 6) 
• “A 1:1 mixture of THF/MeOH provided optimum reaction conditions. A complete solution was formed during the reaction, and on cooling, the product alcohol crystallized from solution.” (p. 7) 
• Table 1 shows 100 % conversion and >98 % ee under the screened conditions.

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: The Mitsunobu reaction traditionally leaves triphenylphosphine oxide and reduced DIAD by‑products that normally require chromatographic purification, which is impractical at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Crystallisation of the sulfonamide product 13 directly from the reaction mixture (acetonitrile) removed triphenylphosphine oxide and reduced DIAD impurities, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The common issues associated with the use of the Mitsunobu reaction, such as removal of triphenylphosphine oxide and reduced DIAD by‑products, have been eliminated through crystallization of the relevant intermediates.” (abstract) 
• “Inspection…product sulfonamide 13 crystallized from acetonitrile, providing the product in excellent purity and free from associated phosphine and reduced DIAD byproducts.” (p. 9) 
• “Residual triphenylphosphine oxide and reduced DIAD impurities were retained in the mother liquors, obviating the need for chromatography.” (p. 10)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: 2‑Nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride (the reagent used to prepare the nosylate 12) tests positive in the Könenen test for Class 1 explosives, imposing storage, transport and handling restrictions.
Solution_Description: The 4‑nitro analogue of the sulfonyl chloride, which is not classified as an explosive, was substituted for the 2‑nitro version, providing the same nosylated intermediate without the safety liability.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “Further work…showed that the corresponding 4‑nitro analogue…does not have explosive properties…The 4‑nitro analogue was utilized in later campaigns.” (p. 8)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of an Asymmetric Synthesis of AZD8186 Using the Fukuyama Modification of the Mitsunobu Reaction
Problem_Description: The original Mitsunobu step required stoichiometric amounts of triphenylphosphine and DIAD (expensive, hazardous reagents) and exhibited sub‑optimal yields when equivalents were low.
