Solution_Description: A co‑expression system pairing PpKR8 with glucose dehydrogenase (BsGDH) was constructed in E. coli, enabling in‑situ regeneration of NADH from inexpensive glucose and dramatically reducing cofactor consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: “The co‑expression of PpKR8 and glucose dehydrogenase from Bacillus subtilis in Escherichia coli allowed up to 300 g L⁻¹ (1.57 M) 24a to be completely converted… with a low cofactor dosage of 0.1 mM and a high total turnover number (15 473).”

Paper Title: Efficient Biocatalytic Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: When the whole‑cell biocatalyst was supplied as a separate GDH‑expressing strain (cell‑coupled system), cofactor transfer between cells was slow, doubling the reaction time compared with the co‑expression system.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Co‑expressing PpKR8 and BsGDH in the same E. coli cell eliminated the inter‑cellular barrier, improving cofactor turnover and halving the time needed for full conversion of 300 g L⁻¹ substrate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The co‑expression system could completely convert 300 g L⁻¹ 24a in 6 h, while the cell‑coupled system required 12 h… cofactor transfer efficiency in the co‑expression system was higher, as cofactors do not need to transfer across cells.”

Paper Title: Efficient Biocatalytic Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: At 300 g L⁻¹ substrate loading, conversion dropped to 95 % after 8 h, indicating incomplete conversion under the initial conditions.
Solution_Description: Optimal reaction parameters were established: 35 °C temperature, pH 6.0 maintained by automated Na₂CO₃ addition, and a biocatalyst loading of 15 g L⁻¹ dry cells, which together afforded >99 % conversion within 6 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “The maximum catalytic activity was observed at 40 °C… the enzyme was most stable at 35 °C… the maximum catalytic activity was reached at pH 6.0… 15 g L⁻¹ co‑expressing cells gave complete conversion of 300 g L⁻¹ 24a in 6 h with 99.9 % ee.”

Paper Title: Efficient Biocatalytic Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Using the standard 0.5 mM NAD⁺ cofactor increased material cost; lower cofactor concentrations prolonged the reaction.
Solution_Description: The NAD⁺ concentration was reduced step‑wise to 0.3 mM (10 h, >99 % conversion) and finally to 0.1 mM (24 h, >98 % conversion), delivering a space‑time yield of 728 g L⁻¹ day⁻¹ while minimizing cofactor expense.
Supporting_Evidence: “A lower concentration of NAD⁺ (0.3 mM) achieved a conversion rate of >99 % in 10 h with a space‑time yield of 728 g/(L day)… Even with 0.1 mM concentrations of cofactors, the conversion rate reached 98 % in 24 h… total turnover number of 15 473.”

Paper Title: Efficient Biocatalytic Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Isolation of the chiral alcohol products required removal of residual cells, solvent, and salts, which could reduce overall yield if not optimized.
Solution_Description: A streamlined liquid–liquid extraction using 1 : 5 ethyl acetate (or methanol for 7b) followed by drying over anhydrous Na₂SO₄ and rotary evaporation gave ≥93 % isolated yields of the target alcohols.
Supporting_Evidence: “The mixture was then extracted three times using an equivalent volume of ethyl acetate… the organic phase was dried using anhydrous sodium sulfate and evaporated to obtain 7b as a yellow oily liquid with a yield of 93 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original Grignard addition of the organomagnesium reagent to ribonolactone stalled at 60‑70 % conversion and generated 15‑25 % of the over‑addition impurity, giving only a 40 % isolated yield after chromatography.
Solution_Description: Screening of lanthanide additives identified LaCl₃·2LiCl (0.6 M in THF) as a promoter that raised conversion to 72 % and reduced the impurity to 2 %; the additive also stabilised the lactol product, improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions stalled between 60 % and 70 % conversion and contained high levels of the over‑addition impurity 6 (15–25 %).”; “The addition of the LaCl₃·2LiCl complex as a 0.6 M solution in THF was found to improve the conversion and purity profile (Table 1, entries 1–2).”; “Notably, the level of over‑addition impurity 6 was suppressed, suggesting that LaCl₃·2LiCl played a role in stabilizing the lactol product.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: The i‑PrMgCl·LiCl reagent used for Grignard formation is expensive and required a lower concentration (1.3 M) that limited throughput.
Solution_Description: Switching to i‑PrMgCl (no LiCl) reduced reagent cost and permitted a higher concentration (2 M), increasing overall throughput without compromising conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “i‑PrMgCl was selected over i‑PrMgCl·LiCl due to its lower cost and higher reagent concentration (2 M versus 1.3 M) allowing for increased throughput.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: On scale‑up, the solid NdCl₃ aggregated, forming an immobile mass at the bottom of the reactor, which raised impurity levels and posed a risk of damaging glass‑lined vessels and blocking valves.
Solution_Description: Addition of an equimolar quaternary ammonium salt (n‑Bu₄NCl) dissolved NdCl₃ completely in THF, preventing aggregation and restoring high conversion and low impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high density of NdCl₃ prevented the solids from dispersing … formed a solid, immobile mass … leading to high levels of over‑addition impurity 6 and … damage to glass‑lined reactor vessels.”; “Quaternary ammonium chloride or bromide additives led to near complete dissolution of NdCl₃ in THF… when exposed to an equimolar amount of quaternary ammonium salt.”; “Application of 1.0 equiv of the solubilized NdCl₃/n‑Bu₄NCl combination … generated lactol 3 in high conversion and good yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: The preferred LaCl₃·2LiCl additive was difficult to source in bulk and relatively expensive compared with other lanthanide salts.
Solution_Description: NdCl₃ was selected as the lanthanide additive because it is commercially available, less costly, and gave comparable conversion and impurity suppression when combined with the quaternary ammonium salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “NdCl₃ was ultimately selected for further development based on availability and cost.”; “Use of commercially available, solid, anhydrous LaCl₃ resulted in … poor conversion … Anhydrous Ce(III) salts … were considered viable alternatives … YCl₃ or NdCl₃ increased conversion >85 % while suppressing impurity 6.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: Initial reaction conditions required prolonged mixing times (up to 9 h) to achieve satisfactory conversion, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Reducing the equivalents of TMSCl (from 2.0 to 1.3 equiv) and adjusting stoichiometry of the Grignard reagents allowed the reaction to reach >90 % conversion in a shorter time, improving overall productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The TMSCl equivalents could be reduced from 2.0 to 1.3 without compromising process performance (Table 2, entry 1). In order to achieve reaction conversion above 90 %, the stoichiometry of 2, TMSCl, PhMgCl, and i‑PrMgCl·LiCl were adjusted … affording 98 % conversion and a modest increase in assay yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: Various lanthanide salts (e.g., LaCl₃, CeCl₃) formed slurries or precipitates with quaternary ammonium salts, limiting their effectiveness as soluble promoters.
Solution_Description: Systematic evaluation of quaternary ammonium salts with different alkyl chain lengths and halide counter‑ions identified n‑Bu₄NBr as a superior promoter that produced clear solutions with NdCl₃ and YCl₃, enhancing additive performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the size of the hydrocarbon substituents on the ammonium counterion led to improved overall solubility of the lanthanide/ammonium salt mixtures; with respect to the impact of the anion identity, bromide demonstrated better dissolution properties, followed by chloride.”; “n‑Bu₄NBr was ultimately selected to replace n‑Bu₄NCl due to the similar reaction performance and the availability of bulk material.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Lanthanide Halide/Quaternary Ammonium Salt System for the Nucleophilic Addition of Grignard Reagents to Carbonyl Groups and Application to the Synthesis of a Remdesivir Intermediate
Problem_Description: The efficiency of the NdCl₃/quaternary ammonium additive system varied with the size of the ammonium ion and the halide counter‑ion, leading to inconsistent yields across substrates.
Solution_Description: Optimization of the ammonium ion size (n‑Bu₄⁺, n‑Pen₄⁺) and choice of halide (Cl⁻ vs Br⁻) standardized the additive system, delivering reproducible high yields for a broad scope of ketone substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the ammonium ion size from n‑Pr₄⁺ and n‑Bu₄⁺ to n‑Pen₄⁺ resulted in a significant increase in yield … while a further increase in size to n‑Hex₄⁺ resulted in diminished reaction performance.”; “The counterion was also found to impact reaction performance, with Cl⁻ providing high yield and BF₄⁻ providing low yield.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: During the magnesium‑bromide exchange on intermediate 6 (Route 1) the reaction gave >99 % conversion but the crude product 9 showed only ~78 % in‑process purity because of proto‑demetallation and over‑addition impurities (≈17 % area). The high impurity load carried over into the Boc‑deprotection step, creating a difficult downstream purification problem and raising safety concerns due to the large amount of acidic work‑up needed.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned Route 1 and pursued Route 2, which moves the Grignard addition to an earlier, simpler bromide (13 → 14) and avoids the problematic magnesiation of the advanced intermediate. This new route eliminates the impurity‑prone exchange step and streamlines the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “Laboratory evaluation of the magnesium–bromide exchange between 6 and i‑PrMgCl·LiCl reached >99 % conversion after 18 h at 0 °C. The in‑process purity of 9 was typically around 78 % because of…proto‑demetallation and overaddition…This high impurity burden…led the team to explore Route 2.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry synthesis of intermediate 8 used a TBS protecting group, required two silica‑gel chromatography steps, proceeded through non‑crystalline intermediates and employed TBAF, a hygroscopic reagent that is incompatible with glassware – all of which are unsuitable for kilogram‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: A survey of alternative phenol protecting groups identified 4‑morpholine‑carbonyl (carbamate) as the optimal choice. The carbamate can be installed and crystallized directly, giving crystalline intermediates (13 → 14 → 8) and allowing isolation without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “While this approach was convenient on laboratory scale, several scale‑up challenges were identified: the process employed two silica gel column chromatography operations, proceeded through noncrystalline intermediates, and utilized TBAF…To address these challenges, alternative protecting groups were surveyed.” “Of the protecting groups surveyed, 4‑morpholinecarbonyl met these criteria…Compound 4 could be efficiently converted to carbamate 13 and subsequently crystallized directly…the isolation of compound 14 was found to be a robust impurity control point…yield …99.8 % area.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: The Grignard addition of i‑PrMgCl·LiCl to the carbamate (13 → 14) at 0 °C gave only 78 % in‑process purity and moderate isolated yield (71 %). Lower conversion was attributed to temperature‑sensitive side reactions and partial decomposition of the organomagnesium reagent.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to –15 °C while maintaining the same reagent equivalents. This increased the area % of 14 to 89 % (71 % isolated yield) and improved overall purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 shows entry 6: i‑PrMgCl·LiCl at –15 °C gave 89.0 % area (71 % yield). The text notes “The lower temperature to –15 °C … gave…higher in‑process purity of 14.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: The alkylation of intermediate 8 with chlorinated intermediate 15 performed in THF, i‑PrOAc or toluene gave poor or no conversion, limiting throughput. Moreover, the heterogenous mixture led to variable reaction rates on scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified polar aprotic solvents (DMAc, NMP, acetone, MeCN) that provided quantitative conversion. Adding a small amount of water to the MeCN system (MeCN/H₂O) further increased rate and reduced impurity 16, demonstrating that improved miscibility/homogeneity benefits the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “Incomplete reaction conversion was observed in THF and i‑PrOAc…no product formation was observed in toluene…complete conversion to 9 was observed in DMAc, NMP, acetone, and MeCN…On a gram scale, the reaction with water proceeded at a slightly higher rate…reduced level of process impurity 16.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: After the alkylation step the reaction mixture contained excess aryl chloride 2, which needed to be removed before the final S_NAr step; traditional aqueous work‑up left residual 2 in the organic layer.
Solution_Description: An extractive work‑up was developed: the crude stream was partitioned between MTBE and dilute HCl to remove bases and azetidine, then treated with aqueous NaOH at 40 °C to hydrolyze residual 2 to sodium nicotinate 21, which partitions into the aqueous phase. This cleanly removes 2, enabling telescoped S_NAr without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “An extractive work‑up was developed to purge excess 2 through selective hydrolysis to the corresponding sodium nicotinate 21…the organic layer was treated with dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide solution and warmed to 40 °C for 1 h to hydrolyze 2 to 21.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: The Boc‑deprotection of intermediate 9 with p‑TsOH·H₂O generated CO₂ and isobutylene, requiring venting and nitrogen flow to prevent over‑pressurization and emissions on pilot scale.
Solution_Description: The deprotection was performed in a glass‑lined reactor equipped with a caustic scrubber vent, nitrogen headspace, and controlled temperature (50 °C) to safely manage gas evolution. Solvent choice (i‑PrOH) also helped trap tert‑butyl cations, reducing isobutylene release.
Supporting_Evidence: “To a 30 gallon glass‑lined jacketed reactor vented to a caustic scrubber…the mixture was heated at 50 °C for 15 h…Adequate venting and nitrogen flow were necessary on the pilot scale to prevent overpressurization…Alcoholic solvents…have been shown to partially trap tert‑butyl cation.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: The S_NAr step using K₂CO₃ as base was heterogeneous, leading to inconsistent conversions and modest yields on scale‑up; the insoluble base also hampered impurity control.
Solution_Description: Soluble organic bases (i‑Pr₂NEt, Et₃N) were evaluated. Triethylamine gave the highest conversion (98 % after 20 h) and improved reproducibility, eliminating the variability associated with the solid carbonate.
Supporting_Evidence: “To avoid scalability issues associated with a heterogeneous base, the soluble amines diisopropylethylamine, triethylamine, and DABCO were evaluated…Triethylamine providing higher conversion after 20 h.”

Paper Title: Early Development and Kilogram Scale-Up of a Non-steroidal FXR Agonist for the Treatment of Non-alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH)
Problem_Description: Isolation of the final API 1 required removal of residual salts and solvents from a large volume mixture after the telescoped S_NAr and hydrolysis steps.
Solution_Description: The crude stream was directly crystallized by seeding with API 1 and adding heptane at 0 °C, followed by filtration and washing with MeTHF/heptane. This avoided chromatography, reduced solvent waste, and enabled multikilogram isolation with 82 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The slurry was cooled to 20 °C…aged for 13 h, and then filtered…The wet cake was washed with a mixture of 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran and heptane…gave 1 (6.1 kg, 9.8 mol) in 82 % yield.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: The anhydride intermediate 6 showed very poor solubility, forcing the imidation step to be run at >190 °C in mesitylene and making the operation difficult to scale up because careful temperature control was required.
Solution_Description: Replacing the high‑temperature mesitylene protocol with a polar‑solvent‑based batch (NMP, then finally inexpensive DMA) allowed the reaction to proceed at 170 °C (or lower) with high yield (≈94 %) and eliminated the need for extreme heating.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Owing to the poor solubility of the anhydride 6, the reaction was required to be carried out at a high temperature (>190 °C) in mesitylene to avoid any crystallization during the reaction.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP), the initially best solvent, is classified as a potential health and safety hazard and is undesirable for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Switched to N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMA), a cheaper and less hazardous solvent that gave comparable or better conversion and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “However, NMP is a potential hazard and needs to be avoided for scale up.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: The literature NaBH₄ reduction of imide 3 gave only a 40.8 % isolated yield of the desired amide 4a, far too low for commercial viability.
Solution_Description: Introduced calcium borohydride (Ca(BH₄)₂) as a more Lewis‑acidic reductant; the Ca²⁺ cation preferentially coordinated to one carbonyl, increasing both conversion and diastereoselectivity (4a/4b = 70:30).
Supporting_Evidence: • “When NaBH₄ reduction of 3 was run at 40 °C for 10 h … the yield (40.8 %) was not high enough …”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: Alternative metal borohydrides (K, Mg, Al) and many alcoholic or ether solvents gave very low conversions (0–20 %) and poor selectivity, making the reduction inefficient.
Solution_Description: Systematic solvent screening identified EtOH as the optimal medium for Ca(BH₄)₂, delivering 100 % conversion and the best diastereoselectivity; other solvents (1‑PrOH, IPA, diglyme) were discarded.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Other borohydrides … gave much lower selectivities … and yields (0–20 %). Screening of the solvent … use of 1‑PrOH gave a similar result … considerably decreased conversions were observed for other alcoholic solvents … ether‑type solvent (diglyme) was found to be much less effective.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: The undesired isomer 4b could not be obtained in sufficient quantity or purity by recrystallisation or chromatography, hindering material balance for the overall process.
Solution_Description: Devised an alternative synthetic sequence (Scheme 3) starting from the same acid 5, using S‑PEA to make the opposite‑configured imide 7, then Ca(BH₄)₂ reduction, lactone formation and ring‑opening to furnish pure 4b monohydrate.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It was quite difficult to obtain enough amount of undesired isomer 4b of high quality … Hence, an alternative synthesis of 4b was devised (Scheme 3).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: A mixture of 4a/4b monohydrates (≈73:27) could not be separated by conventional recrystallisation at ambient temperature, leading to impure product.
Solution_Description: Exploited the temperature‑dependent solubility difference between 4a·H₂O (stable to ~72 °C) and 4b·H₂O (converts to anhydrate at ~45 °C) to crystallise the mixture at 52–55 °C, affording virtually pure 4a monohydrate (99+ % purity).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Selective crystallization of 4a might be possible … within the temperature range of 42.5 and 72.1 °C.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of (+)-Biotin Key Intermediate by Calcium Borohydride Reduction and Temperature-Dependent Purity Upgrade during Crystallization
Problem_Description: The multistep work‑up after reduction required isolation of the crude 4a before crystallisation, adding time and handling steps.
Solution_Description: Performed a telescoped procedure: after Ca(BH₄)₂ reduction, added concentrated HCl and water directly to the reaction mixture and crystallised 4a·H₂O in‑situ at 40–60 °C, giving 63 % isolated yield of diastereomerically pure 4a.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We conducted direct isolation of 4a monohydrate from the reaction mixture by adding concentrated HCl (c‑HCl) and water and concomitant crystallization at a specific temperature (40–60 °C).”

Paper Title: Hydrogen Evolution from Telescoped Miyaura Borylation and Suzuki Couplings Utilizing Diboron Reagents: Process Safety and Hazard Considerations
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Insights into Fast Amide Couplings in Aqueous Nanomicelles
Problem_Description: The formation of the activated carboxylate intermediate is intrinsically slow, leading to low conversion of the carboxylic acid to the amide product.
Solution_Description: Running the coupling in an aqueous 3 wt % PS‑750‑M micellar solution forces EDC·HCl to self‑aggregate with the surfactant, creating mixed‑micelle nanoparticles that concentrate the coupling agent and substrate. The higher local concentration accelerates activation, giving 98 % GC–MS yield in 8 min.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The slower formation of an activated complex of carboxylic acid causes low conversions.” (Intro, p. 3)

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The traditional preparation of the 2‑fluorobenzylzinc reagent by flame‑drying zinc powder and lithium chloride followed by addition of the bromide was not practical or reproducible, and on larger scale the exothermic zinc insertion became difficult to control, creating a safety hazard.
Solution_Description: Adopted zinc activation with 1,2‑dibromoethane as an operationally simpler method and, ultimately, switched to the commercially available 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride reagent to avoid the hazardous exotherm and reproducibility issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The previously employed procedure that involved flame drying zinc powder and lithium chloride followed by the addition of 2‑fluorobenzyl bromide was not found to be practical or reproducible.”; “Zinc activation with 1,2‑dibromoethane proved to be a viable and operationally simpler alternative, allowing for the straightforward generation of the 2‑fluorobenzylzinc bromide reagent which was used in situ.”; “However, on larger scale, controlling the exothermic zinc insertion became challenging, especially given the elevated temperature required to initiate said insertion.”; “Ultimately, the use of commercially available 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride proved more practical.”; “This change avoided the safety‑critical exotherm associated with the in‑situ generation of the zinc reagent.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: Negishi coupling gave significant formation of the bis‑Negishi impurity (7) and the regio‑isomer (8), reducing the isolated yield of the desired product 3.
Solution_Description: Screened a series of palladium sources and ligands; selected Pd(PPh₃)₂Cl₂ as the optimal catalyst that provided the highest conversion and the most favorable product‑to‑impurity ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: “Several commercially available ligands and palladium sources were screened to optimize the ratio of desired product 3 to residual starting material 2, bis‑Negishi product 7, as well as undesired regioisomer 8.”; “Comparable results were obtained with Pd(PPh₃)₂Cl₂… which was chosen for further development.”; “Entry 7 (Pd(OAc)₂, Xantphos) gave 95 % conversion and a 1:96:2:1 ratio (2 : 3 : 7 : 8).”; “As anticipated, driving the reaction to completion without competing formation of the bis‑Negishi impurity 7 proved difficult even under optimal conditions.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: Excess zinc reagent (≥1.3 equiv) and long addition times (>5 h) generated side‑products 9 and 10, decreasing overall yield and complicating purification.
Solution_Description: Reduced the zinc reagent to 1.1 equiv and limited the addition time, enabling higher product yield while suppressing formation of impurities 9 and 10.
Supporting_Evidence: “The difficulty of excluding adventitious water on a small screening scale led to the need for at least 1.3 equiv of zinc reagent to reach the conversions shown in Table 1.”; “However, this excess was not needed on a preparative scale and led to greater amounts of bis‑Negishi impurity (entry 2).”; “Typically, 1.1 equiv of zinc reagent was required to maximize product yield compared to both residual starting material 2 and bis‑Negishi impurity 7.”; “A zinc reagent addition time in excess of 5 h can lead to generation of impurity 9… Small amounts of impurity 10… were also seen, likely due to an impurity in the 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride reagent as levels varied based on a commercial source of this.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The original sequence required isolation and chromatography after each step, extending the overall process time and increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: Implemented a telescoped Negishi‑coupling/cyanation sequence without intermediate isolation, eliminating chromatography and reducing both time and cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “While bromide 3 could be isolated after an extractive work‑up, a telescoped process to the cyanation stage was considered to streamline operations.”; “Addition of zinc cyanide, dimethylformamide (DMF), and 0.02 equiv of dppf to the end‑of‑reaction process stream… allowed for the straightforward substitution of the remaining bromide group to give 4.”; “The streamlined process for generation of high‑purity 4 was defined avoiding the need for any chromatography or intermediate isolations and allowing for significant cost saving based on reduced palladium loading (3 mol % vs 8 % in the previous process) and increased yield.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The earlier route used 8 mol % palladium, leading to higher catalyst cost and higher residual metal levels in the product.
Solution_Description: Reduced palladium loading to 3 mol % while maintaining conversion, decreasing both cost and residual metal impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “After removal of THF by distillation… the overall 82 % yield through the two‑step sequence from 2.”; “The streamlined process … reducing catalyst loading.”; “Typically, 1.1 equiv of zinc reagent was required … and a lower palladium loading of 3 mol % could be used.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The conversion of nitrile 4 to amidrazone 5 required >6 equiv of anhydrous hydrazine, a highly flammable, toxic, carcinogenic reagent, and the isolated amidrazone 5 began to decompose below 30 °C.
Solution_Description: Replaced the hazardous hydrazine step with a Boc‑protected amidrazone route (compound 20) generated from methyl imidate 19 and tert‑butyl carbazate, eliminating the need for anhydrous hydrazine and providing a thermally stable intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “A major challenge … was the use of excess anhydrous hydrazine … Hydrazine has a flammability range between 4 and 100 % and a flash point of 38 °C… It is also acutely toxic and a known animal carcinogen/mutagen.”; “The isolated amidrazone 5 showed multiple decomposition events by DSC with the earliest initiating below 30 °C.”; “Treatment of nitrile 4 with catalytic quantities of sodium methoxide … acid‑catalyzed addition of tert‑butyl carbazate gave complete and clean conversion to the Boc‑protected amidrazone 20… isolated in >90 % yield… no new impurities formed.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The cyclization of Boc‑amidrazone 20 to CY6463 generated a mild exotherm when TFA‑TFE was added; temperature needed to stay <30 °C to avoid decomposition of 20.
Solution_Description: Added DABCO (endothermic) and TFA‑TFE in a controlled, dropwise fashion while jacket‑cooling, keeping the reaction temperature between 30 °C and 35 °C; DABCO also acted as a promoter for the cyclization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of DABCO to the slurry of 20 in MeCN was found to be endothermic.”; “Addition of TFA‑TFE led to a mild exotherm; however, this was easily controlled by jacket cooling and reagent addition rate to ensure the internal temperature of the reaction did not exceed the final reaction temperature of 30 °C.”; “The optimized conditions for the cyclization were the use of 2.2 equiv of both TFA‑TFE and DABCO at 30 °C…”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: The cyclization step required a homogeneous reaction medium for efficient mixing; the substrate and reagents were poorly soluble in many solvents.
Solution_Description: Switched to acetonitrile as the reaction solvent, providing a clear solution that facilitated mixing and allowed the slurry to be efficiently processed.
Supporting_Evidence: “Boc‑amidrazone 20 (1.19 kg …) was charged … anhydrous acetonitrile (7.14 L, 6 vol) was added at room temperature … the slurry was heated to an internal temperature of 35 °C and stirred for 2 h … the reaction became an orange solution.”

Paper Title: Accelerated Development of a Scalable Synthesis of CY6463, a CNS-Penetrant sGC Stimulator for the Treatment of Neurodegenerative Diseases
Problem_Description: Impurities 10 varied in level depending on the commercial source of 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride, leading to inconsistent impurity profiles.
Solution_Description: Standardized the source and quality control of the commercial 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride reagent to ensure consistent impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “Small amounts of impurity 10 … were also seen, likely due to an impurity in the 2‑fluorobenzylzinc chloride reagent as levels varied based on a commercial source of this.”

Paper Title: An Unexpected Incident during the Manufacture of
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the isolated O‑(diphenylphosphinyl)‑hydroxylamine (DPPH) underwent an unexpected thermal decomposition inside an agitated pressure filter/dryer; the exothermic event propagated out of the equipment and into the surrounding area, posing a serious safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The root‑cause investigation identified an electrostatic discharge (ESD) from a non‑grounded scraper as the most likely ignition source; subsequent mitigation actions included grounding all metal tools, adding ESD‑control procedures, and revising the discharge protocol to prevent spark generation.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Scaling up processes … an unexpected thermal decomposition of O‑(diphenylphosphinyl)‑hydroxylamine (DPPH) occurred during its isolation on scale using an agitated pressure filter/dryer.', 'The decomposition propagated outside of the confines of the filter and glovebox used for discharging, resulting in the further decomposition of previously discharged DPPH contained in a bag below the glovebox.', 'The investigation … the most likely the result of an electrostatic discharge during heel removal from the filter.', 'The scraper was designed without a grounding strap, as it was intended for use within a nitrogen‑inerted closed system. The change in the equipment’s operation introduced the potential of an electrostatic discharge event.', 'On the basis of the electrostatic discharge (ESD) test using the ARDEC test method, evidence of “slight decomposition” (a color change from white to brown) was observed with energies down to 30 mJ.']

Paper Title: An Unexpected Incident during the Manufacture of
Problem_Description: The original DPPH synthesis suffered from poor filterability and difficult solid handling, limiting the ability to isolate and wash the product efficiently on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: A modified Laulhé‑Nantz one‑pot protocol was adopted that incorporated low‑temperature filtration (≤ ‑20 °C), extensive washing with cold water and THF, and a Na₂CO₃ slurry step to remove the undesired N‑isomer, which together improved filter cake formation and overall product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: ['...the scalability of its preparation had not been well‑established. This is primarily related to the reaction selectivity (O vs N), instability under the reaction conditions, and poor filterability.', 'We introduced modifications to the one‑pot Laulhé and Nantz method to address these challenges (Scheme 1).', 'The wet cake was washed with subsequent portions of precooled water (2 × 5.0 kg, 3 °C)…', 'The wet cake was reslurried on the filter with a Na₂CO₃ solution … to remove the undesired isomer.', 'The solid was dried under vacuum at NMT 25 °C until the loss on drying was NMT 1 % to obtain DPPH…']

Paper Title: An Unexpected Incident during the Manufacture of
Problem_Description: DPPH exhibits a low onset temperature for its highly exothermic decomposition (≈ 77 °C DSC, T_D24 ≈ 60 °C ARC), requiring drying temperatures to be kept well below this limit to avoid runaway reactions.
Solution_Description: The drying step was performed under vacuum with the internal and jacket set‑points limited to 25 °C, and all filtration and washing operations were conducted at ≤ ‑15 °C to stay safely below the thermal decomposition onset.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Samples … displayed a large exothermic decomposition with an autocatalytic profile… ARC test sample decomposed energetically with a measured onset of 77 °C, and the T_D24 value … was calculated to be about 60 °C.', '…drying of the product under vacuum with a maximum internal and jacket set point temperature of 25 °C.', '…process‑related information (reaction and product isolation (i.e., filtration) performed at temperatures below −15 °C …']

Paper Title: An Unexpected Incident during the Manufacture of
Problem_Description: The presence of residual diphenylphosphinic acid (DPPA) impurity in DPPH lowered the thermal onset temperature and increased the likelihood of decomposition during handling.
Solution_Description: Process adjustments (additional aqueous washes, Na₂CO₃ slurry, and final THF rinses) were implemented to minimise DPPA content to < 1 % in the final product, thereby raising the decomposition onset and reducing the exothermic risk.
Supporting_Evidence: ['DPPA did have lower onsets of self‑heating, albeit with a concomitant reduction in the normalized integral.', 'Samples of DPPH spiked with DPPA displayed lower onset temperatures and/or faster decomposition onsets, as the thermal decomposition is likely catalyzed by the acid.', 'The bulk material did not contain notable levels of DPPA (< 1 %), the possibility that residual DPPA was retained … cannot be ruled out. No issues with filterability/deliquoring were noted in the process.']

Paper Title: An Unexpected Incident during the Manufacture of
Problem_Description: Prior to the incident there was no systematic assessment of low‑temperature energetic hazards for DPPH, leaving the operation vulnerable to ignition from unexpected sources such as static discharge.
Solution_Description: A simple “burning test for solids” (Steinbach method) was adopted for all DPPH batches; compounds with a DSC integral > 500 J g⁻¹ and onset < 150 °C now undergo this test and are assigned a Burning Number (BN) to guide handling, with BN 4–6 triggering additional safety reviews.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The simple burning test for solids … can demonstrate the propagating deflagration potential and is now employed with samples where the decomposition energy is determined by DSC to be > 500 J g⁻¹ and the onset temperature is < 150 °C.', 'Performing further safety assessment is highly recommended before proceeding with a compound rated as 4 to 6 on the burning number (BN) scale.', 'The test for the propagating deflagration potential was based on the simple test described by Steinbach.']

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: The desired enantiopure amino acids would racemize or decompose under traditional harsh conditions (e.g., strong bases, organometallic reagents, high temperature).
Solution_Description: Metallaphotoredox catalysis couples a β‑bromo‑alanine intermediate with aryl bromides under ambient temperature, visible‑light irradiation, and without strong bases, preserving stereochemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: “Photocatalytic cross‑electrophile coupling … is characterized by high efficiency, mild conditions, and extraordinary substrate scope…”; “...the protocol is mild and enantioretentive… without the need to develop novel asymmetric catalytic platforms.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: Using silanes with strong Si–H bonds (Ph₃SiH, Et₃SiH) gave dramatically reduced product yields (34 % or 0 %).
Solution_Description: Switch to tris‑(trimethylsilyl)silane [(TMS)₃SiH] as the hydrogen‑atom source, which provides the optimal Si–H bond strength for efficient silyl‑radical formation.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 6 → 34 % yield with Ph₃SiH; entry 7 → 0 % with Et₃SiH; “The choice of silane proved important… the use of (TMS)₃SiH gave 85 % yield (entry 1).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: Electron‑rich heterocyclic aryl bromides (e.g., 2‑pyridines) coupled poorly under the standard conditions, requiring longer reaction times and giving lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Increase the nickel catalyst loading from 0.5 mol % to 5 mol % for heterocyclic substrates to accelerate oxidative addition and improve conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Higher loadings of the nickel catalyst (>3 mol %) were generally required to achieve good efficiency with heterocyclic substrates.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: 2‑Pyridine substrates gave low yields with the standard (TMS)₃SiH because the rapid radical generation outpaced the nickel catalytic cycle.
Solution_Description: Replace (TMS)₃SiH with the silanol (TMS)₃Si‑OH, which generates the alkyl radical more slowly, matching the rate of nickel turnover and improving yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the case of 2‑pyridines, the silanol reagent (TMS)₃Si‑OH gave superior yields compared to the standard super silane… attributed to slower generation of the alkyl radical species.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: During prolonged flow runs a precipitate of lutidinium bromide formed, causing clogging and limiting continuous operation.
Solution_Description: Switch the solvent from DME to DMA, lower the reaction concentration to 0.2 M, reduce the base loading to 1 equiv, and raise the temperature to 40 °C; these changes increase the solubility of lutidinium bromide and maintain homogeneous flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempts to conduct larger scale flow reactions… were impeded by accumulation of a precipitate, lutidinium bromide… (a) DMA was used… (b) the reaction was run at more dilute concentrations (0.2 M); (c) the base loading was decreased… (d) the reaction temperature was increased from 30 to 40 °C… providing the desired adduct in a synthetically useful yield of 60 %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: Using higher‑wavelength LEDs (≥420 nm) gave slower reaction rates, longer residence times, and lower isolated yields for the Celebrex‑derived amino acid.
Solution_Description: Employ a 385 nm LED, which better matches the absorption maximum of the iridium photocatalyst, dramatically accelerating the reaction and increasing the yield to 90 % under the same residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The lower wavelength light (385 nm)… was found to substantially accelerate the reaction compared with higher wavelength sources… Under the optimal conditions… 1 mol % nickel catalyst and a 385 nm lamp produced 90 % yield within 20 min.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Unnatural Amino Acids by Metallaphotoredox Catalysis
Problem_Description: The batch cross‑electrophile coupling required 4 h of irradiation for acceptable conversion, limiting throughput for large‑scale synthesis.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Translate the reaction to a continuous‑flow photoreactor (Vapourtec E‑series) which provides efficient light penetration, rapid mixing, and 20 min residence time, dramatically increasing productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The flow reaction… led to an excellent 85 % yield within a residence time of 20 min… this result represents a considerable increase in throughput compared to batch conditions.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: Nickel‑catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura couplings of heterocycles suffered from significant side‑reactions such as protodehalogenation and protodeborylation, which lowered the isolated product amount.
Solution_Description: The inclusion of 10 vol % MeOH as a co‑solvent dramatically improved conversion and suppressed the formation of anisole (a protodeborylation by‑product).
Supporting_Evidence: • “...the inclusion of 10 vol % MeOH was found to be vital to obtain high conversion.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: Typical nickel‑based Suzuki couplings rely on expensive, air‑sensitive Ni(0) precatalysts (e.g., Ni(cod)₂) that are difficult to source and handle on multikilogram scale.
Solution_Description: A bench‑stable, inexpensive NiCl₂·6H₂O (US $14 mol⁻¹) was employed as the precatalyst, providing comparable performance while eliminating the cost and handling issues.
Supporting_Evidence: • “...the inexpensive, bench‑stable precatalyst NiCl₂·6H₂O ($14 / mol) provided 86 AP….”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: Earlier nickel‑catalyzed protocols used heterogeneous inorganic bases (K₂CO₃) that generated biphasic mixtures, making stirring and scale‑up problematic.
Solution_Description: Organic‑soluble amine bases (t‑BuTMG, DBU) were substituted for K₂CO₃, delivering homogeneous reaction mixtures and higher conversions (94–100 AP).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Soluble amine bases, such as DBU and t‑BuTMG, were similarly effective (94–100 AP…) and reliably outperformed heterogeneous K₂CO₃ (32–40 AP).”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: Using non‑polar solvents like toluene failed to fully dissolve the heterocyclic substrates, resulting in poor conversions (6–16 AP).
Solution_Description: Polar aprotic solvents (EtOAc, MeCN, NMP, DMAc) that fully solubilize the reactants were adopted, giving 77–99 AP across ligands.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Solvents that did not fully solubilize the substrates gave poor conversion… toluene provided only 6–16 AP, whereas homogeneous reactions with EtOAc, MeCN, NMP, and DMAc provided 77–99 AP.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: The original 24‑reaction screen required 18 h at 80 °C, limiting throughput for rapid process development.
Solution_Description: Increasing the equivalents of the aryl‑boronic acid and raising the overall reaction concentration reduced the required reaction time and improved process‑mass‑intensity (PMI).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Optimization…showed that a slight increase in the number of equivalents of the aryl‑boronic acid coupling partner significantly improved the conversion and reduced the reaction time, while the PMI was improved by increasing the reaction concentration.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base-Metal Catalysis: Development of a Screening Method for Nickel-Catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura Reactions of Pharmaceutically Relevant Heterocycles
Problem_Description: Ligand performance was highly substrate‑dependent, preventing a single universal set of conditions from being applied across all heterocyclic couplings.
Solution_Description: A 24‑reaction high‑throughput screening platform (12 ligands × 2 solvents) was designed to rapidly map the ligand/solvent space, allowing selection of the optimal condition for each substrate pair.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The diversity of reactions…show that the optimal conditions for the formation of 3 are less relevant than the trends in key class variables… HTE identified the ligand as the most influential class variable.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided
Problem_Description: The traditional route uses homopiperazine (or its derivatives) as a key intermediate. Homopiperazine is expensive, its synthesis is complicated, and large amounts are needed, resulting in low atom‑economy and high waste.
Solution_Description: A new six‑step synthesis starting from low‑cost, readily available ethylenediamine and 5‑isoquinoline sulfonyl chloride avoids homopiperazine entirely, reducing material cost and improving scalability.
Supporting_Evidence: “the synthesis of homopiperazine was complicated and excessive homopiperazine was used to obtain the high yield, which led to the low atom economy. In addition, large amounts of waste were produced in this route.”; “the use of expensive homopiperazine or its derivatives as intermediates… limited their application in industrial production.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided

Solution_Description: The redesigned route eliminates the low‑yield reduction by using a direct condensation of ethylenediamine with sulfonyl chloride, delivering the target in 67.1 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield of the reduction step from 9 to 10 is low (42 %), which, in turn, affected the overall yield.”; “we report a new six‑step procedure… affording 1 in 67.1 % overall yield.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided

Solution_Description: Solid NaHCO₃ was used, pH was adjusted in two stages (2.0 then 7.5‑8.0) and the product was precipitated from the aqueous phase, raising the isolated yield to 87.2 % with 93.84 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the reported procedure, the aqueous solution of sodium bicarbonate was used, and 12 was obtained in 60 % yield…”; “we used solid sodium bicarbonate… the pH of the mixture was adjusted to 2.0… then to 7.5–8.0… the white solid was isolated… yield 87.2 %.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided

Solution_Description: Using THF/H₂O as solvent and K₂CO₃ (2.0 eq) with 1.0 eq (Boc)₂O gave 98.5 % isolated yield of protected product 13.
Supporting_Evidence: “Boc‑protected product 13 was obtained in 98.5 % yield using THF/water as a solvent and K₂CO₃ as a base (entry 4).”; Table 1 entries showing lower yields with different bases/solvents.

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided
Problem_Description: Alkylation of 13 with 1,3‑dihalogenated reagents gave poor conversion (no reaction with NaH at rt, 17.5 % yield at reflux) and generated side‑products (elimination product 17 and dimer 18) that complicated isolation.

Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction could not occur in the presence of sodium hydride (NaH) at room temperature… conversion rate… still very low, isolated yield 17.5 %”; “the eliminated byproduct 17 was produced in a 43.1 % yield.”; “the phase transfer catalyst TBAB plays an important role… low conversion was observed in the absence of TBAB”; “when 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane (2.0 eq) was used and water was added as a co‑solvent, the yield of 14b was dramatically improved (84.6 %) and only a trace amount of 18 was observed.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided
Problem_Description: Deprotection of the Boc group in the previous processes employed trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), which is expensive and corrosive.
Solution_Description: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) was used instead of TFA for Boc deprotection at 50–55 °C, providing a cheaper and safer option.
Supporting_Evidence: “First, the cheaper inorganic acid hydrochloric acid (HCl) was used instead of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) for the deprotection of the Boc group at 50–55 °C.”

Paper Title: Unconventional Synthetic Process of Fasudil Hydrochloride: Costly Homopiperazine Was Avoided
Problem_Description: The final fasudil hydrochloride needed to be obtained with ≥99.9 % purity, requiring an efficient isolation step.

Supporting_Evidence: “After recrystallization with methanol/isopropyl ether, fasudil hydrochloride 1 was afforded… yield 78.1 %, purity 99.94 %.”

Supporting_Evidence: “the route via the enol triflate was less suitable for further scale‑up, in part due to the high cost of Ru‑catalysts, whereas the Shapiro route was readily scaled.”

Problem_Description: The Shapiro reaction on the tosylhydrazone 13 gave a moderate isolated yield (≈ 51 %) with olefin 15 as the main by‑product, caused by quenching of the vinyl‑lithium intermediate with adventitious water and required careful temperature control to avoid exotherms.

Supporting_Evidence: “Cryogenic treatment (< −50 °C) of tosyl hydrazone 13 with 4 equiv of n‑butyllithium … followed by a slow warm up to ∼10 °C, formed the vinyl lithium intermediate … Quenching of this active intermediate by slow addition of 1,2‑dibromoethane (3 equiv, controlling the exotherm to maintain the internal temperature below 26 °C) afforded a ∼4:1 mixture …”

Paper Title: Practical Kilogram Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The classical chiral salt‑resolution step (formation of (–)‑di‑p‑toluoyl‑l‑tartaric acid salt of 12) gave an isolated overall yield of 39 % (theoretical 50 %) after two recrystallizations, limiting material throughput.
Solution_Description: The authors developed an improved crystallisation protocol: slow addition of the acid solution to hot ethanol at 67 °C, gradual cooling to 15 °C, followed by a hot‑ethanol reslurry and a second recrystallisation. This sequence raised the diastereomeric ratio to 99.18:0.82 and maintained acceptable recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “A solution of (–)‑di‑p‑toluoyl‑l‑tartaric acid … was added in a single portion to a stirred solution of racemic vinyl bromide 12 … heated to 70 °C … then slowly cooled to 25 °C … The crude was triturated in ethanol … and the solid was dried … affording the desired salt … in 39 % (vs theoretical 50 %) with 99.18:0.82 d.r.”
