Solution_Description: Implement a continuous‑flow packed‑bed reactor (glass column) allowing direct conversion of substrate to product without isolation, reducing residence time to 9.8 min and delivering a space‑time yield of 930.73 g L⁻¹ day⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "the batch reaction (0.5 g of immobilized enzyme in 3 mL reaction volume) required ∼6 h to generate similar conversion results" (Section 3.4.4).  
Solution: "We packed ATA‑W12‑EES into glass columns ... achieved 95 % conversion in 9.8 min of residence ... space–time yield of 930.73 g·L⁻¹·day⁻¹" (Section 3.4.4).

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: The original five‑step synthesis of molnupiravir from uridine gave a very low overall isolated yield of only 17 %, making the process economically unattractive for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A new non‑enzymatic four‑step route from inexpensive cytidine was developed, raising the overall isolated yield to 36–41 % and eliminating the need for the low‑yielding acetonide‑protecting‑group sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the original synthesis of molnupiravir … proceeds in five steps with a low overall yield (17 % overall…)”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Isolation of intermediates 8, 6 and molnupiravir relied on column chromatography, which is labor‑intensive, generates large solvent waste, and is costly and impractical at multigram scale.
Solution_Description: All chromatographic steps were replaced by recrystallization‑based purifications (i‑PrOAc or water as solvents), delivering the products in ≥95 % purity without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “column chromatography was used to isolate the products of Step 2 and molnupiravir.”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: During step 2 (regioselective acylation) a significant amount of the diacylated side‑product 11 formed (up to 6 % LCAP), lowering the yield of the desired mono‑acylated ester 8.
Solution_Description: Optimisation identified DBU as the optimal base, running the reaction at 0 °C, using 1.1 equiv anhydride, and increasing the solvent volume (10 V) which together reduced impurity 11 to ≤2.2 % and raised ester 8 to >94 % LCAP.
Supporting_Evidence: • “key impurities generated in Step 2 were the diacylated side compound 11…”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Hydroxylamine is a known explosion hazard on heating and a severe respiratory, skin and eye irritant, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The safe hydroxylamine sulfate salt was used instead of free hydroxylamine, allowing the transamination to be performed at 72–73 °C without the explosive risk.
Supporting_Evidence: • “There is some safety and environmental concerns related to hydroxylamine. It was reported that hydroxylamine may explode on heating… It is also an irritant to respiratory tract, eyes, skin…”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Removal of the high‑pKa base DBU from the crude reaction mixture required chromatography, which is undesirable on large scale.
Solution_Description: A mild aqueous 10 % acetic‑acid wash selectively protonated and transferred DBU into the aqueous phase, allowing DBU removal without chromatography and with >84 % recovery of ester 8.
Supporting_Evidence: • “...chromatographic separation was used to isolate the pure compound… this will be costly on scale.”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Deprotection of the acetonide (step 4) gave low to modest yields (<50 %) with many protic or Lewis acids, and generated side‑products such as 8 and 13.
Solution_Description: Neat formic acid was found to give >90 % conversion to molnupiravir with consistent results, and recrystallization from water provided the final API in 98.5 % wt purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Only neat formic acid and trifluoroacetic acid provide conversions to molnupiravir in >90 % yield… formic acid was selected for further development.”

Paper Title: Toward a Practical, Nonenzymatic Process for Investigational COVID-19 Antiviral Molnupiravir from Cytidine: Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Finding a solvent that could both dissolve crude product 6 and allow high‑purity recrystallization proved challenging; inappropriate solvents gave low recovery or impure material.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified isopropyl acetate (Method A) as the optimal recrystallization solvent, delivering 66 % mass recovery and 98 % qNMR purity, and acetonitrile (Method B) as an alternative.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Qualitative solubility studies … two methods were identified. Method A involves recrystallization of crude 6 from i‑PrOAc … 66 % mass recovery, 98 % purity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Trifluoromethylation of aldehydes with Ruppert–Prakash reagent (CF₃TMS) is an autocatalytic reaction that caused a rapid temperature jump (0 → 80 °C within seconds), raising a safety concern for heat control on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A two‑stream continuous‑flow system was implemented: stream 1 (acrolein + CF₃TMS) and stream 2 (TBAF catalyst) were mixed in a static mixer and the released heat was removed by a temperature‑controlled heat‑exchange coil, allowing precise temperature control and safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: In‑line monitoring of the turbo Grignard reaction using in‑situ IR spectroscopy: Normalized time-dependent relative concentration trends for amide 28, aryl Grignard reagent 29, and tetrahedral adduct 30 based on univariate (one wavelength) analysis of IR. (Fig 2)===“The temperature of the reaction mixture changed from ca. 0 to 80 °C almost instantaneously (within seconds) even on a relatively small scale (e.g., 1 g) upon addition of a sufficient amount of TBAF to initiate this autocatalytic process.”===“A two‑stream‑flow system … was designed. The two streams were mixed by simultaneous flow through a static mixer, and the released heat was cooled by a subsequent temperature‑controlled heat‑exchange coil.”===“The resulting reactor setup provided the possibility of high production rates of up to 6 kg of 44 per hour and was utilized to produce 45 on a 24 kg scale in a single run.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Stage 3 required lithiation of 1‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzene under cryogenic conditions (below ‑60 °C) to avoid benzyne formation, which limited throughput and increased manufacturing cost.
Solution_Description: The cryogenic lithiation was replaced by a turbo‑Grignard approach: 1‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzene was treated with isopropyl‑magnesium‑chloride‑lithium‑chloride complex (turbo Grignard reagent) to generate the aryl magnesium species at 0 °C, eliminating the need for low‑temperature conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “In Stage 3, the lithiation of 1‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzene required cryogenic conditions (below ‑60 °C) to prevent benzyne formation, which was throughput limiting and increased manufacturing cost.”===“Treatment of 1‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzene with isopropylmagnesium chloride lithium chloride complex (turbo Grignard reagent) provided aryl magnesium complex 29, which then reacted with amide 28 to give tetrahedral adduct 30 at noncryogenic temperatures (0 °C).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Late‑stage Boc‑protected isothiourea intermediates 14 and 15 were unstable, leading to formation of a dimeric urea impurity 22 even at ambient temperature.
Solution_Description: A chemoselective amide coupling was performed via in‑situ protection: 1 equiv of HCl generated from acid‑chloride formation protonated the basic isothiourea moiety of diamine 34, giving an in‑situ‑protected species that coupled cleanly with acid chloride 35, eliminating the need for the unstable protecting groups.
Supporting_Evidence: “Two late‑stage intermediates, Boc‑protected isothioureas 14 and 15, posed handling challenges due to instability. For example, a significant dimeric urea impurity 22 was generated from 15 … at ambient temperature.”===“Diamine 34 … underwent a chemoselective coupling with acid chloride 35 to give E2609 in a quantitative yield … 1 equiv of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in‑situ generated … would selectively protonate the more basic isothiourea amine moiety of 34 … This chemoselective amide coupling eliminated two unstable intermediates (14 and 15) and shortened the overall synthesis by two stages.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Stage 3′ deoxofluorination required the expensive and hazardous reagent Deoxo‑Fluor and special facilities for safe handling, limiting scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The difluoromethyl group was installed via a Reformatsky‑decarboxylation sequence: halo‑pyrazinoic ester 38 was converted to bromide 39, then coupled with a BrZnCF₂CO₂Et Reformatsky reagent in the presence of CuBr, followed by decarboxylation, avoiding Deoxo‑Fluor entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Stage 3′ deoxofluorination has a limitation for scale‑up due to the high cost of Deoxo‑Fluor and the requirement of special facilities for the handling of hazardous reagents.”===“To avoid the hazardous deoxofluorination step, introduction of the difluoromethyl group by Reformatsky reaction … was investigated.”===“According to this method, any special facilities and use of hazardous fluorinating reagents were not required to make further scale‑up manufacturing feasible.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The original route comprised 15 linear synthetic stages with an overall yield of only 4.8 %, resulting in a long production time and low material efficiency.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned: the [3 + 2] cycloaddition and oxime formation were merged into a one‑pot water‑mediated step, the chemoselective amide coupling eliminated two protecting‑group steps, and the turbo‑Grignard replaced cryogenic lithiation. These changes reduced the number of stages to nine and raised the overall yield to 10 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The route contains 15 linear synthetic stages with 4.8 % overall yield, leading to a long production time.”===“The one‑pot, three‑step process reduced two synthetic stages and increased the overall yield from ca. 50 % to ca. 80 %.”===“These process optimization steps resulted in shortening the linear synthetic stage count from 15 to 9 and improving the overall yield to 10 % from 4.8 % in the first‑generation route.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The [3 + 2] cycloaddition gave only moderate yields because the oxime precursor 7 existed mainly as the E‑isomer (Z/E ≈ 2.7:1), and only the Z‑isomer participates in the desired cycloaddition.
Solution_Description: Oxime formation and cycloaddition were performed in water, which promotes Z/E isomerization and suppresses side reactions; the combined one‑pot process increased the Z/E ratio, eliminated the need for separate steps, and raised the isolated yield of the cycloadduct to 81 % (overall ∼ 80 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “One of the reasons for the moderate yield of the [3 + 2] cycloaddition was attributed to be the modest Z/E ratio (2.7/1) of oxime 7.”===“Given that the oxime formation proceeded well in water, the oxime formation and cycloaddition steps were combined into a single step; the desired product 8 was generated … at 100 °C.”===“This one‑pot, three‑step process reduced two synthetic stages and increased the overall yield from ca. 50 % to ca. 80 %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Formation of the aryl Grignard reagent 29 and the tetrahedral adduct 30 could not be monitored by conventional in‑process analytical methods, creating uncertainty in reaction progress and possible variability.
Solution_Description: In‑situ infrared (IR) spectroscopy was employed to directly monitor characteristic absorption bands of the aryl Grignard (1161 cm⁻¹), the adduct (1200 cm⁻¹), and the amide (1635 cm⁻¹), providing real‑time conversion data and enabling precise control of the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “Formation of aryl Grignard reagent 29 and tetrahedral adduct 30 could not be directly monitored using conventional in‑process control (IPC) methods (e.g., HPLC, GC). Therefore, in‑situ IR spectroscopy was employed to monitor these species directly.”===“The peak at 1161 cm⁻¹ for aryl Grignard reagent 29, the peak at 1200 cm⁻¹ for adduct 30, and the peak at 1635 cm⁻¹ for amide 28 … were selected for reaction monitoring.”===“Changes in the absorption intensities … were plotted as a function of time, highlighting how the concentration of each component changed with reaction progress (Fig 2).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE1 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The autocatalytic trifluoromethylation of aldehydes generated a rapid temperature increase (0 → 80 °C) that posed exothermic safety risks.
Solution_Description: Using a flow‑reactor with a static mixer and a temperature‑controlled heat‑exchange coil allowed the exotherm to be removed continuously, maintaining a stable reaction temperature and preventing runaway conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “The temperature of the reaction mixture changed from ca. 0 to 80 °C almost instantaneously … upon addition of a sufficient amount of TBAF to initiate this autocatalytic process.”===“The two streams were mixed by simultaneous flow through a static mixer, and the released heat was cooled by a subsequent temperature‑controlled heat‑exchange coil.”===“The resulting reactor setup provided the possibility of high production rates of up to 6 kg of 44 per hour and was utilized to produce 45 on a 24 kg scale in a single run.”

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: The late‑stage Sonogashira coupling of the electronically mismatched bromocinnamate (compound 14) gave a low isolated yield, creating a major inefficiency and waste burden in the discovery route.
Solution_Description: The diaryl‑acetylene moiety was installed early on an electronically matched p‑bromo‑cinnamate (compound 19) using a standard Pd‑Cu Sonogashira protocol (0.1 mol % PdCl₂(PPhCN)₂, 0.2 mol % tBu₃P·BF₄). This early coupling gave 94 % isolated yield and avoided the low‑yielding late‑stage step.
Supporting_Evidence: The conversion of the benzylic alcohol  4 to chloride 5 … a low‑yielding, late‑stage Sonogashira reaction…was among the lower‑yielding steps in the entire synthesis and a significant opportunity for improvement.

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: The original synthesis required fifteen chromatographic purifications, leading to high solvent consumption, waste generation and elevated manufacturing cost.
Solution_Description: A crystallization‑based strategy was adopted, identifying fourteen crystalline intermediates that could be isolated by simple cooling or antisolvent addition, completely replacing chromatography and reducing solvent use >100‑fold.
Supporting_Evidence: The complete removal of chromatographic purifications was set as a must‑have goal… 15 chromatographies were replaced by 14 crystallization (or precipitation) steps resulting in a greater than 100‑fold reduction in the projected solvent use and waste generation.

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: The Zn‑mediated asymmetric cinnamylation was heterogeneous and highly exothermic, posing a scale‑up safety hazard and giving variable yields depending on the ZnCl₂ source and water content.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to a Zn‑chelate Claisen rearrangement, which proceeds under homogeneous conditions.  Commercial ZnCl₂ dissolved in 2‑MeTHF was used, providing a scalable, water‑controlled system with reproducible high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: The heterogeneous and exothermic nature of the Zn‑mediated cinnamylation, which was deemed a potential hazard for a scale up…A lower yield of the reaction was accompanied with the regeneration of alcohol 24, hinting that a close control of water content was needed. Freshly “fused” ZnCl₂ provided the best yield…but this method of drying was limited to small‑scale reactions. Fortunately, commercially available solutions of ZnCl₂ in 2‑MeTHF … were found to be equally effective and provided a practical option for scale‑up.

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: Iodolactonization of salt 31 initially gave only a 4 : 1 mixture of trans‑trans diastereomers, reducing the amount of the desired product and requiring additional purification.
Solution_Description: Changing the reaction medium to acetonitrile and then to aqueous acetonitrile raised the diastereoselectivity to >20 : 1, delivering the target iodolactone 34 in high purity without extra chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: Treatment of salt 31 with iodine in THF afforded the desired alternating trans, trans‑iodolactone 34 with a 4:1 ratio. Additional experimentation identified that the diastereoselectivity could be increased to 15:1 by conducting the reaction in acetonitrile and ultimately greater than 20:1 in aqueous acetonitrile.

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: Mesylation of bis‑alcohol 36 produced a mixture that preferentially cyclised to an aziridine (38) rather than the intended bis‑mesylate, compromising yield of the downstream azetidine.
Solution_Description: Addition of K‑phthalimide in DMF at ambient temperature promoted clean chemoselective formation of the aziridine, which then underwent regio‑selective SN2 opening and intramolecular cyclisation to give the all‑cis azetidine 39 in >90 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Mass spectral data in the initial experiments indicated this compound exhibited a tendency to form aziridine 38… A treatment of the bis‑mesylate with K‑phthalimide in dimethylformamide (DMF) at ambient temperature smoothly afforded … the desired azetidine 39 with all‑cis stereochemistry (>90 % yield).

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: Removal of the nosyl protecting group from azetidine 39 required a deprotection protocol that left thiol‑containing impurities, preventing direct crystallization of the product.
Solution_Description: Scale‑up deprotection was performed with mercaptoacetic acid and DBU in DMF, followed by a basic aqueous work‑up that removed thiol impurities, enabling isolation of the amine 40 as a crystalline hydrochloride salt (>97 % purity).
Supporting_Evidence: Optimal conditions for scale‑up involved the use of mercaptoacetic acid and 1,8‑diazabicyclo[5.4.0]‑undec‑7‑ene (DBU) in DMF, allowing a removal of thiol‑containing impurities in the basic aqueous workup to afford 40 as an amorphous mass…The crystallization of 40 as the corresponding hydrochloride salt in iPrOAc resulted in an improved purity, that is, greater than 97 %.

Paper Title: Crystallization-Based Synthetic Route to Antimalarial Agent BRD5018: Diazocene Ring Formation via a Staudinger-aza-Wittig Reaction on an Azetidine-Ribose Template
Problem_Description: Overall the discovery route gave an overall isolated yield of ~0.05 % and required >500 000 L kg⁻¹ of solvent, making it economically unviable for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The new crystallization‑based synthetic route (14 steps, 22 linear steps, 0 chromatographies) increased overall isolated yield to 3.20 % (64‑fold improvement) and cut estimated solvent usage to 3 416 L kg⁻¹, reducing API cost by ~30‑fold.
Supporting_Evidence: The new route resulted in an overall yield of 3.20 % vs 0.05 % in the discovery route…most notably, the relative cost of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) was substantially reduced by ca. 30‑fold…15 chromatographies were replaced by 14 crystallization (or precipitation) steps resulting in a greater than 100‑fold reduction in the projected solvent use and waste generation.

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Acetone, used as the traditional solvent for the Finkelstein reaction, remains as a trace impurity in the product iodide 4 and dramatically interferes with the subsequent zinc‑reagent formation, requiring severe in‑process control to obtain reproducible results on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced acetone with a non‑polar solvent (toluene) and added catalytic amounts of tetra‑n‑butylammonium bromide (TBAB) together with a small quantity of water, which catalyse the halide exchange and avoid the need for post‑reaction solvent exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: “even a trace amount of acetone contaminated in 4 was found to considerably affect the zinc reagent formation … severe in‑process (IP) control … was needed to attain a reproducible outcome, especially on scale.”; “we explored an alternative protocol and finally found out a convenient and efficient procedure of the Finkelstein reaction in inert solvents employing tetra‑n‑butylammonium bromide (TBAB) and water as the additives.”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: When toluene was used as the solvent, no detectable amount of the iodide product 4 was formed because NaI (the iodide source) is poorly soluble in non‑polar media.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount (6 mol %) of tetra‑n‑butylammonium iodide (TBAI) was added, converting NaI into the soluble tetra‑alkylammonium iodide and enabling the reaction to proceed (94.7 % conversion at 50 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: “any detectable amount of 4 was not observed … even after stirring at elevated temperature (entry 2).” ; “addition of tetra‑n‑butyl iodide (TBAI) (6 mol %) … the reaction occurred dramatically and reached up to a 94.7 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Using TBAI at 50 °C required 73 h to reach ~95 % conversion, a reaction time that is impractically long for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Increasing the temperature to 80 °C or 100 °C dramatically shortened the reaction time (e.g., 2 h at 100 °C with 6 mol % TBAB gave 99.8 % conversion). Adding 0.05 v/w water further reduced the required time to 2 h at 100 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “To reduce the reaction time, the temperature was increased to 100 °C … but an appreciable amount of 3 (6.0 %) was left …” ; “addition of a small amount of water (0.05 v/w) … has decreased the reaction time considerably (entry 8).”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Excessive water (0.5 v/w or 2.5 v/w) lowered the conversion of the Finkelstein reaction, likely because dissolved NaBr shifts the equilibrium away from product formation.
Solution_Description: Optimised the water amount to 0.025 v/w (0.05 v/w overall) while keeping TBAB at 2.5 mol % to achieve >99 % conversion without compromising the equilibrium.
Supporting_Evidence: “addition of an increased amount of water can dissolve NaBr and retard shift of equilibrium … apparent reduction of conversion was found for the latter one (entry 15).” ; “Despite further reduction of TBAB, water, and toluene … the reaction proceeded very well to give 4 in a 99.7 % conversion (entry 13).”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: TBAI, the initial phase‑transfer catalyst, is relatively expensive for large‑scale use.
Solution_Description: Replaced TBAI with the cheaper TBAB (tetra‑n‑butylammonium bromide) while retaining comparable activity, thereby reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “We then tested exchange of expensive TBAI to a much cheaper TBAB.” ; “entry 12 shows 99.8 % conversion with TBAB (6 mol %).”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Using tert‑butyl methyl ether (TBME) as the solvent gave only moderate conversion (≈40 %).
Solution_Description: Screened alternative solvents (CHCl₃, THF, EtOAc, 1,4‑dioxane, CH₂Cl₂) and identified those that afforded >90 % conversion under the same additive conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 3 shows TBME entry 8 – 40.1 % conversion, whereas CHCl₃ (entry 1) gave 99.8 % and THF (entry 2) gave 99.5 % conversion.

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: The crude iodide 4 obtained after the Finkelstein reaction contained about 10 % residual toluene, which could complicate downstream steps.
Solution_Description: The crude product was used directly in the zinc‑reagent formation and subsequent Fukuyama coupling without further purification, demonstrating that the residual solvent did not impair the downstream chemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: “crude 4 … contained 10.4 wt % of toluene … nevertheless, the residual toluene did not affect the performance of the subsequent reaction …” ; “the crude iodide 4 … was added to a suspension of activated zinc dust … resulted in a smooth zinc reagent formation (98.6 % conversion).”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Trimethylsilyl iodide (TMSI) is highly unstable toward moisture, requiring strictly anhydrous conditions for its preparation and use.
Solution_Description: Prepared TMSI in anhydrous CH₂Cl₂ (or toluene) using TBAB (5 mol %) as the phase‑transfer promoter, and conducted the reaction under nitrogen to avoid moisture‑induced decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “due to instability of 7 to moisture, the reaction was carried out under absolutely anhydrous conditions.” ; “use of TBAB (5 mol %) … gave a 95.4 % conversion (entry 3).”

Paper Title: Finkelstein Reaction in Non-polar Organic Solvents: A Streamlined Synthesis of Organic Iodides
Problem_Description: Conventional batch heating of the Finkelstein reaction required 15 h to achieve only ~35 % conversion.
Solution_Description: Applied microwave irradiation (5–10 W, 1–2 bar) at 100 °C which raised the conversion to 62.5 % in 40 min, and further addition of 0.05 v/w water gave 99.6 % conversion in just 15 min.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2, entry 1: conventional 15 h → 34.7 % conversion; entry 2: microwave 40 min → 62.5 %; entry 3: microwave + water 15 min → 99.6 % conversion.

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: Obtaining the 2‑trifluoromethylphenyl‑magnesium chloride Grignard reagent from 1‑chloro‑2‑(trifluoromethyl)benzene (CTFB) using Mg dust or a metal‑halogen exchange with i‑PrMgBr caused violent reactions and rapid decomposition of the Grignard reagent because of a very exothermic Mg insertion step.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced Mg dust with inexpensive Mg turnings and added 0.3 equiv of LiCl. LiCl promotes Mg insertion into the aryl chloride, giving a stable Grignard complex that can be prepared safely and in high yield (95 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “A previous study reported that it was difficult to obtain the Grignard reagent … using Mg turnings owing to its poor reactivity… However, halogenated trifluoromethylbenzenes can react violently with Mg dust, and the Grignard reagent decomposes because of the strong exothermic reaction.”; “We successfully developed the process for the Grignard reagent synthesis … using Mg turnings in the presence of LiCl. 2‑Trifluoromethylphenyl magnesium chloride Grignard reagent was easily and safely obtained in high yields because LiCl promoted Mg insertion to chlorobenzene… the stability of the Grignard reagent was improved because of the formation of a complex Grignard reagent with LiCl.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: During the homocoupling step, addition of the Grignard reagent to the catalyst solution generated large amounts of gas (from EDC oxidation) and an exotherm that could be difficult to control on a large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The Grignard solution was added dropwise (slowly) to the FeCl₃/EDC/Toluene mixture while keeping the reactor temperature at 50–60 °C (jacket at 5 °C) and later cooled below 10 °C before acid quench. This controlled the rate of gas evolution and limited the temperature rise.
Supporting_Evidence: “To avoid the accumulation of 2, the Grignard reagent solution was added dropwise (slowly) to a metal catalyst solution … while keeping the temperature at 50–60 °C. The generation of outgases was observed … Following the completion of the Grignard reagent solution addition, the reaction was stirred at 50–55 °C for 3 h… then cooled below 10 °C before HCl addition.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: Screening of transition‑metal catalysts (Cu, Ni, Pd, Co) gave low homocoupling yields (≤27 %), and some catalysts (e.g., Pd) are relatively expensive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: FeCl₃ was selected as the optimal catalyst because it afforded 59–56 % yield, is inexpensive, and is readily available in large quantities.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the reaction proceeded with poor yield … with Ni, Pd, Co, or Cu catalyst, the reaction proceeded with a low yield. However, … Fe catalysts … exhibited a relatively high yield… FeCl₃ was selected as a model catalyst for this process because it is inexpensive and readily available.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: Using 1,2‑dichloroethane (EDC) as the oxidant produced a markedly exothermic reaction and gave only 67 % yield, indicating poor reaction control.
Solution_Description: 1,2‑Dichloropropane (DCP) was adopted as the oxidant; it gave a milder exotherm (≤83 % yield) and was judged safer for industrial operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the presence of EDC as the oxidizing agent, the reaction was more exothermic … It is assumed that the lower yield … is due to the difficulty of reaction control. In the case of 1,2‑dichloropropane (DCP), >80 % yield was obtained with a mild exothermic reaction… DCP was chosen as a suitable oxidizing agent … based on industrial operation and safety.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: Nitration in concentrated H₂SO₄ required temperatures >100 °C, generated large amounts of NOx gas, and gave low selectivity (87 % selectivity, 66 % isolated yield).
Solution_Description: The nitration was performed in halogenated solvents (CH₂Cl₂ or DCP) at 20–30 °C, which suppressed NOx formation, improved selectivity to ≥92 % and increased isolated yields to 77–82 %. DCP was finally selected because it is already used in the previous step.
Supporting_Evidence: “In H₂SO₄, the nitration proceeded at ≥100 °C … the selectivity … was insufficient. However, in the halogen solvents CH₂Cl₂ and DCP, nitration proceeded under mild conditions with less NOx generation and high selectivity … Table 3 shows selectivity 92–93 % and yields 77–82 %.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the dinitro‑biphenyl in methanol required a relatively low boiling solvent, raising safety concerns for large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: 2‑Propanol replaced methanol as the hydrogenation solvent; its higher boiling point improves safety while maintaining comparable activity (88–91 % yield).
Supporting_Evidence: “2‑Propanol was found to be a good solvent in the place of methanol … Because of the relatively high boiling point compared with methanol, 2‑propanol was selected for the reaction from the viewpoint of safety.”

Paper Title: Homocoupling of a Grignard Reagent toward the Synthesis of 2,2′-Bis(trifluoromethyl)-4,4′-diaminobiphenyl
Problem_Description: After two cycles the 5 % Pd/C catalyst began to deactivate, lengthening the hydrogenation time and reducing yield to 89 % in the third batch.
Solution_Description: The authors limited catalyst recycling to two batches and refreshed the catalyst thereafter, ensuring consistent activity and yields (≈91 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “In the second batch, the reused catalyst exhibited the same activity as the fresh catalyst … However, in the third batch, catalyst deactivation was observed, resulting in a slightly prolonged reaction time, but the reaction completed with an 89 % yield.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: The conventional batch synthesis of edaravone suffers from low conversion (product content only 82.1 %) and a low isolated yield, while the crude product contains many impurities that require extensive recrystallisation, which further reduces the overall yield.
Solution_Description: A new continuous‑flow process was developed that performs the two‑step synthesis in a single, uninterrupted system, enabling rapid reaction, high conversion and only one recrystallisation step, delivering 88.4 % yield with 99.95 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“Its disadvantages are low yield, complex purification process, and the presence of many impurities.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: In the first flow experiments the target edaravone was not obtained; only the intermediate 7 formed at low temperature, and even at 100 °C the product content was only 76.9 % with a large amount of impurities.
Solution_Description: The reaction was split into two separate steps – an initial rapid formation of intermediate 7 under mild conditions, followed by a second cyclisation step – which avoided the formation of impurity 6 and improved overall conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“The results indicated that the target product edaravone was not obtained, but intermediate 7 was formed… when the temperature was 100 °C, the content of edaravone was only 76.9 %, the content of intermediate 7 was 10.1 %, and many impurities were produced.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: When the concentration of intermediate 7 was increased to 2 mol L⁻¹ at 25 °C, edaravone precipitated inside the micro‑reactor, causing blockage of the flow channel.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The concentration was tuned to 3.84 mol L⁻¹ while raising the temperature to 60 °C and shortening the residence time to 1 min, which kept the product in solution and eliminated reactor fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“when the concentration of intermediate 7 was 2 mol L⁻¹ and the temperature was 25 °C, edaravone solid will precipitate and block the microreactor tube because edaravone reached saturation.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: The choice of base for the cyclisation step affected the solubility of the reaction mixture; K₂CO₃ required excess water, which lowered the solubility of edaravone, while organic bases (CH₃ONa, Et₃N) were difficult to remove and lowered crystallisation yield.
Solution_Description: NaOH was selected as the base because it dissolves in a small amount of water, provides the necessary alkalinity, and is easy to neutralise, allowing the reaction to proceed efficiently at lower temperature with high product solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“K₂CO₃… needs more water to dissolve, which would reduce the solubility of edaravone… Et₃N… not easy to be removed completely compared with other bases.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: After the second step, edaravone did not crystallise readily from the ethanol–water mixture; without pH control the product remained in solution, lowering isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The pH of the reaction mixture was adjusted to 7 with 6 M HCl at 0 °C, and the EtOH/H₂O ratio was optimised to 2.8:1, which induced quantitative precipitation of edaravone (90.2 % yield, 99.0 % purity) before the final recrystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“The last problem was the crystallization of edaravone… eda‑ravone did not precipitate even when the solution cooled.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of a Continuous Manufacturing Process of Edaravone
Problem_Description: Operating the two‑step synthesis as a single‑pot batch required high temperature, which increased impurity formation and caused degradation of phenylhydrazine.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow reactor (microreactor with plunger pumps and back‑pressure regulator) was employed, allowing rapid mixing, precise temperature control and minimal exposure of phenylhydrazine to moisture, oxygen and light, thereby suppressing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】“continuous flow minimizes the decomposition of phenylhydrazine by reducing exposure to moisture, oxygen, and light during the reaction, which is beneficial to improve the purity and yield.”

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: The original route used triphenylmethyl (trityl) chloride as the protecting group, generating large amounts of low‑value by‑product (triphenylmethanol), which reduces atom economy and increases waste‑handling cost.
Solution_Description: Replace the trityl protecting group with formaldehyde (methylene) – a small, inexpensive reagent – giving a much higher atom utilization and avoiding the formation of triphenylmethanol.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The use of trityl protecting group led to low atom economy … large quantities of byproducts such as triphenylmethanol were generated." (intro, lines 70‑73)
- "Formal­dehyde instead of triphenylmethyl chloride was employed in the protection of the secondary amine, resulting in much higher atom economy." (abstract, lines 41‑44)
- "The new method uses methylene as the protecting group … avoided the generation of triphenylmethanol and improved the atom utilization." (conclusion, lines 548‑553)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: During the acylation of 3,5‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride (15) with 2‑aminoethanol (16) in biphasic solvent systems (DCM/water or toluene/water) a significant amount of N,O‑bisacylated by‑product formed, lowering the isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Run the reaction in water alone. The benzamide product precipitates immediately, suppressing the bis‑acylation impurity and giving a higher isolated yield (92.4 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Biphasic solvent systems such as dichloromethane/water and toluene/water were first investigated (entries 1 and 2). Moderate yields were obtained because of the generation of the N,O‑bisacylated by‑product …" (Results, lines 151‑155)
- "Surprisingly, employing water as a single solvent significantly reduced the amount of bisacylation byproduct as a result of precipitation of the generated benzamide 17 from water during the addition of 15." (Results, lines 157‑160)
- Table 1 entry 5 (water, Na₂CO₃, 0–10 °C) gave 92.4 % isolated yield, the highest among the screened conditions. (Table 1, lines 185‑191)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: Direct filtration of the crude benzamide after the acylation at 15–25 °C produced a small spherical solid containing residual impurities.
Solution_Description: Heat the suspension at 75–85 °C for 1 h before filtration; the solid becomes a clean powder with negligible impurity, affording 98.2 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "When the reaction was complete, the direct filtration at this temperature gave a small spherical solid that contained a few amounts of impurities. Fortunately, when the suspension of the reaction mixture was stirred at 75–85 °C for 1 h, a good powder solid was obtained." (Results, lines 168‑172)
- "Under the optimized conditions, benzamide 17 was isolated in 98.2 % yield as a white powder." (Results, line 174)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: Portionwise addition of NaBH₄ during the reduction of benzamide 17 caused violent hydrogen evolution, representing a safety risk on scale‑up. Additionally, dropping acetic acid into the NaBH₄ suspension caused agglomeration.
Solution_Description: Reverse the addition order: add the solution of benzamide 17 + AcOH into the NaBH₄ suspension in THF, keeping the mixture well‑dispersed and avoiding rapid gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The addition of NaBH₄ in portions resulted in a violent reaction, increasing the safety risk for scale‑up production. Additionally, the reaction mixture was agglomerated when dropping acetic acid was attempted." (Results, lines 197‑201)
- "It was found that the reaction proceeded smoothly when the solution of benzamide 17 and AcOH in THF was dropped into the suspension of NaBH₄ in THF." (Results, lines 202‑205)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: In the Friedel‑Crafts cyclization of 18 to 19, the use of KCl as an additive lowered the reactivity, forcing the reaction to 175–185 °C, which caused carbonization and degradation of product; ammonium chloride sublimated, making the process impractical.
Solution_Description: Omit the solid additive and run the cyclization with AlCl₃ alone at 155–165 °C, preventing degradation and giving a 75.6 % yield (optimized work‑up later raised overall yield to 83 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The use of potassium chloride … resulted in some degradation … when the temperature was enhanced to around 180 °C, which led to some degradation (Table 3, entry 1)." (Results, lines 226‑231)
- "The use of ammonium chloride as the additive was also unfeasible because severe sublimation of ammonium chloride was observed (entry 2)." (Results, lines 233‑236)
- "Finally, we decided to attempt aluminum trichloride individually … at 155–165 °C … the product was isolated in 75.6 % yield … The cyclization temperature was restricted to the range of 155–165 °C. A temperature higher than 170 °C caused more carbonization and degradation impurities (entry 4)." (Results, lines 239‑246)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: During the organolithium‑mediated carboxylation of acetal amine 20, bubbling CO₂ caused the reaction mixture to become highly viscous, hampering stirring and mass transfer; the lithium carboxylate (21) showed poor solubility in the reaction medium.
Solution_Description: Add lithium chloride (LiCl) to the reaction; LiCl dramatically increases the solubility of the lithium carboxylate, maintaining a fluid mixture and enabling efficient CO₂ incorporation.
Supporting_Evidence: - "During the bubbling of carbon dioxide proceeded, the reaction mixture gradually became viscous, causing difficulty in stirring. It was found that charging lithium chloride dramatically enhanced the solubility of the formed lithium carboxylate 21." (Results, lines 277‑283)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: Carboxylation temperature and equivalents of n‑BuLi strongly affected conversion: too low temperature (‑70 °C) left unreacted material; too high temperature (‑50 °C) gave more by‑products; reducing n‑BuLi from 2.5 eq to 2.0 eq dropped yield from 88.5 % to 67.5 %.
Solution_Description: Select the optimal temperature window (‑60 ° to ‑70 °C) and use 2.5 equiv of n‑BuLi to achieve the highest isolated yield (88.5 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "More byproducts were produced at −50 to −60 °C, while a lot of raw material remained unchanged at a lower temperature of −70 to −80 °C, resulting in a decrease in the isolated yield … therefore, the suitable reaction temperature range was −60 to −70 °C." (Results, lines 262‑267)
- "When the amount of n‑butyllithium was reduced from 2.5 to 2.0 equiv, the yield dramatically decreased from 88.5 % to 67.5 % …" (Results, lines 269‑271)
- Table 4 entries 7, 8, 9 show 2.5 eq n‑BuLi at −60 ° to −70 °C giving 88.5 % (entry 7) and the effect of time/temperature variations. (Table 4, lines 290‑306)

Paper Title: Scalable Process for Making 5,7-Dichlorotetrahydroisoquinoline-6-carboxylic Acid Using Methylene as the Protecting Group
Problem_Description: The multistep synthesis required prolonged heating periods (e.g., 15 h Friedel‑Crafts cyclization, 5 h organolithium carboxylation, 2 h work‑up), limiting throughput for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Increase reaction concentration and adjust temperature ramps (e.g., higher temperature for cyclization 155‑165 °C, optimized heating time for precipitation of benzamide) to shorten residence times while maintaining yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "AlCl₃ … added in 50 portions … then the mixture was stirred at this temperature for 15 h." (Friedel‑Crafts, lines 242‑244)
- "The carboxylation reaction … was then stirred for 4 h at this temperature. Then excess CO₂ … stirred for an additional 4 h …" (Carboxylation, lines 285‑288)
- The authors report “optimizing temperature” and “concentration tuning” to obtain solid product after brief heating (75‑85 °C for 1 h) rather than long filtration steps (acylation, lines 168‑172).

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: The previously reported syntheses of cGMPS analogues produce diastereomeric mixtures that require chromatographic separations, leading to low overall yields and poor reproducibility on scale.
Solution_Description: A chromatography‑free route was implemented by isolating all intermediates and the final product through crystallization, which enabled a scalable, robust process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In all the abovementioned cases, cNMPSs … were obtained as diastereomer mixtures and later separated by chromatography.”
• “Finally, the chromatography‑free process allowed for a scale‑up, as intermediates and the final product were isolated by crystallization … (13.8 % total yield) with over 99.9 % HPLC purity.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: The phenylethenylation step suffered from poor solubility of the commercial 8‑bromoguanosine (≈8 % water) which required large volumes of DMSO and caused sticky precipitates when water was added too quickly.
Solution_Description: The starting material was vacuum‑dried to <0.5 % water, allowing dissolution in only 5 vol DMSO; water addition was performed slowly (4 vol) and the crude was washed with MeCN to give the product in 71 % isolated yield and >99 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The commercial 8‑bromoguanosine was found to contain ~8 % water … required at least 8 volumes of DMSO for dissolution.”
• “The water content could be reduced to <0.5 % by vacuum drying … the dried material gave clear solutions in 5 volumes of DMSO within 15 min.”
• “Rapid water addition should be avoided, as it caused formation of sticky lumps … performing the reaction in 5 volumes of DMSO and precipitating the product using 4 volumes of water … yielded intermediate 2 as a white solid in 71 % yield.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: Initial silylation with TBDMS‑Cl gave a high amount of trisilylated side‑product (44 %) and no selectivity, while TIPS‑Cl showed slow second‑hydroxyl protection and 2′→3′ silyl migration, resulting in isomer ratios that drifted from 85:15 to ~60:40 over time.
Solution_Description: TIPS‑Cl was employed with 5 equiv imidazole (as a promoter) and 5 equiv TIPS‑Cl, increasing the equivalents and optimizing reaction time (overnight) to obtain a 2′,5′‑disilylated product with an 86:14 ratio, minimizing silyl migration and improving isolated yield (58 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When using 2.5 equiv of TBDMS‑Cl … no selectivity … 44 % of the product composition.”
• “When TBDMS‑Cl was replaced with TIPS‑Cl, less than 1 % trisubstitution … 85:15 ratio … however, a 2′→3′ silyl migration does occur over time, and the isomers generally approached 60:40 ratio over several days.”
• “The most notable result came from using 5 equiv of both imidazole and TIPS‑Cl … the isomer remained at 86:14 … crystallization gave 3 in 58 % yield and >98 % purity.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the disilylated nucleoside gave low isolated yields (33 % with isopropyl acetate) and required multi‑day operations, making the step time‑consuming and inefficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A two‑step crystallization was introduced: first removal of the undesired 3′,5′‑isomer with MeOH, followed by recrystallization of the mother liquor from isopropyl acetate, improving overall yield to ~40 % (though still deemed too time‑consuming for large scale).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Isopropyl acetate gave >98 % pure crystalline material in 33 % isolated yield.”
• “A two‑step crystallization … first removing some of the undesired isomer with a crystallization from MeOH … after evaporation, recrystallizing the mother liquor residue from isopropyl acetate. This gave the product in a somewhat improved yield of 40 %.”
• “Still, this two‑step operation was time‑consuming and therefore not adopted on scale.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: During the cyclization of the H‑phosphonate monoester, the kinetic S_P‑H‑phosphonate diastereomer rapidly epimerizes to the undesired R_P isomer, especially when the reaction is left overnight in pyridine, leading to poor diastereoselectivity (1:9 S_P/R_P).
Solution_Description: 2,6‑Lutidine was used as the base (5 equiv) to suppress epimerization, and 1.5 equiv of pivaloyl chloride was employed to ensure full conversion while avoiding excess that generates side‑products; the coupling step was kept short (45–60 min) before sulfurization.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The initially formed cyclic H‑phosphonate diastereomers … 1:9 S_P/R_P ratio … showing that the kinetic product is the undesired diastereomer.”
• “To preserve the desired kinetic product, 2,6‑lutidine was explored … performed the reaction in DCM with 5 equiv of 2,6‑lutidine … initial 19:1 S_P/R_P ratio.”
• “1.5 equiv of the coupling agent … ensured full conversion and tolerance to adventitious water. A larger excess … side products became more pronounced.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: Sulfurization timing was critical; adding sulfur before the cyclic H‑phosphonate had fully formed left unreacted material, while adding it too late degraded the diastereomeric ratio, reducing the proportion of the desired R_P product.
Solution_Description: Sulfur (1.5 equiv) and Et₃N were added 45–60 min after the coupling reagent, a timing that gave consistent diastereoselectivity and prevented further epimerization.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Charging of sulfur before 45 min left unreacted intermediates, and longer times were associated with degrading diastereomeric ratios.”
• “A 50 % excess of sulfur and Et₃N was found sufficient.”
• “Suitable sulfurization timings were determined by adding reaction aliquots to vials containing sulfur and Et₃N at different times … after addition of sulfur/Et₃N, the reaction mixtures were stable over several nights.”

Paper Title: Preparative Synthesis of an
Problem_Description: The final deprotection with Et₃N·3HF generated a fluoride complex (triethylammonium fluoride) that contaminated the product and required additional washing steps.
Solution_Description: A reslurry in MeCN removed the fluoride and excess Et₃N; the product was then recrystallized from ethanol to give a high‑purity, fluoride‑free material.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The crude product … contained two equivalents of triethylammonium cation … ^19F NMR showed a broad peak … presumably triethylammonium fluoride.”
• “A reslurry in MeCN removed the fluoride, excess Et₃N, and all color, yielding the product in a crude form containing ~1 % of the undesired diastereomer.”
• “After a small solvent screen, ethanol was found to be a suitable recrystallization solvent, from which the product was recovered as a crystalline hemi‑ethanol solvate … >99.9 % LC purity.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: The starting material showed very low solubility in many common organic solvents (IPA, 2‑MeTHF, CPME, MeOH, IPAc, acetone), which led to poor conversion and low product yield (entries 1‑6).
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified MeCN (and other high‑performing solvents) that gave excellent solubility, high conversion and >99 % LCAP for the keto‑alcohol intermediate; MeCN was then selected for the one‑pot through‑process.
Supporting_Evidence: “A key challenge encountered was the low solubility of the starting material in many organic solvents… Use of a number of solvents gave the product in poor yield, due to either low conversion or the formation of impurities (entries 1–6).”; “The low solubility of the starting material was a big driver of the low conversions observed in 2‑MeTHF, IPA, IPAc, and MeOH… (see Table S13 for solubility data).”; “Fortunately, employment of a range of solvents, including … MeCN showed high reaction purity for the formation of keto alcohol intermediate 2….”; “MeCN was chosen as the solvent for the one‑pot through‑process development.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: The original clinical‑supply route required distinct solvents for each transformation, leading to inefficient aqueous work‑ups, multiple solvent switches and a high step PMI (63).
Solution_Description: A single‑solvent, one‑pot through‑process was developed using MeCN, eliminating the need for intermediate work‑ups and solvent swaps, thereby cutting the step PMI to 29 and reducing cycle time by ~30 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Multiple parameters were optimized to reduce the complexity of the original operation, with a particular priority on removing aqueous workups and wasteful solvent switches… criteria… high yield, short reaction times and high EOR stability.”; “The one‑pot, aspirational … was achieved with MeCN as the sole solvent.”; “The newly developed process … improves cycle times and process mass intensity (PMI reduced from 63 to 29).”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: CO₂ generated as a by‑product of the Ru‑DPEN–catalyzed transfer‑hydrogenation reversibly inhibited catalyst turnover, causing slow kinetics, reaction stalling and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Active nitrogen sweeping of the reactor headspace was introduced to continuously strip CO₂, stabilising reaction kinetics and providing scale‑insensitive conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “A plausible mechanism… CO₂ is formed… the equilibrium may be shifted away from the productive Ru‑hydride in the presence of dissolved CO₂… could lead to slower reaction kinetics or even stalled reactions.”; “A strategy relying on active sweeping of nitrogen through the reactor headspace was developed to reliably control the level of CO₂ affecting the kinetics.”; “Across this range of interest, we confirmed the critical importance of nitrogen sweeping to temper the catalyst reactivity by controlling the level of dissolved CO₂.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: Extended aging of the reduction end‑of‑reaction (EOR) stream generated the hydroxy‑ketal amine dimer impurity 4′; higher nitrogen flow rates exacerbated its formation, jeopardising product purity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The nitrogen sweep rate was tuned to a moderate 0.0175 Nm³ h⁻¹ kg⁻¹, providing a wide EOR stability window, and stoichiometric water (1.0–3.33 eq) was added to suppress dimer formation without introducing new species.
Supporting_Evidence: “The data show that this impurity is primarily generated through extended aging of the reduction EOR stream, and its rate of formation is strongly correlated with nitrogen sweep rate.”; “If the CO₂ is removed too aggressively with high N₂ sweeping, there is a risk of generating elevated levels of impurity 4′….”; “A moderate N₂ sweep of 0.0175 Nm³ h⁻¹ kg⁻¹ ensures controlled and fast reaction kinetics (5–7 h) with a wide window of EOR stability (<1 LCAP 4′ after 24 h).”; “Water could suppress the formation of impurity 4′… 1.0 eq of water (<0.1 LCAP after 24 h) and 3.33 eq eliminated it completely.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: Hydrogen generated in the reduction step accumulated to 12 % v after 3 h and 22 % v at EOR, presenting a significant flammability risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The same nitrogen sweep that removed CO₂ also swept away hydrogen, maintaining its concentration below dangerous levels and enabling safe operation at lab, pilot and commercial scales.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrogen is flammable, with a wide flammability range (4–77 % v) … after 3 h, 12 % hydrogen by volume was observed … by EOR the hydrogen concentration had increased to 22 %.”; “Active sweeping of nitrogen through the reactor not only controlled the amount of CO₂ … also removed hydrogen as it was generated, helping mitigate the accumulation of this flammable gas.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: The Ru‑DPEN catalyst is expensive; using the literature 1 mol % loading increased material cost without clear benefit.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was lowered to 0.3 mol % without loss of enantioselectivity or reaction rate, reducing reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “After initial screening, we were able to reduce the catalyst loading from 1.0 to 0.3 mol % with no erosion in enantioselectivity or quality of the isolated intermediate 3 and no significant rate loss.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: Incorrect HCl concentration caused either formation of indenone impurity (>5 M HCl) or precipitation of intermediate 2 (<3 M HCl), leading to inconsistent conversion and impurity profiles.
Solution_Description: The HCl amount was fine‑tuned to a catalytic level (10–20 mol % relative to Et₃N), eliminating both the indenone impurity and the precipitation issue.
Supporting_Evidence: “The HCl concentration was found to be critical; higher concentrations (>5 M) led to higher levels of indenone impurity… Lower concentrations (<3 M) resulted in crystallization of intermediate 2, limiting the solution availability… Only a catalytic amount of HCl was found to be required for conversion… 10–20 mol % excess relative to the triethylamine loading … was selected as the final optimized condition.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: The original reactive crystallization caused solid occlusion of intermediate 2 in the product, giving up to 0.17 LCAP of impurity 2 in isolated 3.
Solution_Description: A seeded antisolvent crystallization (using water as antisolvent) was adopted, providing reproducible crystal form, eliminating solid occlusion and delivering >99.8 % LCAP purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Experiments showed that up to 0.17 LCAP of 2 could be detected in isolated solid 3 … likely as a result of solid occlusion.”; “Instead of a reactive crystallization, the standard procedure was used to induce supersaturation via antisolvent addition. … seeded and self‑seeded crystallizations afforded similar quality, but a seeded process was selected for long‑term manufacturing to ensure a crystallization with predictable kinetics while providing consistent form and purity control.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 4: Nitrogen Flow Criticality for Transfer Hydrogenation Control
Problem_Description: Scale‑up to kilogram and pilot scale showed batch‑to‑batch inconsistency in the amine‑dimer impurity 4 (0.05 → 0.83 LCAP), indicating a lack of robustness in the reduction step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Process modeling (DynoChem) and extensive PAT (FT‑IR, Raman) were employed to understand the impact of nitrogen flow, liquid fill and mass‑transfer coefficients, confirming that normalising nitrogen flow to substrate mass gave consistent kinetics across scales; the optimized flow and water additive eliminated the impurity variability.
Supporting_Evidence: “Batch‑to‑batch inconsistency with respect to amine dimer impurity 4 … led us to focus considerable attention on understanding the scale‑sensitive nature of this impurity … leveraging process modeling, data‑rich experimentation, and PAT.”; “The kinetic profiles over a range of nitrogen flow rates … confirmed the critical importance of nitrogen sweeping.”; “The clean overlay of the kinetic profiles … supports the conclusion that the rate of the reaction is solely dependent on the nitrogen flow rate normalized to the mass of starting material.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 3: Completing a Streamlined Through-Process with a Safe and Scalable Oxidation
Problem_Description: The original clinical‑supply oxidation used DMSO as both solvent and oxidant.  Basic DMSO mixtures at elevated temperature present a thermal‑runaway hazard that could cause vessel failure, and oxidation of the bromide generated dimethyl‑sulfide, a noxious, stench‑producing by‑product.  In addition, the bromide intermediate (compound 2) is mutagenic, imposing extra handling restrictions.
Solution_Description: A modified Kornblum oxidation was developed that replaces DMSO with 2‑picoline N‑oxide in MeCN, eliminating the DMSO‑related exotherm and dimethyl‑sulfide odor while also providing a safer, non‑mutagenic reaction environment.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The oxidation process used in the clinical supply route employed DMSO as the oxidant and solvent … which identified a potential thermal runaway that could lead to vessel failure.”
• “Furthermore, the dimethyl sulfide byproduct posed a stench hazard …”
• “Compounding these issues was the identification of mutagenic activity in bromide 2 …”
• “We report the development of a modified Kornblum oxidation mediated by 2‑picoline N‑oxide … that circumvented safety and stench problems associated with the original clinical supply route conditions.”
• “A robust quench for the crude bromination stream … enabled a single‑solvent through‑process …”
