Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: The original thermal benzylic bromination required heating to 40 °C to decompose AIBN.  This temperature sensitively affected product stability, caused uncontrolled over‑bromination (impurities 3 & 4) and de‑ketalisation (impurity 5), and the reaction could not be rapidly quenched on large scale, leading to batch‑failure risk.
Solution_Description: A visible‑light‑induced benzylic bromination was developed that proceeds at ambient temperature, eliminating the need for a radical initiator and the associated temperature‑control hazards.  The photochemical pathway uses DBDMH as a bromine reservoir and blue‑light activation, providing a safer, more robust process.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The primary drawback of this thermal approach resided in its sensitivity to temperature. A temperature of 40 °C was necessary to initiate the radical mechanism via AIBN decomposition but also impacted the stability of the product...the inability to rapidly and consistently stop the radical reaction via cooling on a large scale triggered uncontrolled overbromination...and deketalization...These safety, environmental, and quality concerns rendered this route unsuitable for long‑term manufacturing."
"This photochemical benzylic bromination en route to belzutifan...circumvents the need for azo radical initiators and proceeds at room temperature."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Ketal‑protected indane 1 exhibited poor solubility in acetonitrile, forcing the use of very dilute conditions for the photobromination.
Solution_Description: Initial trials were performed in 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE).  Subsequent optimisation employed MeCN with a higher concentration (4 mL MeCN per 200 mg 1) once the solubility issue was addressed, allowing the bromination and downstream oxidation to be conducted in the same solvent.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Room‑temperature irradiation of a mixture of starting material 1 and DBDMH in 1,2‑dichloroethane afforded full conversion...The reaction performed similarly in acetonitrile, albeit under more dilute conditions because of the poor solubility of ketal 1."
"The optimized conditions are as follows: 200 mg of 1, 1.05 equiv of DBDMH, in 4 mL MeCN."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Trace copper (≤ 22 ppm) carried over from upstream steps dramatically slowed the photobromination rate (20 min vs 3 min for Cu‑free material), creating lot‑to‑lot variability and potential safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A screening of metal‑chelating additives identified ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) and nitrilotriacetic acid (NTA) as effective scavengers.  Low‑cost carboxylic acids (citric acid, L‑tartaric acid) were later chosen because they also promoted Br₂ generation, restoring the fast reaction rate and eliminating the Cu effect.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Cu has a significant impact on the reaction rate...required a reaction time of 20 min to reach full conversion, as opposed to 3 min in the absence of Cu."
"Both EDTA and NTA emerged as feasible additives to restore an initial reaction rate comparable to what was observed in the absence of Cu."
"Citric acid and L‑tartaric acid as inexpensive and readily available additives...the positive effect on the reaction rate observed in the presence of citric acid surpassed what we had observed with NTA."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Certain batches of starting material contained unknown UV‑absorbing impurities that competed for photons, extending the required irradiation time and leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The material was passed through activated carbon (5–10 wt % relative to 1) to remove the light‑absorbing contaminants, and an acceptable absorbance window was defined for the treated solution.
Supporting_Evidence:
"We thus implemented a carbon treatment of this substrate (activated carbon, 5–10 wt % loading...and set acceptable absorption values for the carbon‑treated solution of compound 1."
"The control strategy proved to be effective in standardizing the reaction performance against lot‑to‑lot variability."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Over‑bromination to the gem‑dibromo by‑product 3 occurs under prolonged irradiation, reducing the isolated yield of the desired bromide 2 and compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: Reaction time was tightly controlled (3 min at 450 nm blue light) to stop the reaction before significant formation of 3.  In flow, precise residence‑time distribution and rapid cooling further limited over‑bromination.
Supporting_Evidence:
"When blue (i.e., 450 nm) light was employed to initiate the reaction, the desired product was obtained in excellent yield within 3 min of irradiation."
"Overbromination to yield byproduct 3 is also a light‑catalyzed process, the impact of which can be minimized by appropriate control of the irradiation time."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Scaling the photochemical step in larger batch reactors is hampered by light attenuation (Lambert–Beer law) and the presence of flammable organic vapours, making uniform irradiation and safe operation difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A tubular plug‑flow photoreactor (8 mm i.d., 890 mL volume) was built with high‑intensity blue LED panels and housed in a glass aquarium for safe cooling.  The design provides short optical path lengths, efficient photon capture, and controlled gas‑liquid environment, enabling safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The tubular reactor (8 mm i.d., 890 mL volume) is housed in a 20.8 L glass aquarium tank and is irradiated with two panels of LEDs...The tight control of the irradiation time and the narrow residence time distribution typical of a PFR are instrumental in ensuring the high conversion and minimal formation of gem‑dibromo impurity 3."
"Implementation of continuous flow technology allowed tight control of irradiation and residence time, resulting in a robust process with minimized byproduct formation."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Different light intensities in batch scale‑up led to disparate reaction times (7 min at 64 W vs 3.5 min at 120 W) for the same conversion, complicating process scheduling.
Solution_Description: The concept of photon equivalents was introduced as a scale‑independent metric; reactions were run to a fixed photon‑equivalent target (0.8 eq), allowing identical conversion regardless of light power or reactor size.
Supporting_Evidence:
"When the product LCAPs from different experiments were plotted as functions of time, poor profile overlap due to the difference in photon fluxes was observed. Conversely, plotting the product LCAP as a function of photon equivalents emitted by the light source results in good profile overlap."
"Delivering 0.8 equiv of photons to this reactor resulted in the same product yield (90 LCAP), although the times necessary for those photons to be emitted are different (7 min at 64 W output vs 3.5 min at 120 W output)."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: Intermediate bromide 2 is unstable on storage, making isolation and handling problematic for downstream steps.
Solution_Description: A quenching protocol using neat 2,6‑lutidine (to neutralise HBr) and 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene (to trap residual electrophilic bromine) was developed, allowing the reaction stream to be fed directly into the subsequent oxidation without isolating 2.
Supporting_Evidence: "The key goal was to ensure that the quenched reaction stream could be used directly in the subsequent synthetic step. This investigation led to the identification of quenching conditions involving the use of neat 2,6‑lutidine and 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene...This approach proved to be useful in improving the long‑term stability of the product in the reaction stream, which could then be carried into the following oxidation step without the need for product isolation."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 2: A Continuous Flow Visible-Light-Induced Benzylic Bromination
Problem_Description: High‑power LEDs and custom‑built flow reactors represent a significant capital investment for large‑scale photochemistry, and suitable light sources must be qualified for GMP use.
Solution_Description: A modular, GMP‑qualified tubular photoreactor train was designed, allowing multiple identical units to be numbered‑up to achieve > 100 kg day⁻¹ productivity while using standardized LED panels and cooling systems, spreading cost and ensuring component availability.
Supporting_Evidence: "We thus built a Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP)‑qualified reactor train meeting all of the safety requirements for operation in a plant setting. The same reactor units were employed, and each reactor was irradiated with two LED panels...With this optimized setup, a productivity of > 100 kg day⁻¹ was achieved."

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: The α‑fluorination reaction released a significant exotherm when heated to the target temperature, creating a safety hazard and threatening stable plant operation.
Solution_Description: Temperature was carefully ramped and the addition sequence was re‑designed (pre‑mixing acid, controlled heating) while switching to methanesulfonic acid in a MeCN/MeOH co‑solvent system, which suppressed the exotherm as confirmed by DSC.
Supporting_Evidence: The fluorination reaction showed some concerning exothermic activity upon heating to the reaction temperature, posing a threat to plant operation<ref id="ref5"/>; Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) indicated that the exothermicity was now suitably suppressed; The best results were observed when methanesulfonic acid was used as the catalyst in MeCN/MeOH.

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: Fluorination often failed to reach its endpoint, requiring additional charges of Selectfluor and producing variable over‑fluorination impurities.
Solution_Description: The amount of Selectfluor was reduced to 1.1 equiv and water content was tightly controlled (< 1500 ppm) to give consistent > 99 % conversion and limit over‑fluorination.
Supporting_Evidence: Fluorination routinely failed to meet its end point and required additional charges of Selectfluor, leading to variability in over‑fluorination impurities; Consistent reaction conversion could now be achieved with a reduced Selectfluor loading (1.1 equiv), which led to much tighter control of over‑fluorination impurities.; The reaction mixture was controlled to a total of <1500 ppm water, which resulted in significantly improved process robustness.

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: Severe glass corrosion (≈ 0.94 mm yr⁻¹) was observed, likely from HF generated under acidic fluorination conditions, limiting reactor material choices.
Solution_Description: Corrosion‑resistant Hastelloy C‑276 reactors were employed for all large‑scale runs, and the chloride content of Selectfluor was controlled to mitigate HF formation.
Supporting_Evidence: Severe glass corrosion was found (0.94 mm year⁻¹), likely as a result of HF formation under acidic reaction conditions; The process was carried out in corrosion‑resistant C‑276 reactors for all large‑scale reactions.; Control of the chloride content in the Selectfluor proved to be critical in order to avoid corrosion of C‑276.

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: In the DKR step, insufficient triethylamine resulted in slow reaction rates, while excess base generated impurity profiles, causing inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The base was optimized to exactly 2 equiv Et₃N (with 2 equiv formic acid) to ensure rapid, clean reduction without impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: Slow reaction kinetics was observed when <2 equiv of Et₃N was used (entry 2), likely because base is required to generate the active Ru species; Excess Et₃N was also deleterious to the reaction purity profile (entry 3).

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: Reducing the Ru‑TsDpen catalyst loading below 0.5 mol % drastically slowed the DKR, leading to incomplete conversion even after 72 h.
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading was fixed at 0.5 mol % (the lowest loading that maintained > 99 % conversion within a practical time frame).
Supporting_Evidence: When the loading was further decreased to 0.25 mol %, the reaction rate decreased significantly, and the reaction failed to reach satisfactory conversion even after 72 h of aging (entry 6).

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: The DKR at 30 °C required a longer aging period to reach full conversion, extending batch time.
Solution_Description: Increasing the DKR temperature to 40 °C reduced the cycle time while preserving > 99 % conversion and 99:1 dr.
Supporting_Evidence: The optimal reaction temperature was set to 40 °C to reduce the process cycle time without impacting the reaction performance (entry 7).

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: The crude EOR stream contained color impurities that would carry over into the final product.
Solution_Description: An activated carbon treatment was introduced to decolorize the EOR stream before crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: A carbon treatment was used to remove color from the EOR stream, which otherwise translated to the product solids.

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for Belzutifan, Part 5: A Streamlined Fluorination–Dynamic Kinetic Resolution Process
Problem_Description: Direct isolation of the fluorodiol required careful control of polymorphic form; uncontrolled water addition led to mixed crystal forms.
Solution_Description: A single‑solvent through‑process was developed in which water served as the antisolvent, the hydrate form was seeded, and the water addition profile (2 vol % then 7 vol %) was optimized to give reproducible hydrate crystallization with > 97 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Water was identified as the optimal antisolvent that allows the direct crystallization of the product from the reaction mixture.; The hydrate form was targeted to achieve robust form control through the course of the aqueous crystallization.; The seed point is reached by adding 2 vol % water and then 7 vol % water over 8 h, delivering the hydrate with 89 % recovery and > 97 % purity.

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 5‑(Aminomethyl)-2-methylpyrimidin-4-amine: A Key Intermediate of Vitamin B

Problem_Description: The second S_NAr reaction required a large excess (2.4 equiv) of aminopiperidine 6 and 80 h at 80 °C in DMF to reach completion, leading to high solvent usage and lengthy processing.
Solution_Description: Screening identified DMSO as the optimal solvent, allowing the use of only 1.2 equiv of 6, raising the temperature to 100 °C, reducing reaction time to 24 h, and cutting the DMSO volume to 7 vol, thereby streamlining the step.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction required elevated temperature in polar solvents…The initial reaction conditions…used DMF and a large excess of 6…A high‑throughput screening…DMSO stood out as the best option…Based on the modeling data, we elected to run the reaction with only 1.2 equiv of 6 and use higher temperature…The reaction could be run at 100 °C for 24 h…the volume of DMSO was reduced to 7 vol to increase the throughput, reaction rate, and workup efficiency.⟨/p⟩

Paper Title: Safety Assessments Supporting Scale-up of Chemistry Involving Hydrogen
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the end‑of‑reaction (EOR) stream and the post‑distillation concentrate generated a large amount of hydrogen gas.  The gas pressure rose to ~56 psi in a ~1.6 mL head‑space and hydrogen concentrations reached 6.3 % (above the lower‑explosive‑limit, LEL).  The gas evolution was accompanied by strong exotherms (≈107 J g⁻¹ for EOR, 253 J g⁻¹ for concentrate) that began near the operating temperature (≈69 °C) and intensified above 160 °C.
Solution_Description: The EOR stream was quenched with methanesulfonic acid (MSA).  Adding 1.0 mol equiv MSA (relative to substrate) protonates residual formic acid and deactivates the Ru catalyst, suppressing formic‑acid decomposition that produces H₂.  This reduces the exotherm dramatically (to 13 J g⁻¹) and shifts the gas‑onset temperature to 125 °C.  The residual pressure after MMC scanning falls to ~11 psi and H₂ drops to 0.3 % (well below the LEL).
Supporting_Evidence: • "significant gas generation from both the EOR and the concentrate streams during the MMC scanning experiments, where a residual pressure of 56 psig built up…" (Fig 1a)

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Cumulative list of the key difficulties encountered during development of the catalytic static‑mixer (CSM) hydrogenation of nitropyridine 2.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Corresponding strategies that were applied to overcome each problem.
Supporting_Evidence: All excerpts are taken verbatim from the article and are grouped per problem‑solution pair below.

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Electro‑plated Pd‑CSMs gave only ~6 % conversion of nitropyridine 2 under the initial screening conditions.
Solution_Description: Switched to Pd/Al₂O₃ slurry‑coated CSMs, which provided full conversion because of their much higher effective surface area (200 m² g⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: “The Pd‑electroplated CSMs displayed only a minimal extent of reaction (∼6 % conversion …), while Pd/Al₂O₃ slurry coated CSMs were substantially more effective under the same conditions (full conversion).”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Catalyst activity decreased over time, especially at higher flow rates, leading to a drop in conversion (e.g., 78 % → 56 % at 80 °C). This was attributed to catalyst inhibition by reaction intermediates.
Solution_Description: Increasing the jacket temperature to 120 °C eliminated the loss of conversion, and adding 1–4 equiv of water to the feed doubled the conversion and prevented deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Temperature appeared to have a significant positive influence on the reaction… the gradient of conversion loss was substantially shallower at 80 °C compared to 60 °C and was not observed at all at 120 °C.”

“The presence of water appeared to significantly improve the rate of reaction, while preventing catalyst deactivation over time. The maximum examined value, 4 equiv, provided almost double the level of conversion versus conditions in the absence of water (38 % vs 73 %).”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Adding methanol as a protic co‑solvent drastically altered the impurity profile, making it unsuitable for the process.
Solution_Description: Instead of methanol, a controlled amount of water was added as a promoter, which improved conversion and maintained a clean impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The approach of adding a protic solvent was also examined, by first adding methanol as a cosolvent. Unfortunately, the reactivity and impurity profile were drastically affected… suggesting that it would not be a viable solution.”

“Using water… the presence of water appeared to significantly improve the rate of reaction, while preventing catalyst deactivation over time.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: There were concerns that the high water content required for catalyst stability could degrade the Al₂O₃ support of the CSMs.
Solution_Description: A control experiment exposing a single CSM to up to 512 equiv of water showed no loss of activity or visible degradation, and ICP‑MS confirmed no Al leaching.
Supporting_Evidence:
“To ensure that this would not cause catalyst degradation, one single CSM was exposed to an increasing quantity of water from 4 to 512 equiv… no loss of activity or visible degradation was observed.”

“ICP‑MS analysis of the reactor effluent showed no elevated levels of palladium, indicating that the CSMs were stable, even in the presence of such high levels of water.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: At the highest throughput (16 CSMs, 30 mL min⁻¹) an internal temperature rise of ~12 °C was observed due to the reaction exotherm.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A heat exchanger was added before the reactor and additional temperature sensors were installed to monitor the exotherm; future scale‑up could also use inactive static mixers or staged H₂ addition to manage heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
“When operating at high throughput, a notable internal temperature rise was observed (∼12 °C)… This study benefited greatly from the additional temperature sensors in the reaction channel, which allowed the behavior over the progress of the reaction to be monitored.”

“For larger scale operation, this exotherm could be managed by a variety of approaches, such as alternating CSMs with inactive static mixers or introducing sub‑stoichiometric quantities of H₂ at multiple positions along the reactor.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Small amounts of precipitation were noted toward the end of a 16 h run, causing minor issues with the real‑time FT‑IR analysis.
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration was limited to 0.4 M to avoid precipitation, and the process continued without impact on conversion or pressure.
Supporting_Evidence: “Some issues in real‑time analysis were observed toward the end of the first day of processing, due to small amounts of precipitation. However, this had no effect on the performance of the reaction itself and no increase in pressure was observed.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Static Mixer-Enabled Hydrogenation of a Key Fenebrutinib Intermediate: Real-Time Analysis for a Stable and Scalable Process
Problem_Description: Pumping issues occurred at the end of the second day of the long‑duration experiment.
Solution_Description: The problematic pump was replaced with an alternative pump, resulting in less than 5 min of downtime.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pumping issues were observed toward the end of the second day of processing, but this was remedied by switching to an alternative pump, resulting in <5 min downtime.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intrinsically Safer Methanolysis/Aromatic Nitro Group Reduction for Step 1 and 2 of Talazoparib Tosylate
Problem_Description: The original methanolysis step used 30 wt % HCl in MeOH – a concentration far above commercially available solutions, which is unstable and decomposes to flammable MeCl and DME, creating off‑gassing and a serious handling risk. Fresh preparation required bubbling anhydrous HCl gas through methanol, posing additional engineering and safety challenges.
Solution_Description: Replaced the 30 % HCl methanolysis with a catalytic acetic‑acid slurry in MeOH and later discovered that a 1:1 v/v anisole/MeOH system (10 vol) gave full conversion. Addition of 3 equiv MeSO₃H (methanesulfonic acid) acted as a promoter, suppressing side‑product formation and eliminating the need for concentrated HCl.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The methanolysis step called for the use of 30 wt % HCl in MeOH, which is a concentration far beyond that of the commonly commercially available solutions..." (SAFETY/AVAILABILITY)

Paper Title: Development of an Intrinsically Safer Methanolysis/Aromatic Nitro Group Reduction for Step 1 and 2 of Talazoparib Tosylate
Problem_Description: The iron‑mediated nitro reduction was strongly exothermic (adiabatic temperature rise of 142 K) and classified as Stoessel Class 5, with off‑gassing of H₂ and hazardous gases during filtration, raising runaway‑reaction and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Switched to a Pt/C hydrogenation catalyst. The Pt‑catalyzed reduction released less heat (T_ad ≈ 123 K at 10 vol and 48 K at 25 vol) and eliminated off‑gassing of hazardous gases, moving the reaction into Stoessel Class 1‑2.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Following completion of the methanolysis step, the reaction mixture ... was charged ... to a suspension of iron powder... This reaction is strongly exothermic... an adiabatic temperature (T_ad) rise of 142 °C was calculated... Stoessel Class 5" (EXOTHERMIC/SAFETY)

Paper Title: First-Generation Asymmetric Synthesis of the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) Featuring a Highly Efficient Pictet–Spengler Reaction and a C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler reaction gave inconsistent conversions and diastereomeric ratios, making it difficult to achieve high isolated yield and to purify the product without chromatographic steps.
Solution_Description: Acetic acid (and salicylic acid) were identified as optimal catalysts and methanol was selected as the reaction solvent, giving 100 % conversion and 95:5 dr. A simple water‑addition at the end of the reaction caused the product to crystallize directly from the mixture in 98 % isolated yield, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The key challenge for this particular transformation was the selection of a suitable catalyst and solvent to promote high conversion and diastereomeric ratio (dr) while simplifying the overall purification and isolation.”
• “Acetic acid … and salicylic acid … were identified as the optimal catalysts. Both acids gave the desired product in >91 A% with >94:6 dr.”
• “By employing MeOH as the reaction solvent, we were able to achieve 100 % conversion with 95:5 dr.”
• “To our delight, simple addition of water crystallized the desired product 14 in 98 % yield with 95:5 dr directly from the reaction mixture.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Asymmetric Synthesis of the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) Featuring a Highly Efficient Pictet–Spengler Reaction and a C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Initial Buchwald–Hartwig C–N coupling between the tetrahydrocarboline and the amino‑azetidine gave only 45 % assay yield and generated up to 87 % area of intramolecular S_NAr side‑products (impurities 15 and 16).
Solution_Description: Switching to the soluble organic base DBU suppressed the S_NAr impurities (<7 % A). Replacing the third‑generation Buchwald G3 precatalyst with [t‑BuBrettPhos Pd(allyl)]OTf further increased conversion and lowered impurity levels, allowing the catalyst loading to be reduced to 2.5 mol % and delivering a 90 % assay yield of the product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “HTE … afforded complete consumption of the starting material 14 but a modest 45 % assay yield … impurities 15 and 16 were formed in levels of up to 87 A%.”
• “Inorganic bases … were found to be ineffective … the soluble organic base DBU … suppressed the formation of both S_NAr impurities to <7 A%.”
• “Replacing the Buchwald G3 precatalyst with [t‑BuBrettPhos Pd(allyl)]OTf … further increased the conversion, reduced the levels of S_NAr impurities, allowed reduction of the catalyst loading to 2.5 mol %, and further improved the reaction outcome to 90 % assay yield.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Asymmetric Synthesis of the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) Featuring a Highly Efficient Pictet–Spengler Reaction and a C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: After the C–N coupling, residual palladium needed to be removed and the free‑base product had to be isolated as the tartrate salt; conventional chromatography would be labor‑intensive and generate metal‑contamination concerns.
Solution_Description: A solid‑supported thiol resin (SiliaMetS Thiol) was employed to scavenge residual palladium. The reaction mixture was then telescoped directly to tartrate salt formation and crystallized from ethanol, delivering the API in 90 % isolated yield and >99 % HPLC purity without any chromatographic purification.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “After aqueous workup and scavenging treatment to purge residual Pd, the mixture was telescoped to tartrate salt formation and crystallization in EtOH.”
• “SiliaMetS Thiol, a proprietary solid‑supported resin … was used as the scavenging agent.”
• “GDC‑9545·tartrate … was isolated in 90 % yield (from 14) with 99.0 A% HPLC purity … without chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: During the Friedel‑Crafts acylation the acid‑chloride intermediate was not stable and epimerized, and the reaction was cryogenic (‑40 °C) and highly exothermic with CH₄ gas evolution, creating safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the Friedel‑Crafts step and replaced it with a convergent sequence that used a C–N coupling and a crystallization‑driven diastereoselective Pictet‑Spengler reaction, eliminating the need for the unstable acid‑chloride and the exothermic cryogenic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the Friedel‑Crafts acylation, the acid chloride intermediate was not stable and would epimerize during the course of the reaction. In addition, the reaction is cryogenic (‑40 °C) and very exothermic with CH₄ gas evolution during the process.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The reduction of ester 5 required a very large excess (600 mol %) of NaAl(OMe)₂H₂, leading to difficult and material‑intensive work‑up.
Solution_Description: The downstream route was redesigned to use a Wenker aziridine synthesis that required only stoichiometric reagents and gave the key tryptamine 11 in 59 % overall yield, simplifying isolation and reducing reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “Meanwhile, the large excess (600 mol %) of NaAl(OMe)₂H₂ used in the reduction led to significant challenges in the work‑up.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The final C–N coupling required at least 2.5 mol % Pd catalyst, creating a burden for residual Pd control and adding expense.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput experimentation identified BrettPhos Pd G3 (1 mol %) as a highly active precatalyst, and a solid‑supported thiol scavenger (SiliaMetS Thiol, 20 wt %) was used to reduce residual Pd to <20 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “A minimum of 2.5 mol % Pd catalyst was required … This created a significant burden on controlling the residual Pd in the API … The crude reaction mixture was subsequently subjected to aqueous workup and Pd scavenging treatment with SiliaMetS Thiol to reduce the residual Pd to <20 ppm.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The indole alkylation route required stoichiometric copper in CH₂Cl₂ at –20 °C and gave only 70 % yield, making it impractical for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the copper‑mediated alkylation and pursued alternative routes (Wenker aziridine synthesis and Larock indolization) that avoided the low‑temperature copper conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “The key indole alkylation reaction … required … a stoichiometric amount of copper in CH₂Cl₂ at –20 °C, and afforded product 20 in only 70 % yield at best.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The Larock indolization method generated significant tar during work‑up, rendering the process unsuitable for large scale.
Solution_Description: The route was discarded in favor of the Wenker aziridine synthesis, which gave the desired tryptamine 11 with clean isolation and high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, significant tar formation during work‑up was observed, which rendered the route impractical on scale.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The chiral resolution of racemic tryptamine 13 gave only 36 % isolated yield of the resolved salt, overall 29 % yield of tryptamine 11.
Solution_Description: The process was replaced by the Wenker aziridine synthesis, which delivered tryptamine 11 in 59 % overall yield on >100 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Treatment of commercially available racemic tryptamine 13 … provided crude 11·l‑CSA in 36 % yield … overall low yield … was not pursued further.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The continuous synthesis of 4‑bromo‑2,6‑difluorobenzaldehyde 7 required cryogenic conditions (‑78 °C) because the organolithium intermediate was unstable, posing safety and operational challenges.
Solution_Description: A continuous flow process was developed where LDA was generated in situ at 5 °C, followed by lithiation at –35 °C with short residence times, allowing production of >100 kg of aldehyde 7 at 74 % yield without the need for extreme cryogenic temperatures.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, this approach suffered from the use of cryogenic conditions (‑78 °C)… To address this issue, we developed a continuous process for this transformation.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The initial C–N coupling of aldehyde 7 and aminoazetidine 9·2HCl gave only 9 % assay yield despite using high catalyst loadings and excess base, and the reaction mixture was difficult to stir at the required high concentration.
Solution_Description: The authors converted aldehyde 7 to its diethyl acetal 33, which avoided imine formation and allowed coupling with free‑base 9 in PhMe using BrettPhos Pd G3 and NaOtBu, achieving >95 % assay yield after increasing the concentration (8 mL g⁻¹) and temperature (60 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: “We hypothesized that aldehyde 7 and aminoazetidine 9 could readily undergo imine formation… Therefore, we turned our attention to the C–N coupling of diethyl acetal 33 and aminoazetidine 9.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: Even after switching to the acetal route, the C–N coupling required high base excess (350 mol %) and a 5.0 mL g⁻¹ concentration, causing agitation difficulties and long reaction times (18 h).
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration was increased to 8 mL g⁻¹ and the temperature raised from 40 °C to 60 °C, which reduced the reaction time from 18 h to 2 h while maintaining >95 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction temperature was also increased from 40 to 60 °C, which allowed a significant reduction of reaction time from 18 to 2 h while maintaining the same reaction profile.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: Residual palladium from the C–N coupling needed to be reduced to meet API specifications, and palladium is an expensive catalyst.
Solution_Description: SiliaMetS Thiol (20 wt %) was employed as a solid‑supported scavenger to lower residual Pd to below 20 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude reaction mixture was subsequently subjected to aqueous workup and Pd scavenging treatment with SiliaMetS Thiol to reduce the residual Pd to <20 ppm.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: After the acetal deprotection, the crude aldehyde 10 contained catalyst‑related impurities that remained in the PhMe layer, complicating isolation.
Solution_Description: A direct phase‑separation work‑up was implemented: the aqueous layer (containing aldehyde 10) was isolated, then pH was adjusted to 6.6‑6.9 and 1 mol % seeds added to induce controlled crystallization, yielding pure aldehyde 10 in ~80 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Impurities remained in the PhMe layer… Direct phase separation improved the purity of 10 … pH of solution was carefully adjusted to 6.6–6.9… addition of 1 mol % seeds then induced a controlled crystallization.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: The initial Pictet‑Spengler reaction using AcOH produced the azetidine‑ring‑opening side product 37 (20 % A) and gave low overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switching to diphenylphosphoric acid as the catalyst, using i‑PrOH as solvent, and performing continuous azeotropic distillation in 2‑MeTHF gave 97 % conversion and 84 % assay yield with no azetidine‑ring‑opening impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “When diphenylphosphoric acid was employed … the reaction proceeded smoothly without azetidine‑ring‑opening impurity 38 … By continuous azeotropic distillation in 2‑MeTHF, the reaction achieved 97 % conversion and 84 % assay yield without azetidine‑ring‑opening impurity 38.”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the Pictet‑Spengler reaction showed slower conversion, and the API formed oligomeric side‑products (up to 6.4 % by SEC) due to acid‑mediated ring‑opening and polymerization.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in EtOH with 150 mol % l‑tartaric acid at 70 °C for 48 h, allowing in‑situ crystallization of the API and suppressing oligomer formation (<0.3 % SEC). Stoichiometry was optimized (100 mol % each of aldehyde and tryptamine) to improve conversion and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “We envisioned that if the acid were changed … the API would simultaneously crystallize … Using EtOH … and 150 mol % l‑tartaric acid … gave API isolated yields 77–83 % and oligomer contents of 0.1–0.3 % … The reaction plateaued at around 90 % conversion … Longer reaction times … were detrimental …”

Paper Title: Efficient Manufacturing Process for the Selective Estrogen Receptor Degrader GDC-9545 (Giredestrant) via a Crystallization-Driven Diastereoselective Pictet–Spengler Condensation
Problem_Description: Increasing the amount of tryptamine 6 beyond 100 mol % improved conversion but raised raw material cost, and excess aldehyde 10 caused gelling and higher oligomer content.
Solution_Description: Optimization identified 125 mol % tryptamine 6 (entry 3, Table 5) as the best compromise, giving 97.6 % conversion, 89 % isolated yield, and 0.28 % oligomer content without excessive cost.

Problem_Description: Quenching the iodination step with sodium thiosulfate generated elemental sulfur, which contaminated the product mixture.
Solution_Description: The quench was switched from sodium thiosulfate to sodium sulfite, eliminating sulfur formation and improving product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Avoiding contaminating 5‑iodo compound 16 with elemental sulfur was important … This was achieved by changing the quench of the reaction from a solution of sodium thiosulfate to that of sodium sulfite.”

Paper Title: Expedited Kilolab Development of AZD7624 Using Kulinkovich-de Meijere Cyclopropanation
Problem_Description: Direct palladium‑catalysed amination of the iodo‑aryl substrate failed because of poor solubility under basic conditions.
Solution_Description: The iodo‑aryl acid was first converted to the methyl ester, after which the amination was performed with benzophenone imine under conditions that gave a homogeneous slurry; the crude ester was slurried in DCM to remove residual acid, improving solubility and reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Limited attempts to aminate iodoarene 16 directly failed … due to the poor solubility of the substrate under basic conditions. After conversion to methyl ester 13, the amino group was instead introduced via a two‑step sequence that started with the palladium‑catalyzed reaction with benzophenone imine.”; “Slurrying the crude iodo acid 16 in dichloromethane conveniently removed the residual 3‑fluoro‑4‑toluic acid 14 and lowered the levels of the regioisomeric 6‑iodo compound.”

Paper Title: Expedited Kilolab Development of AZD7624 Using Kulinkovich-de Meijere Cyclopropanation
Problem_Description: Chlorotitanium triisopropoxide is expensive and its commercial quality was uncertain for large‑scale use.

Supporting_Evidence: “Purchasing the methyltitanium triisopropoxide reagent … was ruled out … These issues could be addressed by freshly preparing the reagent through the reaction of methyllithium with chlorotitanium triisopropoxide.”; “the cyclopropanation protocol was extended to use the reagent prepared in situ from the more readily available titanium tetraisopropoxide and titanium tetrachloride… it proved possible to form and use the putative methyltitanium triisopropoxide in a one‑pot procedure…”

Paper Title: Expedited Kilolab Development of AZD7624 Using Kulinkovich-de Meijere Cyclopropanation
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route required alkylation with 1‑bromo‑2‑chloroethane, a known carcinogen that also generates vinyl chloride under basic conditions.

Paper Title: Expedited Kilolab Development of AZD7624 Using Kulinkovich-de Meijere Cyclopropanation

Paper Title: Expedited Kilolab Development of AZD7624 Using Kulinkovich-de Meijere Cyclopropanation

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: The original Route 1 required a lithium‑bromine exchange at –80 °C to form boronic acid 2. Solution_Description: The process was abandoned in favor of a new convergent sequence (Route 2) that avoids the cryogenic lithium‑bromine exchange altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: "requires cryogenic conditions (−80 °C) to inhibit uncontrolled nucleophilic attack on the sensitive nitrile group"; "The use of cryogenics in large‑scale manufacturing presents various challenges including high energy usage (environmental and economic)… and the potential for the loss of refrigeration… (safety and control)"; "We previously explored alternative routes … route 2 … identified as a potential means of mitigating the issues associated with route 1"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: Boronic acids tend to dehydrate to oligomeric boroxines. In the case of intermediate 2, the undesired boroxine trimer 12 was isolated unintentionally, leading to inconsistent assay results and difficulty charging the next step, jeopardising quality and yield.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to a Miyaura borylation (Miyaura borylation → trans‑esterification → Suzuki‑Miyaura) that generates a more robust boronate ester (11) instead of the unstable boronic acid, eliminating boroxine formation and improving downstream isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Boronic acids are known to readily form oligomeric boroxines via dehydration… Inconsistent isolation of boroxines can lead to overconfidence in purity assay results…"; "... boroxine trimer 12 … was inadvertently isolated…"; "We previously explored alternative routes … route 2 … identified as a potential means of mitigating the issues associated with route 1"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: Boronic acid 2 crystallized as small needle‑like crystals, causing very slow filtration and formation of additional impurities during work‑up.
Solution_Description: Instead of isolating boronic acid 2, the process was redesigned to convert the pinacol boronate 10 directly into the diethanolamine (DEA) boronate 11 via trans‑esterification, which gives a highly crystalline, easily filterable product.
Supporting_Evidence: "Boronic acid 2 was also found to display physical properties (small needle like crystals) that led to slow filtration upon isolation with concomitant impurity formation"; "The application of such conditions enabled successful transesterification and the isolation of boronate 11 in 60 % yield"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: The Miyaura borylation of aryl bromide 8 proceeded extremely rapidly at 80 °C, giving an onset temperature of ~50 °C and an estimated adiabatic temperature rise of ~40 °C, which would overload condenser capacity on scale and posed a safety risk.
Solution_Description: Scale‑up studies introduced a 40 % solvent dilution (14 L kg⁻¹) to increase the heat‑sink and reduced the palladium loading to ≤0.5 mol %, thereby controlling the exotherm and enabling safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Palladium‑catalyzed transformations are known to exhibit exothermic energetic behaviors…"; "Differential scanning calorimetry experiments found the reaction onset temperature… leading to an adiabatic temperature rise of around 40 °C"; "investigations… suggested that a combination of increasing the energy sink via dilution by at least 40 %… and a reduced catalyst loading to 0.5 mol %… would enable safe operation"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: Pinacol boronate 10 is highly soluble in common organic solvents; attempts to crystallise it required large volumes of antisolvent and resulted in low isolated yields and purity with substantial loss of material to the liquor.
Solution_Description: The pinacol boronate was transformed into the DEA‑boronate 11, which is markedly less soluble and readily crystallises, delivering higher isolated yields (≈84 %) and >99.8 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "The isolation of pinacol boronate esters such as 10 via crystallization can prove problematic on an industrial scale due to their high solubility in organic solvents… required large quantities of antisolvent addition and could only be achieved in low yield and low purity"; "The application of such conditions enabled successful transesterification and the isolation of boronate 11 in 60 % yield…"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: During the DEA trans‑esterification of 10 to 11, the reaction consistently gave oiling, phase separation and uncontrolled precipitation, attributed to poor miscibility of DEA in 2‑MeTHF.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A slow addition (1.5 h) of a 80 % w/w DEA solution in IPA to a 3:7 IPA/2‑MeTHF mixture kept at >50 °C maintained a homogeneous phase, allowing clean conversion and crystalline product isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: "...oil­ing, phase separation, and uncontrolled crystallization of 11… irrespective of DEA addition rate… immiscibility of DEA in 2‑MeTHF"; "Data in the ternary diagrams demonstrated that miscibility would significantly improve through temperature increases (from 20 to 60 °C)… slow addition of a solution of DEA (80 % w/w in IPA) over a period of 1.5 h … maintained above 50 °C would maintain homogeneity"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: During the Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling of aryl bromide 3 with DEA‑boronate 11, an impurity 13 (proto‑debromination product) appeared at ~10 % level, reducing isolated yield by ~20 % compared with the original route.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput screening identified that replacing the dual NaOH/Na₂CO₃ base with a weaker base (Na₂CO₃ alone or DIPEA) lowered impurity 13. Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: The target molecule 1 forms a n‑butanol solvate that requires prolonged drying above 190 °C for complete desolvation, which is impractical and energetically costly on a manufacturing scale.
Solution_Description: A continuous atmospheric distillation of the n‑butanol solvate in a methylethylketone (MEK)/water mixture removed the solvent in‑situ, yielding the MEK solvate (form O). Subsequent vacuum drying at 80 °C for 20 h gave the anhydrous form A in high yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Prolonged drying at temperatures in excess of 190 °C … was considered impractical on the proposed manufacturing scale"; "a distillative process was found to be successful… continuous atmospheric distillation… capable of purging n‑butanol… Desolvation … at 80 °C under vacuum for 20 h enabled the isolation of … anhydrous form A in high yield and in high purity"

Paper Title: Process Development, Manufacture, and Understanding of the Atropisomerism and Polymorphism of Verinurad
Problem_Description: Verinurad is a class II atropisomer; racemisation could occur on a timescale comparable to its in‑vivo clearance, raising safety concerns about chiral purity during storage and dosing.
Solution_Description: Kinetic studies (both in‑silico DFT and experimental HPLC/H‑NMR) demonstrated that racemisation half‑lives in biologically relevant media (pH 2.1‑6.5, 37 °C) are <13 min, an order of magnitude faster than the 15 h clearance, thereby showing that any atropisomeric impurity will equilibrate before exposure, mitigating the safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: "Atropisomerism can be a major challenge … time‑dependent racemisation…"; "Kinetic measurement of enantiomerically enriched verinurad salts confirmed that racemisation occurred within the clearance time frame, thus mitigating safety concerns"; "half‑life of compound 1 in biologically relevant temperature (37 °C) and pH ranges was subsequently measured to be less than 13 min… an order of magnitude faster than the in vivo terminal half‑life of 15 h"

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of β‑Lactamase Inhibitor QPX7728 by Sequential Nickel-Catalyzed Boron Insertion into a Benzofuran Substrate and Enantioselective Cyclopropanation of the Resulting Vinylboronate

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Enantioselective Synthesis of JAK Inhibitor Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: During the TFAA‑mediated cyclization of the Cbz‑protected intermediate, significant loss of the Cbz protecting group occurred due to acidic conditions.
Solution_Description: Triethylamine was added to neutralize the generated acid, suppressing Cbz loss. Later, pyridine was introduced as a base additive to accelerate the cyclization while maintaining protection.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Significant loss of the Cbz protective group was seen when only TFAA was used… Adding triethylamine to neutralize the acid significantly reduced this byproduct.”
“The biggest impact on the rate of the cyclization came from changing the organic base additive… switching to pyridine greatly accelerated the rate of cyclization.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Enantioselective Synthesis of JAK Inhibitor Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: In the final urea‑formation step, pH strongly affected reaction rate and impurity formation; high pH gave rapid conversion but produced over‑acylated impurity, while low pH slowed the reaction.
Solution_Description: The reaction pH was optimized to 9 using a potassium phosphate buffer, balancing fast conversion (≈99 % in 1 h) with minimal bis‑acyl impurity (<0.2 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 5 shows: pH 9 → 99.5 % conversion, <0.2 % impurity; pH 7 → 66 % conversion, <0.2 % impurity; pH 11 → 99.9 % conversion, 9.3 % impurity.
“The optimal balance of reaction rate and impurity profile was found to be at pH 9.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original chemical‑development route to the 11β‑HSD‑1 inhibitor gave only 16 % overall yield because it required cyano‑group manipulation (hydrolysis/dehydration) and a late‑stage resolution, resulting in many steps, high material cost ($13 000 / kg API) and a long production cycle.
Solution_Description: A direct asymmetric Ir‑catalysed hydrogenation of the fused tricyclic indenopyridinium salt was developed, eliminating the nitrile‑group manipulations and the resolution step, which raised the overall yield to 38 % and cut cycle time and cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “The key feature of the synthesis is the identification of a unique and effective MeO‑BoQPhos ligand for the Ir‑catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation… This strategy eliminated the nitrile group manipulation steps… provided the API in an overall yield of up to 38 %.”; “Compound 1 was identified… overall yield of 16 % … The process mass intensity (PMI) … material cost was $13 000 for 1 kg of API on a 100 kg scale.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: When existing chiral bisphosphine ligands were used, the Ir‑catalyst gave only 40–50 % ee at 2.5 mol % loading and yielded merely 10–15 % of the desired product when the loading was reduced to 1 mol %, indicating low reactivity and poor consistency.
Solution_Description: A new rigid P,N‑ligand (MeO‑BoQPhos) was designed and synthesized, giving high activity and enantioselectivity even at catalyst loadings as low as 0.1 mol % (1000 ppm).
Supporting_Evidence: “Several chiral bisphosphine ligands provided up to 40–50 % ee when a high [Ir(COD)Cl]₂ catalyst loading of 2.5 mol % was applied. However, when the catalyst loading was decreased to 1 mol %, ... product 10 was isolated in merely 10–15 % yield.”; “The ligand MeO‑BoQphos containing two MeO groups was shown to be the ideal solution for enantioselective reduction… catalyst loading down to 0.1 mol % … the same enantioselectivity of 85:15 er was still maintained.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Using the free‑base substrate 5 in the hydrogenation gave undesired cyano‑group reduction, forming 10–20 % of dimeric side products.
Solution_Description: The substrate was converted to its pyridinium chloride salt (5·HCl) before hydrogenation; the positively charged salt prevented metal coordination of the cyano group and eliminated the side‑reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “Complete consumption of 5 was observed… however, the undesired cyano reduction was also observed with a 10–20 % yield of the corresponding dimers.”; “When 5·HCl was used as the starting material for the asymmetric hydrogenation … no cyano reduction side reaction was observed, and >99 % conversion was observed.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The pyridinium salt 5·HCl showed poor solubility in THF, leading to low conversion under the standard hydrogenation conditions.
Solution_Description: A small amount of water (15 equiv, ∼5 vol %) was added as a co‑solvent to increase the salt’s solubility in THF, which raised conversion to 100 % and improved the enantiomeric ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: “To increase the solubility of 5·HCl in THF, cosolvents were added… addition of water significantly improved the conversion… entry 3 (15 equiv H₂O) gave 100 % conversion and 85:15 er.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Increasing the water content above ∼5 vol % caused hydrolysis of the tetrasubstituted enamine intermediate, generating up to 40 % impurities.
Solution_Description: The water was reduced and an alcohol cosolvent (MeOH) was employed instead; MeOH improved solubility without promoting hydrolysis, giving high conversion and low impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the amount of water was increased to 10 vol % significant amounts of impurities (up to 40 %) were generated… Alcohol cosolvents … did not provide any benefit … MeOH was selected for further studies… MeOH 20 vol % gave 97.6 % yield with 85.2:14.8 er and <1 % impurities.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: High catalyst loadings (≥2.5 mol %) were required with earlier ligands, making the process expensive and giving low product throughput.
Solution_Description: The MeO‑BoQPhos ligand provided sufficient activity to reduce the Ir catalyst loading to as low as 0.1 mol % (1000 ppm) while maintaining >85:15 er and high conversion, dramatically cutting catalyst cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the catalyst loading was decreased to 1 mol %… product 10 was isolated in merely 10–15 % yield.”; “When the catalyst loading was further decreased to 0.1 mol % [Ir(COD)Cl]₂, the same enantioselectivity of 85:15 er was still maintained.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: After the asymmetric hydrogenation, the crude mixture contained high levels of residual palladium (up to 1600 ppm) and iridium (up to 670 ppm); Darco G‑60 charcoal removed Pd modestly but was inefficient for Ir and caused 10–15 % product loss.
Solution_Description: A scavenger based on N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine (0.1 equiv, two treatments) was employed, reducing Pd to 2.8 ppm and Ir to 13 ppm with only 2–5 % product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “Darco G‑60 charcoal was moderately efficient for reducing Pd and inefficient for removing Ir… product loss was relatively high at 10–15 %.”; “N‑acetyl‑l‑cysteine turned out highly effective … after two treatments … metal contents were reduced to 2.8 ppm Pd and 13 ppm Ir … minimal product loss of 2–5 %.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Enantioselective Reduction of 2,3-Disubstituted Indenopyridine Enables a Practical Manufacturing Process for an 11β-HSD‑1 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The final API crystallization in EtOH/HCl generated the genotoxic impurity ethyl chloride (EtCl) and suffered from polymorph control and solvent entrapment; initial batches contained ∼312 ppm EtCl.
Solution_Description: A reactive crystallization was designed using concentrated aqueous HCl added to an EtOH solution of the free base, with limited water (<5 wt %) to suppress EtCl formation; heavy seeding produced the desired anhydrous Form II, and EtCl levels were consistently kept ≤20 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The anhydrous form II was difficult to produce in an aqueous system… EtCl formed mainly during the preparation and storage of HCl in the EtOH solution. Recrystallization … reduced EtCl from ∼312 to 14 ppm.”; “A robust recrystallization process was designed by using concentrated aqueous HCl solution to minimize the introduction of H₂O to ≤5 wt %… EtCl level … ≤20 ppm.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of the C1–C13 Fragment of Eribulin on a Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The original fragment synthesis relied on an intramolecular ring‑closing metathesis (RCM) of intermediate 5.  At the concentrations required for scale‑up the reaction suffered extensive self‑dimerisation and formation of side‑products, giving poor and inconsistent isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the RCM step with a Rh‑mediated 6‑endo‑tet cyclization of vinyl epoxide 6, which cleanly furnishes the tetrahydropyran core on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ‘...the reaction was hindered by self‑dimerization and other side products when executed without considerable dilution, presenting a significant challenge for scale‑up…’ (introduction, paragraph 3) | ‘...Rh‑mediated 6‑endo cyclization of vinyl epoxide 6 and subsequent intramolecular lactol formation enabled an effective and vastly more scalable route…’ (introduction, paragraph 4)

Paper Title: Synthesis of the C1–C13 Fragment of Eribulin on a Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Direct deprotection of the C11‑OTES group in 6 with TBAF gave the desired alcohol 9 but also produced the 5‑exo‑cyclised tetrahydrofuran 10 (16 % yield), decreasing overall material efficiency.
Solution_Description: A buffered mixture of TBAF and imidazole·HCl was employed; the imidazole·HCl neutralises excess base and suppresses the side‑cyclisation, affording 9 in 77 % yield with no detectable 10.
Supporting_Evidence: ‘Treatment of 6 with TBAF afforded the desired deprotected product 9 alongside significant formation of 5‑exo‑cyclized…10 (16 % )’ (Table 1, entry 1) | ‘...treatment of 6 with TBAF buffered by imidazole·HCl yields deprotected free alcohol 9 in high yield… (entry 3, 77 % )’ (Table 1, entry 3)
