Problem_Description: Amine 7·HCl degraded in the presence of excess N‑methylmorpholine in THF, releasing ammonia that reacted with acid 6 to form impurity 9, compromising product purity and safety.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to 10 °C and the addition of NMM was controlled (3.0 equiv, added slowly) to suppress amine decomposition; stability studies confirmed that storing 7·HCl did not affect the reaction, eliminating the need for pre‑treatment.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The formation of 9 was presumably due to the reaction of the starting material 6 with inorganic ammonia … amine 7 was unstable with the alkaline NMM in THF, degrading to ammonia, which resulted in the formation of 9 during amide coupling.” (Impurity 9 discussion) 
• “A lower temperature such as 10 °C was tested … the reaction under 10 °C significantly decreased the impurity 9.” (Table 3) 
• “The storage duration of the solid 7·HCl had no obvious influence on the reaction.” (Table 4)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for a Novel HCV NS3/4A Inhibitor, Furaprevir
Problem_Description: The ring‑closing metathesis (RCM) step gave only 40–50 % isolated yield, produced significant dimeric by‑products, required large solvent volumes for dilution, and needed time‑consuming column chromatography.
Solution_Description: A catalyst screen identified the Hoveyda‑Grubbs 2nd‑generation catalyst as optimal; solvent screening showed toluene gave near‑complete conversion; a feeding strategy using separate reactors (batch‑wise addition) reduced dimer formation and increased overall yield by ≈ 20 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The RCM reaction proceeded in a 40–50 % yield … time‑consuming column chromatography … dimeric impurities.” (Introduction) 
• “The Hoveyda–Grubbs 2nd generation catalyst afforded the highest conversion …” (Table 5, entry 3) 
• “Solvent screen … toluene (entry 5) obtained near‑complete consumption …” (Table 5) 
• “Two feeding modes … the second feeding mode … lower dimer impurity and higher yield.” (Table 6) 
• “The optimized process … improved the yield from 71.5 % to 87.6 %.” (Results, diene 2)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for a Novel HCV NS3/4A Inhibitor, Furaprevir
Problem_Description: The Boc‑deprotection of amine 8 using SOCl₂/MeOH generated genotoxic chloromethane, which had to be removed to meet safety specifications.
Solution_Description: SOCl₂ was chosen because it is easy to store; the purge factor was calculated to be ~10⁶, and the chloromethane was removed by trituration and distillation steps, keeping its level < 0.1 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Boc‑amine 8 was deprotected with SOCl₂/MeOH/THF … genotoxic chloromethane can be removed as many processes such as trituration and distillation were utilized.” (Synthesis of 7·HCl) 
• “The purge factor is around 10⁶, which means less than 0.1 ppm remained after two more steps and is acceptable.” (Experimental section)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for a Novel HCV NS3/4A Inhibitor, Furaprevir
Problem_Description: The work‑up after the RCM used dichloromethane, which is a Class 2 solvent and not process‑friendly; large solvent volumes were required and the product had to be purified from Ru residues and dimeric impurities.
Solution_Description: The coupling for diene 2 was re‑optimized in acetone (process‑friendly) and the Ru catalyst was removed by a silica‑gel plug together with 2‑mercaptonicotinic acid scavenger; subsequent salt‑formation and “acidified–salted–acidified” work‑up gave 87.6 % yield of pure 2.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “DCM was not a process‑friendly solvent, we re‑optimized the coupling condition and found that HATU/NMM/acetone could also work well.” (Synthesis of diene 2) 
• “The residual of ruthenium was finally reduced from 1560 to 5 ppm.” (Ru removal) 
• “The crude solid product 2·Na was further purified by an ‘acidified–salted–acidified’ process … 87.6 % yield and 99.3 % purity.” (Results)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for a Novel HCV NS3/4A Inhibitor, Furaprevir
Problem_Description: Crystallisation of the crude API from ethanol/acetone/water caused ketal formation, lowering purity and yield.
Solution_Description: The final crystallisation was changed to acetone/water only, which avoided ketal formation and gave a final API purity of 99.89 % with 91.3 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When ethanol/acetone/water were used … ketal impurity (ketal formation from ethanol and acetone).” (Crystallisation discussion) 
• “Finally, acetone/water was employed for the crystallization instead of the above mixed solvents … the overall yield … 91.3 %.” (Refining of Product)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for a Novel HCV NS3/4A Inhibitor, Furaprevir
Problem_Description: During the Boc‑deprotection step after amide coupling, the crude product formed a thick solid that was difficult to stir and required large solvent volumes for effective mixing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The THF solution of crude 5 was diluted with additional THF before deprotection, the reaction mixture was then treated with MTBE as an antisolvent to precipitate 3·HCl cleanly, and subsequent filtration gave an 87.4 % yield of pure product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The THF solution was diluted with another part of THF, as a large amount of solid would precipitate in the next Boc‑deprotection step, which made it too thick to stir and mix.” (Synthesis of 3·HCl) 
• “After treating with MeOH, SOCl₂ was then added slowly … The addition of MTBE as the antisolvent made the product 3·HCl precipitate completely.” (Experimental section) 
• “Crude 3·HCl was then fully dissolved … filtered … 87.4 % yield.” (Results)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: The blocking reaction between HDIT and MEKO is highly exothermic (≈190 kJ kg⁻¹) and in batch leads to a rapid temperature increase of >50 °C, creating a risk of overheating and thermal runaway.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow reactor with a high surface‑to‑volume ratio was used; the residence‑time unit is thermostated and temperature set‑points are corrected using inlet/outlet thermocouples, allowing precise heat removal and preventing temperature overshoot.
Supporting_Evidence: “The exothermic reaction between HDIT and MEKO releases 190 kJ kg⁻¹ of material.”; “A strong temperature increase of >50 °C was observed in all cases, accompanied by a rapid drop of the isocyanate IR signal.”; “In a continuous flow reactor, highly efficient (essentially instantaneous) mixing can be achieved… the high surface‑to‑volume ratio… provides excellent heat and mass transfer to the system.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: HDIT is very viscous (≈3000 mPa·s at 25 °C), making it difficult to stir in a batch flask and to achieve uniform mixing with MEKO.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The viscous stream was pumped with a peristaltic pump equipped with a viscous‑solvent kit and pre‑heated to 75 °C (viscosity < 500 mPa·s). A Kenics static mixer together with a modified Y‑connector (central injection of MEKO) provided rapid, homogeneous mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high viscosity of the starting material (ca. 3000 mPa·s at 25 °C) made appropriate stirring at room temperature difficult.”; “Accurate dosing of the highly viscous HDIT … was difficult … The liquid could be satisfactorily pumped using a peristaltic pump … and pre‑heating the starting material to 75 °C.”; “The modified Y‑connector provided excellent mixing within the Kenics mixer and allowed for a significantly reduced length of the mixing unit.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: Traditional batch production requires slow, dropwise addition of the blocking agent over several hours to avoid uncontrolled exotherms, dramatically limiting productivity.
Solution_Description: Switch to continuous flow where the two neat streams are fed at constant rates; mixing occurs instantaneously, eliminating the need for slow addition and allowing full conversion in seconds.
Supporting_Evidence: “Large‑scale preparation … requires slow addition of the reactants over several hours to avoid overheating.”; “In continuous flow, the reactants are pumped separately and mixed … the homogeneous mixture obtained … was fully converted … in a residence time unit downstream of the mixer.”; “The design of the flow reactor therefore focused initially on the proper mixing of the two neat reactants.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: A tin‑based catalyst (dibutyltin dilaurate) is typically employed, posing toxicity, environmental, and cost concerns.
Solution_Description: In the optimized flow process the reaction proceeds to completion without any catalyst; the tin catalyst is omitted, removing the associated safety and cost penalties.
Supporting_Evidence: “1 mol % of dibutyltin dilaurate was added as the catalyst in some of the experiments for comparison purposes.”; “The continuous flow process … has the potential to provide significant benefits … by eliminating the use of a catalyst, a heavy‑metal (tin) containing compound with a substantial environmental impact.”; “The reaction is therefore very fast in the absence of additives even without preheating of the starting materials.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: The blocked product B‑HDIT is extremely viscous (≈100 000 mPa·s at 25 °C); this can cause a severe pressure drop and reactor clogging during batch handling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The outlet tubing was kept very short (≈2 cm) and the product was kept hot enough (by rapid exit from the heated residence‑time unit) to maintain a moderate viscosity, preventing blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high viscosity of the target compound B‑HDIT (over 100 000 mPa·s at 25 °C) could cause a significant pressure drop and blockage of the reactor.”; “The non‑thermostated tubing at the reactor output was kept very short (ca. 2 cm)… the viscous fluid obtained at the reactor output was still hot enough to have moderate viscosity and prevent clogging of the system.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: Batch processes require extensive solvent for cleaning the reactor after each run, contributing to high solvent consumption and waste.
Solution_Description: The continuous flow setup only needs ~10 % of the cleaning solvent (1‑methoxy‑2‑propanol) compared with the large batch vessel, drastically reducing solvent use.
Supporting_Evidence: “The continuous process only requires an estimated 10 % of solvent for cleaning (1‑methoxy‑2‑propanol) purposes with respect to the much larger volume vessel utilized in batch.”; “The lower environmental burden of the continuous process can mainly be ascribed to its reduced amounts of solvent required during the shutdown protocol.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: In batch, temperature overshoot and incomplete mixing can lead to inconsistent conversions and occasional yields below 100 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Precise temperature control (thermostated residence‑time unit, correction factor from two thermocouples) and instantaneous mixing in the static mixer give reproducible full conversion (0 % NCO) and quantitative yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Full conversion (< 1 % NCO) was achieved in less than 2 min in all cases.”; “After the initial rapid drop of the NCO signal… the signal decrease became slower… Full conversion to the desired B‑HDIT compound (with 0 % NCO being detected by FTIR) was obtained in all cases.”; “Accurate temperature measurements using a thermocouple at the inlet and outlet … a correction factor was calculated for the temperature drop and used for the setting of the thermostat temperature.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: Batch blocking reactions, although intrinsically fast (< 2 min), are performed over several minutes to hours due to mixing and safety constraints, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Process intensification by stepwise temperature increase up to 155 °C reduces the required residence time to 15 s while maintaining full conversion, boosting productivity to ~1 kg h⁻¹ in a 4.5 mL reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: “Full conversion after only 15 s of overall residence time has been achieved at 155 °C, providing a productivity of ca. 1 kg h⁻¹ for a reactor of only 4.5 mL volume.”; “The reaction time required to obtain full conversion could be additionally shortened to 15 s by heating the residence time unit to 155 °C.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: Isocyanates are highly toxic and volatile; batch handling requires careful containment and inert gas blanketing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous flow eliminates the need for nitrogen inertisation and reduces the inventory of reactive isocyanate at any moment, increasing safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “The continuous flow process … does not require the tin catalyst … and, owing to the lack of headspace, no inertization steps are needed.”; “The lower amount of chemicals in the reaction zone at a given time in flow in combination with improved heat and mass transfer ensure a reliable process with low risk of thermal runaway.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Blocked Polyisocyanate: Process Intensification, Reaction Monitoring Via In-Line FTIR Analysis, and Comparative Life Cycle Assessment
Problem_Description: No real‑time monitoring of the blocking reaction in batch; product quality can drift without immediate detection.
Solution_Description: Implementation of an in‑line FTIR probe at the reactor outlet provides continuous monitoring of the NCO band, enabling rapid detection of conversion and ensuring consistent product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “In‑line FTIR analysis was implemented to the continuous flow reactor to monitor the concentration of residual NCO at the reactor output and ensuring constant product quality.”; “Real‑time reaction monitoring, via in‑line Fourier‑transform infrared analysis, has been implemented, enabling fast optimization of the reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: The original route relied on 6‑iodotetralone, which suffered from high cost and long lead‑time, making it unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The starting material was changed to inexpensive, commercially available β‑tetralone, removing the cost and availability bottleneck and establishing a new synthetic route.
Supporting_Evidence: “(1) the cost and lead time of 6‑iodotetralone; (2) the introduction of the sulfur at the wrong oxidation state… (3) the need for a classical resolution… (4) the multistep installation of the heptafluoro‑isopropyl group… As we set to explore route options … (1) use of readily available starting materials … (2) an asymmetric synthesis … (3) simple, ideally one‑step, incorporation of the challenging heptafluoro‑isopropyl group.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Sulfur was introduced at the wrong oxidation state in the early sequence, requiring later oxidation adjustments that lowered overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: Sulfur is now introduced as the sulfone from the beginning, eliminating the need for later oxidation steps and simplifying the linear sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “the introduction of the sulfur at the wrong oxidation state, which had to be adjusted in the synthetic linear sequence; … (2) the sulfur was introduced at the desired oxidation state from the beginning.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: A classical resolution step reduced overall material throughput and overall yield of the target intermediate.
Solution_Description: A chiral sulfinamide ambivalent reagent was employed in a highly diastereoselective annulation, providing the desired stereochemistry without the need for a resolution step.
Supporting_Evidence: “a classical resolution approach which reduced overall yield and impacted material throughput; … a novel ambivalent reagent (8b) … provided a highly diastereoselective annulation.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Installation of the heptafluoro‑isopropyl group required a five‑step sequence with protection/de‑protection, leading to long reaction times and higher material cost.
Solution_Description: A direct radical perfluoroalkylation (Onishi conditions) installs the HFP group in a single step, dramatically shortening the sequence and reducing reagents and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “the multistep installation of the heptafluoro‑isopropyl group … an unproductive protection/de‑protection sequence… Gratifyingly, subjecting 3 to aqueous Na2S2O4, (CF3)2CFI, and 1 M NaOH in MTBE afforded the desired 5 as a single regioisomer.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Early metal‑promoted HFP couplings required temperatures above the boiling and decomposition point of the perfluoro‑isopropyl iodide, giving poor reproducibility and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The metallic cross‑coupling was abandoned in favor of a mild radical perfluoroalkylation that proceeds at ambient temperature, eliminating the high‑temperature exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “very high temperatures required, well above the boiling and decomposition point of 4… low reproducibility… none of them proved suitable… because of stability issues of the organometallic species or because of the high tendency of 4 to behave as an oxidant.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Various cross‑coupling attempts failed due to the oxidizing nature of heptafluoro‑isopropyl iodide, leading to side‑reactions and inconsistent outcomes.
Solution_Description: Radical perfluoroalkylation using sodium dithionite and aqueous NaOH was adopted, avoiding oxidative side reactions and providing consistent conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “none of them proved suitable… because of the high tendency of 4 to behave as an oxidant… We turned our attention to radical‑based chemistry approaches.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: The original conditions for forming intermediate 3 caused uncontrolled precipitation and were O2‑sensitive, leading to variable yields on scale.
Solution_Description: Switching to NMP as solvent, charging iodine portionwise, and strict nitrogen atmosphere kept the reaction homogeneous and temperature below 35 °C, delivering reproducible 75 % isolated yield on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “initial literature conditions for the formation of 3 caused uncontrolled product precipitation and were also O2 sensitive resulting in variable results on laboratory scale… A solubility screen revealed that 3 and 2 were fully soluble in NMP… addition of I2 was done portionwise… internal temperature did not rise above 35 °C.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: MTBE‑derived enol‑ether side‑products (3a, 5a) formed during the perfluoroalkylation, complicating isolation and reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Alternative solvents (THF, 2‑MeTHF, MeCN) suppressed formation of the MTBE adducts; acids (TFA, HCl, etc.) were employed to deprotect the remaining adducts back to the desired sulfonyl ketones.
Supporting_Evidence: “significant levels of MTBE‑derived enol ethers 3a and 5a were formed… a variety of alternative ethereal (THF, 2‑MeTHF) and non‑ethereal solvents (MeCN, toluene) provided cleaner reaction profiles… TFA, pTsOH, MSA, and HCl in IPA and concentrated HCl were found to productively deprotect the MTBE adducts.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: A side reaction between heptafluoro‑isopropyl iodide and sodium dithionite generated an unreactive sulfinate, causing reaction stalling and inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A biphasic solvent system was introduced, partitioning HFP‑iodide into the organic phase and sodium dithionite into the aqueous phase, which suppressed sulfinate formation and restored conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction stalling was attributed to an undesired side reaction between heptafluoroisopropyl iodide and sodium dithionite… This side reaction could be suppressed with aqueous/organic biphasic solvent systems, in which heptafluoroisopropyl iodide is largely partitioned into the organic layer and sodium dithionite is largely partitioned into the aqueous layer.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: During the NaBH₄‑mediated reduction, adding MeOH before NaBH₄ generated a large exotherm and vigorous H₂ evolution, posing safety risks.
Solution_Description: The order was reversed – NaBH₄ was added first, followed by a controlled, slow addition of MeOH while keeping the temperature below 10 °C, which eliminated the runaway exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the MeOH was added prior to the NaBH₄, a large (30 °C) exotherm was observed… To manage this safety concern, NaBH₄ was added first followed by the slow addition of MeOH to control the exotherm and H₂ off‑gassing.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Vinyl sulfone 7 could not be crystallized, making isolation difficult and lengthening the process.
Solution_Description: The reaction sequence was telescoped directly from the reduction product to the annulation step, bypassing isolation of 7 and improving overall throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, crystallization efforts did not reveal any crystalline forms of 7… a telescope into the annulation step was explored.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: The addition of iodine generated an exotherm that needed to be controlled to avoid runaway heating.
Solution_Description: I₂ was added portionwise with temperature monitoring, keeping the internal temperature below 35 °C, which prevented uncontrolled heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of I₂ can also be done as a solution in NMP. The exotherm could be easily controlled by the rate of the addition.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Base and temperature strongly influenced diastereoselectivity and yield of the annulation product 9, leading to inconsistent outcomes.
Solution_Description: Screening identified NaO‑t‑Pent and –42 °C as the optimal combination, delivering >20:1 dr and ≥80 % yield, even on multigram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Base screen revealed that NaO‑t‑Pent and –42 °C were the optimal base and temperature, respectively… 5 g, 82 % yield, >20:1 dr.”

Paper Title: A Radical Addition Approach to a Heptafluoro­isopropyl Substituted Arene, Combined with a Highly Diastereoselective Annulation Reaction To Synthesize the Tricyclic Core of BMS-986251
Problem_Description: Using MsCl/pyridine gave only 65 % yield and inconsistent results for mesylation/elimination to vinyl sulfone 7.
Solution_Description: Switching to trifluoroacetic anhydride (TFAA) with NMM as base increased the yield to 95 % and provided a cleaner reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “(a) MsCl/pyridine (65% yield); (b) TsCl/pyridine (60% yield); … (d) TFAA/NMM (95% yield); (e) TFAA/pyridine (75% yield).”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: The original enabling route relied on an enzymatic kinetic resolution that gave low conversion (low throughput) and required a large excess of enzyme, while the directed hydrogenation with the Crabtree Ir‑catalyst needed very high catalyst loadings and showed frequent stalling, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: A dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) using immobilised Lipozyme CAL‑B was introduced to replace the kinetic resolution, and the final directed hydrogenation was switched to a Rh‑DCyPF catalyst system that works with a stronger carboxylic‑acid directing group, allowing lower catalyst loadings (3 mol %) and reliable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the kinetic resolution… low yield… impact on material throughput” ; “high catalyst loadings and proneness to stalling… Crabtree catalyst” ; “Implementing a DKR… and Rh‑catalyzed hydrogenation… gave high yield and diastereoselectivity.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: After the lipase‑catalysed DKR, isolation of the acid product 11 was problematic – water caused decomposition above 15 °C and the solid showed limited stability, making the work‑up difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The crude DKR broth was telescoped directly into the subsequent diastereoselective hydrogenation without isolation, thereby avoiding exposure to water and temperature‑sensitive conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “presence of water decreased the stability… resulting in decomposition” ; “isolated product also displayed limited stability” ; “We decided to explore telescoping the crude acid into the diastereoselective hydrogenation”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the crude acid gave variable conversion; runs without a co‑solvent suffered low conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adding 5 % v/v MTBE to the hydrogenation mixture dramatically improved H₂ solubility and gave consistent full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “conversion rate was variable. Further investigation unveiled that small amounts of MTBE were required for reproducible reaction performance.” ; Table 1 shows 5 % MTBE raising conversion from 13 % to 43 % (2 h) and to 100 % (5 h).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: tert‑Butyl ester formation in the original route required large excesses of POCl₃ and pyridine, which are hazardous and caused epimerisation of the stereocenter.
Solution_Description: The ester was instead formed by reacting the acid with TFAA and t‑BuOH at ≤10 °C, followed by an aqueous NH₄OH reverse quench to control the exotherm; this gave 90 % yield with no detectable epimerisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “large excess of POCl₃ and pyridine… undesirable… also created an epimerisation liability.” ; “Combination of TFAA and t‑BuOH… followed by an aqueous work‑up with ammonium hydroxide… afforded … 90 % yield and with no detectable epimerisation.” ; “A reverse quench was used to control the exotherm.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: The palladium‑catalysed carbonylation of the enol tosylates required cryogenic temperatures, gave variable yields, and generated variable amounts of TsNH₂ which poisoned the reaction; an exotherm (+12 °C) was observed when adding reagents.
Solution_Description: The tosylates were replaced by enol nonaflates prepared with NfF/DBU at 40 °C (no cryogenic conditions). For the tosylate route, the base was changed from NaHMDS to NaO‑t‑Bu, eliminating TsNH₂ formation. The carbonylation was performed with Pd(OAc)₂/DPPP/DIPEA/phenol under 15 psi CO at 55–60 °C, giving >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “process suffered yield variability, low levels of epimerization (<3 %), and the need for cryogenic conditions.” ; “While using NaHMDS… variable amounts of TsNH₂ were formed which hindered the carbonylation reaction.” ; “Treatment of 5 with NfF and DBU at 40 °C afforded the desired mix of enol nonaflates quantitatively.” ; “The use of 15 psi CO was more favorable than 70 psi.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: When NaHMDS was employed as the base for enol tosylate formation, inconsistent amounts of TsNH₂ were produced, leading to unreliable carbonylation.
Solution_Description: The base was switched to NaO‑t‑Bu (2 equiv), which gave a clean tosylate formation and reliable subsequent carbonylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “While using NaHMDS… variable amounts of TsNH₂ were formed which hindered the carbonylation reaction.” ; “Exploration of alternative bases identified NaO t‑Bu as optimal.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: After Rh‑catalysed hydrogenation, the product mixture contained high levels of Rh and colored impurities; over 25 metal‑scavenger materials failed to lower Rh below acceptable limits.
Solution_Description: A crystallisation as the salt with (R,S)-2‑amino‑1,2‑diphenylethanol was employed, which removed Rh/ligand residues and simultaneously purged the undesired diastereomer, delivering the API in 85 % isolated yield, >99 % ee and dr.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempts to directly isolate the product without metal scavenging yielded highly colored material in low purity. Multiple metal scavengers… all failed to reduce the levels of Rh.” ; “Crystallization study revealed that … formed a highly crystalline salt … reduced metal and ligand content … used for final isolation.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: Directed hydrogenation using the Crabtree Ir‑catalyst required high catalyst loadings and showed frequent stalling, making the step expensive and unreliable.
Solution_Description: Switch to a Rh‑DCyPF catalyst system (3 mol % Rh) together with a free carboxylic‑acid directing group (obtained by deprotecting the t‑Bu ester) gave consistent high diastereoselectivity (94:6 dr) and eliminated the need for high catalyst loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: “high catalyst loading requirements and proneness to stalling observed during the directed hydrogenation mediated by the Crabtree catalyst.” ; “Rh catalysts… facilitated the diastereoselective hydrogenation… 94:6 dr” ; “Catalyst loading studies identified 3 mol % Rh as optimal.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: Intermediate 14/15 showed very low solubility in most organic solvents, forcing the use of CH₂Cl₂ for the deprotection and subsequent hydrogenation steps.
Solution_Description: CH₂Cl₂ was selected as the reaction medium to dissolve 14/15 adequately for the deprotection/de‑esterification and the downstream hydrogenation.
Supporting_Evidence: “CH₂Cl₂ was required due to the low solubility of 14/15 in other solvents.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of the Cyclohexyl Fragment in RORγt Inhibitor (BMS-986251) Enabled by a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution of Hageman’s Ester
Problem_Description: During the tert‑butyl ester formation a rapid exotherm of +12 °C was observed upon addition of reagents.
Solution_Description: A reverse quench with aqueous NH₄OH was employed and the reagent addition rate was controlled to keep the reaction temperature below 10 °C, effectively managing the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “Exotherm observed immediately upon addition (+12 °C exotherm, from 22 to 34 °C).” ; “A reverse quench was used to control the exotherm.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required eight steps, gave an overall 0.07 % yield, involved protection/de‑protection sequences and needed multiple chromatographic purifications, making it unattractive for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A convergent synthesis was designed that eliminated protection steps, reduced the step count and removed chromatographic purifications, delivering the target pyrrolidone in high overall yield on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The synthetic route suffered from many drawbacks: a linear sequence with a high step‑count, protection/de‑protection steps, low yields, as well as multiple chromatographic purifications.”; “The development of the synthesis led to decreased route complexity and removal of chromatographic purifications.”; “to support toxicological studies, a new route to access compound of interest 1 on kilogram scale was necessary.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: The C5‑aldehyde (12) is volatile, making it difficult to isolate in pure form after oxidation of the trifluoropentanol.
Solution_Description: The crude aldehyde was used directly in the subsequent Mannich‑type reaction without isolation, avoiding the need for a purification step.
Supporting_Evidence: “As this aldehyde is volatile, it was difficult to isolate the product in a pure form.”; “aldehyde 12 was obtained … and directly engaged in the next step.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: Formation of the hydroxyfuranone suffered from aldol side‑product formation when the aldehyde dissolved too well in organic solvents (DCM, toluene), and attempts to control the addition did not improve selectivity.
Solution_Description: Various solvents (n‑heptane, DCM, toluene, water) were screened; the historical n‑heptane conditions were ultimately retained because they gave acceptable yield (77 %) despite the side‑product, representing a solvent‑change optimisation attempt.
Supporting_Evidence: “Switching n‑heptane to dichloromethane or toluene resulted in an increase of the aldol byproduct… probably due to higher solubility of aldehyde 12 in the organic layer.”; “When the reaction was performed in full aqueous media… a comparable result was surprisingly obtained as the aldehyde was insoluble in this media.”; “Attempts to slowly add either the aldehyde … led to disappointing results.”; “hydroxyfuranone 10 was prepared using historic conditions and was obtained in 77 % yield…”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: The hexamethylenetetramine (HMTA) route to the benzylic amine (11) gave a product contaminated with up to 30 % trimeric impurity (18) that could not be removed by varying work‑up conditions.
Solution_Description: An alternative oxidative pathway via an Ellman sulfinyl‑imine was developed, delivering the amine in 68 % isolated yield and >98 % purity on kilogram scale, eliminating the impurity problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “compound 11 was not isolated in a pure form but contaminated with up to 30 % of an unexpected impurity… Alternative reaction and/or work‑up conditions were investigated, but none of them resulted in the complete absence of this impurity.”; “Another retrosynthetic analysis identified an alternative oxidative pathway via an Ellman sulfinyl‑imine… afforded the desired amine … 68 % yield and 98.2 LCAP over five steps on kilogram scale.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: Standard oxidation methods for the benzylic alcohol (8) gave incomplete conversion or poor selectivity, hindering scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Stahl’s aerobic CuI/TEMPO oxidation was employed, providing a quantitative, clean and scalable oxidation of the alcohol to the aldehyde.
Supporting_Evidence: “Various classic oxidative conditions were investigated… Among those conditions, Stahl’s aerobic oxidative conditions highlighted its superiority with a mild, clean, and scalable reaction in quantitative yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: Imine formation (19 → 20) was highly sensitive to the particle size (granulometry) of cesium carbonate, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: Using finely milled cesium carbonate as the dehydrating agent in isopropyl acetate (an optimal solvent) gave clean, reproducible conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Imine formation was found to be sensitive to cesium carbonate granulometry.”; “Complete and clean conversion was obtained using cesium carbonate as the dehydrating agent in isopropyl acetate, identified as an optimal solvent for processing purposes.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: Sodium borohydride decomposes rapidly in methanol, releasing hydrogen; handling large quantities posed safety and reproducibility concerns.
Solution_Description: The borohydride solution was stabilized with catalytic amounts of sodium methanolate (NaOMe), preventing premature decomposition and improving safety during scale‑up reductions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reduction of esters and lactones at room temperature without solvent‑induced loss of hydride… Stabilization of NaBH₄ in methanol using a catalytic amount of NaOMe.”; “sodium borohydride solution in methanol stabilized by sodium methanolate.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route to a Pyrrolidone Compound via a Hydroxyfuranone
Problem_Description: The one‑pot condensation of hydroxyfuranone (10) with amine (11) generated a highly exothermic reaction that required tight temperature control to avoid runaway conditions.
Solution_Description: The amine was added slowly over 1.5 h while keeping the reactor temperature below 5 °C, and subsequent steps were also performed under controlled temperature ramps to manage the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The mass temperature was maintained below 5 °C during the exothermic addition.”; “The solution was cooled down to 0 °C before adding 11… and the addition was performed over 1.5 h while maintaining the temperature below 5 °C.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Evaluation and Solvent-Based Linear Free Energy Relationship in the Alkylation of ABT-199 Using Di-
Problem_Description: Initial screening of bases showed that inorganic bases gave selective N‑1 alkylation but low conversion, whereas mild organic bases gave complete N‑7 selectivity with little improvement in yield and stronger organic bases caused degradation of the substrate.
Solution_Description: The strong, non‑nucleophilic base 1,8‑bis(dimethylamino)naphthalene (6) was employed; it provided high conversion (94 %) without degrading the substrate, acting as a basic promoter that controls the reaction pH.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem]“When inorganic bases were used at reduced temperatures, the reaction was selective for alkylation at N‑1…When mild organic bases were used … the reaction was completely selective for N‑7.”; “The results showed little improvement in the yield when common trialkylamine bases were used, and increased degradation was observed when stronger organic bases were employed.”
[Solution]“1,8‑bis‑(dimethylamino)‑naphthalene (6) was a strong enough base to drive the reaction to high conversion without degrading 1. The use of 6 resulted in 94 % conversion…”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Evaluation and Solvent-Based Linear Free Energy Relationship in the Alkylation of ABT-199 Using Di-
Problem_Description: Varying the equivalents of the phosphate reagent (3) and base (6) affected impurity formation (7, 8, 9); higher concentrations lowered conversion of the desired product because impurities were difficult to reject during crystallization.
Solution_Description: A design‑of‑experiments study identified the optimal stoichiometry: 3 equiv of phosphate 3 and 1.1 equiv of base 6, which minimized impurity levels while maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem]“Increasing the number of equivalents of 6 has no impact on the conversion, while increasing the amount of 3 leads to improved conversion…Increasing the concentrations of 3 and 6 demonstrated negative synergistic relationships toward impurities 7 and 8…Minimization of the amounts of 7 and 8 was prioritized over the slightly higher yields observed at higher concentrations of 6 because of their minimal rejection during crystallization.”
[Solution]“Taken as a whole…the optimal conditions: 3 equivalents of 3 and 1.1 equivalents of 6.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Evaluation and Solvent-Based Linear Free Energy Relationship in the Alkylation of ABT-199 Using Di-
Problem_Description: The reaction exhibited a rapid zero‑order conversion to 94 % in ~6 h followed by product degradation; to obtain >80 % yield the reaction must be stopped within 30–60 min, making crash‑cooling of large reactors unreliable and posing a scale‑up risk.
Solution_Description: Kinetic data and Arrhenius analysis were used to define a cooling protocol: after reaching target conversion the reactor is cooled 20 °C in ~1 h (10–40 min depending on size) to 60 °C, limiting further degradation.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem]“the reaction would need to be stopped within 30–60 min. This feature of the reaction posed a substantial risk on scale‑up, as crash‑cooling of large scale reactors is not a reliable control mechanism for product quality.”
[Solution]“target cooling of 20 °C over the period of 1 h could be achieved…the reactor would be cooled as quickly as possible to 60 °C, which could be accomplished in 10 to 40 min depending on the reactor size (100 to 800 L).”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Evaluation and Solvent-Based Linear Free Energy Relationship in the Alkylation of ABT-199 Using Di-
Problem_Description: Attempts to trap the hypothesised phosphate radical intermediate with TEMPO, DMPO, or other scavengers failed; spectroscopic attempts also did not detect any phosphorus‑containing product, indicating rapid decomposition or self‑reaction of the intermediate.
Solution_Description: A flow‑reactor was designed based on 31P NMR kinetics to generate the activated phosphate in a controlled residence time; the stream was then mixed with substrate, revealing that the intermediate rapidly converts to a diphosphate (10) rather than the desired product.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem]“Attempts to trap any phosphate radical intermediate with TEMPO, DMPO, and other trapping reagents were unsuccessful…no desired product 4 was observed.”
[Solution]“A flow reactor was designed on the basis of the 31P NMR experiments…the most predominant species was the diphosphate product 10.”

Paper Title: Mechanistic Evaluation and Solvent-Based Linear Free Energy Relationship in the Alkylation of ABT-199 Using Di-
Problem_Description: The reaction rate varied markedly with solvent; conventional polarity descriptors (dipole, dielectric) gave no correlation, making solvent choice ambiguous for process robustness.
Solution_Description: A systematic screen of nine solvents was performed and rates were regressed against Hansen solubility parameters; a strong linear free‑energy relationship with the Hansen polarity parameter was identified, enabling rational solvent selection to favor the radical chain mechanism.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem]“Preliminary inspection of the data suggested a correlation between the solvent polarity and the rate, but no quantified correlation could be determined using standard solvent parameters…no such correlation exists with the hydrogen‑bonding parameter.”
[Solution]“HSPs provided the best correlation…the strong linear free energy relationship between the Hansen polarity parameter and the rate of reaction provides further support for a radical‑based mechanism.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The original (first‑generation) synthesis of DHPN starts from 1,4‑dimethylnaphthalene (cost ≈ 16 €/g) and uses CCl₄ as solvent, giving an overall low isolated yield (≈ 44 % over two steps from the diacid).
Solution_Description: A concise three‑step route from inexpensive 1,4‑dibromonaphthalene was developed. The key step is a ligand‑free Pd‑catalyzed double Mizoroki‑Heck reaction using only 0.05 mol % Pd(OAc)₂ (homeopathic loading) in N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone, avoiding toxic CCl₄ and reducing catalyst cost. Subsequent hydrogenation (Pd/C) and direct amidation give DHPN in 70 % overall yield (four steps).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the high costs of the starting material 3 (16 €/g), the use of CCl₄ as a toxic solvent, and the rather poor overall yield prompted us to evaluate possible alternatives.”
• “the double Heck reaction … using only a remarkably low (‘homeopathic’) catalyst loading … 0.05 mol % of palladium‑(II) acetate without the need for any additional ligand.”
• “the reaction … went to completion … giving the diacrylate … in 80 % yield … without the need for chromatographic purification.”
• “hydrogenation … afforded the dipropionate … in 98% yield.”
• “the final amidation … gave DHPN … in 89% yield … overall 63% from 1‑bromonaphthalene.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The endoperoxide DHPNO₂ is only moderately stable; large‑scale isolation is limited because of its tendency to decompose on warming.
Solution_Description: Photochemical oxidation of DHPN to DHPNO₂ is performed at 4 °C with white‑LED illumination and the product is stored at –20 °C under argon. The low temperature minimizes thermal decay, allowing isolation of up to 1 g batches with 89 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the final conversion … was performed only on a smaller scale (1 g batches) because of the somewhat limited stability of the endoperoxide.”
• “a solution of 1 g of 1 … was irradiated … at 4 °C … after 7 h … the deep‑blue solution was cooled to 0 °C … the product was stored in a freezer at –20 °C.”
• “High‑performance liquid chromatography … indicated a conversion of 89 % of 1 into the target endoperoxide 1b.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: During the final amidation of dimethyl 1,4‑naphthalene‑dipropionate with 3‑amino‑1,2‑propanediol, the reaction mixture becomes highly viscous, which could impede stirring and efficient water removal.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction is carried out in a Dean–Stark apparatus under reduced pressure, allowing continuous removal of methanol and preventing excessive viscosity; the pressure is gradually lowered to 5 mbar to facilitate efficient mixing and removal of solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the mixture … was heated to 110 °C while MeOH was distilled off (into the Dean–Stark trap)… the pressure was slowly reduced to 250 mbar … the viscosity of the mixture increased while the pressure was now gradually further reduced to 5 mbar … then kept at 5 mbar for another 60 min.”

Paper Title: Stereoselective Nickel(II)-Catalyzed Addition of Aryl Grignards to Diphenylacetylene in the Synthesis of Zuclomiphene
Problem_Description: Direct coupling of 4‑(2‑(diethylamino)‑ethoxy)‑magnesium bromide with N‑chlorosuccinimide gave a complex mixture and only 12 % isolated yield of zuclomiphene, attributed to chlorination of the tertiary amine that generated many impurities.
Solution_Description: Switched to the 4‑methoxyphenylmagnesium bromide (16b) route; the nickel‑catalyzed addition proceeded smoothly and the crude product was purified by hot‑trituration in isopropanol, affording the intermediate (18a) in 59 % yield, later converted to zuclomiphene.
Supporting_Evidence: • “This led to a complex mixture of compounds, and zuclomiphene was isolated in only a 12 % yield …”

Paper Title: Stereoselective Nickel(II)-Catalyzed Addition of Aryl Grignards to Diphenylacetylene in the Synthesis of Zuclomiphene
Problem_Description: Methyl deprotection of the 4‑methoxy intermediate using boron tribromide caused double‑bond isomerisation under basic (NaSEt/DMF, 150 °C) conditions and the reagent is unsafe and costly for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Adopted the 4‑fluorophenylmagnesium bromide (16c) route; the addition‑chlorination sequence gave the chloride intermediate (18c) in 72 % yield, eliminating the need for BBr₃.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When basic conditions (2.5 equiv NaSEt, DMF, 150 °C) were employed … isomerization … leading to a mixture of E‑ and Z‑isomers.”

Paper Title: Stereoselective Nickel(II)-Catalyzed Addition of Aryl Grignards to Diphenylacetylene in the Synthesis of Zuclomiphene
Problem_Description: Presence of bromide ions from the aryl‑magnesium bromide caused N‑chlorosuccinimide to convert to N‑bromosuccinimide, generating the bromo‑analog impurity (21) in >20 % of the product after chlorination.
Solution_Description: Generated the chloride Grignard (4‑fluorophenylmagnesium chloride) instead of the bromide; the chloride reagent prevented formation of the brominated impurity, delivering a high‑purity chloride product (18c).
Supporting_Evidence: • “We concluded that the impurity was most likely compound 21 … N‑chlorosuccinimide converts to N‑bromosuccinimide in the presence of bromide ions.”

Paper Title: Stereoselective Nickel(II)-Catalyzed Addition of Aryl Grignards to Diphenylacetylene in the Synthesis of Zuclomiphene
Problem_Description: The desired chloride Grignard is not commercially available; attempts using Rieke magnesium (highly reactive) are unsafe for scale‑up, and lithium‑chloride activation interferes with nickel‑catalyzed addition.
Solution_Description: Implemented an iodine‑mediated sequence (Alternative Route 1): reacted the vinyl intermediate with I₂ to give iodo‑compound 22, then treated with cyclohexylmagnesium chloride to generate the chloride intermediate, sequestering iodine as cyclohexyl‑iodide; this eliminated the need for unavailable chloride reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A simple solution would be to use the chloride version of the Grignard; however, it is not commercially available … Rieke magnesium … safety issues preclude its use … LiCl interferes …”

Paper Title: Stereoselective Nickel(II)-Catalyzed Addition of Aryl Grignards to Diphenylacetylene in the Synthesis of Zuclomiphene
Problem_Description: Residual bromo‑analog and E‑isomer impurities persisted in crude zuclomiphene after the final step, lowering overall purity.
Solution_Description: Converted crude zuclomiphene to the oxalic‑acid salt, which selectively removed the des‑halo impurity (25) and the E‑isomer (2); the oxalate salt was then treated with citric acid to afford zuclomiphene citrate in 95 % isolated yield and ~90 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The two main impurities that are purged during oxalic acid salt formation are the des‑halo impurity 25 … and the E‑isomer 2 … The oxalic acid salt … was free based and treated with citric acid … to furnish zuclomiphene citrate in a 95 % yield.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: The high‑cost protected amino‑acid building block Fmoc‑Har(Pbf)‑OH required large excesses (≥2.5 equiv) to avoid formation of the Des‑Har² impurity caused by incomplete coupling or δ‑lactam formation, which lowered overall yield.
Solution_Description: Coupling was optimized on the 5 mmol scale using a single coupling with exactly 2.5 equiv of Fmoc‑Har(Pbf)‑OH at 90 °C (17–26 W) for 15 min, giving <0.6 % Des‑Har² impurity; the same protocol was scaled to 70 mmol by proportionally increasing microwave power and maintaining the temperature, achieving <0.1 % impurity and high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “We demonstrated that the first coupling should not be performed with <2.5 equiv of Fmoc‑l‑Har(Pbf)‑OH… This is fundamental to limiting Des‑Har²‑linear precursor impurity formation…We succeeded in optimizing the coupling conditions … using 1 × 2.5 equiv, at 90 °C and 17–26 W, obtaining only a 0.6 % Des‑Har²‑linear eptifibatide impurity.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: Industrial‑grade solvents and reagents (DMF, Oxyma Pure) were needed in large volumes; using analytical‑grade material would increase cost and some antisolvents (MTBE) are classified as hazardous SVHCs.
Solution_Description: Industrial‑grade DMF and Oxyma Pure were qualified by comparison with analytical‑grade batches (identical UHPLC purity), permitting cost reduction; iPr₂O was selected as the antisolvent because of its low volatility, acceptable cost (40–50 €/L), and compliance with safety regulations, replacing MTBE and CPME.
Supporting_Evidence: “Industrial‑grade DMF and Oxyma pure quality were tested (use test)…the UHPLC purity…was comparable…we considered it acceptable to use industrial‑grade DMF and Oxyma pure reagent, decreasing the production cost.”; “MTBE…has the disadvantage of being classified in the list of substances of very high concern (SVHC)…After evaluation of all factors, iPr₂O was selected as an antisolvent because of low volatility, facilitating large volume management (crude yield 73.4 % and UHPLC purity 58.8 %) with a competitive cost (40–50 €/L).”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: The initial TFA/TIS/DODT/H₂O cleavage cocktail generated tert‑butyl carbocation side‑products (Imp a, Imp b) that re‑attached to thiol groups, reducing crude purity and requiring hazardous strong acids for cleanup.
Solution_Description: Two‑step cleavage was implemented, testing several scavenger ratios; the optimal mixture (TFA/H₂O/TIS/DODT = 91:2.3:2.3:4.4 (v/v/v/v)) minimized tert‑butyl derivatives, gave the highest UHPLC crude purity (61.5 %), and avoided the need for strong acid treatments.
Supporting_Evidence: “The mixture TFA/TIS/DODT/H₂O 92.5:2.5:2.5:2.5… after cleavage…three main side products…Imp a and Imp b correspond to tert‑butyl derivatives…The best crude UHPLC purity was achieved using entry 1 mixture…the final cleavage mixture selected…TFA/H₂O/TIS/DODT ratio was 91:2.3:2.3:4.4 (v/v/v/v).”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: Precipitation of the peptide crude by adding iPr₂O to the TFA cleavage solution is highly exothermic; uncontrolled temperature rise (>35 °C) can cause safety hazards and degrade product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Precipitation was performed at ≤35 °C using an ice‑bath for lab‑scale and a thermostated jacketed reactor with stirring for the 70 mmol pilot scale, successfully controlling the heat release and preserving crude purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Lab‑scale preliminary tests…temperature was maintained at <35 °C by ice‑bath cooling…In the 70 mmol pilot scale process, the temperature of the mixture was maintained at <35 °C using a thermostated jacketed reactor under stirring to manage the temperature increase developed during the exothermic iPr₂O addition.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: iPr₂O batches with high peroxide content (>1000 ppm) caused severe oxidation of amino‑acid side chains, producing oligomers and lowering crude purity, while peroxide‑free iPr₂O is more expensive.
Solution_Description: Only iPr₂O with peroxide content <350 ppm (ideally peroxide‑free) is used for precipitation; peroxide levels are verified before use to ensure safety and product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “Peroxide content >1000 ppm dramatically affected the purity (32.5 % vs >60 %)… a peroxide content <350 ppm, ideally peroxide‑free, must be performed before precipitation of the eptifibatide linear precursor crude for both safety and purity.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: Flash reverse‑phase chromatography with high column loading (>5 %) led to lower recovery yields (≤24 %) and incomplete removal of impurities, compromising overall process efficiency.
Solution_Description: A linear gradient of 10–37 % B in A with ≤5 % column loading was adopted, improving recovery (34.3 %) and maintaining >98.5 % purity; step gradients and higher loadings were avoided.
Supporting_Evidence: “Starting from 5 % eptifibatide TFA crude column loading, two linear gradients… the 10–37 % linear gradient required slightly lower amount of eluents… yield increased from 24.7 % to 34.3 %… We demonstrated that crude loading should be maintained <5 % to achieve the highest purity and recovery yield.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: The final API must be the acetate salt, but the TFA counter‑ion is hazardous and must be removed; high pH required for ion‑exchange can degrade the disulfide bond.
Solution_Description: An ion‑exchange SPE was performed at pH 8 (NH₄OH added) with isocratic washes (water, 0.5 % AcOH) to exchange TFA for acetate without exceeding pH 8, yielding 99.6 % HPLC purity and TFA residual <5000 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solution… was adjusted at pH 8 adding NH₄OH… Under these conditions, the peptide was completely soluble, and the resulting disulfide bond was stable… Two isocratic elutions… completely removed ammonium trifluoroacetate salt… The resulting homogeneous fractions… lyophilized.”

Paper Title: An Optimized Safe Process from Bench to Pilot cGMP Production of API Eptifibatide Using a Multigram-Scale Microwave-Assisted Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesizer
Problem_Description: Scaling the multistep synthesis from 5 mmol to 70 mmol risked inconsistencies in conversion, impurity profile, and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The same optimized MW‑SPPS protocol, dual‑mode mixing, and detailed risk‑assessment (Ishikawa diagram) were applied on the Liberty Pro microwave synthesizer; equipment was qualified (design, installation, OQ, PQ) and hold points were defined, resulting in comparable purities and yields across scales.
Supporting_Evidence: “Scaling‑up the coupling step… required a proportional increase of MW power… Reproducibility of the MW‑SPPS on the pilot‑scale was unequivocally demonstrated… The scale‑up produced extremely comparable UHPLC crude purities… No new impurities were detected… cGMP peptide API production requires the qualification of manufacturing equipment…”

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Route to a Human Immunodeficiency Virus Maturation Inhibitor by Chromium-Free Allylic Oxidation and an Efficient Asymmetric Henry Reaction
Problem_Description: The original allylic oxidation employed highly toxic sodium dichromate and required overnight heating at 60 °C to reach completion.
Solution_Description: A chromium‑free oxidation was developed using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) and aqueous calcium carbonate in 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2‑MeTHF), avoiding toxic elements and reducing reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The allylic oxidation used highly toxic sodium dichromate and required overnight heating at 60 °C to drive the reaction to completion.”

Paper Title: Engineering a Transaminase for the Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Rimegepant
Problem_Description: The research team encountered a series of scale‑up challenges while developing a transaminase‑catalysed route to the key rimegepant intermediate.  The main issues were: (1) no detectable activity of any wild‑type or variant transaminase toward the bulky ketone 1, resulting in essentially zero conversion; (2) even after initial mutagenesis the bulky substrate was still poorly accepted, giving only trace conversion; (3) acetone generated during the biotransformation accumulated and slowed the reaction; (4) the amine donor i‑PrNH₂ volatilised at 60 °C causing a loss of reagent and lower conversion; (5) high temperature led to enzyme inactivation; (6) initial runs required a high enzyme loading (5 wt/wt) which is costly; (7) the substrate showed limited solubility in aqueous buffer; (8) isolating the product at gram‑ and kilogram‑scale proved difficult; (9) the overall reaction time was long (70‑110 h) for industrially relevant batches.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team resolved these problems through a combination of protein‑engineering and process‑engineering strategies: (1) rational design created a first‑generation variant (M3) that showed trace activity – a new enzymatic route; (2) iterative saturation mutagenesis of a flexible loop (positions 83‑91) generated highly active variants (M6‑M11) that dramatically increased conversion; (3) a mild nitrogen sweep was introduced to strip acetone from the reaction mixture; (4) the reaction temperature was lowered to 45 °C and i‑PrNH₂ equivalents were increased, preventing amine loss; (5) temperature optimisation also avoided enzyme deactivation; (6) reaction conditions (pH, donor loading) were tuned so that enzyme loading could be reduced to 2 wt/wt, cutting cost; (7) DMSO concentration was raised to 15 % to improve substrate solubility; (8) a new work‑up sequence (acid precipitation, diatomite filtration, MTBE extraction and crystallisation) gave a clean product at scale; (9) temperature and feeding adjustments, together with a second enzyme addition, shortened the overall reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem 1 – No activity: "Over 300 transaminases, including the wild‑type and variants, were screened … however, no enzyme with detectable activity was identified" (sec 2.1).  
Problem 2 – Trace activity after first mutations: "the variant L59A/F88A was first detected having activity toward compound 1 with a conversion of 0.02 %" (sec 2.2).  
Problem 3 – Acetone inhibition: "acetone accumulation in the later stage of the reaction might lead to incomplete conversion" (sec 2.3).  
Problem 4 – Amine volatilisation: "volatilization of i‑PrNH₂ at high temperature (60 °C) caused severe loss of i‑PrNH₂ in the late stage of the reaction" (sec 2.3).  
Problem 5 – Enzyme inactivation at high T: "high temperature might also lead to enzyme inactivation" (sec 2.3).  
Problem 6 – High enzyme loading: "an excess amount of i‑PrNH₂ (20 equiv) was added at the beginning … 5 wt/wt enzyme" (sec 2.3).  
Problem 7 – Solubility: "The conversion increased with increasing DMSO concentration" (Fig 2A).

Paper Title: Generation of Tosyl Azide in Continuous Flow Using an Azide Resin, and Telescoping with Diazo Transfer and Rhodium Acetate-Catalyzed O–H Insertion
Problem_Description: The presence of water in the reaction stream (from the use of aqueous sodium azide) dramatically reduces the basicity of DBU, resulting in little or no conversion of the aryl acetate 8 to the desired α‑diazo ester 9. This gives very low yields of the target product and makes the diazo‑transfer step ineffective for less‑acidic substrates.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the aqueous azide protocol with an anhydrous flow‑based generation of tosyl azide using a polymer‑bound azide resin (Amberlite 15 or Dowex 16). This eliminates water from the reaction mixture, restores the high basicity of DBU, and enables rapid, high‑yielding diazo transfer of aryl acetates. In addition, using the resin avoids isolation of hazardous tosyl azide, shortens reaction residence times (especially with Dowex resin), removes polar by‑products by passing the stream through an inline silica‑gel column before the Rh‑catalysed O‑H insertion, and allows the entire sequence (azide generation → diazo transfer → O‑H insertion) to be telescoped in continuous flow without any intermediate isolation, greatly improving safety and product quality.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Evidently, the presence of water in the reaction stream is detrimental for diazo transfer to ester 8 …” (sec 2.1). 
• “The use of aqueous sodium azide … is sufficient to reduce the basicity of DBU …” (sec 2.1). 
• “In order to overcome this challenge a new protocol for generation of tosyl azide in anhydrous acetonitrile … was developed … using an azide resin.” (sec 2.1). 
• “Two azide resins … were explored … the rate of formation … proved faster using the Dowex resin 16 than with the Amberlite resin 15.” (sec 2.1). 
• “The reaction outflow was passed through silica gel … to remove polar components … without noticeably impacting the downstream rhodium‑mediated reaction.” (sec 2.8). 
• “The crude product mixture from the flow process was much cleaner than that recovered from the comparable batch reaction.” (sec 2.6). 
• “The reaction was substantially increased at 35 °C … the reaction proceeded more rapidly at 35 °C … consequently, 35 °C was used for subsequent diazo‑transfer experiments.” (sec 2.1). 
• “Telescoping … without isolation of either tosyl azide 12 or α‑aryl‑α‑diazoacetate 9 … without ever isolating, handling, or indeed having significant amounts of either … present at any point.” (abstract & sec 2.8).
