Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: The original medicinal route required an excessive amount of palladium catalyst (20 mol %) for the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, gave poor reproducibility and low conversion, and the work‑up after the coupling produced a gelatinous mixture that hindered agitation.
Solution_Description: Catalyst screening identified PdCl₂(dt‑bpf) as an active, air‑stable catalyst that worked at 5 mol % loading with no loss of conversion, and the base was changed from Na₂CO₃ to K₃PO₄ to avoid gel formation during extraction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the medicinal synthetic reaction used 20 mol % of Pd(PPh₃)₄.” (Sec 2.2)
• “the reaction could not be reproduced in a satisfactory yield.” (Intro)
• “During liquid separation using EtOAc… the reaction mixture became gelatinous, which we considered to be a problem for agitation.” (Sec 2.2)
• “Evaluation of … PdCl₂(dt‑bpf) … The catalytic amount was reduced to 5 mol % without decreasing the reaction conversion ratio.” (Sec 2.2)
• “use of potassium phosphate instead of sodium carbonate improved the workup process without generating a gelatinous reaction mixture.” (Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: Reductive amination of intermediate 8 gave low and irreproducible yields, required the toxic chlorinated solvent CH₂Cl₂, and demanded three chromatographic purifications to remove residual amine.
Solution_Description: The reducing agent was switched to 2‑picoline‑borane, a stable crystalline reagent that works in THF (a non‑chlorinated solvent); the reaction was heated to 60 °C, cutting the time to 2 h, and the product was isolated by simple filtration/antisolvent crystallisation, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “reductive amination suffered from low yield and poor reproducibility, and use of dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂)… should be avoided.” (Intro)
• “NaBH(OAc)₃ is unstable to moisture and partially degraded during storage.” (Sec 2.5)
• “2‑picoline borane was suitable for this reductive amination reaction.” (Sec 2.5)
• “2‑picoline borane is a mild reducing agent, a very stable crystal, and is easy to handle on a pilot scale.” (Sec 2.5)
• “Using 2‑picoline borane in THF with AcOH, the residual starting material was reduced to 0.1 LC area %.” (Table 5, entry 3)
• “reaction time was shortened to 2 h by heating the reaction mixture to 60 °C.” (Table 5, entry 4)
• “No chromatographic purification was required” (Conclusion)

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: During the palladium‑catalysed hydrogenation of the benzimidazole‑2‑carboxylic acid intermediates 11 and 12, rapid decarboxylation occurred in polar solvents, leading to unwanted impurity peaks.
Solution_Description: The substrates were first converted to their sodium (or potassium) carboxylates using aqueous NaHCO₃ (or K₃PO₄) and the hydrogenation was performed under basic conditions; decarboxylation was completely suppressed and the desired product was obtained in ≈ 90 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “impurity peaks… increased… decarboxylated compounds of the starting material 12 and the target compound 11.” (Sec 2.2)
• “Compounds 11 and 12 were easily decarboxylated at room temperature in a polar solvent like DMSO.” (Sec 2.2)
• “decarboxylation was completely suppressed under basic reaction conditions.” (Sec 2.2)
• “Compound 12 was converted to sodium carboxylate by aqueous NaHCO₃ solution and hydrogenated to 11… No decarboxylated compound was observed under this basic reaction condition.” (Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: Boc deprotection with 5 equiv HCl in DMSO produced a highly viscous slurry that was difficult to stir; using TFA/CH₂Cl₂, while effective, introduced a corrosive, volatile solvent that caused hydrolysis of the product amine 8.
Solution_Description: The deprotection was performed with 4 equiv TsOH·H₂O in DMSO at 60 °C, and a co‑solvent MeCN was added to suppress hydrolysis; the solvent volume was reduced to increase productivity while maintaining clean conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “use of 5 equiv of HCl in DMSO immediately made the reaction solution too viscous to stir.” (Table 4, entry 1)
• “TFA in CH₂Cl₂ showed clean conversion…, but CH₂Cl₂ should be avoided… TFA is highly corrosive, volatile, and poses incineration problems due to the generation of HF.” (Table 4, entry 2)
• “prolonged reaction time caused hydrolysis of 8.” (Table 4, entry 3)
• “reaction proceeded smoothly by heating to 60 °C in DMSO with 4 equiv of TsOH·H₂O.” (Table 4, entry 3)
• “addition of MeCN was effective for suppressing hydrolysis of 8.” (Table 4, entry 4)
• “the solvent volume was reduced to increase productivity.” (Table 4, entry 5)

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: Residual palladium remained in intermediate 16 (78.7 ppm), exceeding acceptable limits for the API and requiring additional purification steps.
Solution_Description: A scavenger, N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine, was added together with silica gel to the reaction mixture; filtration removed palladium, reducing the residual level to < 10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The amount of residual palladium in 7 was reduced from 78.7 ppm in 16 to less than 10 ppm.” (Sec 2.3)\n• “The mixture was treated with 1 equiv of N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine, before adding NaOH for neutralization… One weight of silica gel was added… stirred for 1 h at 2.5 °C.” (Sec 2.3)\n• “N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine and silica gel were used to remove residual palladium.” (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Synthetic Route for the Adenosine Monophosphate-Activated Protein Kinase Activator, ASP4132
Problem_Description: The original route required three chromatographic purifications (for intermediates 6, 7, 10), which are time‑consuming and unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The new process telescoped the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling directly into the hydrogenation step without isolation, and all intermediates were isolated by simple filtration/antisolvent crystallisation, eliminating chromatography entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Three chromatographic purifications were needed to purify 6, 7, and 10 with good quality.” (Intro)\n• “The newly developed process includes an efficient telescoping process consisting of Suzuki–Miyaura coupling and hydrogenation.” (Abstract)\n• “No chromatographic purification was required in any step.” (Conclusion)

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: The preparation of nitroalkene 4 involves nitromethane, a flammable liquid that is shock‑sensitive and can explode at 230 °C, and the nitronate salt which is explosive when dry.  Accelerated‑rate calorimetry showed an exothermic onset at 174.9 °C for pure 4 and a large exotherm at 194.6 °C for the crude stream, creating a serious safety hazard on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow set‑up was implemented for the Henry reaction, base addition, aldehyde addition and acidic quench.  Flow operation limits the inventory of reactive intermediates, provides high‑intensity mixing with static mixers, and allows rapid heat removal, thereby containing the exotherm and eliminating shock‑sensitive bulk handling.
Supporting_Evidence: “the dry salt should not be isolated as it can be explosive… (ref 19)”; “Accelerated Rate Calorimetry showed that it is unstable at moderately high temperature, showing an exothermic onset temperature of 174.9 °C and eventually rupturing the test cell” (sec 2); “The potential hazards of this process can, therefore be mitigated by minimizing the inventory and quickly reacting product 4 onwards into the following organocatalytic reaction” (sec 2); “flow chemistry proved to be viable… high‑intensity mixing… high heat‑transfer capabilities” (sec 2).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: The bifunctional organocatalysts (structure 6) are expensive, and their high loading in literature (≥1 mol %) would make the overall pregabalin process cost‑uncompetitive.
Solution_Description: Screening identified quinidine‑derived squaramide 6i as the most active catalyst, permitting a loading as low as 0.2 mol % (vs 0.5 mol % for earlier catalysts) while maintaining >90 % ee.  The catalyst synthesis was also redesigned to be convergent and inexpensive.
Supporting_Evidence: “the economic viability of the whole process could be hampered by the non‑negligible cost of bifunctional catalysts 6” (intro); “catalyst 6i… full conversion in 18 h at a catalyst loading as low as 0.2 mol %” (sec 2.1); “cost‑efficient convergent synthetic route for organocatalyst 6i” (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: The first batch synthesis of nitroalkene 4 used acetic anhydride or triflic anhydride, both costly reagents and, in the case of acetic anhydride, a controlled substance, making the route unsuitable for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: A new continuous route was developed that replaces the anhydride‑mediated dehydration with a base‑catalysed Henry reaction followed by direct acidic quench using HCl, eliminating the need for acetic/triflic anhydride.
Supporting_Evidence: “This was a short‑term solution… the main two… cost of reagents and the fact that acetic anhydride is a controlled substance” (sec 2); “The chemistry detailed below is for a process carried out… final quench and dehydration to form nitroalkene 4 are exothermic” (sec 2); “flow chemistry was evaluated… individual process steps were all sufficiently fast” (sec 2).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: Nitroalkene 4 is a liquid that cannot be purified by crystallisation; it is unstable (exothermic onset > 170 °C) and prone to oligomerisation, which generates impurities that poison the downstream organocatalytic step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The crude product from the flow reactor is used directly after a simple aqueous bicarbonate wash, avoiding distillation.  High‑intensity mixing in the final quench step ensures rapid dehydration and minimizes polymer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The product is a liquid and, therefore, it cannot be purified by crystallization… its initial purification by distillation or chromatography is not scalable” (sec 2); “Crude 4 can be purified by distillation; however… the preference was to use the crude material in the organocatalytic step” (sec 2); “two liquid phases form… the lighter organic phase containing most of 4” (sec 4.1).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: The Henry reaction (nitromethane + aldehyde + NaOH) generates a very thick slurry that is difficult to stir, especially on scale, leading to poor mass transfer and problematic downstream acid quench.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent system of methanol / water was adopted to keep all components soluble, and static mixers were installed in the tubing to provide intensive mixing and avoid slurry formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the published process… resulted in the formation of a very thick slurry that was challenging to stir – a significant problem, especially on scale” (sec 2); “a more practical process using a mixture of methanol and water (to ensure solubility) was developed” (sec 2); “static mixers… high‑intensity mixing immediately at the joining of the two streams is important for high conversion and good yield” (sec 2).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: Residual acid or base remaining in the crude nitroalkene stream deactivates the organocatalyst and reduces enantioselectivity in the Michael addition.
Solution_Description: After the flow synthesis, the crude stream is neutralised with potassium bicarbonate and washed with water to remove any leftover acid/base before the organocatalytic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “the crude nitroalkene stream is neutralized with potassium bicarbonate followed by a water washing” (sec 2); “Residual acid will deactivate the organocatalyst, while residual base will reduce the enantioselectivity” (sec 2).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: Even with low catalyst loading, the high price of the chiral organocatalyst would still impact the economics of a high‑volume API like pregabalin; a minimum 50 % recycle was set as a target.
Solution_Description: An acidic ion‑exchange resin (Dowex Marathon MSC) is added after the reaction; the catalyst binds to the resin, the product is washed away, and the catalyst is released with methanolic ammonia, achieving ≈ 59 % recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “the resin had to not affect and bind the other reagents… Dowex Marathon MSC proved to be a successful candidate” (sec 2.6); “the catalyst was taken up in DCM and then recrystallized… 59 % assayed recovery” (sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: If nitroalkene 4 is added to the catalyst before the malonate, the catalyst is rapidly deactivated, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The protocol was changed so that the malonate is added to the catalyst first, followed by the nitroalkene, preventing catalyst deactivation and delivering reproducible high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the catalyst 6i is deactivated upon stirring with pure nitroalkene 4; it is therefore critical to add malonate 5 to the catalyst prior to the addition of 4” (sec 2.1); “chosen conditions… 0.5 mol % 6i, no solvent at 20 °C, for 24 h” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Asymmetric Organocatalysis and Continuous Chemistry for an Efficient and Cost-Competitive Process to Pregabalin
Problem_Description: Size‑exclusion membrane (OSN) recycling of the catalyst was investigated but required many stages, large solvent volumes, and suffered from oligomer fouling, making it economically unattractive.
Solution_Description: The OSN approach was abandoned in favor of the acidic‑resin catch‑and‑release method, which is simpler, cheaper and avoids membrane fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: “modeling calculations… showed that a membrane cascade technology was needed… rendered the OSN process noneconomically viable… oligomers would accumulate in the retentate and poison the catalyst” (sec 2.4); “the process appeared simple… resin was added… catalyst released by washing with ammonia” (sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Manufacturing Route for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: Uridine has low solubility in the acetonide‑formation step, leading to incomplete conversion (≈95 %) and up to 5 % uridine co‑crystallizing with the product, which reduces isolated yield to 70–75 %.
Solution_Description: A temperature‑induced dynamic crystallization was introduced: after heating to 55 °C to reach ≈95 % conversion, the slurry is cooled to 0–5 °C and an antisolvent (n‑heptane, 2 L kg⁻¹) is added, driving conversion >99 % and improving isolated yield to 91 % while using 14 % less solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Uridine has low solubility and would cocrystallize with 1, resulting in up to 5 % of uridine in the isolated solid.”; “The mixture is then cooled to 0–5 °C to perform the dynamic crystallization and increase conversion to >99 %… the addition of heptane (2 L/kg) … improves recovery.”; “Compared to the original process, the changes described here improved the yield by 1.3‑fold and resulted in 14 % less solvent use.”

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Manufacturing Route for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The ester‑intermediate (2) tends to crystallize during storage in ethyl acetate, causing a safety risk and causing ≈5 % loss during aqueous work‑up, lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: The solvent volume was reduced (8 → 5 L kg⁻¹), Et₃N, DMAP, and anhydride charges were lowered, and the aqueous work‑up was simplified to a single 2 L kg⁻¹ water wash. The product was azeotropically dried and transferred to MeCN (high solubility > 50 wt % at 20 °C) for the next step, eliminating precipitation hazards and improving overall productivity 1.5‑fold.
Supporting_Evidence: “The product was prone to crystallization upon storage as a solution in EtOAc, which was flagged as a significant risk for large‑scale manufacturing.”; “The aqueous workup was modified to a single 2 L/kg water wash… resulting in less than 2 % loss to the aqueous layer.”; “The EtOAc solution… switched to MeCN… provides much greater solubility… and does not pose a risk of precipitation upon storage.”

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Manufacturing Route for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The original triazole‑phosphate step generated a thick slurry of Et₃N·HCl, formed Et₃N‑adduct side‑products, required a multi‑day isolation sequence with large organic‑solvent waste, and posed exothermic hazards during POCl₃ dosing.
Solution_Description: The base was switched from Et₃N to DIPEA, giving a homogeneous reaction mixture with no slurry and eliminating the Et₃N‑adduct impurity. The product was isolated directly by water antisolvent crystallization, removing the multistep solvent‑switch work‑up and cutting the cycle time from ~10 days to a single operation while greatly reducing solvent waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “The formation of a thick slurry of Et₃N·HCl… was identified as a potential risk for large‑scale manufacturing.”; “To avoid the thick reaction slurry … the base was changed to DIPEA… the entire reaction sequence was homogeneous, and no amine adduct impurities were formed.”; “We explored options to directly crystallize 3a from the reaction mixture… avoids the use of excessive organic solvents and unit operations for the isolation.”

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Manufacturing Route for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The penultimate oxime formation used only 1.0 equiv of hydroxylamine in dilute MeCN, resulting in slow (>18 h) reactions, variable conversion, formation of a dimeric impurity, and required dangerous distillation of aqueous NH₂OH.
Solution_Description: Hydroxylamine loading was increased to 1.3 equiv and the reaction concentration raised to 2 L kg⁻¹ MeCN, giving complete conversion in 2–3 h. The product was isolated by direct water‑induced crystallization, avoiding any NH₂OH distillation and delivering a 10 % yield increase.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of an equimolar amount of NH₂OH not only resulted in slow reaction rates (>18 h) … and a dimeric impurity … was formed in significant levels.”; “We opted to increase the charge of NH₂OH to 1.3 equiv while also maximizing the reaction concentration at just 2 L/kg MeCN… complete conversion… in just 2–3 h.”; “The distillation of aqueous hydroxylamine is known to be dangerous, and thus, avoiding a distillation was deemed to be a necessary practice.”

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Manufacturing Route for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The final acid‑catalyzed deprotection was extremely sensitive to HCl amount and temperature, leading to over‑hydrolysis (10 % N‑hydroxycytidine, 3–5 % isobutyryl uridine), formation of a purple‑colored API due to trace iron, and large off‑gassing when quenched with NaHCO₃.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput screening identified robust conditions (0.85 eq HCl, 5 eq water, 8 L kg⁻¹ MeCN, 60 °C, 12 h) that gave ≥95 % conversion with minimal impurity. The quench was changed to 13.2 wt % Na₂CO₃ (reducing off‑gassing), and a 15 wt % Na₂SO₄/1 wt % Na₂EDTA wash removed iron and residual water. Crystallization was split into controlled azeotropic drying, seeding, and EtOAc addition, producing colorless API with consistent physical properties.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was extremely sensitive … resulting in significant rate and purity profile differences.”; “Two potential operating conditions were identified… the final reaction conditions use 0.85 eq of concentrated HCl, 5 eq of water, 8 L/kg MeCN … at 60 °C for ≈12 h.”; “The aqueous base used in the quench was changed from 5.3 wt % NaHCO₃ to 13.2 wt % Na₂CO₃… avoided the significant off‑gassing … and introduced less than one‑third the amount of water.”; “Iron could be completely sequestered … by incorporating Na₂EDTA in the first aqueous wash.”; “Crystallization of the majority of the API during the slow addition of EtOAc offers more control … and reliably affords high‑purity API.”

Paper Title: Scalable and Safe Transformation of 3‑Hydroxypropionitrile to Its Amidoxime
Problem_Description: Previously reported procedures for the synthesis of 3‑hydroxypropionitrile amidoxime gave either no reported yield, low isolated yields (47 % or 44 %), or required flash chromatography, making the processes irreproducible and unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a new, scalable route that adds 50 wt % aqueous NH₂OH dropwise to a cold (0 °C) solution of the nitrile, keeps the temperature below 7 °C during addition, and avoids any reflux heating, thereby eliminating the exothermic runaway and improving reproducibility and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Previously published procedures were either irreproducible and/or the processes were not practical on larger scales.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: THP is very soluble in water and requires ≥10 extractions with large volumes of CH₂Cl₂; 1,5‑dichloro‑3‑pentanone must be prepared from 3‑chloropropionyl chloride and ethylene in a gas‑liquid‑solid system that is difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned Strategy A and pursued alternative routes (Prins‑type cyclization) that avoid the gas‑liquid‑solid ethylene insertion and the extensive water extractions.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “THP 1 is very soluble in water and needs to be extracted at least 10 times using copious amounts of CH₂Cl₂.”
• “…the insertion of ethylene is carried out in a gas–liquid–solid system, which was expected to be very complex to scale up.”
• “We finally switched to the development of a Prins‑type cyclization…which was deemed more suitable for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: The use of TMDS as a reducing agent in Strategy B leads to a very tedious work‑up and poses safety concerns for large‑scale operations.
Solution_Description: Strategy B was discarded in favor of the Prins‑type cyclization route, eliminating the TMDS reduction step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The use of TMDS as the reducing agent makes the work‑up of this reaction very tedious and essentially ineligible for large‑scale applications.”
• “We finally switched to the development of a Prins‑type cyclization…which was deemed more suitable for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Strategy C involves manipulation of highly electrophilic compounds, which is considered undesirable from a health‑, safety‑ and environment (HSE) standpoint.
Solution_Description: The authors eliminated Strategy C and focused on the Prins‑type cyclization, a safer alternative.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The manipulation of these electrophilic compounds is not desirable from a HSE standpoint, so this route was not selected.”
• “We finally switched to the development of a Prins‑type cyclization…which was deemed more suitable for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: The first route to γ‑pyrone required a large excess of BF₃·OEt₂ and cryogenic conditions, making the process hazardous and costly.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the BF₃‑based route and pursued the Prins cyclization route.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The first step suffered from several drawbacks such as the use of a large excess of BF₃·OEt₂ and the need for cryogenic conditions.”
• “We successfully reproduced the procedures, but all our efforts to reduce the amount of Lewis acid and to perform the reaction under non‑cryogenic conditions failed.”
• “We finally switched to the development of a Prins‑type cyclization…which was deemed more suitable for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Electrochemical allylic oxidation of 3,4‑dihydropyran gave numerous side‑products; the enol ether was oxidized directly, leading to low selectivity and decomposition.
Solution_Description: The electrochemical approach was abandoned and the team moved to a Prins‑type cyclization to access the target.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “This approach failed to afford the targeted compound 11. The electron‑rich enol ether is prone to oxidation via direct electron transfer…resulted in the production of many products, none of which being the expected ketone 11.”
• “We finally switched to the development of a Prins‑type cyclization…which was deemed more suitable for scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Initial Prins‑type cyclization screenings with various additives (LiCl, Zn(OAc)₂, ZnCl₂, no additive) gave incomplete conversion and produced mainly the acetate side‑product 17.
Solution_Description: Switching to TfOH as a Brønsted acid catalyst gave higher conversion; triflate salts (Zn(OTf)₂, Sn(OTf)₂, Sc(OTf)₃) further improved selectivity; raising temperature from 80 °C to 100 °C increased reactivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When LiCl, Zn(OAc)₂, or ZnCl₂ was used, incomplete conversion was observed, and the major product was 3‑buten‑1‑ol acetate 17.”
• “By switching from Zn(OAc)₂ to Zn(OTf)₂, the targeted product 16 was obtained as the major compound.”
• “Other triflate salts…gave higher amount of 16.”
• “TfOH alone was found to be similarly effective…Increasing the amount of TfOH had no influence…Increasing the temperature from 80 to 100 °C had a beneficial effect on reactivity.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Isolation of acetate 16 required multiple solvent‑swap steps; repeated distillations in the presence of residual TfOH produced black sticky tars and reduced overall yield.
Solution_Description: A new isolation protocol was developed: first isolate acetate 16 by fractional distillation using a Raschig‑ring packed column with a high reflux ratio, then neutralize residual acid before downstream steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “These solvent‑swap had to be repeated four times to reach full conversion…degradation of the distillation residue…resulted in black sticky tars and a slightly lower yield.”
• “Distillation simulations…showed that a reflux ratio of not less than 5 was key…column packed with Raschig rings equipped with a reflux head…We were able to separate acetic acid (≤2 % w/w residual AcOH) and isolate a mixture…in 70 % yield.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Oxidation with TCCA/pyridine generates large quantities of cyanuric acid and pyridine‑hydrochloride salts, creating waste handling challenges and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the TCCA method with an Anelli‑type oxidation using solid calcium hypochlorite (low water content) and CH₂Cl₂ as the extraction solvent, eliminating massive salt waste.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The main drawback of this methodology is the production of large quantities of salts…would give a 3 L cake made of pyridine hydrochloride and cyanuric acid.”
• “Given the issues mentioned above, calcium hypochlorite (a solid oxidant containing only 5–10 wt % of water) was selected as the oxidant of choice in the Anelli‑type oxidation.”
• “The solvent selection was dictated by the partition coefficient…CH₂Cl₂ was the best solvent.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, treatment of the crude mixture with hot ethanol caused degradation, formation of polymeric by‑products, and raised safety concerns over possible alkyl‑sulfonate impurities.
Solution_Description: The authors eliminated the ethanol reflux with methane sulfonic acid; instead they isolated acetate 16 first, neutralized residual TfOH with aqueous NaOH, and performed fractional distillation using a high‑efficiency column.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The most problematic issue…is the use of refluxing ethanol in the presence of methane sulfonic acid…The scientific community and the regulatory agencies do have divergent opinions on the likeliness…of the formation of alkyl sulfonate impurities.”
• “Thus, we chose to isolate the acetate 16 first and to develop a separate cleaner and simpler water‑free deprotection protocol…by adding 1.25 equiv of 30 % aqueous NaOH to the reaction mixture.”
• “A reflux ratio of not less than 5…column packed with Raschig rings…We were able to separate acetic acid …and isolate a mixture of acetate 16 and THPol 2 in 70 % yield.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Zemplén transesterification with catalytic NaOMe caused a polymeric by‑product (Claisen‑type condensation of methyl acetate) that hampered distillation and lowered isolated yields to ~40–50 %.
Solution_Description: Addition of a small amount of concentrated HCl (0.38 equiv) efficiently quenched the base, stopped polymer formation, and allowed high‑yield distillation (90–95 % isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “…a yellowish polymer was formed…attributed to the further reaction of the catalytic amount of base with the by‑product methyl acetate in a Claisen‑type intermolecular reaction.”
• “Therefore, the neutralization of the catalyst was mandatory, and concentrated hydrochloric acid was added…The distillation was indeed more efficient and resulted in an isolated yield of 90–95 %.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydro‑4
Problem_Description: Initial calcium‑hypochlorite oxidation on 80 g scale gave only 90 % conversion and a low isolated yield of 46 % after tedious distillation.
Solution_Description: Optimized the reaction temperature to 5 ± 5 °C, added TEMPO in two portions (half at start, half after the first Ca(OCl)₂ addition), and used solid Na₂S₂O₄ to quench TEMPO, which together gave >99.5 % conversion and improved isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Only 90 % conversion was obtained, thus making the purification by distillation very tedious and resulting in a low 46 % isolated yield.”
• “Performing the reaction at 5 ± 5 °C and adding TEMPO in two portions were key to the success of this strategy (the first half of TEMPO was added at the beginning…second half after adding 0.3 equiv of calcium hypochlorite).”
• “A variety of reducing agents and quench conditions were assessed…solid sodium dithionite (Na₂S₂O₄) as the best reducing agent.”

Problem_Description: The fractional distillation of ketone 1 produced a highly exothermic decomposition of the residue starting at 130 °C, posing a safety risk.

Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: To overcome these problems the authors (i) identified a novel ω‑transaminase (ShdTA) that efficiently catalyzes kinetic resolution of rac‑2‑aminobutane at high substrate concentrations, providing a new biocatalytic route; (ii) shortened the reaction time for the 800 mM process to 2 h (vs. 5 h at lower concentration) to limit substrate inhibition; (iii) employed purified ShdTA (261 U, 6 mL) instead of crude cell‑free extract, raising the ee of d‑alanine to 99 %; (iv) coupled ShdTA with l‑threonine deaminase (TD) to generate 2‑ketobutyric acid in situ, avoiding the purchase of the expensive keto‑acid; (v) optimized the enzyme concentrations (TD 20 mg mL⁻¹, ShdTA 40 mg mL⁻¹) to achieve >98 % ee for (S)‑2‑aminobutane and >99 % ee for d‑homoalanine; (vi) maintained a 30 °C temperature and pH 8.0 buffer to keep the mixture fluid and used vigorous orbital shaking (200 rpm) to ensure adequate mixing at >800 mM substrate.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Because of the high solubility in water and high volatility of 1a, a high product concentration is necessary to facilitate effective isolation of product 1a. In this context, Paradisi et al. conducted the reductive amination of butanone… however, it is still a challenge to separate (S)‑1a and the excess isopropylamine." (Introduction) 2. "At higher concentrations (1000 and 1200 mM), lower conversions (47.9 % and 42.1 %) were obtained, which resulted in a decrease in the ee values of product 1a because the R enantiomer was not completely deaminated." (Results, Table 2) 3. "Although (S)‑1a with high optical purity could be obtained when crude ShdTA enzyme was used … the optical purity of d‑alanine was only about 90 % ee. In order to improve the optically purity of d‑alanine, purified ShdTA was applied…" (Results) 4. "…coupled with threonine deaminase (TD), which enabled the in situ generation of expensive 2‑ketobutyric acid from the bulk chemical l‑threonine…" (Introduction/Results) 5. "When a sufficient amount of ShdTA was used, the optical purity of (S)‑1a reached >98 % quickly, but otherwise, lower optical purity was observed… The final enzyme amounts were 20 mg mL⁻¹ TD and 40 mg mL⁻¹ ShdTA after optimization (Table 4)." (Results) 6. "The kinetic resolution of 1a at different concentrations was performed using 30 mg mL⁻¹ cell‑free extracts of ShdTA in potassium phosphate buffer (100 mM, pH 8.0) … at 30 °C." (Results) 7. "The preparative biotransformation … was carried out … stirred at 30 °C for 4 h. At the indicated time intervals, aliquots … were taken, quenched …" (Experimental Section).

Problem_Description: Wild‑type transaminases are strongly inhibited by both acetophenone and the product (R)‑α‑PEA, leading to severe loss of activity (e.g., >80 % inhibition at 12 g L⁻¹ product and complete loss at 20 mM acetophenone). • “Increasing the substrate concentration … allowed to reduce the enzyme concentration as much as possible.”
• “NOX‑34 … led to a > 10‑fold improvement in terms of the amount of enzyme necessary to achieve 50 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: 4‑Hydroxybenzoic acid (6) showed very poor solubility in isopropanol, in isopropanol/H₂SO₄ mixtures and in many other solvents, which caused frequent clogging of the feed lines and gave an unacceptably low product output (g · L⁻¹).
Solution_Description: The authors switched the starting material to methyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate (8), an ester that is far more soluble in isopropanol and compatible with the downstream saponification/decarboxylation steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “It soon became clear that the poor solubility of 6 at room temperature in isopropanol … will lead to either clogging and/or to an unacceptably low g/L output …”; “We then rationalized that the output could be significantly increased by using methyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate (8) considering its greater solubility in isopropanol …”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: Even after moving to methyl 4‑hydroxybenzoate, an almost‑saturated feed (≈2.2 M) tended to precipitate unless kept warm, and the high viscosity of the reacting mixture threatened clogging downstream.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The concentration was lowered to a stable 1.40 M solution of 8 in sulfuric acid/isopropanol, and toluene was added immediately after the reactor via a T‑mixer to reduce viscosity and keep the stream fluid.
Supporting_Evidence: “The second option was preferred … A cooled solution of 1.40 M of 8 in sulfuric acid and isopropanol was optimal to maximize the output.”; “The viscosity of the solution significantly increased … Hence, toluene was introduced via a T‑mixer … to avoid any clogging.”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: The addition of isopropanol to the hot sulfuric‑acid/8 mixture generated a strong exotherm that could lead to uncontrolled temperature spikes and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: Isopropanol was added at a controlled rate to a pre‑cooled acid‑substrate mixture, and the reactor temperature was carefully set (e.g., 56 °C for the 120 min residence) to keep the exotherm in check.
Supporting_Evidence: “The exotherm upon the addition of isopropanol to the sulfuric acid/8 mixture was well controlled …”; “The solution was then pumped into the reactor using an acid‑resistant syringe pump …”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: Increasing temperature or residence time beyond the optimal window caused decomposition of starting material and/or product, lowering assay yields; very short residence times gave poor conversion.
Solution_Description: Two optimized condition sets were identified: 56 °C for 120 min (high conversion with minimal decomposition) and 120 °C for 5 min (process intensification); these balance conversion, reaction time, and stability.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the temperatures as well as the residence time led to a decrease in the overall assay yield due to decomposition …”; “Our optimization led to two sets of conditions … 56 °C, 120 min … 120 °C, 5 min.”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: The decarboxylation step required a biphasic mixture; without an appropriate co‑solvent the system clogged and the reaction failed to proceed efficiently at high temperature.
Solution_Description: 2‑Ethoxyethanol was chosen as the organic co‑solvent/alcohol to act as a phase‑transfer agent, a 1:1 toluene/2‑ethoxyethanol mixture gave the best performance, and the amount of NaOH was increased to 6 equiv to drive complete decarboxylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The alcohol is needed to act as a phase‑transfer agent … 2‑ethoxyethanol emerged as the most suitable alcohol.”; “When the temperature was raised … near‑complete conversion … after increasing the amount of NaOH to 6 equivalents.”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: Attempts to recrystallize propofol as its DABCO complex failed to remove residual 2‑isopropyl‑ and 2,6‑diisopropyl‑phenol impurities, making it difficult to meet pharmacopeial purity (>99.5 %).
Solution_Description: The authors resorted to high‑vacuum fractional distillation after the telescoped two‑step flow process, which afforded propofol at 99.8 % purity and 49 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although fractional distillation is the method of choice … we also explored … DABCO complex. Unfortunately, it was not possible to successfully reduce the impurity level …”; “The oily residue was fractionally distilled … to provide propofol … ≥98 % purity.”

Paper Title: Process Intensive Synthesis of Propofol Enabled by Continuous Flow Chemistry
Problem_Description: Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive, causing incompatibility with PEEK flow‑line components and posing material‑degradation risks.
Solution_Description: All PEEK parts in contact with sulfuric acid were replaced by acid‑resistant PFA or glass components, and glass syringes with stainless‑steel plungers were employed.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sulfuric acid is highly corrosive so all the PEEK components were removed and replaced by acid compatible materials (PFA or glass). Glass syringes with a stainless‑steel plunger … were used.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: Pyridine was used as the original reaction solvent for the condensation of cytidine with DMF‑DMA, but it was deemed unsuitable for industrial application because of safety and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was switched from pyridine to tetrahydrofuran (THF). THF gave comparable yields (90 %) at 65 °C and eliminated the need for pyridine altogether, making the process safer and more amenable to scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Nevertheless, pyridine as a reaction solvent was not suitable for industrial application.”; “Accordingly, pyridine was not necessary for this reaction.”; “THF was considered as the optimal solvent for the condensation reaction of cytidine and DMF‑DMA.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: Intermediates 3 and 4 contain a dimethylaminomethylene (DMAM) group that is unstable, leading to decomposition of the intermediates during the sequence.
Solution_Description: Mild deprotection conditions were employed (i‑PrOH) to remove the DMAM group without affecting other functionalities, preserving the integrity of the intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: “intermediate 3 was unstable, which resulted from the instability of the dimethylaminomethylene (DMAM) at the 2′,3′-dihydroxyls.”; “intermediate 4 was also unstable due to the presence of DMAM.”; “Using methanol as the deprotecting agent … an attempt was made to deprotect DMAM of 4 with i‑PrOH, affording compound 5 smoothly.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: When the isobutyrylation was attempted directly after the condensation, the reaction failed because methanol generated in the first step remained in the mixture and interfered with the acylation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The crude reaction mixture was concentrated and subjected to a solvent‑exchange (two washes with CH₂Cl₂) to remove methanol before adding the acylation reagents, restoring a homogeneous, reactive medium.
Supporting_Evidence: “the acylation reaction did not work. Methanol that was generated from the condensation reaction was speculated to affect this reaction.”; “evaporation of the solvent and the process of solvent exchange with CH₂Cl₂ twice were indispensable when the condensation reaction was completed.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: The hydroxyamination step converting intermediate 5 to molnupiravir proceeded very slowly at 25 °C, giving poor conversion and requiring a long reaction time (≈18 h) for acceptable yield.
Solution_Description: The temperature was raised to 78 °C, which accelerated the conversion of intermediate 5 through 6 and 7 to the final product, delivering the desired yield within the same 18 h timeframe.
Supporting_Evidence: “the expected conversion of intermediate 6 to product 1 did not take place at 25 °C… the conversion of 5 to 1 required a long reaction time (∼18 h).”; “the hydroxyamination reaction was attempted at 78 °C, as reported in the literature.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: Hydroxylamine sulfate showed poor solubility in neat i‑PrOH, leading to low conversion (30 % yield) and longer reaction times when used as the nucleophile for hydroxyamination.
Solution_Description: A mixed aqueous solvent (70 % aq. i‑PrOH) was adopted, providing sufficient water to dissolve hydroxylamine sulfate while maintaining an organic environment, which gave the optimal 92 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield decreased to 30% … which resulted from the low solubility of hydroxylamine sulfate in i‑PrOH.”; “70% aq. i‑PrOH not only was the solvent of the hydroxyamination reaction but could also be used to remove the DMAM of 4.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: The esterification (isobutyrylation) of intermediate 3 proceeded very slowly and gave only 20 % yield in the absence of a catalyst.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount of 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) was added, which dramatically increased the esterification rate and restored the yield to 90 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the absence of DMAP, the isobutyrylation proceeded very slowly and incompletely (entries 1 and 2).”; “a catalytic amount of DMAP was necessary for this esterification.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: Performing the three‑step sequence (protection, esterification, deprotection) in separate vessels required multiple solvent exchanges and work‑ups, reducing overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: A telescoped one‑pot protocol was developed where each step was performed sequentially in the same reactor after appropriate solvent swaps, eliminating isolation of intermediates and streamlining the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “the method may be optimized for the one‑pot synthesis of molnupiravir.”; “the one‑pot process for preparing molnupiravir from cytidine was developed.”

Paper Title: “One-Pot” Synthesis of Molnupiravir from Cytidine
Problem_Description: After the final reaction, crude molnupiravir needed to be purified to pharmaceutical grade, and simple chromatography was impractical on large scale.
Solution_Description: The final product was isolated by crystallization from a mixture of i‑PrOH and tert‑butyl methyl ether (MTBE), delivering material of ≥99.7 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “product 1 … was obtained … crystallized from the mixture of i‑PrOH and tert‑butyl methyl ether (MTBE) (v_i‑PrOH/v_MTB = 1:3).”; “Molnupiravir with high purity (purity up to 99.7% … was obtained in a yield of 63% through crystallization.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: The first‑generation five‑step synthesis of 6‑fluoromenadione gave an overall yield of only ~9 % because the key cyclization step proceeded in very low yield, and it relied on dilauroyl peroxide, a hazardous peroxide that makes the process unsafe and unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation sequence was devised that avoids the peroxide step and instead uses a three‑step condensation/hydrogenation/cyclization cascade (aldol condensation of 4′‑fluoropropiophenone with glyoxylic acid, Pd/C hydrogenation, and PPA cyclization) to afford the tetralone in 59 % yield; the overall six‑step route to 6‑fluoromenadione was then streamlined to 50 % overall yield on a 25 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although this five‑step synthesis was elegant, the overall yield is only about 9 % due to the very low yield of the cyclization step… the use of dilauroyl peroxide, a known hazardous reagent, led to an unstainable method… (a) bromine, acetic acid… (b) potassium O‑ethyl xanthane… (c) dilauroyl peroxide… (d) PTSA… (e) PIDA… (low yields).”; “Through these three simple steps, it is possible to explore a library of new 7‑substituted 3‑methyltetral‑1‑one derivatives … in an overall yield of 59 %… Next, the synthesis was performed with only one purification step … overall yield of 50 %… scalability.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: The original route required chromatographic purification after each intermediate, which made scale‑up time‑consuming and wasteful.
Solution_Description: The improved process telescopes the sequence so that intermediates are not isolated; only a single flash‑chromatography step after the final oxidation is required, dramatically simplifying the work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Each step was followed by a chromatographic purification during the optimization of the methodology… Next, the synthesis was performed with only one purification step after the final oxidation to get 6‑fluoromenadione with an overall yield of 50 %.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: Cyclization of the acid intermediate with polyphosphoric acid (PPA) gave only 23 % yield even after 18 h at 90 °C.
Solution_Description: Switching to triflic acid (TfOH) and subsequently to a combination of TfOH with trifluoroacetic anhydride (TFAA) at room temperature increased the cyclization yield to 95 %.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 entries: “PPA, 90 °C, 18 h, 23 % yield” versus “TfOH, r.t., 4 h, 34 % yield” and “TfOH + TFAA, r.t., 1 h, 95 % yield.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: The radical‑addition/cyclization step in the first‑generation route employed dilauroyl peroxide, a peroxide that is prone to thermal runaway and poses significant safety hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: The peroxide‑based radical step was eliminated entirely in the second‑generation route, which proceeds via aldol condensation, hydrogenation, and acid‑mediated cyclization without any peroxide.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of dilauroyl peroxide, a known hazardous reagent, led to an unstainable method, when it comes to multigram‑scale synthesis… (ref 15 a,b).”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: During hydrogenation of brominated and chlorinated substrates (e.g., 4′‑bromopropiophenone), a mixture of inseparable products formed, with apparent substitution of the halide by hydrogen, leading to poor yields and reproducibility.
Solution_Description: An alternative Heck‑coupling sequence using 1‑bromo‑4‑iodobenzene (or 1‑chloro‑4‑iodobenzene) with 3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol, followed by oxidation, was employed to generate the required intermediates, bypassing the problematic hydrogenation step.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the hydrogenation step, a mixture of several inseparable products was obtained. The substitution of bromide/chloride atom by a hydrogen atom was observed… Another strategy was investigated following Sleebs et al.’s method… A Heck coupling between 1‑bromo‑4‑iodobenzene … was applied to form aldehyde 24e.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: PPA cyclization required 18 h at 90 °C and gave low yield (23 %).
Solution_Description: Moving to room‑temperature conditions with stronger acids (TfOH) and adding TFAA reduced reaction time to 1 h and raised yield to 95 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “PPA, 90 °C, overnight, 18 h, 23 % yield” vs “TfOH, r.t., 1 h, 95 % yield.”

Paper Title: Efficient Multigram-Scale Synthesis of 7‑Substituted 3‑Methyltetral-1-ones and 6‑Fluoromenadione
Problem_Description: The previously reported fac‑Ir(ppy)₃‑catalyzed photoredox route to the naphthol intermediate could not be reproduced under sustainable conditions.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the photoredox approach and instead used a bromination/aromatization sequence followed by oxidation with PIDA to obtain the target menadiones.
Supporting_Evidence: “A fac‑Ir(ppy)₃‑catalyzed photoredox process has recently been described … but its preparation has proved difficult in our hands under sustainable conditions.”

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: The original gold‑I‑catalyzed cyclization route gave a mixture of benzofuran and chromene products (≈2:1) that required chromatography for isolation and showed variable yields (62 % isolated on 20 g scale).  The high‑temperature steps used toxic N,N‑dimethylaniline and were difficult to scale safely.
Solution_Description: A second synthetic route was devised that employed a regioselective 5‑exo Claisen rearrangement performed in flow (Syrris Asia) to give a single trans‑DBF diastereomer, eliminating the need for chromatographic separation and avoiding the hazardous high‑temperature, toxic solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The authors described the substrate‑dependent formation of benzofurans, such as compound 5, as side products… a ∼2:1 benzofuran/chromene ratio … isolated in 62 % isolated yield on a 20 g scale" (Scheme 1 description).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: The Claisen rearrangement of ether 14 in N,N‑dimethylaniline at 194 °C gave variable yields on scale‑up and raised safety concerns because of the high temperature and toxic solvent.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified NMP (and Tamisolve) as safer, higher‑solubility media; the rearrangement was then executed in a 16 mL stainless‑steel coil flow reactor at 250 °C for 3.5 min, providing reproducible, safe conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "High‑temperature (194 °C) rearrangement in toxic N,N‑dimethylaniline … gave variable yields on scale‑up and presented safety issues." (Section 2, bullet list).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: Deoxo‑Fluor‑mediated fluorination of alcohol 19 to alkyl fluoride 27 was capricious (39–76 % yield), used a toxic, thermally unstable reagent, and produced multiple impurities.
Solution_Description: Five alternative fluorinating reagents were screened; XtalFluor‑M and PFBS gave the best performance (78–89 % HPLC yield).  PFBS was selected for further optimisation, reducing reagent equivalents and achieving 78 % isolated yield on 100 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Deoxo‑Fluor‑mediated fluorination was capricious, giving yields from 39 to 76 %… the reagent is toxic and thermally unstable." (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: Aminocarbonylation of bromide 19 in n‑butyl acetate gave moderate, variable yields and precipitated, blocking the CO inlet.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to 1,4‑dioxane (no solubility issues) and the catalyst loading of Pd(OAc)₂/Xantphos was increased to 5 mol % each, delivering 100 % conversion and 95 % isolated yield on 45 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Carbonylation of (±) 19 gave capricious yields… precipitation… blocked the gas inlet." (Section 2.3).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: On multigram scale the final product’s low solubility in CH₂Cl₂ made flash chromatography impractical, leading to poor recovery.
Solution_Description: A SiliCycle thiol‑modified silica scavenger (SiliaMetS‑Thi​ol) was employed to remove palladium, followed by simple trituration in EtOAc to afford the product in 83 % overall yield without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "While we had used flash chromatography at a small scale, we found that on scale, the solubility in the CH₂Cl₂ loading solvent was insufficient… a simple trituration of the crude material in EtOAc… delivered 98.5 g … 83 % from (±) 27." (Section 2.3).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of benzofuran 9 to cis‑DBF 10 failed under atmospheric H₂ pressure, giving no conversion.
Solution_Description: Using an H‑Cube flow hydrogenator at 70 bar/70 °C with a 10 % Pd/C catcart gave excellent yield; subsequent screening identified Pd/C 5R424 that worked at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, simplifying the operation.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Hydrogenation of benzofuran 9 … no reaction observed using palladium on carbon under a hydrogen atmosphere at atmospheric pressure. However, increasing the pressure and temperature to 70 bar and 70 °C … gave an excellent yield … A subsequent catalyst screen showed that hydrogenation could be carried out in high yield (95 %) using Pd/C 5R424 at atmospheric pressure and room temperature." (Section 2).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Tetrasubstituted Dihydrobenzofuran GSK973 Enabled by High-Throughput Experimentation and a Claisen Rearrangement in Flow
Problem_Description: Impurities in ether 14 batches caused inconsistent Claisen rearrangement performance.
Solution_Description: Problematic batches were reslurried with TBME, restoring consistent yields in the flow rearrangement.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "During the development of this process, the purity of ether 14 had a significant impact… resolved by a simple reslurry of the problem batch with TBME, which enabled reproducible yields for the Claisen rearrangement." (Section 2.1).

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: Scaling photochemical reactions is hampered by poor light penetration in larger vessels, secondary photoreactions that appear at long residence times, and difficulty controlling the heat generated by the light source.
Solution_Description: A modular continuous‑stirred‑tank (CSTR) platform equipped with dedicated LED photomodules provides a high surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio for better light penetration, and cooling by natural convection (enhanced with a fan) controls reaction temperature.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Well‑documented issues with scaling photochemical reactions, especially around light penetration into larger reaction vessels, secondary photoreactions at extended reaction times, and control of thermal effects …”
• “The dedicated photounits give a high radiant light output and offer easy and safe operation within the laboratory environment.”
• “Cooling is effected through natural convection around each photomodule unit and can be enhanced with a small external fan.”
• “The fReactor platform … shows high‑mass‑transfer characteristics.”
• “The modular nature of the system facilitates the simple integration of downstream reaction steps.”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: Many practical photochemical processes involve solid‑containing or poorly soluble reagents (e.g., inorganic bases, N‑bromosuccinimide), which are difficult to handle in traditional tubular flow reactors.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The 1.7 mL PEEK CSTRs contain a cross‑stirrer bar and four ports, allowing slurries to be pumped directly and providing intense mixing that keeps solids suspended and enhances mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...a pressing need for photochemical reactors capable of handling solid–liquid biphasic systems has been identified.”
• “Each reaction vessel (PEEK material, volume 1.7 mL) contains a single cross‑stirrer bar and is equipped with four standard ports … allowing flexibility in connecting reactors … and to feed sources, sampling ports and instrumentation.”
• “One of the advantages of CSTRs versus, for example, tubular reactors is the ease with which they can handle solid materials and slurries.”
• “The volume above the midline of the inlet to the CSTR is filled with gas, with liquid sitting below it … the impeller creates a less defined interface.”
• “The fReactor platform … shows high‑mass‑transfer characteristics.”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: When 4‑methoxytoluene is brominated under the standard acetonitrile conditions, unwanted electrophilic aromatic bromination competes with the desired benzylic bromination.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to dioxane suppresses the competing aromatic bromination and restores selectivity for the benzylic position.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In the case of 4‑methoxytoluene 1c, it was found that a solvent switch to dioxane was required to prevent significant competition from electrophilic aromatic bromination.”
• “We began by adopting conditions previously employed … a homogeneous solution of 1.05 equiv of NBS to 0.5 M methylarene (4‑methylacetophenone) in acetonitrile.”
• “Using two reactors … gave an 85 % conversion at steady state, with good selectivity for monobrominated product 2a (a small amount of 1,1‑dibrominated product was also observed).”
• “The more electron‑rich substrates 1b and 1c underwent faster reaction … similar conversions and selectivities … could be achieved at a higher flow rate …”
• “Solvent switch to dioxane … to prevent significant competition …”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) has a low solubility limit, restricting substrate concentration and thus limiting productivity in the benzylic bromination.
Solution_Description: The reaction is run as a slurry (heterogeneous feed) at four‑fold the normal substrate concentration; the CSTR’s vigorous stirring keeps the solid NBS suspended, delivering similar conversion with much higher throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We investigated the intensification of bromination reactions by carrying them out at concentrations higher than the solubility limit of NBS.”
• “Thus, pumping a 4‑fold more concentrated solution of the substrate toluenes 1a‑d through two photochemical reactor modules as a slurry with NBS led to generally similar steady‑state conversions … but with greatly improved productivity (up to 63 g h⁻¹).”
• “The general performance characteristics remove the requirement of specifying a reactor platform for a given combination of phases.”
• “One of the advantages of CSTRs versus, for example, tubular reactors is the ease with which they can handle solid materials and slurries.”
• “A solution containing substituted toluene (500 mM) and NBS (525 mM) was dissolved in the stated solvent… The slurry mixture was injected with constant stirring.”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: The batch photoredox‑catalyzed hydroamination of enecarbamates requires dilute conditions (50 mM), insoluble Ir photocatalyst (2 mol %), and a long reaction time (16 h), giving modest isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading is halved to 0.5 mol % (reducing cost and insoluble material), the solvent mixture is adjusted (20 % v/v THF/toluene or 20 % DCM/toluene) to increase catalyst solubility, substrate concentration is raised to 200 mM, and residence time is shortened to ~1 h by using continuous flow CSTRs.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The discovery‑scale batch reaction conditions represent a challenge … being dilute (50 mM in substrate), heterogeneous (partially insoluble photocatalyst at 2 mol %), and requiring long reaction times for completion (16 h).”
• “We reduced the catalyst loading to 0.5 mol % … to reduce both the cost and amount of insoluble material.”
• “Using 20 % v/v THF/toluene led to a 50 % conversion at 100 mM, but further intensification was not possible as the catalyst solubility limit in this solvent was reached.”
• “Using 20 % dichloromethane/toluene allowed further intensification to 200 mM.”
• “At a flow rate of 50 μL min⁻¹ (overall residence time ca. 1 h), we were able to achieve a steady‑state conversion to product 6a of 42 %, translating to a 37 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: Even after solvent optimisation, the Ir photocatalyst reaches its solubility limit, preventing further increase in substrate concentration for the hydroamination.
Solution_Description: Scale‑out is achieved by adding more CSTR modules (five reactors in series), allowing the same concentration to be processed at higher flow rates, boosting productivity without exceeding solubility limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Further intensification was not possible as the catalyst solubility limit … was reached.”
• “Using five reactors in series, enabling an increase in flow rate to 125 μL min⁻¹; conversion and isolated yield remained essentially unchanged, but productivity increased to ca. 3.7 g day⁻¹.”
• “The ease‑of‑use and flexibility of CSTRs … allow simple integration of downstream chemical transformations.”
• “We chose to use two reactors in sequence to demonstrate the performance of CSTRs in preparative reactions.”
• “The modular nature of the CSTR platform is the ease with which additional operations can be coupled…”

Paper Title: Readily Reconfigurable Continuous-Stirred Tank Photochemical Reactor Platform
Problem_Description: In the photoredox‑catalyzed decarboxylative oxidation, dissolved oxygen is the limiting reagent; using pure O₂ is hazardous, while air provides a safer but less efficient oxidant.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Air is used as the terminal oxidant (eliminating the need for pure O₂), and its flow rate is tuned to control dissolved O₂ concentration; the CSTR’s gas‑headspace design and vigorous stirring enhance gas‑liquid mass transfer, delivering high conversion and yield safely.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We adopted simplified conditions (alternative photocatalyst, no viologen salt additive, and use of air rather than oxygen as the source of terminal oxidant).”
• “The conversion was found to be dependent upon the air flow rate, indicating that the availability of dissolved oxygen was a limiting factor.”
• “In a gas–liquid system within the fReactors, the volume above the midline of the inlet to the CSTR is filled with gas, with liquid sitting below it (although in practice, the impeller creates a less defined interface).”
• “This represents a 5‑fold more productive reaction … using reaction conditions that are simpler (additive‑free) and safer (air vs oxygen as a terminal oxidant).”
• “The CSTR platform … is capable of handling common process‑relevant heterogeneous mixtures (solid–liquid, liquid–liquid, and gas–liquid).”

Paper Title: Modified and Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The sulfonyl chloride 2 is poorly soluble in water, requiring 15 mL H₂O · g⁻¹ of substrate.  The large water volume leads to formation of a hydrate of the sulfinate salt 3 and makes removal of water by evaporation difficult on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A THF co‑solvent is added to the aqueous reaction to keep the mixture homogeneous and avoid hydrolysis.  After reduction, the sulfinate is acidified and the resulting sulfinic acid 6 is extracted with MTBE, allowing the water volume to be reduced and eliminating the need for a dry‑down step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Because sulfonyl chloride 2 is of poor solubility in water, THF was used as a co‑solvent to make the reaction homogeneous…”.

Paper Title: Modified and Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The direct, heterogeneous reaction of sulfinate salt 3 with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) is inconvenient for monitoring and for purification of the sulfinyl chloride 4, especially on larger scales.
Solution_Description: The sulfinate salt is first acidified to the sulfinic acid 6, which is then reacted with SOCl₂.  Converting to the acid form makes the chlorination step homogeneous and simplifies work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “To avoid the heterogeneous reaction, we decide to convert sulfinate salt 3 to its acid form 6 first before its reaction with SOCl₂…”.

Paper Title: Modified and Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: A large excess of corrosive thionyl chloride is employed in the original route, raising safety concerns and increasing reagent cost.

Paper Title: Scaling up a C–H Borylation: Addressing the Safety Concerns of an Iridium-Catalyzed Process for Multikilo Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: HBpin (the stoichiometric by‑product) reacts rapidly with moisture or water in air to generate large volumes of flammable hydrogen gas (≈10.7 m³ for a 400 L batch), creating a serious fire/explosion hazard on scale.
Solution_Description: Increase the B₂pin₂ charge to >1 equiv (1.05 equiv in the final process) so that HBpin is consumed as a borylating agent rather than generating H₂; this eliminates hydrogen evolution during the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “The stoichiometric byproduct … HBpin … can react rapidly with … water … to generate hydrogen gas … for a typical 400 L batch … the stoichiometric quantity of HBpin formed (ca. 25 kg) would have the potential to release up to 10.75 m³ of hydrogen gas on contact with water.”; “When substoichiometric quantities of B₂pin₂ are used … gas evolution is clearly observed … confirmed to be hydrogen.”

Paper Title: Scaling up a C–H Borylation: Addressing the Safety Concerns of an Iridium-Catalyzed Process for Multikilo Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: Direct quenching of HBpin with methanol at –12 °C gave a biphasic mixture, raising mass‑transfer and manufacturability concerns, while the rapid H₂ evolution required careful control.
Solution_Description: Use a controlled, rate‑limited addition of ethanol (instead of methanol) as the quench agent; ethanol is fully miscible with heptane, giving a homogeneous solution and allowing precise control of H₂ release via the addition profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “The safest, most reliable, and effective approach to quenching the residual HBpin … was therefore a controlled addition of a reactive substance, such as alcohol … Anhydrous methanol was found to be an effective quenching agent … however, on completion … two phases were present … Isopropanol … much slower … Ethanol … reaction rate … similar to methanol, but its increased miscibility with heptane allowed for a homogeneous solution at the end of the quench.”; “Hydrogen generation commences simultaneously with the start of the ethanol addition … the addition time of ethanol can be modified to control the rates of both energy and hydrogen release.”

Paper Title: Scaling up a C–H Borylation: Addressing the Safety Concerns of an Iridium-Catalyzed Process for Multikilo Scale Manufacture

Supporting_Evidence: “Further rounds of HTE demonstrated that the reaction performed efficiently … with a dramatic 20‑fold reduction in catalyst loading to 0.0125 mol % … the higher catalyst loading of 0.025 mol % … was employed for further development to mitigate … catalyst deactivation.”; Table 2: “loading of [Ir(COD)Cl₂]₂ and ligand reduced by 10× to 0.025/0.05 mol % … 10‑fold reduction in the use of catalyst and ligand gives environmental and economic improvements.”

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder
Problem_Description: Catalyst deactivation during continuous operation caused a steady decline in citral conversion (from ~100 % to ~60 %) and a drop in menthol selectivity (≈75 % to ≈74 %), indicating loss of active metal and acidic sites over time‑on‑stream.
Solution_Description: A semi‑empirical kinetic model incorporating exponential decay functions for metal and acidic site deactivation (α₁ and α₂) was developed, allowing prediction of performance loss and enabling future catalyst design to mitigate deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: "The time‑on‑stream conversion of citral, which was initially complete, decreased to ca. 60 %… simultaneously high selectivity to menthols (above 70 %)… decreased because of lower conversion." (sec 3.1, Conclusions) ; "The term α₁ reflects catalyst deactivation… modeled… by introducing an exponential decay function of metal sites with TOS" (eq 4) ; "The citral conversion as a function of time‑on‑stream at different temperatures… also demonstrates catalyst deactivation visible through a decrease of the conversion with time‑on‑stream" (sec 2.3, Fig 11).

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder
Problem_Description: Metal leaching (Ni loading fell from 4.76 % to 4.55 % in powder and from 6.30 % to 5.95 % in extrudates) and pore blockage by the sepiolite binder reduced surface area and pore volume, diminishing catalytic activity.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was shaped into extrudates using sepiolite as an inorganic binder, which provided mechanical strength and maintained the mesoporous structure while limiting Ni loss and pore blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: "Nickel loading decreased during citral transformations… 4.76 % → 4.55 % (powder) and 6.30 % → 5.95 % (extrudates)… due to insignificant metal leaching" (sec 2.1, Table 1) ; "The decrease of the surface area from 337 to 149 m² g⁻¹… can be assigned to sepiolite that clogged pores…" (sec 2.1) ; "The mechanical strengths of extrudates were determined to be 32 ± 7 and 4 ± 1 bar… relatively high compared to the mechanical strengths of aluminosilicate extrudates… attributed to the sepiolite binder" (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder
Problem_Description: Batch experiments with 5 wt % Ni/MAS powder gave low overall menthol yield (≈6 %) and high formation of defunctionalized products (≈78 % selectivity) due to insufficient hydrogenation of intermediates and rapid side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: Switching to a continuous trickle‑bed reactor with shaped Ni/(MAS+sepiolite) extrudates and operating at 70 °C improved menthol selectivity to ≈75 % and overall yield to 63 %, while minimizing pressure‑drop problems of powder beds.
Supporting_Evidence: "The catalytic results from a batch experiment… selectivity to menthols after 5 h were only 6 %… high selectivity to DFP products can be explained by… larger Ni particle size" (sec 2.2) ; "One‑pot citral transformation experiments… demonstrated rather high citral conversion and exceptionally high selectivity to menthols of ca. 75 %… yield of menthols of 63 %" (sec 2.3, Fig 7) ; "Continuous menthol production from citronellal requires utilization of either shaped catalyst bodies or structured reactors to avoid high pressure drop…" (sec 1).

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder
Problem_Description: The literature lacked any kinetic analysis of the one‑pot citral‑to‑menthol transformation, making scale‑up predictions and catalyst optimisation difficult.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive kinetic model (including hydrogenation, cyclisation, side‑reactions and deactivation) was built and fitted to batch and continuous data, achieving a 97.1 % degree of explanation, thus providing a quantitative tool for future process development.
Supporting_Evidence: "Kinetic analysis was absent for citral transformations to menthol… the aim of this work was… develop a kinetic model…" (sec 3) ; "The model… gave a reliable description of experimental data… degree of explanation equal to 97.1 %" (sec 3, Fig 14).

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder
Problem_Description: Larger Ni particle sizes in the powder catalyst (≈13 nm) correlated with lower menthol selectivity and higher defunctionalization compared with smaller particles in extrudates (≈9 nm).

Paper Title: Citral-to-Menthol Transformations in a Continuous Reactor over Ni/Mesoporous Aluminosilicate Extrudates Containing a Sepiolite Clay Binder

Solution_Description: The reaction was run in a biphasic mode with controlled addition of TCCA, and the temperature was kept at 22–25 °C using an incubator bath; the contact time was limited to 5 min to avoid excessive heat and solid buildup.
Supporting_Evidence: “After the addition, a rise of temperature (roughly up to 40 °C…) and the reaction lasted around 3 to 5 min from the moment when the exothermicity and the precipitate (cyanuric acid) started to form.” (Results and Discussion, solvent screen).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: During quenching with HCl the cyanuric acid precipitated, risking solid accumulation and clogging of the small‑diameter coil.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Engineered a tee‑piece mixer with a drilled axial hole to allow the acid stream to pass through a PEEK tube, preventing solid buildup in the mixer walls.
Supporting_Evidence: “A simple modification of the mixer can be engineered to allow a contact interface axial to the tubing…a tee‑piece connector was drilled to create a 1.6 mm diameter thru hole…Using this setup the flow system was run repeatedly for over 8 h…without any issue.” (Flow‑system design).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: A significant portion of the starting material was lost to the aqueous phase after quench, leading to inconsistent yields and the need to separate an additional by‑product (2‑hydroxyaniline).
Solution_Description: Increased NaOH to 4 equiv, ensuring complete deprotonation of the substrate and suppressing aromatic chlorination, which raised the isolated yield of 4 to 73.5 % and reduced the amount of chloro‑phenol impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “4 equiv of sodium hydroxide was thought to be required to avoid chloro‑phenol 2 formation…a significant increase in the conversion to the desired product 4 was observed when 4 equiv of NaOH was employed (73.5 % yield).” (Table 2, entry 5).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: When 4 equiv NaOH were used, a new chlorinated by‑product (5) started to appear, complicating purification and lowering the overall yield of 4.
Solution_Description: Reduced residence time from 5 min to 2.5 min, which minimized formation of by‑product 5 and improved the proportion of 4 in the product mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “A new chlorinated byproduct 5 started to form, which increased when lowering the residence times to 2.5 min…Slightly changing the equivalents of the base did not change the yield of 4 ; however, it strongly influenced the composition of the final mixture.” (Table 2, entries 5‑6).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: At higher substrate concentrations (1.5 M) the starting material showed evidence of hydrolysis over prolonged processing, limiting the achievable concentration.
