Solution_Description: Implemented a four‑pump input system (dual NaOH streams, separate TCCA/EtOAc stream) to allow rapid mixing, easy flushing and maintain high concentration without excessive hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “To increase the throughput…a more concentrated solution…1.5 M was found to be the highest concentration to avoid precipitation…Working on such high concentrations was noted to be detrimental to the starting material 1, which showed evidence of hydrolysis…Consequently, we modified the flow setup to become a four‑pump input system.” (Scale‑up section).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: Increasing the total flow rate to 10 mL min⁻¹ (to improve turbulence) did not improve conversion, indicating a mixing limitation rather than residence‑time effect.
Solution_Description: Raised the substrate concentration to 1.5 M and reduced residence time to as short as 0.5 min, achieving >96 % yield and >95 % purity, thereby overcoming the mixing bottleneck.
Supporting_Evidence: “In an attempt to improve the contact surface area…no improvement was obtained…Therefore, we decided to test the scale‑up and concentration of the reaction…after 30 s, the desired material was obtained in over 96.3 % yield (>95 % purity).” (Table 3, entry 1).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Hofmann Rearrangement Using Trichloroisocyanuric Acid for the Preparation of 2‑Benzoxazolinone
Problem_Description: Chlorination of product 4 to obtain 5 gave moderate isolated yields (51 % – 81 %) and required careful purification to remove cyanuric acid and residual TCCA.
Solution_Description: Employed an excess of TCCA (0.66 equiv) together with a concentrated HCl quench (2.6 equiv) to selectively N‑chlorinate 4, followed by filtration and recrystallisation, delivering 5 in up to 81 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of 2.6 equiv of a concentrated HCl solution…resulted in the formation of a white suspension…The material isolated in 51 % yield and 92 % purity…An improved isolated yield of 81 %…was achieved when the equivalents of TCCA (0.66 equiv) were doubled.” (Table 4, entries 2‑3).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: Traditional hydrocyanation uses HCN, a highly volatile, toxic, explosive and corrosive gas.  The HCN concentration required for effective catalysis also leads to catalyst poisoning via formation of an inactive nickel‑dicyanide species, which compromises conversion and scale‑up reliability.
Solution_Description: The authors replace toxic HCN with commercially available aliphatic nitriles (e.g., isovaleronitrile or butyronitrile) as sacrificial HCN donors.  The nitrile coordinates to a cocatalytic Lewis‑acid (AlMe₂Cl) that both activates the C–CN bond of the donor and reduces the Ni(II) precatalyst in situ, keeping cyanide concentrations low enough to avoid nickel‑dicyanide formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...HCN‑free transfer hydrocyanation of alkenes and alkynes that employs commercially available aliphatic nitriles as sacrificial HCN donors...” (Abstract); “...the use of highly volatile HCN in laboratory‑scale settings has been limited due to its extreme toxicity, as well as its explosive and corrosive nature.” (Introduction); “...the demand for careful adjustment of the HCN concentration to avoid catalyst poisoning through the formation of an inactive nickel dicyanide species...” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: The original protocol relied on an air‑ and temperature‑sensitive Ni(0) precatalyst (Ni(cod)₂) that required glove‑box handling and special storage, making the process operationally cumbersome and increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: NiCl₂ (Ni(II)), an inexpensive and air‑stable precatalyst, is employed together with the bidentate ligand DPEphos.  This catalyst can be weighed and set up on the benchtop under a simple nitrogen atmosphere, eliminating the need for glove‑box equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: “In our original report, the transfer hydrocyanation reaction relied on a Ni‑(cod)₂, a Ni(0) precatalyst… handling of the Ni(0) precursor is not trivial… since it is especially sensitive toward oxygen and prone to thermal decomposition… we therefore aimed to establish a more user‑friendly protocol… utilizing an inexpensive and air‑stable Ni‑(II) precursor.” (Introduction); “An inexpensive and air‑stable NiCl₂ precatalyst… the reaction could be set up on the benchtop, without the requirement for any special equipment (e.g., glovebox).” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: Using AlCl₃ as the Lewis‑acid cocatalyst gave only trace conversion (13 % GC conversion, 0 % yield) because AlCl₃ cannot deliver the alkyl groups required for the sequential transmetallation steps that reduce Ni(II) to the active Ni(0) species.
Solution_Description: Alkyl‑aluminum Lewis acids (AlMe₂Cl, Al(iBu)₂Cl, Al(iBu)₃) are employed.  Their alkyl groups enable two successive transmetallation steps to generate a dialkylnickel(II) intermediate that undergoes reductive elimination to the active Ni(0) catalyst, restoring catalytic activity and giving quantitative yields.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 6 – “AlCl₃ instead of AlMe₂Cl … 13 % conversion, 0 % yield.”; “… only alkyl‑aluminum Lewis acids such as AlMe₂Cl, Al(iBu)₂Cl, and Al(iBu)₃ successfully facilitated the transfer hydrocyanation reaction with a NiCl₂ precatalyst.” (Results and Discussion, §3.1).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: Initial scale‑up experiments at 5 mm using 23 equiv of butyronitrile (0.50 M solution) required 2.5 mol % Ni catalyst to obtain quantitative GC yield.  When the catalyst loading was reduced, conversion and isolated yield dropped dramatically.
Solution_Description: The excess of the nitrile donor was lowered to 11.5 equiv (1.0 M solution) and the Ni catalyst loading was reduced to 1 mol % while maintaining excellent GC yields (≈ quantitative) and an isolated 79 % yield on a 100 mmol scale.  The adjustment of reagent stoichiometry and reaction concentration restored high productivity with less catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “...initial experiments to reduce the catalyst loading… led to a significantly diminished conversion and product yield… Gratifyingly, reducing the excess of butyronitrile (11.5 equiv, corresponds to a 1.0 M solution of substrate in butyronitrile) afforded the desired product in excellent GC yields using only 1 mol % of Ni catalyst.” (Results and Discussion, §3.3).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: Typical hydrocyanation reactions require a separate solvent (toluene) in addition to the nitrile donor, increasing solvent waste and processing cost.  Moreover, the presence of two liquid phases can complicate mixing on larger scale.
Solution_Description: When butyronitrile is used in large excess (≥ 11.5 equiv) the reaction can be performed neat, i.e., without any added solvent, simplifying work‑up, reducing waste, and lowering cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “When using more inexpensive butyronitrile as a reagent, the need for an additional solvent could be circumvented by increasing the amount of the butyronitrile donor used.” (Results and Discussion, §3.1); “The decagram scale reaction was performed on the benchtop… using a standard, two‑necked round‑bottom flask.” (Scale‑up of the Transfer Hydrocyanation Reaction, §3.3).

Paper Title: Development of an Operationally Simple, Scalable, and HCN-Free Transfer Hydrocyanation Protocol Using an Air-Stable Nickel Precatalyst
Problem_Description: Even though HCN is not generated in detectable amounts, the handling of aluminum‑based Lewis acids (AlMe₂Cl) and nitrile donors still requires proper personal protective equipment and ventilation due to their toxicity and flammability.
Solution_Description: The authors explicitly state that all operations should be performed in a well‑ventilated fume hood with appropriate safety gear, reinforcing standard laboratory safety practices for the reagents used.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although highly toxic HCN was never observed in significant amounts under our transfer hydrocyanation conditions, appropriate safety measures should nevertheless be implemented.  The handling of all reagents requires the practitioner to wear appropriate safety equipment, and all operations should be executed in a well‑ventilated fume hood.” (Precaution, §2.2).

Paper Title: Leveraging High-Throughput Experimentation to Drive Pharmaceutical Route Invention: A Four-Step Commercial Synthesis of Branebrutinib (BMS-986195)
Problem_Description: The original discovery route was linear (nine steps from commercial nitroarene, seven from a bulk intermediate) and required a lead‑time almost as long as the interval between clinical deliveries, leaving only a very short window to decide on a new route.
Solution_Description: A parallel high‑throughput‑experiment (HTE) campaign was launched to evaluate shortened variants and entirely new disconnections.  This effort identified a four‑step, high‑yielding commercial route that could be developed in the available time window.
Supporting_Evidence: “The linear nature of the synthesis introduced a significant challenge from a timeline perspective.”;

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: During GMP Step 1‑1, two ester‑type by‑products (11a and 11b) were formed in appreciable amounts (up to >30 % HPLC area) when the reaction was run for long times, at 20–25 °C and with ~10 % HCl in 1,4‑dioxane. The impurity formation reduced the isolated yield of the desired product (90–96 %).
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to 15 °C, the HCl/1,4‑dioxane concentration was fixed at 20–22 % wt and the reaction was quenched as soon as conversion was complete (<1 % residual starting material). The crude mixture was then crystallised directly from DCM/MTBE, which removed both esters to <1 % level and gave the product in 90–96 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Impurity 11a can reach >30 % HPLC area percentage in the reaction mixture with prolonged reaction time, 20–25 °C reaction temperature, and ∼10 % HCl concentration (Table 1).”
• “To minimize impurity formation, the reaction temperature was maintained at 15 °C, and 20–22 % HCl/1,4‑dioxane was used … both ester impurities (11a and 11b) were kept at <1 % after an effective crystallization in dichloromethane (DCM)/MTBE.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: In the final de‑protection of the Boc group to give 8‑HCl (Step 8‑3), prolonged reaction times (>10 h) or temperatures above 30 °C caused partial removal of the Cbz protecting group, generating impurity 8e.
Solution_Description: The de‑protection was performed at controlled low temperature (≤30 °C) and the reaction time was limited to the minimum required for complete Boc removal, thereby suppressing formation of the Cbz‑deprotected impurity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Partial removal of the Cbz protecting group to give the impurity 8e … was observed during prolonged reaction times (>10 h) or at high temperature (>30 °C).”
• “To control this undesirable side reaction, which impacts downstream chemistry, temperature, reaction time, and workup are carefully controlled and monitored.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: During the coupling of 5‑O‑tBu/HCl with (S)‑Cbz‑Val (Step 10‑1) a γ‑lactam impurity (10e) formed by intramolecular cyclisation, reducing the isolated yield of the desired product (≈75 %).
Solution_Description: The coupling reagent was changed to CMPI (2‑chloro‑1‑methylpyridinium iodide) and the reaction was run in DMF with controlled base (DIPEA). Alternative coupling reagents (EDCI, HATU) were screened but gave inferior results, confirming CMPI as optimal for suppressing lactam formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The γ‑lactam major impurity 10e … was formed by intramolecular cyclisation of 5‑O‑tBu/HCl in the presence of base.”
• “Other coupling reagents such as EDCI and HATU were also screened, but all gave inferior results.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: In GMP Step 1‑3, hydrolysis of intermediate 13 to 13a and Cbz‑deprotection to 13b increased dramatically with longer reaction times, higher temperatures and higher HCl equivalents, leading to up to >2 % impurity levels.
Solution_Description: The reaction was limited to 2–3 h, temperature was kept at 10–15 °C and HCl/1,4‑dioxane stoichiometry was set to 5.0 equiv. Under these conditions both 13a and 13b were kept below 2 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Longer reaction time, higher temperature, and higher concentration of HCl promoted the undesired side reactions (Table 3).”
• “The optimal reaction conditions (2–3 h, 10–15 °C, 5.0 equiv of HCl/1,4‑dioxane) … resulted in fast completion with minimum (<2.0%) formation of the two by‑products.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: During GMP Step 1‑4, three specified impurities (14a – hydrolysis of 14, 14b and 14c – fate impurities from previous steps) appeared at 0.2‑1 % levels, causing inconsistent impurity control and affecting overall product purity.
Solution_Description: A slight excess of 11‑HCl (1.05 equiv) was used to drive the coupling to completion while excess free base was removed by basic wash, eliminating basic aqueous work‑up that forms 14a. Impurities 14b/14c were controlled upstream. Crystallisation was optimised using EtOAc (6 vol) with antisolvent heptane, achieving >98 % purity and <0.2 % impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A slight excess of 11‑HCl (1.05 equiv) increased the conversion of 13‑HCl …”
• “Formation of impurity 14a is best controlled by avoiding basic aqueous workup. Impurities 14b and 14c are best controlled in the upstream steps …”
• “After a solvent volume screen … it was found that 6 vol of EtOAc provided an optimal result … impurity levels <1.0 % …”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: The final warhead 1‑TFA has very low solubility in most organic solvents, making isolation and purification difficult and requiring a robust crystallisation protocol to obtain a high‑purity product.
Solution_Description: A two‑stage crystallisation was developed: the mono‑TFA salt was generated in IPA, then TFA/IPA was added slowly at 5 °C to induce precipitation of the di‑TFA salt, followed by a second addition at 35 °C. This controlled cooling and solvent composition gave the product as an off‑white solid with >98 % purity and 79 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Due to its stability characteristics, low solubility in the reaction solvent (IPA), and ease of process control, XMT‑1864 was isolated as a bis‑TFA salt (1‑TFA).”
• “A two‑stage crystallization process was developed … 5 °C … then heated to 35 °C … solids formed … filtered … affording 0.73 kg of 1‑TFA … 98.0 % LCAP in 79 % yield.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: The initial Cbz de‑protection required high‑pressure hydrogen (>20 psi), which is not readily available at many CDMOs and poses safety concerns for large‑scale processing of a highly potent compound.
Solution_Description: The de‑protection was re‑optimized to run at atmospheric hydrogen (1 atm) using 10 % Pd/C, completing in <5 h. This eliminated the need for high‑pressure equipment and improved scalability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The initial Cbz deprotection reaction required high‑pressure H₂ (>20 psi). … could not be easily implemented on scale, as there are a limited number of CDMOs …”
• “The current reaction is run at 1 atm H₂, and the reaction proceeds to completion in less than 5 h.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: Penultimate intermediate 14 contained baseline impurities that could not be removed by crystallisation alone; impurity levels varied (0.2‑1 %).
Solution_Description: A short silica‑gel column chromatography step (≈5 % product loss) was introduced before the final crystallisation, reducing all three specified impurities by >50 % and allowing the subsequent recrystallisation to achieve <0.2 % impurity levels and >98 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “It was found that the use of silica gel chromatography to remove baseline impurities, prior to the crystallization, significantly enhanced the effectiveness of crystallization for penultimate impurity control.”
• “Impurity levels were first reduced by >50 % after column purification … and further reduced to <0.5 % after crystallization … >98 % purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Conjugate Warhead: Auristatin F‑HPA-Ala/TFA (XMT-1864/TFA)
Problem_Description: Frequent use of column chromatography on kilogram‑scale batches increased material cost and process time, conflicting with the objective to eliminate chromatography where possible.
Solution_Description: Where feasible, reactions were telescoped (e.g., the Cbz de‑protection of 10 followed immediately by coupling with dimethyl‑L‑valine) without isolation, reducing the number of work‑ups and chromatography steps, thereby lowering cost and improving throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The coupling of 10‑c … was telescoped and reacted with dimethyl‑L‑valine to afford 10.”
• “Improvement of process efficiency by reduction and/or elimination of purification by column chromatography.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route relied on a Buchwald‑Pd‑catalyzed C–O coupling of aryl chloride 11 with alcohol 12 to give the penultimate intermediate 13. On scale this step delivered only 12 % isolated yield and ~90 % purity after reverse‑phase preparative HPLC, making the route impractical for >80 g production.
Solution_Description: A completely new convergent synthesis was devised in which phenol 17 is coupled with the enantioenriched 1,2‑cyclic sulfamidate 18 via nucleophilic cleavage, bypassing the low‑yielding C–O coupling altogether.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “the essential C–O coupling of 11 and 12 provided 13 in only 12 % yield and with approximately 90 % purity after reverse phase preparative HPLC purification.”
- “The key strategy developed for this route involved the nucleophilic cleavage of 1,2‑cyclic sulfamidate 18 with phenol 17.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The discovery route employed a stoichiometric oxidation of olefin 6 with osmium tetroxide (OsO₄) and sodium periodate. OsO₄ is extremely toxic, volatile and expensive, making it unsuitable for kilogram‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The oxidative cleavage step was eliminated by redesigning the sequence: ethyl 4,6‑dichloronicotinate 28 was reduced directly to the alcohol 29, which then entered the amide‑formation/Suzuki sequence, avoiding OsO₄ altogether.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Second, stoichiometric amounts of OsO₄ were used for the oxidative cleavage of olefin 6. This reagent should be avoided in large‑scale preparation due to its extremely toxic, hazardous, expensive, and volatile nature.”
- “To circumvent the difficulty in selectively reducing the ester 20… the strategy of first reducing 28 to alcohol 29… proved to be successful and scalable.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The original route required the vinylboronic anhydride pyridine complex 5, a very expensive reagent with limited commercial availability, driving up material cost and supply risk for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the use of 5 by a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of intermediate 21 with the readily available boronic acid 23, which is inexpensive and commercially stocked, thereby removing the costly reagent from the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Third, vinylboronic anhydride pyridine complex 5 is very expensive with limited availability.”
- “The Pd‑(dppf)‑Cl₂‑catalyzed Suzuki coupling of chloride 21 with boronic acid 23 afforded ester 20 in 94 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The original penultimate chiral resolution discarded roughly half of the material, resulting in a low overall material throughput and waste of valuable intermediate 13.
Solution_Description: An enantioselective synthesis of the sulfamidate 18 was developed, followed by chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) to isolate the (S)-enantiomer in high purity, eliminating the 50 % loss associated with classical resolution and providing >500 g of optically pure 18 in three batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Finally, it is inefficient to perform chiral resolution at the penultimate step as half of the material will be discarded.”
- “Over 500 g of optically pure 18 was prepared by this process in just three batches.”
- “The racemate 37 was resolved by chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC)… to give the desired enantiomer 18.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Selective reduction of ester 20 to the alcohol 19 proved problematic; NaBH₄ gave deacetylated side‑product, LiAlH₄ reduced the amide, and even LiBH₄ gave only 60 % yield on 3 g scale and 40 % on 15 g scale, with a substantial amount of deacetylated alcohol formed.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was redesigned: ethyl 4,6‑dichloronicotinate 28 was reduced with NaBH₄ to alcohol 29, then amidated, Suzuki‑coupled and finally reduced, giving the target alcohol 19 in consistently high yields (≈75 % isolated) without loss of the acetyl group.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Using NaBH₄ in a mixture of MeOH and THF… no desired product 19 was detected… a substantial amount of deacetylated product was formed.”
- “On a 3 g scale, 19 was isolated in 60 % yield. On a 15 g scale, the isolated yield reduced to 40 % with a concomitant increase in the amount of the deacetylated alcohol side product.”
- “The strategy of first reducing 28 to alcohol 29… proved to be successful and scalable.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Phenol 17 displayed very poor solubility in common organic solvents (MeOH, EtOAc, CH₂Cl₂, acetone), complicating its isolation after the one‑pot demethylation/cyclization sequence.
Solution_Description: Compound 17 was isolated by precipitation and trituration rather than chromatography, allowing the preparation of hundreds of grams efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: - “Compound 17 exhibits poor solubility in most organic solvents… Therefore, it can be isolated and purified by precipitation and trituration.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: During the nucleophilic displacement of 18 with phenol 17, temperature strongly influenced the formation of side‑product 38; reactions below 50 °C were sluggish, while above 70 °C gave mostly 38, leading to inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: The optimal temperature window (50–55 °C) was identified, and the order of addition (phenol 17 in NMP, then K₂CO₃, followed by addition of 18) was standardized, delivering a 10:1 ratio of desired product 16 to side‑product 38 and a 72 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Temperature played an important role in the amount of 38 that was formed. Below 50 °C, the reaction was very sluggish, while at temperatures above 70 °C, the major product produced was 38.”
- “The optimal temperature range was found to be 50–55 °C with a 10:1 ratio of 16 and 38…”
- “Ground‑up potassium carbonate… was added… A solution of 18… was added in one portion. The reaction mixture was then stirred at 50 °C for 22 h.”

Paper Title: Development of a Rapid Scale-Up Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The multi‑step conversion of alcohol 19 to phenol 17 involved reagents of differing polarity (BBr₃ in CH₂Cl₂, work‑up in aqueous NaOH), creating biphasic mixtures that risked incomplete phase transfer and material loss.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot telescoped protocol was established where demethylation, cyclization and work‑up were conducted sequentially without isolation, using CH₂Cl₂/BBr₃ followed by aqueous NaOH directly, streamlining the process and minimizing transfers.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Each of the individual reactions in the one‑pot process can be well controlled.”
- “A solution of 19 in ClCH₂CH₂Cl was treated with 7 equiv of BBr₃… heated to reflux… Treatment of the mixture 32 and 17 with 3 N NaOH… cleanly provided 17.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of the Chiral Pyrrolidine Fragment of Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: The initial asymmetric hydrogenation approach gave only 57 % isolated yield of the desired 2,5‑dihydro‑1H‑pyrrole (10) and the product was obtained with only 71 % HPLC purity after a labor‑intensive column chromatography.
Solution_Description: The researchers abandoned the asymmetric hydrogenation route and adopted a chiral‑auxiliary‑directed asymmetric 1,3‑dipolar cycloaddition (Oppolzer’s camphorsultam + TFA‑catalyzed cycloaddition) to build the pyrrolidine core with high diastereo‑ and enantio‑selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the reaction afforded an intractable mixture of products and the desired 2,5‑dihydro‑1H‑pyrrole 10 could be isolated in merely 57 % yield and 71 % high‑performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) purity only after careful column chromatography."; "...the complex reaction mixture obtained while converting ethyl pent‑2‑ynoate to 10, and the subsequent tedious product separation made us scout for an alternate substrate for asymmetric hydrogenation that could be prepared more efficiently."; "...we decided to alter our strategy and access chirally pure pyrrolidine 8 via a chiral auxiliary directed asymmetric 1,3‑dipolar cycloaddition reaction."

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of the Chiral Pyrrolidine Fragment of Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the EtOAc/THF (1:1) solvent system used in the Lindlar hydrogenation led to excessive hydrogen solubility, causing the over‑reduced product to dominate, thus lowering the yield of the desired (Z)‑alkene 20.
Solution_Description: The solvent system was altered to a less polar n‑hexane/EtOAc (≈1:1) mixture, which reduced hydrogen solubility and prevented over‑reduction, delivering the target alkene 20 in excellent yield and selectivity on 100–200 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the solvent combination fared poorly during scale‑up studies with an autoclave and repeatedly afforded the over‑reduced product as the major one."; "We hypothesized that a solvent combination with lower polarity than 1:1 EtOAc/THF might limit the solubility of hydrogen in the reaction milieu and reduce over‑reduction... Eventually, it was found that hydrogenation could be carried out even on a 100–200 g scale with excellent yield and selectivity in the n‑hexane/EtOAc (∼1:1) mixture with 8–10 psig of hydrogen pressure and 5–6 h of reaction time."

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of the Chiral Pyrrolidine Fragment of Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: The commercial batch of (+)-camphorsultam used for the multigram synthesis had only 97 % enantiomeric purity, which reduced the diastereomeric ratio of the cycloadduct 21a/21b and required additional purification steps.
Solution_Description: A reliable recrystallization protocol was developed to isolate pure 21a from the diastereomeric mixture, and the disengaged camphorsultam was recovered (≈83 % yield) and recycled for subsequent batches, restoring consistent chiral purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Unlike the lab runs, the commercial grade of camphorsultam (+)-18, employed for the multigram synthesis of 8, had a chiral purity (er) of only 97 %. While this did affect the obtained diastereomeric ratio of 21a/21b, the efficient recrystallization technique developed for the mixture eventually allowed us to isolate 21 essentially as a single diastereomer."; "...the disengaged camphorsultam (+)-18 could be easily recovered and successfully recycled for reaction with 17 to afford eventually 22a without any significant variation in chiral purity."

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of the Chiral Pyrrolidine Fragment of Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: A reliable HPLC resolution of the diastereomers 21a and 21b could not be achieved, making isolation of a single diastereomer impractical.
Solution_Description: The crude diastereomeric mixture was carried forward without isolation; the subsequent lithium‑hydroxide de‑auxiliary step yielded the acid 22a, whose enantiomeric ratio reflected the diastereomeric composition of the precursor.
Supporting_Evidence: "A reliable resolution of 21a and 21b by HPLC techniques could not be obtained. Hence, the obtained solid was taken into the next step and the diastereomeric ratio was extrapolated from the chiral purity (er) of 22a."

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of the Chiral Pyrrolidine Fragment of Upadacitinib
Problem_Description: Alternative bases (NaH, sodamide, NaOMe) failed to generate the desired acyl‑sultam 19 during the mixed‑anhydride coupling, leading to inconsistent formation of the key intermediate.
Solution_Description: The authors retained n‑butyl‑lithium as the deprotonating agent and controlled its addition rate and temperature (−78 °C to −70 °C) to reliably form 19, ensuring reproducible scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: "Bases such as sodium hydride, sodamide, and sodium methoxide were explored as alternatives to n‑butyl‑lithium for deprotonating camphorsultam. However, no formation of the desired product 19 was observed."; "To a stirred solution of the recovered (1R)-(+)-2,10‑camphorsultam 18...was added n‑butyl lithium (70.26 g, 1.0972 mol, 1.6 M in THF) at such a rate as to maintain an internal temperature of −70 to −78 °C. After 30 min at −78 °C, the lithiated mixture was transferred to the pivaloylated mixed anhydride at −78 °C at such a rate as to maintain the internal temperature of −70 to −78 °C."

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: Using 5 equiv of the TBDPS‑triflate (1b) in toluene at 50 °C gave high conversion of rapamycin (98 % in 23 h) but only 69 % of the desired product (TBDPS‑EVR) and generated a persistent 14 % mixture of dialkylated impurities (TBDPS‑D,E,F). Extending the reaction to 5 days increased the impurity level to 18 % and reduced the product to <65 %. When the reagent excess was lowered to 2.5 equiv, conversion fell below 86 % and the impurity content remained significant.
Solution_Description: The authors reduced the amount of alkylating agent to 2.5 equiv, switched the solvent from toluene to acetonitrile (which provides higher solubility of all components), lowered the reaction temperature to 30 °C (room‑temperature range) and raised the reaction concentration eight‑fold. Under these optimized conditions full conversion was achieved in 40–45 h with a 71–73 % isolated yield of TBDPS‑EVR and a markedly lower impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction in toluene with 5 equiv of 1b and DIPEA at 50 °C resulted in the full conversion of RAP (98 %) after 23 h … accumulation of these impurities started … Prolonging the reaction time to 5 days led to the increased amount of TBDPS‑D,E,F (up to 18 %) while the content of TBDPS‑EVR decreased to less than 65 %.”
• “We failed to achieve RAP conversion of more than 86 % with 2.5 equiv of 1b, while the amount of TBDPS‑D,E,F was still significant.”
• “Replacement of toluene with acetonitrile … higher solubility … 8‑fold increase in concentration … full conversion of RAP was achieved at 40 °C after 26 h … entries 1–4 in Table 4 show yields of 71–73 % under these conditions.”

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: Common bases used in the alkylation (DIPEA, 2,6‑lutidine) undergo undesired alkylation by the triflate reagents, forming quaternary ammonium salts and consuming the base, which leads to incomplete rapamycin conversion and variable impurity formation.
Solution_Description: The study switched to sterically hindered, non‑alkylatable amine bases such as 1,2,2,6,6‑pentamethylpiperidine (PMP) and other tetramethyl‑piperidine derivatives, which remained inert under the reaction conditions. This change eliminated base alkylation, improved conversion, and reduced impurity formation without increasing reagent load.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Heating of triflates 1a–c with bases that were used in most works, DIPEA and 2,6‑lutidine, indeed led to their alkylation with the formation of the corresponding quaternary ammonium salts 2 and 3.”
• “We managed to find suitable bases… which did not react with triflate when heated up to 70 °C.”
• “With literature excess of 1b (5 equiv) and 1,2,2,6,6‑pentamethylpiperidine (PMP) as a base … a maximum TBDPS‑EVR content of 58 % was observed after 23 h, while RAP conversion was about 90 %.”

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: Published procedures for rapamycin alkylation often require high temperatures (up to 80 °C) and large excesses of reagents (up to 8 equiv), which increase energy consumption, raise safety concerns, and drive up material costs while still delivering low overall yields.
Solution_Description: By operating at a milder temperature (30 °C) in acetonitrile and reducing the alkylating agent to 2.5 equiv, the authors achieved comparable or higher conversions with fewer reagents, eliminating the need for high‑temperature operation and decreasing costs.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The major drawbacks of all of these procedures are not only low yields but also the requirement of high temperatures up to 80 °C and numerous excess of reagents up to 8 equiv.”
• “Optimal conditions were chosen as follows: 2.5 equiv of 1b and PMP as a base in acetonitrile at 30 °C for 40–45 h.”
• Table 4 entries 1–4 show >95 % conversion and 71–73 % yield under these milder conditions.

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: Isolation of the three dialkylated impurities (TBDPS‑D,E,F) required flash chromatography and preparative reverse‑phase HPLC. Their dynamic tautomeric equilibrium and overlapping NMR signals made structural assignment difficult, and the reliance on HPLC added considerable expense and waste.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The optimized process increased the loading of crude reaction mixture onto silica (20 g silica per 1 g mixture) enabling flash chromatography to isolate TBDPS‑EVR with >98 % purity, eliminating the need for HPLC. The one‑pot hydrolysis of the labile impurity E directly to the target product further removed a purification step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Impurities TBDPS‑D,E,F were isolated and purified by flash chromatography and preparative reverse‑phase (RP) HPLC, respectively. Isolation and identification were complicated … cannot be isolated individually.”
• “Only 20 g of silica was sufficient to purify 1 g of the reaction mixture. The purity of thus obtained product was more than 98 % … the process mass intensity (PMI) index decreased 2.7 times compared to unoptimized conditions.”
• “Under optimized conditions … the one‑pot hydrolysis of the TBDPS‑E impurity … increased the content of the everolimus intermediate proportionally … without formation of additional impurities.”

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: TBDPS‑EVR is highly soluble in most common solvents, preventing classical crystallization; upon cooling oily phases formed and then froze, giving no purity gain. Direct crystallization of the final API after deprotection also left ~15 % of the silyl fragment.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Instead of attempting crystallization, the team employed a minimal‑silica filtration step after deprotection to remove the non‑polar TBDPS fragment and impurity F, then crystallized the API from heptane/ethyl acetate, achieving >90 % yield and 99.7 % HPLC purity without the residual silyl fragment.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “TBDPS‑EVR was highly soluble in most common solvents and was only separated from nonpolar alkane solids. But this was not classical crystallization, as upon cooling, oily parts were formed followed by their freezing.”
• “We were pleased to find that flash column chromatography was not necessary. A filtration‑like procedure through a minimal amount of silica was sufficient to separate the non‑polar TBDPS fragment and impurity F from EVR with a yield of more than 90 %.”
• “Direct crystallization … resulted in the formation of a product containing about 15 % of the protection group fragment. … a filtration‑like procedure … gave pharmaceutically pure everolimus after crystallization on a large scale.”

Paper Title: Optimization of the Everolimus Intermediate Preparation Process: Impurity Identification Followed by One-Pot Transformation to the Desired Product
Problem_Description: Literature reports show a sharp drop in yield when scaling up the rapamycin alkylation (e.g., from 62 % at small scale to 37 % at 2 kg), indicating poor scalability and variability of the process.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Applying the optimized conditions (2.5 equiv 1b, PMP base, MeCN, 30 °C, high concentration) on a 1 kg rapamycin batch retained a 57 % isolated yield of TBDPS‑EVR, comparable to laboratory yields and far above the literature‑scaled‑down values, demonstrating robust scalability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Preparative yields in the TBS triflate‑utilizing approach do not exceed 36 %, while for the more stable TDS triflate on a laboratory scale, they reach 60 %, but after scaling up, they drop sharply to less than 40 %.”
• “Testing on a rapamycin load of 1 kg was successful and no decrease in yield was observed, and TBDPS‑EVR of high purity was obtained with a yield of 57 % (compared to the literature yield decrease from 62 to 37 % upon scaling up from 6 g to 2 kg of RAP).”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The original Route A delivered a very low overall isolated yield (≈ 6–8 %) and required frequent column chromatography because most Boc‑protected intermediates (4–9) were oily and could not be purified efficiently.
Solution_Description: A new Route B was devised that replaces the Boc protecting group with an (R)‑α‑phenethyl substituent, allowing the key intermediates to be converted into hydrochloride salts that precipitate and can be isolated by simple filtration, eliminating chromatography and raising the overall yield to ≈ 38 % for the intermediate and ≈ 17 % for the API.
Supporting_Evidence:
The total yield was still very low (about 6–8%).
Almost all Boc‑protected compounds from 4 to 9 were oily without efficient purification methods except frequent column chromatography.
Preparative HPLC or SFC was used to purify 9 or 1.
The Boc protecting group was replaced by (R)‑α‑phenethyl, and the latter could help to purify intermediates easily by forming the salt.
The screening results indicated that 13 formed salts with hydrochloric acid in ethyl acetate, while the solid was separated by filtration easily.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The diastereoselectivity of the reduction step from 6 to 7 was poor (3 : 1 dr), which gave a low isolated yield (25–33 %) after resolution of the racemic mixture.
Solution_Description: Magnesium was employed as a reducing agent in methanol, added in portions under inert atmosphere, which gave a much higher diastereoselectivity (≈ 10 : 1 dr) and an 83 % isolated yield for the desired product.
Supporting_Evidence:
The diastereoselectivity from 6 to 7 was poor with 3/1 dr. Even after purification by a silica gel, the target compound in rac‑9 was only above 30–40%.
Magnesium was chosen as the reducing agent, and the reaction risk was reduced by adding Mg in several portions and running the reaction in an inert atmosphere.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Removal of the protecting group by hydrogenation required flammable H₂ gas, raising safety concerns for large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a transfer‑hydrogenation protocol using ammonium formate and Pd/C, which avoids the use of gaseous hydrogen and thus mitigates the safety hazard.
Supporting_Evidence:
The protecting group could be easily removed by reduction in the hydrogen gas; however, in light of safety concerns of flammable hydrogen, eventually the condition of transfer hydrogenation was chosen.
Ammonium formate along with Pd/C in methanol was considered to be the optimal condition for this step.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Both the discovery route and Route A relied on preparative HPLC or SFC to separate isomers, dramatically increasing material cost and making scale‑up impractical.
Solution_Description: Formation of hydrochloride salts of intermediates 13 and 18 allowed the undesired isomers to be removed by simple filtration, eliminating the need for preparative chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
Preparative HPLC or SFC was used to purify 9 or 1.
The Boc protecting group was replaced by (R)‑α‑phenethyl, and the latter could help to purify intermediates easily by forming the salt.
The screening results indicated that 13 formed salts with hydrochloric acid in ethyl acetate, while the solid was separated by filtration easily.
The crude 18·HCl was separated as an off‑white to white solid after treatment with HCl in EtOAc.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Intermediates 13 and 18 were oily liquids, preventing direct recrystallisation and forcing the use of column chromatography for purification.
Solution_Description: Acidification of the reaction mixtures (pH 3‑4) in ethyl acetate generated hydrochloride salts that precipitated as solids; the salts were then isolated by filtration and washed with appropriate solvents (EtOAc, i‑PrOH).
Supporting_Evidence:
Although the Boc group was replaced by the (R)‑α‑phenethyl group, 13 is oily like 7, which cannot be purified by recrystallization directly.
The pH was adjusted to between 3 and 4 at 5‑15 °C and stirred at this temperature for another 12 h.
The screening results indicated that 13 formed salts with hydrochloric acid in ethyl acetate, while the solid was separated by filtration easily.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Conversion of 13 to 16 under several reagent sets failed or gave low conversion because the carbonyl existed predominantly in the enol form, reducing its reactivity.
Solution_Description: The Mannich cyclisation was performed at pH 3‑4 and low temperature (5‑20 °C), which suppressed enolisation and improved both conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
The failure in these conditions might be attributed to the enol form of the carbonyl group in the ring, which reduced the reactivity.
The ring‑closure step was a Mannich reaction, which was very sensitive to pH, so we investigated the pH effect and the results showed that pH 3.0‑4.0 was the appropriate condition for the reaction.
The IPC results indicated that the area percentages of 13 and 13a (isomer) were approximately the same at 5 and 20 °C. As the temperature rose to 45 °C, 13 and 13a both decreased significantly. Ultimately the reaction was run at 5‑20 °C.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The magnesium‑mediated reduction of 15 to 16 releases hydrogen gas, creating a potential explosion hazard on scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Magnesium was added slowly in portions under a nitrogen blanket, temperature was kept at 0‑10 °C, and the reaction was quenched carefully, thereby controlling hydrogen evolution and mitigating safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence:
the operation should be performed very cautiously due to the release of hydrogen gas, and a suitable control strategy should be designed to mitigate the potential safety hazard to an acceptable level.
Magnesium was chosen as the reducing agent, and the reaction risk was reduced by adding Mg in several portions and running the reaction in an inert atmosphere.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route with Efficient Stereoisomer Control to YZJ-1139, an Orexin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Carrying undesired stereoisomers through multiple steps caused material waste and lowered the overall material throughput.
Solution_Description: A telescoped sequence was designed that couples the condensation with 2,5‑difluoropyridine before olefin reduction, allowing the removal of isomers early and avoiding isolation of intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence:
The introduction of 2,5‑difluoropyridine prior to the reduction of olefin in this route could perform the reduction of the olefin and debenzylation simultaneously by hydrogenation.
We proposed a new telescoped route.

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: The original methyl‑chloroformate (MCF)/hydrazine route required 18 eq MCF and up to 50 eq hydrazine, gave very long reaction times (3 days at 95 °C for the hydrazine step, 18 h reflux for carbamate formation) and produced toxic, hazardous waste, making it unsafe and uneconomical for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Adopted an iron‑catalyzed non‑classical Polonovski reaction that uses mCPBA (1.2 eq) and catalytic Fe/FeCl₃ at room temperature in methanol/water, eliminating toxic MCF and hydrazine, shortening the reaction to ≈2 h and using inexpensive, benign reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Intermediate carbamate 3 was formed by refluxing 1 with 18 equiv of MCF in chloroform for 18 h at 60 °C… then treated with up to 50 equiv (!) of hydrazine… 3 days… highly toxic.”
• “The reaction proved capricious… the hydrazine step lengthened to 5 days, and yields deteriorated.”
• “The optimized reaction proceeded via the N‑oxide in 2 h at room temperature in methanol/water using a mild stoichiometric oxidant and catalytic iron…”
• “It avoided the major process concerns of the initial conditions which had required a super excess of toxic MCF and hydrazine, extended reaction times (3–5 days)…”
• “Both this and other alternative methods… were judged to be impractical for even modest scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: The initial screening used 110 relative volumes of a 4:1 chloroform/isopropanol solvent system, which required large amounts of chlorinated solvent (toxicity) and created handling/mixing difficulties at scale.
Solution_Description: Replaced chloroform with methanol (or IPA) and reduced solvent volume to ~30 volumes, eliminating hazardous chloroform and simplifying mixing and heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction had been conducted in 110 relative volumes (!) of 4:1 v/v chloroform/isopropanol… Chloroform was clearly an unacceptable process solvent.”
• “Fortunately, solubility in the MCL‑509 series proved good and the reaction could be successfully performed in 30 volumes of methanol or IPA alone.”
• “The lack of material limited initial studies… reaction times varied… conversions varied… (inconsistent results were linked to the solvent system).”
• “This involved reduction of the batch volume from 110 to 10 volumes and then re‑dilution with chloroform… a strong incentive for minimizing the iron loading because high iron residues also complicated the following step.”
• “In an attempt to simplify this long work‑up and replace the undesired halogenated solvents, a solvent swap from methanol into ethyl acetate was investigated.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: Small‑scale reactions showed erratic induction periods, stalled conversions, and inconsistent product ratios because low‑level iron powder and FeCl₃ could not be measured accurately and iron powder tended to adhere to the stir bar, giving poor dispersion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Prepared a stock solution of FeCl₃ (0.04 M) for accurate dosing, introduced a palladium‑scavenger treatment (30 wt % SiliaMetS Thiol) to remove residual Pd, and employed vigorous mechanical stirring (impeller ~300 rpm) together with chemical pretreatment of iron powder with HCl to keep the powder well dispersed.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A contributing factor may have been the difficulty in accurately charging low molecular weight catalysts at low levels (iron powder at 13 and FeCl₃ at only 2 mol %).”
• “The iron powder could not be solubilized and thus titrated … the small charge of the FeCl₃ cocatalyst could be added as a stock solution (0.04 M) … without any adverse impact.”
• “Residual Pd carried over in starting material 1 … To reduce residual Pd to an acceptable level (<50 ppm), a scavenger treatment … 30 wt % of SiliaMetS Thiol … was used.”
• “Magnetic stirring helped initially on a small scale … iron powder naturally adhered to the magnetic stir bar and so was poorly dispersed … therefore, chemical pretreatment of iron powder with concentrated HCl … was introduced before being added.”
• “The reaction mixture quickly becomes a characteristic red/orange color as the reaction progresses. The reaction solution was mechanically stirred at 20 °C for 30–60 min (variable induction periods have been noted, especially on a larger scale with mechanical stirring).”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: Incorrect amounts of concentrated HCl resulted in either stalled reactions (>1 eq) or incomplete conversion (<0.3 eq), leading to lower yields and variable product ratios.
Solution_Description: Optimised the HCl charge to 0.3–0.8 eq total (0.1 eq for iron pretreatment, 0.4 eq for N‑oxide protonation) yielding pH 3–5 before catalyst addition, which gave full conversion within 30–60 min and 99:1 selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reaction times increased and even stalled in some cases when >1.0 eq was used.”
• “Reactions at pH <2 failed to give full conversion and exhibited poor ratios, while reactions at pH >5 proceeded slowly.”
• “When a small HCl charge was used solely for activation of the catalyst, 30 mol % iron loading gave full conversion … whereas at 10–15 mol % conversions were incomplete.”
• “Reactions performed in the range of 0.3 to 0.8 equiv of HCl … exhibited full conversions with good ratios of 2:1.”
• “Based on these results, the final optimization of the total HCl charge was fixed at 0.5 equiv, split between the iron powder pretreatment (0.1 equiv) and that required for the partial protonation of the N‑oxide 6 (0.4 equiv). This stoichiometry led to a robust reaction, capable of full conversion within 30–60 min, with a 99:1 selectivity.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: Surface iron oxides on the powder reduced its reactivity, causing induction delays; magnetic stirring was ineffective at larger scale because the powder stuck to the stir bar.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Performed a chemical pretreatment of iron powder with 0.1 eq HCl in methanol (mechanical agitation) to remove surface oxides and generate active Fe⁰, then added the activated powder in one portion with vigorous impeller stirring, avoiding magnetic stir bars.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Surface iron oxides would reduce the exposure of Fe(0) metal… This issue could be overcome by either mechanical or chemical action on the iron powder.”
• “Increased magnetic stirring helped initially on a small scale … but could not be relied on at a larger scale … iron powder naturally adhered to the magnetic stir bar and so was poorly dispersed.”
• “Chemical pretreatment of iron powder with concentrated HCl (0.1 equiv) … was introduced before being added … proved reliable on scale‑up, although this pretreatment is moderately exothermic and does generate hydrogen.”
• “The reaction solution was mechanically stirred at 20 °C for 30–60 min (variable induction periods have been noted, especially on a larger scale with mechanical stirring).”
• “Safety note: the activation of iron powder with concentrated HCl releases a small quantity of hydrogen gas and moderate heat; inertion does not appear to be essential, other than for fire safety concerns.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: The original work‑up required multiple solvent swaps (methanol → chloroform → NaOH washes), removal of large quantities of Fe(OH)₂ precipitate, and charcoal treatment, making the isolation steps lengthy and labor‑intensive.
Solution_Description: Implemented a single screening filtration followed by an azeotropic solvent swap from methanol to ethyl acetate, allowing the product HCl salt to precipitate directly and be filtered, eliminating alkaline washes, charcoal adsorption, and halogenated solvents.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The original literature method used a very dilute reaction, which resulted in an extended work‑up regime… Two or three washes with 5 % NaOH were used… very difficult to remove… an aqueous EDTA wash was also tried … without much success.”
• “In an attempt to simplify this long work‑up and replace the undesired halogenated solvents, a solvent swap from methanol into ethyl acetate was investigated.”
• “A screening filtration at the end of reaction removed undissolved iron powder … followed by a partial ethyl acetate/methanol solvent swap via azeotropic distillation … a high yield (84 %) of pure MCL‑509 Amine.HCl could be obtained directly by crystallization.”
• “Residual iron salts appeared to remain in solution and did not interfere with the work‑up.”
• “The finalized process delivered MCL‑509 Amine (…) in ∼84 % yield with reproducible HPLC purity of 96 % and typically 0.5–0.7 % of re‑formed starting material as the largest single impurity.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: High iron loadings (30 mol %) generated large amounts of Fe‑containing precipitates that were hard to filter and required extensive alkaline washes, complicating isolation and increasing waste.
Solution_Description: Reduced iron loading to 13 mol % (with 2 mol % FeCl₃) and employed a methanol→ethyl acetate solvent swap that kept iron residues soluble, allowing clean filtration and direct crystallisation of the product salt.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The original literature method used a very dilute reaction… two or three washes with 5 % NaOH … very difficult to remove … strong incentive for minimizing the iron loading because high iron residues also complicated the following step.”
• “The level of iron in product 2 was acceptable, and while iron is environmentally benign … it must be acknowledged that iron residues left in GLMS reactors might have been difficult to visualize and/or remove.”
• “The reaction was carried out with 13 mol % Fe powder and 2 mol % FeCl₃ … The iron content of 2 and later intermediates was confirmed as <50 ppm.”
• “A solvent swap from methanol into ethyl acetate … a solid formed, confirmed as the HCl salt … high yield (84 %) of pure MCL‑509 Amine.HCl could be obtained directly by crystallization.”
• “Residual iron salts appeared to remain in solution and did not interfere with the work‑up.”

Paper Title: Application of the Polonovski Reaction: Scale-up of an Efficient and Environmentally Benign Opioid Demethylation
Problem_Description: The discovery route used large excesses of toxic methyl chloroformate and hydrazine, generating hazardous waste and requiring careful chromatography for product isolation.
Solution_Description: Replaced the toxic MCF/hydrazine sequence with the iron‑catalyzed Polonovski reaction performed in methanol/water, avoiding halogenated reagents, reducing waste, and enabling direct isolation of the HCl salt without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The specific Discovery method… exploited the methyl chloroformate (MCF)/hydrazine combination of reagents… 18 equiv of MCF … up to 50 equiv of hydrazine … highly toxic.”
• “The reaction proved capricious on scale‑up too … yields deteriorated.”
• “It proved to be a great improvement in every aspect over the chloroformate‑mediated and classical von Braun reactions … especially for environmental, health, safety, and operability reasons.”
• “The optimized reaction proceeded via the N‑oxide in 2 h at room temperature in methanol/water using a mild stoichiometric oxidant and catalytic iron to yield the crystalline amine as its HCl salt directly from the reaction solution … after only a screening filtration and facile solvent swap.”
• “Both this and other alternative methods … were judged to be impractical for even modest scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: Commercially sourced isourea 1 contained 2–10 % residual N,N′‑diisopropylcarbodiimide (DIC), which led to the formation of impurity 4 and prevented the required <1 % DIC level for downstream esterification.
Solution_Description: The team developed an in‑situ copper‑catalyzed preparation of isourea 1 from tert‑butanol and DIC under aerobic conditions, pre‑activating CuCl with O₂ before adding the alcohol, thereby eliminating the need for the impurity‑laden commercial material.
Supporting_Evidence: “…commercial sources…contained high levels of DIC (2–10 %) in excess of this requirement.”; “The use of an aerobic copper‑catalyzed reaction between tert‑butyl alcohol and DIC afforded superior reaction rates and conversion compared with the reported conditions under inert atmospheres.”; “Pre‑mixing … CuCl … with a portion of DIC under air for 60 min … led to higher rates.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: Reactions performed under inert atmosphere were dramatically slower (up to 3 days) and gave low conversion of DIC, making the process unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: An O₂‑containing pre‑activation step (exposing CuCl to O₂ for ~1 h before addition of the remaining reagents) was introduced, eliminating the induction period and achieving >99 % DIC conversion within 24 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reported examples…required…up to 3 days…Our experiments under inert atmospheres confirmed these dramatically lower reaction rates.”; “…trials in which the CuCl was mixed with a portion of the DIC under air for 60 min…led to higher rates.”; “…routinely observed >99 % conversion of DIC within 24 h.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: Using an aerobic atmosphere raised concerns about flammable headspace and uncontrolled exotherms when scaling the reaction.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was limited to 4–5 % O₂ (well below limiting‑oxygen‑concentration limits for t‑BuOH and DIC), employed a static headspace with intermittent 4 % O₂ sweeps, and maintained vessel fill at 33–50 % to provide sufficient headspace while preventing oxygen‑rich combustible mixtures.
Supporting_Evidence: “While beneficial…O₂ poses safety concerns for large‑scale applications…the use of an aerobic atmosphere on scale requires precautions to avoid combustible headspaces.”; “We elected to study 4 % O₂/96 % N₂…which was readily available on laboratory and industrial scales.”; “The decision to run the reaction under static pressure…was based on observations that constant atmospheric sweeps could result in loss of t‑BuOH…Under static atmospheres, O₂ meters showed that the measured O₂ level in the atmosphere gradually declined over time.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: CuCl has poor solubility in tert‑butanol, leading to heterogeneous mixtures and inconsistent O₂ uptake during catalyst activation.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was pre‑activated by mixing CuCl with a limited portion of DIC under O₂ before the bulk addition of t‑BuOH, ensuring the CuCl was fully oxidized in the solid‑state and avoiding reliance on solution‑phase solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: “The poor solubility of CuCl in t‑BuOH may affect the uptake of O₂.”; “During further studies, control experiments revealed that reactions conducted with CuCl under inert atmospheres were dramatically slower.”; “Premixing event … formed a dark‑brown/red‑brown mixture of the active precatalyst.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: O₂ consumption during the reaction generated water, which hydrolyzed isourea 1 to give impurity 2 (N,N′‑diisopropylurea) in 4‑5 % yield, potentially compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: An inline filter was installed to remove trace impurity 2 from the crude stream, and the O₂ concentration was carefully limited (4 % O₂) to keep water formation minimal while still providing the catalytic benefit.
Supporting_Evidence: “The main impurity…was formed in 4‑5 % yield…The primary source of this impurity was the O₂ from the atmosphere…Water formed…reacts with 1 to give 2.”; “On the large scale we passed the stream through an in‑line filter (to remove small quantities of 2) prior to use.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Addition of Alcohols to Carbodiimides: Oxygen as an Accelerant
Problem_Description: Repeated atmospheric sweeps caused loss of t‑BuOH, leading to crystal formation on reactor walls and incomplete DIC conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: After the initial O₂ activation, the reaction was run under a static atmosphere with only 8–10 brief O₂ sweeps over 18–24 h to minimize solvent loss while maintaining sufficient O₂ for catalyst regeneration.
Supporting_Evidence: “The decision to run the reaction under static pressure…was based on observations that constant atmospheric sweeps could result in loss of t‑BuOH…Under static atmospheres, O₂ meters showed…gradually declined…We targeted 8–10 atmosphere exchanges over the course of the reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The first‑generation route to the aniline fragment 7 required the expensive starting material methyl 2‑methoxy‑3‑nitrobenzoate (2) and suffered from poor overall yield (≈26 %) because the triazole‑methylation step gave a mixture of regioisomers that could only be isolated with large material loss.
Solution_Description: A new two‑step sequence was developed that builds the 1‑methyl‑1,2,4‑triazole by a regioselective cyclocondensation of 5‑chloro‑2‑methoxy‑3‑nitrobenzonitrile (28) with in‑situ‑generated N‑methylformohydrazide, avoiding the problematic methylation entirely and using the much cheaper chlorinated starting material 28.
Supporting_Evidence: “The overall yield was modest due to a triazole methylation step plagued by poor regioselectivity.”; “The cost of starting material 2 was prohibitively high…The undesired regioisomers could be removed by crystallization but only under conditions that led to significant losses.”; “The proposed route to 7 depicted…was demonstrated successfully…the starting material 28 was nearly an order of magnitude cheaper than either 25 or 2.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The trideuteromethyl‑amide formation step in the discovery route gave low yield because the intermediate trichloro‑compound 10 was inherently unstable and degraded during work‑up, a problem that worsened on scale.
Solution_Description: Safe, homogeneous conditions were devised to quench POCl₃ after chlorination, using a controlled addition sequence and temperature profile that avoided rapid exotherms and prevented decomposition of the sensitive intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The poor yield was mostly due to the inherent instability of trichloro‑intermediate 10…During the workup of the chlorination reaction, significant decomposition was observed.”; “The development of safe, homogeneous conditions to quench POCl₃ following chlorination of a substrate that is sensitive to nucleophilic and basic conditions.”; “The adiabatic temperature increase due to quenching (+29 °C)…would not result in thermal runaway or decomposition.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The original API step required a palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling on a nitrogen‑rich molecule, leading to low isolated yield and demanding extensive palladium removal (acid washes, thiol‑silica, recrystallization).
Solution_Description: The commercial route was redesigned so that the trideuteromethyl‑amine is introduced in the final amide‑bond‑forming step, eliminating the need for palladium in the API step and thereby improving yield and simplifying metal‑remediation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The poor isolated yield in the API step was attributable to palladium remediation efforts.”; “A final amide bond formation step…would become an amide bond formation step and no longer include a palladium catalyst.”; “The discovery of a robust, scalable ‘dual‑base’ palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling reaction…” (used earlier in the penultimate step but not in the API step).

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The cyclocondensation product 27 (methyltriazole) was a low‑melting solid with high solubility in most organic solvents, making isolation of the free base difficult.
Solution_Description: The free base was converted to its hydrochloride salt (27‑01) by treating an ethyl‑acetate stream of 27 with methanolic HCl, enabling high‑yield, high‑purity isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “27 was a low‑melting solid with high solubility in most organic solvents, complicating isolation of the free base form. As such, an acid salt was targeted for isolation. Initially, the hydrochloride salt (27‑01) was found to be readily isolated in high yield and excellent purity by treating an ethyl acetate stream of 27 with methanolic HCl.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: During the nitration of 27 to 26, a small amount of over‑chlorinated impurity 36 formed because chloride from the hydrochloride salt was oxidized to electrophilic chlorine in the acidic medium.
Solution_Description: The counter‑ion of the methyltriazole was changed from the hydrochloride (27‑01) to the bisulfate salt (27‑02), which eliminated the source of chloride and gave a clean nitration (>99 % in‑process purity).
Supporting_Evidence: “The simplest solution to the chlorinated impurity was to replace hydrochloride salt 27‑01 with bisulfate salt 27‑02. Once this change was implemented, the nitration reaction was extremely clean (typically >99 % in‑process purity of 26).”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: Deoxychlorination of 8 to 18 with POCl₃ in neat POCl₃ or POCl₃/toluene produced >10 % N‑linked dimer impurities and hydrolysis upon quench; scale‑up showed worse hydrolysis due to heterogeneous, exothermic quench conditions.
Solution_Description: Switching to the polar solvent sulfolane with triethylamine reduced dimer formation to ~2 %; later, changing the reaction solvent to acetonitrile (5 L kg⁻¹) and performing a forward water‑addition quench produced a homogeneous mixture, eliminating hot‑spots and limiting hydrolytic impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “The dimerization pathway could be inhibited by the use of a more polar reaction solvent (sulfolane) and by the addition of triethylamine; these modifications reduced the level of the dimers to around 2 % each in‑process.”; “Subsequent optimization efforts targeted a homogeneous quench…by switching the reaction solvent from sulfolane to acetonitrile and increasing the solvent loading from 3 to 5 L kg⁻¹…the quenched reaction mixture would remain homogeneous.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The POCl₃ quench in the forward direction (adding reaction mixture to water) was critical for safety, but the biphasic mixture caused local hot‑spots and inadequate mixing, leading to higher hydrolysis impurity levels on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A controlled, slow addition of the POCl₃‑containing mixture into a cooled aqueous buffer was employed, together with temperature control and slow addition rates, to keep the exotherm manageable and maintain a homogeneous phase throughout the quench.
Supporting_Evidence: “Inverse quench…is not unprecedented…By reducing the POCl₃ charge…we could significantly reduce the amount of heat evolved during the quench.”; “Cooling and slow addition are implemented during the direct quench of the reaction mixture, thermochemical studies have confirmed that the adiabatic temperature increase due to quenching (+29 °C)…would not result in thermal runaway.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: Lithium salt 22‑02 was unstable as the free acid, undergoing spontaneous decarboxylation even at ambient temperature, compromising yield and material handling.
Solution_Description: The lithium salt monohydrate 22‑02 was isolated and used directly; its crystal form was stable, non‑hygroscopic and suitable for downstream processing, avoiding the decarboxylation pathway of the free acid.
Supporting_Evidence: “Investigation…revealed that the lithium salt offered the optimal physical properties: lithium salt monohydrate 22‑02 was a stable, non‑hygroscopic crystalline solid with desirable solubility properties.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The nucleophilic aromatic substitution between 22‑02 and 7 gave moderate conversion (70‑75 %) and produced regioisomer 54 and bis‑adduct 55 as impurities, with variable removal depending on reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: Addition of stoichiometric Zn(OAc)₂ as a Lewis‑acid promoter dramatically improved selectivity (≈92 % desired product, <0.5 % impurity) and caused the product to precipitate as a zinc salt (23‑02) that was less hygroscopic and more stable.
Supporting_Evidence: “Divalent metals were the most promising…stoichiometric Zn(OAc)₂ could mediate the reaction with near‑perfect selectivity…the zinc salt of the product…was less hygroscopic…than the free acid form and was stable against decarboxylation.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: The first‑generation palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling used heterogeneous K₃PO₄; jet‑milling was required for reproducible high conversion, but the material was hygroscopic, not commercially available, and caused inconsistent reaction rates on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The base was changed to off‑the‑shelf 325 mesh K₂CO₃ (a soluble inorganic base) and the reaction rate was boosted by increasing the amide partner to 2.5 eq; later a dual‑base system (DBU + K₂CO₃) was discovered that gave rapid, homogeneous reactions and eliminated the need for a reslurry step.
Supporting_Evidence: “By increasing the stoichiometry of cyclopropanecarboxamide 14 to 2.5 equivalents…enabled the use of ‘off‑the‑shelf’ 325 mesh K₂CO₃.”; “The newly identified DBU/K₂CO₃ ‘dual‑base’ system was selected for the final optimization of the commercial process.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: Product 24 remained as a zinc salt with poor solubility in most solvents, precluding conventional aqueous work‑up and making isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: A solvent system of AcOH and water (13 L kg⁻¹ AcOH, 2.5 L kg⁻¹ water) was added to the reaction mixture to create a homogeneous slurry; subsequent addition of heptane (7 L kg⁻¹) partitioned an organic layer that contained the zinc salt, which was then crystallized by water addition and seeding, giving a fast‑filtering product slurry.
Supporting_Evidence: “The end‑of‑reaction slurry could be made homogeneous by the addition of 13 L kg⁻¹ AcOH and 2.5 L kg⁻¹ water…Upon addition of 7 L kg⁻¹ heptane, an organic layer would split…The product‑rich bottom layer…could then undergo a controlled crystallization…yielding a fast‑filtering product slurry.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: Using PyBroP as the coupling reagent in the final amidation generated a pyrrolidine‑amide impurity 61 that varied with reagent lot and persisted after storage, threatening product purity and raising safety concerns due to the impurity’s unknown toxicity.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to HATU, which eliminated the pyrrolidine impurity but introduced a dimethyl‑amide impurity 62; subsequently, EDC/HOBt was selected as the activator because it gave high yields, low impurity levels, was inexpensive, and showed no lot‑to‑lot variation, solving both the impurity and safety issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of PyBroP as the activator consistently led to the formation of a pyrrolidine amide side product 61…Different lots of PyBroP afforded different, but reproducible, levels…With a clinical delivery pending, we turned to a head‑to‑head comparison of the second‑ and third‑best coupling reagents…When using HATU, pyrrolidine amide impurity 61 was not observed; however, dimethylamide impurity 62 was formed…Because no EDC reagent specification appeared necessary…the decision was made to pursue EDC as the coupling reagent for our third‑generation process.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: Prior to amidation, the zinc carboxylate 24 could decarboxylate to impurity 63 especially when CD₃NH₂·HCl was present, leading to loss of material and lower overall API yield.
Solution_Description: A precise order of addition (N‑methylimidazole → CD₃NH₂·HCl → 24‑02 → HOBt → EDC) and tight control of the time between charges were implemented to keep the free acid from forming and suppress decarboxylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The rate of decarboxylation of 24 prior to the EDC charge was strongly dependent on what else was in solution…The combination of zinc salt 24‑02 with trideuteromethylamine hydrochloride (11) is believed to lead to zinc decomplexation…To control impurity 63 to levels that could be purged…the order of addition was prescribed as follows…The second control implemented was to limit the time between these charges.”

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Process for Deucravacitinib, a Deuterated API for TYK2 Inhibition
Problem_Description: If the EDC addition was interrupted, product 1 could begin to crystallize before complete consumption of 24, entrapping unreacted 24 in the crystals, which required additional downstream processing.
Solution_Description: The EDC charge rate was controlled to avoid prolonged periods where 1 was supersaturated but 24 remained in solution; temperature cycling after crystallization was used to dissolve any entrapped 24 and release it to the mother liquor.
Supporting_Evidence: “The second problematic scenario uncovered by our stress testing was an interrupted EDC charge…If 1 begins to crystallize…entrainment of 24 in the product crystals can be observed.”; “When entrapment was to occur, heat cycling a completed reaction with small amounts of entrapped 24 could dissolve enough 1 to free the entrapped penultimate and facilitate its removal to the mother liquor.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Photochemical Bromination/Alkylation Sequence En Route to AMG 423
