Problem_Description: The original batch Wohl–Ziegler bromination required benzoyl peroxide as an initiator, which generated low‑level peroxide‑derived impurities and posed safety concerns; the process also relied on multiple aqueous work‑ups that created waste and complicated product isolation; the photochemical bromination in batch took ∼6 h to reach conversion, leading to long reaction times; N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) showed limited solubility in many solvents, risking incomplete conversion; using elemental bromine alone gave <1 % product, indicating a low yield; reactions at 80 °C produced noticeable decomposition by‑products; an induction period of 60–90 s was observed, and its length varied with oxygen content, causing variability in the start‑up profile.
Solution_Description: The team replaced the peroxide‑initiated batch reaction with a photochemical bromination that eliminates the need for benzoyl peroxide, thereby removing the impurity source and safety hazard (NEW ROUTE); they telescoped the sequence, avoiding isolation of intermediates and eliminating aqueous work‑ups (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY); acetonitrile was selected as the reaction solvent to fully dissolve NBS (SOLVENT CHANGE); the reaction temperature was tuned (25 °C‑80 °C) to accelerate conversion while avoiding decomposition (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION); a stoichiometric addition of a small amount of bromine or HBr at the start of the reaction removed the induction period and increased the rate (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE); the temperature was finally set at 60 °C for the flow reactors to balance speed and stability (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION); increasing LED light intensity and using nitrogen‑sparged solvent further reduced the induction period (ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “(1) the removal of the need for benzoyl peroxide as the chemical initiator, which was responsible for low‑level impurities in the batch process” (SAFETY, PURIFICATION) 
• “(2) the elimination of all aqueous workups to streamline the process and minimize waste output” (PURIFICATION) 
• “good conversion of 1 to monobromide (FNB) 2 and dibromide (FNBr2) 3 was observed in approximately 6 h” (LONG_REACTIONS) 
• “Acetonitrile was identified as a promising reaction solvent… offering good solubility for N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS)” (SOLUBILITY) 
• “Bromine proved to be ineffective with <1% product seen after 6 h” (LOW_YIELD) 
• “Reactions conducted at 80 °C showed elevated levels of decomposition products” (DECOMPOSITION) 
• “an induction period of approximately 60–90 s… A control experiment… under nitrogen atmosphere… showed a slightly reduced induction period but the same reaction rate” (VARIABILITY) 
• “Increasing the light intensity (use of three LED rings instead of 1) reduced the time of the induction period” (ORDER_AND_RATE_OF_ADDITION) 
• “Adding 5 mol % bromine or 5 mol % HBr… removed the induction period” (STOICHIOMETRY_CHANGE) 
• “Increasing reaction temperature provided clean conversion of 1 to 2 and 3 in only 15 min” (TEMPERATURE_OPTIMIZATION) 
• “The continuous process … eliminating aqueous workups” (TELESCOPE_DIRECTLY) 
• “Acetonitrile … offering good solubility for NBS” (SOLVENT_CHANGE) 
• “A solution of 1, NBS, and TFA was prepared in acetonitrile” (SOLVENT_CHANGE) 
• “The use of AcOH as a cosolvent… allowed reaction completion to be reached in 3 h” (SOLVENT_CHANGE, REACTION_TIME_CHANGE)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Photochemical Bromination/Alkylation Sequence En Route to AMG 423
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the crude PIPN stream after the telescoped process gave a mixture of HCl and HBr salts, making selective isolation of the desired HCl salt difficult; the bromination mixture was found to be incompatible with metal components, raising corrosion and safety concerns; the high viscosity of the reaction mixture and the need for efficient mass transfer in the flow reactors required careful mixing design.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The isolation strategy was changed to target the HBr salt directly by adding concentrated HBr during crystallization, providing a straightforward purification (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE); the flow reactors were constructed from PFA (Teflon) tubing and all metal components were avoided to prevent corrosion (REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS); T‑mixers were used to merge streams and residence times were optimized to maintain consistent mixing and heat transfer (MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Crystallization of PIPN HBr was achieved by the addition of concentrated HBr to crude PIPN streams… it was a mixture of the HCl and HBr salts” (PURIFICATION) 
• “Process modifications for the selective isolation of the HCl salt … proved ineffective, and thus … we targeted the isolation of PIPN as the HBr salt” (NEW_PURIFICATION_PROCEDURE) 
• “Note: The bromination mixture is incompatible with metal and metal components should be avoided at and before the first PFR.” (SAFETY, REACTOR_PLATFORM_AND_MATERIALS) 
• “A mixing T‑joint was used to merge this outcoming stream with the stream of …” (MASS_TRANSFER_MIXING_AND_GAS_ENVIRONMENT_CONTROL) 
• “The outgoing stream of crude PIPN was monitored and maintained a steady‑state concentration… allowing for the production of crude PIPN at a rate of ∼25 g/h” (MASS_TRANSFER_MIXING_AND_GAS_ENVIRONMENT_CONTROL)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Photochemical Bromination/Alkylation Sequence En Route to AMG 423
Problem_Description: The batch photochemical bromination required 15 min at 80 °C for each step, leading to a total residence time that was longer than desired for a high‑throughput continuous process; early experiments using bromine alone gave poor yields (<1 %).
Solution_Description: Temperature was increased to 77 °C in the first PFR to achieve full conversion within a 20 min residence time, and then to 60 °C in the final PFR for efficient alkylation, thereby shortening overall reaction time (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION); sub‑stoichiometric bromine (0.25 equiv) was added alongside NBS to boost conversion rates and yields (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We were pleased to find that under our initial conditions … 15 min … to furnish a crude mixture of PIPN in 85 % assay yield” (LONG_REACTIONS) 
• “Bromine proved to be ineffective with <1% product seen after 6 h” (LOW_YIELD) 
• “The use of AcOH … allowed for reaction completion to be reached in 3 h” (REACTION_TIME_CHANGE) 
• “Increasing the reaction temperature provided clean conversion of 1 to 2 and 3 in only 15 min” (TEMPERATURE_OPTIMIZATION) 
• “NBS in combination with lower amounts of bromine leads to increased reaction rates (entries 8–9)” (STOICHIOMETRY_CHANGE) 
• “A solution of 1, NBS, and TFA was prepared in acetonitrile, and this was then pumped through the first PFR … at 77 °C with a residence time of 20 min” (TEMPERATURE_OPTIMIZATION) 
• “A mixture of 0.25 equiv bromine … gave 80 % assay yield of 2” (STOICHIOMETRY_CHANGE)

Paper Title: Process Development of Enantioselective Imine Reductase-Catalyzed Syntheses of Pharmaceutically Relevant Pyrrolidines
Problem_Description: The researchers faced several scale‑up challenges: (1) the previously reported biocatalytic reductions were performed at low substrate concentrations (10–40 mM), limiting productivity; (2) when the substrate concentration was raised to 50 mM the reaction no longer gave full conversion; (3) the pyrroline substrates have limited solubility in aqueous media; (4) accumulation of d‑gluconic acid from the glucose‑dehydrogenase co‑factor recycle caused pH drift, leading to inconsistent conversions; (5) at 100 mM loading the chloro‑substituted imine 1c gave only ~92 % conversion; (6) conventional reducing agents are expensive, making the process costly; (7) the activities of the imine reductase (IRED) and the glucose dehydrogenase (GDH) in the whole‑cell catalyst were imbalanced, causing variability in performance; (8) overall conversion/yield at higher loadings remained sub‑optimal for some substrates.
Solution_Description: To overcome these issues the authors applied: (1) a systematic increase of substrate loading up to 100 mM, together with concentration‑tuning of the whole‑cell catalyst; (2) a stepwise (portionwise) addition of the imine substrate at 50 mM, which restored >99 % conversion; (3) addition of 4 % v/v methanol (after a cosolvent screen) to improve substrate solubility; (4) continuous pH control by automatic titration with NaOH (Titrino apparatus) to keep the reaction mixture at constant pH; (5) doubling the amount of wet biomass (whole‑cell catalyst) for the chloro‑substrate at 100 mM, raising conversion to >99 %; (6) replacement of expensive stoichiometric reductants by cheap, nontoxic d‑glucose as the reducing agent, lowering material cost; (7) construction of a two‑plasmid whole‑cell system with different copy numbers to balance IRED (low‑activity) and GDH (high‑activity) expression, giving a robust and reproducible catalyst; (8) optimisation of catalyst loading (concentration‑tuning) to achieve quantitative conversion across the substrate series.
Supporting_Evidence: "When raising the substrate concentration to 50 mM, however, in an initial experiment, this type of transformation no longer led to full conversion. We could solve this problem of insufficient conversion by a stepwise addition of the cyclic imine substrate, which then gave an excellent conversion of >99 %"; "The initial experiments were performed with a reaction volume of 40 mL and substrate concentrations of the pharmaceutically relevant substrates 1b and 1c ranging from 20 to 100 mM … During these reactions, the pH value was kept constant by titration with sodium hydroxide"; "4 % methanol was added to achieve a better substrate solubility. Methanol was the cosolvent of choice because, in a cosolvent screening, methanol and DMSO were preferred"; "The developed processes utilizes cheap d‑glucose as an economically favorable and nontoxic reducing agent"; "When utilizing imine 1b as a substrate, full conversion was achieved while, at first, the enzymatic reduction of the chloro‑substituted imine 1c … reached a conversion of 92 %. In order to further increase the conversion … the amount of wet biomass … was doubled"; "The whole‑cell catalyst containing CsIRED and BsGDH was constructed as a two‑plasmid system"; "As a next step, we focused on the increase of the substrate concentration as an important criterion for achieving economically favorable data in technical processes"

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: Even with 10 equiv of triethylphosphite the batch Michaelis–Arbuzov rearrangement gave only 37 % conversion to the target phosphonate 4a after 24 h, and heating above 100 °C for long periods generated unknown impurities that reduced selectivity.
Solution_Description: Increasing the temperature (200–250 °C) and reducing the residence time (10 min → 2 min) while lowering the phosphite loading to 3–5 equiv gave quantitative conversion of both the alkyl bromide and phosphite, eliminating the long reaction time and low yield observed in batch.
Supporting_Evidence:
“even using 10 equiv of the required phosphite source led to only 37 % conversion… after 24 h”
“heating the reaction mixture above 100 °C for a prolonged period… led to the formation of unknown impurities”
“total conversion… was reached by using 5 equiv of triethylphosphite upon heating the reaction mixture for 10 min at 200 °C”
“total conversion… within 2 min of reaction at 250 °C using only 3 equiv of phosphite”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: The batch reaction required 78 h to reach full conversion, producing a yellow mixture and delivering only 37 % isolated yield after distillation.
Solution_Description: Microwave irradiation at higher temperatures dramatically reduced the required reaction time from 78 h to minutes, enabling faster screening and optimization.
Supporting_Evidence:
“showed total conversion… after 78 h of reaction time… the reaction mixture turned yellow… pure 4a could only be recovered in 37 % yield”
“the transposition of the process under microwave irradiation… to decrease the required reaction time by working at higher temperatures”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: Microwave reactors are sealed, pressurized systems; scaling up caused safety concerns and limited the attainable reaction scale because excess pressure could not be safely released.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a high‑temperature/high‑pressure continuous‑flow reactor (ThalesNano Phoenix, 5 mL SS coil) allowing safe operation at up to 500 psi and temperatures above 300 °C, thus removing the scale‑up bottleneck of microwave devices.
Supporting_Evidence:
“microwave processes are scale‑dependent, and increasing the scale usually results in decreased yields… poor scale‑up potential of microwave processes”
“the transposition of the optimized microwave procedure under continuous flow operations… using a low‑footprint commercial high‑temperature/high‑pressure continuous flow reactor…"

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: The competitive ‘homo’ Michaelis–Arbuzov rearrangement generates the side product 4′a, which complicates purification and reduces overall selectivity toward the desired phosphonate 4a.
Solution_Description: Instead of treating 4′a as waste, the researchers deliberately used a 3 equiv phosphite ratio so that the excess phosphite is converted into the valuable side product 4′a, turning a purification issue into a productive step and improving atom economy.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the formation of the competitive … side product 4′a… leads to complex purification protocols”
“the competitive … side product 4′a also finds value‑added purposes as a building block, hence providing a very favorable intensified process”
“the excess of the phosphite derivative is converted into a valuable side product, showcasing the overall low footprint of our process.”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: Reactivity of the halogenated electrophile varied dramatically; the chloro substrate gave only ~58 % conversion even at 340 °C, whereas the bromo and iodo substrates converted quantitatively, making the process substrate‑dependent.
Solution_Description: The bromo derivatives were selected as the optimal electrophiles based on cost, availability, and reactivity; the reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, phosphite ratio) were tuned specifically for bromides to achieve >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the efficiency of the process was strongly dependent on the nature of the substrate… iodide derivatives gave better results… the chloro counterpart only leads to partial conversion”
“the basic cost analysis… converging arguments toward the selection of the bromo derivatives as the most efficient and cost‑effective electrophiles”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: The iodo electrophile (1a‑I) showed the highest reactivity but its price (≈ USD 1400 / 100 g) and limited commercial availability made it impractical for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The bromide (1a‑Br) was chosen instead, offering comparable reactivity at a far lower cost (≈ USD 33 / 100 g) and ready commercial supply.
Supporting_Evidence: “the iodo derivative … was discarded due to its limited availability at a very prohibitive price (USD 1400 / 100 g) … the bromide … USD 33.4 / 100 g”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: When P(OMe)₃ was used, the in‑situ formed methyl bromide (MeBr) preferentially reacted with the phosphite, forming side product 4′b and preventing full conversion of the starting bromide.
Solution_Description: Switching to less reactive phosphites (P(OiPr)₃ or P(OEt)₃) eliminated the MeBr‑induced side reaction; the i‑Pr bromide by‑product is much less electrophilic, allowing quantitative conversion to the desired phosphonate without excessive side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“MeBr is a much more reactive electrophilic species … it reacts preferentially with P(OMe)₃ to yield side product 4′b”
“using P(OiPr)₃ … total conversion … while the side product 4′c is not formed”
“using P(OEt)₃ … ethyl bromide (EtBr) exhibits intermediate reactivity … enables total conversion of both the starting alkyl bromide and the excess phosphite source.”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: Traditional batch work‑ups required column chromatography to remove catalyst residues and side‑products, which is impractical on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow process produced crude streams that could be purified by simple vacuum distillation, delivering 87 % isolated 4a and 94 % isolated 4′a on multi‑hundred‑gram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reactor effluents were collected and then distilled… 4a (324 g, 87 %) and 4′a (478 g, 94 %) were both recovered in great purity, demonstrating the efficiency of such continuous flow process for large‑scale preparation.”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: The electrophilic amination of 4a using DTBAD required 30 min deprotonation at –78 °C in batch, making the downstream step time‑consuming.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Under continuous flow the deprotonation step was performed at ambient temperature in 1 min, and the subsequent amination step required only 5 min overall, accelerating the sequence dramatically.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction time for the initial deprotonation step of 4a was decreased from 30 min at –78 °C under conventional batch conditions down to 1 min at room temperature in continuous flow… the intermediate … was prepared in 87 % conversion after 5 min of reaction time at room temperature.”

Paper Title: Intensified Continuous Flow Michaelis–Arbuzov Rearrangement toward Alkyl Phosphonates
Problem_Description: Monitoring of reaction conversion in flow was needed to ensure steady‑state operation and avoid off‑spec batches.
Solution_Description: An in‑line low‑field ^31P NMR detector was installed downstream of the flow coil, providing real‑time quantitative conversion data for rapid optimization and process control.
Supporting_Evidence: “In‑line low‑field ^31P NMR monitoring was conveniently implemented for rapid optimization and process monitoring.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The palladium‑catalyzed sulfamidation step gave only 66 % isolated yield on plant scale (vs 78 % in the laboratory) because of lower conversion, material losses during work‑up and the need for repeated palladium scavenging to reach <100 ppm residual metal. This step contributed roughly 50 % of the total manufacturing cost due to the expensive palladium source, ligand and scavenger.
Solution_Description: A copper‑catalyzed Ullmann–Goldberg coupling was adopted, replacing the palladium process and eliminating the expensive palladium/ligand/scavenger combination. The copper route was successfully developed and operated in four pilot‑plant batches (>50 kg scale).
Supporting_Evidence:
“The plant‑scale manufacture of AZD5069 involved … palladium‑catalyzed coupling … This step revealed … the difficulty of removing palladium residues … and the increasingly prohibitive costs of the metal, ligand, and scavenger used.”
“An alternative, copper‑catalyzed Ullmann–Goldberg coupling reaction was investigated, developed, and ultimately successfully operated in four pilot plant batches of >50 kg scale.”
“The manufacturing yield of the sulfamidation stage was lower than expected, 66 % versus 78 % in the lab… repeated palladium scavenging required to bring the residual palladium level down to <100 ppm… Cost evaluation … step to prepare 9 contributed approximately 50 % to the overall total manufacturing costs.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The sulfonamide reagent (compound 8) was poorly soluble in all tested solvents, preventing reliable addition as a slurry and leading to inconsistent conversions when the reaction was scaled to ~50 mL. This contributed to variability and lower yields on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to a bromide substrate (compound 11) that could be delivered as a solution in n‑butyl acetate, and the copper/ligand ratio was optimized to 1 : 0.95 (CuI : cyDMEDA) to minimise ligand adduct formation and improve handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the insolubility of 8 in various solvents, limiting opportunities to add it to the reaction vessel. Attempts to add 8 as a slurry were unsuccessful …”
“Therefore, we turned our attention to the previous stage material Diol 4. Treatment of 4 with phosphorus oxybromide afforded 10 … Intermediate 11 was prepared by treating 6 with 10 … as a solution in n‑butyl acetate.”
“The copper/ligand ratio … was set at 1:0.95 to minimize the formation of 12.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The copper‑catalyzed reaction was highly sensitive to oxygen; head‑space O₂ levels above ~2 % v/v caused reaction stalling and required additional catalyst doses. On larger scales the oxygen level could not be maintained at glove‑box (<10 ppm) levels, limiting catalyst loading to ≥15 mol % for reliable conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reactor head‑space was repeatedly purged with nitrogen and kept under a slight positive N₂ pressure to maintain O₂ < 0.1 % v/v. When oxygen‑related slowdown occurred, a second portion of catalyst (10 mol %) was added. The temperature‑ramp and catalyst‑addition sequence were optimized to limit oxygen exposure.
Supporting_Evidence:
“it was known that the catalyst was sensitive to oxygen… if the nitrogen pressure on the reaction vessel was switched off, the oxygen level rose to ~5 % v/v.”
“by purging the vessel with nitrogen and then maintaining a slight positive nitrogen pressure… we were able to control the headspace oxygen levels down to <0.1 %.”
“addition of further portion of catalyst (10 mol %) … saw a continued but slow onward conversion to the product.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Copper removal using ferric sulfate generated precipitated iron salts, causing difficult phase separations and time‑dependent instability of the biphasic mixture. Extended wash times led to precipitate formation and impaired downstream processing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A washing regime employing ferric sulfate with excess sodium sulfate (to keep iron soluble) followed by a sodium bicarbonate wash, and an in‑line filtration step using harborlite filter aid was implemented. This cleaned the organic phase, reduced copper to <15 ppm and provided robust phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Ferric sulfate successfully oxidized copper (I), it led to precipitation of ferric salts… the presence of acid led to hydrolysis of 9 and was not considered further. Hence, sodium sulfate was used as a sulfate ion additive to good effect.”
“a sodium bicarbonate wash was introduced followed by an in‑line filtration through filter aid (harborlite), leading to improved phase separations.”
“The ferric sulfate work up successfully reduced the copper levels to <15 ppm.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Product 9 has high solubility in n‑butyl acetate and a low melting point (~47 °C), making crystallization difficult and leading to low isolated yields (~73 % in the lab). Precise concentration control was required to induce nucleation.
Solution_Description: The crystallization protocol was refined to concentrate the reaction solution to >31 % w/w, add n‑heptane as anti‑solvent, seed with solid 9, and cool to –10 °C. The solution temperature was kept above 30 °C prior to seeding to avoid premature crystallization, resulting in an overall isolated yield of 77 % (217 kg) on pilot scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The crystallization of 9 was challenging due to its high solubility … This required a concentrated solution of 9 in n‑butyl acetate and the addition of anti‑solvent (n‑heptane), seeding, further anti‑solvent addition, and isolation at –10 °C.”
“The concentration was adjusted to 31 % w/w … anti‑solvent added … the slurry was cooled to –10 °C.”
“The overall yield from the four batches was 217 kg (77.2 % of theory).”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Copper-Catalyzed Sulfamidation Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The palladium‑based route required large amounts of expensive Pd₂(dba)₃, XPhos ligand and a palladium scavenger, driving up raw‑material cost to ~50 % of total manufacturing expense and raising concerns about supply of these reagents at scale.
Solution_Description: Switching to a copper‑catalyzed process using inexpensive CuI and the inexpensive diamine ligand cyDMEDA dramatically lowered reagent cost and eliminated the need for costly palladium scavenging.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Cost evaluation … step to prepare 9 contributed approximately 50 % to the overall total manufacturing costs. This was due to the high palladium loading, expensive ligand, and use of a palladium scavenger.”
“The catalytic system selected involved copper (I) iodide and trans‑N,N′‑dimethylcylohexane‑1,2‑diamine (cyDMEDA).”
“These diamine ligands were much cheaper than the corresponding palladium ligands, allowing for a potentially significant cost reduction.”

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: The batch nitration of INT11 to INT11B generates a very high adiabatic temperature rise (108 K) and the nitro intermediates have a huge decomposition heat, creating a serious risk of runaway and explosive decomposition.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to continuous flow where the nitric‑acid stream is added slowly, the temperature is kept at 35–45 °C, and a back‑pressure regulator is used.  Dichloromethane (DCM) was chosen as the reaction solvent to maintain solubility and stability.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The adiabatic temperature rise of the crucial nitration step … is high (108 K), but the reaction temperature can be efficiently controlled by the slow addition rate of nitric acid solution.", "the decomposition heat of nitro compounds is also huge, so not only the reaction heat of the nitration step itself but also the subsequent step holds a safety risk.", "Although starting material INT11B was miscible with acetic acid, its decomposition was observed, and the solubility of product INT12 in acetic acid … was also unsatisfactory. Among several candidates, dichloromethane (DCM) was chosen as the solvent of the nitration step…"]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: The Dakin–West‑type reaction of INT11 could not be performed in flow because of technical difficulties, insufficient conversion and the need for 110 °C, which posed safety and stability concerns.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was rearranged: the Dakin–West reaction is carried out in batch to give INT11B, after which nitration and hydrogenation are performed in flow, providing an uninterrupted four‑step flow cascade.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the Dakin–West‑type reaction of INT11 could not, despite several efforts, be carried out in such manner due to technical difficulties and insufficient conversion, thereby the potential multistep flow synthetic route would have been interrupted.", "To avoid this unwanted outcome, we decided to switch the order of the nitration and Dakin–West reactions, in order to create a potentially uninterrupted 4‑step flow synthesis."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: INT11B decomposes and INT12 shows poor solubility in acetic acid (2 g · 100 mL⁻¹), limiting the usable concentration for the nitration step.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane (DCM) was adopted as the nitration solvent because it dissolves both INT11B and the nitro product INT12 (22.6 g · 100 mL⁻¹) without degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Although starting material INT11B was miscible with acetic acid, its decomposition was observed, and the solubility of product INT12 in acetic acid (2.00 g/100 mL) was also unsatisfactory.", "Among several candidates, dichloromethane (DCM) was chosen as the solvent of the nitration step, since it is compatible with highly acidic conditions, it dissolves INT11B without decomposition, and nitro derivative INT12 also exhibits good solubility in it (22.6 g/100 mL)."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: All tested Pd/C catalysts suffered degradation of the charcoal support, causing catalyst leaching, column clogging and loss of activity during continuous hydrogenation of INT12.
Solution_Description: A 5 wt % Pd on alumina catalyst was selected; it gave >99 % conversion, 87 % isolated yield, no leaching and low pressure drop, solving the stability and safety issues.
Supporting_Evidence: ["after having tested several types of Pd/C catalysts, it was clearly shown that degradation of the charcoal solid supporter led to a constant leaching of the catalyst load and to a clogging in our system, regardless of the particle size of the catalyst.", "5 w% Pd on alumina solid supporter (entry 7) was chosen for further development. This catalyst was suitable considering chemical activity (ca. 100 % conversion and 87 % isolated yield for INT13·HCl), as well as physical properties (no leaching observed, low pressure drop on the catalyst column)."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: During prolonged operation the hydrogenation conversion dropped sharply (INT12 became the main component) because of reversible catalyst poisoning when less polar solvent mixtures (containing DCM) or impure nitro feed were used.
Solution_Description: A solvent blend of THF‑DCM‑MeCN (3:2:1) was introduced, which maintained full conversion and prevented poisoning; the system showed stable performance over several hours.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Afterward … conversion dropped rapidly, and after 3 h nitro compound INT12 became the main component … The decrease in the conversion was a consequence of a reversible catalyst poisoning. This issue was observed when less polar solvent mixtures (containing DCM cosolvent), and/or a less pure nitro compound (INT12), were used.", "Among polar aprotic solvents, acetonitrile (MeCN) gave the best result, leading to a practically full conversion in both the hydrogenation and the cyclization steps when applied in a THF–DCM–MeCN 3:2:1 ratio (entry 8)."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: After flow nitration the reaction mixture contains inorganic acids and residual nitric and acetic acid that must be removed before hydrogenation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A custom glass liquid–liquid separator with a manually controlled valve was employed to continuously extract the organic layer (containing INT12) from the aqueous phase, enabling immediate downstream processing.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For the removal of inorganic impurities and residual nitric and acetic acid, application of a continuous purification technique is necessary.", "As a result, a tailor‑made glass separator equipped with a manually controlled valve was tested, which utilized gravitational force for separation… This tool proved to be essentially universal, the only limiting condition being the difference in the density of the applied phases."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: The heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation step was the throughput bottleneck (≈1.5 g h⁻¹) in the original flow cascade, limiting overall productivity.
Solution_Description: The hydrogenation reactor was upscaled (8.5 mm ID × 250 mm length, 7.5 mL volume) and operated at higher flow rates, allowing a 5‑fold increase in productivity and reaching 11.95 g h⁻¹ after further concentration optimisation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The bottleneck of the procedure in terms of output was the heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenation; therefore, our subsequent process intensification efforts primarily concentrated on this step.", "In order to maintain the conversion rate at higher throughput, an upscaled hydrogenation reactor was designed… This enables a theoretical 5‑times increase in productivity compared to the original, lab‑scale flow reactor.", "Thus, after process intensification, an average productivity of 11.95 g/h was achieved."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: Borohydride reagents (NaBH₄) have very low solubility, preventing their use in a continuous‑flow keto‑reduction step; enzymatic attempts gave <30 % conversion.
Solution_Description: The keto‑reduction was retained as a batch operation after the flow cascade, allowing the reduction to be performed in a conventional stirred vessel while the preceding steps remain continuous.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Since the low solubility of borohydride‑based reagents prevents their utilization in our flow technology, several enzymatic reduction test reactions were conducted… the successful biocatalytic reduction unreachable in this case.", "Further efforts to develop a flow chemistry implementation of the keto reduction step were not undertaken, since the final workup… was intended to be carried out anyhow in batch technology."]

Paper Title: Development and Process Intensification of an Efficient Flow–Cascade Reaction Sequence in the Synthesis of Afizagabar
Problem_Description: After 1 h of continuous hydrogenation the conversion of INT12 fell, indicating reversible catalyst poisoning; the column required regeneration.
Solution_Description: A simple regeneration step—washing the packed‑bed catalyst column with MeOH and water—restored the original activity, demonstrating that periodic cleaning can maintain steady performance.
Supporting_Evidence: ["After thorough washing of the catalyst column with MeOH and water, the original conversion was regained, which indicated that the decrease in the conversion was a consequence of a reversible catalyst poisoning."]

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: All tested amine dehydrogenases (AmDHs) were inactive for the conversion of (R)- or (S)-1‑phenylethane‑1,2‑diol (5) into the corresponding phenylglycinol (7). This resulted in no product formation and forced the researchers to abandon the planned NAD‑dependent alcohol dehydrogenase/AmDH cascade.
Solution_Description: The team switched to an alternative alcohol‑amination strategy that combined a secondary alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) with an ω‑transaminase (ω‑TA). The transamination step was made internally recyclable by adding an alanine dehydrogenase (AlaDH) together with d‑ or l‑alanine as the amine donor, thereby providing the necessary ammonia and restoring NAD⁺/NADH balance.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, all the tested AmDHs proved to be unsuitable for this process (data not shown). Therefore, we turned our attention to the alcohol amination by combining an ADH with an ω‑transaminase (ωTA)…”; “the alanine dehydrogenase from Bacillus sphaericus (Bs‑AlaDH) … internally recycled from NADH and pyruvate, respectively, by an alanine dehydrogenase…”

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: When oxidising racemic 5 with the horse‑liver alcohol dehydrogenase (HL‑ADH), the enzyme acted as a secondary ADH, converting the diol into the hydroxy‑ketone 6 instead of the desired aldehyde 8. The unintended oxidation of the primary alcohol also led to aldehyde 8 decomposing to benzaldehyde (10) and subsequently to benzylamine (11), a side‑product observed in 2‑8 % of the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: The researchers replaced the HL‑ADH/ht‑ADH oxidation step with a choline oxidase variant (AcCO6) that directly oxidises the primary alcohol to the aldehyde without over‑oxidation. To prevent H₂O₂‑mediated enzyme deactivation, a small amount of catalase was added to the reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “We envisioned an alternative strategy … that combined a variant of the choline oxidase (AcCO6) … with an AmDH (Ch1‑AmDH).”; “However, HL‑ADH produced the hydroxyketone isomer 6 rather than the desired product 8…”; “a catalase must be added to prevent the possible deactivation of any enzyme … due to the formation of H₂O₂ as a side product.”

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: The AcCO6‑catalysed oxidation generates hydrogen peroxide, which can inactivate enzymes in the cascade and also leads to the oxidative degradation of the aldehyde intermediate 8, forming benzaldehyde (10) that is subsequently reduced to benzylamine (11).
Solution_Description: A catalase (0.1 mg mL⁻¹) was added to decompose H₂O₂ to water and oxygen, protecting the enzymes and minimising side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, a catalase must be added to prevent the possible deactivation of any enzyme in the reaction mixture due to the formation of H₂O₂ as a side product in the oxidation reaction.”; “The reactions were performed … supplemented with a catalytic amount of NAD⁺ (1 mM) and a catalase (0.1 mg mL⁻¹).”

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: During the one‑pot amination of (R)‑5 to (R)‑9, conversion was consistently lower (70 % at 20 mM substrate) than for the (S)‑enantiomer (≥98 % conversion). This reflected the lower intrinsic activity of the AcCO6 enzyme toward the (R)‑enantiomer of the diol.
Solution_Description: The enzyme loading was optimised: the AcCO6 concentration was increased to 70 µM while keeping Ch1‑AmDH at 35 µM, which raised the conversion of (R)‑5 to >98 % with only trace benzylamine formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The optimal conditions for the amination of (R)‑5 (10 mM) were found to be 70 µM AcCO6 and 35 µM Ch1‑AmDH, which resulted in 98 % conversion into product (R)‑9 and traces of 11 (2 %).”

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: NAD⁺/NADH cofactors are expensive when used in stoichiometric amounts, making large‑scale biocatalytic processes uneconomical if they are not regenerated.
Solution_Description: A formate dehydrogenase (Cb‑FDH) together with sodium formate was employed to recycle NAD⁺ to NADH in situ, providing the reducing equivalents required for both the Fus‑SMO epoxidation step and the final reductive amination, thereby minimising cofactor consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: “NADH … was generated in situ and recycled from NAD⁺ (1 mM) by a formate dehydrogenase (Cb‑FDH) and sodium formate (100 mM, 5 equiv).”; “a catalytic amount of NAD⁺ and a formate dehydrogenase … is required in the second reductive amination step … for the in situ generation and recycling of NADH.”

Paper Title: High-Yield Synthesis of Enantiopure 1,2-Amino Alcohols from
Problem_Description: The biocatalytic epoxidation step uses a biphasic n‑heptane/KPi buffer system. Viscosity and phase separation can affect mass transfer and overall conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 1:1 volume ratio of the organic and aqueous phases was identified as optimal on the analytical scale, providing sufficient inter‑phase mixing for quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The influence of the ratio of the two phases on the conversion was initially tested on an analytical scale (total volume of 1 mL), which showed that a 1:1 volume ratio was the optimal condition (see SI section 3.1).”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: Precipitation of material after the initial MTBE charge of the supersaturated MeOH solution interfered with nucleation and proved to be a liability during isolation of 1‑HCl.
Solution_Description: The process was shortened: seed‑bed aging reduced from 2 h → 0.5 h, MTBE charge reduced from 1.5 h → 0.5 h, and final slurry aging reduced from 2 h → 0.5 h, thereby limiting the time for uncontrolled precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “it was observed that precipitation of the material after the initial MTBE charge of the supersaturated MeOH solution can influence the crystallization of 1‑HCl, which proved to be a liability during the isolation of 1‑HCl.”; “the key changes to the process: (1) form I seed bed aging was shortened from 2 to 0.5 h, (2) the MTBE charge was shortened from 1.5 to 0.5 h, and (3) the final MTBE/MeOH slurry aging time was shortened from 2 to 0.5 h.”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: During a production batch the slurry was aged 15 h after MTBE addition and the undesired polymorph 1‑HCl form II appeared even though the charge was seeded with form I, leading to a change in bulk properties and reduced filtration performance.
Solution_Description: The aging time after MTBE addition was limited (≤ 0.5 h) and the seed‑bed was formed before MTBE addition, preventing the nucleation of the more stable form II.
Supporting_Evidence: “during one of the production batches, the slurry was aged for 15 h after the addition of MTBE…a new polymorph, 1‑HCl form II, was isolated (even though the process was seeded with form I).”; “the final crystallization process…(1) form I seed bed aging was shortened from 2 to 0.5 h, (2) the MTBE charge was shortened from 1.5 to 0.5 h, (3) the final MTBE/MeOH slurry aging time was shortened from 2 to 0.5 h.”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: The metastable 1‑HCl form I seed lot fully converted to form II after seven weeks of ambient storage, raising concerns for long‑term manufacture.
Solution_Description: Future campaigns will employ a cooling crystallization that targets form II (stable at room temperature) by seeding above ambient temperature and applying appropriate hold times; alternative solvents will also be evaluated to influence morphology and bulk density.
Supporting_Evidence: “analysis of 1‑HCl post the campaign demonstrated that the 1‑HCl form I seed lot had completely converted to form II after 7 weeks of storage under ambient conditions.”; “the crystallization process will be modified to a cooling crystallization to isolate form II…seed point will be targeted for a temperature higher than ambient and coupled with proper holding times…alternative solvents would be considered to influence the resulting morphology/bulk properties.”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: In the 3 kg production of intermediate 2, the slurry filtration was extremely slow (~2 h) due to smaller particle size from the newly formed polymorph II, and the material showed lower purity (98.5 % AN) with elevated immunomodulating impurity 7.
Solution_Description: A crystallization was designed using solubility curves: seeding at 50 °C (between the solubility curves of forms I and II) and controlled cooling to favor pure form I; the solvent system (MeTHF/MeCN) was exchanged to MeCN to improve dissolution and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “filtration of the reaction slurry was extremely slow (∼2 h)…purity of this material was lower than expected (98.5 % AN), and the elevated levels of immunomodulating 7 were especially concerning.”; “Utilizing the solubility curves and metastable zone as guidance, a crystallization was developed to ensure form control of form I through a seeding process at 50 °C…the majority of MeTHF is removed via two distillation cycles with MeCN…this rigorous solvent exchange into MeCN ensures a consistent and higher yield for the crystallization process.”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: When the crystallization of 2 was seeded with the metastable form II, the product was a mixture of forms I and II, leading to phase contamination and lower overall yield.
Solution_Description: Seeding was performed with pure form I at the appropriate temperature (50 °C) to lock in the desired polymorph; kinetic conditions (minimal stirring, rapid cooling) were used when the goal was to isolate pure form II.
Supporting_Evidence: “the crystallization was repeated but instead seeded with the metastable form II…the resulting solids…were found to be a mixture of forms I and II, emphasizing the potential for phase contamination as a function of seed.”; “An attempt was made to isolate form II utilizing kinetic conditions (minimal stirring and faster cooling rate)…the solution was then cooled to 5 °C over 10 min…500 mg of form II was added…resulting solids…were pure form II.”

Paper Title: Mapping Polymorphic Behavior of Process Intermediates, an Often-Overlooked Exercise
Problem_Description: The original crystallization of 2 produced form I with acceptable yields (70–80 %) but the scale‑up to 3 kg resulted in slower filtration and a modest drop in purity; impurity 7 levels were above target.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation crystallization was implemented: solvent‑exchange into MeCN, a controlled cooling ramp (45 °C → 0 °C) with staged holds to generate a stable form I seed‑bed, and longer aging steps to suppress form conversion, giving 65–75 % yield and >99 % AN purity on a 15 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “the process starts with a crude stream of 2 in MeTHF/MeCN…the reaction mixture is then cooled to 45 °C over 3 h to generate a seed bed that was consistently found to be form I…the slurry is then aged for an additional 3 h at 45 °C…ramp cooling to 0 °C over 5 h…2 was isolated with 65–75 % yield and >99 % AN purity.”

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: Water‑insoluble organic amines have very low solubility in aqueous electrolytes, which makes direct electrosynthesis inefficient and the use of surfactants (commonly employed to stabilize emulsions) creates difficulties in product isolation and generates waste.
Solution_Description: The authors employed 20 kHz ultrasonication (acoustic emulsification) to generate a surfactant‑free oil‑in‑water emulsion, thereby delivering the hydrophobic substrate as fine droplets in water and avoiding the need for organic co‑solvents or surfactants.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...the use of organic solvents in electrosynthesis reactions is not desirable... However, because a large number of organic materials are generally insoluble or only sparingly soluble in water, the desired reactions are difficult to carry out efficiently in aqueous electrolytes.", "...the presence of surfactants may cause other problems such as difficulty in separating postsynthetic products from the reaction mixtures and the production of additional wastes. Hence, conducting electrosynthetic processes in the absence of surfactants is desirable...", "...we developed a continuous‑flow emulsion electrosynthetic system. This new flow system involves 20 kHz ultrasonication for acoustic emulsification of water‑insoluble organic amines in an aqueous electrolyte without the use of a surfactant..."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: When the flow started, a pre‑existing volume of reaction mixture in the sonication vessel was expelled before being fully sonicated, leading to incomplete emulsification and reduced conversion in the downstream electrolysis.
Solution_Description: A 30‑minute pre‑emulsification step (ultrasonication of the entire volume before resuming flow) was introduced to ensure a homogeneous and stable emulsion before entering the electrochemical microreactor.
Supporting_Evidence: ["If syringe pumping is initiated without any prior treatment, a reaction solution that pre‑existed in the sonication vessel might be expelled before being adequately sonicated, substantially decreasing the efficiency of the emulsification process and, thus, the efficiency of the subsequent electrochemical reaction.", "Therefore, the reaction solution in the sonication vessel should be subjected to a pre‑emulsification treatment before the flow reaction is started.", "...a pre‑emulsification treatment consisting of irradiation with 20 kHz ultrasound for 30 min was applied before connecting to the flow system."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: Using a feed volume ratio of n‑octylamine to 1 M KOH of 2 / 10 resulted in poor emulsification; the oil phase segregated, giving an outlet composition different from the inlet and lowering the product yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The feed ratio was optimized to 1 / 10 or 0.5 / 10, which maintained the two‑phase composition throughout the emulsification stage and produced a uniform emulsion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When the feed ratio was 2/10 (= n‑octylamine/1.0 M KOH aq.) by volume, the emulsification did not proceed sufficiently and some of the n‑octylamine segregated into the upper layer in an unemulsified form.", "However, when the feed ratio was set to 1/10 or 0.5/10 by volume, emulsified solutions were obtained at the outlet of the ultrasonication vessel.", "Therefore, to maintain the composition of the two‑phase solution introduced into the ultrasonication vessel while supplying the solution to the subsequent electrolysis stage, we determined that the feed ratio should be 1/10 or 0.5/10 by volume."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: A flow rate of 26.2 mL h⁻¹ exceeded the emulsification capacity of the sonication vessel, resulting in unemulsified n‑octylamine appearing at the outlet and reducing conversion in the electrolysis step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The flow rate was limited to ≤16.5 mL h⁻¹, ensuring that the ultrasonication could keep up with the feed and produce a stable emulsion for the downstream microreactor.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When the flow rate was 26.2 mL h⁻¹, the emulsification process could not keep up with the feed rate of the two‑phase solution and some unemulsified n‑octylamine appeared at the upper layer of the emulsified solution.", "However, when the flow rate was 16.5 mL h⁻¹ or lower, we attained stable emulsified solutions.", "Therefore, to obtain a homogeneous and stable emulsified solution in the continuous flow system, the flow rate should be limited to a range below 16.5 mL h⁻¹."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: At a high current density of 40 mA cm⁻², the current efficiency dropped dramatically (to 51 %) because water oxidation competed with substrate oxidation, indicating excessive heat/over‑potential and side‑reaction formation.
Solution_Description: The current density was reduced to 10–20 mA cm⁻², where current efficiencies above 70 % were recovered, minimizing water oxidation and improving substrate conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...the efficiency decreased dramatically at 40 mA cm⁻². In this case, oxidation of the water used as a solvent might have occurred because of the high current density.", "...at current densities of 10 and 20 mA cm⁻², the desired oxidation product, octanenitrile, was obtained with high current efficiencies greater than 70 %.", "...high current densities ... lead to decreased current efficiency."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: Varying the KOH concentration in the aqueous phase altered droplet size and ionic conductivity; concentrations below 1.0 M reduced conductivity, while concentrations above 1.2 M increased droplet size, both lowering current efficiency.
Solution_Description: The KOH concentration was optimized to 1.0 M, providing sufficient electrolyte in both phases without causing droplet growth, thereby maximizing current efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: ["As the concentration of KOH in the aqueous phase decreased, the concentration of KOH in the droplets also decreased, resulting in a decrease in the ionic conductivity of the droplets. Therefore, the current efficiency decreased in the case of the 0.5 M KOH aq. solution.", "...when the concentration of KOH in the aqueous phase was increased beyond 1.2 M, the current efficiency also decreased. Because the size of emulsion droplets increased when the concentration of KOH was greater than 1.2 M, the decrease in current efficiency was attributed to the slower kinetics of electron transfer as a result of the decrease in the total interfacial area of the droplets.", "Therefore, to achieve a high efficiency in the emulsion electrolysis, the concentration of KOH in the aqueous phase should be 1.0 M."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: Platinum cathodes, while effective, are expensive and generate hydrogen bubbles that require a draft chamber for safe operation.
Solution_Description: The cathode material was switched from Pt to inexpensive Ni, which delivered comparable current efficiency (79 % vs 78 %) and reduced material cost while maintaining safety with proper venting.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...Pt, which has a low hydrogen overvoltage, was used as the cathode material to prevent re‑reduction of the target product. In fact, hydrogen bubbles were observed at the outlet of the microreactor (for safety, these experiments should be conducted in a draft chamber).", "However, for the cathode of the scaled‑up flow microreactor, an inexpensive and easily available material is needed. Therefore, the cathode material was changed from Pt to Ni.", "...the current efficiency for octanenitrile formation in the emulsion electrolysis of n‑octylamine with the Ni cathode was approximately the same as that with the Pt cathode."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: Scaling the electrode area beyond 16 cm² caused electrode deflection and frequent short‑circuits, posing safety hazards and unreliable operation.
Solution_Description: The electrode area was limited to 16 cm² (2 × 8 cm) with a maintained 80 µm gap, and the microreactor design was retained to avoid short‑circuiting while enabling higher throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The maximum electrode area at which a distance of 80 µm could be maintained between the electrodes without short‑circuiting was 16 cm² (2 cm × 8 cm). When electrodes larger than 16 cm² were used, short circuits due to slight deflection of the electrodes occurred frequently.", "...the electrode area of the flow microreactor was increased from 3 to 16 cm².", "...the electrolysis was performed with the Ni cathode at the scaled‑up electrode area without loss of efficiency."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: After electrolysis, the oil phase contains both unreacted amine and product nitrile; efficient phase separation is required to isolate the product without cross‑contamination.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A liquid–liquid separator equipped with a hydrophilized PTFE membrane was integrated downstream of the microreactor, enabling rapid and effective separation of the oil and aqueous phases.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...the emulsion after the electrolysis was efficiently separated into an aqueous electrolyte and oil product using a liquid–liquid separator.", "A polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) membrane subjected to a hydrophilic treatment... was placed in a liquid–liquid separator... and the oil phase was collected.", "...the liquid–liquid separator could separate the two phases irrespective of the ratio between n‑octylamine and octanenitrile in the oil phase."]

Paper Title: Integrated Flow Emulsion Electrosynthetic System by In Situ Generation of Emulsions, Subsequent Emulsion Electrolysis, and Final Phase Separation
Problem_Description: The original batch acoustic‑emulsification/electrolysis system performed ultrasonication and electrolysis in the same reactor, limiting productivity and requiring long residence times.
Solution_Description: A fully continuous flow platform was built, separating the ultrasonication vessel, the electrochemical microreactor, and the liquid–liquid separator, thereby dramatically increasing throughput and enabling gram‑scale synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...both electrolysis and ultrasonication are performed in the same batch reactor, which limits the productivity of the process.", "...we have developed a continuous‑flow emulsion electrosynthetic system. This new flow system uses 20 kHz ultrasonication for acoustic emulsification... followed by emulsion electrolysis in a flow microreactor; the emulsion is finally separated...", "The product­ivity of the 16 cm² microreactor under the optimum conditions was 0.34 g h⁻¹, which was five times higher than that of the 3 cm² microreactor."]

Paper Title: Continuous Processing of Concentrated Organolithiums in Flow Using Static and Dynamic Spinning Disc Reactor Technologies
Problem_Description: In static micro‑flow reactors the organolithium reactions caused precipitation of salts or polymeric solids (e.g., LiOH, lithiated intermediates) that quickly blocked the narrow channels, leading to reactor fouling and loss of flow.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The researchers switched to a dynamic spinning‑disc reactor (SpinPro) which generates very high shear forces (>1 000 000 Re) and provides alternating PFR/CSTR zones; this device tolerates solid formation, prevents deposition and maintains uninterrupted flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “Many users observed decreasing flow rates and finally blockages… clogging phenomena are attributed to… precipitation of salts… the SpinPro reactor… tolerates salt precipitations and can provide excellent mass transfer conditions.”

Paper Title: Continuous Processing of Concentrated Organolithiums in Flow Using Static and Dynamic Spinning Disc Reactor Technologies
Problem_Description: Commercial 15 % BuLi solutions contain large amounts of hexane (≈15‑30 wt %); the hydrocarbon acts as an antisolvent for polar lithiated intermediates, causing low solubility, precipitation and consequently reduced conversion/yield.
Solution_Description: Highly concentrated BuLi (3–6 M) or diluted BuLi in THF was used, dramatically lowering the hexane fraction in the reaction mixture; the higher organolithium concentration also reduced the overall solvent volume.
Supporting_Evidence: “By reducing the concentration of the non‑polar solvent hexane, the conversion is significantly increased… Using higher concentrated BuLi solutions, hence by introducing less hexane to the reaction mixture, see data in Table 7.”

Paper Title: Continuous Processing of Concentrated Organolithiums in Flow Using Static and Dynamic Spinning Disc Reactor Technologies
Problem_Description: Batch organolithium processes require cryogenic temperatures (‑78 °C to ‑95 °C) and handling of pyrophoric reagents, posing safety hazards and limiting scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reactions were transferred to continuous flow where they could be performed at ambient or mildly cooled temperatures (‑20 °C to 20 °C), eliminating the need for extreme cooling and improving operational safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the flow mode, the observed reactions could be carried out under more convenient conditions, that is, at higher temperatures … the deprotonation reaction even at ambient temperature instead of −78 °C.”

Paper Title: Continuous Processing of Concentrated Organolithiums in Flow Using Static and Dynamic Spinning Disc Reactor Technologies
Problem_Description: In static flow the simple T‑piece mixing of BuLi with substrate gave poor homogenisation, leading to low conversion for the deprotonation/borylation sequence.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The flow system was upgraded to include static tube mixers (Koflo) with larger channels and/or the high‑shear spinning‑disc reactor, providing turbulent mixing that dramatically increased conversion (up to 78 % in static flow and 86 % in dynamic flow).
Supporting_Evidence: “The static mixing devices… are especially vulnerable to clogging… The SpinPro dynamic reactor… high shear forces counteract solid deposition… conversion increased to 86 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous Processing of Concentrated Organolithiums in Flow Using Static and Dynamic Spinning Disc Reactor Technologies
Problem_Description: Static flow required relatively long residence times (up to 20 s) to obtain acceptable conversion, limiting throughput and space‑time yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Residence time was reduced to as short as 5 s in the SpinPro reactor by exploiting its high shear and efficient mass transfer, while still achieving >98 % conversion for bromine–lithium exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: “All experiments showed almost quantitative conversion… a residence time of 5 s… provided excellent results.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: The conventional synthetic route for ENA phosphoramidites required 13 steps, gave an overall yield of only ~12 % and was costly and time‑consuming, making large‑scale manufacturing impractical.
Solution_Description: A divergent synthetic strategy was introduced that places the ethylene‑bridged bicyclic scaffold as a downstream common intermediate (compound 34). This shortens the synthesis to four steps after the common intermediate, dramatically reducing material cost, lead time and number of operations.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since the manufacturing cost of ENA was high in the conventional synthetic method … and the required period for production was very long, an efficient manufacturing method … was strongly required.”; “The most important issue to efficiently reduce the total steps was the construction of the quaternary carbon at the 4‑position.”; “By changing the raw material and applying the new synthetic method, we obtained the common intermediate 34 … in 23 % overall yield for 11 steps by three isolations without performing column purification.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Construction of the quaternary carbon at the 4‑position of the ENA skeleton was difficult, requiring many oxidation‑reduction steps and giving low overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: A stereoselective aldol reaction of ketone 13 with formaldehyde was employed to set the quaternary carbon in a single step, leveraging known literature precedents for high diastereoselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The most important issue … was the construction of the quaternary carbon at the 4‑position.”; “Ketone 13 … could be used for constructing a four‑substituted carbon by a stereoselective aldol reaction.”; “The stereoselective aldol reaction … has also been reported in the literature …”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Deoxygenation of the 5‑hydroxy group on the concave side of the intermediate was very slow, leading to poor conversion and many steps via an aldehyde intermediate.
Solution_Description: The starting material was changed to commercially available glucuronolactone 22; a one‑step deoxygenation/reduction using sodium bis(2‑methoxyethoxy)‑aluminum dihydride (Red‑Al) gave the desired diol 24, avoiding the hazardous lithium aluminum hydride (LAH).
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, these results showed that the reactivity of the 5‑hydroxy group is generally low … The only route was found … and was discontinued from the viewpoint of efficiency.”; “Glucuronolactone 22 was selected as an alternative starting material … When the product was treated with Red‑Al, deoxygenation and reduction proceeded … avoiding the use of LAH made the method safer and scalable.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Five consecutive transformations (tritylation, oxidation, alkylation, reduction, benzyl protection) previously required isolation of intermediates, making the sequence long and labor‑intensive.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: All five steps were performed in a biphasic toluene‑water system without intermediate work‑ups; each step was completed by simple liquid‑liquid separation, allowing continuous conversion of 24→29 in 7 days on multikilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was noticed that most of the reactions can be conducted in the presence of water; we attempted to successfully perform the five steps by the biphasic reaction … As a result, the reaction of a total of five steps could be continuously converted into intermediate 29 … transformation of 24 into 29 was carried out within 7 days on a multikilogram scale.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Attempted SN2‑type cyclization of diol 30 via selective tosylation failed because the secondary alcohol also tosylated, leaving unreacted material.
Solution_Description: A Mitsunobu etherification (DIAD/Triphenylphosphine) was used instead, giving smooth cyclization to the desired bicyclic product 32.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, we tried SN2‑type cyclization … however, this approach was discontinued because it was difficult to suppress tosylation for the secondary alcohol, and even the diol 30 remained.”; “Alternatively, when etherification was tried under Mitsunobu conditions, the desired cyclization reaction smoothly proceeded.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Phosphoramidite formation is highly moisture‑sensitive; residual water hydrolyzes the phosphorodiamidite, leading to impurity formation and safety concerns due to reactive phosphorus species.
Solution_Description: 4 Å molecular sieves were added to remove trace water, and 4,5‑dicyanoimidazole (DCI) was used as a catalytic activator to promote phosphoramidite formation while suppressing over‑reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “This reaction is known as a highly moisture‑sensitive reaction … To prepare the strictly anhydrous conditions, we employed an addition of molecular sieves 4 Å … it was found that the use of 4,5‑dicyanoimidazole (DCI) worked to catalytically activate the phosphoramidite reagent and suppress the over‑reacted impurities under mild conditions.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: β‑Selective glycosylation of pyrimidine bases using TMSOTf gave predominantly the undesired α‑anomer (β:α ≈ 3.7:96.3).
Solution_Description: Switching the Lewis acid to TMSBr or TMSI dramatically increased β‑selectivity (e.g., TMSI gave β:α ≈ 81.7:18.3), providing the desired β‑glycoside.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 shows that with TMSOTf the β‑form was only 3.7 % while with TMSBr and TMSI the β‑form increased to 75.7 % and 81.7 % respectively; “When TMSBr or TMSI were used … the β‑adduct was generated with relatively high selectivity.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Glycosylation of purine bases (N6‑Bz‑adenine, N2‑isobutyryl‑guanine) produced complex mixtures of regio‑ and stereoisomers, making isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: Using 2,6‑dichloropurine as a common building block allowed the reaction mixture to isomerize over time to the desired N9‑β isomer, simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “Complex mixtures containing regio‑ and stereoisomers were given … Thus, an alternative methodology … was required.”; “When the glycosylation reaction was examined using 2,6‑dichloropurine … these mixtures were found to be converted into the desired N9‑β isomer.”

Paper Title: Efficient Divergent Synthesis of 2′‑
Problem_Description: Residual boron reagents from BCl₃ deprotection interfered with subsequent DMTr protection of the diol.
Solution_Description: A post‑treatment with aqueous Rochelle’s salt effectively removed boron species, allowing the DMTr protection to proceed cleanly.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the boron components remained in the next step, the subsequent DMTr protection could not be completed … when the treatment is performed using an aqueous Rochelle’s salt solution, the boron component was almost completely removed and the subsequent reaction proceeded smoothly.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: During batch diazotization‑azidation the reaction mixture formed a suspension (especially the azide 4a) that was unsuitable for flow screening and caused low conversion when water/HCl was used.
Solution_Description: A biphasic mixture of dichloromethane (DCM) and water with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) was employed, keeping all components in solution and giving high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction mixture containing azide <bold>4a</bold> formed a suspension that was clearly unsuitable for flow chemistry screening.; In a biphasic mixture of dichloromethane (DCM) and water in combination with TFA, the reaction mixture remained a solution and high conversion rates were achieved.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Azide 4a shows multiple exothermic events above 100 °C (DSC) releasing 635 J g⁻¹, posing a severe runaway risk and potential nitrogen‑gas explosion if heated to the original 80 °C batch temperature.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to continuous flow with small reactor volumes, precise temperature control, and an inert‑gas back‑pressure regulator to limit the accumulation of hazardous intermediates and manage the exotherm safely.
Supporting_Evidence: Multiple exothermic events are apparent above 100 °C, setting free a total energy of 635 J/g, which could lead to an adiabatic temperature increase of more than 300 K.; A scale‑up in batch at the original jacket temperature of 80 °C was clearly considered to be a severe safety risk, which potentially could lead to a runaway situation.; The development of a continuous flow procedure enabled us to prepare azides in solution, keeping reactor volumes small and allowing precise control of reaction parameters, especially the reaction temperature.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: The diazonium chloride of 2a is highly unstable, decomposing to deazotized aldehyde 7 and giving variable conversion and side‑product formation when nitrite is not fully consumed before azide addition.
Solution_Description: Sodium azide was added only after complete consumption of sodium nitrite, and stoichiometry was optimized (1.2 eq of NaN₃ and NaNO₂, 2.5 eq of TFA) to suppress side‑product formation and achieve full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: A more careful look into this reaction sequence revealed the importance of only adding sodium azide to the reaction mixture when the sodium nitrite is fully consumed.; If sodium azide is dosed in too early, it would be immediately consumed by the unreacted sodium nitrite, observable by the poor conversion of <bold>2a</bold> and even variable amounts of deazotized aldehyde <bold>7</bold>.; With regard to stoichiometry, a 1.2‑fold excess of sodium nitrite and sodium azide and 2.5 equivalents of TFA proved to be efficient for both reactions to proceed to completion.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: A stock solution of amino‑aldehyde 2 in DCM/TFA was unstable, undergoing self‑condensation to dimers and trimers, which compromised reproducibility.
Solution_Description: TFA was introduced in a separate feed stream rather than premixed, preventing premature condensation of 2a.
Supporting_Evidence: The first experiments in the flow mode revealed that a stock solution of aminoaldehyde <bold>2</bold> in the 1:1 mix of DCM and TFA was unstable, yielding dimers and trimers via self‑condensation reactions.; To prevent this, the continuous flow setup was adapted to add TFA in a separate stream to the substrate feed.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Copper(I) oxide (10 mol %) used for the cyclization formed suspensions in DCE and required a 90 min residence at 80 °C, leading to low productivity and unsuitable operation in flow.
Solution_Description: The heterogeneous Cu₂O was replaced by soluble Cu(I) iodide with TMEDA (0.1 eq CuI, 1 eq TMEDA) and later by a copper coil (inner‑diameter 1 mm) acting as a solid catalyst, eliminating precipitation and enabling rapid flow cyclization.
Supporting_Evidence: Copper‑(I) oxide (10 mol %) was used originally as a catalyst for this cyclization reaction, forming suspensions in DCE that were unsuitable for a continuous flow process.; Initial experiments focused on the replacement of insoluble Cu‑(I) oxide by a soluble catalyst system. Therefore, we tested Cu‑(I) iodide in combination with various bases, for example, triethylamine, 1,4‑diazabicyclo[2.2.2]octane (DABCO), and tetramethylethylenediamine (TMEDA) in DCE and in toluene.; As a proof of concept, a 0.32 M solution of <bold>4a</bold>, already mixed with 1.2 equivalents of amine <bold>6</bold> in toluene, was prepared and pumped through a copper coil at 120 °C with a residence time of 20 min.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: The copper‑catalyzed cyclization required 90 min at 80 °C, giving only 70–80 % isolated yield and reducing throughput for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Temperature was raised to 120 °C and residence time shortened to 20 min (30 min for 5b) in flow, while using higher substrate concentrations (0.32–0.45 M), resulting in ≥95 % conversion and improved productivity (up to 16 g h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction time of 90 min at 80 °C was too long for a flow reaction with a small footprint for reasons of safety and would have resulted in an unacceptably low productivity.; Starting with a 0.45 M solution of <bold>4b</bold> in DCE that contained 0.1 equivalent of Cu‑(I) iodide and 1 equivalent of TMEDA, we achieved full conversion to indazole <bold>5a</bold> at 120 °C with a 20 min residence time.; After adjusting the residence time to 30 min, the cyclization to <bold>5b</bold> proceeded to completion, and only 3 % of amino‑imine <bold>8b</bold> was detected as the side product.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Azide 4b and indazole 5b showed poor solubility in toluene, leading to longer residence times, risk of clogging, and lower productivity.
Solution_Description: The process retained DCE as the reaction solvent for both azide formation and cyclization because DCE provided higher solubility for 4b and 5b, allowing higher concentrations (≈0.45 M) and shorter residence times.
Supporting_Evidence: We decided not to do a solvent switch but to keep DCE as the solvent for this process for a couple of reasons. … the solubilities of both, azide <bold>4b</bold> and product <bold>5b</bold> were higher in DCE than in toluene, which allowed the use of higher concentrations and lowered the risk of clogging.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Initial small‑scale flow runs gave acceptable conversion, but scaling to multi‑gram quantities required higher throughput; the original reactor volumes (5 mL/10 mL) limited productivity.
Solution_Description: Reactor volumes were increased (20 mL for the first coil, 40 mL for the second) and larger copper‑coil reactors (two 10 mL coils) were employed, enabling continuous operation at higher flow rates (up to 0.67 mL min⁻¹) and delivering >14 g h⁻¹ of azide 4b and >8 g h⁻¹ of indazole 5b.
Supporting_Evidence: The volume of the cooled reactors was set to 20 mL (2 × 10 mL PFA‑coils, ID: 1 mm), and the volume of the second reactor was enlarged to 40 mL (4 × 10 mL PFA‑coils, ID: 1 mm).; For the scale‑up of 5b, we used a portion of crude solution of 4b … pumped through two 10 mL copper coils (ID: 1 mm) at 120 °C at a flow rate of 0.67 mL min⁻¹.

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Isolation of the hazardous azide intermediate 4a/4b posed safety risks and added purification steps.
Solution_Description: The azide formation step was telescoped directly into the copper‑catalyzed cyclization without isolation of the azide, eliminating the handling of solid azides and simplifying the workflow.
