Supporting_Evidence: We stood firm in our strategy to develop a continuous flow procedure for the synthesis of azide <bold>4a</bold>, keeping it in solution without any isolation, and to use solutions of <bold>4a</bold> for telescoping into the cyclization step to 2H‑indazole <bold>5a</bold>.; ...the new alternative flow procedure not only avoided the isolation of hazardous azides <bold>4a</bold> and <bold>4b</bold>...

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Diazonium Salts and Azides in a Three-Step Continuous Flow Sequence
Problem_Description: Residual copper and palladium from the final Suzuki coupling required removal before the drug substance could be obtained.
Solution_Description: A solid metal‑scavenger was added after the cross‑coupling to remove copper and palladium contaminants, enabling isolation of the final product without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: After treatment with a metal scavenger to remove the potentially remaining copper and palladium contamination, the Boc‑protecting group was cleaved in the final step...

Paper Title: An Efficient Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain Using Chemoenzymatic Catalysis
Problem_Description: Several steps in the synthesis exhibited low conversion, unwanted side‑products, or operational difficulties that limited overall productivity.
Solution_Description: The authors systematically optimized reaction time, concentration, enzyme loading, additives and solvents, and in one case switched to a different biocatalyst to overcome the identified shortcomings.
Supporting_Evidence: See individual Problem_Solution_Pair entries below for specific excerpts.

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Synthetic Process of Clonazepam by Preventing the Formation of a Trimeric Compound in the Presence of HCl
Problem_Description: The original industrial routes for clonazepam suffered from several issues: (1) low conversion of intermediate 3 (< 85 %) due to protonation of the amine by HBr; (2) use of diethyl ether was unsafe (volatile, flammable and prone to oxidation); (3) HBr by‑product was poorly soluble in ether, hampering removal; (4) the one‑pot conversion of 3 + HMTA gave only ~90 % HPLC purity because a trimeric impurity 9 formed during the long reflux (≈ 24 h); (5) polymerisation to trimer 9 also reduced overall yield; (6) a Smiles‑rearrangement impurity 13 formed during dehydration of 7 ·HCl; (7) Route 2 required expensive potassium iodide, raising cost; (8) pyridine used in Route 2 is highly toxic; (9) the one‑pot step required 24 h reflux, greatly limiting throughput; (10) incomplete hydrolysis of 8 ·HCl to 7 ·HCl because of its low water solubility.
Solution_Description: The authors implemented a series of improvements: (1) switched the amide‑coupling solvent from ether to dichloromethane (DCM), achieving > 99 % conversion of 2 → 3; (2) washed the crude 3 with aqueous sodium carbonate to avoid hydrolysis; (3) performed the Delepine reaction (3 + HMTA) in DCM and then hydrolysed the quaternary ammonium salt 4 directly in a mixed aqueous HCl/ethanol medium, which prevented formation of the trimer 9; (4) used ethanol as the co‑solvent for the acidic hydrolysis (Stage 2), giving complete conversion of 8 ·HCl to 7 ·HCl; (5) increased the amount of HCl to 5.76 equiv (4 × 1.2 × 1.2) to ensure full depolymerisation of 9; (6) employed sodium acetate as a weakly basic buffer for the final dehydration–condensation of 7 ·HCl, suppressing the Smiles‑rearrangement to 13; (7) eliminated the costly KI step by using the Delepine route, reducing material cost; (8) replaced toxic pyridine with sodium acetate, improving safety; (9) reduced the overall reaction time (e.g., 4 h reflux for the Delepine step, 2 h for dehydration) to increase throughput; (10) added ethanol to the hydrolysis step to improve solubility of 8 ·HCl, achieving > 96 % 7 ·HCl and eliminating residual trimer.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "the conversion rate was still lower than 85%" (sec 2.1) – low yield problem.
• "diethyl ether was volatile, flammable, and easily produced oxidized byproducts; therefore, we gave up the attempt to prepare 3 in diethyl ether" (sec 2.1) – safety problem.
• "Considering the lower solubility of the byproduct hydrobromic acid in dichloromethane (DCM) than diethyl ether, it can be volatilized and taken out of the DCM under reflux" (sec 2.1) – solubility problem.
• "the HPLC purity of 1 prepared by using one‑pot method reaches only ~90%" (intro) – low purity/yield.
• "The trimer intermediate 9 … polymerized … the depolymerisation … is the rate‑determining step" (sec 2) – decomposition/polymerisation problem.
• "Smiles rearrangement product 13 … detected" (sec 2.3) – purification/impurity problem.
• "the economic cost is significantly increased by the expensive potassium iodide" (intro) – cost problem.
• "Compared with other highly toxic and irritating pyridine in Route 2, sodium acetate is ... a better choice" (sec 2.3) – safety problem.
• "It takes almost 24 h for the reflux to make the second white precipitate…" (sec 2) – long reaction time.
• "the low water solubility may be the main reason that 8·HCl cannot be completely hydrolysed to 7·HCl" (sec 2.2) – solubility problem.
• "Therefore, inert DCM was selected as the reaction solvent, and it was found that the conversion rate … could reach more than 99%" (sec 2.1) – solution: solvent change.
• "a sodium carbonate aqueous solution was selected as the wash" (sec 2.1) – solution: pH control.
• "hydrolysis of 4 in aqueous hydrochloric acid solution did prevent the formation of 9" (sec 2.2) – solution: order and rate of addition.

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: The early‑stage Mitsunobu reaction (DEAD/TPP) used to install the trifluoro‑alkyl tail generated large amounts of by‑products (triphenylphosphine oxide) that required low‑temperature hexane slurries and silica‑gel chromatography, making purification difficult and the step low‑atom‑economy.  Additionally, the azodicarbonyl reagents examined offered no improvement, and the reagents (DEAD, DCC, etc.) present safety and cost concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The Mitsunobu step was replaced by a Williamson‑ether sequence (mesylation of the alcohol followed by SN2‑etherification).  This two‑step protocol gave >90 % overall yield, eliminated the need for purification of the Mitsunobu by‑product, and avoided the hazardous and expensive reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Notable challenges with the synthesis included the early installation of the trifluoroalkyl tail under classical DEAD/TPP Mitsunobu conditions. The byproducts of this reaction plagued purification strategies which involved multiple low‑temperature (‑78 °C) hexane slurries for triphenylphosphine oxide removal, followed by the necessity for silica gel chromatography..."  
"A survey of some of the newer azodicarbonyl reagents… failed to offer an improvement…"  
"The problems associated with the Mitsunobu reaction were effectively addressed by switching to the alternative workhorse method for ether construction, the Williamson‑ether synthesis"  
"Mesylation of alcohol 10 was achieved under standard conditions and product 11 was used crude in the subsequent SN2‑etherification reaction. The overall yield was >90 % for the two steps and eliminated the need for any purification during the sequence."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: The first stereoselective Mannich alkylation of the sulfinyl‑imine gave low conversion (trace product with Ti‑enolate, 39 % with LDA) and poor diastereoselectivity (2:1 dr), leading to an overall low isolated yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑optimized by switching the base to KHMDS, changing the solvent from THF to diethyl ether, using a 3 equiv excess of the acetophenone partner, and premixing the sulfinimine with the ketone before adding KHMDS.  These changes raised the yield to 85 % and improved the dr to 30:1 (97:3).
Supporting_Evidence:
"Only a trace product was identified from the covalent titanium enolate formed via transmetallation of the lithium enolate with ClTi(iPrO)3."  
"Lithium enolate formation with LDA in THF resulted in a modest yield of product but with low diastereoselectivity."  
"A significant improvement in diastereoselectivity was realized when KHMDS was used as the base.  Further notable increases to both yield and diastereoselectivities were observed for KHMDS in diethyl ether."  
"Using these conditions, premixing of sulfimine 6 with 1.2 equiv acetophenone, followed by the addition of 1.1 equiv KHMDS proved superior… and resulted in a further yield improvement to 85 %"

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the sulfinyl ketimine (6) beyond ~50 g gave a reduced isolated yield (≈54 %) and the ketimine proved hydrolytically unstable; traditional purification (silica, alumina) failed, and the recovered ketone indicated decomposition.
Solution_Description: The crude ketimine was carried forward without isolation into the Mannich reaction, allowing telescoping of the step and avoiding the problematic purification.  This approach gave a cleaner reaction profile and restored high conversion on multigram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Increasing the scale to >50 g resulted in a reduced isolated yield (54 %) of the pure ketimine 6. Alternative methods of purification including Celite filtration, neutral alumina, and Et₃N‑doped silica gel failed to improve the outcome…"  
"These optimized conditions performed well on scale and resulted in a cleaner reaction profile which enabled telescoping of the crude reaction mixture into auxiliary cleavage."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: The oxidation of alcohol 4 to ketone 5 originally employed Dess–Martin periodinane, a reagent with significant safety hazards and high cost; alternative oxidants (Moffatt, TEMPO, MnO₂) gave inferior results.
Solution_Description: A classical Jones oxidation (CrO₃) with a 1.3‑fold excess was adopted.  It provided 98 % crude yield, eliminated the safety and cost issues associated with Dess–Martin, and required only a simple Celite filtration for work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Oxidation of 4 had originally used Dess–Martin periodinane to give 5 in 71 % yield, although safety and cost concerns with this reagent prompted us to explore other alternatives."  
"A survey of Moffatt, TEMPO, and MnO₂‑based oxidations all gave inferior results… the classical Jones oxidation… served us well in this case. A 1.3‑fold excess of CrO₃ proved to be efficient and the often cumbersome work‑up… was minimized by simple filtration through Celite. Extractive work‑up gave a 98 % crude yield of the ketone 5."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: The initial intramolecular cyclization using piperidine under reflux in ethanol caused a significant double‑bond migration (5–20 % of migrated product) and delivered only 30 % isolated yield of the desired ADHP core, with additional impurities forming upon tautomerization.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to toluene improved the yield (83 %).  Further optimization identified NaOH/MeOH at 40 °C as the optimal condition, delivering 95 % yield with no migration.  The reaction could also be run at room temperature in NaOH/MeOH, giving 70 % yield without migration, thereby reducing reaction time and temperature exposure.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Initial attempts at cyclization employed piperidine at elevated temperatures which resulted in significant double bond migration… low yield of the desired product (Table 2, entry 1)."  
"Switching solvent to toluene resulted in an improved yield due to a quicker reaction time but the observation of the double bond migrated product…"  
"A brief screen of base/solvents produced the NaOH/MeOH at 40 °C (Table 2, entry 4) showing optimal results… gave a high‑purity API in an 88 % isolated yield."  
"Alternatively, the reaction could be performed at room temperature (Table 2, entry 3) with no migration products detected."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: Purification of the Mannich alkylation product (8) required multiple chromatographic steps; the need for high‑throughput chiral separation slowed material throughput.
Solution_Description: Supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) was implemented for the rapid chiral separation of 8, enabling a throughput of 6 g h⁻¹ and clean removal of the 2–4 % undesired diastereomer.
Supporting_Evidence: "SFC purification of 8 allowed the rapid throughput of material (6 g/h) with the 2–4 % undesired isomer generated in the alkylation step readily removed."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: The first‑generation eight‑step route required extensive chromatographic purifications, leading to a modest 6.5 % overall yield and limiting multigram production.
Solution_Description: The revised route telescoped several intermediates (e.g., crude Mannich product directly to auxiliary cleavage) and eliminated most column chromatography, achieving a 30 % overall yield for >100 g of API.
Supporting_Evidence:
"These improvements facilitated improved yields and less reliance on intermediate purification, which in combination with an optimized stereoselective Mannich alkylation and modified final cyclization‑direct API isolation resulted in a 35 g synthesis in a 30 % overall yield."  
"... resulted in a cleaner reaction profile which enabled telescoping of the crude reaction mixture into auxiliary cleavage."

Paper Title: Synthesis Optimization, Scale-Up, and Catalyst Screening Efforts toward the MGAT2 Clinical Candidate, BMS-963272
Problem_Description: Initial Suzuki coupling of the common intermediate (12) gave poor conversion even with high loadings of a Buchwald precatalyst, preventing reliable scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A high‑throughput 96‑well plate screen of 16 ligands, two bases (K₃PO₄, K₂CO₃) and three solvents identified DPEphos, DCyPF, and PPh₃ with K₃PO₄ as optimal.  This catalytic system delivered high conversion and will guide future scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Initial attempts at Suzuki coupling with the common intermediate proved challenging even with high catalyst loadings of a Buchwald precatalyst…"  
"We decided to perform a high‑throughput catalyst screening… 96‑well plate screen of 16 ligands… each reaction contained 5 % Pd(OAc)₂… heated at 50 °C for 17 h.  The top‑performing ligands… DPEphos, DCyPF, and PPh₃…"  
"Analysis of this data indicates that K₃PO₄ generally provided superior results versus K₂CO₃…"

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: Using NaOMe as the base with Ru‑MACHO (1a) caused base‑promoted isomerisation of d‑glucose to the diastereomer d‑mannitol (2.8 % of product), lowering the selectivity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to the borohydride complex Ru‑MACHO‑BH (1b), which does not require a base for activation, and employed the mild amine N‑methylpyrrolidine (0.05 mol %) as a promoter. This combination suppressed the isomerisation (only 1.2 % d‑mannitol) while maintaining >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Issue – "Since we presumed that isomerization was caused by a strong base, NaOMe, Ru‑MACHO‑BH (1b) was used instead…" (Table 1, entry 1 vs 2).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: When no base was added with Ru‑MACHO‑BH (1b), conversion dropped to 66.2 % (entry 2), indicating insufficient catalyst activation.
Solution_Description: A systematic base screen identified N‑methylpyrrolidine (0.05 mol %) as the most effective additive, restoring >99 % conversion and improving selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: Issue – "significant decrease in conversion was observed with 1b in the absence of a base (entry 2)" (Table 1).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: Reactions performed in methanol displayed lower selectivity and higher formation of the mannose isomer, especially at high catalyst loadings; the substrate’s limited solubility in MeOH contributed to incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to ethanol or isopropanol markedly increased selectivity (≤1.2 % d‑mannitol) and maintained high conversion; the concentration was set to 0.5 M to balance solubility with throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: "Screening of the solvent revealed that ethanol and 2‑propanol gave higher selectivity than methanol (entries 7–11)" (Table 1).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: Lowering the hydrogen pressure to 3 MPa or 1 MPa resulted in insufficient conversion (entries 12–13).
Solution_Description: The optimal pressure of 5 MPa was retained for all subsequent experiments to ensure complete hydrogenation.
Supporting_Evidence: "On the other hand, hydrogenation under lower hydrogen pressure gave insufficient conversion with comparable selectivity (entries 12 and 13)" (Table 1).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: When the catalyst loading was reduced to an S/C ratio of 30 000 in methanol, conversion remained high but the amount of the unwanted diastereomer d‑mannitol increased to 2.3 % (entry 4, Table 2).
Solution_Description: Performing the reaction in ethanol at the same high S/C ratio kept the diastereomer formation below 1 % while preserving >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "the amount of d‑mannitol had to be increased from 1.2 to 2.3 % (entry 4)" (Table 2) and "when hydrogenation was conducted in ethanol, almost no increase in the diastereomer was confirmed" (text).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the disaccharide maltose gave only 55 % conversion under the aldose conditions, attributed to the substrate’s higher acidity and poorer solubility in ethanol.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of N‑methylpyrrolidine to 0.40 mol % and lowering the substrate concentration to 0.25 M improved conversion to 86 %; a further temperature increase to 150 °C raised conversion to >99 % with unchanged selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "the conversion tended to increase when the amount of base was increased up to 0.40 mol %… a lower concentration also had a positive effect… finally, when the reaction temperature was increased to 150 °C, the reaction was completed" (Table 3).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: Lactose required twice the amount of Ru‑MACHO‑BH catalyst to reach quantitative conversion, raising material cost concerns.
Solution_Description: No dedicated solution was reported; the authors simply noted the higher catalyst demand for lactose.
Supporting_Evidence: "Lactose ... required twice as much catalyst as the other disaccharides" (text).

Paper Title: Highly Efficient and Selective Hydrogenation of Sugars Catalyzed by Ru-MACHO-BH: Practical Synthesis of Sugar Alcohols
Problem_Description: On a ~100 g scale, the isolated yield of maltitol was 76 % because a portion of product remained in the mother liquor after crystallisation.
Solution_Description: A single‑crystallisation step from ethanol was employed to recover the product, delivering pure d‑sorbitol and maltitol with >99 % purity, albeit with a modest isolated yield for maltitol.
Supporting_Evidence: "we successfully obtained pure d‑sorbitol (3a) and maltitol (8a) by single crystallization from ethanol on a scale of nearly 100 g. The moderate isolated yield of maltitol (8a) is mainly due to the loss of product to the mother liquor" (Scheme 4).

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: The original third‑generation route uses phosphorus pentasulfide (P₂S₅) to form a thioamide intermediate (5). P₂S₅ generates toxic H₂S gas, has a strong odor, produces waste‑disposal issues, and the thioamide is unstable, leading to decomposition during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the thio‑activation step with a phosphorylative activation using diethyl chlorophosphoridate (DECP) and the phosphazene base BTPP, eliminating P₂S₅ and the thioamide intermediate while delivering the triazole intermediate (6) in high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of P₂S₅ is not optimal from a long‑term manufacturing viewpoint due to the potential for the generation of toxic hydrogen sulfide gas, limited stability of the thioamide, stringent odor abatement requirements, and waste disposal concerns.”; “The improved synthetic route … avoids the need for the formation of a thioamide intermediate… and culminated in the demonstration of the new process at a 750 g scale.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: Lactam 4 shows poor solubility in the reaction medium (MeCN), resulting in low conversion and high levels of residual starting material (∼3 % after 5 h at –10 °C).
Solution_Description: Screening identified the phosphazene base BTPP, which is highly soluble in MeCN and exhibits strong basicity. Using MeCN as the reaction solvent and the appropriate concentration of BTPP/DECP gave higher conversion (up to 76.5 % a/a on 200 mg scale).
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction started with relatively low solution levels of starting material 4 due to poor solubility in MeCN.”; “The best overall combination identified … BTPP in MeCN, yielding 55.1 % a/a of triazole 6. Scale‑up of this hit to 200 mg further increased the product yield to 76.5 % a/a due in part to the better exclusion of moisture from hydrolytically sensitive intermediate 8.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: The chlorination approach (POCl₃) gave acceptable conversion initially but suffered from racemisation of the chiral centre and poor reproducibility when the scale was increased, leading to variable yields and impurity profiles.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the POCl₃ route and adopted the phosphorylative activation (DECP/BTPP), which showed minimal chiral erosion and robust, reproducible performance on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “More reproducible conversions could be achieved using DBU … however, this led to increased epimerisation… the approach was not progressed further.”; “Racemisation was observed in product 6 when relatively forcing conditions … were employed for the chloroimine forming step.”; “Chiral erosion using a phosphorylative approach was of low concern.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: BTPP is a liquid that is poorly miscible with MeCN and, because of a density difference (0.786 g mL⁻¹ vs. 1.022 g mL⁻¹), the reaction becomes a multiphase system at –10 °C, causing mixing/blending challenges during scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A constant‑blending strategy was employed: the addition time of BTPP was extended from 34 min to 1 h when scaling from 70 g to 750 g, ensuring uniform dispersion and preventing stalling.
Supporting_Evidence: “At the intended reaction temperature, the liquid BTPP is poorly miscible with MeCN … the reaction is a complex multiphasic system at –10 °C; therefore, appropriate mixing during the addition of BTPP was critical to avoiding stalling.”; “We proposed to increase the addition time of the BTPP from 34 min to 1 h to allow us to scale from 70 g (1 L) to 750 g (10 L) and therefore give confidence that the process would be scalable.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: Lowering the temperature to –10 °C improves selectivity but slows the reaction rate, extending the required reaction time and reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: The process was optimized to run the initial phosphorylation at –10 °C, then ramp to 20 °C for hydrazone formation and finally to 60 °C for the triazole ring closure (2.5 h), balancing conversion, chiral integrity and overall reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reducing the initial reaction temperature from ambient to −10 °C increased the proportion of 6 from 70.8 % to 78.2 % a/a … however, the decreased temperature reduced the reaction rate, which necessitated increasing the reaction time.”; “The final conditions for ring closure of 60 °C for 2.5 h therefore met the requirements of giving the desired product quality with acceptable throughput.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: Residual BTPP (up to 7.1 % w/w) carried through the aqueous work‑up caused product oiling and reduced isolated yields, and excess base posed safety and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: A work‑up sequence using 5 % w/w aqueous NaHCO₃, followed by a 1 M NH₄Cl wash and a solvent swap to isopropyl acetate/MeTHF, removed BTPP (target ≤2.5 mol % by NMR) and enabled clean crystallization of the benzenesulfonic‑acid salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initial work had shown that if a high level of BTPP (up to 7.1 % w/w observed) was carried through the aqueous work‑up, significant product oiling and lower isolated yields were obtained, so a target of no greater than 2.5 mol % by NMR was set.”; “The existing isolation of the benzenesulfonic acid salt … was well precedented … MeTHF was evaluated … gave a poor recovery … a simple reaction solvent swap into isopropyl acetate was shown to be suitable for both the work‑up and crystallization.”

Paper Title: Use of Phosphazene Base BTPP for Phosphorylative Activation in the Scale-Up of BET Inhibitor GSK525762
Problem_Description: Phosphazene base BTPP is expensive, commercially limited and has poor atom‑economy, which could affect the economic viability of large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors minimized the amount of BTPP used (≈2.8 mol % relative to lactam 4) and designed a work‑up to remove virtually all residual base, thereby limiting cost impact while retaining the performance advantage of BTPP.
Supporting_Evidence: “The phosphazene bases are not an obvious first choice for use in a manufacturing environment due to their high cost, limited commercial availability, and poor atom economy, so we were keen to also explore the use of other, more readily available strong bases. … Therefore, the process of using BTPP and DECP … was considered to be a viable alternative …”; “target of no greater than 2.5 mol % by NMR was set.”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Many commercially available diol and phenol auxiliaries gave poor conversion or low β‑selectivity because of limited solubility in the reaction medium, making it difficult to achieve high‑yielding diester formation on scale.
Solution_Description: A systematic screen of diols and phenols identified catechol as a highly β‑selective, inexpensive, and readily soluble auxiliary that could be installed and removed in high yields, providing a practical route to the desired β‑truxinate precursors.
Supporting_Evidence: “Among a set of acyclic diols… three‑carbon glycols 1,3‑propanediol (5b) and neopentane glycol (5e) showed good conversion (88–95 %) and selectivity (>20:1 d.r.)… Finally, from a handful of phenols… catechol and phthalol provided high conversion and β‑selectivity… With considerations of the cost, solubility, and installation/removal, catechol proved to be the ideal linker for β‑truxinate synthesis.”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: During the second ester‑coupling step, using a slight excess of the second cinnamic acid caused a complex mixture of products due to background trans‑esterification, leading to irreproducible conversions on decagram scale.
Solution_Description: Exact stoichiometric control (1.00 equiv each of TBTU and 3,4,5‑trimethoxycinnamic acid) together with DIPEA (5 equiv) prevented trans‑esterification and afforded the diester in 99 % isolated yield on multigram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “...we found that even slight excess of the second cinnamic acid led to a complex mixture of products. Ultimately, close stoichiometric control of TBTU and 3,4,5‑trimethoxycinnamic acid (1.00 equiv each) along with DIPEA (5 equiv) mitigated background transesterification and provided pure 14 in excellent yields on decagram scale (99 %).”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Traditional metal‑halide UV lamps generate large amounts of heat, making temperature control difficult and requiring long reaction times (≥4 h) for high conversion in batch photocycloadditions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A custom 365 nm LED flow photoreactor (53 mL, 46 W m⁻²) was built, allowing continuous flow at 50 mM EtOAc with a 15 min residence time, eliminating excess heat and dramatically reducing reaction time while maintaining >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Based on this observation, we built a 365 nm LED array, which was used in a 46 W m⁻² 53 mL flow photoreactor… Under optimized conditions (50 mM EtOAc, 15 min), we achieved 5.5 g h⁻¹ production of 15 at steady‑state continuous flow… In contrast, small‑scale batch trials… required longer reaction times and lower concentrations for high conversion (≥4 h at 10–15 mM).”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Batch photocycloadditions required low substrate concentrations (10–15 mM) and extended reaction times (≥4 h), limiting throughput and scalability.
Solution_Description: The flow photoreactor enabled operation at higher concentration (50 mM) with a short residence time (15 min), providing linear scalability and producing 51 g of product in a single 9 h run without loss of conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using this setup… we achieved 5.5 g h⁻¹ production of 15… In a large‑scale trial, we produced 51 g of 15 in a single 9 h run… productivity scales linearly in sequential reactor coils.”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Direct opening of the catechol‑protected cyclobutane (15) with 5,6‑dihydropyridin‑2‑one (DHP) failed to give the desired imide, leading to poor yields.
Solution_Description: The authors first removed the catechol auxiliary to generate a free truxinic acid, then employed more reactive electrophiles (PFP ester) for the imidation step, which proceeded efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: “Several attempts to directly install both imides by direct opening of 15 using DHP were unproductive… Consequently, we opted to remove the catechol linker and test more reactive electrophiles.”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of the cyclobutane ester (15) directly from EtOAc stalled on scales ≥100 mg, and the photochemical step was not operable in THF, necessitating a solvent switch that complicated scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The [2 + 2] reaction was performed in isopropyl acetate (iPrOAc), allowing the subsequent hydrolysis to be carried out directly in a THF/K₂CO₃ biphasic mixture, giving β‑truxinic acid (16) in 83 % yield over two steps without a separate solvent exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrolysis of 15 directly from the [2 + 2] reaction in EtOAc stalled on larger scales… however, by carrying out the [2 + 2] in iPrOAc, we were able to directly hydrolyze 15 using aqueous K₂CO₃ (10 equiv), giving 16 in a satisfactory yield of 83 % (2 steps).”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Attempted conversion of the β‑truxinic acid (16) to a bis‑acyl chloride using thionyl or oxalyl chloride resulted in exclusive formation of a cyclic anhydride (18), preventing further functionalisation.
Solution_Description: Instead of forming the acyl chloride, the authors prepared the bis‑pentafluorophenyl (PFP) ester (17) using EDC·HCl and PFP‑OH. The PFP ester reacted cleanly with lithium‑diisopropylamide‑activated DHP to give the desired mixed imide in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempts to form a bis acyl chloride from 16 resulted in the formation of cyclic anhydride (18)… Fortunately, synthesis of bis‑PFP ester 17 proceeded without issue… Double addition of Li‑DHP to bis‑PFP ester 17 was achieved in high yield (94 %).”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Direct deprotonation of DHP with n‑BuLi at 0–5 °C caused partial decomposition of the DHP reagent, reducing the efficiency of the imidation step.
Solution_Description: Lithium diisopropylamide (LDA), generated in situ, was employed as a milder base, avoiding DHP decomposition and enabling clean double imidation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Trials at 0–5 °C revealed that direct deprotonation of DHP with nBuLi led to partial decomposition of the DHP. Alternatively, using lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) generated in situ as the base, double addition of Li‑DHP… was achieved in high yield (94 %).”

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of Piperarborenines C‑E
Problem_Description: Cinnamic acid 20, needed for the synthesis of piperarborenines C and E, was commercially expensive and scarce, making large‑scale synthesis uneconomical.
Solution_Description: The authors performed an in‑house Doebner–Knoevenagel condensation of myristicin aldehyde (19) to afford cinnamic acid 20 (78 % yield), providing a cost‑effective and readily available source of the required building block.
Supporting_Evidence: “While cinnamic acid 20 is commercially available, its high cost and low availability required its preparation in‑house by Doebner–Knoevenagel condensation (78 %) from myristicin aldehyde (19).”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The original NBS bromination of phenol 2 was performed in THF with strong acid, which can cause THF polymerisation and presents a significant safety risk on scale.
Solution_Description: The reaction was moved to acetonitrile with catalytic triflic acid and run at –15 °C, eliminating THF, reducing exotherm, and providing high monobromination selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initial process employed 2 equiv of NBS in THF catalyzed by sulfuric acid… More concerning was the use of THF in the presence of a strong acid, which can lead to solvent polymerization.”; “To address the dichloromethane challenge… selective monobromination of phenols similar to 2 in MeCN with catalytic triflic acid… Running the reaction at a lower temperature (–15 °C) further improved the selectivity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The early route required column chromatography, hot filtrations, and distillation to dryness to isolate intermediates, which are difficult to scale and lengthen the process.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was devised that inverted the coupling partners and employed crystallizable intermediates (e.g., DEA‑boronate 17) to avoid chromatography and hot filtrations.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original route… featured … difficult to scale unit operations, such as column chromatography, hot filtrations, and distillation to dryness operations.”; “All column operations were eliminated using a seldom utilized, isolable, and crystalline DEA boronate.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The phenol 2 and its monobrominated product have markedly different solubilities in CH₂Cl₂, leading to over‑bromination and poor control.
Solution_Description: Using CH₂Cl₂ exploited the solubility gap; NBS was added in five portions with seeding of the product to keep it crystallised and prevent further bromination.
Supporting_Evidence: “By exploiting this difference, an improved process run with some additional modifications was conceived.”; “Portion‑wise addition of NBS with seeding with the product ensured reactive product crystallization, thereby minimizing its presence in solution and subsequent over‑reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The pinacol boronate 12 was unstable and gave poor physical properties, causing low isolated yields and difficult work‑up.
Solution_Description: Diethanolamine was added post‑reaction to convert the unstable boronate into a stable, filterable DEA‑boronate 17, which could be isolated in high purity and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The end of the reaction mixture containing 12 could be filtered … and then treated with a solution of diethanolamine to form … white slurry of 17 in high area purity.”; “Most importantly, the tetrahedral boron intermediate suffered from none of the stability issues previously observed.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: Boronate 8 decomposed in the solid state, making its isolation and purification problematic.
Solution_Description: The coupling partners were inverted so that the unstable boronate 8 was replaced by its bromide precursor 7, eliminating the need to handle the decomposing boronate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The effect of this change would be … it would eliminate the stability challenges associated with 8 and potentially avoid poorly purging dimer 9.”; “The inversion in coupling strategy … eliminated the generation of 9‑forming the highly purgeable 14 instead.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The use of dichloromethane for the phenol bromination raised safety, environmental, and cost concerns for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to acetonitrile, which is less hazardous; the bromination could be performed with a single NBS charge, simplifying the operation and reducing waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “The continued use of dichloromethane and the requirement for multiple solid charges of NBS … were identified as opportunities to improve process greenness.”; “Switch to acetonitrile further lowered the process safety risks and simplified the unit operations; the reduced adiabatic temperature rise allows for a simple, single charge of NBS.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch variability in the sulfur content of the bromide 7 caused catalyst poisoning and inconsistent cross‑coupling performance.
Solution_Description: Carbon treatment was introduced to lower sulfur levels in 7 to ≤200 ppm and specifications for the upstream material were tightened; an optional Pd‑kicker charge was added when needed.
Supporting_Evidence: “Elemental analysis of failed lots implicates low‑level sulfur as a catalyst poison.”; “We have modified our specifications … implemented a carbon treatment … and modified our cross‑coupling procedure to include an optional kicker charge if required.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: The final API crystallisation sometimes produced a kinetic form‑solvate that reduced yield and required additional processing to convert to the stable form.
Solution_Description: A concurrent charging regime was developed where the API solution, formic acid and water were added slowly over ≥6 h to maintain constant solvent composition, guaranteeing formation of the thermodynamic, non‑solvated form.
Supporting_Evidence: “A concurrent charging regime was established … to access the final form … ensured consistent solvent composition throughout crystallization and was demonstrated to eliminate the generation of the solvated form.”

Paper Title: Development of a Process to a 4‑Arylated 2‑Methylisoquinolin-1(2
Problem_Description: Commercially sourced isoquinolinone 6 showed variable purity, form (gray, brown, waxy) and low‑melting behaviour, hampering reliable scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A telescoped sequence was developed that bypassed isolated 6, converting hydroxy‑isoquinoline 5 directly to bromide 7, thus avoiding the problematic intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sourcing of compound 6 emerged as a thorny problem … variable purity and even form.”; “The team decided to back up production one step to avoid the sourcing and isolation challenges … intending to telescope through this challenging intermediate.”

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: The original pre‑clinical chlorination of acetylquinazolinone 12 used a 48 equiv excess of SOCl₂/DMF. This caused Vilsmeier‑type formylation (impurity 27) and hydrolysis impurity 28, and generated N,N‑dimethyl‑carbamoyl‑chloride (DMCC), a known potential carcinogen.
Solution_Description: The chlorination reagent was switched to POCl₃ (1.2 equiv) in toluene with DIPEA (1.3 equiv). The addition was performed slowly, maintaining the temperature ≤ 70 °C, which eliminated the Vilsmeier side‑reaction and avoided DMCC formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...a high loading (48 equiv) of SOCl₂ was adopted. This system is prone to formylate (Vilsmeier reaction), resulting in the formation of the amination impurity 27 and hydrolysis impurity 28" (p. 5). • "When POCl₃ (1.2 equiv) was used as the chlorination reagent…1.3 equiv of Et₃N helped to increase the conversion…avoiding a large amount of SOCl₂…and the generation of following formylation impurities (27, 28)" (p. 7).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: During quenching of the POCl₃‑mediated chlorination, residual POCl₃ hydrolysed exothermically, raising the temperature from 25 °C to 58 °C and causing partial hydrolysis of chloroquinazoline 11 back to the starting material 12.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: After the reaction, the mixture was cooled to 10 °C before the slow addition of water (controlled 10‑25 °C). The wet solid was filtered and stored at 10‑15 °C, where it remained stable for up to 84 h, preventing degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...hydrolysis of chloroquinazoline 11 to acetylquinazolinone 12 was detected…temperature increasing from 25 to 58 °C due to the exothermic hydrolysis of residual POCl₃" (p. 7). • "When the temperature of the reaction solution was cooled down to 10 °C…slow addition of water for quenching with a controlled temperature of less than 25 °C obtained a stable wet chloroquinazoline 11…no obvious degradation at 10‑15 °C for up to 84 h" (p. 7‑8).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: The nucleophilic substitution of chloroquinazoline 11 with 3‑chloro‑4‑fluoroaniline 10 gave poor conversion in toluene, leaving the majority of 11 unreacted and requiring extensive washing to remove residual material.
Solution_Description: tert‑Amyl alcohol (TAA) was identified as the optimal solvent, providing 81.36 % HPLC yield of aminoquinazoline 9. Additionally, the aniline equivalent was reduced from 1.35 to 1.0 equiv without loss of conversion, improving material efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The vast majority of chloroquinazoline 11 was left (entry 3) …toluene was beneficial to the chlorination reaction…but was not suitable for the substitution reaction" (p. 9). • "The best conversion was obtained with tert‑amyl alcohol (TAA)…81.36 % HPLC yield" (p. 9). • "The amount of 3‑chloro‑4‑fluoroaniline 10 was decreased from 1.35 to 1.0 equiv…conversion could also be efficient" (p. 9).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: During the hydrolysis of aminoquinazoline 9 to hydroxyquinazoline 8, the 41.12 kg scale reaction in methanol suffered from poor stirring, leaving 34.4 % of 9 unreacted after 10 h.
Solution_Description: The methanol volume was increased from 2.5 L kg⁻¹ to 7.5 L kg⁻¹, improving mixing and achieving complete conversion. NaOH was set to 2.5 equiv (instead of 3 equiv) and the final pH adjusted to 5‑6, giving > 95 % isolated yield with minimal residual 9.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The starting material aminoquinazoline 9 cannot stir efficiently…34.4 % remained…Increasing the volume of methanol from 2.5 to 7.5 L kg avoided the incomplete consumption" (p. 10‑11). • "Decreasing the amount of NaOH to 2.5 equiv afforded comparable results…to ensure complete conversion (less than 0.7 % of aminoquinazoline 9 remained)" (p. 11). • "When the pH value was adjusted to 5–6, the yield could reach up to more than 95 %…" (p. 11‑12).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: The etherification of hydroxyquinazoline 8 with 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane produced alkylation impurity 29 and dimer impurity 30, especially when K₂CO₃ was used, leading to high impurity levels and low product purity.
Solution_Description: K₃PO₄·7H₂O was employed as the base instead of Cs₂CO₃, and the reaction temperature was lowered to 10 °C (or 0 °C) which reduced dimer impurity 30 to < 0.5 % area. Switching the solvent to NMP improved purity, and the optimized K₃PO₄·7H₂O/NMP/10 °C system gave consistent high yields (≈ 88‑90 %) and low impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Cs₂CO₃ easily sinks …high level of dimer 30…" (p. 13). • "A slight decrease of dimer 30 can be obtained when K₃PO₄·7H₂O was used …Lowering the reaction temperature to 10 °C furnished a significant decrease for dimer 30…" (p. 13‑14). • "Compared with the K₃PO₄·7H₂O/DMF system, the K₃PO₄·7H₂O/NMP system showed higher purity…" (p. 14).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: 1‑Bromo‑3‑chloropropane is a mutagenic impurity (PGI). Its residual amount must be below 28 ppm, otherwise it can form impurity 29 during drying, posing a safety and regulatory risk.
Solution_Description: The crude chloroalkylquinazoline 7 was triturated twice with ethanol, which removed 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane to < 28 ppm. Subsequent filtration and washing gave product free of impurity 29 and compliant with the TTC limit.
Supporting_Evidence: • "1‑Bromo‑3‑chloropropane was predicted to be a mutagenic substance…limit …28 ppm…residual 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane brings the risk of forming impurity 29…" (p. 15). • "After screening, it was found that triturating with ethanol twice could effectively control the level of residual 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane (less than 28 ppm) in 85% yield" (p. 15).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: In the final nucleophilic substitution to give Larotinib 4, quaternary ammonium impurity 31 persisted (> 2 % area) and a syrupy solid formed when water was added directly, hampering isolation and lowering overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The post‑reaction mixture was diluted with acetone/H₂O (1:30) to precipitate a dispersed powder that could be filtered, avoiding syrup formation. The wet cake was then dissolved in DCM (where Larotinib is soluble but impurity 31 is not) and filtered to remove impurity 31, giving API of 99.51 % purity and 82.9 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A syrupy solid appeared when adding water directly…" (p. 16). • "Adding a little amount of acetone in water … promoted the powdery product to precipitate well…A simple vacuum filtration avoided multiple water washing…Impurity 31 still > 2 %…When the wet cake Larotinib was dissolved in DCM, we could observe some insoluble white flocs…impurity 31 can be effectively removed by the following suction filtration…final API…99.51 % purity, 82.9 % yield" (p. 17‑18).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: The original process relied on labor‑intensive column chromatography to remove impurities and PGIs, which is time‑consuming and unsuitable for kilogram‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A series of simple operations—filtration, water washes, triturations, antisolvent crystallizations (acetone/H₂O), and selective DCM washes—replaced column chromatography, drastically reducing processing time and waste while achieving > 99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...avoiding the use of laborious and time‑consuming column chromatography" (abstract). • "The early stage … washing with DCM/H₂O required nine water washes…An attempt was made to precipitate…different organic solvents/H₂O …dispersed solid appeared…acetone was finally adopted as the auxiliary crystallization solvent…The final API…all solvents and bases …were not detected after the recrystallization step" (p. 17‑19).

Paper Title: Manufacturable Process of a Novel EGFR Inhibitor (Larotinib) for the Treatment of ESCC
Problem_Description: The pre‑clinical route used reagents and steps (e.g., large excess of SOCl₂, nitration/nitroreduction sequences) that are expensive, generate toxic by‑products, and rely on reagents not readily available at large scale.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic route (Route I) was adopted that starts from the commercially available acetylquinazolinone 12 and avoids nitration/nitroreduction. Reagent loadings were minimized (e.g., POCl₃ 1.2 equiv, NaOH 2.5 equiv) and safer reagents (DIPEA, KI) were used, reducing overall material cost and improving scalability.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Route I can avoid dangerous processes…using the commercially available acetylquinazolinone 12 as the regulatory starting material" (p. 4). • "Overall yield of this optimized process increased significantly from 16.2 to 55.6%" (abstract). • "A smaller loading of SOCl₂ (1.2 equiv) was tested…When POCl₃ (1.2 equiv) was used …avoiding a large amount of SOCl₂" (p. 7).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The electrochemical oxidation of cyclohexanol gave very different current efficiencies (31 % vs <10 %) when using nickel anodes from three commercial vendors, indicating inconsistent catalyst performance and low yields.
Solution_Description: A pre‑activation protocol was introduced in which the nickel surface was polished, acid‑cleaned and electro‑oxidised in 0.1 M NiSO₄/0.1 M KOAc/0.005 M KOH to generate a uniform NiOOH layer before the oxidation reaction. This pretreatment restored high and reproducible efficiencies for all electrode sources.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "As anticipated, the efficiency of the oxidation of 1 to the ketone 2 significantly differed between the nickel materials. The best performing anode (entry 1) was the original IKA electrode material… other commercial nickel sources performed poorly… current efficiencies below 10 %" (Table 1, entries 2–3).
- "We anticipated that formation of a NiOOH layer… would improve both the efficiency of the alcohol oxidation and the reproducibility of the results, independent of the source of the nickel material utilized."
- "After this process a black layer could be visually observed… the performance of the three electrode materials was significantly improved… with analogous efficiency after activation" (Table 1, entries 4–6).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: During batch oxidation of nicotinyl alcohol, conversion stopped after 4 F mol⁻¹ because the generated nicotinic acid neutralised KOH, lowering the pH and destabilising the NiOOH active layer.
Solution_Description: The concentration of KOH in the electrolyte was increased (0.2 M then 0.5 M) to supply sufficient base throughout the reaction, maintaining the alkaline environment required for a stable NiOOH layer and restoring full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Reaction progress halted after 4 F mol⁻¹… this issue was ascribed to the fact that the acidic product neutralizes 1 equiv of KOH. Thus, as the reaction progresses, the pH becomes less alkaline than that required to maintain a stable NiOOH layer."
- "Formation of 4a could be improved by increasing the concentration of KOH to 0.2 M (entry 4) and then to 0.5 M (entries 5 and 6)."
- Table 3 shows the increase in HPLC area % when KOH is raised from 0.1 M to 0.5 M (entries 4–6).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: In single‑pass continuous‑flow electrolysis, rapid gas evolution (H₂ at the cathode and O₂ at the anode) coated the electrode surfaces, limiting the effective electrode area and preventing conversions above ~68 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The inter‑electrode gap of the flow cell was enlarged from 0.3 mm to 0.9 mm, increasing the cell volume and reducing gas coverage. Additionally, a three‑step reactor cascade (re‑circulating the reaction mixture through the same cell three times) was employed to release gas between passes and achieve 88 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "...in this process, ... oxygen gas may also form at the anode… the interelectrode gap was increased from 0.3 mm to 0.9 mm. In this manner, the cell volume was increased, thus decreasing the extent of electrode coverage by the gas."
- "A three‑step cascade provided 88 % of 4a… the gas generated during the electrolysis can therefore be released before entering the second unit, thus effectively acting as a gas removal strategy."
- Figure 4b and Figure 5 illustrate the effect of flow rate, charge, gap size and cascade on conversion.

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Homogeneous electron‑proton transfer mediators (e.g., TEMPO, PINO) are expensive, toxic and require downstream removal, offsetting the sustainability benefits of electrochemical oxidation.
Solution_Description: A heterogeneous NiOOH layer on nickel anodes was used as a solid, recyclable electron‑proton transfer mediator, eliminating the need for soluble, costly, and hazardous mediators.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The downside to using these homogeneous mediators is their relatively high cost, toxicity, and the need for downstream removal… An ideal electrochemical oxidation process would use an inexpensive, recyclable heterogeneous EPTM…"
- "Nickel anodes coated with nickel oxide hydroxide (NiOOH) … offers an opportunity for the development of an inexpensive heterogeneous EPTM…"
- The successful oxidation of a range of nitrogen‑heterocycle‑containing alcohols using NiOOH is demonstrated (Table 4).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Nickel salts are classified as carcinogenic, raising concerns about nickel contamination in the product stream.
Solution_Description: The process employs a heterogeneous NiOOH‑coated anode that shows minimal metal leaching (≈20 µg L⁻¹), well below WHO drinking‑water limits, thereby mitigating safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Nickel contamination is of paramount concern… the activated anodes showed very high stability, with no degradation… only a very low amount of Ni leaching was observed… 19.9–22.3 µg L⁻¹… WHO recommends nickel levels below 70 µg L⁻¹ in drinking water."
- "The NiOOH‑coated anodes showed no reduction in catalysis efficiency over 12 h, and minimal Ni metal leaching (22.3 µg L⁻¹) is observed."

Paper Title: Electrochemical Oxidation of Alcohols Using Nickel Oxide Hydroxide as Heterogeneous Electrocatalyst in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Highly polar nitrogen‑containing carboxylic acids were difficult to isolate, leading to moderate isolated yields despite good conversion.
Solution_Description: The authors acknowledge that the work‑up protocol (extraction, acidification, KCl removal) was not optimized for each substrate; further development of a tailored purification strategy is required.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Isolation of the highly polar nitrogen‑containing carboxylic acids proved troublesome in some cases… moderate isolated yields were achieved for some products."
- "Product loss was ascribed to the KCl removal step in EtOH suspension. Yet, the workup protocol was not further optimized for each individual substrate."

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: A control reaction without a photosensitizer gave only 34 % conversion of 2‑fluorotoluene (1) to the desired monochloride (2); the low conversion limits productivity and makes scale‑up unattractive.
Solution_Description: Addition of 0.1 equiv of benzophenone (5) as a photosensitizer increased conversion to 91 % and gave a 10:1 selectivity for the monochloride, demonstrating that sensitized photochemistry overcomes the low‑yield issue.
Supporting_Evidence: “A control reaction was carried out … without a sensitizer … led to a 34 % conversion of 1 into 2 … When 0.1 equiv of benzophenone 5 was introduced … the conversion of 1 reached 91 % and a selectivity of 10:1 in favor of 2.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: The formation of the dichlorinated by‑product (3) makes isolation of the target monochloride (2) difficult because 2 and 3 have similar boiling points, leading to poor overall yield and hard purification.
Solution_Description: A systematic optimisation using one‑factor‑at‑a‑time (OFAT) followed by a design‑of‑experiments (DoE) approach identified a reaction window (60 °C, 5 min residence time, 0.05 equiv benzophenone, 1.05 equiv NCS, 1 M substrate) that reduced the dichloride impurity to ≤3 % GCAP and increased the monochloride yield to 85 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The DoE method was then chosen to identify operating conditions to decrease the formation of 3 … The optimal reaction conditions … allowed a GCAP of 3 inferior or equal to 3 % … experimentally observed … the numerical model enabled a higher value of the GCAP of the targeted 2 (85 % versus 80 %) with a similar value of the GCAP of the dichlorinated by‑product 3 of 7 %.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: During the fractional‑factorial DoE two runs clogged the flow system (1.2 equiv NCS, 1.5 M substrate), preventing data collection and indicating poor mixing/solubility at higher concentrations.
Solution_Description: The experimental space was restricted to ≤1 M substrate concentration while keeping NCS at 1.2 equiv, eliminating clogging and allowing consistent data acquisition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, two of the selected conditions led to the clogging of the flow system … the conditions involving 1.2 equiv of NCS and a concentration of 1.5 mol/L … Therefore, a restriction of the concentration (up to 1 mol/L) was implemented for the other experiments by using only 1.2 equiv of NCS.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: In the larger Corning AFR G1‑LF PHOTO reactor, light attenuation across the channel created heterogeneous concentration fields, limiting conversion; additionally, the product (2) decomposes exothermically above 250 °C, imposing safety limits during downstream processing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the number of fluidic modules (larger reactor volume) and the flow rate improved mixing and photon absorption, raising conversion without needing higher photon flux. Downstream distillation was performed at ≤155 °C (well below the 250 °C decomposition onset) to avoid thermal degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “For a given reactor volume, the conversion … increased with the residence time … conversion increased with the reactor volume … the higher flowrate, the higher the velocity of vortices … better mixing … An exothermal decomposition was observed starting at 250 °C … it is recommended not to exceed 155 °C during the distillation.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: Distillation of 2 (boiling point 178 °C) poses a risk because the compound begins to decompose exothermically above 250 °C; operating at high temperature could lead to safety incidents and product loss.
Solution_Description: A 100 K safety margin was applied: distillation was limited to 155 °C (well under the 250 °C onset) under reduced pressure (2 mbar), protecting against decomposition while achieving 61 % isolated yield and >99.9 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “An exothermal decomposition was observed starting at 250 °C … it is recommended not to exceed 155 °C during the distillation using the 100 K rule as a safety margin … 2‑fluorobenzyl chloride … was successfully distilled off … at 148 °C with a 61 % isolated yield and a GC purity superior to 99.9 %.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: Earlier chlorination procedures used carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), classified as a Class 1 solvent, which is environmentally hazardous and banned in GMP environments.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to acetonitrile as the reaction solvent together with N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) as the chlorinating agent, eliminating the need for CCl₄ and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “Thermal conditions using N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) … furnished 2 … in high yield … However, CCl₄ is a class 1 solvent according to ICH Q3C and should be avoided.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: The conventional route via 2‑fluorobenzyl alcohol (4) is approximately four times more expensive than using 2‑fluorotoluene (1) as the starting material, adversely affecting the cost of goods.
Solution_Description: An alternative synthetic route was developed that starts from the inexpensive 2‑fluorotoluene (1) and uses NCS as the chlorinating agent, reducing raw‑material cost and improving overall economics.
Supporting_Evidence: “The cost of goods evaluation … benzylic alcohol 4 … is almost 4 times more expensive than 1 … an alternative strategy would consist of preparing 2 from 2‑fluorotoluene 1.”

Paper Title: Selective Photochemical Continuous Flow Benzylic Monochlorination
Problem_Description: Traditional chlorination reagents (e.g., t‑BuOCl/FeCl₂) are hazardous and/or generate large amounts of waste, while benzoyl peroxide presents thermal run‑away risks.
Solution_Description: The authors selected inexpensive N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) as a safe, practical chlorinating agent, avoiding hazardous reagents and reducing waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “N‑Chlorosuccinimide (NCS) was selected as an inexpensive, safe, and practical chlorinating agent …”

Paper Title: Discovery and Process Development of a Scalable Biocatalytic Kinetic Resolution toward Synthesis of a Sterically Hindered Chiral Ketone
Problem_Description: When the reaction was scaled to 50 g, it stalled after ~2 h and conversion stopped at ~45 % with a loss of enzyme activity. Microscopic inspection revealed significant protein aggregation after ~0.5 h, indicating that the wild‑type KRED enzyme deactivated/aggregated under the scale‑up conditions.
Solution_Description: An incremental “2 + 2” enzyme addition strategy was employed: after 1–2 h a second portion of KRED (2 wt %) and GDH (0.5 wt %) was added, which restored activity and allowed the reaction to reach >50 % conversion with ≥98 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the reaction significantly slowed down after 2 h. The reaction finally stalled at 45 % conv after 19.5 h with 88 % ee of ketone 2. We reasoned that the stalling of the reaction might be a result of enzyme activity loss after 2 h since we observed a significant amount of protein aggregation at that time."; "...the use of an additional 2 wt % of KRED and 0.5 wt % of GDH after 1–2 h of reaction helped to drive the reaction to ∼50 % conv (entry 4, 60 g scale)."; "Ultimately, we applied the “2 + 2” incremental addition strategy of enzyme additions to our 0.8 kg scale experiment."

Paper Title: Discovery and Process Development of a Scalable Biocatalytic Kinetic Resolution toward Synthesis of a Sterically Hindered Chiral Ketone
Problem_Description: The reaction mixture is biphasic due to incomplete dissolution of the racemic ketone. Low agitation (100 rpm) gave only ~20 % conversion after 1.5 h, whereas high agitation (≥700 rpm) caused excessive foaming and enzyme destabilization, making it difficult to achieve consistent conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mixing studies identified 350 rpm as the optimal agitation, giving ≥50 % conversion in ~2 h. Scale‑up to a 20 L vessel employed Dynochem mixing‑modeling to match the power‑per‑mass (P/m) of the 2 g reference reactor, ensuring appropriate shear and mixing rates.
Supporting_Evidence: "...a low agitation speed (100 rpm) usually leads to slow progression of reaction (20 % conv after 1.5 h)… On the other hand, the use of a high agitation speed (≥700 rpm) often causes the foaming of the reaction solution… the optimal agitation rate should be within the range of 100–700 rpm. For example, the reaction performed at 350 rpm gradually proceeds and eventually reached ≥50 % conv within 2 h."; "...mixing modeling was performed with Dynochem software… matching of the predicted power per unit mass (P/m) with the 50 mL (2 g scale) vessel was used to determine the appropriate agitation rate in the 20 L reactor."

Paper Title: Discovery and Process Development of a Scalable Biocatalytic Kinetic Resolution toward Synthesis of a Sterically Hindered Chiral Ketone
Problem_Description: Addition of the product alcohol (3) at the start of the reaction dramatically reduced the initial rate: 0.5 equiv of alcohol lowered conversion within the first 0.5 h to ~20 % compared with ~35 % in the control, indicating product inhibition of the KRED/GDH enzymes.
Solution_Description: The protocol avoided adding product early; instead the reaction was run without pre‑added alcohol and the enzyme was added incrementally to maintain activity, mitigating product inhibition.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the addition of sodium gluconate barely affects the reaction… the product (alcohol 3) diminishes the initial rate of reaction… when 0.5 equiv of alcohol 3 is introduced, the reaction conversion within the first 0.5 h is significantly decreased (∼20 % conv) as compared to that observed in a control experiment (∼35 % conv)."; "...the use of an additional 2 wt % of KRED and 0.5 wt % of GDH after 1–2 h of reaction helped to drive the reaction to ∼50 % conv…"

Paper Title: Discovery and Process Development of a Scalable Biocatalytic Kinetic Resolution toward Synthesis of a Sterically Hindered Chiral Ketone
Problem_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 40 °C caused rapid loss of KRED activity; the reaction stalled after 0.5 h and never exceeded ~45 % conversion, likely due to thermal deactivation of the wild‑type enzyme.
Solution_Description: The temperature was set to 30 °C, which provided a balance between reaction rate and enzyme stability, giving consistent conversion and high ee.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the reaction performed at 40 °C generally stalls after 0.5 h and is not able to proceed to over 45 % conv. It is possible that KRED 119, as a wild‑type enzyme, decomposes at a faster rate at 40 °C (vs 30 °C) and ultimately loses its activity.
