Paper Title: Integration of Liquid–Liquid Biphasic Flow Alkylation and Continuous Crystallization Using Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Further reduction of the solvent to 5 mL g⁻¹ MIBK and 5 mL g⁻¹ water caused the aqueous phase to contain insoluble salts, jeopardizing smooth flow.
Solution_Description: Add a small amount of water (3 mL g⁻¹) to dissolve the salts, establishing an optimal solvent composition of 5 mL g⁻¹ MIBK and 8 mL g⁻¹ water.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “when the solvent volume was further reduced … the aqueous phase had insoluble salts.”
• “These salts could be dissolved by adding 3 mL g⁻¹ of water and thus the optimized solvent volume was set at 5 mL g⁻¹ of MIBK and 8 mL g⁻¹ of water.”

Paper Title: Integration of Liquid–Liquid Biphasic Flow Alkylation and Continuous Crystallization Using Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Tilting the Taylor‑vortex reactor altered the organic/aqueous volume ratio; at 60° the organic residence time dropped to 75 % of the design value, reducing conversion.
Solution_Description: Operate the reactor horizontally (0° tilt) to maintain the intended phase ratio, residence time, and conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the tilt angle was larger … the volumetric ratio of the aqueous phase was larger … the residence time of the organic phase was shortened … and the reaction conversion was decreased.”
• “In this reaction system, setting the flow reactor horizontally assures appropriate residence time and reaction conversion.”

Paper Title: Integration of Liquid–Liquid Biphasic Flow Alkylation and Continuous Crystallization Using Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: In the fully integrated continuous line the isolated yield fell to 88 % (vs 95 % in batch) because a portion of the organic phase was lost during membrane‑based phase separation, likely due to pressure disturbances.
Solution_Description: Minimize pressure loss at the separator‑crystallizer connection (e.g., re‑design the feed line) to keep the organic phase on the membrane and prevent its discharge with the aqueous stream.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The isolated yield … was lower … resulted from poor phase separation … some organic phase was discarded along with the aqueous phase without penetration of the hydrophobic membrane.”
• “The slight pressure loss due to the connection of the separator and the crystallizer disturbed the balance of the phase separation …”

Paper Title: Integration of Liquid–Liquid Biphasic Flow Alkylation and Continuous Crystallization Using Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: During continuous crystallization of the real organic stream, encrustation formed at the inlet, leading to clogging risk.
Solution_Description: Apply a two‑stage approach: (i) perform antisolvent crystallization at 40 °C (higher temperature) to lower supersaturation and reduce encrustation; (ii) dilute the feed with methanol before mixing with water to decrease local supersaturation; (iii) trial seeded crystallization (up to 10 wt % seed) although seeding alone was ineffective, the temperature and dilution steps proved successful.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “encrustation was observed … clogging … when the actual organic phase after quenching was used.”
• “When the antisolvent crystallization was done at 40 °C, encrustation decreased dramatically.”
• “The prior mixing with methanol increased the flow rate of the organic phase, which would mitigate the risks of the encrustation and clogging.”

Paper Title: Integration of Liquid–Liquid Biphasic Flow Alkylation and Continuous Crystallization Using Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Scaling the Taylor‑vortex reactor to pilot scale required determining a suitable rotating speed; calculations gave 60 rpm (too low) and 1500 rpm (acceptable), indicating uncertainty in scale‑up methodology.
Solution_Description: Adopt a scale‑up strategy based on maintaining constant shear stress (or Reynolds number) across scales, using the derived equations to select the appropriate rotating speed (1500 rpm) for the larger reactor.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The rotating speed in the pilot‑scale Taylor vortex flow reactor was calculated … 60 and 1500 rpm … The rotating speed of 60 rpm was visually too low … The rotating speed of 1500 rpm was tried … the result was the same as that from the laboratory‑scale experiment.”
• “This showed that a reasonable scale‑up strategy was possible … through scaling based on constant shear stress.”

Paper Title: Development of an Ene Reductase-Based Biocatalytic Process for the Production of Flavor Compounds
Problem_Description:
The researchers encountered several scale‑up challenges while developing the ene‑reductase process:
1. Pbr‑ER displayed low solubility in the expression host, limiting the amount of active enzyme available for catalysis.
2. The required nicotinamide co‑factor NADPH is expensive, making the process costly at large scale.
3. Many screened enzymes gave sub‑optimal conversions (>0.2 g product L⁻¹) at the target substrate load of 10 g L⁻¹, i.e., low product yield.
4. The aldehyde substrate 2E‑decenal undergoes autoxidation to 2E‑decenoic acid and decanoic acid, leading to side‑product formation.
5. High‑substrate‑load reactions (40–60 g L⁻¹) required very long reaction times (up to 80 h) to reach acceptable conversion.
6. The same autoxidation issue caused a drop in pH during scale‑up, creating variability in reaction performance.
7. Operating at higher temperatures (≥50 °C) caused loss of enzyme activity, i.e., thermal decomposition of the biocatalyst.
Solution_Description:
To overcome these problems the authors implemented the following measures:
1. Added the GroEL‑GroES chaperone system and 5 g L⁻¹ yeast extract to the R/2 minimal medium (glucose‑based) during Pbr‑ER expression, which improved soluble enzyme production despite the low intrinsic solubility of the protein.
2. Introduced an in‑situ NADPH recycling system using glucose dehydrogenase (GDH) and d‑glucose, thereby eliminating the need for stoichiometric NADPH addition.
3. Selected the most robust enzyme (Pbr‑ER) from the library and performed targeted cultivation‑condition optimisation (medium, carbon source, chaperone co‑expression) to raise its catalytic activity at 10 g L⁻¹ substrate.
4. Performed the biotransformation at 10 °C; the lower temperature suppressed aldehyde autoxidation and prevented formation of 2E‑decenoic acid and decanoic acid.
5. Reduced the overall reaction time by operating at the optimal temperature (22 °C) for the most active enzymes, which gave >80 % conversion in 16 h for 10 g L⁻¹ substrate, compared with 24 h in the initial screen.
6. Implemented automated pH control by dosing 5 M NaOH during scale‑up to neutralise the acidification caused by gluconate formation, maintaining a stable pH throughout the reaction.
7. Chose enzymes with higher thermal stability (e.g., GkOYE) for processes that required elevated temperatures, and limited reaction temperatures to ≤40 °C for Pbr‑ER to retain activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Low solubility: “To enhance Pbr‑ER’s low solubility … cultivation conditions were evaluated … R/2 medium … the addition of yeast extract … the best biotransformation results … when Pbr‑ER was produced together with the GroEL‑GroES chaperone system …”
Problem – Cofactor cost: “the expensive cofactor NADPH … the NADPH recycling system consisting of d‑glucose and glucose dehydrogenase (GDH) … reduce the cost of the biocatalysis reactions.”
Problem – Low conversion: “Thirteen of the 20 screened enzymes were active (>0.2 g product L⁻¹)… only 5 of the 10 selected enzymes were found to transform both substrates with conversions of at least 50 %.”
Problem – Aldehyde autoxidation: “Due to the presence of a labile aldehyde group … led to the formation of side products (2E‑decenoic acid and decanoic acid).”
Problem – Long reactions: “40 g L⁻¹ substrate … 94.2 % conversion after 24 h … 60 g L⁻¹ substrate … 83.6 % after 80 h.”
Problem – pH drift: “To compensate for the acidification caused by the coproduct gluconate, the pH of the reaction was readjusted with the automated addition of NaOH (5 M stock solution).”
Problem – Thermal deactivation: “Only the thermostable GkOYE retained its initial activity at 60 °C … YqiG retained close to full activity at 40 and 50 °C …”
Solution – Chaperones/yeast extract: “The best biotransformation results … when Pbr‑ER was produced together with the GroEL‑GroES chaperone system in glucose‑based R/2 medium supplemented with yeast extract.”
Solution – NADPH recycling: “NADPH was recycled using a GDH system … thus posing no restraints on the industrial applicability of Pbr‑ER.”
Solution – Temperature optimisation: “Running the reaction at 10 °C … no side product formation was observed.”
Solution – Reaction time reduction: “Pbr‑ER and Ppo‑ER3 showed the highest product titers … after a reaction time of 16 h.”
Solution – pH control: “pH was concomitantly controlled through the automated addition of NaOH (5 M stock solution).”
Solution – Thermal stability selection: “Only the thermostable GkOYE retained its initial activity at 60 °C …”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: The original Suzuki coupling used the expensive and poorly available Pd‑PEPPSI‑IPent (CX32) catalyst, which gave low conversion on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A screening campaign identified cheaper palladium catalysts (Pd[(PCy₃)₂]Cl₂ and Buchwald G2/G3 precatalysts). The G2/G3 system gave robust initiation and allowed catalyst loading to be reduced to 0.25 mol % (acceptable for scale‑up).
Supporting_Evidence: Our starting point for this Suzuki optimization was literature conditions using expensive and poorly available Pd‑PEPPSI‑IPent (CX32) as a catalyst.; Around 20 different alternatives to CX32 were tested (mostly palladium and some nickel catalysts).; The Buchwald‑type precursor PCy₃ Pd G2 was much better at initiating this reaction, allowing for the reduction of catalyst loading to 0.25 mol %.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: Scale‑up Suzuki reactions often showed no conversion for 24 h because strict oxygen exclusion prevented the necessary oxidation of PCy₃ to generate the active Pd‑L₁ species.
Solution_Description: A brief introduction of air/oxygen at the start of the reaction (or use of Buchwald G2/G3 precatalysts that generate the active species in situ) restored conversion and gave consistent results.
Supporting_Evidence: Scale‑up reactions regularly failed to even start conversion within 24 h. We realized that better exclusion of oxygen on the scale was causing the reaction to fail to initiate.; Once air was introduced for a short time, the reactions went to completion, even after having shown no conversion for 24 h previously.; The Buchwald‑type precursor PCy₃ Pd G2/G3 were much better at initiating this reaction, allowing for the reduction of catalyst loading to 0.25 mol %.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: Intermediate 5a was extremely unstable under the basic conditions required for the Suzuki coupling, delivering only trace product unless the expensive CsF base was used.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to an early‑Suzuki strategy, performing the coupling before the installation of the sensitive functional groups, thereby avoiding the unstable intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: Unfortunately, 5a proved to be very unstable under the basic conditions of a Suzuki reaction. Only very modest amounts of product were detected in the crude reaction mixture and only when using impractical and expensive CsF as special fluoride base.; With no good options left on the table, we abandoned the most desirable late Suzuki approaches and moved to a less convergent route.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: Early laboratory routes required chromatographic purification of several intermediates, which is impractical on multi‑kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The sequence was telescoped from the Suzuki step through isolation of the racemic alcohol, and all chromatographic steps were replaced by a single solid‑filtration work‑up (precipitation/trituration).
Supporting_Evidence: Early work required purification by silica plug filtration or even chromatography.; We found that concentration of the organic phase to a thick brown slurry and trituration with warm isopropyl acetate, followed by cooling and filtration, gave the product as white powder in ca. 70 % yield over the entire sequence.; The telescoped four‑step sequence removed all chromatographic purification from the previous process, replacing it with a single solid filtration.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: The Grignard formation for the boronic‑acid precursor is highly exothermic (adiabatic temperature rise of 276 °C), posing safety and temperature‑control challenges at large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition was performed in a strictly dose‑controlled manner and the reaction temperature was kept between 65 °C and 75 °C, as determined by calorimetric studies, to avoid runaway heating.
Supporting_Evidence: Keeping the temperature of this step between 65 and 75 °C was one of the major technical challenges encountered. In fact, the high adiabatic temperature increase of 276 °C shown in calorimetric measurements required the reaction to be run strictly dose‑controlled.; Lower temperatures led to stalling of the reaction and accumulation, whereas higher temperatures resulted in increased proto‑dehalogenation of the starting material.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: The oxidation of the pyridine to the N‑oxide using MCPBA required low temperatures (10–15 °C) and suffered from MCPBA decomposition, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A TEMPO/bleach oxidation (using NaOCl, KBr, and TBAB) was adopted, giving a clean reaction profile, high yield (95 %), and eliminating the need for hazardous peracid handling.
Supporting_Evidence: Oxidation of aryl pyridine 1b using MCPBA (1.4 equiv) required 10–15 °C with unwanted decomposition of MCPBA occurring at warmer temperatures.; The procedure using TEMPO (2.5 mol %), bleach, KBr, and TBAB gave 5b with a very clean reaction profile and 95 % isolated yield (compared to 70 % with O₂).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: Dichloromethane, a chlorinated solvent used initially for the TEMPO oxidation, is undesirable for large‑scale production due to environmental and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to methyl acetate; after the oxidation the product precipitated on addition of water, giving >99 % purity without any phase‑transfer catalyst, thus avoiding chlorinated solvents altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: Dichloromethane was first used as a solvent to obtain a foothold into this chemistry. However, chlorinated solvents are not ideal, and a time‑consuming distillative solvent switch to heptane still gave varying yields.; With methyl acetate as a last resort… the reaction with bleach was dose‑controlled, and after completion, the addition of water followed by filtration gave 5b in 97 % yield with >99 % purity. As a bonus, no phase‑transfer catalyst (TBAB) was needed using these conditions.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: The Swern oxidation required −78 °C and produced toxic, odorous waste, making it unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The Swern step was replaced entirely by the TEMPO/bleach oxidation described above, which proceeds at 0–5 °C, avoids low‑temperature operation, and generates minimal hazardous waste.
Supporting_Evidence: The Swern oxidation from racemic alcohol 4b to ketone‑intermediate 5b should be avoided when searching for an efficient process. The use of low‑temperature conditions (−78 °C) and exposing plant workers to odorous and toxic waste products are not ideal.; We were happy to observe that the procedure using TEMPO (2.5 mol %), bleach, KBr, and TBAB gave 5b with a very clean reaction profile and 95 % isolated yield.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of the Chiral Pyridyl-Backbone for the Crabtree/Pfaltz-Type Iridium Complex Used in the Industrial Production of the Novel Fungicide Inpyrfluxam
Problem_Description: The final (S)-alcohol 6b is poorly crystalline, making chromatographic purification impractical and leading to material loss.
Solution_Description: After the transfer‑hydrogenation, the product was converted to its (S)-camphorsulfonic acid salt by a solvent switch from acetonitrile to xylene, precipitating a pure solid that retained the enantiomeric excess and required no chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Unfortunately, the (S)-alcohol 6b proved to be much less crystalline than racemic 4b. Thus, crystallization was only possible by taking unacceptable losses in the mother liquor.; We developed a procedure that precipitates a very pure (S)-camphorsulfonic acid salt of 6b, after a distillative solvent switch from the original acetonitrile to xylene. This protocol removes all side components and the brown color but leaves the enantiomeric excess of 6b completely unchanged.

Paper Title: Regioisomer Formation with Agmatine Guanidino Group, Its Implications for Agmatine Peptide Cyclization, and Application of Bis-Boc-Agmatine
Problem_Description: Agmatine sulfate has very low solubility in common organic solvents, preventing direct coupling to the peptide intermediate. This leads to the need for additional steps and generates significant impurity levels (≈10 % each of regio‑isomeric and dimeric by‑products), complicating purification.
Solution_Description: The sulfate is first neutralized with NaOH to give free‑base agmatine, which is then lyophilised and dissolved in DMF for coupling. This changes the solvent system to one in which the agmatine is soluble and allows the reaction to proceed at reasonable concentration.
Supporting_Evidence: Agmatine sulfate is sparsely soluble in common organic solvents and could not be directly coupled to the complementary peptide in solution at a decent concentration.; Therefore, agmatine sulfate is first neutralized by 2 equiv NaOH in aqueous solution and isolated through lyophilization; 1.92 equiv of thus obtained freebase agmatine are solubilized in DMF and coupled with 1 equiv Intermediate A by 1.05 equiv PyBOP and 2.5 equiv DIPEA.

Paper Title: Regioisomer Formation with Agmatine Guanidino Group, Its Implications for Agmatine Peptide Cyclization, and Application of Bis-Boc-Agmatine
Problem_Description: Neutralized (free‑base) agmatine bears a de‑protonated guanidino group that competes with its 4‑amino group for acylation, forming an acyl‑guanidine regio‑isomer (≈9.5 % of product) and a cross‑linked dimer (≈10.9 %). These side‑reactions reduce overall isolated yield and generate impurity‑heavy material.
Solution_Description: Replace free‑base agmatine with bis‑Boc‑protected agmatine. The Boc groups mask the guanidino nitrogen, preventing it from reacting, so coupling occurs exclusively through the amino terminus, eliminating regio‑isomer and dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: The deprotonated guanidino group from the freebase agmatine poses a competition reaction against its 4‑amino group in the target amidation reaction, giving rise to the formation of an acyl guanidine regioisomeric impurity.; The unpaired amino group on the formed isomer could be entangled in subsequent reactions, further complicating the impurity profile.; Bis‑Boc‑agmatine, a guanidino‑protected species, could be readily fused to peptide molecules exclusively through its amino group without forming regioisomeric impurities.

Paper Title: Regioisomer Formation with Agmatine Guanidino Group, Its Implications for Agmatine Peptide Cyclization, and Application of Bis-Boc-Agmatine
Problem_Description: The cross‑linked dimeric impurity (agmatine‑crosslinked protected linear FE 201836 dimer) consumes material and requires extensive work‑up (multiple precipitation and washing steps), lowering overall isolated yield (~71 % purity for the free‑base route).
Solution_Description: Using bis‑Boc‑agmatine at a strict 1:1 stoichiometry (1.05 equiv) prevents excess free agmatine from being carried into the cyclization step, eliminating the dimer‑forming pathway. The new route with protected agmatine inherently suppresses dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: The stoichiometry of bis‑Boc‑agmatine should be rigorously controlled since the excess bis‑Boc‑agmatine could be carried over to the cyclization step as agmatine, which would interfere with the target amidation cyclization.; No isomeric or dimeric impurities are generated in this process.; The protected linear FE 201836 crude product was analyzed by RP‑HPLC, and two major impurities with abundances of 9.5 and 10.9 % were detected.

Paper Title: Regioisomer Formation with Agmatine Guanidino Group, Its Implications for Agmatine Peptide Cyclization, and Application of Bis-Boc-Agmatine
Problem_Description: The free‑base process yields a product containing ~20 % total impurities that must be removed by labor‑intensive chromatography, increasing process time and material loss.
Solution_Description: The bis‑Boc route isolates the protected linear intermediate by precipitation from cold 20 % iPrOH/H₂O, avoiding chromatography. The subsequent deprotection and cyclization are performed at dilute concentrations (pseudo‑high‑dilution) to keep dimer formation under 1.5 %, simplifying downstream purification.
Supporting_Evidence: The protected intermediate 5 is isolated through the precipitation in a 20 % iPrOH (isopropanol) aqueous solution while maximizing the removal of the excess bis‑Boc‑agmatine.; Less than 1.5 % dimeric impurity is generated in this process.; Pseudo‑high‑dilution strategy to construct the target cyclic product while minimizing the undesired intermolecular reaction and the resultant dimeric impurity.

Paper Title: Regioisomer Formation with Agmatine Guanidino Group, Its Implications for Agmatine Peptide Cyclization, and Application of Bis-Boc-Agmatine
Problem_Description: The free‑base agmatine does not fully dissolve in DMF, forming a suspension that could lead to uneven reaction rates and incomplete conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture is pre‑stirred, and the free‑base agmatine suspension is added to a pre‑dissolved peptide/activator solution, ensuring rapid mixing and consistent conversion within 2 h. Additionally, a cold water quench precipitates the product efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: Freebase agmatine will not be entirely dissolved. The mixture was stirred and transferred to the reactor with freebase agmatine/DMF suspension to start the coupling reaction.; The mixture was stirred for 30 min, and the conversion was controlled with the developed RP‑HPLC method. The reaction was continued until less than 2 % of Intermediate A is detected (maximum reaction time 2 h).

Paper Title: Cost-Efficient, Multigram Scalable Synthesis of Shelf-Stable Electrophilic (Phenylsulfonyl)difluoromethylating Reagents
Problem_Description: The two key starting materials, disulfide 1 and PhSO₂CF₂H, are very expensive (> 2500 €/g) and, when the sulfane 2 was prepared on larger scale (80 g of 1), the isolated yield dropped from 74 % to 42 % and an unknown by‑product had to be removed before the oxidation step.
Solution_Description: The authors devised inexpensive laboratory syntheses (four‑step for 1 and two‑step for PhSO₂CF₂H) to generate the reagents in house, performed a single silica‑gel flash chromatography to remove the by‑product, and then telescoped the crude sulfoxide 3 directly into the triflic‑anhydride step without further purification, thereby reducing cost and minimizing material loss.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Both 1 and PhSO₂CF₂H being rather expensive chemicals (>2500 €/g for 1) … we decided to perform their synthesis following a four‑step procedure for 1 and a two‑step sequence for PhSO₂CF₂H to minimize the global cost of the large‑scale synthesis of I"; "When the reaction was carried out on 80 g of 1 … the yield decreased … the desired product 2 had to be purified from an unknown by‑product, which had a deleterious impact on the next oxidation step."; "The desired product 2 was smoothly synthesized from 1.4 g to 33.8 g … although the yield decreased by increasing the scale of the reaction."; "The crude sulfoxide 3 (35.28 g, quant.) was used without purification for the next step."

Paper Title: Cost-Efficient, Multigram Scalable Synthesis of Shelf-Stable Electrophilic (Phenylsulfonyl)difluoromethylating Reagents
Problem_Description: Scaling the first step to multigram quantities resulted in a lower isolated yield (42 % for entry 3, Table 1) and required a chromatographic purification to remove an unknown impurity that interfered with the subsequent oxidation.
Solution_Description: A single silica‑gel flash chromatography (petroleum ether/dichloromethane gradient) was employed as the sole purification for the whole sequence, and the reaction concentration was adjusted (500 mL DMF for 80 g of 1) to maintain homogeneity and avoid the need for vigorous stirring, improving reproducibility on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The desired product 2 had to be purified from an unknown by‑product, which had a deleterious impact on the next oxidation step."; "The yield decreased by increasing the scale of the reaction… entry 3 (80 g of 1) gave 42 % isolated yield."; "The reaction mixture remained homogeneous and mechanical stirring was not required."; "The residue was purified by silica gel flash column chromatography … to give 2 as a pale yellow amorphous solid (33.84 g, 42 %)."

Paper Title: Cost-Efficient, Multigram Scalable Synthesis of Shelf-Stable Electrophilic (Phenylsulfonyl)difluoromethylating Reagents
Problem_Description: The synthesis needed to avoid hazardous reagents (ozone‑depleting chemicals, metals) and to ensure thermal safety of the electrophilic salts, which could decompose exothermically at elevated temperatures.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free protocol using mCPBA oxidation and triflic anhydride was adopted, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was performed on the key intermediate and final salts to verify that their decomposition temperatures (≈ 163 °C for 3, 123–184 °C for the salts) are well above the reaction temperatures, confirming safe operating windows.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The synthesis of the reagent I was achieved owing to a metal‑free protocol, which did not require ozone‑depleting reagents."; "The DSC studies showed … a high decomposition energy … with a peak very distant from the melting point. The decomposition temperature is about 163 °C … far from the reaction temperature used in the oxidation step."; "The DSC analyses of I, II, III show an exothermic decomposition phenomenon close to the melting temperature … the decomposition of this family of products occurs at temperatures well above those used for their synthesis."

Paper Title: Cost-Efficient, Multigram Scalable Synthesis of Shelf-Stable Electrophilic (Phenylsulfonyl)difluoromethylating Reagents
Problem_Description: The overall three‑step/one‑purification sequence afforded a modest 38 % global isolated yield for the target reagent I, and the oxidation step required a 24 h stir at 21 °C, extending the production time.
Solution_Description: The crude sulfoxide 3 was telescoped directly into the triflic‑anhydride step without isolation, eliminating an additional work‑up and reducing total reaction time; reaction time for the oxidation was monitored and found to give quantitative conversion after 24 h, allowing the authors to set a practical 24 h schedule; the reaction concentrations were kept in a range that maintained a homogeneous mixture, facilitating scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The synthesis of I has been performed on about 43 g scale … with a 38 % global yield."; "The selective oxidation of 2 with mCPBA afforded the sulfoxide 3 at 21 °C … the reaction mixture was stirred at 21 °C for 24 h, allowing full conversion of 2 into the product 3."; "The crude sulfoxide 3 (35.28 g, quant.) was used without any further purification for the next step."; "The preparation of the compound I has been scaled up … to about 43 g (91 % yield)"

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Raney Ni gave a low reactant conversion (78 %) and a low isolated yield (64 %) in batch hydrogenation of syn‑2‑nitro‑1,3‑diol (Table 1, entry 1).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: In traditional batch reactors the alkylation of TNPG produces large amounts of volatile side‑products (ethanol, ethyl formate) that evaporate rapidly. This raises the liquid level, creates a high risk of spill and possible eruption incidents, and forces the use of an elevated jacket temperature to overcome the low heating efficiency of batch reactors, which is unsafe from a thermal‑runaway perspective.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a wiped‑film evaporator/distillation coupled system. This equipment provides a very low liquid hold‑up, a thin moving film that ensures excellent heat transfer, and continuous removal of the low‑boiling side‑products via an integrated distillation column, thereby eliminating the spill‑risk and the need for excessive heating.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Running this alkylation in the traditional stirred reactors has a high risk of spill and eruption incidents because of the evaporation of large amounts of volatile side‑products." (Abstract)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: Batch operation requires heating the reactor well above the boiling points of ethanol (78 °C) and ethyl formate (52 °C) to obtain sufficient conversion. This high jacket temperature creates a safety hazard because a large inventory of high‑energy materials (TNPG and TETNB) is present in the reactor.
Solution_Description: By using the wiped‑film evaporator the jacket temperature can be set at an optimum (≈145 °C) that maximises conversion while keeping the reaction temperature below the decomposition onset of the energetic materials. The superior heat‑transfer capacity of the film evaporator removes the need for excessive heating.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Due to the endothermicity nature of evaporation process and low heating efficiency of batch reactors, an elevated temperature of the heating carrier is required to improve the reaction efficiency in a batch reactor. This is undesirable from the viewpoint of thermal safety..." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: In a previously reported micro‑reactor synthesis, the reaction temperature (90–120 °C) is far above the boiling points of the side‑products, generating gas bubbles that lead to an uncertain residence time distribution.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The wiped‑film evaporator/distillation system provides continuous operation with a thin film that eliminates gas‑bubble formation and yields a well‑defined residence time, removing the variability observed in the micro‑reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Because the reaction temperature of 90–120 °C is significantly higher than the boiling point of side‑products, this synthesis method cannot avoid the generation of gas bubbles in the micro‑reactor, leading to the uncertainty of residence time of reaction mixture in the micro‑reactor." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: When the feeding speed is low (e.g., 3 mL min⁻¹) TETNB crystals form on the bottom of the wiped‑film evaporator; the crystals can stay in the hot zone for a prolonged time, raising the risk of decomposition of the energetic product.
Solution_Description: Increasing the feeding speed (≥8 mL min⁻¹) shortens the residence time and eliminates the crystal buildup, preventing exposure of solid TETNB to high temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "When the feeding speed was low such as 3 mL min⁻¹, a small portion of TETNB was crystalized at the bottom of the film evaporator... This phenomenon should be paid attention because if the solid crystal is exposed to high temperature for a long time, it may cause the decomposition of TETNB. Moreover, increasing the feeding speed was an effective treatment to deal with this problem. Indeed, It is found that when the feeding speed increased up to 8 mL min⁻¹, the crystallization phenomenon completely disappeared." (Section 3.4.2)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: Triethyl orthoformate decomposes at the reaction temperature, causing loss of reagent and risk of supersaturation of TNPG and TETNB, which could precipitate on reactor walls and lead to accidents.
Solution_Description: A large excess of triethyl orthoformate (molar ratio TNPG : triethyl orthoformate ≈ 1 : 19) is used to compensate for its decomposition and to keep the reaction mixture well‑solubilised, preventing solid precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Among these, the amount of triethyl orthoformate far exceeds the stoichiometric ratio, mainly for the following two reasons. One is that triethyl orthoformate will decompose at high temperature to generate ethanol and ethyl formate, resulting in certain losses; the other is the raw material TNPG and products... Insufficient amount of solution will lead to the supersaturation of solids and precipitation on the wall surface, which will lead to accidents when heated for a long time." (Section 2.2.3)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: Batchwise alkylation requires a residence time of >2.5 h, resulting in a large liquid holdup of energetic material and a high probability of runaway or spill incidents.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The wiped‑film evaporator/distillation coupled system reduces the liquid holdup to <8 mL and the total reaction time to <4 min, dramatically improving safety and productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The holdup of reaction liquid in the wiped evaporation is less than 8 mL and the contact time of explosible TNPG and TETNB to heat surface is less than 4 min, which greatly restrain the risk of a runaway reaction... The reaction time needed to complete the alkylation reaction in the coupling technology is lower than 4 min. As a comparison, the semi‑batch operation required at least 2.5 h to complete the alkylation." (Section 3.5)

Paper Title: Continuous and Safe Alkylation of 1,3,5-Trihydroxy-2,4,6-trinitrobenzene using Wiped Film Evaporator/Distillation Coupled Technology
Problem_Description: The alkylation reaction becomes vigorous only above 70 °C; as temperature rises, the rate of gas (ethanol/ethyl formate) generation increases sharply, demanding efficient heat removal.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Operating at a jacket temperature of 145 °C (optimal) provides sufficient heat to drive the reaction while the wiped‑film evaporator’s high heat‑transfer coefficient (τ ≈ 3.6–4.1) quickly removes the generated heat, preventing temperature run‑away.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The heat flow signal was always lower than the baseline, indicating that the alkylation reaction is endothermic… The heat flow curve started to decrease at the temperature of 70 °C and meanwhile the gas bubbles began to be generated. Moreover, the conversion of TNPG can be neglected before 70 °C... With the increase of reaction temperature, the gas production rate increased significantly." (Section 3.1)

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: The reaction mixture became highly viscous (≈5.5× that of neat THF) because of the high concentration of LiBr (3 M) and DMU, which slowed mixing, increased equilibration time (≈80 min) and caused a larger voltage drop; at higher currents the temperature rose, requiring additional cooling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The LiBr and DMU concentrations were reduced (to 1.5 M LiBr/6 eq DMU and 0.75 M LiBr/3 eq DMU), lowering viscosity, shortening the equilibration time (~40 min) and reducing the voltage needed.  Additionally, the reactor was operated at a controlled temperature (10–30 °C) using an aluminum cooling jacket with a copper coil to remove the excess heat generated at higher currents.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The viscosity of the reaction mixture was found to be ca. ×5.5 greater than that of neat THF and high viscosity is clearly undesirable for a flow process."
"We noted that the concentration of LiBr contributed most to the viscosity and decided to investigate the effect of reducing the concentration of DMU and LiBr."
"Reducing the concentration of LiBr and DMU by half (1.5 M LiBr, 6 equiv DMU) and to a quarter (0.75 M LiBr, 3 equiv DMU) of the original amount led to only a slight decrease in the yield of 2a…"
"The productivity of the reaction could be increased by simultaneously increasing the flow rate and current; however, higher currents necessarily required higher voltages leading to increased temperatures of the reactor. Therefore, an aluminum cooling jacket with a copper coil fed by a recirculating chiller was used to maintain a stable temperature in the reactor."

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: When the additive TPPA (10 eq) was used, the reactor operated for only 20–30 min before blockages formed from a black tar‑like material, and the process showed poor repeatability.
Solution_Description: TPPA was omitted from the reaction mixture, allowing uninterrupted flow without tar formation and restoring consistent operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Under these conditions, 1a was consumed and the selectivity was promising; however, repeatability was poor as the reactor could not be operated for more than 20–30 min, at which point blockages were encountered due to the build of a black tar‑like substance."
"The omission of TPPA allowed the reaction mixture to be passed through the reactor without blockage; however, the desired current could not be achieved without increasing the amount of LiBr/DMU."

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: Running the reaction under non‑anhydrous conditions produced a cloudy solution with black/gray particles, leading to inconsistent operation and occasional blockages.
Solution_Description: All reagents and THF were dried and the solution was prepared under strictly anhydrous conditions, giving a clear, particle‑free outflow and stable operation for extended periods (>8 h).
Supporting_Evidence:
"We noted that in some cases, when the reaction was performed under nonanhydrous conditions, a cloudy solution containing black/gray particles sometimes appears in the output stream…"
"By contrast, when the solution is prepared anhydrously, the output stream appears clear and free of insoluble particles and the reactor operated stably, running without problems for extended periods, tested up to 8 h."

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: The sacrificial aluminum outer electrode corroded during operation, releasing Al particles into the reaction mixture; over 8 h the gap widened by ~0.2 mm, raising concerns about blockages and long‑term durability.
Solution_Description: The reactor design places all seals on the outer surface, allowing the aluminum tube to be easily replaced after a defined run time; monitoring of gap size and mass loss ensures safe operation and prevents leaks.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The total mass loss from the Al electrode was 6.73 g (0.25 mol)… the gap size had increased by 0.2 mm over the 8 h period."
"A feature of this reactor Taylor vortex design is that, for a fixed gap size, the ratio of reactor volume to electrode surface area remains approximately constant as the diameter of the reactor is increased. This means that one might expect that the rate of erosion of the sacrificial electrode would be similar to that which we observed if the reactor were to be scaled up by increasing its diameter."
"Because the metal is lost from the inner surface of the cylindrical electrode and all seals are on the outer surface, the loss of aluminum does not cause any leaks from the reactor. Eventually, the electrode will need replacing but the simple design of our reactor makes the replacement quite straightforward."

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: Using a graphite outer electrode gave no reaction, making the process ineffective and requiring a more suitable material.
Solution_Description: An inexpensive aluminum tube (sacrificial anode) was employed as the outer electrode, providing the necessary reactivity and allowing straightforward machining.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Indeed, when the reduction reaction was run with the graphite anode, no reaction took place. We opted for an aluminum anode as it is a commonly used sacrificial electrode and is relatively inexpensive, inert, and easy to machine, making it ideal for use in our reactor design."
"The single‑pass electrochemical reduction of naphthalene has been developed in a continuous flow vortex reactor using inexpensive aluminum and stainless‑steel electrodes."

Paper Title: High-Productivity Single-Pass Electrochemical Birch Reduction of Naphthalenes in a Continuous Flow Electrochemical Taylor Vortex Reactor
Problem_Description: Selectivity between the single‑ring reduction product (2a) and the double‑ring reduction product (3) depended strongly on the applied current; insufficient control led to variability in product distribution.
Solution_Description: Current was precisely controlled (e.g., 520 mA for 2a, 1040 mA or higher for 3) to switch selectivity on demand, achieving >98 % selectivity for the desired product; the stoichiometry of LiBr/DMU was kept constant while adjusting current.
Supporting_Evidence:
"by varying the current, we can switch between high selectivity (>90 %) for either the single ring reduction or double ring reduction"
"When the applied current was doubled, the selectivity could be inverted to produce 3 in 94 % yield."
"With a flow rate of 1.75 mL min⁻¹ and a current of 520 mA, we obtained high conversion of 1 (85 %) with 84 % yield of 2a and 1 % of 3; … When the applied current was doubled, the selectivity could be inverted to produce 3 in 94 % yield."

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: The original laboratory protocol used Bu4NClO4 as the supporting electrolyte. Perchlorate salts are energetic, shock‑sensitive in the presence of organics or metals, and are potent thyroid‑hormone disruptors, making them unsafe and costly for large‑scale use.
Solution_Description: A systematic HT‑eChem screen identified Et4NPF6 as an alternative electrolyte. Et4NPF6 provides homogeneous reaction mixtures, lower toxicity, and reduced cost relative to perchlorate salts while maintaining comparable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of Bu4NClO4 as an electrolyte raises safety concerns... Perchlorates are energetic materials and can be shock‑sensitive... We screened a broad collection of electrolytes... Et4NPF6 and Bu4NPF6 electrolytes gave a clean reaction profile and homogeneous conditions... We ultimately settled on Et4NPF6 as the electrolyte of choice because of its lower molecular weight compared to Bu4NPF6.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: When stainless‑steel electrodes were used, the reaction mixture became heterogeneous, product yields were lower, and significant metal leaching (Fe, Cr, Ni) occurred, indicating electrode corrosion and decomposition of the electrode surface.
Solution_Description: Switch to dimensionally stable anodes (DSA) – RuO2 coated on titanium – which are chemically compatible, highly durable, and give >90 % isolated sulfone yield with minimal metal leaching.
Supporting_Evidence: “Stainless steel provided high yields of the product but resulted in a heterogeneous mixture, possibly due to metal leaching... RuO2 on Ti electrodes... show excellent chemical compatibility, durability, and high Faradaic efficiency… an excellent yield of sulfone 3 and Faradaic efficiency (full conversion after 5 F/mol) were obtained when the oxidation of thioether 1 was performed with RuO2 on Ti.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Initial flow experiments in the micro‑flow cell gave full conversion but only <5 g day⁻¹ productivity at 13 mA cm⁻² (requiring 5 F mol⁻¹), which is far too slow for kilogram‑scale manufacturing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increase substrate concentration from 0.1 M to 0.47 M (reducing electrolyte loading to 0.18 equiv) and maintain moderate temperature (<20 °C). Higher concentration improves current efficiency (4.5–4.75 F mol⁻¹) and overall throughput without sacrificing selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “We sought to intensify our process by decreasing the electrolyte stoichiometry... increasing substrate concentration (from 0.1 to 0.47 M)... this increase in substrate concentration results in a net decrease in catalyst loading... resulting in higher current efficiencies (reactions reach full conversion, including <5 % sulfoxide remaining, with only 4.5–4.75 F/mol).”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Scaling to kilogram quantities introduced hazards from H₂ evolution and possible formation of explosive chlorine‑dioxide (ClO₂). Uncontrolled temperature rise could push the mixture into the ClO₂ explosive regime.
Solution_Description: The kilo‑scale reactor was housed in a custom plexiglass enclosure with N₂ sweep, head‑space cooling (<20 °C), gas scrubbing (NaOH/Na₂SO₃), and a power‑supply voltage limit (10 V) to cap the cell potential and prevent runaway exotherms.
Supporting_Evidence: “The electrochemical cell was housed in a custom‑made plexiglass enclosure… The enclosure was connected to two nitrogen lines to provide a sweep with inert gas… The headspace of the reservoir was continuously swept using nitrogen… finally, we maintained a reaction temperature below 20 °C via active cooling… set our power supply to a maximum potential of 10 V… to minimize any risk of electrocution and to prevent the onset of undesired side reactions.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Using LiCl or KCl electrolytes produced heterogeneous mixtures and complicated downstream isolation of the sulfone due to insoluble precipitates and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Adopt Et4NPF6 in MeCN/0.1 M aq. HCl (6:1 v/v), which maintains a single‑phase homogeneous solution, facilitating both reaction performance and easy work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both Et4NPF6 and Bu4NPF6 electrolytes gave a clean reaction profile and homogeneous conditions, in contrast to heterogeneous conditions observed when using the LiCl or KCl electrolyte.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Batch‐scale screening at low current densities gave inconsistent conversions; poor mass‑transfer limited the current, leading to variable Faradaic efficiencies and sub‑optimal yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Identify an optimal current density of 30 mA cm⁻² in flow (above mass‑transfer limit but below hydrogen‑generation safety limit) and operate in recirculating mode to decouple flow‑rate from conversion, providing reproducible performance across scales.
Supporting_Evidence: “We investigated the electrochemical oxidation of 1 at 20, 30, and 40 mA cm⁻²… similar results were obtained at all current densities… we settled on the use of 30 mA cm⁻² as the optimal current density… recirculating mode… allowing a high flow rate, which provided good mixing and rapid H₂ removal…”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the reaction generated trace pyrimidone impurities (5a–c) and volatile amine/aldehyde side‑products (6, 7, 8) that were difficult to detect by conventional HPLC, complicating product isolation and quality control.
Solution_Description: Couple the flow reactor to an online ¹H/¹³C NMR platform for real‑time monitoring, enabling rapid detection of low‑level impurities and adjustment of residence time and concentration to minimise their formation; employ ion‑chromatography to track chloride‑derived species for informed work‑up decisions.
Supporting_Evidence: “We interfaced our flow electrochemical cell with a recirculating flow NMR… By measuring ¹H and ¹³C NMR data with 10 min temporal resolution, we were able to track the consumption of thioether 1, growth and decay of the sulfoxide intermediate 2, and formation of the sulfone product 3… ion chromatography proved useful to confirm or exclude the presence of different oxidized Cl species in our mixture.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: Certain high‑performance electrode materials (Pt foil, BDD) were not commercially available in the large dimensions required for kilogram‑scale reactors, and their cost would be prohibitive for routine manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Select RuO₂‑coated Ti DSA electrodes, which are widely supplied in large plate formats, inexpensive relative to Pt/BDD, and demonstrably durable under industrial current densities.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pt, glassy carbon, and boron‑doped diamond (BDD) were identified as suitable anodes… however, glassy carbon is not a viable option… Pt foil and BDD are available for the laboratory scale, larger electrodes for kg scale are not readily available and are very costly… RuO₂ on Ti electrodes… provide excellent chemical compatibility, durability, and high Faradaic efficiency.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale Electrochemical Oxidation of a Thioether to a Sulfone: A Workflow for Scaling up Electrosynthesis
Problem_Description: The original reaction required 6 F mol⁻¹ (theoretically 4 F mol⁻¹) to reach full conversion, leading to unnecessarily long electrolysis times and high energy consumption.
Solution_Description: Mechanistic insight revealed a mediated oxidation pathway (Cl⁻ → Cl₂/HOCl) requiring only 4 F mol⁻¹. By optimizing chloride loading (14 mol % mediator) and operating at 30 mA cm⁻², full conversion was achieved at 4.5 F mol⁻¹, reducing reaction time by ~25 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The net double oxidation of sulfide 1 to sulfone 3 is shown in eq 8, which clearly highlights how 4 equiv of electrons (4 F/mol) are required… In batch reactions performed in the absence of HCl gave full conversion after 5 F/mol… With the intensified conditions we observed full conversion… with only 4.5–4.75 F/mol instead of 5 F/mol.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: Previous industrial routes to irbesartan relied on highly toxic sodium cyanide, which poses severe safety hazards and increases the cost of waste handling.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a new four‑step synthetic route that starts from inexpensive glycine methyl ester, thereby avoiding the use of sodium cyanide altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compared with leucine or its derivatives as the starting material … the intermediate 5 could be obtained … from low‑cost and commercially available glycine methyl ester … which also avoided the use of highly toxic cyanide.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: When amide 12 was prepared using DCC as a coupling agent, the resulting urea by‑product was difficult to remove by crystallisation or washing.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to an acid‑chloride protocol (n‑pentanoyl chloride) and introduced a controlled, slow addition (5 mL min⁻¹) of the acid chloride to suppress bis‑acylated side‑products, while also selecting EtOAc as the reaction solvent for easier work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the byproduct urea associated with the use of DCC … was difficult to remove … Therefore, we tried another method … using acid chloride … impurity I was efficiently avoided when the addition rate of n‑pentanoyl chloride was 5 mL/min.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: During the synthesis of amide 12, pyridine gave a comparable yield to Et₃N but is highly toxic, prompting a need for a safer base.
Solution_Description: Et₃N was selected as the base because it provided high conversion without the toxicity concerns of pyridine; the reaction conditions (base loading 2.5 equiv, 0 °C, controlled addition) were optimized accordingly.
Supporting_Evidence: “Et₃N was selected as the base given the high toxicity of pyridine … impurity I was efficiently avoided … when the addition rate of n‑pentanoyl chloride was 5 mL/min.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: In the ammonolysis of ester 12 with biphenyl substrate 7, inorganic bases (Na₂CO₃, NaOH, NaH) gave low conversions and, in the case of NaH, generated large amounts of H₂ gas, creating safety hazards.
Solution_Description: Organic bases (MeONa, t‑BuOK) were screened; t‑BuOK (3 equiv) in MeOH at 65 °C delivered up to 92 % isolated yield, and MeOH was retained as the optimal solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “When inorganic bases … were used the product was obtained in 0–52 % yield … organic bases MeONa and t‑BuOK gave 65 % and 70 % … finally, the reaction proceeded cleanly using 3 equiv t‑BuOK … at 65 °C, achieving a 92 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: Washing of crude 13 with water gave only 90 % HPLC purity, indicating residual impurities that lowered overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: AcOEt was employed as the washing solvent; performing the wash at 15 °C increased the purity to 99.40 % and the isolated yield to 93.2 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 13 was obtained by washing with water … HPLC purity … only 90 % … AcOEt was used as the washing solvent at room temperature … 99.23 % purity … further improvement in yield (93.2 %) was obtained by cooling it to 15 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: Cyclization of diamide 13 to imidazolinone 14 under inorganic acids (H₂SO₄, HClO₄) led to complete decomposition of the substrate and no product formation.
Solution_Description: Organic methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) was identified as the optimal catalyst (1.25 equiv) in refluxing toluene, providing 60–73 % yield of 14 while minimizing decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the reaction was performed in the presence of inorganic acid, none of the products 14 were detected … MsOH gave a 60 % yield … the best yield of 14 was obtained with 1.25 equiv MsOH, but 8.4 % of compound 7 was still present.”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: During the MsOH‑mediated cyclization, hydrolysis generated salts of by‑products 7 and 15, contaminating the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: A direct water wash followed by pH adjustment (8–9) and extraction with DCM efficiently removed the acidic salts, delivering pure 14 with >98 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since the byproducts 7 and 15 … existed in the system under acidic conditions, the reaction system was directly washed with water, … pH of the aqueous phase was adjusted … extraction with dichloromethane … the HPLC purity of 7 was up to 98.6 % …”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: Initial alkylation of 14 with 1,4‑dibromobutane gave only 25–35 % yield in THF with various bases, and higher temperatures caused substrate decomposition (impurities 16, 7).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system THF/DMSO (6:1) with NaOH as base at room temperature (RT) increased the yield to 85 %; replacing THF with 2‑MeTHF further improved sustainability and maintained high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “NaOH as a base catalyzed this reaction to synthesize 5 at 40 °C in THF/DMSO (V/V = 6:1), and 5 was obtained in 74 % yield … the yield … was up to 85 % at room temperature in THF/DMSO … 2‑MeTHF instead of THF gave a similar yield (87 %).”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: 1,4‑Dibromobutane is classified as a mutagenic substance (ICH M7) and must be limited to ≤66 ppm in the final drug product.
Solution_Description: The authors employed methyl‑tert‑butyl‑ether washing of the crude spirocycle 5, which successfully reduced residual 1,4‑dibromobutane below the toxicological limit.
Supporting_Evidence: “1,4‑Dibromobutane is a mutagenic substance … limit … 66 ppm … we controlled the residual amount … when methyl tert‑butyl ether was used as a washing solvent to purify 5 …”

Paper Title: Development of a New Synthetic Route of the Key Intermediate of Irbesartan
Problem_Description: The cyclization step to form imidazolinone 14 required 6 h reflux, and the alkylation step required 3 h stirring, leading to long overall processing times.
Solution_Description: Optimization of reaction temperatures (e.g., performing the alkylation at RT) and careful monitoring reduced the total reaction time while maintaining high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was stirred at 40 °C for 3 h … the yield decreased … when the temperature was increased … the yield of 5 was up to 85 % at room temperature …”

Paper Title: Reactor Design for the Direct Electrosynthesis of Periodate
Problem_Description: Precipitation of paraperiodate during electrolysis coated the anode and diaphragm and blocked the flow‑electrolysis cell, causing clogging, high back‑pressure (up to 17 bar) and damage to the BDD anode.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor (e‑CSTR) operated in steady‑state mode with a loop that isolates the electrolysis step. The process was run at late‑stage conversion so that paraperiodate precipitates out of the anolyte and can be removed by inline decantation, preventing cell blockage and anode coating.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Both precipitates, iodine and paraperiodate, impair the efficiency of electrolysis by coating of the anodic surface and separator… The clogging required disassembling and cleaning of the cell, which resulted in significant maintenance efforts. Back pressures up to 17 bar were generated damaging the anode in some cases.” (Introduction, p. 3) 
• “A tank reactor was preferred over a pure plug‑flow reactor … The concept of steady‑state CSTR … with the electrolytic flow cell, where the actual oxidation takes place (e‑CSTR).” (Introduction, p. 4) 
• “Clogging occurred less frequently at the later stages of electrolysis… therefore we envisioned a continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) design …” (Introduction, p. 5) 
• “The inline separation of the product … decantation … The overall yield was determined … The productivity was doubled … Clogging did not occur after enlargement of the diameter of the outlet to 8 mm.” (Results, Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Reactor Design for the Direct Electrosynthesis of Periodate
Problem_Description: Early‑stage precipitation adhered to the anode causing severe clogging and damage to the BDD electrode, even when the improved cell design was used.
Solution_Description: Redesigned the electrolytic cell with funnel‑shaped inlet/outlet geometry and enlarged the outlet diameter (8 mm) to allow precipitated solids to be removed without high pressure build‑up, eliminating early‑stage clogging and protecting the anode.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Clogging was exceedingly observed in scale‑up experiments due to the formation of a solid periodate precipitate within the electrolysis cell. The clogging required disassembling and cleaning of the cell, which resulted in significant maintenance efforts.” (Introduction, p. 3) 
• “The inlets and outlets were funnel‑shaped and arranged in a linear fashion to enable a simpler unload of precipitates upon the buildup of pressure (p_max set to 17 bar).” (Results, Sec 2.2) 
• “Clogging did not occur after enlargement of the diameter of the outlet to 8 mm.” (Results, Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Reactor Design for the Direct Electrosynthesis of Periodate
Problem_Description: When iodine was used as the feedstock the applied voltage rose to ~12 V, the current decreased, and the overall yield fell to 44 % (0.96 kg product), indicating insufficient electrolysis capacity and poor conversion.
Solution_Description: Increased the NaOH concentration in the anolyte from 1 M to 4 M, which lowered the applied voltage to 6–8 V, improved current efficiency, and raised yields up to 98 %. The higher hydroxide concentration also helped maintain a high pH (>12.6) that favored the oxidation pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When iodine was used … an increased applied voltage up to 12 V … resulted in a lower current… The productivity accounted to 3.9 g h⁻¹ … only a low overall yield of 44 % was obtained.” (Results, Sec 2.2) 
• “In the following steady‑state experiments, the initial NaOH concentration in the anolyte was increased … which resulted in a significantly lower applied voltage of 6.2–7.9 V. … Yields of up to 98 % were obtained.” (Results, Sec 2.3) 
• “A pH above 12.6 indeed lowered the applied voltage from an average of 10 to 8 V, which improved the electrolysis performance as compared to iodine.” (Results, Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Reactor Design for the Direct Electrosynthesis of Periodate
Problem_Description: At high flow rates (30 L h⁻¹) the cell experienced excessive gas evolution (H₂/O₂), which filled the cell volume with non‑conducting gases, increased electrical resistance and caused voltage spikes.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Scaled the flow from 7.5 L h⁻¹ to ~700 L h⁻¹ using high‑capacity Flujo01 pumps, which promoted better gas removal, stabilized the applied voltage at 6.1–6.5 V and improved energy efficiency while retaining throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Currents above 20 A resulted in an increased evolution of gases, presumably H₂ and O₂, leading to a high electrical resistance of the electrolysis cell. The cell volume is then largely filled with non‑conducting gases.” (Results, Sec 2.1) 
• “Finally, the flow rate was increased from 7.5 L h⁻¹ to approximately 700 L h⁻¹ using Flujo01 pumps… A decrease and stabilization of the applied voltage at 6.1–6.5 V was observed.” (Results, Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Reactor Design for the Direct Electrosynthesis of Periodate
Problem_Description: When the flow was increased to 700 L h⁻¹, dark particles were observed in the pump tubes (SiC bearings) and gas evolution indicated decomposition of periodate to O₂, compromising product integrity.
Solution_Description: Identified the SiC pump bearings as a source of decomposition and suggested using pump hardware made from compatible, non‑catalytic materials to avoid periodate degradation.

Problem_Description: In batch mode the homogeneous ionic‑liquid catalysts suffered from poor mass‑transfer because the reaction mixture is highly viscous and the epoxide does not mix well with CO₂, leading to low conversions and yields.
