Solution_Description: The operating pressure was increased to 15–20 MPa, which suppressed catalyst leaching, and the catalyst loading was reduced to 15 wt % (from 30 wt %) to minimise leaching while maintaining activity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["While screening pressures from 6 to 20 MPa (entries 22–25), it turned out that a pressure of 6 MPa (entry 22) led to leaching of 12 %… at operating pressures of 15 and 20 MPa… no leached catalyst was detected.","For this reason, the catalyst loading was reduced to 15 wt %… only traces of leached catalyst were detected via ¹H‑NMR spectroscopy… after the first 27 h, no leaching and a constant output of carbonates were observed."]

Paper Title: Continuous Formation of Limonene Carbonates in Supercritical Carbon Dioxide
Problem_Description: At temperatures of 150 °C the tetrabutylammonium chloride decomposes via Hoffmann elimination to tributylamine, which sharply decreases the carbonate yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was limited to 120 °C (or lower) where no decomposition of the catalyst was observed, preserving activity and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["At 150 °C (entry 21), Hoffmann elimination of TBAC 1 to tributylamine became an issue, resulting in a decrease in yield over time.","Increasing the temperature from 80 °C up to 120 °C (entries 18–20) resulted in increasing and constant outputs… In contrast, at 150 °C (entry 21)… the formation of the elimination product was confirmed via ¹H‑NMR analysis."]

Paper Title: Continuous Formation of Limonene Carbonates in Supercritical Carbon Dioxide
Problem_Description: In batch reactions the acidic silanol groups of the silica support and residual water promoted ring‑opening of the epoxide to limonene diol, decreasing selectivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Water was removed by thorough drying of the silica and the process was transferred to continuous flow, where the shorter contact time prevented diol formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The influence of water was proven by the addition of 10 wt % of water… 20 % of limonene diol was formed… In batch mode using SILP 1… 5 % of limonene diol was formed… however, the diol was no longer formed in continuous flow…" , "The long‑term stability studies… no leaching over 48 h…" ]

Paper Title: Continuous Formation of Limonene Carbonates in Supercritical Carbon Dioxide
Problem_Description: Increasing the catalyst loading to 40 wt % caused agglomeration of the SILP material, loss of free‑flowing properties and pressure spikes, leading to unstable operation and inconsistent yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading was limited to 30 wt % (optimal) and the catalyst cartridge length/residence time were adjusted (250 mm, 125 s) to provide sufficient activity without causing agglomeration.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A higher catalyst loading to 40 wt % (entry 28) ended up in an overpressure in the system during the reaction due to a visible agglomeration and loss in the free‑flowing property of the SILP material.","Increasing the catalyst loading from 20 to 30 wt %… resulted in a slight increase in yield… However, a further increase to 40 wt %… was not suitable.","Using a catalyst cartridge of 250 mm … resulted in a 65 % higher input of SILP and equally longer residence time… an increase of 60 % in maximum yield… was observed."]

Paper Title: Continuous Formation of Limonene Carbonates in Supercritical Carbon Dioxide
Problem_Description: Performing reactions at pressures above the typical batch limit (5 MPa) required a safe, controllable system to avoid hazardous over‑pressurisation.
Solution_Description: A dedicated continuous‑flow scCO₂ setup with a back‑pressure regulator, stainless‑steel HPLC column cartridges and heated zones was employed, allowing safe operation up to 50 MPa and reliable pressure control.
Supporting_Evidence: ["All continuous flow reactions were performed with the following reaction setup… (1) liquid CO₂ supply… (9) back‑pressure regulator… (10) gas–liquid separator…", "In contrast to batch mode conversions of CO₂, in continuous flow chemistry, even higher pressures can be applied under safe conditions. While reactions with normal CO₂ gas cylinders in batch are typically limited to feed pressures of 5 MPa, continuous conversions can be safely realised with pressures up to 50 MPa."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: The original seven‑step synthesis of the pyridoazepine (Scheme 1) gave low overall yields for the key coupling step, required large volumes of solvent and generated significant waste, required the costly and difficult‑to‑scale potassium benzyloxy‑ethyltrifluoroborate (2), and involved a late‑stage H₂SO₄/HNO₃ nitration that posed safety concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was designed that uses a Rh(II)‑catalyzed ring‑expansion followed by nitroacetamide condensation, shortening the synthesis to four–five steps, eliminating palladium‑mediated steps, avoiding chromatography, and improving atom‑economy and waste profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “Key to this approach was a bis‑2‑carbon homologation … while this method provided sufficient material for early discovery work, it was unsuitable for multi‑gram scale‑up due to (i) relatively low yields … (iii) challenges in accessing the trifluoroborate 2 … (iv) safety concerns over the late‑stage H₂SO₄/HNO₃ nitration …”; “In addition to being shorter than the original route, the new route encompasses many of the principals of green chemistry … the route requires no chromatographic purification …”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: p‑Toluenesulfonyl azide (TsN₃) contains a high‑energy functional group; DSC shows an exothermic decomposition onset at 120–128 °C and literature reports of explosions during distillation.
Solution_Description: TsN₃ was employed as an 11–15 % w/w solution in toluene and the CuAAC was carried out at 0 °C (ice bath). TSU analysis showed no exotherm up to 200 °C, confirming safe operation under the chosen order and temperature of addition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) data indicates an initiation temperature for the exothermic decomposition of TsN₃ of between 120 and 128 °C …”; “We deemed TsN₃ in toluene as suitable for this work. This decision was further derisked by … TSU analysis … revealed no untoward thermal or pressure events … the reaction … proceeded at ice‑bath temperature …”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: The Rh(II)‑catalyzed denitrogenative ring expansion of triazole 17 was originally reported at 140 °C (microwave) with a DSC onset for decomposition of 155.5 °C, leaving a narrow safety margin and risking uncontrolled nitrogen evolution.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed at a much lower temperature (50 °C) under conventional heating, using a higher catalyst loading (1–2 mol % vs 0.5–1 mol % in literature). TSU showed no exothermic onset and a gradual pressure rise, providing a comfortable safety window.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was first reported to occur in the microwave at 140 °C … DSC revealed initiation of exothermic decomposition at 155.5 °C … the event provided little margin …”; “When testing the lower temperature limits … conversion proceeds at an acceptable rate at an even milder temperature of 50 °C … higher catalyst loading was beneficial … TSU indicated no undesirable exothermic event … pressure rise … could be managed on scale …”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: Nitroacetamide (20a) and its ammonium enolate (20b) have low DSC onset temperatures (≈94–99 °C) and high decomposition enthalpies (≈‑1866 to ‑2776 J g⁻¹), and internal BAM Fallhammer tests showed shock‑sensitivity, indicating explosive hazard.
Solution_Description: Nitroacetamide was prepared in‑house by reacting the ammonium enolate slurry with a controlled amount of sulfuric acid (pH ≈ 5) in 2‑propanol, precipitating ammonium sulfate and yielding a 0.21 M stock solution of the free acid. The solution is stored cold, avoiding isolation of the neat, shock‑sensitive solid.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC onset for nitroacetamide of 93.8 °C with high energy output … predicted to be potentially capable of explosive propagation.”; “Six trials of BAM Fallhammer testing produced discoloration … nitroacetamide … is potentially explosive.”; “We prepared 20a as a stock solution by treating a 2‑propanolic slurry … with 0.5 mol equiv of sulfuric acid … the solution thus formed was found to be stable for several weeks at 5 °C …”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: During the double‑condensation of sulfonamide 18 with nitroacetamide 20b, the major product was the undesired ammonium adduct 19 (>2:1 vs desired pyridoazepine 9) due to nucleophilic attack by ammonia.
Solution_Description: The reaction was switched to use the triethylammonium enolate 20c (prepared in situ by addition of excess triethylamine to 20b), which suppresses ammonia‑mediated side‑reaction and furnishes the desired product without the ammonium adduct.
Supporting_Evidence: “In initial experiments, reaction … gave the undesired ammonium adduct 19 as the major product … To avoid this … we prepared the corresponding triethylammonium enolate by evaporating … in the presence of excess triethylamine.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Pyridoazepine Scaffold via Rhodium-Catalyzed Ring Expansion and Nitroacetamide Condensation
Problem_Description: Alkylation of pyridoazepine 9 with methyl iodide gave poor selectivity when using potassium carbonate, which afforded predominantly N‑methylation (>95:5 N‑ vs O‑methylation).
Solution_Description: Silver carbonate was employed as the base in dichloromethane, which delivered high O‑methylation selectivity (83 % yield of 8) with negligible N‑alkylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The selective O‑methylation reaction affording 8 was accomplished in dichloromethane with methyl iodide and silver carbonate base, whereas potassium carbonate afforded almost exclusively the N‑methylation (>95:5).”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: The original first‑generation route used commercial L‑(−)‑fucose (1) which costs ~$1000 kg⁻¹ and is difficult to procure in metric‑ton quantities, making large‑scale production impractical.
Solution_Description: The authors switched the starting material to L‑(−)‑rhamnose (7), which is commercially available at multi‑ton scale for ~$70 kg⁻¹, enabling a more economical and scalable synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states: “procuring requisite quantities of L‑(−)‑fucose was an impediment toward scale up… L‑(−) rhamnose… is an attractive substitute given its availability at metric‑ton scale and potential for significant attenuation of the production costs ($70 kg⁻¹ for 7 versus $1000 kg⁻¹ for 1).”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: During the TEMPO/NaOCl oxidation of protected rhamnose (9 → 10) the reaction stalled at ~70 % conversion because the pH dropped sharply in the un‑buffered biphasic system, leading to inconsistent conversion.
Solution_Description: A buffer (0.3 equiv sodium bicarbonate) was added to maintain the reaction pH between 8–9, which restored full conversion and improved product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Excerpt: “the reaction stalled at ∼70 % conversion… an initial rapid drop in pH was observed in the absence of a buffer… buffering the reaction with 0.3 equiv of sodium bicarbonide maintained an optimum pH range (8–9) and induced complete conversion with enhanced product purity.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: The bromination of intermediate 13 under the conditions used for the analogous fucose substrate caused extensive decomposition of the substrate with no detectable bromide product.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced catalytic Zn(II) bromide together with stoichiometric acetyl bromide, which allowed smooth bromination of 13 to give bromide 14 in good yield, avoiding decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: Excerpt: “subjecting 13 to the same conditions led to extensive decomposition… Fortunately, use of catalytic Zn(II) bromide in conjunction with stoichiometric acetyl bromide effected the desired transformation in good yields.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: The Zn‑mediated elimination of bromide 14 to the glycal 4 gave only ~30 % isolated product together with three major side products (15, 16, 17).
Solution_Description: Screens of halide salts identified NH₄I as the optimal additive, increasing the proportion of desired product 4. Acetonitrile was selected as the solvent that consistently delivered the highest purity and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Excerpt: “addition of NaI and Zn in EtOAc furnished 4 in relatively high yield… a subsequent screening of halide salts divulged that ammonium halides indeed enhanced the production of 4… (NH₄I displayed precedence over its chloride and bromide counterparts).” and “we chose MeCN as the optimal solvent for further optimizations.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: When scaling the Zn‑mediated elimination to 2 g of 14 in an EasyMax reactor, the zinc suspension clumped in EtOAc, causing poor mixing, reduced product purity (from ~90 % to 49 %) and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The stirrer blade was reversed (upside‑down) to improve suspension homogeneity; zinc flakes (140‑325 mesh) were identified as the most effective form of Zn, yielding 83 % purity at scale.
Supporting_Evidence: Excerpt: “significant drop in the purity profile… attributing this to inefficient mixing, we reversed the pitch blade (upside down) to enhance the homogeneity of zinc suspension… the best results were obtained from Zn flakes (83 % purity).”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: Silica‑gel column chromatography of the final glycal 4 caused discoloration and decomposition, resulting in lower than expected isolated yields (≈50 %).
Solution_Description: The reaction was quenched, the solvent exchanged to EtOAc, and the organic layer washed twice with saturated NH₄Cl and brine before isolation, avoiding column chromatography and preserving product integrity, giving a 70 % overall yield over the last two steps.
Supporting_Evidence: Excerpt: “silica‑gel column chromatography… observed signs of decomposition… To avoid decomposition, we quenched the reaction before purification by exchanging the solvent to EtOAc and washing the organics twice with saturated ammonium chloride and brine… the resulting residue … furnished 4 in 70 % yield (over two steps).”

Paper Title: An Alternative Route to the Anticancer Agent: 2‑Fluorofucose from Readily Available L‑(−)Rhamnose and Mechanistic Insights into a Zinc/Ammonium Iodide-Mediated Elimination Reaction
Problem_Description: The initial oxidation step using Swern or PCC protocols required extended reaction times and generated hazardous by‑products, making them unsuitable for large‑scale production.

Paper Title: Preparation of Enantiopure 3‑Aminopiperidine and 3‑Aminoazepane Derivatives from Ornithine and Lysine. Consecutive Syntheses of Pharmacologically Active Analogs, Such as Besifloxacin
Problem_Description: Grinding the crude trityl‑protected lactam 21b with diethyl ether gave a very low “solving ability”, leading to poor isolation yields and requiring additional column chromatography.

Solution_Description: Liquid‑assisted grinding (LAG) was employed, first with a manual pestle and then with a planetary ball‑mill, which dramatically improved the overall isolated yield to 94 %.  Methyl‑tert‑butyl ether was also evaluated as a safer grinding solvent with comparable results.

Paper Title: Preparation of Enantiopure 3‑Aminopiperidine and 3‑Aminoazepane Derivatives from Ornithine and Lysine. Consecutive Syntheses of Pharmacologically Active Analogs, Such as Besifloxacin
Problem_Description: Using sodium carbonate as the base for lysine‑derived cyclization gave only 49 % isolated yield because the generated water partially opened the lactam at the elevated temperature.
Solution_Description: The dihydrochloride was neutralized with NaOH pellets (2 equiv) at 0 °C, the free amino ester was extracted with MTBE and directly cyclized in dry methanol without any additive; the reaction proceeded to completion after 32 h reflux, affording 78 % overall yield and avoiding lactam hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only 49 % of 22b was obtained … we assume that the two equivalents of water … partially opened the lactam.”; “The free amino ester could be subjected to lactam formation in dry methanol without any additive. … the amino ester cyclization was only completed after refluxing the reaction mixture for 32 h … enantiopure 22b was isolated in 78 % overall yield.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Enantiopure 3‑Aminopiperidine and 3‑Aminoazepane Derivatives from Ornithine and Lysine. Consecutive Syntheses of Pharmacologically Active Analogs, Such as Besifloxacin
Problem_Description: Cyclization of the lysine methyl‑ester dihydrochloride with sodium methanolate gave incomplete conversion after 4 h reflux, producing significant side‑products.
Solution_Description: The procedure was changed to neutralize the dihydrochloride with NaOH pellets, extract the free amino ester, and then cyclize the ester in dry methanol (no added base).  This eliminated the side‑product formation and gave a reproducible 78 % isolated yield after 32 h reflux.
Supporting_Evidence: “According to Boyle’s protocol, ester dihydrochloride was treated with 2.0 equiv of sodium methanolate … but the conversion to the lactam was incomplete.”; “The free amino ester could be subjected to lactam formation in dry methanol without any additive … enantiopure 22b was isolated in 78 % overall yield.”

Problem_Description: Charging all components together produced a slurry‑to‑slurry process that gave inconsistent M/P ratios and occasional co‑crystallization of the racemate, indicating poor mixing and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: A solution‑to‑slurry protocol was implemented: full dissolution of rac‑1 and (+)-DBTA in 2‑MeTHF at 75 °C, anti‑solvent addition of heptane, seeding, and controlled cooling, which gave >99.9 : 0.1 M/P and robust performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “The experiments executed to this point had been performed by charging rac‑1, (+)-DBTA, and 2‑MeTHF/heptane all at once, which resulted in slurry‑to‑slurry resolutions.”; “It was hypothesized that adjusting the experimental protocol to proceed through a solution‑to‑slurry process may improve the resolution efficiency… resulted in slurry formation… providing a M/P ratio of >99.9:0.1.”

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 1: Development of a Classical Resolution to Prepare an Atropisomerically Pure Sotorasib Intermediate
Problem_Description: Trace amounts of the opposite enantiomer of DBTA ((‑)-DBTA) severely degraded the M/P ratio, introducing variability in product purity.
Solution_Description: A specification was set limiting (‑)-DBTA impurity to ≤0.10 % HPLC area (≥99.8 % ee) to maintain a consistent M/P ratio ≥1994 : 6.
Supporting_Evidence: “As little as 0.10 HPLC area % of (‑)-DBTA relative to (+)-DBTA impacted the selectivity… led us to limit the maximum amount of (‑)-DBTA to not more than 0.10 LC area % (99.8 % ee) to ensure that the required M/P ratio… is consistently met.”

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 1: Development of a Classical Resolution to Prepare an Atropisomerically Pure Sotorasib Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original slurry composition caused fouling and poor flowability during large‑scale operations.
Solution_Description: The volume of 2‑MeTHF was increased from 7.0 L kg⁻¹ to 8.0 L kg⁻¹ and heptane reduced from 2.0 L kg⁻¹ to 1.0 L kg⁻¹, improving slurry physical properties and preventing fouling; seed temperature was lowered to 45 °C to avoid seed dissolution.
Supporting_Evidence: “The amount of 2‑MeTHF was increased from 7.0 to 8.0 L kg, which improved the physical properties of the slurry and prevented fouling. Additionally, the solvent composition at the seed point was adjusted to reduce the heptane content from 2.0 to 1.0 L kg, which would allow for full redissolution via heat cycle if required. … the seed crystal charge temperature was correspondingly reduced to 45 °C to prevent dissolution of the seeds.”

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 2: Leveraging a High-Temperature Thermal Racemization to Recycle the Classical Resolution Waste Stream
Problem_Description: The classical resolution of the sotorasib intermediate generates only the desired atropisomer (M‑1) at a theoretical maximum of 50 % overall yield, discarding the undesired P‑1 enantiomer as waste.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team developed a high‑temperature (>300 °C) continuous‑flow racemization process to recycle the P‑1 waste stream back to racemic‑1, followed by crystallization directly from the reaction stream. This required a new reaction pathway (racemization), selection of a non‑polar solvent (anisole) with low decomposition, an intermediate isolation step to remove the excess (+)-DBTA, inverse addition of the mother liquor to a basic aqueous phase, and a plug‑flow reactor (PFR) with high‑pressure capability and precise temperature control. Concentration and flow were tuned (10 wt % feeds, 11–12 min residence) to avoid clogging, and safety measures (ARC/DSC studies, rupture disc, BPR, interlocks) were implemented.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Inherent to this approach is a theoretical maximum yield of 50%, with the undesired atropisomer (P‑1) being discarded with the supernatant.', 'The high activation barrier to atropisomer interconversion ... required the processing equipment capable of achieving extreme operating conditions, not readily available at traditional batch manufacturing facilities.', 'An aqueous potassium carbonate (K2CO3) proved to be the optimal solution for removal of (+)-DBTA ... inverse addition—slow charge of the mother liquor to an agitated vessel containing 20 wt % aq. K2CO3 ensured a high concentration of base relative to (+)-DBTA and additional control against precipitation of a monopotassium DBTA salt.', 'A small‑scale PFR was built ... a 90 mL tube‑in‑tube heat exchanger ... the reactor design would be capable of effecting racemization of P‑1 with a mean residence time (V/Q) of only 11 min.', 'Solvent choice had an impact on the overall product purity ... anisole was deemed optimal because of its ability to solubilize P‑1, low cost, and favorable safety profile.', 'The high reactor thermal mass ... provided additional confidence in the safe operation of this process.', 'Insulation was insufficient, resulting in the PFR operating at 290 °C rather than the TCU setpoint of 315 °C, decreasing conversion.']

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 2: Leveraging a High-Temperature Thermal Racemization to Recycle the Classical Resolution Waste Stream
Problem_Description: High‑boiling polar aprotic solvents (NMP, DMI, sulfolane) caused significant hydrolytic decomposition of the substrate (2‑chloropyridine moiety) and gave poor solubility for the racemic product, limiting kinetic studies.
Solution_Description: Switching to non‑polar solvents, particularly anisole, eliminated hydrolytic decomposition and provided sufficient solubility for P‑1 while keeping the racemic product less soluble, facilitating crystallization directly from the reaction stream. Concentrations were adjusted (10 wt % feeds) to balance solubility and avoid precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: ['An initial survey of high‑boiling‑point polar aprotic solvents resulted in significant decomposition of the substrate, primarily through hydrolysis of the 2‑chloropyridine moiety.', 'Use of high‑boiling‑point non‑polar solvents delivered similar rates of racemization and minimized greatly the extent of decomposition.', 'In particular, use of diphenyl ether as the reaction solvent at 250 °C for 4 h resulted in nearly complete racemization with retention of achiral purity.', 'The poor solubility of both P‑1 and rac‑1 limited the utility of this solvent for kinetic studies.', 'Solvent choice had an impact on the overall product purity through the course of thermal racemization. A survey of additional nonpolar solvents was conducted, and anisole was deemed optimal because of its ability to solubilize P‑1, low cost, and favorable safety profile.', 'The solubility of rac‑1 in anisole was significantly lower than that of P‑1, encouraging a convenient isolation approach.']

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 2: Leveraging a High-Temperature Thermal Racemization to Recycle the Classical Resolution Waste Stream
Problem_Description: Operating the racemization at >300 °C with volatile solvents (2‑MeTHF, heptane) and high vapor pressures posed safety risks, including potential runaway reactions and pressure buildup.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous plug‑flow reactor constructed from stainless‑steel tube‑in‑tube heat exchangers was selected, allowing precise temperature and pressure control (≥20 bar). Safety hardware (rupture disc, knockout pot, back‑pressure regulator, interlocked solenoid valve, emergency stop) and rigorous thermal hazard assessments (DSC, ARC) were implemented to mitigate runaway and pressure hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The high activation barrier ... highlighted the requirement for processing equipment capable of achieving extreme operating conditions, not readily available at traditional batch manufacturing facilities.', 'An ARC experiment ... exhibited a self‑heating event with an onset of 347 °C and an accompanying pressure increase up to 199 bar, which is the system limit.', 'The higher phi factor afforded by the HTF in a jacketed tubular reactor also differentiates this type of reactor from other methods of heating tubular reactors such as direct electric heating or ovens.', 'The flow reactor system was further assessed using methodology described in the American Petroleum Institute’s API 521 standard.', 'Hazard conditions and mitigation strategies ... include rupture disc, interlock, knockout pot, NC solenoid valve wired to e‑stop, attended operation, and temperature control interlocks.']

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 2: Leveraging a High-Temperature Thermal Racemization to Recycle the Classical Resolution Waste Stream
Problem_Description: In the pilot‑scale flow system, insufficient insulation caused the reactor temperature to drop to ~290 °C, leading to longer residence times and variable conversion; also, precipitation of rac‑1 risked clogging the tubing.
Solution_Description: Improved reactor insulation and heat‑tracing were planned to maintain target temperature (315 °C). Feed concentration (10 wt % in anisole) and flow rates were tuned (80 g min⁻¹) to achieve the required residence time (≈11 min) while avoiding precipitation. Additional heat exchangers were considered to integrate heating and cooling, reducing thermal losses.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Heat loss was observed which resulted in the PFR operating at 290 °C rather than the TCU setpoint of 315 °C.', 'The decreased reactor temperature resulted in an overall decrease in reaction conversion as highlighted by the first data point in Figure 8.', 'The apparent mean residence time (V/Q) was increased … allowing for greater conversion at the lower operating temperature.', 'The set of experiments ... demonstrated that this reactor design would be capable of effecting racemization of P‑1 with a mean residence time (V/Q) of only 11 min.', 'A 10 wt % solution of P‑1 in anisole was fed … to avoid potential clogging from premature crystallization of rac‑1 upon cooling.']

Paper Title: Axial Chirality in the Sotorasib Drug Substance, Part 2: Leveraging a High-Temperature Thermal Racemization to Recycle the Classical Resolution Waste Stream
Problem_Description: Overall process yield was reduced by ~20 % due to losses during the downstream crystallization step and ~2 % loss from thermal decomposition of the atropisomer in the PFR.
Solution_Description: The crystallization protocol was refined: a slurry at the eutectic point was prepared, filtered, and the supernatant diluted to the desired 10 wt % feed; seeds of rac‑1 were added downstream to promote controlled crystallization. Process throughput and solvent handling were optimized to reduce hold‑up and improve mass balance.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Only 2 % yield loss is associated with decomposition of atropisomer 1 in the PFR; the bulk of remaining mass balance (ca. 20 %) is associated with losses to the crystallization, which remains an opportunity for optimization.', 'A 17 wt % slurry in anisole was prepared, allowed to equilibrate to the eutectic point, and filtered to deliver a supernatant with high enantiomeric purity (99:1 P/M) and solids of rac‑1 (50:50 P/M).', 'The supernatant could then be diluted to the desired concentration (10 wt %) and fed through the PFR while the solids were used as seeds in the downstream crystallization.', 'The end‑to‑end workflow … resulted in 1.43 kg (77 % yield) of rac‑1 as a crystalline solid with 99.2 % achiral purity.']

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: The neat reaction of N‑methylimidazole (NMI) with n‑butyl bromide produced an extremely viscous reaction mixture (η ≈ 1486 mPa·s at 298 K), causing irregular flow rates and reactor blockages, and gave low conversion/yield.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent stream of MeCN was added to lower the viscosity and improve the miscibility of the reaction mixture, restoring smooth flow and enabling higher yields (up to 97 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “We began our study targeting [BMIM]Br and attempting neat conditions but quickly observed remarkably high viscosity (η = 1486 mPa·s at 298 K)… which led to irregular flow rates and reactor blockages.”; “we opted to use an additional solvent stream of MeCN.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: During the reaction the imidazolium product was immiscible with the alkylating agent, producing a biphasic mixture that at low flow rates formed sinking dense droplets, causing CSTR‑like back‑mixing and occasional precipitation of dicationic salts that could block the reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The helical tube geometry (Dean vortices) and operating at higher flow rates (>5 mL min⁻¹) were used to keep the phases well mixed (plug‑flow regime) and prevent droplet sinking and solid buildup.
Supporting_Evidence: “The helical geometry of the reactor tube enhances mixing… At low flow velocity… sinking… In the low flow rate CSTR‑like conditions, severe back‑mixing takes place…"; “Using 4 mm ID helical tubes, the reaction mixture was completely carried forward at flow rates >5 mL min⁻¹ where at flow rates <4 mL min⁻¹, sinking droplets could be observed.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Dielectric property changes as the reaction progressed caused the resonant frequency of the single‑mode cavity to shift, leading to uncontrolled frequency switching, reduced heating efficiency, and temperature drops during constant‑power operation.
Solution_Description: A thin PTFE “frequency adjustor” tube was placed around the helical tube to shift one of the absorption bands out of the operating window, stabilising the resonant frequency and improving heating efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: “To avoid this situation of uncontrolled frequency switching, a thin PTFE ‘frequency adjustor’ tube was placed around the outside the helical tube which shifted one of the absorption bands outside the operating frequency window.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: The temperature‑control (auto‑temperature) mode caused local overheating and pulsations at low flow rates, leading to side‑reactions (E2 elimination, formation of NMI·HBr) and a drop in product yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was switched to an isocratic (constant‑power) mode, where the same microwave power is applied continuously, providing more uniform energy input and eliminating temperature spikes, thereby improving reproducibility and yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “As a work‑around, isocratic (constant) power operation was evaluated… The constant power (isocratic) mode … offers potentially more balanced steady‑state conditions…”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Secondary alkyl bromides gave poor conversions because competing E2 elimination pathways were favored at the high temperatures required for MW flow, resulting in yields ≤30 %.
Solution_Description: The study focused on primary alkyl bromides, iodides, activated chlorides and sulfonate esters, which delivered near‑quantitative yields under the same MW flow conditions, while secondary alkyl electrophiles were avoided or used only under more forcing conditions with limited success.
Supporting_Evidence: “Branched and 2° alkyl bromides reacted poorly… more forcing conditions were not applicable for the 2° electrophiles since E2 elimination was promoted, and product yields could not exceed 30 %.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Sulfonate‑ester alkylating agents (e.g., isoprenyl tosylate, ethoxyethyl methylate) were intrinsically unstable, decomposing violently when concentrated in vacuo above rt and discoloring during prolonged heating.
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow MW approach minimized the residence time and the amount of material exposed to high temperature, preventing bulk decomposition; additionally, reactions were performed at controlled temperatures (≤200 °C) with immediate cooling to avoid thermal runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: “Neat isoprenyl tosylate violently decomposed after several minutes of concentrating in vacuo at 80 °C… Thermal decomposition of sulfonate esters presents a grave concern for a high scale batch alkylations, the risk of which is dramatically mitigated using the MW continuous flow approach.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: The crude imidazolium products were yellow‑discolored due to minor side‑products formed from overheating, which is undesirable for electrochemical and photophysical applications.
Solution_Description: A simple work‑up involving filtration through alumina and activated charcoal (3 h, 60 °C) removed the coloration, delivering >99 % pure product; for solids, a single recrystallisation from MeCN/EtOAc was sufficient.
Supporting_Evidence: “A standard procedure… of treating the received mixture diluted with MeCN through alumina and activated charcoal… was sufficient to remove yellow discoloration… and the product obtained… was afforded in >99 % purity.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: When the reaction mixture was pre‑heated with recirculated MeCN, the presence of multiple MW resonance bands caused the system to switch between “solvent” and “reactant” bands, leading to unstable temperature control.
Solution_Description: The frequency adjustor tube (PTFE) eliminated the competing resonance band, keeping the system locked on the desired frequency and stabilising the temperature profile.
Supporting_Evidence: Same as problem 3 evidence above.

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Alkylation of benzothiazole (BZT) with n‑butyl bromide failed even at 200 °C, giving <0.5 % yield because of poor miscibility and phase separation.
Solution_Description: Switching to the more polar methyl benzenesulfonate (a sulfonate ester) as the electrophile and using a 3 mm ID helical tube (higher flow velocity) enabled efficient mixing and gave 95 % yield in <3 min at 210 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “Switching to the more potent methyl benzenesulfonate and a 3 mm ID helical tube… provided the benzothiazolium salt in 95 % yield after 3.0 min at 210 °C.”

Paper Title: Tunable Microwave Flow System for Scalable Synthesis of Alkyl Imidazolium-type Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Reactions using 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane produced a mixture of mono‑ and bis‑adducts; at higher temperature the bis‑imidazolium dication precipitated inside the reactor, causing blockages.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 200 °C improved the mono‑adduct yield (81 % total) and shifted the isomer ratio, while using larger helical tubes prevented precipitation by maintaining higher flow velocity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The temperature drop … The distribution of isomers… was unaffected by temperature. High temperature inside the reactor is expected to decrease selectivity… Using pure CHCl₃ solvent … prevented dication precipitation.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: When exploring acylating agents for the diacylation of 3,4‑diaminopyridine (1), oxalic acid/HCl and oxalyl chloride gave low or inconsistent conversions, whereas only diethyl oxalate afforded acceptable conversion and yield.
Solution_Description: The authors selected diethyl oxalate as the acylating reagent; using this reagent together with a temperature of 100 ± 10 °C and higher concentration gave the highest in‑process control (IPC) conversion and a 74.8 % isolated yield on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: The diacylation of commercially available 3,4‑diaminopyridine 1, we explored diethyl oxalate, oxalic acid with aqueous HCl, and oxalyl chloride as potential acylating agents. Of these three reagents, diethyl oxalate provided the most promising results by IPC (in‑process control).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: The POCl₃/DBF chlorination of intermediate 2 to give dichloropyrido‑[3,4‑b]‑pyrazine 3 is strongly exothermic; uncontrolled addition can raise the temperature above 70 °C, risking side‑product formation and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: DBF was added slowly at 65 °C while monitoring temperature; POCl₃ and DBF were used in controlled stoichiometry (5‑6 vol POCl₃, 3 vol DBF) and the reaction was quenched carefully to keep temperature ≤70 °C.
Supporting_Evidence:
The addition of DBF at 65 °C led to the highest assay purity and yields; due to the exothermic nature of this reaction, DBF was added slowly to the mixture in order to avoid an increase in temperature above 70 °C.
Larger quantities of POCl₃ (5 to 6 volumes) and DBF (3 volumes) gave the best results … the excess of this reagent had to be quenched carefully.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: During the first nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) on dichloropyrido‑[3,4‑b]‑pyrazine 4, several solvents gave biphasic mixtures or sticky precipitates, complicating work‑up and causing loss of material.
Solution_Description: DMAc was selected as the reaction solvent because it gave >82 % conversion, the highest assay yield, and a free‑flowing solid that could be precipitated and filtered easily.
Supporting_Evidence:
While most of these conditions yielded similar conversions in excess of 82 % (HPLC area %), DMAc turned out to be the solvent of choice due to the highest assay yield and the facile workup following the chemical reaction, resulting in a free‑flowing solid.
A simple dilution of the reaction mixture with CH₃CN and water at ambient temperature led to precipitation of the desired product, … other solvents such as CH₂Cl₂ led to a biphasic mixture that would have required an extractive step.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: Residual water (>1 % w/w) in the DMAc reaction mixture slowed the SNAr rate and promoted hydrolysis of the starting material back to intermediate 2, leading to lower conversion and variable impurity profiles.
Solution_Description: Water content was strictly limited to ≤0.1 % on scale‑up; the reaction was performed under dry conditions to maintain high conversion and suppress hydrolytic side‑reactions.
Supporting_Evidence:
We observed that a residual water content of up to 1 % (w/w) was tolerated in this reaction, but higher water concentrations slowed down the reaction kinetics and led to increased hydrolysis of the starting material back to compound 2.
Therefore, on a larger scale, it was ensured that the water content did not exceed 0.1 %.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: The second SNAr (Cl → amine) required heating to 60 °C in DMSO with KF; elevated temperature was needed to avoid accumulation of starting material but DMSO is thermally unstable above ~180 °C, posing safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was set to ~60 °C (well below the DMSO degradation threshold) and maintained for 24 h; temperature limits were enforced (≤65 °C) to ensure safety while achieving >80 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: The mixture was heated to ~60 °C and stirred for 24 h. For safety reasons, the higher temperature was selected to minimize accumulation of starting materials and any potential exothermic effects. However, it was ensured that the reaction temperature never exceeded 65 °C since it has been documented that DMSO is not stable at high temperatures (around 180 °C), constituting a potential safety hazard.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of CVN424, an Inverse Agonist of the GPR6 Receptor
Problem_Description: On the 322.6 g scale, the final one‑pot acetylation/hydrogenation gave only 23 % conversion with substantial starting material and side‑products; the heterogeneous Pd/C suspension showed poor mass‑transfer, leading to inconsistent results.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mechanical stirring at 300 rpm under 5 atm H₂ at 25 ± 5 °C was implemented, dramatically improving conversion and yield (up to 92 % IPC). After reaction, a silica‑thiol scavenger removed residual Pd (41 ppm → ≈12 ppm). Temperature and pressure were carefully controlled to avoid exotherms.
Supporting_Evidence:
Mechanical stirring of the heterogeneous reaction mixture improved the rate of conversion and the yield dramatically. After several attempts, we found that mechanical stirring (300 rpm) under 5 atm H₂ at 25 ± 5 °C provided the most consistent results.
The material was treated with a metal scavenger (silica thiol) to remove potential traces of Pd from the final CVN424 drug substance … the scavenger treatment reduced the Pd content from 41.3 to ∼12 ppm.
The autoclave was kept at 25 ± 5 °C and purged with N₂ three times followed by H₂ (0.5–0.6 MPa) three times… the mixture was stirred for 16 h at 25 ± 5 °C while maintaining the H₂ pressure at 0.4–0.5 MPa.

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Previously reported racemic and chiral‑auxiliary routes gave low overall yields (≈22 % for the racemic approach and 27‑29 % for the chiral‑auxiliary approach) and unsatisfactory stereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: A dual‑chiral‑auxiliary intramolecular double‑stereodifferentiation pathway was devised, delivering the key intermediate with a total isolated yield of 56.2 % over seven steps and >99 % enantiomeric excess.
Supporting_Evidence: ["overall yield around 22%"; "...overall yield of 27–29%"; "selectivity and overall yield of the known chiral auxiliary approaches were not satisfying"; "intramolecular double stereodifferentiation methodology was developed"; "process ... total yield of 56.2% over seven steps"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) gave the highest assay for the lactam but its volatility and strong odor made it unsuitable for pilot‑scale handling.
Solution_Description: Cyclohexane was adopted as the reaction solvent; it provided comparable conversion and purity while offering a low boiling point and high water‑immiscibility, improving safety and work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["MTBE successfully provided product 17 with the highest purity... the volatility and smell of MTBE made it unsuitable for pilot‑scale manipulation"; "cyclohexane, which was able to deliver comparable results... was preferred for its low boiling point and high water immiscibility"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Formation of under‑reaction by‑product acid 18 and intermolecular dimer 19 reduced conversion; acid 18 was suppressed only by increasing DMF loading, while dimer 19 appeared at low temperature (10 °C).
Solution_Description: Increasing DMF to 1.2–1.4 equiv suppressed acid 18, and raising the reaction temperature (30 °C) minimized dimer 19 formation, giving a cleaner reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: ["acid 18 was presumably an under‑reaction byproduct... the formation of acid 18 was also suppressed by the increased loading of DMF"; "Intermolecular dimerized 19 was observed when the reaction was cooled to 10 °C. The content of 19 decreased as the temperature increased"; "1.2–1.4 equiv was regarded as the optimal dosage of DMF"; "temperature increased, implying the intramolecular ... prevailed over the intermolecular version"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Strong bases (NaOH, DBU) caused hydrolysis of the hydrogenation substrate, while moderate bases gave sub‑optimal enantioselectivity.
Solution_Description: Pyridine was selected as a mild, non‑nucleophilic base, delivering the best selectivity (92 % desired isomer) without hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: ["treatment of a base as strong as NaOH led to hydrolysis of the substrate"; "moderate bases, organic or inorganic, tended to offer a selectivity that is less than satisfactory"; "pyridine was found to provide the best result by delivering a 92% formation of the desired isomer"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Using 10 % Pd/C for hydrogenation increased catalyst cost; reducing the loading to 5 % Pd/C maintained performance, but further reduction slowed the reaction and lowered product formation.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was optimized to 5 % Pd/C, preserving conversion while halving catalyst expense.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Replacement of 10% Pd/C with 5% Pd/C gave similar results, providing a possibility to reduce cost"; "further catalyst minimization led to a slower reaction, which resulted in a decreased formation of both desired and undesired products"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Very concentrated reaction mixtures (low solvent volume) adversely affected selectivity; overly dilute conditions also reduced selectivity.
Solution_Description: A solvent volume of 4–6 V was identified as optimal for industrial handling, balancing mixing, selectivity and throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ["lowering the concentration of the reaction mixture by increasing the solvent volume had a contrary effect on the selectivity"; "Considering manipulation convenience on an industrial scale, 4–6 V of solvent would be the most suitable for reagent mixing and mixture transferring"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: Lithium aluminium hydride (LAH) is highly reactive, combustible, and requires extreme caution for storage and handling on a large scale.
Solution_Description: The reduction was switched to a milder NaBH₄–BF₃ system, which delivered comparable yields without the safety hazards associated with LAH.
Supporting_Evidence: ["LAH ... rather unfavorable, especially on an industrial scale, for its high reactivity and combustibility. Both storage and manipulation of LAH require extreme caution"; "NaBH₄–BF₃ met our needs by delivering satisfying outcomes"]

Paper Title: Efficient Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Moxifloxacin Via Intramolecular Double Stereodifferentiation
Problem_Description: During the NaBH₄–BF₃ reduction, a stable amine‑borane complex (compound 23) formed and could not be removed by aqueous work‑up, reducing the isolated yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The amount of BF₃·THF was limited (≤3 equiv) and NaBH₄ was used in excess (>2.25 equiv) to suppress formation of 23; addition temperature was kept ≤0 °C to keep the impurity below 2 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ["amine‑borane complex (23) ... could not be washed away by acidic or basic aqueous solutions"; "the more BF₃·THF it charged, the higher percentage of 23 was formed"; "excess of NaBH₄ (>2.25 equiv) was observed to suppress the generation of amine‑borane 23"; "keeping the adding temperature at no higher than 0 °C was vital to control the content of 23 by at most 2%"]

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Synthesis of Lorazepam
Problem_Description: The bromo intermediate (14) and the cyclization reagents (NH₄X salts) showed poor solubility in many organic solvents, leading to precipitation and clogging of the micro‑reactor chips during continuous‑flow operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors performed extensive solubility screens and selected 2‑MeTHF for the N‑acylation step and ACN/H₂O mixtures for the cyclization, increased the equivalents of NH₄Br to improve its solubility, and switched to larger‑diameter PFA tubing with temperature‑controlled T‑mixers to prevent solid buildup.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The cyclization reaction was performed in ACN:H₂O mixture … due to the higher solubility of NH₄Br in these solvents.” (sec 3.2) 
 • “We observed a clog … where the NH₄Br/NH₄OH feed mixed with the step 1 output … crystallization of intermediate 14 inside the staggered oriented ridge mixer.” (sec 3.2.1) 
 • “We then moved to PFA tubing (internal diameter 0.726 mm) for both steps… it was critical to hold the T‑mixer outlet at higher temperature (110 or 140 °C) to achieve a consistent flow without any clogging.” (sec 3.2.1) 
 • “We performed a 2² full‑factorial design … The most efficient reaction condition was obtained at 20 °C and 10 min using 2‑MeTHF as solvent.” (sec 3.1) 
 • “The bromo acetyl chloride stoichiometry was increased from 1.25 to 1.5 equiv … leading to 95 % 14.” (sec 3.1 Table 1)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Synthesis of Lorazepam
Problem_Description: The direct α‑hydroxylation route using air/oxidants caused evaporation of DMSO and generated an uncontrolled exotherm, resulting in by‑product formation and safety concerns.

Problem_Description: The three‑component 1,3‑dipolar cycloaddition of nitrostyrene 5, l‑serine and 6‑chloroisatin gave the desired spirooxindole 6a in only 30 % isolated yield, while the regio‑isomer 6b was obtained in 44 % yield.  The modest conversion of 6a limited the overall material efficiency of the route.
Solution_Description: The authors exploited the different solubilities of 6a and 6b in dichloromethane.  After removal of solvent, partial evaporation of DCM caused 6a to precipitate as a solid that could be filtered off, providing the pure product without chromatographic purification.  The mother‑liquid was then chromatographed to recover 6b.  This straightforward precipitation‑based isolation replaces a low‑yielding, multi‑step work‑up with a one‑step solid‑formation step, improving material throughput while still delivering the desired scaffold.
Supporting_Evidence: “...precipitation from dichloromethane provided exclusively pure spirooxindole 6a with acceptable 30 % yield.”; “Purification of the mother liquor yielded the regioisomer 6b in 44 % yield…”; “Especially on large scale effortless separation of isomers greatly ensures the feasibility of a synthetic route.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of MDM2-p53 Inhibitor BI-0282 via a Dipolar Cycloaddition and Late-Stage Davis–Beirut Reaction
Problem_Description: On multigram scale the reaction mixture contains both 6a and the regio‑isomer 6b, making it difficult to isolate the desired product without extensive chromatography or loss of material.
Solution_Description: By adding the crude reaction mixture to dichloromethane and allowing selective precipitation of 6a, the authors achieved a simple solid‑liquid separation.  The remaining solution (mother‑liquid) was processed by normal‑phase column chromatography to isolate 6b.  This solvent‑based phase‑separation strategy eliminates the need for large‑scale column chromatography for the major product and streamlines the purification workflow.
Supporting_Evidence: “...precipitation from dichloromethane provided exclusively pure spirooxindole 6a…”; “The filtrate was purified by normal phase column chromatography using cyclohexane and ethyl acetate as solvents to obtain isomer 6b…”; “Effortless separation of isomers… ensures feasibility on large scale.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of MDM2-p53 Inhibitor BI-0282 via a Dipolar Cycloaddition and Late-Stage Davis–Beirut Reaction
Problem_Description: The nitro‑group reduction step required hydrogen gas at 8 bar pressure in the presence of Raney nickel, a potentially hazardous combination on scale due to flammability of H₂ and the pyrophoric nature of Raney nickel.
Solution_Description: The reduction was performed at ambient temperature (25 °C) in a pressure‑rated reactor, limiting the exotherm while maintaining high conversion (92 % over two steps).  Conducting the reaction at room temperature reduced thermal risk, and the use of a sealed pressure vessel provided a controlled environment for handling H₂ safely.
Supporting_Evidence: “Crude intermediate 7 is dissolved … treated with a catalytic amount of Raney nickel… The reaction vessel is pressurized with dihydrogen (8 bar) and the reaction mixture stirred for 24 h.”; “The final step … proceeded smoothly at room temperature in very good yields.”

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: The initial batch reactions suffered from incomplete dissolution of d‑fructose in the reaction medium, leading to the formation of humins, reduced sugar conversion and inconsistent HMF yields.
Solution_Description: A biphasic DMC/TEAB solvent system was introduced (SOLVENT CHANGE) to fully dissolve d‑fructose and extract HMF; the acidic resin Purolite CT275DR was selected (CATALYST OPTIMIZATION) for its high acidity and accessible pores; catalyst loading was reduced to 5 wt % (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE) and TEAB to 10 wt % without loss of selectivity; the reaction time was shortened to 2 h (REACTION TIME CHANGE) at 110 °C (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION) to avoid side‑product formation; a custom crystallization protocol using diethyl ether (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE) gave pure HMF crystals; the HMF‑rich oil was telescoped directly to BHMF by NaBH₄ reduction (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The synergic action of TEAB and DMC, acting as co‑solvents, allowed the complete dissolution of D‑fructose…” (solubility solution) 
• “Purolite CT275DR proved to be the best catalyst… high acidity… large average pore diameter” (catalyst optimisation) 
• “Trials carried out using lower amounts of Purolite CT275DR i.e., 5 % wt., showed an increase in HMF selectivity” (stoichiometry change) 
• “The amount of TEAB could be reduced to 10 % wt. without affecting HMF selectivity” (stoichiometry change) 
• “Reactions performed in an autoclave for 2 h at 110 °C” (reaction time) 
• “Tests conducted at higher temperatures (up to 150 °C) produced similar or worse results… side reactions and product degradation” (temperature optimisation) 
• “A custom‑made crystallization process… diethyl ether proved to be the most efficient one” (new purification) 
• “The brown oil was added to the residual crystallization solution… subjected to reduction by adding NaBH₄… BHMF was isolated” (telescope directly) 
• “To have a complete evaluation … the extracting solvent (DMC) and the workup solvent (ethyl acetate) can be easily recovered and reused” (solvent change/recovery).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: Isolation of pure HMF from the reaction mixture was difficult because the crude product formed a viscous oil that was partly insoluble in common crystallisation solvents, leading to low isolated yields (~50 %).
Solution_Description: A bespoke crystallisation protocol was developed using diethyl ether (and ether/hexane mixtures) to selectively precipitate HMF crystals while the remaining HMF‑rich oil was kept for downstream reduction to BHMF.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A custom‑made crystallization process… diethyl ether proved to be the most efficient one; the use of diethyl ether/hexane and ethyl acetate/hexane mixtures also led to reasonable amounts of crystalline HMF.” (new purification) 
• “~30 % of the crude oil was insoluble in Et₂O… the soluble fraction was left to crystallize… pure HMF in ca 50 % yield.” (problem description).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: Earlier HMF syntheses required long reaction times (up to 168 h) or multiple steps, decreasing throughput and increasing cost.
Solution_Description: The optimized autoclave protocol achieved complete dehydration in 2 h, drastically shortening the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reactions performed in an autoclave for 2 h at 110 °C… after 2 h at 110 °C, the system was cooled down…” (solution) 
• “Motokucho et al. required heating at 90 °C in an autoclave for 168 h…” (problem).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: High market price of HMF and the need for large amounts of expensive reagents limited industrial viability.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was reduced to 5 wt % and TEAB to 10 wt %; DMC and ethyl acetate were recovered and reused, lowering material costs.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Trials carried out using lower amounts of Purolite CT275DR i.e., 5 % wt., showed an increase in HMF selectivity.” (stoichiometry) 
• “The amount of TEAB could be reduced to 10 % wt. without affecting HMF selectivity.” (stoichiometry) 
• “The extracting solvent (DMC) and the workup solvent (ethyl acetate) can be easily recovered and reused… DMC recovered 88 %; EtOAc recovered 75 %.” (solvent change/recovery).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: Operating at temperatures above 110 °C led to side‑product formation (methyl levulinate, OBMF) and HMF degradation.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was set at 110 °C, the highest temperature that maintained high selectivity and prevented decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Tests conducted at higher temperatures (up to 150 °C) produced similar or worse results… side reactions and product degradation.” (problem) 
• “Reactions performed in an autoclave for 2 h at 110 °C… gave 70–73 % HMF yield with minimal by‑products.” (solution).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: Scale‑up beyond 40 g d‑fructose was limited by the maximum capacity of the 220 mL stainless‑steel autoclave.
Solution_Description: The authors employed a larger‑capacity autoclave (220 mL) and demonstrated that the procedure is viable up to the equipment’s limit, suggesting that larger reactors would allow further scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We had to limit our scaling‑up trials to 40 g of d‑fructose due to the constraints of the autoclave maximum capacity.” (problem) 
• “Reactions performed in an autoclave… up to 40 g of d‑fructose” (solution).

Paper Title: Multigram Synthesis of Pure HMF and BHMF
Problem_Description: Inconsistent HMF yields were observed when catalyst loading or TEAB amount deviated from the optimum, indicating sensitivity of the process to stoichiometry.
Solution_Description: Precise control of catalyst (5 wt %) and TEAB (10 wt %) equivalents was established; the reaction mixture was stirred at 1000 rpm in the autoclave to ensure uniform mixing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Trials carried out using lower amounts of Purolite CT275DR… showed an increase in HMF selectivity… however, when 2.5 % wt. catalyst was employed, a significant decrease in HMF yield was noted.” (variability) 
• “Reactions were conducted in a stainless‑steel autoclave … under magnetic stirring (1000 rpm).” (order/rate of addition).

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: The discovery synthesis suffered from low overall isolated yield (6.4 % overall), safety concerns with the radical bromination (over‑bromination, exotherm) and the use of a toxic cyanide reagent in the Pd‑catalyzed cyanation, and required column chromatography to reach purity.
Solution_Description: A new scalable route was devised that starts from a readily available phthalide, converts it to a chloromethyl‑benzoate ester under mild conditions and avoids the hazardous bromination and cyanation steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "While suitable for discovery purposes, several aspects were undesirable for a multikilogram scale synthesis. The radical bromination reaction was susceptible to over‑bromination and also posed safety concerns. The use of a toxic cyanide reagent in a Pd‑catalyzed cyanation, and the reliance on column chromatography to achieve desired purity levels, would also need to be addressed. Furthermore, the overall yield was low…" (p. 3)
- "The route was scaled up … 55 % overall yield …" (p. 7)
- "A key feature of the synthesis was the transformation of a phthalide to the corresponding o‑(chloromethyl)‑benzoate ester while managing the tendency of intermediates to relactonize." (abstract)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: Direct opening of the phthalide with α‑aminoglutarimide failed because the glutarimide moiety decomposes (hydrolyses or ring‑opens) under basic or Lewis‑acidic conditions; the reaction mixture also formed two phases when aqueous NaOH was used, preventing isolation.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to solid KOH pellets in isopropanol (i‑PrOH) with a small water content, forming a poorly soluble potassium benzoate (12) that precipitated directly, avoiding aqueous work‑up and minimizing exposure of the glutarimide to water/strong base.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The use of aqueous NaOH led to the rapid formation of the desired benzoate, but the product was highly water soluble and could not be isolated or readily extracted from water.…" (p. 4)
- "By contrast, potassium salt 12 displayed low solubility in alcohol solvents with minimal water content. Treatment of 10 with solid KOH in i‑PrOH led to the formation of potassium benzoate 12 which crystallized directly from the reaction mixture." (p. 4)
- "The conversion of 10 to 12 required only 1–2 h at Ti = 20–25 °C… the scaled procedure required heating… to improve the filtration rate of 12." (p. 4)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: Intermediate 13 (the methyl ester of the benzoate) is unstable in solution and re‑lactonises back to the phthalide 10 (0.4 % h⁻¹ at 20–25 °C, increasing with temperature or added base). This creates timing‑sensitive batches and risk of impurity formation.
Solution_Description: The methylation was performed at ≤10 °C and Me₂SO₄ was added slowly; the reaction mixture was kept cold throughout to suppress relactonisation. The same low‑temperature protocol was applied to the subsequent mesylation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "While the methylation was initially demonstrated in DMAc at Ti = 20–25 °C, the intermediate alcohol 13 was unstable at this temperature in solution due to lactonization back to 10 at a rate of 0.4 %/h.…" (p. 5)
- "By lowering the reaction temperature to Ti = 10 °C, the rate of relactonization of 13 was decreased to nondetectable levels." (p. 5)
- "1.05 equiv of Me₂SO₄ was added slowly to a slurry of 12 in DMAc at Ti = 5–10 °C…" (p. 5)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: Addition of N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) as a base/scavenger increased the rate of lactonisation of 13 to 10 (0.6 % h⁻¹ at 22 °C).
Solution_Description: NMM was retained because of its lower basicity relative to other tertiary amines, but the reaction temperature was kept ≤10 °C to keep the lactonisation rate below detection.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "NMM was selected as a scavenger of HCl due to its low basicity… Even with this reduced basicity, the presence of NMM increased the rate of lactonisation… to an additional 0.6 %/h at Ti = 22 °C." (p. 5)
- "Fortunately, as with the methylation stream, this rate was temperature dependent and could be reduced to nondetectable levels at Ti ≤ 10 °C." (p. 5)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: During the isoindolinone‑forming step, an undesirable N,N‑dibenzylamino dimer (15) formed (12–15 % area) when KI was used, especially at high temperature, reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switching the halide source from KI to equimolar KBr lowered impurity 15 to 4–5 %, while maintaining high conversion. The reaction temperature was set at 75 °C to balance rate and impurity formation, and 1.0 equiv of KBr was found optimal.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The formation of 15 … was accompanied by the formation of 12–15 % of an N,N‑dibenzylamino ‘dimer’ 15… Neither a slow addition … suppressed the formation of 15…" (p. 6)
- "A study of the Finkelstein reaction … showed the viable use of KBr as an alternative to KI.…" (p. 7)
- "The use of catalytic amounts of KBr was ineffective and 1.0 equiv was found to be optimal. Importantly, the observed levels of 15 were reduced to 4–5 %…" (p. 7)
- Table 1 shows that at 75 °C conversion was 100 % with only 5.3 % 15, comparable to lower temperatures but with faster reaction. (Table 1)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: Conversion of the mesylate intermediate to the benzyl chloride 11 required 36–40 h at 20–25 °C, extending the batch time unnecessarily.
Solution_Description: Addition of 1.0 equiv of solid LiCl and heating the mixture to 35–40 °C accelerated the Finkelstein‑type displacement, completing conversion in 1–2 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The conversion of the mesylate to 11 was accelerated by heating the reaction mixture to Ti = 35–40 °C. Under these conditions, formation of 11 was complete within 1–2 h." (p. 6)
- "To facilitate full conversion of the intermediate mesylate, solid LiCl (1.0 equiv) was added at this point, and the resulting mixture was heated to Ti = 35–40 °C." (p. 6)

Paper Title: Advancing Scalable Chemistry toward Novel CELMoDs: Process Development for the Synthesis of CC-90009
Problem_Description: During hydrogenation of 7 to 8, a dimeric amine impurity (16) and an over‑reduced tolyl derivative (17) formed; the process also involved 10 % Pd/C and required removal of residual metal, raising safety and purity concerns.
