Problem_Description: The cyclopropanation reaction required the additive HFIP to mitigate water effects, but HFIP alone could not prevent O‑H insertion, necessitating an additional drying step.
Solution_Description: HFIP was retained (10 equiv) to preserve catalyst activity and enantioselectivity, while the downstream molecular‑sieve drying removed residual water, allowing the reaction to proceed with high ee and minimal side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “HFIP can be utilized as an additive to minimize the impact of water on the catalytic activity and enantioselectivity of the cyclopropanation reaction.”; “Molecular sieve column drying provided water levels below 100 ppm, thereby ensuring acceptable reactivity, selectivity, and purity in the water‑sensitive cyclopropanation reaction.”

Paper Title: Continuous Process to Safely Manufacture an Aryldiazoacetate and Its Direct Use in a Dirhodium-Catalyzed Enantioselective Cyclopropanation
Problem_Description: Initial extraction designs using a mixer‑settler increased holdup of the energetic diazo intermediate, compromising safety and steady‑state operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A membrane‑based separation (Zaiput) was chosen over a mixer‑settler to minimize residence time and holdup of the diazo‑containing stream, enabling rapid phase separation and continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “While a mixer settler setup was first considered, a desire to minimize aryldiazoacetate accumulation and hold‑up led to the selection of a membrane‑based separation.”; “A Zaiput equipped with 1 µm hydrophobic PTFE membrane was utilized.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: The early‑stage route that used 3‑hydrazinopyridine·2HCl required a diazonium step that is hazardous on scale, and the resulting intermediate (2) was difficult to isolate because it is highly soluble in water; the final alkylation also relied on expensive reagents (ethyl iodide, Cs₂CO₃) making the process uneconomical.
Solution_Description: A middle‑stage Ullmann‑coupling route was adopted. It begins with a palladium‑catalysed reductive chlorination of 4‑nitropyrazole (avoiding diazonium chemistry) followed by acetylation, delivering the key nucleophile in >80 % yield and >99 % purity; the overall five‑step sequence uses inexpensive reagents and was selected as the lead pilot‑plant route.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the synthesis of key raw material 2 from 3‑aminopyridine required hazardous diazonium chemistry, which is undesirable for large‑scale practice.”
• “the isolation of 2 proved to be challenging due to its high solubility in the aqueous phase.”
• “the conditions used for the final alkylation step made it difficult to achieve the economic target … due to the cost of reagents (i.e., ethyl iodide, cesium carbonate).”
• “This route started with a palladium‑catalyzed reductive chlorination reaction of 4‑nitropyrazole … The product was isolated in more than 80 % yield and high purity (>99 % AUC).”
• “The five‑step process using a middle‑stage Ullmann coupling approach … was selected as the lead route for the pilot plant campaign.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: The NaBH₄ reduction of the acetyl‑amide (step 4) gave inconsistent yields (50–80 %) that depended heavily on the quality of BF₃·Et₂O, requiring large excess of both reagents and adding analytical burden.
Solution_Description: The reduction was replaced by a two‑step ethylation/hydrolysis sequence: ethyl bromide and NaOtBu (or related alkoxides) alkylate the amide, then aqueous HCl hydrolysis furnishes the ethyl‑amine. This avoids BF₃·Et₂O, uses cheaper reagents, and delivers >97 % conversion with a robust, scalable process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the yield of this reaction varied significantly from less than 50 % to 80 %.”
• “the performance of this reaction was mostly affected by the quality of BF₃·Et₂O … yielded very different outcomes.”
• “It was envisioned that 23 could also be synthesized via alkylation of 19 followed by hydrolysis …”
• “the combination of EtBr and metal alkoxides … afforded clean conversion … more than 97 % conversion … at 58 °C in a sealed system to prevent loss of EtBr.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: During the CuCl‑catalysed Ullmann coupling in MeCN, the product precipitated prematurely and remained trapped with inorganic solids, giving isolated yields below 70 %.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in DMF instead of MeCN. After completion, water was added to precipitate the product cleanly, eliminating the loss of material and improving isolated yield to 70–75 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The isolation was found to be problematic giving low yield at less than 70 % caused by premature precipitation of the desired product during workup … due to its poor solubility in MeCN.”
• “We found that conducting the reaction in DMF at 100 °C … greatly simplified the isolation process, as the product could be precipitated out by adding water to the reaction mixture upon reaction completion.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: The final amidation employed pyridine as the base, which poses toxicity concerns and generated troublesome emulsions during aqueous workup, hindering scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Pyridine was replaced with sodium bicarbonate (or sodium carbonate) as a non‑toxic base, delivering >98 % conversion across several solvents and eliminating emulsion formation, enabling straightforward workup and crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “handling pyridine on scale in the final step was not desirable due to a toxicity concern. In addition, problematic emulsions during aqueous workup was not suitable for scale‑up.”
• “replacing pyridine with NaHCO₃ or Na₂CO₃ as the base led to clean conversion (>98 %) in a wide range of solvents (EtOAc, DCM, toluene).”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: During the Sandmeyer conversion of the diazonium salt to the chloro‑pyrazole, uncontrolled foaming occurred when copper powder was added to the acidic diazonium solution, creating safety and reproducibility issues.
Solution_Description: The order was reversed: the diazonium solution was added to a pre‑cooled suspension of CuCl in toluene (0–5 °C). This suppressed foaming, controlled gas evolution, and gave cleaner conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Inconsistent yield caused by uncontrollable foaming during addition of copper to the diazonium salt solution in concentrated HCl was a major issue of this step.”
• “Much cleaner conversion was obtained when the diazonium salt solution was added to a suspension of CuCl in toluene. Off‑gassing was observed at ∼0‑5 °C … The use of toluene as the cosolvent significantly suppressed foaming.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for the Insecticide Tyclopyrazoflor. Part I. Evaluation of Strategies using Ullmann Coupling of Pyrazole Derivatives
Problem_Description: The late‑stage ethylation of the secondary amide used ethyl iodide and Cs₂CO₃, which are costly and generate elimination by‑products (impurities 12, 13), leading to low overall yields.
Solution_Description: Ethyl bromide (cheaper) together with NaOtBu (or KOtBu) in THF was employed in a sealed vessel at 58 °C, giving >97 % conversion, minimal elimination, and a higher isolated yield (≈80 % over two steps).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the high cost of reagents (i.e., ethyl iodide, cesium carbonate) … and challenges… to remove impurities (12, 13) from undesired elimination.”
• “the combination of EtBr and metal alkoxides … afforded clean conversion … more than 97 % conversion … at 58 °C in a sealed system to prevent loss of EtBr.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 3 demethylation used a 18‑equiv excess of methyl chloroformate and up‑to‑50‑equiv hydrazine, required > 5 days, gave variable yields (70‑90 %) and required chromatographic purification to remove saturated amine impurity.
Solution_Description: Replaced the toxic MCF/hydrazine sequence with an iron‑catalysed non‑classical Polonovski demethylation (Fe/FeCl₃, mCBPA) and introduced SiliaMetS Thiol scavenger to clean the reaction mixture, delivering 84 % crude yield, 96 % assay and easy isolation as the HCl salt.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Step 3 demethylation … used a very large excess of toxic reagents methyl chloroformate and hydrazine, and typically required more than 1 week per batch …”
2. “The reaction … gave variable quality product after chromatography in variable yield.”
3. “We were able to adapt an iron‑catalyzed non‑classical Polonovski reaction … which proved ideal for this demethylation.”
4. “SiliaMetS Thiol was better than SiliaMetS DMT and much superior to both standard activated carbon treatments …”
5. “The reaction was mild, fast, hazard‑free, and with low overall toxicity … the amine could be isolated as its HCl salt.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 5 oxidation employed 2‑iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX), an expensive, explosive oxidant that gave variable yields (≈ 68 %) and the resulting ketone (8) was unstable, decomposing during chromatography, heating or storage.
Solution_Description: Swern oxidation was introduced (oxalyl‑chloride/DMSO/triethylamine) under controlled low temperature (≤ ‑30 °C) to afford the ketone in 90 % crude yield with quantitative conversion and no detectable side‑products, avoiding explosive reagents and eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Step 5 oxidation … used expensive and potentially explosive 2‑iodoxybenzoic acid (IBX) …”
2. “None of the desired ketone (8) could be isolated on multi‑gram scale … only multiple unidentified side‑products were observed.”
3. “IBX was clearly unacceptable for scale‑up due to its explosion potential, high cost …”
4. “Swern oxidation … gave ketone 8 in 90 % crude yield … without formation of any detectable side‑products or residues.”
5. “Standard Swern reaction conditions … were followed … exotherm of 27 K … toxic dimethyl sulfide generated, but the process was acceptable for up to 1 kg scale.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 6 acid‑catalysed rearrangement required sealed‑tube heating at 95 °C for 1 h, gave moderate yields (≈ 70 %), generated diphenol impurity 19, and demanded a highly dilute aqueous work‑up with > 100 vol water, leading to poor isolation and long cycle times.
Solution_Description: Optimised the rearrangement by running the reaction at 20 °C then 65 °C in methanol/MSA, reduced methanol volume to 1.2 rel vol, employed a rapid aqueous drown‑out with 80 vol water and controlled exotherms during quench and basification, giving quantitative conversion, 95 % LC purity and a streamlined work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Step 6 … required MSA/methanol under ‘sealed tube’ conditions at 95 °C, giving a moderate yield after a dilute work‑up.”
2. “The reaction ... gave a moderate yield after a dilute work‑up.”
3. “Development of the reaction started at 65 °C … Sealed‑tube conditions were not necessary.”
4. “The improved process (1.2 rel vol of methanol, 8.5 vol of MSA, 30 min at 20 °C then 4 h at 65 °C) provided crude MCL‑509 free base… with diphenol 19 at 3.7 % LC area.”
5. “Aqueous drown‑out … 80 vol water were used to obtain a precipitate free from tarry residues; the exotherm on quench was modest and controllable.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 1 (triflation) required multiple aqueous washes, back‑extractions, two concentrations to dryness and a slow CPME distillation; drying the water‑wet product paste took several days.
Solution_Description: Implemented an aqueous drown‑out precipitation of the triflate at pH 9‑10, eliminated the final extractions and a second concentration; switched to CPME (later 2‑MeTHF) to enable co‑distillation and faster removal of DCM, reducing overall processing time by > 3 days per batch.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Isolation of 4 required multiple washes … and a second concentration to dryness.”
2. “When repeating the original research procedure, precipitation of some white solid … was found to be the desired product 4.”
3. “An aqueous drown‑out was attempted … gave product 4 in high yield and purity by direct precipitation at pH 9‑10 … avoided the final set of extractions and the second concentration to dryness.”
4. “CPME was initially chosen … the distillation was slow due to the high bp of CPME (106 °C).”
5. “The aqueous drown‑out was a major improvement, boosting the yield slightly for no loss in quality and filtering well, although the CPME distillation was slow.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 2 hydrogenolysis used DMF (toxic, environmentally undesirable) and a high Pd loading (6 mol %); impurity formation (phosphine adducts 13‑14) and variable yields (65‑82 %) were observed.
Solution_Description: Switched the solvent to 2‑MeTHF (less toxic, water‑immiscible), reduced Pd loading to 4 mol % while maintaining a 2:1 PPh₃:Pd ratio, and lowered Ph₃P equivalents, which suppressed phosphine‑adduct impurities and gave consistent yields (87‑91 % with 91‑93 % LC purity).
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The main issue … was the use of DMF, which led to an extended and dilute work‑up, as well as being undesired for toxicity and environmental reasons.”
2. “Other polar aprotic solvents gave full conversion but did not avoid toxicity … less polar ones (toluene, 2‑MeTHF, CPME, MEK) required longer reaction times.”
3. “A Pd loading of 4 mol % catalyst was found to be robust … impurity 9 was also lower at ∼2.5 %.”
4. “Degassing … improved the sparging and led to higher conversions and lower impurity levels.”
5. “Speculative structures were proposed … phosphine adducts 13 and 14 … Lowering the Ph₃P loading was helpful …”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: Step 4 alkylation employed propyl iodide (toxic, reactive) and produced a dark‑colored product with N,O‑dialkylated impurity 16, requiring chromatography for purification.
Solution_Description: Adopted a reductive amination using propionaldehyde and sodium triacetoxy‑borohydride (STAB) in 2‑MeTHF, eliminating the iodide reagent, avoiding the colored by‑product, suppressing impurity 16, and allowing isolation without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Alkylation … using propyl iodide gave a yellow oil … required chromatography to remove saturated impurities 9‑11 and residual 5.”
2. “It avoided the use of a toxic and reactive alkylating agent (propyl iodide), which was also responsible for the dark colored product.”
3. “The initial reductive amination reaction was considerably faster, being complete within 30 min at room temperature … yielding higher‑quality, lighter‑colored product 7.”
4. “STAB … is mild, selective, and tolerant of other functional groups and has precedent in scale‑up processes.”
5. “No chromatography was required; the product could be isolated as a solid.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of Orally Active Apomorphine Drug Candidates
Problem_Description: After step 6, the free‑base product formed a heavily water‑wet paste that required up to 2 days of drying at 40 °C, and filtration of the precipitate was slow (1‑2 h on 200 g scale) due to small particle size.
Solution_Description: Developed a methanol solvate purification: the crude base was slurried in methanol, precipitated the methanol solvate, filtered, washed and dried, giving a high‑purity product (≥ 99 % LC) with overall corrected yields of 68 % and simplifying downstream handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Crude 1 … was a thick water‑wet paste … drying at elevated temperatures (40–60 °C) led to decomposition …”
2. “Suspending crude 1 in methanol for 1 h at room temperature … gave off‑white precipitate … after filtration and drying gave MCL‑509 MeOH with 95 % LC purity.”
3. “The dried off‑white precipitate … was charged to a reactor, methanol added, heated to 60 °C … after cooling the solid was filtered and washed … gave MCL‑509 MeOH as an off‑white solid (23.4 g, 95 % assay, 63 % corr. yield).”
4. “Overall, this rapidly developed reductive amination proved to be tolerant and robust … the lack of crystallization being the only drawback.”
5. “The final re‑treatment was rapidly developed to deliver API to the requisite quality …”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Traditional amide‑coupling processes for DBO‑derived β‑lactamase inhibitors rely on hazardous organic solvents such as dichloromethane, DMF and NMP, which pose health, safety and regulatory concerns and add to material cost.
Solution_Description: Switch to water as the reaction medium and use the water‑soluble coupling pair EDC·HCl/HOBt, eliminating the need for toxic solvents and dramatically reducing cost and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: • “However, the prior literature for the amide coupling primarily involves hazardous solvents such as dichloromethane (DCM), N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF), and N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP).”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: After coupling, 5–7 % of HOBt remained bound to the product; conventional recrystallisation or solvent washes failed to remove this impurity, jeopardising product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Perform a hot‑water wash (50–55 °C) of the crude solid followed by filtration; the elevated temperature removes the residual HOBt, delivering a highly pure intermediate in the reported isolated yield (85–88 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “HPLC analysis of the isolated product showed that ∼5–7 % HOBt was intact with the product. Neither recrystallization nor solvents/a combination of solvent treatment was successful for the entire purging of HOBt.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The O‑alkylated hydroxylamine (compound 4) is a semi‑solid that required DMF for dissolution on laboratory scale, introducing a non‑greener co‑solvent and complicating scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Change the addition sequence to add the solid hydroxylamine directly to the aqueous EDC·HCl/HOBt mixture, avoiding DMF entirely; the reaction remains high‑yielding and reproducible at kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Initially, the semi‑solid nature of O‑alkylated hydroxylamine (4) posed a challenge. Hence, during lab‑scale reactions, DMF was used to dissolve 4…”.

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Literature protocols employ column chromatography on silica or preparative HPLC for product isolation, consuming large volumes of organic solvents and increasing operational cost.
Solution_Description: Isolate the product by simple vacuum filtration and a hot‑water wash; no organic solvent extraction or chromatography is required, providing a swift, cost‑effective, and greener work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The product was efficiently isolated from the reaction through simple filtration and recrystallized using hot water treatment as a swift and cost‑effective process.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The free DBO acid or its acyl chloride is unstable, difficult to handle, and not readily available on large scale, creating safety and supply‑chain issues.
Solution_Description: Use the bench‑stable sodium salt of DBO acid as the coupling partner; the salt is highly water‑soluble, avoids decomposition, and can be prepared in bulk.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The designed protocol is useful for water‑soluble sodium salts of DBO acids if the corresponding carboxylic acids or acyl chlorides are unstable, challenging to manipulate or isolate, or not readily available commercially.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Amide Coupling in Aqueous Media: Process for the Production of Diazabicyclooctane β‑Lactamase Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Previously reported amide‑coupling methods generate high Process Mass Intensity (PMI > 15) and complete E‑factor (> 14) due to extensive solvent use and chromatographic steps.
Solution_Description: The water‑based EDC·HCl/HOBt protocol delivers PMI = 12.57 and cEF = 11.57, markedly lower than literature values, by eliminating organic solvents and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reported procedure suffers from many factors such as organic solvents … higher PMI (> 15) and cEF (> 14) values were observed … The process with boric acid …”.

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Racemization of the chiral centre occurred during the cyclisation step to give intermediate 10 under the original high‑temperature (80 °C) conditions with only 0.2 eq DMF, leading to loss of enantiopurity and inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: Increasing the DMF charge to 0.6 eq accelerated the reaction so that the temperature could be lowered to 40 °C, which suppressed racemisation and gave consistently enantiopure product.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The uncyclized intermediate 11 … was found to readily racemize under the acidic conditions of the cyclisation reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Use of dichloromethane in the bromination and subsequent steps caused formation of a methylene‑bridged dimer impurity and presented an environmental/health hazard.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane was replaced with 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2‑MeTHF) for the bromination step, and heptane was introduced as the extraction/anti‑solvent for the benzyl‑chloride removal, eliminating the dimer impurity and reducing solvent toxicity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of dichloromethane … had also led to batch failures due to the formation of a methylene‑bridged dimer …”.

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Filtration of intermediate 3 was operability‑limited: the product crystallised as a clay‑like, water‑rich paste (type 2 crystal) that clogged filters and required time‑consuming oven drying.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A dry‑2‑butanol work‑up enabled isolation of the anhydrous form C (or the 2‑butanol solvate type 3) which filtered rapidly; a heating step above 75 °C converted any residual type 3 to form C; continuous‑level vacuum distillation removed water azeotropically, improving filtration speed and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: • “All attempts at improvement of the type 2 crystals failed … the inherited process had originally isolated 3 … as a thick, clay‑like product …”.

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Purification of 2‑butynoic (tetrolic) acid by distillation showed a thermal runaway onset at ~135 °C, making the operation unsafe at scale.
Solution_Description: A recrystallisation protocol was developed to isolate high‑quality tetrolic acid without the need for hazardous distillation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Thermal analysis of the distillation procedure revealed a thermal runaway (onset at approximately 135 °C), which precluded the use of this purification technique.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: The final acylation to give acalabrutinib (1) suffered from over‑/under‑reaction, formation of an N‑acetyl impurity, solvent entrapment (dichloromethane) and oiling during crystallisation, leading to variable yields (~70 %).
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane was exchanged for 2‑MeTHF to avoid aminal formation; a continuous‑level vacuum distillation kept the product in solution at 50 °C while replacing DCM with ethanol, preventing oiling; pH was adjusted to 4.5–5.0 during work‑up to extract residual starting material and impurity 18; seeding and a 50 °C hold gave controlled crystallisation with consistent particle size.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The inherited process used a solvent swap (from dichloromethane to ethanol) … the product 1 was consistently seen to oil/gum before finally crystallising …”.

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Formation of highly toxic dimethylcarbamoyl chloride (DMCC) was possible when thionyl chloride/DMF was used to generate the acyl chloride for intermediate 4, raising carcinogenic‑risk concerns.
Solution_Description: DMF was replaced by tetra‑n‑butylammonium chloride as the catalyst for acyl‑chloride formation, eliminating the DMCC pathway while keeping the existing process flow.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The process to produce 4 … was seen to be undesirable since highly toxic dimethylcarbamoyl chloride (DMCC) is likely to form under the reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: The addition of N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) in the bromination of 9 required careful titration; over‑addition caused impurity 18 and under‑addition left unreacted material, leading to batch failures.
Solution_Description: NBS was added in a controlled “titrate‑in” fashion with frequent in‑process checks; after the coupling step the pH was set to 4.8 so that residual 3 and impurity 18 partitioned into the aqueous phase, allowing relaxed control over the T3P addition.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the N‑bromosuccinimide must be ‘titrated in’ to the reaction, with repeated in‑process control measurements to avoid overreaction.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Oxidation impurity 13 formed during the 8‑step sequence when oxygen entered the reactor, causing discoloration, polymer formation and impurity buildup.
Solution_Description: Strict oxygen control (inerting regime, material‑of‑construction changes) prevented formation of impurity 13 and eliminated the need for a carbon‑treatment step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Control of oxygen levels … was found to be important in preventing discoloration … and an oxidation impurity 13 … Close attention to the inerting regime … gave an improvement in quality, such that a previously used carbon treatment was rendered unnecessary.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: When the palladium scavenger was applied after acylation (step 1), the triple bond of 1 interacted with the propanethiol‑functionalised silica, causing material loss and reduced yield.
Solution_Description: The scavenger treatment was moved upstream to the 3‑step, where it removed palladium efficiently without yield loss.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It is postulated that the presence of the triple bond of 1 can interact with the propanethiol‑functionalised silica, so that increased material is lost to the scavenger when the treatment is performed at that stage, leading to yield loss.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial Manufacturing Processes for Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Polymorphic variability (forms C, type 3, and type 2) caused inconsistent filtration rates and occasional back‑transformation during cooling, requiring careful control of water content and temperature.
Solution_Description: A heating step above 75 °C converted any type 3 to the thermodynamic form C; dry‑2‑butanol work‑up kept water <0.5 % w/w; a temperature cycle (90 °C → 20 °C) fixed the polymorph before isolation, delivering fast filtration and high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Form C is the thermodynamic form at temperatures above 75 °C … By incorporating a heating step prior to cool down and isolation, form C can be routinely produced.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: The literature LiAlH₄ reduction of 1‑bromomethyladamantane (2) required >48 h under reflux, needed up to 20 % excess LiAlH₄, gave conversions below 90 % and produced mixtures of starting bromide and product that could only be separated by recrystallisation, resulting in significant yield loss.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount (1–2.5 mol %) of tributyltin hydride was added to the LiAlH₄ reduction. This shortened the reaction time to 24 h, eliminated residual bromide, limited formation of the hydrolysis product (1‑adamantanol) to 2–5 % and allowed isolation of the pure hydrocarbon by flash chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • "For instance, it requires prolonged reaction times (over 48 h under reflux) and additional portions of LiAlH₄ (must be added over time, up to 20 % excess). Otherwise, conversion remains below 90 %…" (p. 3)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: When the LiAlH₄ protocol was scaled above 100 g of bromide 2, the amount of side‑products (hydrolysis product 1 and other impurities) increased dramatically, giving inconsistent conversion and poor material balance, while handling large quantities of LiAlH₄ is hazardous.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the LiAlH₄ reduction with a zinc‑in‑acetic‑acid (Zn/AcOH) reduction using 4 equiv Zn and 20 mol % KI as an additive. This gave quantitative conversion in 4 h and 94 % isolated yield of 1‑methyladamantane (3) with 96 % purity, eliminating the safety and scalability issues of LiAlH₄.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Reacting 250 g of 2 with 4 equiv of zinc powder in acetic acid in the presence of 20 mol % of KI allowed to achieve 100 % conversion… yielding 94 % of the desired product 3…" (p. 3)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: The literature multistep synthesis of racemic 3‑methyl‑5‑phenyladamantane‑1‑carboxylic acid employed bromination, reflux with HCOOH/H₂SO₄ (8 h) and AlCl₃ (6 h) and generated inseparable regio‑isomeric acids, making the route unsafe, time‑consuming and difficult to purify.
Solution_Description: The authors used triflic acid (TfOH) in benzene (20‑fold excess) with a Dean–Stark water trap to avoid formation of isomeric products and to accelerate the reaction (complete in 6 h). This avoided the use of hazardous AlCl₃ and shortened the overall sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Only the use of triflic acid allowed to avoid the isomerization product formation… The same effect was observed due to the water accumulation… In this regard, the use of the Dean–Stark water trap improved the reaction rate. As a result, refluxing the substrate in an excess of benzene… allowed achieving the reaction completion with a 74 % isolated yield after 6 h." (p. 4)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: During the oxidation steps to convert 1‑methyladamantane (3) to the carboxylic acid, addition of highly concentrated HNO₃ caused rapid temperature spikes, which led to poor preparative yields, especially on larger scale.
Solution_Description: The procedure was modified to add 65 % HNO₃ dropwise while keeping the internal temperature below 25 °C, followed by controlled addition of additional H₂SO₄ and a low‑temperature work‑up; this prevented exotherms and restored high conversion and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • "After the addition of HNO₃, the course of the reaction was controlled… keeping the reaction temperature below 25 °C… rapid temperature growth… led to poor preparative yields, especially when increasing the scale." (p. 4)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: Initial screening of chiral resolving agents (cinchonidine, (R,S)‑2‑amino‑1,2‑diphenylethanol, quinidine) produced either insoluble adducts or oily residues, resulting in low enantiomeric excess (≤92 %) and material loss after crystallisation.
Solution_Description: The authors selected (s)‑1‑(4‑bromophenyl)ethylamine as the resolving agent and screened acetone, acetonitrile and ethyl acetate as solvents; a three‑step crystallisation from ethyl acetate gave the target acid with 96 % ee (entry 3pA) and acceptable isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Only the use of triflic acid… The best results were achieved when 1 equiv of triflic acid…" (p. 4)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: Conventional semi‑preparative normal‑phase chiral chromatography could only resolve ~100 mg per run, making multigram production of the enantiopure acid prohibitively expensive.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A stacked‑injection approach on the Chiralcel OJ‑H column was developed, allowing multiple 30 mg injections per run (up to 180 mg per hour) with the same mobile phase, raising productivity from 165 mg h⁻¹ (single injection) to 315 mg h⁻¹ and cutting the cost of enantioseparation by ~20 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The use of stacked injection… allowed us to isolate pure (98 % ee) … with up to 180 mg of product scale per run (315 mg per hour)… decreased the cost of chromatographic separation…" (p. 6)

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of 1‑Methyladamantane and Its Functionalization as a Key Point for Promising Antiviral Agents
Problem_Description: The final amide coupling to afford the target antiviral agent (20) had to be performed on multigram scale; earlier routes produced low overall yields and required costly chiral resolution steps.
Solution_Description: Using the optimised, enantioenriched acid 18 (98 % ee) obtained by the combined crystallisation‑stacked‑injection protocol, the authors performed a standard HATU‑mediated coupling to give the amide 20 on a 25 g scale in 60 % isolated yield, demonstrating practical multigram synthesis of the antiviral candidate.
Supporting_Evidence: • "We successfully prepared 20 on the gram scale using the sample of acid 18 with 98 % ee previously purified via our combined crystallization‑chiral chromatography approach… The synthetic scale of carboxamide 20 was successfully increased to 25 g per operation with a 60 % preparative yield." (p. 6)

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: The literature‑scale synthesis gave a dark brown crude product with a fine, clay‑like precipitate that required lengthy filtration, gave only 21 % isolated yield, contained CB[5] impurity and excess acid, and generated large amounts of waste (E‑factor 259).
Solution_Description: The amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ was reduced roughly two‑fold (350 mg glycoluril · mL⁻¹ H₂SO₄ instead of 190 mg · mL⁻¹) while keeping reagent concentrations high, which minimized the acid volume and prevented excessive dilution that caused low solubility and fine suspensions.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Using these conditions led to darkening of the reaction mixture… the precipitate obtained was very fine and required long‑time filtration and washing… the yield exceeded the theoretical yield… E‑factor was 259 for the crude product.”
• “First, this can be achieved by reducing its amount for the synthesis in proportion to the amount of starting materials… further reducing amount of sulfuric acid leads to temporary gel formation… the amount of sulfuric acid … should be minimized.”
• Table 1 shows E‑factor dropping from 259 to 6.5 when acid amount was lowered.

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: The condensation of glycoluril with paraformaldehyde in concentrated H₂SO₄ is highly exothermic; uncontrolled temperature caused gel formation and poor mixing, making the reaction difficult to control on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Formaldehyde was added in portions over 1–2 h while maintaining the reaction temperature at 45–55 °C using cooling, followed by a staged temperature ramp (60 °C → 70 °C → 80 °C) for 12–16 h total. This controlled the exotherm and prevented gelation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The mixing process was exothermic; it required as large amounts of methanol… The temperature during the addition of formaldehyde should be maintained at 45–55 °C… higher temperatures lead to an increase in the formation of other homologues, while lower temperatures lead to gelation.”
• “To keep the temperature of the exothermic reaction in this range, cooling is required, and paraformaldehyde should be added in portions over 1–2 h… then the temperature should be gradually… raised to 80 °C over 12–16 h.”

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: Work‑up in the literature required large volumes of methanol (≈0.4 L · g⁻¹ glycoluril) to precipitate the product; the resulting slurry was a fine suspension that was difficult to filter and washed, leading to high waste and low overall yield (30–40 %).
Solution_Description: The crude CB[6] was precipitated directly from the reaction mixture by using maximum reagent concentrations and solid paraformaldehyde, allowing the product to crystallize in‑situ. Only a small amount of methanol (3–4 mL · g⁻¹ glycoluril) or, preferably, water was later used for washing, dramatically reducing solvent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The mixing process… required as large amounts of methanol (∼0.4 L per 1 g of starting glycoluril). The precipitate obtained was very fine… The procedure gave a large amount of waste containing acids and methanol; … E‑factor was 259.”
• “Higher concentrations of the starting materials in sulfuric acid lead to the precipitation of the final product just during the reaction… using maximum concentrations … enables most of the product to be obtained as a precipitate directly from the reaction mixture without the need to precipitate it with large amounts of organic solvents or water.”
• “Using 3–4 mL of methanol per 1 g of starting glycoluril dilutes the remaining sulfuric acid… However, it is preferable to avoid using toxic methanol at all.”

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: Methanol, employed in the traditional work‑up, is toxic, volatile and expensive, and its recovery by distillation gave only 30–40 % efficiency, inflating waste and operating cost.
Solution_Description: Methanol was eliminated from the final work‑up; the filter cake was washed with a small amount of dilute H₂SO₄ followed by water, and the product was finally purified by aqueous recrystallisation. This removed the toxic solvent, cut cost, and lowered the E‑factor.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The procedure gave a large amount of waste containing acids and methanol; the latter could be regenerated by distillation only up to 30–40 % degree.”
• “Using 3–4 mL of methanol per 1 g of starting glycoluril… However, it is preferable to avoid using toxic methanol at all.”
• “The best way to treat the filter cake is its dispersion in an excess of water or methanol… Using 3–4 mL of methanol per 1 g … Nevertheless, it is preferable to avoid using toxic methanol at all.”

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: Even after filtration the crude product retained residual H₂SO₄ (≈5.8 wt %), giving an acidic suspension that was difficult to neutralize and risked corrosion and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: A second washing step with excess water (7–8 mL · g⁻¹ glycoluril) was introduced, allowing the acid‑laden filter cake to recrystallize as coarse CB[6] crystals. The crystals were then washed to neutrality and dried, delivering acid‑free product (≤0.3 pH‑unit shift) and eliminating the safety issue.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “All of the above‑mentioned procedures yielded both crude and purified products containing residual acid, as shown by the acidic pH of their suspensions in water… the fine character of the crude products made washing them to remove acid very hard.”
• “Upon suspension in water, the product still led to acidic pH… The acid can be completely removed… a more thorough washing until neutral, preferably with additional suspension in water, should be utilized.”
• “The acid can be completely removed from the product… the pH of the solution remained neutral… indicating that virtually no acid was present in the product.”

Paper Title: Modified Greener Procedure for the Synthesis of Cucurbit[6]uril
Problem_Description: When the amount of H₂SO₄ was reduced too far, a temporary gel formed during the reaction, preventing proper mixing and temperature control on scale.
Solution_Description: The acid amount was optimized to the lowest level that still kept the reaction mixture fluid (≈350 mg glycoluril · mL⁻¹ H₂SO₄). This avoided gel formation while still allowing high reagent concentration for precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Further reducing amount of sulfuric acid leads to temporary gel formation during the reaction that is unacceptable, especially in the case of large‑scale synthesis, because it disables mixing and temperature control.”
• “First, this can be achieved by reducing its amount for the synthesis in proportion to the amount of starting materials… further reducing amount of sulfuric acid leads to temporary gel formation… therefore, the amount of sulfuric acid … should be minimized.”

Paper Title: Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Sulfonamide Step Speciation Study: Investigation into Precipitation–Dissolution Events during Addition of Chlorosulfonic Acid
Problem_Description: During the extended 16‑h addition of chlorosulfonic acid (CSA) the reaction mixture showed an unexpected series of precipitation‑dissolution events (regions A‑F) that caused the mixture to alternate between solid slurries and clear solutions, indicating poor and irregular solubility of the reacting species.
Solution_Description: A detailed speciation study (offline HPLC, FTIR, FBRM, XRPD, NMR and DFT) was performed to understand the protonated forms of the diaminopyrimidine and sulfonic‑acid intermediate.  The insight enabled the adoption of a controlled, slow CSA addition procedure that avoids the precipitation zones and ensures robust operation at commercial scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “unexpected series of precipitation–dissolution events were observed.”; “letters highlight various regions where changes in solubility behavior were observed during CSA addition (A, C, and E denote precipitation events, while B, D, and F correspond to dissolution events).”; “The full understanding of the speciation and solubility data from this detailed study gave us high confidence that the current process is operating within the optimal conditions to avoid any potential engineering risk.”

Paper Title: Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Sulfonamide Step Speciation Study: Investigation into Precipitation–Dissolution Events during Addition of Chlorosulfonic Acid
Problem_Description: The diaminopyrimidine starting material (1) has very low solubility in acetonitrile (≈ 4 mg mL⁻¹), leading to a solid slurry at the start of the reaction and causing mixing/phase issues.
Solution_Description: Slow addition of CSA converts the poorly soluble 1 into more soluble mono‑ and bis‑protonated salts; the measured concentration of 1 in solution rises to ≈ 100 mg mL⁻¹ after ~1 equiv CSA, effectively increasing solubility without changing the solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Given the low solubility of starting material 1 in acetonitrile, solids were present at the start of the reaction (Region A).”; “compound 1 exhibited very low solubility (ca. 4 mg mL⁻¹) in acetonitrile.”; “The concentration of 1 after 1 equiv CSA added was approx. 101 mg mL⁻¹ at reaction conditions, and a homogeneous solution was eventually obtained as the total amount of CSA added approached 2 equiv.”

Paper Title: Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Sulfonamide Step Speciation Study: Investigation into Precipitation–Dissolution Events during Addition of Chlorosulfonic Acid
Problem_Description: Standard reaction monitoring (FTIR, HPLC) does not detect the solid formation/dissolution events, leaving a blind spot for physical changes that jeopardise process control.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implementation of focused‑beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) as an online probe to monitor particle formation and dissolution in real time, providing immediate detection of slurry formation and guiding process adjustments.
Supporting_Evidence: “FBRM allows for the monitoring of physical changes like particle formation and dissolution events.”; “In this case however, the FBRM data (Figure 1, black line trace) showed interesting trends that prompted us to perform further investigation.”

Paper Title: Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Sulfonamide Step Speciation Study: Investigation into Precipitation–Dissolution Events during Addition of Chlorosulfonic Acid
Problem_Description: The CSA counter‑ion is unstable in the presence of water and hydrolyses to give sulfate and HCl, causing an apparent loss of chloride in ion‑chromatography analyses.
Solution_Description: Developed a specific ion‑chromatography method to monitor sulfate and chloride, and performed a head‑space quench with dilute NaOH to convert any liberated HCl to NaCl for detection, thereby accounting for the counter‑ion loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “due to the instability of the CSA counterion in the presence of water, the resulting hydrolysis products, namely, sulfate and chloride ions were monitored instead.”; “We attributed the initial chloride discrepancy to the instability of the CSA counterion, whereby hydrolysis resulted in loss of HCl.”; “An aliquot of headspace vapor was taken… quenched with dilute aqueous NaOH, to convert any HCl gas to NaCl. Indeed, IC analysis of the quenched sample was positive for chloride ions.”

Paper Title: Gefapixant Citrate (MK-7264) Sulfonamide Step Speciation Study: Investigation into Precipitation–Dissolution Events during Addition of Chlorosulfonic Acid
Problem_Description: At ~3 equiv CSA the reaction forms a thick slurry that is insoluble, preventing acquisition of solution‑state ^13C NMR spectra and obscuring structural information.
Solution_Description: Density‑functional‑theory (DFT) calculations of ^13C chemical shifts were performed on candidate protonated structures; the computed shifts were compared with the limited experimental data to assign the speciation despite lacking solution NMR spectra.
Supporting_Evidence: “At 3 equiv CSA, a thick slurry formed, and an NMR spectrum could not be acquired.”; “DFT calculations were performed for each test structure… to assign the observed species.”; “The NMR spectral changes occurred without accompanying chemical changes… attributed to subsequent protonation events.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: The batch Curtius rearrangement generated explosive azide‑derived impurities 7 and 8 (up to >15 wt % w/w), exceeding the safety limit of 12 wt % and causing low isolated yields (≈61 %).
Solution_Description: The process was moved to continuous flow reactors (FlowStart Evo and later plate reactors) which drastically reduced the inventory of hazardous intermediates, provided precise temperature/pressure control and improved conversion, keeping impurity 8 below 12 wt % and raising yields to 72–78 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “...in batch approaches ... 61% average yield. On scaling up this batch process, increased levels of impurities 7 and 8 were observed... levels exceeding 15% w/w were deemed potentially explosive...”; “...continuous flow … smaller reactor volume… significantly less… could be adequately cooled… further reducing the risk to the operator.”; “...process offers clear advantages to the batch process... Safer scale‑up conditions due to better control of potentially explosive impurities.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: When the batch step was transferred to an Alfa Laval plate reactor, large fluctuations (up to 20 %) in conversion and impurity levels were observed, largely caused by vigorous N₂ off‑gassing that altered the mean residence time.
Solution_Description: The reaction was split into two discrete reactors: (R1) low‑temperature (75 °C) formation of acyl azide 5, and (R2) high‑temperature (165 °C) rearrangement to product 3. This ordering limited N₂ generation in the first stage and allowed independent temperature and residence‑time control, stabilising conversion and impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...off‑gassing… clearly affecting mean residence time… resulted in a lower degree of control, due to the greater quantities of nitrogen produced.”; “...it was postulated that if the steps were separated… each step occurred in a discrete reactor… better degree of control.”; “...suitable amounts of 5 could be formed selectively in R1 with a temperature of 75 °C… R2 … set at 165 °C…"

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: Nitrogen off‑gassing during the high‑temperature rearrangement caused pressure spikes and residence‑time fluctuations, leading to inconsistent product quality and occasional reactor fouling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A cooling loop was installed downstream of R2 and before the back‑pressure regulator to lower the temperature below the boiling point of acetonitrile, stabilising pressure and minimizing gas‑phase disruptions; the Hastelloy plate reactor provided efficient heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: “...a cooling loop was introduced… to maintain a stabilised flow… ensure that the temperature is lowered enough to be below the boiling point of acetonitrile and avoid any fluctuations in pressure….”; “...the Hastelloy reactor… more efficient heat transfer… leading to the violent off‑gassing.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: Product 3 precipitated when the outlet temperature fell below ~70 °C, causing partial clogging of the reactor and interruption of flow.
Solution_Description: The outlet temperature was kept continuously above 70 °C during operation and the flow rate/concentration were adjusted to keep product in solution, preventing solid formation and maintaining steady operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...partial clogging due to precipitation of 3 was observed if the temperature of the outlet dropped below 70 °C, therefore, the outlet temperature was kept above this.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: Initial solvent screens (toluene, anisole, isobutyronitrile) gave high levels of impurity 8 and, in the case of toluene with 4‑methylmorpholine, immediate precipitation of solids, indicating poor solubility/mixability of reagents.
Solution_Description: Acetonitrile (MeCN) was selected as the reaction solvent; it fully dissolved DPPA, base and acid, eliminated precipitation, and allowed reliable temperature control and downstream work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Toluene with 4‑methylmorpholine formed a precipitate as soon as heat was applied… no product was detected.”; “...MeCN was the remaining viable non‑protic polar solvent, it was selected as the solvent of choice for further optimization.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: Direct aqueous work‑up of the acetonitrile reaction mixture using brine led to significant product loss in the aqueous phase, making recovery inefficient.
Solution_Description: A solvent‑swap distillation was developed: acetonitrile was removed under reduced pressure, toluene was added, then water was used as an antisolvent to precipitate product 3, giving >80 % recovery and >97 % w/w purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initial attempts to wash the acetonitrile solution using brine were not efficient… Instead, a solvent swap distillation process was developed… toluene/water gave the best recovery and purity data (80 % recovery, >97 % w/w purity).”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacture of a Curtius Rearrangement Using Continuous Flow towards the Large-Scale Manufacture of AZD7648
Problem_Description: Potential formation of heavy‑metal azides from contact of DPPA/azide intermediates with stainless‑steel and Hastelloy components raised safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Materials of construction (C‑22, 316L, Hastelloy C‑22, gold‑sealed IR probe) were evaluated and confirmed not to corrode under process conditions; the system is flushed with fresh solvent before and after runs and a caustic scrubber removes any liberated hydrazoic acid.
Supporting_Evidence: “Concern was raised about the potential risk of DPPA and the acyl azide intermediates forming heavy metal azides on contact with stainless steel (316L) and Hastelloy C‑22… however, these heavy metals are unavailable to react in solution… A much higher risk would be if heavy metal salts were in solution… All development was carried out in similar equipment… without issues related to corrosion.”; “The system was flushed… a caustic scrubber was also used in the vent… to eliminate any potential hydrazoic acid formed.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route used DBU in steps 4 and 5, which generated high levels of persistent impurities that could not be removed in the downstream crystallization, causing the overall product to fall short of USP/ICH purity specifications.
Solution_Description: DBU was replaced by tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH) in the final synthetic steps, yielding a much cleaner crude API solution that allowed successful optimization of the two‑stage continuous crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Before the chemical process had been finalized, DBU was used … which resulted in high levels of impurities that could not be purged.”
• “Ultimately tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH) replaced DBU which resulted in a higher purity crude API solution.”
• “This change allowed optimization of a continuous two‑stage purification which … met the desired purity specifications.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: The dimethylamino impurity (compound 14) proved to be the most difficult impurity to purge in stage 1; its level varied with temperature, ACN‑v/v and pH, and at low temperature the impurity remained above the 0.07 % specification, reducing overall yield and consistency.
Solution_Description: A series of OFAT/DOE experiments demonstrated that increasing the stage 1 temperature (up to 55 °C) and adjusting the neutralization pH from 7.5 to 8.0 significantly improved impurity purging while maintaining acceptable yields; the optimal condition (45 °C, pH 8.0) was selected for continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The dimethylamino impurity (14) is the most persistent … Increase in temperature or ACN v/v results in the lowest levels of the dimethylamino impurity.”
• “A 50 °C stage 1 neutralization resulted in a yield reduction of 38 % … Raising the pH from 7.5 to 8.0 … shows an increase in yield by 15 % with similar purity results.”
• “Temperature is the only significant parameter affecting the purging coefficient of compound 14 … an increase in temperature leads to increased purging.”
• “The linear model … PC (14) = 0.006033 × Temp + 0.6137411.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: When formic acid was used as the acid component in the stage 2 crystallization solvent (0.35 M HCl in 25/75 v/v formic‑acid/water), a new impurity (compound 17) grew over time, likely due to formylation of the piperazine ring, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: Formic acid was replaced by acetic acid in the crystallization solvent (0.30 M HCl in 40/60 v/v acetic‑acid/water), eliminating the formation of impurity 17 and meeting the impurity specifications.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Only the solution with formic acid present resulted in impurity growth of compound 17 … hypothesized that formylation of the piperazine ring was causing the impurity growth.”
• “From these results, acetic acid was selected to replace formic acid in the solvent mixture.”
• “Acetic acid was used in a 40/60 v/v mixture with water, and hydrochloride was lowered from 0.35 to 0.30 M.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: Continuous operation required a steady supply of crude API solution, but the novel synthetic route could not produce enough material for long‑duration continuous experiments, leading to inconsistent material availability and variability in scale‑up studies.
Solution_Description: Small‑scale (150 mL) batch OFAT experiments were performed to generate a robust data set; a statistically‑significant linear model relating temperature to impurity purging was built and then used to predict performance in scaled‑up continuous runs, allowing process development despite limited material supply.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “There is a lack of consistent supply of representative synthetic material … therefore, small‑scale batch optimization and modeling was performed and subsequently used to predict larger scale continuous performance.”
• “A series of design‑of‑experiment (DOE) and one‑factor at a time (OFAT) experiments led to the optimization … a statistically significant linear model was derived in batch within a 20 °C range … tested in continuous flow and predicted the impurity removal within 5 % accuracy.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: Precise pH neutralization of the high‑pH crude reaction mixture in stage 1 was critical; manual or poorly timed acid addition could cause pH drift, leading to inconsistent impurity removal and yield.
Solution_Description: A feedback‑controlled dosing system was implemented: the acid pump delivered the acetic‑acid/ACN/water solution until the pH probe signaled the target, automating the order and rate of addition and maintaining the set pH throughout the continuous cycles.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Upon addition of the high pH crude reaction mixture … a feedback loop is triggered in order to neutralize the pH. The acid pump is directed to deliver the acetic acid/ACN/water solution until the pH probe sends a signal to terminate pumping once the target level is reached.”
• “The cascade transfers and pH neutralizations repeat continuously taking 5–10 min per cycle based on the recipe used.”

Paper Title: Impurity Purging through Systematic Process Development of a Continuous Two-Stage Crystallization
Problem_Description: Stage 2 crystallization required efficient mixing of the feed solution with isopropanol antisolvent; insufficient agitation could lead to poor crystal growth, needle‑shaped morphology, and reduced yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Both stages employed over‑head stirred 2000 mL mixed‑suspension mixed‑product‑removal (MSMPR) crystallizers in series, with precise temperature control and parallel Nutsche‑style filters, providing robust agitation and reliable mass‑transfer for continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Each stage was equipped with two over‑head stirred 2000 mL mixed suspension mixed product removal (MSMPR) crystallizers in series … Stage 2 utilized filtration, washing, and drying (FWD) operation.”
• “Both stages … a combined working volume of 3600 mL and a residence time of 2 h, with each MSMPR in a stage at the same temperature.”
• “The filtration apparatus was equipped with a Hastelloy agitator …”

Paper Title: Tracking the Isotopologues: Process Improvement for the Synthesis of a Deuterated Pyrazole
Problem_Description: A 15–20 % over‑deuterated C5‑isotopologue (compound 2) is formed together with the target pyrazole 1 in every batch, reducing the overall potency and lowering the effective assay‑corrected yield of the desired material.
Solution_Description: A 10 wt % aqueous NaOH wash performed after the two‑step sequence removes the HOD‑derived deuterium impurity, giving >99 % d³‑product with no measurable d⁴‑contamination and restores high assay‑corrected yield (70–80 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “small amounts of C5‑deuterium incorporation (∼15 to 20%) were lowering the overall potency…overdeuterated isotopologue 2” (p. 3). • “a 10 wt % sodium hydroxide wash…proved effective for removing d⁴ impurities…affording 70–80 % assay‑corrected yield, 100 % purity by HPLC” (p. 8).

Paper Title: Tracking the Isotopologues: Process Improvement for the Synthesis of a Deuterated Pyrazole
Problem_Description: The cheaper deuterated alcohol CD₃OD (≈ $160/10 g) is used as the CD₃ source, but its trace HOD generates the unwanted C5‑deuteration, compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: Switching the CD₃ source from CD₃OD to the more expensive CD₃OH eliminates the HOD impurity, preventing over‑deuteration, albeit at a higher material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “CD₃OD is ∼3× cheaper than CD₃OH…suggesting that the use of CD₃OD is a more cost‑efficient source of CD₃ for manufacture” (p. 4). • “a logical solution…would be to switch CD₃ sources to CD₃OH…guarantee that exchangeable deuterium atoms are not available” (p. 5).

Paper Title: Tracking the Isotopologues: Process Improvement for the Synthesis of a Deuterated Pyrazole
Problem_Description: A brine wash of the tosylate intermediate removes HOD but creates a heterogeneous mixture and incomplete conversion of the tosylate, reducing overall throughput.
Solution_Description: The brine wash was evaluated but ultimately not adopted; instead, a 10 wt % NaOH aqueous wash was chosen because it removes HOD without generating a heterogeneous reaction mass or conversion loss.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A brine wash…proved successful for generating higher‑quality 1, but the overall process suffered from incomplete conversion and heterogeneous reaction conditions due to precipitation of salt” (p. 6). • “The third strategy…performed an aqueous base wash…solved all of these issues in one operation” (p. 7).

Paper Title: Tracking the Isotopologues: Process Improvement for the Synthesis of a Deuterated Pyrazole
Problem_Description: Using 3 Å molecular sieves to dry the reaction mixture removes HOD but introduces difficult filtration steps that are not practical at scale.
Solution_Description: Although molecular sieves successfully removed the HOD impurity, the approach was abandoned in favor of the aqueous NaOH wash because it avoids the problematic filtration step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using 3 Å molecular sieves before the introduction of pyrazole could also remove HOD…resulted in higher‑quality material…however…the use of molecular sieves posed practical filtration issues for scale‑up” (p. 6).

Paper Title: Tracking the Isotopologues: Process Improvement for the Synthesis of a Deuterated Pyrazole
Problem_Description: The addition of tosyl chloride to the sodium hydroxide/THF mixture is highly exothermic; uncontrolled temperature rise can affect reaction conversion and safety.
Solution_Description: The authors controlled the addition rate of the TsCl solution and maintained the reactor temperature below 35 °C (by slow addition and external cooling), thereby managing the exotherm and ensuring consistent conversion.

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of Menthol from Citral over Ni/H-β-38 Extrudates Containing Bentonite Clay Binder in Batch and Continuous Reactors
Problem_Description: The catalytic performance (activity, conversion and selectivity) varied dramatically with the nickel precursor used (nitrate, acetate, chloride, sulfate).  NiS (sulfate) showed very low activity and selectivity because sulfur remained on the catalyst and poisoned active sites; NiCl gave low conversion due to large Ni particles; NiA and NiN gave the best results.  In the continuous trickle‑bed reactor the apparent activation energy (18.6 kJ mol⁻¹) and a Weisz modulus of ≈ 3 indicated strong mass‑transfer limitations, causing slow reaction rates and a gradual loss of conversion over time‑on‑stream.  Catalyst deactivation was observed after several hours as the specific surface area dropped 55‑67 % because of coke/organic oligomer deposition.  Extrudates made with bentonite and methylcellulose showed relatively low mechanical strength (vertical ≈ 2.6 MPa, horizontal ≈ 1.2 MPa) compared with binder‑only extrudates, reflecting difficulties in mixing/viscosity during shaping.
Solution_Description: 1. Choose nickel nitrate (or acetate) as the precursor – these salts decompose at lower temperatures, give smaller Ni particles (6‑11 nm) and produce catalysts with low amounts of strong Brønsted acid sites, thus improving activity, selectivity and reducing sulfur poisoning.  2. Use a bentonite‑based binder and extrude the catalyst (batch → trickle‑bed reactor) to create a mesoporous structure that enhances mass‑transfer and maintains the β‑zeolite framework.  3. Operate the trickle‑bed reactor for a short initial period (≈ 3 h) and then work at steady‑state; the initial rapid deactivation is limited and conversion stabilises, mitigating coke buildup.  4. Avoid sulfate or chloride precursors to eliminate sulfur‑related deactivation and avoid large Ni particles that lower active surface area.  5. Add methylcellulose as an organic binder and optimise the zeolite : bentonite ratio (7 : 3) to improve the rheology of the paste, resulting in extrudates with higher mechanical strength and better shape stability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The effect of nickel precursors (nitrate, chloride, acetate, and sulfate) … demonstrating higher activity for the Ni‑H‑β‑38‑bentonite composite derived from a nickel nitrate precursor … The most efficient catalyst was synthesized from nickel nitrate … second‑best from acetate … low activity of ex‑sulfate and ex‑chloride catalysts could be the lowest volume of mesopores … sulfur … can interact with organic molecules, provoking potentially severe catalyst deactivation.” (Intro & Sec 2.1) 
• “The apparent activation energy … 18.6 kJ mol⁻¹ indicated the presence of mass‑transfer limitations … Weisz modulus … ≈ 3, significantly exceeding the minimum value (i.e., 0.6) for the first‑order reaction.” (Sec 2.3) 
• “The specific surface area observed for the powder catalysts … decreased by 55 % for NiN and 67 % for NiS after reaction … organic deposits caused the catalyst deactivation because of formation of oligomers (C₁₀H₁₆)ₓ.” (Sec 2.2) 
• “The mechanical strength of [(NiN/H‑β‑38)+bentonite] extrudates … 2.6 ± 0.3 MPa (vertical) and 1.2 ± 0.2 MPa (horizontal) … lower compared to extrudates made only from bentonite …” (Sec 2.1) 
• “The 5 wt % Ni‑containing extrudates were prepared … using methylcellulose (viscosity: 4000 cP) as an organic binder to improve the rheological properties of the paste …” (Sec 4.1) 
• “Ex‑nitrate Ni/H‑β‑38‑bentonite extrudates gave the highest surface area (272 m² g⁻¹) and best performance …” (Sec 2.2) 
• “Sulfur was confirmed to be present in the fresh and spent NiS catalysts … the large hydrogen consumption is related not only to metal reduction but also to the partial reduction of sulfur …” (Sec 2.1) 
• “Large Ni particles … observed for NiCl … which are catalytically inactive due to a low number of exposed sites.” (Sec 2.2) 
• “Initially, at 70 °C, defunctionalized menthanes … were formed … their selectivity dropped substantially after 4 h … thereafter selectivities to menthol and hydrogenated acyclic products increased rapidly.” (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Exploiting the Physical Properties of Diethanolamine Boronic Esters for Process Improvements in AZD5718
Problem_Description: The pinacol boronic ester (4) is an oily liquid that cannot be isolated as a solid, forcing a telescoped solution‑phase transfer into the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling. This necessitates a five‑extraction work‑up, acid‑induced precipitation of an amorphous solid, and a 2‑week low‑temperature drying step (150 °C) on 150 kg scale, severely limiting throughput and increasing cycle time.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to a diethanolamine (DEA) boronic ester (9) that crystallises as a free‑flowing solid. This new intermediate can be isolated by filtration, removing the need for telescoping, reducing the number of extractions to one, and enabling a rapid 1‑day drying of a crystalline product.

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Asymmetric Total Synthesis of (−)-Emetine with Pharmaceutical Grade Quality; First Multigram Scale Synthesis
Problem_Description: The original Ito‑type route required silica‑gel column chromatography for every step, many intermediates were non‑crystalline oils, and acrolein (a toxic, strong irritant) was used. Over‑oxidation of intermediate 3 to the isoquinoline occurred, leading to poor reproducibility and low yields. The crystallization of the allylation product gave a gel‑like precipitate that was difficult to filter. Scale‑up of the Pd(OH)2/C deoxygenation step suffered from variable yields due to metal leaching from the autoclave. Reduction of ketone 13 gave undesired lactone/lactol side‑products under standard conditions.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced step‑wise addition of HMTA to suppress over‑oxidation of 3 and give reproducible yields (ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION). They screened cheaper ligands and reagents (TBAF, CuCl) and selected (R)‑DADMP‑BINAP to improve enantioselectivity while reducing cost (CATA LYST OPTIMIZATION, COST). Toxic acrolein was replaced by methyl‑vinyl‑ketone, avoiding a safety hazard (SOLVENT/REAGENT CHANGE). Reaction temperature was raised (50 °C) for the asymmetric allylation to increase conversion without loss of ee (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION). A new work‑up using an upfront HCl salt formation eliminated the gel‑like crystals, giving a readily filterable product (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE). When conversion with (R)‑SEGPHOS was low, extra CuCl and ligand were added to reach >95 % conversion (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE). The protection‑olefin‑metathesis‑deprotection sequence was telescoped, removing the need for column chromatography (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY). Scaling the Pd‑catalyzed deoxygenation required a newer stainless‑steel autoclave to prevent metal leaching and regain yield (REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS). The reduction of ketone 13 was performed at –10 °C with a reverse quench into aqueous citric acid to suppress lactone/lactol formation (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION).

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Substituted 3,4-Propylenedioxythiophene Derivatives

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Substituted 3,4-Propylenedioxythiophene Derivatives
Problem_Description: The traditional Williamson etherification uses sodium hydride in DMF; NaH is explosively reactive, especially on scale, and its quenching generates large exotherms, making batch scale‑up hazardous.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow setup was employed: NaH is delivered as a slurry with a peristaltic pump, reactants are mixed at a T‑mixer, the reaction occurs in a heated static‑mix reactor, and the effluent is immediately quenched with methanol in a downstream loop, safely dissipating the exotherm and minimizing hazardous inventory.
Supporting_Evidence: "The commonly used etherification process involves… sodium hydride as the base in polar solvents like DMF…It is not trivial to scale up this reaction…due to the explosive nature of NaH…the quenching of unreacted sodium hydride…needs to be done with utmost care because of the high exothermicity…Solution…solution B was a slurry, and hence a peristaltic pump…the combined reaction mixture was introduced to a 10 mL ETFE reactor…At the exit…a 2 mL ETFE loop…methanol was introduced…resulting in the continuous quenching of the unreacted sodium hydride inside the loop in a controlled manner…"

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Substituted 3,4-Propylenedioxythiophene Derivatives
Problem_Description: After about 2.5 h of continuous operation the acetone‑protected dibromodiol conversion began to drop, indicating catalyst deactivation.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Substituted 3,4-Propylenedioxythiophene Derivatives
