Paper Title: Aqueous Electrochemical Synthesis of 5‑Trifluoromethyluracil in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: A residence time of 13 min in the flow cell caused anodic fouling due to gas (H₂ and SO₂) buildup, halting the reaction.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The optimal residence time was set to 7 min, which gave the highest yield (55 %) without fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the residence time was adjusted to 13 min, the anodic fouling of the electrode was observed …”; “When the residence time was 7 min, an optimum yield of 55 % was obtained (entry 1).”

Paper Title: Aqueous Electrochemical Synthesis of 5‑Trifluoromethyluracil in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Continuous‑flow electrolysis on a 15 mmol scale afforded only ~50 % yield, lower than the batch process because of incomplete conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors propose moving to a continuous‑stirred‑tank‑reactor (CSTR) configuration to improve mixing, residence‑time distribution and overall conversion for larger scale flow production.
Supporting_Evidence: “the insufficient conversion of uracil 1a during continuous flow electrolysis led to a minor decrease in yield.”; “This could potentially be improved by translating to a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR)‑based system for further scale‑up synthesis.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: The previously reported linear syntheses of eldecalcitol required 27–27 steps (lithocholic acid) or 16 steps (cholesterol) and gave overall yields of only ~0.03 %–0.5 %, making the routes excessively long for practical production.
Solution_Description: A convergent 13‑step route was designed that uses a Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons olefination of an A‑ring fragment (derived from inexpensive d‑mannose) with a C/D‑ring ketone, delivering the key epoxide intermediate 17 in 9 % overall yield and drastically shortening the synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The linear approach … 27‑steps, overall yield: ∼0.03 %… or cholesterol (16‑steps, overall yield: ∼0.5 %). However, the long reaction routes, low yield … make them less than ideal.”
“The novel, practical, and scalable approach … via the Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons (HWE) olefination … was described.”
“...13 steps, 9.0% overall yield… employing d‑mannose as the chiral pool… reducing the complexity of the chiral separation process.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: Direct Williamson ether alkylation of the trityl‑protected intermediate 7a with TBSO‑(CH₂)₃OTf repeatedly failed because of steric hindrance at the reaction site.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Williamson ether step with a Michael addition of methyl acrylate to intermediate 7, using cesium carbonate as base and t‑butanol as co‑solvent, which successfully installed the carboxypropyl side chain.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Although the most straightforward way to install the hydroxypropyl group … we made various attempts to directly alkylate 7a … however, all attempts were unsuccessful, possibly due to the steric hindrance at this position.”
“An alternative approach involves the utilization of a Michael addition reaction … treating 7 with methyl acrylate (10 V), cesium carbonate (4 equiv), and t‑butanol (5 V) … suitable for the manufacturing process.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: Early Michael‑addition experiments gave no conversion with DABCO, and even with inorganic bases the conversion plateaued at 70–78 % despite changing bases, stoichiometry, and temperature, indicating sub‑optimal yield and reproducibility.
Solution_Description: The optimal conditions were identified as 4 equiv cesium carbonate, 10 equiv methyl acrylate, and 5 equiv t‑butanol at 20–30 °C, giving an isolated yield of 78 % for the Michael‑addition product.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initial attempts with DABCO as a base gave no reaction … using cesium carbonate as a base gave satisfactory conversion (70 %). … extending the reaction time did not significantly improve the conversion … changes in temperature showed an adverse effect … Finally, we found that treating 7 with methyl acrylate (10 V), cesium carbonate (4 equiv), and t‑butanol (5 V) … suitable … entry 5) … 78 % yield.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: During the Appel iodination of compound 9, a competing side‑product (furanose 10b) formed in significant amounts, and 10 and 10b could not be separated by TLC, lowering the isolated yield of the desired iodide 10.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen was performed; a 2:1 (v/v) toluene/acetonitrile mixture gave the best selectivity (83 % 10 vs 11 % 10b), improving the overall yield of the iodination step.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The formation of 10b is likely due to the reverse Michael addition … In preliminary experiments, we observed that the solvent plays a crucial role … Several solvents … were investigated … The optimal reaction conditions were determined to be a mixed solvent of toluene and acetonitrile (2:1, v/v). … ratio of 10 to 10b was found to be approximately 83:11.”
Table 2 entries show yields for each solvent; entry 5 (toluene/acetonitrile 2:1) gives 83 % 10 versus 11 % 10b.

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: The Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation used in earlier routes required equimolar tert‑butyl hydroperoxide, a peroxide that poses a safety risk on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The new strategy avoids the Sharpless epoxidation entirely by constructing all three A‑ring stereocenters directly from d‑mannose, eliminating peroxide handling and improving process safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Nevertheless, the use of equimolar amounts of tert‑butyl hydroperoxide in this route presents a potential safety hazard.”
“The improved route … utilizes d‑mannose as the chiral pool to directly assemble all the stereocenters … eliminating the need for asymmetric oxidation required for the construction of the C‑3 stereocenter.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: Many intermediates in the sequence are oily and difficult to isolate, historically requiring column chromatography for most steps, which is labor‑intensive and costly at scale.
Solution_Description: The process was reorganized so that only three key steps require column chromatography; the crude product from the Michael addition and subsequent de‑protection steps are carried forward without isolation, dramatically reducing purification workload.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Although most of the intermediates are oily and difficult to purify and separate, only the key three steps require purification by column chromatography in these 13 reactions.”
“The crude 8 obtained was utilized in the next step without further purification … The crude 9 … was used without further purification … only the key three steps require purification.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: Reduction of the methyl ester with LiAlH₄ is hazardous (pyrophoric, exothermic) and unsuitable for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: LiAlH₄ was replaced with the milder reducing agent DIBAL‑H, which safely reduces the ester under controlled low temperature, making the step amenable to industrial scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “With 12 in hand, instead of LiAlH₄ … DIBAL‑H was chosen to reduce the methyl ester moiety to afford 13, which was more suitable for the industrial‑scale process.”

Paper Title: Novel, Practical, and Scalable Approach for the Synthesis of Eldecalcitol
Problem_Description: Achieving consistent high enantiomeric excess and purity for eldecalcitol on multi‑kilogram batches required precise control; earlier processes showed batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: The authors repeatedly performed the optimized sequence, controlling addition order, temperature ramps, and quench conditions, enabling reproducible production of 3 kg of intermediate 17 with high ee and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Our team has repeatedly performed this process to obtain the key intermediate 17 and subsequently used it in reactions to consistently produce eldecalcitol with high enantiomeric excess and excellent purity, scaling up to a maximum of 3 kg.”

Paper Title: Gram-Scale Synthesis of the C14–C23 Fragment of Eribulin
Problem_Description: The original Kishi synthesis of the C14‑C23 fragment required 18 steps and gave a low overall yield, making large‑scale preparation of eribulin costly and difficult to purify.
Solution_Description: A concise 14‑step route from cheap l‑arabinose was developed, giving an overall 24 % isolated yield and using inexpensive reagents. The new sequence avoids the problematic steps of the original route and provides a more scalable process.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the original Kishi route, this fragment was prepared from 2‑deoxy‑l‑arabinose diethyl thioacetal 4,5‑acetonide in 18 steps… However, it is still necessary to develop a more concise route with easier purification and higher yields for large‑scale preparation… Herein, we report a synthetic route… highlighted by an α‑stereospecific C‑glycosylation… overall 24 % yield.”

Paper Title: Gram-Scale Synthesis of the C14–C23 Fragment of Eribulin
Problem_Description: The α,β‑unsaturated ester (12) normally required column chromatography before use as the C‑glycosylation donor, adding time and material cost.
Solution_Description: The crude ester 12 was isolated by a simple filtration and used directly in the C‑glycosylation without column purification, streamlining the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “…could be directly used as the C‑glycosylation donor after quick filtration without column purification.”

Paper Title: Gram-Scale Synthesis of the C14–C23 Fragment of Eribulin
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of ester 12 over Pd/C is highly flammable and poses a fire risk on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Safety notes advise purging excess hydrogen with nitrogen before filtration and using a non‑flammable solvent (wet DCM) for handling the Pd/C cake.
Supporting_Evidence: “Safety precaution notes: The mixture is highly flammable. It is recommended… to purge the excess hydrogen with nitrogen before filtration. A nonflammable solvent such as wet DCM could be used for filtration…”

Paper Title: Gram-Scale Synthesis of the C14–C23 Fragment of Eribulin
Problem_Description: Quenching of LiAlH₄ reductions is highly exothermic and can cause violent reactions if not performed carefully.
Solution_Description: The authors recommend low‑temperature quench with sequential addition of isopropanol, methanol, then water, and the use of potassium sodium tartrate to avoid emulsions and control the heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “Safety precaution notes: quenching with water is highly exothermic. It is recommended to quench LiAlH₄ at low temperatures through sequential addition of isopropanol, methanol, and water. Aq. potassium sodium tartrate could be used to avoid emulsions.”

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Initial biocatalytic reduction of the bulky, hydrophobic α‑bromo‑ketone 4a gave only 25.7 % conversion at a 5 g L⁻¹ substrate loading.
Solution_Description: A library screen identified KRED‑205 from Lactobacillus kefiri, which provided >99.9 % ee and was selected as the biocatalyst for further development.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Only 6 out of 180 KREDs… displayed activities toward 4a… KRED‑205 showed excellent enantioselectivity… conversion was poor at a substrate loading of 5 g L⁻¹.” (Table 1 description) • “KRED‑205 was thus chosen for further investigation.” (Results and Discussion, p. 3)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: The highly hydrophobic substrate 4a showed poor solubility in aqueous buffer, limiting the achievable substrate concentration and reaction conversion.
Solution_Description: A biphasic MTBE/water system (10 % v/v MTBE) was adopted as the cosolvent to improve substrate dissolution while maintaining enzyme activity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Considering the hydrophobic nature of 4a, an organic cosolvent would be essential to help solubilize the reaction substrate… 12 solvents were evaluated… MTBE gave higher conversions.” (Results and Discussion) • “Hence, MTBE was eventually selected as the cosolvent throughout the following experiments.” (p. 4)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Certain organic cosolvents (EA, DMF, DMSO) caused protein denaturation, dramatically reducing enzyme activity and conversion.
Solution_Description: These denaturing solvents were excluded from the optimization; only MTBE, THF, and toluene were retained, preserving enzyme integrity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction rates were found reduced when treated with ethyl acetate (EA), N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF), and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). The potential explanation was that the addition of these organic solvents led to protein denaturation, which resulted in a loss of enzyme activity.” (p. 4)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Using toluene as the cosolvent required high‑temperature post‑treatment, which generated a dimer impurity that complicated product isolation.
Solution_Description: MTBE replaced toluene as the cosolvent, eliminating the high‑boiling‑point issue and the associated dimer impurity, simplifying downstream work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Although comparable conversions were observed for both toluene and MTBE, the high boiling point of toluene would require a higher concentration temperature during the post‑treatment of product 1a, which resulted in a notable formation of a dimer impurity… thus making it difficult for product purification.” (p. 4) • “MTBE was eventually selected as the cosolvent throughout the following experiments.” (p. 4)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Enzyme activity was highly pH‑dependent; conversions dropped sharply outside the pH 6.0–7.0 window, leading to inconsistent results.
Solution_Description: The reaction pH was fixed at 7.0, which was identified as the optimum for maintaining high conversion across the study.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Wet whole cells with overexpressed KRED‑205 were sensitive to pH changes outside the narrow optimal range of pH 6.0–7.0… To achieve the maximum conversion with the least adjustment, pH 7.0 was selected as the optimum pH value for the rest of the experiments.” (p. 5)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Raising the reaction temperature above 45 °C decreased conversion, likely due to MTBE evaporation and increased substrate/product concentration.
Solution_Description: The optimal temperature of 40 °C was chosen, balancing enzyme activity, substrate diffusion, and solvent stability.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Peak conversions were observed at 40–45 °C… the conversion started to decrease when the temperature continued to increase to 50 °C, possibly due to the evaporation of solvent MTBE, which led to an increased substrate/product concentration.” (Table 2 discussion) • “Therefore, the preferred reaction temperature was set at 40 °C…” (p. 6)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Increasing substrate loading to 80–85 g L⁻¹ together with reduced cofactor loading slowed the reaction, giving <80 % conversion after 23 h.
Solution_Description: The proportion of isopropanol (co‑substrate for NADPH regeneration) was raised to 15.6 % v/v, which boosted conversion. MTBE loading was also optimized (≤42.2 % v/v) to maintain solubility without inhibiting the enzyme.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reduced cofactor loading and the increased substrate concentration led to a decrease in reaction conversion… As shown in Figure 4, the conversion was improved with an increased proportion of isopropanol when the highest conversion was obtained with an IPA proportion of 15.6 % v/v.” (p. 7) • “Higher conversion was not observed when MTBE was added with a proportion larger than 42.2 % v/v (Figure 5).” (p. 7)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Even with optimized conditions, conversions remained sub‑optimal unless a high biocatalyst loading (>50 wt % relative to substrate) was used, raising material cost.
Solution_Description: The biocatalyst loading was increased to 50 wt % (over 850 g of wet cells for the 30 L scale), achieving ≥94 % conversion while balancing cost and productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We had to increase the dosage of the biocatalyst… the reaction was complete when the biocatalyst loading (overexpressed wet whole cell) was above 50 % wt… with a conversion of 94.3 % after 23 h.” (Figure 6, p. 8) • “Considering the overall cost and post‑treatment manipulation efficiency, a biocatalyst loading of 50 % wt was considered to be the optimal choice.” (p. 8)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, emulsification caused by cellular debris and membrane components interfered with product isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A celite co‑filtration step was introduced after MTBE removal, efficiently breaking the emulsion and allowing clean separation of the crude bromohydrin.
Supporting_Evidence: • “After all of the reaction parameters were determined, scale‑up studies were conducted but emulsification was encountered during product isolation… an improved post‑treatment process with celite co‑filtration was developed.” (Scale‑Up Demonstration, p. 9)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Traditional isolation of the bromohydrin 1a was labor‑intensive, requiring multiple solvent exchanges and filtrations.
Solution_Description: The crude 1a obtained after celite filtration was used directly in the subsequent intramolecular epoxidation without further purification, streamlining the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A small level of epoxide 2 was found during the work‑up. As such, the collected filtrate of crude 1a was then used directly without further purification in the next step of epoxidation.” (Scale‑Up Demonstration, p. 9)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: The epoxidation step required careful base selection; some bases gave poor conversion or side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: NaOH was identified as the most suitable inorganic base (1.05 equiv, 15–25 °C), and its addition was optimized to avoid over‑reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A further evaluation of the base was conducted and the results indicated NaOH as the most suitable reagent from a range of common inorganic bases… 1.05 equiv of NaOH and a reaction temperature of 15–25 °C were considered as the optimal reaction parameters.” (Scale‑Up Demonstration, p. 9)

Paper Title: Biocatalytic Asymmetric Reduction of a Sterically Hindered α‑Bromo Ketone for the Synthesis of Key Intermediates of Olodaterol
Problem_Description: Large‑scale production required a robust enzyme source; the study moved from lyophilized cells to wet whole cells for better practicality.
Solution_Description: Wet whole cells were adopted for all subsequent reactions, offering easier handling and lower cost at scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Lyophilized whole cells were used as the enzyme formulation in the early stage… however, lyophilized whole cells used in the early development stage are less favored… Therefore, wet whole cells were subjected to the present and subsequent investigations.” (Results and Discussion, p. 4)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Asymmetric Process for the Synthesis of GLYT1 Inhibitor BI 425809 (Iclepertin)
Problem_Description: The initial racemic synthesis of intermediate 6 produced an equal mixture of the desired product 1 and the undesired diastereomer 8, which could only be separated by a labor‑intensive preparative HPLC – a process unsuitable for scale‑up and driving up material cost.
Solution_Description: An asymmetric synthesis of 6 was developed using a chiral lactone (11) derived from inexpensive bulk chemicals ((R)‑epichlorohydrin and diethyl malonate). The route sets the two stereocenters in a single step with >99 % ee, avoiding the racemic mixture and the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “A main drawback of the non‑asymmetric approach … gave rise to an equal mixture of diastereomers 1 and 8, which could only be resolved through a very labor‑intensive preparative HPLC. As this was not ideal for scale‑up, we sought to develop a streamlined, chromatography‑free, scalable, and asymmetric approach …”; “Although lactone 11 was obtained in a modest yield (45–50%) … their condensation turned out to be a very efficient way to set the two key stereocenters in 11 with high enantioselectivity (>99 % ee) in a single chemical step.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Asymmetric Process for the Synthesis of GLYT1 Inhibitor BI 425809 (Iclepertin)
Problem_Description: Hydrogenolysis of the benzyl protecting group with Pd/C was highly sensitive to the quality of the substrate; some batches failed to reach full conversion, required a charcoal filtration step, and suffered a 5–10 % mass loss.
Solution_Description: The benzyl amine was replaced by aqueous ammonia; the azabicyclic core was formed directly from bis‑mesylate 13 and subsequently protected with Boc, eliminating the problematic hydrogenolysis step altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “the hydrogenolysis failed to reach completion with some batches … required a filtration through a charcoal cartridge … a modest but noticeable mass loss (5–10 %)”; “the formation of the [3.1.0]‑azabicyclic core by addition of ammonia instead of benzyl amine was developed … the resulting azabicyclo[3.1.0]‑hexane was not isolated but instead protected with Boc anhydride … to avoid this potential problem and eliminate the hydrogenolysis step.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Asymmetric Process for the Synthesis of GLYT1 Inhibitor BI 425809 (Iclepertin)
Problem_Description: The Ru‑catalyzed asymmetric reduction of trifluoroacetone required 600 psi H₂ and posed safety concerns because trifluoroacetone can undergo highly exothermic thermal decomposition under solvent‑free conditions.
Solution_Description: A Rh‑catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation of 1‑(trifluoromethyl)‑vinyl acetate (24) using the air‑stable ligand t‑Bu‑SMS‑Phos·2HBF₄ (27) was developed. This method operates at only 15 psi H₂, avoids the exothermic decomposition issue, and delivers the product 25 in 99 % yield with 98–99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “the H₂ pressure required (600 psi) was relatively high and there were safety concerns … highly exothermic thermal decomposition of trifluoroacetone … As a result, an alternative method involving a novel Rh‑catalyzed asymmetric reduction of 1‑(trifluoromethyl)‑vinyl acetate 24 was developed … using the solid and air‑stable ligand t‑Bu‑SMS‑Phos·2HBF₄ (27) gave … 99 % yield and 98–99 % ee.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The homologation of lactam 3 to give lactam 4 using the original LHMDS/LDA‑chloroiodomethane protocol gave highly variable and low isolated yields (15‑50 %) and did not scale well; solid lithium chloroacetate salts precipitated and clogged the flow reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A magnesium (or lithium) enolate of chloroacetic acid was employed instead of LHMDS/LDA, run at –10 °C in batch (40‑50 % yield) and in a plug‑flow reactor (≈60 % yield, 90 % conversion). The use of a more soluble acetate salt prevented solid formation, and the flow‑reactor provided superior temperature and mixing control.
Supporting_Evidence: “The first‑generation homologation protocol was highly variable in yield (∼15–50 % yield) and generally did not scale well using LHMDS and/or LDA with chloroiodomethane.”; “The chloroacetatic acid lithium or magnesium enolate performed much more reliably, providing 40–50 % yield of 4 in a batch mode at −10 °C.”; “When switching over to a plug flow reactor, the isolated yield improved to about 60% with 90% conversion.”; “The lithium enolate had issues with solids forming and clogging the flow reactor… formation of the monolithium salt of chloroacetic acid which then failed to undergo enolization to the more soluble dilithium salt.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: Lactam 3 was only isolable by chromatography because of its poor crystallinity, making large‑scale purification problematic.
Solution_Description: After reduction of intermediate 23, the Boc protecting group was removed with tosic acid to give the tosylate salt of 25, which crystallizes readily from methanol or isopropanol, providing a robust, scalable isolation point.
Supporting_Evidence: “Lactam 3 was prepared… required chromatography for purification due to the relatively poor crystallinity of 3.”; “The tosylate salt of 25 was found to be optimal… crystallized readily from methanol or isopropanol.”; “The tosylate salt of 25 was implemented… after workup, 3 was azeotropically dried… charged anhydrous tosic acid… heated to 45–55 °C to enable Boc cleavage and direct crystallization of 25 as the tosylate salt.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The originally reported route to the indole fragment 9 used high‑energy azide intermediates, posing significant safety hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: A Cu‑catalyzed C–N coupling (ligand‑free) followed by a Cu‑catalyzed C–O coupling using oxalamide ligands (e.g., DPEO, DMAPO) was developed to assemble the indole 9 without azides, providing a safer, scalable process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The route to the indole fragment (9) … not deemed suitable for larger scale manufacture due to the high energy azide intermediates.”; “A new sequence featured a Cu‑catalyzed C‑N ring closure that relies only on the substrate and triethylamine as a ligand … as well as a Cu‑catalyzed C‑O coupling to install the methoxy group.”; “Oxalamide ligands were found to be quite effective… DPEO and DMAPO performed similarly for this coupling.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: Lufotrelvir 2 and its intermediates (1, 8, 13) suffered epimerization at the stereocenter α‑to‑ketone under basic or elevated pH, leading to lower diastereomeric ratios and reduced yields.
Solution_Description: The amidation of 9 with leucine was performed using N‑methylimidazole (a mild base) instead of triethylamine, which prevented epimerization; later, Zn(OTf)₂/EDCI was employed for the coupling of 13 and 5 to further suppress epimerization.
Supporting_Evidence: “With triethylamine, this was more difficult to achieve and required careful matching of the stoichiometry… however, when using N‑methylimidazole, pyridine or a related mild base, epimerization was not observed even when used in excess.”; “It was recognized during screening of Lewis acids that Zn salts could help suppress epimerization of 13.”; “Using stoichiometric amounts of ZnOTf₂ with EDCI (rather than HATU) … delivered a dr of 85:15 to 92:8 in situ on ∼600 g scale.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The phosphorylation step (alkylation of 8 with DTBKPhos) generated insoluble impurity 17 (a pseudodimer) that could precipitate during parenteral formulation, and the reaction gave variable impurity levels depending on solvent and stoichiometry.
Solution_Description: A solvent blend of 85 % MEK / 15 % DMSO was adopted, and the stoichiometry of DTBKPhos was lowered to 1.5 equiv while NaI was kept at 0.2 equiv; the addition was performed at 25–35 °C over ~24 h, which reduced impurity 17 to ≤0.1 % in the final material.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solvent had a profound impact on limiting the formation of 17… By blending a polar aprotic solvent such as DMSO or DMF with acetone or MEK, the alkylation proceeded more cleanly.”; “Using too little sodium iodide would result in more opportunity for 8 to degrade to 13… If the concentration of DTBKPhos is higher, this can preferentially outcompete 13… the solvent blend 85:15 MEK‑to‑DMSO was implemented which typically formed about 1 % of 17 in situ, resulting in a level of about 0.1 % in crude 2.”; “The optimized phosphorylation protocol involved reacting 8 with DTBKPhos (1.5 equiv) with NaI (0.2 equiv) in DMSO (1.5 vol) and MEK (8.5 vol) at 25–35 °C over about 24 h.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The original deprotection of the tert‑butyl protected phosphate used concentrated HCl, which was highly exothermic, gave variable purity, and promoted epimerization and degradation of 2.
Solution_Description: Oxalic acid (5–6 equiv) at 50–60 °C for 6–12 h was employed as a milder deprotecting agent, giving controlled deprotection with only 2–5 % epimer formation (later reduced to <0.2 % after purification).
Supporting_Evidence: “Another concern with the initial process was the use of TFA … could lead to highly variable purity results due to the propensity for epimerization, and degradation.”; “After examining a number of potential acids for the deprotection, oxalic acid emerged as a leading option. The tert‑butyl groups … were smoothly cleaved with oxalic acid (5–6 equiv) at 50–60 °C over 6–12 h … the milder acid limited most side reactions though typically epimer formed at a level of 2–5% in situ which was readily purged to a level below 0.2%.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The MEK solvate of 2, isolated after deprotection, was unsuitable for long‑term storage because it desolvated easily and contained residual organic solvent, and the hydrate form was prone to hydrolysis to 1.
Solution_Description: A DMSO‑solvated form of 2 was discovered by crystallizing from DMSO/MEK (or DMSO/iPrOH) and proved stable (≤0.05 % 1 after 12 weeks) and gave better bulk density; the DMSO solvate was then isolated as a dedicated step after the MEK solvate stage.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was noticed that dissolution in DMSO and crystallization with MEK or iPrOH led to new solid forms… the DMSO solvate was found to be relatively stable to storage even at ambient conditions… level of 1 as an impurity in the DMSO solvate of 2 would remain at NMT 0.05 % over this same time period.”; “The DMSO solvate isolation was integrated into the route as an independent step by redissolving the MEK solvated form of 2 in MEK (∼2 vol) and DMSO (∼1 vol) at ambient conditions and crystallizing 2 as the DMSO solvate with the addition of iPrOH (∼15 vol) as antisolvent.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The initial Claisen homologation of 31 with chloroacetic acid required very high loading (20 equiv) of t‑BuMgCl, leading to low conversion and side‑reactions such as dehalogenation.
Solution_Description: The Grignard loading was optimized to 12–14 equiv and N‑methylpiperidine was used as a more nucleophilic amine ligand, reducing dehalogenation to <5 % and delivering >97 % conversion with 60‑75 % isolated yield for 8.
Supporting_Evidence: “A high loading of t‑BuMgCl was required (originally 20 equiv) which was optimized down to 12–14 equiv.”; “Triethylamine gave acceptable results (7–10% dehalogenation), but much less dehalogenation (<5%) was observed with the more nucleophilic N‑methylpiperidine or N‑methylpyrrolidine.”; “Under optimal conditions… the reaction proceeded to >97% conversion with minimal impurities other than ~3% dehalogenation. After workup, 8 was isolated in 60–75% yield.”

Paper Title: Early Clinical Development of Lufotrelvir as a Potential Therapy for COVID-19
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the final API 2 from the hydrate form suffered from low bulk density (≈0.2 g mL⁻¹) and needle morphology, making handling and downstream processing difficult.
Solution_Description: A two‑step polymorph conversion was employed: the MEK solvate was reslurried in ethanol at 40–45 °C to give the hydrate, then the hydrate was washed and dried; later a 2‑MeTHF/MeOH blend was used to improve solubility and enable a higher‑density, rod‑shaped hydrate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The isolation of 2 as the MEK solvate… was undesirable as a final form… The non‑stoichiometric hydrated form of 2 had been selected for clinical development… Generally, protic solvents favored conversion to the desired hydrate… The bulk density of the hydrated form of 2 was generally about 0.2 g/mL with a needle morphology, while the more favorable DMSO solvated form… was 0.3–0.4 g/mL with a plate‑shaped or rod‑shaped morphology.”; “By starting the process in MEK (4.5 vol), the crude 2 remains as the MEK solvate which upon addition of MeOH (3 vol) can then undergo the transition to the desired hydrate… The solubility of 2 in MeOH is significantly higher than in EtOH which greatly facilitates the form conversion.”

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The oxidative carbonylation reaction is limited by the low solubility of CO in the reaction solvent, leading to poor mass‑transfer of CO from the gas to the liquid phase and consequently low conversion and yield.
Solution_Description: Increase the CO partial pressure to the optimal value and select a solvent with higher CO solubility (e.g., toluene) to improve gas‑liquid mass transfer. The researchers identified an optimal CO concentration and switched to solvents that give measurable reactivity, which raised the turnover number from 7 to 420.
Supporting_Evidence: ["development of scalable processes ... revealed that the reaction is CO‑limited even at elevated pressures"; "If our hypothesis is true, an increase in CO partial pressure should result in an increase in the observed reaction rate"; "solvents characterized by a lower solubility of CO should result in a slower reaction"; "toluene gave measurable reactivity ... ethyl acetate was slower"; "optimal CO concentration for the most effective outcome" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: A catalytically inactive bis‑amine‑palladium complex forms under reaction conditions, giving a negative order dependence on amine concentration and reducing the overall reaction rate and yield.
Solution_Description: Add a nitrogen‑based ligand (Li‑quinoline or pyridine) which coordinates to Pd after the turnover‑limiting step, keeping Pd in solution and preventing formation of palladium black. This ligand addition increased yields by >20 % and allowed higher turnover numbers.
Supporting_Evidence: ["formation of a catalytically inactive bis‑amine‑palladium complex"; "negative order influence of the concentration of the starting material"; "presence of 5 mol % of the ligand, Li‑quinoline, increased the yield of the reaction by more than 20 %"; "pyridine ... achieved even better results ... prevents formation of palladium black"; "ligand likely solubilizes Pd(0) species and prevents insoluble species" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The original protocol used 5–10 mol % Pd(OAc)₂, which is expensive and raises safety concerns due to Pd toxicity and the need for high metal loadings on large scale.
Solution_Description: Optimize conditions (ligand choice, CO pressure, solvent) to lower the Pd loading to 0.2 mol % while maintaining high turnover (TON ≈ 420). This required a longer residence time in batch but dramatically reduced metal cost and toxicity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["amount of catalytic palladium used ... raises issues of sustainability (resource use) and safety (Pd toxicity)"; "a simple and broadly applicable batch process allowed the reduction in Pd loading down to 0.2 mol %"; "entry 7 in Table 3 shows 0.2 mol % Pd with TON = 420"; "longer reaction time (150 min) was accepted to achieve the low loading"; "lower Pd loading decreases environmental impact" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, MeCN) coordinate strongly to Pd(II), forming kinetically stable complexes that block catalytic turnover, resulting in no measurable reactivity.
Solution_Description: Select non‑coordinating solvents with suitable CO solubility (toluene, ethyl acetate, p‑xylene). These solvents avoid Pd deactivation and give measurable yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ["DMF, DMSO, and MeCN presumably coordinated with the Pd(II) species forming kinetically stable complexes, thus prohibiting the reaction"; "only benzene‑ and ester‑derived solvents gave measurable reactivity"; "toluene gave the highest rate, consistent with its higher CO solubility"; "solvents with lower CO solubility resulted in slower reaction"; "solvent selection was guided by predicted CO Henry’s coefficients" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: In batch, the multiphase gas‑liquid–solid system suffers from poor mass transfer and requires operation at elevated CO pressures and temperatures above the solvent boiling point, creating safety hazards.
Solution_Description: Translate the process to continuous‑flow using a copper‑tube‑flow reactor (CuTFR) which provides a heterogeneous Cu(II) source, enhances gas‑liquid mass transfer, and allows operation at safer temperatures and pressures.
Supporting_Evidence: ["continuous‑flow process ... allow us to enhance mass transfer, improve process safety"; "use of a copper‑tube‑flow reactor (CuTFR) as a heterogeneous source of Cu²⁺ oxidant"; "CuTFR resulted in a significant improvement of stability of the system and in the increase in the observed reaction rate"; "operation in batch at elevated pressures of CO mixture and temperatures above the boiling point of the solvent raises safety concerns"; "flow process used toluene at 150 °C, lower pressure" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Switching from toluene to ethyl acetate improved catalyst loading and cost but increased the reaction time from ~120 min to ~300 min, reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: Implement the same chemistry in continuous‑flow (CuTFR) at a higher temperature (150 °C) and short residence time (5 min), restoring high productivity while retaining the benefits of the ethyl acetate solvent system.
Supporting_Evidence: ["reactions in ethyl acetate required much longer reaction times than the reactions under the same conditions in toluene; for the same conditions, we require 300 min in EtOAc vs 120 min in toluene"; "flow (using CuTFR) entry 2 gave a 5 min residence time with 86 % isolated yield"; "continuous‑flow process allowed operation at 150 °C"; "the CuTFR‑enabled flow process provides easy access to the in situ generated Cu(II) species"; "short residence time dramatically increased productivity" ]

Paper Title: Scalable Palladium-Catalyzed C(sp3)–H Carbonylation of Alkylamines in Batch and Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Delivering soluble Cu(II) oxidant to the reaction mixture is problematic due to solid precipitation, potential clogging, and the need for high pressure/gas handling.
Solution_Description: Introduce a solid heterogeneous Cu(II) source (copper wire, later a copper‑tube flow reactor) that oxidizes Pd in situ, eliminating the need for soluble Cu salts and simplifying gas handling.
Supporting_Evidence: ["we experimented with the use of heterogeneous precursors of Cu(II) salts instead of the continuous delivery of solids"; "introducing a copper wire into a tubular reactor ... in situ oxidized metallic copper was able to reoxidize the palladium catalyst"; "system proved to be stable only for short periods of time"; "CuTFR resulted in a significant improvement of stability and increased reaction rate"; "layer of oxidized Cu was regenerated in situ by the oxygen present in the gas phase" ]

Paper Title: Photocatalytic and Photoinduced Phosphonylation of Aryl Iodides: A Batch and Flow Study
Problem_Description: The copper‑photocatalyzed phosphonylation of p‑iodoanisole in batch gave only a modest 50 % isolated yield after 24 h of blue‑LED irradiation and required the use of stoichiometric amounts of triethyl phosphite and base, making the process relatively expensive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Optimization of the batch protocol (1 : 2 : 1.1 ratio of aryl iodide : triethyl phosphite : DIPEA, 5 mol % Cu(DPEPhos)(DMEGqu)PF₆, 0.1 M CH₃CN, 34 W blue LEDs) lowered the amount of phosphite needed and gave the best conversion (≈52 % NMR, 50 % isolated) under the same 24 h reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: "An optimal ratio of 1:2:1.1 between p‑iodoanisole, triethyl phosphite, and DIPEA was the most efficient ... using 5 mol % [Cu‑(DPEPhos)‑(DMEGqu)]‑PF₆ as the catalyst in CH₃CN (0.1 M) under blue LED irradiation for 24 h... allowed the formation of 1 in a decent 50 % isolated yield."

Paper Title: Photocatalytic and Photoinduced Phosphonylation of Aryl Iodides: A Batch and Flow Study
Problem_Description: When the copper‑photocatalyzed protocol was transferred to continuous‑flow (UV‑150 reactor, 365 nm, 0.1 mL min⁻¹) no product was obtained, indicating that the batch‑optimized conditions were not scalable and gave negligible conversion.
Solution_Description: A catalyst‑free, photoinduced phosphonylation was discovered by direct 365 nm irradiation of the reaction mixture (no copper catalyst). Using Et₃N (2 equiv) instead of DIPEA and an equimolar amount of phosphite enabled 70 % isolated yield after a second pass through the flow reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: "We serendipitously discovered an efficient catalyst‑free photoinduced phosphonylation ... direct irradiation of the reaction medium in the absence of the catalyst at 365 nm resulted in the formation of the targeted phosphonate 1. The replacement of DIPEA by readily available Et₃N (2 equiv) in an equimolar quantity with the phosphite ... allowed the conversion of p‑iodoanisole into 1 in a fairly decent 70 % yield at the cost of a second pass through the reactor."

Paper Title: Photocatalytic and Photoinduced Phosphonylation of Aryl Iodides: A Batch and Flow Study
Problem_Description: Even after establishing the catalyst‑free photoinduced protocol, the flow rate of 0.1 mL min⁻¹ could not be increased, which limited residence time and prevented higher productivity on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors transferred the reaction to a commercial Lucent 360 photoreactor (larger volume, higher LED power) and performed scale‑up experiments at 0.2 M concentration. By increasing the flow rates to 6 mL h⁻¹ (190 min residence) and 13 mL h⁻¹ (90 min residence) they achieved 72 % and 61 % conversion respectively, with space‑time yields up to 20 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: "We undertook scale‑up of the photoinduced phosphonylation reaction in batch and in flow using a Lucent 360 apparatus... The flow reaction was studied at two different flow rates, 6 and 13 mL/h, leading to 72 % and 61 % conversion into 1, respectively, on a 4 mmol scale for a reactor volume of 20 mL... These experiments highlighted the interest of using flow chemistry to scale up photoinduced reactions, as the space‑time yield is 7–13 times higher than in batch."

Paper Title: Photocatalytic and Photoinduced Phosphonylation of Aryl Iodides: A Batch and Flow Study
Problem_Description: A series of aryl iodides (p‑iodotoluene, p‑fluoroiodobenzene, p‑iodonitrobenzene, quinoline, pyrazole) gave no conversion or decomposed under the copper‑photocatalyzed conditions, limiting the substrate scope.
Solution_Description: The catalyst‑free photoinduced method proved more tolerant, delivering moderate‑to‑good yields for many electron‑rich and electron‑deficient substrates, and even enabling functionalisation of heterocycles (pyridine, pyrazine, quinoline, indole) that were unreactive in the copper‑catalyzed protocol.
Supporting_Evidence: "Surprisingly p‑iodotoluene and p‑fluoroiodobenzene were not reactive and decomposed in the reaction medium... In contrast, the photoinduced phosphonylation reaction was somewhat broader... heterocyclic scaffolds were readily functionalized under our conditions, as pyridine, pyrazine, quinoline, and indole substrates were converted in fairly decent yields."

Paper Title: Photocatalytic and Photoinduced Phosphonylation of Aryl Iodides: A Batch and Flow Study
Problem_Description: Kinetic studies showed that the photoinduced transformation was photon‑limited; low light intensity drastically reduced the reaction rate, requiring long irradiation times for acceptable conversion.
Solution_Description: The authors increased the photon flux by using higher‑energy (365 nm) LEDs and confirmed that temperature had negligible effect at the early stage, thereby focusing on maximizing light intensity to accelerate the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: "The comparison of the kinetic profiles at different wavelengths confirmed the higher reactivity of our system under higher‑energy irradiation... we also observed that a maximum intensity of irradiation is needed, as the reducing light intensity resulted in a diminution of the reaction rate."

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: Crystallization attempts for the borylated intermediate 6a gave very low recovery, making isolation inefficient.
Solution_Description: A telescoped sequence that combines the Pd‑catalyzed borylation and Suzuki–Miyaura coupling was developed, avoiding isolation of 6a and allowing direct crystallization from the THF‑water mixture, delivering the product 5a in 85 % isolated yield over two steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Unfortunately, preliminary efforts to develop a crystallization process for 6a were not successful due to low recovery.”
 • “Combination of the previously optimized borylation and Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling only generated 49.3 area% (5a)… due to decomposition in the second step (Condition A).”
 • “Full conversions were observed for this telescoped process, and the product 5a was isolated in 85 % yield over two steps after direct crystallization from the THF and water mixture.”

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: When the borylation and Suzuki steps were run sequentially (Condition A), the second step caused decomposition of the intermediate, resulting in only 49.3 % area‑% of product 5a.
Solution_Description: The borylation was changed to a lithiation‑borylation sequence (n‑BuLi/tri‑isopropyl borate) at –70 °C, followed by Suzuki coupling with Pd‑dppfCl₂ and K₂CO₃ in THF/H₂O at 60 °C, which gave full conversion and 85 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Combination of the previously optimized borylation and Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling only generated 49.3 area% (5a)… due to decomposition in the second step (Condition A).”
 • “Inspired by these precedents, we developed a procedure to construct the boronic acid 6b by subjecting pyridooxazine 6 to n‑BuLi and triisopropyl borate in THF at –70 °C… successfully generate the product 5a… Full conversions were observed for this telescoped process, and the product 5a was isolated in 85 % yield.”

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: The original Pd‑catalyzed C–N amidation used 10 mol % catalyst, 9 equiv of tert‑butyl carbamate, and required 4 h at 110 °C to reach full conversion, which was inefficient and expensive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput experimentation identified BrettPhos Pd G3 (5 mol %) in toluene with 3 equiv of carbamate at 110 °C as optimal, reducing catalyst loading, reagent excess and reaction time while maintaining >100 % conversion and >80 % A% of product 2a. The solvent was later switched to toluene only (avoiding 1,4‑dioxane) and the temperature was fine‑tuned to balance conversion and impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In the synthesis of carbamate 2a, high‑throughput experimentation… Using BrettPhos Pd G3 and K₂CO₃, 1,4‑dioxane and toluene emerged as the best solvents… 83 A% and 79 A% HPLC of 2a.”
 • “The amount of tert‑butyl carbamate could be lowered to 3 equiv at 110 °C without compromising the conversion or purity profile.”
 • “The catalyst loading was further reduced to 5 mol % from 10 mol % while providing 100 % conversion and a similar reaction profile (83 A% of 2a).”
 • “Reaction did not reach completion at 90 °C… 6 equiv were required to drive the reaction to completion, which resulted in a slightly improved purity profile (89 A%).”

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: Triphosgene, a highly toxic phosgene surrogate, was originally used to generate the activated carbamate 1a, posing significant safety and handling concerns for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Disuccinimidyl carbonate (DSC) was screened and selected as a safer, non‑toxic coupling agent that gave 98–100 % conversion and an impurity profile superior to triphosgene, enabling a greener and safer penultimate‑intermediate synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Triphosgene, a toxic coupling agent, was used to perform this two‑step transformation in the medicinal chemistry synthesis.”
 • “Among the six coupling agents tested, optimal conversions (98–100 %) were observed in the reactions using 4‑nitrophenyl chloroformate, disuccinimidyl carbonate (DSC), and dipyridyl carbonate… DSC gave the best conversion and impurity profile … and was therefore selected as the reagent of choice for further optimization.”

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: Global deprotection of the final API with TFA in DCM caused decomposition of GNE‑6893, forming an undesired amide product.
Solution_Description: A new deprotection protocol using 12 equiv of HCl in MeCN/H₂O at 60 °C (instead of TFA) removed both Boc groups without decomposition; the mixture was then neutralized with DIPEA, cooled, and crystallized to afford the API in 94 % isolated yield, 99.9 % ee, and 98.0 % A% purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Unfortunately, GNE‑6893 (1) decomposes under these conditions by reacting with TFA to form the corresponding amide.”
 • “A new set of conditions utilizing 12 equiv of HCl in a mixture of MeCN and water at 60 °C to remove both Boc protecting groups was quickly developed… After neutralization … the crystalline compound 1 was isolated in 94 % yield, 99.7 % ee, and 98.0 % A% HPLC purity.”

Paper Title: A Convergent Synthesis of HPK1 Inhibitor GNE-6893 via Palladium-Catalyzed Functionalization of a Tetrasubstituted Isoquinoline
Problem_Description: The deprotection of carbamate 2a originally employed aqueous hydrazine (N₂H₄·H₂O), a hazardous reagent unsuitable for large‑scale operations.
Solution_Description: A safer alternative, aqueous methylamine (MeNH₂), was substituted for hydrazine, providing the deprotected product 2 in 75 % yield over two steps with high purity and eliminating the hydrazine safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “To address process safety in the deprotection of carbamate 2a, we replaced the previously used N₂H₄·H₂O with MeNH₂ after examination of safer alternatives.”
 • “Without isolation, Boc‑amide 2a … was isolated in 75 % yield over two steps and 98.4 % A% HPLC purity …”

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: The reported synthetic route gave an overall isolated yield of only 1 % over 8 steps, which is far too low for clinical and commercial supply and required numerous low‑yielding operations that also increased the consumption of an expensive chiral piperazine intermediate.
Solution_Description: The sequence of bond‑forming events was reordered so that the piperazine is introduced early via a regioselective S_NAr on the most reactive aryl chloride of the pyrimidine core. This eliminates three steps (protection, demethylation, activation) and restores a high‑yielding transformation for the piperazine installation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The low overall yield (1%) clearly must be addressed ..." (sec 1)
- "Introducing the piperazine early could be particularly beneficial. The northern aryl chloride presented itself as the pyrimidine’s most reactive electrophile. Conducting the SNAr in this way eliminates 3 steps related to protection, demethylation, and activation." (sec 1)
- "Successful high‑yielding installation of the piperazine resolved the low yield associated with the hydroxyl activation and ensuing SNAr (9.7 % yield over two steps)." (sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: The palladium‑catalyzed C–O bond formation sometimes stalled, required high loadings of expensive Pd (up to 100 000 $/kg) and of cesium carbonate, making the step costly and inconsistent.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to 2‑MeTHF, the palladium source was switched to Pd₂(dba)₃, the base was changed to K₃PO₄, and the ligand Xantphos was introduced, allowing catalyst loading to be reduced to 0.25–0.5 mol % (essentially negligible palladium cost).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Occasionally, the reaction stalled. ... palladium pricing has risen greatly ... reduction of the original loading was essential." (sec 2.2)
- "To further improve the system, the reaction was run in 2‑MeTHF, Pd₂(dba)₃ replaced Pd‑(OAc)₂, and K₃PO₄ was chosen as the base ... loading to be reduced to 1.5 mol %" (sec 2.2)
- "Screening identified Xantphos as a ligand imparting high catalyst activity. 0.25–0.5 mol % catalyst loading effectively promoted the reaction ... the cost of palladium ... negligible." (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Residual formaldehyde (up to 1.5 % w/w) in the prolinol coupling partner poisoned the palladium catalyst, extending the reaction time to 88 h and generating ~10 % hydrolysis impurity of the aryl chloride.
Solution_Description: Tight control of formaldehyde impurity to ≤0.2 % w/w eliminated catalyst deactivation, reducing the reaction time to 15 h and suppressing the hydrolysis side‑product.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "When present at 1.5 % by weight, the reaction required 88 h to reach completion. ... substantial generation of an impurity resulting from hydrolysis of the aryl chloride (∼10 % A%)." (sec 2.2)
- "At 0.2 % formaldehyde, however, 17 reacted fully within 15 h (0.6 % residual 17)." (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the low‑loading C–O coupling showed poor reproducibility in jacketed vessels; reaction rate depended strongly on the surface area of potassium phosphate, indicating mass‑transfer and mixing limitations.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Phosphate was wet‑milled with a rotor‑stator mixer (or ground by a stir bar) before addition, markedly increasing its surface area and delivering consistent, rapid conversions at kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Reaction kinetics revealed a strong dependence on the stoichiometry of potassium phosphate and concentration of prolinol but no dependence on the concentration of the catalyst. ... phosphate surface area was greatly increased by grinding action of the stir‑bar." (sec 2.2)
- "Wet‑milling the hygroscopic phosphate in 2‑MeTHF with a rotor‑stator mixer before the reaction similarly increased the conversion rate and provided a kilogram‑scale approach to reproduce this effect." (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: The Buchwald–Hartwig amination gave only 80‑90 % assay yield; at >90 % conversion the product began to decompose, and the free‑base of the tosylate salt resisted crystallization, leading to impurity‑control issues.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The catalyst system was changed to (R)‑BINAP/Pd₂(dba)₃ with K₃PO₄ in 2‑MeTHF, and wet‑milling of the phosphate was applied, which together raised the assay yield and gave a robust crystalline tosylate salt.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The installation of naphthyl chloride proceeded cleanly but with only modest to good efficiency (80–90 % assay yield). ... product decomposition pathways competed with the latter becoming more dominant at high conversions (>90 % consumption of 23)." (sec 2.4)
- "RuPhos, Cs₂CO₃, and toluene were replaced with (R)‑BINAP, K₃PO₄, and 2‑MeTHF, respectively. Again, wet‑milling the phosphate improved robustness. These modifications substantially increased the assay yield." (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: Traditional Cbz deprotection with trimethylsilyl iodide generates benzyl iodide, a potentially mutagenic impurity, and forms a quaternary ammonium species that required a silica plug at API stage for removal.
Solution_Description: A novel deprotection using 2‑mercaptoethanol in DMAc with K₃PO₄ cleanly removed the benzyl group as carbon dioxide, producing a benign thioether by‑product and eliminating benzyl iodide formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Trimethylsilyl iodide (TMSI) is a traditional deprotection reagent ... benzyl iodide (BnI), a potentially mutagenic impurity, is coproduced. Although it purged well, elimination of this hazard was desired." (sec 2.5)
- "A new Cbz‑deprotection was developed which avoids BnI production. Reaction of 24 tosylate with 2‑mercaptoethanol cleanly released the benzyl group and carbon dioxide. The coproduct ... is a benign liquid that easily purged." (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: During the Cbz deprotection step, basic conditions without 2‑mercaptoethanol caused epimerization of the cyanomethyl group via deprotonation and subsequent Michael addition.
Solution_Description: Design‑of‑experiments identified temperature and water content as critical variables; by limiting temperature (≤85 °C) and water (≤200 ppm), epimer formation was kept below 4 % and acceptable for downstream crystallizations.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Epimerization of the cyanomethyl group was an unexpected consequence of the reaction under basic conditions ... The deprotected 25 was not prone to epimerization since the amine was a poor leaving group." (sec 2.5)
- "DoE helped determine factors that impacted the reaction ... Epimerization depended primarily upon temperature and water content, where higher values of these factors increased the formation of the diastereomer. The reaction was well controlled by setting appropriate limits on these variables." (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Development of Adagrasib’s Commercial Manufacturing Route
Problem_Description: The initial coupling to install the acrylamide warhead proceeded with low isolated yield, limiting overall productivity.
Solution_Description: Using the sodium salt of 2‑fluoroacrylic acid together with T3P (propylphosphonic anhydride) eliminated the need for external base and raised the assay yield to 89 % (70 % isolated).
Supporting_Evidence: - "Installation of the acrylamide warhead was low‑yielding in the initial developments. Minor refinements led to substantial gains ... The use of the sodium salt of 2‑fluoroacrylic acid promoted both acylation activity and stability of the starting material and eliminated the need for external base (Et₃N). This greatly improved yield to 89 % assay yield and 70 % isolated yield." (sec 2.6)

Paper Title: Improved Synthetic Process of Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediate 3‑Benzyloxy-4-oxo‑4
Problem_Description: The original enamine‑formation step (4b) required a 5‑equivalent excess of the costly reagent DMFDMA (14). The over‑charged reagent decomposes to DMF, generating large volumes of nitrogenous wastewater and raising environmental‑safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The excess of DMFDMA was reduced to 1.8 equiv by continuously removing the by‑product methanol via azeotropic (Dean–Stark) distillation, which also accelerated the reaction. The catalyst was changed from TBAB to TBAC to avoid salt‑related safety issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “the installation of the enamine function group required up to 5 equiv of reagent 14… overcharged reagent 14 could be converted to DMF… leading to significant environmental concerns”; “the reaction stalling of 4b was addressed by the azeotropic removal of the byproduct methanol”; “desublimation of quaternary salt caused by the interaction … catalyst tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB) was avoided by switching to catalytic tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC)”

Paper Title: Improved Synthetic Process of Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediate 3‑Benzyloxy-4-oxo‑4
Problem_Description: When benzyl chloride and acetone replaced benzyl bromide and acetonitrile for the benzyl‑ether formation (compound 3), the mixture agglomerated and could not be stirred properly.
Solution_Description: The solvent volume was increased to 20 V · m⁻¹, water (5 V · m⁻¹) was added as a co‑solvent to aid dispersion, the base was switched to Na₂CO₃, catalytic KI was introduced to shorten the reaction, and finally 2‑butanone at 80 °C was used to restore good mixing and reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “an agglomeration of raw materials, along with the agitation difficulty” (entries 1‑2); “the addition of water as a cosolvent solved the agitation problem… hydrolysis of benzyl chloride” (entries 3‑4); “switching to 2‑butanone as the solvent at an elevated temperature of 80 °C” (entries 7‑8)

Paper Title: Improved Synthetic Process of Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediate 3‑Benzyloxy-4-oxo‑4
Problem_Description: During the NaIO₄ oxidation, acidic conditions caused hydrolytic impurity 16 and its downstream aldol condensation product 17, which appeared at up to 20 % area, compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: The reaction pH was maintained around 6, the temperature set to 70 °C and the total reaction volume increased to 20 V · m⁻¹, and 4b was charged into the oxidant solution (instead of the reverse) to keep the acidity low and suppress formation of 16/17.
Supporting_Evidence: “hydrolytic impurity 16… could transform quantitatively into 16 under an acidic aqueous solution with pH < 2”; “impurity 17 … up to 20.1 area %”; “charging 4b into [O] … reduced impurity 17 to 1.1 %”

Solution_Description: TBAB was replaced with tetrabutylammonium chloride (TBAC), which forms tetramethylammonium chloride that does not sublimate under the reaction conditions.

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of a Continuous Flow Synthesis of Dapagliflozin
Problem_Description: The classic dapagliflozin synthesis requires an ultralow temperature (‑78 °C) for the n‑BuLi Br/Li‑exchange step. This temperature window consumes a large amount of cooling energy, raises the operating cost, and poses safety hazards associated with handling highly reactive organolithium reagents at very low temperature.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Running the Br/Li‑exchange in a continuous‑flow micro‑reactor provides rapid and efficient heat removal, allowing the reaction temperature to be raised to –20 °C while maintaining high conversion. The micro‑reactor’s high surface‑to‑volume ratio also improves safety by limiting the amount of reactive organolithium present at any time.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The ultralow temperature of –78 °C is needed to use n‑BuLi in the reaction, which consumes a lot of energy and greatly increases the cost.” (Abstract)   • “The traditional method … requires an ultralow temperature (‑78 °C) … the high activity of organolithium reagent, ultralow temperature control and adequate mixing are necessary to improve safety.” (Introduction)   • “The mild and efficient synthesis … the reaction temperature could be increased from –78 °C to –20 °C. The high specific surface area, high mass transfer rate, high safety, and linear amplification process of flow chemistry technology … a series of problems in using organolithium reagents can be solved.” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Optimization and Scale-Up of a Continuous Flow Synthesis of Dapagliflozin
Problem_Description: Intermediate 4 is a syrupy oil that is difficult to crystallize, forcing the traditional route to employ an acetylation‑protection step followed by de‑acetylation to obtain a crystallizable intermediate 6. These extra steps increase material cost and process complexity, especially on large scale.
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow sequence directly furnishes methyl C‑aryl glycoside 4, which is then recrystallised from methanol to give a high‑purity solid without the need for protection/de‑protection chemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It is difficult to crystallize intermediate 4 due to its syrupy nature, so it is necessary to prepare acetylated product 6 … however, this refining strategy … is less attractive in large‑scale production.” (Introduction)   • “The continuous flow synthesis … the final product quality is improved, the purity of the product is 99.83 %… the oily crude product 4 … recrystallized with methanol to obtain a white solid.” (Abstract, Section 2.1)
