Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: The original Suzuki–Miyaura coupling gave only a 56 % isolated yield of aniline 4 and required 10 mol % Pd catalyst, making the step expensive and giving poor batch‑to‑batch consistency.
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading was reduced to 1 mol % Pd(dppf)Cl₂·DCM, 2 equiv of TMG base and 10 equiv water were used in MeCN (or MeOH/THF/2‑propanol) giving >97 % in‑situ yield and an isolated yield >90 % after anti‑solvent crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Pd‑catalysed Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of step 1 required a 10 mol % Pd catalyst and afforded aniline 4 in a moderate 56 % yield.”; “After further optimisation, aniline 4 could be obtained in a >98 % in‑situ yield using 1 mol % Pd‑(dppf)‑Cl₂·DCM in the presence of 2 equiv TMG and 10 equiv water in 2‑MeTHF within 4 h at 65 °C.”; “MeCN was finally selected for further development … more than 97 % in‑situ yield.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: The initial biphasic 2‑MeTHF/water reaction mixture caused non‑reproducible conversion profiles on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Switching to a single‑phase solvent (MeCN) eliminated mixing effects and allowed direct anti‑solvent crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion profiles obtained with this biphasic system were not reproducible, which led us to investigate water‑miscible solvents to avoid mixing effects on a larger scale … MeCN was finally selected for further development.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Buchwald–Hartwig impurity 11 repeatedly formed, requiring up to three HBr‑salt formation/free‑basin/re‑slurry cycles to achieve >99.5 % purity of 4.
Solution_Description: The use of TMG as base suppressed impurity 11 and the addition of 1,3,5‑triazine‑2,4,6‑trithiol trisodium (TriNaTMT) at reaction end quenched residual Pd, further reducing the impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Screening the reaction conditions … quickly identified 1,1,3,3‑tetramethylguanidine (TMG) for minimizing impurity 11.”; “The addition of TriNaTMT at the end of the reaction minimized the formation of the Buchwald–Hartwig amination impurity 11 by quenching the active catalyst.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: After isolation, wet solid 4 contained high water (≈0.5 % w/w) leading to long drying times (>12 h) and residual palladium levels of ~1000 ppm.
Solution_Description: The wet solid was dissolved in 2‑MeTHF, washed sequentially with N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine, sodium bicarbonate and brine, then azeotropically distilled to reduce water <0.1 % and palladium ≤100 ppm; TriNaTMT scavenger was also added to lower metal levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “The isolation from MeCN/water also resulted in a low weight assay … and long drying times due to the high water content … These issues were resolved by dissolving wet solid 4 in 2‑MeTHF … performing two washes with an aqueous solution of N‑acetyl cysteine … the water content could be reduced below 0.1 % after an azeotropic distillation, thus reducing the cycle time.”; “On multi‑kilogram scale, the yield for this telescoped process was 93 % … and 55 ppm residual palladium.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Aniline 4 showed poor aqueous solubility, causing the azidation step to fail under standard NaNO₂/NaN₃ conditions.
Solution_Description: 2‑MeTHF (and THF) were used as the organic phase, with MeCN as co‑solvent; the addition order was reversed (add TMS‑azide first, then t‑BuONO) to avoid slurry formation and achieve full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the poor aqueous solubility of aniline 4, the aqueous azidation conditions … did not work. 2‑MeTHF and THF exhibited the highest solubility …” ; “A sharp contrast … when adding t‑BuONO to a mixture of 4 … a thick slurry … low conversion … We hypothesised … When adding slowly t‑BuONO to a solution containing 4 and 1.2 equiv TMS azide, the reaction proceeded smoothly with full conversion.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: During azidation, Pd(II) salts reacted with TMS‑azide to form shock‑sensitive palladium azide (Pd(N₃)₂) that could explode on drying, and hydrazoic acid (HN₃) could accumulate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reactions were run under a constant nitrogen flow with a double aqueous NaOH trap; the headspace was purged, and azide levels were monitored by ion chromatography (typically <3 ppm).
Supporting_Evidence: “All lab and plant scale reactions were run under a constant nitrogen flow to avoid accumulation of the highly explosive and toxic hydrazoic acid (HN₃) … nitrogen flow was passed through a double aq. NaOH trap.”; “Hydrazoic acid content in solution was indirectly measured as sodium azide in the NaOH trap … results were typically below 3 ppm after two washes.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Isolated azide 5 had very low solubility in common organic solvents and a high decomposition energy (1001 J g⁻¹) with autocatalytic behaviour, making its isolation hazardous.
Solution_Description: The crude 2‑MeTHF solution of azide 5 was used directly in the click step (no isolation), avoiding handling of the energetic solid.
Supporting_Evidence: “The potential of this compound to degrade by impact or friction … prompted us to discard the option of isolating 5 on the scale. The resulting 2‑MeTHF solution containing 5 was then used as such in the next step.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Using CuSO₄/ascorbate in the click reaction generated up to 20 % aniline 4 impurity from azide 5, reducing the desired product yield and purity.
Solution_Description: Switching to CuI as copper source (no reductant needed) and using Et₃N as base lowered the aniline impurity to ≤0.4 % area, giving >99 % conversion to triazole 7.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reduction of 5 to 4 was reduced to ≤5 % area when CuI was the copper source.”; “In the presence of K₂CO₃ … aniline impurity 17 % … Switching to Et₃N further decreased the amount of 4 … Using a combination of CuI and Et₃N, we were able to lower the aniline impurity to ≤0.4 % area (entries 4 and 6).”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: The original N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) chlorination required corrosive HBr and gave high exotherms; NCS also presented a high decomposition energy (104 J g⁻¹).
Solution_Description: 1,3‑Dichloro‑5,5‑dimethylhydantoin (DCDMH) was adopted as a safer chlorinating agent; the reaction was run at 5 °C with portionwise addition (0.25 equiv ×3) to control heat and impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “1,3‑Dichloro‑5,5‑dimethylhydantoin (DCDMH) provided full conversion … The reaction temperature turned out to be key … 5 °C was found to be optimal, leading to 0.2 % des‑TMS impurity after 23 h.”; “From a safety perspective, the use of DCDMH is safer than NCS (decomposition energy of 30 vs 104 J g⁻¹).”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Impurity 14 (des‑chloro) appeared up to 3.5 % on 1 kg scale due to loss of TMS‑azide when nitrogen flow removed reagent from the reactor headspace.
Solution_Description: Sub‑surface addition of TMS‑azide ensured full dosing; pH of the azide‑containing stream was kept below 9 (via Na₂SO₄ washes) to suppress cleavage of the Si‑C bond and formation of impurity 15.
Supporting_Evidence: “We found that the nitrogen flow … removed part of the TMS azide … Impurity 14 was controlled by performing sub‑surface addition of TMS azide.”; “It was critical to control the pH … below 9 to minimize the cleavage of the carbon‑silicon bond … Additional washes with aqueous saturated Na₂SO₄… effectively controlled the pH.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: The crude penultimate intermediate 7 retained a brown color and contained non‑polar impurities that limited product acceptance.
Solution_Description: A charcoal treatment of the DCM solution of 7 removed color, and a final DCM/heptane recrystallisation increased purity to 99.9 % area with 94 % recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “A reactor was charged with crude 7 … the mixture was filtered through charcoal … The resulting purified 7 … gave 99.9 % area purity …”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: The final O‑demethylation step originally used corrosive HBr, which is expensive and poses equipment‑corrosion issues.
Solution_Description: HCl (10 equiv) was substituted for HBr; reactions were run at 45 °C overnight, giving >99 % purity of 1 while reducing cost and corrosion risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “HCl was investigated as an alternative to HBr for the O‑demethylation … 10 equiv HCl … gave full conversion … excellent purity.”

Paper Title: Toward the Development of a Manufacturing Process for Milvexian: Scale-Up Synthesis of the Side Chain
Problem_Description: Compound 1 exhibited a high decomposition energy (610 J g⁻¹) with strong gas evolution, requiring a safe maximum operating temperature.
Solution_Description: Isothermal DSC experiments set the maximum allowable temperature at 130 °C, ensuring safe handling during manufacture.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 1 has a very high decomposition energy (610 J g⁻¹) … The maximum allowable temperature was set at 50 °C based on isothermal DSC experiments … The maximum allowable temperature is set at 130 °C based on isothermal DSC experiments.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The electrophilic bromination of methyl‑vinyl‑ketone (MVK) is highly exothermic.  The original laboratory procedure used n‑pentane as a solvent, which is unsafe for large‑scale operations because the heat released can lead to a thermal runaway.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run neat (no solvent) and bromine was added very slowly (≈25 kg h⁻¹) while keeping the bath temperature between –20 °C and –10 °C.  This controlled the heat evolution and eliminated the need for a flammable solvent.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Given the exothermic nature of this reaction, hexanes and n‑heptane were initially evaluated as alternative solvents… the reaction could conveniently be run neat to afford comparable results.”
• “To minimize potential thermal hazards, the reaction mixture was held at –20 to –10 °C while adding neat bromine… at a rate of 25 kg h⁻¹ (for a total of 16.5 h) to maintain the reaction temperature below –10 °C.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: During dehydrobromination (Step 1B) the use of DBU generated a thick, gummy DBU·HBr precipitate that was difficult to stir and filter, causing inconsistent recovery of BMK and variable downstream coupling yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Triethylamine (TEA) was substituted for DBU.  TEA forms a soluble triethylammonium bromide salt, giving a free‑flowing slurry that filters easily and provides more consistent BMK yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “This yielded a thick and gummy DBU·HBr precipitate that was difficult to stir and filter… leading to significant processing and throughput difficulties, and inconsistent amounts of BMK.”
• “Triethylamine was identified as the best replacement for DBU, solving the stirring efficiency problems… triethylammonium hydrobromide, which were easier to filter.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: In the tandem Michael addition/cyclization (Step 1C) the amount of BMK delivered to the reaction varied, causing incomplete conversion, residual dihydronapabucasin (DHNp) impurity, and difficulty removing this impurity by crystallization because of its similar solubility to the product.
Solution_Description: A quantitative ^1H‑NMR (later GC) assay was implemented to accurately determine BMK content.  The BMK/HNQ ratio was then tightly controlled to 1.07–1.17 mol mol⁻¹ and the internal batch temperature was set to 60–70 °C, which drove >95 % oxidation of DHNp to napabucasin.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The relative ratio of MVK to bromine emerged as one of the key factors that impacted the downstream chemistry… inconsistent amounts of BMK required in Step 1C coupling.”
• “A weight % assay for BMK was developed… to ensure that the right amounts of HNQ coupling partner were consistently used.”
• “A breakthrough was achieved… coupling reaction temperature (60–70 °C) was a critical factor in achieving a consistent conversion (>95 %) of DHNp to napabucasin.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Quenching the Step 1C reaction with water caused the crude material to precipitate as a sticky mass that adhered to reactor walls and stir blades, leading to significant product loss during filtration.
Solution_Description: Instead of aqueous precipitation, the crude mixture was subjected to a solvent exchange from THF to ethanol and precipitated directly from aqueous ethanol.  This gave a free‑flowing solid that could be filtered cleanly with minimal loss.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In the original process (Process A), quenching the reaction with water precipitated the bulk of the crude product… generating a sticky material that clung to the reactor walls and stir blades, depending on the ratio of napabucasin to DHNp.”
• “The improved workup (Process C)… a solvent exchange from THF to ethanol was implemented and the product was precipitated directly from aqueous ethanol to produce crude napabucasin.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Recrystallization of the crude product from formic acid (Process A) required large solvent volumes (up to 100 vol) and long cooling periods, making the step difficult to scale and expensive.
Solution_Description: Ethyl acetate was screened and found to give high‑quality crystals, but still required large volumes.  Ultimately acetonitrile was selected for recrystallization (Process C) and the final purification was performed by a hot‑acetate reslurry, which reduced solvent usage and gave >99.9 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “While this procedure afforded good quality API, the recrystallization from formic acid proved difficult to scale, so alternative solvent systems were sought.”
• “From multiple solvents evaluated, acetonitrile was identified and selected as the best solvent for recrystallization in Process C.”
• “Finally, reslurry of the product in hot ethyl acetate yielded the drug substance with consistently high purity (>99.9 % area).”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The external oxidant approach (Process B) employed MnO₂ in hot toluene.  The MnO₂ slurry created a thick filter cake, generated a black tarry residue that clogged the filter, and required a large toluene volume (≈50 vol) leaving >2000 ppm residual toluene in the product.
Solution_Description: Process C eliminated the external oxidant and relied on in‑situ oxidation by dissolved oxygen at 60–70 °C, giving >95 % conversion of DHNp and removing the need for MnO₂ and toluene altogether.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In Process B, the crude Step 1C product containing high levels of DHNp was subjected to further oxidation with manganese dioxide in toluene… the filtration was improved using the higher toluene volume and a pre‑heated filter pad.”
• “A breakthrough was achieved with the observation that the coupling reaction temperature (60–70 °C) was a critical factor in achieving a consistent conversion (>95 %) of DHNp to napabucasin.”

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development of Napabucasin and Impurity Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Residual bromine in the reaction mixture promoted a halo‑form degradation of napabucasin, generating bromoform and a carboxylic‑acid impurity (RRT 0.55).  Bromoform is a hazardous volatile by‑product.
Solution_Description: The bromine : MVK molar ratio was tightened to 0.92–0.95 and the work‑up included aqueous ethanol washes that removed residual bromine, keeping bromide levels ≤1.5 % (ICP‑MS) and suppressing the halo‑form pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The relative ratio of MVK to bromine emerged as one of the key factors that impacted the downstream chemistry… The presence of bromides is confirmed in the crude reaction mixtures at levels of up to 1.5 %.”
• “The optimal purity range for MVK… the optimal bromine molar ratio … was found to be 0.92–0.95.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: The original epoxidation of alkene 15 (or 13) gave a ∼1:1 trans/cis mixture of epoxide 16, providing only ~50 % of the desired trans‑isomer and requiring expensive preparative chiral HPLC for separation – a bottleneck for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Switch to m‑CPBA oxidation in toluene with inverse addition (dropwise addition of substrate to the oxidant) and perform crystallization of the trans‑epoxide from EtOAc followed by short‑path vacuum distillation; this gave dr ≥ 98:2 and overall isolated yield of 39 % on three 50 g batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the reported epoxidation of 15 with m‑CPBA in DCM affords an ∼1:1 ratio … we undertook a survey of alternative oxidation conditions” (Results & Discussion, sec 2.2). 
• “Oxidation with m‑CPBA (1.2 equiv) afforded … 70:30 ratio” (Table 4, entry 2). 
• “inverse addition … dr 79:21” (Table 4, entry 4). 
• “The most non‑polar … toluene led to slightly better results … dr 81:19” (Table 4, entry 6). 
• “vacuum distillation… afforded trans‑16′ as a colorless glassy solid … total yield 39.4 %” (sec 2.2, epoxidation‑crystallization).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: Metal‑catalysed epoxidations (Jacobsen’s catalyst, cat‑2, cat‑3‑5) provided low yields (33–67 %) and poor trans‑selectivity (often favoring the undesired cis‑isomer), making them unsuitable for large‑scale preparation.
Solution_Description: Abandoned metal‑catalysed routes; instead adopted the m‑CPBA oxidation in toluene with controlled addition and temperature, which gave higher conversion, better diastereoselectivity and was industrially acceptable.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Metal‑catalysed epoxidation methods were examined … delivered the epoxide 16 in 33 % yield and 37:63 dr …” (Results & Discussion, sec 2.2). 
• “At this stage, we decided to explore alternative methods … because the tested direct epoxidation reactions had failed to deliver the requisite selectivity …” (sec 2.2). 
• “Oxidation with m‑CPBA (1.2 equiv) afforded … 70:30 ratio …” (Table 4, entry 2). 
• “The most non‑polar … toluene led to slightly better results … dr 81:19” (Table 4, entry 6).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: The stereoselective reduction of (R)‑7 with l‑selectride required cryogenic temperatures (–78 °C) and an oxidative work‑up, and the resulting diastereomeric product was poorly crystalline, necessitating chromatographic separation.
Solution_Description: Switched to Ru‑catalysed transfer hydrogenation of the (S)‑sulfinyl imine 7 using [RuCl₂(p‑cymene)]₂, 2‑amino‑2‑methyl‑1‑propanol and t‑BuOK; the reaction runs at reflux (∼80 °C), gives > 99 % conversion, dr > 99:1 and is readily scalable.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A significant bottleneck … reduction of (R)‑7 with l‑selectride … required oxidative cleavage … low crystallinity …” (sec 2.1). 
• “We searched for alternative more selective reductants … Ru‑catalysed transfer hydrogenation … dr ≥ 99:1.” (sec 2.1). 
• “Ru‑catalyzed transfer hydrogenation proved to be the method of choice … 1 kg scale reduction … de > 99 %.” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: Commercial Ti(OEt)₄ contained up to 10–15 wt % Ti(iPr)₄, which caused trans‑esterification of the sulfinyl imine 7, generating an impurity (S)‑7‑iPr and complicating the reaction work‑up.
Solution_Description: Ensured strict quality control of Ti(OEt)₄ (using reagent free of Ti(iPr)₄) and added N,N,N',N'-tetrakis(2‑hydroxyethyl)ethylenediamine (THEED) before quenching to convert titanium alkoxides to a water‑soluble complex, simplifying extraction and phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “most of the commercially available Ti(OEt)₄ contains … Ti(iPr)₄ … which was found to effect formation of an impurity …” (sec 2.1). 
• “The quality of the titanium reagent had to be strictly controlled.” (sec 2.1). 
• “addition of THEED … greatly simplified extraction using the EtOAc/water system and enhanced separation of the phases.” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: During the Ti‑promoted condensation, formation of a titanium hydroxide gel during aqueous work‑up hindered filtration and caused lengthy work‑up times.
Solution_Description: Added Celite to the reaction mixture to reduce filtration time and, more effectively, introduced THEED to convert the gel to a water‑soluble ligand‑bound form, enabling clean phase separation and filtration.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A common complication … formation of titanium hydroxide gel … usually converted to a filterable solid … but the procedure is not always efficient.” (sec 2.1). 
• “The addition of Celite can help … though an improved approach involves conversion of titanium alkoxides to a water‑soluble ligand‑bound form … addition of THEED … greatly simplified extraction …” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: The original epoxide‑opening step used LiClO₄ in a sealed vessel; LiClO₄ is hygroscopic, caused reproducibility issues, and generated a significant amount of bis‑product, complicating purification.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Performed the epoxide opening in protic solvents (EtOH or i‑PrOH) without added Lewis acid; later added tert‑amyl alcohol (t‑AmOH) as a co‑solvent under reflux in an open system, which gave quantitative conversion and a clean product profile with minimal bis‑by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “formation of a significant amount of bis‑10′ and lack of reproducibility due to hygroscopicity of LiClO₄ forced us to look for a better alternative.” (sec 2.2). 
• “reaction of trans‑16′ in protic solvents (EtOH or i‑PrOH) proceeded with an equally high conversion without the need for a Lewis acidic promoter.” (sec 2.2). 
• “introduction of a protic high‑boiling tert‑amyl alcohol … led to complete consumption of 9 in 6 h at reflux with an acceptable 10′/bis‑10′ ratio.” (Table 5, entry 4).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: Reduction of nitrile 19 with NaBH₄/NiCl₂ was problematic on scale and produced a side‑reaction forming a dimer (bis‑20), making isolation of pure amine 20 difficult; the dimer persisted even after recrystallisation due to low solubility of the product.
Solution_Description: Adopted catalytic hydrogenation of 19 over Raney‑Ni (50 bar H₂, 50 °C) in the presence of excess aqueous NH₃, which suppressed dimer formation and gave 65 % isolated yield of 20; the crude amine was used directly in the subsequent saponification step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “NaBH₄/NiCl₂ system afforded the amine 20, upscaling … problematic.” (sec 2.3). 
• “Hydrogenation of 19 over Raney‑Ni … identified as a more promising method.” (sec 2.3). 
• “Saturation of the reaction medium with ammonia substantially suppressed this process and provided selectivity sufficient for practical large‑scale use.” (sec 2.3). 
• “The highest yield of 65 % was obtained … with 5–7 % content of the dimer bis‑20.” (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: Final API 2 (EBL‑3183) existed predominantly as a crystalline betaine insoluble in common organic solvents, and the residual dimer impurity (bis‑2) could not be fully removed by a single crystallisation due to low solubility of the target.
Solution_Description: Developed a two‑stage purification: (i) pH‑controlled precipitation from concentrated aqueous ammonia followed by acidification to isolate 2 with ~90 % purity, and (ii) antisolvent precipitation from acidic solution using ethanol, yielding a stable EtOH‑solvate of 2 with > 95 % purity and only ~2.5 % dimer.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “target 2 exists predominantly in a crystalline betaine form, which is insoluble in common organic solvents.” (sec 2.3). 
• “Two principal purification methods were developed: precipitation using an antisolvent for acidic solutions or precipitation under pH‑controlled conditions for basic solutions.” (sec 2.3). 
• “pH‑controlled precipitation … 90–93 % content of 2, 3–4 % bis‑2.” (sec 4.12.1). 
• “Antisolvent precipitation … 94.9–95.1 % content of 2, 3.1 % bis‑2.” (sec 4.12.2).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of Indole Carboxylate Metallo-β-Lactamase Inhibitor EBL-3183
Problem_Description: The bromination step to convert 4 to 5 initially used an extractive work‑up that was labour‑intensive and gave impure product.
Solution_Description: Implemented a simple direct precipitation of 5 by adding 5 % aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ to the reaction mixture, which avoided extraction and provided higher purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Direct precipitation of 5 from the reaction mixture by 5 % aq. Na₂S₂O₃ was simpler than the previously employed extractive procedure … and improved the product purity.” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Enones 12 and alcohol 8 were obtained as oils and isolated by column chromatography, which is impractical and unsafe at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The Grignard addition and hydrogenation steps were telescoped without intermediate isolations; the reaction mixture was worked up, the solvent exchanged to MTBE, and the product crystallized from n‑heptane, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since the mixture of enones 12 was an oil that was originally purified by column chromatography, we examined the feasibility of telescoping the Grignard addition step into the hydrogenation step without isolation… (Section 2.1).”; “The mixture was filtered… and the solvent was exchanged with MTBE to furnish a mixture of enones 12… The two‑step telescoped protocol was implemented on a 35 kg scale…”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Quenching the Grignard reaction with 10 % aq NH₄Cl caused a large exotherm (ΔT_ad = 56 °C) and a rapid gas evolution (56 L h⁻¹), exceeding the venting capacity of the pilot‑plant reactor.
Solution_Description: The quench was changed to 10 % v/v water in THF, giving a much lower gas evolution (11 L h⁻¹). A nitrogen sweep was applied to keep methane below its flammable limit, and the quench was performed in‑situ in the same reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: “Quenching… using 10 % aq NH₄Cl … resulted in a spike in heat flow (ΔT_ad = 56 °C) accompanied by a sharp gas release… beyond the venting capacity.”; “The severity of gas release was substantially lower (11 L h⁻¹) when 10 % v/v water in THF was used… a nitrogen sweep was provided to the headspace of the reactor.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: The original Grignard reagent (MeMgBr in Et₂O) posed significant safety hazards and required a large amount of Et₂O, which is costly and difficult to handle safely on large scale.
Solution_Description: MeMgBr was switched to a 1.4 M solution in THF, which gave identical efficiency at 5–15 °C, reducing both safety risk and solvent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the original conditions utilized MeMgBr in Et₂O, we discovered that the reaction was equally efficient using MeMgBr in tetrahydrofuran (THF) (1.4 M) at 5–15 °C.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation using dry 10 % Pd/C presented pyrophoric safety concerns, while wet Pd/C lowered diastereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified MTBE as the optimal medium, delivering quantitative conversion and a 49:1 diastereomeric ratio while allowing the reaction to be run at ambient temperature, mitigating safety and selectivity issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original protocol provided a 12:1 dr… due to safety concerns associated with dry Pd/C… we screened alternative solvents… the use of MTBE as the reaction solvent led to quantitative conversion in a 49:1 ratio of diastereomers.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: During the transesterification of lactam 10 to methyl ester 19, the product was highly sensitive to pH; at pH < 5 the lactam ring opened (impurity 20) and at pH > 10 the methyl ester saponified (impurity 21), causing large yield losses.
Solution_Description: A controlled work‑up was instituted: after reaction, MeOH was removed, the residue was quenched with 10 % aq Na₂CO₃ to maintain pH 6.5–7.5, and subsequent solvent exchanges were performed under low‑water conditions, suppressing both degradation pathways.
Supporting_Evidence: “Methyl ester 19 was highly sensitive to pH… At pH < 5… impurity 20 formed; at pH > 10… impurity 21 formed… We minimized this… by developing a controlled workup protocol… 10 % aq Na₂CO₃ (≈1.5 mL g⁻¹) at 10–15 °C to a pH of 6.5–7.5.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Diastereoselective reduction of ketone 13 with ZnCl₂/NaBH₄ showed a drop in diastereoselectivity from 10:1 on a 2 g scale (magnetic stirrer) to 4:1 on a 10 g scale (overhead stirrer) due to heterogeneous reaction conditions and poor solubility of the ZnCl₂/NaBH₄ complex.
Solution_Description: A solvent system of CPME containing 5 % 2‑MeTHF was identified, providing full solubilisation of the ZnCl₂/NaBH₄ complex, restoring high conversion and a 7:1 dr at kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reactions were heterogeneous… the particle attrition… led to decreased diastereoselectivity… we investigated CPME as the solvent, with varying amounts of THF and 2‑MeTHF… 5 % 2‑MeTHF in CPME afforded the best conversion and diastereoselectivity (7:1).”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Quenching the ZnCl₂/NaBH₄ reduction produced rapid, uncontrolled hydrogen gas evolution (spikes >1000 mL min⁻¹) and an exotherm, posing a safety hazard for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in a pilot‑plant hydrogenator equipped with gas handling capabilities; nitrogen sweep and dose‑controlled acetone quench were used to safely manage gas evolution and heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “The gas evolution was not dosing‑controlled… To ensure safe scale‑up of this procedure, a hydrogenator was chosen where the evolved hydrogen could be handled in a safe manner… the quench was exothermic (ΔH = −597 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 87 °C) with no gas evolution, and ~80 % of the total heat was evolved during the addition of acetone, suggesting that the quench was dose‑controlled.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: The Corey‑Itsuno reduction of ketone 13 using (R)‑2‑methyl‑CBS‑oxazaborolidine and BH₃·PhNEt₂ was moderately exothermic (ΔH = −177 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 34 °C) and generated hydrogen gas on quench, requiring careful temperature control.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run at 65–70 °C with a controlled acetone quench at 35 °C, providing a 67:1 dr and safe, dose‑controlled gas handling.
Supporting_Evidence: “Thermal hazard evaluation… addition of 13 to a mixture… was found to be moderately exothermic (ΔH = −177 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 34 °C)… After quenching, the stream was neutralized… This process was implemented on a 20 kg scale.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Deoxyfluorination of alcohol 8 with PBSF using DIPEA or DBU gave low conversion (≈55 % area) and significant side‑product formation (olefin 17, lactone 18), partly due to a biphasic mixture and ineffective base.
Solution_Description: t‑BuTMG was employed as a stronger, non‑nucleophilic base, and solvents were switched to MTBE, 2‑MeTHF, or i‑PrOAc. The homogeneous i‑PrOAc system gave 85 % isolated yield of fluorinated product 9 with minimal impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “t‑BuTMG afforded complete conversion with minimal impurities… The reaction with t‑BuTMG in toluene… Product… 73.5 % area 9 (entry 3)… Replacing toluene with solvents such as MTBE, 2‑MeTHF, or i‑PrOAc resulted in higher yields… i‑PrOAc was homogeneous and particularly clean, providing 9 in 85 % yield.”

Paper Title: Alternative Approach to the Large-Scale Synthesis of the Densely Functionalized Pyrrolidone BMT-415200
Problem_Description: Reduction of methyl ester 19 to alcohol 2 with NaBH₄ generated a highly exothermic reaction (ΔH = −404 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 74 °C) and considerable gas evolution (up to 14 W kg⁻¹ heat spike, 14 L min⁻¹ gas) during MeOH addition, posing a safety risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: MeOH was added slowly under a nitrogen sweep at 10–20 °C, the reaction was kept cool, and the quench with acetone was performed at 10–20 °C under nitrogen, providing a controlled exotherm and safe gas removal.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was found to be exothermic (ΔH = −404 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 74 °C) … a significant spike in heat flow… and gas flow… Therefore, a nitrogen sweep was maintained… the quench… was exothermic (ΔH = −597 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 87 °C) with no gas evolution, and ~80 % of the total heat was evolved during the addition of acetone, suggesting that the quench was dose‑controlled.”

Paper Title: A Novel and Practical Synthesis of 5‑Fluoro-1-(2-fluorobenzyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The hydrazinolysis of the acyl chloride 23 to give 2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinohydrazide (24) afforded only a 35 % isolated yield after column chromatography because the product was heavily contaminated with N,N′‑bis‑(2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinoyl)‑hydrazine, a side‑product formed due to the high reactivity of the acyl chloride.
Solution_Description: The authors changed the synthetic sequence to first convert 2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinic acid (22) into the methyl ester (25); then hydrazinolysis of 25 with hydrazine hydrate followed by an intramolecular cyclization.  By performing the cyclization in 1‑pentanol under reflux (~104 °C) and using 2.5 equiv of hydrazine, the isolated yield of the target pyrazolopyridin‑3‑ol (26) increased to >74 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The best yield of 24 was only 35% after purification by column chromatography since the product was contaminated by N,N′‑bis‑(2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinoyl)‑hydrazine.', 'Methyl 2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinate (25) was prepared ... then treatment of 25 with hydrazine hydrate ... The precipitated solid was filtered ... affording 26 in an excellent yield (74.2%).', 'When 1‑pentanol was used as the solvent, the reaction reached completion under reflux (≈104 °C) in 18 h, affording compound 26 in an excellent yield (74.2%).']

Paper Title: A Novel and Practical Synthesis of 5‑Fluoro-1-(2-fluorobenzyl)‑1
Problem_Description: When the hydrazinolysis/cyclization was carried out in EtOH or MeCN, the reaction required more than 60 h for the disappearance of intermediate 24 and gave only ca. 30 % yield of 26 due to extensive by‑product formation.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to 1‑pentanol and performing the reaction at reflux (≈104 °C) dramatically shortened the reaction time to 18 h and raised the isolated yield to >74 %. Similar performance was observed with 2‑ethoxyethanol at higher reflux temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Initially, the reaction was conducted in EtOH or CH₃CN, and the reaction time for the nucleophilic substitution was more than 60 h ... it gave 26 in a yield of ca. 30% because of generation of many byproducts.', 'When 1‑pentanol was used as the solvent, the reaction reached completion under reflux (≈104 °C) in 18 h, affording compound 26 in an excellent yield (74.2%).', 'In order to study the solvent effect, 2‑ethoxyethanol was used as the solvent, and the reaction carried out under reflux (≈119 °C) gave similar results (yield and time required).']

Paper Title: A Novel and Practical Synthesis of 5‑Fluoro-1-(2-fluorobenzyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The N‑1 benzylation of 26 with 2‑fluorobenzyl chloride in DMSO/K₂CO₃ produced the desired product 27 together with significant amounts of disubstituted by‑products 27a and 27b, resulting in low isolated yield (37 %) after column chromatography.
Solution_Description: Screening of bases and solvents identified aqueous NaOH (1.1 equiv) at 25–35 °C as the optimal condition. Under these conditions, the reaction gave 27 in 88.7 % isolated yield after simple recrystallisation from isopropanol/heptane, eliminating the need for chromatography and removing the by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['To a solution of compound 26 ... K₂CO₃ ... gave 27 together with N2‑substituted and O3‑substituted byproducts.', 'Different bases and solvents were screened, and NaOH in water was found to be the best (Table 2, entries 1–6).', 'When the amount of 2‑fluorobenzyl chloride was decreased to 1 equiv ... the yield of the crude product decreased.', 'Entry 9: ... NaOH (1.1 equiv) ... gave 150.8 g of 27 (88.7 % yield) after recrystallisation; HPLC purity: 99.45%.']

Paper Title: A Novel and Practical Synthesis of 5‑Fluoro-1-(2-fluorobenzyl)‑1
Problem_Description: Cyanation of bromide 28 with CuCN at 125 °C for 40 h gave only 27.6 % yield of the desired nitrile 9 and produced several cyanated by‑products (9a, 9b, 9c), and CuCN is a toxic cyanide source.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the CuCN system with a palladium‑catalysed cyanation using K₄Fe(CN)₆ (0.5 equiv) as a safer cyanide source, tBuXPhos Pd G3 (0.04 equiv) with tBuXPhos ligand, and KOAc as base in a 1:1 dioxane/water mixture. Conducted at reflux (≈100 °C) for 2.5 h in a Schlenk tube or a three‑neck flask, the reaction afforded 9 in 90.5 % yield (87.7 % on 80 g scale) with >99 % purity and without detectable by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['In entry 1 ... CuCN ... gave 27.6% yield and several by‑products.', 'The reaction was performed with 0.5 equiv of K₄Fe(CN)₆ and catalyzed by tBuXPhos Pd G3 ... at reflux for 2.5 h, gave a good result with a yield of 90.5% without detection of 9a or 9b (entry 6).', 'In order to make the reaction easy for scale‑up, the reaction conditions were changed to refluxing for 15 h in a three‑neck round‑bottom flask, and a similar result was achieved (entry 7).', 'Finally, the reaction was scaled up (80 g of 28) ... gave purified product 9 in a yield of 87.7% with a remarkable purity of 99.9% (99.91% HPLC).']

Paper Title: A Novel and Practical Synthesis of 5‑Fluoro-1-(2-fluorobenzyl)‑1
Problem_Description: The previously reported routes to intermediate 9 required diazotisation and iodination steps that pose significant safety hazards on an industrial scale, and relied on expensive or low‑atom‑economy starting materials.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a concise five‑step synthesis beginning from the commercially available and inexpensive 2‑chloro‑5‑fluoronicotinic acid (22). The new sequence eliminates hazardous diazotisation/iodination, uses inexpensive reagents, and achieves an overall isolated yield of 48.3 % for the target intermediate 9.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The original synthesis ... needed 11 reaction steps, where the main intermediate ... involved diazotisation ... and iodination ... These reactions might bring about safety risks in industrial‑scale production.', 'Another report ... involved seven reaction steps ... poor atom economy ... very expensive material ... 49% yield.', 'All of these problems made it unsuitable for industrial‑scale production, and an alternative synthesis of vericiguat was desirable.', 'Herein we report a novel and practical method to prepare key intermediate 9 ... in five steps with an overall yield of 48.3%.']

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: The initial cryogenic PFA‑tube reactor gave poor mixing of the two liquid feeds at –5 °C, resulting in a very long residence time (80 min) and only 41 % isolated yield (96 % ee).
Solution_Description: The PFA tube and premixer were replaced by an all‑glass microreactor (2.7 mL) that provided much improved mass‑transfer; the residence time fell to 40 min and the yield rose to 94 % (97 % ee).
Supporting_Evidence: “It was speculated that the two feeds were mixed ineffectively in the PFA tube at low temperature.”; “The reaction achieved a total residence time of 80 min with 41 % yield and 96 % ee.”; “The premixer and PFA tubing reactor were replaced with a glass microreactor (2.7 mL)… The yield was significantly increased to 94 % while maintaining a high ee value (97 %).”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: When the cryogenic module was removed and the temperature raised to 35 °C, only two homogeneous liquid feeds entered the reactor; the short residence time (5.4 min) limited mass‑transfer and gave a low 60 % yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Introducing a controlled flow of nitrogen gas created dense bubbles, greatly enhancing turbulence and mixing; this accelerated the reaction to give 98 % yield and 98 % ee in just 48 s.
Supporting_Evidence: “the residence time was significantly decreased to 5.4 min, and 60 % yield … were obtained. … it is presumed that the mass transfer effect … was limited.”; “Uniform and dense bubbles could be observed inside the reactor because of the enhanced liquid turbulence by the introduction of nitrogen gas.”; “the addition of gas did accelerate the reaction process, which ultimately achieved 98 % yield and 98 % ee with a residence time of 48 s.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Without nitrogen gas the reaction gave only 60 % yield, showing that insufficient mixing/turbulence limited conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A nitrogen gas flow of 5 mL min⁻¹ was adopted (maintaining a gas–liquid flow‑rate ratio of 10:1), which provided optimal turbulence and delivered 98 % yield and 98 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “When no nitrogen was fed, the product yield was only 60 % (entry 1).”; “When the gas flow rate was increased to 5 mL min⁻¹ … 98 % yield and 98 % ee were obtained.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Excessive gas flow (10 mL min⁻¹) shortened the residence time to 0.41 min, causing the yield to drop to 90 % despite good mixing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The gas flow rate was optimized to 5 mL min⁻¹, balancing turbulence with sufficient residence time to maintain high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “when the gas flow rate was increased to 10 mL min⁻¹, the reaction yield declined to 90 % … because the increased flow rate led to a significant reduction in the reaction residence time (0.41 min).”; “the optimum gas flow rate was finally chosen to be 5 mL min⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Using too much catalyst (0.4–0.5 equiv) or excess oxidant (1.2 equiv) decreased the yield, either by catalyst deactivation or by‑product formation, and would increase material cost.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was fine‑tuned to 0.3 equiv Ti(O‑iPr)₄ and 1.0 equiv cumene hydroperoxide, the optimum amounts that gave the highest yield (≈98 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “when the catalyst was increased from 0.2 to 0.3 equiv, the product yield increased significantly, though when the catalyst equivalents continued to increase to 0.4–0.5 equiv, the product yield decreased slightly.”; “when the oxidant equivalent was increased to 1.2 equiv, the reaction gave slightly lower product yields because of the formation of byproducts.”; “the optimum catalyst equivalent is 0.3 equiv, and the optimum oxidant equivalent is 1.0 equiv.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Raising the reaction temperature above 35 °C caused catalyst deactivation, reducing both yield and enantioselectivity.
Solution_Description: The temperature was set to 35 °C, which gave the best compromise between rate and catalyst stability, delivering 98 % yield and 98 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “when the reaction temperature reached 50 °C, both the yield and the ee values decreased. This indicates that the high temperature partially deactivates the catalyst.”; “the optimum reaction temperature is 35 °C.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Using solvents other than toluene (EtOAc, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, MeCN) gave markedly lower conversions (22‑62 % yield) because of poorer substrate solubility and/or unfavorable reaction media.
Solution_Description: Toluene was selected as the optimal solvent, affording 98 % yield and 98 % ee under the continuous‑flow conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Among these, toluene reacted most effectively as a solvent (entry 1) and provided a 98 % yield and 98 % ee value.”; Table 2 entries show much lower yields with other solvents.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: At very low system concentration (0.05 g mL⁻¹) the reaction gave only 65 % yield and 82 % ee; at higher concentration (>0.2 g mL⁻¹) the substrate precipitated and could not be fed.
Solution_Description: An optimal concentration of 0.2 g mL⁻¹ was chosen, delivering 98 % yield and 98 % ee while staying fully soluble for continuous feeding.
Supporting_Evidence: “First, we attempted the reaction … 0.05 g mL⁻¹ … 65 % yield and 82 % ee.”; “As the concentration of the system was raised, both the yield and ee values increased substantially … optimum system concentration of 0.2 g mL⁻¹ led to a yield of 98 % and an ee value of 98 %.”; “when the concentration was increased further, the substrate could not be dissolved … unable to be fed.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: Using a large batch of cumene hydroperoxide created a high online volume of oxidant, which poses safety risks at scale.
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow system automatically and slowly added the oxidant via a separate feed, keeping the online oxidant volume small and mitigating safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: “the continuous, automatic, and slow addition of oxidant kept a small online volume, which improved the selectivity of the reaction and addressed the safety concerns of using large quantities of oxidant.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Esomeprazole via Asymmetric Sulfoxidation
Problem_Description: After oxidation, the product needed to be isolated on a multigram scale; batch extraction and crystallization would be inefficient and could affect product quality.
Solution_Description: A continuous extraction‑precipitation train was coupled to the microreactor; the reaction stream was fed directly into a separatory funnel, then pH‑adjusted and precipitated, allowing a 20 g preparation with a productivity of 5.6 g h⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: “extraction and precipitation steps were added after the oxidation process … scale‑up preparation … provided about 20 g of product and achieved a yield of 5.6 g h⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Utilization of Quality by Design, Kinetic Modeling, and Computational Fluid Dynamics for Process Optimization and Scale-Up
Problem_Description: The epimer A content of the budesonide reaction mixture frequently falls outside the required 40‑51 % range, especially after scale‑up, leading to low overall yield of acceptable product.
Solution_Description: The epimerization temperature was lowered (0–10 °C) and the volume of aqueous HBr was tightly controlled (6–8 V) using a design‑of‑experiments (DoE) screening and response‑surface methodology (RSM). Reaction time was fixed at 3 h and butyraldehyde equivalents were set to 1.7 eq to maintain the desired epimer ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The epimer ratio drastically changed to 45:55… when the temperature after the acetalization reaction was increased from –5 °C to 23 °C…" (sec 1.1)

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: The combination of boron trifluoride diethyl etherate and triethylsilane in sulfolane generates diborane in situ, a highly flammable, toxic and reactive gas that also participates in a delayed exothermic event.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in sealed pressure vessels equipped with a back‑pressure regulator set to 50 psig and automatic pressure‑control valve (PCV). Diborane detectors, nitrogen sweep, and controlled venting through flame‑arrestors were installed to sequester and monitor the hazardous gas.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Detailed mechanistic inquisition revealed that in the presence of sulfolane, boron trifluoride is reduced by triethylsilane to generate diborane as the active reductant." (Intro) 
• "Diborane poses many process safety hazards; it is highly reactive, flammable, and acutely toxic." (Intro) 
• "The reaction headspace was studied using infrared spectroscopy and gas chromatography, while the reaction stream was studied using heat flow and adiabatic calorimetry to ensure safe scale‑up of the process." (Abstract) 
• "Reaction pressure was controlled by allowing some venting of the hazardous gases to the atmosphere through an automatic PCV with 50 psig setpoint." (Section 2.2.1) 
• "The reaction was run in a closed, isolated area of the pilot plant with diborane detectors installed strategically throughout the production area." (Section 2.2.1) 
• "The vessel was then purged with nitrogen... diborane meters were activated..." (Section 4.5).

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: Gas evolution (hydrogen and diborane) caused rapid pressure rise in sealed vessels, threatening to exceed the maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP) and creating a potential runaway scenario.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The fill level was limited to 30 % to increase headspace, and a pressure‑control valve was set to maintain pressure below 0.5 × MAWP (<60 psig). Back‑pressure regulators were used to keep pressure at the target 50 psig during the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Significant pressure generation in a sealed large‑scale vessel can pose a hazard as it approaches the maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP)." (Section 2.1.3) 
• "A pressure limit of <0.5 × MAWP (<60 psig, MAWP = 120 psig) was identified as the target margin to ensure safe operation..." (Section 2.1.3) 
• "Operating at low fill volume to increase the headspace volume versus batch mass..." (Section 2.1.3) 
• "The PCV was set to automatic control at 50 psig." (Section 4.5).

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: Increasing nitrogen sweep rates to remove diborane resulted in lower conversion to the product and increased formation of impurity A, compromising yield and purity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed under pressure (no nitrogen sweep) using a back‑pressure regulator, which retained diborane in the liquid phase, restored full conversion and reduced impurity A formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A significant decrease in reaction conversion was observed with increasing nitrogen flowrate... when using 50 sccm nitrogen flow, conversion to 2 decreased by 10–15% after the typical 18 h reaction time." (Section 2.1.2) 
• "Removing diborane negatively impacted the purity of 2 through increased formation of a key impurity, referred to herein as impurity A." (Section 2.1.2) 
• "Running the reaction under pressure significantly decreased the formation of impurity A... and full conversion of 1 was achieved consistently compared to reactions performed at ambient pressure." (Section 2.1.2) 
• Table 1 entry 6 (ambient pressure with nitrogen sweep) shows higher impurity and lower conversion versus pressured runs.

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: A delayed exotherm on heating to ~49 °C caused a rapid temperature and pressure rise (adiabatic temperature rise 31 °C), presenting a thermal runaway risk at larger scale.
Solution_Description: Batch temperature was limited to 40 °C (operating temperature) with a hard‑wired interlock capping jacket temperature at 80 °C, providing a >50 °C safety margin below the diborane auto‑ignition temperature.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The assessment focused on the thermal and pressure hazard associated with a jacket runaway upset scenario..." (Section 2.1.5) 
• "A significant delayed exotherm was observed upon heat up with an initiation temperature of 49 °C and an adiabatic temperature rise of 31 °C." (Section 2.1.5) 
• "The maximum batch temperature was assessed against the AIT of diborane... a safety margin of greater than 50 °C." (Section 2.2.1) 
• "The maximum jacket temperature was also limited to 80 °C using a hardwire interlock..." (Section 2.2.1).

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: The amount of methanol used in the quench affected impurity A entrapment and isolated yield; too little methanol trapped impurity, too much reduced yield.
Solution_Description: Two volumes of methanol were added, the quench was performed at 60 °C for 2 h, which balanced impurity removal and maximized yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Using less methanol during the quench was found to trap excess amounts of the key impurity A in the crystal, while using more methanol was found to significantly decrease the isolated yield of the product." (Section 2.1.6) 
• "Charging two volumes of methanol was found to balance purity and yield, effectively decreasing impurity levels while maintaining the highest possible isolated yield." (Section 2.1.6) 
• "A target temperature of 60 °C with a 2 h age time to ensure full conversion to 2." (Section 2.1.6) 
• Figure 10 shows quench time vs temperature data supporting the 60 °C, 2 h choice.

Paper Title: Integrating Process Development and Safety Analysis for Scale-Up of a Diborane-Generating Reduction Reaction
Problem_Description: Impurity A was incorporated into the crystal lattice during cooling; rapid cooling led to higher impurity levels.
Solution_Description: A slow cooldown (20 °C over at least 15 h) was implemented, allowing impurity rejection and delivering higher purity product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The cooldown rate was found to be the most critical factor affecting impurity rejection during the crystallization." (Section 2.1.6) 
• "Cooling the slurry to 20 °C over at least 15 h." (Section 2.1.6) 
• Table 2 entry 5 (pilot batch with 15 h cooldown) shows the lowest impurity A level (0.07 % area).

Paper Title: Multigram, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of the Flavonol Morin
Problem_Description: The literature‑based two‑step synthesis of tetramethyl‑morin required column chromatography for product isolation and used expensive, corrosive reagents (e.g., BCl₃) that are impractical on a large scale.
Solution_Description: A chromatography‑free work‑up was devised: the crude TBHP oxidation mixture was acidified, extracted with DCM, and the product was recrystallized from n‑butanol to give tetramethyl‑morin and its auronol isomer as sodium salts, eliminating the need for chromatographic purification and allowing the use of technical‑grade solvents.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “we were able to devise a work‑up sequence that avoids chromatography for all reaction steps, employing technical‑grade solvents.”
• “Recrystallization of the crude TBHP oxidation product from n‑butanol allowed the removal of all components besides tetramethylmorin and the isomeric auronol, which were separated as their sodium salts.”
• “Boron trichloride is a corrosive, expensive reagent that would have to be replaced in a technical reactor.”

Paper Title: Multigram, Chromatography-Free Synthesis of the Flavonol Morin
Problem_Description: The oxidative cyclization of chalcone 10 with TBHP gave only an average isolated yield of 39 % for tetramethyl‑morin, with many side‑products (aurone 21, auronol 20, fragmentation products), indicating low conversion and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: The oxidation conditions were optimized by using 10 equiv of 70 % aq. TBHP, performing the reaction at 24 °C for 23 h, and employing ethanol as the reaction solvent, which increased the yield compared with H₂O₂/NaOH (25 %).
Supporting_Evidence:

Solution_Description: The azide feed was basified with 5 mol % pyridine to keep pH > 7, preventing HN₃ formation.  The reaction was performed in continuous flow through a PFA tubing reactor at 100 °C with a 4 min residence time (instead of 120 °C/1 min), reducing the exothermic risk while still achieving quantitative conversion.  A DMSO/H₂O (≥40 % water) homogeneous solvent was used to keep NaCl in solution and avoid solid blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: "A small quantity of base (pyridine, 5 mol %) was added to the sodium azide solution to ensure that toxic and explosive hydrazoic acid could not be formed in the feed vessel."; "DSC analysis ... showed an exothermic event with an onset temperature of 115 °C as well as a highly exothermic event with an onset at 215 °C... therefore, for safety reasons, it was decided to operate at a lower temperature where possible. final process conditions were selected as a 4 min residence time at 100 °C."; "The precipitation of NaCl was observed over time ... an obstacle to operation in a microreactor. Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 1: Azidation and [3 + 2] Cycloaddition

The optimal stoichiometry (equivalents of 2‑cyanoacetamide and TMG) was fixed based on kinetic modelling.
Supporting_Evidence: "Numerous reported bases (e.g., NaOH and NaOMe) were found to be unproductive... simply showing consumption of azide starting material 2 with no triazole formation. This was attributed to the increased acidity of the benzylic protons of tetrazole azide 2, as well as the increased propensity for decomposition."; "Little to no reactivity was observed when using weaker bases... When examining slightly more basic species, such as amidines, guanidines, and carbonates (pKa 13–16), significant quantities of product 4, up to 83 %, were observed... The addition of strong bases (pKa > 25) immediately induced substantial gas formation, and little to no product was observed."; "The five most effective bases were found to be: K2CO3, Cs2CO3, DBU, TBD, and TMG. Due to limited solubility, the carbonate bases were discounted for continuous flow operation. The simple guanidine base, TMG, was selected as the most cost‑effective of the organic bases."
