Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 1: Azidation and [3 + 2] Cycloaddition
Problem_Description: The use of pyridine to basify the NaN₃ feed eliminated HN₃ formation but resulted in a pink coloration of the isolated product, likely due to formation of a pyridine‑derived colored salt, which is undesirable for downstream processing.
Solution_Description: The base for the NaN₃ feed was changed from pyridine to a minimal addition of 2.0 M NaOH (≈50 µL, pH 8‑10), which prevented the pink impurity and still provided effective basification without gas evolution.  This also reduced reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: "The pink color was ascribed to the formation of a colored salt relating to pyridine itself, so alternative bases were examined for the NaN₃ solution. Triethylamine was unsuccessful... On the other hand, when basifying the solution with a minimal quantity of 2.0 M NaOH (≈50 µL, ensuring pH = 8–10), effective reaction was observed and the isolated product was white in color."

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 1: Azidation and [3 + 2] Cycloaddition
Problem_Description: The initial PFR approach required a 12.4 min residence time to achieve the desired conversion, limiting throughput.  When operated at higher concentration, solid precipitation caused blockages and reduced yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A hybrid reactor configuration (short PFR (1.3 min) at 40 °C followed by a room‑temperature CSTR cascade) was implemented.  This allowed higher concentration (0.7 M) without precipitation, improved mixing via a static mixer, and eliminated the long residence needed in a single PFR.  The cascade delivered 79 % isolated yield and 9.5 g h⁻¹ productivity, suitable for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: "The PFR approach was limited to relatively low concentrations due to solubility issues, which prompted the use of a CSTR... The combined PFR + CSTR approach... increasing the concentration of the final reaction mixture to 0.7 M... The corresponding reaction conditions were chosen to be 1.3 min at 40 °C, followed by finishing the reaction in the batch vessel."; "A small static mixer unit (glass beads in 1.6 mm i.d. tubing) was added to ensure the homogeneity of the reaction mixture."

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: The starting triazole carboxamide (1) showed poor solubility in all screened solvents, limiting the maximum substrate concentration to 0.30 M and resulting in low conversion/yield for the N‑pivaloylation step.
Solution_Description: A heterogeneous reaction in MeCN was adopted, allowing concentrations up to 1.5 M; pyridine equivalents were reduced and the stoichiometry of pivaloyl chloride was lowered (1.30 equiv), which gave >94 % isolated yield of product 2.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: DMSO, though a good solvent for 1, reacted with pivaloyl chloride and prevented formation of the desired N‑pivaloylated product.
Solution_Description: Alternative solvents (sulfolane, N‑butylpyrrolidone, and finally MeCN) that do not react with pivaloyl chloride were screened; MeCN gave quantitative conversion under the optimized conditions.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: During N‑pivaloylation the chloride ion released could cause corrosion at the high temperatures required for the subsequent cyclization.
Solution_Description: The pivaloyl chloride addition was slowed and performed at 0 °C, limiting chloride buildup and preventing corrosion of the flow reactor components.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: The previously reported cyclization using heterogeneous KHCO₃ was unsuitable for flow and required 72 h at 90 °C to reach 98 % conversion, delivering only 62 % isolated product.
Solution_Description: Switching to the strong organic base DBU (catalyst optimization) and adding t‑BuOH cosolvent improved homogeneity; increasing the temperature to 140–200 °C (temperature optimization) reduced the residence time to 15–30 min (reaction‑time change), yielding 78–85 % product.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: Chlorination of pyrimidinone 3 with POCl₃ in NBP gave only 9 % yield and the Vilsmeier‑type reagent generated hazardous by‑products (dimethylamine).
Solution_Description: Switching to MeCN as solvent (solvent change) and using POCl₃ or (COCl)₂ in MeCN (reagent optimization) gave up to 95 % yield; the reaction was then transferred to a continuous‑flow coil (reactor platform) for safe, high‑throughput processing.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: Dimethylamine formed from the Vilsmeier reagent during chlorination reacted with the aryl chloride intermediate, generating side‑product 6a and creating a nitrosamine formation risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A cation‑exchange resin (SCX‑2 silica) was employed in a packed‑column to scavenge dimethylamine; the column’s color change was monitored by inline UV/vis (PAT) to ensure complete scavenging and enable continuous operation.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: During the SNAr coupling, insufficient DIPEA caused precipitation of the HCl‑salt of the chiral amine, leading to clogging in flow and reduced conversion.
Solution_Description: The DIPEA equivalents were increased to 4–5 equiv (stoichiometry change) and added prior to the amine feed (order and rate of addition) to maintain a homogeneous mixture and achieve ≥89 % isolated yield of API 6.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow-Facilitated CB2 Agonist Synthesis, Part 2: Cyclization, Chlorination, and Amination
Problem_Description: The solid‑phase amine‑scavenging step required periodic regeneration of the cation‑exchange resin, and performance could vary between cycles.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Two SCX‑2 columns were operated alternately; the spent column was regenerated with 2 M HCl, and inline UV monitoring ensured consistent resin performance across cycles.

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: The original quinoline fragment (9) synthesis required a long linear sequence with low overall yield (≈30 %) and employed hazardous high‑temperature decarboxylation and oxidation with m‑CPBA.
Solution_Description: A Friedlander quinoline synthesis was introduced, reducing the sequence to four steps, using cheaper, scalable reagents and eliminating the high‑temperature decarboxylation/oxidation, thereby improving overall yield to 32 % and removing safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The synthesis of the quinoline fragment 9 entailed a long linear sequence with low overall yield and hazardous chemistry such as high‑temperature decarboxylation and oxidation with m‑CPBA” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: Tosylate intermediate 11 was thermally unstable (onset 106 °C, ΔH = ‑415 J g⁻¹), making its isolation and storage unsafe.
Solution_Description: A tosyl‑swap strategy generated the tosylate in situ from benzylic alcohol 10 and tosylate 36, avoiding isolation of the unstable intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Isolation and storage of tosylate intermediate 11 was deemed unsafe due to its thermal instability with a thermal onset at 106 °C and energy of ‑415 J/g” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: In the Pd‑catalyzed C–O coupling, rapid precipitation of Pd black occurred with the Pd₂dba₃‑tBuXPhos system, leading to inconsistent reaction performance.
Solution_Description: Pre‑complexed catalysts (tBuXPhos Pd G3 and later tBuBrettPhos Pd G6) were employed, eliminating Pd black formation and allowing catalyst loading to be reduced to 0.2 mol %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The rapid precipitation of Pd black in the Pd₂dba₃‑tBuXPhos system likely occurred due to inefficient complexation … despite increasing the ligand‑to‑metal ratio to 2:1, we still observed significant Pd black precipitation.” (Section 2.4)

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: The low‑loading tBuBrettPhos Pd G6 catalyst was expensive and required a multi‑step synthesis from air‑sensitive precursors, raising cost and safety concerns for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: An alternative synthetic route to the G6 catalyst was developed from commercially available allylpalladium chloride dimer, avoiding the air‑sensitive (cod)‑Pd‑(CH₂)TMS₂ precursor and reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Commercial sources of tBuBrettPhos Pd G6 bromide were expensive… The original synthesis… started from air‑sensitive (cod)‑Pd‑(CH₂)TMS₂, and yields were moderate.” (Section 2.4)

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: The C–O coupling product (API 1) had low solubility, and residual THF was trapped as a solvate, requiring multiple solvent‑distillation cycles and leading to high ash content.
Solution_Description: The API was isolated as its HCl salt; treatment with HCl and 2 mol % DPPE lowered residual Pd to 6 ppm and eliminated azeotropic distillation cycles. Later, a salt‑break to free‑base in IPA/water removed THF entirely and reduced ash.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Residual THF was trapped in the API as a solvate and a re‑slurry in ethanol was implemented to purge the THF.” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the tosyl‑swap/SN2 alkylation, prolonged dosing of sodium tert‑butoxide caused an exotherm that generated a dimsyl anion from DMSO, leading to epimerization and a drop in enantiomeric excess (96 % ee on 70 kg scale).
Solution_Description: The addition order was changed: sodium tert‑butoxide was first added to the THF solution (tosyl swap), then DMSO was added to initiate the SN2 step, which controlled the exotherm and restored ee to 98–99 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The main difference between the laboratory and pilot plant operations was the dosing time of sodium tert‑butoxide since the exothermic addition took much longer to accomplish on a large scale… An inverse correlation between dosing time … and product ee.” (Section 2.3)

Paper Title: Route Optimization of the Noncovalent Modulator of Hemoglobin PF-07059013 for Treatment of Sickle Cell Disease through a Palladium-Mediated C–O Coupling, Part II: Pilot Plant Scale Manufacture
Problem_Description: Initial free‑base isolation required THF extraction and caused high residual THF and ash levels, adding cost and processing time.
Solution_Description: A direct slurry of the HCl salt in 1:1 IPA/water was heated, filtered, and neutralized with aqueous NaOH, eliminating THF use, reducing ash, and simplifying the work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Addition of ~10 % water during crystallization drastically reduced both THF and ash content… prompted us to examine the neutralization in an IPA/water mixture without use of THF.” (Section 2.5)

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of Ketoprofen: A Pyrolytic Aromatization Approach
Problem_Description: Claisen condensation of cyclohexanone with dimethyl carbonate gave only 68 % isolated yield, which was deemed unsatisfactory for large‑scale preparation.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a Stork‑enamine alkylation sequence: formation of the pyrrolidine‑derived enamine (92 % yield, 46 g scale) followed by benzylation and hydrolysis, delivering the desired benzyl‑cyclohexanone in 91 % yield on a 65 g scale, i.e. a higher‑yielding, scalable alternative.
Supporting_Evidence: “...Claisen condensation conditions (e.g., NaH, NaOMe, NaOEt, t‑BuOK, or t‑BuONa) with dimethyl carbonate suffered from unsatisfactory efficacy; the best transformation using NaOMe proceeded to deliver 16 with just 68 % yield…”,

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of Ketoprofen: A Pyrolytic Aromatization Approach
Problem_Description: The TiCl₄–Bu₃N mediated aldol/enol‑lactonization annulation initially afforded only 66 % conversion (80 % with Et₃N) and showed a strong dependence on concentration and reagent ratios, indicating poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: Optimization involved (i) switching the base to Et₃N, (ii) using DCM as the optimal solvent, (iii) increasing TiCl₄ to 2.0 equiv, (iv) adding ethyl pyruvate in three 0.5 equiv portions (portionwise addition), and (v) running the reaction from –78 °C to room temperature (30 °C) to give 96 % conversion (entry 11).
Supporting_Evidence: “...the low conversion rate (66 %) was measured … after the reaction proceeded for 12 h from –78 °C to rt…”,

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of Ketoprofen: A Pyrolytic Aromatization Approach
Problem_Description: The key pyrolytic aromatization step required heating the dihydrobenzofuranone with pyridine·HCl at 230–250 °C, posing safety concerns and risk of thermal decomposition.
Solution_Description: Pyridine·HCl was identified as an effective promoter, allowing the sealed‑tube aromatization at 230 °C for 12 h to afford the aryl‑propionic acid in 75 % yield, while avoiding more hazardous reagents and uncontrolled exotherms.
Supporting_Evidence: “...careful screening indicated that pyridine hydrochloride (C₅H₅N·HCl) was an effective promoter at 230–250 °C, thus providing the desired arylpropionic acid 9 in 75 % yield…”,

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of Ketoprofen: A Pyrolytic Aromatization Approach
Problem_Description: Benzylic oxidation of intermediate 9 gave no reaction in low‑polarity solvents (THF, MeOH, MeCN, EtOAc, CH₂Cl₂) and only modest yields in DMF (23 %) or DMSO (55 %).
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to DMSO dramatically improved the yield to 55 % (50 °C) and 68 % (25 °C, 2 h). Lowering the temperature to 25 °C and extending the reaction time to 5 h gave a reproducible 70 % yield on a 12 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the use of the highly polar solvent DMF proved to be effective and provided ketoprofen in 23 % yield…”,

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of Ketoprofen: A Pyrolytic Aromatization Approach
Problem_Description: Conventional ketoprofen syntheses employ hazardous reagents (NaNH₂, propionitrile, benzene) and require multiple isolation/crystallization steps, which are undesirable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The new route avoids these hazards by (i) using TiCl₄–Et₃N mediated annulation, (ii) employing a supported KMnO₄ ion‑exchange resin for the oxidation (avoiding free permanganate), and (iii) telescoping the dihydrobenzofuranone directly into the pyrolytic aromatization without intermediate purification, thereby reducing the number of isolation steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the avoidance of hazardous chemicals and crystallization of several intermediates would be greatly beneficial to the scalable synthesis of ketoprofen.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The original synthesis relied on a Sandmeyer reaction (Step f) to install a bromine atom.  Re‑trying this transformation on scale was impossible – the reaction could not be performed beyond low‑gram quantities, giving inconsistent conversion and making scale‑up futile.
Solution_Description: A completely new synthetic route was designed that starts from 2‑bromo‑6‑fluorobenzoic acid, eliminating the Sandmeyer step altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “Our attempts to scale‑up the original synthesis … proved futile. This route relied on a Sandmeyer reaction at the last step (Step f)… we were unable to execute the reaction beyond low gram scales.”; “A conceptually straightforward synthesis, starting from 2‑bromo‑6‑fluorobenzoic acid (9), would satisfy this requirement.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Acylation of the aminobenzimidazole (4) with acyl chloride 9a at 0 °C gave rapid disappearance of the amine but the intermediate decomposed on aqueous work‑up; heating in DMAc yielded a 7:3 mixture of the desired amide 10 and the undesired isomer 12.
Solution_Description: Switch to an in‑situ acid activation using CDI and the additive HOBT (1.2 equiv), which gave >99 % conversion to the desired amide 10 with only 1.4 % of impurity 12.
Supporting_Evidence: “When amine 4 was treated with acyl chloride 9a … the observed intermediate decomposed upon aqueous work‑up.”; “When amine 4 was converted … heated … two products formed … the purified minor product was identified to be 12.”; “After 24 h at 98 °C … complete conversion … predominant formation of the desired amide 10 (98.6 % A) … a small amount (1.4 % A) of undesired product 12 was also detected.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Screening of common amide‑coupling reagents (EDC/HOBT, HBTU, TBTU) gave either predominant formation of impurity 12 or low conversion to the target amide 10.
Solution_Description: Use of CDI together with HOBT (or DMAP) as a promoter enabled near‑quantitative conversion to amide 10 (entry 7, Table 1).
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entries 1‑4: “undesired compound 12 was produced predominately” or “significant amount of impurity 12 was also produced.”; “When carbonyl diimidazole‑(CDI) was used, no conversion was observed (entry 5).”; “After 24 h at 98 °C … complete conversion … predominate formation of the desired amide 10 (98.6 % A) … 1.4 % 12.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The original hydrogenation of intermediate 3 used 60 wt % of 10 % Pd/C, 40 vol MeOH, and required overnight‑to‑days reaction times with large‑volume filtrations and chromatography, making the step impractical for kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading was reduced to 10 wt % Pd/C, the solvent volume cut from 40 vol to 10 vol by adding 1 vol of acetic acid as a co‑solvent, and the reaction was run at ambient temperature for 4 h at 100 psi H₂.  This dramatically lowered catalyst, solvent, and time requirements and simplified work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: Original protocol: “required 60 wt % of 10 % Pd/C … 40 vol of methanol … overnight to a few days … 90 L of filtrate for a 100 g run.”; Optimization: “included acetic acid as a cosolvent … 10 vol of methanol and 1 vol of acetic acid … with just 10 wt % of catalyst loading, the hydrogenation reached completion in 4 h under 100 psi hydrogen at ambient temperature.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: During work‑up of the hydrogenation product 4, neutralizing the filtrate caused the compound to aggregate into solid blocks, making filtration difficult.
Solution_Description: A staged neutralization/crystallization strategy was adopted: partially neutralize the solution, seed to form a free‑flowing slurry, then add additional water/NaOH to complete crystallization, yielding a free‑flowing solid without aggregation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The isolation of the hydrogenation product 4 … was challenging initially. … compound 4 aggregated into solid blocks.”; “A strategy of inducing crystallization at a partially neutralized stage … seeding produced a uniform free flowing slurry … This process reliably produced compound 4 as an off‑white crystalline solid.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The original Suzuki coupling (Step 1) used 10 mol % Pd(dppf)Cl₂, 1,4‑dioxane, 24 h reaction time, and required distillation, extraction, and column chromatography for work‑up.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was dropped to 1 mol % Pd(dppf)Cl₂, solvent was switched to DMAc with K₂CO₃ as base, reaction time reduced to 3 h at 120 °C, and product was precipitated by adding water, allowing filtration and crystallization instead of chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Original: “required 10 mol % Pd‑(dppf)‑Cl₂ … 24 h at 95 °C … work‑up involved distillation, extraction, and column chromatography.”; Optimized: “1,4‑dioxane was replaced with DMAc and Na₂CO₃ was replaced with K₂CO₃ … reaction reached 98 % conversion in 3 h at 120 °C, with merely 1 % catalyst loading. Product isolation involved adding water to precipitate the product. … further purified by crystallization from methanol‑water.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The Boc deprotection of compound 11 (Step 5) caused product aggregation when performed in 1,4‑dioxane alone, leading to solid chunks that were difficult to filter.
Solution_Description: Inclusion of 1 vol of 2‑propanol as a co‑solvent prevented aggregation, allowing the product to crystallize as a free‑flowing solid during the acid‑mediated deprotection.
Supporting_Evidence: “It should be noted that the inclusion of 1 volume of 2‑propanol as the cosolvent was necessary to prevent the product from aggregating into solid chunks, which occurred when the reaction was carried out in 1,4‑dioxane alone.”

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: HOBT, used as an activating additive in the CDI‑mediated amide coupling, is shock‑sensitive and therefore not ideal for large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: The authors note that HOBT can be replaced by N‑hydroxysuccinimide for future large‑scale work to mitigate the safety issue.
Supporting_Evidence: “HOBT is not ideal for large scale synthesis due to its shock sensitivity. We had subsequently found that HOBT can be replaced by N‑hydroxysuccinimide. This modification is under examination for future use.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: The initial alkylation of 3‑methyl‑1H‑1,2,4‑triazole (3) with benzyl 2‑bromoacetate (2) gave a mixture of N¹‑, N²‑ and N⁴‑alkylated products; the desired N¹‑product (4) could only be isolated in 17 % overall yield after labor‑intensive chromatography to separate the regioisomers.
Solution_Description: A desymmetrization strategy was introduced using inexpensive 3,5‑dibromo‑1H‑1,2,4‑triazole (7). N¹/N²‑selective alkylation followed by regioselective debromination gave a single bromide intermediate (9) that could be carried forward without chromatographic separations.
Supporting_Evidence: ['the desired N¹‑product 4 could only be isolated in 17% yield, as the reaction was unselective with regard to N¹‑, N²‑, and N⁴‑alkylation.', 'The N⁴‑isomer 6 had to be separated by chromatography before the N²‑isomer 5 was then removed by recrystallization.', 'We envisioned to either build up the triazole ring itself in a de novo approach or by starting from a symmetrical 1,2,4‑triazole starting material and performing a desymmetrization after the initial alkylation step.', '3,5‑Dibromo‑1H‑1,2,4‑triazole (7) caught our attention as a starting material for the desymmetrization approach as it is inexpensive and readily available on large scale.', 'Only two different regioisomers can be formed (N¹/N² vs N⁴) in the alkylation step.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: Methylation of bromide 9 proved difficult; most reagents gave poor conversion (≤5 %) and a recurring unidentified polar impurity, while Me₂Zn gave 49 % a/a but still generated the same impurity.
Solution_Description: Screening identified DABAl‑Me₃ as a viable methylating agent; using Pd₂(dba)₃ (0.015 eq) with CyJohnPhos (0.03 eq) in THF (35 vol) gave >99 % conversion and 72 % isolated yield of product 15, eliminating the polar impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Only trimethylboroxine and MeB(OH)₂ showed product formation in the methylation via Suzuki–Miyaura coupling (21%, respectively 1% of desired product 15 formed).', 'Full conversion was observed when Me₂Zn was applied ... but only 49% a/a of product 15 was detected and the formation of an unidentified polar impurity was observed.', '1,4‑Diazabicyclo[2.2.2]‑octan‑bis‑(trimethylaluminium) (DABAl‑Me₃) ... showed 30% conversion (entry 9) and no formation of further impurities other than the same unknown polar impurity.', 'A ligand screening that identified CyJohnPhos as a superior ligand over XPhos, leading to full conversion of 9 after 2 h at 70 °C (entry 2).', 'Solvent screening (entry 3) confirmed that besides toluene and dioxane, THF was the best solvent.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: Quenching the DABAl‑Me₃ methylation with aqueous HCl caused rapid evolution of methane gas, posing a significant safety risk during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: An inverse quench was performed by slowly adding the reaction mixture into 2 M aqueous AcOH while maintaining a strong N₂ flow, thereby controlling gas evolution and eliminating the safety hazard.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The release of methane gas during the quench was considered most safety‑critical and was controlled by performing an inverse quench of the reaction mixture into 2 M aq. AcOH and dilution of the off‑gas with a strong N₂‑flow.', 'We considered the conditions in THF (Table 2, entry 4) as an interesting starting point for a potential scale‑up and started further investigations, including the examination of the quench of the DABAl‑Me₃ reagent, as we hoped to avoid the release of methane gas during the quenching process.', 'It was found that 10% of the tert‑butyl ester of 15 was cleaved when the reaction mixture was quenched onto 1 M aq. HCl and stirred at room temperature for 3 days. This observed ester hydrolysis in aq. HCl was even more pronounced on gram scale, and consequently, we changed to a quench with 2 M aq. AcOH, which triggered no ester hydrolysis in a corresponding stress test.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: During quench of the methylation step with 1 M aq. HCl the tert‑butyl ester of product 15 was partially hydrolyzed, leading to loss of material.
Solution_Description: The quench was changed to 2 M aq. AcOH, which suppressed ester hydrolysis; the pH of the quench medium was thus controlled to avoid acidic decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: ['10% of the tert‑butyl ester of 15 was cleaved when the reaction mixture was quenched onto 1 M aq. HCl and stirred at room temperature for 3 days.', 'This observed ester hydrolysis in aq. HCl was even more pronounced on gram scale, and consequently, we changed to a quench with 2 M aq. AcOH, which triggered no ester hydrolysis in a corresponding stress test.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: The methylation step required expensive palladium catalyst Pd₂(dba)₃ and the uncommon DABAl‑Me₃ reagent, which are costly and have limited commercial availability for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A fully de novo synthesis avoiding the Pd‑catalyzed methylation was developed, using inexpensive reagents (hydrazine, Me‑acetimidate) and eliminating the need for costly reagents, thereby reducing the estimated cost of the API to $4 000 /kg.
Supporting_Evidence: ['the methylation of bromo triazole 9 requires the use of the expensive Pd₂(dba)₃ catalyst and applies the uncommon methylation reagent DABAl‑Me₃, which might be difficult to source on a larger scale.', 'the de novo synthesis via hydrazine 16‑HCl also starts from readily available and inexpensive starting materials. However, it does not include the expensive methylation step and therefore offers a less expensive synthetic alternative toward triazole 1 with estimated costs of only $4 000 /kg.', 'The overall process clearly benefited from its short step‑count and inexpensive reagents and starting materials but suffered from a low overall yield and laborious purification procedures due to the selectivity issues in the alkylation of 3.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: Hydrazine 16‑HCl showed strong exothermic decomposition (‑794 J g⁻¹) and potential shock sensitivity, raising safety concerns for isolation and handling on scale.
Solution_Description: The hydrazine was isolated as a solvent‑wet solid (no drying) and handled as its HCl salt; thorough DSC and falling‑hammer tests were performed, and the material was stored under controlled conditions to mitigate safety risks.
Supporting_Evidence: ['DSC analysis indicated a strong exothermic decomposition (‑794 J g⁻¹) with a left limit at 135 °C.', 'All efforts to telescope hydrazine 16‑HCl into the following condensation step with Me‑acetimidate failed. Therefore, the shock sensitivity of 16‑HCl was assessed with a falling‑hammer test, which turned out to be negative, opening the door for the isolation of solvent‑wet hydrazine 16‑HCl by filtration without further drying.', 'For safety reasons (see above), we only isolated 16‑HCl as solvent‑wet material and directly converted it in the next reaction step.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: The use of Me‑thioacetimidate in the de novo route generated 1‑octanethiol, an odorous and malodorous by‑product, complicating handling and work‑up.
Solution_Description: Me‑acetimidate was substituted for Me‑thioacetimidate; the latter releases methanol, a benign, easily removable by‑product, eliminating the odor issue.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The reaction with Me‑thioacetimidate caused an unpleasant odor, especially during workup.', 'Hence, we investigated nonsmelly alternatives such as octyl‑thioacetimidate and Me‑acetimidate. Even though the desired condensation also worked with octyl‑thioacetimidate, we focused our efforts on Me‑acetimidate due to its straightforward synthesis from two bulk solvents (MeOH and MeCN).', 'In addition, the formed MeOH byproduct from the reaction of Me‑acetimidate with hydrazine 16‑HCl can be easily removed, which is an advantage compared to the high boiling 1‑octanethiol from octyl‑thioacetimidate.']

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route toward an Alkylated 1,2,4-Triazol, a Key Starting Material for CXCR3 Antagonist ACT-777991
Problem_Description: After the alkylation step the reaction mixture contained inorganic salts (KBr, KHCO₃) that caused precipitation and required filtration before telescoping, potentially impacting throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Tenofovir Alafenamide Fumarate Inspired by New Retrosynthetic Disconnection Featuring a Novel Carbon–Phosphorus Bond Construction Methodology

By performing crystallisation (20 °C) and racemisation (160 °C, 4 min) simultaneously in a continuous‑flow set‑up, the (M)‑atropisomer is amplified in situ, eliminating the need for chromatography and delivering 75 % isolated yield at 12 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The only serious deficiency was reliance on chiral chromatography, characterized by low throughput, poor recovery, and low mass utilization.”; “The chromatographic separation of atropisomers, necessary in the original route, was initially replaced by a traditional chiral resolution… Subsequently, efficiency of the chiral resolution process (37 % yield, inherently limited to 50 % maximum yield) was drastically improved with the development of formally dynamic chiral resolution process (SPACE) able to convert the racemate into 98.4 % d.e. MRTX1719•BDP salt in 75 % isolated yield on 12 kg scale.”

Paper Title: Scalable Atroposelective Synthesis of MRTX1719: An Inhibitor of the PRMT5/MTA Complex
Problem_Description: Atroposelective palladium‑catalysed cross‑coupling of enantiopure (M)‑1 with fragment 2 caused severe loss of enantiomeric excess (e.e.).  Even at 80 °C the e.e. dropped by 0.8 % after 2 h, and at 100 °C a loss of 8.1 % was observed; the final coupled product showed only 6 % e.e., indicating rapid racemisation of the axial chirality under the reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: Instead of forcing an asymmetric cross‑coupling, the authors developed the SPACE dynamic resolution, which couples crystallisation (which favours the (M)‑enantiomer) with a rapid high‑temperature racemisation loop.  This simultaneously drives the equilibrium toward the desired atropisomer while preventing its degradation during the high‑temperature step.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the resulting 3 showed only 6 % e.e.”; “A solution of enantiomerically pure (M)‑1 (99.4 % e.e.) was incubated in a range of synthetically relevant temperatures… modest 0.8 % e.e. loss at 80 °C but significant 8.1 % e.e. loss at 100 °C after only 2 h of exposure.”; “The incompatibility of low temperature crystallization (20 °C) and high temperature racemization (160 °C) was resolved by a filter upstream of the PFR …”

Paper Title: Scalable Atroposelective Synthesis of MRTX1719: An Inhibitor of the PRMT5/MTA Complex
Problem_Description: The synthesis of building‑block 1 was driven by two expensive and poorly available raw materials: 4‑chloro‑2,5‑difluorobenzoic acid (5) and cyclopropanol.  The acid suffered from a long lead‑time and limited kilogram‑scale availability, inflating the cost of the API.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic sequence was designed using inexpensive 1,4‑difluorobenzene as the starting material, with an optimized chlorination (SO₂Cl₂/AlCl₃/I₂) and a copper‑catalysed cyanation to give benzonitrile 7.  Cyclopropanol was sourced from cyclopropyl‑methyl‑ketone via a Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, eliminating the costly early‑stage steps and providing a scalable, low‑cost route.
Supporting_Evidence: “Chief offenders were the expensive raw materials 4‑chloro‑2,5‑difluorobenzoic acid (5) and cyclopropanol introduced early in the synthetic sequence. To make matters worse, 5 suffered from a long lead‑time and limited availability on a kilogram scale.”; “The desired product 12 was isolated by distillation… 1,4‑difluorobenzene was identified as a potentially attractive precursor due to its low cost and availability on scale.”

Paper Title: Scalable Atroposelective Synthesis of MRTX1719: An Inhibitor of the PRMT5/MTA Complex
Problem_Description: The Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of cyclopropyl‑methyl‑ketone generated highly energetic peroxides and intermediates, posing significant safety risks on large scale.
Solution_Description: The oxidation was transferred to a continuous‑flow reactor, which safely handles the energetic peroxides, improves heat removal and enables robust scale‑up while mitigating safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: “To alleviate safety concerns related to highly energetic Baeyer–Villiger intermediates, continuous flow operation was adopted on a manufacturing scale.”

Paper Title: Scalable Atroposelective Synthesis of MRTX1719: An Inhibitor of the PRMT5/MTA Complex
Problem_Description: The original Miyaura‑Suzuki borylation of 19b used 1.0 mol % Pd and required a separate palladium‑removal step because residual Pd caused inconsistent performance of downstream cross‑couplings.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was reduced to 0.1 mol % Pd using XPhos, and a direct crystallisation from a 1:4 dioxane/water mixture was employed, which rejects >99 % of Pd (150–170 ppm) while delivering ≥90 % isolated yield, removing the need for a dedicated Pd‑scrubbing operation.

Paper Title: Scalable Atroposelective Synthesis of MRTX1719: An Inhibitor of the PRMT5/MTA Complex
Problem_Description: Low‑temperature crystallisation (20 °C) could not be performed together with the required high‑temperature racemisation (160 °C) because the two operations are antagonistic, leading to process incompatibility.

Paper Title: Optimized Process and Quality Evaluation for Ketamine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The bromination step using HBr/H₂O₂ generated a violent exothermic reaction (temperature jumped from 20 °C to 80 °C within minutes) that posed a safety hazard and resulted in incomplete conversion on kilogram scale (only 84 % of intermediate 5 formed, with 11.6 % of intermediate 4 remaining).
Solution_Description: The bromination reagent was switched to N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) together with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH·H₂O in dichloromethane. This change gave a milder, steadier reaction, raising the conversion of intermediate 5 from 88 % to 99 % and eliminating the violent temperature rise.

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: Key reaction intermediates (aryl nitroso and aryl hydroxylamine) are unstable and decompose during sampling, preventing the preparation of analytical standards and making traditional analytical control (ICH M7 Option 2) impractical.
Solution_Description: A kinetic justification and control strategy were developed (kinetic model, rate‑confirmation test) to demonstrate that the intermediates are fully consumed, eliminating the need for analytical standards.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The relatively large number of these intermediates, several of which were unstable, preventing samples from being maintained and appropriate analytical standards from being prepared… presented a serious challenge for developing traditional analytical methods” (sec 1).

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: Arylnitro hydrogenations are highly exothermic, generating large amounts of heat that pose safety risks and can lead to runaway reactions if not properly managed.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature and pressure were deliberately lowered for kinetic studies (60 °C, 2 bara H₂) and a conservative hold time was added to ensure complete conversion while keeping the reaction under safe thermal conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Aryl nitro reductions are highly exothermic and can generate potentially unstable reaction intermediates, so a keen knowledge of kinetics and thermal and mass transfer is required to ensure safe scale‑up.” (sec 1). 
• “The reaction was performed… at 60 °C and maintaining a hydrogen pressure of 15 psia” (ref 36). 
• “A conservative 12 h reaction kinetic hold time was prescribed for the commercial process” (sec 3).

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: The final product (diamino 2) adsorbs on the catalyst surface, inhibiting further hydrogenation and causing slower conversion rates that vary with the amount of product present.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading and DIEA equivalents were reduced in the “lowest‑rate” test to accentuate the inhibition effect, and the kinetic model incorporated a product‑inhibition term (k₄, K₄) to predict conversion under various product concentrations.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Diamino 2 was observed to impede the rate of hydrogenation and was added to the model.” (sec 3).

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: Ensuring that all potentially mutagenic intermediates fall below the 1 ppm limit required extended reaction times (12 h kinetic hold + 4 h mass‑transfer hold = 16 h total), which could reduce throughput.
Solution_Description: A batch process with robust agitation (80–100 rpm) and appropriate reactor geometry was selected to reliably achieve the required gas–liquid mass‑transfer coefficient (k_L a ≥ 0.011 s⁻¹) and allow the long hold times without scale‑up issues.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A mass‑transfer hold time of 4 h… was used to ensure that potentially mutagenic intermediates are consumed even when operating at the lower limit of k_L a.” (sec 5). 
• “The batch must be operated at or above an agitation rate that can achieve a minimum hydrogen interphase mass transfer coefficient of 0.011 s⁻¹.” (sec 4). 
• “This rate was easily achieved in multiple commercial reactors tested in the 80 to 100 rpm range.” (ref 41).

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation reactors pose a fire/explosion risk if oxygen enters the system after hydrogen consumption.
Solution_Description: A nitrogen pre‑charge (0.1 barg) is introduced before hydrogen addition to maintain a positive pressure and prevent atmospheric oxygen intrusion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “For commercial hydrogenation safety, nitrogen at 0.1 barg … ensures a constant positive pressure … and oxygen from the external atmosphere will not be drawn into the vessel.” (sec 6). 
• “Hydrogen is added at a pressure of 2.9 bara … to a reactor containing 1.1 bara nitrogen for a total pressure of 4.0 bara.” (sec 6).

Paper Title: Development of a Control Strategy for Hydrogenation of Aryl Nitro Analogs by Kinetic Justification
Problem_Description: Potential variability in catalyst activity due to poisons, inhibitors, or lot‑to‑lot differences could lead to insufficient conversion of intermediates.
Solution_Description: A Rate Confirmation Test (RCT) is performed before each commercial batch using the exact lots of catalyst, solvent, and reagents under deliberately slowed conditions; failure to meet the 95 % conversion criterion triggers investigation and material replacement.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The RCT is required to be performed in the laboratory prior to each commercial batch and uses the same lots of catalyst, solvent, raw materials, and reagents … to best detect any potential for insufficient conversion.” (sec 6). 
• “If the combination of material lots does not result in meeting the acceptance criterion, an investigation is initiated … alternate lots … are identified, and the RCT is repeated.” (ref 47).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of the Shelf-Stable Radical Difluoromethylthiolation Reagent
Problem_Description: When the synthesis of benzyldifluoromethyl‑thioether (BnSCF₂H) was scaled from 0.1 mol (≈ 5 g) up to the 5 mol (≈ 481 g) level, the isolated yield dropped dramatically from > 90 % in small‑scale trials to only 49 % on the 0.1 mol run, indicating poor reproducibility and low conversion on larger scale.
Solution_Description: The temperature was lowered from 60 °C to 40 °C and the reaction was run for 6 h. Under these milder conditions the conversion became quantitative and the isolated yield recovered to 77 % on the 5 mol scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield dropped dramatically to 49% when the reaction was conducted in a 0.1 mol scale… Decreasing the temperature to 40 °C, the reaction occurred in full conversion after 6.0 h to give … 77% yield (entry 18).”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of the Shelf-Stable Radical Difluoromethylthiolation Reagent
Problem_Description: Screening of solvents showed that the reaction gave high yields only in toluene (96 %). Substituting toluene with petroleum ether, THF, hexane, acetone or DMF caused the yield to fall to 40–75 %, suggesting poor solubility/mixing of the reagents in those media.
Solution_Description: Toluene was selected as the optimal solvent for the transformation, providing the highest conversion and isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “When toluene was used as the solvent, the yield could reach up to 96 %. The yields of the reaction decreased significantly to 40–75 % when toluene was replaced by other solvents… (entries 1–6).”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of the Shelf-Stable Radical Difluoromethylthiolation Reagent
Problem_Description: Absence of the phase‑transfer catalyst tris‑(3,6‑dioxaheptyl)‑amine (TDA‑1) reduced the formation of BnSCF₂H to < 47 % (entry 7), indicating inefficient contact between the aqueous NaOH phase and the organic substrates.
Solution_Description: Inclusion of 20 mol % TDA‑1 as a PTC restored high conversion, giving up to 96 % yield in toluene.
Supporting_Evidence: “A phase‑transfer catalyst (PTC) tris‑(3,6‑dioxaheptyl)‑amine (TDA‑1) was playing a very important role… In the absence of TDA‑1, the formation of BnSCF₂H … was observed in less than 47 % yields (entry 7).”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of the Shelf-Stable Radical Difluoromethylthiolation Reagent
