Problem_Description: In the single‑temperature‑controlled reactor (MR‑1) larger tube diameters reduce heat‑transfer efficiency, causing hot spots, excessive H₂O₂ decomposition and a drop in MSM yield.
Solution_Description: Select a smaller internal diameter (3 mm × 1 mm), adjust catalyst loading (0.002 mol) and residence time (4 min) to balance kinetic rate and heat removal, achieving a 91.5 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "The overall heat transfer efficiency of the microchannel reactor ... depends on the specific surface area of the PTFE tube."; "When the tube diameter was increased, the heat transfer efficiency reduced, leading to hot spots and lower MSM yield."; "In a larger diameter reactor with a low heat transfer efficiency, an increase in catalyst dosage can accelerate the decomposition side reaction of H₂O₂."; "When the channel diameter was 3 mm × 1 mm, the water bath temperature was 80 °C, the catalyst dosage was 0.002 mol, and the residence time was 4 min, the yield of MSM reached 91.5 %"; "The increase of catalyst dosage will accelerate the process of the oxidation reaction, and on the other hand will cause a small amount of H₂O₂ decomposition."

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of Methyl Sulfone with Microchannel Reactors: A Safer and Efficient Production Strategy
Problem_Description: During MR‑1 operation a violent reaction occurs in the front section of the channel; the external water bath cannot absorb the heat fast enough, producing hot spots and risking thermal runaway.
Solution_Description: Implement a dual‑temperature‑controlled reactor (MR‑2) with a low‑temperature zone at the inlet (e.g., 20 °C) and a higher‑temperature zone downstream (e.g., 75–80 °C), thereby spreading the heat‑release profile and preventing hot‑spot formation.
Supporting_Evidence: "a violent reaction occurred in the front section of the microchannel. This was attributed to the significant amount of heat released in the initial stage of the reaction, which the external water bath environment was unable to remove in time, leading to thermal runaway for part of the reactants."; "MR‑2 was designed to optimize the reaction process through low‑temperature control in the front and high‑temperature control in the back."; "When the first stage temperature is 20 °C and the residence time is 1.0 min, and the second stage temperature is 80 °C and the residence time is 3.0 min, the yield of MSM can reach 98.1 %"; "The temperature of the first zone was defined as Tf and the temperature of the second zone was defined as Ts"; "The dual temperature‑controlled continuous‑flow process can effectively increase the yield of MSM."

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of Methyl Sulfone with Microchannel Reactors: A Safer and Efficient Production Strategy
Problem_Description: Excessive catalyst loading or overly long residence times promote H₂O₂ decomposition, generating oxygen, shortening the actual residence time and reducing MSM conversion.
Solution_Description: Use an optimal catalyst dosage of 0.001 mol and keep the jacket temperature ≤ 60 °C (or 50 °C in the scale‑up reactor) to suppress H₂O₂ decomposition while maintaining sufficient oxidation rate.
Supporting_Evidence: "When the catalyst dosage is 0.002 mol, the increase of catalyst dosage will accelerate the process of the oxidation reaction, and on the other hand will cause a small amount of H₂O₂ decomposition."; "When the residence time exceeded 4 min, the yield of MSM decreased… due to the side reaction of the H₂O₂ decomposition reaction becoming dominant."; "The increase of catalyst dosage and the value of Tj both aggravate the decomposition of H₂O₂… significant oxygen generation… unfavorable for improving the MSM yield."; "To achieve a higher yield of MSM, a catalyst dosage of 0.001 mol and the value of Tj above 60 °C are preferred… ensures a rapid reaction rate and reduces excessive hot spots."; "When Tj exceeds 50 °C, temperatures at monitoring sites are lower than set temperature… high temperature causes H₂O₂ decomposition, producing oxygen that reduces the actual residence time."

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of Methyl Sulfone with Microchannel Reactors: A Safer and Efficient Production Strategy
Problem_Description: At the industrial scale (MR‑4), DMSO solidifies when the inlet temperature is set near its melting point (≈ 18–19 °C), causing tube blockage.
Solution_Description: Set the temperature of the pre‑heating plates at 25 °C (above the DMSO melting range) while keeping the downstream zones at higher temperatures, preventing solidification and maintaining smooth flow.
Supporting_Evidence: "Because the melting point of DMSO is 18–19 °C and the temperature control fluctuation in MR‑4 is ±1 °C, when Tf was set to 20 °C, the DMSO in the microchannel is prone to solidification, leading to tube blockage."; "Therefore, the Tj value of the 1–3 reaction plates was set at 25 °C, and that of the 4–10 reaction plates was set at 80 °C."; "The industrial continuous‑flow process for producing MSM... was conducted on an industrial microchannel reactor plant (MR‑4)."; "The application of microchannel technology can effectively improve the intrinsic safety and productivity of the MSM preparation process."; "A catalyst dosage of 0.001 mol was used, and the total residence time of the reactants in the reactor was 5 min, with a total reaction time of 4 min."

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of Site-Specific Antibody–Drug Conjugates Using AJICAP Second-Generation Technology
Problem_Description: The linker‑cleavage step uses a high concentration of hydroxylamine, which can cleave the antibody‑peptide bond under alkaline conditions, creating a safety/decomposition risk and leaving residual hydroxylamine and peptide fragments in the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: The process switches to an acidic buffer during tangential‑flow filtration (TFF) to quench the hydroxylamine and remove >95 % of residual peptide‑reagents, thereby eliminating the cleavage risk and purifying the product.
Supporting_Evidence: “the present method for cleaving the linker … requires high concentrations of hydroxylamine. However, due to the potential risk of hydroxylamine cleaving the peptide bond of the antibody under alkaline conditions, it was needed to eliminate this risk.”; “TFF purification was employed utilizing an acidic buffer to remove hydroxylamine as much as possible.”; “To remove reaction related impurities (residual hydroxylamine and peptide‑related compounds), trastuzumab‑Lys248‑thiol (3a) was purified by TFF … to remove >95 % of residual 1a.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of Site-Specific Antibody–Drug Conjugates Using AJICAP Second-Generation Technology
Problem_Description: MMAE‑containing payloads are highly hydrophobic, making their removal by a simple TFF step difficult and leading to residual drug‑related impurities.
Solution_Description: The payload loading is reduced from 10 equiv (first‑generation) to 2.7 equiv (second‑generation), decreasing the hydrophobic load and allowing a single TFF operation (with an acidic histidine buffer, pH 5.2) to completely clear MMAE‑related compounds.
Supporting_Evidence: “AJICAP second‑generation technology enabled the reduction of MC‑VC‑MMAE using fewer equivalents (present study: 2.7 equiv of MC‑VC‑MMAE, previous study: 10 equiv)… a single TFF was sufficient to clear the residual payload linkers.”; “removal of MMAE‑related compounds using a simple TFF step was challenging due to the hydrophobicity of MMAE.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of Site-Specific Antibody–Drug Conjugates Using AJICAP Second-Generation Technology
Problem_Description: Aggregation of antibody‑thiol intermediates (especially Lys288‑thiols) can reduce conjugation efficiency and overall process yield.
Solution_Description: Intermediate stability is improved by storing AAPCs and antibody‑thiols in 20 mM histidine buffer with 5 % trehalose at pH 5.2 (‑80 °C for long term) and limiting freeze‑thaw cycles; this reduces aggregation to <5 % and supports >90 % yields in each step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both synthetic intermediates … were sufficiently stable … indicating that each synthetic step is a possible holding point.”; “Lys248‑related compounds were more stable … aggregation rate of trastuzumab‑Lys248‑thiol was less than 5 % even after storage at 4 °C for 4 weeks.”; “Overall product yield was >80 % … each step was >90 %.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Synthesis of Site-Specific Antibody–Drug Conjugates Using AJICAP Second-Generation Technology
Problem_Description: High‑concentration antibody solutions (up to 20 mg mL⁻¹) can become viscous and present mass‑transfer challenges during purification.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A scale‑down manufacturing approach using TFF with controlled diafiltration volumes (10–15 diavolumes) and appropriate buffer exchanges (AcONa → PBSE → histidine) manages viscosity and ensures efficient impurity removal while maintaining high antibody concentrations.
Supporting_Evidence: “The purification processes … were conducted according to a scale‑down approach involving tangential flow filtration.”; “TFF with 10 diavolumes of 20 mM AcONa buffer (pH 5.5) at an antibody concentration of 20 mg mL⁻¹.”; “Subsequent buffer exchange … to afford antibody‑thiol (3a) (13.7 g, 91 % yield).”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: The original eight‑step synthesis of seltorexant suffered from a low overall isolated yield, required several protecting‑group manipulations, and used a LiAlH₄ reduction in refluxing THF that posed a safety risk. Additionally, the key amine intermediate 7 showed stability issues (slow loss of Boc) leading to inconsistent material quality.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was designed that introduced the pyrimidine moiety early (via guanidine‑acetic acid condensation) and eliminated three protecting‑group steps, giving a five‑step sequence with a higher overall yield (≈60 % vs 32 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “four of the eight synthesis steps were protecting group manipulations for three new bond formations; (ii) there was a low‑melting solid and stability issue upon storage of the key intermediate amine 7 due to slow loss of the Boc moiety; and (iii) there was a safety concern for LiAlH₄ reduction in refluxing THF.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: The pivotal (3 + 2) cycloaddition only proceeded at very high temperatures (>250 °C). At such temperatures the oxazolidinone intermediate 21 decomposes above ~70 °C, and the high‑temperature operation raises significant safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A custom high‑pressure continuous‑flow platform equipped with a back‑pressure regulator, stainless‑steel coil reactors, and precise temperature control was built, allowing safe operation above the solvent boiling point and efficient heat‑removal at 250–300 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Since the cycloaddition step reaction proceeds in a temperature range far above the boiling point of the solvent and under high pressure (up to 60 bar), a back‑pressure regulator is essential … appropriate measures must be taken to protect chemists from very hot surfaces and spill of solution in case of leak.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: When the cycloaddition was attempted directly from N‑pyrimidylglycine 19, both 19 and paraformaldehyde were insoluble in toluene, leading to a heterogeneous slurry, low conversion, and modest isolated yields (≈57 %).
Solution_Description: The researchers first isolated the soluble oxazolidinone 21 from 19, then performed the cycloaddition under homogeneous conditions in toluene at ≥250 °C (microwave heating), which gave higher yields of the cycloadduct 17.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Both N‑pyrimidylglycine 19 and paraformaldehyde were insoluble in toluene whereas 2, oxazolidinone 21, and cycloadduct 17 were soluble.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: Oxazolidinone 21 decomposes slowly above 70 °C, and paraformaldehyde sublimates at the reaction temperature, causing incomplete conversion to 21 and limiting the overall yield of the subsequent cycloaddition.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature for forming 21 was carefully maintained between 60 °C and 65 °C, a controlled nitrogen sweep and vacuum were applied to remove water while preserving paraformaldehyde, and excess paraformaldehyde was added to drive the condensation to quantitative yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “maintaining the reaction temperature between 60 and 65 °C provided a much cleaner reaction profile but still with incomplete conversion, presumably due to the loss of formaldehyde by sublimation.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: A one‑pot continuous‑flow process starting from the heterogeneous suspension of 19 gave only ~57 % isolated yield of 17, with decarboxylation of 19 at high temperature forming by‑products 24 and 25.
Solution_Description: A two‑temperature‑zone flow system was introduced: the first zone (180–200 °C) performed the oxazolidinone formation, and the second zone (300 °C) executed the cycloaddition. This decoupled the temperature sensitivity of each step, improving material balance and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “we designed a new flow system consisting of two successive temperature zones, with 21 being formed in the first temperature zone at lower temperature and the cycloaddition occurring in the second one at higher temperature… marginal improvements… but the batch formation of 21 followed by flow cycloaddition gave higher yields.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: Reduction of the imide 17 with Red‑Al gave only 60 % in‑situ yield and significant impurities; silane‑mediated reductions were irreproducible; use of borane (BH₃·THF) raised safety concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: An in‑situ generated borane system (NaBH₄ + BF₃·THF) was employed, delivering 91 % isolated yield with excellent purity while controlling diborane formation via slow BF₃ addition and monitoring headspace, thereby addressing safety and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A reduction with BH₃·THF provided the product in 98% solution yield… we investigated conditions to generate the borane in situ from NaBH₄… found to provide the product in very good yield.”

Paper Title: Exploratory Process Development of a High-Temperature Thermal (3 + 2) Cycloaddition in Continuous Flow for the Synthesis of Seltorexant
Problem_Description: During debenzylation, the presence of acid was required for reliable hydrogenolysis; however, acetic acid generated an N‑acetyl impurity, while stronger acids reduced the pyrimidine ring, creating guanidine impurities.
Solution_Description: Transfer hydrogenolysis using Pd/C and ammonium formate (no added strong acids) was developed, giving 97 % isolated yield of the amine 10 without the acid‑derived impurities, followed by straightforward biphasic acyl‑chloride coupling and antisolvent crystallization to afford seltorexant in 97 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Transfer hydrogenolysis using Pd/C and ammonium formate provided amine 10 in 97% yield.”

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: The laboratory‑scale reactor has a much higher cooling capacity than the 4000 L production vessel, so the heat‑transfer behavior of the large‑scale system cannot be reproduced. This leads to insufficient cooling during the highly exothermic hydrogenation, risking temperature runaway, side‑product formation and loss of yield.
Solution_Description: A 3‑D‑printed stainless‑steel insert (the H/C‑Finger) is installed in the 1.4 L Scale‑Down‑Reactor to reproduce the heat‑transfer coefficient and surface‑to‑volume ratio of the 4000 L reactor. The insert, together with a quasi‑adiabatic safety container, makes the heat‑transfer behavior of the pilot reactor match that of the production plant.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "One of the main challenges for scale‑up/scale‑down is heterogeneous reactions. The other is overcoming the scale‑dependent heat transfer behavior of reactors of different sizes and geometry...the heating/cooling capacity of laboratory reactors is considerably higher than that of reactors at the plant scale, indicating that kinetic effects or degradation on hot/cold vessel surfaces cannot be replicated and examined at the laboratory scale."
Problem: "...insufficient cooling power to control the temperature during an exothermic reaction at the production scale, which is typically not an issue at the laboratory scale due to the substantially higher cooling power per volume."
Solution: "To overcome the challenge of differing heat exchange surface‑to‑volume ratios by incorporating a heating/cooling finger (H/C‑Finger) with limited surface area in a quasi‑adiabatic reactor."
Solution: "The measured cooling power of the H/C‑Finger is remarkably close to the cooling power of the 4000 L production reactor equivalent. This demonstrates that the design of the H/C‑Finger based on CFD computations and a model of the heat transfer of the 4000 L reactor was a success."

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: Gas‑liquid mass transfer of hydrogen to the liquid phase is a key rate‑limiting step in the heterogeneous hydrogenation. Inadequate mass‑transfer leads to side‑product formation, reduced yield and inconsistent performance when scaling up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The Scale‑Down‑Reactor (SDR) is built with geometrically‑similar agitator, baffles and base to the production‑scale vessel, keeping the volume‑specific power dissipation constant. This reproduces the gas‑liquid mass‑transfer coefficient (kL a) of the 4000 L reactor, as confirmed by experimental comparison.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "Heterogeneous reactions in general are a challenge for scale‑up because mass transfer, partial dissolution, and shear forces on particles influence the kinetics of the process. ... A slow mass transfer could lead to increased formation of undesired side products..."
Problem: "The conversion rate of multiphase reactions, such as hydrogenations, is dependent on the rate of interphase mass transfer."
Solution: "The geometry of the agitator, baffles, and the base were kept similar to the geometry of the production vessel. ... the SDR was designed with geometric similarity to its large‑scale counterpart."
Solution: "The comparison reveals a good similarity between the volumetric mass transfer coefficient of the SDR and the production‑scale reactor at constant volume‑specific power dissipation."

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: The original production batch required 22 h to reach completion, limiting throughput and increasing cost.
Solution_Description: A dynamic process model (digital twin) was used to optimise jacket temperature, gas‑phase pressure and stirrer speed. The optimised operating window reduced the reaction time to 12 h while maintaining product quality and yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "...the reaction time could be reduced significantly while maintaining the high product quality."
Problem: "...reaction time reduced from 22 to 12 h."
Solution: "The dynamic process model ... was used to optimise the process parameters for the hydrogenation process. ... The agitation speed (120 rpm) and gas phase hydrogen pressure (10 barg) were chosen to be constant during the process. Compared to the previous process, the reaction time was reduced from 22 to 12 h."
Solution: "Based on the accurate heat transfer model, we were able to define the ideal jacket temperature so that overshooting of the reaction mixture temperature was prevented. This minimized the side‑product formation and improved the overall product quality."

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: Starting material that had been stored for six months in standard laboratory containers showed degraded quality, causing delayed conversion, temperature deviations and mismatched product profiles in the Scale‑Down‑Experiment.
Solution_Description: Store the starting material under protective conditions (e.g., in large containers with inert atmosphere) and use fresh material for experiments, ensuring consistent quality and reproducible reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "The difference in temperature, starting material, and product profile can be attributed to the different storage times of the starting materials used in the production‑scale and SDR experiments. The starting materials used for the large‑scale process were stored in large containers and a protective environment. The starting materials used for the SDR experiment were stored within standard laboratory containers without a protective environment for approximately 6 months."
Problem: "A subsequent laboratory‑scale experiment confirmed the effect of long storage time on the quality of the starting material."
Solution: "The reason for the change in starting material quality has not yet been further investigated but was independently confirmed by laboratory experiments."
Solution (implied): Use protective storage and fresh material to avoid degradation.

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: Existing literature correlations for gas‑liquid mass transfer could not predict the behavior of the 4000 L reactor, leading to inaccurate scale‑up predictions.
Solution_Description: Develop a new correlation equation (Eq. 9) that incorporates fill level, physical properties of the liquid, and agitation speed, fitted to the experimental data, providing accurate mass‑transfer predictions for the specific vessel.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "...none of the equations is able to describe the mass transfer behavior of our agitated autoclave. The correlation equations either show an insufficient dependency on the fill level or a high deviation in the absolute value..."
Solution: "Hence, a new equation that is able to model the mass transfer behavior of this specific agitated vessel was developed. The equation was built up in three steps... The equation developed is able to model the volumetric gas–liquid mass transfer coefficient for hydrogen in the 4000 L agitated vessel as a function of the agitation speed, volume, and physical properties of the reaction mixture."

Paper Title: New Scale-Up Technologies for Multipurpose Pharmaceutical Production Plants: Use Case of a Heterogeneous Hydrogenation Process
Problem_Description: Traditional scale‑up requires pilot‑scale experiments, which are costly and time‑consuming.
Solution_Description: Implement a direct scale‑down approach using a 1.4 L SDR that faithfully reproduces scale‑dependent parameters, combined with a digital twin. This eliminates the need for intermediate pilot runs, reducing cost and timeline.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "Minimizing the effort associated with the pilot and laboratory‑scale experiments needed for a successful scale‑up… is a significant challenge... Efficient scale‑up is becoming increasingly important in process development due to the growing pressure to reduce costs and timelines."
Solution: "Instead of the conventional practice of scaling up from laboratory to plant, our approach focuses on scaling down the designated process from plant to laboratory… The core component of the Scale‑Down‑Reactor is a 3D‑printed metallic insert… To finally prove and validate the concept, a hydrogenation process currently running at the production scale was conducted in the Scale‑Down‑Reactor."
Solution: "By enabling direct and efficient process scale‑up while concurrently optimizing scale‑dependent parameters, the technologies described within this article offer a promising approach to reducing costs and timelines while improving process understanding."

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Debenzylation of benzyl ethers in Pfizer’s routes relied on heterogeneous hydrogenolysis using a packed‑bed reactor (PBR) with H₂ gas; this requires pressure‑rated batch reactors, poses H₂ handling hazards, and suffers from catalyst deactivation (nickel black formation) that limits continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “All debenzylations surveyed required specialized, pressure‑rated batch reactors to enable the use of hydrogen gas and heterogeneous catalysts.”; “The downside to operating these PBR hydrogenation systems is the fact that catalyst activity can depreciate over time due to sequestration of catalyst sites from impurities or catalyst leaching.”; “A single‑phase debenzylation … would offer an alternative continuous method in cases where catalyst deactivation occurs or handling of H₂ gas is restricted.”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: At higher catalyst loadings (20 mol %) and temperatures (≥120 °C) black particles (nickel‑black) formed, indicating catalyst decomposition; the particles rendered the reaction mixture heterogeneous and lowered product formation (e.g., 86 / 14 ratio).
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was reduced to 5 mol % and the temperature lowered to 90 °C. Under these conditions the reaction gave a 6 / 94 ratio but remained homogeneous, preventing clogging while retaining acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 5: “10 mol % … 120 °C … black particles … 9 / 91 ratio.”; “Further decreasing the catalyst loading to 5 mol % resulted in a ratio of 1 / 99.”; “Running the reaction with 5 mol % catalyst and at a reduced temperature of 90 °C resulted in a 6 / 94 ratio and a homogeneous final mixture.”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: The NiCl₂·DPPF precatalyst is insoluble in THF, and after reaction the product mixture precipitates magnesium‑naphthol salts at ambient temperature, causing solid formation that could clog a plug‑flow reactor.
Solution_Description: Six equivalents of acetic acid were added post‑reaction to dissolve the magnesium salts, producing a homogeneous solution that can be safely pumped through a back‑pressure regulator.
Supporting_Evidence: “The substrate … readily dissolves in THF; however, the NiCl₂/DPPF precatalyst is not soluble THF.”; “The resulting solids are hypothesized to be 2‑naphthol magnesium salts… Addition of 6.0 equiv of acetic acid … resulted in rapid dissolution of the formed solids and a homogeneous solution.”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Benzyl butyl ether (2j) showed no conversion across the temperature range 90–130 °C, indicating substrate‑specific reactivity limitations.
Solution_Description: The authors note that future work will explore alternative solvent combinations to improve solubility of catalyst and substrate, aiming to overcome the kinetic barrier.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempted debenzylations of benzyl butyl ether to form butanol (2j) showed no substrate conversion at reaction temperatures ranging from 90 to 130 °C. We hypothesize that the higher kinetic barrier … Future work will explore various solvent combinations …”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Running the Ni‑catalyzed debenzylation in a plug‑flow reactor required a homogeneous feed; nickel‑black formation from the catalyst would clog the reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A three‑feed strategy was employed: (A) substrate in THF, (B) NiCl₂/DPPF + MeMgBr in THF, (C) acetic acid quench. Feeds A and B were mixed before the heated PFR (95 °C, 20 mL), then immediately quenched with Feed C before the back‑pressure regulator, ensuring a single‑phase flow and preventing clogging.
Supporting_Evidence: “The debenzylation reaction was performed in a PFR with three feed solutions … Feed A … Feed B … Feed C … A 100 psi BPR was used at the outlet … stable 96–97% calibrated assay yield …”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Batch reactions originally required 1 h at 80 °C to meet the maximum residence time allowable in the authors’ internal flow facility, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Microwave heating and superheated flow (95 °C) were used to accelerate the reaction, enabling the required conversion within the 1‑hour residence time window.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions were run for 1 h to select for conditions amenable for use in a PFR. After heating the reaction at 80 °C … The reaction solution remains homogeneous at elevated temperatures (50 to 90 °C). The reaction was performed in a PFR … held at 95 °C … residence time of the continuous reaction was 1 h …”

Paper Title: Utilizing Ni-Catalyzed Cross-Coupling as a Reversed Strategy for Homogeneous Deprotection of Benzyl Ethers in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: The original protocol used 20 mol % NiCl₂·DPPF catalyst, which could be cost‑prohibitive for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was lowered to 5 mol % without sacrificing acceptable yield, reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 entries 5–7 show systematic reduction of catalyst loading from 20 mol % to 5 mol % and the corresponding impact on conversion; the authors selected 5 mol % as optimal for flow operation.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Electrophilic Amination Protocol for the Multi-kg Production of 5‑Methyl-2-pyridinesulfonamide: A Regulatory Starting Material of Endothelin Receptor Antagonist Clazosentan
Problem_Description: The original multi‑kg sulfonamide synthesis suffered from a very low isolated yield (29 %), the use of hazardous chlorinated solvents (CH₂Cl₂) and generation of Cl₂ gas, two highly exothermic reagent additions (NaOCl and aq. NH₄OH) that required >24 h slow dosing, instability of the sulfonyl‑chloride intermediate which forced a low‑temperature solvent switch, difficult phase‑splits during isolation, heavy crust formation on solvent exchange to TBME, and large batch‑to‑batch variation in product colour and purity (genotoxic benzyl‑chloride impurity 4 required re‑work).
Solution_Description: A conceptually new one‑pot sequence was developed: (i) oxidation of the thiophenol to a sodium sulfinate using 70 % aq. t‑BuOOH (green, chlorine‑free oxidant) – eliminating chlorine‑based reagents and the sulfonyl‑chloride intermediate; (ii) in‑situ electrophilic amination of the sulfinate with hydroxylamine‑O‑sulfonic acid (HOSA) – avoiding the genotoxic impurity; (iii) controlled, portionwise addition of the oxidant and HOSA (order‑and‑rate‑of‑addition) at modest temperatures; (iv) buffering the mixture with 30 % aq. sodium citrate (pH ≈ 3) to stabilize HOSA and allow the amination at ambient temperature (ph‑control, temperature‑optimization); (v) switching to a green solvent system (iPrOAc extraction, then CPME crystallisation) and removing the EtOH by distillation, delivering the product directly after Na₂SO₃ quench without aqueous work‑up (new‑purification‑procedure, solvent‑change, telescope‑directly); (vi) the entire sequence was telescoped without isolating the sulfinate intermediate, cutting the batch‑time roughly in half (telescope‑directly).
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: {"quotes":["a low isolated yield of 1 of only 29% on 123 kg scale (prior to rework, vide infra)","the use of undesirable CH₂Cl₂ as reaction and extraction solvent and formation of Cl₂‑gas in the oxidation step","two highly exothermic additions (NaOCl and aq. NH₄OH) that required extremely slow additions on scale (up to 24 h dosage time)","stability issues of the intermediate sulfonyl chloride, which necessitated the solvent switch from CH₂Cl₂ to THF to be performed at IT ≤ 25 °C","difficult phase splits (THF/EtOAc and H₂O) during the isolation of 1","heavy crust formation during the solvent switch of the organic layer to TBME to crystallize 1","high variability in the purity and color of the isolated product 1"],"source":"Introduction, list items (a)–(g)"},
Solution: {"quotes":["The new process relied on selectively oxidizing the thiophenol to the intermediate sulfinate salt followed by an electrophilic amination of the nucleophilic sulfinate sulfur‑atom with hydroxylamine‑O‑sulfonic acid (HOSA)","70 % aq. t‑BuOOH solution (45.0 kg) was added … while keeping IT = 24.9–26.5 °C", "solid HOSA (1.5 equiv) was added … followed by warming to IT = 45–50 °C and stirring for 16 h", "adding a 30 % aq. sodium citrate solution (0.5 equiv) prior to HOSA addition proved to be optimal (pH ≈ 3 after addition). Not only could the electrophilic amination step be performed at RT, but also a dramatic rate acceleration was observed and full conversion of the sulfinate 5‑Na was achieved within only 3 h.", "addition of iPrOAc (10 vol) followed by phase split and washing of the organic phase with H₂O (2.5 vol) worked well to remove the salts prior to crystallisation. Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: At high initial concentrations (e.g., 140 mg mL⁻¹, 100 mg mL⁻¹) the tubular reactor became completely blocked before any product could exit, preventing steady‑state operation and causing large loss of material.
Solution_Description: The concentration was reduced to 60 mg mL⁻¹ (test 5) while keeping the flow rate at 30 mL min⁻¹, which allowed continuous slurry production without blockage and enabled easy washing of the reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: • “reactor completely blocked before sample could exit” (Table 1, tests 1–4). • “lower concentrations at flow rates of 30 mL/min were selected (test 5) … slurry coming out, reactor did not block” (p. 8).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: Both adipic acid and lactose have limited solubility in water; lactose required concentrations > 600 mg mL⁻¹ to obtain any crystals, and adipic acid needed temperatures well above the nucleation temperature to dissolve before cooling.
Solution_Description: A two‑step temperature profile was employed: the solution was pre‑heated (60 °C for adipic acid, 85 °C for lactose) to achieve dissolution, then rapidly cooled in the capillary reactor (≈ ‑10 °C s⁻¹) to reach the nucleation temperature, creating the supersaturation needed for nucleation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “adipic acid…70 mg mL⁻¹…solubility data…Figure 3” (p. 8). • “All tests performed at solution concentrations below 600 mg/mL did not result in a crystalline material…high concentrations … needed” (p. 13). • “The temperature drop inside the tubular reactors … to reach −10 °C s⁻¹, it becomes possible to reach spontaneous nucleation conditions” (p. 7).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: Lactose required very long induction and crystal‑growth times (up to 18 h) to reach equilibrium; short residence times produced only a small fraction of the theoretical yield (≈ 50 %).
Solution_Description: The process was adapted to use a very high lactose concentration (850 mg mL⁻¹) and a low nucleation temperature (5 °C) to trigger nucleation, followed by an extended maturation step (18 h) at the same temperature. This gave yields close to the theoretical maximum (≈ 93 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Lactose crystallization requires long induction times” (p. 13). • “Only when the nucleation temperature was lowered to 5 °C at concentrations of 850 mg/mL … crystals were observed” (p. 14). • “The slurry…taken…18 h…yield reaches nearly the maximum obtainable yield of 93 %” (p. 22).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: Small deviations in nucleation temperature, concentration or flow rate produced noticeable shifts in particle‑size distribution, especially for lactose where a 5 °C change altered the median size.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Parameter‑set consistency was enforced by tightly controlling the nucleation temperature (± 0.5 °C), using a pressure regulator (15 bar) to fix the flow rate at 20 mL min⁻¹, and continuously monitoring the flow‑meter valve; this eliminated fluctuations and reproduced laboratory‑scale particle attributes on pilot scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Any deviation in the parameters results in a deviation of the final product” (p. 25). • “The pressure regulator … needed to be set at 15 bar … flow rate … stable” (p. 21). • “Temperature of the bath … must be stabilized … before start of testing” (p. 19).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: During pilot operation a thin layer of dried material accumulated at the reactor outlet, causing intermittent flow dips and risk of complete blockage.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The accumulated encrustation was removed manually every 30 s without changing valve position, preventing flow interruption and maintaining continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Figure 6 B shows a slight decrease in flow rate … dried material … removed without perturbance of the flow rate” (p. 15). • “Avoiding the buildup of the material by removing every 30 s ensured continuous operation” (p. 15).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations
Problem_Description: Up to 30–50 % of the crystallized material adhered to the sampling recipient, filter funnel or reactor internals, making laboratory‑scale yield calculations unreliable.
Solution_Description: A vacuum‑operated filter funnel (for adipic acid) and a pressurized Nutsche cell (for lactose pilot runs) were employed to collect the slurry rapidly and minimize material loss; filtration was performed without washing to avoid loss of fines.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The crystalyzed materials sticking … could even represent up to 30–50 % of the total yield” (p. 7). • “The filtration of adipic acid was very straightforward … performed at a rate of about 250 mL min⁻¹ …” (p. 7). • “Slurries … filtered with a pressurized Nutsche cell … no washing was performed” (p. 19).

Paper Title: Continuous Nucleation Process of Lactose and Adipic Acid: Parameter Optimization from Laboratory- to Kilogram Pilot-Scale Operations

Paper Title: From Chiral Resolution to Diastereoselective Ellman Chemistry to Biocatalysis: Route Evolution for the Efficient Synthesis of the Tetrahydrobenzoazepine Core of BTK Inhibitor BIIB091

The key three‑step sequence (N‑tosylation, N‑alkylation, ester hydrolysis) was performed in 2‑MeTHF as a telescoped process, eliminating NaBH₃CN, reducing the step count, and delivering a 69 % overall yield with far fewer isolations.

Paper Title: From Chiral Resolution to Diastereoselective Ellman Chemistry to Biocatalysis: Route Evolution for the Efficient Synthesis of the Tetrahydrobenzoazepine Core of BTK Inhibitor BIIB091
Problem_Description: The Friedel–Crafts acylation for ring closure was highly exothermic in DCM, posing safety concerns and giving modest isolated yields (43‑50 %) with significant impurity formation.

Paper Title: From Chiral Resolution to Diastereoselective Ellman Chemistry to Biocatalysis: Route Evolution for the Efficient Synthesis of the Tetrahydrobenzoazepine Core of BTK Inhibitor BIIB091
Problem_Description: Initial imine‑reduction screens with NaBH₄, L‑selectride and LiBHEt₃ gave low diastereoselectivity or favored the undesired diastereomer, limiting the overall efficiency of the chiral‑auxiliary step.

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: Large‑scale Birch reduction uses lithium metal and liquefied ammonia at –50 °C to –60 °C.  The excess ammonia (∼25 equiv) and metallic lithium present a serious risk of rapid boil‑off, hydrogen evolution and over‑pressurisation, while calorimetry shows a worst‑case adiabatic temperature rise of ≈ 98 °C (MTSR = 48 °C), indicating a potentially runaway exotherm.
Solution_Description: Lithium was switched to granular sand (0.5–1 cm particles) to improve heat removal, divided into 100 g portions in a glove‑box, and added via a hopper in 200 g sub‑charges.  Reaction temperature was held at –50 °C to –60 °C throughout charging and a controlled warm‑up was used for quench, minimizing the exotherm and avoiding ammonia over‑pressurisation.
Supporting_Evidence: - "the use of lithium metal and liquified ammonia at cryogenic temperatures is typically disfavored on large scale due to concerns over handling of flammable solids and the need for robust temperature control to avoid over‑pressurization" (Intro).

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: After Birch reduction, the MTBE solution of enol ether 4 contained 2.5–3 % w/w water.  Azeotropic drying of this large volume proved impractical – prolonged distillation caused extensive hydrolysis of 4, and a membrane‑filter drying attempt failed because 4 decomposed at the required temperature and residence time.
Solution_Description: A two‑stage drying sequence was employed: (1) batch addition of anhydrous CaCl₂ (2 kg kg⁻¹) reduced water to ≈ 0.7 % w/w; (2) filtration followed by a second drying step with 4 Å molecular sieves (1 kg kg⁻¹) lowered water to < 0.1 % w/w, providing material suitable for the downstream ketalisation without degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: - "Azeotropic drying of solutions containing 4 did not appear feasible on large scale, as significant degradation (primarily via hydrolysis) was observed during the prolonged time scales" (Birch reduction section).

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: During batch electrolysis of arene 1 a black tar formed on the stainless‑steel cathode.  The deposit increased cell voltage, inhibited current flow and risked fouling in a continuous‑flow cell, jeopardising scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The electrolyte was changed from LiCl (poorly soluble, high voltage) to LiOTf, which prevented tar formation by keeping DMU‑derived lithium/magnesium salts in solution.  LiOTf was used alone (1 M) for the scale‑up run, eliminating cathode fouling and stabilising voltage.
Supporting_Evidence: - "We observed the buildup of a black tar on the cathode surface…this buildup can ultimately inhibit electrolysis and result in a continual increase in voltage" (Electrochemical reduction section).

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: Ketalisation of enone 2 produced a 3 : 1 mixture of the desired ketal 3 and the undesired isomer 5.  The presence of 5 lowered overall yield and would require chromatographic separation, which is unattractive at scale.
Solution_Description: A selective hydrolysis step was introduced: 0.25 equiv water was added after ketalisation to convert 5 back to enone 2, then aqueous hydrazine (1 equiv) was used to remove the regenerated enone via formation of a water‑soluble hydrazone.  This sequence removed 5 without chromatography, delivering ketal 3 in > 85 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: - "undesired ketal 5 could be selectively hydrolyzed back to enone 2 simply by adding a small amount of water (∼0.25 equiv) … followed by aqueous hydrazine hydrate (1.0 kg, 1.5 equiv) … allowed for a clear phase split to successfully remove the major by‑products and provide unreacted ketal 3" (Ketalisation section).

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: In the ketalisation step, using 5 equiv ethylene glycol in toluene caused a biphasic system; the glycol layer preferentially solubilised the starting enone 2, making monitoring difficult and leading to inconsistent analytical results.

Paper Title: Demonstration of a Multikilogram-Scale Birch Reduction and Evaluation of Alternative Synthetic Routes to a Ketalized Cyclohexene Derivative
Problem_Description: The electrochemical route required LiOTf as electrolyte, which is considerably more expensive than LiCl, inflating raw‑material cost (≈ $1300 /kg 3 vs $600 /kg for the Birch route).

Paper Title: Formation of a Disulfide Bridge on the Resin during Solid-Phase Synthesis of Terlipressin: Influence of the Boc-Protected and Free N‑Terminal Amino Group
Problem_Description: When the standard on‑resin disulfide‑bond closure was applied to terlipressin bearing a free N‑terminal α‑amino group, the crude material contained only 67.73 % of the target peptide, giving a low isolated yield and poor purity.
Solution_Description: The N‑terminal α‑amino group was protected with a Boc group before cyclisation.  Boc‑protected terlipressin gave a crude purity of 94.70 % (vs. 67.73 % for the free‑amino precursor) and an overall isolated yield of 45–55 % from the starting amino acid.
Supporting_Evidence: “crude product contained only 67.73 % of the target peptide”; “crude terlipressin was obtained with 94.70 % purity against 67.73 % in the case of the free‑amino‑group precursor”; “Boc‑protected amino group drastically decreased the preactivation energy… very close to that of the more reactive DDAVP intermediate.”

Paper Title: Formation of a Disulfide Bridge on the Resin during Solid-Phase Synthesis of Terlipressin: Influence of the Boc-Protected and Free N‑Terminal Amino Group
Problem_Description: Using too little iodine gave incomplete cyclisation, whereas using an excess (≥10 equiv) caused a rise in the linear precursor (up to 15.37 %) and reduced the amount of cyclic product, lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening of iodine equivalents identified the optimal range of 5–10 equiv I₂ (5 equiv chosen for routine work), which affords complete conversion to the disulfide without over‑oxidation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Complete conversion … was observed in the range of 5–10 iodine equivalents”; “when the excess content of the oxidant is increased above 10 equiv, the S–S content of the peptide decreases… the content of the linear precursor increases up to 15.37 %.”

Paper Title: Formation of a Disulfide Bridge on the Resin during Solid-Phase Synthesis of Terlipressin: Influence of the Boc-Protected and Free N‑Terminal Amino Group
Problem_Description: Large‑scale peptide cyclisation can require long reaction times; prolonged heating or extended residence times reduce throughput and increase operational cost.
Solution_Description: A 1 h cyclisation at 25 °C with 5 equiv I₂ was demonstrated to give >95 % conversion for both terlipressin and desmopressin; extending the time to 3 h did not improve conversion, establishing 1 h as the optimal duration.

Paper Title: Formation of a Disulfide Bridge on the Resin during Solid-Phase Synthesis of Terlipressin: Influence of the Boc-Protected and Free N‑Terminal Amino Group
Problem_Description: The conventional Fmoc‑deprotection reagent 4‑MePip/DBU is toxic, posing safety and environmental concerns for scale‑up.

Paper Title: Formation of a Disulfide Bridge on the Resin during Solid-Phase Synthesis of Terlipressin: Influence of the Boc-Protected and Free N‑Terminal Amino Group
Problem_Description: Solution‑phase disulfide cyclisation requires ~1 L of solvent per gram of linear peptide, leading to high solvent consumption and waste at multi‑gram scale.

Problem_Description: Separation of cyclic terlipressin from residual linear peptide and dimeric side‑products is difficult by conventional HPLC because of overlapping peaks.

Solution_Description: The authors diluted tert‑butanol with an equal volume of water to keep it liquid at low temperature. For the nitration, a packed‑bed glass‑bead column was operated with a continuous air feed (10 mL min⁻¹) to ensure efficient liquid‑gas contact and sufficient O₂.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “tert‑Butanol solidifies below 25 °C. Hence, it was diluted with an equal volume of water so that the reaction can be done at low temperatures without any solidification challenges.”
• “Air was found to be essential in getting the optimal conversion; a very low yield was obtained with nitrogen gas (entry 4).”
• “To provide oxygen in the reaction, a packed‑bed column reactor was constructed… air was constantly bubbled by using a mass flow controller (MFC).”
• “The special column reactor provided good liquid‑air contact which has resulted in faster reaction and significant reduction in reaction time from 12 h to 3 min.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Batch nitration of styrene to nitrostyrene required 12–24 h with modest yields (≈85 %). Extended residence time allowed decomposition of the reactive nitrite intermediate, lowering overall conversion.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was tuned to 1.15 equiv NaNO₂ and 1.10 equiv HCl for TBN generation, and the nitration temperature was raised to 120 °C while keeping a 3 min residence time, giving isolated yields of up to 95 % (88 % isolated).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Under optimal conditions, we could get 93 % yield in 1 min residence time with 1.15 equiv NaNO₂ and 1.10 equiv HCl (Table 1, entry 3).”
• “We found the best yield under a 3 min residence time and 120 °C temperature (entry 3, Table 3).”
• “Batch‑vs‑flow comparison… batch time 12–24 h, yield 85 %; flow time 3 min, yield 88 %.”

Problem_Description: The original batch protocol for TBN preparation required a cycle time of 12‑24 h, which is unsuitable for industrial‐scale production.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow PFA tube reactor (2 mL for optimization, 10 mL for scale‑up) with a 5.20 M tert‑butanol solution pumped at 4.15 mL min⁻¹, reducing the residence time to 1 min and achieving a production rate of 127 g h⁻¹ (STY = 13 g h⁻¹ mL⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The current reports for the preparation of TBN… have a higher batch cycle time of 12 to 24 h, limiting its application for commercial production.”
• “Under optimal conditions, we could get 93 % yield in 1 min residence time.”
• “A production rate of 127 g/h or a space‑time yield (STY) of 13 g/h/mL was achieved.”
• Table 2 comparison: batch time 4.5 h, flow 1 min; flow consumption rate 129 mol h⁻¹ L⁻¹ vs 0.75 mol h⁻¹ L⁻¹.

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: When the continuous‑flow reduction was first attempted in glycerol (viscosity ≈ 1499 cP at 20 °C) the reaction mixture became highly viscous, causing pump blockage and over‑pressure, which made the process unreproducible.
Solution_Description: The authors switched the hydrogen‑donor/solvent from glycerol to ethylene glycol (EG), whose much lower viscosity (≈ 16 cP) allowed smooth flow; in addition, they diluted the substrate (0.5 M) to keep the feedable concentration.
Supporting_Evidence: “Preliminarily, the continuous reaction was attempted in glycerol that has a viscosity of 1499 cP at 20 °C; therefore, we heated the starting solution to 100 °C (21 cP) to perform experiments … pumps were blocked for over‑pressure and we decided to perform the reaction in EG alone.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: In batch mode EG gave a slower reaction rate than glycerol, requiring up to 7 h to reach complete conversion, which is impractical for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Increasing the Cu loading on the supported catalyst from 5 % to 10 % w/w and raising the catalyst mass in the packed‑bed reactor (250 mg) dramatically shortened the residence time to ≈ 2 min and gave > 99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the reaction was repeated with 20 mol % of Cu‑supported catalysts, complete conversion was achieved in 1.5 h in EG… we attempted to study the process in continuous flow… the high efficiency heat and mass transfer… would lead to a higher reaction rate than the batch version.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: Using isopropanol (iPrOH) as solvent at 90 °C gave only 22 % isolated aniline and a significant amount of azoxy‑ and azobenzene side‑products.
Solution_Description: The solvent was changed back to ethylene glycol (or EG/Gly 1:1) and the temperature raised to 130 °C, which restored high conversion (> 97 %) and selectivity toward aniline.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was therefore performed with setup B (entry 5) … in iPrOH. A decrease in product conversion was observed (70 %) and the reduction showed a decreased selectivity to aniline… the mixture of diols … acts efficiently as hydrogen donors.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: The strong base (KOH) required to generate the active Cu catalyst caused variability in conversion and side‑product formation, especially for base‑sensitive substrates.
Solution_Description: The amount of base was reduced to the stoichiometric 2 equiv (instead of excess) and the effect of base equivalents was systematically studied, identifying 2 equiv as optimal for complete conversion and minimal side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was recognized that… the use of a strong base can affect the reaction outcome… therefore, we opted for a study aimed to reduce the amount of base… the conversion of nitrobenzene increased from 51 % to > 99 % as the base equiv. increased to 2.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: 1‑Nitronaphthalene crystallised in EG at 0.5 M and clogged the flow tubes, making the reaction and product isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: A 5:2 DMA/EG co‑solvent system was employed and the substrate concentration lowered to 0.4 M, which fully dissolved the nitronaphthalene and gave 85 % isolated amine.
Supporting_Evidence: “1‑Nitronaphthalene crystallized and clogged tubes when dissolved at 0.5 M in EG, whereas it showed solubility at 0.05 M in EG… naphthalene was successfully converted… when dissolved in a 5:2 mixture of DMA/EG.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: The high polarity of EG made conventional liquid‑liquid extraction of the aniline products impractically solvent‑intensive.
Solution_Description: Anion‑exchange resin (Dowex 50 × 8) was used to bind the aniline as its ammonium salt; after washing, the free aniline was released with ammonia/methanol, eliminating the need for large volumes of organic solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude amine solution was purified with a polymeric supported sulfonic resin (Dowex 50 × 8)… the aniline‑bound resin was treated with 4 M ammonia methanolic solution… the pure free anilines were released… without any further purification.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: After ~ 99 h continuous operation the CuNPs/Celite catalyst showed loss of metallic Cu peaks in XRD and a colour change, indicating partial oxidation and activity loss (conversion fell to ~ 87 %).
Solution_Description: The spent catalyst was re‑activated by flowing fresh EG through the packed‑bed at 130 °C, restoring the Cu(0) diffraction peak and the original activity for further cycles.
Supporting_Evidence: “Being that the solvent of our system is a reducing compound, fresh ethylene glycol was then flowed through the exhausted catalyst at 130 °C … the intensity of the main (111) peak of metallic copper was recovered, demonstrating that the Cu(0) species can be easily restored.”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: Scaling‑up the process to larger packed‑bed reactors (up to 5 g catalyst) required higher flow rates, which reduced residence time and lowered conversion, threatening productivity and economic viability.
Solution_Description: The flow rate was adjusted (e.g., 0.6 mL min⁻¹ for a 5 g reactor) to maintain a residence time of ~ 7 min, achieving > 99 % conversion and a productivity of 29.4 mmol h⁻¹ (2 738 g h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: “We evidenced that a residence time of approximately 7 min could provide full conversion… when the flow was increased to 1 mL min⁻¹, aniline was obtained in 93.8 % yield… 720 mmol of nitrobenzene were converted with a productivity of 29.4 mmol/h (2 738 g/h).”

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: Standard liquid‑liquid extraction of the aniline products from EG required large volumes of organic solvents, increasing waste and cost.
Solution_Description: An ion‑exchange resin (Dowex 50 × 8) was employed to capture the aniline as its ammonium salt, allowing washing with minimal methanol/DCM and release of the pure amine, greatly reducing solvent use.
Supporting_Evidence: Same as above (see purification section).

Paper Title: Copper-Catalyzed Continuous-Flow Transfer Hydrogenation of Nitroarenes to Anilines: A Scalable and Reliable Protocol
Problem_Description: Large amounts of fresh EG were discarded after each batch, contributing heavily to the E‑factor and process cost.
Solution_Description: The recovered EG was distilled, its purity checked by NMR, and reused in subsequent runs, resulting in an overall E‑factor of 8.30 for the flow protocol versus 20.19 for the batch process.
Supporting_Evidence: “After capturing the desired aniline… the EG was distilled and reused… the reaction performed in the presence of distilled EG showed 97 % yield… the E‑factor value associated with our flow setup is lower with respect to other alternatives.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: The literature route to intermediate 1 uses the high‑cost spiro‑oxazetidine 5 and a palladium‑catalyzed hydrogenation that is expensive and not widely available on large scale.
Solution_Description: The authors rearranged the synthetic sequence, bypassing 5 and the Pd‑hydrogenation by performing a hydroxide‑facilitated double N‑alkylation of 2‑fluoro‑4‑nitroaniline with BBMO, providing a low‑cost, protecting‑group‑free route to 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “The current route … involves … a sluggish filtration … Isolation of the amine requires a final conversion to an oxalate salt that suffers from stability issues … The key step … is the creation of the azetidine ring through a hydroxide‑facilitated alkylation … avoiding the previous drawbacks … the major cost driver …”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: Initial screening in polar protic solvents (EtOH, H₂O) gave little or no conversion, and acetone with Cs₂CO₃ gave only modest conversion while the reagent was expensive.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to polar aprotic solvents that better solubilize inorganic bases (e.g., DMSO, sulfolane) and used inexpensive NaOH (2 – 2.5 eq) as the base, which dramatically increased conversion to >90 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Polar protic solvents … gave little to no conversion … acetone refluxes … success was predicated on the use of Cs₂CO₃, which is a prohibitively expensive reagent … NaOH is reasonably soluble at elevated temperatures in dimethylformamide (DMF), NMP, diglyme, and DMSO, and these combinations proved to be the most efficient alkylation systems (entries 11–13), with nearly quantitative conversion in DMSO (94 area %).”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: Use of NaH in DMF or DMSO presents explosion and safety hazards, especially at scale.
Solution_Description: The hazardous NaH/DMF combination was abandoned in favor of NaOH in sulfolane, a safer, industrially acceptable solvent system.
Supporting_Evidence: “The results … were not compelling enough to justify the potential safety concerns, especially with the commonly used, but unsafe, combination of NaH/DMF.” … “Sulfolane is generally considered to be a safer solvent under these basic, higher‑temperature reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: A bis‑aniline impurity (compound 6) formed via a second‑order intermolecular alkylation, reducing the yield of the desired spiro‑amine.
Solution_Description: Slow, separate dropwise addition of 50 wt % NaOH (aq) and then the aniline (or a premixed solution of aniline + BBMO) to the hot sulfolane mixture kept the instantaneous concentrations low, suppressing impurity formation and driving the reaction to >90 % product.
Supporting_Evidence: “A major process improvement came when NaOH (as a 50 wt % solution in water) was slowly added … Near complete consumption of 2 was observed … Slow addition appears to limit the amount of base that is available to decompose 3.” … “The most successful … was slow addition of a premixed solution of 3 and 2 to a hot mixture of NaOH in sulfolane … product levels in excess of 90 area % and starting material and impurity both below 5 area %.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: Sulfolane’s high boiling point and water miscibility made product isolation difficult; large volumes of water (40 V) were needed to precipitate 1, which limited throughput.
Solution_Description: Neutralizing the reaction mixture with 1 N HCl to pH 5‑6, followed by addition of a controlled volume of water (10 V), caused efficient precipitation of 1 with high purity and improved recovery (>80 % yield).
Supporting_Evidence: “Neutralization of the crude reaction mixture with 1 N HCl proved to be the key for successful product isolation … after addition of only 10 V of water, with isolated yields between 80 and 85 % and purities of >95 wt %.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: Commercial BBMO (3) is only available in small quantities and at high price, limiting large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: A scalable, low‑cost synthesis of BBMO was developed from the commercially available flame‑retardant TBNPA (4) using Schotten‑Baumann conditions with TBABr as the phase‑transfer catalyst and excess NaOH, followed by vacuum distillation to afford BBMO in 72 % yield and >95 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “A scalable synthesis of 3 was accomplished … treatment of 4 with NaOH under Schotten‑Baumann conditions … with TBABr (3 mol %) and an excess of base (3.5 eq) … crude 3 was obtained … Vacuum distillation … isolated yield … 72 % and >95 % wt %.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223
Problem_Description: Crude BBMO contained a brominated olefin impurity (3‑bromo‑2‑(bromomethyl)‑1‑propene) that lowered assay purity.
Solution_Description: Short‑path vacuum distillation removed the impurity, delivering a near‑pure BBMO fraction (99.7 % GCMS area, 96 % wt %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Crude BBMO was purified by short path vacuum distillation … The major fraction … was found to be a nearly pure product (99.7 % GCMS area % purity; 96 % wt % purity), and the yield … was 72 %.”

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Two-Step Process for 6‑(2-Fluoro-4-nitrophenyl)-2-oxa-6-azaspiro[3.3]heptane: A Key Intermediate of the Potent Antibiotic Drug Candidate TBI-223

Problem_Description: A very large excess (10 equiv) of the diamine (rac‑3) was required to achieve the monobenzylation step, leading to waste of reagent and low material throughput.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was optimized to 1.3 equiv of diamine 3 and 3 equiv of aldehyde 8, providing ~80 % assay yield of the benzylic amine 9 and reducing reagent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “a large excess (10 equiv) of diamine rac‑3 was required to achieve monobenzylation…" (Sec 2). 2. “A quick optimization of the reductive amination… 1.3 equiv of 3 and 3 equiv of 8 as the optimal stoichiometry, resulting in ca. 80 % assay yield of product 9." (Ref 18).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Reactive Immuno-PET Linker-Chelator (1
Problem_Description: The first‑generation route required several chromatographic purifications (silica gel and preparative HPLC) to isolate intermediates and the final RESCA‑TFP, which reduced throughput and increased material loss.
Solution_Description: Salt formation (orotic‑acid salt of 9, HCl salt of 11) and direct isolation by filtration were introduced, eliminating all preparative chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “the process was not efficient, as multiple chromatographic purifications were required" (Sec 2.2). 2. “Extensive screening of salt formation … discovered its orotic acid salt as a crystalline compound…isolated by filtration" (Sec 2.2). 3. “Isolation of 11·HCl … by filtration, without any preparative purification operations" (Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Reactive Immuno-PET Linker-Chelator (1
Problem_Description: Intermediate 9 was unstable during storage, undergoing dimerization/oligomerization and loss of purity over time.
Solution_Description: The benzylic amine was immediately converted to its orotate salt, which was isolated as a stable crystalline solid and used directly in the next step, avoiding storage of the free amine.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Intermediate 9 was unstable during storage as multiple impurities derived from dimerization…" (Sec 2.1). 2. “The wet cake was washed… and dried … to give 9·orotate … 97.1 % A % HPLC purity" (Sec 2.3.1).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Reactive Immuno-PET Linker-Chelator (1
Problem_Description: The TFP‑ester (7) was prone to hydrolysis and residual TFP (6) was difficult to remove, leading to low isolated yields and impurity carry‑over.
Solution_Description: A mild aqueous work‑up with 0.5 M NaHCO₃ at 0 °C was employed, which quenched residual TFP without hydrolysing the labile ester, improving purity and recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “TFP ester 7 was prone to hydrolysis, and the residual TFP (6) was difficult to remove, leading to low yields and purity." (Sec 2.1). 2. “An aqueous workup under mild basic conditions using 0.5 M NaHCO₃ at 0 °C effectively reduced residual TFP (<1 % A % HPLC) without hydrolyzing the labile TFP ester." (Sec 2.1).

Problem_Description: The original trialkylation step gave only 79 % isolated yield, limiting overall material throughput.

Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Trialkylation … afforded 79 % isolated yield of product 10." (Sec 2.1). 2. “The trialkylation reaction … employing K₂CO₃ as the base in PhMe/H₂O gave 90 % yield of ester 10." (Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Reactive Immuno-PET Linker-Chelator (1
Problem_Description: The free‑base RESCA‑TFP (1) required storage at –20 °C to prevent rapid hydrolysis; at higher temperatures purity dropped sharply.
Solution_Description: Transformation of the free base into its HCl·1,4‑dioxane salt produced a solid that remained stable at 20 °C for 23 days with no loss of purity, removing the need for low‑temperature storage.

(Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Efficient Large-Scale Process for Tecovirimat via Reactive Distillation for the Preparation of Cycloheptatriene
Problem_Description: The historic pyrolysis of 7,7‑dichlorobicyclo[4.1.0]‑heptane (9) to cycloheptatriene (2) required temperatures of 490–520 °C, gave only a 35 % yield of 2, and the high temperature caused decomposition of the unstable bicyclic substrate, creating a safety‑critical exotherm.

Supporting_Evidence: “A key intermediate of tecovirimat, cycloheptatriene, was efficiently obtained via a reactive distillation process of 7,7‑dichlorobicyclo[4.1.0]­heptane to give 82% (91.38% purity by GC) on a 44.8 kg scale.”; “This method avoided the high temperatures (490–520 °C) and low yield that detracted from the previous synthesis.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective and Step-Economic Synthesis of the Chiral Amine Fragment in the Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Repotrectinib by Direct Asymmetric Reductive Amination under Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: The previously reported routes to the chiral amine fragment (<italic>R</italic>)-I rely on stoichiometric chiral auxiliaries, protecting‑group manipulations, and hazardous reagents such as BBr₃, giving overall low yields and making the process unattractive for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: A one‑step Ru‑catalyzed asymmetric reductive amination using cheap NH₄OAc as the nitrogen source and H₂ as the reductant was developed, eliminating the need for chiral auxiliaries and protecting groups while delivering high isolated yields and enantioselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: Both of the aforementioned routes suffer from tedious reaction steps, the requirement of quantitative chiral auxiliaries, and unfriendly reagents like BBr₃ as well as low overall yields, all together making them less attractive and inefficient for larger‑scale production.; The target product was obtained in excellent yield and ee from an easily available substrate through Ru‑catalyzed asymmetric reductive amination with cheap NH₄OAc as the nitrogen source and H₂ as the reductant.

Problem_Description: Screening of solvents showed that several alcoholic and aprotic solvents gave poor chemoselectivity or no reaction at all (e.g., TFE gave ketone reduction by‑product, i‑PrOH gave no product, THF gave none), leading to low yields.

Supporting_Evidence: The solvent proved to be critical for the outcome. Among the alcoholic solvents screened, methanol provided both excellent yield and enantiocontrol of I (entries 1–3).; In comparison, using 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol (TFE) as the solvent resulted in worse chemoselectivity, with competitive ketone reduction product 3 dominant (entry 2).; No desired product was observed in i‑PrOH (entry 4), and no reaction occurred in the aprotic solvent THF at all (entry 5).

Problem_Description: Scaling the batch reaction to 1 g caused a drop in isolated yield (65 %) due to formation of the alcohol by‑product 3, and the large amount of H₂ required in batch raised explosion concerns.

Solution_Description: Transition to a high‑pressure continuous‑flow hydrogenation reactor improved mixing, heat and mass transfer, and limited the volume of H₂ present at any time, eliminating the need for column chromatography and restoring high yields and ee on gram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: To solve the amplification issue, we turned our attention to continuous‑flow reactors, which have demonstrated several advantages in hydrogenation reactions.; The high surface area‑to‑volume ratio and efficient mixing increase the reaction efficiency, as reported in previous studies.; Additionally, scaling up a batch reaction would greatly increase the amount of hydrogen used, resulting in a significant explosion hazard. In contrast, the small volume of continuous hydrogenation reactions can prevent the accumulation of a large amount of hydrogen gas.; Scaling up the reaction to 21.6 g was successful, and the desired product (R)‑I was obtained in 93 % NMR yield (17.8 g, 82 % isolated yield) with 99 % ee.

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Quinazoline Organozinc toward KRAS G12C Inhibitor

Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow plug‑flow reactor (PFR) was adopted to give a narrow residence‑time distribution and excellent heat removal, while the reaction temperature was kept in a tight window (–20 °C to 0 °C) and the addition of i‑PrMgCl·LiCl was precisely controlled.
Supporting_Evidence:

Solution: "Converting the existing halogen–metal exchange batch process to continuous flow… offered the simplest solution"; "PFRs offer fast mixing … and exceptional heat transfer… allowing maintenance of a narrow temperature window for this highly exothermic process"; "a properly sized PFR avoids back mixing and provides tight control over residence time".

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Quinazoline Organozinc toward KRAS G12C Inhibitor

Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "The reaction enthalpy of −172 kJ/mol… suggesting a prohibitively slow addition rate… expected to consume an excessive amount of liquid nitrogen, creating a significant environmental impact".
Solution: "While excellent heat transfer and precise residence time control were critical… a properly sized PFR avoids back mixing… allowing maintenance of a narrow temperature window"; "initial reaction temperature ranging from −20 to 0 °C… matching the desired reaction heat transfer profile".

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Highly Functionalized Quinazoline Organozinc toward KRAS G12C Inhibitor

Supporting_Evidence:

Solution: "swapping the transmetalation PFR stage with a single CSTR offered a reliable engineering solution to processing the resulting product slurry"; "crude quinazoline organomagnesium 2 and ZnCl₂ streams were fed to a 100 mL EasyMax reactor modified for use as a CSTR…".
