Paper Title: Developing and Optimizing a Quench-Crystallization Operation in Drug Substance Manufacturing
Problem_Description: The early‑phase reverse quench‑crystallization used methanol as a cosolvent. Methanol partially methanolysed the piperazine fragment, forming impurity 7, and the resulting crystals were small with a broad particle‑size distribution, leading to very slow filtration (4–6 days) on commercial scale. In addition, the DCM‑reaction solution was immiscible with the aqueous basic quench, forming a triphasic system that made droplet formation and mixing difficult, and the standard cooling/antisolvent design‑of‑experiments (seeding, slow addition, lower agitation) gave even poorer filtration performance, indicating poor process consistency.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: 1. **Cosolvent substitution** – Methanol was replaced by N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP). NMP eliminates the methanolysis pathway (removing impurity 7) and yields larger, filter‑friendly crystals. 2. **Solvent‑volume optimisation** – The reaction solvent (DCM) was fixed at 5 L kg⁻¹‑input‑5 and the quench was formulated as 20 L kg⁻¹‑input‑5 water + 1 L kg⁻¹‑input‑5 NMP. This avoids precipitation of the potassium‑TFA salt and provides sufficient phase‑contact while keeping total volume low. 3. **Addition‑time and agitation redesign** – The reaction stream was added to the quench over 30 min (scaled to ~40 ± 20 min at plant) and the quench was vigorously agitated (700 RPM, scaled by turbulent shear‑rate). Faster addition and higher agitation produce smaller, more uniform droplets, increase interfacial area, accelerate the quench reaction, and generate a narrower crystal‑size distribution that filters quickly. 4. **PAT‑guided development** – Focused‑beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) and EasyViewer (EV) imaging were used to monitor chord counts, droplet formation and crystal growth in real‑time, allowing rapid identification of the critical design variables (cosolvent, solvent ratios, addition rate, agitation). 5. **Integration of quench and crystallization (new route & telescoping)** – The quench step was deliberately designed to also serve as the crystallization step, eliminating a separate isolation operation and reducing the number of unit operations. 6. **Other condition change** – The workflow incorporated a systematic, step‑wise design‑space exploration (solubility screening → PAT → small DoE) rather than relying solely on conventional cooling‑crystallization heuristics.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “the cosolvent originally used in the quench, methanol, resulted in low levels of methanolysis … impurity 7” (sec 2.1). 2. “small primary crystal size and broad particle size distribution… resulted in a slow filtration rate requiring multiple (4–6) days” (sec 2.1). 3. “The reaction solvent … is immiscible with the aqueous quench… multiple‑solution phases” (sec 1.2). 4. “seeding, slow addition, and lower agitation… resulted in crystals that filtered significantly slower” (sec 2.2). 5. “NMP … eliminated the challenge associated with methanolysis of 6” (sec 2.7). 6. “reducing the water volumes below 20 L kg⁻¹‑input‑5 could result in undesired potassium–TFA salt crystallization” (sec 2.8). 7. “Increasing agitation … results in smaller reaction‑solution droplets … faster to filter” (sec 2.9). 8. “Linear addition of the reaction solution over 30 min (translated to 40 ± 20 min at scale) to the rapidly agitated quench” (sec 2.10). 9. “FBRM and EV were used … to reveal underlying phase dynamics … to guide design‑space selection” (sec 2.5). 10. “The optimized process … was successfully transferred to three commercial manufacturing sites … 95 % yield, crystal size >200 µm, filtration <12 h” (sec 2.10).

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The original discovery route required chromatography to isolate cyclopropane ester (rac‑4) (28 % yield) and the enantiomers of rac‑1 could only be separated by preparative chiral SFC, which was deemed unsuitable for long‑term scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new three‑step sequence was developed that avoids chromatography altogether: (i) Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to give vinyl‑pyrimidine 3, (ii) nitrogen‑ylide mediated cyclopropanation of 3 to give trans‑ester 13 in 86 % isolated yield, and (iii) ester deprotection to give rac‑1 in 58 % overall yield. The cyclopropanation replaces the hazardous ethyl‑diazoacetate step, eliminating the safety issue and removing the need for chromatographic purification.
Supporting_Evidence: The problem of the inefficient separation of the enantiomers of rac‑1 was partially solved through preparative chiral supercritical fluid chromatography. While this could supply sufficient (S,S)‑1 for further development of structure–activity relationships, it was not considered to be a suitable long‑term solution.  The use of ethyl diazoacetate for the cyclopropanation, in excess and close to its decomposition temperature, was also considered to be a serious safety concern.  An efficient, novel cyclopropanation of 3 was developed through reaction with the nitrogen ylide derived from t‑butyl bromoacetate and DABCO.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: During the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of 2‑chloro‑4‑methylpyrimidine (2) to vinyl‑pyrimidine (3), the product 3 was volatile (bp ≈ 185 °C) and co‑distilled with the pinacol ester and pinacol, while two by‑products (10 and 11) were also formed, complicating isolation.
Solution_Description: The pinacol ester was replaced by potassium vinyltrifluoroborate, and the reaction was run in dioxane/water with Pd(OAc)₂/dppf and potassium carbonate, using a saturated carbonate solution to give a homogeneous mixture that could be filtered and distilled, affording 3 in 77 % yield with minimal impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: To counter the problem of the product volatility, vinylboronic acid pinacol ester was replaced by potassium vinyltrifluoroborate ... The best results were obtained with palladium acetate and dppf as catalyst (entries 7 and 8) in dioxane/water with potassium carbonate as base. ... the overall concentration maximized at 0.66 M without compromising the yield. The amount of water was chosen so that the potassium carbonate formed an approximately saturated solution that could be stirred easily.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: When potassium vinyltrifluoroborate was used, the reaction generated noticeable exotherms and evolved carbon dioxide, presenting a safety hazard on scale.
Solution_Description: The exotherm was mitigated by controlling the addition order (slow addition of the boronate) and by maintaining the reaction at 90 °C with efficient stirring, allowing safe scale‑up to 1–2 mol without runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: One consequence of being forced to use potassium vinyltrifluoroborate (in conjunction with only 2 equiv of potassium carbonate) was the observation of significant exothermic behavior and carbon dioxide evolution, but both were manageable on 2 mol scale.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The nitrogen‑ylide cyclopropanation of 3 did not reach completion even when 2 equiv of the ylide were used; the reaction stalled, giving only partial conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Finely grinding the cesium carbonate to <150 µm and drying it improved slurry homogeneity; after overnight reflux the cyclopropanation went to completion, delivering 13 in 86 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction did not proceed to completion, even with 2 equiv of the nitrogen ylide, and did not respond to the addition of more reagents. The problem was readily solved by grinding the cesium carbonate to <150 µm and drying. In this way, the cyclopropanation was complete after being heated overnight, and compound 13 was obtained in 86 % yield.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Resolution of rac‑1 using the (+)-abietylamine salt gave the undesired (R,R)‑acid as the less soluble salt; the amine is expensive (90 % purity) and not commercially available in the antipode, making the route costly and impractical at scale.
Solution_Description: The resolution was switched to the (S)‑1‑(1‑naphthyl)ethylamine salt, which is cheaper and more readily available. Dimethyl carbonate was employed as the recrystallisation solvent, providing high diastereomeric enrichment (99.8 : 0.2 dr) with only two hot triturations and a 41 % isolated yield on a 50 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: The use of (+)-abietylamine was relatively more expensive than 1‑(1‑naphthyl)‑ethylamine, has higher molecular weight, and the best grade available has only 90 % purity. We therefore turned our attention to the (S)‑1‑(1‑naphthyl)‑ethylamine salt … dimethyl carbonate … gave satisfactory results … the optimized procedure consisted of formation of the salt in dimethyl carbonate … to raise the dr to 99.4 : 0.6. The yield was 41 % (82 % of theory) on ca. 50 g scale.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: During resolution with the (S)‑1‑(1‑naphthyl)ethylamine salt in dimethyl carbonate, an acetamide by‑product (19) formed in the mother liquors, reducing overall yield, especially at larger scale.
Solution_Description: Replacing acetate solvents (ethyl, isopropyl acetate) with dimethyl carbonate eliminated the formation of the acetamide impurity, allowing a straightforward hot trituration purification that gave the desired (S,S)‑acid salt in high diastereomeric purity without additional chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: However, the first two are not ideal owing to their toxicity, and 2‑MeTHF gave poor crystal quality. Consideration of the requisite solvent polarity led us to try dimethyl carbonate … Trial recrystallizations of the diastereomeric mixture of salts with dimethyl carbonate revealed … the ratio of diastereomeric salts was found to be (S,S):(R,R) = 99.4:0.6. The optimized procedure consisted of … to raise the dr to 99.8:0.2. The yield was 41 % (82 % of theory).

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Crystallisation of the (+)-abietylamine salt gave variable yields (23 % adjusted for theory, 46 % of theory) because the unwanted diastereomer precipitated preferentially and the antipode of the amine is not available.
Solution_Description: A more robust resolution was developed using the (S)‑1‑(1‑naphthyl)ethylamine salt in dimethyl carbonate with controlled hot‑reflux trituration and PolyBLOCK‑mediated cooling to 0 °C, achieving consistent 99.8 % ee and 41 % isolated yield on multi‑gram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: The procedure afforded the (S,S)‑acid abietylamine salt (de = 100 %) in 23 % yield (46 % of theory) on a scale of 3 g. However, an improved procedure was subsequently developed using the 1‑(1‑naphthyl)‑ethylamine salt … the optimized procedure consisted of formation of the salt in dimethyl carbonate … to raise the dr to 99.8:0.2 … The yield was 41 % (82 % of theory) on ca. 50 g scale.

Paper Title: N‑Ylide Mediated Synthesis and Resolution of a Chiral Pyrimidinyl Cyclopropane Carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The original discovery route required three steps with chromatography and a 28 % isolated yield for the cyclopropane ester, making the process time‑consuming and low‑throughput for pre‑clinical material supply.
Solution_Description: The new three‑step route (Suzuki‑Miyaura, N‑ylide cyclopropanation, ester deprotection) delivers rac‑1 in 58 % overall yield in only three steps, all chromatography‑free, significantly reducing reaction time and simplifying the workflow for kilogram‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: We now had a way to prepare trans racemic acid in 58 % overall yield, in only three steps, free from its cis isomer, without resorting to chromatography. This process was used to provide rac‑1 on kilogram scale to support preclinical development studies.

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Sodium hydride (NaH) in dimethylformamide (DMF) was used in the batch N‑amination step. NaH is highly reactive, poses explosion hazards, and is not preferred for scale‑up in polar, non‑protic solvents.
Solution_Description: The hazardous NaH/DMF system was replaced by the soluble, process‑friendly base potassium tert‑butoxide (KOtBu) in THF (or diglyme/triglyme) with adjusted equivalents (1.2–1.5 eq) to achieve quantitative conversion without safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sodium hydride is not a preferred reagent for process scale‑up in either batch or continuous flow mode, and its potential safety risk in polar nonprotic solvents was well documented.” (Abstract); “We report the second‑generation synthesis … where sodium hydride was replaced by a soluble and process‑friendly base KOt‑Bu.” (Abstract); “Potassium tert‑butoxide providing the highest yields …” (Section 2.2.1); Table 4 shows >99 % A% with KOtBu vs 30 % with DBU, confirming the improvement.

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Incomplete conversion of POCl₃ during Vilsmeier reagent formation left excess POCl₃, which reacted violently with pyrrole to form polymers that clogged the tubular reactor and caused inconsistent operation.
Solution_Description: The POCl₃ equiv. was reduced from 1.10 → 1.05 → 1.02, minimizing excess reagent. Temperature control (0 °C or room temperature) ensured complete VR formation within ~95 s, eliminating polymer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unreacted POCl₃ reacts vigorously with pyrrole … thereby clogging the tubular reactor” (Sec 2.1.1); “With a decrease in the amount of POCl₃, a decrease in the amount of VR was observed via ReactIR” (Fig 2); “The VR formation was completed after about 95 s at both 0 °C and RT” (Sec 2.1.1).

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Formamidine acetate (FAAc) showed low solubility in IPA, n‑BuOH, and THF even at elevated temperatures, leading to poor mixing and reactor clogging during the cyclization step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: The batch cyclization to the final triazine required 8 h at 95–100 °C, limiting throughput and contributing to a modest overall yield (≈52 %).
Solution_Description: Higher temperatures (up to 140 °C) and increased FAAc equivalents reduced the cyclization time to 0.5–1 h while achieving >90 % A% conversion, thereby increasing overall productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 8 entry 8: 120 °C, 0.3 h gives 21 % A% (low); entries 8–9: 140 °C, 0.5–1 h give 92–93 % A%; “At 140 °C, 92 % and 93 % A% were observed after 0.5 and 1 h, respectively.” (Sec 2.3.2).

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Extraction of 2‑cyanopyrrole (3) at larger scale suffered from poor layer separation and slow filtration through activated carbon, causing product loss.
Solution_Description: MTBE was selected as the extraction solvent, and a MTBE/heptane mixture was used to improve phase separation. The aqueous layer was filtered through activated carbon before organic washes, streamlining isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Solvents ranked worst to best … MTBE was chosen to be applied in the final extraction procedure.” (Sec 2.1.3); “With increasing scale, separation of the layers was not clear, and filtration … was slow … At higher scales, layer separation using the MTBE/heptane mixture was effective.” (Sec 2.1.3).

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Hydroxylamine (NH₂OH·HCl) is thermally unstable and can decompose explosively, posing a safety risk during large‑scale handling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The hydroxylamine solution was prepared as a 50 wt % aqueous solution and used immediately in flow; temperature was kept low (≤ 90 °C) and water content was carefully controlled to suppress decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Particular attention and caution should be exercised when working with hydroxylamine. Hydroxylamine may decompose explosively …” (Sec 4.2); “Hydroxylamine … was used … at temperatures close to the boiling point of the solvents” (Sec 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Development of Continuous Flow Processes to Access Pyrrolo[2,1‑
Problem_Description: Increasing the reactor inner diameter from 1/16″ to 1/4″ caused vapor‑gas bubbles, reduced residence‑time control, and decreased solution yield (from ~92 % to 79 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Operating at higher back‑pressure (14 bar vs 7 bar) reduced bubble formation and partially recovered yield (81 %). The authors suggest static mixers to improve mixing in larger‑diameter reactors.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2 entry 3 vs 4: yield drops from 89.4 % to 79.3 % when moving to 1/4″ at 7.5 bar; “A significant reduction in the proportion of bubbles resulted… solution yield increased by 2 %… (79.3 % → 81.1 %)” (Sec 2.1.2); “The use of a static mixer can potentially improve the mixing…” (Sec 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: Use of NaH/DMF in the original route creates an explosion hazard, making scale‑up unsafe.
Solution_Description: Replace the NaH/DMF protocol with safer reagents (in‑situ bromine generation from HBr/H₂O₂ and a NaI/TFA debromination sequence), eliminating the need for NaH/DMF.
Supporting_Evidence: The synthesis also includes other potentially hazardous or undesirable conditions like the use of NaH/DMF, which can be problematic for scale‑up in a technical process due to the associated explosion risk.; The published process for preparing the starting material 2‑bromo‑4‑nitro‑imidazoline (7) revealed optimization potential with respect to process safety and isolated yield. The use of molecular bromine, difficult on a larger scale, could be replaced with the in‑situ formation of bromine from hydrobromic acid and hydrogen peroxide.; The intermediate 2,5‑dibromo‑4‑nitroimidazole does not require isolation but could be debrominated in a single pot to yield 7 in moderate yields. However, on scaling this one‑pot procedure, a decrease in product purity was observed due to intractable salt contamination, so the final procedure run on kilogram scale involved isolation of 7b and debromination with NaI and TFA to yield 2‑bromo‑4‑nitro‑imidazoline (7) in good yields and very high purity.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: Molecular bromine is difficult to handle and procure on kilogram scale, posing safety and availability concerns.

Supporting_Evidence: The published process for preparing the starting material 2‑bromo‑4‑nitro‑imidazoline (7) revealed optimization potential with respect to process safety and isolated yield. The use of molecular bromine, difficult on a larger scale, could be replaced with the in‑situ formation of bromine from hydrobromic acid and hydrogen peroxide.

Problem_Description: Trityl‑ and TBS‑protected glycidols showed poor solubility in water, leading to incomplete conversion and side‑product formation.
Solution_Description: Select protecting groups (PMBz, Bz) that are water‑compatible; perform the alkylation in water/K₂CO₃ where solubility is sufficient.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: During the first alkylation, product 21 precipitated, causing loss during filtration and low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Remove toluene before work‑up, redissolve the crude solid in ethyl acetate, and carry the crude forward without isolation, thereby preserving material.
Supporting_Evidence: The desired product 21 precipitates during the reaction, causing a beige suspension after 48 h. Filtration and washing with toluene were insufficient as a significant amount of product was lost in the mother liquor. Therefore, toluene was removed prior to redissolving the residue in ethyl acetate to obtain a homogeneous solution.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: Alkylation of 7 with some protecting groups required 48–70 h, significantly extending batch time.
Solution_Description: Switch to water/K₂CO₃ medium, which gives comparable conversions in 44 h (PMBz) or 71 h (Bz) and enables precipitation‑based isolation, reducing overall time.

In contrast to the crystalline PMBz‑derivative 21, crude imidazole 22 was however isolated as a viscous oil (HPLC purity 81 %). Adding MTBE (methyl tert‑butyl ether) to the solution of crude 22 in ethyl acetate led to precipitation of contaminants which increased the purity of imidazole 22 remaining in the organic layer to 87 %.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: During the one‑pot deprotection/cyclation in MeOH, the generated methoxide attacks the substrate, forming side product 27 and causing ring‑opening of pretomanid at extended times.
Solution_Description: Perform the K₂CO₃ addition at –10 °C, keep the mixture at 0 °C overnight, and monitor conversion closely; this limits methoxide attack and yields pretomanid with ≤12 % side product.
Supporting_Evidence: It was important to perform the reaction at low temperatures and follow the conversion carefully by HPLC because 10 was observed to react with in situ generated methoxide to form side product 27.; A methanolic solution of crude 24 or 25 (82 % purity) was cooled to –10 °C, K₂CO₃ (15 equiv) was added in one portion, the suspension was stirred for 2 h at –10 °C and then warmed to 0 °C and stirred for 22 h, giving pretomanid in 30–40 % isolated yield with ≤12 % of side product 27.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (
Problem_Description: Cyclization attempts using NaH in THF gave only 21 % consumption and a complex mixture.
Solution_Description: Abandon the NaH/THF route; instead, use TBAF for TBS deprotection followed by heating for cyclization (THF at –5 °C to reflux for several days) to achieve complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Cyclization attempts using NaH in THF were unsuccessful. Only 21 % consumption (12 % conversion to 1) could be observed when 3.0 equiv of NaH were added. Further addition of NaH led to a complex product mixture.; By addition of TBAF (1 M in THF) at –5 °C, complete deprotection could be observed after 2 h. Direct cyclization after deprotection could be achieved by heating the reaction mixture to reflux for 3–5 days.

Paper Title: Short and Efficient Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Agent Pretomanid from (

After the recrystallization from 2‑propanol/heptane and washing with water, tetrabutylammonium salts were only present in traces but unfortunately, t‑butyldimethylsilanol could not be removed without column chromatography.

Paper Title: Stereoinvertive Deoxyamination of
Problem_Description: The traditional azide‑introduction step (S_N2 displacement of a mesylate with NaN₃) uses large quantities of sodium azide, which is highly explosive and toxic. Differential scanning calorimetry showed an exothermic onset at 220 °C and the process would have to be run below 120 °C for safety, making the step hazardous on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced NaN₃ with diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA) in a Bose–Mitsunobu azidation. DPPA is a non‑explosive azide source, allowing the reaction to be performed at ~25 °C with a controlled, mild exotherm. Reagents were added at 0 °C and the mixture was stirred at 25 °C, eliminating the safety and heat‑release concerns associated with NaN₃.
Supporting_Evidence: “The requisite nucleophile, sodium azide, is highly explosive and toxic… Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) measurements of the azide intermediate 7 showed that the exothermic starting temperature was 220 °C… the process can be carried out at temperatures generally below 120 °C… it can be judged that the process can be carried out at temperatures generally below 120 °C.”; “Since this reaction uses DPPA as a non‑explosive azide source, it is expected to be safer to perform even on a large scale… the reaction is expected to proceed under milder conditions at approximately room temperature.”; “After stirring at 0 °C for 21 h (conversion: 97.7 %, 65.2 % yield)… a strong exothermic reaction and nitrogen generation were observed.”

Paper Title: Stereoinvertive Deoxyamination of
Problem_Description: The original S_N2 azidation (mesylate 6 → azide 7) gave >10 % of undesired diastereomers and side‑products (aziridine 16, olefin 17) even at elevated temperature, resulting in low overall yield and poor diastereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: Running the Bose–Mitsunobu azidation at room temperature (25 °C) dramatically reduced the formation of side‑products and improved the diastereomeric ratio (dr = 1:0.02). Screening of solvents identified MTBE, 1,4‑dioxane, toluene, CPME, and anisole as giving higher yields, while polar solvents (EtOAc, THF, MeCN) gave poor results. Reducing DPPA equivalents from 3.0 → 2.0 equiv restored yield while keeping diastereoselectivity, demonstrating that reagent excess was not required.
Supporting_Evidence: “Stirring a solution of 5… at 25 °C for 21 h afforded the target 7 in a 65.2 % yield… 1.1 % of the diastereomer epi‑7… aziridine 16… also observed… The reaction proceeded smoothly in a wide variety of solvents (entries 2–7)… MTBE afforded the best yield (entry 3).”; “From a cost reduction perspective, the reduction of the reagents… reducing the amount of DPPA resulted in a 20‑point decrease in the yield (entry 9). Further reduction in the amounts of DIAD and PPh₃ had minimal impact on the yield compared with entry 9 (entry 10).”

Problem_Description: Intermediate 4 (the trans‑2‑aminocyclohexanol) is highly polar and could not be efficiently extracted from aqueous solution, leading to low isolation yields and cumbersome work‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: “When acetonitrile was added as a poor solvent to a concentrated aqueous solution containing amine 4… the amine hydrobromide salt 4·HBr precipitated as a white solid… 86.5 % yield (98.9 % area) by filtration alone.”

Paper Title: Stereoinvertive Deoxyamination of
Problem_Description: Amide 19, obtained after coupling thiazole‑carboxylic acid to 4·HBr, was a reddish oil that extracted poorly and contained significant HOBt‑derived impurities, making purification difficult and lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: The crude oil was treated with acetonitrile as a poor solvent at 0 °C; the resulting solid was filtered to give pure 19 (98.6 % area). This simple anti‑solvent precipitation removed impurities without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “When acetonitrile was added to the concentrated reddish oil as a poor solvent, a solid precipitated. After stirring for 30 min at 0 °C, the resulting slurry was filtered to obtain the target product 19 in high quality (98.6 % area).”

Paper Title: Stereoinvertive Deoxyamination of
Problem_Description: During the Staudinger reduction step in the one‑pot sequence, hydrolysis of the iminophosphorane intermediate sometimes stopped midway, limiting conversion and overall yield; the reaction was also highly exothermic when PPh₃ was added.
Solution_Description: Addition of primary or secondary amines (e.g., ethylamine, dimethylamine) accelerated the hydrolysis of the iminophosphorane, completing the Staudinger step. The addition of PPh₃ was performed at 0 °C followed by controlled warming, mitigating the exotherm. Reaction temperature was raised to 50 °C only after the gas‑evolution step, ensuring safe and complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The hydrolysis process could be accelerated and that 23 was consumed by the addition of primary or secondary amines such as ethylamine and dimethylamine, suggesting an iminophosphorane exchange.”; “After stirring at 0 °C for 21 h … PPh₃ was added at the same temperature. [Caution]: evolution of nitrogen gas! After stirring for 2 h at 50 °C…”

Problem_Description: Crystallization of the final salt 20·2CSA in acetone gave low purity because other by‑products (triphenylphosphine oxide, iminophosphorane) co‑precipitated; some acids (H₂SO₄, citric acid, l‑tartaric acid) failed to precipitate the salt at all.

• “the best reaction conditions were DMA, DHFP, and POCl₃ (2:1:40) at 120 °C for 3 h, with an increased yield of 62 %” (Abstract). 
• Table 2 entries show 62 % yield at 120 °C, 3 h, 1:40:2 ratio (Results and Discussion). 
• “The highest yield was obtained with N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMA)” (Results and Discussion). 
• “Reaction time should be 3 h… optimal temperature should be 120 °C” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Synthesis of 5,6-Dichlorofurazano[3,4‑

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Synthesis of 5,6-Dichlorofurazano[3,4‑
Problem_Description: Temperatures above 150 °C cause increased by‑product formation and black solid formation, reducing DCFP yield.

Supporting_Evidence:
• “If the temperature is too high, the proportion of by‑products will increase, resulting in a decrease in yield” (Results and Discussion). 
• “When the reaction temperature was too high (>150 °C), a large amount of black solids formed… lowered the separated yield” (Results and Discussion). 
• Table 2 entries 5‑7 show optimal yields at 120 °C, while entry 7 (150 °C) gives lower yield (42 %) (Results and Discussion). 
• “The optimal reaction temperature should be 120 °C” (Results and Discussion). 
• “Reaction temperature too high… decrease in yield” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Synthesis of 5,6-Dichlorofurazano[3,4‑
Problem_Description: Extending the reaction time beyond 3 h (e.g., 5 h, 10 h, 24 h) leads to black solids and a drop in isolated DCFP yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction time was fixed at 3 h, which gave the highest yield while avoiding solid formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the reaction time was too long (>5 h)… a large amount of black solids formed, … lowered the separated yield” (Results and Discussion). 
• Table 2 entries 1‑4 (1 h‑24 h) show decreasing yields with longer times (46 % at 1 h, 11 % at 24 h) (Results and Discussion). 
• “According to entries 1–4 … the optimal reaction time should be 3 h” (Results and Discussion). 
• “The optimal reaction time … 3 h” (Results and Discussion). 
• “Long reaction times cause black solids” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Synthesis of 5,6-Dichlorofurazano[3,4‑
Problem_Description: The quenching of the POCl₃‑based reaction is highly exothermic; uncontrolled addition of ice water can cause local overheating and product degradation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: During scale‑up, the reaction mixture is poured slowly into ice water with vigorous stirring, temperature is kept below 30 °C, and DMA is added at ≤10 °C to control heat release.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the exothermic nature of the reaction requires thorough stirring to prevent local overheating” (Safety Precautions). 
• “Never add ice water to the reaction solution” (Safety Precautions – warning of rapid quench). 
• Experimental: “DMA was added slowly while maintaining the temperature below 10 °C” (Synthesis of DCFP). 
• “Poured into 5.0 L of ice water, and constantly stirred… temperature was kept below 30 °C” (Synthesis of DCFP). 
• Scale‑up experiment reports “no loss of yield, and no acid fumes are generated during the post‑treatment process” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical and Scalable Synthesis of 5,6-Dichlorofurazano[3,4‑
Problem_Description: Changing the equivalents of POCl₃ and DMA significantly affects the conversion, leading to inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified the optimal stoichiometry of 1 : 40 : 2 (DHFP : POCl₃ : DMA), which consistently produced a 62 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 2 shows variation in yield with different POCl₃/DMA ratios (e.g., 1:20:2 gives 52 %, 1:10:2 gives 46 %) (Results and Discussion). 
• “According to entries 8–12, 2 equiv of DMA and 40 equiv of POCl₃ gave the best yield” (Results and Discussion). 
• “A 62 % yield was reached by the reaction of DHFP, POCl₃, and DMA (1:40:2) at 120 °C for 3 h” (Abstract/Conclusion).
