Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Lysine oligomers are highly soluble in the aqueous phase, so the growing peptide chain remains in solution where it is exposed to secondary enzymatic hydrolysis, leading to poor overall yield and a broad, uncontrolled dispersity.
Solution_Description: A low‑water biphasic system (water ↔ toluene) was adopted; a small aqueous fraction (≈5 % v/v) provides enough water to keep papain active while the organic toluene phase extracts the growing oligolysine away from water, suppressing hydrolysis. The water‑to‑toluene ratio was tuned to optimise both enzyme activity and product partitioning.
Supporting_Evidence: Hydrophilic amino acids ... are highly soluble in the aqueous medium, making them susceptible to secondary enzymatic hydrolysis, thereby lowering the yield and dispersity of the oligopeptide product. (Sec 3.1)“This problem can be solved by conducting the reaction in either (i) a low‑water‑activity medium ... or (ii) a low‑water organic biphasic medium such as the low‑water toluene system reported in this work.” (Sec 3.1)“When the water content was increased beyond this to 2.5 and 5 %, the yield was still maintained at ∼85 %, but higher‑order oligolysines were formed… At 10 % water content, the yield fell to ∼45 % … due to the increasing dominance of the competing secondary hydrolysis reaction.” (Sec 3.6.1)“The organic solvent should be relatively immiscible with water to prevent enzyme denaturation but be able to partition the relatively hydrophilic product away from the aqueous phase… Toluene … was chosen as one of the best choices for this low‑water reaction medium.” (Sec 3.1)

Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Papain loses activity when the reaction is performed in neat toluene (no water), resulting in zero oligolysine formation.
Solution_Description: A minimal aqueous phase (≈5 % v/v) was included to provide essential hydration for papain, preserving its catalytic activity while maintaining a low‑water environment.
Supporting_Evidence: When the reaction was conducted in neat toluene in the absence of any water content, no oligolysine yield was observed. This is most probably due to inactivation of the papain in the organic solvent without any water hydration necessary to maintain activity.

Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Excessive amounts of the additives 2‑mercaptoethanol and DIPEA are toxic to papain, causing enzyme deactivation and sharply reduced yields.
Solution_Description: The concentrations of 2‑mercaptoethanol (0.2 % v/v) and DIPEA (0.8 % v/v) were optimized using OVAT and CCD to provide enough reducing/neutralising capacity without reaching toxic levels, maximizing yield (~85 %).
Supporting_Evidence: The absence of any 2‑mercaptoethanol ... led to a zero yield, as its presence is considered essential for papain activity.

Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: The ion‑pairing agent HSA used in semipreparative LC is non‑volatile and interferes with LC‑MS detection of oligolysine peaks.
Solution_Description: After semipreparative ion‑pair LC, the collected fractions were subjected to solid‑phase extraction (SPE) on a strong cation‑exchange cartridge to remove HSA before LC‑MS analysis.
Supporting_Evidence: The samples contained abundant amounts of the non‑volatile ion‑pairing agent HSA used in the semipreparatory ion‑pair LC analysis. As the non‑volatile HSA was expected to interfere with LC‑MS analysis, the oligolysine peak isolate samples were purified with SPE as described in Sec 2.3.3.

Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: When the process was scaled‑up 10‑fold, the oligolysine yield dropped from ~85 % to ~75 % and the distribution of residues changed, indicating inconsistent performance at larger scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Scale‑up was performed in a 250 mL flat‑bottom flask equipped with a magnetic stirrer, keeping stirring rate, temperature and reactant ratios identical to the laboratory batch, thereby improving mixing and mass‑transfer while preserving the low‑water environment.
Supporting_Evidence: The feasibility of scale‑up of the developed experimental synthesis model was investigated with a 10× upscaling setup. The reaction was conducted as a one‑pot synthesis ... 250 mL flat‑bottom flask with a magnetic stirrer at room temperature... The results (not shown) ... oligolysine is synthesized at these scaled‑up conditions also in ∼75 % yield with the number of residues ranging from 2 to 7.

Paper Title: Papain-Catalyzed Synthesis of Oligolysine in Low-Water Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: The one‑variable‑at‑a‑time (OVAT) approach requires many runs and cannot reveal interactive effects among process variables, limiting the ability to optimise yield and dispersity efficiently.
Solution_Description: A statistical design‑of‑experiments workflow was employed: first a Plackett‑Burman screen to identify the five most significant factors, followed by a Central Composite Design (CCD) to model interactions and locate optimum conditions (∼92 % yield, dispersity 2–10).
Supporting_Evidence: The Plackett–Burman design was used to screen for significant variables ... The five predominant variables ... were the aqueous phase composition (A), 2‑mercaptoethanol (D), DIPEA (E), duration of incubation (F), and substrate concentration (G).

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: The initial milling experiments used large amounts of liquid triethylamine and TMS‑acetylene, producing a mobile slurry that leaked from the milling jar and made post‑reaction handling difficult, leading to poor conversion when solid bases were first tried.
Solution_Description: The liquid base was replaced with solid inorganic bases (K₂CO₃ or DABCO) and the amount of base was adjusted, eliminating the slurry and improving handling while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the large loadings of liquid reagents caused the reaction mixture to be a mobile slurry that could leak from the milling jar and make the post‑reaction handling problematic.”; “Exchanging triethyl amine with these solid bases gave moderate results in initial screening but gave a lead toward conditions that are better suited for mechanochemical processing.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: Using TMS‑acetylene limited the maximum temperature to 45 °C because the reagent (bp 53 °C) decomposed at higher temperatures, preventing further rate acceleration.
Solution_Description: The coupling partner was switched from TMS‑acetylene to the higher‑boiling TES‑acetylene (bp 136 °C), allowing the reaction to be run at 90 °C and 120 °C, which cut the required milling time from 4 h to 30 min while delivering comparable or higher conversions and purities.
Supporting_Evidence: “our upper‑temperature threshold was limited by our coupling partner, TMS‑acetylene (boiling point: 53 °C)”; “A pivot from TMS‑acetylene … to triethylsilyl (TES) acetylene (boiling point: 136 °C) was made, which would allow access to higher temperatures for our milling trials.”; “At elevated temperatures, we observed conversions and purities comparable to multihour reactions in half the time.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: Pd(PPh₃)₄ was found to be air‑sensitive; under extrusion conditions it degraded, preventing full substrate consumption.
Solution_Description: The catalyst system was changed to the more air‑stable Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃ (3 : 1 L/Pd ratio), which gave comparable conversions in extrusion and removed the need for rigorous inert atmosphere.
Supporting_Evidence: “air sensitivity of Pd‑(PPh₃)₄ was a significant limitation.”; “Thus, the more stable Pd‑(OAc)₂/PPh₃ system was evaluated… gave comparable conversions to trials where Pd‑(PPh₃)₄ was used.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: During early extrusion runs a die at the extruder exit became blocked by the solid reaction mixture, causing back‑filling, barrel pressure build‑up and a complete stop of material flow.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The die was removed and the extrudate was collected directly from the barrel opening; a less aggressive screw configuration was later replaced by a more aggressive design with multiple kneading elements to improve mechanical force and prevent blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: “the extrudate blocked the exit port and began backfilling the barrel until the system totally seized.”; “the die was removed, and the samples were collected from the end of the barrel.”; “a more aggressive screw design was implemented… three unique kneading segments… to increase the residence time of the reactive material.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: At extrusion temperatures above 115 °C and higher screw speeds, the undesired bis‑alkyne product increased, reducing the purity of the desired mono‑alkynylated product.
Solution_Description: The optimal extrusion temperature was fixed at 115 °C with a slower screw speed (100 rpm) and lower feed rate (1 cm³ min⁻¹), which limited residence time enough to suppress bis‑alkyne formation while maintaining ≥73 % conversion of the mono‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: “At higher temperatures, we observed increased formation of the bisalkyne product.”; “Ultimately, an isothermal barrel at 115 °C, a slower screw speed of 100 rpm, and a feed rate of 1 cm³ min⁻¹ were implemented as optimum for this system … conversion of 73 %.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: When applying the optimized conditions to pyridine substrates, using K₂CO₃ as base gave only 10 % conversion, indicating that the base was ineffective for this heterocycle class.
Solution_Description: The base was switched to DABCO, and the amounts of alkyne, copper, and Pd catalyst were modestly increased; this restored >99 % conversion and >86 % purity for the pyridine substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “the use of potassium carbonate led to extremely poor conversions ….”; “Because DABCO showed promising activity … we investigated its effectiveness… With a slight increase in alkyne, copper, and catalyst, the coupling reaction performs extremely well with high conversion and purity.”

Paper Title: Investigation of Mechanochemical Sonogashira CouplingsFrom Batch Solution to Continuous Reactive Extrusion through Ball-Milling Optimization
Problem_Description: The original solution‑phase Sonogashira process required 9 V of THF (solvent‑intensive) and gave lower overall yields compared with the mechanochemical route.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a solvent‑free mechanochemical ball‑milling platform and then to twin‑screw reactive extrusion, reducing solvent use to 6 V of EtOAc (a 63 % reduction) while achieving comparable or higher isolated yields and shorter reaction times.
Supporting_Evidence: “The rapid emergence of mechanochemistry … could reduce solvent use.”; “Assay yields were comparable to standard solution‑based methods … solvent used was reduced … from 9 V of THF … to 6 V of EtOAc and a 63 % reduction when compared to work by Rozema …”

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: Coupling of the final Fmoc‑Arg(Ot‑Bu) onto the resin‑bound tetrapeptide SP‑1 gave large amounts of deletion sequence and a guanidine‑transfer side‑product, resulting in only a 3 % isolated yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: Switch to an N‑Pbf protected arginine (instead of the bis‑Boc Arg) eliminated the deletion and guanidine‑transfer side‑products (≤5 % by LC) and gave a clean coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The loading of the last amino acid, Fmoc‑l‑(Boc)₂ Arg‑OH to SP‑1 turned out to be problematic as significant amounts of the deletion sequence 1 and guanidine‑transfer product 3 were formed instead.', 'The reaction proceeded smoothly with the elimination of the deletion sequence side product and reduced formation of the guanidine‑transfer product (less than 5 % by LC).']

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: After Fmoc removal of the Orn‑Nδ on the CTC resin the loading was only ~28 % because a competitive lactamisation cleaved Orn from the resin, generating side‑product 7a.
Solution_Description: Begin the sequence with a CTC‑resin‑bound Orn (SP‑7) and perform an early Alloc deprotection using 10 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄/phenylsilane; this increases the bulk of the ornithine derivative and raises resin loading to ~60 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Upon Fmoc protecting group removal of the Orn‑Nδ, poor loading (∼28 %) was observed presumably due to a competitive lactamisation side reaction which cleaved Orn from the resin to afford side product 7a.', 'Careful treatment of 8 g of intermediate SP‑7b with 10 mol % of Pd‑(PPh₃)₄ and excess of phenyl silane … afforded SP‑7d with an improved resin loading of ∼60 %.']

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: The second‑generation route required two separate protecting‑group removal steps, giving a poor overall isolated yield (6 %) and making the final HPLC purification of API‑1 difficult.
Solution_Description: Perform a single global deprotection after macro‑lactamisation (eliminating one deprotection step) using 1 M HCl in HFIPA; this simplifies the sequence, shortens reaction time and raises the overall isolated yield to 35 % from SP‑7c.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The main issues with this second‑generation synthesis include … two protecting group removal steps … a poor overall yield (6 %) … difficult HPLC purification of API‑1.', 'The overall route to API proceeded … with an overall 6‑fold increase in overall yield from 2‑chlorotrityl‑bound intermediate SP‑7c.', 'The use of 1 M HCl in HFIPA readily cleaved the Boc and t‑butyl protecting groups at rt with minimal formation of the API‑tert‑butyl or the trifluoro acetylated side products.']

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: TFA‑mediated deprotection incorporated a tert‑butyl group (Friedel–Crafts trapping) and acetylated the free hydroxyl of d‑Cha(4‑OH), and the Pbf group on Arg was reluctant to be removed, creating side‑products that complicated purification.
Solution_Description: Use 1 M HCl in HFIPA at 0 °C followed by a basic work‑up (NaOH addition) to remove all four protecting groups cleanly without forming tert‑butyl or trifluoro‑acetyl side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['All of which led to the incorporation of tert‑butyl group into the reaction product (likely resulting from the Friedel–Crafts trapping of the tert‑butyl cation by the indole motif).', 'The free hydroxyl of d‑Cha(4‑OH) was readily acetylated by TFA, which would complicate API‑1 isolation.', 'The use of 1 M HCl in HFIPA readily cleaved the Boc and t‑butyl protecting groups at rt with minimal formation of the API‑tert‑butyl or the trifluoro acetylated side products.']

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: The Alloc deprotection step generates propene gas (CH₂=CHCH₃) which can cause pressure build‑up in the reaction vessel.
Solution_Description: Operate the Alloc deprotection under a well‑ventilated setup and monitor pressure; careful ventilation of the vessel is required during scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Caution: The Alloc removal procedure generates CH₂CHCH₃ gas which can cause pressure build‑up. Careful ventilation of the vessel is required.']

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of a Macrocyclic Peptide-Like C5aR Antagonist for Intravenous Applications
Problem_Description: The macro‑lactamisation originally employed HATU, a relatively expensive coupling reagent.
Solution_Description: Replace HATU with the less expensive HBTU, which gave comparable yields (∼90 % isolated) for the macro‑lactamisation step, reducing material cost on large scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The use of less expensive HBTU as the coupling reagent proved to be just as effective and was subsequently demonstrated on two 35 g batches.']

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: Recrystallisation of crude 4,7‑dichloroquinoline (5) gave only moderate yields (65‑67 %) and required extra steps to remove the 4,5‑dichloroquinoline isomer (12). Hydrocarbon solvents (hexane, heptane) gave good purity but low yield; OH‑containing solvents (EtOH, MeOH) lowered the yield drastically, and addition of water reduced purity.
Solution_Description: A fractional precipitation sequence was developed: after hydrolysis the quinoline acid was isolated at pH 8.2, then slurry‑washed at pH 4.0. By adjusting the pH the two acid isomers precipitate at different points, allowing the 4,5‑isomer to be removed in a single operation with only a 10 % loss in overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "Attempted recrystallization in hexane … afforded the pure product in moderate yields of 65 %" (Table 1, entry 1); "OH‑containing solvents such as ethanol and methanol resulted in a drastic decrease in yield" (entries 3 and 5); "fractional precipitation … pH 8.2 … slurry‑washed at pH 4 … resulted in the target product in 99.3 % purity" (Table 2, entry 6).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: The Mannich reaction of 4‑acetamidophenol (13) with paraformaldehyde and diethylamine gave incomplete conversion in 3 h (60 % yield) and required 24 h to reach 82 % yield. Acid‑catalysed attempts (HCl, p‑TSA) produced double‑Mannich by‑products and reduced yield to 61 %.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to toluene and conducting the Mannich condensation at 85 °C for 15 h gave a 95 % isolated yield with minimal impurities. Toluene is inexpensive, recyclable, and avoids the acid‑catalysed side reactions observed in polar solvents.
Supporting_Evidence: "The first attempt … 2 h at 40 °C … only 60 % yield" (Table 3, entry 2); "reaction was repeated in methanol + HCl … formed unidentifiable impurities"; "the next attempt saw the reaction performed in toluene at 85 °C, which afforded 14 in an excellent yield of 95 % within 15 h" (text).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the 4,7‑DCQ synthesis, the reaction mixture formed a thick heterogeneous slurry at room temperature, which was difficult to stir and filter. Heating the mixture to 45 °C rendered it homogeneous, but large reactors required longer heating times, affecting throughput.
Solution_Description: The pH adjustment step after hydrolysis was performed at 50 °C (hot) rather than at ambient temperature, giving a homogeneous slurry that could be filtered easily. The same temperature was used for the subsequent pH 4 slurry‑wash, eliminating the mixing problem while maintaining product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Reactions were first attempted at room temperature at which a thick heterogeneous slurry formed and rendered the mixture difficult to stir" (text); "as the temperature was increased to 45 °C, the mixture was homogeneous and easy to stir and filter" (text).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: Acetic acid had been reported as an excellent solvent for selective precipitation of quinoline acids, but its harsh reflux conditions, strong odor, and high cost make it unsuitable for commercial scale.
Solution_Description: Instead of using acetic acid, the team employed a water‑based fractional precipitation where the quinoline acid precipitates at pH 8.2 and the remaining salt is removed at pH 4. This avoids the need for refluxing acetic acid, reducing hazards, energy consumption and solvent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: "Acetic acid … is expensive and would require extra care in the plant due to its strong odor and harmful effects" (text); "we envisaged that, owing to the difference in acidity, the two isomers … would precipitate at different pH values" (text).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: 4,7‑Dichloroquinoline (5) accounts for >40 % of the raw‑material cost of amodiaquine, and reliance on commercial suppliers is financially unsustainable.
Solution_Description: A four‑step in‑house synthesis from meta‑chloroaniline (7) was developed, using inexpensive diphenyl ether and toluene, with solvent recovery and recycling. The overall yield (89 %) and material cost ($24.15 kg⁻¹) are significantly lower than market price.
Supporting_Evidence: "A cost‑competitive process for the production of 4,7‑DCQ … was also reported wherein 4,7‑DCQ was prepared in four steps from meta‑chloroaniline" (abstract); "material cost per kilogram for 4,7‑DCQ … calculated as $24.15 versus a market price of $42.00/kg" (text).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of the Antimalarial Amodiaquine Dihydrochloride Dihydrate
Problem_Description: Initial hydrolysis of the quinoline ester (9) required 2 h at 95‑97 °C, followed by a 1 h neutralization at pH 8.2; the subsequent filtration of the acid precipitate was slow and gave modest yields (89 %).
Solution_Description: The hydrolysis was performed with aqueous NaOH at 95 °C for 2 h, then the mixture was held at 45 °C for 1 h while maintaining pH 8.2, producing an almost quantitative conversion (89 % isolated yield). The controlled pH steps eliminated the need for additional work‑up and improved reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: "Hydrolysis of the ester (9) in aqueous sodium hydroxide … was achieved in essentially quantitative yields" (text); "the reaction mixture was heated at 45 °C for 1 h (maintaining the pH 8.2)" (section 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: The traditional batch synthesis of the aziridines gave only moderate isolated yields and required long reflux times (up to 3 h) to reach partial conversion.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow reactor where the residence time could be reduced to minutes and the temperature raised, delivering high isolated yields in a short reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: The abstract notes “suffered from moderate yields, long reaction times … The process can be greatly improved … high yields, short reaction times … in continuous flow” (lines 1‑5 of the abstract).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: In batch mode, poor heat‑transfer control caused excessive exotherms, leading to side‑reactions (formation of oxazolines) and decomposition of the aziridine product.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous flow offered superior heat removal and the ability to superheat the reaction mixture under pressure, which suppressed competing pathways and minimized product degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: The introduction states that “Poor control over heat transfer is the main culprit …” and later the flow system “provides improved heat and mass transfer … and effectively use low‑boiling solvents” (lines 30‑36).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: Batch experiments showed inconsistent conversions and yields, with substantial amounts of unidentified side‑products observed.
Solution_Description: Systematic optimization of flow temperature, residence time, and back‑pressure (100 psi BPR) resulted in reproducible high yields (up to 83 %).
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 shows varying yields with different residence times and temperatures; the text notes “variability … accompanied by substantial amounts of unidentified side products” and later “a reproducible yield of 83 %” after pressure stabilization (lines 70‑92).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: For substrates bearing electron‑withdrawing nitrogen substituents, the required high temperatures caused complete consumption of the starting material but also degradation of the aziridine product.
Solution_Description: By switching to MeCN (higher boiling point) and employing a back‑pressure regulator, the reaction could be superheated (up to 130 °C) while keeping residence times short, thus avoiding decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: The text describes “higher temperatures … resulted in a drop in yield … due to decomposition” and later the solvent study identifies MeCN as the best solvent for both yield and diastereoselectivity (lines 103‑115).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: Isoxazoline 11 m showed limited solubility in MeCN, which reduced the achievable concentration and throughput during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Concentration studies were performed, establishing 0.125 M as optimal for most substrates and attempting higher concentrations (up to 1 M) where feasible, while retaining MeCN as the solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: The scale‑up paragraph notes “limited solubility of isoxazoline 11 m in MeCN” and the earlier concentration study discusses yields at 0.125 M, 0.5 M and 1 M (lines 115‑124).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: Isolation of certain aziridines (e.g., 12 k) by flash chromatography caused near‑complete decomposition, making product recovery difficult.
Solution_Description: The authors acknowledge the difficulty but do not report a successful alternative purification; the issue remains identified for future work.
Supporting_Evidence: The discussion states “isolation was difficult, and column chromatography resulted in almost complete decomposition of the product” for 12 k (lines 124‑127).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: Electron‑rich aryl substrates (e.g., 3,4‑dimethoxyphenyl) degraded under batch reflux, giving low or no yields.
Solution_Description: Milder flow conditions (5 min residence, 125 °C) were employed, which prevented decomposition and afforded good isolated yields for these substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: The text reports “For compounds bearing an electron‑rich aryl ring, it was required to reoptimize … milder reaction conditions (5 min, 125 °C) gave good to high isolated yields” (lines 138‑144).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Baldwin Rearrangement Process and Its Comparison to Traditional Batch Mode
Problem_Description: Fluctuations in back‑pressure (6–8 bar) led to inconsistent yields during repeated experiments.
Solution_Description: A peristaltic pump was used as the back‑pressure regulator, fixing the pressure at 8 bar and delivering reproducible 83 % yields.
Supporting_Evidence: The manuscript notes “pressure fluctuated … To mitigate this … used a peristaltic pump … resulting in a reproducible yield of 83 %” (lines 96‑104).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Acid Hydrazides from Carboxylic Acids in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The initial attempts at continuous‑flow Fischer‑esterification using Amberlyst 15 and Amberlyst 36 ion‑exchange resins gave very low conversion, even at 120 °C with long residence times, producing little to no dimethyl ester.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The researchers switched to a homogeneous catalytic system (catalytic H₂SO₄ in methanol) which afforded the dimethyl ester in 93 % yield on a 5 g scale. To prevent clogging from precipitation during hydrazinolysis they submerged the tubing downstream of the back‑pressure regulator in a sonicating bath and increased the tubing internal diameter, or alternatively added a second heated coil that provided a controlled, step‑wise temperature drop (125 °C → 60 °C → rt). They also raised the overall flow rate and employed a staged temperature profile to keep the product in solution, reduced the equivalents of hydrazine hydrate from 10 eq to 6.4 eq, and replaced the T‑mixer with a Y‑mixer to avoid hydrazine‑sulfate precipitation at the mixing point.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Disappointingly, neither resin proved acceptable. Even at an elevated temperature of 120 °C and with extended residence times, little to no diester was obtained under relevant flow conditions" (Low Yield).

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: The traditional liquid–liquid extraction (LLE) workflow required scientists to prepare samples by hand, measure phase volumes with a ruler, and collect samples for LC analysis. This labor‑intensive process was time‑consuming and resource‑intensive, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: A fully automated LLE platform was built on a Tecan Freedom EVO200 equipped with liquid‑handling and vision‑guided cameras. The platform prepares up to 96 LLE samples, agitates, detects phase boundaries, and aliquots samples automatically, completing a 96‑sample screen in ~5 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The typical workflow involves a scientist preparing LLE samples by hand… The labor‑intensive and monotonous nature of this process has, at times, led to merely functional rather than fully optimized extraction processes.”
• “An automated, high‑throughput workflow was developed for liquid–liquid extraction optimization… The workflow was performed on a Tecan EVO200 platform… allowing rapid evaluation of up to 96 samples per experiment.”
• “The entire automated workflow for a standard 96‑sample LLE screen (i.e., 2 min agitation time and 15 min settling time per sample), excluding LC data collection, can be performed in only 5 h.”

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: During extraction of the biocatalytic cascade, protein and other hydrophilic impurities formed a rag‑layer that floated at the phase interface, preventing a clean phase split and impairing product recovery.
Solution_Description: Additive screening (commercial additive plates) identified polypropylene glycol (PPG 400/2000) and salting‑out agents (ammonium sulfate) that promoted protein settling and provided a clean interface. Optimal solvent ratios (2‑MeTHF/IPA) and appropriate salt loading (≈60 wt % NH₄SO₄) were selected to achieve an 80 %+ recovery with a clean split.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A considerable challenge associated with performing LLE in the presence of enzyme is the tendency for protein rag layer formation… obscuring an otherwise clean extraction interface.”
• “Across the two screens, the only set of conditions that yielded layer separation with a high‑quality interface involved the use of polypropylene glycol (PPG) 400.”
• “When 44 % v/v 2‑MeTHF/IPA was used … a high recovery yield of 80 % was obtained with 60 wt % ammonium sulfate.”
• “At lower concentrations of ammonium sulfate (0–15 wt %) a single miscible phase was observed … increasing to 30–60 wt % gave a clean phase split … raising beyond 60 wt % led to rag layer formation.”

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: The original workup used filtration of the heated reaction mixture through a Celite cake to remove enzyme, which caused up to 7 % product loss on the filter and exhibited slow, inconsistent filtration rates.
Solution_Description: The filtration step was replaced by a direct liquid‑liquid extraction using the optimized solvent/ salt system, eliminating the need for a Celite filter and increasing overall product recovery (up to 90 % on 50 mL scale).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Conditions identified for filtration resulted in product loss of up to 7 % on the Celite waste cake, as well as slow and/or variable filtration rates.”
• “To address process challenges associated with filtration, efforts were undertaken to develop a direct extraction that would enable both protein removal and efficient product recovery.”
• “A clean phase‑cut was performed to recover 90 % 5′‑isobutyryluridine after the first extraction… a 10 % increase in recovery yield was observed on 50 mL scale.”

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: In the nemtabrutinib biaryl‑ether workup, the product tended to partition into an undesired oil phase either during the aqueous workup or after cooling, compromising product morphology and purity.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening of water‑IPA ratios and cooling temperatures identified a solvent composition and temperature window that suppressed oil formation (no oil at 10 °C, oil only observed below 5 °C), enabling a clean phase split and homogeneous crystallization feed.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The starting material … was found to have a tendency to partition out of solution as an undesired oil phase during workup and crystallization.”
• “Higher IPA and lower water charges suppressed oil formation… The presence of the oil phase was hypothesized to be the root cause of poor crystallization performance.”
• “The centerpoint sample behaved as expected… the isolated organic layer did not form an oil layer on cooling to the target crystallization seed temperature of 10 °C, but instead remained a homogeneous solution as desired, eventually oiling out at 5 °C.”
• “Nearly half of the samples formed an oil layer either before the phase‑cut or after cooling… indicating that water and IPA content are the most important parameters responsible for oiling.”

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: Accurate identification of phase boundaries was difficult when both phases were colorless, leading to occasional mis‑classification of hits and failed samples.
Solution_Description: A TubeEyeX camera equipped with configurable pixel‑saturation and color‑range parameters was employed; when necessary, a colored dye was added to one phase to enhance contrast, enabling reliable automated detection of up to two phase boundaries.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Automated phase boundary detection proved less robust on samples containing colorless top and bottom phases, and in many cases, a colored dye… was used to impart a color difference in the aqueous phase.”
• “Through careful adjustment of parameters in the TubeEyeX software, including pixel saturation and color range, the camera was trained to recognize up to two phase boundaries for a biphasic solution.”
• “The camera was able to successfully distinguish these phase boundaries across a broad profile of solutions with varying colors and opacity.”

Paper Title: Vision-Guided Automation Platform for Liquid–Liquid Extraction and Workup Development
Problem_Description: The high volume of visual and quantitative data generated during HTE LLE screens required extensive manual processing, slowing down decision‑making.
Solution_Description: A custom Python script using the Dash library was created to automatically import LC data, merge it with phase‑volume information, and display an interactive heat‑map linking quantitative results with annotated images, dramatically accelerating data interpretation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “To streamline data processing, we designed an interactive heat map that allows for facile aggregation and visualization of both quantitative data and annotated photos.”
• “We have written a streamlined data processing protocol in Python… the script extracts processed LC data… calculates distribution coefficients… links each TubeEyeX image with its representative vial location.”
• “Python was leveraged to develop interactive tools for data visualization using Dash… providing the user with an interactive heat map which displays the extraction yield calculated from each ‘hit’ sample.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: The original early‑scale route generated intermediate 3 as a neat oil after concentration of the esterification reaction, making it difficult to handle and requiring a time‑consuming isolation step.
Solution_Description: The process was changed to use dimethyl carbonate (DMC) as both solvent and desiccant, allowing 3 to be obtained directly as a homogeneous solution that could be carried forward without an oil‑concentration step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The early clinical supply route … was shown … by treating acid 2 with thionyl chloride … the reaction was concentrated to an oil … This intermediate was then treated with phenol …”; “The esterification step employs unique conditions leveraging dimethyl carbonate as a dual‑function reagent, acting as both the solvent and the desiccant to drive the reaction forward.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Use of large excesses of hazardous thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) and methanol (20‑50 V) in the first esterification presented significant safety and cost concerns.
Solution_Description: The route was switched to a Fischer esterification catalyzed by catalytic H₂SO₄ with a reduced solvent volume (3‑5 V). Later, dimethyl carbonate was introduced to serve as both solvent and desiccant, further reducing the need for excess acid and solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Efforts quickly shifted from employing an excess of hazardous SOCl₂ and MeOH as solvents … to the implementation of Fischer esterification.”; “Early versions of the reaction employed catalytic H₂SO₄ and used a large excess of 20–50 L/kg (or volumes, V) of MeOH … to reduce solvent usage, a target of 3–5 V was more desirable.”; “Alternative desiccants … leading to the selection of dimethyl carbonate (DMC) for this purpose.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Reducing the esterification volume to 3 V caused the reaction to plateau at 91 % conversion; increasing H₂SO₄ to 150 mol % gave full conversion but quenching with carbonate base caused CO₂ off‑gassing and a substantial exotherm, raising impurity formation risk.
Solution_Description: DMC was used as a dual‑function solvent/desiccant, allowing only 50 mol % H₂SO₄ to achieve 99 % conversion and eliminating the high‑exotherm carbonate quench. The quench was later performed with a reverse addition of aqueous KHCO₃ after dilution with MTBE to better manage heat and off‑gassing.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reducing the volume of the esterification to 3 V was found to adversely impact the reaction, causing conversion to plateau at 91 % … At 150 mol % H₂SO₄ a reproducible 99 % conversion was achieved. However, quenching this large amount of acid introduced additional challenges. When a carbonate base was used for the quench, CO₂ off‑gassing and appreciable heat of neutralization were observed.”; “Dimethyl carbonate (DMC) … could be used to drive the reaction forward.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: In the SₙAr etherification step, water content strongly affected reaction rate and caused hydrolysis of both the product 4 and the ester 3, leading to inconsistent conversions and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: A water‑adjustment equation was developed to target ~2000 ppm (≈10 mol %) water in the reaction mixture, providing a balance between rate acceleration and minimal hydrolysis. Karl‑Fisher titration was used to verify and adjust water content prior to reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction profiles … demonstrated a rate dependence on the water content, wherein the time to reaction completion decreases with the increasing water content … increasing water content also caused increased hydrolysis of biaryl ether 4 … An optimal water loading was needed to balance the reaction rate and impurity generation.”; “To achieve the approximate desired reaction water content, eq 1 was developed …”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Biaryl ether 4 is highly soluble in both MeOH and heptane, causing significant product loss during the original cold crystallization (‑5 °C) from these solvents.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was redesigned to leave 4 dissolved in DMF, then water was used as an antisolvent. The solution was cooled to 10 °C, seeded, and later further diluted with water before final cooling to 5 °C, yielding a high‑yield crystalline solid with minimal loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “Improvements to the isolation of 4 were required due to the high solubility of the product in both MeOH and heptane, resulting in significant yield losses.”; “Instead, to crystallize 4, the wet DMF solution was cooled to 10 °C, seeded … water (3 V) was added … followed by cooling to 5 °C. This provided 4 as a highly crystalline solid.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: The original DMSO‑based work‑up after the etherification produced a complex triphasic mixture (heptane‑rich, water‑rich, and DMF‑rich layers), making phase separation difficult and risking product loss.
Solution_Description: The reaction was quenched with 0.5 mol % glacial acetic acid, followed by water addition and then 1.6 V IPA as a cosolvent, converting the system to a biphasic mixture that could be cleanly separated with <1 % product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of 0.5 mol equiv of glacial acetic acid … was found to neutralize the remaining K₃PO₄ while minimizing ester hydrolysis.”; “When water was charged to the quenched solution, three phases were observed … To address this challenge, the addition of 1.6 V IPA as a cosolvent afforded a biphasic mixture that could be separated with <1 % loss of product.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Biaryl ether 4 has a low melting onset (28–31 °C) and is non‑hygroscopic, causing balling and agglomeration during conventional heat‑vacuum drying (rotary evaporator), which prevented reliable water removal.
Solution_Description: A two‑stage drying strategy was implemented: first a nitrogen sweep in a vacuum filter pot to bring water content below 0.10 wt %, then gentle blending in a double‑cone rotary dryer. This avoided heating above the melting point, eliminated balling, and produced dry, free‑flowing powder.
Supporting_Evidence: “The low melting point … precluded the use of heat and vacuum to dry the wet cake.”; “An alternative drying strategy … using the filter dryer to apply a nitrogen sweep to convectively dry the cake … then blending the resultant 4 powder in the double‑cone rotary dryer.”; “Photos … showed agglomeration in a rotary evaporator … no balling occurred in the V‑blender … final LOD of 0.04 % after less than 2.5 h of drying under vacuum.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Use of DMSO with strong bases at elevated temperature raised safety concerns (autocatalytic decomposition, formation of toxic dimethyl sulfate) and cost issues due to the need for bulky equipment and handling precautions.
Solution_Description: The etherification step was moved to DMF with K₃PO₄ as the base, eliminating DMSO and its associated hazards while using a cheaper, readily available base.
Supporting_Evidence: “With the goal of avoiding the safety concerns associated with combining the base with DMSO at elevated temperatures … efforts to optimize … began with high‑throughput screening of solvent and base combinations.”; “The combination of K₃PO₄ in DMF was effective …”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process Development for the Biaryl Ether Fragment of Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026)
Problem_Description: Sodium phenoxide and 1,3‑dimethyl‑2‑imidazolidinone (DMI) identified as effective reagents in early screening, but they are expensive and of limited supply at scale.
Solution_Description: K₃PO₄ was selected as a cost‑effective, commercially available base, and DMF was retained as the solvent, providing comparable yields without the expensive reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sodium phenoxide (NaOPh) was promising … but it was found to be prohibitively expensive and of limited supply at the required scale … The combination of 1,3‑dimethyl‑2‑imidazolidinone (DMI) and K₃PO₄ was also effective. However, DMI was also determined to be cost‑prohibitive.”; “Subsequent optimization focused on employing K₃PO₄ as the base in DMF.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: DCQ is a solid and HNDA is a viscous oil, leading to a heterogeneous reaction mixture that is difficult to stir homogeneously on scale; the mixture also showed irreproducibility because the solid DCQ sublimated at temperatures above ~90 °C and accumulated in the head‑space of the reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a liquid co‑solvent (initially i‑PrOH, later dimethyl‑sulfoxide, DMSO) that dissolves both reagents, giving a homogeneous medium.  Reactions were carried out in tightly sealed Schlenk tubes, preventing loss of DCQ by sublimation and assuring consistent mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “Actually, DCQ is a solid and HNDA is a viscous oil; they are not well‑mixed homogeneously in each other, which in turn results in difficulty in an industrial‑scale process.”; “We noticed that sublimates of DCQ accumulated in the upper part of the Schlenk tube, the reaction vessel, at temperatures above ca. 90 °C.”; “A white crystalline product precipitated after a short time … the substitution product 16·HCl … was obtained … at 90 °C … strongly explains the discrepancies …”; “The reaction in i‑PrOH … gave higher yields …”; “DMSO appeared to be superior … to the others.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: High temperatures (≥130 °C) and long reaction times (up to 42 h) were required to obtain acceptable conversion; extending the time increased by‑product formation, making purification of the API difficult and causing irreproducible yields.
Solution_Description: The optimal DMSO loading (1.0 equiv relative to DCQ) and a fixed temperature of 130 °C were identified, giving 99 % conversion in 18 h with 93 % selectivity.  Kinetic profiling was used to stop the reaction at the point of maximum selectivity, avoiding impurity buildup.
Supporting_Evidence: “At least, 130 °C was needed to get ca. 64 % yield after 18 h … Extending the reaction time (up to 42 h) furnished slightly higher yields (ca. 75 % y), but also caused an increase in by‑products that made purification… more difficult.”; “An excess amount of DMSO (ca. >1.00 equiv…) resulted in a decrease in the reaction yield… 1.00 equiv … afforded 99 % conversion and 92 % yield.”; “Kinetic profile … also point out some decrease in selectivity with respect to time.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: DCQ sublimated during heating, causing loss of material and inconsistent conversion; the loss also raised safety concerns because the solid could deposit on reactor walls or vent lines at elevated temperature.
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed in tightly sealed Schlenk tubes (or sealed reactors) that retained both the solid and any volatile solvent, preventing sublimation and ensuring reproducible yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “We noticed that sublimates of DCQ accumulated in the upper part of the Schlenk tube … This might be the main factor that hinders achieving high yields under neat conditions. Apparently, this phenomenon also necessitates design of special reactors for larger‑scale productions of HCQ.”; “These reactions were carried out in tightly sealed Schlenk tubes to ensure that the solvents were retained in the reaction vessel.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: Historical processes required 2–3 equiv of phenol as a catalyst, increasing reagent cost and waste while still giving only modest yields.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount of 3,5‑bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol (F‑phenol) was identified as the most active phenol catalyst (40–50 mol %) and gave high conversions and yields (up to 98 % isolated) at 120–130 °C, converting the process to a truly catalytic route and reducing reagent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: “Among the phenols tested (5–9), 3,5‑bis­(trifluoromethyl)­phenol (F‑phenol, 9) exhibited the highest catalytic activity …”; “A catalytic amount of 3,5‑bis­(trifluoromethyl)­phenol (50–40 mol %) was found to be effective … delivering the corresponding aminopyridines in yields up to 98 %.”; “We thus transformed an overstoichiometric process into a catalytic one.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: Certain amines (e.g., cyclohexylamine, propargylamine) gave very low yields under the standard DMSO‑promoted or F‑phenol‑catalyzed conditions, even after long reaction times.
Solution_Description: For the recalcitrant amines the reaction temperature was raised to 160 °C and, where applicable, the catalyst loading increased to 100 mol % (F‑phenol), which improved the yields (e.g., cyclohexylamine → 48 % at 160 °C, 100 mol % F‑phenol).
Supporting_Evidence: “Cyclohexylamine … did not give rise to formation of the desired product … even in the presence of 1.00 equiv of DMSO. Indeed, even in the presence 100 mol % of F‑phenol as the catalyst, the reaction temperature had to be raised to 160 °C … to obtain the desired product 20c in a reasonable yield (48 %).”; “Propargylamine … 18 h at 120 °C with 50 mol % F‑phenol gave 63 % yield … DMSO provided only 29 % after 40 h.”

Paper Title: High-Yielding Process for the Synthesis of Hydroxychloroquine under Concentrated Conditions: Nucleophilic Amination of Chloropyridines Promoted by Dimethyl Sulfoxide or Catalyzed by 3,5-Bis(trifluoromethyl)phenol
Problem_Description: Prolonged heating led to accumulation of by‑products that complicated API‑quality isolation, which must be performed by extraction/crystallisation rather than chromatography.
Solution_Description: A kinetic study was performed to define the optimal reaction time (≈18 h) that maximized conversion while minimizing impurity formation; the work‑up was adjusted (qNMR monitoring, pH adjustments) to enable efficient extraction and crystallisation of the product.
Supporting_Evidence: “In some cases, prolonged reaction times … result in increase in the concomitant formation of impurities. This makes isolation of the product in API‑quality more and more difficult … monitoring reaction progresses … is of particular importance … kinetic profile … also point out some decrease in selectivity with respect to time.”; “The kinetic profile … was also studied … while showing a selective conversion …”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Process for Lifitegrast
Problem_Description: During the first amide‑bond formation of acid 5 with amine 7, the moisture‑sensitive acid‑chloride of 5 hydrolysed, generating significant amounts of the starting acid (5) and reducing the isolated yield of the desired product 8.
Solution_Description: The researchers replaced the moisture‑sensitive acid‑chloride route with an EDC/HOBt coupling using a stoichiometric amount of HOBt.  In addition, they discovered that adding HOBt first and then EDC (reversing the order of addition) suppressed formation of the N‑acyl‑urea impurity (14) and gave >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A major challenge observed was the significant formation of 5 during amide coupling due to the moisture sensitivity of the acid chloride of 5." (p. 3)

Paper Title: Practical Synthetic Method for Amino Acid-Derived Diazoketones Shelf-Stable Reagents for Organic Synthesis
Problem_Description: Diazomethane is highly toxic and explosive (ΔH_decomp ≈ –5450 kJ kg⁻¹, comparable to RDX). Its danger limits both availability and utility of α‑amino‑acid‑derived diazoketones (AADDKs) on any scale.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow ‘dry‑diazomethane’ platform was developed: MNU is decomposed in a biphasic alkaline solution, the organic CH₂N₂ layer is immediately separated by a hydrophobic membrane and fed to the downstream synthesis. Flow recirculation and precise stoichiometric feeding control the exotherm and avoid accumulation of free CH₂N₂.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the high toxicity and explosiveness of CH₂N₂ strongly limit both the availability and utility of the AADDKs …” (intro, lines 41‑44); “The productivity of the system reached up to 90 g of CH₂N₂ per hour (2.1 mol h⁻¹)… all of the above setups have provided a water solution of CH₂N₂ … suitable only for water‑tolerant reactions.” (intro, lines 56‑65); “Herein we report a continuous flow‑based approach to the generation of ‘dry’ CH₂N₂ with productivity up to 0.45 mol h⁻¹…” (intro, lines 73‑77).

Supporting_Evidence: “MNNG is known for its high carcinogenicity… ten times more mutagenic than MNU… which had been confirmed on mammalian embryos.” (sec 2.1, lines 112‑119); “The transformation of MNU occurred almost instantaneously in this temperature range, whereas Diazald had to be discarded… as it required a higher temperature for decomposition.” (sec 2.1, lines 102‑108).

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development
Problem_Description: Liquid bromine (Br₂) is highly toxic, corrosive and difficult to handle safely on large scale, and its use drove up material cost and operational risk.
Solution_Description: The bromination reagent was replaced with crystalline pyridinium tribromide (pyHBr₃), a safer solid bromine source that can be handled without the hazards associated with liquid Br₂ while delivering comparable conversion and yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Due to its high toxicity and corrosiveness, liquid Br₂ is a cause of serious safety concerns and difficult to handle in large‑scale organic synthesis" (p. 5). 
• "Crystalline pyridinium tribromide … was used for the optimization of alkenyl bromide 6 preparation as a preferred and safer bromination reagent" (p. 5).

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development
Problem_Description: Potassium tert‑butoxide in tert‑butanol (KOtBu/t‑BuOH) is only sold as a dilute solution in THF, a peroxidizable solvent, and is not available in the large quantities required for kilogram‑scale synthesis.

Problem_Description: Aqueous washing after bromination removed pyridinium salts but caused significant product loss and side‑reactions, reducing the overall isolated yield of the alkenyl bromide intermediate.

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development
Problem_Description: The original synthesis employed 20 mol % Pd catalyst for both borylation and Suzuki coupling, resulting in high metal cost and downstream impurity removal challenges.

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development
Problem_Description: The cyclization step originally required 25 equiv of H₂SO₄ and 50 equiv of base, generating a highly exothermic neutralization step that posed safety risks and prolonged reaction time.

Paper Title: Building a Quaternary Stereogenic Center on Dihydroazaindole Carboxylic Acid through Scalable Process Development
Problem_Description: Direct isolation of brominated product 4‑a after bromination in THF resulted in significant product loss to the mother liquor during crystallization and filtration.

Problem_Description: When the aqueous thiosulfate treatment was used after bromination, the alkenyl bromide intermediate decomposed to undesired side‑products, drastically lowering the yield.

Problem_Description: The commercial starting material 4 required a long lead time (6–8 weeks) and was expensive, impacting overall process economics.

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Grignard Reaction to Manufacture a Key Intermediate of Ipatasertib
Problem_Description: The batch Grignard step that converts nitrile 2 to ketone 3 suffered from a modest 61 % isolated yield and required a 6–9 h addition time.  The unstable magnesium chelate intermediate 2b decomposed under the reaction conditions, and the highly exothermic Br/Mg exchange (ΔH ≈ ‑256 kJ·mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad ≈ 73 °C) created safety and heat‑removal concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow cascade of CSTRs was implemented.  The reactors provide excellent heat removal (IT ≈ 27.5 °C) and short residence times (≈15 min per tank) that prevent degradation of 2b and limit the temperature rise.  Back‑mixed CSTRs give uniform concentration profiles and high mass‑transfer efficiency, delivering ≥ 80 % overall yield with consistent quality.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “a modest overall yield of about 61 % was achieved in classical batch mode operation.”
• “The internal temperature (IT) for this one‑pot procedure was defined as +7.5 °C … with an addition time of about 6–9 h at the intended commercial scale.”
• “RC1 calorimetry experiments … revealed a dose‑controlled Grignard reaction with an enthalpy of reaction (ΔH) of ‑256 kJ·mol⁻¹ with a total adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad) of 73 °C.”
• “The cascade of CSTRs can manage a degree of heterogeneity … the residence time distribution (RTD) would require characterization, but … operate on the order of minutes rather than hours (in batch).”
• “Conversions by HPLC were found to be about 75 % in CSTR1, about 95 % in CSTR2, and > 98 % in CSTR3 … the yield increase from 61 % in large‑scale batch mode to approximately 80 % in continuous mode.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Grignard Reaction to Manufacture a Key Intermediate of Ipatasertib
Problem_Description: Early laboratory‑scale flow experiments showed only ~50 % conversion of 2 and significant formation of impurity 6 (1–5 %) and desbrominated impurity 5 (1–10 %).  The poor performance was traced to local concentration “hot spots” at the mixing point and to an insufficiently controlled feed strategy.
Solution_Description: The dosing strategy was revised: i‑PrMgCl was split into two separate feeds (0.96 equiv in CSTR 1 and 0.30 equiv in CSTR 2) to keep the local Grignard concentration low, and the feed ratio was kept constant at the mixing point.  The solvent system was changed to a MeTHF/toluene mixture, which moderated the reaction rate and suppressed impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In every case, we observed incomplete conversion of 2 (∼50 %) and significant formation of 6 (1–5 %) accompanied by desbrominated compound 5 (1–10 %).”
• “The most obvious differences … are (a) dosing mode, (b) concentration profiles … and (c) local concentration and dilution effects.”
• “We hypothesized a bimolecular reaction … To establish evidence … we conducted two batch experiments … experiment 2 … the yield of 6 rose to 5.7 area % … we concluded that a low concentration of the Grignard reagent is essential to mitigate the formation of 6.”
• “A breakthrough was made using i‑PrMgBr in a mixture of MeTHF and toluene … While the formation of 6 was dramatically reduced … we also observed precipitation of the intermediate Mg chelate 2b …”.
• “In flow mode the two feeds ( 2 and i‑PrMgCl) are dosed in parallel, and the stoichiometric ratio at the mixing point is constant.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Grignard Reaction to Manufacture a Key Intermediate of Ipatasertib
Problem_Description: When i‑PrMgBr was employed in MeTHF/toluene, the magnesium chelate intermediate 2b precipitated, raising concerns about possible reactor clogging in the flow system.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The solvent mixture (MeTHF/toluene) was deliberately chosen to induce controlled precipitation of 2b, which actually protected the intermediate from over‑reaction.  The CSTR cascade with overflow junctions and a recirculation loop was shown to handle the solid/liquid suspension without clogging, and intensive mixing in the tanks prevented mass‑transfer limitations.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “While the formation of 6 was dramatically reduced, we also observed precipitation of the intermediate Mg chelate 2b in this less polar solvent combination MeTHF/toluene.  It is usually undesirable to produce solids due to potential clogging issues in a flow process.  In this case, deliberate precipitation of 2b protects the intermediate against degradation and consecutive overreaction, further mitigating the formation of compound 6.”
• “Based on the above‑mentioned attributes, we chose a series of continuous stirred tank reactors (CSTRs) with overflow junctions … The passage time for the reaction mixture through the insulated transfer lines … was on the order of seconds, and clogging was not observed, in part due to the physical nature of the solids in this system.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Grignard Reaction to Manufacture a Key Intermediate of Ipatasertib
Problem_Description: The aqueous acidic hydrolysis of 2b (5 wt % NaHSO₄, pH 2) is a highly exothermic process (ΔH ≈ ‑253 kJ·mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad ≈ 19 °C) that generates a biphasic mixture which is unstable and cannot be held for long; uncontrolled temperature or pH leads to impurity formation and yield loss.
Solution_Description: A fourth CSTR (CSTR 4) was dedicated to the hydrolysis step, operated at 15 °C with a mean residence time of ~5 min.  The pH was kept at the target of 2.0 by a dose‑controlled feedback loop that adjusted NaHSO₄ addition, providing rapid heat removal and stable reaction conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The stream exiting CSTR3 was a suspension, so we opted for a fourth CSTR … to carry out the aqueous hydrolysis reaction in a continuous manner.”
• “The ΔrH value of ‑253 kJ·mol⁻¹ and the ΔT_ad value of 19 °C require excellent heat dissipation capabilities.”
• “The acidic biphasic mixture proved to be unstable and not a suitable hold point; therefore, timely neutralization was important to minimize formation of undesired impurities, color formation, and yield loss.”
• “Active process control was employed to manage the pH adjustments by controlling the addition of acid … Using the pH reading of the emulsion, we could operate with only minor fluctuation around the set point.”
• “Experimental work showed the desired internal temperature of CSTR4 to be IT = 15 °C with a mean residence time of ∼5 min.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Grignard Reaction to Manufacture a Key Intermediate of Ipatasertib
Problem_Description: Accurate pH adjustment during the neutralization step (pH 4.8) is critical; the titration curve shows an inflection around pH 5–6, making fixed‑volume dosing prone to drift and causing color or impurity issues.
Solution_Description: A dose‑controlled feedback loop was implemented for the addition of 2 M NaOH, allowing real‑time pH monitoring and adjustment.  This ensured the product stayed in the organic phase and avoided over‑ or under‑neutralization.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The titration curve … indicates an inflection point around pH 5–6, which poses a challenge for an accurate pH adjustment. Hence, the pH adjustment is dose‑controlled by a feedback control loop (rather than a fixed volume stream) using aqueous NaOH (2 M).”
• “Using the pH reading in the biphasic mixture was found to provide steady values.”
• “At pH ≥ 7, the product proved to be unstable … at pH ≤ 4, product loss to the aqueous layer became evident.”
• “The pH adjustment and imine 2b hydrolysis reaction were dose‑controlled … the ΔrH value … require excellent heat dissipation capabilities.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Oxidation of Alcohols Using TEMPO/NaOCl for the Selective and Scalable Synthesis of Aldehydes

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of an Efficient, Scalable Process to Generate the Western Fragment
Problem_Description: When the lithium carboxylate (10·Li) was generated on scale the slurry formed after LiOH addition would suddenly thicken and stagnate, giving a non‑uniform, shear‑thinning mixture that caused erratic potencies (85.6–94.7 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mixing speed was increased, the addition of LiOH was performed in smaller portions at elevated temperature, and the order of operations was changed (THF/H₂O dissolve 3, then add LiOH in a separate vessel) to generate a seed bed and avoid supersaturation. Temperature ramps and controlled cooling were introduced to improve crystal growth and slurry mobility.
Supporting_Evidence:
The initial process used to generate 10·Li, while operationally simple, was not suitable for scale. When scaled to 1 L in the laboratory, the slurry formed upon the addition of LiOH (and the precipitation of 10·Li) would occasionally thicken suddenly, resulting in stagnation. 
Increasing the mixing speed and stirring for a longer period of time led to a mobile slurry. 
The non‑uniform mixing behavior and stagnation effects observed in this process were a direct result of the shear‑thinning properties of mixtures that emulate non‑Newtonian fluids. 
The addition of 3 to LiOH at an elevated temperature and in smaller portions permitted us to avoid gross supersaturation and allowed a seed bed to form. 
Modeling of mixing in laboratory and manufacturing vessels to ensure sufficient agitation (taking into account the diameter and volume in the vessel) was undertaken to enable the successful operation of the process at varying scales.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of an Efficient, Scalable Process to Generate the Western Fragment
Problem_Description: Lithium‑carboxylate 10·Li was highly hygroscopic, absorbed up to 100 % water, contained LiCl contamination, and had an extremely low bulk density (0.09–0.35 g cm⁻³), making storage, handling and addition to subsequent reactors difficult.
Solution_Description: The salt‑break step was moved to a separate operation: 3 was first treated with TEA in THF/H₂O, the aqueous phase (containing LiCl) was removed, and the organic phase was subsequently hydrolysed and converted to the lithium salt. This eliminated LiCl carry‑over and reduced water uptake.
Supporting_Evidence: To address LiCl contamination and slurry mobility concerns, the process was revised to perform the salt break step in a separate operation. Starting material 3 was first dissolved in THF and water (4:1), and then triethylamine was charged. The aqueous phase was discarded, and the organic phase was transferred to a new reactor for hydrolysis and Li salt formation. With this process, the potency was improved, and the isolated solids exhibited less water uptake.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of an Efficient, Scalable Process to Generate the Western Fragment
Problem_Description: During the amidation of 12 with 10·Li, the presence of water (1–5 %) lowered the isolated yield and increased the formation of the undesired tert‑butyl epimer (13).
Solution_Description: A design‑of‑experiments study varied water content, TsCl equivalents, DMAP loading and temperature. It showed that lower water, lower temperature and higher DMAP gave the best conversion and minimal epimer formation; the optimum conditions were then fixed for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: Results from spiking studies in which 1 or 5 % water was introduced into the reaction revealed a decrease in yield and higher epimer formation. Higher percentages of water, high temperatures, and lower levels of DMAP all had a negative impact on conversion and epimer levels. The amount of TsCl was inconsequential across the range studied.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of an Efficient, Scalable Process to Generate the Western Fragment
Problem_Description: Isolation of the amidated product 7 directly from THF was difficult because the reaction mixture formed an extremely thick slurry that was hard to mix, and solvent exchange to iPrOAc caused gumming and product loss during the water wash.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was changed to a two‑step aqueous citric‑acid quench followed by solvent exchange to iPrOAc, a second water wash to remove inorganic residues, and finally precipitation of 7 as an iPrOAc‑heptane solvate. This avoided the thick THF slurry and eliminated gumming.
Supporting_Evidence: Isolation of the reaction product directly from THF proved to be challenging. A crystallization of the iPrOAc solvate of 7 was developed and would require a solvent exchange from THF to iPrOAc. While performing the entire process in iPrOAc would have been preferable, the reaction generated an extremely thick slurry that was challenging to mix effectively. Initial attempts to perform solvent exchange and crystallization led to gumming of the solids, presumably due to the carryover of inorganic byproducts. A second water wash that was introduced following the partial displacement of THF with iPrOAc eliminated this problem.

Solution_Description: Stirring rates were increased, reaction times extended, and a minimum of two successive in‑process‑control samples were required before the batch could be forwarded, ensuring full conversion.

The immediate problem was resolved by instituting longer reaction stir times, increasing stir rates, and mandating at least two successive in‑process‑control (IPC) sample passes before a batch was moved forward.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of Magnesium Sulfate-Mediated Aminolysis for the Manufacture of the Eastern Fragment
Problem_Description: The first‑generation aminolysis of 12·TsOH required a protecting group, 20‑60 equiv of ammonia and a prolonged 48‑60 h reaction time to reach acceptable conversion. 6·HCl has low solubility in most organic solvents, leading to uncontrolled precipitation, formation of agglomerates, high residual isopropanol (3‑5 wt %), and assay values as low as 87 wt % which posed safety risks during handling and storage.
Solution_Description: MgSO4 was introduced as a cheap, widely‑available Lewis acid to accelerate the aminolysis and suppress impurity formation, eliminating the need for a protecting group and reducing the required ammonia equivalents to ~10 equiv.  This shortened the reaction to ~11 h and gave higher conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “MgSO₄, a material that is widely available at low cost, could be used to accelerate the desired aminolysis of 12·TsOH without the need for a large amount of ammonia and could suppress the formation of impurities without introducing a protecting group.”; “The mixture was stirred at 13 °C for 11–13 h… 7 M solution of NH₃ in MeOH (10.3 equiv) was then added.”; “Even with protection, excess ammonia (20–60 equiv) and a prolonged reaction time (48–60 h) were required… low solubility of 6·HCl… resulted in uncontrolled precipitation… generated materials with assays as low as 87 wt %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of Magnesium Sulfate-Mediated Aminolysis for the Manufacture of the Eastern Fragment
Problem_Description: Removal of magnesium salts (MgCl₂, CaCl₂) generated by the Lewis‑acid catalyzed aminolysis was difficult because they share similar solubility with 6·HCl, compromising purification and causing loss of material.
Solution_Description: A solvent system based on DMF was employed after filtration to dissolve the reaction mixture; subsequent addition of HCl in IPA crystallized 6·HCl while the magnesium salts remained insoluble and were removed by filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: “Based on the solubilities of the reaction components… we determined that dimethylformamide (DMF) would be suitable for purging stoichiometric byproducts including magnesium chloride and p‑toluenesulfonic acid while facilitating high recovery.”; “Reactions performed in the presence of MgSO₄ resulted in a clean profile… The addition of HCl in IPA resulted in the crystallization of 6·HCl. The subsequent addition of DCM as an antisolvent resulted in additional crystallization and increased product recovery.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of Magnesium Sulfate-Mediated Aminolysis for the Manufacture of the Eastern Fragment
Problem_Description: The DMF/DCF isolation route left residual DMF (1.2–3.5 wt %) and required the chlorinated solvent DCM as an antisolvent, which is undesirable for safety and environmental reasons.
Solution_Description: A new isolation protocol using methanol, water, and isopropanol (IPA) as antisolvent was developed. This mixture gave higher potency, lower residual solvents, and eliminated the need for DCM.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Nirmatrelvir: Development of Magnesium Sulfate-Mediated Aminolysis for the Manufacture of the Eastern Fragment
Problem_Description: 6·HCl isomerizes to impurity 15 during solvent exchange (especially methanol → DMF) and at higher temperatures, reducing yield and causing batch‑to‑batch variability.

Supporting_Evidence: “Reducing the hold time after the addition of HCl in IPA resulted in an improved yield and reduced impurity formation… a process temperature of 10 °C offered the most favorable balance between yield (85 %) and product potency and purity.”; “The rate of isomerization increased at higher temperatures… we needed to maintain the temperature of the solution at ≤25 °C during the operations.”

Paper Title: Scaling-up Electroorganic Synthesis Using a Spinning Electrode Electrochemical Reactor in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: Parallel‑plate flow electrolysis cells require fully homogeneous reaction mixtures.  Solids in the feed clog the narrow electrode gap, and the generation of large volumes of H₂ gas at the cathode creates a safety hazard and reduces the effective reactor volume.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A spinning‑cylinder electrode was introduced (new reactor concept).  The rotating inner electrode provides intense bulk mixing, prevents particle deposition and quickly detaches gas bubbles, eliminating clogging and allowing safe operation with an inert‑gas blanket.
Supporting_Evidence: • “(1) … the presence of solids in the reaction mixture should be avoided to prevent clogging … (2) … most electrochemical reactions release gases … Gas evolution is a significant issue … (3) … low flow rates … undermine the mass‑transport properties” (Introduction). • “The efficient mixing … should also enable working with solid suspensions without the risk of clogging … the fact that the central electrode is spinning should provoke rapid detachment of any gas bubbles … effectively overcoming the issues of gas evolution” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Scaling-up Electroorganic Synthesis Using a Spinning Electrode Electrochemical Reactor in Batch and Flow Mode
