Paper Title: Balancing Yield, Purity, and Form: Finding the Sweet Spot for the Rework of the First Clinical Batch of Giredestrant (GDC-9545)
Problem_Description: Acid‑catalysed opening of the azetidine ring generated API‑related oligomers (6.4 wt % by SEC), causing the first GMP batch to fail potency and impurity specifications and reducing overall product recovery.
Solution_Description: Reslurrying the batch in acetone/water mixtures (≥95 v/v % acetone) removed oligomers (down to 1.1 wt % in the final material) while preserving the anhydrous Form I; the solvent composition also limited solvate formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The initial oligomer content was determined by size exclusion chromatography (SEC) to be 6.4 wt %…" 
• "Mass spectrometric analysis… revealed the presence of three major types of API‑related oligomers generated from the opening of the azetidine ring…" 
• "Initial analytical data showed a substantial reduction in oligomer content (by an average of ~5 wt %) upon reslurrying the batch in acetone/water mixtures." 
• "Reslurry using acetone/water (at compositions ≥95/5 v/v) was deemed suitable for use as reslurry solvents." 
• "Final oligomer content of 1.1 % (determined by SEC) and a slightly lower yield of 53 %…"

Paper Title: Balancing Yield, Purity, and Form: Finding the Sweet Spot for the Rework of the First Clinical Batch of Giredestrant (GDC-9545)
Problem_Description: During rework, Form I converted partially or completely to undesired solid forms (Form III acetone solvate, Form IV hydrate, or metastable Form II), leading to inconsistent polymorph outcomes, lower yields and risk of impurity formation.
Solution_Description: A solvent‑composition window (≥95 v/v % acetone, 94:6 v/v for the final protocol) was selected to limit conversion to Form III; a two‑step slurry (acetone/water followed by a short ethanol slurry) was introduced to reconvert any Form III back to Form I, and controlled cooling (−30 °C) was used to promote complete conversion to the desired polymorph.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Form I partially converts to Form IV (hydrate) in 90/10 v/v acetone/water… At compositions ≥95/5 v/v acetone/water, Form I completely converts to Form III (acetone solvate)." 
• "Formation of a mixture of Forms I and II… Form II is the metastable polymorphic form… conversion slow." 
• "There appeared to be a strong likelihood of partial or complete conversion of Form I to Form III during rework." 
• "Reslurry using acetone/water (≥95/5 v/v) was deemed suitable…" 
• "A second slurry in ethanol was proposed to aid form control… Trial ethanol reslurry experiments typically produced a Form I yield of >95 wt %." 
• "The final conditions adopted… acetone/water (94:6 v/v, 5 vol at 50 °C for 2 h), then cooled to 20 °C and held for 12 h…"

Paper Title: Balancing Yield, Purity, and Form: Finding the Sweet Spot for the Rework of the First Clinical Batch of Giredestrant (GDC-9545)

Solution_Description: A new strategy – a salt‑break followed by crystallization of the free base and subsequent salt re‑formation – was adopted, providing a robust pathway to obtain pure Form I with acceptable yield and particle‑size distribution.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A single solvent cooling recrystallization step … led to the formation of mixtures of Forms I and II/IV/V… deemed unsuitable." 
• "Finally, a salt break followed by crystallization followed by salt reformation was adopted as the best path forward to preserve the solid form and obtain the desired yield…"

Paper Title: Flow Photo-on-Demand Synthesis of Vilsmeier Reagent and Acyl Chlorides from Chloroform and Its Applications to Continuous Flow Synthesis of Carbonyl Compounds
Problem_Description: Phosgene (COCl₂) is a highly toxic gas and the Vilsmeier reagent (VR) generated from DMF is extremely unstable in air, rapidly decomposing back to DMF and HCl when exposed to moisture.
Solution_Description: The authors devised a continuous‑flow photochemical oxidation of chloroform (CHCl₃) that generates COCl₂ on‑demand inside a sealed quartz‑tube reactor, allowing immediate consumption of the toxic gas in situ and avoiding isolation of the unstable VR.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "COCl₂ is a gaseous compound with extremely high toxicity, which imposes a safety risk." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Polymorphs, Particle Size, and a Pandemic: Development of a Scalable Crystallization Process for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The original distillative crystallization process relied on variable distillation rates and temperatures, which could not be precisely controlled across different scales and manufacturing sites. This lack of control caused uncontrolled self‑seeding, leading to large batch‑to‑batch variability in API particle‑size distribution, morphology and impurity rejection.
Solution_Description: A defined seeding point was introduced after pausing the distillation at 6 batch volumes, followed by a controlled addition of dry ethyl acetate (EtOAc) and a heat‑cool cycle to dissolve any premature nuclei. This created a reproducible supersaturation ratio (≈1.2) at the seed point and allowed a controlled 6 h EtOAc addition to drive crystal growth.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Only the batch temperature and maximum jacket temperature can be specified. As this is the least controlled portion of the crystallization due to the combination of variable distillation conditions and high supersaturation, it is undesirable, but also very likely, for self‑seeding of the batch to occur during the distillation cycles.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “This can lead to substantial variation in API physical attributes (PSD, morphology, etc.) between vendors and between batches.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “To consistently reach this target seed point, we chose to pause the distillative crystallization once the batch volume is reduced to 6 volumes and proceed with a solvent charge of 2 volumes of dry EtOAc, after which the seed is added.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “We also added a heat and cool cycle immediately before seeding, so any batches that had spontaneously nucleated during the concentration step would fully dissolve prior to the intended seed point.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “By introducing a reliable seed point to the process, as well as a controlled 6 h EtOAc addition … we gave more consistency … of resulting API physical attributes.” (Sec 3.2)

Paper Title: Polymorphs, Particle Size, and a Pandemic: Development of a Scalable Crystallization Process for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: Because the original crystallization relied on repeated distillation/addition steps, the timing and rate of EtOAc addition were inconsistent, producing a wide range of particle‑size distributions (D50 ≈ 20‑137 µm) across vendors and scales.
Solution_Description: After seeding, EtOAc is added in a single, controlled charge of 4 L kg⁻¹ over 6 h with defined mass, temperature and rate, replacing the variable multi‑step distillation/addition sequence. This standardizes the desupersaturation profile and narrows PSD variability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Only the batch temperature and maximum jacket temperature can be specified… leading to an uncontrolled distillation portion… self‑seeding …” (Sec 3.2)  
• “The overall wt % water content of the main batch decreases gradually, driving the product to crystallize and grow on the seed bed.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “To consistently reach this target seed point, we chose to pause the distillative crystallization … and proceed with a solvent charge of 2 volumes of dry EtOAc, after which the seed is added … then an additional charge of 4 L kg⁻¹ EtOAc was added over 6 h.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “The improvements in the consistency of PSD are visible … via the narrowing of the D50 variability when comparing the final commercial batches that utilized the updated crystallization to the early clinical batches.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “The controlled EtOAc addition, the total mass of EtOAc charged, charge rate, batch temperature, and total charge time can be specified.” (Sec 3.2)

Paper Title: Polymorphs, Particle Size, and a Pandemic: Development of a Scalable Crystallization Process for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: During commercial validation a low‑probability stochastic event generated 10‑30 % of the metastable Form 2 polymorph in otherwise Form 1 API, raising concern about potential impact on drug‑product quality.
Solution_Description: A parallel reverse‑addition crystallization using a large Form 1 seed bed and dry EtOAc was explored, but the team elected to keep the simpler, higher‑throughput process because comprehensive derisking demonstrated that any mixture of Form 1 and Form 2 meets the ICH Q6A decision‑tree criteria and does not affect product performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Two separate batches … yielded a mixture of Form 1 and Form 2 … the batches were composed of predominantly Form 1 with ∼10–30 % Form 2.” (Sec 3.5)  
• “Despite the occurrence of these unlikely events, our thorough derisking of form control ensured that API with a mixture of polymorphs would not negatively impact drug product quality and performance.” (Sec 3.5)  
• “An alternative crystallization process was also examined … However, once both crystal forms had been derisked the team chose the simpler more productive process over the increased complexity in setup and seed load.” (Sec 3.5)  
• “The ICH decision tree provides guidance that no acceptance criterion for crystal form is needed if multiple polymorphs are identified but have similar properties including solubility, stability, and melting point.” (Sec 3.3)  
• “Thus, we were able to demonstrate that the API’s physical attributes did not affect the drug product’s critical quality attributes …” (Sec 3.5)

Paper Title: Polymorphs, Particle Size, and a Pandemic: Development of a Scalable Crystallization Process for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: Generating API enriched in the metastable Form 2 at laboratory scale proved difficult; conventional reverse addition of warm acetone into cold heptane failed to maintain the required high supersaturation, especially when scaled to 100 L.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A rotor‑stator wet‑mill (Quadro) co‑feed strategy was employed, delivering the warm acetone/API solution and heptane simultaneously into the mill head at 70 m s⁻¹ tip speed. This created high local supersaturation and rapid mixing, enabling 30‑40 % Form 2 at 100 L scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In theory, metastable Form 2 could only be generated under extremely high supersaturation. However … the final API isolated … was always observed as Form 1.” (Sec 3.4)  
• “The only three methods that were successful … (3) a continuous cofeed process where fresh 20 °C n‑heptane and warm 52 °C acetone/API solution are simultaneously co‑fed via primary and secondary inlets directly into the head of a Quadro rotor‑stator wet mill operating at 70 m s⁻¹ tip speed … was the most effective method at 100 L scale.” (Sec 3.4)  
• “The rapid manual reverse addition method failed to maintain high enough supersaturation at the 100 L scale … the API/acetone solution was charged above the surface … allowed for initial nucleation of Form 1 at lower supersaturations due to relatively poor meso‑mixing.” (Sec 3.4)  
• “By performing the reverse addition in the well‑mixed Quadro mill, API enriched in 30–40 % Form 2 was successfully prepared at 100 L scale.” (Sec 3.4)  
• “The setup utilizing a cofeed addition … was used to maintain high local supersaturation and rapid mixing … the most effective method.” (Sec 3.4)

Paper Title: Polymorphs, Particle Size, and a Pandemic: Development of a Scalable Crystallization Process for Molnupiravir, an Antiviral for the Treatment of COVID-19
Problem_Description: The pandemic‑driven timeline required a rapid manufacturing process; the original crystallization involved lengthy distillation steps and multiple solvent additions, extending overall cycle time and risking delayed delivery of metric‑ton quantities.
Solution_Description: Process modifications included a heat‑cool cycle before seeding to quickly dissolve premature nuclei, a controlled EtOAc addition to target water‑content reduction without lengthy distillations, and the use of MTBE (lower boiling point) for faster drying of the final cake, collectively shortening the production cycle.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The original isolation of API was achieved through a distillative crystallization … the process was modified to give better control around the seeding point and initial desupersaturation, which resulted in more consistent nucleation and growth.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “We also added a heat and cool cycle immediately before seeding, so any batches that had spontaneously nucleated … would fully dissolve prior to the intended seed point.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “MTBE was utilized as part of the final solvent composition because of the lower solubility of the API … and more favorable drying kinetics, as the boiling point of MTBE is 55 °C, while that of EtOAc is 77 °C, so MTBE is easier to remove from the drycake at lower temperatures, which could reduce overall cycle times for processing.” (Sec 3.2)  
• “The improvements in the consistency of PSD are visible … via the narrowing of the D50 variability …” (Sec 3.2)  
• “In addition to examining the typical operating conditions, we also evaluated the potential variability … while the process was scaled up from lab batch to metric ton scale.” (Sec 4)

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: The original stereoselective synthesis (Scheme 1b) suffered from (i) low and inconsistent yields for the condensation of the (R)-phenylglycinol auxiliary with ethyl pyruvate, which required freshly activated molecular sieves, (ii) temperature‑sensitive diastereoselectivity that demanded cryogenic conditions, and (iii) a high loading of Pd‑(OH)₂/C for auxiliary hydrogenolysis that was a significant cost driver.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to use a hydrolase‑catalyzed kinetic resolution of a racemic α,α‑disubstituted amino ester, eliminating the auxiliary‑based sequence altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: ["condensation of the auxiliary (R)-phenylglycinol with ethyl pyruvate to give adduct 2 provided inconsistent/low yields and relied on freshly activated molecular sieves","the diastereoselectivity of the n‑BuMgCl addition to give 3 was sensitive to temperature and required cryogenic conditions","high loading of Pd‑(OH)₂/C for the hydrogenolysis of the auxiliary from intermediate 4 was an undesirable cost driver","This report presents the process development of a sequence featuring a hydrolase‑catalyzed kinetic resolution of a racemic α,α‑disubstituted amino ester")

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: The N‑benzoyl‑protected substrate 7 gave only 8 % conversion after 63 h in the preliminary enzymatic screen; the poor performance was attributed to steric hindrance around the α‑carbon and the extremely low aqueous solubility of 7 (< 1 mg mL⁻¹), which produced heterogeneous reaction mixtures that limited enzyme activity.
Solution_Description: A series of unprotected amino‑ester substrates (11a–c) were prepared, reducing steric bulk and dramatically improving aqueous solubility; the isopropyl ester 11c was selected for scale‑up because of its superior stability and reactivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Efforts to optimize the conditions for Alcalase‑mediated resolution of substrate 7 achieved only 8% conversion to the carboxylic acid product (S)‑6 after 63 h","Two factors were suspected to contribute to the poor conversion observed with substrate 7: (1) the enzyme activity was sensitive to the steric burden of the N‑protected α,α‑disubstituted amino ester and (2) the limited solubility of substrate 7 in predominantly aqueous media and consequently heterogeneous reaction mixtures hindered reactivity","With these challenges in mind, a series of unprotected amino ester substrates that would have reduced steric burden... and improved aqueous solubility were prepared","Each of the three esters exhibited substantially higher reactivity than substrate 7... Based on these results, isopropyl ester substrate 11c was selected for further development")

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: Initial solvent screening for the Alcalase‑mediated resolution showed that MeCN and DMSO gave inferior conversion and selectivity compared with acetone, limiting the overall product recovery.
Solution_Description: Acetone (20 % v/v) was chosen as the optimal co‑solvent, delivering 63–65 % conversion and 98 % ee of the remaining ester under the chosen conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Both the fumaric acid and phosphoric acid salts of substrate 11c were tested with acetone as a cosolvent and performed comparably, giving 63–65% conversion and 98% ee of the remaining ester (entries 1–2)","Acetonitrile and dimethyl sulfoxide cosolvents were also evaluated but gave inferior selectivity (entries 5–6), leading to selection of 20% acetone as the preferred condition for scale‑up (entry 2)"]

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: During the kilogram‑scale enzymatic resolution the reaction pH dropped from the initial value to ~8.1, causing variability in conversion rates and selectivity factors (k_rel).
Solution_Description: The initial pH was systematically varied (7.0–9.1) and adjusted with phosphoric acid or potassium hydroxide before charging Alc­ alase, establishing that an initial pH of 7.5–8.6 gives the best balance of conversion, selectivity, and reaction time; in‑process pH monitoring and base dosing were proposed for further robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The pH of the reaction mixture dropped by approximately 0.4 units over the course of the process, which raised questions about the impact of pH on the efficiency and robustness of the resolution","The initial pH was adjusted within the range from 7.0 to 9.1 with the addition of phosphoric acid or potassium hydroxide prior to charge of the Alcalase solution","At the more basic initial pH 9.1, the reaction proceeded at a comparable rate but with diminished selectivity... At an initial pH of 7.9, the reaction proceeded with greater selectivity... Further reduction of the initial pH to 7.5 further enhanced the selectivity... finally, at an initial pH of 7.0, the selectivity continued to rise, but the reaction time became intractably long")

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: Two separate analytical workflows (¹H NMR for conversion and Fmoc‑derivatization/chiral LC for ee) were required for every time‑point, slowing data acquisition and contributing to inconsistent k_rel calculations.
Solution_Description: A single OPA/N‑Ac‑l‑cysteine (OPA/NAC) derivatization protocol was introduced, allowing simultaneous measurement of conversion and enantiomeric purity of both ester and acid on an achiral LC system, streamlining analysis.
Supporting_Evidence: ["This problem was addressed with the implementation of an amino acid derivatization method that enabled the simultaneous assessment of conversion and enantiomeric purity of amino ester 11c and amino acid 12 with achiral LC analysis (Scheme 6)","An aliquot of the reaction mixture was treated directly with a solution of o‑phthalaldehyde (OPA) and N‑Ac‑l‑cysteine (NAC) in borate buffer, giving the corresponding pair of diastereomeric isoindole adducts of the ester and acid","These four diastereomeric species were fully separable on a single analytical LC method and provided quantitation of the conversion of ester to acid and the enantiomeric ratio of each species")

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Preparation of the Amino Alcohol Fragment of Selgantolimod by Enzymatic Resolution of an α,α-Disubstituted Amino Ester
Problem_Description: The lithium borohydride reduction of Boc‑protected ester 13 gave only 35 % conversion at 20 °C (entry 1) and generated a cyclic carbamate impurity (entry 2) at 40 °C; the reaction also evolved flammable H₂ gas and required careful temperature control to avoid runaway exotherms.
Solution_Description: Methanol (2.2 equiv) was added as a co‑solvent/additive, which suppressed impurity formation and gave >99 % conversion at 40 °C; the reaction was conducted in MTBE or THF with controlled addition of LiBH₄ solution (maintaining < 30 °C) and quenched with aqueous citric acid to safely dissipate the exotherm and capture H₂.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The reduction step was initially tested with LiBH₄ (2.2 equiv) in THF (16 L kg⁻¹) at 20 °C, but inadequate conversion was observed after 18 h (entry 1)","At 40 °C, the conversion improved along with substantial production of cyclic carbamate impurity 15 (entry 2)","Due to these unfavorable results, methanol was employed as an additive to modulate the reactivity of LiBH₄. A solution of amino ester 13 in THF was warmed to 40 °C, charged with LiBH₄, and then charged with methanol (2.2 equiv), and full conversion with reduced formation of impurity 15 was observed (entry 3)","Safety Note: the following procedure uses lithium borohydride and results in the evolution of flammable hydrogen gas. Ensure adequate venting to avoid reactor pressurization and maintain sufficient nitrogen flow throughout the reaction to dilute hydrogen below its lower explosion limit.","The end‑of‑reaction mixture was added into an aqueous citric acid solution to quench, which allowed for control of the exotherm and gas evolution."]

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: All column purifications were eliminated and every attempt to crystallise the final GalNAc‑ligand 1 failed, leaving the product as an oil and limiting isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The product was isolated as an off‑white solid by lyophilisation or by spray‑drying from acetone, providing a practical solid‑form without the need for crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “All column purifications were removed, but unfortunately, all attempts to crystallize 1 were unsuccessful…The GalNAc ligand 1 can be isolated as an off‑white amorphous solid via lyophilization or spray drying.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: The original step‑2 used 10 wt % Pd/C (a 50 wt % aqueous slurry) which introduced a large amount of water that carried into step‑3, potentially affecting the condensation reaction and causing variability.
Solution_Description: Pd/C loading was reduced to 0.8–1.2 wt % (≈1 wt % relative to 4) to minimise water introduction while maintaining catalytic activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Pd/C catalyst comes as a 50 wt % suspension in water, high catalyst usage introduces a significant amount of water…Early laboratory‑scale experiments indicated that 1 wt % Pd/C catalyst loading was sufficient…so this became the new set‑point.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: During step‑1 activation, incomplete conversion of 2 or hydrolysis of the PFP‑ester 3 could generate mono‑acid 8 and cyclic anhydride 9, leading to loss of material and potential critical impurity 10.
Solution_Description: A sufficient excess of PFP‑TFA (3.5–4 equiv) was maintained and the addition rate was controlled to ensure complete activation and suppress hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “If present, 8 continues to react…Monoacid impurity 8 would be expected…if insufficient PFP‑TFA were present…Impurity 8 and 9 were undetectable at the end of the reaction…ensuring a sufficient excess of PFP‑TFA is used.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: The activation step required a minimum reaction time of 5 h to drive the conversion below the 0.2 % mono‑acid threshold, which would be impractical for high‑throughput manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A 5 h (300 min) minimum reaction time was imposed as the standard set‑point for step‑1, balancing conversion and throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “All reactions went to completion within 5 h…the reaction reaches 0.2 % remaining monoacid 8 after 270 min, thus 5 h (300 min) is set as a minimum reaction time.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: In step‑2, high Pd/C loading combined with low TFA produced elevated levels of non‑critical impurity 11, and reaction rates varied widely (20 min to 17 h).
Solution_Description: Pd/C loading was limited to 0.8–1.2 wt % and TFA to ≥1 equiv, providing a robust design space where impurity 11 remains ≤0.8 % and reaction times stay within practical limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “The formation of 11 was mainly affected by the amount of Pd/C, the amount of TFA…Holding the Pd/C amount between 0.8% and 1.2% provides a robust process range that keeps non‑critical 11 impurity at low levels…”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: During step‑3 condensation, using 9 equiv of DIEA failed to achieve complete conversion, leaving mono‑PFP ester 14 and incomplete product formation.
Solution_Description: Base loading was increased to a minimum of 11 equiv DIEA (range 11–16 equiv) which ensured full consumption of the PFP‑ester and complete product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “A minimum of 11 equiv of DIEA were needed for completion of the reaction…After stirring for 18 h, 5 additional equivalents of base were added, which was sufficient for complete reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Repeated bicarbonate washes in the step‑3 aqueous work‑up caused the organic layer to oil out, indicating poor phase separation due to residual DIEA.
Solution_Description: The wash sequence was changed to alternating bicarbonate and phosphate buffers, then to phosphate‑only washes, eliminating oiling and providing clear phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “To try to avoid a large residual of DIEA…we switched from consecutive bicarbonate washes to alternating bicarbonate and phosphate buffer washes, which gave clear phase separation without oiling out.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Low temperature and low buffer volume during the phosphate washes caused precipitation of the buffer, hampering phase separation.
Solution_Description: The wash temperature was raised (≈29 °C for the first buffer wash) and buffer concentration reduced (0.2–0.5 M) to prevent precipitation and maintain clear separations.
Supporting_Evidence: “Higher temperatures reduce the efficiency of DIEA extraction…The phosphate precipitated during the first wash under a combination of low temperature and low buffer volume…lower buffer concentrations (0.2 and 0.5 M) were tried…When a slightly elevated temperature was applied, a clear phase separation was observed.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Step‑4 extraction with MTBE/heptane could either leave PFP and impurity 13 in the aqueous layer (insufficient organic solvent) or cause the product 1 to oil out (excess MeOH, low organic volume).
Solution_Description: A defined MTBE extraction protocol (5 V MTBE) was adopted together with a minimum of 27 % MeOH in the aqueous layer to ensure clear phase separation and quantitative removal of PFP and impurity 13 without product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “We found that two extractions with either 4:1 or 6:1 MeTHF/heptane removed both PFP and 13 without significant loss of 1…MTBE performed identically…High MeOH input solution…27 % MeOH was needed for clear phase separation.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Large amounts of solid NaCl added for phase separation could precipitate and block drains during the final extraction step.
Solution_Description: The NaCl loading was limited to 12.5–17.5 wt % (set‑point 22 wt %) which gave reliable phase separation while keeping precipitation manageable.
Supporting_Evidence: “A minimum of 12.5 wt % NaCl is needed for clear phase separation…a range of 17.5–25 wt % NaCl with a set point of 22 wt % was selected…the amount of precipitation is manageable without concern about drain blockage.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Azeotropic distillation to reach the target water content (<0.2 wt %) could be inefficient if temperature or pressure were not correctly controlled, risking higher residual water and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Five consecutive 50 % solvent removal/distillation cycles were performed at 15 °C internal temperature and ≤40 °C jacket temperature under ~65 mbar, reliably delivering <0.1 wt % water.
Supporting_Evidence: “Modeling suggested that the target water content would be reached by 5‑fold repetition of a process comprising 50 % solvent mass reduction…follow‑up experiment confirmed that azeotropic distillations controlled the amount of water to below 0.1 wt %.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Spray‑drying of 1 gave variable yields; lower feed concentrations produced poorer recovery.
Solution_Description: Feed concentration was identified as the dominant factor and was increased within the operational window, resulting in higher isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Concentration was identified as the main effect, with higher concentrations giving better yields…Half‑normal plot of spray drying.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Process for the Liver-Targeted Triantennary
Problem_Description: Step‑4 hydrogenation rates varied widely (20 min to 8 h) depending on Pd/C loading and temperature, threatening consistent throughput.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was fixed at 6 wt % Pd/C and temperature set to 22.5 °C, delivering a robust rate (~30 min) while still allowing acceptable completion within 8 h at the design space extremes.
Supporting_Evidence: “The amount of Pd/C catalyst showed the biggest effect, followed by temperature…The fastest reaction…high catalyst loading at high temperature…run 17…low catalyst at low temperature took 8 h…The hydrogenation reaction is expected to complete within 2 h under the current set‑point conditions (6 wt % Pd/C and 22.5 °C).”

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: The nitration of naphthalene is a very fast, highly exothermic reaction (ΔH ≈ ‑73 to ‑253 kJ mol⁻¹) that can generate large amounts of heat in a short time, creating a risk of thermal runaway and unsafe operating conditions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow microreactor (inner diameter 0.8 mm) with a large surface‑to‑volume ratio was employed. The small characteristic size and high specific surface area provide intense mixing and rapid heat removal, mitigating the exothermic hazard.
Supporting_Evidence: “Mixed acid nitration … is fast and highly exothermic, with the heat of the reaction ranging from ‑73 to ‑253 kJ·mol⁻¹” (Intro). “Rapid exothermic characteristics of nitration … a quick heat transfer assessment … to obtain the temperature profile” (Abstract). “The continuous flow microreactor with a smaller characteristic size and larger specific surface area is considered an excellent tool for performing such fast and exothermic reactions due to enhanced mixing and heat transfer capacity” (Intro).

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: Using a high molar ratio of nitric acid (M > 1.2) generates a large waste stream of inorganic acid, which is environmentally unfriendly and uneconomical on scale.
Solution_Description: The molar ratio was optimized to M = 1.2, providing sufficient conversion while minimizing excess nitric acid waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “The excessive use of nitric acid … brings a large number of waste inorganic acid stream, which is environmentally unfriendly and hard to dispose of and recover” (Sec 3.1.1). “When the molar ratio increased from 1.2 to 1.6, the selectivity declined more quickly… Therefore, a molar ratio of 1.2 was selected to be the basis for the following research” (Sec 3.1.1).

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: Increasing the nitric‑acid‑to‑naphthalene molar ratio raises the reaction rate but also promotes side reactions (dinitration and formation of 2‑nitronaphthalene), decreasing selectivity of the desired 1‑nitronaphthalene.
Solution_Description: The molar ratio was limited to 1.2 and the reaction temperature was kept at 30 °C–40 °C (with 74 % H₂SO₄) to suppress hot‑spot formation and limit side‑reaction rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “Selectivity decreased with the increase in the molar ratio… hot spots increased, further increasing the possibility of dinitration” (Sec 3.1.1). “When the molar ratio increased… the reaction rate increased… the occurrence of hot spots increased” (Sec 3.1.1). “A molar ratio of 1.2 was selected… sulfuric acid strength of 74 % was selected as the initial … for subsequent research” (Sec 3.1.1).

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: Scale‑up from a 0.8 mm microreactor to a 4 mm mesoscale reactor reduces the heat‑transfer per unit volume, leading to temperature spikes (over‑temperatures up to ≈ 50 °C) and increased dinitration.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A dimension‑enlarging strategy was applied: modular reaction sections, higher volumetric flow rates, and real‑time temperature monitoring were used to balance residence time, improve mixing, and keep the reactor temperature within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the inner diameter of the reactor was enlarged from 0.8 mm to 4 mm, the mass and heat transfer performance would undoubtedly decrease” (Sec 3.3.1). “The temperature profile under different volumetric flow rates… highest temperature measured was 36.17 °C, 37.98 °C, 41.04 °C, and 50.10 °C respectively” (Fig 9). “The highest temperature rise … predicted … was 22.13 °C … however the experimental rise was 17.10 °C, indicating larger heat‑transfer limitations at pilot scale” (Sec 3.3.1).

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: In the conventional semibatch reactor the nitration requires ~80 min of dosing/holding, during which the temperature exceeds the set point by >15 °C for ≈ 2340 s, creating prolonged over‑temperature and safety hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to continuous‑flow operation reduced the reaction time to ~120 s and limited over‑temperature to 30–60 s, increasing space‑time yield by two orders of magnitude and improving inherent safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “The dosing time and holding time were both set to 40 min… The temperature of the reaction system rose rapidly… reached its highest value of 50.93 °C… time when temperature exceeded the setting temperature by 15 °C was 2240 s (93.3 % of dosing time)” (Sec 3.3.2). “Continuous flow reactor could quickly reduce the reaction temperature to below 40 °C… over‑temperature time of continuous flow mode was between 30 to 60 s” (Sec 3.3.3). Table 1 shows reaction time 4800 s (batch) vs 120 s (flow) and space‑time yield 0.0361 vs 1.575 g L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Paper Title: Study on Continuous Flow Nitration of Naphthalene
Problem_Description: Direct temperature measurement inside the 0.8 mm microreactor channel is difficult, preventing real‑time monitoring of the rapid exotherm.
Solution_Description: A rapid heat‑transfer assessment was performed by coupling the energy‑balance equation with the kinetic model, allowing a quick estimate of the temperature profile along the channel without physical thermocouples.
Supporting_Evidence: “For a microreactor with an inner diameter of 0.8 mm, obtaining the temperature profile by a thermocouple is very difficult. Therefore, by coupling the heat balance equation for the nitration of naphthalene with the reaction kinetic equation, the reaction conversion and temperature profile along the channel can be roughly estimated” (Sec 3.2).

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: Using a large excess of hydrogen peroxide (2 equiv) caused a highly exothermic oxidation that generated a rapid temperature rise (ΔT_ad ≈ 58 °C) and posed a flash‑explosion risk; the high peroxide load also increased reactor volume, waste‑treatment costs and safety‑related equipment investment.
Solution_Description: The peroxide loading was reduced to the stoichiometric optimum of 1.02 equiv, which lowered the heat release, eliminated the safety hazard, and cut raw‑material cost while maintaining >95 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “After gradually reducing the amount of hydrogen peroxide from the initial oxidant equivalent of 2 equiv, a yield of 95.2 % was achieved at 1.02 equiv, despite decomposition resulting in an insufficient amount of oxidant.”; “The oxidation reaction liberates 142.1 kJ mol⁻¹ with an adiabatic temperature increase of 58.3 °C… rapid hydrogen peroxide addition could elevate the risk level to 5, necessitating meticulous control to avert material ejection and flash explosion risks.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: 2‑Chloropyridine and 8 % H₂O₂ form a liquid‑liquid heterogeneous system that quickly stratifies (≈20 s), causing poor contact, variable conversion, and material loss at low flow rates.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 3‑D‑printed SMV static mixer was installed in a mixed fixed‑bed reactor to enforce turbulent liquid‑liquid dispersion, eliminating phase separation and delivering >99 % conversion at the same residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The raw materials 2‑chloropyridine and hydrogen peroxide exhibit extremely poor miscibility… under low flow velocity conditions… leads to stratification… The simple internal structure of our first generation reactor is insufficient to ensure complete mixing.”; “We opted for an SMV static mixer… to enhance the mixing between the two liquid phases… The fabricated mixer was connected directly to the original fixed bed reactor… achieving an internal standard yield of 99.6 %.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: In batch mode the TS‑1 powder catalyst had to be filtered after each run, creating a labor‑intensive separation step and escalating waste‑treatment costs, which limited scale‑up feasibility.
Solution_Description: A fixed‑bed reactor loaded with sieved TS‑1 particles (10–20 mesh) retained the catalyst in‑situ; after reaction the catalyst could be regenerated and re‑charged, removing the need for filtration and reducing operational cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “Powder catalysts with small sizes… are used in batch reactions… however, the complexity of separating these catalysts… may hinder scale‑up capability, limit production efficiency, and increase labor costs.”; “The catalyst was regenerated and recharged into the reactor… after three cycles of regeneration, the catalyst activity did not show a significant decline.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: Batch oxidation required 2 h at 55–70 °C and hydrolysis an additional 4 h, giving only moderate yields and limiting throughput for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Continuous flow reactors (mixed fixed‑bed oxidation, CSTR quench, plug‑flow hydrolysis) reduced oxidation to ≤10 min and hydrolysis to 2 h with >97 % overall yield, dramatically increasing space‑time yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The continuous reaction process and post‑treatment process resulted in >90 % isolated yield with no need for additional separation and purification steps… The complete oxidation of 2‑chloropyridine was achieved within 10 min, and the hydrolysis reaction was completed in 60 min.”; Table 2 shows conversion rising from 86.5 % (5 min) to 98.6 % (10 min) with yields of 97 %.

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: Residual hydrogen peroxide exiting the oxidation reactor required safe quenching; uncontrolled peroxide could decompose, generate oxygen, and pose flash‑explosion hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) was fed with a 20 wt % sodium sulfite solution at 80 °C at a calculated 10 mL min⁻¹ flow, ensuring complete peroxide quench and oxygen removal, verified by potassium‑iodide test strips.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sodium sulfite and sodium bisulfite were considered as quenching substances; the former was preferred due to its superior quenching effect… A 20 wt % sodium sulfite aqueous solution was formulated for easy continuous conveyance… The quenching temperature was controlled at 80 °C… Complete quenching was verified by periodic checks with potassium iodide test strips.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: HOPO remained in aqueous solution; direct evaporation would cause premature crystallization and product loss, while its high solubility at neutral pH hindered solid recovery.
Solution_Description: A continuous crystallization CSTR was employed where 12 N HCl was added dropwise to lower pH to 3 at 0–5 °C for 1 h, inducing precipitation of HOPO as a light‑yellow solid that could be filtered and dried, giving isolated yields up to 91 % and >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The optimal post‑treatment procedure involved slowly adjusting the system’s pH to 3 by the dropwise addition of 12 N HCl aq while controlling the temperature between 0 and 5 °C and stirring the solution for 1 h… Light yellow solids could be observed… filtered to obtain a solid product.”; Figure 2 shows isolated yield increasing with decreasing pH and plateauing at pH 3.

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: During long‑term operation the catalyst activity decreased, leading to residual 2‑chloropyridine (~1 % after 20 h) and a slight drop in conversion, indicating deactivation.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was regenerated in‑situ after each run and re‑charged; the mixed fixed‑bed design with 3‑D‑printed mixer allowed consistent contact, maintaining conversion and enabling multiple regeneration cycles without performance loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “The remaining raw materials were 1.2 % after 20 h… According to the method provided in the literature, the catalyst was regenerated and recharged into the reactor. After three cycles of regeneration, the catalyst activity did not show a significant decline.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: The first‑generation fixed‑bed reactor’s simple geometry could not prevent phase segregation at low flow rates, causing 2‑chloropyridine to escape unreacted and lowering overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implementation of a mixed‑fixed‑bed reactor integrating the 3‑D‑printed SMV static mixer provided turbulent dispersion of the two liquid phases, eliminating stratification and achieving 100 % conversion at 10 min residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: “Under low flow velocity conditions, the incompatibility of the two components leads to stratification… the simple internal structure of our first generation reactor is insufficient to ensure complete mixing.”; “The fabricated mixer was connected directly to the original fixed bed reactor… achieving an internal standard yield of 99.6 %.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2‑Hydroxypyridine‑
Problem_Description: Scaling to kilogram‑per‑day production required larger reactors and precise metering; conventional pumps and flow meters were insufficient for accurate delivery at higher throughput.
Solution_Description: The pilot plant employed gear pumps (Tuthill DG.19) and mini CORI‑FLOW mass‑flow meters, enlarged reactor diameters (0.5″ → 2″) and lengths (330 mm → 3.2 m), and introduced a pressure‑filter tank, enabling stable 8 kg day⁻¹ operation with consistent product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “To ensure successful scale‑up, precise component delivery was achieved using Tuthill DG.19 gear pumps and mini CORI‑FLOW mass flow meters… the continuous catalytic oxidation reactor saw an enlargement of its diameter from 1/2″ to 2″ and its length from 330 mm to 3.2 m… The scale‑up isolated yield could reach a maximum of 91.06 %…”

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: The original bedaquiline assembly (BA) reaction using a non‑chiral base gave only 40–70 % conversion of the quinoline and ketone, no stereoselectivity and consequently a very low assay yield, driving up the manufacturing cost.
Solution_Description: Switch to a chiral lithium amide base – lithium (R)‑2‑(methoxymethyl)‑pyrrolidide (derived from d‑proline) – which both deprotonates quinoline 1 and transfers chirality, giving high conversion (up‑to 53 % assay yield in the first test) and strong diastereo‑ and enantio‑control (d.r. ≈ 8:1, ee ≈ 26 %). The additive LiBr further improves the syn/anti d.r. (from 1:1.2 to 2.1:1).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the current synthetic strategy … suffers from low conversion and no stereoselectivity, which subsequently increases the cost of manufacturing BDQ.” (Abstract)  
• “low conversion of starting materials 1 and 2 (40–70 % remains unreacted …)” (Introduction)  
• “lithium (R)‑2-(methoxymethyl)‑pyrrolidide … results in high assay yield … and considerable stereocontrol (d.r. = 13.6:1, ee = 56 %)” (Abstract)  
• “the lithium amide base of (R)-2-(methoxymethyl)‑pyrrolidine (11) promoted quinoline 1 lithiation and afforded a 53 % assay yield … d.r. ≈ 8:1, 26 % ee” (Section 2.2)  
• “the use of lithium bromide (LiBr) as an additive improved the syn/anti d.r. from 1:1.2 to 2.1:1” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: A sub‑stoichiometric (catalytic) amount of the chiral amine 11 was desired to lower material cost, but reducing it below 0.2 equiv caused a severe loss of enantioselectivity, making catalytic use infeasible.
Solution_Description: Systematic stoichiometry study: keep the total amine equivalents at 1.5 equiv but replace part of 11 with lithium pyrrolidide. Increasing lithium pyrrolidide from 0 to 1.3 equiv raised assay yield from 53 % to 75 % while maintaining diastereoselectivity, confirming that excess chiral base is required.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “With the focus on lowering the cost … the usage of a substoichiometric amount of the chiral reagent was explored.” (Section 2.3)  
• “Higher yields … were observed when the amount of lithium pyrrolidide was increased … from 53 to 75 %.” (Section 2.3)  
• “A substantial deterioration of enantioselectivity … when the amount of chiral base 11 was reduced from 1.5 to 0.2 equiv.” (Section 2.3)  
• “These experiments unfortunately concluded that the use of catalytic amounts of the chiral transfer reagent 11 would not be feasible.” (Section 2.3).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: Non‑polar solvents (toluene, hexanes, DCM) could not be used because LiBr, a crucial additive for stereocontrol, is poorly soluble, leading to >85 % of starting material recovered after quench.
Solution_Description: Replace THF with 2‑MeTHF (or binary mixtures) which dissolves LiBr adequately. In 2‑MeTHF at –40 °C the reaction gave 72 % of the syn‑diastereomer pair with a 9:1 d.r.; the less polar solvent also slowed the reaction, reducing retro‑addition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Nonpolar solvents … are not compatible due to the low solubility of LiBr … mostly starting materials (>85 %…) were observed after the reaction quench.” (Section 2.5)  
• “The replacement of the standard solvent THF with the less polar 2‑MeTHF led to the formation of the product … at –40 °C, improved conversion … 72 % of the syn‑diastereomer pair … 9:1 d.r.” (Section 2.5)  
• “When the reaction was carried out at –40 °C, improved conversion was achieved, and 72 % of the syn‑diastereomer pair … was observed.” (Section 2.5).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: Increasing the temperature above –78 °C drives the reversible lithiation equilibrium toward the starting quinoline 1 and ketone 2, causing retro‑addition and enolate formation (compound 16), which reduces conversion and diastereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: Temperatures were carefully tuned: maintain –78 °C for lithiation but allow the 1,2‑addition at –40 °C in 2‑MeTHF. At –40 °C the conversion and d.r. improved (31 % syn at –60 °C, 69 % syn at –78 °C) and enantioselectivity rose to 54 % ee, while still limiting retro‑addition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “carrying out the reaction at temperatures higher than –78 °C strongly favored the retro‑addition … leading the reaction equilibrium to favor 1a and 2.” (Section 2.4)  
• “Enolate 16 begins to disrupt the equilibrium … represents a thermodynamic sink for this reaction.” (Section 2.4)  
• “Higher temperatures … resulted in lower diastereoselectivity and conversion … but the reaction at –40 °C provided higher enantioselectivity (54 % ee) compared to –78 °C (35 % ee).” (Section 2.4).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: The 1,2‑addition step is reversible; prolonged reaction times (>30 min after ketone addition) allow retro‑addition and ketone enolization, lowering yield, while too short times prevent equilibrium and give poor stereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: Systematic time study showed that 20–30 min after ketone addition gives the best balance: assay yield ≈ 80 %, d.r. ≈ 15:1, ee ≈ 50 % and BDQ assay yield ≈ 56 %. Longer (60 min) or shorter (5 min) times worsen either conversion or selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the longer the reaction was carried out (>30 min after the completion of ketone 2 addition), the more the reaction was dominated by the thermodynamically driven enolization, leading to the deterioration of the overall yield.” (Section 2.6)  
• Table 1 entries show optimal results at 20–30 min (entries 2–4) with high d.r. and ee, whereas 5 min and 60 min give poorer selectivity or yield. (Section 2.6, Table 1).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: Changing the reaction concentration alters side‑reaction pathways: high concentration (≤3 V THF) promotes Li‑halogen exchange (desbromoquinoline 17) and subsequent undesired addition (product 18), while very dilute conditions lower throughput.
Solution_Description: Optimize solvent volume to 15–20 V of 2‑MeTHF (vs. 30 V THF). This keeps conversion high, suppresses Li‑halogen exchange, and minimizes side‑product 20 formation, while reducing solvent usage and improving practicality for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the quinoline 1 solution was further concentrated from 5 to 3 V of THF, a higher amount of desbromoquinoline 17 was observed … higher dilutions tend to slow these side reactions.” (Section 2.7)  
• “The use of 2‑MeTHF alone was found to provide superior conversion … and considerably less impurity formation.” (Section 2.7)  
• Figure 3 and associated text describe that 15–20 V 2‑MeTHF gives similar product amount (~70 % HPLC A) as 30 V THF while using less solvent. (Section 2.7).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: The reaction is extremely moisture‑sensitive; water >0.5 % w/w shuts down the 1,2‑addition, dramatically reducing the syn‑diastereomer (2 % only) and increasing side‑product formation.
Solution_Description: Implement rigorous drying: azeotropic distillation of LiBr and quinoline 1, dry ketone 2 under vacuum at room temperature, store reagents over molecular sieves, and only use solvent with ≤0.1 % w/w water (KF). These practices restore high conversion and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the lithiation/1,2‑addition sequence is extremely sensitive to moisture … all components must be freshly distilled and dried.” (Section 2.8)  
• “When water content >0.5 % w/w shuts down the desired reaction, and only 2 % of the syn‑diastereomer pair was detected.” (Section 2.8)  
• “Azeotropic distillation of the LiBr and quinoline 1 … to obtain the lowest water content possible.” (Section 2.8).

Paper Title: Application of Chiral Transfer Reagents to Improve Stereoselectivity and Yields in the Synthesis of the Antituberculosis Drug Bedaquiline
Problem_Description: Commercial batches of chiral amine 11 from different vendors showed variable purity (90 % vs >99 % by GCHS) and inconsistent diastereoselectivity in the BA reaction, likely due to undetected inorganic salts.
Solution_Description: Synthesize amine 11 in‑house from d‑prolinol and purify by distillation, followed by storage over molecular sieves under inert atmosphere. This removes moisture and inorganic salts, providing consistent >99.5 % purity and reproducible dr (≈19:1 to 6:1) across scales.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reproducible results could not be achieved with different sources of the amine … presence of undetected inorganic salts …” (Section 2.8)  
• “Distillation of the chiral amine 11 prior to its use … adopted as the standard procedure.” (Section 2.8)  
• Table 2 shows that vendors A and C gave >99 % purity after distillation, while vendor B gave ~90 % purity and inferior dr. (Section 2.8, Table 2).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Cyclodextrin-Grafted Chitosan: From Laboratory Scale to Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: TsCD undergoes an unwanted hydrolysis reaction with water at temperatures above 60 °C, producing TsOH and reducing the amount of TsCD available for grafting onto chitosan. This side reaction lowers the degree of N‑substitution (DS) and therefore the overall yield of CD‑g‑CS.
Solution_Description: The authors increased the TsCD : CS molar ratio to 0.88 : 1 and selected a reaction temperature of 95 °C, which maximised the grafting rate while minimising the hydrolysis of TsCD. Reaction time was also set to 24 h to ensure complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “An increasing mole of TsCD led to increasing DS because of an abundance of available TsCD molecules to react with chitosan” (Fig 5a). “TsCD could undergo another reaction in the presence of water at a high temperature … The product … TsOH, was noticeable at a reaction temperature over 60 °C” (Fig 6). “The optimum reaction conditions were determined to be 95 °C for 24 h” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Cyclodextrin-Grafted Chitosan: From Laboratory Scale to Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: Temperatures above 95 °C cause chitosan degradation, evidenced by a colour change from yellow to brown and loss of DS, which also raises safety concerns due to possible formation of degradants.
Solution_Description: The process was limited to 95 °C, the highest temperature that gave high DS without observable degradation. For the 500 L reactor an internal heating coil was recommended to improve heat transfer and avoid local hot spots that could degrade chitosan.
Supporting_Evidence: “Beyond 95 °C, the DS dropped concurrently with the change in the mixture colour from yellow to brown due to chitosan degradation” (Sec 3.1). “The colour of CD‑g‑CS from a 500 L reactor was … slightly darker … due to partial degradation of chitosan from the exposure to the high‑temperature reactor wall.” (Sec 3.3). “An internal heating coil installation is recommended to enhance the heat transfer per unit volume and alleviate the high utility temperature requirement.” (Sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Cyclodextrin-Grafted Chitosan: From Laboratory Scale to Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: In the 2 L reactor, low impeller speeds (200–300 rpm) produced dead zones and non‑uniform temperature, while excessive speeds (≥500 rpm) generated bubbles and vortex that broke the grafted polymer, both leading to reduced DS.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Impeller speed was optimised to 450 rpm for the 2 L reactor, 320 rpm for the 10 L reactor and 245 rpm for the 500 L reactor, providing sufficient shear for uniform mixing without inducing vortex or polymer breakage.
Supporting_Evidence: “DS increased with increasing impeller speed from 200 to 450 rpm; however, it dropped when the impeller speed was further increased to 500 and 600 rpm” (Sec 3.2, Fig 7). “The higher impeller speed of 450 rpm, calculated from this scaling method, induced vortex and retrograded grafting.” (Sec 3.3). “The proper impeller speed … required to assist in blending without deteriorating the complex material.” (Sec 3.2).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Cyclodextrin-Grafted Chitosan: From Laboratory Scale to Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: Dialysis (MWCO = 3500 Da) used for laboratory‑scale product isolation is impractical and costly for larger batches (10 L and 500 L).
Solution_Description: A spiral‑wound membrane filtration system (TriSep, MWCO = 3500 Da) replaced dialysis for the 10 L and 500 L reactors, offering scalable, faster and less expensive product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reacted solution was purified by a dialysis bag … for the laboratory scale and 2 L reactors. For 10 and 500 L reactors, the solution was purified through a spiral wound membrane filtration system … for purification.” (Sec 2.2.3).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Cyclodextrin-Grafted Chitosan: From Laboratory Scale to Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: Initial scale‑up calculations based on constant tip speed or power per volume yielded impractically high impeller speeds (900 rpm for 10 L, 2160 rpm for 500 L), making the process unfeasible.
Solution_Description: The scaling strategy was changed to maintain a constant heat‑transfer rate per unit volume. To compensate for the lower practical impeller speeds, the heating‑oil temperature was raised (105 °C for 10 L, 125 °C for 500 L), achieving the required heat‑transfer driving force.
Supporting_Evidence: “Impeller speeds of 900 rpm for a 10 L reactor and 2160 rpm for a 500 L reactor … were impractical.” (Sec 3.3). “The temperature difference … should be applied … 105 and 125 °C hot oil … for 10 and 500 L reactors.” (Sec 3.3). “Constant heat‑transfer rate per volume … was set as a scale‑up objective.” (Abstract, Sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Development of an Early Phase Process for a Potent Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cell Differentiator
Problem_Description: The original discovery route gave a very low overall isolated yield (~13 %) and required a chromatographic purification of ester 5, making the process inefficient for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A completely redesigned synthetic sequence (Scheme 3) eliminated the low‑yield steps and removed the chromatographic isolation of ester 5, delivering a three‑fold overall yield increase (≈38 %) and a chromatography‑free process.

Among its other scale up limitations, a chromatographic purification of ester 5 was required.”; “The improved process … removed a chromatographic purification, and significantly reduced the cost of goods for preparing 14.”

Paper Title: Development of an Early Phase Process for a Potent Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cell Differentiator
Problem_Description: The addition of DIAD in the Mitsunobu reaction released a large amount of heat (ΔT_ad ≈ 196 °C), presenting a safety risk and causing temperature spikes that could degrade the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: DIAD was delivered as a 1 : 1 (w/w) solution in PhMe and added at a controlled rate while maintaining the reactor temperature at 35‑45 °C, preventing heat accumulation and enabling a robust scale‑up.

Problem_Description: Sodium triacetoxyborohydride (STAB) was poorly soluble in EtOAc, causing slurry‑charging difficulties and incomplete mixing during the reductive amination step.

Paper Title: Development of an Early Phase Process for a Potent Oligodendrocyte Precursor Cell Differentiator
Problem_Description: The HCl/2‑PrOH solution used for salt formation in the reductive amination was hygroscopic; moisture ingress caused hydrolysis of the ester 15, forming impurity 22 and reducing product purity.
Solution_Description: Reagent containers were reduced in size, opened only as needed, and the KF and titer were measured before use; only 1.0 equiv of the freshly titrated solution was added, and a strict KF limit (<0.5 %) was imposed, eliminating water‑induced hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reagent’s KF and titer were measured on the day of use to permit addition of 1.0 eq based on the input quantity of 15.”; “The root cause of the hydrolysis was traced to the presence of water… the vendor COA listed a KF limit of <0.5 % for the reagent, while measured KF values were 3.30 %, 8.99 % and 13.99 %.”
