Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of the PARP-1/2 Inhibitor HYDAMTIQ: Synthetic Strategy, Optimization, and Green Metrics Evaluation
Problem_Description: The thermal cyclization step (Curtius rearrangement) shows poor reproducibility, batch‑size dependency and low yields (71 % on 0.5 g, 25 % on 10 g). Conventional batch heating is non‑homogeneous, generates side‑products and requires time‑consuming chromatographic purifications.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The cyclization was transferred to a continuous‑flow stainless‑steel coil reactor (235 °C, τ = 80 min) providing uniform, super‑heated conditions. An in‑line silica‑packed column was placed between the acyl‑azide formation and cyclization to remove DPPA, diphenyl phosphate and salts, eliminating the need for chromatography and raising the isolated yield of the thieno‑isoquinolinone to 90 % with ≥93 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The thermal cyclization of intermediate 6 represents the main issue… poor reproducibility, batch‑size dependency, and low yield… 71 % yield on 0.5 g, 25 % yield on 10 g… non‑homogenous heating…" (sec 3.1) 
• "To improve reaction efficiency, a silica‑packed column was inserted … This in‑line purification … 90 % yield and high purity (≥93 %) without the need of chromatographic purifications." (sec 3.1) 
• "The crude acyl azide intermediate 6 was then directed toward a stainless steel coil reactor heated at 235 °C (τ = 80 min) to promote the Curtius rearrangement and cyclization." (sec 3.1)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of the PARP-1/2 Inhibitor HYDAMTIQ: Synthetic Strategy, Optimization, and Green Metrics Evaluation
Problem_Description: The original demethylation uses boron tribromide (BBr₃) in refluxing CH₂Cl₂, giving only 54 % yield, producing several side‑products that require silica‑gel chromatography, and poses severe safety hazards (high acute toxicity, violent exothermic decomposition, corrosive behavior).
Solution_Description: The hazardous BBr₃ was replaced by an odorless thiolate (1‑dodecanethiol, DodSH) together with AlCl₃ and NaI in 1,2‑dichlorobenzene under continuous flow (70 °C, τ = 38 min). This catalytic system provides 86 % isolated yield, avoids toxic reagents, and suppresses side‑product formation, eliminating the need for chromatographic work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The procedure for the demethylation reaction previously developed… used BBr₃… high acute toxicity, exothermic (violent) decomposition, and corrosive behavior." (sec 3.2) 
• "To solve this problem, we attempted the use of odorless alkyl thiolates… 1‑dodecanethiol (DodSH)…" (sec 3.2) 
• "The reactor outcome was readily mixed with a solution of DodSH… heated at 70 °C (τ = 38 min) allowing the formation of 9 in 86 % yield…" (sec 3.2) 
• "Avoiding the use of BBr₃ due to its high acute toxicity…" (sec 3.2)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of the PARP-1/2 Inhibitor HYDAMTIQ: Synthetic Strategy, Optimization, and Green Metrics Evaluation
Problem_Description: Screening of alternative bases (t‑BuOK, NaHMDS, Proton‑sponge) for the demethylation gave poor solubility and negligible conversion, limiting the reaction efficiency.
Solution_Description: AlCl₃ (3 equiv) was identified as an effective Lewis acid; the addition of NaI (3 equiv) dramatically increased conversion to ≥95 % and reduced the reaction time from 6 h to 2–3 h, allowing the reaction to be performed at 70 °C instead of 130 °C.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The use of alternative bases such as t‑BuOK, NaHMDS, and Proton‑sponge was unsuccessful both in terms of solubility and reaction efficiency." (sec 3.2) 
• "AlCl₃ (3 equiv) gave the desired product 9 in 52 % yield… The addition of 3 equiv of NaI resulted in an increase of the conversion up to 95 %… reduction of the reaction time (2–3 h instead of 6 h) and/or the temperature (70 °C instead of 130 °C)." (sec 3.2) 
• "Reducing the equivalents of DodSH, AlCl₃, and NaI… furnished lower conversions…" (sec 3.2)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of the PARP-1/2 Inhibitor HYDAMTIQ: Synthetic Strategy, Optimization, and Green Metrics Evaluation
Problem_Description: During the work‑up of the demethylation, the sodium salt of intermediate 9 has very low solubility in water, forming a fine suspension that prevents a continuous aqueous extractive work‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A liquid‑liquid membrane separator (Zaiput SEP‑10) replaced gravity phase separation, efficiently removing the aqueous phase. The organic stream was then precipitated by quenching into cold MeOH/Et₂O (1:3, v/v, 0 °C) and filtered, giving the final HYDAMTIQ·HCl without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The formation of a fine suspension due to the low solubility of the sodium salt of intermediate 9 in water prevented the possibility to perform the aqueous extractive workup under flow conditions." (ref 20) 
• "We made use of a membrane separator instead of the previously employed gravity separation. The method was extremely efficient to separate the aqueous stream from the organic phase." (sec 3.4) 
• "The reactor outcome was continuously dropped into a flask containing MeOH/Et₂O (1:3, v/v) cooled at 0 °C… The resulting precipitate was filtered off affording the desired HYDAMTIQ·HCl…" (sec 3.4)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of the PARP-1/2 Inhibitor HYDAMTIQ: Synthetic Strategy, Optimization, and Green Metrics Evaluation
Problem_Description: The batch demethylation required 6 h at 130 °C and subsequent silica‑gel chromatography to isolate the phenol, making the step time‑ and resource‑intensive.
Solution_Description: In flow, the combination of AlCl₃/NaI/DodSH at 70 °C reduced the demethylation time to 3 h (or 2 h at 130 °C) and afforded 86 % yield. The product was isolated by simple precipitation, completely eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The reaction yielded 54 %… along with several side products that required silica gel purification…" (sec 3.2) 
• "The addition of 3 equiv of NaI… reduction of the reaction time (2–3 h instead of 6 h) and/or the temperature (70 °C instead of 130 °C)." (sec 3.2) 
• "The reactor outcome was readily mixed with a solution of DodSH… heated at 70 °C (τ = 38 min) allowing the formation of 9 in 86 % yield…" (sec 3.2) 
• "The resultant precipitate was filtered off… without the need of chromatographic purifications." (sec 3.1)

Paper Title: In Vitro Biotransformation of High-Titer
Problem_Description: Glucaric acid (GA) strongly inhibits myo‑inositol oxygenase (MIOX); even low GA concentrations (0.1 mM) reduce MIOX activity to 60 % and 2 mM GA cuts activity by ~80 %, leading to low GA yields in the one‑pot cascade.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a step‑wise‑added enzyme‑cocktail strategy: first oxidize MI to glucuronic acid (GlcA) with MIOX, then after complete GlcA formation add uronate dehydrogenase (UDH) and NADH‑oxidase (NOX) to convert GlcA to GA. This temporal separation removes GA from the MIOX step and restores high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “GA had a remarkable effect on the activity of MIOX… 2 mM GA led to 80 % decrease in the MIOX activity” (Table 2); “To eliminate the inhibition of GA on MIOX, two‑step oxidation of MI was investigated… MIOX converted 10 mM MI to 9.8 mM GlcA in the first stage… the supplemented added UDH and NOX further converted GlcA to 9.8 mM GA” (Scheme 3, Fig. 3).

Paper Title: In Vitro Biotransformation of High-Titer
Problem_Description: The enzyme set required for myo‑inositol (MI) synthesis (thermophilic) and for GA synthesis (mesophilic) have mismatched optimal temperatures and pH, causing sub‑optimal activity when operated at a single temperature.
Solution_Description: A three‑step temperature regime was implemented: the first step (MI synthesis) runs at 70 °C, after which the thermophilic enzymes are removed; the second and third steps (MIOX, then UDH/NOX) are carried out at 30 °C. This matches each enzyme’s optimum and improves overall conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “stepwise‑added enzyme cocktail strategy … to circumvent … mismatches in enzymes’ properties, such as temperature and pH” (Introduction); “first step … at 70 °C … second step … at 30 °C … third step … at 30 °C” (Scheme 4, Fig. 4).

Paper Title: In Vitro Biotransformation of High-Titer
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the reaction mixture acidifies (pH falls to ≈6.3) as GA and GlcA accumulate, causing MIOX instability and precipitation of enzymes, which stalls conversion.
Solution_Description: A real‑time pH‑control loop was added, automatically dosing 2 M NaOH to maintain pH 7.5 throughout the cascade. The second addition of MIOX was performed after pH stabilization, preventing precipitation and enabling complete conversion to GA.
Supporting_Evidence: “pH gradually decreased … to 6.55 … after 6 h … MIOX was added again … but the addition did not result in an increase … pH dropped to 6.35. Moreover, a large amount of enzyme precipitate appeared” (Sec 2.5); “real‑time pH control strategy … adding 2 M NaOH … maintain the reaction mixture at a pH of 7.5” (Sec 2.5, Fig. 5B).

Paper Title: In Vitro Biotransformation of High-Titer
Problem_Description: Insufficient dissolved oxygen limits the activity of the H₂O‑forming NADH oxidase (NOX), reducing the regeneration of NAD⁺ and thus slowing the GA‑forming oxidation steps.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Stirring speed was increased to ≥600 rpm in the 50 mL bioreactor, giving an estimated k_La ≈ 100 s⁻¹, which provided adequate oxygen transfer for NOX activity and improved GA productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “to ensure adequate oxygen supplies … stirring (600 rpm) … the pH controller” (Sec 2.5); “we optimized the stirring rate from 100 to 800 rpm … When the stirring rate was greater than 600 rpm, it was estimated that the k_La value could be around a level of 100 s⁻¹” (Discussion).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The Core‑Chaykovsky epoxidation of intermediate 2 using sodium methoxide gave very low conversion – up to 70 % of 2 remained unreacted (Table 1, entry 1).
Solution_Description: Switch to a stronger base – potassium tert‑butoxide (1.5–2.0 equiv) or potassium hydroxide (1.5 equiv) – in acetonitrile. Full conversion was achieved (remaining 2 ≤ 0.5 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, we made efforts on reproducing Corey–Chaykovsky epoxidation of 2 by sodium methoxide, but … up to 70 % unreacted 2 was left over” (sec 2.1). “Potassium tert‑butoxide … proved superior to achieve a higher conversion” (Table 1, entry 5). “Potassium hydroxide … gave superior results with full conversion (remaining 2 ≤ 0.5 %)” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Purification of intermediate 3 required high‑temperature (100–102 °C) and high‑vacuum (1 mmHg) fractional distillation; the oil bath had to exceed 150 °C, which is unsafe and impractical for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Fractional distillation was completely eliminated and replaced by a robust crystallization step followed by an aqueous work‑up, giving high‑purity material without extreme temperature/vacuum.
Supporting_Evidence: “Purification of 3 … due to the need of fractional distillation at high temperature (100–102 °C) and high vacuum (1 mmHg)… oil bath even needed to be set at more than 150 °C, which was unacceptable for scale‑up” (sec 2.1). “Fractional distillation has been completely replaced by a robust crystallization method and an aqueous work‑up procedure” (abstract).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The nucleophilic ring‑opening substitution used sodium hydride, which released large amounts of hydrogen gas and required high‑temperature (>170 °C) fractional distillation, posing explosion and safety risks.
Solution_Description: Replace NaH with potassium hydroxide in DMSO (KOH–DMSO ‘superbase’). The reaction proceeds safely at moderate temperature, and DSC shows decomposition only above 235 °C, greatly improving process safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conditions for Step 2 also posed safety risks … due to the release of a substantial amount of overwhelming hydrogen gas caused by the use of sodium hydride” (introduction). “We proposed that a relatively weaker base such as sodium or potassium hydroxide might perfectly balance the reactivity and safety risks… KOH–DMSO combination … proved to be a unique ‘superbase’… DSC test … mixture started decomposition at 235.56 °C” (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The conventional Corey–Chaykovsky reagents TMSI and TMSOI are expensive because they require iodide, making them unattractive for large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: Adopt the inexpensive KOH–DMSO ‘superbase’ as the epoxidizing system, eliminating the need for costly iodide reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both TMSOI and TMSI suffer from higher cost, resulting from the usage of uneconomical and less atom‑economical iodide. Therefore, neither TMSOI nor TMSI was selected for further development” (sec 2.1). “Potassium hydroxide in combination with dimethyl sulfoxide (KOH–DMSO combination) was proven to be a unique ‘superbase’… we also wondered whether potassium hydroxide … could work” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: When NaH was used as the base for the ring‑opening step, impurity 16 accumulated up to 8.1 % (Table 3, entry 1), lowering overall purity and yield.
Solution_Description: Switch to potassium hydroxide (1.5 equiv) which cuts impurity 16 to ≤ 3.8 %; further reduction achieved by controlling the aqueous work‑up pH (≈ 6.84) and using isopropyl ether as the extraction solvent, allowing selective removal of impurity 16.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, impurity 16 could reach up to 8.1 % employing sodium hydride as the base (Table 3, entry 1)” (sec 2.2). “After changing from sodium hydride to potassium hydroxide … impurity 16 was significantly reduced to 3.8 % or 3.4 %” (sec 2.2). “pH of 6.84 yielded superior extraction results… IPE proved superior to MTBE as an extraction solvent” (Table 4, sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Control Strategy of Penehyclidine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Direct salt formation of 1‑HCl failed to precipitate; attempts in various solvents (EtOAc, MeCN, iPrOAc, THF, acetone) gave clear solutions, and addition of antisolvents produced only oily precipitates, hindering isolation.
Solution_Description: Adopt isopropyl ether (IPE) as the antisolvent and adjust the aqueous phase pH to 6.84–7.0 during extraction; this enables effective crystallization of 1‑HCl with ≥ 99.9 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “1‑HCl could not precipitate … could be dissolved … forming a clear solution… only oily precipitate could be obtained” (sec 2.2). “IPE proved superior to MTBE … pH of 6.84 yielded superior extraction results … acceptable levels of material loss and impurity” (Table 4, sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: The conventional synthesis of bis‑benzimidazole 5 uses nitration with nitric/sulfuric acid and a cyclization in polyphosphoric acid (PPA), which generates hazardous acidic waste and poses safety and environmental risks.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic route was designed that eliminates the nitration step and the PPA‑mediated cyclization, proceeding instead from commercially available 3‑methyl‑4‑nitrobenzoic acid and 2‑chloronitrobenzene to the key intermediate 5.
Supporting_Evidence: “...avoids undesired nitration using nitric/sulfuric acid and cyclization in PPA.”; “In the past few decades, several alternative approaches have been evaluated… the common pitfalls… high costs, hazardous processes.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: The previously reported copper‑catalyzed cyclization of o‑haloarylamidines suffers from an unstable chlorination intermediate 16, which decomposes and makes scale‑up unreliable.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to bromination of aniline 10 with elemental bromine, a stable electrophile. Bromine was added portion‑wise via a nitrogen‑purge bag to control exotherm, and the reaction was quenched with sodium bisulfite.
Supporting_Evidence: “unstable chlorination intermediate 16 impedes the scaling‑up…”; “bromine… low cost and ease of product isolation… added via a nitrogen purge bag to control the exotherm… Sodium bisulfite was found to be an effective reagent for quenching unreacted bromine.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: Reduction of nitro groups in compound 9 using iron‑acetic acid gave only a modest 70 % isolated yield with side‑products and was deemed unsuitable for large scale.
Solution_Description: A Pt/C‑catalyzed hydrogenation in ethanol at 90 °C was employed, delivering the desired aniline 10 in 95 % isolated yield and enabling kilogram‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: “initial use of iron–acetic acid… modest yield (70 %)… was deemed less suitable for scale‑up.”; “hydrogenation was performed using Pt/C in ethanol at 90 °C (optimum reaction conditions)… 95 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: Bromination of aniline 10 with N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) or dibromantine gave incomplete conversion, significant dibromination side‑product 11A, and overall isolated yields of 70–82 %.
Solution_Description: Elemental bromine in methanol at 25 °C was used; bromine was added slowly under cooling, and the reaction mixture was quenched with sodium bisulfite, resulting in 96 % isolated yield of 11 with only trace 11A.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using NBS… 82 % isolated yield, dibromination 11A (5–10 % HPLC).” ; “Conversion and isolated yields obtained upon bromine application were found to be significantly higher… 96 % isolated yield… bromine in methanol at 25 °C.” ; “Sodium bisulfite was found to be an effective reagent for quenching unreacted bromine.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: The initial copper‑catalyzed cyclization of 2‑bromoarylamine 11 with n‑butyramide afforded only a 50 % yield of bis‑benzimidazole 5.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified CuI (or CuBr) as the optimal catalyst, t‑BuOK as the most effective base, t‑BuOH as the preferred solvent, and a reaction time of 48 h (optimized by DoE) giving a 95 % isolated yield of 5.
Supporting_Evidence: “CuI… most effective catalyst… 50 % yield of 5.” ; “t‑BuOK… afforded the highest product yield among all the screened bases.” ; “t‑BuOH was identified as the most suitable solvent… 68 % yield.” ; “DoE optimization… optimum reaction time 48 h… predicted and experimental yields of 5 96 % and 95 % respectively.”

Paper Title: Optimized Synthesis of the Key Intermediate of Telmisartan via the Cyclization of 2‑Bromoarylamine with
Problem_Description: The cyclization step required prolonged reaction times (up to 48 h) to reach high conversion, which could limit productivity.
Solution_Description: A Design‑of‑Experiments (DoE) study was used to simultaneously optimize reaction time, t‑BuOK equiv, and nitrile equiv, confirming 48 h as the optimal duration for maximal yield and purity, thereby providing a rational basis for scheduling and scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “A Design of Experiment (DoE) approach was adopted… limits of the three variables as 24–48 h for the reaction time… optimum reaction conditions… 48 h, 4.0, and 2.9… predicted and experimental yields of 5 97 % and 96 % respectively.”

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale GMP Synthesis of Renewable Semisynthetic Vaccine-Grade Squalene
Problem_Description: The low‑temperature (‑78 °C) CuI‑mediated coupling of farnesyl chloride (RSM1) and farnesyl p‑tolylsulfone (RSM2) proceeded poorly, gave significant amounts of a sulfone trimer impurity, and left 10–20 % of starting material unreacted. Moreover, maintaining ‑78 °C was not feasible at kilogram scale, and the required temperature control equipment could only reach ‑45 °C.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Base (KOtBu) was added in eight equal portions while keeping the reactor at –45 ± 5 °C, followed by a controlled warm‑up to 0–5 °C over 5–7 h. This staged addition and temperature ramp minimized trimer formation, drove the reaction to >90 % conversion, and kept impurity levels below the 2.5 % limit required for downstream purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The reactions did not proceed very cleanly, and significant amounts of an unknown byproduct ... were formed..." (Table 1 description)

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale GMP Synthesis of Renewable Semisynthetic Vaccine-Grade Squalene
Problem_Description: The reductive desulfonylation step generated highly pyrophoric trialkyl‑borane species (LiEt₃BH) that are not fully quenched by simple methanol washes, posing a fire and explosion hazard during work‑up.
Solution_Description: After the reduction, the reaction mixture was quenched with cold water and then partitioned with 25 % aqueous NH₄Cl. Multiple heptane/MeOH extractions were performed to remove residual borane by‑products, and the safety note recommends further treatment with excess base followed by H₂O₂ if needed. This thorough quench and extraction sequence eliminates pyrophoric species before solvent removal.
Supporting_Evidence: • "These heptane/MeOH extractions are critical to ensure the removal of boron species ... which are still pyrophoric" (Safety Note)

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale GMP Synthesis of Renewable Semisynthetic Vaccine-Grade Squalene
Problem_Description: The crude squalene obtained after desulfonylation contained ~90 % purity (by GC‑IPC) but required >97 wt % purity for pharmacopeial specifications; conventional fractional distillation could not separate closely related double‑bond isomers and residual sulfone trimer.
Solution_Description: An inclusion‑complex crystallization using thiourea in methanol/heptane was developed. The squalene‑thiourea clathrate precipitates, allowing removal of impurities upon filtration and subsequent decomposition of the clathrate to release >99 % pure squalene, meeting EP specifications without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • "We devised the protocol ... which provided high‑purity squalene (>99%) meeting the EP purity specification" (Sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale GMP Synthesis of Renewable Semisynthetic Vaccine-Grade Squalene
Problem_Description: Many reducing agents caused double‑bond migration and isomerization of the squalene skeleton during desulfonylation, leading to variable product composition and lower purity.
Solution_Description: A Pd(dppb)Cl₂ catalyst (0.0025 equiv) with 1 M LiEt₃BH (1.2 equiv) was employed at 7–15 °C, followed by stirring at ~20 °C until <3 % sulfone remained. This combination gave the highest squalene purity (up to 89 % isolated yield) while suppressing isomerization.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The best conditions identified thus involved treatment of the squalene sulfone at 7–15 °C with Pd(dppb)Cl₂ (0.0025 equiv) and 1 M LiEt₃BH ..." (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Kilo-Scale GMP Synthesis of Renewable Semisynthetic Vaccine-Grade Squalene
Problem_Description: The addition of KOtBu base is slightly exothermic, and uncontrolled addition could raise the temperature above the set point, risking side‑product formation and compromising reaction control at scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Base was added portionwise (in eight portions over 30–45 min) with continuous temperature monitoring, keeping the internal temperature at –45 ± 5 °C. This controlled addition mitigated the exotherm and maintained reaction homogeneity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "As the addition of the base is slightly exothermic, it was added in portions to maintain the reaction temperature around the –45 °C set point." (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Ph
Problem_Description: When the hydrolysis of BrCF₂CO₂Et was performed at temperatures above 20 °C (40–80 °C), an unknown –CF₂– by‑product appeared, making the isolation of the desired BrCF₂CO₂K difficult.
Solution_Description: The authors kept the reaction temperature at ≤ 20 °C by adding BrCF₂CO₂Et slowly over ~2 h to the KOH/EtOH mixture while using ethanol as the solvent, which suppressed the formation of the by‑product and gave clean product.
Supporting_Evidence: “the hydrolysis proceeded very well at different temperatures…especially, the reaction at 20 °C was very clean…under heating conditions (entries 2–4)…an unknown –CF₂– byproduct was detected…difficulties in the purification of BrCF₂CO₂K.”; “the hydrolysis reaction is exothermic…BrCF₂CO₂Et has to be added slowly (about 2 h)…temperature needs to be kept under 20 °C by an ice bath.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Ph
Problem_Description: Mixing BrCF₂CO₂Et with KOH released a large amount of heat (ΔH ≈ ‑138 kJ mol⁻¹), which could raise the reaction temperature enough to decompose BrCF₂CO₂K and generate the unknown impurity.
Solution_Description: The addition of BrCF₂CO₂Et was performed portion‑wise over two hours while the reaction mixture was cooled in an ice bath, keeping the temperature below 20 °C and preventing decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “The hydrolysis reaction is exothermic, and its enthalpy change…has been determined…to be –137.71 kJ mol⁻¹…BrCF₂CO₂Et has to be added slowly (about 2 h)…temperature needs to be kept under 20 °C by an ice bath.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Ph
Problem_Description: BrCF₂CO₂K decomposes even at 40 °C in DMF, producing unknown species; using excess Ph₃P to drive the quaternization would increase material cost without improving yield.
Solution_Description: The quaternization of Ph₃P with BrCF₂CO₂K was carried out at room temperature without heating, avoiding the temperature‑induced decomposition and allowing a 1:1 stoichiometry to keep the process economical.
Supporting_Evidence: “BrCF₂CO₂K would decompose even at 40 °C in DMF to produce some unknown species…Therefore, the quaternization…was carried out without being heated…the reaction temperature was only slightly higher than room temperature…a good yield (77 %) was obtained on kilogram scale.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Ph
Problem_Description: After quaternization, the reaction mixture contains KBr and residual solvents (water, acetone, ethyl ether) that must be removed to isolate pure PDFA.
Solution_Description: A sequential washing protocol—first with water to remove KBr, then with acetone (which does not dissolve PDFA) to eliminate water, and finally with ethyl ether to strip residual acetone—was employed, yielding a dry, analytically pure PDFA.
Supporting_Evidence: “PDFA was purified by a convenient washing process. …Water is used to remove this byproduct. After washing with water, a water‑soluble solvent, acetone, which cannot dissolve PDFA, is used to remove water. Finally, ethyl ether is used as a washing agent to remove residual acetone … allowing easy drying of PDFA under vacuum.”

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Ph
Problem_Description: On kilogram scale the hydrolysis mixture became viscous, making stirring and efficient mass‑transfer difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration was adjusted to ~0.9 M (1.2 L EtOH for 6 mol BrCF₂CO₂Et) and vigorous stirring with an ice‑bath‑cooled jacket was used to maintain homogeneity and adequate heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: “The hydrolysis reaction was performed on kilogram scale using 1.2 L ethanol for 6 mol BrCF₂CO₂Et…the reaction temperature was kept under 20 °C by an ice bath…the solution was concentrated via rotary evaporator.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: Incomplete alkylation of the sodium salt of cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (14) gave only ~86 % conversion and generated side‑products (e.g., 1‑pentanone 19) that raised concerns about robustness and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Isolate and dry salt 14 before alkylation; generate lithium‑diethylamide in‑situ with 10 mol % catalytic amine, which raised conversion to 85‑90 % and reduced side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Isolating and drying salt 14 before alkylation proved most effective.", "Alkylation efficiency improved when lithium diethylamide was used instead of lithium diisopropylamide and additionally when the lithioamide base was generated in situ.", "The post‑alkylation workup was also optimized to selectively remove unreacted salt 14 (or acid 3)."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: Lithium‑based bases (n‑BuLi, LDA) reacted with THF, forming ketone 19 and butenyl acids, indicating lithio‑species decomposition and posing safety/robustness concerns.
Solution_Description: Replace lithio bases with methylmagnesium chloride (MMC) together with catalytic diethylamine (DEA); later‑addition of MMC to the reaction mixture eliminates THF‑related side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The 1‑pentanone derivative 19 was formed at up to 2 % levels.", "Using MMC in conjunction with catalytic quantities of diethylamine (DEA) to mediate deprotonation proved to work very well in the alkylation of nitrile 10.", "Attempts to employ MMC in the alkylation of esters were unsuccessful, as the amine catalyst was consumed in the process of amide formation.", "The principal side‑products formed in MMC‑mediated alkylation of nitrile 10 were acetyl‑cyclohexane (31), aminoenone (32) and the n‑butanol derivative (33). Faster rates of MMC addition increased the levels of side‑products 31 and 32, but all remained <1 %."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of sterically hindered esters 23 and 25 was very slow (up to 42 h at 160 °C) and gave only partial conversion, limiting overall yield (≈75‑80 %).
Solution_Description: Adopt acidic hydrolysis using HBr/acetic acid with catalytic NaI, giving 94 % yield of acid 2 in a shorter time and improving selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For ethyl ester 25, Gassmann’s hydrolysis conditions, which involve the use of potassium tert‑butoxide in the presence of a small amount of water, were superior to using potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol.", "However, these conditions only partially converted isopropyl ester 23 despite prolonged heating, while potassium hydroxide in ethylene glycol yielded 60 % of acid 2 after treatment for 42 h at 160 °C.", "Employing HBr/acetic acid with a catalytic amount of sodium iodide led to a slow but high‑quality conversion to acid 2 (99.3 % by GC area%) in 94 % yield."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: Acidic hydrolysis using nitrosylsulfuric acid (NSA) presented safety hazards (exothermicity, tar formation above 120 °C, limited commercial suppliers).
Solution_Description: Develop an alkaline hydrolysis route with NaOH in methanol/water at 200 °C, which uses inexpensive, widely available reagents and avoids the hazardous NSA step.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Both approaches are discussed in detail in the following section.", "The acidic conditions developed for the hydrolysis of nitrile 12 to acid 2 involved hydrolysis of nitrile 12 to the amide 34 with aqueous sulfuric acid, followed by diazotization and hydrolysis of the amide with nitrosylsulfuric acid (NSA)... Both steps are exothermic, making the control of temperatures and addition rates crucial.", "The two exothermic steps… decomposition into tar‑like material occurs at temperatures exceeding 120 °C.", "The basic approach involved the hydrolysis of 12 to acid 2 with sodium hydroxide in a mixture of methanol and water at 200 °C."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: The two‑step acidic hydrolysis (sulfuric acid then NSA) released large amounts of heat, requiring strict temperature and addition‑rate control to prevent decomposition and formation of hazardous nitrous/nitric acids.
Solution_Description: Implement controlled temperature ramps and slow addition of reagents, maintaining the first step below 120 °C and the second below 70 °C, with cooling and staged addition to manage the exotherms safely.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The preferred sequence involved adding nitrile 12 to a mixture of water and sulfuric acid at approximately 110 °C, partially cooling the resulting amide 34, diluting with water, and then adding NSA for the diazotization step… Both steps are exothermic, making the control of temperatures and addition rates crucial.", "In the first hydrolysis reaction, decomposition into tar‑like material occurs at temperatures exceeding 120 °C.", "In the second reaction, decomposition of NSA occurs at temperatures above 70 °C (particularly at higher water concentrations), which can result in an incomplete reaction."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: All‑water alkaline hydrolysis at 250 °C caused severe corrosion of the Hastelloy C‑22 autoclave, limiting the feasibility of a water‑only process.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to a nickel continuous‑flow reactor equipped with SMX static mixing elements, which resists corrosion and provides efficient mixing, allowing high‑temperature water‑only hydrolysis without reactor damage.
Supporting_Evidence: ["While at 205 °C in methanol/water, no corrosion of Hastelloy C‑22 was detected in either laboratory or plant, at 250 °C in water alone, significant corrosion was observed in the laboratory Hastelloy C‑22 autoclave.", "No corrosion was observed when all parts of the autoclave that came into contact with the reaction mixture were made of nickel.", "Further experiments were thus conducted in a continuous‑flow reactor made from nickel… equipped with SMX static plus mixing elements… to enable continuous mixing of the two solvent streams along the entire heated reaction zone."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: During alkaline hydrolysis in methanol/water, ketone 31 was reduced to 1‑cyclohexylethanol 38, generating an additional impurity that required extra purification steps.
Solution_Description: Perform the hydrolysis in water only (no methanol) to prevent reduction of ketone 31; optionally add a small amount of acid 2 as a phase‑transfer catalyst to improve reaction rate without forming alcohol 38.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In the plant demonstration of the alkaline hydrolysis of nitrile 12, the only impurities present were traces of nitrile 12, amide 34, cyclohexanecarboxylic acid 3, and somewhat surprisingly, 1‑cyclohexylethanol 38.", "It was known that the nitrile 12 used in the campaign contained up to 0.1 % of both acetyl‑cyclohexane 31 and aminoenone 32, and it was expected that under the strongly alkaline conditions, 32 would cleave to 31 and the sodium salt of cyclohexanecarboxylic acid 14. However, it seemed that the reduction of ketone 31 to alcohol 38 had occurred.", "Laboratory runs were conducted using only water as a solvent. Higher temperatures were required than in methanol/water, but reaction completion was achieved in 17 h at 250 °C."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: 2‑Ethylbutyl bromide 4 reacted faster but is more expensive and generates more waste than the corresponding chloride 29, which also required a hazardous chlorination step.
Solution_Description: Use 2‑ethylbutyl chloride 29 as the alkylating agent in the MMC‑mediated alkylation; chloride is cheaper, produces less halogen waste, and integrates better with lithium‑recycling streams.
Supporting_Evidence: ["However, it was observed that bromo compound 4 reacted much faster than chloro compound 29.", "The use of the chloride 29 would also facilitate lithium recycling, as lithium chloride is the principal feedstock in the lithium manufacturing processes.", "The chloride 29 performed as well as the corresponding bromide 4, which is significant as the chlorination step involved in the manufacture of chloride 29 from 2‑ethylbutanol is cleaner than the comparable bromination, and the chloride 29 is potentially significantly cheaper than the bromide 4."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: Early continuous‑flow alkaline hydrolysis required long residence times (up to 4 h) and suffered from blockage due to solid NaOH precipitation, limiting throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Upgrade to a nickel flow reactor with SMX static mixers, increase NaOH equivalents (up to 10 mol), raise temperature to 300 °C, and reduce residence time to 30 min while maintaining >98 % conversion, eliminating blockages and improving space‑time yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Using this improved continuous‑flow setup, reaction conditions were again systematically evaluated… The best results were achieved using nitrile 12 (0.8 M) in tert‑butanol and an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide (1.0 M; pumped at a ratio of 1:4) at 300 °C for 1 h, resulting in 99.2 % conversion to acid 2.", "Employing 10 mol equiv of NaOH (2.0 M solution; pumped at a ratio of 1:4) under identical reaction conditions led to a conversion of 99.9 %, demonstrating the superior mixing behavior of this flow reactor compared to the previous system.", "The improved mixing properties of this system enabled an even further reduction of the residence time down to 30 min, albeit at the expense of an increase of sodium hydroxide to 10 mol equiv in order to achieve a conversion of 98.2 % to acid 2."]

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a High-Volume Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate of Dalcetrapib: Investigations on the Alkylation of Carboxylic Acids, Esters, and Nitriles
Problem_Description: When using undistilled nitrile 12 in the acidic hydrolysis campaign, emulsions formed during work‑up, leading to inconsistent product isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employ freshly distilled nitrile 12 to eliminate impurities that cause emulsions; optimize addition rates, agitation, and cooling during the hydrolysis to obtain reproducible phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A 6‑batch plant hydrolysis campaign was conducted with freshly distilled nitrile 12… past experience had shown that emulsions could pose a problem during workup when undistilled nitrile 12 was used as the starting material.", "Reaction conditions (such as temperature and dosing rate) and engineering aspects (like agitation and cooling) were optimized during the first two batches, yielding excellent results."]

Paper Title: Selectivity of Grignard Reagent Formation: From Semibatch to Continuous Lab and Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: The Grignard reaction shows varying induction periods caused by a passivating Mg‑oxide layer and traces of moisture, leading to unpredictable start‑up times and safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A jogging motor mounted in the reactor cartridge continuously vibrates the magnesium turnings, abrading the oxide layer and providing in‑situ activation, which shortens incubation periods and reduces the risk of moisture‑related delays.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "varying induction periods due to a passivating oxide layer on the magnesium surface or due to traces of moisture"; "Insufficient activation of the magnesium surface or residual moisture can result in extended incubation periods". 
Solution: "jogging motor … abrades the passivating oxide layer … leads to shorter incubation periods, an earlier start of the reaction, and potentially a higher halide conversion".

Paper Title: Selectivity of Grignard Reagent Formation: From Semibatch to Continuous Lab and Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: The Grignard formation is highly exothermic; uncontrolled heat release can cause a thermal runaway, especially when halide accumulates before the reaction starts.
Solution_Description: Continuous flow feeding of the halide maintains a constant concentration and a small reactive volume, while temperature monitoring and automatic pump shut‑off stop the feed if the temperature rises sharply, preventing runaway.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "high exothermicity with the risk of a potential run‑away reaction"; "Accumulated halide can result in a sudden and vigorous start of the reaction and lead to a thermal runaway". 
Solution: "Such an event is less problematic for a continuous production process in which the halide is constantly pumped through a reactor filled with magnesium"; "In case of a thermal runaway, turn off the pump to stop the addition of the halide/solvent mixture".

Paper Title: Selectivity of Grignard Reagent Formation: From Semibatch to Continuous Lab and Pilot Scale
Problem_Description: Formation of the Wurtz coupling side‑product lowers the amount and purity of the desired Grignard reagent, especially for Wurtz‑affine substrates.
Solution_Description: Using a packed‑bed reactor with a large excess of magnesium and a narrow residence‑time distribution reduces back‑mixing, limiting the contact time between halide and already‑formed Grignard and thus suppressing Wurtz coupling.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "side‑product formation such as the Wurtz coupling product … diminishes the Grignard reagent quantity and product quality"; "continuous production process can improve Grignard reagent selectivity and reduce Wurtz coupling". 
Solution: "The continuous process provides higher selectivity … due to the narrow residence time distribution and reduced backmixing"; "Because of the continuous provision of a halide educt and a magnesium excess, the reaction rate remains high, whereas the Wurtz coupling reaction is slower".

Problem_Description: Higher halide concentrations increase the probability of Wurtz coupling, leading to lower selectivity, especially with coarse magnesium turnings.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employing fine magnesium turnings creates a more compact bed with higher surface area and a narrower residence‑time distribution, mitigating back‑mixing and suppressing side‑product formation even at higher concentrations.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "An increased halide concentration leads to increased side product formation"; "Higher concentrations increase the likelihood that the halide and Grignard reagent will meet and form the corresponding Wurtz product". 
Solution: "higher selectivities … can be achieved with the use of fine magnesium turnings"; "fine magnesium turnings … provide a more compact magnesium bed, the narrower particle size distribution, and the higher surface area".

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: The original metal‑halogen exchange step required cryogenic conditions (‑78 °C) with alkyl‑metal reagents, which exceeds the standard process‑equipment temperature window (‑20 °C to 120 °C) and is therefore a temperature‑range limitation.
Solution_Description: Implemented a continuous‑flow plug‑flow reactor (glass static‑mixer) operated at ­50 °C with an 8 s residence time, allowing the metal‑halogen exchange to be performed safely under non‑cryogenic conditions and eliminating the need for batch cryogenic reactors.
Supporting_Evidence: “The metal‑halogen exchange reaction was demonstrated to be amenable to continuous flow…a 2 mL glass static mixer…was used as the PFR reactor at ‑50 °C…the reaction resulted in 94.3 % assay yield.”; “Under the optimized conditions, on a 5 g scale, 1 was obtained in 82.8 % yield following workup and isolation by crystallization.”; “A continuous‑flow cryogenic…potential solution to address the concerns of anion stability and scalability on production scales.”

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: Organolithium (n‑BuLi, n‑HexLi) and isopropyl‑magnesium bromide reagents decompose rapidly at temperatures above ‑40 °C, limiting the metal‑halogen exchange to cryogenic conditions and posing safety hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to continuous‑flow processing, which provides rapid heat removal and precise temperature control, thereby stabilizing the reactive anion and permitting operation at higher temperatures without decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “The metalated species generated from n‑butyl lithium…decomposed rapidly at ‑40 °C and above, limiting the temperature range of the reaction under batch conditions.”; “Continuous flow at cryogenic temperatures was considered a potential solution to address the concerns of anion stability and scalability on production scales.”

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: The reductive dehalogenation using sodium sulfite required 160–180 °C for 5 h and a labor‑intensive work‑up, exceeding temperature limits and causing long equipment occupancy.
Solution_Description: Developed a lower‑temperature dehalogenation using sodium dithionite (10 equiv) in DMF/water (1:1) at 100 °C, albeit with a long reaction time; attempted to accelerate by acid addition, which proved ineffective, highlighting the need for alternative routes.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reductive dehalogenation proceeded at 100 °C with sodium dithionite…but required ∼120 h to reach reaction completion; attempts to reduce the equivalents of reducing agents or increase the reaction rate with the addition of acids were unsuccessful.”; “While both methods were suitable on multikilogram scales, the procedures suffered from production process constraints as the reaction conditions exceeded the standard process equipment temperature range of ‑20 to 120 °C…required strenuous workup and isolation.”

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: Bromination of pyrazole‑4‑carboxylic acid (3) gave tribromopyrazole (2) as the major product; attempts to stop at the dibrominated intermediate failed, leading to low selectivity and longer processing times.
Solution_Description: Switched to the ethyl ester (5) as the starting material; bromination of the ester in ethanol/water with NaOAc gave the desired dibromopyrazole (6) in excellent yield, providing a more selective and efficient pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: “Bromination of 3 did not result in the expected dibromopyrazole 4, and instead, tribromopyrazole 2 was obtained as the major product…We turned our attention toward the use of ethyl ester 5 as the starting material. Dibromopyrazole 6 was obtained in excellent yields when 5 was treated with bromine and sodium acetate in an ethanol/water mixture.”

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: During the one‑pot conversion of dibromopyrazole 6 to the target product 1 under strong acidic conditions in the presence of ethanol, the product underwent N‑ethylation to give impurity 7b, reducing overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: Implemented a two‑stage, one‑pot saponification/decarboxylation: first saponify with aqueous NaOH, then add concentrated H₂SO₄ slowly while keeping the temperature below 60 °C; evaporate ethanol before decarboxylation and raise temperature to ~110 °C for 6 h, which avoids N‑ethylation and affords product 1 in 73 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The saponification was readily achieved using aqueous sodium hydroxide…In the same pot, concentrated sulfuric acid was added. This was a highly exothermic operation but was readily controlled with the rate of addition while keeping the reaction at below 60 °C…Prior to decarboxylation, ethanol generated during the hydrolysis was evaporated completely. The reaction temperature was subsequently increased to ∼110 °C for 6 h to achieve decarboxylation…This one‑pot protocol successfully avoided the formation of 7b and provided 1 in 73 % yield.”

Paper Title: Evaluation and Removal of Production Process Constraints in the Synthesis of 3,5-Dibromopyrazole
Problem_Description: In the continuous‑flow metal‑halogen exchange, longer residence times (11–33 s) reduced assay yield from 94.3 % to 91.0 %, indicating sensitivity to residence time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Economical and Practical Process Development for a Novel Multitarget Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Vorolanib
Problem_Description: The existing patented synthesis uses raw material 5 and the coupling reagent HATU, both of which are expensive, and the patent lacks detailed synthetic and post‑processing procedures, making the route financially unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Raw material 5 was replaced by the cheaper analogue 9 (price $0.75 g⁻¹ vs $1.30 g⁻¹) and the costly HATU ( $0.46 g⁻¹) was substituted with the inexpensive EDCI/HOBt couple ( $0.14 g⁻¹), reducing material cost while preserving high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "the high cost of raw material <bold>5</bold> leads to increased synthesis expenses."; "the high price of HATU hinders its industrial production feasibility."; "the existing patent lacks detailed descriptions regarding Vorolanib’s synthesis and postprocessing procedures."; Solution: "We substituted the costly coupling agent HATU ($0.46/g) with EDCI/HOBt ($0.14/g), resulting in a significant enhancement of industrial production feasibility while ensuring consistently high yields."; "the price of raw material <bold>9</bold> ($0.75/g) was much lower than that of raw material <bold>5</bold> ($1.3/g), which means that the synthesis cost is greatly reduced."

Paper Title: Economical and Practical Process Development for a Novel Multitarget Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Vorolanib
Problem_Description: Raw material 2 and the resulting intermediate 3 exhibit poor solubility in common solvents (DCM, EtOH, EtOAc), causing difficulty in removing excess material and lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: Industrial ethanol was selected as the reaction solvent, and the feeding ratio of 2 to 1 was optimized (≈0.95 : 1) to avoid excess undissolved material, which raised the isolated yield of 3 to 93.8 %.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "raw material <bold>2</bold> showed a low solubility similar to the intermediate <bold>3</bold> in common solvents such as DCM, EtOH, and EtOAc."; "Using an excess of <bold>2</bold> for the reaction will cause the remaining raw material to be difficult to remove after the end of the reaction, increasing the difficulty of postprocessing and leading to a decrease in yield."; Solution: "by adjusting the appropriate feeding ratio, the yield was increased to 93.8%"; "industrial ethanol was established as the solvent of choice for the reaction."

Paper Title: Economical and Practical Process Development for a Novel Multitarget Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Vorolanib
Problem_Description: Screening of bases revealed that inorganic bases gave poor conversion, and the amount of organic base (dimethylamine) dramatically affected the yield of the Claisen–Schmidt step.
Solution_Description: Dimethylamine was identified as the optimal base; using 1.2 equiv gave the best conversion (93.8 % yield), while higher equivalents did not improve the result, establishing a robust and reproducible protocol.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The results demonstrated that the organic base exhibited higher reaction efficiency compared to the inorganic base, highlighting excellent conversion when dimethylamine was employed as a base."; "The variations in the amount of dimethylamine to 1.2 equiv resulted in an increase in the yield, while further increasing it to 1.5 equiv did not lead to any improvement."; Solution: "dimethylamine was deemed as the optimal choice to facilitate the reaction."; "optimized conditions ... dimethylamine (1.2 mmol) in industrial ethanol ... 78 °C for 3 h ... yield 93.8 %"

Paper Title: Economical and Practical Process Development for a Novel Multitarget Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Vorolanib
Problem_Description: The original amide‑coupling step used expensive reagents (HATU, HBTU, TBTU, PyBOP) that gave low to moderate yields and required difficult chromatographic work‑up.
Solution_Description: EDCI/HOBt was adopted as the coupling system, and the additive HOBt (or DMAP) was employed to activate the carboxylate. The urea by‑product is water‑soluble, allowing simple aqueous work‑up and boosting the isolated yield of 10 to 80.5 %.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "high price of HATU ... not conducive to industrial production."; "HBTU and TBTU ... high molecular weight (which translates to a high cost per mole)."; "purfication of the product was difficult, resulting in significant loss and difficulties in achieving a clean removal, ultimately leading to a low yield."; Solution: "use EDCI/HOBt instead of HATU used in the patent for this reaction."; "EDCI/HOBt was more conducive to the reaction."; "the water solubility of the urea byproduct allows for its facile removal during the aqueous workup."

Paper Title: Economical and Practical Process Development for a Novel Multitarget Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Vorolanib
Problem_Description: Coupling at ambient temperature gave modest yields (≈60 %) whereas raising the temperature to 40 °C significantly increased the conversion.

Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "When the temperature in the coupling step was increased to 40 °C, the reaction yield was increased to 75.5 %; however, at 60 °C, the yield was not increased."; Solution: "optimum reaction conditions were obtained by using ... at 40 °C for 8 h."

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2

Supporting_Evidence: • “A cold quench of the reaction was adopted to mitigate the risk of racemization at ambient temperature in the presence of >1.5 equiv of borate salts.”

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2
Problem_Description: Base‑promoted side reactions generated impurity 13 (glutarimide) and its subsequent quaternary ammonium salt 14, which consumed product and lowered overall yield and enantiopurity.
