Solution_Description: Stoichiometry of K₂CO₃ and benzylic chloride 4 was tightly controlled (0.99 equiv 4 per 3, K₂CO₃:4 = 1:1.9). A catalytic amount of Et₄NBr (10 mol %) and a small water loading (4 wt %) were added to improve base solubility and suppress impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of K₂CO₃ required us to impose stoichiometry restrictions to minimize base‑promoted glutarimide formation… The inclusion of Et₄NBr and a small amount of water greatly improved the robustness and imparted stability….”

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2
Problem_Description: Water present in the glutarimide cyclization led to hydrolysis of the intermediate 15 and formation of carboxylic‑acid impurities 15–17, especially when using the monohydrate form of BSA.
Solution_Description: A constant‑volume MeCN distillation (CVD) was employed to remove water via the MeCN/H₂O azeotrope while heating at 82 °C; anhydrous BSA was used, and the reaction time was limited to 3.5 h before seeding, minimizing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We proposed a strategy to perform a constant‑volume distillation with MeCN that takes advantage of the MeCN/H₂O azeotrope… Inclusion of the distillation technique led to demonstrably faster reactions… and lower levels of water‑related impurities 15–17.”

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2
Problem_Description: Higher BSA stoichiometry (≥2 equiv) accelerated the rate of stereochemical erosion of the product 1·BSA at 80–82 °C, reducing enantiopurity.
Solution_Description: The optimal BSA charge was set to 1.3 ± 0.1 equiv, with a fixed 3.5 h constant‑volume distillation at 82 °C followed by rapid cooling and seeding, limiting the exposure time that leads to racemization.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The optimized operational stoichiometry window… was 1.3 ± 0.1 equiv. … The reaction was maintained at 82 °C for 3.5 h… The rate of stereochemical ablation was <0.02 %/h after seeding and cooling.”

Paper Title: Chirality Control in the Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 2
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, prolonged exposure of the cyclized product 1·BSA at 80–82 °C caused linear racemization (0.15–0.27 % h⁻¹), risking failure to meet the ≥98:2 e.r. specification.
Solution_Description: Reaction time at the high temperature was limited (≤3.5 h) and then the mixture was cooled to ≤60 °C before seeding; this reduced the racemization rate to <0.02 % h⁻¹ during the aging step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We preferred short reaction times at T_i = 82 °C… the rate of stereochemical ablation was nearly linear… the reaction was cooled to 60 °C… where the rate of stereochemical ablation was <0.02 %/h.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: During the SN2 alkylation of α,α′‑dichloro‑p‑xylene (14) with morpholine (15) to afford benzylic chloride 11, a bis‑alkylation impurity 16 formed. 16 has low solubility in the reaction medium and co‑exists as a bis‑HCl salt, making it difficult to separate from the desired product and consuming base in downstream steps.
Solution_Description: An exogenous base (K₂CO₃) was added and the stoichiometry of 14 and 15 was tuned (Table 1, entries 3–9). 1.05–1.80 equiv of K₂CO₃ and increased equivalents of 14 shifted the product ratio toward 11 and reduced 16 formation. Iso‑propyl acetate (i‑PrOAc) was retained as the optimal solvent for its balance of reactivity and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The approach resulted in the formation of 11 as well as the bisalkylation impurity 16, which required purging during the isolation of 11.", "The use of i‑PrOAc emerged from a screen where this solvent showed a preferable balance of reactivity and selectivity for 11 versus 16.", "Entries 3–5 demonstrate that for a given charge of K₂CO₃, an increase in the stoichiometry of 14 led to a higher AY of 11 with an associated decrease in the 11:16 ratio.", "The optimal conditions (entry 8) were implemented on scale and delivered 11 in improved AY and 11·HCl in 15% higher isolated yield compared to the enabling route."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: Even after optimizing the SN2 step, residual bis‑alkylation impurity 16 persisted at low levels (<0.25 LCAP) and needed to be removed efficiently before HCl‑salt formation of 11.
Solution_Description: A solubility‑driven salt‑metathesis extraction was developed using aqueous glycolic acid. The glycolic‑acid salt of 16 is highly water‑soluble, while the glycolic‑acid salt of 11 remains in the organic i‑PrOAc phase, allowing selective removal of 16.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The glycolic acid salt of 11 and the mono‑(glycolic acid) salt of 16 were predicted and shown to have considerable solubility in IPAc, whereas the bis‑(glycolic acid) salt of 16 was highly water‑soluble due to polarity.", "A glycolic acid charge of twice the amount of 16 present was predicted to form a mixture of interacting acid–base complexes that would funnel in the organic IPAc phase to the bis‑(glycolic acid) salt of 16, which would partition exclusively into the aqueous phase.", "The loss of 11 (as a glycolic acid salt) to the resulting aqueous phase was typically <2%, while 16 was reduced to <0.25 LCAP in the organic phase."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: The original discovery route formed the α‑amidoglutarimide via a base‑mediated cyclization under cryogenic conditions. The stereocenter was labile to base, causing epimerization and low, inconsistent yields, rendering the step unsuitable for kilogram‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The commercial route was redesigned to use an acid‑catalyzed glutarimide cyclization, eliminating the need for strong base and cryogenic temperatures, thereby preserving stereochemistry and improving robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The α‑amidoglutarimide was formed via base‑mediated cyclization of isoglutamine methyl ester 8 under cryogenic conditions, where retention of the chiral centre was under kinetic control.", "The strict limitations on reaction parameters and, more importantly, the lability of the stereocenter under basic conditions precluded the use of this chemistry on scale.", "An acid‑catalyzed glutarimide cyclization was employed to form 1·BSA."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: The Duff formylation of methyl 3‑hydroxybenzoate (18) generated a mixture of aldehydes (12, 19, 20) and a dimeric amine impurity (21). The target aldehyde 12 could not be crystallized directly, complicating isolation and scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in excess TFA (≥20 vol) at 65 °C, and the crude mixture was neutralized by simultaneous addition of aqueous K₂CO₃ under tight pH control (2.5–4.5). This enabled precipitation of 12 as a crystalline solid while rejecting 20 and 21. The pH‑controlled addition also minimized hydrolytic decomposition of the ester.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Duff formylation was used to prepare the salicylaldehyde building block, and the isolation of this compound was enabled by an innovative simultaneous addition of acidic and basic solutions.", "The targeted pH range was 2.5–4.5 (the former based on arguments above and the latter based on observations that impurity rejection decreased at pH >5.0).", "The AY of 12 was optimal using ≥20 volumes of TFA, as more concentrated conditions led to lower AY of 12 at the expense of 21.", "Variations in reaction temperature from Ti = 55 to 72 °C had only minor effects on the yields and 12:19 ratio."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: Compound 12 is hydrolytically unstable outside the pH 2–8 window; exposure to water or higher pH leads to ester hydrolysis and formation of side products, limiting extractive work‑up options.
Solution_Description: The isolation protocol employed simultaneous addition of the concentrated TFA reaction solution and aqueous K₂CO₃ while maintaining the pH between 2.5 and 4.5, preventing hydrolysis and allowing crystallization from water as antisolvent.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Attempts to isolate 12 were complicated by the hydrolytic instability of the ester moiety outside of the pH range of 2.0–8.0.", "A simultaneous addition of the concentrated final reaction solution of 12 and aqueous K₂CO₃ was adopted, with inclusion of IPA as a cosolvent for impurity rejection.", "The targeted pH range was 2.5–4.5 (the former based on arguments above and the latter based on observations that impurity rejection decreased at pH >5.0)."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: During synthesis of isoglutamine 23, the free acid 23 is unstable under acidic conditions, leading to decomposition if isolated directly from acidic mixtures, which would cause operational risk on scale.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was first isolated as the crystalline salt 27 (stable), then a controlled salt‑break with aqueous H₃PO₄ at pH 4.0 ± 0.2 was performed to generate solid 23, avoiding exposure to low pH bulk solutions.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Attempts to acidify the reaction mixture of 27 and isolate 23 as a neutral compound as part of an extractive workup were hampered by the instability of 23 in solution under acidic conditions.", "Fortunately, 27 was a stable crystalline solid that precipitated directly from reaction mixtures where the MeCN:H₂O volume ratio was >5:1. Therefore, we elected to isolate 27 and perform a separate reactive salt break crystallization to obtain 23.", "A slurry of 27 in MeCN was treated with aqueous H₃PO₄. The solid isoglutamine 23 was stable under these conditions, protected from acidic solution instability by remaining out of solution at pH 4.0 ± 0.2."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: Esterification of 23 to the t‑butyl ester 24 using O‑tert‑butyl‑N,N′‑diisopropylisourea generated large amounts of N,N′‑diisopropylurea and other by‑products; the isourea reagent itself decomposes under acidic conditions, complicating work‑up and lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: A large excess (≈4.4 equiv) of the isourea reagent was employed, and the reaction was run in 2‑MeTHF at 30–40 °C. Insoluble N,N′‑diisopropylurea was removed by filtration, and the remaining soluble impurity was washed away during crystallization from 2‑MeTHF/heptane, delivering 24 in 52–61 % isolated yield with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The reagent was identified as uniquely effective from an extensive screen of published t‑butyl ester formation procedures and was the only one that was reactive under mild conditions.", "The isourea reagent was prepared ... The neat crude reagent (4.4 equiv) was added slowly to a solution of 23 in 2‑MeTHF at Ti = 20 °C, and the resulting solution was heated to Ti = 35 °C.", "Insoluble N,N′‑diisopropylurea (∼90% of all formed) was removed via the filtration of the crude reaction mixture.", "The resulting solution was concentrated ... and the product was isolated via crystallization from 2‑MeTHF and n‑heptane."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: Residual Cu(II) salts from the isourea preparation carried over into 24 and inhibited the subsequent Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogenation of the N‑Cbz protecting group, posing a risk of metal contamination in the API.
Solution_Description: Aqueous NaHCO₃ wash was incorporated after the esterification step to extract Cu(II) ions, reducing Cu levels to <100 ppm and restoring efficient hydrogenation downstream.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The aqueous NaHCO₃ wash also incorporated Cu metal remediation by extracting water‑soluble CuII salts. This was important since residual CuII salts (>800 ppm in isolated 24) from the isourea reagent inhibited the subsequent Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogenation.", "Typical kilogram‑scale results over multiple batches afforded 24 with 99 % purity and >99.95:0.05 e.r. with <100 ppm residual Cu."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: Pd/C‑catalyzed N‑Cbz deprotection of 24 in IPA produced the carbamate by‑product 30, which precipitated and trapped Pd, making Pd removal difficult and generating an impurity burden.
Solution_Description: The hydrogenolysis was transferred to MeOH, where 30 remained soluble and no precipitation occurred. Reaction conditions (15 psi H₂, 25 °C, 2.6 wt % Pd/C) were optimized, and tri‑n‑octylphosphine was added later to keep residual Pd soluble during HCl‑salt formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["MeOH emerged as a promising solvent after parallel CO₂ sparging experiments in MeOH remained homogeneous under otherwise identical conditions to those in IPA.", "The best conditions utilized 2.6 wt % Pd/C (10 wt %), 8 volumes of MeOH, and 15 psi H₂ at Ti = 25 °C.", "An alternative approach was to solubilize Pd during HCl salt formation. Toward this end, tri‑n‑octylphosphine was introduced to this solution at Ti = 40 °C as a ligand for Pd to form a complex that was soluble in the crystallization liquors."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Kilogram-Scale Manufacture of Key Intermediates toward Single-Enantiomer CELMoDs: Synthesis of Iberdomide·BSA, Part 1
Problem_Description: The final HCl‑salt formation of intermediate 13 suffered from residual Pd and Cu contamination; conventional scavenger resins were ineffective, risking metal levels above specification.
Solution_Description: Tri‑n‑octylphosphine was added during the HCl‑salt formation to complex Pd, keeping it soluble in the IPA/IPA‑c solution, allowing removal by filtration and yielding product 13 with <10 ppm Pd and Cu.
Supporting_Evidence: ["An alternative approach was to solubilize Pd during HCl salt formation. Toward this end, tri‑n‑octylphosphine was introduced to this solution at Ti = 40 °C as a ligand for Pd to form a complex that was soluble in the crystallization liquors.", "This process has been executed on a kilogram scale over multiple batches to produce 13 with >99 % purity and >99.95:0.05 e.r. with low residual Pd and Cu (<10 ppm each)."]

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: The palladium‑catalyzed cyanation of triflate 6 gave inconsistent conversions – the reaction stopped at incomplete conversion when the addition of mixture A to mixture B took longer than ~40 min, but proceeded smoothly when the addition was rapid.
Solution_Description: The order of addition was reversed – a pre‑formed solution of Pd₂(dba)₃/dppf in DMF was added to a mixture of triflate 6 and Zn(CN)₂ at 90 °C – shortening the contact time and preventing catalyst deactivation. Pd(dba)₂ was also substituted for Pd₂(dba)₃ to use a readily available catalyst with equivalent activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the time from the preparation of mixture A to the completion of its addition was about 1 h, the reaction stopped at incomplete conversion… In contrast, the reaction proceeded smoothly when this time was less than 40 min.”; “We decided to shorten this contact time as much as possible and examined a new procedure in which a mixture of Pd₂(dba)₃ and dppf in DMF was added to a mixture of triflate 6 and Zn(CN)₂… gave a high reaction conversion (100%)”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required multiple protection/de‑protection steps for the carboxylic‑acid functionality (steps h–k), increasing the number of operations, reaction time and the cost of reagents.
Solution_Description: A shortened two‑step sequence was designed in which the nitrile was hydrolysed after morpholine substitution, eliminating the protection/de‑protection sequence and allowing telescoping of the nitrile‑to‑ester‑to‑acid steps without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The major issues… (2) protection/deprotection steps for the carboxylic acid moiety… (4) chromatographic purification… To streamline these reactions, we explored an alternative route in which hydrolysis of the nitrile moiety is performed after the introduction of the morpholine moiety to avoid the protection/deprotection steps.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: Zinc cyanide (Zn(CN)₂) is toxic and can generate hydrogen cyanide (HCN) gas, posing a safety hazard during large‑scale cyanation.
Solution_Description: After the cyanation, the work‑up incorporated aqueous NH₃ and sodium thiosulfate (Na₂S₂O₃) to quench residual cyanide, and HCN levels were continuously monitored with an external detector; personnel wore protective suits.
Supporting_Evidence: “Zn(CN)₂ is toxic and can liberate hydrogen cyanide (HCN) gas… In the manufacturing campaign, HCN concentration in the air was monitored… operators wore an appropriate chemical protective suit.”; “Na₂S₂O₃ was added to quench the residual cyanide ion.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: During the acetylation step to form amide 4, the reaction mixture became a thick, difficult‑to‑stir slurry when pyridine was used as the base, hampering efficient mixing.
Solution_Description: Pyridine was replaced by 2,6‑lutidine, which gave a lower‑viscosity mixture and improved the isolated yield by ~5 %. The reaction was also performed in THF/DME, which gave cleaner conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pyridine used as a base… turned into a thick, difficult‑to‑stir slurry… the yield was improved by ∼5 % with 2,6‑lutidine.”; “Results revealed a clean conversion in THF and 1,2‑dimethoxyethane (DME).”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: In the intramolecular condensation of amide 4 to pyridone 5, impurity A formed at higher temperatures and the reaction mixture with pyridine was viscous, leading to lower overall yield (≈53 % on the second scale‑up).
Solution_Description: The base was switched to LiHMDS in a THF‑toluene mixture with a low THF volume (3.7 vol % THF, 8 vol % toluene) to suppress impurity A; 2,6‑lutidine also reduced slurry viscosity. The optimized conditions gave impurity A ≤0.1 % and improved yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Impurity A was slightly increased with additional THF… When the reaction was performed without additional THF, the increase in impurity A was further suppressed.”; “Pyridine… turned into a thick, difficult‑to‑stir slurry… 2,6‑lutidine… improved the yield.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: When the scale of the pyridone 5 step was doubled, impurity B rose to 18.2 % HPLC area and overall yield dropped to 53 % due to low LiHMDS concentration and prolonged addition time.
Solution_Description: LiHMDS concentration was increased and the addition time shortened to keep the reaction region homogeneous; the amount of LiHMDS was adjusted to maintain a consistent base excess, limiting impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The level of impurity B increased with a low LiHMDS concentration and a high amide 4 concentration. The addition time of LiHMDS… took about 2 h longer… leading to unfavorable conditions and an increase in impurity B.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: N‑Phenyltrifluoromethanesulfonimide (Tf₂NPh) and Ghosez’s reagent were expensive and difficult to procure in bulk, limiting scale‑up feasibility.
Solution_Description: Tf₂NPh was replaced by the cheaper and commercially available triflic anhydride (Tf₂O) for triflation, and Ghosez’s reagent was substituted with sulfuryl chloride (SOCl₂) for acyl‑chloride formation, eliminating the need for the costly reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Replacing reagents that had procurement issues, such as N‑phenyltrifluoromethanesulfonimide and Ghosez’s reagent, with more commonly used reagents.”; “We found that 13 was cleanly converted to the corresponding acyl chloride with SOCl₂ in MeCN.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: The original route required chromatographic purification of triflate 10, which is inefficient at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: A direct work‑up sequence was developed: after triflation the crude product was precipitated and filtered without chromatography; the subsequent reaction (morpholine substitution) was performed on the isolated solid, eliminating the need for column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Avoidance of the use of halogenated solvents… and no chromatographic purification in any step.”; “Amide 4 is an oily compound and was therefore subjected to the following reaction without purification.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: During the final salt‑formation step, the BsOH·H₂O solution in MEK generated unidentified impurities above 50 °C, likely from MEK aldol condensation, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: The temperature of the BsOH·H₂O/MEK solution was capped at 10 °C during addition and the slurry was kept ≤10 °C until crystallisation, suppressing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The stability evaluation of a solution of BsOH·H₂O in MEK revealed that unidentified impurities increased with a temperature rise (>50 °C)… we decided to set the temperature of this solution at not more than 10 °C.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of nitrile 17 to acid 13 was sluggish in DME and i‑PrOH because the intermediate amide had poor solubility, leading to incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: EtOH was selected as the reaction solvent and the mixture was heated to reflux (≈80 °C) with KOH, which gave quantitative conversion to acid 13 within 45 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction did not proceed in DME… The reaction was sluggish in EtOH, and the intermediate amide was still observed… The reaction rate with KOH was faster than that with NaOH, and the reaction was completed at reflux.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development and Scale-Up of a Positive Allosteric Modulator of the α7 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor
Problem_Description: Acyl‑chloride formation from acid 13 at 40 °C or 60 °C led to increased impurity D, indicating temperature‑induced decomposition of the acyl chloride.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was optimized to 20 °C, which suppressed impurity D formation while maintaining high conversion (≈99 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “An increase in impurity D was observed at 40 and 60 °C… indicating that the acceptable temperature is 20 °C.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: The asymmetric alkylation sequence required cryogenic temperatures, multiple functional‑group interconversions (reduction of the oxazolidone, oxidation of a benzyl ether, etc.) and chromatographic separations, making the route expensive, operationally hazardous and slow for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the alkylation route and adopted a crystallization‑induced dynamic resolution (CIDR) sequence that proceeds under ambient conditions in few steps, eliminating cryogenic reactors, expensive reagents and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “the alkylation of 5 with t‑butyl bromoacetate … under cryogenic conditions … While this reaction was convenient in the drug discovery… the oxazolidone amide … needed to be reduced … and the hydroxyl group protected … had to be oxidized …”
- “we decided to examine the feasibility of catalytic asymmetric hydrogenation and CIDR methodologies … neither oxidation nor reduction should be required in the process”
- “We herein report an efficient asymmetric synthesis of 4 using a CIDR approach”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: Catalytic asymmetric hydrogenation of α,β‑unsaturated acid 8 gave only 46 % ee even with the best Rh/(R)-CyBINAP system and the substrate was found to be unstable on scale, leading to poor reproducibility and low conversion.
Solution_Description: The hydrogenation approach was dropped; instead the CIDR of the aldehyde 9 was pursued, which gave high enantiopurity (96 % ee) and robust, scalable results.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “the best catalyst system … gave (R)-4a … in 46 % ee despite large efforts.”
- “substrate 8 was relatively unstable and should be avoided to be handled in large scale.”
- “In the wake of these unsuccessful results, we shifted our focus to the CIDR of 9.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: Intermediates 8, oxime 4a and compound 17 are energetic substances with low exothermic onset temperatures and high heats of decomposition, posing safety risks during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The team treated these compounds as solutions, used low‑temperature (<3 °C) portionwise addition of solids, and employed controlled quench/kill media to mitigate exotherms and prevent runaway reactions.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Caution: The exothermic onset temperature and the heat of decomposition of 8 on DSC analysis were 91 °C and 868 J/g…”
- “Caution: Oximes (S)-4a and 17 are also energetic substances … heat of decomposition of 1.06 kJ/g and 894 J/g …”
- “To a solution … was added 16 portionwise as a solid at <3 °C …”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: Complex 16 is only stable in the solid state; in solution it decomposes rapidly, leading to partial racemization and loss of optical purity during conversion to oxime 4a.
Solution_Description: The conversion was performed by portionwise addition of solid 16 to a cold aqueous‑acetonitrile mixture (<3 °C), followed by gentle stirring, which preserved the enantiomeric excess (96 % ee).
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The 1H NMR measurement of 16 indicated that this complex was only stable in solid state and rapidly decomposed … This fact implies that partial racemization took place …”
- “To a solution … was added 16 portionwise as a solid at <3 °C, and the resulting mixture was stirred at this temperature for 1 h …”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: The chiral amine (S)-1‑phenylethylamine 14 is an expensive reagent and its loss would increase material cost.
Solution_Description: After the CIDR step, >95 % of 14 was recovered as its sulfate salt by simple filtration, minimizing reagent consumption and cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “More than 95 % of 14 was recovered as sulfate by just filtration.”
- “After completion of oxime formation, an equivalent amount of sulfuric acid was added to the reaction to precipitate out 14 as a solid salt of sulfuric acid.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: The previously reported synthesis of the API intermediate 23 required 17 steps, gave an overall 27 % yield and used cryogenic conditions, making it costly and time‑consuming for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The new 13‑step CIDR‑based route delivers chemically and stereochemically pure 23 in 30 % overall yield (≈13 % improvement) without cryogenic reactors, thereby reducing production cost and time.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The synthesis of 23 in the drug discovery stage consisted of 17 steps, and its total yield was 27 % … In contrast, the new route reported here provides … 30 % overall yield via 13 steps without the need to utilize cryogenic conditions.”
- “We herein reported the highly practical synthesis of chiral 4 via CIDR …”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of Chiral 3‑(Hydroxyiminomethyl)adipic Acid, a Key Intermediate of the ROR‑γ Inhibitor JTE-151, via Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution
Problem_Description: Decarboxylation of the isoxazole carboxyl group traditionally requires high‑temperature, metal‑catalyzed conditions that can be costly (large amounts of Ag₂O) and present handling hazards.
Solution_Description: The authors employed Gooßen’s protocol using only 5 mol % Ag₂O and 10 mol % K₂CO₃ at 135 °C, which gave smooth selective decarboxylation on kilogram scale, reducing catalyst loading and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: - “After screening some of these conditions, we found reaction under Gooßen’s conditions using 5 mol % of Ag₂O; 10 mol % of K₂CO₃ in NMP proceeded quite smoothly at 135 °C for the selective decarboxylation of 20 to afford monoacid 22.”

Paper Title: Efficient Cleaning Method for Flow Reactors in Flow Lithiation Reactions Under Water-free Conditions
Problem_Description: During the first production the pressure in the flow reactor rose rapidly after 3 h and eventually exceeded the diaphragm‑pump pressure limit, causing the process to be stopped for safety reasons.
Solution_Description: The water content in Solution A was strictly controlled to ≤95 ppm (by dehydration with molecular sieves), which prevented the formation of lithium hydroxide and thus avoided fouling‑induced pressure spikes.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The pressure in the flow reactor increased rapidly after 3 h of operation, the raw material solution was fed below the upper pressure limit (≤500 kPa).',
'Neither a pressure increase in the flow reactor nor fouling in Mixer 1 was observed in Run 1 (water content 47 ppm).',
'Consequently, it was concluded that during the first production, the high water content in Solution A precipitated lithium hydroxide in the channel and subsequently increased the pressure in the flow reactor.']

Paper Title: Efficient Cleaning Method for Flow Reactors in Flow Lithiation Reactions Under Water-free Conditions
Problem_Description: The conventional cleaning method (water → THF) required large quantities of organic solvent to remove residual water, and incomplete water removal increased the risk of fouling when the next lot was started.
Solution_Description: A new water‑free cleaning protocol was introduced: a 5 wt % THF solution of a phenolic derivative (p‑hydroxybenzoic acid, PHBA) is passed through the reactor to convert insoluble lithium hydroxide into soluble phenoxylithium, which is then removed with THF.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Although this cleaning method is commonly used to remove the inorganic lithium salts precipitated in flow reactors, it requires a large amount of organic solvent to completely remove the residual water.',
'If the water is not sufficiently removed, the risk of fouling in the subsequent lot increases.',
'The new cleaning method does not require water. Phenolic derivatives convert inorganic lithium salts into organic lithium salts that are readily soluble in organic solvents.']

Paper Title: Efficient Cleaning Method for Flow Reactors in Flow Lithiation Reactions Under Water-free Conditions
Problem_Description: Lithium hydroxide generated in the reactor is poorly soluble in the organic reaction solvent, leading to precipitation, channel fouling and pressure build‑up.
Solution_Description: Screening of phenolic compounds identified p‑hydroxybenzoic acid (PHBA) as the most effective additive; its phenoxide forms phenoxylithium, which is highly soluble in THF, enabling dissolution of the precipitated lithium hydroxide.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The solubility of lithium hydroxide was investigated using several compounds such as BHT, benzoic acid, p‑cresol, PHBA, and phenol to verify the concept of the new cleaning method.',
'A THF solution of PHBA or phenol was more effective as a cleaning solvent. A smaller amount was required to dissolve lithium hydroxide.',
'Given the toxic and corrosive nature of phenol, PHBA was selected as the phenolic derivative.']

Paper Title: Efficient Cleaning Method for Flow Reactors in Flow Lithiation Reactions Under Water-free Conditions
Problem_Description: Residual inorganic lithium salts left after the conventional water‑based cleaning caused immediate pressure spikes on restarting the second lot, forcing an emergency shutdown.
Solution_Description: After each lot the reactor is cleaned by (i) flushing with THF, (ii) passing a 5 wt % THF solution of PHBA through the channel at –20 °C for 5 min (or longer on production scale), and (iii) a final THF flush; HPLC confirms no PHBA remains.
Supporting_Evidence:
['In the second production, a THF solution of PHBA was used as the cleaning solvent. It is noteworthy that no pressure increase was observed during production, even after the cleaning processes.',
'The THF solution of PHBA (ca. 2.3 times the total reactor volume) was then passed through the channel at the same flow rate for 5 min at –20 ± 5 °C to remove inorganic lithium salts, followed by 5 min of THF to remove the remaining PHBA.',
'After cleaning, HPLC analysis confirmed that no PHBA remained in the flow reactor.']

Paper Title: Efficient Cleaning Method for Flow Reactors in Flow Lithiation Reactions Under Water-free Conditions
Problem_Description: Large volumes of THF (tens of kilograms) were required to purge water and residual solvents after each lot, inflating solvent consumption and waste.
Solution_Description: The water‑free PHBA cleaning method reduces the total amount of organic solvent needed because water removal steps are eliminated; only the THF‑PHBA solution and a final THF rinse are required.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Eliminating water from the process greatly reduces the risk of fouling after cleaning while potentially shortening production times and reducing the total amount of organic solvent.',
'The conventional cleaning method...requires a large amount of organic solvent to completely remove the residual water.',

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: The original protocol employed chloroform as the reaction solvent. Chloroform is classified as a carcinogen and is subject to a stringent ICH residual limit of 60 ppm, making it unsuitable for large‑scale pharmaceutical manufacture.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂). Dichloromethane has a much higher allowable residual limit (600 ppm) and is less hazardous, allowing compliance with ICH limits while preserving reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “This approach uses chloroform as the reaction solvent, which is likely to be carcinogenic and has a stringent ICH limit of 60 ppm.”
• “The dichloromethane solvent used for the reactions has an ICH limit 10‑fold higher than that of chloroform (600 ppm vs 60 ppm), making it a more suitable solvent for further development.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: Choline chloride is poorly soluble in most solvents screened; in several cases it precipitated on the vessel walls, forming solid deposits that impeded product isolation.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane was selected because it forms a biphasic mixture in which the product resides in an oily upper phase, avoiding solid precipitation and simplifying phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Choline chloride is not soluble in any of the screened solvent at room temperature.” (Table 1 footnote b)
• “Halogenated solvents such as CHCl₃ and CH₂Cl₂ gave a biphasic reaction mixture; the clear oily upper phase contained product 3.”
• “The experiment described in entry 2 was promising, as product 3 was isolated from the upper oily layer.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: The crude reaction mixture obtained with the initial conditions gave only ~50 % purity and low isolated yield (≈48 % after crystallization attempts).
Solution_Description: A sequence of controlled work‑up steps was introduced: direct addition of IPA to the reaction mixture, gradual water addition via syringe pump to control exotherm and precipitation, followed by polish filtration and a hot slurry treatment to remove residual impurities and improve overall purity to >98 % assay.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The purity of the crude product was low, at 50.32 %. Purifications by crystallization from ten different solvents were attempted and the highest recovery was only 48 %.”
• “After adjusting the pH … 4 equiv of water … added … at a flow rate of 1 mL/min for exothermic control, as well as gradual product precipitation.”
• “The hot slurry treatment … reduced succinyl monocholine from 0.4 wt % to 0.2 wt % and choline from 1 wt % to 0.13 wt %.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: During scale‑up to 25 g, the product‑rich oily layer solidified before IPA addition when the temperature fell below 15 °C, leading to difficult redissolution and inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was altered so that isopropyl alcohol was added directly to the reaction mixture (without a prior DCM phase cut) after cooling to 25 °C, preventing premature solidification and improving impurity removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “…the oily liquid (product‑rich liquid as the upper layer) solidified prior to IPA addition… Once formed, these solids were difficult to redissolve in IPA.”
• “To overcome the issue of premature product solidification, IPA was charged directly into the reaction mixture (without removal of the dichloromethane layer) after it was cooled to 25 °C.”
• “This slight modification… not only avoided premature solid formation but also improved the removal of impurities.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: Residual pyridine in the final API was found at 600–800 ppm, exceeding the ICH limit of 200 ppm, posing a safety/regulatory concern.
Solution_Description: A polish filtration step (cold water dissolution followed by IPA precipitation) was introduced before the hot‑slurry treatment, which reduced pyridine to ≤200 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Scale-Up and Development of a One-Step Process for the Synthesis of Succinylcholine
Problem_Description: DMAP (10 mol %) effectively catalyzed the reaction but its removal added cost and complexity to the purification process.

Paper Title: Process Development of a Novel Route to Rilpivirine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The classical route to rilpivirine relies on two S_NAr reactions performed at 80‑150 °C in polar aprotic solvents (acetonitrile or NMP) and uses POCl₃ and a Pd‑catalyzed Heck step.  Harsh temperatures, toxic waste generation, and residual transition‑metal contamination pose safety and environmental concerns, while the long heating times lengthen the process.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic route was devised that installs a Boc‑protected aniline before the first S_NAr, eliminating the need for POCl₃ and the Pd‑catalysed Heck step.  The chemistry was transferred to greener solvents (2‑MeTHF, isopropanol, acetic acid) and milder temperatures, giving a safer, shorter sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Both S_NAr reactions typically proceed under harsh conditions at elevated temperatures (80–150 °C) in polar aprotic solvents (typically acetonitrile or NMP)" – safety/long‑reaction issue.

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The original literature routes use hazardous reagents such as Raney‑nickel hydrogenation, methylamine gas, nitrous acid (nitrosamine‑forming), iodomethane, n‑butyl‑lithium, titanium tetrachloride, aluminium chloride, urotropine, chromium and mercury, which pose serious security and toxicity risks, and many of the key start‑materials are expensive or difficult to obtain, leading to a long, multistep (8‑step) production cycle with low overall yield (7.9‑10.2 %).
Solution_Description: A concise, five‑step third‑generation process was designed that eliminates the dangerous reagents, replaces them with safer alternatives (e.g., oxalic‑acid‐promoted reductive amination, ethylene‑glycol protection, iodine deprotection) and shortens the synthesis to four distinct intermediates, raising the overall yield to 26.5 % while improving safety and cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the key reactions … such as Raney nickel catalytic hydrogenation … and methylamination of 4 with methylamine gas, which face serious security risks” (Introduction). 
• “the reagents used … such as nitrous acid … may result in the generation of poisonous nitrosamine impurities” (Introduction). 
• “many dangerous reagents, such as iodomethane, n‑butyl lithium, Raney nickel, nitrite, methylamine gas … were employed with serious security risks” (Introduction). 
• “the process ... eight steps ... total yield ranging from 7.9% to 10.2% … too many steps, a much longer production cycle, and complicated operation” (Introduction). 
• “the third‑generation process … delivered midazolam … with an overall yield of up to 26.5% and purity of 99.8%” (Abstract & Conclusions).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Direct condensation of 3‑iodide (16) with amine 12 failed to give the desired imine 17 under all tested conditions, producing only residual starting material and fluorinated by‑products due to steric hindrance and low reactivity of the benzophenone moiety.
Solution_Description: The ketone 16 was first converted in situ to the more active imine 18, which then smoothly reacted with 12 to afford intermediate 17 in 67 % yield over two steps, demonstrating that a step‑wise (in‑situ) approach rescues the transformation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “product 17 could not be obtained … other fluorinated byproducts were detected. We speculated … due to the large steric hindrance and low activity of benzophenone in 16” (Sec 2.1). 
• “the reaction between 18 and 12 proceeded smoothly, and the key intermediate 17 was obtained in 67 % yield over two steps” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Reductive amination of 3 with amine 14 gave no desired product; 3 was reduced instead, and under dehydration conditions a dimer (20) formed, indicating competing side‑reactions and poor conversion.
Solution_Description: Using oxalic acid (2 equiv) as an additive together with NaBH₃CN in DCM enabled the reductive amination to proceed, delivering the product in 87 % isolated yield (Table 1, entry 13). The additive screens (HClO₄, H₂SO₄, TFA, etc.) showed oxalic acid gave the best result, and the reaction was performed with careful addition of reagent 14 in batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the desired product was not obtained … instead of 3 being reduced” (Sec 2.2). 
• “only 20 from dimerization of 3 was obtained under dehydration conditions” (Sec 2.2). 
• “when oxalic acid was used as an additive and sodium cyanide borohydride was used as a reducing agent, the target product could be achieved in up to 87 % yield” (Sec 2.2, Table 1, entry 13).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Scaling the first‑generation reductive amination from 50 g to 200 g resulted in incomplete conversion because ketone 14, the starting ketone 3 and intermediate 19 were also reduced, necessitating a large excess of 14 (up to 1.5 equiv) to maintain conversion.
Solution_Description: The carbonyl of 3 was protected as a thioketal using ethylene disulfide (21) catalysed by TiCl₄ (88 % yield), preventing its reduction. Later the protective group was replaced by ethylene glycol (ketal 23) activated with TMSCl, which gave 61 % yield and avoided the smelly dithiol and the need for toxic mercury deprotection.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Formation of the final midazolam hydrochloride salt required a suitable acid to give a solid, but many acids (fumaric, d‑tartaric, d‑mandelic, methanesulfonic, camphosulfonic, oxalic) gave poor precipitation or no solid, complicating isolation and lowering overall yield.

Paper Title: Development of a Safe, Efficient, and Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Midazolam Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The oxidative dehydrogenation of intermediate 8 to midazolam required excess manganese dioxide and long reaction times (≈24 h) for full conversion, increasing material cost and process time.

Paper Title: Process Study on One-Pot Synthesis of DBX‑1 with High Conversion Rate and Intrinsic Safety
Problem_Description: The traditional multistep synthesis of DBX‑1 from 5‑AT suffers from a low overall conversion (≈57 % in the initial trials) and generates hazardous intermediates (fine‑needle‑like intermediate 1 with very high mechanical sensitivity). The yield varies dramatically with small changes in reagent feed ratios, leading to inconsistent production.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A one‑pot process was designed that telescopes all three steps (5‑AT → intermediate 1 → 5‑NaNT → DBX‑1) without isolating the highly sensitive intermediate. The stoichiometry of NaNO₂ and HNO₃ was optimized (1.3‑fold NaNO₂ feed, 1.2‑fold HNO₃ feed) and the pH was kept above 3.2 to suppress the NO side‑reaction. Fast peristaltic feeding and high‑speed stirring were employed to improve mass‑transfer and keep gas evolution under control. The temperature profile was programmed (5 °C during diazotisation, 25 °C for nitro substitution, 90‑95 °C for the final Cu(I)Cl coupling). These combined changes raised the overall conversion of 5‑AT to NT⁻ to 90 % and the final DBX‑1 yield to >85 % while eliminating the handling of the sensitive intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The conversion rate of 5‑AT to NT⁻ was increased to 90 %.” (Abstract) 
• “The yield should refer to … the yield … was 57.1 % in group 1 … 91.5 % in group 2 … 83.2 % in group 3 …” (Table 2) 
• “Intermediate 1 … is a fine needle‑like crystal with extremely high mechanical sensitivity, which has a long filtration time and high handling risk.” (Introduction) 
• “Increasing the weight of sodium nitrite … significantly increases the rate of the NO side reaction … the side reaction of generating NO starts when the pH is below 3.2.” (Fig 5 discussion)

• “The synthesis of DBX‑1 … the temperature of the circulating bath liquid was increased to 95 °C … a suspension of Cu(I)Cl … was added at a constant rate of 10 mL/min …” (Section 4.9) 
• “The one‑pot synthesis … avoids the transfer of hazardous intermediate 1 and the prolonged filtration of fine CuO.” (Conclusion)

Paper Title: Process Study on One-Pot Synthesis of DBX‑1 with High Conversion Rate and Intrinsic Safety
Problem_Description: Previously reported routes to sodium 5‑nitrotetrazolate (5‑NaNT) required expensive reagents (e.g., precious‑metal catalysts, sulfonic‑acid resins) and long reaction times (several hours to days), giving low overall yields.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the costly catalyst‑based oxidation of 5‑AT with a stoichiometric diazotisation/nitro‑substitution sequence using inexpensive NaNO₂, HNO₃ and CuSO₄·5H₂O. By optimizing the feed ratios (1.3‑fold NaNO₂, 1.2‑fold HNO₃) and shortening the nitro‑substitution step to 20 min at 25 °C, the overall reaction time was reduced from > 8 h to ≈ 2 h while improving the isolated 5‑NaNT yield to > 85 %.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Development and Kilogram-Scale Implementation of a Flavin-Catalyzed Photoredox Fluorodecarboxylation
Problem_Description: The researchers identified several scale‑up challenges: (1) low quantum efficiency of photoredox reactions leading to poor conversion/yield; (2) scarcity and high cost of iridium/ruthenium photocatalysts; (3) heterogeneous reaction mixture before irradiation that could cause clogging/fouling in flow; (4) background decomposition of the fluorinating agent (Selectfluor) in the presence of 2,6‑lutidine, reducing yield; (5) light attenuation and pressure buildup when using highly concentrated solutions; (6) the need for a fast reaction (short residence time) to obtain high space‑time yields; (7) temperature‑control and heat‑removal issues for the LED‑driven reactor; (8) lack of a standardized, modular platform for translating batch photochemistry to kilogram‑scale flow.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A series of strategic actions resolved the above problems: (1) Photo‑HTE combined with DoE‑guided optimization discovered an efficient flavin‑catalyzed fluorodecarboxylation route (new route, catalyst optimization); (2) Replaced expensive Ir/Ru catalysts with inexpensive riboflavin (RF) and its tetrabutyrate derivative (RFTB) (cost, availability, new route, catalyst optimization); (3) Switched to RFTB to obtain a fully homogeneous reaction mixture, eliminating clogging risk (mixability, new route, catalyst optimization); (4) Implemented a two‑feed addition strategy so that SF and 2,6‑lutidine only mix immediately before irradiation, minimizing the background decomposition (order & rate of addition, mass‑transfer/mixing control); (5) Employed a plug‑flow photoreactor (PFP) with highly transparent tubing and a large surface‑to‑volume ratio, and tuned concentration (14 vol %) to mitigate light attenuation and pressure build‑up (reactor platform, mass‑transfer/mixing, concentration tuning); (6) Optimized catalyst loading (0.8 mol % RFTB) and base/fluorinating‑agent equivalents to achieve <2 min full conversion, satisfying the fast‑reaction requirement (reaction‑time change, catalyst optimization); (7) Integrated temperature monitoring and active heat‑removal for the LED panels, reactor housing and pumps to keep inlet/outlet temperatures stable during extended runs (temperature optimisation, reactor platform); (8) Established a modular development workflow (photo‑HTE → DoE batch → lab‑scale flow → kilogram‑scale PFP) that standardises scale‑up and reduces re‑optimization effort (other condition change, reactor platform).
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem evidence:
1. “In general, the main challenges impeding more widespread applications of this technology in process chemistry can be attributed to the low quantum efficiency of the reactions that lead to poor scalability.”
2. “Well‑established Ir‑ and Ru‑polypyridyl complexes… however, due to the scarcity of these late transition metals, they are neither sustainable nor economical solutions for scale‑up.”
3. “…its heterogeneous nature prior to irradiation was a concern due to the potential for clogging or fouling in the eventual flow setting.”
4. “Prolonged mixing of SF and 2,6‑lutidine prior to irradiation resulted in a greatly reduced yield… a background reaction between 2,6‑lutidine and SF occurs at room temperature.”
5. “The use of a highly concentrated solution … will inevitably lead to enhanced light attenuation and pressure buildup due to rapid CO₂ release.”
6. “One important aspect for scaling up photoreactions in flow is a fast reaction rate with short residence time to maximize space‑time yield and throughput.”
7. “Temperature control and heat management of the photoreactor, LED panels, and pumps with increased operation time during the scale‑up process.”
8. “Other factors, such as the lack of a standardized platform and suitable scale‑up system to support a systematic development workflow, provide additional challenges… ”

Solution evidence:
1. “Photo high‑throughput experimentation (photo‑HTE) and design of experiment (DoE)‑guided optimization have enabled the discovery of efficient, homogeneous, and cost‑effective conditions for fluorodecarboxylation.”
2. “RF was prioritized as a more cost‑effective and sustainable option.”
3. “The use of RFTB (1 mol %) produced a clear and homogeneous reaction mixture … and furnished 2a in 92 % yield.”
4. “We implemented a two‑feed approach with separate streams … which are combined in an intermediate vessel before introducing them into the PFP.”

6. “Both RF‑ and RFTB‑catalyzed protocols were highly efficient with less than 2 min for reaction completion.”
7. “Temperature control and heat management … were implemented during the scale‑up process.”
8. “We also discuss the adoption of a general development workflow consisting of (1) photo‑HTE, (2) DoE‑guided optimization in batch, (3) lab‑scale flow assessment, (4) pilot production using a kilogram‑scale PFP.”

Paper Title: Development of a Streamlined Manufacturing Process for the Highly Substituted Quinazoline Core Present in KRAS G12C Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Anthranilic acid 6, a key early intermediate, was not commercially available at kilogram scale and the original batch route required cryogenic (‑65 °C) lithiation and a high‑temperature (150 °C) nucleophilic aromatic substitution with aqueous ammonia, both of which limited scalability and raised safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The authors developed continuous‑flow processes for the LDA‑mediated lithiation/carboxylation and for the S_NAr amination, eliminating the need for cryogenic temperatures and high‑temperature batch reactors. The flow sequence was telescoped, enabling multikilogram production of 6 without the hazardous batch conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Anthranilic acid 6 … lacked commercial availability on a larger scale and thus necessitated a scalable process for its preparation.”
• “Drawbacks of this original approach in batch mode included … cryogenic (‑65 °C) conditions for deprotonation, and a high‑temperature nucleophilic aromatic displacement reaction (S_NAr) at 150 °C, limiting further scalability.”
• “Lithiation was triggered by mixing lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) solution … in a tubular plug flow reactor (PFR) … at −45 to −40 °C.”
• “A continuous process could also be identified for the S_NAr reaction with ammonia … passing ... through a PFR … at 220–230 °C.”
• “These new process adaptations using continuous flow provided access to >100 kg of product 2 and facilitated downstream development and material production.”

Paper Title: Development of a Streamlined Manufacturing Process for the Highly Substituted Quinazoline Core Present in KRAS G12C Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Electrophilic chlorination of aminonitrile 14 with NCS/HCl produced halogen‑scrambling side‑products 4,5‑dichloro (20) and 4,5‑dibromo (21) impurities that were difficult to purge in downstream steps, and their levels varied markedly with reaction time and HCl loading.
Solution_Description: The chlorination was re‑optimized by adding NCS rapidly (<4 h), maintaining the reaction at –10 °C to 0 °C, and using sub‑stoichiometric HCl (0.25 equiv) as a catalytic promoter. Fast addition and tight temperature control limited the formation of the ipso‑substituted bromine species that caused scrambling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A significant concern in this step was the observed formation of halogenated side products 20 and 21 … their formation needed to be controlled by the choice of appropriate reaction conditions.”
• “Fastest conversions and cleanest reaction profiles were seen in DMF, giving dose‑controlled reactions at temperatures <0 °C.”
• “The critical impurities were best controlled through fast reagent addition (<4 h) and temperature control (‑10 to 0 °C), while longer aging led to significantly increased levels of 4,5‑dichloro impurity 20.”
• “Higher contents of 20 were also seen with excess HCl (0.79 area % … with 0.5 equiv).”

Paper Title: Development of a Streamlined Manufacturing Process for the Highly Substituted Quinazoline Core Present in KRAS G12C Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the CO₂/DBU‑mediated cyclization to quinazoline‑2,4‑dione 10, residual DMSO promoted a catalytic dimerization pathway that formed impurity 22, complicating isolation and lowering the overall purity.
Solution_Description: Residual DMSO was reduced to <1 000 ppm by an i‑PrOH/H₂O slurry wash and the cyclization was staged in two temperature steps (25 °C then 70 °C). This limited dimer formation and gave clean product after filtration.

• “At higher levels of residual DMSO, dimerization occurs … at ∼5000 ppm residual DMSO, about 5 area % HPLC of dimer 22 was obtained.”
• “It was found that running the process in a stepwise manner at two different temperatures further reduced dimerization and led to an overall cleaner reaction profile.”

Paper Title: Development of a Streamlined Manufacturing Process for the Highly Substituted Quinazoline Core Present in KRAS G12C Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original Halex fluorination used excess CsF in DMF at high temperature, which required a large amount of toxic DMF, a costly fluorine source, and suffered from poor solubility of KF, leading to inefficient conversion and waste‑generation concerns.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to inexpensive KF in DMSO, adding catalytic DABCO (0.04 equiv) and methanesulfonic acid (0.04 equiv) as a co‑catalyst. This lowered the temperature, eliminated DMF, reduced fluorine reagent cost, and achieved >99 % purity with standard‑grade KF.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Early process conditions used an excess of CsF (2.9 equiv) in DMF, which enabled the delivery of initial multikilogram quantities. Our intent was to use more economical sources of fluoride and replace DMF with a more environmentally benign solvent.”
• “KF was effective at displacing the chloride in DMSO, but high temperatures were needed for obtaining high conversions.”
• “Screened nucleophilic catalysts … revealing much better performance with catalytic amounts of DABCO (0.02–0.10 equiv).”
• “Non‑nucleophilic methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) was subsequently identified as an effective cocatalyst, leading to faster and cleaner conversions to product.”
• “The most optimal performance and control over process impurities were obtained at a loading of 4 mol % DABCO–MsOH … This process allowed the use of standard quality KF (1.3 equiv) and avoided the need for polyether solvents … or crown ether additives.”

Paper Title: Highly Regioselective Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug MMV693183
Problem_Description: The previously published 7‑step synthesis of MMV693183 gave a very low overall isolated yield (≈ 14 %) and required three protection‑deprotection sequences that used wasteful, expensive, and hazardous reagents (Mitsunobu reagents and hydrazine).
Solution_Description: A new three‑step, protecting‑group‑free route was developed that exploits the intrinsic steric difference of the two primary amines in (S)‑1,2‑diaminopropane. No Mitsunobu or hydrazine steps are needed, which eliminates the safety hazard and improves the overall isolated yield to 46 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Overall yield was only ∼14 %” (intro, line ≈ 140‑150). “3 of the 7 steps were used to manipulate protecting groups” (intro). “The Mitsunobu reaction and subsequent hydrazine deprotection … are challenging transformations to scale‑up due to … safety risks associated with handling diazodicarboxylates and hydrazine at scale.” (intro). “We report a three‑step scalable synthesis … avoiding the use of any protecting group.” (Results & Discussion, first paragraph). “The overall yield of the three‑step process … was 46 %.” (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Highly Regioselective Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug MMV693183
Problem_Description: Direct amidation of the diamine with (R)‑pantolactone failed in polar aprotic solvents because the inorganic base (Na₂CO₃) was insoluble, and at lower solvent volumes (5 V) the reaction mass became too viscous to stir.
Solution_Description: A mixed protic solvent system (i‑PrOH/H₂O 7:3) was adopted, which solubilises Na₂CO₃ and gives the desired conversion. A dilution of 10 V solvent was found optimal to keep the mixture fluid; 20 V gave the same conversion, confirming that 10 V is the practical balance between solubility and mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “No reaction was observed in polar aprotic solvents probably due to insolubility of the inorganic base” (Table 1 discussion). “The reaction occurred only in polar protic solvents … i‑PrOH … the addition of water to the solvent system … gave superior results … up to 86 % assay yield” (Table 1 discussion). “Due to the incomplete solubility of all species, 10 V of solvent was necessary to ensure proper mixing … the reaction mixture in 5 V conditions … was difficult to stir.” (Results & Discussion).

Paper Title: Highly Regioselective Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug MMV693183
Problem_Description: After the direct amidation step the crude mixture contained the desired mono‑amide (≈ 9 : 1 regioisomeric ratio) together with ∼ 8 % of a di‑acylated side‑product and inorganic salts from the aqueous work‑up; column chromatography gave a product of relatively low purity because of residual salts.
Solution_Description: Screening of acids identified l‑(+)-tartaric acid as a counter‑acid that precipitates the desired mono‑amide as a crystalline tartrate salt, simultaneously rejecting the undesired regio‑isomer and inorganic salts. The salt formation step provides a clean, high‑purity solid (≥ 97 % qNMR purity) without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “The product isolated by column chromatography … was of relatively low purity. The product was contaminated with inorganic salts, likely due to the high water content …” (Results & Discussion). “Mineral acids tend to cleave the amide bonds before crystallization occurs.” (Table 2 discussion). “When l‑(+)-tartaric acid was utilized, a stable white solid … was formed … 25:1 ratio of desired/undesired amides … 78 % yield, 99 % purity.” (Table 2 discussion). “The optimal conditions … gave a stable tartrate salt … with 86 % isolated yield and 97 % purity.” (Results & Discussion).

Problem_Description: The key starting material 3‑bromo‑L‑phenylalanine (7) was not commercially available on a large scale, limiting the practicality of the previously reported route.
Solution_Description: A completely new chemo‑enzymatic synthetic route was devised that builds the brominated phenylalanine intermediate from inexpensive, readily available 3‑bromobenzaldehyde (2) and N‑acetyl‑glycine (3).

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: Previous routes required expensive transition‑metal catalysts and ligands that are not available industrially, raising the cost of the process.
Solution_Description: The new route replaces metal‑catalyzed steps with a cheap Zn/HCl reduction and an enzymatic resolution, eliminating costly reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “this method involved expensive transition metal catalysts and ligands, which are not available industrially; thus, it restricts the application of the method on an industrial scale.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: During the Erlenmeyer–Ploch reaction, the hydrolysis of intermediate 4 to 5 occurs under the reaction conditions, producing a mixture that made isolation of 4 difficult.
Solution_Description: A telescoped protocol was implemented so that 4 is not isolated; the reaction mixture is directly carried forward to give 5.
Supporting_Evidence: “the formation of compound 5 was concurrently observed during the synthesis of compound 4… A telescoped synthesis was implemented to directly produce compound 5.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: Screening of 32 ene‑reductases (EREDs) gave unsatisfactory conversion of 5 to (L)‑6, providing negligible product.
Solution_Description: The researchers abandoned the enzymatic reduction and adopted a chemical reduction (Zn/HCl) followed by enzymatic resolution, thereby achieving high yield of 6 and subsequent steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “all of the evaluated EREDs demonstrated unsatisfactory conversion… Subsequently, a strategy involving chemical reduction, followed by enzymatic resolution, was selected.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: NaBH₄ reductions of 5 gave a major impurity 6a and low conversion to the desired product 6; other reductants (NiCl₂, CoCl₂, CuCl, etc.) also gave poor selectivity.
Solution_Description: Extensive screening of reductants and solvents led to the selection of Zn powder in acidic AcOH/HCl, which gave clean conversion to 6 with 99 % isolated yield and >90 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 entries 1–5 show low conversion/impurities; “Finally, Zn powder was found to be capable of reducing the double bonds of 5 under acidic conditions… a Zn powder/HCl system was chosen as the reducing agent… product 6 was obtained with a 99 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: Pd/C hydrogenation of 5 at 60 °C produced a debromination impurity 6b rather than the desired reduction product 6.
Solution_Description: The Pd/C conditions were abandoned; the Zn/HCl system was adopted as the superior reductant, eliminating debromination.
Supporting_Evidence: “increasing the reaction temperature to 60 °C did not result in the formation of 6. Instead, a debromination impurity… was generated. The reduction system was changed, and it was found that Zn powder… was capable of reducing the double bonds of 5.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: A panel of commercial lipases, papain and several acylases (AsACY, EcACY, GsACY) showed very low or no activity for hydrolysis of N‑acetyl‑3‑bromo‑phenylalanine 6, limiting the enzymatic resolution step.
Solution_Description: Two novel acylases were identified (GsACY and AmACY); recombinant expression of AmACY in E. coli gave robust activity (46 % conversion, 99.9 % ee), enabling the enzymatic resolution.
Supporting_Evidence: “Through sequence alignment… two novel acylases were identified… recombinant AmACY demonstrated robust enzymatic activity… achieving a maximum conversion of 46.3 % and an ee value of 99.9 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: The high water solubility of phenylalanine made extraction of the product from the aqueous work‑up phase difficult, leading to low recovery.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was optimized by adjusting the aqueous pH to 3‑4, extracting with THF, then basifying to pH 9‑10 and adding Boc₂O to trap the product as a protected intermediate, which could be efficiently isolated.
Supporting_Evidence: “To address this issue, an optimized workup protocol was devised… pH of the aqueous phase was initially adjusted… THF was employed to completely extract… the pH … adjusted to 9‑10, followed by the addition of Boc₂O…”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: Deprotection of the Boc‑protected intermediate with HCl in 1,4‑dioxane/DCM gave only 1.2 % conversion after 8 h, rendering the step impractical.
Solution_Description: Switching to HCl in isopropanol (i‑PrOH) as the solvent dramatically increased conversion to 96 % (entry 7, Table 4) within 8 h, providing a viable deprotection conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction conversion was only 1.2 %… subsequent efforts to switch the hydrogen chloride solution… resulted in low conversions… Notably, the application of a HCl isopropanol solution in this reaction increased the conversion to 96.3 % (Table 4, entry 7).”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: Recrystallization of the final product 1·HCl from DCM/DMF gave only 35 % yield, insufficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen showed that ethyl acetate/MeOH and ultimately ethyl acetate/isopropanol gave substantially higher yields (up to 75 %) and purity (>99 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield of 1·HCl was just 35 %… The yield and purity of 1·HCl could reach 53 and 99.5 % by using EA/MeOH… EA/IPA was the optimal recrystallization system… isolated yield 75 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: The undesired (D)‑6 enantiomer accumulated in the mother liquor, lowering overall material balance.
Solution_Description: A racemization protocol using Ac₂O/AcOH at 90 °C for 8 h efficiently converted (D)‑6 to racemic‑6 (≈50:50), which could be recycled back into the enzymatic resolution, raising overall yield to 59.5 % (two recycles).
Supporting_Evidence: “the unwanted (D)‑6… could be converted back to a racemic mixture via oxazolone formation under AcOH/Ac₂O conditions… Upon extending the reaction time to 8 h, a near‑equimolar racemic mixture… was successfully achieved (Table 3, entry 6).”

Paper Title: Development of a Novel Chemoenzymatic Process for 3‑(Methylsulfonyl)‑
Problem_Description: The final product 1·HCl showed limited precipitation when deprotected in certain alcohol solvents, requiring additional processing steps.
Solution_Description: Using i‑PrOH as the deprotection solvent produced an oily crude that precipitated upon cooling; the precipitate was filtered and then recrystallized from IPA/EtOAc to afford pure 1·HCl.
Supporting_Evidence: “When alcohols were employed as solvents, elevated conversion was observed, but the resultant crude 1·HCl failed to precipitate… Oily crude 1·HCl could be obtained if THF or 1,4‑dioxane were used… finally, the reaction was conducted according to the conditions in entry 7.”

Paper Title: Continuous GMP Manufacturing for Grignard Reagent/Zincate Synthesis and Negishi Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The Grignard reagent (2) is intrinsically unstable over active magnesium and decomposes rapidly at elevated temperatures, releasing heat that can lead to polymerisation and fouling of downstream equipment.  This posed a safety risk because large exotherms could cause uncontrolled temperature spikes and generate hazardous magnesium solids that might release hydrogen on quench.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The Grignard formation was moved to a continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) operated at 30 °C with a 2.5 h residence time.  The jacket temperature was kept at 19–20 °C to absorb the heat of reaction.  Magnesium was added in 4‑equivalent batches every 12 h to maintain >6 equiv in the reactor, and the exotherm was used as a diagnostic for steady‑state operation.  Dip‑tube level control and a magnesium‑settling trap were employed to manage solids and maintain consistent flow.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The Grignard reagent is unstable over active magnesium, and using flow chemistry, the temperature and residence time were well controlled to minimize decomposition." (Abstract)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: The Gewald reaction used to assemble the ACT moiety was nonscalable, giving inconsistent results and widely varying isolated yields when the scale was increased.
Solution_Description: The route was redesigned to install the terminal alkyne before the Gewald reaction and to perform a one‑pot Gewald condensation/cyclisation on the alkyne‑bearing ketone, eliminating the problematic Gewald step in its original form.
Supporting_Evidence: “The assembly of the ACT moiety by way of a Gewald reaction proved to be nonscalable, with inconsistent results and varied isolated yields with scale.”; “Having prepared over 5 kg of 3 via enzymatic resolution … it was desirable to utilize this chiral building block to access 1… To execute this strategy, we envisioned that the terminal alkyne moiety could be prepared through the elimination of an enol triflate… The simpler ketone Gewald precursor … was then tested… the condensation proceeded readily…”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: Malononitrile decomposed under the Knoevenagel condensation conditions, generating polymeric by‑products and reducing conversion to the desired product.

Solution_Description: Malononitrile was added incrementally as a THF solution with vigorous stirring, which kept the temperature low enough to suppress decomposition and gave higher conversion and isolated yield.
