Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: The ethyl ester in the β‑keto ester could undergo side‑reactions with the adjacent nitrile, forming undesired heterocyclic impurities that lowered overall productivity.
Solution_Description: The ester was removed before the condensation step by converting the intermediate to an alkyne‑bearing ketone, thereby eliminating the problematic ester‑nitrile interaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “It is also known that the ethyl ester could cause potential side reactions with the proximal nitrile to form heterocyclic impurities.”; “Having prepared over 5 kg of 3 via enzymatic resolution … we sought to eliminate this concern by transforming the carboxylic ester to the terminal alkyne prior to executing the Gewald reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: A late‑stage chemical resolution of the racemic intermediate gave only ~30‑35 % isolated yield, severely limiting material throughput.
Solution_Description: A classical chemical resolution using (S)‑phenylglycinol was introduced early in the sequence to set the quaternary stereocenter, providing a higher‑yielding, scalable resolution step.
Supporting_Evidence: “A late‑stage, low‑yielding chiral resolution was required to set the stereochemistry… only about 30–35 % yield.”; “A classical chemical resolution emerged to address the practicality of kilogram‑scale production… the same chiral amine … gave excellent selectivity … gave the best isolated yield (44 %).”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: Multiple stages of the discovery route required extensive column chromatography to isolate intermediates, adding cost, time, and complexity.
Solution_Description: The new route replaces chromatography with simple recrystallisation from EtOH for the final product and eliminates chromatographic steps for non‑crystalline intermediates, dramatically reducing cost and processing time.
Supporting_Evidence: “Extensive column chromatographic purifications were needed in multiple stages of the synthesis to preserve the consistent quality… The isolated Crude‑1 (typically in the range of 97–98 % area by HPLC) can be readily and efficiently recrystallized from EtOH to further enhance both chemical and chiral purities.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: The Bestmann–Ohira reagent (11), a high‑energy homologation reagent, posed safety hazards on scale and had storage restrictions.
Solution_Description: The alkyne was installed via a mild vinyl‑triflate elimination (using LiCl) instead of the energetic Bestmann–Ohira reagent, removing the safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “Finally, the discovery team employed the high‑energy reagent 11… The use of 11 not only raises process safety concerns… Hence, an alternative route bypassing the use of 11 was urgently needed.”; “Elimination of the triflate to obtain the corresponding terminal alkyne … the use of excess LiCl successfully provided the desired alkyne in 73 % yield initially and 95 % yield upon further fine‑tuning… eliminated the process safety concerns associated with the use of a highly energetic reagent.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: The asymmetric methylation via chiral enamine required cryogenic temperatures (−50 °C) and the toxic additive HMPA, delivering only 34 % yield.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the cryogenic enamine approach and pursued a chemical resolution/biocatalytic route that avoids low temperature and HMPA, improving safety and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Given the narrow operating temperature window (−50 ± 3 °C) to retain consistent stereochemical outcome, non‑process‑friendly cryogenic conditions, and the requirement of HMPA… the team decided to explore a more environmentally friendly alternative.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: Pig liver esterase (PLE) enzymatic resolution gave only 30‑35 % yield and required careful monitoring; external collaborators could not reproduce consistent results.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry and reaction time were optimized, and process monitoring was tightened; ultimately a chemical resolution using chiral amines replaced the enzymatic step for better reliability.
Supporting_Evidence: “While PLE exhibited significantly higher activity… the low‑yielding enzymatic resolution was performed on an up to 11 kg scale… the enzyme required careful monitoring… external collaborators were unable to demonstrate this enzymatic process with consistent results… prompted the team to investigate a more process‑friendly alternative.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: During the PLE kinetic resolution, prolonged reaction times led to hydrolysis of the desired ester, decreasing overall yield.
Solution_Description: pH was tightly controlled and reaction time limited to stop after desired conversion, preventing over‑hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “pH control for this reaction was critical, it was observed that prolonged reaction time promoted hydrolysis of the desired ester… the process required careful monitoring of consumption of rac‑3 to preserve the reaction yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: Initial base‑mediated elimination of the enol triflate (using LDA or NaHMDS) afforded only trace alkyne, giving poor yield.
Solution_Description: Addition of excess LiCl as a promoter dramatically improved the elimination, delivering up to 95 % isolated yield of the alkyne.
Supporting_Evidence: “Elimination of the triflate to obtain the corresponding terminal alkyne moiety was initially tested using bases such as LDA and NaHMDS; however, only a trace amount of product was detected. Finally, the use of excess LiCl successfully provided the desired alkyne in 73 % yield initially and 95 % yield upon further fine‑tuning.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 1: From Discovery Route to Kilogram-Scale Production
Problem_Description: The one‑pot amidation‑methylation using organo‑aluminum reagents (DIBAL‑H, Red‑Al) produced emulsions and required extensive filtration, complicating scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Direct use of MeLi in a premixed morpholine/MeLi solution eliminated the need for organo‑aluminum reagents, avoided emulsion formation, and streamlined work‑up.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis toward a KRAS G12C Inhibitor Building Block Bearing an All-Carbon Quaternary Stereocenter, Part 2: Asymmetric Synthesis via Shi Epoxidation
Problem_Description: Initial attempts at the Shi epoxidation of TMS‑enyne 14 gave essentially no conversion, even when a large excess of reagents and catalyst were used.  The reaction rate was also highly dependent on the source of the Shi catalyst (D‑Epoxone); only one vendor’s material gave any product, and even then the rate was far slower than reported in the literature.
Solution_Description: The D‑Epoxone catalyst was recrystallised from isopropanol, raising its purity from ~81 wt % to >98 wt %.  With the purified catalyst the epoxidation ran to full conversion in ~20 h using 20 mol % loading and no co‑solvents (ethanol or CH₂Cl₂) were required; the crude product could be carried forward directly after azeotropic heptane distillation with water content <200 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “To our surprise, no conversion was detected from the initial attempts, even with a large excess of reagents and catalyst.”
• “the source of the Shi catalyst (D‑Epoxone) was critical … using the catalyst from one of the vendors, albeit with much lower reaction rates compared to those reported in the literature.”
• “the measured purity (81 wt % by NMR assay) of the commercial Shi catalyst was significantly lower than … 95 %.”
• “upon recrystallization from isopropanol, the catalyst purity can be effectively upgraded to >98 wt %.”
• “the typical cosolvents employed … such as ethanol and dichloromethane, were not needed … the crude product could be used directly … with water content control (<200 ppm) via azeotropic distillation with heptane.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthesis of aminopyridine 1 required a super‑stoichiometric amount of copper(I) iodide and used hazardous solvents (DMF, HMPA).  In addition the sequence was linear, nine‑step, and required many protecting‑group manipulations, giving poor atom economy and a long lead‑time.
Solution_Description: A concise three‑step second‑generation route was developed that replaces the CuI‑mediated trifluoromethylation with a deoxofluorination of inexpensive 2,6‑dichloro‑4‑methylnicotinic acid, a high‑yielding halogen‑exchange bromination and a regio‑selective S_NAr amination, eliminating the need for CuI, DMF/HMPA and many protecting‑group steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “the trifluoromethylation of chloroiodopyridine 6, for instance, employs superstoichiometric amounts of the transition metal reagent CuI.”; “environmentally unfriendly solvents such as DMF and HMPA are required.”; “the route is linear and features an inefficient nine‑step sequence with multiple protecting group manipulations, which results in poor atom economy and a long manufacturing lead time.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Halogen‑exchange of 2,6‑dichloro‑4‑methylnicotinic acid (13) with 33 % HBr/AcOH proceeded slowly (≈50 % conversion after 24 h at 110 °C) and the mixture was highly corrosive.
Solution_Description: Pressurizing the reaction in an autoclave (32 h, 110 °C, 19 kg cm⁻²) gave full conversion (>90 % yield) while containing the corrosive HBr/AcOH mixture; the process was later shifted to bromination of the already‑brominated intermediate 11, which completed in 12 h on a 500 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “At ambient pressure…reached only 50 % conversion…over 24 h at 110 °C.”; “this reaction presented limitations due to the corrosive nature of the HBr/AcOH mixture, high reaction temperature, and long reaction time.”; “Pressurization of the reaction in an autoclave over 32 h at 110 °C resulted in full conversion with a >90 % uncorrected yield.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: During deoxofluorination of acid 13, monofluoro by‑products (15) accumulated (≥5 % HPLC after 24 h, rising to 8 % after 36 h); the original protocol used 3.5 equiv of SF₄ and DCM for work‑up.
Solution_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature to 75–80 °C suppressed formation of fluoropyridine impurities; the SF₄ loading was reduced to 2.5 equiv while maintaining full conversion; DCM was replaced by MTBE for extraction, followed by a charcoal treatment and crystallisation that delivered 77 % isolated 11 (99.3 % HPLC purity).
Supporting_Evidence: “we identified the presence of monofluoro impurities 15 (>5 % HPLC at 24 h)…increasing over time to 8 % HPLC each after 36 h.”; “Lowering the reaction temperature below 80 °C provided control of 2‑ and 6‑fluoropyridine impurities to 0.4 % each.”; “equivalents of SF₄ could be lowered from 3.5 to 2.5 while still achieving full conversion of the acyl fluoride intermediate 16.”; “To avoid using halogenated solvent DCM, we implemented an extractive workup using MTBE.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Direct S_NAr amination of dibromopyridine 12 with (PMB)₂NH gave poor selectivity, producing the undesired isomer 18 and bis‑aminated side‑product 19, especially when inorganic bases (K₂CO₃, K₃PO₄) were used.
Solution_Description: Screening of organic bases identified Et₃N as the optimal base; solvent screening showed N‑butyl‑pyrrolidinone (NBP) gave the best balance of conversion (94 %) and selectivity (85:15 1:18) while being environmentally sustainable.  The optimized protocol uses Et₃N (2.0 equiv) in NBP (5 mL g⁻¹) at 70 °C for 32 h, delivering 95 % conversion and a 70 % assay yield of 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “most reactions were unselective or led to over‑reaction, forming bis‑aminated side product 19.”; “Among the organic bases examined, Et₃N provided the cleanest reaction profile.”; “A marked difference in selectivity was noted among the solvents examined, with NBP emerging as an environmentally sustainable option.”; “When performed in DMSO at 70 °C, the reaction reached 93 % conversion…however these conditions raised process safety concerns…NBP as the solvent…produced 94 % conversion and an 85:15 ratio of 1:18.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: DSC safety profiling of the S_NAr reaction in DMSO (Et₃N, 1.0 equiv) showed a sharp exotherm with an onset at 196 °C, indicating a risk of runaway reaction.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to NBP raised the exotherm onset to 231 °C, significantly reducing the thermal hazard while maintaining high conversion.  The temperature was also limited to 70 °C to stay well below the exotherm onset.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initial DSC safety profiling … indicated a sharp exothermic event with an onset temperature of 196 °C, whereas a reaction in NBP (5 mL g⁻¹) showed weakly exothermic event with onset temperature of 231 °C.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: After the S_NAr step, the reaction mixture contained salts of (PMB)₂NH·HBr and Et₃N·HBr as a slurry, and the product mixture contained 8 % of the regio‑isomer 18, which interfered with downstream Negishi coupling.
Solution_Description: An aqueous work‑up with 20 % citric acid (10 mL g⁻¹, 50 °C) dissolved the salt by‑products, followed by cooling to precipitate the product.  The crude material was then recrystallised from a THF/MeOH (1:10) seed‑crystallisation, and a final reslurry in n‑heptane removed residual MeOH (<500 ppm), delivering >99.0 % HPLC‑pure 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “We implemented an aqueous workup by adding 20 wt % citric acid solution (10 mL/g) at 50 °C to dissolve the salt byproducts, followed by a cooling ramp to 20 °C to allow precipitation of aminopyridine 1.”; “Extensive solvent screening indicated that the differential solubility between aminopyridine 1 and isomer 18 was highest in MeOH…A THF/MeOH mixture (1:10, v/v) was identified as an optimal system for seeded crystallization.”; “An additional reslurry of aminopyridine 1 in n‑heptane was implemented in order to promote fast drying and control the amount of residual MeOH to a <500 ppm level.”

Paper Title: Manufacturing Process for 6‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Alternative routes explored (Guareschi–Thorpe pyridine synthesis, Langlois’ reagent trifluoromethylation, photoredox C–H trifluoromethylation) either failed to give product or gave low conversion and significant degradation.
Solution_Description: These unproductive pathways were abandoned in favour of the deoxofluorination/halogen‑exchange sequence, which proved robust and scalable, ultimately delivering the target intermediate in 45 % overall yield from acid 13.
Supporting_Evidence: “examination of the cyclization … failed to provide evidence of the desired product, leading primarily to the degradation of the starting materials.”; “no desired reaction and/or mild degradation was observed when mixing … with Langlois’ reagent.”; “while attempts involving photoredox‑catalyzed chemical activation … led to degradation, some evidence of trifluoromethylation … was observed… with pronounced product decomposition beyond that point.”

Paper Title: Points of Interest in the Chemistry of the Levomepromazine Drug Substance: Recycling of Undesired Enantiomer, Identification of New Phenothiazine Dimers, Synthesis of a Pharmacopeial Impurity, and an Unexpected Rearrangement
Problem_Description: The original one‑pot recycling of dextromepromazine to 2‑methoxyphenothiazine (Scheme 2) gave only 78 % isolated yield, incomplete conversion (12 % of starting material recovered) and a product whose purity (99.30 % UHPLC, with 0.35 % 8 and 0.17 % 9) was insufficient for pharmaceutical use. Because intermediates were not isolated, a mixture of side‑products accumulated, leading to material loss during multiple recrystallisations.
Solution_Description: Key intermediates (quaternary salt 5b and enamine 7) were isolated and purified before the final hydrolysis step. This stepwise approach removed impurity build‑up and increased the isolated yield of enamine 7 to 90–91 % with UHPLC purity 99.20 %, making the material suitable for levomepromazine synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence: "the incomplete conversion of the procedure (12 % of the starting compound was recovered)"; "multiple recrystallizations of the final product lead to significant material loss, making the recovery process uneconomical"; "compound 7 was isolated in an excellent yield (90–91 %) and quality (UHPLC purity: 99.20 %)"; "the quaternization, trimethylamine elimination and rearrangement… could be carried out in one pot, and compound 7 was isolated"

Paper Title: Points of Interest in the Chemistry of the Levomepromazine Drug Substance: Recycling of Undesired Enantiomer, Identification of New Phenothiazine Dimers, Synthesis of a Pharmacopeial Impurity, and an Unexpected Rearrangement
Problem_Description: Methyl iodide, the methylating agent used in the original sequence, is expensive for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: Methyl iodide was replaced with dimethyl sulfate, a less expensive reagent with a higher boiling point that is common in the pharmaceutical industry.
Supporting_Evidence: "we successfully replaced methylating agent methyl iodide … with dimethyl sulfate … due to its significantly lower price and higher boiling point"

Paper Title: Points of Interest in the Chemistry of the Levomepromazine Drug Substance: Recycling of Undesired Enantiomer, Identification of New Phenothiazine Dimers, Synthesis of a Pharmacopeial Impurity, and an Unexpected Rearrangement
Problem_Description: During processing of 2‑methoxyphenothiazine in THF with t‑BuOK, phenothiazine radicals formed and dimeric impurities 8 (C–N dimer) and 9 (C–C dimer) were generated, contaminating the product and complicating purification.
Solution_Description: The dimers were isolated by column chromatography, characterized, and one dimer (8) was used as a precursor to synthesize the pharmacopeial impurity Imp D. This provided a reliable source of the impurity standard and removed the need to chase unknown side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: "Two new dimer‑type impurities have been detected and these have also been synthesized"; "dimer 8 could be successfully separated by chromatography"; "One of these dimers was used for the preparation of a Pharmacopeial standard Imp. D"

Paper Title: Points of Interest in the Chemistry of the Levomepromazine Drug Substance: Recycling of Undesired Enantiomer, Identification of New Phenothiazine Dimers, Synthesis of a Pharmacopeial Impurity, and an Unexpected Rearrangement
Problem_Description: When attempting to synthesize the pharmacopeial impurity Imp E, an unexpected rearrangement occurred, yielding dimer 15 instead of the intended intermediate 13, indicating poor reaction control and side‑product formation.
Solution_Description: A revised pathway was devised: the unexpected dimer 15 was O‑methylated with methyl p‑toluenesulfonate to give dimer 9, which could then be processed to the desired impurity. The use of methyl p‑toluenesulfonate acted as a functional promoter for the methylation step.
Supporting_Evidence: "Surprisingly, instead of the expected product 13, the formation of a multicomponent mixture… with dimer 15 as the main product"; "Compound 15 was finally transformed to dimer 9 by O‑methylation carried out with methyl p‑toluenesulfonate"

Paper Title: Points of Interest in the Chemistry of the Levomepromazine Drug Substance: Recycling of Undesired Enantiomer, Identification of New Phenothiazine Dimers, Synthesis of a Pharmacopeial Impurity, and an Unexpected Rearrangement
Problem_Description: The original multistep sequence required prolonged heating (e.g., 16 h reflux for dimer formation) and multiple isolated steps, limiting throughput and reducing overall material efficiency.
Solution_Description: One‑pot variants (Methods B and C) combined quaternization, elimination, and rearrangement in a single operation at 35 °C, eliminating the lengthy reflux step and delivering the enamine 7 in >90 % yield with comparable purity, thus shortening the process and improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "When using THF as the solvent, the quaternization…, trimethylamine elimination, and rearrangement of the double bond, could be carried out in one pot"; "Method C… carried out at 35 °C for 3 h, followed by boiling for 2 h, gave enamine 7 in 91 % yield"; "The latter was isolated and transformed… yielding 2‑methoxyphenothiazine with 78 % yield"

Paper Title: Application of Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor Enabling Precise Control of Nucleation in Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: In batch reactive‑crystallization the nucleation timing cannot be controlled, causing rapid supersaturation, fine‑particle precipitation, low slurry fluidity and severe adhesion of solids to the reactor wall, which risks clogging and limits conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A Taylor vortex flow reactor (TVFR) was employed. The rotating axis creates Taylor vortices that generate high shear stress and excellent mixing, accelerating nucleation (from 120 min to 5 min) and reducing supersaturation, thus mitigating adhesion and clogging while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
“A Taylor vortex flow reactor realizes high shear stress and mixing efficiency, which accelerate the timing for nucleation of target imines… This effect enabled precise control of nucleation in reactive crystallization and successfully showed the mitigation of significant adhesion to the flow reactor through a long‑run experiment for 120 min.”
"Our previous work revealed that TVFR significantly accelerated the timing for nucleation from 120 to 5 min because of its high shear stress."
"The high shear stress by TVFR is advantageous for tearing off the adhesion to the reactor wall, leading to the mitigation of the risk of clogging."
"The large cross‑sectional area compared with a standard tube reactor is advantageous for mitigating the risk of clogging."
"The high shear stress generated by Taylor vortices initiated the nucleation in 2 min of residence time at 2000 rpm and within 1 min at 3000 rpm."

Paper Title: Application of Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor Enabling Precise Control of Nucleation in Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: The target imine 3a is highly soluble in common organic solvents (e.g., MeOH, EtOH, DMF), which prevents efficient precipitation and isolation by reactive crystallization.
Solution_Description: Solvent screening identified EtOH/n‑heptane (1:1) and IPA as mixtures that lower the solubility of 3a while maintaining adequate reactant solubility, enabling crystallization and easier downstream isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Typical organic solvents other than alcohols, such as tetrahydrofuran and N,N‑dimethylacetamide, may be used as reaction solvent, but they show the high solubility toward the target product 3a, which were not suitable for the following crystallization.”
"IPA has the lowest solubility of 3a in alcohols (entries 1–3 in Table 2), which is advantageous for isolation after reactive crystallization."
"EtOH/n‑heptane (1/1, v/v) has a lower solubility of 3a than EtOH (entry 2 vs 4 in Table 2)."
"EtOH as a single solvent was further investigated… Reducing the solvent volume to 4 mL g⁻¹ of EtOH led to immediate initiation of the nucleation, and the reaction slurry could not be stirred due to solidification."

Paper Title: Application of Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor Enabling Precise Control of Nucleation in Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: At a low rotation speed (1000 rpm) in the TVFR severe adhesion of the slurry to the reactor wall was observed, and conversion remained comparable to batch despite faster nucleation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The rotation speed was increased to 2000–3000 rpm, which amplified the shear stress generated by Taylor vortices, eliminated adhesion and maintained stable nucleation without loss of conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The severe adhesion to TVFR was observed at 1000 rpm… a higher rotation speed was required.”
"As expected, the high shear stress generated by Taylor vortices initiated the nucleation in 2 min of residence time at 2000 rpm and within 1 min at 3000 rpm."
"Unfortunately, the conversion was not better than the batch result despite the accelerated nucleation."
"Although adhesion to the reactor increased as the running time … was prolonged at 2000 rpm, the adhesion did not increase at 3000 rpm…"

Paper Title: Application of Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor Enabling Precise Control of Nucleation in Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: Even with accelerated nucleation in the TVFR, the overall conversion of the imination (≈43 %) was lower than desired, limiting process productivity.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature was raised to 60 °C and solvent volume reduced to 4 mL g⁻¹ (higher concentration) in batch, which increased conversion and provided a reliable benchmark for comparison with the TVFR; residence time in the TVFR was set to 5 min to match the optimized batch conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
“When the reaction was conducted at 60 °C, the reaction was accelerated, but the timing for nucleation was prolonged to 10 min because of the increased solubility of 3a…"
"The optimized reaction conditions were applied to a TVFR… residence time was set as 5 min."
"The conversion was not better than the batch result despite the accelerated nucleation…"
"The conversion was not better than the batch result despite the accelerated nucleation (Table 1)."
"Reducing the solvent volume to 4 mL g⁻¹ of EtOH led to immediate initiation of the nucleation…"

Paper Title: Application of Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor Enabling Precise Control of Nucleation in Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: After nucleation, the reaction slurry solidified and could not be stirred, preventing proper cooling and filtration.
Solution_Description: n‑Heptane was added as an antisolvent after reaction to decrease slurry concentration without losing product, allowing the slurry to be cooled to 5 °C, maintaining fluidity and enabling filtration.
Supporting_Evidence:
“After the reaction slurry was cooled to 25 °C, the reaction slurry could not be stirred due to its low fluidity. By adding 4 mL g⁻¹ of n‑heptane at 60 °C, the slurry concentration decreased without the increase of loss of 3a…"
"After the addition of n‑heptane, the slurry could be cooled to 5 °C with the fluidity remaining."
"The combined reaction slurry revealed that the reaction proceeded during storage to 86 % conversion. After storage of the reaction slurry, the target imine 3a was isolated under batch conditions."
"The addition of n‑heptane, the slurry could be cooled to 5 °C with the fluidity remaining."

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling
Problem_Description: The original linear‑cooling crystallization of the agrochemical (Needle Z) generated very fine needle‑shaped crystals that caused prolonged filtration, washing and drying times and produced a non‑uniform particle size distribution.
Solution_Description: A model‑based Quality‑by‑Control (mbQbC) strategy was implemented where a two‑dimensional population‑balance model was calibrated and then used in a multi‑objective optimization to design a new temperature‑profile (cascading temperature cycles with reduced cooling rates) that suppresses fine‑particle formation and improves crystal uniformity.
Supporting_Evidence: "linear cooling profile ... generated very fine needles, leading to long filtration, washing, and drying cycle time" (Materials and Experimental Setup, §2.1); "the simulation had a good fit over the experimental data trends" (Results and Discussion, §4.2); "the linear cooling optimized profile reduces the overall objective function to ∼25 % of its original value and showed major improvements in the spanL, spanW, fines (LCR), and mean sizes" (Process Optimization, §4.4).

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling
Problem_Description: Prolonged temperature‑cycling (used to elongate crystals) introduced higher impurity levels and produced a bimodal particle size distribution, which jeopardised downstream filtration and drying consistency.

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling
Problem_Description: Intermittent off‑line sampling of the slurry perturbed the system, inducing undesired nucleation and altering crystal growth kinetics, while also prolonging the experimental campaign.

Supporting_Evidence: "Intermittent sampling of the slurry is a solution to improve model accuracy ... but frequent use of this invasive approach can trigger undesired nucleation" (Introduction, §1); "To address data scarcity, incorporation of inline measurements is the key to improving the resolution of the model" (Introduction, §1); "the ParticleTrack counts trend ... recorded a decrease ... highlighted the drawback of backscattered laser detection of high‑aspect‑ratio particle systems" (Model‑Based QbC Calibration, §4.2).

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling

To further optimize the process while reducing experimental time, cost, and efforts, a model‑based QbC framework was applied" (Abstract); "The digital model was exploited for process intensification via digital design ... a large search space ... different initial conditions are helpful in determining whether there is a global solution" (Process Optimization, §4.4).

Paper Title: Digital Design of an Agrochemical Crystallization Process via Two-Dimensional Population Balance Modeling

Paper Title: Use of a Dynamic Flow Platform To Translate a Batch Immobilized Transaminase Process to a Packed Bed Reactor for the Synthesis of an Intermediate of Nemtabrutinib

Paper Title: Use of a Dynamic Flow Platform To Translate a Batch Immobilized Transaminase Process to a Packed Bed Reactor for the Synthesis of an Intermediate of Nemtabrutinib

Problem_Description: In the initial bubble reactor the up‑flow gas distribution generated large bubbles, limiting gas–liquid interfacial area and giving poor conversion and selectivity.

Problem_Description: A conventional T‑shaped mixer gave very low conversion (13.8 %) because the gas–liquid mass transfer was insufficient.

Problem_Description: Step 3 in batch uses sodium acetate, which creates a heterogeneous mixture that is difficult to handle in continuous flow, leading to low conversion and operational problems.
