Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: The only published method to racemize the levomedetomidine‑enriched waste uses a large excess of benzoyl peroxide in methanol under visible‑light irradiation, which is hazardous and gives only 28 % recovery of the racemic mixture.
Solution_Description: Replace the peroxide‑mediated racemization with a base‑mediated process using potassium tert‑butoxide (t‑BuOK) in isooctanol at 160 °C for 2 h (1.5 equiv). This method is safe, inexpensive, and affords >99 % racemization with >95 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The only one method for racemization… uses a large excess of benzoyl peroxide… the percentage recovery … is only 28.2 %.”; “Potassium t‑BuOK… at 160 °C led to a complete racemization in 2 h.”; “The use of high‑boiling alcohols … allowed us to complete the racemization in a short time… (Runs 8‑11).”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: D‑tartaric acid and its salts are highly water‑soluble, making their recovery from the mother liquor inefficient and expensive; many alternative resolving agents are either unavailable or too costly.
Solution_Description: Identify levamisole and (+)‑ADPE as inexpensive, poorly water‑soluble chiral amines that can serve as resolving agents. (+)‑ADPE gives >99.5 % enrichment of the (S)‑acid salt and is readily regenerated, substantially lowering material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “All our attempts to apply … amines for resolution of acid 5 failed… the salt of acid 5 and levamisole was also a low‑melting, noncrystallizable oil.”; “(1S,2R)‑(+)-2‑amino‑1,2‑diphenylethanol … was found to be the best resolving amine… providing the required (S)‑configuration.”; “Both versions use an expensive d‑enantiomer of tartaric acid… their high cost prevents the resolution process from being commercially viable.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Quenching the cobalt‑catalyzed cross‑coupling with 10 % aqueous HCl at temperatures above 10 °C leads to cobalt(III) complexes that remain in the organic phase, giving variable residual Co levels and poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: Quench with moderately cooled HCl (–3 °C to 0 °C), then wash the organic extract briefly (≤10 min) with concentrated HCl, followed by water and Na₂EDTA washes. This converts Co(III) to water‑soluble Co(II) and reduces residual cobalt to <1 ppm, giving a reproducible process.
Supporting_Evidence: “If the reaction temperature during quenching rises above 10 °C … product 9 was considerably contaminated by cobalt compounds (>100 ppm)… The reverse order of quenching … caused a fast decomposition of Co(III) compounds … to water‑soluble Co(II) compounds, which resulted in producing pale‑yellow extracts with low residual content of Co.”; “Thus, the use of moderately cooled HCl (from −3 to 0 °C), followed by removal of Co(III) compounds… seemed to be a compromise, reproducible, and viable solution.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: When salt 12 is treated with 10 % HCl, the mixture becomes a viscous, rubber‑like phase that prevents extraction of the free acid (S)‑4; both dilute and concentrated acids give the same problem.
Solution_Description: Perform the acidification in a pre‑heated (80 °C) n‑butyl acetate–water or toluene–water binary system. The salt dissolves in the organic layer; subsequent phosphoric‑acid addition keeps the phases clear, allowing clean extraction of (S)‑4 in >96 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The best isolation result was achieved in an n‑butyl acetate–water or toluene–water binary system preheated to 80 °C… the diastereomeric salt 12 was completely dissolved in the organic layer, and … the phases remained transparent and readily mixable.”; “Separation of the organic phase… provided a pure (S)‑enantiomer of 4 in almost quantitative yield (>96 %).”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Base‑mediated racemization of the (R)‑enriched acid 15 using NaOH or KOH required high equivalents and long reaction times (≥20 h) to reach only ~60 % racemization, making the step inefficient and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: Adopt potassium tert‑butoxide (1.5 equiv) in isooctanol at 160 °C for 2 h, which achieves complete racemization (>99 % conversion) in a short, scalable operation.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 6 shows long times and incomplete conversion for NaOH, KOH, etc.; “Potassium t‑BuOK … at 160 °C … led to a complete racemization in a short time (2 h).”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Scaling up the ylide 19 synthesis caused unexpected racemization (96.2:3.8 % ee) due to higher KOH impurity in the commercial t‑BuOK batch, compromising stereochemical integrity.
Solution_Description: Source high‑purity t‑BuOK (≤0.1 % KOH), control humidity, and keep the generation temperature at ≤45 °C. Under these conditions racemization is suppressed and ee >99 % is retained.
Supporting_Evidence: “The batch of potassium t‑BuOK used in scaling up contained a higher amount of free KOH (>1 wt %)… To achieve high enantiomeric purity … one should strictly control the atmospheric humidity and the quality of potassium t‑BuOK.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Generation of the ylide 19 at higher temperatures (45 °C) produced lower yields and a mixture containing sulfoxide 22 (by‑product up to 30 %); the reaction was sensitive to temperature.
Solution_Description: Lower the ylide generation temperature to 45 °C and add acid chloride 16 at –10 °C, which gives 90 % isolated yield of 19 with >99 % ee and suppresses formation of sulfoxide 22.
Supporting_Evidence: “Many authors earlier reported this step is better to be performed upon reflux… however, a temperature decrease at this step to 45 °C favored both the yield and total purity of the product (Run 6).”; “The reaction of bromoketone 21 with HBr … produced sulfoxide 22 up to 30 %.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: The bromination of ylide 19 to give α‑bromoketone 21 also yields sulfoxide 22 (up to 30 %); both products are low‑melting and soluble in organic solvents, hampering isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: After reaction, extract the mixture with heptane and wash repeatedly with water; sulfoxide 22 is highly water‑soluble and is removed, leaving pure 21 (≥99.7 % purity) with only 0.3 % residual impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sulfoxide 22 was found to be very soluble in water. This observation made it possible to remove 22 by multiple washings of a solution of the crude product mixture in an organic solvent using water… After five such washings, the residual content of 22 was <0.3 %.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Azide 30 is potentially explosive; its handling at scale raised safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Perform extensive safety tests (impact, flame, heating >300 °C, friction) showing no detonation; conduct the azidation in a controlled, aqueous‑organic two‑phase system with a phase‑transfer catalyst (TBAI) at 45 °C for 2 h, minimizing isolated azide amount.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of azidoketone 30… gave cause for our concern of its potential explosiveness; therefore, we carried out a number of experiments to study its energy properties. The fall of hammer… caused no detonation of azidoketone 30.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: The Weidenhagen cyclization of α‑hydroxyketone 23 to dexmedetomidine gave only 63 % (S)‑enantiomer due to severe racemization during the imidazole ring formation.
Solution_Description: Replace the Weidenhagen route with the milder Marckwald cyclization of α‑aminoketone salts (derived from the azide route) using potassium thiocyanate; this maintains enantiomeric purity (>95 % ee) and provides high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “The enantiomeric purity of the final product 1 was strongly affected during cyclization due to significant racemization… we sought alternative cyclization methods… the Marckwald reaction … is an alternative …”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Desulfurization of thione 26 with oxidizing reagent combinations (H₂O₂/metal salts, peracids, etc.) gave complex mixtures despite complete conversion, making purification difficult.
Solution_Description: Use Raney nickel (Ra‑Ni) in a water‑ethanol mixture at room temperature under argon; this provides clean, total conversion to dexmedetomidine (99.8 % conversion) with simple filtration and yields a product of >99.8 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “All oxidizing reagent combinations … resulted in the formation of complex reaction mixtures… We succeeded in carrying out the desired transformation using Raney nickel … provided very pure and total conversion of thione 26 under mild conditions.”

Paper Title: Research and Development on the Manufacturing Process of Dexmedetomidine from Chiral Precursors: Resolution–Racemization–Recycle Synthesis Strategy
Problem_Description: Dexmedetomidine HCl is extremely soluble in water; attempts to precipitate it from organic solvents failed because any water trace prevented crystallization, even at –20 °C.
Solution_Description: Seed the supersaturated aqueous solution of 1·HCl with a small amount of crystalline salt (0.1 wt %) and remove water by azeotropic distillation with ethyl acetate under atmospheric pressure; the resulting suspension crystallizes rapidly, giving 97 % yield of high‑purity material.
Supporting_Evidence: “All our attempts to precipitate the product … failed … due to water traces that totally prevented crystallization even when solutions were cooled to –20 °C. However, seeding a supersaturated solution with crystalline hydrochloride (∼0.1 wt %) resulted in fast crystallization. The removal of water traces by azeotropic distillation … afforded 1·HCl as an easily handled suspension in yield of 97.1 %.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: The copper‑catalyzed Ullmann C–N coupling (aryl‑iodide 7 + indazole 8) gave high conversion on a small scale but failed on gram scale – conversion dropped dramatically and the N‑2 arylation impurity (13) increased to >10 a % while a dark‑gray‑brown product containing copper (≈2 wt %) and inorganic salts (≈8 wt %) was obtained.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to a palladium‑catalysed Buchwald–Hartwig coupling (aryl‑bromide 12 + indazole 8) using Pd(dba)₂ (1 mol %) and t‑BuXPhos (2 mol %). This gave >92 a % of the desired phenol 9 with only 0.3 a % N‑2 impurity and no colored copper‑derived impurities.
Supporting_Evidence:
“During the route‑design work, high‑throughput experimentation (HTE) identified copper‑promoted Ullmann reaction conditions … conversion was considerably lower, and higher amounts of the N‑2 arylation… were observed.”
“...the palladium‑mediated Buchwald–Hartwig methodology… gave 92.1 a % of the desired product 9… the colored impurities 15‑17… were not observed by HRMS.”
“Switching to the palladium‑mediated Buchwald–Hartwig reaction… minimized the formation of impurities that caused significant issues with developing a robust control strategy.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: Phenol 9 is extremely insoluble in organic solvents, making aqueous extractions or crystallizations ineffective; basic extraction gave a product contaminated with ∼2 wt % copper, ∼8 wt % inorganic salts and a low assay (≈91.5 wt %).
Solution_Description: After adding THF as a co‑solvent at the end of the reaction the phenol stayed in the organic phase, allowing an aqueous HCl wash, silica‑thiol scavenging, and direct distillation/crystallisation of pure phenol 9 (98.5 a %, 98.1 wt %).
Supporting_Evidence:
“The purification of phenol 9 posed a significant challenge as the compound is extremely insoluble in organic solvents… Initial attempts at isolating phenol 9 via basic extraction… indicated that regioisomer 13 was not completely purged.”
“...after addition of THF cosolvent to the end‑of‑reaction mixture, the solubility of phenol 9 could be maintained in the organic phase while still allowing for an aqueous wash… Phenol 9 was isolated by filtration in 98.5 a % purity, 98.1 wt % assay, and 88 % yield.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: During the copper‑catalysed Ullmann reaction dark‑coloured quinone‑derived impurities (15‑17) formed, likely from oxidative coupling of the indazole under trace‑oxygen conditions, causing black aqueous/organic phases and operability issues.
Solution_Description: Switching to the palladium‑catalysed Buchwald–Hartwig coupling eliminated the formation of the quinone‑derived impurities; no coloured by‑products were detected by HRMS, and downstream phases separated cleanly.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Analysis of this phenol sample by HRMS indicated the presence of oxidatively coupled impurities 15‑17… Attempts to de‑colorize the reaction mixture… were fruitless. … copper has been observed to promote the formation of the quinone‑derived impurities.”
“...the colored impurities 15‑17… were not observed by HRMS, and downstream processes were easier to conduct.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: The early amide‑bond‑formation using CDI required a large excess of difluoropropionic acid (DFPA, 3.5 equiv) to reach completion and generated up to 5 a % of a urea impurity (32), with non‑reproducible crystallisation from 2‑MeTHF.
Solution_Description: The activating agent was changed to pivaloyl chloride (PivCl) to form a mixed anhydride (33) which gave full conversion with only 1.6 equiv of PivCl and 1.6 equiv of DFPA, reducing impurity 34 to <0.6 a % and enabling robust crystallisation from MeCN.
Supporting_Evidence:
“However, several challenges were identified… a large excess of DFPA (3.5 equiv) was required… urea impurity 32 was detected at up to 5 a %.”
“When pivaloyl chloride (PivCl) was used… complete conversion of the amine nucleophile was observed within 1.5 h… the level of impurity 34 was reduced to 0.55 a %.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: In the hydrogenolysis/debenzylation of intermediate 10, MeOH gave fast conversion but formed N‑methyl impurities (28‑29) and over‑hydrogenated by‑products; less polar solvents gave incomplete conversion (≈90 %) and poor impurity profiles.
Solution_Description: MeOH was selected as the optimal solvent, providing the fastest rates and >93 % conversion; the reaction temperature was later lowered to 30 °C which suppressed over‑hydrogenated impurities 26‑27 to <0.1 a % while maintaining high yield (≈98 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
“MeOH was superior as a solvent and provided the fastest reaction rates and high conversion… The impurities 28‑29 were formed at levels up to 0.1 a % when the reaction was conducted at 50 °C.”
“...the reaction temperature was reduced to 30 °C, which resulted in the challenging to purge impurities 26 and 27 being reduced to 0.1 a % at the end of reaction.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: During the PivCl‑mediated amide coupling, a prolonged (30 min–1 h) addition of amine 11 to the mixed anhydride (33) allowed background equilibrium to generate symmetric pivalic anhydride (35), leading to increased impurity 34 (up to 1.15 a %).
Solution_Description: The addition time of amine 11 was shortened to <2 min and the charge of DFPA was increased (1.65 equiv) relative to PivCl (1.3 equiv) to keep mixed anhydride concentration high, reducing impurity 34 to ≤0.55 a %.
Supporting_Evidence:
“A long addition time of 11… was reproduced… and was shown to lead to elevated levels of impurity 34.”
“...an excess of DFPA (1.65 equiv) relative to PivCl (1.30 equiv)… led to a reduction in impurity 34 from 3.4 a % to 0.55 a %.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: Crystallisation of AZD7594 (1) from 2‑MeTHF was inconsistent; the compound showed very low solubility in both 2‑MeTHF and MeCN, hampering reliable nucleation.
Solution_Description: MeCN was chosen as the reaction solvent because it gave a more robust nucleation and higher isolated yield; a controlled crystallisation protocol (70 °C heat‑to‑50 % water, then cooling to 0 °C) gave consistent crystals with impurity 34 <0.05 a %.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The pivaloyl chloride mediated amide coupling was found to perform well in both 2‑MeTHF and MeCN. However, MeCN was selected as the reaction solvent due to a more robust nucleation and crystallisation of AZD7594 (1).”
“...addition of 10 %v/v water and heating to 70 °C … followed by cooling to 0 °C provided a controlled nucleation and cooling crystallisation… achieving impurity 34 <0.05 a %.”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: During the synthesis of bromo‑amide 12, a batch with high water content in amine 6·HCl led to hydrolysis of the acid‑chloride intermediate, giving ∼13 a % of carboxylic acid 18 and a low overall yield (75 %).
Solution_Description: The process was modified to use anhydrous conditions (anisole as solvent, DIPEA as base) and a seeded crystallisation at elevated temperature to avoid hydrolysis and improve yield to 86 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The end‑of‑reaction analysis of this batch showed that significant amounts of carboxylic acid 18 were present (∼13 a %). … a high water content of amine 6·HCl was responsible for the hydrolysis of the acid‑chloride intermediate.”
“...anisole was selected as the formation of acid‑chloride 19… could also be carried out in this solvent… a seeded crystallisation starting at an elevated temperature was developed… resulting in 133.15 kg 12 (86.1 % yield).”

Paper Title: Metal-Catalyzed C–N Bond Forming Reaction Selection and Process Development for the Manufacture of AZD7594
Problem_Description: A previously unseen impurity (36) appeared at ~2 a % during large‑scale hydrogenolysis of intermediate 10; it shared structural similarity with the API and posed a risk to product quality.
Solution_Description: The impurity was successfully removed (<0.1 a %) during the subsequent formation and isolation of 11·Furoate by adjusting the work‑up (additional aqueous washes) and filtration steps, ensuring API specifications were met.
Supporting_Evidence: “The trifluoroacetamide impurity 36 was observed at ~2 a % at the end of the hydrogenation reaction… Because of the close structural similarity… this impurity posed a significant risk to the quality of the final API. … it was found that impurity 36 could be purged to <0.1 a % during the formation and isolation of 11·Furoate.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: The organolithium‑mediated reactions (methyllithium deprotonation and n‑BuLi lithium‑halogen exchange) are fast, highly exothermic and generate reactive gases (methane, H₂).  In batch mode the large heat release and the need to add n‑BuLi over many hours at –27 °C created temperature‑control difficulties and a safety risk of runaway or over‑pressurisation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A tubular flow reactor with insulated static mixers and actively‑cooled residence‑time units was employed.  The flow geometry provides rapid heat removal (high surface‑to‑volume ratio) and maintains a uniform temperature profile, while the inline quench and vent sizing prevent pressure spikes and safely vent generated gases.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction of 2 with n‑BuLi and the subsequent coupling reaction … are both fast and exothermic … control of temperature … is critical to mitigate undesirable side reactions.”
• “The deprotonation reaction is rapid and exothermic, it was determined that this reaction was amenable to being performed in batch mode …”
• “Across the campaign, average isolated yield … was approximately 65 % … The temperature increase across the first and second static mixer was found to be between 4 and 6 °C and 4 and 8 °C, respectively. Ultimately, the precooling of the streams and subsequent rapid cooling after the static mixers was sufficient to control the reaction exotherms.”
• “Standard safety protocols also included ensuring that the venting capacity … was sufficient for the specific process being run. Vent sizing calculations were conducted to ensure the vessels’ process safety valves and rupture disks were sufficient to prevent over‑pressurizing the vessels.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: During early experiments nitrogen dissolved in the pressurised feed tanks and out‑gassed in the reactor, creating two‑phase flow and causing residence‑time fluctuations.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A back‑pressure regulator was installed downstream of the second residence‑time unit to raise reactor pressure, and feed tanks were operated at the lowest feasible pressure (≈20 psig) without agitation to minimise dissolved nitrogen.  These steps prevented bubble formation and stabilised flow.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “One potential concern with the pressure‑driven flow approach used for streams B and C is unwanted two‑phase flow in the reactor caused by nitrogen dissolving into solution … This bubbling behavior was observed during some of our early experiments … can have a considerable impact on the residence time.”
• “Multiple steps were taken … a back‑pressure regulator was installed after Residence Time Unit 2 to increase reactor pressure; feed tanks were kept without agitation at the lowest feasible pressure (about 20 psig) … These efforts were successful, as we observed no significant bubbling during batch operations.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: The n‑BuLi solution occasionally contained solids, and moisture intrusion could generate insoluble lithium hydroxide, raising the risk of clogging and line rupture with a pyrophoric reagent.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Inline filters were placed upstream of each mass‑flow controller; stream B (n‑BuLi) was equipped with parallel backup filters and flush tees to allow rapid switching without stopping flow.  Filters were flushed and dried between batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The parallel filter design enabled rapid switching of the flow pathway from one filter to a backup filter without stopping flow if the filter was fouled during a run. This capability enables a rapid response to clogs without yield loss and safety implications associated with the breaking of the lines containing n‑BuLi during processing.”
• “While only single filters were installed in the flow paths for streams A and C, backup filters in parallel were included in the stream B flow path, as the n‑BuLi solution was observed to occasionally contain solids. Furthermore, small amounts of moisture intrusion could lead to the formation of insoluble lithium hydroxide.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: Variations in reagent concentrations (especially n‑BuLi) and flow‑rate control led to inconsistent stoichiometry, causing under‑ or over‑delivery of n‑BuLi, which directly affected impurity levels and product yield.
Solution_Description: An in‑process startup sample was taken after three residence times; its UPLC analysis guided immediate adjustment of the stream B flow rate (n‑BuLi) to correct stoichiometry before directing product to the collection vessel.  The corrected flow rate was then maintained for the remainder of the batch.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Small variations in solvent or reagent charges … can potentially compound and lead to an undesired reaction stoichiometry. For example, the impurity profile … is significantly impacted by the stoichiometry of n‑BuLi relative to 2.”
• “An in‑process sample was implemented prior to collecting the product stream. … when the desired values were achieved and maintained for at least three residence times, a startup sample … was collected … to ensure the calculated flow rates of the feed streams delivered acceptable reagent stoichiometry.”
• “If the impurity profile … was unacceptable, the stream B flow rate was adjusted up or down … The startup and sampling procedure would be repeated to ensure an outlet stream of acceptable quality.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: During solvent‑only test runs the temperature set‑point of –27 °C could not be reached simultaneously for streams A and B because they shared a cooling loop but had very different flow rates, limiting the ability to verify process conditions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A jacketed hose on an independent cooling loop was installed on the highest‑flow stream A, allowing independent temperature control of each feed line.  After this modification, both streams achieved the target temperature.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “During an initial solvent‑only run, it was found that the desired temperature of –27 °C could not be reached for streams A and B simultaneously … Because streams A and B were on the same cooling loop and had significantly different flow rates, simply adjusting the chiller set point would not result in both streams reaching the desired target.”
• “To address this issue, a jacketed hose on an independent cooling loop was installed before the heat exchanger of the highest flow rate stream, stream A … Installing the jacketed hose and repeating the solvent‑only runs allowed the chiller set points to be determined such that the desired temperature could be achieved for all three streams.”

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: The original flow‑rate calculation required solving three coupled equations for each batch, which was time‑consuming and introduced potential for calculation errors and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: A simplified approach was adopted: stream A flow was fixed (determined once from equipment sizing) and only streams B and C flows were recalculated to meet target stoichiometry, eliminating the need for solving the full set of equations each batch.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The initial strategy called for an assay of the stream C solution after preparation to confirm concentration. … Using this method, tight control over both residence time and stoichiometry could be achieved … Once it was determined that the process could handle moderate variability in reactor residence time without impacting product quality, a simpler approach … where the flow rate of stream A is fixed and only the flow rates of streams B and C need to be calculated …"

Paper Title: Pilot-Scale Operation and Characterization of an Organolithium-Mediated Coupling Reaction in Flow to Form a Ketone Intermediate on the Route to Nemtabrutinib
Problem_Description: Routine concentration assay of stream C (the ester solution) added analytical workload without improving control, as the stoichiometry tolerance was ±15 % and the calculated concentration from charge was acceptable.
Solution_Description: The concentration assay for stream C was eliminated; the process now relies on calculated concentrations based on weighed charges of 4 and THF, reducing analytical cost and simplifying startup.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Initial process development called for an assay of the stream C solution after preparation to confirm concentration. Analysis … indicated that calculation of stream C concentration based on the charges of 4 and THF … had only a slightly wider range of uncertainty than the analytical concentration assay. … this would allow for the removal of this concentration assay from the process, further simplifying the activities required for reaction startup.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Cyclopropanol (5) has a limited supply chain and high cost because it is produced from cyclopropyl bromide, a scarce starting material.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a supply‑centered route that begins from highly available cyclopropyl‑methyl‑ketone (6).
Supporting_Evidence: “Cyclopropyl alcohol (5) has a limited supply chain and high cost.”; “Supply‑centered synthesis ensures robust and economical access … including cyclopropyl‑methyl‑ketone (6).”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Typical 90 % hydrogen peroxide is not commercially available at the required scale and poses significant storage and handling hazards.
Solution_Description: Urea‑hydrogen peroxide (UHP) was adopted as a safer, anhydrous peroxide source that is commercially available and not listed as shock‑sensitive.
Supporting_Evidence: “Even at lab scale, such high peroxide concentrations are not available…considerable concern with storage and handling…UHP is an attractive alternative because … it is not listed as shock‑sensitive on safety data sheets.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: The Baeyer–Villiger oxidation generates a strong exotherm (adiabatic temperature rise of 263 °C), creating a Stoessel‑Class‑4 thermal hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to continuous‑flow equipment (CSTR and later a plug‑flow reactor) to limit the reacting inventory and improve heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: “A strong exotherm was apparent…adiabatic temperature rise is found to be 263 °C…classified as a Stoessel Criticality Class 4 hazard.”; “Running the reaction under a continuous regime…limits the amount of material reacting at a given time and improves the risk profile.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: When phosphate buffer is present the reaction mixture becomes a thick, difficult‑to‑stir gum that hampers mixing and conversion.
Solution_Description: The phosphate buffer was omitted, which gave either a clear biphasic mixture or a well‑behaved slurry depending on DCM content.
Supporting_Evidence: “The typical prescription of dibasic hydrogen phosphate buffer lowered the assay yield and caused the reaction to be a thick and difficult‑to‑stir gum. Removal of the phosphate results in either a clear biphasic mixture or a well‑behaved slurry.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: UHP particles settle rapidly in dichloromethane, leading to clogging and uneven dosing when attempting to pump a slurry.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A high‑molecular‑weight poly(ethylene oxide) (POLYOX) rheology modifier was added (0.1 wt %) to create a gel‑like suspension that prevents settling and can be pumped reliably.
Supporting_Evidence: “UHP particles were large and dense. They settled very quickly in DCM…Grinding…was only partially acceptable…The best solution was to use a rheology modifier…UHP settling was negligible at only 0.5 wt % loading…the gel‑like mixture could be pumped at the lowest flow rate of the peristaltic pump indefinitely.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Initial oxidation conditions used 10 equiv of UHP, giving high peroxide consumption, elevated cost, and still only ~90 % combined assay yield.
Solution_Description: Peroxide loading was reduced to ≤2.5 equiv (optimal 2 equiv UHP with 2 equiv TFAA) without loss of conversion, lowering material cost and exotherm risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “The peroxide loading of initial results were quite high (10 equiv)…Optimization identified safer conditions using much less peroxide (≤2.5 equiv…).”; Table 2 shows high yields with 2 equiv UHP.

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Cyclopropanol is volatile, water‑soluble, and has a boiling point similar to the trifluoroacetate ester, making isolation by evaporation difficult (co‑distillation loss).
Solution_Description: Three strategies were developed: (i) falling‑film evaporation at low temperature and reduced pressure; (ii) short‑path distillation; (iii) telescoped amine‑mediated cleavage followed by solvent exchange, each mitigating loss and decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Isolation of cyclopropyl alcohol is nontrivial. It is a volatile, water‑soluble liquid…The trifluoroacetate has a boiling point similar to that of DCM…gentle evaporation…nearly complete codistillation…The falling‑film evaporator limits heat exposure…short‑path distillation…telescoped procedure can greatly reduce the cycle time.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Cyclopropanol decomposes when heated in strongly acidic or basic media, threatening product integrity during isolation.
Solution_Description: A mild ester‑cleavage using a high‑boiling amine (DETA or NH₃) was implemented instead of strong bases (NaH) to avoid degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Cyclopropyl alcohol is prone to decomposition upon heating in strongly acidic or basic medium…The milder ester cleavage with a high‑boiling amine might be more appropriate.”; “After addition of a more mildly basic amine (DETA, NH₃)…Cyclopropanol is generated.”

Paper Title: Access to Cyclopropanol via Supply-Centered Synthesis
Problem_Description: Traditional isolation required multiple evaporation and distillation steps, prolonging cycle time and causing material loss.
Solution_Description: The crude cyclopropanol from the ammonium‑hydroxide route was telescoped directly into the subsequent SNAr coupling without any intermediate distillation, sharply reducing the overall process time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The cyclopropyl alcohol made via the ammonium hydroxide route could be directly telescoped into the SNAr reaction, without any distillation…This can greatly reduce cycle‑time during manufacturing.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: The key condensation step between aminosulfone (3) and 3‑acetamidophthalic anhydride (4) suffered from very low solubility of the anhydride in the traditional THF/AcOH solvent system (≈32 mg mL⁻¹ in THF, 22 mg mL⁻¹ in AcOH).  This produced a thick suspension that was difficult to stir, caused non‑uniform feed‑tank transfer, and required >30 L kg⁻¹ of solvent to achieve dissolution, dramatically lowering throughput.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF, DMAc, NMP) that gave >100 mg mL⁻¹ solubility for 4.  DMSO was selected for its lower toxicity and greener profile, enabling homogeneous feed solutions and eliminating the thick suspension.
Supporting_Evidence:
["low solubility of the starting materials and intermediates in the primary reaction solvent (THF)"],
		["poor solubility of 3‑acetamidophthalic anhydride (3‑AA, 4) in the reaction solvents THF and acetic acid (AcOH), at 32 and 22 mg mL⁻¹, respectively"],
		["A range of polar aprotic solvents proved to be appropriate for this purpose; dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), dimethylformamide (DMF), dimethylacetamide (DMAc), and N‑methylpyrrolidinone (NMP) all demonstrated greater than 100 mg mL⁻¹ solubility for 3‑AA (4)"],
		["DMSO was chosen because of its lower toxicity and better greenness compared to the other polar aprotic options" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: The batch condensation required >18 h at 72 °C to reach the target apremilast conversion (>98 % LCAP).  The lengthy residence time limited productivity and increased exposure to side‑reaction pathways (formation of de‑acetylated impurity 7).
Solution_Description: Conversion was transferred to a plug‑flow reactor (PFR) operated at 130 °C, which reduced the required reaction time to 15 min (entry 5, Table 1).  The PFR’s high surface‑to‑volume ratio provided superior heat‑transfer, enabling the higher temperature while maintaining control.
Supporting_Evidence:
["resulted in a shorter reaction time to reach the target conversion (>18 h in batch to 30 min in flow)"],
		["increasing the reaction temperature from 70 to 130 °C led to a reduction in reaction time from 10 h to 15 min"],
		["A plug‑flow reactor (PFR) provides improved heat‑ and mass‑transfer properties relative to a traditional batch reactor owing to the higher surface area‑to‑volume ratio"],
		["A residence time of 25 min was necessary to achieve full conversion" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: The legacy batch process required a series of four aqueous work‑ups, a distillative solvent‑swap and a final antisolvent crystallisation, totaling nine primary unit operations and generating large solvent waste.
Solution_Description: Direct addition of water (40 wt % final composition) to the hot PFR effluent served as an antisolvent, precipitating apremilast in a single step.  The continuous three‑stage MSMPR crystalliser replaced the multiple batch work‑ups, cutting the number of unit operations from nine to three and reducing both water and organic solvent PMI.
Supporting_Evidence:
["extensive postreaction unit operations contributing to significant solvent waste"],
		["The number of primary unit operations reduced from nine to three (67 % reduction)"],
		["Initial proof‑of‑concept batch crystallisation experiments demonstrated that adding water directly to post‑PFR crude reaction streams provided apremilast in excellent yield and purity"],
		["The antisolvent water drastically reduces the need for aqueous work‑ups and distillation steps" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: Attempted slurry transfer of the 3‑AA/THF mixture via peristaltic pumps showed non‑uniform flow, frequent clogging, and high sensitivity to particle size, posing a reliability risk for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: By moving to a fully dissolved DMSO feed (after the solvent change) the need for slurry pumping was eliminated, removing the clogging risk and allowing stable, low‑variance mass‑flow control with diaphragm pumps.
Supporting_Evidence:
["nonuniformity of transfer based on various tube diameters and pumping rates as well as the risk of clogging"],
		["reliance on transfer of a 3‑AA (4) feed‑tank slurry was deemed a risk to development and production campaigns"],
		["The change had no effect on conversion and purity profile compared to flow conditions with water" (implying dissolved feed) ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: DMSO decomposes thermally in the presence of strong acid at high temperature; ARC data showed decomposition onset at 149 °C and a TD₍₂₄₎ of 108 °C, only 22 °C below the intended 130 °C reaction temperature, indicating a significant exothermic runaway risk.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive safety assessment introduced crash‑cooling and line‑flushing protocols, continuous temperature monitoring, and a maximum residence time (25 min) that is < 1/10 TD₍₂₄₎.  The PFR material was changed to PFA tubing to avoid metal‑catalysed decomposition, and the process includes a rapid shut‑down procedure if temperature excursions occur.
Supporting_Evidence:
["ARC data of the reaction stream highlights thermal decomposition with an onset temperature of 149 °C"],
		["The phi‑corrected TD24 … was calculated to be 108 °C, which is 22 °C below the desired reaction temperature of 130 °C"],
		["No temperature excursions were observed over hundreds of hours of run time"],
		["additional safety measurements were designed into the production skid, such as crash‑cooling and line‑flushing protocols"],
		["PFA tubing was chosen to replace the 316L stainless steel in process characterization and end‑to‑end CM demonstration" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: Operating the PFR constructed from 316 SS caused progressive colour change (light yellow → orange/brown) in the product stream.  ICP analysis revealed increasing leached Fe, Cr, Ni, Mn and Mo, indicating metal contamination from the reactor wall.
Solution_Description: The reactor tubing was switched from stainless‑steel to perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) tubing, eliminating metal leaching and stabilising product colour and impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
["A colour change was observed in the collected material… the hypothesis was that the colour change … might be related to metal content"],
		["Concentrations of the metals… increase as the solution colour darkens in the stainless steel PFR process"],
		["Obvious colour change was observed in 316L stainless steel and Hastelloy C276 cases…"],
		["PFA tubing was chosen to replace the 316L stainless steel in process characterization and end‑to‑end CM demonstration" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: Continuous crystallisation in the MSMPR system exhibited fouling after ~5 h, leading to blockages and risking shutdown.  High supersaturation at 30 wt % water in MSMPR1 was identified as the cause.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The water content in MSMPR1 was lowered from 30 wt % to 25 wt % to reduce supersaturation, and the mean residence time of each MSMPR was increased to 90 min (up from 60 min).  This moderated crystal nucleation, eliminated fouling, and restored stable operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Fouling was observed after the 5 h time point in MSMPR1 on Day 1 … minimized significantly … after adjusting the water content from 30 to 25 wt %"],
		["The change … successfully achieved this goal"],
		["Mean residence times of each MSMPR were set to 90 min"],
		["These antisolvent amounts were determined based on the observed behaviour during batch crystallisation" ]

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part I: Process Development and Intensification by Utilizing Flow Chemistry Principles
Problem_Description: The final solid‑form stage (filtration, washing, drying) of apremilast crude required manual, time‑intensive batch filtration and overnight drying, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: A dual‑centrifuge‑in‑tandem isolation strategy was introduced, allowing simultaneous deliquoring, washing and spin‑drying of slurry streams in a staggered schedule, dramatically shortening the isolation time and enabling continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
["A dual‑centrifuge‑in‑tandem system is particularly enabling in filtering apremilast crude … deliquoring, washing, and spin‑drying tasks can be performed in parallel with a staggered time schedule"],
		["The centrifuges would continue to alternate this slurry fill‑and‑filter and wash/spin‑down/discharge sequence through the end of manufacturing"],
		["Important to the execution of such a strategy is the assurance that the crystal population generated … will consistently filter, be washed, and spun down within the set schedule" ]

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: The legacy batch process for the acetal‑deprotection step gave only a 57 % isolated yield and, because the stage was run in relatively small 416 kg batches, it became a throughput bottleneck for the overall DB Mesylate synthesis.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow platform was introduced, allowing residence times of ≤10 min (target <1 h) and thereby increasing conversion and overall yield to ≈75 % while providing a scalable high‑throughput operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The current process … average yield of 57 % …”
• “A general target for reaction time of less than 1 h, and preferably less than 10 min, was set …”
• “Implementation of a new flow process … enabled a 20 % increase in yield”
• “The continuous process … meet the projected commercial demand”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: Both the reaction and downstream work‑up required large volumes of solvent, which limited the ability to scale the process economically.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified glacial acetic acid (with controlled water content) as a suitable reaction medium; the flow protocol uses defined relative volumes (RV) to keep solvent usage low and to maintain high reactant concentrations.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “high solvent volumes were required for both the reaction and the workup process. This limited the extent to which the process could be scaled up effectively.”
• “An initial solubility screen … determined that the starting material was readily soluble (>100 mg mL⁻¹) in MeCN, MeOH, THF, and AcOH … most yielded poorer results than the current process that had acetonide (1) suspended in acetic acid.”
• “Acetonide (1) was dissolved … in acetic acid with varied levels of water … the stability data suggested that the flow process could be run with the proposed two‑feed configuration.”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: Elevated temperatures and prolonged residence times promoted degradation of the desired glycol (2) to the undesired tetraol (3), increasing impurity levels.
Solution_Description: Temperature was screened between 15 °C and 50 °C; 30 °C gave the best balance of conversion (≈75 %) with minimal tetraol formation. The water content in the formic‑acid feed was tuned to 0.32 RV to further suppress degradation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Elevated temperatures appeared to result in increased levels of tetraol (3) relative to conversion.”
• “As the temperature increased to 30 °C, the conversion (area %) to the desired glycol (2) increased, with yield peaking around ∼75 % … Further temperature increases lead to degradation of glycol (2) with a significant increase in levels of tetraol (3).”
• “The relative volume of water … optimal conversion to glycol (2) was obtained at 0.32 RV of water.”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: Acetonide (1) was unstable in acetic acid when water content was high, leading to premature conversion to glycol (2) and by‑products during feed storage.
Solution_Description: Water content in the acetic‑acid feed was strictly controlled (≤ 0.2 % w/w) and a two‑feed configuration (separate acetonide‑AcOH and water‑formic‑acid streams) was adopted to preserve feed stability over 48 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Acetonide (1) … sampled over 48 h … As the level of water in acetic acid increased, the rate of degradation … also increased.”
• “Provided water levels are controlled, the stability data suggested that the flow process could be run with the proposed two‑feed configuration.”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: Direct quenching of the acidic reaction mixture with 15 % aqueous KOH generated large exotherms (≈55 kJ mol⁻¹) and required impractically high quench volumes, creating safety and equipment‑sizing concerns.
Solution_Description: Instead of a direct quench, the mixture was first extracted into toluene (removing the acids into the aqueous phase) and only the organic glycol phase was subsequently neutralised with a reduced volume of KOH, lowering the adiabatic temperature rise to ~15 °C and achieving a Stoessel class 1 safety rating.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A large exotherm was observed … exotherms of 55.25 and 58.8 kJ mol⁻¹ for reaction of potassium hydroxide with acetic acid and formic acid, respectively.”
• “The direct quench also proved to be impractical for equipment sizing … 31 RV of 15 wt % quench solution being required.”
• “An extraction with toluene … reduced the amount of potassium hydroxide required to quench the final organic product stream.”
• “An adiabatic temperature rise of 15.7 °C was calculated for the post‑extraction quench … giving an inherently safe Stoessel class rating of 1⁸ for the final process.”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: When the total flow rate was reduced below 25 % of the development rate, inadequate mixing caused lower glycol (2) conversion and higher tetraol (3) formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Agitation rates were maintained at ≥ 120 % of the calculated just‑dispersed speed (Njd) in both the laboratory CSTRs and the plant mixers, ensuring sufficient dispersion and preventing mixing‑limited impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Poor mixing resulted in reduced glycol (2) and increased acetonide (1) and tetraol (3).”
• “Both micro‑ and macro‑mixing were expected to be affected … End‑of‑reaction performance due to reduced mixing was only impacted when flow rates were dropped to below 25 % of the flow rate used throughout development.”
• “Agitation rates for the CSTRs were operated above 120 % Njd …”

Paper Title: Going with the Flow: Implementation of a New Continuous Process for a Selective Acetal Deprotection
Problem_Description: Scaling from the 87 mL SiC micro‑reactor to the 1080 mL Hastelloy plant reactor introduced uncertainties in Reynolds number, heat‑transfer, and residence‑time distribution, potentially affecting robustness.
Solution_Description: A low‑volume (20 kg) confirmatory run was performed in the plant reactor; parallel 3 mm channels were used to match the laboratory Reynolds number, and RTD measurements (TiS ≈ 31) confirmed comparable flow behaviour before full‑scale manufacture.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reactor available for manufacture was manufactured by a different supplier … geometry similar … providing a consistent Reynolds number between scales.”
• “A low‑volume, 20 kg confirmatory run … was used to assess performance prior to continuing with the manufacturing campaign.”
• “The laboratory development reactor showed an average value of 29 TiS, while the plant average was 31 TiS … comparable performance gave confidence in a successful scale‑up.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Because many primary operating parameters affect multiple secondary process parameters, the integrated continuous‑manufacturing (CM) process exhibits strong inter‑parameter connectivity.  A one‑factor‑at‑a‑time (OFAT) study is insufficient; cross‑variations must be explored to understand how simultaneous changes impact the reaction and crystallization outcomes.
Solution_Description: The team performed fixed‑set‑point multifactor‑at‑a‑time (FSV‑MFAT) experiments that varied two or more process parameters together (e.g., flow rates Q1/Q2) to map the combined effects and define proven‑acceptable ranges (PARs) for the integrated CM process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The interconnectivity of parameters is illustrated … the full set of binary cross variations is quite expansive; we therefore took a risk‑based approach for selecting a specific subset of cross variations to study … The first FSV‑MFAT experiment set consisted of just four experiments varying Q1 and Q2 at ±15 % of their set points … each experiment gave passing results, with no process upsets and isolated Apremilast solid passing the release specifications.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Several process parameters are time‑dependent (mass‑flow ratios, MRT, temperature, axial‑dispersion number).  Temporary deviations (pump failures, loss of heat) could push a parameter outside its proven‑acceptable range (PAR) and trigger a deviation if a conservative strategy were used.
Solution_Description: Temporary‑disturbance (TD) experiments were carried out (e.g., Q1 = 0 % SP for 30 min, Q2 = 0 % SP for 20 min, removal of PFR from the temperature bath for 20 min) to determine tolerable time‑duration (TTD) limits for each time‑dependent parameter without affecting product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “To avoid formulating an overly conservative control strategy, we also implemented temporary disturbance process characterization experiments … The goal of these experiments is to identify tolerable time durations (TTD) for which the process parameters can be outside of the given PARs without compromising the quality of the produced material.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: When agitation power per unit mass (PPUM) in the MSMPR crystallizers was set too low (0.03 W kg⁻¹), mixing was very poor, leading to fouling and temporary clogging of the system.
Solution_Description: The agitation level was increased to a modest 0.09 W kg⁻¹, which restored adequate mixing and eliminated fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: “When a power‑per‑unit‑mass (PPUM) of only 0.03 W/kg was applied, the mixing was observed to be very poor and ultimately resulted in fouling and temporary clogging. This was deemed unacceptable, and a less‑extreme low agitation (0.09 W/kg PPUM) was tried; the mixing at this PPUM was observed to be significantly better and no process upsets were observed.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: When agitation PPUM in the MSMPRs was set too high (1.26 W kg⁻¹), the solid product filtered and dried significantly slower than under baseline conditions, which is undesirable for throughput.
Solution_Description: The agitation level was lowered to 0.59 W kg⁻¹, achieving normal filtration and drying rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “When a very high PPUM of 1.26 W/kg was applied for the mixing, the produced solid was observed to filter and dry significantly more slowly … a more moderate PPUM of 0.59 W/kg was applied, resulting in normal filtration and drying times.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: The axial‑dispersion number (ADN) of the plug‑flow reactor (PFR) could not be varied independently from other process parameters without redesigning the reactor geometry, limiting the ability to study its effect directly.
Solution_Description: The ADN was measured for the baseline lab‑scale PFR and held constant (≤0.0013) while other parameters were varied; the process was later modeled to understand its impact without needing to change the reactor configuration during experiments.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ADN, our measure of RTD, was not varied independently across this first set of experiments as doing so required reconfiguration of the PFR … the axial‑dispersion number was recorded for each experiment but could not be varying independently from the other listed process parameters without changing the reactor configuration.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: A control strategy that relied on many in‑process controls (IPCs) would increase operational complexity and waste, which is undesirable for a continuous manufacturing process.
Solution_Description: A parametric‑only control strategy was implemented, using the defined PARs and TTDs for the primary operating parameters, eliminating the need for IPCs and enabling discrete‑lot batch release of the drug‑substance intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The data collected across the PC experiment sets … support a control strategy that relied on parametric control only … no in‑process controls (IPCs) were required.”

Paper Title: A Continuous Process for Manufacturing Apremilast. Part II: Process Characterization to Establish a Parametric Control Strategy
Problem_Description: Standard batch‑reactor laboratory setups are not directly applicable to integrated continuous processes, making it challenging to perform process‑characterization (PC) experiments across all unit operations.
Solution_Description: A dedicated lab‑scale continuous setup was constructed, featuring PFA‑tubing PFR, diaphragm pumps with mass‑flow controllers, inline sampling/dilution cart, FBRM probe, and peristaltic pumps for MSMPR transfer, allowing realistic PC of the integrated CM process.
Supporting_Evidence: “To conduct PC experiments for such processes, an appropriate dedicated lab scale setup must be established … The feed tank and PFR setup … consists of two feed vessels, pumped into a 120 mL PFR … The MSMPR crystallization setup ... consists of a series of three 100 mL vessels … A focused‑beam reflectance measurement (FBRM) probe was added to the first MSMPR …”

Paper Title: Concomitant Precipitation of Solid-State Miscible Product-Impurity Phases in Solution Crystallization – Part 2: Industrial Case Studies
Problem_Description: When the API synthesis was transferred from laboratory scale to pilot‑plant scale, the crude API contained 6–7 a % of a regio‑isomer impurity that could not be removed by the standard toluene crystallisation. The impurity level varied widely (2–7 a %) and the process gave an unacceptable product yield, causing an out‑of‑specification (OOS) result.
Solution_Description: A different crystal form (tert‑butanol solvate) was selected, breaking the solid‑state miscibility with the impurity. The crystallisation was moved to a tert‑butanol/H₂O solvent system with a cooling/antisolvent operation. This gave >90 % product yield and reduced the impurity to <0.3 a %.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "...upon scale‑up suddenly, the regioisomer could not be purged using the standard work up and toluene crystallization, which led to an out‑of‑specification (OOS) result. The regioisomer was obtained in the crude API at 6.2 a %..." 
- "...multiple API batches/lab lots could not purge the regioisomer anymore leading to it being present in variable levels from 2 a % to 7 a % in the crystallized crude API. Obviously, the regioisomer impurity posed a serious challenge..." 
- "...the lack of consistency in the crude API crystallisation was alarming." 
- "...impurity could be rejected to some extent but not enough with respect to the desired yield..." 
Solution:
- "...a switch of the crystal form was feasible as this was the crude API isolation and not the final API isolation..." 
- "...the solvent selection was based on finding the highest separation efficiency... tert‑butanol/H₂O..." 
- "...the combined cooling/antisolvent crystallisation was quickly developed in tert‑butanol/H₂O... The entire process was executed at a max Vp of 13 L kg⁻¹ API giving a theoretical yield of 94.5 %...the impurity was completely rejected..."

Paper Title: Concomitant Precipitation of Solid-State Miscible Product-Impurity Phases in Solution Crystallization – Part 2: Industrial Case Studies
Problem_Description: A regio‑isomer impurity formed at ~14 w % in the crude API after the final synthetic step. The impurity was significantly less soluble than the API and solid‑state miscible, so crystallisation from n‑propanol/H₂O could not achieve the required impurity rejection without using large solvent volumes, leading to low overall product yield.
Solution_Description: A polish filtration in dichloromethane (DCM) was employed to physically separate the impurity‑rich CSS‑β phase, reducing the impurity to 4.5 w % in the filtrate. The filtrate was then switched to a THF/MTBE antisolvent system, enabling a second crystallisation that lowered the impurity to <0.5 w % with an overall yield of ~75 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "...approximately 20 w % of the regioisomer was formed in the final synthetic step... The impurity was significantly less soluble than the API, rendering its rejection via crystallisation under thermodynamic control elusive in the chosen solvent system." 
- "...the impurity level from the final reaction step was so high, it was questionable whether crystallisation by itself could control the impurity level..." 
Solution:
- "...a polish filtration was carried out in DCM that physically filtered the regioisomer phase (CSS‑β) from 14 w % down to 4.5 w % in the filtrate." 
- "...the solvent switch was therefore required to a solvent system that is more amenable to purification by crystallisation. ... THF/MTBE would be ideal for an antisolvent crystallisation..." 
- "...the final crystallisation could thermodynamically reject the remaining 4.5 w % regioisomer to below 0.5 % in yield exceeding 70 %..."

Paper Title: Concomitant Precipitation of Solid-State Miscible Product-Impurity Phases in Solution Crystallization – Part 2: Industrial Case Studies
Problem_Description: During a pilot‑plant campaign, the impurity level in the solid product increased from 0.40 a % to >3 a % over the course of the batch (heat/cool cycle and ageing). The slow formation of a second CSS‑β phase (SLIP 2/CSS) caused batch‑to‑batch variability and loss of yield.
Solution_Description: The material was reslurried in ethanol, which dissolves the impurity‑rich CSS‑β phase and converts the mechanism to SLIP 1/CSS. This reslurry step removed the impurity to 0.45 a % and provided a stable, reproducible process.
Supporting_Evidence:

- "...the impurity was reslurried in ethanol in order to increase the level of the impurity so that the intermediate could be successfully used..." 
- "...the SLIP tests show that increasing Vp in wet MeTHF leads to a reduction in product purity... ethanol is more favourable in terms of impurity rejection... the impurity was not isolated... the reslurry in ethanol changed the mechanism to SLIP 1/CSS..."

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 1Process History and Development Strategy
Problem_Description: Starting material 1 was a supply‑chain risk because its preparation required dimethyl disulfide, a hazardous reagent.
Solution_Description: A new, shorter synthesis of the indanone core was developed from the commodity dihydrocoumarin 11, eliminating the need for dimethyl disulfide.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Starting material 1 was a supply chain risk due to the use of dimethyl disulfide in its preparation.”
“To avoid these concerns, an improved synthesis of 5 was developed, starting from the commodity reagent dihydrocoumarin 11.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 1Process History and Development Strategy
Problem_Description: The commercial supply route used dichloromethane (a chlorinated solvent) in a Friedel–Crafts acylation, posing environmental and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The chlorinated solvent was removed by redesigning the sequence (using the dihydrocoumarin‑derived route) and substituting safer solvents for the Friedel–Crafts step.
Supporting_Evidence:
“dichloromethane was employed in a Friedel–Crafts acylation to form indanone 5.”
“Removing dichloromethane from the commercial process is preferable to achieve our green chemistry goals.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 1Process History and Development Strategy
Problem_Description: The original methyl‑sulfone installation relied on a peroxide‑based oxidation and stoichiometric copper/sodium methanesulfinate, both hazardous and expensive.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 1Process History and Development Strategy
Problem_Description: Early enzyme variants over‑oxidized indanone 22 to an indanedione, giving low assay yields, poor mass balance and reaction stalling.
Solution_Description: Directed evolution of FoPip4H focused on chemoselectivity, increased enzyme loading, and a 40‑fold increase in reaction concentration, delivering >99 % ee and >90 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence:

Problem_Description: Belzutifan has an extremely low solubility in water (0.2 mg mL⁻¹), making isolation by conventional work‑up difficult.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 2Development of a Scalable Nickel-Catalyzed Sulfonylation
Problem_Description: The nickel‑catalyzed sulfonylation is a doubly heterogeneous reaction involving two insoluble salts (K₂S₂O₅ and KCO₂H). When the process was scaled from the 4 g EasyMax vessel to a 15 g round‑bottom flask, the reaction profile changed dramatically – the desired product conversion dropped and impurity 7 rose to >20 % even though the same reagents, stoichiometry and impeller speed were used. The heterogeneous mixture caused poor mixing, particle‑size‑dependent mass‑transfer limitations, and inconsistent conversion on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A controlled‑addition strategy was implemented: a solution of K₂S₂O₅ (1.7 equiv) in ethylene glycol was added slowly rather than dosing a solid slurry. The addition rate was tuned (10 h for the formate charge, 24 h for the K₂S₂O₅ solution) and the impeller speed/vessel geometry were optimized (four‑blade pitched turbine, 400 rpm). This eliminated the mixing‑related scale‑up failures and restored the conversion/impurity profile observed in the DoE experiments.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The doubly heterogeneous nature of the reaction proved difficult to scale due to mixing and particle size issues." (Abstract)
• "We were disappointed to discover a vastly different reaction profile ... <bold>7> 23% ... the potential mixing issue of this heterogeneous reaction had finally manifested" (Sec 2.4)
• "Controlled addition of a solution of potassium formate in ethylene glycol was found to mitigate all scaling issues" (Abstract)
• Table 2 shows that changing vessel/impeller and rpm dramatically alters % 2 and % 7, confirming the mixing sensitivity.
• "The investigation began by looking at both the suspension and particle size of the K₂S₂O₅..." (Sec 2.4)
• “The reaction was demonstrated on a multikilogram scale with robust kinetics between scales.” (Abstract) – after the controlled‑addition solution was applied.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 2Development of a Scalable Nickel-Catalyzed Sulfonylation
Problem_Description: Impurity 7 (hydrodehalogenation product) formed in significant amounts when potassium formate was added in a single charge or when excess K₂S₂O₅ was used. This impurity reduced isolated yield of the desired sulfone and complicated downstream purification, especially at larger scale where impurity levels reached 23 % in some runs.
Solution_Description: Formate was introduced as a dilute aqueous or ethylene‑glycol solution and charged continuously over 4–24 h. The slow, controlled feed kept the concentration of free formate low, suppressing the competing hydro‑dehalogenation pathway and limiting impurity 7 to ≤5 % (entries 2–5 of Table 4). Using ethylene‑glycol as the solvent also avoided water‑related gumming.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 1 shows that using KCO₂K gave higher % 7 (9.1 %) compared with KNaCO₂ (1.5 %).
• Table 4 entry 1 (4 h aqueous charge) gave 20.0 % 7, whereas entry 2 (24 h aqueous charge) gave only 4.4 % 7.
• "Upon charging the remaining reagents and reaching the reaction temperature, HCO₂K (1.2 equiv in MeCN) was added over 10 h…" (Sec 2.5)
• "The slow addition of HCO₂K over 20 h ultimately solved both issues of controlling impurity 7 and removing the need to mill either of the two salts." (Sec 2.5)
• "Ethylene glycol was found to be able to dissolve HCO₂K… delivering results similar to those of the aqueous solution charge but with no observable gumming." (Sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 2Development of a Scalable Nickel-Catalyzed Sulfonylation
Problem_Description: Milling K₂S₂O₅ to a fine particle size (D₅₀ = 12 µm) improved impurity control but added a unit‑operation step and did not fully resolve the mixing problem; higher agitation rates still increased impurity 7. The extra milling step increased material‑handling cost and equipment wear.
Solution_Description: Instead of milling, the process was switched to a continuous charge of a K₂S₂O₅/ethylene‑glycol solution combined with a slow formate feed. This eliminated the need for any solid‑state particle‑size control, removed the milling operation, and still achieved low impurity levels on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • "While we were pleased to discover that this led to less 7 (entry 5), we were disappointed to find that the agitation issues remained unresolved (entry 6)." (Sec 2.4, Table 2)\n• "The addition of an aqueous solution of HCO₂K to the reaction mixture did not inhibit the reaction, but it did lead to 20.0 % of impurity 7 when charged over four hours… The slow addition of HCO₂K over 20 h ultimately solved both issues of controlling impurity 7 and removing the need to mill either of the two salts." (Sec 2.5)\n• "Incredibly, this was achieved without the need to mill K₂S₂O₅, thus removing a unit operation from the process." (Sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 2Development of a Scalable Nickel-Catalyzed Sulfonylation
