Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 6Development of a Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution in Water
Problem_Description: The early‑stage S<sub>N</sub>Ar reaction suffered from several practical and performance issues: (1) product inhibition between the newly formed belzutifan and phenoxide limited conversion, giving low yields; (2) the originally employed formamide solvent raised safety concerns (toxicity, impurity profile, removal, REACH restrictions); (3) visual glass corrosion due to in‑situ HF generation; (4) reactions often produced oily or biphasic mixtures that behaved as poorly‑stirred slurries; (5) slow filtration of the crude slurry because undissolved trifluoride and phenol formed an oil layer; (6) hydrolysis of belzutifan to benzamide (4) reduced purity and overall yield; (7) conversion and impurity levels were highly sensitive to the composition of the head‑space (CO₂ pressure, N₂ venting), leading to inconsistent performance on scale; (8) the use of solid additives (Celite, alumina) introduced heterogeneity and complicated downstream isolation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
[MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: To overcome the identified shortcomings the team implemented a series of targeted changes: (1) switched the reaction medium from formamide to water (highly polar, low product solubility) to eliminate product inhibition and enable reactive crystallization; (2) introduced fluoride‑scavenging solid additives (Celite, alumina) to capture HF and prevent glass corrosion; (3) added small amounts of isopropanol or 2‑methyl‑3‑buten‑2‑ol to improve solubility and give a well‑behaved slurry; (4) employed 20 mol % Na pyruvate (and, where needed, acidic alumina) as an antioxidant/promoter that suppressed belzutifan hydrolysis; (5) controlled head‑space pressure and nitrogen‑sweep rate (vented vs sealed, 5 psig back‑pressure, 1 HT h⁻¹ sweep) to regulate CO₂ levels, thereby stabilising conversion and impurity profiles; (6) applied the same gas‑environment control at pilot‑scale, confirming that pressure‑sweep tuning reproduced the small‑scale performance; (7) used a Hastelloy C‑276 reactor to withstand HF and avoid glass corrosion; (8) performed carbon treatment followed by MeCN/H₂O recrystallisation to remove colour and residual impurities, delivering API of >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: • "Through the judicious choice of solvent, product inhibition could be overcome using formamide…" (p. 3). • "Due to reaction sensitivity to the vapor phase composition, engineering controls around the headspace pressure and sweep rate were tuned…" (Abstract). • "visual glass corrosion stemming from hydrofluoric acid generation" (Table 1 discussion). • "These reactions resulted in oils and/or biphasic mixtures" (Table 1 discussion). • "slow filtration was observed when the batch was directly isolated… we postulated that the slow filtration was due to an oil layer" (Isolation section). • "major impurity formed… benzamide 4… 0.6–2.9 % yield" (p. 4). • "We observed different reaction kinetics when the vial was sealed or vented" (p. 4). • "concerns surrounding potential HF generation and glass corrosion… gram scale processing needed to be carried out in a reactor constructed from Hastelloy C‑276" (ref 18). Solution: • "we investigated water as a solvent…" (p. 3). • "Additives such as Celite or alumina could provide improvements in the yield … and no visual corrosion of the vials" (Table 1). • "addition of 0.5 V isopropanol (IPA)… could afford belzutifan in 83 and 86 % yield… well‑behaved slurry" (Table 1). • "The use of Ca pyruvate as an additive could decrease the hydrolysis to 0.60 %" (Table 2). • "controlled nitrogen flow as a measure to improve the reaction conversion…" (Figure 4, Table 3). • "A slightly elevated temperature (90 °C), K₂CO₃ (0.9 equiv)… 5 psig nitrogen back‑pressure… 1 HT h⁻¹ sweep" (Figure 7). • "…Hastelloy C‑276 reactor…" (ref 18). • "carbon treatment of crude belzutifan… followed by MeCN/H₂O recrystallisation… pure belzutifan was obtained with >99 % purity" (p. 7).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: The original batch process using the Li/Li synergistic organolithium system suffered from poor repeatability and safety concerns when scaled‑up because organolithium reagents are highly reactive and can lead to uncontrolled exotherms.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved the synthesis to a continuous‑flow platform built from corrosion‑resistant 316 L/PTFE tubing and plunger pumps, which provides rapid heat removal and precise temperature control, thereby mitigating the safety risks and improving reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: "scaling up the process presents significant challenges due to its poor repeatability and safety concerns associated with the commercial scale use of organolithium reagents"; "materials used must (1) be corrosion resistant, (2) be low temperature resistant, and (3) enable rapid heat transfer"; "pumps and reaction tubes made with 316 L or PTFE materials were used"; "the design of the flow chemistry system incorporates three reactors immersed in separate cooling baths"; "continuous flow chemistry has enabled a safer regime for the employment of organometallics"

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: In batch mode the lithiation/addition sequence generated by‑products because the slow heat dissipation and inadequate mixing caused localized hot spots and poor mass transfer.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Three temperature‑controlled reactors (‑25 °C/‑35 °C/‑85 °C) were employed and an arrow‑type static mixer was installed to ensure uniform mixing, which eliminated hot spots and suppressed by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: "byproduct formation due to poor mixing and limited heat dissipation"; "To accommodate these different temperature requirements, the design of the flow chemistry system incorporates three reactors immersed in separate cooling baths"; "Lowering the temperature for all three steps resulted in higher yields and enantiomeric excess"; "An arrow mix was used for sufficient mixing"

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: The batch process required a 5 h residence time to reach acceptable conversion, and initial flow trials gave only 73 % isolated yield despite a much shorter reaction time.
Solution_Description: Residence times were shortened to 7.5 min/7.5 min/5 min for the three stages, and the temperature profile was optimized (‑25 °C/‑35 °C/‑85 °C), which restored the yield to >90 % while cutting the overall reaction time to ~2 h on a 100 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: "reaction time of 5 h vs 40 min"; "The continuous flow process allowed for smooth progression of the reaction; however, the results were less satisfactory (73 % yield)"; "When the reaction temperature was increased from −35 to −15 °C, the dr ratio changed… with higher yield"; "The highest yield and enantiomeric excess (ee) were achieved with a residence time of 7.5/7.5/5 min"; "Scale‑up ... 100 g ... 94 % yield ... 2 h"

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: The original work‑up relied on silica‑gel chromatography, which is labor‑intensive and unsuitable for large scale; the product’s solubility varied dramatically with solvent and temperature, complicating isolation.
Solution_Description: A telescoped purification was developed that acidifies the crude mixture to the HCl salt, precipitates it with anti‑solvent (heptane/methanol), and finally recrystallizes from EtOH, eliminating the need for column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: "difficulty isolating products due to high solubility or presence of impurities"; "The product exhibited high solubility in toluene, but as the anti‑solvent methanol was gradually added, the solubility decreased noticeably"; "We successfully developed a workup process … acidified into hydrochloride (HCl) salt … EtOH was added … the desired TBAJ‑876 (99 % ee) was obtained"; "purification process obviating the need for silica gel chromatographic purification has also been developed"

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: Water present in the solvent led to incomplete formation of the achiral base and inconsistent lithiation, reducing conversion.
Solution_Description: The water content was controlled by using freshly distilled solvents and by increasing the equivalents of n‑BuLi (up to 1.6 equiv) and L1 (up to 1.8 equiv), which restored full conversion and improved yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "We envisaged that the water content of the organic solvent is crucial in this lithiation reaction"; "some water in the solvent is present … insufficient preparation of the achiral base was observed"; "Increasing the quantity of n‑BuLi from 1.3 equiv to 1.6 equiv improved the yield to 90 %"; "When 1.8 equiv of L1 was employed, the reaction proceeded with 92 % yield"

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for the Efficient Preparation of Anti-Tuberculosis-Specific Drug TBAJ-876
Problem_Description: Low temperatures in the final reactor (‑85 °C) caused a risk of freezing and clogging of the flow line.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A downstream continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) operating at 0 °C was installed for quenching, allowing the reaction mixture to be safely warmed and preventing blockages.
Supporting_Evidence: "To address the risk of freezing due to the low temperature in PFR‑03 and the possibility of clogging, a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) was designed for quenching the reaction"; "After the reaction, the system was run in a CSTR‑01 where it was quenched simultaneously with Solution E"; "The continuous flow system was constructed … plunger pumps … no clogging occurred during the whole process"

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: Initial hydrochlorination of 1‑methyl‑1‑cyclohexene with 1.2 equiv HCl (37 % aq.) at rt for 20 min gave only 11 % isolated yield, indicating poor conversion under the tested stoichiometry.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of HCl to 2 equiv per mmol of alkene raised the GC yield to 84 %; addition of 0.5 mL acetic acid further boosted the yield to 96 %, showing that both excess acid and AcOH act as rate‑enhancing promoters.
Supporting_Evidence: “afforded tertiary chloride 2 within just 20 min, albeit with a low 11 % yield (entry 1).”; “When we increased the hydrochloric acid quantity from 0.1 to 2.0 mL per mmol of alkene, the GC yield reached 84 % (entries 2‑4).”; “Indeed, the inclusion of 0.5 mL of acetic acid increased the yield from 61 % (entry 2) to 96 % (entry 5).”

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: The reaction required vigorous agitation; lowering the stirring speed from 1500 rpm to 0, 500 or 1000 rpm caused a sharp decrease in GC yield, indicating mass‑transfer limitations in the biphasic HCl/AcOH/alkene mixture.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed with a digital overhead stirrer (1500 rpm, PTFE blade) in a 2 L round‑bottom flask, ensuring intense mixing and stable emulsion; the same setup was used for scale‑up to 1 mol without loss of conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “From the start, we worked with a high stirring speed (1500 rpm). Decreasing this speed to 0, 500, and 1000 rpm resulted in a sharp decrease in the GC yield (entries 10–12).”; “Figure 1 illustrates the reaction of styrene on a large scale… stirred at 1500 rpm with a digital overhead stirrer … equipped with a PTFE stirrer blade.”

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: Screening of other carboxylic acids (dichloroacetic acid, trifluoroacetic acid) showed they were efficient additives but their high price made them unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Acetic acid, a cheap bulk chemical, was selected as the optimal additive, providing comparable rate acceleration without the expense of stronger acids.
Supporting_Evidence: “We also tested several other carboxylic acids and found that dichloroacetic acid and trifluoroacetic acid are also efficient additives; however, these acids are significantly more expensive than acetic acid, and therefore, they were no longer pursued in our studies.”

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: Hydrochlorination of a benzonitrile led to nitrile hydrolysis, delivering mainly the corresponding carboxylic acid and low yield of the desired chloride.
Solution_Description: Addition of FeCl₃ (catalytic amount) suppressed nitrile hydrolysis, preserving the nitrile group and affording the target chloride in a satisfactory 62 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Standard conditions, hydrochlorination of a benzonitrile was accompanied by hydrolysis of the nitrile, resulting in a low yield of carboxylic acid … To our delight, iron trichloride emerged as a beneficial additive, preserving the integrity of the nitrile group and enabling the isolation of targeted product 20 with a satisfactory yield of 62 %.”

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: Para‑methoxy‑styrene produced a gel‑like polymeric material under standard conditions; even after dilution in CH₂Cl₂ and reducing HCl to 5 equiv, only 42 % NMR yield was obtained accompanied by oligomer/polymer side‑products.
Solution_Description: Diluting the reaction mixture with dichloromethane and using a reduced amount of HCl (5 equiv) lowered the concentration of reactive species, mitigating polymerization and improving the isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “para‑methoxy styrene gave only a gel‑like product. Dilution of the styrene in dichloromethane and only 5 equiv of hydrochloric afforded 11 in 42 % NMR‑yield accompanied by what appears to be an oligo‑ or polymer side‑product.”

Paper Title: Hydrochlorination of Alkenes with Hydrochloric Acid
Problem_Description: Reproducibility tests showed that stirring rate requirements depended on substrate polarity; some substrates formed homogeneous solutions (no stirring dependence) while others required vigorous agitation, leading to inconsistent guidelines.
Solution_Description: The authors mapped substrate polarity to optimal stirring conditions, establishing that homogeneous mixtures (polar alkenes) can be run at low rpm, whereas biphasic systems still need high stirring, thereby standardising the protocol for each substrate class.
Supporting_Evidence: “After the submission of the manuscript, one of the reviewers pointed out that the stirring rate is very likely dependent on the character of the mixture … we found for most cases biphasic mixtures … some of the more polar alkenes … gave homogeneous solutions … conversion was independent of stirring rates.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 4Applications of Process Analytical Technology in Heterogeneous Biocatalytic Hydroxylation
Problem_Description: Indanone has a very low aqueous solubility (<1 g L⁻¹) so that, even when 100 vol % of water is used, the reaction mixture is a thin slurry containing solid indanone, liquid organic phase, aqueous phase and gas.  The slurry makes the reaction kinetics difficult to predict and causes sampling problems for offline analysis.
Solution_Description: A small amount of 1‑octanol (6 vol %) was added as an amphiphilic cosolvent/additive.  The 1‑octanol forms droplets that wet the surface of indanone particles, preventing their aggregation and keeping them finely dispersed, which maintains the dissolution rate of indanone despite its low intrinsic solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: The limited solubility of indanone (<1 g/L) results in a thin slurry with multiple phases (aqueous liquid, organic liquid, solid, and gas).

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 4Applications of Process Analytical Technology in Heterogeneous Biocatalytic Hydroxylation
Problem_Description: In the dense‑slurry regime (25 vol % water) the autosampler frequently clogs, giving inconsistent offline data and a complete failure to withdraw samples at later times.
Solution_Description: Real‑time FTIR monitoring was implemented (PAT).  A calibrated univariate FTIR model predicts the dissolved hydroxy‑indanone concentration and, by correlating the succinate signal, the total product concentration, eliminating the need for reliable offline sampling.
Supporting_Evidence: The autosampler failed to withdraw samples at 15 h and 20 h due to clogging (Fig 3B).

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 4Applications of Process Analytical Technology in Heterogeneous Biocatalytic Hydroxylation
Problem_Description: Reaction rates differed dramatically depending on the particle‑size distribution of the indanone solid; larger particles gave slower conversion and a prolonged oxygen‑mass‑transfer‑limited phase.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Oxygen kLa was set to 0.02 s⁻¹ by controlling agitation speed, and indanone was sieved to defined size ranges (125–300 µm or 350–500 µm) to obtain reproducible kinetics.  Larger particles were either milled or the reaction was simply aged longer to reach completion.
Supporting_Evidence: Large particles show slower kinetics than small particles (Fig 6A).

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 4Applications of Process Analytical Technology in Heterogeneous Biocatalytic Hydroxylation
Problem_Description: When indanone becomes depleted, the enzyme over‑oxidizes hydroxy‑indanone to a diketone impurity that inhibits enzyme activity.
Solution_Description: Directed‑evolution of FoPip4H (round 9–14) produced variants with reduced over‑oxidation, and the presence of 1‑octanol kept indanone dissolution steady, preventing substrate limitation that leads to the diketone side‑reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: Variants from round 6 show over‑oxidation to a diketone impurity; keeping dissolved indanone concentration constant suppresses this pathway.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 4Applications of Process Analytical Technology in Heterogeneous Biocatalytic Hydroxylation
Problem_Description: The original commercial route required five separate chemical steps to install the required hydroxyl group, leading to high material cost and a large environmental footprint.
Solution_Description: A single‑step biocatalytic hydroxylation using the engineered FoPip4H enzyme replaces the five‑step sequence, cutting raw‑material cost and improving sustainability.
Supporting_Evidence: The new commercial route replaces five chemical steps with a single biocatalytic hydroxylation, reducing cost‑of‑goods and environmental impact.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: When the reaction volume was reduced from 100 vol water to a more concentrated regime the reactants (indanone 1, enzyme, cofactors) showed poor solubility, leading to a heterogeneous slurry, slow filtration, and low conversion/yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: 1 Octanol (6 vol %) was added as a cosolvent/additive to improve the physical nature of the mixture, increase substrate dissolution, and suppress enzyme inhibition; protease papain (5 wt %) was used to hydrolyze protein residues; Celite 545 was employed as a filter aid together with thermal denaturation to accelerate filtration; enzyme evolution generated a more active FoPip4H variant allowing reduction of enzyme loading to 7.5 wt % and water volume to 25 vol; the presence of 1‑octanol also acted as a functional additive that lowered surface tension and prevented over‑oxidation of the product; higher agitation (up to 800 rpm) and particle‑size reduction (sieving/wet milling) were used to improve mixing and dissolution of indanone 1.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Reduction of reaction volumes introduced additional complexity for large‑scale operations due to the low solubility of the reaction components." (Abstract)
• "Attempts at direct filtration of the hydroxylation stream resulted in exceedingly slow filtrations, which would pose a significant challenge during large‑scale operations." (Sec 2.1)
• "When the heterogeneous reaction mixture was treated with concentrated HCl, H₂SO₄, or H₃PO₄ at 90 °C, most of the protein was hydrolyzed into smaller peptide fragments, resulting in a nearly homogeneous solution. However, degradation of hydroxyindanone 2 under these harsh hydrolysis conditions was observed. … When the oxidation stream was treated with 5 wt % of papain at 60 °C for 2 h, the heterogeneous batch became a nearly homogeneous solution." (Sec 2.1)
• "Filtration with Celite 545 was several times faster compared to filtration with Standard Super‑Cel NF… Without Celite 545, filtration was not possible at both 25 and 60 °C.... a much faster filtration was observed when the enzyme was first thermally denatured at 60 °C." (Table 1)
• "The best result was 94.9 % conversion with 1‑octanol… the boiling point of 1‑octanol is 195 °C and its flash point is 81 °C… 1‑octanol was selected as the most suitable cosolvent." (Table 2 discussion)
• "The addition of 1‑octanol reduced the surface tension… allowing removal of the antifoam agent." (Ref 13)
• "At 1000 rpm, the dissolution rate of the indanone 1 with a large particle size was now similar to that of the indanone 1 with a small particle size… demonstrating that proper mixing mitigates particle‑size effects." (Fig 3)
• "Enzyme evolution… to increase activity under more concentrated conditions… the use of 1‑octanol allowed us to obtain high conversions at lower reaction volumes and enzyme loadings" (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: Direct filtration of the reaction mixture to remove residual protein was impossible due to membrane fouling and formation of emulsions; large amounts of protein precipitated during phase separation, leading to slow filtration and loss of product.
Solution_Description: Proteolytic digestion with papain hydrolyzed the protein into soluble fragments; Celite 545 was identified as an effective filter aid; a short thermal denaturation step (heating to 60 °C) prior to filtration dramatically reduced filtration time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Attempts at direct filtration of the hydroxylation stream resulted in exceedingly slow filtrations…" (Sec 2.1)
• "When the oxidation stream was treated with 5 wt % papain at 60 °C for 2 h, the heterogeneous batch became a nearly homogeneous solution." (Sec 2.1)
• "Filtration with Celite 545 was several times faster compared to filtration with Standard Super‑Cel NF…" (Table 1)
• "A much faster filtration was observed when the enzyme was first thermally denatured at 60 °C." (Table 1 entry 4)
• "During the workup, a significant amount of protein precipitated out during phase separation, and the formation of an emulsion was observed." (Sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: Over‑oxidation of hydroxy‑indanone 2 produced a diketone impurity that strongly inhibited the enzyme, causing rapid loss of activity and low overall conversion.
Solution_Description: Adding 1‑octanol (6 vol %) suppressed formation of the over‑oxidation product and maintained enzyme activity; increasing the initial substrate loading (higher equivalents of indanone 1) reduced the relative amount of diketone formed and improved conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Overoxidation of the desired hydroxyindanone 2 was observed to generate a diketone impurity… which strongly inhibits enzyme activity." (Sec 2.2)
• "The presence of 1‑octanol also helped to maintain enzyme activity and stability during hydroxylation… the addition of 1‑octanol potentially reduced or even prevented this enzyme inhibition." (Sec 2.2)
• Table 4 shows that adding 3 vol % 1‑octanol at the onset of the reaction markedly increased conversion even with low substrate loading (e.g., entry 6: 36.6 % vs 12.8 % without 1‑octanol).
• "Higher amounts of initial indanone 1 resulted in lower levels of the diketone impurity. Thus, maintaining a consistent dissolution of indanone 1 is critical to minimizing the formation of diketone and achieving high conversion." (Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: The original process required 50 wt % enzyme loading and 100 vol water, making the process expensive and impractical for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Through enzyme evolution a more active FoPip4H variant was obtained; combined with the addition of 1‑octanol the enzyme loading could be lowered to 7.5 wt % and water volume to 25 vol, dramatically reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Prior to optimization, hydroxylation reactions required dilute conditions (100 volumes of water) and high enzyme loading (50 wt %)… unsuitable for a long‑term manufacturing process." (Abstract)
• "With the expectation that filtration time would ultimately be improved from enzyme evolution efforts to increase activity and lower enzyme loading…" (Sec 2.1)
• "Using 35 wt % of enzyme without 1‑octanol gave 93.1 % conversion… With 1‑octanol, reactions run in 30 vol water now gave 91.3 % conversion… Enzyme loadings could also be reduced where oxidations with 1‑octanol gave 92.5 % conversion in 50 vol water and 15 wt % enzyme." (Table 5)
• "After further optimization and successful enzyme evolution, reaction conditions using 7.5 wt % enzyme in 25 volumes of water could be achieved providing 96–97 % conversion…" (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: Large particle size of indanone 1 caused slow dissolution, poor mixing, and inconsistent conversion across batches.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Particle size was reduced by sieving or wet milling; agitation speed was increased to 800 rpm (or higher) to achieve proper suspension (N_js) as indicated by mixing models; the reactor fill volume was adjusted to maintain kLa while increasing agitation to ensure uniform mixing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The batches of indanone 1 with larger particle size gave poor conversion…" (Table 6)
• "When the enzyme was first thermally denatured at 60 °C…" (Table 1) – shows temperature effect on filtration not mixing.
• "Reactions run at 480 rpm with large particles… resulted in poor conversion… increasing agitation to 800 rpm improved performance." (Table 6 entries 5 and 9)
• "Mixing modeling… estimated N_js for different particle sizes… 299 μm particles would require ∼800 rpm." (Table 7)
• "At 1000 rpm, the dissolution rate of the indanone 1 with a large particle size was now similar to that of the indanone 1 with a small particle size…" (Fig 3)
• "The reaction was performed on a 2.0 g scale… agitation of 480 rpm with subsurface air sparging to achieve the target kLa 0.02 s⁻¹…" (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 3Development of a Scalable Enzymatic Oxidation Process
Problem_Description: Foaming caused by antifoam agent and high surface tension hindered efficient mixing and required excess antifoam.
Solution_Description: The addition of 1‑octanol reduced the surface tension of the aqueous phase, eliminating the need for the antifoam agent.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The surface tension of water was reduced from ∼70 to ∼32 mN/m in the presence of antifoam… and ∼26 mN/m in the presence of 1‑octanol (0.5–4 vol % 1‑octanol in water tested)." (Ref 13)\n• "Thus, the antifoam agent, Glanapon 2000 Konz, could be removed from the reaction system." (Sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: The ketoreductase (KRED) identified in the initial screening was not stable in the MeCN/MeOH solvent system required for the electrophilic fluorination step, leading to loss of catalytic activity and inconsistent conversion.
Solution_Description: Enzyme evolution was employed to generate KRED variants (e.g., KRED‑12, KRED‑14, KRED‑15) with markedly improved tolerance to MeCN/MeOH, restoring activity and enabling one‑pot operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the KRED hit identified in the screening panel was not natively tolerant to MeCN/MeOH.”; “tolerance toward MeCN/MeOH had not yet been achieved, meaning that a distillation was needed to solvent switch from MeCN/MeOH to water prior to beginning the enzymatic DKR.”; “The KRED solvent tolerance was enabled by enzyme evolution.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Residual Selectfluor remaining after the fluorination step interfered with the downstream KRED‑DKR, causing side‑reactions, low conversion and the formation of hydroxymethylated impurities (8a/8b).
Solution_Description: Initially 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene (DMB) was added to quench Selectfluor; later methyl‑acetoacetate (MAA) was adopted as a more effective quench that also scavenges the formaldehyde generated from methanol oxidation, drastically reducing 8a/8b levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “Residual Selectfluor needed to be quenched prior to introducing the KRED/NADP+ cocatalyst mixture to avoid interference…”; “DMB was initially chosen to quench Selectfluor… DMB reacted with formaldehyde to only a minor degree.”; “Use of MAA as the reaction quench reduced the level of formation of 8a/8b considerably and did not affect the conversion of 2a/2b to 3.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Direct liquid–liquid extraction of the aqueous reaction mixture failed because the target fluoro‑alcohol (3) is highly water‑soluble, the denatured enzyme sticks to vessel walls, and reduced Selectfluor is not efficiently removed, leading to low product recovery and a heavy water‑removal burden.
Solution_Description: A protein precipitation protocol was introduced using Na₂CO₃‑treated Celite and 35–40 wt % (NH₄)₂SO₄, followed by addition of an organic solvent at 45–55 °C to generate a biphasic slurry that can be filtered, effectively separating enzyme and by‑products from the product‑rich organic phase.
Supporting_Evidence: “A liquid–liquid extraction without filtration … was initially pursued … not ideal due to the relatively high water solubility … sticking of the denatured enzyme … low rejection of reduced Selectfluor, and distillation burden.”; “protein precipitation and filtration proved to be more successful … Na₂CO₃‑treated Celite … (NH₄)₂SO₄ … generated a biphasic slurry that was readily filtered.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: When MeCN/MeOH/2‑propanol remained in the reaction mixture, addition of (NH₄)₂SO₄ caused a phase split and the enzyme localized at the interface, resulting in inconsistent protein precipitation and filtration.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture is first distilled to remove MeCN/MeOH/2‑propanol before protein precipitation, restoring consistent denaturation and filtration performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “The protein denaturation and filtration performed inconsistently with MeCN/MeOH present; however, when MeCN/MeOH/2‑propanol was removed by distillation before denaturing, robust enzyme filtration performance was observed.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: During crystallization, oiling and a dark black coloration were observed, traced to oligomeric/polymeric impurities generated in the fluorination step, which also caused reactor fouling and reduced product yield.
Solution_Description: An activated carbon treatment (CUNO #5) of the azeotropically dried organic stream was implemented to adsorb polymeric impurities, eliminating oiling, discoloration, and fouling in subsequent crystallizations.
Supporting_Evidence: “Oiling and dark black solution color were observed … associated with oligomeric impurities generated during the fluorination reaction.”; “a carbon (CUNO #5) treatment of the azeotropically dried organic stream removed the dark color and oligomeric impurities and oiling and reactor fouling were no longer observed.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Using 2‑MeTHF as the work‑up and crystallization solvent caused >150 mg mL⁻¹ solubility of the product, leading to substantial loss of product in the mother liquor, caking on vessel walls and low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: EtOAc was selected as a superior work‑up and crystallization solvent, eliminating the need for a solvent switch prior to seeding and providing tighter solubility control, which improved recovery and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high solubility of 3 in 2‑MeTHF (>150 mg/mL) … product losses to the mother liquor and cake washes were substantial (12%).”; “EtOAc was identified as a suitable alternative … removed the need for a partial solvent switch prior to seeding and provided tighter solubility control.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Seeding the crystallization at 60 °C with 6 L kg⁻¹ resulted in large particle sizes, fouling of product on reactor walls, and >4 % loss, making the process unreliable.
Solution_Description: Seeding temperature was reduced to 30 °C while increasing the batch volume to 10 L kg⁻¹, which minimized particle growth, prevented fouling and lowered total losses to <4 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “seeding and antisolvent dosing operations were performed … at higher concentration and temperature (6 L kg⁻¹ and 60 °C) … large particle size and yield losses.”; “the seeding temperature was lowered to 30 °C (and consequently target batch volume was increased to 10 L kg⁻¹) to reduce particle growth and promote nucleation.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Early process iterations required high loadings of KRED (up to 35 wt %) and NADP⁺ (5 wt %) to achieve acceptable conversion, which is economically undesirable at scale.
Solution_Description: Further enzyme evolution produced more active KRED variants, allowing the loadings to be reduced to 4 wt % KRED and 1.5 wt % NADP⁺, decreasing material costs while maintaining performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Further improvement to KRED activity allowed the process to be performed with 5 wt % KRED‑14 rather than with 10 wt % KRED‑12.”; Table 1 shows reduction of KRED loading from 35 % to 4 % and NADP⁺ from 5 % to 1.5 % across process iterations.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for Belzutifan: Part 5Chemoenzymatic Diastereoselective Fluorination/DKR
Problem_Description: Reaction pH strongly influenced both conversion rate and impurity formation; low pH (≈7.1) gave impractically slow rates, while high pH (≈9.7) accelerated the reaction but generated dimeric impurities (6, 7) at unacceptable levels.
Solution_Description: The pH was set to an intermediate value (≈8.3) during the DKR, providing a fast reaction rate while keeping dimer impurity levels low, thus balancing yield and purity.

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthetic Process to an Advanced GPR40 Agonist
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthesis of API 1 suffered from low conversion of the nitrile to the carboxylic acid, required reverse‑phase preparative HPLC because of many impurities, and the oxidative hydrolysis step decomposed the molecule.  The route also required a chiral separation and a lengthy 12‑step sequence, used expensive (–)-sparteine, and relied on reagents (2,2‑dimethoxyacetaldehyde, dibutylboron triflate) that were not commercially available at scale.  The work‑up of the Weinreb‑amide intermediate was problematic because of its high water solubility, and the O‑alkylation step gave only modest yields and generated an exotherm when reduced with DIBAL‑H at –78 °C.  Several steps required cryogenic temperatures, raising safety and operational concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team switched to a second‑generation convergent route that built the pyrrolidine core de novo (NEW ROUTE).  TiCl₄ replaced the unavailable dibutylboron triflate (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE).  A TMEDA/DIPEA mixture was found to give quantitative conversion and high diastereomeric ratio for the Evans aldol step (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE).  The undesired isomer was removed by a recrystallization in CH₂Cl₂/hexane (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE).  For the O‑alkylation, NaH replaced NaOH and the mesylate 37 was employed, giving 87 % isolated yield (ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION, OTHER CONDITION CHANGE).  The dangerous DIBAL‑H reduction was replaced by lithium di‑tert‑butoxyaluminum hydride (LDBBA) generated in situ, allowing the reaction at 0 °C with controlled addition and buffered citric‑acid quench (FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE /PROMOTER, ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION, PH CONTROL).  A lead‑poisoned Lindlar catalyst in THF/pyridine suppressed over‑reduction in the final olefination (CATALYST OPTIMIZATION).  The Still–Gennari phosphonate was replaced by the Ando HWE reagent, giving >20:1 Z/E selectivity without cryogenic conditions (NEW ROUTE, OTHER CONDITION CHANGE).  Several steps were telescoped (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY) and the final API was isolated by simple acid‑base work‑up and lyophilization, eliminating the need for preparative HPLC (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY, NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE).
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "The KOH hydrolysis of nitrile 19 under forcing conditions was low yielding… The final product required reverse phase preparative HPLC purification due to the significant number of impurities…" (sec 2.1).  
2. "Acidic hydrolysis with HCl/AcOH under microwave conditions provided higher conversions and yields but racemized the chiral center… oxidative hydrolysis methods caused the decomposition of the molecule." (sec 2.1).  
3. "The synthesis of the chiral piperidinol fragment was lengthy and included a chiral separation, resulting in additional loss of material after five steps." (sec 2.1).  
4. "(‑)-Sparteine is costly…" (sec 2.2).  
5. "2,2‑Dimethoxyacetaldehyde … was no longer commercially available… dibutylboron triflate was not available in a large supply…" (sec 2.2).  
6. "The reaction mixture was slowly added to a saturated aqueous Rochelle’s salt solution to allow a safe release of the gaseous by‑product… Exotherms were observed during the addition of the DIBAL‑H solution to the LiOt‑Bu solution as well as during the quench…" (sec 2.3).  
7. "The secondary hydroxyl was unreactive with 1‑bromo‑3‑methoxypropane… we replaced NaOH with the stronger base NaH… eventually the optimized condition … gave 87 % isolated yield." (sec 2.2).  
8. "To overcome the concerns of the other methods, the Ando modification of the HWE olefination… led to >20:1 Z/E selectivity with an acceptable 79 % yield." (sec 2.3).  
9. "LDBBA resolved both issues as the reduction could be performed at 0 °C, and no epimerization was observed upon quench… The exotherms were found to be addition‑controlled and easily managed by extending the addition time…" (sec 2.3).  
10. "A lead‑poisoned Lindlar catalyst… significantly decreased the over‑reduced by‑product to 6–9 %…" (sec 2.3).  
11. "The final product was isolated by reverse phase MPLC… The modified second‑generation route was successfully scaled up to deliver more than 100 g API." (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required repeated column chromatography for product isolation and employed hazardous reagents such as NaClO₂ and BBr₃; transition‑metal catalysts generated elemental‑metal impurities that exceed ICH‑Q3D limits.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the intramolecular Friedel–Crafts cyclisation (Approach A) the N‑tert‑butyl‑amide group proved unstable under the strong‑acid conditions, leading to cleavage (impurity 25) and further dehydration to a nitrile (impurity 26) that could not be removed, reducing overall purity and yield.
Solution_Description: Approach A was abandoned and Approach B was adopted, which constructs the tetracyclic core earlier and uses a more robust dimesyl‑protected aniline that tolerates the acidic cyclisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The N‑(tert‑butyl)‑amide group on 24 proved unstable under the acidic conditions required for the Friedel–Crafts reaction, and during the reaction, cleavage of the tert‑butyl group occurred to form the corresponding amide 25 as an impurity… Neither impurity was purged during crystallization, and both persisted in the final drug substance at initial levels.”
“Because the types of reactions employed in both approaches were the same, the knowledge gained from development following Approach A could be fully utilized, streamlining the progress of Approach B.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Using mesyl, acetyl or Boc protecting groups on the aniline nitrogen during the S_NAr step gave a mixture of the desired product and a double‑substituted side‑product (33) because the remaining N‑H participated in a second substitution.

“The S_NAr reaction of these substrates with 2‑fluoro‑5‑iodonitrobenzene (29) under basic conditions, however, gave a mixture of desired adduct 32 along with undesired double‑substituted product 33 that was generated due to the remaining N‑H function reacting with 29.”
“Treating methyl ester 21 with N,N‑dimethylformamide dimethyl acetal (DMF‑DMA) … produced amidine 34 … A subsequent S_NAr reaction of 35 with 29 … proceeded smoothly to afford 28 with a clean profile.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The intramolecular cyclisation of intermediate 36 was essentially inactive at 40 °C (only trace benzofuran 38) and required higher temperature; K₂CO₃ was ineffective as a base.

“...K₂CO₃ was not effective in promoting intramolecular cyclization (condition 3).”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the Sonogashira coupling to form 2‑ethynylpyridine 11, dissolved oxygen caused a Glaser‑type coupling, producing bis‑ethynyl impurity 46 that was hard to separate; on scale‑up, residual AcOEt led to product aggregation and a tar‑like precipitate during crystallisation.

Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was repeatedly degassed under reduced pressure to remove O₂, preventing formation of 46. Crystallisation was switched to a non‑aqueous solvent pair (CPME + n‑heptane) which eliminated the tar‑like aggregates and gave a pale‑yellow product.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The Sonogashira coupling to install the ethynyl fragment is exothermic (ΔT_ad ≈ 29 °C); uncontrolled heat could cause thermal runaway.
Solution_Description: Acetate ethyl (bp 77 °C) was selected as the solvent and the jacket temperature was set to 50 °C, providing sufficient heat removal and keeping the internal temperature within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “This coupling reaction is exothermic (ΔT_ad = 29 °C), and once the reaction starts at around 40 °C, it is promoted by the exothermic nature of the reaction itself. In order to prevent thermal runaway … AcOEt (boiling point: 77 °C) was used as a solvent and the jacket temperature was set at 50 °C.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Residual palladium in the final API exceeded the target (<10 ppm); conventional scavengers (N‑acetyl‑cysteine, TMEDA) were ineffective, especially in the presence of aqueous ammonia.
Solution_Description: The palladium catalyst loading was lowered from 5.0 mol % to 0.3 mol % and isopropyl acetate was introduced as a cosolvent for the crystallisation step, which together reduced Pd levels below 100 ppm (and <1 ppm after final recrystallisation).
Supporting_Evidence: “We conducted a comprehensive investigation on Pd scavengers … but we found no reagent that could effectively reduce residual Pd levels… Therefore, the loading of Pd catalyst was reduced to 0.3 mol % from the initial condition of 5.0 mol % … and isopropyl acetate was employed as a cosolvent for the crystallisation. This approach successfully reduced the residual Pd levels … below 10 ppm after recrystallisation.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor

Paper Title: Early Process Development of CH7057288, a Benzofuran-Containing Selective NTRK Inhibitor

Paper Title: Stereochemical Editing via Coupled Epimerization and Optical Resolution to Sustainably Manufacture a Key Adagrasib Building Block

Paper Title: Early Process Development of Two Vanin‑1 Inhibitors: Solid Form Challenges and Control of Ambident Reactivity

Paper Title: Process Development and Kinetic Analysis in the Green Synthesis of Lomustine
Problem_Description: The original telescoped route used dichloromethane (DCM) as the reaction solvent. DCM is a Class 2 solvent (toxic, likely carcinogenic, ozone‑depleting) and is prohibited for pharmaceutical manufacturing, making the process unsafe and non‑green.
Solution_Description: All reaction steps were transferred to a green solvent blend of 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2MeTHF) and acetic acid (7:3 v/v), eliminating the need for DCM.
Supporting_Evidence:

• "The green route uses 2MeTHF and acetic acid" (introduction)

Paper Title: Process Development and Kinetic Analysis in the Green Synthesis of Lomustine
Problem_Description: When the intermediate (1‑(2‑chloroethyl)‑3‑cyclohexylurea) was dissolved in 2MeTHF its solubility was low (≈20 mg mL⁻¹). At higher loadings the intermediate precipitated, causing reactor clogging and limiting the attainable concentration to 15 mg mL⁻¹, which gave only 31–33 % isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent (20 % v/v acetic acid) was added to 2MeTHF (7:3 2MeTHF/AcOH). This increased the intermediate solubility 9.3‑fold (to 140 mg mL⁻¹) and allowed higher reactant concentrations without clogging.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "...the reactor by precipitation of the intermediate… resulted in a yield of 31 % due to clogging of the reactor by precipitation of the intermediate" (Results – Part A) 
• "When the concentration was increased to 40 mg mL⁻¹ with sonication, we obtained no product due to immediate clogging" (Results – Part A) 
• "The addition of as little as 20 % acetic acid increased the intermediate solubility by 9.3‑fold compared with 2MeTHF alone" (Results – Part A) 
• Table 2 shows 140 mg mL⁻¹ intermediate concentration with 7:3 2MeTHF/AcOH (expt 6) 
• "...enable the process to run at 140 mg mL⁻¹ and give 85 % yield" (Conclusions)

Solution_Description: The reactor configuration was changed so that the intermediate is formed in 2MeTHF and, immediately downstream, a T‑mixer injects the 7:3 2MeTHF/AcOH stream, instantly solubilising the intermediate. Paper Title: Transition-Metal-Free Synthesis of a Densely Functionalized Benzodioxole Intermediate toward Lotiglipron
Problem_Description: The reaction of 3‑bromocatechol (2) with ketone 3a gave no observable conversion, and the analogous reaction with methyl 2,2‑dichloropropanoate (3d) afforded only 7 % of the desired acid 4 with complete loss of the expected methyl ester 5.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput screening identified K₂CO₃ in methyl‑isobutyl‑ketone (MIBK) as a suitable solvent/base combination; slow, portion‑wise addition of the catechol solution was employed to limit its base‑induced degradation, and raising the reaction temperature to 100 °C increased the isolated yield of 4 to 71 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “A broad initial screen of 24 diverse bases in 4 solvents … K₂CO₃ in MIBK … gave 36 % yield of 4… It was found that 3‑bromocatechol rapidly decomposed in MIBK under basic conditions at elevated temperatures, and slow addition of a 3‑bromocatechol solution … gave 55 % yield… An increase in the reaction temperature to 100 °C also improved the yield, and a 71 % yield of 4 could be reliably achieved.”

Paper Title: Transition-Metal-Free Synthesis of a Densely Functionalized Benzodioxole Intermediate toward Lotiglipron
Problem_Description: Crude acid 4 was obtained as a dark‑brown, highly soluble low‑melting solid; attempts to purify it by trituration or recrystallization failed because of its high solubility in most organic solvents and limited solubility only in heptane.
Solution_Description: A salt‑trapping strategy was adopted: formation of the dibenzyl‑amine (Bn₂NH) salt of 4 in MIBK/MTBE gave an isolatable solid that could be freed quantitatively with 2‑MeTHF/2 M H₂SO₄, providing a high‑purity product without chromatography.

An HTE salt screen … MIBK proved superior … Bn₂NH was preferred … The yield of 4·Bn₂NH was improved by addition of MTBE solvent … this salt could be freed … and recovered nearly quantitatively with 2MeTHF and 2 M H₂SO₄ (aq).”

Supporting_Evidence: “…large‑scale access to both 2,2‑dichloropropanoic acid derivatives 3b and 3c were challenging to source, due to their status as controlled substances… however, we were able to secure vendors for ton‑scale supplies of methyl 2,2‑dichloropropanote and sought to further optimize the reaction of 3‑bromocatechol with methyl 2,2‑dichloropropanoate (3d).”

Solution_Description: Redesign of region 1 – larger 1/4 in. tubing, removal of the 1/8 in. injectors, separation of the two feed inlets by 15 cm, and installation of a heated seeding loop with a dedicated pump – eliminated dead‑zones, reduced blockage, and allowed long uninterrupted runs (> 390 min).

• “The 1/8″ injector of feed 1 was prone to clogging and was only able to run for 240 min total … before blockage occurred.”
• “check valves of the flusys WADose pump (feed 2) began to fail, likely due to the constant and intense pressure oscillations throughout the system.”
• “In order to improve the run times from setup 3a, the 1/8″ injectors were removed from the 1/4″ four‑way junction.”
• “The positions of the inlets for feed 1 and feed 2 were separated such that they were 15 cm apart and were no longer pointed directly at one another.”

• “higher seeding temperature of 173 °C … reduced the amount of amorphous content in the product.”
• “full intensity oscillation (Reₒ/Reₙ = 175) was necessary to produce the correct ZS‑9 product.”
