Problem_Description: The flusys WADose pump used for feed 2 suffered check‑valve failure under the high‑pressure oscillatory conditions, leading to unreliable operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Replaced the WADose pump with two intermittently operated ISCO 260D syringe pumps that operate with a single large syringe, providing stable dosing and resistance to pressure oscillations.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “check valves of the flusys WADose pump (feed 2) began to fail, likely due to the constant and intense pressure oscillations throughout the system.”
• “In order to improve the run times … the flusys WADose pump was replaced with two intermittently operated ISCO 260D syringe pumps. These pumps were more stable under the oscillating pressure of the system.”
• “The result … was an extension of system run times before clogging, where 1415 min of intermittent running time … were possible before the first clog appeared.”

Paper Title: Continuous Production of an API Suspension (ZS-9) under Oscillatory Flow at Intensified Temperature and Pressure
Problem_Description: Extended crystallization residence times increased the conversion of ZS‑9 to the less‑desired ZS‑7 polymorph and left significant amorphous solid, diminishing overall yield of the target API.
Solution_Description: Reduced the fluid space time in the crystallization coil from 1.5 h to 1 h (and examined 30 min) and adjusted the crystallization temperature (245 °C–252 °C) to stop the ZS‑9 → ZS‑7 transition, while maintaining high oscillation intensity to preserve product purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the space time is cut in half to 30 min … the result is pure ZS‑9 with a large portion of amorphous content.”
• “When the space time is extended further to 1.5 h, the resulting product is primarily composed of ZS‑7.”
• “At the highest‑intensity oscillation produced significantly more ZS‑9 with only a small amount of ZS‑7.”
• “A 1 h crystallization fluid space time at 245 °C … produced pure cubic ZS‑9 crystals with no amorphous content.”

Paper Title: Continuous Production of an API Suspension (ZS-9) under Oscillatory Flow at Intensified Temperature and Pressure
Problem_Description: The benchmark batch synthesis required 72 h at 200 °C, resulting in low throughput and high solvent consumption.
Solution_Description: Through continuous oscillatory flow, the authors achieved the required conversion in a 1 h crystallization residence time at elevated temperature (245‑252 °C), dramatically increasing productivity (40 g h⁻¹) and reducing solvent waste.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Previous methods of ZS‑9 generation have been performed via semibatch operation … over the course of 72 h at 200 °C …”
• “The final operating conditions … 1 h crystallization fluid space time at 245 °C … produced pure cubic ZS‑9 … with a production rate of 40 g h⁻¹.”
• “When the space time is cut in half to 30 min … the result is pure ZS‑9 …”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: The original synthesis relied on oxetane‑3‑carboxaldehyde (4) which is extremely expensive (several thousand $/kg), highly water‑soluble (complicating work‑up), and has a low thermal onset that limits safe distillation.
Solution_Description: A new seven‑step sequence was developed that completely bypasses aldehyde 4, using a widely available bromodichlorofluoro‑benzene and an oxidative decyanation strategy to generate the oxetanyl‑ketone intermediate. This route reduces raw‑material cost > 3‑fold and eliminates the troublesome aldehyde.
Supporting_Evidence: “There were several challenges with the use of the oxetane aldehyde 4: the high cost of the precursor 3‑oxetanemethanol in the range of multiple thousands of dollars per kilogram, water solubility of the aldehyde (which complicated reaction workups), and limits on distillation parameters due to the high energy and low thermal onset associated with the oxetane moiety.”; “This process was demonstrated on a large scale to produce up to 50 kg of our key intermediate … a cost reduction above 3 times when compared to the previous route.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: During the SNAr step the reaction stalled on gram scale because the mixture became heterogeneous, leading to incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from DMSO to sulfolane, giving a homogeneous reaction medium, and the addition of tert‑butyl cyanoacetate was performed in a dose‑controlled manner to maintain temperature and avoid hot spots.
Supporting_Evidence: “Milligram‑scale reactions reached 96 % conversion … the reaction stalled on a gram scale due to heterogeneity (entry 3).”; “Sulfolane was replaced … to address safety concerns.”; “Upon performing this process on a multikilo scale, a dose‑controlled addition of tert‑butyl cyanoacetate was proven ideal to maintain a safe reaction profile.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: DMSO, used in the initial SNAr screening, posed safety concerns for large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: The reaction was moved to sulfolane, a higher‑boiling, less hazardous solvent, and potassium carbonate was substituted for the expensive and potentially more hazardous cesium carbonate, while DBU was identified as an effective base at lower equivalents.
Supporting_Evidence: “DMSO was replaced with sulfolane to address safety concerns.”; “Cesium carbonate was replaced with cheaper potassium carbonate (entry 2).”; “DBU was finally identified as a suitable base that led to high conversions within 1 h (entries 4 and 5).”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: The deprotection/decarboxylation sequence was very slow in several solvent systems (up to 48 h), limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: A solvent mixture of DMSO/H₂O (or dioxane/H₂O) was selected, delivering full conversion in 6 h at 90 °C, dramatically shortening the reaction time while maintaining product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “A mixture of acetonitrile or propionitrile with water led to high conversions, albeit at a slow rate (entries 1 and 2, 48 h). … A combination of dioxane or DMSO with water offered the best balance of reaction time and product formation (entry 7).”; “On a 384 kg scale … 99.5 % conversion was achieved in 6 h.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: When the decarboxylation was scaled up, CO₂ and isobutylene accumulated, causing a dramatic drop in reaction rate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Running the reaction under a slight vacuum efficiently purged the gases, restoring the rapid conversion observed at smaller scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Upon scaling the decarboxylation process … a dramatic decrease of reaction rate was observed … Various strategies … The most impactful process modification was to run the process under a slight vacuum, which efficiently purged the isobutylene and CO₂ generated … 99.5 % conversion was achieved in 6 h.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: During the alkylation of intermediate 11, water accelerated an autocondensation side‑reaction forming by‑product 13, reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Limiting water content and using 2 equiv of 3‑iodooxetane (or 1 equiv for cost) suppressed the side‑reaction and gave 78 % isolated yield on a 212 kg batch.
Supporting_Evidence: “The presence of water was found to accelerate the formation of this side product.”; “78 % yield of the desired oxetane product 12 was obtained when 2 equiv of 3‑iodooxetane was utilized.”; “Using 3‑iodooxetane in a 1:1 ratio … provided slightly lower yield (65 %) but afforded an overall 3 % cost reduction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: The oxidative decyanation step generates cyanide, a highly toxic species, raising safety concerns on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was kept basic and coupled with a basic/oxidative scrubber to capture cyanide; 10 % O₂ in N₂ was used to balance rate and selectivity while minimizing over‑oxidation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Maintaining the reaction streams as basic and using a basic/oxidative scrubber was essential to avoiding any HCN exposure.”; “In order to minimize the flammability of the reaction media, oxygen in nitrogen was employed. 10 % O₂ in nitrogen provided the best compromise between reaction rate and selectivity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: Methylation with dimethyl sulfate or methyl iodide is hazardous for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Methyl tosylate, a solid, less volatile reagent, was selected; it gave 97 % assay‑corrected isolated yield with a much safer handling profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “While dimethyl sulfate and methyl iodide provided full conversion … those reagents were not favored on a large scale due to concerns regarding workers’ safety.”; “Methyl tosylate offered a good safety profile given the solid nature of this reagent (entry 4).”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: The traditional halogen‑magnesium exchange using n‑BuLi is hazardous at multi‑kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Isopropylmagnesium chloride·LiCl complex was employed instead; it is safer to handle while delivering quantitative exchange at –16 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “The isopropylmagnesium chloride lithium complex was preferred over n‑BuLi given that it is safer to handle at scale and for the stability of the resulting metalated species.”

Paper Title: Development of a Cost-Efficient Process Toward a Key Synthetic Intermediate of the EZH2 Inhibitor PF-06821497
Problem_Description: During acidic quench of the carboxylation product, low pH caused oxetane ring opening to a 1,3‑diol, lowering purity.
Solution_Description: A buffered quench using acetic or citric acid kept pH > 2 at 0 °C, preventing ring opening and delivering > 98 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “We found that keeping the pH above 2 was important to suppress ring opening of the oxetane functionality … For this reason, acetic acid or citric acid was preferred as they each provided a buffered and controlled quench.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: The original annulation of ethyl 5‑bromo‑2‑methylnicotinate with triazine under basic conditions generated cyanide and a large exotherm (≈ +60 °C). Heating strong bases in polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO is known to cause autocatalytic decomposition, creating a risk of thermal runaway with toxic HCN in a skin‑penetrating solvent.
Solution_Description: A completely new route was devised that replaces the triazine‑based cyanation with a dehydrative condensation of 2‑bromo‑malonaldehyde and the ester under acidic conditions (pTsOH/H₂SO₄). No cyanide or strong base is used, eliminating the hazardous exotherm and decomposition pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the first step, 3‑bromo‑1,6‑naphthyridin‑5‑(6H)‑one … is generated via an annulation … and triazine … a significant exotherm, an increase of 60 °C, was also observed.”; “Heating strong bases in polar aprotic solvents such as DMSO is undesired due to potential exothermic decomposition.”; “The work was prioritized … to avoid the highly hazardous cyanation/cyclization sequence that also exhibited a significant exotherm.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: The second step of the literature route required N‑alkylation with alkyl halides (e.g., MeI) in the presence of strong bases at high temperature, reagents that are highly toxic, genotoxic and generate hazardous waste.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the alkyl‑halide/KOtBu system with dimethyl‑sulfonate (Me₂SO₄) or ethyl‑sulfonate (Et₂SO₄) together with KOH in water, allowing the N‑alkylation to proceed at much lower temperature without toxic halides.
Supporting_Evidence: “N‑alkylation of (5) required high‑temperature conditions with the use of alkyl halides … which is undesirable due to their toxicity.”; “Me₂SO₄ and KOH in water … provided 3‑bromo‑6‑methyl‑1,6‑naphthyridin‑5‑one … in 77 % isolated yield.”; “These conditions eliminated the need for higher temperatures and a strong base.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Early attempts at the acidic condensation gave only 35–45 % isolated yield of the pTsOH salt and suffered from reaction mixture thickening when H₂SO₄ was used, which limited conversion.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening of acid type, amount, and addition protocol identified pTsOH as the optimal additive; careful reagent addition and solvent control raised the isolated yield to 81 % and avoided viscosity problems.
Supporting_Evidence: “The best physicochemical behavior and fastest kinetics were observed with H₂SO₄ and pTsOH … pTsOH emerged as advantageous to avoid thickening of the reaction and affording slightly better, despite quite low, overall yield (35–45 %).”; “The amount of pTsOH, reagent addition protocol, and solvent was investigated, … the isolated yield … improved to 81 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: A previously reported enamine synthesis used NaH in DMF, which caused vigorous hydrogen evolution and presented safety concerns (NaH‑DMSO/DMF explosivity).
Solution_Description: The authors adopted the Batcho–Leimgruber sequence: treatment of the ester with DMF‑DMA and pyrrolidine at 80 °C in DMF, eliminating NaH and the associated hydrogen evolution while still delivering the enamine as a stable, isolatable solid (70 % yield on 1 g scale).
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction employed the use of NaH in DMF, a combination with known safety issues … It also showed vigorous hydrogen evolution and resulted in a moderate to low yield of 48 %.”; “Following the Batcho–Leimgruber sequence … afforded the desired enamine intermediate … in 70 % yield … eliminated NaH/hydrogen evolution from the process.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Cyclization of the enamine with primary amines required lengthy reflux times (up to 64 h) to reach acceptable yields, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Optimization showed that as little as 1.5 equiv of amine gave >90 % conversion in 24 h at reflux in isopropanol, reducing both reagent excess and reaction time while maintaining high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Further studies indicated that the cyclization could be achieved in high yields with as little as 1.5 equiv of the desired amine.”; Table 3 shows 1.5 equiv gives 94.5 % conversion in 24 h; “All reactions were conducted in IPA at reflux.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Some amine substrates required large excess (up to ~6 equiv) for acceptable yields, which would be cost‑prohibitive on kilogram scale for expensive amines.
Solution_Description: Through systematic screening, the equivalent of amine was lowered to 1.5 equiv without loss of conversion, reducing material cost and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “More volatile amine sources worked best when used as amine salts.”; Table 3 shows that 1.5 equiv gives 94.5 % conversion; the text states “This is particularly important if a more expensive complex amine is to be used.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Method to Prepare 3‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the enamine formation required careful temperature control and phase handling to avoid foaming and uncontrolled exotherms in a 10 L jacketed reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a jacketed vessel with argon purging, controlled addition, and temperature holds (25 °C → 80 °C → 30 °C) plus staged work‑up; concentration (2 vol DMF) was chosen to keep viscosity manageable. DSC/TSU studies confirmed no thermal events, enabling safe kilogram‑scale production (6.6 kg of product).
Supporting_Evidence: “A 10 L jacketed vessel… was purged with argon… the mixture was stirred at 80 °C for 8 h. The mixture was then cooled to 30 °C… temperature was controlled to keep the contents between 20 and 25 °C throughout.”; “DSC and TSu studies … showed no thermal events … repeated on a 2.5 kg scale … isolation of the product as a yellow crystalline solid.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: The initial synthesis used super‑stoichiometric amounts of both alkylating agents (methyl 4‑bromobutanoate and 2‑bromo‑N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide) leading to high reagent cost and low overall assay of the target β‑ketoester 1.
Solution_Description: The new process cuts the equivalents of the alkylating reagents by more than 50 % by telescoping the two alkylations in a single pot, thereby reducing material cost and delivering an overall isolated yield of ~70 % (vs 45 % originally).
Supporting_Evidence:
["both alkylating agents were used in superstoichiometric amounts; (1) both alkylating agents were used in superstoichiometric amounts"]
["reduction of both alkylating agents … by more than 50 %"]
["the overall yield of 70 %"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: The Weinreb bromide (2‑bromo‑N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide) is not commercially available, requiring an extra in‑house production step and adding cost.
Solution_Description: The Weinreb amide was replaced by a readily available 4‑(chloroacetyl)‑morpholine, which after alkylation gives morpholine amide 5; this substitution removes the need for the unavailable reagent and lowers material cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
["commercial unavailability of 2‑bromo‑N‑methoxy‑N‑methylacetamide necessitated an extra production step"]
["Morpholine amide hypothesis… the corresponding morpholine amide 5 was prepared using the commercially available 4‑(chloroacetyl)‑morpholine"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: Large amounts of organic bases (triethylamine and DIPEA) were employed as cosolvents in both alkylation steps, inflating cost and creating highly viscous reaction mixtures.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount of tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBAB) was introduced as a phase‑transfer promoter together with sodium bicarbonate, drastically accelerating the reactions while using only 10 mol % TBAB and eliminating the excess organic base.
Supporting_Evidence:
["use of a substantial amount of organic base as a cosolvent in both alkylation steps"]
["TBAB drastically increased the reaction rate and conversion when used in a catalytic amount"]
["10 mol % of TBAB proved to be the optimal amount"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: The original sequence required several aqueous washes and large solvent volumes, generating waste and increasing operational cost.
Solution_Description: The two alkylation steps were telescoped, eliminating the intermediate aqueous work‑up and cutting the total solvent volume to 3.0 V for each step, which reduced waste and improved process mass intensity.
Supporting_Evidence:
["multiple aqueous washes"]
["telescoped protocol… demonstrated on a >100 kg batch"]
["solvent reduced to 3.0 V for both alkylation steps"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: The Dieckmann condensation originally employed the expensive potassium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (KHMDS).
Solution_Description: KHMDS was replaced with the cheaper lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (LiHMDS), which also provided superior conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
["use of expensive potassium bis‑(trimethylsilyl)‑amide [KHMDS]"]
["replacement of costly KHMDS with the cheaper LiHMDS"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: The intramolecular Dieckmann condensation was run at near‑cryogenic temperatures (‑30 °C), complicating scale‑up and extending reaction time.
Solution_Description: The condensation temperature was raised to –10 °C (still low enough for selectivity) which simplified temperature control and shortened the operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
["final intramolecular condensation performed at near cryogenic temperature"]
["final Dieckmann condensation performed at −10 versus −30 °C"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: Formation of a dimeric impurity 1d occurred via formaldehyde generated from the unstable Weinreb amide under strong base, compromising product quality and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switching to the morpholine amide eliminated the formaldehyde pathway; no dimer 1d was detected in the new sequence, restoring high assay of the target material.
Supporting_Evidence:
["dimeric species 1d was formed via formaldehyde generation and subsequent trapping by some of the reaction intermediates"]
["the instability of Weinreb amides under strong basic reaction conditions… generate the corresponding aldehyde – in our case formaldehyde"]
["thorough analysis of the successful reaction mixtures failed to detect the dimeric species 1d using morpholine amide 5"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: On scale‑up, water generated from NaHCO₃ neutralization accumulated, causing hydrolysis of the alkylating agent, agglomeration of solid salts, and reaction stalling.
Solution_Description: A Dean–Stark water‑removal setup (azeotropic toluene) was introduced and the reaction temperature was raised to 110 ± 3 °C, efficiently stripping water, preventing slurry formation, and restoring conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
["the detrimental agglomeration phenomenon (of inorganic salts with water forming a pasty semisolid) was additional evidence that water removal had to be addressed"]
["the most attractive solution was to use a Dean–Stark apparatus allowing us to efficiently remove the produced water"]
["the internal temperature was increased to 110 ± 3 °C to ensure rapid elimination of water"]

Paper Title: Process Development and Manufacture of the Core Starting Material of Adagrasib (MRTX849)
Problem_Description: Impurity 10 formed during the Dieckmann step could not be fully removed by the primary crystallization, risking specification breach.
Solution_Description: A re‑processing step was developed: the crude solid was reslurried in aqueous MeOH (35 % v/v water) at 55 °C, which removed impurity 10 to below LOQ with >97 % recovery of product 1.
Supporting_Evidence:
["impurity 10 … was more challenging to remove during the crystallization process"]
["reprocessing method was quickly identified by reslurrying isolated 1 in aqueous MeOH (35 % v/v water) at 55 °C"]
["sample … reprocessed … fully eliminate impurity 10 to below LOQ level with a recovery of 1 higher than 97 %"]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: The conventional aldehyde and acetyl routes to thiophene‑2‑carbonyl chloride (TCC) generate significant side‑product streams, require large waste‑handling operations and give overall yields of only 50–63 %, making the material expensive and difficult to meet the cost‑of‑goods target.
Solution_Description: Develop a new three‑step sequence that uses a homogeneous liquid‑phase aerobic oxidation of 2‑acetylthiophene (AcT) (the MC oxidation) to give thiophene‑2‑carboxylic acid (TCA), followed by telescoped work‑up and chlorination, thereby avoiding the high‑waste, low‑yield steps of the legacy processes.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Current manufacturing routes to TCC suffer from side product formation and significant waste generation, which lead to high manufacturing costs.",
"Both processes produce TCC in a reasonable overall yield (50‑63 %), and both processes use inexpensive reagents. In addition, both routes have been used to generate large volumes of TCC. However, drawbacks are associated with each of these processes.",
"A new and potentially more cost‑effective process to prepare TCC from thiophene has been developed."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: Using the literature Hartough‑Kosak acylation with only 1 equiv of acetic anhydride gave low conversion (≈83 %) and required a time‑consuming 21 h aqueous work‑up to remove phosphoric acid, while the original protocol needed a 3‑fold excess of anhydride.
Solution_Description: Replace the homogeneous phosphoric‑acid catalyst with Amberlyst® 15 (a solid‑acid resin) and employ 2.0 equiv of acetic anhydride; this raises conversion to >97 % in 4 h, eliminates the aqueous work‑up, and permits direct telescoping of the crude AcT into the oxidation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
["In our hands, using Hartough and Kosak’s conditions with an equal amount of acetic anhydride led to a reduced conversion of thiophene (Table 2).",
"From the literature, ortho‑phosphoric acid gave the highest yield of 2‑acetylthiophene (94 %) but required three equiv of acetic anhydride.",
"We were able to repeat Bando’s experiments and obtain AcT in similar yields. Importantly, the use of the resin catalyst eliminated the need for an aqueous work‑up.",
"Running the acylation reaction with excess acetic anhydride produced two beneficial changes: the acylation reaction proceeded at a faster rate (4‑5 h vs 21 h), and the amount of condensation side product (ATAP) produced was lowered."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: When the MC oxidation was scaled from 5 g to 10 g in pressure tubes, a brown gas burst caused an uncontrolled exotherm, pressure rise and metal precipitation, leading to only 40 % conversion and catalyst deactivation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch from nitrate salts to the thermally‑stable Co(II)‑ and Mn(II)‑acetates, construct a 500 mL Ace pressure reactor equipped with overhead stirring, a gas sparger and a vent‑relief system, and continuously purge and back‑fill with fresh O₂ during the run to maintain catalyst activity and control the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence:
["When the reaction was scaled to 10 g in the same pressure tubes, a brown gas would abruptly form about an hour into the reaction. The gas formation led to an exotherm that caused an increase in both pressure and temperature.",
"For safety reasons, we discontinued the use of metal nitrates and focused on the corresponding metal acetates.",
"The pressure tubes did not allow an effective means of continuously sparging oxygen into the reactor with simultaneous off‑gassing. Furthermore, the pressure tubes did not promote good agitation, which was essential for achieving a good mass transfer.",
"To test this hypothesis, we set up a 10 g reaction, purging the reaction every 60 min and backfilled the system with fresh oxygen. Happily, conversions returned to those seen in the 5 g reactions (entry 5)."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: Even in the 500 mL pressure reactor the aerobic oxidation released a noticeable exotherm that could threaten reactor integrity.
Solution_Description: Feed AcT slowly through an addition funnel to limit the rate of heat generation and install a reflux condenser to provide evaporative cooling, keeping the temperature under control throughout the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The exotherm was effectively controlled in two ways: (1) the concentration of AcT in the reactor was limited by feeding it into the reactor via an addition funnel, and (2) a reflux condenser was installed that provided adequate evaporative cooling."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: Synthetic thiophene contained trace mercaptan impurities (detected by a strong odor) that poisoned the Co/Mn catalyst, giving low conversion and precipitation, whereas petroleum‑derived thiophene performed well.
Solution_Description: Apply Levitt’s nitric‑acid treatment to the synthetic thiophene, removing >99 % of sulfur‑containing impurities and restoring catalytic activity; alternatively, source petroleum‑based thiophene which is already clean.
Supporting_Evidence:
["The thiophene that gave low conversion had a strong mercaptan odor, whereas the thiophene that gave high conversion had no mercaptan odor.",
"Levitt has described a method for thiophene purification involving nitric acid treatment.",
"GC‑MS indicated that Levitt’s method removed >99 % of all nonaromatic sulfur impurities.",
"Fortunately, using Levitt’s method, our synthetic thiophene produced AcT that performed identically to AcT prepared from petroleum‑based thiophene."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: Formic acid accumulates in the oxidation broth (≈65–75 % of TCA on a mole basis) and impairs conversion of AcT to TCA.
Solution_Description: Add 1 equiv of acetic anhydride to the reaction mixture to convert formic acid to acetyl‑derived by‑products, reducing the residual formic acid to 30 % and raising conversion from 92 % to 97 %; further improve by delivering a portion of the anhydride 1 h after AcT addition, achieving >99 % conversion and >99 % destruction of formic acid.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Formic acid levels were typically 65–75 mol % that of TCA on a 100 mol % basis.",
"We were pleased to find that adding acetic anhydride to the MC oxidation of AcT did result in a higher conversion. For instance, when 1.0 equiv of acetic anhydride was added together with AcT to the reaction, formic acid was reduced by 60 % and conversion increased from 92 to 97 % (Table 5, entry 2).",
"By delaying the introduction of a portion of the acetic anhydride to 1 h post addition of AcT, full conversion of AcT was realized and >99 % of formic acid was destroyed (entries 4 and 5)."]

Paper Title: A New Process To Prepare Thiophene-2-Carbonyl Chloride, a Key Raw Material in the Synthesis of Tioxazafen, Utilizing a Catalytic Liquid Phase Aerobic Oxidation Reaction
Problem_Description: When acetic anhydride is added all at once, new side products TGDA (thiophene‑glyoxal diacetyl acetal) and MDA (methylene diacetate) appear at 3–4 % and 5 % levels, respectively.
Solution_Description: Introduce the second half of the acetic anhydride 1 h after the initial addition of AcT; this staged addition suppresses formation of TGDA and MDA to <2 % each.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initially, levels of TGDA were averaging 3‑4 % (w/w based on TCA).",

Paper Title: Supervised Machine-Learning Algorithm using Low Data Sets: Flow Chemistry Optimization of the Key Urea Moiety Construction in Larotrectinib
Problem_Description: The heteroarene 2 is poorly soluble in the originally used solvent DCM, giving a heterogeneous reaction mixture that is difficult to stir in batch and flow.

Paper Title: Practical Manufacturing Process for Baloxavir Marboxil: Effective Selection and Replacement of Protective Group toward Enhancement of Crystallization-Induced Diastereomer Transformation

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Acetylquinazolinone (10) has low solubility in DCE, forming a solid suspension that clogs the feed tube and the interior of the micro‑channel reactor, making the instrument inoperable.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred from the micro‑channel reactor to an agitated tube reactor (ATR). The ATR’s internal stirring shaft and ability to accept solid inputs enable efficient mixing of gases, liquids and fine solids, preventing blockage and improving mass‑ and heat‑transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: “due to the low solubility of acetylquinazolinone 10 in DCE, a significant suspension clogged the feed tube and the interior of the MR, rendering the instrument inoperative.”; “Fortunately, the application of an agitated tube reactor (ATR) was successful. In contrast to conventional tubular reactors, an ATR is appropriate for mixing gases, liquids, and fine solids since it can be coupled to a peristaltic pump…"

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: (COCl)₂ has a low boiling point and is volatile in batch reactors, leading to inaccurate stoichiometry control and sub‑optimal substrate conversion.
Solution_Description: In the continuous‑flow ATR the amount of (COCl)₂ was fixed at 2 equiv and the residence time optimized to 10 min at 70 °C, delivering a 92.7 % isolated yield and reliable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because (COCl)₂ has a low boiling point, it is quite volatile in batch processes, making material stoichiometry control inaccurate and leading to suboptimal substrate conversion profiles.”; “An optimal residence period of 10 min gave a yield of 90.6 %… 70 °C, 2 equiv of (COCl)₂… The yield of 92.7 % is higher than any obtained in the batch experiments.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Batch chlorination in many solvents produced numerous unanticipated impurities and low selectivity; the product was especially difficult to isolate when DMSO or NMP were used.
Solution_Description: Switching to DCE as the reaction solvent with (COCl)₂ and performing the reaction in an ATR greatly improved selectivity and isolated yield (60.7 % in batch, 92.7 % in flow).
Supporting_Evidence: “numerous unanticipated impurities were produced and the reaction selectivity was very low… The desired product was considerably harder to separate when using DMSO or NMP as solvents.”; “Hence, optimal conditions using DCE and (COCl)₂ provided the highest yield of 60.7 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Slow flow rates caused solid accumulation, leading to peristaltic‑pump tube rupture and obstruction during the chlorination step.
Solution_Description: Increasing the solvent volume from 100 : 1 to 200 : 1 (mL g⁻¹) reduced the solid content below 30 % and restored smooth flow, eliminating pump blockages.
Supporting_Evidence: “we frequently ran into issues like peristaltic pump tube rupture and obstruction, in part due to the excessively slow flow rate…"; “The fluidity of the mixture significantly improves, and pipeline blockage is resolved when the solvent volume is increased from 100 to 200 times the mass of the raw material (Table 3, entry 16)."

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Extended residence times caused the reversible chlorination to revert to starting material 10 due to moisture ingress, decreasing conversion.
Solution_Description: A residence time of 10 min at 70 °C was identified as optimal, giving a 90.6 % yield while preventing back‑hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “conversion indeed shows a downward trend with prolonged reaction… because the chlorination of quinazolinone is reversible and the longer the residence… the more likely external moisture will … hydrolyze the chlorinated quinazoline, reverting it into feedstock.”; “An optimal residence period of 10 min gave a yield of 90.6 % (Table 3, entry 8)."

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: In the amination step, too‑long residence times allowed solids to settle, clogging the system and lowering product yield.

Supporting_Evidence: “If the residence time is too long, solids in the pipeline settle, clog the system, and hinder conversion.”; “The yield of 7 increased as the residence time decreased from 15 to 2.5 min… optimal conditions… residence time of 2.5 min, temperature 30 °C, 1.2 equiv 8… 96.1 % yield.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Excess aniline (≥1.3 equiv) required additional solvent for washing, leading to product loss during post‑treatment.

Supporting_Evidence: “excess unreacted aniline required more solvent to wash the cake… leading to concomitant loss of product 7.”; “Using 1.0–1.2 equiv of aniline, the yield increased gradually… optimal 1.2 equiv gave maximum yield 96.1 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: The batch hydrolysis required 3 equiv of NaOH, generating excess waste and increasing reagent cost.

Supporting_Evidence: “under batch process conditions… required 3 equiv NaOH… could be reduced to 2.0 equiv on scale‑up.”; “the yield of 6 increases as the stoichiometry of NaOH increases… maximum yield with 2.0 equiv NaOH (Table 5, entry 3).”; “Optimal conditions … 2 equiv NaOH at 30 °C with a residence period of 6 min… maximum yield 85.1 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key Intermediate Common to Gefitinib and Larotinib
Problem_Description: Isolation of the final product 6 required an appropriate pH to maximize recovery.

Paper Title: An Intramolecular Diels–Alder Approach to the Isoindolinone Core of AZD8154
Problem_Description: The historic benzylic bromide intermediate used in the discovery‑chemistry route presented safety concerns and limited scalability, and the original synthesis of the sulfone‑acrylamide dienophile gave only a 13 % isolated yield with poor purity.

Paper Title: An Intramolecular Diels–Alder Approach to the Isoindolinone Core of AZD8154
Problem_Description: Acid‑mediated dehydration/aromatization of cycloadduct 6 (using MSA, PTSA, HCl, or BF₃·Et₂O) resulted in extensive decomposition and gave either no product or an unexpected sulfone‑migration product.

Problem_Description: Initial base‑mediated aromatization gave moderate but variable isolated yields (57‑75 % by UHPLC, 23‑62 % isolated) and side‑product formation.

Paper Title: An Intramolecular Diels–Alder Approach to the Isoindolinone Core of AZD8154

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: Traditional cathodic reductions of disulfides require either sacrificial anodes (generating metal waste) or divided cells equipped with ion‑exchange membranes (expensive and not suited for organic solvents).
Solution_Description: Adopt a “quasi‑divided” cell concept where a very small anode relative to the cathode creates a mass‑transfer barrier, eliminating the need for sacrificial electrodes or ion‑exchange membranes.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Both strategies avoid reoxidation and degradation of the reduction products. Sacrificial electrodes have a negative impact on the sustainability of the process, as they essentially act as a stoichiometric reductant and generate metal waste.","Divided cell setups, particularly on technical or commercial scales, rely on the use of ion exchange membranes such as Nafion, which are not well suited to operate in organic solvents.","To solve these issues, we have recently reported an electrochemical method for the reduction of disulfides to thiols in undivided cells that does not require sacrificial electrodes."]

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original reactor used a stainless‑steel outer shell, which can corrode under acidic conditions and is not compatible with the organic solvent system required for the disulfide reduction.
Solution_Description: Replace the stainless‑steel outer shell with a PTFE (poly‑tetrafluoroethylene) reactor body, providing chemical resistance and allowing the use of standard fluidic fittings for the counter‑electrode rods.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In this modified version, the stainless steel outer shell of the reactor, which together with the base acted as the reactor vessel, was substituted by a PTFE piece with an inner pipe‑shaped cavity.","The outer surface of the PTFE reactor wall had a pentagonal prism shape, with 5 connections for 1/4–28 flat‑bottom fittings on each side."]

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: A fixed anode configuration limits the cathode‑to‑anode surface‑area ratio, which is critical for achieving the mass‑transfer imbalance required for quasi‑divided operation.
Solution_Description: Design the reactor with modular graphite counter‑electrode rods (up to 25) that can be inserted into standard fittings, allowing rapid adjustment of the anode surface area and thus the desired cathode/anode ratio (47:1 to 1190:1).
Supporting_Evidence: ["Each of the fittings implemented an electrode surface of 7.9 mm², and by incorporating a variable number of fittings into the reactor, counter electrode surfaces ranging from 7.9 to 198 mm² could be achieved.","As the spinning working electrode features a surface area of 94 cm², working/counter electrode surface ratios of 47:1 to 1190:1 could be realized using this scalable setup."]

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: During batch electrolysis the reaction mixture heated to ~50 °C because of Joule heating, whereas in flow‑recirculation mode the same cell dissipated heat and the temperature dropped to near room temperature, leading to only 82 % conversion of the disulfide.

Supporting_Evidence: ["Internal temperature monitoring of the reaction mixture with a temperature probe revealed that the electrolysis experiment in flow mode was taking place at nearly room temperature instead of the 50 °C observed in the batch.","This issue could be solved simply by heating the electrolyte reservoir to 50 °C during the electrolysis process, counteracting the heat dissipation from the connections.","When the reaction was carried out using the thermostated reservoir … a full conversion of 7 and an excellent yield (96 %) of thiol 8 were obtained."]

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: Disulfide 7 is only partially soluble in MeOH; in the continuous‑flow cascade the suspension tended to settle and cause clogging of tubing, especially with large‑diameter or very narrow tubing.

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: At a cathode spinning speed of 900 rpm the current efficiency dropped (54 % conversion at 4 F mol⁻¹) compared with 600 rpm, likely due to vortex formation that reduced electrode‑solution contact.

The effect might be ascribed to the generation of a vortex and, consequently, less contact between the spinning electrode and the reaction mixture.", "Thus, a 600 rpm reaction was selected for further experimentation."]

Paper Title: Scalable Quasi-Divided Cell Operation Using Spinning Cylinder Electrode Technology: Multigram Electrochemical Synthesis of an Axitinib Intermediate
Problem_Description: Scaling the process from a 3 mL batch to multi‑10 g batches required larger electrolyte volumes and continuous operation without re‑optimising reaction parameters; maintaining conversion and selectivity was a challenge.

Problem_Description: The Schlenk equilibrium is highly sensitive to the quality of BiBr₃, leading to poor reproducibility between runs.
Solution_Description: Controlled, inverse addition of the organozinc intermediate to BiBr₃ together with external cooling (water‑bath) limits temperature spikes and mitigates sensitivity to BiBr₃ quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “The protocol exhibits poor reproducibility, presumably due to … the sensitivity of the key Schlenk equilibrium (step 3) to the quality of the BiBr₃.”; “Both the lithiation and the Li‑to‑Zn transmetalation steps were observed to be accompanied by moderate exotherms … limited to < 2 °C in subsequent repetitions … simply by controlling the rate of addition and by applying external cooling with an ambient temperature water bath.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a New Sulfone-Based Bismacycle as a Universal Precursor for Bi(V)-Mediated Electrophilic Arylation
Problem_Description: Copper salts used in the CuCl‑mediated transmetalation lead to copper contamination of the product, requiring additional filtration steps and posing a risk of unwanted side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: The copper transmetalation was replaced by a ZnCl₂‑mediated pathway, eliminating copper residues and simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Given the environmental toxicity of copper salts … efforts were instead focused on the use of organozinc intermediates.”; “Bismacycle 1‑Br was formed in reproducibly high yields and purities when dilithiodiphenyl sulfone 4 was transmetalated to a solution of 2.2 equiv of ZnCl₂ before addition to BiBr₃.”
missing_information: [DECOMPOSITION], [REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS], [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a New Sulfone-Based Bismacycle as a Universal Precursor for Bi(V)-Mediated Electrophilic Arylation
Problem_Description: Lithiation of diphenyl sulfone and the subsequent Li‑to‑Zn transmetalation generate moderate exotherms, raising reaction temperatures by 11–14 °C on a 10 mmol scale.
Solution_Description: The addition rates of n‑BuLi and ZnCl₂ were slowed and external cooling with a water bath was applied to keep temperature rises below 2 °C on the 100 mmol scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both the lithiation and the Li‑to‑Zn transmetalation steps were observed to be accompanied by moderate exotherms, with reaction temperatures increasing by 14 and 11 °C (respectively) on a 10 mmol scale. These temperature increases were limited to <2 °C … simply by controlling the rate of addition and by applying external cooling with an ambient temperature water bath.”

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: The original batch‑based ketone‑formation required 2 equiv of n‑butyllithium, demanded cryogenic temperatures (‑60 °C) to control a highly exothermic organolithium addition, gave only a modest 61 % isolated yield and generated a major dehalogenated impurity (4).
Solution_Description: A new sequential deprotonation/lithium‑halogen‑exchange protocol was introduced: first deprotonate with 1 equiv of MeLi, then add n‑BuLi (≈1 equiv). This changes the order of addition and reduces the total equivalents of organolithium, suppressing the internal quench that forms impurity 4 and raising the isolated yield by ~15 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “An initial synthetic supply route … relied on the use of n‑butyllithium. Cryogenic temperatures (‑60 °C) were also required to achieve a modest 61 % yield, with one major impurity … dehalogenation …” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: Grignard‑based coupling of aryl iodide 5 to generate the bismagnesium intermediate 1D produced extremely thick slurries that were difficult to stir, showed rapid loss of activity on standing, and gave low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The Grignard approach was abandoned in favor of a revised organolithium sequence (sequential deprotonation/lithium‑halogen exchange).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Extremely thick slurries were observed that were difficult to stir… the stability of 1D was problematic, as yields decreased upon extended age times.” (Results and Discussion, paragraph on Grignard).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: Friedel–Crafts acylation gave only 6–11 % assay yield and required toxic solvents (dichloroethane or nitro‑benzene).
Solution_Description: The Friedel–Crafts route was dismissed; development continued with the organolithium pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The low assay yield (AY) of 6–11 % and the requirement of either dichloroethane or nitrobenzene … led us to eliminate Friedel–Crafts chemistry as a viable alternative.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the batch reaction to kilogram quantities showed inconsistent assay yields, required very long organolithium addition times to keep the reaction cold (because of the exotherm), and increased overall cycle time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was moved to continuous flow. First a CSTR configuration was used to handle the heterogeneous slurry, then a plug‑flow reactor (PFR) was adopted, providing superior heat removal and allowing operation at higher temperatures (‑35 °C → ‑28 °C) with much shorter residence times.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Potential issues … reproducibility … long addition times would be required to maintain cryogenic temperatures during organolithium addition due to the exothermicity … leading to longer addition times and longer cycle times.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: The dianionic intermediate 1C was poorly soluble in THF, forming a slurry that risked clogging in flow reactors.
Solution_Description: Lithium bromide was added as a functional promoter; it increased the solubility of lithium aggregates, rendered the reaction mixture homogeneous and enabled a clean transition from CSTR to PFR operation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Poor solubility of dianionic intermediate 1C in THF, which resulted in a slurry… Lithium bromide was ultimately identified as a suitable additive to maintain homogeneity, and it enabled our successful transition from CSTR to PFR.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: CSTR operation required broad residence‑time distributions, giving longer overall residence times (≈27 min) compared with the desired short reaction window.
Solution_Description: Switching to a PFR reduced the combined residence time ten‑fold (2.7 min total) and allowed a modest temperature increase, dramatically improving throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Combined residence time … reduced 10‑fold, from 27 to 2.7 min (CSTR vs PFR) … The operating temperature for the PFR could be increased slightly from −35 to −28 °C.” (Results and Discussion, Scheme 6).

Paper Title: Development of a Green and Sustainable Manufacturing Process for a Key Intermediate to Nemtabrutinib (MK-1026): Sequential Deprotonation–Lithiation as a Batch–Flow Process
Problem_Description: Incorrect stoichiometry of MeLi and n‑BuLi led to incomplete conversion or excess by‑product formation, affecting yield and consistency.
Solution_Description: Systematic stoichiometry screening identified ~1.08 equiv of n‑BuLi (with 0.95–1.0 equiv MeLi) as optimal, delivering maximal product formation with minimal impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When 0.95 and 1.0 equiv of MeLi were used … n‑BuLi equivalents screened from 0.85 to 1.3 … formation of ketone 3 was maximized when approximately 1.08 equiv of n‑BuLi was employed.” (Results and Discussion, Scheme 5).

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: The condensation of chiral triazinanone R‑3 with thiepin alcohol 4 gave a very low diastereoselectivity (5 : 5′ ≈ 1 : 1), producing a mixture that required HPLC separation to isolate the desired product, which reduced overall yield and made purification difficult on scale.
Solution_Description: A combination of 2,4,6‑tripropyl‑1,3,5,2,4,6‑trioxatriphosphorinane‑2,4,6‑trioxide (T3P) and methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) was introduced, the amount of T3P was reduced and the reaction temperature lowered to 80 °C. This adjustment increased the coupling rate, improved the diastereomeric ratio up to ≥99 : 1, and allowed the desired diastereomer 5 to be isolated by simple crystallisation rather than HPLC.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The coupling reaction … using T3P … was unselective (5 : 5′ ≈ 1 : 1) … HPLC separation was necessary …” (Problem) 
• “Addition of methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) was found to be good for the coupling reaction rate and improving the diastereoselectivity … When the amount of T3P was reduced to 2.5 equiv and the reaction temperature was lowered to 80 °C … diastereomer ratio improved to about 3 : 2 … Further reduction … ratio to about 2 : 1 … Crystallisation … gave 5 in 40 % yield (5 : 5′ = 98 : 2) … 49 % yield (5 : 5′ ≥ 99 : 1).” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route to rac‑3 required silica‑gel column chromatography for key intermediates, which is impractical and unsafe for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The ethyl ester group of intermediate 11 was replaced by a p‑nitrobenzyl ester, which markedly improved crystallinity and enabled purification by simple recrystallisation instead of chromatography, facilitating kilogram‑scale synthesis.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Although this synthetic method gave rac‑3 in good yield, it was difficult to achieve a scaled‑up synthesis due to the purification by silica gel column chromatography …” (Problem) 
• “We tried to improve the crystallinity by changing the ethyl group … to a p‑nitrobenzyl group. As expected, the benzyl ester intermediates showed improved crystallinity and could be purified by crystallization. This process was successfully performed on a kilogram‑input scale …” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: Optical resolution of rac‑3 by chiral HPLC was viable for medicinal‑chemistry studies but required long cycle times and was expensive, making it unsuitable for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A diastereomeric crystallisation strategy was adopted: rac‑3 was condensed with chiral carboxylic acid 21a to give two diastereomeric hydrazides, the desired solid diastereomer 26 was isolated by filtration and subsequently deprotected to afford R‑3 with >95 % ee, while the undesired diastereomer 28 was recycled. This eliminated the need for HPLC and reduced cost and time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “HPLC separation … requires long cycle times and is costly, making it unsuitable for scaled‑up synthesis.” (Problem) 
• “The condensation of rac‑3 with 21a … gave diastereomers 26 and 28 as a 1 : 1 mixture. Filtering … gave the desired diastereomer 26 … Crystallisation … afforded R‑3 in 95 % yield … The undesired diastereomer 28 was converted to rac‑3 …” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: The thiepin alcohol 4 decomposes under the basic conditions required for an SN2‑type coupling with R‑3, preventing the desired S_N2 pathway.
Solution_Description: The reaction was switched to an SN1‑type coupling using T3P in the presence of the strong Brønsted acid MsOH, avoiding the basic conditions that caused thiepin degradation and enabling efficient coupling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We could not find suitable reaction conditions due to the instability of the thiepin moiety under the basic coupling conditions …” (Problem) 
• “Since each diastereomer … could not be separated … For the scaled‑up synthesis … we first considered the reaction solvents and additives … Addition of methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) was found to be good for the coupling reaction rate and improving the diastereoselectivity …” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: The initial coupling of R‑3 and 4 using T3P was performed in sealed tubes with explosion‑proof shields, which is unsuitable and hazardous for kilogram‑scale operations.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to an open‑batch system using ethyl acetate as solvent; T3P was added dropwise at 30 °C and the mixture was stirred at 25 °C, eliminating the need for sealed tubes and improving safety for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The coupling reaction … using T3P … was performed in a sealed tube …” (Problem) 
• “To a suspension of 21a and rac‑3 … T3P (50 % w/w in ethyl acetate) was added … the mixture was stirred at 25 °C for 7 h …” (Solution) 
• “The coupling reaction in DMF, 1,4‑dioxane, toluene and EtOAc proceeded without the use of a sealed tube if the reaction time was extended.” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: Triazinanone 3 undergoes oxidation during the deprotection step, leading to degradation of the product.
Solution_Description: 2,6‑Di‑tert‑butyl‑p‑cresol (BHT) was added as an antioxidant to suppress oxidation of triazinanone 3 under the reaction conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • “2,6‑Di‑tert‑butyl‑p‑cresol (BHT) was added to prevent oxidation of triazinanone 3 under the reaction conditions.” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: The undesired diastereomer 28 generated in the resolution step represented a loss of material and increased waste.
Solution_Description: The undesired diastereomer 28 was treated with DBU in ethanol at 70 °C for 6 h, effecting deprotection and racemisation back to rac‑3, which could then be recycled, improving overall material efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The recycling of undesired diastereomer 28 … DBU (61.6 mL, 409 mmol) at 25 °C … after the mixture was stirred at 70 °C for 6 h … the precipitated solid … afforded rac‑3 (87.5 % yield).” (Solution)

Paper Title: First-Generation Process Development for the Synthesis of Baloxavir Marboxil: Early-Stage Development of Synthetic Methods to Prepare Baloxavir Marboxil Intermediates
Problem_Description: During large‑scale synthesis of intermediate 5, benzylated‑sulfur by‑products formed, complicating purification of the target diastereomers.
Solution_Description: N‑Ethylpiperazine was added after benzylation to convert the over‑benzylated sulfur compounds back to the desired diastereomers 5 and 5′, simplifying the downstream purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • “During this benzylation, a small amount of overreacted compounds … the sulfur atom … was benzylated, but these benzylated‑sulfur‑atom compounds could be returned to 5 and 5′ by treatment with N‑ethylpiperazine.” (Solution)

Paper Title: High-Speed Circulation Flow Platform Facilitating Practical Large-Scale Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
Problem_Description: When the C–N coupling reaction was attempted in a capillary reactor packed with mpg‑CN (1–3 µm particles), the solid photocatalyst settled, causing severe clogging and a very low product yield. Ni‑black formation further blocked light penetration, compounding the low conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A custom high‑speed circulation flow reactor was employed. By circulating the reaction slurry at high linear velocities (≥1.65 m min⁻¹), solid sedimentation was prevented, clogging was eliminated, and mixing efficiency was dramatically improved, delivering full conversion and high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high flow rate set in a circulation flow reactor overcomes solid sedimentation to prevent clogging and improve the mixing efficiency.”; “initial attempts … yielded a very low product yield, with significant Ni‑black contamination after just an hour of flow operation, thus blocking light penetration.”; “At a flow rate of 1.10 m min⁻¹, the flow was interrupted after 2 h of reaction due to clogging, resulting in only 35 % conversion.”; “when the flow rate was raised to 1.65 m min⁻¹, full conversion was achieved in 12 h… at a flow rate of 2.2 m min⁻¹, complete conversion was accomplished in just 8 h, and aggregation was entirely prevented.”

Paper Title: High-Speed Circulation Flow Platform Facilitating Practical Large-Scale Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
Problem_Description: During the capillary‑packed run, the Ni catalyst decomposed to Ni‑black, which not only blocked light but also lowered the overall conversion and yield of the C–N coupling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the circulation flow rate reduced the residence time of solids at any given point and kept the Ni catalyst uniformly dispersed, suppressing Ni‑black formation and restoring high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “significant Ni‑black contamination after just an hour of flow operation, thus blocking light penetration.”; “At a flow rate of 1.65 m min⁻¹, full conversion was achieved…; at 2.2 m min⁻¹, aggregation was entirely prevented.”; “The high flow rate … prevents clogging and improves the mixing efficiency.”

Paper Title: High-Speed Circulation Flow Platform Facilitating Practical Large-Scale Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
Problem_Description: The heterogeneous slurry’s opacity and short residence time in a conventional gas‑liquid‑solid microbatch setup led to poor light penetration and conversion (<5 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The circulation flow platform continuously recirculates the slurry, providing uniform irradiation throughout the PFA tubing and allowing the reaction to proceed to full conversion. Optimization of LED number (reducing from nine to five) retained efficiency while simplifying the light source.
Supporting_Evidence: “introducing argon gas to flow a gas–liquid–solid suspension … less than 5 % conversion achieved due to the short residence time.”; “The high-speed circulation flow platform … improves mixing efficiency and light irradiation.”; “It was observed that the number of 64 W LED lamps could be reduced from nine to five without compromising the reactivity.”

Paper Title: High-Speed Circulation Flow Platform Facilitating Practical Large-Scale Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
Problem_Description: Heterogeneous photocatalytic C–N, C–S, and three‑phase C–C couplings typically require prolonged reaction times (several hours), limiting throughput on scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: By operating the reactor in a semicontinuous mode with high circulation speeds, the reaction time is decoupled from reactor volume, enabling long‑duration reactions to be run efficiently. Automated feeding and collection allowed 210 h of uninterrupted operation, producing kilogram quantities with high productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “circulation flow reactors … allow it to re‑enter the reactor until the reaction reaches completion.”; “Semicontinuous production can be simply achieved through automated feeding and collection.”; “Production for 210 h … afforded the product trifluridine in an overall 43.2 % yield and 63.8 g day⁻¹ productivity.”

Paper Title: High-Speed Circulation Flow Platform Facilitating Practical Large-Scale Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
Problem_Description: Scaling heterogeneous photoreactions traditionally requires specialized equipment (packed‑bed reactors, oscillatory flow reactors) that are costly and not readily available for many laboratories.
Solution_Description: The high‑speed circulation flow system uses simple, inexpensive components (peristaltic pump, PFA tubing, LED arrays) that are easy to assemble and scale, removing the need for custom‑built, high‑cost reactors.
Supporting_Evidence: “A custom‑designed circulation flow system was assembled as a proof of concept… comprising a reagent reservoir, peristaltic pump, perfluoroalkoxyalkane (PFA) tubing coil, and multiple sets of 64 W LEDs.”; “The high‑speed circulation flow reactor … simple infrastructure, ease of operation and automation, significant efficiency improvement compared to conventional batch reactors.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Crystallization Research of Voclosporin
Problem_Description: The original acetylation of cyclosporin A using Ac₂O/pyridine/DMAP in CH₂Cl₂ gave only 90.67 % conversion after 2 days, required 96 h to reach <1 % starting material, and the presence of silicon reagents caused emulsification that made work‑up difficult.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to isopropyl acetate (IPAc), increasing DMAP loading to 0.8 equiv and running the reaction at 55–60 °C reduced the reaction time to 15 h and raised the conversion to 97 % (entry 9, Table 1).
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was conducted at room temperature for a duration of 2 days… the content of 3 was only 90.67 %… (Table 1, Entry 1).”, “Silicon reagents could lead to emulsification of the reaction mixture, making it challenging to carry out subsequent workup procedures.”, “The reaction results reveal that the content of 3 was 95.25 % in IPAc…”, “By increasing the amount of DMAP from 0.2 to 0.8 equiv… conversion efficiency… 97.01 % within a shorter time frame of 15 h (Table 1, Entry 9).”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Crystallization Research of Voclosporin
Problem_Description: The Wittig reaction with allyl‑triphenylphosphonium bromide (5) afforded only 49 % of the desired diene (6) and an E/Z ratio of 45:55, necessitating column chromatography to enrich the E‑isomer.
Solution_Description: A Peterson elimination using γ‑trimethylsilyl‑allyl‑boronate (8) was employed. This gave >90 % conversion and an E/Z ratio of 98:2, and the product could be isolated by simple crystallisation from MTBE without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Wittig reaction yielded a ratio of the E isomer (6) to the Z isomer (7) at 45:55… requiring the use of column chromatography… (ref 8).”, “Compound 8 was used as the allyl reagent… the content of intermediate 6 increased to 93.0 %… after crystallisation using MTBE, the yield improved to 85.5 % and the E/Z ratio reached 98:2 (Table 2, Entry 7).”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Crystallization Research of Voclosporin
Problem_Description: During hydrolysis of acetyl‑voclosporin (6) many bases (K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, NaHCO₃, LiOH, NaOMe, t‑BuOK, Et₃N/LiBr, HCl) gave incomplete conversion, low product levels, and significant E→Z isomerisation (e.g., 95:5 to 1:99 depending on base strength).
Solution_Description: DBU was identified as a mild deprotection base; using 4 equiv DBU in MeOH/H₂O at 35–40 °C (or 20 equiv in MeOH/H₂O at 35–40 °C) gave >93 % isolated product with an E/Z ratio of 97:3, maintaining stereochemistry and high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “When sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) or sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) was used… the content of 1 declined to 85.51 % and 34.03 % respectively.”, “LiOH… resulted in a shift … 85:15…”, “The method of using boron trifluoride… did not result in product formation.”, “Notably, the content of 1 increased to 93.46 % when DBU was used… with the ratio of the E to Z isomer being 97:3 (Table 3, Entry 11).”, “We achieved a content of 1 at 94.10 % when using DBU in combination with a MeOH/water mixture (20:1) at a temperature range of 35–40 °C (Table 3, Entry 14).”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Crystallization Research of Voclosporin
Problem_Description: Previous processes relied on semi‑preparative HPLC or column chromatography for the final product, which is expensive and generates large solvent waste at industrial scale.
Solution_Description: A crystallisation protocol using ethanol/water (8 v : 8 v) gave Voclosporin of 98.87 % HPLC purity, 73 % isolated yield and eliminated the need for chromatography, reducing cost and solvent waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “In a previous report, semipreparative HPLC purifications were performed… however, this procedure has a high cost in industrial production.”, “Crystallizing Voclosporin using methanol/water, ethanol/water, or isopropanol/water… yielded purities of 97.51 %, 98.87 % and 98.01 % respectively (Table 4, Entries 1–3).”, “The use of an ethanol/water solvent mixture demonstrated superior results … the purity of the solid was 98.87 % with a yield of 73 % (Table 4, Entry 2).”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Crystallization Research of Voclosporin
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 80 °C the acetylation reaction in IPAc led to a drop in conversion (content of 3 decreased to 86.76 %) indicating thermal degradation of cyclosporin A, while the low‑boiling CH₂Cl₂ gave a viscous mixture that impeded stirring.
Solution_Description: The optimal temperature range of 55–60 °C in IPAc was selected; this avoided degradation and provided a homogeneous, low‑viscosity mixture that could be efficiently stirred and worked up.
Supporting_Evidence: “If the reaction temperature was increased to 80–85 °C when using IPAc, the content of 3 declined to 86.76 %… indicating that high temperatures may deteriorate the structure of cyclosporin A (Table 1, Entry 8).”, “The lower reaction temperature and the reduced polarity of the reaction solvent… contributed to the lower conversion rate.”

Paper Title: PAT Application in the Expedited Development of a Three-Step, One-Stage Synthesis of the Dipeptide Intermediate of HCV Protease Inhibitor Faldaprevir
Problem_Description: The mixed‑anhydride coupling using isobutyl‑chloroformate or pivaloyl chloride gave incomplete regio‑selectivity (≥15 % of undesired by‑products 6 and 7) and a moderate isolated yield (≈70 %). Moreover, the conversion of the mixed anhydride with hydroxy‑proline required 16 h at 5 °C, making the step very slow on scale.
Solution_Description: Switch to sulfonyl‑mixed anhydrides (TsCl) using N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) as base in acetonitrile. The new conditions gave fast, clean conversion to the desired dipeptide ester 5 in >90 % isolated yield with no detectable isomerisation. The change involved a different halogen‑sulfonyl reagent (TsCl), a different base (NMM) and a more polar aprotic solvent (MeCN) that improved reaction rate and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...incomplete regioselectivity was observed…more than 15 % of the undesired products 6 and 7 formed, which accounted in part for the moderate yield (70 %)…required 16 h to reach 95 % conversion.”
• “Screening of different organic bases and solvents identified N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) as a suitable base in acetonitrile, resulting in a fast and selective conversion to the desired dipeptide 5 in >90 % isolated yield without detectable isomerisation.”
• “Acetonitrile was selected due to the rapid and clean reaction profile and its compatibility with the subsequent saponification step.”

Paper Title: PAT Application in the Expedited Development of a Three-Step, One-Stage Synthesis of the Dipeptide Intermediate of HCV Protease Inhibitor Faldaprevir
Problem_Description: The original peptide‑coupling route used EDC/HOBt. HOBt is classified as shock‑sensitive in Europe, posing a safety risk for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Replace the HOBt‑based coupling with a tosyl‑mixed‑anhydride protocol (TsCl/NMM) that uses inexpensive, non‑explosive reagents, thereby eliminating the hazardous HOBt component while maintaining high conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In addition to our primary goal of replacing HOBT, which is classified as shock sensitive in Europe, further process considerations had to be addressed in developing a scalable, safe, and economical process.”
• “Tosyl chloride (TsCl) was added…resulted in a fast and selective conversion to the desired dipeptide 5 in >90 % isolated yield without detectable isomerisation.”

Paper Title: PAT Application in the Expedited Development of a Three-Step, One-Stage Synthesis of the Dipeptide Intermediate of HCV Protease Inhibitor Faldaprevir
Problem_Description: The three‑step, one‑stage sequence involves highly exothermic addition steps (mixed‑anhydride formation, amide formation, saponification). Uncontrolled heat release could jeopardise safety and product quality on multikilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Implement controlled, portion‑wise addition of TsCl and hydroxy‑proline under tight temperature control (≤5 °C for the first two steps, ≤15 °C for saponification). Use MultiMax IR and calorimetric tools (RC1e, DSC, ARSST) to monitor reaction heat and keep the temperature rise below safe limits (ΔT < 6 °C for steps 1&2, ΔT ≈ 14 °C for saponification).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The temperature profile of the reaction in step 1 indicated a low exotherm (T_r – T_j < 6 °C) after addition of solid TsCl to the reaction mixture at 0 °C.”
• “The saponification step…value of T_r – T_j = 14 °C was attributed to sensible heat from addition of a higher temperature (RT) solution of the base.”
• “RC1e experiments indicated an adiabatic temperature rise of 61 °C, 38 °C, and 17 °C for the three steps in the process, respectively.”
• “The mixture was cooled to 0–5 °C before addition of NMM…maintaining the internal temperature below 5 °C while adding TsCl.”

Paper Title: PAT Application in the Expedited Development of a Three-Step, One-Stage Synthesis of the Dipeptide Intermediate of HCV Protease Inhibitor Faldaprevir
Problem_Description: Using pivaloyl chloride as the activating agent required 16 h at 5 °C for the mixed‑anhydride to react with hydroxy‑proline, dramatically extending the overall process time.
Solution_Description: Adopt the TsCl/NMM system which enables completion of the coupling in ~1 h at 5 °C, reducing the step time by >15 h and allowing the whole three‑step sequence to be finished within 10 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...slow reaction of the mixed anhydride with hydroxyproline at 5 °C, required 16 h to reach 95 % conversion.”
• “...resulted in a fast and selective conversion to the desired dipeptide 5 in >90 % isolated yield…The mixture was then stirred for 1 h at 5 °C…complete conversion to 5 after 1.5 h at 0 °C.”

Paper Title: PAT Application in the Expedited Development of a Three-Step, One-Stage Synthesis of the Dipeptide Intermediate of HCV Protease Inhibitor Faldaprevir
