Paper Title: Identification, Synthesis, Characterization, and Control Strategy Establishment for Process Impurities of Baloxavir Marboxil
Problem_Description: Imp‑H remained in the crude product after the coupling (2.73 %); standard filtration was insufficient to meet the <0.10 % impurity specification.
Solution_Description: A slurry wash with increasing volumes of EtOAc (2–6 vol) efficiently removed Imp‑H; 5 vol EtOAc gave 0.02 % Imp‑H and >99.8 % API purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 8 shows impurity levels decreasing with EtOAc volume: 2 vol → Imp‑H = 1.15 %; 5 vol → Imp‑H = 0.02 %.
• “5 vol of EtOAc as the slurry solvent is sufficient to purge Imp‑H to <0.10 % …”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: Thiomorpholine (TM) is the most expensive structural component of the existing route and its early incorporation inflates the overall cost, making the previous routes impractical for low‑cost production.
Solution_Description: A lower‑cost synthetic strategy was implemented that replaces TM with inexpensive diethanolamine (DEA) and sodium sulfide, which also serve as the nucleophile for ring closure and as the reductant for the nitro group (Zinin reduction), thereby eliminating the costly transition‑metal reduction step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Incorporation of this fragment early in the synthetic route further inflates its overall cost contribution, rendering these early routes impractical from a cost perspective.”; “This sulfide treatment has the added benefit of affecting a Zinin reduction of the nitro functional group, which alleviates the need for the transition metal reduction used in previous routes.”; “The key step in this process is the construction of the thiomorpholine ring by a nucleophilic sulfide ring closure…”,

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: The S_NAr reaction between 3,4‑difluoronitrobenzene (DFNB) and DEA is highly exothermic, causing a rapid temperature rise that presents a safety risk on scale.
Solution_Description: The addition of DFNB was performed slowly (30 mL h⁻¹) into hot DEA, and the reactor jacket temperature was adjusted to keep the internal temperature within ±5 °C of the set point, thereby controlling the heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “When DEA (3 equiv) and DFNB are mixed at room temperature and then heated, a rapid increase in the internal temperature is observed starting at ∼50–60 °C.”; “A common method employed to control exothermic reactions… slow addition of the reactive reagent to the hot reaction mixture… DFNB was added at a rate of 30 mL/h… the internal reaction temperature did not exceed the set temperature by more than ∼5 °C.”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: Early S_NAr conditions using near‑stoichiometric DEA with trialkylamine bases gave sluggish conversion even at 80 °C and produced a significant amount of the double‑substitution impurity 6.
Solution_Description: Using DEA as both reactant and base at 3 equiv in CH₃CN (10 V) and heating to 80 °C achieved near‑complete conversion in 3 h, minimizing impurity 6; alternative solvents (toluene, DMF, water) were screened, confirming CH₃CN gave the best performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions conducted with near stoichiometric DEA and trialkylamine bases… are sluggish, even at temperatures up to 80 °C.”; “With K₂CO₃ or DBU… complete consumption… but the product mixture contains a significant portion of impurity 6.”; “Near complete conversion was obtained with 3 equiv of DEA in only 3 h at 80 °C (entry 7).”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: Running the S_NAr reaction under neat DEA at lower temperatures made the mixture very viscous, reducing stirring efficiency and reaction rate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A slight excess of DEA (3 equiv) was retained and the reaction temperature was kept between 80 °C and 90 °C, which improved mixing and maintained acceptable conversion rates while avoiding excessive viscosity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Lowering the reaction temperature… the mixture becomes considerably more viscous, reducing the reaction rate and limiting efficient stirring.”; “A slight excess of DEA (3 equiv) and temperatures between 80 and 90 °C were chosen for further scale‑up optimization.”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: Mesylation of intermediate 4 using inorganic bases (K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, KOtBu, NaOtBu) and imidazole was sluggish with low conversion, even after reflux overnight.
Solution_Description: Triethylamine (Et₃N) was employed as the base in CH₃CN (or DCM), delivering full conversion to the mesylate 5 without external heating, simplifying the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reactions with inorganic bases and imidazole were sluggish after several hours at RT, and heating to reflux overnight did little to improve conversion.”; “Et₃N afforded full conversion to the desired product in both CH₃CN and DCM without the need for external heating.”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: During mesylation scale‑up, varying solvent‑antisolvent ratios either gave low isolated yields or produced a sticky reaction mass that hindered filtration.
Solution_Description: An intermediate water addition (3.5 V water to 5 V MeCN) provided a good balance of yield (≈85 %) and filterability, while larger water volumes improved yield but caused stickiness.
Supporting_Evidence: “With the smallest charge of antisolvent… modest yield (82.9 %). Isolated yields improved with equal volume ratios… but the reaction mass became sticky, making filtration difficult.”; “A compromise … with an intermediate addition of water (3.5 V) … good yield and purity (85.2 % and 99.6 %).”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: In the tandem ring‑closure/reduction step, basic conditions promoted hydrolysis of the mesylate and formation of morpholinylaniline 8, while polysulfide impurities in sodium sulfide generated impurity 9.
Solution_Description: A two‑step sulfide addition was adopted: a slow first addition of Na₂S·9H₂O followed by a batch addition, with 0.5 equiv Na₂SO₃ added beforehand to reduce polysulfides; the reaction pH was kept around 10 – 11 to limit base‑promoted side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “To facilitate a selective ring closure with sulfide, slow addition of the first equivalent of sulfide was attempted… entry 1 showed a dramatic improvement (96.5 % area).”; “A substoichiometric charge of Na₂SO₃ (0.5 equiv)… eliminated the remaining traces of impurity 9.”; “The pH of the reaction was adjusted to 11… to limit the formation of morpholinylaniline 8.”

Paper Title: A Tandem Ring Closure and Nitrobenzene Reduction with Sulfide Provides an Improved Route to an Important Intermediate for the Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Candidate Sutezolid
Problem_Description: The crude product from the final step displayed a tan color and contained inorganic impurities, reducing assay purity to ≈71 %.
Solution_Description: A simple charcoal treatment (20 wt % activated charcoal at 80 °C for 3 h) was applied, followed by filtration, which increased assay purity to 94.2 % and removed discoloration.
Supporting_Evidence: “The tan color of the crude isolated product suggested that a charcoal treatment may be effective… after treatment, an off‑white solid with assay purity of 94.2 % was obtained.”

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The original amide‑coupling step used HATU, a reagent that is hazardous, expensive and not readily available on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Replace HATU with the safer, inexpensive and widely‑available coupling reagent EDC·HCl (1‑ethyl‑3‑(3‑dimethylamino)propyl‑carbodiimide hydrochloride).
Supporting_Evidence: “Replace HATU with a safer, widely accessible, inexpensive reagent that can be readily purged during workup or isolation” (Intro, list item (1)).; “Early investigation into alternative coupling reagents led us to the identification of 1‑ethyl‑3‑(3‑(dimethylamino)‑propyl)‑carbodiimide hydrochloride (EDC·HCl) as a promising substitute for HATU.” (Sec I, p 5).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The amide‑coupling was originally performed in DMF, a toxic and difficult‑to‑remove solvent.
Solution_Description: Switch the reaction solvent from DMF to MeCN, a greener solvent that is easier to remove and gave comparable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Replace DMF with a greener alternative solvent.” (Intro, list item (1)).; “Employing acetonitrile (MeCN) led to near‑identical results to the reaction in DMF … with the benefits of being a greener solvent that is easier to remove at the end of the reaction.” (Sec I, p 5).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: Ester side‑product S‑5 formed during the coupling and was not removed by the acidic aqueous work‑up, sometimes becoming enriched and lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: Add a post‑reaction aqueous LiOH (or NaOH) hydrolysis step that cleaves S‑5 back to the desired amide S‑4, followed by a slight excess of acid 2 to drive complete conversion, giving a clean 98 % assay yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Ester S‑5 was not removed at all and, in certain cases, even became enriched.” (Sec I, p 6).; “Treating a typical end‑of‑reaction stream with 1 M LiOH led to clean hydrolysis of S‑5 and an increased yield of penultimate S‑4.” (Sec I, p 7).; “...this procedure gave a significantly improved 98 % assay yield (AY) of S‑4.” (Sec I, p 7).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: During post‑work‑up batch concentration the intermediate 4 spontaneously crystallized as an IPAc‑solvate, posing a risk of gumming and loss of material.
Solution_Description: Maintain water content > 24 000 ppm by spiking water (≈0.2 V) before the final concentration step; this keeps 4 soluble in IPAc and eliminates undesired crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “An IPAc‑solvate of 4 spontaneously crystallized while performing a post‑workup batch concentration.” (Sec I, p 8).; “Karl Fischer titration … indicated that water content had an important impact on the solubility of 4 in IPAc.” (Sec I, p 9).; “Spiking 0.2 V of water … resulted in a solution of 4 that no longer crystallized upon seeding.” (Sec I, p 9).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: The original Dess‑Martin periodinane (DMP) oxidation is highly exothermic and can undergo unsafe decomposition on scale.
Solution_Description: Replace DMP with a TEMPO/NaOCl oxidation, which is safer, scalable and uses inexpensive reagents. Use IPAc as the organic cosolvent instead of DCM.
Supporting_Evidence: “Differential scanning calorimetry data … indicate that these exothermic reactions can initiate unsafe decomposition.” (Sec II, p 13).; “A safe, widely scalable TEMPO/NaOCl oxidation … presented an attractive option.” (Sec II, p 13).; “Running the reaction with IPAc as an organic cosolvent led to the formation of 1 in high purity … at a much faster rate compared to DCM.” (Sec II, p 15).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: During the TEMPO/NaOCl oxidation, the α‑keto‑amide stereocenter epimerized to give epi‑1, especially if the biphasic mixture was agitated for extended periods.
Solution_Description: Control the reaction temperature at 15 °C (or 5 °C for reverse addition), limit agitation time, perform a phase split immediately upon completion, and optionally use solid NaOCl·5H₂O (lower pH) to suppress epimerization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Undesired epimerization … could occur … a phase cut upon reaction completion was required to suppress continued epimerization.” (Sec II, p 13).; “Epimerization could be better controlled at 15 °C, even upon extended agitation … the amount of epi‑1 could be held below 1 % LCAP.” (Sec II, p 16).; “Reverse addition … afforded 95 % LCAP of 1 after 3 h … continuing agitation overnight at 5 °C afforded only 1 % LCAP of epi‑1.” (Sec II, p 19).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: A suitable quench for residual NaOCl was required; some quench agents (Na₂S₂O₃, NaHSO₃) caused epimerization or impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Adopt a sodium sulfite (Na₂SO₃) aqueous quench (4 % w/w, pH ≈ 11) which did not increase epimerization and gave clean product.
Supporting_Evidence: “Evaluated several aqueous solutions … Na₂SO₃ afforded no increase in typical EOR epimerization when held at 5 °C.” (Sec III, p 22).; Table 4 shows Na₂SO₃ with LCAP epi‑1 = 0.6 % after 5 °C aging. (Sec III, p 22).

Paper Title: Rapid End-Game Process Development and First GMP Production of MK-7845: An Experimental Antiviral Treatment for COVID-19
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the API 1 suffered from gumming, oiling, and agglomeration due to high water content and inappropriate solvent ratios.
Solution_Description: Control water content to < 1 000 ppm, use an IPAc/n‑heptane solvent system (final ratio ≤ 1:1.75), maintain temperature ≤ 25 °C, and add n‑heptane in stages with proper seeding to obtain consistent crystalline Form 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addressed challenges associated with gumming, oiling, and agglomeration.” (Abstract).; “Control of water content … required to prevent gumming and improve robustness of the seeding process.” (Sec IV, p 24).; “Solvent composition of up to 1:2 IPAc:n‑heptane minimized mother‑liquid losses … temperature had minimal impact between 5 and 25 °C.” (Sec IV, p 26).

Paper Title: What Does It Take to Develop Structurally Complex Molecules by Total Synthesis? Rapid Process Development and GMP Manufacturing of E7130 Drug Substance for First-in-Human Clinical Study
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthetic route gave very low isolated yields (often <10 %) in the final assembly and required long deprotection times under harsh conditions, which generated a multitude of by‑products. The resulting crude material was so complex that high‑pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC) was required to obtain material of acceptable purity.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route was designed that changed the protecting‑group pattern (TES replaces TBS at C35/C48 and TBS replaces MPM at C41).  The new groups are removed cleanly with TBAF, shortening the deprotection step and eliminating many side‑products, thereby raising the overall yield and removing the need for HPLC purification.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “low‑yielding reactions (usually less than 10 % yield) at the final assembly phase… ”
• “deprotection of robust protecting groups such as TBS or MPM … required a long reaction time as well as harsh conditions, resulting in a significant generation of undesirable byproducts… ”
• “high pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC) purification was necessary due to the complex mixtures in crude material … ”
• “substituting the TBS group with a triethylsilyl (TES) group … allowed easy removal using TBAF, consequently reducing the reaction time.”

Paper Title: What Does It Take to Develop Structurally Complex Molecules by Total Synthesis? Rapid Process Development and GMP Manufacturing of E7130 Drug Substance for First-in-Human Clinical Study
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the key Zr/Ni‑mediated ketone coupling, the originally used zinc reductant caused slow competitive degradation of the C1–C37 fragment (e.g., reductive deiodination and pyran ring‑opening), especially when the reaction was prolonged, leading to loss of material and variability in conversion.
Solution_Description: The reducing agent was switched from Zn to Mn, which has a more appropriate redox potential and suppressed fragment degradation.  In addition, the unnecessary additives (DTBMP and EtOAc) were removed, simplifying the protocol and improving robustness.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “zinc caused slow competitive degradation of the C1–C37 fragment… via the C1–C37‑ZnI intermediate … during the coupling reaction.”
• “When zinc was replaced with manganese … the coupling product could be obtained without degradation at the C37 position, which mitigated the risks of failure.”
• “2,6-di‑tert‑butyl‑4‑methylpyridine (DTBMP) and ethyl acetate (EtOAc), originally used … were not necessary for the ketone coupling.”

Paper Title: What Does It Take to Develop Structurally Complex Molecules by Total Synthesis? Rapid Process Development and GMP Manufacturing of E7130 Drug Substance for First-in-Human Clinical Study
Problem_Description: The penultimate intermediate C52‑alcohol was obtained as an 8:1 mixture of C38 epimers together with other diastereomeric impurities generated upstream, and conventional HPLC purification would have been required to reach the API purity specification.
Solution_Description: C52‑alcohol was isolated by octadecyl‑silane (ODS) column chromatography, which removed the unwanted C38 epimer and upstream impurities.  Because many key intermediates were obtained as crystalline solids, the final API could be delivered with >99.8 % purity without any HPLC step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “C52‑alcohol … afforded a ca. 8:1 epimers mixture at the C38 position. This undesired C38 epimer could be removed by octadecylsilane (ODS) column chromatography.”
• “Many key intermediates … were found to be crystalline compounds … highly pure C52‑alcohol and the API could be efficiently obtained without using HPLC purification.”

Paper Title: What Does It Take to Develop Structurally Complex Molecules by Total Synthesis? Rapid Process Development and GMP Manufacturing of E7130 Drug Substance for First-in-Human Clinical Study
Problem_Description: In the final three steps to the API, dissolved CO₂ in the solvent promoted side‑reactions, and solvent impurities from lower‑grade solvents could also generate unforeseen by‑products, jeopardizing batch‑to‑batch consistency.
Solution_Description: The final step was performed with more stringent solvent quality (higher‑grade solvents) and the reaction mixture was thoroughly degassed to remove dissolved CO₂, which suppressed side‑reactions and yielded a reproducibly pure API.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “apply more strict criteria for main fraction in chromatographic purification”
• “use higher‑grade solvents for preventing unforeseen contamination… ”
• “conduct the reaction of the final step … with careful degassing to remove the dissolved carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the solvent for suppressing side reaction.”

Paper Title: What Does It Take to Develop Structurally Complex Molecules by Total Synthesis? Rapid Process Development and GMP Manufacturing of E7130 Drug Substance for First-in-Human Clinical Study
Problem_Description: Residual thio‑esterification by‑products (PyS₂ and Ph₃P=S) in the C38–C52 fragment inhibited the Zr/Ni ketone coupling, requiring careful control of impurity levels before scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A spike‑study‑based acceptance limit was established and the manufacturing process was adjusted to keep residual PyS₂ and Ph₃P=S below the set limits, ensuring the coupling reaction proceeded without inhibition.
Supporting_Evidence: • “residual (PyS)₂ and Ph₃PS in the C38–C52 fragment … were found to inhibit the coupling reaction. Therefore, the residual levels of these contaminants were controlled at less than the acceptable level, which had been set by spike study conducted in advance.”

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: Entrapment immobilization of cells (cellulose membrane, PVA, calcium alginate) gave a ~20‑fold lower fatty‑alcohol yield than free cells because the long‑chain fatty alcohols diffuse slowly through the entrapment matrix, and a large fraction of product becomes trapped in the hydrogel.
Solution_Description: Switch to adsorption‑based immobilization using PEI‑coated polyester fabrics, which places the cells on the surface of the support, eliminating the diffusion barrier and restoring yields comparable to free cells.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "All three materials gave a considerably lower yield than that of the free cells (by 20‑fold)… This could be explained by the slow diffusion of the long‑chain fatty alcohol… through the entrapment layer." (Fig. 3) 
• "For the case of alginate hydrogels, a major fraction of the fatty alcohols were trapped in the alginate… 10–14‑fold higher than that found in the dodecane phase." 
• "Adsorption would mitigate the effects of mass transfer limitations by enabling cells to be at the surface of the support materials…" 
• "Polyester fabrics yielded the highest levels of fatty alcohol production… the adsorption led to a minimal mass transfer limitation."

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: Cells immobilized on nylon fabric showed ineffective fatty‑alcohol production, giving very low yields and inconsistent performance across cycles.
Solution_Description: Replace nylon with polyester fabric as the support material; polyester provided higher cell loading, brighter bioluminescence, and stable activity over multiple reuse cycles.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Fatty alcohol production was ineffective when the cells immobilized onto the nylon fabrics were used." (Fig. 4A) 
• "Cells immobilized onto both polyester fabrics yielded the highest levels of fatty alcohol production… production dropped after two cycles on nylon but remained stable on polyester." 
• "The blue bioluminescent light intensity… showed that cells immobilized onto the polyester fabrics appeared to be the brightest, indicating the highest loading."

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: Increasing glucose concentration above 5 g L⁻¹ caused substrate inhibition, decreasing fatty‑alcohol productivity.
Solution_Description: Optimize glucose feed to 5 g L⁻¹, which gave the highest steady‑state productivity (7.7 mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A higher glucose concentration was likely to cause substrate inhibition…" (Section 2.2) 
• "The optimal glucose concentration was 5.0 g/L, resulting in the productivity of 7.7 mg/(L·h)." (Fig. 5A)

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: Low‑log P solvents such as ethyl acetate and hexane were toxic to the engineered cells, while high‑log P solvents (e.g., isopropyl myristate) limited oxygen transfer, both reducing fatty‑alcohol production.
Solution_Description: Select dodecane as the in‑situ extraction solvent; it has an appropriate log P, low toxicity, and provides good mass‑transfer of fatty alcohols without oxygen limitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A low log P value tends to be toxic to cells, causing damage to cell membrane proteins…" (Section 2.2) 
• "A long‑chain hydrocarbon (e.g., isopropyl myristate) … gave a lower fatty alcohol production possibly due to the oxygen diffusional limitation." 
• "Dodecane was found to be an effective in situ extraction solvent, yielding the highest production as compared to other solvents with a low log P value."

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: The membrane‑based liquid‑liquid separator required precise pressure control; excessive pressure could damage the membrane or lead to phase breakthrough.
Solution_Description: Implement a self‑regulating pressure controller that automatically keeps the trans‑membrane pressure between 1–4 psi, safely within the capillary and permeation limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The membrane has a self‑regulating pressure controller to maintain a pressure difference across a membrane within the operating range…" 
• "The self‑tuning pressure control adjusted the pressure difference across the membrane to be around 1–4 psi, which was less than and greater than the capillary and permeation pressures, respectively." (Section 2.2)

Paper Title: Integrated Continuous-Flow Production of Wax Esters Combining Whole-Cell and
Problem_Description: Longer residence times (higher flow rates) reduced fatty‑alcohol productivity, indicating sub‑optimal reaction time for the bioconversion step.
Solution_Description: Operate the packed‑bed reactor at a flow rate of 0.2 mL min⁻¹ (residence time giving highest productivity), rather than 0.3 or 0.4 mL min⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The operation with 0.2 mL/min gave the highest productivity (8.2 mg/(L·h)) as compared to the productivities of 3.3 and 2.4 mg/(L·h) for those with 0.3 and 0.4 mL/min." (Fig. 5B)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: The oxidative cyclisation (Step 2) is highly exothermic (ΔT_ad = +211 °C for 50 % H₂O₂ addition) and is classified as an E‑category reaction, presenting a serious runaway‑reaction risk if cooling fails.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow platform where the temperature was limited to 50 °C, the addition of H₂O₂ was controlled by a syringe pump with a back‑pressure regulator, and the residence time was tuned to keep the reaction under safe thermal limits.
Supporting_Evidence: - "The formation of 1‑amino‑1,2,3‑triazole (step 2) was found to be highly exothermic (−525 kJ) with an adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad) of 211 °C during the addition of 50 % hydrogen peroxide…" (Section 2.1.1)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: When the two raw materials (glyoxal and hydrazine) were mixed directly in the larger 1/4‑in. PFA tubing, a solid by‑product formed from oligomerisation, causing clogging of the flow reactor.
Solution_Description: The feeds were premixed in a sealed bottle before entering the reactor (premixing), which prevented the solid formation and allowed the use of larger tubing without blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: - "For the 1/4 in. PFA tubing (o.d. = 6.4 mm, i.d. = 4.8 mm) … clogging issues in the system" (Section 2.2.1)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: Addition of concentrated HCl in Step 3 produced a large amount of solid precipitate, leading to flow blockage and raising safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition sequence was reversed – NaNO₂ was added first, then a diluted HCl solution – which suppressed solid formation. The HCl concentration was reduced, and the process was operated under controlled flow with a back‑pressure regulator.
Supporting_Evidence: - "In the established batch conditions, the addition of concentrated HCl into the reaction mixture would generate a significant number of solids. The incompatibility of solids poses a huge challenge in continuous flow systems. After various evaluations, we discovered that altering the addition sequence by adding the aqueous NaNO₂ first and reducing the concentration of aqueous HCl effectively mitigated the challenge of solid formation." (Section 2.2.3)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: Batch processing of the three‑step sequence involved handling of energetic intermediates (hydrazine, hydrogen peroxide, 1‑amino‑1,2,3‑triazole) and required high‑temperature vacuum distillation, presenting significant safety hazards at scale.
Solution_Description: The entire synthesis was migrated to a continuous‑flow platform using water as the sole solvent. Water’s high specific heat absorbed reaction heat, minimizing runaway risk, and the smaller reactor inventory reduced exposure to hazardous intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: - "The main basis of safety for this process was underpinned by the exclusive use of water as a solvent throughout all steps, leveraging its high specific heat…" (Section 2.1.1)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: The original batch oxidation step (Step 2) gave only ~50 % isolated yield and showed poor reproducibility when a WO₃ packed‑bed reactor was used in flow.
Solution_Description: WO₃ was replaced by inexpensive, water‑soluble Na₂WO₄·2H₂O as a homogeneous catalyst, the H₂O₂ equiv. were increased from 2 to 3, and the reaction temperature was tuned to 50 °C, delivering yields up to 70 % in flow and consistent performance.
Supporting_Evidence: - "In an effort to seamlessly transition to the flow system, we initially attempted the oxidation reaction using a WO₃ packed‑bed reactor…only ~50 % yield…poor reproducibility…" (Section 2.2.2)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: Large volumes of gas generated in Step 2 (from H₂O₂ decomposition) entered the syringe pump and altered the flow rate of Step 3, compromising reaction control.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A degassing chamber (with ultrasonic assistance) was placed after Step 2 to remove dissolved gases before feeding into Step 3, restoring stable flow rates.
Supporting_Evidence: - "The generation of a significant volume of gas in Step 2…adversely affected the flow rate in Step 3…degassing the reaction mixture after Step 2 was deemed essential." (Section 2.2.3)

Paper Title: 1,2,3-Triazole Synthesis: Development of Safe and Effective Batch and Continuous Manufacturing Processes
Problem_Description: The final batch work‑up required high‑temperature vacuum distillation of 1,2,3‑triazole, which is energetically demanding and posed a risk of thermal degradation.
Solution_Description: An in‑line liquid–liquid separator (Zaiput SEP‑200) with pH control (NaHCO₃, pH 8‑9) was employed for continuous extraction of the product, eliminating the need for high‑temperature distillation and improving overall purity.
Supporting_Evidence: - "To facilitate the continuous extraction and isolation of 1,2,3‑triazole from the reaction mixture, we incorporated an in‑line purification module using a commercially available liquid–liquid separator (Zaiput)…the pH value was regulated within the range 8–9 by employing a saturated aqueous NaHCO₃ solution, thereby optimizing the extraction efficiency." (Section 2.2.4)

Paper Title: Highly Productive Flow Synthesis for Lithiation, Borylation, and/or Suzuki Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Increasing concentration and lowering temperature in the flow lithiation‑borylation step caused precipitation of solids, leading to reactor clogging and a risk of operation failure.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Problem_Description: The legacy processes for the key intermediate required a large excess of toxic NaN₃ (up to 6.5 equiv) and gave only ~32 % yield of the desired cis‑diamine, with the remaining material forming the trans‑isomer that could be separated only by demanding column chromatography.
Solution_Description: A new nine‑step synthetic route was devised that uses an enzymatic asymmetric reductive amination to set the stereocenters, eliminates the need for NaN₃‑driven azide displacements, and telescopes several intermediates (precipitation, in‑situ work‑ups) so that isolation steps and chromatographic separations are avoided.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The known synthetic methods suffer from drawbacks, such as low yield, long reaction times, as well as excessive use of NaN₃… The yield of 7 is low, approximately 32%, and is contaminated… with the undesired trans‑isomer … column chromatography …” (Intro, lines 1‑7). • “The new method includes a total of nine steps… The critical intermediate… was synthesized on a scale of up to 10 kg…” (Results, lines 1‑5).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: The azide displacement step is mildly exothermic; solid NaN₃ added over 60 min caused a 1–2 °C temperature rise, raising safety concerns especially at larger scale.
Solution_Description: The addition time was extended to 120 min (or 15 min using 25 % aq NaN₃) and a cooling device was employed to keep the reaction within 0–10 °C, eliminating the temperature spike and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: • Table 2 entry 1: 60 min solid NaN₃ addition → 1–2 °C rise. • Table 2 entry 2: 120 min addition → temperature maintained at rt. • Table 2 entry 4: 15 min addition of aq 25 % NaN₃ at rt → no exotherm (Results, lines 106‑119).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: Swern oxidation of the azide‑derived alcohol required ultra‑low temperatures (‑80 °C to ‑60 °C) and generated malodorous Me₂S, making large‑scale operation impractical.
Solution_Description: TEMPO/NaClO oxidation was adopted, delivering the ketone in 95 % isolated yield at 0 °C – 5 °C without the need for cryogenic conditions or hazardous reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: • Swern gave 64–73 % yield but required unpleasant odor and −80 °C (Results, lines 140‑145). • “TEMPO oxidation proved an efficient approach, transforming 26 to 27 in high yield (95 %)” (Results, line 148).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: The ketone 27 has poor solubility in aqueous buffer, causing precipitation and incomplete conversion in the biocatalytic asymmetric reductive amination.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: 10 % DMSO (v/v) was added as a cosolvent to improve substrate solubility; higher temperatures (up to 50 °C) were tolerated, and substrate loading was optimized to 50–100 g L⁻¹ with appropriate enzyme loading.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Considering the poor solubility of ketone 27 in water, an organic cosolvent was required… 10 % DMSO at 30 °C gave satisfactory conversion” (Results, lines 180‑186). • Table 5 entries 6, 7, 8 show 10 %–20 % DMSO with 50–100 g L⁻¹ substrate (Results, lines 190‑211).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: The ω‑transaminase–catalyzed amination is reversible; without shifting the equilibrium, conversion stalls at ~70 % on kilogram scale, especially at high substrate concentration (125 g L⁻¹).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 3.5 equiv excess of isopropylamine donor was employed, and the acetone by‑product was continuously removed by a 1 fps nitrogen sweep or a mild vacuum (0.5 atm) to drive the equilibrium toward product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A substantial excess of the amine donor… 3.5 equiv … sufficient for good conversion” (Results, lines 210‑215). • Table 5 entry 7: 1 fps N₂ headspace sweep gave complete conversion; Table 6 entry 1‑5: vacuum removal of acetone improved HPLC area to ≥85 % (Results, lines 224‑242).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: During the work‑up of the TEMPO oxidation, residual NaClO can react with HCl to generate Cl₂ gas, posing an inhalation hazard.
Solution_Description: A chlorine‑absorption device was recommended for the acid‑wash step to capture any generated Cl₂, ensuring safe handling on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It is strongly recommended to implement a chlorine absorption device during the acid washing process due to safety considerations.” (Results, lines 166‑168).

Paper Title: New Method to Large-Scalable Preparation of the Key Chiral Cyclohexane
Problem_Description: Neutralization of the oxalate salt 20 with a tertiary amine caused the free base 12 to form a gel, hardening the reaction mixture and making stirring difficult.
Solution_Description: By telescoping the step and avoiding isolation of the free base (direct precipitation or solvent‑swap), the gel‑formation issue was bypassed.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Upon neutralization of 20 with the tertiary amine, the free base 12 forms a gel, hardening… making stirring quite difficult.” (Intro, lines 73‑77).

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: Compound 2 is insoluble in toluene, leading to crystallisation and blockage of the reaction chips during the first‐step chlorination.
Solution_Description: Dichloroethane (DCE) was selected as the reaction solvent for all steps despite its green‑chemistry drawbacks, because it keeps compound 2 in solution and prevents chip clogging.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "compound 2 was insoluble in toluene, posing a risk of crystallization and blockage in the reaction chips."[Solution] "In spite of the inconsistency with the principle of green chemistry, dichloroethane (DCE) was chosen as a fitting solvent for the subsequent optimization of batch reaction conditions and exploration of continuous flow reactions."

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: Powdered MgSO₄ in the drying column agglomerates after absorbing moisture, causing flow‑path blockage; a single pass through a 4 Å molecular‑sieve column does not completely remove water, giving low purity of ester 3.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The moisture‑removal step was redesigned: MgSO₄ was replaced with a 4 Å molecular‑sieve column and the effluent was recycled through the column (1 → 4 passes) to raise the purity of ester 3 from 73 % to 84 %.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "the powdered MgSO₄ tended to agglomerate after absorbing a large amount of moisture, leading to the blockage of the flow path (Entry 1)."[Problem] "the use of 4 Å molecular sieve proved to be a failure to completely remove the water, even the cycles passing through the column were raised from 1 to 4 (Entry 2–5)."[Solution] "Entry 2–5 … number of recycles … 4 Å MS … purity 73 % → 84 %"

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: The literature batch synthesis of tiadinil and methiadinil uses five different solvents, making work‑up cumbersome and increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: A single solvent (DCE) was employed for all steps in the continuous‑flow sequence, and the integrated chip‑based platform allowed on‑line filtration and liquid–liquid membrane separation, eliminating multiple solvent exchanges and column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "this synthetic route suffered from the use of five different solvents, leading to cumbersome separation and purification."[Solution] "DCE was chosen as a fitting solvent for the subsequent optimization…"[Solution] "all the reaction steps and tedious workup process were achieved via an integrated continuous flow system"

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: Generating the acyl chloride 5 with SOCl₂ requires distillation of excess SOCl₂ and redissolution of the resulting slurry, which is hazardous and difficult to handle in flow.
Solution_Description: Instead of the SOCl₂ route, the carboxylic acid 4 was activated with methanesulfonyl chloride (MsCl) and later converted to the amide using HOBt/EDCI, avoiding the need to distill SOCl₂ and eliminating slurry handling.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "it is necessary to distill the excessive SOCl₂ after the generation of acyl chloride 5 and the resulting slurry needs to be redissolved to proceed to the subsequent step."[Solution] "we changed the reaction condition and used a combination of 1‑hydroxybenzotriazolein (HOBt) and 1‑ethyl‑3‑(3‑dimethylaminopropyl)‑carbodiimide (EDCI) as the condensation reagent, which gave the desired product 6 in 91 % yield after only 15 min."

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: Activation of acid 4 with MsCl gave low conversion and required long residence times (up to 10 h) while producing side‑product 6a.
Solution_Description: Switching to HOBt/EDCI as the coupling reagents reduced the reaction time to 15 min and raised the isolated yield of tiadinil to 91 % (and methiadinil to 88 %).
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "the separation yield of 6 was a mere 54 %, and the overall reaction time was too long, making it impractical for continuous synthesis."[Solution] "using a combination of HOBt and EDCI… gave the desired product 6 in 91 % yield after only 15 min"

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: EDCI is poorly soluble in DMF, causing pumping difficulties and risk of clogging in the flow chip during the final amide‑formation step.
Solution_Description: Adding 10 % water to the DMF solution dramatically improved EDCI solubility without affecting the coupling reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "the poor solubility of EDCI in DMF… led to pumping and clogging issues."[Solution] "the problem was addressed by adding 10 % water to the solution, which both improved the solubility of EDCI and particularly had no side effects on the reaction."

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: Water generated in the first chlorination step reacts with excess SOCl₂ to form HCl, which destroys intermediate 2 and reduces the overall ester 3 yield.
Solution_Description: A drying column packed with 4 Å molecular sieve was placed before the SOCl₂ addition; the effluent was passed through the column 1–4 times to remove water, thereby protecting compound 2 and increasing ester 3 purity.
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "residual water would react with SOCl₂, impeding our target reaction. Meanwhile, the acid generated from water and SOCl₂ would destroy compound 2."[Solution] "the first reaction chip was connected with a drying column filled with either 4 Å molecular sieve or MgSO₄… the use of 4 Å molecular sieve … short retention time … failure to completely remove the water, even the cycles passing through the column were raised from 1 to 4 (Entry 2–5)."

Paper Title: On-Demand Production of Two Commercial Plant Activators, Tiadinil and Methiadinil, under an Integrated Continuous Flow System
Problem_Description: The batch synthesis required 56 h to complete five steps, giving low overall yields (≈ 40 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implementation of Baker’s‑type 3‑D reaction chips enabled rapid mixing and heat removal, allowing the multistep sequence to be telescoped without intermediate isolation; the total process time fell to 9 h with overall yields of 62 % (tiadinil) and 58 % (methiadinil).
Supporting_Evidence: [Problem] "the overall process time was decreased from 56 to 9 h, thanks to the high mixing efficiency and mass transfer in a Baker’s type 3D reaction chip."[Solution] "the multistep continuous flow synthesis… was realized in an integrated continuous flow system… the retention time of the final condensation was only 81 s… yields of 88 % and 81 % respectively"

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: The organolithium intermediate generated by deprotonating 2,6‑dichloropyrazine (1) with TMPLi was poorly stable during formylation, leading to low conversion to aldehyde 2 (13 % assay yield) and significant recovery of starting material.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the unstable organolithium with the Turbo‑Hauser base i‑Pr₂NMgCl·LiCl (MgDA), a more robust organomagnesium species, and employed inverse addition of 1 into the MgDA solution over 1 h to suppress formation of the dimeric side‑product 1‑dimer.
Supporting_Evidence: “the organolithium intermediate suffered from poor stability during the formylation reaction” (Intro, p. 2); “an encouraging 42 % NMR assay yield of the aldehyde product 2 was achieved … with TMPMgCl·LiCl” (Sec 2.1); “inverse addition of 1 to a solution of TMPMgCl·LiCl over 1 h prevented the formation of dimeric side products” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: TMPMgCl·LiCl and its TMP precursor are expensive and not reliably available on an industrial scale, limiting the practicality of the metalation step.
Solution_Description: A cost‑effective and readily available alternative base, i‑Pr₂NMgCl·LiCl (MgDA), was identified and shown to give comparable performance to TMPMgCl·LiCl in batch and flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high cost and unreliable availability of TMPMgCl·LiCl and its TMP precursor on industrial scale prompted us to explore alternative magnesium bases” (Sec 2.1); “identified the less commonly employed base i‑Pr₂NMgCl·LiCl (MgDA)… to be optimal, giving comparable performance to TMPMgCl·LiCl” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: MgDA solutions began to precipitate when the deprotonation temperature was lowered to –20 °C, causing pressure spikes and solid formation in the feed lines.
Solution_Description: The deprotonation temperature was set between –10 °C and –15 °C where a 0.35 M MgDA solution in THF remains fully soluble, avoiding precipitation and pressure spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: “When pyrazine deprotonation was performed at –20 °C … white solids were observed … precipitation was a risk at this temperature” (Sec 2.2); “we thus chose to set the deprotonation temperature between –10 and –15 °C, at which a 0.35 M solution of MgDA in THF was fully soluble” (Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: The aldehyde 2 is highly reactive and unstable; it decomposes (up to 20 % loss) during storage and its hydrate/hemiacetal side‑products reduce overall yield.
Solution_Description: The aldehyde was immediately converted to a bench‑stable sodium bisulfite adduct 3, which also serves as a convenient purification handle, improving overall isolated yield to 56 % from 1.
Supporting_Evidence: “low assay yields of aldehyde product 2 were achieved via isolation as a bench‑stable bisulfite adduct 3” (Intro, p. 2); “Given the previously observed instability of aldehyde 2 … we decided to redevelop its isolation as a crystalline, bench‑stable sodium bisulfite adduct 3” (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: The originally reported cyclization used hydrazine monohydrate at 100 °C in DMSO, generating highly energetic nitrogen‑rich intermediates and posing a significant safety risk on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a continuous stirred‑tank‑reactor (CSTR) cascade operated at 30–35 °C with acid‑promoted cyclization (AcOH) to keep temperatures well below the DSC‑defined safety limits (30 °C for intermediate 5), thereby minimizing energetic buildup while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the subsequent cyclization step … use of hydrazine monohydrate at 100 °C … posed significant process safety risks on scale” (Intro, p. 2); “we therefore attempted to convert … via an acid‑promoted cyclization at reduced temperatures… AcOH showing optimal reactivity at 30 °C” (Sec 2.5); “maximum recommended safety temperature … is 30 °C … for the highly energetic intermediates” (Ref 40).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: During aqueous work‑up of the final product 4, red‑colored precipitates formed, hindering extraction into the organic layer and reducing overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Prior to aqueous dilution, a quench with 4.5 equiv acetic anhydride was introduced to acylate and scavenge excess hydrazine, stabilizing the crude product and preventing red precipitate formation; the downstream work‑up then employed K₃PO₄ aqueous extraction and crystallization from i‑PrOH/H₂O to give >99 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “we implemented a quenching step prior to aqueous dilution using acetic anhydride (Ac₂O, 4.5 equiv), which effectively scavenged excess hydrazine and enhanced the stability of crude pyrazolopyrazine 4” (Sec 2.6); “Compound 4 was extracted into MTBE … giving an excellent purity of >95 % (HPLC)” (Sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 6‑Chloro‑1
Problem_Description: The bisulfite adduct 3 forms a DMSO solvate that precipitates below ~55 °C, leading to fouling and potential blockages in the CSTR cascade during the hydrazine addition step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Feed lines delivering 3 to the CSTR train were actively heated to 60–65 °C, maintaining solubility of the DMSO solvate and preventing solid formation throughout the continuous process.
Supporting_Evidence: “heated feed lines were required to maintain solubility of bisulfite adduct 3 during transfer to CSTR 1, thus preventing precipitation of its corresponding DMSO solvate, which occurs below 55 °C” (Sec 2.7).

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: The Wacker oxidation used to convert olefin 11 into methyl ketone 12 required stoichiometric CrO₃ and catalytic Pd, reagents that are toxic and generate large amounts of waste, making the step unsafe and uneconomical on large scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Wacker oxidation with a metal‑free oxidative cleavage sequence: epoxidation of the protected citronellol using magnesium monoperoxy‑phthalate (MMPP) followed by periodic‑acid cleavage to give aldehyde 20, then a TEMPO/iodobenzene‑diacetate oxidation to the aldehyde needed for downstream steps.  This avoids CrO₃/Pd and uses inexpensive, safer reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Wacker oxidation to convert olefin 11 into methyl ketone 12 was not desirable, given the use of stoichiometric CrO₃ and catalytic palladium.”; “Consequently, a 2‑step sequence of epoxidation using magnesium monoperoxy phthalate (MMPP) … followed by oxidative cleavage of the epoxide 19 with periodic acid … was pursued and provided aldehyde 20 in 98 and 91% yields, respectively.”; “Among the plethora of possible oxidation conditions … we selected a metal‑free protocol involving catalytic (10 mol %) TEMPO with iodobenzene diacetate … “

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: In the original Discovery route the methyl stereocenter was formed non‑selectively, giving a ∼1:1 mixture of diastereomers that required preparative SFC separation, a step that is low‑throughput and gives variable yields on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A chiral‑pool approach was adopted: (S)‑citronellol provides the required methyl stereocenter, and a diastereoselective aryl Grignard addition to an Ellman N‑sulfinyl aldimine installs the second stereocenter with >95:5 dr, eliminating the need for SFC separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Given the nonselective formation of the linker methyl stereocenter … we sought an asymmetric route to this fragment.”; “The diastereoselective aryl Grignard addition to an Ellman sulfinyl aldimine… gave the sulfinamide 22 in 95:5 diastereoselectivity…”; “Reduction of the ester and SFC separation of the diastereomers gave the pure S,S‑diastereomer 14 in 33% yield overall… not desirable for large scale.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: Attempted direct C–H arylation of 4‑methylthiazole with intermediate 23 failed completely under a variety of conditions, giving no usable product.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a Suzuki cross‑coupling of 23 with a pre‑made thiazolyl boronate 25, which furnished the desired biaryl 24 in 59 % isolated yield after chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, under a variety of conditions, this reaction failed to yield any significant amount of desired product 24.”; “Given the failure of the C–H arylation, the biaryl motif was prepared by a Suzuki cross coupling of 23 with thiazolyl boronate 25… product 24 was isolated in a moderate yield (59%).”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: The thiazolyl boronate 25 required for the Suzuki coupling is expensive and not readily available in the quantities needed for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot borylation/Suzuki sequence was developed: aryl bromide 23 is first borylated in situ to give pinacol‑boronate 26, then coupled with bromothiazole 27 under Pd(dppf)Cl₂ catalysis and Cs₂CO₃/H₂O. This eliminates the need for isolated 25 and improves overall yield (80 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “While the above process enabled access to the required biaryl, the high cost and limited availability of the boronate ester 25 were not desirable for larger scale.”; “It was found optimal to borylate aryl bromide 23 to give the pinacol boronate 26 and subsequently introduce bromothiazole 27… These conditions furnished 24 in 80% yield after chromatography.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: The original alkylation strategy for joining the linker fragment to the SMARCA2 binding motif gave inconsistent yields on multigram scale, likely because the reaction mixture was highly heterogeneous, and the crude product 16 was difficult to purify, requiring multiple silica chromatography steps.
Solution_Description: A reductive amination route was adopted: oxidation of alcohol 14 to aldehyde 31 (TEMPO/PhI(OAc)₂), followed by condensation with amine 4 and NaBH(OAc)₃ reduction. This gave product 16 in 78 % isolated yield, and a crystalline form of 16 was isolated, simplifying downstream purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, the alkylation strategy … gave inconsistent yields on scaling up … the crude product 16 proved difficult to purify, necessitating multiple chromatographic purifications on SiO₂.”; “An alternative strategy involving reductive amination was therefore explored… resulted in clean formation of 16.”; “Importantly, after extensive screening, a crystalline form of 16 was found … gave a convenient crystalline intermediate prior to the final steps.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: The final amide‑bond formation using HATU generated HOAt, tetramethylurea and PF₆⁻ counter‑ions, which complicated the work‑up and introduced safety and environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: The crude product was washed with aqueous K₂CO₃ to remove the PF₆⁻ salt, followed by an EtOH slurry to isolate pure API 1. The authors note that future scale‑up will replace HATU with a safer coupling reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: “The coupling reagent HATU contains the PF₆⁻ counterion, which likely formed a partial salt with 1 … The HPF₆ was removed by washing a CH₂Cl₂ solution of 1 with aqueous K₂CO₃ …”; “Due to the safety concerns … further development would have necessitated replacing HATU as the coupling reagent in the final step.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: Hydrogenolysis of benzyl ester 37 with Pd/C required high catalyst loadings and on 70 g scale produced a cyclopropane‑opened, hydro‑defluorinated impurity 39 (≈12 %) that could not be removed by chromatography or crystallization.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned hydrogenolysis and instead performed a direct saponification (LiOH in THF/H₂O) of 37 to give the free acid 2 in 75 % overall yield with no detectable epimerization or side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “This procedure gave the desired product but often required additional dosing of a Pd/C catalyst … a byproduct … 39 was formed in significant amount (12%). This impurity proved impossible to separate.”; “Hydrolysis was explored … clean conversion of 37 to 2 occurred with no detectable epimer formation.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: During basic hydrolysis of the dipeptide ester 37, the use of MeOH or other alcoholic cosolvents led to epimerization at the proline ester stereocenter, generating an isomeric impurity difficult to remove.
Solution_Description: The hydrolysis was performed in a 2:1 THF/water mixture (no alcohol) with LiOH·H₂O at ≤5 °C, followed by careful acidification and crystallization, which gave pure 2 in high yield and without epimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found critical to avoid the use of MeOH or other alcohols as cosolvents for the hydrolysis, as an isomeric product was formed … likely due to epimerization.”; “When the solvent was changed to a 2:1 v/v mixture of THF and water … clean conversion of 37 to 2 occurred with no detectable epimer formation.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: The originally planned dihydroxylation of the olefin using catalytic OsO₄ was rejected because osmium is highly toxic, even in catalytic amounts.
Solution_Description: The authors substituted the OsO₄‑catalyzed dihydroxylation with a two‑step sequence: epoxidation using magnesium monoperoxy‑phthalate (MMPP) followed by oxidative cleavage of the epoxide with periodic acid, delivering aldehyde 20 in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Nonetheless, the use of toxic osmium, even in catalytic amounts, was not desirable.”; “Consequently, a 2‑step sequence of epoxidation using magnesium monoperoxy phthalate (MMPP)… followed by oxidative cleavage… was pursued and provided aldehyde 20 in 98 and 91% yields, respectively.”

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: Large‑scale ozonolysis of the protected citronellol olefin was not feasible because of limited internal equipment and safety considerations for handling ozone.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced ozonolysis with the MMPP/periodic‑acid oxidative cleavage sequence described above, which is scalable and uses reagents that are readily available and safer to handle.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although ozonolysis of similar substrates is known … the lack of internal options for large‑scale ozonolysis prompted us to seek alternatives.”; Same MMPP/periodic‑acid evidence as above.

Paper Title: A Chiral Pool Strategy for the Synthesis of a SMARCA2 Degrading PROTAC
Problem_Description: During the T3P‑mediated coupling of the dipeptide fragments, formation of a doubly‑acylated impurity 38 was observed (up to 5 % without i‑PrOH), complicating purification.
Solution_Description: A stoichiometric amount of i‑PrOH was added as a decoy secondary alcohol to compete with the hydroxy group of the protected leucine, suppressing formation of impurity 38 to <0.75 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The inclusion of i‑PrOH as a decoy secondary alcohol to compete with the hydroxy group in 33 suppressed the formation of 38 to less than 0.75%.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: The SNAr approach failed on fluoro‑indazole‑derived substrates, giving poor conversion.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned SNAr and developed a copper‑catalysed Ullmann‑type biaryl ether coupling, selecting copper as the catalyst to achieve higher conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original SNAr approach was unsuccessful on all fluoroindazole‑derived substrates… the copper‑catalysed reaction with acid 3a and fluorophenol 4 outperformed palladium‑catalysed conditions and achieved conversions up to 68%.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: Initial copper‑catalysed conditions required high copper loadings (10 mol %), raising material cost and waste‑disposal concerns.
Solution_Description: Screening identified CuBr as the optimal copper source and allowed the loading to be reduced to 6 mol % without loss of conversion, lowering cost and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “CuBr was selected for further development based on its favorable cost, ease of sourcing, atom efficiency, and disposal… it was found that loadings could be reduced to 6 mol % without detriment to the reaction.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: Mixing CuBr with NaOtBu before adding the substrates led to moisture‑induced hydrolysis and dimerisation impurities, reducing conversion.
Solution_Description: A new addition protocol was instituted: azeotropically dried solutions of 2,4‑difluorophenol 4 and NaOtBu in THF were added to a pre‑dried CuBr/3a slurry in toluene at 80 °C, keeping water levels low and preventing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction performance decreased when CuBr and NaOtBu were mixed prior to the addition… Azeotropic distillation of both input solutions… enabled robust control of water content… a procedure involving the addition of an azeotropically dried solution of 2,4‑difluorophenol 4 and NaOtBu in THF to an azeotropically dried mixture of 3a and CuBr… achieved a conversion of 97%.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: Elevated temperatures (> 80 °C) promoted SNAr‑type side reactions and substrate degradation, generating impurities.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was limited to 80 °C, the highest temperature that gave a good rate while minimising side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “High temperatures also resulted in increased impurities from SNAr‑type reactions and substrate degradation, and a temperature of 80 °C was found that provided a good reaction rate while minimizing their formation.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: Post‑reaction mixtures contained high residual copper (≈ 1200 ppm) and conventional washes gave poor phase separation and required additional back‑extractions.

Supporting_Evidence: “Washing with saturated NH₄Cl followed by 5 % citric acid was sufficient to purge residual copper to 3 ppm… A single combined wash comprising 10 % NH₄Cl/5 % citric acid was also effective… a second wash was maintained … increasing the reliability of copper purge down to < 1 ppm.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Key Copper-Catalyzed Biaryl Ether Formation for the Multikilogram Synthesis of Emprumapimod
Problem_Description: Isolation of the biaryl ether as its potassium salt produced a waxy solid with poor copper and impurity removal, and the free acid showed limited solubility in non‑polar solvents.

Paper Title: Development of the Synthetic Route to PF-06878031 Part 2: Amide Reduction Route

Paper Title: Development of the Synthetic Route to PF-06878031 Part 2: Amide Reduction Route

Paper Title: Development of the Synthetic Route to PF-06878031 Part 2: Amide Reduction Route

Paper Title: Development of the Synthetic Route to PF-06878031 Part 2: Amide Reduction Route

Paper Title: High Enantioselective and Large-Scale Production of Ursodeoxycholic Acid by Combination of Pd- and Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase-Catalyzed Hydrogenation

Paper Title: High Enantioselective and Large-Scale Production of Ursodeoxycholic Acid by Combination of Pd- and Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase-Catalyzed Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: A patent route using Pd‑OH₂/carbon under 6 bar H₂ gave only a 68 % isolated yield and was performed at very low substrate concentration (≈1 g, 14 g L⁻¹, 37 mM), making the process inefficient and unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors increased substrate loading (up to 100 g L⁻¹) and switched to the more active Pd/CaCO₃ catalyst in a MeOH/CH₂Cl₂ (1:4) mixed solvent, which improved both conversion and isolated yield to >95 % on kilogram scale.

Paper Title: High Enantioselective and Large-Scale Production of Ursodeoxycholic Acid by Combination of Pd- and Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase-Catalyzed Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: Compound 5 existed in multiple tautomeric forms depending on the solvent; in polar solvents (DMSO, MeOH‑d₄) the enol forms dominated, while in CDCl₃ the keto form was predominant, leading to inconsistent hydrogenation outcomes.

Paper Title: High Enantioselective and Large-Scale Production of Ursodeoxycholic Acid by Combination of Pd- and Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase-Catalyzed Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: In the enzymatic hydrogenation of intermediate 7, the substrate exceeds its critical micelle concentration (CMC), forming sticky micellar aggregates that increase viscosity and impair mass transfer, potentially leading to incomplete conversion and operational difficulties.
