Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: When the reaction scale was increased, the limited solubility of the hydrophobic substrate 2‑acetyl‑6‑bromopyridine (1) in water prevented concentrations above 20 mM unless more than 20 % (v/v) DMSO was used, which in turn limited conversion.
Solution_Description: A biphasic reaction medium was introduced by using water‑immiscible organic solvents (toluene, isopropyl acetate, MTBE) as the organic phase. The substrate was dissolved in the organic phase, allowing concentrations up to 100 mM while keeping the aqueous phase for the enzyme.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Nonetheless, when we tried to increase the scale, the limited solubility of the starting material in water posed a problem when the DMSO was kept at less than 20 % (v/v).”
“the suitability of EP403/S‑TsRTA was evaluated in biphasic systems with three selected water‑immiscible organic solvents: toluene and two greener alternatives, isopropyl acetate (IPAc), and methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE).”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: The use of DMSO (or large amounts of methanol) as a cosolvent created downstream work‑up problems because the solvent is difficult to remove and complicates isolation of the amine product.
Solution_Description: By switching from DMSO/methanol to a biphasic organic‑aqueous system the need for organic‑solvent removal was eliminated; the product and unreacted ketone could be separated by a simple inline acid‑base extraction, providing a clean work‑up without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
“However, DMSO is challenging to remove in the reaction workup and downstream processing.”
“The system, while not able to surpass the 55 % conversion of the initial substrate 1, allowed for the implementation of a simple and efficient strategy to recover the unreacted ketone and isolate the amines … by coupling an acid inlet of 2 M HCl downstream to acidify the aqueous phase.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: In the biphasic continuous transamination the conversion plateaued at 55–60 % regardless of substrate concentration or amine‑donor equivalents, likely because the amine donor (R‑MBA) and the product inhibit the enzyme.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A recirculation loop was implemented: after the first pass the organic and aqueous streams were collected and pumped back through the packed‑bed reactor, extending the total contact time to 6 h. This increased the residence time without changing the reaction composition and mitigated mass‑transfer limitations.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Within 20 min of contact time, TsRTA was able to aminate >10 % of the 2‑Ac‑6‑BrPyr 1 … a plateau was observed after 60 min of contact time, reaching a maximum conversion of ~50 %.”
“A recirculating strategy was applied. In this case, after the first pass through the column, both phases were collected and recirculated for a total contact time of 6 h.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: Di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (Boc₂O) formed micelles in water and its phase (liquid/solid) depended strongly on temperature, causing inconsistent Boc‑protection in batch.
Solution_Description: Boc₂O was prepared as a 2 M solution in acetonitrile and added to the aqueous phase together with NaOH (1.5–2 equiv). The reaction was run at a controlled temperature, giving quantitative conversion in <30 min residence time in flow (1.1 equiv Boc₂O, NaOH 2 equiv).
Supporting_Evidence:
“Boc₂O formed micelles in the aqueous environment, and its original state, either liquid or solid, was highly dependent on the temperature.”
“Boc₂O was initially prepared as a 2 M solution in acetonitrile (MeCN) and added to the water phase. In flow, full conversion was achieved with 1.1 equiv and 30 min of residence time.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: Initial attempts to perform the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling using Pd/C as catalyst gave no detectable product, even after 20 h, indicating an ineffective catalyst system.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was changed to Pd(OAc)₂ (0.1 equiv) together with PPh₃ (0.3 equiv) in a 1‑propanol/water mixture (later a toluene/1‑propanol 1:1 mixture). This gave >99 % conversion after heating at 100 °C overnight, and the same conversion could be achieved in flow within 30 min.
Supporting_Evidence:
“No product formation was ever observed” with Pd/C.
“[Pd(OAc)₂]₃, worked with excellent conversions (99 %) after heating at 100 °C overnight.”
“With the same reaction conditions, similar conversions were obtained in only 30 min of residence time.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: The optimized batch Suzuki coupling required long reaction times (20 h) and relatively high catalyst loading (0.1 equiv Pd(OAc)₂), which is inefficient for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was reduced to 0.015 equiv Pd(OAc)₂, residence time shortened to 5 min, and a trisolvent mixture (toluene/1‑propanol/ water) was employed, maintaining >99 % conversion while lowering reagent consumption and process time.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Optimization of catalytic loading, temperature, and residence time … reduced the residence time to 5 min and reduced the equivalents of [Pd(OAc)₂]₃ from 0.1 to 0.015 equiv.”
“[Pd(OAc)₂]₃, worked with excellent conversions (99 %) after heating at 100 °C overnight.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: Traditional multistep syntheses require isolation and chromatography after each step, which is time‑consuming and adds waste, limiting overall throughput of the chemo‑enzymatic sequence.
Solution_Description: All three transformations (transamination, Boc‑protection, Suzuki coupling) were linked in a continuous flow platform without intermediate isolation. Inline extractions and solvent switches provided the necessary phase separations, allowing the final product to be isolated after the last step only.
Supporting_Evidence:
“We offer a solution to the integration of chemo‑ and biocatalytic steps in continuous flow.”
“After fully telescoping all reaction steps, no change in individual step conversions were observed … the final step afforded the product 6a with a 57 % yield after column chromatography.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: When the substrate solution was prepared in 40 % (v/v) methanol, the immobilized TsRTA lost activity after only 2 h of contact, showing rapid deactivation in high‑alcohol media.
Solution_Description: The enzyme was immobilized on epoxy‑functionalized methacrylic resin (EP403/S) and operated in a biphasic system (organic phase + aqueous buffer). The immobilized biocatalyst retained activity for >12 h on stream, demonstrating robustness to organic solvents when the substrate resides mainly in the organic phase.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Surprisingly, while the catalyst did not seem to lose activity despite the presence of 40 % (v/v) methanol, the conversion dropped significantly after the first few cycles, with no reactivity observed after only 2 h of contact time.”
“TsRTA could be immobilized through epoxy linkage … with >99 % of immobilization yield … and immobilized activities of 12.4 and 6.8 U g⁻¹ … indicating the high stability and reusability of TsRTA once it is immobilized.”

Paper Title: Solvent Switching in Continuous Multistep Chemoenzymatic Synthesis: Telescoping Enzymatic Synthesis of Chiral, Pyridine-Containing Amines with Cross-Coupling as a Case Study
Problem_Description: Previous chemo‑enzymatic routes for similar substrates required DMF as a cosolvent, which is costly, hazardous, and not readily compatible with continuous flow.
Solution_Description: Greener, water‑immiscible solvents (isopropyl acetate, MTBE, toluene) were selected for the biphasic transamination, removing the need for DMF and enabling a more sustainable and scalable process.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Bornscheuer et al. reported … DMF had to be used as a cosolvent, and the process was not in continuous mode.”
“The suitability of EP403/S‑TsRTA was evaluated in biphasic systems with three selected water‑immiscible organic solvents: toluene and two greener alternatives, isopropyl acetate (IPAc), and methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE).”

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: The aldehyde impurity (5‑H‑dibenzo[b,f]‑azepine‑5‑carbaldehyde) generated during the continuous synthesis persisted at moderate levels in the isolated form‑I solid, limiting overall purity and reducing the usable yield of carbamazepine.
Solution_Description: A design‑of‑experiments (DOE) study was performed for the antisolvent crystallization step, varying temperature and water equivalents to simultaneously maximise isolated yield and minimise aldehyde impurity (LCAP). The optimal DOE conditions (e.g., –10 °C, 1 vol eq H₂O) were then applied during scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Two main impurities (aldehyde impurity and impurity‑2) were generated during continuous synthesis.', 'The aldehyde impurity was initially present at higher levels, the focus of the DOE was minimisation.', 'A DOE was conducted for antisolvent crystallization conditions ... with the dual objective of maximizing the isolated yield ... minimizing impurities.', 'The data set was analyzed ... objectives of maximizing yield and minimizing the aldehyde impurity.', 'The Pareto front shows the achievable conditions for yield and aldehyde impurity levels.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: A partial clog of the cyanate pump caused a temporary rise in unreacted iminostilbene (ISB) during the COBR run, risking product quality and forcing material diversion.
Solution_Description: Real‑time in‑line Raman spectroscopy was employed to monitor ISB concentration; when the concentration exceeded the detection limit the stream was automatically diverted to waste, preventing contaminated solid from being collected.
Supporting_Evidence: ['a partial clog in the cyanate pump led to a temporary increase in ISB that was detected by the in‑line Raman method in real time and manually diverted from the MSMPR to waste without impacting the solid product quality.', 'The COBR permitted the utilisation of in‑line Raman spectroscopy for real‑time PAT analysis.', 'The detection limit (DL) of the Raman method was about 0.061 mg mL⁻¹ ISB, indicating that the concentration of ISB could be quantified up to around 99 % conversion.', 'During startup, the synthesis product was manually diverted to waste until the in‑line Raman method confirmed that ISB had stabilised below the DL of the method.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: Evolution of gaseous by‑product during the KOCN reaction reduced the effective fill volume of the continuous oscillatory baffled reactor (COBR), shortening the actual residence time and limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: The process was scaled up using a larger‑volume (≈ 679 mL) COBR, which accommodated the gas‑phase volume loss and restored the intended residence time for quantitative ISB conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['gaseous reaction by‑product reduced the fill volume and consequently the real residence time significantly.', 'The synthesis was scaled up from a 16 mL stainless‑steel coil to a COBR with an approximately fill volume of 679 mL.', 'The COBR was next demonstrated as an effective tool for reaction scale‑up and material generation.', 'The residence time was increased from the smaller scale PFR in part to help ensure quantitative conversion of ISB.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: Insufficient agitation (500 rpm) in the first hour of continuous crystallisation caused crystals to settle at the vessel bottom, producing a transient concentration spike of CBZ in the filtrate and poor crystal growth control.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The stirring speed was increased to 750 rpm after the initial hour, promoting uniform suspension of crystals, eliminating the concentration spike, and stabilising the crystallisation performance.
Supporting_Evidence: ['overhead stirring rate set at 500 rpm appeared to be insufficient, as a disproportionate number of crystals began to accumulate on the bottom of the vessel.', 'The decreased amount of solid material lowered the rate of crystallisation in the first hour, leading to the concentration spike.', 'After the first hour, the stirring rate was increased to 750 rpm, and the solids were observed to become more evenly distributed in the vessel.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: Direct cooling crystallisation of the reaction mixture in acetic acid yielded only the undesired form‑I polymorph; form‑III (the pharmaceutically required form) could not be obtained without an additional step, causing extra processing and yield loss.
Solution_Description: A two‑step crystallisation strategy was adopted: (1) antisolvent crystallisation with water to isolate form‑I, followed by (2) dissolution of form‑I in an organic solvent and a controlled cooling crystallisation (seeding with form‑III) to convert to the target form‑III polymorph.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The cooling crystallisation of CBZ in acetic acid resulted in form I with and without seeding form III.', 'Therefore, two crystallisation steps were designed in this study to obtain the desired polymorph form III of CBZ from the crude reaction mixture.', 'In the first crystallisation step, the CBZ form I polymorph was isolated from the reaction product with an antisolvent crystallisation via the addition of water.', 'Second, the form I product was redissolved in an organic solvent for a cooling crystallisation to CBZ polymorph form III.', 'The seed loading, cooling rate and starting concentration were varied to achieve different supersaturation profiles.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: The mixed‑suspension‑mixed‑product‑removal (MSMPR‑1) crystalliser volume (1 L) limited the achievable crystallisation residence time, reducing overall product yield.
Solution_Description: The residence time in MSMPR‑1 was deliberately extended (e.g., up to 25.9 min in COBR‑2 and 21.2 min in COBR‑3) to allow more complete crystallisation and improve adjusted yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ['MSMPR‑1 volume was primarily the limiting factor for reaction throughput at the laboratory scale production.', 'An extended residence time for crystallisation would be beneficial in a further scale‑up effort.', 'In COBR‑3, further effort was made to increase the yield by extending the crystallisation residence time.', 'The crystallisation residence time (min) for each COBR trial is shown in Table 5.']

Paper Title: Impurity Profiling for a Scalable Continuous Synthesis and Crystallization of Carbamazepine Drug Substance
Problem_Description: Impurity‑2 was not completely removed during the antisolvent crystallisation, especially under more aggressive conditions, leading to detectable impurity in the final solid.
Solution_Description: The DOE optimisation of water equivalents and temperature was used to locate conditions (e.g., higher water equivalents) where impurity‑2 could be fully purged, while still maintaining acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Preliminary data also suggested that trace amounts of ISB and impurity‑2 would be less problematic during the crystallisation stages.', 'Specifically, many antisolvent crystallisation conditions could purge impurity‑2 entirely.', 'In Table 2 the experimental results include the isolated yield, aldehyde impurity LCAP and filtrate concentration; impurity‑2 was not reported because it was fully removed under those conditions.']

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route gave a very low overall yield (7.2 %) because the O‑alkylation of intermediate 3 to give 8 proceeded in only 35 % yield, and the sequence required a benzyl protecting group that added extra steps, used expensive Pd/C for deprotection and introduced safety hazards on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new five‑step route was devised that starts from commercially available chrysin 4 (98 % purity) and eliminates the benzyl‑protect‑deprotect sequence.  By removing the protecting group the number of steps and the need for costly Pd/C hydrogenation were avoided, raising the overall yield to 29.1 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "conversion of 3 to 8 in the O‑alkylation step was poor, with a yield of only 35 %" (Introduction). 
• "the incorporation and subsequent removal of the benzyl protecting group contributed negatively to the process mass intensity, resulting in poor atom economy and low synthetic efficiency; the use of hydrogenation and the expensive Pd/C catalyst for the deprotection… increased the economic cost and introduced potential safety risks" (Introduction). 
• "Industrial‑scale production of 4 has been well developed… redundant protection and de‑protection steps were eliminated to streamline the overall process" (Improved Route description). 
• "Overall, the improved route… gave an overall yield of 29.1 %" (Abstract).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: Initial attempts at the direct O‑alkylation of intermediate 5 with 1,4‑dibromobutane gave only 36 % conversion and produced a large amount of the dibromo‑substituted by‑product 10 because both bromides reacted equally.
Solution_Description: The reaction was optimized by increasing the amount of 1,4‑dibromobutane to 7 equiv, raising the temperature to 80 ± 5 °C, and using potassium carbonate (2 equiv) as a mild base in DMF.  These changes raised the desired product conversion to 80.1 % (area %) and suppressed by‑product 10.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "initial attempt resulted in a poor desired conversion of only 36.1 area %" (O‑alkylation section). 
• "higher amounts of 1,4‑dibromobutane led to an increased formation of the desired product 9… The use of 7 equiv of 1,4‑dibromobutane at 60 ± 5 °C provided … a conversion of 80.1 area % to the desired product 9" (Table 1, entry 4). 
• "Increasing the temperature from 60 ± 5 to 80 ± 5 °C had a beneficial effect on the conversion … while simultaneously suppressing the formation of by‑product 10" (O‑alkylation discussion). 
• "potassium carbonate (2 equiv) … in DMF under 80 ± 5 °C" (Optimal conditions).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: When a strong base (KOH) was used for the O‑alkylation, DMF decomposed, generating many unknown side‑products and posing safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Potassium carbonate, a weaker base, was employed instead of KOH.  This eliminated DMF decomposition while still providing adequate deprotonation for the O‑alkylation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "replacement of potassium carbonate with a strong base potassium hydroxide led to more side reactions and the generation of many unknown side products… this observation corroborated the known decomposition of N,N‑dimethylformamide in the presence of strong bases" (O‑alkylation section). 
• "Conversely, when potassium carbonate was replaced with the weaker base potassium bicarbonate, the reaction conversion was incomplete…" (Table 1, entry 9). 
• "optimal reaction conditions … potassium carbonate (2 equiv) in DMF" (final O‑alkylation conditions).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: Compound 5 had poor solubility in neutral/weakly acidic water, making its isolation difficult, while by‑product 14 showed very different solubility from product 12, complicating purification after methylation.
Solution_Description: A salting‑out precipitation with NaCl was used to isolate 5 from water after heating, and a 1:1 MeOH/DMF mixture (8 vol) was employed to selectively dissolve 12 while leaving impurity 14 insoluble, allowing simple filtration to remove 14.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Considering the poor solubility of 4 in neutral and weakly acidic aqueous solutions… we devised a recrystallization strategy for compound 5 in water… the hot aqueous solution… efficiently removed 4…" (Elbs oxidation purification). 
• "We found that 12 could be effectively solubilized in 8 volumes of an equivolume mixture of methanol and DMF, while 14 remained largely insoluble… By employing a simple filtration step… the content of by‑product 14 was reduced to less than 3 area %" (Purification of 12).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: Tetramethylammonium hydroxide, used as the base in the Elbs oxidation, is classified with a fatal H‑phrase and requires strict protective measures.
Solution_Description: The addition of potassium persulfate was performed in 12 equal portions every 20 min while maintaining the temperature at 15–20 °C, and the cooling system was refreshed with ice‑water before each addition to keep the reaction within a safe temperature window.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Tetramethylammonium hydroxide is classified with a fatal H‑phrase; it is crucial for operators to take strict protective measures…" (Safety assessment). 
• "the addition rate of potassium persulfate should be strictly controlled for safety concerns… potassium persulfate (2 equiv) was added every 20 min in 12 equal portions while cooling, and reaction temperature was well maintained at 15–20 °C" (Elbs oxidation). 
• "the reactor jacket was refreshed with a new batch of ice water (0–5 °C) prior to each addition of potassium persulfate. The reaction temperature was maintained at 15–20 °C" (Scale‑up cooling optimization).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the Elbs oxidation, the cooling system sometimes over‑cooled the reaction mixture, dropping the temperature below the set point and affecting conversion.
Solution_Description: The cooling jacket was refreshed with fresh ice‑water before each persulfate addition, and the addition was paced in 12 equal portions to keep the temperature stable at 15–20 °C throughout the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "...the reaction mixture was cooled below the set reaction temperature when the cooling process was applied" (Scale‑up Results). 
• "we optimized the cooling procedure that the reactor jacket was refreshed with a new batch of ice water (0–5 °C) prior to each addition of potassium persulfate. The reaction temperature was maintained at 15–20 °C" (Scale‑up solution).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: On multikilogram scale, filtration after the O‑alkylation was extremely slow because the inorganic salts formed a fine particulate slurry that could not be efficiently centrifuged.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Instead of centrifugation, the mixture was allowed to settle; the clear supernatant was pumped to a second reactor, and the precipitate was rinsed with DMF.  This settling‑pumping strategy eliminated the bottleneck.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "the filtration rate was exceptionally slow, and the fine particulate nature of the inorganic salts made centrifugation an unsuitable option" (Scale‑up Results). 
• "we proposed allowing the reaction mixture to undergo thorough settling, followed by pumping the supernatant into a separate reactor vessel… the precipitate… was rinsed with DMF" (Scale‑up solution).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: In the large‑scale methylation step, the reaction mixture became increasingly viscous, causing the reaction rate to drop and extending the reaction time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An extra 0.1 equiv of dimethyl sulfate was added and the paddle speed was increased, which restored the conversion of 12 to 8 and kept the reaction time comparable to laboratory scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • "reaction rates experienced a significant slowdown over time due to increasing viscosity… extra Me₂SO₄ (0.1 equiv) was added, and the mixing speed of the paddle was increased, which helped promote conversion of 12 to 8" (Scale‑up Results).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: During the N‑alkylation, strong bases such as NaOH caused a Wessely–Moser rearrangement of product 2 to by‑product 17 and also generated quaternary ammonium salt 18.
Solution_Description: Pyrrolidine was used in 2.2 equiv as both the alkylating reagent and a mild base, and the solvent was switched from DMF to acetonitrile.  These changes suppressed formation of 17 (to 3.4 area %) and 18 (to 4.2 area %).
Supporting_Evidence:
• "compound 2 was susceptible to undergoing a Wessely–Moser rearrangement… and the formation of quaternary ammonium salt 18…" (N‑alkylation section). 
• "we envisioned that employing 2.2 equiv of pyrrolidine would be conducive to suppressing by‑product formation…" (N‑alkylation optimization). 
• "formation of 17 and 18 reached the minimal level in acetonitrile… 3.4 and 4.2 area % respectively" (Table 4, entry 5).

Paper Title: Practical, Facile, and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of the Flavonoid Derivative GL-V9
Problem_Description: Dimethyl sulfate (Me₂SO₄) was selected as the methylation agent despite its higher toxicity because it is cheaper and more stable than methyl iodide on an industrial scale.
Solution_Description: Me₂SO₄ was adopted as the preferred methylating reagent for the large‑scale methylation, and appropriate safety controls were implemented to mitigate its toxicity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Me₂SO₄ is a commonly used methylation agent in industrial‑scale production due to its superior chemical stability and convenience for storage compared to CH₃I, as well as its lower production cost… this decision was made with the understanding that appropriate safety measures… would be implemented" (Methylation section).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: The original discovery route gave a very low overall isolated yield (3–6 % over eight steps, 7–14 % on kilogram scale) and required many steps, making the process inefficient for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A redesigned four‑step process avoided the low‑yielding steps, introduced oxidative cleavage of the C‑17 side‑chain as the first transformation, followed by selective hydrogenation and stereoselective reductions, thereby increasing the overall isolated yield to 21–28 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The initial discovery route … achieved a 3–6 % yield over eight steps” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: Luche reduction of intermediate 17 gave the undesired C3 epimer, necessitating a Mitsunobu inversion step that gave highly variable yields (66–91 %).
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to eliminate the Luche reduction entirely; oxidative cleavage of the C‑17 side‑chain was performed first, followed by hydrogenation and a direct stereoselective reduction, removing the need for epimer inversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Luche reduction of 17 … provided the undesired epimer at C3” (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: During the hydrogenation/hydrolysis of enol ether 14 to 15 the C‑17‑hydroxyl group was highly acid‑sensitive, leading to significant elimination (Δ¹⁶‑¹⁷) by‑product.
Solution_Description: The weaker acid pyridinium p‑toluenesulfonate (PPTS) was employed as a promoter, which minimized elimination of the C‑17‑OH; EtOH was retained as solvent to maintain adequate solubility while avoiding harsh conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the C17‑hydroxy moiety was highly acid‑sensitive … eliminated by‑product … detected” (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: When K₃PO₄ was used on larger scale the reaction mixture became heterogeneous; material stuck to the reactor and agitator, leading to poor conversion and reproducibility.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to sodium methoxide (2.5 equiv) in 1,4‑dioxane gave a homogeneous solution, eliminated sticking, and provided consistent >95 % conversion; overhead stirrers and appropriate agitation were employed to ensure proper mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: • “homogeneity of the reaction was an issue when using K₃PO₄ … material sticking to the reactor and agitator” (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: The original work‑up relied on silica‑gel column chromatography, which is impractical and costly at kilogram scale and gave low mass recovery.
Solution_Description: Alternative purification methods were developed: filtration through activated carbon (100 wt % or with silica), and adsorption onto silica (100–200 wt %) followed by filtration, which provided ≥93 % purity with substantially higher mass recovery (up to 81 % on 100 g scale).
Supporting_Evidence: • “In an effort to avoid column chromatography, other methods of purification were explored … filtration through activated carbon … gave the best‑isolated yields” (Table 3 B).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch variability of the reductant (Na‑/K‑selectride) caused fluctuations in diastereoselectivity of the final C3‑α‑OH reduction (dr ranged from 5:1 to >20:1).
Solution_Description: Each new batch of reductant is now screened on milligram scale before scale‑up; the stoichiometry was adjusted (1.1 equiv of K‑selectride) and alternative suppliers were evaluated to maintain consistent dr ≥20:1.
Supporting_Evidence: • “batch variability of the reductant was a key factor affecting diastereoselectivity” (Section 2.5).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: Using Pt, Pd, or Rh catalysts on enone 25 led to over‑reduction to ethyl ether 29, lowering product yield and purity; this side‑reaction was temperature‑dependent.
Solution_Description: Cooling the hydrogenation to 0 °C suppressed formation of over‑reduced product; Rh/C (30 wt %) was identified as the optimal catalyst giving >95 % conversion and >20:1 dr for the desired product 24.
Supporting_Evidence: • “over‑reduced ethyl ether 29 now observed … cooling the reaction to 0 °C minimized the production of this unwanted product” (Section 2.4).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 11β-Hydroxyandrosterone
Problem_Description: At larger scales (≥50 g) the reduction of 27 to 24 showed slower conversion, requiring longer reaction times and resulting in lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Reaction times were increased (up to 40 h) and temperature raised to 30 °C for larger batches, restoring full conversion and maintaining >74 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “rate of conversion dropped at larger scales … longer reaction times and warming the reaction to 30 °C enabled the complete conversion … 74 % yield” (Table 7).

Paper Title: Chemoselective Saponification in the Synthesis of Danuglipron Facilitated with Trifluoroethanol
Problem_Description: The original saponification of the methyl ester (compound 2) with TBD/MEK‑water gave poor chemoselectivity; up to 14 % amide (compound 3) and up to 2.4 % di‑acid were formed, forcing the reaction to be stopped at ~80 % conversion to keep impurities <3 %, which greatly reduced overall yield (≈52.7 %).
Solution_Description: A new transamidation route was introduced: the methyl ester was first converted to a trifluoroethyl ester using 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol (TFE) and then hydrolysed with K₃PO₄/H₂O. This solvent change and altered stoichiometry gave a much cleaner profile (≤3 % amide, ≤2 % residual ester) and higher isolated yield (70–75 %).
Supporting_Evidence: 【1】"The saponification of methyl ester 2 resulted in modest chemoselectivity due to the competing nitrile hydrolysis. In lab pilots, 5–14 % of the amide byproduct (3) was observed, along with 0.20–2.4 % of a diacid species…"【2】"All reactions showed that amide byproduct 3 started growing… The reaction needed to be stopped at ∼80 % conversion. Obviously, this would greatly lower the yield…"【3】"We were attracted by a transamidation method facilitated with 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol (TFE)… The reaction gave a superior profile than the previous condition (TBD/MEK‑H₂O)."【4】"A quick base screen… K₃PO₄ outperformed…"【5】"With the improved reaction profile… 70–75 % yields and >98.5 % purity were obtained."

Paper Title: Chemoselective Saponification in the Synthesis of Danuglipron Facilitated with Trifluoroethanol
Problem_Description: Free‑base danuglipron has very poor solubility in the reaction feed, making silica‑gel chromatography inefficient. The process required ~100 vol of eluent, an isopropylamine co‑eluent, multiple solvent exchanges (MEK → EtOAc → MEK → EtOH/H₂O), and isolation of an isopropylamine salt, leading to a high process mass intensity (PMI = 455).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A new work‑up was developed: after reaction, water and toluene were added; the unreacted ester partitioned into toluene and was removed, while the product stayed in the basic aqueous TFE phase. After pH adjustment to 5 with citric acid, the product was extracted and directly isolated as the tris‑amine salt after a simple DMSO exchange, eliminating chromatography entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: 【1】"Due to the poor solubility of free base danuglipron in the feed solution, the column chromatography was highly inefficient and required the use of ∼100 vol of the eluent…"【2】"Isopropylamine was used as a coeluent, which necessitated the isolation of the isopropylamine salt (1‑CC) as an intermediate…"【3】"Water and toluene were added to the reaction mixture, and the unreacted starting material (2) was rejected in the toluene phase; whereas, the product was retained in the basic, aqueous TFE phase."【4】"After pH adjustment with aqueous citric acid to pH 5 and extractive workup, the product was isolated from DMSO/water as the desired trisamine salt (1) directly."

Paper Title: Chemoselective Saponification in the Synthesis of Danuglipron Facilitated with Trifluoroethanol
Problem_Description: The original method showed a narrow reaction window: higher temperature, excess water, or excess base accelerated both desired ester hydrolysis and undesired amide formation, requiring careful timing to meet impurity specifications. This limited scalability and robustness.
Solution_Description: A full‑factorial DOE was performed to map the effect of water and base equivalents in TFE, identifying conditions (e.g., 3 equiv H₂O, 2.5 equiv K₃PO₄, 8 mL g⁻¹ TFE) that gave a 10–12 h reaction window satisfying both conversion and impurity limits. The optimized protocol was successfully scaled in a 100 mL Flexycube reactor, demonstrating consistent performance at larger scale.
Supporting_Evidence: 【1】"Thus, a design of experiments (DOE) was carried out with a two‑level full factorial design…"【2】"From the DOE data, the reaction met targets on conversion and purity (<5 % residual ester and <2.5 % amide) within the investigated range…"【3】"The condition … struck a good balance between the reaction window and cycle time, which was scaled up on the basis of 10 g of input into a 100 mL Flexycube reactor… provides about 10–12 h when both metrics are met."

Paper Title: Synthesis and Impurity Profiling of a Vital Intermediate in Gabapentin and Bispidine Derivative Pathways by Response Surface Methodology
Problem_Description: Low solubility of dinitrile 7 in water at low sulfuric‑acid concentrations caused poor conversion to the target spiro‑product 8, giving a low reaction yield.
Solution_Description: Increasing the H₂SO₄ concentration to the 50–70 % (v/v) range (optimally ~65 %) raised the acidity of the medium, improving the solubility of 7 and consequently the yield of 8.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Since 7 is insoluble in water, the acid percentage directly affects its solubility.”
• “As a result, the solubility was enhanced with an increase in the acid percentage.”
• “The reaction yield was low at 40 % acid concentration, which could be related to the weak initial solubility of compound 7…"

Paper Title: Synthesis and Impurity Profiling of a Vital Intermediate in Gabapentin and Bispidine Derivative Pathways by Response Surface Methodology
Problem_Description: At high acid concentrations (80 %) and high temperatures (≥120 °C) the reaction generated significant amounts of impurity 13 (2,4‑dioxo‑3‑azaspiro[5.5]‑undecane‑1‑carboxamide) and impurity 14 (1,1‑cyclohexanediacetic acid), lowering the isolated yield and raising safety concerns (impurity 14 is a respiratory irritant).
Solution_Description: Optimising the process to 65 % H₂SO₄, 102 °C and a 22 h reaction time minimized the formation of 13 and 14, delivering a high‑purity product with an 89 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A high acid concentration (80 %) produced 13 as an impurity in addition to 8.”
• “At 120 °C, a mixture of compounds 8, 13, and 14 (CDA) … was obtained.”
• “Impurity 14 has also been reported to cause respiratory irritation.”
• “The optimum temperature range was determined to be between 90 and 110 °C … 65 % acid concentration … produced the best conversion results.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Impurity Profiling of a Vital Intermediate in Gabapentin and Bispidine Derivative Pathways by Response Surface Methodology
Problem_Description: Literature procedures using 60 % H₂SO₄ at 120–140 °C for 10–15 min gave only ~40 % isolated yield of 8 and required concentrated acid, making the process uneconomical, unsafe and unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A Box–Behnken response‑surface design was employed to identify optimal conditions (≈65 % H₂SO₄, 102 °C, 22 h) that lifted the yield to ~89 % while using a less aggressive acid concentration and longer, controlled reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Schön et al. described that… to produce 8 in only 40 % yield… 60 % sulfuric acid at 120–140 °C for 10–15 min.”
• “the earlier processes were environmentally unfriendly and unviable for the commercial production of the target molecule 8.”
• “The optimal reaction conditions of 65.5 % sulfuric acid concentration, 22 h time, and 102 °C temperature were obtained… experimental yield 89.25 ± 1.31 %.”
• “Box–Behnken design (BBD)… was conducted to explore the most suitable operating conditions.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Impurity Profiling of a Vital Intermediate in Gabapentin and Bispidine Derivative Pathways by Response Surface Methodology
Problem_Description: The reproducibility of the optimized laboratory protocol needed verification before scale‑up, as variability in yield or impurity levels could impede reliable manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A 20 g batch was performed using the same optimized conditions; the reaction delivered 88.4 % yield with purity comparable to the 1 g laboratory run, confirming consistent performance at a larger scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “An experiment was carried out on a 20 g scale to evaluate the scalability of the optimum reaction condition.”
• “NMR analysis confirmed the formation of compound 8 with a yield of 88.4 %.”
• “The purity profile in the 20 g scale was almost the same as the 1 g scale.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: Cs₂CO₃ is dense and difficult to agitate on scale, leading to settling of the solid and loss of product; the reaction mixture is a viscous oil that cannot be directly isolated, and chromatography was required for purification in the original lab‑scale route.
Solution_Description: The addition mode was changed – MeCN was charged first, the reactor cooled below the flash point of MeCN, and solid Cs₂CO₃ was added portion‑wise with constant agitation to keep it suspended; the work‑up was simplified to a filter‑and‑telescope step, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Cs₂CO₃ can be difficult to agitate on scale because of its density…the product was an oil, and direct isolation was not possible…To circumvent potential agitation issues associated with the use of Cs₂CO₃ on scale, the mode of addition was changed…solid Cs₂CO₃ (4 equiv) was charged portion‑wise to the reactor with constant agitation…the process to be scaled would simply involve filtering the mixture…and telescoping the filtrate directly to step 2.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: m‑CPBA is hazardous, costly, and difficult to ship on large scale; the original DCM solvent is undesirable, and the epoxidation in MeCN/H₂O led to oiling‑out of the product.
Solution_Description: Switched to peracetic acid (an inexpensive oxidant) and performed the epoxidation in MeCN only (no water) to avoid oiling out; adjusted base and oxidant equivalents to improve conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “mCPBA was used … Use of mCPBA on scale was not desirable…The initial focus … was on peracetic acid‑mediated epoxidation…peracetic acid is an inexpensive oxidant…Use of a MeCN/H₂O solvent mixture to maintain solubility … led to oiling out of the product, which did not occur when MeCN was the sole reaction solvent…The best reaction conditions employing peracetic acid (1.2 equiv) with Na₂CO₃ (1.2 equiv) in MeCN (10 vol) provided a ratio of 81:19 2:13.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: The epoxide product contained water which promoted formation of the undesired cyclic ether (15) during HCl‑catalyzed ring‑opening, and high water content gave low selectivity.
Solution_Description: The epoxide was dried by toluene azeotroping before HCl addition; HCl was generated in situ from AcCl/IPA and used in MeCN as solvent, with reduced equivalents of HCl to suppress cyclization; the reaction was performed in dry MeCN to avoid water‑mediated side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Drying the epoxide via toluene azeotroping prior to reaction with HCl led to a reduction in 15 formation…the use of polar protic solvents mediated the undesired cyclization…A more concentrated (10 M) stock solution of HCl was generated in situ from AcCl with IPA and then diluted to 1 M with MeCN. An improved ratio of 90:10 3:15 was obtained…Reducing the quantity of HCl to 0.5 equiv further favored the desired product.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: During mesylation/halogenation (step 4a) a quaternary ammonium salt (22) formed when Et₃N was added before MsCl, leading to a 20 % impurity; also the reaction mixture was viscous and difficult to work up.
Solution_Description: Reversed the order of addition (MsCl added before Et₃N) and increased MsCl/E₃N equivalents (up to 2.5 equiv MsCl and 2.45 equiv Et₃N) which eliminated the ammonium salt; MeCN was used as the solvent for both mesylation and bromination to improve handling.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of the reverse order of addition, the use of excess MsCl (1.8 equiv) with Et₃N (1.75 equiv) was found to eliminate the formation of 22…A reduction in the quantity of 22 from 20 to 8 %…Use of 2.5 equiv of MsCl and 2.45 equiv of Et₃N mediated the complete consumption of 3, and critically no ammonium salt 22 was generated.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: Intermediate aldehyde 18 decomposes at low temperature (onset 53 °C), making solvent swap by distillation from MeCN to t‑BuOH unsafe; also poor solubility of Na₂CO₃ in MeCN caused precipitation.
Solution_Description: Introduced DMSO as HOCl scavenger and reduced NaClO₂ equivalents; used a mixed MeCN/t‑BuOH solvent system (6 vol MeCN : 2 vol t‑BuOH) to keep the mixture homogeneous and avoid high‑temperature distillation; overall solvent volumes were lowered.
Supporting_Evidence: “DMSO was evaluated as an alternative scavenger…using DMSO (2 equiv) with NaClO₂ (1.5 equiv) in a mixture of t‑BuOH (10 vol), KH₂PO₄ (2 vol), and H₂O (1 vol) was found to mediate the complete conversion…Use of MeCN as the sole reaction solvent for step 6a led to oiling out…A mixed MeCN/t‑BuOH (6:2 vol) solvent system yielded a homogeneous mixture, and a 99 % conversion was achieved.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: After Pinnick oxidation (step 6a) ordinary salt formation and ion‑exchange resin treatments failed to isolate the product; residual non‑volatile impurities remained.
Solution_Description: A silica slurry in EtOAc/heptane (1:3) was employed to adsorb non‑volatile impurities, giving a 34 % impurity removal with 99 % product recovery; the mixture was later concentrated and handled with minimal solvent swaps.
Supporting_Evidence: “Silica (entry 4) yielded better purity uplift than alumina…The best balance between recovery and purity uplift was achieved in an EtOAc/heptane mixture with silica as the adsorbent…The treatment successfully adsorbed 34 % of non‑volatile impurities, with a 99 % recovery of 19.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: Allyl deprotection (step 7a) required expensive Pd(PPh₃)₄ and generated dimedone‑related impurities; palladium levels remained high (∼3266 ppm) after work‑up.
Solution_Description: Reduced Pd loading to 2–5 mol % and dimedone to 1.5 equiv; introduced a K₂CO₃ base wash (0.5–1 equiv) prior to deprotection, which proved essential for full conversion; performed a sequential charcoal filtration, NaHCO₃ wash, and basic ion‑exchange resin treatment to remove Pd and dimedone impurities, lowering Pd to <100 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction completion was achieved on reducing the equivalents of dimedone from 3.5 to 2.5…The basification of step 6a product was crucial…K₂CO₃ could be used at 1.0 equiv or 0.5 equiv…Catalyst loading of 3.5 mol % …also gave complete conversion…Charcoal filtration, NaHCO₃ wash, and resin treatment gave a 96 % yield of the available 7‑COOH CBD while removing 279 kg of non‑volatile impurities…Analysis by ICP‑MS indicated that 3266 ppm Pd remained after step 7a resin treatment, which reduced to 84.2 ppm Pd after salt formation and dissociation.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: Formation of the DCHA salt produced a high‑viscosity oil that could not be agitated; the salt precipitated only after IPA addition and required long standing times.
Solution_Description: Added IPA (1 vol) to the EtOAc solution of the DCHA salt to solubilize the viscous oil; after 16 h solid formed and could be filtered; subsequent MeOH slurrying and MeOH/H₂O slurries were used to improve purity and recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of IPA (1 vol) solubilized the oil, and solid formation was observed after 16 h…The DCHA salt was then slurried in MeOH, EtOH, and MeOH/H₂O mixtures…A higher proportion of MeOH gave better purity uplift with lower recovery.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: The final free‑acid 7‑COOH CBD contained residual EtOAc (∼5 %) after salt dissociation; removal of EtOAc required long drying times.
Solution_Description: Switched the final crystallization solvent from EtOAc to isopropyl acetate (iPrOAc), which left only 1.6 % residual solvent; MTBE was also evaluated as an alternative solvent for salt cracking, giving comparable purity with lower residual solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “iPrOAc was investigated…quantitative yield…HPLC purity of 95.0 %…QNMR assay for the 7‑COOH CBD obtained from iPrOAc was 97.8 % with only 1.6 % iPrOAc remaining…MTBE was also examined…off‑white solid obtained…HPLC purity 95.6 % with 2.1 % MTBE residual.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: On production scale, the addition of allyl bromide and CBD over 8–13 h was required to keep temperature 20‑25 °C, which prolonged the process but was necessary to control impurity (triallyl CBD).
Solution_Description: Extended the addition time for the allyl bromide/CBD solution, keeping the reaction temperature within the target range; the longer addition reduced the triallyl impurity from 16‑18 % (pilot) to 8‑10 % (production).
Supporting_Evidence: “The target addition temperature for allyl bromide was 20–25 °C and maintaining the mixture in this range led to extended addition times (8–13 h)…the level of triallyl CBD 9 in these batches (8–10 %) was lower than in the pilot plant campaign (16–18 %).”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of 7‑COOH CBD Synthesis, a Key Cannabinoid Metabolite
Problem_Description: Chromatography was required for the original 9‑step laboratory route, making scale‑up impractical.
Solution_Description: The protecting‑group strategy was revised to stay with the allyl group through to step 7a, reducing the synthesis from 9 to 7 steps; multiple steps were telescoped without isolation; purification was achieved by base washes, resin treatment, DCHA salt formation and MeOH slurry rather than chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “The route was shortened from 9 to 7 steps by altering the protecting group strategy…Chromatography was circumvented, and purification was achieved through base washes, resin treatment, dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) salt formation, and methanol slurry at the final step.”

Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Under the standard conditions the addition of aniline 1 to a slurry of TCDI in THF at –14 °C created a heterogeneous mixture for the first half of the addition; the reaction of 1 to form isothiocyanate 2 proceeded faster than the dosing rate, resulting in missing kinetic data and a difficult‑to‑fit model.
Solution_Description: The reaction was diluted ten‑fold (200 mL g‑1 THF) which gave a fully homogeneous mixture throughout the addition and slowed the reaction enough to capture all kinetic events.
Supporting_Evidence: “the standard conditions … the reaction is heterogeneous for the first half of the addition … reaction is faster than the rate of dosing … To alleviate both issues, the reaction was diluted 10‑fold. This modification leads to both homogeneous conditions throughout the entirety of the reaction as well as slowing the reaction sufficiently to observe all relevant kinetic phenomena.”

Paper Title: Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Impurity 5 (over‑reaction product) forms when a second equivalent of aniline 1 reacts with intermediate 2; impurity 5 has very low solubility under the isolation conditions, causing loss of material during work‑up and reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Four levers were identified and optimized: (1) lowering the reaction temperature (–14 °C → –20 °C); (2) increasing the TCDI stoichiometry by ≈4 %; (3) decreasing the total reactor volume (raising concentration); and (4) adding one equivalent of imidazole at the start, which catalyzes formation of 2 but has negligible effect on formation of 5, thereby suppressing impurity 5 formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the primary goal … was to reduce the level of formation of 5 … All four factors proposed to minimize 5 formation were experimentally validated: decreased temperature, increased stoichiometry of TCDI, increased reaction concentration, and addition of imidazole.”; “The addition of 1 equivalent of imidazole leads to an approximately 40 % predicted reduction in impurity 5.”

Paper Title: Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Calorimetry of the standard process showed that ≈70 % of the observed heat (≈10 kJ) is generated by the dosing of the aniline solution, creating a sizable exotherm that could lead to temperature spikes and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: In addition to cooling the reactor to –14 °C, the feed solution of aniline 1 was cooled (to the same temperature) to reduce the heat of dosing and keep the overall adiabatic temperature rise low.
Supporting_Evidence: “about 70 % of the heat of this process is due to dosing and only about 30 % … Thus, cooling the feed solution of 1 in addition to cooling the reaction will lead to reduced levels of impurity 5.”

Paper Title: Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Increasing the amount of imidazole in the reaction slurry caused an exponential increase in the solubility of both the desired product 4 and impurity 5; during the IPA‑wash isolation step this led to catastrophic loss of material when four equivalents of imidazole were present.
Solution_Description: The process was limited to adding only one equivalent of imidazole (instead of 4 eq.) and the isolation solvent system (THF → IPA) was retained, avoiding the solubility‑driven loss while still benefitting from the catalytic effect of a single equivalent of imidazole.
Supporting_Evidence: “the solubility of 4 (left) and impurity 5 (right) increase exponentially as a function of imidazole concentration… catastrophic yield loss in the presence of four additional equivalents of imidazole.”; “while four equivalents of imidazole proved to lead to catastrophic yield loss, the losses associated with one additional equivalent of imidazole are predicted to be minimal (6 % vs 5 % based on equilibrium solubilities).”

Paper Title: Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Product 4 is relatively stable under normal conditions but at elevated temperatures in the presence of two equivalents of imidazole it decomposes to impurity 5 (and to impurity 6), a pathway that is accelerated by increased solubility of the species.
Solution_Description: The reaction and work‑up temperatures were kept below the temperatures where imidazole‑catalyzed decomposition becomes significant (e.g., –14 °C to –20 °C), thereby suppressing the decomposition pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: “degradation of 4 into 5 is observed… only at elevated temperatures beyond the reaction or isolation temperatures in the presence of imidazole.”; “operating at lower temperature… reduces the formation of 5.”

Paper Title: Development of a Mechanism-Based Kinetic Model and Process Optimization Incorporating Imidazole Autocatalysis in a 1,1′-Thiocarbonyldiimidazole-Mediated Thiocarbonyl Transfer
Problem_Description: Initial kinetic data fitted poorly to a simple two‑step model, showing an un‑accounted induction period that masked the true reaction behavior.

Supporting_Evidence: “The poor fitting … led to a re‑evaluation … Once an autocatalytic step was added to the mechanistic model, a dramatically better fit to the experimental data was observed.”

Problem_Description: The original epoxidation of 1,5‑hexadiene with a stoichiometric amount of mCPBA in chloroform gave a large amount of undesired bis‑epoxide (≈ 20 %) and a low isolated yield of the desired mono‑epoxide (41 %).  Chloroform is a class‑2 solvent with a very low permitted daily exposure (0.6 mg day⁻¹) and strict concentration limits, making it unsafe for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from chloroform to dichloromethane (DCM) (higher PDE, 6 mg day⁻¹).  The reaction temperature was lowered to ≤ 3 °C (regular addition) to suppress over‑oxidation.  A DOE study identified the optimal solvent volume (5 V) and a 2.0 equiv excess of 1,5‑hexadiene, giving > 90 % mono‑epoxide and < 10 % bis‑epoxide.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the formation of a significant amount of undesired bis‑epoxide 7 (≈ 20 %)… (1) …the isolated yield of mono‑epoxide 1‑rac was only 41 %.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Process Development of (
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the epoxidation step, a large loss of product occurred during solvent purge and atmospheric distillation because the epoxide (bp ≈ 120 °C) and 1,5‑hexadiene (bp ≈ 60 °C) co‑distilled, resulting in a corrected isolated yield of only 42 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The distillation temperature was reduced and a gentle N₂ flow (0.1 N L min⁻¹) was applied throughout the purge, which dramatically increased the recovery yield (71 % isolated).
Supporting_Evidence: • “a drastic amount of product loss occurred during the solvent purge and distillation due to the low boiling point of the epoxide (∼120 °C) … To improve the recovery yield, we decreased the distillation temperature; meanwhile, N₂ flow was used throughout the distillation process. This operation increased the recovery yield dramatically.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Process Development of (
Problem_Description: The hydrolytic kinetic resolution (HKR) of racemic epoxide on 60 g scale proceeded much slower than on 8–20 g scale (160 h versus 16 h), giving only 49 % assay yield and a low overall isolated yield (33 %).  The long reaction time and poor conversion made the route unattractive for larger scale.
Solution_Description: Screening confirmed that the originally reported catalyst loading (0.5 mol %) was optimal; no further catalyst or stoichiometric changes improved the reaction, indicating that the HKR step remains a bottleneck for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the experiment with 0.5 mol % of catalyst loading was complete after 16 h, affording compound 1 in up to 99.6 % ee… however, the 60 g scale batch proceeded much slower… The reason for the slow reaction on the large scale is unknown…”.

Paper Title: Synthetic Process Development of (
Problem_Description: The literature method for the epichlorohydrin route (CuI‑catalyzed ring opening with allylMgCl) gave only ~60 % yield of intermediate 10 and required column chromatography; side‑products (1,5‑hexadiene, 1,8‑nonadien‑5‑ol, dichlorohydrin) were formed, especially when CuI was present.
Solution_Description: CuI was removed, the addition order was inverted (epichlorohydrin added to Grignard), and the equivalents of reagents were fine‑tuned (1.05 equiv epichlorohydrin 6, 1 equiv allylMgCl 9).  Running the reaction at 0 °C in THF (1 V) gave 81 % yield of 10 with only 1.1 % 1,5‑hexadiene and no detectable 11 or 12, eliminating the need for chromatographic purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • “With 2 mol % CuI … the bis‑epoxide impurity … the formation of 1,5‑hexadiene … up to 22 %…

Paper Title: Synthetic Process Development of (
Problem_Description: When the optimized CuI‑free protocol was scaled to 25 g, the impurity dichlorohydrin 12 increased to ≈ 9 %, indicating that the reaction pathway became more competitive at larger scale.
Solution_Description: The regular addition mode (adding Grignard to epichlorohydrin) with a stoichiometric 1:1 ratio, temperature 0 ± 5 °C and a low solvent volume (1 V THF) was reinstated; under these conditions the 25 g run gave 94 % in‑solution yield of 10 with only 2.5 % dichlorohydrin, restoring reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: • “As a result, the regular addition approach (adding the Grignard reagent to the epichlorohydrin) was revisited… with a stoichiometric reaction … affording the desired product 10 in 94 % in‑solution yield, … impurity 12 was only 2.5 %.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Process Development of (
Problem_Description: The ring‑closure of chlorohydrin 10 to epoxide 1 using solid NaOH pellets at 60 °C caused glass‑reactor etching and was not practical for large‑scale operations.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An aqueous 2 N NaOH solution (1.2 equiv) in MTBE was employed at 50 °C for 12 h (or 2 h at 50 °C with MTBE) with N₂ sparging, delivering > 98 % conversion and > 99 % ee while avoiding solid NaOH handling and glass etching.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Solid NaOH is not amenable to scale‑up… glass etching… NaOH (2 equiv, pellets)… not amenable… The aqueous solution of NaOH (2 N) … heated to 50 °C … gave an in‑solution yield of 77 % … the epoxide … 98.6 % A % and ee 99.9 %.”
