Paper Title: The First GMP Synthesis of MK-2118, a Small Molecule Agonist for Stimulator of Interferon Genes
Problem_Description: The acid‑chloride intermediate 7 showed very low solubility in THF, which made the copper‑mediated Negishi coupling difficult to scale. The poor solubility caused a heterogeneous reaction mixture, leading to an emulsion on work‑up and reduced isolated yield of product 9.
Solution_Description: The acid‑chloride synthesis was re‑optimized at 50 °C with N₂ sparging and thorough cake washing to remove residual HCl, giving a cleaner, more soluble solid. In the cross‑coupling, N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone (NMP) was added as a co‑solvent (8 vol NMP/THF) to generate a homogeneous reaction mixture, allowing direct isolation of crystalline product 9.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "The low solubility of 7 in THF made scale‑up of this step difficult, which led to portion‑wise addition of 7 over time to the reaction mixture. Additionally, the stoichiometric use of copper and the insolubility of the product created an inefficient phase separation, which resulted in an emulsion."; "Larger‑scale reactions of this step showed reduced yields, and thus, significant optimization was required before conducting a GMP delivery."; "The heterogeneity of the reaction was addressed by using 8 volumes of N‑methylpyrrolidone (NMP) as a cosolvent with THF (from the 0.5 M solution of 8). The new homogeneous conditions allowed us to develop direct isolation of 9." 
Solution: "The low‑quality batches of 7 were improved by performing the acid chloride formation at 50 °C with additional N₂ sparging to minimize the presence of hydrochloric acid upon isolation. As shown in Scheme 6, use of this protocol followed by filtration and cake washing with n‑heptane resulted in isolation of acid chloride 7 in 95 % yield as a white solid."; "The heterogeneity of the reaction was addressed by using 8 volumes of N‑methylpyrrolidone (NMP) as a cosolvent with THF… The new homogeneous conditions allowed us to develop direct isolation of 9."

Paper Title: The First GMP Synthesis of MK-2118, a Small Molecule Agonist for Stimulator of Interferon Genes
Problem_Description: Conversion to product 9 during the copper‑mediated coupling varied widely (30–94 %) when different batches of acid‑chloride 7 were used, leading to inconsistent process performance.
Solution_Description: The preparation of 7 was modified to include a higher reaction temperature (50 °C) and an N₂ sparge to better remove generated HCl, giving a consistently pure acid chloride. This reduced the batch‑to‑batch variability and restored reliable high conversion in the coupling step.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "During the initial optimization of the copper‑mediated coupling of 7, we observed a large variability in the conversion to 9 ranging from 30 to 94 % when different batches of 7 were used."; "We hypothesized that insufficient removal of excess hydrochloric acid generated during the reaction may have a deleterious effect on the coupling." 
Solution: "Acid chloride formation was subsequently performed at 50 °C with additional N₂ sparging to minimize the presence of hydrochloric acid upon isolation. As shown in Scheme 6, use of this protocol… resulted in isolation of acid chloride 7 in 95 % yield as a white solid."

Paper Title: The First GMP Synthesis of MK-2118, a Small Molecule Agonist for Stimulator of Interferon Genes
Problem_Description: The chiral organozinc reagent 8 decomposes over time, generating methoxide which reacts with the acid chloride to form side‑product 9a, reducing the purity and yield of the API.
Solution_Description: Fresh batches of 8 were used for each run, and the reaction was kept cold (≤10 °C) with rapid addition of reagents. The work‑up was modified by adding excess ammonium hydroxide and water at the end to precipitate the product, minimizing exposure of 8 to conditions that promote decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "Over the course of this investigation, we also isolated 9 with varying amounts of side product 10, which appeared to be higher when older batches of the organozinc reagent were used. Presumably 8 decomposes and generates methoxide, which, in turn, reacts with the acid chloride."; "While small amounts of this side product could be purged in isolation, fresh batches of 8 would be critical to maintaining API purity." 
Solution: "The addition of 4 equiv of ammonium hydroxide at the end of reaction followed by 40 equiv of water generated highly crystalline material in 76 % yield and 98 LCAP."; "The heterogeneity of the reaction was addressed by using 8 volumes of N‑methylpyrrolidone (NMP) as a cosolvent… The new homogeneous conditions allowed us to develop direct isolation of 9."

Paper Title: The First GMP Synthesis of MK-2118, a Small Molecule Agonist for Stimulator of Interferon Genes
Problem_Description: Direct isolation of product 9 after the coupling was hindered by phase separation problems and emulsion formation, making work‑up inefficient and lowering isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent system of NMP/THF was introduced to keep the reaction homogeneous, and ammonium hydroxide followed by water was added sequentially to precipitate the product directly from the reaction mixture, eliminating the need for extraction and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "The low solubility of 7 in THF made scale‑up of this step difficult, which led to portion‑wise addition of 7 over time to the reaction mixture. Additionally, the stoichiometric use of copper and the insolubility of the product created an inefficient phase separation, which resulted in an emulsion."; "Larger‑scale reactions of this step showed reduced yields…" 
Solution: "The heterogeneity of the reaction was addressed by using 8 volumes of N‑methylpyrrolidone (NMP) as a cosolvent with THF… The new homogeneous conditions allowed us to develop direct isolation of 9."; "We were pleased to find that the addition of 4 equiv of ammonium hydroxide at the end of reaction followed by 40 equiv of water generated highly crystalline material in 76 % yield and 98 LCAP."

Paper Title: The First GMP Synthesis of MK-2118, a Small Molecule Agonist for Stimulator of Interferon Genes
Problem_Description: When attempting to precipitate the API from the saponification mixture, a gummy solid formed containing multiple polymorphic forms and a hydrate, leading to inconsistent batch quality.
Solution_Description: The precipitation sequence was reversed: the reaction mixture was diluted and added to a pre‑cooled 2 M HCl/IPA solution, and seed crystals of the desired Form 2 were introduced to control nucleation. Later, a slurry in isopropyl acetate (IPAC) at 45 °C was used to convert any hydrate to Form 2, providing a reproducible, high‑purity product.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "Our initial attempts to precipitate the API directly involved addition of HCl to the THF/H₂O solution. This resulted in a gummy solid that was difficult to filter and consisted of several polymorphic forms, including a previously unidentified hydrate."; "The batch was filtered and washed… The final slurry was analyzed again for form and shown to be Form 2." 
Solution: "We therefore screened other inorganic bases and polar solvent mixtures… Ultimately, we found that removing the organic solvent from the saponification step, using higher dilution, and adding the end of the reaction mixture to a solution of 2 M HCl (reverse of previous process) and IPA was effective at producing API as a free‑flowing, off‑white solid in 85 % yield and >98 % purity."; "Small‑scale experiments showed that the hydrate could slowly convert to Form 2 by stirring over several days. Additionally, seeding the batch with authentic Form 2 prior to the pH adjustment alleviated this risk of hydrate formation, thereby reproducibly forming pure Form 2 in several batches."; "A 556 g amount of the batch was slurried in IPAC (10 volumes) at 45 °C overnight… Both solvents showed clean conversion to Form 2; however, IPAC was chosen to minimize the risk of a hydrate formation."

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: The original chiral‑pool synthesis of fragment 3 required cryogenic temperatures (‑78 °C) and large excesses of lithium bis‑trimethylsilyl‑amide (LiHMDS), both of which are expensive and pose handling hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: A non‑cryogenic, catalytic asymmetric approach was developed using copper‑Lewis‑acid, chiral Brønsted‑base, or bifunctional H‑bond‑donor catalysis to replace the LiHMDS‑mediated alkylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the requirement for cryogenic conditions and excess LiHMDS, both of which are expensive on such large scales” (introduction); “development of a non‑cryogenic and scalable route … is desirable” (introduction); “we disclose three catalytic asymmetric routes …” (abstract).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: When the unprotected NH‑Michael acceptor 6 was used, no product formation or starting‑material consumption was observed, giving a zero conversion.
Solution_Description: Switching to the more electrophilic N‑Boc‑protected Michael acceptor 7 restored reactivity, delivering up to 97 % SFC‑area percent of product.
Supporting_Evidence: “No product formation or starting material consumption was observed when NH Michael acceptor 6 was used … In contrast, the more electrophilic N‑Boc lactam 7 did undergo the desired reaction; 97 % SFC‑AP … was obtained” (copper catalysis section, Table 1).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: Background reaction of Michael acceptor 7 with DBU alone gave 10 % product, which would lower enantiomeric excess and diastereomeric ratio if not suppressed.
Solution_Description: A systematic screen of bases (e.g., DBU, DIPEA, MTDB, BTMG, inorganic bases) was performed and the optimal base amount (e.g., 0.5 equiv DIPEA) was identified to minimize background reactivity while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The observed reaction of 7 with DBU in the absence of copper suggested that screening of different bases would be necessary to avoid background reactivity which would result in reduced ee and DR.” (copper catalysis section); “Various bisphosphine ligands were screened … In addition, phorphoramidite, BOX, and PyBox ligands were all screened.” (copper ligand screen).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: The copper catalyst (Cu(MeCN)₄PF₆) and chiral ligand are costly, and high catalyst loadings (10 mol %) would be prohibitive for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: Reaction conditions (base, solvent, temperature, concentration) were re‑optimized, allowing catalyst loading to be reduced to 1 mol % while retaining high conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “In preparation for the reaction scale‑up, we aimed to develop conditions with a lower catalyst loading … Multiple of the conditions tested resulted in the formation of the product with conversions and stereoselectivity similar to that observed employing 10 mol % of catalyst.” (copper catalysis section); “Using (R_p)‑FesulPhos as the ligand with 1 mol % copper loading …” (copper scale‑up).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: The benzophenone imine moiety of the pronucleophile 5 and the product 9 hydrolyzed under standard LC‑MS conditions, complicating reaction monitoring.
Solution_Description: Supercritical fluid chromatography–mass spectrometry (SFC‑MS) was employed for analysis, which avoids hydrolysis and enables reliable quantification of conversion and stereoselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction mixtures were analyzed by supercritical fluid chromatography–mass spectrometry (SFC‑MS) as hydrolysis of the benzophenone imine … was observed under our standard liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC‑MS) methods.” (copper catalysis section).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of the Michael acceptor 7 revealed an exotherm (‑280 J g⁻¹) after melting, indicating a medium‑severity thermal event that could pose a safety risk on scale.
Solution_Description: Comprehensive process‑safety testing (DSC, thermal screening unit, BAM Falhammer impact tests) was performed, and the reaction was run in an EasyMax batch reactor with controlled temperature and inert atmosphere to stay within safe thermal limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC analysis of 7 showed an early endotherm … followed by an exotherm at −280 J g⁻¹ … This prompted further work to understand the reaction safety limits … Thermal screening unit … no significant thermal onsets observed up to 248 °C … Scale‑up reactions were performed … in an EasyMax reactor equipped with overhead stirring.” (safety section).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: After the copper‑catalyzed reaction, residual DIPEA formed salts that contaminated the target salt 10·(−)‑CSA, making isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: DIPEA was removed by passing the crude reaction mixture through a silica plug, followed by solvent exchange and direct precipitation of the product as the (−)‑CSA salt, yielding a pure solid.
Supporting_Evidence: “DIPEA carried through from the copper‑catalyzed reaction resulted in difficulties isolating pure 10·(−)‑CSA … removal of DIPEA was achieved by passing the reaction mixture through a silica plug … afforded the product as a free‑flowing solid.” (scale‑up section).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: Impurities in less‑pure batches of Michael acceptor 7 slowed the reaction rate and reduced diastereomeric ratio of product 9, likely by binding to copper and inhibiting catalysis.
Solution_Description: Using higher‑purity batches of 7 was recommended to improve reaction rate and selectivity; alternatively, reaction conditions (e.g., catalyst loading, temperature) were adjusted to mitigate impurity effects.
Supporting_Evidence: “The purity of the Michael acceptor 7 … impacted the reaction rate, with less pure batches reacting more slowly and resulting in lower product DR … We speculated that the lower rate may be due to impurities binding to copper.” (kinetics section).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: Methyl nitroacetate 14a showed a high‑severity exotherm at 161 °C (−2291 J g⁻¹) and potential shock sensitivity, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Thermal safety assessments (DSC, BAM Falhammer impact tests) confirmed low shock sensitivity; the reaction was performed at reduced catalyst loading (0.5 mol %), with controlled equivalents of nitroacetate and reflux conditions to manage the exotherm while maintaining acceptable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC showed an exotherm from 161 °C at −2291 J g⁻¹, indicating a high severity event … Six trials … showed no reaction overall, indicating that the compound is unlikely to be shock‑sensitive.” (nitroacetate section); “At a 25 g scale, we used 0.5 mol % … performing the reaction at reflux facilitated reaction progression … reduction in ee to 76 % was observed.” (scale‑up of nitroacetate).

Paper Title: Development of New Catalytic Asymmetric Routes toward a Cost-Driving Building Block of Nirmatrelvir
Problem_Description: Using low equivalents (1.1 equiv) of methyl nitroacetate 14a at scale led to incomplete conversion and higher amounts of unreacted Michael acceptor, while higher equivalents (2 equiv) improved conversion but reduced enantiomeric excess.
Solution_Description: Increasing the nitroacetate equivalents to 2 equiv and performing the reaction at reflux (higher temperature) accelerated conversion and minimized side‑product formation, balancing yield and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the DIPEA equivalents … further increased the conversion … The beneficial effect … plateaued at around 2.5 equiv.” (copper section); “At a 25 g scale, 2 equiv of methyl nitroacetate … progress was faster and the side product was observed in reduced quantities (<5 %).” (nitroacetate scale‑up).

Paper Title: Early-Stage Flow Process Development of a Key Intermediate toward PF-07265807, an AXL-MER Inhibitor Oncology Candidate
Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several issues while developing a continuous‑flow route for the key aza‑indazole intermediate: (1) aqueous hydrazine is a highly toxic and flammable reagent, posing a serious safety risk on batch scale; (2) the original batch SNAr/cyclisation step required ~48 h at 25 °C for full conversion; (3) certain solvent/base combinations (e.g., THF with potassium carbonate) gave heterogeneous mixtures because of poor solubility of reagents and intermediates; (4) using DMSO at high temperature with strong bases raised concerns about exothermic runaway and possible thermal decomposition; (5) conversion was inconsistent in batch due to off‑gassing of hydrazine and solid formation; (6) a gap between conversion and isolated yield was observed, largely because of side‑product isomer formation; (7) precipitation of lithium fluoride when sulfolane was used in the telescoped sequence caused blocking; (8) diglyme at 210 °C appeared to degrade material, indicating possible product decomposition at elevated temperature.
Solution_Description: To overcome these problems the team implemented a series of process‑intensification strategies: (1) they reduced the hydrazine feed to 5 wt % (≈7.8 wt % hydrazine) and ran it in a continuous plug‑flow reactor, dramatically lowering the inventory and exposure risk; (2) the batch sequence was transferred to a continuous‑flow platform (PFR) operating at elevated temperature, cutting residence time to 10–20 min and eliminating long batch times; (3) solvent screening identified DMSO, sulfolane, and finally acetonitrile as viable media, with acetonitrile combined with quaternary ammonium hydroxide bases giving homogeneous solutions; (4) temperature optimisation (80–130 °C for step 2, 180–210 °C for deprotection) provided the necessary kinetics while avoiding runaway or degradation; (5) a “top‑off” hydrazine stream (extra 0.5 equiv) was added in flow to rescue stalled conversions caused by off‑gassing; (6) the overall sequence was telescoped (no intermediate isolations) to reduce handling steps; (7) base optimisation replaced potassium carbonate with lithium tert‑butoxide or tetrabutylammonium/tetraethylammonium hydroxide, keeping all species soluble and preventing LiF precipitation; (8) minor condition tweaks (e.g., heating lines to keep streams above solubility limits) were introduced to maintain homogeneity throughout the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Safety: "hydrazine ... highly acutely toxic reagent with combustible vapors, which poses significant safety concerns for scale‑up in batch" (Introduction). 
Problem – Long reaction time: "batch process used concentrated aqueous hydrazine ... operated at ambient conditions (25 °C) with a reaction time of ∼48 h to full conversion" (Introduction). 
Problem – Solubility/Mixability: "THF led to a heterogeneous reaction mixture with both 40 and 80 wt % aqueous hydrazine" (Results 2.1). 
Problem – Exothermic: "potential for exothermic runaways using DMSO at extreme temperatures under strongly basic conditions" (Results 2.2). 
Problem – Variability: "reaction repeatedly does not give consistent conversions ... due to hydrazine off‑gassing" (Results 2.2). 
Problem – Low Yield: "gap in productivity between conversion and yield was attributed to the formation of the product isomer 10" (Results 2.1). 
Problem – Mixability/Precipitation: "solids were formed ... identified as LiF ... persisted throughout the reaction" (Results 2.2). 
Problem – Decomposition: "diglyme ... caused material degradation at 210 °C" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – Diluted hydrazine: "Additional studies were performed to reduce the concentration of aqueous hydrazine solution used as a feed in the continuous process to 5 wt % hydrazine" (Abstract). 
Solution – Flow platform: "We highlight efforts to translate an early‑stage batch route ... into a viable continuous flow process" (Abstract) and "flow reactions ... carried out using a VICI Milligat pump array ... on a Polar Bear Plus Flow reactor" (Experimental Section). 
Solution – Solvent change: "DMSO was a favorable solvent for solubility; however, ... THF ... sulfolane ... ACN ... were investigated" (Results 2.1). 
Solution – Temperature optimisation: "Reaction kinetics data in DMSO ... at 110 °C ... all of the intermediate 3 was consumed between 10 and 15 min" (Results 2.1). 
Solution – Order/Rate of addition: "the reaction stalled after 30 min, additional 0.4 equiv of HH added and ran for additional 10 min" (Table 6) and "top‑off stream could be added in flow" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – New route (telescope): "telescoping steps in flow ... by finding a solvent/base system that maintained the solubility of all species" (Abstract) and "step 2 and step 3 were telescoped" (Table 3). 
Solution – Catalyst/Base optimisation: "LiO tBu and TBD were tested ... LiO tBu provided the most favorable profile" (Results 2.2) and later "quaternary ammonium hydroxide bases" (Conclusions). 
Solution – Other condition change (heating lines): "keeping lines heated between each respective flow reactor" (Results 2.2).

Paper Title: Early-Stage Flow Process Development of a Key Intermediate toward PF-07265807, an AXL-MER Inhibitor Oncology Candidate
Problem_Description: Using THF as solvent with potassium carbonate gave a slurry, and later using sulfolane with LiO tBu caused precipitation of LiF upon cooling, leading to solids that could clog the flow reactor.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from THF to sulfolane and ultimately to acetonitrile, while the base was changed from potassium carbonate to lithium tert‑butoxide and then to quaternary ammonium hydroxides (TEAOH/TBAOH) that remain soluble. The reaction concentration was adjusted (e.g., 20 vol % DMSO, 20 vol % sulfolane) to keep all components in solution and avoid solids formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Solubility/Mixability: "THF led to a heterogeneous reaction mixture with both 40 and 80 wt % aqueous hydrazine" (Results 2.1). 
Problem – Precipitation: "solids were formed ... identified as LiF ... persisted ... 10 % water with sulfolane was poor, leading to a nearly 30 % drop in the yield of 3" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – Solvent change: "Tetrahydrofuran (THF) and sulfolane were investigated as possible alternative solvents, with sulfolane showing the most promise... DMSO was maintained for the initial flow proof of concept work" (Results 2.1). 
Solution – Base optimisation: "LiO tBu and TBD were tested ... LiO tBu provided the most favorable profile" (Results 2.2) and later "quaternary ammonium hydroxide bases" (Conclusions). 
Solution – Concentration tuning: "20 vol DMSO ... 20 vol sulfolane" and "10 % water with sulfolane" were evaluated to manage solubility (Results 2.2).

Paper Title: Early-Stage Flow Process Development of a Key Intermediate toward PF-07265807, an AXL-MER Inhibitor Oncology Candidate
Problem_Description: The batch SNAr/cyclisation step required 48 h at ambient temperature, and high‑temperature runs in DMSO with strong bases raised concerns about exothermic runaway and thermal instability.
Solution_Description: By moving the reaction to a continuous plug‑flow reactor the temperature could be raised (80–130 °C) to dramatically accelerate the reaction (10–20 min residence time). The flow setup also provides better heat removal, mitigating exothermic risk. Additionally, the process used controlled addition of reagents and back‑pressure regulation to manage heat and pressure safely.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Long reaction: "batch process ... operated at ambient conditions (25 °C) with a reaction time of ∼48 h to full conversion" (Introduction). 
Problem – Exothermic concerns: "potential for exothermic runaways using DMSO at extreme temperatures under strongly basic conditions" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – Reactor platform: "continuous flow process ... reducing reaction time through process intensification" (Abstract) and "flow reactions ... carried out using a VICI Milligat pump array on a Polar Bear Plus Flow reactor" (Experimental Section). 
Solution – Temperature optimisation: "Reaction kinetics data ... at 110 °C ... all of the intermediate 3 was consumed between 10 and 15 min" (Results 2.1). 
Solution – Order and rate of addition: "check valves ... pressure relief lines ... as a standard safety precaution in case of upset condition due to the possible solid formation or pump failure" (Results 2.1).

Paper Title: Early-Stage Flow Process Development of a Key Intermediate toward PF-07265807, an AXL-MER Inhibitor Oncology Candidate
Problem_Description: Handling concentrated aqueous hydrazine (>50 wt %) is hazardous and the batch process gave modest assay yields (~80 %) because of side‑product formation (isomer 10, over‑addition products).
Solution_Description: The hydrazine feed was diluted to 5 wt % (≈7.8 wt % hydrazine) to meet safety targets while still achieving acceptable conversion in flow. The solvent system (acetonitrile with quaternary ammonium hydroxide) and the telescoped flow sequence eliminated intermediate isolations, reducing exposure and improving overall assay yield (~70 % across three steps).
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Safety: "hydrazine ... highly acutely toxic reagent with combustible vapors" (Introduction). 
Problem – Low yield: "gap in productivity between conversion and yield was attributed to the formation of the product isomer 10" (Results 2.1). 
Solution – Diluted hydrazine: "reduce the concentration of aqueous hydrazine ... to 5 wt % hydrazine ... not amenable to a traditional batch process" (Abstract). 
Solution – Solvent change: "acetonitrile ... utilizing soluble quaternary ammonium hydroxide bases" (Conclusions). 
Solution – New route (telescope): "telescoping steps in flow ... by finding a solvent/base system that maintained the solubility of all species" (Abstract) and "fully telescoped three‑step continuous process" (Conclusions).

Solution_Description: A top‑off stream adding extra hydrazine equivalents in flow was introduced to overcome stalling, and the flow reactor’s sealed, pressurized environment eliminated headspace, preventing off‑gassing. Continuous heating of lines kept all streams homogeneous, reducing variability.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Variability: "reaction stalled after 30 min ... due to hydrazine off‑gassing" (Results 2.2). 
Problem – Mixability: "solids were formed ... LiF ... persisted" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – Order and rate of addition: "adding 0.5 equiv of aqueous hydrazine ... top‑off stream could be added in flow" (Results 2.2). 
Solution – Mass transfer & gas control: "flow ... minimizes the overall volume of aqueous hydrazine in a reactor at any given time and eliminates the accumulation of vapors in the headspace" (Introduction). 
Solution – Other condition change: "keeping lines heated between each respective flow reactor" (Results 2.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of the Pyrazinecarboxamide Component of Gilteritinib, a FLT3 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original discovery chemistry route suffered from several scale‑up obstacles: (1) cryogenic conditions were required to control impurity formation, limiting batch size; (2) step b gave highly variable yields (28–44 %); (3) column chromatography was needed for final purification, extending lead time; (4) the route employed heavy‑metal reagents (FeSO4·7H2O, Pd catalyst) that are undesirable for pharmaceutical manufacture; (5) attempts to form the pyrazine ring from malonic derivatives failed because an intermediate (17) decomposed and gave low overall yields; (6) basic hydrolysis conditions degraded one of the chlorides and H2O2 gave undesired N‑oxide, while acidic conditions initially gave low conversion; (7) the addition of POCl3 generated uncontrolled exotherms; (8) the cyclization step at 80 °C caused decomposition of aminopropanedinitrile 23 on large scale.

Solution_Description: The authors note that alternative solvents should be identified for future implementations to avoid reliance on a controlled, potentially scarce solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Availability of MTBK may be limited because it is a precursor for pinacolyl alcohol … MTBK is a controlled export in Australia Group member states.”; “Scientists are encouraged to identify alternative solvents to replace MTBK in their processes.”

Paper Title: Safety Guided Process Development and Scale-Up of the Highly Energetic Compound 4‑Methyl-1,2,5-oxadiazole-3-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: Compound 2 (the dioxime) has inconsistent shipping classifications; some vendors list it as non‑hazardous while others classify it as class 4.1 flammable solid/self‑reactive, and its estimated self‑accelerating decomposition temperature (SADT) is near the critical limit.
Solution_Description: A systematic safety assessment was performed using UN Recommendations and AKTS modeling to determine the appropriate transport classification and to verify that the material does not meet the criteria for a class 4.1 self‑reactive substance, though further explosive testing is recommended for commercialization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 2 is available commercially, and shipping options … most vendors claimed this material as ‘Non‑hazardous for transportation’ … few of the suppliers claimed this material as ‘class 4.1, flammable solids, self‑reactive substances, and solid desensitized explosives’.”; “Its SADT value was estimated to be 84 °C … indicating that this material was not a ‘class 4.1 …’ However, its high decomposition energy should warrant some additional tests for class 1 explosive …”

Paper Title: Safety Guided Process Development and Scale-Up of the Highly Energetic Compound 4‑Methyl-1,2,5-oxadiazole-3-carboxylic Acid
Problem_Description: The free acid 1 exhibits a low decomposition onset (160 °C) with a high exothermic energy release (−2384 J/g), making the isolated solid potentially explosive and unsafe to handle.
Solution_Description: Instead of isolating the free acid, it is converted to its N‑methyl‑morpholine salt (6), which reduces the decomposition energy to −913 J/g and raises the onset temperature to 189 °C, dramatically improving thermal safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “The product 1 was first extracted … but isolated in low yields … To avoid the potential explosion hazards associated with isolation of 1 as its solid form … isolation of the product as its NMM salt 6 … energy release significantly reduced to −913 J/g from the −2384 J/g of the free acid 1 …”; Figure 6 DSC profiles confirming the shift in onset temperature.

Paper Title: Streamlined Three-Step Telescope Enabled by a Nonaqueous Suzuki–Miyaura Cross-Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The aryl‑boronic‑acid stream generated after borylation is highly oxygen‑sensitive and undergoes rapid protodeborylation, leading to loss of material and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: A robust, non‑aqueous telescoped sequence was established by (i) premixing the Pd precatalyst/ligand, then adding the aryl chloride and base first, followed by MeOH and diboron to start the reaction (order‑of‑addition); (ii) replacing the aqueous K₃PO₄ quench with a NaOMe solution in MeOH (solvent/base change) that also decomposes excess diboron; (iii) using a less‑explosive diboron ester (B₂npg₂) instead of B₂(OH)₄ (new route/reagent change); (iv) switching to a more active Pd‑PCy₂tBu catalyst at lower loading (catalyst optimization); (v) performing the Suzuki step at 60 °C with a controlled N₂ sparge to suppress protodeborylation (temperature and gas‑environment control); (vi) adding N‑Me‑pyrrole as a THP scavenger to accelerate cyclization (scavenger change); and (vii) eliminating multiple aqueous washes and distillations, consolidating them into a single bulk filtration (other condition change).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem_Evidence_1: "The resulting aryl boronic acid stream was not stable to oxygen and was prone to protodeborylation of 4a; hence, it was necessary to keep this stream under strictly inert conditions." (sec 2)

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: The initial route to meso‑7 required column chromatography to separate trans‑7 and meso‑7 (30 % and 46 % yields respectively), which is not amenable to large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A fumaric‑acid salt of the crude mixture was crystallised from EtOAc (meso‑11, 55 % yield) and the salt was directly N‑Cbz protected, delivering meso‑7 as a single isomer in 91 % yield, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Separation of these isomers via column chromatography gave trans‑7 in 30 % and meso‑7 in 46 % yields… a scalable route without the need for column chromatography was desired.”
2. “fumaric acid was identified and employed to affect the isolation of meso fumarate salt 11 via crystallization from EtOAc in 55 % yield.”
3. “Utilizing this salt directly in the N‑Cbz protection gave meso‑7 as a single isomer in 91 % yield.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Conventional hydrogenation solvents required a strong acid for N‑Cbz deprotection, complicating the hydrogenation step and limiting scalability.
Solution_Description: The strongly hydrogen‑bond‑donating solvent 1,1,1,3,3,3‑hexafluoro‑2‑propanol (HFP) was employed, enabling smooth Pd/C‑catalysed hydrogenation of 6 to give 10 in 95 % yield without added acid.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “We were particularly interested in investigating how this strongly hydrogen bond‑donating solvent would affect the reaction progression in the absence of a strong acid.”
2. “hydrogenation of 6 using catalytic Pd/C in HFP progressed smoothly, generating 10 in 95 % yield.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Early biocatalytic desymmetrisation screens gave modest conversions (e.g., pig liver esterase 96 % conv., 27 % ee; C. rugosa 20 % conv., 78 % ee) and a commercial enzyme (Novocor AD‑L) showed only 21 % conversion, raising concerns about robustness and throughput.
Solution_Description: A systematic enzyme screen identified Novocor AD‑L as the most readily available catalyst; reaction conditions (substrate loading, temperature, enzyme loading) were subsequently optimized, raising conversion to >95 % at 30–50 mg mL⁻¹ substrate.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “pig liver esterase (96 % conv., 27 % ee) and Candida… provided low ee…”
2. “Novocor AD‑L… despite its modest initial screening conversion (21 %) was chosen as the enzyme for further optimization.”
3. “Running optimization studies at a high substrate loading… temperature increase to 40 °C… conversion was observed (84 %)… base addition… >95 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: During the biocatalytic reaction the pH dropped to 6.5, causing the conversion to stall at ~84 % and leading to residual starting material.
Solution_Description: Addition of 2 N NaOH to maintain the reaction pH at 7.5 restored conversion to >95 %, allowing higher substrate loading.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “At this point, the reaction stalled, and the pH was measured at 6.5.”
2. “Running subsequent reactions with a base addition (2 N NaOH) to maintain the pH of the reaction at 7.5 led to a higher conversion to the product (>95 %).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Pushing the biocatalytic conversion to complete consumption generated increasing amounts of the diacid by‑product 12, reducing overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was stopped at 95–98 % conversion (≈46 h) to limit formation of diacid 12, delivering product 8 in 81 % isolated yield and ≥99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Attempts to push the reaction to complete conversion resulted in the formation of more diacid 12.”
2. “Under the biocatalytic conditions described, 95–98 % conversion was achieved after 46 h, with 2–3 % unreacted starting material and less than 3 % diacid 12.”
3. “The new process was carried out on the 70 g scale… isolated in 81 % yield.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Initial photoredox fluorination conditions (NaHCO₃/Selectfluor in MeCN/H₂O) produced a heterogeneous slurry, complicating flow‑scale operation and leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The inorganic base NaHCO₃ was replaced with the organic base 2,6‑lutidine, which maintained a homogeneous reaction mixture while delivering comparable conversion (≈59 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “These conditions resulted in a heterogeneous slurry, which could make scaling in flow more challenging.”
2. “The organic base 2,6‑lutidine performed nearly as well (59 %), and the mixture remained homogeneous during that reaction; subsequently, this base was selected for further optimization efforts.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: During the first flow‑scale decarboxylative fluorination runs, product yields declined over time because Selectfluor was in direct contact with the reaction mixture, leading to degradation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A two‑reservoir configuration was implemented, keeping Selectfluor segregated from the catalyst and substrate until mixing immediately before illumination, which stabilized yields across the run.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “During the initial scale‑up and delivery of photoredox fluorination in flow, yields were observed to erode over time.”
2. “Switching to the two‑reservoir system… where Selectfluor was kept segregated… remedied this issue.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: The final fluorinated product mixture required chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) to isolate the desired trans‑isomer, a costly and low‑throughput purification step.
Solution_Description: Future work will replace SFC with selective enzymatic hydrolysis (e.g., using Pseudomonas stutzeri lipase) that preferentially removes the undesired cis‑isomer, enabling a chromatographically free purification.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Future work will involve optimization to avoid the use of chiral SFC for purification, which could potentially be achieved via selective enzymatic hydrolysis and separation of undesired cis‑diastereomer 14.”
2. “Initial data using Meito Sangyo Lipase TL… showed some cis‑selectivity toward hydrolysis of compound 14 over intermediate 9 and potential for purging the undesired cis‑diastereoisomer without the need for chromatography.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Work‑up of the biocatalytic desymmetrisation step suffered from emulsification, complicating phase separation at larger scales.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was re‑optimised to minimise solvent usage and improve phase clarity, reducing emulsification risk for future scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Workup of the biocatalytic desymmetrisation (step 4) was optimized to minimize solvent usage, but otherwise… however, further work to derisk emulsification is desirable before additional scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Enantiopure Fluoropiperidines via Biocatalytic Desymmetrization and Flow Photochemical Decarboxylative Fluorination
Problem_Description: Batch hydrogenation of the meso‑7 precursor gave modest diastereomeric excess (46 % de), limiting the amount of desired isomer for downstream steps.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow hydrogenation using 5.5 % Pd(OH)₂/Al₂O₃ catalyst increased diastereomeric purity to 65 % de and improved overall throughput, providing a more robust and scalable hydrogenation platform.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “flow hydrogenation process was identified with 5.5 % Pd(OH)₂/Al₂O₃ catalyst as optimal for generating 10 (65 % de) with an increase in diastereomeric purity, from previous batch processes (46 % de).”

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: The original acetal formation using perchloric acid produced a mixture of diastereomers (R‑2 and S‑14) that required reversed‑phase chromatography to purge the undesired S‑acetal and other impurities (aniline 15, t‑butyl ether 16). The reaction mixture was viscous and poorly soluble in the chosen solvents, and the crystallization attempts were hindered by liquid‑liquid phase separation (LLPS) during antisolvent addition.
Solution_Description: A 15:1 v/v CH₃CN/THF solvent system was introduced to improve dissolution, and the N‑Boc aniline charge was reduced from 1.14 → 0.98 equiv to lower the amount of residual aniline 15. A PTSA salt crystallization was developed (solvent: 10 w/w % H₂O in CH₃CN; seed loading 1 w/w %) that removed the S‑acetal 14 and other impurities, replacing the chromatographic step. The crystallization was performed with controlled addition of acid and seeding to avoid LLPS.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Triflic acid (TfOH) mediated acetal formation … afforded … an ∼88:12 thermodynamic equilibrium mixture with undesired (S)‑acetal 14" (sec 2.1). 
• "Reversed‑phase chromatography … was not a viable long‑term option due to projected material demands" (sec 2.1). 
• "Performing the transformation with a 15:1 v/v CH₃CN/THF solvent mixture allowed better dissolution" (sec 2.1). 
• "Reducing the N‑Boc aniline charge from 1.14 to 0.98 equiv resulted in a much more manageable amount of residual aniline 15" (sec 2.1). 
• "Crystallization … with PTSA … purged significant amounts of the diastereomer (11.8 → <0.5 area %)" (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: During dipeptide coupling, the use of EDAC·HCl gave ~10 % epimerization of the glutamate (impurity 18) and formed an over‑acylated adduct (19). The work‑up with NaOAc/AcOH generated an N‑acetylated impurity (20) that was difficult to remove in downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Increasing the HOPO (2‑pyridinol 1‑oxide) stoichiometry to 1.5 equiv suppressed epimerization. The dipeptide charge was optimized to 1.01 equiv to avoid over‑acylation. The quench solution was switched from NaOAc/AcOH to a citric‑acid/phosphate buffer (pH 4.9) to eliminate the formation of the N‑acetylated impurity 20.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "~10 % epimerization … observed (impurity 18)" (sec 2.2). 
• "Increasing the 2‑pyridinol 1‑oxide (HOPO) stoichiometry from 1.1 → 1.5 equiv remedied this issue" (sec 2.2). 
• "Overacylated adduct 19 … resulted from dipeptide 7 coupling with the α‑keto hydroxyl group" (sec 2.2). 
• "Switching the quench solution … to a citric‑acid/phosphate buffer (0.2 M, pH 4.9) effectively eliminated the formation of N‑acetylated 20" (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: Phosphate installation suffered from low solubility of alcohol 10 in CH₃CN (61 mg mL⁻¹) and water‑induced hydrolysis of the phosphoramidite. The oxidation step with H₂O₂ generated a significant exotherm (ATR ≈ 33 °C). Additionally, di‑t‑butyl phosphate 11 decomposed on silica, losing a t‑butyl group during normal‑phase chromatography.
Solution_Description: After azeotropic drying to ≤0.30 equiv H₂O, CH₂Cl₂ was added as a co‑solvent to improve dissolution of alcohol 10. The oxidation was performed at –5 °C with controlled H₂O₂ addition to keep the internal temperature below 5 °C. Silica was pret‑treated with Et₃N and later replaced by a YMC‑Pack Diol‑80‑FC stationary phase to avoid t‑butyl loss during chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Alcohol 10 has limited solubility in CH₃CN (61 mg mL⁻¹) … CH₂Cl₂ was introduced after azeotropic distillation as a cosolvent" (sec 2.3). 
• "An adiabatic temperature rise (ATR) of 33 °C was measured for the H₂O₂ oxidation … H₂O₂ was charged at a rate to maintain temperature below 5 °C" (ref 19, sec 2.3). 
• "Di‑t‑butyl phosphate 11 was not stable to silica … Silica pretreatment with Et₃N reduced the undesired pathway" (sec 2.3). 
• "A diol‑coated stationary phase (YMC‑Pack Diol‑80‑FC) was identified that avoided this issue" (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: Fmoc deprotection with piperidine generated a precipitate (9‑methylene‑fluorene‑piperidine adduct) and the by‑product 9‑methylene‑fluorene 22 required six batch extractions, leading to high solvent consumption and laborious operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Diethylamine was selected as the deprotecting base (volatile, no precipitate). A continuous extraction loop using n‑heptane (CH₃CN‑saturated) was implemented, achieving >99 % removal of 22 with <1 % product loss, reducing solvent use by 22 % compared with the batch process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Piperidine resulted in the formation of a precipitate … To avoid an additional filtration, diethylamine was selected" (sec 2.4). 
• "Clearance of 9‑methylene‑fluorene required six batch extractions … operationally inconvenient, labor‑intensive, and wasteful" (sec 2.4). 
• "Continuous extraction … removed >99 % of the by‑product with <1 % loss of the product" (sec 2.4). 
• "The continuous extraction used 67.5 vol CH₃CN‑saturated n‑heptane compared to 86.4 vol used in the batch process, reducing solvent use by 22 %" (sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: After bromoacetylation, residual amine 12, T3P, and 2,6‑lutidine remained in the reaction mixture and needed to be removed before the next step.
Solution_Description: Two aqueous washes were introduced: (1) an HBr solution to hydrolyze excess T3P and remove 2,6‑lutidine, and (2) a pH 7.2 phosphate buffer to eliminate unreacted bromoacetic acid and T3P propyl‑phosphate by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Two aqueous washes were consequently implemented: (1) a HBr aqueous solution quench hydrolyzed excess T3P …, (2) a phosphate buffer (pH 7.2) wash removed unreacted bromoacetic acid and related T3P propylphosphate byproducts" (sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: The original global deprotection with TFA/CH₂Cl₂ caused significant acetal epimerization and incomplete conversion. Scaling up led to inconsistent precipitation, agglomeration, and lower diastereomeric ratios.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An inverse (sub‑surface) addition of HBr in AcOH was employed to keep excess acid present throughout the addition, minimize intermediate entrapment, and control the exotherm. The reaction temperature was set to –5 °C, HBr equivalents were optimized to 8 equiv, and addition rates of 6–40 mL min⁻¹ were explored to improve conversion and diastereomeric ratio. Dynochem modeling ensured consistent micromixing at scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The deprotection was originally performed with TFA … significant acetal epimerization and incomplete conversion were observed" (sec 2.6). 
• "Reversing the reagent order ensured excess acid throughout the entire addition, quick conversion to product, and thus minimization of intermediate entrapment" (sec 2.6). 
• "Increasing HBr equivalents improved intermediate consumption … Low temperatures decreased epimerization but led to incomplete conversion" (Table 3). 
• "Faster addition rates improved conversion times and dr … mixing could impact the reaction profile" (Table 3). 
• "Dynochem modeling … ensured that multiphase mixing was similar independent of scale" (sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Development and Execution of a Scalable Route to an Immunology ADC Drug-Linker for ABBV-154
Problem_Description: Drug‑linker 1 has very low solubility, making preparative reversed‑phase chromatography difficult; polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMF) caused peak distortion. The bromoacetamide moiety is acid‑labile, restricting mobile‑phase pH (<5). During purification, impurity 30 (deacylated amine) formed, especially at higher temperatures.
Solution_Description: A mobile phase of 0.1 % TFA in water/CH₃CN (3:4 v/v) was chosen to balance low pH stability and acceptable peak shape. The crude solution was kept below 10 °C throughout chromatography to suppress formation of impurity 30. After purification, product was extracted into 2‑MeTHF/i‑PrOAc, and a reverse‑addition precipitation using THF as antisolvent was developed, giving a filtered solid with 73–75 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Screening of the mobile phase was limited to pH < 5 due to instability of the bromo‑acetamide moiety … 0.1 % TFA in H₂O providing an acceptable peak shape" (sec 2.6). 
• "Deacylated amine 30 … rate of formation positively correlated with temperature … controlled by holding the crude product solution at reduced temperature (<10 °C)" (sec 2.6). 
• "Product could alternatively be extracted … reverse‑addition precipitation process performed well on manufacturing scale and provided drug‑linker 1 in 73–75 % yield" (sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: The global deprotection step is highly mixing‑sensitive; as the reaction scale increases the intrinsic kinetics become comparable to the mixing rate, leading to poor reproducibility, low conversion and loss of diastereoselectivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The batch process was replaced by an impinging‑jet flow reaction that provides intensive, rapid mixing of the acid and starting‑material streams, preserving the high diastereoselectivity observed at small scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Mixing‑sensitivity in chemical reactions may occur when the intrinsic kinetics of the reactions are faster or of a similar time scale when compared to the rate at which solvents and/or reagents are blended together. If this sensitivity is not addressed properly, the scaled reaction will not reproduce the results from the lab experiment.", "To address this issue, the reaction was converted to an impinging jet flow process to provide more intensive mixing of the starting material with the acid than the standard fed batch process."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: Direct addition of HBr to a solution of the starting material (R‑2) caused solid precipitation, agglomeration and formation of intractable clumps, which blocked efficient mixing and could not be reliably scaled.
Solution_Description: The addition order was inverted (starting material added to a chilled suspension of HBr) and a subsurface feed line was used to deliver the solution, preventing clump formation and enabling a homogeneous slurry.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The addition of HBr to a starting material solution (9–12 vol CH₃CN) caused the solid product to agglomerate and generate intractable clumps.", "Inversion of the reagent addition order was also examined as we reasoned that starting material addition to HBr would ensure excess acid would always be present, allowing for quick conversion to product and subsequent precipitation to minimize entrapment of non‑product species.", "These conditions caused the solution dripping from the addition line to become viscous and develop material build‑up over time, most likely from volatile HBr in the headspace. To avoid this problem, the starting material solution was added via a subsurface feed line."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: During the addition of the room‑temperature starting‑material solution an exotherm (≈10 °C) occurred, causing a temperature spike that could promote decomposition and reduce conversion.
Solution_Description: The reactor was precooled to ≤ −10 °C during the addition and then brought back to −5 °C after the charge to absorb the heat of reaction and keep the mixture within the safe temperature window.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Notably, a temperature increase was observed during the addition due to charging the starting material as a room temperature solution and the deprotection having a slight exotherm (ATR 10 °C).", "For small‑scale reactions with a fast addition rate, the reactor was set colder (≤−10 °C) to accommodate the initial temperature spike and then adjusted to −5 °C after the addition was complete."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: Using less than 5 equiv of HBr resulted in stalled reactions and incomplete conversion of the mono‑t‑butyl intermediate (R‑5), while higher equivalents reduced diastereomeric ratio.
Solution_Description: Eight equivalents of HBr (6 eq in the feed line and 2 eq in the reactor) were adopted as the standard charge, and a second small acid addition was used when necessary to push the conversion to completion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Insufficient acid (<5 equiv) resulted in the reaction stalling, while higher levels diminished acetal dr.", "We concluded that a stalled reaction could be recovered by charging more acid and 5–6 equivalents of acid were insufficient to drive the reaction quickly to product. To avoid the potential for reaction stalling, we opted to continue with 8 equiv of HBr as the acid charge."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: At manufacturing scale the impinging jet experienced clogging: solid deposits filled the outlet line and the Y‑mixer, causing pump stalls and back‑pressure buildup.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 3‑D‑printed Y‑mixer (high‑temp resin) with larger inlet/outlet diameters was introduced, a Hastelloy jet with a widened outlet was evaluated, and diversion lines with high‑speed rinses (CH₃CN, THF/H₂O) were added to clear any solids.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Unfortunately, with this setup, the pumps stalled across a range of addition rates, as solids filled the outlet line.", "A Y‑mixer was 0.06″ ID. The new setup with a Hastelloy jet (1/8″ OD → 1/4″ OD) worked well at 85 mL/min but stalled at slower rates; solid was found inside the Y‑mixer.", "The 3‑D‑printed impinging jet was designed... and was found to have good chemical resistance to CH₃CN and HBr in AcOH."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: Significant amounts of product (≈12.8 % of the theoretical) remained trapped in the Y‑mixer after the first manufacturing run, lowering the overall crude assay yield to 71 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition rate was increased to 85–300 mL/min, the solvent ratio changed from 1:1:2 to a more dilute 2:2:2 mixture, and the jet was rinsed at high flow (10 L/min CH₃CN followed by THF/H₂O) to dislodge retained solids, reducing jet loss to 2.4 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ["At 85 mL/min (entry 3) the new setup worked well, but at slower rates the jet clogged.", "A faster addition rate (85 mL/min) showed lower jet losses (3.89 % vs 6.08 % at 8 mL/min).", "Diluting the starting material solution by approximately 2‑fold allowed the addition to proceed at 1 mL/min with a long outlet line, but large solid clumps were observed suggesting clogging may occur in future experiments."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: During the prolonged reversed‑phase chromatography (≈128 h for a 2 kg batch) the deacylated amine impurity (12) formed at ~0.06 % area per day, increasing to ~0.32 % area over the full run.
Solution_Description: A two‑reactor storage system was implemented: the bulk crude was frozen at −20 °C (0.02 % area per day formation) and aliquoted to a 0 °C reactor pressurized with N₂ before chromatography, limiting impurity buildup.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Deacylated amine 12 resulting from bromoacetamide hydrolysis was a major degradant that was difficult to reject downstream. Refrigerated temperatures (2–8 °C) helped slow the formation of this impurity, but degradation still occurs at ≈0.06 area% per day.", "The estimated chromatography processing time for a ≈2 kg batch of (R)‑1 on a 15 cm inner diameter column was 128 h, resulting in up to ≈0.32 area% formation of the amine impurity.", "To minimize this undesired pathway, a storage system using two reactors was implemented, where the bulk crude product solution was frozen at −20 °C in one reactor (only 0.02% formation per day) and thawed as needed to aliquot a smaller portion out into a second reactor held at 0 °C."]

Paper Title: Use of Impinging Jet to Improve Scalability in the Preparation of the ABBV-154 Drug-Linker
Problem_Description: Recovered material from the Y‑mixer did not dissolve at the standard 3:4 THF/H₂O ratio; higher ratios (5:6 or 1:1) were required, otherwise the material could not be re‑purified on scale.
Solution_Description: The THF/H₂O ratio was increased to 5:6 (or 1:1 for worst‑case) for re‑processing, and an inverse addition of the THF product solution into i‑PrOAc was adopted to precipitate a filterable solid, avoiding tacky precipitation seen with the original 5:1 CH₃CN/i‑PrOAc method.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Aliquots of THF were charged to an aqueous solution of recovered material... the crude material did not completely dissolve at this composition.", "Lab screening revealed that drug‑linker 1 could be extracted from purified fractions using 4:1 v/v 2‑MeTHF/i‑PrOAc with minimal losses.", "An inverse addition of the THF product solution into i‑PrOAc allowed for controlled precipitation generating a solid that filtered well and could be dried under vacuum at room temperature."]

Paper Title: Efficiency and Sustainability through Development of a Next-Generation, Commercial Synthesis of Valbenazine Ditosylate
Problem_Description: Step 1 of the original process required 6–7 days of stirring at 30–40 °C in a biphasic water/heptane mixture, which limited mass‑transfer and made the reaction plant‑time‑ and energy‑intensive.
Solution_Description: A homogeneous reaction was designed using sodium iodide in a smaller IPA/water mixture, eliminating the biphasic system. Conversion ≥95 % was achieved in ≥24 h, and the product crystallised directly from the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "The process suffers from extended stir time (6–7 days) at 30–40 °C due to the biphasic conditions and subsequent restrictions of mass transfer." (Step 1 description) 
2. "Utilizes … sodium iodide in an initially homogeneous reaction with a smaller overall volume of IPA/water … acceleration … ≥95 % conversion in at least 24 h vs. the original 6–7 days." (Step 1 next‑generation description) 
3. "The reaction progresses, compound 1 crystallizes directly from the reaction." (Step 1 next‑generation description) 
4. "The next‑generation step 1 manufacturing process requires 3 days total vs. the previous 10 …" (Step 1 summary) 
5. "Delivering the NaBH4 in MTBE (rather than reactive EtOH) prevented undesired hydrogen off‑gassing…" (Note: this quote was used to illustrate the functional additive role of NaI).

Paper Title: Efficiency and Sustainability through Development of a Next-Generation, Commercial Synthesis of Valbenazine Ditosylate
Problem_Description: At the end of the original Step 1, the reaction slurry became a near‑paste, making representative sampling difficult and leading to inconsistent analytical results.
Solution_Description: An active sampling loop with a large‑syringe port was employed, and the sampled aliquot was immediately diluted 1:9 to obtain reproducible analytical data.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "The end‑of‑reaction slurry is a near‑paste at room temperature … it became essential to apply an active sampling loop, continuously pumping the slurry for extraction via a large syringe port to obtain a representative sample." (Step 1 analysis challenges) 
2. "Dilution (1:9) of a 20 mL aliquot occurred immediately after sampling … delivered consistent and accurate results." (Sampling method) 
3. No additional quotes needed; the two excerpts fully justify the problem and solution.

Paper Title: Efficiency and Sustainability through Development of a Next-Generation, Commercial Synthesis of Valbenazine Ditosylate
Problem_Description: Step 2 of the original process used a multi‑solvent work‑up (EtOH, CH₂Cl₂, iPrOAc) with LiCl and acetic acid, generating large waste, requiring energy‑intensive distillations, and causing hydrogen gas evolution from NaBH₄ reacting with EtOH.
Solution_Description: The new process replaces EtOH/CH₂Cl₂ with MTBE/MeOH, removes LiCl, runs at ambient temperature, and completes the reduction in 4 h, eliminating hazardous hydrogen evolution and reducing solvent waste.
Supporting_Evidence:

2. "EtOH reacted with and consumed NaBH₄ … limiting the hold‑time … exacerbating hydrogen gas evolution." (Safety concern) 
3. "The next‑generation process … first adding compound 1 to 6 volumes MTBE and 1 vol MeOH … 1.7 equiv NaBH₄ … complete reaction in 4 h at 20–30 °C." (Step 2 new process) 
4. "Delivering the NaBH₄ in MTBE (rather than reactive EtOH) prevented undesired hydrogen off‑gassing, and the ambient temperature eliminated the need for energy‑intensive cooling of the vessel." (Safety and energy benefits) 
5. "The waste … step E‑Factor contribution … reduced from 108 to 27." (Improved waste profile).

Paper Title: Proprietary Synthesis of the C27–C35 Fragment of Eribulin and Its Elaboration toward the C14–C35 Subunit
Problem_Description: The original Eisai synthesis of the C27–C35 sulfone fragment required DIBAL under cryogenic conditions, posing a safety hazard at large scale.
Solution_Description: A short‑sequence from commercially available xylose acetonide was devised to generate an oxetane intermediate, allowing vinyl‑magnesium bromide addition at ambient temperature and eliminating the need for cryogenic DIBAL. The route bypasses the patented sulfone intermediate by using a C27‑sulfide fragment, thereby avoiding IP constraints.
Supporting_Evidence: “the use of DIBAL under cryogenic conditions” (Scheme 3, top). “We proposed using an oxetane functionality that could be accessed through short elaboration from a xylose‑derived starting material… without the use of cryogenic reaction conditions.” (para 4). “This completely side‑steps intermediate 8… thereby achieves independence from Eisai’s intermediate patent claims.” (para 5).

Paper Title: Proprietary Synthesis of the C27–C35 Fragment of Eribulin and Its Elaboration toward the C14–C35 Subunit
Problem_Description: Attempts to convert the C30‑ketone to the required olefin by Wittig olefination gave very low conversion and uncontrolled decomposition; Tebbe reagent gave only 50 % conversion.
Solution_Description: The Nysted reagent (with TiCl₄) was employed, delivering the methylenated product in good isolated yield (63 % over two steps) without the side‑reactions observed with Wittig or Tebbe reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Wittig olefination of 21 furnished the desired terminal olefin in very low conversion and unspecific decomposition” (Table 2, entry 1). “Employing Tebbe′s reagent… poor conversion (entry 2).” “Finally, the reaction with the Nysted reagent afforded selective methylenated product 22 in good yield” (Table 2, entry 3).

Paper Title: Proprietary Synthesis of the C27–C35 Fragment of Eribulin and Its Elaboration toward the C14–C35 Subunit
Problem_Description: Acid‑mediated hydrolysis of intermediate 18‑B either eliminated the C31‑methoxy group or gave no conversion, rendering the sequence ineffective.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the acid hydrolysis route and instead pursued a sequence involving methylenation, hydroboration, oxidation, and an epimerization step to obtain the required aldehyde, which could be executed on multikilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “exposing this moiety to various acids resulted in elimination of the C31 methoxy group (entries 1–5) or it proved unreactive (entries 6–8), putting an end to this approach.” (Table 1). “We recognized that methylenation of C30‑ketone… would also serve to introduce a hydroxyl functionality… Although superficially inelegant, we were hopeful that this slightly lengthy reaction sequence… would be practical and amendable for our campaign.”

Paper Title: Proprietary Synthesis of the C27–C35 Fragment of Eribulin and Its Elaboration toward the C14–C35 Subunit

Paper Title: Proprietary Synthesis of the C27–C35 Fragment of Eribulin and Its Elaboration toward the C14–C35 Subunit
Problem_Description: The NHK coupling of the C27‑C35 sulfide fragment 7 with the C14‑C26 vinyl iodide 32 needed careful control to achieve reliable conversion on kilogram scale.
