Solution_Description: The authors employed a finely tuned order of addition (formation of the Cr‑Ni catalytic system, followed by slow addition of the substrates under an argon atmosphere with oxygen monitoring) and maintained low temperatures during the coupling, ensuring consistent yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “A 3 L five‑neck round‑bottom flask… was equipped with a magnetic stir bar, oxygen detector… To the reaction mixture was added CrCl₂… and NiCl₂… the solution comprising 32 and 7 in THF was added… the reaction mixture was stirred at rt overnight… oxygen detector was turned on, and argon flow was maintained to sustain a level of oxygen below 200 ppm.” (sec 2.25).

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: The methylation of compound 1 using dimethyl carbonate (DMC) showed poor reproducibility on scale‑up. Formation of large amounts of methanol caused the temperature to drop, and the reaction stalled before reaching full conversion.
Solution_Description: A completely new route was adopted that bypasses the problematic methylation step. The halo‑form reaction of N‑methylpyrrole (9) with trichloroacetyl chloride (11) furnishes the trichloromethyl ketone 13 in high conversion, eliminating the need for the DMC methylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “First, a more classical synthesis route was developed… The methylation… performed using dimethylcarbonate… reproducibility issues hampered the methylation step… the reaction temperature decreased, and the reaction stalled…”; “The haloform reaction… allowing direct coupling between electron‑poor aniline and trichloromethylketone… The desired amide intermediate was obtained in high yield…”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: The second step of the original sequence required a large excess of an expensive base, driving up the cost of goods.
Solution_Description: Base loading was optimized by switching to potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) at 1 equiv, which gave higher yields without the need for excess expensive base.
Supporting_Evidence: “The second step required an excess of an expensive base.”; Table 4 shows that “K₂CO₃ (1.0 equiv) … gave 85 % in‑situ yield, whereas other bases performed poorly.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: Compound 4 showed very low solubility in toluene, making its isolation difficult and leading to poor phase separation and product precipitation during work‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was changed to acetonitrile, which greatly improved the solubility of the amide. After the reaction, concentrated HCl and water were added as antisolvents to crystallize the product, enabling simple filtration isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solubility of compound 4 in toluene was low, making its isolation difficult to control.”; “We decided to add concentrated aqueous HCl followed by water addition, as an antisolvent, to crystallize product 4 and facilitate direct isolation by filtration. MeCN appeared to be the best solvent…”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: The sulfonylation step generated chlorinated impurities whose levels depended on the quality of the chlorosulfonic‑acid batch, requiring recrystallization of compound 5 and giving only moderate isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Instead of the problematic sulfonylation, the route was redesigned to convert the trichloromethyl‑ketone 13 to the carboxylate 19, then activate it with SOCl₂ and couple with aniline, avoiding the need for the sulfonylation and its impurity issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The impurity profile of the sulfonylation step was linked to the quality of the batch of chlorosulfonic acid… Recrystallization of compound 5 was needed… leading to a moderate isolated yield.”; “The use of the carboxylate salt 19 allowed us to overcome the instability of carboxylic acid 17… After activation with SOCl₂… the desired amide 4 was obtained in high yield and purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: Formation of the acyl‑chloride intermediate 18 (from trichloromethyl‑ketone 13) was problematic; the reaction gave black mixtures and precipitated material, indicating instability, and the acidic conditions caused degradation of the product.
Solution_Description: The acyl‑chloride was generated in situ with thionyl chloride, and the resulting solution was added dropwise to a slurry of aniline and K₂CO₃ (reverse addition). This controlled the reaction environment and prevented decomposition, delivering high isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Formation of the activated species 18 using thionyl chloride or oxalyl chloride appeared to be difficult… black reaction mixtures…” ; Table 4 entry 8: “Reverse addition… acyl chloride solution was added dropwise to a slurry containing compound 3 with K₂CO₃… amide 4 was formed with a very high in‑situ yield of 93 %.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the haloform‑type amidation, the reaction in dry toluene stalled at 92 % conversion and product precipitated, leading to poor phase separation and low isolated yield (34 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to acetonitrile, which kept the product in solution; DBU was added slowly over 30 min to control the exotherm, and an aqueous HCl quench was used to crystallize the product after the reaction, giving 79 % isolated yield with >96 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction did not reach full conversion… product precipitated… After increasing the amount of DBU… we turned our attention to other solvents… MeCN appeared to be the best solvent… DBU was then added over 30 min to control the exotherm… amide 4 isolated in 79 % yield and a purity of 96.7 %.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 1: Route Scouting Effort toward a Key Amide Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original amide‑formation step required a two‑step ester‑aminolysis using an expensive base (LiHMDS), leading to a long overall reaction time and high cost.
Solution_Description: A shorter two‑step sequence was developed: trichloromethyl‑ketone 13 is directly converted to the lithium carboxylate 19, activated with SOCl₂, and coupled with aniline in a one‑pot operation, reducing the step count by half and cutting the PMI from 73 to 17.
Supporting_Evidence: “The second approach utilized an innovative extension of the haloform reaction, allowing direct coupling … The desired amide intermediate was obtained in high yield and purity via a simple two‑step synthesis … a significant PMI reduction was reached … from 73 to 17.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: The original haloform‑type amidation required 2 equiv of DBU, an excess that increased material cost and generated large amounts of waste that needed to be quenched with HCl.
Solution_Description: Switch to a catalytic amount of TBD (as low as 0.2 equiv) dramatically reduced the amount of base required while maintaining high conversion, lowering both cost and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the use of an excess of 1,8‑diazabicyclo[5.4.0]‑undec‑7‑ene (DBU) prompted us to investigate potential alternatives… the catalytic use compensated for the price difference.”; “...TBD was chosen… catalytic version… using 0.2 equiv gave 91 % conversion.”; “TBD being much more expensive than DBU, its catalytic use compensated for the price difference.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: Trichloromethyl ketone 3 sublimated on drying, making its isolation difficult and causing losses of material.
Solution_Description: The solid ketone 3 was used directly and the reaction mixture was switched to acetonitrile after azeotropic drying, improving handling and avoiding sublimation losses.
Supporting_Evidence: “We used our standard reaction conditions (excess of 2 equiv of DBU)… trichloromethyl ketone 3 sublimates upon drying, thus hampering its isolation.”; “After a solvent switch to acetonitrile in the presence of aniline 4, enabling the azeotrope drying of the reaction mixture…”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: Screening of multiple bases gave low conversions (e.g., TMG 4 % conversion), indicating poor yields with many reagents.
Solution_Description: TBD was identified as a highly active base/catalyst, giving near‑quantitative conversion even at catalytic loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: “Little conversion was obtained with TMG… After careful analysis, we found a new impurity….”; “A clear cut‑off was obtained with 1,5,7‑triazabicyclo[4.4.0]‑dec‑5‑ene (TBD), and nearly full conversion was reached after only 2 h of reaction at 30 °C (entry 8).”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: In MTBE the reaction mixture formed crusts on the reactor wall and impeller, causing non‑homogeneous material and reduced product purity (88.6 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Raising the temperature to 45 °C dissolved the crusts and restored homogeneous stirring, improving conversion and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “We also noticed that the conversion to the desired product was hampered by the crusting… An increase in temperature from 20 to 45 °C allowed us to overcome the crusting issue without impacting the reaction profile while also increasing the coupling kinetics.”; “Crust formation… led to a nonhomogeneous material, low product purity, and concerns regarding upscaling.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: The Friedel–Crafts acylation generated HCl that required aqueous quenching, posing safety and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: HCl was removed by controlled distillation (boiling off) instead of aqueous quench, eliminating the hazardous aqueous work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “We wondered whether we could eliminate the basic wash by inverting the stoichiometry… and then boiling off the HCl from the reaction mixture.”; “The reaction mixture was equipped with a distillation setup, and the temperature was increased to 95 °C… to distill chloroform from the reaction mixture.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: Amide 5 exhibited high solubility in MeCN, leading to significant losses in the mother‑liquid during isolation.
Solution_Description: Switching to MTBE for the second step reduced amide 5 solubility; concentrated reaction conditions and addition of water as an antisolvent precipitated the product, improving recovery and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solubility of amide 5 is rather low in acetonitrile at 30 °C… the addition of water as an antisolvent allowed us to reach a higher physical yield of 79 % with a very high solid purity of 98.9 %.”; “Only two solvents provided lower solubility for our compound: MTBE and toluene… MTBE was investigated as a solvent also in the second step.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: The original DBU‑mediated amidation required 22 h stirring after base addition, significantly lengthening the process.
Solution_Description: Using catalytic TBD reduced the reaction time to 2 h at 30 °C, and higher temperatures were employed when necessary to accelerate conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the reaction required an additional 22 h after DBU addition.”; “At 0.5 equiv, the conversion was still high after 2 h and reached 89 % (entry 12).”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the catalytic TBD reaction sometimes stalled, giving inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction concentration and improving agitation helped maintain consistent conversion at larger scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Upon scale up, we noticed that at 20 mol % base loading, the reaction was stalling at different levels of conversion… To investigate the isolation procedure, catalytic loading was increased, and the reaction was run under more concentrated conditions… Pleasingly, conversions to the desired product above 98 % were reached.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Bersacapavir, Part 2. Early Game Route Selection: Catalytic versus Stoichiometric Haloform-Type Amidation
Problem_Description: Removal of chloroform generated from the haloform reaction posed a risk of carbene formation when treated with base.
Solution_Description: Chloroform was removed by distillation rather than basic treatment, eliminating the carbene formation hazard.
Supporting_Evidence: “Even if low, the risk of carbene generation (coming from the reaction between hydroxide and chloroform) became critical… Our solution was to remove the chloroform from the reaction mixture by distillation.”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: The original C–N coupling of iodide 1 with tetrahydropyran‑protected amine 2 gave low conversion on kilogram scale, required a large excess of the expensive Cs₂CO₃ base and a high palladium loading, and the work‑up relied on silica‑gel chromatography, resulting in only 65–75 % isolated yield of product 3.
Solution_Description: The catalyst system was changed to Pd(OAc)₂/Xantphos with a reduced 3 mol % Pd loading. K₃PO₄ (3 equiv) was used as base with a 0.3–0.5 % water additive to improve solubility, and 2‑MeTHF was selected as the reaction solvent. The work‑up was switched to a simple aqueous citric‑acid/quench and NaHCO₃ washes, followed by removal of residual Pd with ammonium pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (APDTC). Crystallization of 3 was performed directly from the concentrated 2‑MeTHF solution, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “additional challenges surfaced upon kilogram scale‑up…high conversion while reducing the amount of palladium precatalyst required, developing a more robust and practical workup, and eliminating chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: The first‑generation S_NAr reaction used heterogeneous K₂CO₃ in DMSO; this caused severe mass‑transfer limitations, required long reaction times (3–10 h) and presented an exothermic safety hazard (onset 170 °C, max operating temperature 70 °C).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A biphasic Schotten‑Baumann protocol was adopted using 2‑MeTHF as the organic phase and aqueous KOH (or NaOH) as the base. This homogeneous‑compatible system gave >99 % conversion in 2 h at 60 °C, removed the DMSO safety issue, and avoided mass‑transfer bottlenecks.
Supporting_Evidence: • “S_NAr reaction suffered from mass transfer limits due to the use of a heterogeneous base in DMSO, which also posed a safety concern… strongly exothermic decomposition… onset 170 °C suggested a maximum operating temperature of 70 °C.”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: Intermediate 5 (the diastereomeric mixture) was highly soluble in most organic solvents; attempts to precipitate gave amorphous, oily slurries that required long drying times and gave variable particle‑size distribution, making isolation inefficient on multikilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The crude reaction mixture was not isolated; instead it was diluted, washed, and directly transferred (telescoped) into n‑propyl‑alcohol for the subsequent THP deprotection. A controlled azeotropic solvent swap (2‑MeTHF → DMSO → water → n‑PrOH) enabled a stable solution that could be processed without a drying step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We were unable to reduce the equivalents of amine 4 significantly without also reducing conversion… The isolation of intermediate 5… was unsuccessful, leading to gumming or oiling out of the product(s) and no effective way to generate seed crystals.”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: The THP deprotection required 20–60 equiv of HCl/MeOH, generating large volumes of waste, and the use of MeOH/HCl risked formation of mutagenic methyl chloride. Multiple distillation steps made the operation time‑intensive.
Solution_Description: In‑situ HCl was generated from acetyl chloride in a 2:1 PhMe/n‑PrOH mixture (avoiding MeOH). Only 10 equiv of AcCl were needed, eliminating the methyl‑chloride risk. The reaction was seeded with crystalline GDC‑1971·3HCl at 0 °C and then heated to 80 °C over ~12 h, effecting a reactive crystallization that gave >99 % isolated yield of the HCl salt.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the first‑generation process… required multiple wasteful cycles of distillation and recharge of HCl/MeOH (∼20–60 equiv) … risk of forming methyl chloride (a genotoxic impurity).”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: Residual palladium remained >3000 ppm after the C–N coupling; silica‑supported thiol scavenging only lowered it to ~800 ppm and activated carbon was ineffective, while APDTC worked on lab scale but did not scale linearly.
Solution_Description: Ammonium pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate (APDTC) was employed in two successive charges (6 mol % each) at 45–55 °C, bringing palladium levels below the target 250 ppm. Additional water washes removed any APDTC‑derived degradation products.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The next challenge was to find an acceptable means of reducing the level of residual catalysis… silica‑supported thiol … only partly effective, ~800 ppm … APDTC identified as a viable alternative… this stoichiometry did not scale linearly… a repeat APDTC treatment (2 charges of 6.0 mol % each) was successful in achieving the <250 ppm [Pd] target.”

Paper Title: Streamlined Synthesis of SHP2 Inhibitor GDC-1971 Enhanced by a Telescoped Schotten-Baumann S
Problem_Description: Final API crystallization from the original 2:1 H₂O/MeOH system required large solvent volumes, produced sticky films on vessel walls, and gave variable particle‑size distributions with large agglomerates, leading to extended drying times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The antisolvent was switched to n‑PrOH/H₂O (1:1 and 1:2 v/v) which lowered the total solvent volume (~12 mL/g) and eliminated wall‑cake formation. A seeded crystallization at 70 °C followed by temperature cycling (70 → 25 → 70 °C) gave consistent polymorph and PSD. The slurry was passed through an IKA magic‑LAB wet mill (2G/4M/6F rotor‑stator, 5 passes) to achieve D₁₀ = 20 µm, D₅₀ = 55 µm, D₉₀ = 111 µm.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The original 2:1 (v/v) H₂O/MeOH system… high‑volume process (V_max ∼ 30 mL/g), sticky films… PSD was also found to be variable… We instead achieved success by using n‑PrOH as a slightly less polar substitution for MeOH, together with H₂O as a miscible antisolvent… the wet‑milling process was repeated… tightened the PSD of the isolated material.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis to Enable Rapid, Multigram Deliveries of Peptides
Problem_Description: Uronium‑based coupling reagents (HATU, HBTU, COMU) gave markedly lower isolated yields and LC area % purities, likely because of incomplete activation of the amino acids.
Solution_Description: Switch to the DIC/Oxyma coupling system, which provides comparable yields with a lower cost and a safer safety profile.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reactions with analogous uronium reagents, HATU and HBTU, gave appreciably lower yields and purities likely due to incomplete activation of the amino acids.”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: The earliest batch synthetic routes to azvudine required 14 steps (overall yield 2.6 %) or 9 steps (overall yield ~2 %) with total reaction times >136 h and involved hazardous chlorination, fluorination and azidation reactions, as well as multiple column‑chromatography purifications.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A fully continuous‑flow process was developed that performs the six‑step synthesis of the key intermediate 2′‑deoxy‑2′‑fluoro‑arabinoside (FAU) in a series of micro‑reactors with in‑line extraction and neutralisation, eliminating batch‑wise hazardous steps, reducing reaction time to 156 min and raising the overall yield to 32.3 %.
Supporting_Evidence: The abstract reports a fully continuous flow synthesis with total residence time of 156 min and a total yield of 32.3 % compared with batch conditions where the total reaction time was >136 h and yield <3 % ("The earliest synthetic route… total yield 2.6 %… total reaction time over 136 h…"; "Under the optimized process conditions, the total yield was 32.3 % with a total residence time of 156 min…" )

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: Initial chlorination of FR‑0 gave only 65.4 % conversion, limiting the overall yield of FR‑Cl.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature, residence time and SOCl₂ equiv were optimized via a Box–Behnken design; the optimum (80 °C, 42 min, 1.54 equiv SOCl₂) gave 97.9 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the preliminary studies… conversion (65.4 %). … prolonging the reaction time and increasing the reaction temperature… could improve the reaction conversion… the optimal process parameters… reaction temperature 80 °C, residence time 42 min, SOCl₂ 1.54 equiv, conversion rate 98.2 %… verified… 97.9 %”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: Increasing the temperature of the hydrolysis step above 50 °C promoted 1′‑position side‑hydrolysis, lowering the yield of FR‑1 despite longer residence times.
Solution_Description: A temperature of 50 °C and a residence time of 15 min were selected, giving a total two‑step yield of 90.4 % for FR‑1.
Supporting_Evidence: “With the increase of reaction temperature, the yield of FR‑1 increased… when the temperature reached 50 °C, the yield hardly increased… At 50 °C, prolonging the residence time… yield… 90.4 %… Under 70 °C, more 1′‑position hydrolysis by‑products formed… therefore, the reaction temperature of 50 °C, and the residence time of 15 min were selected as the optimal conditions… total yield… 90.4 %”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: The fluorination reagent DAST decomposes at temperatures >80 °C, limiting the temperature window and posing safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed at 75 °C with 2.5 equiv DAST; the substrate concentration was doubled, affording a 97.1 % isolated yield of FR‑F.
Supporting_Evidence: “Considering that DAST would decompose at higher temperatures (>80 °C)… we did not choose to continue increasing the temperature… the final yield reached 97.1 % under the following conditions… 2.5 equiv. of DAST. To further increase the production capacity, we doubled the concentration of the reaction substrate… final yield 97.1 %”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: Bromination of FR‑Cl using HBr/AcOH in DCM gave only 11.1 % yield at room temperature; raising temperature was limited by DCM’s low boiling point, and the reaction suffered from poor phase mixing.
Solution_Description: Temperature was raised to 80 °C, HBr equiv increased to 4.0, and substrate concentration was increased to 0.4–1.0 M, delivering >99 % yield with residence times as short as 2.5 min.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yield was only 11.1 % at room temperature… reached 81.5 % when the reaction temperature was raised to 80 °C… As the HBr equivalent increased… yield increased… By further prolonging the residence time… highest yield 93.2 %… It was found… the residence time could be greatly shortened by further increasing the concentration… with the temperature of 80 °C and a residence time of 2.5 min, the yield… 99.9 %”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: The condensation of FR‑Br (in DCM) with silylated uridine required a compatible solvent; initial attempts with DCM, DCE, CHCl₃ gave low conversion, while MeCN worked best but introduced a biphasic system.
Solution_Description: MeCN was used for the Si‑uridine stream, reaction temperature set to 120 °C, Si‑uridine at 1.2 equiv and 25 min residence gave a 91.3 % yield of FAU‑Bz.
Supporting_Evidence: “We screened DCM, DCE, CHCl₃ and MeCN… MeCN reacted most effectively… the condensation reaction was carried out… temperature increased (entries 1–5)… 120 °C selected… 1.2 equiv Si‑uridine more appropriate… residence time 25 min gave 91.3 % yield”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: Deprotection required a base; methanol‑ammonia gave unstable operation, prompting the need for a more reliable base system.
Solution_Description: NaOMe (1.4 equiv) in MeOH at 80 °C for 1 min gave a 99.8 % isolated yield of FAU with consistent performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Methanol ammonia and NaOMe were screened… NaOMe was selected… increasing the temperature had a positive effect… optimum conditions… temperature 80 °C, residence time 1 min, NaOMe 1.4 equiv, yield 99.8 %”

Paper Title: Fully Continuous Flow Synthesis of 2′-Deoxy-2′-fluoro-arabinoside: A Key Intermediate of Azvudine
Problem_Description: In the fully continuous flow set‑up, feeding SOCl₂ as a DCM solution introduced extra solvent, diluting the reaction mixture and lowering the yield of module A.
Solution_Description: SOCl₂ solution was replaced by hydrogen‑chloride gas, eliminating the extra DCM, allowing a 30 min residence, gas–liquid molar ratio 1.4, and achieving 98 % conversion for chlorination.
Supporting_Evidence: “We replaced the stream of SOCl₂ in DCM with hydrogen chloride gas to reduce the introduction of solvent… optimum conditions… residence time 30 min, gas–liquid molar ratio 1.4, conversion 98.0 % (Table 8, entry 9)”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthesis of the tricyclic diazepine core gave an overall isolated yield of only 5.6 % with 17 steps and high estimated material cost, making it unviable for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: A completely redesigned eight‑step route was developed that uses a metal‑catalyzed C–N coupling/reductive cascade to form the core, improved fragment couplings and a dynamic N6‑acylation, delivering the API in 27 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “overall yield (5.6 %), total step count (17), and estimated cost were not viewed to be viable on multikilogram scale.”
[Solution] “The optimized route involves a metal‑catalyzed C–N coupling/reductive cascade to form the central diazepine core, improved entries to both the zigzag morpholine and cyclohexyl acid peripheral pieces…”.

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Selective acylation of the unprotected tricyclic core at N6 was not scalable using the original HCl‑mediated conditions; low conversion and mixtures of N‑acyl isomers were observed on larger scale.
Solution_Description: A dynamic equilibration protocol was introduced: 1.03 equiv of acid chloride is added to the core in dioxane (or 1,2‑DCE/DMA), the mixture is heated to 100 °C to allow reversible acyl transfer, and the HCl salt is isolated by simple filtration, giving high selectivity and scalability.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “These conditions were not scalable.”
[Solution] “Treatment of tricyclic cores with 1.03 equiv of benzoyl or cyclohexane carbonyl chloride followed by aging at 100 °C funneled product to the desired N6 isomer.”
[Solution] “1,2‑DCE (or DMA) was found to be a viable alternative to dioxane…”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original C–N coupling approach (route a) required large excess LiHMDS, which caused cis–trans epimerisation of the cyclohexyl group and hampered isolation of the final API.
Solution_Description: Switch to the N6‑acyl‑N11‑Boc protected core (route b option 2) allowed the use of milder carbonate bases, eliminating epimerisation while maintaining high coupling efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “required a large excess of a strong base (LiHMDS), which caused some cis–trans epimerization of the cyclohexyl group and compromised an effective isolation of 1.”
[Solution] “a variety of catalyst systems were active and worked with milder carbonate bases, avoiding cis–trans epimerization of the cyclohexyl group.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The NiXantPhos ligand required for the Ni‑catalyzed C–N coupling (approach A) was expensive and difficult to source in the quantities needed for kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The route was shifted to approach B using Pd₂(dba)₃/XantPhos with reduced catalyst loading (1 mol % Pd, 0.5 mol % NiXantPhos), lowering material cost while preserving high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “high cost and limited availability of the NiXantPhos ligand, which was critical for obtaining acceptable yields of 32.”
[Solution] “the catalyst loading could be decreased to as low as 0.5 mol % but afforded the cleanest reaction profile at 1 mol % loading.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Intermediate 32 exhibited very low solubility in common organic solvents, leading to a heterogeneous reaction mixture and difficult extractions during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction volume was increased to 35 equivalents of 2‑MeTHF, providing a homogeneous solution and facilitating downstream Boc‑protection and work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “Because the low solubility of 32 in organic solvents resulted in heterogeneity throughout the reaction as well as difficulties with extraction, the solvent was increased to 35 volumes.”
[Solution] “the solvent was increased to 35 volumes, and the crude material was directly carried forward to the Boc protection.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During large‑scale Boc‑protection of 32 to give 25‑Cl, conversion dropped sharply; additional Boc₂O/DMAP charges were ineffective, leading to inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: A controlled acid‑base work‑up sequence (pH 6 → 8 → 3 → 8) was instituted, DMAP loading was limited, and EcosorbC‑941 was employed to remove residual Pd, restoring full conversion and giving a reproducible 72 % overall yield after crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “a sharp decrease in conversion was observed. The addition of a second charge of Boc₂O and DMAP was ineffective.”
[Solution] “the batch was filtered, and an aqueous workup was performed. Resubjection to 0.7 equiv of DMAP and 0.8 equiv of Boc₂O resulted in full conversion…”
[Solution] “EcosorbC‑941 was added… to remove residual Pd.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of 25‑Cl with Pd/C gave almost quantitative dehalogenation (product 27) and negligible formation of the desired 26‑Cl, resulting in poor material balance.
Solution_Description: Switching to Pt–V/C (0.1 equiv) in a MeOH/THF mixture under 20–30 psi H₂ at 10–20 °C for 16 h gave >99 % conversion to 26‑Cl with 80 % isolated yield and low metal impurities after a CUNO polish.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “Pd/C demonstrated high reactivity, it almost exclusively generated dehalogenated product 27….”
[Solution] “We decided to move forward with Pt–V/C… quantitative yields could be attained over just 16 h with 0.1 equiv of Pt–V/C in MeOH (10 vol)/THF (10 vol) under 20–30 psi H₂.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Excess DMAP present after Boc‑protection caused re‑conversion of 25‑Cl back to the unprotected intermediate 32, threatening material loss.
Solution_Description: DMAP charge was limited, and CO₂ generated during the reaction was shown to neutralise excess DMAP, preventing reversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “excess DMAP could cause reversion of the desired product 25‑Cl to the unprotected intermediate 32.”
[Solution] “control experiments… suggested subtle protective effects of liberated CO₂ during the reaction which could neutralize excess DMAP.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Securing a multi‑kilogram supply of the bridged morpholine fragment 10 was problematic; the previously published routes required SFC or long, low‑throughput sequences.
Solution_Description: A double‑inversion crystallisation‑induced diastereomer transformation (CIDT) starting from (S,S)‑HPA supplied the required (R,R)‑morpholine, and the benzoate salt 39 was chosen for improved solubility and coupling performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “One of the most challenging aspects … securing a supply of 10 … required supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) and would have had an unacceptably long cycle time.”
[Solution] “This was resolved by returning to HPA as a key starting material and developing a double‑inversion crystallisation‑induced diastereomer transformation (CIDT) process to afford the (R,R) isomer.”
[Solution] “We chose to enable access to the benzoate salt 39, as it had improved solubility versus the oxalate 10 and performed better in the C–N coupling.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Tricyclic Diazepine-Based IDH1 Mutant Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Residual palladium remained in the C–N coupled product 24 after work‑up, necessitating an additional purification step.
Solution_Description: The product was taken up in acetonitrile and passed through MP‑TMT resin, reducing Pd to <100 ppm before the deprotection step.
Supporting_Evidence: [Solution] “Removal of residual Pd was accomplished by taking up the product in acetonitrile after workup and subjecting it to MP‑TMT resin.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Replicating manufacturing conditions (procedure, process parameters, equipment) across geographically distant sites caused variability in the protein‑refolding performance and raised concerns about consistent mixing behavior.
Solution_Description: Identical suitcase‑sized portable flow microreactors (FMR) were shipped and installed at both the Japan and US sites, providing the same reactor geometry, pumps and control electronics, thus eliminating equipment‑related gaps.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “One of the primary challenges in TT is replicating manufacturing conditions … across geographically diverse sites.”
• “The Portable FMR allows the use of identical equipment at multiple sites worldwide.”
• “Successful process transfer … streamlined using portable FMR. Employing identical FMR units at both the sending (Japan) and receiving (US) sites allowed for uniformity.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Potential voltage differences between Japan and the United States could affect the mixing efficiency of the FMR, leading to variable refolding outcomes.
Solution_Description: Mixing performance was verified with the Villermaux–Dushman reaction and a feedback loop based on flow‑versus‑pressure (or viscosity) measurements was implemented to monitor and control mixing in real time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Potential issues related to voltage differences … necessitating an evaluation of mixing efficiency using the Villermaux–Dushman reaction.”
• “In the process qualification of the Portable FMR, the Villermaux–Dushman reaction was employed to critically evaluate mixing efficiency.”
• “The optimized design includes a feedback mechanism based on flow versus pressure or viscosity measurements.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: A pump malfunction caused by sticking rubber packing and air entrapment in the diaphragm system threatened reliable operation and could lead to unsafe run conditions.
Solution_Description: The portable FMR is designed for rapid disassembly; the malfunctioning pump was serviced on‑site by cleaning the diaphragm, restoring full functionality and minimizing downtime.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “During the validation process … a notable challenge was faced with a pump malfunction, primarily caused by sticking rubber packing and air entrapment … resolved by disassembling and servicing the diaphragm system.”
• “A key advantage of the Portable FMR is its design that facilitates easy disassembly, enabling rapid on‑site maintenance and repair.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: SEC analysis of refolded IL‑6 showed overlapping monomer/dimer peaks, making product isolation ambiguous.
Solution_Description: The SEC column and chromatographic conditions used at the originating site were imported and applied at the receiving site, providing clear separation of monomer and dimer species.
Supporting_Evidence: • “An overlapped peak phenomenon was discerned. Consequently, it was decided to adopt the sender’s conditions … and import the SEC column along with a Portable FMR from Japan.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Differences between the Vivaflow cassette (Japan) and the Saltflow TFF system (US) – membrane type, trans‑membrane pressure (TMP) and flow rate – created inconsistencies during the protein‑concentration step.
Solution_Description: The membrane material was matched to regenerated cellulose, and TMP (1.5 ± 0.5 bar) and flow rate (2 mL·min⁻¹) were set based on the receiver’s experience to harmonize performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The sender used a Vivaflow cassette … the receiver used a Saltflow TFF system. Major gaps were identified in membrane type, trans‑membrane pressure (TMP), and flow rate.”
• “We matched the membrane material … set the TMP based on the receiver’s experience, agreeing to optimize parameters as needed.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Protein concentration measurements differed between sites (Nanodrop at the sender vs. Solo‑VPE at the receiver), risking inconsistent data for downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Both sites agreed to validate concentration using standard samples and adopt a unified analytical method (Solo‑VPE) for higher accuracy.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Protein concentration measurements differed, with the receiver using Solo‑VPE for higher accuracy compared to the sender’s Nanodrop.”
• “To bridge this gap, we agreed to validate concentration variability using standard samples.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Traditional batch refolding of IL‑6 gave a low monomer yield (~68 %), limiting process efficiency.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow FMR with 0.25 mm inner‑diameter V‑shaped mixers and higher flow rates (10 mL·min⁻¹) was employed, raising monomer yield to ~89 % and demonstrating superior mixing‑driven refolding.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “batch … 68% yield in the batch process.”
• “FMR process … 89% monomer yield … narrower mixer I.D and higher flow rates substantially enhance refolding efficiency.”

Paper Title: Implementing an Efficient Technology Transfer for Biomolecule Production: A Case Study on Continuous-Mode Processes
Problem_Description: Typical technology‑transfer projects require 3–6 months, prolonging product availability.
Solution_Description: Deploying the portable FMR reduced the on‑site demonstration and training period to roughly 2 weeks, dramatically shortening the overall TT timeline.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The TT process, which typically takes 3–6 months, was significantly reduced (e.g., the on‑site visit was completed in 2 weeks).”

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The key intermediates (compound 16, the free base 6 and the ketone 17) showed very poor solubility in most common organic solvents.  When the Friedlander cyclisation was attempted in DMF, NMP or acetic acid a black‑tar solid formed, the reaction mixture became highly viscous and only a small fraction of material remained in solution, giving low conversion and difficult work‑up.
Solution_Description: A binary solvent system of toluene/NMP (95:5) was adopted for the Friedlander step, which kept the mixture fluid and prevented tar formation.  The amount of PPTS was reduced to 1 equiv and a Dean–Stark trap was used to continuously remove the water generated in the condensation, thereby suppressing side‑reactions and improving conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The starting materials exhibited poor solubility in most solvents, and when the reaction was tried in either DMF, NMP, or acetic acid, a black tar formed as the reaction progressed.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The SNAr displacement of fluorine in route A required 5 bar of 7 N ammonia at 120 °C in a sealed pressure reactor, generating hydrogen fluoride as a by‑product.  The reaction gave only 25 % yield of the amine and posed significant handling hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: Route A was abandoned in favour of route B, which avoided the high‑pressure SNAr step and HF generation.  The desired nitro intermediate was obtained by conventional nitration followed by crystallisation of the regio‑isomeric impurities, improving safety and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Using ammonia (7 N) at 5 bar and 120 °C in a sealed pressure reactor gave a 25 % yield of compound 22.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The final amide‑coupling of the free drug 6 with the highly polar linker 19 proceeded at 1 % w/w concentration in DMF/MeCN and required >100 vol solvent per gram of drug.  The reaction gave only ~50 % conversion and each batch needed multiple chromatographic purifications, resulting in an overall route yield of 1 % and a PMI of ~102 000.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route (routes C/D) was designed that moved the linker‑attachment step later in the sequence and employed DIC/DIPEA as the coupling reagent at a higher concentration (95:5 DCM/MeOH).  The crude product was filtered, pre‑filtered over silica and precipitated from MTBE, eliminating the need for repeated chromatography and raising the overall yield to 7.8 % (PMI ≈ 7 100).
Supporting_Evidence: ['The only suitable solvents were DMF, acetonitrile, and DCM, but in each case, 100 volumes (relative to 6) was needed for the reaction.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: Nitration of ketone 24 produced a mixture of the desired nitro‑compound 25 and the regio‑isomer 29 (4:1) together with a small amount of dinitrated impurity 30.  The mixture was difficult to separate and the dinitro impurity posed a potential safety hazard if accumulated.
Solution_Description: The nitration mixture was added slowly to the substrate under controlled temperature (5 °C) to avoid local accumulation of reactive intermediates.  The resulting mixture was crystallised first from acetone/water to remove the insoluble regio‑isomers, then the solvent was swapped to ethanol to isolate pure 25 (≈19:1 25/29).
Supporting_Evidence: ['The reaction hazards were carefully considered, and we developed the reaction with a controlled addition of the nitration mixture into the substrate to avoid any potential accumulation of material.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: Deprotection of 16 to give the free base 6 gave low solubility of the product in most solvents, hindering isolation of the free base and leading to only 46.9 % yield over the two‑step deprotection/coupling sequence.
Solution_Description: The deprotection was performed using 1.5 M HCl in IPA (6.5 equiv) at 85 °C, followed by basification and extraction into DCM/MeOH (95:5).  The mixed HCl‑salt was isolated directly, avoiding the need to isolate the free base, which improved the isolated yield to 94.5 % (mixed HCl salt).
Supporting_Evidence: ['The free base would be useful as the starting material for the final reaction and could couple directly without the addition of a further base.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: Alloc deprotection of 39 required Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5 mol %) and pyrrolidine, generating palladium residues and triphenylphosphine oxide that complicated work‑up and increased material cost.
Solution_Description: The Pd loading was lowered to 5 mol % (2.5 mol % proved incomplete) and the reaction mixture was precipitated with n‑heptane, allowing the palladium‑containing phase to remain in solution.  The solid product was filtered and washed, avoiding extensive chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The reaction worked well with 5 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₄ but did not go to completion when 2.5 mol % was used.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The activated linker 41 (Mal‑PEG8‑acid) and its intermediate 19 were unstable as lyophilised solids; rapid formation of oligomeric impurities was observed during storage at 5 °C.
Solution_Description: The lyophilisation step was omitted; the linker was kept as a dilute solution in acetonitrile and stored frozen, which suppressed oligomer formation and maintained purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['When the lyophilized solid was stored at ~5 °C, the impurity level was observed to increase quite rapidly; this was believed to be due to the formation of oligomers.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The final drug‑linker coupling required handling of a highly potent molecule in a high‑containment facility, limiting batch size to 60 g and demanding multiple chromatographic purifications, which reduced throughput.
Solution_Description: Routes C and D were selected because they moved the high‑potency steps later and reduced their number.  The intermediate 37 was obtained by a direct‑drop crystallisation (telescoped into the next step) and the final coupling was performed in a larger 50 L reactor, allowing larger batches while maintaining containment.
Supporting_Evidence: ['We prioritized investigating routes C and D as the best alternative options.',

Paper Title: Route Design and Scale-Up of a Topoisomerase I Inhibitor Antibody–Drug Conjugate Payload
Problem_Description: The initial Friedlander cyclisation of deacetylated 16 gave only 36 % conversion to 6 and the product could not be fully separated from PPTS, leading to low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑optimised by deprotecting 16 first (to give 33) and then performing the Friedlander step under the original conditions; this avoided the low conversion issue and improved overall yield of the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: ['When bisaniline 33 was reacted under Friedlander conditions, only 36% conversion to 6 was observed, and the product could not be fully separated from the PPTS reagent.',

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The Pinnick oxidation generated a large exotherm during addition of sodium chlorite; the heat accumulation was so severe that a cooling failure would raise the temperature from 10 °C to >80 °C, entering the decomposition zone.
Solution_Description: The oxidant was added in four controlled portions (10 % + 20 % + 30 % + 40 %) at 5–10 °C, keeping the internal temperature below 15 °C and spreading the heat over time. The addition rate and temperature set‑point were optimized to avoid a runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The addition rate was controlled carefully, and the reaction mixture was held for at least 1 h after the addition of each portion to keep the internal temperature below 15 °C.”

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Aldehyde 6 displayed limited solubility in the reaction medium, forming a slurry at the start of the oxidation; this delayed the exotherm and caused uneven heat release.
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration was lowered by increasing 2‑MeTHF from 10 vol to 15 vol and water from 5 vol to 7 vol, fully dissolving the starting material before oxidant addition.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction mixture being a slurry at the initial stage… More 6 became solubilized… Therefore, performing the oxidation under a more dilute condition should allow the full dissolution of 6.”

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original TMS deprotection step employed TBAF, which can generate hydrogen fluoride and cause reactor etching on scale.
Solution_Description: TBAF was replaced by alkaline protodesilylation (KOH) performed after oxidation, eliminating HF formation and corrosion concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of TBAF for silyl cleavage carried the risk of hydrogen fluoride formation and reactor etching.”

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Hydrogen peroxide as a hypochlorite scavenger required a large excess that had to be quenched, enlarging the reaction volume and complicating work‑up.
Solution_Description: DMSO was selected as the hypochlorite scavenger; it reacts rapidly, does not need excess quench, and partitions into the aqueous layer on work‑up, simplifying isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Hydrogen peroxide offered the fastest reaction rate, excess reagent must be quenched… Limonene… problematic for product purification… DMSO provided both fast reaction rates and ease of workup as it was washed away into the aqueous layer upon quench.”

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During acid‑adjustment with HCl, atmospheric oxygen oxidized dissolved SO₂ to sulfuric acid, which decomposed the acid‑sensitive thiophene core and caused browning of the solid API.
Solution_Description: HCl was retained as the protonation acid, but the reaction was performed under inert atmosphere (oxygen exclusion) to prevent formation of sulfuric acid, eliminating browning.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Sulfur dioxide partitions… prone to oxidation by atmospheric oxygen, generating sulfuric acid… exposure to concentrated sulfuric acid leads to browning. When the reaction was protected from atmospheric oxygen, no spontaneous slow exotherm was observed, … no significant browning of solids on the wall.”

Paper Title: Pinnick Oxidation on Scale: Process Development of a BDK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Quenching the oxidation with sodium thiosulfate caused gelling of the reaction mixture, complicating phase separation and downstream processing.
Solution_Description: Sodium bisulfite was used instead of thiosulfate for quench; it gave a clean phase split and avoided gel formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Quenching the excess oxidant with a sodium thiosulfate solution led to gelling. In contrast, quenching with sodium bisulfite solution gave a clean phase split.”

Problem_Description: Using sodium hydroxide for protodesilylation produced a thick, sticky slurry that often formed a solid cap in the reactor, impeding mixing.
Solution_Description: Potassium hydroxide was selected as the base for the TMS cleavage, producing a mobile slurry without sticking issues.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Sodium hydroxide produced a thick, sticky slurry… Potassium hydroxide gave a mobile slurry without sticking issues.”

Supporting_Evidence: • “Silyl cleavage with lithium hydroxide… considering the bioactivity and potential toxicity of lithium salts, this option was less attractive. Therefore, potassium hydroxide was selected.”

Paper Title: Design of Experiments-Based Optimization of an Electrochemical Decarboxylative Alkylation Using a Spinning Cylinder Electrode Reactor
Problem_Description: Visible corrosion of the graphite anode was observed when the reaction was performed in the small‑scale undivided IKA ElectraSyn vial. The porous graphite allowed the reaction mixture to penetrate the electrode surface and CO₂ bubbles detached particles, causing electrode degradation. This effect was also seen when molecular sieves were omitted, indicating water oxidation‑driven corrosion. High current density (13 mA cm⁻²) further accelerated anode degradation.
Solution_Description: The authors substituted porous graphite with non‑porous impervious graphite (resin‑filled) to eliminate corrosion; they added 3 Å molecular sieves to remove trace moisture, which prevented water oxidation and protected the electrodes; the supporting electrolyte concentration was increased from 0.025 M to 0.05 M n‑Bu₄NPF₆ to keep cell voltage low (7 → 12 V drop avoided); the current density was limited to ≤ 10 mA cm⁻² (optimal 6.6 mA cm⁻²) to avoid rapid anode degradation; a Design‑of‑Experiments (DoE) factorial study was performed to identify the optimal combination of spinning speed, charge, flow rate and current density, thereby removing the inconsistent conversion observed at high rpm alone.
Supporting_Evidence: "visible corrosion of the surface of the graphite anode was observed" (Table 1, entry 1) ; "the reaction mixture can penetrate the porous graphite material and react … detaching electrode particles as CO₂ bubbles are generated" (p. 5) ; "no corrosion was observed under the same conditions when the standard graphite was substituted by nonporous resin‑filled impervious graphite" (Table 1, entry 2) ; "a reduction of the supporting electrolyte loading to 0.025 M … resulted in a significant increase in the cell voltage from 7 to 12 V" (p. 5) ; "increase of the current density to 10 mA cm⁻² slightly decreased the selectivity… a further increase to 13 mA cm⁻² resulted in rapid degradation of the anode surface" (Table 1, entries 9‑10) ; "high spinning speeds (i.e., 900 rpm) are detrimental to the reaction conversion when paired with low charge… the DoE model showed that high spinning speeds are favorable when combined with larger amounts of charge" (p. 9‑10).

Paper Title: Design of Experiments-Based Optimization of an Electrochemical Decarboxylative Alkylation Using a Spinning Cylinder Electrode Reactor
Problem_Description: Scaling‑up electrochemical reactions that involve solid suspensions (molecular sieves) in conventional parallel‑plate flow cells leads to clogging and electrode fouling because of the very narrow inter‑electrode gap (< 1 mm). Moreover, the electrolysis generates stoichiometric H₂ gas, which poses an explosion risk when not properly diluted. In the initial small‑scale studies, low conversion was observed at high electrode‑spinning speeds (900 rpm) when the charge passed was insufficient, leading to poor yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors employed a spinning‑cylinder electrode reactor (SCER) with a 5 mm inter‑electrode gap and a rotating inner electrode that provides vigorous mixing and can handle solid suspensions without clogging. Continuous recirculation flow mode with matched inlet/outlet pump rates kept the reaction mixture well‑stirred and prevented solid settling. Safety was addressed by diluting the generated H₂ with N₂ to keep the gas composition below the explosion limit. Finally, the DoE‑derived optimal parameters (spinning speed ≈ 900 rpm, charge ≈ 6 F mol⁻¹, current density ≈ 5.3 mA cm⁻², flow ≈ 50 mL min⁻¹) gave full conversion and 94 % isolated yield, eliminating the low‑yield issue.
Supporting_Evidence: "traditional parallel‑plate flow reactors … the presence of solids can easily cause clogging of the reactor and electrode fouling" (p. 4) ; "the spinning cylinder electrode reactor … provides excellent mixing and enables very efficient agitation of solids in a suspension" (p. 4) ; "electrochemical oxidations described herein produce stoichiometric amounts of H₂ gas … dilution with N₂ … recommended … especially during multigram experimentation" (p. 15) ; "high spinning speeds … poor conversion values at 900 rpm … DoE model showed that high spinning speeds are favorable when combined with larger amounts of charge" (p. 9‑10) ; "full conversion … 94 % isolated yield … 600 mL reaction mixture … 50 mL min⁻¹ flow" (p. 11‑12).

Paper Title: Application of Experimental Design (DoE) to Improve a Very Dilute Workup Procedure
Problem_Description: The original acid‑catalysed rearrangement required an extremely dilute aqueous drown‑out work‑up (∼100 relative volumes of water and NH₄OH) to precipitate the product, making isolation cumbersome and generating large waste streams.
Solution_Description: A face‑centered central‑composite DoE was used to increase the concentration of ketone 1 in methanesulfonic acid (MSA) from 0.4 M to 0.8 M, keep methanol at 9 equiv and operate at 65 °C. This cut the total work‑up volume from 101 RV to 45 RV while preserving product quality.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “extremely dilute aqueous drown‑out process … totaling ∼100 relative volumes (RV)” (Background). 
• “The aim … to decrease the very dilute work‑up procedure required for isolation … without compromising yield, quality” (Abstract). 
• “increase the concentration of ketone 1 in MSA up to 0.8 M … while keeping the level of product 2 formed … ≥93 %” (Results and Discussion). 
• “total volume of the aqueous work‑up could be decreased from 101 RV to 45 … (MSA/methanol reaction mixture 5.4 RV; aqueous NH₄OH 4.5 RV; water 35 RV)” (Drown‑Out Study).

Paper Title: Application of Experimental Design (DoE) to Improve a Very Dilute Workup Procedure
Problem_Description: Running the reaction at lower temperatures (55 °C) gave acceptable impurity levels but required considerably longer reaction times (up to 26 h), reducing throughput; higher temperatures introduced exotherms and increased impurity formation.
Solution_Description: The DoE identified 65 °C as the optimal temperature, balancing reaction rate (≈19 h) and impurity profile. The procedure also stipulated pre‑stirring at ∼20 °C before heating and controlled addition of methanol and ketone to limit temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “Higher temperatures (85 and 95 °C) had given higher levels of diphenol 3 …” (Introduction). 
• “An exotherm of 15 K resulted on this scale without cooling … a more substantial exotherm which must be controlled …” (Experimental Section). 
• “The reaction mixture was stirred at 20 °C for 70 min … before heating to 65 °C as rapidly as possible” (Experimental Section).

Paper Title: Application of Experimental Design (DoE) to Improve a Very Dilute Workup Procedure

Paper Title: Micelle-Enabled Hofmann Rearrangement in Water
Problem_Description: Initial attempts at the Hofmann rearrangement in conventional organic solvents gave poor conversion (33 % yield in MeCN, 58 % in THF, <5 % in DCM, etc.), and even the best organic solvent (DMSO, 91 % yield) was unsuitable for pharmaceutical production because its polarity made the work‑up tedious. Moreover, many organic solvents are flagged under REACH as substances of very high concern, creating regulatory safety issues. When moving to water, the reaction mixture became a white suspension that needed proper physical handling for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors switched the reaction medium to water (solvent change) and added 2 wt % surfactants (TPGS‑750‑M, Triton X‑100, Tween‑80, and finally PS‑750‑M) to create nanomicelles that dramatically increased the assay yield to >90 % (functional additive/promoter). After the reaction, 31 % HCl aqueous solution was added to quench the reaction and generate the amine as its HCl salt (order and rate of addition). The scale‑up was carried out in a 1 L Radley reactor with mechanical stirring, followed by simple aqueous work‑up, toluene extraction, slurry, filtration and drying (reactor platform and materials).
Supporting_Evidence:
“When acetonitrile was selected as the solvent … the desired product 2a was obtained with only 33 % yield … Screening of other organic solvents did not have any improvement, resulting in inferior yields … DMSO was found to produce 91 % yield … this solvent is not recommended in the pharmaceutical industry due to its polar nature, resulting in tedious efforts during the workup process (entry 10).”

“To our delight, when water was used as the sole reaction medium, the desired product could be obtained in 67 % assay yield (entry 13). … the yield was significantly increased to above 90 % when 2 wt %‑TPGS‑750‑M in water … Finally, the best surfactant was identified as PS‑750‑M … producing 95 % assay yield and 93 % yield after isolation (entry 18).”

“Upon completion of the reaction … a 31 % HCl aqueous solution was added to obtain a yellow emulsion … Toluene was added to remove the organic impurity (e.g., phenyl iodide), and the product was collected in the aqueous layer … Filtration and drying allow 52.1 g of product to be produced as a white solid in 90 % yield.”

“With the best conditions in hand, the scale‑up reaction … was performed in a reactor with mechanical stirring.”
