Paper Title: Scale-Up Investigation of Aggarwal Enal Bicyclic Intermediate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Higher hydrolysis (115 °C) and distillation (135 °C) temperatures gave only 66 % dry succinaldehyde; temperature‑related loss of volatile product.
Solution_Description: Lower the hydrolysis temperature to 105 °C and the subsequent distillation steps to 115 °C, which increased the isolated succinaldehyde yield to 75 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “Further improvement … lower temperature was used for hydrolysis (105 °C) and distillation steps (115 °C). The optimized method gave 75 % yield.”; “triple azeotropic distillation … yielded 66 % of dry succinaldehyde.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Investigation of Aggarwal Enal Bicyclic Intermediate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The crude succinaldehyde contained 5–7 % residual water, which negatively impacted the subsequent aldol reaction and promoted polymerisation.
Solution_Description: After azeotropic removal, dry the product with Na₂SO₄ and keep the material frozen (dry‑ice/acetone bath) throughout vacuum distillation to prevent degradation and eliminate water‑induced side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “succinaldehyde produced … was not completely dry (5–7 % water content), which negatively affected the subsequent aldol reaction.”; “It is crucially important to keep collected succinaldehyde frozen during the entire distillation time to prevent its degradation.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Investigation of Aggarwal Enal Bicyclic Intermediate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Succinaldehyde is unstable, exhibiting slow polymerisation and the risk of sudden exothermic polymerisation, which can lead to safety hazards during handling.
Solution_Description: Collect the distilled succinaldehyde at –78 °C in a dry‑ice/acetone bath and store it frozen to suppress polymerisation and avoid exothermic run‑away.
Supporting_Evidence: “Succinaldehyde is a rather unstable liquid, which has a tendency to undergo slow polymerisation … or sudden fast exothermic polymerisation depending on its handling.”; “It is crucially important to keep collected succinaldehyde frozen during the entire distillation time to prevent its degradation.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Investigation of Aggarwal Enal Bicyclic Intermediate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The enal isolation required removal of long‑chain oligomers and residual succinaldehyde; conventional aqueous extractions and column chromatography gave only 32 % overall yield.
Solution_Description: Employ a salt‑out step with aqueous Na₂SO₄, treat the concentrated phase with wet silica gel to adsorb oligomers, and finally recrystallise the enal from toluene, delivering >99 % purity and >90 % recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only two extractions … allow for full recovery of the enal product.”; “wet silica gel … is crucial to adsorb even more oligomers and also part of residual succinaldehyde.”; “toluene was the best solvent for recrystallisation delivering … highly pure (99 %) enal with greater than 90 % product recovery.”

Paper Title: Scale-Up Investigation of Aggarwal Enal Bicyclic Intermediate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Commercial proline batches contain varying amounts of monohydrate (0.5–10 %) and differing crystal habits, leading to inconsistent catalyst dissolution and reaction performance.
Solution_Description: Select a dry proline batch with minimal water content and uniform small crystals; if necessary, recrystallise proline from toluene to obtain the desired polymorph that dissolves readily.
Supporting_Evidence: “PXRD analysis … revealed the presence of a small amount of proline monohydrate (0.5–10 %) in several samples.”; “Generally, the older the sample, the more water it contains due to the high hygroscopicity of proline.”; “Fluorochem proline … was fully soluble in EtOAc under overhead stirring conditions.”

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: The original 14‑step medicinal chemistry route gave only ~0.05 % overall isolated yield, making the sequence impractically low‑yielding and time‑consuming for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Through a series of process‑level optimisations (improved yields of individual steps, streamlined work‑ups, safer reagents and temperature controls) the same sequence was executed on decagram scale delivering the API in 4 % overall yield – an 80‑fold improvement.
Supporting_Evidence: "This sequence consisted of a 14‑step process with a ∼0.05 % overall yield."; "The implementation of these improvements and changes to the synthesis allowed for the preparation of 46 g of KRAS inhibitor 1 in 4 % overall yield which, represents an 80 fold increase in productivity vs the original route."

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: The Rh‑catalysed Hayashi arylation set two stereocenters as a racemic mixture, requiring chiral SFC to isolate the desired diastereomer. This added a costly purification step and lowered material throughput.
Solution_Description: A fully asymmetric synthesis was devised by preparing enantiopure (R)‑4‑methylcyclohex‑2‑en‑1‑one via an Ir‑catalysed asymmetric monohydrogenation and using it in the Hayashi arylation, which gave (R,R)‑5 directly in comparable yield with no need for downstream SFC separation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Hayashi arylation selectively provided a racemic mixture… separated by chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC)"; "Using enantiomerically pure (R)‑4 we were able to access (R,R)‑5 directly… without any loss of stereochemical integrity and in similar yields… proof‑of‑concept for an asymmetric synthesis suggests … could be completed without the necessity of any SFC separations."

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: The nucleophilic aromatic substitution of the sulfone with (S)‑1‑methylpyrrolidin‑2‑yl‑methanol originally employed NaH in DMF, a combination known to present explosion hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: The hazardous NaH/DMF system was replaced by NaHMDS in THF, delivering the desired product in good isolated yield while eliminating the safety risk associated with NaH.
Supporting_Evidence: "the use of NaH in DMF was replaced with a safer option (NaHMDS in THF), providing good yields of the desired product"; "Explosion Hazards of Sodium Hydride in Dimethyl Sulfoxide, N,N‑Dimethylformamide, and N,N‑Dimethylacetamide" (ref 4).

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: Regioselective metalation of the fluorinated aniline proved erratic; direct borylation, Miyaura borylation, and magnesiation all gave incomplete conversion, high impurity levels or poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: A regioselective ortho‑deprotonation was achieved using LiTMP (a strong, sterically hindered base) followed by trapping with tri‑isopropyl borate, affording >99 % of the desired aryl‑boronic acid 14 in a single step.
Supporting_Evidence: "Formation of the fluorinated arylboronic ester… proved challenging… All suffered from incomplete reactions, high impurity levels and/or reproducibility issues."; "We found that a regioselective ortho‑deprotonation using LiTMP, followed by trapping with triisopropyl borate provided >99 % of fluoro‑arylboronic acid 14 after an acidic quench."

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: The aryl‑boronic acid 14 is unstable on scale; its decomposition during handling reduced the efficiency of the subsequent Hayashi arylation step (47 % yield of product 5).
Solution_Description: The crude, unpurified boronic acid 14 was used directly in the rhodium‑catalysed conjugate addition, avoiding isolation steps that exacerbate decomposition and giving the desired ketone 5 in the highest practical yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "The lower yield observed in this step is due to the instability/decomposition of the arylboronic acid 14."; "Use of the crude boronic acid product directly in a subsequent Hayashi arylation… provided the desired cyclohexanone 5 in 47 % yield."

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: Installation of the acrylamide warhead at the end of the sequence generated side‑products unless the addition was tightly controlled, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: The acrylic anhydride was added slowly at –20 °C, which suppressed impurity formation and afforded the final API in >99 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "Finally, installation of the acrylamide was examined under several conditions… we found that at a lower temperature (−20 °C), slow addition of a solution of acrylic anhydride… led to clean profile and high yield (>99 %) of 1."

Paper Title: Fit-for-Purpose Synthesis of a KRAS
Problem_Description: Screening of ~50 Ir‑based catalysts for the asymmetric monohydrogenation of a 1,4‑diene showed widely varying conversion, regio‑ and enantio‑selectivity, making catalyst choice uncertain.
Solution_Description: SimplePHOX ligand (catalyst C1) emerged as the optimal Ir catalyst, delivering the best conversion, regio‑selectivity and 99 % ee across the substrate scope.
Supporting_Evidence: "We performed a preliminary microscale screen of ∼50 selected iridium catalysts… promising results were obtained with catalysts bearing SimplePHOX (C1)… Ultimately, among all tested modifications, SimplePHOX catalyst C1 gave overall the best conversion, regioselectivity and %ee."

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: Batch benzylic photo‑oxidations required long reaction times (up to 24 h) and the use of pure O₂, which poses fire‑risk safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow set‑up using a Corning Advanced‑Flow Reactor (AFR) and compressed air was adopted, providing rapid gas–liquid mixing and reducing the residence time to ~1 min, thereby eliminating the need for pure O₂ and long batch times.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Traditional methods tend to use stoichiometric oxidants… or hypervalent iodine… Direct utilization of oxygen gas… is a much more desirable and sustainable method… This offers safer reaction conditions, as excess oxygen is prevented, reducing the risk of fire by solvent ignition.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: Increasing the liquid flow rate without a corresponding increase in gas flow reduced the amount of oxygen available, lowering conversion and yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Gas flow was increased proportionally to maintain 2.2 equiv of O₂, and the AFR’s heart‑shaped cells ensured effective gas–liquid mixing, preserving conversion at higher throughputs.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When the liquid flow rate was increased to 1.6 mL min⁻¹, the gas flow rate had to also be increased to maintain 2.2 equiv of oxygen…this reduced the residence time, which caused a reduction in yield for 2a.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: At higher catalyst loadings the water‑soluble SAS showed reduced solubility in the reaction solvent.
Solution_Description: The MeCN:H₂O co‑solvent ratio was adjusted from 3:1 to 1:1 to maintain full catalyst solubility when the loading was increased to 40 mol %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When increasing the amount of catalyst to 40 mol % and adjusting the solvent mixture to ensure full solubility (i.e., 1:1 MeCN:H₂O) a notable increase in product yield was observed.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: Using 20 mol % SAS for aldehyde‑forming substrates gave low yields (≤27 %).
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was increased to 40 mol % and the solvent composition was changed to a 1:1 MeCN:H₂O mixture, which raised conversion and product yield to 77 % for the aldehyde series.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When using 20 mol % of SAS similarly to our standard conditions, lower yields for aldehyde 2n were obtained… however, when increasing the amount of catalyst to 40 mol % and adjusting the solvent mixture… a notable increase in product yield was observed (entry 3).”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: For substrate 1k, C–C bond cleavage occurred under the standard 375 nm illumination, producing benzaldehyde as a major side product.
Solution_Description: Alternative LED wavelengths (340, 395, 422 nm) were screened in an attempt to suppress the cleavage, although the undesired product remained dominant.
Supporting_Evidence: • “C–C bond cleavage giving benzaldehyde as a side product (∼40 %) was observed at 375 nm. Alternative wavelengths (340, 395, and 422 nm) were trialed to reduce the amount of C–C bond cleavage, however, this was not successful…”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Approach for Benzylic Photo-oxidations Using Compressed Air
Problem_Description: When the reaction was performed without a stream of air, only 10 % conversion was observed and a dimer of diphenylmethane formed.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
[MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Maintaining a continuous flow of compressed air (2.2 equiv O₂) restored high conversion (>99 %) and prevented dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Performing the reaction without a stream of air resulted in only 10 % substrate conversion with no ketone product observed, instead a dimer of diphenylmethane was observed (entry 6).”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The first‑generation Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation gave the undesired stereoisomer as the major product (6a) with a 1:3–1:4 ratio of desired 6 to undesired 6a, leading to low isolated yield of the target.
Solution_Description: Switching the ester protecting group from a methyl ester to a benzoyl ester reversed the stereochemical preference of the Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation, delivering the desired stereoisomer as the major product (95:5–97:3) and enabling a scalable second‑generation route.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation exhibited opposite stereoselectivity with a benzoyl ester … resulting in the desired stereoisomer as the major product.”; “The latter gratifyingly yielded the desired product with a remarkable 95:5–97:3 selectivity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Both the first‑generation route required silica‑gel column chromatography after methylation and cyclopropanation to separate the desired product from by‑products; this step was inefficient and not amenable to scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A benzylamine‑salt crystallization was introduced to selectively precipitate the desired diastereomer, eliminating the need for column chromatography and providing a practical isolation method for large scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The benzylamine salt was identified … to enable the effective separation of the desired stereoisomer in a reasonable yield.”; “The benzylamine salt formation was a purification step that was key to achieve the desired chemical purity and eliminating undesired stereoisomers.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The generation‑1 process relied on multiple isomerization and recycling cycles, achieving only ~40 % overall recovery of the desired benzylamine salt, making the sequence inefficient and time‑consuming.
Solution_Description: By employing the benzoyl‑ester substrate, the second‑generation route generated the correct stereoisomer directly, removing the need for repeated isomerization/recycling and dramatically improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The process to carry out the benzylamine salt break initially employed … total recovery … was ∼40 %.”; “The use of the benzoyl ester substrate for the cyclopropanation enabled obtaining the desired stereoisomer as the major product.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The cyclopropanation step with diethylzinc and chloroiodomethane is highly exothermic, raising safety concerns for heat removal and reagent handling at scale.
Solution_Description: Process safety data (calorimetry) were collected; the addition of diethylzinc and chloroiodomethane was staged and temperature‑controlled (−25 °C → 0 °C) to keep adiabatic temperature rises mild and to safely quench residual reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Heat evolution was monitored by reaction calorimetry … the adiabatic temperature rises associated with each reaction stage are mild and can be scaled‑up safely.”; “Diethylzinc was added … at −25 °C … chloroiodomethane added in four portions … mixture warmed to 0 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Bredereck’s reagent showed inconsistent performance depending on the commercial source, leading to variable yields (52 %–91 %) in the Bredereck’s/hydrogenation sequence.
Solution_Description: A pre‑use test of each reagent batch was implemented to qualify source quality before scale‑up, ensuring consistent high yields (up to 91 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “We observed high variability in reaction performance depending on the source of Bredereck’s reagent … 52 %–91 % yields.”; “Hence, a use‑test prior to utilization was incorporated.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: During the oxidation of the primary alcohol to the acid, deviation from the required simultaneous addition of NaClO and NaClO₂ generated two unknown impurities at ~5 % level.
Solution_Description: The oxidation was optimized to add NaClO and NaClO₂ simultaneously at a controlled rate, eliminating impurity formation and delivering the desired product in high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “If not added simultaneously, two unknown impurities … will be generated.”; “Simultaneous addition of NaClO and NaClO₂ at a controlled rate … was required.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Initial solvent screens for benzylamine‑salt formation gave poor yields or solid‑handling issues; the choice of solvent strongly influenced diastereomeric purity and isolation yield.
Solution_Description: An optimized solvent system of acetonitrile (or toluene) was identified, providing the highest yield (66 %) and excellent stereochemical purity for the benzylamine salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acetonitrile and toluene were found to have the most favorable combination… Yield 66 %.”; Table 5 showing solvent comparison.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of Cyclopropyl-Methyl-Proline with Complex Stereochemistry: A Key Building Block of Factor D Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Oxidation using TPAP or CrO₃ gave high yields but involved expensive metals and added downstream metal‑removal steps.
Solution_Description: The oxidation was switched to a TEMPO/NaClO/NaClO₂ catalytic system, which is inexpensive, avoids metal waste, and maintains high yields (75 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “TPAP and CrO₃ gave the best results … however, to avoid the higher costs associated with metals … we selected TEMPO as the oxidizing agent.”; Table 4 entries 7–9 showing 75 % yield with TEMPO.

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: Conjugation work with the native maleimide‑linked cytotoxic payloads (e.g., MMAE‑based linkers) requires handling highly toxic compounds.  Specialized isolators and dedicated laboratories are needed, raising capital expense, limiting the number of experiments that can be performed, and creating occupational‑exposure concerns.
Solution_Description: Replace the toxic linker/payload with commercially available, nontoxic ADC‑mimic maleimides that retain the required conjugation chemistry and HIC‑shifting behavior, allowing work to be performed in standard process‑development labs.
Supporting_Evidence: • “For process development of ADCs, the cytotoxic nature of the linker/payloads (LPs) is a significant challenge… experimental work is often confined to specifically designed laboratories… The space in potent laboratories is constrained, which limits the number and type of studies …” (Intro, p. 1)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: A first test set of eight commercially available maleimides (MAL‑1 – MAL‑8) gave no discernible HIC retention‑time shift, indicating insufficient lipophilicity and therefore poor utility as HIC‑shifting mimics.
Solution_Description: Assemble a larger, diverse maleimide collection (> 90 compounds) guided by filter rules that prioritize hydrophobic substituents remote from the maleimide core, increasing the chance of obtaining HIC‑shifting mimics.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Unfortunately, no significant shifts … were observed. This suggests … due to insufficient lipophilicity.” (Sec 2.1)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: Some screened maleimides (e.g., MAL‑45) produced broad, non‑resolved HIC peaks, suggesting decomposition or formation of multiple conjugate species, making data interpretation unreliable.
Solution_Description: Select only those maleimides that give clean, well‑resolved HIC peaks with consistent DAR‑0 → DAR‑2 shifts (e.g., MAL‑27, MAL‑75, MAL‑78, MAL‑82, MAL‑83, MAL‑85, MAL‑97).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Figure 3 compares … a nonshifting maleimide (B), a strongly shifting maleimide (E), … a maleimide that results in the appearance of multiple broad, nonresolved peaks (A)… could be indicative of the formation of multiple mAb conjugates …” (Sec 2.2)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: Conjugation efficiency and the distribution of DAR species varied dramatically with pH, maleimide equivalents, and the specific mimic used; some mimics (e.g., MAL‑85 at low equivalents) gave almost no conjugation.
Solution_Description: Perform a three‑factor high‑throughput screen (pH 5.5 vs 7.0, 2.5–7.8 equiv maleimide, seven mimics) to identify optimal pH (7.0) and stoichiometry that maximize DAR‑2 formation while minimizing side‑product peaks.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The results … reveal that conjugations generally proceed more readily at pH 7.0… The LP mimics show similar but not identical reactivity… MAL‑85 is almost unreactive at 2.5 equiv …” (Sec 2.5)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: MAL‑78 showed poor stability in the water/DMSO dosing mixture, leading to very low DAR in flow runs; MAL‑83 precipitated during flow, causing reactor clogging.
Solution_Description: Prepare mimic solutions in water/DMSO 9:1 just before the run to minimize degradation; adjust concentration to stay below solubility limits (e.g., avoid high‑concentration MAL‑83 solutions) to prevent precipitation and clogging.
Supporting_Evidence: • “MAL‑78 … poor stability … aged solutions … showed either poor or no conversion, both in batch and in flow.” (Sec 2.8)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: When low equivalents of MAL‑27 were used together with sub‑stoichiometric TCEP, increased low‑molecular‑weight fragments (2.7 % LMW) were observed, likely due to uncontrolled TCEP reduction and side‑reaction of TCEP with the maleimide.
Solution_Description: Use an excess of maleimide (≥ 4.5 equiv) to quench residual TCEP after reduction, thereby preventing mAb fragmentation and ensuring robust conjugation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Elevated fragmentation (2.7 % LMW) is observed when treating the mAb with 2.1 equiv TCEP + 3.0 equiv MAL‑27. This suggests that the lower amount of MAL‑27 … leads to fragment formation, likely via uncontrolled TCEP reduction… the excess of maleimide used … prevents damage to the mAb structure by quenching the remainder of non‑oxidized TCEP.” (Sec 2.7)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: Scaling flow conjugation required a reactor capable of reliable mixing at low flow rates (µL min⁻¹) and construction from materials compatible with protein solutions; commercial glass chips were prohibitively expensive and not readily available.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Design and fabricate custom PDMS micromixers via 3‑D‑printed molds and evaluate geometries (connected‑groove design) to achieve rapid mixing; later transfer to an in‑line static mixer (1.6 mm ID PTFE) for gram‑scale operation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Rather than relying on commercially available yet expensive glass microchips, we chose to focus on the design and fabrication of custom‑made micromixers… The decision … enabled rapid turn‑around and testing of different mixer geometries… Efficient mixing was achieved with the connected‑groove mixer geometry…” (Sec 2.8)

Paper Title: “Build Your Own” ADC Mimics: Identification of Nontoxic Linker/Payload Mimics for HIC-Based DAR Determination, High-Throughput Optimization, and Continuous Flow Conjugation
Problem_Description: Continuous‑flow ADC conjugation traditionally demands large amounts of toxic payload, increasing process‑mass‑intensity and operator exposure.
Solution_Description: By using the nontoxic LP mimics, the amount of toxic payload can be minimized; the high‑throughput studies identified conditions where low equivalents (2.5 – 3.5) of mimic still afford high DAR, lowering material usage and exposure risk.
Supporting_Evidence: • “This is an important consideration for conjugation processes, especially when using toxic LPs for ADC production: in such situations, minimizing the equivalents of LP would result in a lower process mass intensity (PMI) and minimize the potential for exposure to toxic process intermediates.” (Sec 2.8)

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: During the large‑scale opening of (R)‑epichlorohydrin with allyl‑magnesium chloride (AMC) the exothermic addition of the substrate to the cold AMC solution required a 32 h addition time on a 367 kg scale. The long addition led to >10 % bis‑addition by‑product formation, lowering the isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The addition mode was reversed – AMC was charged to a cooled solution of epichlorohydrin – which allowed the addition time to be shortened, reduced the bis‑addition impurity to 0.5 % by area and lowered the AMC equivalents from 1.4 to 1.1 while maintaining >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Adequate temperature control during the exothermic addition of the substrate to the cold AMC solution required a 32 h addition time on a 367 kg scale … This long addition time resulted in the formation of >10 % UPLC area percent … This issue was addressed in subsequent batches by charging AMC to a cooled solution of 9, leading to low levels (0.5 % by area) of this by‑product … Employing this mode of addition also enabled the equivalents of AMC to be lowered from 1.4 to 1.1 equiv while achieving >99 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: The initial protocol for the epoxy‑olefin Hodgson substrate employed 0.05 equiv copper‑I iodide; copper catalysis added cost and caused inconsistent performance on scale.
Solution_Description: Copper‑free conditions were discovered to give improved conversion and higher purity, eliminating the need for the copper catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although 0.05 equiv copper‑(I) iodide was used in the first 180 kg manufacturing batch … it was found that the copper catalysis often employed for such reactions was not required, and the reaction performance improved under copper‑free conditions to afford chlorohydrin 10 …”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: The C‑H oxidation using NaClO/N‑hydroxyphthalimide generated chlorine dioxide gas; a lab‑scale incident showed sparking and required emergency cooling, indicating a serious safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the sodium‑chlorite oxidation and developed alternative α‑oxidation sequences (PIDA‑mediated, Albright‑Goldman oxidation, nitrite oxidation) that proceeded at ambient temperature without hazardous gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: “A preliminary process safety evaluation … demonstrated that the addition of sodium chlorite was exothermic … An incident … observed sparking … it was hypothesized chlorine dioxide had formed … Because of this event, development of an alternative approach … was prioritized … The first oxidation condition discovered … PIDA‑mediated transformation … Cryogenic Swern oxidation … the Albright–Goldman oxidation … was found to afford high conversion and purity at ambient temperature using less‑expensive inputs.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: Bicyclic ketone 13 readily formed a bisulfite adduct, making direct isolation difficult and leading to impurity carry‑over.
Solution_Description: Formation of the bisulfite adduct 16 allowed extraction of the ketone into the aqueous phase, rejecting organic impurities; subsequent regeneration with KOH gave pure ketone 13 in MTBE.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the strained nature of the bicyclic ketone, we found that 13 readily formed a bisulfite adduct 16 which could be extracted into the aqueous layer, rejecting most organic impurities to the MTBE layer … Treating the resulting aqueous bisulfite layer with potassium hydroxide reverted adduct 16 to 13, which could be taken up in MTBE with the rejection of inorganic impurities.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: Alkyl nitrite reagents (iso‑amyl, tert‑butyl nitrite) used in the nitrite oxidation were toxic, highly flammable, energetically unstable and had limited commercial supply.
Solution_Description: The oxidation step was re‑engineered to use inexpensive, non‑explosive sodium nitrite under acidic conditions, eliminating the need for hazardous alkyl nitrites.
Supporting_Evidence: “A concern with the second‑generation route … was the supply chain availability and process safety of the alkyl nitrite reagents … isoamyl nitrite … was found to have a decomposition onset of 156 °C with an exotherm of –1758 J g⁻¹ … therefore, an alternative approach was sought to avoid the use of alkyl nitrites in favor of safer sodium nitrite, for which no exotherm was observed up to 350 °C.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: The oxidative desulfurative fluorination with DBDMH and HF·pyridine was highly exothermic; manual sampling caused temperature spikes, variable quenching, and posed corrosion hazards to reactor materials.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The oxidant mixture (DBDMH + HF·pyridine) was pre‑formed and aged; the addition of the dithiolane substrate was performed slowly at –12 °C; Hastelloy C22 reactors replaced corrosion‑prone stainless/ glass; an automated EasySampler was introduced for safe, reproducible sampling.
Supporting_Evidence: “For this reaction, it was determined that preformation of the active oxidant mixture greatly improved reaction performance … after the oxidant mixture was aged, a dry DCM solution of 7 was then charged slowly … to control the resulting exotherm … The fluorination reaction is rapid, and any warming of samples can bias the EoR conversion … an EasySampler … was used to sample the reaction mixture autonomously, safely, and reliably.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: The original fluorination work‑up required >65 L kg⁻¹ of water due to the large excess of DBDMH (3.4 equiv) and HF·pyridine (17 equiv), generating massive salt loads and limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: The oxidant charge was reduced to 2.4 equiv DBDMH (20 % overage) and HF·pyridine to 17 equiv, cutting the aqueous quench volume in half (to 14 L kg⁻¹) and eliminating filtration of the biphasic mixture, which raised throughput by 32 % and lowered PMI.
Supporting_Evidence: “By reducing the oxidant charge, the sodium metabisulfite could be reduced to 1.0 equiv and the potassium hydroxide to 24 equiv. This lower salt burden allowed the total amount of water needed … to be reduced by half to 14 L kg⁻¹ … The improvement led to a 32 % increase in throughput, with a new Vmax of 42 L kg⁻¹ and reduced PMI.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: After fluorination, the crude product solution was amber and contained colored impurities, resulting in colored solids and poor appearance.
Solution_Description: Treatment of the ethanolic solution with Darco KB‑G activated carbon removed color; the clarified solution was then crystallized to give light‑yellow, filterable solids with low liquor loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “Evaluation of scavengers … identified KB‑G activated carbon in EtOH as a preferred treatment for color removal. After the aqueous workup, the stream of 1 was solvent‑exchanged … and treated with activated carbon … to afford a clarified light‑yellow solution … followed by seeding and crystallization to afford filterable solids as large granular particles with excellent impurity rejection.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: The lithium salt 25 of the enolate formed a fine needle, hygroscopic solid that filtered slowly and was difficult to handle on scale.
Solution_Description: Screening of alternative amine salts led to the diisopropylamine (DIPA) salt 26, which gave a crystalline, less hygroscopic solid with better filtration properties and high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The lithium salt 25 … was found to have poor solid properties … filtration of the solid was very slow … and the resulting solid was very hygroscopic … To improve these properties, alternative salts … were explored … the DIPA salt was chosen … affording enolate 26 in high yield and purity.”

Paper Title: Synthetic Development and Scale-Up of a Complex Pyrazole Fragment of Lenacapavir
Problem_Description: When the fluorination process was transferred to a third manufacturing site, an elevated ketone 6 impurity (13 %) appeared, traced to trace water or methanol in equipment.
Solution_Description: Equipment conditioning and removal of residual water/methanol were implemented (no successful water scavenger), allowing subsequent batches to meet quality specifications.
Supporting_Evidence: “... the first manufacturing batch contained an elevated amount of ketone 6 impurity at 13 % … root cause was linked to one piece of equipment containing a trace amount of either water or methanol … a water scavenger … was attempted … not successful … minor adjustments to the reactor train … were made to ensure that water or methanol was fully removed prior to operation.”

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Batch chlorosulfonation of 4‑methoxy‑phenylacetone gave low isolated yields (32 %‑50 %) and produced a brown solid/oil. The reaction is highly exothermic when the acidic mixture is added to cold water and the viscous reaction mixture is difficult to transfer, creating operational challenges on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors moved the chlorosulfonation to a continuous‑flow reactor using DCM as solvent, maintained the reaction at 30 °C and directly quenched the stream into an ice‑water/DCF mixture. Flow operation reduced the hazardous exotherm, eliminated the viscous transfer problem and afforded a white crystalline sulfonyl chloride intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: Batch problems: “Adding ClSO₃H to 4‑MPA … gave yields of 32 and 22–50 % … The reaction mixture’s high viscosity makes transfer difficult, thereby posing operational challenges.” (Results and Discussion, paragraph 2). Flow solution: “Switching to flow would increase the safety surrounding the use of chlorosulfonic acid and reduce the time required for quenching.” (Results and Discussion, paragraph 5).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: The initial batch chlorosulfonation runs (entries 1‑3) produced only 32 %–50 % isolated sulfonamide, far below the reported ~50 % and with colour impurities due to oversulfonation and self‑condensation of the ketone.
Solution_Description: Continuous flow chlorosulfonation in DCM gave a cleaner white product (sulfonyl chloride) with comparable or higher yield, minimizing oversulfonation and improving colour and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Batch low yields: “Adding ClSO₃H to 4‑MPA … gave yields of 32 and 22–50 % … the product was not stable … oversulfonation and self‑condensation …” (Results and Discussion, paragraph 2). Flow improvement: “Continuous chlorosulfonation produced a white crystalline solid … the colour of isolated sulfonamide 6 was significantly improved … white solid without requiring recrystallization.” (Results and Discussion, paragraph 7).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Whole‑cell E. coli transaminases (ArR‑ATA, ArRmut‑ATA, AtR‑ATA) gave modest conversions (40 %–43 %) and insufficient enantioselectivity, indicating poor catalytic performance for the key asymmetric step.
Solution_Description: A systematic screening of lyophilised ATAs from the Codex® Transaminase Kit identified ATA‑412, which delivered 97 % conversion with >99 % ee, providing a superior biocatalytic route.
Supporting_Evidence: Whole‑cell low conversion: “The highest conversion achieved (ArRmut‑ATA) was only 43 % and without sufficient enantioselectivity (91 % R). ArR‑ATA gave an excellent ee (>99 % R) albeit with a moderate conversion of 40 %.” (Enzyme Screening). Successful new enzyme: “The highest conversion (97 %) was achieved with ATA‑412 while maintaining perfect enantiomeric selectivity.” (Enzyme Screening).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Long‑term stability tests showed rapid deactivation of ATA‑117 (50 % loss after 4 h, complete loss after 48 h) and partial loss for ATA‑P2‑A07/B01, compromising consistent performance on scale.
Solution_Description: The more robust ATA‑412 was selected for further development, as it retained full activity after 48 h incubation, providing a stable biocatalyst for the process.
Supporting_Evidence: Stability problem: “ATA‑117 showed the most severe inactivation; after just 4 h … its activity had decreased by 50 %, and 48 h … completely deactivated the ATA.” (Long‑Term Stability). Stable enzyme choice: “ATA‑412 … provided the same conversion both without incubation and after 48 h of incubation; therefore, this ATA was stable for a total of 72 h.” (Long‑Term Stability).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Reducing the amine‑donor excess (from 75 equiv to 7.5 equiv) dramatically lowered conversion for most ATAs, limiting the process efficiency.
Solution_Description: Switching the amine donor from isopropylamine to sec‑butylamine (15 % v/v) restored high conversion for ATA‑412 (57 % → 74 %) and maintained >99 % ee, demonstrating the importance of donor identity and stoichiometry.
Supporting_Evidence: Low conversion with reduced donor: “Reducing the donor equivalent resulted in significantly reduced conversion in all cases.” (Long‑Term Stability). Improved donor choice: “With 7.5 equiv of sec‑butylamine, ATA‑412 operated with twice the conversion as compared to isopropylamine.” (Long‑Term Stability, Table 4).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Sulfonamide 6 exhibits low solubility (<100 mg mL⁻¹) in most organic solvents, limiting substrate concentration and causing substrate‑ or product‑inhibition that reduced conversion at higher concentrations.
Solution_Description: DMF (10 % v/v) was employed as a cosolvent to improve reaction homogeneity, and substrate concentration was limited to ≤50 mM with 15 % v/v isopropylamine, balancing solubility and conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Solubility issue: “Sulfonamide 6 exhibits low solubility … less than 100 mg mL⁻¹; consequently, a 50 mM substrate concentration … resulted in a heterogeneous reaction mixture.” (Cosolvent). Conversion drop: “With increasing substrate concentration, the conversion decreased consistently by 15–20 % … indicating substrate‑ or product‑induced inhibition.” (Substrate Concentration Screening).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: At 50 mM substrate concentration the transamination conversion fell, suggesting either substrate inhibition or insufficient catalyst loading.
Solution_Description: Doubling the amount of ATA‑412 from 2 mg to 4 mg per reaction improved conversion by 15 % (isopropylamine) and 8 % (sec‑butylamine), indicating higher enzyme loading mitigates the inhibition effect.
Supporting_Evidence: Enzyme loading test: “Doubling the enzyme concentration only led to a 15 % increase in conversion with isopropylamine and 8 % increase with sec‑butylamine; therefore, the enzyme was maintained at 2 mg mL⁻¹ for further experiments.” (Enzyme/Substrate Ratio).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Covalently immobilized ATA‑412 on magnetic nanoparticles (MNPs) suffered progressive activity loss (≈14 % after 120 h) due to exposure of the enzyme surface to the reaction medium, limiting long‑term reuse.
Solution_Description: A second immobilization method using porous polymeric Resindion ReliZyme beads provided better enzyme shielding, resulting in >90 % activity retention after 5 × 24 h cycles and only a 6 % loss after 10 cycles.
Supporting_Evidence: MNP deactivation: “… in the fifth cycle, only 80 % conversion was detected … meaning approximately 14 % activity loss in 120 h of operation.” (Stability Testing of the ATA412@MNP). Resin performance: “After 5 cycles, the initial activity was maintained … only a 6 % decrease … after the 10th cycle.” (Stability Testing of the ATA‑412@ReliZyme).

Paper Title: Step-Economic Synthesis of Tamsulosin Hydrochloride via Continuous Chlorosulfonation and Biocatalytic Transamination
Problem_Description: Sulfonamide 6 is poorly soluble and the chiral amine (R)‑2 is highly water‑soluble; isolating the amine from the aqueous biocatalytic mixture would require cumbersome extractions, reducing overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: The authors telescoped the transamination directly into the N‑alkylation step without isolating the amine, filtering off the immobilised enzyme and proceeding with the downstream reaction in the same pot.
Supporting_Evidence: Telescoping rationale: “To avoid the need for isolating (R)‑2 … a telescoping reaction was envisioned … Following transamination, ATA‑412@ReliZyme was filtered off and recycled for the next round.” (Telescoping of the Asymmetric Synthesis and N‑Alkylation).

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Batch reactions using inorganic azide generate hydrazoic acid (HN₃) that can accumulate in the headspace of the reactor, creating a toxic and explosive hazard especially at elevated temperatures.
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a continuous‑flow micro‑reactor equipped with a 250 psi back‑pressure regulator and a downstream NaOH quench flask. The plug‑flow geometry prevents head‑space formation, and the pressure regulator suppresses evaporation and gas‑phase HN₃ formation, making the operation safe.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Even small, laboratory‑scale reactions pose serious safety issues … due to the toxic and explosive hydrazoic acid (HN₃) that can accumulate in the headspace of the reactor.”
• “The pressure was regulated by incorporating a 250 psi back pressure regulator (BPR) after the reactor. This prevented evaporation and hazardous gas formation, even at high temperatures.”
• “At the output, the product was collected in a stirred flask containing sodium hydroxide solution … to avoid the liberation of HN₃ gas.”
• “Continuous‑flow technology … preclude headspace formation in microreactors.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: When benzylamine was used, the desired 1‑substituted tetrazole (5a) was only a minor product; the reaction mainly gave formamidine (6) and formamide (7) as kinetic by‑products.
Solution_Description: Guided by DFT calculations, the temperature was raised to 150 °C and the residence time shortened to 11.25 min, while keeping the optimal 3 equiv of TMSN₃ and 3.6 equiv of TMOF. Under these conditions the thermodynamically favored tetrazole became the major product (73 % isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The analysis of the reaction mixture … showed that the targeted tetrazole … was only a minor product … by‑products … formamidine (6) and formamide (7) …”
• “According to the calculations, the tetrazole … is the thermodynamically most stable product, but this may require overcoming a high energy barrier … leading to kinetic by‑products.”
• “The maximum yield of the product was reached at a residence time of 15 min. This could be somewhat shortened (11.25 min) when the reaction temperature was raised to 150 °C … and the product was isolated with 73 % yield.”
• “Any deviation from the initially applied 3 equiv of TMSN₃ and 3.6 equiv of TMOF resulted in poorer performance.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Aromatic amine 2‑chloroaniline gave a significant drop in tetrazole yield because the reaction preferentially formed N‑acetyl (8) and N‑methylcarbamate (9) by‑products, which are thermodynamically favored.
Solution_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature to 100 °C and using an 8‑min residence time suppressed by‑product formation and restored high conversion and selectivity to the desired tetrazole (11c).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Analysis of the reaction mixture showed … formation of different by‑products … N‑acetyl (8) and N‑methylcarbamate (9) … thermodynamically favored instead of the targeted tetrazole.”
• “Suppression of by‑product formation and better product yields were achieved at lower temperatures … High selectivity with good conversion was shown at 100 °C with a residence time of 8 min.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Certain benzylamines (e.g., 4j) are insoluble in acetic acid, preventing homogeneous reaction conditions and leading to lower yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent mixture of acetic acid and N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (AcOH:NMP, 1:5) was employed to dissolve the substrate, enabling the continuous‑flow reaction to proceed with acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Due to the insolubility of 4j in acetic acid, a mixture of acetic acid and N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) in a 1:5 ratio was applied. The product (5j) could be isolated with a somewhat lower yield from this solvent mixture.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Traditional 1‑substituted tetrazole syntheses rely on hazardous inorganic azides and expensive metal catalysts, limiting scalability and increasing risk.
Solution_Description: A catalyst‑free continuous‑flow method using liquid trimethylsilyl‑azide (TMSN₃) as a safer, more soluble azide source was developed, eliminating the need for expensive catalysts and reducing safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The available synthetic strategies … typically lengthy … requiring the use of hazardous inorganic azides, as well as expensive catalysts … Even small, laboratory‑scale reactions pose serious safety issues …”
• “We report the development of a safe, one‑step, catalyst‑free, continuous‑flow method for the synthesis of 1‑substituted‑1H‑tetrazoles.”
• “Liquid trimethylsilyl‑azide (TMSN₃) was selected as the azide source … organic azides … are more soluble … TMSN₃ is reported to have adequate thermal stability.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Batch cyclizations of amines to tetrazoles require prolonged heating (several hours), limiting throughput for process development.
Solution_Description: Transition to a micro‑flow reactor (1.5 mL volume) allowed residence times of 8–15 min while maintaining high conversion, dramatically increasing the production rate (e.g., 384 mg h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Even small, laboratory‑scale reactions pose serious safety issues … the required reaction times are excessive.”
• “The aim of the optimization was to reach a short residence time while maximizing tetrazole productivity within a small sized (1.5 mL) reactor …”
• “Running the optimized reaction for several hours … gave 84 % yield (1.73 g, 384 mg h⁻¹ productivity).”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Potential loss of azide through PTFE reactor walls could lead to uncontrolled azide exposure and variability in azide consumption.
Solution_Description: Control experiments using glass reactors and a microchip flow reactor demonstrated that azide loss through PTFE was insignificant, confirming safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “To investigate possible HN₃ losses by penetration through the PTFE reactor wall, we carried out control reactions … In these cases, similar quantities of azide were required to reach sufficient conversion, showing that azide loss through penetration was insignificant.”

Paper Title: One-Step, Catalyst-Free Continuous-Flow Method for the Rapid and Safe Synthesis of 1‑Substituted 1
Problem_Description: Thermal decomposition of tetrazole products could pose an explosion risk during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) of representative tetrazoles revealed no significant exothermic decomposition up to the reaction temperature range, confirming low explosive potential.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The analysis suggested that these products exhibit a low explosive potential, as no significant exothermic decomposition was detected over the temperature range applied in the synthetic methods described here.”
• “Together with the thermal stability of TMSN₃ and other starting materials … this ensured safe operation in laboratory‑scale continuous‑flow reactors.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Initial Sonogashira‑type alkynylation using 3 mol % Pd(PPh₃)₂Cl₂ and CuI gave variable conversion and generated alkyne dimer (Glaser coupling) while copper loading further reduced conversion and purity.
Solution_Description: Copper was omitted and the reaction was run at 75 °C in 2‑MeTHF with NEt₃ as base, which restored high conversion (93 %) and cleaner product.
Supporting_Evidence: ["these conditions suffered from variable reaction performance and oxidation of the copper‑alkyne species which resulted in elevated levels of alkyne dimerization (Glaser coupling).","CuI ranging studies up to 6 mol % loading indicated that both reaction conversion and purity profile were negatively impacted when copper was present.","omitting CuI (entry 3) led to a significant reduction of the reaction rate at 50 °C. By elevating the temperature from 50 to 75 °C (entry 4), conversion of this Heck alkynylation reaction could be improved to 93%.","2‑MeTHF was chosen for further development because it would allow for an aqueous palladium extraction during the workup.","NEt₃ was ultimately chosen as the base for this reaction."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: When the alkynylation was performed in MeCN, cooling caused premature precipitation of NADL and the isolated product contained high palladium (>2500 ppm) and low assay due to the NADL impurity.
Solution_Description: A small amount of water (0.5 part) was added at elevated temperature to keep NADL in solution, then N‑acetyl‑L‑cysteine (NAC) scavenger was used, reducing palladium to ≤121 ppm and giving 99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["cooling the contents led to the premature precipitation of N‑acetyl‑d‑leucine (NADL)... isolated 14 had low purity and assay due to the presence of NADL.","14 isolated using this process had a palladium content >2500 ppm.","to solubilize NADL and limit the premature precipitation, a small amount of water (0.50 part) was added to the end of the reaction mixture at elevated temperature.","This produced a homogeneous solution to which metal scavengers could be added to control the palladium content.","Aging various scavengers at 50 °C for 4 h reduced the palladium level from 2789 ppm to considerably lower levels, with NAC (entry 2) providing the best palladium purge."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: The initial amide coupling using EDC·HCl/HOBt·H₂O generated EDU and HOBt by‑products that poisoned the Pd catalyst in the downstream Suzuki step, causing incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: Propanephosphonic acid anhydride (T3P) in MeCN/DMF was adopted as the coupling reagent; it required only 1 equiv of the expensive acid component, gave fast reaction, and its by‑products were compatible with the Suzuki reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: ["byproducts from the initial process, 1‑ethyl‑3‑(3‑(dimethylamino)‑propyl)‑urea (EDU) and HOBt, were found to poison the Pd‑catalyst in the downstream Suzuki coupling, leading to incomplete conversion.","propanephosphonic acid anhydride (T3P) was chosen for further development due to the fast reaction time and need for only 1.0 equiv of the complex and expensive coupling partner 12.","T3P and its byproducts were well tolerated in the downstream Suzuki reaction."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: The first Suzuki cross‑coupling (Generation 1) required >24 h at reflux to reach >95 % conversion and produced a heterogeneous mixture that needed filtration through diatomaceous earth before work‑up.
Solution_Description: Switching to n‑BuOAc allowed higher reaction temperature, KHCO₃ replaced K₂HPO₄·3H₂O, and the product was isolated as a bis‑methanesulfonic‑acid (MsOH) salt by crystallisation using n‑Bu₂O as antisolvent, eliminating the need for diatomaceous‑earth filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The penultimate step... required >24 h at reflux to reach a conversion of >95%.","For the next scale‑up, n‑BuOAc was substituted for i‑PrOAc in order to allow for a higher reaction temperature to drive the reaction to completion while still using Pd‑(PCy₃)₂Cl₂ as the catalyst.","KHCO₃ was substituted for K₂HPO₄·3H₂O which provided a similar reaction purity profile using less mass and fewer equivalents of base.","crystallization of a bis‑methanesulfonic acid (MsOH) salt was developed.","n‑Bu₂O was chosen as the antisolvent, as it delivered better palladium purge compared to alkane solvents and minimized losses to liquors compared to other ethereal solvents."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Generation 2 Suzuki still required a lengthy heterogeneous work‑up and exhibited variable palladium removal; emulsions formed during aqueous NAC treatment reduced the palladium purge by ~50 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A homogeneous catalysis system (PdCl₂ + CyPPh₂) in 2‑MeTHF at 70 °C with 2 mol % Pd and 4 mol % ligand gave 100 % conversion in ~12 h; addition of EtOH as a cosolvent in the NAC washes prevented emulsion formation and restored consistent palladium removal.
Supporting_Evidence: ["While most catalysts evaluated did not provide high conversion at 75 °C in i‑PrOAc, PCy₃ Pd G2 and PdCl₂ + CyPPh₂ allowed for full conversion.","PdCl₂ + CyPPh₂ was chosen for further development due to the clean reaction profile, lower cost, fewer by‑products, and easier sourcing of this precatalyst and ligand.","PdCl₂ + CyPPh₂ (2 mol %) and CyPPh₂ (4 mol %) in 2‑MeTHF at 70 °C (entry 10) provided 100 % conversion with high purity in ∼12 h and afforded a homogeneous solution at the end of the reaction.","When emulsions were observed, the palladium purge was reduced by about half, and a recrystallization had to be implemented.","It was discovered that the addition of EtOH as a cosolvent in the NAC treatments allowed for consistent, clean phase splits."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Oxygen ingress during the alkaline NAC work‑up of intermediate 16 caused inconsistent impurity profiles (higher levels of impurities 20 and 21) compared with manufacturing scale where oxygen is better controlled.
Solution_Description: All reactions, work‑ups and crystallisations were performed in a glove‑bag or under strict oxygen‑exclusion to reproduce manufacturing‑scale impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When oxygen was present during the alkaline NAC workup of 16 on a laboratory scale, the impurity profile was inconsistent with what was observed during manufacturing where control of oxygen is easier to achieve.","Impurities 20 and 21 were observed up to 0.44 area% higher during manufacturing than what was routinely observed in the laboratory.","To obtain laboratory results that better represented manufacturing scale observations, reactions, workups, and crystallizations were run in a glovebag or under strict control to prevent oxygen incursion."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: During the bis‑methanesulfonylation/hydrolysis sequence, using EtOH/NaOEt for hydrolysis generated ethyl‑methanesulfonate, which alkylated the API to give impurity 22, reducing assay and yield.
Solution_Description: Hydrolysis was switched to an aqueous NaOH addition in 2‑MeTHF, producing non‑reactive sodium methanesulfonate that could be removed by aqueous washes, eliminating impurity 22.
Supporting_Evidence: ["hydrolysis was performed by exchanging the solvent from DCM to EtOH, adding NaOEt in EtOH, and isolating 1 by adding n‑heptane. Under these conditions, stoichiometric amounts of ethylmethanesulfonate were formed, which reacts with 1 to form an ethylated impurity 22.","In order to avoid this side reaction, the hydrolysis was later performed by addition of an aqueous NaOH solution to the reaction stream in 2‑MeTHF. Under these biphasic conditions, a nonreactive byproduct, sodium methanesulfonate, was generated which was removed via aqueous washes."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Trace 5‑hydroxy‑2‑pentanone (5H2P) in 2‑MeTHF reacted with intermediate 16 to form a hemiaminal that stalled the bis‑methanesulfonylation, preventing full conversion.
Solution_Description: Sodium carbonate was added to the final aqueous brine washes to keep the mixture basic and the wash was performed in a separate reactor to avoid acid‑catalysed condensation, allowing the reaction to tolerate 5H2P without stalling.
Supporting_Evidence: ["It was observed that the reaction could not be driven to full conversion and that the starting material 16 was always present between 0.2 and 1.4 area% by LC, even when a large excess of MsCl and base was used.","The root cause of this reaction stalling was eventually determined to be the presence of 5‑hydroxy‑2‑pentanone (5H2P), a low‑level impurity in 2‑MeTHF which accumulates during azeotropic distillations.","In order to minimize this potential acid source, sodium carbonate was introduced to the final aqueous brine washes to maintain a basic pH, and this wash was performed in a separate reactor to reduce the risk of residual 16·MsOH being present during distillations."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of Lenacapavir Sodium: Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Commercial methanesulfonyl chloride (MsCl) contained trace chloromethanesulfonyl chloride (CMSC) that produced impurity 24, an ICH M7 class 5 impurity.
Solution_Description: Only MsCl batches with ≥98 % purity and ≤0.20 % CMSC were used, keeping impurity 24 below 0.20 % area.
Supporting_Evidence: ["commercial MsCl contains varying trace levels of chloromethanesulfonyl chloride (CMSC) which reacts with 16 to form compound 24.","After this alkyl chloride impurity was confirmed to be non‑mutagenic, it was effectively controlled to <0.20 area% as an ICH M7 class 5 impurity by using commercial MsCl (≥98.0% pure with no more than 0.20% CMSC)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Method for the Synthesis of Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene
Problem_Description: The previously reported routes for synthesising ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (1) start from hexafluorocyclotriphosphazene (2), which is very expensive and not readily available in bulk, making the process uneconomical for industrial production.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic route was devised that begins with the cheap, commercially available hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene (3). The sequence uses sodium fluoride (NaF) for fluorination and an ethoxylation step with ethanol/NaOH, eliminating the need for costly intermediate 2.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "the price of 2 is too high for industrial production of 1" (Introduction, paragraph 3) 
• "hexachlorocyclotriphosphazene (3) as the starting material for this synthesis process" (Introduction, paragraph 4)
• "The overall yield of 76%" (Abstract)
• "The process uses easily available starting materials 3, NaF, EtOH, and NaOH" (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Method for the Synthesis of Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene
Problem_Description: Earlier methods employed hazardous reagents such as PF₅ gas and anhydrous HF, which pose severe health and environmental risks and are unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The hazardous fluorination reagents were replaced with solid NaF, a far less toxic and easier‑to‑handle material, and the ethoxylation step was performed under mild, room‑temperature conditions with ethanol and NaOH, removing the need for dangerous gases.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "PF₅ is a colorless and foul‑smelling gas… has a strong irritant effect… extremely dangerous" (Introduction, paragraph 3)
• "HF… still a kind of hazardous chemical" (Introduction, paragraph 4)
• "For safety reasons, highly toxic anhydrous hydrogen fluoride was first excluded… highly active potassium fluoride (KF) was chosen as the fluorinating reagent" (Results, section 2.1)
• "NaF… much weaker hygroscopicity… applied as the fluorinating reagent for subsequent research" (Results, section 2.1)

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Method for the Synthesis of Ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene
Problem_Description: Using KF as the fluorinating agent gave unstable and low yields (46‑78 %) due to its strong hygroscopicity; water >300 ppm generated hydroxyl‑substituted impurity 2A, reducing conversion.
Solution_Description: NaF (6.5 equiv) was selected as the fluorinating reagent; its particle size and water content were strictly controlled (≤300 mesh, ≤200 ppm). The amount of NaF was further increased to 8.5 equiv and the reaction temperature was optimised (70‑75 °C) to give a consistent 91 % isolated yield on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "yields of 2 were unstable due to the strong hygroscopicity of KF… water content ≥300 ppm… generate hydroxyl‑substituted impurities 2A" (Results, section 2.1)
• "NaF possessed much weaker hygroscopicity…" (Results, section 2.1)
• "NaF can only be used… particle size ≤300 meshes and water content ≤200 ppm" (Results, section 2.1)

Solution_Description: A modified Photochemical Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor (PhotoVortex) was employed. The rapid rotation of a central rotor generates Taylor vortices, providing intense mixing and short diffusion paths, which restored high conversions and yields (>90 %) at larger reactor volumes.
Supporting_Evidence: ["...due to suspected mass transfer/mixing limitations, the yield decreased upon scale‑up in some cases.", "We applied a modified version of our previously reported photochemical Taylor Vortex Flow Reactor (PhotoVortex), where Taylor vortices and a short‑irradiated path length allow photochemical reactions to be performed efficiently via excellent mixing.", "In a small PhotoVortex (8 mL irradiated volume), we have demonstrated projected productivities around 1 kg day⁻¹ and >10 kg day⁻¹ in a large PhotoVortex (185 mL irradiated volume) with good product yields (>90 %)."]

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Continuous Metallaphotoredox Catalyzed C–O Coupling to a 10 kg-Scale Using Small Footprint Photochemical Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Operating the flow reactor at temperatures above 70 °C caused the formation of a black precipitate identified as Ni⁰ (Ni‑black), which deactivates the catalyst and fouls the reactor.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was optimized to 60 °C (the temperature generated by LED heating), which gave the best yields while avoiding Ni‑black formation. Additionally, the outlet tubing was externally heated to >40 °C to keep the TMG‑salt in solution, preventing blockages.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The outlet stream from the 80 °C experiments contained a black precipitate, likely attributable to the aggregation and precipitation of Ni(0) as Ni black—a deactivation pathway previously identified.", "The increased temperature probably resulted in more efficient quenching of the excited state...", "The yields at 60 °C were comparable to those obtained without the application of a heating/cooling fluid.", "For similar conditions a lower yield was observed in the larger bore tubing reactor compared to the smaller bore reactors.", "The outlet tubing needed to be externally heated using a heating cell to maintain the temperature above 40 °C to avoid precipitation of the TMG‑salt formed in the reaction."]

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Continuous Metallaphotoredox Catalyzed C–O Coupling to a 10 kg-Scale Using Small Footprint Photochemical Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: The original PhotoVortex design employed white LEDs whose emission did not overlap the absorption of the Ir photocatalyst, leading to inefficient photon usage and requiring higher light intensities, which raises safety concerns for eye and skin exposure.
Solution_Description: The LED array was replaced with three high‑intensity 410 nm blue‑violet LED blocks (3 × 200 W), providing spectral overlap with the catalyst and enabling high productivities while maintaining proper safety shielding.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the reactor was equipped with white light LEDs (i.e., broadband visible light). However, there was poor overlap between the photocatalyst absorption bands and the emission profile of the white light LEDs.", "we modified our original design using three high‑intensity blue‑violet LED blocks (3 × 200 W 410 nm) and we were able to obtain high productivities in the PhotoVortex."]

Paper Title: Scale-Up of Continuous Metallaphotoredox Catalyzed C–O Coupling to a 10 kg-Scale Using Small Footprint Photochemical Taylor Vortex Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: In batch, the C–O coupling required 24 h reaction time, leading to low throughput for manufacturing‑scale production.

Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the process would generate large volumes of waste containing the expensive Ir photocatalyst, raising sustainability concerns.

Alternative recovery routes (heterogenized catalysts, membrane separations) are being investigated.

Paper Title: Development of a Safer Continuous Flow Process for B
Problem_Description: Addition of B₂(OH)₄ and 4,4′‑bipyridine to the reaction mixture caused a rapid temperature spike (22 °C → 62 °C at 0.5 g scale) and generated non‑condensable gases, indicating a highly exothermic and potentially hazardous decomposition event.
Solution_Description: The addition was divided into three portions and the reaction mass was cooled to 0 °C, which limited the temperature rise to < 20 °C while still giving complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the internal temperature increased to 62 °C from 22 °C even at only a 0.5 g scale.”; “The addition was exothermic, with a rapid temperature rise observed during the initial 25 % addition.”; “Following this mode of addition, the exotherm was controlled below 20 °C and complete conversion of the starting material was observed after 5 min.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safer Continuous Flow Process for B
Problem_Description: Solutions of B₂(OH)₄ in aprotic polar solvents (DMF, DMSO) generated a fine stream of gas bubbles (presumed H₂) on standing, indicating unsafe gas evolution and secondary exothermic decomposition events.
Solution_Description: A protic cosolvent (EtOH) was introduced, forming a B₂(OH)₄/EtOH mixture (up to 60 vol % EtOH) that showed no visible gas evolution and significantly reduced exothermic peaks in DSC/ARSST studies.
Supporting_Evidence: “formation of a fine stream of gas bubbles, presumably hydrogen gas… was noted.”; “noncondensable gases were generated.”; “B₂(OH)₄ did not completely dissolve in EtOH… no noticeable gas generation.”; “clear solution of B₂(OH)₄ with EtOH… no detectable gas generation even upon standing the solution for 12–16 h.”

Problem_Description: B₂(OH)₄ displayed limited solubility in several solvents (DMF < DMAc < DMSO) and poor dissolution in EtOH, leading to precipitation and potential instability of the reagent.
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system of DMSO/EtOH (3 : 4 v/v) was selected, providing higher solubility for B₂(OH)₄, a stable stock solution, and lower exothermicity.
Supporting_Evidence: “B₂(OH)₄ has decreased solubility in the order of DMSO > DMAc > DMF.”; “B₂(OH)₄ did not completely dissolve in EtOH even at higher volumes.”; “DMSO/EtOH … was applied for further evaluation of chemoselective nitro reduction in continuous flow mode.”

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Pd-Catalyzed C–S Coupling for the Synthesis of Janus Kinase Inhibitor GDC-9918

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Pd-Catalyzed C–S Coupling for the Synthesis of Janus Kinase Inhibitor GDC-9918

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Pd-Catalyzed C–S Coupling for the Synthesis of Janus Kinase Inhibitor GDC-9918

Paper Title: Development of a Robust Pd-Catalyzed C–S Coupling for the Synthesis of Janus Kinase Inhibitor GDC-9918

Paper Title: Development of a Mild and Efficient Process for Ir-Catalyzed
Problem_Description: The classical oxidation‑reductive amination route gave only ~52 area % product and isolated yields <30 % because the 2‑aminopyridine (1) is a poor nucleophile toward the aldehyde (4). The protocol also required the hazardous reductant NaBH₃CN.

Supporting_Evidence: “... resulted in ∼52 area % of the desired product … low isolated yields (<30 %).”; “In addition to the poor performance of the reaction, the process required the use of the hazardous NaBH₃CN.”; “Ir (III) catalyst in combination with LiO‑t‑Bu as a base was found to provide optimal conversion.”
