Problem_Description: During the scaling‑up experiments (runs 5–6) the productivity plateaued at ≈14 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ despite increasing the circulation rate and feed‑tank size; the feed‑tank could not dissolve rac‑IMG‑P fast enough to maintain the target 17 wt % concentration.
Solution_Description: The feed‑tank volume was increased (from 500 mL to 1 L) to give more residence time for dissolution, and the vessel size of the crystallizers was also enlarged (500 mL vessels used). This alleviated the dissolution bottleneck and allowed higher product output in subsequent runs.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We hypothesized that production of the feed solution (i.e., dissolution of rac‑IMG‑P solids in the feed tank) was not fast enough, so we tried increasing the volume of the feed tank in run 5.", "Note that we continued to scale up while adjusting the seeding procedure. We increased the seed amount and circulation rate in run 4, and we tried a larger feed vessel in run 5."]

Paper Title: Coupled-Batch Preferential Crystallization of Imeglimin Propionate on a 200 g Scale
Problem_Description: In the 14 h runs (runs 6–8) the productivity dropped to ≈11.6 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ and the mother‑liquor concentration fell. The authors linked this to water uptake by the hygroscopic rac‑IMG‑P (≈0.8 wt % water) which raised the solubility and reduced supersaturation.
Solution_Description: Water content was tightly controlled when recycling the mother‑liquor: the recycled stream was adjusted back to the target 8:2 IPA/MeOH ratio and the amount of water was measured and minimized before the next run.
Supporting_Evidence: ["One possible explanation for the lower productivity is the water content. The rac‑IMG‑P starting material used in this study is slightly hygroscopic and contains 0.8 wt % water…the actual solubility may have been higher than intended.", "We also conducted CB‑PC using recycled mother liquors…Control of the water content in recycled liquors was identified as an issue to address."]

Paper Title: Coupled-Batch Preferential Crystallization of Imeglimin Propionate on a 200 g Scale
Problem_Description: When the runs were extended to 14 h the slurry became very thick (≈20 wt % solids) and clogged the filters, requiring filter cleaning every ~10 min (instead of once per 20 min) and frequent nitrogen‑pulses, which limited the effective circulation rate and reduced overall throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The filter size was increased (from 13 × 20 mm to 23 × 39 mm) and nitrogen‑blowing was employed more regularly to clear the filters. The authors also noted that the apparatus design (half‑moon impeller, jacketed lines) had to be operated near its physical limits, prompting the suggestion of larger vessels for future work.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Filter size was also increased (from 13 mm × 20 mm to 23 mm × 39 mm).", "The slurry thickness became a limitation of our apparatus. Filter clearing went from 1 time/20 min in the 6 h runs to 1 time/10 min in the latter half of the 14 h runs. This became operationally troublesome.", "During operation, crystals would accumulate on the filter surfaces. Filters were cleared…by blowing N₂ gas into the filter."]

Paper Title: Coupled-Batch Preferential Crystallization of Imeglimin Propionate on a 200 g Scale
Problem_Description: Even after implementing the improved seeding protocol, occasional drops in crystal optical purity were observed late in the 14 h runs (e.g., run 6 and run 8) suggesting uncontrolled nucleation sources such as excessive supersaturation or nitrogen‑bubble cleaning.
Solution_Description: The authors propose future work to operate at lower supersaturation (time > 0 h) and to investigate potential nucleation sources (e.g., filter‑cleaning procedure, line incrustation). No concrete change was made within the present study, but the recommendation itself is recorded as a planned condition change.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A common cause of off‑isomer nucleation is excessive supersaturation; future work should investigate the process conditions at other less supersaturated points in the metastable zone.", "Nucleation sources in the apparatus could include the filter cleaning procedure (where nitrogen bubbles are blown into the solution) or incrustation of solids (even in small amounts) in the circulation lines."]

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: AllylZnBr is highly sensitive to moisture and oxygen, causing a loss of organozinc concentration over time and promoting Wurtz‑type dimerisation (6–10 % side‑product), which reduces the isolated yield of the desired homo‑allyl alcohols.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot continuous flow sequence was implemented where the organozinc reagent is generated and immediately consumed in the Saytzeff reaction, eliminating storage of the reactive intermediate. Fresh zinc is continuously fed to the packed‑bed reactor to keep the active surface available.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “AllylZnBr shows a high sensitivity to moisture and oxygen, which manifests itself in a reduction of the zinc organyl concentration over time … the formation reaction of allylZnBr has a high affinity for Wurtz formation. Studies have shown that this can be 6–10 %…” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The one‑pot synthesis … avoids the upstream production and storage of the reactive intermediate, which minimizes the risk of concentration reduction due to moisture, oxygen or dimerisation.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The addition of fresh zinc during the ongoing synthesis allows a theoretically unlimited conversion time.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The one‑pot synthesis … combines two reaction steps in one reactor … no additional pump … required compared to two‑step synthesis.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The pilot reactor … allows the addition of fresh zinc during the ongoing synthesis.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: When attempting a one‑pot conversion at 2.0 M 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde the reaction mixture precipitated, causing a pressure rise and clogging of the IR flow cell and the reactor.
Solution_Description: The concentration of the aldehyde was reduced to 0.56 M, which prevented precipitation. The authors also suggest that adding a polar co‑solvent such as DMA or DMF could improve solubility for future runs.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “During the conversion, an increase in pressure was observed as a result of clogging … It is questionable whether the solubility was exceeded … which ultimately caused a solid to precipitate.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The reaction could not be transferred to a 1.36 M 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde solution … No increase in pressure was observed … a reduced 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde concentration of 0.56 M was reacted with 1.0 M allylBr.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The observed excess solubility … could be remedied by … adding a polar solvent, such as DMA or DMF.” (sec 2.1.2)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: High‑concentration (2 M) allylZnBr/acetophenone reactions released more heat, leading to an increased formation of by‑products and a lower isolated yield (83 % vs. 92 % at lower concentration).
Solution_Description: The thermostatic bath temperature was lowered to 15 °C to improve heat dissipation while keeping the residence time at 2 min, allowing complete conversion with acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Due to the high initial concentrations … the thermostatic bath temperature was reduced to 15 °C to ensure sufficient heat dissipation. … a yield of 83 % … lower than 92 % … the higher heat release … is not unlikely.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The temperature progression … shows the reactor was then tempered to the operating temperature of 25 °C … slight fluctuations … due to the decrease in zinc …” (sec 2.1.2, fig 4) 
• “In the pilot scale … the thermostatic bath temperature was reduced from 25 °C to 20 °C in order to dissipate the heat released during the formation and conversion reaction to a sufficient extent.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: Previous literature examples for organozinc conversions used very low flow rates (0.5–0.2 mL min⁻¹), giving low productivities and long overall reaction times.
Solution_Description: The authors employed a continuous‑flow packed‑bed reactor (lab‑scale and pilot‑scale) with higher flow rates (up to 13 L h⁻¹ pilot throughput) and used highly concentrated organozinc solutions (up to 2 M) to markedly increase productivity while keeping residence times short (2 min or less).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The work presented … low productivity … flow rates of 0.5 mL/min … low productivity.” (sec 1) 
• “In the Saytzeff reaction, residence times of 2.0 min were sufficient … isolated yields of 66–98 %.” (abstract) 
• “The pilot reactor … allowed a liquid throughput of 13 L/h … The scale‑up factor … approximately 33.” (sec 2.2) 
• “Highly concentrated 2.0 M organozinc compounds … the reactor volume is better utilized, and the synthesis is more efficient at the same time.” (sec 1)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: In the Negishi cross‑coupling at 2.0 M benzZnBr, homocoupling to bibenzyl increased, lowering the isolated yield of the cross‑coupled product (79 % vs. 92 % at 0.5 M).
Solution_Description: The thermostatic bath temperature was raised to 80 °C for the highly concentrated runs to keep Zn‑containing by‑products in solution and prevent reactor clogging, while the concentration was kept at 2.0 M to demonstrate feasibility despite a lower yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “During the Negishi coupling, the corresponding zinc salt was formed … In order to keep this in solution and avoid clogging … the thermostatic bath temperature was increased to 80 °C for the highly concentrated conversion reactions.” (sec 2.1.3) 
• “Yield was significantly lower at 79 % … The higher concentration presumably favored the undesired homocoupling to bibenzyl … which can clog the reactor.” (sec 2.1.3) 
• “The residence time was only slightly higher … however, the yield was significantly lower at 79 % … compared to 92 %.” (sec 2.1.3)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: At high concentrations the reaction mixture sometimes cooled in the IR flow cell or upper reactor region, leading to unforeseen precipitation and pressure spikes, indicating inconsistent mixing and temperature control.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors propose improving mixing and temperature control (e.g., adjusting coil length, adding a capillary for residence‑time extension, or employing a co‑solvent) to avoid local cooling and precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “It is questionable whether the solubility was exceeded … or whether the reaction solution merely cooled down too much in the IR flow cell … which ultimately caused a solid to precipitate.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The capillary allowed the residence time to be doubled while the flow rate remained unchanged … only affected the conversion … not the formation of RZnX.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The addition of a polar solvent … could provide a remedy.” (sec 2.1.2)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: Organozinc reagents are highly reactive toward moisture and oxygen, posing safety risks during storage and handling on large scale.
Solution_Description: By coupling organozinc formation directly to the downstream conversion step in a continuous flow set‑up (one‑pot), the intermediate is never stored, dramatically reducing the exposure of reactive species to air and moisture.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The one‑pot synthesis … avoids the upstream production and storage of the reactive intermediate, which minimizes the risk of concentration reduction due to moisture, oxygen or dimerization.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “The directly connected conversion … reduced storage times of the reactive intermediates … greater process reliability … especially with regard to industry‑relevant quantities.” (sec 5) 
• “Both syntheses yielded comparable results … the one‑pot synthesis was defined as the method of choice … particularly advantageous for reactive and Wurtz‑affine RZnX formation reactions.” (sec 2.1.2)

Paper Title: Organozinc Reagents: Highly Efficient Scalable Continuous Conversion in Various Concentrations and Reaction Types
Problem_Description: The tertiary homoallyl alcohol from 3‑pentanone gave a low isolated yield (66 %) despite complete conversion, suggesting loss during purification.
Solution_Description: The authors acknowledge that the low yield may stem from downstream purification; they suggest that optimizing the work‑up or chromatographic conditions could improve recovery.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The conversion of the ketone was complete … isolated yield of only 66 % … It is questionable whether the low yield of the tertiary alcohol is due to the reaction itself or to the downstream purification and separation.” (sec 2.1.2) 
• “Further parameter adjustment is expected to improve the target product yield.” (sec 2.1.3, Negishi high‑concentration discussion)

Paper Title: Continuous Sonocrystallization Process for Controlling the Polymorphs and Particle Size of Perampanel
Problem_Description: When continuous crystallization of perampanel anhydrate type I was performed without ultrasound (Run 1), a large amount of fouling built up on the crystallizer wall and agitator blades. The fouling reduced product quality, lowered the precipitation yield and caused blockage of the transfer tube, threatening slurry overflow.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous ultrasound irradiation of the crystallizer (immersed in an ultrasonic bath) eliminated fouling completely. Cavitation promoted immediate consumption of supersaturation in the bulk solution, prevented solid deposition on the reactor surfaces and increased the precipitation and recovery yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In Run 1, when continuous crystallization was attempted … a large degree of fouling was observed on the crystallizer wall and agitator blades … Fouling not only reduces the quality and yield of the product but also clogs the transfer tube, resulting in the risk of slurry overflow …”
• “In Run 5 … the crystallizer was immersed in an ultrasound bath … No fouling was observed on the crystallizer wall and agitator blades during the entire operation, demonstrating that the problem was completely solved.”
• “Immediate consumption of supersaturation occurs in the solution rather than on the crystallizer walls … Ultrasound irradiation also improved the precipitation yield, resulting in a higher recovery yield.”

Paper Title: Continuous Sonocrystallization Process for Controlling the Polymorphs and Particle Size of Perampanel
Problem_Description: In batch reslurry experiments aiming to convert perampanel hydrate to the stable anhydrate type V, the transformation failed when only 0.01 wt % seed crystals were added, giving low yield of the desired polymorph. Even with 1.00 wt % seed crystals, the conversion required long times, indicating difficulty achieving consistent polymorph control without ultrasound.
Solution_Description: Ultrasound irradiation of the hydrate slurry (without any seed crystals) promoted nucleation of the anhydrate type V crystals, enabling complete transformation within a few hours and yielding the desired polymorph with high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The transformation from hydrate to anhydrate type V was not observed with 0.01 wt % seed crystals … the transformation was observed with 1.00 wt % seed crystals …”
• “In Run 3, the crystallizer was immersed in an ultrasound bath … XRD peaks of anhydrate type V crystals appeared, and the hydrate crystals began to dissolve. After 4 h of irradiation, the hydrate peaks disappeared completely.”
• “The results of Run 3 suggest that ultrasound promotes the nucleation of anhydrate type V crystals in a saturated solution of hydrate crystals.”

Paper Title: Continuous Sonocrystallization Process for Controlling the Polymorphs and Particle Size of Perampanel
Problem_Description: During continuous crystallization of perampanel hydrate, a residence time of 30 min was insufficient for the hydrate → anhydrate type V transformation; the process yielded mainly hydrate crystals, showing that the reaction time was too short for reliable polymorph conversion.
Solution_Description: Extending the residence time to 120 min (by reducing pump flow rates while keeping slurry volume constant) allowed the ultrasound‑mediated transformation to proceed to completion, giving the stable anhydrate type V polymorph.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When continuous crystallization was performed … a short residence time of 30 min … hydrate crystals were obtained even under ultrasound irradiation … Since a residence time of 30 min was found to be insufficient for the transformation … the residence time was extended to 120 min … Consequently, anhydrate type V crystals were obtained.”

Paper Title: Continuous Sonocrystallization Process for Controlling the Polymorphs and Particle Size of Perampanel
Problem_Description: Scaling the sonocrystallization process to a 10 L ultrasonic crystallizer required direct transducers attached to the vessel wall, raising concerns about metal erosion and possible contamination of the API product, which could pose safety and cost issues.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 10 L stainless‑steel (SUS316L) crystallizer equipped with multiple ultrasonic transducers was used. Post‑run ICP‑MS analysis showed Ni levels below the quantification limit, confirming that erosion was negligible and the approach was safe and cost‑effective for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Because the 10 L scale equipment could not be immersed in an ultrasound bath, a system with multiple ultrasonic transducers attached directly to the outer bottom of the crystallization vessel was utilized.”
• “The amount of metal impurities (Ni) … was below the lower limit of quantification (0.3 ppm) … in Run 3 … thus, the concept for scaled‑up continuous sonocrystallization was successfully demonstrated.”

Paper Title: Continuous Sonocrystallization Process for Controlling the Polymorphs and Particle Size of Perampanel
Problem_Description: Without ultrasound, the continuous crystallization runs produced crystals with a broad particle‑size distribution (large D90 and high span), leading to less uniform products and lower overall precipitation yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing ultrasound power (up to 260–330 W) in the 10 L reactor promoted nucleation over crystal growth, resulting in smaller, more uniform particles (reduced D10, D50, D90 and span) and higher precipitation and recovery yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In Run 1, when continuous crystallization was performed without ultrasound … large crystals with a broad particle size distribution were obtained.”
• “When the ultrasound power was increased stepwise (Runs 2 and 3), smaller and more uniform crystals were obtained in increased yields.”
• “When the ultrasound power was set to the maximum (260–330 W), particle sizes and yields similar to those in the small‑scale experiments were reproduced.”

Paper Title: Impurities from Hydroxyproline Derivatives in the Synthesis of Modified Oligonucleotides
Problem_Description: A +293 Da impurity appears when the trans‑4‑hydroxy‑L‑prolinol‑derived amino linker is subjected to the strongly alkaline ammonia/methylamine (AMA) deprotection. The authors infer that the pyrrolidine ring breaks under these conditions, generating a fragment that is difficult to separate from the desired oligonucleotide.
Solution_Description: Pre‑load the amino linker onto the solid support as a succinate ester (compound B) before the oligonucleotide synthesis. This bypasses the unstable phosphoramidite derived from the hydroxyprolinol and eliminates the +293 Da by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: “Another uncommon +293 Da impurity was also found… may be related to the amino‑modified alkyl chain on pyrrolidine… When phosphoramidite A is placed at the terminal 5′‑nucleotide, this impurity does not appear.”; “To address the difficulty and instability associated with preparing such phosphoramidite monomers on a large scale, we recommend preloading them onto the resin in the form of succinate.”; “Using the two commonly employed de‑protection conditions mentioned above, impurities related to unylinker can be excluded (Table 2, entries 1 and 2).”

Paper Title: Impurities from Hydroxyproline Derivatives in the Synthesis of Modified Oligonucleotides
Problem_Description: Acrylonitrile (+53 Da) and acetylation (+42 Da) adducts form during the cleavage‑and‑deprotection step. Their amount depends on the ammonolysis conditions: they are absent in the AMA (40 % MeNH₂/NH₄OH) system but appear under milder NH₄OH/EtOH conditions, and increase when the tri‑ethylamine (NEt₃) pretreatment is omitted.
Solution_Description: Add a strong nucleophilic scavenger (methylamine) to the de‑protection mixture. Methylamine traps the released acrylonitrile and acetyl groups, preventing their addition to the oligonucleotide.
Supporting_Evidence: “These impurities do not appear in the AMA system but do under relatively mild conditions… When the ONA‑support triethylamine treatment was not performed, the occurrence of impurity significantly increased… methylamine can trap cyanoethyl and acetyl groups that break down from bases.”; “For linkers with primary amine groups, it is advisable to use a system with scavengers for C&D, such as methylamine, to reduce the addition reactions of removed protective groups.”

Paper Title: Impurities from Hydroxyproline Derivatives in the Synthesis of Modified Oligonucleotides
Problem_Description: During a 10‑fold scale‑up of the synthesis, the acrylonitrile adduct remained undetectable, but the acetylation adduct increased modestly compared with the small‑scale reaction, indicating inconsistent impurity profiles upon scaling.
Solution_Description: Introduce a portion of aqueous methylamine (40 % wt., 15 equiv) into the de‑protection step at scale. The added scavenger suppresses the formation of the acetylation adducts observed on larger batches.
Supporting_Evidence: “After scaling up the synthesis 10‑fold… there was a slight increase in the formation of the acetylation adduct… Upon adding a portion of methylamine aqueous solution, the formation of the acetylation adducts decreased, indicating that methylamine serves as an effective scavenger in this system.”

Paper Title: Impurities from Hydroxyproline Derivatives in the Synthesis of Modified Oligonucleotides
Problem_Description: The amount of acrylonitrile and acetylation adducts correlates with the amount of tri‑ethylamine used in a pre‑wash of the solid support. Insufficient NEt₃ leads to higher impurity levels, which compromise product purity and yield.
Solution_Description: Increase the equivalents of NEt₃ in the pre‑wash (up to 2700 equiv) and perform the wash as a defined pretreatment step (NEt₃/CH₃CN, steady flow, 15 min) before the standard NH₄OH/EtOH de‑protection. This reduces both the acrylonitrile (+53 Da) and acetylation (+42 Da) adducts.
Supporting_Evidence: “Washing the oligonucleotide‑bound solid support with a solution of triethylamine in acetonitrile before cleavage and deprotection prevents the formation of acrylonitrile adducts. Increasing the dosage of triethylamine gradually reduced this impurity… Table 3 shows decreasing acrylonitrile adducts with 450–2700 equiv NEt₃.”; “Pretreatment with 50 % (v/v) NEt₃–CH₃CN, steady flow, 15 min, followed by NH₄OH/EtOH‑3:1 (v/v), 45 °C, 20 h.”

Paper Title: Impurities from Hydroxyproline Derivatives in the Synthesis of Modified Oligonucleotides
Problem_Description: The phosphoramidite derived from the hydroxyprolinol linker (compound A) is difficult to prepare on a large scale because it is unstable and requires careful handling, limiting its practical availability for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Instead of synthesizing and using the unstable phosphoramidite, the authors load the succinate derivative (compound B) onto an aminomethyl resin and then carry out the oligonucleotide synthesis, avoiding the need for the problematic phosphoramidite altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “The adverse effects of complex synthesis, purification, and preservation of special monomers are also unacceptable. Therefore, we synthesized succinate (B) and preloaded it onto aminomethyl resin, where ONA‑1 was subsequently synthesized.”; “This approach avoids impurities related to unylinker and addresses the difficulty and instability associated with preparing such phosphoramidite monomers on a large scale.”

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: Previous electrochemical cyclopropanations required toxic mercury cathodes and expensive platinum anodes, creating safety and cost concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the hazardous electrodes with inexpensive graphite cathodes (and a zinc sacrificial anode when needed), eliminating the need for toxic or costly electrode materials.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Overall, this approach eliminates the necessity for a divided cell and the use of hazardous or costly electrodes.”
- “use of toxic (mercury) and/or expensive (platinum) cathodes and the need for a divided cell…" (Introduction).
- “graphite cathodes outcompete metal‑based ones with nickel and platinum cathodes affording low yields of only 10 % and 15 %, respectively.” (Optimization, entry 11‑12).
- “When substituting the graphite anode with a zinc anode… 75 % yield of product 2 were obtained.” (Optimization, entry 14).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: A divided cell was previously required to prevent oxidation of the substrate at the anode, adding operational complexity and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: The authors adopted an undivided cell and employed alternating polarity (AP) every 60 s, which suppresses anode buildup and removes the need for a divided cell.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Overall, this approach eliminates the necessity for a divided cell …” (Abstract & Conclusions).
- “Alternating polarity was necessary to avoid any buildup at the anode… Without AP, the yield dropped from 69 % to 46 %.” (Optimization, entry 2).
- “The reaction was performed in an undivided cell at room temperature…” (Optimization, first paragraph).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: Metal cathodes (nickel, platinum) gave very low product yields (10–15 %) compared with graphite, making them unattractive for large‑scale use.
Solution_Description: Switching to a graphite cathode dramatically increased the isolated yield to 69 % (GCMS 89 %), providing a cost‑effective and efficient electrode material.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “graphite cathodes outcompete metal‑based ones with nickel and platinum cathodes affording low yields of only 10 and 15 %, respectively.” (Optimization, entry 11‑12).
- “After 5 F /mol, desired cyclopropane 2 was obtained in an 89 % GCMS (69 % isolated) yield.” (Optimization, entry 1).
- “The method hinges on the integration of a sacrificial reductant alongside cost‑effective cathode and anode materials.” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: In flow mode the reaction suffered from low conversion (12–16 %) and inconsistent results due to a deposit layer forming on the cathode, which inhibited the reaction.
Solution_Description: Lowering the current density from 6.25 → 3.5 mA cm⁻² increased conversion to 62 % and reduced deposit formation; the authors also propose using alternating‑current electrolysis as a future way to prevent the cathode layer.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “A concomitant increase of the cell resistance was also observed along with the presence of a deposit layer at the cathode… low conversion… 12 %… 16 %.” (Flow and Scale‑Up).
- “A decrease of the current density from 6.25 to 3.5 mA cm⁻² proved beneficial with a significant increase of the conversion (62 %).” (Flow and Scale‑Up).
- “the scale‑up of this reaction requires the minimization of the formation of the cathode layer, and alternating current electrolysis could be a potential solution.” (Flow and Scale‑Up).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: Earlier electrochemical protocols needed 5–10 F mol⁻¹ to reach full conversion, translating into long reaction times and low throughput.
Solution_Description: The optimized protocol reached high conversion in only 3 F mol⁻¹ (batch) and even 3 F mol⁻¹ on a 1.35 mmol scale, dramatically shortening the required charge and reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “complete conversion requiring an electrical charge of 5–10 F mol⁻¹.” (Introduction, discussion of prior work).
- “The reaction profile… indicated that a high conversion was obtained after 3 F mol⁻¹ and then the reaction reached a plateau.” (Optimization, Figure 1B).
- “Only 3 F mol⁻¹ was required compared to 5 F mol⁻¹ when the reaction was performed on a small scale.” (Scale‑Up, IKA Carousel).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: Using triethylamine as the base led to significant elimination side‑reactions, lowering the isolated cyclopropane yields.
Solution_Description: Switching to N‑N‑diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA) suppressed elimination pathways and restored high yields (up to 69 % isolated).
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The base and its nature proved critical, with DIPEA effectively minimizing elimination side reactions that were more prevalent when triethylamine was used.” (Optimization, entries 16‑18).
- “DIPEA… offered the best result; reducing it to 4 equiv was counter‑productive.” (Optimization, entry 19).

Paper Title: Electrochemical Cyclopropanation of 1,3-Dialkyl Bromides
Problem_Description: In the flow cell the electrode gap (0.25 mm) differed from batch (70 mm), affecting cell resistance and requiring adjustment of electrolyte concentration.
Solution_Description: The amount of NaBr was reduced to 0.5 equiv to match the smaller gap, decreasing resistance and improving conversion under the new geometry.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “We also decided to decrease the amount of NaBr to 0.5 equiv since the gap between the electrodes is smaller in our electrochemical flow cell (0.25 mm) compared to the batch mode (70 mm), thus minimizing the cell resistance.” (Flow and Scale‑Up).
- “Changing the amount of NaBr or DIPEA … was ineffective in improving the conversion.” (Flow and Scale‑Up).

Paper Title: Catalytic Activity of Triphenylphosphine for Electrophilic Aromatic Bromination Using
Problem_Description: N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) shows limited solubility in most organic solvents (except DMF) and must be added in portions to avoid large solvent volumes; the reaction is highly exothermic, causing a rapid rise in internal temperature that can exceed the flash point of the solvent, creating a safety hazard.
Solution_Description: A broad solvent screen identified DMF, MeCN, AcOEt, MEK and THF as suitable media; NBS was added sequentially (four‑portion or twelve‑portion dosing) to spread the heat release, and the reaction was run at 0 °C (or kept below the flash point) to suppress temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “NBS has limited solubility in various organic solvents except for amide solvents … therefore, NBS should be added in portions to the reaction mixture to control the reaction and ensure process safety.” (Introduction)  
• “The characteristic behavior of the reaction heat made it difficult to suppress the increase of the internal temperature.” (Abstract)  
• “A sudden exotherm was observed from 70 to 80 min … the internal temperature rose rapidly.” (Results & Discussion – Fig. 1)  
• “In DMF, the increase was suppressed to 5 °C … sequential addition of NBS in four portions.” (Section 2.6, Fig. 3a)  
• “When the reaction mixture was cooled to 0 °C, the reaction rate slightly decreased but the reaction was completed in 120 min.” (Table 1, entry 5)  
• “Various organic solvents … the reaction proceeded smoothly and reached completion.” (Section 2.4, Table 3)  
• “DCM is a hazardous organic solvent and should be avoided on a manufacturing scale.” (Section 2.4)
missing_information: COST, AVAILABILITY, LONG REACTIONS, MIXABILITY, PURIFICATION

Paper Title: Catalytic Activity of Triphenylphosphine for Electrophilic Aromatic Bromination Using
Problem_Description: NBS decomposes (partly to HBr) under the reaction conditions, consuming reagent without producing product and leading to incomplete conversion or need for excess NBS, which in turn lowers yield and can cause over‑bromination.
Solution_Description: The loading of triphenylphosphine was reduced to 0.05 equiv, which limited the side reaction that consumes NBS and allowed quantitative conversion with 1.2 equiv of NBS; NBS was then delivered in controlled portions to avoid excess reagent in the mixture.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The remaining amount of substrate 5d did not change … NBS was consumed due to decomposition.” (Table 1, entry 1)

Paper Title: Solving Gas–Liquid Mixing-Induced Clogging in Continuous-Flow Hydrogenation Synthesis of an API Intermediate
Problem_Description: When the feed solution (substrate 1) is mixed with dry H₂ in a standard tee‑mixer (configuration a) the poorly soluble substrate precipitates in the gas‑rich region, rapidly forming solid plugs that cause an immediate pressure rise (tₛ < 0.5 h) and shutdown of the continuous‑flow hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: A second tee‑mix is installed upstream of the main gas‑liquid mixer. A low‑flow solvent stream (0.04 mL solvent per mL feed) is introduced to the H₂ line to pre‑wet the gas. The resulting two‑phase gas stream can carry the solvent into the mixing zone, dramatically reducing the drying power of the gas and washing any nascent precipitate, which prevents clog formation for >56 h (lab) and >1.5 h (25× scale‑up).
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Using a standard tee‑mixer (config a), clogging was noted almost immediately (tₛ < 0.5 h) …”
- “A simple, yet practical, approach … pre‑wet gas with a solvent (0.04 mL mL⁻¹ feed) prior to contacting the feed … resulted in a clog‑free 56 h continuous run (config d, entry 9).”
- “The amount of solvent added … was inconsequential and could be easily borrowed from the feed solution to maintain the same overall process concentration.”

Paper Title: Solving Gas–Liquid Mixing-Induced Clogging in Continuous-Flow Hydrogenation Synthesis of an API Intermediate
Problem_Description: Adding a dip tube for liquid entry in the tee‑mixer (configuration b) increased the gas‑liquid interface area (A_g = 29.7 mm²) and delayed pressure rise, but after ~13 h the pressure became unstable and eventually triggered a shutdown, indicating that the modification did not fully eliminate solid accumulation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The dip‑tube was repositioned so that the gas, rather than the liquid, flowed through the dip tube (configuration c). This altered the gas‑liquid flow paths and reduced the residence time of the gas‑rich phase in the clog‑prone region, but the smaller gas‐cross‑section (A_g = 1.2 mm²) led to earlier pressure spikes, showing that flow‑path redesign alone was insufficient.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Adding a dip tube for liquid entry in the standard tee‑mixer design (config b, entry 6) raised tₛ further, although ΔP started to become unstable eventually after 13 h.”
- “Altering the gas and liquid flow paths (config c, entry 7), where gas was flown through the dip tube instead of liquid, resulted in a shorter tₛ.”
- “It is worth noting that, in all these examples, ΔP rise was solely due to changes in USP reading, whereas DSP remained stable.”

Paper Title: Solving Gas–Liquid Mixing-Induced Clogging in Continuous-Flow Hydrogenation Synthesis of an API Intermediate
Problem_Description: Reducing the feed concentration and delivering the liquid from the bottom of the tee (entry 5) lowered the rate of precipitation and extended the clog‑free run time, but the pressure still increased to >100 psi, causing automatic shutdown; the approach required additional solvent use and longer flushing cycles, increasing operational cost.
Solution_Description: The feed concentration of substrate 1 was lowered (≈5 wt % instead of ~6 wt %) and the liquid was introduced from the bottom of the tee‑mix to keep the gas line wetted, which modestly increased tₛ (< 1 h) but did not fully prevent clogging. Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Process Development for the Manufacture of a Topical Pan-Trk Inhibitor Incorporating Decarboxylative sp

Supporting_Evidence: “LiCl was shown to be necessary for the reaction, with the Grignard reagent poorly soluble in the absence of LiCl, leading to it precipitating out and resulting in poor reaction conversion.”; “Alternative additives to DMPU were screened, but DMPU performed better than the alternative additives tested (NMP, DMI, TMEDA).”

Supporting_Evidence: “The Grignard reagent … was added in a single portion within 20 s resulting in an exotherm (32–38 °C) and off‑gassing.”; “No significant impact was observed in the range of THF volumes explored, so more dilute conditions were chosen for process safety reasons (greater dilution preferred for inherent safety of exothermic processes).”; “Scale‑up was performed in a stepwise fashion for safety reasons, monitoring exotherm and gas evolution…”

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: The previous route required the expensive and poorly sourced starting materials 2‑aminoaryl iodide (2) and aldehyde 4, which had limited suppliers and high per‑gram prices, making large‑scale production financially and logistically untenable.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced 2 and 4 with inexpensive, commercially available methyl 5‑fluoro‑2‑methyl‑3‑nitrobenzoate (6) and 4‑cyanobenzaldehyde (7), which are low‑cost and readily sourced, thereby removing the cost and supply bottlenecks.
Supporting_Evidence: “the expensive starting materials 2 and 4, their high cost and the limited number of suppliers present significant challenges for large‑scale synthesis” (Scheme 1 b). “Methyl 5‑fluoro‑2‑methyl‑3‑nitrobenzoate (6) and 4‑cyanobenzaldehyde (7) were identified as suitable surrogate… cost‑effective starting materials” (Scheme 2 a).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: The earlier synthesis required two column‑chromatography steps for product isolation, which are inefficient and impractical at manufacturing scale.
Solution_Description: All intermediates and the final product in the new route were isolated by simple recrystallization, eliminating chromatography entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: “the final two of the three separation steps require column chromatography, which is not ideal for product isolation in the pharmaceutical industry” (Introduction). “All intermediates and the final product could be isolated through recrystallization” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: The oxidation of compound 10 with m‑CPBA is highly exothermic, posing safety and temperature‑control concerns during scale‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: “meta‑chloroperoxybenzoic acid (70 %, 20 g, 82.5 mmol) at 0 °C (ice/water) … <bold>Caution: This process is exothermic</bold>” (Scheme 3 a). “The reaction mixture was stirred at the same temperature …” (Scheme 3 a).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: Formamide 15, the methyl‑group precursor, is poorly soluble in THF, limiting its reactivity in the chemoselective reduction step.
Solution_Description: Addition of L‑selectride dramatically increased the solubility of 15 in THF, forming a clear solution that enabled efficient reduction with Red‑Al.
Supporting_Evidence: “Formamide 15 was barely soluble in THF, which likely contributed to its low reactivity and poor selectivity during reduction” (Results). “We observed an unexpected increase in the solubility when l‑selectride was added” (Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: Direct monomethylation of desmethyl rucaparib 8 with methyl iodide or via the Eschweiler–Clarke reaction gave mixtures of over‑methylated product Me‑1 or the undesired cyclic amine 16, leading to poor yields of the target rucaparib 1.
Solution_Description: An indirect methylation strategy was adopted: conversion of 8 to formamide 15 using acetic formic anhydride, followed by chemoselective reduction of the formamide to the methyl group, which furnished rucaparib 1 in high yield and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “When we treated 8 with one equivalent of methyl iodide, no selectivity was observed… affording a 1:1:1 mixture of 8, 1, and Me‑1” (Scheme 5 a). “The direct monomethylation… proved challenging” (Discussion). “The indirect methylation approach… formamide 15 as a reliable precursor… chemoselective reduction… yielded rucaparib 1” (Results).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: The Strecker reaction employed trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) and the imino‑Stetter reaction used sodium cyanide, both of which generate toxic hydrogen cyanide and require strict safety precautions.
Solution_Description: All cyanide‑handling steps were conducted in a fume hood equipped with HCN detectors, personnel wore detector necklaces, and cyanide‑containing waste was deactivated with sodium hypochlorite before disposal.
Supporting_Evidence: “Trimethylsilyl cyanide is a toxic reagent… appropriate protective gears… HCN detector… residual cyanide in wastewater could be deactivated by the treatment with sodium hypochlorite” (Experimental section). “Sodium cyanide is a toxic reagent… appropriate protective gears… HCN detector… residual cyanide in wastewater could be deactivated” (Scheme 4 b).

Paper Title: Practical and Efficient Approach to Scalable Synthesis of Rucaparib
Problem_Description: Initial reductive attempts on formamide 15 with LiAlH₄ or DIBAL‑H gave low conversion and produced the over‑reduced cyclic amine 16, reducing the overall yield of rucaparib 1.
Solution_Description: A combination of L‑selectride (to increase solubility) and Red‑Al (a milder, selective hydride donor) at 25 °C gave 70 % conversion with a 10:1 1 : 16 ratio, leading to an isolated 84 % yield of rucaparib 1 on decagram scale.

Paper Title: Impurity Control Strategy of TMS-Triol in the Manufacture Development of Islatravir
Problem_Description: The original gas‑chromatography (GC) release method (DB‑1701 column) could not detect the non‑volatile impurities TMS‑Ketal and TMS‑Hexol that were generated in the TMS‑Triol step, leading to undetected impurity build‑up and inconsistent batch quality.
Solution_Description: Orthogonal HPLC‑UV methods (Cortecs T3 at 205 nm for TMS‑Triol step, SeQuant Zic‑Hilic for the triol/phosphorylation step and a second Cortecs T3 method for the final API) were developed and validated, enabling reliable detection and quantification of TMS‑Ketal and TMS‑Hexol.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “These impurities, defined as TMS‑Ketal and TMS‑Hexol, were observed … were non‑volatile and were not previously detected by the GC release method employed.” (sec 2.1) 
• “The GC method used for analyzing TMS‑triol was not suitable for detecting impurities such as TMS‑ketal … To overcome the limitation … an HPLC method was established.” (sec 2.1) 
• “HPLC analysis was performed on Waters Cortecs T3 … UV detection at 205 nm … retention times are TMS‑hexol at 8.87 min, TMS‑triol at 9.76 min, and TMS‑ketal at 13.52 min.” (sec 4.2.1) 
• “The HILIC column operates … is proficient at retaining these highly polar compounds effectively.” (sec 2.3) 
• “An orthogonal HPLC method has been incorporated using the Cortects T3 column and UV detection at 205 nm in the final API step.” (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Impurity Control Strategy of TMS-Triol in the Manufacture Development of Islatravir
Problem_Description: During the de‑silylation (hydrolysis) of TMS‑Triol, a poorly water‑soluble TMS‑Ketal precipitated on reactor walls and impellers, leading to fouling, incomplete hydrolysis and the possibility of impurity carry‑over to the API.
Solution_Description: The hydrolysis temperature was raised from 50 °C to the upper permissible exposure limit of 70 °C, increasing the solubility of TMS‑Ketal and accelerating its hydrolysis so that the ketal no longer remains on the vessel interior.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “TMS‑ketal… accumulates on the reactor walls and impellers, and most of it is not hydrolyzed.” (sec 2.3) 
• “Simply increasing the temperature to the current upper permissible exposure limit (PAR limit) of 70 °C can increase the solubility of TMS‑ketal and promote the hydrolysis reaction kinetics.” (sec 2.4) 
• “The original hydrolysis process involved … 50 °C for approximately 4 h.” (sec 2.4) 
• “The increase in temperature resulted in nondetectable levels of TMS‑Ketal left in the reaction solution, and the formed Ketal can be washed away from the final product.” (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Impurity Control Strategy of TMS-Triol in the Manufacture Development of Islatravir
Problem_Description: The catalytic amount of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) used in the DHA‑cracking step, together with higher temperature and longer residence time, promoted formation of the trimeric TMS‑Ketal impurity, increasing impurity levels up to > 1 % area.
Solution_Description: TFA loading was reduced, the cracking temperature was lowered, and the residence time shortened, which together suppressed the equilibrium shift toward the dimer/ketal‑forming pathways.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Increased formation of TMS‑ketal … is observed with a prolonged reaction time under DHA cracking conditions. Higher temperatures and TFA can also elevate TMS‑Ketal formation.” (sec 2.2) 
• Table 1 shows a clear increase in TMS‑ketal area% with higher temperature, longer time and higher TFA equiv. (e.g., 70 °C, 24 h, 0.04 eq → 1.75 % area). (tbl 1) 
• “The formation of TMS‑ketal … can be minimized … by controlling the amount of TFA and minimizing the reaction temperature and time of the DHA cracking step.” (sec 2.4) 
• “The root cause … was the catalytic action of TFA … temperature and holding time … influence the formation of TMS‑ketal.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Impurity Control Strategy of TMS-Triol in the Manufacture Development of Islatravir
Problem_Description: TMS‑Hexol was formed via an aldol‑type side reaction during the base‑catalyzed alkynylation step; its level was strongly affected by the amount of Grignard reagent and the alkynylation temperature.

Supporting_Evidence:

• “The DOE study identified that the alkynylation temperature and the number of Grignard equivalents had the strongest effects on the formation of TMS‑hexol.” (sec 2.2) 
• Table 1 shows low TMS‑hexol area% under most conditions, confirming temperature/time control suppresses its formation. (tbl 1) 
• “The base‑catalyzed mechanism appears to be more likely for the formation of TMS‑Hexol.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Impurity Control Strategy of TMS-Triol in the Manufacture Development of Islatravir
