Problem_Description: Pulsating flow caused inconsistent pressure profiles in the electrolysis cell and led to fluid leakage during operation of the parallel‑plate reactors.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Replaced the pneumatic diaphragm pump with an electrically‑controlled centrifugal pump and eliminated the downstream pulse‑damper, providing smooth, pulsation‑free flow up to ~50 L min⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of an electrically controlled centrifugal pump instead of a pneumatic diaphragm pump…provides smooth flow and is controlled using a variable frequency drive…access to flow rates up to ~50 L/min without pulsation, in contrast to the 16 L/min attainable…with a diaphragm pump.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Leaking of the reaction mixture from the parallel‑plate reactor due to porous graphite electrodes and inadequate gasket design.
Solution_Description: Fabricated custom impervious graphite electrodes (resin‑filled) and used larger‑area EPDM rubber gaskets to eliminate the need for porous spacers and improve sealing.
Supporting_Evidence: “Custom‑made impervious graphite electrodes…obviating the need for the polypropylene spacers…avoiding the leaking issue associated with using porous graphite electrodes.”; “EPDM rubber gaskets were cut to expose a larger surface area…doubling the surface area…enabled doubling the productivity…and avoided leaks.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Poor solubility of 1,2‑bis(diphenylphosphino)ethane (DPPE) required a higher reaction temperature (18 °C vs 5 °C) for the electrolysis.
Solution_Description: Adjusted the reaction temperature to 18 °C to improve DPPE dissolution and maintain consistent conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the synthesis of 4, the electrolysis was conducted at 18 °C instead of 5 °C due to the poor solubility of the 1,2‑bis‑(diphenylphosphino)‑ethane (DPPE) starting material.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Product 3 showed decomposition after reaching a maximum yield at ~2 F mol⁻¹, indicating over‑electrolysis leads to product degradation.
Solution_Description: Monitored voltage and charge in real time with PAT tools to terminate the electrolysis at the optimal charge before product degradation occurs.
Supporting_Evidence: “Figure 4B illustrates that the amount of product 3 reaches a maximum after approximately 2 F/mol…further electrolysis of the mixture results in decomposition of the product.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Gradual formation of phosphine‑oxide impurity during the electrolysis, which grew throughout the reaction rather than appearing in a single burst.
Solution_Description: Implemented continuous voltage monitoring and data logging to understand impurity growth kinetics and adjust reaction parameters accordingly.
Supporting_Evidence: “The phosphine oxide impurity in each reaction grows in over the entire course of the electrolysis and is neither generated as a burst at the start…nor in a disproportionate amount near the end of the electrolysis when the cell voltage is the largest.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Platinum‑clad niobium cathodes are expensive, increasing the cost of the electrochemical process.
Solution_Description: Substituted the platinum cathode with a 316 stainless‑steel cathode, which offers comparable overpotential for proton reduction at a much lower cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “Given that the cathodic reaction is a proton reduction…we explored substitution of the platinum cathode for a 316 stainless‑steel (SS) electrode.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Tetramethylammonium acetate supporting electrolyte showed limited solubility in the NMP/MeOH solvent system and was less available on large scale.
Solution_Description: Replaced tetramethylammonium acetate with tetrabutylammonium acetate, which has improved solubility and greater commercial availability.
Supporting_Evidence: “The supporting electrolyte was changed from tetramethylammonium acetate…to tetrabutylammonium acetate, which has improved solubility in the NMP/MeOH mixture, thus enabling operation under more concentrated conditions…and is more widely available on a larger scale.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: High solubility of products 1 and 2 prevented direct crystallization from the reaction mixture, requiring aqueous work‑up to remove supporting electrolyte, NMP and MeOH.
Solution_Description: Developed an aqueous work‑up protocol to remove the supporting electrolyte and solvents, allowing isolation of 1 and 2 despite their high solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high solubility of 1 and 2 precluded this approach; instead, an aqueous workup was required to remove the supporting electrolyte (Bu₄NOAc), NMP and MeOH from the product.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Use of Bu₄NPF₆ as supporting electrolyte resulted in insolubility in water, causing contamination of the isolated solid despite acceptable product formation.
Solution_Description: Switched to water‑soluble supporting electrolytes (KPF₆, LiOAc, Et₄NPF₆) and ultimately selected Et₄NPF₆ for improved isolation, avoiding water‑insoluble contamination.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of Bu₄NPF₆ as a supporting electrolyte and its insolubility in water resulted in Bu₄NPF₆ contamination in the isolated solid despite providing acceptable performance for product formation.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: When Et₄NPF₆ was used for the synthesis of (R,R)‑5, assay yield dropped to 49 % and the product crystallized as an amorphous, poorly filterable solid containing residual electrolyte.
Solution_Description: Developed a new direct‑crystallization protocol (addition of water as antisolvent) that gave crystalline product with improved yield and filterability.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of Et₄NPF₆ for the synthesis of (R,R)‑5 not only provided worse performance…The product came out of solution as an amorphous form that demonstrated poor filterability…The team developed a new crystallization process that provided crystalline material and enabled facile filtration.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Corrosion of the titanium current collector in the kilogram‑scale Electro Syn Cell caused incomplete conversion of the P(III)–P(V) intermediate and introduced titanium leached into the product, raising safety and quality concerns.
Solution_Description: Applied an Ebonex (Ti sub‑oxide) coating (~0.008–0.012 in. thick) to the titanium current collector to protect against corrosion and embrittlement.
Supporting_Evidence: “Corrosion was observed on the titanium current collector…We postulated…application of a protective coating…Ti suboxide coatings such as an Ebonex coating…A coating of Ebonex…was applied on the titanium current collector…no visual evidence of corrosion was observed on the Ebonex‑coated titanium current collector sections.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Use of 0.5 mm ePTFE gaskets in the kilo‑scale reactor caused leaks at lower temperatures due to thermal swelling, compromising reactor integrity.
Solution_Description: Replaced ePTFE gaskets with 1 mm EPDM rubber gaskets, which have better thermal‑swelling properties and provide a more reliable seal.
Supporting_Evidence: “EPDM rubber gaskets were used in the Electro Syn Cell instead of extended PTFE (ePTFE)…The combination of thicker gaskets (1 vs 0.5 mm) and change in material from ePTFE to EPDM provided a cost reduction and, more importantly, improved sealing due to EPDM having better thermal‑swelling properties.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: At kilogram scale, the electrolysis required 6.42 F mol⁻¹ to reach >99 % substrate consumption but still left ~5 % of the P(III)–P(V) intermediate unreacted, likely due to Ti current collector corrosion.
Solution_Description: Implemented improved temperature control (recirculating jacket, larger cooling lines, high‑surface‑area heat exchanger) and used Ebonex‑coated Ti current collectors to prevent corrosion, thereby achieving complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “To improve cooling capacity, two key changes were made…larger diameter insulated cooling lines…larger‑surface‑area tube‑in‑shell heat exchanger…Applied a protective Ebonex coating…no visual evidence of corrosion was observed on the Ebonex‑coated titanium current collector.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: The original turbulence promoter mesh in the parallel‑plate reactors varied in geometry and pore size across reactor sizes, affecting mixing efficiency and mass transfer.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Designed a custom 3‑D‑printed nylon gyroid‑infill turbulence promoter that maximized strength while minimizing obstruction, standardizing mixing across scales.
Supporting_Evidence: “A custom 3D printed turbulence promoter made of nylon was used…The 3D printed pattern used was a gyroid infill, which maximized strength of the mesh while minimizing the surface area that obstructs access to the electrode.”

Paper Title: Scalable Flow Electrosynthesis of Iminophosphoranes
Problem_Description: Large‑scale use of platinum cathodes increases material cost and limits process economics.
Solution_Description: Adopted stainless‑steel cathodes for all scales, leveraging comparable overpotential for proton reduction while dramatically reducing electrode cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “While platinum clad on niobium is generally robust…we explored substitution of the platinum cathode for a 316 stainless‑steel (SS) electrode. This substitution is usually feasible for electrolyses where the cathodic reaction is the reduction of protons…overpotential…on platinum or stainless steel is both small and comparable.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The original commercial synthesis used stoichiometric silver carbonate in DMSO at 120 °C for a decarboxylation, which would be prohibitively expensive and posed a potential explosion risk upon thermal decomposition of DMSO at larger scale.  The subsequent reduction of an intermediate required 10 mol % Pd/C at high pressure, demanding specialized equipment.  The final Sugasawa Friedel–Crafts step gave only 24.8 % isolated product and required chromatographic purification.
Solution_Description: A completely new four‑step route was devised that replaces the silver‑carbonate decarboxylation with a Buchwald‑Hartwig amination (Pd(OAc)₂/BrettPhos, 1 mol % catalyst, K₂CO₃ base) and the Sugasawa step with a GaCl₃‑mediated Friedel–Crafts acylation.  The new sequence eliminates high‑pressure reductions, removes the need for stoichiometric silver, and raises the overall isolated yield to 32 % (an 18.6 % absolute increase).
Supporting_Evidence: The abstract states “An improved synthesis … features a Buchwald‑Hartwig amination … and a GaCl₃‑mediated Friedel–Crafts acylation… The new route reduced the commercial synthesis by three steps and increased the overall yield by 18.6 %.”; The background paragraph notes “the use of stoichiometric silver carbonate in DMSO at 120 °C … would be prohibitively expensive and poses a potential explosion risk… reduction of 6 used 10 mol % Pd/C at high pressures… Sugasawa reaction of 8 yielded only 24.8 %… and required chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The AlCl₃‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts acylation required three equivalents of both AlCl₃ and chloroacetyl chloride (CAC) to obtain modest conversion.  The aqueous quench of excess AlCl₃ was highly exothermic, generated large volumes of hot HCl/aluminum salt emulsion, and left behind volatile, carcinogenic CAC, raising safety and waste‑handling concerns.
Solution_Description: Screening of Lewis acids identified GaCl₃ as a superior catalyst; only 1.5 equiv of CAC was needed for >90 % conversion, and GaCl₃ hydrolysis is markedly less exothermic than AlCl₃, allowing a smaller quench volume and eliminating the need for ice‑water cooling.
Supporting_Evidence: The text reports “Initially, AlCl₃ and CAC were used… three equivalents of both Lewis acid and CAC were required… the required aqueous quench … was highly exothermic and raised safety concerns… excess CAC, a volatile lachrymator and carcinogen, persisted throughout the workup.”; Later it states “GaCl₃ … rapid, clean conversion… hydrolysis is less exothermic than that of AlCl₃, it was expected that quench volume could be reduced and safety improved.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The lithiation‑cyclization of dibromophenyl ether produced hydrodehalogenated by‑product as the major side‑reaction, giving only 62 % isolated yield of the desired benzofuran and requiring normal‑phase chromatography for purification.
Solution_Description: A future development goal is to replace the chromatography step with a direct crystallization of the benzofuran intermediate, simplifying work‑up and improving overall material throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors write “Hydrodehalogenation was the major side reaction, thus normal‑phase chromatography was required to purify 12.” and later note “A future development goal is to perform crystallization to isolate this intermediate.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The intermediate acetamide product (compound 3) was insoluble in water and heptane, complicating isolation, while the pre‑cyclization material (12) was soluble in heptane, leading to mixed solubility profiles that required careful precipitation and washing steps.
Solution_Description: A work‑up protocol was implemented where the crude reaction mixture was precipitated with heptane, washed with brine and heptane, and dried, affording compound 3 in quantitative yield and 97 % purity without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states “Solubility data showed that 3 was insoluble in water and in heptane. Fortunately, 12 was soluble in heptane… a procedure was developed where the crude product was precipitated with heptane, washed with brine and heptane, and dried to provide 3 in quantitative yield and 97 % purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: Aqueous quench of the AlCl₃‑catalyzed Friedel‑Crafts reaction generated large amounts of heat, HCl, and aluminum salts, producing an emulsion that required large solvent volumes and cooling with ice, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Switching to GaCl₃ reduced the exotherm of the quench, eliminated the need for ice‑water cooling, and avoided emulsion formation, simplifying the work‑up and improving operational safety.
Supporting_Evidence: The text notes “the required aqueous quench … was highly exothermic and raised safety concerns… significant quantities of heat, HCl, and aluminum salts… prone to emulsion formation.” Later, “GaCl₃ … hydrolysis is less exothermic than that of AlCl₃, it was expected that quench volume could be reduced and safety improved.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: Use of Cs₂CO₃ as base in the Buchwald‑Hartwig amination introduced cost and hygroscopicity issues, and water present in the reaction mixture inhibited conversion, leading to lower yields.
Solution_Description: K₂CO₃ was substituted for Cs₂CO₃; it is cheaper, less hygroscopic, and performed equally well, restoring high conversion while reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors write “due to the risk of hygroscopicity … cost, and density of Cs₂CO₃, we decided to use K₂CO₃, which performed equally well in the amination reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The AlCl₃ Friedel‑Crafts quench generated a biphasic mixture that formed stable emulsions, requiring large volumes of organic solvent for separation and making isolation of the product cumbersome.
Solution_Description: GaCl₃, being more soluble in DCE and water, produced a cleaner phase separation after quench, eliminating emulsion formation and allowing direct precipitation of the product with MTBE.
Supporting_Evidence: The manuscript states “Gallium salts were more soluble in DCE and water, thus, reducing workup volumes and eliminating emulsion problems experienced with AlCl₃ quenches.”

Paper Title: Process Development to Synthesize SGD-11275 Utilizing a Pd-Catalyzed Acetamide Arylation and Gallium-Mediated Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The traditional route employed a decarboxylation using silver carbonate in DMSO at 120 °C, which poses a thermal explosion hazard on scale.
Solution_Description: The decarboxylation step was removed entirely; the core benzofuran fragment was assembled via an alkylation‑cyclization sequence followed by a Buchwald‑Hartwig amination, avoiding the dangerous silver‑carbonate/DMSO step.
Supporting_Evidence: The background notes “the use of stoichiometric silver carbonate in DMSO at 120 °C … would be prohibitively expensive and poses a potential explosion risk …” and the new route description emphasizes “a Buchwald‑Hartwig amination … and a GaCl₃‑mediated Friedel‑Crafts acylation” without any mention of the silver‑carbonate step.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The tetracyclic core formed early in the medicinal‑chemistry route has very low solubility in any solvent, making material handling difficult on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was redesigned so the indole‑containing tetracyclic core is assembled at the end of the sequence via an S_NAr reaction followed by intramolecular reductive cyclization, avoiding early exposure of the poorly‑soluble core.
Supporting_Evidence: “construction of the tetracyclic core ... causes difficulty in material handling due to its low solubility in any solvent” (Introduction, p. 2); “We sought to address the critical issues … by altering the synthetic strategy … compound 12 … allows the installation of the tetracyclic core at the end of the synthesis” (Introduction, p. 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The Fischer indolization step gives a 1:1 regioisomeric mixture, providing low overall yield and requiring a trituration step to remove the undesired isomer.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic route was adopted that avoids the Fischer indolization step entirely, building the indole moiety later through S_NAr and reductive cyclization, thereby eliminating the regio‑selectivity problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “low regioselectivity (1:1 isomeric mixture) is observed in the Fischer indolization step” (Introduction, p. 2); “compound 12 … allows the installation of the tetracyclic core at the end of the synthesis” (Introduction, p. 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: A demethylation step in the original route required heating to 190 °C, which is impractical and unsafe for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The route was completely redesigned (new synthetic strategy) to eliminate the high‑temperature demethylation, using milder conditions in later steps such as TFE/TMSCl for t‑butyl ester cleavage performed at ≤10 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “high reaction temperatures are required (i.e., 190 °C for the demethylation process), which are not feasible for scaling up” (Introduction, p. 2); “TMSCl as a source of HCl in the presence of TFE provided optimal results … 98 % conversion … at 0–10 °C” (Step 4, Table 5).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The original Claisen condensation using i‑PrMgCl required 19 h to reach full conversion and employed a large excess of an expensive, moisture‑sensitive Grignard reagent.
Solution_Description: Replacing i‑PrMgCl with MgCl₂ and Et₃N in DME reduced the reaction time to 5 h while using inexpensive, air‑stable reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “reaction rate was extremely low (i.e., it took 19 h to reach 99 % conversion). In addition, the necessity of a large volume of expensive and moisture‑sensitive i‑PrMgCl solution is a disadvantage” (Step 1); “concomitant use of MgCl₂, a stable reagent … and triethylamine allowed the reaction to complete within 5 h at 75 °C” (Step 1, Table 1, condition 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: During the S_NAr reaction, product 13 decomposes under basic conditions, undergoing a retro‑Claisen reaction that generates bis‑aryl impurity 24 and reduces the purity of the desired intermediate.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of Cs₂CO₃ to three equivalents and keeping the reaction temperature ≤ 45 °C suppressed the retro‑Claisen pathway and provided high‑purity product 13.
Supporting_Evidence: “product 13 decomposes … a retro‑Claisen reaction … forming bis‑aryl 24” (Step 2); “using three equivalents of Cs₂CO₃ is optimal, in combination with a temperature not exceeding 45 °C” (Step 2, Fig. 3).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: Residual Mg²⁺ ions from the previous step inhibited the S_NAr reaction, giving only 68 % conversion.
Solution_Description: A thorough removal of magnesium ions prior to the S_NAr step was implemented (e.g., washing), restoring full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “When 0.2 equiv of MgCl₂ was added … the reaction reached only 68 % conversion. This indicates that it is crucial to thoroughly eliminate magnesium ions prior to step 2.” (Step 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The nitro‑reduction with Na₂S₂O₄ generated sulfonic‑acid impurities 26 and 27 via a Piria reaction, which were difficult to purge in downstream work‑up.
Solution_Description: In‑process control measures, including pH monitoring and a crystallization step, were introduced to limit the formation of these impurities and ensure high‑purity indole 22.
Supporting_Evidence: “sulfonic acids 26 and 27 were formed … these impurities were not effectively purged … in‑process control measures to limit the levels of impurities were implemented” (Step 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The intramolecular Friedel–Crafts cyclization of acid 12 led to decarboxylation (impurity 30) and formation of regio‑isomer 31, reducing the isolated yield of the tetracyclic core 10.
Solution_Description: Optimized conditions employed Ac₂O (4 equiv) with DIPEA in DMA (5 v/w), using dilute reaction conditions and higher Ac₂O loading to suppress decarboxylation and improve regio‑selectivity, giving 76 % isolated yield of 10.
Supporting_Evidence: “Ac₂O in the presence of DIPEA resulted in a complete conversion of substrate 10, with satisfactory selectivity (condition 4). … increasing the amount of Ac₂O notably suppressed decarboxylation (condition 4). … highly dilute conditions (condition 3) appeared to improve regioselectivity” (Step 5, Tables 6 and 7).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: Traditional crystallization of acid 12 was time‑consuming; prolonged stirring caused in‑situ generation of HCl from tert‑butyl chloride, lowering the isolated yield from 91 % to 71 %.
Solution_Description: A rapid crystallization protocol at pH ≈ 6 was adopted, limiting the stirring time and preventing HCl buildup, thereby preserving high yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “when the crystallization mixture was stirred for 3 days … final isolated yield dropped to 71 %. This observation can be attributed to the in‑situ generation of HCl … These results suggest that the crystallization process must be conducted quickly … to ensure a high yield.” (Step 4).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: Conventional addition of aqueous HCl to a solution of free‑base 10 caused simultaneous precipitation of both the free base and its HCl salt, contaminating the final salt 1 with unconverted base.
Solution_Description: A reverse‑addition protocol was developed where a solution of free‑base 10 was added slowly to an aqueous HCl/EtOH mixture, ensuring immediate conversion to the salt and minimizing free‑base contamination.
Supporting_Evidence: “conventional solvent/antisolvent crystallization were unsuccessful … prompting us to alter our approach to a reverse addition method (adding a solution of 10 to an HCl solution). As free base 10 is immediately converted into HCl salt 1 … there is only negligible risk of 10 contaminating 1.” (Step 6).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: The original process used palladium catalysts and toxic transition metals in the final step, raising safety and cost concerns for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The final amination employed a palladium‑NHC precatalyst (CX21) at low loading (2 mol %) and an aqueous work‑up with N‑acetyl‑l‑cysteine to scavenge residual palladium, reducing metal usage and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “investigated NHC ligands … identified CX21 … high reactivity … reducing the catalyst loading to 2 mol % improved the selectivity” (Step 3, Table 4); “Aqueous workup with N‑acetyl‑l‑cysteine (NAC) to reduce the residual Pd content afforded the crude compound 11” (Step 3).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Manufacturing Process for Alectinib with a Concise Preparation of the Indole-Containing Tetracyclic Core
Problem_Description: Column chromatography was required for isolation of several intermediates in the medicinal chemistry route, which is time‑consuming and unsuitable for kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The new manufacturing sequence eliminates column chromatography by telescoping reactions (e.g., using the crude β‑keto ester 20 directly in the next step) and relies on crystallization for product isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “workup techniques required for the isolation of intermediates (e.g., column chromatography) are time‑consuming.” (Introduction, p. 2); “The product is an oil, and it was used in the next step without purification.” (Step 1).

Paper Title: Identification of a Novel Process Impurity, Root Cause Investigation, and Its Control Strategy in Process Chemistry of Nevirapine API
Problem_Description: During routine HPLC related‑substance testing of nevirapine API an unknown peak (RRT 6.4) was sometimes observed at >0.10 % (the unspecified‑impurity limit) and was difficult to be removed in the downstream crystallisation work‑up because of its structural similarity to the API.
Solution_Description: 1. The final two reaction steps were cooled from the original 140 ± 5 °C to 120–125 °C, which lowered the RRT 6.4 impurity to 0.04 % and increased the nevirapine yield to ~80 %. 2. The NaH loading was reduced from 3.0 equiv (the theoretical 2.0 equiv) to 2.7 equiv; under these conditions the impurity fell to 0.02 % while the API yield rose to 81.4 %. 3. By combining the lower temperature and the reduced NaH loading (both TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION and STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE) the impurity level was consistently ≤0.02 % and the overall process yield improved by 16 % relative to the original manufacturing route. 4. The original Method 1 (nitration of CAPIC) suffered from a low‑yield nitration step and required chromatographic purification, making scale‑up expensive and environmentally problematic; the process was therefore abandoned in favour of Method 3 (a revised CAPIC condensation route) which gave higher overall yield and lower material cost. 5. Method 2, which relied on 2‑cyclopropylamino‑nicotinic acid, required multiple intermediate isolations and incurred high raw‑material and operation costs; the same drawbacks were avoided by adopting Method 3, a more concise and cost‑effective synthetic pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "An unknown peak ... was sometimes above 0.10% and difficult to be purged in the downstream of the existing manufacturing process of nevirapine, most likely due to its structural similarity to the API." (Abstract)
2. "When the reaction temperatures were set at 120–125 °C, levels of RRT 6.4 impurity could be controlled in relatively low levels, while the yield of nevirapine was progressively improved..." (Section 2.5)
3. "When the molar ratio of NaH was lowered to 2.7, the level of the RRT 6.4 impurity decreased to 0.02 %, while the yield of nevirapine increased from 65.4 % to 81.4 %" (Section 2.5)
4. "Method 1 becomes environmentally problematic due to the low yield of the nitration step... chromatographic purification was needed, which hindered its further development for scale‑up and commercialization." (Introduction)
5. "Method 2... carried high raw material and operation costs due to multiple intermediate isolations and unit operations to prepare 2‑CAN." (Introduction)
6. "Method 3 ... was shown to have the highest yield with reasonable cost ... therefore, it was adopted as the initial process and subsequently improved in our company for the commercial manufacturing of nevirapine API." (Introduction)
7. "Cyclopropylamine can undergo rearrangement via ring opening to form propan‑1‑imine … the imine product formed from the ring opening of cyclopropylamine could react with the core of nevirapine to eventually lead to the formation of 8‑n‑propyl nevirapine." (Section 2.4)
8. "Ten grams of cyclopropylamine were heated to ∼140–150 °C for 12 h … two new degradants … identified as (E)‑N‑propylidenecyclopropanamine (10) and (Z)‑N‑propylidenecyclopropanamine (10′)." (Section 2.5, Experimental)
9. "When the reaction temperature was decreased to 120–125 °C, the level of the RRT 6.4 impurity could be controlled … while the yield of nevirapine was progressively improved as compared to the existing manufacturing process." (Section 2.5)
10. "The existing manufacturing process … uses NaH (3.0 equiv) … the theoretical molar ratio of NaH to nevirapine condensate is 2, suggesting that the molar ratio could be lowered." (Section 2.5)

Paper Title: Identification of a Novel Process Impurity, Root Cause Investigation, and Its Control Strategy in Process Chemistry of Nevirapine API
Problem_Description: Method 1 required a low‑yield nitration step and chromatographic purification, while Method 2 involved many intermediate isolations, both leading to high material and operational costs for multikilogram production of nevirapine.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to Method 3, which uses the same raw materials as Method 1 but with an improved CAPIC condensation step, delivering the highest overall yield (∼65 % in the original process and up to 81 % after optimisation) with reasonable cost and without the need for chromatographic purification.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Method 1 becomes environmentally problematic due to the low yield of the nitration step... chromatographic purification was needed, which hindered its further development for scale‑up and commercialization." (Introduction)
2. "Method 2 ... carried high raw material and operation costs due to multiple intermediate isolations and unit operations to prepare 2‑CAN." (Introduction)
3. "Method 3 ... was shown to have the highest yield with reasonable cost... therefore, it was adopted as the initial process and subsequently improved in our company for the commercial manufacturing of nevirapine API." (Introduction)
4. "The improved process ... gave a nevirapine yield of 81.4 % with impurity at 0.02 %" (Section 2.5, Table 2).

Paper Title: Identification of a Novel Process Impurity, Root Cause Investigation, and Its Control Strategy in Process Chemistry of Nevirapine API
Problem_Description: Cyclopropylamine undergoes thermal ring‑opening at ∼140–150 °C to give propan‑1‑imine and related imine derivatives (10 and 10′), which act as electrophiles that generate the 8‑n‑propyl nevirapine impurity.
Solution_Description: Operating the final steps at a lower temperature (120–125 °C) and using a reduced NaH loading (2.7 equiv) limit the formation of the cyclopropylamine degradation products, thereby suppressing the downstream impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Cyclopropylamine can undergo rearrangement via ring opening to form propan‑1‑imine ... under heating ... the imine product could react with the core of nevirapine to eventually lead to the formation of 8‑n‑propyl nevirapine." (Section 2.4)

Paper Title: Use of Population Balance Modelling to Derisk Scale-Up of an Integrated Crystallization–Wet Milling Process
Problem_Description: Intermittent wet‑mill operation (only after seed‑age or during antisolvent addition) could not reduce the PSD sufficiently; agglomeration was observed when milling was omitted, leading to inconsistent particle sizes.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Redesign the process to run the wet mill continuously (throughout seed‑age and antisolvent addition) so that breakage counteracts growth and prevents agglomeration, thereby stabilising the PSD.
Supporting_Evidence: “Intermittent wet milling … also failed to deliver material within target PSD; … milling was needed during the antisolvent addition to avoid agglomeration, which had been observed to occur without milling.” (p. 3‑4) | “iCWM … with wet milling occurring throughout the entire process.” (p. 4‑5)

Paper Title: Use of Population Balance Modelling to Derisk Scale-Up of an Integrated Crystallization–Wet Milling Process
Problem_Description: Scaling up iCWM is difficult because crystal growth is scale‑independent while wet‑mill breakage is scale‑dependent, causing batch‑to‑batch PSD variations when batch size or mill geometry changes.
Solution_Description: Build a first‑principles‑based PBM that explicitly includes growth, breakage, and equipment‑scale correlations (shear number) to predict how mill tip speed, rotor diameter and batch size affect D90, enabling rational scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “iCWM introduces additional complexity … as it couples scale‑independent growth with scale‑dependent milling and is therefore more difficult to scale‑up in a reproducible manner.” (p. 2‑3) | “Population balance modeling … indicated that mill size and batch size, in addition to wet‑mill tip speed, had a large impact on final PSD.” (p. 2‑3)

Paper Title: Use of Population Balance Modelling to Derisk Scale-Up of an Integrated Crystallization–Wet Milling Process
Problem_Description: In‑process particle‑size monitoring using FBRM failed due to severe probe fouling, preventing reliable real‑time PSD data.
Solution_Description: Rely on offline PSD measurements (laser diffraction, SEM) and incorporate them into the PBM; the model replaces the need for continuous FBRM data during scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Collection of reliable FBRM data was not successful due to severe probe fouling.” (p. 8‑9) | “The PBM … utilizes first‑principle‑based fundamental kinetics, it is more robust to changes in scale …” (p. 3‑4)

Paper Title: Use of Population Balance Modelling to Derisk Scale-Up of an Integrated Crystallization–Wet Milling Process
Problem_Description: The PBM over‑predicted D90 for the 10 m/s tip‑speed condition, indicating a mismatch between model and experiment at low shear rates.
Solution_Description: Refine the breakage‑rate correlation (shear‑number) and include additional data points at low tip speeds to improve model accuracy across the full operating window.
Supporting_Evidence: “The overall match is good, albeit with an overprediction of D90 for the 10 m/s wet‑mill tip speed.” (p. 13‑14) | “The breakage‑rate constant … is described by the shear‑number correlation …” (p. 12‑13)

Supporting_Evidence: “The route originally developed for the preparation of 2′‑fluoroarabinoadenosine … involved the use of DAST to introduce the 2′‑fluorine… The hazards associated with aminotrifluorosulfurane reagents such as DAST are well known.”; “We desired a shorter route that did not require an aminotrifluorosulfurane reagent… A more direct approach from adenosine was envisioned.”

Problem_Description: During the six‑step route, the desilylation and subsequent fluoride‑displacement steps caused base‑mediated cleavage of the adenine base, resulting in loss of product and reduced overall yield.
Solution_Description: The authors redesigned the sequence to employ a single protection‑deprotection strategy based on dynamic kinetic crystallization of the N⁶,3′,5′‑tripivaloyladenosine, which avoids the base‑sensitive desilylation step and preserves the adenine moiety.
Supporting_Evidence: “Another issue was the observation of base cleavage during the desilylation and fluoride displacement steps with the loss of adenine… If a route involving only one protection/deprotection could be found, a greater improvement would be realized.”; “The dynamic kinetic crystallization of 9 gave the desired acylation regiochemistry and the stereoselective fluorination of the corresponding triflate 10.”

Problem_Description: Fluoride displacement of the diol‑triflate intermediate led to rapid elimination, forming 3′‑ and 2′‑ketones and the unsaturated ketone 5, giving poor conversion to the desired fluorinated product.
Solution_Description: Screening identified that using NaHF₂ together with Cy₂NMe in toluene at 50 °C for 41 h provided a high assay yield (81 %) and reduced elimination side‑reactions, delivering the fluorinated product with improved selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The possibility of fluoride displacement on the diol triflate was stymied by its facile elimination… Strongly basic conditions such as with KF, CsF, and Me₄NF gave elimination… Further improvement in the fluoride displacement was achieved (4 equiv of NaHF₂, 6 equiv of Cy₂NMe, 10 vol of toluene, 50 °C, 41 h… obtaining 81 % assay yield.”

Paper Title: Selective Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Acylation of adenosine with pivaloyl chloride initially gave a mixture of di‑ and tri‑pivalates (6 : 1 ratio) and trace tetra‑pivalate, making it difficult to isolate the desired N⁶,3′,5′‑tripivaloyladenosine.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot sequence was devised: (i) pivaloylation of the 2′‑ and 5′‑hydroxyls, (ii) capping of remaining alcohols with TMSCl, (iii) second pivaloylation of the N⁶‑amine, followed by NaHCO₃‑mediated trans‑esterification and crystallization in the presence of trace NaHCO₃ and a catalytic amount of acid. This dynamic kinetic crystallization drives the equilibrium toward the tripivalate, which can be isolated in 89 % yield and >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Treatment of adenosine with 2.5 equiv of PivCl in pyridine converts adenosine mostly to the di‑ and tripivalates… Treatment of the mixture with 2 equiv TMSCl caps the alcohols allowing subsequent complete pivalation… The addition of trace acid prevents any reisomerization… Crystallization in the presence of trace NaHCO₃ drives the ratio further in our favor, since N⁶,3′,5′‑tripivaloyladenosine 9 crystallizes out with >99 % purity.”

Problem_Description: Heating a solution of the isolated tripivalate 9 in EtOAc to reflux for 3 h caused up to 4 % conversion back to the di‑pivalate 8, indicating thermal instability of the product.

Supporting_Evidence: “The product was stable in pyridine with trace Pyr·TfOH, allowing the subsequent triflation to proceed without isomerization… Once isolated as a crystalline solid, 9 was found to be stable for years, but upon heating a solution of 9 to reflux in EtOAc for 3 h up to 4 % of 8 was formed.”

Paper Title: A Tribute to Ullmann’s Work: Expanding Copper Coil Reactor Applications toward the Hydroxylation of Aryl Bromides

Paper Title: A Tribute to Ullmann’s Work: Expanding Copper Coil Reactor Applications toward the Hydroxylation of Aryl Bromides

Supporting_Evidence: “The limited solubility of the organic substrates tested in the DMF/water system forced dilution of the reaction mixture for the compounds in entries 6 and 7.”; “DMF … resulted in a 55 % conversion …”

Paper Title: A Tribute to Ullmann’s Work: Expanding Copper Coil Reactor Applications toward the Hydroxylation of Aryl Bromides

Supporting_Evidence: “One of the main concerns about using a self‑consuming coil … is related to the lifetime of the coil and whether this will be safe to operate.”; “The lifetime of our reactor was determined to be 1.6 years … proving that copper coil reactors are feasible to operate under safe conditions.”; “The lifetime … can be further increased by using thicker copper coils.”

Paper Title: Three-Step Continuous Flow Synthesis of the Intermediate 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxy-5-nitrophenol of Linzagolix
Problem_Description: The esterification step used benzyl chloride and acetyl chloride as protecting‑group reagents. In addition, the reaction generates solid salts that precipitate and clog the PTFE coil, causing pressure buildup and possible reactor failure.
Solution_Description: The protecting group was changed from benzyl chloride/acetyl chloride to propyl‑chloroformate (new protecting‑group route). The substrate concentration was lowered to 0.1 M, which prevented solid‑salt formation and coil clogging while still giving quantitative conversion.

Therefore, there are safety concerns in the dropping process in batch reactors."; "The solid salts formed in the esterification reaction can clog the reaction coil, which can lead to problems such as pressure buildup, equipment failure, and interruption of the flow process."; "We chose propyl chloroformate as a protective reagent instead of benzyl chloride and acetyl chloride …"; "The concentration of 3 was chosen as 0.1 M, as the increase in the concentration of 3 caused the solid salts formed in the reaction to clog the PTFE coil (see Figure S2)."

Paper Title: Three-Step Continuous Flow Synthesis of the Intermediate 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxy-5-nitrophenol of Linzagolix
Problem_Description: The batch nitration of the protected phenol required long residence times at low temperature (‑15 °C to 20 °C) and employed fuming nitric acid, which is hazardous. Conventional nitration is highly exothermic; poor temperature control can cause sharp pressure spikes or explosions.
Solution_Description: The nitration was moved to a continuous‑flow micro‑reactor, providing superior heat removal and safe handling of mixed acids. The molar ratio of sulfuric acid to nitric acid was optimized (2.1 : 1) and the reaction temperature was set to 20 °C, reducing residence time to 24 s and eliminating the exothermic safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: "The following nitration reactions … needed a prolonged reaction time. The low temperature required for the reaction … increased the energy consumption. And the use of fuming nitric acid… has a high safety hazard."; "conventional nitration reactions are fast and highly exothermic, poor control … cause the pressure in the batch reactor to rise sharply or even explode."; "Due to the remarkable temperature rise and high safety risk of nitration in batch, we attempted to use the continuous flow reactor to address these issues."; "When the molar ratio of sulfuric acid to nitric acid increased from 1.5 to 2.1, the conversion and yield reached the maximum 100 % and 91.3 % … The reaction temperature was set to 20 °C … residence time 24 s."

Paper Title: Three-Step Continuous Flow Synthesis of the Intermediate 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxy-5-nitrophenol of Linzagolix
Problem_Description: During batch nitration the rapid, highly exothermic addition of mixed acids generated a large heat‑release rate, leading to a significant adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad ≈ 30 °C) and a maximum reaction temperature of ~48 °C, posing a serious safety hazard.
Solution_Description: A reaction‑calorimetry study quantified the heat evolution; the process was then transferred to a continuous‑flow reactor where the addition of acids is precisely controlled (steady dropwise addition) and the reactor temperature is maintained at 20 °C, eliminating the dangerous temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: "The specific reaction heat (ΔHr) was 89.2 kJ mol⁻¹, the adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad) was 29.9 °C, and the maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction (MTSR) was 47.7 °C."; "The nitration solution and the quenched nitration solution were relatively stable… no obvious thermal decompositions."; "We attempted to use the continuous flow reactor to address these issues."; "Temperature = 20 °C, residence time = 24 s, conversion = 100 % – the exothermic risk was mitigated by the flow platform and controlled addition."

Problem_Description: In the batch hydrolysis of the nitrated intermediate, the organic phase (DCE) and aqueous NaOH were immiscible, resulting in no product formation; even with Et₃N as base, no conversion was observed without a co‑solvent.

Paper Title: Three-Step Continuous Flow Synthesis of the Intermediate 4‑Fluoro-2-methoxy-5-nitrophenol of Linzagolix
Problem_Description: Batch nitration produced significant amounts of isomeric impurity 11 (up to 35 % at high substrate concentration) and impurity 10, reducing overall yield and complicating purification.

Supporting_Evidence: “Method two… using Ni(COD)₂ as a starting material… still carries all of the previously stated issues of synthesis, storage, and cost associated with Ni(COD)₂… we pursued an inexpensive, straightforward synthesis… that avoids both AlMe₃ and Ni(COD)₂.”

Supporting_Evidence: “Ni(tmeda)(o‑tol)Cl and the by‑product … could then be separated, given that the latter is soluble in a variety of solvents … Isolation of Ni(tmeda)(o‑tol)Cl was thereby achieved by simple filtration in air, followed by washing …”

Paper Title: Practical, Large-Scale Preparation of Ni(tmeda)(
Problem_Description: At lower temperatures (0 °C) the reaction yield dropped markedly, and no conversion was observed at –78 °C, indicating temperature‑dependent variability.
Solution_Description: All subsequent optimizations were performed at ambient temperature (room temperature), which gave the highest and most reliable yields.

Problem_Description: Using three equivalents of tmeda gave a slight yield increase but added unnecessary reagent cost.
Solution_Description: The optimal protocol employs only one equivalent of tmeda, balancing cost and performance.

Paper Title: Can a Simple Surrogate Model System Be Used to Develop a Continuous Flow Packed Bed Hydrogenation for a Complex Molecule?
Problem_Description: Catalyst deactivation occurs during hydrogenolysis of the real glycopeptide (Cbz‑GP), leading to a plateau in conversion and low overall yield. The deactivation is attributed to CO₂ adsorption on Pd/C, peptide adsorption on the carbon support, and accumulation of CO₂ at higher pressures.
Solution_Description: The deactivation was mitigated by (i) raising the temperature (to 50 °C) to keep the catalyst active, (ii) adding water as a co‑solvent to displace CO₂ from the catalyst surface, and (iii) lowering the liquid hourly space velocity (LHSV) to reduce oversaturation of the catalyst pores, which together restored >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "the conversion reaching a plateau ... indication of catalyst deactivation"; "adsorption of species onto the carbon support"; "formation of CO₂ ... could be responsible for this drop". 
Solution: "A lower pressure can also help to reduce catalyst deactivation by lowering the concentration of CO₂ in the liquid phase"; "A strategy to avoid catalyst deactivation by CO₂ is to use water as a cosolvent to displace CO₂ from the catalytic sites"; "The deactivation was most likely caused by pore blocking ... therefore, a lower LHSV (<45 h⁻¹) was used to obtain a steady process".

Paper Title: Can a Simple Surrogate Model System Be Used to Develop a Continuous Flow Packed Bed Hydrogenation for a Complex Molecule?

Supporting_Evidence:

Solution: "We selected to use Cbz‑protected lysine methyl ester (Cbz‑Lys) as a surrogate ... because its solubility resembled that of Cbz‑GP"; "MeOH was selected due to its lower viscosity, which was considered beneficial for the translation of the conditions to the larger molecular weight Cbz‑GP".

Paper Title: Scalable Process Development of Ceritinib: Application of Statistical Design of Experiments
Problem_Description: The originally reported syntheses of ceritinib suffered from several serious issues: (i) the use of sodium hydride (NaH) in DMSO or DMF presented an explosive hazard; (ii) a high‑temperature (150 °C) sealed‑tube microwave step required dangerous sealed‑vessel conditions; (iii) the nitro‑to‑amine reduction required high‑pressure H₂ and palladium carbon, which is unsafe and costly on scale; (iv) column chromatography was required for purification, leading to massive solvent use, low reproducibility and poor isolated yields (≈21 %); (v) overall yields were low and the sequence was long, with many transformations and long reaction times (≈8 h for complete conversion, longer times causing degradation); (vi) the TCP addition was strongly exothermic, creating heat‑removal challenges; (vii) the reaction mixture showed mixing limitations (viscosity, heat removal) that led to variability in conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: To overcome these obstacles the authors implemented a suite of changes: (i) replaced NaH with lithium tert‑butoxide (LiO‑t‑Bu) as a safer, effective base; (ii) switched the reaction solvent to N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMAc), which gave better solubility and safety profile; (iii) controlled the exothermic TCP addition by diluting TCP in 2 vol DMAc and employing controlled, portion‑wise addition (two‑lot addition) to mitigate heat release; (iv) eliminated the microwave step and high‑pressure hydrogenation by redesigning the second step to avoid palladium‑catalyzed conditions and expensive ligands (xantphos, Pd(OAc)₂); (v) removed column chromatography altogether, opting for conventional crystallization to isolate the product, dramatically reducing solvent use and improving yield; (vi) applied statistical design of experiments (DoE) and QbD principles to identify optimal temperature (≈25 °C), solvent volume (10 vol DMAc), and reagent equivalents, fixing reaction time at 8 h to avoid degradation; (vii) increased mixing speed to ensure homogeneity and consistent conversion. Paper Title: Pd-Catalyzed Miyaura Borylations Mediated by Potassium Pivalate with Alcohol Cosolvents
Problem_Description: Traditional inorganic carboxylate bases (KOAc, KEHA) have poor solubility in organic solvents, creating heterogeneous reaction mixtures that lead to mass‑transfer limitations, batch‑to‑batch variability (particle size, water content) and sub‑optimal conversion of aryl halides in the Miyaura borylation.
Solution_Description: Switch to potassium pivalate (KOPiv), a more lipophilic carboxylate with higher solubility, and employ a polar protic alcohol cosolvent (2‑PrOH or MeOH) to keep the base in solution and homogenize the reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of carboxylate bases with low solubility in organic solvents often poses a challenge … due to variability in the kinetic behavior … stemming from scale‑dependent mass‑transfer effects.”

Paper Title: Pd-Catalyzed Miyaura Borylations Mediated by Potassium Pivalate with Alcohol Cosolvents
Problem_Description: When KOPiv is combined with B₂(pin)₂ in aprotic solvents, a very thick, viscous suspension forms that adheres to the vessel wall and is difficult to agitate, causing poor mixing and reduced reaction rates.
Solution_Description: Add 30 % (v/v) 2‑propanol (or 10 % MeOH for THF/PhMe) as a cosolvent, which converts the thick gel into an easily‑stirred thin slurry without surface adhesion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In most aprotic solvents tested, the combination of KOPiv and B₂(pin)₂ formed a very thick, viscous suspension … difficult to agitate when alcohol cosolvent was not present.”

Paper Title: Pd-Catalyzed Miyaura Borylations Mediated by Potassium Pivalate with Alcohol Cosolvents
Problem_Description: The original process used 6 mol % (PPh₃)₂PdCl₂ and 2.5 equiv CsOAc, an expensive, hygroscopic base that required silica‑gel and Ecosorb filtration aids, making the process costly and operationally cumbersome.
Solution_Description: Reduce Pd loading to 1.5 mol % (XPhos)‑Pd‑crotyl‑Cl, replace CsOAc with 1.5 equiv KOPiv, lower reaction temperature to 40 °C, and simplify work‑up (no silica/Ecosorb needed), resulting in a 75 % reduction in catalyst loading, 40 % reduction in base loading, and easier filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: • “While this process successfully delivered >50 kg of high‑quality material, the high loadings of both the palladium catalyst and expensive base were considered drawbacks … removal of the cesium salts on the scale required silica gel and Ecosorb as filtration aids.”

Paper Title: Pd-Catalyzed Miyaura Borylations Mediated by Potassium Pivalate with Alcohol Cosolvents
Problem_Description: Using MeOH as the cosolvent gave high protodeborylation (16 % RAP) and homocoupling (2 % RAP) impurities, and higher alcohol fractions slowed the reaction and introduced an induction period due to poor solubility of the Pd precatalyst.

Paper Title: Development of an Inherently Safe and Scalable Nickel-Catalyzed Borylation Process of an Aryl Sulfamate

Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to a Ni‑catalyzed system (Ni(NO₃)₂·6H₂O + Cy‑JohnPhos) that gave higher conversion; later replace the nitrate salt with NiCl₂·6H₂O, a more robust precatalyst that does not decompose the diboron. Add the amine base last (order‑of‑addition) to avoid formation of insoluble Ni(OMe)₂ or Ni(OH)₂ that coat the reactor. Use a MeOH/isopropanol co‑solvent system (and later cyclohexane as a cosolvent) to improve solubility and phase behavior. Develop a cooling‑induced crystallization followed by water antisolvent addition to isolate A with high purity (new purification procedure). Add the diboron/amine solution over 10–15 L min⁻¹ to control the rate of hydrogen evolution (order‑and‑rate of addition). Replace the nitrate‑based Ni salt with NiCl₂·6H₂O, reducing catalyst degradation and off‑gassing. Employ N‑acetyl‑cysteine (instead of citric acid) as a nickel scavenger to remove residual Ni from product and reactor walls. Install a mass‑flow meter‑controlled vent and N₂‑blanketing to safely vent H₂ generated during scale‑up (mass‑transfer/gas‑environment control). Problem_Description: The original two‑step synthesis of intermediate 7 uses 6 vol · mol⁻¹ of high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMAc).  DMAc is difficult to recover by distillation because the Boc protecting group decomposes under the concentrated PPTS conditions used, and the aqueous work‑ups generate >15 vol · mol⁻¹ of nitrogen‑containing wastewater (≈40 % DMAc).  At temperatures >60 °C, >50 % of product 7 is deprotected, dramatically increasing impurity 10.
Solution_Description: A PPTS‑organic‑base buffering system (Strategy III) was introduced, using triethylamine (TEA) as a weak Lewis base.  This allowed replacement of DMAc with low‑boiling, easily recovered THF (or 1,4‑dioxane) while maintaining the required acidity for the condensation.  The TEA‑PPTS buffer suppresses Boc‑deprotection and improves solubility of all components.
Supporting_Evidence: "Both reaction steps require a total of 6 volumes (based on starting material 5) of the high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent N,N‑dimethylacetamide (DMAc), which is difficult to recover via distillation due to the instability of the Boc protecting group under concentrated PPTS conditions";"Aqueous workups in both steps generate over 15 volumes of nitrogen‑containing wastewater (containing 40 % DMAc)";"At temperatures above 60 °C, more than 50 % of the product 7 was deprotected under concentrated PPTS catalysis, resulting in a sharp increase in impurity 10";"The use of a PPTS‑organic base buffering system (Strategy III) enabled the replacement of the polar aprotic solvent DMAc with readily recoverable THF";"Cyclic ethereal solvents like THF and 1,4‑dioxane showed high solubility for substrate 6, tert‑butyl carbazate, and PPTS, making them viable alternatives to DMAc"

Supporting_Evidence: ["Both the preparation of the zinc reagent and the subsequent Negishi reaction require strict anhydrous and anaerobic conditions, making this route less optimal for scale‑up despite higher yields.", "We utilized this method to form the C–C bond. For the third step, a visible‑light‑promoted Ir/Ni‑catalyzed C(sp²)–C(sp³) cross‑coupling reaction was implemented."]

Paper Title: A Concise Flow Synthesis of the IKZF2 Glue Degrader DKY709
Problem_Description: The longer Suzuki‑coupling/H‑hydrogenation sequence increased yield but required isolation and purification between steps, adding labor, waste, and decreasing throughput.
Solution_Description: By performing all four transformations in a single continuous‑flow platform and telescoping the intermediates directly into the next reaction, purification steps are avoided, streamlining the process and improving space‑time yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["An alternative, longer pathway from compound 3 to compound 4 involved Suzuki coupling and hydrogenation, which increased the yield to 34%. However, purification was necessary between these steps.", "A continuous two‑step injection protocol, executed at a 100 g scale, achieved an overall yield of 71%, surpassing the 50% yield observed for discrete batch operations."]

Paper Title: A Concise Flow Synthesis of the IKZF2 Glue Degrader DKY709
Problem_Description: During the high‑temperature amination‑cyclization step, increasing the temperature above 220 °C caused product degradation and inconsistent conversion, while changes in base or residence time also led to variable yields.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified 220 °C, 3 equiv DIPEA and 1.5 equiv 3‑aminopiperidine‑2,6‑dione as optimal; residence time of 5 min gave the best conversion (73 % area).
Supporting_Evidence: ["When the temperature was increased from 180 to 220 °C, the product area increased from 45 to 73%.", "A further temperature increase resulted in a decrease of the target product, likely due to product instability at higher temperatures.", "Lowering the equivalent of DIPEA also led to decreased conversion.", "Variations in residence time (1, 3, or 10 min) similarly diminished conversion efficiency."]

Paper Title: A Concise Flow Synthesis of the IKZF2 Glue Degrader DKY709
Problem_Description: The traditional acidic de‑Boc followed by reductive amination required aqueous work‑ups, salt‑breaks and multiple unit operations, which increase processing time, waste and expose operators to corrosive acids at high temperature.
Solution_Description: A single high‑temperature (220 °C) flow step combined de‑Boc and alkylation using TBAA as base in HFIP, delivering the final product in 58 % isolated yield and eliminating acid work‑ups; the homogeneous reaction mixture was achieved only with TBAA, demonstrating the importance of the functional additive.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For the last de‑Boc and nucleophilic substitution reaction, we attempted to combine these two steps into one step using a continuous‑flow, high‑temperature reaction.", "Only TBAA produced a homogeneous solution in hexafluoroisopropanol (HFIP). Initial conditions afforded a 39% product area percentage.", "Elevating the TBAA stoichiometry from 0.5 to 1.0 equiv enhanced the product ratio from 39 to 57%.", "Thermal optimization revealed superior performance at 220 °C.", "Implementation of this methodology for a 70 g scale reaction enabled one‑pot synthesis of DKY709 with 58% isolated yield."]

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: Large quantities of trifluoromethyl‑diazomethane (TFDM) are dangerous to handle because the reagent has highly unfavorable energetic properties, making batch processes a significant safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The authors moved TFDM generation to a continuous‑flow platform with an in‑line liquid‑liquid membrane phase separator (Zaiput Sep‑10) that delivers a dry, acid‑free TFDM solution directly to the downstream reactor, eliminating the need to store or handle bulk TFDM.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “large quantities of TFDM in batch processes presented a significant safety hazard, as the unfavorable energetic properties of TFDM are well‑documented.” (Abstract) 
• “Inclusion of an in‑line liquid–liquid membrane phase separator… allowed for the production of concentrated TFDM dichloromethane solutions free of acidic impurities.” (Concluding paragraph) 
• “The critical component … was the inclusion of a Zaiput liquid–liquid membrane phase separator.” (Results) 
• “The membrane phase separators are available in various sizes, allowing for facile scale‑up of the reactor volume.” (Flow setup description)

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: Adapting the aqueous TFDM generation to flow required efficient extraction into an organic solvent and removal of water; inadequate extraction gave low TFDM concentrations and residual acidic aqueous waste that poisoned the catalyst.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A biphasic system of aqueous TFEA/NaNO₂ and CH₂Cl₂ was optimized (flow rates, residence time, 2:1 aqueous‑to‑organic ratio) together with a static mixer and the Zaiput membrane separator to provide a dry, ≈0.7 M TFDM solution with <1000 ppm water and no acidic impurities.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The main drawback … was the necessity to extract the TFDM using organic solvents and remove the aqueous waste.” (Results) 
• Table 3 shows systematic variation of flow rates, concentrations, and residence times to reach up to 0.72 M TFDM with 58–62 % isolated yield. (Table 3) 
• “The static mixer … provides a clear biphasic separation with no emulsions observed.” (Flow setup) 
• “The organic stream … afforded a dry solution (∼1000 ppm residual water content by Karl Fischer titration).” (Flow description)

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: Acidic impurities, specifically acetic acid used in some TFDM preparation protocols, completely shut down the Ru‑(S)‑Pheox catalyst, indicating that the carbenoid or catalyst decomposes in the presence of acid.
Solution_Description: The authors deliberately omitted acetic acid from the TFDM generation step, using only TFEA·HCl and NaNO₂, thereby delivering an acid‑free TFDM stream that maintained catalytic activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The presence of acetic acid… resulted in an almost complete shutdown of the reaction, which indicates that the presence of acidic impurities is deleterious to the catalytic system.” (Table 1, entry 4) 
• “The optimal TFDM generation method … avoided the use of acetic acid, allowing for the production of highly concentrated solutions of TFDM.” (Results) 
• “The inclusion of a Zaiput liquid–liquid membrane phase separator… allowed for the production of … free of acidic impurities.” (Concluding paragraph)

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: When TFDM was added too quickly (e.g., 2 h addition) the reaction gave incomplete conversion and side‑product formation (bis‑trifluoromethyl‑ethene), showing that reaction rate control is critical for consistent performance.
Solution_Description: The addition of TFDM was slowed to a 4 h continuous feed (≈20 mL h⁻¹ in batch, 4 h in flow) to ensure complete consumption of the diazo species, preventing side reactions and giving >99 % conversion and high ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the TFDM addition time was shortened from 4 to 2 h, incomplete conversion (87 %) was observed … loss of carbenoid to undesired reaction pathways.” (Table 1, entry 2) 
• “Kinetic Studies … indicated that TFDM is rapidly consumed … and bis(trifluoromethyl)ethene is generated when TFDM is added too quickly.” (ref 24) 
• “Slow addition of a preformed solution of TFDM … over 4 h … resulted in complete conversion … 77 % isolated yield.” (Batch experiment description) 
• “The PFR–BTR system could be monitored by ReactIR … due to the slow addition rate of TFDM, there was no observable exotherm …” (Process description)

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: In the flow reactor, the biphasic mixture risked forming emulsions that could impair phase separation and lead to water carry‑over into the organic TFDM stream.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A stainless‑steel helical static mixer (Stamixco PTFE) was installed downstream of the Y‑junction to promote efficient mixing and rapid phase disengagement, ensuring a clear organic layer for downstream use.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The resulting free‑flowing biphasic mixture ages … and passes through a Stamixco PTFE helical mixing element … which provides a clear biphasic separation with no emulsions observed during our studies.” (Flow setup) 
• “The static mixer outlet stream was then connected to a Zaiput …” (Process flow diagram) 
• “The mixture … provides the optimal extraction efficiency (entries 5 and 8–10).” (Table 3 discussion)

Paper Title: Continuous Preparation of Trifluoromethyl Diazomethane in Flow Using In-Line Membrane Phase SeparationApplication to the Catalytic Asymmetric Cyclopropanation of Substituted Styrenes
Problem_Description: Previously reported tube‑in‑tube or other flow reactors for TFDM generation suffered from low productivity (<2 mmol h⁻¹) and required specialized gas‑permeable membranes that are hard to scale, limiting practical large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the tube‑in‑tube design with a simple, scalable PTFE tubing loop and a commercial membrane phase separator, achieving higher throughput (≈0.7 M TFDM at 0.5 mL min⁻¹ flow) without the need for specialized gas‑permeable reactors.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We anticipated that a tube‑in‑tube reactor would be difficult to scale, especially considering its low productivity (less than 2 mmol h⁻¹).” (Background) 
• “Both Jamison … and Koenigs … utilize acetic acid, which is detrimental … Given the limitations … we explored developing a novel flow‑based approach.” (Rationale) 
• “The membrane phase separators are available in various sizes, allowing for facile scale‑up of the reactor volume.” (Flow description) 
• “The PFR–BTR system was run for 4 h … generated >150 g of cyclopropane 3a.” (Scale‑up result)

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: The penultimate intermediate (compound 1) is a costly and scarcely‑available solid that dissolves very slowly, causing the overall reaction to be controlled by dissolution and leading to long batch times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature (40 → 80 °C) speeds up the dissolution of 1 and accelerates the chemical steps; raising the stirring speed (300 → 1000 rpm) improves solid suspension and mass‑transfer; and loading more Pd/C catalyst (up to 7.8 wt %) further enhances dissolution by increasing particle collisions.
Supporting_Evidence: “The penultimate expensive and scarcely available intermediate is characterized by a slow dissolution rate … the standard Area Percentage method … was found misleading” (Abstract).; “Increasing the temperature from 40 to 80 °C reduced the batch time by 58%” (Abstract).; “Stirring rate controlled the initial reaction phases when reagent dissolution is critical” (Abstract).; “Increasing the catalyst loading was proved to affect the reagent dissolution rate, by increasing the collision frequency between reagent and catalyst particles” (Abstract).; “The time required to reach 98% of 5 final concentration (τ98) values decrease exponentially from 40 to 80 °C” (Section 4.4).

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: Using the relative‑area (LCAP) HPLC method gave a misleading view of the reaction progress because it assumes equal detector response for all species, masking the increase of dissolved reagent 1.
Solution_Description: All data were re‑analyzed with absolute peak areas calibrated against standards, and a mass‑balance correction factor was applied to enforce stoichiometric closure.
Supporting_Evidence: “The LCAP method … provides the relative, not the absolute amount of species … it could lead to erroneous assumption of the response factors … the analysis … leads to a dramatic misunderstanding of the physical and chemical processes” (Section 4.1).; “It is essential to highlight that … a calibration curve is required to accurately quantify the amount of the reagent present in the liquid phase” (Section 4.1).; “All of the collected data in this work have been analyzed through the absolute peak area, coupled with calibration lines” (Section 4.1).; “The correction was applied to each experiment… The limitation of this correction is that it is based on liquid‑phase concentrations alone” (Section 4.1).

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: Higher reaction temperatures increase the formation of undesired intermediate 2, lowering the purity of the target Argatroban isomers 5 and 6.
Solution_Description: A temperature optimum (≈ 60 °C) was identified that balances faster conversion with acceptable impurity levels, avoiding the loss of selectivity observed at 80 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “Higher temperatures promoted the formation of undesired impurities” (Abstract).; “Temperatures higher than 80 °C were detrimental to product purity, as they favor the formation of the undesired intermediate” (Section 5).; “Increasing the temperature … enhances dissolution and kinetics … but the variation from 40 to 80 °C reduced the batch time by 58%… temperatures higher than 80 °C were detrimental to product purity” (Section 4.4).; “Figure 8 … shows that temperature favors the reaction path through the intermediate 2, suggesting a higher activation energy” (Section 4.4).

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: Insufficient stirring (300 rpm) provides only partial suspension of the solid phases, limiting the solid‑liquid mass‑transfer coefficient and extending the dissolution period of 1.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the impeller speed to 1000 rpm (well above the predicted just‑suspended speed) improves particle suspension, reduces the diffusion film around the solids, and shortens the time needed for reagent 1 to dissolve.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solid/liquid mass transfer coefficient kSL is related to the degree of particle suspension … increasing N will lead to a substantial improvement in mass transfer coefficients” (Section 4.5).; “Two experiments at constant N were performed to assess its impact at 300 and 1000 rpm” (Section 4.5).; “At the highest stirring speed, 1 dissolves completely in a shorter time … 5 concentration reaches the highest value at N = 1000 rpm” (Section 4.5).; “Stirring rate appears to affect also the selectivity… production of intermediate 2 is favored at higher N” (Section 4.5).

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: Using the reference catalyst loading (3.9 wt %) results in a batch time of 311 min to reach 98 % conversion, which is sub‑optimal for industrial throughput.
Solution_Description: Doubling the Pd/C loading to 7.8 wt % reduces the batch time to 97 min while maintaining comparable selectivity, demonstrating a linear relationship between catalyst amount and product formation rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The impact of the catalyst amount was assessed doubling (7.80 wt %) and halving (1.95 wt %) the reference loading” (Section 4.6).; “Doubling the amount of the catalyst reduces the batch time by approximately 2/3” (Section 4.6).; Table 1 shows τ98 of 97 min at 7.80 wt % versus 311 min at 3.90 wt % (Section 4.6).; “The apparent rate of production of 5 … is linearly proportional to the mass of the catalyst charged” (Section 4.6).

Paper Title: Impact of Reactant Dissolution in the Kinetics of a Catalytic Hydrogenation for the Production of Argatroban
Problem_Description: The previously developed first‑principles kinetic model failed to predict the concentration profile of 1 when catalyst loading changed, because it omitted the catalyst‑induced enhancement of the dissolution mass‑transfer coefficient.
Solution_Description: A semi‑empirical correlation (eq 5) linking kSL to the catalyst amount was incorporated into the model, yielding accurate predictions of reagent 1 and product 5 across all catalyst loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: “Model predictions did not reasonably explain the experimental results … especially for dissolving reagent 1” (Section 3.1).; “A correlation between the solid–liquid mass transfer coefficient for dissolution and the catalyst amount was added” (Abstract).; “The correlation … was incorporated in the model and calibrated with the experimental data” (Section 4.7).; Figure 11 shows improved agreement of the modified model with data for all catalyst loadings (Section 4.7).

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: The oxidation of ethylene sulfite (ES) with H₂O₂ in the TS‑1 system is a strongly exothermic reaction that can lead to unsafe temperature spikes and rapid decomposition of the product (DTD) by hydrolysis, especially at higher temperatures.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A fixed‑bed reactor was employed, allowing efficient removal of reaction heat through jacket cooling and enabling precise temperature control (gradient of 10 °C and 5 °C). The reactor geometry also improves mixing and mass‑transfer, suppressing hydrolysis and making the process safe for continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the reaction is violently exothermic which poses safety and product hydrolysis problems.”
• “The reaction is categorized as strong exothermic, and cooling water is passed through the jacket to effectively remove the heat of the reaction.”
• “Under the optimized experimental conditions…gradient temperatures of 10 and 5 °C…the hydrolysis of the product was effectively suppressed.”
• “The application of the fixed‑bed reactor to the oxidation reaction of ES effectively addresses the challenges posed by the exothermic reaction process and product hydrolysis.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: The TS‑1 catalyst consists of very small particles (≈2 mm) that are difficult to separate from the reaction mixture, and the multiphase (oil–water–solid) system complicates product isolation.
Solution_Description: Using a packed‑bed fixed‑bed reactor eliminates the need for downstream catalyst filtration; the catalyst stays inside the reactor column. A continuous liquid‑phase separation unit downstream removes the organic and aqueous phases instantly, enabling fast isolation of DTD.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the TS‑1 catalyst is characterized by a relatively small particle size, which poses a challenge for catalyst separation.”
• “The fixed‑bed reactor effectively removes the heat of reaction, achieves a safe reaction…avoids catalyst segregation.”
• “A continuous separation unit was built to separate the products in time…the organic phase was then washed, dried, and concentrated, resulting in an isolation yield of 96%.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Reaction rates varied strongly with the polarity/solubility of the organic solvent in water; low‑solubility solvents gave poor ES conversion.
Solution_Description: Dimethyl carbonate (DMC) was selected as the reaction solvent because its moderate polarity gives sufficient miscibility with water to promote contact between the TS‑1/H₂O₂ phase and ES, while still keeping DTD out of the aqueous phase to limit hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence:
