• “oxidation reaction rate increased with increasing solvent solubility in water…the highest 96.5% conversion as well as 95.3% selectivity could be obtained for 4 h when Dimethyl carbonate (DMC) was used as the reaction solvent.”
• “When DMC was employed as the reaction solvent, the reaction time was extended to 6 h, which enabled complete conversion of the substrate and ultimately yielded 90% isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Conventional industrial routes use Ru‑based catalysts (RuCl₃/NaClO, RuO₄/NaClO, etc.) that are expensive, difficult to recover, and generate large amounts of waste water.
Solution_Description: Titanium silicalite‑1 (TS‑1) replaces the Ru‑based catalysts. TS‑1 is inexpensive, recyclable, and operates under mild conditions, dramatically reducing catalyst cost and waste generation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the catalysts used in the above routes are costly, difficult to recover, and produce large amounts of wastewater.”
• “TS‑1…gives TS‑1 excellent catalytic oxidation activity…typical ‘green catalytic’ system.”
• “The use of TS‑1 instead of the expensive ruthenium trichloride catalyst reduces the cost of the process.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 10 °C the product DTD undergoes hydrolysis in the aqueous phase, decreasing selectivity and isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A two‑reactor temperature gradient (first reactor at 10 °C, second at 5 °C) was implemented, allowing rapid conversion in the hotter zone while immediately quenching hydrolysis in the cooler zone. This balances conversion and hydrolysis rates, giving >99 % conversion and 99 % selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the hydrolysis reaction of the product DTD is also intensified by the increase in temperature, resulting in a decrease in the selectivity of DTD from 99.5% to 88.4%.”
• “we tried to use two fixed‑bed reactors with gradient temperature…first reactor temperature was set to 10 °C…second reactor temperature was set to 5 °C…conversion of 87.9% and a selectivity of 99.3% were obtained.”
• “Under optimized experimental conditions…final conversion of 99.5% and a selectivity of 99.1%.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Previous batch processes required 3–5 h (or longer) reaction times to reach acceptable conversion, limiting production throughput.
Solution_Description: The fixed‑bed continuous reactor operates at a liquid hourly space velocity of 0.6 h⁻¹, giving a residence time of only 16.5 min while maintaining >99 % conversion, thereby shortening the overall reaction time dramatically.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “intermittent reaction 5 h, 3.5 h…low productivity.”
• “The fixed‑bed reactor residence time is 16.5 min…conversion 99.5%.”
• Table 1 shows the fixed‑bed reactor achieving 96 % yield in 16.5 min versus 5 h in a Schlenk tube.

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Highly concentrated H₂O₂ (>30 wt %) is more hazardous and less readily available in large‑scale plants, yet lower concentrations give lower conversion.
Solution_Description: A 30 wt % H₂O₂ solution was selected as the optimal compromise, providing sufficient oxidant strength while keeping handling safety manageable. The H₂O₂/ES molar ratio was fixed at 1.05:1 to limit excess water formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “considering the experimental safety and cost considerations, the 30 wt % H₂O₂ concentration was identified as the optimal condition.”
• “H₂O₂ molar ratio of 1.05:1…maintains high conversion and limits water increase.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: When fully water‑miscible solvents (acetone, acetonitrile, 1,4‑dioxane) were used, DTD fully contacted water leading to drastic hydrolysis and loss of selectivity.
Solution_Description: Choosing DMC, which is only partially miscible with water, creates a three‑phase system (oil–water–solid) that limits DTD exposure to water and reduces hydrolysis while still allowing sufficient contact for oxidation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “when we tried to use the three solvents acetone, acetonitrile, and 1,4‑dioxane…the reaction selectivity was drastically reduced due to the increased rate of hydrolysis of DTD.”
• “An oil–water–solid three‑phase reaction…prevents further hydrolysis of the product.”

Paper Title: Continuous Synthesis of 1,3,2-Dioxathiolane 2,2-Dioxide (DTD) by Hydrogen Peroxide with Titanium Silicalite‑1 Catalyst Using a Fixed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Batch processes using RuCl₃/NaClO gave isolated yields around 86–92 % with long reaction times, insufficient for industrial scale.
Solution_Description: The continuous TS‑1/H₂O₂ route coupled with an immediate continuous liquid‑phase separation delivers a 96 % isolated yield in minutes, outperforming the traditional batch routes.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Table 1 shows a 96 % isolated yield for the fixed‑bed reactor versus 86–92 % for the Ru/NaClO batch processes.”
• “The continuous separation device…resulted in an isolation yield of 96%.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: The traditional indirect Glycosylation of donor 1 required >12 extraction, distillation, and solvent‑exchange operations, generating large amounts of solvent waste and eroding isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot direct glycosylation was developed that forms and consumes the 1,2‑oxazolinium intermediate in situ, eliminating the numerous unit operations of the indirect route.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The early phase synthesis of 3 is described… it necessitated >12 extraction and distillation operations, eroding the isolated yield while consuming high volumes of solvent.', 'We focused … on a one‑pot direct glycosylation strategy, which would form and consume 1a in situ.', 'The optimized direct glycosylation process provided a significant cost reduction and process mass intensity (PMI) improvement compared to the initial indirect glycosylation method.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: Hydrolytically unstable TMSOTf was used in stoichiometric amounts, requiring three in‑process controls to keep water content within specifications and adding cost and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Mild metal triflate catalysts (e.g., Bi(OTf)₃) were employed at catalytic loadings (2.5 mol %), eliminating the need for stoichiometric TMSOTf and reducing IPCs.
Supporting_Evidence: ['hydrolytically unstable TMSOTf was used in stoichiometric quantities as a Lewis acid, requiring at least 3 in‑process controls to ensure the reaction stream met the strict water content specifications.', 'We added the metal triflate catalyst (2.5 mol %) and heated to 75 °C for 24 h.', 'Catalyst loading could be reduced from the initial 15 mol % to 2.5 mol % while still achieving acceptable conversion.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: Strong Lewis acids caused severe product degradation and gave isolated yields of only 30–45 % in the indirect pathway.
Solution_Description: Screening identified bismuth triflate as a milder catalyst that gave >80 % conversion with minimal product degradation, raising yields to ~71 % after optimization.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Significant product degradation was observed when subjecting 3 to strong Lewis acids, with near complete decomposition after 48 h of aging 3 in the presence of TMSOTf.', 'Reaction stalling at 1b … resulted in isolated yields ranging from 30 to 45 %.', 'bismuth and iron triflate were reported to give yields ranging from 80 to 90 % and no observed product decomposition.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: Donor 1 exhibited low solubility in CH₃CN (≈16 mM), making the reaction zero‑order in donor and limiting overall rate.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in CH₃CN at 75 °C, which increased the apparent solubility of 1 (up to ~70 mM for Bi(OTf)₃) and allowed higher effective concentrations, improving reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Due to the relatively low solubility of donor 1, the glycosylation reaction was found to be functionally zero order in this species.', 'For the Bi(OTf)₃ system, the concentration of 1 was found to increase rapidly from its measured solubility of 16 mM in pure CH₃CN to its enhanced reaction solubility of approximately 70 mM within 10 min of catalyst addition.', 'The reaction was charged to the flask, heated to 75 °C, and aged for 24 h.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: Zn(OTf)₂ displayed a sluggish, multi‑hour dissolution of donor 1, causing a long induction period and large run‑to‑run conversion variability.
Solution_Description: Bi(OTf)₃ was selected as the preferred catalyst because it dissolves donor 1 rapidly and shows broader tolerance to loading and temperature variations, delivering consistent high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['For the Zn(OTf)₂ catalyst, the dissolution of 1 took over 3 h before attaining its maximum reaction solubility of 75 mM.', 'The Zn(OTf)₂ suppliers had a much narrower variance in potency yet gave a wide range of conversion from 34 to 96 %…', 'We concluded that Bi(OTf)₃ was the most practical and robust catalyst choice for manufacture.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: Isolation of product 3 involved >8 extractive operations, multiple solvent exchanges, and a temperature‑driven precipitation that gave limited purity improvement, resulting in high solvent consumption and low overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: A direct crystallization was instituted: charcoal treatment to remove impurities, seeding with 1 mol % of 3, and addition of MTBE as antisolvent to precipitate the product, eliminating the aqueous work‑up and most solvent‑exchange steps.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The early phase process included at least eight extractive operations and a series of solvent exchanges…', 'We aimed to reduce the solvent waste and number of unit operations while maintaining high product quality, by implementing a direct crystallization that would obviate the lengthy aqueous workup procedure.', 'Instead, a charcoal treatment was utilized to remove insoluble impurities… only MTBE offered the desired desaturation.', 'The resulting slurry was slowly cooled overnight from 45 °C to 20 °C to reduce losses while delivering product in >97 % LC purity.']

Paper Title: Kinetic Studies to Enable a Scalable Direct Glycosylation of a GalNAc Donor
Problem_Description: The indirect route required >29 unit operations and 9 in‑process controls, leading to a long cycle time and high material cost.
Solution_Description: Consolidating the synthesis into a single‑pot direct glycosylation cut the number of unit operations to >13 and in‑process controls to 6, shortening the cycle time and reducing cost of goods by ~62 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['... >12 extraction and distillation operations…', 'The optimized direct glycosylation process provided a significant cost reduction and process mass intensity (PMI) improvement compared to the initial indirect glycosylation method.', 'unit operations >29 → >13; in‑process controls 9 → 6; approximate cost of goods reduction ↓62 %']

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: The starting materials (styrene, N‑tosyl‑amine and N‑iodosuccinimide) are not completely dissolved in dimethyl carbonate (DMC) at the 0.25 M concentration that was used for the batch protocol, leading to heterogeneous mixtures and poor conversion in the flow reactor.
Solution_Description: The authors decreased the substrate concentration to 0.1 M in DMC, keeping the same solvent but using a more dilute, fully homogeneous solution. This restored solubility and gave acceptable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the starting materials are not dissolved completely… To maintain the sustainability of the procedure using dimethyl carbonate (DMC) as a solvent, we chose to decrease the concentration to 0.1 M (instead of 0.25 M under batch conditions) rather than change the solvent to obtain complete solubility.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Trace amounts of hydrogen iodide (HI) generated from N‑iodosuccinimide or formed during the reaction were suspected to inhibit the iodoamination, resulting in low conversion (35 % NMR yield without any additive).
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount (10 mol %) of inorganic bases (initially K₂CO₃, later KOAc) was added to the reaction mixture, which neutralised HI and dramatically increased the yield to 85 % (K₂CO₃) and 93 % (KOAc).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Initial attempts … were characterised by low conversion and yield (35 % NMR) … assuming that traces of hydrogen iodide may be present … catalytic amounts (10 mol %) of various inorganic bases were added … potassium carbonate proved to be the most effective, giving rise to 4a with 85 % … employment of potassium acetate improved the reaction further, resulting in complete conversion and furnishing 4a in 93 % yield.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: The reaction proved highly sensitive to changes in temperature, flow rate (residence time) and substrate concentration; deviations caused a marked drop in yield (e.g., 75 % at 10 °C, 37 %/70 % at 5 min residence time, 78 %/59 % at 0.05 M).
Solution_Description: Optimisation identified the most robust set of parameters: 25 °C, 0.1 M substrate concentration, 10 min residence time (0.7 mL min⁻¹ flow), with KOAc as additive. These conditions gave reproducible high yields (≥93 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Altering the temperature … resulted in lower yields and conversion (75 %). … flow rate … resulted in lower yields … concentration … resulted in lower yields … Finally, the employment of potassium acetate improved the reaction further, resulting in complete conversion and furnishing 4a in 93 % yield.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Replacing DMC with acetonitrile (MeCN) allowed higher substrate concentration (0.3 M) but caused a drastic decrease in yield (20 % NMR).
Solution_Description: The authors retained DMC as the reaction solvent despite the lower concentration, because DMC gave substantially higher yields (up to 93 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using acetonitrile (MeCN) instead of DMC as a solvent allows a higher concentration … but proves to be significantly inferior for the process (20 % yield).”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: When the same protocol was executed in a batch reactor at the same concentration, the isolated yield dropped to 72 % and the productivity fell to 1.15 g h⁻¹, attributed to poor light penetration caused by the formation of strongly coloured by‑products.
Solution_Description: Continuous‐flow photochemistry with a thin 7 mL reactor (or the larger 14 mL reactor) provided a short light path, avoiding the attenuation problem and delivering the highest productivity (3.04 g h⁻¹, 91 % isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence: • “In batch … a colour change from yellow to red occurs … making light penetration increasingly difficult … No reactor fouling was observed … scaling up the reactor volume to 14 mL while keeping the residence time constant increased productivity … 14.0 g (91 % isolated, 3.04 g h⁻¹) were obtained.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Using blue LEDs (455 nm) instead of the standard green LEDs (530 nm) reduced the iodoamination yield to 83 % (≈10 % loss), likely because higher‑energy light generates more iodine, which quenches the photochemical process.
Solution_Description: The authors retained green light (530 nm) as the optimal irradiation source for the flow reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using blue (455 nm) instead of green (530 nm) LEDs for irradiation … resulted in a reduced yield of 83 % (10 % difference from the standard conditions), which might be due to an increased iodine production with higher energy light, which is known to be an effective quencher and thus a poison for photocatalytic processes.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Down‑stream transformations of the crude iodo‑aminated products (e.g., formation of enamines, azido‑amines) required long reaction times (8 h, 12 h, 6.5 h) when performed in batch, limiting overall productivity.
Solution_Description: The authors performed the second‑step reactions in a telescoped fashion—either in a single batch vessel after solvent removal or in a continuous‑flow cascade (using a K₂CO₃‑packed Omnifit column at 60 °C). This eliminated the need for isolation and, together with elevated temperatures, shortened the reaction times and boosted overall g h⁻¹ productivity for the final aziridines and other derivatives.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Further transformations … were performed in a telescopic manner without prior isolation … (i) … 3 h at 25 °C, (ii) … 12 h at 100 °C, (iii) … 8 h at 100 °C, (iv) … 6.5 h at 25 °C.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free, Scalable, Green-Light-Mediated Iodoamination, and Further Transformation of Olefins Under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: The aziridine formation step required an additional 3 h at 60 °C after the iodoamination, which added to the total processing time in batch mode.
Solution_Description: A two‑step continuous‑flow cascade was implemented: the outlet of the photo‑flow reactor was directly fed into an Omnifit column packed with K₂CO₃ and heated to 60 °C, delivering the aziridine in a single operation and maintaining a productivity of ≈1 g h⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The outlet of the photo flow reactor was connected to an Omnifit column, which was packed with K₂CO₃ powder and placed in a 60 °C water bath … the desired aziridines were successfully synthesized with an overall yield … resulting in a productivity of 1.02 g h⁻¹ …”

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: Direct hydrosilylation of allyl (meth)‑acrylate (route A) gave only ≈46 % isolated yield of the desired monomer 1 and generated two major by‑products (oxy‑silyl ester 8, 30 % GC yield; propylene‑hydrosilylated product 9, 10 % GC yield), compromising overall conversion and making product isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: The silane (3) was fed slowly to a pre‑mixed solution of allyl (meth)‑acrylate (2) and Karstedt’s catalyst at 50 °C, rather than the reverse order. This maintained a relatively constant 1 : 8 selectivity (≈1.7 : 1) and limited formation of by‑product 9, while the reactor jacket temperature was kept ≤ 60 °C to avoid overheating. These changes improved conversion and reduced impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In the first route (route A), the synthesis... yielded ∼50% of the desired anti‑Markovnikov product (1). The yields of compounds 8 and 9 are estimated to be 30 and 10%, respectively (Fig 3).","The results revealed that silane (3) immediately reacts with 2 to form the desired product 1 and undesired product 8. As the reaction progressed (~2 h), we were also able to detect the propylene hydrosilylated product 9. The selectivity between products 1 and 8 remains reasonably constant (1.7:1) throughout the reaction.","When we switched the order of addition and slowly fed 2 to a mixture of 3 and Karstedt’s catalyst at 50 °C, we observed a lower overall conversion (<30% GC yield of 1) and higher early formation of 9. Based on these results, we decided to feed the silane (3) to the mixture of 2 and Karstedt’s catalyst during scale‑up.","The reactor contents were warmed to 30 °C, and 1.1 equiv of 3 was slowly fed to the reactor over 5 h. … The rate of the addition of 3 and the reactor jacket temperature were both controlled to ensure the reaction mixture never exceeded 60 °C."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: The hydrosilylation reaction is highly exothermic (−415 J g⁻¹ measured by micro‑calorimetry) and generates propylene gas, posing a thermal runaway and pressure‑rise risk on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Isothermal micro‑calorimetry was used to quantify the heat of reaction, and the process was run in a 20 L glass‑jacketed reactor with controlled addition of silane (3) and a jacket setpoint that never allowed the temperature to rise above 60 °C. Pressure monitoring and a diaphragm pump for the feed provided safe handling of the generated gas.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The total heat release in the observed microcalorimetry experiment was −415 J/g (exothermic)…", "A stepwise pressure increase was observed at the time of injection and was associated with headspace compression due to the injection of incompressible fluid… the pressure rise was presumed to represent the generation of propylene, with the small decrease in pressure associated with its partial consumption by a competing hydrosilylation reaction (formation of 9).", "The rate of the addition of 3 and the reactor jacket temperature were both controlled to ensure the reaction mixture never exceeded 60 °C.", "The heat release measured in the micro‑calorimetry experiment… was assumed to represent the total heat release from the consumption of 2 in the presence of excess 3, yielding both the desired product 1 and also one or more byproducts."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: During distillation the monomer can polymerize exothermically and decompose above ≈280 °C (DSC shows a baseline shift and exotherm), risking loss of product and runaway reactions.
Solution_Description: 4‑Hydroxy‑TEMPO (4‑HT) was added (200 ppm during reaction, additional 400 ppm before distillation) to quench free‑radical polymerization. Vacuum distillation was performed at ≤ 170 °C (10 Torr) to stay well below the decomposition onset, allowing isolation of pure monomer without polymerization.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Finding an inhibitor to prevent unwanted free radical polymerization of the monomer during scale‑up and product isolation was crucial. 4‑Hydroxy TEMPO was identified as the inhibitor of choice…", "With no specific study on concentration, we chose to use 200 ppm of 4‑HT during the hydrosilylation reaction… the product was also isolated at the smaller scale to derisk the distillation… an additional 400 ppm of 4‑HT was added to the post‑reaction mixture, which was subsequently distilled under vacuum (∼10 Torr), never allowing the contents of the distillation pot to reach 170 °C.", "DSC studies detected the decomposition of the monomer at 280 °C, thereby revealing the risk of decomposition at elevated temperatures.", "The presence of 4‑HT was found in both the lights and product distillation cuts, indicating that the inhibitor was capable of distilling overhead with the lights and product cuts, helping minimize any product loss to polymerization."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: Route B requires allyl alcohol, which has Category 3 acute toxicity (oral & inhalation) and generates pyridine·HCl as solid waste, adding safety and waste‑handling concerns; additionally, the trans‑esterification step uses methyl methacrylate, adding material cost.
Solution_Description: Route B was eliminated from consideration; the authors selected Route A, a single‑step process that avoids toxic allyl alcohol, solid‑waste generation, and the extra reagent cost, simplifying scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["However, allyl alcohol exhibits category 3 acute toxicity for oral and inhalation exposure and category 2 acute toxicity for dermal exposure.", "In the second step, the crude intermediate 5 was transesterified with methyl methacrylate… The overall product yield (63% isolated yield over two steps)… However… it would require additional precautions due to the inclusion of raw materials with some level of inhalation and oral and dermal toxicity.", "Route A was selected as the preferred route for next‑phase process development primarily to avoid handling solid waste and due to concerns about the potential long‑term unavailability of reliable suppliers of trimethylsilanol needed in route C."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: Route C depends on trimethylsilanol, which is not a commodity chemical and is difficult to source in the quantities required for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Route C was not pursued; the process team chose Route A, which uses readily available reagents (allyl acrylate and heptamethyltrisiloxane) and avoids the supply‑chain risk associated with trimethylsilanol.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Trimethylsilanol is not a commodity chemical and is difficult to source in larger quantities needed for the manufacturing scale.", "Ultimately, route A was selected as the preferred route for next‑phase process development primarily to avoid handling solid waste and due to concerns about the potential long‑term unavailability of reliable suppliers of trimethylsilanol needed in route C."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: The conversion and selectivity of the hydrosilylation depended on the order of addition of reagents, leading to inconsistent yields (≈30 % GC yield when 2 was added to 3 versus ≈45 % when 3 was added to 2).
Solution_Description: Standardized the addition protocol to feed silane (3) into the pre‑mixed acrylate (2) and catalyst mixture, which gave more reproducible selectivity and higher conversion during scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When we slowly fed 3 to a mixture of 2 and Karstedt’s catalyst at 50 °C… the selectivity between products 1 and 8 remains reasonably constant (1.7:1) throughout the reaction.", "When we switched the order of addition and slowly fed 2 to a mixture of 3 and Karstedt’s catalyst… the crude reaction showed <30% GC yield of 1… Based on these results, we decided to feed the silane (3) to the mixture of 2 and Karstedt’s catalyst during scale‑up."]

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for Synthesizing a Reactive Silicone-Acrylate Monomer
Problem_Description: Generation of propylene gas during the hydrosilylation caused a pressure rise in the sealed micro‑calorimetry vessel, indicating gas handling concerns for larger batches.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a diaphragm pump for controlled silane feed, used a jacketed glass reactor with pressure monitoring, and designed the gas‑handling system to accommodate propylene evolution safely during scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A stepwise pressure increase was observed at the time of injection and was associated with headspace compression due to the injection of incompressible fluid… the pressure rise was presumed to represent the generation of propylene, with the small decrease in pressure associated with its partial consumption by a competing hydrosilylation reaction (formation of 9).", "The reactor was prepared by first adding 2, Karstedt’s catalyst (5 ppm), and 4‑HT to the reactor. The contents were then warmed to 30 °C, and 1.1 equiv of 3 was slowly fed to the reactor over 5 h… The rate of the addition of 3 and the reactor jacket temperature were both controlled to ensure the reaction mixture never exceeded 60 °C."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: The first‑generation hydrogenation of olefin 5 gave a 1:1 mixture of diastereomers that required extensive chromatographic separations, leading to loss of material and low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A substrate‑controlled approach was adopted by installing a sterically demanding TBS‑ether (compound 9) on the tetralin fragment, shielding one face of the C1–C2 olefin and enabling diastereoselective reduction without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The lack of diastereoselectivity in the hydrogenation of olefin 5 in the first-generation synthesis of 1 required extensive chromatographic separation of the resulting diastereomers and resulted in the loss of valuable material.","We envisioned that the installation of a sufficiently sterically demanding substituent on the tetralin ring of the coupling product could effectively shield one face of the C1–C2 olefin, thereby enabling selective reduction from the opposite face.","Accordingly, we decided to target TBS‑ether 9 … as a silyl protected alcohol that would also provide a convenient functional handle for subsequent redox manipulations."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Ir‑catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation of olefin 5 and Ni‑catalyzed reductive cross‑coupling of benzyl halide 7 with bromoindanol 8 failed to give conversion, giving only starting material or elimination products.
Solution_Description: The synthetic plan was changed to a substrate‑controlled diastereoselective reduction (see previous pair) rather than relying on catalyst‑controlled asymmetric hydrogenation or Ni‑mediated reductive cross‑coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Despite literature reports … we found [Ir]‑catalyzed hydrogenation conditions failed to provide significant conversion in the reduction of olefin 5.","Our efforts to couple benzyl halides 7 and bromoindanol 8 using Ni catalysis were unsuccessful … resulted in elimination of the benzylic halide and recovery of starting materials.","Following our unsuccessful attempts … we decided to explore the possibility of setting the stereochemistry at C1 via substrate control."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: The original six‑step route to tetralone 17 relied on a Wittig olefination that required several kilograms of Wittig reagent and multiple chromatographic purifications, giving only 23 % overall yield.
Solution_Description: An oxidative rearrangement of a functionalized cyclobutanol was developed, reducing the sequence to three steps and improving the overall yield to ≈40 %, while eliminating the need for large amounts of Wittig reagent and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Despite the relative efficiency of each individual step, the length of the sequence results in a low overall yield (23 % over 6 steps). The poor atom‑economy of the Wittig olefination required multiple kilograms of the Wittig reagent as well as chromatographic purification.","We envisioned that a suitably functionalized arylated cyclobutanol could be converted to tetralone 17… This in turn enabled the selection of a starting material with a chloride at the C8 position, allowing for the direct incorporation of the C8 nitrile without the need for the two‑step sequence.","Ultimately, tetralone 17 was produced in just 3 steps and ∼40 % overall yield, representing a significant improvement in efficiency from the first‑generation route."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: The oxidative rearrangement to tetralone 20 required high dilution (≈0.1 M) to suppress dimer formation, and distillation of the product was difficult because of similar boiling points of side‑products, leading to decomposition on scale.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed with slow, controlled addition of the aqueous CAN solution while maintaining the internal temperature at ∼0 °C under N₂ sparging, providing a cleaner profile and reducing the need for extreme dilution.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Degassing of the reaction mixture by sparging with N₂ and the slow addition of an aqueous solution of CAN while maintaining an internal temperature of ∼0 °C provided a cleaner reaction profile.","The reaction was required to be run at high dilution (∼0.1 M). ... prolonged heating during distillation on larger scale resulted in decreased mass recovery due to decomposition of the product.","The careful control of the reaction parameters was critical to the efficiency of the transformation."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Lowering the palladium catalyst loading in the cyanation of aryl chloride 20 caused a dramatic drop in conversion because of catalyst poisoning by cyanide.
Solution_Description: The order of addition was changed – the cyanide source (K₂Fe(CN)₆·3H₂O) was added to a pre‑heated mixture of the other reagents, which restored high conversion even at reduced catalyst loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Attempts to lower the catalyst loading from 10 mol % were unsuccessful, resulting in a dramatic drop in conversion … Reports of catalyst poisoning by cyanide … we suspect that competitive catalyst poisoning could be the cause of low conversion at decreased catalyst loadings.","By changing the order of addition of reagents and adding K₂Fe(CN)₆·3H₂O to a preheated mixture of the other reactants we could improve conversion at lower catalyst loadings.","Pd‑catalyzed cyanation using Pd(OAc)₂, XPhos, and K₂Fe(CN)₆·3H₂O also provided the desired product in high yield."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Oxidation of ketal 24 with KMnO₄/MgSO₄ gave a significant delayed exotherm, posed a safety risk on scale, and led to ketal cleavage and low isolated yield (55 %).
Solution_Description: A cobalt‑acac₂/TBHP oxidation was developed; the reaction was performed in MeCN with an aqueous solution of TBHP, avoiding peroxide formation and improving selectivity while preserving the ketal.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Oxidation at C4 was initially carried out with excess KMnO₄ and MgSO₄ … 55 % isolated yield (100 g scale), significant exotherm.","Co‑(acac)₂‑catalyzed oxidation using tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) provided the cleanest reaction profile with limited cleavage of the ketal and modest conversion of starting material.","While the reaction was run in acetone, which presented the potential for formation of hazardous acetone‑peroxide species. Fortunately, using an aqueous solution of TBHP and running the reaction in acetonitrile provided comparable results, mitigating a potential safety hazard."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: The Co(acac)₂/TBHP oxidation of ketal 24 stalled after ~48 h, required multiple catalyst/oxidant charges (kicker) and gave only 48 % isolated yield, making scale‑up inefficient.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was increased, a second charge of catalyst and TBHP was added after the reaction stalled, and the reaction was quenched at partial conversion (≈70 %) to allow recovery and recycling of starting material, improving overall throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ["reaction progress stalled after ∼48 h irrespective of initial reagent quantities. Addition of a kicker charge of catalyst and oxidant was effective at further improving conversion.","To strike a balance between isolated yield and material throughput, the reaction was quenched at partial conversion (∼70 %) and starting material was recovered during isolation.","Increasing the catalyst loading and equivalents of TBHP provided a modest improvement in conversion, we found that reaction progress stalled after ∼48 h…"]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Triflation of ketone 28 to vinyl triflate 10 required removal of excess Comins’ reagent, which previously necessitated extensive column chromatography.
Solution_Description: After the triflation, the reaction was quenched with an aqueous solution of N,N‑dimethylethylenediamine, forming a soluble triflimide diamine adduct that could be removed by aqueous washes, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Separation of vinyl triflate 10 from excess Comins’ reagent following aqueous workup required extensive column chromatography.","Quenching the reaction with an aqueous solution of N,N‑dimethylethylenediamine generated a triflimide diamine adduct. Subsequent concentration of the reaction mixture and partitioning … removed the acidic triflimide byproducts … affording vinyl triflate 10 in 70 % yield and >95 % purity over 4 steps without column chromatography."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the heterogeneous hydrogenation of olefin 34 gave inconsistent conversion due to residual Pd and Fe from the preceding Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, poisoning the Pd/C catalyst.
Solution_Description: The crude product was treated with a silica/ethylenediamine mixture and later with silica‑based thiol or dimercaptotriazine scavengers together with activated charcoal, which removed >90 % of residual metals and restored quantitative hydrogenation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["ICP‑OES analysis of the Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling product 34 indicated high levels of residual Pd and Fe… leading to the observed variability in reaction performance.","Treatment of olefin 34 with 100 wt % silica and 10 wt % ethylenediamine … dramatically improved conversion …","The combination of activated charcoal and SiliaMetS Thiol and DMT were comparably effective at consistently accelerating the rate of the reduction … without the introduction of additional impurities."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Deoxy‑fluorination of fluorohydrin 38 with DAST caused formation of a C4‑chloride impurity (≈5 %) and the reaction was exothermic and hazardous, leading to difficult purification and variable diastereoselectivity.
Solution_Description: An in‑situ generated morpholine‑DeoxoFluor complex was used for the deoxy‑fluorination, giving >20:1 dr, eliminating the chloride impurity and providing a safer, more controllable process.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Fluorination of fluorohydrin 38 with DAST … resulted in formation of significant quantities of a putative C4‑chloride impurity (∼5 %) which was also challenging to remove.","Stereoselectivity was improved to >20:1 by affecting the deoxyfluorination of 38 using an in situ generated morpholine‑DeoxoFluor complex … This approach also eliminated the formation of previously observed chloride impurities.","DeoxoFluor is volatile and a respiratory hazard and must be handled in a well‑ventilated hood. … operators performing the reaction on larger scales should be aware of potential safety risks."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: Limited commercial availability of 6,8‑difluoro‑1‑tetralone required a new scalable synthesis of a functionalized tetralone precursor.
Solution_Description: A three‑step oxidative rearrangement route starting from readily available aryl bromide 18 was developed, providing tetralone 17 in three steps with ~40 % overall yield, bypassing the need for the scarce starting material.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the limited commercial availability of 6,8‑difluoro‑1‑tetralone necessitated that we develop a scalable route to supply a suitably functionalized tetralone precursor.","We envisioned that a suitably functionalized arylated cyclobutanol could be converted to tetralone 17… This in turn enabled the selection of a starting material with a chloride at the C8 position.","Ultimately, tetralone 17 was produced in just 3 steps and ∼40 % overall yield, representing a significant improvement in efficiency from the first‑generation route."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of Casdatifan (AB521), a Potent, Selective, Clinical-Stage Inhibitor of HIF-2α
Problem_Description: The original Pd‑catalyzed cyanation used relatively expensive palladium precursors and high loadings, prompting consideration of cheaper alternatives.
Solution_Description: Ni‑catalyzed cyanation was investigated, delivering high yields on test scale and offering a lower‑cost catalyst alternative for large‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Pd‑catalyzed cyanation using Pd(OAc)₂, XPhos … also provided the desired product in high yield.","We found that Ni‑catalyzed cyanation afforded tetralone 17 in high yield on 5 g test scale.","This presented an attractive alternative given the relative costs of Pd and Ni catalysts."]

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The indole‑containing heterocycle gave poor conversion to the aryl‑boron product under all tested conditions, preventing a reliable borylation of this fragment.
Solution_Description: The screening platform identified Ph‑DavePhos as the optimal ligand for this substrate and the nickel source was changed to NiCl₂·6H₂O, which gave higher conversion and a more reproducible reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “the indole‑containing fragment showed poor conversion to the corresponding aryl boron species under an array of reaction conditions.”; “Ph‑DavePhos … was the top‑performing ligand and was chosen for further optimization.”; “Based on our previous tetrahydroxydiboron (BBA) stability studies, we have changed the nickel precursor to NiCl₂·6H₂O, which performs equally well… but provides improved stability of the diboron reagent.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: During the nickel‑catalyzed borylation of the triazole bromide a significant amount of protodehalogenated product (compound 4) formed, consuming the aryl halide and lowering the isolated yield of the desired boronate.
Solution_Description: 1,3‑Propanediol was added to all reactions to stabilize the diboron reagent and methanol was chosen as the preferred solvent, which together reduced the formation of the dehalogenated side‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: “the mass balance for most borylation conditions was the species derived from protodehalogenation (4) of the starting aryl halide.”; “1,3‑propanediol was added to all of the reactions in the screen… While the impact of added 1,3‑propanediol is sometimes minimal, we have observed few if any cases where its inclusion has a detrimental impact.”; “For this substrate, methanol was a better solvent than ethanol for each ligand tested in the borylation.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: An exotherm occurred when DIPEA was added to the borylation mixture, causing a rapid temperature rise (0 → 23 °C) and generating heat that could pose safety risks during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The addition of DIPEA was performed over a controlled 5‑minute period with temperature monitoring, and the reaction was subsequently held at 20 °C to manage the exotherm safely.
Supporting_Evidence: “A significant exotherm is observed at the start of the reaction after the addition of DIPEA, resulting in a rapid product formation… as it warmed from 0 to 23 °C to control the exotherm.”; “The base solution was then transferred to the Chemglass reactor via vacuum under a stream of N₂ over 5 min (an exotherm of 6 °C was observed). The batch was then warmed to 20 °C and aged for 16 h.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The pre‑formed Pd‑A‑caPhos complex was poorly soluble in the 1:1:1 MeTHF/MeOH/H₂O solvent system at 60 °C, resulting in a sluggish Suzuki coupling and increased protodeboronation of the aryl‑boronate.
Solution_Description: The catalyst system was switched to in‑situ generated SPhos/Pd(OAc)₂, which is soluble under the reaction conditions, and the solvent ratio was kept at 1:1:1 MeTHF/MeOH/H₂O with increased methanol volume (10 vol) to ensure a homogeneous mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “A‑caPhos is not readily soluble in 1:1:1 MeTHF/MeOH/H₂O at 60 °C… resulting in increased protodeboronation.”; “We elected to change the catalyst system to SPhos/Pd(OAc)₂ to improve the robustness of the transformation.”; “we increased the volumes of methanol in the borylation process from 5 to 10 vol… which afforded a homogeneous reaction at room temperature and removed any mixing sensitivity.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The presence of unreacted B₂‑npg₂ in the borylation stream could lead to uncontrolled hydrogen evolution during the quench step, presenting a safety hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The stream was cooled to 0 °C and the diboron reagent was quenched slowly with 5 M aq. K₃PO₄ (or 25 wt % NaOMe) while maintaining a nitrogen sweep to capture any hydrogen evolved, thereby controlling the exotherm and ensuring safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “To ensure consumption of the unreacted diboron reagent… a quench operation was performed… we cooled the stream to 0 °C and slowly added 5.0 equiv of 5 M aq. KOH or 25 wt % NaOMe in MeOH.”; “Safety testing was completed for the telescoped process, and significant amounts of hydrogen were not detected during the quench. However, a full N₂ sweep was completed during the quench to ensure that if a small amount of hydrogen was generated, it would be removed from the reactor headspace.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: The aryl‑boronate intermediate degraded under the Suzuki conditions (60 °C, base KOH), leading to loss of material and lower overall isolated yield of the final API.
Solution_Description: The base in the Suzuki step was changed from KOH to K₃PO₄, the reaction temperature was lowered to 50 °C, and the Pd loading was reduced to 2.5 mol % while still achieving >95 % in‑process yield, thereby preserving the boronate and improving product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “We decided to investigate catalysts generated in situ… we elected to change the catalyst system to SPhos/Pd(OAc)₂.”; “Based on these stability data, we decided to utilize K₃PO₄ as the base in the Suzuki reaction.”; “Further optimization showed that we could decrease the Pd loading to 2.5 mol % and the reaction temperature to 50 °C without impacting the quality or conversion, leading to finalized conditions that afforded an in‑process yield of the Suzuki step of ∼95 %.”

Paper Title: Advancing Base Metal Catalysis: Development and Execution of a Ni-catalyzed Borylation/Pd-catalyzed Suzuki Telescoped Process
Problem_Description: Isolation of the final product required removal of homodimers and residual boronate, and conventional work‑ups gave only 70 % isolated yield with variable purity.
Solution_Description: A reactive crystallization was employed directly on the reaction mixture, followed by filtration and a final toluene recrystallization to afford the API in 70 % isolated yield, >99 % purity, and low residual metals; the telescoped approach avoided intermediate isolations.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Suzuki reaction was a reactive crystallization, with the product crystallizing out of the solution as the reaction proceeded… the crude product was isolated by filtration… we completed a recrystallization in toluene to increase potency to 99 %.”; “Since the Ni catalyst in a borylation stream can be removed by an aqueous wash… no scavenger was required to control the Pd or the Ni to 20 and <10 ppm, respectively.”

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: Glycerol (1) and acetic anhydride are immiscible liquids. Their non‑miscibility prevents efficient phase‑dispersion in a solvent‑free batch or continuous‑flow reactor, leading to poor homogenisation, uncontrolled exothermic spikes and hazardous splashes of acetic acid.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors transferred the reaction to the Impact‑in‑Continuous‑Flow‑Heated‑Mechanochemistry (ICHeM) platform. Continuous‑flow bead‑mechanochemistry with 0.7 mm zirconia beads creates intense mechanical impact that instantaneously disperses the two immiscible phases, eliminates the need for external heating, and allows the reactor to be cooled (rather than heated) to suppress thermal runaway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Due to the nonmiscibility of glycerol and acetic anhydride, none of these heterogeneous catalysis methods can be transposed to solvent‑free continuous flow to date..." (Sec 2, first paragraph). 
• "The cylindrical geometry of the ICHeM system, coupled with the DYNO bead accelerator technology, allows these two compounds to be mixed in a continuous flow process using homogeneous catalysis" (Intro). 
• "The reaction is triggered by mechanical transfer and by auto‑heating and then autotriggered by exothermicity, and it is notable that using a cooling regulation of the reactor has a negative effect on conversion due to energy dissipation" (Sec 2.4). 
• "The WAB rotation system only needs to be cooled, no temperature regulation of the reactor is needed to avoid thermal runaway or projections" (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: Most Brønsted and Lewis acids (AcOH, CoSO4·7H2O, ZnCl2, CuCl2·2H2O, FeCl2·4H2O, etc.) give ≤ 2 % conversion of glycerol at ≤ 65 °C, requiring either very high temperatures (130 °C) or long reaction times to reach acceptable yields.
Solution_Description: Screening identified Fe(OTf)2 (1 mol %) and H2SO4 (1 mol %) as highly active homogeneous catalysts that afford 100 % glycerol conversion at room temperature within 2 min in batch and ≤ 15 min in a planetary ball mill, eliminating the need for high temperature or prolonged heating.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 2, entry 25 – Fe(OTf)2 (1 mol %) gives 100 % conversion at 25 °C in 2 min. 
• Table 2, entries 7–9 – H2SO4 gives 100 % conversion at 25 °C, 40 °C and 65 °C (2 min). 
• "When strong Brønsted acid H2SO4 is used as a catalyst, glycerol conversion is complete whatever the temperature (25, 40, and 65 °C)" (Sec 2.1). 
• "At 65 °C for 2 min, polyol conversion reached 33 % in the presence of CoSO4·7H2O, 100 % in the presence of ZnCl2 or CuCl2·2H2O..." (Sec 2.1) – indicating variability and need for optimisation.

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: In a microfluidic (1.6 mL) continuous‑flow mixer the immiscible glycerol and acetic anhydride streams do not mix; Fe(OTf)2 even precipitates inside the channel, and acetic anhydride degrades at higher flow rates, resulting in zero conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the microfluidic approach and employed the ICHeM continuous‑flow mechanochemical reactor, which can handle non‑miscible liquids and prevents catalyst precipitation, while allowing adjustment of flow rate, residence time and rotation speed to achieve full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "In our conditions, the reactants remained nonmiscible, and no reaction occurred even with long residence times" (Sec 2.3). 
• "It is notable that Fe(OTf)2 can precipitate in the microreactor" (Sec 2.3). 
• "The WAB DYNO‑MILL RESEARCH LAB... features continuous flow cylinder bead reactors... allowing these two compounds to be mixed in a continuous flow process" (Intro). 
• Table 5 demonstrates full conversion (100 %) in ICHeM with optimized residence time and rotation speed.

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: The acetylation of glycerol with acetic anhydride is a highly exothermic, essentially explosive reaction that generates a rapid temperature rise to 125–130 °C and can cause dangerous splashes of acetic acid, posing a serious safety risk in batch reactors.
Solution_Description: By using the ICHeM system the reaction is initiated by mechanochemical energy; the reactor is operated under cooling with no external heating, and the exotherm is self‑controlled by the bead impact, eliminating the need for high‑temperature heating and reducing the risk of thermal runaway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "When the reaction occurred, the synthesis of triacetin ... was a quantitative exothermic reaction with a temperature rise to 125–130 °C and, above all, dangerous splashes of acetic acid" (Sec 2.1). 
• "The WAB rotation system only needs to be cooled, no temperature regulation of the reactor is needed to avoid thermal runaway or projections" (Sec 2.4). 
• "The reaction is triggered by mechanical transfer and by auto‑heating and then autotriggered by exothermicity" (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: In the ICHeM continuous‑flow process a long equilibration/fill period (40–60 min) is required before steady‑state operation because the reactor volume is constantly crossed by non‑laminar flows, reducing productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimization of rotation speed (4.6 m s⁻¹ sufficient) and residence time (14–28 min) together with appropriate bead filling (55 % of 0.7 mm beads) shortened the equilibration time and provided homogeneous mixing, allowing steady operation without additional heating.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "An equilibration/fill time of 40–60 min was required before the system reached a steady state, depending on the flow rate and rotation speed" (Sec 2.4). 
• "High rotational speed is not necessary in a steady state; a speed of 4.6 m s⁻¹ was sufficient for homogenization and reaction to occur" (Sec 2.4). 
• Table 5, entries 1–3 show full conversion with 4.6 m s⁻¹ rotation and 14–28 min residence.

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: At high total flow rates (4 mL min⁻¹) acetic anhydride degrades at the reactor exit, giving zero conversion and loss of valuable reagent, which also raises operating cost.
Solution_Description: The authors reduced the total flow rate to 1.3 mL min⁻¹ and increased the residence time to 28 min, while adding a slight excess of acetic anhydride (3.2 equiv) to compensate for any degradation, thereby achieving 99–100 % yield with lower reagent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 5, entries 4–5 (4 mL min⁻¹) show 0 % conversion, indicating degradation. 
• "A slight excess of acetic anhydride (3.2 equiv) was used to compensate for its possible degradation during the reaction" (Sec 2.4). 
• Entries 1–3 (1.3 mL min⁻¹, 14–28 min) give 100 % conversion and 99–100 % selectivity.

Paper Title: Solvent-Free Production of Triacetin from Glycerol through Complementary Mechanochemical, Biphasic, and Catalytic Approaches Using ICHeM Technology
Problem_Description: Conventional magnetic agitation in batch reactors consumes ~0.85 kW, which is higher than the power required for the ICHeM process, increasing energy cost for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The ICHeM continuous‑flow mechanochemical reactor requires only 0.57 kW (0.55 kW for bead rotation + 0.018 kW for pumps), delivering the same or higher conversion with significantly lower energy consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The electrical power required for the ICHeM continuous flow process was estimated to be 0.57 kW... In comparison, the estimated power requirement for a conventional magnetic agitator in a batch reactor is 0.85 kW..." (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: Traditional solid‑phase synthesis (SPOS) produced sgRNA batches with only 44‑45 % HPLC purity, which is insufficient for clinical material.
Solution_Description: A chemo‑enzymatic ligation process (single‑point T4 RNA ligase 2‑mediated assembly of two RNA fragments) gave consistently higher purity (10‑15 % improvement) and 3‑4 × higher overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Inheriting a traditional SPOS process… we had mg‑scale sgRNA batches… assessed at 44–45 % HPLC purity."  
2. "This level of quality was not considered acceptable for sgRNAs entering the clinic."  
3. "Our method leverages ligase‑mediated assembly… consistently achieves higher purity (10–15 % improvement…) and significantly greater yield (3–4 times higher) compared to traditional linear solid‑phase synthesis."

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: Achieving high purity required two successive orthogonal chromatographic steps, a resource‑intensive operation that limited throughput and increased cost.
Solution_Description: The ligation‑based route eliminates the need for the dual‑purification workflow, enabling a more streamlined, higher‑throughput process.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "A true step change in purity to 75 % HPLC levels was achieved when we expanded the purification process to include two successive but orthogonal chromatographic separations… the effort… would limit the throughput of operations."

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: Increasing the number of ligation sites would require more fragments and monitoring steps, compromising process consistency and robustness.
Solution_Description: A single ligation point in the middle of the 100‑mer was chosen, balancing fragment purity and simplifying the process design.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The greater the number, the more fragments must be synthesized… However, every ligation would need to be monitored… We decided to opt for a single ligation point in the middle of the 100‑mer structure to balance the purity… and the simplicity of process design."

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: Short DNA adaptor oligonucleotides (<20 nt) gave low ligation conversion rates.

Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: Standard ligation protocols use a massive excess of enzyme or fragments, leading to high reagent cost and potentially lower conversion when scaled.
Solution_Description: The process was optimized to use approximately equimolar fragments, reduced enzyme loading, and higher reactant concentrations (adjusted Mg²⁺ and ATP) while maintaining full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "A major focus… was to obtain a reproducible process while maintaining 1) an approximately equimolar ratio of fragments… 2) reducing the loading of T4‑RNA Ligase 2 while preserving full conversion… 3) reducing the reaction volume factor."

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs
Problem_Description: During purification at pH 10 with 50 mM n‑butyl‑ammonium acetate, partial sgRNA degradation occurred due to base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the 2’‑OH groups.

Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Partial decomposition of the sgRNA would occur when the purification was conducted using n‑butyl ammonium acetate 50 mM at pH 10… The problem was solved by lowering the pH of the mobile phase to 7.5 to prevent the base‑catalyzed hydrolysis."

Paper Title: Development of a Broadly Applicable Enzymatic Ligation Process for the Production of Single Guide RNAs

Supporting_Evidence: 1. "Initially, we sought to digest the DNA template with DNase I… Subsequently, we determined that the DNA digestion step could be omitted and the DNA adaptor carried forward as it was efficiently removed during purification."

Problem_Description: Microbial growth was observed in the ligation buffer over time, posing a contamination risk.

Supporting_Evidence: 1. "As part of our microbial control strategy investigations, it was found that 10 % acetonitrile was sufficient to significantly delay microbial growth in the media while having negligible impact on the ligation efficiency."

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: The residual trifluoro‑ethanol (TFE) remaining in the cocrystal after crystallisation and vacuum drying far exceeded the regulatory limit (≈3300 ppm). Even exhaustive drying at 80 °C for 12 h left >4000 ppm TFE, making the material unsafe for pharmaceutical use.
Solution_Description: Replace TFE with alternative solvents (acetone or ethyl formate). Ethyl formate was finally selected as the production solvent because it yields acceptable residual levels (≈840 ppm) and eliminates the toxic TFE issue.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...its residual concentration in the final product is constrained, particularly to a maximum of 3300 ppm… even after exhaustive drying at 80 °C … the quantity of trifluoroethanol remained in excess of 4000 ppm.” (Abstract/Results) 
• “...none of the solvents were effective in reducing the trifluoroethanol concentration to below the specified limits… Consequently, an alternative solvent was devised.” (Results – Crystallisation from Trifluoroethanol) 
• “The residual solvent in the sample fell within the acceptable limits for pharmaceutical use… 1400 ppm for acetone and 840 ppm for ethyl formate.” (Results – Purity) 
• “The optimized process, which employs ethyl formate at 25 °C, offers several advantages…” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: Washing the freshly‑crystallised cocrystal with most candidate solvents caused the cocrystal to dissociate back to rivaroxaban form I, preventing removal of TFE without destroying the product.
Solution_Description: Identify solvents that do not dissolve the cocrystal (heptane, methyl tert‑butyl‑ether, ethyl acetate). These were screened, but ultimately the process was abandoned in favour of a completely different solvent (ethyl formate) that both crystallises the cocrystal and removes the need for a wash‑step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Only three of the seven employed solvents yielded a pure cocrystal phase: heptane, methyl tert‑butyl‑ether, and ethyl acetate. The remaining solvents resulted in the dissociation of the cocrystal into crystalline form I of the pure API.” (Results – Crystallisation from Trifluoroethanol) 
• “The highest reduction was observed … methyl tert‑butyl‑ether, with a concentration of 3400 ppm.” (Results – Solvent washing) 
• “Consequently, an alternative solvent was devised.” (Results – Solvent wash) 
• “Acetone and ethyl formate were effective in producing the cocrystal.” (Results – Solvent Screening)

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: The rivaroxaban‑oxalic‑acid cocrystal displays incongruent behaviour: in pure solvents it converts back to the API, so stoichiometric solutions of API and co‑former do not give the cocrystal and yields are poor.
Solution_Description: Determine the critical co‑former concentration from solubility data (≥0.1 g mL⁻¹ in acetone, ≥0.016 g mL⁻¹ in ethyl formate) and run the crystallisation with a controlled excess of oxalic acid. This stabilises the cocrystal in solution and enables quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The cocrystal exhibited incongruent behaviour… the cocrystal also transforms into the pure API when placed in a pure solvent.” (Results – Solubility Measurement) 
• “It was determined that the cocrystal is stable in acetone solutions with concentrations exceeding 0.1 g mL⁻¹ and in ethyl formate solutions with concentrations exceeding 0.016 g mL⁻¹ at 25 °C.” (Results – Solubility Measurement) 
• “The manipulation of saturated solutions is hindered by their high viscosity and proclivity for crystallisation… the formation of a cocrystal was unsuccessful when stoichiometric amounts… were used.” (Results – Solubility Measurement) 
• “The data were subsequently employed to construct the ternary phase diagram… to ascertain the critical concentration at which the cocrystal remains stable.” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: Highly saturated solutions of oxalic acid are very viscous and tend to crystallise during handling, making stirring and accurate dosing difficult.

Solution_Description: Work with less‑concentrated (but still supersaturated) solutions and adjust the solvent volume to reduce viscosity; this also improves agitation and avoids premature crystallisation during the solubility experiments.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The manipulation of saturated solutions is hindered by their high viscosity and proclivity for crystallisation.” (Results – Solubility Measurement) 
• “The solubilities of the two components and the cocrystal were determined… by varying the temperature… The data indicate that lower temperatures would be conducive to shifting to the cocrystal side for both systems, given the requisite co‑former excess.” (Results – Solubility Measurement) 
• Implicit in the design of the ternary phase diagrams where concentrations were systematically varied.

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: When crystallising from acetone at 25 °C or 50 °C, the transformation to the cocrystal requires several hours (up to >17 h at 25 °C), dramatically reducing productivity.
Solution_Description: Select ethyl formate as the solvent and operate at 25 °C; under these conditions the cocrystal forms within 21 min, providing a much faster and higher‑yielding process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...the transformation into a cocrystal in the system with acetone was markedly prolonged, with the process taking approximately five hours at 50 °C… at 25 °C… pure rivaroxaban form I was present even after 8 h, … it was necessary for 17 h for full transformation.” (Results – In Situ Study) 
• “...the complete transformation into a cocrystal was observed in the system with ethyl formate after 21 min at 50 °C. At a lower temperature of 25 °C, the transformation was slower, taking approximately 1 h to complete.” (Results – In Situ Study) 
• “The process of crystallisation is advantageous in terms of both the rate of reaction and the quantity of the co‑former required, as well as the smaller crystal size of the product.” (Results – Conclusions) 
• “The optimized process, which employs ethyl formate at 25 °C…” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Development of the Crystallization Process for Rivaroxaban–Oxalic Acid Cocrystal Preparation Using a Combination of Phase Diagrams and In Situ Measurements
Problem_Description: Extended heating at high temperature risks degradation of the API and formation of impurities.
Solution_Description: Use a rapid temperature ramp to 25 °C (or 50 °C only briefly) and monitor conversion in real time with in‑situ Raman spectroscopy. This avoids unnecessary prolonged heating, protecting product integrity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The in situ Raman probe was employed… the transformation … was monitored to minimise costs and theoretical risks associated with the inappropriate setting of these parameters (e.g., degradation during prolonged heating).” (Results – In‑situ Study) 
• “The temperature of 50 °C was employed to circumvent the boiling of the solvent… however, this temperature was selected to be sufficiently high to observe the effect of intensive heating on the kinetics of the transformation.” (Results – In‑situ Study) 
• “The optimized process… offers several advantages, including an increased reaction rate, a reduced quantity of co‑former, and a smaller crystal size of the product.” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: The original Daiichi‑Sankyo route used inorganic NaCN to introduce the cyano group, which generated toxic HCN gas that had to be tightly controlled on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the NaCN‑based nitrile addition with a 1,4‑selective addition of lithioacetonitrile generated in‑situ from inexpensive n‑BuLi and MeCN, eliminating HCN formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The generation of toxic HCN gas during the introduction of the cyano group was a concern, where the amount of generated gas needed to be controlled.” (Intro, p. 4)  |  “Encouraged by the successful 1,4‑selective addition of lithioacetonitrile… using only inexpensive n‑BuLi and MeCN” (Results, p. 9)  |  “Since the amount of generated gas needed to be controlled… could be avoided in a single stroke by changing the strategy to introduce a two‑carbon unit bearing a carbamoyl group” (Results, p. 5‑6).

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: The original process required a high‑pressure hydrogenation of the nitrile using pyrophoric sponge cobalt, which posed safety risks and left residual heavy‑metal contaminants in the product.
Solution_Description: The nitrile reduction step was eliminated by introducing a one‑carbon degradation (Hofmann rearrangement) that used inexpensive sodium hypochlorite pentahydrate as the oxidant, removing the need for cobalt and high‑pressure equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: “Controlling the residual heavy metals during reduction with pyrophoric sponge cobalt was also necessary.” (Intro, p. 4)  |  “Pressure‑resistant equipment is needed for nitrile reduction to achieve efficient hydrogenation.” (Intro, p. 4)  |  “Sodium hypochlorite pentahydrate as one of the least expensive reagents was used as the oxidant. The reaction proceeded smoothly under the standard reaction conditions.” (Results, p. 13)  |  “The Hofmann rearrangement… eliminates the nitrile reduction step.” (Results, p. 13).

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: High‑pressure hydrogenation required pressure‑rated reactors, increasing equipment cost and operational risk.
Solution_Description: Switching to the Hofmann rearrangement removed the high‑pressure hydrogenation requirement, allowing the process to be run in standard equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pressure‑resistant equipment is needed for nitrile reduction to achieve efficient hydrogenation.” (Intro, p. 4)  |  “The Hofmann rearrangement… eliminates the nitrile reduction step.” (Results, p. 13).

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: Attempts to add soft carbon nucleophiles (ethyl cyanoacetate, Meldrum’s acid, diethyl malonate) to the alkylidene malonate gave poor or no conversion because of steric hindrance and competing reverse reactions.
Solution_Description: A mono‑ester nucleophile (acetonitrile) was selected; lithioacetonitrile was generated with n‑BuLi (strong base) at –78 °C, then added to the substrate. Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: During the one‑pot decarboxylation/hydrolysis of intermediate 10, the dicarboxylic acid 14 formed as a by‑product that was difficult to remove by liquid‑liquid extraction or crystallisation, lowering overall purity and yield.

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate

Paper Title: Stereoselective Synthesis of Mirogabalin via 1,4-Selective Addition of Lithioacetonitrile to Alkylidene Malonate
Problem_Description: Selectivity of the 1,4‑addition varied with substrate structure; simple cinnamate ester 15a gave only 1,2‑adduct, whereas malonate‑activated 15b gave high 1,4‑adduct, indicating the need for electronic activation.

Paper Title: Continuous Flow for the Photochemical Synthesis of 3‑Substituted Quinolines
Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several scale‑up and reaction‑performance issues: the explosive/ toxic nature of azides makes batch processing unsafe; a long induction period (>1 h) delayed reaction start; conventional radical initiators gave poor conversion; many solvents (ethers, EtOAc, MeCN) gave low conversion or side‑products, indicating solubility/phase problems; increasing reactant concentration caused clogging in the flow reactor; the required excess of NBS raised cost concerns; optimizing residence time and light intensity was needed to obtain acceptable yields; higher concentrations again led to precipitation; and product isolation required an efficient work‑up to quench bromine and separate phases.
Solution_Description: To address safety, the batch azide step was transferred to a continuous‑flow photoreactor, providing a small reactor volume and excellent heat/mass transfer. The long induction was eliminated by adding a catalytic amount of HBr, which generates bromine in situ and initiates the radical cascade instantly. Conventional initiators were dismissed in favor of the HBr/NBS system. Solvent screening identified DCM as the optimal medium, improving solubility and selectivity. Reactant concentration was tuned to 0.071 M to avoid precipitation and clogging. NBS loading was reduced from 2.05 eq. to 1.5 eq. (and later fine‑tuned to 3.5 eq. in a saturated solution) to lower reagent cost while preserving yield. Residence time and LED wavelength were optimized (2 min, 527 nm green LED) to maximize conversion and minimize side‑products. A larger 3 mL FEP coil was employed for scale‑up without loss of selectivity. Finally, an inline Zaiput liquid‑liquid membrane separator quenched residual bromine and facilitated phase separation, providing a fast and robust purification step.

Safety issue – “the use of sodium azide poses serious safety issues in batch equipment, due to the presence of the toxic and explosive hydrazoic acid (HN₃) … the safe and efficient scale‑up of such a reaction step in batch mode is not feasible …”
Long induction period – “we experienced a relatively long induction period before the initiation of the reaction (>1 h), when an orange‑brown color accompanied by nitrogen extrusion were observed.”
Ineffective initiators – “the application of usual radical initiators… such as dibenzoyl peroxide, AIBN, molecular iodine… proved equally ineffective.”
Solvent problems – “the ether type solvents were inefficient… while in ethyl acetate (EtOAc) and acetonitrile (MeCN) multiple side products were formed.”
Clogging – “increasing the reactant concentration to 0.081 M… resulted in clogging in the flow system.”
Cost of NBS – “In batch, the equivalence of NBS used was 2.05… Reduction of the NBS loading to 1.5 eq resulted in a decrease in yield… increasing the amount to 3.0 eq did not change the selectivity… using a saturated solution of NBS… increased the yield.”
Residence‑time optimization – “the shortest residence time of 0.5 min gave 31% … Longer residence time increased the yield… The highest yield … achieved by applying 2.0 min residence time.”
Light‑wavelength effect – “At 370–390 nm … low product … When wavelength was shifted to the visible range, formation of the desired product increased … highest yield … at 527 nm (Green LED).”
Reactor scaling – “This modification did not affect the selectivity of the reaction, maintaining the desired product yield at 77%.”
Inline work‑up – “We then extended the continuous system with an in‑line workup procedure using a Zaiput liquid–liquid membrane separator… yielding an organic phase and an aqueous phase at separate outlets.”

Problem_Description: The batch oxidation proceeded slowly, requiring multiple additions and long residence times.
