Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: The aryllithium (11) generated by bromine‑lithium exchange is unstable on scale – it turns from green to black, leads to side‑product formation and a very low isolated corrected yield (≈33 %). The exchange reaction is also highly exothermic, creating safety and heat‑removal challenges.
Solution_Description: The phenolic hydroxyl was protected as a THP ether and directed ortho lithiation (DoM) was used instead of bromine‑lithium exchange. This gives a stable aryllithium (5) that can be generated at 0 °C (instead of –78 °C), eliminating the instability and improving yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Instability of aryllithium <bold>11</bold>, which manifested itself by a color change from green to black, became an issue with increasing scale… resulting in a low isolated corrected yield of 33 %" (section 2.2). • "The charge of Boc₂O… was exothermic…" (exothermic context). • "Protecting the phenolic hydroxy group as tetrahydropyran (THP) ether… generated the desired aryllithium in a stable form, suitable for use in a batch process on a large scale" (abstract). • "Metalation temperature of around 0 °C instead of previously required cryogenic conditions of –78 °C reduces plant infrastructure requirements" (section 2.3).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: The addition of solid Boc₂O to the esterification reaction is highly exothermic, posing a safety risk and making temperature control difficult.
Solution_Description: Boc₂O was added as a 51 % (w/w) solution in toluene at 60 °C, allowing controlled dosing and preventing a delayed exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The charge of Boc₂O as a solid to the reaction mass was found to be exothermic, and this was mitigated by dosing a 51 % (w/w) solution of Boc₂O in toluene at 60 °C, allowing better control of the addition rate and thereby avoiding a delayed exotherm" (section 2.2).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: Commercially supplied mixed mono‑ester 7 contains ~5 % of the undesired isomer 14, requiring an additional purification step to meet the >99.5 % purity needed for the route.
Solution_Description: A recrystallization from methanol was introduced early in the sequence to isolate pure 7, avoiding later chromatographic separations.
Supporting_Evidence: • "When the commercial material 7 arrived, it contained 5 % undesired isomer 14, and … a recrystallization from methanol was introduced to ensure a purity of >99.5 %" (section 2.2). • "Separating regioisomers 7 and 14 by crystallization at the beginning of the route… compared favorably" (section 2.2).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: Routes through phthalic anhydride or mixed diester 22 suffer from substantial over‑addition of the aryllithium, giving complex product mixtures and low isolated yields (18 % for the anhydride route, 25–40 % for the diester route).
Solution_Description: The THP‑protected directed ortho lithiation route avoids the use of bromine and the formation of stoichiometric n‑bromobutane, producing a more stable aryllithium and eliminating the over‑addition problem, thereby improving overall yield and simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Substantial overaddition… low isolated yield of 18 %" (section 2.4). • "Overaddition… 38 % (a/a) by LCMS" (section 2.4). • "Protecting the phenolic hydroxy group as THP ether… directed ortho metalation generated the desired aryllithium in a stable form" (abstract). • "Formation of stoichiometric n‑bromobutane… is avoided" (section 2.3).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: Hydrazine (N₂H₄) is a toxic, carcinogenic, and highly flammable reagent, presenting serious health and process safety hazards, especially in its anhydrous form.
Solution_Description: Hydrazine hydrate (64 % w/w) was used together with an additional water charge to dilute the reagent, greatly reducing toxicity and explosion risk while maintaining reactivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Hydrazine is toxic and a carcinogen… highly hazardous, particularly in the anhydrous form…" (section 2.3). • "Sufficient dilution with water reduces these risks considerably, and … an additional water charge was introduced before performing the distillation operations" (section 2.3).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: The bromine‑lithium exchange and subsequent acylation are fast, highly exothermic reactions that are difficult to control on kilogram scale, leading to variability in conversion and limiting scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous flow setup with two cooled tube reactors (first for bromine‑lithium exchange, second for acylation) was employed; the high surface‑to‑volume ratio enables efficient heat removal and short residence times, improving safety and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: • "High exothermicity of the bromine lithium exchange reaction… turned to flow processing for increased reaction control. The high surface to volume ratio in flow reactors allows efficient heat removal" (section 2.2). • "Two 10 mL cooled tube reactors … with the bromine lithium exchange taking place in reactor 1 at –70 °C, followed by acylation in reactor 2" (section 2.2).

Paper Title: Access to Phenolic Pyridopyridazinones and Phthalazinones Using THP Ether-Directed Ortho Lithiation
Problem_Description: The original route relied on palladium‑catalyzed cross‑coupling and bromine‑containing substrates, which are expensive and generate hazardous by‑products (e.g., n‑bromobutane).
Solution_Description: A palladium‑free, telescoped two‑step sequence (ketone formation via acylation of mixed diester followed by cyclisation with hydrazine) was developed, reducing material cost, eliminating the need for precious metal catalysts, and simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Final process, a palladium‑free, telescoped two‑step sequence… demonstrated in our kilogram laboratory" (abstract). • "This route… does not require the use of precious transition metals such as palladium, saving resources and facilitating purification" (section 2.3).

Selective and Scalable
Problem_Description: Conventional O‑alkylation of N‑protected serine/threonine suffers from side‑reactions (Fmoc de‑protection and intramolecular cyclisation to oxazolidinone) and uses hazardous, high‑energy reagents such as aziridine‑2‑carboxylates and NaIO₄.

Problem_Description: Using MeCN as a polar additive gave a homogeneous mixture but dramatically lowered conversion because MeCN is a strong Lewis base that interferes with Ti‑mediated chelation.
Solution_Description: HFIP, which is polar but far less Lewis basic than MeCN, was chosen as the additive, restoring both homogeneity and high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:

Supporting_Evidence: “The literature conditions… failed to cleanly yield the desired ketone 9… either unreacted starting material (6) was isolated… or decomposition occurred.”; “The mixture was exposed to a TEMPO/NaClO oxidation to yield 11 kg of 9 with 91 % purity as a yellow solid in a 40 % yield over three steps.”

Supporting_Evidence: “6 was treated with n‑BuLi at –78 °C… The desired product, 18, was not obtained; however, a 1:1 mixture of 19 and 20 was observed.”; “In light of these results… efforts were refocused on developing the discovery route to enable the production.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of an ORL‑1 Receptor Antagonist via a Radical Bromination and Deoxyfluorination to Afford a

The reagents were added to a slurry of 6 in CH₂Cl₂ and heated at 40 °C for 5 h, giving complete consumption of 6 and enabling kilogram‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the challenges of conducting batch photochemical reactions at scale… the conditions to conduct a thermally induced radical bromination were reevaluated. It was determined that DBDMH (0.8 equiv) in the presence of AIBN (0.07 equiv) would lead to complete consumption of 6.”; “The suspension was heated at 40 °C for 5 h before quenching…”

Paper Title: Synthesis of an ORL‑1 Receptor Antagonist via a Radical Bromination and Deoxyfluorination to Afford a
Problem_Description: The bromide intermediate 7 was unstable to isolation (hydrolyzed to alcohol 8) and could not be purified by chromatography without significant yield loss.

Therefore, it was stored as a solution in DMSO and used without further purification.”; “Since development efforts did not yield a process to isolate 7 without chromatography and significant yield loss, it was telescoped directly into the subsequent step after solvent exchanging from CH₂Cl₂ into DMSO.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of an ORL‑1 Receptor Antagonist via a Radical Bromination and Deoxyfluorination to Afford a

The crude product was washed with water to remove boron, followed by recrystallization from IPA, delivering API of >98 % purity and meeting the residual‑boron specification.
Supporting_Evidence: “The best results were obtained with 3 equiv of lithium triethylborohydride (Super‑Hydride) at –20 to –15 °C… The slurry was filtered… To remove the boron residue, 1 was slurried in 10 volumes of water for 4 h, filtered, and recrystallized from IPA to yield 4.19 kg (59 %)… with >98 % purity.”

Supporting_Evidence: “CAUTION: Appropriate safety data should be collected prior to conducting this reaction at scale.” (multiple sections); “Bis(2‑methoxyethyl)aminosulfur trifluoride is a fuming liquid… reacts violently with water, and generates HF. Supporting_Evidence:
“The literature approach for the synthesis of 2 consists of coupling the amino acid derivatives with isocyanate or phosgene which are highly toxic, unstable, and difficult to handle.”
“The developed process involved the coupling of tert‑butylamine with N,N‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) in the presence of toluene … to give 82% of urea 2.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: In the first attempted routes, the oxidized intermediate 12 was unstable and could not be isolated, and the conversion of intermediate 11 to 6 gave only 20–30 % yield with poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: The problematic route was abandoned and an alternative sequence was adopted that couples the deprotected intermediate 11 with fragment 2, followed by telescoping the remaining steps without isolating intermediates, leading to a robust, higher‑yielding process.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The oxidized intermediate 12, however, was unstable and not isolable.”
“Conversion of 11 to 6 gave 20–30% inconsistent yield; therefore, we did not optimize this route further.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: The previously reported syntheses use restricted solvents (CH₂Cl₂) and water‑miscible solvents (acetonitrile, THF) that are difficult to recover and are not acceptable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: All coupling and hydrolysis steps were redesigned to use an industrially acceptable solvent system (toluene/DMF mixture, ethyl acetate, heptane) and the process was telescoped to avoid isolation of intermediates, eliminating the need for restricted solvents.
Supporting_Evidence:
“All of these schemes involve CH₂Cl₂/acetonitrile solvents … CH₂Cl₂ is a restricted solvent in the industry, and there is a problem of recovery with acetonitrile and THF.”
“...we describe the cost‑effective and scalable process for boceprevir 1 as shown in Scheme 4.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: Coupling reagents like CDI, TBTU, DCC and BOP gave modest yields (62–85 %) and required long reaction times (8–15 h).
Solution_Description: EDC·HCl with N‑methylmorpholine in a 1:1 DMF–toluene mixture at 0–10 °C was found to give 90 % isolated yield in only 5 h, dramatically improving efficiency and reducing cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
“With coupling reagents like CDI, TBTU, DCC, and BOP, the yield and purity were less and required longer reaction times (entries 1–4).”
“Eventually EDC·HCl was found to be a good coupling reagent … at 0–10 °C (entry 5) … 90% yield and 99.3% purity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: Initial hydrolysis conditions gave lower yields and poor purity; many bases required additives to achieve acceptable conversion.

Supporting_Evidence:
“In the presence of Bu₄NOH … gave product in good yield and purity (entries 3–4). When reaction was carried out in the presence of methanol and NaOH … gave a good yield and purity (entry 6).”
“...we found 47% NaOH solution in the presence of 1 volume of methanol gave 92% yield of 5 at room temperature (entry 9).”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug

The crude product was converted to a sodium bisulfite adduct, which was filtered and regenerated to pure boceprevir (>99.4 % purity).
Supporting_Evidence:
“Under Moffatt conditions, the reaction gave a displeasing odor of dimethyl sulfide … TEMPO oxidation … genotoxicity … DMP … when more than 1.6 equiv … α,β‑unsaturated carbonyl 14 was forming as a major impurity.”
“DMP (1.6 equiv) was added in three lots at equal intervals of 45 min at 5–10 °C … the reaction mass … filtered … sodium bisulfite solution … to achieve >99.4% purity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: Conventional solvent extraction and crystallization failed to give pure boceprevir; the final isolated yield after the last step was only 40 % despite high purity.
Solution_Description: A bisulfite adduct formation followed by regeneration of boceprevir was employed, delivering the target drug with >99.4 % purity and simplifying the purification workflow.
Supporting_Evidence: “All of the attempts for the purification of boceprevir 1 through solvent extraction and crystallization methods were unsuccessful. Finally, we moved towards sodium bisulfite adduct formation … >99.4% purity … The adduct was regenerated to boceprevir with >99.4% purity and 40% yield.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Process Optimization of Boceprevir: A Protease Inhibitor Drug
Problem_Description: The stepwise isolation process gave an overall yield of only 23 % and a high manufacturing cost (~ 30 000 USD kg⁻¹).
Solution_Description: By telescoping the first three and the last two steps, removing intermediate isolations, and using industrially acceptable solvents, the overall yield increased to 35 % and the cost dropped to ~ 22 000 USD kg⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Optimization of oxidation … The overall yield of the telescoped process of boceprevir was found to be 35% in comparison to the 23% yield obtained from the stepwise isolation process.”
“Cost (USD/kg) … isolated process 29984 → telescoped 21882.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: The older FBRM S‑series probes suffered from probe fouling (stuck particles), non‑linearity, bearing reliability issues and outdated software, which caused noisy, unreliable chord‑length data and made it difficult to interpret crystallization behavior consistently.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team upgraded to the new FBRM G400 probe (which includes a stuck‑particle correction feature, improved linearity, and a more reliable bearing) and paired it with in‑line PVM. For the LDA‑formation step they implemented a controlled‑addition dosing strategy (slight over‑charge of PIP‑P), used stoichiometric excess to consume all LDA, and ran the n‑butyllithium charge at –18 °C with real‑time ReactIR247 monitoring to precisely track LDA consumption and prevent impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “probe fouling (e.g., stuck particles) often occurs… instrument nonlinearity, reliability of bearings, bias of surface features… are among the limitations … of the older S series.”
• “The new FBRM G400 probes address several problem areas… higher accuracy… less noise due to surface features… improved bearing design… correction feature for fouling or stuck particles.”
• “When PIP‑P is overcharged slightly… all of the LDA is consumed completely, eliminating the risks of forming impurities.”
• “The n‑butyllithium charge takes ∼7 h, which is controlled by holding the batch temperature around –18 °C… LDA profile increases continuously as more n‑butyllithium is added… When the LDA has been entirely consumed, its profile levels off… This allows the reaction end point to be determined… to ensure the complete consumption of LDA when PIP‑P is slightly overcharged at ∼1 % equivalent.”
• “The FlowIR sensor is connected to a flow reactor… The reactor and IR flow cell are thermally controlled at 42–44 °C to control this exothermic reaction… In a continuous process mode, the risk that a Grignard reaction will run away can be substantially reduced because the size or volume involved in the reaction is much smaller than in a batch process.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: Using the older FBRM S400 probe during crystallization of MK‑A, MK‑B and MK‑C gave noisy chord‑length distributions, mis‑interpreted nucleation events, and failed to detect phase‑separation or oil droplets, leading to inconsistent particle‑size data across lots.
Solution_Description: Switching to the G400 probe (with enhanced digital signal processing and stuck‑particle correction) together with simultaneous PVM imaging restored accurate particle‑size distributions, correctly distinguished growth from nucleation, and reliably identified lot‑to‑lot differences such as oil‑droplet phases or sharp‑edge artifacts.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In the older S400 instrument… stuck particles on the surface of the probe is a common problem… data under the same circumstances because of stuck particles (see Figure 5e).”
• “The new FBRM G400 probes address several problem areas… higher accuracy… less noise due to surface features… correction feature for fouling or stuck particles.”
• “The G400 Primary electronics provide a more accurate distribution that represents the particle observations in PVM… The G400 electronics resolves the phase separation on the surface of the probe (droplet mode, lot 21) in the chord length distribution, whereas the S400 F electronics does not.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: Grignard reactions are highly exothermic and present safety hazards when scaled up in batch mode; uncontrolled heat release can lead to runaway conditions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved the Grignard step to a continuous flow reactor equipped with FlowIR monitoring, kept the reaction temperature at 42–44 °C, and maintained inert nitrogen coverage on reagents, thereby reducing reaction volume, controlling heat removal, and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Because of the potential exothermic nature of these reactions, process scale‑up of Grignard reactions inherently carries potential safety hazards.”
• “In a continuous process mode, the risk that a Grignard reaction will run away can be substantially reduced because the size or volume involved in the reaction is much smaller than in a batch process.”
• “The reactor and IR flow cell are thermally controlled at 42–44 °C to control this exothermic reaction. In addition, both starting materials are prepared under nitrogen coverage to avoid potential moisture impact.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: During the LDA‑PIP‑P step, any unreacted LDA carries over to subsequent steps, reacting with downstream species and forming impurities; over‑charging PIP‑P wastes material.
Solution_Description: A dosing strategy was adopted where PIP‑P is slightly over‑charged (≈1 % excess) and added after LDA formation, ensuring complete consumption of LDA while minimizing excess PIP‑P, thereby reducing impurity formation and material waste.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When PIP‑P is undercharged… not all of the LDA is consumed, resulting in the formation of impurities when the active LDA reacts with species such as diphenyl methanone in the subsequent step.”
• “When PIP‑P is overcharged slightly… all of the LDA is consumed completely, eliminating the risks of forming impurities… the slight excess of PIP‑P can be removed downstream and does not impact the impurity profile.”
• “The dosing strategy is to have all of the LDA reacted away at low temperature with PIP‑P slightly overcharged.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: In the Grignard flow reaction, insufficient Grignard equivalence (below 2.0 eq) left unreacted starting material, leading to incomplete conversion and impurity formation; IR monitoring lacked sensitivity for low‑level impurities.
Solution_Description: The reaction was programmed to incrementally increase the Grignard feed (0.8 → 2.0 eq) while keeping total flow rate constant at 1.2 mL min⁻¹, allowing full conversion and minimizing impurities; FlowIR was used to track the concentration profiles in real time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction starts with 0.8 eq of Grignard reagent, and every 3 min the amount of Grignard reagent is increased by 0.2 eq, up to 2.0 eq… As the amount of Grignard reagent is increased… the formation and consumption of components are tracked by IR… the reaction does not reach completion until 2.0 eq of Grignard agent has been added (excess Grignard agent is added to avoid impurity formation).”
• “IR has insufficient sensitivity to accurately monitor either impurity in this study.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Control with Recent New FBRM, PVM, and IR
Problem_Description: Interpretation of FBRM data alone could misclassify particle‑growth events as nucleation, leading to inconsistent process understanding.
Solution_Description: Concurrent use of in‑line PVM provided visual confirmation of crystal morphology, allowing correct discrimination between nucleation and growth and improving reliability of particle‑size analysis.
Supporting_Evidence: • “FBRM data alone are not straightforward to interpret… may appear to be nucleation‑dominated because the mean of the chord length distribution appears to be shifting to the left… PVM clearly shows the growth of rods… With the addition of PVM, the FBRM results can be interpreted more reliably… the crystallization process can be described as a smooth, growth‑dominated process.”

Paper Title: Control Strategy for the Manufacture of Brivanib Alaninate, a Novel Pyrrolotriazine VEGFR/FGFR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The sodium salt of intermediate 6 degrades slowly when isolated as a solid or stored as a solution, leading to loss of material and reduced overall yield.
Solution_Description: Acetonitrile was chosen as the reaction solvent, allowing the sodium‑salt intermediate to be telescoped directly into the alkylation step without isolation, thereby avoiding degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "If isolated as solid or stored as a solution, the salt of intermediate 6 slowly degraded." (Section 3.1)

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The vinyl‑Grignard addition step in the Astra‑Zeneca route was highly dependent on the quality of the vinyl Grignard reagent and required cryogenic temperatures (‑20 °C).  The reaction also gave variable yields and generated a thick, difficult‑to‑stir slurry that needed extensive filtration of titanium‑derived salts.
Solution_Description: The team replaced the vinyl‑Grignard step with a Ti(OiPr)₄‑catalyzed Kulinkovich cyclopropanation followed by oxidative fragmentation, which avoids the need for vinyl‑magnesium bromide and provides higher, reproducible yields on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “We found that the outcome of this step was highly dependent on the quality of the vinyl Grignard, and in addition, cryogenic temperatures (‑20 °C) were necessary.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The original oxidation of N‑Boc‑4‑hydroxyproline (8) to ketone 9 used sodium periodate and catalytic RuO₂, which involved an expensive metal catalyst and raised safety and waste concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free TEMPO/bleach oxidation was adopted, adding the bleach portion‑wise at low temperature (0–5 °C) to control the exotherm and avoid Ru‑catalyst use.
Supporting_Evidence: “We wanted to avoid using ruthenium or other metals to oxidize 8 to 9, so a TEMPO/bleach oxidation was examined.”; “No reaction occurred using the conventional TEMPO/bleach reaction system … but ketone 9 formed when KBr and NaHCO₃ were omitted.”; “When performed below 10 °C, the reaction went to completion and the heat flow … was relatively constant … indicating that the catalyst was not being significantly deactivated.”; “When the reaction was performed at 20 °C, there was incomplete conversion … and the height of the heat flow spikes decreased … suggesting that the catalyst was decomposing.”; “The bleach was added at a rate that maintained the reaction temperature between 0 and 5 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: During the TEMPO/bleach oxidation, higher temperatures (≈20 °C) caused catalyst decomposition and uncontrolled heat release.
Solution_Description: Bleach was added in seven small portions over 24 h while keeping the reactor temperature ≤10 °C, thereby preventing catalyst degradation and managing the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “A total of 1.0 equiv of bleach was added in seven smaller portions over 24 h … while the reaction and jacket temperatures were monitored.”; “When performed below 10 °C, the reaction … went to completion and the heat flow … was relatively constant.”; “When the reaction was performed at 20 °C … the height of the heat flow spikes decreased … suggesting that the catalyst was decomposing.”; “The process temperature could be readily controlled by varying the rate of the bleach addition to maintain the reaction temperature between 0 and 5 °C.”; “The bleach was added at a rate that maintained the reaction temperature between 0 and 5 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: Ketone 9 has low solubility in 2‑MeTHF (≈73 g L⁻¹), making solid addition cumbersome on kilogram scale and leading to filtration delays.
Solution_Description: Ketone 9 was supplied as a concentrated solution in N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone (NMP, 500 g L⁻¹), eliminating the need for solid handling and improving throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the initial kilo‑lab runs, ketone 9 was added to the reaction mixture as a solid … because of the relatively low solubility of 9 in 2‑MeTHF (73 g/L).”; “For the pilot plant, ketone 9 was added as a concentrated solution in NMP (500 g/L).”; “A 20 wt % solution of potassium tert‑butoxide … was added to a suspension of methyltriphenylphosphonium bromide …” (showing need for soluble reagents); “The aqueous layer was extracted … and acidified … to afford 6·t‑BuNH₂.”; “The mixture was filtered … and dried … to give 6·t‑BuNH₂ as a colorless solid (91 % yield).”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The 3 + 2 cycloaddition produced a 4:1 mixture of spirocycle diastereomers that previously required chromatography for separation.
Solution_Description: The free‑base mixture was treated with HCl in dioxane, directly crystallizing the HCl salt of the desired diastereomer (>99:1 dr) without any chromatographic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “We needed to replace the chromatography that was used to separate the 4:1 mixture of diastereomers produced in the 3 + 2 cycloaddition.”; “Treatment of the initial Boc‑protected cycloadduct product 15 with anhydrous 4 M HCl in 1,4‑dioxane … resulted in salt 2·HCl crystallizing directly … with a diastereomeric ratio of >99:1.”; “The procedure was successfully demonstrated on a 200 g scale, but further scale‑up to 2 kg surprisingly afforded only a 94:6 mixture.”; “Subsequent studies showed that the >98:2 selectivity was obtained only when the solid was rapidly filtered after addition of the maleic acid.”; “This new salt crystallization eliminated the need for chromatography.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: Final compound 1 could not be isolated by chromatography on kilogram scale, and the product existed only as an amorphous solid, complicating isolation and raising impurity‑control concerns.
Solution_Description: The crude oxidation mixture was treated with acetic acid to form a crystalline acetic‑acid solvate (1·HOAc); the solvate was filtered, washed and subsequently dried under controlled vacuum/temperature to give neat amorphous 1 with <50 ppm residual TEMPO.
Supporting_Evidence: “The purification and isolation of 1 were achieved in the kilo‑lab campaign by forming a cocrystalline material with acetic acid (1·HOAc).”; “With this crystallization procedure, the TEMPO level in 1·HOAc was consistently <50 ppm.”; “Preliminary studies of the drying and stability of 1·HOAc showed that the acetic acid could be removed under vacuum at elevated temperature to afford neat amorphous 1.”; “The cocrystal was broken by dissolution of the solid in i‑PrOAc and washing with base to remove the acetic acid.”; “Scraping the solid out of the rotary evaporator bulb was tedious but was the fastest way to obtain 1 for use in the non‑clinical studies.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: During a large‑scale coupling of spirocycle 2·HCl with N‑Boc‑tert‑leucine, the reaction mixture became too thick, broke the PTFE paddle, and generated by‑product 19, reducing yield to 64 % and purity to 96 % AUC.
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed at lower concentration, with reagents added at 0–5 °C (instead of 30 °C), and the order of addition was adjusted (charging NMM last) to avoid thick slurries and suppress impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “One batch of the coupling … became so thick that it could not be mixed completely and eventually broke the pin holding the PTFE paddle onto the glass stirring rod. This led to the formation of many new byproducts, the most abundant being impurity 19 … the yield … fell to 64 % and the purity decreased from >98 % to 96 % AUC.”; “A study of the effect of the reaction temperature … showed that it was necessary to charge NMP first, cool it to 0–5 °C, and then charge the reagents.”; “If the reagents were charged at 20–25 °C, 1–2% AUC impurity 19 formed via double addition … Only 0.2–0.4% impurity 19 formed when reagents were added to NMP at 0–5 °C.”; “The optimal amount of NMM … was 3.0 equiv … Slower reaction was observed when 2.5 equiv …”; “The reaction was heated to 35 °C … but significant degradation … was observed in DMF at 35 °C, so NMP was selected.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: During Boc deprotection of intermediate 16, the aqueous workup generated substantial diketopiperazine impurity 18 and acetamide 20 (from EtOAc hydrolysis), both undesirable for safety and purity.
Solution_Description: The deprotection was changed to a direct 4 N HCl in 1,4‑dioxane addition, avoiding any aqueous workup and completely suppressing formation of 18 and 20.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original Boc deprotection procedure … used methanesulfonic acid in THF … significant quantities of diketopiperazine 18 formed under all of the conditions studied.”; “The original medicinal‑chemistry Boc removal procedure directly precipitated the hydrochloride salt of 17 using 6 N HCl in dioxane, and diketopiperazine 18 was not observed as a major process impurity.”; “We reverted back to this direct‑drop process to avoid the aqueous workup.”; “When the EtOAc was not fully removed … it inhibited the precipitation of 17·HCl and afforded a sticky product containing acetamide 20 … poorly rejected … leading to contamination of the final product 1.”; “The use of CH₂Cl₂ and MTBE for the aqueous workup eliminated the formation of acetamide 20.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The chloro‑oxime 7 is thermally unstable above 120 °C and the addition of solid NCS generated a large, uncontrolled exotherm, posing safety risks at pilot‑plant scale.
Solution_Description: Instead of isolating 7, a safe in‑situ generation was performed by adding bleach to a solution of oxime 14 and olefin 11, immediately forming the cycloadduct 15; the process avoided high‑temperature isolation and controlled the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) showed that the solid was thermally unstable above 120 °C. As a result, we decided that it was safer not to isolate the solid but to telescope a solution of chloro‑oxime 7 in DMF directly into the 3 + 2 cycloaddition.”; “Initial attempts … adding NCS … led to a strong and rapid exotherm once the mixture was heated again above 35 °C.”; “We added a catalytic amount of concentrated HCl … the reaction went to >95 % conversion within 5 min … and the exotherm was readily controlled.”; “The final pilot‑plant route used bleach in the presence of olefin 11 so that the chloro‑oxime would react immediately to form cycloadduct 15.”; “Heat flow measurements showed a readily controlled exotherm during the addition of bleach … and no significant exotherm during the rest of the reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The concentration of active bleach in commercial solutions varied, leading to inconsistent conversions in the in‑situ chloro‑oxime generation.
Solution_Description: A stoichiometric excess of NaOCl (2.0 equiv) was deliberately used to ensure complete conversion despite variability in bleach concentration.
Supporting_Evidence: “Studies indicated that 1.5 equiv of NaOCl could be used to complete the reaction, but because of the variability of the concentration in aqueous bleach solutions, typically 2.0 equiv of NaOCl was used to be certain that enough base was present to convert the chloro‑oxime to the reactive dipolar nitrile oxide.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: Residual TEMPO (≈300 ppm) remained in the crude oxidation product 1, exceeding acceptable limits due to its genotoxicity.
Solution_Description: Intermediate 24 was isolated as a solid before the final oxidation, allowing a precipitation step that removed >99.5 % of TEMPO and reduced its level in the final drug substance to <50 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude product contained approximately 5000 ppm TEMPO, which was unacceptably high … A study was carried out … an MTBE/heptane solvent mixture precipitated 1 out of solution containing 300 ppm of residual TEMPO … the material obtained was a noncrystalline sticky solid …”; “When 24 was isolated, the TEMPO level in 1·HOAc was consistently <50 ppm.”; “The EDCI/HOBt process was used in the pilot plant because insufficient time was available to ensure that the CDMT process would perform acceptably on a kilogram scale … The EDCI/HOBt procedure afforded isolated solid hydroxyamide 24 in 99.7 % AUC purity with less than 0.04 % ureas 26 and 27.”; “The isolated solid 24 removed the TEMPO impurity before the oxidation step.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The final HCl salt 17·HCl retained 8–12 % residual 1,4‑dioxane, making the product hygroscopic and promoting formation of diketopiperazine 18 and amino‑acid impurity 21 over storage.
Solution_Description: Storage under nitrogen at 5 °C was mandated and the product was used within a week; attempts to slurry the solid in t‑BuOH, EtOAc, or THF reduced dioxane content but caused mass loss, so the operational schedule was adjusted rather than further solvent‑exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: “The product 17·HCl contained 8–12 % residual 1,4‑dioxane, which increased the solid’s hygroscopicity, thereby promoting the formation of diketopiperazine 18 and amino acid 21.”; “Samples of 17·HCl could be stored for up to a month at 5 °C under a blanket of nitrogen to prevent formation of the impurities.”; “Attempts were made to remove the residual 1,4‑dioxane by slurrying 17·HCl in various solvents … but in each case at least 15 % of the mass was lost … the best course of action was to plan the pilot‑plant processing schedule … used within a week of isolation.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: The original 3 + 2 cycloaddition in the kilo‑lab required 18 h, limiting throughput for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to MTBE (or CH₂Cl₂) allowed the cycloaddition to be telescoped directly from the in‑situ generated chloro‑oxime, reducing the reaction time to 8 h (CH₂Cl₂) or 18 h (MTBE) while simplifying the workflow.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the pilot‑plant campaign, the process to make oxime 14 was further simplified to remove the need to concentrate the mixture to dryness … The mixture was telescoped directly into the cycloaddition.”; “The pilot‑plant campaign showed that the reaction could be run in MTBE (18 h reaction time, 78:22 diastereomer ratio) or CH₂Cl₂ (8 h reaction time, 75:25 diastereomer ratio) at ambient temperature.”; “MTBE was selected as the preferred solvent because the sequence could be telescoped through all of the steps … without needing to swap solvents.”; “The largest batch performed … gave 22.5 kg of 2·HCl in 46 % yield from 11 …”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Process for an HCV Protease Inhibitor Candidate Molecule
Problem_Description: Alternative coupling reagents (T3P, oxalyl chloride, isobutyl chloroformate) were evaluated but gave lower conversions or higher costs, threatening overall process economics.
Solution_Description: After brief screening, the established EDCI/HOBt system was retained for pilot‑plant scale because it offered the best balance of cost, conversion, and impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “2‑Propanephosphonic acid anhydride (T3P), oxalyl chloride, and isobutyl chloroformate were briefly assessed … none was as effective as EDCI/HOBt.”; “The coupling reaction in NMP, DMF, or DMA gave greater than 97 % conversion … DMA was ruled out … the purity of the product in the reaction mixture was only 92 % AUC, compared with 97–98 % AUC for DMF and NMP.”; “Despite the testing, the EDCI/HOBt‑mediated coupling was selected for the pilot plant.”; “The EDCI/HOBt process was used in the pilot plant because insufficient time was available to ensure that the CDMT process would perform acceptably on a kilogram scale and generate no new impurities …”

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: When no rinse step was performed, bulk micron‑sized ibuprofen crystals remained on the surface of the CPG particles, inflating the measured loading far above the theoretical pore capacity.
Solution_Description: A brief rinse with a small amount (2.5 mL) of cold ethanol is applied after imbibition to wash away excess solution on the particle exterior before solvent evaporation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...the highest percentage weight loss ... column: no rinse ... indicates the presence of excess, bulk micron‑sized crystals of IBP present in those samples."

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: Increasing the volume of the ethanol rinse solvent dramatically reduces the amount of ibuprofen that remains loaded in the pores, because the rinse solution diffuses into the pores and extracts the drug.
Solution_Description: Maintain a minimal rinse volume (2.5 mL) to remove surface liquid while preserving the drug retained inside the pores.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The loading of IBP within CPG decreases dramatically with increasing volume of solvent used to rinse the exterior of the CPG particles. The loading halves when going from 2.5 to 5 mL..."

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: Applying heat (35 °C) to the column during solvent removal caused the formation of a solid cake that stuck to the column walls and produced non‑uniform loading and bulk surface crystals.
Solution_Description: The heating jacket is omitted; the drying step is performed at ambient temperature with controlled air flow, eliminating the exotherm and preventing cake formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "In early experiments we applied heat (35 °C) to the column ... generated a distinct cake of IBP and CPG ... the caked phase also contained the presence of a bulk IBP melting peak... Use of the heated jacket was avoided in subsequent experiments."

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: Bench‑top imbibition‑evaporation experiments required ~15 h of drying time to completely remove solvent, severely limiting throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A column equipped with pressure‑driven air flow and vacuum rapidly removes solvent; air is introduced at <2 SCFH for 10 min, then increased to 4 SCFH for 50 min, achieving full drying in ~1 h.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Pressurized air at the fumehood was then opened, sending air upwards into the column regulated at <2 SCFH for the first 10 min. Thereafter the air flow was increased to 4 SCFH for the next 50 min to fully evaporate the solvent and crystallize IBP within the pores... total dry time of 1 h."

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: There was concern that the 20 min imbibition time might be insufficient for more viscous solutions to fully wet the nanopores, potentially leading to lower and inconsistent loadings.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A short vacuum pull (2 min) before solution introduction and a 20 min residence time are employed to enhance capillary wetting and ensure complete pore filling regardless of solvent viscosity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Vacuum was pulled on the column for 2 min before pumping in the solution to encourage wetting of the pores... The solution was initially allowed to wet the CPG material in the column and then pumped out again... an extra 20 min of imbibition time was allowed to ensure that the solution had fully imbibed the pores."

Paper Title: A Process for the Formation of Nanocrystals of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients with Poor Aqueous Solubility in a Nanoporous Substrate
Problem_Description: Higher ibuprofen loading was limited when low‑viscosity carrier solvents were used, as the solution was not retained well in the pores during drying.
Solution_Description: More viscous carriers (i‑PrOH, n‑BuOH) are selected; their higher viscosity improves solution retention in the pores, leading to higher % w/w loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: • "An increase in the % (w/w) loading of nanocrystalline IBP within CPG was achieved with increasing solution concentration used to load CPG during the process and also with increasing viscosity of the carrier solution."

Paper Title: Concise Preparation of a Stable Cyclic Sulfamidate Intermediate in the Synthesis of a Enantiopure Chiral Active Diamine Derivative
Problem_Description: The 10‑step discovery route relied on (L)-N‑Boc‑pipecolic acid, a raw material that is expensive and not readily available in metric‑ton quantities.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to start from cheap, readily available 2‑benzoyl‑pyridine, eliminating the need for the costly Boc‑pipecolic acid.
Supporting_Evidence: “Availability and price of the (L)-N‑Boc pipecolic raw material at metric ton scale;” “The intent was to prepare the amino alcohol from a cheap and available raw material, and so the study was focused on 2‑benzoyl‑pyridine 15….”

Problem_Description: Attempted synthesis of the sulfamidate directly from the amino‑alcohol using sulfuryl chloride gave low yield and produced numerous degradation products.

Paper Title: Concise Preparation of a Stable Cyclic Sulfamidate Intermediate in the Synthesis of a Enantiopure Chiral Active Diamine Derivative
Problem_Description: The thionyl‑chloride/triethylamine method for making sulfamidite 22 was irreproducible, yielding a tarry, purple oil that was difficult to purify.

Supporting_Evidence: “When pyridine/DMAP was used, the product could be isolated as a white solid with a good yield (90 %) and a very good purity (95 %).” “When pyridine alone was used, the product was isolated as a brownish solid… with the concomitant presence of tar.”

Problem_Description: The oxidation of sulfamidite 22 with RuCl₃/NaIO₄ generated ruthenium tetroxide, which darkened the organic phase and posed safety and waste‑handling concerns.

After filtration, a clear and colorless organic phase was obtained with less than 10 ppm of residual ruthenium.”

Problem_Description: Final palladium‑catalyzed deprotection in the discovery route left up to 100 ppm palladium in the API, requiring multiple crystallisations to meet purity specifications.

Paper Title: Intensified Co-Oligomerization of Propylene Oxide and Carbon Dioxide in a Continuous Heat Exchanger Loop Reactor at Elevated Pressures
Problem_Description: The PO/CO₂ oligomerization is highly exothermic. Combined with the high CO₂ pressure, the PO feed had to be limited to keep the reaction stable, which forced long batch times and gave very low space‑time yields (< 0.1 kg·L⁻¹·h⁻¹) in the laboratory semibatch reactors.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a 0.4 L shell‑and‑tube heat‑exchanger loop reactor equipped with static CSE‑XR mixers. The loop provides very high surface‑to‑volume heat‑transfer and intense mixing, enabling isothermal control of the exotherm and allowing much higher PO feed rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “its highly exothermic character in combination with significant CO₂ pressures PO feed rates had to be limited … long batch times and typical space‑time‑yields of less than 0.1 kg·L⁻¹·h⁻¹ resulted from this kind of semibatch approach.”; “A continuous heat‑exchanger loop reactor … is the flow setup of choice for this novel process… exothermic statistical oligomerization was performed in bulk while CO₂ pressures up to 100 bar were applied.”; “the combination of flow reactor and heat exchanger enables outstanding performances in isothermal reaction control while homogenizing the bulk reaction mixtures.”

Paper Title: Intensified Co-Oligomerization of Propylene Oxide and Carbon Dioxide in a Continuous Heat Exchanger Loop Reactor at Elevated Pressures
Problem_Description: Cyclic propylene carbonate (3) is formed as a side product; it consumes PO and CO₂, reduces the amount of valuable polyol, and is a high‑boiling compound (TB = 242 °C) that makes downstream thin‑film evaporation difficult.
Solution_Description: After reaction, the crude mixture is degassed and then fed to a thin‑film evaporator (TFE) operated at 120 °C and 0.1 mbar to strip off cyclic carbonate 3, facilitating isolation of the polyol.
Supporting_Evidence: “A general drawback of this process is the formation of cyclic propylene carbonate (3) as side product… valuable PO (and CO₂) … are lost… Moreover, typical workup by thin film evaporator (TFE) gets more challenging with (increasing amounts of) high‑boiling 3 (TB = 242 °C).”; “After proper degassing of the obtained reaction mixture a TFE unit was used to remove the side product 3 at 120 °C and 0.1 mbar.”

Paper Title: Intensified Co-Oligomerization of Propylene Oxide and Carbon Dioxide in a Continuous Heat Exchanger Loop Reactor at Elevated Pressures
Problem_Description: When the total pressure fell below ≈ 67 bar, the reaction mixture became biphasic with vigorous gas evolution, which could threaten uniform contact of PO, CO₂, catalyst and polymer chains.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Operating the loop at pressures ≥ 76 bar (monophasic region) together with high recycle ratios (ν = 20–80) and static mixers maintains a bubble‑free, quasi‑homogeneous phase and provides strong internal mixing, preventing phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Starting from 100 bar, p was reduced stepwise revealing a bubble‑free, slightly hazy … down to 67 bar. By further reducing … a stable biphasic reaction mixture existed (p < 67 bar).”; “The influence of flow and mixing in terms of the recycle ratio … intense (internal) flow results in reduced c/l.”

Paper Title: Intensified Co-Oligomerization of Propylene Oxide and Carbon Dioxide in a Continuous Heat Exchanger Loop Reactor at Elevated Pressures
Problem_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature to increase carbonate incorporation and suppress the cyclic carbonate (3) causes a sharp drop in PO conversion (down to 68.9 % at 105 °C) and higher molecular‑weight distribution (MWD up to 1.64), making the process unattractive.
Solution_Description: An optimal temperature of 130 °C was identified, balancing high PO conversion (> 99 %) with acceptable carbonate incorporation and narrow MWD (≈ 1.1), while still limiting side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In an attempt to further increase the carbonate content … the temperature was reduced … PO conversion dropped from 99.9 % at 130 °C to 68.9 % at 105 °C … and relative high MWD up to 1.64 render operation conditions … unattractive.”; “Very narrow and monomodal MWDs from 1.08 to 1.15 were obtained as a benefit of the relatively high reaction temperature of 130 °C.”

Paper Title: Intensified Co-Oligomerization of Propylene Oxide and Carbon Dioxide in a Continuous Heat Exchanger Loop Reactor at Elevated Pressures
Problem_Description: The DMC catalyst requires a conditioning step (batch activation) before it becomes active; performing this step separately complicates continuous operation and can lead to inconsistent activity.
Solution_Description: The catalyst conditioning sequence was incorporated directly into the flow loop (in‑situ activation), ensuring the catalyst reaches its active state just before the PO/CO₂ feed enters the reactor, thus maintaining consistent activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “the initial catalyst conditioning sequence, which is performed (in batch) to transform complex DMC‑type catalysts into an active working mode had to be integrated into the flow synthesis itself… the essential catalyst conditioning sequence is performed in situ.”

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: LiAlH4, historically used for lactam reduction, is flammable, explosive and causes undesirable side‑reactions, making it difficult to handle on plant scale.
Solution_Description: Adopt NaBH₄ in combination with TFA as the reducing system, which is easier to handle and scalable.
Supporting_Evidence: LiAlH₄ is difficult to handle in plant‑scale manufacturing because it is flammable and explosive and causes undesirable side reactions (p. 2). The combination of NaBH₄ and additives is equivalent to LiAlH₄ in reducing power and is easy to handle in a manufacturing plant (p. 2).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: BH₃·THF provides good reduction but is a high‑cost reagent and poses a storage hazard due to its explosion risk.
Solution_Description: Replace BH₃·THF with the NaBH₄/TFA system, which is less expensive and safer to store.
Supporting_Evidence: BH₃·THF is difficult to handle as a storage hazard due to the risk of explosion (p. 2). NaBH₄ combined with TFA was used because it is easier to handle than either LiAlH₄ or BH₃·THF (p. 2).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: The lactam reduction with NaBH₄/TFA is highly exothermic, releasing large amounts of heat and gas, which creates safety concerns on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Add TFA slowly (1 h‑2 h dropwise) to a suspension of NaBH₄ and substrate in THF, keeping the reaction temperature below 10 °C during addition, then hold at 20 °C. This controls the heat release and limits gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction is highly exothermic, and evaluation of the safety during addition of TFA therefore means evaluating the safety of the reduction process (p. 5). TFA (3.5 equiv) was added to a mixture of 1 (0.35 M) and NaBH₄ over 60 min at 15 °C; the adiabatic temperature rise was estimated at 93 K (p. 5). The heat output ratio was in good agreement with the TFA addition ratio (p. 5).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: Direct addition of solid NaBH₄ to the reactor is unsafe, especially on large scale.
Solution_Description: Prepare a solution of NaBH₄ in THF beforehand and add TFA to this solution (semibatch), avoiding the handling of solid NaBH₄.
Supporting_Evidence: Solid NaBH₄ addition was an unsafe operation (p. 4). The semibatch approach by addition of TFA avoided the need to add solid NaBH₄ (p. 4).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: When NaBH₄ and TFA are mixed before the substrate, the reaction does not go to completion, giving low conversion and variable yields.
Solution_Description: Add TFA to the reaction mixture *after* the substrate is present, ensuring that the most reactive mono‑trifluoroacetoxyborohydride species is generated in situ and can reduce the lactam efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: The lactam reduction reaction was not completed when NaBH₄ and TFA were mixed before 1 was added (p. 4). Adding TFA avoids the deactivation of the active species involved in the reduction process (p. 5).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: The reduction generates diborane (B₂H₆) together with hydrogen; diborane is toxic and must be eliminated before venting.
Solution_Description: Install a double‑scrubber system using 15 % aqueous NaOH to convert diborane to boric acid, and dilute the off‑gas with steam before release; a reducer pipe controls the TFA addition rate to limit gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: Diborane gas was released; it must be decomposed to boric acid before purging because of its toxicity (p. 7). A double scrubber system with 15 % NaOH reduced diborane to below detection (p. 7). Gas was diluted with steam to avoid static ignition (p. 7).

Paper Title: Process Safety Evaluation and Scale-up of a Lactam Reduction with NaBH
Problem_Description: On pilot‑plant scale, uncontrolled heat release could lead to runaway conditions.
Solution_Description: Use a pilot‑scale reactor equipped with a reducer pipe for precise TFA addition, temperature monitoring, and heat‑removal capability; maintain the internal temperature below 10 °C during addition and keep the process within the measured maximum temperature of synthesis (34 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: The addition of TFA was controlled in the pilot plant using a reducer pipe (p. 7). The plant temperature profile data revealed that the conditions employed were successful in maintaining the process temperature within the desired range (p. 7).

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: During early chemistry development, many solvents gave poor conversion because the starting material, intermediate and product were not fully dissolved; only low‑molecular‑weight alcohols solubilised all reaction components.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified methanol as the optimal reaction medium; methanol fully dissolved all reactants and gave the lowest level of over‑reduced impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “During early chemistry development, adequate conversion to product was found only when low‑molecular‑weight alcohols were used as the solvent, and these also fully solubilised all of the reaction components, excluding the catalyst.”; “The level of over‑reduced impurity for a given conversion was found to be lowest using methanol, so this was selected as the solvent for the reaction.”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: The reaction end‑point varied from batch to batch; off‑line HPLC sampling was required and a fixed reaction time could not be used for commercial scale.
Solution_Description: In‑situ mid‑infrared (MIR) spectroscopy coupled with a MATLAB curve‑fitting algorithm was implemented to monitor the intermediate in real time and trigger sampling at a defined reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “During a previous API manufacturing campaign, frequent samples for off‑line HPLC analysis were required… the variable reaction end point also meant that a fixed reaction time approach was not suitable.”; “The optimisation of the process and development of in situ MIR spectrometry as a control based on the consumption of the intermediate will be discussed.”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Using a dry Pd/C catalyst led to large batch‑to‑batch variations in activity, causing inconsistent reaction times and potential safety concerns when stopping the reaction.
Solution_Description: A high‑throughput screen identified wet‑compatible catalysts (Evonik E4 and Johnson Matthey 424) that gave consistent activity without the need for drying.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that the catalyst drying process caused significant variation in the catalyst activity between batches, and therefore, the time period for stopping the reaction… also varied significantly.”; “Evonik E4 and Johnson Matthey 424 catalysts were selected for further development.”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Over‑reduction of the aromatic ring formed an impurity that needed to be kept below spec; the amount of this impurity changed with temperature and catalyst loading.
Solution_Description: A full‑factorial DoE identified that low catalyst loading (4 % w/w) and low temperature (30 °C) minimized the over‑reduced impurity while maintaining acceptable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reduction of the aromatic ring system can also occur, leading to an over‑reduced impurity.”; “From the DoE study it was found that the experiments with low catalyst loading and high temperature gave the lowest levels of over‑reduced impurity… Conversely, the highest levels of over‑reduced impurity… were found with low catalyst loading and low temperature… We therefore chose to proceed with a system using both a low catalyst loading (4% w/w) and a low temperature (30 °C).”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: At low impeller speeds the uptake of H₂ on the Pd/C surface slowed, making the formation of the intermediate mass‑transfer limited and extending the reaction time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Higher agitation rates (up to 800 rpm) were employed during scale‑up to ensure rapid H₂ dissolution and consistent intermediate formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “At lower impeller speeds, the H₂ is absorbed onto the catalyst surface much more slowly, resulting in slower conversion of the starting material to the intermediate; however, the conversion of the intermediate to the product did not appear to be mass‑transfer‑limited.”; “When the correct temperature was attained, the vessel was purged with H₂ at 2 bar, and the agitation rate was increased to ensure efficient mixing (rpm dependent on scale).”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Crystallization from alcohol/antisolvent mixtures produced non‑crystalline or unstable polymorphs, compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: A solvent‑exchange to dry THF via constant‑volume distillation was introduced, and seeding was performed at 8 % w/w methanol (within the metastable zone) to obtain a stable crystalline form.
Supporting_Evidence: “All of the investigated crystallization systems that incorporated an alcohol solvent resulted in the isolation of noncrystalline or unstable polymorphs of the product.”; “A stable, crystalline form of the product could be isolated from THF as long as the methanol and water contents were kept below 0.3 and 0.1% w/w, respectively… The seed point was chosen at the centre of the metastable zone, with 8% w/w methanol remaining.”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Long fibre‑optic runs for MIR were previously avoided because attenuation could lead to loss of signal and unreliable monitoring of an exothermic hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: A 4 m fibre‑optic conduit was successfully used with the iC15 spectrometer, enabling direct probe insertion into the reaction vessel and reliable in‑situ monitoring at 1 L and 20 L scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Until recently, longer fibre optic cables for MIR spectrometry had been avoided because of poor attenuation of MIR light over long distances; however, recent advances in fibre technology have allowed longer fibers to be used without significant signal loss.”; “The utilisation of longer fibers allows for direct insertion into reaction vessels, which means that processes where recirculation is not feasible… are now becoming accessible.”

Paper Title: Using PAT To Understand, Control, and Rapidly Scale Up the Production of a Hydrogenation Reaction and Isolation of Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Determining the exact methanol concentration during constant‑volume distillation was difficult using off‑line methods, hampering controlled seeding.
Solution_Description: A partial‑least‑squares (PLS) regression model based on in‑situ NIR spectra was developed to predict methanol content in real time and trigger seeding.
Supporting_Evidence: “A feasibility study was carried out at a 1 L scale to ascertain whether NIR spectrometry could be used to monitor the removal of methanol during the CVD… the model was successful in determining the solvent concentration at the seeding point.”; “During 20 L scale batches 2 and 3, the process was successfully seeded solely on the basis of NIR feedback, with retrospective confirmation by off‑line NMR analysis.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Biocatalytic Oxidations Applying Alcohol Dehydrogenases
Problem_Description: High cost of the pyridine cofactors (NAD⁺/NADP⁺) makes their stoichiometric use uneconomical for preparative oxidations.
Solution_Description: Couple the alcohol dehydrogenase with an engineered NAD(P)H oxidase that regenerates the cofactor in situ, providing a catalytic (rather than stoichiometric) route.
Supporting_Evidence: - "Because of the high costs of these pyridine cofactors, in situ cofactor regeneration is required for preparative applications…" (Abstract)

Paper Title: Process Development for Biocatalytic Oxidations Applying Alcohol Dehydrogenases
Problem_Description: Insufficient dissolved oxygen limits the rate of cofactor regeneration, giving low conversion (≈ 15 U mL⁻¹ at 700 rpm) and poor overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Raise stirring speed to create vortex‑driven bubbles and/or feed pressurised air through a tube; this improves oxygen transfer (k_La) and boosts the initial volumetric activity up to ≈ 195 U mL⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: - "For a stirring rate of 700 rpm, an initial volumetric activity of just 14.7 U/mL was reached, compared to 47.9 U/mL for 1600 rpm and even 246.3 U/mL for the highest applied stirring rate of 3000 rpm…" (Sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Process Development for Biocatalytic Oxidations Applying Alcohol Dehydrogenases
Problem_Description: At the highest stirring rate (3000 rpm) intense foam formation over‑flows the reactor within the first minute.
Solution_Description: Add 5–10 µL of an inert antifoaming agent to destabilise the gas‑liquid interface and suppress foam, allowing safe high‑speed agitation.
Supporting_Evidence: - "Without the addition of antifoaming agent, the liquid surface was immediately covered with foam bubbles, and the reactor was overflowed by foam already within the first minute…" (Sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Process Development for Biocatalytic Oxidations Applying Alcohol Dehydrogenases
Problem_Description: Higher reaction temperatures can accelerate enzyme denaturation, potentially reducing catalytic turnover.
Solution_Description: Run the reaction at 28 °C–35 °C where the enzymes retain activity for the required time while still benefiting from the Q₁₀ increase in rate; avoid temperatures that cause rapid loss of activity.
Supporting_Evidence: - "With higher temperature the activity of an enzyme increases … simultaneously, the enzyme stability usually decreases with rising temperature…" (Sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Process Development for Biocatalytic Oxidations Applying Alcohol Dehydrogenases
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction to 1 L without external aeration lengthens the conversion time from ~2.5 h to ~28 h, drastically lowering productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Use a gassed stirred‑tank reactor (fixed‑tube bubble aeration) with a controlled air flow of 4 L min⁻¹; the increased k_La compensates for the reduced surface‑to‑volume ratio and restores a fast reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: - "The reaction with additional air supply proceeds much faster… full conversion of the (R)-enantiomer was already reached after 2.5 h; … without air inlet it took around 28 h…" (Sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) showed that the second step (conversion of dibromide 2 to bromodiene 3) is highly energetic – dibromide 2 has an onset temperature of 145 °C (360 J g⁻¹) and bromodiene 3 an onset of 226 °C (500 J g⁻¹). The operating temperature (150 °C) left < 100 °C safety margin, violating the lab’s safety practice.
Solution_Description: Dibromide 2 was isolated and the second step was run separately in a continuous‑flow reactor (Hastelloy tubing). The exotherm was tamed by slow (4 h) addition of bromoform to a slurry of olefin 1/t‑BuOK at –9 → 0 °C, and the reaction mixture passed through a heated flow tube (150 °C, 12.5 min residence). This platform removed the hazardous batch exotherm and allowed safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: The DSC analysis revealed that the second part of the reaction is highly energetic. The dibromide 2 has an on‑set temperature of 145 °C with energy of 360 J g⁻¹. The bromodiene 3 has an on‑set temperature of 226 °C with energy 500 J g⁻¹…These results…were deemed unsafe for standard batch operations.; Based on these observations, we decided to isolate dibromide 2 and perform the second part…as a separate stage.; the exotherm was controlled by the slow addition of bromoform (over 4 h)…; Therefore, we employed a continuous flow reactor (CFR)…Processing was complete in 3.5 h…effectively addressed our safety concerns and minimized the reaction time for this step.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: The original carbene‑addition to olefin 1 used large excesses of heptane (≈10 vol), N,N‑dimethylaniline (≈3 vol) and olefin (2.0 equiv), inflating solvent and reagent costs at scale.
Solution_Description: The volumes were reduced to 3 vol heptane, 1.5 vol N,N‑dimethylaniline and olefin equiv lowered from 2.0 to 1.5 (later to 10 mol % excess). This cut material consumption and improved the cost profile without sacrificing conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: The level of heptanes was decreased to 3 volumes; The volume of N,N‑dimethylaniline was decreased to 1.5 volumes relative to bromoform; The amount of olefin was decreased from 2.0 to 1.5 equiv.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: Potassium bromide generated in the carbene‑addition could not be removed by filtration even with filtration aids, leading to a solid residue that complicated work‑up.
Solution_Description: The salts were removed by an aqueous wash performed under buffered conditions to neutralize excess t‑BuOK and avoid product discoloration.
Supporting_Evidence: An attempt to remove the side product, potassium bromide, by filtration was unsuccessful even when filtration aids were employed. Hence, the salts were removed by aqueous wash.; Dibromide 2 was found to be sensitive to water at a high pH. Thus, aqueous workup conditions which properly buffer against t‑BuOK are important to prevent discoloration and preserve yield.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: Dibromide 2 hydrolyzes under basic aqueous conditions (high pH), causing discoloration and loss of material during work‑up.
Solution_Description: A buffered aqueous quench (using saturated NaHCO₃/sodium bicarbonate) was employed to keep the pH low, protecting dibromide 2 from base‑catalyzed decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: Dibromide 2 was found to be sensitive to water at a high pH. Thus, aqueous workup conditions which properly buffer against t‑BuOK are important to prevent discoloration and preserve yield.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: At a reduced temperature (100 °C) the conversion of dibromide 2 to bromodiene 3 required 30 h, which was unacceptable for a production route.
Solution_Description: Screening showed that 10 min at 150 °C gave quantitative conversion. Implementing the step in a continuous flow reactor allowed safe, rapid (10 min residence) processing on kilogram scale, cutting the overall step time from days to hours.
Supporting_Evidence: The conversion of 2 to 3 at a lower temperature (100 °C) took 30 h to reach completion.; A screening of reaction time (10, 20, 40 min)… showed that efficient conversion…can be achieved in 10 min at 150 °C…Therefore, we employed a continuous flow reactor (CFR)…Processing was complete in 3.5 h…effectively addressed our safety concerns and minimized the reaction time for this step.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: When performed in diethyl ether, the copper‑mediated addition to give compound 7 gave only ~50 % yield unless freshly prepared CuBr·DMS was used; the reaction was also sluggish (≈2 h).
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent from diethyl ether to THF accelerated the reaction (complete in 2 h) and permitted the use of commercially available CuBr·DMS (which previously failed), raising the isolated yield to 85 %.
Supporting_Evidence: Preparation of 7… proceeded with 50 % yield only if freshly prepared CuBr·DMS complex was used.; Thus, when diethyl ether was replaced by THF, the reaction was complete in 2 h. Moreover, running the reaction in THF made it possible to use commercially available CuBr·DMS complex, which had failed earlier in our studies.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of (‑)-9 using literature conditions failed; brief exposure of the highly acidic reaction mixture to atmospheric moisture during quench was suspected to cause irreproducibility.
Solution_Description: A reverse quench (adding the acidic quench to the reaction mixture rather than the opposite) was introduced, maintaining an acidic environment and preventing moisture ingress; this gave a consistent quantitative yield on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: Although successful on small scale, the literature conditions failed upon attempted scale‑up…It was speculated…brief exposure…to atmospheric moisture during the quench. Implementation of a reverse quench allowed the reaction to be scaled up with a consistently quantitative yield.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: The crude Diels–Alder product (+)-13, after silica‑plug purification, contained co‑eluting impurities that could not be removed by column chromatography and would contaminate downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Direct crystallization of (+)-13 from heptanes was developed, providing a high‑purity solid and eliminating the problematic impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: The crude material after silica plug purification was contaminated with several coeluting impurities, which would not purge in the next step…we found that the desired product (+)-13 can successfully be crystallized from heptanes.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: The overall isolated yield of (+)-13 after the Diels–Alder step was low (22 %), jeopardizing material throughput.
Solution_Description: Crystallization from heptanes not only removed impurities but also boosted the isolated yield and provided material of sufficient quality for the final steps.
Supporting_Evidence: The material was crystallized from heptanes to afford (+)-13 (4.3 g, 22 % yield) as a white solid…This crystallization step was essential to obtain taxadienone (+)-16 in high quality.

Paper Title: Route Optimization and Synthesis of Taxadienone
Problem_Description: The Negishi coupling of triflate 15 with dimethylzinc was moisture‑sensitive; residual water would deactivate the Pd catalyst and lower yield.
Solution_Description: Azeotropic drying of the triflate intermediate by co‑distillation with fresh THF was performed before the coupling to assure anhydrous conditions, enabling the reaction to proceed with 82 % isolated yield after crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: Azeotropic drying by distillation while adding fresh THF was done to ensure moisture would not interfere with the next step. The Negishi reaction…afforded the product (+)-16 in 82 % yield after crystallization from methanol.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: The original preparation of the amide (1) used a lengthy linear sequence with multiple solvent systems, could not isolate the final amide in a usable form and gave a modest overall yield of only ~23 %.
Solution_Description: A more convergent synthetic route was designed that eliminated multiple catalyst charges and solvents, simplifying the sequence and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: The original preparation … suffered from a relatively lengthy linear sequence of reactions, multiple solvent systems, … modest overall yields (∼23%).; Initial efforts focused on a more convergent process, eliminating multiple catalyst charges, solvents, and unnecessary protection schemes.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: The earlier nitro reduction required multiple catalyst charging steps, increasing safety hazards and cost.
Solution_Description: The nitro group was reduced using an iron–acetic acid system, removing the need for additional catalysts and improving processing safety.
Supporting_Evidence: Reduction of crude nitrobenzene (12) to aniline (13) was achieved under Fe–HOAc conditions. This resolved the issue of multiple catalyst charging, thus significantly improving processing safety.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the hydrolysis/decaboxylation of ester 20 to acid 10 in 2‑MeTHF under strongly basic conditions caused amide hydrolysis because the acid became overly soluble, leading to decomposition.
Solution_Description: A base/solvent screen identified potassium carbonate as an acceptable base and ethanol (or MeOH/THF) as a suitable solvent, eliminating decomposition and giving >99 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Significant amide hydrolysis occurred … due to the increased solubility of acid (10) in 2‑MeTHF exposed to strongly basic conditions.; Once K₂CO₃ had been determined to be an acceptable base …; Ethanol avoided the formation of mixed esters and allowed for easy isolation by distillation of the solvent.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: When esterification was carried out with EDCI, a minor impurity (the EDCI adduct 22) formed, compromising purity and requiring additional purification.
Solution_Description: The impurity was controlled by dose‑controlled addition of EDCI·HCl, minimizing temperature excursions and preventing adduct formation.
Supporting_Evidence: … a minor impurity started to develop. This impurity was isolated and characterized as the EDCI adduct (22).; Formation of the impurity was readily managed by dose‑controlled addition of EDCI·HCl … minimizing significant changes in reaction temperatures.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: The final API (1) was exceptionally soluble in all common solvents except heptane and water, making isolation as a solid difficult.
Solution_Description: The product‑rich solution was concentrated to a low volume and precipitated by addition of excess water, yielding an amorphous powder that could be filtered.
Supporting_Evidence: The product (1) had exceptional solubility in all common solvents aside from heptanes and water.; Thus, in order to isolate the API, the product‑rich solutions were concentrated to a low volume and charged to an excess of water.
