The solids were ultimately isolated as an amorphous powder.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: Several steps required hazardous reagents (oxalyl chloride) or elevated temperatures, posing safety risks and lengthening cycle times.
Solution_Description: ReactIR was deployed for online monitoring, reducing worker exposure and allowing rapid determination of reaction endpoints.
Supporting_Evidence: … required the use of hazardous reagents (oxalyl chloride) or elevated temperatures (decarboxylation), ReactIR monitoring was extensively utilized to minimize worker exposure and reduce cycle time during the development and scale‑up.; The ReactIR results correlated with off‑line UPLC analysis results well.

Paper Title: Utilization of ReactIR in Fit for Purpose Process Enablement
Problem_Description: Early LC methods suffered from overlapping peaks, forcing a conservative 18 h reaction time to ensure full conversion of the final coupling step.
Solution_Description: A multivariate ReactIR model tracked reactant disappearance and product formation in real time, showing >75 % conversion after 1 h and >98 % after 6 h, enabling a much shorter, controlled reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: Early LC methods were complicated by overlapping peaks which relegated the team to letting the reaction progress for 18 h to ensure completion.; The ability of ReactIR to simultaneously track these reactants and products in real time … allowed the team to determine that the reaction was ca. 75 % complete within the first hour and >98 % complete within 6 h … thus affording the team greater confidence in scaling.

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: The batch hydrogenolysis generated the defluorination impurity (desF 5) at ~0.04 % area h⁻¹ after the reaction ended, increasing to ~0.1 % h⁻¹ at lower H₂ pressure. This impurity rejected poorly downstream and threatened product specifications.
Solution_Description: Residence time inside the packed‑bed catalyst was reduced to 15–30 min (nominal 4 h batch time → 1 h flow residence) which suppressed the formation of desF 5 to <0.05 % and gave steady‑state conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initially developed batch conditions produced the desF impurity 5 at approximately 0.04 area % per hour of additional reaction time…The target specification was <0.1 % of 5 formed in the reaction…Control of a critical defluorination impurity … has been achieved by reducing residence time inside the catalyst bed to 15–30 min.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Batch runs required 17 h reaction time plus catalyst filtration, with 10 vol n‑propanol / water per substrate and a 630 L autoclave, resulting in only 1 kg product day⁻¹ and a high process‑mass‑intensity (PMI).
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow packed‑bed reactor was implemented. The high catalyst exposure in the packed bed shortens the effective reaction time to minutes, raising throughput to 550 g h⁻¹ (206 kg h⁻¹·m³), a >150‑fold increase over batch.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was successfully scaled up…demonstrating heat/mass transfer sufficiency…The reactor volume throughput of 206 kg h⁻¹·m³ was attained…superior to the 1.3 kg h⁻¹·m³ volume throughput obtained in batch…The pilot‑scale…processed 5 kg of substrate at a rate of 550 g h⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Powdered Pd/C catalysts caused excessive pressure drop and poor gas‑liquid mixing when packed into a flow column, preventing efficient reaction.
Solution_Description: Large‑particle catalysts (granules, beads, extrudates) were selected and ground only to <1 mm to maintain low pressure drop while keeping sufficient surface area; the 5 % Pd/C granules (S4336) gave the best conversion and impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “The powdered catalysts typically used for batch reactions are not suitable…due to high pressure drop…larger particle catalysts…are typically used…The initial screen used 100 wt % catalyst…Catalyst S4336 was the best of those screened.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Catalyst activity declined after ~90 h on‑stream, giving slower conversion in the third reuse experiment despite constant reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: Residence time was increased twice during the long run to compensate for activity loss, maintaining high conversion while the catalyst was still active; later a column‑conditioning step (solvent + H₂ soak) was added for fresh catalyst batches to restore performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “The time‑course reaction profiles showed identical profiles for the first two reactions but slower conversion in the third reaction…Residence time was increased twice during the duration of the run to compensate for catalyst activity over time…The observed difference was resolved by altering the column conditioning procedure…several hours of contact time with n‑PrOH and H₂ to properly condition the column.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Significant adsorption of substrate 2 and intermediate 3 onto the Pd/C surface reduced the apparent liquid residence time and required long solvent pushes to recover bound material during startup/shutdown.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adsorption studies quantified the binding (≈10 % loss after 1 h) and informed the design of a static soak‑then‑flow conditioning step; a fast solvent flush (3–4 L) after packing removed fines and freed adsorbed species before reaction start‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Solutions of the starting material…were stirred with catalyst at 50 °C…the strongest binding was with 3, the solution concentration decreased by about a quarter overnight…It is expected to require several hours of contact time with n‑PrOH and H₂ to properly condition the column…A great deal of fines was seen in the solvent run, although they were flushed out after 3–4 L of solvent, resulting in clear effluent afterwards.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: The starting material 2 showed limited solubility in 1:1 n‑PrOH : water, restricting how concentrated the feed could be and thus limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: A solvent system of 85 % n‑PrOH / 15 % water was selected, giving a maximum solubility of ≈158 mg mL⁻¹ (operated at ≈130 mg mL⁻¹), improving feed concentration without compromising stability.
Supporting_Evidence: “Solubility data…showed maximum solubility in 85:15 n‑PrOH:water…Thus, this solvent system was selected for the flow reaction to maximize throughput with minimized solvent use.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Deacetylation impurity (desAc 6) formed when the substrate solution was exposed to HCl in the feed, especially during long‑term storage, reducing product purity.
Solution_Description: Two separate feed streams (neutral substrate solution and aqueous HCl) were combined only at the reactor inlet, preventing acid‑induced deacetylation before the catalytic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “It is simpler to pump a single feed solution, but the starting material is unstable toward deacetylation in the presence of acid…whereas the neutral starting material solution in 85:15 n‑PrOH:water is stable for at least 10 months.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: The batch process required handling large volumes of pressurised hydrogen and palladium catalyst, raising safety concerns for hydrogen inventory and catalyst exposure.
Solution_Description: Continuous packed‑bed operation dramatically reduced the amount of hydrogen present at any instant and eliminated catalyst filtration steps, improving overall process safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “The continuous process…provides reduced handling of hydrogen and of palladium catalyst relative to equivalent substrate throughputs in a typical batch process…Safety was improved due to lower levels of H₂ present within the system at any given time and higher turnover numbers.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Corrosion of stainless‑steel components by the HCl/HF environment generated by the reaction threatened equipment integrity.
Solution_Description: All wetted reactor parts were fabricated from Hastelloy C‑22 (or C‑276) which exhibits excellent resistance to concentrated HCl and low fluoride levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “A corrosion study…found it highly corrosive to stainless steel but not to Hastelloy C‑276…The reaction has been run in the more robust Hastelloy C‑22…which was shown to have lower corrosion rate in concentrated HCl.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Fresh catalyst contained a large proportion of fine particles that caused channeling and pressure fluctuations during flow.
Solution_Description: A filtration pack (Whatman filter paper, Teflon sieve, glass wool) was installed to retain fines, and a solvent flush removed residual particles before reaction start‑up; a DARCO filtration pad was proposed for future runs.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reactor was most efficiently packed using Whatman filter paper…Two pieces of filter paper were placed…Even so, a great deal of fines was seen in the solvent run, although they were flushed out after 3–4 L of solvent…For future runs, the use of a layer of DARCO catalyst filtration material…is recommended.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: The hydrogenolysis is highly exothermic (total ΔH ≈ 407 kJ mol⁻¹). In large‑scale flow the adiabatic temperature rise (≈ 37 °C) could generate hot spots and cold spots, risking catalyst degradation and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Steam heating with a copper‑tube jacket and temperature‑controlled steam flow was used; a thermal well provided axial temperature monitoring, allowing real‑time adjustment of steam flow to keep the reactor within the desired 100 °C window.
Supporting_Evidence: “The total heat of reaction was calculated as 406.8 kJ mol⁻¹…For a flow reactor, without preheating…this exotherm could result in a cold spot…and a hot spot…During the pilot‑scale run…temperature was controlled by a saturated steam heating system…Figure 9 shows the temperature profiles…adjusted to return to desired operating conditions.”

Paper Title: Development of Pilot-Scale Continuous Production of an LY2886721 Starting Material by Packed-Bed Hydrogenolysis
Problem_Description: Multiphase, trickle‑bed flow caused difficulty in defining a single residence time; liquid and gas phases travelled at different velocities, and adsorption altered effective residence for different species.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Online HPLC (Waters PATrol) with fast dilution and an internally built automation cart provided real‑time concentration data; a marker compound (1 % isopropanol) was used to calibrate nominal residence times, and push‑out samples were taken to verify actual component residence.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was monitored by online HPLC…providing real‑time reaction information…Fast dilution, precise sample preparation, and minimum carryover…were required for successful online analysis…During most reaction shutdowns, a set of samples were taken from the solvent pushout to determine the actual component residence times.”

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: The aqueous reaction system suffers from low substrate solubility, requiring an extractive work‑up that denatures the enzyme and often creates an emulsion, complicating product isolation.
Solution_Description: Covalent immobilisation of ketoreductase P1B2 on the EC‑HFA resin enables the reaction to be run in a 50/40/10 hexanes/IPA/water organic‑solvent mixture; the product is isolated by a simple filtration, eliminating the extractive work‑up and preserving enzyme activity for reuse.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A drawback of the aqueous reaction system, which is common to many aqueous enzymatic reaction systems, is the need for an extractive reaction workup to isolate the product away from the enzyme catalyst. The extractive workup results in denatured enzyme that cannot be reused and that has the possibility to generate an emulsion layer that can complicate the product isolation."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: The free (lyophilised) ketoreductase loses activity rapidly in high‑percentage organic solvent; it tolerates only up to ~60 % IPA, and the reaction fails completely in 90 % IPA.
Solution_Description: Covalent attachment of the enzyme to the EC‑HFA polymer resin stabilises it, allowing operation in 90 % IPA (with 10 % water) while maintaining >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • "While the soluble lyophilized KRED P1B2 can tolerate up to 60% IPA cosolvent, the enzyme stability drops dramatically with increasing levels of organic solvent, and the reaction fails in 90% IPA."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: Initial immobilisation protocol required a 48 h incubation at 5 °C, leading to a slow development cycle.
Solution_Description: Raising the immobilisation temperature to ambient (room) temperature reduced the incubation time to 6 h without loss of activity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The lyophilized ketoreductase P1B2 and cofactor NADP+ were dissolved in buffer and incubated with each resin at 5 °C for 48 h."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: Repeated addition of the expensive NADP⁺ cofactor for each batch adds cost and operational complexity.
Solution_Description: Washing the immobilised resin with buffer containing NADP⁺ binds the cofactor to the carrier, eliminating the need for fresh cofactor addition in subsequent cycles.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Washing the resin with buffer solution containing the NADP+ cofactor helped increase the activity of the immobilized enzyme."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: After the first three recycle rounds the initial 1‑h conversion rate dropped slightly, raising concerns about consistent performance.
Solution_Description: Demonstrated that the immobilised enzyme retains >94 % of its activity over ten recycle batches (total ≈ 200 h), confirming stable performance once the resin is properly washed and the water content is maintained.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Although the initial rate of the reaction (1 h) decreased slightly after the first three rounds of recycling, the reaction rate over the next 7 rounds remained consistent. In total, we demonstrated 10 consecutive recycles of the immobilized ketoreductase over a 200 h time period."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: The immobilised enzyme shows almost no activity without water in the organic solvent; lack of a water phase severely reduces conversion.
Solution_Description: Introducing 2–10 % water (by volume) into the IPA‑based solvent system raises conversion from <10 % to >70 % within 2 h.
Supporting_Evidence: • "When no water was added, the immobilized ketoreductase showed minimal reactivity, with <10% conversion after 2 h. However, with the addition of only 2% water, the conversion jumped to 40% in 2 h. Good activity (70% conversion in 2 h) was observed in IPA with a water concentration of 10%."

Paper Title: Development of an Immobilized Ketoreductase for Enzymatic (
Problem_Description: Reaction conversion is temperature‑dependent; sub‑optimal temperature reduces rate and throughput.
Solution_Description: Identified 40 °C as the optimal temperature for the immobilised ketoreductase, giving the highest conversion; higher temperatures (60 °C) decrease conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A study of the effect of reaction temperature showed that 40 °C is the optimal reaction temperature with the highest conversion. The conversion slightly decreased when the temperature was increased to 60 °C."

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: When the amount of lipase added to the immobilisation mixture was increased, a sizeable fraction (∼40 %) of the protein did not become covalently bound to the support, reducing the effective enzyme loading and overall catalytic yield.
Solution_Description: The enzyme‑to‑polymer ratio was optimised to 1 : 100 (protein : poly‑(GMA‑co‑HDDMA)), which gave quantitative (100 %) binding of the lipase to the support.
Supporting_Evidence: • “using a 1:100 ratio of protein to polymer, 100 % binding of protein to poly‑(GMA‑co‑HDDMA) copolymer was observed.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: Higher enzyme loadings (up to 3 mg) caused a drop in catalytic efficiency, attributed to diffusional limitations that prevent substrate molecules from reaching all immobilised enzyme sites.
Solution_Description: A porous polymer with larger pores and higher surface area (poly‑(GMA‑co‑HDDMA), 26 nm pores, 27 m² g⁻¹) was selected instead of Eupergit C, reducing mass‑transfer restrictions and restoring activity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “This value decreased when the amount of enzyme was increased up to 3 mg. This fact is suggesting the presence of diffusional problems for the substrate upon reaching the enzyme molecules on the derivative having a higher enzymatic loading, maybe as consequence of enzyme clustering.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: The free lipase loses activity rapidly at 50 °C (half‑life ≈ 9 h), which limits its use in dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) that requires elevated temperature for the metal‑catalyzed racemisation step.
Solution_Description: Covalent immobilisation of the lipase on the epoxy‑functional polymer increased thermal stability, enabling operation at 50 °C with minimal deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “native enzyme shows a clear deactivation with half‑life times of 14 and 9 h at 37 and 50 °C, respectively.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: Acetaldehyde generated from the vinyl‑ester acyl donor interferes with the Shvo’s ruthenium catalyst during DKR, leading to side‑reactions and reduced efficiency.
Solution_Description: The acyl donor was switched from vinyl butyrate to trifluoroethyl butyrate, which does not release acetaldehyde and thus eliminates the interference.
Supporting_Evidence: • “in order to avoid the described interference of acetaldehyde produced from vinyl esters during KR with the hydrogen transfer catalyst, trifluoroethyl butyrate was used as acyl donor.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: Repeated use of the free enzyme would be economically prohibitive and would require long reaction times for each batch, limiting scalability.
Solution_Description: Immobilising the lipase on the porous polymer produced a recyclable biocatalyst (TL‑PGcH‑2) that could be reused for at least 15 cycles with > 70 % activity retained, dramatically lowering catalyst cost and process time.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The experimental results shown in Figure 3 illustrate the excellent reusability in 2‑MeTHF for the immobilized enzyme, which retained 74 % of its initial activity after the 15th catalytic cycle.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: Scaling the kinetic resolution from analytical to preparative scale raised concerns about diffusion limits and longer reaction times in larger volumes.
Solution_Description: Two reactor configurations—batch and packed‑column—were evaluated; the column reactor gave a 90 min residence time and slightly higher productivity, demonstrating that reactor design can maintain short reaction times at scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • “KR of benzoin was scaled‑up 5 times … testing two types of bioreactors (batch and column). … In the case of the batch reactor, a final conversion of 49 % after 2 h was observed… For the KR protocol in a column reactor … yielding a 50 % conversion with an enantiomeric excess above 99 % … The optimal reaction time was 90 min … productivity … slightly higher than that one obtained employing in a batch reactor.”

Paper Title: Covalent Immobilization of
Problem_Description: The Shvo’s ruthenium catalyst (10 mol %) is expensive and highly sensitive to trace oxygen, which can cause deactivation when the reaction is performed on a larger scale.
Solution_Description: When the reaction volume was increased, the ruthenium loading was reduced from 10 mol % to 2.5 mol % without compromising conversion, lowering material cost and reducing oxygen‑sensitivity issues.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Increasing the reaction volume allows the decrease of the ruthenium catalyst loading… Thus, catalyst loading was decreased from 10 % mol to 2.5 % mol.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthesis of LY2886721 required a very long sequence (nine steps) and gave a poor overall isolated yield of only about 1 % (≈0.02 % per step).
Solution_Description: A completely new five‑step synthetic pathway was designed that starts from the asymmetric nitrone cycloadduct and avoids the late‑stage resolution, delivering the API in 46 % overall yield (≈17 % over nine steps).
Supporting_Evidence: “long synthesis and low overall yield (1%);” “A key impurity control point was the hydrogenolysis in Step 2… The five‑step process developed for synthesis of LY2886721 … overall yield was 46 % for these five steps and 17 % over 9 steps.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: During catalytic hydrogenolysis of the isoxazolidine, significant formation of a defluoro impurity (des‑F) and an acetyl‑loss impurity (des‑Ac) occurred, reducing product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in the presence of controlled amounts of HCl (≥1 equiv) to suppress defluorination, and 20 mol % ZnCl₂ was added to accelerate the hydrogenolysis and further limit des‑F formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “one of the best ways to minimize the des‑F impurity was to perform the hydrogenolysis in the presence of acid… more acid suppressing des‑F, but increasing hydrolysis of the acetyl group” “ZnCl₂ accelerated the reaction… slowed the defluorination.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: Product 8 (the HCl salt of the amino alcohol) showed very low solubility in MeOH, leading to a high‑volume process and difficult downstream processing.
Solution_Description: Water was introduced as a co‑solvent (1:1 n‑PrOH/H₂O) to improve solubility, and azeotropic removal of water was employed to isolate the product efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: “low solubility of the product 8 in MeOH led to a high volume process. Water was chosen as a cosolvent to improve product solubility, with azeotropic removal after the hydrogenation reaction.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: Catalyst poisons (iodide, copper, phosphate) introduced during the amidation step caused variability in hydrogenolysis conversion rates and could halt the reaction at high levels.
Solution_Description: A work‑up involving partitioning into 10 % aq. NH₄Cl and isopropyl acetate was developed to extract copper, iodide and phosphate, keeping their residual levels below specified limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “Partitioning between 10 % aqueous NH₄Cl and isopropyl acetate was useful for extracting the copper residue into the aqueous phase… residual levels of inorganics in the isolated product were below the acceptance limits (≤100 ppm iodide, ≤250 ppm Cu, ≤250 ppm phosphate).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: Use of excess benzoylisothiocyanate (BzNCS) in the thiourea formation step generated several by‑products (benzoyl transfer, alcohol addition) that reduced the isolated yield of the desired thiourea.
Solution_Description: The BzNCS charge was limited to 1.0 equiv and added over 1.5 h at 50 °C, while the CDI charge was also monitored by HPLC and added incrementally only when residual thiourea remained, preventing over‑activation and by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The desired mono‑activated BzNCS adduct 11 was obtained … using 1.0 equiv of BzNCS and a slight excess of Et₃N… If the IPC showed >2.0 % remaining thiourea, an additional charge of CDI … was added.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: The HCl salt of intermediate 8 was poorly soluble in organic solvents, causing a slurry‑to‑slurry process in the aminothiazine formation that limited reaction kinetics.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The BzNCS charge was performed at 50 °C to increase solubility, and the reaction mixture was maintained as a slurry with controlled agitation (k_La) to ensure adequate mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: “To increase the solubility and improve the kinetics of freebasing, the BzNCS charge was conducted with the slurry at 50 °C.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: Peptide coupling of diamine 21 with acid 28 gave significant amounts of regio‑isomer 29 and bis‑acylated by‑product 30, especially when using the free‑base diamine, leading to low isolated yield and batch‑to‑batch inconsistency.
Solution_Description: The coupling was switched to an acid‑chloride (Schotten–Baumann) protocol performed in protic solvent mixtures (THF/H₂O or EtOH/H₂O) with the HCl salt of the diamine, which suppressed regio‑isomer formation and minimized bis‑acylation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The acid chloride coupling provided a more robust control of the regioisomer and bis‑acylated by‑product… HCl salt of diamine 21 gave better selectivity and a faster reaction… THF/H₂O or EtOH/H₂O prevented bis‑acylated product formation.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: The free‑base API 1 had extremely low solubility in common organic solvents, preventing conventional thermal or antisolvent crystallization and leading to needle‑like crystals with poor flow properties.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The API was generated as its HCl salt and a reactive crystallization was performed by co‑addition of the salt solution and NaOH through two high‑shear mixing elbows, followed by in‑situ terminal milling and two pH‑cycle treatments to control crystal shape, aspect ratio and bulk density.
Supporting_Evidence: “A crystallization process that controlled both chemical purity and physical properties … the HCl salt 1·HCl … reactive crystallization … mixing elbows … terminal milling … pH cycles … reduction in crystal aspect ratio from 2.4 to 1.7 and improved powder flow.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of BACE Inhibitor LY2886721. Part II. Isoxazolidines as Precursors to Chiral Aminothiazines, Selective Peptide Coupling, and a Controlled Reactive Crystallization
Problem_Description: The acidic deprotection step using methanesulfonic acid (MeSO₃H) introduced a mutagenic reagent (MeSO₃Me) and generated an N‑methyl impurity, raising safety and regulatory concerns.
Solution_Description: A two‑stage deprotection was adopted: first a basic LiOH treatment to remove the benzoyl group, followed by acidic MeSO₃H to remove the acetyl group, minimizing exposure to the mutagenic acid and controlling impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Screening of various acidic hydrolysis conditions identified MeSO₃H/MeOH as the best acid option… a two‑stage base, acid deprotection … was selected.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: The original medicinal route required expensive palladium catalyst (5 mol %), large amounts of boronic acid, and BBr₃/CH₂Cl₂, giving a low total yield (49 %) and raising serious environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: A new two‑step synthesis using the Hurtley reaction with inexpensive copper (CuI) and simple bases reduced the number of steps by one, increased overall yield to 59.5 % and lowered material cost from USD 3 057 kg⁻¹ to USD 196 kg⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: “manufacturing costs are extremely high, and there are serious environmental concerns due to the use of 5 mol % of palladium catalyst and the extensive use of boronic acid 2 and BBr₃/CH₂Cl₂.”; “total yield of 49 %”; “new route via the Hurtley reaction reduced the number of steps by one and improved the total yield from 49.0 % to 59.5 %”; “reagent cost is reduced… Cu, resorcinol, Na₂CO₃… total cost USD 196 kg⁻¹”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: Using the free amino substrate 6a in the Hurtley reaction gave only trace product and a large amount of by‑products, making the yield impractically low.
Solution_Description: Acetyl‑protecting the amino group (forming 6b) suppressed side reactions and increased isolated yield to 39 % (entry 2).
Supporting_Evidence: “significant number of byproducts occurred with the use of a free amino substituent; consequently, it was considered that improving the yield would be difficult.”; “acetyl protection of the amino substituent … was affordable and … yield 39 %”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: Initial stoichiometry gave modest conversion; the reaction required more reagent to reach acceptable yield.
Solution_Description: Increasing the equivalents of resorcinol (to 3 equiv), NaOH (to 3.3 equiv) and CuSO₄ (to 0.3 equiv) raised the isolated yield to 50 % (entry 3).
Supporting_Evidence: “When the amount of reagents was increased (3.0 equiv of 7, 3.3 equiv of NaOH, and 0.3 equiv of CuSO₄) the yield improved to 50 %”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: The reaction temperature strongly affected conversion; lower temperatures gave poorer yields.
Solution_Description: Screening showed the optimal temperature was 60 °C, which gave the highest isolated yield (65 % with CuSO₄, 73 % with CuI).
Supporting_Evidence: “temperature screening at 40 and 60 °C, a superior yield was obtained at 60 °C (entry 4, 5).”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: Different copper counter‑ions gave similar yields but varying amounts of by‑products A, B and C, indicating catalyst‑related side reactions.
Solution_Description: CuI was identified as the best copper source, providing a slightly higher yield (67 %) and the lowest levels of by‑products, likely because CuI promotes the desired C–C/O bond formation while suppressing decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “CuI resulted in a slightly higher yield as a consequence of the reduced generation of all byproducts.”; Table 2 shows CuI giving 67 % yield with only 10 % A, 12 % B, 2 % C.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: Base choice impacted both conversion and the impurity profile; stronger hydroxide bases reduced by‑product C but others affected A and B.
Solution_Description: A weak carbonate base (Na₂CO₃) together with CuI gave the best balance, delivering 73 % yield at 60 °C and markedly fewer by‑products compared with hydroxide bases.
Supporting_Evidence: “KOH, LiOH … almost equal yields… carbonate bases improved the yield slightly… carbonate bases inhibited production of by‑product C.”; Table 4 entry 1 shows CuI/Na₂CO₃ → 73 % yield with low A/B/C.

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: When a carbonate base is added directly to the bromobenzoic acid solution, vigorous foaming occurs, which is problematic for large‑scale operations.
Solution_Description: The process was split: first 1 equiv NaOH aq was added to generate the sodium carboxylate, then 2.3 equiv Na₂CO₃ was added later, eliminating foaming and improving scalability.
Supporting_Evidence: “These separate additions avoided the foaming that is generated by mixing benzoic acid and a carbonate base, which is a consideration for a scaled‑up synthesis.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: Residual copper (>5000 ppm) remained after conventional slurry washing on kilogram scale; extended washing caused filter clogging and long filtration times.
Solution_Description: A scalable copper‑removal method was developed: the reaction slurry was treated with 4 M NaOH aq (5 v/w) and water at 60 °C, converting the product to soluble sodium salt 8 while copper stayed insoluble and was removed by filtration; subsequent acidification regenerated 1b with only 4 ppm Cu.
Supporting_Evidence: “removing copper was found to be difficult in a large‑scale process… residual copper >5000 ppm… longer filtration time… A more effective scalable method was investigated.”; “1b could be solved in 4 M NaOH aq … sodium salt 8 formed … copper salt did not solve … removed by filtration … residual copper 4 ppm.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of 8‑Amino-3-hydroxy‑6
Problem_Description: If the reaction mixture is not kept fully dissolved, 1b precipitates, leading to loss of assay yield during the post‑reaction hold.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Maintaining the solution at 60 °C with 4 M NaOH/H₂O kept 1b in solution; assay yields remained above 70 % for at least 10 h, preventing precipitation‑related loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “If a sufficiently dissolved state was not maintained, the loss of yield was observed resulting from the precipitation of insoluble 1b.”; “Assay yield was maintained at more than 70 % for 10 h.”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the Ullmann coupling the amount of O₂ required to oxidise Cu⁺ to Cu²⁺ varied with batch size, making the oxidative work‑up inconsistent.  The combination of residual Cu, KOH and O₂ gave rise to the undesired oxidative dimer impurity (product 4), which lowered the isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The team introduced dithiocarbamate (DTC) scavengers (e.g., APDTC) that chelate Cu⁺/Cu³⁺ under low‑O₂ conditions, preventing formation of impurity 4.  DTC was added as a solid (2.2 equiv) under N₂ followed by a small amount of water, causing immediate precipitation of a Cu–DTC complex.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “As the process was scaled up, the amount of O₂ needed varied depending on the scale, and thus, our process to provide the oxidative conditions to remove the Cu was inconsistent.”
- “Our experimental data showed that the formation of the undesired side product 4 required the combination KOH, O₂, and Cu.”
- “We hypothesized that if we could effect Cu removal under low O₂ levels, the formation of 4 could be minimized.”
- “An excess of each DTC was added as a solid under an atmosphere of N₂, and a dark solid precipitated immediately.”
- “The addition of solid DTC led to faster filtering of the material compared with the addition of an aqueous solution of DTC.”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Screening of solid‑supported scavengers (SiliaMetS Thiol/Thiourea) gave highly variable Cu removal results, and conventional metal‑hydroxide or metal‑sulfide precipitation methods degraded the desired product (compound 3).
Solution_Description: The researchers replaced the unreliable solid supports with dithiocarbamates, adding the solid DTC directly to the reaction mixture followed by water (as an antisolvent) to precipitate the metal‑DTC complex without degrading the product.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “A variety of solid‑supported reagents were tested, but the results were highly variable.”
- “Metal hydroxides have been used to precipitate transition metals, but these methods caused further degradation of 3.”
- “The formation of metal sulfides has been used, but with our system, further degradation was seen.”
- “DTCs are air‑stable solids that possess high water solubility, which makes removal of any residual DTC from the reaction train straightforward.”
- “Once the reaction was complete … DTC (2.2 equiv wrt the metal) was added as a solid, followed by the addition of water (2 mL g⁻¹).”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Precipitation of the Cu‑DTC (and other metal‑DTC) complexes produced fine particles that passed through coarse filter media (5–10 µm), leading to incomplete removal of metal and potential loss of product on larger scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A two‑stage filtration set‑up was implemented: first a nutsche filter packed with Celite to capture bulk precipitate, followed by an in‑line 1 µm polish filter (used throughout scale‑up). This ensured quantitative removal of the metal‑DTC solids and consistent product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Since the precipitation is rapid, it is difficult to control the particle size. Thus, small particles are obtained.”
- “When solid APDTC was used, the filtration flux was 1100 L m⁻² h⁻¹… With an aqueous solution of APDTC, the filtration flux was 700 L m⁻² h⁻¹.”
- “At least a 1 µm filter had to be used in order to remove all of the solids.”
- “We utilized a nutsche filter with a Celite bed to remove a majority of the DTC complex followed by an in‑line polish filter (1 µm).”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: The dithiocarbamate NaDMDTC is classified as a genotoxic impurity (GTI), which is unacceptable for pharmaceutical intermediates.
Solution_Description: The team selected ammonium pyrrolidinedithiocarbamate (APDTC), which was demonstrated to be Ames‑negative and therefore not a GTI, meeting safety requirements for large‑scale API production.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “NaDMDTC has been extensively studied and is considered to be a genotoxic impurity (GTI), whereas the NaDEDTC has been found to be Ames‑negative.”
- “We recently tested APDTC and found it to be Ames‑negative, and thus, it is not considered to be a GTI.”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: For certain metals (Co(acac)₂, Rh complexes) the Cu‑DTC analogue showed only partial removal (≈100 ppm) and the solubility of the resultant metal‑DTC complexes was not measured, limiting their effectiveness.
Solution_Description: The authors acknowledge the limitation and suggest that further optimization (e.g., alternative solvents, DTC structures, or temperature adjustments) would be required to improve solubility and removal efficiency for these metals.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Co(acac)₂ was removed to only ~100 ppm. This system was not studied beyond these screens, and the solubility of the Co–DTC complex was not measured.”
- “Rh catalysts also were not purged completely, and the solubility of the Rh–DTC complex was not measured.”

Paper Title: Dithiocarbamates: Reagents for the Removal of Transition Metals from Organic Reaction Media
Problem_Description: Scaling the Cu‑removal protocol from gram to 156 kg batches required consistent control of Cu levels (<10 ppm) and suppression of impurity 4; any variability would jeopardise yield and product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was optimized by (i) using 2.2 equiv of APDTC per Cu, (ii) performing the scavenging step at 50 °C (maintaining product solubility), and (iii) applying the validated 1 µm filtration train at each scale, achieving Cu levels as low as 3 ppm at 156 kg with no detectable impurity 4.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “We found that in each case the amount of Cu was reduced to <100 ppm, and no product degradation was observed.”
- “Experimental results… led us to use 2.2 equiv of DTC with respect to the amount of CuI used.”
- “The reaction mixture was cooled to 50 °C… the mixture was stirred at 50 °C for 1 h and then filtered….”
- Table 2 shows Cu levels of 3 ppm at the 156 kg scale and consistent control of 4.

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Handling carbon monoxide (CO) gas is hazardous, and the use of CO‑equivalents in the literature requires harsh reaction conditions (strong base, high temperature, long reaction times).
Solution_Description: The authors employed a press‑urised microwave reactor that allows safe, direct use of CO gas under controlled pressure, dramatically shortening the reaction time (90 min) and eliminating the need for CO‑releasing reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: * "its true potential has not been fully realised in lab‑scale synthesis due to the troublesome handling of CO gas."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Metal carbonyl CO‑releasers are relatively expensive and require near‑stoichiometric amounts of an additional transition metal, complicating product purification.
Solution_Description: A recyclable heterogeneous Pd(II)/TPP‑β‑cyclodextrin cross‑linked catalyst (CβCAT) was developed, eliminating the need for extra metal carbonyl reagents and simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: * "These inorganic metal carbonyls and their derivatives are nevertheless CO releasers and relatively expensive. Moreover, they require near stoichiometric amounts of an additional transition metal to work, which can encumber the purification of the desired products."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Using homogeneous Pd(OAc)₂ under conventional heating gave only 69 % isolated amide after 8 h, far lower than the desired rapid, high‑yielding process.
Solution_Description: Switching to microwave‑assisted conditions (125 °C, 90 min) with the CβCAT catalyst increased the yield to >80 % in a fraction of the time.
Supporting_Evidence: * "Complete conversion was obtained after 8 h of heating at 100 °C, and the desired product was collected in a 69 % yield."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Polar, non‑nucleophilic solvents (MeCN, THF, dioxane, DMF) gave markedly lower conversions and yields compared with toluene.
Solution_Description: Toluene was selected as the optimal solvent for the homogeneous protocol; later, MeCN was found optimal for the heterogeneous CβCAT system, showing that solvent choice must be matched to the catalyst environment.
Supporting_Evidence: * "A reduction in reaction yields was noticed … as we moved from toluene to more polar non‑nucleophilic solvents (such as MeCN, THF, dioxane, or DMF)."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Increasing CO pressure above 1 bar increased formation of the undesired keto‑amide side product, lowering the amide yield.
Solution_Description: The CO pressure was kept at 1 bar (total 10 bar with N₂) to minimise side‑product formation while maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: * "a slight increase in ketoamide (3b) formation (up to 25 %) was observed when the reaction was carried out over 5 bar of CO."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Omission of the TPP ligand or the base Et₃N led to very poor or no product formation.
Solution_Description: Both TPP (0.1 %) and Et₃N (3.5 equiv) were added to the reaction mixture, ensuring efficient Pd‑catalysed aminocarbonylation.
Supporting_Evidence: * "without the TPP ligand, only a poor (3a) yield was obtained, and no reaction product was detected when Et₃N was omitted even when 0.1 % Pd was employed."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Traditional homogeneous Pd catalysis risks metal contamination of the amide products, requiring extensive purification.
Solution_Description: The cross‑linked β‑CD support immobilises Pd and the TPP ligand; filtration of the solid CβCAT after reaction gave products with <6–8 ppm Pd and no detectable phosphine oxide, eliminating the need for metal‑removal steps.
Supporting_Evidence: * "Metal content was measured by ICP, and a 0.65 % average was obtained. Moreover, ICP analysis indicated negligible metal leaching, while the absence of TPP or TPPO in the reaction filtrate demonstrated the potential of this catalyst for recycling."

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Microwave-Assisted CO Aminocarbonylation with a Recyclable Pd(II)/TPP-β-Cyclodextrin Cross-Linked Catalyst
Problem_Description: Repeated recycling of CβCAT caused a gradual decline in isolated amide yield (from 83 % to 64 % over four cycles).
Solution_Description: The catalyst was recovered by simple filtration, washed and dried, and reused under identical conditions; the modest loss was attributed to handling loss rather than deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: * "The recovered catalyst was reused at least five times and gave consistent isolated amide yields (83 %, 75 %, 70 %, and 64 %, respectively). The slight change may be due to a loss of catalyst during handling of the β‑CD catalytic system."

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: The conventional chiral reduction methods (e.g., Corey–Bakshi–Shibata (CBS) reduction) rely on stoichiometric boron reagents, which are impractical for manufacturing because they generate hazardous waste and increase cost.
Solution_Description: A catalytic, ruthenium‑mediated asymmetric transfer hydrogenation (ATH) was introduced, using sub‑mol % of the Ms‑DENEB Ru‑amide catalyst instead of a stoichiometric boron reagent, thereby eliminating the hazardous boron waste and improving the process economics.
Supporting_Evidence: These methods can be developed to prepare useful compounds in excellent yields, but the key asymmetric reduction methods are impractical for manufacturing. In the development of our drug candidates, we wished to avoid using a stoichiometric boron reagent. (section 2. paragraph 3).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: When α‑chloroketone 1b was reduced with HCO₂H/NEt₃, the formic acid acted as a nucleophile, causing SN2 substitution on the bromo group and generating a large amount of side‑products, leading to very low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The nucleophilic substitution was suppressed by replacing soluble HCO₂H with the insoluble salt HCO₂K, which dramatically improved the yield of the desired alcohol.
Supporting_Evidence: reduction of the ketone proceeded with the S_N2 substitution on the bromo functional group with HCO₂H, giving a large amount of nucleophilic substitution compounds as major side products. (Table 1, entry 3‑4). To prevent nucleophilic substitution, HCO₂K was used as an insoluble salt, which improved the yield dramatically (entry 6).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: CHCl₃ was identified as the best cosolvent for ATH, but it is an environmentally unfriendly chlorinated solvent, raising safety and waste‑disposal concerns for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The process was re‑optimized to run without CHCl₃, using a high concentration of the hydrogen donor (HCO₂H/NEt₃) in the absence of a cosolvent, thereby eliminating the use of the hazardous solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: CHCl₃ was a preferable solvent for the ATH… However, we also managed to avoid using CHCl₃, which is not an environmentally friendly solvent. (section 2. paragraph 5).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: The initial ATH of ketone 1c gave product 2c with 92 % ee, which was insufficient for the drug‑candidate program that required >99 % ee.
Solution_Description: Addition of i‑PrOH as an antisolvent caused crystallization of the mother liquor, resulting in product 2c with >99 % ee and high isolated yield, while alternative antisolvents gave lower enantiopurity.
Supporting_Evidence: the addition of i‑PrOH to the reaction mixture directly as an antisolvent gave the desired product (R)-2c in 73 % isolated yield with >99 % area% and 99 % ee (Scheme 3). The enantiopurity of the mother liquor was much higher than that of the solid when alternative antisolvents such as acetonitrile, dichloromethane, and EtOAc were used.

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Using an N‑Bn protecting group on the amine led to olefin reduction during hydrogenation, generating by‑product 6 that is extremely difficult to remove by crystallization.
Solution_Description: The protecting group was switched to N‑Cbz, which is easy to deprotect under mild hydrogenation conditions and avoids formation of the problematic olefin‑reduction by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: The Cbz group is a much more practical protecting group for amine in terms of easy deprotection at the subsequent step… Hydrogenation of the N‑Bn moiety instead of Cbz gave a troublesome by‑product via olefin reduction. (section 2. paragraph 8).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Asymmetric transfer hydrogenation generates CO₂ gas, and vigorous gas evolution was observed on scale‑up, requiring safe venting and pressure control.
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed under nitrogen with explicit venting steps; the reactor was equipped for gas handling and the procedure included multiple evacuation/back‑fill cycles to control pressure and avoid over‑pressurization.
Supporting_Evidence: All reaction carried out under nitrogen. Asymmetric transfer hydrogenation generates CO₂ gas, so the reactor should be vented. (General Information). Caution!! Generating gas… Caution!! Vigorous gas evolution! (preparation of 2c).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Residual Ru catalyst could contaminate the final API, and removal of Pd/C after hydrogenation required an effective filtration step.
Solution_Description: The post‑hydrogenation mixture was filtered through Celite to remove Pd/C and was analyzed by XRF, confirming that no residual ruthenium was present in the final product 5.
Supporting_Evidence: The filter cake was washed… to remove Pd/C. No residual ruthenium in (R)-5 was detected by XRF. (section 2. paragraph 14).

Paper Title: Scalable Ruthenium-Catalyzed Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for the β2-Adrenergic Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature improved enantioselectivity but extended the reaction time to 24 h, reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: A compromise temperature (50 °C) with an increased concentration of the hydrogen donor allowed quantitative conversion in 2 h while still delivering high ee, eliminating the long reaction times associated with low‑temperature runs.
Supporting_Evidence: The reduction reactions were carried out at lower temperatures to achieve slightly better enantioselectivity, but the reaction time was longer in each case (entries 9 and 10). Finally, asymmetric reduction with (S,S)-3b gave the corresponding chiral alcohol (R)-2c in quantitative chemical yield with high enantio purity (entry 13).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of a Serotonin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The original route employed methyl iodide as the methylating reagent for compound 4, which is a known carcinogen and therefore unsuitable for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Methyl p‑toluenesulfonate was substituted for methyl iodide as the methylating agent. The reaction in acetonitrile at 82 °C for 24 h cleanly gave the tosylate salt 10, which precipitated on addition of isopropyl acetate and could be isolated by filtration on kilogram scale (93 % yield, 99 % purity).
Supporting_Evidence: “First, methyl iodide is not a desirable methylating agent… because it is a potential carcinogen.”; “We found that methyl p‑toluenesulfonate is an excellent alternative. Methylation of 4 with methyl p‑toluenesulfonate in acetonitrile at 82 °C for 24 h cleanly generated tosylate salt 10… employed on a 47‑kg scale … 93 % yield…”.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of a Serotonin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Using dibenzoyl‑L‑tartaric acid for the chemical resolution of racemic 11 gave only a 28.6 % isolated yield of the desired diastereomeric salt (overall synthesis yield ≈10.8 %).
Solution_Description: D‑camphoric acid was introduced as a new resolving agent. In an EtOH/isopropanol mixed‑solvent system the resolution afforded the diastereomeric salt 14 in 47 % isolated yield (94 % theoretical) with a diastereomeric ratio of 98.6:1.4, which was further improved to 99.9:0.1 after recrystallization, giving an overall 41 % isolated yield on a 40‑kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Resolution with dibenzoyl‑L‑tartaric acid afforded … 28.6 % yield… overall yield … 10.7 %.”; “We found that D‑camphoric acid consistently gave superior results… best diastereomeric ratio of 98.6:1.4 … 47 % yield (94 % theory)… scaled up on 40‑kg scale … 41 % yield of 14 with 99.9 % diastereomeric purity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of a Serotonin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Catalytic hydrogenation of tosylate 10 to piperidinium salt 11 produced side products 12 and 13 (≈25 % each) when hydrogen concentration and mass‑transfer were insufficient, leading to inconsistent product profiles and reduced overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The hydrogenation was re‑optimized to 30 °C, 75 psi H₂ pressure and 450 rpm agitation. Under these conditions the reaction gave product 11 with no detectable 13 and only 14 % of 12 (which could be removed by crystallization), delivering 71 % isolated yield on a 20‑kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Conversion of … could generate side products 12 and 13 … about 25 % each, if the hydrogen concentration and its mass‑transfer rate are not sufficient.”; “Employing the improved conditions (30 °C, 75 psi, and 450 rpm), we were able to generate 11 containing no detectable amount of 13 and 14 % … side product 12 … protocol was utilized on 20‑kg scale … 71 % yield of 11.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of a Serotonin Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The amidation step using a biphasic Schotten‑Baumann protocol (aqueous K₂CO₃ or NaHCO₃) generated a Michael‑addition impurity (compound 15) in 33–42 % of the reaction mixture, complicating purification and lowering the overall yield of the API.
Solution_Description: An anhydrous amidation was implemented: the free base 8 was azeotropically dried, and solid K₂CO₃ was used as the acid scavenger in isopropyl acetate. This reduced the impurity to 1.3 % (further <0.1 % after crystallization) and afforded the API (1) on a 16‑kg scale in 83 % isolated yield with 99.1 % purity and 99.8 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “Amidation … resulted in the formation of a side product in 33–42 % range… characterized as a Michael adduct 15.”; “Replacing the … with an anhydrous system employing K₂CO₃ as the acid scavenger … side product 15 was decreased to 1.3 %… further reduction to less than 0.1 % was achieved by crystallization… amidation … on 16‑kg scale … 83 % yield, 99.1 % purity.”

Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was raised to 50 °C, which increased solubility to give a clear 8 % (w/v) solution, and the substrate concentration was set at 0.32 M (8 % w/v) for the scale‑up.

Problem_Description: CAL B loses activity rapidly at temperatures above 50 °C (complete loss within 30 min at 60 °C).
Solution_Description: The optimal temperature of 45 °C was chosen, where the enzyme remained stable for >72 h and gave the highest enantioselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The enzyme itself is stable at 45–50 °C for more than 72 h but loses its activity rapidly at 60 °C within 30 min.', 'Based on these results, 45 °C was chosen as the optimal temperature for further studies.']

Problem_Description: During hydrolysis the pH drops because acid is formed; localized over‑addition of NaOH can raise the pH above 10 and denature the enzyme.

Solution_Description: A five‑step chemical sequence (hydrolysis, re‑esterification, N‑chlorination, de‑hydrochlorination, hydrogenation, acetylation) was employed to recycle the unwanted isomer back to the racemic diester, recovering 75 % overall yield.

Paper Title: Investigation of a Kumada Cross Coupling Reaction for Large-Scale Production of (2
Problem_Description: Initial attempts to prepare the Grignard reagent of alkyl chloride 3 were unsuccessful; the reaction gave no Grignard formation and the starting chloride or its reduced alkane 5 were recovered.
Solution_Description: A moisture‑free Mg activation strategy using 0.15 equiv of 1,2‑dibromoethane together with methyl‑magnesium‑chloride (MeMgCl) was introduced. MeMgCl quenches residual moisture (releasing CH₄) and weakens the MgO layer, allowing initiation at 50–55 °C and stable Grignard formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “All of our attempts to prepare the Grignard reagent were unsuccessful, and the reactions ended up with no reaction, leaving behind alkyl chloride (3) or the corresponding alkane compound.”
• “In our study a safer Mg metal activation as well as a moisture‑free system was created by using MeMgCl reagent, which improved the efficiency of Grignard formation.”
• “MeMgCl reacted with moisture and liberated methane gas… the initiation was achieved at low temperature (50–55 °C) and stabilized the Grignard reagent.”
• “The addition of moisture‑free alkyl halide solution not only quenched the moisture present in the Grignard system but also weakened the MgO layer and exposed the reactive Mg surface.”
• “This moisture‑free controlled strategy not only succeeded in the gram scale (lab) but also demonstrated the process robustness in the large scale (50 kg) batches.”

Problem_Description: Excess 1,2‑dibromoethane (≥0.3 equiv) caused a sudden temperature rise to ~70 °C during Mg activation, leading to Grignard degradation and poor coupling performance.
Solution_Description: DBE loading was reduced to 0.075 equiv (total 0.15 equiv) and added slowly together with the alkyl halide, keeping the temperature below 60 °C and providing controlled initiation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Excess moles of (0.3) DBE … lead to a sudden rise of the temperature to 70 °C, and that subsequently effected the Grignard reagent and the coupling reaction.”
• “Viable 0.15 equiv of DBE is viable for the activation of magnesium… the viable 0.15 equivalence of DBE was used as 0.075 equivalence for Mg initiation, and 0.075 mol was mixed with alkyl halide 3 and slowly added to Mg.”
• “Fast addition (∼15–20 min) of alkyl solution at 55–60 °C lead to an uncontrolled exothermic and incomplete Grignard reaction.”
