Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The final amidation step of the first‑generation route gave low isolated yield (≈61 %) and required >24 h on kilogram scale, with incomplete conversion and formation of side‑products.
Solution_Description: A new reductive amination protocol was developed using 2‑picoline·BH₃ (1.2 equiv) added in three portions together with HC(OCH₃)₃ (10 equiv) and 0.5 equiv acetic acid to suppress alcohol impurity 15; the reaction was run at 50 °C for 1 h, giving 79–86 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Na(OAc)₃BH … required addition of Na(OAc)₃BH in multiple portions and use of molecular sieves.”
“2‑picoline·BH₃ … proceeded smoothly and fewer impurities formed.”
“Best conversion and the lowest A% of the alcohol impurity 15 was achieved when the reaction was run … at 50 °C … addition of 2‑picoline·BH₃ in three portions was effective.”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The final step of the first‑generation synthesis produced des‑lactate (8) and dilactate (9) impurities (1.8 % and 3.7 % by HPLC) and the overall isolated yield of the step was only 61 % because of losses during reslurrying and work‑up.
Solution_Description: The crude product was reslurried in MeOH/THF to lower impurity levels, followed by an acid/base extraction to remove residual HOBt and DIPEA; residual Pd was reduced by treatment with Florisil and Thio‑Silica, and later by activated‑carbon filtration of the crude API solution.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The crude product was then reslurried in a mixture of methanol (7.5 vol) and THF (2.5 vol) and the impurities were reduced to 0.53 % and 1.1 %.”
“Residual HOBt (0.89 wt %) and DIPEA (0.1 wt %) could be readily purged by an acid/base extraction procedure.”
“The crude product typically contained 200–1000 ppm residual Pd which was then treated with Florisil … and Thio‑Silica … to reduce residual Pd to <20 ppm.”
“Activated carbon cartridge filtration … to reduce residual Pd to 20–40 ppm.”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The boronate intermediate 5 required a Boc protecting group and was very expensive (≈ $25 000 kg⁻¹), making the first‑generation process financially unattractive for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: The protecting‑group‑free boronic acid 10 was prepared in a single step directly from 2‑amino‑5‑bromopyrimidine, eliminating the need for the expensive protected boronate 5.
Supporting_Evidence:
“A protecting group was needed for the boronate 5 to improve the solubility … As such, a common Boc protection scheme was introduced for the boronate 5.”
“One of the starting materials, the boronate 5, was highly expensive ($25 000 kg⁻¹).”
“The boronic acid 10 was produced from 2‑amino‑5‑bromopyrimidine in a one‑step and protecting‑group‑free approach.”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Isolation of aldehyde 2 after metalation/formylation was hindered by very slow filtration of the crude mixture, leading to low throughput.
Solution_Description: Removal of THF prior to filtration and a controlled ripening step (aging 1–2 h at 50 °C) induced a crystal‑form change that accelerated filtration by ~10‑fold (specific cake resistance dropped from 1.3 × 10¹¹ to 4.2 × 10⁹ m kg⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence:
“Isolation of the aldehyde product proved challenging because of slow filtration of the crude mixture.”
“Removal of THF was beneficial to the filtration.”
“After aging for 1–2 h at 50 °C, the filtration was about 10× faster, as the specific cake resistance was reduced …”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Residual sodium salts (NaOEt/NaOMe) and trace piperazine in oxalate 14 led to downstream des‑lactate impurity 8 and reduced overall material balance.
Solution_Description: Oxalic acid was used to convert the material to the insoluble disodium oxalate salt, which precipitated while the API remained in solution; the pH was adjusted (7–7.5) to precipitate residual piperazine as its oxalate salt, enabling removal by filtration and giving oxalate 14 in 59 % isolated yield and >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
“We found that 0.25 equiv of oxalic acid was able to generate the disodium oxalate salt which is insoluble in ethanol and could therefore be readily removed by filtration.”
“The residual piperazine in 14 would react … leading to the des‑lactate impurity 8 … we set a specification of no more than 0.2 % of piperazine in 14.”
“Direct treatment of the resultant filtrate with excess oxalic acid (1.12 equiv) afforded the desired oxalate 14 in 59 % isolated yield and >99 % purity.”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: In the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling, the use of Na₂CO₃ or Cs₂CO₃ as base generated amide‑hydrolysis impurity 8 (7–17 %).
Solution_Description: Switching to K₃PO₄ as the base eliminated des‑lactate formation, and using the protecting‑group‑free boronic acid 10 further improved the impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
“In the presence of Na₂CO₃ or Cs₂CO₃, a significant amount of amide hydrolysis byproduct des‑lactate 8 (7–17 %) was generated.”
“With K₃PO₄ no des‑lactate 8 was detected in the reaction with the boronate ester 5 or when we later made the switch to the corresponding boronic acid 10.”

Paper Title: A Practical, Protecting-Group-Free Synthesis of a PI3K/mTOR Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Residual palladium (<200 ppm) from the Suzuki coupling needed to be reduced to meet regulatory limits.
Solution_Description: Pd catalyst loading was lowered to 0.15 mol % and the crude API solution (1‑propanol/water) was passed through an activated‑carbon cartridge, achieving Pd levels of 20–40 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “We reduced the Pd catalyst loading to 0.15 mol % … in combination with an activated carbon cartridge filtration of crude API solution … to reduce residual Pd to 20–40 ppm.”

Paper Title: Multi-Kilo Delivery of AMG 925 Featuring a Buchwald–Hartwig Amination and Processing with Insoluble Synthetic Intermediates
Problem_Description: The three late‑stage intermediates (compounds 3, 4, and AMG 925) exhibit very low solubility in the majority of common process solvents, forcing the use of slurry‑based operations, very large solvent volumes (>20 L kg⁻¹) and/or elevated temperatures to keep the material in a workable form.
Solution_Description: Solvent systems were switched to mixtures that substantially increase solubility (e.g., 80 % v/v toluene/MeOH, N‑methyl‑pyrrolidin‑2‑one (NMP), AcOH/H₂O), and operating concentrations were adjusted (higher temperature, higher solvent‑to‑solid ratios) to maintain homogeneous slurries throughout the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The last three synthetic intermediates (Scheme 1) and the drug substance AMG 925 hydrochloride (AMG 925 HCl) have limited solubility in preferred process solvents." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: Conventional substrate‑coupled NADH regeneration requires a large molar excess (10–20 equiv) of cheap alcohols (e.g., ethanol, isopropanol) to drive the equilibrium, making the process economically unattractive at scale.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a “smart‑cosubstrate” strategy using 1,4‑butanediol (1,4‑BD). Oxidation of 1,4‑BD generates a thermodynamically favored lactone (GBL), which pulls the equilibrium toward product formation and allows the use of only 0.5 equiv of cosubstrate.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the reversibility, and the poor thermodynamic driving force of the reaction necessitate significant molar surplus (usually 10–20 equiv) of the cosubstrate, e.g., ethanol and isopropanol.” (Introduction) 
• “we have introduced a “smart cosubstrate” approach… 1,4‑butanediol… The use of a lactone‑forming diol as a cosubstrate leads to a thermodynamically favorable lactone coproduct, which shifts the overall equilibrium towards more products.” (Introduction) 
• “This approach offers a significant economic advantage by avoiding high surpluses of the cosubstrate and hence tedious product recovery from the excess amounts of cosubstrate/coproduct.” (Introduction) 
• “Using this approach, full conversion … with only half‑molar equivalent of 1,4‑BD … was accomplished.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: Full conversion of the keto‑ester to the chiral alcohol required 5 days (0.5 L scale) to 7 days (2 L scale), which is excessively long for an industrial process.
Solution_Description: Although the authors did not change the reaction time, they highlighted that reducing the reaction time is highly desirable to limit sampling‑induced losses and increase throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “full conversion … was accomplished in 5 days.” (Abstract) 
• “After 5 days, the solvent was separated … 150 g of isolated product … (≥99 % ee).” (Results) 
• “Hence, reduced reaction times would be highly desirable to reduce the number of samples.” (Results)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: An endogenous NADH oxidase present in the crude enzyme preparation oxidises 1,4‑BD to GBL without coupling to ketone reduction, lowering the overall product yield.
Solution_Description: The authors note the issue but do not implement a specific mitigation; they suggest that future work may involve enzyme purification or removal of the oxidase activity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the increase in product formation … was lower than the increase in GBL synthesis … this observation was attributed to the presence of an endogenous NADH oxidase, found in the crude enzyme preparation, which would promote oxidation of 1,4‑BD to GBL without coupling it to reduction of the ketone.” (Results)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: The product alcohol (S‑2) and the lactone coproduct (GBL) co‑distilled, giving a GBL content of 22 % in the product fraction when using conventional fractional distillation.
Solution_Description: A column‑head (distillation‑swamp) approach was employed, enabling a significantly cleaner separation: only 4 % GBL remained in the product fraction at the 2 L scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the separation of the product 2 and GBL was not possible … under the distillation conditions applied.” (Results) 
• “Therefore, in order to improve DSP, column head distillation was performed to purify the product.” (Results) 
• “…the separation of 2 and GBL could be significantly improved (only 4 % of GBL found in the fraction instead of 22 % in sub‑fraction no. 2).” (Results) 
• Table 3 shows the revised composition after column‑head distillation.

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: High concentrations of substrate (100 g L⁻¹) and cosubstrate in MTBE required careful mixing to avoid phase‑separation and ensure sufficient mass‑transfer at 1000 rpm.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reactions were performed at 30 °C with vigorous stirring (1000 rpm) in sealed three‑neck flasks, which provided adequate mixing and prevented phase‑separation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction mixture … was kept at 30 °C and 1000 rpm using a magnetic stirrer.” (Experimental Section) 
• “The substrates … were added to the incubated enzyme, and the reaction mixture … was kept at 30 °C and 1000 rpm using a magnetic stirrer.” (Scale‑up Step 2) 
• “The reaction conditions … 1000 rpm.” (Table 1 footnote)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: The use of large excesses of conventional alcohol cosubstrates (ethanol, isopropanol) generates hazardous waste streams, increasing environmental and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The smart‑cosubstrate (1,4‑BD) operates at only 0.5 equiv, reducing waste by ~40‑fold and improving the safety profile of the process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “This approach offers a significant economic advantage by avoiding high surpluses of the cosubstrate and hence tedious product recovery from the excess amounts of cosubstrate/coproduct. This concept is also less harmful to the environment by 40‑fold … reduction in the waste generated for >95 % conversions.” (Introduction) 
• “Using half‑molar equivalent of 1,4‑BD … full conversion … was accomplished.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Scaling-Up of “Smart Cosubstrate” 1,4-Butanediol Promoted Asymmetric Reduction of Ethyl-4,4,4-trifluoroacetoacetate in Organic Media
Problem_Description: The target keto‑ester and the lactone coproduct have limited solubility in many organic solvents, necessitating the selection of a solvent that can dissolve both at high concentration (100 g L⁻¹).
Solution_Description: Methyl‑tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) was selected for its low boiling point and ability to maintain high enzyme activity while providing adequate substrate solubility.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Various organic solvents … were screened, and among them, we chose methyl‑tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) owing to its low boiling point and offering the highest enzyme activity.” (Introduction) 
• “Substrate concentrations of 100 g/L were applied by using half‑molar equivalent of 1,4‑BD in MTBE.” (Abstract) 
• Reaction conditions footnote lists MTBE as the solvent.

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: The original synthesis of the target 2,3‑disubstituted‑4,7‑diazaindole gave an overall isolated yield of only ~12 %. The key intermediate 2‑propylpyrazine (4) had to be made by ethyl‑iodide alkylation under cryogenic conditions and required a tedious fractional distillation to remove unreacted material and side‑product, giving rise to downstream impurities that were difficult to remove.
Solution_Description: The team replaced the ethyl‑iodide alkylation with an iron‑catalyzed n‑propyl‑magnesium‑halide cross‑coupling to 2‑chloropyrazine. 1.2 equiv of n‑PrMgCl was added over 2 h at 10–25 °C in THF (optimal solvent), giving >97 % conversion and allowing isolation of 4 in 62–77 % yield after a simple aqueous work‑up and short‑path distillation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The overall yield of 1 was only about 12 %" (Introduction).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: Methylation of 4‑acetylbenzonitrile with CH₃MgBr gave partial enolisation of the ketone, producing 5‑10 % aldol side‑product 9 and leaving 2–15 % unreacted starting material. The magnesium enolate and the resulting magnesium alkoxide were poorly soluble in ether solvents (especially MTBE), limiting conversion and making the downstream distillation of the tertiary carbinol 8 unreliable because the product partially dehydrated to a styrene impurity and batch‑to‑batch variability was observed.
Solution_Description: An in‑situ generated organotitanium reagent, CH₃TiCl₃ (from TiCl₄ + CH₃Li), was employed as a nucleophile that is a poor base. It gave chemoselective addition to the ketone without enolisation, producing 8 as the sole product. The reaction was run in anisole at –10 to 0 °C, providing >98 % conversion and eliminating the aldol side‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Partial enolization ... resulted in about 5–15 % of the aldol side‑product 9" (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: When CH₃TiCl₃ was prepared from TiCl₄/CH₃MgBr, the methylation proceeded much slower (20 h vs 2 h) and gave only 1–5 % conversion even with excess reagent; higher temperature led to impurity formation. The use of CH₃MgBr also raised safety concerns due to the larger amount of organometallic reagent and its moisture sensitivity.
Solution_Description: The route was switched to generate CH₃TiCl₃ from TiCl₄ and CH₃Li, which afforded complete conversion in 2 h with a clean impurity profile, eliminating the need for excess Grignard reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: • "CH₃TiCl₃ produced from TiCl₄/CH₃MgBr was less efficient … 20 h vs 2 h" (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: Certain commercial CH₃Li solutions (e.g., in diethoxymethane) produced a mixed‑acetal impurity (11) on quench and raised the risk of formaldehyde formation, a genotoxic impurity. Metalated impurities in the CH₃Li stock led to addition products 12 and 13 at higher reaction temperatures.
Solution_Description: The formulation CH₃Li in cumene/2‑MeTHF was selected as the preferred reagent. Quenching was performed at ≤ –15 °C to suppress formation of the mixed acetal 11, and the methylation was kept at –10 to 0 °C to keep the cumenyl side‑products below 0.1 %. This solvent choice also avoided the need for diethoxymethane, eliminating the formaldehyde risk.
Supporting_Evidence: • "About 6 % of the mixed acetal 11 formed … quenching at < –15 °C avoided it" (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: The intramolecular Chichibabin cyclization initially used solid KHMDS (4 equiv) in MTBE. The solid reagent showed lot‑to‑lot quality variation and limited availability, leading to inconsistent conversions (55–72 % after 24–120 h) and formation of the isopropyl side‑product 15 when THF from the KHMDS solution increased the solubility of the product.
Solution_Description: A 32 wt % KHMDS solution in CPME (with ≤ 5 wt % THF after codistillation) was adopted, which gave a homogeneous reaction mixture, suppressed side‑product 15, and allowed the temperature to be raised to 70–75 °C. This reduced the reaction time to 5–6 h and increased isolated yield to 81–87 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • "KHMDS solid had inconsistent quality … yields of 55 % and 72 % after 24 and 120 h" (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of a 2,3-Disubstituted 4,7-Diazaindole Including Large-Scale Application of CH
Problem_Description: Quenching the CH₃TiCl₃ methylation generated large amounts of methane; uncontrolled addition caused vigorous gas evolution and an exotherm that could not be safely managed at pilot‑scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The quench was performed by adding water slowly over 45 min while the reaction was kept at –10 to 0 °C, thereby controlling the exotherm and limiting methane evolution. The controlled addition also allowed safe scale‑up to kilogram batches.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The reaction was quenched by the addition of water over a period of 45 min to control the exotherm and evolution of methane" (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Effect of Reaction Parameters on the Synthesis of 5‑Arylidene Barbituric Acid Derivatives in Ball Mills
Problem_Description: At low rotation frequencies (νrot = 450 min⁻¹) the Knoevenagel condensation did not reach full conversion within 60 min, resulting in low yields and long reaction times.
Solution_Description: Increase the rotation frequency; increasing νrot to ≥650 min⁻¹ dramatically reduced the time needed for quantitative yields (full conversion achieved after 30 min at 550 min⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: • "full conversion was not observed within 60 min at 450 min⁻¹" (sec 2.1.1).

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route relied on an acyl‑azide (intermediate 4) generated from the carboxylic acid using sodium azide, which is highly energetic, decomposes exothermically (ΔH ≈ ‑200 kJ mol⁻¹, T_onset ≈ 40 °C) and can release toxic hydrazoic acid, posing a serious safety hazard on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the azide‑based Curtius rearrangement with a CDI‑mediated Lossen rearrangement that proceeds via a hydroxamic‑acid/dioxazolone sequence, eliminating the need for hazardous azide chemistry and avoiding the formation of unstable acyl‑azide intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: “TGA analysis of acyl azide 4 showed a 10% loss of mass at 70–90 °C … DSC analysis showed that 4 decomposed with T_onset of 40 °C with a sharp exotherm measured at –200 kJ/mol, clear indications that handling 4 on scale would be problematic.”; “Effecting the Curtius rearrangement via dose‑controlled addition of DPPA mitigated process safety risks such as accumulating and handling large amount of acylazide. However, the potentially hazardous acyl azide was still an intermediate … Therefore, a protocol for preparing 1 that avoided the use of azide chemistry was desired.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The dimethylation step in the original route used sodium hydride in DMF with excess iodomethane, which raised safety concerns (NaH reactivity, DMF toxicity) and left residual DMSO/DMF in the product, while also requiring chromatographic purification to remove impurities.
Solution_Description: The process was changed to use potassium tert‑butoxide and iodomethane in THF, allowing a cleaner reaction, easier work‑up, and removal of the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initial attempts to replace the hazardous NaH/DMF reagent system involved evaluating iodomethane and 50 % aqueous NaOH in DMSO… there were concerns regarding the use of aqueous NaOH in glass‑lined equipment and the presence of residual amounts of DMSO in the isolated product.”; “After screening a variety of bases and solvents, an alternative process utilized potassium tert‑butoxide and iodomethane in THF… the reaction was essentially an instant reaction… Remaining monomethylated impurity 8 was monitored at very low level (<0.1 %).”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The thiazole formation (ethyl 4‑chloroacetoacetate + 4‑fluorothiobenzamide) is exothermic (ΔH ≈ ‑98 kJ mol⁻¹, adiabatic temperature rise ≈ 33 °C) and initiates at ~40 °C, creating a risk of runaway on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A dose‑controlled addition of the chloroacetoacetate over 2 h while maintaining reflux temperature kept the reaction temperature in check, preventing uncontrolled heat build‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original batch‑mode process … was found to be exothermic with initiation at about 40 °C… The heat of reaction was –98 kJ/mol, and the adiabatic temperature rise was 33 °C. … Ethyl 4‑chloroacetoacetate was then added over a period of 30 min… The reaction was found to commence immediately with little accumulation of reagent.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The early route required three chromatographic purifications across four steps, which are time‑consuming, costly, and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: The redesigned four‑step synthesis eliminated all chromatographic steps; product isolation was achieved by crystallization and solvent‑swap extractions, dramatically simplifying downstream processing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The early synthetic route posed challenges for scale up … the need for chromatographic purifications in multiple steps… The elimination of all chromatographic purification steps.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The CDI‑mediated activation of the acid to the hydroxamic acid (first CDI addition) is highly exothermic (ΔH ≈ ‑260 kJ mol⁻¹) and must be carefully temperature‑controlled to avoid decomposition.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed at 0–3 °C with slow addition of a 50 % aqueous hydroxylamine solution, keeping the temperature below 15 °C and using dilute conditions to manage the heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “This amide bond formation reaction was found to be highly exothermic (‑260 kJ/mol). Thus, more preferably performed under more dilute conditions and under dosing control on larger scales. Accordingly, a commercially available 50 % aqueous solution of hydroxylamine was added … at 0–3 °C … keeping the temperature < 15 °C.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: During isocyanate formation a minor amount of symmetrical urea (≈3 % of product) formed, lowering purity and overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A final crystallization from isopropyl acetate/heptane removed the urea impurity, delivering the carbamate in 71–83 % yield with >99.8 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Approximately 3 % of symmetrical urea 11 was formed … Fortunately, 11 was readily removed during the crystallization of 1 from isopropyl acetate and heptane (1:1).”

Paper Title: Process Development of a GCS Inhibitor Including Demonstration of Lossen Rearrangement on Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The Curtius‑azide route required handling of free hydrazoic acid (bp 37 °C), a volatile and highly explosive material that can be generated from both the acyl‑azide and DPPA.
Solution_Description: The authors moved to a CDI‑mediated Lossen rearrangement, which avoids azide intermediates altogether, removing the hydrazoic‑acid risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both 4 and DPPA can potentially generate hydrazoic acid, a volatile (bp 37 °C), explosive, and highly toxic material … Therefore, a protocol for preparing 1 that avoided the use of azide chemistry was desired.”

Paper Title: Leveraging an Industrial–Academic Partnership To Optimize Small Molecule Process Development within the Pharmaceutical Industry
Problem_Description: Hazardous chloromethylation step (bis‑chloromethyl ether by‑product) in the synthesis of benzyl alcohol 1; use of highly toxic cyanogen bromide and polar aprotic solvents (DMF, NMP) in the cyclization to 2‑aminopyridoimidazoles/benzimidazoles; need for high‑temperature (130‑170 °C) microwave‑driven decarboxylative Pd‑cross‑coupling; cryogenic (‑50 °C) lithiation step for the synthesis of ketone 4.
Solution_Description: Telescoping the Bouveault formylation and hydride reduction into a single step, eliminating the chloromethylation; replacing cyanogen bromide with phosphorus oxychloride and using acetonitrile as a greener solvent; developing a mild Pd‑catalyzed decarboxylative coupling at 80 °C (no copper, no microwave); moving the lithiation from –50 °C to –10 °C and swapping TEMPO for low‑loading AZADO catalyst, reducing PMI.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem – Safety (chloromethylation): "...highly hazardous chloromethylation chemistry that produces bischloromethyl ether as a byproduct, which is dangerous on all scales of operation.";

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis of a Nucleoside Phosphoramidate Prodrug Inhibitor of HCV NS5B RdRp: Challenges in the Production of a Diastereomeric Mixture
Problem_Description: The API (IDX184, 1) shows very low solubility in both pure aqueous and pure organic solvents, and its amphiphilic nature makes the reaction mixture viscous or prone to phase‑separation, leading to poor conversion and handling problems (crystallization impossible, sticky/coagulated powder).
Solution_Description: Use mixed aqueous‑organic solvent systems (e.g., MeCN/H₂O, EtOH/H₂O, EtOAc/MeCN/H₂O) to keep the drug in solution during work‑up, and replace the final RP‑chromatography with a dual liquid‑liquid extraction that removes non‑polar and polar impurities while maintaining the 1:1 diastereomeric ratio. Adjust concentration to ~10 % w/v to aid precipitation and filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: The abstract notes that “its preferred solubility in mixed aqueous–organic solvents presented additional processing challenges.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: The impurity profile for the N⁷‑benzylation impurity (6) was inconsistent; a 4 kg GMP batch exceeded the specification limit of 0.2 % HPLC area. The low selectivity for N⁹‑alkylation also gave only ~70 % of the desired product (3).
Solution_Description: The pyridine hydrochloride (2) was added in three or more portions into a stirred mixture of 1 and K₂CO₃ in DMSO, which eliminated the 0.5–3 h induction period and gave reproducible conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It was necessary to charge the pyridine hydrochloride 2 in portions into the mixture of K₂CO₃ … and the chloropurine compound 1 in dimethylacetamide (DMA).”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Benzylation of 1 with 2 gave poor N⁹‑selectivity; the N⁷‑benzylated impurity (6) had low solubility (≤1.4 mg mL⁻¹ in DMF) and precipitated, making isolation of the desired product difficult and lowering overall yield (45–56 %).
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium from DMF/DMSO to DMA and running the reaction at 40 °C (avoiding temperatures ≥65 °C that increased bis‑alkylated impurity 8) improved both solubility of intermediates and selectivity for N⁹‑product 3.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The main N⁷ benzylation impurity 6 had low solubility (≤1.4 mg/mL) in DMF …”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Using 2.2 equiv of K₂CO₃ in the salt‑formation step generated up to 1.4 % residue‑on‑ignition (ROI) from inorganic salts, degrading the purity of crude API 4.
Solution_Description: The K₂CO₃ charge was reduced to 1.1–1.3 equiv, which lowered ROI to <0.1 % without affecting impurity profile, thereby improving the purification step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Use of 2.2 equiv of K₂CO₃ resulted in crude 4 containing high levels of inorganic salts (up to 1.4 % ROI). … ROI was reliably reduced to <0.1 % by decreasing the amount of K₂CO₃ to 1.1–1.3 equiv.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: During the MsOH salt‑formation, up to ~20 % of the API degraded in 30 min, forming ethoxypurine 5 and the genotoxic ethyl‑mesylate impurity, causing batch‑to‑batch yield variation.
Solution_Description: The salt‑formation was performed in DMA at ≤40 °C (the slowest degradation rate) with MsOH added below 20 °C, which limited API decomposition and avoided generation of the genotoxic impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The rates of degradation and impurity formation were slowest in DMA at 40 °C… the MsOH (1.4 equiv) was added over 15 min at <20 °C.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Filtration of the precipitated product after antisolvent addition with water was very slow, leading to low yields and unacceptable purity on scale‑up (10 kg runs took several days).
Solution_Description: A 1:1 (v/v) mixture of H₂O–IPA was employed as the antisolvent, which accelerated filtration and gave reproducible recovery of 1–2 kg batches.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Water was an effective antisolvent, but filtration of 3 was very slow. An improved filtration was observed using a 1:1 (v/v) mixture of H₂O–IPA as the antisolvent.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Impurity 6 (N⁷‑benzylated) hydrolyzed to impurity 9 during the salt‑formation step and could not be removed by downstream filtration, contaminating the final API.
Solution_Description: A telescoped process was developed in which the benzylation and MsOH salt‑formation were run consecutively in DMA without isolating the free base 3, allowing impurity 6 to be removed by early filtration before salt formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The best point of the process to remove 6 was during the filtration.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: API 4 degraded in DMSO solutions at 22 °C, forming impurity 10 (hydroxy‑purine); the impurity level rose linearly with residence time, causing variable yields and purity in recrystallization batches.
Solution_Description: Seeding (0.5–1.0 wt % seed) together with a high supersaturation step (adding 8 vol EtOAc to the DMSO solution) forced rapid crystallization (onset <2 min), minimizing the time API stayed in solution and suppressing impurity 10 formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Higher degree of supersaturation due to higher volumes of the first portion of EtOAc significantly reduced onset times.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: Initially no recrystallization route existed for crude API 4, limiting overall purity and yield of the final drug substance.
Solution_Description: A DMSO–EtOAc recrystallization was developed (5 vol DMSO, 8 vol EtOAc, seed, then additional EtOAc) that gave 84 % isolated yield and reduced impurity 10 to <0.05 % after scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A recrystallization was developed … DMSO–EtOAc … gave 84 % yield and impurity 10 <0.05 %.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an N‑Benzylated Chloropurine at the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: During large‑scale batches, occasional lack of seeding produced thin slurries, delayed crystallization, and gave low yields (e.g., 40 % in one 6 kg run).
Solution_Description: A deliberate seeding step (0.6 kg seed, 1 wt %) was instituted together with a staged EtOAc addition (8 vol then 7 vol) to ensure rapid and consistent crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: • “An improved recrystallization procedure … seed crystals (0.6 kg) … 8 vol EtOAc … then 7 vol EtOAc … gave robust and consistent results.”

Paper Title: A DMAP-Catalyzed Approach to the Industrial-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: In the bicarbonate‑mediated reaction, traces of water react with Troc‑Cl (2) to generate HCl and carbonate intermediates. The generated HCl further reacts with KHCO₃/NaHCO₃, creating a self‑sustaining HCl‑and‑water cycle that produces side‑products (2,2,2‑trichloroethanol, symmetric and asymmetric carbonates). These impurities lower product assay and can protonate the cyclic nitrogen of 1, halting the desired N‑demethylation.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount of DMAP (5 mol %) was introduced as a nucleophilic base catalyst. The reaction mixture was rigorously dried (azeotropic removal of water) and any HCl formed was purged with nitrogen before adding substrate 1. DMAP suppresses the HCl‑generating cycles, prevents side‑product formation and affords a high‑purity product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the concomitant presence of bicarbonates and traces of water triggers side reaction cycles that produce and accumulate hydrochloric acid and water … formation of multiple carbonate and alcohol‑type side products”
• “the huge access of the released HCl would eventually stop the primary N‑demethylation reaction”
• “application of DMAP as a catalyst and the use of a reaction medium free of water … allowed operation on an industrial scale … with higher yields, shorter reaction times, and improved product quality”

Paper Title: An Improved and Practical Synthesis of Tranexamic Acid
Problem_Description: During the monohydrolysis of dimethyl terephthalate (9) to potassium 4‑(methoxycarbonyl)benzoate (10), the product 10 precipitated as a thick suspension, giving poor stirring and heat accumulation, which led to the formation of the side‑product potassium terephthalate (16) and a drop in isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A mixed‑solvent system of methanol/toluene (1 : 1.1 v/v) was introduced as an antisolvent. The added toluene kept 10 in solution, eliminated the thick suspension, and raised the crude purity to 97.8 % (99.1 % isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: ["The possible reason is that 10 precipitated from methanol as thick suspension which made the stirring quite inefficient and resulted heat accumulation with increased formation of the byproduct potassium terephthalate 16."]

Paper Title: An Improved and Practical Synthesis of Tranexamic Acid
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of nitrile 13 under basic Raney‑Ni conditions gave a complex mixture (44.3 % 18, 21.9 % 19, 6.2 % 20, plus unidentified side‑products) because the methyl ester was hydrolysed to 19 and the primary amine dimerised to 20.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to an acidic one‑pot hydrogenation/acylation using Ni–Al₂O₃ catalyst, anhydrous sodium acetate as a cocatalyst, and acetic anhydride as solvent (50 °C, 1 MPa). The amine generated in‑situ was immediately acylated, preventing ester hydrolysis and dimerisation, and delivering 14 in high yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: ["The reaction mixture contained 44.3% methyl 4-(aminomethyl)benzoate 18, 21.9% 4-(aminomethyl)benzoic acid 19, 6.2% methyl 4-((4-(aminomethyl)benzamido)methyl)benzoate 20, and trace amounts of unidentified side products."]

Paper Title: An Improved and Practical Synthesis of Tranexamic Acid
Problem_Description: Earlier routes relied on expensive metal catalysts (PtO₂, Raney cobalt, Ru‑Rh‑Pd/C) and toxic reagents/solvents (CrO₃, Cl₂, CCl₄), making the processes uneconomical and hazardous for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The new synthesis employed inexpensive, readily available catalysts Ni–Al₂O₃ for the key hydrogenation/acylation step and Ru–Al₂O₃ for the final hydrogenation, eliminating the need for PtO₂, Raney cobalt and toxic reagents, thereby reducing cost and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: ["…using toxic reagents (CrO₃, Cl₂), solvent (CCl₄), and expensive catalyst (PtO₂), etc., that plagued the previous methodologies."]

Paper Title: An Improved and Practical Synthesis of Tranexamic Acid
Problem_Description: The intermediate 4‑(aminomethyl)benzoic acid (4) contains both carboxyl and amino functionalities; its isolation was highly pH‑dependent, rendering downstream purification difficult.
Solution_Description: The authors combined hydrolysis and isomerisation of intermediate 15 in a single step, followed by simple pH adjustments, charcoal treatment and crystallisation, providing the final product 1 with 99.6 % purity without elaborate purification of 4.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: ["Additionally, containing both carboxyl and amino group, the success of purification of 4 was highly dependent on the pH value, making the post‑process difficult to handle."]

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: The second Migita coupling has a very narrow optimum operating window; under the standard conditions symmetrical sulfides 6 and 7 are formed (up to several percent). 7 cannot be removed by crystallisation and requires chromatography, and the impurity level rises as the reaction proceeds, forcing the reaction to be stopped within 3 h at 70 °C.
Solution_Description: Switch to Pd₂(dba)₃/Xantphos as the catalyst/ligand system, which suppressed formation of the symmetrical sulfides and therefore reduced the purification burden while maintaining good conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The first one is the narrow optimum operating range of the second Migita coupling…symmetrical sulfides 6 and 7 form readily (up to several percent…) 7 could not be purged by crystallisation and could only be removed by chromatography.”
• “Pd₂(dba)₃/Xantphos appeared to minimise formation of the symmetrical sulfides, which greatly reduced the burden on product purity upgrade.”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: Tri‑isopropyl‑silyl‑thiol (TIPS‑SH) is the traditional sulfur source but it is only available from a single vendor on multikilogram scale, is expensive and has a strong rotten‑egg odor that poses an environmental and safety risk.
Solution_Description: Replace TIPS‑SH with iso‑octyl 3‑mercaptopropionate (17), a cheap, bulk‑available, odorless commodity chemical that behaves similarly in the Migita coupling, providing a cost‑effective and safer sulfur source.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Triisopropylsilanethiol (3, TIPS‑SH)…its availability on scale is limited…at a relatively high price. In addition, the reagent has a pungent rotten egg odor, which is an environmental risk.”
• “From availability and cost perspectives, 17 had the advantage of bulk availability…All alkyl 3‑mercaptopropionates exhibit very similar reactivities, 17 was finally chosen for development.”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: Alternative sulfur sources (S₈, ClSSCl, thiourea, NaSCN/NBS, etc.) gave complex mixtures such as sulfide, disulfide and trisulfide by‑products (11‑13) or decomposed intermediates (e.g., thioamidine → sulfide 11) and failed to deliver the desired thiophenol efficiently.
Solution_Description: Adopt the 3‑mercaptopropionate family (specifically iso‑octyl 3‑mercaptopropionate, 17) as the sulfur reagent for the initial Pd‑catalysed Migita coupling, which cleanly delivers the thiophenoxide after deprotection and avoids the problematic side‑reactions observed with the other candidates.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Among all the candidates, molecular sulfur (S₈) is the most desirable… however, metalation… proceeded to 9 prior to reaction with S₈…
• “Reaction with S₈ or ClSSCl afforded a mixture of sulfide, disulfide, and trisulfide products 11‑13.”
• “Thiourea coupled successfully… but the resulting thioamidine decomposed to sulfide 11.”
• “Since all alkyl 3‑mercaptopropionates exhibit very similar reactivities, 17 was finally chosen for development.”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: Impurity 27, generated from aryl‑phosphine exchange on the Pd catalyst, could not be removed by any solubility‑based purging study and persisted at 0.15–0.25 % in the crude product.
Solution_Description: Operate the second Migita coupling at a lower temperature and reduce the n‑PrOH‑to‑toluene ratio, which lowers solvent polarity and hinders phosphine dissociation, thereby suppressing the C–P reductive elimination pathway that leads to impurity 27.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Structure elucidation work identified the impurity as 27… Extensive solubility‑based purging studies… did not afford any conditions that consistently remove this impurity.”
• “The kinetic analysis also offered a rationale for the empirically discovered conditions that minimised the formation of 27 (i.e., performing the reaction at lower temperature and reducing the n‑PrOH to toluene ratio).”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: PF‑04191834 exists as three anhydrous polymorphs (A, B, C) and two solvated forms; the initial crystallisation from THF provides limited purity upgrade when the material is impure, and uncontrolled polymorph formation can compromise API specifications.
Solution_Description: Develop a recrystallisation protocol in a 23.7 % n‑PrOH/toluene binary solvent system, seed with 0.2 wt % Form A, and control cooling (20–45 °C) to convert any Form B to Form A, followed by filtration and solvent washes, delivering the desired polymorph with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Several polymorphs have been identified…Form A was the most stable…When the API is already present in high purity, it crystallises out of THF as Form A; however, this process offered very limited purity upgrade when less pure material was employed.”
• “The resulting pale‑yellow filtered solution was cooled below 40 °C…seeded with 0.2 wt % of Form A crystals…Extended stirring between 20–45 °C allowed for polymorph conversion to the desired Form A.”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834
Problem_Description: Palladium and Xantphos constitute the biggest cost drivers; reducing catalyst loading is needed to improve the cost‑of‑goods, but lowering the loading to 0.5 mol % elongates the reaction time.
Solution_Description: Decrease the Pd₂(dba)₃/Xantphos ratio from 1:2 to 1:1 (and ultimately to 0.5 mol % Pd) while extending the reaction time (up to 18 h for the second coupling) to retain high conversion, thereby cutting catalyst expense.

• “1 mol % Pd₂(dba)₃ and 2 mol % Xantphos performed quite well… we were able to reduce the Pd/Xantphos ratio from 1:2 to 1:1 without much change in performance; however, longer reaction times were necessary when lowering the catalyst loading to 0.5 mol %.”

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834

Paper Title: Development of the Commercial Route for the Manufacture of a 5‑Lipoxygenase Inhibitor PF-04191834

Paper Title: Practical Assessment Methodology for Converting Fine Chemicals Processes from Batch to Continuous

Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Practical Assessment Methodology for Converting Fine Chemicals Processes from Batch to Continuous
Problem_Description: In the reagent‑formation step of Process 1 excess Zn⁰ solids are required to provide surface area; the solids settle rapidly and can block downstream lines, creating safety and operability concerns.
Solution_Description: Use a continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) with liquid overflow or a packed/ fluidised bed that maintains solids in suspension; size the tube/pipe diameter so the linear velocity stays above the particle settling velocity and, if needed, lower the reactant concentration to keep the slurry mobile.

• “Continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) with liquid overflow … can be used to keep solids in suspension.” (Section 2.5).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: When the step‑wise synthesis was scaled to hundreds of grams, the peptide chain became increasingly insoluble after the fourth amino‑acid insertion, leading to accumulation of impurities (mainly O‑acylisourea and N‑acylurea), difficulty removing DCU, and an overall crude pentapeptide purity of only 40‑60 %. The isolated overall yield of the final product was only 25‑35 %.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the linear route and adopted a convergent “3 + 2” fragment‑coupling strategy, which reduces the length of each linear sequence and limits impurity buildup.  The activated‑ester method was used with near‑stoichiometric DCC/HOSu so that excess carbodiimide was avoided, minimizing DCU formation.  The reaction medium was tuned to a 30 % (v/v) water/THF biphasic mixture to keep the hydrophilic glycyl‑glycine dissolved while maintaining solubility of the tripeptide ester.  Coupling of the acid‑sensitive residues (Tyr, Phe) was performed at 0 °C using the OSu ester to suppress racemisation.  After condensation the crude protected pentapeptide was purified by cation‑exchange chromatography followed by desalting on an MCI column, delivering a pure product in 45 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "when it was applied to hundreds of gram‑scale preparation, some impurities gradually accumulated and the solubility of peptide chain decreased substantially, especially after four links of amino acids were completed" (para 2).  
• "the purity of crude pentapeptide obtained after all side‑chain deprotection was about 40–60 %... overall yield of product at 25–35 %" (para 2).  
• "the peptide chain was finally divided into two different sequences: Fmoc‑Tyr‑(tBu)‑Gly‑Phe‑OH (2) and H‑Gly‑Gly‑OH (6)" (para 4).  
• "The tripeptide ester (3) is freely soluble in organic solvent, while glycylglycine (6) was hydrophilic, undissolving in the organic layer, the fragment condensation must be carried out in two miscible liquids. Consequently, the proportion of mixed solvents directly affects the yield" (para 5).  
• "The optimum water proportion ... approximately 30 % (v/v)" (Fig 2).  
• "The amount of base had substantial effects on the yield... NaHCO₃, TEA, DIEA gave high yield, while Na₂CO₃ gave lowest" (Fig 3).  
• "Tyrosine and phenylalanine must be activated as −OSu in ice bath… to reduce racemisation" (para 8).  
• "The crude product was purified on cation exchange chromatography to yield the pure pentapeptide (9)" (para 4).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: The tripeptide ester is soluble in organic solvent whereas glycyl‑glycine is only soluble in water, creating a biphasic mixture that can cause incomplete mixing and lower yields. Conventional work‑up required removal of DCU and other water‑soluble by‑products, which was time‑consuming on large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A mixed water/THF solvent system (23‑38 % water) was adopted to keep both fragments in solution, providing a homogeneous reaction phase.  After coupling, the product was precipitated by adjusting the aqueous phase to pH 3 with citric acid, allowing the hydrophobic peptide acid to separate from the bulk aqueous phase containing excess amino acid, base, and DCU.  This simple precipitation/filtration avoided chromatographic purification of intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "the tripeptide ester (3) is freely soluble in organic solvent, while glycylglycine (6) was hydrophilic, undissolving in the organic layer, the fragment condensation must be carried out in two miscible liquids" (para 5).  
• "The expected yield was not obtained when a lower percentage of water was added… The yield was satisfactory when the proportion of water was between 23 % and 38 %…" (Fig 2).  
• "We have envisioned that this problem could be easily solved by reacting the full‑protected peptide ester with excess free amino acid to produce hydrophobic peptide acid products… which could be precipitated by addition of 10 % aqueous solution of citric acid (pH 3) after remove the organic phase by reduced pressure distillation" (para 6).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: The linear approach required protected phenylalanine and excessive DCC/HOSu, making the process expensive for kilogram‑scale production.  The authors noted that protected phenylalanine is comparatively costly, while the resin‑based solid‑phase route is also unaffordable for large batches.
Solution_Description: The convergent “3 + 2” route uses inexpensive free glycine and phenylalanine directly, and employs Boc₂O (cheap) for the Boc‑protection step.  Stoichiometric activation (1.2 equiv DCC/HOSu) reduces reagent excess and waste, lowering material cost and simplifying waste handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "most of the described synthesis have been based on the solid‑phase chemistry… it is not the most cost‑effective method to produce kilograms… due to limitation of resin carriers" (intro).  
• "the protected phenylalanine… is comparatively expensive, while Boc₂O is much less expensive in ‘3 + 2’ strategy" (para 4).  
• "the activated ester was obtained in a nearly stoichiometric yield and used in the next step without further purification" (para 4).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: Excess DCC generates N,N′‑dicyclohexylurea (DCU) which precipitates and is difficult to remove; trace DCU accumulates with scale‑up and poses handling and disposal concerns.
Solution_Description: Reducing the amount of DCC to 1.2 equiv and performing the activation in a single pot (no isolation) limits DCU formation.  The DCU precipitate is filtered off early, and the remaining activated ester is used directly, avoiding an extra purification step and minimizing safety hazards associated with handling large amounts of solid urea by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Due to excess carbodiimide is used, traces of DCU are accumulated gradually and are difficult to be removed" (para 2).  
• "the activated ester was obtained in a nearly stoichiometric yield and used in the next step without further purification" (para 4).  
• "the precipitate of DCU was removed to leave the Fmoc‑Tyr‑(tBu)‑OSu in 1,4‑dioxane as a colorless transparent liquid" (sec 4.1).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: Using 1,4‑dioxane as solvent for kilogram‑scale coupling of Fmoc‑Tyr‑(tBu)‑Gly‑Phe‑OH gave lower coupling yields because 1,4‑dioxane forms azeotropes with water, preventing complete removal of water and thus incomplete precipitation of the tripeptide ester.
Solution_Description: The authors switched from 1,4‑dioxane to a water/THF mixed solvent system, which avoids azeotrope formation, facilitates water removal, and improves precipitation and recovery of the tripeptide ester, thereby raising the coupling yield to 70‑80 % for the fragment‑coupling step.
Supporting_Evidence: • "a low coupling yield would be obtained if 1,4‑dioxane was used as a solvent during the kilograms preparation of Fmoc‑Tyr‑(tBu)‑Gly‑Phe‑OH (2). It is because 1,4‑dioxane can easily form azeotropes with water which makes it hard to be distilled, result in the uncomplete precipitation of the tripeptide, and ultimately lead to the loss of product during the post‑treatment" (para 6).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: Active ester hydrolysis competes with aminolysis during the “3 + 2” condensation, especially when strong bases are used in excess, leading to loss of the ester and lower yields.
Solution_Description: Mild base NaHCO₃ (1.0‑1.5 equiv) was selected to promote aminolysis while suppressing ester hydrolysis.  The base level was optimised to avoid excessive alkalinity that accelerates hydrolysis, thereby improving the coupling yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The hydrolysis of active esters is performed under the same condition… the amount of base had substantial effects on the yield… When the amount of base was added to 1.0‑1.5 molar quantity, NaHCO₃, TEA, and DIEA resulted in a high yield, whereas Na₂CO₃ generated the lowest yield (30 %) followed by DEA (40 %). This result was due to the strong basicity that makes the hydrolysis of the ester faster than the coupling reaction" (para 5).  
• "To be environmentally friendly, sodium bicarbonate was often used as a additional base with 1.2 equiv in our research" (para 5).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: The O‑acylisourea intermediate can rearrange to N‑acylurea, an irreversible side‑product that consumes starting amino acid and reduces overall conversion.
Solution_Description: Using HOSu/N‑hydroxysuccinimide as a coupling additive stabilises the active ester, reducing the formation of the O‑acylisourea and its rearrangement.  Performing the activation at 0 °C further suppresses side‑reactions and racemisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "O‑acylisourea tends to be the primary source of impurities… it could be rearranged into the N‑acylurea, which is irreversible and consumes starting amino acid without generating product" (para 2).  
• "HOSu is a relatively stable additive to HONp, while HONp is more prone to peptide‑coupling than other additives. Both of them are less reactive than the O‑acylisourea toward peptide bond formation" (para 8).  
• "Tyrosine and phenylalanine must be activated as −OSu in ice bath. Although such procedures could possibly reduce racemization during the activation reaction" (para 8).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of Osteogenic Growth Peptide (10–14) Using a Fragment Coupling Approach
Problem_Description: Column chromatography was required to isolate the crude pentapeptide after deprotection, which is time‑consuming and limits throughput on multi‑kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a cation‑exchange (SP‑sepharose) column followed by desalting on an MCI resin, allowing rapid bulk purification without silica gel chromatography and achieving >97 % purity for the final peptide.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The crude product was purified on cation exchange chromatography to yield the pure pentapeptide (9)" (para 4).  
• Detailed description of SP‑sepharose and MCI column steps in the Experimental section (sec 4.9).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: The original four‑step synthesis of Isoclast (starting from 5‑chloromethyl‑2‑(trifluoromethyl)pyridine) gave an overall isolated yield of only 2.4 % after silica‑gel chromatography and required a costly, commercially limited starting material.
Solution_Description: A de novo pyridine construction by an enamine‑mediated Michael cyclization was developed, using inexpensive, readily available 3‑(methylthio)‑butanal, pyrrolidine, and a trifluoro‑acetyl vinyl ether, thereby eliminating the expensive 5‑chloromethyl‑2‑(trifluoromethyl)pyridine and raising the three‑step overall yield to ~66 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The overall yield (four chemical steps) was a low 2.4%… Although this route was optimized to provide gram quantities… an aggressive commercialization plan included rapidly escalating kilogram sample requirements.”; “Since the cost of 5‑chloromethyl‑2‑(trifluoromethyl)‑pyridine (2) was considered to be prohibitive for scale‑up, an investigation of alternative starting points… The most promising… was enamine‑mediated Michael additions.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: Oxidation of the sulfilimine to the sulfoximine with m‑CPBA was unpredictable on scale, required handling of a hazardous peroxide, and the reagent cost made it unsuitable for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A catalytic RuCl₃/NaIO₄ oxidation was introduced, which proved more robust and scalable, and later replaced by a sodium permanganate oxidation that avoided costly reagents and peroxide hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: “Perhaps the most troublesome aspect… oxidation of the sulfilimine to the corresponding sulfoximine. Although mCPBA… produced numerous small‑scale samples, we found chemical yields… unpredictable upon scale‑up… cost, together with safety concerns, made this approach unsuitable for large‑scale sample production.”; “Initial efforts were focused on catalytic ruthenium‑based sodium periodate oxidations… This method proved to be more robust than the mCPBA approach and was eventually scaled to multikilograms.”; “Either sodium or potassium permanganate… the cheaper sodium salt was chosen based on the cost of future scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: The sulfilimine formation using iodobenzene diacetate was expensive and generated large quantities of iodobenzene waste that required extensive extractions and disposal.
Solution_Description: A cheaper halogen source—commercial bleach (NaOCl)—was employed together with cyanamide to generate the sulfilimine, dramatically reducing reagent cost and simplifying work‑up by eliminating the iodobenzene extraction step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of iodobenzene diacetate presented the problems of using an expensive reagent as well as disposal or recycle of large quantities of iodobenzene on a process scale.”; “When the bleach/cyanamide procedure was investigated… the workup was simplified… eliminating extraction into methylene chloride, thus eliminating its use.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: During the RuCl₃/NaIO₄ oxidation the reaction became very viscous, formed a thick black rind on the reactor walls, generated off‑gassing and a black residue, and occasionally stalled, creating heat‑removal and filtration problems at scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition order was reversed—aqueous sodium permanganate was added to the sulfilimine solution (or vice‑versa, depending on the version)—and the reaction was run more dilute. This eliminated the thick rind, lowered viscosity, and allowed temperature control (10–20 °C) via controlled addition rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the reaction mixture became more viscous from manganese byproduct formation. This brown precipitate exhibited fine particles that were difficult to filter quickly… formation of such a thick rind layer could possibly insulate the reaction mixture from the appropriate heat transfer… It was found that by reversing the addition order of reagents and running the reaction more dilute these process issues were eliminated.”; “The addition rate was adjusted so that the internal reaction temperature could be maintained between 10 and 20 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: Bleach‑derived sulfilimine reactions generated higher levels of sulfoxide and, under alkaline conditions, led to formation of a methyl‑ketone impurity (20) during the subsequent permanganate oxidation; impurity levels varied with water content and pH.
Solution_Description: Acetic acid was added to neutralize the alkaline head‑space from the permanganate oxidation, suppressing ketone formation; solid calcium hypochlorite (instead of liquid bleach) reduced sulfoxide formation; water content was minimized by using an aqueous cyanamide solution and controlling addition order.
Supporting_Evidence: “Methyl ketone (20) formation can be suppressed by controlling the pH during permanganate oxidation… the iodobenzene diacetate route… generates 2 equiv of acetic acid… neutralizing the sodium hydroxide that was formed.”; “Use of solid calcium hypochlorite appeared to give better conversion to sulfilimine 17 with less formation of sulfoxides 19.”; “The level of sulfoxide 19 increased… when the reaction was run with 50 % aqueous cyanamide … water appeared to have a detrimental effect.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: Vacuum distillation of pyridine sulfide 10 produced hot spots; the distillation bottoms contained tars that decompose exothermically at ~170 °C, posing a safety hazard if temperature limits were exceeded.
Solution_Description: Distillations were limited to an internal pot temperature of <155 °C based on DSC/ARC data, preventing runaway decomposition of the tars while still providing high isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and accelerated rate calorimetry (ARC) data on the distillation bottoms indicated a potential exothermic decomposition starting as low as 170 °C. For this reason, distillations were kept at an internal pot temperature of less than 155 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Crop Protection Agent Isoclast
Problem_Description: The RuCl₃/NaIO₄ oxidation left residual ruthenium (≈270 ppm) in the final sulfoximine, giving a gray product and requiring additional removal steps.
Solution_Description: The product was passed through neutral alumina to adsorb ruthenium, followed by recrystallization from 2‑propanol, delivering an off‑white, higher‑purity material.
Supporting_Evidence: “The grey color of the product was caused by residual ruthenium. The ruthenium level in the material was about 270 ppm… The gray color (ruthenium) could be removed from the product by treatment with neutral alumina.”

Paper Title: Real-Time Monitoring and Control of Critical Process Impurities during the Manufacture of Fostamatinib Disodium
Problem_Description: The SNAr coupling shows a very steep temperature‑dependence: between 115 °C and 125 °C the reaction time varies from 5 h to 15 h, with no useful rate below 115 °C and unacceptable impurity formation above 125 °C.  At the intended 600 kg scale there were concerns about controlling the batch temperature and heat‑up profile, making the process both slow and unpredictable.
Solution_Description: A real‑time UV/vis PAT tool (ATR probe) was deployed to monitor the reaction progress in‑line.  The model‑based EoR determination allowed the reaction to be stopped after ~4 h (instead of the nominal 8 h) without offline sampling, thereby shortening the residence time while keeping impurity levels under specification.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction rate is highly sensitive towards temperature in the range 115–125 °C with reaction times varying from 5 to 15 h… Uncertainties regarding batch temperature control and heat‑up times at the proposed 600 kg scale gave serious concerns about processing time and EoR analysis.”; “The reaction was judged to be complete after 4 h (versus the expected 8 h)… The combined levels of 5 + 6 were 0.26 %; significantly less than the specification limit <1.0 %.”

Paper Title: Real-Time Monitoring and Control of Critical Process Impurities during the Manufacture of Fostamatinib Disodium
Problem_Description: An induction period of ~30 min is observed before any conversion, giving a sigmoidal kinetic profile that indicates an incompletely understood mechanism and creates risk of batch‑to‑batch variation or failure.
Solution_Description: Mechanistic studies using the inline data revealed that the reaction is autocatalytic in HCl.  Adding a measured amount of HCl at the start removed the induction period (no improvement in final purity), confirming the role of HCl as a catalyst and allowing the reaction to be initiated more reliably.
Supporting_Evidence: “The observed sigmoidal data curve is a clear indication that the reaction pathway is not fully understood… The process is autocatalytic wrt hydrogen chloride with an induction period being observed whilst sufficient hydrogen chloride is accumulated in the system.”; “Addition of hydrogen chloride at the start of the reaction reduced the observed induction period (with no improvement in the eventual purity of 4).”

Paper Title: Real-Time Monitoring and Control of Critical Process Impurities during the Manufacture of Fostamatinib Disodium
Problem_Description: Mass balance (full recovery of start material and product) is only achieved at the very beginning or end of the reaction; between 20 % and 80 % conversion a large fraction of material is unaccounted for, indicating loss of material to an undetected intermediate and resulting in sub‑optimal yields.
Solution_Description: Multivariate analysis (PCA, MCR‑ALS) of the inline UV/vis data uncovered a fourth UV‑active component (intermediate X), a tetrahedral adduct that is unstable to offline HPLC.  Recognising this species explained the mass‑balance gap and permitted a more accurate kinetic model and yield prediction.
Supporting_Evidence: “A three‑component model left significant structure… suggesting the presence of a fourth UV active chemical component… The fourth reaction component indicated by the analysis above (intermediate X) is most‑likely a tetrahedral adduct… and is clearly unstable to the attempted (aqueous) HPLC analyses causing erroneous kinetic analysis and incomplete mass balance.”

Paper Title: Real-Time Monitoring and Control of Critical Process Impurities during the Manufacture of Fostamatinib Disodium
Problem_Description: Phenol side‑products (5 and 6) form toward the end of the reaction and continue to increase after the main conversion is complete.  Repeated offline sampling caused fouling of the sampling loop at large scale, leading to inconsistent HPLC results and difficulty controlling impurity levels.
Solution_Description: An ATR‑based inline UV/vis probe was selected because it samples only the solution phase, avoiding contact with solids and eliminating loop fouling.  The in‑line model provides a reliable EoR signal, removing the need for frequent offline sampling and enabling tight control of phenol levels (<1 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “As the reaction in question is heterogeneous, attenuated total reflectance (ATR) sampling was deemed to be a robust and reliable way to make the process measurement by minimizing the risk of probe fouling due to heterogeneity (solids).”; “Repeated reaction sampling of this process (for offline analysis) has been shown previously to lead to problems with fouling of the sampling loop at large scale resulting in inconsistent analyses.”

Paper Title: Real-Time Monitoring and Control of Critical Process Impurities during the Manufacture of Fostamatinib Disodium
Problem_Description: During the manufacturing campaign an erroneous charge of input material caused the reaction rate to increase unexpectedly, which would have been missed without real‑time monitoring, risking excess phenol formation and batch failure.
Solution_Description: The same inline UV/vis PAT system was used to detect the abnormal kinetic profile in real time, allowing operators to intervene before the reaction passed EoR and to avoid a failed batch.
Supporting_Evidence: “The inline analysis tool proved of even greater value… allowing for real‑time identification of a non‑standard reaction profile arising from erroneous charging of input materials… Without inline analysis, it is probable that this error… would not have been identified until after EoR had been passed, greatly increasing the risk of batch failure.”

Problem_Description: Using an ester instead of the Evans oxazolidinone chiral auxiliary gave very poor diastereoselectivity in the epoxidation step, reducing the usable product yield.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to the Evans chiral auxiliary (oxazolidinone) as the protecting group, which restored high diastereoselectivity (>99 % de) and excellent yield (91 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
- “When the oxazolidinone was replaced by the ester, the diastereoselectivity of the epoxidation reaction was very poor.”
- “We were pleased to find out that the following epoxidation reaction of 6 could be carried out smoothly and gave 7 in 91 % yield with excellent diastereoselectivity (d.e. >99 %).”

Paper Title: A Facile, Six-Step Process for the Synthesis of (3
Problem_Description: The S_N2 ring‑opening of epoxide 7 with bromide failed under a variety of halide sources (NaBr, KBr, LiBr, KI) – only starting material was recovered, giving essentially zero conversion.
Solution_Description: The conversion was rescued by (i) adding an acidic additive (2 equiv HBr) to generate an acidic medium, (ii) using Mg(ClO₄)₂ (3 equiv) as a Lewis‑acid promoter, (iii) switching the solvent to THF and (iv) increasing the equivalents of LiBr (5 equiv) and Mg(ClO₄)₂ (10 equiv) to 5 equiv/10 equiv respectively, which gave 82 % isolated yield of bromide 8.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The bromination of (4S,5S)-epoxide 7 using sodium bromide in DMF/H₂O was initially attempted, but only the starting material was recovered even after heating to 120 °C for 24 h (Table 1, entry 1).”
- “An enhancement in the conversion to 8 was achieved with the use of 2 equiv of HBr as the bromide source (Table 1, entry 5).”
- “Mg(ClO₄)₂ proved to be the best acidic additive (Table 1, entry 10).”
- “After screening of the solvent and the reaction temperature, THF was finally chosen as the reaction solvent at 80 °C (Table 1, entry 16).”
- “Consequently, 5 equiv of LiBr/10 equiv of Mg(ClO₄)₂ was used (Table 1, entry 18)… gave 82 % yield.”

Paper Title: A Facile, Six-Step Process for the Synthesis of (3
Problem_Description: When the loading of LiBr and Mg(ClO₄)₂ was increased beyond a certain point, the reaction mixture became too viscous to stir smoothly, limiting further scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors limited the equivalents of LiBr to 5 equiv and Mg(ClO₄)₂ to 10 equiv (instead of higher amounts) to keep the reaction mixture fluid enough for efficient stirring while still maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- Footnote g of Table 1: “The reaction mixture was too viscous to be stirred smoothly.”
- “Considering the cost and the fact that adding more LiBr and Mg(ClO₄)₂ made the reaction mixture too viscous to be stirred smoothly (Table 1, entry 19).”

Paper Title: A Facile, Six-Step Process for the Synthesis of (3
Problem_Description: The direct azidation of bromide 8 with NaN₃ under basic conditions gave low conversion and generated significant amounts of elimination by‑products 9a and 9b.
Solution_Description: A quaternary ammonium salt, n‑C₈H₁₇₃NMeCl, was added as a weak buffer to moderate the basicity of the reaction medium; this suppressed elimination, eliminated by‑product formation, and afforded the azide 9 in 95 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “An increase of reaction temperature and the amount of NaN₃ (3 equiv) accelerated the conversion… but the eliminated by‑products 9a and 9b were formed preferentially. The formation of 9a and 9b was caused by the alkaline reaction conditions (Table 2, entry 2).”
- “We found that (n‑C₈H₁₇)₃NMeCl gave the best results and promoted the azidation reaction to give 9 in 95 % yield without any by‑products formation (Table 2, entry 6).”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of an Edivoxetine·HCl Intermediate via an Efficient Diazotization Process

Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors replaced 2‑CAN with d‑serine as the chiral feedstock, devised a controlled‑addition, low‑temperature diazotization protocol with venting, limited drying temperatures for the epoxide, swapped MTBE for the greener 2‑MeTHF solvent, telescoped bromohydrin generation directly into the epoxidation step, exploited the differential solubility of epoxide 7 and KBr in methanol for purification, selected tert‑amyl alcohol for the ring‑closure to avoid ether side‑products, employed a water‑addition strategy to improve mixing and reduce diol impurity formation, and used T3P coupling at ≤5 °C in toluene/DIEA to suppress Hofmann‑elimination impurities.

For this reason, the maximum drying temperature for epoxide 7 was restricted to not more than 50 °C.", "A known purification method is an ethanolic recrystallization of epoxide 7, but this procedure has low throughput due to the poor solubility of both the epoxide and KBr in ethanol.", "Potassium bases such as potassium tert‑butoxide, potassium tert‑amylate, and potassium hydroxide in alcoholic solvents resulted in complete conversion but also caused partial racemization.", "The addition of more water beyond the nominal amount brought in by the 50 % aqueous base improved the conversion but produced higher levels of diol impurity 14, which suppressed the yield.", "The ring‑closure was performed in 16 volumes of tert‑amyl alcohol with 2 equiv of 50 % NaOH‑aq and the addition of 17 equiv of water after 1–2 h of reaction time. Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of an Edivoxetine·HCl Intermediate via an Efficient Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: During the diazotization step the addition of aqueous sodium nitrite generated a large exotherm (≈290 kJ mol⁻¹) and caused rapid pressure buildup and foaming; the extraction of bromohydrin with MTBE required ≈30 volumes of solvent, making the work‑up inefficient and environmentally unfriendly.
