Supporting_Evidence: ["Colorimetric measurements revealed a 290 kJ/mol exotherm for the sodium nitrite addition, which translated to a potential adiabatic heat rise of 70 °C.", "The diazotization step was operated safely on scale by using a carefully controlled addition rate of the sodium nitrite solution and temperature control (<5 °C reaction temperature) in combination with adequate venting.", "These were mass‑inefficient, requiring ∼30 volumes (L kg⁻¹) of MTBE, which is a solvent of environmental concern.", "Several potential replacement solvents were screened, and 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2‑MeTHF) was found to be a superior extraction solvent, allowing 90 % partitioning of bromohydrin 6 into the organic layer with two extractions."]

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of an Edivoxetine·HCl Intermediate via an Efficient Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Epoxide 7 is thermally sensitive (decomposes above 130 °C) and has low solubility in ethanol, while the co‑product KBr is also poorly soluble, leading to a sluggish recrystallization and low throughput.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to methanol, where epoxide 7 is ≈10‑fold more soluble than KBr, allowing removal of the bulk of KBr by filtration and obtaining a 90 % recovery of epoxide 7; the process also avoided the low‑throughput ethanolic recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A known purification method is an ethanolic recrystallization of epoxide 7, but this procedure has low throughput due to the poor solubility of both the epoxide and KBr in ethanol.", "Since the optimal solvent in the next processing step is methanol, we decided to telescope the purification of 7 with the subsequent nucleophilic addition reaction.", "It should be noted that other literature references mentioned the use of methanol for the preparation of 7, but the yield and purity from these procedures were unclear.", "Since the optimal solvent in the next processing step is methanol, we decided to telescope the purification of 7 with the subsequent nucleophilic addition reaction."]

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of an Edivoxetine·HCl Intermediate via an Efficient Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Using potassium bases for the ring‑closure caused partial racemization and formation of ether impurities when primary or secondary alcohols were employed; the reaction also generated diol impurity 14 when insufficient water was present.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Sodium bases (NaOt‑Bu, NaOt‑Amyl, NaOH) were adopted to avoid racemization; tert‑amyl alcohol, a tertiary alcohol, was selected as the solvent to suppress ether formation; additional water (≥8 equiv) was added after 1–2 h to improve slurry dissolution and eliminate the diol impurity, addressing mass‑transfer limitations on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Potassium bases such as potassium tert‑butoxide, potassium tert‑amylate, and potassium hydroxide in alcoholic solvents resulted in complete conversion but also caused partial racemization.", "Sodium bases ... all gave good conversion without racemization.", "Because this side reaction is prevented with a tertiary alcohol, tert‑amyl alcohol became the preferred solvent for the cyclization reaction.", "The addition of more water beyond the nominal amount brought in by the 50 % aqueous base improved the conversion but produced higher levels of diol impurity 14.", "We found that the addition of at least 8 equiv of water after 1–2 h of reaction time solved this problem.", "We surmised that on larger scales mass transfer issues were prevalent and that large particles of starting material were not efficiently broken up by the mechanical agitation."]

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of an Edivoxetine·HCl Intermediate via an Efficient Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: During the final amide‑formation with T3P, the Hofmann‑elimination pathway generated impurity 18 (>0.1 %) when the reaction temperature exceeded 5 °C, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: The coupling was performed in toluene/DIEA, adding T3P slowly at 0 °C and maintaining the reaction mixture below 5 °C throughout, which suppressed formation of impurity 18 to <0.05 %; the chosen solvent also simplified work‑up and was compatible with the downstream isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initial evaluation of T3P as a coupling reagent produced levels of amide impurity 18 (>0.1 %), likely via a Hofmann elimination‑type mechanism.", "We found that the formation of this impurity could be suppressed (<0.05 %) by maintaining the reaction mixture at less than 5 °C.", "Ultimately toluene/DIEA was the best solvent/base combination for the amide formation.", "The reaction components were combined, and the solution was cooled to 0 °C, after which 1.2 equiv of T3P was slowly added, keeping the reaction temperature below 5 °C."]

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Synthetic and Purification Process of S‑2367 (Velneperit), a Novel Neuropeptide Y (NPY) Y5 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The early synthetic route required six chemical steps, gave an overall isolated yield of only 59 % and used a large amount of solvents (seven solvent types, including toxic DMF), resulting in high material cost and safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was revised to start from commercially available trans‑1‑ethoxycarbonyl‑4‑aminocyclohexane hydrochloride (12), eliminating the esterification‑isomerization sequence, reducing the number of steps to four, and replacing DMF with toluene/water. The telescoped sequence also simplified work‑up and lowered solvent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The process could be tolerable for scale‑up, but there was still room for improvement in synthetic route, yield, and productivity.”
• “The overall yield from the starting material was increased from 59 % to 83 %… The number of chemical reactions was reduced from 6 to 4.”
• “DMF… could be substituted by toluene and water.”
• “The starting material was changed from 5 to trans‑1‑ethoxycarbonyl‑4‑aminocyclohexane hydrochloride salt (12)… The change could remove esterification and isomerization from the manufacturing process.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Synthetic and Purification Process of S‑2367 (Velneperit), a Novel Neuropeptide Y (NPY) Y5 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Controlling the residual impurity 14 in intermediate 10 required either extending the oxidation time or adding excess H₂O₂/catalyst, which would increase processing time and material cost.
Solution_Description: Switching the catalyst from (NH₄)₆Mo₇O₂₄·4H₂O to inexpensive Na₂WO₄·2H₂O and performing the Na₂WO₄/H₂O₂ oxidation under weakly basic pH 9.0–9.5 accelerated the reaction, eliminating the need for longer reaction times or higher reagent loadings.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “It could be achieved by extending reaction time and increasing the amount of H₂O₂ and/or catalyst, but they might increase the processing time and the material cost.”
• “We changed the catalyst … because the latter was more inexpensive.”
• Table 2 shows that at pH 9.0 the residual 13 after 2.5 h was 0.00 % versus 0.07 % at pH 8.0, indicating faster conversion.
• “The oxidation reaction in the weakly basic condition … was faster than that under nearly neutral conditions.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Synthetic and Purification Process of S‑2367 (Velneperit), a Novel Neuropeptide Y (NPY) Y5 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The Na₂WO₄/H₂O₂ oxidation is highly exothermic (total heat 332 kJ mol⁻¹) and generates oxygen gas, creating a combustion risk if flammable toluene vapor is present.
Solution_Description: The process controls heat by adding H₂O₂ slowly, removes toluene vapor prior to reaction (partial pressure ≤0.012 atm), and operates at temperatures well below the maximum temperature of synthesis reaction (87.6 °C) and water’s boiling point, thus keeping the reaction safe.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “As oxygen gas was continuously released by decomposition of H₂O₂ in the reaction, we removed flammable toluene before the reaction (partial toluene vapor pressure/atmospheric pressure ≤0.012).”
• “Reaction heat could be controlled by addition of H₂O₂ (Figure 3), and the maximum temperature attainable by the synthesis reaction (MTSR; 87.6 °C) was lower than the boiling point of water (100 °C).”
• “Total reaction heat; 332 kJ mol⁻¹, process temperature; 25 °C adiabatic temperature; 62.6 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Synthetic and Purification Process of S‑2367 (Velneperit), a Novel Neuropeptide Y (NPY) Y5 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: During pilot scale recrystallization in 95 % acetone/water, the crude product hydrolyzed, increasing impurity 10 (acid) from ≤0.04 % to ≈0.08 %–0.09 %, a deviation that was not observed in flask‑scale batches because the hold time was not controlled.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A slurry‑washing step was introduced that uses only acetone and water to effect a solvent‑mediated polymorphic transformation (form II → form I) while simultaneously removing the entrapped acid, eliminating hydrolysis and stabilising the product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The impurity 10 in purified 1 was 0.08 w/w %… which did not meet the specification.”
• “We compared the increase… in 95 % acetone/water … the increase … about five times higher than that in 100 % acetone.”
• “The dissolution of crude 1 in 95 % acetone/water was highly acidic … it was thought to cause acidic hydrolysis.”
• “The solvent‑mediated polymorphic transformation by slurrying … prevented hydrolysis and removed the residual acid.”
• “By the clever polymorph control using only acetone and water, the purified 1 including 0.00 % of 10 could be produced in the pilot manufacturing.”

Paper Title: Development of an Optimized Synthetic and Purification Process of S‑2367 (Velneperit), a Novel Neuropeptide Y (NPY) Y5 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Even with slurry washing, the removal rate of impurity 10 during recrystallization varied widely (36 %–73 %) because the acid could interact ionically with the basic pyridyl group of 1, limiting its precipitation.
Solution_Description: A weak‑base (NaHCO₃) was added to neutralise the residual acid, forming a salt of impurity 10 that stays soluble in the 80 % acetone/water mixture; the process then uses staged concentration‑and‑water‑addition to precipitate pure 1 while keeping the impurity salt in solution, raising the removal rate to > 83 % with a reproducible 94.7 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The removal rate of 10 … fluctuated … considered to be the possible weak interaction of acid 10 with the basic pyridyl group of 1.”
• “We examined several weak bases … NaHCO₃ … improved the removal rate to 80 % due to the completion of salt formation.”
• “The precipitation point of form I was set at 80 % acetone/water … the solubility of the sodium salt of 10 was sufficiently large.”
• “By the changes, the removal rate of 10 was dramatically and reproducibly increased to more than 83 %.”
• “Using the recrystallization procedure, we could produce purified 1 with no 10 at an average 94.7 % yield.”

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: The originally reported Pd‑catalyzed coupling of 4‑bromobenzothiophene with unprotected piperazine generated impurities 2 and 3 that were difficult to remove by crystallization, and it required an expensive palladium catalyst.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the palladium‑coupling step by a nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorobenzaldehyde with tert‑butyl‑piperazine‑1‑carboxylate, eliminating the need for the costly catalyst and avoiding the troublesome impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the first step, 4‑bromobenzo[ b ]thiophene was coupled … using tris‑(dibenzylideneacetone)‑dipalladium … this process suffered from the formation of impurities 2 and 3 … which are difficult to remove via a crystallization method.”; “An alternative process … using protected piperazine and an expensive catalyst …”; “The strategy of replacement rather than coupling was used … to avoid the formation of impurities … and the use of an expensive catalyst.”

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: During the SNAr step, using too little tert‑butyl‑piperazine (9) gave incomplete conversion of 2‑chloro‑6‑fluorobenzaldehyde (11), while excess 9 produced impurity 16, lowering overall purity.
Solution_Description: The optimal stoichiometry was identified as 1.1 equiv of compound 9 per equiv of 11, delivering 93 % of the desired arylpiperazine (12) with only ~1 % impurity 16.
Supporting_Evidence: “Lower amounts of compound 9 gave incomplete conversion … higher amounts gave more of impurity 16.”; “HPLC result indicated the reaction mixture contained 93 % of compound 12 … 1 % of impurity 16.”; “Finally, optimum equivalent of compound 9 was found to be 1.1 equiv, based on compound 11.”

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: Acetonitrile proved unsuitable for the SNAr reaction, giving very low conversion of dihalide 11 to arylpiperazine 12 even at its boiling point (81 °C).
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidinone (NMP) provided high conversion and good product quality, making it the preferred solvent for this step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of acetonitrile was avoided since very low conversion of dihalide 11 to arylpiperazine 12 was observed even at its boiling point (81 °C).”; “N‑Methyl‑2‑pyrrolidinone was found to be a good solvent for this step in terms of both product yield and quality.”

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: The work‑up of arylpiperazine 12 required careful precipitation; an excessive acetone‑to‑water ratio reduced yield, and the product needed a clean isolation step.
Solution_Description: An optimized acetone/water mixture was employed to precipitate 12, followed by a reslurry in n‑heptane (which is recovered and reused), affording 94 % isolated yield with only 4 % of by‑product 15.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ratio of acetone and water was important for the precipitation of compound 12 … a higher ratio of acetone resulted in a yield reduction.”; “The precipitated compound 12 was purified by reslurrying in n‑heptane, which can be recovered in high yield and reused in the next batch… (94 % yield).”

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: Using DIPEA (or triethylamine) as the base in the cyclization of 12 with thioglycollic acid ethyl ester gave only ~30 % conversion, even with excess electrophile.

Paper Title: An Improved Synthesis of 4‑(1-Piperazinyl)benzo[
Problem_Description: Attempts to replace DMF with greener solvents (toluene, dioxane, acetonitrile, ethanol) in the cyclization step resulted in low conversion and reduced yields.

Problem_Description: The tert‑butoxycarbonyl (Boc) protecting group on piperazine (compound 14) partially decomposes in heated DMF, generating ~6 % impurity 17, which required removal.

Problem_Description: Isolation of the final product 18 required efficient removal of solvents and impurities to reach >99 % purity.

Paper Title: Selection of a Suitable Physical Form and Development of a Crystallization Process for a PDE10A Inhibitor Exhibiting Enantiotropic Polymorphism
Problem_Description: During crystallization the opposite polymorph (Form 1) could appear when trying to isolate the desired Form 2. Solution_Description: Implemented a controlled seeded antisolvent crystallization where the antisolvent (water) is added to a hot DMSO solution of the API and 1 wt % Form 2 seed is introduced. This inverse‑addition protocol forces growth of the thermodynamically stable Form 2 and eliminates the risk of accidental Form 1 nucleation.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: The hydrochloride salt of the amino‑alcohol (2·HCl) has an extremely low solubility in THF (< 0.01 mg/g at 50 °C), resulting in a slurry‑to‑slurry free‑basing step where 2·HCl, free base 2 and Et₃N·HCl are only partially dissolved. This limits mass transfer and creates a heterogeneous mixture that makes the reaction difficult to control on scale.
Solution_Description: The model explicitly incorporated a solid‑liquid mass‑transfer term and the low solubility of 2·HCl (set to 0.01 mg/g) and the process was run at a slightly higher THF volume (3.04 L mol⁻¹) to reduce concentration of the slurry components, improving mixing and mass transfer without changing the solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Since the measured solubility of 2·HCl is very low … the solubility of 2·HCl was set to 0.01 mg/g” (Section 2.2.1).

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: Excess benzoyl isothiocyanate (BzNCS) and triethylamine (Et₃N) in step 7a generate side‑products (impurities 9, 10, 11) and consume the starting material, lowering overall yield and causing batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: The optimal stoichiometry was identified as 1.05 equiv Et₃N and 1.15 equiv BzNCS (instead of 1.1 and 1.0). BzNCS addition time was increased to 120 min and free‑basing was set to 30 min, allowing the thiourea to form before excess BzNCS is present; reaction time was limited to 60 min to avoid over‑conversion to impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The optimized conditions reduced Et₃N equiv and increased BzNCS equiv compared to the original conditions” (Section 3.1).

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: Prolonged step 7b/7c reaction times lead to additional formation of impurity 13 and unknown by‑products, decreasing the isolated yield of the aminothiazine.
Solution_Description: CDI was limited to 1.02 equiv (instead of 1.0–5.0) and added in three 20‑min shots; the cyclization step was performed immediately after CDI addition with a rapid temperature ramp to 68 °C (near reflux) and no hold time, eliminating the need for a separate step 7b hold.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The CDI equiv were set to 1.02 equiv … The optimized step 7b reaction time was set to zero minutes, and the step 7c reaction temperature was set close to reflux (68 °C)” (Section 3.3).

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: Changing THF volume away from the original 9.5 volumes caused either a concentration‑driven increase in impurities 9/10 (low volume) or a slowdown of step 7a leading to unreacted 2 and impurity 8 (high volume).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A modest increase to 10 volumes of THF (≈1.1× the original) was selected, balancing concentration to keep impurity formation low while maintaining acceptable mass‑transfer rates.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A higher THF volume decreases the BzNCS concentration and decreases the reaction rate… The model predicted that if the reaction volume was increased … to 1.5–2 times … would lead to an increase in yield … it was decided to slightly increase the reaction volume to 10 volumes” (Section 3.4).

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: BzNCS slowly hydrolyzes in the presence of trace water (and Et₃N as catalyst) to form N‑benzoyl‑benzamide (16), consuming reagent and generating a potentially hazardous impurity.
Solution_Description: Water content was limited (Karl Fischer < 0.05 % w/w) and Et₃N‑catalyzed decomposition pathways were explicitly modeled; the process was kept dry to suppress BzNCS hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The decomposition of BzNCS in the presence of water and triethylamine to form N‑benzoylbenzamide (16) was added to the model” (Section 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Optimization of an Aminothiazine Ring Formation: Integrating Modeling with Experiments to Maximize Yield by Minimizing Impurity Formation
Problem_Description: Charging solid CDI followed by rapid heating could generate localized exotherms, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: CDI was added in three small portions (0.34 equiv each) over 20‑min intervals while maintaining the mixture at a lower temperature; the temperature was only ramped to reflux after the last CDI addition, minimizing instantaneous heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: • “For safety reasons, it was preferred to charge CDI and then increase the temperature of the batch” (Reference 20).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-Up of a Benzoxazepine-Containing Kinase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the discovery synthesis of bromobenzoxazepine 2, reduction of the lactam with complexed lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) gave variable levels of debromination, up to 40 % on a 500 g scale, resulting in low overall yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The reduction step was changed to a borane·THF reduction, which avoids the debromination and gives higher conversion. The addition of borane was performed slowly at controlled temperature (35 °C) to manage heat evolution and hydrogen gas formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reduction of the lactam to the amine was accomplished using complexed lithium aluminum hydride… however, varying levels of debromination were observed… on a 500 g scale, up to 40 % yield of the by‑product 12…”, "The problem of debromination… could be mitigated by using borane as the reducing agent…", "The reaction mixture was stirred for 4 h at 35 °C… a large excess of borane was required…", "Calorimetric evaluation showed that the heat evolution… could be controlled by the rate of addition"

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-Up of a Benzoxazepine-Containing Kinase Inhibitor

Solution_Description: The work‑up was changed to precipitate the imide from heptane after cooling, avoiding the aqueous basic quench that caused hydrolysis. The acidic quench was performed with a controlled addition of acid to keep the pH low and prevent formation of the acid‑amide.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: During the first amidation (addition of aniline 3 to squarate diester 2) a significant amount of the bis‑amide by‑product 9 formed (up to 12 area % in early campaigns), reducing isolated yield and purity of intermediate 7.
Solution_Description: The addition protocol was changed to a slow, controlled addition of the aniline solution into a basic squarate solution, keeping the reaction homogeneous and preventing local excess that leads to over‑addition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Control of the bis‑amide impurity 9 in the following amination step remained a key concern… the ideal 1:1 stoichiometry… was more easily achieved by ensuring that a homogeneous solution of the aniline was slowly added to a basic solution of the squarate diester… limiting over‑reaction.”; “Table 1 shows the bis‑amide impurity falling from 12 area % (research) to <0.1 area % (clinical) with the new addition strategy.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: In the kilogram‑scale campaign the drug substance 1 (choline salt) did not fully dissolve in ethanol prior to antisolvent addition, preventing true crystallization and leading to a lower isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Crystallization was switched to a methanol/isopropanol solvent system with seeding and n‑heptane as antisolvent, allowing complete dissolution, true crystal formation and high purity (≥99.9 area %).
Supporting_Evidence: “...incomplete dissolution of substance 1 in ethanol prior to addition of n‑heptane as antisolvent… Isolated purity was nonetheless high at 99.03 area % with 93 % recovered yield.”; “For the second preclinical campaign an additional crystallization of 1 from methanol/isopropanol was initiated, which substantially purged the structural isomer present as major impurity (98.5 area %).”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Squarate diester 2 and several intermediates decompose violently at elevated temperature (e.g., 170 °C for 2, >‑1000 J g⁻¹ for other intermediates), presenting a serious thermal‑runaway hazard on scale.
Solution_Description: Maximum jacket temperatures were set for each step, and a head‑tank solvent reservoir was added as a boiling‑barrier in the pilot plant. Comprehensive hazard analyses and temperature‑monitoring safeguards were implemented.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 2 undergoes decomposition from 170 °C, releasing considerable energy… each pure compound providing greater than –1000 J g⁻¹ at temperatures starting from 100 °C… maximal jacket temperatures were implemented… a head‑tank of solvent was connected to provide an additional boiling‑barrier in case of thermal runaway.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: A structural isomer impurity appeared during the kilogram campaign due to poor purge efficiency, necessitating a recrystallization from acetonitrile/ethanol that reduced the step yield to 74 %.
Solution_Description: Supplier quality control of 3‑pentylamine 4 was tightened to prevent formation of the isomer, and later a crystallization using methanol/isopropanol antisolvent was adopted, eliminating the impurity without sacrificing yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Very poor purge efficiency… a new byproduct… was observed… Very rapid development of a recrystallization from acetonitrile/ethanol (reduction to 1.1 area %), but at the cost of yield on this step (74 %).”; “Tighter control at the supplier of the 3‑pentylamine 4 was sufficient to control quality downstream in later campaigns.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The original route required a tri‑ethylammonium phenolate salt isolation, a subsequent acid‑base salt exchange, and a separate choline addition, adding material cost and process variability.
Solution_Description: The tri‑ethylammonium phenolate salt was isolated and used directly in the second amination, eliminating the salt‑exchange step. Later, choline hydroxide was employed as both base and salt‑forming agent, collapsing two steps into one.
Supporting_Evidence: “Further reduction of 9 was achieved by directly isolating the triethylammonium phenolate salt… Eliminating the salt exchange operation led to an increase in isolated yield (81 %) and purity (99 %).”; “Choline hydroxide is highly basic… and was used as both base during the addition of aniline 3 to the new intermediate 11 as well as salt‑forming agent to directly arrive at compound 1 without need for the former salt‑switching.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: In the second amination, the tri‑ethylammonium phenolate salt of 7 displayed limited solubility in the ethanol/THF mixture, hindering reaction progress and productivity.
Solution_Description: The solvent system was switched to methanol, which fully dissolved the salt and allowed addition‑controlled amination, raising the isolated yield of 8 to 98 % with high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the second amine addition… the triethylammonium phenolate salt of compound 7 was again directly taken, but due to the limited solubility in ethanol (the solvent used in the second preclinical campaign), a switch was made to methanol which thereby increased the productivity of the reaction and rendered it addition‑controlled.”

Paper Title: Early Process Development of a Squaramide-Based CXCR2 Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Multiple isolated work‑up steps (isolations, filtrations, solvent swaps) introduced batch‑to‑batch variability and increased operational complexity.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot telescoped sequence was developed where 3‑pentylamine 4 and aniline 3 (as choline salt) are added sequentially to the squarate diester 2 in the same reactor, delivering the final drug substance 1 directly after a single antisolvent addition.
Supporting_Evidence: “A one‑pot variant starting from the 3‑pentylamine 4 and obtaining the drug substance 1 from the same reactor by simple sequential addition of amines… was highly feasible.”; “The product 1 was precipitated from solution by addition of n‑heptane as antisolvent rendering the sequence highly streamlined.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: The reaction of compound 6 with methyl formate uses NaH as the base.  NaH is considered unsafe and unattractive for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A systematic screen for alternative bases was performed, leading to the selection of a safer, more scalable base (e.g., NaOMe).
Supporting_Evidence: “First, the use of NaH is not attractive, and as such screening for an alternative base to mediate this reaction would be required to evaluate more attractive options.”; “sodium (25.7 g, 1.12 mol) was added in portions … NaOMe (prepared as described above) …”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: During the Pinner‑type condensation, formamidine acetate sublimates, building up solids that clog the condenser, making the step difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the Pinner condensation and devised a three‑step route that bypasses this problematic transformation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the Pinner reaction on the laboratory scale, we observed sublimation of the formamidine acetate from the reaction mixture leading to build‑up and clogging of the condenser.”; “The newly developed route mitigates the safety concerns, reduces the number of steps from five to three, avoids column chromatography…”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: The literature sequence gave only a 30 % overall yield over two steps and required chromatographic purification of intermediate 8, which is a major obstacle for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new three‑step synthesis from inexpensive 4,6‑dichloro‑5‑methoxypyrimidine was developed, eliminating chromatography and increasing the overall yield eight‑fold.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the overall yield of 30 % over the two steps and the required chromatographic separation of 8 were a major obstacle to scale‑up this compound.”; “The newly developed route… reduces the number of steps from five to three, avoids column chromatography, leads to an 8‑fold improvement in yield…”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: Chlorination with POCl₃ traditionally uses a large excess of the reagent, which creates a hazardous exothermic quench and generates a large waste burden.
Solution_Description: The method was redesigned to employ stoichiometric‑level POCl₃ with careful control of addition order and rate, minimizing excess, heat release, and waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “Typically in the research setting, a large excess of POCl₃ at reflux is employed… leading to a hazardous exothermic quenching operation… the reaction only requires a slight excess of POCl₃ to proceed.”; “In our initial studies on multigram scale… removed the bulk of the excess POCl₃ through distillation… The issue now becomes carrying out the controlled quench on the residual gum.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: The O‑demethylation step uses n‑BuSH (toxic, flammable, extremely odorous) together with NaH (thermal runaway risk), and affords only modest yields requiring chromatography.
Solution_Description: The thiol was replaced with odorless 1‑dodecanethiol and NaH was replaced by NaOMe; the reaction in DMF at 120 °C gave 87 % isolated yield with a simple aqueous work‑up and no chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Concerns with handling n‑BuSH based on its toxicity, flammability and the fact that it is a known irritant… the use of DMF and NaH is known to present a thermal hazard on scale.”; “Switching NaH for NaOMe and reacting … in the presence of 1‑dodecanthiol … gave … 87 % yield … with no column chromatography.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of 4‑Aminopyrimidin-5-ol, a Versatile Intermediate
Problem_Description: Buchwald and Ullmann couplings of 4‑aminopyrimidine (11) failed to give useful product; the free amine likely chelates the metal catalyst, and Boc‑protected substrate showed deprotection and poor conversion.
Solution_Description: The synthetic plan was switched to the readily available 4,6‑dichloro‑5‑methoxypyrimidine (17), avoiding the problematic amine and enabling a robust three‑step sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “In none of these reactions could synthetically useful levels of the product be detected… We hypothesized that perhaps the aminopyrimidine was inhibiting the desired reaction… Across the series of reaction conditions evaluated, the desired product was readily observed; however, competing loss of one of the Boc protecting groups…”.; “At this time, we switched our attention to utilize 4,6‑dichloro‑5‑methoxypyrimidine 17 as an alternative pyrimidine‑based starting material.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Reactions performed in THF or acetonitrile gave very poor results because 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid (and other additives) were insufficiently soluble, causing heterogeneous slugs and difficult mixing.
Solution_Description: Switch to N‑methyl‑2‑pyrrolidone (NMP) as the reaction solvent, which fully dissolves the aryl‑boronic acid and additives, enabling a homogeneous flow and reliable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["reactions conducted in tetrahydrofuran or acetonitrile (ACN) were very troublesome due to the lack of solubility of the 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid and other additives.", "An NMP solution of 4‑methoxyphenylboronic acid (1 mmol) and cyclohex‑2‑enone (3 mmol) was placed in the first inlet."]

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 70 °C (especially >120 °C) a substantial amount of black palladium precipitation formed, which frequently blocked the microchannel and interrupted the oxidative dehydrogenation step.
Solution_Description: Identify 70 °C as the optimal temperature to avoid palladium black formation and employ the Pd(CH₃CN)₄(BF₄)₂/6,6′‑dimethyl‑2,2′‑bipyridyl catalyst system, which gave high conversion with minimal precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The yields in the range 40–70 °C increased with increasing reaction temperature… a significant amount of black precipitation was observed in the microchannel over 120 °C.", "The combination of Pd(CH₃CN)₄(BF₄)₂ and 6,6′‑dimethyl‑2,2′‑bipyridyl was found to be superior for both conversion and selectivity."]

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: In the conventional batch reactor the oxidative Heck step required up to several days (360 min) to reach 90 % yield, and only 20 % yield was obtained after 20 min, making the process inefficient for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implement a capillary microreactor (T‑junction + simple capillary) that provides a high surface‑to‑volume ratio, dramatically improving O₂ mass transfer and cutting the total sequence time from 2160 min to 130 min.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The capillary microreactor ... enabled oxidative Heck/dehydrogenation on a microgram scale with a shortened reaction time; the total sequence time … was optimized from 2160 min in a traditional batch system to 130 min in the microchemical system.", "Increased surface‑to‑volume ratio in the microchemical systems allows greater mass transfer."]

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Scaling the oxidative Heck reaction was hindered by the limited contact area between gaseous oxygen and the liquid phase; as reactor volume increased, the contact area per volume dropped, reducing feasibility for industrial scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopt a tube‑in‑tube microreactor (gas‑permeable AF‑2400 inner tube) that separates gas and liquid streams while maintaining high O₂ permeability, providing consistent mass transfer and enabling gram‑scale synthesis without the need for large gas‑liquid contact interfaces.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The tube‑in‑tube microreactor … successfully performed a gram‑scale synthesis under the optimized safety and economic conditions.", "The working volume in the tube‑in‑tube microreactor is consistent due to the separation of the gas and liquid channels."]

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: High‑pressure batch reactions (>5 atm O₂) required special reactors, were difficult to handle, and consumed >100‑fold excess reagents, raising safety and economic concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Operate the microreactors at moderate oxygen pressures (1.3–5.0 atm) with precise pressure control, and use stoichiometric amounts of reagents (microgram‑scale in capillary, gram‑scale in tube‑in‑tube) to minimize reagent waste and avoid the hazards of high‑pressure vessels.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The oxygen pressure in the microchemical system was one of the key parameters; it was much more important above 50 °C.", "high‑pressure reaction in a traditional batch system requires a special reactor that suffers from somewhat difficult handling and high reagent consumption (>100 times)."]

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Uncontrolled bubble formation in the tube‑in‑tube reactor led to inconsistent residence times and occasional channel blockage, compromising reproducibility.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adjust injection rates (500–1000 µL min⁻¹) and operating conditions to suppress bubble formation, ensuring a steady dissolved‑gas environment and consistent product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["bubble formation in tube‑in‑tube microreactor should be suppressed to obtain consistent results.", "The injection rates were varied in the range 500–1000 µL/min, and bubble formation … should be suppressed."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Previously reported routes (enzyme‑catalysed exchange, S‑acetyl‑thiophenol, thioacetic acid) gave low isolated yields (≈70 % or less), required tedious post‑treatment and enzyme dependence, and involved costly reagents, making them unsuitable for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: A new one‑step acylation was devised using CoCl₂ as catalyst in a DMF/TFA (1:1) mixed solvent, which afforded the target S‑acetyl‑l‑glutathione in 89–91 % isolated yield with easy work‑up, eliminating the need for enzymes and expensive reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “...the initial method … is unsuccessful in isolating product from the reaction mixture… 70 % yield… enzymatic processes … not suitable for industrial scale….”
2. “...the process would result in poor quality and difficult recycling of the relatively expensive solvent trifluoroacetic acid….”
3. “...CoCl₂ is an effective catalyst for the acylation of GSH by acetyl chloride in the mixed solvent of TFA/DMF (1:1, v/v) at room temperature… The current process increased the overall productivity by 6 %.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: The Galzigna route generated a side‑product (compound 3) up to 0.78 % area by HPLC, which compromised the stability, safety and overall yield of S‑GSH.
Solution_Description: Screening identified CoCl₂ (0.5 % mol) as the optimal catalyst; acetyl chloride was added over 5 min at 0–5 °C and the reaction was run 10 min at 20–30 °C, reducing the impurity to 0.02 % and raising the yield to 89 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Byproduct 3 was formed in the reaction (up to 0.78 area %) and difficult to be removed during purification, which affected the stability and safety of the S‑GSH.”
2. “The best result was obtained on treatment of GSH with acetyl chloride in the presence of 0.5 % mol CoCl₂. The yield of S‑GSH was 89 % in 10 min… impurity content was minimal (0.02 %).”
3. Table 1 (entry 6) shows 0.5 % CoCl₂, 10 min, 100 % conversion, 89 % isolated yield, 0.02 % impurity.

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: ZnCl₂ and ZnO, though active for some thiol‑acetylations, failed to catalyse the acylation of glutathione efficiently, giving only ~80 % conversion and lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: A systematic catalyst screen demonstrated that CoCl₂ and BiCl₃ are highly active; CoCl₂ gave the highest conversion (100 %) and yield (89 %) under the same conditions, solving the low‑yield issue.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “ZnCl₂ is not effective in catalyzing acylation of GSH… The results indicate that CoCl₂ and BiCl₃ are very active for the acylation reaction and CoCl₂ is more effective than BiCl₃.”
2. Table 1 entries 2–4 (ZnCl₂) show 81‑77 % isolated yields, whereas entry 6 (CoCl₂) shows 89 % yield with 100 % conversion.

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Using excess acetyl chloride beyond the stoichiometric requirement did not improve the yield, while insufficient equivalents led to lower conversion.
Solution_Description: The optimum amount of acetyl chloride was identified as 1.1 equiv; this gave an isolated yield of 89 % without further benefit from higher equivalents, balancing material cost and conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “It was found that the yield of compound 1 increased with an increase in amount of acetyl chloride up to 1.1 equiv… at 1.1 equiv, compound 1 was obtained in 89 % yield… a further increase… showed no difference in the yield.”
2. Table 2 entries 1–5 illustrate the plateau in yield at 1.10‑1.20 equiv (all 89 %).

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is expensive and its recovery from DCM/TFA mixtures is difficult; DCM/TFA also leads to solvent‑separation challenges and poor solubility of the GSH‑TFA salt in some co‑solvents.
Solution_Description: A DMF/TFA (1:1, v/v) mixed solvent was selected because DMF dissolves the GSH‑TFA salt, gives high yields (≈91 %) and purity (≥99.6 %), and simplifies TFA recovery compared with DCM/TFA.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “…the mixed solvent of DMF/TFA exhibited even better results… the yield and purity were not obviously decreased… the mixed solvent of TFA/DCM showed satisfactory results, but it was challenging to separate TFA from the recovered solvent.”
2. Table 3 entries 10–13 (DMF/TFA) show yields 90.5–91.0 % and purities ≥99.6 %.
3. “Recycling of solvent TFA could further increase the economic benefits.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Quenching the reaction with water left residual water in recycled TFA that could not be removed by atmospheric distillation; P₂O₅ also failed to dry the recovered acid, jeopardising product quality and safety.
Solution_Description: Methanol (or ethanol) was used as the quenching agent; the excess alcohol is converted to methyl (or ethyl) acetate by treatment with acetyl chloride, and methyl acetate can be easily separated from TFA because of a large boiling‑point gap, delivering dry, reusable TFA.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The recycled TFA was not able to be reused, because the residual water … was not able to be removed by atmospheric distillation.”
2. “Then P₂O₅ was added … but failed to remove the water. To avoid the water, we decided to use alcohol as the quencher… both methanol and ethanol gave promising results.”
3. Table 4 shows methanol quench gives 91 % yield, 99.5 % purity; methyl acetate is easily separated from TFA.

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Using ethanol as the quencher gave ethyl acetate after acetyl‑chloride treatment, which is difficult to separate from TFA because of similar boiling points.
Solution_Description: Methanol was selected over ethanol as the quencher; the resulting methyl acetate can be removed cleanly, avoiding the ethyl‑acetate/TFA overlap.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Methyl acetate was easily separated from the recycled TFA because of the big gap between their boiling points, while ethyl acetate was difficult to be separated due to the similar boiling points. So, we chose methanol as the quencher.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Preparation of
Problem_Description: Initial TFA recovery with 1 equiv acetyl chloride gave only 97.6 % TFA purity; residual methanol remained, lowering recycle efficiency.
Solution_Description: Increasing acetyl chloride to 2 equiv fully acetylates residual methanol, converting it to methyl acetate and raising TFA purity to >99 % (99.2 % at 2 equiv), enabling efficient reuse.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. Table 5 entry 1 (1 equiv) shows TFA purity >97.6 % with <1.2 % methanol.
2. Table 5 entry 3 (2 equiv) shows TFA purity >99.2 % with <0.1 % methanol.

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: The racemic alcohol RS‑1 was not fully soluble in the reaction solvent (2‑methyltetrahydrofuran) at the start of the lipase‑catalysed succinylation, which limited the effective concentration of substrate and contributed to sub‑optimal conversion and yield.
Solution_Description: 2‑Methyl‑THF was selected as the reaction medium because of its low peroxide‑formation risk and ability to become miscible with the substrate as the reaction progressed; the substrate loading was increased to 50 g L⁻¹ (≈0.23 M) to keep the reaction mixture saturated once the substrate dissolved, improving overall conversion and allowing yields of 35‑43 % (theoretical 50 %).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The racemic alcohol RS‑1 was not completely soluble in 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran in the beginning of the reaction; however, with the progress of the reaction, it most likely became completely soluble."; "The improved conditions (i) substrate input 50 g/L … (iv) 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran as solvent were implemented, and five lab batches … were carried out in 5.5–8.5 h at 4 °C to prepare the desired alcohol S‑1 in yields of 35–43 % (maximum possible yield 50 %)."

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: Initial screening of many lipases for the succinylation of RS‑5 gave poor enantio‑selectivity (ee < 70 %) and low conversion, making the process unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Novozym 435 (immobilised Candida antarctica lipase B) was identified as a robust, commercially available biocatalyst that gave >97 % ee for the R‑alcohol despite a slower reaction; the enzyme‑to‑substrate ratio was adjusted (1 : 4) and the reaction was run at 25 °C to balance rate and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Enzymatic succinylation screening experiments identified lipase PS 30 … gave solution yield 30–40 %, ee > 99 % … but hydrolysis of racemic acetate 2 by the same enzymes gave poor ee for both alcohol (ee < 35 %) and the remaining acetate (ee < 14 %)."; "Among the different kinds of kinetic resolutions, enzymatic succinylation is preferred … Enzymatic succinylation screening identified lipase PS 30 …". Solution: "Novozym 435 (lipase from Candida antarctica) catalyzed the resolution of the racemic acetate RS‑4a … the ee of the alcohol R‑5 was >97 %; Novozym 435 is a robust, well‑characterized, commercially available immobilized enzyme, tolerant to a wide range of reaction conditions…"

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: The hemisuccinate (succinate) derivative of the R‑enantiomer degraded during the extractive work‑up, causing loss of enantiopurity and making isolation of high‑ee R‑5 infeasible by the desuccinylation route.
Solution_Description: The process was redirected to a direct enzymatic hydrolysis of the racemic acetate (RS‑4a) followed by silica‑gel chromatography, avoiding the unstable succinate intermediate; later, a longer‑chain ester (hexanoate) was employed, enabling simple solvent extraction instead of chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "However, due to poor stability of the succinate derivative in an extractive workup, the preparation of alcohol R‑5 with ee > 99 % was not feasible. The desuccinylation route was ruled out because >99 % ee of the chiral intermediate R‑5 is necessary for drug development studies. Even 1 % degradation of the homochiral succinate derivative could reduce the ee of R‑5 by 2 %."; Solution: "We reasoned that it might be possible to separate longer chain esters … The enzymatic hydrolysis process from hexanoate does not require column chromatography, and simple solvent extraction was sufficient to separate the desired enantiomer from the undesired enantiomer."

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: The enzymatic hydrolysis of the racemic acetate RS‑4a required 24–28 h to reach only ~48 % conversion, limiting throughput and giving modest isolated yields (≈37 %).
Solution_Description: Temperature was set to 25 °C (optimal balance of rate and energy use) and water content was lowered to 1 % (v/v) to accelerate the reaction; the enzyme‑to‑substrate ratio was reduced from 1 : 4 to 1 : 25, decreasing enzyme loading while maintaining >99 % ee, thereby reducing reaction time to ~5 h for ≥45 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The reaction was fast in the beginning (conversion 35 % in 7 h) … was stopped after 28 h (solution yield 49.5 %, ee …)"; "The improved conditions … 5.5–8.5 h at 4 °C … yields of 35–43 %". Solution: "The impact of temperature … no significant benefit … thus, the temperature 25 °C was preferred for a greener … process"; "A series of 1.0 g scale (20 g/L) reactions … 0.5 % ≅ 1 % (optimum) … a ≥2‑fold increase in reaction rate was seen just by reducing water from 10 % to 1 %"; "An enzyme‑to‑substrate ratio of 1:20 conversion > 45 % and ee > 99 % was achieved in 6–8 h… further reaction aging to 24 h reduces the ee".

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: The first pilot‑scale campaign required 250 g of Novozym 435 per kilogram of racemic acetate (≈250 g kg⁻¹), leading to high enzyme cost and limited availability for larger batches.
Solution_Description: By lowering the water content to 1 % and increasing substrate concentration to 100 g L⁻¹, the enzyme loading was reduced stepwise to 40 g kg⁻¹ in the second campaign and finally to 5 g kg⁻¹ for the hexanoate route, drastically cutting reagent cost while preserving >99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: Table 1 – enzyme g kg⁻¹ of RS‑ester: 250 g (campaign 1).; "The enzymatic hydrolysis process from acetate requires chromatography … The enzyme loading was reduced from 250 g kg⁻¹ of ester to 40 g kg⁻¹ in the second campaign to 5.0 g kg⁻¹ of RS‑ester in the hexanoate process."; Solution: "Under the modified conditions (1 % water in acetonitrile …) >45 % conversion was achieved in ∼5 h, suggesting that still lower enzyme load could be sufficient … the enzyme loading was reduced by 6‑fold when water concentration was reduced from 10 % to 1 %"; "The improved conditions were implemented in the second pilot plant campaign … enzyme loading was reduced from 250 g kg⁻¹ of ester to 40 g kg⁻¹ …"

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: For the R‑alcohol product (R‑5) the separation from the S‑acetate by silica‑gel chromatography was time‑consuming (∼16 h solvent‑swap) and added substantial cost to the process.
Solution_Description: Switching to a longer‑chain ester (hexanoate) allowed the undesired S‑hexanoate to be extracted into toluene, while the desired R‑alcohol remained in the aqueous phase and could be recovered by a single dichloromethane extraction, eliminating the chromatography step and the solvent‑swap operation.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The enzymatic hydrolysis process from acetate requires chromatography for the separation of the desired alcohol R‑5 from the acetate S‑4a which reduces throughput and increases the cost of the overall process."; "In the first campaign, the solvent swap … taking ∼16 h of pilot plant time". Solution: "The enzymatic hydrolysis process from hexanoate does not require column chromatography, and simple solvent extraction was sufficient to separate the desired enantiomer from the undesired enantiomer."; "The undesired hexanoate S‑4d was extracted into toluene, and the desired R‑5 was extracted into dichloromethane …"

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: Many of the screened lipases (e.g., PS 30, Sprin lipo, Sprin epobond) were not available in bulk quantities or at a price suitable for kilogram‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Novozym 435, a widely stocked immobilised Candida antarctica lipase, was selected for its commercial availability, robustness, and tolerance to the required organic‑solvent/temperature conditions, enabling scale‑up without supply constraints.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Some enzymes showed good selectivity but they were not available in large scale and/or reasonable cost to move forward with the process development."; Solution: "Novozym 435 is a robust, well‑characterized, commercially available immobilized enzyme, tolerant to wide range of reaction conditions … Immobilized Novozym 435 can easily be removed from the reaction mixture for reuse by a simple filtration."

Paper Title: Enzymatic Process for
Problem_Description: The reaction of the hexanoate substrate initially formed a heterogeneous mixture; after several hours the mixture became homogeneous, indicating mixing/phase‑transfer limitations that could affect scale‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "In the beginning, the reaction mixture was heterogeneous. After 4 h, the reaction mixture became homogeneous…"; Solution: "The optimized reaction conditions for enantioselective RS‑hexanoate 4d resolution were established as follows: substrate input 100 g L⁻¹, acetonitrile 98 %, water 2 %, enzyme‑to‑substrate ratio 1:200 at 45 °C (the reaction was complete in ∼15 h)."

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel MC1R Agonist
Problem_Description: The original Grignard addition of o‑tolylmagnesium bromide to Boc‑azetidinone was performed at –78 °C in THF, requiring cryogenic conditions that are unsafe and impractical on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The Grignard step was moved to –20 °C and the solvent was changed from THF to 2‑methyl‑tetrahydrofuran (MeTHF).  An aqueous HCl wash was added to quench excess Grignard reagent, and after concentration the organic phase was switched to heptane, inducing in‑situ crystallisation of intermediate 3.

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: 5‑Aminotetrazole (5‑AT) is poorly soluble in nitric acid; during dosing lines it precipitates as the energetic 5‑AT nitrate, creating a safety hazard and a source of 5‑AT impurity in the product.
Solution_Description: Switch the reaction solvent for the Sandmeyer step from nitric acid to aqueous sulfuric acid, which provides at least twice the solubility for 5‑AT and eliminates formation of 5‑AT nitrate in the dosing lines.
Supporting_Evidence: “...attempting to dose solutions of certain concentrations of 5‑AT in nitric acid resulted in the nitrate salt of 5‑AT precipitating in the dosing lines… 5‑AT is at least twice as soluble in aqueous sulfuric acid as it is in aqueous nitric acid… the improved solubility of 5‑AT in sulfuric acid combined with eliminating the energetic 5‑AT nitrate solids present in the dosing lines made sulfuric acid a very attractive choice.”

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: The copper‑(II) 5‑NT complex (intermediate 1) forms a gelatinous solid that is difficult to filter and wash; when dry it is highly impact‑sensitive, exposing operators to serious safety risk and adding a cumbersome purification step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employ a filter‑reactor equipped with an internal filter and add diatomaceous earth as a filtration aid. This allows the solid to remain wet, be filtered, washed and converted to NaNT without ever being removed from the reactor, thus simplifying mass‑transfer, reducing handling of the sensitive solid, and eliminating a manual purification operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “…we envisaged using a reactor with an internal filter that would enable us to isolate 1, perform washes of that material, and convert it to NaNT, all without removing 1 from the reactor… We charged diatomaceous earth to the reactor prior to filtering 1 to assist in filtering that material and left the diatomaceous earth in place to assist the filtration of copper oxides from the NaNT solution. The sensitive intermediate 1 remained wet at all times and was never handled by the operator.”

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: NaNT obtained from the original process contains ~5 wt % residual 5‑AT impurity, requiring a separate isolation/purification step that reduces overall yield, adds cost, and increases operator exposure.
Solution_Description: By using sulfuric‑acid dissolution of 5‑AT, the resulting NaNT solution is obtained with 5‑AT below the detection limit, allowing direct conversion to DBX‑1 without any additional purification, thereby improving yield, lowering cost, and removing an extra handling step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The improved solubility of 5‑AT in sulfuric acid… led to the production of 1 that could be converted to NaNT solutions that had levels of 5‑AT that were typically below our limit of detection… We were able to convert these solutions directly to DBX‑1 without any additional purification steps.”

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: Conversion of NaNT to DBX‑1 is erratic; some batches show a long, unpredictable induction period or fail to crystallize, leading to low or zero yield, especially at larger scale.
Solution_Description: Introduce authentic DBX‑1 seed (1–25 wt % of theoretical yield) before adding sodium ascorbate to dramatically shorten the induction period, and dose the ascorbate in two stages (15 % slow, then 85 % faster) to maintain control over nucleation and growth, giving reproducible high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “The most significant modification is that we seed our reactions with authentic DBX‑1 before dosing sodium ascorbate… This dramatically reduces the length of the induction period and reduces the likelihood of a batch of NaNT not converting to DBX‑1… we dose our sodium ascorbate solution in two portions. The first portion… is dosed slowly… After this dose, the reaction mixture is stirred until the gelatinous brown material transforms to DBX‑1. This effectively increases the amount of seed for the second dose… which can then be dosed at a faster rate.”

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: Using the stoichiometric amount of NaOH to neutralize 5‑NT leads to an excessively high pH because the copper‑(II) complex already contains sodium; the high pH prevents formation of DBX‑1 and reduces overall NaNT yield.
Solution_Description: Adjust the NaOH dose to a sub‑stoichiometric level (≈0.75 equiv relative to 5‑NT) based on the measured sodium content in intermediate 1, thereby maintaining the target pH (~9–10) needed for efficient conversion to NaNT.
Supporting_Evidence: “…dosing a full equivalent of sodium hydroxide with respect to 5‑NT leads to a very high pH (>12) and a NaNT solution that does not produce DBX‑1… we stopped our dose with 0.75 equiv of NaOH dosed with respect to 5‑NT present in 1… The 5‑AT concentration of this solution was 0.04 % (w/w), an order of magnitude less than… solutions of purified NaNT used for DBX‑1 synthesis in our previous publication.”

Paper Title: Development of a Lean Process to the Lead-Free Primary Explosive DBX‑1
Problem_Description: Handling of the dry explosive intermediate 1 poses a severe safety risk to operators and limits scalability.
Solution_Description: Conduct the entire sequence in a closed, internally‑filtered reactor that keeps 1 wet throughout, coupled with remote‑control operation, removing the need for manual transfer of the sensitive solid.
Supporting_Evidence: “The sensitive intermediate 1 remained wet at all times and was never handled by the operator… Future work will focus eliminating ‘dead space’ below the filter plate… eliminating the necessity of an operator interacting directly with the reactor for manual operations… increases the overall safety of the process and is an absolute requirement for transition to manufacturing at larger scales.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 2‑Ethylphenylhydrazine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Batch diazotization of aromatic amines is highly exothermic and presents safety hazards (potential for explosive intermediates) when scaled‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopted a continuous‑flow reactor platform that provides a much smaller reaction volume, high surface‑to‑volume ratio and precise temperature control, thereby minimizing the exotherm and associated safety risks.
Supporting_Evidence: “Diazotization of aromatic amines is usually exothermic and fast… Research has confirmed that diazotization presented potential safety hazards for scale up.”; “Continuous‑flow technology offers many advantages… precise control of… temperature; the much higher surface area to volume ratio … renders highly efficient heat transfer.”; “safety hazards in handling exothermic reactions… are minimized because they involve a much smaller volume in the reaction train.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 2‑Ethylphenylhydrazine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Intermediate diazenesulfonate (3) has poor water solubility, leading to precipitation and tube clogging during the continuous process.

Solution_Description: Increased the inner diameter of the reacting tubes (from 3 mm to 6 mm) to accommodate the low‑solubility solid and maintain smooth flow.
Supporting_Evidence: “The primary challenge of this continuous process was the poor solubility of diazenesulfonate 3 and the problem of a clogging tube.”; “Therefore, we chose to increase the diameter of the reacting tube to improve the process.”; “Inner diameters of residence loops II and III were both 6 mm.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 2‑Ethylphenylhydrazine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt at higher temperatures (or long residence) generates a black tar and severely reduces product yield.
Solution_Description: Implemented a temperature‑programmed reduction: generate diazenesulfonate 3 at a lower temperature, then raise the temperature for the subsequent reduction step, avoiding decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Maximum yield was 80 % when τ₂ = 30 min, T₂ = 100 °C due to the formation of a black tar. The main reason could be thermal decomposition of diazonium chloride 2 during formation of 3.”; “Because of the thermal decomposition problems of the initial method, an improved process was developed by temperature‑programmed reduction. Diazenesulfonate 3 was generated at a slightly lower temperature, and intermediate 4 was formed at a higher temperature.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 2‑Ethylphenylhydrazine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Product required recrystallization after isolation; the original work‑up was labor‑intensive and gave only 99 % purity after recrystallization.
Solution_Description: Added toluene directly to the hydrolysis reactor to extract impurities in situ; the product precipitated as bright white crystals, giving >99 % purity without a separate recrystallization step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Toluene was added in the hydrolysis reactor, and impurities were extracted into an organic layer with hydrolysis by hydrochloric acid. Bright white crystals of the target product precipitated while the mixture cooled, and after filtration and drying, a purity of more than 99 % was directly obtained.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 2‑Ethylphenylhydrazine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Initial stoichiometries of sodium nitrite and sodium sulfite gave sub‑optimal yields (≤75 %).

Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 shows maximum yield (75 %) at 1.03 equiv NaNO₂; “Sodium nitrite can be slightly excessive to 1.03 equiv….”; Table 2 shows 81 % yield at 2.8 equiv Na₂SO₃; “The yield of 1 was 81 % when 2.8 equiv of sodium sulfite was used.”

Paper Title: Careful Navigation of the Crystallographic Landscape of MK-8970: A Racemic Acetal Carbonate Prodrug of Raltegravir
Problem_Description: Uncertainty existed whether crystalline form 1 was a true racemic crystal or a conglomerate, preventing confident selection of the thermodynamically preferred polymorph.
Solution_Description: Single‑crystal X‑ray diffraction of form 2 together with comparative crystallization of the pure (R)- and (S)-enantiomers established that form 2 is a true racemic crystal and gave strong indirect evidence that form 1 is also racemic, resolving the ambiguity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Crystals of form 2 suitable for structure determination were grown … Form 2 crystallizes in the monoclinic centrosymmetric space group … the crystal is a true racemate.”; “Samples of the pure (R)- and (S)-enantiomers … XRPD patterns … were different from forms 1 and 2 … indicating that form 1 is not a conglomerate …”; “Form 1 is likely to be a true racemic crystal, although definitive proof has remained elusive.”

Paper Title: Careful Navigation of the Crystallographic Landscape of MK-8970: A Racemic Acetal Carbonate Prodrug of Raltegravir
Problem_Description: During scale‑up crystallization, mixtures of forms 1 and 2 appeared even when seeding with form 2, leading to inconsistent product form and reduced isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Solubility curves of both polymorphs in ethyl acetate were measured; crystallization was performed at concentrations and cooling rates that remain below the supersaturation line for form 1, guaranteeing exclusive nucleation of form 2.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initial cooling crystallizations from EtOAc resulted in mixtures of forms 1 and 2… Hence, a plot of the solubility in EtOAc as a function of temperature was constructed… to improve form control.”; “The solubility curves … show that cooling the system too rapidly can readily enable crystallization of the metastable form 1. Isolation of pure form 2 can be achieved by maintaining the system concentration below the supersaturation curve for form 1.”

Paper Title: Careful Navigation of the Crystallographic Landscape of MK-8970: A Racemic Acetal Carbonate Prodrug of Raltegravir
Problem_Description: An imidate impurity (1‑2 % by HPLC) appeared in the first GMP batch, giving an unexpected XR‑PD peak and compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: A solubility screen of the imidate versus MK‑8970 in several solvents identified isopropyl acetate (IPAc) and IPAc saturated with water as media where the impurity’s solubility is markedly lower than the API, allowing its rejection while maintaining high product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “The XRPD of some laboratory runs showed an unexpected peak … associated with an elevated amount (1–2 % area) of an imidate impurity.”; “In this study, the imidate and MK‑8970 solubility was interrogated across a range of potential processing solvents … Interestingly, in EtOAc, the solubility of the imidate was observed to be substantially lower than that of MK‑8970 form 2 … The most desirable scenario … would be obtained using either pure IPAc or IPAc saturated with water.”

Paper Title: Careful Navigation of the Crystallographic Landscape of MK-8970: A Racemic Acetal Carbonate Prodrug of Raltegravir
Problem_Description: The imidate impurity crystallizes as a hemi‑ethyl‑acetate solvate (imidate form 1) that is poorly soluble in ethyl acetate, leading to poor rejection during the MK‑8970 crystallization step.
Solution_Description: Imidate form 1 was annealed at 166 °C to convert it to imidate form 2, which exhibits a distinct XR‑PD peak and a higher solubility profile, facilitating its identification and removal in subsequent batches.
Supporting_Evidence: “Imidate form 2 was subsequently isolated by annealing a sample of imidate form 1 at 166 °C.”; “XRPD of imidate form 2 possessed a very intense peak at 7.2° 2θ, making this crystalline form a better candidate to account for the extra peak in the first GMP batch pattern.”

Paper Title: Careful Navigation of the Crystallographic Landscape of MK-8970: A Racemic Acetal Carbonate Prodrug of Raltegravir

Problem_Description: The classical dibenzylation procedures rely on solvents that are either toxic, banned, or unsuitable for large‑scale manufacturing (benzene, carbon tetrachloride, benzyl alcohol, toluene).

Paper Title: Enantiomerically Pure Dibenzyl Esters of
Problem_Description: When toluene or benzyl‑alcohol are used, the dibenzylation gives significant racemization, leading to low enantiomeric excess (≤10 % ee) and lower effective yield of the desired enantiomer.
Solution_Description: Using cyclohexane, which provides a lower‑boiling water azeotrope, keeps the reaction temperature around 80 °C and suppresses racemization, delivering >94 % ee and high isolated yields.
