Supporting_Evidence: “Since the C–H amidation was found to be highly exothermic (−290 kJ mol⁻¹), a careful control of reaction rate was required to prevent uncontrollable heat and CO₂ emission.”; “2‑phenylpyridine … was added using a syringe pump over 3.5 h while maintaining the reaction temperature under 45 °C.”; “When 2‑phenylpyridine was added at once, a surge of heat and CO₂ emission was observed … the resulting temperature elevation caused further rate amplification; thus a loss of control was witnessed.”

Paper Title: Study of Sustainability and Scalability in the Cp*Rh(III)-Catalyzed Direct C–H Amidation with 1,4,2-Dioxazol-5-ones
Problem_Description: CO₂ generated during the reaction can build up pressure in a sealed flask, potentially causing over‑pressurization.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Install a 22‑gauge needle as a CO₂ outlet (or a balloon vent) to vent gas and monitor pressure, preventing pressure accumulation.
Supporting_Evidence: “With a placement of needle of 22 gauge as a CO₂ outlet, no sign of pressure accumulation was detected.”

Paper Title: Study of Sustainability and Scalability in the Cp*Rh(III)-Catalyzed Direct C–H Amidation with 1,4,2-Dioxazol-5-ones
Problem_Description: Protic solvents (alcohols, acids) gave low conversion for ketoxime‑directed substrates, limiting product yield.
Solution_Description: Select ethyl acetate (a polar aprotic, green solvent) which provides high conversion for both pyridine‑ and ketoxime‑directed arenes.
Supporting_Evidence: “Protic solvents such as alcohols and acids showed good efficiency with 2‑phenylpyridine, but low conversion was observed with ketoxime‑containing arene … Delightfully, excellent reactivity was observed in ethyl acetate …”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Pd‑(S)/C gave a very low conversion (<10 % after 4 h) for the model substrate, providing insufficient yield of the desired iodo‑aniline.
Solution_Description: The catalyst screen was refocused on Pt–V/C (high activity) and Raney Co (high selectivity), which delivered substantially higher conversions and reduced dehalogenation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“low conversion was observed for Pd‑(S)/C, which shows less than 10 % conversion of 1‑iodo‑4‑nitrobenzene after 4 h”
“Particularly Pt–Fe and Pt–V based catalysts on activated carbon gave promising results… The most selective catalyst… was Raney Co”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: During hydrogenation the product 4‑iodoaniline undergoes hydrodehalogenation to aniline, reducing selectivity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Raney Co was chosen as the catalyst because it shows <1 % overall dehalogenation. In addition, using a low substrate concentration (0.05 M) further suppresses dehalogenation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The most selective catalyst… Raney Co with less than 1 % overall dehalogenation”
“At 0.05 M substrate concentration … dehalogenation decreased … from 27 % over 8 % to 1 %”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Alcoholic solvents showed very low solubility of the halogenated nitroarenes, risking precipitation and clogging in continuous reactors.
Solution_Description: THF (and 2‑methyl‑THF) were selected as the reaction solvent because they dissolve >0.5 M of the substrate and give fast turnover without precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Alcohols have not been investigated due to very low solubility of the substrates… Solubility is especially important for continuous reactions… At ambient temperature… 1‑iodo‑4‑nitrobenzene was soluble in THF in concentrations of approximately 0.6 M”
“Using alkyl ethers like THF… resulted in high reaction rates together with good substrate solubility”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: When Pt–V/C was used in continuous flow its activity dropped continuously (e.g., 88 % → 51 % conversion over 5 h), preventing stable long‑term operation.
Solution_Description: The flow experiments were shifted to Raney Co, which maintained stable conversion for >20 h, demonstrating that catalyst choice is critical for continuous processing.
Supporting_Evidence:
“conversion ... with Pt–V/C usually decreased rapidly over time… conversion dropped from 88 to 51 % over 5 h”
“Raney Co showed higher long‑term stability in comparison to Pt–V/C”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Scale‑up from 10 mL to 200 mL and then to 1 L caused slower heating and longer reaction times, attributed to hydrogen mass‑transfer limitations.
Solution_Description: Continuous‑flow microreactors were employed to improve gas‑liquid contact; pressure was increased to 85 bar and temperature lowered to 80 °C to achieve >90 % yield in shorter residence time.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Heating was slower for larger reaction volumes… assumed that the decreased performance might be due to a hydrogen mass transfer limitation.”
“in continuous flow conditions… increasing the pressure to 85 bar and lowering the temperature to 80 °C, increased the yield of 4‑iodoaniline … to 90 %”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Raney Ni is highly pyrophoric when freshly prepared and can ignite during drying, posing a serious safety hazard for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Raney Co was preferred over Raney Ni for large‑scale operations because it is less pyrophoric and retains activity over long storage periods.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Raney Ni, which is highly pyrophoric when freshly prepared… the material eventually ignited.”
“Raney Co showed stable catalytic activity after up to 1.5 years of storage… Raney Co was less pyrophoric than freshly prepared Raney Ni.”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: Residual catalyst on the walls of a multipurpose autoclave caused unwanted background hydrogenation (≈10 % conversion) even without added Raney Co, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: Dedicated reaction equipment (cleaned and passivated) was used for sensitive batch hydrogenations to eliminate background activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
“hydrogenation experiments … without Raney Co … 10 % of substrate were converted… Further suppression of the background reactivity could not be achieved by cleaning.”
“Therefore, using highly selective Raney Co on sensitive substrates in batch processes might necessitate the use of designated equipment.”

Paper Title: Selective Hydrogenation of Halogenated Nitroaromatics to Haloanilines in Batch and Flow
Problem_Description: The crude reaction mixtures contained internal standards, unreacted material and trace dehalogenated aniline, requiring efficient isolation of the halogenated aniline products.
Solution_Description: A two‑step work‑up (acid–base extraction followed by crystallization) was developed to remove impurities and afford the pure anilines in 78–98 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“acid–base extraction was used in order to separate the crude products … The crude product was dissolved … washed … After crystallization … overall yield of 78 %”
“Removal of the dehalogenated aniline … was possible by crystallization (entry 9), giving … overall yield of 88 %.”

Paper Title: Two-Phase Flow Oxidation of Valeraldehyde with O
Problem_Description: The oxidation of valeraldehyde is limited by the low solubility of oxygen in the liquid phase, resulting in a mass‑transfer bottleneck that restricts conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A Hastelloy microstructured reactor equipped with periodic channel narrowings was employed. The geometry creates a large gas‑liquid interfacial area and intense mixing, thereby overcoming the oxygen‑mass‑transfer limitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
【1】“Due to the low solubility of oxygen in aldehydes… the progress of reaction… is limited by the mass transfer of O₂.”
【2】“One‑A Engineering… microreactor… with periodical narrowings to increase the mixing performance for an improved mass transfer.”
【3】“These process parameters were selected to achieve a high mass transfer rate, since the oxidation process is described with a mass transfer limitation.”
【4】“The microreactor is especially suited for multiphase oxidations… the degree of mixing and the generation of the gas–liquid interface can be seamlessly adjusted.”
【5】“A rapid conversion of valeraldehyde … conversion: 95 % (residence time 82 s).”

Paper Title: Two-Phase Flow Oxidation of Valeraldehyde with O
Problem_Description: The aldehyde oxidation is highly exothermic, raising concerns about thermal runaway and safety when run in conventional batch reactors.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a metal‑based microreactor (Hastelloy) that provides a very high surface‑to‑volume ratio, enabling rapid heat removal and eliminating hot‑spot formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
【1】“Microstructured reactors are the ideal device for highly exothermic reactions.”
【2】“Due to the efficient heat transfer, a critical hot spot or a thermal runaway is unlikely.”
【3】“The catalytic oxidation… demonstrated using a Hastelloy microreactor.”
【4】“The used microreactor is ideal for scale‑up… with the benefits of microreaction technology… safe oxidation process.”
【5】“The reaction is highly exothermic… the fast removal of reaction heat improves safety.”

Paper Title: Two-Phase Flow Oxidation of Valeraldehyde with O
Problem_Description: Conventional processes often require dilution of the aldehyde to reduce flammability/flammable vapour risks, which lowers productivity.
Solution_Description: By operating the microreactor at modest temperatures (0–40 °C) and exploiting its excellent heat‑dissipation capability, the authors achieved a safe oxidation without any prior dilution of the aldehyde.
Supporting_Evidence:
【1】“A safe oxidation process with oxygen has been developed. A dilution of valeraldehyde for safety reasons is not necessary.”
【2】“The oxidation is performed at 0 to 40 °C with a catalytic amount of manganese‑(II) acetate.”

Paper Title: Two-Phase Flow Oxidation of Valeraldehyde with O
Problem_Description: Using a very low catalyst loading (50 ppm Mn(II) acetate) caused the reaction rate to drop dramatically, requiring unacceptably long residence times.

Paper Title: Two-Phase Flow Oxidation of Valeraldehyde with O
Problem_Description: Without any promoter, the conversion and selectivity were poor (≈50 % selectivity), indicating insufficient reaction rate and uncontrolled radical pathways.

【5】“An annular flow pattern can be assumed…”

Paper Title: Application of Safety by Design Methodology in Evaluating Process Safety for a Duff Reaction Using Predictive Process Simulators
Problem_Description: Hexamine (the formylation reagent) shows an exothermic DSC peak at 219 °C with a decomposition enthalpy > 500 J g⁻¹, and the Duff reaction mixture exhibits an adiabatic temperature rise of 159 °C in the ARSST, indicating a strong potential for runaway.
Solution_Description: A Safety‑by‑Design workflow was applied: DSC, isoperibol‑RC and adiabatic‑calorimetry were used to obtain reaction enthalpies and kinetic parameters; DynoChem regression fitted activation energies and rate constants; the kinetic model was then used in process simulators to define safe temperature limits and TMR margins.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “hexamine has an exothermic peak … at an exothermic onset temperature (T_onset) of 219 °C … indicates a potential risk.”
• “When the model reaction mixture was scanned in an adiabatic calorimeter … exothermic decomposition with an adiabatic temperature rise of ΔT_ad = 159.09 °C …”
• “The experimental data were analyzed by simultaneous numerical methods … using the DynoChem software package.”
• “This evaluation was accomplished using response surface methodology … providing a quantitative measure of thermal risk.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: The original Cu‑source, [Cu(MeCN)4]OTf, is expensive and generates fluorine‑containing waste (triflate), making the process costly and environmentally unfriendly.
Solution_Description: Replace the expensive copper source with inexpensive CuI, eliminating the need for fluorinated waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “[Cu‑(MeCN)4]OTf should be replaced with an inexpensive copper halide salt to lower the catalyst cost and avoid fluorine‑containing waste from the triflate counter‑ion.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: The bidentate ligand MeO‑bpy is costly, adding significantly to the catalyst cost.
Solution_Description: Substitute MeO‑bpy with the inexpensive monodentate ligand N‑methyl‑imidazole (NMI).
Supporting_Evidence: “The ligand should be replaced with a low‑cost alternative, such as bpy or, preferably, a monodentate nitrogenous ligand.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: ABNO loading of 1 mol % is high, increasing operating costs.
Solution_Description: Reduce ABNO loading to 0.05–0.3 mol % without loss of activity for many substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ABNO loading should be reduced from 1 mol % to minimize operating costs.”; “For electron‑rich benzylic alcohols, ABNO can be lowered to 0.05 mol % without loss of activity.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: Acetonitrile has a low flash point and is flammable, posing safety risks when using air as the oxidant in batch processes.
Solution_Description: Adopt N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone (NMP), a high‑flash‑point solvent, for batch reactions to enable safe operation with air.
Supporting_Evidence: “Use of a high flash point solvent, N‑methyl‑pyrrolidone, enables safe operation in batch reactions with air as the oxidant.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: A solid precipitates from the CuI/ABNO/NMI stock solution in MeCN, threatening clogging in the flow reactor.
Solution_Description: Increase NMI loading three‑fold (to 15 mol %) to keep all components soluble and prevent precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “A solid precipitated from the stock solution of CuI, ABNO, and NMI in MeCN. Increasing the NMI loading threefold (i.e., 15 mol % under the reaction conditions) prevented solid formation in the catalyst solution.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: CuI corrodes stainless‑steel components in the slug‑flow reactor after < 24 h, causing equipment failure.
Solution_Description: Switch to a PTFE membrane flow reactor (and PTFE loop) to avoid metal contact and corrosion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The new CuI‑based system led to noticeable stainless steel corrosion… As a result, a PTFE membrane reactor was used to test the CuI/ABNO/NMI catalyst in flow.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: Original batch reactions were run at 0.1 M and low temperature, giving modest yields and requiring 1–6 h reaction times.
Solution_Description: Increase reaction concentration to ≥0.5 M and raise temperature to 60 °C, which together boost conversion and shorten reaction times.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction concentration should be increased from 0.1 M to ≥0.5 M to maximize throughput and minimize waste.”; “Increasing the temperature to 60 °C … provided the best results for a 2° aliphatic alcohol.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: After batch oxidation, CuI, NMI, and NMP remain in the reaction mixture, making product isolation tedious.
Solution_Description: Develop a work‑up involving aqueous extraction, washing with sodium bisulfite, and optional silica‑gel chromatography or crystallization to remove catalyst residues.
Supporting_Evidence: “Isolation of the product … was accomplished with aqueous extraction to remove CuI, NMI, and NMP. The organic layer was washed with sodium bisulfite or passed through activated carbon … Removal of ABNO from the product may be accomplished with silica gel column chromatography … or crystallization.”

Paper Title: Process Development of CuI/ABNO/NMI-Catalyzed Aerobic Alcohol Oxidation
Problem_Description: In flow, gas–liquid mixing and gas pressure needed to be optimized to achieve fast oxidation; inadequate mixing leads to low conversion and long residence times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Use slug‑flow or membrane reactors with controlled gas dispersion (e.g., 9 % O₂ in N₂ at elevated pressure) to ensure efficient gas‑liquid contact and short residence times (≈6 min).
Supporting_Evidence: “Continuous‑flow reaction methods … smaller reactor volume, effective and reproducible gas–liquid mixing, and the ability to operate at high gas pressures can promote faster aerobic oxidation on large scale.”; “A 6 min residence time provided the highest product yield … steady‑state yield of ≥98 % was maintained over a 3 h period.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Process for Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-7-azaindole
Problem_Description: During the iodination of 2‑amino‑5‑nitropyridine, excessive evolution of elemental iodine caused condensation of iodine on the condenser surface, creating operational difficulties.
Solution_Description: The addition of KI was slowed – only 0.8 equiv were added dropwise over ~2 h – which reduced iodine evolution; the mixture was then refluxed for 1 h to consume remaining material.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “excessive evolution of iodine resulted in the condensation of iodine on the condenser surface leading to complications in the reaction.”
• “evolution of iodine was comparatively less when 0.8 equiv of KI was added dropwise for about 2 h. The reaction mixture was refluxed over 1 h after KI addition to ensure complete consumption of the starting material.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Process for Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-7-azaindole
Problem_Description: The original Sonogashira coupling protocol gave the alkyne product in 81 % yield but required column chromatography for isolation, which is unattractive on scale.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in a mixture of triethylamine and DMF (instead of THF/TEA) and the product precipitated directly on cooling, allowing simple filtration. Catalyst loadings were also reduced (PdCl₂(PPh₃)₂ to 0.002 equiv, CuI to 0.008 equiv) without loss of yield, decreasing metal residue.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “However, isolation and purification of the compound were problematic.”
• “We obtained the required product by simple filtration in good yield.”
• “It was found that the yield of the product was not affected at all when the amount of bis‑(triphenyl‑phosphino) palladium(II) chloride was reduced to 0.002 equiv… The Sonogashira coupling reaction offered compound … in 89 % yield using catalysts … in a 0.002:0.008 molar ratio.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Process for Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-7-azaindole
Problem_Description: Initial cycloisomerization attempts with strong bases (e.g., KOt‑Bu) gave only ~50 % yield and the product required chromatographic purification; many other bases gave no reaction at all.
Solution_Description: A systematic base screen identified morpholine (and pyrrolidine) in combination with water as effective promoters; carrying out the reaction at 90 °C for 24 h in a 1:1 morpholine/water (later optimized to 10:2) mixture afforded up to 88 % isolated yield of the azaindole without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “With strong bases … we were able to obtain required compound … in 50 % yield… quality and purity … not good and required column chromatography.”
• “...using various bases ... none of the bases afforded desired 5‑nitro‑7‑azaindole 6.”
• “Morpholine/water (1:1) … 73 % yield … Morpholine/water (10:2) … 88 % yield … The product was isolated by filtration as a yellow solid in high purity (>97 % area by HPLC).”

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Process for Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-7-azaindole
Problem_Description: Residual palladium and copper from the Sonogashira step posed a contamination risk and added cost for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loadings were minimized (PdCl₂(PPh₃)₂ to 0.002 equiv, CuI to 0.008 equiv) while maintaining >84 % yield, thereby reducing metal usage and downstream purification burden.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We optimized the molar equivalents of the catalysts … to minimize the residual metal contamination in the product.”
• “Yield of the product was not affected at all when the amount of bis‑(triphenyl‑phosphino) palladium(II) chloride was reduced to 0.002 equiv… The Sonogashira coupling reaction offered compound … in 89 % yield using catalysts … in a 0.002:0.008 molar ratio.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Scalable Process for Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-7-azaindole
Problem_Description: Previous literature routes for 5‑nitro‑7‑azaindole required heavy‑metal catalysis, microwave irradiation, or extensive chromatographic work‑up, making them unsuitable for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free cycloisomerization of the alkyne intermediate was developed; the product precipitates on cooling and can be isolated by simple filtration, eliminating the need for chromatography and metal reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We have developed a simple and straightforward methodology for the synthesis of 5‑nitro‑7‑azaindole … using metal‑free cycloisomerization … without using column chromatography and heavy metals for cycloisomerization.”
• “The reaction was carried out on multikilogram scale … 5‑nitro‑7‑azaindole was isolated as a yellow solid by filtration in >97 % purity.”

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: The lithiation of difluorobenzene (230 kJ mol⁻¹) and of the DFT intermediate (480 kJ mol⁻¹) is highly exothermic, creating hot‑spots inside the IKSM mixing modules; temperature spikes lead to runaway and risk of decomposition of the organolithium intermediate.
Solution_Description: The production load was reduced (≈50 % throughput cut‑back) and the cooling‑medium temperature was lowered (‑45 °C → ‑55 °C) so that the reactor temperature stayed below the decomposition limit; residence time was increased accordingly to retain full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Reaction of difluorobenzene with hexyllithium has a reaction enthalpy of 230 kJ mol⁻¹ and hence is highly exothermic.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Solid salts (Li‑based salts, polymeric deposits) and jelly‑like material accumulate in the hexyllithium filter, IKSM reactor and residence‑time modules, causing blockage and flow interruption after 20–40 h of operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A clean‑in‑place (CIP) concept was introduced using two parallel reactor trains; the blocked line is purged by a temporary temperature increase, after which residual water is removed. The hardware was upgraded (new filters, redesigned mixers) to tolerate solid deposits.
Supporting_Evidence: The hexyllithium filter (1) was frequently blocked by a jellylike buildup.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Gas bubbles generated in the pumps and micro‑reactor channels cause pulsating flow and occasional plugging, leading to unstable operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Three parallel piston‑membrane pumps together with Coriolis flow‑meters and pressure monitoring were installed to dampen pulsations and detect early pressure spikes; flow rates were carefully balanced to minimise gas entrainment.
Supporting_Evidence: The problem of clogging in microreactors by gas bubbles is seldom discussed, but it seems to be an important issue.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Hexyllithium precoolers became blocked when the coolant temperature was set too low, causing impurities to freeze and form solid plugs.
Solution_Description: The precooler temperature was raised to a level that prevents freezing of impurities, restoring uninterrupted flow.
Supporting_Evidence: The hexyllithium precoolers (3) were frequently blocked due to the freezing of impurities if the temperature was too low.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: An aged DMS‑THF solution caused precipitation and clogging of the DMS precooler.
Solution_Description: Fresh DMS‑THF solution was used, eliminating the precipitate‑induced blockage; the solvent system was kept under inert, dry conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: the DMS precooler was susceptible to clogging when using an aged DMS–THF solution (7).

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Moisture in the starting materials generated lithium hydroxide, a solid that quickly fouled the reactors and raised pressure.
Solution_Description: Reactants were rigorously purified and dried; the feed streams were kept strictly anhydrous and inert, preventing lithium‑hydroxide formation.
Supporting_Evidence: increase of pressure was observed after this period, which was related to the presence of moisture in the starting materials.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Replacing a capillary with a residence‑time module altered flow and heat‑exchange characteristics, causing deviations in conversion and yield.
Solution_Description: Operating windows (temperature, throughput) were re‑optimised for the new hardware; the reactor design was standardised to keep hydraulic and thermal profiles consistent.
Supporting_Evidence: some pieces of equipment had to be replaced by different types; for example, a capillary was replaced by residence time modules.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Lower cooling‑medium temperatures required a doubling of residence time to achieve full conversion, decreasing throughput and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The cooling‑medium temperature was increased (‑45 °C → ‑55 °C) which shortened the necessary residence time while still providing complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: a reduction of the cooling temperature by 10 °C required almost a doubling of the residence time in order to complete the first stage.

Paper Title: Experience with Scale-Up of Low-Temperature Organometallic Reactions in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: At high throughputs the DFT route (reaction enthalpy 480 kJ mol⁻¹) experienced runaway in the second stage, making the process unstable.
Solution_Description: Throughput was cut by ~50 % (1.07 → 0.5 kg h⁻¹) and the cooling‑medium temperature was lowered to keep reactor temperature below the runaway threshold.
Supporting_Evidence: throughput for the DFT synthesis had to be reduced by almost 50 % from 1.07 to 0.5 kg h⁻¹ in order to sustain stable operation.

Paper Title: Preparation of β‑hydroxy-α-amino Acid Using Recombinant
Problem_Description: The original chemical synthesis of the API used toxic ethyl isocyanoacetate and, because it was a racemic resolution, the theoretical maximum yield was only 50 % resulting in low overall yield and large waste generation.
Solution_Description: A recombinant d‑threonine aldolase‑catalysed aldol addition of glycine and pyridine‑4‑carboxaldehyde was developed, providing a high‑yielding, enantio‑ and diastereoselective route that avoids the toxic reagent and reduces waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initial synthesis also used toxic ethyl isocyanoacetate… Since a theoretical maximum of 50 % possesses the correct stereochemistry in the racemic synthesis, the initial process had low yield and generated significant waste.”; “The chiral β‑hydroxy‑α‑amino acid … was synthesized by a recombinant d‑threonine aldolase‑catalysed condensation… an environmentally friendly process …”

Paper Title: Preparation of β‑hydroxy-α-amino Acid Using Recombinant
Problem_Description: The AXDTA gene cloned into the pBMS2004 (tac‑promoter) vector gave almost no protein expression, whereas the same gene in the pET30a (T7‑promoter) vector expressed well.
Solution_Description: The expression construct was changed to the pET30a vector (T7 promoter) which restored high enzyme activity in shake‑flask cultures.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only background activity was present in extracts of BL21Gold (pBMS2004‑AXDTA)… while both genes could be efficiently expressed using the T7 promoter of pET30a.”; “We have not investigated the reason for these results… 5′ end of a gene might influence mRNA folding… which may explain the lack of expression for pBMS2004 and AXDTA.”

Paper Title: Preparation of β‑hydroxy-α-amino Acid Using Recombinant

Paper Title: Seeded Crystallization of β‑
Problem_Description: Unseeded continuous crystallizations in the COBC caused severe encrustation of the glass walls, leading to blockages, loss of temperature control, back‑pressure increase and eventual process shutdown.
Solution_Description: A continuously seeded operation was introduced, adding a controlled stream of β‑LGA seed crystals directly into the reactor to suppress primary nucleation and prevent crystal deposition on the vessel surface.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Encrustation of crystallization vessel surfaces during the crystallization of LGA … led to loss of control of PSD, blockages and ultimately process shut‑down.”
• “The approach used eliminates the need for primary nucleation … through the use of continuous seeding using seeds produced from a continuous antisolvent process.”
• “Over each of the four continuously seeded experiments encrustation was not observed … operation for at least 10 h.”

Paper Title: Seeded Crystallization of β‑
Problem_Description: In unseeded runs the COBC consistently produced the metastable α‑LGA polymorph, and even when seeding was used, high supersaturation (experiment 3) triggered primary nucleation of α‑LGA, giving a mixed‑phase product.
Solution_Description: Operating temperatures and feed concentrations were tuned so that bulk supersaturation remained in the range 2–3, avoiding the metastable zone (≈3–5) and ensuring only the thermodynamically stable β‑polymorph formed.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When bulk supersaturation remained in the range 2–3, the polymorphic phase purity of the thermodynamically stable β polymorph was retained.”
• “Experiment 3 … exceeded this range … primary nucleation of the metastable α polymorph was observed, and product crystals were a mixed phase.”
• “Final SS values from experiments 1, 2, 4 (ranging from ca. 2–3) … resulted in pure β‑LGA.”

Paper Title: Seeded Crystallization of β‑
Problem_Description: The product crystals collected from seeded runs were heavily agglomerated, complicating particle‑size‑distribution (PSD) measurements and obscuring the relationship between seed loading, concentration and crystal growth.

Solution_Description: The authors acknowledge the need for improved agitation or anti‑agglomeration strategies (e.g., adjusting oscillation parameters) and plan further work on population‑balance modelling that includes agglomeration effects.

• “The overall particle growth mechanism did not follow that of individual crystals; therefore this posed challenges in drawing firm conclusions …”
• “Further work to develop a PFR PBM which can also account for agglomeration is ongoing …”

Paper Title: Seeded Crystallization of β‑
Problem_Description: The seeding strategy relied on an off‑line turbulent jet reverse antisolvent process to make β‑LGA seeds, requiring separate production, isolation and resuspension steps.
Solution_Description: Seeds were generated continuously by a turbulent jet antisolvent method, producing ~10 µm β‑LGA crystals that could be fed directly into the COBC, reducing the need for batch seed preparation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Seeds were prepared using a turbulent jet reverse antisolvent process … β‑LGA seeds with a mean size ca. 10 µm were produced.”
• “The approach used eliminates the need for primary nucleation … through the use of continuous seeding using seeds produced from a continuous antisolvent process.”

Paper Title: Seeded Crystallization of β‑
Problem_Description: Achieving sufficient crystal growth required a residence time of ≈80 min, which is long for continuous crystallization and could limit throughput.
Solution_Description: The COBC’s plug‑flow character and oscillatory mixing allowed the residence time to be extended without sacrificing mixing intensity, enabling the required crystal growth while maintaining a compact reactor volume.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “COBC operating conditions were selected to ensure a sufficient RT was available for particle growth (ca. 80 min) alongside the operation within a near plug‑flow domain.”
• “The ability to extend the mean residence time, under plug‑flow conditions, at a similar mixing intensity … is advantageous to slow processes such as crystallization.”

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: During the acidic work‑up of the first‑generation sequence, hydrogen fluoride (HF) was generated, posing a safety hazard and risking corrosion of equipment.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the original sequence that required acidic work‑up and devised a new second‑generation route that avoids the HF‑forming step entirely, eliminating the safety issue.
Supporting_Evidence: In the first step, hydrogen fluoride is formed at acidic workup.; The route was successfully scaled up … however, the route needed to be improved for future material supply due to the following three problems: i. In the first step, hydrogen fluoride is formed at acidic workup.

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: After the Wittig reaction the phosphine oxide impurity could only be removed by silica‑gel column chromatography, which is costly and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: A Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons (HWE) reaction using t‑BuOK was introduced, which does not generate phosphine oxide, thereby eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: After the Wittig reaction, silica gel column chromatography was needed to remove phosphine oxide.; We were delighted to find that the selective decarbonylative Heck reaction … The HWE reaction with t‑BuOK proceeded with minimum isomerization of the double bond and also avoided the use of silica gel column purification.

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: The hydrogenation step required 40 wt % of an expensive 10 % Rh/C (50 % wet) catalyst to reach full conversion, leading to high material cost and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was switched to 5 % Pt/C (10 % of 50 % wet slurry) and the solvent changed from 2‑propanol to ethyl acetate, reducing catalyst loading to 13 wt % and improving safety and cost profile.
Supporting_Evidence: At the hydrogenation step, 40 wt % (vs starting material 9) of expensive 10 % Rh/C (50 % wet) was needed for full conversion.; 5 % Pt/C was found to be promising with only 10 % wt loading (entry 6).; Switching the solvent from 2‑propanol to ethyl acetate was effective but gave only 1.1 % of debrominated 18 when reaction completed (entry 7).

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: The decarbonylative Heck coupling gave only ~50 % yield and the crude product required a second recrystallization for acceptable purity, making the route unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the decarbonylative Heck pathway and adopted a second‑generation route based on an HWE coupling that provided higher overall yield and reproducible purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Although this route was shorter than the first generation procedure, the yield from the coupling reaction was moderate (∼50 %). The purity of 10 was also not satisfactory, and so a second recrystallization at the final step was necessary to improve its purity.; we decided to move to another process for further scale‑up.

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: During the HWE step, the by‑product 17 formed (phosphonate impurity) and tri‑isopropyl phosphite carried over acted as a catalyst poison for the subsequent hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: Running the HWE reaction with t‑BuOK at ≤5 °C suppressed formation of 17 to ~3 %; the resulting product 9 was recrystallized from aqueous 2‑propanol, fully removing tri‑isopropyl phosphite.
Supporting_Evidence: With higher loading of t‑BuONa, the reaction still did not complete … Gratifyingly, about 3 % of 17 was formed with t‑BuOK when the reaction was performed below 5 °C, while the starting material was consumed in 6 h.; triisopropyl phosphite could be completely removed when the product 9 was recrystallized from aqueous 2‑propanol.

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: Residual water in the Pt/C slurry promoted debromination of the substrate, forming impurity 18 and also slowed the hydrogenation rate.
Solution_Description: The water content of the Pt/C slurry was tightly controlled (50 % wet, limited addition) and powdered K₂CO₃ was added during hydrogenation to scavenge HBr, minimizing debromination while maintaining reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: The use of Pt/C slurry in water is normally desirable … however, it was revealed that the addition of water significantly increased the formation of debrominated 18.; The formation of this compound was suppressed by addition of powdered K₂CO₃ during the hydrogenation without affecting the reaction rate.

Paper Title: A Second Generation Synthesis of Benzyl Piperidine Derivatives: A Key Intermediate for the Preparation of SERT/5-HT
Problem_Description: Impurities present in 1‑bromo‑2‑methoxyethane (15) generated a series of material‑derived impurities (20‑26) in the final product.
Solution_Description: Reagent 15 was sourced with controlled impurity levels; the authors limited its impurity content and employed basic washing steps to remove related by‑products, ensuring product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Analysis of the reagent grade 15 revealed that it contained corresponding bromides … formation of these compounds could be avoided by limiting its impurity levels.; It was found that 14 could be easily removed to 0.03 % (HPLC area %) by basic washing at workup of 6.

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Potent NAE Inhibitor Pevonedistat
Problem_Description: The original discovery synthesis of pevonedistat required >20 linear steps, many chromatographic purifications, a low‑yielding resolution, removal of an extra hydroxyl group, and a ketal protecting‑group installation, resulting in poor overall efficiency.
Solution_Description: A completely revised retrosynthetic plan was adopted that introduced the labile sulfamoyl group at a late stage and used commercially available amino‑indane 6 and 4‑chloropyrrolopyrimidine 3, eliminating the inefficient steps of the discovery route.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The original Discovery synthesis toward pevonedistat involved 20+ linear steps … Poor efficiency resulted from a low yielding resolution, removal of an extra chiral hydroxyl group, and installation of a ketal protecting group.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Potent NAE Inhibitor Pevonedistat
Problem_Description: The Sharpless epoxidation route to amino‑diol 4 gave modest yields, produced a 1:1.3 mixture of regio‑isomers (13/14) after reductive opening, and required multiple chromatographic purifications to isolate pure 13, making the sequence unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The route was abandoned in favor of a bromolactonization‑based synthesis of 4‑HBr, which provided a high‑yielding, telescoped sequence with only a single isolation step, eliminating the need for chromatography and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The regioselectivity of the subsequent reductive epoxide ring opening was an obstacle … resulted in a mixture of 13 and 14 (1:1.3)… Attempts to separate 13 from 14 by column chromatography proved difficult.”

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Potent NAE Inhibitor Pevonedistat

Problem_Description: Late‑stage sulfamoylation of intermediate 2 with reagents 22/23 gave a mixture of the desired product 1, a regioisomer 1′ and bis‑sulfamoylated by‑product 24, requiring chromatographic purification and presenting safety concerns due to the handling of aggressive sulfamoyl chlorides.

Problem_Description: Isolation of the Burgess‑type reagent 28 from the reaction mixture was difficult because it co‑precipitated with DABCO·HCl salt and could not be separated by standard crystallisation.

Paper Title: Process Development and GMP Production of a Potent NAE Inhibitor Pevonedistat
Problem_Description: The final API (pevonedistat) needed a chromatography‑free method to meet GMP purity specifications for salt formation.
Solution_Description: Free base 1 was dissolved in ethanol, heated to 50 °C, and seeded with 1 % (w/w) pevonedistat prior to slow addition of ethanolic HCl; cooling induced precipitation of the hydrochloride salt with >98 % a/a purity, eliminating chromatography.

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed Coupling of Sulfonylhydrazones with Heteroaromatic 2‑Amino-Halides (Barluenga Reaction): Exploring the Electronics of the Sulfonylhydrazone
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route to the key intermediate 1 required a long sequence that involved the expensive and difficult‑to‑purify ketone 3c, its conversion to a nonaflate (3b) and then to a vinyl boronate (3a) before the final coupling – a step‑inefficient process with costly reagents and problematic purification.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was devised that avoided the protection/de‑protection steps and used the free‑amino substrate 2 directly.  The optimized protocol employed Pd(OAc)₂ with the electron‑rich phosphine ligand t‑Bu₂MeP‑HBF₄ (6.5 mol %), milled K₂CO₃, and DMA as solvent, delivering the target in 85 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the rather expensive and difficult to purify ketone 3c had to be converted to the nonaflate 3b… which was converted to the vinyl boronate 3a, which could then be coupled with 2 to form the desired product.” (Introduction) 
• “Given the observations above, we decided to focus our attention on the free amino derivative 2… we were able to achieve good yields… by using di‑tert‑butyl methyl phosphine as the ligand and milled K₂CO₃ as the base and by using 1.1–1.2 equiv of the sulfonylhydrazone. … the reaction works best in dimethylacetamide which is not the preferred solvent for Barluenga reactions.” (Results and Discussion) 
• The final isolated yield of 1 was 85 % (Experimental Section).

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed Coupling of Sulfonylhydrazones with Heteroaromatic 2‑Amino-Halides (Barluenga Reaction): Exploring the Electronics of the Sulfonylhydrazone
Problem_Description: When the unprotected amino substrate 2 was coupled with tosylhydrazone 4 under the standard Barluenga conditions (LiOBu‑t, XPhos, dioxane), only 2 % of the desired product 1 was obtained; the major products were the dimer 5 and reduced 6, and >44 % of 2 remained while <6 % of 4 was recovered, indicating rapid hydrazone decomposition.
Solution_Description: Replacing XPhos with the more electron‑rich di‑tert‑butyl‑methyl‑phosphine ligand and switching the solvent from dioxane to DMA suppressed the side‑reactions, while using 1.1–1.2 equivalents of the sulfonylhydrazone (instead of a large excess) restored high conversion and reduced by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Indeed when the unprotected 2 was reacted with 4 … the desired product … was observed as the minor component … 2 % … while the dimeric and reduced compounds 5 and 6 were the main reaction products. … 44 % of the starting material 2 remained, while less than 6 % of the tosylhydrazone 4 could be detected … indicating that decomposition of 4 … was faster than the desired cross‑coupling path.” (Results and Discussion) 
• “We were able to achieve good yields … by using di‑tert‑butyl methyl phosphine as the ligand and milled K₂CO₃ … and by using 1.1–1.2 equiv of the sulfonylhydrazone. Surprisingly the reaction works best in dimethylacetamide …” (Results and Discussion) 
• Entry 9 in Table 1 shows that two equivalents of the expensive sulfonylhydrazone were required for useful yields, prompting the stoichiometry change. (Table 1 footnote).

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed Coupling of Sulfonylhydrazones with Heteroaromatic 2‑Amino-Halides (Barluenga Reaction): Exploring the Electronics of the Sulfonylhydrazone
Problem_Description: Earlier experiments showed that acceptable yields could only be obtained when two equivalents of the sulfonylhydrazone (an expensive reagent) were used, dramatically increasing material cost for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑optimized to work with 1.1–1.2 equivalents of the sulfonylhydrazone and an increased substrate‑to‑hydrazone (S/C) ratio of 100–150 without loss of efficiency, thereby cutting reagent cost while maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed Coupling of Sulfonylhydrazones with Heteroaromatic 2‑Amino-Halides (Barluenga Reaction): Exploring the Electronics of the Sulfonylhydrazone
Problem_Description: A slow, 8‑hour addition of the hydrazone was required to obtain even modest yields (≈15 %); such prolonged addition at elevated temperature is tedious and poses safety hazards on medium‑ to large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: By redesigning the addition protocol (using the more active phosphine ligand and DMA solvent) the reaction could be run with a shorter addition time and at a controlled temperature, eliminating the need for an 8‑hour slow addition and improving safety and throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed Coupling of Sulfonylhydrazones with Heteroaromatic 2‑Amino-Halides (Barluenga Reaction): Exploring the Electronics of the Sulfonylhydrazone
Problem_Description: Under condition B, electron‑rich sulfonylhydrazones (e.g., 24b) gave substantial amounts of the anisole adduct 28b (up to 30 % yield), consuming starting material and lowering the isolated yield of the desired product.

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Low conversion at low catalyst loading and temperature gave sub‑optimal yields; at higher conversion the reaction also produced an over‑reduced impurity (compound 2) that was not detected by the original UV method, reducing purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The D‑optimal DoE showed that raising the catalyst loading to 2.8 mol % and the temperature to 60 °C gave complete conversion in 1 h.  Reaction time and temperature were then limited (≤ 4 h, ≤ 40 °C) and conversion capped at ≈ 99 % to avoid over‑reduction, thereby improving yield and impurity profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “Higher temperature, catalyst loading, and substrate concentration all resulted in better conversion… (Table 1).”; “Combination of high catalyst loading (2.8 mol %) and high temperature (60 °C) resulting in complete conversion after 1 h.”; “Over‑reduced side product (compound 2) only forms in appreciable amount after all of compound 1 has been consumed.”; “Over‑reduction only becomes significant once > 99 % conversion is observed.”

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The initial DoE could not be augmented because the new analytical method (LC‑MS/GC) required to quantify the over‑reduced impurity was not compatible with the original data set, forcing a complete redesign of the experiment.
Solution_Description: A second, independent D‑optimal study was launched that incorporated reaction time, temperature, catalyst loading and H₂ pressure as factors, using LC‑MS and GC to monitor conversion and the over‑reduction impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “This first DoE was not able to take the formation of compound 2 into consideration… it was not possible to leverage the existing data set and augment the DoE design.”; “A new DoE study… was established… to investigate the following variables: (1) reaction time, (2) reaction temperature, (3) catalyst loading, and (4) hydrogen pressure.”; “All experiments were designed… and the responses were (1) yield …, (2) conversion, and (3) over‑reduction … using a GC w/w assay.”

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The SiliaMetS Triamine scavenger removed insufficient Pd and Pt on scale (> 40 g), and the Thiourea‑based scavenger, although effective, posed a genotoxicity risk in the final drug‑substance step.
Solution_Description: The PhosphonicS STA3 scavenger (1 wt % of charge, 50 ± 5 °C, 18 h) was selected; it achieved < 1 ppm Pd/PT on lab scale and has a benign ligand profile, eliminating the safety concern associated with thiourea.
Supporting_Evidence: “SiliaMetS Triamine… afforded unsatisfactory Pd and Pt removal during preliminary scale‑up to beyond 40 g.”; “SiliaMetS Thiourea… was ruled out because of the concern over genotoxicity risk posed by leached thiourea.”; “The PhosphonicS STA3 scavenger… was ultimately chosen for its superior removal of both platinum and palladium (to < 1 ppm) and benign ligand profile.”; “After removal of the bulk catalyst… the mixture was heated to 50 ± 5 °C, and the batch temperature was maintained for 18–24 h.”

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original HCl‑addition/salting protocol used a very small, arbitrarily‑chosen seed (1.5 % of batch) and a very slow HCl addition (7–8 h), making the operation cumbersome, variable and time‑inefficient.
Solution_Description: Seed loading was raised to 5 % based on solubility data, HCl equivalents were fixed at 1.2 equiv, and the addition rate was changed to moderate/slow (1–2 h).  Heat/cool cycles (25 → 55 → ≈ 84 °C) were introduced to control crystal growth and improve filterability.
Supporting_Evidence: “The seed was added after an initial addition of the HCl… the addition rate of the HCl was very slow (took a very long time in production).”; “The amount of seed used was increased from 1.5 % and fixed at 5 % based on the solubility of IPI‑926·HCl in 2‑PrOH.”; “The equivalents of HCl… were set to 1.2 equiv.”; “After a number of experiments probing… the highest purity material was obtained after multiple heat/cool cycles of the IPI‑926·HCl crystals in 2‑PrOH.”

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Fast HCl addition caused uncontrolled supersaturation, leading to rapid precipitation that trapped impurities; this reduced product purity and mass balance.
Solution_Description: Addition rate was moderated (1 h) or slowed (2 h) to allow controlled nucleation, which yielded higher purity crystals and improved overall mass balance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Purity was most affected by the rate of HCl addition… the most pronounced effect being observed when the addition rate was slowed down from ‘fast’ to ‘moderate’.”; “Mass balance was also affected by the rate of HCl addition… a prolonged exposure to the reaction conditions (i.e., through a slow HCl addition) could result in impurity formation.”

Paper Title: A Design of Experiments Approach to a Robust Final Deprotection and Reactive Crystallization of IPI-926, A Novel Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Two new impurities (RRT 1.10 and 1.11) appeared during salting, especially when the overall mass balance was low, threatening product purity and yield.
Solution_Description: Optimized HCl stoichiometry (1.2 equiv) and controlled addition rate (moderate/slow) eliminated the formation of the new impurities; the optimized conditions were applied at production scale with no detectable RRT 1.10/1.11.
Supporting_Evidence: “Yield was most affected by the stoichiometry of the HCl added… the purity was most affected by the rate of HCl addition.”; “The salting procedure was effective… but two new impurities at RRT 1.10 and 1.11 were generated in the process… higher levels of the RRT 1.10 and 1.11 impurities were observed in the solid, the mother liquor, or both (but primarily in the mother liquor).”; “With these optimal conditions, the formation of the RRT 1.10 and 1.11 impurities is kept to a minimum, and they have typically not been observed in production.”

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Initial batch reactions using NaN₃ or TMSN₃ with concentrated H₂SO₄ in water‑miscible polar solvents (MeCN, MeOH, dioxane, AcOH, NMP) gave essentially no sulfoximine product – LC‑MS showed only Pummerer‑type rearrangement products and a strong, unpleasant odor. Conversions were < 20 % and selectivity for the desired sulfoximine was ≈ 10 % after 14 h.
Solution_Description: Switching to fuming sulfuric acid (20 % SO₃, “superacid”) dramatically increased the rate and selectivity (≈ 90 % selectivity after 10–15 min at 50 °C). The reaction time was cut from ≈ 14 h to ≤ 15 min and the product formed cleanly.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Reactions with NaN₃ or TMSN₃ and concentrated sulfuric acid under literature conditions provided low conversions and poor selectivities."
• "Sulfoxide 1 was fully consumed after a reaction time of only 90 min … no desired sulfoximine was produced."
• "Reactions with fuming sulfuric acid afforded the sulfoximine with a selectivity of ∼90 % after a reaction time of only 10–15 min at 50 °C."
• Table S4 shows product selectivities up to 87 % after ∼30 min at 50 °C.

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: When Lewis acids (BF₃·OEt₂, Yb(OTf)₃, Cu(OTf)₂, ZnBr₂) were employed in non‑polar toluene with TMSN₃, no sulfoximine formed after 1 h at 50 °C. In MeOH, TMSN₃ hydrolyzed rapidly to HN₃, yielding only an unidentified side product after 5 h (38 % conversion). The reaction therefore decomposed rather than delivering product.
Solution_Description: Adopting a biphasic CH₂Cl₂/H₂SO₄ system (organic phase transports substrate and TMSN₃; acid phase conducts the imidation) prevented premature hydrolysis/decomposition and allowed the reaction to proceed with high conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "No reaction was observed under these conditions after a reaction time of 1 h at 50 °C."
• "A reaction with TMSN₃ in MeOH … gave an unidentified side product in a slow reaction (38 % after 5 h at 50 °C)."
• "The sole purpose of the inert organic phase … is to carry the reagents into the reactor."
• ">99 % conversion was obtained with fuming sulfuric acid after a reaction time of only 10 min at 50 °C."
• "The reaction was considerably faster and significantly cleaner with fuming sulfuric acid compared to reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid."

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Using concentrated H₂SO₄ in CHCl₃ produced an immiscible two‑phase system; the sulfoxide was extracted into the acid phase and partially precipitated as a sticky solid, severely hindering stirring and giving only 19 % conversion and 10 % product selectivity after 14 h.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employing CH₂Cl₂ (instead of CHCl₃) as the organic carrier and introducing fuming H₂SO₄ in a controlled biphasic flow configuration provided homogeneous segments, eliminated the large precipitate, and allowed efficient mass transfer of substrate into the acid phase, sharply improving conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Sulfuric acid is not soluble in CHCl₃ and forms a separate, immiscible phase. … a sticky precipitate was formed … rendering stirring difficult."
• "The mixture was then added … to a well‑stirred solution of fuming sulfuric acid. Two separated, homogeneous phases were obtained …"
• "The reaction worked equally well using CH₂Cl₂ as solvent."
• ">99 % conversion was obtained with fuming sulfuric acid after a reaction time of only 10 min at 50 °C."

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: When the sulfoxide was dissolved directly in neat concentrated H₂SO₄ for continuous‑flow feeding, it decomposed slowly, making the approach impractical for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The substrate was pre‑dissolved in CH₂Cl₂ (feed A) and mixed with fuming H₂SO₄ only inside the reactor (feed B). This limited the residence time of the sulfoxide in the strong acid, preventing decomposition while still delivering high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Preliminary experiments suggested that 1 slowly decomposes in conc H₂SO₄, rendering this approach impractical."
• "The flow reactor was assembled … feed A … CH₂Cl₂, feed B … fuming sulfuric acid. … the mixture was combined only in the reactor."
• "A reaction on a 4 mmol scale confirmed that the reaction provides full conversion with similar product selectivity as obtained under batch conditions."

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Quenching the fuming H₂SO₄ stream with H₂O is extremely exothermic and can cause violent temperature spikes, posing a safety hazard even on small scale.
Solution_Description: The quench was performed in‑line within an ice‑cooled segment of fluoropolymer tubing, with the flow rates adjusted to keep the temperature at or below room temperature and a back‑pressure regulator (3–7 bar) used to manage gas evolution and residence time, thereby controlling the exotherm safely.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Caution: the quench of fuming sulfuric acid with H₂O is extremely exothermic and must be done very carefully."
• "The temperature of the cross‑mixer and the subsequent tubing … did not increase above about room temperature."
• "All supply lines, fittings, and T‑ and X‑pieces were made of fluoropolymers (H₂SO₄ is not compatible with PEEK)."
• "Back pressure was adjusted to 3 bar … later to 7 bar to control residence time and gas evolution."

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Sulfoxide Imidation Protocol Using Azide Sources under Superacidic Conditions
Problem_Description: Batch reactions under literature conditions required ≈ 14 h at room temperature to reach only 19 % conversion and gave a mere 10 % isolated product, making the process unsuitable for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Raising the temperature to 50 °C and employing fuming H₂SO₄ reduced the reaction time to 10–15 min while achieving ≈ 90 % selectivity, effectively eliminating the long‑reaction bottleneck.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Reactions with concentrated sulfuric acid under literature conditions gave a slow reaction and poor selectivity (10 % product after 14 h at room temperature)."
• "Reactions with fuming sulfuric acid afforded the sulfoximine with a selectivity of ≈ 90 % after a reaction time of only 10–15 min at 50 °C."
• Table S4 shows product selectivities up to 87 % after ~30 min at 50 °C.

Problem_Description: The standard Ugi protocol gave <10 % of the desired product because the enolizable aldehyde degraded and Passerini side‑reactions occurred, leading to poor conversion and inconsistent results.

Supporting_Evidence: “Application of the standard protocol…resulted in a complex mixture with less than 10 % …the desired product” (p. 7). “A search…revealed a description of the amine added as the last component…formed product 14 almost quantitatively.” (p. 8). “We found that the aldehyde can be added last…highly exothermic salt formation…When the order is changed a clean and rapid transformation can be essentially completed in less than 30 min.” (p. 9).

Problem_Description: Methoxyacetaldehyde 8 is volatile, water‑soluble, and not commercially available in usable quantity; commercial samples were completely decomposed.
Solution_Description: Prepare 8 by hydrolysis of its dimethyl acetal 8a in water (reflux 8 h), giving a stable ≈2 M aqueous solution that can be stored for months and used directly without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Methoxyacetaldehyde…cannot be obtained on scale and a commercial sample turned out to be entirely decomposed.” (p. 10). “The simple heating of the acetal in water for 6–10 h leads to almost complete conversion obtaining the aldehyde as an approximately 2 M solution in water. This aqueous solution is stable…for at least two years.” (p. 12).

Paper Title: Development of Scalable Conditions for the Ugi ReactionApplication to the Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Removal of many chiral auxiliaries (e.g., naphthylethylamines) failed under hydrogenolysis, giving no conversion or decomposition, making the de‑protection step a bottleneck.
Solution_Description: Use formic acid (16 eq) with anisole at 82 °C to cleave the auxiliary; the resulting non‑polar bis‑aryl by‑products are removed by simple MCH extraction, delivering the API in 82 % isolated yield, >99.9 % purity and ee.

Problem_Description: The Ugi condensation is highly exothermic, especially the acid‑amine salt formation, which can lead to temperature spikes on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Neutralize the chiral amine with acetic acid at 15 °C first, then add the isocyanide solution at 10 °C, and finally add the aldehyde at −10 °C; this staged addition removes the heat of salt formation before the main Ugi exotherm and enables safe scale‑up.

Problem_Description: The Boc‑protected penultimate intermediate was found to be labile; under the planned downstream chemistry the Boc group decomposes, creating safety‑concerned impurity and loss of material.
Solution_Description: The protecting‑group strategy was changed to an ethoxy‑ethyl (EE) group, which is more stable to the required reaction conditions and can be removed in high yield later in the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although successful, lability concerns with the Boc group led us to explore alternative protecting groups… it was decided that an ethoxy ethyl (EE) protecting group would be explored, as it was believed that it would withstand the desired chemistry, while also being able to be deprotected in high yields.”

Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction is heated above the solvent’s boiling point, so back pressure must be applied… The feed was pumped through a 12 L Hastelloy tube heated to 150 °C at a residence time of 2 h… 94 % isolated yield, >99.8 % purity.”

Supporting_Evidence: Table 1: entry 1 (none) – 2 % conversion; entry 5 (NH₄Cl) – 100 % conversion, 0 % aniline. “NH₄Cl looked very promising.”
