Problem_Description: Running the deprotection above THF’s boiling point creates a high‑temperature, high‑pressure environment that requires equipment able to withstand 250 psi and poses safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A stainless‑steel/Hastelloy tubular plug‑flow reactor was employed with an inline back‑pressure regulator (250 psi) to keep the reaction mixture liquid and safely manage the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction is heated above the solvent’s boiling point, so back pressure must be applied to ensure the contents stay a liquid… 250 psi… The equipment used must be able to withstand pressures above those needed.”

Paper Title: Development of an NH
Problem_Description: Potential drift in conversion during long continuous runs could lead to off‑spec material, especially because the process is run for many hours.
Solution_Description: An online HPLC system with automated sampling/dilution was integrated to monitor the % of starting material in real time, allowing immediate corrective action if the profile deviated.
Supporting_Evidence: “Online HPLC data of wt % starting material (3) remaining over time… The results were very consistent across the 90 h… In addition to analysis of the collected final product, online HPLC was also in place to monitor the reaction in real‑time.”

Paper Title: Development of an NH
Problem_Description: The final product existed as THF‑solvate and monohydrate forms; eliminating these required six successive distillations, a time‑consuming operation.
Solution_Description: A series of six controlled distillations (alternating IPA addition and reflux concentration) were performed to remove solvent‑solvate water, yielding the anhydrous, nonsolvated merestinib with 94 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The slurry was heated to reflux and concentrated… repeated six times… to obtain 1 (26.7 kg, 94 % yield) as a white solid.”

Paper Title: Development of an NH
Problem_Description: Residual palladium from the Suzuki coupling needed to be removed before downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Silica‑thiol Pd‑scavenging resin (41 kg) was added to the organic layer after the coupling; the slurry was heated to 60 °C for 6 h, filtered, and the filtrate was concentrated.
Supporting_Evidence: “41 kg of silica‑thiol Pd‑scavenging resin was added… heated to 60 °C for 6 h, and the resin was removed by filtration.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: The aza‑Henry product precipitates during the reaction, giving a low‑solubility solid that clogs plug‑flow reactors and makes continuous operation impossible.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An automated intermittent‑flow CSTR was adopted. The reactor runs as a repeating batch with semi‑batch filtration of the solid product and recycle of the filtrate, eliminating plugging and allowing solids handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The product precipitates during the course of the reaction… PFRs generally cannot handle solids in flow due to plugging and clogging.”
• “An automated intermittent flow stirred tank reactor was selected instead… the az­a‑Henry product continuously crystallizes… and is intermittently filtered while the mother liquor… is returned to the reactor.”
• “The answer to this reactor design challenge was an intermittent‑flow CSTR… the feed pumping, product slurry pumping to the filter, filtration, and recycle… are all fully automated.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: Batch aza‑Henry reactions require ~24 h per cycle, limiting throughput and process intensity.
Solution_Description: Reaction time was shortened to 4 h by increasing catalyst loading (0.5 % w/w) and running at higher temperature (−20 °C to −13 °C), which together allowed a 40‑min intermittent‑flow cycle.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Batch organocatalytic aza‑Henry reactions can require long reaction times (∼24 h)… Reduced cycle times on the order of 30–40 min would provide an opportunity for translation.”
• “It was found that reaction time can be shortened from 24 to 4 h, and the catalyst loading was reduced to 0.5 % without loss of yield or selectivity.”
• “The automated intermittent‑flow unit … achieved a 40 min total turnover time.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: Organocatalyst loadings of 5–10 % are economically unattractive for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: Catalyst recycle was implemented (80 % recycle ratio) together with lower catalyst loadings (0.38 % overall) by feeding fresh catalyst each cycle, maintaining high concentration in the reactor while using far less catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Generally high catalyst loadings (5–10 %) are considered unattractive… With high catalyst loadings, economical constraints play an important role.”
• “The recycling number 80 % indicates that only 80 % of the catalyst was recycled, but 20 % of fresh catalyst was introduced at the beginning of each cycle.”
• “Overall catalyst loading was 0.38 %… Significant intensification of the process was achieved by reduction of the reaction time… while maintaining high concentrations of the catalyst in the flask due to 80 % recycling.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: Low‑molecular‑weight nitroalkanes are high‑energy, potentially explosive compounds; handling the full batch inventory poses a safety risk.
Solution_Description: The intermittent‑flow platform introduces the nitroalkane slowly and keeps only a small quantity in the reactor at any time, dramatically reducing the amount of hazardous material present and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Low molecular weight nitroalkanes can be high‑energy compounds… hazards… are largely unstudied.”
• “Operating an automated intermittent flow reactor affords the safety benefit of only having small amounts of nitroalkane present at any given time, as opposed to a batch reaction where the full amount… is subjected to the reaction from the start.”
• “The mode of reagent addition was designed to keep concentration of the imine low relative to nitroalkane… while simultaneously maintaining excess nitroalkane acid in a range that does not affect activity of the Brønsted basic catalyst.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: The α‑amido sulfone intermediate (compound 8) has very low solubility in non‑polar solvents, making chromatographic purification difficult and leading to product loss.
Solution_Description: The sulfone was isolated by filtration and trituration with diethyl ether, avoiding chromatography; the precipitation step was exploited for easier collection despite low solubility.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Purification of these sulfones is generally a challenge due to low solubility in a majority of non‑polar organic solvents, and significant decomposition is often observed upon crystallization from protic solvents.”
• “Filtration and trituration with diethyl ether to remove residual aldehyde provided the desired amido‑sulfone 8 in 80–82 % yield overall.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: Oxidation of the oxime to the nitroalkane using m‑CPBA is highly exothermic and requires large excess of the aggressive oxidant, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The oxidant was switched to peracetic acid (a milder oxidant) which gave a less exothermic profile, reduced side‑product formation and allowed a simpler work‑up, albeit with still limited direct crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Extensive chromatographic purification was required, and excessive amounts of meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid raised safety concerns. An alternative oxidant was considered…”
• “Based on literature precedent we attempted the same reaction using peracetic acid solution… these conditions have shown a slightly better reaction profile with decreased reaction times, diminished side product formation and a simple purification protocol.”
• “However, direct crystallization of the product with desired purity from the crude reaction mixture was unattainable, and an exothermic profile of the reaction was a concern.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: When 100 % catalyst recycle was used, enantioselectivity dropped after 4–5 cycles, indicating loss of active catalyst or deactivation.
Solution_Description: A recycle ratio of 80 % was adopted with addition of fresh catalyst (1.25 % initial, 0.25 % each subsequent cycle), stabilizing enantioselectivity throughout the sequence.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “With 100 % recycle, good enantioselectivity could be maintained only during the first 4–5 iterations and usually dropped (10–15 %) after the fifth or sixth iteration.”
• “We conducted a sequence with 1.25 % of the catalyst in the flask and an 80 % recycling ratio… The enantioselectivity and diastereoselectivity of the process remained high throughout the entire sequence.”
• “The recycling ratio 80 % indicates that only 80 % of the catalyst was recycled, but 20 % of fresh catalyst was introduced at the beginning of each cycle.”

Paper Title: Development of an Intermittent-Flow Enantioselective Aza-Henry Reaction Using an Arylnitromethane and Homogeneous Brønsted Acid–Base Catalyst with Recycle
Problem_Description: Cooling nitroalkane to –20 °C leads to its partial crystallization, causing feed blockages and inconsistent stoichiometry.
Solution_Description: The nitroalkane was used with a slight excess (1.2–1.5 equiv) at a concentration of 0.10–0.15 M to keep it in solution while avoiding catalyst deactivation from excessive acid.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “While cooling nitroalkane to –20 °C, in concentrations between 0.5 and 0.7 g per 1 mL, slow crystallization of the starting material was observed.”
• “Experiments were usually performed with a slight excess of nitroalkane (1.2–1.5 eq at 0.10–0.15 M). High stoichiometric amounts of nitroalkane proved to be detrimental to selectivity…”
• “An attempt to increase concentration further resulted in lower selectivity.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: The epoxidation mixture existed as three immiscible phases (organic, aqueous, solid Amberlite) and the high viscosity made stirring difficult, causing inconsistent mixing and variability in conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The stirrer gap was increased from 1 mm to 2.5 mm and a stirring speed of 400 rpm was used to keep Amberlite beads suspended. H₂O₂ was added via an automated syringe pump over 2.5 h, ensuring a controlled addition rate and uniform mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The epoxidation mixture remains in three phases (organic, aqueous, and solid) during the reaction and proper mixing is very important … Mixing at 400 rpm was deemed sufficient as solid brownish Amberlite could be seen throughout reaction mixture.” ; “The H₂O₂ addition rates were 0.91, 0.68, or 0.46 g min⁻¹ mol⁻¹ unsaturation …”, “The mechanical stirrer … gap … was increased to 2.5 mm to prevent the Amberlite IR 120H catalyst beads from being damaged during epoxidation.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: Epoxidation is highly exothermic; during the first 15 min of H₂O₂ addition the reactor temperature rose sharply, creating a risk of overheating and oxirane bond cleavage.
Solution_Description: A jacketed reactor with an automated temperature‑control system (Huber Cryostat) was employed; the controller continuously adjusted the jacket fluid temperature to keep the reaction at the set point (55–65 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: “The increase was due to the exothermic reaction. But the controller adjusted the jacket temperature to bring the reaction back down to the set point temperature.” ; “The temperature–time profile … shows the exothermic nature of the reaction … ΔT was 16.3 °C at 45 min.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: Hydrogen peroxide is the most expensive reagent and is not recyclable, contributing significantly to the production cost of epoxidized sucrose soyate.
Solution_Description: Design‑of‑experiments modeling identified the minimum H₂O₂, acetic acid, and Amberlite amounts that still gave >98 % conversion, allowing a reduction of all reagents by 18–20 % while maintaining resin quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion greater than 98 % also indicates that side reactions were negligible at 60–65 °C and 4.5–5 h of reaction.” ; “The results … indicate that a conversion of greater than 98 % can still be achieved even with a significant reduction of up to 20 % of the amount of reagents.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: Typical epoxidation runs required 3.5–5.5 h, limiting throughput for industrial production.
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 60–65 °C and using optimal catalyst loading accelerated the reaction, enabling >95 % conversion in as little as 3.5 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction temperature was a relatively important source of variation … increasing temperature increases the rate of epoxidation.” ; “The model shows that up to 95 % conversion can be achieved in just 3.5 h when other factors are at the optimal level.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: Inconsistent H₂O₂ addition rates and inadequate stirring caused batch‑to‑batch variability in conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A Chemspeed AutoPlant system provided automated control of pump flow, stirring speed, and temperature, ensuring reproducible addition of H₂O₂ and consistent mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Chemspeed operational Autosuite … provide automatic control of the pump flow rate, stirring speed, and temperature.” ; “H₂O₂ was added using the syringe pump over 2.5 h… The reaction timer started when H₂O₂ addition started.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction to a 3 kg batch introduced a higher heat‑generation rate, challenging temperature control and posing safety risks.
Solution_Description: A 10 L jacketed glass reactor equipped with a dual‑impeller stirring system and an automated temperature‑control loop was used; the controller modulated the jacket fluid to keep the bulk temperature at 60 °C throughout the scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “A 10 L jacketed glass reactor … was used to scale up … The reactor system has a chemical metering pump … Stirring is provided by an Optichem stirring motor …” ; “The temperature of the reaction mixture remained constant at 60 °C … the controller adjusted the jacket temperature to bring the reaction back down to the set point temperature.”

Paper Title: Optimizing Process Parameters of Epoxidized Sucrose Soyate Synthesis for Industrial Scale Production
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 65 °C oxirane bonds can cleave, forming hydroxyl groups and reducing resin quality.
Solution_Description: The process window was limited to 55–65 °C and H₂O₂ was added well before the end of the reaction, minimizing water‑induced oxirane cleavage; hydroxyl values were monitored to confirm minimal degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Oxirane cleavage … especially above 65 °C … The hydroxyl values were less than 2.8 mg KOH g⁻¹ of resin, indicating minimal oxirane cleavage.” ; “The model shows that at 55 °C, conversion cannot attain 90 % and up to 99 % conversion can be achieved at 60 °C.”

Paper Title: A Three-Step Synthesis of Acotiamide for the Treatment of Patients with Functional Dyspepsia

Paper Title: A Three-Step Synthesis of Acotiamide for the Treatment of Patients with Functional Dyspepsia
Problem_Description: Aminolysis of ester 5a gave poor chemoselectivity; competing displacement of the amide produced impurity 9, and the initial salt‑formation step gave only 69 % yield with sub‑99 % purity.
Solution_Description: A staged addition protocol was employed: first 5b was aminated at low temperature in the presence of DCC (a scavenger that converts 5b into the desired product), then the temperature was raised to 120 °C under solvent‑free conditions to complete conversion of 5a. Excess amine was removed by vacuum distillation and the insoluble dicyclohexylurea (DCU) was filtered off. The final HCl salt was isolated by pH‑controlled crystallisation from DCM, which gave >99 % purity and a 92 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “the purification of 1 by crystallization from DCM… resulted in practically all major impurities removed.”

Paper Title: Enabling Synthesis of Triple Reuptake Inhibitor (+)-BMS-820836, a Potential Therapeutic Agent for the Treatment of Depression
Problem_Description: The acid‑mediated Friedel–Crafts cyclization of intermediate 5 gave a 1:1 mixture of the undesired C‑5 and the desired C‑7 tetrahydro‑isoquinoline, resulting in low isolated yield of the target isomer and the need for chromatographic separation.

Paper Title: Evolution of a Manufacturing Route to Omarigliptin, A Long-Acting DPP‑4 Inhibitor for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes

Paper Title: Evolution of a Manufacturing Route to Omarigliptin, A Long-Acting DPP‑4 Inhibitor for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes
Problem_Description: During Boc‑deprotection of intermediate 4 the mesyl group was cleaved, forming impurity 2, and the BSA salt used in earlier routes is mutagenic (genotoxic).
Solution_Description: Screened acids/solvents and identified benzenesulfonic acid (BSA) in CH₂Cl₂ as the best deprotection medium, suppressing impurity 2 to ~3 % A. Later, trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) was adopted, giving negligible demesylation (0.0–0.3 % A) and avoiding the mutagenic BSA salt altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: "Deprotection of the Boc group within 4 proved to be challenging…due to competitive cleavage of the mesyl group to form undesired byproduct 2"; "From a screen of acid and solvent combinations, benzenesulfonic acid (BSA) in dichloromethane…suppressed 2 to around 3.0 % A"; "Trifluoroacetic acid proved to be an excellent solution…negligible demesylation (0.0–0.3 % A)"; "Mesyl pyrazole BSA salt…was found to be AMES‑positive…to avoid handling of mutagenic 1‑mesylpyrazole BSA salt 8"

Paper Title: Evolution of a Manufacturing Route to Omarigliptin, A Long-Acting DPP‑4 Inhibitor for the Treatment of Type 2 Diabetes
Problem_Description: Reductive amination of pyranone 5 with mesyl‑pyrazole 8 gave variable yields (50–80 %) because both starting materials decompose in DMAC at room temperature, generating many low‑level impurities and polymeric by‑products.
Solution_Description: Developed a telescoped Boc‑deprotection/ reductive amination sequence: TFA deprotects 14 to the mesyl‑pyrazole TFA salt, which is transferred directly into DMAC/Et₃N and NaHB(OAc)₃ at –15 °C. This avoids isolation of the unstable BSA salt, keeps the product soluble, and gives consistent 85–90 % isolated yields with ≥30:1 diastereoselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Both starting materials in DMAC were decomposing at a rate of ∼2–3 wt % per hour…led to variable yield"; "To avoid handling of mutagenic 1‑mesylpyrazole BSA salt 8…we designed a through‑process for the Boc deprotection of Boc mesyl pyrazole 14 and in‑situ reductive amination"; "Boc‑deprotected TFA solution was simply added to DMAC…gave an improved yield of reductive amination product (∼84 %)"; "This new process…improved the diastereoselectivity to ≥30:1 and the isolated yield to 85–90 %"

Problem_Description: During the final Boc‑deprotection (H₂SO₄ in DMAC) the viscous slurry foamed when nitrogen was sparged, entraining gases and causing process instability.

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: The Grignard reaction is intrinsically hazardous because it requires activation of metallic magnesium and releases a large amount of heat (ΔHrxn = –340 kJ mol⁻¹), presenting a risk of runaway and safety incidents.
Solution_Description: The researchers moved the reaction to a continuous‑stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR). The CSTR operates at only 2.5 % of the batch volume, giving a larger surface‑area‑to‑volume ratio that improves heat removal and limits the amount of activated magnesium present at any time, thereby mitigating the exotherm and safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A Grignard reaction is a hazardous reaction due to the need for magnesium (metal) activation and the overall exothermic nature of the reaction." (Introduction)

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: Facility policy required that steps 2C‑2E be performed in a hydrogenation unit because hydrogen is evolved when excess magnesium is quenched, creating scheduling pressure and limiting flexibility for throughput.
Solution_Description: An alternative continuous‑flow unit operation (CSTR) was developed that sequesters magnesium inside the reactor, eliminating the need for a downstream hydrogenator and freeing the hydrogenation facility for other jobs.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The mandate also required mitigating the potential risk of acid mischarge during the Grignard reaction due to equipment set up issues or operator error... thus, an alternative unit operation was developed to form the Grignard reagent in a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR)." (Background)

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: Excess activated magnesium that is not retained in the reactor can react with residual acid, generating hydrogen and creating a pressure‑build‑up hazard; the solid‑liquid separation was insufficient in early designs.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A settling‑pipe (Mg trap) was designed using CFD to maximize solid‑liquid separation; the pipe geometry (60° bend, optimized diameter) and placement were chosen to keep Mg particles inside the CSTR, thereby reducing hydrogen evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The settling pipe allows Mg particles to drop to the bottom of the pipe by gravity and then slide back down into the CSTR... the first was the settling pipe geometry, designed to maximize the solid–liquid separation..." (Settling Pipe Design)

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: Variability in the concentration of Compound D and in the mass of magnesium charged each batch creates uncertainty in the Mg level inside the CSTR, risking under‑charging (loss of conversion) or over‑charging (excess solid load).
Solution_Description: A magnesium‑recharge strategy was built from the kinetic model: periodic Mg charges (two per 12 h shift) at a predefined amount (5 kg) were selected, and the timing of each charge was calculated to keep Mg above the critical level throughout the campaign.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Statistical analysis … suggested that the incoming Compound D concentration can vary up to ±2.6 wt % and the Mg charges can vary up to ±1 wt %… 1000 simulations… The simulation results suggested having two Mg recharges per shift coupled with a higher Mg level provides the lowest probability of over‑consuming Mg…" (Mg Recharge Strategy)

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: There was no real‑time measurement of Mg concentration, making it difficult to detect when conversion would fall below the target during operation.
Solution_Description: Reactor temperature was identified (via the kinetic‑energy balance) as a sensitive indicator of conversion; a 1.5 °C rise signals a drop below the 95 % conversion threshold, so temperature monitoring was adopted as the primary on‑line control metric.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The main concern for the project team was whether reactor temperature is sensitive enough to detect a drop in conversion rate… the model simulations showed that reactor temperature is sensitive enough to be used to monitor the CSTR conversion rate… a 1.5 °C difference… is above typical measurement noise…" (Reaction Monitoring)

Paper Title: Operation Strategy Development for Grignard Reaction in a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor
Problem_Description: High agitation speeds caused Mg particles to be entrained into the outlet stream, reducing sequestration efficiency.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: CFD flow‑field simulations guided the placement of the settling‑pipe inlet away from the impeller flow and toward the high‑pressure zone near the reactor wall; this positioning reduced particle entrainment and improved Mg capture.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The placement of the settling pipe away from the flow direction was favored to limit the number of Mg particles entering the settling pipe… The settling pipe is also best positioned in the high pressure zone…" (Positioning of Settling Pipe)

Paper Title: Process Research and Development of an Enantiomerically Enriched Allyic Amine, One of the Key Intermediates for the Manufacture of Synthetic Tetracyclines
Problem_Description: The original Myers‑Brubaker route relied on acetylene dicarboxylic acid methyl ester (4), a very expensive starting material (> $1000 kg⁻¹), and the isoxazole‑forming step gave only ~50 % isolated yield on laboratory scale. Subsequent benzylation of the iso­xazole produced significant amounts of the N‑benzyl regio‑isomer (10–20 %) that required chromatography. Reduction of the benzyl ether (6) with DIBAL generated over‑reduced alcohol (19) and unconsumed starting material, again needing chromatographic purification. The asymmetric vinylation using divinyl‑zinc formed large amounts of insoluble solids, causing very slow filtration and racemic product when the solids were not removed. The mesylation/displacement step gave two major impurities (vinyl‑mesylate 31 and linear amine 32). The bromination of dimethyl maleate (12) showed a pronounced exotherm at bromine addition and, if the quench was not carefully controlled, the dibromide (10) was partially reduced back to the fumarate (13). During the cryogenic DIBAL reduction of 6 to 7, precipitation of 6 caused over‑reduction and low conversion. The vinylation of the sulfinyl imine (34) displayed batch‑to‑batch variability in diastereoselectivity. Finally, the cleavage of the chiral auxiliary and reductive methylation using conventional borohydrides produced emulsions, side‑reduction products and required large excess of reagent.
Solution_Description: A new, cost‑effective route was developed beginning with cheap dimethyl maleate (12). Bromination was accelerated with AIBN, a small amount of water and light, and the addition of bromine was temperature‑controlled to manage the exotherm. Using dilute (5 wt %) Na‑thiosulfate at 0–5 °C during quench prevented undesired debromination to fumarate (13). The dibromosuccinate (10) was isolated by precipitation with heptane, avoiding chromatography. For the benzylation of isoxazole (5), the solvent was switched to NMP, DBU (or K₂CO₃) was used as base, benzyl chloride replaced benzyl bromide, and the addition of electrophile was performed slowly at 60 °C; the crude product was passed through a silica pad to remove the N‑benzyl impurity (16) without chromatographic work‑up. The reduction of 6 to 7 was performed as a two‑step sequence: NaBH₄ reduction to the alcohol (19) followed by a cryogenic Swern oxidation (oxalyl chloride/DMSO/Et₃N) at –70 °C, giving > 90 % isolated yield and avoiding over‑reduction. The problematic divinyl‑zinc vinylation was replaced by a one‑pot asymmetric vinylation using an ephedrine‑derived amino‑alcohol (26), diethyl zinc and vinyl‑MgBr, with careful order of addition (zinc‑ligand pre‑complex → vinyl‑Magnesium → aldehyde) and temperature ramps (–85 °C to –55 °C), eliminating solid by‑products and furnishing the allylic alcohol (8) in high ee. Mesylation and displacement were performed at –20 °C to 0 °C in DCM with dimethylamine in ethanol, minimizing formation of side‑products 31 and 32. The chiral‑auxiliary cleavage and reductive methylation were combined in a one‑pot protocol using 2‑picoline‑borane as the hydride source (functional additive), with pH adjusted by NaOAc before addition, providing 80–90 % isolated yield of the amine (3) with minimal side‑products. Finally, the final product was crystallized as its l‑tartaric acid salt from acetone/toluene, affording a solid, stable material with > 99 % ee.

Problem_Description: The batch Grignard process presented several safety hazards: the organic halide (benzyl bromide) is a strong lachrymator and mutagen, the Grignard reaction is highly exothermic and potentially violent, and hydrogen gas evolves during the quench because of excess magnesium.

Paper Title: Mitigating the Risk of Coprecipitation of Pinacol during Isolation from Telescoped Miyaura Borylation and Suzuki Couplings Utilizing Boron Pinacol Esters: Use of Modeling for Process Design

Paper Title: Development of Suitable Plant-Scale Drying Conditions That Prevent API Agglomeration and Dehydration
Problem_Description: During the first production run on the larger 1.0 m² agitated filter dryer (site B) the API showed significant agglomeration, producing a bimodal particle size distribution and a markedly reduced in‑vitro dissolution rate.  Simultaneously, the monohydrate API lost crystal‑bound water (Karl‑Fischer < 3.2 wt % H₂O) indicating dehydration of the target hydrate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A new drying window was established: jacket temperature 45 °C, absolute pressure 50 mbar, and elimination of nitrogen flow‑through (leak‑rate ≤ 1.3 mbar · min⁻¹).  The agitation regime was fixed at 5 rpm with 10 min of agitation per hour followed by a short smoothing step.  These conditions removed solvent quickly, kept the wet‑cake composition above the “sticky‑point” region, prevented formation of liquid bridges, and preserved the monohydrate form.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Higher pressures resulted in greater agglomeration" (Table 1, entries 2, 4, 3, 5).  
    • "Dehydration … was shown … at lower temperature (27 °C) and with nitrogen flow‑through" (intro, site B description).  
    • "Drying at 45 °C and pressure > 50 mbar … very robust with respect to dehydration" (Sec 4.3).  
    • "The revised conditions… jacket 45 °C, vacuum 50 mbar, no N₂ flow‑through, leak‑rate ≤ 1.3 mbar/min" (Table 2).  
    • "Aggitation speed 5 rpm … 10 min every 1 h, followed by 5–10 min smoothing" (Table 2, pilot‑plant).

Paper Title: Development of Suitable Plant-Scale Drying Conditions That Prevent API Agglomeration and Dehydration

Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Washing was changed from static displacement to an agitated wash (15–20 min at 5 rpm) that uniformly contacts the entire cake, removes residual water more efficiently and reduces the water content that drives agglomeration.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Static displacement washes … resulted in cracking of the wet‑cake and consequently channeling of the solvent" (Sec 4.2).  
    • "Agglomeration … correlated with the amount of water in the wash" (Table 1, entries 2–3 and 4–6).

Supporting_Evidence: ['One of the specific challenges associated with the development of a scalable continuous process for Buchwald–Hartwig reactions is the solid salt formation resulting from the necessary use of inorganic or alkali metal alkoxide bases.', 'The challenge of this workup methodology for continuous processing is the sensitivity of the catalyst to water; although the chosen process solvent, toluene, has very low solubility for water, the sensitivity of the reaction to ppm levels of water poses some technical challenges in terms of continuous drying, which was not feasible in this small setup.', 'the PTFE coil reactor (10.9 mL volume and 1.5 mm internal diameter) placed into an ultrasonic bath at 70 °C to avoid tube clogging by surface crystallization of the potassium bromide byproduct.', 'the observed loss of catalyst activity, attributed to the increase in water content of the feed catalyst solution, could potentially be compensated for in future operation by increasing the flow rate of the base feed as conversion begins to drop.', 'Moving beyond lab‑scale operation, our reaction required an alternative reactor approach; use of microreactor technology or lab‑scale equipment would not provide sufficient throughput to produce the larger quantities of material required due to the limited internal volume and the challenges of handling solids at high concentrations in such reactors.', 'The original batch process used a Pd‑(OAc)2/BINAP catalyst system, sodium tert‑butoxide as base... Our new flow process also uses an alternative base, potassium tert‑amylate, and reduced quantities of NMP.', 'All previous experiments had been run at 50 °C; however, Figure 7a demonstrates that a slight increase in temperature to 60 °C results in a sharp increase in reaction rate, thus halving the residence time required for full conversion.', 'The pressure peaks observed in Figure 12b occurred after taking samples from AB202... To avoid this for the remaining runs, the manual back‑pressure regulator was adjusted, and no further samples were taken until the end of operation.']

Problem_Description: The DIBAL‑H reduction of ester 2 to aldehyde 3 shows a rapid loss of selectivity at temperatures above –70 °C, leading to significant over‑reduction to alcohol 10 and lower overall conversion of the desired aldehyde.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Supporting_Evidence: Problem – "The main disadvantage with this reaction is the unwanted generation of over‑reduced alcohol 10... selectivity achieved decreased with increasing reaction temperature" (Table 1, Entries 2‑4).

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow for DIBAL‑H Reduction and
Problem_Description: The validated process requires three cryogenic steps (including the DIBAL‑H reduction), which demand costly cooling equipment, high energy consumption, and pose safety concerns for large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: In continuous flow the DIBAL‑H reduction can be performed at –50 °C (instead of –70 °C) and operated continuously for 87 min, delivering the aldehyde with 96.5 % isolated yield. The higher temperature reduces cooling load and the short, steady‑state run cuts overall operation time.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem – "cryogenic processing remains inconvenient because of the high operating costs associated with the long operation time and high energy requirements for cooling of the reactor" (Introduction).

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow for DIBAL‑H Reduction and
Problem_Description: Increasing the concentration of ester 2 three‑fold to improve throughput caused a very high solution viscosity, which limited the achievable flow rates and the ability of the syringe pumps to deliver the feed reliably.

Solution_Description: The use of high‑pressure plunger pumps (Shimadzu LC8A/LC10AD) allowed flow rates up to 27 mL min⁻¹ without pulsation, and connecting two COMET X‑01 micromixers in tandem further enhanced mixing, enabling the high‑viscosity feed to be processed efficiently.

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow for DIBAL‑H Reduction and
Problem_Description: The n‑BuLi‑mediated coupling of aldehyde 3 with sulfone 4 gave insufficient conversion to the target sulfone‑diol 5 under batch conditions, even after extensive optimization.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: In continuous flow, the residence time and mixing were improved by raising the flow rate from 10 to 20 mL min⁻¹ and using a CMPS‑α02 micromixer, while the temperature was optimized to 10 °C. An n‑BuLi loading of 2.15 equiv (with 1.10 equiv of aldehyde 3) gave 96.5 % conversion (only 3.5 % unreacted 4), the best result reported.

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow for DIBAL‑H Reduction and
Problem_Description: During the coupling step, the anion generated from sulfone 4 can deprotonate the α‑proton of product 5 or of aldehyde 3 before coupling, leading to side reactions and loss of material.
Solution_Description: Careful stoichiometric control (2.15 equiv n‑BuLi, 1.10 equiv aldehyde 3) combined with a modest temperature (10 °C) suppressed premature deprotonation, delivering the desired product with minimal by‑product formation (96.5 % conversion, 3.5 % residual 4).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem – "possible causes of this incomplete conversion were that the active anion of 4 deprotonated the α‑proton of product 5 or coupling partner 3 before it had reacted" (Section 3).

Paper Title: Rapid and Scalable Access into Strained Scaffolds through Continuous Flow Photochemistry
Problem_Description: Photocycloaddition of precursor 6a gave mixtures of the “crossed” product 7 and the “straight” product 8 in all screened solvents, leading to a low‑selectivity outcome and difficulty isolating the desired product.

Paper Title: Rapid and Scalable Access into Strained Scaffolds through Continuous Flow Photochemistry
Problem_Description: Photocycloadduct 9 was found to decompose slowly even at low temperature when stored.

Paper Title: Rapid and Scalable Access into Strained Scaffolds through Continuous Flow Photochemistry
Problem_Description: The small‑scale Rayonet flow reactor gave a low material throughput (≈5.6 g day⁻¹), insufficient for library production.

Paper Title: Rapid and Scalable Access into Strained Scaffolds through Continuous Flow Photochemistry
Problem_Description: Products 7 and 8 displayed almost identical chromatographic behaviour; product 8 could not be isolated in pure form even after extensive silica‑gel chromatography.

Paper Title: Continuous, Fast, and Safe Aerobic Oxidation of 2‑Ethylhexanal: Pushing the Limits of the Simple Tube Reactor for a Gas/Liquid Reaction

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: During the Suzuki‑Miyaura borylation of bromide 2 to the pinacol boronate 1a, the crude product hydrolysed to the free boronic acid during aqueous work‑up, causing low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: A non‑aqueous isolation was adopted: the reaction mixture was hot‑filtered to remove inorganic salts and the filtrate was crystallised from ethanol. 1,4‑Dioxane was replaced by 2‑MeTHF, which facilitated the hot‑filtration and gave >95 wt % pure 1a after ethanol crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “pinacol boronate hydrolysis to the corresponding boronic acid during the aqueous washes was observed, leading to low recoveries.”; “non‑aqueous isolation for these reactions was pursued … by performing a hot filtration of the reaction mixture to remove the inorganic salts, followed by crystallization from ethanol.”; “Replacing 1,4‑dioxane with 2‑MeTHF allowed for a more efficient removal of the inorganics with the hot filtration and provided 1a in high purity (>95 wt %) after crystallization.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: The original protocol used the Class 2 solvent 1,4‑dioxane and a relatively high loading of PdCl₂(dppf) (0.5 mol %) on a multi‑kilogram scale, creating cost and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to 2‑MeTHF and the catalyst system was changed to Pd₂(dba)₃ (0.1 mol %) combined with Fc(PtBu)₂‑HBF₄ (0.2 mol %). This reduced both the amount of expensive palladium material and eliminated the use of a regulated Class 2 solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “the use of the Class 2 solvent 1,4‑dioxane and high catalyst loading persuaded us to conduct a further screening to render the process efficient for operation at larger scale.”; “Replacing 1,4‑dioxane with 2‑MeTHF allowed for a more efficient removal of the inorganics…”; “the catalyst source was replaced with Pd₂(dba)₃ (0.1 mol %) / Fc(PtBu)₂‑HBF₄ (0.2 mol %) … also afforded complete conversion.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: When the borylation was scaled to 1 kg the reaction stalled at 0.5 mol % PdCl₂(dppf) and required an additional catalyst charge to reach completion.
Solution_Description: The catalyst system was changed to the more active Pd₂(dba)₃/Fc(PtBu)₂‑HBF₄ combination, allowing complete conversion with the lower loading and eliminating the need for a second catalyst charge.
Supporting_Evidence: “when the process was scaled to 1 kg, the reaction stalled with the lower catalyst loading (0.5 mol %), and an additional charge of catalyst was required to drive the reaction to completion.”; “the catalyst source was replaced with Pd₂(dba)₃ (0.1 mol %) / Fc(PtBu)₂‑HBF₄ (0.2 mol %) … also afforded complete conversion.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: Literature amine‑protecting strategies (Boc, imine, benzyl) required multiple isolation steps and gave only modest overall yields for the target boronic acid.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot bis‑silylation using tetramethyldisilylazacyclopentane (STABASE) was employed to protect the amine in situ, giving the N‑protected intermediate 3 in >96 % yield and eliminating the separate de‑protection step.
Supporting_Evidence: “those methods suffered from modest yields and required two or three isolation steps as well as a deprotection step.”; “Our attention thus turned to the potential use of tetramethyldisilylazacyclopentane (STABASE)… the desired N‑protected substrate 3 was readily obtained… in excellent yield (>96 %).”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: STABASE is not commercially available in bulk and is expensive, making it unsuitable for multi‑kilogram production.
Solution_Description: Trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) was introduced as a cheap, readily available alternative for bis‑silylation, providing the same N‑protected intermediate 4 in >95 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the STABASE reagent was not readily available at low cost on large scale” ; “TMSCl was thus explored as a potential alternative to STABASE.” ; “When compound 2 was treated with TMSCl (2 equiv) … a quantitative formation of the bis‑TMS adduct 4 was observed by ¹H NMR.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: The NaH‑mediated silylation generated exotherms (35–40 °C) and H₂ gas evolution, posing safety and temperature‑control issues.
Solution_Description: A controlled sequence was developed: NaH was added first, followed by TMSCl in two portions, and a catalytic amount of i‑PrOH (7 mol %) was employed to moderate the exotherm and suppress uncontrolled gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sodium hydride … was charged … Caution!! exotherm to 35–40 °C with gas evolution!”; “when bromide 2 was treated with NaH … the deprotonation reaction initiated with a mild exotherm and concurrent H₂ gas evolution.”; “a process was thus developed whereby sequential addition of NaH and TMSCl (2×) furnished > 95 % conversion to the desired bis‑TMS adduct.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Synthesis of (2-Aminopyrimidin-5-yl) Boronic Acid
Problem_Description: Extraction of the free boronic acid 1b with EtOAc failed because the product is highly soluble in water under basic conditions, giving poor recovery.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was redesigned: THF was removed by distillation, the aqueous phase was acidified to pH 1–1.5, washed with heptane/EtOAc to strip non‑polar impurities, then the pH was raised to 5.5–6 to precipitate the boronic acid, which was isolated by filtration and hot water reslurry.
Supporting_Evidence: “Extraction of the boronic acid 1b with EtOAc failed to provide high recovery due to the high solubility of 1b in water under basic conditions.”; “A practical purification was found by first removing THF by distillation and then adjusting the pH to 1–1.5 using HCl… finally, the pH of the aqueous layer was adjusted to 5.5–6 … which provided boronic acid 1b as a precipitate.”

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: The initial batch crystallization of the raw material (de₂,₄ ≈ 26 %) gave a very low overall recovery of the target racemate (≈ 29 % yield) because only a small fraction of the desired stereoisomer was present in the feed and the solid‑solution nature of the system gave little solubility contrast between the racemates.
Solution_Description: A multistage cross‑current crystallization cascade (four stages) was designed and operated isothermally at 20 °C using acetone as solvent. By modelling the solid‑liquid equilibrium and adjusting the solvent‑to‑solid ratio at each stage, the target racemate was enriched to > 99 % purity and the crystallization‑only yield rose to 84 % when coupled with recycling.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The crystallization process ... was realized isothermally at 20 °C" (sec 3.2).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: After the first crystallization stage the mother liquor was depleted of the target racemate; if discarded it would represent a loss of material and keep the overall process yield low.
Solution_Description: The depleted mother liquor was fed to a recycling loop (process II) that included conversion of the oxalate salt to the free base, a fast base‑catalysed diastereoisomeric conversion (BCDC) with NaH to an equimolar mixture of all four stereoisomers, and re‑formation of the oxalate salt. The recycled stream was mixed back with the fresh feed for the next crystallization stage, raising the total yield to 84 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The mother liquor, which was depleted with the target racemate, was transferred into an equimolar mixture of all stereoisomers by a fast base‑catalyzed diastereoisomeric conversion" (abstract).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: Nafronyl oxalate salt is scarcely soluble in the mobile phase normally used for chiral chromatography, which limits the achievable column load and productivity.
Solution_Description: The oxalate salt was first converted to the free base before chromatography. The free base is far more soluble (≈ 50 g L⁻¹) in the hexane/2‑propanol/diethylamine mobile phase, allowing high‑overload, medium‑pressure CSP separations.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The maximum solubility of nafronyl free base in the mobile phase is about 50 g L⁻¹, whereas nafronyl oxalate salt is scarcely soluble in the mobile phase used for chromatography" (sec 4.4).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: The base‑catalysed diastereoisomeric conversion (BCDC) using sodium hydride gave only a 65 % isolated yield and involved a pyrophoric reagent (NaH) that poses safety hazards at scale.
Solution_Description: BCDC was performed in a sealed flask under a nitrogen blanket, with the NaH added as a 60 % dispersion in mineral oil, and the mixture heated to 90 °C for 3 h. The controlled addition and inert atmosphere mitigated safety risks, while the temperature profile ensured complete conversion, giving a reproducible 90 % conversion of free base to an equimolar mixture (overall process II yield ≈ 65 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • "A 0.69 g ... of sodium hydride ... were placed into a tightly closed flask. Then, dry nitrogen was blown through the mixture for 15 min. After that, the flask was sealed and heated up to 90 °C for 3 h" (sec 5.3.2).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: Direct chiral chromatography of the quaternary stereoisomeric mixture required high‑pressure analytical equipment and very low column loads, resulting in low productivity and long processing times.
Solution_Description: The quaternary mixture was first pre‑enriched by crystallization to isolate the racemate (2,4). The binary racemate was then separated by medium‑pressure semipreparative CSP chromatography, which operates at lower pressure but supports higher column loads, giving 99 % purity and a productivity of 1.27 g h⁻¹ L⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The pure racemate 2,4 obtained from the crystallization process was further processed by enantioselective chromatography … under high mass overloading conditions" (sec 4.4).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: The stereoisomeric mixture forms a solid solution; the solubility of the two racemates in acetone is very similar, which reduces the driving force for selective crystallization.
Solution_Description: SLE measurements in acetone at 20 °C identified a composition window (x̅₂,₄ ≈ 0.37 g g⁻¹) where the target racemate preferentially crystallizes. The process was therefore operated isothermally at 20 °C with solvent volumes adjusted to keep the mixture within this window, enabling multistage cross‑current crystallization to reach 99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The SLE pattern indicated that stereoisomers of nafronyl oxalate form solid solution … the minimum solubility for the pure target racemate … Therefore, multistage cross‑current crystallization was designed" (sec 1).

Paper Title: Separation of Stereoisomeric Mixtures of Nafronyl as a Representative of Compounds Possessing Two Stereogenic Centers By Coupling Crystallization, Diastereoisomeric Conversion and Chromatography
Problem_Description: Sodium hydride, used in the BCDC step, reacts violently with moisture and must be handled under strict inert conditions.
Solution_Description: The NaH dispersion was purged with dry nitrogen for 15 min before sealing the reaction flask, and the reaction was carried out in a closed system at 90 °C, eliminating exposure to moisture and minimizing the risk of uncontrolled exotherms.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Then, dry nitrogen was blown through the mixture for 15 min. After that, the flask was sealed and heated up to 90 °C for 3 h" (sec 5.3.2).

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Adenine is insoluble in most solvents, restricting the choice of reaction medium to high‑boiling‑point polar aprotic solvents (DMF, NMP, DMSO).
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in DMF (or NMP/DMSO) to keep adenine in solution, and later a virtually solvent‑free approach was developed to avoid the use of these high‑boiling solvents.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The insolubility of adenine in most solvents restricts the solvent choice to high boiling point polar aprotic solvents; DMF, NMP, and DMSO were screened.", "In contrast, when performed in DMF, HPA (6) can be readily precipitated from the reaction mixture.", "A goal of this research was to reduce the need for undesirable solvents. Unfortunately the insolubility of HPA severely limits the choice of solvents to that of high boiling point aprotic polar solvents like DMF, NMP, and DMSO."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Magnesium tert‑butoxide (MTB) is expensive, its quality varies, and the resulting magnesium salt by‑products form a sticky salt cake that traps up to 15 % of the product, making work‑up and purification difficult.
Solution_Description: MTB was replaced by a 1 : 1 combination of a Grignard reagent (phenyl‑ or methyl‑magnesium chloride) and tert‑butanol, providing a lower‑cost, more robust base system.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Magnesium tert‑butoxide (MTB) has been commonly used affording high conversions in excess of 90%... it is expensive, the transformation is highly dependent on the quality of the MTB, and the magnesium salt byproducts makes the reaction workup and purification difficult.", "The use of MTB and a range of inorganic and organic bases not previously reported... confirmed the previously reported findings that MTB is the optimal base of choice affording excellent conversions (92%).", "The use of a Grignard in combination with tert‑butanol affords good conversions for stage 2a."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: When DMF or DMSO are used, the product PPA cannot be isolated directly because these solvents are highly solvating and difficult to remove, leading to low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: A virtually solvent‑free reaction was developed and a new work‑up protocol involving aqueous quench, chloroform extraction, acid/base washes and dichloromethane extraction was implemented to isolate pure PPA in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The key issue seemed to be the use of NMP and DMSO as a solvent system both of which are not easily removed and are highly solubilizing of PPA (8).", "The development of the virtually “solvent‑free” approach allowed us to develop a workup and purification protocol that affords the isolation of pure PPA (8) in high yields.", "The workup protocol involves solubilizing the solvent‑free reaction mixture in water followed by continuous extraction into chloroform, allowing the removal the water‑soluble unreacted HPA and magnesium salts present at the end of the reaction."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Under solvent‑free conditions the reaction mixture becomes increasingly viscous, forming a thick sticky residue that is difficult to stir and process.
Solution_Description: A small amount of low‑boiling non‑polar solvent (cyclohexane) was added to reduce viscosity; reaction concentration was also optimized (0.25–1 M) to keep the mixture manageable.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Under the solvent‑free conditions, the reaction mixture becomes increasingly viscous over time eventually forming a thick, sticky residue which is difficult to stir and process.", "The use of cyclohexane as a solvent to reduce reaction mixture viscosity was further screened at 0.5 and 1 M. The process performed similarly at both concentrations.", "Beyond 2 M the solubility of HPA became a limiting factor."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Extended reaction times (>3 h) lead to the formation of unidentified impurities and product decomposition when the temperature is increased to 120 °C.
Solution_Description: The temperature was set to 75 °C and the reaction time limited to ~105 min to achieve ~60 % total conversion while minimizing impurity formation and avoiding decomposition observed at 120 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Significant amounts of unidentified impurities started to form after 3 h. When performed at 120 °C conversions peaked at 72% after only 90 min but product decomposition started becoming a limiting factor, with significant decomposition observed after 120 min.", "A standard reaction temperature of 75 °C was adopted for all further optimizations.", "The reaction was monitored by LCMS every 15–20 min for 3 h… the overall conversion to PPA (8) + PPA‑HH (9) started to slow significantly after 105 min corresponding to a conversion of ~60 %."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Changing the order of addition of reagents (DESMP before Grignard, or premixing Grignard with tert‑butanol) caused a drop in conversion, indicating sensitivity to addition sequence.
Solution_Description: The optimal sequence was established: suspend HPA and tert‑butanol in NMP, add methyl‑magnesium chloride dropwise, then add DESMP after 30 min, which gave the highest conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The standard procedure involved the preparation of a suspension of HPA (6) and tert‑butanol in NMP, to which was added methyl magnesium chloride dropwise, followed within 30 min by the dropwise addition of DESMP (7).", "If the DESMP (7) was introduced prior to the addition of the methyl magnesium chloride, the process showed a slight drop in conversion from 86% to 80%.", "If the methyl magnesium chloride and the tert‑butanol are premixed prior to the addition to the HPA and DESMP (7), the conversion drops to 77%."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Chloroform, used in the first extraction step, is a known mutagen and environmentally unfriendly.
Solution_Description: Chloroform was replaced with dichloromethane for the first extraction; although yields were somewhat lower, dichloromethane is less hazardous and preferred for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Chloroform is a potential mutagen and is environmentally unfriendly; as such the use of chloroform is best avoided on scale if possible.", "When we attempted the process by replacing the chloroform in the first extractive process with dichloromethane and running the extraction for the same time (24 h), the overall yield of isolated PPA (8) fell to 55% after the first continuous extraction."]

Paper Title: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate
Problem_Description: Alternative bases (NaOtBu, KOtBu, various magnesium salts) gave little or no conversion, resulting in low overall yields for stage 2a.
Solution_Description: A Grignard reagent (phenyl‑ or methyl‑magnesium chloride) in combination with tert‑butanol was employed, providing high conversions (up to 92 %) and improving overall yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ["All three solvent choices afforded >90% conversions when used with NaOH, KOH, K2CO3, and LiOH. ... Paper Title: Selective Olefin Reduction in Thebaine Using Hydrazine Hydrate and O
Problem_Description: Thebaine shows very low solubility in most organic solvents (including common alcohols), which limited the achievable substrate concentration and caused the reaction mixture to become biphasic after addition of hydrazine hydrate.
Solution_Description: A toluene/ethanol 2:1 solvent mixture was employed to raise the thebaine concentration to 0.33 M, and the sample‑loop was pre‑heated to 70 °C before injection to ensure a completely homogeneous feed.
Supporting_Evidence: “The low solubility of thebaine in most organic solvents … caused us to use a toluene/ethanol mixture (2:1) to reach a suitable substrate concentration (0.33 M). Since the solution slowly became biphasic after the addition of hydrazine hydrate (4 equiv), we decided to preheat the sample loop to 70 °C for injecting a totally homogeneous solution into the flow system.”

Paper Title: Selective Olefin Reduction in Thebaine Using Hydrazine Hydrate and O
Problem_Description: At 100 °C the reaction generated N‑oxides of thebaine and the hydrogenated analogue, attributed to H₂O₂ formed during hydrazine oxidation, which reduced the selectivity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The residence‑time unit was changed from a PFA coil to a stainless‑steel coil, which (i) eliminates gas‑permeability‑induced residence‑time variation and (ii) provides Fe²⁺ sites that decompose H₂O₂, suppressing N‑oxide formation. In addition, dimethyl sulfide (Me₂S) was added as an antioxidant to trap any remaining peroxide.
Supporting_Evidence: “We therefore decided to evaluate the applicability of a stainless steel coil … This would not only allow working at higher temperatures/pressures … but also results in a better control of the residence time as gas permeability is not an issue anymore.” and “We additionally speculated that under the applied corrosive conditions small amounts of Fe²⁺ may be formed on the coil surface which would readily decompose generated H₂O₂ … the formation of the respective N‑oxides was avoided by addition of dimethyl sulfide as antioxidant.”

Paper Title: Selective Olefin Reduction in Thebaine Using Hydrazine Hydrate and O
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the continuous flow system showed irreproducible conversions; after several runs the conversion dropped dramatically, traced to fouling/corrosion of the stainless‑steel coil.
Solution_Description: The coil was subjected to an acid‑passivation treatment with 20 % v/v HNO₃, which restored the original performance and eliminated the variability.
Supporting_Evidence: “After trying several washing cycles … we discovered that after a steel passivation procedure using HNO₃ (20 % v/v) the original results could be successfully reproduced. We therefore assume that corrosion of the coil surface or reactor fouling is responsible for the observed deviations.”

Paper Title: Selective Olefin Reduction in Thebaine Using Hydrazine Hydrate and O
Problem_Description: The batch protocol required a very large excess of hydrazine hydrate (53 : 1 hydrazine : thebaine) and involved a gaseous O₂/hydrazine mixture, posing a serious explosion hazard and making the process economically unattractive.
Solution_Description: A multi‑injection strategy was introduced, whereby fresh portions of hydrazine hydrate are added continuously along the reactor (four separate feeds, totalling 12 equiv). This reduces the instantaneous hydrazine concentration, limits diimide disproportionation, and avoids the need for the massive excess while achieving >95 % conversion in <1 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “A multi‑injection strategy applying periodic additions of fresh hydrazine hydrate … enabled an increased effective residence time … In the case of the optimized setup (entry 5) the reaction mixture passed the first coil within ~6 min … a conversion >95 % was obtained using four liquid feeds …”

Problem_Description: During the benzylation of phenol 23, use of coarse K₂CO₃ particles slowed the reaction and increased formation of homodimeric by‑products, BnOH, and Bn₂O.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Fine‑powder K₂CO₃ was employed to increase surface area and improve reaction rate, minimizing side‑product formation and ensuring high (99 %) isolated yield of product 9.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Fine powder K₂CO₃ to facilitate the benzylation.”

“The particle size of potassium carbonate is critical. Reaction is slow if larger‑particle of K₂CO₃ is used, resulting in more homodimer, Bn₂O, and BnOH.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of Fully Synthetic Tetracycline TP-2758: A Potent Antibacterial Agent with Excellent Oral Bioavailability
Problem_Description: Formation of the aldimine 32 required heating at 45 °C for six days, making the step time‑inefficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was increased and the amount of CuSO₄ was adjusted, reducing the reaction time while maintaining high yield and purity of aldimine 32.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The reaction mixture was heated to 40 °C and stirred at this temperature for 6 days… Additional copper sulfate (120 g) was added and the reaction mixture was stirred at 40 °C for another day.”

“The aldimine 32 was obtained in 76.8 % yield after correction for solvent.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of Fully Synthetic Tetracycline TP-2758: A Potent Antibacterial Agent with Excellent Oral Bioavailability
Problem_Description: The Michael–Dieckmann (M‑D) coupling of LHP 10 with enone 7 gave only 70–75 % yield on 200 g scale, dropping to 49 % on 4 kg scale due to poor mixing, solid formation, and inadequate temperature control in a near‑full 50 L reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Scale‑up was improved by using a larger vessel, ensuring vigorous agitation, maintaining the reaction mixture at cryogenic temperatures during anion transfer, and adjusting concentrations to avoid solid precipitation; yields rose to >85 % on >20 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
“In an in‑house kilo‑lab campaign (∼4 kg scale), a lower yield (49 %) was obtained presumably caused by poor mixing and temperature control … The capacity and cylindrical shape of the reactor … made agitation very inefficient.”

“After scaling up this reaction to >20 g, we have consistently obtained 36 in 85 % to 90 % yield…”

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of Fully Synthetic Tetracycline TP-2758: A Potent Antibacterial Agent with Excellent Oral Bioavailability
Problem_Description: The Negishi coupling route employed s‑BuLi, a pyrophoric and highly hazardous reagent, and the overall coupling gave only 50 % isolated yield with significant side‑products, making the process unsafe and non‑robust for manufacturing.

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of Fully Synthetic Tetracycline TP-2758: A Potent Antibacterial Agent with Excellent Oral Bioavailability
Problem_Description: During the final hydrogenation, impurities 40 (M‑18) and 41 (M‑16) accumulated to >5 % total, and catalyst poisoning was suspected from trace contaminants, leading to additional purification steps that reduced overall material recovery.

Supporting_Evidence:
“The crude product 37 was purified by acid/base extraction… impurity 40+41 reduced to 1 % (entry 5).”

“Adding 1 to 1.5 vol of water into the hydrogenation reaction… impurity 40 could be reduced by half.”

“The readily available catalyst of 10 % Pd/C (wet) from Aldrich… was the best for this hydrogenation.”

“The filtrate was polished filtered via a 0.2 µm in‑line filter and then stirred with SiliaBond DMT (56 g) for 2 h.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of Fully Synthetic Tetracycline TP-2758: A Potent Antibacterial Agent with Excellent Oral Bioavailability
Problem_Description: The crystallization of TP‑2758 di‑HCl salt required removal of residual epimers 39 and 42; water content critically affected recovery, and without careful water addition the yield dropped to ~80 %.

Supporting_Evidence:
“The final recrystallization procedure… using MeOH/EtOH/MTBE… after addition of ~3.5 equiv of water the yield was boosted from ~80 % to ~90 % without compromise of the purity.”

“The recrystallization can effectively purge ~90 % of epimer 42, ~50 % of side chain epimer 39, and ~40 % of impurity 40.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: The indoloboronic acid 7 is unstable on scale; decomposition during work‑up caused low isolated yields and forced the use of large excess of the reagent.
