Supporting_Evidence: The route to chloroindolopyridine 2 progressed through the unstable indoloboronic acid 7; further process development would be necessary to support the handling times required on scale.; We surmised that the moderate yield of boronic acid 7 was a result of decomposition during processing rather than a low‑yielding borylation reaction.; Indeed, the addition of triisopropyl borate to a mixture of lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) and indole 6, followed by acidic work‑up, provided a solution of indole‑boronic acid 7 in quantitative yield.

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: The synthesis of benzofuran 19 required a long linear sequence with seven chromatographic purifications, giving low overall isolated yield and a cumbersome operation.
Solution_Description: Chromatographic steps were eliminated by crystallizing intermediates (e.g., bromide 11 from MTBE/heptane) and by optimizing the Claisen condensation base, enabling a through‑process sequence that delivered benzofuran 19 in 33 % overall yield (90 % per step).
Supporting_Evidence: Benzofuran 19 was synthesized via a long linear sequence with multiple chromatographic separations.; The Claisen condensation and benzofuran formation, in particular, were targets for optimization.; We intended to eliminate all of the chromatographic purifications (seven out of 16 steps) and identify through‑processing opportunities to increase yields without sacrificing purity.; Bromination of methyl ester 20 with TBATB reproducibly achieved >90 % solution assay yield and afforded 11 in 88 % yield after crystallization from MTBE and n‑heptane.; Benzofuran 15 was purified by crystallization from CH₂Cl₂/MeOH in 65 % yield from phenol 11 (average of 90 % yield per step).

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: Initial palladium‑catalysed borylation of bromobenzofuran 19 gave poor conversion and left a large amount of desbromo‑arene 28; the reaction also required elevated temperature in dioxane, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A smaller bis‑(boronic acid) 25 was employed as the borylation reagent in methanol with PCy₃‑based Buchwald precatalyst 26; temperature (55–65 °C) and concentration (7–13 vol MeOH) were optimised via DoE, giving >93 % assay yield of aryl‑boronic acid 27 and minimal desbromo‑arene 28.
Supporting_Evidence: The borylation of benzofuran 19 proved to be low‑yielding using the discovery chemistry conditions.; We hypothesised that both approaches proved suboptimal because of the steric hindrance about the aryl bromide conferred by the o‑sulfonamide group. Therefore, we evaluated the much smaller bis‑(boronic acid) (25) as an alternative borylation reagent.; Gratifyingly, a significant increase in assay yield of arylboronic acid 27, with a concomitant decrease in the amount of desbromoarene 28, was accomplished utilizing this reagent.; Early screening efforts identified conditions that utilised the second‑generation Buchwald tricyclohexylphosphine (PCy₃) precatalyst 26 and a base at elevated temperature in methanol.; The reaction temperature and concentration were identified as the significant factors from the study.

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: The final Suzuki–Miyaura coupling originally used 1,4‑dioxane, an ICH‑Q3C class‑2 solvent with a low permitted daily exposure, posing operational and safety issues.
Solution_Description: The coupling was transferred to acetonitrile (later THF) with aqueous K₃PO₄ and a second‑generation SPhos precatalyst 29, delivering quantitative conversion; the coupling and subsequent solid‑form change were telescoped into a single operation.
Supporting_Evidence: The final Suzuki–Miyaura coupling utilized dioxane as the reaction solvent, leading to both operational and safety concerns.; The reaction was carried out in acetonitrile with aqueous K₃PO₄ (2.5 M) and provided the desired product in excellent yield.; Replacement of acetonitrile with THF (10 volumes) as the reaction solvent for the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling provided a successful solution: conversion to the desired product occurred in essentially quantitative yield.; To streamline isolation of the desired form, we sought to combine the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling and form change into a single step.

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: During the high‑temperature Suzuki coupling, MK‑8876 crystallised into the undesired polymorph 2, leading to inconsistent API form and requiring additional processing.
Solution_Description: A biphasic THF/water system was exploited to keep the product in solution after coupling; subsequent concentration, seeding and antisolvent addition of 2‑propanol gave a high‑yield crystallisation of the desired form 1, eliminating the undesired form 2 and removing desbromo‑arene 28.
Supporting_Evidence: The Suzuki–Miyaura coupling process in acetonitrile produced MK‑8876 in high yield and purity, the high reaction temperature coupled with the reactive crystallisation generated the undesired form 2.; THF and water mixtures conferred unique solubility properties on MK‑8876 that were utilised to generate a high‑yielding, volume‑efficient crystallisation process on a multikilogram scale.; 2‑Propanol was identified as the optimal antisolvent for the crystallisation of MK‑8876 form 1.; The new isolation process was developed by first concentrating the post‑workup solution to 6 volumes while reducing the water content (11–19 wt %) via distillation, heating the concentrated mixture to 40–50 °C, seeding, and finally charging the antisolvent slowly (2‑propanol, 7 volumes).

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: Bulk batches of the API contained palladium levels (≈100 ppm) exceeding acceptable limits for clinical material.
Solution_Description: A 50 wt % loading of MP‑TMT resin was used to treat the crude borylation stream, lowering palladium from 34.7 mg L⁻¹ to 6.7 mg L⁻¹ (≈81 % removal) with minimal product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: Experimental batches of the active pharmaceutical ingredient contained unacceptably high levels of palladium for use in clinical trials.; MP‑TMT resin was identified from a multiresin screen as the optimal treatment for the borylation stream, significantly reducing the palladium content with minimal product loss.; The batch was cycled through MP‑TMT resin ... the palladium level was lowered from 34.7 to 6.7 mg/L, an 81 % purge.

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: Reduction of nitro‑arene 16 with iron powder was performed by a single charge, causing a delayed exotherm (13 °C rise) that risked exceeding cooling capacity.
Solution_Description: Iron powder was added portion‑wise at 60–65 °C, controlling the temperature rise and providing an additional safety margin.
Supporting_Evidence: Initially, we conducted this reaction by charging Fe powder in a single portion ... a delayed exotherm was observed under these conditions.; Reaction calorimetry measurements of this single‑charge process revealed an adiabatic temperature rise of 13 °C ... we altered the process to add the iron powder portionwise to the remainder of the reactants at 60–65 °C as an additional safety control.

Paper Title: Process Development of the HCV NS5B Site D Inhibitor MK-8876
Problem_Description: Using Na₂CO₃ in the iodination of pyridine 9 gave poor conversion because the carbonate was insufficiently soluble in the aqueous THF mixture.
Solution_Description: Switching to K₂CO₃ and performing the iodination in pure water increased base solubility, enabling isolation of pyridine 9 in 89 % yield after crystallisation from n‑heptane.
Supporting_Evidence: Altering the base from Na₂CO₃ to K₂CO₃ and running the iodination reaction in pure water as opposed to aqueous tetrahydrofuran (THF) led to improved performance and isolation of pyridine 9: elimination of THF simplified the work‑up for this step, and iodide 9 was isolated in 89 % yield by crystallisation from n‑heptane.

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Gas–liquid mixing in the flow reactor was insufficient, leading to low CO partial pressure in solution and consequently reduced regio‑ and enantio‑selectivity. The reaction uses synthesis gas (CO/H₂), which is toxic and flammable, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A vertical‑pipes‑in‑series plug‑flow reactor was employed. Its design (small‑diameter 0.56 mm tubing, bubble‑flow vertical pipes, and high vapour‑liquid mass‑transfer rates) provides vigorous gas–liquid mixing, maintaining CO at its Henry‑law equilibrium and mitigating safety risks by containing the high‑pressure syngas in a closed flow system.
Supporting_Evidence: "One of the challenges of performing gas–liquid reactions in flow is effecting good mixing of the gaseous and liquid reagents" (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Styrene feed solutions that were degassed and stored in a drybox became viscous over time due to polymerisation, losing potency and causing inconsistent reaction performance.
Solution_Description: Degassing was performed immediately before feeding the reactor (or in‑line degassing), avoiding prolonged exposure of the deoxygenated styrene to conditions that promote polymerisation, thereby stabilising the feed and restoring consistent conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "When styrene was degassed and held in the drybox, we observed that the material became viscous over time with loss of potency" (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: The synthesis gas (CO/H₂) used in hydroformylation is flammable and CO is highly toxic, presenting intrinsic scale‑up hazards.
Solution_Description: The reaction was moved to a continuous‑flow, closed‑system reactor, which limits the inventory of hazardous gases at any moment and provides better containment, thereby reducing the overall safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence: "Hydrogen is a flammable gas… Carbon monoxide is also a flammable gas. In addition, CO is a poisonous gas…" (Ref 5).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Increasing reactor pressure to 800 psi unexpectedly lowered both branched/linear selectivity and enantio‑selectivity, with the cause not identified; the system also failed to fully recover its original selectivity after pressure cycling.
Solution_Description: The authors retained the baseline pressure of 400 psi (where selectivity was optimal) and focused on the temperature that gave the best balance (70 °C) while keeping residence time (~8 h) constant, thereby stabilising selectivity across runs.
Supporting_Evidence: "The pressure of the flow system was increased to 800 psi… we saw a drop in both branched/linear selectivity and enantioselectivity. The reasons for these decreases remain unclear" (Sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: During long‑term operation (multiple start‑stop cycles) the branched/linear selectivity did not fully recover after returning to the original 400 psi condition, suggesting possible feed instability or accumulation within the reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reactor was designed with optional pre‑activation loops and sampling points to monitor and adjust gas‑liquid mixing in real time; the authors emphasised careful control of feed composition and pressure to maintain steady‑state performance.
Supporting_Evidence: "After returning to the initial flow conditions of 400 psi without preactivation, the branched/linear selectivity increased; however it did not recover to its initial value" (Sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: The solubility of the substrate, intermediates, and product in toluene under high‑pressure syngas conditions needed careful control to avoid precipitation or phase separation that could impair conversion.
Solution_Description: Toluene was selected as the reaction solvent and the substrate concentration was adjusted (≈0.5 M) to ensure a single, homogeneous liquid phase throughout the reactor, facilitating reliable mass transfer and consistent reaction rates.
Supporting_Evidence: "[2‑Vinyl‑6‑methoxy‑naphthalene]₀ = 0.502 M… reactions performed in toluene" (Table 1 footnote; Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Achieving high conversion required residence times of 6‑8 h, which could limit throughput in batch but was acceptable in a continuous reactor.
Solution_Description: The vertical‑pipes‑in‑series reactor provides adjustable residence times (0.5‑12 h) while maintaining high catalyst turnover, enabling the long reaction to be performed continuously with steady output.
Supporting_Evidence: "The reactor was designed to give a long residence time… adjustable between 0.5 to 12 h… Most of the flow hydroformylation experiments used an ∼8 h τ" (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 2: Asymmetric Hydroformylation with Rhodium-Bisdiazaphos Catalysts in a Vertical Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: After oxidation, the crude product needed isolation of (S)-Naproxen with high purity; traditional work‑up could be cumbersome on scale.
Solution_Description: A Pinnick oxidation was chosen (mild, pH‑neutral) followed by standard aqueous work‑up and extraction, providing an efficient route to the acid without harsh reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: "We elected to use a Pinnick oxidation due to its mild nature and relatively pH neutral conditions… oxidation of the aldehyde yielded Naproxen in 82 % overall yield" (Sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: The first‑generation coiled‑tube reactor gave much slower reaction rates (47‑65 % conversion) than batch and showed low selectivity, which the authors traced to poor vapor‑liquid mixing caused by large liquid slugs and an oversized 1.75 mm i.d. tubing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to smaller‑diameter tubing (≈0.5 mm i.d.) in the second‑generation reactor to increase interfacial area and improve gas‑liquid mass‑transfer rates.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The first generation coiled tube reactor system gave slower reaction rates than batch."
"low selectivity in flow pointed to poor vapor liquid mixing."
"The large internal diameter of the tubing (1.75 mm) was another reason for the larger liquid segment volume."
"A picture of … the bubble lengths and liquid slug lengths could be directly observed."
"The second generation coiled tube reactor achieved an about 10–300× smaller liquid segment size and thus much higher interfacial surface area for gas/liquid mass transfer."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: In the first‑generation system the gas‑mass‑flow rate and reactor pressure were poorly controlled (pressure oscillated 198‑202 psig), producing long liquid slugs and inconsistent residence times.
Solution_Description: A custom pressure‑control scheme using sequenced block valves, finite‑volume chambers and pressure transmitters eliminated the need for commercial regulators and kept pressure within ±0.1 % of set‑point, stabilising gas flow.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The commercially available back pressure regulator was allowing the pressure to vary between about 198 and 202 psig."
"Changes to the reactor inlet and outlet side flow control and pressure control resulted in less oscillations in pressures and gas flow rate."
"The redesigned method of pressure control allowed the reactor outlet pressure to be held very close to set point, with less than 0.1 % variation."
"Custom design and automation were used to control the reactor pressure, gas mass flow ... The reactor pressure was controlled within 0.1 % of set point."
"No pressure regulators were used for pressure control, only sequenced automated block valves, finite volume chambers, and pressure transmitters."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: Both the first and second‑generation coiled‑tube reactors failed to satisfy several design criteria (adjustable residence time, intermediate sampling, syngas equivalence changes, optional pre‑activation, and scalability > 1000 L). The low solubility of H₂/CO required high pressure, raising safety concerns and catalyst cost.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A third‑generation ‘pipes‑in‑series’ reactor was created: 20 vertical bubble‑flow pipes (large‑diameter) in series with short, sub‑mm‑diameter jumper tubes, providing high gas‑liquid mass‑transfer, low axial dispersion, and a scalable geometry that meets all listed criteria.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The second generation coiled tube reactor … fail to meet design criteria 3, 9, 10, 11, and 13."
"We had previously developed a pipes‑in‑series reactor platform … capable of achieving the design criteria proven at scales up to 360 L."
"Thus, 20 vertical pipes in series were installed … The vertical pipes remained almost completely liquid filled at all times because the H₂/CO reagent gas bubbled up through the liquid in each pipe."
"The revised reactor easily operated with an 8 h τ. The total reactor volume was 23.8 mL … High vapor–liquid mass transfer was achieved by establishing very small liquid segments …"
"The research scale version … met design criteria: low liquid volume, long residence time, high mass‑transfer rates, optional pre‑activation, and scalability."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: The process required an optional catalyst‑pre‑activation step in flow, which could not be performed with the earlier reactor designs.
Solution_Description: A dedicated 14.3 mL 0.56 mm i.d. coiled‑tube section was added with three‑way valves to allow optional pre‑activation of catalyst/ligand with syngas at reaction pressure and temperature before entering the main reactor.
Supporting_Evidence:
"A 14.3 mL 0.56 mm i.d. 316 L stainless steel tube was installed for optional preactivation in flow."
"Three‑way valves were installed so that the operator could switch to either flow through preactivation tubing section or bypass it."
"The small diameter tubing was selected for segmented flow, so that the catalyst molar flow rate was independent of the amount of toluene that strips off into the syngas in the preactivation section."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: Real‑time monitoring of conversion, enantiomeric excess and branched/linear ratio was lacking, making it difficult to confirm steady‑state operation after each parameter change.
Solution_Description: A custom online HPLC system was built by converting an offline Agilent 1100 HPLC, adding an automated sampling/diluting/parking unit to provide continuous analytical data.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Online HPLC was achieved by converting an off‑line Agilent 1100 HPLC into an online HPLC by implementing a custom built and automated sampling/diluting/parking system."
"The custom system was described in the Experimental Section and Supporting Information."
"The unit took a 0.33 mL sample … diluted it 30× … then pushed the diluted sample to an online HPLC."
"The average total delay time from the time the sample exited the continuous reactor to the time it was injected on the Agilent HPLC was 15 min."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: Hydrogen is an explosion hazard and CO is highly toxic; both gases have low solubility in organic solvents, necessitating high reactor pressures and increasing the risk of a gas release.
Solution_Description: The vertical bubble‑flow pipe‑in‑series design operates > 98 % liquid‑filled, minimizing the volume of hazardous gas present and allowing safe operation at high pressure with low internal gas volume.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Hydrogen is an explosion hazard, and carbon monoxide has high toxicity. They both have relatively low solubility … therefore often require high reactor pressures, which increases the risk of gas releases."
"The vertical bubble flow pipes in series reactors are designed to operate more than 98 % liquid filled, which minimizes the mass of hazardous reagent gas that could be released in the event of a leak or rupture."
"Continuous reactors made of pipes and tubing are relatively low cost for achieving high pressure rating and sufficient heat and mass transfer rates, with low internal gas volume."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid Vapor Reactions Part 1: Design and Characterization of a Reactor for Asymmetric Hydroformylation
Problem_Description: Rhodium catalyst is expensive; the process sought to minimize catalyst loading while maintaining high conversion.
Solution_Description: Design of a research‑scale reactor with long residence times (2–20 h) enables very high substrate‑to‑catalyst ratios, thereby reducing the amount of precious metal required.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The reason for the long reaction times was to achieve a high substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio and minimize the quantity … and removal burden of precious metals."
"One of the main challenges … was to design … long reaction times (2 to 20 h residence time) … while maintaining low liquid volume."
"The continuous reactor achieved high k_La, low axial dispersion, and an 8 mL liquid holdup volume … suitable for high‑pressure asymmetric hydroformylation."

Paper Title: Design of a Numbering-up System of Monolithic Microreactors and Its Application to Synthesis of a Key Intermediate of Valsartan
Problem_Description: The five parallel monolithic microreactors exhibited different pressure drops (channel resistances), leading to non‑uniform flow distribution and variable conversion among reactors.
Solution_Description: A split‑and‑recombine‑type flow distributor (SRFD) was designed using a pressure‑drop‑compartment (PDC) model; channel resistances were equalized by adding dummy channels, and the SRFD was built from stainless‑steel tubes and T‑joints to enforce uniform flow.
Supporting_Evidence: Pressure drops of microreactors were examined beforehand, and it was shown that there were some variations in pressure drops, namely, channel resistances, among the reactors MR1–MR5.; The channel resistances of the reactors were made the same by adding channels without reactions.; The channel resistances (R1 … R15) of the SRFD were derived to minimize the flow maldistribution under the constraints on design and operation conditions.; Based on this result, the SRFD composed of round stainless steel channels and T‑joints was constructed.; The flow uniformity of the SRFD was evaluated experimentally using a mixed solvent of THF and MeOH (3 mL/min, 1:1) and the difference between maximum and minimum flow rate was lower than 5%.

Paper Title: Design of a Numbering-up System of Monolithic Microreactors and Its Application to Synthesis of a Key Intermediate of Valsartan
Problem_Description: Short residence times in the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling gave poor conversion and low isolated yield (e.g., 61 % conversion at 1.9 min, 29 % conversion at 0.96 min).
Solution_Description: Residence time was increased by reducing the total flow rate to 0.5 mL min⁻¹ (≈3.9 min residence), which provided >94 % conversion and >85 % yield; the reaction temperature was kept at 120 °C to maintain activity.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 4 shows conversion % and yield % decreasing sharply with shorter residence times (1.9 min → 61 % conversion, 0.96 min → 29 % conversion).; High yields were obtained with longer residence times, such as 6.4 min (0.3 mL/min) and 3.9 min (0.5 mL/min).; Although an increase of residence time caused an increase in the yield, it is saturated when the residence time is longer than 4 min.; Thus, we chose to carry out the reaction at the flow rate of 0.5 mL/min for each reactor.; The coupling reaction was carried out at 120 °C.

Paper Title: Design of a Numbering-up System of Monolithic Microreactors and Its Application to Synthesis of a Key Intermediate of Valsartan
Problem_Description: Operating multiple parallel reactors traditionally requires several pumps or flow regulators, creating a complex system prone to malfunction and making it difficult to detect a blocked reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The SRFD provides a single‑point flow control that automatically balances flow to all reactors and incorporates a small number of flow sensors to monitor for blockages, eliminating the need for multiple pumps and simplifying safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence: Use of multiple pumps or multiple flow regulators to enable the control of the flow rate of each parallelized reactor leads to a complicate system which may cause various troubles during operation.; Unlike such flow distributors, the SRFD can also be used for detection and diagnosis of a blocked parallelized reactor by using a small number of flow sensors.; The SRFD was connected to a plunger pump (Shimadzu, LC‑20AT) to control the total flow rate of the system.

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: TNT shows poor solubility in the aqueous NaClO oxidation medium, limiting its conversion to HNBB.
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system of ethyl acetate/ethanol (1:2, 0.25 mL EA / 1.25 mL EtOH per mmol TNT) was introduced to improve TNT solubility while keeping the reaction homogeneous.
Supporting_Evidence: “The problem that still existed is to improve the solubility of TNT in aqueous system… The ideal cosolvent was found to be ethyl acetate/ethanol (1:2)…”; “TNT (30/100/1000 g) was added into the mixed solvent of ethyl acetate (0.25 mL mmol‑1) and ethanol (1.25 mL mmol‑1).”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: Conventional HNS syntheses employ highly toxic solvents (benzene, pyridine) and hazardous bromine as the oxidant.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to replace bromine with green oxidants (NaClO for HNBB formation and O₂ for the dehydrogenation step) and to substitute benzene/pyridine with ethyl acetate and DMSO, greatly reducing safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: “The HNS preparation step… employed high toxic oxidant bromine… To solve this problem, an alternative method employing … was investigated.”; “Oxygen gas was employed as green oxidant instead of high hazard bromine… Benzene and pyridine solvents of high toxicity were also replaced by ethyl acetate (EA) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO).”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: The first‑step oxidation of TNT to HNBB gave only modest yields (≈35‑40 %) when using traditional THF/EtOH or benzene/EtOH systems because of side reactions and incomplete dissolution of TNT.
Solution_Description: Optimising the solvent polarity (EA/EtOH 1:2) and adjusting the NaClO alkaline pH (12.4–13.9) maximised HNBB yield to >80 % by promoting Meisenheimer‑complex formation and suppressing side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only 35–40 % of yield was obtained… The polarity of mixed solvent and pH were two main factors affecting the yield.”; “With dielectric constant used as the index of polarity… the ideal cosolvent was found to be ethyl acetate/ethanol (1:2)…”; “The optimized pH value was relatively low with cosolvents of high polarity… the highest yield of curve a and curve b was obtained with completely the same pH value.”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: HNBB is insoluble in several potential solvents (ethyl acetate, benzene, acetonitrile, amides, cyclohexylamine), leading to negligible HNS formation.
Solution_Description: DMSO was selected as the dehydrogenation solvent because it fully dissolves HNBB and the TEMPO/FeCl₂ catalyst, delivering the highest HNS yields (up to 68.7 % at 15 mL DMSO).
Supporting_Evidence: “Almost no product was obtained in ethyl acetate or benzene as HNBB could not be dissolved… DMSO was determined as the best solvent for dehydrogenation of HNBB.”; Table 1 shows 68.7 % yield with 15 mL DMSO.

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: Using amide or amine solvents (DMF, hexamethylphosphoramide, cyclohexylamine) generated large amounts of by‑products and a viscous red solid, complicating product isolation.
Solution_Description: These solvents were discarded in favour of DMSO, which gave clean reactions with minimal by‑product formation and allowed straightforward filtration and washing of HNS.
Supporting_Evidence: “When amides (DMF and hexamethylphosphoramide) or amine (cyclohexylamine) were used… a great quantity of byproducts was detected… So after screening, DMSO was determined as the best solvent.”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: Excess DMSO (>15 mL) reduced the contact between HNBB and the catalyst, lowering the HNS yield; too little DMSO (<5 mL) failed to dissolve the substrate.
Solution_Description: A DMSO volume of 15 mL (for 2.2 mmol HNBB) was identified as optimal, balancing solubility and mass‑transfer to maximize yield (68.7 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “At least 5 mL of DMSO was required to dissolve the substrate… the yield of HNS increased with further addition of DMSO, and a maximum yield was observed when 15 mL of DMSO was used. … excessive solvent hindered the contact between substrate and catalyst.”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: During catalyst/solvent recycling, loss of TEMPO and FeCl₂ caused a rapid decline in HNS yield after more than five cycles (dropping below 60 %).
Solution_Description: The authors limited recycling to five runs and replenished the lost amounts of TEMPO and FeCl₂ after each cycle, preserving yields above 85 % while reducing waste of expensive catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the 5 times’ recycling, small amount of TEMPO and FeCl₂ would be washed away… If they were not supplemented after each recycling, the yield would decreased much more quickly, and less than 60 % yield were obtained.”

Paper Title: A Green and Effective Approach of Two-Step 2,2′,4,4′,6,6′-Hexanitrostilbene Preparation and Its Industrial Scale Study
Problem_Description: Scaling up the first step (HNBB formation) encountered diffusion limitations due to the fast reaction rate, requiring longer residence times to maintain conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A stirred batch reactor equipped with a kenics static mixer was employed to improve bulk mixing and mass transfer, allowing the reaction to proceed efficiently at larger scales (up to 1000 g).
Supporting_Evidence: “In the first step, due to the high reaction rate and short reaction time, kenics static mixer was reported to be a good choice… Its advantage was continuous flow and well‑mixed; however, the low yield of HNS… limited its industrial application.”

Paper Title: Technical Process for Preparation of Genistein
Problem_Description: The original route required large amounts of hazardous and corrosive HCl (gas) and the flammable, toxic solvent 1,2‑dimethoxyethane (DME).
Solution_Description: HCl (gas) was bubbled directly into the reaction mixture (eliminating the need for a DME solution) and the solvent volume was cut by ~50 %, simplifying the operation and lowering waste and cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “required the use of large amounts of such inconvenient and corrosive materials as HCl gas or 1,2‑dimethoxyethane (DME).”; “The introduced important technological modification consisted in direct saturation of the reaction mixture with HCl gas, instead of charging HCl as a solution in DME.”; “the amount of solvent was reduced by almost 50 %.”

Paper Title: Technical Process for Preparation of Genistein

Supporting_Evidence: “overall reaction time of step A was 96 h”; “Applying a temperature of 17–28 °C and cutting the reaction time to 27–32 h allow us to obtain 3 of suitable purity….”

Paper Title: Technical Process for Preparation of Genistein

Problem_Description: A minor C‑2 methyl analogue impurity formed during the formylation/acylation step and could not be removed by standard cleaning.

Paper Title: Technical Process for Preparation of Genistein
Problem_Description: The crude genistein obtained as a hemihydrate needed to be converted into the required crystalline API form.

Supporting_Evidence: “Crystallization from anhydrous ethanol … to obtain a desired crystal structure (marked as ‘genistein after crystallization’)… yield of this process was in the range of 70–82 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis and Kinetic Study of Diphenyl Sulfoxide in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: The oxidation of diphenyl sulfide (DPS) by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is extremely exothermic (ΔH_rxn ≈ ‑240 kJ·mol⁻¹). Supporting_Evidence: “The oxidation of diphenyl sulfide (DPS) by hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) ... is extremely exothermic and has a high thermal risk. … therefore, a microreactor was adopted to reduce reaction thermal risk …” (Abstract). “Microreactors possess high surface‑to‑volume ratio and low total inventory … superior heat and mass transfer performance … enable them to handle demanding process requirements and improve reaction safety.” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis and Kinetic Study of Diphenyl Sulfoxide in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: When the reaction temperature exceeds about 70 °C, H₂O₂ begins to decompose, producing bubbles and consuming oxidant. This decomposition not only reduces the available oxidant but also adds an uncontrolled exothermic event that limits further temperature increase and conversion.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was limited to a maximum of 70 °C (later 80 °C as an upper bound) to stay below the onset of H₂O₂ decomposition, thereby preserving oxidant availability and preventing uncontrolled heat release.
Supporting_Evidence: “Experimental observations revealed that temperatures exceeding 70 °C induced H₂O₂ decomposition accompanied by bubble formation… Consequently, the upper temperature limit for this study was established at 80 °C.” (Section 3.1.1). “The selected temperature for the kinetic study should be lower than the decomposition temperature of H₂O₂ (71.98 °C).” (Section 3.2).

Supporting_Evidence: “A shorter residence time (3 min) and a lower temperature (30 °C) were tested … conversion was extremely low. … With the increase of residence time from 5 to 25 min, the reaction conversion increased …” (Section 3.1.1). “The conversion of DPSO was always higher under higher reaction temperature at the same residence time.” (Section 3.1.1).

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis and Kinetic Study of Diphenyl Sulfoxide in a Microreactor

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis and Kinetic Study of Diphenyl Sulfoxide in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: Insufficient oxidant (low H₂O₂/DPS molar ratio) limits the amount of active oxygen species, leading to lower conversion and possible variability in product selectivity.
Solution_Description: The molar ratio of H₂O₂ to DPS was increased (up to 2:1 and examined up to 10:1 in kinetic studies), providing enough oxidant to generate •OH radicals, enhancing the reaction rate while maintaining >99 % selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “With the increase in molar ratio, the conversion of DPS gradually increased … an increase in feed molar ratio meant an increase in the content of H₂O₂ … ensuring sufficient oxidant for the reaction.” (Section 3.1.3).

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis and Kinetic Study of Diphenyl Sulfoxide in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: Scaling up the channel diameter (1/8 in. → 1/2 in.) reduces the surface‑to‑volume ratio, degrading heat removal and causing significant temperature rises (up to ~10 °C) that could create hot spots and jeopardize safety.
Solution_Description: Larger‑diameter channels were fabricated from materials with higher thermal conductivity (stainless‑steel 316 L or quartz glass) to improve heat transfer. The heat‑transfer coefficient was recalculated (U) and the temperature profile re‑predicted, limiting temperature rise to acceptable levels for safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “The temperature rise … was 0.30, 1.78, 4.16, and 9.70 °C for 1/16, 1/8, 1/4, and 1/2 in. channels respectively … The higher the thermal conductivity, the faster the heat transfer efficiency.” (Sections 3.3, Figures 14‑15).

Paper Title: Novel Baeyer–Villiger Oxidation of Nucleosides Applied to the Large-Scale Synthesis of MeMOP: A Key Amidite in the GalXC Platform
Problem_Description: The original multistep synthesis of MeMOP phosphoramidite gave an overall isolated yield of only ~4.6 % and required a stoichiometric excess of toxic lead tetraacetate (Pb(OAc)4), generating hazardous waste.  Multiple column‑chromatographic purifications were needed, and several intermediates (e.g., the lactol 17) were unstable, decomposing during work‑up.  During the ozonolysis step the substrate precipitated at –78 °C, preventing efficient conversion, and the reaction mixture became heterogeneous, leading to poor mixing and emulsification during aqueous work‑up.  Some key transformations (e.g., the MeMgBr addition to the Weinreb amide) required long reaction times (up to 16 h) to reach completion, further lowering throughput.
Solution_Description: A convergent Baeyer–Villiger oxidation route was developed to replace the Pb(OAc)4 oxidation, using mCPBA/NaHCO3 (or DAIB/TEMPO/NaHCO3) to generate the lactone in high yield.  The solvent system was switched from DCM to acetonitrile (or 2‑Me‑THF) to improve solubility, avoid precipitation, and eliminate emulsions.  The order of addition for the MeMgCl methylation was reversed (adding the organometallic to a cooled solution of the Weinreb amide) and the stoichiometry was lowered (2.4 equiv MeMgCl) to achieve quantitative conversion in a shorter time.  Temperature profiles were optimized (‑40 °C to ‑20 °C for the Grignard addition, 5–15 °C for the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation) to suppress side‑reactions and decomposition of sensitive intermediates.  pH/acid–base control (NaHCO3 quench, citric‑acid work‑up) was introduced to stabilize labile lactols and prevent uracil elimination.  A single chromatographic purification was retained for the penultimate intermediate, and the final product was isolated by crystallization (DCM/MTBE) to replace the many column steps.  An enzymatic Baeyer–Villiger oxidation (immobilized CAL‑B with 30 % H2O2) was also demonstrated on >10 kg scale as a greener alternative.  Overall, the process yield increased to 12 % with reduced reaction time, lower cost, and improved safety profile.

Paper Title: Decagram-Scale Synthesis of the Novel Bacterial Topoisomerase Inhibitor OSUAB-0284
Problem_Description: The original discovery route gave an overall 1.8 % isolated yield over the longest linear sequence (LLS) and required >25 g of the cost‑limiting bromonaphthyridine 12 per gram of final API. The sequence relied on >10 flash chromatography steps, large solvent volumes, and showed run‑to‑run fluctuations in conversion and reaction time.
Solution_Description: A fit‑for‑purpose 4‑phase redesign was implemented. Key changes included (i) installing the cost‑limiting fluoronaphthyridine 12 later in the sequence on a Boc‑protected intermediate (new route); (ii) reducing the Pd loading in the Heck step from 20 mol % to 2 mol % and using ligand‑free Pd(OAc)₂ in DMF (catalyst optimisation); (iii) increasing base equivalents and lowering the temperature to suppress side‑product formation (stoichiometry and temperature optimisation); (iv) switching several steps to more soluble solvents (e.g., n‑BuOH, DMF, DCM) to improve solubility and enable precipitation‑based isolation (solvent change, concentration tuning); (v) eliminating all but one silica‑plug chromatography by employing precipitation, trituration and direct filtration (new purification procedures). These combined changes raised the overall isolated yield to >20 % (a 16‑fold increase), cut the use of bromonaphthyridine 12 by 21‑fold and removed >90 % of chromatographic work‑ups.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Over the longest linear sequence (LLS) of 10 steps to 2, we obtained an average yield of 1.8 % … the discovery approach required >25 g of bromonaphthyridine 12 (cost‑limiting reagent) per gram of final product.”
• “...11 or more flash columns were needed…poor solubility plagued this route…”
• “We sought to install 12 with boc‑protected material, improving its economy by two steps.”
• “Reducing the loading of Pd(OAc)₂, reasoning that a lower concentration of Pd⁰ would prevent agglomeration…initial success with similar conversion and reduced Pd black/mirror formation, even at Pd loadings of 1–2 mol %.”
• “The optimized Heck conditions afforded only one side product…To avoid this issue, we instead poured the reaction mixture into ice water…purified by trituration with MTBE…isolated yield of 84 %.”
• “The overall yield was increased >2‑fold (44.3 vs 19.2 %) over 5 steps…10‑fold reduction in Pd use …entirely eliminated chromatography from the 5‑step process.”

Paper Title: Decagram-Scale Synthesis of the Novel Bacterial Topoisomerase Inhibitor OSUAB-0284

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Process To Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Sotorasib
Problem_Description: Adding a second equivalent of iPr₂NEt (total 2 eq) during acylurea formation gave a large anilide impurity (9) (~ 50 % LC area) and dramatically lowered the yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The amount of iPr₂NEt was limited to 1 equiv (the amount needed for isocyanate formation) and no extra iPr₂NEt was added in the acylurea step, preventing impurity formation and restoring yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "addition of another 1 equiv of iPr₂NEt (2.0 total equivalents) resulted in a significantly reduced yield of 3·HCl and formation of anilide impurity 9 in approximately 50 LC area percent"; "the iPr₂NEt charged amount for the formation of 5·HCl was controlled at 1.0 equiv to avoid carryover into the subsequent reaction"; "This reactivity is widely known for the reaction of carboxylic acids with isocyanates ..."; "The addition of another 1 equiv of iPr₂NEt ... resulted in a significantly reduced yield"; "Limiting iPr₂NEt to 1.0 equiv avoided the formation of impurity 9"

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Process To Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Sotorasib
Problem_Description: Sodium tert‑butoxide had to be carefully titrated to avoid formation of the tert‑butyl‑ether impurity (10) through SNAr displacement of the heteroaryl chloride, leading to batch‑to‑batch variability and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The base was switched to DBU (a non‑nucleophilic guanidine base) and the loading reduced to 4.5 equiv, which gave high conversion to rac‑4 with minimal ether impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: "require to carefully titrate the NaOtBu due to the risk of the tert‑butyl ether impurity"; "Alternative base to promote the cyclization... amidine or guanidine bases proved particularly effective"; "DBU provides crude rac‑4 in 95 LC area percent with minimal byproducts"; "DBU equivalents could be lowered to 4.5 equiv"; "After addressing the issues presented by carryover of phosgene and iPr₂NEt, our focus was shifted to identifying conditions for the crystallization and isolation"

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Process To Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Sotorasib
Problem_Description: Inconsistent self‑seeding of the acylurea reaction caused some batches to remain homogeneous for the entire 18 h period, resulting in diminished purity or fouling.
Solution_Description: A seeding protocol was introduced: 0.5 mol % of acylurea 3 added after ~ 3 h to enforce slurry formation and ensure consistent product isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: "inconsistent self‑seeding of the reaction mixture occurred, resulting in instances where batches would remain homogeneous well into the 18 h reaction, resulting in a diminished purity profile or fouling"; "a seeding protocol was developed where 0.5 mol % of 3 was added approximately 3 h into the reaction to ensure that a consistent slurry was obtained"; "The final process to prepare acylurea 3·HCl is summarized"; "The final process to prepare acylurea 3·HCl is summarized in Scheme 5"; "Seeding of 0.5 mol % of 3 at 3 h"

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Process To Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Sotorasib
Problem_Description: When DBU encountered upstream nitrile impurity 8, it generated new impurities (12 and 13), showing that DBU can act as a nucleophile under certain conditions and leading to batch‑to‑batch impurity variation.
Solution_Description: Upstream impurity levels were tightly controlled (by nitrogen sparge and other safeguards) and DBU loading was limited to 4.5 equiv to minimize formation of impurities 12 and 13.
Supporting_Evidence: "incoming crude reaction stream can lead to several new impurities … DBU is typically regarded as non‑nucleophilic but ... resulted in N‑acylamidine 12 and polyheterocyclic 13"; "The formation of these impurities highlights the need to have proper controls in place upstream"; "DBU equivalents could be lowered to 4.5 equiv"; "Impurities 12 and 13 were confirmed by single crystal X‑ray crystallography"; "These downstream impurities arise from DBU reacting with impurity 8"

Paper Title: Development of an Improved Process To Prepare a Key Intermediate in the Manufacture of Sotorasib
Problem_Description: Isolation of rac‑4 required removal of solvent and careful crystallization; without an optimized acid‑addition strategy the product loss and impurity rejection were problematic.
Solution_Description: A controlled addition of 4.5 M H₃PO₄ with pH monitoring (target pH 3.5–4.5), seeding at pH ≈ 7 and subsequent acid addition gave rapid desaturation, high recovery (75 % yield) and > 99.5 % LC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "addition of a number of aqueous acids was evaluated. The addition of 4.5 M H₃PO₄ to the crude reaction mixture proved to be most effective"; "A notable feature of this crystallization procedure was the self‑seeding and rapid desaturation of rac‑4 at around pH 7"; "Upon achieving pH 7, the batch is seeded with 1 mol % rac‑4 to promote controlled desaturation"; "The final target pH range of 3.5–4.5 is achieved by addition of a total of 4.5 equiv of 4.5 M H₃PO₄"; "After filtration, cake washing, and drying, rac‑4 is obtained in 75 % yield > 99.5 % LC purity"

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The original literature route relied on a Claisen rearrangement of the olefin intermediate that required 200 °C for 10 h and gave only 53 % isolated yield.  The high temperature and long reaction time also raise safety and scalability concerns.
Solution_Description: A new practical route was developed that avoids the Claisen rearrangement altogether.  The sequence now uses regio‑selective para‑bromination of 2‑isopropylphenol, followed by esterification, a Fries rearrangement under mild TfOH conditions, a mild Pd/C‑catalyzed hydrogenolysis, and a Ru‑catalyzed asymmetric hydrogenation.  This redesign eliminates the high‑temperature step, shortens the overall process, and improves the overall isolated yield to 60 %.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The olefin intermediate is produced by a Claisen rearrangement reaction, which requires 200 °C over 10 h with 53 % yield… the high temperature is not ideal for industrial production, and the low yield significantly decreases the efficiency…”(Intro, p. 2). 2. “The low yield of the Claisen rearrangement and the use of costly and corrosive reagents in the previously reported synthesis were avoided.” (Abstract). 3. “Herein, we report an atom‑economical and cost‑efficient manufacturing process… the overall yield was improved significantly to 60 %.” (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The previously reported Simmons–Smith reaction uses Zn‑Et₂/CH₂I₂/CF₃CO₂H, a highly reactive mixture that generates a violent exotherm when scaled, posing significant safety hazards.
Solution_Description: The hazardous Simmons–Smith step was replaced by a regio‑selective para‑bromination using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS), which is safe, inexpensive and easily controlled on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The use of highly reactive Zn‑(Et)₂/CH₂I₂/CF₃CO₂H reagent in the Simmons–Smith reaction introduces safety concerns due to its exothermic nature of the reaction at scale.” (Intro, p. 2). 2. “The bromination of 2‑isopropylphenol could be easily achieved on a kilogram scale using N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) in acetonitrile…” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The earlier route required 1‑chloro‑2‑butene as a starting material, which is expensive and inflates the material cost of the process.
Solution_Description: The new process starts from cheap, commercially available 2‑isopropylphenol and inexpensive NBS for bromination, eliminating the costly 1‑chloro‑2‑butene.  Additionally, a low‑loading Pd/C catalyst (0.5 wt %) and a Ru‑based system for the asymmetric hydrogenation were chosen to keep reagent costs low.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “In addition, the high cost of starting materials, particularly cyclopropylacetylene, makes the route less suitable for large‑scale production.” (Intro, p. 2). 2. “The synthesis began with commercially available chemical 2‑isopropylphenol…” (Sec 2.1). 3. “We reduced Pd/C loading to 0.5 wt % … offers a mild and efficient way to replace bromine with hydrogen.” (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The initial Fries rearrangement gave poor regio‑selectivity, producing 92 % of the undesired para‑isomer and only 8 % of the target ortho‑isomer, resulting in a low overall yield of the desired phenol intermediate.
Solution_Description: A para‑blocking bromine atom was introduced before the Fries step.  This prevents para‑substitution, forcing the rearrangement to occur exclusively at the ortho‑position and delivering the desired phenol in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Initial attempts at the Fries reaction resulted in the formation of both ortho‑ and para‑regioisomers, giving 92 % of the undesired para‑regioisomer as the major product and only 8 % of the target intermediate 5.” (Sec 2.1). 2. “We wondered if the side reactions could be avoided by introducing a blocking atom/group to selectively occupy the para‑position… halogens were chosen to serve the role of blocking the para‑position of phenol.” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The bromination reaction gave an oily crude mixture containing residual bromine and succinimide, which was difficult to isolate as a pure solid.
Solution_Description: The crude bromophenol was converted into a cocrystal with 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP).  The cocrystal solidified, could be filtered and washed with n‑heptane, delivering a white solid of >99.9 % purity (compound 2).  This cocrystallization step serves as a new purification method and uses a non‑polar solvent (heptane) to induce crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The purification was challenging since the crude product was an oil that contained residual bromine and succinimide… Peng et al. previously demonstrated that cocrystal formation with DABCO was essential… We conducted a quick screening… both DMAP and DABCO successfully produced the eutectic compound… bromophenol‑DMAP cocrystal solidified with higher purity (99.9 %) and yields (95 %).” (Sec 2.1). 2. “To the above oily substance 2a, 2.2 kg of DMAP was added… mixture was heated to 50 °C, … n‑heptane was added… filtered under vacuum… dried … giving 5.94 kg of product 2 (yield: 95 %).” (Experimental Sec 4.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: Using AlCl₃ as the acid for the Fries rearrangement generated a heterogeneous reaction mixture with an aluminum colloid that was difficult to separate and work‑up.
Solution_Description: Trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (TfOH) was adopted as a homogeneous Brønsted acid.  The amount of TfOH was reduced to 1 equiv and the reaction temperature raised to 50 °C, providing clean conversion to the desired phenol (98 % yield) with straightforward aqueous work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “AlCl₃ (entry 2) offered phenol 4 in a good yield, but the reaction was heterogeneous and formed an aluminum colloid, which is hard to workup.” (Sec 2.3). 2. “Using 4 equiv of TfOH at 25 °C afforded phenol 4 in 77 % yield, but the reaction was slow… Increasing the reaction temperature to 50 °C offered a clean reaction profile and gave desired product 4 in 96 % yield (entry 5). Reducing the amount of TfOH to 1 equiv and heating the reaction at 50 °C led to full conversion of ester 3 with product 4 in 98 % yield (entry 7), which was chosen as the optimal condition.” (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: TfOH at low temperature (25 °C) gave a sluggish Fries rearrangement that failed to reach full conversion even after 24 h, resulting in modest yields.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was increased to 50 °C and the TfOH loading reduced to 1 equiv, which accelerated the rearrangement and delivered quantitative conversion with 98 % isolated yield of phenol 4.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Using 4 equiv of TfOH at 25 °C afforded phenol 4 in 77 % yield, but the reaction was slow and could not complete even for 24 h (entry 4).” (Sec 2.3). 2. “Increasing the reaction temperature to 50 °C offered a clean reaction profile and gave desired product 4 in 96 % yield (entry 5). Reducing the amount of TfOH to 1 equiv and heating the reaction at 50 °C led to full conversion … 98 % yield (entry 7).” (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: Quenching the TfOH‑mediated Fries reaction with aqueous NaHCO₃ generated an exotherm that raised the temperature of a 5 kg batch by up to 5 °C, posing a safety risk on larger scale.
Solution_Description: The quench was performed by slow, staged addition of the NaHCO₃ solution while actively monitoring temperature, limiting the temperature rise and ensuring safe heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “When the reaction mixture was washed with a NaHCO₃ solution, the exothermic nature of the quenching process was evident, but the temperature increased no more than 5 °C in a 5 kg scale reaction, indicating safe and efficient heat management.” (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The Wittig reaction generated a large amount of triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO), which is difficult to remove and can contaminate the product if not fully eliminated.
Solution_Description: A precipitation method was developed by adding a 20:1 (v/v) mixture of n‑heptane/ethyl acetate to the crude reaction mixture, causing TPPO to crystallise on cooling.  The precipitate was removed by filtration, reducing residual TPPO to <0.5 % and delivering the desired intermediate 6 in 98 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “To remove the big amount of triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO), we developed an efficient purification method using a mixture of n‑heptane and ethyl acetate (20:1 v/v), which allowed TPPO to precipitate upon cooling to room temperature and was removed easily through filtration.” (Sec 2.5). 2. “The filtrate was concentrated to yield 2.6 kg of compound 6 … (yield: 98 %).” (Experimental Sec 4.7).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: An alternative sequence (4 → 5a → 6) gave incomplete reduction of 5a even at 4 MPa and 10 wt % Pd/C, leading to only 65 % overall yield of intermediate 6 and formation of an undesired ring‑opened by‑product 6a.
Solution_Description: The authors reverted to the preferred sequence (4 → 5 → 6), where the para‑bromo reduction (using 0.5 wt % Pd/C at 0.1–0.2 MPa) proceeded to 98 % yield, followed by the Wittig reaction, giving a robust 98 % overall yield of intermediate 6.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Applying the Wittig reaction under the same conditions led to the production of alkene 5a in a high yield. However, … the conversion remained incomplete, resulting in a 65 % yield of intermediate 6, along with an undesired ring opening byproduct 6a in 10 % yield.” (Sec 2.5). 2. “The reduction was carried out at 0.1–0.2 MPa for 6 h … gave phenol 5 in 98 % yield.” (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: During asymmetric hydrogenation, using methanol as the solvent generated a methanol‑derived by‑product (1b), decreasing product purity.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to sterically hindered t‑butyl alcohol, which suppressed formation of the methanol by‑product and gave a cleaner reaction profile with 91 % isolated yield of Ciprofol (1) and 76 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “In entry 4, a methanol‑related by‑product 1b was observed, which might be avoided if switched to other solvents.” (Sec 2.6). 2. “To test this hypothesis, we replaced methanol with more sterically hindered t‑butyl alcohol, which effectively reduced the formation of 1b and gave 91 % yield of product 1 with 76 % ee as the optimal condition (entry 9).” (Sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: Iridium‑based catalysts reported in the literature give high enantioselectivity but are expensive, raising the material cost of the hydrogenation step.
Solution_Description: A ruthenium‑based catalyst (RuCl₂(COD) with R‑BINAP) was selected.  Ruthenium is cheaper and more readily available, and the optimized system delivered full conversion and good enantioselectivity (91 % yield, 76 % ee) at lower catalyst cost.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The use of the iridium catalyst would greatly improve the yield and enantioselectivity; however, it also significantly increases the overall cost.” (Sec 2.6). 2. “The screening began with commercially available chiral ruthenium catalysts … The combination of RuCl₂(COD) and R‑BINAP gave 91 % yield of product 1 with 76 % ee (entry 9).” (Sec 2.6).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The initial hydrogenolysis of para‑bromophenol used 5 wt % Pd/C, a relatively high catalyst loading that adds to material cost.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was lowered to 0.5 wt % Pd/C without compromising conversion or purity, thereby reducing catalyst expense.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Initially, reduction … was carried out using 5 wt % Pd/C loading … Full conversion was achieved … After further optimizing the catalyst loading, we found that 0.5 wt % Pd/C loading could successfully afford phenol 5 with the same quality on a 4 kg scale.” (Sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical and Scalable Manufacturing Process for Ciprofol
Problem_Description: The previously reported five‑step synthesis of Ciprofol gave an overall isolated yield of only 14 %, making the process impractical for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The newly designed eight‑step route (para‑bromination → esterification → Fries rearrangement → hydrogenolysis → Wittig → asymmetric hydrogenation → carbamate formation → hydrolysis) achieves an overall isolated yield of 60 % (68 % from intermediate 6 to Ciprofol), a more than four‑fold improvement.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The overall yield of 14 % for five steps could be further optimized.” (Intro, p. 2). 2. “The overall yield was improved significantly to 60 %… the process offers an increased overall yield (68 % from 6 to 1).” (Abstract & Conclusions).

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: During diazotization of 2‑naphthylamine‑1,5‑disulfonic acid (NADA) the diazonium salt (NADA‑DS) precipitates, forming solid particles that can clog the reactor and create explosion‑type safety hazards.
Solution_Description: A continuous dynamic tubular reactor was employed and operated at low temperature (≈20 °C) with carefully tuned feed concentrations so that the slurry remains stable and the solid does not accumulate, while the reactor design (dynamic tube, high‑low temperature circulating chiller, PLC‑controlled pumps) accommodates the heterogeneous mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the production of C.I. Reactive Red 195, the precipitation of diazonium salts may pose potential safety hazards.”; “Considerable diazonium salt may precipitate, posing potential safety risks.”; “We established a continuous dynamic tubular reaction system to achieve the multistep continuous heterogeneous synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195.”; “The reaction temperature is then controlled by a high–low temperature circulating chiller to maintain the desired temperature throughout the process.”; “The mechanical stirrer is activated first to ensure proper mixing of the reactants.”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: The diazotization of NADA is highly exothermic; a rapid heat release (maximum 345 W) causes a swift temperature rise that could lead to thermal runaway if not properly managed.
Solution_Description: Reactants (NADA, HCl, NaNO₂) are fed simultaneously from precisely timed pumps (PLC control) to spread heat generation, while a high‑low temperature circulating chiller removes the released heat; the dynamic tubular reactor geometry further improves heat dissipation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The exothermic nature of the NADA diazotization process was determined using this instrument.”; “During the reaction, a significant amount of heat is rapidly released, causing the reaction temperature (Tr) to rise quickly… maximum heat release rate of 345 W.”; “The pumps delivering NADA, hydrochloric acid, and sodium nitrite solutions are activated simultaneously to transport the three raw materials to the bottom of the tubular reactor.”; “To mitigate the temperature increase, the reaction calorimeter lowers the jacket temperature (Tj) to dissipate the heat.”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Poor mixing in the tubular reactor leads to non‑uniform residence times and variability in conversion, potentially reducing product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The rotational speed of the reactor’s impeller was optimized to 100 rpm, which lowered the segregation index to ~0.03, indicating near‑ideal mixing; this speed balances energy consumption with mixing efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: “With an increase in rotation speed, the segregation index (XS) decreases, indicating better mixing performance.”; “The minimum XS value is approximately 0.03, close to zero, indicating that the reactor provides nearly ideal mixing conditions.”; “Considering both energy consumption and reaction efficiency, a rotation speed of 100 rpm was selected as the optimal condition.”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Using excess sodium nitrite (NaNO₂) in the diazotization step reduces diazonium‑salt yield because extra nitrous acid promotes decomposition of NADA‑DS.
Solution_Description: The NaNO₂/NADA molar ratio was optimized to 1.05:1, providing the highest diazonium‑salt yield while avoiding decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yield of diazonium salts initially increased, peaking at a ratio of 1.05, then decreased… excess sodium nitrite produces extra nitrous acid, leading to diazonium salt decomposition.”; “Therefore, the optimal NaNO₂/NADA molar ratio is 1.05:1.”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Dye purity (and thus overall yield) is highly sensitive to reaction temperature and pH of the coupling component (CTN); temperatures above 20 °C or pH > 10 cause hydrolysis and lower purity.
Solution_Description: The coupling reaction was performed at 20 °C and pH 10, the conditions that maximized dye purity (~90 %) while preventing hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the reaction temperature from 5 to 20 °C accelerated the reaction… further temperature rise significantly increases the hydrolysis of the dye and diazonium salt, causing a decrease in dye purity.”; “Increasing the pH of the CTN solution from 7 to 10 also improved dye purity to approximately 90%… a further increase in the pH led to reduced dye purity due to dye hydrolysis.”; “The optimal conditions are as follows: Tp = 20 °C, pH = 10…”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: Long residence times (overall ~287 s) limit throughput for industrial production.
Solution_Description: The total volumetric flow rate was increased from 1000 mL min⁻¹ to 2000 mL min⁻¹, halving the residence time to ~144 s without compromising dye purity, thereby boosting productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Varying the total flow rate from 1000 to 2000 mL/min had little effect on dye purity… As the total flow rate increased, the reaction times for each step decreased… overall residence time from 287 to 144 s.”; “In conclusion, the optimal conditions are … Q = 2000 mL/min.”

Paper Title: Multistep Continuous Heterogeneous Synthesis of C.I. Reactive Red 195 and Safety Evaluation of the Continuous Diazotization Process
Problem_Description: NADA‑DS exhibits thermal decomposition (T_init = 71.9 °C, ΔH_d = 228 J g⁻¹) and could, in principle, pose an explosive hazard.
Solution_Description: Comprehensive DSC and TGA analyses were performed; the decomposition enthalpy was found to be below the 400 J g⁻¹ hazard threshold, and impact‑sensitivity correlations gave negative values, confirming low explosion risk. These data informed the safety assessment and justified operation at 20 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC was used to preliminarily assess the thermal hazards… initial decomposition temperature (T_init) of 71.89 °C, decomposition enthalpy (ΔH_d) of 227.95 J g⁻¹, indicating a decomposition heat risk level of 1 and a potential explosive hazard.”; “According to the Yoshida correlation, NADA‑DS has an IS value of −0.53 and an EP value of −0.61… indicating that NADA‑DS is not prone to impact sensitivity or explosive propagation.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: The traditional Arndt‑Eistert step uses diazomethane, an extremely hazardous reagent that poses serious safety risks on scale.
Solution_Description: Diazomethane is generated in‑situ in a continuous‑flow diazomethane generator and fed directly to the downstream photoreactor, eliminating the need to bottle or manually handle bulk diazomethane and thereby greatly improving the safety profile of the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the first step for preparing diazoketones, the reaction employs diazomethane, an extremely hazardous chemical.”; “Our method leverages the power of flow chemistry, which improves the transformation safety profile by mitigating the risks associated with the generation and handling of diazomethane.”; “The flow generation of diazomethane, diazoketone preparation, and subsequent photoflow Wolff rearrangement without intermediate isolation.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: When scaling the previously reported telescopic cascade, a homogeneous diazoketone solution could not be formed from the diazomethane/THF/CH₂Cl₂ mixture, and the mixed anhydride required additional residence time for complete conversion, leading to unreliable flow operation.
Solution_Description: A short batch “transitional” step is inserted after diazomethane addition: excess diazomethane is quenched with formic acid, CH₂Cl₂ is removed by evaporation, and the mixture is diluted with fresh THF to the optimal 0.1 M concentration (plus 10 equiv H₂O) before entering the photoreactor. This ensures a fully homogeneous feed and provides the needed residence time for anhydride‑to‑diazoketone conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “We cannot prepare the homogeneous diazoketone solution on the water addition step… and we need some residence time for the mixed anhydride to fully convert… This leads us to the necessity of having a batch step, where we allow the reaction to complete, remove the excess diazomethane by quenching it with formic acid, and reduce the CH₂Cl₂ content via evaporation. Then, we dilute the mixture … to reach the 0.1 M concentration of diazoketone, which we found optimal.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: N‑Fmoc‑protected α‑amino acid diazoketones exhibit poor solubility in the THF reaction medium, which reduces their reactivity in the Wolff rearrangement compared with N‑Boc analogues.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent is modified to THF containing 10 equiv of water, which improves the dissolution of the Fmoc substrates. The temperature of the coil is kept at –10 °C (cooler set point) to maintain consistent conversion while preventing precipitation, allowing the photochemical rearrangement to proceed efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: “We assume that the reasons for such a decreased reactivity might lie in the overall worse solubility of the N‑Fmoc amino acids… The photoreactor uses a diazoketone solution (0.1 M, THF) supplemented with 10 equiv of water.”; “Effective temperature control within the set boundaries enabled safe switching from test to large‑scale loads without reducing the conversion while maintaining the side products at a minimum.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: High conversion of diazoketones in flow generates heat that, if not properly removed, can lead to temperature excursions, increased side‑product formation, and safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The external thermostat of the photoreactor is set to a cooler temperature of –10 °C, and a 3 atm back‑pressure regulator maintains pressure. The LED block is actively cooled, and the system shuts down LEDs automatically on overheating, ensuring the reaction mixture stays within a narrow temperature window and side‑product levels remain low.
Supporting_Evidence: “The external thermostat controls the temperature inside the reaction coil… the LED block is equipped with a system for cooling the LEDs and controlling the temperature of the reaction solution… For safety reasons, when the lid … is opened, the LED panels automatically switch off. The coil’s temperature is maintained by an external thermostat, and the LED array is also cooled by an external cooler.”; “The main criteria… were the completion of the diazoketone conversion, control over side product formation, and the productivity of the cooling loop.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: Thermal or metal‑catalyzed Wolff rearrangements fail on sterically hindered or functional‑group‑sensitive substrates, giving low yields or no conversion.
Solution_Description: Replacing the high‑temperature/metal‑catalyzed approach with a photo‑induced Wolff rearrangement (365 nm LEDs) performed under mild, metal‑free conditions expands the substrate scope, delivering good‑to‑excellent yields even for sulfur‑containing, olefinic, or Fmoc‑protected substrates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Arndt‑Eistert process suffers from issues related to safety, efficiency, and substrate scope… High temperature or metal catalysis is necessary, which leads to structural limitations… The photo‑Wolff rearrangement is milder than thermal and catalytic modifications… our photoflow process provides even milder reaction conditions at 365 nm LED light versus previously employed 254 nm irradiation… This accommodates a broader range of substrates on a significantly elevated scale.”

Paper Title: Up-Scale Pseudotelescopic Photoinduced Arndt-Eistert α‑Amino Acid Homologation in a Flow Reactor Cascade
Problem_Description: Scaling the batch Arndt‑Eistert sequence required long reaction times and multi‑hour operations, limiting throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A pilot‑scale continuous‑flow photoreactor (UOSlab FlowReactor UF365/450) operates at 20 mL min⁻¹ flow rate and –10 °C coolant temperature, enabling a steady‑state production of 0.12 mol h⁻¹ (≈20‑30 g h⁻¹) of β‑amino acids. Continuous operation removes the time bottleneck of batch steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “We selected Entry 6… flow rate of 20 mL/min at the cooler temperature set at –10 °C… such a flow rate ensured the formation of the final compound on a 20–30 g scale per hour… Under these conditions, despite a relatively high flow rate, the substrate has sufficient time to absorb enough light for complete conversion.”

Paper Title: Soft and Sustainable Synthesis of Perylene Diimides through Soluble Surrogates of Perylenetetracarboxylic Acid Dianhydride
Problem_Description: Perylene‑3,4,9,10‑tetracarboxylic dianhydride (PDA) is extremely insoluble in common organic solvents because of strong π‑π stacking, which makes its reaction with primary amines slow at room temperature and forces the use of harsh, high‑temperature conditions (>140 °C) and toxic, high‑boiling solvents (NMP, DMF, imidazole, quinoline).
Solution_Description: The authors devise a new synthetic route that first converts PDA into soluble surrogates (MESAC or AMAC) by treating PDA with a non‑nucleophilic volatile amine (tert‑butylamine) in methanol at room temperature. The soluble intermediates are then reacted with the desired primary amine and cyclized in isopropanol under reflux, eliminating the need for high‑temperature, toxic solvents.

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Procedure for Stages 1 and 2 of the Buprenorphine Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: The Diels‑Alder adduct (1) and the hydrogenated product (2) have very low solubility in isopropanol (≈7 % w/w for 1 and ≈4 % w/w for 2 at 50 °C).  This limits the usable concentration, forces large dilutions to keep the solids in solution, and causes catalyst blinding during the heterogeneous hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent (tetrahydrofuran) was added to the IPA reaction bulk (1 : 2 IPA/THF).  This raised the solubility of 2 to 25–37 % w/w at 50 °C, allowing higher reaction concentrations and preventing catalyst fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states: “The biggest barrier to developing a volume‑efficient telescoped process … was the relatively low solubility of both compounds 1 and 2 in IPA… At 50 °C, alkene 1 has a solubility in IPA of approximately 7 % w/w, whereas for alkane 2, the solubility drops to 4 % w/w.” (Problem) ; “The solubility of compound 2 in 1:1 IPA/THF at 50 °C was determined to be 25 % w/w, increasing to 37 % w/w in 1:2 IPA/THF.” (Solution) ; “A successful hydrogenation of alkene 1 was achieved in 1:2 IPA/THF at 50 °C.” (Solution)
