Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Solid‑phase oligonucleotide synthesis (SPOS) is limited to ~10 kg batch sizes because the columns become too large, the flow rates become non‑linear and the process requires large excesses of expensive phosphoramidites and solvents, leading to an extremely high process‑mass‑intensity (PMI ≈ 4300 kg kg⁻¹ for a 20‑mer).
Solution_Description: A scalable one‑pot liquid‑phase oligonucleotide synthesis (OP‑LPOS) was developed that uses only 1.5 equiv of phosphoramidite per coupling, telescopes coupling, sulfurisation and detritylation into a single pot and employs one membrane‑based purification per cycle, reducing solvent/reagent consumption and the PMI to ~718 kg kg⁻¹ (or as low as 108 kg kg⁻¹ with solvent recovery).
Supporting_Evidence: “SPOS requires large excesses of solvents and reagents, notably the expensive phosphoramidite monomers… PMI ∼ 4300 kg kg⁻¹ for a 20mer oligo” (Introduction). “OP‑LPOS employs sequential coupling, sulfurisation, and detritylation, followed by a single membrane purification step per chain‑extension cycle… using just 1.5 equiv of phosphoramidites” (Abstract, Section 2.5). “Overall, the yields for each chain extension were nearly quantitative… PMI per nucleotide for our developed process was 718 kg kg⁻¹” (Sections 3.4, 3.7).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Precipitation has been the dominant intermediate‑purification method for LPOS, but on large scale it suffers from poor control of particle size and precipitation rate, making scale‑up difficult and unreliable.
Solution_Description: Organic‑solvent‑resistant (OSR) ceramic nanofiltration and ultrafiltration membranes were introduced as a continuous, solvent‑based purification alternative to precipitation, providing >99 % rejection of the growing PEG‑oligo and low impurity passage in only 5–10 diavolumes.
Supporting_Evidence: “There are drawbacks to precipitation… scaling up industrial precipitation may be limited by the extensive process development required to control particle size and precipitation rate” (Introduction). “Ceramic organic solvent nanofiltration (OSN) and ultrafiltration (OSU) membranes were used to selectively retain the growing oligonucleotide… enabling purification of intermediate products in just 5 diavolumes” (Abstract). “The NF 750 Da membrane could remove all reagents and by‑products during LPOS in 14 diavolumes… The UF 2000 Da membrane removed all reagents and by‑products in just 5 diavolumes” (Sections 3.3.1, 3.3.2).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: The earlier membrane‑assisted LPOS (nanostar sieving) gave a low overall process yield (39 % for a 9‑mer) because product rejection was insufficient, PEG‑oligo solubility dropped at longer chains and detritylation by‑products were not fully removed.
Solution_Description: A 4‑arm branched PEG support (5–20 kDa) with higher solubility was selected and ceramic NF 750 Da and UF 2000 Da membranes with >99 % PEG‑oligo rejection were employed, enabling stepwise filtration yields of 97–100 % and high crude purity (≈ 72 % for 18‑mer).
Supporting_Evidence: “low overall process yield (39 % for 9mer) due to insufficient product rejection, poor PEG‑oligo solubility… and incomplete removal of detritylation by‑products” (Introduction). “4‑arm PEG was used… shows close to quantitative membrane rejection… The developed platform was demonstrated… with high stepwise filtration yields (97–100 %)” (Abstract, Section 3.1, 3.3).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Loading the 4‑arm PEG with 2,6‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride (DcbCl) created a Dcb‑ester impurity that could not be separated by chromatography, complicating analysis of later LPOS steps.
Solution_Description: The Steglich esterification (DCC/DMAP) was adopted for loading, which avoids formation of the Dcb‑ester impurity and gives clean NMR spectra for subsequent reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: “This loading method produced a Dcb‑ester impurity… Attempts to separate this impurity chromatographically were unsuccessful.” (Section 3.1). “DCC/DMAP was preferred as the DcbCl coupling reagent formed a Dcb‑ester impurity… Loading was achieved by Steglich esterification with DCC/DMAP” (Section 3.1).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: During chain extension the membrane permeance dropped (from 2.2 → 1.1 L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹ for the 6‑mer and from 20.2 → 7.3 L m⁻² h⁻¹ bar⁻¹ for the 18‑mer) and impurity (Dmtr‑CySH) rejection increased, indicating concentration‑polarisation and/or precipitation at the membrane surface.

Solution_Description: The diafiltration solvent was switched to a MeCN/MeOH mixture (9:1 or 4:1 v/v) which increased PEG‑oligo solubility, broke hydrogen‑bonding networks, raised permeance and reduced Dmtr‑CySH rejection, restoring efficient filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: “permeance decreased… and the rejection of Dmtr‑CySH increased… A sudden drop in filtration yield was observed… To increase the solubility of the PEG‑oligo, the diafiltration solvent was swapped to MeCN:MeOH (9:1 v/v), where permeance increased… and the Dmtr‑CySH rejection lowered to 26 %” (Sections 3.3.1, 3.3.2, Figure 6).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Sulfurisation reagents DDTT and XH have very low solubility in neat acetonitrile (0.02 M and 0.005 M), causing precipitation on the membrane surface and fouling.
Solution_Description: POS (3‑phenyl‑1,2,4‑dithiazoline‑5‑one) was selected (and PADS used in excess) because both are highly soluble in acetonitrile, giving complete sulfurisation in under 30 min without precipitation.

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Cross‑flow velocities of 0.2–1 m s⁻¹ used during diafiltration are well below the manufacturers’ recommended 3–5 m s⁻¹, providing insufficient turbulence to prevent solute buildup and membrane fouling at longer chain lengths.

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: The dimethoxytrityl (Dmtr) protecting group generates a hydrophobic Dmtr‑CySH impurity that is poorly soluble in acetonitrile (≈ 20 mg mL⁻¹) and is increasingly rejected by the membrane, causing fouling and removal difficulties.
Solution_Description: Replace the Dmtr group with a smaller, acid‑labile, non‑reversible protecting group such as 2‑isopropoxyprop‑2‑ylacetal (IIP), which produces a more polar by‑product that can be removed efficiently by the hydrophilic ceramic membrane.
Supporting_Evidence: “Dmtr‑CySH impurity… may pose a risk for membrane fouling due to its poor solubility… Switching to a smaller, acid‑labile and nonreversible group, such as the 2‑isopropoxyprop‑2‑ylacetal (IIP) protecting group, may be beneficial…” (Section 3.6).

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Detritylation of longer chain oligomers becomes slower, requiring higher equivalents of acid (30–180 eq) and longer reaction times (up to 130 min) to reach completion.

Paper Title: Scalable Membrane Enabled One-Pot Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis
Problem_Description: Even with high PEG‑oligo solubility in bulk acetonitrile, at the membrane interface precipitation and concentration‑polarisation occur, limiting filtration performance at later chain‑extension steps.

Paper Title: Quality Management of Diastereomeric Impurity for Complex Peptide Manufacturing: A Case Study of Corticorelin Ovine
Problem_Description: For long peptides (≥ 15 residues) synthesising a separate reference standard for each possible diastereomeric impurity becomes impractical – the corticorelin ovine peptide (41 residues) would require 41 individual diastereomeric impurity standards.
Solution_Description: An orthogonal impurity‑management strategy was introduced: the peptide is fragmented into five overlapping C‑terminal sequences that are directly analysed by de‑uterated HCl hydrolysis‑GC‑MS (chiral amino‑acid analysis). This avoids the need to prepare every individual diastereomeric reference standard.
Supporting_Evidence:

"When the peptides of interest contain more amino acids, they will pose substantial challenges to the preparation of individual diastereomeric impurity reference standards…".
"We developed an orthogonal diastereomeric impurity management strategy… five overlapping fragments… are prepared".
"The fragments are not purified but directly applied to the analyses of deuterated HCl hydrolysis‑based GC‑MS".

Problem_Description: The original route I uses multiple hazardous reagents (dimethyl sulfate, phosphorous acid, chlorosulfonic acid) and requires many steps, resulting in higher material cost and a moderate overall yield (≈61 %).

Supporting_Evidence: “Route I… suffers from long reaction steps and environmental unfriendly reagents like dimethyl sulfate, phosphorous acid, chlorosulfonic acid… With the second route, the cost of chemical materials is relatively higher, and its yield is moderate.… We chose the second approach to modify for its convenience in terms of operation and showed promising potential for improving yield.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Reduction side‑products (compound 6, ~12 %) arise from the use of excess sodium thiomethoxide, decreasing the purity and overall yield of m‑nitrothioanisole.
Solution_Description: The equivalents of sodium thiomethoxide were lowered from 1.2 equiv (batch) to ~1.03 equiv in flow, which reduced the formation of reduction by‑products while slightly increasing the product yield to 89 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “sodium thiomethoxide is the most likely reducing agent… the usage of sodium thiomethoxide may be reduced (which is 1.2 equiv in batch chemistry)… the molar equivalent of sodium thiomethoxide was reduced to 1.03 with a slight increase of yield. A maximum yield of 89 % was achieved, and the purity of crude product was 91 %.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The dediazoniation step is slow and out‑gassing; providing sufficient residence time would require an excessively long tube, causing an unacceptable pressure drop in the flow system.
Solution_Description: Dediazoniation was moved out of the flow tube into a separate heated collection vessel, eliminating the need for a very long coil and avoiding pressure‑drop limitations while maintaining sufficient reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “dediazoniation is a time‑consuming and outgassing process, the reaction tube needs to be extremely long to give adequate residence time, and in that case, the pressure drop was beyond our acceptance range. Therefore, dediazoniation was rearranged in a collection vessel.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Initial optimization of diazotization showed that yield varied with temperature and residence time, with a peak yield at 30 °C and 30 s; longer times or higher temperatures led to decomposition of the diazonium intermediate.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified the optimal temperature (30 °C) and residence time (30 s) for the diazotization step, giving a stable maximum yield of 68 % and preventing over‑decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “The maximum yield (68 %) of 1 was achieved at about T1 = 30 °C and τ1 = 30 s… the yield was increased to a constant value with prolonged residence time at low reaction temperature (less than 10 °C), while it was increased to a peak value followed by a decrease with prolonged residence time at relatively high reaction temperature (excess than 20 °C).”

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: The bromide substrate (compound 3) showed poor solubility in most organic solvents, requiring a high‑boiling, low‑water‑content solvent to keep it in solution at ambient temperature.
Solution_Description: THF was selected as the reaction solvent to provide sufficient solubility of the bromide feed at room temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: ["given the poor solubility of the bromide in many organic systems, the feed stream of 3 required a strong solvent with low water content to remain in solution at ambient temperature, and THF was selected.", "Initial solvent screening focused on trying to obtain a fully homogeneous system, but given the poor solubility of the bromide in many organic systems, the feed stream of 3 required a strong solvent with low water content to remain in solution at ambient temperature, and THF was selected."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: The reaction is biphasic (organic/aqueous) and the two layers are essentially immiscible, leading to poor mass‑transfer and slow reaction rates.
Solution_Description: A catalytic amount (0.05 equiv) of tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr) was added as a phase‑transfer agent, more than doubling the observed reaction rate.
Supporting_Evidence: ["These layers differ significantly in density and are for all practical purposes immiscible.", "The addition of 0.05 equiv of tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr), a phase transfer catalyst, served to more than double the apparent reaction rate and was adopted into the standard protocol."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: PdCl₂[dtbpf] is poorly soluble in the organic feed and shows reduced activity when mixed with the organic/aqueous streams, likely due to catalyst precipitation/formation of Pd(0).
Solution_Description: The catalyst feed was kept as an independent stream (3–5 % w/w in DCE) and combined with the organic and aqueous feeds only inside the reactor, allowing precise control of catalyst charge and avoiding premature deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The insolubility of PdCl₂[dtbpf] was problematic in that catalyst solutions of practical concentration (3–5 wt %) could only be achieved in 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE), dichloromethane (DCM), or aqueous THF.", "It was decided that the catalyst feed should be kept separate from the organic and aqueous feeds as preliminary stability data on organic feed solution that contained catalyst indicated that catalyst performance suffered relative to a catalyst‑only feed.", "With the third feed stream, the catalyst charge could be varied during the course of continuous runs to probe catalyst loading effects."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: Conventional PAT (IR, Raman, UV‑vis) were ineffective for a fast, biphasic Suzuki coupling, making it difficult to determine reaction completion on a cycle‑by‑cycle basis.
Solution_Description: A non‑contact, colorimetric monitoring system using a simple web‑camera was implemented; RGB values of the reaction mixture were extracted in real‑time and correlated to conversion, providing an automated end‑point decision.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A unique noncontact colorimetric method was used to monitor reaction completion.", "Due to the biphasic nature of the reaction, infrared, Raman, and UV–vis methods proved problematic for reaction monitoring.", "When an inexpensive web camera was used to monitor the reaction in real time, the image of the stirred reaction could be broken into red, green, and blue values, which could then be exported to Excel for data analysis and trending."]

Problem_Description: The product stream becomes supersaturated with the target compound below 40 °C, creating a risk of fouling in downstream tubing and vessels.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A transfer‑zone architecture was added; the reactor was periodically evacuated and pressurised, providing high‑frequency head‑space turnover that limits solid precipitation and removes dissolved oxygen.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the product stream becomes supersaturated with 2 below 40 °C, so concerns existed surrounding potential fouling of tubing and vessels downstream of the reactor.", "The transfer zone consisted of a chamber or “zone” connected to the reactor and isolated by a number of automated valves. The zone could be evacuated or pressurized and would be used to move the product mixture from the reactor into the chamber with vacuum, then pushed into a bulk holding vessel with nitrogen pressure.", "One advantage of this method of transfer was that the headspace in the reactor was turned over at a high frequency due to the transfer zone evacuations. This meant that any oxygen from the feed streams, which were not perfectly inerted, could not build up in the reactor headspace over time."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: Significant amounts of palladium and iron remain in the reaction mixture after the Suzuki coupling, posing toxicity and regulatory concerns for the final API.
Solution_Description: A packed thiosilica (20 % w/w) column was employed to scavenge residual Pd and Fe; metal levels were reduced from 51 ppm Pd / 12 ppm Fe to <3 ppm Pd / 5.9 ppm Fe.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Removal of the residual Pd and Fe from the ferrocene catalyst was desired prior to crystallization.", "After removal of the phosphate layer, thiosilica (20% by mass) was added and the slurry agitated at 40–45 °C overnight.", "Thiosilica treatment of the organic solution resulted in reduction of Fe from 12 to 5.9 ppm and Pd from 51 ppm to <3 ppm."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: The catalyst solvent DCE is toxic and has undesirable environmental impact, limiting its use in a GMP production environment.
Solution_Description: Current investigations are shifting the catalyst solution to DCM, which is less hazardous and acceptable in the small quantities required for production.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For the purposes of this demonstration, DCE was used as the catalyst solvent, although its toxicity and environmental implications deter its use in production.", "Current investigations are focused on catalyst solutions in DCM, as the small quantities that would be used in production are viewed as acceptable in this case."]

Paper Title: An Automated Intermittent Flow Approach to Continuous Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: Reaction times varied widely (10–30 min) with changes in temperature, catalyst loading, or base concentration, reducing throughput and consistency.
Solution_Description: Systematic adjustments—raising reactor temperature from 60 °C to 67 °C and increasing base load or catalyst equivalents—reduced the average cycle time to 16–17 min, providing a faster and more consistent process.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Increase temp, TJ = 65 °C … reaction time reduced to 17 min for the same feed.", "Reduce catalyst loading to 0.0025 equiv resulted in a much longer reaction (74 min) and required an additional catalyst charge to complete the reaction.", "Decrease base load by 10%, TJ = 60 °C … reaction times were 21–22 min."]

Problem_Description: During continuous crystallization the product feed tube accumulated solid material, leading to blockages and potential shutdowns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A tube‑in‑tube arrangement was implemented; periodic injection of THF (10 mL/hr) through the outer tube dissolved the deposited solids and prevented blockage.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the tip of product feed tube gradually built up a solid mass of crystallized product (likely due to evaporation and cooling at that point), which could eventually lead to tube blockage.", "In order to correct this liability, a tube‑in‑tube system was devised to encase the feed tube in a larger tube and use 10 mL aliquots of THF, delivered by syringe pump once per hour, to dislodge the solids."]

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the lithiation / alkylation of 2,6‑dichloropyridine with salicylaldehyde gave a dramatic loss of conversion (only 19 % isolated yield of azaxanthene 17 compared with 56 % on laboratory scale).  The reaction stalled when the aldehyde was added slowly, and the exotherm at larger scale made temperature control difficult.
Solution_Description: The salicylaldehyde was added in a single, rapid charge while keeping the batch temperature below –40 °C.  This fast addition prevented hemiaminal formation that masked the aldehyde and maintained >90 % conversion on the 0.5‑kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Upon initial scale‑up to a 20 L vessel, a dramatic drop in reaction conversion to 16 was observed resulting in only a 19 % isolated yield of 17.”; “Subsequent laboratory experiments identified the addition rate of the salicylaldehyde as a critical parameter for achieving high conversion. When salicylaldehyde was added in a single, rapid charge, >90 % conversion was observed, whereas slower additions resulted in reaction stalling.”; “The preparative formation of 16 was carried out by charging the salicylaldehyde at the maximum possible rate while maintaining a batch temperature below –40 °C to prevent degradation of the pyridyllithium species.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Quenching the TiCl₄‑mediated Lewis‑acid alkylation generated a titanium hydrogel that was difficult to filter, complicating work‑up and product isolation.
Solution_Description: The reaction stream was treated with wet ethyl acetate at a controlled pH, precipitating the titanium by‑products as filter‑able solids.  The solids were removed by a polish filtration, giving a clear solution for downstream processing.
Supporting_Evidence: “The removal of titanium byproducts proved to be problematic as the direct aqueous quench of TiCl₄ in the reaction mixture formed a difficult‑to‑filter titanium hydrogel.”; “We found that the titanium salt could be easily removed by polish filtration after treatment of the reaction stream with wet ethyl acetate at controlled pH… which resulted in the precipitation of the titanium byproducts as filterable solids.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Residual palladium remained in the penultimate intermediates (20 and 21) after Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling, exceeding the acceptable limits for API production.
Solution_Description: The carboxylic acid was converted to its dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) salt, which crystallised cleanly and reduced palladium to ~200 ppm.  After acid‑liberation and a final crystallisation, palladium levels were <10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “We were unable to achieve our target levels for palladium by treatment of MeTHF streams… We then turned our attention to palladium removal via crystallisation… the dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) salt of 20 was a highly crystalline solid that, when isolated, reduced palladium levels to 200 ppm.”; “Liberation of 20 from the DCHA salt… provided a white, fluffy solid with >99.7 % LCAP purity and <10 ppm of palladium.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling of the electron‑deficient 2‑chloro‑azaxanthene (10a) with aryl‑boronic acids (18/19) gave low conversion and extensive homocoupling under standard conditions.
Solution_Description: High‑throughput screening identified tricyclohexylphosphonium tetrafluoroborate as the optimal ligand, potassium carbonate as the base, and tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr) as an additive.  These conditions gave >99 % LCAP of the desired cross‑coupled product with no detectable homocoupling.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initial Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling… led to low conversion of the 2‑chloroazaxanthene fragment or homocoupling of the arylboronic acids.”; “When tricyclohexylphosphonium tetrafluoroborate was employed with more basic potassium carbonate and tetrabutylammonium bromide (TBABr), 99 % LCAP of cross‑coupled product 20 was observed with no detectable 31.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Impurities derived from dimethylamine and ethyl‑methylamine (present in the amine reagents) required a second chiral SFC purification after the final amidation step.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was reordered so that the Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling was performed on the azaxanthene core before incorporation of the amide.  The dialkyl‑amide groups were introduced early, eliminating the need for amine‑derived impurities at the boronic‑acid stage and removing the second SFC step.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the original process… a second SFC purification… required due to contaminants in the corresponding amines… To minimise the formation of the impurities… we turned our attention to developing processes to prepare the requisite nucleophilic Suzuki–Miyaura coupling partners 18 and 19.”; “Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling using 18 and 19 with the dialkyl amide moieties already incorporated was envisaged to provide greater control of impurities associated with dimethylamine and ethylmethylamine.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: A partial classical resolution of the racemic carboxylic acid mixture using cinchonidine gave a salt enriched in the undesired enantiomer (10b).
Solution_Description: A partial classical resolution was combined with a preparative chiral SFC step using the 85:15 mixture of 10a:10b, affording sufficient quantities of the desired enantiomer (10a) for further development.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, the only crystalline salt prepared from cinchonidine was enriched with the undesired enantiomer 10b… Coupling of our optimized partial classical resolution with a chiral preparative SFC process using the 85:15 mixture of 10a:10b as feedstock allowed the production of enough material to support the initial development of both 1 and 2.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: The amorphous APIs (1 and 2) exhibited very low aqueous solubility (≈0.01 mg mL⁻¹), limiting formulation options for oral dosing.
Solution_Description: A non‑ionic surfactant (Polysorbate 80) was added to the aqueous media, increasing apparent solubility by roughly an order of magnitude. Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of Functionalized Azaxanthene-Derived Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators

Supporting_Evidence: “Our initial attempt… to prepare amorphous 1 by dissolution in methanol followed by rotary evaporation… was not completely successful… it was possible using EtOH as the solvent.”; “We also acknowledge Dr. Chiajen Lai for performing the spray drying studies to prepare amorphous materials.”

Paper Title: A Partial Classical Resolution/Preparative Chiral Supercritical Fluid Chromatography Method for the Rapid Preparation of the Pivotal Intermediate in the Synthesis of Two Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: The original preparative SFC scale‑up using a 50:50 8a/8b feed gave a processing rate of only ~31 g day⁻¹ of the desired enantiomer, meaning that the required 1.3 kg of 8a would have taken ≥42 days – far beyond the aggressive clinical timeline.

Supporting_Evidence: • “At this rate, however, processing 1.3 kg of 8a would have taken at least 42 days, failing to meet our delivery timeline.”

Paper Title: A Partial Classical Resolution/Preparative Chiral Supercritical Fluid Chromatography Method for the Rapid Preparation of the Pivotal Intermediate in the Synthesis of Two Nonsteroidal Glucocorticoid Receptor Modulators
Problem_Description: Commercial preparative SFC columns of the required size were not readily available, which limited the ability to scale the chiral separation.

Supporting_Evidence: • “...their application in process development… has been limited in part by column availability.”

Paper Title: Development of a Multi Kilogram-Scale, Tandem Cyclopropanation Ring-Expansion Reaction en Route to Hedgehog Antagonist IPI-926

• “Nitrogen sweeps were used to prevent accumulation of ethane.”

Paper Title: Development of a Multi Kilogram-Scale, Tandem Cyclopropanation Ring-Expansion Reaction en Route to Hedgehog Antagonist IPI-926

The authors propose a revised mechanism (Scheme 13) that “assumes that 19 and 34 … can react to give 35 … leading to 50 % conversion … and 96 % e.p.” (p. 9).

Paper Title: Proposed Mechanism for the Enantioselective Alkynylation of an Aryl Trifluoromethyl Ketone, the Key Step in the Synthesis of Efavirenz
Problem_Description: Changing the order of addition to 9 → DEZ → 3 reduced the enantioselectivity by 3‑5 % compared with the standard sequence, indicating that the addition order is critical for consistent performance.
Solution_Description: The authors identified the problematic sequence and recommended the standard order (DEZ → 3 → 9) or avoiding the 9‑DEZ‑3 order to preserve high enantioselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: It is reported that “the single exception to be the sequence 9–DEZ–3, which gave 3–5 % lower enantioselectivity.” (p. 5).  The discussion of “sequence of addition of DEZ, 3, and 9” (p. 5) led to the conclusion that the order must be controlled.

Paper Title: Proposed Mechanism for the Enantioselective Alkynylation of an Aryl Trifluoromethyl Ketone, the Key Step in the Synthesis of Efavirenz
Problem_Description: Using excess Grignard reagent (10) (up to 1.3 equiv) caused a drop in enantioselectivity, suggesting that disproportionate deprotonation of the alkyne or side reactions were occurring.
Solution_Description: The optimal Grignard loading was identified (≈1 equiv) and controlled via precise dosing; the DoE work defined the maximal tolerated excess to avoid loss of selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: The article notes that “addition of excess Grignard 10 (up to 1.3 equiv) led to a drop in enantioselectivity but … no formation of alcohol 17 as a by‑product.” (p. 5).  The DoE experiments “provided the information (including reagent‑charging accuracy and precision requirements) required to define the process.” (p. 5).

Paper Title: Proposed Mechanism for the Enantioselective Alkynylation of an Aryl Trifluoromethyl Ketone, the Key Step in the Synthesis of Efavirenz
Problem_Description: When sub‑stoichiometric amounts of DEZ and amino alcohol 3 were used, the reaction proceeded more slowly and did not reach full conversion in the first cycle, indicating a rate limitation.
Solution_Description: A catalytic pathway was proposed in which a small amount of DEZ/3 initiates a chain of cycles; the stoichiometric ratios were tuned to exploit this catalytic turnover, improving overall conversion while using less reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors observed that “Employing substoichiometric amounts of the reagents DEZ and 3 resulted in slower reaction, but the conversion … was higher than expected.” (p. 6).  They then describe “a catalytic process … initiated by extrusion of chloromagnesium salt 15 … and the formation of complex 33 … could react … to form … 15.” (p. 9‑10).

Paper Title: Proposed Mechanism for the Enantioselective Alkynylation of an Aryl Trifluoromethyl Ketone, the Key Step in the Synthesis of Efavirenz
Problem_Description: The predictive spreadsheet model initially over‑predicted conversion when using equimolar reagent amounts, because the real system required excess of certain components for high conversion.
Solution_Description: The model was refined by incorporating empirical correction factors and narrower stoichiometric ranges (±1 %) derived from extensive experimental data, improving its accuracy for troubleshooting.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors note that “equimolar stoichiometry settings (1.00 mol of each reagent) predict ideal results … whereas experimental work showed that molar excesses of some reagents are required.” (p. 8).  They then state that “the simulation … was extended to include 64 sets of calculations … to define half‑ranges (Δ) … some ranges must be as narrow as ±1 % to ensure a successful reaction outcome.” (p. 8‑9).

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: Initial coupling of Boc‑protected intermediate 5 with cystamine using PPh₃/I₂/imidazole in CH₂Cl₂ gave only 15–20 % isolated yield, and the phosphine‑oxide by‑product co‑eluted with the desired product on silica‑gel chromatography, making purification difficult.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a carbodiimide‑mediated coupling using EDCI/HOBt in DMF at room temperature with dropwise addition of cystamine.  This gave 95 % isolated yield of product 6 and eliminated the need for column chromatography by performing liquid‑liquid extractions to remove HOBt and the urea by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Initial attempts using PPh₃, I₂, and imidazole in CH₂Cl₂ gave 6 in only 15–20% yield; in addition, the phosphine oxide byproduct had nearly the same mobility on silica gel chromatography as 6.', 'We achieved smooth coupling of 5 and cystamine by employing EDCI and HOBt.', 'DMF at room temperature proved best along with dropwise addition of cystamine.', 'Most importantly, we eliminated column chromatography by judicious extractions that removed both HOBt and the carbodiimide byproduct and provided 6 in 95% yield with no need for further purification.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: During the enzymatic cascade at high substrate concentration the Mg²⁺‑pyrophosphate complex precipitated, causing loss of material and interfering with the PPAT‑catalyzed step.
Solution_Description: The solid Mg·PPᵢ precipitate was removed by simple filtration before the addition of the next enzyme, allowing quantitative conversion in the subsequent steps.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The limited solubility of pyrophosphate in the presence of Mg²⁺ caused precipitation during reactions with PPAT at high substrate concentrations, which interfered with the enzymatic reaction.', 'The Mg·PPᵢ complex that precipitated during the reaction was removed by filtration.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: Free thiol intermediates (pantetheine) are prone to oxidation by atmospheric oxygen, leading to unstable products and undesired sulfur‑oxide by‑products.
Solution_Description: The authors employed the disulfide dimer pantethine as the biocatalytic precursor.  The disulfide masks the thiol, eliminates the need for protection/de‑protection steps, and reduces the formation of oxidation by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The dimeric intermediates were organic‑soluble, which allowed the desired products to be isolated by solvent extraction with no need for chromatographic purification.', 'To avoid side‑reactions involving the free thiol of 1 and its derivatives, we employed disulfide 8 as an alternate substrate.', 'The disulfide also diminishes the chances of forming sulfur oxidation byproducts during the synthetic operations.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: Final purification of CoA‑disulfide by reversed‑phase HPLC gave very low loading capacity, making scale‑up impractical and costly.
Solution_Description: A Dowex anion‑exchange column (low‑cost, high‑capacity resin) was used with a LiCl gradient to bind the product and elute CoA‑disulfide with 600 mM LiCl, providing high recovery and material throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Reversed‑phase HPLC, while effective, had very low capacity that greatly limited its practical scalability.', 'Dowex anion exchange resin combined low material cost, high loading capacity, and simple operation.', 'After binding, increasing concentrations of LiCl were used to separate CoA disulfide 11 from byproduct.', 'A linear LiCl gradient yielded individual fractions containing AMP, ADP, ATP, and 11, which allowed recovery of the adenosine byproducts and regeneration into ATP if desired.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: Even after ion‑exchange, inorganic salts (mainly LiCl) remained with the product, limiting its measured purity (~82 %).
Solution_Description: The crude product was adsorbed onto activated charcoal, washed to remove salts, and then eluted with 40 % aqueous acetone containing a small amount of ammonia; a second adsorption/desorption cycle raised the analytical purity to ~90 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['CoA disulfide was desalted by absorption on activated charcoal.', 'Excess LiCl was removed by rinsing the activated charcoal with deionized water; then CoA disulfide was eluted with a 40% acetone solution containing 0.028% ammonia.', 'The adsorption onto activated charcoal was repeated a second time to provide analytically pure 11 (1.89 g, 95%).', 'The purity of CoA disulfide could be raised to 90% by a second adsorption/desorption treatment with activated charcoal.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: Pantolactone can racemize under basic, high‑temperature conditions, potentially compromising the stereochemical integrity of the final product.
Solution_Description: The coupling of pantolactone was performed in ethanol with a limited amount of Et₃N at reflux; control reactions showed no detectable racemization, confirming that the conditions preserve stereochemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Base‑catalyzed racemization of d‑pantolactone, e.g., when heated in DMF, has been reported.', 'Because our conversion of 7 to 8 involved heating an ethanolic solution of d‑pantolactone in the presence of Et₃N, we carried out a control reaction to determine whether racemization might have occurred.', 'Chiral‑phase GC analysis of the reaction mixture revealed only a single peak for pantolactone within the detection limits of the instrument.', 'We believe that our reaction product is diastereomerically pure and that no significant racemization took place.']

Paper Title: An Efficient Chemoenzymatic Synthesis of Coenzyme A and Its Disulfide
Problem_Description: The disulfide‑CoA product is susceptible to oxidation when exposed to air, which can generate unwanted by‑products.
Solution_Description: A slight excess of TCEP was added directly to the reaction buffer to quantitatively reduce the disulfide to free CoASH in situ, allowing the stable disulfide to be stored and only reduced when needed.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The disulfide bond of 8 was reduced quantitatively by a slight molar excess of tris(2‑carboxyethyl)‑phosphine (TCEP) in the buffer used for the enzyme‑catalyzed reactions (75 mM Tris‑Cl, 25 mM KCl, 250 mM MgCl₂, pH 7.5).', 'When a slight molar excess of TCEP was added to the sample of CoA disulfide prior to HPLC analysis, only one peak was observed at the tᵣ corresponding to free CoASH.', 'This allows the cofactor to be stored as the stable disulfide, then reduced in situ as needed for biochemical applications.']

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: When scaling the synthesis of BB13H to multigram quantities the reaction gave slightly lower yields with a standard magnetic stirrer; efficient stirring was needed for proper mixing and diffusion of species.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Use a mechanical stirrer (overhead stirrer) for large‑volume batches to ensure vigorous agitation and uniform mass transfer, which restored the high isolated yields (up to 89 %).
Supporting_Evidence: ["With the biggest quantity, the amount of final product slightly decreases with a standard magnetic stirrer (entry 3), whereas an optimal yield is obtained under mechanical stirring, certainly due to a more efficient stirring, and species diffusion, with larger volume.", "The production of this first reagent has been scaled up to 17 g without major issues, following the initially described procedure."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: The transient difluoro‑(trifluoromethyl)-λ⁴‑sulfanamine intermediate is prone to degradation if the temperature is not kept low.
Solution_Description: Run the first step at –20 °C (maintaining –20 °C to –10 °C during reagent additions) to suppress decomposition and give optimal formation of the intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: ["It is noteworthy that the low temperature (−20 °C) is necessary to well control the first step and to observe an optimal formation of the transient difluoro‑(trifluoromethyl)-λ⁴‑sulfanamine without degradation."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: The original methylation of BB13H used NaH/MeI; handling large amounts of NaH is hazardous and alternative bases gave poor conversion.
Solution_Description: Retain NaH/MeI as the methylation system for multigram batches (ensuring safe handling protocols) and avoid weaker bases that give low yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initially, the methylation step had been performed with NaH and MeI. To try to avoid the manipulation of large amount of NaH, a few other systems has been tested.", "In a practical point of view, during the synthesis of BB23 reagent, the chromatographic purification of intermediates 1b is highly recommended to achieve optimal yields."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: Skipping purification of BB13H before methylation led to lower methylation yields and poorer quality BB13 product.
Solution_Description: Introduce a systematic flash‑chromatography purification of BB13H prior to the methylation step, which restores high yield (≈90 %) and product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: ["However, several attempts have shown that not only the methylation yield was slightly lower but that the final BB13 product was of lesser quality, even after purification.", "Consequently, it is recommended to systematically purified BB13H by chromatography before the methylation step."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: Tosylamide, the starting material for BB23, becomes poorly soluble in ethyl acetate at larger scales, causing inconsistent yields and difficulty in handling.
Solution_Description: Switch to solid addition of tosylamide (pre‑weighed solid added to the hot reaction mixture) instead of trying to dissolve it, which eliminates the solubility bottleneck and gives reproducible yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The solubility of tosylamide is a major issue in this multigram extrapolation. Indeed, if with a small amount, a homogeneous solution in ethyl acetate is easy to obtain, with larger quantities tosylamide must be solubilized in hot solution... this technical issue is source of variability in the observed yields.", "To better control this critical addition, a solid addition has been envisaged. To validate this modification, the reaction has been first performed in small scale (entry 6). The obtained results are in accordance with the previous “liquid addition”. Then, this strategy has been scaled up to 50 g of starting tosylamide with good, and reproducible, results."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: The first‑generation reagents (BB13H and BB13) are more expensive per gram than the second‑generation BB23, primarily because pentane is used for chromatography.
Solution_Description: Replace pentane (expensive) with cyclohexane for the purification of BB23, thereby reducing solvent cost and overall reagent price.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Surprisingly, despite a lower step number, the first generation of trifluoromethanesulfemanide reagents (BB13H and BB13B) is more expensive than the second generation (BB23). This is mainly due to the pentane, used for chromatographic purifications, which is a more expensive solvent than cyclohexane, used for BB23."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: Acidic rearrangement of 1b initially used trifluoroacetic acid, a relatively costly reagent.
Solution_Description: Substitute trifluoroacetic acid with cheaper sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) without loss of yield, lowering material cost for large‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The acidic treatment of 1b led to BB23H with good reproducible yields at around 30 g scale (entries 1–2). Nevertheless, to try to reduce costs at larger scale, trifluoroacetic acid has been successfully substituted by less expensive sulfuric acid (entry 3)."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: Methylation of BB23H with NaH/Me₂SO₄ gave satisfactory results on a small scale but yielded poor conversions on larger batches; also the deprotonated species is unstable.
Solution_Description: Adopt iPr₂NEt/TfOMe methylation system and add TfOMe rapidly (≈5 min) after deprotonation to capture the unstable intermediate before it decomposes, delivering consistent high yields (≈90 %) on multigram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["With the iPrNEt₂/TfOMe system, excellent, and reproducible, results were obtained whatever the starting quantities (from 7 to 91 g). It is noteworthy that TfOMe must be added rapidly following the deprotonation (around 5 min after) because of the relative instability of deprotonated species.", "In general, NaH, as s base, did not lead to satisfactory yields, whatever the methylating agent."]

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Syntheses of First and Second Generation of Trifluoromethanesulfenamide Reagents
Problem_Description: During the large‑scale rearrangement and methylation steps for BB23, insufficient agitation led to lower yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employ mechanical stirring (overhead stirrer) throughout the BB23 synthetic sequence to ensure uniform mixing and improve yields (up to 95 % for BB23H and 88 % for BB23).
Supporting_Evidence: ["From the experience acquired from BB13 synthesis, this step has been systematically performed under mechanical stirring as, also, the following steps.", "Again, a mechanical stirring seems to improve the yield."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of an Azaindolyl-Pyrimidine Inhibitor of Influenza Virus Replication
Problem_Description: The enzymatic desymmetrization of the diester required a very high lipase loading (42 wt %) on a 400 g scale, which generated a persistent emulsion and a difficult aqueous work‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The lipase loading was reduced to 10 wt % (consistent with literature precedent). The reaction still proceeded to completion overnight, and the emulsion was largely eliminated, simplifying isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...we encountered a significant emulsion using the same work‑up procedure. This may have been due to the scale on which we were performing the reaction (400 g) and the large loading (42 wt %) of the lipase.”; “Since the enzymatic reaction conditions used in initial synthesis caused isolation problems, we lowered the lipase loading to 10 wt % and found that reaction went to completion overnight and much less emulsion was observed during work‑up.”; “Same 10 wt % enzyme loading was used by Yoshida with a similar lipase in an enzymatic hydrolysis reaction on half‑ton scale.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of an Azaindolyl-Pyrimidine Inhibitor of Influenza Virus Replication
Problem_Description: The Hofmann rearrangement step generated copper salts (CuBr₂/LiO‑tBu) that were difficult to remove, complicating the work‑up and raising safety/environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: The second Curtius rearrangement/Hofmann sequence was eliminated; instead, the acid was directly converted to the morpholinyl urea via a DPPA/TEA Curtius rearrangement followed by addition of morpholine, avoiding copper reagents altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “...a second Curtius rearrangement to convert 8 to 9 was unsuccessful and led to an unidentified byproduct. Alternatively, 8 was converted to the corresponding primary amide and subsequent Hofmann rearrangement using CuBr₂/LiO‑tBu worked efficiently…although the presence of copper salts made the work‑up challenging.”; “The advantage of this route is that the morpholine‑based urea is installed in a more direct manner and both the Hofmann rearrangement and Boc deprotection steps have been eliminated.”; “Compound 14 was treated with DPPA/TEA, followed by the addition of morpholine to form the desired urea.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of an Azaindolyl-Pyrimidine Inhibitor of Influenza Virus Replication
Problem_Description: The original synthesis required 12 steps, gave an overall yield of only 8.7 %, and needed chromatographic purification after six of those steps, making the process inefficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A redesigned retrosynthetic route shortened the sequence to seven steps, improved the overall yield to 32 %, and limited chromatography to a single final step. Key changes included a direct Curtius‑to‑urea conversion, avoidance of Boc deprotection, and precipitation‑based isolations.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the need to supply hundreds of grams of compound 2 for advanced studies required that we address the weaknesses of the synthetic route. Most notably…the long overall sequence (12 total steps) and 8.7 % overall yield; the requirement for chromatographic purification after 6 of the 12 reactions.”; “The sequence was shortened from 12 steps to 7 steps, and overall yield was improved from 8.7 % to 32 %.”; “All steps were run on 100+ g scale, and no chromatography was needed except at the final step.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of an Azaindolyl-Pyrimidine Inhibitor of Influenza Virus Replication
Problem_Description: Several intermediates required chromatographic purification, and some reactions (e.g., SNAr displacement) risked forming emulsions or difficult separations.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The SNAr displacement was performed using Hunig’s base and the product isolated by a simple silica‑gel plug; ester hydrolysis and tosyl deprotection were carried out with LiOH, causing the target acid to precipitate and be filtered, eliminating the need for chromatography for those steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “The S_NAr displacement of sulfoxide 11 with amine 15 in the presence of Hunig’s base gave 16 in 73 % yield by simple silica gel plug purification.”; “Both ester hydrolysis and tosyl group removal were successfully carried out using LiOH, and compound 14 was precipitated out after acidification and collected by filtration.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis of an Azaindolyl-Pyrimidine Inhibitor of Influenza Virus Replication
Problem_Description: Direct conversion of mono‑acid 6 to the amine 15 under Curtius conditions with HCl was messy and gave low yields, indicating side‑reactions and decomposition.
Solution_Description: The isocyanate formed from the Curtius rearrangement was trapped with benzyl alcohol to give a protected intermediate, which after hydrogenation cleanly afforded the amine 15 as an HCl salt in quantitative yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Efforts were made to directly convert monoacid 6 to amine 15 under Curtius conditions using HCl; however, the reaction was messy and low‑yielding.”; “So the intermediate isocyanate was trapped with benzyl alcohol, followed by hydrogenation to cleanly give amine 15 as an HCl salt.”

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: The desired polymorph A04 could not be obtained reproducibly; only the less‑stable A02 form was obtained on scale‑up because A03 and A04 have very similar solubilities, making selective crystallization of A04 difficult and leading to low yields of the target form.
Solution_Description: A solvent‑mediated polymorph transformation was introduced, selecting highly polar, non‑hydrogen‑bond‑donating solvents (e.g., MEK, acetone) at elevated temperatures (≈323 K) to shift the equilibrium toward A04, thereby providing a new route to the desired crystal form.
Supporting_Evidence: “...only the A02 form—not the desired polymorph A04—could be reproducibly obtained.”; “...solubility between these two forms does not markedly differ, hampering selective crystallization of A04.”; “A04 was obtained at high temperatures using highly polar non‑hydrogen‑bond‑donating solvents, while A03 was obtained at low temperatures using low‑polarity or hydrogen‑bond‑donating solvents.”

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Induction times for the A02 → A04 transformation were excessively long (up to several hundred hours) with several solvents, making the process impractical for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The use of ketone and ester solvents (MEK, acetone) at the higher temperature of 323 K dramatically shortened the induction period (as low as 1.4 h with MEK), enabling a time‑efficient process.
Supporting_Evidence: “Induction time significantly shortened as temperature increased from 298 to 323 K...value at 323 K was shortest when using MEK, followed by AcOEt, acetone, MIBK, …”; “No solvent‑mediated polymorph transformation of A02 was observed even after 300 h when using IPA, 50% acetone–water, or 50% EtOH–water.”

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Residues on ignition (e.g., NaCl) remained in the crude A02 crystals after crystallization with organic solvents, exceeding the specification limit of 0.2 % and posing a quality‑safety issue.
Solution_Description: Crystallization was switched to a 50 % acetone–water mixture, which successfully removed the inorganic residues and met the acceptance criteria.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude crystal A02 contained residue on ignition…this residue proved difficult to remove via crystallization using organic solvents such as MEK and acetone.”; “Therefore, 50 % acetone–water was ultimately selected as the crystallization solvent for ASP3026.”

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the reaction mixture remained a slurry; inadequate agitation could lead to poor mixing, incomplete transformation, and variable product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A scaled‑down glass reactor matching the pilot‑plant geometry was used to determine the appropriate agitation rate (500 rpm lab, 125 rpm pilot) based on constant power per volume, ensuring sufficient mixing and reliable transformation on scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “The agitation rate was considered crucial, as this process system was always slurry during the polymorph transformation of A02 to A04.”; “Experiments using the scaled‑down glass reactor … were first conducted to verify process conditions for scale‑up manufacturing.”; Table 4 shows agitation rates for lab (500 rpm) and pilot‑plant (125 rpm).

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: When using 50 % acetone–water, the induction period was still relatively long, risking delayed nucleation of A04.
Solution_Description: A small amount of A04 seed crystals (≈25 mg) was added to the slurry to initiate nucleation, effectively shortening the overall transformation time.
Supporting_Evidence: “After 25 mg of A04 had been seeded, the slurry was agitated at a constant temperature of approximately 335 K for predetermined duration.”

Paper Title: Effect of Temperature and Solvent of Solvent-Mediated Polymorph Transformation on ASP3026 Polymorphs and Scale-up
Problem_Description: Accurate quantification of low‑level A03 impurity (≈10 % or less) was needed to ensure product purity, but DSC could not reliably detect A03 below ~1 %.
Solution_Description: Raman spectroscopy calibration curves were employed alongside DSC to detect and quantify A03 contamination down to ~10 % of the total, providing a practical analytical workaround.
Supporting_Evidence: “The heat‑of‑fusion of A03 was not actually detected by DSC analysis. Therefore, the limit of quantification using Raman spectroscopy was considered to be approximately 10 % of A03 contamination.”

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: Using the original PdCl2(dppf) catalyst gave isolated yields of 75–82 % and produced several hard‑to‑purge impurities (des‑bromo 4, vinyl 5, regio‑isomers 6 and 7) up to 1 % total.
Solution_Description: Screening identified a Pd(OAc)₂/DPEPhos catalyst (4 % Pd, 4.8 % ligand) that delivered 80–82 % isolated yield with <0.05 % of each impurity, eliminating the impurity problem.
Supporting_Evidence: • "These conditions can be used to produce enol ether 3 in 75–82 % isolated yield. However, several key impurities are also formed…" (Catalyst Selection section)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: Oxygen ingress oxidised the bidentate phosphine ligand, lowering α‑regioselectivity and increasing formation of des‑bromo, vinyl and regio‑isomer impurities.
Solution_Description: Reactions were rigorously purged with nitrogen and the head‑space O₂ level was controlled (≤3000 ppm, later ≤5000 ppm) and monitored with an O₂ probe to keep oxygen below the level that caused impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Elevated levels of 4, 5, 6, and 7 resulted if oxygen was not rigorously excluded…" (Reaction Parameter Optimization)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: Water present in the starting material (≤0.75 % w/w) promoted formation of the regio‑isomers (6 + 7) by oxidising Pd(II)‑phosphine complexes to Pd(0) and phosphine oxides.
Solution_Description: The process was modified to dry the bromide starting material (target ≤0.2 % water) and water was limited in all reagents, keeping water at ≤0.6 % for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Water has been shown to react with Pd‑II phosphine complexes…" (Reaction Parameter Optimization)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: After the standard aqueous work‑up and filtration the product contained ~500 ppm palladium (visible black specks), exceeding the acceptable limit.
Solution_Description: A 0.45 µm polyamide membrane filter removed solid palladium; an aqueous wash with 5 equiv 1,2‑diaminopropane chelated soluble palladium, reducing residual Pd to <200 ppm on 30–70 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The dull yellow solids contained tiny black specks…" (Palladium Removal)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: Initial crystallizations produced Form A (high‑aspect‑ratio needles/rods) or Form B (slow‑filtering needles) that either fractured or gave very high filtration resistance, threatening throughput.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive polymorph study identified Form C as the low‑energy, fast‑filtering crystal. Seeding with Form C, controlling seed size, and applying a staged cooling protocol (60 → 30 → 20 °C) consistently yielded only Form C.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Form B…filter very slowly. Form C…filter much faster…" (Crystallization)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: Crystallization kinetics were strongly dependent on seed particle size; large block‑like seeds gave >8 h desaturation whereas finely pulverised seeds gave <2 h.
Solution_Description: Seed particle size was reduced (D₄,₃ ≈ 45 µm) and dry‑seeding (instead of slurry) was adopted, shortening desaturation time to ≤3 h while still delivering Form C.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Desaturation time decreased to <2 h when seeds were pulverised…" (Form C Crystallization Kinetics)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part II: Regioselective Heck Coupling with Polymorph Control for Processability
Problem_Description: A stepwise cooling profile occasionally allowed supersaturation of Form A, leading to its nucleation and the need for post‑process heating to convert Form A to Form C.
Solution_Description: A model‑predictive controller used mid‑IR concentration feedback to keep the solution undersaturated with respect to Form A; a simplified two‑ramp cooling (2.5–8 °C/h then 0.8–4 °C/h) emulated the feedback profile for routine manufacturing.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Supersaturation control keeps the process undersaturated in Form A…" (Crystallization Cooling Protocol)

Paper Title: Palbociclib Commercial Manufacturing Process Development. Part I: Control of Regioselectivity in a Grignard-Mediated S
Problem_Description: The original discovery route used a Stille coupling that gave only 38 % isolated yield and required an expensive, toxic vinyl‑tin reagent.
Solution_Description: The Stille step was replaced by a Heck coupling, eliminating the need for the vinyl‑tin reagent and improving overall yield and safety.
