Paper Title: TCDA: Practical Synthesis and Application in the Trifluoromethylation of Arenes and Heteroarenes
Problem_Description: The trifluoromethylated products were difficult to isolate in high yield or purity because they are volatile and have polarity similar to the iodo‑arene starting materials.
Solution_Description: Yield determination was performed by ^19F NMR; for selected examples the authors employed silica‑column chromatography followed by preparative HPLC to obtain isolated material.
Supporting_Evidence: “it was difficult to isolate the trifluoromethylated products … due to their high volatility or similar polarity to the iodoarene”; “All of the yields … were determined by ^19F NMR spectroscopy”; “Purification via silica column … then Pre‑HPLC, afforded the title compound as a clear oil”.

Paper Title: TCDA: Practical Synthesis and Application in the Trifluoromethylation of Arenes and Heteroarenes
Problem_Description: The original laboratory synthesis of TCDA required 6 h at 60 °C and gave only 43 % isolated yield.
Solution_Description: By lowering the reaction temperature to 50 °C, shortening the reaction time to 2 h and conducting the reaction solvent‑free, the isolated yield increased to 58 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “reaction time was reduced from 6 to 2 h with decreased temperature from 60 to 50 °C, and the yield was increased from 43 % to 58 %”.

Paper Title: TCDA: Practical Synthesis and Application in the Trifluoromethylation of Arenes and Heteroarenes
Problem_Description: Scaling the synthesis of TCDA to decagram quantities required a practical, inexpensive, and readily available route.
Solution_Description: A one‑step, solvent‑free mixing of sodium chlorodifluoroacetate and TMSCl was executed on a 50 g scale, followed by a single distillation to give >95 % pure TCDA, using inexpensive commercially available reagents and no observed decomposition on storage.
Supporting_Evidence: “TCDA is prepared in a one‑step process by mixing sodium chlorodifluoroacetate and chlorotrimethylsilane without solvent”; “reaction was executed on 50 g scale, followed by one distillation to afford TCDA with purity above 95%”; “starting materials are commercially available and inexpensive”.

Paper Title: TCDA: Practical Synthesis and Application in the Trifluoromethylation of Arenes and Heteroarenes
Problem_Description: For electron‑rich substrates the earlier protocol (AgF 5 equiv, TMEDA) gave only moderate yields.
Solution_Description: The authors reduced AgF to 4 equiv, raised the temperature to 100 °C and extended the reaction time (up to 6 h), which delivered higher conversions for electron‑rich aryl iodides.
Supporting_Evidence: “AgF was reduced to 4 equiv to obtain the higher yield at 100 °C than 90 °C”; “longer reaction time gave better yields (entries 7, 8, 9)”.

Paper Title: Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase-Catalyzed Synthesis of (1
Problem_Description: The recombinant pig liver esterase (rPLE) isoenzymes showed large differences in activity, stability, and enantioselectivity. ECS‑PLE03 lost activity rapidly (half‑life ≈1.7 h) while ECS‑PLE06 remained stable (half‑life ≈91 h). At pH 9 the substrate autohydrolyses, reducing ee. At substrate concentrations >200 mM the material becomes insoluble, forming an emulsion, and at high pH the reaction rate drops. The first enantioselective crystallization gave only 33 % practical yield, far below the theoretical maximum (≈66 %).
Solution_Description: The authors switched from natural PLE to recombinant isoenzymes (NEW ROUTE) and screened six commercial rPLEs, selecting ECS‑PLE06 because of its high specific activity and long‑term stability (CATALYST OPTIMIZATION). Reaction temperature was raised to 50 °C to accelerate conversion without loss of ee (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION). The pH was fixed at 7.5 to avoid base‑catalyzed substrate autohydrolysis (PH CONTROL). Organic cosolvents were eliminated; reactions were run in pure 100 mM phosphate buffer (SOLVENT CHANGE). Substrate loading was limited to 230 mM (≈100–200 mM workable range) to keep the substrate soluble (CONCENTRATION TUNING). Finally, the low‑yield crystallization step was improved by performing multiple enantioselective crystallizations and a final recrystallization to isolate the enantiopure product (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE).
Supporting_Evidence: ["ECS‑PLE03 lost activity significantly faster with a remaining activity of 19 % after only 4 h, which converts to a very low half‑life stability of only 1.7 h (Fig 3).", "ECS‑PLE06 possesses at 50 °C a consistent stable enzyme activity over 23 h and a remaining activity of 24 % after 168 h, which translates to a half‑life stability of 91 h.", "At pH 9 a much lower ee of 68 % was observed, caused by autohydrolysis of the substrate at elevated pH conditions.", "The substrate was not soluble at higher concentrations, and thus an emulsion was formed (Table 1 footnote a).", "The first crystallization entry 5 and 6 of the scale‑up reactions were used. … yielded pure (1 S,4 R)‑4‑hydroxy‑2‑cyclopentenyl acetate (ee ≥ 99.5 %) with a moderate yield of 33 % (entry 1). Since an enantiomeric excess of 71 % ee remained in the mother liquor, this process was terminated too soon, and the theoretical maximum yield of 66 % was not achieved.", "The reaction temperature was set to 50 °C … >80 % conversion was achieved at 50 °C … a relative high enantiomeric excess of 83 % remains nearly constant at all reaction temperatures.", "The pH level was set to pH 7.5 for all further experiments, which is relatively similar to an early report of Brüsehaber et al.", "Organic cosolvents were not applicable for the scale‑up of the investigated ECS‑PLE06 catalyzed process.", "Substrate concentrations between 100–200 mM were successfully converted … while even higher concentrations of 500 mM significantly inhibited ECS‑PLE06 (entry 7).", "Crude product 2a was dissolved in n‑heptane, conditioned to 50 °C, and continuously cooled … yielded (1 S,4 R)‑4‑hydroxy‑2‑cyclopentenyl acetate with excellent enantiomeric excess (>99 % ee)."]

Paper Title: Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase-Catalyzed Synthesis of (1
Problem_Description: At high substrate loadings (500 mM) the reaction mixture formed an emulsion, indicating poor mixing and phase separation that hindered conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The substrate concentration was limited to ≤230 mM for scale‑up to avoid emulsion formation, thereby improving mixture homogeneity. No specific mixing hardware was described, but the limitation of concentration implicitly controls the mass‑transfer challenge.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The substrate was not soluble at higher concentrations, and thus an emulsion was formed (Table 1 footnote a).", "Substrate concentrations between 100–200 mM were successfully converted … while even higher concentrations of 500 mM significantly inhibited ECS‑PLE06 (entry 7)."]

Paper Title: Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase-Catalyzed Synthesis of (1
Problem_Description: The biocatalytic reaction produces acidic by‑products that lower pH, requiring continuous pH monitoring and addition of base to maintain optimal conditions, which could pose safety concerns on large scale.
Solution_Description: An external base (0.5 M NaOH or KOH) was added via an autoburet to keep the reaction at pH 7.5 throughout the scale‑up, ensuring enzyme stability and preventing uncontrolled acid build‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The solution was kept constant at pH 7.5 by addition of 0.5 M sodium hydroxide solution via an autoburet.", "The solution was kept constant at pH 7.5 by addition of 0.5 M potassium hydroxide solution via an autoburet."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: During the early enzyme screening several enzyme families (acylase and esterase) gave no conversion and the best protease and lipase hits only reached ∼40‑50 % conversion, resulting in low isolated yields of the desired chiral acid.
Solution_Description: The team focused on protease B and protease C from *Bacillus subtilis* (which showed the highest ee and conversion) and discarded the inactive families; later the enzyme loading was increased to 10‑15 % w/w to push conversion higher.
Supporting_Evidence: ["No conversion was observed with the acylase and esterase families.","The best results were obtained with lipase and protease families, especially alkaline protease B and protease C from Bacillus subtilis with 97–98% ee.","Conversion close to 50%, a high ee for the desired product 6 and also a higher E value.","The back‑up from the lead enzyme alkaline B n°2 and the protease C from Bacillus subtilis (type 1) gave poor results in the conditions tested."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The enzymatic resolution required a cosolvent; some solvents (cyclohexane, toluene) gave poor conversion or no reaction, indicating solubility/mixability limitations for the substrate and enzyme.
Solution_Description: Alternative cosolvents (dimethyl‑sulfoxide, acetone) and the option of running the resolution without any cosolvent were evaluated, giving comparable or improved conversions and simplifying downstream work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The influence of alternative cosolvents and the absence of a cosolvent were also evaluated on the four identified hits.","Dimethyl sulfoxide and acetone emerged as alternative cosolvents to methyl tert‑butyl ether used in the screening.","The absence of a cosolvent also led to similar good results."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The two lead enzymes (protease alkaline B and protease C type 2) were not immediately available at the 2 kg scale, creating a supply bottleneck and a cost concern.
Solution_Description: Alternative enzyme batches (alkaline B n°2, protease C type 1 and type 2) from the same supplier stocks were qualified and used for the scale‑up, allowing the project to continue without delay.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the most promising enzymes…could unfortunately not be provided immediately by the supplier at 2 kg scale.","alternative enzymes from the same strains available from the supplier’s stock were therefore quickly evaluated.","The back‑up protease C from Bacillus subtilis (type 2) gave acceptable results whereas poorer than the best results obtained during the screening phases."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: When the pH was controlled with a strong base, an overshoot caused significant chemical hydrolysis of the ester substrate (≈12 % loss), posing a safety and product‑quality risk.
Solution_Description: A pH‑stat system using a 0.1 M phosphate buffer and a controlled 2 M NaOH feed was implemented in a 10 L jacketed vessel, allowing tight pH regulation and preventing hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Controlling the pH of the reaction mixture during the resolution by adding a NaOH solution might lead to the ester hydrolysis as a side‑reaction in case of pH overshoot.","A stress test…showed a significant amount of chemical hydrolysis was observed (ca. 12%).","The phosphate buffer solution…was replaced by water with a pH‑stat Metrohm Titrando 902 using a NaOH solution in order to control the pH and to limit the overall dilution."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: During work‑up, extraction of the unreacted (S)‑methyl ester caused loss of ~12 % of the desired succinic‑acid product, reducing overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The pH of the reaction mixture was adjusted to 9 before the cyclohexane extraction, keeping the product ionized in the aqueous phase; later the pH was shifted to 1 for selective extraction of the acid, improving recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the unreacted (S)‑methyl ester derivative 8 was extracted with cyclohexane. The analysis of the discarded organic layer showed that ca. 12 % of the succinic acid derivative 6 was also eliminated.","To circumvent that issue, the pH was adjusted at 9 before the extraction. In these conditions, the product 6 was totally ionized into the succinate form and remained in the aqueous phase without any racemization identified.","The pH is then adjusted to pH 1…to extract the product 6 with isopropyl acetate."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: At pH 1 during work‑up, the enzyme denatured and formed a protein‑rich slurry that caused foaming and difficult filtration.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The slurry was pre‑filtered with celite (diatomaceous earth) which adsorbed the protein material and allowed smooth filtration of the product‑containing phase.
Supporting_Evidence: ["During both liquid–liquid separations at pH 9 and pH 1, some foaming was observed probably due to protein material but also due to amphiphilic properties of the product 6.","Moreover, at pH 1, the precipitation of the denatured enzyme was observed.","The most appropriate solution found was to prefilter the biphasic mixture prior to separation with addition of diatomaceous earth (celite) which enhances the filtration by adsorbing the protein material."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The biocatalytic resolution required 16‑20 h to reach ∼43 % conversion, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Increasing the enzyme loading to 10‑15 % w/w and raising the reaction pH to 8.5 accelerated the rate, allowing the same conversion in ∼17 h and giving a modest yield increase.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The resolution was also tested with 15% w/w of enzyme loading. As expected, the initial rate was higher compared to 10% w/w.","When the resolution was conducted at pH 8.5, the yield (42%) and enantiomeric excess (97%) were reproducible in a shorter time without any chemical hydrolysis observed. The usual conversion (ca. 43%) was obtained after ca. 17 h at pH 8.5 compared to ca. 20 h at pH 8.0."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The enzymatic resolution at 10 L scale gave a modest isolated yield (≈42 %) mainly because of multiple extraction, pH adjustments and filtration steps.
Solution_Description: Running the resolution without any cosolvent eliminated the need for solvent removal and simplified the work‑up, while the pH‑stat system allowed telescoping directly to the next step, improving overall material throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The opportunity to conduct the resolution without any cosolvent was prioritized to simplify the workup.","It was worthwhile to note that the absence of a cosolvent gave similar good results than the resolution using a cosolvent. This option without a cosolvent could be attractive to simplify the workup of the reaction."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The alternative salt‑resolution route gave only 26 % overall isolated yield of the chiral salt, far lower than the enzymatic route.
Solution_Description: The project abandoned the salt‑resolution approach in favour of the biocatalytic resolution, which provided 42 % yield and higher ee, making it the preferred stereocontrolling strategy.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The overall resolution and recrystallization sequence gave the salt 9 in 26% yield and 95.2% de.","After preliminary parallel development, the enzymatic resolution appeared to us significantly more attractive than the salt resolution."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: During the reduction‑cyclisation of the acid to the lactone, methanol addition at temperatures above –20 °C led to formation of a methyl‑ester impurity (2‑4 %).
Solution_Description: The temperature was kept below –20 °C, a slight excess of triethylamine (1.2 eq) was used to avoid acidic methanol, powdered NaBH₄ was employed for better control, and the methanol feed rate was carefully regulated to suppress impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A side‑reaction occurred above –20 °C with the addition of methanol onto the activated chloroformate derivative to generate the methyl ester impurity 12—typically 2–4%.","From a safety perspective, the use of a slight excess of triethylamine (1.2 eq vs 1.1 eq) avoided the presence of acidic methanol in contact with sodium borohydride.","Furthermore, the use of powdered sodium borohydride versus a granular form ensured that the reduction started at the beginning of the methanol addition without any accumulation of reducing agent.","The evolution of hydrogen gas during the reduction was accompanied by foaming, both controlled with the rate of addition of methanol."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: A supply shortage of HBr gas prevented the planned one‑pot ring‑opening/esterification sequence.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a two‑step protocol: HBr in acetic acid for ring opening to the brominated acid, followed by a separate esterification, preserving the overall synthetic plan.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Due to a supply shortage of HBr gas lecture bottle at the time of the study, the transformation was performed in two steps: a ring opening with HBr in acetic acid to give (R)-γ‑bromo‑3‑propylbutyric acid 13 followed by a standard esterification."]

Paper Title: A Biocatalytic Route to the Novel Antiepileptic Drug Brivaracetam
Problem_Description: The final condensation of the bromo‑ester with (S)‑2‑aminobutanamide gave only 32 % overall step yield of the API, with difficult removal of salts and residual lactone impurity.
Solution_Description: The authors employed tetrabutylammonium iodide as a phase‑transfer catalyst and refluxing isopropyl acetate to drive the reaction; however, they note that further optimisation of this step is required (listed under missing information).
Supporting_Evidence: ["The condensation of 14 with (S)-2‑aminobutanamide was catalyzed with tetrabutylammonium iodide in refluxing isopropyl acetate.","The condensation was the less optimal step from the demonstration with a 32% overall step yield."]

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: The long‑lived commercial silica‑alumina catalyst gave only ~40 % DABCO mole‑selectivity (≈39.8 % yield) despite 100 % HEP conversion, resulting in low overall productivity (STY≈0.79 mol DABCO L⁻¹ h⁻¹).
Solution_Description: Discovery and deployment of a strontium hydrogen phosphate (SrHPO₄) solid‑acid catalyst that raised DABCO selectivity to 83–94 % and doubled the STY (≈1.6–1.8 mol L⁻¹ h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: “The SrHPO₄ catalyst exhibited very significantly improved performance in terms of HEP conversion and DABCO yield and selectivity… The STY for the SrHPO₄ catalyst ranges from 1.64 to 1.83… about a 2‑fold increase in productivity” (Table 2; discussion).

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: The silica‑alumina process generated large amounts of piperazine, dimers, trimers and high‑molecular‑weight “tars”, increasing waste‑disposal costs and complicating product recovery.
Solution_Description: The SrHPO₄ catalyst dramatically reduced non‑selective by‑products (piperazine fell from ~13–18 wt % to ≤7 wt % in pilot runs) and lowered the burden on downstream separation, cutting feed‑stock and disposal expenses.
Supporting_Evidence: “Piperazine had some marketable coproduct value… Other byproducts and ‘tars’ presented a significant waste disposal burden… The DABCO mole selectivity of the commercial silica–alumina… was only around 40 %… The SrHPO₄ catalyst… greatly reduced the formation of piperazine and high‑molecular‑weight materials” (Results & Discussion).

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: Frequent catalyst deactivation limited the usable lifetime of the silica‑alumina bed, causing unplanned shutdowns and increasing catalyst replacement cost.
Solution_Description: The SrHPO₄ catalyst demonstrated a long operational life (>78 days continuous with unchanged conversion) and retained performance after scale‑up, eliminating frequent catalyst swaps.
Supporting_Evidence: “Over the course of 78 days of continuous operation, no loss in conversion was observed… The physical hardness of the catalyst also increased slightly and surface area was but little changed” (Life Test discussion).

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: Scaling the precipitation of SrHPO₄ and forming 0.125‑in extrudates was difficult; the slurry required precise order‑of‑addition, stirring, washing, and drying to produce hard, durable pellets suitable for a fixed‑bed reactor.
Solution_Description: The team optimized the precipitation sequence (stirring Sr²⁺ and HPO₄²⁻ solutions together with good mixing), washing, and drying steps, and introduced an inert additive to enable formation of mechanically strong extrudates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The questions around what is the most effective Sr²⁺ and HPO₄⁻¹ precursors … the order and rates of combination, how to efficiently wash … were all addressed … addition of the phosphate component to the strontium component with good stirring worked well. Forming the washed and dried SrHPO₄ into 0.125″ diameter extrudates presented some serious challenges which were finally overcome largely by selection of an effective and catalytically inert additive” (Scale‑up discussion).

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: Coated (core‑shell) SrHPO₄ catalysts (25 % active shell on Al₂O₃ core) performed markedly worse in conversion and selectivity than the bulk catalyst.
Solution_Description: The process was altered to use the bulk (uncoated) SrHPO₄ granules directly, eliminating the inert coating step and restoring high activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Coated versions of the catalysts are generally less effective and selective than the bulk forms of the same catalyst… This observation remains a mystery; possibly due to a low exotherm from the cyclization since coated catalysts are most effective where large exotherms are seen.” (Table 4 discussion).

Paper Title: Synthesis of 1,4-Diazabicyclo [2,2,2] Octane with Alkaline Earth Phosphate Catalysts
Problem_Description: Initial high‑throughput screening of many solid acids showed no clear correlation between measured surface area, acidity, and catalytic performance, leading to inconsistent selection of promising candidates.
Solution_Description: The research focus was narrowed to materials possessing a single type of Bronsted acidity (hydrogen phosphates, arsenates, sulfates), which quickly yielded active catalysts and reduced variability in screening outcomes.
Supporting_Evidence: “The only feature that all of the catalysts had in common was that they had a wide range of surface areas … The probable correlation between the acidity required for DABCO selectivity and that known to be exhibited by common solid phosphates… This realization led … focus on materials that have only one type of acidity… the focus would be on surfaces with single types of Bronsted acidity.” (Results & Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Robust Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of a Vinyl Bromide from a Ketone Using a (PhO)
Problem_Description: During the first‑generation batch run the addition of molecular bromine to a solution of triphenyl phosphite in dichloromethane was highly exothermic.  To keep the temperature below –60 °C the addition had to be spread over ~8 h, followed by an additional 8–9 h warm‑up period.  The long addition and hold‑up caused temperature drift, safety‑concern for uncontrolled heat release and gave only 55 % isolated yield of the vinyl bromide.
Solution_Description: A semi‑continuous flow platform was introduced in which bromine and triphenyl phosphite were mixed in a precooled Hastelloy coil (−50 °C to −60 °C, 1.35 min residence).  The active brominating species was generated in situ and then transferred to a batch reactor containing substrate and base.  This eliminated the large exotherm, reduced the addition time to minutes and allowed precise temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Addition of molecular bromine … was exothermic, such that the addition rate needed to be controlled carefully to maintain the reaction temperature below −60 °C; one plant‑scale batch (17 kg input) required an 8 h addition sequence … and resulted in a significantly lower yield (55 %)” (exothermic, long addition, low yield).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Robust Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of a Vinyl Bromide from a Ketone Using a (PhO)
Problem_Description: The active brominating reagent 2a (bromotriphenoxyphosphonium bromide) slowly converts to the inactive covalent form 2b when the temperature rises above –50 °C.  When 2a was held at –35 °C for 16 h before adding substrate, only ~45 % product was obtained, versus ~75 % when kept at –60 °C, indicating temperature‑dependent loss of activity.
Solution_Description: The active reagent was generated in flow and immediately mixed with the ketone substrate (and base) inside the same coil, thus telescoping reagent formation and consumption.  This “instantaneous” reaction prevented the degradation of 2a and gave ~85 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The ionic species 2a is reported to convert to the inactive covalent form … over time even at low temperatures … The ratio … is temperature‑dependent (4:1 at −60 °C, 1:3 at −20 °C).” (decomposition, variability).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Robust Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of a Vinyl Bromide from a Ketone Using a (PhO)
Problem_Description: In the original batch protocol the elimination step required a 24 h warm‑up to ambient temperature to achieve complete conversion to the vinyl bromide, limiting throughput and giving only 55–74 % overall yield.
Solution_Description: The addition temperature was raised to –20 °C to –5 °C and the overall reaction temperature to 20 °C.  With bromine added at the warmer range the reaction completed within 1 h, delivering 90 % isolated yield and reducing the total batch cycle to ~1 day.
Supporting_Evidence: • “After further parameter screening, we were able to increase the reaction temperature … molecular bromine was charged at –20 to –5 °C … This reaction proceeded to completion within 1 h at 20 °C and generated vinyl bromide … in 90 % yield.” (temperature optimum, short reaction, high yield).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Robust Process for the Large-Scale Preparation of a Vinyl Bromide from a Ketone Using a (PhO)
Problem_Description: The first‑generation batch required cryogenic operation (–75 °C to –50 °C) and a dedicated low‑temperature reactor, increasing equipment cost, operational complexity, and safety risk associated with handling large quantities of bromine at very low temperatures.
Solution_Description: By modifying the addition sequence (charging bromine to a pre‑cooled mixture of substrate, phosphite and base) the process could be run without any reactor below –20 °C, eliminating the need for cryogenic hardware and simplifying the operation while still delivering >90 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The modified addition sequence … gave a further improvement in yield and quality … providing 5 in ~90 % yield… The operating temperature moved from –75 °C to –20 °C, removing the requirement for cryogenic conditions.” (cost and safety benefit).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The original Dieckmann‑type condensation of 4 to 5 using NaH at –40 °C gave a mixture of the desired regioisomer 5 and the undesired regioisomer 7. The by‑product 7 could only be removed by silica‑gel chromatography or high‑vacuum distillation, which is impractical on multi‑kilogram scale and caused low overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A robust, scalable procedure was developed using TiCl₃(OiPr) as a Lewis‑acid promoter together with triethylamine. This combination gave 5 as a single regioisomer in 96 % isolated yield, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “...under strongly basic conditions (sodium hydride, DME) at low temperature (‑40 °C) resulting in the desired product along with varying amounts of the undesired regioisomer 7… the undesired regioisomer ( 7) could only be removed by silica gel chromatography or high vacuum distillation… making this approach undesirable for multi‑kilo scale synthesis.”; “…utilized TiCl₃(OiPr) and triethylamine to give 5 as a single regioisomer from 4 in 96 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The early route to pyrimidine‑2,4‑diol 9 required two equivalents of the relatively expensive ethyl‑isothiourea hydrobromide 13, gave only 60–70 % yield, caused decomposition of intermediate 5 under basic conditions, and released foul‑smelling ethanethiol during hydrolysis.
Solution_Description: A cost‑effective process was designed that replaces ethyl‑isothiourea with inexpensive urea. The new sequence eliminates the ethanethiol odor, avoids decomposition of 5, and provides the solid intermediate 6 in 95 % yield, improving overall material cost and safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “One key issue with this approach was the synthesis and hydrolysis of 8; preparation of this intermediate required two equivalents of the relatively expensive ethylisothiourea hydrobromide 13… and the yield was a modest 60–70 %… there was significant decomposition of 5 under the basic reaction conditions… the hydrolysis of 8… resulted in the release of ethanethiol that also caused a strong unpleasant stench.”; “To overcome the issues stated above, a new streamlined and cost‑effective process… in which inexpensive urea was used in place of the much more costly ethyl‑isothiourea hydrobromide 13… eliminated the strong stench… overall cost … significantly reduced… provided a stable, easy‑to‑purify, solid intermediate 6.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The chlorination of 9 to give 10 originally employed 10 equivalents of POCl₃ at 85 °C, leading to uncontrolled exotherms, accumulation of unreacted POCl₃, and a large amount of hazardous reagent to quench.
Solution_Description: The amount of POCl₃ was reduced to 2 equivalents, and the reaction temperature was increased to 105–110 °C. This controlled the exotherm, lowered the quantity of hazardous POCl₃, and improved throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “…reduction of the amount of POCl₃ from 10 to 2.0 equiv. and by increasing the reaction temperature from 85 to 105–110 °C to afford 10 in 88 % yield… These changes facilitated the workup, increased the throughput and improved the inherent safety of the process both by having less reagent to quench and giving more control over a notable exotherm present during the reaction.”; “At 85 °C unreacted POCl₃ accumulated… At a higher temperature POCl₃ reacted as it was being added and the reaction could be carried under a controlled fashion.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The SNAr displacement of 10 with 4‑aminotetrahydropyran produced a mixture of regioisomers (≈15 % C2‑substituted product). Conventional chromatographic separation would be cumbersome on scale.
Solution_Description: The undesired C2‑isomer was found to be considerably more soluble than the desired C4‑product. Simple filtration removed the impurity, allowing isolation of 11 as a single regioisomer in ~82–85 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The S_NAr displacement… was not completely regioselective and approximately 15 % of the product resulting from displacement of the chlorine at C2 was observed… the undesired regioisomer was significantly more soluble than 11 and was completely removed from the product during the isolation by filtration.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The original asymmetric oxidation of sulfides to sulfoxide 12 used hazardous solvents (chloroform or carbon tetrachloride), low substrate concentration, and required high catalyst loading, leading to costly, long, and unsafe operation.
Solution_Description: The protocol was revised to use dichloromethane as solvent, increase reaction concentration, reduce catalyst loading, and streamline isolation by a solvent switch to isopropanol followed by filtration. The process now delivers 12 in 80–90 % yield with >99 % ee on large scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Key improvements over earlier protocols include an increase in concentration/throughput, a reduction of the catalyst loading, replacement of the solvent from chloroform or carbon tetrachloride to dichloromethane, and streamlining of the isolation procedure… the product is isolated as a crystalline solid by filtration following a solvent switch from dichloromethane to isopropanol… provided 12 in good yield (80–90 %) and excellent enantioselectivity (>99 %).”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: Achieving a reproducible crystal form of API 1 was difficult; polymorph control is critical for API quality and stability.
Solution_Description: Extensive solvent screening identified an acetic‑acid/water system that consistently gave the desired stable polymorph. The crystallization was successfully scaled to multi‑kilogram quantities with 80–85 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Extensive solvent screening studies were carried out for 1 until a solvent system consisting of acetic acid and water was found to reproducibly and exclusively provide a suitable and stable polymorph… implemented on multi‑kilogram scale to provide the desired polymorph of 1 in 80–85 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The original two‑step synthesis of the 4‑(4‑chlorophenoxy)‑piperidine moiety 21 required a protected piperidin‑4‑ol intermediate, adding steps and cost.
Solution_Description: A streamlined, atom‑economic O‑selective SNAr using unprotected piperidin‑4‑ol was developed, delivering 21 in 83–86 % yield, reducing steps, material cost, and improving overall efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: “Later, a more streamlined atom‑economic and inexpensive O‑selective SNAr procedure was developed… with unprotected piperidin‑4‑ol (22) that gave 21 in 83–86 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Process for the Synthesis of PDE4 Inhibitors
Problem_Description: The TiCl₄‑mediated regioselective formation of 5 generated numerous impurities from chlorination/dehydrohalogenation and produced large amounts of solid waste that were difficult to remove during work‑up.
Solution_Description: Alternative Lewis acids (TiCl₃(OiPr), TiCl₂(OiPr)₂, etc.) and amine bases were screened, leading to a practical TiCl₃(OiPr)/Et₃N protocol that avoided the formation of solid by‑products and gave clean product.
Supporting_Evidence: “In addition, the workup procedure resulted in the formation of vast quantities of solids that had to be laboriously removed… Hence, given the limitations of the TiCl₄ procedure, alternative Lewis acids… were evaluated resulting in a robust and practical procedure that utilized TiCl₃(OiPr) and triethylamine to give 5 as a single regioisomer….”

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required evaporation of the reaction mixture to dryness to isolate intermediate 4, used the carcinogenic solvent 1,4‑dioxane and the mutagenic reagent 2‑aminophenol, and demanded a high‑temperature (240‑250 °C) cyclization followed by chromatographic purification of intermediate 7.
Solution_Description: The process was revamped by (i) telescoping the crude solution of 4 straight into the next step, eliminating the evaporation step; (ii) swapping 1,4‑dioxane for a THF/MeOH mixture and replacing acetyl chloride with acetic anhydride while substituting the expensive EDC·HCl with inexpensive SOCl₂; (iii) lowering the cyclization temperature to 130 °C under azeotropic dehydration with methanesulfonic acid and avoiding chromatography by crystallising the product directly as its fumarate, followed by recrystallisation for purity control.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: In the direct C–H/C–Br coupling of benzoxazole with heteroaryl bromide 8, the addition of CuI gave a low 29 % isolated yield, and the use of costly reagents such as EDC·HCl added to the expense.
Solution_Description: Screening of copper salts showed that Cu(OTf)₂ (or other Cu(II) salts) dramatically improved the yield to 87 % and was chosen as the additive; the Pd loading was reduced to 5 mol % while maintaining activity, thereby lowering catalyst cost.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: Many ligands examined for the Pd‑Cu‑catalyzed coupling gave poor conversions; the reaction did not proceed without a ligand.
Solution_Description: Triphenylphosphine (PPh₃) was identified as the optimal ligand, delivering complete conversion (<1 % residual bromide) and consistent performance across scales.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: The original sequence to compound 11 required isolation of intermediate 10 to remove triethylamine hydrochloride, adding an extra filtration and drying step.
Solution_Description: The base was switched from triethylamine to potassium carbonate, which can be filtered away, allowing the crude solution of 10 to be telescoped directly into the subsequent step without isolation.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: Use of the expensive and less readily available reagent EDC·HCl in the first‑generation route raised cost and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: EDC·HCl was replaced with inexpensive thionyl chloride (SOCl₂), reducing material cost and simplifying waste disposal.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: The high‑temperature (240‑250 °C) cyclization to form 7 required chromatographic purification, which is cumbersome on scale and reduces overall yield.
Solution_Description: Cyclization was performed at 130 °C in the presence of methanesulfonic acid under azeotropic dehydration, and instead of chromatography, the product was directly crystallised as the fumarate of 7, giving a high‑purity API after recrystallisation.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: The original route involved multiple solvent exchanges and evaporations, leading to long batch times and handling of viscous mixtures.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Concentrations were adjusted to allow direct hand‑offs between steps (telescoping) and solvent systems (THF/MeOH, toluene) were chosen to provide good miscibility, reducing batch time and simplifying agitation.

Paper Title: Direct Synthesis of a PDE4 Inhibitor by Using Pd–Cu-Catalyzed C–H/C–Br Coupling of Benzoxazole with a Heteroaryl Bromide
Problem_Description: Trace palladium and copper residues in the final product needed to be reduced to meet pharmaceutical specifications.
Solution_Description: Activated carbon and ISOLUTE Si‑Thiol were employed as metal scavengers to lower Pd and Cu levels to <1 ppm.

Paper Title: A Facile Route of Synthesis for Making Flibanserin
Problem_Description: The original flibanserin synthesis required a 200 °C thermal rearrangement, needed special equipment, produced impurity 6, generated a genotoxic O‑substituted impurity 7, gave an overall isolated yield of only 16 % over five steps, suffered from poor solubility of potassium carbonate in polar media, used DMF (an EHS concern), produced an elimination impurity when NMP was used, and relied on the expensive tetramethyl orthocarbonate.
Solution_Description: The team replaced ethyl benzoylacetate with cheaper ethyl acetoacetate, introduced a benzimidazole cyclization using inexpensive tetraethyl orthocarbonate (masked O‑atom) to avoid impurity 7, switched the alkylating reagent to 1‑bromo‑2‑chloroethane, optimized its amount to 2.5 equiv, selected K2CO3/acetone as the scale‑up base/solvent system, switched the nucleophilic substitution solvent to water (with K2CO3/NaI), removed bis‑substituted impurities by recrystallization from n‑heptane, and overall adopted a new five‑step route that gave ~45 % overall yield with >99.9 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem-1: "The original preparation of flibanserin ... used benzene‑1,2‑diamine (2) and ethyl benzoylacetate to prepare 3 at 200 °C."; "The harsh conditions involved in the thermal rearrangement required special equipment and tedious operations..."

Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: The original 1,3‑dipolar cycloaddition between ethyl trifluorobutyno‑2‑ate and the nitrile‑oxide dipole gave the undesired regio‑isomer 7 as the major product (85 : 15), leading to low isolated yield of the desired isoxazole (8) and requiring chromatographic separation.
Solution_Description: Regiochemistry was inverted by replacing the alkyne dipolarophile with 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑yn‑1‑ol, which delivered a 9 : 1 ratio of the desired isomer 8 and a typical isolated yield of 60–65 % after chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】"Unfortunately, this reaction favored the undesired regioisomer 7 in a ratio of 85:15"; "the 9:1 ratio ... required chromatographic separation to isolate pure isomer 8, which would be undesirable on scale." 【Solution】"replacing ethyl trifluorobut‑2‑ynate with 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑yn‑1‑ol ... resulted in a mixture ... ratio 9:1 ... typical yield of 60–65 % after chromatographic separation."

Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: The regio‑selective route relied on the non‑commercial 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑yn‑1‑ol, which is a low‑boiling liquid requiring distillation; batch‑to‑batch variations in yield and purity were observed.
Solution_Description: A commercially available (E)‑ethyl 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑enoate was used as the starting material; a new cycloaddition/oxidation sequence employing brominated enoate 14 gave the desired isoxazole ester without the need for the unavailable alkyne.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】"this approach relies on synthesizing non‑commercially available 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑yn‑1‑ol"; "low boiling point crude product required a distillation for purification, which could result in variations in both yield and purity from batch to batch." 【Solution】"Since (E)‑ethyl 4,4,4‑trifluorobut‑2‑enoate is commercially available at a low cost, we planned to synthesize the corresponding dihydroisoxazole ... the dihydroisoxazoles were readily prepared in high yield."

Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: During the optimized [3 + 2] cycloaddition, a dimerization side‑product (15) formed, limiting the overall isolated yield of the desired ester 6 to ≈60 % in early experiments.
Solution_Description: The rate of nitrile‑oxide generation was slowed by using KHCO₃ (a sparingly soluble base) in ethyl acetate, keeping enoate 14 in large excess; this suppressed dimer formation and raised isolated yields to 72–82 % with high regio‑selectivity (20 : 1).
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】"the yield was still low as a result of the formation of dimerization byproduct (15) during the reaction." 【Solution】"KHCO₃ and ethyl acetate provided an optimal combination for this [3+2]-cycloaddition, which was further scaled up with isolated yields in the range of 72–82 % and with high regioisomer selectivity (6:7 = 20:1)."

Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: After the cycloaddition, the mixture contained ~4 % of the undesired regio‑isomer 7 and residual dimer 15; these non‑polar impurities were difficult to remove by flash chromatography.
Solution_Description: A selective, mild hydrolysis was developed that converted the desired ester 6 to the acid while leaving 7 and the dimer untouched, allowing their removal by simple aqueous work‑up and eliminating the need for column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】"the presence of ∼4 % of the undesired regioisomer 7 and residual dimer 15 were difficult to separate by flash chromatography due to the nonpolar nature of these compounds." 【Solution】"we developed a robust, selective hydrolysis to remove all impurities, eliminating the need for column chromatography."

Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: The original deprotection of the tert‑butyl group with neat TFA followed by neutralisation using 1 N NaOH produced very fine particles that filtered slowly and required two MeOH trituration steps to achieve the desired purity.
Solution_Description: Neutralisation was switched to 1 N aqueous NH₄OH, generating larger particles for rapid filtration; a new recrystallisation (NMP/EtOH) gave high‑purity product with smooth filtration and no need for multiple slurrying steps.
Supporting_Evidence: 【Problem】"producing very fine particles that resulted in very slow filtration that could trap impurities. Paper Title: An Efficient Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-520, a Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: The penultimate oxadiazole formation used cyanuric fluoride (highly corrosive) and Hunig’s base, leading to glassware erosion risk and a long reaction time.
Solution_Description: Cyanuric fluoride was replaced by thionyl chloride to give the acyl chloride 18 in quantitative yield; a DMAP‑catalysed oxadiazole cyclisation was developed that furnished the product 17 by direct crystallisation (>99 % purity, 72–84 % yield) in a much shorter time.

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Initial screening of a variety of N‑oxide heterocycles gave excellent regioselectivity but very low isolated yields for many substrates (e.g., pyridine‑N‑oxide, pyrazine‑N‑oxide, pyridazine‑N‑oxide, pyrimidine‑N‑oxide).
Solution_Description: The researchers shifted focus to fused‑ring N‑oxides (quinoline‑N‑oxide, quinoxaline‑N‑oxide) which provided significantly higher yields (60‑71 %). This substrate change, combined with subsequent statistical optimisation, constituted a new reaction route that overcame the low‑yield limitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “while pyridine N‑oxide … could be arylated with outstanding regioselectivity but disappointing yield (Table 1, entries 1 and 2)… only traces … were detected … pyridazine N‑oxide and pyrimidine N‑oxide … (Table 1, entries 3 and 4).”; “fused‑ring systems displayed significantly more promise… quinoline N‑oxide … 60 % yield, quinoxaline N‑oxide … 71 % yield (Table 1, entries 5 and 6).”

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Screening of common organic solvents showed that most gave negligible conversion (0‑7 % HPLC yield), indicating poor solubility/miscibility of the reactants in those media.
Solution_Description: Systematic solvent screening followed by OPLS modelling identified acetonitrile as the optimal solvent, delivering a 60 % isolated yield. The selection was based on solvent polarity descriptors that correlate with higher conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction did not proceed well in heptane, toluene, 1,4‑dioxane, tetrahydrofuran, ethyl acetate, DMSO, ethanol, and water as only low yields were observed… DMF, acetone, and dichloromethane gave 16, 31, 42 % yield… acetonitrile gave the product in 60 % isolated yield (Table 2, entry 12).”; “The model revealed that solvents with high dipole moment, dielectric constant … resulted in high yield whereas increased lipophilicity was detrimental.”

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: The original protocol required 17 h reaction times and used an excess of ascorbic acid (promoter), adding cost and time without clear benefit.
Solution_Description: Design‑of‑experiments (DoE) showed temperature to be the dominant factor; running the reaction at 40 °C with minimal ascorbic acid (1 mol %) gave comparable yields, reducing promoter loading and reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The half‑normal plot revealed that the temperature (D) had the greatest influence as reactions performed at elevated temperatures gave the best results.”; “the loading of ascorbic acid (A) had no impact… minimum quantities … could be used to render this metal‑free process even more sustainable.”

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Previous reports required ascorbic acid as a promoter; its use added material cost and raised safety concerns regarding additional reagent handling.
Solution_Description: Control experiments demonstrated that the arylation proceeds with identical yields in the absence of ascorbic acid, allowing its complete omission and simplifying the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “identical results were obtained regardless of the presence or absence of ascorbic acid and confirm that neither the ascorbic acid, nor the N‑oxide functionality are required to promote the generation of an aryl radical intermediate.”; Table 4 entries 2 and 3 show 52 % and 53 % yields with/without ascorbic acid.

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Scale‑up calorimetry revealed a strongly exothermic event during the dropwise addition of tert‑butyl nitrite, with a predicted adiabatic temperature rise of 81 °C and substantial gas evolution, posing a safety risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors propose either increasing the reaction temperature to accelerate conversion or reducing the addition rate of tert‑butyl nitrite to better match the reaction rate, thereby controlling the exotherm and gas release.
Supporting_Evidence: “subsequent controlled addition of tert‑butyl nitrite … strongly exothermic event … calculated 81 °C adiabatic temperature rise.”; “The reaction was intrinsically slower than the rate of addition. This issue could be addressed by increasing the rate of reaction (for example by increasing reaction temperature) or by reducing the rate of tert‑butyl nitrite addition.”

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: On a 5 g multigram scale the isolated yield dropped to 39 % despite optimized conditions, indicating variability and incomplete conversion possibly due to mismatch between addition rate and reaction rate.
Solution_Description: Adjusting the temperature upward or slowing the addition of tert‑butyl nitrite are recommended to synchronize reagent addition with reaction kinetics, thereby improving conversion and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: “the product … was isolated … in 39 % yield … accumulation … 88 % of the total heat output occurring after the addition of tert‑butyl nitrite was complete, implying that the reaction was intrinsically slower than the rate of addition.”; “This issue could be addressed by increasing the rate of reaction (for example by increasing reaction temperature) or by reducing the rate of tert‑butyl nitrite addition.”

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Initial product isolation relied on silica‑gel column chromatography, which is time‑consuming and less scalable.

Paper Title: C–H Arylation of Heterocyclic
Problem_Description: Aryldiazonium salts are high‑energy, potentially explosive intermediates; their isolation poses safety hazards on large scale.
Solution_Description: The methodology generates the aryldiazonium species in situ from cheap aniline and tert‑butyl nitrite, avoiding isolation of the unstable salt and thereby improving safety.

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: High catalyst loading (2 mol % Au) normally required for gold‑catalyzed oxazoline‑to‑oxazole oxidations, leading to expensive reagent consumption on scale.

Solution_Description: Reduced catalyst loading to 0.5 mol % IPrAuCl/AgNTf₂ (stoichiometry change + catalyst optimisation), enabling inexpensive, scalable gold catalysis.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “most gold‑catalyzed reactions are performed at much smaller scales and with higher catalyst loadings” (introduction). 2. “The published conditions … could be optimized to 0.5 mol % IPrAuCl/AgNTf₂ … with a very good yield of 92 % within 24 h” (section 2, Table 1).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: Molecular oxygen can form explosive mixtures and peroxide intermediates with common solvents, posing severe safety hazards for batch processes.
Solution_Description: Implemented a micro‑structured reactor (PTFE‑T‑Mixer, capillary) that safely tolerates high temperatures (up to 100 °C) and pressures (up to 18 bar a) while handling O₂, thereby eliminating explosion risk.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Molecular oxygen as an oxidizing agent is often neglected because of its propensity to form explosive mixtures or peroxides …” (introduction). 2. “This can be prevented by executing the reaction in microstructured reactors, where high temperatures and pressures can be applied in a safe and simple fashion.” (introduction).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: Batch oxidation of oxazoline 2 with O₂ required 48 h and gave only ≈13 % conversion without a radical initiator, leading to unacceptably long reaction times and low product yield.
Solution_Description: Added 10 mol % azobis(isobutyronitrile) (AIBN) as a radical initiator, which accelerated the oxidation dramatically (conversion >95 % in 48 h and >31 % in 3 h with AIBN vs. 13 % without).
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The addition of 10 mol % of the radical starting reagent AIBN could significantly accelerate the reaction to obtain conversions of more than 95 % within 48 h.” (section 2). 2. “The conversion of oxazoline 2 was increased from 13 to 31 % within a total reaction time of 3 h” (Results).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: The original THF solvent has a low boiling point, restricting the reaction temperature and promoting peroxide formation, which limits conversion and safety.
Solution_Description: Replaced THF with 2‑methoxyethyl acetate, a higher‑boiling solvent that does not readily form explosive peroxides, allowing safe operation up to 100 °C and faster reactions.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The published conditions (THF, 50 °C, 48 h) could be modified to allow the use of 2‑methoxyethyl acetate, which is a solvent with higher boiling point, that does not typically form explosive peroxides, thereby enabling reaction temperatures of up to 100 °C.” (section 2).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: The oxidation step requires 4–5 h residence time, which is long for a continuous microreactor and would lead to low throughput if operated in a single‑pass mode.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a liquid‑recycle loop with a 5 mL head‑space reservoir and automated switching of the pump inlet, allowing the reactor to be loaded once and then operated continuously while maintaining the required residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Due to the relatively long reaction time (4–5 h) for a chemical conversion in a microstructured reactor, a process setup with a recycle‑loop of the liquid stream was chosen.” (section 3). 2. Detailed description of the recycle‑loop operation (Figure 1, text).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: The hydroperoxide product 3 is sensitive and can decompose, making isolation and handling problematic.
Solution_Description: Performed an in‑situ reduction of 3 to the corresponding alcohol 4 by passing the reactor effluent through a fixed‑bed of granular NaBH₄, thus telescoping the oxidation and reduction steps and avoiding isolation of the unstable peroxide.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The generated hydroperoxide functionality … the reduction of the generated hydroperoxide functionality … demonstrates the capability of this setup for follow‑up transformations.” (abstract). 2. “To obtain a continuous reduction, the reaction solution was passed through a fixed‑bed column filled with granular sodium borohydride … the oxazole peroxide 3 peak vanished and a new peak appeared … indicating that 3 was converted.” (section 4).

Paper Title: Safe and Fast Flow Synthesis of Functionalized Oxazoles with Molecular Oxygen in a Microstructured Reactor
Problem_Description: Scaling up the microreactor could alter the flow regime (slug‑flow vs. dispersed flow), potentially affecting conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: Scaled the reactor by increasing the inner diameter while keeping the diameter‑to‑length ratio constant, thereby preserving the residence time and slug‑flow characteristics; the scaled‑up experiment reproduced conversion and yield of the laboratory‑scale reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “A scale‑up of the reaction was conducted … the ratio of the inner diameter to capillary length was not changed … scale‑up factor of 3.46 … the conversion and yield were reproduced.” (Results, Figures 3–4).

Paper Title: Preparative Scale Demonstration and Mechanistic Investigation of a Visible Light-Mediated Radical Smiles Rearrangement
Problem_Description: Tributylamine (NBu₃) is poorly soluble in DMSO; the reaction becomes biphasic and highly dependent on stir rate, requiring 45 min for full conversion at half the normal stir rate (vs. 15 min at normal stirring).
Solution_Description: Replacement of NBu₃ with triethylamine (NEt₃) gives a homogeneous solution in DMSO, delivering comparable yields (≈66 %) and simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Due to the poor solubility of tributylamine (NBu₃) in DMSO … a reaction carried out at half the normal stir rate required 45 min for full starting material consumption … compared to the normal 15 min reaction time” (Table 1, entry 1). • “Triethylamine (NEt₃) provided a homogeneous reaction solution, leading to a comparable yield of 66 %” (Table 1, entry 2).

Paper Title: Preparative Scale Demonstration and Mechanistic Investigation of a Visible Light-Mediated Radical Smiles Rearrangement
Problem_Description: An exotherm of ≈10 °C occurs over 5 min (25 → 35 °C) during the reaction, which accelerates formation of the sulfonic‑acid side product (6).

Problem_Description: On preparative scale (100 g) the large volume of DMSO hampers efficient removal and recovery of product 5, limiting overall isolated yield.

Paper Title: Tale of Two Protecting GroupsBoc vs SEMfor Directed Lithiation and C–C Bond Formation on a Pyrrolopyridazinone Core
Problem_Description: The standard Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling of the Boc‑protected aryl iodide 6 (and its analogues 6a, 6b) under the usual Pd(PPh₃)₄/K₂CO₃/dioxane‑H₂O conditions gave no desired biaryl product; the starting material was consumed but only dehalogenated pyrrole 3 was observed.

Problem_Description: When the PdCl₂(dppf)‑mediated Suzuki coupling was performed on gram scale, the isolated yields fell sharply (≈35 % vs. 60 % on 10–100 mg scale), indicating poor reproducibility and scale‑up reliability.

Supporting_Evidence: ["isolated yields dropped substantially when scaled to gram‑scale","Boc protecting group strategy led to poor yields ... especially on a large scale","Using the SEM group gave excellent yields ... and could be successfully scaled up to 5 g without a drop in product yield"]

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Strongly exothermic magnesium activation and Grignard reaction steps generate large amounts of heat, creating safety hazards especially at scale.
Solution_Description: Moving to a continuous‑flow strategy (CSTRs for Grignard formation) limits the reaction volume and performs metal activation only once per campaign, greatly reducing the heat released at any time.
Supporting_Evidence: "strongly exothermic magnesium metal activation and reaction steps; (2) heterogeneous reactions with potential difficulties in suspending and mixing; and (3) operational hazards posed by solvents with low vapor pressures." (Introduction) ; "The continuous strategy reduces hazards by operation at a small reaction volume and performing metal activation only once for each campaign." (Introduction) ; "For highly exothermic transformations, continuous stirred tank reactors (CSTRs) have emerged as a preferred platform if the reaction is heterogeneous with solid reagents." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Solid magnesium particles can escape the CSTR, leading to fines in the product stream and fluctuating residence times that cause conversion drops.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A settling pipe and external fines trap retain magnesium solids; recovered fines are recycled back to the reactor, stabilising flow and conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "A key operational challenge is the prevention of fine magnesium particles exiting the CSTR. The settling pipe is the primary method for keeping magnesium solids inside the CSTR... Magnesium fines from the settling trap are recycled periodically back to the CSTR, for example, once per day." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development) ; "The conversion drop observed in the last hour of processing... magnesium relative to the steady state concentration of 1 in the CSTR. This explains the conversion drop observed in the last hour of processing." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: During the two‑CSTR Grignard run, the formylation intermediate (INT 2) oiled out in CSTR 2, halting further processing.
Solution_Description: Switching the formylation solvent to 10 % (w/w) DMF in THF eliminated the oiling problem and gave >99.5 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "Unfortunately, within hours INT 2 oiled out in CSTR 2, making this approach unamenable to further processing." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development) ; "A solvent screen revealed that the best solvent system for the flow Bouveault formylation was a 10 % (w/w) DMF solution in THF at 40–45 °C… these conditions completely eliminated the oiling of INT 2 and were demonstrated during a 6 h continuous run that produced INT 2 in >99.5 % conversion." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Residual boron salts remained in the product at up to 0.2 % (w/w), compromising purity.
Solution_Description: Replacing the acetic‑acid quench with methanolic sulfuric acid completely removed boron residues.
Supporting_Evidence: "One item which required improvement … was the reduction of residual boron levels, which were seen as high as 0.2 % (w/w). This was addressed by replacement of the acetic acid quench with methanolic sulfuric acid, which completely eliminated all residual boron salts in the product." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Pumping alkyl‑lithium solutions caused premature seal failure in conventional pumps because of inorganic precipitates and the highly reactive nature of n‑BuLi.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A feed coil pre‑filled with hexanes was used; n‑BuLi was drawn into the coil and displaced by inert solvent, keeping the pump seals in contact only with hexane.
Supporting_Evidence: "Exposure of common mechanical pump seals to these salts can result in premature failure of the seals… In this work… Teledyne Isco 1000D syringe pumps were used for n‑BuLi pumping. In order to prevent destruction of the pump seals, a feed coil was prefilled with hexanes, and then the alkyl lithium solution was pulled into the coil. The n‑BuLi was displaced from the feed coil into the reactor by feeding the syringe pump with inert solvent. This method allows the pump seals to interact with hydrocarbon solvent only." (Results and Discussion – Flow Lithiation Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Alkyl‑lithium reagents in PFRs generated solids and gels at cryogenic temperatures, risking fouling and blockage.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Static‑mixing elements were installed in the PFRs and a dome‑type back‑pressure regulator (later replaced by expansion chambers) were used to tolerate transient solids and maintain pressure.
Supporting_Evidence: "The use of static mixers… The PFRs can handle traces of small solids in flow for a brief time without clogging… System 2 used a dome‑type back pressure regulator, which is prone to clogging with solids… To maintain back pressure, System 3 used expansion chambers in series and required automated block valves, which can tolerate some solids." (Results and Discussion – Comparative Analysis of Experimental Setups for Cryogenic Lithiation)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: During the lithiation runs, pressure rose from 160 psig to 244 psig, indicating a possible blockage and uncontrolled exotherm.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The back‑pressure system was changed from a dome‑type regulator to series expansion chambers that can be emptied periodically, preventing pressure buildup.
Supporting_Evidence: "System pressure was measured … increased from 160 to 244 psig… This may have indicated the start of a blockage, potentially at the back‑pressure regulator… In the second run… back‑pressure regulation mechanism … series of chambers … allowed regular cleaning and prevented fouling." (Results and Discussion – Flow Lithiation Development)

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Anisole impurity (5) formed, attributed to moisture ingress or incomplete Grignard reaction.
Solution_Description: Using anhydrous MeTHF and maintaining low temperatures (20–40 °C for Grignard, –70 °C for lithiation) reduced water‑related side reactions and minimized anisole formation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Anisole 5… could result from water contamination or incomplete reaction of the Grignard reagent prior to quench." (Results and Discussion – Continuous Grignard Process Development) ; "The lithiation approach… low temperature … avoids side reactions, impurity formation, and process failure." (Introduction) ; "The acute hazards… solvents with low vapor pressures" (Introduction) – implies need for dry, low‑boiling solvent.

Paper Title: Flow Grignard and Lithiation: Screening Tools and Development of Continuous Processes for a Benzyl Alcohol Starting Material
Problem_Description: Reduction of the lithiation intermediate stalled at ~10 % residual aldehyde when hexanes were present in the solvent system.
Solution_Description: An additional 0.5 equiv of LiBH₄ was added (stoichiometry change) and the hexanes were effectively removed, restoring full reduction.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the reduction stalled at approximately 10 % residual aldehyde 3. It is postulated that the hexanes present in the solvent system had a detrimental impact on the reduction kinetics relative to borohydride degradation or caused LiBH₄ precipitation." (Results and Discussion – Flow Lithiation Development) ; "Additional LiBH₄ (0.5 equiv) was added, which resulted in complete reduction." (Results and Discussion – Flow Lithiation Development)

Paper Title: Selective Amidation of Unprotected Amino Alcohols Using Surfactant-in-Water Technology: A Highly Desirable Alternative to Reprotoxic Polar Aprotic Solvents
Problem_Description: Reagents and intermediates are poorly soluble in water, producing highly viscous emulsions or oil‑out phases that hinder stirring, reproducibility and product isolation.
Solution_Description: Addition of the non‑ionic surfactant TPGS‑750‑M (2 wt % in water) creates micellar domains that solubilize the organic substrates, eliminating the emulsion and enabling high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The use of surfactant TPGS‑750‑M (2 wt % in water)… conversion was complete within 20 h… and a minimum amount of the undesired diacylation by‑product 3b was observed (Table 1, entry 5).”
- “In the control experiment (entry 6) using pure water… 17 % of the by‑product 3b was observed, and the physical properties of the reaction mixture made it challenging to process. Indeed emulsion problems as well as oiling out were systematically observed… resulting in poor reproducibility or limited generality.”
- “Organic reactions are often times very sensitive to solvent effects, and the major drawback of using water as medium … is the lack of solubility of the reagents … The addition of simple amphiphilic molecules such as surfactants can partially “solubilize” organic materials in an aqueous medium and therefore promote the reaction.”

Paper Title: Selective Amidation of Unprotected Amino Alcohols Using Surfactant-in-Water Technology: A Highly Desirable Alternative to Reprotoxic Polar Aprotic Solvents
Problem_Description: Strong, highly basic amines (e.g., pyridine, carbonate bases) deprotonate the free alcohol, leading to a nucleophilic alkoxide that undergoes undesired O‑acylation, generating significant amounts of the di‑acylated side‑product 3b and reducing chemoselectivity.
Solution_Description: Switch to the weaker base N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) (pK_a ≈ 7.5) and adjust its equivalents (2–3 eq) to suppress alcohol deprotonation while maintaining amide formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Strong base (pK_a > 10) generates a substantial amount of the undesired diacylation product 3b… The low chemoselectivity observed when pyridine was used can be attributed to a change in mechanism, where a highly activated acyl‑pyridinium intermediate is generated, leading to non‑selective attack by the free alcohol (entry 1).”
- Table 2, entry 11: “NMM (7.5) 3.0 equiv → >99 % conversion, 1 % 3b.”
- “Increasing the amount of NMM in the mixture slowed down the conversion and increased the amount of by‑product generated (entries 12 and 13).”

Paper Title: Selective Amidation of Unprotected Amino Alcohols Using Surfactant-in-Water Technology: A Highly Desirable Alternative to Reprotoxic Polar Aprotic Solvents
Problem_Description: Running the amidation at temperatures below 40 °C dramatically slows the reaction rate, often failing to reach full conversion even after several days, thereby limiting throughput and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Perform the coupling at 40 °C for 20 h (or 20 h at room temperature when using the optimized surfactant/base combination), providing complete conversion within a practical timeframe.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The use of surfactant TPGS‑750‑M (2 wt % in water) and N‑methylmorpholine as base at 40 °C led to the most desirable outcome; conversion was complete within 20 h at room temperature…”
- “It should be noted that running the reaction at lower temperature led to a slower rate and full conversion was usually not observed even after several days.”

Paper Title: Selective Amidation of Unprotected Amino Alcohols Using Surfactant-in-Water Technology: A Highly Desirable Alternative to Reprotoxic Polar Aprotic Solvents
Problem_Description: Aminophenol substrates (both para‑ and meta‑) give poor conversion and high levels of di‑acylated by‑product because the phenolic OH competes with the amine for acylation, and no improvement is observed in DMF or MeCN.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “Surprisingly, full conversion cannot be achieved with both the para‑ or meta‑aminophenol derivatives. High amounts of the corresponding diacylation by product were also observed, reaching 60 % in the case of meta‑aminophenol 13.”
- “The lack of reactivity in the use of aminophenols can, therefore, be attributed to the presence of the phenolic alcohol. In the latter case, the use of acetonitrile or DMF did not deliver better results and a mixture of product and by‑products were isolated.”

Paper Title: Selective Amidation of Unprotected Amino Alcohols Using Surfactant-in-Water Technology: A Highly Desirable Alternative to Reprotoxic Polar Aprotic Solvents
Problem_Description: When the reaction is performed without surfactant, the aqueous mixture forms stable emulsions and oil‑out phases that prevent efficient work‑up and lead to poor reproducibility on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: With TPGS‑750‑M present, the crude reaction mixture can be filtered directly and the solid product washed with water, eliminating the need for organic extractions and streamlining the isolation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
- “The use of surfactant was clearly essential in this reaction, as exemplified in the control experiment (entry 6) using pure water. … emulsion problems as well as oiling out were systematically observed … resulting in poor reproducibility or limited generality.”
- “Scale‑up experiment … The product was isolated directly as a solid by a simple filtration and washed with water. This very simple protocol reliably provides yield above 15 g of product (>95 % yield) in ≥98.5 % purity.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: Impurities (4‑chloro‑containing species 4b‑4d and 7) generated in the Fe‑catalyzed butenyl‑magnesium bromide coupling poisoned the downstream Pd‑catalyzed Heck cyclization, causing the reaction to stall and requiring impractically high Pd loadings.
Solution_Description: A post‑coupling work‑up with N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine (DMEDA) effected a quantitative SNAr displacement of the residual 4‑chloro groups. The resulting adducts were removed by aqueous acid wash, delivering a high‑purity alkene (4) that performed reproducibly in the Heck step.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that impurities generated during this step had a significant deleterious effect on the downstream Heck reaction… The reaction tended to stall, and impractical Pd‑catalyst loadings were required… A screen of readily available amines quickly identified N,N′‑dimethylethylenediamine (N,N′‑DMEDA) as an appropriate nucleophile that quantitatively scavenged all of the remaining species bearing the 4‑chloro functionality via an SNAr displacement… Incorporation of this simple procedure into the work‑up post Fe‑catalyzed coupling yielded 4 in higher purity… and the resulting stream was found to perform reproducibly in the ensuing Heck reaction.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: The DPE‑Phos ligand displayed poor solubility in acetonitrile, leading to inconsistent Heck cyclization performance and an unwanted ligand‑free background reaction that produced the endocyclic olefin 3a.
Solution_Description: An excess of DPE‑Phos (2 : 1 ligand : Pd) was pre‑complexed with Pd(OAc)₂ in a small volume of CH₂Cl₂ before addition to the reaction mixture in MeCN, suppressing the background reaction and giving consistent exocyclic olefin selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The problem was further exacerbated by the low solubility of free DPE‑Phos ligand in the reaction solvent, acetonitrile… It was critical to employ an excess amount of DPE‑Phos relative to Pd‑OAc₂ (2 : 1 ratio)… and it was necessary to precomplex these two species in a small volume of CH₂Cl₂ prior to mixing with the substrate and other reagents in MeCN… ensured an assay yield of 80% and 9 : 1 ratio of exocyclic 3 vs endocyclic 3a.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: Using excess BH₃·THF in the hydroboration step caused over‑reduction of the pyrimidine ring, reducing overall yield of the alcohol intermediate 8.
Solution_Description: The amount of BH₃·THF was limited to a maximum of 0.4 equiv, preventing over‑reduction and giving an 86 % isolated yield of the alcohol 8.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydroboration was conducted using BH₃·THF complex, and it was necessary to limit stoichiometry of this reagent to a maximum of 0.4 equiv in order to avoid over‑reduction of the pyrimidine ring… Overall yield of the product alcohol 8 from this sequence was 86%.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: During oxidation of the primary alcohol 8 to the carboxylic acid, the commonly used 2‑methyl‑2‑butene scavenger generated volatile, pungent by‑products and promoted over‑oxidation.
Solution_Description: Limonene was employed as a milder scavenger for hypochlorite, suppressing over‑oxidation and improving operational safety.
