Supporting_Evidence: “Limonene was added as the scavenger for the hypochlorite by‑product instead of the more pungent and volatile 2‑methyl‑2‑butene, which helped suppress overoxidation at scale.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: Commercial PMB‑Cl was not available in the required multi‑kilogram quantities, and the thionyl chloride chlorination of PMB‑OH released a large exotherm (‑172 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad ≈ 76 K).
Solution_Description: A new short route was developed: thionyl chloride (1.3 equiv) added to PMB‑OH at –10 °C over 30 min, with a controlled addition rate and a jacket temperature limited to 20 °C during concentration. This gave near‑quantitative PMB‑Cl (99 % yield) on >50 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “A brief in‑house assessment of chlorination conditions identified thionyl chloride (1.3 equiv) as the most suitable reagent. Triethylamine (1.05 equiv) was found to be the optimal base with dichloromethane (DCM) as the optimal solvent… The reaction exotherm produced upon addition of SOCl₂ to the PMB‑OH solution was quantified by reaction calorimetry as −172 kJ mol⁻¹ with an adiabatic temperature rise of 76 K… When this reagent was added over a minimum of 30 min the reaction could be controlled by the rate of addition of thionyl chloride.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: Initial Cu‑mediated cyclization of iodopyrimidine 14 gave inconsistent conversions (6–99 %) due to sensitivity to catalyst loading, base amount, solvent composition, and temperature.
Solution_Description: The superior ligand L2 (2‑picolinic acid) was selected, CuI loading reduced to 0.25 equiv, Cs₂CO₃ optimized to 4 equiv, and the reaction run at 60 °C (or 50 °C in THF) to achieve >99 % conversion with minimal by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “L2 was identified as a superior ligand… Increasing the catalyst loading and Cs₂CO₃ charge afforded 100% conversion… Switching the solvent to THF at a reduced temperature of 50 °C gave similar results with 99% conversion… Reducing the catalyst loading to 25 mol %… further reductions… were not investigated.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: When bulk Cs₂CO₃ (different particle size and lower water content) was used, the Cu‑cyclization conversion dropped to 31 % because of poorer base solubility and surface area.
Solution_Description: Adding 1 equiv of water restored base solubility and matched lab‑scale performance, eliminating the conversion loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was identified to be a consequence of a combination of two factors… The bulk material being almost spherical particles… lower surface area and base solubility… The solution identified was addition of 1 equiv water to help solubilize the Cs₂CO₃… this change gave comparable performance with the lab control.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: After distillation of the vinylpyrimidine intermediate 11, a significant loss in assay yield (from 68 % to 53 %) was observed; polymerization of the product was suspected but the exact cause was not determined.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: N/A – the issue was noted but not fully resolved in the article.
Supporting_Evidence: “After distillation to 6.5 volumes toluene the assay yield had dropped to 53% (17.2 kg)… Polymerization of the product was suspected, but the cause remains unknown.”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: Formation of tetrazole 1 from TMS‑azide generates hydrazoic acid (HN₃), a shock‑sensitive gas that accumulated to 0.5 % v/v in the headspace during the original scale‑up, posing an explosion risk.
Solution_Description: The TMS‑azide charge was reduced from 1.8 to 1.2 equiv, addition was performed over 2 h at 25 °C under a nitrogen sweep, and a carbon filtration step (CUNO R53SP) was added to remove residual azide, keeping headspace HN₃ well below the lower decomposition limit.
Supporting_Evidence: “The main safety concerns associated with the formation of tetrazole 1 derived from the use of trimethylsilylazide (TMS‑azide)… the approach was deemed suitable for scale up… Reducing the TMS‑azide charge from 1.8 to 1.2 equiv was possible while maintaining the assay yield at 92%… Trimethylsilylazide (2.60 kg, 1.2 equiv) was charged over 2 h maintaining the temperature at 25 °C… a vessel headspace nitrogen sweep… passed through a CUNO carbon filtration system…”

Paper Title: Two Approaches to the Chemical Development and Large-Scale Preparation of a Pyrimidyl Tetrazole Intermediate
Problem_Description: The dried tetrazole 1 exhibited a large exotherm (≈1040 J g⁻¹) starting at its melt (135 °C) and was positively tested in drop‑weight impact tests at 30 J, indicating potential energetic hazard if heated above ambient.
Solution_Description: Drying and processing temperatures were limited to ≤25 °C, and the material was stored at 5 °C. DSC, isothermal aging, and drop‑weight testing confirmed stability under the defined conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “DSC analysis of dried 1 indicated a very large exotherm (1040 J g⁻¹) initiating from a melt at 135 °C… we elected to limit operating and drying temperatures to a maximum of 25 °C… Dropweight testing on 1 was conducted… and was found to be negative at 30 J.”

Paper Title: Design and Comparison of Tubular and Pipes-in-Series Continuous Reactors for Direct Asymmetric Reductive Amination
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: The growing oligonucleotidyl homostar rapidly loses solubility in neat acetonitrile as the chain length increases; 2‑mer is moderately soluble but 4‑mer is almost insoluble, requiring the addition of methanol to dissolve the material.
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system of MeCN containing 5‑20 % MeOH (or MeOH/MeCN) was employed, which restored adequate solubility for all chain lengths and allowed constant‑volume diafiltration to be performed.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was observed that their solubility in neat MeCN rapidly decreased with chain length… however, upon the addition of MeOH to the solution, the oligo solubility was markedly enhanced (5–20 % MeOH in MeCN).”; “The solubility of the oligonucleotidyl homostars was excellent in mixed MeOH–MeCN solvent.”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: After the first diafiltration step, the neutral amidate (6b) and other monomer‑derived impurities were only partially removed (≈85 % rejection), leading to lower product purity and a loss of material in early cycles.
Solution_Description: The excess of PADS was reduced from 10 equiv to 3 equiv per 5′‑OH, which suppressed formation of the problematic thioamidate and amidate species; a membrane‑cascade configuration was also proposed to improve impurity removal without sacrificing yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Reducing the excess of PADS from 10 to 3 equiv per 5′‑hydroxyl consistently reduced the proportion of thioamidate generated to undetectable levels.”; “Alternative membrane cascade can increase the yield without compromising the product purity.”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: The bulky 4,4′‑dimethoxytrityl (Dmtr)–pyrrole adduct persisted after detritylation (rejection > 90 %) and could not be removed by the PBI membrane, necessitating a separate precipitation step.
Solution_Description: A different, less‑bulky acid‑labile protecting group (e.g., methoxy‑isopropyl acetal) is being investigated to avoid the Dmtr‑pyrrole issue; alternatively the residual Dmtr‑pyrrole can be eliminated by precipitation of the homostar into diethyl ether.
Supporting_Evidence: “The only significant contaminant remaining… Dmtr‑pyrrole… required a precipitation step.”; “The use of a different protecting group… should be explored.”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: Overall isolated yield was limited (≈50 % for a 23‑mer) because the first three chain‑extension cycles contributed roughly half of the total loss, even though product rejection at the dimer stage was already 99 %.
Solution_Description: Implementing a membrane cascade (two‑stage OSN configuration) or increasing membrane area can raise the effective rejection for early‑stage oligomers and recover material lost in the first cycles.
Supporting_Evidence: “The major loss in the overall yield resulted from the first three chain extension cycles, contributing half of the total loss.”; “A simplified membrane cascade… can increase the yield without compromising purity.”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: Each iterative cycle required a solvent‑exchange step and a separate precipitation after detritylation, making the overall process cumbersome, time‑consuming, and difficult to scale.
Solution_Description: The detritylation reaction and the subsequent CVD can be combined in a single membrane‑reactor vessel, eliminating the need for intermediate solvent exchanges and precipitation (single‑pot operation).
Supporting_Evidence: “The current challenges… redundant solvent exchange steps and a precipitation step, rendering the practical operation of the process cumbersome and time‑consuming.”; “bypass the detritylation reaction in DCM, and perform the de‑protection reaction and membrane CVD in the rig (the membrane reactor concept).”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: Use of 1 vol % dichloroacetic acid (DCA) during detritylation caused extensive capping of the 5′‑OH and acid‑catalysed N‑deacetylation of cytosine, generating unwanted side‑products.
Solution_Description: Replacing DCA with 1 vol % pyridinium dichloroacetate (Py·DCA) reduced the capping reaction while still promoting detritylation, improving product purity and lowering the acidity risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “High concentration of DCA caused significant capping of the 5′‑OH… low N‑deacetylation was observed when 1 vol % Py·DCA was used.”

Paper Title: Organic Solvent Nanofiltration (OSN): A New Technology Platform for Liquid-Phase Oligonucleotide Synthesis (LPOS)
Problem_Description: The constant‑volume diafiltration (CVD) step is highly solvent‑intensive; solvent (MeCN) accounts for the largest fraction of the per‑kg production cost when not recovered.
Solution_Description: A 90 % solvent‑recovery unit (steam distillation) was incorporated, cutting the solvent‑related cost by roughly 50 % and making the process economically competitive.
Supporting_Evidence: “CVD is a highly solvent‑intensive process… solvent accounts for a large proportion of the overall cost.”; “Implementing a 90 % solvent recovery via distillation… reduces the overall cost.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: The original synthetic routes to the target benzofuran (compound 3) required 9–12 steps and suffered from a very low yield (≈15 %) in the key oxidative coupling of 4‑bromophenol with the keto‑ester.
Solution_Description: A concise, two‑step one‑pot sequence was developed that combines an SNAr displacement of an ortho‑fluoride (using a DMAc‑water mixture) with an intramolecular Cu(I)‑catalyzed C–O coupling. CuI is added after formation of the SNAr adduct and the mixture is heated to 55 °C, giving the benzofuran intermediate in 69 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “While relatively short, the former route suffers from low yield of the key oxidative coupling step (15%).”; “The substitution of the fluoride on compound 16 by the enolate of 17 proved very facile … in a DMAc–water mixture (97.5/2.5)…”; “the cyclization could be effected by simply adding CuI to the reaction mixture and heating to 55 °C to form the key benzofuran intermediate 19… 69% yield over the two steps.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Attempted oxidative coupling of the pre‑installed N‑methyl‑methanesulfonamide substrate 9 gave poor conversion and low regio‑selectivity toward the desired benzofuran 10.
Solution_Description: The researchers abandoned the oxidative coupling route and instead used a substrate that already contains the bromide and nitrogen (compound 16) followed by a Cu(I)‑catalyzed intramolecular C–O coupling, which proceeds efficiently and reproducibly.
Supporting_Evidence: “The oxidative coupling gave low yield of 10 … The substrate 9 suffered from poor reactivity and low regioselectivity toward the formation of the desired regio isomer of the substituted benzofuran 10.”; “We were encouraged by the fact that the Cu(I) catalyzed intramolecular C‑O coupling worked well.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Key intermediates 13 and 15 required for the Cu(I)‑mediated cyclization were not readily available on large scale, and bromination of intermediate 10 proved difficult, forcing a pre‑installed bromide.
Solution_Description: The team selected inexpensive commercial tetrasubstituted benzene 16 (≈ $100 kg⁻¹) which already bears the required bromide and nitrogen functionalities, eliminating the need for separate bromination and providing a scalable raw material.
Supporting_Evidence: “the two substrates 13 and 15 are not as readily available as we would desire.”; “due to difficulties with the bromination of 10 to make 11, a preinstalled bromide at the 5‑position … would be required.”; “the tetrasubstituted benzene 16 is readily available at very low cost (∼$100 kg on scale) providing a raw material with both the desired bromide and nitrogen functionalities.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Standard nitro‑reduction conditions (Pd/H₂ or metal reductions) also reduced the bromide, leading to undesirable side‑products and low isolated yield of the desired amine 20.
Solution_Description: A vanadium‑doped platinum catalyst was identified that selectively reduces the nitro group with <1 % bromide loss. The optimal medium was THF–water with 2 equiv acetic acid, which also controlled pH and suppressed over‑reduction.
Supporting_Evidence: “This reaction is complicated by the presence of bromide, which is readily reduced under a variety of typical conditions… we identified a vanadium‑doped platinum catalyst that gave clean reduction with <1 % bromide reduction.”; “The best conditions were identified after screening solvents and acid additives, and we found that THF–water in the presence of 2 equiv of acetic acid worked well.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Addition of common nitrogen ligands (e.g., 1,10‑phenanthroline, TMEDA) to the Cu(I)‑catalyzed C–O coupling generated a significant amount of des‑bromo side‑product, decreasing the overall yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed without any added ligand; simple CuI alone gave clean cyclization and avoided formation of the des‑bromo impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Addition of common ligands … resulted in much higher levels of the des‑bromo side product which significantly reduced the yield.”; “Gratifyingly, we found that a one‑pot through process was possible … after formation of intermediate 18, the cyclization could be effected by simply adding CuI to the reaction mixture.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Mesylation of the benzofuran amine 20 gave poor reaction profiles and impurity formation when carried out in solvents other than dichloromethane (DCM).
Solution_Description: DCM was identified as the optimal solvent for the mesylate formation; other solvents (DMF, THF, MeCN) were avoided.
Supporting_Evidence: “Mesylate formation was accomplished using mesyl chloride and pyridine in DCM to produce 21 in 97% isolated yield. Attempts to replace DCM with other solvents such as DMF, THF, or MeCN led to much less clean reaction profiles.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: The route via Meldrum’s acid to keto‑amide 17 gave very low yield, and excess base carried over from the potassium enolate preparation inhibited conversion to the desired amide.
Solution_Description: A scalable route using the potassium enolate of acetophenone (prepared with K‑t‑BuO) was developed; the crude enolate was precipitated, neutralized with 1–2 equiv HCl before addition of methylamine, and the resulting enamide was hydrolyzed at pH 2 to afford 17 in 82 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction between Meldrum’s acid and 4‑fluorobenzoyl chloride gave the desired intermediate 22, the subsequent reaction … resulted in very low yield.”; “the potassium enolate 24 was precipitated … When this mixture was used directly … the excess base carried over … prevented complete conversion to the keto‑amide. When the excess base was neutralized with 1–2 equiv HCl, the conversion … proceeded well.”; “the enamide was easily hydrolyzed to the keto‑amide 17 by adjusting to pH 2 with HCl.”

Paper Title: Concise Cu (I) Catalyzed Synthesis of Substituted Benzofurans via a Tandem SNAr/C–O Coupling Process
Problem_Description: Some reagents (e.g., palladium catalysts for C‑N coupling) were not economical for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to avoid palladium entirely by employing a copper‑I‑catalyzed C‑O coupling, which is cheaper and more readily available on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling … worked well, the oxidative coupling gave low yield … We were encouraged by the fact that the Cu(I) catalyzed intramolecular C‑O coupling worked well.”

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: Initial small‑scale continuous‑flow trials gave moderate success but conversion dropped quickly and results were difficult to reproduce, suggesting catalyst leaching or degradation.
Solution_Description: The reactor was modified to include a high‑vacuum pump and an argon purge, providing an oxygen‑ and water‑free environment that stabilized catalyst activity and gave a higher total TON (≈ 935) with > 98 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Results were however difficult to reproduce, showing stable enantioselectivity but a relatively fast decrease in conversion, suggesting catalyst leaching or degradation.”
2. “Due to the sensitivity of the catalyst system toward oxygen and moisture, we modified our reactor setup by incorporating a high‑vacuum pump and an argon purge to ensure oxygen- and water‑free conditions…"

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: The substrate enamide (4) has low solubility in ethanol (0.4 mol L⁻¹), limiting substrate concentration and thus space‑time yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was switched from ethanol to tetrahydrofuran (THF), in which substrate solubility rises to ca. 1.0 mol L⁻¹, allowing a ten‑fold increase in concentration and higher productivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The solubility of 4 in ethanol is relatively low (0.4 mol L⁻¹), thereby counter‑acting the productivity in terms of space‑time‑yield.”
2. “To enhance catalyst productivity, the reaction solvent was switched to tetrahydrofuran (THF)… the solubility of 4 in THF is as high as 1.0 mol L⁻¹ allowing an up to 10‑fold increase in concentration.”

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: During early experiments rhodium leaching was detected (5–15 ppm), raising concerns about metal contamination of the product and the need for downstream metal‑scavenging steps.
Solution_Description: An on‑line anchoring procedure was developed: the PTA/Al₂O₃ support was dehydroxylated at 200 °C under vacuum, then the air‑sensitive catalyst solution was pumped through for ion‑exchange immobilisation. This gave catalyst retention with rhodium ≤ 0.77 ppm in the product.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “A straightforward ‘on‑line anchoring procedure’ was then developed whereby the PTA/Alox support was first loaded… dehydroxylated at 200 °C under vacuum… the organometallic catalyst was pumped… efficiently trapped in situ by ion exchange.”
2. “This procedure … resulted in enhanced catalyst retention with far lower levels of catalyst leaching … rhodium content in the product mixture ≤ 0.77 ppm.”

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: The original batch hydrogenation required high catalyst loadings and a Boc‑derivatization step to extract the amine product because of its high aqueous solubility, increasing material cost and downstream work‑up complexity.
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow process uses the same commercial Rh‑(S,S)‑EthylDuphos catalyst immobilised on a solid support, cutting catalyst usage to ≈ 10 % of the batch amount and eliminating the Boc‑derivatization, giving a virtually metal‑free product stream.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The hydrogenation route… required relatively high loadings of the chiral catalyst Rh‑(S,S)‑EthylDuphos and still needed the same boc‑derivatization strategy for product extraction.”
2. “The continuous flow… eliminated the need for additional solvent, metal scavenging, and labor‑intensive workup procedures… catalyst loading in the flow process is approximately 10 % of the quantity required by the batch methodology.”

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: During kilogram‑scale operation the substrate pump failed (ruptured seal) and the H₂ mass‑flow controller malfunctioned, causing sudden drops in conversion and off‑spec product.
Solution_Description: A fully automated control system with online GC monitoring automatically adjusted substrate flow, diverted sub‑standard product and switched to a fresh catalyst cartridge when needed, maintaining product specifications.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “There was a sudden drop in conversion due to a malfunction of the H₂ mass‑flowmeter… the system quickly detected the problem and diverted the substandard product until the problem was fixed.”
2. “The unit … enables real‑time control of performance criteria… adaptation of the substrate flow to ensure predefined threshold conversion; switch of the catalyst cartridge in case of unmet enantioselectivity.”

Paper Title: Enabling the Scale-Up of a Key Asymmetric Hydrogenation Step in the Synthesis of an API Using Continuous Flow Solid-Supported Catalysis
Problem_Description: When operating at higher temperature/pressure to increase throughput, there was a risk of catalyst detachment and loss of enantioselectivity, limiting the usable operating window.
Solution_Description: The process was optimized by selecting THF (less polar, less interference with electrostatic anchoring), increasing substrate concentration to 0.6 M, and using a larger 8 mL reactor, which together gave a stable catalyst performance (TON ≈ 5000, STY ≈ 520 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹) without loss of ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The less polar and aprotic THF should interfere less with the electrostatic catalyst anchoring, and hence a longer catalyst lifetime is expected.”
2. “The productivity was further enhanced by increasing the substrate concentration to 0.6 M and using a setup … larger reactor … gave an overall TON of ca. 5000 … STY of 520 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: Intermediates 2a (sulfinyl‑protected nitrile) and 3a (oxime) showed low thermal stability: DSC revealed an exotherm onset near 140 °C with high released energies (‑1118 J g⁻¹ and ‑1095 J g⁻¹) and they were predicted to be shock‑sensitive (explosion risk).
Solution_Description: Replace the sulfinyl protecting group with Boc or Cbz protecting groups (2b/2c, 3b/3c). The new intermediates displayed much higher exotherm onsets (≈190‑200 °C for 2b/2c, ≈160 °C for 3b/3c) and substantially lower decomposition energies (‑270 J g⁻¹, ‑415 J g⁻¹, ‑460 J g⁻¹, ‑727 J g⁻¹), eliminating the explosion hazard.
Supporting_Evidence: “compounds 2a and 3a were found to be energetic… onset of an exotherm at ∼140 °C with significant energy being released (‑1118 and ‑1095 J g⁻¹)”; “based on the Yoshida‑Bodman correlation… shock sensitive and … explosion risk”; “Boc‑ and Cbz‑protected amines 2b and 2c showed a relatively high onset of exotherm (∼190–200 °C) and a significantly lower decomposition energy (‑270 and ‑415 J g⁻¹)”; “Boc‑ and Cbz‑protected oximes (3b and 3c) displayed a higher onset temperature (∼160 °C) with lower decomposition energies (‑460 and ‑727 J g⁻¹)”.

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: The hydroxylamine addition to the Cbz‑protected nitrile (2c → 3c) was highly exothermic (ΔH = ‑188 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔT_ad = 72 °C). 92 % of the heat remained “unreleased” during addition, creating a risk of vaporising 2‑propanol (bp = 83 °C) if cooling failed, and the safe addition profile required ≥6 h dosing times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Kinetic modelling with DynoChem was used to predict heat‑accumulation versus feed‑time/temperature. The optimal profile (≥6 h feed at ≤80 °C or 10 h feed at ≤66 °C) reduced heat accumulation to ≈20 %. The process was run in a glass reactor with aggressive cooling (jacket set ≈52 °C, ΔT ≈ 15 °C) to keep temperature rise under control.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was found to be exothermic… heat of reaction (‑188 kJ mol⁻¹) and adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad = 72 °C)”; “92 % of the heat still ‘unreleased’ … could vaporize the solvent 2‑propanol (boiling point = 83 °C) in case of cooling failure”; “minimum feed time of 6 h and temperature of 80 °C, or a feed time of 10 h and temperature of 66 °C is required to reduce the accumulation to 20%”; “maximum ΔT observed during a 2.5 kg batch was 15 °C, very close to the model prediction”.

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: Cyclisation of the Boc‑protected oxime (3b) with triethyl orthoformate produced >50 % impurity area, whereas the Cbz‑protected oxime (3c) gave a clean reaction but the Boc route suffered poor purification and low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Adopt the Cbz protecting group for the oxime (3c) which gave complete conversion in 16 h with good isolated yield (≈90 % solution yield) and allowed facile work‑up, eliminating the impurity problem.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although the Boc‑protected oxime 3b underwent the desired cyclisation, the reaction was plagued by the presence of significant impurities (>50 area %)”; “clean cyclisation was observed for the Cbz‑protected oxime 3c, with complete reaction in 16 h…, providing the protected oxadiazole 4c in good yield”.

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: Hydroxylamine solutions are catalysed to decompose by iron (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) present in stainless‑steel equipment, posing a safety hazard during the 2c → 3c step.
Solution_Description: Perform the hydroxylamine addition in glass or glass‑lined reactors (instead of stainless steel) to avoid iron‑catalysed decomposition, as recommended by literature.
Supporting_Evidence: “Glass or glass‑lined reactors are recommended for this process (over stainless steel reactors), as it has been reported that iron (Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺) can catalyze the decomposition of hydroxylamine solution”.

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: The HCl salt of the final product (5·HCl) was hygroscopic, low‑melting (48 °C) and exhibited a high‑energy exotherm (onset ≈ 122 °C, ‑1453 J g⁻¹), creating handling, storage and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Switch to the HBr salt (5·HBr) via deprotection with 33 % HBr in AcOH. 5·HBr has a higher melting point (93 °C), lower decomposition energy (‑1049 J g⁻¹), is not shock‑sensitive, and shows acceptable thermal stability.
Supporting_Evidence: “5·HCl was a low melting solid (mp = 48 °C) that was found to be hygroscopic, and DSC analysis … onset of major exotherm around 122 °C with an energy of ‑1453 J g⁻¹”; “Deprotection … using 33 % HBr in acetic acid… provided 5·HBr… moderately reduced decomposition energy (‑1049 J g⁻¹) … higher melting point (93 °C) … not shock or friction sensitive”.

Paper Title: A Scalable Synthesis of 2‑(1,2,4-Oxadiazol-3-yl)propan-2-amine Hydrobromide Using a Process Safety-Driven Protecting Group Strategy
Problem_Description: Drying 5·HBr above 50 °C leads to significant thermal decomposition (ADT₍₂₄₎ = 55 °C, SADT ≈ 40 °C), risking material loss and safety hazards.
Solution_Description: Limit the drying temperature to ≤50 °C, use a low‑boiling solvent (CH₂Cl₂) for the final reslurry, and store the dried product at <5 °C, thereby staying below the ADT₍₂₄₎ and SADT thresholds.
Supporting_Evidence: “the ADT24 was predicted to be 55 °C … it is not advisable to dry the material at a higher temperature”; “the process was designed using a low boiling solvent (dichloromethane) for the final reslurry in order to facilitate drying below 50 °C”; “the compound was stored at low temperatures (<5 °C)”.

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: The free amino acid cis‑2 has a very low solubility in organic solvents, resulting in an extremely slow enzymatic acetylation that is impractical for large‑scale operation and gives a low isolated yield.
Solution_Description: The amino acid was first converted to its isopropyl ester (cis‑3), which is a non‑viscous oil with high solubility in most organic solvents; the ester then undergoes efficient Novozym 435‑mediated acetylation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...the amino acid cis‑2 had a very low solubility in organic solvents resulting in a very slow process which was deemed inconvenient and impractical to execute on a large scale.” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “...the corresponding i‑Pr ester cis‑3 was prepared which gave an easily handled nonviscous oil which has high solubility in most organic solvents...” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “...using the ester cis‑3 and EtOAc as acyldonor/solvent, the Novozym 435 catalyzed the formation of the corresponding acetamide 4.” (Sec Results & Discussion)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: Impurities present in the commercially sourced racemic mixture of amino acid 2 carried through to the ester and gave unknown impurities in the acetylated product 4, causing variable yields and lower enantiomeric purity.
Solution_Description: A crystallization screen identified a c‑pentyl‑methyl‑ether/c‑hexane solvent system that removed the impurities and delivered product 4 with >99 % ee and improved overall recovery.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...various unknown impurities were detected which presumably originated from the chemically impure starting material 2.” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “After a solvent screen for crystallization of 4, it was found that when a mixture of c‑pentyl‑methyl‑ether/c‑hexane was used, the product 4 was obtained in >99 % ee...” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “...the product 4 was isolated essentially pure after extractive workup.” (Sec Results & Discussion)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: Reducing the enzyme loading to 2.5 % w/w lowered the rate dramatically, requiring >24 h for ~44 % conversion and giving a lower isolated yield of the acetamide.
Solution_Description: Enzyme loading was increased to 5 % w/w (or 8 % w/w for fast screening) to achieve ~50 % conversion within 2 h, allowing a shorter reaction time while maintaining high ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Loading of the enzyme could be reduced to 2.5 % w/w with only a minor change in enantiopurity, but the reaction time required increased significantly (entry 8).” (Table 1) 
• “...isopropyl acetate was chosen as solvent/acyldonor for further studies. The loading of the enzyme could be reduced to 2.5 % w/w… however… the reaction time required increased significantly.” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “Using a loading of 5 % w/w of Novozym 435 at 20 °C gave 51 % conversion in 18 h on 2.1 kg scale.” (Scale‑up description)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: The enzymatic resolution was not scalable and gave inconsistent results when moving from bench‑scale to multi‑kilogram batches.
Solution_Description: A telescoped one‑pot hydrogenation/esterification of cheap 3‑aminobenzoic acid 5 was developed to generate the required cis‑isopropyl ester 3 directly, eliminating the need for the problematic enzymatic route at scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...the enzymatic route was not scaleable and gave inconsistent results.” (Introduction) 
• “Thus, starting from amino acid 5 in an acidic (HCl) mixture of 2‑propanol … furnished in one pot a ∼80/20 cis/trans mixture …” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “...a practical large‑scale method was developed for a telescoped one‑pot hydrogenation and esterification …” (Conclusion)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: Direct hydrogenation of amino acid 2 in water or ethanol gave low solubility, leading to complex mixtures, catalyst removal difficulties, and poor isolation of the product.
Solution_Description: The substrate was first esterified to the i‑Pr ester 6, which was hydrogenated in 2‑propanol with Rh/Al₂O₃; this solved solubility issues and allowed clean isolation of the cis‑ester 3.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...hydrogenation using Pd, Pt or Rh as catalyst in water gave a complex mixture… due to the low solubility of the amino acid 2 in alcohols, removal of the catalyst and isolation of the product was troublesome.” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “Starting from the corresponding iPr‑ester 6 … using Rh as catalyst in 2‑propanol at 80 °C solved the solubility problems and the product 3 was easily isolated…” (Sec Results & Discussion)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: Esterification of the hydrogenation product was incomplete after the initial 3‑day hydrogenation, limiting overall yield of the cis‑ester 3.
Solution_Description: An additional portion of HCl was added and the mixture was heated for two more days, completing the esterification and raising the isolated yield of cis‑3 to 46 % overall.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Using a small excess of HCl, it was found that the hydrogenation was complete within three days whereas the esterification only had reached ∼20 % conversion. To obtain full conversion … additional HCl was added followed by heating for an additional two days.” (Ref 8 note) 
• “...furnished in one pot a ∼80/20 cis/trans mixture … corrected yield cis isomer = 48 %.” (Sec Results & Discussion)

Paper Title: Development of an Enantioselective Novozym 435 Mediated Acetylation for the Preparation of (1
Problem_Description: Commercially available cis‑2 or its ester are scarce, expensive, and difficult to purchase in kilogram quantities, limiting the supply of the key intermediate.
Solution_Description: A cost‑effective route from cheap 3‑aminobenzoic acid 5 was devised, employing Rh‑catalyzed hydrogenation and in‑situ esterification to generate the required cis‑isopropyl ester 3 on multikilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Suppliers of compound cis‑2 are few, the prices are high, and it is difficult to purchase in large quantities.” (Sec Results & Discussion) 
• “Starting from cheap and readily available 3‑aminobenzoic acid 5, a practical large‑scale method … was developed.” (Conclusion) 
• “...hydrogenation of 5 … in the presence of 5 % Rh on Al₂O₃ (0.5 mol %) … gave a ∼80/20 cis/trans mixture …” (Sec Results & Discussion)

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: Tartaric acid (1) exhibits very poor solubility in the reaction mixture; the process therefore proceeds under excess benzoyl chloride and, when the chloride is almost consumed, the system becomes highly viscous and tends to solidify.
Solution_Description: Toluene was introduced as a co‑solvent to improve the dissolution of tartaric acid and to keep the suspension fluid, thereby preventing excessive viscosity and solidification.
Supporting_Evidence: “In fact, due to the bad solubility of tartaric acid 1, at the beginning, the process proceeds under the excess of chloride 2… The addition of solvent, e.g., toluene, is necessary to prevent too high viscosity and solidification of the system, when nearly all of the chloride 2 has been consumed.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: The reaction is highly corrosive and generates gaseous hydrogen chloride; without a catalyst the reaction does not start until >100 °C, posing a thermal‑safety risk.
Solution_Description: Sulfuric acid was added as an acid catalyst; its presence lowers the onset temperature to ca. 40 °C, reducing the thermal load and the risk associated with high‑temperature operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Without catalyst the reaction begins >100 °C (no hydrogen chloride releasing was observed at lower temperature), while with catalyst, e.g., sulfuric acid, it already begins at ca. 40 °C.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: Only two of the three benzoyl groups are incorporated into the product; one equivalent is lost as benzoic acid (4) which must be separated, lowering overall yield and increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: A stoichiometric excess of benzoyl chloride (3 equiv) is intentionally used to drive the complete conversion despite the loss of one equivalent as benzoic acid, simplifying product isolation by filtration of the solid anhydride.
Supporting_Evidence: “A disadvantage of such a method is utilization of only 2 equiv of benzoyl groups, while 1 equiv is lost in benzoic acid 4 which has to be separated… The filtration cake is anhydride 3.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: The heterogeneous solid–liquid–gas system releases large amounts of HCl gas, creating a hazardous environment and requiring safe handling of the exothermic reaction.
Solution_Description: A dedicated laboratory absorption setup (absorption column, recirculation pump, buffer tank, alkaline scrubber) was built to safely capture released HCl and maintain isothermal conditions during kinetic experiments.
Supporting_Evidence: “A laboratory absorption setup was designed and made to operate under slight under‑pressure conditions and to ensure the receipt of HCl… The setup consists of an absorption column, a hydrochloric acid recirculation pump, an acid buffer tank… and an alkaline protective scrubber.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: Mass‑transfer limitations (mixing intensity and particle size) strongly affect the overall conversion rate, making the reaction rate difficult to reproduce consistently.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow design was replaced by a cascade of well‑stirred CSTRs, each equipped with its own agitator, to ensure uniform mixing, reduce mass‑transfer resistance, and provide more reproducible residence times.
Supporting_Evidence: “The experience… shows that the rate … is influenced by mixing intensity and tartaric acid particle size. This indicates that the process of mass transfer is limited… In this case, a cascade of CSTRs … enables to efficiently mixing the high solid‑content suspension.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: Determining the kinetics required many batch experiments at various temperatures (80–100 °C) and long reaction times to achieve near‑complete conversion.
Solution_Description: The reaction was studied at lower temperatures and the kinetic data were extrapolated to the industrial temperature range (110–120 °C) using the Arrhenius equation, thus avoiding long high‑temperature runs.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction kinetics at 110–120 °C (process temperature in the batch industrial process) was determined by the extrapolation of data obtained at lower temperatures… The activation energy … was obtained from the Arrhenius correlation.”

Paper Title: Kinetic Research of
Problem_Description: Separating the anhydride (3) from benzoic acid (4) and other impurities is challenging because of similar solubility characteristics.
Solution_Description: Toluene was used as a selective solvent in which benzoic acid dissolves while the solid anhydride remains as a filterable cake, allowing simple solid‑phase filtration for product isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The advantage… is the effective separation of anhydride 3 (before its hydrolysis) from the benzoic acid 4 and impurities by straightforward filtration (benzoic acid dissolves in toluene). The filtration cake is anhydride 3.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: Leaching of Pt from the solid Pt/C catalyst in batch prevented a smooth transition to flow; in flow the Pt leaching caused low conversion and high levels of the cis‑impurity 8.
Solution_Description: Switch to a homogeneous Ir‑catalyzed reductive amination (Ir‑COD‑Cl₂) that does not suffer from Pt leaching, enabling a continuous‑flow process.
Supporting_Evidence: “One key observation in the batch reaction that prevented a smooth transition to flow was leaching of Pt from the solid support.”; “Low conversion and high levels of the cis impurity 8 were consistently observed in flow.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: During early flow runs Ir(0) precipitated as a black coating on reactor walls, causing loss of catalyst activity and inconsistent conversion.
Solution_Description: Addition of 0.5 equiv TBAI (tetrabutylammonium iodide) stabilized the Ir(I) species and prevented black residue formation; the catalyst was introduced last after hydrogen was already present, eliminating Ir(0) formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “A fine black coating within the reactor tubes … we suspected … Ir(0) … deposited on the metal surface.”; “The use of TBAI provided a beneficial stabilization effect on the catalyst system.”; “It was clear that the initial charge of catalyst was inactive … only after second charge … product formed.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: Long mixing loops (T1, T2) caused extended residence of the catalyst with hydrogen before aldehyde and amine were added, leading to Ir plating and poorer start‑up transitions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a background aldehyde test and delayed the start‑up of the catalyst pump so that the catalyst and hydrogen only mix after the aldehyde/amine stream has arrived, minimizing Ir plating during start‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “When starting a reaction with a solvent filled reactor … there was evidence of Ir plating … all pumps were being started simultaneously … this results in segments of solution that contained just catalyst, acid, and hydrogen.”; “The origin of the problem was not entirely clear … order of addition was something that needed to be examined.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: The mixing time between the amine/aldehyde feed and the acetic‑acid/water stream strongly affected the level of the cis‑impurity 8, raising impurity levels above specification.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reduced both mixing loop volumes (T1 and T2) to shorten residence times; the optimized mixing gave < 0.1 % cis‑impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 10 shows “It is clear that decreasing both mixing times nicely reduced the cis levels in the product.”; “Overall the 3/5 mix time had a larger impact on the resulting cis content in the product.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: The traditional coiled‑tube PFR design is limited to ∼150 L because larger coil tubing is difficult to fabricate and install, making scale‑up expensive and impractical.
Solution_Description: Developed a pipes‑in‑series reactor architecture that can be built from standard stainless‑steel pipe sections, allowing easy scale‑up to 360 L and beyond with modest capital cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “The coiled tube PFR … is limited to ∼150 L because it is difficult to construct larger coiled tube reactors.”; “The pipes‑in‑series reactor provides three practical advantages … it is more feasible to scale up to large (>150 L) reactor volumes.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: Exposure of the reaction mixture to oxygen generated the iminium impurity 11, leading to oxidative degradation of product 6 and loss of yield.
Solution_Description: All work‑up and handling steps were performed under nitrogen; the sodium‑carbonate wash was degassed before use, eliminating oxygen ingress and suppressing formation of impurity 11.
Supporting_Evidence: “The 6 reaction mixture degrades in the presence of oxygen.”; “The problem was addressed by storing and handling all processing under a nitrogen atmosphere and degassing the sodium carbonate wash prior to introduction.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: During crystallization, a high supersaturation at ambient temperature resulted in poor rejection of the cis‑impurity 8.
Solution_Description: Adjusted the crystallization temperature (heated to 20‑25 °C before seeding) and controlled the distillation end‑point and antisolvent addition to achieve ~20‑30 % supersaturation, improving impurity 8 rejection to > 50 % and overall product quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “Heating to 40 °C would have reduced the amount of supersaturation and increased the particle growth rate … leading to better rejection of 8.”; “Target conditions with approximately 20‑30 % supersaturation … were met by targeting a final distillation volume of 2.75 L kg⁻¹ and adding 1.0 vol EtOH prior to seeding.”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: Residual water from the carbonate wash formed an aqueous phase during distillation, causing processing difficulties and variability in the crystallization step.
Solution_Description: Increased carbonate concentration to 10 wt % and reduced wash volume to 2 vol to lower water carry‑over; additionally, the distillation was stopped at a tighter volume (2.5‑3.0 L kg⁻¹) to avoid excessive water in the product stream.
Supporting_Evidence: “When using a 5 % carbonate wash, the water content of the organic phase was measured at 7.0 wt % … The wash study … 10 % sodium carbonate was selected … to reduce waste volumes.”; “The distillation target … was 2.5–3.0 L kg⁻¹ … at 3.0 volumes no issue is expected; at 2.5 volumes self‑nucleation …”

Paper Title: Development and Manufacturing GMP Scale-Up of a Continuous Ir-Catalyzed Homogeneous Reductive Amination Reaction
Problem_Description: The batch STAB process required handling of large quantities of the water‑reactive, hydrogen‑evolving reducing agent (STAB), presenting safety hazards and high material handling costs.
Solution_Description: Adopted the Ir‑catalyzed continuous process that uses hydrogen gas (handled externally) instead of STAB, eliminating hazardous solid handling and reducing waste streams.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of STAB as a long‑term manufacturing route was not appealing … handling, dispensing and storage of STAB, poor atom economy, and hydrogen evolution during reaction and workup.”; “The continuous process uses hydrogen gas, but storage, reaction, and venting is all outside the building … dramatically reduces the safety risk.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: The selective hydrolysis of the diester (compound B) to the half‑ester (compound C) reported in the innovator’s patent was not reproducible and gave low overall yields in the authors’ hands.
Solution_Description: The authors abandoned the problematic hydrolysis step and adopted a regio‑selective mono‑amidation of the diester using 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine, a route that proved easier, reproducible and scalable.
Supporting_Evidence: “We observed that this selective hydrolysis route however did not appear to be reproducible and high‑yielding in our hands (Table S1…)”. “Therefore, alternatively reported mono‑amidation of diester using 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine was explored and identified to be comparatively easier, reproducible and scalable.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: During the first stage (ring‑opening of 2 with aminoacetaldehyde dimethyl acetal) conversion was low and many impurities (Imp‑1, Imp‑2) formed, giving only low‑to‑moderate yields.
Solution_Description: Addition of an organic base (DIPEA) together with sodium sulfate as a water‑trap improved the reaction conversion and suppressed impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yields of all of the stages were low to moderate during the initial optimization either due to lower conversion or due to formation of more impurities.” “Surprisingly the addition of base to the reaction mass conveniently improved the yield and minimized the formation of impurities during the cyclization of acyclic intermediates.” “organic bases, preferably diisopropylethylamine, was employed instead of inorganic bases (sodium bicarbonate) in the final optimized process.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: In‑situ conversion of intermediate 3 to 4 required high temperature and was inconsistent; excess 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine was needed, which generated impurity Imp‑3.
Solution_Description: Portion‑wise dosing of 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine toward the end of the reaction gave consistent completion and reduced the formation of Imp‑3.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction completion was however observed to be always be inconsistent and required higher mole equivalents of 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine which in turn generated more of Imp‑3.” “This bottleneck was overcome by portion‑wise dosing of 2,4‑difluorobenzylamine toward the termination of the reaction.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: Crude intermediate 4 was highly soluble in most solvents, preventing efficient isolation by crystallization.
Solution_Description: Crystallization was achieved by using isopropyl alcohol, which allowed removal of many impurities, including Imp‑3, in a practical manner.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude reaction mass was highly soluble in most of the solvents and did not crystallize out easily.” “Effective and practical crystallization of 4 was achieved in isopropyl alcohol that enabled the removal of many impurities along with Imp‑3.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 4 to the aldehyde 4a gave side‑reactions leading to O‑debenzylated hemiacetal / lactol impurities (Imp‑4, Imp‑5) and reduced yield.
Solution_Description: Fine‑tuning of reaction temperature and the equivalents of methanesulfonic acid, together with portion‑wise acid addition, gave clean conversion with <1 % of Imp‑4/Imp‑5.
Supporting_Evidence: “The major side reaction was identified to be formation of O‑debenzylated hemiacetal or lactol impurities (Imp‑4 and Imp‑5).” “Fine tuning of the reaction parameters (temperature of reaction mass and mole equivalents of methanesulfonic acid …) afforded clean conversion of 4 to 4a with a minimum of Imp‑4 and Imp‑5 (typically less than 1.0 %).”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: During cyclization to form benzyl‑dolutegravir 5, the persistent impurity Imp‑6 could not be removed by conventional purification and was carried forward, compromising overall purity.
Solution_Description: Selective silylation of the primary alcohol of Imp‑6 using tert‑butyldimethylsilyl chloride (TBDMSCl) and imidazole converted it to a silyl‑ether (Imp‑6a) that could be completely removed during work‑up, delivering pure 5.
Supporting_Evidence: “After failing with regular methods of removing Imp‑6, control strategy based on chemoselective derivatization of the Imp‑6 was investigated.” “Finally the more facile silylation of the primary alcohol was identified as a derivatization strategy… TBDMSCl… demonstrated successful derivatization followed by the complete removal of the impurity.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: Conventional catalytic hydrogenation (Pd/C) for O‑debenzylation of 5 suffered from poor solubility of substrate and product and caused defluorination side‑reactions, generating difficult‑to‑remove des‑fluoro impurities.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free acidic deprotection using 5 equiv. TFA in dichloromethane afforded clean conversion to the free acid without defluorination, and the by‑product benzyl‑trifluoroacetate was removed by recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Most of the literature methods use the conventional catalytic hydrogenation… poor solubility… potential aromatic defluorination side reactions generating isomeric desfluoro impurities.” “It was found that 5.0 mol equivalent of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in dichloromethane gave clean conversion.”

Paper Title: Identification and Control of Critical Process Impurities: An Improved Process for the Preparation of Dolutegravir Sodium
Problem_Description: An unknown impurity (Imp‑8, m/z 509) formed during the TFA‑mediated debenzylation, originating from electrophilic benzylation by benzyl‑trifluoroacetate, threatened final API purity.
Solution_Description: Adding 10 % (v/v) toluene as a sacrificial solvent suppressed the electrophilic benzylation, reducing Imp‑8 from 0.08 % to 0.02 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The presence of an additional benzyl group… suggests mechanism… addition of 10 % (v/v) of toluene… reduced the level of Imp‑8 from 0.08 % to 0.02 %.”

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: The original convergent route to GSK1292263A (1) generated significant hydroperoxide impurities (10‑12).  Two of these (11 and 12) were mutagenic in Ames tests, making the impurity profile a safety‑critical issue that also required extensive purification to meet API specifications.
Solution_Description: A two‑step mitigation was adopted.  First, a polymer‑bound triphenylphosphine (TPP) resin was used to scavenge hydroperoxides (≈98 % removal in 1 h at rt).  Second, the sulfide‑to‑sulfone oxidation was moved one step earlier in a new synthetic sequence and the final API was recrystallised from anhydrous 2‑MeTHF (seeded) with BHT as a stabiliser, which dramatically reduced hydroperoxide formation during the polymorph‑control recrystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The API 1 contained relatively high levels of various hydroperoxide impurities.', 'These hydroperoxide impurities arose partly because the oxidation procedure used to synthesize the methyl aryl sulfone portion of 1 was the last step of the molecule’s synthesis.', 'Two of the three hydroperoxides identified ... were shown to be mutagenic via Ames testing.', 'Treating a THF solution of 1 containing hydroperoxides … with commercially available styrene–divinylbenzene polymer resin … eliminated approximately 98 % of the hydroperoxides.', 'The second route … reduced the levels of these hydroperoxide impurities by moving the sulfide‑to‑sulfone transformation one step earlier.', 'A seeded recrystallisation of the API 1 from anhydrous 2‑MeTHF afforded the desired polymorph with minimal hydroperoxide formation.', 'The presence of the stabiliser butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) in the anhydrous 2‑MeTHF solvent was hypothesised as playing a role in minimising the hydroperoxide formation.']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: Even after moving the sulfone oxidation earlier, the modified route still employed methanesulfonate 8, a known genotoxic impurity that had to be controlled at very low levels.
Solution_Description: A completely new synthetic sequence was later developed that omitted the methanesulfonate step, thereby eliminating the genotoxic impurity risk.
Supporting_Evidence: ['This modified route still included the use of potentially genotoxic methanesulfonate 8 which needed to be controlled at low levels in the drug substance.']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: The initial scale‑up route to GSK2041706A (15) suffered from a low‑yielding Mitsunobu reaction (≈50 % yield) that also generated an olefin by‑product and required removal of triphenylphosphine oxide, and the sequence created a potentially hazardous aryl‑diazonium intermediate.
Solution_Description: The Mitsunobu step was replaced by a high‑yielding S_NAr coupling of alcohol 31 with aryl chloride 29 under basic conditions, eliminating the diazonium intermediate and the need for phosphine oxide removal.  The chiral reduction was performed with the opposite enantiomer of the Ru‑DPEN catalyst (same cost) to retain stereochemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The initial synthesis of API 15 suffered from a couple of challenges … low‑yielding Mitsunobu reaction between 19 and 20.', 'Improving the yield of the low‑yielding Mitsunobu reaction was challenging primarily because of a concomitant olefin side‑product formation.', 'The yield of the Mitsunobu reaction was also low due to the inherent difficulties of isolating 15 away from the triphenylphosphine oxide produced in the reaction.', 'Generation of potentially dangerous aryl diazonium salt intermediate during the conversion of pyrazinamine 23 to pyrazinol 20.', 'The low‑yielding Mitsunobu reaction was successfully replaced with a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction (S_NAr) … to afford 15 in very high yield.', 'Chiral alcohol 31 was synthesised … using a catalyst containing the opposite enantiomer of that in 24, and the cost of this second catalyst was identical to its enantiomer.']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: Attempts to couple 5‑bromopyrazin‑2‑ol (25) with the boronic acid via Suzuki‑Miyaura failed despite extensive screening, giving no viable high‑yielding route for that fragment.
Solution_Description: Instead of the problematic Suzuki coupling, the fragment was assembled by first preparing the aryl chloride 29 (via a reliable Pd‑catalysed coupling) and then employing an S_NAr reaction with the pre‑made alcohol, bypassing the recalcitrant bromopyrazin‑2‑yl partner.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Attempts to synthesise pyrazinol 20 directly from coupling boronic acid 21 and 5‑bromopyrazin‑2‑ol (25) were surprisingly disappointing … could not be found.', 'The low‑yielding Mitsunobu reaction was successfully replaced with a nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction (S_NAr) …']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: The early Suzuki‑Miyaura step for 33 used a relatively high palladium loading (0.05 eq of Pd(PPh₃)₄) which would be expensive at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The palladium catalyst was switched to Pd(t‑Bu₃P)₂, allowing the loading to be reduced to 0.0025 eq (≈95 % reduction), cutting catalyst cost dramatically while maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The Suzuki reaction … was initially carried out using in‑situ prepared tetrakis‑(triphenylphosphine)‑palladium(0).', 'Subsequent experimentation showed that the palladium loading could be reduced from 0.05 equiv to 0.0025 equiv by switching to Pd(t‑Bu₃P)₂.']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: Residual palladium needed to be removed from intermediate 33 before isolation, and the crude product contained metal and by‑product impurities that could affect downstream steps.
Solution_Description: A palladium‑scavenging step using aqueous l‑cysteine was introduced, followed by filtration, to clean the reaction mixture before final work‑up, providing a high‑purity product.
Supporting_Evidence: ['l‑cysteine (a palladium scavenger) was dissolved in water and added to the 33 solution. The resulting mixture was stirred at about 60 °C for 1 h. The reaction mixture was filtered…']

Paper Title: Development of Large-Scale Routes to Potent GPR119 Receptor Agonists
Problem_Description: Large‑scale crystallisation of API 1 required precise temperature control and a solvent system that would not promote hydroperoxide formation; the previous use of MEK gave high impurity levels.
Solution_Description: The recrystallisation solvent was switched to anhydrous 2‑MeTHF (seeded) with BHT as an antioxidant; temperature ramps (0 °C → 35 °C → 0 °C) were programmed to control nucleation and growth, delivering the desired polymorph with low impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Hydroperoxide impurities were still found to form in the final recrystallisation procedure used to control the polymorphic form of the API, especially when the solvent utilized was methyl ethyl ketone (MEK).', 'A seeded recrystallisation of the API 1 from anhydrous 2‑MeTHF afforded the desired polymorph with minimal hydroperoxide formation in comparison to the previous solvent.', 'The presence of the stabiliser butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) in the anhydrous 2‑MeTHF solvent was hypothesised as playing a role in minimising the hydroperoxide formation.']

Paper Title: Feasibility Study on Continuous Flow Controlled/Living Anionic Polymerization Processes
Problem_Description: Maintaining a precisely defined relative flow‑rate of the initiator and monomer streams is difficult in continuous‑flow operation; slight drifts cause changes in molecular‑weight, dispersity and overall yield over time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors controlled the monomer/initiator ratio by adjusting the flow‑rates of each feed (order‑and‑rate‑of‑addition) and by changing the stoichiometry (mol ratio) of monomer to initiator; the micro‑reactor’s T‑shaped micromixers and short micro‑tube reactors provide rapid, efficient mixing, eliminating residence‑time variations.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the molecular weight and molecular weight distribution of polymer products are quite sensitive to the relative flow rate of an initiator solution and that of a monomer solution.” (abstract)

Paper Title: Crystallization-Induced Dynamic Resolution of a Diarylmethylamine toward the Synthesis of a Potent TRPM8 Inhibitor

Problem_Description: The magnetic‑stir method, while effective on small scale, does not translate directly to larger batches; a scalable analog for particle‑size reduction and solid‑liquid mass transfer was needed.

Solution_Description: Identified formaldehyde as the optimal racemization agent; its high electrophilicity accelerates iminium‑ion formation, providing rapid epimerization and enabling a practical CIDR workflow.

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine
Problem_Description: The original palladium‑mediated cyanation of intermediate 4 gave >1 % bis‑cyano impurity (2‑CN) on laboratory scale and >1 % on scale‑up, which could not be removed by crystallisation and required HPLC‑purification, reducing overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: Replace the Pd‑catalysed cyanation with a copper‑mediated cyanation of the iodo‑pyridone 6 using CuCN in NMP/DMF at 105–110 °C. This route eliminates the bis‑cyano impurity, proceeds in a single step, and avoids the need for a glove‑box.
Supporting_Evidence: “...several palladium catalysts were screened for the cyanation of 4… >1 % bis‑cyano impurity… outside the glovebox environment.”; “Treatment of iodo‑pyridone 6 with CuCN in DMF or NMP at 120 °C readily afforded complete conversion to the desired pyridone with no observed formation of the bis‑cyano impurity.”; “Cyanation of iodopyridone 6 using the aforementioned CuCN process in NMP at 105–110 °C provided full conversion… The bis‑cyano pyridone impurity 2‑CN could not be detected in material obtained from this route.”

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine
Problem_Description: The iridium‑catalysed C–H borylation used 4,4′‑di‑tert‑butyl‑2,2′‑bipyridyl (dtbpy), a high‑cost, long‑lead‑time ligand that limited large‑scale production of the 3‑chloro‑5‑iodophenol intermediate.
Solution_Description: Substitute dtbpy with inexpensive 2,2′‑bipyridine and lower the iridium loading from 1.5–3.0 mol % to 0.8–1.0 mol %, maintaining catalyst activity while reducing cost and improving availability.

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of chloropyridine 5 with potassium hydroxide caused agglomeration of potassium salts, forming a poorly‑agitated slurry that was not amenable to kilogram‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: Switch the base to sodium hydroxide; the reaction mixture remains a well‑agitated slurry throughout the process, enabling reliable large‑scale operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrolysis of chloropyridine 5 to pyridone 6 could be accomplished using either sodium or potassium hydroxide, but the latter resulted in agglomeration of potassium salts and was not amenable to large‑scale synthesis. In contrast, the use of sodium hydroxide provided a reaction mixture that remained a well‑agitated slurry throughout the course of the reaction.”

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine

Supporting_Evidence: “Screening of base and solvent for the final methylation step immediately revealed that the highest levels of conversion to product could be obtained in DMAc or DMSO… This is most likely due to the very low solubility of pyridone 2 in many organic solvents.”; “We elected to not drive the reaction to completion and instead opted to quench the reaction once >90 % conversion was reached.”; “Additional bis‑methylated impurities were observed when the reaction was carried out at 40 °C, keeping the reaction between 5 and 10 °C provided an optimal balance of reaction time and purity profile.”

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine
Problem_Description: After the methylation step, the crude mixture required a labor‑intensive aqueous work‑up to isolate the API, adding waste and process time.

Supporting_Evidence: “Moving from DMAc to NMP as the reaction solvent further enhanced the process… enabling direct isolation of the crude compound after addition of water and obviating the need for an aqueous workup.”

Paper Title: A Robust Kilo-Scale Synthesis of Doravirine

Paper Title: Compact and Integrated Approach for Advanced End-to-End Production, Purification, and Aqueous Formulation of Lidocaine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Initial extraction using ethyl acetate, toluene, or methyl‑isobutyl‑ketone formed stable emulsions, giving poor phase separation and low recovery of lidocaine (5). Hexane gave only 30 % recovery in a single‑stage extraction, while diethyl‑ether gave higher recovery (≈60 %) but caused downstream purification difficulties.
Solution_Description: Hexane was selected as the extraction solvent because it separates cleanly, and its limited solubility for lidocaine was acceptable at the low upstream concentration.  A co‑addition of aqueous sodium‑chloride (salt‑out) further boosted extraction efficiency to >80 % yield while keeping the organic phase simple for downstream steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “Ethyl acetate, toluene, and methylisobutyl ketone each formed a stable emulsion, with a significant impact on the extraction efficiency, hence giving low yields.”; “Hexane led to only 30 % recovery for the extraction of 5 after a one‑stage extraction … Diethyl ether performed extremely well … but led to major issues further downstream … Hexane was therefore selected as extraction solvent …”; “DI water increased the extraction of 5 up to 80 %.”; “The best results were obtained by salting out 5 with aqueous sodium chloride … 95 % yield was obtained by combining hexane (3 mL min⁻¹) and saturated aqueous sodium chloride (≈40 wt % …).”

Paper Title: Compact and Integrated Approach for Advanced End-to-End Production, Purification, and Aqueous Formulation of Lidocaine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: When the NaCl‑salted hexane extraction (Method A) was used, a large fraction (up to 40 %) of diethyl‑amine (4) co‑extracted into the organic phase, which later caused impurity‑related purification problems and low overall yield of lidocaine‑HCl.
Solution_Description: A second extraction strategy (Method B) added ammonium chloride to the aqueous co‑feed.  The weak acid kept diethyl‑amine protonated in the aqueous phase while allowing lidocaine to partition into hexane, delivering ≈90 % yield of pure lidocaine (5) free of 4.
Supporting_Evidence: “Method A forced significant amounts of 4 (up to 40 %) to transfer into the organic phase, hence causing purification issues …”; “The best results were obtained using ammonium chloride as an additive … ammonium chloride enabled the selective extraction of 5 … while 4 remained protonated in the aqueous phase.”; “Extraction Method B … afforded 5 with 90 % yield (HPLC) and, more importantly, free of 4.”

Paper Title: Compact and Integrated Approach for Advanced End-to-End Production, Purification, and Aqueous Formulation of Lidocaine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: During reactive crystallization, a fast addition of the 0.5 M HCl solution (≥1 mL min⁻¹) caused rapid supersaturation, leading to the formation of an amorphous, gum‑like lidocaine‑HCl that coated the impeller, shaft and reactor walls, creating processing fouling and poor crystal quality.
Solution_Description: The addition rate of the HCl solution was reduced to 0.1 mL min⁻¹ and the residence time was extended (≈8 h) to allow controlled nucleation and growth.  This produced highly crystalline lidocaine‑HCl, eliminated incrustations, and improved yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Faster flow rates caused the precipitation of an amorphous and gum‑like 5·HCl leading to massive incrustations on the impeller, shaft, and reactor walls.”; “Slower addition rate drastically increased the crystallinity of 5·HCl …”; “A prolonged holding time of 8 h supported the formation of a suspension of finely divided crystals … prevented incrustation of the impeller, shaft, reactor wall, and transfer line.”

Paper Title: Compact and Integrated Approach for Advanced End-to-End Production, Purification, and Aqueous Formulation of Lidocaine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The presence of large amounts of diethyl‑amine hydrochloride (4·HCl) in the feed (extraction Method A) caused severe corrosion of the stainless‑steel crystallization tank used for the antisolvent cooling step.
Solution_Description: Switching to extraction Method B (ammonium‑chloride additive) eliminated diethyl‑amine from the organic stream, preventing corrosion and allowing clean downstream purification of lidocaine‑HCl.
Supporting_Evidence: “Extraction Method A ultimately led to severe corrosion issues … due to the presence of large amounts of 4·HCl.”; “Reactive crystallization on the solution obtained from Method B led to a crystalline material containing exclusively 5·HCl … No corrosion issues were noticed while using Method B.”

Paper Title: Compact and Integrated Approach for Advanced End-to-End Production, Purification, and Aqueous Formulation of Lidocaine Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Attempts to crystallize lidocaine‑HCl by direct cooling or evaporative crystallization at the low feed concentration (≈34.6 mg mL⁻¹) required impractically long residence times and caused extensive wall incrustation, resulting in very low product yield.

This generated rapid, uniform supersaturation, produced 88 % isolated yield with 97.7 % purity, and avoided wall fouling.
Supporting_Evidence: “Attempts of cooling and evaporation crystallization … led to extensive incrustation on the wall … and thus very low yield.”; “Antisolvent cooling crystallization … was achieved by adding hexane at a flow rate of 2 mL min⁻¹ to a 34.6 mg mL⁻¹ feed solution … under moderate stirring (200 rpm) while cooling from 50 to 5 °C … afforded crystals of 5·HCl (88 % yield, 97.7 % HPLC purity), … without major incrustation issues.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Doebner–Miller Reaction and Isolation Using Continuous Stirred Tank Reactors
Problem_Description: The Doebner–Miller reaction forms a sticky polymeric solid (poly‑crotonaldehyde) that precipitates and clogs tubular or micro‑channel reactors, making the reaction mixture turbid at temperatures < 85 °C and causing handling difficulties in flow reactors.

Solution_Description: A series of continuous stirred‑tank reactors (CSTRs) were employed, each equipped with a disk‑type turbine impeller to keep the polymer in suspension and prevent clogging. Problem_Description: Batch experiments required ∼200 min residence time to obtain modest yields (≤ 76 % isolated) and the work‑up was time‑consuming with handling losses.

The work‑up was performed continuously in two downstream CSTRs with pH‑adjusted NaOH addition, eliminating batch isolation steps and reducing losses.

Problem_Description: Use of phosphoric acid as a homogeneous catalyst in Doebner–Miller reactions is economically unattractive because it cannot be recovered and is highly corrosive.

Paper Title: Manufacturing Development and Genotoxic Impurity Control Strategy of the Hedgehog Pathway Inhibitor Vismodegib

Paper Title: Multigram Scale Synthesis of A21, A New Antibiotic Equally Effective and Less Toxic than Amphotericin B
