Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: Photolysis in batch suffers from scale‑limitations: light penetration drops with distance from the lamp, giving non‑uniform irradiation that forces long residence times and causes product over‑irradiation and decomposition.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow photochemical system was built by wrapping narrow‑diameter FEP tubing around a quartz immersion well (triple‑wrapped) so that every molecule experiences uniform UV light; the flow reactor also improves mass‑transfer and eliminates dead zones.
Supporting_Evidence: “The drawback to this method is the use of photolysis… Light penetration… leads to nonuniform irradiation… This inefficiency can lead to long reaction times and product decomposition from overirradiation.”; “The photochemical flow system consisted of… FEP tubing wrapped around the immersion well.”; “The narrow diameter of the tubing leads to uniform irradiation of the reaction.”

Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: When cyclohexane was used as solvent the oxaziridine and the FEP tubing decomposed, forming an orange‑brown solid that fouled the reactor and lowered product yield.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium from cyclohexane to acetonitrile prevented the observed decomposition and eliminated solid precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “We found that performing the reaction in cyclohexane led to various levels of decomposition of both the compound and the tubing… The decomposition products precipitated… Changing the solvent to acetonitrile minimized the decomposition.”

Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: Water cooling of the immersion well was insufficient; elevated temperatures caused substrate and tubing degradation and generated solvent vapor bubbles because the system was not pressurised.
Solution_Description: The cooling was supplemented with a stream of chilled nitrogen introduced into a surrounding Dewar flask, keeping the reactor exterior at ambient temperature and preventing overheating.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, water was run through the immersion well to cool the reaction, but this proved to be insufficient… high temperatures led to substantial decomposition… While a commercial chiller would have sufficed… a simple, inexpensive solution was to augment the water‑cooling with a stream of cooled nitrogen… The flow of nitrogen was maintained at a rate that easily kept the outside of the reactor at room temperature.”

Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: Running very concentrated oxaziridine solutions at high flow rates gave acceptable throughput (≈7 kg day⁻¹) but substantially reduced yields because of decomposition that precipitated in the tubing.
Solution_Description: The reaction concentration was lowered to 0.1 M and the reactor was triple‑wrapped in FEP tubing, which together gave higher, reproducible yields while still allowing continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “We successfully ran very concentrated solutions and very high flow rates… the yields suffered… so we elected to use more dilute solutions of oxaziridine.”; “The best results were obtained with more dilute solutions (0.1 M) and by triple‑wrapping the reactor in FEP tubing to maximize exposure of the substrate to the UV light.”

Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: The original synthesis of the target chiral bicyclic lactam required a hydrazoic‑acid step (a safety hazard) and gave low overall yields, including a demanding classical resolution.
Solution_Description: A four‑step asymmetric route was designed that uses the Lattes‑Aubé oxaziridine‑photochemistry, thereby avoiding hydrazoic acid and providing a strong chromophore in each step, which improved safety and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original route… suffered from low yields… the generation of hydrazoic acid… was a potential safety hazard.”; “We proposed a short, four‑step asymmetric route… using the Lattes‑Aubé chemistry… avoided the dangerous hydrazoic acid used in the original route.”

Paper Title: Photochemical Rearrangement of Chiral Oxaziridines in Continuous Flow: Application Toward the Scale-Up of a Chiral Bicyclic Lactam
Problem_Description: Photolysis of the bicyclic oxaziridine (13) on a 0.1 M scale proceeded more slowly than for the monocyclic substrates, leaving a significant amount of starting material after one pass.
Solution_Description: The unreacted oxaziridine was recovered by simple column chromatography, allowing isolation of the lactam (14) in 51 % yield and enabling reuse of starting material.
Supporting_Evidence: “Photolysis of 80 g of 13… proceeded at a slower rate… there was a significant amount of starting material remaining. However, this material was easily separated from the product by column chromatography to provide over 40 g of the chiral lactam 14 in 51 % yield…”

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The initial chemo‑enzymatic route using Novozyme 435 (Candida antarctica Lipase B) to esterify 5‑AD‑diol proceeded very slowly and required an impractically high enzyme loading (60 h, 100 % w/w enzyme) to reach full conversion.
Solution_Description: The researchers abandoned the lipase‑mediated esterification (Route A) and adopted an oxidoreductase‑based pathway (Route B) that employed a highly regio‑ and stereoselective ketoreductase from Sphingomonas wittichii to perform the key reduction step.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states: "our initial trials with 5‑androstene‑3,17‑diol (5‑AD‑diol, 6) indicated that with Novozyme 435 (Candida antarctica Lipase B) the reaction progressed slowly and required high enzyme loading (60 h, 100 % w/w enzyme, complete conversion to 28)."; "we turned our attention to oxidoreductases (Route B…)"; "identified a short‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase from Sphingomonas wittichii…"

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The base‑promoted isomerization of 4‑AD to 5‑AD showed poor reproducibility, with the amount of desired 5‑AD ranging from 50 % to 95 % by HPLC area in different batches.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a controlled kinetic quench into excess acetic acid, carefully regulated the addition rate, ensured efficient mixing, and kept the temperature below 30 °C to avoid localized high‑pH hotspots and improve conversion consistency.
Supporting_Evidence: "Initially, we observed great variability in the reaction outcome, with the relative amount of the desired 5‑AD varying from 50 to 95 % (by HPLC area %)."; "The exposure of the 5‑AD to basic conditions could be minimized by quenching the enolate into an excess of acetic acid… The addition rate, efficient mixing and temperature (<30 °C) have to be carefully controlled to achieve high yields and to prevent localized high‑pH ‘hotspots’ during the quench."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Oxygen‑dependent autoxidation during the isomerization step generated oxygenated impurities (19–23), compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: A rigorous nitrogen‑sparging protocol was introduced to maintain an oxygen‑free environment, dramatically reducing the levels of these oxidative side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: "The main impurities were ... oxygenated impurity ... autoxidation of the steroid backbone by molecular oxygen present in the reaction."; "Thus, the introduction of a rigorous nitrogen sparging protocol during the reactions reduced the levels of these impurities sufficiently; on a 300 g scale we were able to prepare crude 5‑AD of acceptable purity."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Use of 2 M NaOH or 1.7 M Na₂CO₃ caused localized high‑pH “hotspots” and occasional line blockages in the pH‑control system, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The base was switched to 1.4 M K₂CO₃, which has higher aqueous solubility and eliminates line‑blocking problems, providing more reliable pH control and better reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: "We replaced 2 M NaOH with 1.7 M Na₂CO₃ to avoid localized high‑pH ‘hotspots’… ultimately, we preferred 1.4 M K₂CO₃ solution as it possesses higher solubility in water… which improved process reproducibility and eliminated the risk of line blockage in the pH control apparatus."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The first‑generation ketoreductase preparation exhibited low specific activity (17–35 U/g), required high enzyme loadings (3–5 % w/w) and generated emulsions, raising material costs and complicating work‑up.
Solution_Description: Gene codon optimization, expression in a phage‑resistant E. coli BL21‑(DE3) host, high‑density fermentation, and ultrafiltration yielded a second‑generation liquid cell‑free extract with 39 U/mL activity, reducing enzyme loading and eliminating emulsions.
Supporting_Evidence: "The first generation ketoreductase preparation … had relatively low activity, 17–35 U/g … high enzyme loadings (3–5 % w/w) were required … resulting in emulsions."; "We optimized the gene … 90 % of the ketoreductase was solubly expressed. … high optical density fermentation … resulted in second‑generation enzyme produced as liquid cell free extract of 39 U/mL activity."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The enzyme preparation lost ~75 % of its activity after one month storage at 2–8 °C, compromising process robustness.
Solution_Description: Lyophilization of the enzyme was implemented, which restored long‑term stability and retained high activity (400–500 U/g) in the third‑generation powder.
Supporting_Evidence: "Upon storage for 1 month at 2–8 °C, we observed that the enzyme preparation lost 75 % of its activity… We discovered that lyophilization improved its storage and stability over time. Consequently, later batches of the enzyme were lyophilized to give third generation ketoreductase powder with 400–500 U/g activity."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: During the bioreduction, elevated temperatures (> 40 °C) and exposure to air increased the formation of oxygenated impurities (19–23) and caused partial reconversion of 5‑AD to 4‑AD, reducing purity.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was kept below 35 °C, pH was maintained between 6–7, and the reaction mixture was sparged with nitrogen to suppress oxidative degradation and maintain high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "During these bioreductions, we observed the formation of similar impurities… increased significantly at elevated temperatures (> 40 °C)… Maintaining the pH at 6–7 and temperature < 35 °C ensured an efficient biotransformation and minimized the reverse isomerization… Sparging of the bioreduction solutions with nitrogen was necessary to keep the level of the oxygenated impurities below 8 % from the initial 4–6 % present in the input crude 5‑AD."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: Attempts to crystallize crude DHEA after biotransformation gave low recoveries (10–55 %), making the isolation step inefficient.
Solution_Description: The crude DHEA was telescoped directly into the acetylation step, avoiding isolation; the subsequent acetylation and crystallization of DHEA acetate provided high overall yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Initially we intended to develop an efficient crystallization of crude DHEA… recoveries were low (10–55 %). Therefore, we decided to telescope the crude DHEA to the subsequent acetylation step… The acetylation of DHEA to its acetate proved to be a facile reaction… the modifications considerably simplified the process and provided both cost and operational benefits."

Paper Title: Development of a Chemoenzymatic Process for Dehydroepiandrosterone Acetate Synthesis
Problem_Description: The use of 2‑MeTHF as a cosolvent raised safety concerns due to its tendency to form explosive peroxides and increased enzyme loading requirements.
Solution_Description: Ethyl acetate (EtOAc) was selected as the preferred organic phase because it is cheaper, requires only modestly higher enzyme loading, and does not pose peroxide‑formation hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: "EtOAc was selected as the best solvent overall, since it was significantly cheaper, although it required 10–20 % higher enzyme loadings. Moreover, EtOAc offered a process safety advantage, as 2‑MeTHF may form explosive peroxides."

Paper Title: Improved Procedures for Gram-Scale Synthesis of Galeterone 3β-Imidazole and Galeterone 3β-Pyridine Methoxylate, Potent Androgen Receptor/Mnk Degrading Agents
Problem_Description: The original synthesis of galeterone 3β‑imidazole (2) gave a very low overall isolated yield (11 %) and produced several side‑products (3α‑isomer, 6β‑isomer, elimination products) that required tedious flash column chromatography and preparative HPLC to isolate the desired compound.
Solution_Description: A new four‑step synthetic route was developed that proceeds via a stereospecific 3β‑azide intermediate (8) using a Lewis‑acid‑mediated i‑steroid/retro‑i‑steroid rearrangement. The mesylation step was switched to anhydrous DCM with triethylamine as base, affording the mesylate (4) in 100 % yield, and the subsequent azidation was optimized to give 93 % isolated yield of 8. This route avoided the formation of the unwanted 6β‑isomer and eliminated the need for extensive chromatographic purification, delivering galeterone 3β‑imidazole (2) in 63 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “...treatment of 3β‑mesyl galeterone (4) with imidazole in refluxing toluene afforded the desired compound 2 (11 %), stereo 3α‑isomer (5, 3 %), positional 6β‑isomer (6, 35 %), and uncharacterized elimination products.”
• “...the mesylation of galaterone... was modified, by replacing DCM as solvent and using triethyl amine (TEA) as base. This modification gave 4, in 100 % yield after simple solvent removal...”
• “...the best yield (93 %), was obtained when 15 and 27 equiv of TMSN3 and BF3·OEt2, respectively, were used… 3β‑azido product (8) was isolated by filtration after neutralizing the reaction mixture (exothermic)…”
• “Finally, reduction of 3β‑azide (8) to 3β‑amine (10), followed by its cyclization … gave the desired 3β‑imidazole (2) in 75 % yield… overall yield 63 %.”

Solution_Description: Switch to a bubble‑column reactor where the gentle gas‑flow causes no carrier damage, enabling robust scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Occasional destruction of the enzyme carrier by the stirring device during reactions performed in the stirred tank reactor … should consider this issue as well as the energy input.”; “During reaction performed in the bubble column reactor no such effect of carrier destruction was observed.”

Paper Title: Process Characterization Studies for Solvent-Free Simultaneous Epoxidation and Transesterification of Fatty Acid Methyl Esters
Problem_Description: Simultaneous epoxidation + trans‑esterification required ≥ 24 h (up to 30 h) because water removal and phase‑property changes slowed the epoxidation step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimize reaction time by (i) applying the staged vacuum profile, (ii) using a 20 % excess of iso‑nonanol and 4 % excess of H₂O₂, and (iii) setting the gas flow to 40 L h⁻¹ in the bubble column to accelerate water removal and keep the organic phase less polar.
Supporting_Evidence: “The main reason for the long simultaneous reaction is the presence of high amount of water which has to be removed for complete esterification.”; “Best results were achieved with an excess of iso‑nonanol and H₂O₂ of 20 % and 4 %, respectively.”; “The reaction in the bubble column was performed under a gas flow of 40 L h⁻¹ … leading to a faster transesterification reaction and a slower epoxidation reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Characterization Studies for Solvent-Free Simultaneous Epoxidation and Transesterification of Fatty Acid Methyl Esters
Problem_Description: Epoxidation of methyl linoleate gave overlapping HPLC peaks (9,10‑ and 6,7‑epoxy isomers), preventing clear analysis of conversion.
Solution_Description: Switch the model substrate to methyl oleate, which provides well‑resolved chromatographic peaks and allows reliable monitoring of the simultaneous reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “The model system was not suitable for detailed description due to overlapping peaks in the HPLC chromatograms.”; “From this knowledge, it was decided to continue with the methyl oleate as a model system for the description of the simultaneous epoxidation and transesterification.”

Paper Title: Process Characterization Studies for Solvent-Free Simultaneous Epoxidation and Transesterification of Fatty Acid Methyl Esters
Problem_Description: Significant hydrolysis of the methyl ester produced free fatty acids (≈ 38 % for oleate), lowering the overall yield of the desired epoxide ester.
Solution_Description: Add a 20 % excess of iso‑nonanol (and 4 % excess H₂O₂) to drive the trans‑esterification forward, suppressing ester hydrolysis and reducing free‑acid formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulting product mixture shows about 38 % free acid content which originates from the hydrolysis of the methyl ester during reaction.”; “Best results were achieved with an excess of iso‑nonanol … of 20 %.”

Paper Title: Process Characterization Studies for Solvent-Free Simultaneous Epoxidation and Transesterification of Fatty Acid Methyl Esters
Problem_Description: During bubble‑column operation volatile components (H₂O₂, iso‑nonanol) are stripped with the gas, causing undesired loss of reactants.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimize the gas flow to 40 L h⁻¹, which balances removal of water/methanol while minimizing loss of H₂O₂ and iso‑nonanol; the chosen flow was experimentally determined as optimal.
Supporting_Evidence: “During aeration … removal is beneficial for by‑products … but it is undesired for the starting materials such as hydrogen peroxide and iso‑nonanol.”; “The reaction in the bubble column was performed under a gas flow of 40 L h⁻¹ which was determined as an optimum gas flow in respect to mixing and removal of byproducts as well as reduction of the unwanted removal of starting materials.”

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis and Purification of Acetylated Phosphatidyl Choline Headgroup
Problem_Description: Literature procedures for DAcPC required hydrophobic carboxylic acids and multistep sequences, which made scale‑up difficult and forced purification by column chromatography on a small‑scale (milligram‑gram) basis. The use of a long‑chain fatty acid was specifically employed to aid product isolation, but this adds cost and limits throughput.
Solution_Description: A one‑step synthesis was developed using inexpensive, bulk‑available GPC, acetic anhydride and DIPEA, followed by vacuum stripping of excess reagents and crystallization from water/acetone. This eliminates the need for hydrophobic fragments and chromatography, providing a scalable, high‑yielding process.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Typically, the compounds were prepared in small quantities—milligrams to few grams per reaction. However, for large‑scale synthesis (100 g to 1 kg), these purification approaches may not be ideal.", "The process typically uses a long chain fatty acid to facilitate the purification of the product among other synthetic goals.", "The one‑pot, scalable DAcPC synthesis using commercially available GPC, acetic anhydride (Ac₂O), and N,N‑diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA) was performed at 50–60 °C for 5 days.", "Excess reagents and byproducts were stripped off under high vacuum at 110 °C (6 h) and 120 °C (2 h). The resulting waxy solid was dissolved in water and crystallized from acetone.", "The crude product was purified by distillation, crystallization and washing, eliminating column chromatography."]

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis and Purification of Acetylated Phosphatidyl Choline Headgroup
Problem_Description: The modified Ichihara procedure used GPC adsorbed on kieselguhr; a gram‑scale reaction required >1 L of methanol to wash DAcPC off the solid support and column chromatography showed severe tailing, consuming ~7 L of solvent to recover only 650 mg of product.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was changed to a solvent‑based protocol: after reaction completion the mixture was vacuum‑distilled, the residue was dissolved in water, and DAcPC was crystallized from acetone. This removes the solid support and chromatography steps, dramatically reducing solvent usage.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A gram‑scale reaction needed more than a liter of methanol to wash DAcPC off the kieselguhr.", "DMAP as the product seemed to have severe tailing when column chromatography was attempted with even 100% methanol containing 5% ammonia (∼7 L of solvent required to recover ∼650 mg of DAcPC).", "Excess reagents and byproducts were stripped off under high vacuum at 110 °C (6 h) and 120 °C (2 h). The resulting waxy solid was dissolved in 2 mol equiv of water and crystallized from acetone.", "The purification by distillation, crystallization and washing gave 94–95 % HPLC purity without any column chromatography."]

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis and Purification of Acetylated Phosphatidyl Choline Headgroup
Problem_Description: Use of DMAP as catalyst in the original procedure caused severe tailing of DAcPC on silica columns, making isolation inefficient and requiring large solvent volumes.
Solution_Description: DMAP was replaced by the cheaper, less nucleophilic base DIPEA (3 mol equiv) and the stoichiometry of acetic anhydride was adjusted (4 mol equiv), which prevented tailing and simplified work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The modified procedure… treated with excess acetic anhydride (2.5 mol equiv) in the presence of N,N‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) for 60 h… the procedure showed severe tailing of DAcPC during column purification.", "DIPEA was used instead of DMAP as the base.", "About 4 mol equiv of Ac₂O and 3 mol equiv of DIPEA were added to GPC."]

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis and Purification of Acetylated Phosphatidyl Choline Headgroup
Problem_Description: DAcPC crystals absorb atmospheric water over time; after standing for days or weeks the water content rises from the monohydrate (≈5 % wt) to nearly a dihydrate (≈9 % wt), causing batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: Water content was quantified by TGA and Karl Fisher titration, and crystals were stored as the monohydrate under desiccated conditions; prior to use the material can be re‑lyophilized to ensure a defined water level.
Supporting_Evidence: ["If crystallized DAcPC monohydrate is left standing for days or weeks without desiccation, the water content increases to almost two molecules of water per DAcPC.", "Thermogravimetric analysis… showed a weight loss of 7.9 % between 77.6 °C and 117.5 °C, more than expected for a monohydrate.", "Karl Fisher titration of the air‑exposed DAcPC crystals showed the water content of 9.3 %, almost double that of monohydrate."]

Paper Title: Scalable Synthesis and Purification of Acetylated Phosphatidyl Choline Headgroup
Problem_Description: The one‑pot acetylation of GPC required 5 days at 55 °C to reach completion, which limits throughput for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: While the authors retained the 5‑day reaction, they emphasized that the single‑step nature eliminates subsequent multistep operations, effectively reducing total process time compared with prior multistep routes.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The one‑pot, scalable DAcPC synthesis… was performed at 50–60 °C for 5 days.", "Previous multistep procedures required several isolated intermediates and additional purification steps, extending the overall time."]

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: No reliable large‑scale source for the chiral phthalimido epoxide (compound 2) and the pilot‑plant reactors were not equipped to handle epichlorohydrin safely.
Solution_Description: Developed two alternative synthetic routes to the epoxide: (a) a seven‑step sequence starting from commercially available (S)-(+)-solketal and (b) a shorter two‑step Sharpless‑type procedure using readily available (R)-(‑)-3‑chloro‑1,2‑propanediol.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “the available reactors were not equipped to handle epichlorohydrin safely, so two alternate syntheses of this compound were evaluated for the first batches at pilot scale.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required six chemical steps to give the epoxide with only 27 % overall yield, making the process inefficient for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: Implemented a concise two‑step synthesis of the epoxide from (R)-(‑)-3‑chloro‑1,2‑propanediol, raising the overall yield of the epoxide stage to 62.4 % and cutting the number of steps in half.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “The first epoxide 2 batches were prepared from (S)-(+)-solketal 10 in six chemical steps in about 27 % overall yield.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: Isolation of the quaternary ammonium salt 6 was difficult because the product is highly water‑soluble, hygroscopic and tended to oil out, leading to low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Switched the reaction medium to α,α,α‑trifluorotoluene, telescoped the alkylation/mesylation/quaternization steps without intermediate isolation, and crystallized the final salt directly, giving an average 74 % isolated yield on 60 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “the remaining challenge was isolation of quaternary ammonium salt 6 from the rather complex reaction mixture, taking into account its high water solubility and hygroscopicity … to limit the yield of isolation of quaternary ammonium salt 6.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: The original de‑protection of the phthalimido group used catalytic hydrogenolysis followed by hydrazine hydrate, both hazardous reagents for large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: Replaced the two‑step hydrogenolysis/hydrazine sequence with a one‑pot acid‑mediated de‑protection using 20 % HCl, eliminating the need for hydrazine and improving safety and industrial hygiene.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “Our strategy for simplifying this into a one‑pot reaction was to use hydrochloric acid as a single reagent. Additionally, the elimination of hydrazine hydrate … was considered beneficial with regard to safety and hygiene.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: The literature synthesis of acid 9 required handling of chlorine gas, which posed significant safety and equipment challenges on pilot scale.
Solution_Description: Adopted an alternative five‑step sequence that starts from inexpensive bromination of 1,4‑benzodioxan‑5‑carboxylic acid, avoids chlorine gas, and uses N‑chlorosuccinimide for the final chlorination, delivering 43.7 kg of acid 9 safely.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “the only published procedure to synthesize … required special safety equipment compatible with chlorine gas manipulation … this route was deemed impractical in our facility.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: Final amide coupling with DCC generated by‑products that required chromatographic purification, adding cost, waste and operational complexity.
Solution_Description: Switched to a mixed‑anhydride coupling using pivaloyl chloride/triethylamine at 0 °C, which gave the desired amide without DCC‑related by‑products and eliminated the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “this reagent presented an important disadvantage due to the generation of byproducts that required removal by chromatography.”

Paper Title: Pilot Scale Process Development of SL65.0102-10, an
Problem_Description: During recrystallization of the epoxide 2 in ethanol, partial degradation was observed, reducing overall isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Optimized the one‑pot epoxidation by using equimolar amounts (1.5 equiv) of sodium methoxide and chlorotrimethylsilane, and avoided the recrystallization step, which gave 65–74 % yields with >98 % purity on pilot scale.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: “we showed that the epoxide 2 partially degraded during the recrystallization in ethanol.”

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The Phase‑II manufacturing route used a hazardous combination of sodium hydride and DMSO for the conversion of 2 → 6 and generated a large amount of the undesired cis‑isomer of intermediate 3, which required wasteful downstream processing.
Solution_Description: The process was re‑engineered by replacing NaH/DMSO with potassium tert‑butoxide, reducing reaction volumes, eliminating the isolation of intermediate 6, and telescoping directly to the trans‑oxalate salt of 3, which could be crystallised from a methanol/IPA/ethyl‑acetate mixture. This removed the unsafe reagents, cut waste, and gave a clean isolated trans‑isomer.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Key problems within the route were the potentially hazardous combination of sodium hydride and DMSO in the transformation of 2 to 6 and the wasteful onward processing of the undesired cis‑isomer of 3.', 'After much development, the key changes involved substituting the base (for potassium tert‑butoxide)... and the isolation of the first intermediate 6 could be eliminated.', 'It was surprisingly possible to isolate the pure trans isomer of 3 very cleanly by directly crystallizing the oxalate salt from a methanol/IPA/ethyl acetate mixture.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Conversion of 3 → 4 gave poor yields (<30 %) on scale because the strained electrophilic urea had to be introduced before ester hydrolysis; selective hydrolysis of the trans‑isomer required tight temperature, pH and time control, which was difficult to reproduce at larger scale.
Solution_Description: A counter‑intuitive protecting‑group strategy was introduced: the piperidine nitrogen of 3 was protected with FMOC, the amide was formed first, then CDI acylated the hydroxylamine nitrogen, and FMOC deprotection with diethylamine triggered spontaneous cyclisation to the urea. The steps are quantitative, telescoped, and give >90 % yield on commercial scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The conversion of 3 to 4 proved difficult to scale; the introduction of the fragile electrophilic strained urea prior to treatment with nucleophilic reagents required to convert the ester moiety to the primary amide meant that yields were seen to fall as the process was scaled.', 'Both BOC and FMOC protection can be readily achieved on the piperidine nitrogen, with subsequent quantitative acylation of the hydroxylamine nitrogen with CDI.', 'Deprotection of FMOC using diethylamine allows spontaneous cyclization to form the urea, and the addition of aqueous acid facilitates removal of the basic species and promotes crystallization.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The debenzylation‑sulfation sequence (4 → 5) suffered from rapid degradation of the unstable hydroxylamine intermediate 10, which poisoned the Pd/C catalyst, forcing use of a very high (20 % wt) dry catalyst and a DMF/DCM solvent system that required a labor‑intensive solvent swap to xylene; the sulfating agent SO₃·DMF was also moisture‑sensitive.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A one‑pot deprotection/sulfation was developed using a 1:1 iPrOH/water solvent blend (lowering the pKₐ of the hydroxylamine), a catalytic amount of NEt₃, and the more stable SO₃·NMe₃ reagent. This allowed simultaneous debenzylation and sulfation, reduced Pd loading to ~2 % rel wt (wet catalyst tolerated), and controlled hydrogen addition via nitrogen inerting and slow H₂ dosing, eliminating the solvent swap and catalyst poisoning.
Supporting_Evidence: ['By changing the solvent mixture from DMF/DCM to 1:1 iPrOH:water, the pKa of the intermediate hydroxylamine 10 was lowered, such that the anion could be formed by introducing a catalytic amount of mild base (NEt₃).', 'This resulted in a dramatic reduction in the amount of catalyst required; to approximately 2 % rel wt loading (of 10 % Pd/C), since poisoning by degradation products of 10 was significantly lowered.', 'By inerting the starting mixture with nitrogen at ambient pressure and controlling the flow of hydrogen slowly into the vessel, the effective rate of debenzylation was greatly decreased, so that 10 was slowly produced, and quickly sulfated.', 'Hydrogen was rapidly consumed as it was dosed into the vessel, until debenzylation was complete. At this point the pressure began to rise as the unreacted hydrogen remained in the headspace.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original commercial process had a process‑mass‑intensity (PMI) of 6480 and required environmentally undesirable reagents such as DMF and triphosgene, leading to high raw‑material costs and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A completely new manufacturing sequence was implemented that removed DMF and triphosgene, replaced them with safer, cheaper solvents (e.g., chlorobenzene for the urea step and iPrOH/water for sulfation), and employed a lower‑load, wet Pd/C catalyst. The overall PMI fell to 526 (≈92 % reduction) and raw‑material costs dropped ~4‑fold, meeting commercial cost‑of‑goods targets.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The PMI calculation for the synthesis (from 2) has been reduced from 6480 to 526, which represents a 92 % improvement in efficiency, and several environmentally undesirable reagents (such as DMF and triphosgene) have been removed.', 'An approximately 4‑fold reduction in costs has been demonstrated, and the commercial targets for cost of goods have been achieved.', 'Chlorobenzene was chosen as the solvent, to facilitate the exceptionally operable processing described.', 'It also allowed the use of cheaper and more safely handled wet catalyst, and made the work up considerably simpler.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: High agitation speeds during the hydrogenation step increased the rate of debenzylation relative to sulfation, causing buildup of the unstable intermediate 10 and lowering overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reaction agitation was moderated, the vessel was inerted with nitrogen, and hydrogen was fed slowly, allowing the rate of debenzylation to be matched to sulfation; pressure monitoring was used as a real‑time indicator of reaction progress.
Supporting_Evidence: ['High agitation speeds led to buildup of the intermediate 10 and lower yields through increased rate of debenzylation.', 'By inerting the starting mixture with nitrogen at ambient pressure and controlling the flow of hydrogen slowly into the vessel, the effective rate of debenzylation was greatly decreased, so that 10 was slowly produced, and quickly sulfated.', 'The reaction could thus be easily controlled and furthermore, could be monitored by observing the pressure in the vessel.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The earlier route produced a mixture of trans‑ and cis‑isomers of intermediate 3, requiring separate processing of the undesired cis‑isomer, which reduced overall yield and added purification steps.
Solution_Description: The process was telescoped to avoid isolation of intermediate 6 and the trans‑isomer of 3 was isolated directly as an oxalate salt by crystallisation from a methanol/IPA/ethyl‑acetate mixture, reducing solvent usage and improving overall yield to 56 % for 3.
Supporting_Evidence: ['It was also found that isolation of the first intermediate 6 could be eliminated and that, surprisingly, the pure trans isomer of 3 could be isolated very cleanly by directly crystallizing the oxalate salt from a methanol/IPA/ethyl acetate mixture.', 'Ultimately, a fully telescoped procedure to a single isomer of 3 from 2 was realized.', 'The route was successfully scaled to 340 kg (input) scale to produce a total of 1080 kg of 3 in five batches with an overall yield of 56 %.']

Paper Title: Development of a Manufacturing Route to Avibactam, a β‑Lactamase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The sulfating reagent SO₃·DMF is moisture‑sensitive and required handling of a highly toxic, non‑commercial reagent, adding safety and cost burdens.
Solution_Description: The sulfation agent was switched to the more stable, water‑compatible SO₃·NMe₃, which could be used in the iPrOH/water solvent system with a catalytic base, thereby improving safety and lowering reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The handling of the highly moisture sensitive and non‑commercial sulfating agent, sulfur trioxide‑N,N‑dimethylformamide complex (SO₃·DMF) was also problematic, but made necessary, since the reactivity of alternative (more stable) sulfur trioxide complexes were not sufficient to react with the weakly nucleophilic hydroxylamine 10.', 'By changing the solvent mixture from DMF/DCM to 1:1 iPrOH:water, the pKa of the intermediate hydroxylamine 10 was lowered, such that the anion could be formed by introducing a catalytic amount of mild base (NEt₃) to the reaction. The resultant anion was seen to be nucleophilic enough to react with water‑stable sulfur trioxide‑amine complexes, specifically the commercially available sulfur trioxide‑trimethylamine (SO₃·NMe₃).']

Paper Title: A Small-Footprint, High-Capacity Flow Reactor for UV Photochemical Synthesis on the Kilogram Scale
Problem_Description: FEP tubing is not completely UV‑transparent; kinks, abrasions or photochemical damage create weak spots that can rupture under pressure and must be replaced, and the material is prone to fouling and blockage when scaling up.
Solution_Description: Replace the FEP coil with a modular array of quartz tubes that are UV‑transparent, chemically durable and can be assembled around the UV lamp as a single high‑surface‑area reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "although FEP is a versatile material, it is not completely UV transparent, and any kinks or abrasions leads to weak spots that rupture under pressure requiring the whole length of FEP tubing to be replaced."

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: The original synthesis used a 10 % Pd/C hydrogenolysis to remove the O‑benzyl protecting group. This required prolonged treatment with metal scavengers (Smopex 243) to reduce palladium to <10 ppm, creating safety concerns due to palladium handling and long exposure to metal‑scavenger waste.
Solution_Description: A completely new two‑step route was designed that avoids Pd‑catalyzed hydrogenation and the associated scavenger treatment, using suberic acid and methyl paraben as inexpensive building blocks.
Supporting_Evidence: “final protective group removal with 10% Pd/C required prolonged metal scavenger treatment … to reduce palladium levels to <10 ppm.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: During activation of the carboxylic acid 9 with isobutyl chloroformate (IBCF) in NMP, the reaction was highly exothermic and SHP‑141 (1) proved unstable under the low‑temperature conditions, forming oligomeric self‑condensation products (19) and N‑O cleavage product (20).
Solution_Description: The activation was performed at ≤ –10 °C, the hydroxylamine solution was buffered to pH 5–6 with acetate/acetic acid, and the addition of the IBCF‑derived intermediate (18) was performed inversely (adding 18 to the hydroxylamine mixture) to minimise exposure of 1 to excess reagent and heat.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both the activation of 9 with IBCF/NMM and the addition of aqueous NH₂OH to 18/NMP were exothermic reactions and thus required low temperature, i.e., ≤ –10 °C, and efficient mixing.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: When DIPEA was added in a single bolus on 40 g scale, the reaction mixture precipitated DIPEA·HCl and DIPEA·MsOH salts, becoming too thick to stir and leading to low and inconsistent yields of the desired product 9.
Solution_Description: The base addition was split: a reduced initial charge of DIPEA (1.3 equiv) was added before the first step, followed by staged additions after heating, which kept the slurry fluid and gave reproducible yields (≈ 40–42 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “when DIPEA (2 equiv) was added in one portion on 40 g scale … the heterogeneous reaction mixture became too thick to stir … Comparable yields … observed when the first charge of organic base (DIPEA) was added in a single portion … or divided between Step 1a and Step 1b.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: Crude SHP‑141 (1) was unstable in acetonitrile at ≥ 45 °C and in strongly acidic media (pH < 3), leading to degradation and poor isolated yields after precipitation.
Solution_Description: A stabilising package of 0.1 % citric acid and 4 % water was added to the ACN solution, which markedly reduced decomposition and allowed high‑purity precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “crude 1 was stabilized for recrystallization in acetonitrile (ACN) solution by the addition of 0.1 % citric acid and 4 % water.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: Precipitation of 1 from the reaction mixture produced very fine particles that filtered slowly (≈ 1 h for 25 g) and caused filtration bottlenecks.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent system (pre‑cooled toluene with 8 % brine) was employed during precipitation, generating larger granular aggregates that filtered rapidly (≤ 1 min) and reduced degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “pre‑cooled 8 % brine/toluene … produced a granular solid … reduced filtration time to < 1 min compared with ≥ 1 h for water‑only precipitation.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: Recrystallisation of 1 with high percentages of water in ACN gave high purity but lower overall recovery (≤ 64 %).
Solution_Description: The water content was limited to 4 % (v/v) with 0.1 % citric acid, and a four‑step temperature‑cycling profile (45 °C→30 °C→35 °C→10 °C) was applied, improving recovery to 72 % while maintaining > 99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “higher percentages of water … could negatively impact the recovery … 0.1 % citric acid/4 % water in ACN … 45 °C … temperature cycles … 72 % recovery, 100 % area.”

Paper Title: Process Development of the Soft Histone Deacetylate Enzyme Inhibitor SHP-141: Acylation of Methyl Paraben and Suberyl Hydroxamic Acid Formation
Problem_Description: Separating the side‑product methyl‑paraben bis‑ester 12 from the desired 9·DIPEA salt was cumbersome using standard aqueous work‑up.
Solution_Description: A hot toluene extraction was introduced after Stage 1b to partition 12 into the organic phase, leaving purified 9·DIPEA in the aqueous layer.
Supporting_Evidence: “implementation of a hot toluene extraction to separate 12 from 9·DIPEA salt (Stage 1b).”

Paper Title: A Simple Scale-up Strategy for Organolithium Chemistry in Flow Mode: From Feasibility to Kilogram Quantities
Problem_Description: Batch organolithium reactions at cryogenic temperature (JT = −78 °C) gave a poor 21 % HPLC yield because the aryl‑lithium intermediate decomposed rapidly; operating at −78 °C is also expensive and technically demanding on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to a continuous‑flow ‘flash‑chemistry’ platform, performing the halogen/lithium exchange and borylation at a non‑cryogenic temperature (JT = −30 °C) with a residence time of 0.5 s per step, which raised the isolated HPLC yield to ca. 90 % and avoided the need for cryogenic equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Experiments under traditional batch conditions at cryogenic temperatures (JT = −78 °C) resulted in poor yield (21% HPLC yield) due to rapid decomposition of the generated Li‑species (3a).”

Paper Title: A Simple Scale-up Strategy for Organolithium Chemistry in Flow Mode: From Feasibility to Kilogram Quantities
Problem_Description: Scaling batch organolithium reactions can produce hot‑spots, poor mixing, and longer residence times, leading to variable yields, impurity formation and decomposition of the sensitive aryl‑lithium intermediate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopt simple PFA tubing (instead of stainless steel) that limits heat‑removal, combined with short residence times (0.5 s) to keep the process quasi‑adiabatic and use a highly efficient static‑mixing element array to guarantee rapid mixing and uniform temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The exact exotherm of the reaction is only of minor importance when the robustness and safety of the reaction can be guaranteed over a broad temperature range.”

Paper Title: A Simple Scale-up Strategy for Organolithium Chemistry in Flow Mode: From Feasibility to Kilogram Quantities
Problem_Description: Potential clogging and pressure build‑up could arise if the reactants, intermediates or product are insufficiently soluble at the chosen concentrations, jeopardising continuous operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Maintain the same 0.3 M THF concentration that was proven soluble in the lab‑scale system and employ a T‑piece feed arrangement that minimizes premixing, allowing the static mixers to handle the mixing without forming solids.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction is feasible in flow mode as no pressure built‑up was observed during different runs, demonstrating the solubility of all reaction partners and intermediates at the applied concentrations.”

Paper Title: A Simple Scale-up Strategy for Organolithium Chemistry in Flow Mode: From Feasibility to Kilogram Quantities
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the heat‑dissipation capacity changes, potentially leading to fully adiabatic temperature rises that could exceed the stability window of the aryl‑lithium intermediate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Measure the internal temperature with an in‑line thermocouple at the reactor exit to confirm the adiabatic temperature increase (ΔT_ad ≈ 28 °C) and keep the jacket temperature low enough (−30 °C) so that the maximum internal temperature remains within the safe region.
Supporting_Evidence: • “As the heat‑dissipation capability of the setup will change toward fully adiabatic reaction conditions during scale‑up, the adiabatic temperature increase … become highly important, and the stability of intermediates and product at MTSR has to be ensured.”

Paper Title: A Simple Scale-up Strategy for Organolithium Chemistry in Flow Mode: From Feasibility to Kilogram Quantities
Problem_Description: A robust scale‑up required a mixing strategy that could be linearly expanded without loss of performance; simple T‑piece scaling was deemed insufficient for larger diameters.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implement commercially available PTFE static‑mixers (minimum 12 elements for <10 mm ID tubing) to guarantee complete mixing at the chosen scale, thereby preserving the 0.5 s residence‑time chemistry.

Paper Title: Handling Hazards Using Continuous Flow Chemistry: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The triazole products formed in the telescoped sequence often have poor solubility in common organic solvents, leading to precipitation during the flow process.  In addition, the generation of nitrogen gas during the diazotization/azidodediazotization steps creates a segmented (gas‑liquid) flow that makes it difficult to keep accurate stoichiometric ratios when the subsequent reagents are introduced.  When the aryl‑azide stream was combined directly with the dipolarophile (as in the Stazi method) the reaction suffered from imbalanced dipole/dipolarophile ratios and, in the Ley polymer‑supported approach, solid plugs formed inside the column, hampering isolation and steady‑state operation.  Finally, performing the Cu(I)‑catalyzed azide‑alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) at room temperature gave only 46 %–12 % conversion, indicating a low‑yield problem, while the overall sequence involves highly energetic diazonium and aryl‑azide intermediates that pose safety concerns on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors solved the solubility issue by performing all steps in dimethyl‑sulfoxide (DMSO) and, when necessary, diluting the reaction mixture to 0.33 M and adding a dedicated neat‑DMSO stream (Method B) to keep the triazole in solution.  An ultrasonic bath was employed during the diazotization‑azidodediazotization sequence to degas the mixture and produce a well‑segmented, gas‑free stream that could be collected in an intermediate reservoir.  The reservoir, together with a custom‑controlled continuous‑flow unit (CFU) and in‑house software, allowed the aryl‑azide stream to be re‑combined with the downstream reagents in a continuous, stoichiometrically‑balanced fashion, eliminating the imbalanced addition problem of the Stazi method and the plug formation observed with the Ley column.  For the CuAAC step, the temperature was raised to 60 °C and 1,10‑phenanthroline (2.5 mol %) was added as a cheap and efficient ligand, delivering quantitative conversion even at low catalyst loadings.  Overall, the continuous‑flow platform kept only milligram quantities of the high‑energy diazonium and aryl‑azide intermediates at any time, greatly enhancing safety.

Problem_Description: The reaction of sodium aryl sulfinates with hydrophobic nitriles (e.g., benzyl cyanide) forms a biphasic mixture that readily generates a stable emulsion when stirred, making pumping and mixing in continuous‑flow microwave‑heated reactors difficult; the heterogeneous mixture also hampers temperature control because conventional thermocouples cannot be used inside the microwave field, leading to uncertain heat‑up profiles; metal precipitation on the inner surface of the borosilicate‑glass (BSG) reactor and the possibility of microwave‑induced hot‑spots raise safety concerns and can cause reactor cracking; at low flow rates (0.5 mL min⁻¹) the residence time is longer but temperature control becomes erratic, giving lower and variable yields; at higher flow rates (2 mL min⁻¹) the shorter residence time reduces conversion, also lowering the isolated yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A single‑stock solution containing all reagents was prepared and vigorously stirred to generate a segmented flow that could be pumped reliably, thereby overcoming the emulsion problem; an infrared Optris CSmicro 3 M sensor (and, for AlOx/SiC reactors, an Optris CT sensor) was employed to monitor the reaction temperature through the microwave‑transparent tube, providing reliable temperature feedback without intrusive thermocouples; aluminum‑oxide (AlOx) reactors were introduced as a safer, more thermostable alternative to BSG (no metal precipitation, higher maximum temperature, resistance to MW‑induced super‑heating); silicon‑carbide (SiC) reactors were also tested as a conventional‑heating analogue, confirming that the process does not rely on a specific microwave effect; the optimal flow rate of 1 mL min⁻¹ (50 s residence time at 120 °C) was selected to balance conversion and heat management, improving yield relative to both slower (0.5 mL min⁻¹) and faster (2 mL min⁻¹) conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem – Mixability: “the use of hydrophobic nitriles such as benzyl cyanide results in a biphasic reaction mixture… vigorous stirring produced an emulsion which could be pumped into the reactor in a controlled fashion.”
Problem – Exothermic/temperature monitoring: “conventional methods like thermocouples and mercury thermometers … are affected by the electromagnetic field … Consequently, the available options for accurate monitoring … are limited.”
Problem – Safety (metal precipitation): “metal precipitation on the surface as well as particle build‑up complicated the use of the AlOx reactor. In the BSG reactor we observed no metal precipitation on the glass; however, some particle build‑up was present.”
Problem – Safety (reactor cracking): “BSG reactors have previously been reported to undergo thermal cracking under MW processing.”
Problem – Low yield (0.5 mL min⁻¹): “The reaction temperature also proved more difficult to control at 0.5 mL min⁻¹, probably due to the different MW absorbing characteristics of the heterogeneous system… gave a lower yield (Entry 3).”
Problem – Low yield (2 mL min⁻¹): “Increasing the flow rate to 2 mL min⁻¹ resulted in somewhat reduced yield (Entry 5).”
Solution – Mixing: “we decided to use a simplified reaction setup with one stock solution … vigorous stirring produced an emulsion which could be pumped …”
Solution – Temperature monitoring: “we opted for an Optris CSmicro 3 M IR sensor … This sensor has a spectral response that allows measurement of reaction temperatures through BSG.”
Solution – AlOx reactor: “AlOx reactors may serve as a safe and useful alternative … AlOx reactors were identified as a safe and thermostable alternative to BSG reactors.”
Solution – SiC reactor: “By using a SiC reactor … we could mimic conventional heating and thus comment on a potential MW‑activated liquid interface.”
Solution – Flow‑rate optimization: “The best yield … was obtained at 120 °C and at a flow rate of 1 mL min⁻¹ … flow rate of 1 mL min⁻¹ (Entry 4) … chosen for investigation … providing a good balance between process control, production rate and product yield.”
