Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: During the Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation the chiral epoxide 9 is highly water‑soluble; aqueous work‑up caused substantial loss of 9 and the isolated epoxide is prone to polymerisation, giving low isolated yields of the subsequent intermediate 11.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the two‑step isolation of 9 and performed an in‑situ derivatization of 9 with p‑nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride 10 (or later with p‑trifluoromethoxyphenol 7) directly after epoxidation, avoiding aqueous work‑up and eliminating the polymerisation pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: “Following completion of the epoxidation reaction, the usual aqueous workup resulted in substantial loss of 9 owing to its high water solubility.”; “Nonaqueous workup involving vacuum distillation was unsuitable for scale‑up due to the viscous nature of the pot residue and the tendency of epoxide 9 to undergo polymerisation.”; “the in situ reaction of epoxide 9 with p‑nitrobenzenesulfonyl chloride 10 … was extremely tedious…”, “In situ reaction of epoxide 9 with p‑trifluoromethoxyphenol 7 proceeded smoothly…”.

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: Quenching the excess tert‑butyl hydroperoxide (TBHP) generated during epoxidation required the addition of trimethyl phosphite under very low temperature (≤ ‑20 °C); the reaction is violently exothermic and poses safety hazards on large scale.
Solution_Description: Instead of quenching TBHP with trimethyl phosphite, the process was redesigned to avoid quenching altogether; the epoxide was directly transformed in‑situ with phenol 7, and any residual TBHP was later destroyed by a controlled aqueous dilute H₂SO₄ wash after the epoxide ring had been opened.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because of the violent and exothermic reaction, it was necessary to quench the excess TBHP very carefully over a long period of time under cold conditions (below ‑20 °C) to avoid any unsafe situation.”; “We felt that… ignoring TBHP during in situ reaction of 9 with 7 and later destroying it with dilute sulfuric acid would be both safe and the most convenient option.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: The previously reported ester route required column chromatography for intermediates 16, 18 and the final product 2, leading to low overall yields and high solvent consumption on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new four‑step route (Scheme 4) was developed that avoids column chromatography; intermediates are isolated by simple crystallisation or precipitation, drastically reducing solvent use and improving isolated yields (e.g., 43 % for 19, 92 % for 21, 51 % overall for 2).
Supporting_Evidence: “This route was lengthy and unsuitable for scale‑up as the purification of compounds 16, 18, and 2 needed column chromatography.”; “In our hands, attempts to purify these compounds by recrystallization resulted in lower yields.”; “The new process… greatly simplified isolation procedures, economy due to savings on solvents required for chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: After the epoxidation‑diol sequence the organic layer contained residual TBHP, tartrate ester and molecular sieves, giving a cloudy, non‑phase‑separating mixture that hindered work‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was filtered through Celite before phase separation, and the organic layer was washed sequentially with dilute aqueous sulfuric acid (to destroy TBHP), aqueous NaOH (to remove phenol 7 and tartrate ester), and brine, giving a clear, phase‑separated product stream.
Supporting_Evidence: “The two‑phase mixture appeared translucent and did not give a clear phase separation, presumably due to the presence of molecular sieves and titanium tetraisopropoxide… Clear phase separation, however, was achieved after filtering the reaction mixture through Celite.”; “It occurred to us that TBHP in the organic layer could be removed if the organic layer was washed with dilute aqueous sulfuric acid.”; “The unreacted phenol 7 and tartrate ester were easily removed by washing the organic layer with 25 % aqueous sodium hydroxide solution.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: Preparation of anhydrous TBHP from the commercial 70 % aqueous solution traditionally uses azeotropic distillation, which is flammable, explosive and requires a blast‑shield – impractical and unsafe for kilogram‑scale batches.
Solution_Description: A safer, scalable protocol was introduced: the aqueous TBHP was extracted repeatedly with DCM, dried over anhydrous Na₂SO₄, filtered through activated molecular sieves and stored under nitrogen at 4 °C, eliminating the need for azeotropic distillation and reducing fire‑hazard risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “Procedures to prepare anhydrous TBHP in dichloromethane or toluene… involve azeotropic distillation… need to be carried out behind a blast shield… The safety concerns associated with azeotropic distillation on a large scale led us to devise a simpler procedure to obtain anhydrous TBHP.”; “The organic layer was carefully separated, stirred with anhydrous sodium sulfate for 30 min… activated molecular sieves (4 Å) were added… stored in an airtight HDPE container under nitrogen at 4 °C.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: Multiple recrystallisations of intermediate 11 (nosylate) were required to reach acceptable purity, which caused a substantial loss of material and reduced the overall yield of the sequence.
Solution_Description: The synthetic strategy was shifted to a pathway that avoids the isolated nosylate 11 altogether; instead, epoxide 9 is opened with phenol 7 to give diol 19, which is directly sulfonylated and cyclised in situ to afford oxirane 21, thereby eliminating the low‑yield recrystallisation step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The multiple recrystallizations needed to obtain substantially pure intermediate 11 inevitably resulted in lower yields of 11.”; “We therefore began to explore the possibility of making a derivative of 9 in situ by opening the epoxy ring… The in situ reaction of epoxide 9 with 7 proceeded smoothly to give the diol 19 in 45 % yield… The subsequent base‑catalyzed ring closure proceeded smoothly to give oxirane 21 in high enantiomeric excess and >95 % purity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the Synthesis of DNDI-VL-2098: A Potential Preclinical Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Visceral Leishmaniasis
Problem_Description: The aqueous work‑up of the Sharpless epoxidation caused loss of the water‑soluble epoxide 9, leading to low material throughput.
Solution_Description: The epoxidation was performed in dry DCM with activated molecular sieves, and the crude reaction mixture was directly transferred into the phenol 7/K₂CO₃ solution (no aqueous quench), thus keeping the epoxide in an organic phase and preserving material.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction mixture obtained after Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation of 8 was added slowly to a mixture of 7 and anhydrous potassium carbonate in dry methanol at ambient temperature.”; “The reaction mixture … was added into a 200 L reactor … without exothermicity.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: The original discovery route employed a palladium‑catalyzed cyclopropanation using diazomethane. Diazomethane is highly toxic, explosive, and unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production, and the vendor lead‑time for outsourcing the step was prohibitive.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to use a Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation (Shi‑modified) on the alkene substrate, eliminating diazomethane and providing a safer, more readily available reagent set.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although the cyclopropanation was high‑yielding (92%), safety concerns regarding the use of diazomethane on kilogram scale and vendor lead times associated with outsourcing this transformation required the evaluation of alternative routes toward 4.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: The early cyclopropanation routes required tributyltin hydride/AIBN for bromine removal, which are toxic, generate hazardous by‑products, and are costly on large scale.
Solution_Description: A direct Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation was adopted, removing the need for tributyltin hydride and AIBN, thereby avoiding toxic reagents and reducing cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although the key transformations proceeded in high yields, detractors from this strategy are the required five steps… and the use of toxic tributyltin hydride and AIBN.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: Cyclopropanation of the N‑sulfonyl‑amide substrate (12) showed a narrow stoichiometric window; >3 equiv of Simmons–Smith reagent gave ethylated side‑products, while slightly lower equivalents left unreacted alkene, leading to inconsistent conversions (1 %–2.6 % residual alkene) and formation of a thick Zn‑salt slurry that hindered mixing and isolation.
Solution_Description: The reagent equivalents were precisely tuned (3.20 equiv dichloroacetic acid and diiodomethane, 3.39 equiv Et₂Zn) and added at ≤0 °C, followed by a controlled warm‑up to 15 °C with a 6 h hold to allow complete conversion without premature Boc‑deprotection or precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The stoichiometry range tolerated… was narrow… slightly greater than three equivalents… required to obtain >98 % conversion… A larger excess… led to ethylated impurities… Under the acidic reaction conditions, concomitant Boc‑removal occurred… As the reaction progressed, a thick slurry composed of Zn complex 13 and inorganic zinc salts formed.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: The EDTA–based isolation of the Zn‑complexed product required strict control of EDTA stoichiometry; over‑addition caused product loss, under‑addition left zinc salts in the product, and residual EDTA remained, while the process involved multiple filtrations and gave only a <10 % reduction of the alkene impurity.
Solution_Description: A solvent‑swap isolation was developed: after reaction completion, methanol was added to dissolve the slurry, followed by a continuous DCM → MeOH distillation that precipitated the Zn‑complex (15) cleanly, eliminating EDTA, reducing steps to a single filtration, and providing a defined solid form.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of methanol to the crude solid led to rapid solubilization… the product would selectively crystallize leaving the unwanted inorganic zinc salts in solution… only one isolation was necessary to produce product free of inorganic Zn salts, and difficulties associated with using EDTA were eliminated.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: Even after optimized cyclopropanation, residual alkene impurity (14/16) persisted (up to 2.6 % in batch 1) and could not be sufficiently removed by the Zn‑complex isolation, jeopardizing API impurity specifications.
Solution_Description: A downstream impurity‑removal strategy was introduced: (i) N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) treatment of intermediate 19 to convert the alkene to bromide (later removed by crystallization), and (ii) a palladium‑catalyzed intramolecular amino‑acetoxylation that transformed the alkene into a bicyclic acetate (20 → 22–24), which could be purged during crystallization with >99.9 % removal and without generating genotoxic bromides.
Supporting_Evidence: “A removal strategy was developed that utilized downstream, in‑process aminoacetoxylation to convert the alkene contaminant to structurally dissimilar compounds that purged in the crystallization.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: The NBS oxidation of the alkene impurity produced alkyl bromide products (e.g., 21) that are potential genotoxic impurities, necessitating additional toxicology testing and delaying the campaign.
Solution_Description: The NBS method was abandoned in favor of the palladium‑catalyzed amino‑acetoxylation, which installs a less labile acetate instead of a bromide and avoids the generation of genotoxic by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of the aminoacetoxylation eliminated the concerns associated with the generation of alkyl bromide impurities encountered with the NBS procedure.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: After aminoacetoxylation, residual palladium (≈1100 ppm) remained, exceeding acceptable limits for clinical material and requiring an effective removal step.
Solution_Description: N‑methylthiourea‑impregnated silica was screened and found to reduce palladium to <10 ppm after a short filtration, providing a safe and scalable scavenging approach.
Supporting_Evidence: “N‑methylthiourea impregnated silica gel … proved to be the most effective… Pd level after crystallization was determined to be <10 ppm.”

Paper Title: Preparation of a Tricyclopropylamino Acid Derivative via Simmons–Smith Cyclopropanation with Downstream Intramolecular Aminoacetoxylation for Impurity Control
Problem_Description: Addition of co‑solvents (THF, H₂O, MeOH) or use of alternative reaction solvents (EtOAc, toluene) prevented precipitation of the Zn‑complex but dramatically reduced cyclopropanation conversion, creating a trade‑off between mixability and yield.
Solution_Description: The optimal protocol retained DCM as the reaction solvent and employed a controlled methanol‑addition post‑reaction to dissolve the slurry, thereby maintaining high conversion while allowing clean isolation without altering the reaction medium during the cyclopropanation step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The addition of THF, H₂O, or MeOH… inhibited precipitation of the product, but at the expense of conversion.”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: The phase‑transfer catalyst TBAB is highly soluble in the alcoholic starting material but becomes poorly soluble in the ether product, causing the catalyst to partition unfavorably and preventing efficient reaction when only two liquid phases are present.
Solution_Description: Increase the ionic strength of the aqueous phase (by adding water or NaCl) so that a stable third liquid layer forms; the catalyst preferentially resides in this middle layer, allowing it to be recovered and reused.
Supporting_Evidence: • “TBAB is known to prefer alcoholic solvents … In our solvent‑less reaction, the change of bulk medium from starting material (an alcohol) to product (an ether) is likely to create an unfavorable environment for the catalyst (i.e., reduce its solubility in the reaction mass).”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: Formation of the catalyst‑rich middle layer was not consistent; small changes in water addition caused the layer to appear or disappear, leading to unpredictable catalyst recovery.
Solution_Description: Control the ionic strength of the aqueous phase precisely (target 0.87–3.71 mol kg⁻¹) by adding measured amounts of water or solid NaCl, ensuring reproducible middle‑layer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The results showed that the indistinct interface becomes a stable third liquid phase below the ionic strength of 3.71 mol kg⁻¹ and that the middle layer dissolves … when the ionic strength is further decreased beyond 0.98 mol kg⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: The batch O‑alkylation required ~150 min for completion, limiting throughput and increasing inventory.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Shift to a continuous 5 L liquid–liquid extractor (LLE) with a residence time of ≈1 min; adjust lute height to maintain phase separation and achieve steady‑state conversion of ~93 % within 3 h.
Supporting_Evidence: • “With a designed residence time of about 1 min … we were able to observe a steady state flow after approximately 3 h… conversion achieved at steady state was approximately 93 %.”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: ≈10 % of TBAB was lost in the 50 % w/w NaOH aqueous layer after phase separation, reducing overall catalyst utilization.
Solution_Description: Back‑extract the residual catalyst from the water washes with the starting alcohol (3‑phenyl‑1‑propanol) and NaCl to raise ionic strength, using either a centrifugal extractor (CE) or a mixer‑settler (MS) for continuous recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The residual catalyst in the water washes could be recovered using the starting material (alkyl alcohol) as the extractant … by adjusting the aqueous ionic strength with NaCl …”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: TBAB is toxic to aquatic life; disposing of it with the waste stream generates hazardous waste handling costs and VOC emissions.
Solution_Description: Recycle TBAB either via the middle layer (direct reuse with a fresh TBAB top‑up) or via water extraction; both routes keep the catalyst out of the waste stream, lowering VOC emissions and waste‑treatment cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The sustainability benefits of catalyst recovery from a third liquid layer … reduces equipment footprint, product loss through the waste, and VOC emissions …”

Paper Title: Sustainability Improvements through Catalyst Recycling in a Liquid–Liquid Batch and Continuous Phase Transfer Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: Continuous schemes (C1–C3) required substantially higher capital investment (≈90 % increase) compared with the batch process.
Solution_Description: Implement a four‑phase decanter that continuously isolates the middle layer and pipes it directly back to the reactor, eliminating separate storage tanks and reducing the number of extra separators, thereby lowering equipment footprint and in‑process inventory.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Using the four‑phase decanter, the different phases could be maintained at certain height by proper pressure balances. This will ensure a consistent extraction of the middle layer and hence a constant amount of TBAB for continuous recycling.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: The original Miyaura borylation using bis‑(pinacolato)diboron (B₂Pin₂) gave low and variable isolated yields (60‑75 %), required a long batch cycle (~9.25 days), and involved many labor‑intensive unit operations including a separate hydrolysis step, removal of pinacol waste and polish filtration, which together increased cost and reduced robustness.
Solution_Description: A new route was developed that replaces B₂Pin₂ with tetrahydroxydiboron (BBA).  The BBA process eliminates the hydrolysis step and pinacol waste, removes the polish filtration, reduces the number of reactors from two to one, and shortens the overall batch time to ~2.5 days while raising the isolated yield to 80‑90 % and cutting the overall cost by 47 %.  The palladium‑XPhos‑G2 catalyst (Pd‑168) was retained but its loading was reduced 5‑fold (0.05 mol %).  These changes together streamline the process and lower material and processing costs.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The process was greatly simplified and successfully scaled‑up in the pilot plant on a 65 kg scale, reducing plant cycle time and resulting in a 47 % overall cost reduction.', 'A total of five batches were manufactured according to this process on a 20–50 kg scale that afforded product with good overall purity (95.8–97.5%) with the main impurities being the debrominated (3) and homocoupled (4) side products ... The process yield was also low and variable, between 60 and 75 %, which was of great importance as the boronic acid is a significant cost contributor, accounting for approximately 19 % of the overall active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) cost.', 'The 2‑butanol distillation was removed, as was the polish filtration previously needed to remove inorganic residues. The synthesis directly afforded the boronic acid and avoided the intermediary boronic ester.', 'The yield also improved from 60 % in the first generation B₂Pin₂ process to 80 % in the second generation BBA process, and finally to 90 % with the third generation ethylene glycol‑BBA process.', 'The overall processing time dropped from 9.25 to 2.5 days.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: Attempting the metal‑halogen exchange of the aryl bromide with sec‑BuLi generated a rapid heat evolution that made the step unsuitable for batch processing and presented a safety risk.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to a palladium‑catalyzed Miyaura borylation, which avoids the highly exothermic organolithium step and uses milder conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Treatment of boc‑protected aryl bromide 1 with stoichiometric quantities of sec‑BuLi ... resulted predominantly in debromination.', 'A rapid reverse addition of the aryl‑bromide to an excess of sec‑BuLi was shown to enable both complete lithium‑halogen exchange and nitrogen deprotonation. However, the rapid heat evolution associated with this approach makes it unsuitable for batch processing.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: Tetrahydroxydiboron (BBA) showed very low solubility in methanol; attempts to add BBA as a solution gave poor conversion, and when added as a solid the mixture became viscous, leading to incomplete mixing.
Solution_Description: BBA was added directly as a solid to the methanol slurry (order‑of‑addition) and, when a co‑solvent was needed, a small amount of DMAc was used to improve solubility without compromising the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Alternative nonprotic solvents were also considered, and after an extensive solubility screen, BBA was found to be only appreciably soluble in DMAc.', 'The borylation was unsuccessful in pure DMAc but found to proceed to 53.6 % conversion when a solution in 4 vol of DMAc was added to 10 vol of MeOH.', 'When the BBA solution in MeOH was aged for 16 h prior to being added to the remainder of the reagents, the conversion dropped to 27.4 %, highlighting its instability in the reaction solvent.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: BBA decomposes rapidly in the presence of palladium and oxygen, producing boric acid and causing inconsistent conversions, especially at higher temperatures.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adding 1‑15 equiv of ethylene glycol stabilises BBA by forming a less Lewis‑acidic boronate ester, the reaction temperature was lowered to ≤35 °C to suppress polymerisation, and the head‑space oxygen level was rigorously controlled (<0.5 % O₂) using vacuum/N₂ purge cycles.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The addition of ethylene glycol therefore allowed for the amount of BBA required to achieve the target conversion specification of NLT 99.0 % to be reduced from 2.0 to 1.15 equiv, greatly improving the efficiency of the process.', 'Significant base and Pd‑catalysed protodeboronation of 2 was observed at 65 °C, which could account for the varying levels of 3 observed. However, under the reaction conditions at 25 °C, boronic acid 2 was found to be stable for >22 h, suggesting that elevated temperatures should be avoided for this reaction.', 'The process in the absence of ethylene glycol using 2.0 equiv of BBA and 0.25 mol % Pd‑168 catalyst was not found to be particularly sensitive to oxygen, tolerating up to 5 % without an appreciable impact on the overall conversion or reaction impurity profile. Above 5 %, the conversion dropped significantly.', 'The process was found to be greatly dependent on the reactor headspace oxygen levels, as a significant drop in the overall conversion was observed at levels above 0.5 %.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: Running the reaction at 65 °C caused BBA polymerisation, producing black particulates that adhered to reactor walls and required extensive mechanical cleaning.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was reduced to 35 °C, which markedly decreased polymerisation, and the presence of ethylene glycol further suppresses particulate formation.
Supporting_Evidence: ['It was also observed that at 65 °C a large amount of black particulates were formed that were very difficult to clean from the reactor walls, requiring extensive mechanical scrubbing.', 'Gratifyingly, complete conversions were achieved within 16 h at temperatures as low as 35 °C ... the levels of impurities of 3 and 4 were further reduced.', 'The use of ethylene glycol therefore allowed for the amount of BBA required to achieve the target conversion specification of NLT 99.0 % to be reduced ... The addition of ethylene glycol therefore allowed for the amount of BBA required to achieve the target conversion specification of NLT 99.0 % to be reduced from 2.0 to 1.15 equiv, greatly improving the efficiency of the process.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: Higher agitation speeds increased the mass‑transfer of dissolved O₂, accelerating BBA degradation and causing conversion to fall when the headspace contained O₂.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Agitation speed was adjusted (250 rpm preferred) when O₂ was present, and rigorous inert‑gas purging was employed to keep headspace O₂ <0.5 % so that mixing‑induced O₂ transfer would not impact conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Surprisingly, the reaction agitation speed only had an impact on conversion when the process was run under a headspace containing some amount of O₂. For example, when run under an atmosphere of 0.5 % O₂, the overall conversion dropped from 98.0 to 91.8 % as the agitation speed increased from 250 to 600 rpm.', 'This mixing dependency suggested that the observed degradation was O₂‑mediated, as at higher agitation speeds the mass transfer of the O₂ gas to the liquid is higher, leading to faster dissolution of the gas into the liquid layer and therefore faster degradation.']

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of an Efficient Miyaura Borylation Process Using Tetrahydroxydiboron
Problem_Description: Large‑scale inerting of a 2 800 L reactor using simple head‑space gas flow would be time‑consuming and could lead to solvent loss or air ingress.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A variable‑pressure vacuum/N₂ purge cycle (200 mbar vacuum, 400 L/min N₂ flow) was adopted, providing rapid and efficient removal of O₂ while limiting methanol loss, and the process was validated at pilot scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Both are typically performed while the liquid mass is being agitated to maximize the gas‑liquid mass‑transfer rate.', 'Agitated variable‑pressure vacuum and release cycles were selected as the inertion technique. The vacuum set‑point was 200 mbar, to minimize solvent loss (the vapor pressure of methanol at 20 °C is 130 mbar), and the nitrogen gas flow rate was set to 400 L/min to vigorously mix the headspace and ensure homogeneity and efficient dilution.', 'The validated inertion protocol was successfully applied on a pilot scale at 65 kg and achieved, after five cycles, a headspace oxygen level of 0.2 % and a dissolved oxygen level of 0.18 ppm.']

Problem_Description: After BBA addition, the in‑situ dissolved‑oxygen probe stopped returning a reading, likely due to interference from the boron species.

Paper Title: Comparison of a Batch and Flow Approach for the Lipase-Catalyzed Resolution of a Cyclopropanecarboxylate Ester, A Key Building Block for the Synthesis of Ticagrelor
Problem_Description: When the reaction was scaled from milligram‑scale liquid lipase to gram‑scale immobilised TLL the enantioselectivity dropped dramatically (E = 108 → 52) and conversion was lower, which the authors attribute to limited transport of substrate to the enzyme surface on the support.

Supporting_Evidence:

• “One gram was found to be optimal for this system, and thus reactions were carried out using this loading.”
• “The reaction solvent was chosen to be a 1:1 mixture buffer and cosolvent (heptane). The addition of 50 % cosolvent allowed the beads to be constantly washed lest the adsorption of the ester to the beads cause any substrate inhibition.”

Paper Title: Comparison of a Batch and Flow Approach for the Lipase-Catalyzed Resolution of a Cyclopropanecarboxylate Ester, A Key Building Block for the Synthesis of Ticagrelor

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of an Epoxy Substituted Reactive Mesogen
Problem_Description: The original kilogram‑scale alkylation used 5 vol NMP (expensive and toxic). Filtration of the inorganic salts (K·HCO₃, KBr) was time‑consuming, required extensive equipment, and the product acid precipitated as a fine sludge that filtered poorly, necessitating repeated NMP washes to avoid loss.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The NMP volume was reduced to 1.6 vol and the reaction time shortened by running at a higher temperature. The methyl‑ester intermediate was extracted into toluene, allowing the inorganic carbonate to be removed in an aqueous wash using TBAB as a phase‑transfer catalyst. The acid was then crystallised from toluene (new purification point) and neutralised with sulfuric acid (compatible with both glass and stainless‑steel vessels).
Supporting_Evidence:
The alkylation reaction was performed in 5 volumes of NMP, an expensive solvent with toxicity concerns. ... Filtration of the potassium bicarbonate and potassium bromide produced in the first alkylation was unattractive on scale due to the time and equipment required. ... The intermediate acid was precipitated not crystallized, resulting in small particles which could be slow to filter and wash.  
The volume of NMP could be reduced to 1.6 volumes, and the reaction time shortened to 1.5 h at higher temperature.  
... we instead extracted the methyl ester into toluene then removed the bicarbonate in an aqueous wash using TBAB as a phase‑transfer catalyst.  
A final controlled crystallization of the acid 3 from toluene removed previous issues of filtration and inorganic content.  
We also moved to neutralize acid 3 with sulfuric acid rather than HCl to allow compatibility with either glass or stainless‑steel production vessels.

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of an Epoxy Substituted Reactive Mesogen
Problem_Description: The DCC‑mediated esterification gave >99 % conversion but generated large quantities of dicyclohexylurea (DCU) that required tedious filtration and extensive cake washing. DCC itself is a potent sensitiser, raising safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The carbodiimide coupling was switched from DCC to 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI). Heating to 85 °C with a controlled ramp (to 50 °C, hold 15 min, then to 80‑84 °C) managed CO₂ evolution. After reaction the diaryl ester solution was washed with dilute sulfuric acid to remove imidazole, and the product stream was telescoped directly into the epoxidation step, eliminating a solid‑filtration work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
The DCC esterification gave excellent conversion (>99% by HPLC), but filtration of the voluminous DCU by‑product was tedious, and required extensive washing of the cake to liberate all the desired product. Handling the potent sensitiser DCC was also not attractive on production scale.  
We were initially interested in the water‑soluble carbodiimide EDCI … the cost of the EDCI was considerably more than DCC.  
We were interested in the precedented use of CDI for esterification. The CDI mediated reaction was sluggish at the moderate temperatures … but proceeded smoothly to completion on heating to 85 °C. … Control was achieved by heating to ca. 50 °C at a defined rate, then holding at this point for 15 min before completing the ramp to reaction temperature.  
Post reaction, washing with dilute sulfuric acid removed the imidazole by‑product and the solution of the diaryl ester thus produced could be telescoped into the epoxidation without isolation.

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of an Epoxy Substituted Reactive Mesogen
Problem_Description: Epoxidation of the diaryl ester in dichloromethane gave poor aqueous separations; trace aqueous droplets were entrained in the organic layer, producing a darker product that failed purity specifications for liquid‑crystal materials.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The solvent was changed from DCM (or chlorobenzene) to toluene, which afforded cleaner phase separations. A dense aqueous phase of 36 wt % K₃PO₄ was used to pull the aqueous layer down sharply, followed by a cheap potassium carbonate wash to remove residual 3‑chloro‑benzoic acid, giving reproducibly clear separations.
Supporting_Evidence:
The mCPBA epoxidation in DCM … gave poor aqueous separations … minor entrainment of the coloured aqueous phase … gave a darker isolated product – unacceptable for liquid crystal materials.  
We focused on toluene as it was perceived to give better separations than DCM or chlorobenzene. … It was found that the use of a concentrated aqueous solution of tripotassium phosphate (36 %wt/wt) gave a very dense lower phase which separated cleanly and reproducibly. This removed the vast majority of the 3‑chlorobenzoic acid … with a facile subsequent wash with a cheaper potassium carbonate solution accounting for the rest.

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of an Epoxy Substituted Reactive Mesogen

Solution_Description: Instead of neutralising in situ, the methyl ester was extracted into toluene and the bicarbonate removed via an aqueous wash in a biphasic system using TBAB as a phase‑transfer catalyst. This avoided CO₂ evolution in the reactor and reduced the amount of acid needed for final neutralisation.
Supporting_Evidence: Neutralization of the KHCO₃ produced in the alkylation evolved copious CO₂ (g) which could have resulted in pressurisation if not adequately vented on larger scale. … we instead extracted the methyl ester into toluene then removed the bicarbonate in an aqueous wash. This obviated the off‑gassing risk, and vastly reduced the amount of acid needed for the final neutralisation. … this was readily achieved in a toluene/NaOH (aq) biphase using TBAB …

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of an Epoxy Substituted Reactive Mesogen
Problem_Description: During later scale‑up trials the epoxidation showed inconsistent conversion and impurity levels, and residual starting olefin (compound 4) was difficult to remove during crystallisation of the epoxide, leading to yield loss and product‑quality variation.
Solution_Description: The process was altered so that the alkylation and CDI esterification were telescoped, then the alkene 4 was isolated and purified before the epoxidation. This provided a consistent, impurity‑free substrate for the epoxidation, improving robustness and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
We observed in further trials inconsistent reaction profiles in the epoxidation with minor variations in reaction completion and more significant variations in impurity generation. This was compounded by the fact that residual starting olefin 4 could be difficult to purge in the crystallization of the epoxide 1.  
The solution proved to be moving the isolation point. … instead of isolating acid 3 and telescoping the esterification and epoxidation, we instead combined the bromopentene alkylation with the CDI esterification. The isolation and purification of the alkene 4 gave a more consistent starting point for the epoxidation reaction which went on to perform as desired.

Paper Title: Development and Scaling-Up of the Fragrance Compound 4‑Ethylguaiacol Synthesis via a Two-Step Chemo-Enzymatic Reaction Sequence

Paper Title: Development and Scaling-Up of the Fragrance Compound 4‑Ethylguaiacol Synthesis via a Two-Step Chemo-Enzymatic Reaction Sequence

Problem_Description: During scale‑up to 100 mM FA, the reaction slowed after 2 h; product concentrations >10 mM in the aqueous phase likely caused enzyme deactivation, reducing final yield.

Paper Title: Regioselective Epoxide Ring Opening for the Stereospecific Scale-Up Synthesis of BMS-960, A Potent and Selective Isoxazole-Containing S1P
Problem_Description: The original convergent synthesis of BMS‑960 suffered from several scale‑up drawbacks: (a) the N‑alkylation step (Step 1) gave only a moderate isolated yield; (b) the use of isopropyl alcohol in Step 3 generated an ester‑exchange by‑product, complicating purification; (c) the oxadiazole‑forming step (Step 4) afforded low yield (≈50 %) because the free secondary alcohol interfered with cyclisation; (d) the acyl‑fluoride reagent was prepared from cyanuric fluoride, a highly caustic material that corroded glassware; (e) the route required a chiral‑separation step after a racemic chemical reduction, adding cost and waste; (f) the bromohydrin intermediate (14) proved unstable and had to be handled quickly; (g) the enzymatic reduction of the bromoketone originally required long reaction times when performed at low enzyme loading.
Solution_Description: The team redesigned the process: (1) they introduced a new convergent route centred on a common epoxide intermediate (S‑4‑(oxiran‑2‑yl)‑benzonitrile, 15), eliminating the low‑yield N‑alkylation sequence and providing a flexible platform for analogue synthesis (NEW ROUTE). (2) To stop ester‑exchange, isopropyl alcohol was replaced with ethanol and the reaction was run at ambient temperature rather than reflux, removing the by‑product (SOLVENT CHANGE, TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION). (3) The free secondary alcohol was protected as a TBDMS ether before oxadiazole formation; this change raised the cyclisation yield from 50 % to 88 % (FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE/PROMOTER – protecting‑group strategy). (4) The corrosive acyl‑fluoride step was swapped for an acyl‑chloride preparation, avoiding cyanuric fluoride and the associated safety hazards (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE, SAFETY). (5) A biocatalytic reduction using ketoreductase KRED‑NADH‑110 provided the chiral bromohydrin (14) with >99 % ee in a single step, removing the need for a costly chiral‑separation step (CATALYST OPTIMIZATION, STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE, FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE/PROMOTER – co‑factor recycling). (6) The unstable bromohydrin was immediately converted to the epoxide under basic conditions (sodium t‑butoxide) at 40 °C, preventing decomposition (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE). (7) Reaction time was shortened to 5 h by using a low enzyme loading (500 mg KRED‑NADH‑110 for 100 g substrate) with a 200:1 substrate‑to‑enzyme ratio and efficient NADH recycling, dramatically improving throughput (REACTION TIME CHANGE, STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE).
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Step 1 N‑alkylation yield was only moderate" – low conversion for the original route. (LOW YIELD) 
• "Step 3 used isopropyl alcohol which generates the ester exchange byproduct" – impurity formation during work‑up. (PURIFICATION) 
• "Step 4 oxadiazole formation yield was low, probably due to the presence of an unprotected OH group" – poor cyclisation efficiency. (LOW YIELD) 
• "Acyl fluoride was prepared from an unfavorable reagent, cyanuric fluoride, which is very caustic and could even corrode the glassware during scale‑up" – safety hazard. (SAFETY) 
• "Chiral separation was required after a racemic reduction, which was not favorable for a large scale" – added cost and waste. (COST) 
• "The secondary alcohol 14 was unstable and was directly converted to the racemic epoxide 15" – decomposition risk if isolated. (DECOMPOSITION) 
• "A very low loading of ketoreductase KRED‑NADH‑110 was sufficient to effect the complete reduction of 100 g of α‑bromoketone 8 in 5 h" – original longer times improved. (LONG REACTIONS)

• "An alternative synthesis was proposed to efficiently scale up BMS‑960" – new convergent design (NEW ROUTE). 
• "IPA was replaced with EtOH at RT rather than reflux to avoid ester exchange" – solvent and temperature change (SOLVENT CHANGE, TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION). 
• "The oxadiazole formation yield was improved from 50% to 88% with this protecting group change" – use of TBDMS protecting group (FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE/PROMOTER). 
• "During the oxadiazole formation, acyl chloride rather than acyl fluoride was prepared to avoid the corrosive reagent, cyanuric fluoride" – safer reagent (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE). 
• "Ketoreductase KRED‑NADH‑110 was selected… very low loading… 5 h at 40 °C… substrate to enzyme ratio of 200:1" – enzymatic route (CATALYST OPTIMIZATION, STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE, REACTION TIME CHANGE). 
• "The chiral alcohol 14 was extracted in MTBE, then readily converted to (S)‑epoxide 15 by sodium tert‑butoxide" – immediate conversion prevents degradation (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE).

Paper Title: Double Heck Route to a Dibenzoxepine and Convergent Suzuki Cross-Coupling Strategy for the Synthesis of an MR Antagonist

Supporting_Evidence: "A temperature exotherm of 2 °C was observed with the addition [of I₂]... Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Flow Barbier Process for a Pharmaceutical Intermediate

Problem_Description: Conversion drift was observed when the feed lot changed (different water content), indicating sensitivity of the process to feed quality.
Solution_Description: Real‑time PAT monitoring (online HPLC and micro‑GC) was employed to quickly detect conversion changes, allowing operators to adjust feed specifications as needed.
Supporting_Evidence: "The only change in the conversion occurred at approximately 43 h into the run when the feed was switched to a different lot of starting material. The only known difference with the two feeds is that the second can had slightly less water."; "The analytical sample burden is high... PAT is utilized extensively for the key reactions and unit operations that appropriate data are collected."

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Flow Barbier Process for a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Suspending and mixing magnesium solids in the CSTR proved challenging; inadequate mixing could lead to poor metal activation and local hotspots.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The CSTR was equipped with vertical flat baffles and a specially designed settling pipe with a suction tube to keep magnesium particles suspended and to recycle settled metal back into the reaction zone.
Supporting_Evidence: "The four vertical flat baffles helped with the Mg solid suspension."; "The settle pipe was angled… The suck tube allowed about 30 s τ for the liquid flowing up the settling pipe. As the product solution moved up… the magnesium particles settled by gravity and moved back down into the reactor."

Paper Title: Development of a Commercial Flow Barbier Process for a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: The post‑quench liquid–liquid separation required continuous operation; any inefficiency could lead to product loss or impurity carry‑over.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous gravity decanter system was installed downstream of the quench CSTR, allowing rapid phase separation (≈10 min) and direct feeding of the organic layer to the carbonate wash CSTR, minimizing impurity entrainment.
Supporting_Evidence: "The time for separation of the two liquid phases was about 10 min."; "The organic layer continuously flowed to the sodium carbonate wash CSTR... The aqueous layer continuously flowed by gravity to a waste container."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Significant formation of the by‑products n‑butanol (BOL) and the cyclic ether 2‑(4‑hydroxybutoxy)‑tetrahydrofuran (HBOTHF) reduced the overall 1,4‑butanediol (BAD) yield and created difficult‑to‑remove impurities.
Solution_Description: The authors lowered the reaction temperature (100 °C‑110 °C) and increased the feed pH (8 → 10) to suppress the acid‑catalysed dehydration that forms BOL and HBOTHF; they also introduced the P3 promoter, which selectively reduces HBOTHF formation while maintaining high activity.
Supporting_Evidence: "...BAD and BOL concentrations are stabilised at 95.3 and 4.2 wt %, respectively, but significant amounts of HBOTHF (0.4 wt %) were also formed. Reducing the temperature ... eliminated the HBOTHF formation..."; "Increasing the pH of the feed slowed the reaction rate ... but caused a nearly 2‑fold decrease in the BOL level ... and a nearly 10‑fold reduction in HBOTHF..."; "The P3 promoted catalyst ... shows significant improvement in the BAD selectivity, a moderate reduction in the BOL level, and a nearly complete depression of the reactions leading to HBOTHF."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Higher liquid flow rates increased the wetted fraction of the catalyst particles, decreasing hydrogen gas‑to‑solid mass transfer and lowering conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reactor was operated at lower liquid flow rates (≤ 0.233 mL min⁻¹) to keep residence time sufficient and to limit the film thickness; the up‑flow configuration and pre‑heating zone with fine stainless‑steel filters improved gas–liquid mixing and ensured adequate hydrogen transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the loss in conversion with increasing the liquid flow rate is usually associated with the shortening of the residence time..."; "...at lower liquid flow rates, the catalyst particle is partially wetted which makes possible the direct gas to solid diffusion. In contrast, increasing the liquid flow rate will increase the wetted fraction of the catalyst surface, thus lowering the rate of hydrogen transport from gas phase to the catalyst surface..."; "The pre‑heating zone is fitted with three 10 µm stainless steel filters used for pre‑heating and mixing the aqueous BYD and hydrogen."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Insufficient conversion of the γ‑hydroxy‑butanal (γ‑HALD) intermediates (detected as U1 and HTHF) resulted in lower overall BAD production.
Solution_Description: The liquid hourly space velocity (LHSV) was reduced (≈ 0.44 g BYD mL⁻¹ cat h⁻¹) by lowering the feed flow rate and/or BYD concentration, providing longer residence time and higher conversion of the hemiacetals.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the liquid flow rate should be kept at or below 0.233 mL·min⁻¹ to prevent the appearance of unreacted γ‑HALD, detected as the two hemiacetals, U1 and HTHF."; "Increasing the liquid flow rate ... resulted in lower WHSV of 0.40 g BYD mL⁻¹ cat h⁻¹, the overall conversion dropped to 96.7 % (the two hemiacetals U1 and HTHF were detected at the combined level of 3.3 wt %)."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: The rate of BAD formation varied with catalyst surface area; low‑area catalysts gave inconsistent conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: Catalysts with higher BET surface area (33–44 m² g⁻¹) were prepared by varying NaOH leaching conditions, which consistently increased the rate of U1 consumption and BAD formation across temperatures.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the catalyst activity is a direct function of the metal surface area – increasing the surface area of the Ra Ni catalysts leads to drastic reduction in the level of the unreacted U1, to improvement in the BAD content..."; "Increasing the temperature for each catalyst increases the conversion. For example, in the case of the high surface area Ni 37 and Ni 44 catalysts, the reaction went to completion with the U1 nearly eliminated when the temperature was raised to 110 °C."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Raney nickel is a cheaper alternative to precious‑metal catalysts, but earlier literature reported limited use of Raney Ni for BYD hydrogenation.
Solution_Description: The study demonstrated that particulate Raney Ni, when appropriately promoted and operated under optimized conditions, can replace Ru‑Pd/C, Pt/CaCO₃, etc., providing a cost‑effective catalyst system for continuous BAD production.
Supporting_Evidence: "...very few reports are found in the open literature describing the use of Raney nickel as a catalyst for this transformation..."; "The work describes the results on the hydrogenation of 2‑butyne‑1,4‑diol to 1,4‑butanediol over both slurry and particulate Raney nickel catalysts (Ra Ni) in batch and in a fixed‑bed reactor system."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: High hydrogen pressure (2000 psi) and exothermic hydrogenation present safety hazards in large‑scale operation.
Solution_Description: A fixed‑bed, up‑flow reactor with automated pressure monitoring, abort logic (shutdown if any parameter deviates >10 %), and staged temperature control was employed to manage heat removal and safely handle high‑pressure hydrogen.
Supporting_Evidence: "Data acquisition and control system ... Special attention was paid to the safety of the flow system so that when any of the process parameters varied by more than 10 % from the set values, the system was programmed to enter into an abort regime that terminates the power to all heaters and mass flow delivery systems."; "The reactor is fitted with four band heaters and independently controlled temperature zones … maintaining the temperature of each zone within ±0.2 °C."

Paper Title: Continuous Liquid-Phase Hydrogenation of 1,4-Butynediol to High-Purity 1,4-Butanediol over Particulate Raney Nickel Catalyst in a Fixed Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 110 °C, BAD selectivity declined because of acid‑catalysed dehydration of intermediates to BOL and HBOTHF (decomposition pathways).
Solution_Description: Operating the reactor at 100–105 °C and adjusting the feed pH to neutral‑basic values (pH 8–10) minimized acid‑catalysed decomposition, preserving BAD yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "Raising the temperature to 110 °C led to a loss in BAD selectivity and enhanced both the rate of hydrogenolysis (BOL) and the dehydration (HBOTHF) reactions..."; "Increasing the pH of the feed slowed the reaction rate ... but caused a nearly 2‑fold decrease in the BOL level ... and a nearly 10‑fold reduction in HBOTHF."

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: Reproduction of the literature conversion of morpholine amide 5a to the bicyclic side‑chain 7 gave isolated yields of only 30‑35 % (instead of the reported 71 %), and quenching the LAH reduction with aqueous methanesulfonic acid or NaHSO₄ produced a gel‑like mixture that made product isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: The authors screened alternative amide substrates and identified N‑methyl‑aniline amide 5b as the optimal partner, which gave a 70‑75 % isolated yield after LAH reduction. They also reduced the LAH loading to 4 equiv (balancing cost vs. yield) and adjusted the quench pH to 4‑5 with aqueous NaOH, allowing selective extraction of the N‑methylaniline impurity with toluene.
Supporting_Evidence: ["However, we were unable to obtain the reported yield at 71% for the conversion of morpholine amide 5a to furofuranol 7. … isolated yields were typically in the range 30–35%.", "Quenching the lithium aluminum hydride (LAH) reduction reaction mixture with either aqueous methanesulfonic acid (MSA) or aqueous NaHSO4 produced gel‑like mixtures, which made isolation of the product from the byproduct salts difficult.", "The use of 4 equiv of LAH gave the highest isolated yield of furofuranol 7 at ∼70%.", "In order to resolve this issue, the pH of the quenched acidic aqueous solution was adjusted to 4–5 using aqueous sodium hydroxide after holding the cyclization mixture for 3 h.", "Based on the yields of bicyclic acetal 7, we presume that the reduction of N‑methyl aniline amide 5b was more efficient than reduction of the morpholine amide 5a."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: The aqueous work‑up after LAH reduction left ~5‑10 wt % N‑methylaniline in the crude product, requiring additional extraction steps to reach acceptable purity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The pH of the acidic aqueous mixture was brought to 4‑5 with NaOH and the N‑methylaniline was removed by multiple toluene extractions. To avoid tedious batch extractions, the authors later employed a continuous DCM extractor, which gave comparable yields with streamlined work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In order to resolve this issue, the pH of the quenched acidic aqueous solution was adjusted to 4–5 using aqueous sodium hydroxide after holding the cyclization mixture for 3 h. This slightly acidic solution was extracted with toluene to remove N‑methylaniline.", "As an alternative to the tedious multiple extractions, continuous extraction of the aqueous solution was carried out with DCM in a continuous extractor for 16 h, and furofuranol 7 was isolated in 74% yield."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: The originally reported amide‑formation step used 2‑chloro‑4,6‑dimethoxy‑1,3,5‑triazine (CDMT) together with N‑methylmorpholine; CDMT is expensive and its by‑products are difficult to remove on large scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the CDMT coupling with an in‑situ formation of the acyl chloride using oxalyl chloride and catalytic DMF, followed by coupling with N‑methyl‑aniline and pyridine. This reagent set is cheaper and the by‑products are easier to handle.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For the formation of amide, the higher cost of the CDMT coupling reagent, and challenges with the removal of CDMT coupling byproducts, prompted us to seek an alternative.", "Oxalyl chloride with a catalytic amount of N,N‑dimethylformamide (DMF) in dichloromethane (DCM) was found to be suitable for the acyl chloride formation. The acyl chloride thus formed was reacted in situ with N‑methylaniline in the presence of pyridine to give crude amide 5b."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: Neutralizing potassium isocitrate with Amberlyst 15 ion‑exchange resin required large volumes of water, and the subsequent removal of water to drive lactonisation was cumbersome for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to direct acidification of the salt with aqueous HCl, followed by azeotropic removal of water using 2‑methyl‑THF (MeTHF). MeTHF allowed removal of water and precipitation of KCl, simplifying the work‑up and providing a scalable route.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The use of ion‑exchange resin to generate the free acid requires a substantial amount of water, which then must be removed in order to drive the lactonization to completion. While this procedure provided material for downstream research, it would be challenging at scale…", "The alternative procedure neutralized the potassium isocitrate with aqueous hydrochloric acid, and water was then removed by azeotropic distillation with 2‑methyl tetrahydrofuran (MeTHF) to drive the formation of lactone‑diacid 2.", "The solvent selection was key here, with MeTHF providing a medium where the triacid and the lactone are solubilized, where the byproduct salt is essentially insoluble, and where removal of water by azeotropic Dean–Stark distillation is possible."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: Preparation of the cyclic anhydride 3 by refluxing neat acetic anhydride at 139 °C was harsh and required large excess of the costly reagent, making it unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors developed two milder alternatives: (i) using trifluoroacetic anhydride (TFAA) at ambient temperature in MeTHF (yield 68 %) and (ii) using acetic anhydride (1.2 equiv) in cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) at 105 °C, which gave a 97 % isolated yield and benefited from the higher boiling point of CPME.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The literature procedure for preparation of cyclic anhydride 3 used refluxing neat acetic anhydride (at 139 °C)… however, these conditions seemed unnecessarily harsh for scale‑up.", "We first employed a milder procedure in which the MeTHF solution of lactone diacid 2 was treated with stoichiometric trifluoroacetic anhydride (TFAA) at ambient temperature to give the anhydride 3.", "Alternatively, the cyclic anhydride formation was carried out by reacting isolated 2 with 1.2 equiv of acetic anhydride in cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) at 105 °C for ∼3 h. After cooling… the cyclic anhydride 3 was isolated in 97% yield by filtration."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: The reduction‑cyclisation sequence required prolonged heating (16 h LAH reduction, 3 h cyclisation, and several hours of extraction), limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: The authors optimised the reduction time (16 h) and explored telescoping the three‑step sequence (lactone‑diacid → anhydride → hemiester → amide) in a single pot, reducing handling steps and overall processing time.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The optimized reduction/cyclization process, the crystallized amide 5b was treated with LAH (1 M) at −10 to 20 °C for 16 h. … The mixture was then … extracted … to give about 70–75% yield of furofuranol 7.", "Some efforts have been made toward streamlining the conversion from lactone‑diacid 2 to ethyl … amide 5b by using cyclopentyl methyl ether (CPME) as the solvent in three reactions. … gives amide 5b in the same pot. After aqueous workup … amide 5b was obtained in 56% overall yield."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: Crude amide 5b contained trace regio‑ and diastereomeric impurities (≤2 % total) that required removal before further steps.
Solution_Description: The impurity‑laden crude was recrystallized from toluene, affording amide 5b with 99.5 % purity by GC‑MS.
Supporting_Evidence: ["These impurities were effectively purged by recrystallization from toluene to give amide 5b in 99.5 % purity by GC‑MS."]

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of the Bicyclic Darunavir Side Chain: (3
Problem_Description: During the work‑up of the reduction‑cyclisation, the product partitioned poorly into toluene (≈2 % of 7 in toluene/water), making extraction inefficient.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous extractor using DCM as the organic phase was employed, providing vigorous reflux and efficient phase contact, which gave a high yield (74 %) of product with streamlined operations.
Supporting_Evidence: ["As an alternative to the tedious multiple extractions, continuous extraction of the aqueous solution was carried out with DCM in a continuous extractor for 16 h, and furofuranol 7 was isolated in 74% yield."]

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: The initial one‑pot cascade (70 °C → 150 °C, 3 equiv. Amberlyst H15, 4 equiv. Zn) gave the target 2,2‑diphenylethanol (6a) in only 55 % isolated yield and a large amount of the undesired benzylic alcohol 3a (28 % of the aldehyde conversion).
Solution_Description: The amount of Zn was lowered to 2 equiv. (reducing the direct reduction pathway) and the temperature profile was changed to a single‑step at 180 °C for 1 h, while the supported Brønsted acid was switched to Amberlite IR120 (5 equiv.) which gave 80 % yield of 6a with only 16 % 3a.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Starting aldehyde 1a was completely converted. Target 2,2‑diphenylethanol (6a) was obtained … 55 % yield… a high amount of benzylic alcohol 3a … 28 % yield" (Table 1, entry 1).
• "Decreasing the amount of zinc to 2 equiv allowed to limit the amount of benzylic alcohol 3a to 24 %… but with a partial conversion" (Table 1, entry 5).
• "Using 1 equiv of Amberlyst H15 decreased the global conversion (89 % vs 100 %) and hindered the pinacolic rearrangement…" (Table 3, entry 2).
• "The more selective was based on the reactivity of AmberliteIR120 at 90 °C then 160 °C… 80 % yield of 6a with 16 % 3a" (Table 5, entry 1).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Changing the metal reductant (Mg, Al, Mn) did not improve either the yield of 6a or the selectivity, and some metals gave no conversion at all.
Solution_Description: The focus was shifted from the metal to the acidic promoter; supported Brønsted acids (Dowex 50WX8, Amberlite IR120) were screened, identifying Amberlite IR120 as the most selective catalyst for the cascade.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Changing the metal source did not allowed better selectivity nor yield in 6a (Table 1, entries 2–4)." 
• "As a consequence, different sources of acid were screened to master the reduction side reaction (Table 2)."
• "Comparing these four supported acidic media led to the conclusion that AmberliteIR120 displayed the higher potential in terms of selectivities" (text).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Strong homogeneous acids (NH₄Cl, AcOH, CH₃SO₃H) either gave no pinacol rearrangement or promoted the undesired direct reduction, resulting in poor selectivity for 6a.
Solution_Description: Supported Brønsted acids (Dowex 50WX8, Amberlite IR120) were employed instead of homogeneous acids, improving both the pinacol coupling and the subsequent rearrangement while maintaining water as the reaction medium.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Acetic acid … favored the direct reduction … 73 % yield of 3a" (Table 2, entry 3).
• "Methanesulfonic acid … allowed the cascade reaction but with a low selectivity toward pinacol coupling" (Table 2, entry 4).
• "Dowex50WX8 … allowed the pinacol coupling reaction and the pinacolic rearrangement… 39 % of target 6a" (Table 2, entry 7).
• "AmberliteIR120 … gave 80 % yield of 6a" (Table 5, entry 1).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Using only 1 equiv. of supported acid lowered overall conversion (89 %) and slowed the pinacolic rearrangement, leading to residual pinacol 2a and lower 6a yield.
Solution_Description: The acid loading was increased to 5 equiv. of Amberlite IR120, and a two‑step temperature program (90 °C for 1 h followed by 160 °C for 50 min) was applied at 0.3 M concentration, giving quantitative conversion and 72 % isolated 6a.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Using 1 equiv of AmberlystH15 decreased the global conversion (89 % vs 100 %)…" (Table 3, entry 2).
• "The reaction was realized in a sole step at the higher temperature… 50 % of target 6a…" (Table 3, entry 16).
• "The optimized protocol… 90 °C for 1 h then 160 °C for 50 min… gave 72 % of target product 6a" (Table 4, entry 9).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Replacing water with absolute ethanol (or high ethanol fractions) reduced the conversion of the aldehyde and increased side‑product formation, likely due to poor miscibility and different reaction environment.
Solution_Description: Water was retained as the primary solvent; only small amounts of ethanol were used in mixed H₂O/EtOH experiments, but the optimal conditions reverted to pure water to maximize conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Ethanol, reported as able to limit the reduction side reaction, was evaluated… lower amounts of benzyl alcohol were observed, conversions decreased, and a lot of unpreviously observed side products were obtained" (Table 3, entries 7‑8).
• "As a consequence, the replacement of water by biosourced ethanol… was abandoned" (text).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Even after optimization, a small amount of pinacol 2a remained at the end of the reaction, limiting the isolated yield of 6a.
Solution_Description: Increasing the second‑step temperature to 180 °C and extending the heating time (or raising the acid loading to 5 equiv.) allowed complete conversion of 2a, raising the isolated yield of 6a up to 80 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Increasing the temperature of the second step to 180 °C … did not help" (Table 3 entries 1‑5).
• "A second attempt … 180 °C … had a dramatic impact on conversion and yield of 6a" (Table 4, entry 10).
• "With this amount of acid, 16 % of benzyl alcohol … and less than 1 % of deoxybenzoin … 80 % yield of 6a" (Table 4, entry 11).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Scale‑up required a safe and controllable heating method; the microwave approach was not practical for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The cascade was transferred to sealed autoclave reactors (glass, Teflon, steel) operated under conventional heating, preserving yield and selectivity while providing a scalable, industrially relevant platform.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Considering that flow microwave devices are less industrially used than autoclaves, some experiments in sealed vessels have been carried out using the optimized protocol" (text).
• "Scaling up in 60 mL then 300 mL Teflon reactors … gave similar yields and selectivity" (Table 7, entries 3‑4).
• "Conducting the cascade reaction on a 12 g scale in a steel reactor gave the expected results … 79 % yield" (Table 7, entry 5).

Paper Title: Selective One-Pot Three-Step Cascade Reaction: From Aromatic Aldehydes to 2,2-Diphenylethanol Derivatives
Problem_Description: Typical metal‑hydride reductions use expensive or stoichiometric reagents, making the process costly for large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: A cheap, readily available reductant (Zn metal) was employed together with a regenerable supported acid, dramatically reducing reagent cost while maintaining high efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Zinc was selected as electron supplier, and Amberlyst H15 was chosen as a supported acid…" (Results & Discussion).
• "The originality of this medium is the use of AmberliteIR120 as a heterogeneous regenerable proton supplier and zinc as a cheap electron supplier" (Conclusion).

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: The diphenhydramine synthesis is endothermic and requires a large heating duty, especially for the solvent‑based route, leading to high operating costs.
Solution_Description: Use the neat (solvent‑free) synthesis which eliminates the carrier solvent and dramatically reduces the required heating duty; also select operating conditions (temperature, flow rates) that minimise the energy input.
Supporting_Evidence: “Calculated reaction enthalpies (Table 11) show that the reaction is endothermic; thus, heating is required for both PFRs… The duty for the neat synthesis is significantly lower than for the solvent synthesis due to the lower throughput…”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: Only a limited number of experimental data points are available for the kinetic study, preventing accurate determination of reaction orders and rate constants.
Solution_Description: Fit the available conversion versus residence‑time data using linearised forms (ln C vs. t for first‑order, 1/C vs. t for second‑order) and select the model with the highest coefficient of determination (R²).
Supporting_Evidence: “Kinetic parameter estimation ... By plotting different functions ... coefficients of determination (R²) have been calculated to estimate reaction orders and rate constants for each reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: Chloroform, although giving the best extraction performance, is classified as a Class 1 solvent with high toxicity, making it unsuitable for large‑scale continuous manufacturing.
Solution_Description: Replace chloroform with a less toxic solvent such as methyl‑cyclohexane, which still provides good API recovery while satisfying safety and regulatory requirements.
Supporting_Evidence: “Chloroform emerges as a potent separation solvent … but its high toxicity prohibits any recommendation for CPM consideration… Methylcyclohexane … its lower toxicity renders it significantly more acceptable for CPM implementation.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: Several candidate extraction solvents (n‑hexane, n‑heptane) show poor API solubility and low recovery yields, especially at higher temperatures.
Solution_Description: Increase the solvent‑to‑feed (S:F) ratio or select solvents with higher polarity (e.g., dichloromethane, chloroform) based on UNIFAC/NRTL predictions to improve API solubility and recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: “From Fig. 8 it can be seen that the extraction performance of all candidate solvents decreases as temperature increases… n‑hexane and n‑heptane achieve unacceptably low API recoveries of 60.6 % and 53.1 %… the best recoveries (≈ 99 %) are obtained with dichloromethane and chloroform at low S:F.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: The neat reaction mixture (no carrier solvent) has a high viscosity, raising concerns about flow uniformity, possible clogging, and accurate residence‑time control.
Solution_Description: Operate the micro‑reactor with internal diameters ≥ 2.5 mm and maintain the reaction temperature high enough to keep the mixture fluid, thereby mitigating viscosity‑related flow issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The viscosity of the reaction mixture for the synthesis without carrier solvent is of concern… we assume that the reaction mixture viscosity variation does not significantly affect PFR flow patterns or conversion.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: For several candidate solvent systems no UNIFAC/NRTL interaction parameters are available, preventing thermodynamic modelling of liquid‑liquid equilibria.
Solution_Description: Rely on experimentally measured LLE data where available and exclude solvents lacking sufficient interaction data from the screening study.
Supporting_Evidence: “The lack of required interaction parameters for both UNIFAC and NRTL models makes theoretical modelling unavailable for these systems.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: Two side‑reactions (benzhydrol formation and dibenzhydryl ether) are reported for the diphenhydramine synthesis but kinetic data are not available, potentially lowering overall yield.
Solution_Description: Perform additional experimental studies to obtain kinetic parameters for the side‑reactions and incorporate them into the reactor model for accurate yield prediction.
Supporting_Evidence: “The original paper ... also describes two side reactions … The publication did not provide enough information to estimate kinetic parameters of these side reactions, so the model described here only accounts for the synthesis reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Modeling, Simulation, and Technoeconomic Evaluation of Separation Solvents for the Continuous Pharmaceutical Manufacturing (CPM) of Diphenhydramine
Problem_Description: The capital expense of conventional batch‑type reactors is high; large reactor volumes are required to meet the target throughput.
Solution_Description: Adopt plug‑flow micro‑reactors with small diameters (2.5–15 mm) and short lengths, which provide high surface‑to‑volume ratios, efficient heat removal and lower material costs.
Supporting_Evidence: “Plug flow reactors are the most common microreactor type used in CPM … the reactor volumes obtained for both syntheses are small … demonstrating the benefit of reduced equipment sizes offered by CPM.”

Paper Title: S
Problem_Description: Solid material (sticky precipitate) formed during the first SNAr reaction, immobilizing the stir bar and preventing efficient stirring.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A cosolvent (THF) was added at 10–15 % v/v, which reduced the amount of solid, eliminated oiling‑out, and restored smooth stirring of the reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence:

• "Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl), and osmium tetroxide (OsO₄)… did not lead to a significant amount of product (Table 1, entries 2–4)." (Results & Discussion) 
 • "Treatment of compound 4 with KMnO₄ (3 equiv), TBAB, 0 °C afforded crude compound 5 … best yield (85 %)." (Results & Discussion) 
 • Table 1 entries 2–4 show 12 % (OsO₄), 19 % (H₂O₂/Na₂WO₄), 23 % (NaOCl/TMCAC) yields, whereas entry 5 (KMnO₄, 0 °C) gives 85 % yield. 
 • "A lower yield was found at room temperature (entry 6, 62 % yield)." (Oxidative‑cleavage paragraph)

Paper Title: An Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Literature routes relying on Pauson–Khand cyclocarbonylation required high temperatures, long reaction times, and expensive cobalt or ruthenium reagents, delivering only 35–57 % overall yield and making scale‑up uneconomical.
Solution_Description: The authors avoided the Pauson–Khand step entirely by employing a four‑step sequence (reduction, Boc‑protection, KMnO₄ oxidative cleavage, Dieckmann condensation) that uses inexpensive reagents and gives a 54 % overall yield on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The process involved expensive ruthenium‑(IV) oxide (RuO₂) as an oxidizing agent…" (Intro) 
 • "The Pauson–Khand reaction requires a high temperature and long reaction time due to slow decarbonylation and expensive reagents." (Intro) 
 • "A patent from Vertex… reported an overall 35 % yield (Route 1)…" (Intro) 
 • "Becker et al. reported a synthesis… with a 57 % yield…" (Intro) 
 • "The improved process involves transformation of isoindole 4 to diacid 5, using an inexpensive KMnO₄ mediated oxidative cleavage as a key step… four steps with a 54 % overall yield…" (Abstract & Conclusion)

Paper Title: An Efficient and Scalable Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The earlier processes consumed large volumes of organic solvents (≈1 518 L per kg of product) and required expensive raw materials, resulting in a raw‑material cost of ≈ $3 950 kg⁻¹ for intermediate 1.
Solution_Description: By switching to the KMnO₄ oxidative cleavage and simplifying work‑ups, total solvent consumption dropped 77 % (to 347 L per kg) and the raw‑material cost fell to ≈ $1 439 kg⁻¹ (64 % reduction).
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Data analysis … revealed 77 % reduction (4.4‑fold, from 1518 to 347 L) in the total solvent consumption with our improved process." (Results & Discussion) 
 • "RMC of 1 would be approximately $3950 kg⁻¹, whereas … the RMC comes to around $1439 kg⁻¹ (64 % of cost reduction)." (Results & Discussion) 
 • "The improved process is cost‑effective, high yielding, kilogram scalable, and commercially viable…" (Abstract) 
 • "The developed process was cost‑effective, high yielding, kilogram scalable, and commercially viable for synthesis of 1." (Abstract)

Paper Title: Asymmetric Oxidation of a Dihydrothienopyrimidine
Problem_Description: The asymmetric oxidation showed poor reproducibility of enantioselectivity; small changes in temperature, water amount, or catalyst‑aging time caused large variations in ee, and the reaction mixture was heterogeneous at the standard 0.5 M concentration, leading to mixing difficulties.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
