Solution_Description: A robust protocol was developed in which Ti‑i‑PrO4, water and the ligand are added sequentially to a toluene slurry, the mixture is stirred for a defined short period (15 min) before cooling and peroxide addition; the reaction was also run at 0.25 M to give a quasi‑homogeneous system that improves stirring and reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: La variabilidad en la enantioselectividad se debió a pequeñas variaciones en las condiciones de reacción (p. 3).

Paper Title: Development of a Modified Process for the Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of c‑Met/ALK Inhibitor HS-10168
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry Suzuki coupling of bromopyridine 1 with phosphorus‑containing phenylboronic acid 2 did not go to completion and produced a complex mixture; the isolated product after semipreparative HPLC gave only 28 % overall yield.
Solution_Description: A redesigned synthetic sequence replaced the problematic phenylboronic acid 2 with para‑phenol boronate 9 and the original halide 1 with nitro‑containing bromopyridine 6.  The new route eliminates the homocoupling side‑product, removes the need for semipreparative HPLC, and delivers the intermediate 10 in 89 % isolated yield, giving a much higher overall productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Suzuki coupling between 1 and 2 failed to go to completion and gave a complex mixture of products… The yield of the final product obtained by semipreparative HPLC was very low (28%).”; “Our strategy was to use para‑phenol boronate 9 instead of 2 to couple with 6… avoided the formation of the homocoupling side product.”; “The process features a robust Suzuki coupling reaction… followed by… affording 10 in 89 % yield.”

Paper Title: Development of a Modified Process for the Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of c‑Met/ALK Inhibitor HS-10168
Problem_Description: The first attempt at the Suzuki coupling of nitro‑bromopyridine 6 with phenol boronate 9 using Pd(PPh₃)₄ in DME/water at 80 °C gave incomplete conversion after 19 h, producing a complex mixture; the catalyst’s air‑sensitivity was cited as a possible cause of the failure.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was switched to PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂ (5 mol %) which is more robust and air‑stable; the solvent system was changed to a MeOH/DME/water mixture; the reaction was run under reflux (higher temperature) and the catalyst loading was reduced to 1 mol % (longer time) to give complete conversion in 1 h (5 % loading) with a clean profile and 89 % isolated yield of 10.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pd(PPh₃)₄ is often a capricious catalyst… because of its air sensitivity, which might led to the failure of Suzuki coupling.”; “A more robust and active catalyst PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂ (5 mol %) was tried… gave a complete reaction… within 1 h.”; “Further investigation indicated that 1 mol % of PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂ was enough for completion… although a longer reaction time of 5 h was required.”

Paper Title: Development of a Modified Process for the Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of c‑Met/ALK Inhibitor HS-10168
Problem_Description: Coupling of triflate 11 with dimethylphosphine oxide 8 using PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂ (5 mol %) and triethylamine in acetonitrile at reflux gave only ~60 % conversion after 24 h, requiring an impractically long reaction time for acceptable conversion.
Solution_Description: Increasing the palladium catalyst loading to 10 mol % accelerated the reaction to completion within 1.5 h, providing full conversion to intermediate 12; alternative palladium sources were screened but the optimized PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂ system proved superior.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction successfully provided desired intermediate 12 but with low conversion of 11 being ∼60% even after 24 h.”; “Increasing the loading of catalyst to 10 mol % led to a complete reaction within 1.5 h.”; “Other palladium catalysts … were also tested, but none of them showed superior results over those of PdCl₂(dppf)₂·CH₂Cl₂.”

Paper Title: Development of a Modified Process for the Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of c‑Met/ALK Inhibitor HS-10168
Problem_Description: The original preparation of phosphorus‑containing phenylboronic acid 2 via palladium‑catalyzed coupling of 2‑fluoro‑4‑bromo‑phenylboronic 7 with dimethylphosphine oxide 8 suffered from extensive self‑coupling of 7, giving only 38 % isolated yield of 2 and generating difficult‑to‑remove impurities.
Solution_Description: Instead of synthesizing 2, the authors employed para‑phenol boronate 9 (derived from 4‑bromo‑3‑fluorophenol 13) as the coupling partner with nitro‑bromopyridine 6, thereby bypassing the self‑coupling problem and obtaining the desired intermediate 10 in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The coupling of 2‑fluoro‑4‑bromo‑phenylboronic 7 and dimethylphoshine oxide 8 also gave a complex mixture… low yield of 38%.”; “Our strategy was to use para‑phenol boronate 9 instead of 2 to couple with 6… avoided the formation of the homocoupling side product.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: The dinitro‑FPAA intermediate (3) is potentially explosive (Könen tube test) and unstable, making its isolation, handling and storage on large scale hazardous.
Solution_Description: The dinitration is performed in a continuous flow micro‑reactor and the resulting dinitro‑FPAA is immediately transferred to the hydrogenation step without isolation, eliminating the need to store the explosive material.
Supporting_Evidence: “The first intermediate in the sequence, dinitro‑FPAA (3), is a potentially explosive material as indicated by the Könen tube test.”; “To overcome these limitations, we have developed a fully integrated continuous… protocol… the dinitro intermediate … was extracted… and directly hydrogenated without isolation.”; “The unstable nature of the nitro and amino intermediates… makes this procedure exceedingly difficult to perform on industrial scale.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: Nitration reactions are highly exothermic, generating large amounts of heat that are difficult to control and pose safety risks.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was optimized to 60 °C and carried out in a heated micro‑structured flow device, which provides efficient heat removal and safe temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence: “Nitration reactions are generally highly exothermic and constitute one the most hazardous industrial processes.”; “We expected to face several issues regarding temperature control…”; “The temperature was then increased to 60 °C… Under these conditions good results were obtained.”; “Control of the reaction exotherm… achieved using a glass static mixer… and a micro‑structured device heated to 60 °C.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: The nitrating mixture and substrate are very viscous liquids, leading to inefficient mixing in a standard T‑mixer and a non‑constant conversion/purity profile over time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A glass static mixer (Uniqsis) with active mixing geometry was installed, providing constant, high‑purity conversion of the dinitro product.
Supporting_Evidence: “The nitrating mixture in oleum as well as the neat FPAA (2) substrate are very viscous liquids… resulting in a non‑constant composition of the crude reaction mixture.”; “Improved conversion profile was obtained when the T‑mixer was sonicated… Excellent and constant conversion… were achieved when a glass static mixer … was installed.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: Small amounts of water formed during nitration can cleave the ArO–CF₂ bond, leading to decomposition of the substrate.
Solution_Description: Concentrated H₂SO₄ was replaced by 20 % oleum (free SO₃) to scavenge water generated in the nitration, preventing substrate decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “As small amounts of water in the reaction mixture can easily cleave the ArO–CF₂ bond 98 % H₂SO₄ was substituted by oleum (20 % free SO₃) to scavenge the water which is formed during the nitration.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: The diamino‑FPAA (4) product is insoluble in toluene, causing clogging of the hydrogenation reactor.
Solution_Description: Methanol was added (toluene/methanol 2:1) to the reaction mixture, providing sufficient solubility of the diamino intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulting diamino‑FPAA (4) product is not soluble in toluene and clogging of the reactor may occur… Solubility tests indicated that diamino‑FPAA (4) is well soluble in a toluene/methanol 2:1 mixture even at a concentration of 0.2 M.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: Large amounts of H₂ gas generated in the hydrogenation/cyclization step interfere with residence‑time control and present an explosion hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A Teflon‑AF2400 tube‑in‑tube reactor was used to remove excess H₂ inline, allowing safe, constant flow and precise control of residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The hydrogenation reaction mixture… contains a large amount of H₂ gas… we performed an inline removal of the excess of H₂ after the reduction using gas permeable Teflon AF2400 tubing.”; “The advantage of using a tube‑in‑tube reactor is that the H₂ released … can be readily removed by the ventilation system.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: The H‑Cube Pro hydrogenator is limited by the fixed volume of the pre‑packed Pd/C CatCart, restricting throughput and scale‑up.
Solution_Description: All other reactor sections (nitration, extraction, cyclization) were adapted to the maximum flow rate of the hydrogenation step, and additional residence‑time units were added to maintain residence time at higher overall flow rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “The scale of the hydrogenation reaction… is limited by the size of the commercially available CatCart… optimal productivity of 0.2 mmol min⁻¹ can be obtained. All other reactor parts… will therefore have to be adapted to the optimal flow rate of this reaction step.”; “To demonstrate that the dinitration process can be readily scaled… an additional residence time unit … was installed… flow rates increased while keeping residence time constant.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: Gradual Pd leaching and catalyst poisoning during extended operation cause a slight decrease in conversion.
Solution_Description: Periodic catalyst cleaning/recovery with additional solvents was suggested to restore activity and extend catalyst lifetime.
Supporting_Evidence: “ICP‑MS analysis… revealed a Pd content of 14.6 ppm… we ascribe the small decrease in conversion observed to poisoning of the heterogeneous catalyst… To achieve longer process operation recovery of the catalyst by cleaning with additional solvents has been described.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: Cyclization at 120 °C produced a small amount of hydrolysis by‑product, reducing selectivity.
Solution_Description: The cyclization temperature was lowered to 80 °C and the residence time reduced to 5 min, eliminating hydrolysis and delivering >99 % conversion with high selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “…a small amount (1 %) of hydrolysis product was also observed possibly due to the high temperature used in this process.”; “Reaction temperature and residence time were gradually decreased… to ultimately reveal 80 °C and 5 min residence time as optimal conditions for the cyclization.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of a Key 1,4-Benzoxazinone Intermediate via a Nitration/Hydrogenation/Cyclization Sequence
Problem_Description: After nitration, phase separation of the organic product from the aqueous nitrating mixture is required; batch extraction is cumbersome and inefficient at scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous liquid–liquid membrane separator (Zaiput) was employed to achieve rapid, efficient phase separation inline.
Supporting_Evidence: “A membrane based liquid–liquid separator (Zaiput) was utilized to separate the organic and aqueous phases in continuous flow.”; “The continuous flow setup incorporated a membrane based liquid–liquid separator technology.”

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: The nitro‑containing substrate (1‑chloro‑4‑nitrobenzene) is a highly crystalline solid that is poorly soluble in pure water, leading to heterogeneous mixtures and low conversion at higher substrate concentrations.
Solution_Description: A small amount of THF (≈156 µL per 78 mg of substrate) is added as a cosolvent to dissolve the nitro compound before it is introduced to the 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M/H₂O micellar solution, giving a stable, milky emulsion and improving conversion (99 % vs 4 % without cosolvent).
Supporting_Evidence: “Materials containing nitro functionality are typically highly crystalline solids, often unfavorable for reactions in which water is used as the reaction medium… we sought to employ the use of a cosolvent that would aid in dissolving crystalline material and stabilize the starting material emulsion.”; “THF was found to be the cosolvent of choice… slightly better conversion on a 78 mg scale than literature conditions.”; Table 1 entry 2 shows 99 % isolated product with THF vs 4 % without cosolvent.

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: Direct addition of the substrate‑in‑THF solution to the surfactant mixture gave a sluggish reaction (only 18 % product after 18 h) because the emulsion was not formed efficiently.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The substrate solution is added to the surfactant mixture while stirring at >800 rpm, forming a ‘milky’ emulsion before catalyst activation; this high‑speed, portionwise addition ensures rapid dispersion and full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “When a solution of 2 in THF was added directly to the reaction mixture, the progress of the reaction suffered significantly… only 18 % product was observed after 18 h (entry 6).”; “Dissolution in THF prior to addition to 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M/H₂O achieves the desired ‘milky’ appearance much faster… should be done at high stirring rates (>800 rpm).”

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: The reduction can generate azoxy (6) and diazo (7) by‑products, which are genotoxic and carcinogenic, and their removal adds purification burden.
Solution_Description: Diluting the reaction from 0.5 M to 0.25 M suppresses the condensation pathway; addition of 1 equiv KCl further eliminates formation of the hazardous by‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: “The condensation of 4 and 5 to 6 is a concern… these byproducts are both genotoxic and carcinogenic.”; “Within 1 h, 100 % conversion of 2 was achieved… free of by‑products.”; “We considered the entropic factor of condensation by diluting the system from 0.5 to 0.25 M.”; Table 5 entry 5 shows that NaBH₄ + KCl gives 91 % product with no azoxy detected.

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: Catalyst activation with KBH₄ releases large volumes of gas (foam) that can increase the reaction volume up to four‑fold, raising pressure and safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Add the nitro‑substrate emulsion before charging KBH₄; the later addition of KBH₄ after the substrate is present eliminates significant foam formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Foaming has been observed to increase the reaction volume up to four times the original solvent level during catalyst activation… addition of KBH₄ that is charged to the system after the substrate is present will not lead to the generation of any significant amount of foam.”

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: Reducing catalyst loading (0.5 % Pd) or using fewer equivalents of the reductant slows the reaction, giving incomplete conversion and lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Increase Pd loading to 200 ppm and raise KBH₄ loading to 3.0 equiv; this accelerates the reaction (full conversion within 1 h) and restores high yields (94 % on 100 mmol scale).
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulting rate of the reaction was slower from both modifications, and the undesired azoxy byproduct 6 was observed yet again.”; “We changed the nature of the hydride source from NaBH₄ (1.5 equiv) to the more reactive KBH₄ and increased its loading (3.0 equiv). The catalyst loading was increased to a 200 ppm Pd loading… Within 1 h, 100 % conversion of 2 was achieved… affording 3 in 94 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: Potassium borohydride (KBH₄) is significantly more expensive than sodium borohydride (NaBH₄).
Solution_Description: Use NaBH₄ together with 1 equiv KCl; the additive recovers the reactivity of KBH₄ while keeping the cheaper NaBH₄ as the reductant.
Supporting_Evidence: “Price comparison… NaBH₄ $9.04/mol vs KBH₄ $16.20/mol.”; Table 5 entry 5 shows NaBH₄ + KCl gives 91 % product (comparable to KBH₄ alone) with lower cost.

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: Traditional nitro reductions often require high‑pressure hydrogen gas and specialized equipment not readily available in standard process‑development labs.
Solution_Description: Perform the reduction in aqueous micellar media at ambient temperature and pressure using KBH₄ as the hydrogen source, eliminating the need for high‑pressure reactors.
Supporting_Evidence: “Preferred use of KBH₄ as the hydride source, at ambient temperature and pressure, lends this process suitable for a standard reaction vessel alleviating the need for specialized hydrogenation equipment.”

Paper Title: Sustainable and Scalable Fe/ppm Pd Nanoparticle Nitro Group Reductions in Water at Room Temperature
Problem_Description: The nitro reduction is highly exothermic (‑850 kJ mol⁻¹), potentially leading to temperature spikes.
Solution_Description: Run the reaction at room temperature; calorimetric studies show the maximum adiabatic temperature rise is ≈62 °C, well below water’s boiling point, so no special cooling is required.
Supporting_Evidence: “Calorimetric analysis measured the energy … the heat of reaction… approx. –896 to –850 kJ/mol. The theoretical adiabatic temperature increase … about 62 °C… well below the boiling point of the solvent (water) and would not be a safety matter.”

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: Impurities 15–18 were introduced from low‑level contaminants in the commercial reagents 3‑CFA (7) and 2‑chloro‑N‑methyl‑acetamide (14) and from over‑alkylation of the intermediate in the final step of the first‑generation route.
Solution_Description: A new Dimroth rearrangement pathway was developed that avoids the late‑stage introduction of the methyl‑amide side chain and therefore eliminates the formation of impurities 15–18.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: During the kilogram‑scale etherification of phenol 20 to give piperidine 26 the reaction formed an extremely thick slurry that could not be stirred effectively, limiting scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The solvent system was changed to a mixture of water, PEG‑400 and MIBK, which gave a mobile reaction mixture, faster reaction rates and complete conversion.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: The borrowing‑hydrogen alkylation of piperidine 26 with glycolic amide 27 gave only 45 % isolated yield of 21 and generated several by‑products that were difficult to remove.
Solution_Description: The alkylation was re‑optimized using triethanolamine as base in ethanol (4.0 rel vol), followed by direct antisolvent crystallisation of 21 from the reaction solution, which gave >80 % yield and clean product.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: Nitration of intermediate 21 produced trace nitro‑regioisomers that could carry through the sequence and generate regio‑isomeric AZD8931 impurities.
Solution_Description: A safe nitration protocol was established using controlled equivalents of HNO₃ (1.05 eq) and H₂SO₄ (8 eq) at 45 °C, with a staged addition and quench, giving <0.1 % regio‑isomers and high conversion.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the sodium dithionite reduction of nitro compound 28 caused a viscous slurry, crystallisation of acetic acid on vessel walls, and safety concerns when adding the solid reductant all at once.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reduction was replaced by a mixed Pt (1 %)/V (2 %) catalytic hydrogenation in acetonitrile, with controlled hydrogen pressure, increased agitation, and reduced vessel fill level to improve gas‑liquid mass transfer and suppress impurity formation.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: During the final crystallisation of AZD8931 the product oily‑ly plated the reactor walls, gave a sticky solid and low purity when residual water in 2‑MeTHF was >4 %.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to 2‑MeTHF, water was reduced to <1 % by distillation, a small amount of IPA was added to form an IPA solvate which crystallised cleanly, and a partial solvent swap into IPA was used to dry the product, delivering high‑yield, high‑purity API.

Paper Title: The Development of a Dimroth Rearrangement Route to AZD8931
Problem_Description: The synthesis of the dimeric amidine 33 in ethanol/ethyl‑orthoformate required a distillation step to remove ethanol, which was operationally cumbersome on large scale.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to cyclohexane allowed the process to proceed without a distillation step; the reaction progressed directly to product 33 with high yield (96 %).

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: The hydroboration of amorpha‑4,11‑diene (AD) using 9‑borabicyclo[3.3.1]‑nonane (9‑BBN) provides reasonable yields and diastereoselectivity, but the reagent is prohibitively expensive for commercial‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The hydroboration route was abandoned.  The authors redirected the synthesis toward a functional‑group‑protected epoxide strategy that employs inexpensive reagents (e.g., H₂O₂, formic acid) and avoids costly 9‑BBN altogether.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...required the use of an expensive reagent, 9‑borabicyclo[3.3.1]‑nonane (9‑BBN), to perform a hydroboration … making the process practically and economically unappealing.”
“...we initiated our studies by examining methods for the selective functionalisation of the isopropenyl group…the protection of the active double bond…"

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Amyris’ alternative epoxidation of the exocyclic double bond using a metalloporphyrin or metallosalen catalyst is attractive in principle but is also costly and impractical for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The authors screened inexpensive oxidants and identified a hydrogen‑peroxide/formic‑acid system that gives ≥99 % regioselectivity and quantitative yields, eliminating the need for expensive metal catalysts.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...another route...involving regio‑ and stereoselective epoxidation of the exocyclic double bond…was also found to be expensive and ultimately impractical.”
“...zeroed in on the green as well as most economical epoxidising agent, H₂O₂…excellent regioselectivity toward the endocyclic double bond (≥99 %) and almost quantitative yields of 3.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Epoxidation of AD with m‑CPBA delivers only ~80 % conversion and 80 % isolated yield; the reagent is also very expensive, making the process unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Switching to a 50 % aqueous H₂O₂ solution (1 equiv) with NaOAc (0.1 equiv) in 4‑chlorophenol (4‑CP) gave 98 % conversion and 94 % yield.  Further optimisation using 2.5 equiv H₂O₂ with formic acid (0.25 equiv) raised conversion >99 % and yield to 96 %, all with inexpensive, readily available reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 1, entry 1 (m‑CPBA) – 80 % yield; entry 2 (50 % aq. H₂O₂/NaOAc) – 94 % yield; entry 3 (50 % aq. H₂O₂/HCOOH) – 96 % yield.
“...the observed regioselectivity toward the endocyclic double bond…appeared to be too low…Another reason for not considering m‑CPBA was the very high cost of this reagent.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Attempts to functionalise the isopropenyl side‑chain by free‑radical halogenation using N‑chlorosuccinimide, N‑bromosuccinimide or SO₂Cl₂ failed to give any useful conversion, and the reagents are either hazardous or expensive.
Solution_Description: Chlorination was instead achieved by ionic conditions using inexpensive calcium hypochlorite (bleach) or trichloroisocyanuric acid (TCCA).  Both reagents gave >90 % isolated yields of the chloro‑epoxy product, with TCCA offering a safe, stable, and recyclable cyanuric‑acid by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 2, entry 2 (Ca(OCl)₂) – 90 % yield; entry 3 (TCCA) – 94 % yield.
“Under ambient conditions, TCCA is not only safe, stable, and inexpensive but also gives easily recyclable cyanuric acid as a by‑product, thus offering a green alternative to chlorine or other agents.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Oxidation of chloro‑epoxy‑AD (4) to aldehyde (5) using N‑methyl‑morpholine N‑oxide (NMO) is expensive and provides no yield advantage over other methods.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced NMO with dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as both solvent and oxidant (K₂HPO₄ as base).  This change gave quantitative conversion (>99 %) and increased isolated yield to 95 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 3, entry 3 (DMSO/K₂HPO₄) – >99 % conversion, 95 % yield.
“NMO is expensive and its use … was found to inflate the cost of the product considerably while offering no yield advantage.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: De‑epoxidation of the protected intermediate (6) using lithium metal, which worked for earlier steps, unexpectedly reduced the exocyclic α,β‑unsaturated double bond, giving a mixture of DHAA diastereomers and the desired artemisinic acid, compromising selectivity.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was re‑designed so that the exocyclic double bond is saturated **before** epoxide removal (formation of intermediate 7).  This pre‑saturation prevents unwanted reduction during the later de‑epoxidation, delivering clean DHAA in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the conditions used were also favorable for reducing the exocyclic α,β‑unsaturated double bond…the reaction yielded a mixture of both isomers of DHAA…This understanding turned out to be handy for quickly solving the problem and reframing the synthesis, which involved saturation of the α,β‑unsaturated double bond…prior to the removal of the epoxy group, resulting in a good conversion efficiency and high yield of 8.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: The commercial photochemical route to artemisinin requires expensive photoreactors, high‑energy light sources, and a porphyrin‑based photocatalyst, making the process capital‑intensive and unsuitable for low‑cost manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A purely chemical oxidation sequence was employed: esterification with dimethyl sulfate, oxidation with 30 % H₂O₂ in the presence of Na₂MoO₄ (triplet‑oxygen catalyst), and a Hock rearrangement catalysed by benzenesulfonic acid on Indion 225H resin.  This eliminates the photochemical step, reduces capital cost, and improves overall yield to ≈60 % (vs. 41 % for the earlier chemical route).
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion of 8 to 9 is accomplished by esterification with the help of dimethyl sulfate…hydrogen peroxide in the presence of sodium molybdate…The highest overall yield of 61 % was reported…but we achieved 60 % without photoreactors.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: The strong‑acid cation‑exchange resin Dowex 50WX8‑200 used in the original Amyris process is expensive.
Solution_Description: The authors substituted Dowex 50WX8‑200 with the cheaper Indion 225H resin, which performed equivalently in the Hock rearrangement step while reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “we decided to use Indion 225H cation exchange resin, a cheaper alternative to the Dowex 50WX8‑200 resin used by Amyris.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Benzenesulfonic acid (PhSO₃H) is a more economical acid catalyst compared with alternatives such as trifluoroacetic acid used in some literature procedures.
Solution_Description: Benzenesulfonic acid was employed as the catalyst for the final Hock rearrangement, lowering reagent cost without sacrificing yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “We decided to use…benzenesulfonic acid as the catalyst in the step involving triplet oxygen.”

Paper Title: Amalgamation of Synthetic Biology and Chemistry for High-Throughput Nonconventional Synthesis of the Antimalarial Drug Artemisinin
Problem_Description: Initial oxidation steps (e.g., epoxidation, chlorination, oxidation to aldehyde) required lengthy reaction times (30–40 h) and gave modest isolated yields, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperatures were raised (e.g., 55–58 °C for H₂O₂ epoxidation; 80–85 °C for DMSO oxidation) and oxygen exposure times were extended, which increased conversion rates and overall isolated yield of artemisinin to ~60 % while shortening batch times.
Supporting_Evidence: “Increasing the duration of singlet as well as triplet oxygen exposure improved the conversions…thus ultimately giving close to 60 % isolated yield of the desired product.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Scalable Synthesis of a Glucokinase Activator via Diastereomeric Resolution and Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The original ring‑opening iodination of ketal 4 to give iodide 5 using TMSI gave only moderate conversion (≈60 % HPLC area) and generated impurity peaks, and TMSI is a highly corrosive and unstable reagent that poses safety hazards on large scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: TMSI was replaced by TMSCl together with NaI as a safer iodide source; the reaction was performed in CH₃CN with 0.1 equiv water to increase NaI solubility, and the temperature was optimized (−42 °C to 23 °C) to improve selectivity and yield (up to 88 % HPLC area).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When we tried ring‑opening iodination of 4 to give 5 using the original method… the yield was moderate because of the generation of impurities” (Table 1, entry 1). 
• “Performing the reaction at a lower temperature using sodium hydrogen carbonate led to an improved yield… despite the use of 2.2 equiv of TMSI” (Table 1, entry 2). 
• “Chlorotrimethylsilane (TMSCl) together with sodium iodide (NaI)… achieved an acceptable result” (Table 1, entry 3). 
• “Eventually, 0.1 equiv of water was added to the reaction mixture to increase the solubility of NaI for industrial use without detriment” (Table 1, entry 8).

Paper Title: A Practical and Scalable Synthesis of a Glucokinase Activator via Diastereomeric Resolution and Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Diastereomeric resolution of the α‑arylpropionic acid precursor 7 by forming salts with various chiral amines gave low diastereomeric excess (de ≤ 30 %) and in many cases no solid formed, indicating poor solubility of the desired diastereomer under the tested conditions.
Solution_Description: It was discovered that the desired (R)‑7 crystallizes directly from solution without any chiral auxiliary because it is less soluble than its S‑enantiomer; EtOH was identified as the optimal solvent and two recrystallizations raised the de to 99 %, eliminating the need for chiral amine auxiliaries.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Salt formation of 7 with (R)‑(+)-1‑phenylethylamine… gave a little‑improved de of 30 %” (Table 2, entry 1). 
• “Unexpectedly, the desired diastereomer (R)‑7 was crystallized in the absence of chiral amine… suggesting that (R)‑7 is less soluble than the diastereomer (S)‑7” (Table 2, entry 8). 
• “Two recrystallizations with EtOH increased the de to 99 %” (Table 3, entry 2).

Paper Title: A Practical and Scalable Synthesis of a Glucokinase Activator via Diastereomeric Resolution and Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: Attempts to epimerize the undesired (S)‑7 using various strong bases (t‑BuOK, LiNH₂, LHMDS, LDA) either gave low epimerization conversion or caused significant decomposition of the substrate.
Solution_Description: Sodium hydride (NaH) at 60 °C provided sufficient epimerization with minimal decomposition, and a mild ketene‑forming protocol using p‑TsCl and 1‑methylimidazole at 25 °C gave complete epimerization without major side‑reactions; the latter was adopted for pilot‑scale recovery of (R)‑7.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Sodium methoxide and sodium ethoxide did not lead to sufficient epimerization even at 60 °C” (Table 4, entries 1‑2). 
• “Although epimerization was observed using potassium t‑BuOK, concomitant decomposition occurred” (Table 4, entry 3). 
• “Sufficient epimerization was observed using sodium hydride at 60 °C, and a diastereomeric mixture was obtained” (Table 4, entry 4). 
• “Epimerization proceeded completely in CH₂Cl₂ or CH₃CN with slight degradation when treated with p‑TsCl and 1‑methylimidazole” (Table 4, entries 8‑9).

Paper Title: A Practical and Scalable Synthesis of a Glucokinase Activator via Diastereomeric Resolution and Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route to the 2‑aminopyrazine fragment 3 involved steps that emitted hydrogen cyanide (HCN) and required multiple chromatographic purifications, leading to safety concerns and low overall yield (≈38 %).
Solution_Description: A new scalable route was developed starting from commercially available 16, using a palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling with benzophenone imine as the amine source; after imine cleavage the product 3 was isolated as a fumarate salt, which could be crystallized in high purity (≥99 % area) without chromatography, raising the overall yield to 71 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We required a new synthetic approach for 3 to avoid emitting HCN.” (Section 2.4). 
• “The palladium‑catalyzed C–N coupling reaction with benzophenone imine… gave 73 % yield after imine cleavage” (Table 5, entry 5). 
• “Because 3 was oily, we screened various acids for salt formation and concluded that fumaric acid salts were the best from the aspect of stability.” (Section 2.4). 
• “61.1 kg of 3 fumarate was obtained with a purity of 99 % area … yield 71 % based on 16, which was significantly improved compared with that of the medicinal chemistry synthesis (38 %).” (Section 2.4).

Paper Title: A Practical and Scalable Synthesis of a Glucokinase Activator via Diastereomeric Resolution and Palladium-Catalyzed C–N Coupling Reaction
Problem_Description: The medicinal‑chemistry synthesis required nine chromatographic purifications, which are impractical and costly at production scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: All chromatographic steps were eliminated by using crystallization‑based separations (e.g., recrystallization of 7, formation of fumarate salt of 3, and direct precipitation of the final API), allowing the entire process to be performed in batch reactors with simple filtration and washing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The medicinal chemistry synthesis of (R)‑1 involved 15 steps and nine chromatographic purifications.” (Introduction). 
• “In addition, the requirement of several chromatographic purifications… were avoided” (Conclusion). 
• “Crystallization of 7 … two recrystallizations with EtOH increased the de to 99 %.” (Section 2.2). 
• “Fumaric acid salts were the best… most of the impurities were present in the filtrate.” (Section 2.4). 
• “The final product (R)‑1 was obtained by filtration and drying without any chromatography.” (Section 2.5).

Paper Title: One-Step Continuous Flow Synthesis of Antifungal WHO Essential Medicine Flucytosine Using Fluorine
Problem_Description: High manufacturing cost of flucytosine due to the existing four‑step process; difficulty separating unreacted cytosine from the product; formation of a difluorinated side‑product that reduces overall yield; the fluorination reaction is highly exothermic; handling of toxic fluorine gas presents safety concerns at scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Develop a one‑step continuous‑flow direct fluorination of cytosine with inexpensive fluorine gas (new synthetic route); use excess fluorine to drive >99 % conversion and simple water recrystallisation to isolate product (new purification, stoichiometry change); employ narrow‑bore stainless‑steel and silicon‑carbide flow reactors that give rapid gas–liquid mixing and resistance to corrosion (reactor platform, mixing); run the silicon‑carbide reactor at 10 °C with external cooling to control the exotherm (temperature optimisation).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “flucytosine … is manufactured by an expensive four‑step manufacturing process” (Abstract).
• “the separation of unreacted starting material from the desired flucytosine product proved to be very difficult” (Batch results).
• “significant quantities of difluorinated product leads to considerable waste which would contribute to higher production costs” (Batch discussion).
• “silicon carbide … has excellent heat exchange properties appropriate for controlling exothermic processes” (Scale‑up description).
• “fluorine gas (10 % in nitrogen) … was passed … at 10 °C, … no exotherm observed” (Pilot‑scale method).
• “after addition of 1.75 equiv of fluorine … pure flucytosine was isolated … 38 % yield” (Batch optimisation).
• “100 % conversion … 63 % isolated … using flow reactor” (Flow results, Table 1).
• “the reactor … ensures good gas–liquid mixing” (Flow reactor description).

Paper Title: Intensification of Nitrobenzaldehydes Synthesis from Benzyl Alcohol in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: The direct nitration/oxidation of benzyl alcohol in the conventional batch reactor is highly exothermic.  The oxidation step releases ≈ 1100 J·g⁻¹ and the nitration ≈ 1185 J·g⁻¹, leading to rapid temperature spikes (up to 83 °C) and an estimated adiabatic temperature rise of ~380 K.  Such heat release can trigger explosive thermal runaway and cause decomposition of intermediates.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a commercial glass microreactor (embedded static mixer, heat‑exchange channels).  The micro‑scale geometry provides a very high surface‑to‑volume ratio, enabling fast heat removal and uniform mixing, which suppresses hot‑spot formation and prevents thermal runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "...the direct nitration of benzaldehyde the process could easily undergo explosive thermal runaway, due to the exothermic oxidation and nitration reactions occurring in the acid mixture..." (Introduction). 2. "...temperature can very rapidly increase up to 83 °C" (Figure 3 description). 3. "...adiabatic temperature rise is estimated to be ΔT_ad ≈ 380 K..." (Batch Reactions and Evaluation of Reaction Hazard). 4. "The adoption of a commercial microreactor enabled us to carry out the process under unusual conditions of high temperatures and strongly acidic media" (Conclusions). 5. "...glass microreactor with embedded heat transfer and static mixer..." (Microreactor Performance).

Paper Title: Intensification of Nitrobenzaldehydes Synthesis from Benzyl Alcohol in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: Traditional batch nitration of benzaldehyde gives only up to 20 % yield of the ortho‑nitrobenzaldehyde because the reaction must be run at low temperature (5–10 °C) and low acid concentration to keep the exotherm manageable, limiting conversion.
Solution_Description: Using the kinetic model, the authors increased the nitric‑acid molar fraction to 0.350 and sulfuric‑acid fraction to 0.450 and raised the operating temperature to 68 °C.  This stoichiometric enrichment and temperature optimization raised the ortho‑isomer yield to ~42 % and the meta‑isomer yield to ~96 %.  Substrate concentration was also tuned (0.05–0.5 M) to balance conversion and solubility.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "...3‑Nitrobenzaldehyde is traditionally produced ... yields up to 20 %" (Introduction). 2. "...the molar fractions of nitric and sulfuric acids were increased up to 0.35, 0.45, and temperature to 68 °C, which was impossible to do under batch conditions" (Abstract). 3. "Figure 5 shows the effect of nitric acid ... and sulfuric acid ... on the yield of 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde" (Results and Discussion). 4. "The optimal temperature ... fixed at x_n = 0.350; x_s = 0.450; T = 68 °C" (Results). 5. "The average experimental 2‑nitrobenzaldehyde percentage yield was 41.6 %" (Results).

Paper Title: Intensification of Nitrobenzaldehydes Synthesis from Benzyl Alcohol in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: When the organic substrate concentration is increased (up to 0.5 M), benzaldehyde becomes poorly soluble in the less‑acidic mixed‑acid phase, leading to the formation of a biphasic (liquid–liquid) flow.  This demixing limits the amount of benzaldehyde available for nitration and forces longer residence times.
Solution_Description: The authors limited the substrate concentration in the homogeneous runs (≤ 0.05 M) and noted that further work is required to improve solubility (e.g., co‑solvent addition, phase‑transfer agents).  No definitive remediation was implemented in the current study; the issue is flagged for future investigation.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "...a significant increase in the organic substrate concentration can easily lead to the formation of a biphasic system, affecting the residence time necessary to achieve complete conversion" (Conclusions). 2. "...the formed benzaldehyde is poorly soluble under less acidic conditions such that the amount of converted benzaldehyde is limited by the solubility of the organic in the aqueous phase" (Results). 3. "...experiments carried under the same experimental conditions ... but with higher concentrations of 3‑nitrobenzaldehyde (up to 0.5 M) resulted in formation of liquid–liquid heterogeneous flow" (Results). 4. "...no significant differences were measured in the samples collected with residence times up to about 18 s" (Results), indicating that low concentration was used to avoid biphasic flow. 5. "Further study of the solubilities of the organics ... is in progress" (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Intensification of Nitrobenzaldehydes Synthesis from Benzyl Alcohol in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: Batch experiments required very low reactant concentrations and long reaction times (several minutes to hours) to stay isothermal, which dramatically reduces throughput and is unsuitable for industrial production.
Solution_Description: Switching to a microreactor allowed operation at higher temperatures (up to 68 °C) and higher acid concentrations while maintaining safe temperature control, thus shortening the required residence time to the sub‑second regime (model predicts complete conversion in < 2 ms; practical residence time ≈ 9 s).
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "...the results shown in Figure 6c. However, the lowest residence time attainable in the microreactor was about 9 s" (Results). 2. "...a complete conversion is achieved in less than 2 ms according to the model simulation" (Results). 3. "...experiments carried out at low concentrations of the reactants and long reaction times, to allow for heat transfer, thus operating at isothermal conditions" (Batch Reactions). 4. "...the microreactor enables us to carry out the process under unusual conditions of high temperatures and strongly acidic media" (Conclusions). 5. "...temperature, acid composition were increased ... which was impossible to do under batch conditions" (Abstract).

Paper Title: Intensification of Nitrobenzaldehydes Synthesis from Benzyl Alcohol in a Microreactor
Problem_Description: The rapid, highly exothermic oxidation of benzyl alcohol generates a gas phase (NO_x and water vapor) which can cause pressure spikes and vessel pressurisation, raising safety concerns in batch reactors.
Solution_Description: While the authors did not implement a specific addition strategy in batch, the microreactor design inherently provides continuous, controlled feed of both acid mixture and organic, eliminating sudden addition and associated pressure spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "...the very fast rate of the highly exothermic oxidation step and the consequent nitration..." (Batch Reactions). 2. "...temperature can very rapidly increase up to 83 °C" (Figure 3). 3. "...the formation of a gas phase... will necessarily affect the residence time distribution" (Results). 4. "...the microreactor with embedded static mixer, heat exchange..." (Experimental Section). 5. "...adoption of a commercial microreactor enabled us to carry out the process under unusual conditions..." (Conclusions).

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: The initial oxidation of 5‑bromo‑2‑aminopyridine to the nitro compound showed low conversion, high impurity levels and poor reproducibility in laboratory trials.
Solution_Description: A premixed “Piranha” oxidant (H2SO4/H2O2) was prepared and the amine solution was added slowly (6 h) at 20–25 °C using a Teflon‑coated pump; the oxidant ratio was increased to ≥2.2 mol equiv and the addition temperature was raised to 30 °C when needed, giving complete conversion and reducing impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “initially showed low conversion, high impurity content and lack of reproducibility in lab trials.” (Abstract) 
• “no conversion at the end of the addition and full conversion necessitated 40 h at 20 °C… When the reaction temperature was increased to 30 °C, the reaction was completed after 8–10 h.” (Oxidation reaction section) 
• “Addition of amine solution over the oxidant… only 22 % of starting material left at the end of the addition… greatly reduced (5–8 % HPLC area).” (Premixed oxidant experiments) 
• “The addition of hydrogen peroxide 30 % over concentrated H2SO4 was performed via Teflon‑coated metering pump… in any case the overall addition time must not be faster than 6 h.” (Experimental section) 
• “The oxidant ratio was increased to 2.2 mol equiv and addition time to 6 h, resulting in complete conversion.” (Section 2.4)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: When solid N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) was added directly to the cooled amine solution, an instantaneous heat spike occurred, a thick succinimide precipitate formed, and significant polybromination (up to 15 % HPLC) was observed, leading to poor yields and difficult heat removal on larger batches.
Solution_Description: NBS was delivered as a 6 w/w acetonitrile solution and added gradually over ~1 h, which lowered the exotherm, reduced the dibromo impurity to 4 % (vs 14 % with solid NBS) and allowed higher addition temperatures (0 to +5 °C) and better heat transfer.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “As was quite foreseeable, polybromination was observed… up to 15 % area HPLC.” (Bromination reaction) 
• “Reaction calorimetry… addition of a single portion of NBS resulted in an instantaneous heat generation. The sharp heat spike… are the likely cause of a high level of impurity.” (Bromination reaction) 
• “After approximately 70 % of the total amount of brominating agent was added, a precipitate formed… resulting in a thick suspension and consequently difficult heat exchange.” (Bromination reaction) 
• “We modified the protocol to accommodate the addition of the brominating agent… as acetonitrile solution (6 w/w with respect to NBS).” (Bromination reaction) 
• “Lower amounts of the dibromo impurity (4 % … vs 14 % … when solid NBS used) were obtained when this protocol was followed and a higher temperature could be used (2–5 °C vs previous –5 to –8 °C).” (Table 1)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: A “batch‑type” addition of the entire oxidant mixture (H2O2/H2SO4) generated a large adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad ≈ +107 K) and a rapid self‑heating rate (17 °C min⁻¹), creating a serious runaway risk.
Solution_Description: The oxidant was premixed and added slowly (6 h) while continuously monitoring temperature; the addition was paused if the temperature exceeded set‑points, thus keeping ΔT_ad below dangerous levels and staying within Criticality Class 1.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “An undesired ‘batch‑type’ reaction will quite clearly result in large heat generation (ΔT_ad = +107 K…)” (Oxidation reaction calorimetry) 
• “The addition of hydrogen peroxide 30 % over concentrated H2SO4 was performed via Teflon‑coated pump while maintaining the temperature below 10 °C. In case of temperature increase, the dosing must be interrupted and restarted only when the temperature is below the set point.” (Experimental section) 
• “Two experiments were conducted by varying the addition rate of 5‑bromo‑2‑aminopyridine solution (3 h and 6 h)… the extent of the accumulation decreased with the increasing addition time (32 % and 23 %).” (Oxidation reaction calorimetry) 
• “The resulting robust reaction conditions and appropriate safety boundaries allowed to develop a reproducible, safe protocol…” (Abstract) 
• “The safety limit can arbitrarily be defined as the temperature at which the TMR is equal to 24 h (T_D,24).” (Criticality discussion)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: Metal ion contaminants (from gold‑plated or Hastelloy test cells) catalyzed the decomposition of the oxidant mixture, lowering the onset temperature from ~86 °C to ~46 °C and increasing the criticality class of the process.
Solution_Description: Glass‑lined reactors and inert glass test cells were employed for the preparation and use of the oxidant mixture, eliminating metal‑catalyzed decomposition and maintaining the process at Criticality Class 2.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “DSC analyses… detected a lower onset when the sample was left in a gold‑plated crucible (46 °C) versus a clean one (56 °C), indicating metal‑catalyzed decomposition.” (Table 5) 
• “Hastelloy C22 possesses limited chemical resistance toward strongly oxidizing acidic mixtures… onset increased to 93 °C in glass test cell.” (Table 5) 
• “It appears evident that a reactor train free from any metal ion contamination is of utmost importance.” (Section 2.8.1) 
• “Glass‑lined reactors were utilized after extensive washing with water.” (Industrial scale‑up results) 
• “The criticality class definition holds true if and only if no metal ion contaminants are present; otherwise the process becomes Criticality Class 5.” (Section 2.8.1)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: Direct addition of 30 % H2O2 to the amine solution gave little to no conversion during the addition period and generated red bromine fumes, indicating a competing decomposition pathway and poor productivity.
Solution_Description: The oxidant was premixed with sulfuric acid (Piranha solution) and the amine was added over 1 h; the oxidant equivalence was increased to ≥2.2 mol equiv and the reaction temperature was allowed to reach 30 °C, achieving complete conversion in 8–10 h without bromine fumes.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Direct addition of hydrogen peroxide 30 % over a solution of 5‑bromo‑2‑aminopyridine… no conversion was observed at the end of the addition; full conversion necessitated 40 h at 20 °C.” (Oxidation reaction) 
• “Red fumes… identified as molecular bromine… hypothesized to arise from oxidative decomposition of the pyridine ring.” (Oxidation reaction) 
• “A premixed solution of H2SO4 95–98 %/H2O2 30 % (Piranha) … addition of amine solution over the oxidant … only 22 % of starting material left at the end of the addition, greatly reduced (5–8 % HPLC area).” (Premixed oxidant) 
• “Increasing the amount of oxidant to 2.2 mol equiv and increasing the addition time to 6 h resulted in complete conversion.” (Section 2.4) 
• “When the reaction temperature was increased to 30 °C, the reaction was completed after 8–10 h.” (Oxidation reaction)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: Using a lower sulfuric‑acid to hydrogen‑peroxide ratio (3:1 w/w) generated an “azo‑oxy” impurity and decreased product yield.
Solution_Description: The optimal H2SO4/H2O2 ratio was experimentally determined to be ≥5.6:1 w/w (final acid concentration 82.6 % w/w), which suppressed the formation of the azo‑oxy impurity and improved yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A reaction run with sulfuric acid/hydrogen peroxide ratio (3:1 vs 5.6:1 w/w)… produced a large amount of an impurity… identified as the ‘azo‑oxy’ derivative.” (Section 2.5) 
• “The optimal ratio of sulfuric acid 98 % and H2O2 30 % was experimentally found to be ≥5.6:1 w/w… lower ratio invariably resulted in slow reactions and higher side‑product formation.” (Section 2.4) 
• “The critical role played by the sulfuric acid was also supported by the following experimental observations… (1) direct addition of hydrogen peroxide 30 %… high impurity levels; (2) more diluted sulfuric acid (50–80 %)… reactions invariably met with failure.” (Section 2.5) 
• Table 3 shows enthalpy data confirming the formation of the active peroxosulfuric species only at higher acid concentrations. (Table 3) 
• “The oxidation reaction gave comparable purity (99.92 % HPLC) after optimization of the acid ratio.” (Industrial scale‑up results)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: The quench of the reaction mixture with sodium metabisulfite generated an exothermic event and SO₂ gas that required gas‑scrubbing to avoid safety hazards.
Solution_Description: The quench was performed by adding metabisulfite solution at controlled rate, followed by a scrubber to remove SO₂, ensuring safe temperature control and gas handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The quench was highly exothermic, and the gas generation (SO₂) from metabisulfite acidification must be controlled through the use of a scrubber.” (Product isolation) 
• “Sodium metabisulfite (1 w/w) was added to the water phase prior to quench followed by semiquantitative peroxide test (limit < 10 ppm).” (Product isolation) 
• “The quench could be performed on a solution containing a very small amount of oxidant left due to its almost complete decomposition.” (Section 2.8.1) 
• “Reaction calorimetry showed no degree of accumulation… so the process could be considered perfectly dose‑controlled.” (Product isolation) 
• “The addition of hydrogen peroxide 30 % over concentrated H₂SO₄ was performed via Teflon‑coated pump… in case of temperature increase, the dosing must be interrupted.” (Experimental section)

Paper Title: Handling Hydrogen Peroxide Oxidations on a Large Scale: Synthesis of 5‑Bromo-2-nitropyridine
Problem_Description: The original oxidation protocol required up to 40 h at 20 °C to reach full conversion, which was impractical for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: By increasing the reaction temperature to 30 °C, employing the premixed oxidant, and raising the oxidant equivalence to 2.2 mol equiv with a controlled 6 h addition, full conversion was achieved in 8–10 h, dramatically shortening the reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “No conversion was observed… full conversion necessitated 40 h at 20 °C… When the reaction temperature was increased to 30 °C, the reaction was completed after 8–10 h.” (Oxidation reaction) 
• “A premixed solution of H₂SO₄ 95–98 %/H₂O₂ 30 %… addition of amine solution over the oxidant … only 22 % of starting material left at the end of the addition, greatly reduced (5–8 % HPLC area).” (Premixed oxidant) 
• “Increasing the amount of oxidant to 2.2 mol equiv and increasing the addition time to 6 h resulted in complete conversion.” (Section 2.4) 
• “The addition of the oxidant mixture was performed via Teflon‑coated pump while maintaining the temperature below 10 °C… the overall addition time must not be faster than 6 h.” (Experimental section) 
• “The resulting robust reaction conditions… allowed to develop a reproducible, safe protocol…” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: When the API and impurity have similar molecular weights and structures, the impurity readily incorporates into the crystal lattice, giving low crystal purity and forcing multiple batch crystallizations to reach acceptable impurity levels.
Solution_Description: Add a selective complexing agent that binds the impurity (but not the API) to form a higher‑molecular‑weight complex that is sterically excluded from the API crystal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "For crystal‑impurity systems with similar structures and molecular weights, the impurity has a strong tendency to incorporate into the crystal lattice…" (Intro). 
• "The net yield of the two steps is 51.58 ± 0.57 % … final impurity level is more than 1 %… suggesting a potential to use complexation for further purification." (Results, batch experiments). 
• "The batch crystallization experiment was repeated for a single step with the addition of DOTG…yield …73.32 ± 0.26 %… No impurity and complexing agent were detected in the crystals… DOTG proves to be an effective complexing agent for the isolation of NBA from BAM." (Section 3.2.1).

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: Several potential complexing agents (e.g., hydrazide, benzotriazole) were eliminated because of toxicity or poor stability, limiting the pool of usable additives.
Solution_Description: Screen guanidine‑based agents (DOTG, DPG) that are stable, non‑toxic and show very high binding constants to the impurity; select the agent (DOTG) based on ITC‑measured K‑values and batch performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "hydrazide and benzotriazole were rejected for concerns of stability and toxicity" (Section 3.2.1). 
• "The guanidine‑containing agents bind to NBA 3 orders of magnitude stronger than to BAM… The batch crystallization experiment…with DOTG…yield …higher than two‑step batch without complexation." (Section 3.2.1). 
• "The K‑values for DOTG … 23235.28 ± 1524.73 … clearly superior to the API‑impurity pair (16.08 ± 1.95)." (Table 3).

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: A membrane must reject the impurity‑complex while allowing the lower‑MW API to permeate; inappropriate MWCO leads either to excessive API loss or inadequate impurity rejection.
Solution_Description: Screen two polybenzimidazole‑based OSN membranes (22‑PBI‑DBX, 24‑PBI‑DBX); select the 22‑PBI‑DBX membrane because it gives the lowest API rejection while still providing high impurity‑complex rejection.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Two OSN membranes were screened…22‑PBI‑DBX (MWCO ≈ 300–400 Da) and 24‑PBI‑DBX (MWCO ≈ 200–300 Da)." (Section 3.3.1). 
• "Since the impurity level was already below 1 ppm after complexation, the focus … was to improve yield. This required the selection of a membrane with the lower rejection factor for the API, and hence the 22‑PBI‑DBX membrane was chosen for nanofiltration." (Section 3.3.1). 
• Figures 7 and 8 show the rejection ratios that guided the decision.

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: Concentrating the permeate stream before recycle normally requires solvent evaporation, a time‑consuming step that complicates solvent composition control at scale.
Solution_Description: Implement a simulated‑recycle approach (mixing fresh feed with a calculated concentrate in‑line) to demonstrate the effect of recycle without performing an actual evaporation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The permeate stream … must first be concentrated. … for a proof‑of‑concept demonstration, a simulated recycle, instead of actually concentrating the stream by evaporation … was used instead of actual solvent evaporation." (Section 2.2). 
• "It was decided to simulate a case where the API concentration in the recycle stream was the same as that in the fresh feed… the yield … 80.68 ± 0.04 % … higher than the 65.74 ± 0.04 % obtained without recycle." (Section 3.4.1).

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: Strong complexing agents (DOTG, N‑phenylurea) bind not only the impurity but also the API, leading to API‑complex incorporation into the crystals and loss of selectivity.
Solution_Description: Choose a less‑strong agent (4,4′‑bipyridine, BPY) that selectively complexes the impurities; employ a 1:2 (BPY/impurity) molar ratio to ensure sufficient binding of impurities while avoiding API complexation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Simple vial‑scale cooling crystallization … with DOTG and N‑phenylurea yielded crystals incorporating the complexing agents, suggesting against the use of such strong complexing agents." (Section 3.2.2). 
• "The complexing agent of choice was BPY for yielding crystals with the least impurity incorporation… No detectable incorporation of BPY in the crystals, implying that its concentration was below 1 ppm." (Section 3.2.2). 
• "BPY had a feed concentration of 1:2 (BPY/impurity) by mole…" (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: Continuous Crystallization with Impurity Complexation and Nanofiltration Recycle
Problem_Description: Operating the membrane cell at low temperature risks fouling and precipitation due to higher solution viscosity and reduced solubility.
Solution_Description: Run the membrane cell at a higher temperature (45 °C for BAM–NBA, 25 °C for KETO‑IBU‑DMPAA) within membrane compatibility limits to minimize fouling and maintain good mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A higher temperature (well within the membrane compatibility limits) is preferable to minimize issues with fouling and precipitation at the membrane." (Section 2.2). 
• "The temperature in the cell was maintained at 45 °C for the BAM–NBA system and at 25 °C for the KETO–IBU–DMPAA system." (Section 2.2).

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: Building a conventional continuous‑flow system (pump, mixers, reactors, back‑pressure regulator and tubing) is time‑consuming and requires a large amount of lab‑space and hardware, limiting practical use in R&D labs.
Solution_Description: A suitcase‑sized Mobile Reactor Unit (MRU) (<10 kg) was designed from standard HPLC parts, allowing rapid transfer into a fume hood and operation as a single, stand‑alone flow platform.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Constructing a specific flow setup … is inherently time‑consuming.”
• “the major one being practicality.”
• “mobile systems would allow the R&D chemist to rapidly move the flow reactor system into the fume hood.”
• “A suitcase sized mobile reactor unit (MRU) weighing in at less than 10 kg was designed …”.
• “The concept behind the MRU is a robust, yet simple design based on HPLC parts.”

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: Using hydrogen gas requires pressurised cylinders, poses safety hazards and gives a two‑phase flow because of its very low solubility in common solvents.
Solution_Description: A transfer‑hydrogenation strategy was adopted: cyclohexene, a liquid hydrogen donor, is introduced together with the substrate, eliminating the need for gaseous H₂.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Hydrogen is typically stored and transported in pressurised cylinders compromising the desired simplicity …”.
• “the use of hydrogen will always result in two‑phase systems due to the low solubility of this gaseous reagent …”.
• “We therefore decided to apply a transfer hydrogenation approach …”.
• “Cyclohexene (bp 83 °C) proved highly useful as this hydrogen donor”.
• “A 1:1 mixture of cyclohexene with a cosolvent … was used as the hydrogen source”.

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: γ‑Terpinene (the initial hydrogen donor) and its oxidised products have very high boiling points (≈ 180 °C), making their removal from the reaction mixture difficult and time‑consuming.
Solution_Description: Cyclohexene was selected as an alternative donor; its oxidation products (cyclohexadienes, benzene) have low boiling points and can be removed easily by rotary evaporation, simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “γ‑Terpinene … removal … is complicated by high boiling points of this compound and its fully oxidised counterpart (182 and 177 °C)”.
• “Cyclohexene (bp 83 °C) proved highly useful as this hydrogen donor … oxidation products … could be removed by simple rotary evaporation”.
• “… eliminating the need to perform workup on the crude reaction mixture”.

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: Transfer hydrogenation with cyclohexene generates benzene as a by‑product, a known carcinogen that raises safety and regulatory concerns.
Solution_Description: 1‑Methyl‑ or 4‑methyl‑cyclohexene were proposed as alternative donors; their dehydrogenation yields toluene rather than benzene, providing a less toxic by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Benzene, which is most likely formed during transfer hydrogenation, is a toxic substance and a known carcinogenic.”
• “If benzene is to be completely avoided … 1‑ or 4‑methyl‑cyclohexene could possibly be used … leading to the formation of more benign toluene instead.”

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: A packed‑bed reactor containing only Pd/C exhibits a high pressure drop, which can impede flow and cause particle loss.
Solution_Description: Pd/C was mixed with silica to lower the pressure drop and both column ends were sealed with silica‑cotton plugs to prevent Pd‑C particles from escaping.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Pd/C was mixed with silica in order to reduce the pressure drop over the packed bed reactor.”
• “Both ends of the HPLC column were sealed with additional silica and cotton plugs to prevent small particles of Pd/C from exiting the reactor.”
• “The packed‑bed reactor designs differed in the method of packaging and the amount of Pd/C catalyst loaded.”

Paper Title: A High Mobility Reactor Unit for R&D Continuous Flow Transfer Hydrogenations
Problem_Description: During prolonged operation the Pd/C packed‑bed shows catalyst leaching/deactivation; after ~90 min conversion drops sharply, limiting the number of runs before repacking.
Solution_Description: The system is operated with a super‑stoichiometric Pd/C loading (0.054 mol % Pd, TON ≈ 1850) to maintain activity for hundreds of 1–2 mmol batches, and the reactor is scheduled for periodic repacking when conversion falls.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “catalyst deactivation, palladium leaching … were considered to be most significant problem”.
• “Full conversion was retained for the first 90 min … after this point catalyst activity drops dramatically”.
• “A catalytic palladium loading of 0.054 mol % (TON = 1851)”.
• “… running hundreds of 1–2 mmol scale transfer hydrogenations on the MRU before maintenance would be required”.

Paper Title: Process Research and Development of TP-808: A Key Intermediate for the Manufacture of Synthetic Tetracyclines
Problem_Description: The original Myers–Brubaker route required a 7‑day Diels–Alder reaction, gave only ~30 % overall isolated yield, involved cryogenic Swern oxidations that are hazardous, and required multiple chromatographic purifications (silica gel) for the coupled alcohols (8a/8b) and for the final enone (1).
Solution_Description: 1) Replace the cryogenic metalation with TMPMgCl·LiCl‑mediated magnesiation at –25 °C and perform the coupling at –70 °C → –10 °C, which improves conversion and stereoselectivity while avoiding unsafe –100 °C conditions. 2) Use DMSO as the Diels–Alder solvent (30 vol), which accelerates the cycloaddition to 2 days and gives higher endo‑selectivity, allowing the reaction mixture to be telescoped directly into the oxidation step (one‑pot). 3) Switch the oxidation from Swern to a room‑temperature Parikh–Doehring (SO₃·Py/DMSO) or Omura–Sharma–Swern (TFAA/DMSO) protocol; the former gives quantitative conversion with milder conditions. 4) Eliminate all chromatographic purifications by developing a recrystallization of the oxidation product (10a) from toluene/heptane and a final silica‑/charcoal work‑up followed by IPA/water crystallization of the enone (1). 5) Quench the coupling with saturated NH₄Cl (instead of strong acids) and use a reverse quench with aqueous K₃PO₄ for the BCl₃ demethylation, keeping the reaction mixture basic throughout. 6) Adjust reagents stoichiometry (1.1 equiv TMPMgCl·LiCl, 1.2 equiv aldehyde, 1.1 equiv SO₃·Py) to minimise waste and improve yields. 7) Condense neat BCl₃ vapor from a cylinder directly into the reactor head‑space rather than using commercial BCl₃/solvent solutions, which resolves availability and cost issues.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The originally reported Diels–Alder conditions for the conversion of 8a/b to 9a–d required 7 days and provided modest endo selectivity (≤6.2:1).","The Swern oxidation of alcohols 9a–d to ketones 10a/b using oxalyl chloride and DMSO under cryogenic conditions was reported to proceed with good yield; on multiple occasions in our hands this reaction condition gave significant by‑products.","Regioselective deprotonation of 6 proceeded rapidly at 0 °C using 1.2–1.4 equiv of TMPMgCl·LiCl... the reaction was quenched with 670 kg of saturated NH₄Cl.","We proceeded to investigate the direct magnesiation of 6 using a magnesium base... TMPMgCl·LiCl was chosen for further investigation and scale up.","The reaction could be accelerated at higher temperature by using a sealed tube or microwave reactor (entries 6 and 7). Notwithstanding the lower selectivity at higher temperature, this provided quick access to Diels–Alder products.","The Diels–Alder reaction in DMSO was completed after 2 days at 95 °C. After the reaction reached completion, it was stressed by keeping the reaction at 100 °C for additional 2 days. Even after this extended reaction time, yield and purity were not compromised.","We investigated the possibility of using vaporized neat BCl₃ (13.2 kg, 1.14 equiv) from a cylinder... As a cost‑effective and practical alternative, we developed the direct use of vaporized BCl₃ from a cylinder.","A recrystallization of 10a/b was developed using an ethanol/MTBE mixture yielding pure 10a. This process is capable of purging impurities... An alternative recrystallization/reslurry process using toluene and heptane was developed.","The product is not stable under acidic conditions, sufficient base should be added first to ensure that the mixture never becomes acidic.","The use of saturated aqueous K₃PO₄ solution at 30–40 °C for work‑up gave high yields."]

Paper Title: Process Research and Development of TP-808: A Key Intermediate for the Manufacture of Synthetic Tetracyclines
Problem_Description: During the magnesiation/coupling step the 6‑anion showed nonspecific decomposition (≈15 % assay loss) and the reaction was inconsistent at larger scale; the BCl₃ demethylation gave variable amounts (up to 40 %) of side‑product 18a/b, which depended on the quality and source of BCl₃.
Solution_Description: 1) Reduce the equivalents of TMPMgCl·LiCl to 1.1 equiv and add the aldehyde 0.3 equiv excess to consume any residual base, which suppresses decomposition of the 6‑anion. 2) Perform the magnesiation at –25 °C (instead of 0 °C) to limit concurrent base‑induced degradation. 3) For the BCl₃ step, use −40 °C to −30 °C and a controlled addition of neat BCl₃ vapor, avoiding local excesses that cause decomposition. 4) Implement a reverse quench with aqueous K₃PO₄ to keep the mixture basic during work‑up, preventing acid‑catalysed breakdown of the borate intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Although the deprotonation would not achieve completion without the extra 0.2–0.4 equiv of base suggested that at 0 °C the decomposition occurred concurrently to the deprotonation and consumed base.","The magnesiation of 6 using 1.4 equiv of TMPMgCl·LiCl was carried out at approximately −25 °C and was complete in ∼40 min.","The reaction rate at different temperatures was studied using 1.3 equiv of BCl₃... The reaction was rapid at 0 to −25 °C (entries 1–2) but slower below −35 °C (entries 3–5).","The quality of BCl₃ is critical for this reaction. We have encountered a very low yield (<30 %) of 11a with older BCl₃ solution presumably due to the HCl generated from the hydrolytic decomposition of BCl₃.","To ensure a basic environment during the work up a reverse quench was instituted for manufacturing. The addition of the reaction mixture into an aqueous potassium phosphate tribasic solution at 30–40 °C consistently gave high yields."]

Paper Title: Process Research and Development of TP-808: A Key Intermediate for the Manufacture of Synthetic Tetracyclines
Problem_Description: Commercial BCl₃ solutions in DCM are not available in large quantities and are expensive; older solutions generate HCl that reduces yield.
Solution_Description: Generate BCl₃ in‑situ by vaporizing neat BCl₃ from a high‑pressure cylinder directly into the reactor headspace and condensing it into the reaction mixture. This eliminates the need for costly BCl₃/solvent solutions, provides a readily available reagent stream, and improves material cost and operational simplicity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["High‑quality BCl₃ solution in DCM is not commercially available on large scale and therefore must be freshly prepared from neat BCl₃ and used immediately.","As a cost‑effective and practical alternative, we developed the direct use of vaporized BCl₃ from a cylinder. In contrast to BCl₃ in DCM solution neat BCl₃ in a cylinder is stable, readily available in large quantities, and easy to handle during manufacturing."]

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: The original discovery synthesis of GDC‑0994 gave only a 12 % overall isolated yield, suffered from modest selectivity in several steps and required tedious distillation and flash‑chromatography for product isolation.
Solution_Description: A practical seven‑step scalable route was developed that increased the overall isolated yield to 41 % and eliminated the need for high‑boiling distillations and flash chromatography by employing a biocatalytic asymmetric ketone reduction and telescoped later steps.
Supporting_Evidence: The initial discovery synthesis … produced the target molecule … in 12 % overall yield. ... the chemistry suffered from low yields and modest selectivity ... tedious purification procedures such as distillation and flash chromatography were required ... Issues revolving around process efficiency, reaction safety, and robustness deterred the chemistry from being used on the multikilogram scale.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: The S N2 displacement of methanesulfonate 4 with pyridone 5 gave only 50‑60 % conversion to the desired N‑alkylated product and generated a thick slurry in non‑polar solvents, making agitation difficult.
Solution_Description: A solvent system of 1,4‑dioxane with 5 % NMP was adopted, which gave a thin slurry and allowed full conversion, while the use of metal hexamethyldisilazide (MHMDS) as base improved regioselectivity toward the N‑alkylated product.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction … produced N‑alkylation adduct … in modest 50–60 % yields ... The addition of 5–10 % NMP as a cosolvent helped to alleviate the mixing issue... Full conversion was obtained in 18 h with an acceptable level of N vs O selectivity (entry 7).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: Oxidation of sulfide 6 with m‑CPBA generated a pyrimidine N‑oxide impurity 13 (∼1 % HPLC) that persisted through the final API and required four recrystallizations to lower its level below 0.15 %.
Solution_Description: The m‑CPBA oxidation was replaced by a Na₂WO₄‑catalyzed tungstate oxidation using aqueous H₂O₂, which gave >99 % conversion to the sulfone with negligible N‑oxide formation; subsequent crystallization steps efficiently removed residual impurity.
