Supporting_Evidence: The reaction yields were consistently high, pyrimidine N‑oxide impurity 13 (∼1 % HPLC) was observed ... The rejection of 13 after the oxidation step was attempted via a crystallization of 7 ... four recrystallizations were required to reduce the level of 13 ... As an alterative to m‑CPBA, aqueous hydrogen peroxide ... Na₂WO₄‑catalyzed oxidation ...

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: The tungstate‑H₂O₂ oxidation is exothermic and can lead to peroxide accumulation, causing temperature spikes (adiabatic rise of 12.7 °C) and potential runaway.
Solution_Description: Charging H₂O₂ at 80 °C with a fast reaction rate minimized peroxide buildup and reduced the post‑addition enthalpy, while reaction calorimetry guided safe temperature and addition profiles.
Supporting_Evidence: Two reaction conditions were examined. When H₂O₂ was charged … at 40 °C … 45 % conversion … high heat accumulation … adiabatic temperature rise of 12.7 °C. In contrast, when H₂O₂ was added … at 80 °C … >95 % conversion … post‑addition enthalpy was significantly reduced.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: The benzenesulfonate salt of GDC‑0994 showed very low solubility in MEK (<5 mg mL⁻¹), hindering impurity removal during the final crystallization.
Solution_Description: A small amount of water (3–4 wt %) was added to MEK, creating a biphasic medium that improved solubility and enabled efficient removal of impurities 18 and 19 during salt crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: GDC‑0994·benzenesulfonate has a low solubility in methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) (<5 mg mL⁻¹). ... The introduction of water as a cosolvent enabled a significant reduction of both impurities. ... 3–4 % of water in MEK was chosen for the salt formation step to balance the recovery of API and the purge of impurities.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: Formation of the genotoxic impurity methyl benzenesulfonate occurred during the benzenesulfonate salt‑formation step when methanol was present.
Solution_Description: Methanol content was reduced to <0.3 % by concentration and solvent swap before salt formation; later a one‑pot desilylation/salt formation using benzenesulfonic acid in non‑alcoholic solvent eliminated the need for methanol altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: ... there was a quality concern associated with the introduction of the genotoxic impurity methyl benzenesulfonate as a byproduct from the reaction of the acid in methanol. MeOH levels were reduced to below 0.3 % GC through concentration and solvent swap before the benzenesulfonate salt formation step. ... envisioned that benzenesulfonic acid could serve a dual purpose as a catalyst for deprotection and acid for salt formation. ... it is ideal to avoid alcoholic solvents in the salt formation step and completely eliminate genotoxic impurity concerns.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: During the tungstate‑catalyzed oxidation, acidic H₂O₂ caused desilylation of the silyl ether (impurity 15) and hydrolysis (impurity 16).
Solution_Description: Addition of 10 mol % 2,6‑lutidine as a base additive suppressed desilylation and minimized formation of hydrolysis impurity 16.
Supporting_Evidence: The acidic nature of H₂O₂, desilylated sulfone byproduct 15 was observed ... A base screen was performed ... we found that 2,6‑lutidine (entry 6) was efficient to minimize desilylation without significantly increasing the level of 16.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: The S NAr displacement of sulfone 7 with aminopyrazole 8 gave only ~60 % conversion and generated hydrolysis byproduct 17 (15‑20 % HPLC).
Solution_Description: Switching to LiHMDS as a strong base in THF at –30 °C dramatically increased conversion to 100 % and reduced impurity 17 to <1 % HPLC; careful control of LiHMDS equivalents (2.1 eq) avoided over‑base‑induced elimination byproducts 18/19.
Supporting_Evidence: The reaction … suffered from a modest conversion … average yield … approx. 60 %. ... LiHMDS … reaction rate was dramatically increased … 100 % conversion (entry 2). … the level of hydrolysis byproduct 17 was reduced from 15‑20 % to 3 % HPLC. … The stoichiometry of the base is critical … only 50 % conversion was observed when 1 eq of LiHMDS was applied (entry 1). … When slight excesses of LiHMDS were employed … no significant byproducts were formed (entry 2).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of ERK Inhibitor GDC-0994
Problem_Description: Non‑polar solvents in the S N2 step gave low solubility of methanesulfonate 4, leading to thick slurries and poor mixing.
Solution_Description: Adding 5‑10 % NMP as a cosolvent to non‑polar media generated a homogeneous mixture and improved agitation, enabling full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: Nonpolar solvents … enable a reaction with reasonable selectivity … however, due to the low solubility of 4, thick slurries were obtained and made the agitation challenging. The addition of 5‑10 % NMP as a cosolvent helped to alleviate the mixing issue.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: The original bromination of 4‑fluoro‑2‑methylbenzonitrile (2) using 1.5 eq NBS in 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE) gave a mixture dominated by the dibromide 3′ (≈50 % of the product) and left a significant amount of starting material, resulting in low overall yield of the desired bromomethyl compound 3. DCE is a Class 1 solvent with safety and cost concerns.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂), which gave a higher conversion of 2 to 3 with less residual starting material. The NBS/2 ratio was optimized to 1.5 eq, and the amounts of diethyl phosphite and DIPEA were reduced to 0.5 eq and 0.2 eq respectively, which were sufficient to convert the dibromide 3′ completely to 3 without further purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ratio of N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) and compound 2 was set at 1.5, and the Class 1 solvent DCE was replaced by chloroform or dichloromethane… dichloromethane was a better solvent since less starting material remained.”; “0.5 eq of diethyl phosphite and 0.2 eq of DIPEA … adequate for complete conversion of 3′ into 3.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: In the key nucleophilic substitution (4 → 5) the use of DMF as solvent gave a low crude yield (72 %) and generated several by‑products (11d, 9, unknown impurities). Protic solvents also led to additional side‑products (11a–11d). DMF is a hazardous solvent, and the impurity profile complicated purification.
Solution_Description: A systematic solvent screening identified isopropanol as the optimal medium, delivering the highest purity (94.9 % of 5 in the crude) and minimal formation of the 11‑series impurities. Sodium bicarbonate was retained as the base, providing a clean reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the reaction was run in DMF … the yield of the crude product was poor (72.1 %) and the byproducts included … 14.5 % of unknown impurities.”; “Methanol was too active … isopropyl alcohol was found to be the best, giving the desired 5 with 94.9 % purity in the crude product (98.6 % of yield), and 11c was almost negligible.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: Using the protected (R)‑3‑N‑protected‑aminopiperidine required a de‑protection step that produced additional cyano‑hydrolysis impurities, complicating the isolation of trelagliptin.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was redesigned to employ the unprotected (R)‑3‑aminopiperidine directly in the substitution step, eliminating the de‑protection stage and its associated impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the following deprotection step may produce additional impurities resulting from the cyano‑hydrolysis. In this paper, the improved synthesis … was based on the original company route … using unprotected (R)‑3‑aminopiperidine.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: The original work‑up used the Class 1 solvent 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE) for recrystallization and work‑up, posing safety and regulatory issues.
Solution_Description: The overall process was redesigned to use only three organic solvents (CH₂Cl₂, THF, i‑PrOH) throughout all reactions and recrystallizations, removing DCE from the route and simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “In addition, only three kinds of organic solvents (CH₂Cl₂, THF, i‑PrOH) were used in the whole process … avoiding the Class 1 solvent 1,2‑dichloroethane.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: Isolation of the final trelagliptin succinate required high purity (>99 %) and efficient removal of residual solvents and impurities.
Solution_Description: The crude product 5 (≥94 % purity) was directly converted to the succinate by treatment with succinic acid in isopropanol, followed by recrystallization from a 9:1 isopropanol/water mixture, affording the succinate with 99.93 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Trelagliptin succinate was formed by mixing crude 5 and succinic acid in isopropyl alcohol and then recrystallized with a mixture of isopropyl alcohol and water (9:1) in a purity of 99.93 %.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Trelagliptin Succinate
Problem_Description: Scaling the nucleophilic substitution from 5 g to 80 g could potentially alter the impurity profile and yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed on a 80 g scale under the same optimized conditions (i‑PrOH, NaHCO₃) and yielded comparable purity and conversion, confirming robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “Finally, the reaction was scaled up according to the condition in entry 5, and a similar outcome was obtained (entry 9).”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: The traditional synthesis of 5‑aryltetrazoles using hydrazoic acid is extremely hazardous because HN₃ is toxic, volatile (bp = 37 °C) and a powerful explosive; it also reacts with metals to form shock‑sensitive metal azides.
Solution_Description: A safer buffered protocol was devised that replaces free HN₃ with a mixture of benzylamine, benzylamine·HCl and NaN₃.  The higher‑mass benzylammonium azide generated in‑situ is far less volatile and is thermally stable, eliminating the need to handle hydrazoic acid directly.
Supporting_Evidence: “Up until the middle of the 20th century, the most direct method … was by reacting an aryl nitrile with hydrazoic acid … However, hydrazoic acid is not only toxic … but also explosive.”; “The search for a faster, safer protocol … led to the discovery of a buffered system comprised of BnNH2, BnNH2·HCl, and NaN3.”; “All three of these amine hydrochloride salts have significantly higher molecular weights than ammonium chloride, suggesting that the corresponding azide salts should be much less volatile and thus safer to work with.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: Using the classic NaN₃/NH₄Cl protocol in DMF gave a very slow reaction (>40 h at 120 °C) for ortho‑substituted nitriles and produced a sub‑limate identified as ammonium azide, a volatile and explosive salt.
Solution_Description: Screening of twelve amine‑HCl promoters identified benzylamine·HCl (and morpholine·HCl, DABCO·HCl) as far more reactive. The higher‑mass ammonium azide formed from benzylamine·HCl reduced volatility and improved conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “While nitrile 1 was successfully transformed to 2 under these conditions, the reaction was unfortunately very sluggish … Full consumption of the nitrile … required >40 h at 120 °C … a sublimate … likely ammonium azide (NH₄N₃).”; “we found that three amine hydrochloride salts demonstrated a significantly faster reaction rate than the original NH₄Cl conditions … benzylamine hydrochloride … has the highest C:N ratio and is also commercially available.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: During scale‑up in a 20 L jacketed reactor with overhead stirring, the heterogeneous mixture failed to reach full conversion, unlike the small‑scale magnetic‑stir experiments.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A water co‑solvent (15–20 % v/v) was added to the NMP or THF reaction mixture. The water increased the solubility of NaN₃ and provided the grinding action necessary for complete conversion with overhead agitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Upon transitioning to jacketed glass reactors … the reaction no longer reached completion … the grinding action of a magnetic stir‑bar was necessary … As further corroboration … a scalable process was designed by incorporating 15–20 % water as a cosolvent into the reaction mixture. Reactions conducted in either 5:1 NMP–water or 5:1 THF–water reached complete conversion.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: Initial aqueous NaOH extractions of the NMP reaction stream removed only ~43–46 % of the residual azide, leaving unsafe levels of NaN₃ in the organic phase prior to acid work‑up.
Solution_Description: THF was introduced as a cosolvent to lower the polarity of the organic layer, dramatically improving azide partitioning into the aqueous washes. Multiple 25 % NaOH washes (up to four) were employed, ultimately achieving >98 % azide removal with minimal product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: “Aqueous extraction of sodium azide from the reaction stream in NMP was surprisingly inefficient, with less than 50 % of the azide ion removed … A survey of other polar aprotic solvents revealed a similar trend. Gratifyingly, reducing the polarity of the organic layer by introducing tetrahydrofuran (THF) as a cosolvent improved the purge of sodium azide to the aqueous layer.”; Table 2 entries showing 98.9 % and 99.6 % removal with 4–5 × 25 % NaOH washes.

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: Head‑space HN₃ concentrations peaked at ~17 000 ppm during the benzylamine‑promoted reaction, posing a potential explosion risk if nitrogen flow were interrupted.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A slow nitrogen purge (≈1 headspace volume per 10 min) was maintained throughout the reaction; an additional 0.5 equiv of free benzylamine was added as a buffer, raising the pH from ~5 to ~9 and cutting the peak HN₃ level five‑fold. The reactor was equipped with a head‑space trap containing 2.5 % aqueous NaOH to scavenge any escaped HN₃.
Supporting_Evidence: “In‑line MS analysis … headspace HN₃ peaked early … 17 000 ppm … This level is below … 120 000 ppm … Any disruption in headspace nitrogen flow … could allow … explosion hazard.”; “buffering the reaction mixture with 0.5 equiv of added benzylamine … a 5‑fold reduction in peak headspace hydrazoic acid.”; “slow above‑surface nitrogen purge (500 mL min⁻¹ …) … an effluent gas trap containing 2.5 wt % aqueous NaOH … to remove any HN₃ prior to venting.”

Paper Title: Development and Demonstration of a Safer Protocol for the Synthesis of 5‑Aryltetrazoles from Aryl Nitriles
Problem_Description: The phenyl nitrile substrate (1) required long reaction times (≈18 h at 110 °C) compared with the phenol nitrile (5), which converted rapidly under the same conditions.
Solution_Description: Switching the substrate to the more reactive phenol nitrile (5) allowed the reaction to be run at lower temperature (100 °C) and drastically reduced the reaction time to 30 min, while also decreasing the required NaN₃ loading.
Supporting_Evidence: “Full consumption of the nitrile … required >40 h at 120 °C … When phenol substrate 5 was subjected to the reaction conditions, >99.8 % conversion was achieved after only 30 min at 100 °C.”; “These modifications … led to a large reduction in peak headspace hydrazoic acid detected …”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: The originally reported batch method required long reaction times and used a large excess of reagents (up to 9 equiv of the amine nucleophile) to obtain reasonable conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow system with two sequential micro‑reactors was built.  The micro‑reactors provide excellent mixing and short residence times (≈30–70 s) under mild (room‑temperature) conditions, dramatically reducing reaction time and allowing the reagent equivalents to be lowered.
Supporting_Evidence: "A continuous‑flow system consisting of two sequential microreactors was developed for the synthesis of nonsymmetrically substituted ureas... Short reaction times could be achieved under mild conditions."; "The first reaction step was sufficiently fast to reach completion in a 250 µL reactor... These conditions correspond to low residence times in both steps (t_R1 = 32 s, t_R2 = 68 s)"

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride (Tf₂O) is highly corrosive; it rapidly degraded plastic storage vessels, syringes and tubing, limiting the choice of reactor and pump components.
Solution_Description: All parts that contacted Tf₂O were made from PTFE (for tubing) or glass (for the syringe) and a custom stainless‑steel connector was used to join the syringe to PTFE tubing, ensuring chemical compatibility.
Supporting_Evidence: "Even in dilute solutions, Tf₂O rapidly degraded the plastic parts ... only PTFE proved to be resistant."; "An infusion syringe pump (P2) was used with an all‑glass and PTFE syringe for the handling of the Tf₂O reagent. A custom‑made stainless steel connector ... was employed to attach the syringe to the PTFE tubing."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: When HPLC pumps were employed, harmful pulsation was observed, interfering with the smooth delivery of reagents.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous syringe pumps (Syrris P1 and P3) were used for all reagent feeds, providing steady, pulsation‑free flow.
Supporting_Evidence: "The use of HPLC pumps (Knauer AZURA P 2.1S) was also attempted, but harmful pulsation occurred, due to interference with the infusion syringe pump."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Standard in‑line FT‑IR sensors (silicon ATR probes) corroded in the presence of Tf₂O, and diamond sensors had a blind spot overlapping the isocyanate band, making them unsuitable for monitoring.
Solution_Description: A transmission flow cell featuring ZnSe windows was introduced, which is chemically resistant and provides a broad spectral range without the blind‑spot problem.
Supporting_Evidence: "The commonly used sensor materials (silicon sensors are prone to corrosion, while the more robust diamond sensors have a “blind spot”, which overlaps with the characteristic vibration of the isocyanate group) were unsuitable for this study. These issues were avoided by employing the versatile (but previously neglected in continuous‑flow synthesis) transmission flow cell (FC) using highly resistant ZnSe windows."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Sharp fluctuations in product composition were observed after any major change in flow parameters, requiring a period of stabilization before reliable data could be recorded.
Solution_Description: The system was allowed to reach steady‑state by collecting at least three reactor volumes (≈4 mL) before measuring conversion, ensuring reproducible results.
Supporting_Evidence: "Severe fluctuation ... occurred in the composition of the product mixture after any major changes in reaction parameters (e.g., flow rate). This phenomenon gradually ceased as the system approached steady state. In order to obtain reproducible results, conversion was measured after reaching a steady state (after collecting 3 times the total reactor volume)."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Initial FT‑IR monitoring of the first step (carbamate → isocyanate) suggested full conversion, but after the second step significant starting material remained, indicating that the first step was not truly complete.
Solution_Description: The crude mixture from the first microreactor was immediately quenched by adding a high excess of the amine in the second reactor; the FT‑IR probe was placed after this quench, allowing the true conversion of the first step to be measured via the urea signal.
Supporting_Evidence: "Optimization was required in order to reduce the high excess of reagents ... The FT‑IR signal of the carbamate vanished, but considerable amounts of the starting material were still observed after addition of 6a. ... the optimization of the first step was realized by continuously in‑line quenching its crude mixture using high excess (9 equiv) of amine 6a in the second reactor ... the ratio of signals of 4a and 7a reflects the conversion in the first step."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: The original protocol required a large excess of base (3 equiv 2‑ClPy) and Tf₂O (1.5 equiv), inflating material cost.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was optimized: 2 equiv of 2‑ClPy and only 1.1 equiv of Tf₂O (minimal excess to avoid water) were sufficient for quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "The excess of 2‑ClPy was investigated ... a 2‑fold excess was found to be optimal. ... the optimized amount of base was used, while molar ratio of Tf₂O was varied ... we decided to use a minimal excess (1.1 equiv) to prevent instability due to traces of water."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: The second step originally required 9 equiv of the amine nucleophile, leading to high material cost and waste.
Solution_Description: The amine excess was lowered to 4 equiv without loss of yield.  A portion of the necessary base was supplied by cheaper triethylamine (TEA), replacing part of the expensive amine while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "The excess of 6a could be reduced to 4 equiv ... excellent isolated yield (97%) was obtained."; "In order to reach even lower consumption of reagent 6a, TEA was used as an additional base. These experiments ... revealed that a part of the total amount of base (4 equiv) needed can be replaced by a cheaper base."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: When the Boc‑protected intermediate for cariprazine was processed, the nucleophilic amino group partially decomposed Tf₂O, leading to incomplete formation of the isocyanate intermediate.
Solution_Description: Higher equivalents of Tf₂O (1.8 equiv) and 2‑ClPy (3 equiv) were employed to compensate for the loss and achieve full conversion in the first microreactor.
Supporting_Evidence: "When the carbamate (8) was subjected to the conditions ... incomplete conversion to the corresponding isocyanate (10) was observed ... the reduced reactivity can be explained by partial decomposition of the Tf₂O reagent ... consequently, higher excess of both Tf₂O and 2‑ClPy had to be used (1.8 and 3 equiv, respectively) to reach total conversion in the first step."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: Isolation of the basic API (cariprazine) from the TEA‑containing reaction mixture proved difficult, compromising product recovery.
Solution_Description: TEA was omitted and solid potassium phosphate was added to liberate dimethylamine. The phosphate salts were insoluble in dichloromethane, allowing them to settle and be filtered, which greatly simplified purification and improved isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "TEA could be omitted, and solid potassium phosphate could be used instead. The basicity of the trivalent phosphate ions was enough to shift the equilibrium to full liberation of dimethylamine base, and both the phosphate and the formed hydrogen phosphate salts were insoluble in dichloromethane. This allowed conveniently letting the solid salts settle ... the product could be isolated in 83% yield."

Paper Title: Synthesis of Urea Derivatives in Two Sequential Continuous-Flow Reactors
Problem_Description: For the bulky diisopropylamine substrate (6e) a high excess (9 equiv) was required and precipitation occurred, preventing complete conversion in the flow microreactor.
Solution_Description: The authors noted that flow conditions were unsuitable for this substrate and resorted to a longer batch reaction to obtain reasonable yield, acknowledging the limitation of the flow setup for highly hindered amines.
Supporting_Evidence: "The rather bulky diisopropylamine (6e) led to incomplete conversions in the continuous flow microreactor, even at high excess (9 equiv). Therefore, the product (7j) of the flow procedure was not isolated. Longer reaction time using batch processing was required to obtain the product with reasonable yield, while slight precipitation was observed in the reaction mixture, emphasizing the inapplicability of flow conditions in this exceptional case."

Paper Title: Development of Commercial-Ready Processes for Antibody Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Product heterogeneity (varying drug‑to‑antibody ratio, DAR, and drug‑load distribution) makes the ADC difficult to control and compare with early‑stage material.
Solution_Description: The amount of activated calicheamicin added (stoichiometry) is tightly limited and the hydrophobic‑interaction chromatography (HIC) fractions are pooled only after meeting strict criteria for protein concentration, DAR and aggregation, thereby fixing the drug‑load profile.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A major challenge…is the control of product heterogeneity to ensure comparability to early clinical and toxicology material.”
• “Results showed that the total drug load (DAR) and drug load distribution were mainly controlled by calicheamicin input in the conjugation reaction and fraction pooling in the HIC purification step.”
• “Acceptable ranges for calicheamicin input and HIC fraction pooling criteria were then established based on the target specifications for drug substance heterogeneity.”
• “The collected HIC fractions were then pooled based on the criteria regarding to protein concentration, drug load, and aggregation level…"

Paper Title: Development of Commercial-Ready Processes for Antibody Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: The conjugation reaction is extremely fast (complete in ~2 min at 10 mg mL⁻¹) and requires uniform mixing; poor mixing (low agitation or surface addition) leads to incomplete conjugation and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Blend‑time studies, CFD simulations and salt‑spiking experiments were used to define agitation rates and subsurface addition of the calicheamicin solution; these mixing parameters are applied at all scales to guarantee rapid, homogeneous mixing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the conjugation reaction at 10 mg/mL mAb concentration reached completion within 2 min… The fast reaction kinetics demands adequate mixing of the reaction mixture at all scales.”
• “Blend time data demonstrated that consistent mixing profiles were achieved in each reactor with comparable agitation settings.”
• “A low agitation rate and above surface addition resulted in poor mixing… when the calicheamicin solution was added subsurface, the conjugation reaction proceeded efficiently even at low agitation rates.”
• “Computational fluid dynamics simulations were used to characterize mixing at various scales.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial-Ready Processes for Antibody Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: The payload (calicheamicin) and its intermediates are highly cytotoxic, requiring special handling to protect personnel and prevent cross‑contamination.
Solution_Description: The process uses single‑use, closed‑system reactors, chromatography skids and filtration devices, together with dedicated isolators/glove boxes for weighing and solution preparation, eliminating cleaning validation and minimizing exposure.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The highly toxic materials must be handled in appropriate facilities during development and manufacture.”
• “Single‑use systems… reduce the potential for exposure of workers to the cytotoxic agents… closed modules… do not have to be disassembled after use.”
• “Standard operating procedures (SOPs) must be in place… isolators/glove boxes for weighing and preparing solutions.”
• “Dedicated suite… facilitates safe charging of the L/P solution into the conjugation reaction and handling of the ADC through purification and UF/DF operations.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial-Ready Processes for Antibody Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: The activated ester on the calicheamicin derivative hydrolyses readily in the presence of water, destroying the conjugatable functionality.
Solution_Description: Raw‑material specifications limit water in the ethanol used for dissolution to ≤0.2 % and the solvent is tightly controlled to suppress ester hydrolysis before the conjugation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The activated ester… are susceptible to hydrolysis under the aqueous/organic conditions of RP‑HPLC… hydrolysis can be controlled by HPLC mobile phase pH and therefore minimized.”
• “The specification for water in ethanol is set to ≤0.2 %… To minimize hydrolysis, the water in ethanol used for dissolution is tightly controlled by the raw material specification.”
• “Hydrolysis of the activated ester is detrimental to the conjugation reaction since the L/P will not react once it is hydrolyzed.”

Paper Title: Development of Commercial-Ready Processes for Antibody Drug Conjugates
Problem_Description: Scaling the HIC purification step to manufacturing scale risked loss of resolution and inconsistent drug‑load profiles.
Solution_Description: The column height was kept constant while cross‑sectional area and flow rate were scaled proportionally, preserving linear velocity and chromatographic performance; fraction‑pooling criteria were transferred from lab scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Scale‑up of the column to manufacturing scale was accomplished by keeping the column height constant and increasing the cross‑sectional area proportional to the reaction amount, while maintaining constant linear velocity.”
• “All other operations and buffers within the chromatography step were kept constant.”
• “Based on the comparability between scales of the UV traces, yield, and quality attributes… the chromatography step was shown to be scalable and robust.”

Paper Title: Practical Large-Scale Regioselective Zincation of Chromone Using TMPZnCl·LiCl Triggered by the Presence or Absence of MgCl
Problem_Description: During scale‑up the regioselectivity of the zincation dropped when the reaction temperature rose; fast addition of the organozinc reagent generated a noticeable exotherm, and temperatures below –5 °C caused MgCl₂ to precipitate, both leading to inconsistent selectivity.
Solution_Description: The authors slowed the addition of TMPZnCl·LiCl to 30 min while controlling the temperature (0 °C for the C‑3 zincation; –5 °C for the MgCl₂‑mediated C‑2 zincation) thereby suppressing the exotherm and avoiding MgCl₂ precipitation, which restored consistent regioselectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When the reaction was scaled up to 50 mmol, TMPZnCl·LiCl … was added over 30 min at 0 °C … The lower reaction temperature and the slow addition rate are necessary to avoid a decrease in regioselectivity presumably caused by an increase of the reaction temperature.”

Paper Title: Practical Large-Scale Regioselective Zincation of Chromone Using TMPZnCl·LiCl Triggered by the Presence or Absence of MgCl
Problem_Description: Coupling of the C‑3‑zincated chromone with electrophiles required considerably longer times on the 50 mmol scale (up to 48 h) compared with the 2 mmol scale (typically ≤ 12 h).
Solution_Description: The authors accepted the longer reaction times for the larger scale and proceeded with the extended periods (12–48 h) to obtain the desired products in good isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction of the resulting C(3)-zincated chromone 3 with various electrophiles generally required longer reaction times for the 50 mmol scale than in the case of the 2 mmol scale … 91 % yield after 12 h … 60 % yield after 48 h … Pd‑catalyzed Negishi cross‑coupling … after 18 h … (83 % yield).”

Paper Title: Practical Large-Scale Regioselective Zincation of Chromone Using TMPZnCl·LiCl Triggered by the Presence or Absence of MgCl
Problem_Description: Cooling the MgCl₂/THF solution below –5 °C caused MgCl₂ to precipitate, which led to lower regioselectivity in the C‑2 zincation.
Solution_Description: The temperature was maintained at –5 °C (not lower) during the addition of TMPZnCl·LiCl, preventing MgCl₂ precipitation and preserving the desired C‑2 selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We noticed that lower reaction temperatures than –5 °C caused the precipitation of MgCl₂ and therefore provided also lower selectivities.”

Paper Title: Process Development and Good Manufacturing Practice Production of a Tyrosinase Inhibitor via Titanium-Mediated Coupling between Unprotected Resorcinols and Ketones
Problem_Description: The original discovery route relied on 4‑bromoresorcinol, an expensive raw material that is difficult to source on a large scale, and required cryogenic temperatures (‑70 °C) and chromatographic purifications, leading to high material cost and safety/operational challenges.
Solution_Description: A new retrosynthetic strategy was adopted that uses cheap, readily available reagents (unprotected resorcinol and N‑Boc‑4‑piperidone) and an operationally simple Ti(IV)‑mediated coupling, eliminating expensive bromoresorcinol, cryogenic steps and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Discovery chemistry synthesis … started from 4‑bromoresorcinol, an expensive raw material, difficult to source on a large scale."

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: When the fine Raney‑Co particles were packed into the 40 mL reactor a pronounced inlet‑pressure buildup occurred (up to 30 bar for pure solvent and >70 bar during the hydrogenation), creating a safety hazard and non‑uniform process conditions that limited the achievable throughput.
Solution_Description: The inlet‑pressure was mitigated by (i) increasing the reactant concentration to 0.2 M (allowing a lower liquid‑flow rate) and (ii) lowering the back‑pressure regulator set‑point from 40 bar to 20 bar, which together reduced the baseline pressure and kept the pressure increase within acceptable limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “A pronounced inlet pressure buildup resulted from the presence of the fine Ra–Co catalyst bed particles at this reactor scale, e.g., 24 mL/min pure solvent induced 30 bar inlet pressure.” (sec 2.3) ‣ “In order to minimize the expected inlet pressure buildup, the amount of H₂ applied in the process was reduced to 3.4 equiv… The inlet pressure recorded at the beginning of the experiment was 59 bar indicating ≈20 bar pressure buildup under the applied process conditions.” (sec 2.3) ‣ “Accordingly, the next experiment (exp. 2) was performed with a 0.2 M DIM‑NA solution and a back pressure lowered to 20 bar… The effect of these measures on the pressure characteristics of the system was desired (exp. 2)… a notable inlet pressure reduction (−20 bar) resulted from the combined effects of lower liquid flow rate and back pressure.” (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature above 60 °C improved conversion but caused a rise in the amount of desiodinated side‑product (desiodo‑DIM‑DAB), lowering the overall selectivity and therefore the usable yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: A temperature of 60 °C was selected as the optimal set‑point because it gave >93 % conversion while keeping desiodination at ≤1.6 wt % and suppressing other side‑products, providing a good balance between conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “While 92 % conversion of 1 was already achieved at 40 °C, the selectivity of the reaction was rather poor with 1.2 wt % desiodo‑DIM‑DAB and 5.5 area % additional side products… temperatures ≥60 °C are required to suppress side product formation other than desiodination.” (Table 1, sec 2.2) ‣ “Full DIM‑NA conversion was reached at 80 °C. The amount of 3 further increased (1.8 wt %), while the formation of other side products remained approximately constant.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: After full conversion of DIM‑NA, the product stream remained in contact with the excess catalyst bed, leading to over‑hydrogenation and a follow‑up deiodination reaction that raised the desiodo‑DIM‑DAB content.
Solution_Description: The liquid flow rate was increased (e.g., from 11 mL min⁻¹ to 16 mL min⁻¹ and then to 22 mL min⁻¹) to shorten the residence time, keeping conversion just below 100 % (≈98–99 %) and sharply reducing the desiodination level to ≤1.0 wt % in later experiments.
Supporting_Evidence: “The degree of desiodination observed for samples 1.1 [8.0 wt %], 1.2 [3.8 wt %], and 1.3 [1.8 wt %]… indicates a run‑up phase for the Ra‑Co catalyst.” (sec 2.3) ‣ “To suppress this follow‑up reaction, the liquid flow rate was increased by 45 % (16 mL/min, exp. 3)… desiodination … barely reached the acceptable limit for downstream processing (<1.0 wt %).” (sec 2.3) ‣ “In the following experiments the flow rates were subsequently increased to 22 mL/min (exp. 4) and 26 mL/min (exp. 5)… the degree of desiodination further dropped to 0.9 wt % and 0.8 wt % respectively.” (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: During the long‑term kilogram‑scale run the inlet pressure showed unpredictable increases and decreases (e.g., from 80 bar down to 57 bar), and at one point a breakthrough of unreacted DIM‑NA occurred, threatening product quality and safe operation.
Solution_Description: An online UV–vis monitoring module was installed upstream of the product collector; real‑time absorption data allowed immediate detection of conversion drift and rapid corrective actions (adjusting flow rates or hydrogen feed), stabilising the process without shutdown.
Supporting_Evidence: “The inlet pressure recorded at the beginning of the experiment was 59 bar indicating ≈20 bar pressure buildup… the inlet pressure steadily increased to 88 bar… then surprisingly dropped to 67 bar… Full scale deflection of the online UV‑absorption… indicated the breakthrough of high concentrations of DIM‑NA… Online analysis has proven highly useful… not only by rapidly indicating an unexpected process instability, immediate measures were taken.” (sec 2.5) ‣ “Accordingly, suitable analytical methods were evaluated, and the experimental setup eventually extended with an online UV–vis analysis module.” (sec 2.4) ‣ “Changes in DIM‑NA conversion following variations of the reactor throughput are nicely reflected by the UV–vis absorption.” (sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: ICP‑OES analysis after a 0.4 M run revealed cobalt leaching (28 ppm in the crude product, 470 ppm in the evaporated concentrate), posing a metal‑contamination risk for the API intermediate.
Solution_Description: A downstream work‑up consisting of concentration and precipitation with water was employed, which reduced the cobalt content in the isolated product to 9 ppm, well within acceptable limits, and also removed most residual impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: “The extent of Co leaching was assessed… 28 ppm of Co were detected in the product solution… In the crystallized product, the amount of Co is significantly lower (9 ppm of Co)… The off‑white precipitate was isolated and dried to yield 831 g (89 %) DIM‑DAB, which contained only 0.09 wt % of the desiodo side product and clearly fulfilled the product specification criteria–also with regard to residual trace metal amount (9 ppm of Co).” (sec 2.5) ‣ “Workup of the product solutions (not optimized) was performed by a downstream procedure including concentration of the product solutions and precipitation by water addition.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Continuous Selective Hydrogenation of Refametinib Iodo-nitroaniline Key Intermediate DIM-NA over Raney Cobalt Catalyst at kg/day Scale with Online UV–Visible Conversion Control
Problem_Description: When a fresh Raney‑Co catalyst was first introduced, the initial product batches contained higher amounts of desiodo‑DIM‑DAB (up to 2.3 wt %) due to catalyst activation effects, leading to lower selectivity at the start of each run.
Solution_Description: The first few fractions (containing higher desiodination) were discarded and only product collected after the catalyst run‑up period, ensuring that the final product met the stringent impurity specifications.
Supporting_Evidence: “The relatively high amount of desiodo‑DIM‑DAB (2.3, 1.0 wt %) in the first two product samples was attributed to a catalyst initiation effect as previously observed for all fresh catalyst loadings. Desiodination then steadily decreased in the further course of the process reaching values <0.5 wt %.” (sec 2.5) ‣ “The initial high desiodination was observed for fresh catalyst loadings and decreased after a run‑up phase.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: Low acrylate selectivity for APA esters that contain a β‑hydrogen (ethyl, butyl, isobutyl) because a competing elimination pathway (Path b) generates free acrylic acid and free APA, which decompose or polymerize, reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Use APA esters lacking β‑hydrogen (methyl or benzyl) as feedstocks; these do not undergo Path b, giving >70 % acrylate selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “those esters with hydrogen on the β‑carbon… exhibit significantly lower selectivity to acrylates” (Sec 3.2); “Path (b)… elimination of the alkyl ester group as an alkene… leads to free acrylic acid… significantly more reactive toward undesired decomposition or polymerization” (Sec 3.2); “experiments with methyl or benzyl APA ester feeds gave acrylate selectivity of 70+ % under the same conditions” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: When nitrogen is used as the diluent gas, carbon deposits build up on the contact material, causing a decline in acrylate selectivity with time on stream.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Replace N₂ with CO₂ as the diluent; CO₂ reacts with deposited carbon via the Boudouard reaction, continuously removing carbon and maintaining high acrylate selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “CO₂ increases acrylate selectivity relative to N₂… acrylate selectivity with N₂ clearly declines with time on stream” (Sec 3.1); “CO₂ continually removes these carbon deposits from the contact material… results in higher acrylate selectivity” (Sec 3.1); “CO formation … 8‑fold greater … explained by the Boudouard reaction of CO₂ with this deposited carbon” (Sec 3.1).

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: Feeding the diluent gas through a separate annular line gave poor vaporization of the liquid APA feed, which lowered acrylate yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
[MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Feed both the liquid APA stream and the diluent gas together through the same 1/16″ tube; this improves liquid‑feed vaporization and raises acrylate yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, diluent gas was fed through the annulus… however, it was found that better vaporization of the liquid feed took place and higher acrylate yields were obtained when the liquid feed and diluent gas were both fed through the 1/16″ tube” (Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: Porous silica (Spherosil) traps feed material in its pores; trapped reactants decompose to carbon and gases, giving a very low acrylate selectivity (≈5 %).
Solution_Description: Use non‑porous, low‑surface‑area quartz or silicon carbide as the contact material; these provide short contact times and do not trap feed, giving higher selectivity (≈30–35 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “The porous silica contact material clearly does not perform well, most likely because any feed material entering the pores is trapped and decomposes to carbon and gases… total acrylate selectivity was 5.1 %” (Sec 3.4); Table 1 shows quartz (34.9 %) and SiC (29.4 %) give much higher selectivity than Spherosil (5.1 %).

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: Operating above 620 °C causes acrylic acid to decompose rapidly, eliminating any acrylic‑acid product at 690 °C and lowering overall acrylate yield.
Solution_Description: Maintain the reactor temperature in the 550–620 °C window where APA conversion is complete, acrylate selectivity is maximal, and acrylic‑acid decomposition is minimal.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acrylic acid decomposition predominates above 620 °C such that no acrylic acid exits the reactor at the highest temperature examined (690 °C)” (Sec 3.3); “Total acrylate yield remains nearly constant at its maximum value between 550 and 620 °C” (Sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Enhanced Acrylate Production from 2‑Acetoxypropanoic Acid Esters
Problem_Description: Using acetic anhydride to synthesize APA esters is prohibitively expensive for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Produce APA esters from lactic acid using acetic acid in a reactive‑distillation step; this cheaper co‑feed also aids volatilization and improves selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although the use of acetic anhydride to form APA is prohibitively expensive, the ability to make APA from acetic acid via reactive distillation makes acrylate production via this route worthy of consideration” (Intro).

Paper Title: Synthesis of Tegafur by the Alkylation of 5‑Fluorouracil under the Lewis Acid and Metal Salt-Free Conditions
Problem_Description: Triethylamine (TEA) and pyridine failed to promote the alkylation without a Lewis‑acid additive, leading to negligible product formation.
Solution_Description: Screening of stronger, non‑nucleophilic amine bases (TMG, DBU) provided effective promotion of the reaction, removing the need for TEA/pyridine or additional Lewis acids.
Supporting_Evidence: “triethylamine required a Lewis acid additive… Our preliminary experiments showed that triethylamine did not promote the reaction… pyridine… not satisfactory.”; “The use of TMG or DBU resulted in a significant increase of the yields.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Tegafur by the Alkylation of 5‑Fluorouracil under the Lewis Acid and Metal Salt-Free Conditions
Problem_Description: Alkylation of pyrimidines with 2,3‑dihydrofuran under literature conditions required very long reaction times (up to 90 h) and high temperature (≥178 °C), often in a steel autoclave.
Solution_Description: The new DBU‑mediated method achieves comparable or higher yields within 24 h at 90 °C, cutting reaction time by more than half and avoiding high‑pressure equipment.
Supporting_Evidence: “In our hands, a very long reaction time was required… 90 h in a steel autoclave…”; “The DBU‑mediated alkylation… for 24 h at 90 °C.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of Tegafur by the Alkylation of 5‑Fluorouracil under the Lewis Acid and Metal Salt-Free Conditions
Problem_Description: Quantitative NMR analysis of the reaction mixture was hindered by overlapping signals (5.8–7.5 ppm), making it difficult to assess conversion and product ratios accurately.
Solution_Description: The authors pre‑purified the alkylation mixture by extraction and used a telescoped second step (direct transformation to tegafur) followed by crystallization, thus bypassing the need for precise NMR quantification during process development.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of NMR spectroscopy to determine the molar ratio… was not successful owing to poor separation of diagnostic signals… The occurrence of the rotamers…”; “To transform the 1,3‑disubstituted derivative 4 into tegafur without separation of the alkylation products, the prepurified mixture… was treated…”.

Paper Title: Synthesis of Tegafur by the Alkylation of 5‑Fluorouracil under the Lewis Acid and Metal Salt-Free Conditions
Problem_Description: Overall two‑step process gave a 72 % yield of tegafur, slightly lower than the 78–82 % reported for silyl‑based methods.
Solution_Description: The authors accepted the modest loss in overall yield in exchange for higher atom economy and greener metrics (lower waste, no metal salts); they suggest that further optimisation of reagent concentrations could close the yield gap.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yield was slightly lower than the yields of the silyl methods (Table 2). On the other hand, our method generates savings resulting from a significant limitation of auxiliary substances.”

Paper Title: Screwing NaBH
Problem_Description: Aromatic aldehydes have negligible water‑solubility; when an aqueous alkaline NaBH₄ solution is used the substrates float on the liquid surface, creating mass‑transfer limitations that give sluggish or incomplete reduction (conversion < 100 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to an aqueous alkaline NaBH₄ solution (water instead of THF) and perform the reaction in a high‑shear twin‑screw granulator. The intense mechanical shearing/kneading continuously disperses the solid aldehyde and NaBH₄ particles, eliminating the floating‑substrate issue and delivering rapid, high‑yield reductions (90–98 % in 20 s).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Aromatic aldehydes were chosen as substrates due to their negligible water solubility resulting in problematic behavior in batch when aqueous systems were used as solvent medium (the substrates “float”, causing mass transfer limitations)."
- "Under these reaction conditions, the target products were obtained swiftly and in high yield (90–98 %)."
- "The reduction of aromatic aldehydes in solid state was attempted... The reduction went off sluggishly in both ethereal solvents without reaching completion within 5 h, perhaps due to mass transfer limitation of the NaBH₄ granules under magnetic stirring."
- "When a drop of water or NaOH solution was added, a vigorous effervescence was observed together with an adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT ≈ 60 °C) and product formation, supporting the idea of mass transfer limitation in the absence of either thorough mixing or an aqueous medium."
- "The process continuous reactive extrusion, we were able to control both the heat generated during the exothermic transformation at the pilot scale and collect the product in high yield (89 %)."

Paper Title: Screwing NaBH
Problem_Description: The carbonyl reduction of aromatic aldehydes with NaBH₄ is strongly exothermic (ΔH ≈ 60 kJ mol⁻¹ for the main reaction and up to ≈ 160 kJ mol⁻¹ for the runaway secondary reaction), raising the risk of thermal runaway and H₂ generation in scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Operate the granulator with a jacket set to 15 °C, model barrel temperature rise to keep material temperatures < 30 °C, and introduce the aqueous NaBH₄ feed after the solid aldehyde has entered the barrel (controlled addition). The continuous extruder provides high heat‑removal capacity (U·A ≈ 0.16 W K⁻¹) that limits temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The exothermic nature of the carbonyl reduction posed some challenges in the quest of an adequate understanding of the boundaries for running a continuous process safely, at scale."
- "APTAC results. Heat of main reaction ≈60 kJ/mol NaBH₄. Heat of runaway reaction ≈160 kJ/mol NaBH₄."
- "By starting with a low jacket temperature (15 °C) … we could keep the internal temperature below 30 °C allowing the starting material to react and leave the barrel within the designed residence time of 16 s."
- "The granulator screws were set to a rotational speed of 200 rpm and the granulator bridge breaker set to run at 80 %. The barrel jacket temperature was set to 15 °C."
- "A portionwise/ordered addition of the alkaline NaBH₄ solution via a rear liquid‑feeding port (instead of feeding both streams simultaneously) helps control the exotherm."

Paper Title: Screwing NaBH
Problem_Description: During the 17‑min continuous run, material accumulated and caked at the custom‑made liquid feed nozzle, partially obstructing NaBH₄ flow and causing a drop in conversion (from 94 % to ~78 % in later samples).
Solution_Description: Propose redesign of the liquid‑feed nozzle with higher precision (collaboration with the equipment manufacturer) to eliminate dead‑volume and prevent caking/rouging of the SS316 screws. This mechanical improvement removes the intermittent blockage and stabilises conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "We noticed some caking occurred at the custom‑made liquid feed nozzle, partially obstructing the flow of NaBH₄…"
- "Light “rouging” was noticed on the SS316 screws in correspondence of the modified solid feed port…"
- "The authors suspect that building a high precision liquid feed in collaboration with the manufacturer would avoid the occurrence of both caking and “rouging”."
- "The cavity underneath the liquid nozzle was large enough to let material accumulate… leading to a compact mass of product that might have affected the screws’ surface."

Paper Title: Screwing NaBH
Problem_Description: In batch mode the heat‑removal capacity is low; the exothermic reduction cannot be cooled efficiently, limiting the achievable conversion and requiring long residence times (up to 5 h) in THF or solvent‑less conditions.
Solution_Description: Replace batch reactors with a continuous twin‑screw granulator (high heat‑removal, high shear). The continuous platform removes heat rapidly (U·A ≈ 0.16 W K⁻¹) and allows short residence times (≈ 16 s) while maintaining > 90 % conversion, eliminating the need for long batch runs.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Low heat removal capacity" (batch) vs "High heat removal" (continuous) – Table 2.
- "The heat of reaction was assumed to be about 160 kJ/mol NaBH₄…" and the model predicted only a ≈ 2 °C barrel temperature rise for the continuous run.
- "During the continuous run… we were able to continuously reduce an aromatic aldehyde using an aqueous solution of NaBH₄ in a controlled manner on a kilogram scale (1.41 kg of product was collected in 17 min, 89 % purity)."
- "The continuous granulator… high shear… eliminates the need for long‑duration batch processes."

Paper Title: Screwing NaBH
Problem_Description: The fed‑batch process relies on a water‑miscible organic solvent (THF) and additional quench steps, generating organic waste, higher energy demand for solvent removal, and associated safety/environmental hazards.
Solution_Description: Eliminate THF completely by using only aqueous alkaline NaBH₄ solution; the reaction proceeds under solvent‑free conditions (water only), removing the need for large‑scale THF handling, distillation, and associated waste, thereby lowering material cost, energy consumption, and safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "In industry, such a chemical transformation is typically performed using a water‑miscible solvent such as THF… However, we felt that the need of organic solvents to solubilize the substrates and the use of a packed column that have to be regenerated… might not be the greenest option."
- "The continuous process… does not use an organic solvent, leading to a lower PMI value."
- "The batch process required solvent removal (vacuum distillation) which was 33 times more energy intensive than the continuous process."
- "The raw material cost for batch process was higher than continuous because of THF and additional water for quenching."

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: The methanol/ethanol solvates obtained from initial solid‑form screening contain >5 % methanol, exceeding ICH Q3C‑R6 limits and making them pharmaceutically unacceptable.
Solution_Description: The researchers employed solid‑state solvent exchange – humidifying the solvates to replace methanol/ethanol with water, producing a hydrate or water‑containing cosolvate that meets ICH limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “solvates which are pharmaceutically undesirable due to ICH limits on solvent content” (Intro, p 1); “the methanol/ethanol solvate could be readily crystallized… then converted to hydrate by humidification” (Sec 3.2.1).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: Conventional drying of the methanol‑containing solvate leads to loss of the crystalline lattice and formation of an amorphous product.
Solution_Description: Instead of drying, the team used humidification (solid‑state solvent exchange) to retain the crystal framework while swapping the solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “Traditional drying techniques resulted in conversion to amorphous form.” (Sec 3.1); “solvent exchange proved successful and resulted in a more stable, predominantly hydrated form” (Sec 3.1).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: During humidification, high temperature/high humidity caused the material to become gummy, whereas low temperature/low humidity gave slow solvent exchange, leading to inconsistent crystal forms (Form‑Y, Form‑β, or a gummy mass).
Solution_Description: A QbD‑driven design‑of‑experiments identified an optimal operating window (20–30 °C, 40–55 % RH) that balances conversion speed without causing gumming or unwanted polymorphs.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 and discussion: “High temperatures and high humidity resulted in the powder becoming gummy… high temperature and low humidity resulted in conversion to Form‑β… optimal operating range … ambient temperature (20–30 °C) with humidity of 40–55 % RH.” (Sec 3.1.1).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: Larger crystals (>15 µm) exhibited slower methanol‑to‑water exchange, leaving higher residual methanol and reducing the overall yield of the target hydrate.
Solution_Description: The DoE varied crystallization temperature (‑20 °C to ‑5 °C), antisolvent (MTBE) addition time (45–180 min), and agitation to promote high supersaturation, generating finer crystals (~5–10 µm) that diffuse solvent faster and achieve <2 % methanol.
Supporting_Evidence: “Faster addition at lower temperatures leading to lower methanol content… lower temperature and faster addition rates of antisolvent lead to a higher degree of supersaturation, favoring nucleation rather than growth, resulting in smaller crystal size distribution.” (Sec 3.1.2).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: Very rapid MTBE addition at low temperature caused the slurry to become gummy rather than crystallize.
Solution_Description: The addition time of MTBE was limited to a minimum of 45 min for the second DoE to avoid gumming while still achieving fine crystals.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2 note: “If MTBE is added very rapidly, it results in gumming out rather than crystallization, particularly at low temperatures… the minimum addition time was increased to 45 min for the second DoE.” (Sec 3.1.2).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: Imatinib mesylate shows a steep drop in solubility from 5 °C to ‑20 °C, making it difficult to control crystallization and solvent exchange at higher temperatures.
Solution_Description: Crystallization was performed at sub‑ambient temperatures (‑5 °C to ‑20 °C) to exploit the low solubility and drive nucleation of fine crystals, which subsequently improve solvent exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: “There is a significant drop in solubility of imatinib mesylate Form‑Y in methanol from 5 °C to ‑20 °C… lower temperatures … favoring nucleation rather than growth.” (Sec 3.1.2).

Paper Title: Development of Pharmaceutically Acceptable Crystalline Forms of Drug Substances via Solid-State Solvent Exchange
Problem_Description: Scaling the humidification step requires equipment capable of delivering controlled temperature and humidity, which may not be readily available in all API plants.
Solution_Description: The authors propose using conventional agitated nut‑shell filter dryers (ANFD) or fluidized‑bed dryers (FBD) with humidified nitrogen/air, noting that FBD are more effective at larger scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Solvent exchange processes that require humidification can be readily scaled up with conventional drying equipment such as agitated nutsche filter dryers (ANFD) or fluidized bed dryers (FBD).” (Sec 3.4).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the Friedel–Crafts acylation of the protected pyrrole (1) with chloroacetyl chloride gave a precipitous drop in isolated yield (from ~74 % on 100 g scale to <35 % on 450 kg scale) with a large fraction of the pyrrole disappearing as unaccounted material, later traced to polymerization of a pyrrole‑AlCl₃ complex.
Solution_Description: The electrophile was changed from chloroacetyl chloride to acetyl chloride. AcCl binds more strongly to AlCl₃, eliminating the unproductive pyrrole‑AlCl₃ equilibrium and polymerization, and delivering quantitative conversion and >99 % C3:C2 selectivity on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “a precipitous drop in yield was observed for the acylation of a protected pyrrole with chloroacetyl chloride upon scale‑up.”; “The remaining 21 % of the input pyrrole 1 could not be accounted for.”; “Initial attempts at kilogram scale led to yields far below 50 %…”; “Despite these changes, the yield decreased from 71 % at a 120 kg scale to 35 % at a 450 kg scale.”; “By changing the acylating agent to acetyl chloride, a more robust process was obtained.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The Friedel–Crafts acylation with chloroacetyl chloride was highly sensitive to the order and rate of addition of reagents; slow addition (180 min) gave only 50 % yield and poor selectivity, whereas rapid addition gave 74 % yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimized the charge sequence: AlCl₃ and ClCH₂COCl were first combined in CH₂Cl₂, then the solution of pyrrole 1 was added rapidly (≤15 min) under maximum agitation. This controlled the formation of the AlCl₃‑pyrrole complex and improved conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The optimal results were found by first charging AlCl₃ and chloroacetyl chloride… then rapidly adding a solution of pyrrole 1…”; “The rate of addition of pyrrole 1… was also critical… charging the solution of 1 over 180 min resulted in a decreased yield and selectivity relative to faster additions.”; “All other permutations of this charge sequence resulted in lower and variable yields.”; “ensure that the agitation rate was always set to maximum.”; “The reaction required 5 h to reach full conversion and afforded 2 in 74 % yield and 16:1 C3:C2 selectivity.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: Dissolved HCl in the reaction mixture acted as a scale‑dependent factor: removing HCl gave almost full consumption of pyrrole 1 but <5 % desired product, while saturating the solvent with HCl completely shut down both the desired reaction and pyrrole decomposition, indicating a narrow and volatile HCl concentration window.
Solution_Description: A four‑factor Definitive Screening Design was employed that included HCl equivalents as a variable; the study identified HCl as the key factor controlling yield and allowed its level to be balanced (low enough to avoid complete inhibition, high enough to suppress polymerization).
Supporting_Evidence: “purging HCl resulted in complete consumption of pyrrole 1, but <5 % yield of the desired product 2!”; “performing the reaction in a sealed vessel with DCE that had been saturated with anhydrous HCl completely inhibited both the desired reaction and the decomposition of 1.”; “The dramatic difference in reaction performance… attested to the strong effect of HCl.”; “Four‑factor Definitive Screening Design… identified HCl as the key factor in controlling yield.”; “An unexpected nonlinear dependence of yield on HCl amount suggested that at low conversion dissolved HCl could be beneficial, whereas at higher conversions its presence could be detrimental.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The α‑chlorination of ketone 6 using Oxone required a very high solids loading (≈1.2 g mL⁻¹). In a 3000 L reactor the minimum agitation rate to keep Oxone fully suspended was almost at the maximum motor speed, leading to incomplete suspension, particle‑size‑dependent kinetics and poor reproducibility; the reaction also generated increasing amounts of by‑product 8 with time.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A specification for Oxone particle size was introduced and agitation was maximized (≈110 rpm, ~8 % below the motor limit) to ensure full suspension. The reaction concentration was tuned to keep Oxone in suspension and to limit by‑product formation, improving robustness at scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “Oxone is a relatively dense solid (∼1.2 g mL⁻¹), and a high loading (3 kg kg⁻¹ of substrate) was required to achieve complete conversion.”; “The minimum agitation rate for complete suspension (Njs) of Oxone was calculated as 110 rpm ± 20 % for a 3000 L reactor… within 8 % of the maximum agitation rate.”; “reaction kinetics were greatly affected by the particle size of Oxone.”; “the reaction stream was not stable, and the level of 8 and other by‑products increased with reaction time.”; “These factors were a major challenge for the translation of this chemistry into a robust process.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) α‑chlorination was highly sensitive to the amount of NCS and to residual water; excess NCS (>1.1 equiv) produced over‑chlorination (compound 8) and higher water (1 equiv) gave over‑chlorination and slower rates, leading to inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run with NCS at 1.05–1.10 equiv and water ≤0.08 equiv; 0.1 equiv methanesulfonic acid (MSA) was added as a catalytic promoter to accelerate the rate and improve yield to >90 % in‑process, delivering a clean product profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “Two key factors were found for achieving a high yield… NCS equivalents and water content.”; “Elevated levels of 8 were obtained when the NCS charge exceeded 1.1 equiv.”; “Significant amounts of overchlorination products were observed when 1.0 equiv of H₂O was added.”; “the reaction rate is enhanced by the addition of catalytic amounts of acid… 0.1 equiv of methanesulfonic acid (MSA)… significant improvement in rate and yield was observed.”; “Under these optimized conditions, complete conversion was achieved in 6 h at 30 °C with a 90 % in‑process yield.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The final amidation generates an equivalent of NaCl, and the crystallization of the target pyrrolopyridine 5 required careful removal of this inorganic salt while maximizing product recovery; yields were highly dependent on the IPA/water antisolvent composition.
Solution_Description: A crystallization map was generated using a two‑step antisolvent addition (first 30 % water to dissolve NaCl, then 70 % IPA to drive product precipitation). This new purification protocol, coupled with controlled solvent volumes, gave reproducible isolated yields of ≥ 98 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The amidation reaction results in a reactive crystallization which also generates 1 equiv of NaCl as a byproduct.”; “A crystallization was devised that utilized the addition of an antisolvent mixture of isopropanol/water to the Me‑THF process stream to maximize the yield and potency of 5 while also purging NaCl.”; “The plot shows the isolated yield is a weak function of water content and a much stronger function of IPA concentration.”; “The isolated yield and potency could be maximized by first charging 30 vol % of water… then charging 70 vol % of IPA.”; “The optimized amidation step… allowed isolation of 5 in ≥ 98 % HPLC AP.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 3. Mechanistic Studies Enable a Scale-Independent Friedel–Crafts Acylation
Problem_Description: The original two‑step sequence (Friedel–Crafts acylation with ClCH₂COCl followed by amidation) delivered only 34 % overall isolated yield on commercial scale, with poor robustness and scale‑dependent performance.
Solution_Description: A three‑step route was introduced: (1) AcCl‑mediated Friedel–Crafts acylation, (2) high‑yielding α‑chlorination of the resulting ketone, and (3) amidation. Steps 1 and 2 were telescoped, eliminating isolation of intermediates and improving overall yield to ≈ 75 % with excellent purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “A counterintuitive choice to switch to a longer, but scale‑independent, three‑step route was made.”; “With this promising result in hand, the reaction of AcCl with 1 was optimized… nearly quantitative yields… not subject to the scale dependence observed in the original ClCH₂COCl process.”; “The first two steps were telescoped, thus avoiding the isolation of compounds 6 and 2.”; “The improved yield and scalability of this three‑step process supported the addition of one linear step to the route… consistently achieved a 62–75 % overall yield for the three‑step telescope with excellent purity (>98 % HPLC AP).”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: The free‑acid form of the parent drug BMS‑626529 crystallised as long, thin needles giving extremely poor filtration rates; a multi‑week filtration was required on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Formation of the lithium salt of BMS‑626529 produced a new crystal form with rod‑like morphology that filtered easily and could be isolated in high purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the crystal form of the free acid of BMS‑626529 (1) had a long, thin, needle morphology—resulting in extremely poor filtration rates. The issue was so significant that a multi‑week filtration of indole 1 was needed on kilo‑scale.”
• “The first, and most obvious, omission from the previous studies was lithium; thus, this was the first salt investigated. To our delight, the initial experiment yielded a new crystalline form of indole 1.”
• “Further optimization and development of the new process resulted in an easily filtered and readily isolated compound with a rod morphology.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: Several genotoxic intermediates (GTIs) were introduced, most notably the chloromethylene compound 5, which was identified as a highly potent dermal sensitiser and posed a safety risk given the projected high daily dose of the final drug.
Solution_Description: A new low‑oxidation‑state synthetic route was designed, starting from a simple pyrrole derivative, which avoided the formation of the chloromethylene GTI and eliminated other genotoxic steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “several new genotoxic compounds (GTIs) were introduced into the sequence, including the chloromethylene compound 5 (which, when tested, was also found to be an extremely potent dermal sensitiser).”
• “The introduction of several GTIs was especially problematic due to the high expected dose of this compound (which at the stage of development was projected to be in the range of 1.2–1.6 g/day).”
• “The genesis of this concept was to electronically disconnect the C4‑methoxy from the C7‑triazole… starting from a simple commercially available pyrrole derivative.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: The pro‑drug installation required the use of corrosive chlorine gas and chloromethyl chlorosulfate (CMCS), reagents that are hazardous, difficult to handle, and suffered from long‑term supply‑availability issues.
Solution_Description: New protocols were developed for the preparation of CMCS, potassium di‑tert‑butyl phosphate and chloromethyl‑di‑tert‑butyl phosphate, providing safer, more readily available reagents for the pro‑drug step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “use of corrosive and hazardous reagents (i.e., chlorine gas), which is not only difficult to handle, but also difficult to charge accurately.”
• “Several issues for the long‑term supply and availability of chloromethyl chlorosulfate (CMCS) were evident and caused by reagent limitations.”
• “new protocols for the preparation of CMCS, potassium di‑tert‑butyl phosphate, and chloromethyl‑di‑tert‑butyl phosphate were discovered, developed, and reported.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: The traditional SNAr sequence required neat POCl₃ (5 L kg⁻¹), high temperature (~140 °C) and long reaction times (~60 h), giving only modest yields and generating hazardous waste and impurity profiles (13 and 14).
Solution_Description: A low‑oxidation‑state approach using a Pictet–Spengler cyclisation with formaldehyde avoided the POCl₃ SNAr step; the subsequent aromatisation employed cumyl hydroperoxide (CHP) as a safe, commodity radical initiator.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the demethylation/chlorination was performed in neat POCl₃ (5 L per kg of input) posing fundamental problems of safety, handling, workup efficiency, waste disposal, and environmental impact.”
• “the displacement of the resulting chloride with triazole 12 was similarly problematic, requiring high temperatures (~140 °C) over the course of several days (~60 h), generating two key impurities 13 and 14.”
• “Only formaldehyde functioned with appropriate reactivity (i.e., a classical Pictet–Spengler cyclisation).”
• “We selected cumyl hydroperoxide (CHP) over reagents such as AIBN, because it is a commodity chemical… the lack of toxic by‑product formation, and ease of use.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: Using pyridine as the key starting material forced multiple functional‑group interconversions, leading to a 14‑step sequence, low overall yield (≈4 %), high material cost and poor step‑ideality.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was re‑designed to start from a commercially available pyrrole, shortening the route to 11 linear steps, improving overall yield and reducing cost‑of‑goods.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “functionalisation of pyridine… required both positions meta to the ring nitrogen to be functionalised… The formation of a tetra‑ipso system… required a large number of functional‑group manipulations, low ideality, high step count, challenging technology, low overall yield, and ultimately higher cost.”
• “The genesis of this concept was to electronically disconnect… starting from a simple commercially available pyrrole derivative.”
• “We quickly prepared amino‑ketone 27, which could be easily elaborated to several substrates (28–33) to test the desired cyclisation to the core azaindole skeleton.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: Traditional triazole installation via SNAr required 140 °C for >48 h and produced significant impurities (13, 14), resulting in low isolated yield and difficult purification.
Solution_Description: A copper‑mediated Ullmann‑Goldberg‑Buchwald coupling using CuI (15 mol %) and trans‑dimethylamino‑cyclohexane (DMCHDA) ligand gave high regioselectivity and isolated yield of the triazole‑substituted product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the displacement of the resulting chloride with triazole 12 … requiring high temperatures (~140 °C) over the course of several days (~60 h), generating two key impurities 13 and 14.”
• “Cu‑mediated Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald conditions quickly showed promise, with simple diamine ligands giving the best regioselectivities, favouring our desired isomer.”
• “trans‑dimethylamino cyclohexane delivered the desired product in high yield and acceptable regioselectivity.”
