Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 2. Strategic Selections in the Transition from an Enabling Route to a Commercial Synthesis
Problem_Description: Selective functionalisation at C7 proved difficult; conventional metalation gave mixtures and low conversion, jeopardising convergent side‑chain installation.
Solution_Description: Turbo‑Grignard (iPrMgCl·LiCl) enabled selective metalation of the C3 bromide over the C7 chloride, allowing a convergent route to introduce the full side‑chain via copper‑mediated coupling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The selective metalation of the C3 bromide (over the C7 chloride) could be easily accomplished using iPrMgCl·LiCl (Turbo Grignard) following the selectivity patterns established by Knochel et al.”
• “In this manner, the entire side chain of 71 could be installed, with obvious advantages in convergency.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: In batch electrochemical cells scaling up is hindered by inefficient mixing, poor heat removal, and low surface‑to‑volume ratio, which lead to low conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the batch vessel with a highly modular continuous‑flow cell that provides intensive mixing via a dendritic feeder and excellent temperature control through the Teflon‑encased electrode geometry.
Supporting_Evidence: “Larger systems face some major drawbacks: First, efficient mixing… can be challenging in larger vessels. Second, heat transfer is hampered… Third, the volume‑to‑surface ratio decreases…”. “To tackle these issues, a transfer to a continuous flow setup is desirable and advantageous.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: No standardized, commercially available electrochemical flow equipment existed, forcing each laboratory to rely on custom‑made setups.
Solution_Description: A novel modular flow cell was designed and later commercialized (ElectraSyn flow), providing interchangeable electrodes, adjustable gaps and the option for divided or undivided operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “So far, there is no commercially available system with a modular setup… Therefore, a highly modular electrochemical flow cell is presented, which is now commercially available.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: During the domino oxidation–reduction of 2,6‑dichlorobenzaldoxime in the flow cell, a large amount of dehalogenated by‑product and unconverted intermediate 2 were observed, indicating poor selectivity and incomplete reduction.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors (i) added a controlled amount of water (CH₃CN:H₂O = 4:1) to suppress dehalogenation, (ii) lowered the supporting‑electrolyte concentration, and (iii) reduced the electrode gap from 1 mm to 0.12 mm, which improved diffusion of the intermediate between anode and cathode.
Supporting_Evidence: “By the addition of water… the dehalogenated by‑product could be efficiently suppressed.”; “Increasing the supporting‑electrolyte concentration… promoted dehalogenation.”; “We replaced the EPDM‑based spacer… with a Teflon spacer providing a gap of 0.12 mm… no nitrile‑N‑oxide 2, but more product 3 was identified.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: When a high concentration of supporting electrolyte was used without water, a film of nitrile‑N‑oxide crystallized on the graphite anode, causing voltage increase and loss of conversion.
Solution_Description: Water was removed from the anolyte (to prevent film formation) and added together with triethylamine and the dipolarophile after electrolysis, thereby restoring conductivity and allowing efficient cyclization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Water in the electrolyte decreased the solubility of 2… we excluded the water from the anolyte.”; “By applying acetonitrile and MTPS as an anolyte and the addition of water, triethylamine, and 4 upon electrolysis, we achieved the desired isoxazole 5 in a high selectivity.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: Potentiostatic electrochemical methods reported in the literature require prolonged reaction times, making them unsuitable for technical‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The process was switched to galvanostatic operation, fixing the current density and allowing rapid, reproducible conversions on scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “One of the major disadvantages of many electrochemical methods… are that potentiostatic methods are applied. Upscaling… results in prolonged reaction times. Therefore, only galvanostatic methods are used on a technical scale.”

Paper Title: Highly Modular Flow Cell for Electroorganic Synthesis
Problem_Description: Single‑cell operation gave limited productivity (≈110 mg h⁻¹) for the nitrile synthesis.
Solution_Description: Two flow cells were connected in series, doubling the electrode surface from 12 cm² to 24 cm² and allowing the flow rate to be doubled while halving residence time, raising productivity to 220 mg h⁻¹.
Supporting_Evidence: “By applying two separate cells… the electrode surface can be increased from 12 to 24 cm²… the flow rate can be doubled… productivity increased from 110 mg/h to 220 mg/h.”

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: The original Cottet procedure required a large excess of Friedel‑Crafts AlCl₃ catalyst and an exothermic aqueous quench, making the reaction unsafe and impractical on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Friedel‑Crafts route with a two‑step sequence: acylation of halo‑anilines with inexpensive methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate (NaHMDS, THF) followed by cyclisation in sulfuric acid, avoiding the hazardous AlCl₃ step.
Supporting_Evidence: “This procedure was not suitable for scale-up due to the large amount of the Friedel–Crafts catalyst and the concomitant problematic exothermic aqueous quench.” (Introduction)  ;  “The heterocycles are easily accessed from inexpensive halo anilines in a two‑step sequence. The anilines are acylated … followed by cyclisation in sulfuric acid.” (Abstract & Results)  ;  “The basic aminolysis of methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate with aniline should give access to the desired starting material for the Knorr quinolinone synthesis.” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: A reported palladium‑catalysed cyclisation gave only sub‑gram scale (≤200 mg), required 36 h reaction time and chromatographic purification, making it unsuitable for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The authors discarded the palladium method and adopted the classical Knorr protocol (acylation → sulfuric‑acid cyclisation), which proceeds rapidly (≈30 min) and affords products that can be isolated by precipitation, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Unfortunately, the procedure was only demonstrated on a scale <200 mg, the reaction time was 36 h, and chromatographic purification was required.” (Introduction)  ;  “The crude amides undergo cyclization in sulfuric acid to the desired halo quinolin‑2(1H)‑ones in 28–93 % yield (2 steps).” (Abstract)  ;  “The products precipitated and were collected by filtration. A slurry in isopropanol or acetonitrile afforded the products in good purities as yellow solids.” (General cyclisation procedure A)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: Turner’s method required two low‑temperature steps at –78 °C and used reagents that are expensive or not available at scale.
Solution_Description: By switching to the Knorr condensation using cheap methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate and performing the reactions at ambient or mildly elevated temperatures, the need for cryogenic conditions and expensive reagents was eliminated.
Supporting_Evidence: “The major drawback was that two steps had to be carried out at low temperature (−78 °C), which is not desirable for scale‑up.” (Introduction)  ;  “Either an aniline derivative was reacted with diethoxyacryloyl chloride, which is an expensive reagent, or it was coupled with dimethoxypropanoic acid, which is not available on scale.” (Introduction)  ;  “The basic aminolysis of methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate with aniline … was further investigated.” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: Halo‑anilines bearing strong electron‑donating groups (Me, OMe, vinyl) showed poor reactivity, gave complex mixtures and incomplete conversion, leading to low and inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: The authors limited the scope to substrates that performed well (halogenated, nitro, cyano, keto) and did not pursue further optimisation for the poorly reacting electron‑rich examples.
Supporting_Evidence: “Anilines with electron donating groups such as methyl, methoxy, or vinyl were less reactive and gave complex product mixtures… The starting material was never fully consumed.” (Results – Formation of the 3,3‑Dimethoxy‑N‑arylpropanamides)  ;  “Anilines 1k–p substituted with two halogens were good substrates, too.” (Results)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: During the NaHMDS‑mediated amidation, partial elimination of methanol from the dimethoxypropionate generated methyl 3‑methoxyacrylate, which reacted with the aniline to give impurity B (and further impurities C, D) that reduced product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed at 0–5 °C with controlled addition of NaHMDS (1.5 eq) and overnight stirring, followed by aqueous citric‑acid quench, mitigating formation of the eliminating side‑product and allowing the crude amide to be used directly in the cyclisation step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Under the reaction conditions, 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate was partly eliminating methanol and forming the methyl 3‑methoxyacrylate, which reacted with 1g to form impurity B.” (Results)  ;  “Substituted halo‑anilines 1 (1.0 equiv) and the propionate (1.2 equiv) were dissolved in THF and treated with 40 % NaHMDS in THF (1.5 equiv) at 0–5 °C … The reaction was usually kept overnight at room temperature and quenched by addition of an aqueous citric acid solution.” (General amide formation procedure)  ;  “The crude product was introduced in the cyclization step without further purification.” (Results)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: Fluoro‑substituted anilides gave modest yields (21‑37 %) under the standard cyclisation conditions (0 °C, 15 eq H₂SO₄).
Solution_Description: Increasing the cyclisation temperature to 22 °C (yield 58 %) and 80 °C (yield 74 %) markedly improved conversion. For the p‑fluoro substrate, raising H₂SO₄ from 15 eq to 33 eq increased yield to 75 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yields of the quinolones substituted with a fluorine atom (3d, h) were only moderate with 21–37 % … Therefore, a test … was carried out … The yield increased from 21 % at 0 °C to 58 % at 22 °C and peaked at 80 °C with 74 %.” (Results – Formation of Quinolin‑2(1H)‑ones)  ;  “When the equivalents of sulfuric acid were raised from 15 to 33 eq, the cyclization step was improved and the product was obtained in 75 % yield.” (Results – Formation of Quinolin‑2(1H)‑ones)  ;  “An increase … to 33 eq … improved … to 75 % yield.” (General cyclisation procedure A footnote e)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: 2,4‑dihalo‑anilides cyclised poorly (28‑40 % yield) and were partially cleaved back to the starting anilines, indicating decomposition under the reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: Higher cyclisation temperatures (80‑120 °C) and an increased acid load (33 eq H₂SO₄) were employed, which raised yields (e.g., iodo‑fluoro 3n from 35 % to 69 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “The four anilides … with a 2,4‑substitution pattern were found to be more deactivated, and they cyclized only at higher temperatures (80–120 °C). The yields were only moderate with 28–40 %.” (Results – Formation of Quinolin‑2(1H)‑ones)  ;  “LC‑MS revealed that the 2,4‑dihalo anilides were not completely cyclized … they were cleaved to form the corresponding anilines.” (Results)  ;  “By increasing the amount of sulfuric acid from 15 to 33 eq, the yield for the iodo‑fluoro heterocycle 3n improved significantly from 35 to 69 %.” (Results)  ;  “The yield for the iodo‑chloro heterocycle 3o improved from 0 to 49 %.” (Results)

Paper Title: Scalable and Practical Synthesis of Halo Quinolin-2(1
Problem_Description: The traditional Knorr starting material required diethoxyacryloyl chloride (expensive) or dimethoxypropanoic acid (not commercially available on scale).
Solution_Description: The authors adopted a cost‑effective synthesis of the amide precursor by direct basic aminolysis of methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate with halo‑anilines using NaHMDS, eliminating the need for costly or unavailable reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “Either an aniline derivative was reacted with diethoxyacryloyl chloride, which is an expensive reagent, or it was coupled with dimethoxypropanoic acid, which is not available on scale.” (Introduction)  ;  “The basic aminolysis of methyl 3,3‑dimethoxypropionate with aniline should give access to the desired starting material for the Knorr quinolinone synthesis. This strategy was further investigated.” (Introduction)  ;  “NaHMDS (1.5 equiv) … at 0 °C … gave quantitative yield of the amide.” (General amide formation procedure)

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: Traditional O‑methylation of vanillin uses hazardous alkylating agents (dimethyl sulfate, methyl halides, diazomethane) and toxic solvents such as DMF, generating large amounts of waste and posing safety risks.
Solution_Description: Replace the toxic reagents with dimethyl carbonate (DMC), a sustainable, nontoxic and biodegradable methylating agent, providing a greener synthetic route.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The traditional synthesis of O‑methylation reactions involved harmful alkylating agents such as dimethyl sulfate, methyl halides, and diazomethane… These reagents are hazardous, which produce a large amount of waste.", "Dimethyl carbonate (DMC) is a sustainable, nontoxic, and biodegradable reagent."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: Homogeneous base catalysts (e.g., K₂CO₃, 18‑crown‑6) require neutralization after reaction, cannot be recycled, and generate large quantities of dissolved solids, leading to pollution and impurity issues.
Solution_Description: Introduce a heterogeneous potassium‑promoted La₂O₃–MgO mixed‑oxide catalyst that can be easily separated, washed and reused, eliminating neutralization steps and improving product purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["These homogeneous catalysts have to be neutralized and cannot be recycled, thereby making the process polluting.", "From a Green Chemistry point of view, the replacement of homogeneous catalysts by heterogeneous ones is most desirable, since the catalyst can be easily recovered and reused."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: The parent La₂O₃–MgO mixed oxide has low basicity and surface area, resulting in sub‑optimal conversion of vanillin to veratraldehyde.
Solution_Description: Load the mixed oxide with 2 wt % potassium (via K₂CO₃ impregnation) to generate additional moderate‑strong basic sites and improve dispersion, thereby increasing catalytic activity and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Lanthanum oxide (La₂O₃) is a strongly basic oxide, but the activity is low due to its low surface area.", "2 wt % K/La₂O₃–MgO showed the best activity and selectivity due to high dispersion of potassium and high basicity."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: Increasing potassium loading beyond 2 wt % blocks pores and decreases surface area, causing a drop in conversion.
Solution_Description: Optimize the potassium loading to the optimum 2 wt % level, avoiding excess promoter that would cover active sites and reduce porosity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The further increase in the loading of potassium leads to a decrease in the conversion, possibly due to blocking of pores by an excess amount of potassium.", "2 wt % K/La₂O₃–MgO is the best and gives 96 % conversion."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: At low agitation speeds (≤600 rpm) external mass‑transfer resistance limits reactant contact, leading to lower and inconsistent vanillin conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Operate the autoclave at ≥800 rpm (the point where conversion plateaus) to ensure sufficient mixing and eliminate mass‑transfer limitations.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The agitation speed was studied at 400, 600, 800, and 1000 rpm… beyond 800 rpm there is no effect on the conversion of vanillin, signifying that the mass transfer resistance was absent.", "The calculated mass transfer rates were found to be very high in comparison to the reaction rate, which confirms that there is no effect of external mass transfer resistance at and beyond 800 rpm."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: Catalyst loading below the optimum provides insufficient active sites, while loading above 0.03 g cm⁻³ offers no further conversion benefit, leading to inefficient use of catalyst.
Solution_Description: Set the catalyst concentration to the optimum 0.03 g cm⁻³ (based on total liquid volume) to maximize conversion without wasting material.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Vanillin conversion increases with the increase in catalyst loading… upon catalyst loading from 0.03 to 0.04 g cm⁻³, there is no appreciable change in the conversion of vanillin.", "Therefore, further reaction was performed upon 0.03 g cm⁻³ catalyst loading."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: During product isolation, 11 % of the formed veratraldehyde is lost, reducing the isolated yield to 89 %.
Solution_Description: After reaction, filter the catalyst, wash it with methanol (4 mL × 2) to retrieve any adsorbed product and evaporate the filtrate under reduced pressure, improving product recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The isolated yield was 89 % because of loss of product during the isolation procedure.", "The catalyst was washed with methanol (4 mL × 2) to confirm that no product was adsorbed on the catalyst."]

Paper Title: Green Synthesis of Veratraldehyde Using Potassium Promoted Lanthanum–Magnesium Mixed Oxide Catalyst
Problem_Description: Scaling the batch process without a predictive model could lead to deviations in conversion and selectivity at larger volumes.
Solution_Description: Develop and apply a kinetic model (pseudo‑first‑order) for the O‑methylation reaction, enabling reliable prediction of scale‑up parameters and ensuring consistent performance.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Scale‑up was done using the kinetic model to observe that the process could be scaled up using the process parameters.", "The reaction follows pseudo‑first‑order kinetics… The energy of activation was found to be 13.5 kcal mol⁻¹."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 5. Selective C‑7 Bromination of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: High raw‑material cost of the MTO/UHP oxidation reported for the N‑oxidation of 2; extensive work‑up and safety concerns with m‑CPBA and Ac₂O/H₂O₂ oxidations; thermal instability, high decomposition energy and mutagenicity of N‑oxide 3; variability in oxidation yield (75–95 %) and poor mass‑balance caused by pH‑dependent decomposition of 3 in the presence of excess H₂O₂; decomposition of 3 during work‑up when K₃PO₄ is added before peroxide quench; particle‑size and solubility limitations of K₃PO₄ in trifluorotoluene leading to inconsistent bromination rates and low selectivity; formation of pyrrolidine impurity 12 from degraded PyBroP, especially when stored improperly; generation of the genotoxic isopropyl‑benzene‑sulfonate impurity during the IPA‑based hydrolysis step and the need for multiple back‑extractions; high slurry viscosity and slow filtration when NMP is used as the hydrolysis cosolvent; exothermic nature of the oxidation (ΔH = ‑120 kJ mol⁻¹) and of the bromination stream, raising safety concerns; pH‑dependent decomposition of 3 by peroxide anion causing batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: Adopt phthalic anhydride/H₂O₂ as an inexpensive, safe oxidant; maintain the same oxidation solvent (CH₂Cl₂) while simplifying work‑up; avoid isolation of the energetic N‑oxide by telescoping the oxidation, bromination and de‑protection steps; add the aqueous H₂O₂ solution slowly over 2 h at 35 °C and reduce the H₂O₂ equiv. to 1.2 equiv to limit exposure of 3 to excess peroxide; modify the aqueous quench sequence to add Na₂SO₃ first (to reduce peroxide) followed by K₃PO₄ (to extract acid), preventing decomposition of 3; replace K₃PO₄ with soluble organic bases (DIPEA or N,N‑dimethyl‑p‑toluidine) and run bromination in toluene; add N,O‑bis‑(trimethylsilyl)‑acetamide (BSA) as a functional additive that scavenges moisture and suppresses formation of the bis‑phosphonium by‑product 11, improving conversion and selectivity; store PyBroP under freezer conditions, limit exposure to air/moisture and recrystallize from EtOAc to eliminate pyrrolidine impurity 12; switch the hydrolysis cosolvent from IPA to tert‑amyl alcohol, eliminating the GTI isopropyl‑benzene‑sulfonate, reducing the number of back‑extractions and improving product partitioning; employ a partial solvent switch to ≥75 % tert‑amyl alcohol to lower slurry viscosity, speed up filtration and avoid hard‑cake formation; control the exotherm of the oxidation by running at 35 °C with slow peroxide addition and evaluate thermal hazards with ARSSt; adjust the pH of the oxidation work‑up (basic aqueous quench) to suppress peroxide‑anion‑driven decomposition; overall, temperature optimisation, stoichiometry adjustment, order‑of‑addition changes and the use of functional additives together gave reproducible, high‑yielding processes.
Supporting_Evidence:
See excerpts:
- "high raw material costs made it inadequate for large‑scale implementation" (Table 1, MTO/UHP entry) – COST.
- "intensive workup" and "potential safety issues" for m‑CPBA and Ac₂O/H₂O₂ – SAFETY, COST.
- "N‑oxide 3 was found to be thermally unstable" and "tested positive in the bacterial reverse‑mutation assay (AMES)" – SAFETY, DECOMPOSITION.
- "The initial scale‑up of the oxidation revealed variability in the yield (75–95 %)" and "N‑oxide 3 decomposes in the presence of aqueous H₂O₂" – VARIABILITY, DECOMPOSITION.
- "presence of K₃PO₄ before the complete quench of excess peroxides could cause product decomposition" – DECOMPOSITION, LOW YIELD.
- "particle size of K₃PO₄ was critical" and "low solubility of K₃PO₄ in trifluorotoluene" – SOLUBILITY, MIXABILITY.
- "formation of the pyrrolidine containing impurity 12" in poorly stored PyBroP – PURIFICATION, SAFETY.
- "initial conditions employed IPA as a cosolvent and aqueous NaOH resulting in the formation of high levels of isopropyl‑benzene‑sulfonate, a known genotoxic impurity" – SAFETY, PURIFICATION, LONG REACTIONS.
- "slow filtration was observed during isolation and formation of hard lumps during drying" when NMP used – MIXABILITY, LONG REACTIONS.
- "reaction was evaluated by calorimetry … exothermic, ΔH_rxn = –120 kJ mol⁻¹" – EXOTHERMIC, SAFETY.
- "addition of Na₂SO₃ first … followed by K₃PO₄" improves yield – ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION.
- "slow addition of H₂O₂ over 2 h … fast consumption of H₂O₂ prevented exposure of 3 to excess peroxide" – ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION.
- "BSA (1 equiv) … gave 85–90 % solution yield … >10:1 selectivity" – FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE/PROMOTER.
- "tert‑amyl alcohol … eliminated need for back extractions and reduced product loss" – SOLVENT CHANGE.
- " azeotropic distillation to achieve water content <1 wt % before crystallization" – CONCENTRATION TUNING.
- "temperature set‑points of 35 °C for oxidation and 10 °C for bromination" – TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION.
- "pH‑dependent decomposition … basic aqueous quench extracted the acid by‑products" – PH CONTROL.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: The Friedel–Crafts acylation originally used nitromethane as a cosolvent. Nitromethane is highly energetic, creating safety concerns on scale, and its removal resulted in a thick, un‑agitated gel‑like reaction mixture that prevented efficient mixing and gave poor conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Nitromethane was replaced with catalytic tetra‑n‑butylammonium bisulfate (Bu₄N⁺HSO₄⁻). The ionic additive increased the polarity of the medium, prevented gel formation, and allowed the AlCl₃‑catalyzed acylation to proceed as a thin slurry with high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "...nitromethane, a commonly used, but highly energetic cosolvent, was employed which was eventually replaced by catalytic tetra‑n‑butylammonium bisulfate to overcome gelling issues encountered during the reaction when nitromethane was omitted." (Abstract)
2. "AlCl₃‑catalyzed acylation of azaindole 1 with methylchloro‑oxalate in a solvent system devoid of nitromethane resulted in a difficult‑to‑agitate reaction mixture due to the formation of a thick gel." (Results and Discussion – Friedel–Crafts section)
3. "The presence of the ionic ammonium salts in the reaction media would increase the polarity of the solvent and potentially resolve the gelling issue due to increased solubility of the catalyst." (Results and Discussion – screening of tetraalkylammonium salts)
4. "Several ammonium salts provided good reaction conversion and produced reaction mixtures that were visually thin slurries that were readily agitated... tetra‑n‑butylammonium salts offered the best results" (Table 3 discussion)
5. "The ammonium salt effectively replaced the highly energetic solvent nitromethane" (Conclusion).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: Attempts to replace AlCl₃ with alternative catalysts or to run the acylation without any Lewis acid gave <5 % to ~19 % conversion and produced thick gels, indicating poor reactivity and inconsistent results.
Solution_Description: The AlCl₃ catalyst was retained, but a catalytic amount of tetra‑n‑butylammonium bisulfate (0.35 equiv) was added. The additive increased the solubility of AlCl₃, eliminated the gel, and raised conversion to >85 % with a homogeneous slurry.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Our attempts to replace AlCl₃ catalyst were unsuccessful. ... resulting in a difficult‑to‑agitate reaction mixture due to the formation of a thick gel." (Results and Discussion – Table 1)
2. "Entry 5 ... 70 % conversion with AlBr₃; all other AlCl₃‑free conditions gave <20 % conversion." (Table 1)
3. "The low conversions were attributed to poor solubility of the acylation catalyst because all of the reaction mixtures again displayed a thick gel‑like consistency." (Results and Discussion)
4. "Several ammonium salts provided good reaction conversion and produced reaction mixtures that were visually thin slurries that were readily agitated. ... tetra‑n‑butylammonium salts offered the best results" (Table 3 discussion).
5. "Having identified a viable substitute for nitromethane, we next focused our attention on the optimization of the acylation reaction conditions." (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: The CDI‑mediated amidation required a two‑stage activation of the acid, and the acyl‑imidazole intermediate was unstable at the reaction temperature, leading to variable product purity, impurity formation (imidazole), and lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The amidation was changed to a single‑pot process using diphenylphosphinic chloride (DPPCl) as the coupling reagent. DPPCl activated the acid in situ and allowed direct reaction with piperazine, eliminating the unstable intermediate and delivering consistent yields and purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "CDI‑mediated amidation led to variable product purity. ... the acyl imidazole intermediate was not stable at the reaction temperature." (Results and Discussion – Amidation)
2. "It was subsequently determined that comparable yields and good purity could be obtained using n‑propylphosphonic anhydride (T3P), which did not require pre‑activation of acid 2a." (Table 6 discussion)
3. "We subsequently demonstrated that a single‑pot, homogeneous transformation could be achieved through the use of the cost‑effective coupling reagent diphenylphosphinic chloride (DPPCl)." (Abstract)
4. "During initial studies of the DPPCl mediated amidation process, a mixture of acid 2a and 1.4 equiv of piperazine ... was treated with 1.7 equiv of DPPCl." (Experimental Section – Amidation).
5. "The isolated product contained low levels of imidazole, leading to reduced potencies of amide 3." (Results and Discussion – CDI).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: The original aqueous work‑up using THF and 15 % Rochelle salt caused 8 % loss of the ester to the aqueous phase and generated inorganic solids that created a rag‑layer, complicating phase separation and filtration on scale.
Solution_Description: Aqueous (NH₄)₂HPO₄ (20 % w/w) was employed as the wash solution. This salt gave a rapid, clean phase split with no precipitated solids or rag‑layer, reducing product loss to ≤4 % and simplifying isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Table 5 entry 1 ... resulted in a substantial loss of the desired product to the aqueous phase (8 %)." (Results and Discussion – Workup)
2. "Utilizing a 20 wt % Rochelle salt solution reduced the product loss ... however, inorganic solids precipitated ... undesirable on scale." (Results and Discussion)
3. "Conducting the workup with an aqueous solution of (NH₄)₂HPO₄ ... was found to be optimal. Both rapid phase splits and minimal product loss were achieved. Additionally, no precipitated solids or rag layers were observed during the workup." (Results and Discussion – Table 5 entries 12–13)
4. "The aqueous (NH₄)₂HPO₄ solution is inexpensive and used as a fertilizer and a fire retardant." (Reference 18 note).
5. "The workup with THF/15 % Rochelle salt gave rag layers; the (NH₄)₂HPO₄ workup eliminated this problem." (Table 5).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of the methyl ester with NaOH occasionally generated solid sodium oxalate, which precipitated and interfered with phase separation and downstream purification.
Solution_Description: The base was switched from NaOH to KOH. Potassium oxalate has higher aqueous solubility, preventing solid formation and allowing a clean hydrolysis work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Solid sodium oxalate was occasionally formed in the reaction mixture ... the presence of these solids in the process stream was undesirable ... This issue was resolved by switching the base for the hydrolysis from NaOH to KOH because the resulting potassium oxalate has increased solubility in water, and therefore, no solids were observed during the hydrolysis." (Results and Discussion – Hydrolysis)
2. "The treatment of the rich organic stream from the acylation reaction with NaOH (1 N, 4.5 equiv) cleanly furnished the desired acid 2b in 3 h. However, solid sodium oxalate was occasionally formed..." (Experimental Section – Hydrolysis).
3. "After warming to 60–65 °C and acidified ... the slurry was filtered." (Experimental Section – Hydrolysis).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: During the DPPCl‑mediated amidation, the amount of diphenylphosphinic acid (DPPOH) in the isolated product varied widely (0.1–41 AP) and longer quench times caused large losses (up to 44 %) of product to the mother liquor.
Solution_Description: The quench was changed to an aqueous quench with no added base, and the DIPEA loading was optimized to 4.0 equiv (narrow 3.8–4.1 equiv). Later, a weaker base (N‑methylmorpholine, pKa 7.4) was employed, providing consistent low DPPOH (<1 AP) and minimal mother‑liquor loss (<5 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Entry 1 ... 2 h quench gave 90–92 % isolated yield with 0.1 AP DPPOH. Entry 2 ... 18 h quench gave 48 % isolated yield, 44 % mother‑liquid loss, but still 0.1 AP DPPOH." (Table 7)
2. "Using an aqueous quench with no additional base consistently provided low mother‑liquid loss and high isolated yields ... however, the amount of residual DPPOH was once again highly variable, with levels in the isolated product reaching as high as 41 AP." (Results and Discussion)
3. "The ideal base needed to be sufficiently weak ... N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) ... could use four to six equivalents of NMM and obtain consistent mother‑liquid losses of <5 % ... >98 % AP and <1 AP DPPOH observed." (Table 9 discussion)
4. "The optimal charge of DIPEA was 4.0 equiv, with a narrow acceptable range of 3.8–4.1 equiv to obtain amide 3 in both high purity and high yield." (Results and Discussion).
5. "The quench with NaOH caused high loss; removal of base from the quench eliminated the loss issue." (Table 7).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: When the DPPCl charge was performed rapidly or agitation was insufficient, a self‑condensation side reaction occurred, generating a red insoluble solid and reducing overall yield (as low as 58 % at 50 rpm).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The addition of DPPCl was slowed (30–60 min charge) and the reactor agitation was maintained at ≥250 rpm. This ensured that sufficient free piperazine was present to capture the activated intermediate and prevented the self‑condensation pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "When the agitation rate was reduced to 50 rpm, a sharp erosion in the isolated yield to 58 % was observed ... the yield could not be improved by increasing the agitation after the initial age..." (Results and Discussion – mixing study)
2. "The reaction was performed in the absence of the piperazine coupling partner 4, acid 2b was consumed, and a red, insoluble solid was isolated, further supporting the hypothesis that another molecule of the azaindole was reacting with the activated intermediate 11." (Results and Discussion – self‑condensation)
3. "Because the activated intermediate 11 does react rapidly with piperazine 4b, we could eliminate the undesired self‑condensation by charging DPPCl slowly over 2 h, which ensured that there was sufficient piperazine 4b available in solution." (Results and Discussion).
4. "The addition rate of DPPCl to the reaction mixture had to be carefully controlled due to the substantial exotherm that was encountered..." (Reference 26 note).
5. "Typical reaction conditions in a 1 L reactor with an agitation rate of 250–300 rpm gave the desired product in 95 % isolated yield." (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 6. Friedel–Crafts Acylation/Hydrolysis and Amidation
Problem_Description: Crystallization of amide 3 from an acetonitrile‑water slurry gave very fine particles (<20 µm), resulting in a filtration flux ≤100 L m⁻² h⁻¹, which was unsuitable for large‑scale isolation.
Solution_Description: The solvent composition was adjusted (increase water to 15 vol, reduce NMP to 14 vol), seeding was performed at 60 °C with a controlled relative supersaturation (~30 % RSS), and the hold time at 60 °C was set to 3 h. This produced larger crystals, restored flux to >1 000 L m⁻² h⁻¹, and maintained >99.8 % AP purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "The initial crystallization conditions ... resulted in a very low filtration flux of ≤100 L m⁻² h⁻¹. The reason for this was apparent from the small particle size of the isolated product, generally <20 µm." (Results and Discussion – Crystallization)
2. "Upon adjusting the solvent composition (NMP 15 vol, water 14 vol) and seeding after adding 2.5 vol of water at 60 °C, the relative supersaturation was reduced to 30 % and larger particles were observed." (Table 11 entry 2 discussion)
3. "A prolonged hold at 60 °C for 3 h enabled control of the particle size distribution and increased the rate of desaturation which minimized mother‑liquid losses." (Results and Discussion).
4. Table 11 shows entry 3 (NMP 17 vol, water 2.5 vol at seed, total water 12 vol, 3 h hold) giving a flux of 1 381 L m⁻² h⁻¹.
5. "The optimized conditions gave us excellent control over the particle size while maintaining product losses at <5 % and flux <100 L m⁻² h⁻¹... overall, the amidation process routinely provided amide 3 in 94 % yield with a purity of 99.8 AP." (Conclusion).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: The crystalline intermediate 2 (the parent API) exhibited very low solubility and needle‑like morphology, causing filtration to be extremely slow (more than two weeks for 26 kg on two parallel Nutsche filters).
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route was developed that avoided isolation of 2 altogether.  The process installs the pro‑drug on the late‑stage thioether intermediate (43) and proceeds directly to the final API, eliminating the problematic low‑solubility filtration step.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...due to its very low solubility and needle‑like morphology, the filtration of 2 was extremely slow; on 26 kg scale using two Nutsche filters in parallel the filtration required >2 weeks!” – Section 2.3.
“...to eliminate the problematic isolation of the parent API and synthesis of di‑t‑butyl‑(chloro‑methyl)‑phosphate, a second‑generation pro‑drug installation route was developed...” – Abstract and Conclusion.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: The nitration of 18 (derived from 2‑amino‑4‑picoline) was highly exothermic, presenting safety concerns and requiring careful temperature management.
Solution_Description: The addition of the nitrating agent was performed in a controlled fashion (rate‑controlled addition) while maintaining the reactor temperature between 10 °C and 20 °C to limit the heat released.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...highly exothermic nitration… led to pyridine 18 in good yield.” – Section 2.3.
“...the reaction was judged complete by HPLC… after an additional 8 h.” – Experimental details showing controlled addition and temperature ranges.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Copper contamination in intermediate 21 (>200 ppm) poisoned the downstream hydrogenation step, reducing catalyst activity.
Solution_Description: An aqueous NH₄Cl work‑up was implemented, consistently affording 21 with <200 ppm Cu without the need for recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “...high levels of copper in 21 led to poisoning in the downstream hydrogenation, we implemented an aqueous NH₄Cl workup to consistently afford 21 with <200 ppm of Cu without the need for recrystallization.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: The original hydrogenation employed Pt/C, an expensive catalyst, increasing material cost for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Pt/C was replaced with less expensive Pd/C; both high‑pressure and transfer‑hydrogenation processes were evaluated, with the high‑pressure Pd/C protocol giving improved yields (88 % vs 80 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “...we opted to investigate replacing Pt/C with less expensive Pd/C, as well as both high‑pressure and transfer‑hydrogenation processes… the high‑pressure process (1.8 bar) afforded improved isolated yields (88 % vs 80 %).” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: During the aqueous NH₄Cl phase‑separation step for 21, yields dropped from 80 % (<0 °C) to 50‑65 % (>10 °C) due to formation of hydrolysis by‑products, indicating temperature‑sensitive mixing behavior.
Solution_Description: The phase‑separation temperature was strictly controlled to stay below 0 °C, preserving the high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “...while we obtained 80 % yield when the temperature was kept <0 °C, the yield dropped to 50–65 % at >10 °C due to the formation of multiple hydrolysis byproducts.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Intermediate phosphate salt 26 was not free‑flowing after >12 h storage and residual POCl₃ caused oiling of product 11 upon MeOH addition.
Solution_Description: Residual POCl₃ was removed from 26 before work‑up; the reaction sequence was modified to combine demethylation and chlorination into a single step, minimizing the handling of the unstable phosphate salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “...it was critical to remove the residual POCl₃ in 26 to prevent oiling of 11 due to the formation of PO‑(OMe)₃ upon addition of MeOH to the wet cake of 26.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Triazole incorporation (conversion of 11 to 13) originally required a melt at 110‑120 °C, giving modest 55 % isolated yield and a mixture of isomers.
Solution_Description: The melt was replaced by refluxing 11 and 12 in 4‑methyl‑2‑pentanol (132‑145 °C), delivering 13 in ~65 % LCAP (51 % isolated) with >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “...to eliminate the previous melt conditions at 110–120 °C to install triazole 12, we first explored…addition in 4‑methyl‑2‑pentanol at reflux (132 °C). Under these conditions, 13 was generated in ~65 % LCAP, along with 22 % triazole isomers… final recrystallization gave 13 in 51 % yield with >99 % LCAP.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Direct conversion of 13 to 2 via acid chloride 29 gave only ~50 % conversion; 29 was highly moisture‑sensitive, and required >5 equiv oxalyl chloride, leading to difficult removal and low overall yield.
Solution_Description: The route was abandoned in favor of the original two‑step sequence (13 → 14 → 2), which afforded higher yields and operational robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “...only ~50 % conversion could be achieved using 29… 29 was highly moisture sensitive… we did achieve proof‑of‑concept (∼55 % yield) … this approach was not further explored.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: The t‑BuONO mediated nitration generated a large adiabatic temperature rise (≈27 °C) and gas evolution, posing safety risks.
Solution_Description: The nitration was performed at ≤20 °C with a controlled 7‑hour addition of t‑BuONO, limiting the heat evolution and keeping the reaction within safe temperature limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
“DSC supported the onset temperature following t‑BuONO addition = 181 °C, with the heat of reaction = 368 J/g. Data from RC1 calorimetry supported the adiabatic temperature rise during t‑BuONO addition = 27.1 °C, with gas evolution = 20.9 L/mol.” – Ref 37.
“...highly exothermic nitration... led to pyridine 18 in good yield.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Late‑stage pro‑drug installation required compound 16, whose synthesis had low overall yield (48 %) and depended on the difficult‑to‑source chloromethyl chlorosulfate.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route was designed that bypasses 16 entirely, using thioether intermediate 43 → chloromethyl derivative 44 → displacement with di‑t‑butyl potassium phosphate, thereby eliminating the low‑yielding and scarce reagent.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...to eliminate the problematic isolation of the parent API and synthesis of di‑t‑butyl‑(chloro‑methyl)‑phosphate, a second‑generation pro‑drug installation route was developed… involving conversion of a late‑stage common intermediate to an N(1)‑thioether derivative followed by chloromethylation….” – Abstract.
“...the synthesis of 16... was not optimized… 48 % in‑process yield… the low yield and sourcing issues prompted the development of a route that does not require 16.” – Section 2.3.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Compound 2 is highly static‑prone (volume resistivity > 10¹² Ω·cm) and has a low minimum ignition energy (<10 mJ), making it dangerous as a dust cloud.
Solution_Description: Special handling procedures were instituted: bonding, grounding, and avoidance of milling; equipment was grounded and antistatic measures applied.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to electrostatic hazards, the milling of 2 was not feasible. 2 is highly susceptible to the accumulation of static charge (volume resistivity > 10¹²) and has a low (<10 mJ) minimum ignition energy… Suitable bonding and grounding when handling this material should be provided.” – Ref 19.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Work‑up after alkylation to form 48 required five aqueous HCl washes, leading to difficult phase separations and emulsion formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑engineered to use acetonitrile as solvent with K₂CO₃ base, eliminating NMP and the Finkelstein step; phase separations became rapid and clean, reducing the number of washes needed.
Supporting_Evidence:
“...five aqueous washes were necessary to remove both the NMP and 49 prior to crystallization, and these phase separations were challenging due to the formation of emulsions.” – Section 2.3.
“...switching to K₂CO₃ eliminated the side reaction... also eliminated NMP, making washes rapid and clean.” – Ref 35.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: Genotoxic impurities (44, 52) formed during chlorination and phosphate displacement steps needed strict control to meet regulatory limits.
Solution_Description: A robust GTI monitoring and control strategy was implemented, keeping impurity levels well below the allowed thresholds (e.g., <0.2 ppm for 46/47, <0.3 ppm for 52, 4‑16 ppm for 44B).
Supporting_Evidence: “Both 44 and 52 were shown to be Ames positive and thus needed to be monitored as genotoxic impurities (GTI) … process embodied a robust GTI control strategy; affording 37 with <0.2 ppm 46 and 47, <0.3 ppm 52, and 4–16 ppm 44B.” – Section 2.4.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: The original nitration step using t‑BuONO gave modest yields (77 % for 9) and required a large excess of the nitrite source, increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: A sodium nitrite / in‑situ generated HCl protocol was developed, eliminating the formation of hydroxyl by‑product 20 and allowing comparable yields with fewer equivalents of nitrite.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Development efforts for the Sandmeyer methoxylation using t‑BuONO led to a significant yield improvement (44 % → 77 %); however, 15‑17 % of hydroxyl by‑product 20 was also generated… An alternative process using sodium nitrite and in situ generated HCl was developed. This modification eliminated the potential for formation of 20…” – Section 2.3.
“...it was necessary to control the addition rate of the nitrite source in both processes to prevent stalling due to decomposition of the resulting HNO₂.” – Ref 13.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: During the final chloromethylation of 43, the intermediate 44A was highly susceptible to hydrolysis, leading to stability issues.
Solution_Description: The free‑base form 44B (instead of the HCl salt 44A) was isolated, which was stable under storage conditions, avoiding hydrolysis problems.
Supporting_Evidence: “Stability studies of 44A demonstrated that the material was highly susceptible to hydrolysis. Fortunately, the corresponding freebase (44B) did not hydrolyze under identical storage conditions.” – Section 2.4.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 1. Evolution of Enabling Strategies
Problem_Description: During the telescoped conversion of 43 to 37, residual phase‑transfer catalyst (PTC) in the organic layer precipitated during crystallization, causing variability in product purity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Et₄NBr was selected as the optimal PTC based on its high conversion rate and low partitioning into the aqueous layer, minimizing precipitation and improving consistency.
Supporting_Evidence: “We observed that the reaction rate increased according to the nature of the counterion… Et₄NBr afforded the best combination of reaction rate and partitioning into the aqueous layer.” – Table 1 and Section 2.4.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: The lithium salt (compound 1) exhibited poor solubility in acetonitrile, which limited its reactivity in the alkylation step and gave low conversion (≈30 % RAP) when added without pre‑treatment.
Solution_Description: A small amount of water (0.5 wt %) was added to CH₃CN and Et₄NI together with 325‑mesh K₂CO₃. The water promoted in‑situ formation of the more soluble potassium salt of 1, dramatically increasing its solubility and reactivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “the addition of 0.5 wt % water to the acetonitrile resulted in both reactivity and regioselectivity comparable to the initial conditions utilizing potassium salt 6” (Table 1, entry 7); “The solubility of 1 in wet CH₃CN was greatly enhanced in the presence of K₂CO₃” (Figure 1); “the root cause for the observed rate enhancement was related to the solubility of 1” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: Cesium carbonate (Cs₂CO₃) and other granular bases formed difficult suspensions in NMP, causing poor mixing and low yields in the original alkylation protocol.
Solution_Description: Switch to milled 325‑mesh potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) together with tetra‑ethylammonium iodide (Et₄NI) eliminated the suspension problem and gave consistent ∼80 % in‑process yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “the challenge of Cs₂CO₃ suspension and the multiple washes necessary to remove the NMP… eliminated… by using K₂CO₃ and Et₄NI” (Table 1, entry 2); “325‑mesh K₂CO₃ and milled K₃PO₄ were uniquely effective… because of the significantly lower solubilities of Li₂CO₃ and Li₃PO₄ versus their potassium counterparts” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: Alkylating agent 2 (di‑tert‑butyl chloromethyl phosphate) decomposes under the reaction conditions, reducing overall conversion and generating side‑products.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed at 45 °C with a 3 h pre‑age of the Li‑salt/K₂CO₃/Et₄NI mixture before addition of 2, which both protected 2 from decomposition and improved conversion to >95 % RAP.
Supporting_Evidence: “increased stability of 2… allowed for a reduction in the equivalents from 1.7 to 1.3” (Table 1, entry 2); “implementing a 3 h age at 45 °C prior to the addition of 2… eliminated the observation of slow reaction rates” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: When 2 was added at ambient temperature without a pre‑age step, conversions were highly variable (up to 35 % RAP) across repeat runs.
Solution_Description: A controlled pre‑age (metathesis) of the Li‑salt mixture for 3 h at 45 °C before addition of 2 produced consistent conversions (<3.5 % RAP) in all trials.
Supporting_Evidence: “highly variable conversions (i.e., up to 35 % RAP) were observed… when 2 was added at ambient temperature” (Figure 4); “incorporating a 3 h pre‑age… led to <3.5 % RAP for all reactions” (Figure 4).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: The undesired N‑6 regio‑isomer 4 co‑purified with product 3, and the presence of the genotoxic impurity 14 (chloroiodomethane adduct) required selective removal to meet API specifications.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An aqueous work‑up using NaHSO₄ (0.5 eq) with 5 wt % brine at 5 °C efficiently hydrolyzed 4 while leaving 3 intact; citric‑acid addition adjusted the pH to 7–8, reducing water usage and overall Vₘₐₓ.
Supporting_Evidence: “use of NaHSO₄ in combination with 20 wt % aqueous NaCl led to improved selectivity for the hydrolysis of 4… <1 % hydrolysis of 3” (Table 3, entry 6); “addition of 0.4 eq citric acid… adjusted pH from 11 to 7–8 and led to complete dissolution of the salts” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: The original aqueous work‑up required 34 L kg⁻¹ of solvent (toluene + water) to dissolve inorganic salts, limiting batch size and causing 5–7 % product loss.
Solution_Description: By adding 0.4 eq citric‑acid monohydrate to the first water wash, the pH was lowered, allowing full salt dissolution with only 5 L kg⁻¹ water, reducing Vₘₐₓ to 25 L kg⁻¹ and increasing throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “after charging 10 L kg⁻¹ toluene, and only 5 L kg⁻¹ water… addition of 0.4 eq citric acid… reduced Vₘₐₓ from 34 to 25 L kg⁻¹” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: Product 3 is hydrolytically unstable; elevated temperatures during the final distillation caused ester hydrolysis and purity loss.
Solution_Description: The distillation was performed under 40 °C internal temperature (jacket ≤45 °C) to minimize hydrolysis of 3.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was important to keep the internal temperature <40 °C during this first stage in the distillation to minimize hydrolysis of 3” (ref 12).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 8. Installation of the Phosphonoxymethyl Prodrug Moiety
Problem_Description: Use of IPAc as the organic phase in the work‑up caused solvent hydrolysis, generating impurity 18 and required multiple crystallization attempts.
Solution_Description: IPAc was replaced by toluene; maintaining >25 vol % CH₃CN in the toluene/CH₃CN/water mixture prevented precipitation of 3 and eliminated the hydrolysis pathway that formed 18.
Supporting_Evidence: “IPAc was replaced by toluene… solubility of 3 in toluene was only 0.80 wt %… but in 35 vol % wet CH₃CN in toluene the solubility was 18.5 wt %” (Figure 7); “the IPAc was susceptible to hydrolysis and led to increased levels of the mixed i‑Pr/t‑Bu impurity 18” (text).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: In the acetone‑water (3:2 v/v) system the BMS‑663068‑acid has limited solubility (≈22 mg mL⁻¹). As the reaction proceeds the product precipitates, forming a thick slurry that also entrains the intermediate (compound 2). This slurry‑to‑slurry transformation makes the reaction mass‑transfer‑limited, creates batch‑to‑batch variability (reaction end‑point varies 2–5 h) and stretches the overall reaction time to 9–12 h.
Solution_Description: Switch to an AcOH‑water (2:1 v/v) solvent system. Acetic acid (Class 3) solubilizes the acid (∼30 mg mL⁻¹) and, at 2:1 AcOH‑water, the solubility exceeds 400 mg mL⁻¹, producing a homogeneous reaction mixture that eliminates slurry formation and gives consistent conversion in 10–11 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “the reaction stream evolved from an initial slurry … began to precipitate due to its limited solubility (22 mg mL⁻¹), forming a thick slurry.”
2. “When precipitation … occurred, intermediate 2 … precipitated as well … This variability resulted in a large time window (9–12 h) required to complete the solvolysis reaction, since the consumption of intermediate 2 became mass‑transfer limited.”
3. “Acetic acid … solubilized BMS‑663068‑acid (∼30 mg mL⁻¹)… The solubility of 3 dramatically increased … >400 mg mL⁻¹ at a 2:1 AcOH–water ratio.”
4. “The homogeneous reaction conditions consistently reached completion within 10–11 h …”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The solvolysis generates ∼0.5 equiv of isobutylene, leading to off‑gassing rates up to 0.2 L min⁻¹ kg⁻¹. Although a thermal oxidizer can treat the emissions, the high rate and quantity limit process flexibility and raise safety/environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: The AcOH‑water solvent reduces the amount of isobutylene formed (≈30 % lower) and lowers the peak off‑gas rate. In conjunction, a thermal oxidizer is used at pilot scale to destroy the remaining isobutylene.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The remainder (∼0.5 equiv) formed isobutylene and resulted in off‑gassing from the process stream.”
2. “Maximum off‑gassing rate of 0.2 L‑min‑kg⁻¹ achieved within 15 min … the amount and maximum rate … were within the capability of the thermal oxidizer … but a further reduction … was desirable.”
3. “The maximum rate of off‑gassing was reduced, and the quantity of isobutylene generated decreased by ∼30 %.”
4. “Acetic acid … allowed the transformation … at lower temperature (35 °C) …”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: Under the original conditions (50 °C, acetone‑water) water‑mediated hydrolysis of the benzoyl amide and methylene‑phosphate generates impurities 5 and 6; a zwitterionic impurity 7 forms via intramolecular tert‑butyl transfer. These impurities have very low solubilities (<0.01 mg mL⁻¹) and cannot be adequately purged during crystallization, compromising API purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature to 35 °C in the AcOH‑water system (still homogeneous) suppresses hydrolytic pathways, reducing impurity 5 and 6 by ~50 % and increasing the solubility of impurity 7 (0.4 mg mL⁻¹) so it can be purged during crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Hydrolysis of the benzoyl amide … forming impurity 5.”
2. “Hydrolysis of the methylene phosphate … impurity 6.”
3. “Impurity 7 … low solubility (0.01 mg mL⁻¹) … could not be adequately purged.”
4. “The lower reaction temperature enabled by the addition of acetic acid improved control of these impurities.”
5. “Impurity 5 and 6 reduced by 50 % due to decreased temperature.”
6. “Impurity 7 solubility increased to 0.4 mg mL⁻¹ … allowing purge in the crystallization step.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The initial drying operation (full vacuum, 50 °C, intermittent agitation) required 45–55 h to achieve residual‑solvent levels <0.5 wt % and produced a low bulk density (<0.10 g mL⁻¹) because the needle‑like crystals were highly susceptible to attrition during prolonged agitation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Raising the dryer jacket temperature to 70 °C halved the drying time, while switching to continuous agitation (instead of intermittent) increased bulk density (>0.18 g mL⁻¹) and maintained solvent removal performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “drying required ∼30 h … increased to ∼50 h … to ensure removal of water, acetic acid, and acetone.”
2. “Needle‑like morphology … highly susceptible to particle attrition during agitated drying.”
3. “Increasing the jacket temperature from 50 °C to 70 °C reduced the drying time by roughly half.”
4. “Continuous agitation … increased bulk density to >0.18 g mL⁻¹.”
5. “Target bulk density of ≥0.15 g mL⁻¹ … achieved in more than 30 batches using the defined drying agitation protocol.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the TRIS salt yields brittle needle crystals with high specific surface area (SSA). Higher relative supersaturation (RSS) and higher seed load increase SSA, leading to poor flow and low bulk density. Seed‑property variability further exacerbates SSA differences between batches.
Solution_Description: A design‑of‑experiments study identified RSS as the dominant factor; controlling RSS, seed load, and applying a minimum seed‑age of 2 h (allowing crystal ripening) consistently reduced SSA. The optimized protocol yields a product with lower SSA and acceptable bulk density.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Higher RSS and seed load increase the specific surface area of the isolated product.”
2. “Longer seed age times resulted in lower surface areas … across a wide range of RSS.”
3. “DOE confirmed that RSS was the most significant factor, and also identified the seed age time as an important factor.”
4. “A seed age of at least 2 h was appropriate to achieve the maximum reduction in surface area.”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 9. Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient Process Development and Powder Properties
Problem_Description: Wet milling was introduced to shorten needle length and improve bulk density, but the milled particles regrew to long needles within 72 h, negating the benefit and adding an extra operation that was difficult to control at scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The wet‑milling step was removed entirely. Bulk density control was instead achieved by using continuous agitation during drying, which provides sufficient attrition to raise density without the regrowth issue.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Wet milling reduced needle length … but particles regrew to long needles after 72 h.”
2. “The wet mill was removed from the process and the focus shifted to using the filter dryer agitation mode to control final powder bulk density.”
3. “Continuous agitation increased bulk density to >0.18 g mL⁻¹.”
4. “The variability in bulk density is similar regardless of whether wet milling was applied … supporting the decision to remove wet milling.”

Paper Title: Continuous Microflow Synthesis of Fuel Precursors from Platform Molecules Catalyzed by 1,5,7-Triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene
Problem_Description: Mineral and solid base catalysts exhibit poor activity for the aldol condensation of furfural with long‑chain aliphatic carbonyl compounds, preventing formation of the desired double‑condensation product.
Solution_Description: Replace the mineral/solid bases with 1,5,7‑triazabicyclo[4.4.0]‑dec‑5‑ene (TBD), a highly efficient and recyclable organic‑base catalyst that gives >90 % yield of the double‑condensation product under the same conditions.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “mineral base and solid base catalysts showed poor activity for this reaction, and double condensation product … cannot be obtained.”
2. “These catalysts showed poor catalytic performance for the reaction with long‑chain aliphatic carbonyl compounds.”
3. “TBD was found to be a recyclable and highly efficient organic base catalyst for the aldol condensation… 93 % yield in 2 h.”
4. “Under the situation of using 10 mol % TBD … the desired double condensation product … has 93 % yield in 2 h.”

Paper Title: Continuous Microflow Synthesis of Fuel Precursors from Platform Molecules Catalyzed by 1,5,7-Triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene
Problem_Description: Using DBU as the catalyst requires >30 mol % loading, a 10 h reaction time, and the homogeneous catalyst is difficult to separate from the reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: Switch to TBD, which operates at 10 mol % loading, gives high conversion in ≤2 h, and can be recovered by simple aqueous extraction because it is water‑soluble, enabling catalyst recycling.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “a high dosage of catalyst (>30 mol %) had to be used to obtain double condensation… long reaction time… difficult to separate this homogeneous catalyst.”
2. “TBD was found to be a recyclable and highly efficient organic base catalyst… 10 mol % TBD gave 93 % yield in 2 h.”
3. “TBD is completely soluble in water, but has poor solubility in EtOAc… using EtOAc to extract the mixture resulted in the separation between the condensation products and the catalyst TBD.”

Paper Title: Continuous Microflow Synthesis of Fuel Precursors from Platform Molecules Catalyzed by 1,5,7-Triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene
Problem_Description: In the micro‑flow system, THF, EtOAc and CH₂Cl₂ fail because TBD is poorly soluble in EtOAc and the double‑aldol product precipitates in THF or CH₂Cl₂, leading to solid formation that can block the slit‑plate mixer and tubing reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopt a MeOH/H₂O (1:1, v/v) co‑solvent system that dissolves furfural, the ketone, the double‑aldol product and TBD, eliminates solid formation, and suppresses methanol‑ether side reactions.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “using THF, EtOAc, or CH₂Cl₂ … was not successful … due to the poor solubility of TBD in EtOAc, and the poor solubility of double aldol condensation product in CH₂Cl₂ or THF.”
2. “One of the chief concerns in the fluidic experiment is the formation of solids in the reactor, which could block the slit plate mixer and tubing reactor.”
3. “MeOH meets the above conditions… however, methanol could react… After further screening, a mixed solvent of methanol and water inhibited this side reaction effectively.”
4. “MeOH–H₂O (v/v = 1:1) … the desired double condensation product … was obtained in 87 % yield.”

Paper Title: Continuous Microflow Synthesis of Fuel Precursors from Platform Molecules Catalyzed by 1,5,7-Triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene
Problem_Description: Batch reactions suffer from side‑reactions (etherification, resinification, Cannizzaro, Michael addition) that force the use of excess furfural (≥2.5 equiv) to obtain acceptable yields of the double‑condensation product.
Solution_Description: Implement the continuous micro‑flow system, which under rapid mixing and efficient heat removal suppresses the side‑reactions, allowing the use of the stoichiometric furfural ratio (2 equiv) without loss of yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “side reactions such as resinification of furfural, Cannizzaro reaction, and Michael addition … may happen during the reaction. To obtain the double condensation product … an overdose of furfural (at least 2.5 equiv) has to be used.”
2. “These side reactions were effectively suppressed under the present flow system, and the dosage of furfural could be decreased to its theoretical ratio (2 equiv) without loss of yield of 1b.”
3. “The flow technique … high mixing and heat transfer rates … the reaction time … reduced dramatically … only needs 20 min … about 6‑fold compared to the batch system.”

Paper Title: Continuous Microflow Synthesis of Fuel Precursors from Platform Molecules Catalyzed by 1,5,7-Triazabicyclo[4.4.0]dec-5-ene
Problem_Description: When using longer‑chain aliphatic carbonyl substrates (e.g., 2‑hexanone), the aldol condensation conversion decreases because steric hindrance hampers the enolate attack on the carbonyl partner.
Solution_Description: The article notes the trend but does not provide a definitive remedy; further optimization (e.g., higher temperature, alternative catalysts, or modified residence time) would be required.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “For aliphatic straight‑chain compounds, the reaction reactivity decreased with the increase of carbon chain length… steric effect: the longer alkyl side chain may prevent the carbonyl donor to attack enol and hence reduce the reaction efficiency.”

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: Batch ortho‑lithiation must be performed at –70 °C to avoid fast side‑reactions and uncontrolled exotherms; the highly reactive n‑BuLi and the large adiabatic temperature rise (>55 °C) pose severe safety risks and cause decomposition of the organolithium reagent if mixing is insufficient. Poor mixing (low agitation) also leads to low overall conversion and high impurity formation, while the need for cryogenic cooling makes the process costly and difficult to scale. In flow reactors, precipitation of lithium salts can clog micro‑channels, and the limited syringe volume restricts run time, causing long‑duration experiments for low‑throughput operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved from a batch stirred‑tank reactor to continuous‑flow T‑reactor and spinning‑disc reactor (NEW ROUTE) operating at ambient temperature (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION) to eliminate cryogenic cooling and its associated safety and cost issues. High‑speed impinging T‑mixers and the thin‑film flow on the SDR provide rapid micromixing (MASS TRANSFER, MIXING AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL), dramatically shortening residence time (< 1 s) and suppressing exothermic hot‑spots. DMF was added at a controlled, slower rate or in excess (ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION, STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE) to ensure homogeneous mixing in Step 2 and avoid side‑product formation. The T‑reactor was built from inexpensive PTFE tubing and T‑mixers (REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS) and operated with a silicone‑oil bath that absorbs heat (OTHER CONDITION CHANGE). Multiple T‑reactors in parallel were proposed to mitigate channel clogging, and the SDR’s free‑surface film reduces the risk of blockage (REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Ortho‑lithiation is typically conducted in batch mode under cryogenic temperatures (−78 to −40 °C) to minimize the side reactions arising from the highly reactive organolithium intermediates… The challenges of safely handling both the highly reactive chemicals and a highly energetic reaction in scaled‑up operations constitute a major disadvantage of such batch processes.”

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: In the batch STR, low agitation speeds (50–100 rpm) caused poor mixing, leading to localized high n‑BuLi concentrations, increased decomposition of n‑BuLi in THF, and consequently low overall conversion and product yield (7 % yield at 50 rpm).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the impeller speed up to 400 rpm raised the power dissipation to 0.053 W kg⁻¹, improving mixing and raising conversion to 99 % (Table 2). In flow reactors, the use of T‑mixers and higher Reynolds numbers (Re > 2400) created turbulent flow, providing homogeneous mixing and higher yields (up to 99 %). The DMF addition rate was also lowered to the “usual dosing rate (2 mmol min⁻¹)”, which prevented inhomogeneous mixing and side‑product formation (Table 3).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Mixing is also very important for ortho‑lithiation which is a fast reaction… Poor mixing not only led to an increase in impurities but also lower overall conversion.” (Sec 3.1.2)

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: n‑BuLi rapidly decomposes in THF if not well‑mixed, especially at higher temperatures, and its uncontrolled presence can lead to violent side reactions and safety hazards.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Rapid micromixing in the T‑reactor (mixing times 0.02–0.125 s) and the SDR (micromixing times 0.02–0.125 s) limits the time n‑BuLi is exposed to THF alone, preventing its decomposition. The controlled, staged addition of n‑BuLi after the amide stream (order of addition) ensures that n‑BuLi meets the substrate immediately, minimizing its residence in THF. Although not explicitly pH‑controlled, the use of an inert argon blanket maintains a non‑protic environment, reducing the risk of quenching by water.
Supporting_Evidence: • “n‑BuLi tends to decompose or get consumed in the reaction with THF when n‑BuLi is not well‑mixed.” (Sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: When DMF is added too fast (one‑shot dosing), poor mixing in Step 2 creates hotspots and leads to incomplete quenching of the lithiated intermediate, resulting in lower conversion (63 % overall) and higher impurity (33 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The DMF addition rate was reduced to the “usual dosing rate (2 mmol min⁻¹)”, which provided homogeneous mixing and increased overall conversion to 99 % with only 3 % impurity (Table 3). In the T‑reactor, the head‑on mixing in the second T‑mixer ensures that the DMF stream rapidly contacts the reaction mixture, effectively eliminating local concentration gradients.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The high charging rate of DMF might have caused inhomogeneous mixing and hotspot formation… This explains the lower overall conversion of amide 1 at fast DMF dosing rate.” (Sec 3.1.3)

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: Cryogenic cooling for the batch STR requires an elaborate cascade refrigeration system, increasing capital cost (CAPEX = 48 USD kg⁻¹) and operating cost (OPEX = 456 USD kg⁻¹). Additionally, the batch process operates only 50 % of the year due to cooling‑system limitations.
Solution_Description: Switching to ambient‑temperature flow processes (T‑reactor and SDR) eliminates the need for the cascade refrigeration system, cutting CAPEX to 31 USD kg⁻¹ (T‑reactor) and OPEX to 406 USD kg⁻¹, while enabling 100 % operation time. The T‑reactor was assembled in‑house from inexpensive PTFE tubing, dramatically lowering equipment cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The conventional method is to operate the reaction at −70 °C… The cryogenic cooling… is a costly requirement.” (Abstract)

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: Enclosed micro‑channels in the T‑reactor are prone to clogging from lithium‑salt precipitation over extended runs, which could halt production and require costly replacement of the reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors propose parallel T‑reactors that can be switched when pressure build‑up is sensed, allowing rapid replacement of clogged units (REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS). The low‑cost PTFE T‑mixers and tubing make the reactors inexpensive to replace. Additionally, operating at higher flow rates reduces residence time of lithium salts, lowering the probability of precipitation (MASS TRANSFER AND MIXING).
Supporting_Evidence: • “One possible option to get around this problem is to build in several T‑reactors that can be easily switched to another when pressure build up is sensed. The clogged T‑reactors can then be disposed and replaced swiftly as the T‑mixers and tubes are relatively cheap.” (Sec 3.4)

Paper Title: Intensification of Continuous Ortho-Lithiation at Ambient ConditionsProcess Understanding and Assessment of Sustainability Benefits
Problem_Description: In the SDR, the free‑surface film creates a vapor space where volatile butane can accumulate; if inert‑gas supply fails, flammable vapors could build up, posing an explosion risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A secondary inert‑gas (nitrogen) supply is recommended to back‑up the primary argon system, providing continuous dilution of vapors. The disc’s rapid film turnover and small volume limit the amount of vapor that can accumulate, reducing the severity of any leak. Operating without back‑pressure also prevents pressure spikes that could force vapors out of the reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: • “If there was failure in the inert gas supply or insufficient inert gas to dilute the organic vapor, there would be an accumulation of flammable vapor in the SDR vapor space. This risk can be mitigated by setting up an alternative inert gas supply which can be placed in operation if failure in primary inert supply was detected.” (Sec 3.5)

Paper Title: Use of a Polymer Additive To Enhance Impurity Rejection in the Crystallization of a Pharmaceutical Compound
Problem_Description: An impurity (Impurity D) formed during a pilot‑plant Sonogashira coupling at 3.5 area % – far above the regulatory limit of 0.1 % – and could not be removed by the originally planned crystallization of Intermediate C. The impurity’s lower equilibrium solubility caused it to nucleate and crystallize before the desired product, compromising impurity rejection and reducing usable product.
Solution_Description: A low‑level, non‑adsorbing polymer additive (copovidone, 3 % w/w) was introduced into the antisolvent crystallization.
