The polymer raised the solubility of Impurity D (≈2‑fold) and increased its nucleation energy barrier, thereby delaying its crystallization for >40 h while allowing Intermediate C to crystallize.  The process was implemented as an antisolvent‑crystallization route (distill to 6 mL g⁻¹ THF, add 24 mL g⁻¹ i‑PrOH) at 0 °C, with a 2‑hour, temperature‑controlled antisolvent addition to keep the slurry cold.  The polymer loading (stoichiometry) was optimized to ≥1.5 % (selected 3 %) to achieve <0.2 % impurity after a 16‑h hold.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Impurity D … formed at a level of 3.5 area % … could not be adequately rejected using conventional crystallization processes.” (sec 1)

Paper Title: Use of a Polymer Additive To Enhance Impurity Rejection in the Crystallization of a Pharmaceutical Compound
Problem_Description: When hydroxypropyl‑methyl‑cellulose (HPMC) was added as a polymer additive, the crystallization mixture became highly viscous and the isolated solids were sticky and difficult to dry, creating handling and filtration problems.
Solution_Description: The HPMC additive was replaced by copovidone (Kollidon VA 64), which dissolved well in the solvents and caused no noticeable change in mixture viscosity or solid handling.  This change eliminated the mixing issue while preserving the impurity‑rejection benefit.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The addition of HPMC to the product solution caused the solution to become viscous and the isolated solids to be sticky and difficult to dry.” (sec 3.1.2)

Paper Title: Use of a Polymer Additive To Enhance Impurity Rejection in the Crystallization of a Pharmaceutical Compound
Problem_Description: Impurity D began to crystallize within a few hours after antisolvent addition, limiting the available time window for filtration; a longer hold was needed to allow the product to fully desupersaturate without impurity precipitation, yet the original process could not sustain such a delay.
Solution_Description: The crystallization temperature was lowered to 0 °C and the antisolvent addition was stretched to ~2 h, which slowed the overall crystallization kinetics and extended the induction period for Impurity D to >40 h.  The final slurry concentration (6 mL g⁻¹ THF) was retained to keep product supersaturation high enough for >80 % yield while still permitting the longer residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We further improved the yield … by reducing the crystallization and isolation temperature to 0 °C … without adversely impacting the rejection of Impurity D.” (sec 3.1.3)

Paper Title: Use of a Polymer Additive To Enhance Impurity Rejection in the Crystallization of a Pharmaceutical Compound
Problem_Description: Residual copovidone remained in the isolated Intermediate C (~0.5 % w/w), which would be undesirable for a pharmaceutical intermediate and required an extra processing step.
Solution_Description: A reslurry step was introduced: the isolated product was suspended in i‑PrOH at 60 °C for 2 h, then cooled to 20 °C and filtered.  i‑PrOH dissolves copovidone but has very low solubility for Intermediate C, allowing polymer removal to <0.1 % w/w with negligible product loss.
Supporting_Evidence: • “To further reduce the residual polymer content, we introduced a reslurry process … The resultant product … contained less than 0.1 %w/w copovidone … The yield loss … was negligible.” (sec 3.1.3)

Paper Title: Use of a Polymer Additive To Enhance Impurity Rejection in the Crystallization of a Pharmaceutical Compound
Problem_Description: The initial screening of >60 solvent/antisolvent combinations revealed that THF was the only solvent capable of providing reasonable solubility for Intermediate C, limiting the flexibility of solvent choice and potentially increasing reliance on a single, relatively expensive solvent.
Solution_Description: Rather than seeking an alternative primary solvent, the process was redesigned to use THF as the starting solvent and apply antisolvent addition (i‑PrOH) to induce crystallization, thereby leveraging the unique solubility profile while avoiding the need for costly solvent swaps.
Supporting_Evidence: • “THF was unique in affording reasonable solubility of Intermediate C, and alternative solvent choices for readily solubilizing the product were not available.” (sec 3.1)

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Separation of the trans‑ and cis‑sulfoxide isomers by preparative HPLC was deemed impractical for scale‑up, limiting the amount of material that could be obtained for drug‑candidate evaluation.
Solution_Description: A stereoselective oxidation of the Ns,Boc‑protected substrate (Ns,Boc‑2c) with Oxone was developed, delivering the trans‑sulfoxide as the major product and eliminating the need for HPLC separation.
Supporting_Evidence: “In many cases, the sulfoxides are prepared by separating a mixture of isomeric sulfoxides by HPLC, which would not be a suitable or practical synthesis approach to obtain the requisite quantity of a drug candidate required for its further evaluation and development.”; “Oxone gave rise to trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c in excellent yield and with good selectivity.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Oxidation with NaIO₄ (and later with H₂O₂, MMPP, CHPO) gave only moderate conversions (39–77 %) and poor trans‑selectivity, with cis‑isomers predominating for several protected substrates.
Solution_Description: Switching to Oxone as the oxidant (0.55–1.1 eq.) and performing the reaction at 0 – 10 °C dramatically increased conversion (up to 98 %) and the trans‑/cis‑ratio (up to 92/8), providing a robust and scalable oxidation protocol.
Supporting_Evidence: “Treatment of 2a–2c with NaIO₄ in aqueous MeCN gave corresponding mixtures of isomeric sulfoxides … in 39–77 % yield… the oxidation reactions of Ns,Boc‑2c with various oxidizing reagents … aqueous H₂O₂, MMPP, CHPO afforded trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c in insufficient yield and/or with poor selectivity.”; “Oxone (0.55 equiv) … gave 97 % conversion and a 92/8 trans/cis ratio.”; “Oxone was added at 0 – 10 °C and the mixture was stirred at 0 – 10 °C for 2 h.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: The trans‑sulfoxide (trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c) and its cis‑counterpart had to be isolated by silica‑gel column chromatography, which is labor‑intensive and unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A crystallization/recrystallization protocol from acetonitrile/water was introduced, affording the trans‑sulfoxide in 81–90 % overall yield as a pure solid without any chromatographic step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Method A: Purification by Column Chromatography … gave trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c (62 %) and cis‑Ns,Boc‑4c (16 %).”; “Method B: Purification by crystallization … afforded trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c (81 %) as a white crystalline solid.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Oxidation with Oxone on kilogram scale is highly exothermic, posing safety and heat‑removal challenges.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was conducted at 0 – 10 °C with controlled addition of Oxone, using large‑scale cooling and vigorous stirring to manage the heat release and ensure uniform temperature throughout the reactor.
Supporting_Evidence: “To a stirred mixture of Ns,Boc‑2c … Oxone (80 g) was added at 0 – 10 °C. After stirring at 0 – 10 °C for 2 h …”; “A solution of Oxone … was added to a mixture … at 0 – 10 °C over 30 min …”

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Conversion of the trans‑sulfoxides to the corresponding cis‑isomers required separate de‑protection steps and gave low overall yields when performed sequentially.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot hydrogen‑chloride‑catalyzed isomerization was developed, which simultaneously promoted the sulfoxide isomerization and removed the Boc protecting group, delivering the cis‑sulfoxides in 57–76 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrogen chloride catalyzed the isomerization of the trans sulfoxides into the more stable cis isomers.”; “A mixture of trans‑3 and 2 M methanolic HCl solution … was stirred at 60 °C for 16 h … conversion and the ratio … were determined by ¹H NMR.”; “Runs 1 and 2 were successful, and recrystallization … yielded analytically pure cis‑Ns‑4a and cis‑4d‑HCl.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Stereoselective Syntheses of Isomerically Pure 4‑Aminotetrahydro‑2
Problem_Description: Oxidation outcomes varied dramatically with the nature of the protecting group; substrates bearing only Ns or Boc gave cis‑major products, whereas the dual Ns,Boc protecting group (Ns,Boc‑2c) afforded a trans‑major product, indicating steric effects were not fully understood.
Solution_Description: Adoption of the dual Ns,Boc protecting strategy (Ns,Boc‑2c) provided steric control that consistently favored formation of the trans‑sulfoxide under the same oxidation conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Ns,Boc‑2c yielded trans‑Ns,Boc‑3c as a major product (runs 4 and 5) under the same reaction conditions, suggesting that the tert‑butyl‑N‑(2‑nitrophenyl)sulfonyl carbamate group might provide steric control in the formation of sulfoxides.”; “In contrast, oxidation of 1, Ns‑2a, and Boc‑2b … the corresponding cis 4 products were the major ones obtained (runs 1–3).”

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: Ketalization of ketopyrrole 2 gave low conversion in non‑polar aprotic solvents because the substrate and intermediates were poorly soluble, leading to heterogeneous mixtures that stopped after ~50 % conversion.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in methanol with sulfuric acid and trimethyl‑orthoformate; MeOH both deprotects the N‑formyl group and forms the dimethyl ketal, giving a homogeneous mixture and high‑yielding conversion (≈88 % on 500 kg scale).
Supporting_Evidence: ["Ketalization of <bold>2</bold> ... was achieved most efficiently in MeOH with sulfuric acid and trimethyl‑orthoformate.", "The use of nonpolar aprotic solvents led to low conversions, even under azeotropic drying or strictly anhydrous conditions.", "We believe that MeOH serves multiple roles during this transformation by first facilitating deprotection ... and second via the formation of the corresponding dimethyl ketal.", "The reaction begins as a heterogeneous mixture and fully dissolves after ~50 % conversion of <bold>2</bold> to <bold>7</bold>.", "The low solubility of <bold>3</bold> in methanol resulted in a reactive crystallization that allowed for a facile direct isolation."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: When the Pictet–Spengler cyclization was scaled (>5 kg) impurity levels rose, isolated yield dropped to 65 % (vs 85 % lab scale), a TFA kicker charge was sometimes required for full conversion, and significant product crusting on reactor walls caused 8–15 % loss.
Solution_Description: Premixing paraformaldehyde (PFA) with TFA for at least 2 h dissolved polymeric PFA and gave a clear solution; the premixed solution was then added to substrate 3, eliminating the need for a TFA kicker, reducing impurity formation, and giving consistent yields (≈81 % on 480 kg scale) with <1 % crust loss.
Supporting_Evidence:
["This procedure enabled initial material deliveries but presented a number of issues on larger scales (i.e., >5 kg). First, increased levels of multiple impurities were observed on scale resulting in lower isolated yields (65% vs 85%).",
 "Finally, significant crusting of <bold>4</bold> on the reactor wall occurred during the crystallization leading to high product losses (8–15%).",
 "The use of tight purchase specifications during the sourcing of PFA was deemed impractical and costly, and therefore, we focused on options for a reproducible reaction performance regardless of the polymer molecular weight.",
 "Premixing the PFA and the TFA led to a hazy or clear solution due to the reactive dissolution of the polymeric material.",
 "This solution was then subjected to <bold>3</bold>, resulting in a scale‑independent rapid transformation (<60 min) to form <bold>4</bold> in consistent yields with reduced levels of impurities and without the need for additional kicker charges of TFA."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: Different batches of paraformaldehyde (PFA) exhibited varying particle sizes and degrees of polymerization; high‑MW polymeric PFA was poorly soluble in DCM, slowing the Pictet–Spengler reaction and increasing impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Premixing PFA with TFA before addition to the reaction mixture allowed the polymeric material to dissolve, decoupling reaction performance from PFA physical properties and giving reproducible rates and yields regardless of PFA batch.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The rate of the desired transformation was affected by the low solubility of PFA in DCM as the reaction started out heterogeneous and turned homogeneous as it progressed.", "A cursory analysis of the data suggested that better yielding reactions correlated with faster conversion of the input <bold>3</bold>, which occurred when PFA with a smaller particle size was utilized.", "We determined that the more significant difference in performance arose from the variation in the molecular weight of polymeric PFA.", "No polymeric PFA was detected in solution for poorly performing lots of PFA.", "Premixing the PFA and the TFA led to a hazy or clear solution due to the reactive dissolution of the polymeric material."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: Product 4 was highly soluble in DCM, requiring a labor‑intensive solvent exchange with MTBE/IPAc to crystallize; during this exchange up to 15 % of product crusted on reactor surfaces, causing large yield losses.
Solution_Description: A solubility model was applied to reduce DCM volume (from 10 L/kg to 4 L/kg), achieve a supersaturation of 120 %, and use a single antisolvent (isopropanol) for seeding and crystallization. This eliminated the solvent‑exchange step, reduced crust loss to <1 % and gave 81 % yield with >99 % purity on 480 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["DCM served as an ideal solvent for the reaction; however, the high solubility of product <bold>4</bold> in DCM required a labor and volume-intensive solvent exchange with MTBE/IPAc (10:1 v/v) to achieve acceptable yields at the crystallization end point.", "more importantly, a large amount of product (∼15%) was lost to the reactor surface through crusting due to the large solubility swing during the solvent exchange.", "We developed and applied a solubility model ... which allowed for the maximization of the recovery of <bold>4</bold> while still maintaining acceptable solvent levels for production equipment.", "The application of these learnings resulted in the concentration of the DCM stream from 10 to 4 L/kg to achieve a relative supersaturation (C/C*) of 120%, followed by seeding and slow addition of a single antisolvent (isopropanol, IPA), which allowed for isolation of the product with only 8% loss to the filtrate.", "This dramatically simplified the procedure, reduced the waste generation, and reduced losses from crusting to <1%."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: At 50–60 °C the radical aromatization step caused rapid depletion of trimethyl‑orthoformate (TMOF) via methylation of methanesulfonic acid (MSA), compromising reagent availability and reaction robustness.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to 30 °C, and the loadings of MSA (>1.5 equiv) and TMOF (5 equiv) were increased to offset slow decomposition and maintain conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Initially, high temperatures were used (50–60 °C) to increase the rate of the reaction, but this depleted the TMOF via methylation of MSA.", "Table 2 indicates that significant consumption of TMOF occurs in MeOH with MSA at 50 °C, independent of the water content.", "We therefore reduced the reaction temperature to 30 °C to balance reagent stability with reaction rate.", "DOE experiments demonstrated that a more consistent conversion was observed with >1.5 equiv of MSA and a relatively high charge of TMOF (5 equiv) provided desirable robustness to combat exogenous water and reduce the effect of the slow decomposition of TMOF."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: Using oxygen or air as the radical initiator for the aromatization step posed safety concerns at scale and generated over‑oxidation by‑products that were difficult to purge.
Solution_Description: Cumene hydroperoxide (CHP) was selected as a safer, readily available radical initiator; it gave >95 % conversion with <0.5 % over‑oxidation by‑products and was used successfully on 200–345 kg batches.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The aromatization step is a radical‑mediated process that can be induced by oxygen or other radical initiators.", "Although the use of oxygen was efficient on the lab scale, its use for large‑scale production posed concerns regarding safety and reproducibility, as well as the formation of difficult to purge over‑oxidation byproducts.", "We thus chose the readily available cumene hydroperoxide (CHP) as an optimal alternative.", "Table 3, entry 10 — CHP — 95 % conversion, <0.5 % over‑oxidation by‑products.", "The CHP protocol has been demonstrated on several 200–345 kg scale batches in which >99 % conversion was consistently achieved."]

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 4. Synthesis of the 6‑Azaindole Core
Problem_Description: During work‑up of the final aromatization, acidic conditions could lead to product loss and generation of genotoxic methyl methanesulfonate impurity.
Solution_Description: Triethylamine was added to maintain pH > 8 throughout the crystallization, minimizing losses to the mother liquor; an aqueous sodium thiosulfate antisolvent was then used to precipitate the product and quench residual CHP.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We isolated azaindole <bold>5</bold> by first adding triethylamine to the MeOH solution to maintain a basic pH (>8) throughout the crystallization which minimized losses to the mother liquor.", "An aqueous solution of sodium thiosulfate was then added as antisolvent leading to the crystallization of the product and the reduction of any remaining CHP.", "The optimized process yielded <bold>5</bold> in 90–92% with excellent product quality."]

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: Traditional batch or flow reactors using pure O₂ are hazardous and provide poor O₂ mass‑transfer when only air is supplied, leading to low conversion of oxygen‑dependent photochemical reactions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A vortex reactor with a rapidly rotating inner cylinder generates Taylor vortices that create a large gas‑liquid interfacial area; the reactor draws air directly from the laboratory atmosphere, eliminating the need for pressurised O₂ and dramatically increasing O₂ dissolution.
Supporting_Evidence: The reactor uses a rapidly rotating cylinder to generate Taylor vortices for continuous flow thermal and photochemical reactions…The reactor offers an alternative to traditional setups as it efficiently draws in air from the lab without the need specifically to pressurize with oxygen…The rapid mixing generated by the vortices enables rapid mass transfer between the gas and the liquid phases allowing for a high efficiency dissolution of gases.

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: During the photo‑oxidation of α‑terpinene, rotation speeds above 3000 rpm increase O₂ availability but also promote over‑oxidation to p‑cymene, reducing the yield of the desired ascaridole.
Solution_Description: Doubling the Rose Bengal photosensitiser loading from 2 mol % to 4 mol % at 4000 rpm restores selectivity for singlet‑oxygen formation and suppresses the competing oxidation that forms p‑cymene.
Supporting_Evidence: Without any rotation, the yield of 2 was 35 %; this improved…up to 3000 rpm where the yield was 91 %…At 4000 rpm, when the concentration of Rose Bengal was doubled (to 4 mol %) the ratio of 2 to 3 improved from 3.5:1 (at 2 mol %) to 9:1 (at 4 mol %).

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: Photoredox hydroxylation of phenyl boronic acid gives substantial triphenylboroxine by‑product when O₂ availability is low (slow rotation), resulting in incomplete conversion to phenol.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Increasing the rotor speed to 4000 rpm raises the O₂ concentration in the reactor, suppressing trimer formation and delivering quantitative phenol.
Supporting_Evidence: At lower rotation speeds the conversion of 6 was incomplete and resulted in significant quantities of triphenylboroxine…as the rotational speed was increased from 1000 to 4000 rpm…and the formation of this trimeric by‑product was suppressed, and phenol (7) was formed as the major product.

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: The Ru(bpy)₃Cl₂ photosensitiser used in the artemisinin synthesis is poorly soluble in toluene, leading to low conversion of dihydroartemisinic acid.
Solution_Description: Switching to photosensitisers with better solubility in non‑polar media (9,10‑dicyanoanthracene or tetraphenylporphyrin) restores catalytic activity and raises the overall artemisinin yield.
Supporting_Evidence: When toluene was used…[Ru] had poor solubility…Switching the photosensitizer to 9,10‑dicyanoanthracene (DCA) afforded a remarkably clean … when tetraphenylporphyrin (TPP) was used…full conversion was observed, and a 45 % yield of artemisinin was obtained.

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: The Hock‑cleavage/oxidation step of the artemisinin route proceeds slowly in the polar THF/H₂O (3:2) solvent system, giving low overall conversion and requiring up to 24 h of stirring under O₂.
Solution_Description: Using non‑polar toluene as the reaction medium favours the enol tautomer of the peroxide intermediate, accelerating the second oxidation; additionally, operating at 25 °C (rather than 30 °C) further improves the TPP‑catalysed step, giving up to 50 % isolated artemisinin in a single pass.
Supporting_Evidence: When toluene was used as the reaction solvent, the yield of 8 increased to 20 %…When tetraphenylporphyrin (TPP) was used…At 25 °C the yield increased further to 50 %.

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: Prolonged irradiation of the artemisinin reaction mixture (≥6 h) leads to degradation of the product, causing the isolated yield to fall after a peak at 4 h.
Solution_Description: The process is performed as a single continuous pass (telescoped steps) with residence times limited to 2–4 h, minimising exposure to light and preventing product degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: When the material was recycled for a 4 h period, the yield of 8 peaked at 22 %, but after 6 h the yield began to fall suggesting product degradation was occurring under prolonged irradiation…the photo‑oxidation step could be completed in one pass through the reactor…

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: Room‑temperature Stahl aerobic oxidation of benzyl alcohol gives little conversion, limiting productivity.
Solution_Description: Raising the reactor temperature to 80 °C (using the jacketed reactor and recirculating chiller) increases the oxidation rate, affording 85 % isolated benzaldehyde.
Supporting_Evidence: At room temperature the reaction gave little conversion, but increasing the temperature enhanced the conversion. At 80 °C the product was obtained in a 85 % yield directly from the reactor.

Paper Title: Continuous Photo-Oxidation in a Vortex Reactor: Efficient Operations Using Air Drawn from the Laboratory
Problem_Description: Increasing the liquid flow rate (0.5 → 2 mL min⁻¹) reduces residence time and counteracts the benefits of higher rotation speeds, leading to similar low yields despite faster stirring.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimising the flow rate (e.g., maintaining 0.5 mL min⁻¹) ensures sufficient residence time for O₂ uptake, while high rotor speeds maintain vigorous mixing, delivering the highest yields.
Supporting_Evidence: Increasing the flow rate, hence decreasing the residence time in the reactor, led to a decrease in the yield of 1 at all rotation speeds…the higher upward flow rates have a greater or overriding effect on the vortices.

Paper Title: Potential Safety Hazards Associated with Using Acetonitrile and a Strong Aqueous Base
Problem_Description: Acetonitrile, when mixed with a strong aqueous base (NaOH), undergoes rapid base‑catalysed hydrolysis that releases heat and can self‑heat to the onset temperature of a secondary exothermic event, leading to a runaway reaction.
Solution_Description: The acetonitrile solvent was removed after the cyclisation step by a solvent‑exchange to 2‑methyl‑THF before the NaOH quench/de‑protection, eliminating the hydrolysis pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Acetonitrile … can be hydrolyzed in the presence of a strong aqueous base … which can propagate into a runaway reaction.” (Abstract)  
• “The sodium hydroxide quench and deprotection … has an ATR of 66 °C and a MTSR of 89 °C, which is above Tonset … This means that the reaction has the thermal potential to self‑heat to the onset temperature of the exothermic event.” (Results)  
• “The cyclization reaction proceeded in THF and 2‑methyl THF, but it was slow and resulted in unacceptably low yields and additional impurities.” (Discussion)  
• “After completion of the cyclization, a solvent exchange to 2‑methyl THF was performed to mitigate the process safety risk during the quench of TFAA and deprotection.” (Discussion)  
• “DSC testing of the post TFAA quenching and deprotection reaction mixtures using 2‑methyl THF … did not detect any exothermic event until ∼260 °C.” (Discussion)

Paper Title: Potential Safety Hazards Associated with Using Acetonitrile and a Strong Aqueous Base
Problem_Description: During the NaOH quench/de‑protection step, two large exothermic events (≈40 °C and ≈210 °C) were observed; the first occurs close to the reaction temperature, giving a Stoessel criticality Class 5 (high‑risk) and making scale‑up unsafe.
Solution_Description: Conduct the quench and de‑protection in 2‑methyl‑THF rather than acetonitrile; this raises the criticality index from Class 5 to Class 1 and removes the runaway hazard.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Two exothermic events were detected in the DSC … at 56 °C and near 265 °C … the first exothermic event was near the reaction temperature.” (Results)  
• “The NaOH quench and deprotection has an ATR of 66 °C and a MTSR of 89 °C … this falls into criticality Class 5.” (Results)  
• “DSC testing of the post TFAA quenching and deprotection reaction mixtures using 2‑methyl THF … did not detect any exothermic event until ∼260 °C.” (Discussion)  
• “The modified process … reduced the Stoessel criticality risk level from Class 5 … to Class 1.” (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Potential Safety Hazards Associated with Using Acetonitrile and a Strong Aqueous Base
Problem_Description: The original process required ~20 equiv of NaOH (≈0.33 equiv relative to acetonitrile) for quench and de‑protection; high base concentration lowers the hydrolysis onset temperature (≈57‑74 °C), increasing runaway risk while also using a large amount of reagent.
Solution_Description: Systematic reduction of NaOH equivalents was investigated; lowering NaOH to ≤0.025 equiv raised the exotherm detection temperature to >150 °C (when water is in excess), demonstrating that base stoichiometry directly influences safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In the cyclization reaction, approximately 20 equiv of NaOH … was used.” (Discussion)  
• Table 4 shows exothermic events at 57‑74 °C for NaOH ≥0.1 equiv, but only at 157 °C for NaOH = 0.025 equiv with 2 equiv water. (Table 4)  
• “The test results suggest that NaOH concentration could be used to reduce the hydrolysis rate… but only at concentrations well below the level required to perform the desired chemical transformation.” (Discussion)

Paper Title: Potential Safety Hazards Associated with Using Acetonitrile and a Strong Aqueous Base
Problem_Description: Strong bases (NaOH, KOH, LiOH) catalyse acetonitrile hydrolysis at 60‑72 °C, creating a low‑temperature exotherm; weaker bases raise the onset temperature but may not effect the required de‑protection.
Solution_Description: Screening of weaker bases and salts (e.g., K₃PO₄, Na₂CO₃, NH₃) showed that bases with pKa ≤ 9.3 did not generate observable heat, indicating that adjusting base strength/pH can mitigate the hazard.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When combined with strong bases … exothermic events were detected between 60 and 72 °C.” (Discussion)  
• Table 5 lists bases with their pKa and detection temperatures; K₃PO₄ (pKa = 12.4) shows an event at 112 °C, Na₂CO₃ (pKa = 10.3) at 137 °C, and NH₃ (pKa = 9.3) showed no detectable exotherm. (Table 5)  
• “With a pKa of 9.3 or below, heat generation due to hydrolysis of acetonitrile was not observed.” (Discussion)

Paper Title: Potential Safety Hazards Associated with Using Acetonitrile and a Strong Aqueous Base
Problem_Description: Attempting to run the cyclisation step in alternative solvents (THF, 2‑methyl‑THF) resulted in slow reaction rates, low isolated yields and additional impurities, making those solvents unsuitable for the cyclisation stage.
Solution_Description: Retain acetonitrile for the cyclisation step (where it gives high conversion) and perform a solvent exchange to 2‑methyl‑THF only after cyclisation, thereby preserving yield while eliminating the safety issue in the subsequent quench.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The option of removing acetonitrile was also explored. The cyclisation reaction proceeded in THF and 2‑methyl THF, but it was slow and resulted in unacceptably low yields and additional impurities.” (Discussion)  
• “To achieve a maximum yield … we decided to conduct the cyclisation in acetonitrile. After completion … a solvent exchange to 2‑methyl THF was performed … produced a quality product with comparable yield.” (Discussion)  
• Figure 12 shows DSC of the final process showing only minor exotherms, confirming the safety of the solvent‑switched route. (Discussion)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: The original batch‐manufacturing route relies on trimethylsilyl‑propyne (TMS‑propyne) as a surrogate for propyne and requires the use of TBAF as an additive and a high (30 mol %) loading of CuI.  This makes the process expensive, involves a hazardous liquid surrogate and an overnight reflux, giving only 66 % isolated yield of the key intermediate.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the TMS‑propyne/TBAF batch protocol with a continuous‑flow Sonogashira coupling that uses propyne gas directly (cheaper and more atom‑efficient) and reduces the CuI loading to 10 mol %.  The process is run at 160 °C for 10 min residence time, eliminating the overnight step and the need for TBAF.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Instead of the currently used batch manufacturing process for this intermediate that utilizes TMS‑propyne as reagent, we herein demonstrate the safe utilization of propyne gas, as a cheaper and more atom efficient reagent, using an intensified continuous‑flow protocol under homogeneous conditions." (Abstract)  
"The batch manufacturing process for the Pd‑catalyzed Sonogashira cross‑coupling reaction shown in Scheme 1 involves heating at reflux overnight to proceed to >99 % conversion and typically affords approximately 80 % of the desired product … and 66 % yield.\n The loading of the Cu co‑catalyst was reduced from 30 to 10 mol % …" (Introduction)  
"The concentration of CuI was decreased from 30 to 10 mol % to reduce the loading to levels that are more acceptable for commercial manufacture." (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"The continuous‑flow process compares favorably with the batch process, which uses TMS‑propyne and requires overnight processing, TBAF as an additive, and a significantly higher loading of Cu co‑catalyst." (Abstract)  
"The optimal conditions for a single‑pass experiment were 1.6 equiv of propyne at 160 °C and 10 min residence time to give the mono product 3 in 85 % GC assay yield." (Flow Reactions – Final Optimization)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: Propyne is a gaseous, highly flammable reagent (bp −23.2 °C).  In batch microwave vessels a large portion of the gas remains in the headspace, giving low liquid‑phase concentration and only 10–15 % conversion even with excess propyne.  This creates safety hazards (large reactive gas inventory) and poor yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow reactor equipped with a back‑pressure regulator (3 bar) forces propyne into solution, eliminating headspace.  Propyne is first dissolved in an anhydrous NMP stock solution (predissolved) and fed continuously, which maintains constant concentration and pressure, increasing conversion to >80 % in a single pass.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Propyne is a gas at room temperature (bp −23.2 °C) and is highly hazardous due to its potential flammability and explosive properties…" (Introduction)  
"Much of the gas is in the headspace; therefore, the reactor needs to be pressurized to maximize the amount of gas in solution…" (Introduction)  
"The flow reactor was assembled… a back‑pressure regulator (BPR) at 3 bar… The BPR was submerged in a water bath heated at 90 °C to prevent solid accumulation." (Flow Reactions – Setup)  
"When the system was not under pressure (no BPR used), the conversion was significantly lower… indicating that the positive pressure was essential for maintaining propyne dissolution." (Table 4, entry 1 vs entry 2)  
"The propyne gas was introduced using the same method as described in the microwave section by predissolving in a stock solution (see above)." (Flow Reactions – Procedure)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: During continuous‑flow operation the Pd catalyst deactivates by oxidation of the triphenylphosphine (TPP) ligand to TPPO, causing the reaction to stall and lower product formation, especially at temperatures above 160 °C.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature was kept ≤ 160 °C and anhydrous NMP (99.5 % purity) was used; technical NMP (99 %) was further dried over 3 Å molecular sieves.  These measures suppress ligand oxidation and maintain catalyst activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The oxidation of the triphenylphosphine (TPP) ligand to triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO) was observed by GC‑MS, causing the reaction to stall. The ligand oxidation could be prevented by using anhydrous solvent and keeping the reaction temperature below 160 °C." (Flow Reactions)  
"Anhydrous NMP (99.5 % purity) from a commercial supplier provided the best catalyst stability (toward preventing ligand oxidation). The catalyst stability could also be improved by storing technical NMP (99 % purity) over 3 Å molecular sieves." (Flow Reactions)  
"Increasing the temperature appeared to have no effect … decomposition was observed at higher temperatures (entries 1 and 2)." (Table 5)  
"No loss due to decomposition or other side reactions were observed at 160 °C (entry 3). However, decomposition was observed at higher temperatures (entries 1 and 2)." (Flow Reactions – Final Optimization)  
"The reaction could be driven to completion by performing the reaction in two steps…" (Microwave Experiments – Propyne)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: Screening of solvents for the 1‑hexyne model reaction revealed that MTBE and toluene gave heterogeneous mixtures, THF/Me‑THF caused precipitation of amine salts, and MeCN led to Pd black formation, all of which lowered conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: Homogeneous reaction media were identified: DMF, DMA and NMP.  DMA gave the best conversion (85 %) and selectivity (15 % bis‑adduct) and was thus selected for further development.
Supporting_Evidence:
"MTBE and toluene produced a heterogeneous mixture before reaction and gave only moderate formation of the desired product (54 and 59 %)." (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"THF, Me‑THF, and DME provided homogeneous solutions before the reaction… precipitation of amine salts at the end of the reaction was observed. THF and Me‑THF showed the lowest reactivity… DME as solvent resulted in significant dehalogenation…" (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"Pd black formation was observed with MeCN, which is indicative of some catalyst deactivation." (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"Homogeneous mixtures throughout could be achieved with either DMF, DMA, or NMP, with DMA providing the best conversions and selectivities (2 % < 1 % 2, 85 % 4, 15 % 5)." (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"DMA as solvent resulted in significant dehalogenation to provide 3‑bromopyridine (13 %) as a minor product." (Table 1)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: In batch, full conversion of the aryl bromide could not be achieved even with 2 equiv of propyne; a two‑step addition (initial 2 eq then 0.64 eq after cooling) was required, making the process longer and less efficient.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow setup maintains constant pressure and dissolved propyne, allowing a single‑pass reaction (1.6 eq, 160 °C, 10 min) to reach 85 % assay yield.  For complete conversion, a recirculation step was employed where the reactor effluent is mixed with additional propyne (0.6 eq) and fresh catalyst, giving >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Even with 2 equiv of propyne the reaction could not be driven to full conversion. This is likely a consequence of the fact that more propyne (bp −23.2 °C) will be in the headspace…" (Microwave Experiments – Propyne)  
"The reaction could be driven to completion by performing the reaction in two steps… initially, 2 equiv of propyne was used; then, the reaction mixture was cooled… an additional 0.64 equiv of propyne was added, and the reaction was heated for another 10 min." (Table 2, entry 5a/5b)  
"When the system was not under pressure (no BPR used), the conversion was significantly lower… indicating that the positive pressure was essential for maintaining propyne dissolution." (Table 4, entry 1 vs 2)  
"The optimal conditions for a single‑pass experiment were 1.6 equiv of propyne at 160 °C and 10 min residence time to give the mono product 3 in 85 % GC assay yield (entry 3)." (Table 5)  
"Full substrate conversion could ultimately be achieved by recirculating the reaction mixture with additional propyne (0.6 equiv) and fresh catalyst (1.5 mol %)." (Table 6)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: The original batch process required a high (30 mol %) CuI loading, increasing material cost and potentially generating more metal waste, while also needing TBAF (expensive, hygroscopic, and fluoride‑containing).
Solution_Description: CuI loading was reduced from 30 mol % to 10 mol % without loss of conversion, and TBAF was completely eliminated from the continuous‑flow protocol, simplifying work‑up and lowering cost and safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The concentration of CuI was decreased from 30 to 10 mol % to reduce the loading to levels that are more acceptable for commercial manufacture." (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"We used TBAI instead of TBAF because it displayed better solubility…" (Microwave Experiments – 1‑Hexyne)  
"The loading of the Cu co‑catalyst was reduced from 30 to 10 mol %, giving additional cost and environmental improvements." (Conclusions)  
"No TBAF additive was required under these conditions. TBAF is expensive, difficult to handle, and causes potential accommodation issues for manufacture due to the presence of fluoride and its effect on borosilicate glass." (Conclusions)  
"The concentration of CuI was decreased from 30 to 10 mol % …" (Initial Continuous Flow Procedure)

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous-Flow Sonogashira Cross-Coupling Protocol using Propyne Gas under Process Intensified Conditions
Problem_Description: Scaling the microwave batch reaction proved problematic: increasing the reaction volume doubled the headspace, causing over‑pressure (≈30 bar) and temperature spikes to 194 °C, which introduced safety hazards and inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a continuous‑flow reactor (4 mL stainless‑steel coil, heated, with back‑pressure regulation).  The small channel dimensions provide efficient heat removal and precise residence‑time control, eliminating over‑pressure events and delivering reproducible conversions.
Supporting_Evidence:
"One of the limitations of microwave batch reactors is the difficultly associated with scaling this technology to production quantities… increasing the volume… significant over‑pressure (30 bar) and temperature rise (to 194 °C) were observed." (Microwave Experiments – Propyne)  
"The flow reactor was assembled consisting of a single syringe pump, a 2 mL injection loop, a heated 4 mL 316 stainless steel reactor… a back‑pressure regulator at 3 bar…" (Flow Reactions – Setup)  
"The small channel dimensions of continuous‑flow reactors provide a high surface‑to‑volume ratio, enabling the generated heat to be dissipated quickly…" (Introduction)  
"The flow process could be operated consistently over a period of 20 min… No buildup of pressure or pressure oscillations were observed for the long‑run flow reaction." (Results & Discussion)  
"Temperature appeared to have no effect… however, decomposition was observed at higher temperatures (entries 1 and 2)." (Table 5)

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: The legacy synthesis of thioamide 4 started from pyruvonitrile, a material that liberates toxic hydrogen cyanide on contact with water and requires highly toxic hydrogen‑sulfide gas; the raw material is difficult to store, transport and supply on scale, and the thioamide product is unstable, especially when concentrated.
Solution_Description: A new two‑step route was developed using the stable, commercially‑available 2,2‑diethoxypropionitrile (10) as the starting material, eliminating the need for pyruvonitrile and H₂S gas and providing a safer, more readily available feedstock.
Supporting_Evidence: "The previous route to thioamide 4 started from pyruvonitrile (9), a material that liberates hydrogen cyanide on contact with water…its manufacture, storage, and transport present challenges…the thioamide 4 is unstable, particularly when concentrated, and its manufacture uses hydrogen sulfide, a highly toxic…"; "Scheme B outlines a new route to thioamide 4 using 2,2‑diethoxypropionitrile (10), which is inherently more stable than pyruvonitrile (9), and there are no long‑term supply issues with this raw material."

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: Conversion of 10 to thioamide 11 gave poor yields with Na₂S or without acid (0 % yield) and stronger acids caused ketal hydrolysis of the substrate, leading to low conversion and impurity formation.
Solution_Description: Screening identified NaHS as the effective H₂S surrogate and imidazole‑HCl (pKa 7.0) or triethylammonium‑HCl (pKa 10.7) as suitable acids; the optimal combination (NaHS + Et₃N·HCl, 1 equiv acid) gave up to 76 % yield while avoiding ketal hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: "Entries 1–2 highlight the requirement for an acid in the formation of hydrogen sulfide…pyridine hydrochloride (entries 3–4) failed…imidazole hydrochloride…provided 69 % yield with NaHS (entry 6)…triethylamine hydrochloride…gave 76 % yield (entry 12)…stronger acids may lead to hydrolysis of the ketal in 10…"

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: At low solvent volumes the heterogeneous mixture contained a large amount of solid inorganic salts, leading to sluggish stirring, balling, and reaction times >40 h; increasing dilution slowed the reaction further.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A mixed THF/EtOH (6:2 v/v) co‑solvent was introduced, which solubilised NaHS/H₂S and prevented solid balling, dramatically accelerating the reaction (complete in 12 h) while maintaining high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "significant balling of the inorganics was observed…we therefore sought to improve the physical issues of suspending the solids by employing a hydrophilic cosolvent…We opted for ethanol…resulted in complete suspension of the solids, and no balling…serendipitously discovered that employing the mixed THF/EtOH solvent system significantly increased the rate of reaction, with the reaction being complete within 12 h (vs >40 h)."

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: Attempts to isolate thioamide 11 by antisolvent crystallisation from THF/heptane led to oiling out and partial decomposition of the product; narrow metastable zones made crystallisation difficult.
Solution_Description: Crystallisation from an ethanol/water antisolvent system (25–30 % EtOH) after solvent swap to 100 % ethanol gave a clean, isolated crystalline product (87 % yield) without decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: "Attempts to isolate 11 from heptane proved fruitless…oil‑out…In EtOH/water, the metastable zone widths were similarly narrow; however, no decomposition of the samples was observed…The addition of water (antisolvent) and cooling resulted in crystallization of 11 as a white crystalline solid."

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: Residual H₂S gas accumulated in the headspace of the sealed reactor, posing a toxic hazard and causing loss of reagent during sampling, while extended reaction times increased exposure risk.
Solution_Description: In‑situ FTIR monitoring (ReactIR) was employed to track conversion in real time, allowing the reaction to be stopped precisely at >97 % conversion, and the process was transferred from a parallel Biotage Endeavor to a glass hydrogenation vessel with pressure‑rating to safely vent H₂S through aqueous NaOH.
Supporting_Evidence: "In‑situ FTIR monitoring…enabled us to profile the reaction without having to sample the vessel content, which would have impacted the conversion due to loss of hydrogen sulfide…Reaction pressure 0.66 barg…vetted through an aqueous 6 M NaOH solution to safely quench the residual H₂S from the headspace."

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: Variability in the ketal de‑protection step (formation of 4) resulted from uncontrolled water content, leading to incomplete conversion or formation of ketal by‑products and reduced overall yields (63 % vs 83 %).
Solution_Description: A controlled acidic hydrolysis (10 mol % 4 M HCl, 1.41 mol % water) at 30 °C for 2 h gave >98 % conversion; excess acid was quenched with diisopropylethylamine before distillation, and trimethyl orthoformate was later used as a drying agent to obtain an anhydrous isopropanol solution of 4 without loss.
Supporting_Evidence: "The optimal conditions were 10 mol % of aqueous 4 M HCl…30 °C for 2 h…reached >98 % conversion (87 % solution yield)…we decided to quench the acid prior to the azeotropic distillation using diisopropylethylamine…trimethyl orthoformate (TMOF) can effectively dry the isopropanol solution without tedious distillations…the dry isopropanol solution was charged directly into the next stage…provided dihydroimidazole 5 with <2 % thione…In contrast, the cyclization using 4 derived from pyruvonitrile afforded 63 % isolated yield and 86 % purity.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of 2‑Oxopropanethioamide for the Manufacture of Lanabecestat: A New Route for Control, Robustness, and Operational Improvements
Problem_Description: The original process required stoichiometric zinc acetate as a H₂S scavenger and used large excesses of reagents to drive the imidothioic acid formation, increasing material cost and waste generation.
Solution_Description: The new process replaces zinc acetate with a catalytic amount of acid (Et₃N·HCl) and uses NaHS (1‑equiv acid per H₂S generated), reducing reagent consumption and overall material cost.

Problem_Description: Formation of toxic side‑products (MMS and DMS) during esterification when too much sulfuric acid is used, and the associated safety risk of dimethyl sulfate (genotoxic).
Solution_Description: The acid catalyst loading was reduced to 0.73 wt % (2 wt % H₂SO₄ in the feed) and the acid was added in a single portion below the liquid surface near the impeller for good micromixing, keeping the reaction temperature ≤ 65 °C (the maximum allowable temperature determined from kinetic studies).
Supporting_Evidence: “the larger amount of sulfuric acid used in esterification could raise the level of side products such as MMS and DMS… The low concentration of 2 wt % sulfuric acid used for esterification… had completely prevented the presence of MMS and DMS in all the final products.”; “The reaction temperature was below the maximum allowable limit of 65 °C as determined by reaction kinetics to avoid the runaway situation.”; “once fumaric acid was dissolved, to initiate the reaction, 0.96 mL of sulfuric acid… was fed into the stirred tank… for good micromixing.”

Paper Title: Round Granules of Dimethyl Fumarate by Three-in-One Intensified Process of Reaction, Crystallization, and Spherical Agglomeration in a Common Stirred Tank
Problem_Description: The esterification of fumaric acid with methanol is highly exothermic; if heat is not removed the temperature can exceed methanol’s boiling point, creating a runaway‑reaction hazard.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was limited to 65 °C (below methanol’s bp) and conducted in a water‑jacketed glass stirred tank with adequate agitation (600 rpm in the 0.5 L reactor, 350 rpm in the 10 L reactor). This ensured sufficient heat removal and avoided runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction temperature was below the maximum allowable limit of 65 °C as determined by reaction kinetics to avoid the runaway situation.”; “Since our stirred tank was water jacketed, equipped with a stirrer, and containing only a small volume of 100 mL methanol, it was safe to run the reaction to as high as 65 °C due to sufficient heat transfer and heat removal.”

Paper Title: Round Granules of Dimethyl Fumarate by Three-in-One Intensified Process of Reaction, Crystallization, and Spherical Agglomeration in a Common Stirred Tank
Problem_Description: Achieving high supersaturation and controlling crystal size during crystallization was difficult because dimethyl fumarate is poorly soluble in the methanol–water antisolvent mixture, leading to rapid nucleation and aggregation of primary crystals.
Solution_Description: Cold water (300 mL at 5 °C or 25 °C) was rapidly added as an antisolvent to the hot methanol solution, creating a large supersaturation jump; the mixture was then cooled (0.86 °C min⁻¹) to sustain nucleation. The antisolvent volume and temperature were tuned to obtain the desired primary‑crystal size distribution.
Supporting_Evidence: “A portion of 300 mL of cold water as an antisolvent at either 5 or 25 °C was rapidly fed into the same stirred tank… The cooling rate of 0.86 °C min⁻¹ for 3 h… the dissolution rate of primary crystals… was strongly affected by the antisolvent addition and temperature cooling schemes during crystallization.”; “The solubility value of dimethyl fumarate in 1:3 (v/v) methanol–water solution became <0.05 mg mL⁻¹ at 5 °C… a large supersaturation ratio (≈ 2000) was generated.”

Paper Title: Round Granules of Dimethyl Fumarate by Three-in-One Intensified Process of Reaction, Crystallization, and Spherical Agglomeration in a Common Stirred Tank
Problem_Description: The agglomerates produced by the disconnected spherical‑agglomeration (SA) step showed lower agglomerate yield, higher friability and lower fracture force compared with the three‑in‑one process, indicating weak mechanical properties.
Solution_Description: The authors propose lengthening the SA maturation time, adding polymeric binders to the toluene bridging liquid, and adjusting the bridging‑liquid‑to‑solid ratio (BSR) to improve bridge formation and increase granule strength.
Supporting_Evidence: “The mechanical properties of the round granules produced from the disconnected SA were weaker than the ones from the three‑in‑one intensified process.”; “In the future work, granule strength would be optimized by increasing the maturation time, adding polymers as a bridging liquid, and decreasing the size of the primary particles.”

Paper Title: Round Granules of Dimethyl Fumarate by Three-in-One Intensified Process of Reaction, Crystallization, and Spherical Agglomeration in a Common Stirred Tank
Problem_Description: When the process was scaled‑up from 0.5 L to 10 L, the spherical agglomerates shifted to smaller sizes because the longer travel distance reduced particle–particle, particle–impeller and particle–baffle collisions during the fixed 2 h maturation period.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: For larger tanks the impeller diameter and speed were increased (Zwietering equation) and the impeller clearance was adjusted to enhance mixing and collision frequency; additional bridging liquid can be added or the maturation time prolonged to recover the desired size range.
Supporting_Evidence: “Spherical agglomerates produced from 10 L sized tank were shifted to the smaller sizes… the number of collisions would be drastically reduced for traveling a longer distance in a larger tank during the same 2 h of maturation time.”; “The three‑in‑one intensified process was carried out in a 10 L sized jacketed glass stirred tank… the agitator was set to 350 rpm based on the Zwietering equation.”

Paper Title: Round Granules of Dimethyl Fumarate by Three-in-One Intensified Process of Reaction, Crystallization, and Spherical Agglomeration in a Common Stirred Tank
Problem_Description: Conventional spherical‑agglomeration required separate filtration and drying after crystallization and again after SA, increasing overall batch time and equipment usage.
Solution_Description: The authors integrated reaction, crystallization and SA in a single stirred‑tank (three‑in‑one) so that filtration and drying were performed only once after SA, eliminating redundant steps and shortening the overall process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The three‑in‑one intensified process… filtration, and drying steps are needed only once after SA, whereas in the previous studies… filtration and drying steps were carried out twice, one after the chemical reaction and crystallization, and the second one after SA.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: The 4‑pyridylmagnesium halide reagent (2b) generated in situ is unstable at the reaction temperature, leading to rapid decomposition, inconsistent conversions, and a marked drop in isolated yield when the reaction is scaled from gram‑ to kilogram‑scale batches.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow tandem system was implemented: the halogen‑metal exchange step is performed in a precooled coil (‑5 °C) and the cross‑coupling step in a downstream heated coil (60–65 °C). The flow platform provides precise control of residence time, temperature, and mixing, and a back‑pressure valve (5 psi) suppresses gas‑bubble formation, minimizing exposure of the labile Grignard reagent to elevated temperatures.
Supporting_Evidence: “We identified flow chemistry as a first solution to avoid extensive exposure of the sensitive 4‑pyridylmagnesium halide reagent at elevated temperatures.”; “The halogen‑metal exchange can be completed in a 12 min residence time at –5 °C…The optimal conditions … were found to be a 14 min residence time at 60–65 °C.”; “In order to suppress off‑gassing in the tube reactor, a back‑pressure valve (5 psi) was mounted at the collector.”; “The tandem continuous flow process system was then demonstrated on multiple 40 g scale runs…78% HPLC assay yield…similar to the batch mode on 2 kg scale.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: When the high‑temperature batch Kumada–Corriu coupling was scaled up (30–40 kg), the reaction failed to reach completion, giving only 61 % and 40 % HPLC assay yields respectively, attributed to the labile nature of 2b and its prolonged exposure during longer processing times.
Solution_Description: A low‑temperature Kumada–Corriu protocol was developed using an XantPhos‑π‑allyl Pd precatalyst (0.5 mol %) that delivers full conversion at ≤25 °C, thereby preserving the Grignard reagent and providing consistent 80–82 % assay yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “We aimed for a more efficient catalyst that could facilitate the Kumada–Corriu cross‑coupling reaction at a lower temperature, offering greater stability of the 4‑pyridylmagnesium halide reagent.”; Table 2 shows XantPhos‑π‑allyl precatalyst (0.5 mol %) gives >99 % conversion and 82 % assay yield at 25 °C; “The low temperature Kumada–Corriu cross‑coupling reaction was demonstrated on preparative scale…82% HPLC assay yield…similar profile as the continuous flow process.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: The original Suzuki–Miyaura route to pyridone 1 required a three‑day Soxhlet extraction to remove inorganic impurities; crude material gave only 10 % conversion in a downstream SN2 displacement, whereas the Soxhlet‑purified material gave 97 % conversion.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Suzuki–Miyaura step with a palladium‑catalyzed Kumada–Corriu cross‑coupling, which directly affords a high‑quality intermediate without the need for the lengthy Soxhlet extraction.
Supporting_Evidence: “A lengthy and cumbersome Soxhlet extraction was required to ensure a good purity of 1…When crude pyridone 1 was used directly in the SN2 reaction, only 10% conversion…In contrast, pyridone 1, purified by a 3‑day Soxhlet extraction, gave 97% conversion.”; “We envisioned that an alternative coupling reaction could produce a high quality intermediate and avoid the tedious purification or harsh reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: Acidic hydrolysis of 2‑fluoropyridine 5 generates hydrofluoric acid, which is toxic, highly corrosive to glass‑lined reactors, and poses safety concerns for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: A two‑step basic hydrolysis was introduced: an SNAr displacement of 5 with potassium tert‑butoxide followed by acidic work‑up to give pyridone 1, thereby avoiding HF formation and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrofluoric acid presumably forms in the hydrolysis of fluoropyridine 5 under acidic conditions…the generation of HF was regarded as a disadvantage for large scale manufacturing, due to safety concerns and its highly corrosive properties toward glass‑lined reactors.”; “We found that the SNAr displacement of 2‑fluoropyridine 5 with potassium tert‑butoxide was performed smoothly under mild reaction conditions…the two‑step sequence avoided formation of toxic and corrosive hydrofluoric acid and produced pyridone 1 with a high quality.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: During flow‑scale experiments the reaction temperature in the second reactor approached the boiling point of THF, causing gas generation that formed bubbles in the coiled tube, leading to uncontrolled residence time and inconsistent mixing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A 5 psi back‑pressure valve was installed downstream of the heated reactor to suppress off‑gassing, maintaining stable flow and consistent reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “We observed gas generation in the second reactor, as the reaction temperature was nearly the boiling point of the reaction solvent THF…In order to suppress off‑gassing in the tube reactor, a back‑pressure valve (5 psi) was mounted at the collector.”

Paper Title: Kumada–Corriu Heteroaryl Cross-Coupling for Synthesis of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Comparison of Batch Versus Continuous Reaction Modes
Problem_Description: After the cross‑coupling step, crude 5 was isolated as a THF solution and used directly in the next step without further purification, which could risk carry‑over of impurities.
Solution_Description: The process was telescoped: the crude reaction mixture containing 5 was transferred directly to the hydrolysis step without isolation, simplifying the workflow and reducing material handling.
Supporting_Evidence: “The organic layer was separated, and crude 5 was afforded as a THF solution…The THF solution was concentrated and then solvent‑switched…The organic layer was separated and used directly to the next step without further purification.”

Paper Title: Developing an Asymmetric Transfer Hydrogenation Process for (

Paper Title: Chemoselective Continuous Ru-Catalyzed Hydrogen-Transfer Oppenauer-Type Oxidation of Secondary Alcohols
Problem_Description: Inorganic bases (e.g., NaOH, K2CO3) are poorly soluble in acetone, which would compromise downstream processing and reduce reaction yields.

Problem_Description: The reaction effluent contained soluble ruthenium residues that required removal to obtain product of high purity.

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: Thermal SNAr coupling of the triazole gave poor regio‑selectivity (multiple N‑isomers) and low overall conversion, making it unsuitable for the commercial route.
Solution_Description: A copper‑mediated Ullmann‑Goldberg‑Buchwald coupling (CuI/DMCHDA) was introduced, delivering >10:1 N‑1 regio‑selectivity and high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: - "the high‑temperature S_NAr reaction… produced a poor regiochemical outcome with respect to the three triazole nitrogens" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: The required 7‑bromo‑azaindole (compound 1) could not be accessed before the α‑bromination invention, blocking the coupling strategy.
Solution_Description: A novel α‑bromination of the azaindole core was developed, providing bromide 1 in sufficient quantity.
Supporting_Evidence: - "Prior to the invention of the α‑bromination process, the corresponding bromide 1 had been difficult to prepare, inhibiting its exploration as a coupling partner" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: The initial Cu‑mediated conditions required 20 mol % CuI and 1.6 equiv of the expensive diamine ligand DMCHDA, driving up material cost.
Solution_Description: Ligand loading was cut to 0.80 equiv while CuI was increased to 30 mol % (Cu : ligand ≈ 1 : 2.7), halving the ligand cost with no loss of conversion or selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: - "CuI was found to be the most efficient source of copper, though with the requirement for high ligand loadings (ca. 20 mol % of CuI and 1.6 equiv of DMCHDA)" (Table 1).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: Reactions frequently stalled when run anhydrous; conversions fell dramatically and regioselectivity deteriorated.
Solution_Description: Adding 10–30 equiv of water (or using a 40–45 wt % aqueous KOH solution) restored reaction rate and slightly improved the N‑1 : N‑2 ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: - "the addition of water (10 equiv) restored the expected reaction rate… regioselectivity improved slightly (to ~15:1)" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: Copper‑catalyzed oxidative dimerization (compound 8) and product hydrolysis (compound 9) increased when residual copper remained in the reaction stream.
Solution_Description: An EDTA/KOH wash removed ~95 % of copper, lowering dimer formation; later, ammonium pyrrolidine‑dithiocarbamate (APDTC) was adopted, achieving <20 ppm copper and eliminating oxidative dimerization.
Supporting_Evidence: - "EDTA/KOH treatment… remove 95 % of the charged copper during the first wash… reduce formation of oxidative dimer 8" (Table 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: The free acid of the coupled product (compound 3) formed long needles that were difficult to filter; multiple crystal forms of the potassium salt (3a) caused poor recovery.
Solution_Description: A salt‑metathesis to the lithium salt (3b) was introduced; Li‑salts have very low solubility in MeCN (<0.5 mg mL⁻¹), enabling efficient filtration and >60 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: - "Isolation of the free acid 3 was not feasible owing to the long needle morphology… the lithium analogue 3b… low solubility… offered the potential of high product recovery" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: On pilot‑scale, the EDTA‑based copper removal failed because the lower oxygen level left copper predominantly as Cu(I), which EDTA does not complex efficiently, causing residual copper (≈8300 ppm) and poor crystallization.
Solution_Description: APDTC (a dithiocarbamate) was selected; its insoluble Cu‑complex precipitates and can be removed with a 1 µm filter, delivering consistent low‑copper product at kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: - "efficiency of the EDTA extraction was highly dependent on the oxidation state of the copper… lower O₂ resulted in preservation of Cu(I)… APDTC… reduced Cu levels to <20 ppm" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: Using LiBr for the lithium metathesis gave uncontrolled precipitation and sticky solids, leading to poor filterability and lower yields.
Solution_Description: LiI was employed instead; the LiI solution (1.05 equiv) was added in two portions (35 % then 65 %) with seeding, giving controlled crystallization, higher potency, and reproducible yields.
Supporting_Evidence: - "LiBr resulted in uncontrolled precipitation producing sticky solids… LiI… portion‑wise addition… provided the desired product 3b with significantly improved potency" (Table 3).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: The triazole precursor (compound 2) contained >5 wt % of carcinogenic impurities (DFH, FH, hydrazine), posing safety and regulatory concerns.
Solution_Description: An internal process optimisation reduced DFH/FH/hydrazine levels and allowed a reduction of KOH from 2.05 equiv to 1.8–1.9 equiv, also decreasing the formation of hydrolysis impurity 9.
Supporting_Evidence: - "high levels (>5 wt %) of the carcinogens diformyl hydrazine (DFH), formyl hydrazine (FH), and hydrazine… were observed in several batches of 2" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Preparation of the HIV Attachment Inhibitor BMS-663068. Part 7. Development of a Regioselective Ullmann–Goldberg–Buchwald Reaction
Problem_Description: The Ullmann coupling was heterogeneous, with viscosity and precipitation concerns that could limit further scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to EtOH/KOH as solvent and adjusting concentrations (e.g., higher CuI loading, controlled LiI addition) improved mixing, reduced precipitation, and enabled smooth scale‑up to 25 kg batches.
Supporting_Evidence: - "reaction was heterogeneous, which raised concerns for potential challenges for further scale‑up… controlled crystallization… EtOH was chosen…" (Sec 2).

Paper Title: Identification of a Robust Carbonyl Reductase for Diastereoselectively Building

Paper Title: Identification of a Robust Carbonyl Reductase for Diastereoselectively Building
Problem_Description: Previously reported ketoreductases showed insufficient activity toward the water‑insoluble, bulky substrate 7 at high substrate loading, giving low conversion and poor productivity.

Paper Title: Identification of a Robust Carbonyl Reductase for Diastereoselectively Building
Problem_Description: Substrate 7 is water‑insoluble; at the desired high loading (300 g L⁻¹) the reaction mixture becomes highly concentrated (≈35 % v/v), raising concerns about phase separation and mixing.

Paper Title: Identification of a Robust Carbonyl Reductase for Diastereoselectively Building
Problem_Description: LbCR loses activity rapidly at elevated temperature (half‑life of 1.2 min at 40 °C), which could cause deactivation and inconsistent performance during scale‑up.

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Structurally-Challenging 5‑Lipoxygenase Activating Protein (FLAP) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The cyanation of tertiary alcohol 3 to nitrile 4 was not robust, giving low isolated yields (23‑47 %) and forming impurities that required extensive chromatography to remove.

Problem_Description: The current industrial synthesis of Lobesia botrana pheromone is a linear multistep route that requires isolation of four intermediates and affords only 11 % overall isolated yield with 75 % isomeric purity, making it economically unattractive.

Paper Title: From Reaction Solvent to Crystallization Solvent, Membrane Assisted Reaction Workup and Interpretation of Membrane Performance Results by Application of Spiegler–Kedem Theory

Paper Title: From Reaction Solvent to Crystallization Solvent, Membrane Assisted Reaction Workup and Interpretation of Membrane Performance Results by Application of Spiegler–Kedem Theory

Paper Title: From Reaction Solvent to Crystallization Solvent, Membrane Assisted Reaction Workup and Interpretation of Membrane Performance Results by Application of Spiegler–Kedem Theory

Paper Title: From Reaction Solvent to Crystallization Solvent, Membrane Assisted Reaction Workup and Interpretation of Membrane Performance Results by Application of Spiegler–Kedem Theory

Paper Title: From Reaction Solvent to Crystallization Solvent, Membrane Assisted Reaction Workup and Interpretation of Membrane Performance Results by Application of Spiegler–Kedem Theory

Problem_Description: Using methylene blue (MB) or tetrakis‑(4‑carboxyphenyl)‑porphyrin (TCPP) as photosensitizers gave only partial conversion of methionine under the same conditions.

Paper Title: Highly Productive Continuous Flow Synthesis of Di- and Tripeptides in Water
Problem_Description: The 0.4 M sodium‑borate buffer precipitates at the required 0–2 °C reaction temperature, leading to solid formation that blocks mixing and creates a heterogeneous slurry. The precipitation also dilutes the reaction when ice is added for cooling, worsening mixing. The exothermic nature of NCA hydrolysis and the heat generated by the high‑shear mixer raise the reactor temperature (0.85 °C · min⁻¹ from mixing, 0.54 °C · min⁻¹ from reaction), risking side‑reactions and safety concerns. Low mixer speeds (≤1200 rpm) allow solid NCA to accumulate on the vessel wall, giving low and inconsistent conversions. Precise stoichiometric control is difficult because continuous solid addition can be uneven (e.g., cohesive l‑Val NCA required hopper tapping). NCA is intrinsically unstable in water, hydrolysing and decarboxylating to give side‑products that are hard to separate. Use of the sodium‑borate buffer adds waste and health‑hazard concerns. Finally, ion‑exchange chromatography does not fully separate unreacted amino acid from the di‑peptide, making purification problematic.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The buffer was eliminated and an in‑line proportional‑integral pH controller was installed to add 6 M KOH as needed, maintaining pH 10.2 without excess buffer. Continuous solid dosing of NCA was achieved with an automated powder dispenser (≈7 wt % accuracy) to provide a steady, controlled feed. High‑shear mixing at 4000 rpm was employed to break the solid boundary layer and keep NCA particles fully dispersed, eliminating NCA buildup on the reactor wall and raising conversion to >70 %. An internal cooling coil removed both the reaction exotherm and the heat generated by the mixer, keeping the bulk temperature at 0 ± 1 °C. A custom stainless‑steel CSTR (single‑stage, 300 mL volume) was used, providing the necessary solids‑addition capability and superior heat removal compared with a PFR. Stoichiometry was tuned to 1.1 equiv NCA (instead of 1.5 equiv) to suppress tripeptide formation and improve selectivity. The use of THF as a solvent for NCA was avoided; solid NCA was added directly to aqueous streams, improving yield. Purification was upgraded by combining ion‑exchange chromatography with a final silica‑gel flash step, which successfully removed salts and residual amino acid for all di‑peptides except one case that still required additional silica polishing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "the sodium borate buffer precipitates; ... addition of ice dilutes the reaction and causes problems with mixing" (Intro, p. 2). 
• "heat from the mixer at 4000 rpm ... reaction exotherm ... 0.85 °C·min⁻¹ … 0.54 °C·min⁻¹" (Results, p. 3). 
• "At 1200 rpm, product formation was low and inconsistent with the solid NCA building up on the surface" (Fig. 3 discussion). 
• "Above 3000 rpm, 70 % of the crude dipeptide was produced" (Results, p. 3). 
• "Automated pH controller ... rapid measurement and adjustment of pH ... variation 0.2 pH units vs 1 pH unit for manual" (Fig. 4). 
• "continuous powder dispenser to continuously dose the NCA … accurate to 7 wt %" (Reactor description). 
• "internal cooling‑coil required to maintain the desired temperature of 0–2 °C" (Reactor description). 
• "1.5 equiv of NCA led to over‑reaction, with tripeptide ... while an undercharge caused problems with amino acid and dipeptide separation; all subsequent experiments used 1.1 equiv of NCA" (Table 1 discussion). 
• "The addition of l‑Ala NCA dissolved in THF gave a significantly lower yield, 39 % compared to 72 % with solid addition" (Results, p. 4). 
• "Ion exchange chromatography was successful in separating the salts ... but did not usefully separate the unreacted amino acid from the desired dipeptide" (Purification discussion).
