Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Carbonylated Heterocycles via Pd-Catalyzed Oxidative Carbonylation Using CO and O
Problem_Description: The original batch protocol used PdI₂ and KI, both of which are poorly soluble in organic solvents, leading to heterogeneous mixtures and precipitation of Pd(OAc)₂ when mixed with the substrate. This caused clogging, inconsistent conversion, and deposition of palladium black on reactor surfaces, which reduced catalytic activity and lowered product yields. The use of pure CO/O₂ mixtures without inert dilution also raised significant explosion hazards in batch autoclaves, and the batch process required long reaction times (≈24 h) and high catalyst loadings (5 mol %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors switched to Pd(OAc)₂ and tetra‑n‑butylammonium iodide (TBAI), which are fully soluble in acetonitrile, and fed the catalyst and substrate as two separate liquid streams to avoid precipitation. A stainless‑steel micro‑reactor with a four‑way mixer and back‑pressure regulator provided intense heat‑ and mass‑transfer under segmented gas‑liquid flow, safely handling the explosive CO/O₂ mixture. Reaction temperature (120 °C) and pressure (20 bar) were optimized, and a 1:1 CO:O₂ ratio was identified as optimal to balance carbonylation rate and Pd(0) re‑oxidation, allowing a residence time of only 24 min. The reactor coil was cleaned with 20 % HNO₃ after each run to remove residual Pd black and ensure reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Both PdI₂ and KI proved poorly soluble in organic solvents… Pd(OAc)₂ and tetra‑butyl‑ammonium iodide (TBAI) were used as a catalyst and cocatalyst, respectively, because of their good solubility in organic solvents.” (sec 2.1) 
• “1a and Pd(OAc)₂ form a precipitate within a few minutes of mixing… therefore, the Pd catalyst and substrate were introduced as two separate feed streams.” (sec 2.1) 
• “A stainless steel coil… fitted with a temperature control unit… back‑pressure regulator… was utilized as the reactor.” (sec 2.1) 
• “The optimized continuous flow conditions (120 °C, 20 bar pressure, 24 min residence time) were used to prepare a number of… heterocycles in good overall yield and purity.” (abstract) 
• “The internal surface of the reactor coil became coated with some of the Pd catalyst… The Pd deposited on the reactor coil can be reoxidized by I₂ (from TBAI) to reform the active Pd(II) catalyst… the residual Pd black inside the reactor was removed after each experiment by washing the reactor with 20 % HNO₃ (aq) at 70 °C.” (sec 2.2) 
• “Doubling the gas flow rates resulted in a decrease in conversion, probably from the reduced reaction time.” (fig 4, sec 2.2) 
• “The presence of too much CO can also cause faster deactivation of the Pd(II) catalyst by reduction to Pd(0). A higher O₂ concentration is necessary to maintain the presence of iodine, which reoxidizes Pd(0) to Pd(II)…” (sec 2.2) 
• “The continuous‑flow process enables the safe and scalable oxidative carbonylation using CO/O₂ under elevated pressures and temperatures.” (abstract) 
• “The reaction time was shortened from 24 h to merely 24 min.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Carbonylated Heterocycles via Pd-Catalyzed Oxidative Carbonylation Using CO and O
Problem_Description: Handling a flammable CO/O₂ mixture at high temperature and pressure in batch reactors poses a serious explosion risk. Direct mixing of the gases with organic solvent creates a potentially ignitable mixture, and the high exotherm of oxidative carbonylation can aggravate safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: By moving to a continuous‑flow microreactor built from stainless steel, the reaction volume is minimized and the high surface‑to‑volume ratio enables rapid heat removal, dramatically reducing the risk of thermal runaway. Segmented gas‑liquid flow provides efficient mass transfer while keeping the explosive gas mixture confined within the narrow channels, allowing the use of pure CO/O₂ without inert dilution. The back‑pressure regulator maintains a constant pressure, further improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “O₂ cannot reoxidize Pd(0) directly in the liquid phase; thus, a cocatalyst… is introduced… However, the utilization of O₂ in the presence of an organic solvent as a fuel and an ignition source often results in a potentially flammable mixture.” (intro) 
• “A strategy to improve the operational safety is to dilute the mixture either with an inert gas… However, the use of pure gases without dilution typically provides higher reaction rates and process efficiency.” (intro) 
• “The characteristic features of flow reactors (i.e., fast heat and mass transfer, precise control over reaction time…) facilitate operation under extreme conditions… The safety of the operation is guaranteed… even for a worst case scenario, since a properly designed metallic microreactor is able to sustain an explosion event for a mixture of flammable gases and O₂.” (intro) 
• “A stainless steel coil… fitted with a temperature control unit… A back‑pressure regulator (BPR) was installed downstream of the reactor to control the system pressure.” (sec 2.1) 
• “The continuous‑flow process enables the safe and scalable oxidative carbonylation using CO/O₂ under elevated pressures and temperatures.” (abstract) 
• “CAUTION: Risk of explosion and CO poisoning! … All of the experiments must be performed in a well‑ventilated fume cupboard with a fitted CO detector.” (sec 4.1)

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of Carbonylated Heterocycles via Pd-Catalyzed Oxidative Carbonylation Using CO and O
Problem_Description: Low catalyst loadings (≤1 mol %) led to poor conversions and significant formation of oxidation by‑product 7a, indicating incomplete turnover and catalyst deactivation. Increasing catalyst loading improved conversion but raised material cost concerns.
Solution_Description: The catalyst loading was increased to 5 mol % Pd(OAc)₂ while keeping 20 mol % TBAI, which restored high conversion (>94 %). The substrate concentration was adjusted (0.20 M feed, 0.10 M in reactor) and liquid flow rates were halved to increase residence time, thereby improving yield without excessive catalyst excess. The optimal CO/O₂ ratio (1:1) was also identified to prevent Pd reduction and suppress by‑product formation.

Solution_Description: The process was changed to use toluene as a single solvent for all five steps. Toluene is compatible with the acid‑chloride formation, the amidation, the reduction, cyclisation and the salt‑formation, eliminating the need for dichloromethane and simplifying removal of volatiles.

Supporting_Evidence: ["Formation of enamine 15 resulted in an unacceptable exotherm at the intended reaction temperature of 120 °C.", "development using the original reagent, DMF‑DMA, was re‑evaluated and found to be safe when carried out at a lower temperature (95 °C instead of 120 °C)."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Reduction of nitroalkene 34 to nitroalkane 17 gave only 33 % yield on scale.
Solution_Description: Replace the electrophile with phthalimidoacetaldehyde diethyl acetal; perform a one‑pot TFA‑mediated condensation in CH₂Cl₂ at 20 °C for 28 h, affording product 37 in 43 % yield, followed by cyclisation to 18 in 82 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["To address the safety issues with use of 1‑(dimethylamino)‑2‑nitroethylene and the poor yield in the reduction of 34 to 17, alternate reagents and conditions were probed for conversion of indole 16 to tricycle 18.", "Screening of two‑carbon electrophiles identified phthalimidoacetaldehyde diethyl acetal as the only promising alternative. After further development, the corresponding aldehyde 36 was found to be more reactive and gave a cleaner reaction. The optimized process involved dissolution of indole 16, aldehyde 36, and triethylsilane in dichloromethane; then TFA in dichloromethane was added over 30 min and the reaction stirred at 20 °C for 28 h. Product 37 crystallized from the reaction mixture and was isolated in 43 % yield."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Suzuki coupling of bromide 19 with 4‑formylbenzene boronic acid was sluggish and required higher catalyst loading.
Solution_Description: Identify Pd(dppf)Cl₂ in MeCONMe₂ as optimal catalyst/solvent; heat to 95 °C for 1 h, employing a two‑vessel protocol to ensure catalyst activation and consistent coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: ["For the Suzuki coupling of 19 with 4‑formylbenzene boronic acid, screening experiments identified Pd(dppf)Cl₂‑CH₂Cl₂ as the optimum catalyst, but the reaction was capricious depending on the source of reagents used.", "a reproducible process was devised by combining bromide 19, 2.5 mol % of the Pd catalyst, and solvent MeCONMe₂, then heating to 95 °C for 1 h. This procedure ensured activation of the catalyst (reduction of PdII to Pd0) and oxidative insertion of Pd with the aryl bromide."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Use of Na(CN)BH₃ for reductive amination releases HCN, a toxic gas.
Solution_Description: Replace Na(CN)BH₃ with NaBH₄; perform a two‑step reduction via isolated imine 38 to avoid HCN generation, and scrub any evolved H₂.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Use of sodium cyanoborohydride for reduction amination of 20 was undesirable due to the release of HCN.", "Sodium borohydride was found to be a suitable replacement for Na(CN)BH₃; however, alcohol byproduct 39 was also generated and could not be completely purged from rucaparib when the reductive amination was carried out as a one‑step process. Therefore, the imine 38 was prepared and crystallized from MeOH, removing all residual aldehyde 20 and then reduced with NaBH₄ in MeOH/THF."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Methyl bromide (MeBr) generated during deprotection of the carbamate could pose a safety hazard.
Solution_Description: Trap MeBr using an aqueous ethanolamine scrubber.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The MeBr generated during this reaction could be trapped using an aq. ethanolamine scrubber."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: A low‑yielding (+‑) resolution (≈20 %) of the chiral intermediate gave only 80–90 % ee, requiring an extensive SFC step.
Solution_Description: Develop chiral SFC purification for the final product and later implement an asymmetric transaminase route that avoids the resolution entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A low‑yielding resolution (20 %) that provided product with 80–90 % ee after several recrystallizations, requiring an ee upgrade by preparative chiral SFC chromatography at the end of the synthesis.", "While the optimization of the Medicinal Chemistry route provided kilogram quantities of niraparib for early development activities, a number of opportunities remained for an improved route... An alternate route employing an asymmetric transaminase and a late‑stage C–N bond coupling was designed and developed by Merck process chemists."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Azide chemistry at 90 °C posed a risk of hydrazoic‑acid formation and possible runaway.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Perform the azide reaction at 110 °C under basic conditions with 2,6‑lutidine and a nitrogen sweep to prevent HN₃ accumulation; use a nitrogen sweep to vent gases safely.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Safety concerns carrying out the azide chemistry at 90 °C.", "The reaction was carried out under basic conditions using 2,6‑lutidine and a nitrogen sweep to avoid formation of hydrazoic acid, which can form explosive gas mixtures at a concentration above 10 %.", "Thermal analysis indicated the reaction could be safely carried out at 110 °C, instead of the original 90 °C, allowing for a reduction in azide to 1.0 equiv."]

Paper Title: Patent Review of Manufacturing Routes to Recently Approved PARP Inhibitors: Olaparib, Rucaparib, and Niraparib
Problem_Description: Isolation of the final niraparib as an amorphous, hygroscopic HCl salt required lyophilisation and gave a low‑solubility product.
Solution_Description: Develop a solid‑dispersion tablet formulation (copovidone, hot‑melt extrusion) and switch to the p‑tosylate salt, which is non‑hygroscopic and gives higher bioavailability.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Isolation of the final product via lyophilization as an amorphous, hygroscopic HCl salt.", "A second generation oral formulation is described in U.S. Patent 8,475,842 in which olaparib is formulated as a solid dispersion in copovidone, then compressed into 150 mg tablets. The solid dispersion is manufactured using a hot‑melt extrusion process which involves mixing of olaparib with copovidone, increasing the temperature above the melting point of copovidone (140 °C) to produce a melt, then extrusion of the melt to form a solid dispersion.", "A survey of final forms of the API identified the p‑tosylate salt as a stable and non‑hygroscopic salt."]

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of a Selective M
Problem_Description: The deprotonation of compound 2 with NaH in DMSO at 80 °C (step 2→3) and the deprotection of the benzyl group (step 5→6) create an exothermic environment that can lead to explosion on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Replace NaH with KOH (2 equiv) in DMSO and run the reaction at 30 °C (ambient temperature). The same base change is applied to the benzyl deprotection step, using milder conditions and avoiding hazardous reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The preparation of compound 3 required the use of NaH, compound 7 in DMSO, and a temperature of 80 °C. These reaction conditions can cause explosion at scale‑up.”

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: Low solubility of triethylsilane in the acidic reduction step caused poor reactivity and led to formation of a dimeric impurity (15) that was difficult to remove by crystallization.
Solution_Description: Switch to dichloromethane as the reaction solvent (poorly soluble for both substrate and product) and add TFA slowly at 0 °C, then warm to 25 °C while maintaining agitation; use a 10 vol CH₂Cl₂/triethylsilane/TFA ratio to limit dimer formation and improve conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "...triethylsilane was insoluble...or competitive formation of dimer impurity 15...difficult to remove by crystallization"; ***Solution*** "Methylene chloride, although undesirable as a class‑2 solvent, had the advantage of poorly solubilizing both starting material and product, thus minimizing the formation of 15. Optimized conditions were 10 volumes of CH₂Cl₂, 1.3 equiv of triethylsilane, and 6 equiv of TFA. To avoid the formation of dimer 15, the slow addition of TFA at 0 °C, followed by warming to 25 °C...gave clean, complete conversion."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: The original Grignard‑mediated coupling of sesamol and isatin required excess isopropylmagnesium chloride, a moisture‑sensitive and costly reagent that emitted propane, posing safety and cost concerns on scale.
Solution_Description: Replace the Grignard base with a slight excess of potassium carbonate (fine‑particle) in THF or DMF, using only 1.1 equiv of base; this eliminated the need for the moisture‑sensitive Grignard, reduced cost, and removed propane emissions.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "...only a slight excess of one equivalent of Grignard reagent was necessary...this amount of metalating reagent seemed insufficient...suggested it was merely acting as a base...emission of propane"; ***Solution*** "A quick base screen demonstrated that the chemistry could be performed in THF or DMF using a slight excess of potassium carbonate...This improvement removed a costly, moisture‑sensitive base from the synthesis. This also provided a safer process which avoided the emission of propane."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: Attempts to form the spiro‑furan ring via traditional chlorination (e.g., thionyl chloride, mesylate) failed due to the congested neopentyl centre, giving poor conversions and side‑product formation, and the PBr₃ route produced a phosphine‑oxide impurity and racemization at the quaternary center.
Solution_Description: Adopt a diphenyl‑phosphine leaving group (chlorodiphenylphosphine) which completely consumed the intermediate at 37 °C without the need for base, giving clean conversion and preserving ee; oxidize the resulting diphenylphosphine odorant with 30 % hydrogen peroxide before work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "All attempts to cleanly synthesize chloro or mesylate intermediates were unsuccessful…Traditional reagents such as thionyl chloride failed…PBr₃ gave an oxidized version of intermediate A as the phosphine oxide…scrambling of ee…"; ***Solution*** "Chlorodiphenylphosphine completely consumed 24 when heated to 37 °C and provided the product 1 without an intermediate observed by HPLC. No scrambling of ee was observed…To remove the stench associated with trace amounts of diphenylphosphine, 30 % hydrogen peroxide in water was added…oxidized the malodorous by‑product to diphenylphosphinic acid."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: The asymmetric aldol step using Sharpless ligands gave inconsistent conversions and low ee, especially at higher temperatures, and longer reaction times led to increased impurity formation, including hemiaminal side‑products.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to thiourea catalysts (21/22) with oxindole‑substituted substrates, operate at 25 °C in n‑heptane with high agitation to limit solubility of the product, and use only 1.1 % catalyst loading; this gave 70 % ee on a 47 h scale (plant) and allowed later enantiopurity upgrade by crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "Significant levels of impurities were observed when long reaction times occurred…hemiaminal formation…longer reaction times resulted in lower ee…"; ***Solution*** "The key asymmetric conversion of 18 to 19 was found to perform best with a mixture of solid paraformaldehyde and aqueous formaldehyde using only 1.1 % of 22 at 25 °C. High agitation in n‑heptane was needed…On a small scale, an increase in temperature allowed for shorter reaction time but resulted in lower enantioselectivity."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: During the early-stage coupling of sesamol and isatin, using only isopropylmagnesium chloride gave incomplete conversion because the reagent acted mainly as a base, and the reaction required fine‑particle potassium carbonate for best results.
Solution_Description: Implement potassium carbonate (small particle size) in DMF at 48 ± 3 °C, adding the electrophile (6) first, then sesamol later, to ensure complete consumption of isatin and avoid over‑addition.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "...only a slight excess of one equivalent of Grignard reagent was necessary to complete the reaction...this amount of metalating reagent seemed insufficient and suggested that it was merely acting as a base."; ***Solution*** "A quick base screen demonstrated that the chemistry could be performed in THF or DMF using a slight excess of potassium carbonate....Under the optimized conditions, 1.01 equiv of 6 was added to a slurry of K₂CO₃ and isatin in DMF at 48 ± 3 °C followed by heating for 1 h. Once the consumption of isatin was confirmed…a DMF solution of sesamol was added at 25–35 °C…Product 16 was isolated in 94–97 % yield."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: The final cyclization to the API required prolonged heating (21 h) with PBr₃, resulted in low overall yield, and caused racemization at the quaternary stereocenter.
Solution_Description: Adopt a one‑pot deprotection/cyclization sequence in acetonitrile using HBr followed by chlorodiphenylphosphine addition at 37 °C; this eliminated the need for separate Mitsunobu steps, reduced reaction time, and preserved ee (>99 %).
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "The closure of 24 to provide 1 proved to be problematic…All attempts to cleanly synthesize chloro or mesylate intermediates were unsuccessful…PBr₃ gave an oxidized version of intermediate A as the phosphine oxide…scrambling of ee…"; ***Solution*** "The final step of the synthesis could be successfully telescoped when performed in acetonitrile…added 47–49 % HBr in water and heated to 37 °C…then chlorodiphenylphosphine added…no scrambling of ee was observed…overall yield 80.7 % and purity 99.6 % with 100 % ee."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: Initial large‑scale couplings required extensive chromatography (including SMB) to isolate the racemic drug substance, which is impractical and costly at pilot scale.
Solution_Description: Design a route that avoids chromatography entirely by telescoping steps (e.g., direct isolation of intermediates by precipitation or filtration) and employing crystallization for enantiopurity enrichment, thus eliminating the need for SMB.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "Coupling of 5 with 6 was mediated by cesium carbonate and required large‑scale chromatography to purify the crude racemic drug substance prior to SMB chromatography."; ***Solution*** "The overall synthesis uses mild, process‑friendly reagents…no chromatography was used for any of the steps, and all intermediates were isolated through direct isolation…The removal of the undesired isomer is achieved through preferential precipitation…"

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: Use of thionyl chloride and other harsh reagents for the cyclization step posed safety concerns due to their corrosive and toxic nature.
Solution_Description: Replace hazardous chlorinating agents with a phosphine‑based leaving group (chlorodiphenylphosphine) that operates under mild, aqueous conditions without need for strong acid/base, reducing safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "All attempts to cleanly synthesize chloro or mesylate intermediates were unsuccessful…Traditional reagents such as thionyl chloride failed."; ***Solution*** "Chlorodiphenylphosphine completely consumed 24 when heated to 37 °C…No base was needed…The use of the diphenylphosphino group offered a cleaner alternative to the Mitsunobu reaction, avoiding the use of azodicarboxylate reagents in the final step."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: During the PBr₃ mediated cyclization an oxidized phosphine oxide (A) formed, indicating decomposition of the intended intermediate, and the mechanism of ee scrambling was not elucidated.
Solution_Description: Abort the PBr₃ route and adopt the chlorodiphenylphosphine method which proceeds without detectable decomposition or ee loss, thereby sidestepping the unknown decomposition pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "...mass spectral analysis and NMR revealed an oxidized version of intermediate A as the phosphine oxide…The mechanism for the scrambling was not elucidated and remains unclear…"; ***Solution*** "Chlorodiphenylphosphine completely consumed 24 when heated to 37 °C and provided the product 1 without an intermediate observed by HPLC. No scrambling of ee was observed with this leaving group…"

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: The initial asymmetric aldol using protected phenol 3 suffered from poor reactivity due to the insolubility of triethylsilane and competitive dimer formation, leading to low yields.
Solution_Description: Employ neat TFA (no cosolvent) for the reduction step to force the reaction toward product formation; later, for the aldol, use CH₂Cl₂ as solvent and add TFA slowly to control reaction progress.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "Attempts to alter the conditions resulted in poor reactivity due either to the insolubility of triethylsilane or competitive formation of dimer impurity 15."; ***Solution*** "Methylene chloride...had the advantage of poorly solubilizing both starting material and product, thus minimizing the formation of 15. Optimized conditions were 10 volumes of CH₂Cl₂, 1.3 equiv of triethylsilane, and 6 equiv of TFA. To avoid the formation of dimer 15, the slow addition of TFA at 0 °C...gave clean, complete conversion."

Paper Title: The First Asymmetric Pilot-Scale Synthesis of TV-45070
Problem_Description: The initial asymmetric route required cryogenic temperatures (−20 °C) and an allylated Corey variant of the catalyst, which was not scalable and gave low overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switch to ambient temperature asymmetric aldol using Sharpless ligands or thiourea catalysts, eliminating the need for low temperature control and improving overall yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ***Problem*** "...asymmetric alkylation promoted by the Lygo phase‑transfer catalyst...provided the desired center in 90 % ee when performed at −20 °C. No attempts with the allylated Corey variant…"; ***Solution*** "Employing Sharpless ligands gave encouraging results under mild conditions…The key asymmetric conversion of 18 to 19 was found to perform best…using only 1.1 % of 22 at 25 °C…"

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: The process could not produce azithromycin dihydrate crystals in the desired large size range (425–850 μm) when using the acetone‑water mixture; previous attempts succeeded only after changing the solvent, which is prohibited by cost and regulatory constraints.
Solution_Description: A multi‑stage water‑addition strategy combined with a very slow cooling ramp (0.01 °C min⁻¹) was implemented. Small increments of water (12.5 % then three 2.7 % batches) were added before cooling, followed by a slow temperature drop and a final high‑rate water feed to grow large dihydrate crystals (D₅₀ ≈ 433 μm).
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "previous efforts failed in producing crystals of the size range 425–850 μm directly through crystallization using the mixture of acetone and water as the solvent, unless the solvent was changed. Solvent change was constrained by administrative and environmental considerations as well as cost."  
Solution: "The crystals in the size range 425–850 μm ... were obtained ... 12.5 % water was first added … further water was added … 0.01 °C min⁻¹ … 60 % water was added ... to the solution at the rate of 1.5 % … The obtained crystals had a median diameter (D₅₀) of 542 μm."

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: The solution‑mediated phase transition (SMPT) from monohydrate to dihydrate was inconsistent; insufficient antisolvent amount or inappropriate addition method caused partial or no transition, jeopardising the final crystal size distribution.
Solution_Description: Real‑time PAT (ATR‑FTIR and online imaging) was used to monitor the SMPT, allowing immediate adjustment of the water‑addition rate and amount to ensure complete conversion before the second water feed.
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "If any aberration occurs in the process, the transition might not be able to come to completion. The key factors are the amount of antisolvent and the ways the antisolvent is introduced."  
Solution: "Coordinated utilization of ATR‑FTIR and online imaging allows the direct observation and real‑time measurement ... Unexpected deviations ... can be detected in a timely manner by the PAT instrument and immediate remedial adjustment can be made."

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: Rapid addition of water generated very high supersaturation, leading to excessive secondary nucleation and crystal aggregation, which produced smaller particles than the target size range.
Solution_Description: The feed rate of the second water portion was reduced (e.g., 0.5 % w/w min⁻¹) to lower supersaturation, suppress secondary nucleation, and obtain a narrower, larger‑particle distribution.
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "high supersaturation ... resulted in a high nucleation rate due to the initial high supersaturation. A high nucleation rate produces a large number of nuclei, which means a small crystal size at the end of crystallization."  
Solution: "The feeding rate of the second portion of water could have an impact on the final crystal size ... the highest feeding rate, 1.5 %, corresponds to the largest D₅₀, while the lowest feeding rate is linked to the smallest D₅₀ ... This experimental result could not be fully explained. One speculative explanation is that the large particle size corresponding to 1.5 % was due to aggregation of crystals induced by more small crystals ..."

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: Scaling the process from 1 L to 25 L risked changes in mixing intensity and heat removal, potentially altering supersaturation profiles and crystal size distribution.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Scale‑up was performed using a constant tip‑speed criterion (stirring speed set to 48 rpm), preserving the hydrodynamics and ensuring that the operational spaces identified in the 1 L reactor remained valid at 25 L.
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "The operational spaces derived in the 1 L reactor were then validated in a 25 L crystallizer. According to the principle of scale‑up based on constant tip speed, the stirring speed was set to 48 rpm."  
Outcome: "Similar results were obtained when the same three operating conditions were applied on the 25 L scale. ... Similar median diameters were achieved while the unimodal CSDs of the 25 L scale were even narrower than those of the 1 L scale."

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: Changing the solvent to achieve larger crystals was not permissible because of administrative, environmental, and cost constraints.
Solution_Description: Process parameters (water amount, addition profile, and cooling rate) were optimized within the existing acetone‑water system, eliminating the need for a solvent change while still delivering the three target crystal size ranges.
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "Solvent change was constrained by administrative and environmental considerations as well as cost."  
Solution: "By adopting these conditions, dihydrate products with the three desired CSDs were obtained in a 1 L crystallizer. The developed process allowed for streamlined steps and cost reduction compared to the current sieving method, especially for the largest size range, 425–850 μm."

Paper Title: Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Aided Identification of Operational Spaces Leading to Tailored Crystal Size Distributions in Azithromycin Crystallization via Coordinated Cooling and Solution Mediated Phase Transition
Problem_Description: Without real‑time monitoring, deviations in supersaturation, temperature, or phase transition could go unnoticed until the final product was out of specification.
Solution_Description: Implementation of PAT tools (online imaging and ATR‑FTIR) provided continuous, in‑situ measurement of concentration, supersaturation, and crystal morphology, enabling timely corrective actions.
Supporting_Evidence:
Issue: "Unexpected deviations of the operation from the ideal situation during crystallization ... can be detected in a timely manner by the PAT instrument."  
Solution: "Coordinated utilization of ATR‑FTIR and online imaging allows the direct observation and real‑time measurement of azithromycin polymorph transition ... and crystal growth behavior."

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: The first‑generation synthesis used selenium‑oxide oxidation, a diazonium‑acetate ring‑expansion, and a low‑temperature bromine‑lithium exchange/air oxidation sequence. Selenium reagents and mercury‑containing lead reagents are toxic, the sequence required low‑temperature operations and gave modest yields, making it unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A completely new second‑generation route was designed that replaces the selenium oxidation, diazonium chemistry and low‑temperature organolithium steps with a manganese (or manganese‑copper) catalysed Grignard coupling followed by a semi‑pinacol rearrangement of an epoxide, a sequence that is both safer and scalable.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The original synthesis of this structural motif employed a selenium oxide mediated oxidation, the use of diazoacetate and aryl lead reagents, and a low temperature oxidation of an aryl lithium intermediate, so it was not well suited to large scale synthesis.', 'Although the aryl lead coupling route was relatively high yielding and short, scale up issues throughout the synthesis precluded any work beyond gram scale.', 'In conclusion a straightforward synthesis of two aryl‑1,3‑dione building blocks was realized on kilogram scale employing manganese and manganese‑copper catalyzed alkyl Grignard couplings and a semi‑pinacol rearrangement of an epoxide as the key steps.']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: When substrate 25 was coupled with ethyl‑magnesium bromide in the presence of MnCl₂, the reaction gave a 4:1–5:1 mixture of the desired coupling product (18) and a reduction by‑product (26) arising from β‑hydrogen elimination, limiting overall yield and producing a decomposition pathway.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Selectivity was improved by (i) adding the Grignard reagent slowly over 45 min with vigorous stirring to avoid localized high concentrations, (ii) performing the addition under a controlled ethylene atmosphere to occupy a vacant coordination site on manganese, and (iii) adding a small amount of methyl‑magnesium bromide before the ethyl reagent to block β‑hydrogen elimination, which raised the coupling : reduction ratio to 8:1.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Best results regarding the 18 vs 26 selectivity were obtained adding ethyl magnesium bromide slowly (over 45 min) and vigorous stirring to limit localized concentration of the Grignard reagent.', 'Reaction under atmosphere of ethylene gave improved selectivity.', 'Addition of methyl Grignard (1.5 equiv) followed by the addition of ethyl Grignard (1.5 equiv) gave improved selectivity of the ethyl Grignard coupling (8:1 = coupling:reduction) and no coupling of methyl Grignard at all.']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: The mixture of coupling product 18 and reduction by‑product 26 proved difficult to separate on scale, creating a purification bottleneck.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to an alternative substrate (27) that, under the same coupling conditions, gave the desired product 28 without any detectable reduction by‑product, thereby eliminating the difficult purification step.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The challenges in separating compounds 18 and 26 led us to consider an alternative approach.', 'Coupling of 27 with ethyl Grignard provided 28. As before, there was no conversion to the desired product in the absence of the catalyst (Table 2, Entry 1). In the presence of anhydrous MnCl₂ (10 mol %) clean conversion to the desired product was observed with no reduction by‑product, but the reaction was unfeasibly slow (Table 2, Entry 2). Pleasingly, addition of lithium chloride (2 equiv) significantly increased the reaction rate and provided the desired coupling product in excellent yield (Table 2, Entry 3).']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: Coupling of substrate 27 with ethyl‑magnesium bromide in the presence of MnCl₂ proceeded very slowly, giving only 25 % conversion after 15 h, which is impractical for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The addition of lithium chloride (2 equiv) dramatically increased the rate and conversion, delivering quantitative conversion and >90 % isolated yield of product 28.
Supporting_Evidence: ['In the presence of anhydrous MnCl₂ (10 mol %) clean conversion to the desired product was observed with no reduction by‑product, but the reaction was unfeasibly slow (Table 2, Entry 2).', 'Pleasurably, addition of lithium chloride (2 equiv) significantly increased the reaction rate and provided the desired coupling product in excellent yield (Table 2, Entry 3).']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: Methyl‑magnesium bromide coupling of substrate 25 gave only trace product with MnCl₂ alone, and only 41 % yield when both MnCl₂ and CuCl were used at room temperature.
Solution_Description: A bimetallic MnCl₂/CuCl catalyst system (20 % MnCl₂, 10 % CuCl) was employed and the reaction temperature was raised to reflux, which increased conversion to 100 % and isolated yield of the methyl‑coupled aldehyde 17 to 95 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Combining both metals gave 41% of the desired coupling product 17 after 20 h at room temperature (Table 4, Entry 3).', 'The yield was further improved by running the reaction at reflux for 1.5 h (Table 4, Entry 4).', 'Manganese–copper catalysis is known, but to the best of our knowledge has previously been employed only in sp³–sp³ couplings.']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: When MeMgBr was used in MeTHF for the methyl‑magnesium coupling, up to 20 % of a dehalogenation by‑product was observed, indicating undesired side‑reactions.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent from MeTHF to diethyl ether (Et₂O) eliminated the dehalogenation pathway and gave a cleaner reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Reaction employing methyl magnesium bromide solution in MeTHF was slightly less clean, giving up to 20% of dehalogenation by‑product (Table 4, Entry 5).']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: The semi‑pinacol rearrangement step required the exothermic addition of hydrogen peroxide (40 % aq.) at 50 °C, presenting a potential safety hazard on large scale.
Solution_Description: The peroxide was added slowly with a dosing pump while maintaining the reaction at 50 °C, limiting the temperature rise and controlling the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Hydrogen peroxide (342 mL, 40 % in water, 4.80 mol, 1.25 equiv) was added slowly over a period of 15 min at 50 °C using a dosing pump (exothermic) and the reaction mixture was stirred at 50 °C for additional 15 min.']

Paper Title: Optimization of Manganese Coupling Reaction for Kilogram-Scale Preparation of Two Aryl-1,3-dione Building Blocks
Problem_Description: The acid‑catalyzed semi‑pinacol rearrangement of epoxide 30 with concentrated H₂SO₄ in toluene gave only 46 % yield of dione 31, limiting overall throughput.

Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several issues when scaling the p‑cresol synthesis: (1) the highly energetic diazonium intermediate posed an explosion risk if accumulated; (2) at temperatures above 20 °C the diazonium salt decomposed faster than it formed, lowering conversion; (3) nitration, sulfonation and azo‑coupling side‑reactions generated up‑to 12 % impurities, reducing overall yield and product purity; (4) excess nitrous acid from sodium nitrite generated nitric acid, causing nitration of both product and solvent; (5) high acid concentration promoted sulfonation of p‑cresol; (6) viscous crude oil stuck in the downstream tube, causing pressure spikes and pump shutdown; (7) uncontrolled pressure rise in the reactor threatened safety; (8) the traditional batch process required long residence times (hours) and gave only 75‑80 % isolated yield; (9) the stoichiometry of NaNO₂ to p‑toluidine needed fine‑tuning for consistent conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: To address these problems the team implemented: (1) a fully continuous‑flow reactor network that never allows the diazonium salt to accumulate, dramatically improving safety; (2) careful temperature control of the diazotization step (20 °C, τ₁ = 20 s) to stay below the decomposition threshold; (3) addition of a slight excess of aqueous urea upstream of hydrolysis to scavenge nitrous/nitric acid, which suppressed nitration (<0.5 % S₁); (4) dilution of the diazonium feed (≤2 % salt) and reduction of sulfuric‑acid concentration, which eliminated sulfonation (S₂); (5) raising the hydrolysis temperature to 130 °C (τ₃ ≈ 30 s) to increase the hydrolysis rate relative to azo coupling, dropping S₃ from 12 % to 7 %; (6) introduction of a second organic phase (toluene, later replaced by cyclohexane) to create a biphasic flow, lowering viscosity and preventing tube fouling; (7) installation of a 145 psi back‑pressure regulator and pumps with automatic shut‑down to keep pressure within safe limits; (8) conversion of the whole sequence to continuous flow, compressing total residence time to 70 s and raising isolated yield to 91 %; (9) fine‑tuning the molar flow ratio of NaNO₂ to p‑toluidine to 1.02, which gave the highest conversion.

Paper Title: Enabling the Multigram Synthesis of (2-Cyclooctyn-1-yloxy)acetic Acid

Paper Title: Enabling the Multigram Synthesis of (2-Cyclooctyn-1-yloxy)acetic Acid
Problem_Description: During the dibromocyclopropanation of cycloheptene, incomplete conversion left residual cycloheptene as the major impurity, indicating mass‑transfer limitations in the reaction mixture.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors increased the base equivalents and used efficient mechanical stirring (anchor‑style stirrer) to enhance mass transfer, and replaced pentane with hexane to lower flammability while maintaining comparable solvent properties. These changes gave complete conversion and allowed the crude product to be carried forward without purification.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A detailed analysis of the crude product stream … revealed that the starting cycloheptene was the main contaminant as the result of an incomplete conversion.” (p‑2)  
• “We found that a slight increase in the base stoichiometry coupled with the use of efficient mechanical stirring to facilitate mass transfer limitations directly led to improved conversion.” (p‑2)  
• “Moreover, pentane was replaced with hexane with the intent to reduce the hazards associated with the flammability and volatility of this solvent.” (p‑2)

Problem_Description: The original Matsuda–Heck protocol (Correia) required high palladium catalyst loadings (up to 7 mol %) and elevated reaction temperatures (up to 60 °C), which increase material cost and raise safety concerns on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A novel Pd(OAc)₂/AlPO₄ catalytic system was developed that operates with only 2 mol % Pd and at a reduced temperature of 40 °C, providing comparable or better yields while lowering catalyst consumption and thermal load.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "the synthetic approach suffers from the utilization of high catalyst concentrations up to 7 mol % and elevated temperatures up to 60 °C" (p. 2).

Problem_Description: Only electron‑rich aryldiazonium salts were reported as viable electrophiles, limiting the synthetic scope and the availability of suitable substrates for bis‑aryl‑olefin synthesis.
Solution_Description: The Pd(OAc)₂/AlPO₄ catalyst showed high activity toward a broader range of aryldiazonium salts, including electron‑deficient and deactivated substrates, thereby expanding the usable scope.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "only the bis‑arylation using electron‑rich aryldiazonium salts as electrophiles was reported" (p. 2).

Problem_Description: Nitro‑substituted cinnamic esters displayed poor solubility under the reaction conditions, leading to only mono‑arylated products and low overall yields.
Solution_Description: The authors noted the limitation and suggested that alternative solvents or co‑solvents could be required to improve solubility of nitro‑aryl substrates (solution not fully explored in the article).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "the diarylation of the nitro substituted aryldiazonium salts provided only monoarylated Heck products in excellent yields due to the modest solubility of the nitro cinnamic esters" (p. 8).

Problem_Description: Extended prereduction times of Pd(OAc)₂ before the Matsuda–Heck step decreased catalyst activity, lowering bis‑arylated product formation.
Solution_Description: DoE optimization identified a prereduction time of 34 min (at 25 °C) as optimal, preserving Pd(0) activity and maximizing bis‑arylated product yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "an extended prereduction time has a negative impact on the formation of bis‑arylated product" (p. 9).

Problem_Description: Increasing the molar amount of aryldiazonium salt beyond the optimum caused a negative impact on yield, likely due to mass‑transport limitations and inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: The DoE model established the optimal diazonium quantity (≈21.5 mmol for a 10 mmol substrate scale) to balance reactivity and mass transfer, improving reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "excessive usage of diazonium salt has a negative impact on the outcome" (p. 9).

Problem_Description: The original protocol required lengthy reaction times (several hours) and multiple work‑up steps (filtration, extractions, flash chromatography) that limited throughput.
Solution_Description: Implementing a 40 °C isothermic reaction in an automated EasyMax batch reactor reduced reaction time to 3.5 h and streamlined isolation by simple filtration and solvent extraction.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "All reactions were run over 3.5 h… After separation of the catalyst, quenching with water, and extraction with methylene chloride…" (p. 11).

Problem_Description: Matsuda–Heck reactions are highly exothermic due to the rapid oxidative addition of aryldiazonium salts, posing heat‑removal challenges on scale.
Solution_Description: The protocol employs a rapid, controlled addition of the aryldiazonium salt after a 34 min prereduction step and raises temperature only to 40 °C, allowing safe heat management and preventing runaway exotherms.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "During the reaction… heat flow control and gas evolution were monitored" (p. 12).

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The original Adachi‐type synthesis used 1,2‑diiodobenzene ($461/25 g) and 3‑(trimethylsilyl)‑phenylboronic acid ($257/5 g), which are very expensive, making the route unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors substituted these reagents with inexpensive commodity chemicals – 1,2‑dibromobenzene ($260/500 g) and 3‑methoxyphenylboronic acid ($100/100 g) – dramatically lowering material cost and improving availability.
Supporting_Evidence: “both the starting materials were very expensive… which resulted in low total yields… the improved practical synthetic route… starting from inexpensive commodity chemicals 1,2‑dibromobenzene ($260/500 g) and 3‑methoxyphenylboronic acid ($100/100 g) with high total yields of 48.6% and 47.2%, respectively.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The Adachi route suffered from low conversion in the bromination and Scholl oxidation steps, giving an overall poor yield for the key intermediate (17.6 %).
Solution_Description: The authors redesigned the substrate by using an o,p‑directing methoxy group (1,2‑bis‑(3‑methoxyphenyl)‑benzene) which stabilises the arenium cation intermediate, thereby facilitating the Scholl oxidation and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the bromine atom was a weakly deactivating substituent… could result in low conversion… o,p‑directing methoxy group could stabilise the arenium cation and lower the transition‑state energy… we employed 1,2‑bis‑(3‑methoxyphenyl)‑benzene as the substrate for the Scholl oxidation, which could be efficiently synthesised… in 96 % yield.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Scholl oxidation using FeCl₃ or DDQ gave unsatisfactory yields, and demethylation methods required very high temperatures (220 °C), presenting safety and efficiency concerns.
Solution_Description: An improved MoCl₅‑promoted Scholl oxidation was developed: two equivalents of MoCl₅ were added sequentially with a 24 h interval, affording the dimethoxy‑triphenylene in 82 % yield while operating at ambient temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: “1 equiv of MoCl₅ could not oxidise 5 completely… adding 2 equiv of MoCl₅ at once or separately in a short time generated unsatisfied yields. However, a good yield of 82 % could be achieved if the two equiv MoCl₅ were added at intervals of 24 h.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Demethylation with BBr₃ or pyridine·HCl required complicated work‑up procedures and high reaction temperatures, increasing operational risk and purification burden.
Solution_Description: The authors employed concentrated hydrobromic acid in acetic acid for demethylation, delivering the dihydroxy‑triphenylene quantitatively with a simple work‑up and without the need for high temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: “Thus, demethylation of 6 using concentrated hydrobromic acid in acetic acid gave 2,7‑dihydroxyl‑triphenylene 7 in quantitative yield, which further reacted… It was encouraging to find that pure products of both 6 and 7 could be separated easily with column chromatography free.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The final Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to afford BPyTP‑2 showed sub‑optimal conversion unless the reaction was run for an extended period.
Solution_Description: Extending the reflux time to 2.5 days increased the isolated yield of BPyTP‑2 to 97 % for the step (47.2 % overall), demonstrating that longer reaction time improves conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the mixture was stirred at refluxed temperature for 2.5 days… a slight yellow solid of 5.67 g in 97 % yield… It was worth mentioning that prolonging the reaction time could increase the yield of the last step.”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Electron Transport Material and Its Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Typical purification of intermediates required column chromatography, adding time, solvent use and cost.
Solution_Description: Both the dimethoxy‑triphenylene (6) and the dihydroxy‑triphenylene (7) could be isolated by simple slurry‑washing without chromatographic separation, streamlining the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was encouraging to find that pure products of both 6 and 7 could be separated easily with column chromatography free.”

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Intermediate 4 proved to be a low‑melting, tacky, intractable solid that could not be purified by conventional solvent‑crystallisation, leading to low isolated yield and impure final API.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to isolate the open‑ring intermediate 12 instead of 4; 12 crystallises readily from THF/toluene giving >99 % HPLC purity and high isolated yield, which then allowed clean downstream conversion to canagliflozin.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The intermediate 4 was a low melting tacky intractable solid in our hands that did not allow for any useful purification.","In contrast, intermediate 12 ... greatly eases the purification problems encountered in the conventional syntheses.","Crystallization of 12 from a mixture of THF and toluene afforded high HPLC purity (>99 %) of compound 12 in 84 % yield."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Use of dichloromethane (DCM) and acetonitrile introduced safety hazards (low‑boiling, volatile, toxic) and incurred high solvent‑abatement cost at scale.
Solution_Description: Chlorobenzene was selected as a single high‑boiling solvent for the Friedel–Crafts and reduction steps, eliminating low‑boiling DCM, reducing vapor losses, and lowering overall solvent‑cost and handling hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: ["After examining the solvent screening results, chlorobenzene was found to be a suitable solvent for both Friedel–Crafts and hydride reduction reactions.","Its higher boiling point allows excellent recovery to be achieved… helps in reducing the cost and reduces issues around solvent abatement.","This avoids usage of low boiling DCM or hazardous acetonitrile."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: When the chlorobenzene volume was low, the reaction mixture became a thick slurry, leading to poor stirring, low conversion and reduced yield in the Friedel–Crafts stage.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run with 12 vol of chlorobenzene (instead of ≤8 vol) to keep the mixture homogeneous, improving conversion and giving yields >90 % and purity >80 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ["At lower volume of chlorobenzene, poorer yield and purity were observed, while, at higher volume of chlorobenzene (>8 vol), the obtained purity and yield were >90 % and >80 % respectively.","The reason… thick slurry… difficult to stir… lower conversion and lower yield.","we opted to use 12 volumes of chlorobenzene and 4.25 equiv of TMDS for this reaction."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Deshalo impurity 13 formed (~10 % in early screens) during the n‑BuLi mediated C‑arylation, reducing product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: DoE identified that lower reaction temperatures (–75 °C to –50 °C) and a controlled excess of n‑BuLi (1.4–1.6 equiv) suppress impurity 13, delivering >99 % purity and >80 % yield of intermediate 12.
Supporting_Evidence: ["During screening… around 10 % of potential deshalo impurity 13 was observed.","The purity of 12 is a function of reaction temperature and amount of n‑BuLi.","A moderate volume of THF (∼7 vol) … to control the formation of impurity 13 up to <6 %.","Optimization of temperature and n‑BuLi equivalents gave >80 % yield and >99 % purity."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Furanose impurity 14 formed during the final reductive elimination, compromising API purity and requiring additional purification steps.
Solution_Description: Control of reaction temperature (–45 °C to –35 °C) together with increasing BF₃·Et₂O loading (1.75–2.0 equiv) reduced impurity 14 to <0.1 % and raised purity >96 %; TES was employed as a cheaper silane hydride source.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The major impurity 14 forms during the final reduction step.","Formation … depends on the reaction temperature and the amount of BF₃·Et₂O.","A lower reaction temperature (−45 to −35 °C) … to obtain higher purity and to control the formation of impurity 14.","Increasing the amount of BF₃·Et₂O … decreasing impurity 14.","We have used a relatively less expensive and readily available silane, TES, for this reduction reaction."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: The originally employed sterically hindered silane for the stereoselective reduction was expensive and limited the process economics.
Solution_Description: Triethylsilane (TES), a cheaper, readily available silane, was substituted for the expensive sterically hindered silane, maintaining high β‑selectivity while reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We have used a relatively less expensive and readily available silane, TES, for this reduction reaction to obtain canagliflozin 1 with high selectivity for the β‑anomer."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Performing isolation and purification after each of the six steps increased batch time, waste generation and lowered the overall process yield (~35 %).
Solution_Description: The first three steps (acylation, reduction, C‑arylation) and the last two steps (methoxylation, reduction) were telescoped, eliminating intermediate work‑ups, increasing overall yield to ~47 % and reducing process time.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The process was telescoped by avoiding the isolation of intermediates in the first three and last two steps.","A telescopic strategy was executed for the first three and last two steps in a total six‑step sequence.","The overall yield of the telescoped process is increased from 35 % to 47 %."]

Paper Title: Synthesis and Optimization of Canagliflozin by Employing Quality by Design (QbD) Principles
Problem_Description: Final API required removal of residual furanose‑14, deshalo‑13 and other trace impurities to meet ICH specifications (>99.8 % purity).
Solution_Description: A two‑stage purification using a DCM/isopropyl‑acetate solvent system followed by crystallisation from MTBE/water effectively removed >99.9 % of all impurities, delivering API of >99.8 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We screened different solvents and mixtures… a combination of DCM and isopropyl acetate was suitable to attain purity >99.80%.","The crude isolation and purification process for the final stage is highly efficient and capable enough to wash up to 10 % of furanose impurity 14 to the extent of less than 0.1%."]

Paper Title: A New Synthetic Route to Avibactam: Lipase Catalytic Resolution and the Simultaneous Debenzylation/Sulfation
Problem_Description: Previous reported routes (Routes A, B, C) gave very low overall yields (≈ 9‑11 %), required many steps (long synthetic procedures), used expensive double‑chiral piperidine starting materials, and employed hazardous reagents such as diphosgene, leading to cumbersome purifications.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a new synthetic route (Route D) that starts from the inexpensive and readily available ethyl‑5‑hydroxy‑picolinate, avoids the ring‑opening/cyclisation steps of earlier routes, and therefore cuts cost, length and exposure to toxic reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
["In this process, double‑chiral piperidine derivatives were used … with about 9.0 % total yields… raw materials … are expensive and a number of environmentally undesirable reagents … are required.",
"The Wockhardt developed route B … total yield of about 11.0 %… drawbacks limiting the large‑scale synthesis: (a) a long synthetic procedure, (b) complicated purification process, and (c) the employment of excessive environmentally unfriendly reagents such as diphosgene.",
"Three key changes are made: (1) the commercially available and affordable ethyl‑5‑hydroxy‑picolinate was used as the starting material, avoiding the ring‑opening and carbonized cyclization reaction steps used in previous reported routes.",
"An efficient synthesis of avibactam was completed in 10 steps and 23.9 % overall yield."]

Paper Title: A New Synthetic Route to Avibactam: Lipase Catalytic Resolution and the Simultaneous Debenzylation/Sulfation
Problem_Description: A direct chemical hydrogenation of intermediate 3 to the protected piperidine 5 gave poor stereoselectivity (cis/trans d.r. ≈ 1:1), leading to low usable yield of the desired enantiomer.
Solution_Description: A lipase‑catalyzed kinetic resolution using Lipozyme CALB was employed, delivering the (2S,5S)‑hydroxy‑piperidine acid 4 as a single enantiomer (d.r. ≥ 99:1) and enabling a higher overall isolated yield for the three‑step sequence (42.9 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
["Chemical catalytic methods to prepare 5 directly from 3 were also tried, but the stereoselectivity is relatively poor (d.r. ≈ 1:1).",
"The crude 3 underwent the lipase (Lipozyme CALB)-catalyzed resolution to successfully give compound 4 as a single enantiomer with d.r. ≥ 99:1.",
"Overall, compound 5 was obtained using relatively environmental friendly methods, and the total yield for the above three steps is up to 42.9 %."]

Paper Title: A New Synthetic Route to Avibactam: Lipase Catalytic Resolution and the Simultaneous Debenzylation/Sulfation
Problem_Description: Attempts to install the urea moiety directly on compound 9 using triphosgene or alternative phosgenating agents (CDI, chloroformates) failed, giving either no reaction or very low conversion, and involved toxic reagents.
Solution_Description: The nitrogen atoms were protected with a Boc or FMOC group; the FMOC‑protected route was selected. Using chlorobenzene as solvent under the new protecting‑group strategy afforded the urea product 10 in 89 % yield, eliminating the need for hazardous phosgene‑type reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Initially, we tried the direct urea‑unit formation using triphosgene, but it proved to be unsuccessful. Use of alternative phosgenating agents (such as CDI and various chloroformates) also failed.",
"We predict that the introduction of the Boc or FMOC protecting groups on the nitrogen might favor the formation of 10 directly from 9. … the FMOC approach was selected for further studies.",
"Many solvents were screened, and chlorobenzene was found to be suitable and facilitate the operable processing. Under the optimized reaction conditions, compound 10 with high quality was successfully prepared in 89 % yield."]

Paper Title: A New Synthetic Route to Avibactam: Lipase Catalytic Resolution and the Simultaneous Debenzylation/Sulfation
Problem_Description: Traditional sequences required separate debenzylation and sulfation steps, each followed by isolation and solvent‑intensive work‑ups, increasing cost, time, and waste generation.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot, simultaneous catalytic debenzylation (Pd/C, H₂) and sulfation (SO₃·NMe₃) was developed in a water/isopropanol (1:1) mixture, delivering the sulfonated intermediate 12 without intermediate purification and using a greener solvent system.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Typically, the simultaneous catalytic deprotection of the Bn group with Pd/C as catalyst and sulfation gave the intermediate 12.",
"Without further purification, compound 12 was subjected to a cation exchange reaction to give compound 13.",
"Another advantage of the transformation is that a more environmentally friendly water/isopropyl alcohol (1:1) system was used to replace other organic solvents."]

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: Batch nitration of TFMB with mixed acid is extremely fast and highly exothermic (‑73 to ‑253 kJ·mol⁻¹). To keep the reaction mild, the temperature must be kept at 263 K, the TFMB concentration is kept low and the acid is added over 28 h, making the process very time‑consuming and unsafe on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved the nitration to a continuous‑flow microreactor (micro‑channel reactor) which provides a large surface‑to‑volume ratio, rapid heat removal and precise control of reaction parameters, thus eliminating the need for long acid addition times and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: • "...the nitration reactions are often difficult to control due to its extremely fast rate and highly exothermic nature, with the reaction heat ranging from −73 to −253 kJ·mol⁻¹" (Intro).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature raises the selectivity of undesired meta‑nitro (m‑NB) and dinitration (DNB) products because the activation energies for ortho‑ and meta‑nitration become more accessible, leading to variability in product distribution.
Solution_Description: The temperature was optimized (e.g., kept at 273 K) to suppress formation of m‑NB and DNB while maintaining high conversion, thereby stabilizing selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "With the increase of reaction temperature, the selectivity of p‑NB decreases, while those of m‑NB and o‑NB increase… higher reaction temperature would be conductive to promote the ortho‑ and meta‑nitrations" (2.1.1).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: Short residence times give incomplete TFMB conversion, whereas long residence times lead to over‑nitration and side‑product formation; mass‑transfer limitations in the micro‑channel further hinder conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Residence time was tuned by changing channel length and flow rates; a packed‑bed microreactor (quartz sand microparticles) was introduced to improve interfacial area and mass transfer, allowing full conversion without excessive side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Residence time is another important parameter which affects the reagent conversion and product selectivity… a longer residence time will result in a higher conversion of TFMB" (2.1.2).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: During scale‑up (Strategy A) a sharp temperature rise in the first coiler caused high DNB formation, indicating insufficient heat removal and a safety risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The size of packed quartz sand in the first coiler was increased (Φ3 × 3 mm) to reduce interfacial area, lower the reaction rate and distribute heat more evenly; further adjustments of particle size were made to balance conversion and temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The temperature rise of the flowing stream in the first coiler was found to be evidently high due to the fast nitration reaction… To avoid the sharp temperature rise, the reaction should proceed in a controlled manner" (Strategy A).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: Enlarging the packed particle size (Φ3 × 3 mm) in Strategy A entry 3 decreased TFMB conversion to 95.29 % because the slower reaction rate reduced heat generation but also lowered overall conversion.
Solution_Description: A compromise was reached by selecting particle sizes that keep the reaction fast enough for high conversion while still mitigating the temperature spikes, thereby preserving yield and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Unfortunately, the conversion of TFMB also decreased (95.29 %), which demonstrated that enlarging the size of the packed particles would slow down the reaction rate and further decrease the reaction heat" (Strategy A).

Paper Title: Process Development and Scale-up of the Continuous Flow Nitration of Trifluoromethoxybenzene
Problem_Description: Strategy B required precise temperature control (< ‑2 °C) to keep DNB formation low when scaling to kilogram‑scale, highlighting the need for better heat‑removal design.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A distributed packed‑tubular reactor with smaller diameter tubes and Φ2 × 2 mm quartz sand was employed; the reactor was immersed in a cold NaCl bath (‑9 °C) and temperature was actively controlled, yielding high conversion (99.6 %) and low by‑product levels.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A distributed design of the tubular reactors would be beneficial for the heat transfer of the reaction… controlling the reaction temperature below ‑2 °C… 91.08 % of p‑NB, 7.05 % of o‑NB, and only trace of m‑NB (0.08 %) and DNB (1.34 %) were obtained" (Strategy B).

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The key transamination substrate (compound 9) showed poor solubility in the aqueous buffer required for the transaminase, forcing the use of high concentrations of DMSO (up to 1:1 DMSO/H₂O) which limited reaction concentration and throughput.
Solution_Description: The reaction medium was adjusted to contain a controlled amount of DMSO to improve substrate solubility, and the transaminase was engineered (directed evolution) to tolerate higher DMSO levels while retaining activity, enabling higher substrate concentrations.
Supporting_Evidence: “the enzyme was engineered to tolerate higher DMSO concentration in order to avoid limitations due to low substrate solubility under the more aqueous conditions used previously; the lactam formation minimizes the reaction reversibility and drives the equilibrium towards the product.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The initial transaminase variant ATA‑301 gave only 38 % conversion even at high enzyme loading, resulting in low overall yield and inconsistent performance.
Solution_Description: A directed‑evolution campaign with Codexis generated improved variants (CDX‑017, ATA‑401, ATA‑404, ATA‑412, ATA‑426) that increased conversion to >90 % and diastereomeric ratio to 61:1, providing a robust, high‑yielding biocatalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “ATA‑301 as an initial lead providing the desired syn‑lactam 10 with a 7:1 dr and >99 % ee at C‑6. Unfortunately, the activity of the enzyme was low and afforded only 38 % conversion… The first round of evolution resulted in a variant that produced 10 with an ∼9‑fold increase in dr to 61:1… In the subsequent rounds of evolution, we continuously improved the transaminase’s reactivity… final variant ATA‑426 afforded the desired lactam 10 in 92 % assay yield and 61:1 dr in <24 h.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: Alkylation of mesylate 6 was sluggish; the mesylate rapidly eliminated to alkene 7, and the desired product 8 formed in modest yield due to competing conjugate addition of the enolate of 4‑bromo‑phenyl‑acetone.
Solution_Description: The alkene 7 was isolated before the alkylation step and the base amount was optimized to 0.5 equiv Cs₂CO₃ in DMSO, giving an 85 % isolated yield of 8 under the refined conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was subsequently found that mesylate 6 was rapidly converted to alkene 7 under the alkylation conditions… It was found to significantly improve the alkylation step offering an 85 % yield when enolization was performed with 0.5 equiv of Cs₂CO₃ in DMSO.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The N‑alkylation of lactam 10 with trifluoroethyl triflate generated a substantial amount of the undesired N,N‑dialkylated by‑product 12, complicating isolation of the mono‑alkylated product 11.
Solution_Description: An excess of lithium‑tert‑butoxide base and the alkylating reagent were used, and the reaction was carried out at sub‑ambient temperature (16–22 °C), which suppressed dialkylation and afforded a 94 % conversion with a 9.3:1 ratio of 11 to 12, leading to an 87 % isolated yield of 11.
Supporting_Evidence: “The best base was lithium tert‑butoxide… optimization showed that an excess of LiOtBu and triflate were required to achieve a high conversion in THF. The reaction was sensitive to temperature, and it was found that the best results were achieved when it was performed at subambient temperatures… optimal levels of selectivity were observed, with the reaction affording a 94 % conversion after 18 h. The ratio of 11 to 12 was 9.3 to 1, and the yield of 11 was 87 %.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The original spiro‑acid route employed a SEM protecting group (expensive) and suffered polymerization during the double‑alkylation/spirocyclization sequence, raising safety and scalability concerns.
Solution_Description: The protecting group was switched to a cheaper tert‑butyl group and the synthetic sequence was redesigned to a stepwise bond‑formation route, using a novel doubly‑quaternized phase‑transfer catalyst (22) that enabled mild, fast spirocyclization without polymerization, using less solvent and lower base loading.
Supporting_Evidence: “The N‑protecting group was switched from the relatively expensive SEM group to tert‑butyl… to avoid polymerization during the spirocyclization… the novel N,N′‑doubly quaternized PTC 22 was serendipitously discovered as the most potent catalyst… The spirocyclization with 22 required less solvent and only a slight excess of base… this novel bis‑quaternary PTC reaction is mild, fast, robust, and highly reproducible.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The C‑3 stereocenter in the lactam fragment existed as a 1:1 mixture of β/α diastereomers that readily epimerized under basic conditions, leading to inconsistent stereochemical outcomes.
Solution_Description: A crystallization‑induced diastereomeric transformation (CIDT) was employed: the crude mixture was treated with p‑toluic acid and 1 mol % 3,5‑dichlorosalicylaldehyde at 50 °C, precipitating the pure β‑isomer salt in 86 % yield and >99.6 % de.
Supporting_Evidence: “The stereochemistry of the C‑3 center in 13 was set by a crystallization induced diastereoselective transformation (CIDT)… when crude 13 was treated with p‑toluic acid in the presence of 1 mol % of 3,5‑dichlorosalicylaldehyde at 50 °C, crystals precipitated as the pure β‑isomer… in 86 % yield and with a 99.6 % de.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: The original amide‑coupling protocol (EDC/triethylamine/HOBt) caused >1 % epimerization of the newly formed amide bond, compromising product purity.
Solution_Description: The coupling was re‑optimized using EDC (1.2 equiv) with catalytic HOPO (0.1 equiv) at pH 6.0–6.5 in aqueous acetonitrile, eliminating epimerization; after reaction completion the product was directly crystallized from the crude stream, giving ubrogepant in 95 % isolated yield as the trihydrate.
Supporting_Evidence: “After the reaction was complete, the product could be directly crystallized by slow addition of the crude reaction stream into a mixture of ethanol and water… Ubrogepant 1 was isolated directly as its trihydrate in a 95 % yield with excellent optical and chemical purities… Over 1 % of epimerization was observed under the original coupling conditions… The coupling reaction proceeded smoothly with EDC (1.2 equiv) and a catalytic amount of HOPO, without epimerization at the α carbon center of the newly formed amide bond.”

Paper Title: Practical Asymmetric Synthesis of a Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide (CGRP) Receptor Antagonist Ubrogepant
Problem_Description: Early PTC‑catalyzed spirocyclizations required strict stirring, high temperature, and large excess of base, leading to poor reproducibility and potential exothermic runaway on scale.
Solution_Description: Implementing the doubly‑quaternized PTC 22 reduced the required solvent volume and base excess, delivering >94 % ee and 87 % isolated yield with a mild, fast, and robust protocol suitable for large‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: “The ease of reaction is in direct contrast to monoquaternized PTC catalyzed reactions which often require strict reaction conditions, such as well controlled stirring rate, temperature, high base concentrations and high catalyst loading; this novel bis‑quaternary PTC reaction is mild, fast, robust, and highly reproducible. Employing these conditions on scale gave the desired spiro compound 23 (94.4 % ee with 100 % assay yield) in an 87 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: The previously reported synthetic route used a Pd‑catalysed coupling that left a palladium residue >20 ppm, which is not acceptable for API manufacture and also required an expensive palladium catalyst.
Solution_Description: A completely new convergent synthesis was developed that avoids any Pd‑coupling step, thereby eliminating metal‑contamination concerns and the cost of palladium reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: • “This procedure gave a Pd residue >20 ppm, which does not conform to API preparation.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: During the preparation of intermediate 12, higher equivalents of KOH or inappropriate temperature gave extensive side‑product formation and reduced isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The optimal conditions were found to be 0.4 equiv KOH (stoichiometric change), ethanol as the solvent, and 78 °C (temperature optimisation), which gave an isolated yield of 83 % for 12.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Enhancing the molar ratio of KOH will consume more dicyandiamide … the isolated yield was reduced …”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
