Problem_Description: A one‑pot addition of 12, 13 and NaH gave only ~40 % isolated yield and generated foam when the temperature reached ≈50 °C, indicating mixing/phase‑behavior problems.
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑designed so that a solution of 12 and 13 in DMF was added via a peristaltic pump to the NaH suspension over 2 h at 65 °C, preventing foam formation and improving yield to 77 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “when the materials were mixed (one‑pot operation)… isolated yield was only around 40 %.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: Using weak bases (TEA or K₂CO₃) failed to generate the desired product in the 12 → 14 conversion.
Solution_Description: Switching to NaH as the base (stronger, stoichiometric change) gave a clean reaction and a 41 % yield that was later increased to 77 % after further optimisation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “TEA or K₂CO₃ was too weak to give product, while NaH/DMF would give a better yield.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: Intermediate 14 and the reduced product 6 showed poor solubility in alcohol solvents, hindering the hydrogenation step.
Solution_Description: Tetrahydrofuran (THF) was employed as the reaction medium for the hydrogenation, providing sufficient solubility for both substrate and product.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Because material 14 and product 6 have poor solubility in alcohol solvents, THF … was chosen as the solvent.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: A one‑pot approach to form the phenyl carbamate (15) from 6, 16 and triphosgene in acetonitrile failed completely.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to a stepwise carbamate formation using phenyl carbonochloridate under dichloromethane, which afforded the intermediate 15 in 91 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “a one‑pot method … treating compounds 6, 16, and triphosgene … failed.”

Paper Title: New and Practical Synthesis of Gedatolisib
Problem_Description: The NaH‑mediated coupling of 12 with 13 is highly exothermic, generating gases and heat that could pose safety risks on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reaction calorimetry, gas‑evolution monitoring and a controlled peristaltic‑pump addition were employed to keep temperature and pressure within safe limits, demonstrating a controllable process.
Supporting_Evidence: • “To investigate the safety of this step, the reaction calorimetry, gas evolution rate, and volumetric measurement data were detected.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: In the early route the Miyaura borylation of bromide 3 gave incomplete conversion, requiring multiple charges of Pd(dppf)Cl₂. The high palladium (and iron) loadings made metal removal difficult and forced several labor‑intensive solid‑phase scavenging and chromatography steps.
Solution_Description: The route was changed to a tandem borylation–Suzuki sequence using tetrahydroxydiboron and the commercially available AtaPhos‑PdCl₂ catalyst (0.2 mol %). The low‑loading catalyst eliminated the need for repeated catalyst charges and reduced metal residues, simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Incomplete conversion, which was often observed during the borylation step … necessitated additional catalyst charges of Pd‑(dppf)Cl₂.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of the ethyl ester 7 with NaOH/EtOH produced the desired acid 1 but also generated significant solvolysis by‑products (ethyl carbamate 8 and heteroarylamine 9). To keep these impurities acceptable the hydrolysis was stopped before full conversion, which lowered overall throughput.
Solution_Description: Potassium trimethylsilanolate (TMSOK) was employed as a milder base for the ester hydrolysis. The milder conditions gave full conversion with dramatically lower amounts of by‑products, allowing the reaction to run to completion without sacrificing yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Hydrolysis of the ethyl ester 7 using NaOH in EtOH gave … significant solvolysis by‑products … the reaction was stopped before full conversion … decreasing the overall throughput.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: A lithium‑halogen exchange followed by triisopropyl borate quench gave 75 % yield on ~100 g lab scale, but on manufacturing scale the yield became variable because of undesired protonolysis of the aryl‑Li intermediate.
Solution_Description: The n‑BuLi step was eliminated entirely. A one‑pot tandem borylation/Suzuki sequence using tetrahydroxydiboron and AtaPhos‑PdCl₂ was developed, providing reproducible high conversion without the hazardous organolithium reagent.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Variable yield was observed on manufacturing scale with significant undesired protonolysis of the intermediary aryl lithium.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: The previous route required high Pd loading (≥2 mol %) and multiple solid‑phase metal scavenging steps to meet metal‑spec limits, making the process expensive and operationally burdensome.
Solution_Description: Switching to AtaPhos‑PdCl₂ allowed the Suzuki coupling at 0.2 mol % Pd. Residual palladium was reduced to <20 ppm by an extractive aqueous N‑acetylcysteine wash, removing the need for extensive solid‑phase scavenging and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “By replacing Pd‑(dppf)Cl₂ with (AtaPhos)₂PdCl₂ … catalyst loading as low as 0.2 mol %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: For certain heteroaryl bromides (e.g., 3‑bromothiophene) the borylation gave low and variable yields due to dimeric biaryl side‑reaction.
Solution_Description: Increasing the equivalents of tetrahydroxydiboron to ≥3 equiv markedly improved yields for these challenging substrates, suppressing dimer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Increasing the stoichiometry of tetrahydroxydiboron to at least 3.0 equiv resulted in significant yield improvement.”

Paper Title: Development of a Concise Multikilogram Synthesis of LPA‑1 Antagonist BMS-986020 via a Tandem Borylation–Suzuki Procedure
Problem_Description: Early borylation attempts using traditional Miyaura conditions required excess diboron reagents and gave modest conversions, increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: Optimized the borylation to use only 1.2‑1.5 equiv of tetrahydroxydiboron in a MeOH/THF (30‑40 % v/v MeOH) co‑solvent system at 50‑55 °C, achieving near‑quantitative conversion with minimal reagent waste.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Near‑quantitative yield of boronic acid 10 with as low as 1.2 equiv of tetrahydroxydiboron.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original tetrazole‑10 synthesis used in‑situ generated hydrazoic acid (HN₃) from NaN₃/NH₄Cl at >100 °C in DMF.  Hydrazic acid is highly toxic, shock‑sensitive, and has a low detonation threshold; its boiling point (37 °C) and possible condensation in reactor plumbing raise explosion risk.  The reaction also produced ammonium azide as a by‑product, an additional energetic material.
Solution_Description: A water co‑solvent was introduced (DMF/water 2:1) and the temperature lowered to 90 °C.  The aqueous phase increased solubility of inorganic salts, desensitized any HN₃ in the gas phase and eliminated the need for high‑temperature conditions.  The modified protocol gave >99.5 % conversion in 16 h and isolated tetrazole 10 in 88–93 % yield with no detectable impact sensitivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The original conditions used to prepare tetrazole 10 relied on the treatment of nitrile 8 with hydrazoic acid generated in situ from NaN₃ and NH₄Cl in DMF at temperatures above 100 °C…Hydrazoic acid is highly toxic and is a sensitive energetic compound…low detonation threshold.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Quenching the original NaN₃/NH₄Cl reaction with nitrous acid produced a solid mass that clogged the reactor and impeded stirring.  The resulting slurry required extensive washing of the precipitated inorganic salts before tetrazole 10 could be isolated, reducing throughput and increasing labor.
Solution_Description: After reaction completion the mixture was diluted with water, then neutralised with nitrous acid under a controlled, cooled condition.  Switching the final acid quench from H₂SO₄ to aqueous HCl prevented formation of poorly soluble Na₂SO₄, giving a clean precipitation of tetrazole 10 that could be filtered and washed efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The excess azide was neutralized with nitrous acid…the quenching resulted in the formation of a solid mass that impeded stirring…necessitated extensive washing of the solids obtained by filtration before isolation of tetrazole 10.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, hydrazoic acid generated in the reactor headspace presented a serious safety hazard.  Uncontrolled release could lead to toxic exposure or explosive conditions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous nitrogen sweep was directed through a 25 % NaOH scrubber to trap HN₃.  Gas‑phase FTIR was used to monitor head‑space concentrations, confirming that only trace HN₃ (<200 ppm) formed.  The scrubber‑sweep system allowed safe operation without impacting conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The inlet and outlet were positioned at opposite sides of the glass lid, and the reactor content was swept with nitrogen to a 25% NaOH scrubber…The FTIR profile…showed that no detectable level of hydrazoic acid is present in the head space prior to heating…The average concentration of 410 ppm corresponds to a mass flow rate of 2.1 mg/h of hydrazoic acid.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Using ZnBr₂ as catalyst in THF/water gave modest conversions (<40 %) even after prolonged reflux, making the process too slow for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: Screening identified isopropanol (IPA) as a superior co‑solvent; ZnBr₂/IPA/water gave 89 % conversion in 24 h at 80 °C.  Adjusting the water : IPA ratio to 1 : 1 further improved conversion to 97 % in 48 h, providing a practical, high‑yielding route.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We were pleased to find that DMF and IPA both led to high conversion…we thus selected IPA as the cosolvent of choice for the system under evaluation.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The three‑component dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) of tetrazole 10 with acetaldehyde and isobutyric anhydride stalled when only 1 mol % of the chiral DMAP catalyst was used, leaving ~15 % starting material unreacted and giving inconsistent enantiomeric excess.
Solution_Description: Increasing the catalyst loading to 3 mol % and performing the DKR at 0 °C (instead of ambient) gave quantitative conversion and an ee of 92 % (↑93 % at –20 °C).  Dilution to 50 mL g⁻¹ was adopted to balance mixing and heat removal, delivering the hemiaminal ester 12 in quantitative yield and 97:3 er.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The use of 1 mol % of catalyst led to reaction stalling…For the enantioselectivity to be optimized on a large scale…Holding the reaction temperature at 0 °C led to improved enantioselectivity…Ultimately, 50 mL/g and 0 °C were chosen for scale‑up conditions.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the Negishi coupling of hemiaminal 12 with bromide 5, addition of the palladium catalyst generated a rapid temperature spike (31–47 °C in 1 min), risking uncontrolled reaction rates and potential decomposition of the base‑labile hemiaminal.
Solution_Description: The Pd catalyst was premixed with ligand and added as a pre‑formed slurry under nitrogen, allowing the temperature to be held at 45–50 °C after the initial exotherm.  The reaction time (25 min) and temperature were tightly controlled to achieve 96.5 % conversion without degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The mixture was warmed to 45–50 °C for 25 min…After 10 min, the assay showed 96.5 % conversion…The addition of palladium catalyst created an exotherm (31–47 °C over 1 min).”

Paper Title: A Scalable Route for the Regio- and Enantioselective Preparation of a Tetrazole Prodrug: Application to the Multi-Gram-Scale Synthesis of a PCSK9 Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Final isolation of the enantiopure hemiaminal 12 and the Negishi coupling product 13 required chromatography on chiral support, which is labor‑intensive, costly, and unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors note that further optimization of the acylation and coupling steps would be required to avoid the late‑stage chromatography, suggesting future work on alternative protecting groups or telescoped sequences, but no concrete solution was implemented in this study.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Chromatography on chiral support was required to purge the undesired enantiomer…Further optimization of the acylation would be required to avoid chromatography.”

Paper Title: Process Safety Assessment of the Iron-Catalyzed Direct Olefin Diazidation for the Expedient Synthesis of Vicinal Primary Diamines
Problem_Description: All of the isolated vicinal diazides (3, 6‑9) are moderately impact‑sensitive, as shown by the fall‑weight (drop‑weight) test, making their isolation and handling a safety liability on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors re‑designed the workflow so that the crude diazide is not isolated. After the iron‑catalyzed diazidation the reaction mixture is directly reduced (PPh₃) and protonated (TsOH) to give the diaminium salt, which is then isolated by simple recrystallisation. This telescoped sequence eliminates the need for chromatographic purification of the hazardous diazide intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “All of the aforementioned diazides are moderately sensitive to the DTW….” (p 9) 
• “Guided by these process safety studies … we improved our original … workup procedure, such that purification of diazide intermediates can be excluded and the diaminium salts can be directly isolated through recrystallization.” (p 11) 
• Scheme 4 shows the gram‑scale indene diazidation/diamination sequence that excludes chromatography purification.

Paper Title: Process Safety Assessment of the Iron-Catalyzed Direct Olefin Diazidation for the Expedient Synthesis of Vicinal Primary Diamines
Problem_Description: Azido‑iodinane 1b, a commonly used azide‑transfer reagent, undergoes a violent exothermic decomposition beginning at 126 °C (ΔH = ‑417 kJ mol⁻¹), raising concerns about uncontrolled energy release if it were to accumulate during the iron‑catalyzed diazidation.
Solution_Description: The process employs bench‑stable benziodoxole 1a as the stoichiometric oxidant instead of 1b. 1a is thermally robust (melts at 175 °C and does not decompose until 245 °C).  The reaction is run at ambient temperature with low catalyst loading (5 mol % Fe(OAc)₂), thereby avoiding any exotherm associated with high‑temperature decomposition of 1b.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Azidoiodinane 1b … strong decomposition starting at 126 °C … ΔH = ‑417 kJ mol⁻¹.” (p 7) 
• “Benziodoxole 1a … starts to melt at 175 °C and does not decompose until 245 °C.” (p 7) 
• “The Fe(OAc)₂‑catalyzed diastereoselective indene diazidation … at room temperature in good yield.” (p 5) 
• Scheme 1 and Scheme 2 illustrate the use of 1a rather than 1b.

Paper Title: Process Safety Assessment of the Iron-Catalyzed Direct Olefin Diazidation for the Expedient Synthesis of Vicinal Primary Diamines
Problem_Description: Prior to scale‑up there was insufficient information on the thermal and mechanical stability of the reagents, intermediates and the reaction mixture, which could mask hidden hazards.
Solution_Description: A comprehensive process‑safety assessment was performed using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and drop‑weight testing on every component (Fe(OAc)₂, L1, TMSN₃, 1a, 1b, diazides, diaminium salts) as well as on a ‘blank’ reaction mixture mimicking the catalytic system.  The data demonstrated thermal stability up to >300 °C and low impact sensitivity for the bulk reagents, providing a safety basis for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis of the reagents, products, and intermediates …” (p 4) 
• “The drop weight test (DWT) … all samples were analyzed by dropping a 5 kg weight from 0.8 m.” (p 9) 
• Figures 2 and 4 present DSC curves and Dewar‑test results showing minimal exotherm (ΔTₐd ≈ 1.9–4.2 °C).

Paper Title: Process Safety Assessment of the Iron-Catalyzed Direct Olefin Diazidation for the Expedient Synthesis of Vicinal Primary Diamines
Problem_Description: The original protocol required chromatographic isolation of the diazide intermediate, a step that is labor‑intensive and exposes operators to a mechanistically impact‑sensitive material.
Solution_Description: The work‑up was redesigned so that after the diazidation the reaction mixture is directly reduced and protonated, allowing the final diaminium salt to precipitate and be isolated by simple filtration/recrystallisation.  This telescoped approach removes the hazardous chromatography step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Guided by these process safety studies … we improved our original … workup procedure, such that purification of diazide intermediates can be excluded.” (p 11) 
• Scheme 4 (Gram‑Scale Indene Diazidation/Diamination Sequence) shows the single‑pot conversion without any intermediate purification.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: The Michael addition of benzylamine to the Morita–Baylis–Hillman adduct gave a mixture of trans‑ and cis‑isomers with a low trans‑to‑cis dr (72:28 at rt, 82:18 at 0 °C). The trans‑isomer (rac‑4) is an oily liquid while the undesired cis‑isomer (rac‑4′) is a crystalline solid, making isolation of the desired product difficult and resulting in low effective yield.
Solution_Description: Screened solvents and found MeOH to give the best dr; lowering the temperature to 0 °C improved the dr to 82:18. The trans‑isomer was isolated as a maleic‑acid salt (rac‑4·MA) which precipitated as a white solid, enabling efficient removal of the cis‑isomer and affording the product in 80 % isolated yield with 95:5 dr.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The solvent screening showed that MeOH was the best solvent and gave rac‑4 in 72:28 dr at room temperature.”; 2. “When the reaction temperature was decreased to 0 °C, the dr increased up to 82:18.”; 3. “rac‑4 is an oily compound and the undesired cis isomer rac‑4′ is a crystalline solid.”; 4. “Screening of acids showed that maleic acid (MA) formed a good salt … isolation of the salt was effective for purging the cis isomer.”; 5. “rac‑4·MA was isolated in 80% yield with 95:5 dr from rac‑3.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: During the reduction of rac‑4 to rac‑5 using CaCl₂/NaBH₄, the order of addition was critical. Adding CaCl₂ to NaBH₄ caused vigorous gas evolution and a rapid exotherm, leading to transesterification and low yield of the desired alcohol.
Solution_Description: The reagents were added in the reverse order: NaBH₄ portionwise to a suspension of CaCl₂ at 0 °C, generating Ca(BH₄)₂ in situ before adding rac‑4. This controlled the exotherm, prevented side‑reactions, and afforded rac‑5 in 85 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “When 5.0 equiv of NaBH₄ was added portionwise to 2.5 equiv of CaCl₂ … gave rac‑5 in 85% yield.”; 2. “In contrast, when CaCl₂ was added to NaBH₄ … vigorous gas evolution and rapid exotherm were observed.”; 3. “Probably due to the failure of generation of Ca(BH₄)₂, addition … gave ethyl ester … as the main product.”; 4. “The order of addition of reagents was found to be crucial.”; 5. “On completion of the reaction led by the addition of reagents in the proper order, the reaction mixture was quenched …”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: Reduction of lactam 8 with AlCl₃/LiAlH₄ was hazardous on scale, and attempts to use Red‑Al gave poor reproducibility and generated a dechlorinated by‑product that was difficult to remove.
Solution_Description: A safer NaBH₄/I₂ reduction was adopted. In THF, 2.0 equiv I₂ was added dropwise at 0 °C followed by 4.2 equiv NaBH₄, giving oxazepane 9 in 91 % yield without formation of the dechlorinated by‑product, and the reaction proceeded to full conversion in 1 h.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Considering safety issues related to the use of LiAlH₄ on a large scale …”; 2. “When Red‑Al was used … the reduction did not proceed … poor reproducibility, forcing us to give up this reagent system.”; 3. “Finally, the NaBH₄/I₂ reagent system … was adopted … gave oxazepane 9 in 91% yield … without generation of the dechlorinated byproduct.”; 4. “A solution of 2.0 equiv of I₂ in THF was added dropwise at 0 °C … the reaction reached full conversion in 1 h.”; 5. “The reaction was completely quenched by dropwise addition of MeOH …”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: Methyl ester 12a (the 2‑pyridone‑3‑carboxylic acid methyl ester) was highly soluble in water, making aqueous work‑up and extraction problematic.
Solution_Description: The methyl ester was replaced with less‑water‑soluble isopropyl (12b) and n‑butyl (12c) esters. These derivatives were readily extracted with EtOAc and washed with water/brine, allowing isolation in 86 % yield each.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “workup was found to be difficult due to high solubility of 12a in water.”; 2. “Thus, we decided to synthesize isopropyl ester 12b and n‑butyl ester 12c, which were expected to have relatively low solubility in water.”; 3. “As expected, compounds 12b and 12c were amenable to extraction with EtOAc and washing with water/brine.”; 4. “12b and 12c were crystallized … to provide 12b and 12c in 86% yield and 86% yield, respectively.”; 5. Table of yields confirming the isolates.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: The SN2 reaction of mesylate 20 with 2‑pyridone‑3‑carboxylic acid esters gave comparable amounts of N‑alkylated product 16b and O‑alkylated product 16b′ (≈35 % each), resulting in low overall yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: Screening identified MeCN as the optimal solvent and a lower temperature (25–40 °C) to improve N‑selectivity. Under these conditions the reaction afforded the desired N‑alkylated product 16 in 75–77 % isolated yield after simple column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “both the nitrogen atom and the oxygen atom … gave 16b and 16b′ in 35% yield and 35% yield, respectively.”; 2. “MeCN was found to be the best solvent for the reaction (entry 1–6).”; 3. “when the reaction temperature was decreased to 25–40 °C, the N,O‑selectivity increased.”; 4. “Finally, the reaction was conducted in MeCN at 25–40 °C to give the desired product 16 in 75–77% yields after column chromatographic separation.”; 5. Table 1 entries 9–11 confirming the improved selectivity and yield.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: Intermediate 9, obtained after reduction, is an oily liquid that proved difficult to isolate and purify, hindering downstream processing.
Solution_Description: The oily intermediate 9 was converted in situ to the hydrochloride salt 15·HCl by treatment with 4 M HCl in EtOAc (40–50 °C). The resulting solid salt precipitated and was isolated by filtration in 76 % overall yield with >98 % purity, providing a handle for subsequent steps.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Since 9 is also an oily compound and was found to be difficult to isolate, we decided to convert 9 to another isolable intermediate …”; 2. “treatment of the obtained EtOAc solution of 9 with 3.0 equiv of 4 M HCl in EtOAc at 40–50 °C for 2 h gave 15·HCl as a white solid, which was easily isolated by filtration.”; 3. “Although the synthesis of 15·HCl … was achieved through fully telescoped processes, 15·HCl was isolated in good yield (total 76%) with good purity.”; 4. “HPLC purity: 98.2 area % … Optical purity: >99% ee.”; 5. Procedure details confirming the salt formation.

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Peripherally Selective Noradrenaline Reuptake Inhibitor Possessing a Chiral 6,7-
Problem_Description: The final drug candidate 1 exhibited very low solubility in common organic solvents, making its extraction after hydrolysis of 17b extremely difficult.
Solution_Description: Hydrolysis of 17b was performed with concentrated HCl (3 equiv) in 2‑butanone at 70 °C. The product precipitated as its HCl salt (1·HCl) during the reaction, allowing isolation by simple filtration after dilution with diisopropyl ether. The process gave 1·HCl in 84 % yield with >99.9 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “the extraction of 1 was found to be difficult due to low solubility of 1 in common organic solvents.”; 2. “we changed our strategy and tried to conduct the hydrolysis using hydrochloric acid in organic solvents and to isolate the generated hydrochloric acid salt 1·HCl by filtration.”; 3. “hydrolysis of 17b with 3.0 equiv of concentrated hydrochloric acid in 2‑butanone proceeded well at 70 °C, and precipitation of the desired 1·HCl was observed during the reaction.”; 4. “The reaction mixture was diluted with diisopropyl ether, and 1·HCl was isolated by filtration in 84% yield with excellent chemical and optical purity.”; 5. “Optical purity >99.9% ee (chiral HPLC condition D).”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Preparation of γ‑Butyrolactone Scaffolds from Renewable Fumaric and Itaconic Acids under Photosensitized Conditions
Problem_Description: Dimethoxy‑benzophenone (DMBP) showed poor solubility in isopropanol, forcing the use of low substrate concentrations (0.05 M) that limited overall productivity of the continuous‑flow photoaddition.
Solution_Description: Switch to benzophenone (BP) as the photosensitizer; BP is much more soluble (up to 0.04 M) allowing feed solutions of fumaric acid at 0.2 M and thus higher reaction throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Despite these promising results, the lower solubility of DMBP negatively affected the productivity of the continuous‑flow process since it imposed low concentrations of 1.”

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Traditional oxidative cyclizations of phenolic imines to benzoxazoles rely on strong, often hazardous oxidants, toxic solvents (e.g., CH₂Cl₂, toluene, EtOAc) and elevated temperatures, making the process unsafe and costly for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a heterogeneous OMS‑2 catalyst together with H₂O₂ (a green oxidant) and dimethyl carbonate (DMC, a biobased, non‑toxic solvent) to perform the oxidative cyclization at room temperature, eliminating the need for toxic reagents and high‑energy conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “Traditional methodologies... using acid or harsh reaction conditions… base additives, elevated reaction temperatures or toxic catalyst and reaction solvents were employed” (Intro, p. 2) ; “OMS‑2 was found to be an efficient and recyclable heterogeneous catalyst… H₂O₂ and biobased reagent dimethyl carbonate (DMC) were successfully employed as the environmentally friendly oxidant and solvent” (Abstract).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: When EtOH was used as solvent with OMS‑2, the reaction gave 85 % yield but produced a yellow pigment impurity, complicating product isolation.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium from EtOH to DMC eliminated the pigment formation and allowed the product to be isolated by simple catalyst filtration and solvent removal, avoiding column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using ethanol as the solvent… provided benzoxazole 2a in good yields… with some yellow pigment” (Results, Table 1, entry 3) ; “Delightedly, EtOH was successfully replaced by biomass‑derived reagent DMC… 78 % yield… without yellow pigment” (Results, Table 1, entry 11) ; “Without column chromatographic isolation, 95 % yield… was readily obtained by filtration of solid catalyst followed by removal of DMC” (Results).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: The reaction failed completely when water or ethanol was used as the solvent in the presence of H₂O₂, indicating poor compatibility of the aqueous oxidant with these solvents.
Solution_Description: Adopting DMC as the reaction solvent provided a medium in which H₂O₂ could be used efficiently, leading to full conversion and high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction did not proceed at all when EtOH or water was used as the reaction solvent in the presence of H₂O₂” (Results, Table 1, entry 12) ; “DMC was successfully replaced… H₂O₂ could be a highly efficient oxidant for the aerobic cyclization in DMC under mild conditions” (Results).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Various OMS‑2 preparations (different synthesis routes, ion‑exchanged forms) and other Mn oxides (AMO, α‑MnO₂) gave inconsistent or lower yields (70‑85 %).
Solution_Description: The authors retained the standard OMS‑2 (as prepared) as the optimal catalyst and focused on reaction condition tuning (solvent, oxidant, time) rather than alternative catalyst formulations.
Supporting_Evidence: “Several OMS‑2 materials… with different properties were tested, and the results were unfruitful” (Results, Table 1, entries 5‑8) ; “Amorphous manganese oxide (AMO) and α‑MnO₂ did not lead to higher yields” (Results, Table 1, entries 9‑10).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Using air as the oxidant required longer reaction times (12 h) and gave only ~40 % conversion (≈35 % yield).
Solution_Description: Replacing air with H₂O₂ dramatically accelerated the reaction, allowing full conversion and 95 % isolated yield in just 6 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “In air, the reaction provided nearly 40 % conversion and 35 % yield… H₂O₂ could accelerate the reaction significantly and offered full conversion … in 6 h” (Results, Fig. 1).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Low catalyst loading (5 mol %) and an inert N₂ atmosphere decreased the yield to ~70 % and required longer times.
Solution_Description: Increasing the catalyst loading to 10 mol % and conducting the reaction under air restored high conversion and 95 % yield within 6 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “Low catalyst loading (5 mol %) and N₂ atmosphere was deleterious… decreased reaction time also slashed the yield” (Results, Table 1, entries 16‑17) ; “Standard conditions (10 mol % OMS‑2, air) gave 95 % yield in 6 h” (Results, Table 1, entry 13).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Nitro‑substituted phenolic imines did not undergo the oxidative cyclization and were recovered unchanged, indicating incompatibility with the oxidative conditions.
Solution_Description: The authors note the limitation but do not provide a remedy within this study; the issue is highlighted as a scope limitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sensitive group nitro‑substituted phenolic imine could not react under the standard conditions, and it was recovered after the reaction.” (Scope discussion).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: N‑substituted 2‑aminophenol (3a) did not give product under the standard OMS‑2/H₂O₂/DMC system, even at elevated temperature, because OMS‑2 alone could not oxidatively dehydrogenate the C–N bond.
Solution_Description: Introducing Cu(OH)ₓ onto OMS‑2 (Cu‑OMS‑2) enabled oxidative dehydrogenation of 3a, and performing the reaction at 80 °C for 18 h gave up to 70 % yield of the desired benzoxazole.
Supporting_Evidence: “The standard catalytic system could not give desired product… then, the introduction of a transition metal in the OMS‑2 showed an obvious fruitful effect… Cu‑(OH)ₓ/OMS‑2 made the reaction proceed under heating conditions… yield … 70 %” (Results, Scheme 5, discussion).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Isolation of the benzoxazole product on gram‑scale could be cumbersome if conventional chromatography were required.
Solution_Description: The authors employed a simple filtration of the heterogeneous catalyst followed by removal of DMC under reduced pressure, yielding the product in 96 % isolated yield without any column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Without column chromatographic isolation, 95 % yield … was readily obtained by filtration of solid catalyst followed by removal of DMC under reduced pressure” (Results, gram‑scale synthesis).

Paper Title: OMS-2/H
Problem_Description: Repeated use of homogeneous catalysts or stoichiometric oxidants would be expensive and generate waste, limiting industrial feasibility.
Solution_Description: The heterogeneous OMS‑2 catalyst was recycled seven times in gram‑scale batches with no loss of activity, demonstrating cost‑effective and scalable operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The catalyst was readily recycled by filtration, washing, and drying… the catalyst was employed in seven successive runs without any loss of activity” (Results, Table 3).

Paper Title: An Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Hypericin Improved by a Low Power LED Based Photoreactor
Problem_Description: The protohypericin → hypericin photocyclization performed with high‑power, multifrequential lamps suffers severe photobleaching of hypericin, giving low isolated yields (≤10 % in early reports, 79 % with a 400 W mercury‑vapor lamp) and a rapid drop in product concentration on prolonged irradiation.
Solution_Description: A low‑power red‑LED photoreactor (0.6–12.5 mW cm⁻²) with a narrow, well‑defined emission band was employed, dramatically reducing the overlap with hypericin’s absorption band and limiting photobleaching; quantitative conversion (≈98 % yield) was achieved with minimal degradation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The photobleaching effect… is relatively pronounced… high‑power multifrequential mercury‑vapor lamp sources… lead to a dramatic yield decrease of 96 % (entry 7).”
“...low‑power LED light sources… enable the photoproduct to be obtained in excellent yield even with a prolonged irradiation time… minimized hypericin photobleaching effect.”
“Using a red‑LED based photoreactor… quantitative photoconversion of protohypericin to hypericin.”
“...the rate of the hypericin photobleaching effect is minimum relative to the time needed to reach its maximum yield irradiation with low‑power LED sources.”
“Table 1… red LED quantitative; blue LED 97 %...”

Paper Title: An Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Hypericin Improved by a Low Power LED Based Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Traditional scale‑up of hypericin uses open reaction vessels, large‑power lamps and organic solvents, creating fire, exposure and containment hazards when handling the photoreaction at multigram scale.
Solution_Description: A closed‑loop flow‑photoreactor was designed: modular aluminum chassis with heat‑sink, a transparent Pyrex zig‑zag flow cell, PEEK fittings and sealed tubing, allowing safe recirculation of the reaction mixture under inert atmosphere while irradiating with low‑power LEDs.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The closed system overcomes safety issues related to scale‑up hypericin preparation… which combines the use of open systems, organic solvents, and high‑power light sources.”
“The photoreactor… vertically arranged modular units… flow cell… PEEK fittings… recirculate the reagent into the flow cell… closed system.”
“...the present design… allows that the hypericin can be prepared in an even higher scale overcoming the limitations related to open irradiation systems previously reported, which requires a wide contact surface… limiting the large‑scale production.”
“...the photoreactor designed allows a solution to… the intrinsic effect of hypericin photobleaching… implying an increase in the yield… and consequently the final cost.”
“...the modular unit consists of a three‑bay aluminum chassis… multiple heat sink cooling system…”

Paper Title: An Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Hypericin Improved by a Low Power LED Based Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Earlier protocols did not describe a purification step for protohypericin, resulting in impure material and only ~70 % isolated yield after oxidative dimerization.
Solution_Description: Size‑exclusion chromatography on a Sephadex LH‑20 column using ethanol as eluent was introduced, affording pure protohypericin in 70 % yield suitable for the subsequent photoconversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
“In this precedent work the authors did not report a purification procedure for isolation of protohypericin… here we employed size‑exclusion column chromatography and ethanol as the mobile phase yielding 70 % of pure protohypericin.”
“…the crude product was purified by size‑exclusion column chromatography (SEC) using Sephadex LH‑20 matrix and EtOH as the mobile phase to yield 5.60 g (70 %) of purple crystals.”
“...the crude product was purified by size‑exclusion column chromatography… yielding 70 % of pure protohypericin.”
“...the protohypericin solution… was photoconverted to hypericin in excellent yield by employing the low‑power red‑LED photoreactor.”
“...the high‑efficiency photoconversion to both LED systems, and with reproducibility of the optimized experimental conditions set in microscale.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Hypericin Improved by a Low Power LED Based Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Hypericin’s commercial price is extremely high (≈ USD 815 / mg) due to poor overall yields and expensive, multistep synthetic routes, making large‑scale supply uneconomical.
Solution_Description: The integrated low‑power LED photoreactor, together with optimized reaction parameters (concentration, light dose, time), raised the overall isolated yield to ≈ 98 % on multigram scale, thereby dramatically reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The main problem presented in such a process resides in a low yield and degree of purity… incurring high commercial cost for the final product.”
“…hypericin multigram synthesis can be achieved in excellent yields, near 98 %, for all kinds of LEDs…".
“...hypericin multigram synthesis can be achieved in excellent yields, near 98 %, for all kinds of LEDs, dependent on all of these photonic parameters.”
“...the overall yield of hypericin synthesis provided by preceding works can be significantly improved if the protohypericin photocyclization reaction is performed with low‑power LED sources.”
“...quantitative photoconversion… yield: 4.85 g, 97 %.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Hypericin Improved by a Low Power LED Based Photoreactor
Problem_Description: Photoconversion efficiency was sensitive to the wavelength, light dose, concentration and exposure time; without systematic control the reaction gave inconsistent yields across different light sources.
Solution_Description: A systematic microscale screening of LED colors (blue, green, orange, red), doses, and reaction times was performed; optimal conditions (red LED, 0.6 mW cm⁻², 74 min) were selected and then transferred to gram‑scale, providing reproducible, high‑yielding conversions.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The intrinsic factors should be taken into account as wavelength emission and power LED light source, light dose, time of irradiation, prodrug concentration, and the spectral overlap…”
“...the microscopic studies… showed excellent yields (>97 %) independently of the LED type.”
“Table 1… red LED quantitative (629 nm, 0.6 mW cm⁻², 74 min).”
“...the gram‑scale supply experiments… high‑efficiency photoconversion to both LED systems, and with reproducibility of the optimized experimental conditions set in microscale.”
“...the optimized conditions for the photoconversion… did not result in a 20 % photodegradation of hypericin in the first 3 min of LED irradiation when compared to the usual light sources (mercury vapor‑lamp).”

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: Conventional equipment cannot safely combine high‑pressure, high‑temperature, and intense UV irradiation.  The high photo‑energy and reactive intermediates create severe safety constraints and the process traditionally requires long residence times (≈15 min) that limit productivity and lead to low conversion because the reaction must be stopped early to avoid side‑product formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A micro‑flow photoreactor built from a quartz capillary (0.5 mm ID) surrounded by reflective aluminium enables safe operation at 34 bar and up to 260 °C while delivering uniform UV illumination.  The short residence time (as low as 43 s) and the combined photo‑high‑p,T window shift the equilibrium toward product, dramatically increasing conversion and reducing side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: The process intensification by both photochemistry and thermal intensification may open additional options for photoreactions, yet is difficult to be combined in one step using conventional procedures and equipment because of safety risks.; "severe safety constraints are given due to the high photoenergy introduced and the highly reactive intermediates generated".; "previous comparable flow studies set the residence time at around 15 min".; "The main result is a reduction of the reaction time to 43 s, which means orders of magnitude shorter times than in the case of the same process carried out in batch".; "Quartz (HOQ: 90 % transparency at 280 nm) coil 0.5 mm ID and 3.2 mm ED was used…"; "The setup allows operation at a reaction temperature above a solvent’s boiling point (super heating)"

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: Diethyl ether, the solvent traditionally used for the photochemical step, forms dangerous peroxides at the high temperatures required for the combined process, posing safety and degradation hazards.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched to tert‑butyl‑methyl‑ether (t‑BME), which is sterically hindered and therefore far less prone to peroxide formation while remaining UV‑stable during the short irradiation periods.
Supporting_Evidence: "Due to the dangerous properties of ether peroxides generated by diethyl ether at high temperatures, in this study tert‑butyl methyl ether (t‑BME) is used to minimize as much as possible these inconveniences because of steric hindrance".; "The formation of tert‑butyl radicals as a result of thermal and UV‑irradiation is minimized due to the short residence times, and the absence of interfering compounds and oxygen inside the microchannels, which gives t‑BME supplementary UV‑stability".

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: 7‑Dehydrocholesterol (7DHC) begins to decompose significantly above 200 °C, limiting the usable temperature range and causing loss of material and reduced vitamin‑D₃ yield.
Solution_Description: The operating temperature was kept just below the decomposition threshold (≈200 °C) and the irradiation time was tuned (43 s – 5 min) to maximise conversion while avoiding thermal degradation of 7DHC and the product.
Supporting_Evidence: "Losses of 7DHC are relevant only above 200 °C. Also some important changes in the range between 240 and 260 °C were found. This could suggest a critical stability point for 7DHC in this range".; "Working conditions close to 200 °C were found to be optimal".; "The maximum conversions achieved are in the range 40–80 %… with a maximum yield of VD₃ around 20–25 %"; "Above this temperature… the amount of VD₃ decreases at the expense of increasingly formed side compounds… This phenomenon may be caused by VD₃ decomposition"; "The optimum conditions for P₃ include a 2 min IT… the thermal isomerization is also carried out"

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: Extended irradiation leads to the formation of tachysterol, lumisterol and other toxisterols, which lower selectivity and make isolation of vitamin‑D₃ difficult; conversion varies with residence time and temperature.
Solution_Description: Short irradiation times (43 s) were adopted to suppress side‑product formation, while a modest temperature (≈180–200 °C) provided sufficient thermal driving force for the equilibrium shift, effectively merging the photochemical and thermal steps into a single continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: "The process must be stopped after short irradiations because of the synthesis of tachysterol (T₃)… long irradiations can also give toxisterols".; "Below 200 °C the shorter the IT is, the lower the yield is. Nevertheless, the optimum conditions for P₃ include a 2 min IT, and therefore its conversion to mainly VD₃ can explain why the VD₃ yield at the 2 min IT is higher than the yield at the longest residence time above 200 °C".; "The selectivity of the reaction has a decreasing tendency… At low conversions (low temperatures) high selectivity is found, while at medium and especially high temperature the selectivity becomes very low because of the side compounds and decomposition".

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: The solubility of 7DHC in the reaction solvent limits the maximum achievable concentration, and higher concentrations could theoretically reduce light penetration, potentially decreasing conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Experiments were performed up to the solubility limit of 0.22 M (84.5 mg mL⁻¹) and showed that conversion remained essentially unchanged because the quartz micro‑capillary (≥90 % transmission at 280 nm) and internal reflective aluminium ensured uniform photon flux even at the highest concentration.
Supporting_Evidence: "The solubility limit of 7DHC in t‑BME was experimentally determined and found to be 0.22 M (84.5 mg mL⁻¹) at room temperature".; "the excellent light penetration in the quartz made microcapillaries (transparency above 90 % at 280 nm) … there are even at high concentration enough photons for reaction at any place within the capillary".; "Thus, the highest concentration used was close to the solubility limit the solvent used".

Paper Title: Microflow High-p,T Intensification of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: The relative importance of temperature, irradiation time and concentration on vitamin‑D₃ yield was not initially clear, leading to inconsistent optimisation.
Solution_Description: A principal‑component analysis (PCA) was performed on the experimental data, revealing that irradiation time accounts for 72 % of the variability and temperature for 28 %, while concentration has a negligible effect; this guided the focused optimisation of the key variables.
Supporting_Evidence: "PCA shows the irradiation time (IT) accounts for 72 % of the variability of the VD₃ yield, while the temperature only accounts for 28 %… concentration is in the centre of the axis, confirming it slightly contributes to the variability".

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Very low enantiomeric excess (<20 %) was obtained when attempting resolution of rac‑2 with various chiral acids, and acceptable material was only recovered after a single crystallisation from an already enantioenriched batch, indicating poor overall yield.
Solution_Description: A specific chiral HPLC method was developed and employed to separate the desired enantiomer from the racemic mixture, providing a reliable high‑purity isolation route.
Supporting_Evidence: “Very low ee’s were observed in the best cases (<20 %), and enantiopure material was only obtained after one crystallisation from enantioenriched (>75 % ee) material, suggesting an eutectic.”; “chiral HPLC was preferred and a specific method was developed to separate the desired enantiomer from the racemic mixture of diastereoisomers.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Commercially available rac‑4 (tetrahydrothiophene‑2‑carboxylic acid) is only supplied on gram scale, preventing scale‑up of the discovery route.
Solution_Description: A scalable synthesis of rac‑4 was devised via condensation of ethyl thioglycolate with 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane, followed by intramolecular cyclisation in DMF at –15 °C and subsequent distillation, delivering multikilogram quantities of rac‑4.
Supporting_Evidence: “starting tetrahydrothiophene‑2‑carboxylic acid rac‑4 is only commercially available on gram scale;” “we developed an access to this important building block… ethyl thioglycolate was first condensed… intramolecular cyclisation… at −15 °C, yielding rac‑15… purification by distillation… to obtain pure rac‑4 in 46 % overall yield.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The use of DPPA in the Mitsunobu reaction generates azido intermediates that pose a risk of forming toxic, highly explosive hydrazoic acid.
Solution_Description: DPPA was replaced by phthalimide as the nucleophile under standard Mitsunobu conditions (DIAD, PPh₃), eliminating the azido intermediate and associated safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: “safety concerns associated with azido intermediates and reagents (DPPA);” “use of DPPA could be advantageously replaced by phthalimide as a nucleophile under standard Mitsunobu conditions (DIAD, PPh₃).”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Reduction of the azido group required high catalyst loadings and long reaction times because sulfur poisons the metal catalyst, increasing material cost and decreasing throughput.
Solution_Description: The azido intermediate was avoided altogether by employing the phthalimide Mitsunobu approach, removing the need for the problematic reduction step.
Supporting_Evidence: “high catalyst loading required for the reduction of the azido group;” “We decided to target ketone 12… to avoid the use of the azido intermediate and its challenging reduction.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The lack of crystalline intermediates in the early routes forced reliance on chromatographic purifications, which are inefficient and costly at scale.
Solution_Description: The sequence was re‑designed to include steps that afford crystalline intermediates (e.g., oxime formation) and to replace chromatography with crystallisation or distillation, thereby streamlining purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “absence of crystalline intermediates… chromatographies, lack of crystallinity…;” “Condensation of various hydroxylamines… leading in some cases to crystalline intermediates which enabled an easy isolation and a good impurity rejection.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The one‑pot THF/t‑BuOK cyclisation used in the first‑generation route produced a high level of alkene impurity due to chloride elimination, limiting scalability.
Solution_Description: The condensation was performed in acetone, the cyclisation in DMF at –15 °C, and the product was purified by reduced‑pressure distillation, eliminating the impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “one‑pot process… could not be scaled‑up because of the formation of alkene impurity (from chloride elimination) in high levels;” “ethyl thioglycolate was first condensed in acetone… intramolecular cyclisation… in DMF at −15 °C… purification by distillation under reduced pressure (116 °C, 0.2 mbar) to obtain pure rac‑4.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Reductive amination of rac‑12 with ammonia or other amine surrogates failed because the sterically hindered ketone is thermally unstable, preventing imine formation.
Solution_Description: Alternative functional‑group interconversions (oxime, sulfinamine, hydrazone, semicarbazone) were investigated; oxime formation gave crystalline intermediates that could be isolated cleanly.
Supporting_Evidence: “Direct conversion of rac‑12 into rac‑2 proved challenging: reductive amination… failed… due to the thermal unstability and steric hindrance of the ketone;” “Condensation of various hydroxylamines… leading in some cases to crystalline intermediates which enabled an easy isolation.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Oxime reduction required harsh conditions, gave low diastereoselectivity, and employed toxic reagents such as diethyl chlorophosphate and zirconium salts, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: A free oxime was formed in ethanol (50 °C) and subsequently alkylated with bromoethane (avoiding MeI/Me₂SO₄). Reduction was performed with a borane–THF complex below 35 °C, providing a safer and more selective process.
Supporting_Evidence: “the best compromise was found to be a free oxime formation in ethanol at 50 °C… After alkylation with bromoethane… reduction was performed on scale using a Borane–THF complex. For safety reasons… reduction was performed below 35 °C.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: The racemic route required chiral HPLC for final resolution of 2, a costly and labor‑intensive operation at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: A diastereoselective (stereoselective) route was developed that establishes both stereocenters without chiral HPLC, using an enzymatic resolution followed by quinine salt crystallisation and sulfinimine chemistry.
Supporting_Evidence: “Chiral HPLC was preferred… after optimisation… chiral HPLC separation;” “the diastereoselective route… obviates the need for chiral HPLC separation.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Enzymatic resolution of rac‑15 gave only 41 % conversion and 73.7 % ee after 6 h, with variable conversion rates throughout scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Proteus esterase was screened and selected; the reaction was run in a 250 L bioreactor with controlled pH, temperature (30 °C) and periodic addition of base, and the unreacted ester was recovered and recycled to improve overall material balance.
Supporting_Evidence: “Enzymatic resolution… conversion was 41.5 % and ee 73.7 % after 6 h;” “A 250 L bioreactor… pH adjusted to 7.2… temperature 30 °C… ester recycling by racemisation and transesterification.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Oxime formation under the previously optimised basic conditions caused significant epimerisation of (R)‑12, dropping ee from 96 % to 85 % and could not be mitigated by changing base, temperature, or solvent.
Solution_Description: The synthetic plan was switched to a sulfinimine approach performed under acidic conditions with titanium(IV) ethoxide; nitrogen flow (or vacuum) was used to remove volatile by‑products, allowing full conversion at lower temperature (60 °C) without epimerisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “oxime formation… led to significant epimerisation (ee dropped from 96 to 85 %);” “We decided to re‑evaluate amine formation via a sulfinimine intermediate… acidic conditions… nitrogen flux (4 L/min) was applied… full conversion was reached after 24 h.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Sulfinimine intermediates degraded at elevated temperature; reactions were sluggish and required up to 2 days for acceptable conversion, making scale‑up unattractive.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Scale‑up to 10 g showed faster conversion (85 % in 48 h) using 10 equiv Ti(OEt)₄; at 50 g scale, open‑vessel nitrogen flow and a constant volume regime gave 99 % conversion in 7 h with only 5 equiv Ti(OEt)₄, dramatically improving rate and reducing degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “At 10 g scale an improved 85 % conversion was reached after 2 days… at 50 g scale full conversion was reached in 7 h with only 5 equiv of titanium ethoxide… nitrogen flux… allowed removal of a volatile byproduct.”

Paper Title: Early Development Scale-Up of a Novel CXCR Antagonist: Focus on Racemic and Stereoselective Routes of a Key Intermediate
Problem_Description: Quenching the borane‑THF reduction with methanol generated a strong exotherm and rapid gas evolution, posing a safety risk.
Solution_Description: Methanol was added slowly over one hour while keeping the internal temperature below 35 °C, controlling both the addition rate and temperature to prevent uncontrolled gas release.
Supporting_Evidence: “Quench was performed by the slow addition of MeOH… an exotherm was observed… MeOH addition was carefully controlled with the internal temperature maintained below 35 °C.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: The majority of heterogeneous Pd catalysts (Pd/Al₂O₃, Pd/N@Gr, Pd/ZSM‑5, etc.) gave very low product yields (22–48 % NMR yield), far below the homogeneous benchmark (77 %). In addition, the established Pd‑catalyzed amidocarbonylation required a large excess of lithium bromide (35 mol %) as a co‑catalyst, which markedly increases material cost.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to inexpensive Pd black as the heterogeneous catalyst (new route) and, after systematic optimisation, increased the sulfuric‑acid loading to 10 mol % (stoichiometry change) while lowering the reaction temperature to 80 °C (temperature optimisation). Under these conditions Pd black afforded 87 % NMR yield, comparable to the homogeneous system, thereby eliminating the need for more expensive or less‑active supported catalysts.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When the reaction was carried out with 1 mol % of simple palladium black, 52 % of the desired surfactant was detected.” (Table 1)

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Reducing the palladium loading below 1 mol % caused a pronounced drop in conversion; 0.5 mol % Pd black gave only 52 % yield and 0.25 mol % gave 26 % yield.
Solution_Description: The optimal palladium loading was identified as 1 mol % Pd black (stoichiometry change), which restored full conversion and high isolated yield (95 % on multi‑gram scale).
Supporting_Evidence: • “A catalyst content of 1 mol % is required to achieve approximately full conversion. A reduction to 0.5 mol % palladium black led to a diminished output of 52 %.” (Table 2)

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Repeated recycling of Pd black resulted in a steady loss of activity – about 10 % drop in yield per run, attributed either to catalyst deactivation or loss of active material during handling.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was recovered by centrifugation, washed repeatedly with NMP and reused directly in the next run. Although activity declined, this simple recovery protocol allowed assessment of reusability.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A loss of activity of ca. 10 % was detected after every run.” (Chart 2)

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Significant palladium leaching was observed in the crude product (80–460 ppm Pd), raising concerns about metal contamination of the final surfactant.
Solution_Description: An additional acid–base extraction step reduced the residual palladium to 150 ppm, thereby improving product safety and meeting purity requirements.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In all samples a significant amount of palladium was observed ranging from 80 to 460 ppm.” (Chart 3)

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: On a 10 g scale the initial work‑up left the starting material as the main impurity (<2 % remaining) and did not meet the desired >98 % overall yield for the industrial surfactant.
Solution_Description: The scale‑up was performed in a mechanically‑stirred high‑pressure autoclave and the product was isolated by a modified work‑up that included a water‑wash followed by an acid–base extraction, delivering >98 % yield and high purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Our improved protocol can be easily performed on a 10 g scale… the compound is obtained in >98 % overall yield with the starting material as the major impurity (<2 %). An additional acid–base extraction further enhanced the purity of the product while the yield decreased to 95 %.” (Fig 4)

Paper Title: Synthesis of
Problem_Description: Certain substrate/amidocarbonylation combinations (e.g., PFA with acetamide, 2‑pyrrolidinone, benzamide) gave no product under the mild “conditions A”.
Solution_Description: Applying more forcing conditions (120 °C, 35 mol % LiBr, 1 mol % H₂SO₄ – “conditions B”) enabled formation of the corresponding glycine derivatives, demonstrating that higher temperature and increased co‑catalyst loading can overcome substrate‑specific limitations.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction of PFA with acetamide, 2‑pyrrolidinone, and benzamide using conditions A did not provide access to the corresponding glycine derivatives. On the other hand, the corresponding products were obtained when the reaction was carried out at 120 °C with 35 mol % lithium bromide and 1 mol % sulfuric acid (conditions B).” (Fig 2)

Problem_Description: Operating at 40 °C resulted in a dramatically reduced yield (only 8 % of the desired surfactant).

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: The first acetylation step (2 → 3) required a large excess of pyridine (7.3 equiv) and acetic anhydride (6.2 equiv), which makes the process expensive and introduces a toxic, volatile base that compromises eco‑sustainability.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the excess pyridine/Ac₂O system with silica‑supported H₂SO₄ as a heterogeneous acid catalyst.  Using the supported acid allowed the acetylation to be run with Ac₂O as both reagent and solvent (4.2–4.5 equiv) at 100 °C for 3 min, removing the need for pyridine and dramatically cutting reagent cost and toxicity.
Supporting_Evidence: "requirement for excess pyridine (7.3 equiv) and Ac₂O (6.2 equiv) in the first step … strongly impacts the ecosustainability of the process."; "the selective formation of the fully acetylated intermediate 3 could be realized using Ac₂O (4.2–4.5 equiv) as the reagent and solvent in the presence of a catalytic amount of ZnCl₂ … or more conveniently silica‑supported H₂SO₄ (5 wt %)."; "Using the latter method, we were able to quantitatively produce 3 at moderate temperature (100 °C) and within a short reaction time (3 min)."

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: Intermediates 3 and 4 are highly polar and cannot be isolated by ordinary extraction or crystallisation; batch work‑up required large volumes of toluene and multiple water washes, creating a time‑consuming bottleneck.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous counter‑current extraction (ACR) unit was implemented.  The crude stream of 7 was mixed with toluene and water in a cascade of mini‑CSTR chambers, achieving rapid phase separation and >90 % removal of acetic acid with minimal aqueous waste.
Supporting_Evidence: "The optimized batch workup procedure demanded the use of a nonideal solvent, toluene… required several aqueous washes … laborious and time‑consuming."; "We focused our efforts on developing a counter‑current extraction method using a commercially available AM technology ACR device."; "The initial setup led to excellent phase separation, albeit delivering a poor extraction efficiency … The best results … were obtained using solid cylinder inserts … yielding high quality material suitable for the subsequent step."

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: The methanolysis/alkaline rearrangement of intermediate 4 is highly sensitive to the rate of base addition and reaction time; in batch it required precise dosing and rapid acid quench, leading to reproducibility problems on scale.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to solid‑supported basic resins (Ambersep 900, Amberlyst 26) in a packed‑bed flow column.  The resin provides the hydroxide in situ, eliminating the need for liquid NaOH dosing, giving consistent conversion and simplifying quench handling.
Supporting_Evidence: "The inherent instability of intermediate 4 … under the required alkaline methanolysis conditions further impinges upon the robustness of the synthesis, as it necessitates a rapid acid quench …"; "In line with this approach, we evaluated the bases Amberlyst 26 … and Ambersep 900 … to promote this transformation while avoiding time‑consuming extractions and water washing steps."; "Passing the solution through a heated glass column containing 8 g of Ambersep 900 resin … consistently isolated the cyclopentenone in good yield (74–78 %) and high purity after simple evaporation."

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: Intermediate 4 decomposes rapidly under alkaline methanolysis, necessitating an immediate acid quench that is difficult to control at larger scale.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned so that the base‑mediated rearrangement was performed after an in‑line aqueous work‑up, allowing the unstable intermediate 4 to be isolated as the more stable enone 7 before the base step.  This telescoped sequence removes the need for a fast quench on‑stream.
Supporting_Evidence: "The inherent instability of intermediate 4 … necessitates a rapid acid quench of the product which introduces further timing issues upon scale‑up."; "We therefore reverted to our original plan …, where the scheduled extraction of compound 7 with toluene had worked well and evaluated a heterogeneously promoted methanolysis step."; "The necessity of removing the excess acetic acid … allowed us to telescope the individual stages together in a unified flow process."

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: During the peracetylation, adding the solid silica‑supported catalyst to a suspension of d‑glucono‑1,5‑lactone (2) in Ac₂O caused a sudden temperature jump >100 °C within seconds, a runaway exotherm that is hard to control in batch.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A semi‑batch CSTR configuration was adopted, where the solid substrate is fed by a gravimetric powder‑doser (LAMDA DOSER) at a controlled rate while the catalyst remains in the reactor.  This decouples addition of the two phases, limits the heat release, and provides continuous removal of product.
Supporting_Evidence: "reaction’s run‑away exothermic profile combined with the poor solubility of the starting material 2 in the reagent/solvent Ac₂O … a sudden temperature rise to >100 °C was encountered after only a few seconds."; "To circumvent such issues … we decided to exploit powder dosing equipment for the introduction of the substrate into the reactor … The instrument allows controlled gravimetric solid feeding …"; "The widely adopted solution to overcome this issue at scale involves the development of a semibatch process that allows for better control of the heat released through the slow addition of the reactive species."

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: d‑Glucono‑1,5‑lactone (2) is insoluble in Ac₂O, making it impossible to prepare a homogeneous feedstock required for most flow reactors.
Solution_Description: A continuous powder‑dosing system (LAMDA DOSER) was integrated with a CSTR to deliver the solid substrate directly into the reaction mixture, turning the insolubility issue into a controlled solid‑feed operation.
Supporting_Evidence: "the necessity of working with homogeneous and particle‑free feedstocks … represents a stringent requirement … To circumvent such issues … we decided to exploit powder dosing equipment for the introduction of the substrate into the reactor."; "We incorporated the solid feed unit with a CSTR constructed using standard laboratory equipment … delivering 2 g min⁻¹…"

Paper Title: Sustainable Flow Synthesis of a Versatile Cyclopentenone Building Block
Problem_Description: The fully continuous telescoped process (stage 4) gave only 71 % isolated yield of cyclopentenone 1 with modest purity (~79 %); extensive purification was required to reach acceptable quality, defeating the purpose of a streamlined flow process.
Solution_Description: The final rearrangement was moved to a heterogeneous packed‑bed column packed with Ambersep 900 resin, operated at 85 °C.  This provided a high‑yield, high‑purity product (87 % isolated yield, 78 % purity) without the need for post‑reaction chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: "the desired cyclopentenone product 1 was obtained in 71 % yield … purity … modest (∼79 %)."; "We therefore reverted to … heterogeneous promoted methanolysis step using Ambersep 900 … consistently isolated the cyclopentenone in good yield (74–78 %) and high purity after simple evaporation."; "After a total processing time of 4.2 h … the desired product 1 was obtained … isolated yield of 87 % and a purity of 78 %"

Paper Title: A Convenient and Safer Synthesis of Diaminoglyoxime
Problem_Description: The traditional two‑step synthesis of DAG gave an overall isolated yield of only 44 % and required two recrystallizations to obtain a pure product.
Solution_Description: A new one‑step aqueous procedure was developed in which a large excess (10 equiv) of 50 % hydroxylamine is reacted with 40 % aqueous glyoxal at 95 °C for 72–96 h, delivering DAG in 77–80 % yield without any recrystallization or decolorizing‑carbon treatment.
Supporting_Evidence: “Overall yield for the two‑step procedure is 44 %.”; “Two recrystallizations were needed to obtain the desired product in pure form.”; “The new disclosed procedure … without recrystallization or decolorizing carbon in 77–80 % yield.”

Paper Title: A Convenient and Safer Synthesis of Diaminoglyoxime
Problem_Description: The earlier one‑step method (glyoxal + 4 equiv NH₂OH·HCl + 4 equiv NaOH at 95 °C) frequently suffered from thermal runaway and gave maximal isolated yields of only ~40 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Glyoxal is added dropwise over 30 min to a pre‑heated (≈90 °C) aqueous hydroxylamine solution, keeping the reaction temperature close to the jacket set‑point and allowing the bulk of the heat to be released instantaneously as each drop is consumed, thus preventing runaway and improving conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Yields are typically a maximum of ca. 40 % … prone to thermal runaway.”; “By adding the glyoxal over a period of 30 min … minimizing the number of molecules reacting at any given moment. Thus, the likelihood of thermal runaway is mitigated.”; “Heating was controlled by maintaining the jacket temperature between 95 and 100 °C … approximately 90–95 °C in reaction temperature.”

Paper Title: A Convenient and Safer Synthesis of Diaminoglyoxime
Problem_Description: During early optimization, addition of glyoxal to hydroxylamine caused precipitation of glyoxime, creating a heterogeneous mixture; dissolution around 75 °C led to a rapid increase in the reaction temperature, raising concerns of uncontrolled exotherms.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Temperature ramps were controlled via the reactor jacket (using T_j control) while monitoring the reaction temperature (T_r); the control software reduced jacket heating when the temperature rise accelerated, preventing runaway and keeping the mixture homogeneous.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was heterogeneous … at approximately 75 °C, the solids went into solution and the rate of T_r increase doubled.”; “When T_r was used to ramp temperature, the heating rate of the jacket was immediately reduced … no thermal runaway would occur.”; “When T_j was used … the same pattern … no runaway reactions observed … only aqueous reagents were used.”

Paper Title: A Convenient and Safer Synthesis of Diaminoglyoxime
Problem_Description: Using only 5 equiv of hydroxylamine led to significant discoloration and impurities that could not be removed by recrystallization; the product showed a depressed melting/decomposition point, indicating incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: Increasing the hydroxylamine loading to >5 equiv (ultimately 10 equiv) drove the reaction to completion, eliminating discoloration and impurities; if minor discoloration persisted, a second treatment with aqueous hydroxylamine was performed to obtain pure, colorless DAG.
Supporting_Evidence: “More than 5 equiv of hydroxylamine were necessary to drive the reaction to completion due to significant discoloration … and the presence of impurities inseparable by recrystallization.”; “In some cases where only 5 equiv were used, discoloration was not observed, but the recovered material had a significantly depressed melting/decomposition point.”; “Resubmission of this material to heating in additional aqueous hydroxylamine led to a pure, colorless DAG material.”

Paper Title: A Convenient and Safer Synthesis of Diaminoglyoxime
Problem_Description: Scaling the process to 250 g required careful control of temperature to avoid overheating and to maintain consistent product quality across batches.
Solution_Description: A glass‑jacketed reactor equipped with an overhead stirrer and a Mettler‑Toledo RX‑10 control system provided programmable temperature profiles, automatic over‑temperature shutdown, and precise dosing of glyoxal, ensuring reproducible scale‑up without thermal excursions.

Paper Title: Concise Synthesis of Versatile Imidazo[5,1‑
Problem_Description: The classical Dakin–West‑based synthesis of imidazo‑[5,1‑f]‑[1,2,4]‑triazin‑4(3H)‑ones suffers from low overall conversion (<20 % to triazinone intermediate 6) and poor isolation of the acyl‑amino‑α‑keto‑ester 4, giving low‑purity material on scale.

Problem_Description: Four commonly used electrophilic aminating reagents (11‑14) presented safety hazards: high energetic release (especially O‑4‑nitrophenyl hydroxylamine 11), low onset temperatures requiring cryogenic operation, limited commercial availability and high cost, making them unsuitable for large‑scale manufacture.
