Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: The original route required a large excess of tert‑butanol to trap the isocyanate; tert‑butanol had to be melted before charging and warm water (>30 °C) was needed in the condenser to prevent blockage, and trace alcohol congeners caused contamination of the Boc‑carbamate (4).
Solution_Description: Replaced tert‑butanol with the more reactive benzyl alcohol, forming a benzyl carbamate (10) in a cleaner fashion; azeodried the toluene solution of the acid and benzyl alcohol before use to avoid isocyanate hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of a large excess of tert‑butanol… inconvenience of melting the tert‑butanol prior to charging…”; “Small quantities (0.1–0.2 % wt/wt) of alcohol congeners in the tert‑butanol… contamination of Boc carbamate 4"; “The substitution of the tert‑butanol by the more reactive benzyl alcohol led to the formation of the corresponding carbamate product 10 in a cleaner fashion. Azeodrying toluene solutions… prevented any isocyanate hydrolysis…"

Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: Boc‑carbamate 4 showed thermal lability under Curtius rearrangement conditions, leading to premature formation of the amine (1) that was trapped as a urea impurity (6).
Solution_Description: Switched to benzyl carbamate (10), which is more thermally stable, eliminating the urea side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Boc carbamate 4 also showed some thermal lability… This led to the premature formation of a small quantity of 2‑amino‑5‑methylpyrazine (1) which was unproductively trapped as a urea impurity 6."; “The substitution of the tert‑butanol by the more reactive benzyl alcohol… prevented the formation of urea 6 as a by‑product."

Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: The target amine (1) is appreciably water‑soluble, requiring four n‑propyl‑acetate extractions and generating a dilute, waste‑intensive work‑up.
Solution_Description: Using the benzyl carbamate intermediate and subsequent hydrogenolysis avoided an aqueous work‑up, eliminating the need for multiple extractions and reducing waste.
Supporting_Evidence: “2‑Amino‑5‑methylpyrazine (1) also had an appreciable water solubility. This meant multiple (4) extractions with n‑propyl acetate… a dilute process … generated a large amount of waste.”; “The substitution of the tert‑butanol by the more reactive benzyl alcohol… eliminated the need for an aqueous work‑up, making it easier to isolate the water‑soluble 2‑amino‑5‑methylpyrazine (1) in high yield."

Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: The acyl‑azide intermediate (5) and its addition of DPPA are thermally hazardous; uncontrolled addition is exothermic and the acyl‑azide can decompose to generate explosive nitrogen gas.
Solution_Description: Implemented a controlled addition of DPPA over ≥2 h with temperature capped at 17 °C, a quench‑to‑NaOH strategy if bulk temperature exceeds 30 °C, and a fast‑dump safety vent to manage gas evolution.
Supporting_Evidence: “The toluene solution of the acyl azide intermediate 5 poses a thermal and pressure hazard… EXOTHERM if addition is not controlled.”; “The heat of reaction… −77.2 kJ mol⁻¹… adiabatic temperature rise of 30 °C… self‑heating… could occur at ambient plant temperatures.”; “Controlled the addition of the DPPA … over at least 2 h… limiting the temperature of the batch to no more than 17 °C… fast dump into aqueous sodium hydroxide solution … if the batch temperature exceeds 30 °C.”

Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: Trace acidic impurities promoted over‑reduction of the amine (1) to dihydropyrazine (11), generating an impurity that lowered overall yield.

Supporting_Evidence: “An impurity… attributed to the overreduction … promoted by trace quantities of acidic impurities… discouraged by hydrogenolyzing in the presence of a catalytic amount (1 mol %) of sodium hydroxide.”; “The small quantities (0.10–0.15 % LCAP) of dihydropyrazine that did form… could be oxidized back to 2‑amino‑5‑methylpyrazine (1) by passing a stream of 1 % oxygen in nitrogen through the batch.”

Paper Title: Use of a Curtius Rearrangement as Part of the Multikilogram Manufacture of a Pyrazine Building Block
Problem_Description: The original Curtius sequence using Boc‑carbamate did not effectively reject impurities originating from the starting acid, necessitating a strict acceptance criterion on the level of pyrazine‑2‑carboxylic acid.

Paper Title: Identification and Elimination of an Unexpected Catalyst Poison in Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: In GMP campaign 2 the Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling gave almost no desired product 1; the reaction stalled after the methoxylation step and mainly produced hydrolysis product 3, indicating a severe loss of conversion compared with the successful campaign 1.
Solution_Description: A purification protocol for the nicotinate starting material 2 was introduced: the material was dissolved in MTBE, washed with water (to hydrolyse residual SOCl₂), and then recrystallised from heptane. On a 100 g scale the purified material gave complete Suzuki coupling with the original 0.5 % Pd catalyst loading.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “The main product was 3, resulting from the hydrolysis of intermediate 4.”
• “The only stress test that gave a similar profile as observed in GMP campaign 2 was when the Pd(OAc)₂ catalyst was intentionally omitted.”

• “On 100 g scale, the Suzuki coupling step worked very well with the original 0.5 % catalyst loading.”

Paper Title: Identification and Elimination of an Unexpected Catalyst Poison in Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: When the reaction stalled, the team rescued it by adding extra Pd catalyst and ligand, but the higher catalyst loading caused a significant increase in residual palladium in the product, jeopardising downstream steps and raising material cost.
Solution_Description: In‑process controls were implemented to detect stalling within 1–2 h; upon detection, additional catalyst (up to 5 %) and ligand were added to complete the reaction. An optional palladium‑scavenging step using a Si‑Thiol scavenger in toluene reduced residual Pd to <200 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We found that a stalled Suzuki coupling could almost always be ‘revived’ if enough additional catalyst and ligand were added.”
• “It should be noted that although increasing the catalyst loading might appear to be a simple solution, it would lead to other issues downstream. We found that a higher catalyst loading significantly increased the residual Pd level in product 1.”
• “The optimal conditions were found to be a Si‑Thiol metal scavenger in toluene, which reduced the Pd level to below 200 ppm.”
• “Additional catalyst and ligand (up to 5 %) would be added if stalling was detected.”
• “In‑process controls were implemented to detect stalling within 1–2 h.”

Paper Title: Identification and Elimination of an Unexpected Catalyst Poison in Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: The catalyst poison could not be identified by conventional ¹H NMR, HPLC‑MS, or elemental analysis, making it difficult to pinpoint the root cause of the low conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The mother liquor from the first purification was repeatedly recrystallised to enrich the poison (Scheme 3). Enriched batches were analysed by ICP‑OES, which detected low‑level sulfur (down to 0.13 % wt) and demonstrated a clear correlation between sulfur content and the amount of Pd required for full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The mother liquor was concentrated to give batch ML1… ¹H NMR, GCMS, and CHN elemental analysis still showed very high purity.”
• “We decided to process batch ML1 through two more heptane recrystallizations… The five batches were also tested for sulfur content. Interestingly, sulfur was now detected in all batches.”
• “Based on the data, we suspected that sulfur was actually present in the initial batch of 2 … ICP‑OES found 0.13 % of sulfur, which is just below the sensitivity of conventional sulfur elemental analysis.”
• “Correlation of sulfur content with Pd loading (Table 1).”

Paper Title: Identification and Elimination of an Unexpected Catalyst Poison in Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: Sulfur contamination originated from the esterification of nicotinic acid 5 with SOCl₂/DMF; elemental sulfur (S₈) formed as a by‑product, poisoning the Pd catalyst and rendering the material unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A completely new “sulfur‑free” synthetic route was devised that avoids SOCl₂/DMF. The sequence uses bromination of 6‑hydroxynicotinic acid, double chlorination with POCl₃ (or triphosgene), methanol quench, and a telescoped methoxylation to give the final intermediates 2 and 4. The route uses inexpensive reagents, is scalable, and the final product contains <5 ppm sulfur, restoring full catalyst activity at the original 0.5 % loading.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Elemental sulfur was identified as the catalyst poison.”
• “Sulfur could be generated from the reaction between SOCl₂ and DMF … SCl₂ can react with DMF to generate dimethyl carbamoyl chloride (DMCC), along with sulfur as the stoichiometric by‑product.”
• “Esterification of both acids 5 and 6 with excess SOCl₂/DMF … the isolated products contained a significant amount of sulfur (1.9 % and 6.8 %).”
• “Developed a ‘sulfur‑free’ synthesis … bromination … POCl₃ or triphosgene … methoxylation … high yield and purity.”
• “The product contained no sulfur (<5 ppm). A Suzuki coupling use test on 100 g scale was complete within 1 h with the original 0.5 % catalyst loading.”

Paper Title: Identification and Elimination of an Unexpected Catalyst Poison in Suzuki Coupling
Problem_Description: The original route to nicotinate 2 relied on costly reagents (SOCl₂) and a multi‑step sequence that was not easily scalable, making the material one of the most expensive building blocks in the overall synthesis.
Solution_Description: The new route replaces the expensive, sulfur‑generating steps with bromination (bromine in acetic acid) and double chlorination using POCl₃ or triphosgene, followed by a one‑pot methoxylation and telescoped isolation. This reduces reagent cost, improves scalability, and enables kilogram‑scale production of the downstream intermediate 4 without sulfur contamination.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We needed an alternative synthesis that does not involve SOCl₂/DMF … also would like to develop a more scalable route that can lower the cost of goods, because compound 2 is one of the more expensive starting materials.”
• “The first step is the bromination of readily available 6‑hydroxynicotinic acid … bromine in acetic acid gave the best results.”
• “Nicotinic acid intermediate 5 was then doubly chlorinated with POCl₃ or triphosgene … the resulting acid chloride 9 was quenched with methanol … telescoped to give advanced intermediate 4.”
• “The product contained no sulfur (<5 ppm). A Suzuki coupling use test … complete within 1 h with the original 0.5 % catalyst loading.”

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The original acid‑methanol crystallization of TAK‑117 suffered from very poor solubility of the API in most organic solvents (only sparingly soluble in acidified methanol), which limited achievable productivities and caused low isolated yields (56–69 %). In addition, extensive filtration steps on carbon and scavenger slurries resulted in large material losses and produced an agglomerated product that was difficult to dry and sieve.
Solution_Description: A new crystallization route was developed using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at elevated temperatures (≈100 °C) followed by controlled cooling and thermal cycling.  The solvent change provided sufficient solubility, the high temperature accelerated dissolution and enabled high recovery, while the thermal‑cycling step tuned crystal aspect ratio and reduced agglomeration during drying.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Opportunities to explore a wide array of possible crystallization routes and solvent options were limited because TAK‑117 is sparingly soluble in most commonly used organic solvents, apart from DMSO and acidic systems." (Abstract) 
• "Two 5 kg batches were manufactured … affording TAK‑117 in 56 and 69 % yield … This process was very effective in removing residual Pd but resulted in significant loss of material … the isolated product had a very small particle size and was highly agglomerated." (Results) 
• "Reasonable productivities were achieved using DMSO at elevated temperatures (100 °C), and the optimized process leveraged thermal cycling to improve the aspect ratio of the isolated crystals, minimizing agglomeration during drying and improving the powder bulk properties." (Conclusions)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: When 50 wt % aqueous NaOH was added quickly to the formic‑acid suspension, a large exotherm was generated, leading to uncontrolled supersaturation, high agglomeration, and inconsistent yields and potencies.
Solution_Description: The base concentration was lowered (5–25 wt % NaOH) and the addition rate was prolonged (up to 24 h) to attenuate the exotherm and limit supersaturation, giving better control of precipitation, reduced agglomeration and higher assay values.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The use of 50 % w/v aqueous NaOH was quickly deemed unsuitable because of the distinct lack of control it provided over the process end point and the large exotherm it produced." (Results) 
• "Reduced base concentrations (5, 10, 25 % w/v aqueous NaOH) were therefore investigated as a means to restrain the levels of localized supersaturation… the majority of the agglomeration could be controlled by a combination of lowering the concentration of NaOH used and extending the addition time." (Results) 
• "A two‑part addition profile… first half added rapidly… second half added over 6 h to minimize agglomeration and maximize product purity." (Results)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The aggressive precipitation from formic‑acid/NaOH produced dense suspensions of fine, agglomerated particles that were difficult to transfer, resulted in excessively long filtration times, and retained large amounts of solvent and inorganic impurities in the wet cake.
Solution_Description: A two‑step NaOH addition (fast‑then‑slow) and reduced base concentration were employed to moderate supersaturation, yielding a less agglomerated suspension that filtered more readily and exhibited lower solvent/impurity carry‑over.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Dense suspensions of fine and agglomerated particles were produced that were difficult to transfer, resulted in excessively long filtration times, and caused varying degrees of encrustation on the interior of the crystallizer." (Results) 
• "Extending the hold time made it possible to break up the agglomerates … but the degree of deagglomeration was entirely variable and not a reliable additional control to obtain a consistent product." (Results) 
• "A two‑part addition profile… the second half was added over 6 h to minimize agglomeration and maximize product purity." (Results)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The first‑generation DMSO crystallization showed batch‑to‑batch variability in particle‑size distributions and formation of >2 mm agglomerates during filtration/drying, which compromised downstream drug‑product manufacturability.
Solution_Description: Process parameters were adjusted (e.g., water addition rate, cooling profile) and a seed‑addition step was introduced to control nucleation, resulting in more consistent crystal sizes and reduced agglomerate formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "PSD analysis indicated variability… a large amount of material (~20 %) was retained on the 2 mm screen… these agglomerates must have been generated during filtration and drying." (Results) 
• "It was anticipated that nucleation could be controlled by the implementation of a seeding step… the seed was added as a slurry in DMSO, and the resulting suspension was aged for 30 min before cooling to 25 °C at 10.8 °C/h." (Results) 
• "For all of the batches manufactured … particle size remained consistent, and secondary nucleation was minimal." (Scale‑up section)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: At pilot‑plant scale, inconsistent seed quality (size distribution, impurity level) and variations in DMSO holdup after carbon filtration led to variable supersaturation and PSD, causing batch‑to‑batch inconsistency.
Solution_Description: A controlled cooling‑driven crystallization (primary supersaturation generated by cooling from 100 °C) combined with a defined seed loading (≈1 wt % micronized seed) reduced reliance on antisolvent addition and limited variability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Variation at plant scale may have impacted the PSD… could have been attributed to either differences in mixing, the presence of varying impurities… or slight variations in the solvent composition resulting from variation in the DMSO holdup during the filtration of the large amounts of carbon, Celite, and scavenger." (Results) 
• "Sufficient supersaturation for seeding (≈10 %) was generated by cooling a saturated solution of TAK‑117 in DMSO from 100 °C to 90 °C… the seed was added as a slurry in DMSO, … cooled to 25 °C at 10.8 °C/h." (Impact of Seed) 
• "The temperature of antisolvent addition was not studied in detail, but it was expected that higher temperatures would allow faster growth kinetics…" (First‑generation design)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: Thermal cycling, while improving aspect ratio, caused crystal cementation and aggregation that varied with the number of cycles, potentially affecting downstream handling.
Solution_Description: Thermal‑cycling parameters (temperature range 50–70 °C or 60–80 °C, heating/cooling rates of 20 °C/h and 10 °C/h, respectively) were optimized to obtain a balance between improved aspect ratio and acceptable aggregate formation; a limited number of cycles (3) was chosen to keep cycle time reasonable.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Thermal cycling was investigated… Approximately 30 % of the crystal mass was thermal cycled over two different temperature ranges (50–70 °C and 60–80 °C)." (Impact of Thermal Cycling) 
• "Relatively fast thermal cycle heating and cooling rates of 20 and 10 °C/h, respectively, were investigated, resulting in a 3 h cycle time, which was an acceptable time extension to the process." (Impact of Thermal Cycling) 
• "By application of thermal cycling, the latter type of aggregation appears to become more prevalent, and the bulk width of the crystal morphology increases… material of acceptable quality was obtained that was sufficiently large as to pose no risk of subsequent agglomeration during drying." (Impact of Thermal Cycling)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Crystallization Process To Improve an API’s Physiochemical and Bulk Powder Properties
Problem_Description: The pilot‑plant did not have a wet‑mill capable of processing the required seed quantity, forcing reliance on externally supplied micronized seed and complicating the supply chain.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was adapted to use micronized seed directly (prepared off‑site) and the crystallization was redesigned to minimize the need for in‑plant wet‑milling, relying instead on controlled cooling and seeding to achieve the desired PSD.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Unfortunately, the pilot plant used for the manufacture of TAK‑117 was not equipped with a suitable wet mill for the intended operating scale, and therefore, micronized seed was used." (Scale‑up Studies) 
• "The suspension was cooled to 90 ± 5 °C, seeded with a suspension of micronized TAK‑117 dispersed in DMSO, and aged…" (Scale‑up Studies) 
• "Thus, while the morphology was far from ideal, thermal cycling was incorporated into the process." (Conclusions) – indicates adaptation rather than adding new equipment.

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: The filtered periodate/iodate waste cake generated after the oxidation of diallyl tartrate has a very high thermal potential.  When the solids were packed in a plastic container at 400 L scale an exothermic event occurred that generated enough heat to melt the container and produced vigorous iodine formation.
Solution_Description: Rinse the waste solids with dichloromethane (DCM) and then store the DCM‑rinsed cake in water.  The DCM rinse removes residual organic material that can be oxidized, raising the DSC onset temperature from ~113 °C to ~258 °C and reducing the heat of decomposition from 1.2 kJ g⁻¹ to 0.2 kJ g⁻¹, thereby eliminating the dangerous exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Within hours following the pack‑out, an exothermic event was observed that led to vigorous iodine formation.  This event was exothermic enough to melt part of the plastic container holding the solids.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: In the original MtBE solvent the sodium periodate solids aggregate and cake at the bottom of the reactor, limiting oxidant surface area.  This caused the need to use a large excess of periodate (50–100 % molar excess) and resulted in inconsistent conversions and lower product yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Replace MtBE with DCM, which provides a higher liquid density (1.336 g mL⁻¹) and greatly improves suspension of the periodate solids.  Coupled with an upward‑pumping impeller design the solids remain dispersed, allowing the oxidant to be used at lower equivalents while maintaining complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “With MtBE, as with most ether solvents, there is always concern for peroxide formation… The second choice for reaction solvent, DCM, … provides a much lower flammability (NFPA 704 flammability 1).”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: MtBE and i‑PrOAc are highly flammable (NFPA 704 flammability 3) and are used together with a strong oxidant, increasing the fire/exotherm hazard of the process.
Solution_Description: Adopt DCM as the reaction solvent (NFPA 704 flammability 1).  The lower flammability together with the reduced thermal potential of the waste solids (see above) mitigates fire and exotherm risks.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Both MtBE and i‑PrOAc are highly flammable (NFPA 704 flammability 3), and DCM has a much lower flammability rating.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: The original batch protocol required heating the whole mixture to 35 °C and took ~22 h to reach completion.  The prolonged exposure caused product degradation (formation of allyl alcohol and glyoxylic acid) and lowered isolated yield.
Solution_Description: Implement a temperature‑ramp profile (charge reagents at 15 °C, then ramp to 25–40 °C) and add the sodium periodate in three 10‑min portions.  This reduces the instantaneous heat load, shortens reaction time to 3–4 h, and suppresses formation of degradation products.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction held at constant temperature is considerably less energetic… Reaction times vastly different between the constant temperature (22 h) and the temperature‑ramp procedures (3 h).”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: Charging all reagents at once deposits a large amount of reactive periodate in the reactor, creating a sharp, uncontrolled exotherm that exceeds safe temperature limits.
Solution_Description: Dose the sodium periodate portion‑wise (three 10‑min additions) while maintaining modest temperature (≤30 °C).  This spreads the heat evolution over time, keeping reactor temperature within a safe envelope.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The original procedure places all the reagents in the reactor initially… observed temperature rises in the laboratory of 15 °C above the desired reaction temperature.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and Scalable Process for the Preparation of Allyl Glyoxalate
Problem_Description: Running the reaction with 1.8 equiv of sodium periodate (≈167 g for 100 g substrate) generates a large amount of oxidant waste, driving up material cost and disposal burden.
Solution_Description: Reduce the periodate loading to as low as 1.2 equiv when using DCM (which provides better suspension).  The lower oxidant load cuts raw‑material cost and waste volume while still delivering full conversion (reaction time increases modestly but remains acceptable).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Sodium periodate charge can be within the target range of 1.2–1.8 equiv. A lower amount … extends the reaction time to ∼10–12 h on this scale.”

Paper Title: Application of New Technology to a Mature Piroxicam Crystallization Process To Gain Process Understanding and Control, via Industrial–Academic Collaboration
Problem_Description: Trace amounts of the stable polymorph FII were present on the surface of seed material. Because two of the four seeding points were in an undersaturated region of the solubility curve, those seed charges dissolved, providing insufficient surface area and leading to spontaneous nucleation of the metastable polymorph FI. The result was an increasing level of FII contamination in the final product and batch‑to‑batch failures.
Solution_Description: A new seeding regime was introduced: the first seed charge was front‑loaded (≈1.5 kg at ~94 °C) to consume most of the supersaturation, followed by three smaller charges (0.5 kg each at 90, 86 and 82 °C). Seed loading at each charge was increased (up to 2 % w/w at lab scale, 1.5 % w/w overall at plant) to ensure that seed remained in the supersaturated region and to provide sufficient surface area. In addition, all seed batches were screened by ATR‑FTIR to select those with the lowest surface FII content before use.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Comparison of the seed points with the experimentally generated solubility curves demonstrated that two seed points were located in an undersaturated region of the solubility space, indicating that both of these seed loads would dissolve when added to the solution" (sec 3.3). 
2. "The presence of FII in the seed material could explain the polymorphic failures in the final product… each batch that was seeded with “bad” seed was effectively seeded with small amounts of FII" (sec 3.2). 
3. "The seed charge was front‑loaded to the first charge (1.5 kg, typically 94 °C) … followed by three smaller charges (0.5 kg) at fixed temperature points (90, 86, 82 °C)" (sec 3.4). 
4. "An ATR‑FTIR evaluation of all potential seed batches was conducted in order to identify those seed batches that had the least FII contamination" (sec 3.4). 
5. "As the seed loading increased from 4 × 25 mg (black) to 4 × 200 mg (red), the amount of FI seen in the product decreased significantly" (sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Application of New Technology to a Mature Piroxicam Crystallization Process To Gain Process Understanding and Control, via Industrial–Academic Collaboration
Problem_Description: The conventional FTIR method required grinding of seed samples, which removed the surface‑enriched FII and therefore failed to detect the contaminant. This analytical blind spot masked the root cause of the polymorph failures.
Solution_Description: ATR‑FTIR was adopted for seed screening because it probes only the surface of the raw material, preserving the surface‑enriched FII signal and reliably identifying contaminated seed batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Conventional FTIR analysis detected a slight difference … the presence of a small peak at 3398 cm⁻¹ for the latter… Prior to this study, this difference was not thought to be significant" (sec 3.2). 
2. "ATR‑FTIR analysis of the ‘bad’ seed sample supported this hypothesis, revealing characteristic peaks of FI and FII… Grinding the sample significantly reduced the amount of FII detected" (sec 3.2). 
3. "An ATR‑FTIR evaluation of all potential seed batches was conducted in order to identify those seed batches that had the least FII contamination" (sec 3.4).

Paper Title: Application of New Technology to a Mature Piroxicam Crystallization Process To Gain Process Understanding and Control, via Industrial–Academic Collaboration
Problem_Description: Reducing the cooling rate was shown to suppress spontaneous nucleation of FI, but a slower cooling profile would lengthen the overall process time, increasing the window for solution‑mediated transformation of FI to FII and contradicting manufacturing throughput requirements.
Solution_Description: The cooling rate was retained at the existing plant value (0.41 °C min⁻¹) to avoid extending the batch time, while other process changes (seed loading, real‑time monitoring) were used to control supersaturation and polymorph outcome.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "Decreasing the cooling rate … did not have an effect on the polymorphic content … all three cooling rates generating FI" (sec 3.3). 
2. "At higher cooling rates, FI was detected … The lower cooling rate reduces the speed … However, a lower cooling rate also corresponds to a longer overall process duration… Therefore, it was decided not to increase the length of the cooling time in the manufacturing environment" (sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Application of New Technology to a Mature Piroxicam Crystallization Process To Gain Process Understanding and Control, via Industrial–Academic Collaboration
Problem_Description: Prior to the study there was no in‑situ analytical tool to determine the point at which the solution became saturated, resulting in seed being added when the system was still undersaturated and causing seed dissolution.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An online mid‑IR ReactIR probe was installed on the production vessel, providing real‑time monitoring of solution concentration. This allowed operators to add seed precisely when the solution reached supersaturation, preventing seed dissolution.

This allowed for the identification of the solution saturation point in a qualitative manner and determined when seeding could be initiated so as to avoid seed dissolution" (sec 3.4). 
2. "Mid‑IR data from the first plant crystallization were compared directly to the lab scale data, and excellent agreement was observed" (sec 3.4).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow In-Line Solvent-Swap Crystallization of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: The high solubility of Vitamin D₃ in the photoreaction solvent tert‑butyl‑methyl‑ether (t‑BME) prevents any crystallization, and the low‑pressure solvent‑swap step makes segmented‑flow operation difficult, leading to inconsistent crystallization and potential channel blockage.
Solution_Description: A continuous in‑line solvent‑swap is introduced: the reaction mixture (t‑BME/VD₃) is mixed with acetonitrile (ACN) in a T‑mixer, then the t‑BME is selectively evaporated under controlled temperature (40 °C) and pressure (280 mbar) while the ACN‑rich solution proceeds to crystallization. The flow‑valve counters the vacuum forces to keep a constant flow rate, ensuring stable mixing and preventing phase separation.

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow In-Line Solvent-Swap Crystallization of Vitamin D
Problem_Description: Batch crystallization of Vitamin D₃ from the final resin requires days of processing and gives low overall crystal yields (≈50 % w/w), making the process unsuitable for a continuous manufacturing line.
Solution_Description: The continuous flow set‑up uses a short 1 min cooling period at 7 °C in a capillary immersed in an ethylene‑glycol bath, with a 130 mm PFA tube (ID 0.55 mm) to achieve rapid supersaturation and crystal formation. The solvent‑ratio (t‑BME : ACN = 1 : 3 v/v) and feed concentration (0.22 M VD₃) are tuned to maximize nucleation while keeping the solution below the solubility limit of VD₃ in ACN (8 mg mL⁻¹ at 7 °C).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow In-Line Solvent-Swap Crystallization of Vitamin D

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow In-Line Solvent-Swap Crystallization of Vitamin D

For multicycle operation, a 1 : 4 ratio improves flowability and stabilises yields (~55 % per cycle). Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Manufacturing Route for the Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor GSK2248761A (IDX-899): Synthesis of an Advanced Key Chiral Intermediate
Problem_Description: Initial palladium‑catalyzed couplings suffered from competing reductive dehalogenation, hydrolysis of the methyl phosphinate, and protecting‑group cleavage, resulting in low conversion and product loss.
Solution_Description: Optimized the catalyst (Pd(dppf)Cl₂), used 3‑aminopropyltrimethoxysilane as the methyl donor, and selected reaction temperatures (77–82 °C) that minimized side‑reactions, achieving >80 % conversion to the desired product.
Supporting_Evidence:

• "Our best results were obtained when we used Pd(dppf)Cl₂ and 3‑aminopropyltrimethoxysilane…" (Optimization)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Manufacturing Route for the Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor GSK2248761A (IDX-899): Synthesis of an Advanced Key Chiral Intermediate
Problem_Description: During the telescoped two‑step coupling, the generated dicyclohexylammonium iodide and polymeric silane by‑products formed hard, insoluble balls that threatened reactor integrity and complicated downstream work‑up.
Solution_Description: Performed a weakly acidic aqueous work‑up to quench the iodide salt, filtered the slurry (adding Celite when needed) to remove polymeric silane, and switched the final solvent to toluene for easier isolation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "...the dicyclohexylamine hydrogen iodide produced…in combination with polymeric silane byproducts, produced large hard balls that we anticipated would cause damage to our vessels…" (Scale‑up discussion) 
• "We elected to perform a weakly acidic workup…followed by a filtration to remove the problematic silane byproducts, and we changed the solvent to toluene…" (Process description) 
• "...overcome with the addition of Celite to the vessel." (Pilot‑plant runs)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Manufacturing Route for the Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor GSK2248761A (IDX-899): Synthesis of an Advanced Key Chiral Intermediate
Problem_Description: When using triethylamine in ethyl acetate, the liberated iodide caused S_N2 demethylation of the product and ethyl‑to‑methyl exchange, generating undesired ethyl phosphinate 7 and loss of material.
Solution_Description: Replaced triethylamine with dicyclohexylamine (forming an insoluble iodide salt) and switched the reaction solvent from ethyl acetate to isopropyl acetate, which suppressed both demethylation and ethyl exchange pathways.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "A large amount of demethylation of 8 occurred…hypothesized that the iodide liberated…was responsible via S_N2 attack…" (One‑pot coupling discussion) 
• "The demethylation pathway was shut down when triethylamine was replaced with dicyclohexylamine…" (Optimization) 
• "Ethyl acetate was not completely inert…caused methyl to ethyl phosphinate ester exchange…The solvent was switched to isopropyl acetate to retard this pathway…" (Solvent change)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Manufacturing Route for the Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor GSK2248761A (IDX-899): Synthesis of an Advanced Key Chiral Intermediate
Problem_Description: Inconsistent chiral enrichment during the cinchonidine salt formation/reslurry step was traced to a solid‑form change of the salt, leading to variable diastereomeric ratios and yields.
Solution_Description: Developed a controlled reslurry protocol (acetone → ethyl acetate sequence) that deliberately induced the favorable salt polymorph (form II), giving a reproducible upgrade to >99.5 % d.r. and allowing scale‑up without loss of chiral purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Comparison of the powder X‑ray diffraction traces…revealed that a form change upon reslurrying was a potential source of the irreproducibility…" (Resolution investigation) 
• "When the reslurrying was performed in this order a chiral upgrade…was observed…" (Polymorph effect) 
• "The new reslurry protocol performed as expected to give acid 10 with 99.8% e.r. in 39% overall yield…" (Scale‑up)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-Up of a Manufacturing Route for the Non-nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor GSK2248761A (IDX-899): Synthesis of an Advanced Key Chiral Intermediate
Problem_Description: Late‑stage use of dichloromethane and oxalyl chloride generated large volumes of hazardous waste and required special handling, increasing cost and safety burden.
Solution_Description: By adopting the telescoped palladium‑catalyzed H‑phosphinate coupling, the process eliminated the need for DCM and oxalyl chloride, reducing waste generation and associated safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "These steps involved the use of dichloromethane, a non‑preferred solvent, and the combination of oxalyl chloride and DMF…presented potential engineering/safety issues…" (First‑generation route) 
• "The new route…eliminates most of the materials of concern for production…" (Summary)

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: When the original aminolysis of the imidazolide (2) was scaled‑up to an 8 kg batch the process could not meet the clinical‑grade specification because three significant impurities – phosphinic acid (4), N‑acyl‑urea (8) and indoloyl‑carboxamide (6) – appeared in the product.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was changed to an inverse‑addition mode – the imidazolide solution was added to a pre‑pressurised ammonia/THF gas mixture – and the ammonia feed was precisely controlled with a mass‑flow controller. This eliminated impurity 8 and gave consistent, specification‑grade API.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “original process was unable to produce API within clinical specification when run on an 8 kg scale” (abstract).  
[Problem] “three significant impurities … were formed during the reaction … the original process was unable to produce API within clinical specification” (p. 1).  
[Solution] “To circumvent this engineering challenge, we considered inverse addition… no impurity 8 was formed” (sec 1.1).  
[Solution] “Ammonia was supplied via a mass flow controller… at 30 mL min⁻¹ impurity 8 = 0.54 % a/a, at 60 mL min⁻¹ impurity 8 = 0.35 % a/a” (sec 1.1).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: Phosphinic acid (4) was generated by over‑exposure of the finished API to excess ammonia after the aminolysis was complete, slowly converting product into impurity 4.
Solution_Description: The reaction was stopped as soon as conversion to API was complete and the mixture was quenched with a pH 10 aqueous buffer, which efficiently extracted phosphinic acid and prevented further decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “phosphinic acid 4 was formed by overexposure of the product … once the required reaction was complete… formed slowly on the reaction time scale” (sec 1.1).  
[Solution] “was readily removed by extraction with a pH 10 aqueous buffer” (sec 1.1).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: During activation of indole acid (1) with CDI, variable amounts of the diketopiperazide side‑product (5) were formed; 5 reacts with ammonia to give impurity 6, which consumes material and reduces API yield.
Solution_Description: The process was adjusted to use a large excess (8 equiv) of dilute aqueous ammonia (28 % v/v) after imidazolide formation; the excess ammonia efficiently converts any formed diketopiperazide (5) to API, eliminating impurity 6 and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “variable amounts of the diketopiperazide 5 were formed … this intermediate … reacts with ammonia to give the indoloyl carboxamide 6” (sec 1.1).  
[Problem] “impurity 6 … was found subsequently to react slowly with further ammonia to give GSK2248761A” (sec 1.1).  
[Solution] “using 28 % aqueous ammonia (8 equiv) we were able to isolate GSK2248761A within specification” (sec 1.2).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: Impurity 8 formation was highly sensitive to the ammonia‑gas supply rate; on pilot‑plant scale the addition of the required ammonia equivalents required ~100 min because the gas‑feed line limited the flow, leading to batch‑to‑batch variability and higher impurity levels.
Solution_Description: A high‑flow ammonia feed was implemented using a mass‑flow controller (30–60 mL min⁻¹), which reduced impurity 8 from >0.5 % to <0.35 % and shortened the addition step.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “addition of the required molar equivalents of ammonia took approximately 100 min … limited by the constraints of the gas supply configuration” (sec 1.1).  
[Problem] “impurity 8 … was strongly suspected that the ammonia gas supply rate was influencing impurity 8 formation” (sec 1.1).  
[Solution] “at an ammonia flow rate of 30 mL min⁻¹ impurity 8 = 0.54 % a/a, at 60 mL min⁻¹ impurity 8 = 0.35 % a/a” (sec 1.1).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: The inverse‑addition strategy required multiple interruptions to repressurise the vessel and occasional evacuation of headspace, creating operational complexity and pressure‑limit safety concerns that made scaling difficult.
Solution_Description: The process was later redesigned to avoid gaseous ammonia altogether by using an aqueous ammonia (28 % v/v) solution together with 2‑MeTHF as solvent, eliminating the high‑pressure gas handling and simplifying scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “several interruptions to the imidazolide addition were required in order to repressurize the vessel with ammonia… felt that this process was not amenable to straightforward changes in scale and equipment” (sec 1.1).  
[Solution] “the overall volume inefficiency of the process (maximum 90 volumes)… Substituting THF with 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran… it was possible to increase the reaction concentration … and avoided the use of gaseous ammonia entirely” (sec 1.2).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: The original route required up to 90 solvent volumes (large THF usage) and an expensive gas‑handling layout, leading to high material‑handling costs and waste.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent from THF to 2‑MeTHF (which is immiscible with water) eliminated the need for TBME in the work‑up and allowed the reaction concentration to be increased from 40 volumes to 15 volumes without loss of purity, dramatically reducing solvent cost and waste.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “of specific concern was the use of ammonia gas and the overall volume inefficiency of the process (maximum 90 volumes)” (sec 1.2).  
[Solution] “Substituting THF with 2‑methyltetra­hydrofuran also significantly improved the process… it was no longer necessary to use TBME in the aqueous workup” (sec 1.2).  
[Solution] “it was possible to increase the reaction concentration from 40 volumes to 15 volumes with no adverse effect on product purity” (sec 1.2).

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process to GSK2248761A API
Problem_Description: At higher concentrations the imidazolide dimerised to more diketopiperazide (5), which could lower the overall conversion to API if not addressed.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of concentrated aqueous ammonia (8 equiv) drove the rapid conversion of the accumulated diketopiperazide (5) to API, maintaining high conversion even at 15‑volume concentration.
Supporting_Evidence:
[Problem] “at this higher concentration, imidazolide 2 dimerized to the diketopiperazide 5 in greater amounts … could affect conversion” (sec 1.2).  
[Solution] “under these conditions diketopiperazide 5 reacted efficiently with concentrated aqueous ammonia to give GSK2248761A within specification” (sec 1.2).

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: The batch nitric‑acid oxidation of 2,4‑dichloro‑5‑fluoroacetophenone (AP) is a violent exothermic reaction that requires drop‑wise addition, generates large amounts of nitrogen dioxide, and needs extensive circulating cooling water, while the reaction time is several hours.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to a continuous‑flow tubular reactor (PFA tubing) provides a high surface‑to‑volume ratio, excellent heat‑ and mass‑transfer, and eliminates the safety hazards of the batch exotherm, allowing rapid (≈9 min) oxidation with safe temperature control.
Supporting_Evidence: ['In the traditional batch reaction to prepare BA with nitric acid, nitric acid oxidation is an intense exothermic reaction; therefore, nitric acid was added dropwise into substrate solution of AP below 50 °C ... a large amount of nitrogen dioxide were released.', 'The heat of reaction had to be removed by a large amount of circulating cooling water.', 'The continuous‑flow system includes advantages such as good mass and heat transfer to ensure the safety of the reaction.', 'Compared with the batch process ... the continuous flow was safer and easy to operate and gave a high product yield with high purity.']

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: Conventional oxidation methods rely on heavy‑metal oxidants (e.g., KMnO₄, Na₂Cr₂O₇) that are toxic and generate hazardous waste.
Solution_Description: Nitric acid was employed as a cheap, easy‑to‑recover homogeneous catalyst, eliminating the need for toxic metal oxidants.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Many synthetic methods ... required the use of harsh conditions and toxic reagents, such as heavy metal oxidants.', 'We chose nitric acid as the reaction catalyst which is a cheap and easy‑to‑recover catalyst.']

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: Conversion in the flow reactor is limited by insufficient oxygen mass transfer; low oxygen availability at low temperature/pressure gives poor conversion (<100 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Operating in a Taylor‑flow regime (slug flow with elongated gas bubbles) enhances internal recirculation, dramatically improving O₂ mass transfer and enabling full conversion at 70 °C and 2 bar O₂.
Supporting_Evidence: ['By analyzing the experimental data, we could infer that the whole conversion rate was controlled by the mass transfer of oxygen showing the limit of the Taylor flow regime.', 'Taylor flow is a special case of slug flow where the liquid slugs are separated by elongated bubbles. Compared with single‑phase laminar flow, Taylor flow has been shown to increase the transfer of heat and mass because of the recirculation within the liquid slugs.']

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: Substituting pure O₂ with ambient air lowers the oxidant concentration, leading to reduced conversion (maximum ~93 % vs 100 % with O₂).
Solution_Description: Air is used as the oxidant for economic and safety reasons; conversion is maximized by increasing nitric‑acid loading and pressure within safe limits, achieving ~93 % conversion while avoiding pure O₂ handling.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The use of ambient air to replace oxygen had both economic and safety advantages, so we diverted our attention to the presence of air in a continuous flow reaction.', 'Air gave lower conversion … maximum conversion of AP was accomplished as 93 % using 5 bar of air and a 9 min residence time by using 50 % nitric acid.']

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: Repeated recycling of the reaction filtrate leads to a gradual loss of nitric‑acid concentration, causing declining conversion and product purity over successive runs.
Solution_Description: The deficiency is corrected by adding the appropriate amount of fresh nitric acid to the recycled filtrate, restoring conversion and purity.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The quality of the product significantly decreased. The decrease in purity was mainly attributed to the decreasing conversion rate, and the decrease in conversion rate was mainly attributed to the decreasing nitric acid concentration.', 'It could be solved by adding the proper amount of nitric acid.']

Paper Title: Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of 2,4-Dichloro-5-fluorobenzoic Acid by Air Oxidation under the Continuous-Flow Process
Problem_Description: Batch oxidation requires 5 h residence time to reach ~81 % yield, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 70 °C and reducing residence time to 9 min in the flow reactor accelerates the reaction, delivering near‑quantitative yields at kilogram‑scale rates.
Supporting_Evidence: ['When the reaction temperature was below 50 °C, the reaction rate was slow with a low conversion rate.', 'As the reaction temperature was increased (higher than 70 °C), conversions up to 100 % were obtained for AP in acetic acid with a residence time of 9 min.', 'The output of the continuous‑flow process was 2.7 kg/h in a 402 mL reactor and can easily be scaled up…']

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of Monocyclic β‑Lactam Core 17
Problem_Description: The original 17‑step route gave an overall yield < 0.2 %, required hazardous reagents (e.g., tetrabutylammonium azide) for the hydroxyl‑to‑amine conversion, demanded extensive chromatography, produced non‑crystalline intermediates and an amorphous API, and suffered from unstable intermediates and inconsistent yields, rendering the sequence unscalable.
Solution_Description: A new five‑step route was designed that introduces the 4‑aminomethyl group early via a Staudinger ketene‑imine [2 + 2] cycloaddition, enabling telescoped operations and eliminating isolation steps. All intermediates are obtained by crystallization or precipitation, avoiding normal‑ and chiral‑phase chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "There were several issues in this original synthesis: (1) the overall yield was less than 0.2%, and most notably, alcohol 5 required a three‑step conversion to the amine functionality utilizing hazardous reagents, including tetrabutylammonium azide; (2) several steps in the synthesis required extensive chromatography (four normal‑phase, one reversed‑phase, and one chiral‑phase); (3) all of the advanced intermediates lacked crystallinity; and (4) the final form of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) was amorphous. The initial synthesis was further hampered by unstable intermediates and inconsistent yields in many steps and was therefore deemed unscalable."; "The efficiency of the route could be greatly improved by early introduction of the 4‑aminomethyl group. With this approach in mind, we envisioned a Staudinger ketene–imine reaction to prepare the β‑lactam core…"; "All of the isolated intermediates were obtained through crystallization or precipitation and filtration, avoiding chromatographic steps."

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of Monocyclic β‑Lactam Core 17
Problem_Description: Traditional phthalimide deprotection by hydrazinolysis was unsafe at scale and caused epimerisation or β‑lactam ring opening, generating side‑product 16.

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of Monocyclic β‑Lactam Core 17
Problem_Description: During the classical resolution of racemic amine 15, the slurry became a non‑stirrable gel at temperatures < 40 °C and showed ∼30 % decomposition at reflux, leading to a modest isolated yield (45 %) of the resolved salt 17.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Diatomaceous earth was added as a filter aid to prevent gelling and to adsorb insoluble impurity 16; the reaction temperature was set to 60 °C for 45–60 min (avoiding decomposition); a high solvent‑to‑solid ratio (30 vol EtOAc) reduced viscosity and facilitated agitation.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Stress testing of the reaction showed that ∼30 % decomposition occurred at reflux for 1 h and that a non‑stirrable gel resulted at temperatures below 40 °C."; "The mixture was heated at 60 °C for 1 h…"; "Treatment of 15 with diatomaceous earth (2.40 kg)…"; Solution: "The mixture was stirred at 20 °C for 1 h, treated with diatomaceous earth (2.40 kg), and stirred for 30 min while the temperature was maintained at 20 °C. The solids were filtered…"; "The slurry was heated at 60 °C for 1 h, cooled to 20 °C, and held at 20 °C for 1 h with stirring."; "...30 vol ethyl acetate to reduce the viscosity for effective agitation."

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of Monocyclic β‑Lactam Core 17
Problem_Description: Removal of the dibenzoyl‑l‑tartaric acid salt 17 to obtain the free amine 18 risked β‑lactam ring opening under strongly basic conditions.
Solution_Description: The salt was basified gently with 5 % aqueous K₃PO₄ at pH 8–9, followed by recrystallisation from a heptane/ethyl acetate mixture, delivering free amine 18 (99 % ee, 80 % yield) with no detectable degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...to liberate the free amine without degrading the sensitive β‑lactam ring…"; "...potential ring opening observed with other basic deprotection methods."; Solution: "Basification of salt 17 with 5 % aqueous K₃PO₄ at pH 8–9 followed by recrystallisation from ∼7:1 heptane/ethyl acetate provided free amine 18 (99 % ee) in 80 % yield as a white powder with no detectable presence of side products from ring opening or epimerisation."

Paper Title: Process Development for the Synthesis of Monocyclic β‑Lactam Core 17
Problem_Description: The aldehyde intermediate 8, obtained from diethyl acetal 7, required isolation of a solid product; initial conditions gave a non‑crystalline material that would complicate scale‑up.
Solution_Description: After TFA deprotection in DCM, the reaction mixture was swapped to a 1:3 toluene/heptane mixture, which crystallised 8 in 94 % isolated yield, enabling filtration and drying without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "In the first step, commercially available diethyl acetal 7 was treated with trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) under anhydrous conditions in dichloromethane to afford aldehyde 8. A solvent swap to 1:3 toluene/heptane gave 8 in good yield (94 %) as a crystalline product."; "The mixture was crystallised over 2 h. The batch was filtered, and the solids were washed…"; Solution: "A solvent swap to 1:3 toluene/heptane gave 8 in good yield (94 %) as a crystalline product."; "The mixture was crystallised over 2 h. The batch was filtered…"

Problem_Description: When DBU was added at 10–15 °C the pyrmetazole‑DBU salt was not fully soluble, leading to incomplete conversion; using < 0.8 equiv DBU also gave low conversion.

Problem_Description: Reslurry of the product in a filter‑dryer (≈30 rpm) gave only 98.4 % ee, attributed to poor mixing; a higher stirring speed improved optical purity.
