Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: Low solubility of the solid ketone 10,10‑DMA (1) in toluene limited the attainable concentration for the Grignard addition.
Solution_Description: Replace toluene (or toluene/THF mixture) with THF, which provides a ≈100 g L⁻¹ higher solubility for 10,10‑DMA, allowing a 1.8 M (~400 g L⁻¹) feed concentration.
Supporting_Evidence: “The solubility of 10,10‑DMA 1 in THF shows a significantly higher solubility than toluene or MeTHF… The significantly higher solubility of 10,10‑DMA 1 in THF makes it obvious to use THF.”

Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: During the HCl addition step the THF solvent boiled, producing vapour and loss of a homogeneous liquid phase.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Install a 100 psi back‑pressure regulator (BPR) downstream of the HCl coil to raise the system pressure, suppress THF boiling and keep all streams liquid.
Supporting_Evidence: “Implementation of the HCl stream caused boiling of the THF solvent… A back pressure regulator (BPR) of 100 psi was added to prevent the boiling of the THF (65 °C at STP).”

Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: The one‑step hydrolysis‑dehydration with concentrated HCl generated a large amount of heat and immediate precipitation of a white solid.
Solution_Description: Use 12 M HCl (stoichiometric) to minimize the volume of acid added, and operate the coil at ambient temperature under the 100 psi BPR so the exotherm is dissipated without temperature runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: “The experiment with hydrochloric acid resulted in significant heat development and an immediate precipitation of solids… From a production perspective, the more concentrated hydrochloric acid is the optimal choice; less aqueous waste is generated if the acid used is stoichiometric.”

Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: Grignard reagent DMPC‑MgCl (2) reacts violently with residual moisture; a clogged IR flow‑cell caused a tube burst when moisture entered the stream.
Solution_Description: Use PTFE‑gasket‑lined pump heads specifically ordered for Grignard reagents and place the water‑sensitive addition (HCl) after the acetic‑acid coil where the mixture is already basic, reducing exposure of the Grignard to water.
Supporting_Evidence: “The tube burst was a result of a clog formed from the Grignard reagent reacting with residual water in the IR flow cell… The two Knauer pumps were specially ordered with a PTFE gasket intended for Grignard reagents and THF solvent.”

Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: Crystallization of Melitracen HCl in the T‑mixer caused clogging and loss of product due to premature solid formation.
Solution_Description: Separate the two streams (organic phase and 2 M HCl/Et₂O) and feed them directly into the collection flask rather than mixing in a low‑pressure T‑mixer, preventing crystallization inside the mixer and preserving yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, mixing of the two streams was attempted in a T‑mixer… the clogging was caused by evaporation… and the crystallization of Melitracen HCl happening in the T‑mixer… As an alternative, the two streams were pumped individually into the collecting bottle.”

Paper Title: Redesign of a Grignard-Based Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) Batch Synthesis to a Flow Process for the Preparation of Melitracen HCl
Problem_Description: The magnesium alkoxide intermediate (3) is moisture‑sensitive; attempting to isolate it for solubility testing was unfeasible because it decomposes on exposure to water.
Solution_Description: Rely on a qualitative visual test of solution stability rather than isolation; keep the reaction mixture under inert atmosphere and proceed directly to hydrolysis without isolation, effectively telescoping the step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Magnesium alkoxide 3 is not easily isolated, as the magnesium halide part easily reacts with water and moisture… a qualitative first estimate of its capability to stay in solution could be sufficient.”

Paper Title: Regioselective Functionalization of 4‑Methyl‑1
Problem_Description: The original Strategy I route required many steps, gave a low overall isolated yield, used a costly trisubstituted phenyl precursor, and employed a potentially explosive azido reagent (N₃CH₂COOEt), making the process unsafe and economically unattractive on scale.
Solution_Description: The key indole‑forming Hemetsberger–Knittel cyclization was transferred to continuous flow, allowing high temperature operation with a very short residence time. This limited exposure to the hazardous azide, improved safety, and boosted the isolated yield to ~78 %.
Supporting_Evidence: We first used substrate 10 for a model study. Under conventional heating, batch reactions afforded low yields of indole product 11 (Table 1, entries 1, 2). Switching to flow conditions, by increasing the reaction temperature while limiting the residence time (entries 3–5), an excellent yield (78 %) of indole product 11 was obtained. The flow conditions significantly improved the original route, addressing the main issues of the indole formation step.

Paper Title: Regioselective Functionalization of 4‑Methyl‑1
Problem_Description: Attempts to install a formyl group directly at the 5‑position of indole 11 using Vilsmeier conditions failed, giving poor conversion and low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: Regioselective bromination was achieved by using excess NBS to give bis‑brominated product at the 3‑ and 5‑positions, followed by selective monodebromination to afford the desired mono‑bromo intermediate in good yield.
Supporting_Evidence: After largely unsuccessful efforts to directly install the formyl group on the 5 position under Vilsmeier conditions, attention switched to the bromination reaction. Increasing the equivalence of NBS yielded complete bis‑bromination, regioselectively at the 3 and 5 positions to afford 12. Taking advantage of the higher reactivity at the 3 position, monodebromination was achieved to afford 13 in good yield.

Paper Title: Regioselective Functionalization of 4‑Methyl‑1
Problem_Description: Formylation of bromide 13 under a variety of standard conditions gave only trace product due to competing deprotection of the PhSO₂ group and nucleophilic addition of base to the nitrile, even at –78 °C.
Solution_Description: A Pd‑catalyzed Suzuki cross‑coupling of the 5‑bromo‑indole 19 with vinyl boronate 21, followed by oxidative cleavage of the vinyl group, generated the aldehyde and simultaneously removed the protecting group, providing the target aldehyde in acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Pd‑catalyzed Suzuki cross‑coupling of 19 with vinyl boronate 21 worked well to afford 22. Oxidative cleavage of the vinyl group exposed the aldehyde followed by deprotection to provide desired product A in decent yields.

Paper Title: Regioselective Functionalization of 4‑Methyl‑1
Problem_Description: The Suzuki‑derived three‑step sequence required the expensive vinyl boronate 21 and still needed three operations to reach the aldehyde, limiting overall efficiency and cost‑effectiveness.
Solution_Description: A Pd‑catalyzed carbonylation (formylation) of the more reactive iodo‑indole 20 using CO and Na₂CO₃ gave the aldehyde directly; the mild base also removed the PhSO₂ protecting group in one pot, delivering the final product in 80 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Finally, a Pd‑catalyzed formylation reaction worked beautifully with the more reactive iodo‑substrate 20 whereas the same conditions afforded only a trace amount of A with bromide 19. Furthermore, the mild base (Na₂CO₃) used in the reaction effectively removed the PhSO₂ protecting group concurrently in a one‑pot fashion to afford an excellent 80 % isolated yield of target compound A.

Paper Title: Regioselective Functionalization of 4‑Methyl‑1
Problem_Description: The overall original sequence was long, gave low overall yield, and relied on expensive, non‑commercial phenyl precursors, making kilogram‑scale production impractical.
Solution_Description: Strategy II was adopted: inexpensive, kilogram‑grade 4‑methyl‑indole 15 was sequentially functionalized (ortho‑lithiation‑cyanation, regioselective bromination, Pd‑catalyzed formylation) to afford the target indole in a concise, high‑yielding, and economically viable route suitable for large‑scale manufacture.
Supporting_Evidence: Nevertheless, we were encouraged by the feasibility of the regioselective functionalization of the indole core and turned our attention to inexpensive indole 15 that is commercially available on kilogram scale. The new route is much shorter, higher yielding, and more economical for kilogram scale production.

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: The previously used Heck‑type approach required a protecting group that had to be removed with hydroxylamine and a non‑selective hydrogenation step, adding extra reagents, work‑up, and waste.
Solution_Description: A diastereoselective 1,4‑conjugate addition of alkyl cuprates to the α,β‑unsaturated ester derived from Vince lactam was developed, eliminating the protecting‑group/hydrogenation sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although this method worked well on a small scale, it suffered from the need for a troublesome protecting group, which required hydroxylamine for its removal, and a nonselective hydrogenation of the double bonds.”; “Thus, we searched for a more general alternative approach where both the benzyl and isobutyl side chains could be introduced efficiently with good diastereoselectivity.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: Benzyl cuprates are short‑lived and are prone to Wurtz‑type coupling, which can lower the desired product yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed with trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) as an additive to stabilize the cuprate and enhance reactivity, and the copper loading was carefully controlled.
Supporting_Evidence: “It is also well‑known that the benzyl cuprates required for this study are short‑lived species and that Wurtz coupling is a common side reaction.”; “In the presence of trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) as an additive, enhanced reactivity of a weakly reactive α,β‑unsaturated ester is sometimes observed.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: Endocyclic α,β‑unsaturated esters show lower reactivity than simple alkenes, giving modest conversion in the cuprate addition step.
Solution_Description: Methanol was employed as a common solvent for esterification, Boc‑protection, and isomerisation, enabling a telescoped three‑step sequence without intermediate isolations and giving an overall 84 % yield to the key ester.
Supporting_Evidence: “such α,β‑unsaturated esters are of lower reactivity compared with mono‑ and disubstituted alkenes.”; “We believed that all of the steps from 4 to 3 could be performed in the same solvent… No purification other than extraction of 3 was needed… overall yield … 84 %.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: The conjugate addition produced mixtures of diastereomers; low diastereoselectivity would necessitate time‑consuming chromatographic separations.
Solution_Description: A post‑reaction epimerisation with catalytic NaOMe in MeOH converted the minor diastereomers to the thermodynamically favoured one, and subsequent salt formation (e.g., with dicyclohexylamine) followed by crystallisation gave the stereoisomerically pure product without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “the 1,4‑conjugate addition reactions gave the products as mixtures of diastereomers… would in the worst case require time‑consuming chromatographic purifications.”; “the crude mixture of 5 in MeOH was treated with sodium methoxide… giving an approximately 95:5 diastereomeric mixture in favor of the desired one.”; “dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) formed a crystalline solid with 1… The mixture was filtered … to give the title salt 7 … >99 % stereoisomeric purity.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: During the work‑up of the benzyl‑cuprate reaction, precipitated copper salts formed at the phase interface, blocking filtration and preventing clean liquid‑liquid separation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was altered to use MTBE as the organic solvent (instead of THF) and the copper salt loading was reduced (catalytic CuI), which improved phase separation and eliminated the need for problematic filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: “Precipitated copper salts at the interface prevented clean separation of the layers. Removal of copper salts through filtration was attempted but abandoned because of blockage of the filter.”; “The use of tetrahydrofuran (THF) as the reaction solvent made it harder to obtain clear, well‑separated phases in the extraction.”; “Using a catalytic amount of CuI (21 mol %) and MTBE as the solvent… TMSCl as an additive… was not necessary for the reaction to occur.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: The isobutyl route originally employed excess copper salt and several additives, leading to a labour‑intensive work‑up and higher material cost.
Solution_Description: The process was revised to use only catalytic CuI (21 mol %), eliminated the TMSCl additive, switched to MTBE (non‑miscible with water) to simplify extraction, and employed a salt‑screen (R‑1‑phenylethylamine) to crystallise the final product, removing the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “the excess of copper salt used as well as the additives resulted in a time‑consuming, troublesome workup.”; “We aimed for a process in which we could have as few additives as possible and ideally use only a substoichiometric amount of the copper salt to simplify the workup.”; “TMSCl as an additive … was not necessary for the reaction to occur.”; “(R)-1‑phenylethylamine gave a salt with suitable solid properties and most of the undesired diastereomers were removed in one single crystallisation.”

Paper Title: Diastereoselective 1,4-Conjugate Addition of Alkyl Cuprates to Methyl Cyclopent-1-enecarboxylates
Problem_Description: Direct crystallisation of the free carboxylic acids was hindered by accumulated minor impurities from the linear six‑step sequence.
Solution_Description: A salt‑screen was performed; the chosen amine formed a crystalline salt that could be isolated cleanly, allowing the free acid to be liberated later by simple acid‑base work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Various minor impurities had accumulated in the synthesis and made direct crystallization of carboxylic acid 1 challenging.”; “We believed that a salt screen would give us a better chance to identify suitable conditions for crystallization. … dicyclohexylamine (DCHA) formed a crystalline solid with 1 …”

Paper Title: Dehydration of an Insoluble Urea Byproduct Enables the Condensation of DCC and Malonic Acid in Flow
Problem_Description: N,N′‑Dicyclohexyl urea (DCHU), a solid by‑product, has very low solubility in most solvents, leading to a heterogeneous mixture and potential clogging in flow reactors.
Solution_Description: Switch to THF, where the desired product is highly soluble, and add phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) as a dehydrating agent that converts insoluble DCHU into a soluble salt (5), giving a homogeneous reaction mixture suitable for flow.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "...handling of N,N′‑dicyclohexyl urea (DCHU), a solid which we found to have very low solubility in a wide range of solvents …"; "Table 1 shows DCHU solubilities of 0.0–7.3 mg mL⁻¹".
Solution: "...addition of POCl₃ to the reaction mixture enabled the development of homogeneous conditions…"; "...using THF (in which 2 was most soluble) as solvent".

Paper Title: Dehydration of an Insoluble Urea Byproduct Enables the Condensation of DCC and Malonic Acid in Flow
Problem_Description: Using only 1 equiv of DCC gave poor isolated assay yields (≈21 %), because malonic acid was not completely consumed.
Solution_Description: Employ 2 equiv of DCC to drive full consumption of malonic acid, achieving 84 % assay yield; additionally, run at 80 °C to improve reaction robustness and prevent incomplete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "low yield derived from incomplete consumption of malonic acid"; "Entry 2 (1 eq DCC) gave 21 % assay yield".
Solution: "using 2 equiv of DCC gave complete consumption of malonic acid, giving 2 in 84 % assay yield"; "increasing the temperature to 80 °C increased the robustness of the process".

Paper Title: Dehydration of an Insoluble Urea Byproduct Enables the Condensation of DCC and Malonic Acid in Flow
Problem_Description: Screening of dehydration reagents showed that most additives (e.g., P₂O₅, Ph₃P, Ac₂O) either gave no reaction or low assay yields; DCHU was not recycled to DCC, causing low overall yield when attempting to reduce DCC loading.
Solution_Description: Identify POCl₃ as the only additive that afforded a homogeneous mixture and the highest assay yield (49 %) among the screened reagents, even though DCHU recycling did not occur.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "POCl₃ (entry 7) was the only reagent that gave a homogeneous reaction mixture…moderate assay yield, indicating that DCHU was not recycled to DCC as intended"; "we were unable to find an additive that gave high yield with reduced DCC loading".
Solution: "addition of POCl₃ to the reaction mixture enabled the development of homogeneous conditions".

Paper Title: Dehydration of an Insoluble Urea Byproduct Enables the Condensation of DCC and Malonic Acid in Flow
Problem_Description: During flow operation, slow accumulation of insoluble DCHU caused reactor clogging, especially at 60 °C; impurity 7 formation was sensitive to the malonic‑acid addition rate, leading to variable impurity levels.
Solution_Description: Prime the reactor with a POCl₃‑THF stream before introducing DCC/malic acid to keep the system homogeneous; increase the reactor temperature to 80 °C to suppress DCHU buildup; use a plug‑flow reactor with a 3.6 min residence time, providing sufficient conversion while avoiding clogging.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem: "slow accumulation of DCHU over time was observed when the reaction was run at 60 °C; increasing the temperature to 80 °C increased the robustness of the process, and the reactor was run without clogging for over 8 h"; "Slow dosing of malonic acid … caused an increase in [7]… rapid addition of malonic acid at elevated temperature reduced the level of 7".
Solution: "priming the reactor with POCl₃–THF prior to introduction of DCC and malonic acid was required to prevent clogging"; "increasing the temperature to 80 °C increased the robustness"; "The residence time in the flow reactor … 3.6 min was sufficient to provide complete reaction without clogging".

Paper Title: Dehydration of an Insoluble Urea Byproduct Enables the Condensation of DCC and Malonic Acid in Flow
Problem_Description: The product needed to be isolated from the continuous‑flow stream without interfering with downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Add the reactor effluent to isopropanol, causing the product to precipitate as a solid that can be filtered and washed, providing a simple isolation method compatible with flow.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Samples of 2 could be isolated by addition of the product stream to iPrOH… white solid formed, which could be collected by filtration".

Paper Title: Catalytic Enantioselective Synthesis of Key Propargylic Alcohol Intermediates of the Anti-HIV Drug Efavirenz
Problem_Description: The original catalytic alkynylation of the amino‑substituted trifluoromethyl ketone 1a with Δ‑Ru1 gave only modest conversion (58 % isolated yield) and enantioselectivity (91.6 % ee) even after 48 h at 60 °C; further attempts did not improve these figures.
Solution_Description: The researchers changed the substrate to the electron‑withdrawing nitro‑ketone 1c and switched to the simpler Δ‑Ru2 catalyst (which is cheaper and equally active). Under the same loading (0.5 mol %) the reaction gave 93 % yield and 99.6 % ee in 16 h at 60 °C; the catalyst can also be run at room temperature with comparable results.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the Merck intermediate (S)‑2a with 58% yield and 91.6% ee…we were not able to significantly improve these results.”; “…using just 0.5 mol % Δ‑Ru1, the propargylic alcohol (S)‑2c was obtained in a yield of 93% with 99.6% ee after 16 h at 60 °C (entry 2).”; “Interestingly, using a simplified catalyst devoid of the two 3,5‑dimethylphenyl moieties (Δ‑Ru2), an almost unchanged yield and enantioselectivity were observed (entry 3).”; “Since the synthesis of Δ‑Ru2 is less time‑consuming and less expensive compared to Δ‑Ru1, the simplified catalyst Δ‑Ru2 is apparently the catalyst of choice.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Enantioselective Synthesis of Key Propargylic Alcohol Intermediates of the Anti-HIV Drug Efavirenz
Problem_Description: Reducing the catalyst loading below 0.2 mol % caused the reaction to stall (e.g., 0.1 mol % Δ‑Ru2 gave only 42 % yield after 64 h), indicating that insufficient catalyst amount leads to poor conversion and higher material cost per batch.
Solution_Description: The authors identified 0.2 mol % Δ‑Ru2 as the optimal loading that balances high yield (≥95 %) with minimal catalyst consumption; the use of the cheaper Δ‑Ru2 further mitigates cost concerns.
Supporting_Evidence: “A lower catalyst loading of 0.1 mol % led to a decreased yield, even after prolonging the reaction time to 64 h (entry 5).”; “Even at a reduced catalyst loading of 0.2 mol %, a yield of 95% with 99.4% ee was obtained (entry 4).”; “Since the synthesis of Δ‑Ru2 is less time‑consuming and less expensive compared to Δ‑Ru1, the simplified catalyst Δ‑Ru2 is apparently the catalyst of choice.”

Paper Title: Catalytic Enantioselective Synthesis of Key Propargylic Alcohol Intermediates of the Anti-HIV Drug Efavirenz
Problem_Description: The alkynylation was highly sensitive to exposure to air; performing the reaction under air dropped the isolated yield to 21 % (entry 8).
Solution_Description: All reactions were carried out in sealed Schlenk tubes under a nitrogen atmosphere with magnetic stirring, ensuring an inert environment and preventing oxidative deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction is sensitive to air (entry 8) but not to the presence of small amounts of water (entry 9).”; “All reactions were carried out under an atmosphere of nitrogen with magnetic stirring unless otherwise indicated.”; “Performed under air.” (Table footnote f).

Paper Title: Catalytic Enantioselective Synthesis of Key Propargylic Alcohol Intermediates of the Anti-HIV Drug Efavirenz
Problem_Description: The initial protocol for substrate 1a required 48 h at 60 °C to achieve modest conversion, which is impractically long for manufacturing.
Solution_Description: By switching to the nitro substrate 1c and utilizing the more active Δ‑Ru2 catalyst, the reaction time was reduced to 16 h (or even 16 h at room temperature) while delivering >93 % yield and >99 % ee.
Supporting_Evidence: “…the reaction…provided … 58% yield … after 48 h at 60 °C (entry 1).”; “…using just 0.5 mol % Δ‑Ru1, … 93% yield … after 16 h at 60 °C (entry 2).”; “At a catalyst loading of 0.5 mol % Δ‑Ru2, the reaction can be executed at room temperature to afford (S)‑2c with 96% yield and 99.4% ee after 16 h (entry 6).”

Paper Title: Catalytic Enantioselective Synthesis of Key Propargylic Alcohol Intermediates of the Anti-HIV Drug Efavirenz
Problem_Description: Running the reaction at a lower concentration (0.2 M) lowered the isolated yield to 76 % (entry 7 in Table 2).
Solution_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration to 1.0 M restored the yield to ≥94 % without compromising enantioselectivity, demonstrating the importance of concentration optimization.
Supporting_Evidence: “A reduced overall concentration also afforded a decreased yield (entry 7).”; “An increased concentration (entry 8) … provided comparable results.”

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: The key hydroxylamine intermediate 2 has very limited solubility in common organic solvents (e.g., only 31 mg mL⁻¹ in THF at rt).  This forces the use of large solvent volumes to keep the material in solution, which in turn makes catalyst separation and downstream distillation very time‑consuming on a manufacturing scale.
Solution_Description: An in‑situ trimethylsilyl (TMS) protection strategy using N‑O‑bis‑(trimethylsilyl)‑acetamide (BSA) converts 2 into the silylated intermediate 5, which is much more soluble.  After hydrogenolysis the TMS group is removed and the free hydroxylamine precipitates from the same solvent (isopropyl acetate, IPAc) because 2 is poorly soluble in IPAc, enabling a single‑solvent process, lower reaction volumes and a fast crystallization step.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The solubility of 2 in organic solvents is limited, and even in THF the solubility of 2 was only 31 mg/mL at room temperature.","Since a reaction at elevated temperature was not desirable, separation from the heterogeneous catalyst required a relatively large volume of solvent, and consequently an extended time cycle for distillation at manufacturing scale.","Protection was expected to stabilize 2 and improve the solubility of the intermediate thereby minimizing reaction volume and improving cycle time.","We identified isopropyl acetate (IPAc) as an ideal candidate, since the solubility of 2 in IPAc is low (2.1 mg/mL) and hydrogenolysis in IPAc under optimized conditions proceeded with a similar rate and impurity profile to the reaction in THF."]

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: The free N‑hydroxyl intermediate 2 is unstable; if the hydrogenolysis stalls it decomposes, which would lower overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: BSA rapidly silylates the liberated hydroxylamine, converting it to the more stable TMS ether 5.  This protects the intermediate during the reaction and results in quantitative conversion after deprotection.
Supporting_Evidence: ["If the hydrogenolysis reaction were to stall, degradation of 2 was anticipated to be a significant competing process which could compromise yield and purity.","The TMS protected hydroxyl urea 5 was cleanly formed in nearly quantitative yield by hydrogenolysis of 4 with solid supported Pd catalysts.","The role of BSA is to ensure rapid conversion of 2 to TMS protected 5 in situ."]

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: Without additives the benzyl‑ether hydrogenolysis proceeds extremely slowly (≤4 % conversion after 4 h), making the process unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Adding sub‑stoichiometric amounts of DABCO (≈1–2 mol %) accelerates the reaction dramatically (up to 64 % conversion in 4 h, a 16‑fold increase), enabling practical reaction times and higher isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The use of DABCO resulted in 64% conversion after only 4 h, a 16‑fold increase in conversion over the control reaction.","At a charge of only 0.5 mol % DABCO a significant rate acceleration was observed, with hydrogen uptake essentially plateauing after 1 h and a quantitative yield determined by HPLC after 3 h."]

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: Different batches of BSA contained variable levels of triethylamine (TEA) impurity, leading to inconsistent hydrogenolysis rates.
Solution_Description: The rate‑enhancing effect of TEA was traced to a basic additive, and DABCO was adopted as a defined additive to replace the uncontrolled TEA impurity, standardising the process.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Certain lots of BSA were contaminated with up to 2 mol % of triethylamine (TEA), while other samples contained none of the amine impurity.","The hydrogenolysis reaction was significantly accelerated when TEA contaminated BSA was employed.","After DABCO was identified as the most efficient additive among this set, a loading study was performed..."]

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: High palladium loading (≥2.4 mol % Pd/C) was required for complete conversion, increasing material cost and complicating catalyst recovery.
Solution_Description: In the presence of 1–2 mol % DABCO the same conversion is achieved with only 0.72 mol % Pd/C; Pd/C is also preferred over Pd/Al₂O₃ for easier filtration, reducing both catalyst cost and downstream processing burden.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In the presence of DABCO a catalyst loading of only 0.72 mol % (3 wt %) Pd/C was required to reach complete conversion in a few hours, where in the absence of DABCO more than 12 h were required for reaction completion even with 2.4 mol % of Pd/C (5 wt %).", "After establishing the optimal DABCO charge, other solid supported Pd catalysts were evaluated... In all cases, a significant increase in yield was observed when 2 mol % DABCO was present."]

Paper Title: Improved Preparation of a Key Hydroxylamine Intermediate for Relebactam: Rate Enhancement of Benzyl Ether Hydrogenolysis with DABCO
Problem_Description: The original process required a solvent switch (THF for hydrogenolysis, a different solvent for isolation), adding operational complexity and time.
Solution_Description: Switching to isopropyl acetate as the sole reaction solvent satisfies both the hydrogenolysis step and the subsequent reactive crystallization, eliminating the need for a solvent exchange.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We identified isopropyl acetate (IPAc) as an ideal candidate, since the solubility of 2 in IPAc is low (2.1 mg/mL) and hydrogenolysis in IPAc under optimized conditions proceeded with a similar rate and impurity profile to the reaction in THF.","A single solvent (IPAc) process for the formation of 2 was developed which relies on an in situ TMS ether formation during hydrogenolysis, and reactive crystallization of 2 by acidic deprotection after catalyst removal."]

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: The crystallization of intermediate 9·DCHA required an oil‑solid conversion at 5 °C in a poor solvent, which could not be reproduced on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The route was redesigned to avoid isolation of 9·DCHA altogether by telescoping steps 1–7 and performing a through‑process, eliminating the need for the problematic crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since the crystallization was an unusual oil–solid conversion in a poor solvent at 5 °C, we could not perform the crystallization on a large scale.”; “we decided to maintain the quality of the API by avoiding the generation of the critical contaminants…without isolation of compound 9·DCHA.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Step 2 (O‑2‑butynylation) gave low conversion when water content was uncontrolled, leading to residual starting material and lower overall yield.
Solution_Description: Fine‑particle K2CO3 was used and the water content of the reaction was tightly controlled (≈0.055 % w/w), raising conversion to >99.9 % at manufacturing scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion rate was improved by using fine‑particle K2CO3 and controlling the water content in the reaction system…More than 99.9 % conversion was achieved at manufacturing scale.”; Table 1 showing conversion vs. water content.

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Residual 1‑bromo‑2‑butyne after step 2 caused formation of Impurity‑3 during work‑up of compound 5, decreasing its yield.
Solution_Description: Diethylamine was added after the reaction to quench any remaining alkylating agent completely.
Supporting_Evidence: “This problem was solved by adding diethylamine to quench the alkylating agent thoroughly after the reaction was complete.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Impurity‑4 originated from 1‑bromo‑2‑butyne containing 1,3‑dibromo‑2‑butene when purchased from early‑stage suppliers.
Solution_Description: The standard for the reagent was raised, specifying high‑quality 1‑bromo‑2‑butyne for all subsequent batches.
Supporting_Evidence: “This concern was addressed by setting the standard as high‑quality at the time of purchasing the reagent.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Residual intermediate 5 carried into the condensation step generated Impurity‑5 in the final API.
Solution_Description: After the coupling, the crude mixture was washed twice with aqueous citric acid, reducing residual 5 to 0.23 % and the API impurity to 0.07 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “the amount of residual 5 was decreased to 0.23 % by washing with aqueous citric acid twice. As a result, Impurity‑5 in the API was reduced to 0.07 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Impurity‑6 formed under the acidic conditions used for simultaneous TBS and ketal deprotection (step 5).
Solution_Description: The deprotection sequence was reordered: TBS was removed first under neutral conditions with TBAF/AcOH, followed by separate ketal deprotection after oxidation, preventing lactone formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since the generation of Impurity‑6 was inevitable under acidic conditions, the route was modified to cleave the TBS group first under neutral conditions…and to deprotect the ketal separately after oxidation of the alcohol to avoid the formation of the lactone.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Using TFA/CH₂Cl₂ for the final deprotection imposed a high environmental and equipment burden.
Solution_Description: The reagents were switched to H₂SO₄/MeCN, which reduced both the environmental impact and the strain on the apparatus.
Supporting_Evidence: “In step 7, the reagent was changed from TFA/CH₂Cl₂ to H₂SO₄/MeCN in order to reduce the burden on the environment and the apparatus.”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: The final API required high‑purity isolation; single crystallization gave limited recovery.
Solution_Description: A three‑stage purification was introduced: (1) high‑recovery aqueous crystallization with elevated NaCl, (2) saponification to hydrolyze residual impurities, and (3) a second aqueous MeCN crystallization, delivering 99.62 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “we established a subsequent purification process that involved (1) high‑recovery crystallization, (2) saponification, and (3) quality‑increasing crystallization…The second crystallization from aqueous MeCN afforded the API (99.62 % purity).”

Paper Title: Development of a Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of a Novel Anti-HCV Agent, CH4930808
Problem_Description: Viscous mixtures and phase‑separation during the telescoped steps caused handling difficulties and variable yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reaction mixtures were diluted with appropriate solvents (e.g., MeCN/H₂O 1:1) and agitated under controlled temperature to maintain homogeneity and improve mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: “MeCN (0.45 kg) was added to adjust the MeCN/water = 1:1 (v/v)…the solution had been stirred at 5 °C for 2 h, the solid was filtered….”

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: The commercially sourced acid 4 (chloropyrazine precursor) sometimes arrived with residual moisture and required drying before it could be converted to the acid chloride 5, causing batch‑to‑batch variability and handling difficulties.
Solution_Description: The team elected to manufacture acid 4 in‑house from diaminomaleonitrile, eliminating the need for a drying step and providing a more consistent, on‑demand supply.
Supporting_Evidence: “While a further 430 kg of chloropyrazine 2 were delivered starting from acid 4, the latter occasionally required drying on receipt before it could be successfully engaged in the transformation to acid chloride 5” (Sec 4); “It was proposed that it would be cheaper to manufacture it in‑house” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Azetidine hydrochloride showed an exothermic decomposition onset at ~71 °C (half‑life ≈ 24 h at 29 °C) and is classified as a self‑reactive solid (UN 3238), creating a safety risk on large‑scale handling.
Solution_Description: The acid chloride 5 was added to a basic azetidine solution (pH > 9, maintained with potassium carbonate) to keep the azetidine in its de‑protonated form and suppress the exotherm, while controlling the addition rate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The accelerating rate calorimetry of this salt indicated an onset of exothermic activity from ∼71 °C… 29 °C was evaluated as the temperature at which it would take 24 h for the decomposition to reach its maximum rate” (Sec 3); “Adding the acid chloride 5 solution to a basic solution of azetidine was found to be important in limiting the ring opening… by chloride” (Sec 3).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Impurity 7 (derived from 3‑chloropropylamine) appeared in chloropyrazine 2 when the azetidine hydrochloride feed contained up to 10 wt % of the amine, leading to variable impurity levels.
Solution_Description: The aqueous azetidine solution was washed with toluene before coupling, effectively removing 3‑chloropropylamine and stabilising impurity levels.
Supporting_Evidence: “3‑Chloropropylamine in the azetidine hydrochloride input material was identified as the principal source of impurity 7… 10 wt %/wt was detected in one batch” (Sec 3); “it proved possible to control levels of 3‑chloropropylamine by washing the aqueous azetidine solution with toluene prior to use” (Sec 3).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: During neutralisation of the bisnitrile intermediate, uncontrolled exotherms led to a dark‑coloured sodium salt Na·16 and inconsistent assay values.
Solution_Description: Sodium hydroxide was added slowly while keeping the temperature ≤ 10 °C, preventing the exotherm and the formation of dark product.
Supporting_Evidence: “Controlling the exotherm associated with the sodium hydroxide addition (T ≤ 10 °C) prevents dark coloured sodium salt Na·16 from being isolated” (Ref 17); “The batch was then aged for a further 6 h at 100 °C… the pH was adjusted to 2… resulting in the crystallisation of monosodium salt Na·16” (Sec 6.2).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Thermal decarboxylation of Na·16 required temperatures > 180 °C, beyond the capability of standard plant reactors, and the use of Brønsted acid produced a dark, low‑strength product.
Solution_Description: Phase‑transfer catalysts (Aliquat HTA‑1 or Aliquat 336) were employed to lower the required temperature and avoid excessive darkening; water content was reduced by azeotropic distillation with toluene before catalyst addition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Sodium salt Na·16 could be decarboxylated… beyond the capability of standard reactor vessels… catalytic amounts of Brønsted acid … formed a dark product” (Sec 4); “The replacement of the Brønsted acid by phase‑transfer catalysts Aliquat HTA‑1 or Aliquat 336 allowed the decarboxylation to proceed without excessive darkening” (Sec 4); “Controlling the water content of the reaction mixture… achieved through azeotropic distillation with toluene” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Residual sulfolane in the isolated Na·13 caused cake balling during drying and lowered the yield of the subsequent conversion to acid 4.
Solution_Description: The slurry was filtered hot at 70 °C to keep sulfolane liquid, then washed with toluene; later the free acid 13 was isolated (instead of the sodium salt) to avoid sulfolane altogether, improving downstream yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “These issues were overcome by filtering the slurry produced at the end of the reaction at 70 °C… and then washing the cake with toluene.” (Sec 4); “The presence of residual sulfolane… implicated in balling… significantly lowering the yield… The discovery that the yield… could be increased … by switching from (sulfolane‑free) sodium salt Na·13 to the corresponding free acid… guided the decision to target the isolation of acid 13 itself.” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Double chlorination of acid 13 using thionyl chloride alone proceeded incompletely, giving poor conversion to acid chloride 5.
Solution_Description: Phosphorus pentachloride was added as an accelerator and the reaction was run in two temperature stages (50 °C for acid‑chloride formation, then 85 °C for ring chlorination), leading to complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The double chlorination of acid 13 to acid chloride 5 using just thionyl chloride did not proceed to completion. The finding that it could be accelerated using phosphorus pentachloride as an additive led to the use of phosphorus pentachloride in toluene.” (Sec 4); “In the optimized procedure, the reaction was initially run at 50 °C … before it was heated to 85 °C in order to chlorinate the pyrazinone ring.” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Redesign of the Synthesis and Manufacture of an Azetidine-Bearing Pyrazine
Problem_Description: Acid 4 obtained after chlorination was reddish‑brown due to impurity formation, requiring extra treatment before use.
Solution_Description: The acid chloride solution was treated with activated charcoal before hydrolysis, yielding a lighter‑brown, > 99.5 wt % acid 4 suitable for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “Acid 4 formed … was not deemed to be of sufficient quality… The treatment of the acid chloride 5 solution with charcoal, prior to the hydrolysis, allowed material that was a lighter brown and displayed a strength of > 99.5 wt %/wt to be reproducibly isolated.” (Sec 4).

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Deposition of an unidentified insoluble material at the point where substrate 2 contacts n‑hexyllithium caused an increased pressure drop through the first static mixer, fouling the reactor.
Solution_Description: The deprotonation was moved to a separate batch reactor: lithium anion 4 was generated in batch, kept at low temperature, and then pumped as a homogeneous solution into the flow‑mixing zone. This eliminated the fouling interface while retaining the benefits of a continuous ketimine addition.
Supporting_Evidence:
"One way to circumvent this issue would be to generate lithium anion 4 in a batch reactor and subsequently flow that solution into a mixer where it would be combined with ketimine 3." 
"The subsequent addition of n‑hexyllithium proceeded several times more quickly than when the vessel wall was coated with 2, improving our plant time cycle and minimizing the length of time anion 4 was aged before the start of the continuous process." 
"lab experiments designed to mimic the redesigned process demonstrated that it was sufficiently robust to enable steady‑state operation for multiple hours."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Substrate 2 has very poor solubility in THF at the low temperatures required to suppress fouling, limiting the ability to cool the feed streams without causing solid deposition.
Solution_Description: The addition sequence was altered: THF was first charged and cooled, then substrate 2 was added. This kept 2 as a free‑flowing slurry and prevented crystallization on the vessel wall, preserving efficient heat transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: "Cooling a solution of 2 in THF to –20 °C before charging n‑hexyllithium led to crystallization of 2 on the vessel wall, reducing the cooling efficiency of the jacket... By charging THF to the vessel, cooling to –20 °C, and then charging 2, the insoluble 2 remained a free‑flowing slurry."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Lithium anion 4 slowly loses potency (2–4 % per day) even when stored at –20 °C, jeopardising product quality for longer batch runs.
Solution_Description: The anion stream was kept at –20 °C using jacketed transfer lines and a dedicated chill‑unit; the process flow was accelerated so that the anion was consumed shortly after preparation, minimizing exposure time.
Supporting_Evidence:
"A solution of 4 held at –20 °C for 3 days lost 2–4 % of its potency each day." 
"In our first pilot‑plant batch, the flow reaction began approximately 16 h after the start of the n‑hexyllithium charge; in subsequent batches we were able to more than halve this time."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: At pilot scale a new crystalline polymorph of lithium anion 4 formed, creating a slurry that could not be fed into the flow reactor and was thermodynamically favored in the operating window.
Solution_Description: Addition of 0.8–1.0 equiv of DMPU (a strong donor solvent) disrupted higher‑order aggregation of the organolithium, solubilising the polymorph and delivering a clear, homogeneous solution without affecting reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence:
"A panel of ... additives ... were tested, and DMPU was most effective in solubilizing 4 at the desired operating concentration and temperature." 
"Between 0.8 and 1.0 equiv of DMPU was required to generate a homogeneous solution of 4 that resisted crystallization even upon addition of isolated 4 as a seed." 
"Importantly, the addition of DMPU did not measurably impact the performance of the reaction, nor did it significantly alter the stability of the lithium anion feed solution."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Insufficient micromixing at lower total flow rates resulted in poor conversion (as low as 64 %) and lower diastereoselectivity, limiting productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Systematic increase of the total flow rate (55.5 → 250 kg h⁻¹) enhanced mixing efficiency, raising conversion across the temperature range. Concurrently, feed temperatures were lowered (–10 → –62 °C) to further improve conversion and reduce the sensitivity to flow‑rate changes.
Supporting_Evidence:
"At all of the temperatures studied, the reaction conversion consistently improved as the total flow rate, and thus the quality of mixing, increased." 
"The conversion increased from 64.2 % to 82.1 % when the total flow rate was raised from 55.5 to 250.0 kg/h." 
"As the feed temperature of 3 was lowered, the overall reaction temperature was consequently reduced, leading to higher reaction conversions and a progressive decrease in the impact of the total flow rate on conversion."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Pulsations from pump‑driven feeds caused variability in feed ratios, threatening reaction conversion and potential fouling.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Both reactants were delivered from pressurised vessels through independent, automatic mass‑flow controllers, eliminating pulsations and stabilising the feed ratio throughout the run.
Supporting_Evidence: "Both reactants were delivered by pressurizing the feed vessels and delivering the solutions through independent and automatic mass‑flow controllers. Feeding from pressurized vessels rather than using pumps (as we had at lab scale) eliminated any pulsing that could vary the feed ratio, which we believed might deleteriously affect the reaction conversion given the mere millisecond mixing time frame."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Static‑mixer geometry affected pressure drop and mixing efficiency, influencing throughput and conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Three mixer designs (Y‑shaped, T‑shaped with standard diameter, and T‑shaped with reduced diameter) were fabricated and evaluated; the wider Y‑shaped mixer (A) provided the best balance of conversion and pressure drop, and the equipment train was upgraded to allow precise temperature control at each stage.
Supporting_Evidence:
"A Y‑shaped mixer was fabricated from 1/4 in. Schedule 40 pipe (316L stainless steel), and a Koflo static mixing element was installed..." 
"The subsequent addition of n‑hexyllithium proceeded several times more quickly than when the vessel wall was coated with 2..." 
"Enhancements to the equipment train enabled rigorous temperature control at each point along the flow path, and improvements in our ability to execute the entire process rapidly enabled us to significantly shorten the length of time between the start of the n‑hexyllithium charge to 2 and the beginning of the flow reaction."

Paper Title: Development of an Organometallic Flow Chemistry Reaction at Pilot-Plant Scale for the Manufacture of Verubecestat
Problem_Description: Sampling of the hot, reactive flow stream posed safety and environmental hazards.
Solution_Description: An in‑line IR probe was installed for real‑time, non‑intrusive monitoring, correlating with offline HPLC and eliminating the need for manual sampling.
Supporting_Evidence: "Before the product stream was transferred to the quench vessel, it was passed through a flow cell equipped with an IR probe, allowing for real‑time analysis of the reaction’s performance... the method is well‑suited to real‑time monitoring of a continuous reaction in a commercial manufacturing environment, where such process analytical technology can provide instantaneous feedback on the reaction, enable a rapid response to maintain the target design space, and reduce the safety and environmental hazards associated with sampling."

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: The S_NAr displacement of chloro‑azaindole 4 with piperidine 5 required a large excess of the nucleophile (≥200 mol %) and the reaction mixture showed poor homogeneity in many solvents, leading to inconsistent conversion and difficulties scaling the reaction.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to tert‑amyl alcohol (t‑AmOH) gave a homogeneous solution and the best assay yield (87 %). Adding the organic base N‑methyl‑morpholine (NMM, 100 mol %) further improved conversion to 98 % while maintaining homogeneity and reproducibility on multikilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “We found the reaction in tert‑amyl alcohol (t‑AmOH) gave the cleanest reaction profile with an 87 % assay yield… the reaction mixture in t‑AmOH provided a homogeneous solution upon heating and until reaction completion.”; “The almost complete conversion (98 %) using N‑methyl‑morpholine (NMM) with comparable assay yield to the best condition without any extraneous bases added.”; “excess amounts of piperidine 5 of at least 200 mol % were required for complete conversion… The reaction mixture in t‑AmOH provided a homogeneous solution…”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, the solvent‑switch crystallization of intermediate 3 produced a paste‑like slurry that experienced severe particle attrition when agitated for the required long duration, slowing filtration and reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: A cooling‑crystallization with seeding at 70 °C was developed using a t‑AmOH/CH₃CN (40:60) binary mixture, followed by addition of water as an antisolvent to reach t‑AmOH/CH₃CN/H₂O = 16:24:60 (v/v/v). This minimized attrition, reduced processing time, and gave a rapid (≈30 min) filtration on 5 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “the slurry was found to exhibit paste‑like consistency on multikilogram scale… significant attrition of the crystals when the product slurry was deliberately agitated… To overcome this issue, we designed … a cooling crystallization with seeding at 70 °C … water was further introduced … to maximize the crystallization yield… total processing time dramatically reduced, resulting in a much improved filtration rate (ca. 30 min) on 5 kg scale.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: The amino‑azaindole intermediate 2 produced after hydrogenative nitro‑reduction is extremely oxygen‑sensitive, rapidly decomposing to azaisatin 6 and other side‑products, making reaction monitoring and work‑up problematic.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was quenched immediately after nitro‑reduction with a cyclopropane‑carbonyl acylating reagent under an inert nitrogen or argon atmosphere, avoiding exposure to air and preserving product integrity.
Supporting_Evidence: “the desired amino‑azaindole product 2 was found to be extremely oxygen‑sensitive, rapidly decomposing… To overcome this stability issue… the resulting reaction mixture after completion of the nitro‑reduction was immediately quenched with a cyclopropane‑carbonyl acylating reagent in the same pot after exchanging out the hydrogen with an inert gas such as nitrogen or argon.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: Hydrogenolysis of the 5‑bromo substituent competes with the desired nitro‑reduction when palladium‑based catalysts are used, leading to loss of material and lower yields.
Solution_Description: Platinum‑based heterogeneous catalysts (1 % Pt–2 % V/C) were selected over palladium catalysts, providing chemoselective nitro‑reduction without bromine hydrogenolysis and delivering higher assay yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pt‑ over Pd‑based heterogeneous catalysts were deliberately chosen… to minimize the competitive hydrogenolysis of the 5‑Br group… 1 % Pt–2 % V/C was found to be optimal based on the reaction performance and the catalyst loading.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: During basic free‑basing of the API, nucleophilic attack of the liberated API on intermediate III generated impurity 8b, which was difficult to purge and reduced overall purity.
Solution_Description: A sacrificial amine nucleophile, piperazine (highly water‑soluble), was added during the free‑basing step to out‑compete the API for reaction with intermediate III, suppressing formation of impurity 8b to <0.05 % and allowing easy removal of the resulting piperazine adduct during crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “We thus selected piperazine as a highly water‑soluble amine for evaluation. Gratifyingly, the formation of 8b was effectively inhibited to <0.05 % at 60 °C in a mixture of THF/H₂O or EtOH/H₂O… the corresponding piperazine adduct 8c could be easily purged in the EtOH/H₂O system during crystallization.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: Using hydrochloric acid for Boc deprotection in alcohol or THF solvents can generate chloroalkane genotoxic impurities (GTI).
Solution_Description: Sulfuric acid (300 mol % of 4.5 M H₂SO₄) was chosen instead of HCl, eliminating the risk of GTI formation while achieving >99.5 % deprotection conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Considering the potential formation of chloroalkanes genotoxic impurities (GTI) when hydrochloric acid was used… sulfuric acid was chosen for further development… 300 mol % of 4.5 M H₂SO₄ … to achieve a >99.5 % conversion.”

Paper Title: An Efficient Through-Process for Chk1 Kinase Inhibitor GDC-0575
Problem_Description: The original S_NAr work‑up required organic cosolvents for phase separation and solvent switch, increasing material cost and handling complexity at scale.
Solution_Description: After the S_NAr step, excess piperidine was removed by aqueous citric‑acid washes; the low solubility of t‑AmOH in water allowed easy phase separation without additional organic cosolvents, simplifying scale‑up and reducing cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “excess amounts of nucleophile 5 could be effectively removed to <5 % by aqueous citric acid washes. Owing to the low solubility of t‑AmOH in water (99 mg mL⁻¹), the layers were easily separated during the aqueous workup with no organic cosolvents required.”

Problem_Description: The standard SPPS solvent DMF (and related solvents NMP, DMA, DCM) is reprotoxic and classified by REACH‑ECHA as a Substance of Very High Concern, creating a regulatory and safety hurdle for large‑scale peptide manufacture.
Solution_Description: Replace DMF with N‑butylpyrrolidinone (NBP), a non‑reprotoxic, high‑polarity aprotic solvent that can be used on a 1:1 basis for SPPS with polystyrene‑based resins.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "the practice of SPPS requires the use of significant amounts of toxic process solvents… DMF, NMP, DMA, and DCM"; "Due to their reprotox characteristics, polar aprotic solvents like DMF, NMP, and DMA, have been labeled by REACH‑ECHA as Substances of Very High Concern (SVHC)."; "The goal of the current investigational work was to evaluate the feasibility of replacing DMF with a less toxic solvent…"   Solution: "According to the results presented in this paper, it is clear that N‑butylpyrrolidinone (NBP) is the best green solvent candidate to replace DMF in SPPS."; "NBP is compatible with the most popular polystyrene‑based resins… this situation facilitates the switch from DMF to NBP… as a direct 1:1 replacement."

Problem_Description: Many screened solvents failed to swell the polystyrene‑based resin (AMRES) sufficiently, leading to poor resin swelling and low reaction conversion.
Solution_Description: Select only solvents that show good resin swelling (Group 1 in Table 2) for further evaluation, thereby ensuring adequate swelling of the polymer support.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The first solvent selection criterion applied was the ability of the solvent to swell a polystyrene‑based resin (in this case, Aminomethyl‑PS (AMRES))."; "The solvents in Table 2 are divided into 3 groups… Group 1… considered as solvents with good resin swelling properties."; "The ability of a solvent to keep the resin swollen during the complete SPPS process is a key parameter for a successful process."   Solution: "Solvents with good swelling (Group 1) were selected for further testing."; "All solvents in this group were subject to further testing."

Problem_Description: Several promising solvents (e.g., anisole, toluene, EtOAc) could not dissolve key SPPS reagents such as the DIU by‑product, causing precipitation and potential resin clogging.
Solution_Description: Exclude solvents with poor reagent solubility and retain only those (NBP, DMI, TMU, etc.) that keep DIU and other reagents fully soluble during coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "In the case of the coupling system DICI/oxyma, the by‑product DIU is generated, and in an ideal solvent, this by‑product should remain soluble… anisole and toluene… are not able to dissolve properly SPPS related reagents, such as DIU."; "DIU precipitation during coupling…"   Solution: "anisole, propyl acetate, DEC, toluene, and EtOAc were excluded because of their poor solubility of SPPS reagents."; "NBP, DMI, TMU… retained because they keep reagents soluble."

Problem_Description: Coupling reactions in polar aprotic solvents like NBP, DMI, TMU, and NEP proceeded slower than in DMF, lengthening the required coupling time and increasing the risk of incomplete couplings (lower yields).
Solution_Description: Accelerate the coupling by optimizing reaction parameters—increase temperature, extend coupling time, and apply design‑of‑experiments (DoE) to find the best combination of temperature, time, and stoichiometry.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "In polar aprotic solvents like NMP, TMU, DMI, NEP, and NBP, the coupling reaction is slower compared with DMF… the slower reaction can be overcome by optimization of reaction parameters."; "Longer coupling times are avoided…"   Solution: "this small difference can be overcome by optimization of reaction parameters"; "We are using Design of Experiments (DoE) models to find optimized reaction parameters…"; "Potential further development work… could consider the use of heated SPPS, increasing process temperature could have beneficial effects."

Problem_Description: Fmoc deprotection is very slow in non‑polar/aprotic solvents (anisole, THF, Me‑THF, toluene, EtOAc), leading to incomplete cleavage and higher levels of deletion sequences.
Solution_Description: Switch to a stronger base (e.g., DBU) for Fmoc removal or retain a polar aprotic solvent (NBP, DMI, DMSO) that enables rapid deprotection.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "for nonpolar aprotic solvents… the Fmoc cleavage reaction was slow because it was not complete after 30 min."; "In THF… cleavage very slow… 36.6 % deprotected after 30 min."   Solution: "it could be convenient to consider the use of a stronger Fmoc cleavage reagent, for example, DBU instead of 4‑methylpiperidine."; "In polar aprotic solvents like DMF, DMI, DMPU, TMU, NMP, DMSO… the Fmoc cleavage reaction is complete in less than 5 min."

Problem_Description: THF was identified as a potential toxic solvent (hazard statement H351) and therefore unsuitable for replacement of DMF in a regulated manufacturing environment.
Solution_Description: Exclude THF from the list of candidate solvents for SPPS.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "THF… its suspected toxicity (H351), THF was also excluded for the final test even if THF is already recommended as DMF replacement."   Solution: "THF was excluded from further consideration as a candidate solvent."

Problem_Description: NBP has a higher viscosity (4.0 cP at 25 °C) than DMF (0.8 cP), causing slower liquid transfers and requiring longer cycle times on small‑scale synthesizers.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adapt the synthesizer cycle times and, when possible, employ heated SPPS to lower viscosity and improve mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The important difference in viscosity (NBP = 4.0 cP, DMF = 0.8 cP) is enhanced in small peptide synthesizers… transfers… is slower and therefore the definition of cycles has to be adapted."; "In large‑scale equipment… the high viscosity of NBP is not a technical problem."   Solution: "definition of cycles has to be adapted to ensure full transfers"; "potential further development work… could consider the use of heated SPPS, increasing process temperature could have beneficial effects."

Problem_Description: During coupling of Fmoc‑Arg(Pbf)‑OH in NBP, Arg undergoes lactamization during activation, leading to incomplete couplings and lower overall peptide purity.
Solution_Description: Increase the number of coupling repetitions (double or triple couplings) or adjust activation conditions to suppress lactamization.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "During the coupling of Fmoc‑Arg(Pbf)‑OH, it was found… it was necessary to double and in some cases triple couplings… inefficient Arg coupling could be explained by lactamization of Arg during its activation in NBP."   Solution: "it was necessary to double and in some cases triple couplings…"; "this side reaction also occurs in DMF, but since the coupling is faster in DMF…"

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: The bis‑alkylation of nitrile 9 with NaH in DMSO to give cyclopropyl nitrile 10 is highly exothermic, requiring cooling below the freezing point of pure DMSO, and the NaH‑DMSO combination poses significant safety hazards on scale.
Solution_Description: Scale‑out was achieved by conducting the reaction in batches of <10 g, maintaining the temperature below 0 °C (often sub‑zero) and controlling the addition rate of NaH, which mitigates the exotherm and improves safety.
Supporting_Evidence: ['This exothermic reaction required cooling below the freezing point (pure) DMSO, and safety concerns about the use of NaH–DMSO led us to synthesize compound 10 in batches of less than 10 g as a safety precaution.', 'Efforts to identify base–solvent combinations that would be more amenable to scale … were not successful (LiHMDS, KHMDS, …).', 'The NaH–DMSO conditions provided the cleanest overall reaction profile.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: The NaH‑DMSO bis‑alkylation generated significant amounts of nitrile “dimers”, reducing the isolated yield of the desired product and complicating purification.
Solution_Description: The process was retained with NaH‑DMSO because it gave the cleanest profile; the reaction conditions (temperature, addition order) were optimized to suppress dimer formation, and the product was isolated by crystallization after work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The main reaction byproducts were nitrile “dimers” arising from addition of an intermediate anion to the nitrile functional group of another molecule (of either the starting material or desired product, in varying ratios depending on the specific reaction conditions).', 'The NaH‑DMSO conditions provided the cleanest overall reaction profile.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: The free‑base form of the triamine intermediate 8 is unstable to air, undergoing discoloration that cannot be removed from the final API.
Solution_Description: Instead of isolating the free base, the intermediate was converted to and isolated as its dihydrochloride salt, which proved stable on storage for several months.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The free base of this electron‑rich compound was unstable to air, and 8 was therefore isolated as its dihydrochloride salt.', 'The salt proved to be stable to storage for at least a few months.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: Imidate 11 is hygroscopic and readily hydrolyzes to the ethyl ester byproduct, especially in the presence of adventitious water.
Solution_Description: Fresh ethanolic HCl (or NaOEt) solutions were prepared immediately before use to suppress ester formation, and the imidate was used without isolation in the subsequent cyclization step.
Supporting_Evidence: ['In both cases, the primary byproduct was the ethyl ester resulting from hydrolysis of the imidate, presumably due to adventitious water.', 'Preparation of fresh ethanolic solutions of HCl (from acetyl chloride or trimethylsilyl chloride) or NaOEt (from sodium metal) mitigated ester formation.', 'The imidate 11 … was used immediately without purification in cyclization with the dihydrochloride salt of 8.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: Amide 17, formed from reduction of nitro‑amide 17, is very labile and hydrolyzes during aqueous work‑up, leading to run‑to‑run yield variation and scale‑up concerns.
Solution_Description: A new route was devised that bypasses the unstable amide: the nitro intermediate 7 was reduced and protected as a carbamate (22), then amidated with the carboxylic acid 15 using T3P at 40 °C (instead of 110 °C), followed by deprotection and cyclization under milder acid conditions. This avoids the labile amide and gives higher, reproducible yields.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The amide bond of 17 was very labile and was hydrolyzed back to the starting amine and carboxylic acid under exposure to mildly acidic or basic aqueous conditions, such as during the reaction workup.', 'The need for vigorous cyclization conditions was presumably a result of the low nucleophilicity of the 2‑amino group …', 'Amidation of 7 with 15 was effected by T3P at 110 °C in moderate yield.', 'Reduction of the nitro group with zinc … led directly to cyclized imidazopyridine product 1.', 'To avoid all of these potential problems, an alternative synthesis of the fused imidazole ring utilizing the corresponding carboxylic acid in place of the imidate was developed.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: Commercially available tert‑butyl 2,4‑dibromobutanoate 12, a key precursor for the cyclopropyl‑carboxylic acid 15, was difficult to source in multi‑kilogram quantities.
Solution_Description: The synthetic team adjusted the scale‑up plan to accommodate limited availability, performing a base‑solvent‑temperature screen to identify optimal conditions (KOTMS in THF‑2‑MeTHF) that allowed preparation of sufficient material despite sourcing challenges.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Commercially available tert‑butyl 2,4‑dibromobutanoate 12 was a useful starting material for route development, although sourcing multiple kilograms was difficult.', 'A base, solvent, and temperature screen of the reaction of 12 with 13 revealed that … potassium trimethyl‑silanolate as base (2.0 equiv) in THF‑2‑MeTHF at 15–22 °C led to the two desired alkylations …']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: During the reduction‑cyclization of nitro‑amide 17 to form compound 2, heating at 100 °C in acetic‑d₄ led to complete epimerization (deuterium incorporation) at the methyl‑bearing stereocenter.
Solution_Description: Milder cyclization conditions were employed: methanesulfonic acid (5 equiv) at 70 °C for 12 h, with buffering by NH₄OAc, which prevented detectable epimerization and gave high diastereomeric excess.
Supporting_Evidence: ['Compound 2 … was not configurationally stable when heated at 100 °C in acetic‑d₄ for 2 h … as demonstrated by complete incorporation of deuterium at the methine stereocenter.', 'Deprotection with methanesulfonic acid (5 equiv) in dichloromethane followed by addition of aqueous ammonium acetate solution (6 equiv) to buffer the acidity led to smooth cyclization to 2 without detectable epimerization.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: The NaH–DMSO bis‑alkylation reaction mixture became viscous and difficult to stir at sub‑zero temperatures, complicating scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in small batches (<10 g) and maintained at temperatures below the freezing point to keep the mixture fluid, with careful addition of NaH to ensure proper mixing and heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: ['This exothermic reaction required cooling below the freezing point (pure) DMSO, and safety concerns about the use of NaH–DMSO led us to synthesize compound 10 in batches of less than 10 g as a safety precaution.', 'Addition of the substrate 9 to the base did have some influence on formation of the nitrile dimers, but did not eliminate these byproducts; the NaH–DMSO conditions provided the cleanest overall reaction profile.']

Paper Title: Route Selection and Optimization in the Synthesis of Two Imidazopyridine Inhibitors of DGAT‑2
Problem_Description: Several steps (e.g., T3P amidation, cyclization) required prolonged heating (up to 12 h) and multi‑hour work‑ups, limiting throughput for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The team telescoped three steps (amide formation, Boc deprotection, cyclization) without intermediate isolations, reducing overall reaction time and simplifying the process.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The ethyl acetate solution of amine 22 … was telescoped directly into the amidation step, with T3P at 40 °C (as compared to 110 °C for amidation of 2‑amino‑3‑nitro substrate 7).', 'After aqueous workup and a solvent switch … cleavage of the Boc group of 23 and subsequent cyclization were effect…', 'The resultant three‑step telescoped sequence afforded 1 ·MsOH in 47 % yield (3.1 kg) over the two steps from compound 7.']

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: The chloro‑oxazole (5) was found to decompose at moderate temperature and the Stille coupling that used this substrate required organotin reagents that are volatile and generate toxic by‑products, making the sequence unattractive on the multikilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Stille coupling with a Negishi coupling that uses the more stable oxazole ester (9) and an organozinc reagent (10), eliminating the need for the unstable chloro‑oxazole and the organotin reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: • “chlorooxazole 5 was susceptible to decomposition at moderate temperatures, and scaling up organotin chemistry with volatile byproducts to multikilogram scale was unattractive.” (p. 3)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: The initial Miyaura borylation of heteroaryl bromides using PdCl₂(dppf) in DMF required >8 h at 100 °C and gave ca. 30 % protodeboronation, leading to poor yields and long reaction times.
Solution_Description: Switching to a more active catalyst system (Pd(dba)₂/​tricyclohexylphosphine) in dioxane reduced the reaction time to <30 min and lowered protodeboronation to 5 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The reaction took upward of 8 h at 100 °C to complete, and 30 % protodeboronation was observed …” (p. 5)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the Miyaura borylation, the reaction sometimes stalled because palladium black precipitated, which was attributed to high local concentrations of unligated Pd(0).
Solution_Description: The authors halved the palladium (2 % → 1 %) and ligand (10 % → 5 %) loadings and diluted the reaction from 10 to 20 vol dioxane, thereby lowering the Pd(0) concentration four‑fold and preventing precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Larger‑scale reactions sometimes stalling after precipitation of palladium black … increasing the Pd:ligand ratio from 1:2 to 1:4 led to much slower reactions. This problem was eventually solved simply by halving the loadings of palladium (from 2 to 1 mol %) and ligand (from 10 to 5 mol %) and diluting from 10 to 20 volumes of dioxane …” (p. 5)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: In the Suzuki coupling of pinacolboronate 21 with aryl chloride 19, significant protodeboronation and homodimerization required the use of 2 equiv of the boronate to achieve full conversion.
Solution_Description: The authors converted the pinacolboronate to the potassium trifluoroborate 27 (or added 2 equiv KHF₂ to the reaction) which suppressed protodeboronation and homodimerization, allowing the reaction to proceed with only 1.1 equiv of the boron partner.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Significant protodeboronation and homodimerization of boronate 21 were observed, and 2 equiv was required to fully consume all of the aryl chloride.” (p. 6)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: Use of potassium bifluoride (KHF₂) caused severe glass etching, presenting a safety and equipment‑compatibility issue on pilot‑plant scale.
Solution_Description: Pilot‑plant reactions that required KHF₂ were performed in Hastelloy vessels rather than glass to avoid etching.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Reactions carried out with KHF₂ resulted in severely etched glassware. Pilot‑plant‑scale reactions were carried out in Hastelloy vessels.” (ref 23)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: The oxazole ester intermediate (9) is unstable at elevated temperatures, leading to side‑reactions during its formation.
Solution_Description: Methanol was selected as a co‑solvent because it gave a much faster reaction than ethanol, allowing the transformation to be completed before substantial decomposition could occur, even though some trans‑esterification was observed.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Methanol gave a much faster reaction than ethanol and was thus selected, despite the fact that partial transesterification was observed.” (p. 4)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: Indole product 30 is sparingly soluble in aqueous media, making the sulfonate deprotection step difficult.
Solution_Description: Elevated temperature together with a phase‑transfer catalyst (cetyltrimethylammonium bromide) enabled efficient deprotection of the sulfonate group.
