Supporting_Evidence: • “Indole 30 is sparingly soluble in aqueous media, and thus, elevated temperature and a phase transfer catalyst were required to cleave the sulfonate group.” (p. 8)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: Isolation of the potassium trifluoroborate 27 proved difficult because the product remained mixed with inorganic salts after crystallisation attempts.
Solution_Description: The water content of the aqueous dioxane slurry was reduced to 5 % to allow the inorganic‑rich layer to separate and be decanted; the organic phase was then azeotropically dried to give the trifluoroborate as a solid (≈90 % yield, corrected for purity).
Supporting_Evidence: • “The trifluoroborate salt was eventually isolated by reducing the water content in aqueous dioxane to 5 %, thus allowing an inorganic‑rich aqueous layer to separate and be decanted. Azeotropic drying … afforded trifluoroborate 27 … in 90 % yield after correction for purity.” (p. 6)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: Crude products 19 and 20 sometimes contained impurities that lowered the yield and reproducibility of the subsequent Suzuki coupling.
Solution_Description: Both amines were optionally recrystallised from DMSO (or water) before the Suzuki step, which improved the isolated purity and gave more consistent outcomes.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Less than 5 % quaternization was observed, and the products 19 and 20 were subsequently crystallized by addition of water … An optional recrystallization of both products from DMSO was also introduced, dependent on the outcome of user tests in the downstream chemistry.” (p. 5)

Paper Title: Development of Flexible and Scalable Routes to Two Phosphatidinylinositol-3-kinase Delta Inhibitors via a Common Intermediate Approach
Problem_Description: The sulfonamide‑protected intermediate 26 is acidic enough to be deprotonated but its solubility in water at ambient temperature is limited, complicating the final deprotection.
Solution_Description: Sodium hydroxide (5 M) was added to a suspension of 26 to deprotonate the sulfonamide, enabling deprotection in water at ambient temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In contrast, the sulfonamide group in 26 is acidic enough to be deprotonated by sodium hydroxide, which allows solubility and deprotection in water at ambient temperature.” (p. 9)

Paper Title: Total Synthesis of Entecavir: A Robust Route for Pilot Production
Problem_Description: During the Favorskii‑rearrangement/tosylate‑elimination‑epimerization sequence the epimerization step was incomplete even after 24 h stirring at room temperature on a 50 g scale, giving only partial conversion to the thermodynamically more stable cyclopentanecarboxylate (8).
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to a 1 : 4 mixture of methyl‑t‑butyl ether (MTBE) and methanol accelerated the epimerization; the reaction became complete in < 17 h on the same scale.
Supporting_Evidence: This product was treated with sodium methoxide in methanol to initially provide the cis‑substituted Favorskii rearrangement product 8a, which upon isomerization gave the thermodynamically more stable cyclopentanecarboxylate 8 under the reaction conditions, though the epimerization was incomplete even after being stirred for 24 h (50 g scale) at room temperature. Fortunately, the problem was solved by using methyl t‑butyl ether (MTBE)/methanol as the solvent, and the reaction was complete in less than 17 h (50 g scale).

Paper Title: Total Synthesis of Entecavir: A Robust Route for Pilot Production
Problem_Description: In the Baeyer–Villiger oxidation of ketone 10, the commonly used peracids (m‑CPBA, CF₃CO₃H, CH₃CO₃H) preferentially epoxidised the alkene present in the molecule rather than delivering the desired BV oxidation, leading to low isolated yield of the lactone 11.
Solution_Description: The authors adopted a nucleophilic oxidation protocol (30 % H₂O₂/NaOH, basic conditions) which avoided olefin epoxidation and provided the targeted BV product on kilogram scale (45 % isolated yield after chromatography).
Supporting_Evidence: The Baeyer–Villiger oxidation (BV Oxidation) of ketone 10 was more challenging. Although peracids such as CF₃CO₃H, mCPBA, or CH₃CO₃H are popular reagents for this purpose, all of them underwent alkene epoxidation rather than the desired BV oxidation. For olefin epoxidation to be avoided, nucleophilic oxidation conditions were applied. To our delight, hydrogen peroxide under basic conditions (H₂O₂/NaOH) was found to be an efficient oxidant, and a kilogram scale reaction afforded compound 11 after chromatographic separation in 45 % yield.

Paper Title: Total Synthesis of Entecavir: A Robust Route for Pilot Production
Problem_Description: The addition of aqueous hydrogen peroxide to the reaction mixture during the BV oxidation is highly exothermic; uncontrolled temperature rise can lead to safety hazards and decomposition of sensitive intermediates.
Solution_Description: The peroxide was added dropwise while maintaining the temperature below 5 °C, and the subsequent neutralisation with NaOH was also performed at controlled temperature (65–70 °C), thereby mitigating the exotherm and ensuring safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: H₂O₂ (30 wt %, 1.86 kg) was slowly added over 0.5 h. After being warmed to 60 °C, NaOH(aq) (2.50 mol/L, 2.53 L, 0.86 equiv) was added dropwise during 1.5 h. The reaction mixture was stirred at 65–70 °C for 0.5 h. The addition of H₂O₂ (30 wt %) and NaOH(aq) was repeated 3 times at which point no compound 10 was detected (monitored by TLC).

Paper Title: Total Synthesis of Entecavir: A Robust Route for Pilot Production
Problem_Description: Several steps of the route employ highly reactive and potentially hazardous reagents (e.g., LAH, n‑BuLi, MeONa, TiCl₄‑type reagents) on kilogram scale, which pose safety risks if not properly controlled.
Solution_Description: Reactions with these reagents were conducted in well‑ventilated, temperature‑controlled glass reactors under nitrogen, with slow, portion‑wise addition, quench steps (e.g., Na₂SO₃ for peroxide quench, aqueous Na₂SO₄ for LAH work‑up), and appropriate filtration/evaporation protocols to safely manage exotherms and reactive intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: All reactions were carried out under a nitrogen atmosphere unless otherwise stated. All of the solvents and reagents were purchased at the highest commercial quality and used without further purification unless otherwise stated. ... LAH (0.33 kg, 1.10 equiv) was added to the solvent under nitrogen. ... Na₂SO₄ (1.32 L) was added slowly to quench the reaction. ... MeONa (30 % in methanol, 4.55 kg, 3.20 equiv) was added dropwise while keeping the temperature below 5 °C. ... Na₂SO₃ (0.3 kg) was added to quench the excess peroxide.

Paper Title: Total Synthesis of Entecavir: A Robust Route for Pilot Production
Problem_Description: Multiple steps required extended reaction times (e.g., 20 h for epimerization, 5 h for LAH reduction, 10 h for final acidic hydrolysis), limiting throughput and contributing to an overall modest 9 % isolated yield over 15 steps.
Solution_Description: Optimization of solvent composition (MTBE/MeOH) and temperature (maintaining 0–5 °C for sensitive steps) reduced reaction times (epimerization < 17 h) and allowed operation at higher concentration where feasible, improving throughput without sacrificing selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: The epimerization was incomplete even after being stirred for 24 h (50 g scale) at room temperature. Fortunately, the problem was solved by using methyl t‑butyl ether (MTBE)/methanol as the solvent, and the reaction was complete in less than 17 h (50 g scale).

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: Previously reported syntheses of tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine employed iodomethane‑d₃, a genotoxic alkylating agent, and required expensive reagents such as (2‑acetyl‑4‑methylpentyl)‑trimethylammonium iodide (compound 7).
Solution_Description: The new process replaces iodomethane‑d₃ with inexpensive, commercially available methanol (for 1) or deuterated methanol (MeOH‑d₄, for 2) as the methyl source, eliminating the genotoxic reagent and reducing reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “...the genotoxic iodomethane‑d₃... and the necessity of tedious column chromatography in the previously developed methods.”

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: Earlier methods isolated the product by column chromatography, giving low overall yields (e.g., 35 % for deutetrabenazine) and making the process unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a Mitsunobu‑based O‑methylation followed by simple filtration, solvent‑evaporation, and recrystallisation (ethyl acetate/heptane) to afford the final APIs in >96 % yield and >99.5 % HPLC purity without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The product was isolated by column chromatography in 35 % yield… it was not feasible for industry.”

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: Compound 7 (DTTSC) was identified as the main cost driver; the initial stoichiometry required 1.21 equiv (vs 1.0 theoretical) to achieve full conversion, and low conversions were observed with many bases.
Solution_Description: DoE studies optimized the molar equivalent of 7 to 1.05 equiv, set the water:MeOH ratio to 3:3, used 1.0 equiv K₂CO₃, and fixed the temperature at 65–70 °C for 6–10 h, raising conversion of 6→9 to >95 % and reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • “...1.21 molar equivalents is required (compared with the theoretical requirement of 1.0 molar equivalent) for the complete conversion … The reaction was comparatively slow at low temperature…”

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: At low temperature the reaction proceeded slowly and generated impurities (impurities 4 and 5); yields dropped to 62 % when bases such as TEA, DIPEA, DBU, NaOH, KOH, Na₂CO₃ were used.
Solution_Description: Screening identified K₂CO₃ as the optimal base; temperature was increased to 65–70 °C, and reaction time extended to 6–10 h, eliminating impurity formation and delivering consistent high yields.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Yields were found to be significantly low when bases such as TEA, DIPEA, DBU, NaOH, KOH, and Na₂CO₃ were used. The yield obtained was 0.9 w/w (62 %)…”

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: The Mitsunobu reaction generated triphenylphosphine oxide (TPPO) and residual triphenylphosphine (TPP) that had to be removed to meet API purity specifications.
Solution_Description: A work‑up sequence using aqueous washes, pH adjustment, and a final recrystallisation from ethyl acetate/heptane removed TPPO/TPP, delivering product 2 with >99.5 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “TPPO was formed as a by‑product, and it was removed selectively during the work‑up operation to obtain highly pure deutetrabenazine (2) that was free from TPP and TPPO impurities.”

Paper Title: Novel Process for Preparation of Tetrabenazine and Deutetrabenazine
Problem_Description: Deuterated methanol (MeOH‑d₄) was a major cost contributor; the initial stoichiometry of 2 equiv was insufficient for full conversion.
Solution_Description: DoE optimization increased MeOH‑d₄ to 10 equiv, achieving 84 % HPLC conversion while maintaining overall process economics; reactions were performed on parallel synthesizers to control material usage.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Since deuterated methanol was found to be a major cost‑contributing factor… 10.0 molar equivalents of deuterated methanol gave the best conversion of 84 % area by HPLC.”

Paper Title: Characterization of a Unique Co-crystal of the BACE1 Inhibitor Verubecestat and a Reaction Intermediate: Implications for the Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: During the second multikilogram production batch a previously unseen co‑crystal formed between the HBr salts of the starting amine 2 and the product 1.  This solid phase precipitated, removed amine 2 from the solution, halted the reactive crystallization at ~80 % conversion and generated unusually high levels of cyanamide 3 in the supernatant, lowering overall isolated yield of verubecestat.
Solution_Description: A staged, two‑step sequence was introduced: (i) chemoselective conversion of amine 2 to cyanamide 3 under basic conditions, (ii) quenching residual CNBr with aqueous sodium thiosulfate (scavenger), followed by intramolecular cyclisation of 3 to 1 using aqueous NaOH (pH control).  This order‑of‑addition prevents the HBr‑salt co‑crystal from ever forming and restores high isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the second production batch showed unusually high levels of cyanamide 3… after 48 h” (Fig 1, ref 6).  • “the solid … was a co‑crystal of the HBr salts of 2 and 1 … causing the reaction progress to stall” (Sec 1).  • “a staged approach whereby 2 would first be converted chemoselectively to cyanamide 3 before quenching the residual CNBr and promoting intramolecular cyclisation in a subsequent operation” (Sec 3).  • “the stream was washed with aqueous sodium thiosulfate, which served to reduce residual CNBr” (Scheme 3).  • “treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide to promote intramolecular cyclisation … only trace amounts of over‑cyanated 4” (Sec 3).

Paper Title: Characterization of a Unique Co-crystal of the BACE1 Inhibitor Verubecestat and a Reaction Intermediate: Implications for the Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: When the reaction was run under basic conditions to avoid HBr‑salt formation, over‑cyanation of the product occurred, giving impurity 4 and reducing the isolated yield of verubecestat.
Solution_Description: The basic‑condition route was abandoned in favor of the two‑step route above; the final cyclisation step is performed under controlled basic pH (aqueous NaOH) after removal of CNBr, which suppresses formation of over‑cyanated impurity 4.
Supporting_Evidence: • “this approach did generate 1, cyanation of the product in the presence of soluble organic bases … led to over‑cyanated impurity 4, limiting the overall yield” (Sec 3).  • “treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide … only trace amounts of over‑cyanated 4” (Sec 3).

Paper Title: Characterization of a Unique Co-crystal of the BACE1 Inhibitor Verubecestat and a Reaction Intermediate: Implications for the Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: KH₂PO₄, an inorganic base that gave good conversion, was found to be hygroscopic and difficult to handle safely on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: NaHCO₃ was selected as the preferred inorganic base because it is non‑hygroscopic, easier to handle, and gave comparable or higher conversion in the screened solvents.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We chose to optimise the reaction with NaHCO₃ rather than KH₂PO₄, as the latter presented handling challenges on scale because of its hygroscopicity” (Sec 3).  • Table 6 shows high conversions with NaHCO₃ (e.g., >99 % in 2‑MeTHF, entry 12).

Paper Title: Characterization of a Unique Co-crystal of the BACE1 Inhibitor Verubecestat and a Reaction Intermediate: Implications for the Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: Prolonged reaction times in MeOH or DMAc with NaHCO₃ led to noticeable degradation of the desired cyanamide 3.
Solution_Description: 2‑MeTHF was identified as the optimal solvent, allowing rapid (>99 % in 24 h) conversion at 45 °C without observable decomposition, thereby shortening reaction time and protecting product integrity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Some product decomposition was observed at extended reaction times in MeOH or DMAc when using NaHCO₃” (Sec 3).  • “high levels of conversion were achieved using 2‑MeTHF when the process was conducted at 45 °C” (Sec 3).  • Table 6, entry 12 (>99 % conversion at 45 °C).

Paper Title: Characterization of a Unique Co-crystal of the BACE1 Inhibitor Verubecestat and a Reaction Intermediate: Implications for the Development of a Commercial Manufacturing Process
Problem_Description: The co‑crystal displayed extremely low solubility in the reaction solvent mixture, restricting the usable region of the ternary phase diagram to a tiny area and making the reactive crystallisation unreliable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The process was shifted away from the reactive‑crystallisation end‑game entirely; instead, the reaction was performed wholly in solution (2‑MeTHF) with controlled temperature and concentration, eliminating the need to navigate the narrow solubility window of the co‑crystal.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The low solubility of the co‑crystal … rendered the existing end‑game chemistry untenable for future production campaigns” (Sec 3).  • “Single solubility measurements … showed that the region … is extremely limited” (Fig 8, Table 5).  • “We have described … a revised end‑game … chemoselective alkylation followed by intramolecular cyclisation” (Conclusion).

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: The bromination step for installing the C‑6 bromide used dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂) and bromine.  Dichloromethane is regarded as highly undesirable for long‑term manufacturing because of its toxicity and environmental impact, and its use adds to process cost and waste handling.
Solution_Description: The authors propose replacing CH₂Cl₂ with a more sustainable solvent (e.g., heptane for extraction) and ultimately eliminating it from the work‑up.  A solvent‑screening study is underway to identify a greener alternative.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Although the use of dichloromethane and bromine for the bromination step proved optimal … for environmental reasons dichloromethane is considered highly undesirable for long‑term manufacturing use at Eli Lilly.”
• “It should be noted that dichloromethane was used as the extraction solvent to enable a rapid proof of concept, and a study to replace it with a more sustainable solvent is ongoing.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: The Cu‑catalyzed Ullmann indazole ring‑closure suffered from poor and inconsistent performance on plant scale (yield 37–57 %), required a rigorously oxygen‑free atmosphere, and generated >50 detectable impurities, making the step unsafe and unpredictable.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the Ullmann route and developed an intramolecular S_NAr cyclisation that does not need metal catalysis or an oxygen‑free environment, thereby eliminating the source of variability and the safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “For the Ullmann indazole ring closure, a rigorously oxygen‑free atmosphere is necessary to avoid low product recovery… this step still exhibited substantial variability … and yield (37–57 %).”
• “At least 50 discrete impurities are formed during the Cu‑catalyzed indazole ring formation!”
• “We focused on alternative means to close the indazole ring… an intramolecular S_NAr reaction… The new synthesis avoids the need for any tedious cleanup procedures such as metal scavenging during manufacturing.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: The Ullmann cascade required a lengthy purification train (technical‑grade crystallisation, carbon treatment, recrystallisation) that limited throughput and added substantial time to the overall process.
Solution_Description: By switching to the S_NAr‑based route, the authors eliminated the need for the extensive Ullmann‑specific purification, and the final diaryl‑ether formation could be isolated with a simple base‑mediated work‑up and a single crystallisation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The long cycle time during the extensive purification process limited the throughput.”
• “The new synthesis avoids the need for any tedious cleanup procedures such as metal scavenging during manufacturing.”
• “Optimised conditions used K₂CO₃ as the base and THF as the solvent at 55 °C for 14 h to give >90 % assay yield of 2. After aqueous work‑up, crystallisation from toluene afforded a 72 % yield of purified 2.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Batch nitration of 4‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzaldehyde with KNO₃ in concentrated H₂SO₄ was strongly exothermic (temperature jump 0 → 30 °C in <5 min), raising concerns about thermal runaway on scale.
Solution_Description: The exotherm was mitigated by switching to controlled addition of concentrated HNO₃ and by moving the nitration to a continuous‑flow plug‑flow reactor (PFR) with efficient heat removal, thus limiting the reactive inventory and providing safer scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Although high yield … the portion‑wise addition of KNO₃ … was noted to be strongly exothermic… an exotherm from 0 to 30 °C occurred in a span of <5 min, which gave us great concern for runaway potential.”
• “The exotherm was reduced by switching from KNO₃ to concentrated HNO₃ (65 % w/w). Upon controlled addition… the internal temperature did not exceed 10 °C.”
• “A continuous‑flow nitration… the small reactor dimensions would impart superior heat and mass transfer… limiting the potential for thermal runaway.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Initial attempts at intramolecular S_NAr cyclisation with an unactivated substrate (compound 17) failed to give the desired indazole, giving no product formation.
Solution_Description: Activation of the aromatic ring was achieved by installing a nitro group (strong electron‑withdrawing) and using K₂CO₃ (1.5 equiv) as a base in IPA/H₂O (2:1) at 80 °C, which provided >95 % conversion to the indazole.  Solvent screening (IPA/H₂O, THF, 2‑MeTHF) and temperature variation (50 °C vs 80 °C) further optimized the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A brief investigation of the S_NAr approach with unactivated substrate 17 … failed.”
• “A strongly electron‑withdrawing group at the 5‑position was crucial.”
• “Addition of 1.5 equiv of K₂CO₃ was found to promote the S_NAr reaction, providing 20 as the dominant product.”
• “A mixture of isopropyl alcohol (IPA) and water proved optimal, as it gave the highest conversion rate and HPLC purity of the isolated product (entry 7).”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Reduction of nitroindazole 20 with Raney Ni required handling a pyrophoric metal catalyst and generated dense metal suspensions that were difficult to mix and posed significant waste‑handling burdens.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced Raney Ni with Pt/C (5 % w/w) under hydrogen pressure, performing the reduction in EtOH/H₂O (5:1) at 25 °C.  This eliminated the pyrophoric catalyst, simplified mixing, and reduced metal waste, while still delivering high conversion and clean product.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Scale‑up of Ra‑Ni reductions can prove challenging because of the difficulty of suspending the dense metal catalyst… a process safety assessment indicated a high level of concern with regard to the use of pyrophoric Raney nickel in combination with a hydrazine.”
• “In the metal‑catalyzed hydrogenolysis approach… Pt/C catalyst (5 % w/w) … at 25 °C provided a 6:1 ratio of the desired product 23 and debrominated by‑product 24.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of aminoindazole 23 to hydroxyindazole 13 required heating at 200 °C for 1 h in a Hastelloy B‑2 PFR, which led to corrosion of the coil (0.35 % w/w metal loss) and raised concerns about reactor integrity and long residence times.
Solution_Description: A PFA tube with a stainless‑steel outer jacket was used instead of Hastelloy, allowing operation at 160 °C with a 10 h residence time and eliminating metal leaching.  The lower temperature also reduced the reaction time needed for complete conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Contamination of the collected reaction mixture with nickel…indicating corrosion of the Hastelloy coil.”
• “A corrosion study … showed a 0.35 % w/w loss for a Hastelloy coupon … while a tantalum coupon showed 0.015 % w/w loss … No weight loss … observed for a PFA coupon.”
• “Hydrolysis … next accomplished using a stainless‑steel‑encompassed PFA PFR … at 160 °C with a residence time of 10 h, affording 13 in 77 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Three different nitro‑reduction methods (Bechamp Fe/NH₄Cl, Raney Ni with hydrazine, catalytic hydrogenolysis) gave varying impurity profiles and required different work‑ups, creating process inconsistency.
Solution_Description: Catalytic hydrogenolysis with Pt/S‑C in THF at 60 °C gave clean conversion to the amine 23 with minimal by‑product 24, followed by simple filtration and precipitation to isolate the product, providing a consistent and scalable reduction step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In all three nitro reduction methods, debrominated byproduct 24 was observed. Fortunately, 24 is largely purged during subsequent steps.”
• “In the metal‑catalyzed hydrogenolysis approach … Pt/S‑C catalyst … in THF achieved completion and generated only a small amount of 24. After filtration … the product was isolated in 83 % yield with 98.6 % HPLC purity.”

Paper Title: An Alternative Indazole Synthesis for Merestinib
Problem_Description: Batch nitration of substrate 19 was limited to 100 g because the exothermic nature of the reaction prevented safe scale‑up, whereas continuous flow could process 540 g.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implementation of a PTFE plug‑flow reactor (6 mm ID, 24 m length) operated at 3 °C with a 23 min residence time enabled >98 % conversion and safe handling of larger material loads, demonstrating the inherent safety benefit of continuous processing.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The exotherm … gave us great concern for runaway potential.”
• “A continuous‑flow nitration … The small reactor dimensions would impart superior heat and mass transfer … limiting the potential for thermal runaway.”
• “The continuous nitration process was demonstrated at 540 g scale, whereas the batch process was not developed beyond 100 g batch size.”

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Batch photoredox decarboxylative arylations required 12–72 h to reach conversion and typically gave low isolated yields (<50 % for many substrates). Reaction performance was inconsistent because of poor light penetration and lack of standardized equipment.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved the chemistry to a segmented‑flow “microslug” reactor equipped with a custom photochemistry module. Thin FEP tubing (1.6–3.2 mm O.D.) ensured uniform illumination, improved heat‑mass transfer, and reduced residence time to ~20 min while delivering comparable or higher yields.
Supporting_Evidence: "the reactions are generally slow in a batch setting (12–72 h) and often prone to substrate‑dependent anomalies"; "Flow chemistry conducted in transparent 1/16″ to 1/8″ O.D. (1.6 mm to 3.2 mm) fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) tubing not only ensures exposure of the reaction mixture to sufficient photonic flux but also provides better heat and mass transfer, which can result in improved reaction yield and scale‑up robustness"; "The photochemistry module is water‑cooled and is heated … resulting in an operating temperature between 20 and 70 °C …"; "Through the deployment of a self‑optimizing algorithm, optimal flow conditions for the model reaction were rapidly developed…"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Using sodium tert‑butoxide as the base caused the reaction mixture to form gel‑like precipitates (the base is highly hygroscopic), creating a clogging risk for the tubular flow reactors.
Solution_Description: The authors screened alternative organic bases (guanidines, DBU, TMG, t‑Bu‑TMG) that gave homogeneous solutions and prevented precipitation, thereby eliminating the clogging issue.
Supporting_Evidence: "sodium tert‑butoxide … is highly hygroscopic. Without proper sealing of the reaction vessel, the reaction mixture tends to form gel‑like precipitates, which introduces a clogging risk for flow reactors"; "These bases led to yields ranging from 83 % to 91 % with complete consumption of starting material"; "Both bases led to homogeneous reaction mixtures"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: When the batch reaction was scaled up four‑fold (0.5 mmol, ~100 mg), conversion slowed dramatically and yields dropped because the larger vessel reduced effective light penetration.
Solution_Description: The process was transferred to a Vapourtec UV‑150 continuous‑flow photoreactor that uses the same thin‑wall tubing dimensions as the microslug platform, providing uniform illumination and restoring high yields at higher throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: "An initial attempt to scale‑up the reaction (4‑fold, 0.5 mmol) … became sluggish, requiring prolonged reaction time and leading to low yields. This was likely due to inefficient irradiation as a result of using larger reaction vessels"; "The segmented flow reactor … tubing dimensions … are identical to those of the Vapourtec scale‑up system"; "The Vapourtec UV‑150 flow reactor could generate 345 to 435 mg of product per hour"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Reaction rates were highly temperature‑dependent; insufficient temperature control caused competing side‑reactions (dehalogenation, aldol condensation) and inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: A self‑optimizing algorithm scanned temperature (30–50 °C) and residence time, identifying 43 °C (21 min) for maximal yield (97 %) and 50 °C (12 min) for optimal productivity (91 % yield, 12 min residence).
Supporting_Evidence: "Without proper temperature control, competing side reactions (e.g., dehalogenation, solvent couplings, and homo couplings) have been reported"; "We found that the two guanidine type bases … afforded the highest reaction yield (95 %) in 30 min. By elevating the temperature from 30 to 50 °C, we observed the acceleration of the reaction"; "the system successfully predicted the conditions leading to the maximum of 97 % yield using Barton’s base at 43 °C with a residence time of 21 min… optimal productivity condition … 50 °C with a residence time of just 12 min"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Uncertainty over the optimal catalyst loading for Ir and Ni made it difficult to predict reaction performance; varying catalyst ratios produced inconsistent rates.
Solution_Description: Systematic screening of Ir (0.5–2 mol %) and Ni (2.5–20 mol %) loadings using the self‑optimizing platform revealed that Ir loading had little effect, while increasing Ni loading significantly accelerated the reaction, pinpointing the rate‑determining catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: "The Ir catalyst was dosed from 0.5 to 2.0 mol % … The reaction did not exhibit a significant change … suggesting that the Ir catalyst was robust"; "The Ni catalyst loading was varied from 2.5 to 20 mol % … The reaction rate increased significantly with increasing Ni catalyst loading, suggesting the involvement of this catalyst in the rate‑determining step"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Iridium‑based photocatalysts are expensive, raising cost concerns for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors evaluated the organic dye 4CzIPN as a cheaper, metal‑free photoredox catalyst. Although maximum yields were slightly lower (60–70 % vs 95 % with Ir), the dye offered a cost‑effective alternative for further investigation.
Supporting_Evidence: "4CzIPN … is relatively easy and less expensive to prepare, making it a potential replacement for the expensive metal‑based (Ir or Ru) catalysts"; "The conditions using the organic dye seemed to reach maximal yields faster, but the conversion flattened after 15 min, giving final yields ranging from 60 to 70 %…"

Paper Title: Photoredox Iridium–Nickel Dual-Catalyzed Decarboxylative Arylation Cross-Coupling: From Batch to Continuous Flow via Self-Optimizing Segmented Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Aryl halides lacking electron‑withdrawing groups (e.g., 4′‑chloroacetophenone, bromopyridine, bromide/iodide substrates) performed poorly in batch (<50 % yield, 16–72 h), limiting their utility.
Solution_Description: By applying the microslug platform with elevated temperatures (up to 65 °C) and optimized residence times (5–40 min), yields for these challenging substrates were raised dramatically (up to 94 % isolated yield) and production rates increased to several hundred mg h⁻¹ in flow.
Supporting_Evidence: "These aryl halides are less reactive … typically exhibiting low yields (<50 %) and long reaction times (16–72 h)"; "At 65 °C with a residence time of 40 min, the original 14 % yield … was improved to a 78 % isolated yield in flow"; "With 5, the 45 % yield … was optimized to 94 % yield at 40 °C and a residence time of 30 min"

Paper Title: Nitration Using Fuming HNO
Problem_Description: Fuming HNO₃ is incompatible with many common organic solvents (e.g., acetonitrile, dichloromethane, DMSO) and can cause severe thermal events, making scale‑up hazardous.
Solution_Description: Sulfolane was selected as a solvent because it is stable toward strong acids/oxidizers, fully miscible with fuming HNO₃, and permits a homogeneous reaction mixture. The nitration was then moved to a continuous‑flow Hastelloy C‑22 coil, which provides superior heat‑removal and limits the amount of energetic material present at any time.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The incompatibility of this reagent with various organic solvents was a serious limitation that needed to be overcome prior to scale‑up… [SOLUBILITY]”

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: The Mitsunobu reaction previously used to join fragments 3 and 4 generated large amounts of alkene impurities, required column‑chromatographic removal of by‑products, and involved azodicarboxylates that pose thermal hazards, making the step unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Adopt a palladium‑catalyzed C–O cross‑coupling to forge the C–O bond, which eliminates the Mitsunobu reagents, avoids the formation of the alkene impurity, removes the need for chromatography, and eliminates the thermal risk of azodicarboxylates.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "The Mitsunobu reaction employed by Discovery Chemistry to join fragments 3 and 4 … was considered a potential scale‑up liability because of the formation of significant amounts of alkene impurities ( 7 ), the challenges associated with removing the Mitsunobu by‑products (in this case requiring column chromatography), and the thermal hazards associated with the use of azodicarboxylates."; "Solution: "The application of a palladium‑catalyzed C–O coupling presented significant challenges… Process development was able to address these limitations and enable production of kilogram quantities of the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) in greater efficiency than a Mitsunobu reaction for formation of the key bond."

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: During early Pd‑catalyzed C–O coupling experiments, a biaryl ether by‑product (compound 12) formed in roughly equal amount to the desired product due to adventitious water in the K₃PO₄ base, compromising purity.
Solution_Description: Dry the K₃PO₄ base (vacuum‑dry at 110‑150 °C) and use jet‑milled K₃PO₄ to ensure consistent particle size; switch to a mixed solvent system (trifluorotoluene/CPME) that improves solubility and reduces water content, thereby suppressing formation of compound 12 (< 1 AP).
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...they also led to the formation of biaryl ether 12… in roughly equal amounts to 2. Biaryl ether 12 likely arises from an initial Pd‑catalyzed hydroxylation of 6 with adventitious water present in the K₃PO₄ base… We subsequently found that the formation of 12 could be minimized by using K₃PO₄ that had been dried under vacuum at 110–150 °C…"; "Solution: "Ad‑BippyPhos gave significantly reduced levels of 12 (< 1 AP) relative to what we had previously observed with tBu‑BrettPhos and RockPhos…" and “To ensure consistent reaction rates, we utilized jet‑milled K₃PO₄… the mixture of trifluorotoluene (13 vol) and CPME (10 vol) was selected on the basis of the higher solubilities of 5 and 6…"

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: Literature C–O couplings required 2 equiv of the sterically hindered secondary alcohol (compound 5), which is synthetically complex and costly, leading to sub‑optimal material throughput.
Solution_Description: Increase the equivalents of the alcohol to 1.1 equiv (using the free‑flowing MSA salt) to drive conversion while simultaneously employing the more active ligand Ad‑BippyPhos, which provides higher turnover at lower loadings.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "First, the reported examples utilized 2 equiv of the secondary alcohol, a requirement that we hoped to avoid because of the complexity of alcohol 5…"; "Solution: "We selected the methanesulfonic acid (MSA) salt of 5 … requiring a salt break … and increasing the secondary alcohol coupling partner (5·MSA) to 1.1 equiv to improve the reaction rate/conversion…" and "Ad‑BippyPhos… gave > 50 liquid chromatography area percent (AP) of the desired C–O product 2…"

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: Input compound 5 was an amorphous, sticky, glassy solid that could not be weighed accurately without heating, causing handling and dosing difficulties on scale.
Solution_Description: Convert 5 to its methanesulfonic acid (MSA) salt, which is a free‑flowing powder, and perform a discrete salt‑break operation prior to coupling, eliminating the need for heating and improving material handling.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Input 5 was not crystalline but was in fact a sticky, glassy, and amorphous solid that required warming in an oven at 65 °C to render the material fluid for weighing…"; "Solution: "We investigated various salt forms… selected the methanesulfonic acid (MSA) salt of 5 (5·MSA), a free‑flowing powder that required a salt break and subsequent azeotropic drying operation prior to the coupling reaction."

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: Work‑up of the coupling reaction generated a thick, difficult‑to‑break emulsion when washed with 1 N HCl; the emulsion was caused by the HCl salt of deschloro compound 10, complicating phase separation and downstream processing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Eliminate the 1 N HCl wash and instead use a phosphoric‑acid quench; when an emulsion still forms, add hexanes to split the layers, allowing removal of the problematic salt‑derived layer and simplifying the work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...a thick emulsion resulted that could not be broken by extended standing, heating, or addition of brine. Fortunately, it was found that adding hexanes to the reactor caused the layers to split…the cause of the emulsion was the HCl salt of deschloro compound 10."; "Solution: "...forego a 1 N HCl wash…the coupling stream after the H₃PO₄ wash was directly subjected to hydrolysis…addition of hexanes to the reactor caused the layers to split, with a third, dark‑red minor layer…identified as the cause of the emulsion…"

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: High loading of the phosphine ligand (compound 8) during coupling resulted in residual ligand remaining in the final API after work‑up, exceeding acceptable impurity limits.
Solution_Description: Reduce the ligand loading from 5 mol % to 3 mol % (and Pd from 2.5 mol % to 2.0 mol %), decreasing the amount of ligand that must be removed downstream.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...the crystallization and recrystallization were not effective at reducing residual ligand 8, which was not fully removed during the workup to an acceptable level…"; "Solution: "reducing the amount of both Pd(OAc)₂ (2.0 vs 2.5 mol %) and ligand 8 (3 vs 5 mol %) to reduce the burden of the ligand removal during the workup and isolation."

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: Multiple pH adjustments (acid/base swings) and prolonged reaction times were required to control impurity formation (especially deschloro 10), making the process operationally inefficient and variable.
Solution_Description: Implement a streamlined work‑up with fewer pH swings—use a single phosphoric‑acid quench, avoid the 1 N HCl wash, and control the pH only where necessary—to reduce reaction time and improve reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "Although the use of multiple pH swings was inefficient from an operations standpoint…"; "Solution: "...the operations found to be unnecessary were removed in second‑generation workup…" and "The phosphoric acid (6 M) was added… after which the layers were separated, and the organic layer was washed with water…"

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: Residual palladium from the coupling catalyst remained in the API (up to 37 ppm), posing a potential safety and regulatory issue.
Solution_Description: Treat the crude product with a phosphonic thiol‑silica scavenger resin (SPM‑36) followed by a second thiol‑silica resin to bind and remove palladium, lowering the metal content to ≤ 23 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...the crude residue contained 37 ppm Pd…"; "Solution: "The residue was dissolved in MTBE (28 L), and Phosphonics SPM36 (3‑mercaptopropyl ethyl sulfide silica gel, 500 g, 37 equiv vs Pd) was added… The slurry was stirred… then the resin was removed… after a second scavenger treatment the final API contained 23 ppm Pd."

Paper Title: Palladium-Catalyzed C–O Coupling of a Sterically Hindered Secondary Alcohol with an Aryl Bromide and Significant Purity Upgrade in the API Step
Problem_Description: The initial process required isolation of the coupling intermediate (compound 2) by column chromatography, which is impractical at kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Telescoping the C–O coupling directly into the subsequent ester hydrolysis eliminates the need to isolate compound 2, allowing the API (compound 1) to be obtained in a single sequence without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: Problem: "...the coupling was performed on a larger scale highlighted issues that would need to be addressed before the subsequent clinical campaign… it was not feasible to purify compound 2 via chromatography…"; "Solution: "necessity dictated that we telescope the coupling stream directly into the hydrolysis reaction to produce compound 1…"

Paper Title: Flow-Assisted Synthesis of Bicyclic Aziridines
Problem_Description: Batch photochemical transformation of pyridinium salts gave very low productivities (0.0027–1.33 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹) and only milligram‑scale amounts of bicyclic aziridines, limiting downstream synthesis.
Solution_Description: Three homemade continuous‑flow reactors (FEP4, PQT4, PQT2) were built and placed inside a Rayonet‑type UV reactor, providing higher surface‑to‑volume ratios, better light penetration and straightforward scalability.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The photochemical transformation of pyridinium salts … under batch conditions gives low productivities of 0.0027–1.33 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹… only a few milligrams (less than 100 mg) of bicyclic aziridines are produced” (Abstract, batch discussion).  
• “Three homemade continuous‑flow reactors were developed… The first was a fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) reactor… The second was a flow reactor… PQT4… The third reactor, PQT2…” (Design of Flow Reactors).

Paper Title: Flow-Assisted Synthesis of Bicyclic Aziridines
Problem_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration to about 300 mM caused a strong drop in conversion (e.g., 13–33 % after 8 h) because photon absorption follows the Bouguer‑Lambert‑Beer law.
Solution_Description: The concentration was reduced to ~60 mM for the flow experiments, a level at which photon penetration is not limited and conversions above 90 % are obtained.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “At a concentration of ca. 300 mM the conversion after 8 h of irradiation was lower (17 % for QT4 vs 33 % for QT2 vs 13 % for FEP…) which can be explained by the Bouguer‑Lambert‑Beer law” (Batch Experiments).  
• “Since at a concentration of ca. 60 mM the absorption of photons was not affected, this concentration was chosen for the flow studies.” (Batch Experiments).

Paper Title: Flow-Assisted Synthesis of Bicyclic Aziridines
Problem_Description: The FEP reactor’s coiled geometry reduced light penetration on the inner side, giving lower conversions (56 % at 0.56 mL min⁻¹) than predicted from batch data.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The flow rate was lowered to 0.28 mL min⁻¹ (residence time 17.9 h), which restored high conversion (93 %) and maintained productivity over multi‑day operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The low conversion … is related to the geometry of FEP4, as the reaction mixture receives less radiation since the light penetration in the inner side of the reactor is reduced.” (Recirculating Continuous‑Flow Experiments).  
• “At a flow rate of 0.28 mL/min, … the conversion increased to 93 % and remained above 60 % throughout the operation period of 3.8 days.” (Continuous‑Flow Experiment).

Paper Title: Flow-Assisted Synthesis of Bicyclic Aziridines
Problem_Description: The quartz‑tube reactors (PQT4, PQT2) contain numerous connections that generate a considerable dead volume, preventing their use without recirculating the reaction mixture and decreasing overall productivity.
Solution_Description: The FEP4 reactor, which has a single continuous tube and no dead‑volume connections, was employed for a non‑recirculating continuous‑flow run, allowing higher throughput and longer‑time operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Because of construction limitations of the connections between the quartz tubes, the PQT4 and PQT2 reactors have a considerable dead volume that limits their use without recirculating the reaction medium.” (Continuous‑Flow Experiment).  
• “On the other hand, this limitation is absent for the FEP4 reactor, and therefore, we explored the transformation of 1a at 62 mM without recirculating the reaction medium.” (Continuous‑Flow Experiment).

Paper Title: Flow-Assisted Synthesis of Bicyclic Aziridines
Problem_Description: Prolonged irradiation required to achieve full conversion in oversized reactors can lead to over‑irradiation, promoting formation of by‑products.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Continuous‑flow operation with precisely controlled residence times limits the exposure of the reaction mixture to UV light, thereby reducing over‑irradiation and side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction time necessary to drive the reaction to completion … increases considerably, leading to overirradiation of the reaction mixture, which can potentiate the formation of byproducts.” (Scale‑up limitation paragraph).  
• “The recirculating continuous‑flow experiments … allowed the determination of conversion as well as the product mass and the productivity,” demonstrating that flow control mitigates over‑irradiation.

Paper Title: UV PhotoVap: Demonstrating How a Simple and Versatile Reactor Based on a Conventional Rotary Evaporator Can Be Used for UV Photochemistry
Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several scale‑up issues when converting a rotary‑evaporator into a UV photochemical reactor: (1) intense UV radiation required safe containment; (2) the high‑power mercury lamps raised the reaction temperature (≈3.5 °C min⁻¹) risking overheating; (3) modest yields (≈40–80 %) for the intermolecular [2+2] cycloaddition were observed, especially with quartz glassware; (4) productivity varied with flask material and volume, indicating inconsistent conversion; (5) the thin‑film rotating flask sometimes formed a viscous layer that limited mixing and caused fouling; (6) over‑irradiation led to by‑product formation and possible degradation of the substrate or product; (7) isolation of the bicyclic product was difficult because of co‑eluting polymeric by‑products.
Solution_Description: To address the above challenges the authors implemented a suite of engineering and operational modifications: (1) the reactor was enclosed in a fume‑hood with a removable dark‑red filter that blocks hard UV and visible light ([SAFETY]); (2) a circulating water bath kept the flask at 37 °C and limited solvent loss (<2 mL), mitigating the exotherm ([TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION]); (3) EtOAc (UV cut‑off < 256 nm) was screened as an alternative solvent to quartz, but gave comparable results, highlighting solvent choice as a variable ([SOLVENT CHANGE]); (4) increasing the irradiated volume from 30 mL to 100 mL raised productivity and reduced polymeric fouling, showing that larger reaction volumes improve mass‑transfer and heat dissipation ([CONCENTRATION TUNING]); (5) quartz flasks gave higher conversion than borosilicate; the authors therefore selected quartz for optimum light transmission and demonstrated that flask material directly influences yield ([REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS]); (6) external aqueous CuSO₄/KI filters were tested to attenuate excess UV, giving modest productivity gains, illustrating the use of additive filters to curb over‑irradiation ([FUNCTIONAL ADDITIVE/PROMOTER]); (7) semi‑continuous operation (fill‑irradiate‑empty cycles) and adjusting lamp power (1 × 1.4 kW → 2 × 1.4 kW → 1 × 1.4 kW + 1 × 2.0 kW) allowed fine‑tuning of photon flux and residence time, improving throughput and consistency ([ORDER AND RATE OF ADDITION]).
Supporting_Evidence: • "Safety is paramount in UV photolysis experiments, particularly the containment of high‑power UV sources and radiation... the glass sash is equipped with a removable dark‑red plastic filter that provides enhanced blocking of hard UV light" (Results & Discussion, p. 3).   • "Typically, during the course of operation the temperature increased (at a rate of ca. 3.5 °C min⁻¹). Despite any increase in temperature, the amount of solvent evaporation was found to be minimal (ca. <2 mL)." (p. 3).   • "Moderate yields of 5 (42 %) were obtained using a single 1.4 kW lamp… Switching to borosilicate gave a drop in productivity of ca. 50 %" (p. 5).   • "Increasing both the irradiated solution volume we observed a corresponding increase in both productivity and mass balance… considerably less reactor fouling was observed when a larger irradiation volume was used" (p. 5).   • "Using a quartz flask gave high conversion; using a borosilicate flask required twice the irradiation time to reach comparable conversion" (Table 1, entry 4; p. 4).   • "External filters were also applied, this time by using the thin film that is generated on the outside of the flask as it rotates… with minimal improvements in productivity" (p. 6).   • "Semi‑continuous operation gave productivities of 170.5 g h⁻¹ (entry 8) and scaling lamp power (1 × 1.4 kW + 1 × 2.0 kW) gave the highest productivity of 210.6 g h⁻¹ (entry 7)" (Table 1, p. 4).

Paper Title: UV PhotoVap: Demonstrating How a Simple and Versatile Reactor Based on a Conventional Rotary Evaporator Can Be Used for UV Photochemistry
Problem_Description: The original PhotoVap platform required high‑power mercury lamps (1.4–2.0 kW each) and quartz flasks, both of which are relatively expensive for routine large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: The authors demonstrated that comparable productivity can be achieved with a single 2 kW lamp and smaller irradiated volumes, reducing the number of lamps needed for a given throughput, and note that the reactor can be built from standard laboratory equipment, minimising capital cost.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Using a single 2 kW Hg lamp, moderate to high conversion and yields could be obtained in less than 1 min" (Table 1, entries 1‑3).   • "The simplicity of the design and availability of the equipment makes this a viable and inexpensive option" (Conclusion, p. 7).

Problem_Description: UV‑transparent tubing (e.g., FEP) and custom flow reactors are not universally available, limiting the transfer of existing UV‑flow technologies to other labs.
