Paper Title: Continuous Flow Synthesis of 16-Dehydropregnenolone Acetate, a Key Synthon for Natural Steroids and Drugs
Problem_Description: The original acetylation/acetolysis of diosgenin required reflux in an autoclave at 250 °C and 5 bar for 10–14 h, causing harsh reaction conditions, potential safety hazards and extensive decomposition of the starting material leading to side‑product formation and low yields.
Solution_Description: A milder protocol was developed using acetic trifluoro‑acetate anhydride (ATFAA) with BF₃·Et₂O at room temperature in CH₂Cl₂, followed by DBU (or p‑TSA) to promote conversion. The reagents were introduced by loop‑injection and mixed in a T‑junction before flowing through a coil reactor, eliminating the need for high temperature/pressure.
Supporting_Evidence: S1: “The method consists of refluxing 2 in an autoclave with Ac₂O in xylene for 14 h at 5 bar… which strongly affect the sustainability of the process and the quality of the end product.”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of boronate ester 3 with 4‑bromopyrimidine (4) using Pd(PPh₃)₄, an impurity (compound 6) was formed in ~8 % yield via an aryl‑aryl exchange between the aryl group on palladium and the phosphine ligand, complicating isolation of the desired pyrimidine 5.
Solution_Description: The impurity was removed by precipitating the product 5 as its hydrochloride salt (addition of aqueous HCl); the authors therefore did not pursue changes to the catalyst or ligands, accepting the existing route while using the salt‑precipitation work‑up to obtain >97 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The impurity was likely formed from a side pathway … aryl–aryl exchange … The impurity could be removed upon precipitation of 5 as a hydrochloride salt by adding aqueous hydrochloric acid to the reaction solution”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Use of potassium tert‑butoxide as the base in the Buchwald–Hartwig coupling of 5 and 9 caused trans‑esterification side‑reactions and gave only trace coupled product (entry 1, Table 1).
Solution_Description: The base was switched to milder inorganic bases (Cs₂CO₃, K₃PO₄) and solvents were screened (toluene, dioxane). Cs₂CO₃ in toluene with Xantphos gave the best conversion (33 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “Using potassium tert‑butoxide as the base complicated the reaction because of transesterification and afforded only a trace amount of the coupled product (entry 1)”; “Under conditions without this complication, the reaction generally suffered from low conversions… Xantphos was identified as the best ligand”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The Buchwald–Hartwig coupling of pyrimidine 5 with aryl bromide 9 consistently stalled at ~33 % conversion despite variations in catalyst loading, solvent, and base.
Solution_Description: To push the reaction to completion, the authors added 3 mol % Xantphos every 2 h (total eight additions, 27 % Xantphos overall). This incremental ligand addition compensated for ligand oxidation to the phosphine oxide during the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction under selected conditions always stopped at around 33 % conversion… charging the entire 27 mol % loading of Xantphos up front did not give complete conversion… complete conversion was eventually achieved by charging 3 mol % Xantphos every 2 h up to eight times”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The first‑generation coupling required repeated addition of the expensive bis‑phosphine Xantphos to achieve full conversion, making the process economically unattractive for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation route was designed using aryl chloride 12 and aniline 15 as coupling partners. This combination gave rapid (≈2 h), complete conversion without Xantphos, using inexpensive Pd(OAc)₂/BINAP in DMF, enabling scale‑up to >100 g.
Supporting_Evidence: “The synthesis is convergent but suffers from a sluggish Buchwald–Hartwig coupling that was only driven to completion by repeatedly charging expensive Xantphos… A more efficient and scalable synthesis was needed… Consistent with the prediction, the new partners 12 and 15 underwent smooth coupling with complete conversion within 2 h under catalysis of Pd(OAc)₂/BINAP. DMF was selected as the reaction solvent because it allowed direct product precipitation”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the iron‑powder reduction of nitro‑benzyl intermediate 14 to aniline 15, the exothermic nature of the reaction required portion‑wise addition of iron to avoid uncontrolled heat buildup.
Solution_Description: Iron powder (3.5 equiv) was added in four equal portions at 5 min intervals, allowing the reaction temperature to be controlled and preventing thermal runaway.
Supporting_Evidence: “Iron powder (100 μm) (39 g, 0.70 mol, 3.5 equiv) was added in four equal portions at 5 min intervals… portion‑wise charging of iron powder was needed to avoid heat accumulation in the reaction.”

Paper Title: Exemplifying Prediction of Preferred Coupling Partners in Developing a Buchwald–Hartwig Coupling for the Synthesis of a c‑Kit Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Residual palladium (~800 ppm) remained in the coupled product 10 after the Buchwald–Hartwig step, exceeding acceptable limits for drug substance.
Solution_Description: The product was treated with 10 wt % Smopex 234 in hot toluene, refluxed for 2 h, followed by cooling and filtration, reducing palladium to 21 ppm (acceptable for the final API).
Supporting_Evidence: “To a 5 L three‑neck round‑bottom flask were added 10 (120 g, 800 ppm Pd level), Smopex 234 (12 g), and toluene (2.4 L). The suspension was heated to reflux for 2 h… The filter cake was washed… affording 10 (91 g, 21 ppm Pd level, 76 % yield).”

Paper Title: Ir-Catalyzed Borylation as an Efficient Route to a Nicotine Hapten
Problem_Description: Ir‑catalyzed borylation gave inconsistent conversion on scale; the [Ir(COD)OMe]₂ precatalyst was unstable during ambient storage making it unreliable.
Solution_Description: Switched to the more stable [Ir(COD)Cl]₂ precursor, changed the supporting ligand from dtbpy to tmphen (more active and cheaper) and lowered the Ir loading from 6 mol % to 2 mol %; also ran the reaction in n‑heptane which eliminated the induction period and allowed direct crystallisation of the borylated product.
Supporting_Evidence: • "one of the primary concerns was that the Ir‑catalyzed borylation was inconsistent in achieving complete conversion on scale" (VARIABILITY)

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: The Suzuki coupling of aldehyde 12 with boronate 7 gave a poorly soluble intermediate, requiring very dilute conditions (≈75 vol % solvent) and resulting in incomplete conversion and low isolated yield; isolation required HPLC.
Solution_Description: The aldehyde was introduced **after** the Suzuki coupling (using boronic acid 16) and the reaction solvent was changed from acetonitrile to a 2‑MeTHF/DMSO mixture, which dramatically improved solubility, allowed full conversion, and enabled isolation by simple crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “low solubilities of the coupling product led to high dilutions (75 vol %), incomplete conversion … and difficulties in isolation, as HPLC purification was employed for the first syntheses.”
• “switching from acetonitrile … to 2‑MeTHF/DMSO … led to full conversion of the starting material to greatly facilitate isolation of the final product.”
• “the Suzuki coupling between boronic acid 16 and bromoindole 9 proceeded under standard conditions, … recrystallization … provided… 55 % yield… and a consistent purity profile.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: The boronate ester 7 required chromatography for removal of excess potassium acetate to reach >95 % purity, adding cost and time to the process.
Solution_Description: The synthetic sequence was redesigned to produce the **boronic acid** 16 instead of the ester; the acid can be extracted into a basic aqueous phase, washed, and crystallised, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “isolation of 7 was complicated by the presence of excess potassium acetate, and chromatography was required to achieve >95 % purity.”
• “Synthesis of the corresponding boronic acid 16… was proposed to facilitate isolation without chromatography. … the resultant boronic acid 16 … was extracted into an aqueous basic medium, allowing many of the organic impurities to be purged with an MTBE wash. Neutralization and crystallisation then produced boronic acid 16 in an isolated yield of 72 %.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: The initial reduction of difluoroindole 9 using borane gave only 31 % overall yield, with over‑ and under‑reduced by‑products and difficult chromatographic separations.
Solution_Description: An asymmetric CBS reduction at –20 °C was employed, affording the alcohol 14 in 95 % yield (98.4:1 er); subsequent cyclisation gave tetrahydropyran 15 without chromatography, improving overall yield and purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “reduction with borane afforded the indole in low yield (31 % over two steps). Difficulty in controlling the reduction … contributed to the low yield.”
• “CBS reduction … was selected … On a 50 g scale, alcohol 14 was obtained as a solid product after aqueous workup (95 % yield, 98.4:1.6 er), with temperature control (−20 °C) being a critical variable to ensure high enantioselectivity.”
• “Subsequent cyclisation generated tetrahydropyran 15 without the need for chromatography.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: When 5‑bromo‑4,6‑difluoro‑1H‑indole 9 was formed by adding compound 19 to potassium tert‑butoxide, a rapid exotherm (33 → 87 °C) occurred, posing safety concerns and leading to impurity formation when addition was slowed.
Solution_Description: The addition was performed in a **single portion** to keep the exotherm short (≈1 min) and the reaction essentially adiabatic; the temperature rise was accepted and process parameters (cooling, quench) were controlled to obtain >0.75 kg of pure product without excessive impurities.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “addition of 19 in one portion … was accompanied by a rapid exotherm, from 33 to 87 °C on a 100 g scale.”
• “Attempts to moderate this exotherm by slow addition … resulted in greater formation of impurities.”
• “With addition in one portion, the exotherm was complete within 1 min, such that the conditions were close to adiabatic … enabled the formation of >0.75 kg of pure indole 9.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: During saponification of ester 38 to give acid 2, decarboxylation increased sharply at higher temperatures (≥ 70 °C) or with long reaction times, leading to variable yields and impurity levels.
Solution_Description: The saponification temperature was limited to 50–55 °C and the reaction time to 36–48 h, which reduced decarboxylation to ≤ 2 % while still delivering acceptable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “decaboxylation was observed at higher temperatures (3–4 % at 60 °C, 20–24 h; > 15 % at 70 °C, 15 h) or with long reaction times (4 % at 50 °C, 110 h).”
• “decaboxylation byproduct formation was reduced (2 %) by maintaining the temperature between 50–55 °C and employing a moderate reaction time (36–48 h).”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: The kilogram‑scale synthesis of 3 originally required the expensive Pd‑XPhos G2 precatalyst, which has limited commercial availability, inflating material cost.
Solution_Description: The catalyst was switched to the inexpensive Pd(PPh₃)₂Cl₂, which gave comparable conversion and allowed a high‑yielding process while dramatically lowering catalyst expense.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “high cost and limited availability of the catalyst (Pd‑XPhos G2 precatalyst) … alternative solutions desirable.”
• “Pd(PPh₃)₂Cl₂ was chosen because of its low cost.”
• “These improved coupling conditions enabled a decreased reaction time (5 h) on the kilogram scale.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: Boronic acid 48 was identified as a weak mutagen, requiring its residual level in the final API to be ≤ 30 ppm, imposing strict impurity‑control constraints.
Solution_Description: A silica‑supported thiol scavenger was employed after the Suzuki step to remove residual palladium and lower boronic‑acid impurity levels to < 30 ppm, satisfying safety specifications.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “boronic acid 48 was identified as weakly mutagenic; therefore, its concentration needed to be reduced to ≤ 30 ppm for the planned studies.”
• “After treatment with a silica‑supported thiol to scavenge residual Pd, the Suzuki product was isolated … Boronic acid and Pd residues were quantitated at acceptable levels (< 30 and 45 ppm, respectively).”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: The early synthesis of bromopyridine 28 suffered from poor regioselectivity in SNAr (5:1) and required difficult chromatographic separation of regioisomers, giving low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: A new route started from inexpensive 2,6‑difluoropyridine, performing two sequential SNAr reactions to give 28 in 99 % yield after simple aqueous work‑up and trituration, eliminating the regioisomer problem and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The regioselectivity of the methoxide addition was ~5:1 … leading to low isolated yields … primarily due to the difficulty in chromatographic separation of the closely eluting regioisomers.”
• “Starting from less expensive, symmetrical 2,6‑difluoropyridine … bromination … afforded crystalline 41 in 83 % yield … The second SNAr … provided 1.4 kg of the desired product 28 as a crystalline solid in 99 % yield after aqueous work‑up.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: Indole 9 obtained from the Sonogashira‑then‑cyclisation sequence required silica‑gel chromatography to reach purity > 95 %, making scale‑up cumbersome and decreasing overall yield.
Solution_Description: A revised sequence employed potassium tert‑butoxide in NMP to achieve simultaneous desilylation and cyclisation in one pot, producing crude 9 (~85 % purity) without chromatography; the material was later isolated by trituration, improving throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When this conversion was carried out … crude indole 9 was obtained with ∼85 % purity, but this addition was accompanied by a rapid exotherm … For project expediency, this material was isolated by silica gel chromatography … full optimisation … not completed.”
• “subsequent cyclisation conditions were simplified by employing potassium tert‑butoxide in NMP … crude indole 9 was obtained with ∼85 % purity, … the material was isolated by silica gel chromatography … full optimisation of the conditions to precipitate the product directly was not completed.”

Paper Title: Evolution of the Synthesis of AMPK Activators for the Treatment of Diabetic Nephropathy: From Three Preclinical Candidates to the Investigational New Drug PF-06409577
Problem_Description: Enantiomeric separation of the racemic acid 1 required chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC), an expensive and low‑throughput purification step.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was redesigned to give enantioenriched intermediate 15 via CBS reduction; the downstream steps delivered the final API 1 with > 99.5 % purity by simple recrystallisation, eliminating chiral SFC.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “SFC purification on a chiral phase was then used to isolate the eutomer … Although this route was successful for milligram‑scale synthesis … several problems needed to be addressed … the use of SFC on a chiral phase to isolate the final product.”
• “The enantioselective approach … CBS reduction … 95 % yield, 98.4:1.6 er … Sub‑sequent cyclisation generated tetrahydropyran 15 without the need for chromatography.”
• “After aqueous work‑up, the product acid 1 was isolated in 80 % yield after precipitation … slurrying in ethanol/water (95:5) led to isolation of crystalline 1 … 96 % yield, > 99:1 er … suitable for exploratory toxicology studies.”

Paper Title: Crystallization of a Metastable Solvate and Impact of the Isolation Method on the Material Properties of the Anhydrous Product
Problem_Description: Large‑scale batches of the metastable EtOH solvate required a disproportionate amount of drying time – up to several days for a 50 kg batch – making the temperature‑driven desolvation step impractical for commercial manufacture.
Solution_Description: A post‑filtration wash with ethyl acetate was introduced; the EtOAc wash instantly converts the EtOH solvate to the anhydrous form, eliminating the need for prolonged vacuum drying.
Supporting_Evidence: ['larger batch sizes required a disproportionate amount of drying time, ultimately on the order of days for the largest attempted scale (50 kg).', 'The temperature‑driven desolvation method was found to be time‑consuming and undesirable.', 'EtOAc was found to be a successful solvent to effect the desired change on a very rapid time scale.']

Paper Title: Crystallization of a Metastable Solvate and Impact of the Isolation Method on the Material Properties of the Anhydrous Product
Problem_Description: The particle‑size distribution measured in‑situ (CLD > 100 µm) did not match the final product (d₅₀ < 50 µm) because crystals fractured during desolvation, leading to inconsistent PSD and unpredictable powder attributes.
Solution_Description: A screening of post‑filtration wash solvents identified ethyl acetate as the only solvent that gave immediate formation of the anhydrous polymorph, aiming to reduce the time crystals spend in the lattice‑collapse step and therefore limit breakage.
Supporting_Evidence: ['chord length distribution (CLD) with a median of >100 µm, whereas the final isolated material yielded d₅₀ values of <50 µm.', 'The discord in PSD between the in situ and final crystalline materials was unexpected, and the ability to control and manipulate the PSD of the final product became a priority.', 'A range of solvents ... With the exception of EtOAc, all of the solvents resulted in either retention of the 1‑EtOH form ... The use of relatively small volumes of EtOAc resulted in the exclusive formation of the targeted 1‑anh form.']

Paper Title: Crystallization of a Metastable Solvate and Impact of the Isolation Method on the Material Properties of the Anhydrous Product
Problem_Description: The EtOAc‑wash route produced a powder with a broader PSD span, higher inter‑particulate friction, lower bulk density and poorer flowability, making it unsuitable for downstream tablet manufacturing despite high chemical yield.
Solution_Description: The original ethanol‑wash followed by controlled temperature‑driven vacuum drying was retained; this route yields denser, platelike crystals with superior flow properties, despite the longer drying time.
Supporting_Evidence: ['The most notable difference in the PSD data for the processes is the greatly increased span associated with the EtOAc‑process material.', 'EtOAc‑process powder has higher cohesive strength, lower bulk density, and poorer flow compared with the EtOH‑process material.', 'The temperature‑driven desolvation method ... yields platelike crystals that are denser and exhibit better powder flow.']

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: The conventional industrial route to cefotaxime uses an activated acid intermediate generated from dithiobis‑benzothiazole and triphenylphosphine, which creates a large amount of waste and involves hazardous reagents.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the activated‑acid pathway by a direct amidation of 7‑ACA with the non‑activated acid (Z)‑(2‑aminothiazol‑4‑yl)‑methoxyiminoacetic acid using 4‑toluenesulfonyl chloride as the coupling reagent, generating only benign toluenesulfonic acid as by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states that “the use of 4‑toluenesulfonyl chloride as a coupling reagent leads to a process with only toluenesulfonic acid as an easy‑to‑separate byproduct” and that the standard activated‑acid route “lead[s] to a large amount of waste … reagents like dithiobis‑(benzothiazole) and triphenylphosphine are used.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: 7‑Aminocephalosporanic acid (7‑ACA) is almost insoluble in most organic solvents; its dissolution requires triethylamine, and the mixed anhydride (5) forms a suspension that can cause plugging in continuous flow.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Dimethylacetamide was selected as solvent 1 to dissolve the acid component, while methanol (or water) was identified as a suitable solvent 2 for 7‑ACA, providing a clear solution with triethylamine. In the flow set‑up a tube reactor with a 4 mm inner diameter and peristaltic pumping at ≥5 mL min⁻¹ was used to keep the mixed anhydride in suspension and avoid sedimentation.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors note that “7‑ACA is nearly insoluble in organic solvents, and only in combination with triethylamine solutions of 7‑ACA can be obtained” and that “the mixed anhydride 5 … leads to a suspension, which was stirred all the time to avoid sedimentation.” They further report that “the best results were achieved using polar aprotic solvents like dimethylacetamide … methanol leads to a near‑full conversion … the tube of fluorinated ethylene propylene … with a diameter larger than that in common microreactors to prevent fouling and blocking problems because the mixed anhydride 5 is not completely soluble.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: The traditional batch process employs chlorinated solvent (methylene chloride) and dimethylacetamide, both of which raise health and environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: Methanol was introduced as an alternative to methylene chloride for solvent 2, eliminating the use of a chlorinated solvent while maintaining high conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: The text states “the use of methanol leads to a nearly full conversion to 1, which is comparable to the use of methylene chloride… methanol represents an interesting alternative to methylene chloride because the use of a chlorinated solvent can be avoided.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: The amide‑formation step is highly exothermic and traditionally required temperatures below –30 °C, leading to expensive cooling (e.g., liquid nitrogen) and scale‑up heat‑removal difficulties.
Solution_Description: Operating the reaction in a continuous tube reactor allowed the temperature to be raised to –10 °C while maintaining isothermal control, drastically reducing cooling costs and improving safety. The high surface‑to‑volume ratio of the flow reactor provides superior heat‑transfer (k) and specific surface area (a₍v₎).
Supporting_Evidence: The authors describe that “the reaction between 5 and 2 is highly exothermic… the temperature of the second step was selected to be below –30 °C… the continuous mode leads to a decrease in energy consumption because of the higher reaction temperature… the heat transfer coefficient k in the tube reactor is expected to fall between those of the plate heat exchanger and the stirred tank reactor… the flow process operates at –10 °C instead of –30 °C, which reduces energy demand.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: The batch process requires a 30 min residence time for the amide formation, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: In the flow mode the residence time was reduced to 1 min, providing comparable conversion (≈80 %) while increasing space‑time yield by ~400‑fold.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 5 shows a 1 min residence time at –10 °C giving 80.9 % yield, and the discussion notes “the flow reaction leads to a lower yield compared with the batch reaction, … it has to be taken into account that the flow process operates at a much shorter reaction time of only 1 min instead of 30 min.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: Batch scale‑up suffers from poor heat removal, leading to temperature gradients and inconsistent conversions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to a millimetre‑scale tube reactor (FEP) provides a high surface‑to‑volume ratio, improving heat dissipation and ensuring uniform temperature, thereby reducing run‑to‑run variability.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors explain that “the surface to volume ratio … affects the heat exchange … the continuous tube reactor … provides a higher heat transfer … This allows exothermic reactions to be run at higher temperature under isothermal conditions, leading to… higher space‑time yields.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode
Problem_Description: Cooling to temperatures below –20 °C in batch requires expensive cryogenic media, representing a major cost factor for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: By operating the flow reactor at –10 °C the need for deep cooling is eliminated, significantly lowering utility costs and improving overall process economics.
Supporting_Evidence: The article states “cooling is a very expensive step … temperatures of less than –20 °C represent a significant cost factor … the continuous process … can be adjusted to the more convenient –10 °C… This represents a further advantage of the flow process.”

Paper Title: Process Development for Synthesizing the Cephalosporin Antibiotic Cefotaxime in Batch and Flow Mode

- "One of the problems with the use of aryl fluorides in the SNAr reaction is the fluoride salt byproduct that can cause damage to glass‑lined vessels during repeated batch manufacture."
- "Calcium propionate has been identified as an effective in situ HF scrubber, generating calcium fluoride byproduct, which is simply removed by precipitation/filtration after the reaction."
- "Several calcium salts were initially tested ... Calcium propionate was preferred ... The S_NAr reaction rates with any of the calcium salts tested were identical to that without, indicating the absence of a thermodynamic equilibrium between fluoride, product, and the Meisenheimer complex."
- "Fluoride analysis ... showed minimum detectable levels compared to the theory amounts or control reactions without Ca(EtCO₂)₂."

Paper Title: Development of an S

- "MTBE was charged to the reaction vessel, and the mixture was stirred ... the precipitate was collected via vacuum filtration."

Paper Title: Development of an S

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of Kinase Inhibitor AKN028

Supporting_Evidence: “Initially, a 5 % solution based on the dibromo compound in DMSO was used, but it was found that a 10‑fold reduction in DMSO gave the same purity and increased the reaction rate.”; “Considering the cost of 5‑aminoindole, 1.3 equiv appeared to give optimal performance.”; “When the reaction was run at multikilogram scale, the conversion was 88 %… Workup … returned 2 in 81 % yield with 96 % purity.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of Kinase Inhibitor AKN028
Problem_Description: Extensive screening of palladium catalysts and solvents for the Suzuki coupling gave little or no conversion, and the reaction was highly sensitive to oxygen, which caused dehalogenated by‑product 4 and left residual palladium (~5000 ppm) after work‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: “Pd(dppf)Cl₂… satisfactory 100 % conversion within 2 h.”; “The reaction supported by this catalyst was sensitive to oxygen… dehalogenated compound 4… when oxygen was carefully excluded, the reaction was complete within 1 h and dehalogenation was not observed.”; “Attempts to decrease the catalyst loading from 4 to 1 or 1.5 % gave significantly slower conversion.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of Kinase Inhibitor AKN028
Problem_Description: The final kinase inhibitor (AKN028) displayed very low solubility in most solvents (≤10 mg mL⁻¹), degrading in acetone at elevated temperature and giving poor crystal yields, while residual palladium remained high after the Suzuki step.

Supporting_Evidence: “The desired kinase inhibitor 1 has very low solubility in most solvents… Small crystals were formed when 1 was crystallized from acetone/n‑heptane… the assay and purity remained unsatisfactory.”; “It was decided to use a solution of 1 in 2 M acetic acid and treatment with Hyflo Super Cel… After filtration, almost complete removal of 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran… addition of DMF and scavengers… resulted in an acceptable residual palladium level of 5 ppm.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthesis of Kinase Inhibitor AKN028
Problem_Description: Initial attempts to remove palladium using encapsulated Pd(II)‑EnCat30NP beads failed due to catalyst leaching (≈7000 ppm Pd) and high ligand loadings; scavenger screening alone could not lower Pd below 10 ppm because of the large palladium load in the crude material.
Solution_Description: A two‑step approach was adopted: first treat the crude material with Hyflo Super Cel to precipitate palladium‑rich solids, then apply a combination of two thiol‑based scavengers, which together reduced palladium to <10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “A Suzuki coupling with Pd‑EnCat30NP… product contained about 7000 ppm palladium… In all cases, a substantial reduction of palladium occurred, but it was not possible to reach the desired level of <10 ppm.”; “When a mixture was pretreated with Hyflo Super Cel and then treated with a combination of two different scavengers, the residual level of palladium was well below 10 ppm.”

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Intermediate 9 (hydroximinoacetone) exhibits a large exothermic hazard (≈2450 J g⁻¹, 58 % of TNT) and can undergo a temperature spike >1400 K under adiabatic conditions; it also decomposes on storage (formation of by‑products 11/12) making batch operation on >100 g scale unsafe and low‑yielding.
Solution_Description: Implemented a continuous‑flow nitrosylation of acetone using in‑situ generated nitrosyl chloride (tert‑butyl nitrite + HCl) at 10 °C in a PFA coil, followed by immediate quench with aqueous ammonia; the flow platform limits inventory, controls heat release, and avoids storage of 9.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) analysis of intermediate 9 identifies exothermic activity between 140 and 275 °C with a heat output of ca. 2450 J g⁻¹, a value that represents 58 % of the energy output of TNT.", "Under adiabatic conditions, isolated 9 has the potential to result in a temperature rise greater than 1400 K.", "For safety concerns, could only be operated in batch mode on limited scales (≪100 g).", "We strongly recommend avoiding such a batch process on any scale and guide the reader toward the alternative described later where intermediate 9 is continuously generated and continuously consumed.", "We could develop a continuous flow setup where tert‑butyl nitrite and catalytic quantities of HCl are combined, leading to the in situ formation of nitrosyl chloride… The ideal temperature of the reactor being set at 10 °C… the reactor output was directed toward a Y‑piece where it was then combined with a concentrated aqueous ammonia solution to quench the reaction."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Route A (pyruvaldehyde → 9) gave poor regioselectivity; by‑products 11 and 12 were always formed (70:30 9 : (11+12)), and these impurities could not be removed efficiently, leading to low overall yield and batch‑to‑batch variability.
Solution_Description: Abandoned Route A and selected Route C (nitrosylation of acetone) as the practical pathway to 9, later adapted to continuous flow for robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: ["A regioselectivity issue could be identified in the planning stage, since it is known that the aldehyde moiety is substantially hydrated in aqueous solution.", "by‑products 11 and 12 (see Scheme 4) were always competitively observed (70:30 9:(11+12)).", "Given the difficulty in purging any of these undesired by‑products from 9, it was concluded that this approach was not optimal.", "Route C was therefore selected for our initial preparation of 9.", "The approach was based on the use of 2‑oxapropanal oxime 9, as the primary building block… The reaction mixture appeared to gradually become triphasic owing to CO₂ evolution… which would cause reactor pressurization."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Route B (acetone nitrosylation) was deemed unsafe for batch scale‑up because acetone can generate explosive peroxides under oxidising conditions, making large‑scale batch processing prohibitive.
Solution_Description: Implemented the nitrosylation in continuous flow, generating nitrosyl chloride in‑situ from tert‑butyl nitrite + HCl, which removes the need to handle bulk oxidising acetone and tightly controls reagent addition.
Supporting_Evidence: ["significant safety hurdles inhibited the delivery of 9 via this route in batch mode.", "Under oxidizing conditions acetone can lead to the formation of explosive triperoxides…", "We could develop a continuous flow setup where tert‑butyl nitrite and catalytic quantities of HCl are combined, leading to the in situ formation of nitrosyl chloride.", "The reactor output was directed toward a Y‑piece where it was then combined with a concentrated aqueous ammonia solution to quench the reaction.", "The ideal temperature of the reactor being set at 10 °C."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: During batch trials of Route C, the reaction mixture became triphasic due to CO₂ evolution and solid precipitation, causing pressure build‑up and inconsistent operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switched to a continuous‑flow nitrosylation platform (PFA coil, interdigital mixers) that maintains a single liquid phase, efficiently removes CO₂ and avoids solid fouling, delivering stable operation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Reaction mixture appeared to gradually become triphasic owing to CO₂ evolution (which would cause reactor pressurization) and precipitation of various solids.", "We foresaw these issues to be potentially problematic for the translation into a flow process.", "We therefore re‑examined Route B and developed a continuous flow setup…", "The reactor output was directed toward a Y‑piece…", "The reactor coil (PFA, 1/16′, 2 mL volume) kept at 10 °C."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Intermediate 10 (O‑methyl oxime) is unstable under basic conditions; batch distillation resulted in thermally unstable residue and exothermic decomposition (≈1870 J g⁻¹), posing safety hazards and requiring multiple purification steps.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Performed the O‑methylation in continuous flow using neat dimethyl sulfate, high‑concentration NaOH/9 streams (4 M/4 M), interdigital mixers for efficient biphasic mixing, and chlorobenzene as the extraction solvent (safer than CH₂Cl₂). This avoided batch distillation, improved yield (≈72 % isolated) and eliminated the exothermic hazard.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Intermediate 10 is not stable under basic conditions.", "Batch distillation… residue … found to be thermally unstable.", "DSC analysis of intermediate 10 indicated … heat release was ca. 1870 J g⁻¹.", "Use of a diluted stream of dimethyl sulfate (up to 1.0 M) did not yield more than 7–10 %…, whereas neat dimethyl sulfate gave highest yield.", "Chlorobenzene was chosen as an extracting solvent as it is (a) easier and safer to handle on scale than CH₂Cl₂…", "Interdigital mixers… afforded improved reliability compared to simpler T‑piece mixing units."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Using a diluted dimethyl‑sulfate feed (≤1.0 M) in the O‑methylation step gave only 7–10 % conversion, attributed to poor mass transfer in the biphasic system.
Solution_Description: Switched to neat (undiluted) dimethyl sulfate as the methylating agent, increasing its concentration and thereby improving mass transfer and conversion to 10.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Use of a diluted stream of dimethyl sulfate (up to 1.0 M) did not yield more than 7–10% of the desired product 10.", "Increasing the concentration of the dimethyl sulfate feed significantly influenced the conversion to the desired product 10, with yield being highest when using neat dimethyl sulfate."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: Batch bromination of 10 to 7 suffered from poor selectivity (mono‑ vs dibromo), decreasing yields on scale (>200 g gave 25–35 % yield), generation of gaseous MeBr (safety issue), and apparent mass/heat‑transfer limitations.

Solution_Description: Developed a continuous‑flow bromination using syringe pumps to deliver precise stoichiometry of 10 and Br₂ in chlorobenzene, interdigital mixers for rapid mixing, reactor coil at 40 °C, and in‑line NMR monitoring; this gave 89 % yield with only 2 % dibrominated by‑product and eliminated MeBr evolution by immediate quench.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The bromination step… proved to be very difficult to control and poorly reproducible during initial scale‑up in batch mode.", "Selectivity in the bromination (mono‑ vs dibromination) was the main issue encountered.", "Methanol… introduced the undesired generation of gaseous MeBr as a byproduct.", "Yield decreased to 25–35% on >200 g scales, suspected to be related to mass and/or heat transfer issues.", "A 0.81 M solution of 10 … combined with a 0.81 M solution of Br₂ … heated at 40 °C, to provide 7 in 89% yield with just 2% of the dibrominated by‑product."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C

Supporting_Evidence: ["To refine our setup, we integrated a workup process to quench in‑line any remaining Br₂ and neutralize the acidity of the post‑reactor stream.", "The reaction output was merged with an aqueous feed containing a phosphate buffer (2 M) and sodium bisulfite (0.5 M)."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C

Supporting_Evidence: ["Intermediate 7 cannot be stored for long period of time.", "We observed gradual decomposition (color change and strength erosion on storage) of compound 7 over time, which led us to always use freshly generated material.", "We demonstrated that 7, generated on‑demand in a continuous manner, can be immediately elaborated into the targeted thiazoles. Such generation and consumption on demand greatly mitigates any decomposition of 7 over time."]

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C

Paper Title: A Convergent Continuous Multistep Process for the Preparation of C
Problem_Description: The multistep sequence required isolated intermediates (9, 10, 7) leading to variable inventories of unstable, hazardous compounds.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a fully telescoped continuous‑flow process linking steps 1–3 (and subsequently steps 4–5) without isolations, thereby keeping inventories of unstable intermediates low, improving robustness and safety.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We further exemplify the potential streamlining of the whole sequence and demonstrated that each step could be telescoped into an effective sequence.", "The setup … avoided any accumulation of unstable intermediates 10 and 7 and only used stable feedstocks.", "It avoided any accumulation of unstable intermediates 9, 11, and 7 at any given time during the process, so as to mitigate safety risks."]

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: The double‑conjugate addition of ethanolamine to divinyl‑sulfone is highly exothermic (ΔH = 33.9 kcal mol⁻¹) with an adiabatic temperature rise of ~79 °C, creating a serious thermal‑runaway hazard for batch operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow reactor (small‑diameter tubing, static mixer) was employed so that the large surface‑to‑volume ratio provides rapid heat removal, keeping reactor temperature near the set‑point and preventing uncontrolled temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: “the highly exothermic reaction … could be safely executed in an equal volume of water as the only solvent, despite an adiabatic temperature rise of 142 °C” (abstract); “process hazard evaluation … revealed an exothermic reaction … large adiabatic temperature rise of 79.2 °C” (Introduction); “continuous process … heat generated … could be readily dissipated due to the high surface area and heat transfer rate, minimizing the chance of an uncontrolled reaction” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: The batch protocol required a very slow addition of divinyl‑sulfone; as scale increased the surface‑to‑volume ratio fell, making the addition time impractically long for kilogram‑scale production.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to a continuous flow mode eliminated the need for a prolonged, time‑consuming addition step; reagents are metered by syringe/pumps and mixed instantly in a static mixer.
Supporting_Evidence: “While this batch process … could be controlled by slow addition of DVS, it did not appear amenable to large scale production due to excessively long addition times as the surface area to volume ratio decreased” (Introduction); “continuous process … where the heat generated … could be readily dissipated” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: During early experiments an unidentified side‑product (10–20 % of the mixture) persisted after the initial 1 min residence time, reducing immediate product yield.
Solution_Description: Increasing the residence‑time temperature (e.g., heating to 80 °C) or allowing the stream to age (12 h at 20 °C) fully converts the oligomeric intermediates to the desired thiomorpholine‑dioxide, restoring quantitative yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “an unidentified species was observed at a level of 10–20 % … this species completely converted to 1 within 12 h at 20 °C, or within 10 min at 80 °C” (Results and Discussion); “the oligomers … converted to product with extended aging or heating” (abstract).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: 4‑(2‑hydroxyethyl)‑thiomorpholine 1,1‑dioxide is extremely water‑soluble (>1250 mg mL⁻¹), making aqueous extraction inefficient and causing large product losses during work‑up.

Supporting_Evidence: “Isolation of 1 was complicated by its extremely high water solubility … leading us to study the impact of solvent, pH, and salt addition on an extractive workup” (Results and Discussion); “extraction with 3 × 11 vol DCM resulted in 29 %, 8 %, and 2 % of 1 remaining … EtOAc was much less efficient … pH of 10‑11 … addition of KCl … gave ∼10 % better recovery per extraction” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: The original batch process required a water‑distillation step (6 → 3 vol) before extraction, an energy‑intensive and time‑consuming operation that reduced overall process efficiency.
Solution_Description: By running the continuous reaction in only 3 volumes of water (rather than 6 vol) the downstream water‑distillation unit was eliminated; the flow reactor’s high heat‑transfer capacity safely handled the larger adiabatic temperature rise (142 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: “distillation of water from 6 to 3 volumes was an energy intensive and time‑consuming operation … A modification was investigated whereby the continuous process could be run in 3 volumes of water … while the estimated adiabatic temperature rise of 142 °C … would still be suitable for a continuous process” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: High exotherm combined with the toxic, hyper‑toxic nature of divinyl‑sulfone raised concerns of over‑pressurization, thermal degradation, and operator exposure during scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The plant‑scale flow system incorporated check‑valves, pressure‑relief valves, a back‑pressure regulator, automatic pump cutoff, and continuous IR monitoring to quickly detect and mitigate pressure spikes or runaway conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “continuous reactor was equipped (1) check valves … (2) ReactIR flow cell … (3) temperature and pressure monitors … (4) mechanical pressure relief valves … (5) a 30 psi automatic cutoff on the pumps … (6) a 5 psi back‑pressure regulator” (Results and Discussion); “Divinyl sulfone … classified as an acute toxin … hyper‑toxic …” (References).

Paper Title: Development of a Safe and High-Throughput Continuous Manufacturing Approach to 4‑(2-Hydroxy­ethyl)­thiomorpholine 1,1-Dioxide
Problem_Description: After extraction the product still needed to be isolated as a solid; direct crystallisation from DCM was inefficient and led to material loss.
Solution_Description: The organic phase was concentrated, the solvent exchanged to MTBE, a small seed of product (0.5 wt %) was added, and the mixture was cooled to –10 °C, giving a high‑yield (71 %) crystalline product.
Supporting_Evidence: “The DCM was exchanged for MTBE through distillation … seeded with 0.5 % 1 … cooled to –10 °C … gave 2.45 kg of 1 in 71 % yield” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane

Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to target the free‑base 2 as an isolated solid rather than the salt 2·2HCl. The free base performed better in metal‑catalyzed couplings and eliminated the impurity‑related poisoning.
Supporting_Evidence: “low and variable purity of 2·2HCl derived from this sequence impeded development of subsequent transition‑metal‑catalyzed C–N bond‑forming reactions… Indeed, several instances of catalyst poisoning were observed… It was also envisioned that an improved synthetic process would instead target the free base, 2, as an isolated solid, which was found to perform better in metal‑catalyzed couplings.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: The dihydrochloride salt 2·2HCl is highly water‑soluble but essentially insoluble in most organic solvents, which prevented recrystallisation and limited options for impurity removal.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was altered to isolate the free base 2 directly. A free‑basing protocol using K₃PO₄·H₂O in MeOH (or toluene with K₂CO₃) was developed, allowing the free base to be precipitated from methanol/dioxane mixtures without aqueous washes.
Supporting_Evidence: “the solubility profile of 2·2HCl provides limited options to upgrade its purity via recrystallization… we sought alternative non‑aqueous freebasing conditions… When K₂CO₃ in toluene was employed… free base 4 could be isolated… The optimized freebasing process was eventually performed on a 30 kg scale to provide the target … 2 in 91 % yield with 98 wt % purity.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: The commercially available building blocks 4 (N,N‑dimethylformamide azine) and 5 (tert‑butyl‑protected azabicycle) are only supplied on modest 1–10 kg scales, raising concerns about cost and supply for multi‑kilogram production.
Solution_Description: A scalable Kulinkovich–de Meijere cyclopropanation (route C) was adopted, enabling preparation of the precursors from inexpensive starting materials on >100 kg scale, thus mitigating cost and supply issues.
Supporting_Evidence: “Consideration toward long‑term cost and supply of 2 prompted evaluation of their preparation on a larger scale… we investigated route C as the expedient choice for short‑term production and future optimization.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: During the synthesis of DMFA 4, addition of SOCl₂ to a solution of 1,2‑diformylhydrazine generated a massive exotherm (~100 °C adiabatic temperature rise) and risk of unreacted SOCl₂ accumulation.

Supporting_Evidence: “addition of SOCl₂… generated an exotherm (a large adiabatic temperature rise of approximately 100 °C)… We therefore implemented an addition‑controlled protocol in which SOCl₂ was added … at 15–25 °C over 6 h before heating to 35–40 °C… reaction was safely conducted over ~14 h for production on a >200 kg scale (89 % yield).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: Liberating free‑base DMFA 4 from its dihydrochloride salt required extensive liquid–liquid extractions (e.g., 2‑day Et₂O continuous extraction) and led to low recovery, while residual base after NaOEt deprotection impeded the downstream transamination.

Supporting_Evidence: “When K₂CO₃ in toluene was employed at 60–90 °C… free base 4 could be isolated by filtering off inorganic solids and then concentrating the filtrate to dryness (85 % yield) … or telescoping the toluene solution into the transamination reaction.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: Direct transamination of 4·2HCl with 5 gave a messy reaction profile and low assay yield; use of HCl as catalyst was especially poor.
