Supporting_Evidence: “While 1 mol % HCl was effective… the reaction profile was observed to be cleaner overall and higher‑yielding with the originally reported p‑TsOH, the loading of which could be lowered to ca. 1–3 mol %… Slow addition of DMFA into the solution of 5 resulted in a slightly higher assay yield (entry 8).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: Free‑basing of 2·2HCl with K₂CO₃ in MeOH produced substantial amounts of carbamic acid 28 (50:50 2:28 ratio), contaminating the product.
Solution_Description: Switching to anhydrous K₃PO₄ (and later K₃PO₄·H₂O) as the base dramatically reduced carbamic acid formation (91:9 → 98:2 2:28 ratios). Degassing the reaction mixture further suppressed impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “significant amounts of carbamic acid 28 were also observed… Switching from K₂CO₃ to anhydrous K₃PO₄ and later the more air‑stable K₃PO₄·H₂O… successively decreased the observed amount of 28 to acceptable levels (entries 2 and 3).”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: During large‑scale filtration of the Boc‑deprotection step (formation of 2·2HCl) filtration was slow, compromising throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Incorporation of 1‑propanol as a cosolvent improved slurry fluidity, accelerating filtration and enabling efficient isolation of 2·2HCl on >75 kg scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “On a larger scale, slow filtration was observed, which was improved by incorporation of 1‑propanol as a cosolvent.”

Paper Title: Practical Synthesis of a 6‑Triazolylazabicyclo[3.1.0]hexane
Problem_Description: Isolation of triazole 6 required multiple aqueous citric‑acid washes and back‑extractions with EtOAc/CH₂Cl₂, leading to product loss and operational complexity.
Solution_Description: A solvent screen identified toluene as optimal: direct crystallisation from the reaction mixture at 60 °C (with seeding) removed excess DMFA without aqueous washes, delivering 6 in 61 % isolated yield and >95 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “A solvent screen for 6 indicated that toluene itself (entry 10) offered an appropriate range of solubility… a direct crystallization from the reaction mixture could be performed; 60 °C was subsequently identified as a robust seeding point… the moderate excess of DMFA (30 mol %) could be purged into the crystallization filtrate without the need for aqueous washes.”

Paper Title: Adsorbent-Based Downstream-Processing of the Decarboxylase-Based Synthesis of 2,6-Dihydroxy-4-methylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: The biocatalytic carboxylation suffered from low substrate loading (≤5 mmol L⁻¹) giving only ~80 % conversion and required removal of the large excess of bicarbonate (3 mol L⁻¹) by strong acidification followed by column chromatography, which lowered overall atom‑efficiency and added cost.
Solution_Description: An adsorbent‑based downstream‑processing route was introduced: the strong‑base anion‑exchange resin Dowex 1x2 (Cl) selectively adsorbs both product (DHMBA) and residual substrate from the bicarbonate‑rich reaction mixture, allowing direct product precipitation after a simple HCl/acetone elution without any column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: "major limitations are low substrate loading and the requirement to remove the entire excess bicarbonate via acidification during downstream‑processing, followed by column chromatography"; "The product DHMBA was herein purified by an adsorption–desorption cycle and subsequently obtained with purities >99% without a full elimination of the excess bicarbonate"; "The developed process concept herein enables the synthetic use of the biocatalytic carboxylation reaction without the full removal of excess bicarbonate during downstream‑processing"; "After a single filtration, pure DHMBA was yielded"; "Dowex 1x2 (Cl) was subsequently used throughout the study"

Paper Title: Adsorbent-Based Downstream-Processing of the Decarboxylase-Based Synthesis of 2,6-Dihydroxy-4-methylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration to 50 mmol L⁻¹ (desired for higher productivity) caused a drop in equilibrium conversion to ~60 % and at larger scale CO₂ loss during sampling further reduced conversion, leading to inconsistent yields.
Solution_Description: The biocatalyst loading was increased to 60 mg mL⁻¹ whole‑cell catalyst to drive the equilibrium at higher substrate levels, and the reaction was performed in a closed‑vessel batch reactor (1 L flask, 600 rpm) to retain CO₂ and provide reproducible conversions.
Supporting_Evidence: "higher substrate concentrations of 10 and 50 mmol L⁻¹ result in only 80 % and 68 % conversion"; "for 50 mmol L⁻¹ a significantly higher catalyst loading of 60 mg whole cell biocatalyst mL⁻¹ is required to reach equilibrium conversion"; "the reaction time course of the up‑scaled application differs ... causes multiple losses of gaseous carbon dioxide ... induces lower equilibrium conversions"; "a closed vessel reaction setup was preferred throughout this study"; "30 °C and a substrate concentration of 50 mmol L⁻¹ and 3 mol L⁻¹ KHCO₃ resulted in a conversion of 60 %"

Paper Title: Adsorbent-Based Downstream-Processing of the Decarboxylase-Based Synthesis of 2,6-Dihydroxy-4-methylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: Desorption of DHMBA from the loaded resin was incomplete when using low acetone content, giving only ≤50 % recovery of product and higher co‑elution of the substrate, which limited overall yield.
Solution_Description: An optimized elution mixture of 2 mol L⁻¹ HCl/acetone (20:80 v/v) was employed and applied in three consecutive 30‑min elution steps, achieving ≥90 % recovery of both product and substrate while minimizing orcinol leaching.
Supporting_Evidence: "By increasing the ratio of 2 mol L⁻¹ HCl from 10 % to 40 % (v/v) the initial desorption of DHMBA increases… to a maximum of 50 % … with a simultaneous reduction of orcinol elution…"; "a solvent mixture of 2 mol L⁻¹ HCl/acetone (20:80 v/v) was sufficient with at least three desorption steps to reach a recovery rate of ≥90 % for both reactants"; "Desorption of orcinol and DHMBA from loaded anion‑exchange resin Dowex 1x2 (Cl) at different mixtures of 2 mol L⁻¹ HCl/acetone at 30 °C after 30 min for each desorption step"; "The mixture was filtered off and the permeate evaporated… until white crystals appeared"

Paper Title: Adsorbent-Based Downstream-Processing of the Decarboxylase-Based Synthesis of 2,6-Dihydroxy-4-methylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: The presence of 3 mol L⁻¹ bicarbonate in the reaction solution required traditional acidification and chromatography to isolate DHMBA, which caused complete loss of the bicarbonate and reduced atom‑efficiency.
Solution_Description: The anion‑exchange resin Dowex 1x2 (Cl) shows >99 % affinity for DHMBA even at >3 mol L⁻¹ bicarbonate, allowing product capture without prior bicarbonate removal and preserving the carbonate for possible recycling.
Supporting_Evidence: "significant excess of 3 mol·L⁻¹ bicarbonate, which is required to push the reaction equilibrium… this excess is afterward removed via acidification, resulting in a full loss of bicarbonate and thus lowering the atom efficiency"; "Dowex 1x2 (Cl) … showed affinities >99 % even at bicarbonate concentrations of >3 mol·L⁻¹"; "The developed process concept… enables the synthetic use of the biocatalytic carboxylation reaction without the full removal of excess bicarbonate"; "After loading, the adsorbent including both reactants was removed from the reaction mixture to facilitate its separation from the remaining concentrated bicarbonate solution"

Paper Title: Adsorbent-Based Downstream-Processing of the Decarboxylase-Based Synthesis of 2,6-Dihydroxy-4-methylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: Screening of ten different adsorbents revealed many resins with low affinity (<50 % adsorption) for DHMBA or orcinol, making them unsuitable for efficient downstream recovery.
Solution_Description: Systematic adsorption screening identified Dowex 1x2 (Cl) as the best performer (≥99 % adsorption at 0.1 g mL⁻¹), which was then selected for all subsequent scale‑up experiments.
Supporting_Evidence: "Ten adsorbent resins were studied… the strong anion exchange resin Dowex 1x2 (Cl) in its chloride form showed affinities >99 %"; "Table 1 shows adsorption of DHMBA and orcinol onto 10 different adsorbers… Dowex 1x2 (Cl) requires only 0.1 g adsorber per mL reaction solution to fully remove both main reactants"; "The highest adsorption affinity toward orcinol and DHMBA was found for Dowex 1x2 (Cl)"; "Thus, Dowex 1x2 (Cl) was subsequently used throughout the study"

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Process for Preparation of N,O-Chelated Diarylborinates
Problem_Description: The one‑pot preparation of the diarylborinic acid using B(OiPr)3 gave a crude mixture contaminated with p‑tolylboronic acid, resulting in only 31 % overall isolated yield of the target N,O‑chelated diarylborinate.
Solution_Description: The boron source was changed to less‑sterically demanding trimethylborate (B(OMe)3) and finally to tributylborate B(OBu)3, which completely suppressed formation of the aryl‑boronic acid impurity and restored high conversion (≈93 %).
Supporting_Evidence: "Direct treatment of the crude di‑(p‑tolyl)‑borinic acid prepared by a one‑pot reaction … gave di‑(p‑tolyl)‑boron picolinate (1) in 31 % overall yield, significantly lower than that (93 %) by reaction of authentic di‑(p‑tolyl)‑borinic acid…"; "A ¹¹B spectrum indicated that the crude bis‑(p‑tolyl)‑borinic acid was contaminated by p‑tolylboronic acid…"; "The formation of p‑tolylboronic acid could be completely suppressed when tributylborate B(OBu)₃ was used as the boron source, leading to excellent selectivity for bis‑(p‑tolyl)‑borinic acid."

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Process for Preparation of N,O-Chelated Diarylborinates
Problem_Description: Commercial B(OMe)₃ contains trace MeOH; the methanol destroys the in‑situ generated p‑tolylmagnesium species, decreasing both selectivity and yield of the diarylborinic acid.
Solution_Description: Tributylborate B(OBu)₃, which does not contain MeOH, was employed as the boron source; this eliminated the deleterious effect of water and restored high product yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "The presence of MeOH in the reaction mixture was found be deleterious to the yield and the selectivity of bis‑(p‑tolyl)‑borinic acid through destroying the in situ generated p‑tolyl magnesium species."; "The formation of p‑tolylboronic acid could be completely suppressed when tributylborate B(OBu)₃ was used as the boron source…"

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Process for Preparation of N,O-Chelated Diarylborinates
Problem_Description: Acidifying the reaction mixture to pH 1‑2 to liberate the diarylborinic acid generated large amounts of solid material and required excessive dilute HCl, creating an acidic slurry that had to be neutralized before adding the N,O‑chelate ligands.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Instead of acid work‑up, the crude one‑pot mixture was treated with water, precipitating magnesium salts as Mg(OH)₂ under non‑acidic conditions; the precipitate was removed by filtration, and the N,O‑chelate ligands were added directly to the clear diarylborinate solution, giving the target product in 75 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "To release free diarylborinic acids, the reaction mixture … had to be acidified to pH = 1–2. This procedure not only generated and redissolved copious solid intermediates consuming a large amount of dilute 1 M HCl‑(aq.) but also led to the presence of excess acid, which had to be removed before being subjected to N,O‑chelate ligands."; "Accidentally, it was found that magnesium salts (MgX₂ and/or Mg(OR)X) in the reaction mixture could be removed as precipitate Mg(OH)₂ under non‑acidic conditions. Hence, the one‑pot reaction mixture was treated with water instead of 1 M HCl‑(aq.) to precipitate magnesium salts. After filtration, equivalent 2‑picolinic acid was then added … to give … 75 % yield."

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Process for Preparation of N,O-Chelated Diarylborinates
Problem_Description: Residual magnesium salts remaining in the reaction mixture hindered isolation of the N,O‑chelated diarylborinate, making purification difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The magnesium salts were precipitated as insoluble Mg(OH)₂ by adding water, then removed by filtration (or centrifugation) prior to ligand addition, delivering a clean diarylborinate solution ready for crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Accidentally, it was found that magnesium salts (MgX₂ and/or Mg(OR)X) in the reaction mixture could be removed as precipitate Mg(OH)₂ under non‑acidic conditions. Hence, the one‑pot reaction mixture was treated with water instead of 1 M HCl‑(aq.) to precipitate magnesium salts. After filtration, equivalent 2‑picolinic acid was then added …"

Paper Title: Development of a Telescoped Process for Preparation of N,O-Chelated Diarylborinates
Problem_Description: When 4‑bromobenzonitrile or 4‑bromoacetophenone were used, no N,O‑chelated diarylborinate could be obtained, likely because the –CN or –COCH₃ groups are incompatible with the in‑situ generated aryl‑magnesium species.
Solution_Description: The authors noted this limitation; no specific remedy was presented in the article, indicating a need for alternative conditions or protecting‑group strategies for such functional groups.
Supporting_Evidence: "However, when 4‑bromobenzonitrile or 4‑bromoacetophone was used as the original aryl source, no N,O‑chelated four‑coordinate diarylborinate could be obtained, possibly due to the incompatibility of the CN and Ac groups with the in situ generated aryl magnesium species."

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Peracetic acid is a highly reactive peroxide that degrades at room temperature (1‑2 %/24 h) and is listed with severe health and reactivity hazards (HMIS: Health 3, Flammability 2, Reactivity 4). Its instability and exothermic decomposition create serious safety and handling issues for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors generated peracetic acid in situ continuously using an ion‑exchange (Amberlite IR‑120) packed‑bed reactor (PFA tube‑in‑tube). This avoids storage of the unstable peroxide, limits decomposition, and provides a safe, on‑demand source of the oxidant.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Peracetic acid is a commercially available and relatively inexpensive peracid. However, a solution of this reagent represents an equilibrium mixture…peracid is relatively unstable and degrades at room temperature (via reversible reaction to give hydrogen peroxide and acetic acid) at a rate of ∼1–2 % over 24 h.',
'The poor safety and stability of this reagent not only create additional challenges for storage and handling but also affect the quality and reliability of the oxidation process.',
'Using 10–20 mass % of the resin at 50 °C, we could generate a 15 mass % solution in a 3 h period…consistently generated peracetic acid with maximal equilibrium concentration and without any sign of activity deterioration.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: The oxidation of oximes to nitroalkanes is strongly exothermic (heat of reaction –112.8 J g⁻¹, adiabatic temperature rise ≈ 99 °C) and poses a medium‑risk thermal hazard in batch or semibatch operation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous pipes‑in‑series PFA reactor provides efficient heat removal, controlled temperature (95 °C) and rapid mixing, mitigating the exotherm and preventing runaway.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The heat of the reaction was determined to be −112.8 J g⁻¹ for the reaction mass, and the adiabatic temperature rise was calculated to be +99 °C.',
'The newly developed continuous platform not only delivered appropriate solutions to all of these questions…',
'We designed a uniquely constructed pipes‑in‑series plug‑flow tube reactor…which addresses a range of process challenges, including stability and safe handling of peroxides and nitroalkanes.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Peracetic acid reacts with metal reactor surfaces, generating gas pockets and leading to poor conversion and variable product distribution (benzoic acid formation).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching from stainless‑steel PFR to a non‑metallic PFA pipes‑in‑series reactor eliminates metal incompatibility; a nitrogen carrier gas removes evolved gases and stabilizes the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Gas pockets were observed at the outlet of the reactor, highlighting the incompatibility of the peroxide reagent with the metal surface of the reactor.',
'Substituting the metal PFR with a PFA PFR resulted in a slightly improved result, with nitroalkane and benzoic acid representing the major products of the process.',
'The major role of the carrier gas in this application is to remove oxygen and other gaseous products from the reaction mixture.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Initial continuous runs in simple PFRs (3–30 min residence) gave very low nitroalkane formation (≤ 11 % yield) due to insufficient residence time and poor peroxide distribution.
Solution_Description: The peracetic acid feed was split into multiple streams (2‑, 4‑, or 6‑portion dosing) across the series of pipes, increasing effective residence time and improving conversion to 69‑85 % nitroalkane yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
['very little nitroalkane was formed under these conditions (Table 2, entries 1–3).',
'By dividing the peracetic acid feed into two equal streams and then into four equal streams introduced between the pipes. The yield of nitroalkane improved to 80 %…',
'Feeding 60 % up front and 13.3 % after the fourth, eighth, and 12th pipes was the most successful distribution… giving maximum product (82–85 %) and minimal amounts of starting material and benzoic acid.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Isolating low‑molecular‑weight nitroalkanes on scale is hazardous because of their explosive nature and the need for large handling volumes.
Solution_Description: A continuous three‑stage liquid‑liquid extraction (toluene/water/NaOH) provided a purified nitroalkane solution that was fed directly into the aza‑Henry reaction without isolation, eliminating the risky intermediate handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The subsequent continuous extraction generates a solution of purified nitroalkane, which can be directly used in the following aza‑Henry chemistry… thus completely avoiding isolation of the potentially unsafe low‑molecular‑weight nitroalkane intermediate.',
'The toluene solution of the nitroalkane could be directly used in the subsequent aza‑Henry chemistry… without further manipulation or addition of an isolation procedure.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Traditional nitroalkane syntheses rely on expensive peracids such as MCPBA, which are unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Peracetic acid (low‑cost, readily available) was selected as the oxidant; its in‑situ generation via a cheap ion‑exchange resin further reduces reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Most recently developed alternatives…remain impractical from safety and economic standpoints.',
'Among alternative oxidants considered, a solution of peracetic acid offers the benefits of low molecular weight, low cost, and ease of removal from the product stream…',
'Using 10–20 mass % of the resin… produced peracetic acid…without any sign of activity deterioration.']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Electron‑poor oximes required longer reaction times and higher peroxide equivalents to reach acceptable conversion, leading to prolonged batch times and reduced throughput.
Solution_Description: For electron‑withdrawing substrates the authors increased the peracetic acid equivalents (up to 2 equiv) and adjusted the temperature (90‑95 °C) to accelerate the oxidation while maintaining selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Reactions of aromatic oximes with electron‑withdrawing substituents…the kinetics of the reaction were slower, and conditions with an additional 2 equiv of peracetic acid were therefore utilized.',
'The oxidation of ketoximes is notable, as these are known to be recalcitrant substrates.',
'Further optimization of the reaction conditions for each substrate could be beneficial to achieve optimal yield…']

Paper Title: Continuous Platform To Generate Nitroalkanes On-Demand (in Situ) Using Peracetic Acid-Mediated Oxidation in a PFA Pipes-in-Series Reactor
Problem_Description: Gas evolution from peroxide decomposition created a two‑phase mixture that trapped gases, causing pressure spikes and safety concerns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The pipes‑in‑series design incorporated a nitrogen carrier that continuously sweeps out gases, while the PFA construction prevents gas entrapment, ensuring safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The major role of the carrier gas in this application is to remove oxygen and other gaseous products from the reaction mixture.',
'Gas pockets were observed at the outlet of the reactor, highlighting the incompatibility of the peroxide reagent with the metal surface of the reactor.',
'Using a neutral gas carrier (nitrogen) enables mixing inside the pipes and carries small liquid slugs through the jumpers into the next pipe while providing effective gas/liquid mixing.']

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: When the target boronic acid 3a was prepared in batch by a bromine‑lithium exchange, a major side reaction (butylation, 5a) and protonation of the organolithium by THF (4a) occurred, giving low isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The authors moved the lithiation–borylation sequence into a continuous‑flow platform, allowing precise control of the residence time (≈4 s) and temperature (0 °C). This suppressed both protonation and butylation, dramatically improving the yield of 3a.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When <bold>3a</bold> was synthesized in batch, a side reaction was found to be unavoidable … with butylation being a major issue even when the reaction was carried out at −25 °C.”
 • “The side reactions in the lithiation step that occur in batch were suppressed, and unstable lithium intermediates were handled safely.”
 • “The flow synthesis of boronic acid <bold>3a</bold> was achieved in good yield through minimization of the major side reactions.”
 • “When less than 1 s was allowed for lithiation, not all of the raw materials were converted… as the residence time was increased, more raw material was consumed… the side reaction (butylation, <bold>5a</bold>) increased as the residence time increased.”
 • “The conditions … entry 3 were used as the optimized conditions for the halogen–lithium exchange reaction at 0 °C…”

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: In batch, avoiding the side reactions required cryogenic temperatures and long residence times, leading to inconsistent conversion and impractical processing for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Flow chemistry provided rapid mixing and short, well‑defined residence times, eliminating the need for cryogenic conditions and delivering consistent conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In order to partially suppress the side reaction in batch, cryogenic conditions were required, and thus, a flow reaction was investigated to develop milder conditions.”
 • “The initial experiments … residence times of 0.24–31.42 s… when less than 1 s was allowed for lithiation, not all of the raw materials were converted.”
 • “When the residence time was increased, more raw material was consumed … the side reaction increased as the residence time increased.”
 • “The flow synthesis … was achieved in good yield through minimization of the major side reactions.”
 • “The flow chemistry process for <bold>3a</bold> was successfully developed at lab scale.”

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: Scaling up the lithiation‑borylation sequence increased the concentration and flow rates, reducing the reactor’s ability to dissipate heat and raising safety concerns about uncontrolled exotherms.
Solution_Description: During kilogram‑scale production the reaction temperature was lowered to –15 °C while the concentration of the feedstocks and the flow rates were increased. The stainless‑steel tubing and cooling bath ensured adequate heat removal and safe operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In order to improve the productivity, the concentrations of raw materials and the flow rates were increased … because of concern about the reduced capacity for thermal exchange, the reaction temperature was lowered to −15 °C.”
 • “Scaled‑up production of boronic acids <bold>3a</bold> and <bold>3b</bold> was conducted … 0 °C … the product showed good quality and did not include side products <bold>4a</bold> and <bold>5a</bold>.”
 • “The reactors were fabricated from SS tubing … the reactors for both the lithiation and borylation steps were submerged in a cooling bath set at 0 °C.”
 • “The residence time for the lithiation step was set to 5 s … the temperature in the plug flow reactors was monitored and maintained at approximately 0 °C.”
 • “As a result, 0.76 kg of <bold>3a</bold> was manufactured in good yield with an operation time of 2 h 25 min for the flow mode.”

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: Large‑scale use of n‑BuLi (1.6 M in hexane) and high equivalents of reagents raised concerns about reagent cost and procurement for kilogram‑scale runs.
Solution_Description: The authors optimized the equivalents of n‑BuLi (≈1.07 eq for simple aryl bromides, >2 eq when a Boc‑protected nitrogen was present) and adjusted the concentration of the borate solution to the minimum needed for efficient conversion, reducing reagent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The initial experiments … were conducted with 1.07 equiv of n‑BuLi … When less than 1 s was allowed for lithiation, not all of the raw materials were converted … about 1.07 equiv of n‑BuLi was sufficient for the bromine–lithium exchange reaction.”
 • “When the bromine–lithium exchange reaction was conducted on aryl bromides that included heteroaromatic rings, the optimized residence time was 0.25 s, even though more than 2 equiv of n‑BuLi was required … 1 equiv of n‑BuLi was consumed to remove the proton on the Boc‑protected nitrogen.”
 • “Feedstock B was commercially available 1.6 M n‑BuLi in hexane used directly from the supplied bottle … concentrations of raw materials and the flow rates were increased … 0.75 M solution of aryl bromide, 0.55 M B(OiPr)3.”
 • “All of the chemicals were purchased … used without further purification.”
 • “The concentration of the borate solution was varied (1.8 M, 1.0 M, 0.55 M, etc.) to find the optimal loading.”

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: After flow synthesis, the crude mixture contained trace amounts of side‑products (4a, 5a) that needed to be removed before isolation of the boronic acid.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The product stream was quenched with aqueous HCl and extracted into toluene (or ethyl acetate for 3b). The organic layer was washed, concentrated, and the product precipitated with n‑heptane under cooling, giving high‑purity crystalline boronic acids.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The collected product stream from the FC process was quenched with 1 M aqueous HCl … to allow for efficient liquid–liquid extraction, as compound <bold>3a</bold> was found to stay in the organic phase.”
 • “The organic layer was then further washed with water … and then concentrated.”
 • “The resulting residue was dissolved in toluene, precipitated with n‑heptane, and agitated in an ice bath. The resulting slurry was filtered … to afford <bold>3a</bold> as a white crystalline powder in 79 % yield (0.76 kg) with 97.4 % purity.”
 • “For <bold>3b</bold> the quench used 2 M aqueous HCl and ethyl acetate … precipitated with n‑heptane … 84 % yield (1.55 kg) with 97.0 % purity.”
 • “The obtained product showed good quality and did not include side products <bold>4a</bold> and <bold>5a</bold>.”

Paper Title: Effective Utilization of Flow Chemistry: Use of Unstable Intermediates, Inhibition of Side Reactions, and Scale-Up for Boronic Acid Synthesis
Problem_Description: Aryl bromide, n‑BuLi and the borate reagent needed rapid and homogeneous mixing; insufficient mixing could cause incomplete lithiation or local over‑reaction.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The flow set‑up employed wedged tee mixers (0.50 mm and 1.0 mm i.d.) and narrow‑bore stainless‑steel tubing to ensure efficient micromixing; the short residence times prevented concentration gradients.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A Shimadzu‑GLC tee piece (0.50 mm i.d.) was used as a mixer for feedstocks A and B, and a Shimadzu‑GLC tee piece (1.0 mm i.d., custom‑made) was used as a mixer for feedstock C and the resulting solution after lithiation.”
 • “The reactors were fabricated from stainless‑steel (SS) tubing with an internal diameter (i.d.) of 1 mm and an appropriate length defined by the desired residence time (τ) and flow rates.”
 • “To ensure that the reactants were sufficiently cooled before mixing, precooling loops (L = 50 cm, i.d. = 1.0 mm) were used, and the reactors for both the lithiation and borylation steps were submerged in a cooling bath set at 0 °C before the three pumps were initiated.”
 • “Three diaphragm pumps (TACMINA, TPL1M) were used to pump the solutions … reactors … i.d. of 2.17 mm … the precooling loops (L = 1 m, i.d. = 2.17 mm) and reactors for both the lithiation and borylation steps were submerged in a cooling bath set at 0 °C.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Scale-Up Synthesis to a Potent GluN2B Inhibitor and Its Prodrug
Problem_Description: The first‑generation alkylation of racemic bromolactam (±)-7 gave only a 49 % isolated yield and required a late‑stage chiral SFC step that discarded ~50 % of material as the undesired isomer.
Solution_Description: A chiral route was developed starting from enantiopure (S)-3‑hydroxypyrrolidin‑2‑one (18) to give the mesylate 22 in >99 % ee and high isolated yield, eliminating the need for the racemic bromolactam and the two SFC purifications.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The synthesis of chiral mesylate 22 in four high‑yielding steps…circumvented the need for SFC purification, and we were pleased to find that the chiral integrity of 22 (>99 % ee) remained intact upon storage.”
“Attempts to separate the enantiomers were successful using preparative chiral supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC); however, each enantiomer quickly racemized back to (±)-7…thus necessitating the use of the racemic material…with 50 % of the material discarded as the undesired isomer in each of these steps.”

Paper Title: Evolution of a Scale-Up Synthesis to a Potent GluN2B Inhibitor and Its Prodrug
Problem_Description: Late‑stage fluorination of the fully elaborated molecule with DAST proceeded in low yield (34 %) and gave a complex mixture due to side‑reactions and potential degradation of the substrate.
Solution_Description: Fluorination was moved to an earlier stage and the reagent was changed to bis‑(2‑methoxyethyl)‑aminosulfur trifluoride (Deoxo‑Fluor). Optimized temperature (‑78 °C → 0 °C) and stoichiometry (1.5 eq) gave a 75 % isolated yield of the desired product 24 with minimal by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“We were able to demonstrate the synthesis of chiral mesylate 22 in four high‑yielding steps…
“DAST gave only 34 % yield…

Paper Title: Decoration of an α‑Resorcylate Nucleus as Part of the Manufacture of a Glucokinase Activator
Problem_Description: Alkylation of methyl α‑resorcylate with tosylate 20 suffered from poor conversion and low selectivity, giving mixtures of mono‑ and bis‑alkylated products.

Supporting_Evidence: “Alkylations with tosylate 20 … suffered from poor conversions or selectivity (monoalkylation vs bisalkylation).”; “The use of cesium carbonate … the dosed addition of a slight subcess (0.97 mol equiv) of chloropyrazine 3 … led to a useful level of selectivity for ether 23 versus bisether 22.”

Supporting_Evidence: “These efforts were soon found to be complicated by the ability of the newly installed pyrazine of ether 23 to intermolecularly migrate… leading to regeneration of a quantity of bisether 22.”; “Prestirring the methyl α‑resorcylate … prior to the addition of the electrophile, led to useful selectivities… After some optimization which included switching to the use of cesium carbonate as the base, the dosed addition … gave a useful level of selectivity.”

Paper Title: Decoration of an α‑Resorcylate Nucleus as Part of the Manufacture of a Glucokinase Activator

Paper Title: Decoration of an α‑Resorcylate Nucleus as Part of the Manufacture of a Glucokinase Activator
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the monobenzoylation, batches showed up to 20 % LCAP of bis‑benzoylated product due to poor correlation between pH probe reading and local reaction pH.

Paper Title: Decoration of an α‑Resorcylate Nucleus as Part of the Manufacture of a Glucokinase Activator
Problem_Description: Ester 27 isolated from the monobenzoylation step contained ∼0.5 % wt water, which impeded its consumption in the subsequent Mitsunobu reaction.

Supporting_Evidence: “Activating acid 12 as an acid chloride generated hydrogen chloride which, without scavenging, was found to open the azetidine ring … The pyridine additive (3 equiv) … could simultaneously be used to scavenge the hydrogen chloride generated as a by‑product.”

Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction conversion was found to be adversely affected when particularly dry acetonitrile (20 ppm) was used… water had a role in hydrolysing the excess thionyl chloride … preventing the excess reagent from transforming aminopyrazine 4 into an N‑sulfinyl imine 39.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: The direct nitration route to IS‑5‑MN generates a large amount of undesired nitrated impurities (~40 %) and acetylated impurities (~3 %), leading to low overall selectivity and the need for additional purification steps.
Solution_Description: A work‑up based on solubility differences was implemented: after neutralisation the water‑insoluble ISDN is filtered, the filtrate is neutralised with acetic acid to precipitate NaOAc·3H₂O, and the target IS‑5‑MN is finally obtained by acidification and crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the inevitable side products including nitrated impurities (∼40 %) and a small amount of acetylated impurities (total, ∼3 %) are generated during the direct nitration process”; “the current workup was designed according to the different solubilities of the compounds…After the reaction mixture is neutralized, the water‑insoluble component ISDN is removed by filtration…an aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide is then added…to form sodium IS‑5‑MN hydrate…Subsequently, the target compound can be obtained by an acidification process.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Hydrolysis of IS‑2‑MN in the wastewater is extremely slow at low temperatures (0 °C and 20 °C), requiring days of reaction time and giving poor conversion.
Solution_Description: The hydrolysis temperature was raised to 50 °C, providing complete conversion within 8 h while keeping impurity formation acceptable.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction rate was too slow at low temperature (0 and 20 °C), where the transformation could hardly be achieved (entries 1 and 2)”; “Although higher temperatures could promote the process…a milder temperature of 50 °C was employed for the hydrolysis of IS‑2‑MN.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Higher hydrolysis temperatures (65–80 °C) accelerate the reaction but generate additional undesired impurities, reducing product purity and overall yield.
Solution_Description: A compromise temperature of 50 °C was selected to balance conversion rate and impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although higher temperatures could promote the process (entries 4 and 5), a series of impurities were generated. Therefore, a milder temperature of 50 °C was employed for the hydrolysis of IS‑2‑MN.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Recovering sodium acetate trihydrate from the wastewater is limited by its solubility in the chosen solvent system, affecting crystallisation yield.
Solution_Description: Crystallisation was performed with 95 % EtOH; lower temperatures (25 °C) and minimal solvent volume gave the highest recovery (86 % yield, 58.6 % NaOAc content).
Supporting_Evidence: “crystallization of NaOAc was examined according to its different solubility in 95 % EtOH…The results showed that the recovery rate was higher at lower crystallization temperature, but room temperature (25 °C) was a better choice…Increasing the amount of solvent used resulted in a decline in the recovery rate.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: After NaOAc removal, isosorbide (IS) remains in the aqueous phase and must be isolated in high purity for reuse.
Solution_Description: IS is recovered by vacuum distillation (140–160 °C, 10–18 mm Hg) yielding a 55 % recovery of high‑purity IS.
Supporting_Evidence: “Finally, high‑purity IS was recovered by vacuum distillation (140–160 °C, 10–18 mmHg), affording a recovery rate of 55 % of IS which could be used directly as the starting material.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Direct crystallisation of ISDN from solid waste using water gives excellent yield (93.4 %) but insufficient purity (91.5 %).
Solution_Description: Methanol was selected as the crystallisation solvent, delivering an acceptable compromise of 85.9 % yield with 99.0 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that water could give an excellent yield, but the purity did not meet our requirement (entry 1)…Acetone and EtOH gave considerable purity…however, because of their poor yield, methanol was chosen as the optimal solvent for high yield and purity.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Initial catalytic hydrogenation of ISDN with Pd/C gave a low IS‑5‑MN yield (<40 %) and a poor IS‑5‑MN/IS‑2‑MN ratio (2.5:1).
Solution_Description: Passivated Pd/C and Lindlar‑type catalysts (Pd/BaSO₄, Pd/CaCO₃) were screened; Pd/CaCO₃ gave the best performance (≈58 % isolated yield, IS‑5‑MN/IS‑2‑MN ≈ 14:1).
Supporting_Evidence: “considerable quantities of IS‑2‑MN and IS were generated during our initial attempts using Pd/C…the yield of IS‑5‑MN was less than 40 %…significant increases…when passivated catalyst was used…Lindlar catalysts such as Pd/BaSO₄ and Pd/CaCO₃ gave considerable selectivity…Pd/CaCO₃ was determined to be the optimal choice.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: During catalyst recycling, the reaction mixture became acidic (pH 5–6) and nitrite accumulated, corroding CaCO₃ and causing Pd leaching up to 15 %.
Solution_Description: Four bases were screened; the weak base NaHCO₃ effectively neutralised the acidity, suppressing Pd leaching while preserving IS‑5‑MN yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the solution was acidic (pH 5–6) and NO₂⁻ was accumulated…the weak acidic environment corroded calcium carbonate, leading to the Pd leaking…four commonly‑used bases were tested…considerable improvements were observed…the weak base NaHCO₃ was the optimal choice.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Use of a strong base (NaOH) in the hydrogenation work‑up hydrolysed IS‑5‑MN, reducing the isolated product yield.
Solution_Description: The weak base NaHCO₃ was employed instead of NaOH, preventing IS‑5‑MN hydrolysis while still neutralising the acidic medium.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, strong base (e.g., NaOH) would mediate the hydrolysis of IS‑5‑MN, affording a lower yield…Therefore, the weak base NaHCO₃ was the optimal choice.”

Paper Title: An Improved Process for Industrial Production of Isosorbide-5-mononitrate: Recycling of Wastes
Problem_Description: Full recovery of ISDN from solid waste would create an oversupply relative to market demand, while the alternative route (hydrogenation to IS‑5‑MN) consumes more reagents and energy.
Solution_Description: A hybrid strategy was proposed: partially recover ISDN by crystallisation and partially convert the remainder to IS‑5‑MN, balancing product supply with economic and environmental considerations.
Supporting_Evidence: “the recovered ISDN would face the problem of oversupply…the overall consumption of reagents and energy was higher than the first one…the optimal process may incorporate both routes, where some solid waste is treated to provide the market‑required amount of ISDN and the rest is treated by the second process.”

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: The coupling of the fifth amino‑acid (fourth Arg from the C‑terminus, cycle 5) proceeded more slowly than the other coupling cycles, giving sub‑optimal conversion and requiring long reaction times to reach acceptable yields.

Solution_Description: Vigorous agitation was employed to improve mass‑transfer into the resin beads, and the originally used reagent charges (1.5 eq Arg‑OH, 2.3 eq Oxyma, 2 eq DIC with an extra 1 eq DIC after 30 min) were retained as optimal. 【"The conversion of resin‑bound free‑amine peptide to product peptide at different time points… after 4 h the conversion was 99.2 %… after 18 h the reaction was complete."】
【"Additional experimental results demonstrated that vigorous agitation is needed to generate a high enough coupling rate to have the coupling reaction completed in an overnight run."】
【"The original reagent charges used in the manufacturing process seemed optimal… 1.5 eq Arg‑OH, 2.3 eq Oxyma, and 2.0 eq DIC followed by an additional 1.0 eq DIC after 30 min."】

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: The activated Arg‑Oxyma intermediate can undergo intramolecular cyclisation to give a δ‑lactam side‑product, consuming reagent and lowering the amount of material available for the desired peptide coupling.
Solution_Description: Portion‑wise addition of DIC (or Arg‑OH) was investigated to keep the concentration of Arg‑Oxyma low, thereby suppressing lactam formation; however, this also slowed product formation, leading to the decision to retain the original stoichiometry and addition schedule as the optimal balance.
Supporting_Evidence:
【"The carboxy‑activated arginine amino acid intermediate is known to form δ‑lactam by‑products… The kinetics of this competing side reaction had to be understood in order to improve the efficiency of the overall coupling process."】

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: Colour‑test (Kaiser/TNBS) interpretation is highly subjective, leading to inconsistent assessment of reaction completion and impurity levels across batches.
Solution_Description: A quantitative solution‑phase ^1H‑NMR assay was developed (using a cryoprobe and DMSO‑d6) to directly measure the ratio of reactant‑ and product‑peptide peaks, providing an objective correlation with the colour‑test results.
Supporting_Evidence:
【"The Kaiser and TNBS colour‑tests are useful and are standard practice, but interpretation of their results is often highly subjective because of the nature of visual inspection… Both approaches add cost and processing time to the manufacturing process."】
【"By using the solution NMR technique and the ‘cleave and analyse’ approach, we have modeled the kinetics… NMR assay for determination of the reaction conversion in solid‑phase peptide synthesis (SPPS) can be developed by comparing the peaks…"】
【"The NMR assay was correlated to the colour‑test results; the Kaiser test turned from dark‑blue to colourless as conversion approached 99.4 % and the TNBS orange colour disappeared accordingly."】

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: On‑bead HR‑MAS NMR gave broad resin peaks and no identifiable peptide signals, hindering direct monitoring of the resin‑bound species.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to solution‑phase NMR of the supernatant (using DMF‑d7/DMSO‑d6 as solvents) and performed a ‘cleave‑and‑analyse’ micro‑cleavage to obtain clear peptide spectra; this telescoped the analysis directly from the reaction mixture without needing isolated solid‑phase spectra.
Supporting_Evidence:
【"On‑bead analysis can be performed… HR‑MAS NMR… however the results still depend on the characteristics of the solid support and solvent used; the spectra showed signals from the resin, but no peptide signals could be identified…"】
【"Therefore, in this study we employed solution NMR spectroscopy to monitor the arginine species present in the supernatant and the traditional ‘cleave and analyse’ approach to observe the peptide buildup on the resin at different time points."】
【"Solution NMR spectroscopy offers high specificity, quantitation and can be performed with cryoprobes to increase sensitivity (compared with HR‑MAS probes)."】

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: Variation in resin quality produced occasional small amine, amide or aromatic impurity peaks in the NMR spectra, requiring additional purification steps (capping) to meet in‑process control criteria.

Supporting_Evidence:
【"In another set of data, the spectra of some cycles showed small amine, amide, or aromatic peaks… additional purification efforts were needed… indicating that the resin quality could vary and affect the impurity profiles."】
【"These cycles of peptides that had amine‑related impurities were also subjected to the capping procedure on the basis of positive colour‑test results… the acetylation procedure should generate peptides that have the N‑terminal acetyl methyl peak at around 1.867 ppm…"】

Paper Title: Studies of Coupling Kinetics and Correlation of Reaction Conversions to Color Tests for Solid-Phase Peptide Synthesis of AMG 416 by NMR
Problem_Description: Achieving >99.9 % conversion for all coupling cycles required up to 18 h reaction time, which could limit manufacturing throughput.
Solution_Description: Using the kinetic model and NMR data, an in‑process‑testing (IPT) time limit of 18 h was defined for full‑scale production, while noting that >99.2 % conversion could be reliably attained after 4 h, allowing flexibility in scheduling.
Supporting_Evidence:
【"The data showed that after 18 h of reaction, the conversion for all cycles achieved >99.9 %, demonstrating the robustness of the SPPS process…"】
