Paper Title: Development of Kilogram-Scale Synthesis of EGFR Inhibitor EAI045
Problem_Description: Multiple bottlenecks were encountered during scale‑up: (a) the original two‑step sequence gave only ~12 % overall yield, (b) the use of trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) is highly toxic, (c) almost every step required silica‑gel column chromatography, (d) the key building block isoindolin‑1‑one is not commercially available in bulk, (e) the three‑component coupling initially afforded <20 % isolated yield, (f) raising the temperature to 60 °C caused a drop in yield (51 %) suggesting a heat‑sensitive step, and (g) the BopCl‑mediated amide formation gave modest yield (52 %) and required expensive reagents, while the work‑up/purification steps caused variable losses (overall step yields 51‑67 %).
Solution_Description: To overcome these issues the authors (i) devised a convergent three‑component coupling route that bypasses the toxic TMSCN step, (ii) eliminated the need for TMSCN altogether, (iii) telescoped the three‑component reaction and streamlined work‑up to avoid repeated chromatography, (iv) prepared kilogram quantities of isoindolin‑1‑one by a carbonyl‑monoreduction of phthalimide, (v) changed the reaction medium to pure acetic acid and added catalytic H₂SO₄ to dramatically improve conversion (up to 62 % isolated yield), (vi) lowered the temperature to 25 °C for the acid‑promoted coupling to prevent the yield loss observed at 60 °C, (vii) replaced the BopCl/DIPEA system with a cheaper DIC/HOBt/DIPEA protocol, and (viii) introduced a recrystallization‑based purification sequence that removed the need for silica‑gel chromatography and reduced material loss.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Although the above‑mentioned synthetic route is amenable for a small‑scale preparation of EAI045, there were a few issues to address before it could be efficiently scaled up: (a) the total yield of steps 1 and 2 were too low (∼12%) to be accepted on kilogram scale; (b) the trimethylsilyl cyanide (TMSCN) used in the synthesis of 2 is very toxic; (c) purifications by silica gel column were needed in nearly every step; (d) in‑process controls (IPCs) of those steps with low purities required complex workup processes.',
'The key starting material 10 … cannot be acquired in large supply. Accordingly, it is essential to develop a preparation method to provide enough 10 in kilogram scale.',
'First, isoindolin‑1‑one (10) and glyoxylic acid monohydrate were dissolved … The reaction mixture was stirred at 20–30 °C for 16–20 h … The isolated yield was 51 % (purity 96.8%).',
'When this reaction was performed in pure acetic acid, the yields were increased slightly (entries 4 and 5).',
'To promote the conversion, we considered that a stronger acid might be useful. Thus, sulfuric acid was added to the reaction mixture, and the yield improved in the THF/CH₃COOH/H₂SO₄ system (entry 6, 39%). Subsequently, we attempted the coupling in CH₃COOH/H₂SO₄, and a better yield was observed (entry 7, 62%).',
'It was noteworthy that when the reaction was conducted at 60 °C, the yield was dropped to 51%, perhaps due to the relatively harsh reaction conditions.',
'The alternative conditions for BopCl‑mediated amide coupling … the DIC/HOBt/DIPEA condition was adopted for the preparation of EAI045 (entry 3).',
'The reaction was scaled up on kilogram scale with such conditions, although the scale‑up batch yield (62%) was lower than that for the screened conditions; we still obtained 1.5 kg of EAI045 in overall 21 % yield for three steps.',
'The relatively low yields for the three steps (51%, 67%, 62%) were due to the loss both in the water phase of the work‑up and in the mother liquid of the purification process.']

Paper Title: Scoping the Enantioselective Desymmetrization of a Poorly Water-Soluble Diester by Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase
Problem_Description: The diester substrate is poorly water‑soluble (≈60 mM in water at 25 °C) which limits the rate of substrate transfer to the aqueous phase and makes the reaction mass‑transfer‑limited at enzyme loadings > 6 U · mL⁻¹.
Solution_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration to 400 mM (while keeping the enzyme dose at 6 U · mL⁻¹) eliminates the mass‑transfer bottleneck; the authors also suggest that raising the reaction temperature or adding a water‑miscible cosolvent could further improve substrate solubility and reduce the limitation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the poorly water‑soluble nature of the substrate (approximately 60 mM in water at 25 °C…) remained elusive.”

Paper Title: Scoping the Enantioselective Desymmetrization of a Poorly Water-Soluble Diester by Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase
Problem_Description: When substrate concentrations exceed ≈0.5 M the enzyme aggregates and loses activity, indicating enzyme deactivation/denaturation at high substrate load.
Solution_Description: The substrate was fed in three 400 mM batches at 3 h intervals (fed‑batch) or continuously with a syringe pump at a lower instantaneous concentration, keeping the local substrate level below the denaturation threshold.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Substrate concentrations greater than 500 mM caused the enzyme to agglomerate and denature.”

Paper Title: Scoping the Enantioselective Desymmetrization of a Poorly Water-Soluble Diester by Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase
Problem_Description: In fed‑batch experiments the reaction stopped after ≈400 mM product formation; mass‑balance indicated that no further conversion occurred, pointing to product‑inhibition or product‑induced enzyme deactivation.
Solution_Description: The authors propose in‑situ product removal (ISPR) – e.g., reactive crystallisation of the mono‑ester as a metal‑bicarbonate salt, ion‑exchange resins or a crystallisation loop – to eliminate product inhibition and allow higher conversions.
Supporting_Evidence: • “product formation ceased after 7 h… this result indicated that indeed the reaction had stopped after 400 mM product formation… product inhibition or product induced deactivation was the most likely cause of activity loss.”

Paper Title: Scoping the Enantioselective Desymmetrization of a Poorly Water-Soluble Diester by Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase
Problem_Description: At the original 80 mM substrate level the biocatalyst yield was only 0.89 g · g⁻¹ biocat, far below the desired industrial productivity.
Solution_Description: Raising the substrate loading five‑fold to 400 mM (with the same enzyme dose) increased the biocatalyst yield 4.9‑fold to 4.36 g · g⁻¹ biocat while maintaining the space‑time yield, demonstrating that higher substrate concentration improves overall efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The resultant 4.9‑fold improvement in biocatalyst yield from 0.89 to 4.36 g·g⁻¹ biocat⁻¹ at an almost identical maximum space‑time yield….”

Paper Title: Scoping the Enantioselective Desymmetrization of a Poorly Water-Soluble Diester by Recombinant Pig Liver Esterase
Problem_Description: Maintaining a stable pH in the aqueous biocatalytic system is required; conventional base titration can lead to local pH spikes and handling of corrosive reagents on scale.
Solution_Description: A simple ‘self‑healing’ pH control was used: an oversaturated NaHCO₃ buffer reacts with the acidic product, generating CO₂ and automatically stabilising the pH without external base addition.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A simple method of pH control was implemented that made use of inexpensive sodium bicarbonate degradation in the presence of the carboxylic acid product… the pH remains stable within nonsaturated bicarbonate solutions.”

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: In batch mode the accumulation of isoamyl nitrite and the energetic diazonium salt can lead to violent decomposition, formation of toxic nitric oxide, yellow smoke, and explosion risk due to back‑mixing and high‑temperature zones.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The researchers replaced the batch esterification with a continuous‑flow reactor equipped with a static mixer and a liquid‑liquid separator; the on‑line volume of the hazardous intermediates was kept to a minimum, and the product was removed continuously under nitrogen protection.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The continuous‑flow process minimized the accumulation of dangerous isoamyl nitrite and the energetic diazonium salt" (Abstract).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: Back‑mixing in the batch vessel caused violent decomposition of isoamyl nitrite and release of toxic gases, creating safety hazards and poor reaction control.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A PTFE static mixer and a short residence loop were introduced in the flow system, providing efficient mixing while preventing back‑mixing and keeping the reaction volume small.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The strong action of back‑mixing on the solution of isoamyl nitrite and hydrochloric acid… resulted in yellow smoke and violent decomposition" (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: The diazonium salt (3) has very low solubility in many solvents, leading to pipe clogging and unstable flow during continuous‑flow diazotization.
Solution_Description: Diethylene‑glycol dimethyl ether (DG) was selected as the reaction medium because it provided markedly better solubility for the diazonium intermediate, eliminating clogging.
Supporting_Evidence: • "DG was an ideal medium since 3 had better solubility in it than in the other solvents, thereby avoiding pipe clogging" (sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: The traditional batch route required reflux overnight and gave only 58 % (literature) to 72 % yield of the target benzonorbornadiene, making the process slow and inefficient.
Solution_Description: By optimizing residence times (τ₁ = 200 s, τ₂ = 20 s, τ₃ = 30 s) and temperatures (0 °C for diazotization, 120 °C for the Diels–Alder step), the continuous‑flow process delivered 85 % isolated yield in a total reaction time of only 250 s.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The highest yield of 75 % was gained with τ₂ = 20 s and T₂ = 0 °C… With this restructuring, the yield of 1 increased to 85 % with 99 % purity for τ₃ = 30 s and T₃ = 120 °C" (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: Isoamyl nitrite decomposes rapidly at elevated temperatures, producing toxic nitric oxide and accelerating the breakdown of the diazonium intermediate, which compromises safety and product purity.
Solution_Description: The esterification was run at 0 °C and the stoichiometry of sodium nitrite was fine‑tuned to just above 1.05 equiv; isoamyl nitrite was used at 1.02 equiv of the amine, which minimized its decomposition while maintaining full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The maximum purity of 96 %… was gained with τ₁ = 200 s and T₁ = 0 °C… The amount of sodium nitrite needed to be slightly higher than 1.05 equiv, while much lower doses led to a low conversion rate" (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Continuous-Flow Process for the Synthesis of 5‑Nitro-1,4-dihydro-1,4-methanonaphthalene
Problem_Description: Generation of nitrogen and carbon dioxide during the cycloaddition caused uncontrolled residence time and pressure fluctuations in the flow reactor.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A back‑pressure regulator (BPR) set to 100 psi was installed at the reactor outlet to stabilize the pressure and reliably control gas evolution, ensuring consistent reaction times.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Thus, a back‑pressure regulator (BPR) was installed … the back pressure was set to 100 psi" (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Run Parameters for a Continuous Hydrogenation Process Using ACMC-Pd To Replace Commercial Batch Reactor Processes
Problem_Description: During the nitrobenzene hydrogenation at 82 °C the reaction generated a large temperature rise (27 °C standard deviation) that threatened isothermal operation and could lead to hot‑spots and catalyst degradation.
Solution_Description: The temperature of the inlet, middle and outlet zones of the reactor was actively controlled (heaters set to limit the inlet‑outlet ΔT to ≤15 °C) to keep the exotherm within a safe range.
Supporting_Evidence: “In a separate run with an average run temperature of 82 °C, the conversion was >99 % in four passes… However, this run showed a significant exotherm, with a 27 °C standard deviation in the inlet and outlet temperatures… The temperature rise… was controlled by managing the temperature of the inlet, middle, and outlet zone heaters of the reactor as the chemistry progressed.”

Paper Title: Run Parameters for a Continuous Hydrogenation Process Using ACMC-Pd To Replace Commercial Batch Reactor Processes
Problem_Description: A single pass through the 30.5 cm monolith bed gave only modest conversion for all substrates; >97 % conversion required multiple passes (e.g., 17‑21 passes).
Solution_Description: The process was operated in a “multiple‑pass” mode, circulating the liquid through the same catalyst bed repeatedly until the required conversion was reached, effectively simulating a longer commercial tube.
Supporting_Evidence: “A typical reactor run comprised multiple passes of the reaction solution (1 L) through a 2.54 cm diameter catalyst bed of length 30.5 cm to simulate the performance of a longer reactor bed in a commercial reactor… The chemistries studied… can be run to >97 % conversion in a number of passes corresponding to practical catalyst bed lengths (e.g., 4.3‑6.1 m).”

Paper Title: Run Parameters for a Continuous Hydrogenation Process Using ACMC-Pd To Replace Commercial Batch Reactor Processes
Problem_Description: The neat olefin/aromatic substrate (100 % substrate, no solvent) presented very high viscosity and a high density of unsaturated bonds, leading to potential mixing and mass‑transfer limitations.
Solution_Description: The reaction was split into two temperature stages: a low‑temperature step to form an intermediate, followed by a higher‑temperature step to complete hydrogenation, helping to control viscosity and maintain adequate gas‑liquid contact.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that the reaction was best managed in a two‑step process involving a low‑temperature reaction to form an intermediate followed by a higher‑temperature process… The first four passes… were done using condition set 1, and in the remaining reactor passes condition set 2 was used.”

Paper Title: Run Parameters for a Continuous Hydrogenation Process Using ACMC-Pd To Replace Commercial Batch Reactor Processes
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the neat substrate required high hydrogen flow rates (up to 19 SLM) and elevated pressure (3.45 MPa), raising safety concerns and potential for excessive heat release.
Solution_Description: Hydrogen flow was increased incrementally (2 → 19 SLM) only during the high‑temperature stage to supply the needed hydrogen while avoiding a sudden exotherm; pressure was maintained at the required level but only after the low‑temperature step was completed.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the high‑temperature part of the run, the hydrogen flow rate was increased in increments from 2 to 19 SLM and then back to 2 SLM to simulate the addition of high levels of hydrogen for the complete conversion… The reaction rate increases with the addition of more hydrogen and that the reaction is hydrogen‑limited for the first five passes at the higher reaction temperature.”

Paper Title: Run Parameters for a Continuous Hydrogenation Process Using ACMC-Pd To Replace Commercial Batch Reactor Processes
Problem_Description: Achieving sufficient gas‑liquid mass transfer required a specific liquid‑to‑hydrogen flow ratio; too high a liquid rate would lead to film flow with limited hydrogen solubility, while too low a ratio could cause bubble flow and poor mixing.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The liquid linear velocity was set to 0.086 cm s⁻¹ (≈0.1 mm s⁻¹) to promote thin‑film (annular) flow, providing a thin liquid layer that efficiently transports hydrogen to the catalyst surface.
Supporting_Evidence: “The linear velocity of liquid flow in this work was selected to enable >97 % conversion… The liquid to gas ratios were mostly 0.1 to 0.16 and as low as 0.02… In both the bubble flow and annular film flow configurations, there is the advantage of a thin liquid layer that connects a hydrogen gas reservoir… facilitating efficient gas‑ and liquid‑phase mass transfer to the catalyst while removing hydrogen solubility limitations.”

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: The originally disclosed Acerta‑Pharma route used sulfuryl chloride for chlorination and Raney‑Ni hydrogenation.  Handling of the chlorination reagent caused skin irritation and, on scale, the hydrogenation gave uncontrolled over‑reduction (loss of the chloro group) leading to poor material throughput.
Solution_Description: A new four‑step telescoped sequence based on a literature route was adopted.  Diphenylmethanimine was employed in acetonitrile (replacing benzophenone/DIPEA/toluene and DMF) to give an almost quantitative imine formation and allowed direct telescoping into the next step.  The sequence was carried out without isolating intermediates, eliminating the hazardous chlorination step and the over‑reduction problem.
Supporting_Evidence: "reports of skin irritation when handling <bold>2</bold>, and difficulties in controlling over-reduction (loss of the chloro group) of <bold>3</bold> on scale,"; "Use of diphenylmethanimine in acetonitrile (to replace benzophenone/DIPEA/toluene) to form <bold>18</bold> gave an almost quantitative solution yield and also allowed an operationally simple, direct telescope into the next step"; "meaning that environmentally undesirable N,N‑dimethylformamide could be replaced"; "Through this work, a four‑step telescope procedure was realized ... which delivered <bold>5</bold> in 72% overall yield"

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Attempted reduction of intermediate 7 with sodium dithionite gave a mixture of products and, together with the known thermal instability of both 7 and nitromethane, made the step unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The problematic dithionite reduction was abandoned and the authors switched to the literature‑based route via intermediate 19, which avoided the unstable species and provided a clean, high‑yielding transformation.
Supporting_Evidence: "Sodium dithionite was used to reduce <bold>7</bold>, but the reaction was not clean, and coupled with concerns around the thermal stability of both <bold>7</bold> and nitromethane"; "The route to <bold>3</bold> via <bold>19</bold> is known in the literature and was developed by OSI Pharmaceuticals... The reported reaction conditions were confirmed, and then work was performed to optimize this chemistry"

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Formylation of compound 14 afforded product 13, which was reported and experimentally confirmed to be unstable, precluding its use in downstream steps.
Solution_Description: The unstable 13‑containing pathway was discarded in favor of the alternative literature route that bypasses the formylation step.
Supporting_Evidence: "Formylation of <bold>14</bold> is known in the literature, but the resultant <bold>13</bold> is reported to be unstable, and this was confirmed by the work performed in our group"; "The route to <bold>3</bold> via <bold>19</bold> is known in the literature..."

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Efforts to elaborate the unstable intermediate 13 (as an oxime or via Ellman chemistry) succeeded only partially and required a large number of steps, making the overall sequence long and low‑yielding.
Solution_Description: Because of the lengthy step count and modest conversion, this pathway was abandoned and the more concise literature‑derived sequence was adopted.
Supporting_Evidence: "were only partially successful, and this route was also considered undesirable due to the lengthy step count"; "The route to <bold>3</bold> via <bold>19</bold> is known in the literature..."

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: The methyl tert‑butyl acetate/LHMDS approach generated a chloro‑analogue of 16 that presented handling difficulties and failed to give the desired primary amide, causing safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The problematic sequence was dropped in favor of the literature route that avoids the hazardous intermediate 16 and provides a robust, high‑yielding conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "Handling issues meant that the chloro‑analogue of <bold>16</bold> appeared undesirable for further scale‑up"; "The route to <bold>3</bold> via <bold>19</bold> is known in the literature..."

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: Addition of trimethyl sulfoxonium anion to 6 gave no detectable reaction under the conditions tested, resulting in zero conversion.
Solution_Description: Because this transformation failed, the authors discontinued the approach and pursued the alternative literature pathway that proceeds efficiently.
Supporting_Evidence: "Addition of trimethyl sulfoxonium anion onto <bold>6</bold> gave no reaction under the conditions attempted"; "The route to <bold>3</bold> via <bold>19</bold> is known in the literature..."

Paper Title: A Manufacturing Process to an Intermediate in the Synthesis of Acalabrutinib
Problem_Description: The original process required DMF as a solvent and isolated the imine intermediate before subsequent steps, increasing waste, exposure to a toxic solvent, and extending overall reaction time.
Solution_Description: The process was re‑engineered to use acetonitrile (replacing DMF) and to perform a one‑pot, telescoped sequence where imine formation, ester hydrolysis, and decarboxylation were combined in a single step with concentrated HCl, eliminating isolated intermediates and reducing the number of discrete operations.
Supporting_Evidence: "Use of diphenylmethanimine in acetonitrile (to replace benzophenone/DIPEA/toluene) ... gave an almost quantitative solution yield and also allowed an operationally simple, direct telescope into the next step"; "meaning that environmentally undesirable N,N‑dimethylformamide could be replaced"; "Simultaneous imine and ester hydrolysis and decarboxylation (to yield <bold>3</bold>) were performed using concentrated aqueous hydrochloric acid in one step (rather than sequentially)"

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: The Atherton–Todd reaction traditionally uses carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄) as the chlorinating agent, which is a known carcinogen, ozone‑depleting substance and is banned or heavily restricted in many regions, making it unsafe and unavailable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Replace CCl₄ with chlorine gas (Cl₂) as the chlorinating agent. Cl₂ is industrially produced, inexpensive, and avoids the toxic and regulatory issues associated with CCl₄.
Supporting_Evidence:
“CCl₄ … is a carcinogen and also both an ozone‑depleting and greenhouse gas which prohibits its industrial usage… Its usage in Switzerland is banned and restricted in Europe.”
“Cl₂ gas is industrially produced and commonly used in industry to prepare useful intermediates and final products… the fact that Cl₂ gas is industrially produced … makes it very interesting for the chlorination reaction of P–H bonds.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: When trichloroisocyanuric acid (TCCA) was investigated as a chlorinating agent, the chlorination reaction was found to be highly exothermic, creating safety concerns and making scale‑up difficult.
Solution_Description: Use a controlled flow of Cl₂ gas with temperature monitoring (≤ 20 °C) and a dropwise addition protocol to keep the reaction temperature low and manage the exotherm safely.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the chlorination reaction using TCCA was found to be very exothermic which makes it difficult to scale up in industry.”
“Cl₂ gas was then introduced to the reaction vessel at a flow rate (20 L/h) so that the reaction temperature does not exceed 20 °C.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: N‑chlorosuccinimide (NCS) gave high conversion for P–N bond formation but provided relatively low yields for the one‑pot synthesis of P–O bond containing phosphonates.
Solution_Description: Switch the chlorination step to Cl₂ gas, which gives consistently high yields (≈ 90 %) for both P–N and P–O bond containing derivatives.
Supporting_Evidence:
“NCS showed high efficacy for one‑pot synthesis of P–N bond containing derivatives… the reaction yield of one‑pot synthesis of P–O bond containing derivatives … was relatively low.”
“All target compounds in this study were then synthesized … using 2 mol equiv of Cl₂ … Yield: 90 % for EDA‑DOPO and 76 % for DOPO‑PEPA.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: Sulfuryl chloride (SO₂Cl₂) requires refluxing in CH₂Cl₂, releases Cl₂ and SO₂ as by‑products, and the generated SO₂ presents handling and disposal hazards.
Solution_Description: Eliminate SO₂Cl₂ by adopting Cl₂ gas as the sole chlorinating reagent, thereby removing the need for reflux and eliminating SO₂ formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
“SO₂Cl₂ … involves refluxing … which releases a useful product such as Cl₂ and a byproduct SO₂.”
“The use of Cl₂ gas … simplifies the reaction, avoids by‑products and reduces overall costs.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: Dichloromethane (CH₂Cl₂) is employed as the reaction solvent; its high vapor pressure requires special handling, ventilation, and an additional recycling apparatus, increasing operational cost and safety burden.
Solution_Description: Investigate alternative, less volatile solvents compatible with Cl₂ chlorination to replace CH₂Cl₂, aiming to lower handling hazards and recycle costs.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The only drawback of this synthetic procedure is the use of dichloromethane as a reaction solvent. It has high vapor pressure and requires special handling in large‑scale synthesis and an additional recycling apparatus for its recovery.”
“Accordingly, alternative solvents suitable for a Cl₂‑based synthesis procedure to replace dichloromethane are under further investigation.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: The diastereomeric ratio of ETA‑DOPO influences its melting point and thermal behavior, leading to variability in product specifications.
Solution_Description: Modify the work‑up (solvent choice, washing steps, and precipitation conditions) to separate diastereomeric sets, giving reproducible purity and physical properties.
Supporting_Evidence: “Due to the different solubility behavior of the diastereomer set of ETA‑DOPO, they could be isolated by modifying the synthesis workup procedure… The white precipitate (first crop)… The filtrate was then poured in water, forming a white powder (second crop) … both crops gave the same mass yield.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: Accurate dosing of Cl₂ gas is critical for consistent conversion; any deviation can lead to incomplete chlorination or excess waste.
Solution_Description: Monitor the weight loss of the Cl₂ gas bottle and control the flow rate (20 L h⁻¹) to deliver a stoichiometric 1:1 Cl₂ : DOPO ratio, ensuring reproducible conversion at scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
“For industrial upscaling, a bottle of pure Cl₂ gas was used and the accurate amount of consumed Cl₂ was controlled by monitoring the weight difference of the Cl₂ gas bottle.”
“Cl₂ gas was then introduced … at a flow rate (20 L/h) so that the reaction temperature does not exceed 20 °C.”

Paper Title: Industrial Upscaling of DOPO-Based Phosphonamidates and Phosphonates Derivatives Using Cl
Problem_Description: Isolation of the key intermediate DOPO‑Cl is required before downstream amination; removal of volatiles and residual HCl must be efficient to obtain a pure, isolable solid.
Solution_Description: After Cl₂ addition, volatiles are removed under N₂ flow, yielding a quantitative white solid of DOPO‑Cl without further purification, which can be stored and used directly.
Supporting_Evidence: “After 30 min, the Cl₂ flow was stopped and the volatiles were completely removed under N₂ flow affording a white solid in quantitative yield. The product was analyzed and used without further purification.”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: Catalyst deactivation occurs when acrylate esters are used as the olefinic partner; an inactive betaine species (10) forms, leading to rapid loss of catalytic activity and low product yields.
Solution_Description: The olefinic partner was changed from methyl acrylate to methyl‑vinyl‑ketone (MVK). This avoids formation of the betaine species, preserving catalyst activity and giving higher isolated yields (up to 95 %).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Although polyDMAP provided good results for the MBH reaction the catalytic activity dropped rapidly … the formation of an inactive betaine species 10 upon mixing of acrylates with DABCO …”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: Initial flow experiments with low reactant concentrations (0.2 M aldehyde, 0.3 M MVK) and 20 min residence time gave only 12 % ^1H‑NMR yield, indicating insufficient conversion and long reaction times required for acceptable yields.
Solution_Description: Temperature was raised to 60 °C, reactant concentrations were increased (up to 0.4 M aldehyde and 2.4 M MVK), and residence time was extended to 45‑60 min. These changes raised the ^1H‑NMR yield to 72 % (61 % isolated).
Supporting_Evidence: • “A stock solution of 3 (0.2 M) and MVK (0.3 M) … resulted in a disappointing 12 % yield … Increasing the concentrations … to 0.4 M and 1.2 M at 50 °C afforded 32 % … Further increases … to 2.4 M … gave 43 % and 45 % … Performing the reaction at 60 °C and prolonging the retention time to 45 min resulted in an increase … to 56 % … Finally, doubling the retention time … led to a satisfactory 72 % yield.”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: During extended operation the pressure drop across the polyDMAP packed‑bed reactor increased steadily, attributed to swelling of the cross‑linked polymer beads, which caused clogging and unstable flow.
Solution_Description: The solid support was changed from polymer‑bound DMAP to DMAP immobilized on silica particles (Si‑DMAP). The silica matrix eliminates swelling, stabilizes the pressure drop, and maintains catalyst activity over long runs.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Although polyDMAP provided good results … the pressure drop over the PBR steadily increased as a function of time … most likely related to the swelling of the polyDMAP beads … Examination of the packed bed reactor content … indicated the column material to have become tightly packed … Following this concept, it was decided to change the solid reactor material to DMAP bound on silica particles (Si‑DMAP).”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: For highly reactive substrate combinations (e.g., terephthalaldehyde + MVK) prolonged residence times lead to rapid formation of over‑addition side‑products, reducing the desired product yield.
Solution_Description: Retention time was precisely reduced (down to 10 min) to outpace side‑product formation, which increased isolated yield to 71 % while minimizing over‑reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: • “When performing this reaction with a retention time of 60 min only a meager 24 % … reducing the retention time to 30 min provided a lower conversion … however, this was counterbalanced by small increase in product selectivity … finally, application of a retention time of only 10 min nearly outpaced the formation of side‑products, and 25 was secured in a good 71 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: Certain aldehydes (e.g., 1‑butanol‑soluble substrates) were poorly soluble in the reaction stock solution, hindering smooth flow and conversion.
Solution_Description: A co‑solvent mixture of CH₂Cl₂ (3:1 with 1‑butanol) was added to fully solubilize the starting aldehydes in the stock solution, improving miscibility and reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Some of the reactions required the addition of CH₂Cl₂ as a cosolvent to fully solubilize the starting aldehyde in the stock solution.”

Paper Title: Studying the Morita-Baylis-Hillman Reaction in Continuous Flow Using Packed Bed Reactors
Problem_Description: Potential catalyst deactivation over long operation times could lead to loss of activity and inconsistent product formation.
Solution_Description: A scale‑out experiment (20 h continuous flow) using the Si‑DMAP packed bed demonstrated stable catalyst performance with >90 % yield throughout, confirming robustness of the reactor/catalyst system.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Both the overnight run and the final sample contained 20 in 93 % ^1H‑NMR yield, thereby proving the high stability of the catalyst in the PBR … The setup continuously afforded 20 in a greater than 90 % yield… over 20.5 h … with no sign of catalyst deactivation.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Farnesyltransferase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original discovery synthesis used borane/THF for the reduction of benzodiazepine 5 to diamine 6. Borane is a hazardous, pyrophoric reagent and difficult to handle safely on kilogram scale, and the reagents and work‑up are cost‑intensive.
Solution_Description: The borane reduction was eliminated by redesigning the synthetic route (new route starting from 2‑nitro‑5‑cyanotoluene 9) that bypasses the borane step entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion of 5 to 6 was performed with borane, which is an undesirable reducing reagent with respect to scalability.”; “The new synthesis ... started with commercially available 2‑nitro‑5‑cyanotoluene 9.”; “The new route ... eliminated the need for the borane reduction and cyanide introduction steps.”

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Synthesis of a Farnesyltransferase Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original route required a cyanide‑based cyanation of 6 to 7 using excess cyanide (CuCN or Zn(CN)₂/Pd). Large‑scale handling of cyanide poses serious safety and environmental hazards, and the waste stream is difficult to manage.
Solution_Description: A new synthetic sequence was devised that starts from nitro‑cyanotoluene 9, which already contains the cyanide functionality, thus avoiding any cyanide addition step.
Supporting_Evidence: “Another scale‑up concern with the discovery synthesis was the use of excess cyanide… safety … disposal of the reaction waste stream.”; “We initially proposed a new synthesis with commercially available 2‑nitro‑5‑cyanotoluene 9 … obviated the need for developing and conducting cyanation chemistry on‑scale.”

Problem_Description: Direct sulfonylation of 12 with 2‑thienylsulfonyl chloride/triethylamine gave aziridine 20 as the major product (≈90 %), indicating that the primary alcohol reacts faster than the secondary amine, leading to low yield of the desired sulfonamide 13.

Problem_Description: The TMS‑protected sulfonylation generated side‑product 28 (5–25 %) from nucleophilic attack of chloride on the benzylic position of the TMS ether, lowering the isolated yield of 13.

Supporting_Evidence: “A major side product 28 was observed … generated from an S_N2 reaction of 27 and chloride.”; “When TMSCl was substituted with BSA (0.75 equiv) … significantly less 28 (∼5 % versus 25 %). The best results were obtained … 83 % yield of sulfonamide 13.”

Solution_Description: By directly forming sulfonamide 13 via in‑situ TMS protection and then reducing the nitro group of 13 to aniline 15 (with Na₂S₂O₄) before cyclization, the step count was reduced and the overall yield improved (overall 29 % for the 8‑step sequence).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Direct chemical acetylation of isosorbide gave < 70 % yield and low isomeric purity because the two hydroxyl groups are too similar, leading to formation of undesired isomers (isosorbide‑5‑acetate and di‑acetate).
Solution_Description: Switch to a biocatalytic approach – enzymatic hydrolysis or alcoholysis of isosorbide‑2,5‑diacetate with immobilized lipases – which delivered ∼92 % isolated yield and > 99.5 % diastereomeric excess, eliminating the regio‑selectivity problem of the chemical route.
Supporting_Evidence: “Direct acetylation of 3 was not efficient enough… < 70 % yield with low isomeric purity” (Introduction). “Using immobilized lipase, we developed an enzymatic synthesis…high yield (~92 %) with excellent regioselectivity (>99.5 % d.e.)” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: The previously reported enzymatic process using SAM II required 12 days for alcoholysis and incurred high enzyme cost because recycling was inefficient.
Solution_Description: Adopt readily available immobilized enzymes (Novozym 435 for hydrolysis, lipase PS IM for alcoholysis) and optimize conditions, reducing reaction times to 12 h (hydrolysis) and 24 h (alcoholysis) and enabling enzyme reuse.
Supporting_Evidence: “...long reaction time (e.g., 12 days for alcoholysis) and high enzyme costs...” (Introduction). “The reaction time was shortened to 48 h … and the immobilized lipase could be recycled five times” (Introduction). “Hydrolysis could be completed within 12 h… alcoholysis 24 h” (Results & Discussion).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: The prior immobilized‑lipase method suffered from low substrate concentration (62 g L⁻¹) and high enzyme loading (50 g L⁻¹), limiting productivity and increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: Increase substrate loading to 400–500 g L⁻¹ while reducing enzyme loading to ≤ 15 g L⁻¹ (hydrolysis) or 20 g L⁻¹ (alcoholysis), achieving > 90 % conversion with < 10 wt % enzyme‑to‑substrate ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: “...low substrate concentration (62 g/L) and high enzyme loading (50 g/L) still restricted the application” (Introduction). “Hydrolysis could be completed within 12 h even at a substrate concentration of up to 500 g/L with an enzyme concentration of 50 g/L… acceptable conversion even when the enzyme loading was reduced to 15 g/L” (Section 2.1.3). “Substrate concentration could be increased to 400 g/L… enzyme loading of 20 g/L … for the alcoholysis process” (Section 2.2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Adding THF as a cosolvent to the hydrolysis mixture decreased the activity of Novozym 435, suggesting enzyme deactivation in the presence of organic solvent.
Solution_Description: Omit the cosolvent; perform hydrolysis in aqueous sodium‑phosphate buffer only, which preserves enzyme activity and simplifies work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the hydrolysis reaction could be completed within 6 h, the activity of Novozym 435 decreased in the presence of an organic cosolvent… Therefore, sodium phosphate buffer alone was used as the hydrolysis medium.” (Section 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Strongly hydrophilic solvents (e.g., MeOH) stripped essential water from the immobilized lipase, causing enzyme denaturation and loss of conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: Select moderately or strongly hydrophobic solvents; THF was chosen as the optimal solvent for alcoholysis because it maintained enzyme activity and gave good conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “In strongly hydrophilic solvents, both the conversion and the regioselectivity were decreased… attributed to stripping of essential water… resulting in enzyme denaturation.” (Section 2.2.1). “On the basis of the solvent consumption and space‑time yield, THF was the preferred choice for subsequent studies.” (Section 2.2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Using n‑hexane as the reaction solvent gave poor product isolation because isosorbide‑2‑acetate is insoluble in n‑hexane, making enzyme recovery difficult.
Solution_Description: Replace n‑hexane with THF, which dissolves the product sufficiently for straightforward work‑up while still being compatible with the immobilized enzyme.
Supporting_Evidence: “...in n‑hexane… target compound 1 was also insoluble… difficult to isolate and recover the enzyme… THF was the preferred choice for subsequent studies.” (Section 2.2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Lipase PS IM lost activity rapidly on recycling; conversion fell below 70 % by the third reuse, necessitating addition of fresh enzyme.
Solution_Description: Add 20 % fresh lipase PS IM at each recycle (instead of larger bolus additions) to sustain activity over five cycles, balancing cost and performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “The biocatalytic activity of lipase PS IM obviously decreased… conversion dropped to < 70 % by the third recycle… 30 % fresh enzyme was added at both the fourth and the fifth recycles… an alternative method in which 20 % fresh enzyme was added at each recycle was adopted.” (Section 2.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: Alkaline pH (> 8) caused unintended hydrolysis of the 2‑exo ester group, reducing conversion and regioselectivity.
Solution_Description: Maintain the reaction at weakly acidic pH 6.0 ± 0.5 using 1 M NaHCO₃ (a weak base) instead of NaOH, preventing side‑reactions and preserving enzyme activity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Both the conversion and regioselectivity decreased under alkaline conditions… the acetic acid generated… was better neutralized by a weak base… a weakly acidic medium (pH 6.0 ± 0.5) was the optimum choice, and the pH was controlled using a NaHCO₃ solution (1 M) instead of a NaOH solution.” (Section 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Development of a Practical Enzymatic Synthesis of Isosorbide-2-acetate
Problem_Description: At temperatures above 45 °C the di‑acetate substrate melted, affecting stirring and potentially mass‑transfer.
Solution_Description: Select 50 °C for hydrolysis (ensures substrate is molten for good mixing) and 55 °C for alcoholysis (enhances substrate solubility and conversion).
Supporting_Evidence: “When the temperature was > 45 °C, the starting material 5 melted… therefore, a milder temperature of 50 °C was selected… increasing the temperature improved the conversion… 55 °C was considered the optimal temperature.” (Sections 2.1.1 and 2.2.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Process A used n‑BuOH and required numerous, lengthy phase separations with water, a solid‑supported palladium scavenger step, a difficult solvent swap from n‑BuOH to n‑BuOAc and uncontrolled crystallization, making the route unsuitable for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new Suzuki route (Process B/Process C) eliminated the solvent swap, avoided the solid‑supported scavenger, removed the uncontrolled crystallization and employed aqueous ethanol as the reaction medium, simplifying work‑up and improving robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was performed in n‑BuOH, and the workup involved numerous and lengthy phase separations with water … solid‑supported scavenger step, a challenging solvent swap from n‑BuOH to n‑BuOAc, and an uncontrolled crystallization … all of which were undesirable for scale‑up.”; “The challenging solvent swaps, phase separations, solid‑supported scavenger step, and uncontrolled crystallization were all removed from the process.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Charging the boronic acid (2a) was problematic: under‑charging gave incomplete conversion (low yield) while over‑charging produced the over‑coupled impurity (3). The acid is a fine, amorphous powder that is difficult to handle and to assay accurately, creating a narrow ±0.02 mol equiv CPP that exceeded equipment control limits.
Solution_Description: The boronic acid was replaced by the crystalline diethanolamine boronic ester (2b), which is monomeric, stable and can be weighed and charged with much greater accuracy, widening the acceptable charge range to ±0.05 mol equiv and removing the quality risk.
Supporting_Evidence: “Undercharging the boronic acid led to an incomplete reaction and that an overcharge gave rise to the overcoupled impurity … narrow range of ±0.02 mol equiv … equipment had a control range of ±0.04 mol equiv … quality risk.”; “The diethanolamine boronic ester (2b) was selected … monomeric and crystalline species that could be assayed, and charged, with greater accuracy than the boronic acid.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Switching to the boronic ester (2b) slowed the Suzuki coupling, extending reaction time and allowing competitive non‑palladium‑catalyzed hydrolysis of the ester to an amide impurity (4), which is time‑ and temperature‑dependent.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was raised from 70 °C to 80 °C and the reaction time shortened, which reduced the extent of hydrolysis to an acceptable level while maintaining high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “A drawback … was that the rate of reaction was reduced … an amide impurity (4) … formation … was time‑ and temperature‑dependent.”; “The extent of hydrolysis was reduced to an acceptable level by increasing the reaction temperature to 80 °C (vs 70 °C) and reducing the reaction time.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Palladium catalyst cost and the need for low residual metal levels required high catalyst loadings (0.4 mol %) in earlier processes, increasing cost‑of‑goods and complicating palladium removal.
Solution_Description: A new pre‑formed Pd(AmPhos)₂Cl₂ catalyst was adopted, allowing the loading to be reduced to 0.15 mol % (with maintained activity), decreasing both catalyst expense and theoretical palladium residues.
Supporting_Evidence: “The catalyst loading could be reduced from 0.4 mol % … to 0.15 mol % with Pd(AmPhos)₂Cl₂ … based on its cost, reactivity, availability, and safety.”; “The Pd(AmPhos)₂Cl₂ catalyst was chosen for further development based on its cost, reactivity, availability, and safety.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Removal of residual palladium traditionally required a solid‑supported scavenger, an expensive and high‑risk step that added cost and handling concerns.
Solution_Description: The diethanolamine released from the boronic ester forms a soluble Pd–DEA complex, acting as an internal scavenger and dramatically lowering residual palladium (e.g., 48 ppm without any solid scavenger), thereby eliminating the need for the discrete scavenger step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reduction in residual palladium level when we changed to the diethanolamine boronic ester may be explained by the formation of a palladium–diethanolamine complex … advantageously removed the requirement for a scavenging step in the process.”; Table 2 shows palladium levels dropping from 166 ppm (Process B with scavenger) to 48 ppm (Process C with ester, no scavenger).

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: Addition of diethanolamine (DEA) to the reaction slowed the Suzuki coupling, indicating deactivation of palladium by DEA and causing inconsistent reaction rates.
Solution_Description: When DEA was present, the palladium loading was doubled, restoring the reaction profile to that of the standard conditions, demonstrating that adjusting stoichiometry can compensate for DEA‑induced deactivation.
Supporting_Evidence: “When diethanolamine (1 equiv) is charged … the reaction is slower … consistent with deactivation … charging 1 equiv of DEA while doubling the palladium loading should give a reaction profile similar to the standard conditions. This was indeed the case.”

Paper Title: Process Development of a Suzuki Reaction Used in the Manufacture of Lanabecestat
Problem_Description: The original n‑BuOH based work‑up generated a biphasic system that required multiple, time‑consuming separations, hampering throughput.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction medium to aqueous ethanol created a single‑phase, well‑mixed system that eliminated the need for extensive phase separations.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction was performed in n‑BuOH, and the workup involved numerous and lengthy phase separations with water … The challenging solvent swaps, phase separations … were all removed from the process.”; “Process C employed aqueous ethanol, simplifying mixing and work‑up.”

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: The back‑pressure regulator (BPR) clogged periodically from precipitation of LiF formed in the difluoromethylation mixture. The clogging caused pressure fluctuations of ±2 bar and an unsteady delivery of fluoroform, which prevented precise stoichiometric control and gave inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: A Zaiput BPR with a gas‑chamber design and larger internal channel was installed. The new regulator reduced pressure fluctuations to ±0.1 bar and eliminated clogging, allowing stable fluoroform flow and consistent reaction performance.
Supporting_Evidence: “The formation of solids resulted in pressure fluctuations of ±2 bar … and an unsteady delivery of fluoroform into the reaction mixture; therefore, the stoichiometry could not be carefully controlled.” (sec 2.1, Table 1, entry 2) ‑ “The flow reaction performed most consistently with a Zaiput BPR … Pressure fluctuations were decreased to only ±0.1 bar with no clogging … therefore, the fluoroform flow rate did not fluctuate to compensate for pressure changes.” (sec 2.1, Table 1, entry 3)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: The original protocol used 3 equiv of fluoroform to compensate for pressure fluctuations. This excess waste conflicted with the Kyoto protocol’s restriction on fluoroform emissions and increased material cost.
Solution_Description: The fluoroform input was reduced to 1.05 equiv and the surplus was consumed by an excess of base (LiHMDS). Improved pressure control with the new BPR allowed the lower stoichiometry without loss of conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “One of the main objectives of this work was to reduce the fluoroform input … The main reason for using 3 equiv of fluoroform … was the pressure fluctuation caused by accumulation of inorganic precipitate inside the Swagelok back‑pressure regulator (BPR).” (sec 2.1) ‑ “Gratifyingly, decreasing the amount of fluoroform to equimolar amounts only had a small effect on yield … The use of 1.25 equiv of fluoroform afforded the highest yield with the product formed in 67 % yield.” (sec 2.4, Table 3)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: Increasing the total flow rate (shorter residence time) caused the isolated yield of the difluoromethylated product to drop dramatically to 16 %. The fast flow reduced mixing efficiency and contact time between the enolate and fluoroform.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The amount of LiHMDS was increased from 2 equiv to 3 equiv, restoring conversion. A 2 mL static glass mixer plate was installed after the first reactor to improve mixing, and the residence coil volume was increased to maintain sufficient residence time at higher flow rates.
Supporting_Evidence: “An increase of flow rates and shorter residence time resulted in a considerable drop in yield to just 16 % … We could improve the yield back to acceptable levels (87 %) … by increasing the amount of base from two to three equivalents.” (sec 2.2, Table 2, entries 3 and 5‑6) ‑ “…we exchanged the Y‑shaped connector after reactor 1 for a 2 mL borosilicate static glass mixer plate (Uniqsis).” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: The original solvents (THF and CHCl₃) are classified as hazardous (THF is a CMR‑substance and CHCl₃ is carcinogenic), and THF’s high solubility for fluoroform increased the risk of membrane fouling and handling of a toxic gas.
Solution_Description: THF was replaced with 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2‑MeTHF), a greener, renewable‑derived solvent that offers comparable or better solubility for the substrate, limited water miscibility for easier work‑up, and no CMR classification.
Supporting_Evidence: “...we were interested in increasing the sustainability of the process by finding alternatives to the use of THF and CHCl₃ as solvents as they are classified as highly hazardous and problematic, respectively.” (sec 1) ‑ “Subsequently, the reaction was also investigated by using 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran (2‑MeTHF) as the solvent … 2‑MeTHF is not classified as CMR‑substance.” (sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: LiHMDS, the preferred base for enolate formation, is expensive on large scale. Attempts to replace it with cheaper bases (n‑BuLi, LDA, KOtBu, LiOtBu) resulted in negligible product formation (1‑2 % yield).
Solution_Description: Although alternative bases were explored, LiHMDS remained the only viable option; the process was retained with LiHMDS while other parameters (stoichiometry, solvent, mixing) were optimized to offset its cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of LiHMDS clearly contributes most to the overall cost of the process; therefore, we tried to replace it with a more cost‑effective alternative. Unfortunately all our attempts employing n‑BuLi, LDA, KOtBu, and LiOtBu were largely unsuccessful and yielded only negligible amounts of product (1–2 %).” (sec 2.3) ‑ “Best results apart from LiHMDS could be obtained by using 5 equiv of LiN(cyHex)₂ which afforded compound 7 in 10 % yield.” (sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: Acidic hydrolysis of the difluoromethylated intermediate generates hydrofluoric acid (HF), which can corrode stainless‑steel or glass reactor components.
Solution_Description: Perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) tubing, which is resistant to HF corrosion, was employed for the high‑temperature deprotection coil.
Supporting_Evidence: “PFA was used as small amounts of hydrofluoric acid might form during the addition of HCl which corrodes steel coils over time.” (sec 2.8) ‑ “The inorganic fluoride content … measured … corresponds to a maximum concentration of HF … which poses no risk to health and safety but may contribute to corrosion of steel and glass.” (sec 2.6)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: The original microwave deprotection required 45 min at 150 °C with 6 M HCl, yielding long residence times and high pressures that pose safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The HCl concentration was increased to 12 M, the temperature raised to 160 °C, and the reaction time shortened to 10 min, achieving >99 % conversion while maintaining manageable pressure (11 bar).
Supporting_Evidence: “We thus opted for concentrated HCl (12 M) instead and could achieve full conversion … in 10 min at 160 °C with 12 bar internal pressure.” (sec 2.7, Table 4, entry 11) ‑ “Entry 1–3 … were unsuccessful employing 6 M HCl …” (sec 2.7)

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Flow Process for the Synthesis of Eflornithine Using Fluoroform as Difluoromethyl Source
Problem_Description: When the two continuous‑flow steps (difluoromethylation and deprotection) were telescoped, precipitation after mixing the reaction streams caused blockages, limiting the ability to run the process for extended periods.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A smaller static glass mixer with narrower channels and a larger 40 mL PFA heated coil were used, allowing higher total flow rates (3 mL min⁻¹) and faster mixing, which minimized precipitation and enabled a 4 h continuous run at 24 mmol h⁻¹ throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “The heated coil was exchanged for a 40 mL PFA coil … so that a higher total flow rate (3 mL min⁻¹) could be used … Precipitation after mixing the difluoromethylation feed and HCl feed … was minimized due to faster mixing from the higher overall flow rates used.” (sec 2.9) ‑ “The previously used 2 mL static glass mixer was exchanged for a smaller 1 mL static glass mixer … to ensure an improved temperature control.” (sec 2.9)

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: The conventional preparation of the benzyl carbonate 9c using methyl chloroformate was very slow, required multiple charges of the toxic reagent and pyridine, and generated quaternary ammonium salt 36 (from residual methyl chloroformate or methyl chloride). This raised safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A safer, non‑hazardous carbonate synthesis was developed using dimethyl carbonate (DMC) with 5 mol % NaOMe (or K‑t‑BuO) as base; the reaction gave 90–95 % conversion to 9c without side‑product formation. The crude product was quenched with Et₃N·HCl and crystallised from MTBE/n‑heptane, delivering 96 % isolated yield and >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The most straightforward approach to prepare carbonate 9c was via treatment of benzyl alcohol 9b with methyl chloroformate… The reaction was surprisingly sluggish… various levels of quaternary ammonium salt 36 were observed… More alarmingly, … methyl chloride.”; “N‑Heterocyclic carbene (NHC)‑catalyzed transesterification… prompted us to investigate dimethyl carbonate (DMC)… With catalytic potassium t‑butoxide as the base, similar conversions were observed… It was also found that cheaper NaOMe performed similarly… Typically, 5 mol % NaOMe was used, affording a reaction mixture containing desired product 9c (90–95 %)… Quenching the reaction with Et₃N·HCl… gave isolated carbonate 9c in 96 % yield with ∼96 % purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: Negishi coupling of aryl bromide 26c with the in‑situ generated alkylzinc 28 gave poor conversion when conventional zinc activation methods (DIBAL‑H, LHMDS/NiCl₂, etc.) were used; many additives gave low zincation conversion and the reaction was irreproducible on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Addition of 10 mol % trimethylsilyl chloride (TMSCl) alone activated the zinc dust, giving quantitative zincation (entry 6, Table 2). Adding 0.05–0.5 equiv of LiCl dramatically accelerated the subsequent Negishi coupling (98 % conversion with 0.5 equiv LiCl versus 10 % without). On kilogram scale the mixture of TMSCl (5–10 mol %) and LiCl (≈0.5 equiv) was added gradually to control the exotherm and ensure reliable zinc activation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Laboratory trials with many of these reagents gave poor results… (Table 2, entries 1–5).” ; “When TMSCl (10 mol %) was added… high conversion was observed… Subsequent experiments showed that TMSCl alone is sufficient… Adding as little as 0.05 equiv of LiCl… afforded 98 % conversion versus 10 % without LiCl… The optimal charge of LiCl was 0.5 equiv, allowing the reaction to reach full conversion in ∼2 h.”; “On larger scales with mechanical stirring both TMSCl (5–10 mol %) and LiCl (∼0.5 equiv) were added to provide more reliable zincation.”

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: During the Negishi coupling the palladium catalyst was rapidly deactivated by the alkylzinc reagent if the alkylzinc was added to the catalyst before the aryl bromide, leading to a dark mixture and loss of activity.
Solution_Description: The alkylzinc solution was added slowly to a pre‑mixed suspension of Pd catalyst and aryl bromide 26c, which prevented catalyst deactivation and moderated the highly exothermic reaction. A small pre‑dose of alkylzinc was also used to scavenge residual oxygen before catalyst charging, allowing catalyst loading to be reduced to 0.1 mol % while maintaining robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “The palladium catalyst was readily deactivated by alkylzinc 28 in the absence of aryl bromide 26c: the reaction mixture turned dark rapidly… Therefore, a THF solution of alkylzinc 28 was slowly added to a mixture of the catalyst and the aryl bromide.”; “The catalyst loading was further reduced to 0.1 mol % by scavenging residual oxygen in the reaction system with a small amount of 28 prior to catalyst charge…”

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: In the key sp³‑sp² Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling, a 5–10 % side‑product (imidazolinone 38) was formed via cyclodehydration of the diamide side chain; impurity increased with temperature and aging, and the acetate groups were cleaved by strong bases or nucleophiles, limiting reaction conditions.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent from DMF/MeCN to i‑propyl alcohol (i‑PrOH) suppressed acetate cleavage while maintaining conversion. The reaction temperature was lowered to ≤50 °C (optimum 50 °C) to minimise imidazolinone formation. Using 0.5 mol % [Pd‑allyl]Cl₂ with 1.1 mol % DPP‑butane as ligand gave high conversion and clean product.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the overall transformation was fairly clean, a major side product (5–10 %), imidazolinone 38, formed via cyclodehydration… imidazolinone impurity 38 increased with temperature and aging time… The liability of the acetate groups to strong bases… also limited the scope of reaction conditions.”; “EtOH performed most efficiently, it also readily cleaved the acetate groups… Therefore, reaction optimization was continued with i‑PrOH as the solvent…” ; “Preforming the active catalyst complex by stirring [Pd‑allyl]Cl₂ and DPPbutane… resulted in a palladium‑allyl‑ligand complex 39… Ultimately, only 0.5 mol % [Pd‑allyl]Cl₂ and 1.1 mol % DPPbutane were required under the optimized reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route to LX2761 relied on a Heck coupling that required expensive methyl 3‑butenoate, microwave heating, olefin hydrogenation and preparative HPLC purification, making the process costly and impractical for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A convergent retrosynthetic disconnection was designed, linking two fully elaborated fragments via a late‑stage sp³‑sp² Suzuki coupling of a benzyl carbonate with a hindered arylboronic ester. This route avoided the expensive reagents, eliminated the need for HPLC purification, and was successfully scaled to kilogram quantities for toxicology and pre‑clinical studies.
Supporting_Evidence: “The Heck coupling approach required expensive methyl 3‑butenoate… preparative HPLC purification to obtain LX2761 with acceptable purity.”; “Our revised retrosynthetic analysis dissected the target at the central diarylmethane linkage… a less conventional approach featuring a late‑stage sp³‑sp² Suzuki coupling… intensive experimentation ultimately yielded a scalable process route to LX2761.”

Paper Title: Process Development for a Locally Acting SGLT1 Inhibitor, LX2761, Utilizing sp
Problem_Description: The final API, LX2761, exhibited very low solubility in water and high affinity for aqueous layers, leading to large material losses during extraction and difficulties in obtaining a crystalline solid suitable for formulation.
Solution_Description: Screening of ~40 pharmaceutically acceptable acids identified l‑proline as a suitable co‑former; the free base was converted to the target by saponification, and the resulting mixture was treated with l‑proline in EtOH/H₂O. Addition of MTBE as antisolvent and cooling gave the LX2761·l‑proline cocrystal, which was isolated in 91 % yield with >99 % purity, providing a stable solid form for downstream processing.
Supporting_Evidence: “While LX2761 was not very soluble in pure water, high losses to the aqueous layers were observed during extraction… It also proved challenging to reproducibly obtain crystalline LX2761 directly… A screening of approximately 40 pharmaceutically acceptable acids… identified a well‑defined LX2761·l‑proline cocrystal (1:1) that exhibited acceptable physicochemical properties.”; “The penultimate intermediate 35 was treated with catalytic sodium methoxide… Subsequently, a solution of l‑proline in EtOH/H₂O was prepared… Upon addition of MTBE… the LX2761·l‑proline cocrystal crystallized smoothly… performed successfully on a kilogram scale in 91 % yield with >99 % purity.”

Paper Title: Asymmetric Synthesis of a Key Intermediate for Tofacitinib via a Dynamic Kinetic Resolution-Reductive Amination Protocol
Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several scale‑up obstacles: (1) previously reported ARA‑DKR methods required high catalyst loadings, expensive reductants, protective groups and long reaction times, making them unsuitable for manufacturing; (2) attempts to promote racemisation with a strong base (t‑BuOK) caused rapid catalyst deactivation; (3) early catalyst screens gave low enantiomeric excess, indicating insufficient racemisation and variable stereocontrol; (4) water generated in the imine‑formation step led to hydrolysis and formation of the undesired alcohol side‑product, lowering overall yield; (5) low substrate‑to‑catalyst (S/C) ratios produced poor ee and incomplete conversion, again hurting cost efficiency; (6) excessive acetic‑acid additive reduced the observed ee, showing sensitivity to reagent stoichiometry.
Solution_Description: The team resolved these issues as follows: (1) High‑throughput screening identified an Ir/BiPheP catalyst that delivers high activity at very low loadings, meeting cost targets; (2) They switched from basic to mildly acidic conditions (acetic acid) to effect racemisation, avoiding catalyst decomposition; (3) The optimized protocol performs the reductive amination in one pot, telescoping the imine formation and hydrogenation and eliminating isolation steps; (4) Raising the reaction temperature to 70 °C accelerated both hydrogenation and racemisation, removed the need for excess acid, and improved conversion and selectivity; (5) Raising the S/C ratio (up to 10 000 : 1) increased ee and overall productivity while further lowering catalyst usage; (6) Reducing the amount of acetic acid (to 0–1 equiv) eliminated its negative impact on ee.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem 1: “All of these protocols, however, are arguably not directly applicable for production at scale due to their high catalyst loadings or relatively high‑cost reducing agents … or long reaction times.”
Problem 2: “very low yield… indicating a strong catalyst deactivation by t‑BuOK… the chiral catalyst decomposed under basic conditions into an achiral Ir species.”
Problem 3: “Enantiomeric excesses (E.e.) were overall low… low E.e. indicate that very little to no racemisation… took place.”
Problem 4: “small amounts of alcohol 5 are observed in MeOH and IPA due to the residual water … leads to hydrolysis of 4 back to 3.”
Problem 5: “Increasing S/C from 50 to 1000 mol mol⁻¹ lead to a significant increase in enantiomeric excess.”
Problem 6: “large excess of acetic acid appeared to be detrimental to the enantiomeric excess (entry 6)."
Solution 1: “high‑throughput experimentation was key to identify a catalyst based on Ir and BiPheP … active at loadings compatible with the severe cost requirement imposed on industrial manufacturing.”
Solution 2: “we needed to verify … that the imine 4 could be formed in the presence of acetic acid… many catalysts were active under acidic conditions.”
Solution 3: “high yields … were obtained, achieving the direct conversion from ketone 3 into the desired amine without isolation of the imine 4, that is, truly an asymmetric reductive amination process.”
Solution 4: “by increasing the temperature to 70 °C, full conversion … additional acetic acid was no longer needed … slight increase in D.e. and E.e. …”
Solution 5: “At a remarkably high substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio of 10 000, a yield of a single diastereomer (84 % assay yield) was obtained … indicating that the catalyst was sufficiently active and robust for a cost‑effective implementation at scale.”
Solution 6: “large excess of acetic acid appeared to be detrimental …” (implies the corrective action of lowering the acid equiv).

Paper Title: Development of Asymmetric Transfer Hydrogenation with a Bifunctional Oxo-Tethered Ruthenium Catalyst in Flow for the Synthesis of a Ceramide (
Problem_Description: Initial asymmetric transfer hydrogenation (ATH) of methyl 2‑acetamido‑3‑oxooctadecanoate (5) using the Ru‑DPEN catalyst gave only 62–77 % diastereomeric excess (de) and 88–97 % ee after an 8 h reaction, indicating sub‑optimal conversion and a long reaction time for acceptable selectivity.
Solution_Description: Switch to the oxo‑tethered Ru complex (R,R)-Ts‑DENEB, which provided >98 % conversion and 74 % de in entry 2 of Table 1, and extend the residence time to 20 h (entry 4) to achieve complete conversion without loss of selectivity.

2. "Compared with the prototype catalyst (entry 1), the Ts‑derivative oxo‑tethered Ru(II) complex ((R,R)-Ts‑DENEB) exhibited superior activity (entry 2) and optimal catalytic performance in terms of the yield and enantioselectivity. When the reaction time was increased to 20 h, the reaction completed without loss of diastereoselectivity or enantioselectivity (entry 4)." (Results and Discussion, p. 3-4)

Problem_Description: The NaBH₄‑mediated ester reduction of the crude ATH product 7 gave almost no conversion to the reduced diol 8 when the reaction mixture contained 3 equiv of triethylamine (basic conditions).

Problem_Description: In batch autoclave experiments the larger gas headspace (~30 % N₂) caused CO₂ accumulation, which inhibited the asymmetric transfer hydrogenation and reduced conversion compared with the flow reactor (conversion dropped to 82 %).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Maintaining the cryogenic temperatures (‑95 °C to ‑100 °C) required for the Matteson lithiation step becomes increasingly difficult at larger scale, and poor mixing in the batch reactor can lead to local hot spots and incorrect local stoichiometries, causing by‑product formation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow concept was adopted. The flow reactor uses stainless‑steel tubing immersed in a cooling bath, providing uniform low‑temperature control and high‑shear turbulent mixing, which eliminates hot spots and enables safe handling of the cryogenic organolithium species.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The conversion of this step from a batch to a flow process was necessitated by the low temperature requirements of this transformation. Achievement of such low temperatures becomes increasingly difficult in a plant setting with increasing scale" (Sec 1). 
- "poor mixing may result in by‑product formation, due to local hot spots and/or incorrect local stoichiometries" (Sec 1). 
- "The continuous flow setup ... mixing elements ... reactors placed in a cooling bath" (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Initial experiments at –40 °C gave poor conversion of substrate 3 (only ≈10 % product, entries 1–2 in Table 1), leading to low isolated yield of the desired α‑chloroboronic ester 4.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was lowered to –78 °C and the residence time in reactors R3 and R4 was increased, which shifted the product distribution to >90 % conversion and gave an isolated yield of 86 % for 4.
Supporting_Evidence:

- Table 1 data showing low conversion at –40 °C and improved conversion at –78 °C with longer residence times.

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: Using a larger excess of ZnCl₂ to improve diastereoselectivity caused precipitation and clogging of reactor R4, especially when the rearrangement was performed at lower temperature.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The zinc‑catalyzed rearrangement was moved out of the flow line; the stream exiting the flow reactor was quenched in a batch vessel containing a precooled ZnCl₂ solution, and both the substrate and n‑BuLi streams were diluted with THF to prevent solid formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Improvement of the diastereoselectivity ... larger excess of zinc chloride resulted in clogging of reactor R4" (Sec 2.2). 
- "the zinc‑catalyzed rearrangement reaction was no longer performed in a flow reactor. Instead, the process stream ... was quenched in a batch reactor containing a precooled zinc chloride solution. Undesired precipitation of solid material was further prevented by diluting both the substrate and n‑BuLi solutions with THF" (Sec 2.2).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: A relatively large excess of n‑BuLi was required at the low operating temperature; if the mixture warmed prior to quench, side‑product formation increased, raising safety concerns and reagent cost.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was fine‑tuned (≈1.4 equiv n‑BuLi) and the reaction temperature optimized to –80 °C, allowing full conversion while minimizing excess organolithium, thus reducing side‑product formation and reagent cost.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: During scale‑up, increasing reactor length without changing diameter risked blockage by solid particles; maintaining residence time while avoiding clogging was a key challenge.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The pilot reactor was built with a larger diameter and longer tubing, keeping residence times constant; additional internal mixing elements were installed to promote turbidity‑free flow and prevent solid buildup.
Supporting_Evidence:

- "Turbulent mixing of the flows at the low temperature is required … the viscosity … is rather high … we decided to use additional mixing elements" (Sec 2.3.3).

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: The zinc‑chloride quench step was performed in batch mode, creating a volume and time bottleneck that limited overall throughput and raised operational cost.

Solution_Description: Two continuous‑quench concepts were designed – a loop reactor and a cascade of CSTRs – allowing the quench to be performed continuously, eliminating the bottleneck and improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Development of a Continuous Flow Process for a Matteson Reaction: From Lab Scale to Full-Scale Production of a Pharmaceutical Intermediate
Problem_Description: When choosing between the loop reactor and CSTR quench designs, the CSTR required high‑cost pressure‑resistant Hastelloy hardware, while the loop reactor could be built from simple tubing, offering a safer, lower‑cost solution.
Solution_Description: The loop reactor was selected for scale‑up because it is highly pressure‑resistant, inexpensive (tube, pump, heat‑exchanger only), and offers a safe operating mode, meeting the commercial needs.
Supporting_Evidence:
- Table 6 comparison: "Process safety – Highly pressure resistant, safe mode of operation" for loop; "Costs – Low costs as it simply consists of a tube, a pump and a heat exchanger" (Sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Multikilogram-Scale Preparation of AZD4635 via C–H Borylation and Bromination: The Corrosion of Tantalum by a Bromine/Methanol Mixture

Paper Title: Scaling Up UV-Mediated Intramolecular Photodehydro-Diels–Alder Reactions Using a Homemade High-Performance Annular Continuous-Flow Reactor
