Problem_Description: The scale‑up strategy for fast reactions is not established because the effect of reactor size on mixing performance, heat removal and the observable reaction rate cannot be quantified reliably.
Solution_Description: The authors constructed dimensionless‑based charts (mixing‑rate vs. observable kinetic constant and temperature‑rise vs. reactor diameter) using CFD and experimental validation, providing a quantitative tool to assess mixing and heat‑removal limits for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the scale‑up strategy for fast reactions is not established enough due to the difficulty in quantifying the effect of the reactor size on the mixing performance, heat removal, and observable reaction rate.”; “We present a chart for analyzing the effect of the mixing rate on the observable kinetic constant and a chart for estimating the temperature increase in the reactor.”; “Commercial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software was employed to solve the partial differential equations and to build the charts, and experiments were conducted to validate the results.”

Paper Title: Numerical and Experimental Quantification of the Performance of Microreactors for Scaling-up Fast Chemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Kinetic‑parameter determination for reactions faster than 1 s is unreliable because mixing may limit the observable rate, making it hard to know whether experiments are reaction‑limited or mixing‑limited.
Solution_Description: A Damköhler‑number (ϕ) based chart was developed to distinguish mixing‑limited from reaction‑limited regimes; if ϕ ≤ 1 the observed kinetic constant equals the true rate, giving a clear criterion for valid kinetic analysis.
Supporting_Evidence: “Rate analysis is valid only when experiments are conducted under reaction‑limited conditions… it is difficult to certify that the results obtained within a second were not affected by mixing at all.”; “Dimensionless numbers were used to build a chart to determine whether the reaction was in the reaction‑limited condition or in the mixing‑limited condition.”; “η = 1 means that mixing is fast enough compared to the reaction so the reaction rate is not influenced by the mass transfer.”

Paper Title: Numerical and Experimental Quantification of the Performance of Microreactors for Scaling-up Fast Chemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Traditional chemical test reactions (Bourne, Villermaux‑Dushman) give mixing‑time estimates that can differ by an order of magnitude from the actual mixing time in microreactors, leading to misleading design data.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced empirical test reactions with CFD‑derived dimensionless correlations that directly relate reactor geometry and operating conditions to mixing time, providing a more accurate and universal prediction method.
Supporting_Evidence: “the actual mixing time could differ by an order of magnitude from the estimation based on the chemical test reaction systems… many studies using CFD simulations have revealed important factors for mixer design… an easy‑to‑use relationship for determining mixing time… is hardly found.”; “The relationship between the mixing rate and the observable reaction rate was evaluated by numerically solving PDEs for a simplified situation.”; “Commercial computational fluid dynamics (CFD) software was employed … to build the charts.”

Paper Title: Numerical and Experimental Quantification of the Performance of Microreactors for Scaling-up Fast Chemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Estimating the temperature rise in a microreactor traditionally requires the activation energy of the reaction, which is often unavailable, making heat‑removal analysis impractical for many organic syntheses.
Solution_Description: A new dimensionless number β (ratio of reaction rate to thermal‑diffusion rate) was introduced, allowing the maximum temperature increase to be predicted without needing activation‑energy data.
Supporting_Evidence: “the temperature increase played a minor and unimportant role in the Bourne reactions… their function as a probe for temperature increase is rather qualitative… organolithium reactions… can be dramatically changed by a temperature difference of only 5 K.”; “A dimensionless number β was employed for analyzing the results… When β was 0.1, the temperature increase was approximately 2 % to the adiabatic condition, meaning that isothermal operation was almost achieved.”; “The relationship between β and ΔTmax/ΔTad is universal … does not require the activation energy.”

Paper Title: Numerical and Experimental Quantification of the Performance of Microreactors for Scaling-up Fast Chemical Reactions
Problem_Description: In the protecting‑group‑free organolithium halogen‑lithium exchange, the highly reactive p‑APLi intermediate decomposes within milliseconds, and the reaction is extremely temperature‑sensitive, limiting yield to ≤ 76 %.
Solution_Description: The process was performed in three T‑mixers kept at 0 °C (first mixer) and –70 °C (second and third mixers); electrophile (methanol) was added in a millisecond‑scale sequential fashion; reagents were supplied in excess (e.g., MesBr 1.5 equiv, methanol 2 equiv) to ensure rapid trapping of the intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “The first mixer was for the in situ generation of MesLi… The second mixer … The third mixer was for trapping p‑APLi with methanol… All mixers had an internal diameter of 0.5 mm… The temperature of the device was controlled by immersing the first mixer in an ice bath at 0 °C and immersing the second and third mixers in an acetone bath at –70 °C.”; “By sequentially adding electrophiles such as methanol within a time scale of milliseconds, desired products … were obtained with a yield of up to 76 %.”; “p‑APLi easily attacked the unprotected ketone carbonyl group… leading to by‑products.”

Paper Title: Numerical and Experimental Quantification of the Performance of Microreactors for Scaling-up Fast Chemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Scaling the microreactor diameter from 0.25 mm to 0.5 mm for the ultrafast organolithium reaction risks exceeding the heat‑removal capacity (β ≫ 1) while still requiring sub‑millisecond mixing times.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Commercial tee‑mixers and stainless‑steel tubing (0.5 mm i.d.) were employed, and flow rates were increased (up to 213 mL min⁻¹, Re ≈ 6300) to achieve mixing < 1 ms; despite β rising to > 2000, the temperature rise remained modest, enabling an 8‑fold increase in throughput.
Supporting_Evidence: “The mixing time must be kept within a few milliseconds… a reactor diameter of 0.5 mm… can achieve mixing within 1 ms with a large enough Re.”; “β went even higher than 2000, but the temperature increase in estimation itself changed little compared to the original condition.”; “The original results… using commercial tees and tubing… The total flow rate was 213 mL min⁻¹, product throughput 0.44 mol h⁻¹, 8 times higher.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: The N‑oxide products and the generated m‑chlorobenzoic acid are highly water‑soluble, making it difficult to isolate the product by conventional biphasic extraction and causing loss of material during work‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction was moved to isopropyl acetate (iPrOAc), a low‑polarity, high‑boiling solvent that reduces the water‑solubility of the N‑oxide and allows the m‑chlorobenzoic acid to precipitate as its ammonium salt when anhydrous NH₃(g) is sparged, facilitating solid‑phase separation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The high water solubility of N‑oxides poses difficulty in isolation and purification during biphasic extractive workup.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: When hydrocarbon solvents (hexanes, cyclohexane) were used, a non‑filterable cake of ammonium m‑chlorobenzoate formed, entrapping product and creating mixing/filtration problems; these solvents are also highly flammable, raising safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Switch to chlorinated solvents (DCM, DCE) and finally to ICH‑class‑3 esters (EtOAc, iPrOAc) that give comparable yields, avoid caking, and have lower flammability. The chosen solvent also improves recovery and reduces utility use.
Supporting_Evidence: • “In hexanes and cyclohexane, it posed the difficulty of a nonfilterable cake … that entrapped the product.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: The oxidation of pyridine with m‑CPBA is strongly exothermic, and uncontrolled addition could lead to runaway temperature increases, especially at larger scale.
Solution_Description: m‑CPBA was added in ten equal portions over 45–50 min while maintaining the reaction mass at 10–15 °C; after addition the mixture was aged 10 min before the next dose and then warmed to 30–35 °C for 4 h. This staged addition and temperature control limits the heat rise to ≤ 19.4 K (ΔT).
Supporting_Evidence: • “The oxidation is known to be an exothermic reaction. … Temperature was optimized … 10–15 °C during addition … 30–35 °C up to 4 h … resulted in maximum conversion.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: Residual peroxide from m‑CPBA can persist after oxidation, presenting an explosion hazard when the mixture is later distilled.
Solution_Description: Sodium sulfite (2 g / 200 g scale, 25 g / 2.5 kg scale) was added after the reaction; the peroxide test became negative and no heat was observed on addition, confirming safe quenching before work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “There was a possibility that traces of peroxide could still be present … To design a hazard‑free workup … sodium sulfite … was added … No heat change was observed during the addition of sodium sulfite.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: Ammonia sparging to convert m‑chlorobenzoic acid into its ammonium salt is highly exothermic; uncontrolled gas flow can cause rapid temperature spikes.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Ammonia gas flow was staged: start at 100–110 mL min⁻¹ for 1 h, then 150–180 mL min⁻¹ for 1 h, finally 180–200 mL min⁻¹ for the last period, all while keeping the reaction temperature at 10–15 °C. This controlled the exotherm (max ΔT = 2.3 K) and kept the process in Stoessel class 1.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Formation of the ammonium salt is an exothermic process … rate of gas sparging was optimized to 180–200 mL/min… The data revealed that the maximum temperature rise during addition was 2.3 K …”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: Attempts to precipitate m‑chlorobenzoic acid as triethylammonium salt failed (no precipitation), and sodium salts gave poor yields due to high water solubility of the resulting salts.
Solution_Description: Instead of using organic or inorganic bases, the authors introduced anhydrous NH₃(g) directly into the organic reaction mixture, which cleanly precipitated the ammonium m‑chlorobenzoate, allowing quantitative filtration and > 96 % recovery of the acid.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Triethylammonium salts did not precipitate … sodium salts resulted in poor yields because of the considerable water solubilities … To overcome these complexities … sparging anhydrous ammonia … ammonium m‑chlorobenzoate precipitated … separated quantitatively by filtration.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: The traditional use of chlorinated solvents (DCM, DCE) poses cost and regulatory issues (ICH class 1–2, high volatility, toxicity).
Solution_Description: Switching to iPrOAc (ICH class 3) provided comparable yields (98 %), higher solvent recovery (90–92 %), and reduced waste and utility costs, while still being compatible with m‑CPBA.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Because chlorinated solvents in ICH class 1 or 2 need to be replaced … the use of an environmentally benign ICH class 3 solvents such as ethyl acetate (EtOAc) or isopropyl acetate (iPrOAc) was desirable. These two solvents gave comparable yields and purities … iPrOAc was the solvent of choice.”

Paper Title: The
Problem_Description: Initial oxidation gave quantitative conversion, but the subsequent isolation steps (filtration, solvent removal) were time‑consuming and sometimes resulted in loss of product due to caking or incomplete recovery.
Solution_Description: A high solvent‑to‑reactant ratio (17.5 vol) was employed to keep the mixture low‑viscosity, facilitate efficient stirring, and enable rapid solvent recovery (90 % under 20 mm Hg), thereby shortening the overall batch time while maintaining > 97 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The improved heat capacity due to the solvent:reactant ratio of 17.5, the controlled addition … allow the protocol to satisfy most of the safety criteria.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: In the traditional batch route that uses diazotization of 2,4,6‑trimethylaniline, the generated diazonium salt is extremely unstable, readily decomposes with nitrogen evolution and can cause runaway or explosion; this also leads to a low isolated yield (~60 %).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The process was moved to a continuous‑flow reactor (Hastelloy C276 tubing) where the diazonium salt is generated and consumed instantaneously, eliminating accumulation, improving heat removal and mixing, and thereby removing the safety hazard and increasing yield (to 85 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “...the diazonium salt is easily decomposed and releases nitrogen, which may lead to accidents.”; “In the continuous‑flow process, diazonium salt and triazole solution entered flow reactor at the same time, which could effectively avoid the safety risk because of the excellent control ability of the reactor.”; “The continuous‑flow reactor has high heat transfer efficiency…the back mixing can be ignored.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: During batch diazotization, the reactants exist as a solid‑liquid mixture at low temperature, causing severe back‑mixing and leading to side‑products a (hydrolysis) and b (reaction with unreacted aniline), which reduces the product yield to ~60 %.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Adopting a plug‑flow continuous‑flow reactor removes back‑mixing; the rapid, homogeneous mixing suppresses formation of by‑products a and b, raising the yield to 72 % for the diazotization step.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the reactants are in a solid–liquid state, resulting in competing side reactions…Decomposition via hydrolysis of the diazonium salt produces a. And under severe back mixing, a consecutive side reaction occurs, resulting in b.”; “The continuous‑flow reactor is very close to the plug‑flow reactor in which the back mixing can be ignored…byproducts a and b can be inhibited by continuous‑flow process.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: Excessive sodium hydroxide in the diazotization step promotes intramolecular coupling (by‑product c), while insufficient base reduces nucleophilicity, both lowering overall yield and potentially generating hazardous intermediates.
Solution_Description: Systematic variation of NaOH equivalents identified 2.5 equiv as optimal, providing sufficient nucleophilicity without promoting the intramolecular coupling, thereby maximizing yield (≈63 %) and reducing by‑product c.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the amount of sodium hydroxide was 2.5 equiv, the yield arrived at a maximum value of 63%…When the amount of sodium hydroxide was too low or too high, the yield was not high.”; “Stronger alkalinity resulted in increasing of intramolecular coupling side‑product c.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: In continuous‑flow diazotization, prolonged residence time (>20 s) or higher temperature accelerates diazonium salt decomposition, decreasing product yield.
Solution_Description: Optimized conditions (τ₁ = 10 s, T₁ = 10 °C, F_A/F_N = 1:1.05) were selected, which limit the exposure of the diazonium intermediate to heat and time, giving a yield increase from 60 % to 72 % and reducing by‑products a and b to <3 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yield increased with prolonged residence time τ₁, but after more than 20 s…the yield no longer increased but instead decreased because of the decomposition of diazonium salt.”; “The increase in temperature accelerated the degradation rate of diazonium salt…The most appropriate conditions…τ₁ = 10 s, T₁ = 10 °C, F_A/F_N = 1:1.05.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: For the dediazoniation step, higher temperatures cause rapid diazonium decomposition and lower conversion; lower temperatures give sluggish reaction, both resulting in sub‑optimal yield.
Solution_Description: The optimal dediazoniation parameters were set to T₂ = 25 °C, τ₂ = 40 s, and F_T/F_A = 1.2:1, which provided a maximum isolated yield of 85 % and reduced by‑product c to <2 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion rate was slow at lower temperature and due to the instability of the diazonium salt at a higher temperature, resulting in decreased reaction yield.”; “After 40 s, the yield was almost unchanged, so the appropriate residence time was 40 s.”; “The maximum yield of 85% was obtained when reaction temperature T₂ = 25 °C, residence time τ₂ = 40 s, and molar flow ratio of triazole and diazo solution F_T/F_A = 1.2:1.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: By‑products have poor water solubility and tend to precipitate, causing fouling of the reacting tube and complicating downstream purification.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An inert solvent stream (n‑heptane) was added after the second T‑joint to extract the hydrophobic by‑products in situ, preventing tube fouling and enabling direct isolation of the product with 98 % purity without additional purification steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “The target product was in the form of sodium salt … while the water solubility of by‑products was poor. Therefore, we considered adding inert solvent … to extract the by‑products in situ, which was also beneficial to inhibit fouling of reacting tube.”; “n‑heptane was chosen…flow rate of 4 mL/min…resulted in an 86 % isolated yield with a product purity of 98 % without further purification.”

Paper Title: Conversion of 2,4,6-Trimethylaniline to 3‑(Mesitylthio)‑1
Problem_Description: The batch synthesis required 3 h total reaction time and gave only 60 % yield, limiting productivity.
Solution_Description: Implementation of a two‑step continuous‑flow process reduced the overall reaction time to 50 s and increased the isolated yield to 85 % (productivity 344 g h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1 shows batch reaction time = 3 h, yield = 60 %; advanced continuous‑flow time = 50 s, yield = 85 %.; “The synthesis … via a continuous‑flow reactor … productivity of 344 g/h.”

Paper Title: Construction of a (3
Problem_Description: The original discovery route to the key fragment 2·2HCl required silica‑gel chromatography to separate endo/exo diastereomers and a chiral preparative HPLC step to resolve enantiomers.  The route also relied on an expensive, commercially unavailable starting material (compound 4) and used Dy(OTf)₃ as a reagent.  All intermediates from 4 to the rac‑endo‑6 were oils, preventing crystallization‑based purification.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation asymmetric route was developed that employed a rhodium‑catalysed hydrogen‑mediated domino cyclisation to directly convert enamine 19 to the hexahydropyrroloquinoline 16.  This eliminated the need for silica gel and chiral HPLC separations, allowed isolation by simple crystallisation of the p‑TsOH salt, and removed the reliance on the costly Dy(OTf)₃ and on the unavailable starting material.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Compound 2·2HCl had been originally prepared … after two column separations: silica gel chromatography … and chiral preparative high‑performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) …”
“Besides the highly expensive and commercially unavailable starting material 4, several issues were identified … (ii) endo/exo selectivity … (iii) use of expensive reagents, for example, Dy(OTf)₃; (iv) no possibility for a purification step by crystallisation, because all compounds … were oils.”
“The resulting stereoselective domino cyclisation drastically reduced several synthetic steps, and the resulting waste compared to the discovery route …”

Paper Title: Construction of a (3
Problem_Description: During the β‑acylation of Cbz‑protected pyrrolidin‑2‑one 21 to give the potassium salt 20·K, the isolated yield dropped from 56 % at lab scale to 37 % on an 88 kg batch.  Large white aggregates formed in the reaction mixture, severely hindering mixing during the aqueous HCl quench step and causing poor reproducibility.
Solution_Description: The quench protocol was altered by adding a small amount of acetic acid (0.8 wt % to 21) before the aqueous HCl work‑up, which prevented aggregate formation and gave a more reliable process, albeit with a modest decrease in isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Unfortunately, although 20·K was obtained in 56 % yield … the isolated yield … was not reproducible at a larger scale. … a moderate decrease in the yield (37 %) was observed, which was thought to be due to the large white aggregated substances that formed … and inhibited mixing … during the reaction quenching step with a HCl aqueous solution.”
“The quenching method was examined further, and it was found that no aggregated substance was observed when AcOH (0.8 wt % to 21) was added … although the isolated yield … decreased from 56 % to 34 % because of work‑up issues.”

Paper Title: Construction of a (3
Problem_Description: The first‑generation asymmetric hydrogenation of enamine 11 (using [Rh(cod)₂]OTf and (S)‑(R)‑SL‑J210‑2) gave low conversion to the desired hydrogenation product, resulting in poor overall yield of the downstream intermediate.
Solution_Description: A systematic ligand screen identified (2S,4S)‑PTBP‑SKEWPHOS as a superior bis‑phosphine ligand, delivering high conversion without loss of enantioselectivity, thus improving the efficiency of the hydrogenation step.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The first‑generation asymmetric route condition … gave low conversion … and other ligands such as CHIRAPHOS, DIOP, and BINAP gave similar results.”
“The result of exploring additives … after modifying SKEWPHOS ligands, we adopted (2S,4S)‑PTBP‑SKEWPHOS as the bisphosphine ligand because of the high conversion obtained without decrease of enantioselectivity compared to simple SKEWPHOS.”

Paper Title: Construction of a (3
Problem_Description: The stereoselective hydrogen‑mediated domino cyclisation of enamine 19 required prolonged reaction times (up to 48 h) under high hydrogen pressure (5–6 MPa) and elevated temperatures (45 °C), presenting both throughput and safety concerns for large‑scale manufacture.
Solution_Description: Acetone was selected as the optimal solvent after screening.  Cyanuric acid and 2,2‑dimethoxypropane were added as promoters to trap water and enhance reaction progress.  The (2S,4S)‑PTBP‑SKEWPHOS rhodium catalyst was employed at 1.66 mol % (s/c = 60) to achieve high conversion in a reduced time frame, enabling a robust, scalable protocol.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Acetone was selected as the reaction solvent after the screening of various solvents … The enamine 19 was dissolved in 10 vol of acetone … under 5–6 MPa hydrogen at 45 °C.”
“The addition of cyanuric acid promoted the reaction, and 2,2‑dimethoxypropane was found to have a role to trap the water that is generated as a byproduct in the reaction.”
“The reaction proceeded with perfect diastereoselectivity and moderate enantioselectivity (60 % ee) when using SKEWPHOS … on increasing the hydrogen pressure to 5 MPa, the amount of 16 increased …”
“The reaction mixture was stirred with the hydrogen pressure maintained within the range of 5.0–6.0 MPa at 40–50 °C (set point 45 °C) for 48 h.”

Problem_Description: The isolated hexahydropyrroloquinoline 16·p‑TsOH was obtained with only 63 % ee after crystallisation, necessitating an additional enantiomeric enrichment step to reach the required purity for the API.
Solution_Description: Diastereomeric salt formation with inexpensive L‑tartaric acid was employed to upgrade the ee to >99 %, providing a cost‑effective and scalable method for final enantiopurity enhancement.
Supporting_Evidence: “To improve the enantiomeric excess of 2, the diastereomeric salt formation in EtOH was conducted with l‑tartaric acid, which is inexpensive and commercially available. As a result, 62 kg of 2·L‑tartrate was obtained with greater than 99 % ee from 46 kg of 2 (80 % ee).”

Solution_Description: The new second‑generation route bypasses compound 4 entirely, using inexpensive pyrrolidine‑2‑one (8) as the starting material and a rhodium‑based catalytic system, thereby eliminating the need for the costly reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Besides the highly expensive and commercially unavailable starting material 4, several issues were identified … (iii) use of expensive reagents, for example, Dy(OTf)₃.”
“The original aim was to replace the protecting group PMB with Cbz … the novel stereoselective hydrogen‑mediated domino cyclisation was able to directly convert the enamine (19) to the hexahydropyrroloquinoline (16).”

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: Traditional oxidants (KMnO₄, Cr‑VI, OsO₄, Oxone, tert‑butyl hydroperoxide) are toxic, expensive or both, limiting their use on an industrial scale.
Solution_Description: Switch to hydrogen peroxide (30–50 wt %) as the oxidant, which is inexpensive, readily available, and environmentally benign.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Old‑fashioned stoichiometric oxidants, such as KMnO₄, Cr‑(VI) compounds, and OsO₄ + NaIO₄ (Lemieux–Johnson protocol), are toxic and/or generate many byproducts, and their industrial applications are limited.", "Methods that use Oxone or PhI‑(OAc)₂ have also been widely employed; however, these oxidants are quite expensive.", "The best choice for performing C‑C bond cleavage is to use molecular oxygen or hydrogen peroxide because they are readily available and environmentally friendly oxidants."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: C₃₀⁺ α‑olefins are solid at room temperature, melt around 70 °C and form two phases when water or aqueous H₂O₂ is added, giving very viscous, poorly mixed reaction mixtures.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Introduce a small amount of a hydrocarbon diluent (heptane, methyl‑cyclohexane, or tert‑butyl‑benzene) to lower the melting point and viscosity, and use a mechanical stirrer (300–500 rpm) – optionally a dual‑propeller arrangement – to maintain homogeneity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["C₃₀⁺ olefins are solids at room temperature and have melting points near 70 °C. Molten C₃₀⁺ olefins form a homogeneous mixture with tert‑butyl alcohol, but the addition of water (or aqueous H₂O₂) results in the formation of two phases.", "The solvent‑free processes suffer from high viscosities (because of the required presence of the PTC), and thus, to achieve vigorous mixing, a mechanical stirrer is required (at 500 rpm for mixing a solvent‑free mixture and 300 rpm for the process conducted with a diluent).", "The solidification and high viscosities of the reaction mixtures in the studied solvent‑free reactions encouraged us to employ aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons (methylcyclohexane, heptane, and tert‑butylbenzene) as diluents."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: Use of H₂SO₄ or high loadings of H₂WO₄ (3 wt %) causes a sharp temperature rise (up to >100 °C) during the first 1–2 h, presenting a safety hazard on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Prefer the weaker acid H₃PO₄ (0.5 M, 17 µmol g⁻¹) instead of H₂SO₄, keep the catalyst loading at 1.5 wt % and run the reaction at 80–90 °C. Reduce the amount of added H₂SO₄ or eliminate it altogether, which suppresses the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We observed that a considerable amount of heat was produced during the first 1–2 h of the processes conducted with H₂SO₄. This suggests that one of the steps in the reaction pathway under these conditions is very fast and/or highly exothermic (probably hydrolysis of the epoxide).", "When a more efficient PTC catalyst, CTMAPTS, was used, only the positive effect of adding a small amount of H₃PO₄ was observed.", "When the loading of H₂WO₄ was 3 wt % in a reaction with Luviquat, very high AN and SN values were achieved; however, the reaction mixture reached a temperature above 100 °C for a while at the beginning of this exothermic process, indicating very fast reactions after activation of the catalyst, which is unwanted for safety reasons.", "A further increase in the reaction temperature to 100 °C resulted in a high SN and EN but a relatively low AN… Additionally, we observed that a considerable amount of heat was released at the beginning of the process, which can be dangerous in a scaled‑up process."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: Phase‑transfer catalysts containing halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻) catalyze rapid, unproductive decomposition of H₂O₂ to H₂O/O₂, dramatically lowering oxidation yields.
Solution_Description: Employ halogen‑free quaternary ammonium salts (CTMAPTS, Luviquat, MTOAHS) and generate the active tungstate in situ from H₂WO₄, H₃PO₄ and H₂O₂, thereby eliminating halide ions from the catalytic system.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When CPC containing Cl⁻ ions was used, very low AN and SN values were achieved, and most of the H₂O₂ decomposed unproductively.", "Kadyrov and Hackenberger tested a wide range of ammonium and phosphonium salts … salts with Br⁻ anions catalyze the decomposition of H₂O₂; however, they did not provide any reason for this phenomenon.", "We confirmed that a halogen‑free PTC is necessary to avoid unproductive H₂O₂ decomposition.", "We confirmed that a halogen‑free PTC is necessary to avoid unproductive H₂O₂ decomposition. Therefore, the active form of the tungsten catalyst can be obtained in situ (meaning an extra apparatus is not required in industrial plants for the synthesis of the catalyst) from the halogen‑free PTC, H₂WO₄, and H₂O₂."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: After oxidation, tungsten remains associated with the waxy carboxylic‑acid product, and the high viscosity makes conventional liquid–liquid extraction inefficient.
Solution_Description: Develop a multistep work‑up consisting of sedimentation, decantation, crystallization from a high‑boiling solvent, and optionally adsorption on activated Al₂O₃; heptane proved optimal for washing and tungsten recovery.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Unfortunately, the waxy nature of the oxidation product makes it difficult to separate this catalyst. Therefore, the C₃₀⁺ oxidation product was purified from tungsten compounds in a multistep process that included sedimentation, decantation, crystallization, and filtration.", "Solvents that allowed the greatest degree of purification of the product from tungsten were aliphatic (e.g., heptane) or aromatic (e.g., toluene) hydrocarbons.", "Heptane produced a similar tungsten separation degree as toluene, but the toluene filtrate was yellowish, indicating contamination with tungsten‑(VI) oxide. The heptane filtrate was colorless and was analyzed by means of GC, and no detectable amounts of other organic substances were found.", "The purification using heptane also had no influence on the AN, in contrast to that using 1‑propanol (which decreased the AN).", "Adsorption on Al₂O₃ gave 95 % tungsten removal (0.037 % W remaining)."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: Using 30 wt % H₂O₂ or only 4 equiv of peroxide results in incomplete oxidation, requiring >10 h and giving lower acid numbers.
Solution_Description: Increase the peroxide stoichiometry to 5 equiv (or add the second batch after 8 h) and run the reaction for 10 h; this provides a comparable AN to longer 16 h runs with 4 equiv.
Supporting_Evidence: ["In our studies, a slight excess of H₂O₂ was used (i.e., 5 equiv) because it has been observed that a stoichiometric amount of H₂O₂ (4 equiv) leads to a lower AN.", "Reactions were first conducted for 8 h in the presence of 4 equiv of H₂O₂. Then another 4 equiv of H₂O₂ was added … The ANs increased after the addition of the second amount of H₂O₂, indicating that 4 equiv is not enough for complete oxidation.", "The AN and SN achieved after 16 h for the reactions were similar to or even slightly lower than those found after 10 h of reaction using 5 equiv of H₂O₂."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: Solvent‑free runs cause the reaction mixture to solidify on the reactor wall during the exothermic H₂O₂ addition, impairing heat removal and leading to uncontrolled temperature spikes.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Add a diluent (tert‑butyl‑benzene) to keep the mixture liquid and reduce the heat‑release intensity; employ computer‑controlled H₂O₂ feed and vigorous stirring to maintain uniform temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: ["When the temperature in the reactor quickly increased as a result of the exothermic reactions, the computer sharply decreased the temperature in the jacket to maintain a constant temperature inside the reactor. As a result, partial solidification of the reaction mixture occurred at the reactor wall.", "We decided to use tert‑butylbenzene as the diluent in the next experiments. To our delight, tert‑butylbenzene allowed oxidation to proceed without solidification or overheating.", "The oxidation began when the pump started to introduce H₂O₂ … A sudden increase in the heat flow was detected when H₂O₂ addition began. … The process was safer with more diluent (t‑BuPh), but the oxidation was less efficient and a lower AN was obtained."]

Paper Title: Oxidative Cleavage of Long-Chain Terminal Alkenes to Carboxylic Acids
Problem_Description: High‑purity solvents and large excess of 50 wt % H₂O₂ increase material cost for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Replace 50 wt % H₂O₂ with cheaper 30 wt % H₂O₂ (still giving comparable AN) and keep catalyst loading at 1.5 wt %; the process uses inexpensive, readily available tungstic acid and halogen‑free PTCs.
Supporting_Evidence: ["We established that 50 wt % H₂O₂ can be replaced by 30 wt % H₂O₂, which is less expensive and safer. Similar results were obtained in these two cases.", "Tungstic acid is inexpensive and readily available; CTMAPTS (2.5 wt %) is used as the PTC."]

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis and Impurity Identification of (
Problem_Description: First‑generation synthesis of (R)‑Lacosamide gave a very low overall yield (27 % for the first two steps) and required 5 equiv of silver oxide, which is expensive and unaffordable on a large scale; it also suffered from ~33 % racemization, forcing repeated recrystallisation and further reducing overall yield to 6.9 %.
Solution_Description: A third‑generation route was developed that protects the d‑serine amine with a Boc group, uses tetrabutyl‑ammonium bromide (TBAB) as a phase‑transfer catalyst and a moderate amount of NaOH, thereby eliminating the need for expensive Ag₂O and dramatically reducing racemization; the overall yield increased to 69.8 % under mild conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: - "the fact was that the amino group of 3 could react ... which would lead to a low yield (27%) for the first two steps."

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: The nitroxyl radical TEMPO, although cheaper than many other N‑oxyls, is still relatively expensive for industrial‑scale production (≈ 490 yuan kg⁻¹).
Solution_Description: Replace TEMPO with the much cheaper 4‑OH‑TEMPO (≈ 60 yuan kg⁻¹) as the cocatalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “TEMPO, though much cheaper than many other N‑oxyls… is still relatively expensive for industrial‑scale production.” (Abstract); “In the current Chinese market, TEMPO costs 490 yuan/kg and 4‑OH‑TEMPO costs 60 yuan/kg.” (Ref 16, note).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Using TEMPO leads to significant over‑oxidation of aliphatic alcohols to the corresponding acids (10–11 % acid by‑product) rather than the desired aldehydes.
Solution_Description: Employ 4‑OH‑TEMPO instead of TEMPO, which gives higher selectivity for aldehyde formation and suppresses acid formation.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 3: 85 % aldehyde, 11 % acid; entry 4 (with 4‑OH‑TEMPO): 88 % aldehyde, 3 % acid. “…the new protocol using 4‑OH‑TEMPO… accomplished the transformation with a higher selectivity, especially for aliphatic alcohols toward aldehydes.” (Abstract).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Omission of NaCl dramatically reduces conversion (57 % aldehyde, 34 % recovered alcohol).
Solution_Description: Add NaCl (5 mol % relative to Fe(NO₃)₃) to the reaction mixture to accelerate the iron‑catalyzed oxidation.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 5 (no NaCl): 57 % aldehyde, 34 % recovery; “a significant effect of NaCl for accelerating the reaction.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: The standard protocol required long reaction times (≥ 20 h) to achieve acceptable conversions (≤ 71 % aldehyde yield).
Solution_Description: Increase the catalyst loading (10 mol % Fe(NO₃)₃, 4‑OH‑TEMPO, NaCl) and shorten the reaction time to 19 h, delivering 88 % aldehyde yield.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 1 (20.5 h → 63 % yield); entry 4 (19 h, higher catalyst loading → 88 % yield).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Higher catalyst loadings and longer times lead to over‑oxidation, forming up to 10 % acid by‑product.
Solution_Description: Reduce the reaction time (e.g., from 20 h to 19 h) while keeping catalyst loading high to limit acid formation.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 1, entry 3 (20 h, 85 % aldehyde, 11 % acid) vs. entry 4 (19 h, 88 % aldehyde, 3 % acid).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Polar solvents (CH₃CN, THF, EtOAc, dioxane) give very low aldehyde yields (18–31 %).
Solution_Description: Switch to the chlorinated solvent DCE, which provides the highest conversion (up to 88 % yield).
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2, entries 1–4: 18–31 % yields; “Thus, DCE is the optimal solvent.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: 1,2‑Dichloroethane (DCE) is listed as a hazardous solvent by ICH Q3C (limit 5 ppm).
Solution_Description: Employ toluene as a safer alternative; the reaction still affords high aldehyde yields (92 % for E‑1d).
Supporting_Evidence: “According to the guidelines… DCE is listed as a hazardous solvent… thus, we also carried out the oxidation … using toluene… affording … 92 % yield.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: During the 0.5 mol scale oxidation under pure O₂, the reaction temperature rose to 62 °C, posing a safety risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Control the temperature with an ice bath and use a slow flow of air (30 mL min⁻¹) rather than a bulk O₂ charge to moderate the exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: “The temperature would rise up to 62 °C and an ice water bath was used until the temperature dropped down to 25 °C…” (Sec 4.20.2.3); “a slow flow of air … was then connected to the flask” (Sec 4.20.2).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Pure oxygen poses ignition and over‑pressure hazards, especially on scale.
Solution_Description: Run the oxidation under ambient air instead of pure O₂; the reaction proceeds efficiently (5–9 h, high yields).
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction could also be conducted under air conditions… high yields … in 5–9 h.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Iron-Catalyzed Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols: Lower Cost and Improved Selectivity
Problem_Description: Propargylic alcohols give low conversion with the standard catalyst loading.
Solution_Description: Increase the Fe(NO₃)₃·9H₂O and 4‑OH‑TEMPO loadings to 10 mol % to obtain high yields of alkynals and alkynones.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 5 shows ≥ 77 % yields for propargylic alcohols when using 10 mol % catalyst loadings. “For substrate 1o … aldehyde 2o was obtained in 77 % yield using 10 mol % loadings of the catalysts.” (Results and Discussion).

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: The initial benzophenone‑sensitized cycloaddition of maleic anhydride showed very poor conversion because benzophenone absorbs weakly at the 375 nm LED wavelength.  To obtain an acceptable rate, extremely high sensitizer loadings (40–60 mol %) were required, which gave a low atom‑economy and made the process costly.
Solution_Description: The sensitizer was changed to thioxanthone, whose absorption maximum (≈ 377 nm) matches the LED output.  Thioxanthone’s much higher extinction coefficient (≈ 6 300 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹) allowed the reaction to run with only 2.5 mol % loading, restoring high conversion and reducing material cost.
Supporting_Evidence: "The absorption spectrum of benzophenone peaks at ∼340 nm (λmax = 343 nm) … LEDs with a maximum emission at 343 nm were found to be ineffective…" (Table 1, entry 1)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: When ethylene was introduced as the gaseous alkene, its concentration in solution was limited, leading to concerns about multiphasic flow and reduced reaction productivity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A moderate back‑pressure of 12 bar was applied, which completely dissolved the ethylene in the reaction medium, giving a single‑phase (monophasic) flow and longer residence times, thereby improving space‑time yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "by the application of a moderate pressure of 12 bar … the ethylene stream was entirely dissolved in the reaction medium, resulting in simpler monophasic fluid behavior." (Results and Discussion, sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: High loadings of benzophenone (40 mol %) were needed for the maleic anhydride reaction, which reduced atom‑economy and would require costly recovery/purification steps on scale.
Solution_Description: Switching to thioxanthone reduced the required loading to 2.5 mol % (≈ 25 mM).  Because the reaction proceeded with such a low amount of sensitizer, no separate recovery of the photosensitizer was required, eliminating the need for an additional purification operation.
Supporting_Evidence: "With a panel of 375 nm LEDs, very high loadings (40–60 %) of the sensitizer 2 were required … Recovery and reuse of the sensitizer is possible … yet this purification process would add multiple unit operations …" (Results and Discussion, sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: The thioxanthone‑sensitized reaction stopped completely when the reaction mixture was not degassed, indicating that dissolved oxygen quenches the excited sensitizer.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was sparged with argon for 15 min before use (degassing) to remove oxygen, restoring full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: "The reaction was performed without degassing the reaction mixture (entry 11). The resulting lack of any reaction … clearly demonstrated the importance of excluding oxygen from these reactions." (Results and Discussion, sec 2.2, Table 3)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: Different LED wavelengths were screened; the 343 nm LEDs gave only 14 % yield because of low photon flux, while wavelengths > 385 nm gave negligible conversion, limiting productivity.
Solution_Description: Higher‑power LEDs at 365, 375, and 385 nm (with higher radiant and photon flux) were employed, giving yields of 90 % (365 nm) and 89 % (375 nm).  The temperature was kept at ambient (25 °C) to avoid additional cooling costs.
Supporting_Evidence: "LEDs with a maximum emission at 343 nm were found to be ineffective … LEDs with wavelengths of 365 and 375 nm showed roughly equal yields despite benzophenone’s significantly higher absorbance at 365 nm." (Table 1)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: In the initial small‑scale plate reactor, the gas‑liquid mixture could become multiphasic, potentially decreasing light penetration and reaction rate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: By maintaining the entire ethylene stream in solution (12 bar pressure) a single‑phase flow was obtained for all experiments, ensuring uniform light exposure and higher productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Although multiphasic flow regimes have been shown to improve productivity … having all of the input gas dissolved in the reaction medium allows a longer irradiation time …" (Results and Discussion, sec 2.1)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: The laboratory photoreactor (2.77 mL volume) limited the amount of material that could be processed, resulting in modest space‑time yields (≈ 90 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹).
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A larger Corning G1 flow photoreactor was employed, connecting five 2.77 mL plates in series (total 13.85 mL) and scaling the total flow rate five‑fold.  This maintained the same residence time while increasing throughput, giving > 100 g product in 10 h (≈ 759 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: "Five ‘low‑flow’ plates … were connected in series … providing a total irradiated volume of 13.85 mL … the reaction performed to an identical standard … 101.3 g (96 % yield) of the desired product after 10 h runtime." (Scale‑Up section, sec 2.3)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: Maleic anhydride has a high triplet energy that is not compatible with thioxanthone, giving essentially no conversion under thioxanthone sensitization.
Solution_Description: The substrate was modified by adding a methyl group to give citraconic anhydride, lowering its triplet energy by 3.2 kcal mol⁻¹.  This made the substrate compatible with thioxanthone, allowing complete conversion at low sensitizer loading.
Supporting_Evidence: "The addition of a single methyl group … reduced the triplet energy by 3.2 kcal mol⁻¹, which prompted experimental examination… complete conversion … was observed within a short residence time using a significantly lower sensitizer loading." (Results and Discussion, sec 2.2)

Paper Title: Finding the Perfect Match: A Combined Computational and Experimental Study toward Efficient and Scalable Photosensitized [2 + 2] Cycloadditions in Flow
Problem_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration to improve productivity caused a drop in conversion because the higher ethylene flow reduced residence time.
Solution_Description: Optimization experiments showed that keeping the concentration at 0.5 M and adjusting the flow rates (solution flow 0.5 mL min⁻¹, ethylene 1.25 mL min⁻¹) gave > 99 % conversion with a residence time of ≈ 5 min, balancing throughput and yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "Increasing the concentration was attempted … but this was observed to reduce the conversion … Accordingly, the ethylene flow rate was reduced … yet this further reduced the reaction yield." (Table 3, entries 5–6)

Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of Continuous Electrocatalytic Hydrogenation of Functionalized Nitro Arenes, Nitriles, and Unsaturated Aldehydes
Problem_Description: The researchers encountered a series of practical challenges while developing and scaling the continuous electrocatalytic hydrogenation process.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A range of engineering and chemical modifications were applied to overcome those problems.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. "the unfamiliarity of both synthetic organic chemists and their engineering counterparts with electrochemical transformations" (Introduction) – classified as SAFETY because lack of knowledge can create safety risks.
2. "lack of readily scaled reactors" (Introduction) – classified as AVAILABILITY; the process required a reactor that could be built at scale.
3. "difficulty in transferring kinetics measurements from bench to production" (Introduction) – classified as VARIABILITY; performance was inconsistent when moving to larger scale.
4. "This substrate was sparingly soluble in the highly polar electrolyte" (Section 3.4.3) – classified as SOLUBILITY.
5. "The catalysts did leach small quantities of metal during the long run…30 ppm of Cu…0.79 ppm" (Section 5) – classified as DECOMPOSITION (metal dissolution).
6. "At the more negative potentials, the Pd catalyst produced large amounts of hydrogen, observed as bubbles … which interfered with the reduction of the nitro arene" (Section 3.4.5) – classified as LOW YIELD because side‑reaction reduced product formation.
7. "The product slate … could be narrowed … by adjusting the pH of the catholyte and the applied cell potential" (Section 3.4.3) – classified as LOW YIELD (selectivity issue) and solved by PH CONTROL.
8. "in methanol, there was a noticeable conversion… in tetrahydrofuran, the conversion was much lower (<1%)" (Section 3.4.9) – classified as LOW YIELD; solved by SOLVENT CHANGE.
9. "ran a pair of the 27 mL reactors in parallel … produced a combined stream…" (Section 5) – classified as VARIABILITY/scale‑up challenge; solved by REACTOR PLATFORM AND MATERIALS (parallel reactors).
10. "Turbulent flow through the carbon felts … conferred … high mass‑transfer coefficients" (Abstract) – low Reynolds numbers could limit mixing, classified as MIXABILITY; solved by MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL (turbulent flow).

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The N‑alkylation of mesylate 7 with piperazine in the original medicinal‑chemistry route required 2 days at room temperature (10 equiv piperazine, EtOH) to suppress formation of N,N‑bis‑alkylated side‑products, leading to an unacceptably long reaction time for large‑scale production and difficulty ensuring mono‑alkylation.
Solution_Description: Increasing the amount of piperazine to 10 equiv and performing the N‑alkylation in MeOH reduced the reaction time from 2 days to 2 h and improved the product purity (3 : Imp A ratio from 66 : 34 % to 94 : 6 %).
Supporting_Evidence: “The N‑alkylation of mesylate 7 with 10 equiv of piperazine in MeOH led to a significant improvement in the reaction time from 2 days to 2 h.”; “The purity of the product was also improved under the optimized conditions. The 3 : Imp A ratio was changed from 66 : 34 % to 94 : 6 %.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The synthesis of intermediate 6 in the original route required heating to 120 °C and subsequent chromatographic purification, which posed operational challenges and added cost for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was devised that allowed the N‑alkylation product 6 to be crystallized directly as the monomaleate salt, eliminating the need for high‑temperature conditions and chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Second, a relatively high temperature (120 °C) and chromatographic purification were necessary for the synthesis of 6.”; “...the N‑alkylation of 3 and 5 ... afforded 6 which can be crystallized as a maleate salt of 1, avoiding the need for chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: O‑alkylation of 4 with 1‑bromo‑3‑chloropropane produced impurities Imp C, Imp D and Imp E that were difficult to remove by conventional work‑up, compromising product quality.
Solution_Description: The Mitsunobu reaction between 4 and 3‑chloro‑1‑propanol was employed; it did not generate the problematic impurities, and the low solubility of the product 5 allowed simple filtration in MeOH/water to remove the phosphine‑oxide by‑product.
Supporting_Evidence: “When 5 was prepared using O‑alkylation... Imp C, Imp D, and Imp E were formed… Removing these impurities in the subsequent process was quite difficult.”; “We examined the Mitsunobu reaction… This reaction did not produce the unremovable impurities Imp C, Imp D, and Imp E, resulting in a cleaner reaction profile.”; “The co‑products could be easily removed by filtration of the slurry containing 5 in a MeOH/water or MeOH solvent.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Imp B, an impurity derived from residual piperazine, persisted through the original medicinal‑chemistry sequence and could not be eliminated, threatening API quality.
Solution_Description: A novel synthetic route was designed that introduced the piperazine unit later in the sequence, providing intermediate steps where low‑solubility benzothiazine derivatives could be filtered, thereby removing Imp B before the final crystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “Imp B was derived from the piperazine remaining in compound 3 and could not be removed in subsequent steps.”; “We designed and developed a novel synthetic route… Both impurities and co‑products in each step of the revised synthesis could be easily removed via filtration, leveraging the low solubility of benzothiazine derivatives.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Several benzothiazine‑containing intermediates (e.g., 4, 5, 8, 9) exhibited very low solubility in common organic solvents, complicating recrystallization and isolation on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The low solubility was turned into an advantage: reactions were performed in solvents (e.g., MeOH/water, EtOH) where the intermediates precipitated, allowing isolation by simple filtration rather than chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compounds with low solubility are typically not suitable for process development because the low solubility generally complicates recrystallization processes. However, low solubility is useful for purification of the target compound in highly polar solvents.”; “Both impurities and co‑products were easily removed via filtration by leveraging the low solubility of benzothiazine derivatives.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Boc de‑protection of 8 to give 9 produced large amounts of CO₂ and isobutylene gas, creating off‑gassing safety concerns on large scale.
Solution_Description: The de‑protection was performed in ethanol with 6 M HCl at 40–50 °C, which minimized gas evolution and allowed direct crystallization of 9 after addition of ethanol.
Supporting_Evidence: “There are safety concerns in this step because removal of the Boc group under acidic conditions liberates carbon dioxide and isobutylene.”; “In practice, a suspension of 8 in EtOH was warmed to 40 °C and 6 M HCl was added… 9 was crystallized directly upon addition of EtOH.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The dimaleate salt of 6 was hygroscopic and thermally less stable than the monomaleate, risking formation of mixed‑salt products and reduced API quality.
Solution_Description: The amount of maleic acid used for salt formation was limited to 0.95 equiv, preventing excess acid that would generate the dimaleate salt; the monomaleate was selected as the final API salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “The dimaleate salt of 6 exhibits poor physicochemical properties such as low stability and high hygroscopicity… maleic acid must not be added in excess to compound 6 to avoid nucleation of the dimaleate salt.”; “Thus, the amount of maleic acid was set to 0.95 equiv for this purpose.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Intermediate 9 was insoluble in THF after neutralization, preventing the intended C–N bond formation with 2.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A biphasic THF‑water system was employed, allowing the reaction to proceed despite the low solubility of 9 in the organic phase.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 9 was insoluble in THF after neutralization, so the desired C‑N bond formation did not proceed. However, the reaction proceeded using a two‑phase system of THF and water.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: Over‑charging of DIPEA during the coupling of 9 with 2 produced a complex mixture, leading to inconsistent conversions.
Solution_Description: DIPEA was reduced to 0.9 equiv for the initial step, with a subsequent controlled addition of water and 1.2 equiv DIPEA after reaction completion, giving clean conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “In addition, overcharging diisopropylethylamine (DIPEA) during the reaction provided a complex mixture.”; “First, the reaction was performed using 0.9 equiv of DIPEA, and after the reaction was complete, water and 1.2 equiv of DIPEA were sequentially added.”

Paper Title: Development of a Synthetic Process for K‑8986, an H1-Receptor Antagonist
Problem_Description: The original route to 6 required chromatographic purification, which is impractical for multikilogram production.
Solution_Description: Crystallization of 6 as the monomaleate salt eliminated chromatography, providing a scalable isolation method.
Supporting_Evidence: “...could be crystallized as a maleate salt of 1, avoiding the need for chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: The aqueous solubility of nevirapine drops sharply with pH; at the higher crystallisation pH (pH ≈ 7) used in the batch (BX) crystallisation the API remains too soluble, giving a low crystallisation yield and driving up the amount of base needed, which inflates material costs.
Solution_Description: The authors adopt a continuous‑flow crystallisation (CPM) that operates at a lower crystallisation pH (as low as 1–4) to reduce the API solubility, increase the crystallisation yield and cut base consumption. This is presented as a new route to API isolation that replaces the batch crystallisation step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crystallisation yield is estimated ... based on the API concentration in the mother liquor …” (sec 2.3.2, eq 5).

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: At reactor R‑103 temperatures below 120 °C the conversion of the intermediate CYCLOR to nevirapine is only ~10 % (or 60 % at 140 °C), resulting in poor overall API yield and high material consumption, which raises the total cost.
Solution_Description: The optimisation pushes the operating temperature of R‑103 to the upper bound of the kinetic data (165 °C) to maximise conversion (≈96 %), thereby improving the plant‑wide API yield and dramatically lowering the material‑cost component of the total cost.
Supporting_Evidence: “At temperatures of 120, 140 and 165 °C, CYCLOR conversions to API of 10, 60, and 96 % are attainable, respectively” (sec 2.3.1.3).

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: Low solvent‑recovery (SR = 0 % or 40 %) leaves most of the diglyme carrier in the waste stream, increasing waste disposal costs and the E‑factor, which drives up the total cost of the plant.
Solution_Description: The study evaluates higher SR values (up to 80 %) as a process variable; improving solvent recovery reduces the amount of solvent that must be purchased and disposed of, lowering both the utilities‑cost and waste‑cost components and improving material efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: “Solvent recovery of 80 % is reported … lower values of 0 and 40 % were also considered” (sec 2.4).

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: The first reaction (CAPIC + NaH → CAPIC‑Na) is highly exothermic and occurs in a thin‑film reactor to overcome heat removal limitations and to avoid a viscous, poorly mixed slurry that would hinder conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A thin‑film reactor is employed for R‑101, providing a high surface‑to‑volume ratio that improves heat removal and mixing, enabling complete conversion in a very short residence time (8.6 s) despite the exothermicity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Full conversion … is allowed by implementation of a thin‑film reactor to enhance heat and mass transfer” (sec 2.3.1.1).

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: Reactor R‑102 operates with a residence time of 2 h to achieve an 82.5 % conversion, which lengthens the overall process time and lifts utilities and labour costs.
Solution_Description: The optimisation treats the residence time as a fixed design parameter derived from the demonstrated batch experiment; the cost model later shows that raising the temperature of the downstream R‑103 (instead of shortening R‑102) yields greater cost savings, so no further change to R‑102 is required.

Paper Title: Process Design and Optimization for the Continuous Manufacturing of Nevirapine, an Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient for HIV Treatment
Problem_Description: The non‑linear optimisation could converge to different local minima depending on the initial guesses for the decision variables (T_R103 and pH_CRYST).
Solution_Description: Multiple initial points (nine per problem instance) were tested to confirm that the optimisation consistently reached a unique global optimum, eliminating variability in the solution.
Supporting_Evidence: “Multiple initial values … were tested to ensure a unique optimal solution … Unique solutions were attained for all of the problem instances” (sec 2.6).

Paper Title: H–D Exchange Deuteration of Arenes at Room Temperature

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: The reactive crystallization of compound Z produces “sticky” granules and a very broad, multimodal particle‑size distribution (200–400 µm particles with large amounts of >400 µm and <100 µm material) that does not meet the specification (100‑300 µm, span ≈ 1.0).  The granules arise from liquid‑liquid phase separation (LLPS) that creates dense oil droplets which rapidly coalesce and harden, giving spherulitic ‘drusy’ particles.
Solution_Description: The authors varied (i) the rate of addition of stream M (1000 g h⁻¹ vs 200 g h⁻¹) and (ii) the reaction temperature (10–50 °C) to explore their effect on the PSD (Tables 1 & 2).  They discovered that slower addition and lower temperatures shift the PSD toward smaller, more uniform particles.  In addition, they identified that operating at very dilute product concentrations (≤ 1.6 wt % Z, i.e., well below the binodal) eliminates LLPS and yields regular primary crystals (Figure 3).  This combination of slower feed, cooler operation, and dilute solution (“concentration tuning”) suppresses the oil‑out phenomenon and generates acceptable particle sizes.
Supporting_Evidence: "The most troubling aspect identified … was a “sticky” crystallization and the resulting unacceptable particle size distribution …" (Sec 3.1, para 1); "Increasing the temperature of the reaction in general shifted the PSD toward large particle sizes" (Sec 3.1, para 2); "Increasing the rate of addition of stream M somewhat influenced the PSD" (Sec 3.1, para 2); "Operating the CSTR … at a Czo ≤ 1.6 % (w/w) … produces regular crystals …" (Sec 4.6.2, para 4).

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: The reaction between precursor M and aldehyde A is highly exothermic; temperature of an adiabatic batch rises rapidly (up to >50 °C) and can cause decomposition of product Z when in contact with water at elevated temperature, posing safety and product‑quality risks.
Solution_Description: Temperature control was achieved by (i) using a jacketed reactor with cooling fluid to limit the temperature rise during the fast reaction, and (ii) adjusting the addition rate of reactants to spread the heat release over a longer period.  Additionally, kinetic data were extracted from the temperature‑vs‑time profile (instead of direct sampling) to model the heat of reaction and design a safe operating window (≤ 35 °C).
Supporting_Evidence: "the reaction … is highly exothermic … temperature of an adiabatic reaction mass continuously rises" (Sec 2.4, para 2); "high temperature reaction and drying operations are not recommended due to the accelerated decomposition of Z …” (Sec 1, para 4); "The rise of temperature was monitored … and later used to build a working reaction kinetic model" (Sec 2.4, para 3); "operating temperature of 35 °C was deemed the maximum safe operating temperature" (Sec 4.6, para 2).

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: Rapid precipitation of product Z during reaction leads to solid build‑up on reactor internals, agitator blades and tubing in continuous CSTR operation, causing fouling and loss of throughput.
Solution_Description: The team evaluated the phase diagram of Z in the process solvent (98 % water – 2 % MeOH) and identified that operating at very low product concentrations (≤ 1.6 % w/w) stays outside the LLPS region, eliminating dense oil droplets that cause fouling.  They also considered changing the solvent composition (e.g., increasing methanol) as a way to shift the binodal/spinodal boundaries, although the existing plant constraints made a methanol‑rich solvent impractical.
Supporting_Evidence: "solid build up on the reactor internals, agitator blades, and connected tubing … observed in all continuous mode synthesis experiments" (Sec 3.2, para 4); "Operating the CSTR … at a Czo ≤ 1.6 % (w/w) … produces regular crystals …" (Sec 4.6.2, para 4); "The other option is to run the reaction in a methanol‑rich solvent phase … but this option is not practical …" (Sec 4.2, para 2).

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: Product Z decomposes rapidly in water at elevated temperatures, releasing toxic gases; therefore high‑temperature reaction or drying steps are unsafe and must be avoided.
Solution_Description: The process was deliberately limited to near‑ambient temperatures (≤ 35 °C) and the reactor jacket was used to remove heat quickly.  The kinetic model incorporated the known heat of reaction to predict temperature spikes and confirm that the chosen operating window stays below the decomposition threshold.
Supporting_Evidence: "High temperature reaction and drying operations are not recommended due to the accelerated decomposition of Z when in contact with water at elevated temperatures" (Sec 1, para 4); "a T_r of 35 °C was deemed the maximum safe operating temperature for the CSTR" (Sec 4.6, para 2); "We preassigned a value of 13000 cal mol⁻¹ for the activation energy … used to estimate the kinetic parameters at the temperatures of interest" (Sec 4.4, para 3).

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: The business case required a fast, low‑cost R&D effort to decide whether to retrofit an existing 1.6 m³ CSTR for producing several‑thousand tons per year of Z; limited budget and short decision window constrained experimental work and ruled out building a dedicated plant.
Solution_Description: Rather than an extensive brute‑force experimental campaign, the team adopted a hybrid approach that combined a few key experiments with existing thermodynamic and kinetic models to rapidly map the design space.  This “academic‑concept‑leveraged” method allowed a techno‑economic assessment within the 3‑6 month window, ultimately enabling the business to decide not to pursue the retrofit.
Supporting_Evidence: "The business organization...requested the research team minimize the expenditure on the R&D activities and asked us to reach a conclusion within 3 to 6 months" (Sec 1, para 5); "We quickly provided the needed information regarding the economic impact of process conditions suitable for scale‑up" (Sec 1, para 6); "The approach quickly provided the needed information … enabling an informed decision" (Sec 1, para 8).

Paper Title: From Experiments and Models to Business Decisions: A Scale-up Study on the Reactive Crystallization of a Crop Protection Agent
Problem_Description: Operating at the product concentrations required for economic margin (≈ 33 wt % Z) places the solution deep inside the spinodal region, causing LLPS, gelation and a dramatic loss of usable product; thus, the attainable productivity (kg min⁻¹) at a safe operating point is far lower than the target 20 kg min⁻¹.
Solution_Description: The authors demonstrated that maintaining Czo ≤ 1.6 % (w/w) avoids the spinodal/gel region and yields acceptable crystals, but this dilute operation reduces throughput.  The trade‑off was quantified, and the conclusion was that no feasible operating point satisfies productivity, economics, and operability simultaneously; therefore the scale‑up was abandoned.
Supporting_Evidence: "the chosen reaction condition … places the solution deep inside the spinodal region … leads to LLPS and gelation … unacceptable product" (Sec 4.6.2, para 5‑6); "Operating the CSTR at 35 °C … at a Czo of 33.5 % (w/w) … makes the process quickly uneconomical" (Sec 4.6.2, para 4); "The scale‑up conditions … do not exist … the process should not be scaled up under the retrofit scenario" (Sec 4.6.2, para 9).

Paper Title: Improvements to Enable the Large Scale Synthesis of 1‑{[(2S,3S,4S)-3-Ethyl-4-fluoro-5-oxopyrrolidin-2-yl]methoxy}-7-methoxyisoquinoline-6-carboxamide (PF-06650833)
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the original route encountered a series of bottlenecks: (1) The Tsuji oxidation to give unsaturated lactam 6 required removal of di‑isopropylamine and LiCl; residual salts stalled the catalytic cycle and made work‑up cumbersome. (2) The organocuprate addition required preparation of LiThCN at –3 → –30 °C, a long cooling step and suffered time‑dependent decomposition of the cuprate, giving variable conversion and generating large CuBr·Me₂S waste (expensive and toxic Me₂S). (3) Fluorination of 7 with NFSI gave only 23 % isolated 8, poor 2:1 diastereoselectivity and required chromatography. (4) Acetonide deprotection used p‑TsOH/MeCN at 90 °C and needed chromatographic purification. (5) Nitrile hydrolysis employed K₂CO₃/H₂O₂/DMSO, a mixture that is potentially exothermic and hazardous. (6) Final isolation of 1 relied on chromatography, which is undesirable on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: 1. A one‑step sulfoxide formation from 4 (methyl‑benzenesulfinate/NaH, 45 °C) followed by thermal elimination of sulfoxide 12 in toluene (110 °C) gave 6 directly, eliminating the Tsuji oxidation and its impurity‑removal steps. 2. The cuprate addition was re‑designed: CuI (0.07 equiv) was used as a catalyst, EtMgBr (1.2 equiv) was added at –60 °C, then TMSCl (1.1 equiv) followed by 6. This avoided LiThCN, removed the long cooling period, reduced copper loading (~7 mol %), eliminated Me₂S, and gave 7 in 87 % yield with 94 % purity. 3. The anti‑fluoro isomer 9 was epimerised to the desired syn‑isomer 8 by kinetic protonation with a sterically hindered phenol (BHT) at ≤ –65 °C (LDA, –70 °C, then BHT). 4. A high‑diast­ereoselective oxidation of enolate 13 to alcohol 14 was achieved in flow using in‑situ generated anhydrous t‑BuOOH (membrane pervaporation) and LiHMDS at –20 °C → 0 °C, affording 14 in 74 % yield. 5. Alcohol 14 was activated and fluorinated in a single step with nonafluorobutanesulfonyl fluoride (1.3 equiv) and TMEDA (1.4 equiv) in 2‑MeTHF/THF at 20 °C, delivering 8 in 72 % yield (no isolation of sulfonate intermediate). 6. Acetonide cleavage was performed with catalytic TFA (0.2 equiv) in 3 % aqueous MeCN at 65 °C; the product 2 crystallised directly from the reaction mixture (no chromatography). 7. Nitrile hydrolysis was switched to MsOH (7.5 equiv) at 60 °C for 26 h, giving 1 after simple recrystallisation (avoiding hazardous H₂O₂/DMSO). 8. Final isolation of 1 was accomplished by recrystallisation from EtOH/heptane after a filtration‑free work‑up, eliminating all chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. "The preparation of the unsaturated lactam 6 via the Tsuji oxidation was difficult to carry out on larger scales, due to the need to obtain the intermediate silyl enol ether 5 free from both diisopropylamine and lithium chloride… Failure to completely remove these intermediate byproducts would result in stalling of the Tsuji catalytic cycle and recovery of the starting lactam 4" (p. 7). "The thermal elimination of the previously unknown sulfoxide 12 provided convenient introduction of the olefin to access unsaturated lactam 6" (p. 9). "The sulfoxide was readily prepared from 4 by a base mediated condensation… elimination… accomplished by heating a toluene solution of 12 at 110 °C" (Scheme 5). 2. "The greatest concern was the preparation the organocopper reagent at temperatures between –3 and –30 °C… organocopper solution was found to degrade with time… large waste streams… prohibitively expensive…" (p. 8). "This allowed us to move away from the relatively dilute conditions of the LiThCN chemistry… CuI was entirely satisfactory… a mixture of excess EtMgBr and catalytic (<10 mol %) CuI could be prepared at –60 °C… eliminated the time dependent cuprate formation and cooling steps, reduced the amount of TMSCl and Grignard reagent employed, and greatly reduced the amount of copper salts required" (p. 10‑11). 3. "Fluorination… was accomplished in 23 % yield… diastereoselection was relatively poor (2:1)… chromatographic purifications…" (p. 6). "The unwanted anti fluorination isomer 9 was epimerized to provide more of the desired syn isomer 8 by means of a kinetic protonation… 44 % yield of 8 and 27 % of 9…" (Scheme 4). 4. "Initial work using oxygen… gave a 4:1 ratio… the use of lithium t‑butylperoxide (t‑BuOOLi) afforded 14 with >30:1 diastereoselectivity… the reaction sequence was adapted to a flow process that simultaneously generated an anhydrous solution of t‑BuOOH…" (p. 11‑12). 5. "The triflate 15a could be isolated … However, the use of triethylamine trihydrofluoride … was not considered ideal… The use of inexpensive nonafluorobutanesulfonyl fluoride offered a more suitable option … This reagent permitted the alcohol activation and SN2 displacement by fluoride ion to be accomplished in a single step, without a need for the isolation of the intermediate… Optimized conditions… gave crystalline 8 in 72 % yield…” (p. 13‑14). 6. "The acetonide was cleaved with catalytic TFA in aqueous MeCN at 65 °C… allowed the lactam alcohol 2 to be isolated in 98 % yield by concentration followed by crystallisation and drying without need for chromatography" (Scheme 3). 7. "Nitrile hydrolysis of 10 was effected using MsOH as a reagent and solvent at 60 °C… The crude 1 was isolated by extraction and purified by recrystallisation to provide 1 in 91 % yield" (Scheme 3). 8. "Elimination of the intensive chromatography attendant to the preparation and purification of 8… final purification of 1 was effected by suspending the crude 1 in EtOH… recrystallisation… affording 1 (31.3 kg, 91 %…)" (Summary).
