Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: When the first step (carbamylation) was run in ACN, toluene, or Et₂O, the low solubility of the product and/or reagents caused severe chip clogging, preventing continuous operation.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to THF (which gave good solubility for all components) eliminated clogging and allowed stable flow.
Supporting_Evidence: Product yields dropped sharply in EtOH due to ethanolysis (entries 1‑3). Though the yield in ACN was significant, its low solubility led to chip clogging (entries 4‑6). Similar clogging problems were found for toluene and Et₂O, even at low concentrations (entries 7‑8). The yield increased to 50‑62 % with longer residence times in THF, reaching a maximum at τ = 30 s, 50 °C (entries 9‑14).

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: In EtOH the 1‑chloro‑2‑isocyanatoethane undergoes ethanolysis, and at temperatures above 50 °C the desired product decomposes, both leading to poor isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The reaction was moved to THF as the solvent and the temperature was kept at 50 °C (or lower) to suppress both ethanolysis and product decomposition, giving a maximum isolated yield of 91.7 % under optimized conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: Product yields dropped sharply in EtOH at longer residence times due to ethanolysis of the 1‑chloro‑2‑isocyanato‑ethane (entries 1‑3). The yield decayed rapidly with increased temperature (entries 13‑14) due to increased product decomposition at elevated temperatures. Consequently, a maximum yield of intermediate 3 (92 %) was achieved under conditions of τ = 60 s, T = 50 °C, and 1.4 equiv of 1‑chloro‑2‑isocyanatoethane (entry 20).

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: During nitrosation of intermediate 3 with NaNO₂/HCO₂H, longer residence times (>5 min) led to increased decomposition of lomustine and lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: The residence time was limited to 5 min (or less) and the temperature was kept at 0 °C, which minimized decomposition and gave isolated yields up to 79 % (Method 1) and 74 % (Method 3) after purification.
Supporting_Evidence: A systematic evaluation of residence times led to good lomustine yields and starting‑material conversions; however, longer residence times appeared to enhance the decomposition of lomustine (Table 2, entries 2‑6). Consequently, we kept the temperature constant at 0 °C to avoid NaNO₂ decomposition to the diazonium salt that occurs at higher temperatures.

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Residual triethylamine (TEA) from the first step interfered with the nitrosation step, consuming the nitrosation reagent and lowering product yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An in‑line Zaiput liquid‑liquid extractor was installed between the two reactors to remove the aqueous TEA phase before the nitrosation step, restoring reagent efficiency and improving overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence: An extraction was required between the steps to remove the TEA present in the first reaction to avoid competitive consumption of the nitrosation reagent in the second step. We achieved this objective by incorporating a commercially available Zaiput liquid–liquid extractor to remove the base before the nitrosation step and by re‑optimizing the synthesis using a FEP tubing reactor (Section 2.4).

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: The intermediate cyclohexylurea (3) has low solubility in several solvents, causing blockage in the telescoped flow sequence.
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system (ACN/EtOH 3.7:1 for nitrosation with TBN, or THF/H₂O for NaNO₂) was employed to keep intermediate 3 in solution throughout the telescoped process, preventing fouling and enabling continuous operation.
Supporting_Evidence: Mixed solvents were used in the telescoped reaction to avoid clogging due to the low solubility of 3. tert‑Butyl nitrite, 5, was found to be a milder and more efficient nitrosation reagent in this process to enable the isolation of pure lomustine via simple extraction, filtration, and washing.

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Both the starting isocyanate and the final lomustine are highly toxic alkylating agents, posing inhalation and exposure hazards during handling.
Solution_Description: Using closed microreactor chips and continuous flow reduced operator exposure; additionally, protective equipment (inhalation masks, impermeable gloves) and light‑protected syringes were used for light‑sensitive reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: The 1‑chloro‑2‑isocyanatoethane (2) and cyclohexylurea product (3) are potent alkylating agents. Appropriate chemical inhalation masks and impermeable gloves must be worn while handling all reaction operations and product analyses in a ventilated hood. (Section 4.8).

Paper Title: Rapid On-Demand Synthesis of Lomustine under Continuous Flow Conditions
Problem_Description: Initial attempts to telescope the two steps without an in‑line work‑up suffered from inconsistent conversions because residual TEA varied between runs.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implementing the Zaiput extractor standardized removal of TEA and adjusting the TEA equivalents (down to 0.01 equiv) stabilized the nitrosation step, yielding reproducible high conversion (up to 63 % overall isolated yield).
Supporting_Evidence: Efforts to improve the lomustine yield by changing the residence times of either the first or second steps were unsuccessful using 4 as the nitrosation reagent. Subsequent telescoping experiments indicated that 5 was a better nitrosation reagent. The final optimized conditions included a 1 min reaction time at 50 °C for the first step and an 8 min reaction time at 25 °C for the second step. As the small amount of extracted TEA from the first step negatively impacted TBN activity, lowering the amount of TEA used led to an increased production of lomustine (Table 4, entries 7‑9).

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Ruthenium residues remain in olefin metathesis (OM) products after the reaction, promoting decomposition/isomerisation of the desired product and often exceeding the strict regulatory limit (<10 ppm) for transition‑metal contamination in APIs.
Solution_Description: A semi‑heterogeneous purification protocol was developed that non‑covalently immobilises the commercially available isocyanide QA on unmodified silica (QA@SiO₂) and removes Ru residues by simple filtration, giving products normally below 5 ppm Ru.
Supporting_Evidence: A low‑waste, time‑economical, and scalable semiheterogeneous purification protocol for the removal of ruthenium residues from olefin metathesis (OM) reactions has been developed. … the new purification protocol was effective on a gram scale … leading to a product containing only 0.29 ppm Ru.

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Previously reported homogeneous Ru scavengers (H₂O₂, mercaptonicotinic acid, DMSO, etc.) must be used in large excess (>10 equiv) and require long binding times (>1 h), yet they fail to lower Ru below 10 ppm.
Solution_Description: The new protocol uses only 4.4 equiv of QA (≈ 5 % excess) and a short treatment time (30–60 min) while still achieving Ru levels <10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: A small excess of QA (4.4 equiv) and a short treatment time (30–60 min) are sufficient to obtain OM products with Ru contents less than 10 ppm after a simple filtration of the post‑reaction mixture …

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Heterogeneous scavengers reported previously need large excess of scavenger, long treatment times and suffer from steric diffusion limitations; immobilised scavengers also require multistep syntheses, making them expensive.
Solution_Description: By adding silica first, then QA (method D), the authors obtained the best Ru removal (82 ppm) with minimal scavenger loading, eliminating the need for large excesses and simplifying the procedure.
Supporting_Evidence: The use of silica gel first, followed by the isocyanide treatment (method D) gave the best result, affording a product with 82 ppm Ru.

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Isocyanides hydrolyse to formamides in the presence of acids; silica gel adsorbs water and its surface hydroxyls can catalyse this hydrolysis, risking loss of the QA scavenger.
Solution_Description: QA@SiO₂ is generated in situ during the purification step, minimising exposure of the isocyanide to water and acid and thus preventing decomposition while simplifying the protocol.
Supporting_Evidence: We decided to synthesize the heterogeneous scavenger QA@SiO₂ in situ during the purification process, which not only minimised the risk of decomposition of the isocyanide groups over time but also significantly simplified the purification protocol and reduced the cost of the entire process.

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Removal of Ru from olefin metathesis performed in aqueous media is especially difficult; conventional scavengers give very high residual Ru (≈ 10 000 ppm).
Solution_Description: Applying the same QA scavenger in water (QA + silica) reduced Ru from 9 977 ppm to 21 ppm within 30 min, showing the method works also in aqueous media.
Supporting_Evidence: Finally, QA was used in an aqueous medium and reduced the metal contamination from 9977 to 21 ppm.

Paper Title: Semiheterogeneous Purification Protocol for the Removal of Ruthenium Impurities from Olefin Metathesis Reaction Products Using an Isocyanide Scavenger
Problem_Description: Scaling up traditional column‑chromatography‑based scavenger protocols is time‑consuming and costly for gram‑scale preparations.
Solution_Description: The semi‑heterogeneous protocol D was demonstrated on a 5 mmol (1.38 g) scale, giving the target intermediate with only 0.29 ppm Ru, proving the method is scalable and time‑efficient.
Supporting_Evidence: To demonstrate that purification protocol D is effective on a large scale, RCM was performed with Ru6 (1.0 mol %) using 5 mmol (1.38 g) of diene 12a … after purification, the ruthenium content … was only 0.29 ppm.

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Batch deacylation requires extraction and filtration steps to remove the catalyst, and product loss can occur during liquid–liquid separation of water‑soluble hydroxy compounds.
Solution_Description: A continuous packed‑bed flow reactor containing an anion‑exchange resin was developed; the substrate is fed directly through the catalyst bed, eliminating the need for extraction/filtration and simplifying work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["batch mode requires complicated processes including extraction and filtration to remove the catalyst prior to the next step","product loss might be observed at the liquid–liquid separation step in the case of highly water‑soluble hydroxy compounds","we established an efficient and practical packed‑bed reactor system for undertaking the deacylation reaction using an anion‑exchange resin that provides a simple process compared with batch processing","desired hydroxy compounds can be readily obtained by feeding acyl compounds into a column loaded with the catalyst, thus avoiding the need for extraction and filtration"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: In batch mode the anion‑exchange resin showed poor filterability during the purification step.
Solution_Description: Immobilizing the resin in a packed‑bed column for continuous flow overcame the filterability issue and provided stable operation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["poor filterability of the resin was observed in the purification process","the deacylation efficiency was highly improved by the use of the packed‑bed reactor system and that this system gives good operability over the conventional batch conditions"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Bulky substrates such as benzyl isobutyrate gave low conversion (75 % yield) at 25 °C.
Solution_Description: Raising the reaction temperature to 50 °C increased the yield to 90 % (and 93 % for benzyl butyrate).
Supporting_Evidence: ["a decrease in the reaction yield was observed (75 %); run 4","increase the reaction temperature from 25 to 50 °C (90 %); run 5","good results were also obtained in the case of benzyl butyrate (93 %); run 6"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: The highest‑performing resin (DOWEX 1X2) has a very high unit cost, making it unsuitable for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: DIAION PA 306s, which is less expensive and readily available, was selected as the optimal catalyst despite a modest loss in yield (87 % vs 92 %).
Supporting_Evidence: ["unit cost of this resin is very high compared with other tested resins, thus making it not ideal for scaled processing","we chose DIAION PA 306s as the optimal anion‑exchange resin for this study in terms of the economics and availability for bulk scale, despite the fact that the reaction yield was slightly lower"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: After ~94 h of continuous operation the resin lost activity because the methoxide ion was displaced by pivalate ion from the substrate, causing catalyst deactivation.
Solution_Description: A regeneration protocol (NaOH treatment → water flush → methanol flush) restored the resin to methoxide form, recovering >99 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["high catalytic performance was maintained for 94 h, after which a decrease in the reaction conversion due to deactivation of the resin was observed","deactivation of the catalyst occurred over an extended reaction period because the methoxide ion, which is an active species, was replaced by an inactive pivalate ion","A sodium hydroxide solution was supplied to the column packed with deactivated resin to exchange the pivalate ions into hydroxide ions on the resin, followed by water flushing... finally, methanol was used to flush and replace the hydroxide with methoxide","It was found that the reaction conversion increased to 99.9%"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Inconsistent catalytic performance was observed when the resin activation (chloride → methoxide) was insufficient, leading to lower yields.
Solution_Description: Two activation protocols were implemented (Method A: NaOMe in methanol; Method B: NaOH in water followed by methanol) to ensure complete ion exchange before the main reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Prior to the main reaction, sodium methoxide in methanol or aqueous sodium hydroxide was fed into the column... causing the chloride to exchange to methoxide","Method A: sodium methoxide dissolved in methanol (1 M, 2.5 volumes/resin volume) was fed into the column...","Method B: sodium hydroxide (1 M, 2.5 volumes/resin volume) was fed into the column... then methanol was fed to replace hydroxide with methoxide","It was found that a comparable reaction yield (97 %) was obtained in spite of the difference in the pretreatment method"]

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Deacylation Reaction System in a Continuous Packed-Bed Reactor
Problem_Description: Scaling the process to larger columns could lead to pressure drop or loss of conversion if not properly designed.
Solution_Description: A larger glass column (22 mm ID, 51 × resin volume) was operated at the same space velocity and temperature, delivering comparable yields without high pressure drop, demonstrating scalable packed‑bed operation.
Supporting_Evidence: ["a large‑scale experiment was performed using a wide inner diameter (22 mm, ca. 2.4 times that of run 4) and high throughput (198 mL/h throughput of 7b: 72 mmol/h, ca. 51 times that of run 4)","A large‑sized glass column with a jacket was prepared, and 198 mL of resin (ca. 51 times that of run 4) was filled into the column","After catalyst activation, 7a dissolved in methanol was transferred into the large column using a diaphragm pump with SV = 1 h⁻¹ at 50 °C","The total of 32 g of the desired product 7b was successfully obtained in a yield comparable to that in the small‑scale experiment without a high‑pressure drop"]

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: The substitution of the aryl iodide with pyrazole (coupling step) proceeded only when the head‑space of the reaction vessel was filled with an inert gas and the gas‑flow rate was properly controlled; otherwise the reaction was very slow (5 h) or failed, especially on larger scale where the head‑space volume increased.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Optimised the gas‑exchange by using a continuous Ar flow set to 89 mL min⁻¹ L⁻¹ headspace (later increased to 133 mL min⁻¹ L⁻¹) which dramatically reduced reaction time to 5–6 h even at multi‑kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “filling the headspace of the reaction vessel with Ar gas and controlling the flow rate of the gas were found to be important to complete the substitution…”, “the reaction time was longer for larger volumes of headspace…”, “When the flow rate of Ar per headspace volume was set up as 89 mL min⁻¹ L⁻¹, the reaction time for amidation was 6 h… Increasing the rate to 133 mL min⁻¹ L⁻¹ reduced the reaction time to 5 h…

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: Regioselective lithiation/alkylation of 1‑phenylpyrazole (9) gave only 57 % isolated yield at –70 °C; higher temperatures decreased conversion and the reaction did not proceed at –70 °C without additives.
Solution_Description: Added 1.5 equiv of BF₃·OEt₂, HMPA (2 % v/w) or t‑BuOK (1.5 equiv) to stabilise the lithiated intermediate, allowing the reaction to run at –70 °C (or –20 °C with BF₃·OEt₂) and increasing the isolated yield to 90 % (run 8).
Supporting_Evidence: “Reaction of the lithiated compound derived from 9… at –70 °C gave 57 % yield… reaction did not proceed at –70 °C (run 1)”, “Increasing the amount of n‑BuLi to 4.0 equiv increased the yield to 77 %…, but 9 was incompletely consumed”, “When BF₃·OEt₂… was added… it was necessary to raise the reaction temperature to –20 °C for the reaction to proceed (run 5)”, “the addition of HMPA… or t‑BuOK… allowed the reaction to proceed at –70 °C (runs 6 and 7)”, “increasing the amounts of n‑BuLi and t‑BuOK improved the conversion… affording 11 in 90 % isolated yield (run 8)”.

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: Oxidation of intermediate 11 to ketone 12 failed with several common oxidants (SO₃·pyridine, Me‑AZADO/NaOCl, N‑tert‑butylphenylsulfenamide/N‑chlorosuccinimide/DBU), resulting in complete consumption of 11 without formation of 12.
Solution_Description: Swern oxidation using TFAA/DMSO/NEt₃ in EtOAc at 0 °C–room temperature was employed, delivering 12 in 75 % isolated yield after chromatographic work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the case of SO₃·pyridine as the oxidant, 11 was completely consumed, but ketone 12 was not detected.”, “The system of Me‑AZADO/NaOCl… and the combination of N‑tert‑butylphenylsulfenamide/N‑chlorosuccinimide/DBU did not produce 12, and 11 mainly remained.”, “Swern oxidation of 11 using TFAA/DMSO/NEt₃ in EtOAc was carried out to give 12 as an oily product in 75 % yield”.

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: The coupling step to form 14 required three separate chromatographic purifications, which made the route impractical for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: An alternative synthetic route (Route C) was developed that bypassed the problematic coupling, allowing the target to be assembled in fewer steps without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was thought that route B would be difficult to apply for a large‑scale preparation because three chromatographic purifications were required.”

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: The sodium salt of intermediate 19 was hygroscopic and poorly filterable, complicating isolation and work‑up.
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was switched from THF to toluene, and the aqueous work‑up was adjusted (pH 10 adjustment with HCl then NaOH) to obtain a 57 % assay yield of 19 as an aqueous solution, which could be used directly in the next step without isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, 19 was used as an aqueous solution… because the sodium salt showed high hygroscopicity and poor filterability.”, “To enable efficient extraction into the aqueous layer, the reaction solvent was changed to toluene. After the reaction in toluene, aqueous HCl was added… to give 19 in 57 % assay yield.”

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: During the cyclisation of 20 to 21, by‑product 22 formed (≈5 % LCAP) and several other minor impurities (23–25) persisted, reducing overall yield and purity.
Solution_Description: Lowering the reaction temperature from 80 °C to 60 °C suppressed formation of 22 while maintaining conversion; subsequent crystallisation and recrystallisation steps removed residual impurities, delivering 21 in 89 % overall yield and >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction of 20 with DMFDMA… gave 21… and the undesired product 22… in 5 % LCAP.”, “The reaction temperature was changed to 60 °C to suppress the production of byproducts while maintaining the conversion of 21.”, “Crystallisation of 21… gave 77 % yield, followed by recrystallisation… gave 61.2 kg of pure 21 (99.6 % purity) in 89 % yield.”

Paper Title: Practical Preparation of a 1,3,5-Trisubstituted Pyridazin-4(1
Problem_Description: Phenylhydrazine is a mutagenic impurity; trace amounts needed to be controlled (<10 ppm) in the final product 1, requiring careful removal during work‑up.
Solution_Description: After the cyclisation, the crude product was washed and recrystallised from DMSO/EtOH, then from EtOH/TFA/water, effectively removing phenylhydrazine and other impurities, yielding >99.9 % pure 1 with phenylhydrazine below 10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “the residual amount of phenylhydrazine, which is strictly controlled as a mutagenic impurity, was not more than 10 ppm.”, “crude 1 … recrystallised … to give pure 1 (more than 99.9 % purity, LCAP) in 91 % yield.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: Long‑term storage of the heptane solvate of amide 3 caused loss of heptane and generated a flammable‑solvent hazard; drying the solvate for 40 h at 60 °C produced a degradant that converts to the undesired atropisomer impurity.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature in the API‑forming cyclization was raised from 20 °C to 30 °C to lessen the negative impact of residual DMF and water, allowing a faster, lower‑temperature drying step without excessive degradant formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “long‑term storage of the heptane solvate posed a significant stability risk.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: The EDAc coupling used a high DMF content (≈7 mL g⁻¹) which generated a DMF‑adduct impurity of aniline 1, decreasing overall yield and increasing solvent waste.
Solution_Description: A mixed solvent system of MeTHF and DMF (40 % DMF) was adopted, reducing DMF consumption by ~40 % and, together with revised equivalents of reagents, lowered the DMF‑adduct impurity from 1.5 AP to <0.6 AP while maintaining full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We envisioned using a mixture of API reaction solvent 2‑methyl‑tetrahydrofuran (MeTHF) and DMF to not only decrease the amount of DMF from the initial 7 mL g⁻¹ …”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: In the first‑generation telescoped process residual DMF (0.026 mL g⁻¹) and >6 wt % water were carried into the API reaction, leading to ~4.7 RAP atropisomer formation and inconsistent product quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: High‑throughput extraction (HTEx) was employed to redesign the three early aqueous washes: (i) the first wash used 1 M HCl with a reduced MeTHF volume (10 mL g⁻¹) to capture >90 % DMF; (ii) the second wash volume was increased to 10 mL g⁻¹ to further remove DMF; (iii) the third wash added brine (1 mL g⁻¹) to improve split velocity and limit emulsions, raising overall DMF removal to 99.7 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “HTEx was utilized for the rapid optimization of the extractions, the first three washes improved the removal of DMF from 97.4 % to 99.7 %.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: During the work‑up ~1 mL g⁻¹ of MeTHF was lost to the aqueous phase each split, causing slower phase separation, emulsion formation and product loss.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The wash volumes were adjusted (10 mL g⁻¹ MeTHF after the first split and 10 mL g⁻¹ water in the second split) and 1 mL g⁻¹ brine was added after the third wash to increase aqueous density, which eliminated emulsions and reduced product loss to <0.1 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Approximately 1 mL g⁻¹ of MeTHF is lost to the aqueous phase at each split, leading to … increased risk for emulsions.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: Using 9 M LiCl as the fourth‑wash salt left residual LiCl in the MeTHF stream, which dramatically increased atropisomer formation (~6 AP) in the API step.
Solution_Description: The fourth wash was changed to saturated NaCl (brine), which removed water efficiently, did not introduce deleterious lithium, and kept atropisomer levels low while allowing a single 15 mL g⁻¹ azeotropic distillation to reach <500 ppm water.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The workup was scaled with 9 M LiCl, but residual LiCl … produced nearly 6 AP of atropisomer 5.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: Early telescoping attempts gave inconsistent reaction stalls and variable atropisomer levels because of fluctuating LiOt‑Bu base potency, residual salts, and varying DMF/water content.
Solution_Description: The LiOt‑Bu charge was increased from 5 mol % to 7 mol % based on the linear model from the API DoE, which stabilized the reaction rate and suppressed atropisomer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Initial attempts … gave inconsistent results … due to … inconsistent LiOt‑Bu potency.”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: The fourth wash left ~6.6 wt % water in the organic stream, requiring a >45 mL g⁻¹ MeTHF azeotropic distillation (≈45 h) to reach the <500 ppm water specification.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A saturated NaCl brine wash was introduced as the fourth wash, reducing water to ~2.5 wt % and enabling a single 15 mL g⁻¹ put‑and‑take distillation to achieve the water target, cutting solvent demand and cycle time dramatically.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The fourth wash ... resulted in an organic stream with ∼6.6 wt % water … necessitated over 45 mL g⁻¹ of MeTHF …”

Paper Title: Systematic Optimization of a Robust Telescoped Process for a BTK Inhibitor with Atropisomer Control by High-Throughput Experimentation, Design of Experiments, and Linear Regression
Problem_Description: The original two‑step process required a crystallization step (heptane solvate) that added 5 % yield loss and extra solvent use, inflating cost and PMI.
Solution_Description: The two final steps were telescoped—directly feeding the crude amide 3 into the API cyclization without isolation—eliminating the crystallization loss, cutting PMI by 41 % and raising overall yield by 13 %.
Supporting_Evidence: • “We envisioned developing a telescoped process that subjected a solution of 3 directly to the final reaction.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Asymmetric Process for
Problem_Description: Ellman’s original route to tert‑butanesulfinamide (TBSA) generates toxic, foul‑smelling tert‑butyl‑thiol (4) during the cleavage of the S–S bond, and the large‑scale preparation of LiNH₂/NH₃ requires handling a very thick slurry of Li metal in liquid ammonia, causing severe agitation problems, safety hazards, and a very slow NH₃ evaporation step. Quenching the LiNH₂/NH₃ reaction with solid NH₄Cl is highly exothermic, releasing large amounts of heat.
Solution_Description: A second‑generation chiral sulfinyl‑transfer reagent (8 → 9) was designed that can be cleaved with the milder nucleophile lithium bis‑(trimethylsilyl)‑amide (LHMDS) instead of LiNH₂/NH₃, eliminating the need for cryogenic liquid ammonia and avoiding toxic gas evolution. The new process runs at −10 °C to 20 °C, uses LHMDS in THF, and the order‑of‑addition of reagents was optimized to keep the reaction exotherm under control.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Our initial attempt to synthesize TBSA using Ellman’s method encountered the release of the toxic and foul‑smelling gas tert‑butylthiol (4).”
• “The NH₂Li/NH₃ needs to be freshly prepared in situ … at −78 °C. In the preparation of LiNH₂ on a large scale, a very thick slurry is formed that causes serious agitation problems and potential safety concerns.”
• “The quenching of the reaction with solid NH₄Cl is very exothermic, and this reagent has to be added very slowly.”
• “A more practical and economical means … avoiding low‑temperature reaction conditions and replacing NH₂Li/NH₃ with a milder nucleophile, such as LHMDS.”
• “The entire process is performed under mild reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Asymmetric Process for
Problem_Description: During the conversion of template 8 to sulfonyl chloride 9 the quench with NaHCO₃ is highly exothermic and generates copious gas from SOCl₂ neutralization; pyridine is difficult to remove by aqueous wash, which reduces product recovery.
Solution_Description: The quench was changed from NaHCO₃ to water, and the work‑up was modified by adding a 5 % Na₂HPO₄ aqueous wash followed by a water wash to set the pH to ~7, which eliminates gas evolution and allows efficient removal of pyridine.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The quenching process was exothermic and produced large amounts of gas from the reaction of NaHCO₃ with the excess SOCl₂.”
• “Pyridine could not be efficiently removed from the organic phase with an aqueous wash.”
• “Under these conditions, the reaction could be quenched with water instead of NaHCO₃… a 5 % sodium hydrogen phosphate (Na₂HPO₄) aqueous wash followed by another water wash… gave a final pH of about 7.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Asymmetric Process for
Problem_Description: Concentration of the crude 9 by azeotropic distillation at 40 °C caused 5–10 % racemization of 9 and partial hydrolysis back to starting material 8.
Solution_Description: Distillation was performed at a lower temperature (≈20 °C) under vacuum to keep the water content below 0.03 % (KF) and avoid racemization; the process also incorporated a toluene co‑solvent to aid solvent switching and protect 9 from hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Concentration of the resulting organic phase by azeotropic distillation at 40 °C under vacuum … caused 5–10 % racemization of the title compound 9.”
• “The subsequent organic phase concentration by distillation avoided the racemization of 9, but decomposition of 9 to 8 occurred in this process. This issue was then solved by introducing a 5 % sodium hydrogen phosphate … under which both the hydrolysis and racemization of 9 during the distillation process were found to be minimal.”

Paper Title: Development of a Large-Scale Asymmetric Process for
Problem_Description: During the Grignard ring‑opening step, over‑addition of t‑BuMgCl led to formation of the undesired template 8 (≥6 % yield), reducing the overall yield of sulfinate 10.
Solution_Description: In‑situ React‑IR monitoring was introduced to precisely determine the endpoint of Grignard addition, allowing the use of only 1.05 equiv of t‑BuMgCl and eliminating over‑addition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Compound 8 was found in the reaction mixture in more than 6 % yield as a result of the further addition of the extra Grignard reagent to the product 10.”
• “To minimize this side reaction, the end point of the Grignard addition was therefore determined by applying in‑situ React‑IR monitoring of the reaction.”

Problem_Description: The original discovery route required multiple rounds of silica‑gel chromatography, used a potentially explosive nitration step, and proceeded through a long linear sequence (12 steps, 12 isolations) that gave only 10 % overall yield.
Solution_Description: A convergent, telescoped synthesis was designed, eliminating many chromatographic purifications and shortening the sequence to nine steps with only three isolations, increasing overall yield to 64 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The discovery route … is not particularly attractive for large‑scale manufacturing because of: (i) the requirement of several rounds of silica‑gel column chromatography; (ii) a potentially explosive nitration reaction; (iii) a long linear route.”; “We focused on these issues and planned the convergent route shown in Scheme 3.”; “The overall yield … increased from 10 % to 64 % over nine steps with three isolations.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The first N‑acylation sequence of mono‑Boc‑ethylenediamine (17) produced hygroscopic intermediate 19, which degraded the acid‑anhydride form of 15, giving only 38 % isolated yield of 20.
Solution_Description: Re‑ordering the steps – performing the first N‑acylation, then Boc deprotection, followed by the second N‑acylation in one pot – gave 94 % isolated yield of amide 21 (crystallizable) and, after inverse addition of the acid chloride, 99 % purity of 20 in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “In the first instance … secondary N‑acylation of 19 … presented 20 in 38 % isolated yield. The hygroscopic property of 19 led to degradation …”; “In the alternate sequence, amide 21 … could be isolated by crystallization … in 94 % yield with >98 % HPLC purity.”; “One‑pot Boc deprotection followed by the second N‑acylation … provided 20 in high yield with >99 % purity through crystallization.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During O‑alkylation of 23 with 20, a Smiles rearrangement produced an aniline by‑product 25 that increased over time, lowering the isolated yield of the desired product 24 (79 %).
Solution_Description: Switching the base to tBuONa and using a toluene/1‑BuOH (3:1) solvent system suppressed the formation of 25, delivering 24 in 88 % yield with >98 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The aniline compound (25) … increased over time via Smiles rearrangement. The aniline 25 was removed completely by crystallization to give the crystalline 24 in 79 % isolated yield.”; “We found that using tBuONa as a base and toluene/1‑BuOH = 3/1 (w/w) as a solvent could suppress generation of this impurity. This optimized condition gave target compound 24 in 88 % yield and >98 % HPLC purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The Pd‑catalyzed C–N coupling step showed lot‑to‑lot variability; with some catalyst lots the starting material was not fully consumed and by‑products increased, compromising yield (69 % isolated).
Solution_Description: In‑situ generation of the active catalyst from Pd(OAc)₂ (2 mol %) and PtBu₃ (6 mol %) in xylene gave consistent high conversion (75 % isolated yield of 26) and allowed reduction of Pd loading to 5 mol % on kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “When a different lot of Pd(PtBu₃)₂ was used … the starting material was not consumed and a larger amount of by‑products were observed.”; “In situ preparation of the catalyst was investigated, and it was achieved with 2 mol % Pd(OAc)₂ and 6 mol % PtBu₃ … provided 26 in 96 % yield and >99 % HPLC purity.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Friedel–Crafts acylation of 26 to afford 29 generated a highly exothermic quench (≈243 kcal mol⁻¹) during addition of 1 N HCl, posing safety concerns and giving low production efficiency (≈17 g L⁻¹).
Solution_Description: A slow addition of 1 N HCl over 3 h while maintaining the temperature below 25 °C was implemented, and the reaction mixture was diluted with additional solvent to control the heat release, improving safety and allowing reliable scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “During quenching, a considerable exothermic reaction (243 kcal/mol …) was observed. A slow addition of 1 N HCl over 3 h and a large amount of reaction solvent were therefore required.”; “The reaction was cooled to −5 °C … 1 N HCl aq. (466.8 kg) was added over 4 h with maintenance of the internal temperature below 25 °C.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Acyl‑chlorination of 29 with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) involved hazardous reagents, required removal of excess SOCl₂, and produced variable brown coloration needing decoloration with activated carbon.
Solution_Description: The reagent was replaced by 1‑chloro‑N,N‑2‑trimethyl‑1‑propenylamine (CTPA), a bulk‑available, less hazardous chlorinating agent that gave clean conversion without removal of excess reagent or decoloration, reducing cost and improving safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “Through screening of acyl chlorination reagents, 1‑chloro‑N,N‑2‑trimethyl‑1‑propenylamine (CTPA) was found to be suitable for the reaction, and this reagent can be obtained in bulk quantity at reasonable cost. Compared with SOCl₂, acyl chlorination with CTPA did not require removal of excess reagents and/or decoloration with activated carbon.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the N‑alkylation of 33 to 34, a number of bases and solvents gave poor conversion, low selectivity, or generated by‑product 37 (≈10 %); some bases gave no reaction.
Solution_Description: Optimisation identified K₃PO₄ in DMA at 70 °C as the best combination, delivering >98 % conversion to 34 with high selectivity and suppressing the formation of 37.
Supporting_Evidence: “Less expensive K₃PO₄ and less toxic DMA showed almost identical reactivity and N/O selectivity … Heating to 70 °C increased reactivity, although regioselectivity was decreased slightly.”; Table 2 entries 2‑3 show K₃PO₄/DMA at 50 °C (92.2 %) and 70 °C (98.9 %).

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During amidation to form 13, dimer 44 formed (up to 4.2 %); the acid chloride precipitated and clogged the transfer line when added dropwise, reducing yield.
Solution_Description: An inverse addition—adding the acid chloride to a solution of amine—combined with a lower temperature (20‑25 °C) caused the acid chloride to precipitate, lowering its concentration in solution and suppressing dimer formation to <0.5 %; the amount of amine could also be reduced to 1.05 equiv without extending reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “Inverse addition … could reduce formation of dimer 44 from 4.2 % to 0.5 % … The acid chloride 28 solution in toluene was supersaturated, and the precipitated acyl chloride was clogged during transfer. However, it was proposed that precipitation … could lead to suppression of dimer formation.”; Table 3 shows dimer % decreasing with lower temperature (entry 2 30 °C, 0.33 %; entry 3 20 °C, 0.22 %).

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Use of toxic and environmentally unfriendly solvents (CHCl₃, DMF) in several steps conflicted with green‑chemistry goals and required extensive work‑up.
Solution_Description: CHCl₃ was replaced by toluene for extractions and DMF was replaced by NMP or DMA where appropriate, removing hazardous solvents from the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “Undesirable solvents such as CHCl₃ and DMF needed to be avoided considering the environmental, toxicological, and quality concerns.”; “Hanging the solvent from DMF to NMP … suppressed formation of by‑products.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient and Cost-Effective Telescoping Route to a Key Synthetic Precursor for the Preparation of a Renin Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The overall process still required isolation of multiple intermediates (e.g., 13, 29) causing product loss and lower efficiency.
Solution_Description: Key steps were telescoped (e.g., 13 → 2, 24 → 26 → 29) so that intermediates were not isolated, reducing the number of isolations from 12 to 3 and raising overall yield to 64 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “For the following four steps and final two steps, we developed telescoped processes to avoid the isolation of intermediates.”; “The overall yield to 2 approached 64 % over nine steps.”

Paper Title: Scalable Preparation of Methylated Ando-Type Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons Reagent
Problem_Description: A concise description of each issue.
Solution_Description: A concise description of each fix.
Supporting_Evidence: All excerpts that justify the classification.

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: The reaction mechanism of ammonium‑salt‑accelerated hydrazinolysis of unactivated amides was not understood, hindering reliable scale‑up and optimization.
Solution_Description: Kinetic experiments combined with DFT calculations were performed to elucidate the cooperative role of the hydrazinium salt and hydrazine in the rate‑determining step.
Supporting_Evidence: “We first studied the reaction mechanism by kinetic experiments and DFT calculations and found that cooperation of the hydrazinium salt and hydrazine is important for promoting the cleavage of unactivated amides.”; “The initial‑rate experiment results indicated that the reaction was first‑order with respect to amide 1a, hydrazinium bromide, and hydrazine monohydrate… suggesting that these three molecules are involved in the rate‑determining step.”; “The activation parameters… ΔH‡ = 17.5 kcal mol⁻¹, ΔS‡ = −33.3 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, ΔG‡ = 27.4 kcal mol⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: Batch processing of the hydrazinolysis required strong acids or bases and long heating times, posing safety hazards and low productivity for large‑scale synthesis.
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous microwave flow reactor, providing safer, smaller reaction volumes and faster heating, which facilitates scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “The application of continuous flow synthesis is a potential solution to this problem of batch reactions… flow method is safer than the batch system because the reaction volume of the reactor is smaller than that of the batch system.”; “We next attempted to scale up this reaction by using a microwave flow reactor.”; “The continuous flow system can constantly provide products, and because the reaction scale depends on the operation time, scale‑up of the flow system… is easier than scale‑up of the batch system.”

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: Residence time in the flow reactor is limited, requiring a rapid reaction to achieve high conversion.
Solution_Description: Microwave power and temperature were increased (up to 60 W, 161–170 °C) and substrate concentration raised to 0.67 M, which accelerated the hydrazinolysis and gave >90 % conversion within the 5.5 min residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: “We explored the reaction conditions… at a flow rate of 1.0 mL min⁻¹… 96 % conversion under microwave irradiation conditions (40 W)… To improve the productivity per unit time, we tried a higher amide concentration… 45 W at 0.67 M… Further increasing the irradiation power to 50 W gave the optimal result of 97 % conversion.”; “The optimal result (93 % conversion) was obtained with 60 W microwave irradiation (entry 9).”

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: Conventional batch heating gave only 75 % conversion, indicating a low yield compared with microwave heating.
Solution_Description: Switching to microwave heating (40 W, 134 °C) increased the conversion to 96 %, demonstrating that rapid, uniform heating improves yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “For comparison, we performed the same reaction under batch conditions, and the reaction proceeded with 75 % conversion (entry 4), most likely because of the inefficient heat transfer under conventional heating conditions in comparison with the microwave heating conditions.”; “The reaction proceeded with 96 % conversion under microwave irradiation conditions (40 W) at 0.50 M 1b (entry 1).”

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: Using ammonium salts in the flow reactor would generate gaseous ammonia, creating a safety risk.
Solution_Description: Ammonium salt was replaced with commercially available hydrazinium bromide, which acts as the active species without releasing NH₃ gas.
Supporting_Evidence: “We replaced the ammonium salt with commercially available hydrazinium bromide, a proposed active species generated from the ammonium salt and hydrazine, to prevent the generation of gaseous ammonia in the reactor.”

Paper Title: Ammonium Salt-Accelerated Hydrazinolysis of Unactivated Amides: Mechanistic Investigation and Application to a Microwave Flow Process
Problem_Description: The reaction mixture contains excess hydrazine hydrate, making isolation of the amine products challenging.
Solution_Description: Products were isolated either by flash silica gel chromatography or by aqueous work‑up (e.g., basification and extraction), providing a reliable purification route.
Supporting_Evidence: “It is noted that the product 3 could be separated from the excess hydrazine hydrate by either silica gel column chromatography or aqueous workup.”

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: The original starting material 2,4‑dichloro‑1,3,5‑triazine (6) was considerably expensive and had low commercial availability, making the first‑generation route uneconomical for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The starting material was switched to cyanuric chloride (9), which is inexpensive and readily available in bulk, enabling a cost‑effective and practical synthesis of ASP3026.
Supporting_Evidence: “(1) starting 1,3‑dichlorotriazine (6) was considerably expensive and had low commercial availability” (sec 2.2). “A change of starting material from 2,4‑dichloro‑1,3,5‑triazine (6) to cyanuric chloride (9)…significantly improved the economic efficiency of the process” (abstract & sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: Intermediate 8 generated in the SNAr step was unstable under air, preventing its isolation and leading to low overall yield.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed as a telescoped sequence (no isolation of 8) by switching directly from the 2‑butanone solution of 8 to the SNAr reaction with 5·TFA, thus avoiding exposure of the unstable intermediate to air.
Supporting_Evidence: “A reaction with 8 and 5·TFA had to be conducted continuously…since 8 was unstable under air” (sec 2.1). “The reaction was conducted continuously…without any isolation of 8” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: The SNAr reaction between 10 and 5·TFA gave poor conversion and low isolated yield (≈17 % overall) owing to side‑reactions and instability of the product 11.
Solution_Description: THF was identified as the best solvent and the reaction temperature was optimized (40 °C) to improve conversion, although the route was ultimately abandoned because of impurity formation and decomposition of 11.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2 entries show THF at 40 °C gave the highest conversion (entry 11, 69.9 % HPLC area) (sec 2.3). “Despite the sequence of investigation…the efficiency of the SNAr reaction was not improved sufficiently…extreme instability of resulting 11…poor yield” (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: In the cyanuric‑chloride‑based route, intermediate 11 decomposed during the subsequent hydrogenation step, causing a drop in overall yield to 17 %.
Solution_Description: The cyanuric‑chloride route was abandoned in favor of a new second‑generation route that delayed introduction of the piperazine moiety to a later stage, avoiding the decomposition of 11.
Supporting_Evidence: “ 11 easily decomposed under a condition of following hydrogenation, and the subsequent yield…fell 17 %” (sec 2.3). “We relinquished this synthetic route” (sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: Aniline 5·TFA (the TFA salt of 5) was unstable under air, causing difficulties in quality control, storage, and transportation.
Solution_Description: The TFA salt was generated in‑situ after hydrogenation of 4 and used directly in the SNAr step without isolation, eliminating the need to store the unstable salt.
Supporting_Evidence: “TFA was embedded into the synthetic scheme by obtaining 5 as a TFA salt after a hydrogenation of 4 and using such salt directly in a substitution reaction with 8” (sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: Crude API obtained from the second‑generation route frequently crystallised as a mixed polymorph (Forms A02/A04/A06) and the ratio of Form A03/A04 was inconsistent, jeopardising product specification.
Solution_Description: Recrystallisation from 2‑butanone was implemented (solvent‑mediated polymorphic transformation) to reliably convert the mixture to the thermodynamically stable Form A04.
Supporting_Evidence: “2‑Butanone was selected…because 1 was soluble enough in 2‑butanone to conduct recrystallisation within a practical solvent volume” (sec 2.7). “Recrystallisation with 2‑butanone was incorporated in a process to consolidate polymorphic mixture into Form A04” (sec 2.7).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: Use of activated carbon to remove impurity 18 during recrystallisation reduced the overall yield of the final API from 90 % to 75 % and introduced a yellow colour and a new oxidation impurity.
Solution_Description: After optimisation of the SNAr step (stoichiometry and temperature) that eliminated impurity 18, the activated‑carbon step was removed; recrystallisation alone gave pure Form A04 with higher yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The yield of recrystallisation step was decreased from 90 to 75 % because of adsorption loss on activated carbon…purified 1 was colored yellow…new impurity generated possibly because of oxidation by the activated‑carbon–molecular oxygen system” (sec 2.7). “When 19 was completely eliminated…crude 1 can be reproducibly converted to pure Form A04 by same recrystallisation condition…without an activated carbon process.” (sec 2.9).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: The overall yield of the first‑generation route was only 31 % (overall), leading to inefficient material usage and higher manufacturing cost.
Solution_Description: The second‑generation route introduced a late‑stage reductive amination to install the N‑methyl‑piperazine, reduced the equivalents of the nucleophile 15 (to 0.95‑0.5 eq.) and lowered the SNAr temperature to –10 °C, raising the overall yield to 45 % and cutting the cost roughly in half.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 3 shows overall yield 31 % (first) vs 45 % (second) and cost ~½ (sec 2.5). “Decrease of 15 to 0.95 eq…and change of the reaction temperature to 0 °C effectively inhibited 19…When –10 °C was adopted, 19 was best controlled to ND” (sec 2.9, Table 5).

Paper Title: Improved Manufacturing Route and Polymorphic Control of a Potent and Selective Anaplastic Lymphoma Kinase (ALK) Inhibitor ASP3026
Problem_Description: Several steps (e.g., hydrogenations, SNAr reactions) required long reaction times (up to 18 h) that limited throughput.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Reaction times were shortened by increasing catalyst loading (10 % Pd/C), using efficient stirring and temperature ramps, and by performing reactions in larger, well‑mixed reactors, thereby maintaining productivity despite the added steps in the second‑generation route.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrogenation…with 10 % Pd/C…at 25 °C for 5 h” (sec 4.7.1.2). “A 1500 L autoclave…stirred at 40 °C for 7 h” (sec 4.7.3.5). “Production lead time was not affected…as a result of the optimization of work‑up and isolation protocol” (sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Very low furfuryl‑alcohol yield (8 %) when furfural is reduced in 0.5 M H₂SO₄/CH₃CN using a Cu/SS electrode pair.
Solution_Description: Replace the aprotic acetonitrile with the protic solvent ethanol, which raised the yield to 29 % under the same acidic conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Only a yield of 8 % was obtained for the targeted furfuryl alcohol" (Table 1, entry 1).

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Acidic conditions (HCl) give modest yields (33–41 %) and very poor Faradaic efficiencies (≈ 18–19 %) because competing hydrogen‑evolution consumes electrons.
Solution_Description: Introduce a stronger acid (HCl) as the electrolyte and keep the reaction basic rather than strongly acidic; this increases the yield to 41 % and improves selectivity toward furfuryl alcohol.
Supporting_Evidence: • "In the presence of hydrochloric acid… yield 33 % (entry 3) and 41 % (entry 4)."

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Microreactors are often claimed to work without supporting electrolyte, but in this system a small amount of electrolyte was required for acceptable conversion.
Solution_Description: Add 0.05 M of a supporting electrolyte (either the ionic liquid Ammoeng 110 or n‑Bu₄NBr), which raises the yield to 55 % under the same HCl/EtOH conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Small amounts of electrolyte… such as Ammoeng 110 or n‑Bu₄NBr, were beneficial to increase the overall yield (entries 9–10, 55 %)."

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Acidic media lead to low Faradaic efficiencies (≈ 18–19 %) because the hydrogen‑evolution reaction dominates, wasting electrons and lowering product yield.
Solution_Description: Switch to a basic reaction medium (K‑ethoxide in ethanol) which suppresses H₂ evolution and provides a 90 % isolated yield with 90 % Faradaic efficiency.
Supporting_Evidence: • "A substantial increase in the reaction yield was observed… best results were obtained with a copper/graphite couple yielding 90 % (Table 2, entry 3)."

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Batch electrochemical reduction of furfural requires 6 h residence time and delivers only 18–31 % yield, far inferior to the flow system.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Employ the micro‑channel flow reactor (high electrode surface‑to‑volume ratio, short diffusion distances) delivering quantitative conversion in 10 min residence time.
Supporting_Evidence: • "When we carried out the reaction in a batch electrochemical cell, the yield dropped to 18 % … and requires 6 h of reaction time."

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: During continuous operation the furfural‑reduction yield gradually declines due to fouling/deposition on the electrode surfaces.
Solution_Description: Introduce a periodic cleaning and surface‑treatment step (e.g., washing the electrode) and operate two reactors in parallel—one in reaction mode, the other in cleaning mode—to maintain constant productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: • "The decline can be attributed to erosion of the electrode efficiency… restored by incorporating an adequate cleaning and surface treatment step."

Paper Title: Efficient Electrocatalytic Reduction of Furfural to Furfuryl Alcohol in a Microchannel Flow Reactor
Problem_Description: Optimizing electrolyte concentration and reaction conditions would require many separate experiments, causing variability and low throughput.
Solution_Description: Use the 8‑channel parallel microreactor to screen eight electrolyte concentrations simultaneously, allowing rapid identification of the optimal 0.10 M HCl / 0.05 M C₂H₅OK conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • "Our homemade electrochemical reactor design provided a clear and unique advantage as eight reaction conditions can be screened simultaneously in parallel…"

Paper Title: Self-Assembled Polymeric Pyridine Copper Catalysts for Huisgen Cycloaddition with Alkynes and Acetylene Gas: Application in Synthesis of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: The previously reported MPPI‑Cu heterogeneous catalyst gave very poor conversion for the Huisgen cycloaddition of benzyl azide (4b) with acetylene gas when the reaction was performed in water (only 11 % yield without catalyst and low conversion with MPPI‑Cu).
Solution_Description: A new self‑assembled polymeric Cu(I) catalyst, PVPy‑Cu‑SO₄ (3a), was employed. Under the same aqueous conditions (90 °C, 16 h) the reaction afforded the desired 1‑phenylmethyl‑1H‑1,2,3‑triazole (8b) in 92 % isolated yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “MPPI‑Cu did not efficiently promote the cycloaddition in water.”
• “The reaction of benzyl azide (4b) with acetylene gas … using 3a in water at 90 °C for 16 h … 92 % yield, whereas only 11 % of the product was obtained without a catalyst.”

Paper Title: Self-Assembled Polymeric Pyridine Copper Catalysts for Huisgen Cycloaddition with Alkynes and Acetylene Gas: Application in Synthesis of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: When the aliphatic azide 4a was reacted with acetylene gas in water, the substrate’s poor solubility gave a very low conversion (only 51 % yield).
Solution_Description: The reaction solvent was switched from water to methyl‑isobutyl‑ketone (MIBK), which improved the reaction outcome, delivering the product 8a in 51 % yield under otherwise identical conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Although water was not an appropriate solvent in the reaction of aliphatic azide 4a, the reaction in methyl isobutyl ketone (MIBK) provided the product 8a at a 51 % yield (entry 11).”

Paper Title: Self-Assembled Polymeric Pyridine Copper Catalysts for Huisgen Cycloaddition with Alkynes and Acetylene Gas: Application in Synthesis of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: During the attempted synthesis of the tazobactam intermediate 9 in water, the azide precursor decomposed, preventing formation of the desired triazole.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed in MIBK instead of water and the sodium‑ascorbate reductant was omitted. Under these conditions, protected tazobactam 10 was obtained in 91 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the decomposition of 9 was observed.”
• “Finally, the reaction in MIBK without the addition of sodium ascorbate provided protected tazobactam 10 at a 91 % yield, whereas larger amounts of 3a were necessary to efficiently promote the reaction.”

Paper Title: Self-Assembled Polymeric Pyridine Copper Catalysts for Huisgen Cycloaddition with Alkynes and Acetylene Gas: Application in Synthesis of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: Using a conventional CuI catalyst (10 mol %) for the acetylene‑gas cycloaddition gave a very low isolated yield of the product (26 %).
Solution_Description: Replacing CuI with the polymeric PVPy‑Cu‑SO₄ (3a) dramatically increased the yield to 91 %, demonstrating the superior activity of the new catalyst system.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In contrast, the reaction with CuI (10 mol %) under similar conditions gave 10 in 26 % yield.”
• “The reaction in MIBK … provided protected tazobactam 10 at a 91 % yield … using 3a.”

Paper Title: Self-Assembled Polymeric Pyridine Copper Catalysts for Huisgen Cycloaddition with Alkynes and Acetylene Gas: Application in Synthesis of Tazobactam
Problem_Description: At the very low catalyst loading (100 mol ppm Cu) the tazobactam synthesis gave sub‑optimal conversion; higher catalyst loading was required for efficient turnover.
Solution_Description: The amount of PVPy‑Cu‑SO₄ (3a) was increased (up to 10 mol % Cu) which restored quantitative conversion and enabled isolation of tazobactam in 91 % overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “larger amounts of 3a were necessary to efficiently promote the reaction.”
• “The reaction … provided protected tazobactam 10 at a 91 % yield.”

Paper Title: Modeling and Design of a Flow-Microreactor-Based Process for Synthesizing Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: When the inner diameter of the tubular reactor is increased, mass‑transfer becomes the rate‑limiting step and the product yield drops; simultaneously the larger diameter reduces heat‑removal capacity so that the reaction temperature exceeds 180 °C, causing product discoloration and loss of quality.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
[MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Static (helical) mixers were built into the second half of the 4.35 mm‑i.d. reactor. The additional mixing elements restored mass‑transfer rates, recovered the high conversion/yield and allowed operation at the same temperature without overheating. The reactor with built‑in static mixers increased the production volume ≈ 39‑fold while maintaining > 99 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “It was found that as the inner diameter becomes large, the product yield becomes low because the mass transfer approaches the rate‑limiting step of the reaction process.” (Abstract) 
• “The reaction temperature in the reactor having an inner diameter of 7.53 mm greatly exceeded 180 °C as a result of the decrease in the heat exchange performance, and the product quality was deteriorated because of coloration.” (Sec 3.2) 
• “The use of SMs makes it possible to solve the problem of decreased product yield when the inner diameter of the reactor is large.” (Sec 3.3) 
• “The production volume of the reactor with built‑in SMs was improved about 39 times compared with the conventional one without lowering the product yield.” (Fig 10 & Table 2) 
• “Temperature distribution … was almost uniform for the 0.75 mm reactor, whereas the 7.53 mm reactor showed temperatures > 180 °C.” (Fig 8) 
• “Mass‑transfer performance is necessary when the inner diameter is increased … static mixers … were proposed …” (Sec 3.3)

Paper Title: Modeling and Design of a Flow-Microreactor-Based Process for Synthesizing Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: The T‑shaped micromixer produced slightly lower product concentrations than the V‑ and vortex‑shaped mixers, indicating insufficient mixing efficiency at low flow rates.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: CFD simulations compared T‑, V‑, and vortex‑shaped mixers; the V‑shaped mixer was selected because it provided mixing performance comparable to the vortex design while having a simpler geometry, thus improving mass‑transfer without increasing complexity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The V‑shaped mixer showed the same results as the vortex‑shaped mixer… the T‑shaped mixer results were slightly lower… because the V‑ and vortex‑shaped mixers are superior in mixing efficiency.” (Sec 3.1)

• “From the results of this CFD simulation study, it was decided to select the V‑shaped mixer because it has a simpler channel structure but exhibits the same mixing performance as the vortex‑shaped mixer.” (Sec 3.1)

Paper Title: Modeling and Design of a Flow-Microreactor-Based Process for Synthesizing Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Process development relied on trial‑and‑error experimentation, which required many repeated runs and prolonged the time needed to optimize the flow‑microreactor synthesis of the ionic liquid.
Solution_Description: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were employed to predict temperature, concentration, and velocity fields, enabling rapid virtual screening of mixers and reactor geometries and thereby reducing the number of physical experiments required.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Modeling and Design of a Flow-Microreactor-Based Process for Synthesizing Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: The synthesis of BMIM.Cl is highly exothermic; insufficient heat removal in larger‑diameter reactors leads to temperatures above 180 °C, causing product discoloration (quality loss) and potential safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The operating temperature of the oil bath and flow rates were fixed at 170 °C, and reactor designs (inner‑diameter selection and inclusion of static mixers) were optimized to maintain uniform temperature profiles and avoid overheating.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “However, since the synthesis of ILs is highly exothermic, it is necessary to efficiently remove the heat of reaction to avoid quality decay or runaway conditions.” (Introduction) 
• “The reaction temperature in the reactor having an inner diameter of 7.53 mm greatly exceeded 180 °C … product quality was deteriorated because of coloration.” (Sec 3.2) 
• “The temperature of the oil bath was set to 170 °C … the other design and operation conditions were set in the same way as the experimental conditions.” (Sec 3.1) 
• “Temperature distribution … was almost uniform for the 0.75 mm reactor, whereas the 7.53 mm reactor showed temperatures > 180 °C.” (Fig 8)

Paper Title: Modeling and Design of a Flow-Microreactor-Based Process for Synthesizing Ionic Liquids
Problem_Description: Increasing production volume by numbering‑up many parallel microreactors adds considerable equipment cost and operational complexity.
Solution_Description: Instead of scaling out with many parallel channels, the authors enlarged the inner diameter of a single reactor and introduced static mixers to boost throughput, thereby achieving a 39‑fold increase in production volume without the need for multiple reactors.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of an Irreversible Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) T790 M Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Removal of the N‑7‑SEM protecting group (steps 6‑7) gave low conversion and many impurities; the crude product could not be isolated cleanly by silica‑gel chromatography and the overall yield dropped dramatically on scale (41 % < 100 mg → 11 % on 3 g). Residual formaldehyde was identified as a root‑cause, making the process inconsistent.
Solution_Description: A large excess of ammonium‑hydroxide was added in a biphasic system (CH₂Cl₂/tert‑amyl‑alcohol/water) with slow addition (0‑20 °C) to cleave the N‑7‑hydroxymethyl group, trapping formaldehyde as water‑soluble hexamethylenetetramine. The resulting crude 12 was crystallised as the dihydrochloride (12·2 HCl) from isopropanol, providing >90 % pure, formaldehyde‑free material and eliminating the scale‑dependent loss.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of an Irreversible Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) T790 M Inhibitor

Solution_Description: A new amidation was developed using K₃PO₄ as base in a 1:1 water/tert‑amyl‑alcohol biphasic mixture at ca. 20 °C. The reaction completed within 5 min with minimal side‑products. The crude mixture was passed through a silica pad (2:1 i‑PrOH/MeOH) and the API was crystallised from hot isopropanol (two‑stage cooling), delivering the API in 65 % isolated yield (overall) and >95 % purity.

Paper Title: Early Process Development of an Irreversible Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) T790 M Inhibitor

Paper Title: Early Process Development of an Irreversible Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) T790 M Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Initial Buchwald–Hartwig C‑N coupling gave incomplete conversion (24 h with K₃PO₄) and required high catalyst loading, limiting throughput.

Problem_Description: Final API required high‑purity isolation; conventional silica chromatography gave only ~95 % purity.

Paper Title: Industry-Oriented Route Evaluation and Process Optimization for the Preparation of Brexpiprazole
Problem_Description: In the original O‑alkylation of quinolinone 2 with 1‑bromo‑4‑chlorobutane, a dimeric impurity 6 formed inevitably, and basic‑condition side‑products 7 and 8 were generated.  These impurities persisted into later steps (forming 9 and 10), lowering the overall conversion and making the crude mixture difficult to purify.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to a revised three‑step sequence that starts from dihydroquinolinone 11 (O‑alkylation → oxidation → N‑alkylation).  The O‑alkylation was performed in DMF at 10–20 °C, which suppressed formation of the dimeric impurity 13 (the analogue of 6) and avoided side‑products 7/8.  The lower temperature and DMF solvent improved both conversion and impurity profile.

"In the revised route ... O‑alkylation of dihydroquinolinone 11 produced chlorobutoxy‑dihydroquinolinone 12 ... which was then oxidated to chlorobutoxy‑quinolinone 4.",
"DMF gave a relatively small amount of 13, so it was chosen for further condition optimizations.",
"With respect to the reaction temperature, as shown in entries 5 and 6, lower levels of 13 and 12a were observed at 10–20 °C, but longer reaction times were required."]

Paper Title: Industry-Oriented Route Evaluation and Process Optimization for the Preparation of Brexpiprazole

The reaction was run at 20–30 °C with DDQ (1.2 equiv) and the work‑up employed hot ethyl acetate, providing a cleaner product.

Problem_Description: Several alternative oxidation solvents (acetonitrile, 2‑MeTHF, CPME) failed to fully convert intermediate 12 even after prolonged heating, resulting in low yields and extended reaction times.

Paper Title: Industry-Oriented Route Evaluation and Process Optimization for the Preparation of Brexpiprazole
Problem_Description: The dimeric impurity 13 produced during O‑alkylation had very poor solubility in common work‑up solvents, making its removal by conventional extraction difficult and lowering overall isolated yield of intermediate 12.

Paper Title: Industry-Oriented Route Evaluation and Process Optimization for the Preparation of Brexpiprazole
Problem_Description: In the N‑alkylation step, using 2.1 equiv of K₂CO₃ (high base loading) produced high levels of process‑related impurities 15 and 16 and required 15 h at reflux, leading to low overall yield and increased material cost.
Solution_Description: The reaction medium was changed to EtOH/H₂O (1:2.5) and the base loading reduced to 1.2 times the stoichiometric amount.  Together with using 1.1 equiv of arylpiperazine 5, impurity levels dropped below 0.05 % and the reaction proceeded efficiently at 80–85 °C (15 h).

"It was also discovered that the two impurities were further reduced by increasing the equivalents of arylpiperazine 5 ... finally, the conditions were defined as 1.1 equiv of arylpiperazine 5 and 1.2 times the molar ratio of K₂CO₃ in EtOH/H₂O (1:2.5)."]

Paper Title: Industry-Oriented Route Evaluation and Process Optimization for the Preparation of Brexpiprazole
Problem_Description: Residual impurity 6 persisted after the N‑alkylation, and conventional crystallization did not fully eliminate it, risking the final API purity.
Solution_Description: A multi‑step acid–base work‑up was introduced: formation of the HCl salt, treatment with activated carbon in refluxing ethanol/water, followed by basification and recrystallization.  This sequence removed impurity 6 completely, delivering API of ≥99.90 % HPLC purity.
