Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: The original synthetic sequence required ZnBr₂ as a debromination inhibitor during the nitro‑group hydrogenolysis. Using ZnBr₂ together with a sulfided Pt/C catalyst created a poisoned catalyst system that raised robustness and safety concerns for a trickle‑bed reactor.
Solution_Description: The route was re‑ordered so that the Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling (step 1) was performed before the hydrogenolysis, eliminating the need for ZnBr₂ and allowing a straightforward continuous‑flow hydrogenolysis.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The most recent cGMP production… began with reduction of a nitrobenzene 2 to aniline 3… with the use of a sulfided Pt/C catalyst in the presence of ZnBr₂.”
• “The desire to reduce the dehalogenation potential during hydrogenolysis prompted reordering of the synthetic sequence… which obviated the need for use of ZnBr₂ as a debromination inhibitor.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: The nitro‑group hydrogenolysis is highly exothermic; controlling the temperature in a packed‑bed reactor required careful heat removal. The reaction also required a very dilute (19:1 THF/water) feed to stay homogeneous, leading to high solvent consumption and operational inefficiency.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A custom trickle‑bed reactor (63 mm ID, 1.8 m length) with large particle‑size Pd/Al₂O₃ catalyst and a central cooling tube was employed to improve heat removal and maintain uniform gas‑liquid distribution. Temperature was actively controlled based on online HPLC and thermocouple data.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The reaction is exothermic… the reactor temperature was controlled… to manage the exotherm and maintain the temperature below 90 °C.”
• “A 63 mm‑ID reactor… with a 13 mm × 1.3 m cooling tube installed in the centre of the catalyst bed.”
• “The reactor temperature was adjusted based upon real‑time monitoring of the reaction exotherm and online analysis of the reactor outflow by HPLC.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Scaling down the continuous hydrogenolysis reactor to small diameters caused poor flow regime, channeling and inconsistent conversion, while diameters smaller than ten times the catalyst particle size led to unreliable performance.
Solution_Description: The reactor was scaled up to a 63 mm internal diameter (≈10 × catalyst particle size) and non‑porous Al₂O₃ packing was added above and below the catalyst bed to promote uniform flow and reduce channeling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reducing reactor internal diameter to less than 10× catalyst particle diameter led to inconsistent results.”
• “The smallest practical reactor scale was found to be 10 mm internal diameter when using 1 mm catalyst beads.”
• “Non‑porous Al₂O₃ beads... were packed to promote a more uniform distribution of the flow of hydrogen with the solution of 8.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Catalyst aging in the trickle‑bed reactor caused a progressive loss of activity, requiring higher jacket temperatures to maintain conversion and raising concerns about catalyst lifetime.
Solution_Description: Jacket temperature was incrementally raised during the run to compensate for catalyst deactivation, and the need for a defined catalyst‑bed lifetime was identified for future campaigns.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “As the catalyst aged in the reactor, there was a progressive need to increase the reactor jacket temperature to offset the reduced rate of reaction.”
• “Important concerns surrounded… catalyst bed lifetime… a single bed should last an entire campaign (≈150 kg).”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: The Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling was highly sensitive to mixing; insufficient liquid‑liquid mass transfer led to incomplete conversion and required precise control of catalyst loading.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: An automated intermittent‑flow stirred‑tank reactor with refilling capability was employed to guarantee vigorous mixing. Catalyst charge was modulated (0.5 mol % → 0.19 mol %) to study its effect on conversion, and peristaltic pumps provided controlled feeding.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Due to the mixing sensitivity… the most rapid scale‑up… would employ the automated, refilling stirred tank reactor… designed… to be approximately 15 min.”
• “After 76 h of operation, the catalyst charge was intentionally reduced to 0.19 mol %… slowed the reaction to afford only 93 % conversion.”
• “Solutions … were preheated … and charged via peristaltic pumps … the reaction was allowed to progress at 64–65 °C for 25 min.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Dichloromethane (DCM) was used as the solvent for the palladium catalyst solution, raising safety and regulatory concerns for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: The catalyst solution was switched to a 1:1 (v/v) THF/water mixture, eliminating DCM from the process while maintaining catalyst performance.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Because of concerns surrounding the use of DCM in commercial manufacturing… a solution of catalyst 4 in 1:1 (v/v) THF/water was prepared and charged manually to the reactor for two cycles; the reaction was found to reach completion in 16 min.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Residual palladium and iron from the Suzuki coupling needed to be reduced to <20 ppm and <12 ppm respectively to meet impurity specifications and avoid toxic metal exposure.
Solution_Description: A three‑stage mixer–settler extraction using sodium diethyldithiocarbamate (DDC) as a scavenger was implemented, followed by inline 10 µm filtration and a final 1 µm polishing filter to achieve the required metal removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “A heated three‑stage mixer–settler extraction system… DDC (0.02 equiv) was introduced… to aid in the layer separation…”
• “ICP‑MS analysis … showed the inline filter to be effective in removal of Fe to below 12 ppm.”
• “An additional 1 µm polish filtration was needed … to achieve removal of Pd to <20 ppm.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Continuous crystallization of intermediate 8 experienced minor solid build‑up on reactor walls, baffles and probes, which could potentially impair operation over longer campaigns.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Two mixed‑suspension, mixed‑product‑removal (MSMPR) crystallizers were operated with controlled antisolvent addition and temperature, and automated dual‑filter systems performed in‑line solid removal without manual handling.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Pyrazole 8 was continuously crystallized by adding 1:1 (v/v) ethanol/water antisolvent … in two mixed suspension, mixed product‑removal crystallizers (MSMPRs).”
• “Minor solid accumulation … did not interfere with processing during the 100 h operation.”
• “The slurry from the second MSMPR was transferred to one of two parallel filters, which were fully automated and operated in duty/standby mode.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: During step 3 a partial blockage formed in the anhydride feed line due to accumulation of TEA·HCl salt, causing a spike in unreacted aniline 9 and reducing conversion.

Solution_Description: The blockage was cleared by switching to a fresh feed solution and the root cause (incomplete anhydride formation) was addressed by improving the crystallization of anhydride 10 to obtain a stable, solid feed, thereby preventing salt buildup.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “The blockage developed from the gradual accumulation of TEA·HCl salt that had formed in the 10 feed can and was attributed to incomplete anhydride formation prior to solution filtration.”
• “An effective crystallization procedure for anhydride 10 was identified, which allowed for use of higher PivCl levels … Crystalline 10 exhibits excellent stability under ambient conditions.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: After step 2 the reaction mixture was concentrated using a rotary evaporator, a batch‑wise operation that is time‑consuming and not suitable for scale‑up, increasing cycle time and solvent usage.
Solution_Description: The authors plan to replace the batch rotary evaporator with a continuous liquid‑liquid solvent‑exchange/concentrator unit for future production, enabling uninterrupted operation and reduced solvent waste.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Use of the rotary evaporator for the step 2 concentration was not envisioned as a permanent solution. A simple continuous concentrator would be implemented for future production.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: The high‑temperature deprotection step required operation at 170 °C; temperatures above this risked amide bond hydrolysis, while the reactor pressure limit prevented higher temperatures.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run at 170 °C (below the pressure‑limited ceiling) with residence times ~29 min, and stability studies confirmed no degradation up to 185 °C, ensuring safe operation within the defined window.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Material reacted for an average residence time of 29 min… conversion of 7 to consistently exceed 99.90 % … Temperatures above 170 °C were not investigated due to reactor jacket pressure limitations, but 16‑mL‑scale lab experiments demonstrated the reaction product to be stable to at least 185 °C.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 1. Process Development and Demonstration
Problem_Description: Genotoxic impurity (GTI) control required driving the hydrogenolysis and amide formation steps to near‑quantitative conversion; any residual aniline 9 or its deprotected analogue had to be kept below 80 ppm in the API.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometry was set to 1.05–1.10 equiv of mixed anhydride 10 relative to aniline 9, reaction temperature was maintained at 60 °C for 60 min, and online HPLC monitoring ensured conversion >99.9 %, satisfying GTI limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “High conversion of 9 was integral to the GTI control strategy… at 60 °C, a reaction time of 60 min with 1.05 equiv of 10 was sufficient to achieve <0.1 % HPLC area of 9 in the product stream.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 2. Technology Transfer and cGMP Manufacturing
Problem_Description: The hydrogenolysis step (step 2) suffered from poor reproducibility and occasional reactor fouling when attempted in continuous mode. Supporting_Evidence:

2. “Lack of development time to characterize catalyst bed life, the high dilution required to achieve a homogeneous feed stream, the criticality of adjusting process conditions to control for purity, and occasional episodes of reactor fouling.”
3. “Operation in batch mode also decoupled the process cycle time for step 2 from the throughput of the downstream continuous unit operations, and thus the hydrogenolysis reaction time could be lengthened on the basis of in‑process control (IPC) sampling.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 2. Technology Transfer and cGMP Manufacturing
Problem_Description: Continuous crystallization of the amide 7 in the first MSMPR crystallizer at 20 °C gave poor impurity rejection compared with batch mode, leading to lower overall yield and insufficient removal of the aniline impurity 5.
Solution_Description: The temperature of the first MSMPR crystallizer was increased to 50 °C while maintaining the second at 20 °C (non‑isothermal operation).  This significantly improved impurity rejection (>90 % for aniline 5) and restored the desired product quality.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Isothermal crystallization … resulted in relatively poor rejection of many impurities … Upon increase of the temperature of the first MSMPR crystallizer to 50 °C … impurity rejection was observed to greatly improve.”
2. “Use of a combined antisolvent and cooling continuous crystallization afforded high rejection efficiency for many significant process impurities, including >90 % rejection of the aniline 5.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 2. Technology Transfer and cGMP Manufacturing
Problem_Description: The deprotection step (step 4) required operation at high temperature (150–185 °C) and elevated pressure (25 bar), presenting safety concerns related to thermal runaway and over‑pressurization.
Solution_Description: The reactor was operated within the 150–185 °C window where ≥99.8 % product purity was achieved; the PFR was built from Hastelloy C276, pressure‑tested with nitrogen, and equipped with pressure‑relief valves set at 100 bar to safely divert material in case of over‑pressurization.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “A univariate study of reaction temperatures demonstrated that acceptable product purity of ≥99.8 % could be achieved between 150 and 185 °C.”
2. “The reactor … was maintained at 25 bar and heated to 170 °C … pressure relief valves were installed that would divert material to waste in the event of overpressurization to 100 bar.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 2. Technology Transfer and cGMP Manufacturing
Problem_Description: Manual filtration, washing, and dissolution during the continuous campaign required ~5 h of operator time per 8 h cycle and used vacuum filtration, which slowed the process and increased labor costs.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Feedback‑controlled mass flow controllers (Coriolis) were installed to regulate feed rates of aniline, anhydride, and antisolvent, improving flow accuracy and reducing the need for frequent manual adjustments.  The authors also suggested moving to an electronic batch record to streamline documentation and reduce staffing demands.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Coriolis mass flow controllers … were installed and configured … to enable feedback control of the feed rates … offered a significant improvement in flow rate regulation compared to previous Lilly processes … which, without a controller, required routine calibration to prevent drift over time.”
2. “The paper batch record had to be subdivided … implementation of an electronic batch record that would alert operators of when tasks were due to be performed would have greatly simplified the activity of batch record maintenance.”

Paper Title: Small-Volume Continuous Manufacturing of Merestinib. Part 2. Technology Transfer and cGMP Manufacturing
Problem_Description: In step 3 amide bond formation, residual aniline 5 could remain in the product stream, threatening impurity limits and overall yield.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The anhydride 6 stoichiometry was increased to 1.10 equiv and the residence time was extended to 140 min (90 min in first PFR segment, 50 min in second).  Online HPLC monitoring was used for real‑time control, and feedback mass‑flow control ensured accurate feed rates.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The robustness of the step 3 reaction … was improved by increasing the target feed stoichiometry of the anhydride 6 to 1.10 equiv … and by extending the reaction time in the PFR to 140 min.”
2. “The cGMP step 3 reactor was divided into two stages … At 60 °C, a reaction time of 90 min was sufficient to achieve less than 0.1 HPLC area % of 5 in the product stream.”
3. “Coriolis mass flow controllers … were installed … to enable feedback control of the feed rates of aniline 5, anhydride 6, and the antisolvent cyclohexane.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: The original medicinal‑chemistry route required heating POCl₃ (a hazardous reagent) at 100 °C and a subsequent cyclization at 140 °C, creating safety and heat‑management concerns that prevented reliable scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new manufacturing route (Route D) was selected that performed the condensation and cyclization under much milder, scalable conditions, eliminating the use of POCl₃ and high‑temperature steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “(1) heating (100 °C) in a solvent volume of hazardous POCl₃, (2) cyclization at high temperature (140 °C)”; “In both routes, coupling and cyclization via cyclic amidine intermediate (±)-9 proceeded under mild, scalable conditions…”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Resolution of the racemic intermediate relied on silica‑gel chromatography and chiral‑HPLC, which are labor‑intensive, generate large solvent waste, and are unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A chiral‑salt‑based resolution was introduced using dipivaloyl‑d‑tartaric acid (d‑DPTA), providing the desired enantiomer in high yield and ee without any chromatographic steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “the use of silica gel chromatography, and resolution by chiral HPLC.”; “dipivaloyl‑d‑tartaric acid (d‑DPTA) was identified as the resolving agent, and the corresponding salt… could be obtained in a practical yield with excellent optical purity.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Chiral routes B and C gave low optical purity of (S)-5 because the cyclic amidine intermediate racemised, leading to inconsistent product quality.
Solution_Description: The racemic route (Route A then D) was adopted, avoiding the problematic chiral intermediates; the base and equivalents were adjusted to keep the reaction mixture neutral, suppressing racemisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “the optical purity of the isolated product (S)-5 was found to be low…racemization of the cyclic amidine intermediate (S)-9 was strongly indicated.”; “Thus, the racemic approach was selected for further development… Route D was selected as a future development route.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: When a weak base (pyridine) or no base was used, the oxadiazole impurity (±)-29 formed in significant amounts, decreasing overall yield and complicating purification.
Solution_Description: More basic amines (imidazole or Et₃N) were introduced at appropriate equivalents, which fully suppressed oxadiazole formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “formation of (±)-29 increased significantly when no base or less basic pyridine was employed… whereas it was almost completely suppressed when a more basic amine (imidazole or Et₃N) was employed.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: The regio‑isomer (±)-28 was generated in the cyclisation step at higher temperatures, reducing the amount of desired product.
Solution_Description: The cyclisation temperature was lowered to the lowest operationally feasible value and Et₃N was added to accelerate cyclisation, avoiding prolonged exposure to high temperature and thus minimizing regio‑isomer formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The regioisomer significantly increased at higher temperature… negligible at room temperature.”; “addition of Et₃N was also effective for accelerating the cyclization phase, thus minimizing the formation of the regioisomer.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Initial condensation/cyclisation runs required >25 h and used expensive reagents (e.g., imidazole) in large excess, increasing both time and cost.
Solution_Description: The base was switched from imidazole to cheaper NaOAc, the amount of NaOAc was optimised (12 → 6 equiv), and the order of addition (stepwise addition of Et₃N after condensation) shortened the overall reaction time while maintaining yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “Entry 5 shows that imidazole could be replaced with cheaper NaOAc… addition of Et₃N was also effective for accelerating the cyclization phase… Entry 6… comparable result could be obtained by reducing the amount of NaOAc to 6 equiv.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Route E required the expensive reagent TMSOTf and involved a labile hydrazone intermediate (±)-21, raising cost and safety concerns.
Solution_Description: Route D, which does not employ TMSOTf and uses a more stable intermediate, was chosen for manufacturing, reducing reagent cost and improving process robustness.
Supporting_Evidence: “the cost of TMSOTf in Route E was relatively high, and there was also a quality concern associated with the instability of the hydrazone intermediate (±)-21… Therefore, Route D was selected as a future development route.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Batch photo‑isomerisation of the olefin could not be scaled because light penetration fell with increasing volume, the UV lamp generated significant heat, and long irradiation times led to degradation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A continuous flow photoreactor was built by winding PTFE tubing around a UV lamp, enabling short residence times (≤ 60 s), efficient light exposure, and active cooling of the tubing to control temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: “attention was turned to a flow system… a single‑path flow system consisting of a PTFE tube wound around a traditional photoreactor… By variation of the flow rate and the tube length… the temperature of the cooling medium was kept at −5 to −1 °C… the flow and irradiation were continued for 17 h… with comparable results on the larger scale.”

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient Manufacturing Process for E2212 toward Rapid Clinical Introduction
Problem_Description: Extended irradiation of the E‑isomer in batch caused gradual degradation of the product, compromising purity.
Solution_Description: High‑dilution (1000 vol) conditions with a short 10‑min irradiation were employed, minimizing exposure time and suppressing degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Highly diluted (1000 volume) conditions resulted in fast and clean conversion, in contrast to concentrated (10 volume) conditions… degradation gradually proceeded with extended irradiation time… therefore, a short reaction time under high‑dilution conditions was considered necessary.”

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: Traditional Minisci amido‑alkylations rely on strong acids and transition‑metal catalysts, which generate large amounts of acidic waste, introduce metal traces into the final drug substances, and raise safety and cost concerns.
Solution_Description: A metal‑free, acid‑free protocol was devised that uses sodium persulfate as the sole oxidant/promoter, eliminating the need for external acids or metals while delivering the desired products in high yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "In the last few decades, many efforts have been made to make chemical processes more sustainable and reduce their environmental impact... the α‑amidoalkylation ... has been performed in the presence of sodium persulfate ... without using acids and transition metals."

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: Previously reported Minisci amido‑alkylations required prolonged heating (50–80 °C) to reach acceptable conversion, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: Running the reaction at 80 °C furnishes complete conversion within 15 min (and even at 50 °C for certain substrates), dramatically shortening the reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Very surprisingly, the reaction of lepidine … at 80 °C provided 87 % yield of the desired product … within only 15 min."
"The protocol was then extended … all reactions were carried out within 2 h."
"Encouraged by the fact that the reactions at 80 °C were generally so fast, we decided to decrease the temperature to 50 °C; surprisingly, we found that quinaldine … was completely converted in only 15 min."
"A longer reaction time did not significantly affect the conversion and yield."
"A longer reaction time resulted in an increased amount of by‑products."

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: The rate and conversion varied widely with the amide employed (e.g., DMA gave rapid persulfate decomposition and high conversion, whereas NMA showed slower rates and lower yields), causing inconsistency across substrates.
Solution_Description: Stoichiometric ratios of persulfate were tuned (e.g., 2 : 1 vs 3 : 1), reaction times were adjusted, and temperature was optimized to balance conversion and selectivity for each amide/substrate pair.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The reaction of lepidine with NMA gave a very high yield … in a short time. Under the same reaction conditions, the experiment with DMF afforded complete conversion… A longer reaction time resulted in an increased amount of by‑products."
"The reaction of quinoline with DMA was performed in the presence of a larger amount of persulfate (3:1 instead of 2:1) to maximize the selectivity toward the 2,4‑disubstituted derivative."
"A longer reaction time resulted in lower selectivity due to the formation of side products."
"The reaction of quinoline … gave 81 % conversion within only 15 min, with 58 % yield … Longer reaction time resulted in lower selectivity."
"The persulfate decomposition was 40 % after 15 min at 50 °C in the DMA/H₂O system, whereas it was only 3 % in NMA/H₂O."
"The order of the reaction becomes 3/2, showing that amide‑based induced decomposition of persulfate occurs."

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction to gram quantities required efficient isolation of the product without the acidic work‑up steps traditionally needed to remove metal salts or acid residues.
Solution_Description: Products were isolated directly by aqueous work‑up and dichloromethane extraction, followed by flash chromatography or simple distillation of residual amide, eliminating the need for additional neutralization steps.
Supporting_Evidence:
"Products 2b … were isolated from reactions carried out by the standard procedure on a scale of 2 mmol … after the extraction of the reaction mixtures, respectively, in 84 and 78 % yields, whereas product 2c was purified by extraction and flash chromatography and obtained in 50 % yield."
"In the case of the reactions with DMA and DMF, dichloromethane was removed under reduced pressure, and a major part of the residual amide present in the extract was distilled off at a pressure of 60 mbar."
"The larger scale allowed the isolation of a small quantity of the carboxamido derivative 2d."
"The reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature, and ~0.2 mmol of 1,4‑dimethoxybenzene or benzophenone (utilized as internal standard) was added… Another portion … was diluted in aqueous NaHCO₃ and extracted with dichloromethane (DCM, 3 × 10 mL); then, the combined organic layers were dried with sodium sulfate. A sample of this solution was analyzed in GC–MS, and from the remaining part DCM was removed under reduced pressure."

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: Substrates such as 4‑ethylpyridine and 4‑hydroxyquinazoline showed <3 % conversion, attributed to competing oxidation of the amide radical or inhibition by the hydroxy group, leading to poor yields.
Solution_Description: The authors identified the mechanistic cause (oxidation competition and radical chain inhibition) and suggest that future work could employ additives or promoters to suppress these pathways, although such additives were not tested in the current study.
Supporting_Evidence:
"We think that the very low reactivities shown by 4‑ethylpyridine … could be ascribed to the competition between the oxidation of the amide radical intermediates by persulfate and their trapping by the heteroaromatic base."
"In the case of 4‑hydroxyquinazoline, the low reactivity could be due to the presence of the hydroxy group … that could act as a free‑radical chain inhibitor."
"The low yield of 8b was isolated to establish the substituted positions, as they were not reported in the literature."

Paper Title: Revisiting the Minisci Reaction: New Mild Amidoalkylation of Benzo-Fused
Problem_Description: Maintaining consistent conversion and yield when moving from milligram to gram scale could be problematic due to heat‑mass transfer and mixing differences.
Solution_Description: Scale‑up experiments were performed in a 100 mL round‑bottom flask with vigorous stirring, reproducing the small‑scale results and confirming that the batch platform is suitable for larger batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
"The reactions of quinaldine with DMA, NMA, and DMF … were scaled‑up on the gram scale, and the results were consistent with those performed on a lower scale."
"General Scale‑Up Procedure (for Products 2a, 2b, and 2c): In a 100 mL round‑bottomed flask, 10 mmol of quinaldine was added … heated to 80 °C and stirred for 15 min."

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: The originally reported Grubbs second‑generation catalyst (G2) could not be scaled beyond 100 mg; reactions gave <5 % isolated yield regardless of concentration (5–50 mM) or solvent at 50 °C.
Solution_Description: The Stewart–Grubbs (SG) catalyst was screened and provided the best conversion (up to 57 % isolated yield).  The reaction was performed in PhMe at room temperature, which also avoided the need for high‑temperature conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the macrocyclization described a challenging process that employed Grubbs second generation catalyst G2 … could not be reliably scaled beyond 100 mg regardless of concentration (5 to 50 mM) or solvent (at 50 °C)”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: Using G2, GH2 or GHiPr catalysts with slow addition gave only trace or ≤11 % yield of the desired macrocycle, even when catalyst loading was increased.
Solution_Description: Switching to the SG catalyst (10 mol %) in PhMe gave a markedly higher yield (11 % initially, then 57 % on 500 mg scale).
Supporting_Evidence: • “yields were very low (∼5 %) and attempts at improving the process via slow addition were not successful”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: The batch macrocyclization required 5 days at room temperature to reach acceptable conversion, limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow set‑up (Vapourtec R4 reactor, 150 °C, 5 min residence) reduced reaction time dramatically while still delivering product (up to 32 % yield).
Supporting_Evidence: • “the batch macrocyclizations provide the highest yields … however, the reactions are the most dilute (5 mM) and require very long reaction times (5 d)”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: Running the flow macrocyclization at 150 °C caused complete decomposition of the Ru‑based catalyst, complicating downstream work‑up.
Solution_Description: A downstream packed bed of silica/charcoal was employed to remove Ru decomposition products, simplifying purification of the macrocycle.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The high temperatures used resulted in complete decomposition of the Ru‑based catalyst, and the silica/charcoal reactor was effective at removing Ru‑based byproducts to simplify purification.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: Increasing the concentration of the batch reaction (from 5 mM to 10 mM or 20 mM) caused a steady decrease in macrocycle yield (57 % → 11 % → <5 %).
Solution_Description: Maintaining a high‑dilution (5 mM) condition in batch was retained as the optimal concentration; flow experiments explored a range (5–20 mM) and identified 10 mM as the best compromise (32 % yield).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Increasing the concentration (5 → 10 → 20 mM) resulted in a steady decrease of the yield of 1.”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: Microwave‑assisted macrocyclization at 70 °C for 60 min gave only 32 % yield (10 mM) and 23 % yield (20 mM), lower than the 57 % batch result.
Solution_Description: Microwave heating was used to accelerate the reaction (higher temperature, shorter time), but the authors noted the limitation in scalability and modest yields compared with the flow route.
Supporting_Evidence: • “At a concentration of 10 mM, the microwave experiment afforded a 32 % yield … while at 20 mM the yield decreased further (23 % …).”

Paper Title: Synthesis of a Renewable Macrocyclic Musk: Evaluation of Batch, Microwave, and Continuous Flow Strategies
Problem_Description: After batch reactions, catalyst quenching and removal of Ru residues were essential to avoid impurity formation and simplify isolation of the macrocycle.
Solution_Description: All batch reactions were quenched with ethyl vinyl ether before concentration, effectively deactivating the metathesis catalyst and preventing olefin‑migration side products.
Supporting_Evidence: • “All batch macrocyclizations were quenched with the addition of ethyl vinyl ether before concentrating the reaction mixture.”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: The aerobic oxidation of alcohols with AZADOL/NOₓ in acetic acid can generate enough heat to raise the reaction temperature above the flash point of the solvent (39 °C), creating a fire‑hazard when operated in ambient air.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature is deliberately kept well below the flash point (e.g., 22 °C) by using an ethylene‑glycol/water bath and maintaining at least a 15 °C safety margin, thereby preventing ignition.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because the AZADO/NOₓ‑catalyzed aerobic alcohol oxidation proceeds efficiently at room temperature in ambient air (balloon) and the flash point of acetic acid (39 °C; closed cup) is higher than room temperature, we assumed that controlling the reaction temperature at a value sufficiently lower than the flash point of acetic acid should prevent fire even in ambient air.”; “The maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction (MTSR) at this ΔT_ad was 49.9 °C, which is higher than the flash point of the acetic acid solvent (39 °C). These results indicate that removing heat is necessary to operate this reaction safely.”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Addition of NaNO₂ to acetic acid produces HNO₂, which leads to in‑situ formation of nitric acid that deactivates AZADOL/AZADO and reduces conversion.
Solution_Description: The amount of NaNO₂ was lowered from 10 mol % to 5 mol % (entry 2, Table 1), minimizing nitric‑acid generation while still achieving quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “To reduce nitric acid generated in situ, which is known to deactivate AZADO/AZADOL, the amount of NaNO₂ was reduced.”; “As a result, quantitative conversion was achieved in 24 h (entry 2).”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Initial conditions (1 mol % AZADOL, 10 mol % NaNO₂, air balloon) gave only 96 % conversion after 24 h, which was unsatisfactory for process scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was increased to 2 mol % AZADOL and 10 mol % NaNO₂, and a positive O₂ pressure of 10 kPa was applied using a Mitos P‑Pump to maintain 27 % O₂ in the reaction mixture. The temperature was kept at 22 °C, resulting in complete conversion in 8 h (entry 6).
Supporting_Evidence: “When the amounts of AZADOL and NaNO₂ were increased to 2.0 mol % and 10.0 mol % respectively, the reaction was completed in 8 h (entry 6).”; “A 10 kPa positive pressure of O₂ was applied to a reaction flask… using a Mitos P‑Pump… the resulting concentration of O₂ should be maintained at 27 %.”; “Increasing the reaction temperature to 27 °C shortened the reaction time to 5 h (entry 7).”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: When NaNO₂ is added in a single portion an instantaneous heat spike of 114.7 J occurs, potentially driving the temperature toward the solvent flash point.
Solution_Description: Portion‑wise (controlled) addition of NaNO₂ is recommended to spread the heat release over time and keep the temperature within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “An instantaneous heat output of 114.7 J was observed when NaNO₂ was added in one portion (Figure 2, left). This heat output arises from the reaction between NaNO₂ and acetic acid to give HNO₂ and NaOAc.”; “The corresponding adiabatic temperature rise (ΔT_ad0) was 0.48 K.”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Continuous O₂ supply can cause uncontrolled heat evolution and potential runaway, as indicated by temperature rise after O₂ addition.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Pulse‑feeding of O₂ (stopping the gas flow, allowing temperature to fall, then restarting) was used to regulate the exotherm and keep the reaction under control.
Supporting_Evidence: “After the supply of O₂ was stopped at 0.27 h, the reaction temperature decreased, which indicates slowing the reaction… Resupplying O₂ at 0.8 h caused the temperature to increase again… These results indicate that pulse feeding of oxygen can control the reaction rate and the exotherm.”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Scaling the reaction to 1000 L requires removal of ~13 kW of heat to keep the temperature below the flash point, otherwise the process would over‑heat.
Solution_Description: A conventional glass‑lined (GL) reaction tank with a calculated heat‑transfer area of 4.559 m² and a coolant jacket (U ≈ 200 W m⁻² K⁻¹) was used, providing a coolant temperature of ~7.6 °C to maintain the reaction at 22 °C safely.
Supporting_Evidence: “When aerobic alcohol oxidation is operated in a 1000 L GL reaction tank… the required heat‑removal capability is estimated as 13 098 W.”; “Using a heat transfer area (A) of 4.559 m² and a heat transfer coefficient (U) of 200 W m⁻² K⁻¹… ΔT = 14.4 K… a mean coolant temperature of 7.6 °C is estimated to be required to maintain the temperature of the reaction mixture at 22 °C.”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Isolation of the product (Shi’s catalyst) on multihundred‑gram scale typically requires column chromatography, which is impractical and costly at large scale.
Solution_Description: A work‑up involving neutralization, aqueous Na₂CO₃ wash, extraction, and crystallization from heptane gave the product in 84 % isolated yield without any column chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Compound 2 was isolated using 170 g of 1. An 84 % yield of 2 was obtained without column chromatography.”; “The residual solid was completely dissolved in heptane… cooled to –10 °C for crystallization… washed with cold heptane and then dried…”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Large‑scale availability of the AZADOL catalyst could be a bottleneck for process development.
Solution_Description: AZADOL is commercially supplied by Nissan Chemical (kilogram‑scale batches) and can be obtained through the company’s custom‑chemicals department for quantities > 100 g.
Supporting_Evidence: “AZADOL was synthesized by Nissan Chemical Corporation… AZADOL is prepared on a kilogram scale by Nissan Chemical Corporation. Readers that want to use more than 100 g of AZADOL should contact the Custom Chemicals Department…”

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Aerobic Oxidation by 2‑Azaadamantan-2-ol (AZADOL)/NO
Problem_Description: Precise control of dissolved O₂ concentration is required; simple balloon feeding leads to variable O₂ levels and inconsistent conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A Mitos P‑Pump was employed to regulate O₂ pressure at 10 kPa, providing a constant O₂ concentration (27 %) throughout the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “O₂ was bubbled through the solution using a Mitos P‑Pump (Dolomite Microfluidics) at a 10 kPa positive pressure to maintain the concentration of O₂ at 27 %.”

Paper Title: A Tailor-Made Self-Sufficient Whole-Cell Biocatalyst Enables Scalable Enantioselective Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The conventional chemical routes use expensive chiral metal catalysts and require subsequent removal of trace metals, while enzymatic kinetic‑resolution routes give ≤50 % yield, making them unattractive for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors designed a single bifunctional whole‑cell biocatalyst (MLG) that combines a ketoreductase and a glucose‑dehydrogenase in one polypeptide, eliminating the need for separate enzymes and expensive metal catalysts.
Supporting_Evidence:
“These procedures usually suffer from some disadvantages including the high cost of chiral metal catalysts, subsequent removal of trace metals, the oft‑time lengthy process for screening and synthesis ligand, and the unsatisfactory ≤50 % yield for enzymatic resolution.”
“...we created a highly efficient bifunctional enzyme which exhibited good catalytic activities for (R)-3‑quinuclidinol synthesis and cofactor regeneration of great capacity in the same polypeptide chain.”

Paper Title: A Tailor-Made Self-Sufficient Whole-Cell Biocatalyst Enables Scalable Enantioselective Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: Previously reported biocatalytic processes for (R)-3‑quinuclidinol gave very low product titers (as low as 2 g L⁻¹) and required prolonged reaction times.
Solution_Description: The self‑sufficient whole‑cell catalyst was operated at much higher substrate concentrations (up to 486 g L⁻¹) while maintaining complete conversion in ≤5.5 h, dramatically increasing space‑time yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“But most of them proceed at low product titer, even only 2 g/L, and needed a prolonged conversion time.”
“...impressive substrate concentration of 486 g L⁻¹, and high space‑time yield of (R)-3‑quinuclidinol up to 1505.5 g L⁻¹ d⁻¹…”

Paper Title: A Tailor-Made Self-Sufficient Whole-Cell Biocatalyst Enables Scalable Enantioselective Synthesis of (
Problem_Description: The ArQR reductase, although effective, displayed poor thermal stability and required a high dosage of lyophilized cells, resulting in an unfavourable substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio.
Solution_Description: Engineering a bifunctional MLG enzyme that retains the activity of both domains while being more thermally stable and active at low biocatalyst loading (∼1.65 %).
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: Initial N‑alkylation of 3‑methyl‑1H‑1,2,4‑triazole 8 gave a 60:40 intractable mixture of isomers 7 and 7′ with only 53 % isolated yield, and the ratio was unchanged at lower temperature, giving poor material efficiency.
Solution_Description: A regioselective synthesis of triazole 7 was developed via condensation of isopropylhydrazine·HCl with acetamidine·HCl (forming IPAA 10) followed by tri‑ethyl‑orthoformate, delivering 21 kg of pure 7 in 52 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the alkylation proceeded to give a 60:40 intractable mixture of 3‑methyl‑triazole 7 and 5‑methyl‑triazole 7′ in 53 % yield.”; “treatment of IPAA 10 with tri‑ethyl‑orthoformate afforded the desired triazole 7 regiospecifically… 21 kg of 7 was synthesized in 52 % yield.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: During the synthesis of α‑chloroketone 11, the reaction mixture darkened and the assay yield dropped when the temperature was allowed to rise to 0 °C, indicating temperature‑sensitive degradation of the Weinreb amide intermediate.
Solution_Description: The reaction was kept at –20 °C and the lithiated triazole was added to the Weinreb amide solution (instead of the inverse), giving a 10‑15 % yield increase and preserving product stability.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction mixture at 0 °C darkened over time and resulted in significant lower assay yield of the product 11 relative to the reaction performed at −20 °C.”; “The –20 °C temperature was also essential to maintain for the quench to prevent degradation of 11.”; “When the lithiated triazole was added to a THF solution of Weinreb amide IV at −20 °C, there was a 10–15 % increase in assay yield relative to the inverse mode of addition.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: The isolated α‑chloroketone 11 sublimated under vacuum drying (40 °C/150 mm Hg) and was identified as a lachrymator, making isolation hazardous and leading to material loss.
Solution_Description: A telescoped procedure was implemented where the crude α‑chloroketone 11 solution was directly transferred to the amidine condensation step, avoiding isolation of the volatile, lachrymatory intermediate.
Supporting_Evidence: “When the solids were dried under vacuum (40 °C/150 mmHg), sublimation of the product was observed.”; “The product was also determined to be a lachrymator.”; “Subsequently, this resulted in the development of a telescoped procedure in which α‑chloroketone 11 intermediate could directly be used in the reaction with aryl amidine 12.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: The final alkylation/S_NAr sequence gave low and inconsistent conversion to benzoxazepine 1, with polyether impurity 16 and regio‑isomer 18 forming when excess ethylene carbonate was used, and reaction times >30 h were required.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switching to neat 1‑methylimidazole as solvent (with 6 equiv ethylene carbonate), lowering the carbonate amount to 6 equiv, and employing a biphasic 2‑MeTHF/50 % aqueous NaOH system with n‑Bu₃NMeCl as a phase‑transfer catalyst gave rapid, reproducible conversion (90 % in 3.5 h) with minimal impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only 1‑methylimidazole resulted in significant product 1 formation (35 % by HPLC)…”; “The conversion to 1 was poorly reproducible… Two major impurities… polyether derivative 16 and regioisomer 18.”; “With 5 equiv of ethylene carbonate, the reaction required >30 h… with ≥15 equiv, significantly higher amount of polyether 16 was formed.”; “the use of a second base… aqueous NaOH with n‑Bu₃NMeCl… gave 90 % conversion to 1 after only 3.5 h with 5 % impurity 17.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: Sodium hydride (NaH) gave excellent conversion in the SNAr step but was deemed unsuitable for scale‑up because the NaH/DMF mixture is hazardous.
Solution_Description: Safer bases were screened; aqueous NaOH (50 % aq.) with n‑Bu₃NMeCl proved effective, eliminating the need for NaH and improving safety while achieving comparable conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “NaH initially gave a clean conversion… but it was not considered for scale up due to the hazardous nature of that mixture.”; “NaHMDS was less effective… KOtBu required extensive reaction time… ultimately, controlling the reaction time led to the optimized conditions, using 50 % aqueous NaOH, 3.5 mol % of n‑Bu₃NMeCl.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: During the telescoped final sequence, the combination of 2‑MeTHF with aqueous NaOH caused poor phase separation and emulsions, hindering work‑up.
Solution_Description: The solvent was changed from 2‑MeTHF to toluene for the second step and dilute aqueous KOH (25–35 %) replaced NaOH, providing clean phase separation and avoiding emulsions.
Supporting_Evidence: “the second step required to replace 2‑MeTHF with toluene, since this did not allow good phase separation with the aqueous phase when charged with the 1‑methylimidazole from the first step.”; “the second modification… use dilute (25–35 %) aqueous KOH, instead of NaOH, to facilitate phase separation and avoid emulsions during workup.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 1: Early-Stage Development Routes to the Bromobenzoxazepine Core
Problem_Description: Trace N‑vinyl impurity 17 persisted in the isolated benzoxazepine 1, requiring a final high‑purity step.
Solution_Description: A slurry of the crude cake in EtOH/H₂O at 60 °C was performed, followed by filtration and drying, which removed impurity 17 and delivered product 1 at >99.9 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “To remove this impurity, a slurry in EtOH and water at 60 °C was implemented and afforded bromobenzoxazepine core 1 (34.75 kg, 99.9 % purity by HPLC…) in 88 % yield.”

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: The S_NAr displacement of the aryl fluoride using t‑BuOK was highly exothermic and required long addition times (up to 30 min for a 5 g scale), making the scale‑up difficult.
Solution_Description: The aminoalkoxide was pre‑formed and added to a solution of the aryl halide, the order of addition was reversed, and THF was replaced by the greener 2‑MeTHF, which gave a completely dose‑controlled exotherm.
Supporting_Evidence: "The reaction was found to be very exothermic and required long addition times of t‑BuOK (up to 30 min for a 5 g scale reaction). This exotherm resulted from deprotonation of the ethanolamine and could be successfully controlled by preforming the aminoalkoxide and adding that mixture to a solution of 4‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzonitrile. Thus, for scale‑up tetrahydrofuran (THF) was replaced with the greener alternative 2‑MeTHF, and a solution of 4‑bromo‑2‑fluorobenzonitrile in 2.5 volumes (V) of 2‑MeTHF was instead added to a solution of the preformed aminoalkoxide in 7.6 V of 2‑MeTHF at 0 °C. With this order of addition, the exotherm was completely dose‑controlled."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: During formation of the HCl salt of 7, HF was generated, etching the glassware, and the product showed a high residue on ignition (up to 15.5 %).
Solution_Description: Aqueous washes with water and 13 wt % NaCl were performed before acidification to remove KF, and acidification was carried out with HCl in 1‑propanol (instead of ethanol) to avoid formation of the mutagenic impurity EtCl.
Supporting_Evidence: "...the glassware was being etched by the formation of HF during acidification to form the HCl salt. For these reasons, aqueous washes with water and 13 wt % NaCl solution prior to acidification were implemented to remove the residual KF salt. Finally, acidification was performed with HCl in 1‑propanol instead of ethanol to avoid the formation of the potential mutagenic impurity EtCl."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Cyclization of 7·HCl using Zn(ClO₄)₂ gave low conversion and dimer formation; CuCl suppressed dimer but gave only 13 % amidine on gram scale.
Solution_Description: Switching to 130 mol % trimethylaluminum (AlMe₃) in toluene produced a homogeneous reaction mixture, delivering 83 % amidine conversion with only 1 % dimer, and the stoichiometry was adjusted to 130 mol % AlMe₃.
Supporting_Evidence: "In the presence of 20 mol % Zn(ClO₄)₂ in dioxane at 80 °C, 24 % conversion to 3 was obtained alongside formation of dimer 8 after 24 h... CuCl (100 mol %) resulted in complete suppression of dimer formation. However, when these conditions were performed on gram scale, the heterogeneous reaction stalled, and only 13 A % HPLC of amidine was obtained... Switching to a solution of 130 mol % of trimethylaluminum in toluene resulted in a homogeneous reaction mixture that was reproducible on gram scale, giving 83 A % HPLC of 3 and only 1 A % HPLC of the dimer."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: AlMe₃ is pyrophoric, posing a safety hazard on large scale.
Solution_Description: A screen of alternative Lewis acids identified Mg(OEt)₂ as a safe, non‑pyrophoric reagent that mediated the cyclization in high yield; 2‑MeTHF was employed as a co‑solvent to improve handling.
Supporting_Evidence: "The hazardous pyrophoric properties of AlMe₃ led us to try and find an alternative reagent. After a number of Lewis acids were screened... only Mg(OEt)₂ proved to mediate the cyclization in high yield."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Work‑up of the Mg(OMe)₂‑mediated cyclization produced gels upon water addition (presumably Mg(OH)₂), giving a low isolated yield (56 %).
Solution_Description: Introducing 2‑MeTHF as a co‑solvent prevented gel formation, allowing isolation of the amidine in >97 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: "the addition of water resulted in the formation of gels (presumably Mg(OH)₂) rendering the extraction of amidine 3 very difficult. This was reflected in the low isolated yield (56 %)... Using 2‑MeTHF as a cosolvent solved the gelling issues, and amidine 3 could then be isolated in more than 97 % yield."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Crystallization of acid 13 from HCl caused foaming and corrosion; the acid had low solubility leading to foaming during acid addition.
Solution_Description: The precipitation acid was switched from HCl to H₂SO₄, and 1‑propanol was added to the aqueous lithium salt solution before re‑acidification, eliminating foaming and reducing corrosion.
Supporting_Evidence: "The isolation of acid 13 initially was complicated by foaming of the material upon crystallization by acid addition... The acid to precipitate the product was changed from HCl to H₂SO₄ due to corrosivity issues. The foaming issue was solved by addition of 1‑propanol to the aqueous solution of 13‑lithium salt before reacidification."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: The imidazole product obtained by the BPA alkylation/condensation was a dark purple solid, an undesirable color impurity.
Solution_Description: BPA was added as a solution in 2‑MeTHF and a carbon treatment was performed prior to isolation with aqueous HCl, yielding a lighter‑colored solid.
Supporting_Evidence: "while the yield using this technique was high (91 % yield), the material obtained was a dark purple colored solid. Adding BPA as a solution in 2‑MeTHF (2 V) and implementing a carbon treatment prior to isolation with aqueous HCl resulted in a lighter colored solid."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Controlled crystallization of taselisib to the desired polymorph (Form B) required precise seeding, cooling ramps and solvent composition; inconsistent crystal size and polymorph formation were observed.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A controlled crystallization protocol was established using isoamyl alcohol as solvent, seeding between 75–90 °C, slow cooling (0.05–0.3 °C/min), and an in‑line NIR PAT measurement to monitor concentration and avoid operator exposure.
Supporting_Evidence: "crystallization was then initiated with seeding (45 g of taselisib Form B) at 92 °C, and the mixture was aged for 2 h. The resulting suspension was cooled to 23 °C within 7 h and filtered... the optimal seeding point to promote secondary nucleation was found to be between 75 and 90 °C; by using a slower cooling ramp (0.05 to 0.3 °C/min), desired crystal growth was promoted... an in‑line process analytical technology (PAT) near‑infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method was implemented as an in‑process control (IPC) test prior to crystallization to avoid any operator exposure."

Paper Title: Manufacture of the PI3K β‑Sparing Inhibitor Taselisib. Part 2: Development of a Highly Efficient and Regioselective Late-Stage Process
Problem_Description: Taselisib is a highly potent compound (HHC band 3B); sampling the hot, supersaturated solution posed an exposure risk to operators.
Solution_Description: An in‑line near‑infrared (NIR) PAT method was deployed to monitor the solution concentration and polymorph formation, eliminating the need for manual sampling.
Supporting_Evidence: "an in‑line process analytical technology (PAT) near‑infrared (NIR) spectroscopy method was implemented as an in‑process control (IPC) test prior to crystallization to avoid any operator exposure from sampling of the supersaturated hot solution with a highly potent compound."

Paper Title: A Scalable Total Synthesis of Halofuginone
Problem_Description: The N‑substitution of compound 7 with ethyl 4‑bromobutyrate gave poor conversion when conventional organic bases (Et₃N, DIPEA, DBU) were used in organic solvents (MeCN or toluene).
Solution_Description: Switched the base to anhydrous Na₂CO₃ and added a catalytic amount of tetrabutylammonium iodide (TBAI) in toluene, which raised the conversion to 92 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “While the reaction did not work well when an organic base (Et₃N, DIPEA, or DBU) was used in an organic solvent (acetonitrile or toluene), a high conversion rate (92 %) was observed when anhydrous Na₂CO₃ was used in the presence of a catalytic amount of TBAI in toluene.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Total Synthesis of Halofuginone
Problem_Description: The Dieckmann condensation of intermediate 8 failed or gave low yields (<50 %) under the originally tried conditions (NaOMe in MeOH, NaOEt in EtOH, NaOMe/NaOEt in THF or toluene).
Solution_Description: Screened bases/solvents and found that using t‑BuONa (34.5 mol) in THF (polar aprotic) gave an 89 % isolated yield of the cyclized product 9 on a 15 g scale, which was then employed for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was surprising that the seemingly straightforward Dieckmann condensation turned out to be problematic… no condensation product was observed when compound 8 was treated with NaOMe in MeOH or with NaOEt in EtOH… treated… with either NaOMe or NaOEt in either THF or toluene afforded the desired product 9 in less than 50 % yield.”; “After a brief screening, we found that t‑BuONa in THF gave 89 % yield (15 g scale compound 8).”

Paper Title: A Scalable Total Synthesis of Halofuginone
Problem_Description: Removal of the Cbz protecting group from intermediate 17 gave side‑reactions: catalytic hydrogenolysis caused debromination, Bronsted‑acid treatment gave a mixture of two products, and Lewis‑acid treatment gave a different major product, making the deprotection step unreliable and low‑yielding.
Solution_Description: Switched the protecting group on the piperidine nitrogen from Cbz to Fmoc. Fmoc‑protected intermediate 13 could be brominated with NBS and subsequently coupled, and the Fmoc group was removed cleanly with diethylamine, eliminating the problematic deprotection pathways.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hydrogenolysis of the Cbz of 17 was accompanied by debromination… treating 17 with a Bronsted acid afforded two major compounds 20 and 21… treating 17 with a Lewis acid afforded compound 22 as a major product.”; “Fortunately, this purpose was served when Fmoc was used to protect the piperidine nitrogen… Protection of the N‑atom of 12 with Fmoc‑Cl afforded compound 13… deprotection of the Fmoc group with diethylamine afforded isohalofuginone 3.”

Paper Title: A Scalable Total Synthesis of Halofuginone
Problem_Description: Isohalofuginone 3 partially isomerized to halofuginone 1 during the solvent‑evaporation work‑up, causing batch‑to‑batch variability and impurity formation (ratio of 3 : 1 changed over time).
Solution_Description: Performed a controlled isomerization by refluxing the crude mixture in EtOH (94 % conversion to halofuginone 1) followed by crystallization to afford the product at >98.5 % HPLC purity, thus fixing the conversion and providing a clean final material.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was found that 3 was isomerized to 1 during the solvent evaporation process because the ratio of these two compounds gradually changed… Isohalofuginone 3 was further isomerized to halofuginone 1 in refluxing EtOH in 94 % conversion. After crystallization, 1.65 kg of halofuginone 1 (>98.5 % HPLC purity) was obtained.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: The Sonogashira coupling of aryl halides to form the protected alkynes (B) gave low isolated yields (<50 %) and produced variable amounts of diyne homocoupling by‑products (D) due to Cu/Pd residues, even when oxygen was excluded.
Solution_Description: Abandon the Sonogashira approach and adopt the Corey–Fuchs dibromo‑methylenation followed by LDA‑mediated elimination to obtain the target alkyne (C).
Supporting_Evidence: “The robust and efficient access to the targeted aryl alkynes was challenging due to the facile Glaser–Hay homocoupling… frequently afforded varying amounts of diyne byproducts D.”; “We concluded that… the tested variants of the Sonogashira coupling were not suitable.”; “We decided to further investigate this approach as a means to synthesize alkynes C.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: During the deprotection of the protected alkyne intermediates (B) carried over from the Sonogashira step, transition‑metal residues were difficult to remove because of polar carbamate groups, and the deprotection stage gave rise to further dimer by‑products (D).
Solution_Description: Switch to a metal‑free pathway (Corey–Fuchs) that avoids protecting‑group deprotection and associated metal‑contamination problems.
Supporting_Evidence: “Transition metal residues… were difficult to completely remove due to polar substituents… we frequently observed varying amounts of the dimer byproducts D.”; “We concluded… the tested variants of the Sonogashira coupling were not suitable.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: A route that employs acetyl‑substituted aromatic intermediates and phosphazene‑base elimination of enol nonaflate esters was deemed impractical because the reagents required are too expensive for multigram or kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Reject the high‑cost phosphazene‑base route and adopt the Corey–Fuchs method using inexpensive reagents (CBr₄ and trimethyl phosphite).
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the high cost of the necessary reagents would prevent the application of this method on a larger scale.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: Applying the Ohira–Bestmann protocol on a gram scale of aldehydes (E) gave only 50–60 % isolated yield of the alkyne and a high level of impurities.
Solution_Description: Replace the Ohira–Bestmann approach with the Corey–Fuchs dibromo‑methylenation, which gave higher yields and crystalline intermediates amenable to non‑chromatographic purification.
Supporting_Evidence: “The initial test experiments… resulted in high levels of impurities, and the desired alkynes C were formed in only 50–60 % yield.”; “The Corey–Fuchs method… was quite appealing due to the use of readily attainable reagents and the potential for high yields.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: B‑alkyl Suzuki coupling to make aldehydes (E) left boron‑derived impurities that could not be removed without oxidizing the aldehyde to the acid, and attempts with various oxidants led to rapid oxidation or incomplete removal.
Solution_Description: Postpone the oxidation step until after formation of the dibromo‑methylenation intermediate (F); perform oxidative work‑up on F (H₂O₂/NaOH) which cleanly removed boron residues without degrading the aldehyde.
Supporting_Evidence: “These conditions were not effective due to rapid oxidation of the aldehydes to acids and/or incomplete removal of the 9‑BBN‑derived impurities.”; “We hoped that an oxidative workup performed on the dibromomethylene intermediate F… might be a good option… and this turned out to be the case.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: The classic Ramirez dibromo‑methylenation using triphenylphosphine oxide generated a by‑product that required chromatographic purification, and the harsh acidic hydrolysis required for tri‑isopropyl phosphite removal caused decomposition of the target molecules on scale.
Solution_Description: Replace tri‑isopropyl phosphite with trimethyl phosphite (P(OMe)₃) and conduct the reaction in toluene; the resulting phosphite is hydrolysed under mild conditions, eliminating the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “Triisopropyl phosphite is not, in fact, easily removed after the reaction… harsher conditions… were not compatible… leading to decomposition.”; “We discovered that trimethyl phosphite/CBr₄ in toluene… offered both a very fast and clean dibromo‑methylenation reaction at room temperature, as well as ease of the hydrolysis step.”; “Another improvement… was made in the area of reaction solvent: we determined that toluene was the solvent of choice.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: During the quench of the dibromo‑methylenation mixture with 2 N NaOH and during the addition of the commercial 2.0 M LDA solution, strong exotherms were observed, posing safety and scale‑up concerns.
Solution_Description: Insert the quench and the LDA addition as inverse (slow) additions, control temperature (maintain –40 °C for LDA addition), and monitor the exotherm to keep it manageable.
Supporting_Evidence: “2 N NaOH/H₂O (… N M) addition… is strongly exothermic!”; “Addition of LDA… a strong exotherm develops!”; “The mixture was cooled under argon to (–39 to –43 °C)… a strong exotherm develops!”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: Screening of various bases for the conversion of dibromo‑alkene 5 to alkyne 1 gave many entries with poor conversion, extensive decomposition, or formation of gummy precipitates, especially at higher temperatures.
Solution_Description: Select LDA (a strong, non‑nucleophilic base) at –40 °C, which gave quantitative conversion and high purity of the alkyne while maintaining stability of the reaction mixture.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 3 entries 1–3 show 100 % conversion with LDA at –40 °C; “Other bases… gave poor conversion, decomposition, or precipitates.”

Paper Title: Preparation of Ethynylbenzene Derivatives from Substituted Benzaldehydes
Problem_Description: The dibromo‑methylenation intermediates (F) and some final alkynes were prone to loss of material during silica‑gel chromatography, giving yields 20 % lower than crystallization.
Solution_Description: Avoid chromatography of the dibromo intermediates; isolate them by crystallization and telescope directly to the next step, thereby preserving material and simplifying the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The use of P(OMe)₃/CBr₄… allows the synthesis … without a problem.”; “Crystallization … as a means for non‑chromatographic removal of the impurities.”; “We suggest that chromatography of dibromomethylene compounds F should probably be avoided, and that the purification… by way of crystallization is therefore preferred.”

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of
Problem_Description: Free CALB‑I189K is easily deactivated in the reaction mixture and shows poor reusability; the free enzyme also gives low overall conversion when the substrate concentration is high (e.g., 486 g L⁻¹), leading to poor productivity.
Solution_Description: Covalently immobilize the mutant CALB‑I189K on a glutaraldehyde‑activated amino resin (ESR‑3). The immobilized enzyme displays a half‑life of 247.5 h at 30 °C, retains >85 % activity after 50 cycles, and tolerates substrate concentrations up to 400 g L⁻¹, eliminating the deactivation problem and raising conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "the free CALB‑I189K is easily deactivated and difficult to recover in the reaction system" (Sec 1, paragraph 3).
- "1 M cis‑(±)‑1 was completely resolved in 5 h by 0.1 g L⁻¹ purified free CALB‑I189K… however, the upscale application… is still hampered because the free CALB‑I189K is easily deactivated" (Sec 1, paragraph 3).
- "high substrate concentration (486.52 g L⁻¹) would cause the inactivation of the free CALB‑I189K" (Sec 3.3.2).
- "the immobilized CALB‑I189K exhibited improved thermal stability, with a half‑life of 247.5 h at 30 °C… retained 85.7 % of the initial conversion capacity after 50 cycles" (Abstract & Sec 3.5.2).
- "specific activity of the immobilized CALB‑I189K was increased… after optimization" (Sec 3.2).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of
Problem_Description: Previous chemical routes to the chiral moxifloxacin precursor use expensive chiral induction reagents or resolving agents, and the chemical resolution step gives low overall yields.
Solution_Description: Adopt an enzymatic resolution of racemic cis‑(±)‑dimethyl 1‑acetylpiperidine‑2,3‑dicarboxylate using immobilized CALB‑I189K, which eliminates the need for costly chiral auxiliaries and provides higher conversion (≈50 %) with excellent enantioselectivity (E > 200).
Supporting_Evidence:
- "...chemical methods... suffered from expensive starting materials" (Sec 1, paragraph 2).
- "the chemical resolution process requires expensive resolving agents and results in low yield" (Sec 1, paragraph 2).
- "enzymatic route... offers a great advantage due to the excellent enantioselectivity (E > 2000)" (Sec 1, paragraph 3).
- "the immobilized CALB‑I189K… average productivity of 49.6 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ (batch) and 59.4 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹ (RPBR)" (Abstract).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of
Problem_Description: Earlier enzymatic resolutions using CALB required excessively long reaction times (e.g., 140 h for 80 g L⁻¹ substrate), which is unsuitable for industrial throughput.
Solution_Description: Optimize reaction conditions (pH 7.5, 40 °C, 150 rpm) and employ the immobilized CALB‑I189K, which reduces the reaction time to 2 h for 100 g L⁻¹ substrate in batch mode and achieves comparable conversion in semi‑continuous packed‑bed operation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "80 g L⁻¹ cis‑(±)‑1 was successfully resolved … but the reaction time was not satisfied (140 h)" (Sec 1, paragraph 3).
- "1 M cis‑(±)‑1 was completely resolved in 5 h by 0.1 g L⁻¹ purified free CALB‑I189K… however, the upscale application… is still hampered" (Sec 1, paragraph 3).
- "The resolution reaction was also performed in a recirculating packed bed reactor… average productivity reached 59.4 g L⁻¹ h⁻¹" (Abstract).
- "reaction time was prolonged from 40 min to 2 h" after 50 cycles (Sec 3.4).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of
Problem_Description: At high substrate concentrations (300 g L⁻¹) in the stirred‑tank reactor, the enzyme suffered mechanical damage and substrate diffusion limitations, causing a rapid loss of activity and lower conversion.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Switch to a recirculating packed‑bed reactor (RPBR) operated at an optimal flow rate (8 mL min⁻¹) and enzyme loading (4 g) to improve mass‑transfer, minimize mechanical shear, and maintain conversion (>49 %) while preserving >85 % activity after 50 cycles.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "higher substrate concentration… noticeable deactivation occurred, and half of the initial activity was retained after 14 cycles because of the damage caused by mechanical agitation and substrate" (Sec 3.4, paragraph 2).
- "The effect of flow rate… initial reaction rate increased at 4–8 mL min⁻¹… optimal flow rate was selected as 8 mL min⁻¹" (Sec 3.5.1).
- "The RPBR bioconversion system has high operational stability and conserved over 85.7 % of the initial conversion capacity after 50 cycles" (Abstract & Sec 3.5.2).
- "increase of immobilized CALB‑I189K amount… improved conversion… beyond 4 g the reaction became diffusion‑limited" (Sec 3.5.1).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of
Problem_Description: Recovering the free CALB‑I189K after reaction is difficult, leading to enzyme loss and increased downstream processing costs.
Solution_Description: Covalently bind CALB‑I189K to a solid support (ESR‑3 amino resin), enabling easy filtration and reuse of the biocatalyst, thus simplifying product isolation and reducing enzyme consumption.

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: The initial quinoxaline synthesis from 4‑fluoro‑1,2‑diaminobenzene (15) and ethyl chloroacetoacetate (16) gave a poor regio‑isomer ratio (7 : 17 = 1 : 9), indicating inconsistent selectivity and formation of an undesired by‑product.

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: During the condensation of intermediate 8 with 80 % hydrazine monohydrate the hydrazone (18) and product 9 showed very low solubility in MeOH or EtOH, causing sudden solidification and poor stirring.

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: Intermediate 11 (the pyrazolo[1,5‑a]pyrimidin‑5‑(4H)‑one) is highly hygroscopic; on scale‑up it formed a gelatinous slurry, complicating filtration and dramatically lengthening drying times.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot tandem sequence was developed that converts aminopyrazole 8 directly to the dichloropyrazolo[1,5‑a]pyrimidine 12 via POCl₃ activation of malonic acid, avoiding isolation of the hygroscopic intermediate 11 altogether.
Supporting_Evidence: “We discovered an alternative synthetic approach for 12 without isolating 11. Malonic acid was converted … to give a high yield of 12.”; “The intermediate 11 is so hygroscopic that the reaction mixture became more gelatinous … caused a complicated filtration process and a prolonged drying time.”

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: The deprotonation of quinoxaline 7 with LHMDS to afford β‑ketonitrile 8 is highly exothermic (145 kJ mol⁻¹) and the resulting salt is unstable above 20 °C, requiring strict temperature control.
Solution_Description: The addition of the LHMDS solution was performed slowly while maintaining the reactor temperature between –10 °C and 0 °C, and the mixture was kept below 10 °C throughout the work‑up to prevent decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “This reaction was exothermic (145 kJ/mol per 7)… required a relatively low reaction temperature after adding a solution of LHMDS… the addition rate was controlled to keep the mixture below 10 °C.”; “The resulting salt of 8 was not stable above 20 °C.”

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: The POCl₃‑mediated chlorination of 11 to give 12 released a large amount of heat (≈ 584 kJ mol⁻¹) and the low solubility of the monochloride intermediate caused dimerisation when i‑Pr₂NEt was used as an additive.
Solution_Description: The addition of 11 was staged in quarter‑portions to moderate the exotherm, i‑Pr₂NEt was omitted to suppress dimerisation, and the pH of the quench was tightly controlled (pH 4–5) using aqueous NaOH. A new route employing POCl₃‑activated malonic acid directly generated 12 without isolating 11, further reducing heat load and variability.
Supporting_Evidence: “Each quarter of 11 was added to the reaction mixture at regular intervals… i‑Pr₂NEt as an additive… accelerated the dimerisation of 12 (up to 20 % relative HPLC area %).”; “Dichloride 12 was crystallized … with control of the pH of the resulting suspension (pH 4–5).”; “We discovered an alternative synthetic approach for 12 without isolating 11… activated malonic acid.”

Paper Title: Scalable Process Design for a PDE10A Inhibitor Consisting of Pyrazolopyrimidine and Quinoxaline as Key Units
Problem_Description: The original route required expensive mono‑ethyl malonate for the construction of the pyrazolo[1,5‑a]pyrimidine core and used > 2.5 equiv of costly (R)‑3‑fluoropyrrolidine hydrochloride, inflating material cost at scale.
Solution_Description: Dimethyl malonate, a cheaper and more readily available reagent, replaced mono‑ethyl malonate for the condensation step. Introduction of an oxazolidinone protecting group on the pyrazolo[1,5‑a]pyrimidine increased its electrophilicity, allowing the SNAr coupling to proceed with only 1.2 equiv of (R)‑3‑fluoropyrrolidine, dramatically lowering reagent consumption and cost.
