Paper Title: Development and Scale-up of a Route to ATR Inhibitor AZD6738

Supporting_Evidence: “The process mass intensity (PMI) for the Curtius rearrangement step and the SFC resolution alone in the original approach was estimated to be 3839… In contrast, the process outlined in Scheme 4 decreased the PMI for the Curtius rearrangement and classical resolution to 98.7.”
missing_information: [SOLUBILITY], [ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT], [LONG REACTIONS], [COST OF REAGENTS (T3P, H₂O₂)], [SCALING OF CONTINUOUS H₂O₂ Dosing]

Paper Title: Thermal Stability of 2‑Butynoic Acid (Tetrolic Acid)
Problem_Description: During the n‑butyllithium/Tetrahydrofuran deprotonation step, higher temperatures lead to degradation of the n‑BuLi/THF mixture, forming acetaldehyde that subsequently produces impurity 2 in the 2‑butynoic acid product.
Solution_Description: The temperature of the deprotonation was kept low (below –70 °C) to suppress n‑BuLi/THF degradation, thereby limiting formation of impurity 2.
Supporting_Evidence: • “higher temperature during the deprotonation of propyne appeared to give increased levels of 2.”

Paper Title: Thermal Stability of 2‑Butynoic Acid (Tetrolic Acid)
Problem_Description: Short‑path vacuum distillation of 2‑butynoic acid (120–130 °C) triggers exothermic decomposition (onset ≈123 °C, ΔH ≈‑2300 J·g⁻¹) leading to rapid pressure rise and rupture of the calorimeter, indicating a thermal‑runaway hazard at scale.
Solution_Description: Distillation was abandoned; the product was instead purified by recrystallization from methyl tert‑butyl ether/heptane, which removed impurity 2 and avoided the high‑temperature vacuum step.
Supporting_Evidence: • “short‑path distillation … was used … but subsequent … investigation … revealed the potential for thermal runaway, ruling out this method of purification for future manufactures.”

Paper Title: Thermal Stability of 2‑Butynoic Acid (Tetrolic Acid)
Problem_Description: When dried in a vacuum oven at temperatures above ambient, 2‑butynoic acid sublimes, causing loss of material.
Solution_Description: Drying was performed at ambient temperature under a gentle nitrogen flow or by tray‑drying under vacuum, preventing sublimation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It was observed that the 2‑butynoic acid sublimes when drying in the vacuum oven at temperatures above ambient. Production on a pilot scale was performed using a flow of nitrogen (or by tray drying under vacuum) at ambient temperature to dry the product.”

Paper Title: Thermal Stability of 2‑Butynoic Acid (Tetrolic Acid)
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the literature route was unsafe because the product’s thermal instability limited the maximum safe operating temperature to ~74 °C (T_D24), far below the temperature needed for vacuum distillation.
Solution_Description: A recrystallization‑based purification route was developed, eliminating the need for high‑temperature distillation and enabling safe large‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Scale‑up … was problematic because of the thermal instability of the product, which prevented the use of short‑path distillation … a recrystallization procedure … was developed to facilitate this.”

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: Diazomethane (CH₂N₂) is best soluble in diethyl ether, but the use of this solvent is strongly discouraged or prohibited in industrial laboratories, limiting the ability to achieve high CH₂N₂ concentrations.
Solution_Description: The authors switched the reaction solvent to methyltert‑butyl ether (MTBE), which is industrially acceptable, even though it has lower CH₂N₂ solubility, and they compensated by optimizing other parameters (e.g., residence time, flow rates).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Although CH₂N₂ is best soluble in diethyl ether, its use as a solvent is strongly discouraged, if not forbidden, in industrial laboratories.” (sec 2, p 3)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: Diazomethane is extremely toxic, carcinogenic, and prone to explosive decomposition, making storage, isolation, and large‑scale handling hazardous.
Solution_Description: A continuous on‑site‑on‑demand generation of anhydrous CH₂N₂ was implemented using a membrane‑based tube‑in‑CSTR system, eliminating the need to store or transport the hazardous gas.
Supporting_Evidence: • “CH₂N₂ is extremely toxic and a potent carcinogen…Because of high volatility and extreme sensitivity to explosive decomposition, it is also challenging to handle or to store CH₂N₂.” (intro)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: The tube‑in‑tube reactor delivered a very low productivity (1.25 mmol h⁻¹), insufficient for the slow diazoketone formation step.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the tube‑in‑tube geometry with a cascade of two continuous stirred‑tank reactors (CSTRs) containing the AF‑2400 membrane, which increased the overall throughput to 1.54 g h⁻¹ (5.2 mmol h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: • “Its limitation is a very low productivity (1.25 mmol h⁻¹)…we decided to employ a CSTR concept…Throughput of 1.54 g h⁻¹ could be reached.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: The back‑pressure regulator (BPR) in the CSTR setup repeatedly blocked after >3 h, interrupting flow and causing operational downtime.
Solution_Description: The BPR was removed from the tube‑in‑CSTR configuration because the applied 4–5 bar back‑pressure had no measurable effect on membrane performance, thus eliminating the bottleneck.
Supporting_Evidence: • “the BPR was omitted in the tube‑in‑CSTR setup, since the BPR blocked at ambient temperatures when being used for a longer period of time (>3 h). … membrane performance tests revealed that the applied 4–5 bar back pressure had no effect on the performance of the membrane.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: At lower flow rates in the second CH₂N₂ generator, precipitation of Diazald and/or the by‑product PPTS was observed, leading to potential clogging of the membrane tubing.
Solution_Description: The concentration of the Diazald feed was reduced to 0.5 M and flow rates increased to 0.2 mL min⁻¹, which prevented precipitation while still delivering sufficient CH₂N₂ for the second CSTR.
Supporting_Evidence: • “By applying lower flow rates, occasional precipitation of Diazald and/or PPTS was noticed. … the concentration of the Diazald solution was minimized to 0.5 M to increase the flow rate to 0.2 mL min⁻¹ and thus prevent blockage of the membrane.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: A fraction of CH₂N₂ (up to ~30 % in some runs) was unrecovered, attributed to aqueous decomposition of the diazo compound during its residence in the membrane tubing.
Solution_Description: The residence time in the membrane was optimized (shorter for fast consumption) and an excess of CH₂N₂ (3 equiv) was supplied to ensure immediate reaction with the substrate, reducing the amount of CH₂N₂ that could decompose.
Supporting_Evidence: • “unrecovered CH₂N₂ (Δ), most likely due to decomposition under aqueous conditions, increased with prolonged residence times…The best conditions…involved a residence time of 4 min inside the membrane which relates to a total flow rate of 0.626 mL min⁻¹.” (sec 2.3, 2.5)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: Introducing concentrated aqueous HCl directly into the CSTR caused phase separation and solvent‑level rise due to high surface tension, compromising reaction performance and safety.
Solution_Description: The final halogenation step was performed in batch after collecting the CSTR effluent; the mixture was quenched with HCl, extracted, washed, and the product isolated by simple extraction rather than attempting a continuous CSTR halogenation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “…the goose neck was not reliable, since the surface tension of water is too high…resulted in a rising solvent level…the α‑chloroketone synthesis was conducted in batch by quenching the collected fractions with 3 equiv of concentrated HCl…simple extraction procedure…yield 80–85 %.” (sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Design and Optimization of a Continuous Stirred Tank Reactor Cascade for Membrane-Based Diazomethane Production: Synthesis of α‑Chloroketones
Problem_Description: Accurate real‑time measurement of CH₂N₂ concentration was hindered because the FTIR probe could not detect water (blind spot) and the CH₂N₂ and diazoketone peaks overlapped, leading to potential variability in process control.
Solution_Description: FTIR monitoring was implemented using the characteristic C≡N stretch at 2100 cm⁻¹ for CH₂N₂ and a calibration against benzoic‑acid conversion; later, the FTIR probe in the second CSTR was used to monitor the diazoketone formation at 2107 cm⁻¹, providing reliable PAT data.
Supporting_Evidence: • “FTIR spectroscopy allows accurate monitoring of the generation and consumption of CH₂N₂ based on the characteristic C≡N stretch at 2100 cm⁻¹…The FTIR spectrum … indicates that after ca. 6 h a steady state is reached.” (sec 2.2, 2.5)

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The original synthetic route kept the N‑N‑bis‑chloroethylamine alkylating group throughout the entire sequence, requiring all operations to be performed in containment because the material is highly toxic.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned so that the bis‑chloroethylamino pharmacophore is introduced only at a late stage, eliminating the need to handle the toxic alkylating group during earlier steps.
Supporting_Evidence: The authors state that “Carrying the alkylating pharmacophore from the very beginning means that manufacturing must be performed with containment for all operations… our strategy aimed at introducing the N,N‑bis‑chloroethylamine functionality at a later stage.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: When scaling the amide‑coupling step, an adhesive incrustation formed in the reaction mixture, which lowered the conversion rate.
Solution_Description: Changing the reaction solvent from ethyl acetate to acetone eliminated the incrustation and allowed high conversion at room temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: The text reports “Increasing the scale showed the limitations… incrustations formed… An improvement was observed by changing to acetone as solvent for the reaction, which could now be performed with high conversion at room temperature without forming any adhesive incrustations.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: The nitropeptide intermediate (8) obtained after coupling was insufficiently pure, making downstream hydrogenation and bis‑alkylation unreliable.
Solution_Description: Antisolvent crystallization with n‑heptane was introduced, providing the nitropeptide in 89 % yield and 99.9 % purity, eliminating the need to telescope the steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “Antisolvent crystallization with n‑heptane produced (8) in good yield (89 %) and excellent purity (99.9 %).”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the nitropeptide in ethanol suffered from very low substrate solubility, requiring large solvent volumes and making catalyst removal difficult; using THF/EtOAc also generated impurities.
Solution_Description: A solvent mixture of ethanol/ethyl acetate (70/30) was first employed, and later 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran was adopted, improving solubility, eliminating impurities, and giving full conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “The drawback with ethanol was the low solubility… When we employed a mixture of ethanol and ethyl acetate, the product was more soluble, and none of the impurities were detected… later solvent was changed to 2‑methyltetrahydrofuran, with the primary benefit being increased solubility.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Residual palladium from the hydrogenation catalyst exceeded the allowable limit of 10 ppm in the API.
Solution_Description: A silica‑based trimercaptotriazine scavenger (Si‑TMT) was added post‑hydrogenation, reducing palladium levels from 21 ppm to <1 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: “Among the scavengers, the silica‑based trimercaptotriazine, Si‑TMT, was most promising… Using a loading of 3 % of the Si‑TMT scavenger decreased the palladium content from 21 to less than 1 ppm.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: In the reductive alkylation step, the Boc protecting group was unintentionally removed, generating a complex impurity profile and low‑purity product.
Solution_Description: Adding a large excess of sodium chloroacetate (15 equiv) suppressed Boc deprotection, and the order of addition (dissolve substrate, add chloroacetic acid, then sodium chloroacetate, followed by slow addition of borane‑dimethyl‑sulfide) prevented by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “A clear effect in suppressing deprotection… was evident… The following order of addition protected (6) from by‑product formation; dissolution of (6) in THF, addition of chloroacetic acid for protonation, followed by the addition of sodium chloroacetate and slow addition of borane dimethyl sulfide complex.”

Paper Title: Development of a Safe Process for Manufacturing of the Potent Anticancer Agent Melflufen Hydrochloride
Problem_Description: Using a large excess of HCl in ethanol generated chloroethane, a genotoxic impurity, and the excess acid hindered crystallization of the final API.
Solution_Description: The HCl equivalents were reduced to 7 eq, the reaction was performed at ambient temperature then cooled to 5 °C, and methyl‑tert‑butyl ether was added as an antisolvent to induce crystallization, limiting impurity formation and improving yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “A compromise was found in treating Boc‑melflufen (5) with 7 eq of 2.7 M HCl… Storage at 5 °C was necessary… methyl‑tert‑butyl ether was added to increase the yield.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Glutathione (GSH) shows poor solubility in common organic solvents and high solubility in water, making it difficult to perform acylations in typical organic media.
Solution_Description: The authors performed the acylation in a weakly basic aqueous solution (1 M Na₂CO₃, 0.4 M GSH) using butyric anhydride at room temperature, avoiding organic solvents altogether.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Because of the poor solubility of GSH in common organic solvents and its high solubility in water, we decided to treat GSH with different acylating agents in weakly basic aqueous solution at room temperature.”
2. “The best result was obtained with treatment of 1 dissolved in 1 M aqueous Na₂CO₃ solution (final concentration of GSH, 0.4 M) with butyric anhydride (2.05 equiv) at room temperature … full conversion with a very high purity was achieved.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Traditional routes to N‑acyl‑glutathiones rely on protecting‑group chemistry, expensive reagents and multiple purification steps, leading to high material cost and reduced overall yields.
Solution_Description: The new two‑step sequence uses inexpensive, bulk‑available reagents (butyric anhydride and sodium methoxide) and eliminates protecting groups, delivering C4‑GSH in 61 % overall isolated yield without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “...the synthesis of GSH derivatives requires clever manipulation of protecting groups. However, a protection/de‑protection event introduces at least two steps into a sequence, incurring costs from additional reagents and waste disposal, and generally leads to a reduced overall yield.”
2. “The process ... employed inexpensive reagents such as butyric anhydride and sodium methoxide … and does not require the use of expensive reagents or chromatography.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Screening of many acyl donors gave highly variable conversions (from scarce to excellent) and often produced mixtures of mono‑ and di‑acylated products.
Solution_Description: Optimization identified butyric anhydride (2.05 equiv) with 1 M Na₂CO₃ as the optimal combination, giving complete ( > 99 %) conversion in 2 h and high isolated yield of the mono‑acylated product.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “All tested acyl donors afforded a mixture of mono‑ and double‑acylated products … in scarce to excellent conversion … the exception of 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl esters.”
2. “Butyric anhydride … turned out to be a very suitable donor substrate leading to product 2 with complete conversion and with high yield.”
3. “The best result was obtained … with butyric anhydride (2.05 equiv) … full conversion …”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Using strong bases (e.g., NaOH 5 M) or prolonged reaction times caused decomposition of the GSH substrate.
Solution_Description: The authors limited the base strength to carbonate (1 M Na₂CO₃), kept the reaction at ambient temperature and limited the residence time (2 h for acylation, 1 h for methanolysis), preventing degradation.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. Table 1 entry 15 – “NaOH (5 M) … decomp”.
2. “The solution was acidified … and the reaction was performed at room temperature.”
3. “Stirred at room temperature for 2 h (100 % conversion …) … sodium methoxide … for 1 h at room temperature … gave the desired product in 69 % yield.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Large‑scale production of C4‑GSH would traditionally require column chromatography, which is impractical, waste‑intensive and costly.
Solution_Description: A chromatography‑free work‑up was developed: after acylation the mixture was acidified (pH 3.5), washed with MTBE to remove sodium butyrate, re‑acidified (pH 1.5), filtered and washed, yielding the pure product as a solid. The second step used a Dowex 50WX8‑(H) resin to capture the product and avoid extraction.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “The solution was acidified to pH 3.5 with 6 N HCl … washed with methyl tert‑butyl ether (3 × 2.6 L)… acidified to pH 1.5 … filtered … to give 2 as a white amorphous solid.”
2. “Treatment … with sodium methoxide … followed by removal of methanol … and acidification with Dowex 50WX8‑(H) resin … gave the corresponding N‑acyl glutathione in 69 % yield.”
3. Abstract: “This chromatography‑ and salt‑free synthesis of C4‑GSH … easy to scale up.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: Several entries in the screening required up to 20 h to reach conversion, which would limit throughput on manufacturing scale.
Solution_Description: Optimized conditions reduced the acylation to 2 h (full conversion) and the methanolysis to 1 h, providing a rapid two‑step process suitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. Table 1 entry 1 – “time (h) 20”.
2. “Butyric anhydride … was added dropwise over 2 h and stirred at room temperature for 2 h (100 % conversion).”
3. “Sodium methoxide … added portionwise in 1 h … stirred for 20 min at room temperature.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Preparation of
Problem_Description: The need for large‑scale supply of C4‑GSH is hampered by the high price of existing synthetic routes, which use costly reagents and generate large waste streams.
Solution_Description: By selecting inexpensive bulk reagents (butyric anhydride, sodium methoxide) and water/methanol as solvents, the overall material cost was dramatically lowered; the process also generated only ~9.4 kg waste per kg of product (E‑factor ≈ 9.4) compared with much higher waste from conventional routes.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. Abstract: “...highlights the use of inexpensive reagents such as butyric anhydride and sodium methoxide as well as environmentally acceptable solvents such as water and methanol.”
2. “The current process generates ∼9.4 kg of waste/kg of C4‑GSH (E‑factor value, not including water).”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: The traditional route uses 3‑pentanone, a volatile ketone that is difficult to handle on large scale and suffers from poor recovery of the starting material, driving up material cost.
Solution_Description: Replace 3‑pentanone with cheap, bulk‑available tetrahydrothiopyran‑4‑one (≈ 3–5 USD kg⁻¹) as the five‑carbon source; the cyclo‑ketone is non‑volatile, easily recovered, and lowers the overall cost of the process.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reactions are mostly based on diethyl ketone (3‑pentanone)... 3‑Pentanone is a volatile compound, and the quantities required are greater and the recovery of the starting material lower.”; “It occurred to us that thiopyran‑4‑one (available at 3–5 USD/kg on bulk pricing) could be the best five‑carbon equivalent… The synthetic operation from cheaply available tetrahydrothiopyran‑4‑one 6 provided an added advantage of scale up at a lower cost than the acyclic strategy.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: During preparation of the Grignard reagent from magnesium and 3‑bromoanisole a rapid heat evolution was observed after 10 min, creating a safety risk on scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Generate the Grignard reagent by slow, dropwise addition of 3‑bromoanisole solution to activated Mg in THF under nitrogen, cool the mixture for 1 h before addition, then add the Grignard to the ketone substrate at 0 °C while maintaining vigorous stirring to control temperature and heat removal.
Supporting_Evidence: “...heat generation was observed after 10 min; then, it was allowed to cool for 1 h.”; “the Grignard reagent was slowly dropwise added to the … substrate … at 0 °C, and the stirring was continued for 12 h at room temperature.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: Attempts to achieve a catalytic asymmetric Mannich addition with l‑proline failed to give any enantioselectivity, making the chiral route impractical.
Solution_Description: Abandon the asymmetric organocatalytic pathway; perform the Mannich reaction with inexpensive aqueous formaldehyde (37 % aq.) and dimethylamine (40 % aq.) without a chiral catalyst, delivering the desired adduct in 76 % isolated yield on 100 g scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction with l‑proline did not result in the preferential formation of any one enantiomer… Attempts to use organocatalytic reactions resulted in good yields with no enantioselectivity.”; “The first step of the synthesis, Mannich addition, was carried out using 37 % aqueous formaldehyde and 40 % aqueous dimethylamine … to yield 5a in 76 % yield.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: Initial de‑hydroxylation conditions gave modest yields and poor control of the 7 : 8 product ratio (e.g., 70 % yield, 9 : 1; other entries gave 0 % of the desired isomer).
Solution_Description: Adopt a TFA/CH₂Cl₂ (2 : 1) solvent system with NaBH₄ (15 equiv) at room temperature for 6 h; this delivered the desired de‑hydroxylated product in 81 % combined yield with an improved 8 : 2 7 : 8 ratio.
Supporting_Evidence: Table 2 entry 5: “TFA … NaBH₄ … rt … 6 h … 8:2 … 81 %.”; “Among all conditions, the best was found to be the conversion of compound 4 in TFA/CH₂Cl₂ (2:1) solvent in the presence of NaBH₄ to realize a mixture of 7 and 8, where 8:2 selectivity was observed with 81 % yield.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: Isolation of the Grignard‑derived tertiary alcohol 4 by chromatography would add time and cost; however, the crude material is sufficiently pure for the next step.
Solution_Description: Carry the crude tertiary alcohol directly into the de‑hydroxylation step without chromatographic purification, thus eliminating a purification bottleneck.
Supporting_Evidence: “…generated a single diastereomeric tertiary alcohol 4 in 82 % of crude yield, which was used for the next step without purification.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: The Raney‑Ni hydrogenation requires handling hydrogen gas and a solid catalyst, posing safety concerns on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Conduct the hydrogenation in an autoclave at 80 °C under a mild hydrogen pressure of 1 bar, allowing safe, controlled reduction and easy filtration of the Raney‑Ni catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “The crude 1‑(4‑(3‑methoxyphenyl)… ) was dissolved … treated with a suspension of Raney Ni … heated to 80 °C in an autoclave with an internal hydrogen pressure of 1 bar for 12 h.”

Paper Title: Tetrahydrothiopyran-4-one as Five-Carbon Source for Scalable Synthesis of (±)-Tapentadol
Problem_Description: The overall isolated yield of (±)‑tapentadol from the new sequence is only ~37 %, indicating room for improvement in step efficiency.
Solution_Description: Adopt the cyclic ketone (tetrahydrothiopyran‑4‑one) approach, which provides higher diastereoselectivity and better material recovery, laying a foundation for future yield‑enhancing optimizations.
Supporting_Evidence: “The advantage of the current strategy using ketone 6 was the higher de obtained as compared with previous routes… overall ∼37 % yield.”

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Enzyme stability was identified as the limiting factor; activity drops rapidly during the reaction, causing low conversion and yield at larger scale.
Solution_Description: Select a more stable IRED (IRED‑18) for the process; this enzyme retains activity longer, increasing turnover number and product yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Enzyme stability was identified to be the limiting factor." (abstract)  
- "The in‑process stability for the IREDs was studied… IRED‑18 specifically stood out… activity retained over time; other enzymes dropped by 50 % after 16 h" (stability study).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Increasing substrate concentration (>200 mM cyclohexanone) causes accumulation of the imine intermediate, which inhibits the IRED and prevents formation of the desired amine.
Solution_Description: Implement a fed‑batch feeding strategy for the ketone and amine, keeping their instantaneous concentrations low while achieving a high final substrate load.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The presence of higher substrate concentrations (>200 mM 1) led to the accumulation of the imine intermediate… leading to low or no formation of 3" (scale‑up discussion).  
- "fed‑batch reaction setup was used to allow slow feeding 1 and 2… the fed‑batch strategy was extremely successful and unlocked the potential for scale‑up" (fed‑batch results).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Higher concentrations of the co‑solvent DMSO negatively affect enzyme activity, reducing conversion and yield.
Solution_Description: Limit DMSO to 0–5 % (v/v) or remove it altogether; the DoE identified lower DMSO as a key factor for higher conversion.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The optimum reaction conditions revealed by the DoE… 0–5 % (v/v) DMSO" (DoE results).  
- "lower concentration of 1 and cosolvent significantly improves both the conversion and the yield" (DoE discussion).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Operating at pH ≥ 9 causes irreversible deactivation of the IRED, compromising enzyme robustness.
Solution_Description: Use potassium phosphate or Tris‑HCl buffers within the pH 6.5–8.0 window (phosphate) to maintain enzyme stability while still promoting imine formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Higher pH, in the range of 9 or more, was observed… to be detrimental to the IRED stability and led to its irreversible deactivation." (pH study).  
- "Both buffers provided full conversion under the pH range 6.5 to 8.0 for potassium phosphate…" (buffer comparison).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: The reaction required extended times (up to 40 h) to reach high conversion at high substrate loading, reducing process throughput.
Solution_Description: Operate at the optimal temperature (25 °C) identified by DoE and adjust reaction time based on conversion targets, shortening overall processing time while preserving enzyme activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The most significant parameters were identified… 25–35 °C reaction temperature" (DoE).  
- "After feeding completion (16 h), conversion was ∼93 %… values gradually increased to 99 % and 97 %… by running the reaction for 40 h" (fed‑batch kinetic data).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Insufficient enzyme loading reduces the catalytic capacity, leading to incomplete conversion, especially at higher substrate concentrations.
Solution_Description: Increase the IRED concentration (e.g., from 5 mg mL⁻¹ to 10 mg mL⁻¹) to boost catalytic turnover and improve conversion rates.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The most significant parameters were identified to be … IRED loading, followed by the concentration of DMSO" (DoE).  
- Table 1 entries show higher IRED loading correlates with higher conversion (e.g., entry 1 vs 2).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: Whole‑cell preparations were explored to mitigate substrate inhibition, but initial trials gave modest conversion and side‑product formation (cyclohexanol).
Solution_Description: Employ lyophilized whole‑cell biocatalysts containing IRED‑18 to buffer the enzyme against substrate‑induced inhibition; monitor and control endogenous ketoreductase activity to avoid by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "lyophilized whole cells containing IRED‑18 were used… conversion was ∼57 % and yield 13 %" (whole‑cell experiment).  
- "∼4 % cyclohexanol was also formed… This is not an issue because it can be shifted back toward the ketone" (by‑product note).

Paper Title: Technical Considerations for Scale-Up of Imine-Reductase-Catalyzed Reductive Amination: A Case Study
Problem_Description: At very high substrate loading (1.5 M ketone, 3 M amine) the reaction stalls with predominant imine formation, indicating substrate‑induced deactivation.
Solution_Description: Combine fed‑batch feeding with the more robust IRED‑33 (high activity, acceptable stability) to maintain low instantaneous substrate concentrations while achieving high overall loading.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Further increasing the substrate concentration to ∼1.5 M did not prove successful… main product was the imine intermediate" (high‑load trial).  
- "Using IRED‑33… feeding was completed in 6.5 h… full conversion… turnover number of 48 279" (successful fed‑batch with IRED‑33).

Paper Title: Revisiting the Cleavage of Evans Oxazolidinones with LiOH/H

Supporting_Evidence: "up to 4.6 HPLC area percent (AP) hydroxyamide 10 was formed"; "LiOH in THF gave optimal selectivity for the desired acid 9"; "Biphasic conditions gave no conversion, while among water‑miscible solvents THF was clearly optimal"

Solution_Description: Tetrabutylammonium hydroxide (TBAOH) was employed as a stronger base, providing >99 % conversion in <5 min.  This high rate enabled the design of a single‑tank continuous stirred‑tank reactor (CSTR) that could operate at practical residence times.

Paper Title: Revisiting the Cleavage of Evans Oxazolidinones with LiOH/H
Problem_Description: The peracid intermediate formed after nucleophilic attack of LiOOH decomposes rapidly via reduction by excess H2O2, generating a stoichiometric amount of O₂ gas that exceeds the allowable head‑space limit.
Solution_Description: Lowering the overall water concentration (making the reaction “drier”) slowed the peracid decomposition and improved selectivity, while slow, controlled addition of LiOH in a semibatch mode limited the instantaneous O₂ evolution rate.
Supporting_Evidence: "the peracid is rapidly reduced by the excess H₂O₂… leading to the release of a stoichiometric amount of oxygen"; "Plotting kobs versus the H₂O concentration clearly showed that “drier” reaction conditions lead to a slower reaction but give improved selectivity"; "The other option, in which LiOH was slowly added to the batch… to control the reaction rate and therefore the O₂ flow rate"

Paper Title: Revisiting the Cleavage of Evans Oxazolidinones with LiOH/H

Solution_Description: Two engineering strategies were implemented: (1) a continuous CSTR with N₂ sweep that could be shut down if O₂ rose too high, and (2) a semibatch process with gradual LiOH addition, allowing N₂ flow to dilute O₂ and keep the system within safe limits.
Supporting_Evidence: "O₂ level ever exceeded a safe value in the CSTR reactor, the flow could be stopped, and maintaining the N₂ flow… would return the system to a safe state"; "If the O₂ level exceeded a safe operating level, the flow of LiOH could be stopped to allow the N₂ flow… to return the system to a safe operating state"; "the gas being formed was O₂… exceeded our acceptable safety limit in the reactor headspace"

Problem_Description: The researchers encountered several obstacles while developing a scalable synthesis of eliglustat: (1) preparation of α‑dibenzylamino β‑ketoester 6 required cryogenic conditions (−60 °C); (2) a direct amidation of intermediate 5 with pyrrolidine failed because of steric hindrance, giving low conversion; (3) the same amidation also suffered from retro‑aldol decomposition of the product; (4) conventional amide‑coupling reagents (EDCI/HOBt, CDI, etc.) gave poor conversion when coupling the sterically hindered acid 14; (5) the historic reduction of amide 4 with LiAlH₄, although effective, posed significant safety hazards on pilot‑scale.

Problem_Description: Diaryliodonium salts display exothermic decomposition (initiation 139‑199 °C, magnitude up to 845 J g⁻¹).  Handling at temperatures above 80‑90 °C poses safety risks, especially on scale.

Under the typical dilution (≈ 20 mL DCM g⁻¹), the calculated adiabatic temperature rise is < 2 °C, keeping the process within the “safe” region of the Yoshida correlation.

Paper Title: Anion Metathesis of Diaryliodonium Tosylate Salts with a Solid-Phase Column Constructed from Readily Available Laboratory Consumables

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530
Problem_Description: The phenol impurity 7 continued to form after the reaction had reached > 99.5 % conversion, lengthening the time needed to stay within the safety window.

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530

Supporting_Evidence: ["Guided by the model, new nominal conditions for the amidation reaction were identified and a broad and robust operational space was established.", "The most significant difference between the new and old nominal conditions is the use of a lower reaction temperature (82 °C vs 88 °C) and higher loading of Pd(OAc)₂ (1.10 mol % vs 0.90 mol %) in the reaction.", "The lower bounds of 78 °C for temperature and 1.00 mol % palladium acetate were selected to ensure acceptable reaction conversion was achieved within 12 h."]

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530

Paper Title: Development of an Operational Space Using Mechanistic Models for a Pd-Catalyzed Amidation Reaction Used in the Synthesis of ABT-530
Problem_Description: The multivariate interactions of eight reaction parameters made it difficult to intuitively design experiments and define a robust design space.

Solution_Description: Operate the flow‑flash sequence at a lower temperature (–60 °C) and with reduced flow rates using gear pumps.  The lower temperature and slower streams limit heat buildup and pressure rise, providing a safer operating window for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow-Flash Chemistry to Scale-up Synthesis of 5‑Cyano-2-formylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: Increasing the substrate concentration of 8c above 0.4 M (e.g., 0.8 M) caused a marked drop in the isolated yield of 1, likely due to side‑reactions and increased formation of by‑products 10c/11c.
Solution_Description: Maintain the 8c concentration at 0.4 M (the optimum identified) and use a smaller‑diameter microtube reactor (ϕ = 0.5 mm) for the lithiation step to improve mixing and heat removal.  Adjust flow rates (10 mL min⁻¹ for 8c and 2 mL min⁻¹ for BuLi) to keep residence time around 70 ms, giving the best balance of conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Higher concentration of the 8c solution (0.8 M in THF) … resulted in significant decrease in the yield of 1 (entry 6).”
• “To deliver the highly reactive aryllithium intermediate rapidly … a reaction tube (L1) with a smaller diameter (ϕ_i.d. = 0.5 mm) was employed.”

Paper Title: Application of Continuous Flow-Flash Chemistry to Scale-up Synthesis of 5‑Cyano-2-formylbenzoic Acid
Problem_Description: Large‑scale preparation of 1 required an efficient isolation method because column chromatography is impractical for multi‑hundred‑gram batches.
Solution_Description: After the flow‑flash reaction, the mixture is treated with aqueous 2 N HCl, extracted, and the crude product is recovered by back‑extraction and crystallisation (or by washing with isopropyl ether).  This avoids any chromatographic step and provides >98 % HPLC purity.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The collected reaction mixture was extracted with aqueous saturated NaHCO₃ solution and the aqueous layer was acidified … before it was extracted back with EtOAc … It was found that 9c was converted easily into 1 … to afford crude 1 as crystals in ca. 40 % yield with sufficient purity (>98 % HPLC area) for use in the subsequent step.”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: Low isolated yield (50‑60 %) of intermediate 8 caused by a tedious three‑to‑four‑extraction work‑up in acetone and the poor solubility of the water‑soluble product, which also made the mixture viscous and difficult to stir.
Solution_Description: Switched the starting material from N‑(4‑oxocyclohexyl)‑acetamide (2) to commercially available Boc‑4‑aminocyclohexan‑1‑one (13), providing a more hydrophilic, easily de‑protected intermediate and eliminating the low‑yield extraction step.

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: The methylsulfonyl chloride (MsCl) used for mesylation of intermediate 23 is hazardous, expensive to transport, and difficult to handle on a kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: Replaced MsCl with methanesulfonic anhydride, a less volatile and safer reagent that can be shipped easily; the new reagent gave comparable yields (up to 88 %) after optimisation of base, DMAP, and solvent.
Supporting_Evidence: “The hazardous and expensive transportation of methanesulfonyl chloride limits its use at large scale.”; “Methanesulfonic anhydride was chosen as the alternative acylating agent due to the characteristics of good reactivity, low volatilization, and convenient transportation and storage.”; Table 2 entry 8 shows 88 % isolated yield with methanesulfonic anhydride in DMF.

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: Olefinic impurity 31 co‑eluted with the API 12 because the two compounds have very similar polarity, making conventional recrystallization ineffective (purity only reduced from 99.92 % to ≈99.3 %).
Solution_Description: Implemented a salt‑formation step using oxalic acid (acid‑base control) followed by recrystallization; the acid selectively protonated the API, allowing removal of impurity 31 to <0.1 % HPLC, and the process was then telescoped into the final salinization/recrystallization sequence.
Supporting_Evidence: “The direct recrystallization method was attributed to the similar polarities of 12 and 31… barely improved.”; “Oxalic acid … was efficient (31 = 0.08 % HPLC) and chosen as the optimal acid because of its purity (99.92 % HPLC) and yield (80 % isolated yield).”; “The successful optimization was applied for the scale up … with high HPLC purity (>99.9 %).”

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: The sulfonylation of intermediate 23 with alternative sulfonyl chlorides (compounds 25–28) gave very low isolated yields (≤28 %) and large amounts of unconverted starting material, due to poor solubility and inadequate mixing in the chosen solvents.

Solution_Description: Screened solvents and selected acetonitrile as the optimal recrystallization solvent, providing a high trans/cis ratio (517:1) and acceptable isolated yield (58 %) while using a relatively low solvent volume (21 vol).

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: The original stepwise sequence required separate work‑ups after each transformation, leading to a long overall process (nine separate operations) and multiple solvent exchanges that reduced throughput.
Solution_Description: Combined the Wittig–Horner reaction, hydrogenation, Boc de‑protection, and furoyl acylation into a one‑pot three‑step sequence in the same THF/CH₂Cl₂ solvent system, cutting the step count to three and improving overall isolated yield to 70 % for intermediate 19 on >11 kg scale.

Paper Title: Process Development of an Efficient Kilogram-Scale Preparation of a Preferential Dopamine D
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of the vinyl intermediate produced trace amounts of unreduced olefin 16, which could potentially decompose under the subsequent basic conditions or give rise to olefinic impurity 31.

Paper Title: Enzymatic Synthesis of Trimethyl-ε-caprolactone: Process Intensification and Demonstration on a 100 L Scale

Paper Title: Development of an Efficient and Scalable Biocatalytic Route to (1
Problem_Description: The original synthesis of yimitasvir relied on a kinetic‑resolution/crystallization step that limited the theoretical yield to 50 % and caused a large loss of chiral material.  Enzymatic esterification with a vinyl‑ester acyl donor gave no product, and using succinic anhydride gave only a mono‑ester in poor ee and moderate yield.  At high substrate loading the reaction formed stubborn emulsions when ether co‑solvents were used, and the ee values fluctuated in toluene/buffer mixtures, making data unreliable.  Manual pH adjustments were cumbersome and gave inconsistent control.  High enzyme loadings (≥1 %) caused over‑hydrolysis of the desired mono‑ester (product degradation) and increased material cost, while higher reaction temperatures increased the formation of a hydrolysis by‑product that lowered overall conversion.  The diester substrate 3b showed low solubility in water, necessitating a co‑solvent, and some substrates (e.g., 3i) showed no enzymatic activity, leading to variability in conversion.
Solution_Description: A biocatalytic desymmetrization route was developed that avoids the crystallization‑resolution step and gives essentially quantitative theoretical yield; this new route is also cost‑effective.  The strategy was changed from an unproductive esterification to a direct enzymatic hydrolysis of the diester, providing the desired mono‑ester with high ee.  Ether co‑solvents that caused emulsification were replaced by ethyl acetate, which gave a clear system and stable ee values.  Ethyl acetate also eliminated the ee fluctuations observed with toluene/buffer.  pH was regulated by a single addition of sodium bicarbonate, allowing automatic pH control without manual titration.  Enzyme loading was reduced to 0.2 % (wt % of substrate) to prevent over‑hydrolysis of the product and to lower reagent cost.  The reaction temperature was lowered to 15 °C to suppress formation of the hydrolysis by‑product and improve conversion.  Because 3b is poorly soluble in water, ethyl acetate was employed as a co‑solvent and the substrate concentration was tuned to 110 g L⁻¹ for optimal performance.  Substrates that showed no activity (e.g., 3i) were omitted in favor of the more reactive 3b/3c pair, streamlining the process.
