“Impurity 2 was greater than 0.2 % whether 1.2 or 1.5 equiv NaOH were used … however, 2 was present at no more than 0.2 % if the hydrolyzation … was performed at 25 °C for 1 h.”
“Impurity 2 increased continually with prolonged time (entries 3 and 4).”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy for Obeticholic Acid, a Farnesoid X Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of 9 to 9a was incomplete; Pd/C was poisoned by the colored impurity and higher temperatures increased impurity 2, while insufficient hydrogen pressure slowed the reaction.
Solution_Description: Hydrogenation was run at 25 °C, 3 atm H₂, with 10 wt % Pd/C (10 % loading) for 10 h; Pd/C was filtered off before the subsequent configuration‑inversion step to prevent catalyst poisoning.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The reduction was initially carried out at 25 °C/1 atm with 5% Pd/C … 9.93 % 9 remained.”
“When the reaction was carried out at 25 °C/3 atm with 10% Pd/C for 10 h, only 0.42 % 9 remained.”
“The Pd/C filtered off and washed with water twice …”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy for Obeticholic Acid, a Farnesoid X Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: During configuration inversion (9a → 10) the coexistence of Pd/C and air generated diketone impurity 7 (≈1 %); the impurity increased with longer reaction time.
Solution_Description: The inversion was performed either under a hydrogen atmosphere or after filtering off Pd/C, thereby avoiding the Pd/C‑air interaction that formed impurity 7.
Supporting_Evidence: “The coexistence of Pd/C with air should be avoided for the configuration inversion … two approaches could be used: … the configuration inversion process could be performed in a hydrogen atmosphere, and second, the Pd/C filtered off prior to the reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy for Obeticholic Acid, a Farnesoid X Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: NaBH₄ reduction of 10 at 95 °C for 3 h produced impurity 12 (> 3 %) and gave low conversion of 10 to 1.
Solution_Description: The reduction was optimized to 75 °C for 6 h with NaBH₄ 1.1 equiv, NaOH 2 equiv, delivering > 96 % conversion to 1 and keeping impurity 12 ≤ 0.1 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
“When the reduction was performed at 95 °C for 3 h, Imp‑12 was produced, resulting in a content greater than 3.0%.”
“The optimized reaction conditions were carried out with NaBH₄ (1.1 equiv), NaOH (2 equiv), and H₂O at 75 °C for 6 h.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy for Obeticholic Acid, a Farnesoid X Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Recrystallization of crude 1 using n‑butyl acetate alone gave a sticky slurry that was difficult to filter and gave only ~60 % recovery, with residual impurities remaining in the mother liquor.
Solution_Description: A 1:1 (v/v) mixture of n‑butyl acetate/n‑heptane was used for the two‑stage recrystallization, producing a free‑flowing solid that filtered smoothly and raised overall yield to ~70 % with ICH‑grade purity.
Supporting_Evidence: “The recrystallization mixture was too sticky to filter… the crude 1 was recrystallized twice with n‑butyl acetate and n‑heptane (1:1, v/v), which provided a good yield (∼70 %) of OCA with ICH‑grade quality, and the recrystallization mixture was filtered smoothly.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy for Obeticholic Acid, a Farnesoid X Receptor Agonist
Problem_Description: Process‑related impurities (Imp‑1, Imp‑8‑11, etc.) varied between batches, and conventional chromatography would be required to reach ICH limits.
Solution_Description: A robust impurity‑control strategy was implemented: double recrystallizations at defined steps, strict impurity limits per intermediate, and the use of high‑performance LC–CAD for assay, enabling consistent ICH‑grade OCA without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
“The control strategy and impurity limit of process‑related impurities were proposed… The purification processes of 7, 9, 10, and 1 were efficient, which were reported for the first time.”
“Three HPLC methods were developed… The developed process was robust and suitable for manufacturing scale‑up.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Formation of the imidate ester (6) from nitrile 5 using NaOMe in MeOH proved reversible, leaving 15‑20 % unreacted nitrile that later gave fully deprotected side‑product 11, reducing overall yield.
Solution_Description: Switch to a dimethylsulfamoyl protecting group (13) on the indazole nitrogen. This electron‑withdrawing group allowed near‑quantitative conversion to the imidate (14) with only 1.2‑1.5 % residual nitrile, and the unstable imidate was telescoped directly into the next step to avoid isolation losses.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The formation of imidate ester 6 using sodium methoxide in methanol proved to be reversible, resulting in an equilibrium mixture containing 15–20% of unreacted nitrile 5 which downstream ended up as fully deprotected analog 11, a major side product in the synthesis of 9.", "After going through a list of possible protecting groups the dimethylsulfamoyl group (−SO2NMe2) was identified as a suitable candidate... Reaction with 1 equiv of NaOMe in MeOH afforded near complete conversion to methyl imidate ester 14 with just 1.2–1.5% of unreacted nitrile 13.", "Because of its instability, imidate 14 was telescoped directly into the next step."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The THP protecting group on the indazole required acidic deprotection that was reversible, producing mixtures of protected/deprotected material, polymerizing dihydropyran to black tar and necessitating chromatographic purification.
Solution_Description: Replace the THP group with the dimethylsulfamoyl protecting group, which is stable to both strong bases and mild acids, eliminating reversible deprotection, polymer formation, and the need for chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the deprotection with aqueous acid at the last stage of this sequence was also reversible and resulted in partial conversions and mixtures of THP‑protected and deprotected derivatives.", "the polymerization of the liberated DHP and related compounds under the reaction conditions, therefore shifting the equilibrium toward fully deprotected intermediate 9. ... necessitating chromatographic purification.", "Dimethylsulfamoyl‑protected indazole 13 ... is stable under both basic (including alkoxides) and acidic conditions (strong aqueous acids, such as HCl or H2SO4, do not hydrolyze it at room temperature)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During imidazole cyclization in methanol, the amidine intermediate undergoes solvolysis, giving up to 35 % methyl ester (17) as a side‑product, lowering material throughput.
Solution_Description: Perform the cyclization in isopropanol (IPA) instead of methanol; the more hindered solvent suppresses methanolysis, reducing ester side‑product formation to 5‑10 %.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the solvolytic instability of the amidine manifested itself at this point as well, leading to methanolysis and resulting in the formation of substantial amounts (up to 35%) of methyl ester 17.", "the imidazole cyclization step in IPA reduced the amount of solvolysis side‑product 18 to 5–10%."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The final API (1) and its salt (19·H2SO4) are poorly soluble in most organic solvents; consequently, a high‑boiling polar solvent (NMP) is required, leading to high residual NMP levels in the product and difficult isolation.
Solution_Description: Crystallize the API from methyl ethyl ketone (MEK) with a small water co‑solvent; this antisolvent system removes NMP (down to 0.01 % residual) and yields a solid suitable for filtration.
Supporting_Evidence: ["As both the free base and salts of 19 as well as amide product 1 have low solubility in most organic solvents, a polar solvent such as NMP had to be used to achieve good conversion.", "The MEK crystallization had the additional benefit of lowering the amount of residual NMP in crude 1.", "The residual solvent content was high: NMP: 0.2%; MeOH: 5.9%; and AcOH: 0.4% (all weight% determined by quantitative NMR)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Crystallization of the desired polymorph (Form 1) from MEK alone is extremely slow (several days at 75‑80 °C) because of the very low solubility of the API in MEK.
Solution_Description: Add 1.5‑2 % water to MEK, which modestly raises solubility and accelerates polymorph conversion, allowing complete crystallization in ~24 h at 70‑80 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The crystallization protocol ... required several days of heating at a temperature close to reflux (MEK bp = 80 °C).", "The addition of small amounts of water to the MEK did increase the solubility of both Form 1 and the low crystalline material.", "The mixture was heated to 50 °C and seeded ... temperature was increased to 70 °C and stirred at this temperature until complete polymorph conversion to Form 1 was observed as determined by PXRD analysis (24–30 h)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Addition of concentrated aqueous HCl during the deprotection of the sulfamoyl group generates a large exotherm, presenting a thermal runaway risk.
Solution_Description: Perform the acid addition at 0‑15 °C with controlled addition rate, followed by immediate cooling and staged temperature ramps (0 °C then 50 °C) to manage the heat evolution safely.
Supporting_Evidence: ["the addition of concentrated aqueous HCl solution (37%, 17 L, 204 mol, 13 equiv) ... the ensuing exotherm warmed the batch to 14 °C.", "added 1 equiv of glacial acetic acid, and the reaction solvent (MeOH) was displaced with IPA by vacuum distillation.", "cooling was required to mitigate the large exotherm associated with the addition."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original amide‑bond‑forming step used HATU, a costly coupling reagent unsuitable for kilogram‑scale production.
Solution_Description: Screened common coupling reagents and identified 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) as an inexpensive, process‑friendly alternative, providing comparable conversion and selectivity.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The last bond‑forming step ... was initially carried out with HATU as coupling reagent.", "A screen of common coupling reagents (T3P, acid chloride) identified 1,1′‑carbonyldiimidazole (CDI) as a scale‑friendly alternative."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Formation of the Grignard reagent from aryl bromide 2 and Mg turnings is highly exothermic and uses toxic 1,2‑dibromoethane as an activator, posing safety concerns on scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Run the magnesium insertion in semibatch mode, adding the aryl bromide solution at a rate that keeps the reaction temperature only 5‑15 °C above the jacket temperature; maintain inert atmosphere and monitor temperature spikes carefully.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The magnesium insertion is highly exothermic, and its safe execution requires that it be run in a semibatch mode; that is, most aryl bromide should react as it is being added to avoid accumulation of unreacted material and a potential runaway reaction.", "1,2‑Dibromoethane is a toxic material and required additional safety precautions when handling.", "The batch temperature was closely monitored during this addition to ensure the spike in batch temperature indicative of the exothermic reaction between magnesium and dibromoethane was observed (11 °C spike was recorded)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Using HATU generated bis‑acylated side‑products ( >6 % each) when triethylamine was present, lowering the overall yield of the API.
Solution_Description: Perform the amidation without added base; the intrinsic basicity of the imidazole by‑product suffices to deprotonate the amine, eliminating the bis‑acylated impurities.
Supporting_Evidence: ["There are several functional groups in 19, besides the piperidine nitrogen, which can get acylated ... we consistently observed the formation of two of those bis‑acylated side‑products at levels over 6% each with triethylamine as the base; however, removing the base from the reaction brought their level down to under 1%.", "The reaction also worked perfectly well without any added base (perhaps due to the imidazole coproduct acting as base)."]

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Synthesis for an Inhaled pan-JAK Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The borylation‑Suzuki sequence required two different Pd catalysts (PdCl₂(dppf) for borylation at 10 mol % and a different ligand system for Suzuki), necessitating isolation of the pinacol ester and adding process complexity.
Solution_Description: Keep the two steps separate, isolate the pinacol boronate (3) after borylation, and switch to a Pd(OAc)₂/dtbpf catalyst (2 mol %) for the Suzuki coupling, thereby achieving high conversions without excessive Pd loading.
Supporting_Evidence: ["PdCl₂(dppf) was identified as the optimal precatalyst for the borylation step, and a rather high loading (up to 10 mol %) was needed to consistently drive the reaction to completion.", "This catalyst worked very poorly in the Suzuki coupling, and further screening identified either AmPhos or dtbpf as a much better choice of ligand.", "Pinacol ester 3 had to be isolated after the borylation steps to ensure good performance in the subsequent Suzuki coupling."]

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: On multikilogram batch scale the magnesium–bromine exchange gave incomplete conversion, leading to low overall yield of the aryl‑sulfonamide intermediate.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors moved the Grignard formation into a continuous‑flow reactor, which provided rapid mixing, precise residence‑time control and improved heat removal, thereby delivering >98 % conversion and higher isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “the batch process to produce arylsulfonamide 2 … showed significant robustness concerns above 1 kg scale, we developed a scalable continuous manufacturing process…”; “the continuous process … offered faster mixing, improved temperature control, and consistent residence times inherent to a flow process.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: At –20 °C the substrate 3 has a solubility limit in THF; it crystallized at the inlet of the glass‑chip reactor, causing blockages in the flow system.
Solution_Description: Dimethoxyethane (DME) was added as a co‑solvent (4:1 THF/DME) to keep 3 in solution while maintaining the same overall volume.
Supporting_Evidence: “because of the solubility limit of 3 in THF at –20 °C, 3 sometimes crystallized at the inlet of the glass chip… To improve the solubility of 3 at –20 °C… dimethoxyethane (DME) was successfully employed as a cosolvent.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: The sulfonylation step with sulfuryl chloride is highly exothermic (adiabatic temperature rise of ~51 °C) and poses a risk of thermal decomposition and hazardous gas evolution.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was raised to 0 °C (instead of –20 °C) and the addition of SO₂Cl₂ was performed via a static‑mixer with controlled flow rates to keep the exotherm manageable.
Supporting_Evidence: “The sulfonylation step displayed an adiabatic temperature rise of 51 °C… we decided to conduct the reactions at 0 °C, as this temperature offered the highest conversion… and capability to control the exotherm.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Sulfone impurity 12 has extremely low solubility (<1 mg mL⁻¹) in the crystallization solvents, leading to its enrichment in the solid product and a 10 % yield loss during crystallization.
Solution_Description: A two‑step work‑up was introduced: (i) a MeOH wash/polish‑filter to remove most of impurity 12, followed by (ii) crystallization from MeOH/H₂O where 12 remains insoluble, giving >98 % purity and acceptable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “the major quality concern … sulfone 12 … extremely low solubility … In the best scenario … result in ∼25 % yield loss… we proposed filtration of the crude mixture … MeOH was selected to maximize the solubility differences between 2 and 12… polish‑filtered … to effectively reduce variable levels of 12 to 1.0–1.2 %.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Residual starting material 3 and low‑level impurity 9 (formed by moisture‑induced quenching of the Grignard) remained in the crude reaction mixture.
Solution_Description: A sequential aqueous‑acid wash (2.0 M HCl) was applied to the crude stream to protonate and extract impurity 9, followed by a basic wash (1.0 M NaHCO₃) to neutralize excess amine before isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Because of its higher pKa, 9 could be completely removed from the stream by a wash with 2.0 M aqueous HCl… the crude mixture was washed with 2.0 M aqueous HCl to remove impurity 9 and excess tBuNH₂, followed by a wash with 1.0 M aqueous NaHCO₃.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Impurity 11 (3‑bromo‑5‑chloropyridine) varied 2.2 %–12.0 % depending on the batch of sulfuryl chloride, affecting overall yield.
Solution_Description: High‑purity sulfuryl chloride was sourced and tested before production; a colorimetric UV method was developed to monitor chlorine content and ensure consistent reagent quality.
Supporting_Evidence: “SO₂Cl₂ batches from different suppliers would produce variable amounts of 11… sourcing SO₂Cl₂ that was of high quality became important to avoid such process variability.”; “the sourced sulfuryl chloride reagent was use‑tested… a color method (UV spectrometry) can be developed.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Decomposition of SO₂Cl₂ generated H₂SO₄ and HCl, which corroded the peristaltic‑pump head and caused leaks, disrupting flow and posing safety hazards.
Solution_Description: The SO₂Cl₂ solution was freshly prepared each day to avoid standing‑time decomposition, and pump‑head tubing was inspected and replaced regularly to prevent corrosion.
Supporting_Evidence: “the acidic solution corroded the pump head adapter… the SO₂Cl₂ solution was freshly prepared to avoid the introduction of moisture during standing, and the pump head tubing was frequently inspected for leaking.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Alternative routes (A, B, C) evaluated for making intermediate 2 gave poor yields (52 % for route A, low for B and C), making them unattractive for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The team abandoned the alternative routes and returned to the Grignard‑based sequence, improving it via continuous processing rather than pursuing the low‑yielding routes.
Supporting_Evidence: “For route A … 52 % yield… route B … only low yields… route C … only moderate yields… After evaluation… we decided to refocus our efforts on understanding the Grignard process better and solving the issues observed during scale‑up.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: The batch process required cryogenic temperatures (‑20 °C) and large volumes of THF and DCM, increasing energy and solvent costs for larger scales.
Solution_Description: Operating at 0 °C eliminated the need for cryogenic cooling, and the flow reactor’s high surface‑to‑volume ratio allowed the use of more concentrated solutions, reducing solvent consumption.
Supporting_Evidence: “Fast mixing and rapid heat removal in a continuous process would likely allow the reaction temperature to be raised, avoiding the cryogenic (−20 °C) conditions employed for the batch reaction, thereby saving infrastructure and energy costs.”

Paper Title: A Practical and Robust Multistep Continuous Process for Manufacturing 5‑Bromo‑
Problem_Description: Handling of the highly reactive Grignard reagent and sulfuryl chloride in an open batch set‑up posed exposure and over‑pressurization risks.
Solution_Description: A fully enclosed PFA‑tubing flow system was employed, which can withstand high pressure and contain the reactive intermediates, mitigating safety hazards.
Supporting_Evidence: “the hazardous and reactive nature of both the Grignard reagent and sulfuryl chloride could be controlled through the use of a fully enclosed flow system, compared with a batch process, where open handling could occur.”

Paper Title: Quantitative Link between Secondary Nucleation and Mixing Hydrodynamics in Batch Cooling Crystallization: A New Approach in Process Development
Problem_Description: The link between mixing hydrodynamics and crystallization kinetics is poorly understood, causing variable nucleation behavior and inconsistent product quality when scaling‑up agitated batch crystallizers.
Solution_Description: Particle Imaging Velocimetry (PIV) was introduced to map the turbulent shear stress (TSS) at the seed‑crystal surface, providing a quantitative relationship between mixing conditions and secondary‑nucleation thresholds (SNT).
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Mixing in an agitated stirred tank and its link with crystallization kinetics under the influence of the agitation rate has remained a challenge in process scale‑up because the problem has been tackled mainly by means of semi‑empirical methods." 
• "Variations in mixing quality can be attributed to the lack of a clear understanding of the mixing processes due to the complex nature of fluid flow structures."
• "Crystallization in agitated vessels is often carried out without a detailed optimization of the hydrodynamic conditions which makes statistics on the nucleation kinetics difficult to use for a reliable process scale‑up."
• "Using particle imaging velocimetry, a constant TSS was obtained across different scales which resulted in a constant SNT because of crystal nuclei breeding."
• "PIV was used to determine the TSS at the seed surface which enabled to determine the required agitation rates in a scale‑up from 1 to 5 L reactors."

Paper Title: Quantitative Link between Secondary Nucleation and Mixing Hydrodynamics in Batch Cooling Crystallization: A New Approach in Process Development
Problem_Description: Conventional suspended‑seed crystallizations allow large seed crystals to break during impeller‑seed collisions, generating fines and a broad particle‑size distribution that are undesirable for downstream processing.
Solution_Description: A single large paracetamol seed crystal was held stationary in the stirred vessel using a custom‑machined 316 L stainless‑steel holder, eliminating attrition‑enhanced secondary nucleation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Considering that seed crystals of large sizes could break, this can lead to unfavorable outcomes such as fines generation which is not desirable in industrial processes."
• "In traditional approaches where the seeds are suspended in bulk and may be prone to breakage."
• "A large single seed crystal of paracetamol was held stationary in the agitating reactor."
• "The 316L stainless‑steel crystal holders … were custom designed to fit a specific reactor setup."
• "The approach … using a large single seed crystal held stationary … resulted in a uniform PSD."

Paper Title: Quantitative Link between Secondary Nucleation and Mixing Hydrodynamics in Batch Cooling Crystallization: A New Approach in Process Development
Problem_Description: When the reactor volume is increased, the agitation speed required to achieve the same nucleation behavior changes; without proper adjustment the secondary‑nucleation threshold (SNT) drifts, leading to inconsistent particle‑size distribution across scales.
Solution_Description: Agitation rates were tuned (425 rpm for 1 L, 335 rpm for 5 L) to maintain a constant turbulent shear stress of ~0.67 N m⁻², as identified by PIV, thereby fixing the SNT independent of scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The baseline agitation rate employed was 425 rpm which resulted in Re = 8960…"
• "From PIV experiments, a constant TSS of approximately 0.67 N m⁻² was achieved at both scales which was then used as a function of scale‑up involving cooling crystallization experiments at different agitation rates."
• "The required agitation rate for 5 L reactor was found to be approximately 345 rpm. The corresponding shear stress at 345 rpm was validated… finally resulted in a required TSS… that occurred at 335 rpm."
• "The agitation rates employed were 425 and 335 rpm for 1 and 5 L scales, respectively."

Paper Title: Quantitative Link between Secondary Nucleation and Mixing Hydrodynamics in Batch Cooling Crystallization: A New Approach in Process Development
Problem_Description: Supersaturation measured by in‑line FTIR is unreliable during cooling because the IR signal is strongly temperature‑dependent, causing delayed or inaccurate detection of nucleation events.
Solution_Description: Real‑time FBRM total‑count data were used as the primary nucleation indicator, providing earlier detection (≈20 min before supersaturation peak) and more reliable MSZW/SNT determination.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "Supersaturation measurements are difficult in cooling crystallization experiments because IR spectra can be significantly affected by the change in temperature."
• "The determination of MSZW and SNT has been referenced from FBRM statistics which measured the onset of nucleation approximately 20 min before the maximum supersaturation could reach its peak value."
• "FBRM data were logged with respect to time for the tracking of particle counts. Simultaneously, the concentration of the solution was monitored through FTIR spectroscopy."

Paper Title: Quantitative Link between Secondary Nucleation and Mixing Hydrodynamics in Batch Cooling Crystallization: A New Approach in Process Development
Problem_Description: In the 5 L reactor the FBRM probe recorded lower total particle counts, initially interpreted as poor suspension; the true cause was reduced probe coverage in a larger volume, possibly misleading kinetic interpretation.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The agitation speed was briefly increased to 500 rpm and then to 750 rpm to ensure full suspension; the unchanged particle count confirmed that the lower counts were a detection artifact rather than a mixing issue.
Supporting_Evidence:
• "The number of particle total counts generated was observed to decrease at 5 L scale. Initially, it was assumed that the uniform suspension was not achieved…"
• "When no change in particle counts was observed, the agitation rate was further increased to 750 rpm and sustained for 10 min. No change in the particle total counts was observed."
• "This investigation eliminated any possible misperception associated with uniform suspension, which rather suggested that the answer lies in the nucleation kinetics of the present system."

Paper Title: Model-Based Scale-Up Predictions: From Micro- to Millireactors Using Inline Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy
Problem_Description: The deprotonation reaction of a CH‑acidic compound with n‑butyllithium is highly exothermic; when the reactor inner diameter is increased from 0.5 mm (lab micro‑reactor) to 2 mm (pilot millireactor) the heat‑transfer time scale grows by a factor of ≈ 16, making rapid removal of the released heat impossible and creating a risk of hot‑spot formation at the reactor entrance.

Solution_Description: A model‑based scale‑up was implemented that explicitly incorporates heat‑transfer calculations (using a constant Nusselt number Nu = 3.66) together with kinetic data, allowing the prediction of temperature profiles and ensuring that the reactor is operated within safe thermal limits.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “highly exothermic organometallic reaction… [Abstract]”
• “When increasing the inner channel diameter … the characteristic time needed for heat transfer increases by a factor of 16. Hence, efficient heat removal … can no longer be assumed, and a possible hot spot formation … has to be considered.” [Section 4.3]
• “Heat transfer parameters … were calculated for the lab microreactor and the pilot millireactors. In all cases, α was defined by assuming fully developed laminar‑flow heat transfer with Nu = 3.66 (constant wall temperature).” [Section 4.3]

Problem_Description: Hot‑spot formation at the reactor entrance of the highly exothermic lithiation could raise the temperature by several Kelvin, potentially leading to unsafe conditions if not accounted for during scale‑up.

Problem_Description: During mid‑scale runs, a substantial amount of solid settled at the reactor bottom after decantation, making complete recovery difficult.
Solution_Description: The 50 L and 2000 L reactors were designed with conical bottoms and chevron impellers, which eliminated the solid‑settling issue in the large‑scale campaign.
Supporting_Evidence: “During the mid‑scale pilot plant campaign, a large amount of solids remained on the reactor bottom… The issue did not arise during the large‑scale pilot plant campaign… due to the configuration of the large‑scale reactor, which had a conical bottom and a lower chevron impeller.”

Paper Title: Design and Scale-up of a Co-processing Technology to Improve Powder Properties of Drug Substances
Problem_Description: Variations in the input theophylline particle‑size distribution (different grades) lead to differences in the bulk density and PSD of the final co‑processed material.
Solution_Description: API grade selection and pre‑milling were used to control the initial PSD (e.g., using milled API with D90 ≈ 21 µm) before co‑processing, stabilising the final CPM properties.
Supporting_Evidence: “The input API with slightly lower D10 and higher D90 resulted in slightly lower bulk density and smaller particle size.”; “Various batches were generated using 325M grade… 200M grade… and milled theophylline (D90 = 21.5 µm).”

Paper Title: Design and Scale-up of a Co-processing Technology to Improve Powder Properties of Drug Substances
Problem_Description: Increasing polymer loading from 15 wt % to 20 wt % reduces the API potency of the CPM (to ~78 wt %) and raises residual MTBE and KF, potentially increasing material cost.
Solution_Description: The optimal polymer loading was fixed at 15 wt % (≈ 17.6 wt % of API) to balance bulk density, flow, potency and residual solvent levels while minimising polymer usage.
Supporting_Evidence: “The batch with a higher polymer loading generated a material with a higher bulk density, better flow… The potency of the CPM with a higher polymer loading was lower (77.7 vs 84.5 wt %).”

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The coupling of quinoline 6 with ketone 7 required cryogenic temperatures (‑75 °C) and gave low and variable isolated yields of 37‑47 % for the alcohol 8.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from diethyl ether to MTBE and the amount of n‑BuLi was increased to 2.5 equiv per substrate, which raised the in‑process yield to 86 %. The reaction order was also changed to add n‑BuLi to a mixture of quinoline and excess ketone.
Supporting_Evidence:
["The coupling of 7 with 6 required cryogenic conditions and suffered from low and variable yields (37–47%).",
 "In the revised procedure, the reaction solvent was switched to methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE), and 2.5 equiv of n‑BuLi were added to a mixture of quinoline 6 and 2.5 equiv of ketone 7. The in‑process yield significantly increased to 86%."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Hydrogenation of olefin 9 in ethanol over‑reduced the fluorine, forming des‑fluoro impurity 5b that was difficult to purge downstream, leading to low overall yields.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was re‑optimized using 10 mol % Pd/C in THF under a low‑pressure H₂ (0.15–0.20 MPa), which minimized formation of 5b to <0.03 % and gave near‑quantitative conversion. The change in solvent and pressure also improved gas‑liquid mass transfer.
Supporting_Evidence:
["The original Pd‑catalyzed reduction to 10a ... went to completion in 5–6 days ... a more significant challenge was the tendency to over‑reduce and generate a des‑fluoro impurity 5b.",
 "It was found that running with 10 mol % Pd/C in tetrahydrofuran (THF) with 0.15–0.20 MPa of H₂ was very effective and minimized over‑reduction to the des‑fluoro impurity 5b to <0.03%."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the ketone reduction to alcohol 11, the reaction produced only a 5:1 trans/cis ratio and generated a borane‑amine complex impurity 23 that persisted into the next step.
Solution_Description: Addition of cerium(III) chloride heptahydrate increased diastereoselectivity to >13:1 and allowed the reaction to complete in <1 h. The quench was changed from aqueous NH₄Cl to acetic acid, which broke up the borane complex, and DCM was employed as a solvent to improve extraction.
Supporting_Evidence:
["The reduction of 5a with 1.5–2.0 equiv of sodium borohydride ... afforded only a 5:1 trans/cis isomeric ratio.",
 "The addition of cerium(III) chloride heptahydrate improved the selectivity to >13:1 and allowed for the reaction to complete in <1 h.",
 "The quench was changed to acetic acid, which minimized product degradation.",

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Mesylate 4 was unstable during the original crystallization (heating in water/MeOH) and underwent elimination, causing low isolated yields on scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new crystallization was developed where mesylate 4 was dissolved in DCM and hexanes were added at 25 °C, giving a robust process with minimal elimination and high purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
["It was quickly discovered that mesylate 4 was not stable under these conditions and resulted in the elimination of the mesylate to form the alkene.",
 "An alternative crystallization was developed, in which 4 was dissolved in dichloromethane and hexanes were added at 25 °C until crystallization was achieved. This proved to be a much more robust process and led to minimal epimerization and elimination of the mesylate."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The initial synthesis of carboxylic acid 3 employed NaH in DME, both hazardous on large scale, and gave >10 % epimerization during decarboxylation.
Solution_Description: NaH was replaced with non‑nucleophilic tertiary alkoxides (NaOtBu, KOtBu) and finally NaOtPent; DME was replaced with toluene; the reaction temperature and work‑up were adjusted (use of methanesulfonic acid, sulfolane, KOH work‑up) to suppress epimerization and improve safety.

["The use of sodium hydride was deemed not practical; there were safety concerns with using dimethoxyethane on scale, and there were robustness concerns due to epimerization leading to >10% of the trans isomer 25 during the decarboxylation step.",
 "Non‑nucleophilic tertiary alkoxides (e.g., LiOtBu, NaOtBu, KOtBu) were safe, scalable, and effective replacements for NaH.",

 "The finalized process used sodium tert‑pentoxide, di‑tert‑butyl malonate in toluene to complete the SN2, decarboxylation in the presence of methanesulfonic acid and sulfolane ..."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the S_NAr coupling of 14 with keto‑ester 13, raising the temperature above –10 °C caused the enolate to decompose to a ketene, leading to side‑product 19.
Solution_Description: The reaction temperature was limited to –25 °C to –15 °C and the polar aprotic co‑solvent system DMF/THF (with optional toluene) was employed to keep the enolate stable and promote coupling.
Supporting_Evidence:
["If alternative counterions (LiHMDS or KHMDS) were used or if the temperature was raised to greater than –10 °C, the ester enolate 17 would decompose to the proposed ketene intermediate 18.",
 "Thus, the reaction temperature range was established to be between –25 and –15 °C.",
 "The polar, aprotic cosolvent system dimethylformamide (DMF)/tetrahydrofuran (THF) promoted the coupling."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Acid‑catalyzed trans‑esterification of ethylene glycol with keto‑ester 13 produced impurity 20 (up to 12 % HPLC area) during the Dean‑Stark distillation, and the impurity level was sensitive to water content.
Solution_Description: A slight vacuum (80–380 mbar, 45–85 °C) was applied during the Dean‑Stark step to lower the reaction temperature and reduce water content, which limited impurity 20 to <0.5 % area.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Acid‑catalyzed trans‑esterification of ethylene glycol and 13 to form 20 was observed at up to 12 HPLC area percent during the atmospheric pressure Dean–Stark distillation.",

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During the free‑base crystallization of carboxylic acid 3, rapid precipitation produced sticky solids and gave only ~95 % HPLC purity because impurities were not removed.
Solution_Description: The crude stream was basified with aqueous KOH, allowing most non‑acidic impurities to partition into the toluene layer. The aqueous phase was then acidified slowly with aqueous acetic acid, promoting controlled crystal growth and achieving >99 % purity.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Initial attempts at charging aqueous sodium acetate resulted in the precipitation of very sticky solids.",
 "An alternate workup and crystallization sequence was developed, which involved using aqueous potassium hydroxide to basify the crude decarboxylation stream. At basic pH, a majority of the impurities ... partition to the upper toluene layer and are discarded during the phase split. This phase split affords in‑process purity of up to ~99 HPLC area percent. The pH is then adjusted using the slow addition of aqueous acetic acid, promoting slow crystal growth and more controlled particle formation. An isolated product purity of >99 HPLC area percent is consistently achieved by this method."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The original Pd‑catalyzed hydrogenation of 9 required 5–6 days, and the long exposure to H₂ posed safety concerns.

["The original Pd‑catalyzed reduction to 10a was conducted in ethanol and went to completion in 5–6 days.",

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: During Evans‑auxiliary cleavage (formation of 2), excessive oxygen off‑gassing from the LiOH/H₂O₂ reaction presented a safety hazard.

Supporting_Evidence:
["We were quite surprised to see a high level of oxygen off‑gassing. ... The details of this investigation are described elsewhere.",

 "It was found that the oxygen off‑gassing was addition‑controlled when the lithium hydroxide is added at room temperature, and oxygen off‑gassing quickly stops when lithium hydroxide addition is paused."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Quenching the pivaloyl chloride step with aqueous NH₄Cl generated pivalamide, which persisted as an impurity in later steps.
Solution_Description: The quench was changed to a simple water addition (pH ≈ 8) producing pivalic acid that could be removed in aqueous washes, eliminating pivalamide formation.

["Aqueous ammonium chloride, the original quench solution, led to the formation of pivalamide from excess pivaloyl chloride. Pivalamide would generate impurities in the methylation step and impact quality downstream.",

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: In the methylation of imide 32, the in‑situ generated sodium enolate decomposed over time, and quenching with aqueous NH₄Cl caused the product to decompose to a ring‑opened impurity 35.

["Stress experiments and IR studies indicated, the in situ‑generated sodium enolate of 32 decomposes over time.",

 "Charging NaHMDS last mitigates the challenge of enolate instability, and the new reaction conditions also provide a cleaner reaction profile. The quench was changed to acetic acid, which minimized product degradation."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: Alcohol 11 exhibited poor solubility in most solvents, complicating the work‑up after reduction.
Solution_Description: Dichloromethane was selected as the extraction solvent, providing good solubility for 11 and enabling an effective aqueous work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The relative insolubility of alcohol 11 in most solvent systems; however, dichloromethane (DCM) was found to be an excellent solvent for 11, which allowed for an effective aqueous workup."]

Paper Title: Rapid Development of a Commercial Process for Linrodostat, an Indoleamine 2,3-Dioxygenase (IDO) Inhibitor
Problem_Description: The free‑base crystallization of penultimate 2 suffered from phase separation and oiling‑out when water was added, leading to inconsistent product quality.

Solution_Description: A phase map was generated to define a safe region (25 wt % water, 40 °C) for seeding, avoiding oiling‑out. The process controls temperature, water content, and solvent composition to obtain consistent crystals.
Supporting_Evidence:
["Phase separation was observed, presumably due to the poor solubility of the quinolinium salt in toluene.",

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The original route required a stoichiometric oxidation with toxic selenium dioxide, formation of a triflate using toxic boron tribromide and an expensive phosphonium reagent, and a low‑yielding carbonylation step.
Solution_Description: A completely redesigned synthetic sequence was implemented that avoids SeO₂, BBr₃ and the expensive phosphonium reagent, thereby eliminating the hazardous steps.
Supporting_Evidence: • “oxidation was not feasible due to the usage of a stoichiometric amount of toxic selenium dioxide, formation of triflate 7 required toxic boron tribromide and expensive N‑phenylbis‑(trifluoromethanesulfonimide), and the carbonylation reaction to 8 was low yielding.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: Acid‑chloride formation with SOCl₂ generated a highly exothermic reaction (23 kJ kg⁻¹) and required careful DMF addition to control temperature and gas evolution.
Solution_Description: SOCl₂ was replaced by oxalyl chloride; addition of the reagent and DMF was performed at a controlled rate to keep the temperature below the critical set‑point.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Addition of DMF led to a globally exothermic process with a moderate heat output (23 kJ kg⁻¹ of reaction mass) … A close watch on DMF addition rate was mandatory in the beginning of the process to control both heat release and gas evolution.”
• “Replacement of SOCl₂ with oxalyl chloride was favorable in terms of robustness and chemical purity.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The reduction of amides with NaBH₄/BF₃·THF was highly exothermic (155 kJ kg⁻¹ for BF₃ addition, 168 kJ kg⁻¹ for hydrolysis) and required a 60 h operating time on a 4.5 kg scale.
Solution_Description: The reducing agent was changed to Red‑Al (65 % in toluene) and the solvent to toluene; the reaction was run at 50 °C for 1 h, cutting the process time to ~16 h.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Safety of this process was also evaluated in a RC1 experiment and revealed that BF₃ addition was highly exothermic (heat output of 155 kJ kg⁻¹ …) Hydrolysis turned out to be also highly exothermic with a heat output of 168 kJ kg⁻¹.”
• “However, a total operating time of approximately 60 h combined with safety concerns prompted revision of these reducing conditions.”
• “Red‑Al was finally selected … The amount of Red‑Al was also surveyed … 5 equiv was found to give the best impurity profile … total operating time was about 16 h.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch variation during Cbz removal was traced to poisoning of Pd/C by residual sulfur from the previous step.
Solution_Description: The acid‑chloride step was switched from SOCl₂ to oxalyl chloride, eliminating the source of sulfur and providing a more robust, reproducible process.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “batch‑to‑batch variation was observed during the Cbz removal and was attributed to poisoning of Pd/C by residual sulfur.”
• “Replacement of SOCl₂ with oxalyl chloride was favorable in terms of robustness and chemical purity.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: Overall isolated yield of the first‑generation route to the acid moiety was only 6 % over nine steps, making scale‑up impractical.
Solution_Description: A new convergent route was designed that shortened the longest linear sequence to 13 steps with an overall yield of 8.4 % and enabled kilogram‑scale batches.
Supporting_Evidence:

• “In summary, we developed a synthesis of key intermediate 2 … that proceeded in 13 steps … in an overall yield of 8.4 %.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The need for chiral resolution of racemic intermediate 14 by simulated moving‑bed chromatography added cost and limited material throughput (46 % isolated yield of the desired enantiomer).
Solution_Description: An asymmetric hydrogenation of a quinoline ester using an Ir‑(R)‑Segphos catalyst (2.5 mol % Ir, 5 mol % I₂) gave 100 % conversion and up to 91 % ee, eliminating the resolution step.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In order to get desired enantiomer 14, a chiral separation was performed … 97.1 % ee.”
• “Iridium‑catalyzed hydrogenation of ester derivative 29 … provided the corresponding tetrahydroquinoline with a moderate 43 % ee.”
• “Asymmetric hydrogenation proceeded smoothly and led to a 100 % conversion and up to 91 % ee.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: Saponification of ester 27 with NaOH gave poor conversion (≤42 %); variability was observed with different solvent systems.
Solution_Description: Switching the nucleophile to LiOH and adding THF as co‑solvent increased conversion to >98 % (entries 6‑8), providing reliable and high‑yielding hydrolysis.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Conversion using NaOH as nucleophile remained low (entry 1 and 2). Switching to more nucleophilic LiOH provided encouraging results … Addition of THF was beneficial and helped to solubilize the starting material (entry 6 and 8).”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The benzyl chloride intermediate 26 is mutagenic (positive Ames test) and its handling as a solid powder posed safety and regulatory concerns.
Solution_Description: The synthesis was redesigned to keep 26 in solution (toluene) and to telescope the Suzuki coupling, chlorination, and N‑alkylation steps without isolation, reducing exposure to the mutagenic solid.
Supporting_Evidence:

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The original Suzuki coupling employed a homogeneous Pd catalyst with a patented phosphine ligand, which was costly, raised intellectual‑property issues and gave variable results.
Solution_Description: A ligand‑free, heterogeneous Pd/C catalyst was employed in water; screening identified K₂CO₃ as the optimal base and 60 °C as the temperature, delivering >95 % conversion with consistent performance across catalyst batches.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “In order to develop a greener process, a first survey was carried out … using Pd/C type 91 as catalyst and water.”
• Table 3 shows entries 3‑5 with >94 % conversion using K₂CO₃ in water at 60–80 °C.
• “The use of hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) was unnecessary … Heating at 80 °C seemed to enhance the formation of impurity 34.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The Suzuki coupling at 80 °C generated impurity 34 at higher levels, indicating temperature‑dependent side reactions and safety concerns due to excess heat.

Supporting_Evidence:
• “Heating at 80 °C seemed to enhance the formation of impurity 34 (isolated and identified by NMR).”
• “Entry 3 … 94.5 % conversion at 60 °C.”
• “Entry 5 … 95.4 % conversion at 80 °C, but impurity 34 was higher; therefore 60 °C was chosen as optimal.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The carboxylation of bromide 20 via metal–halogen exchange required cryogenic conditions (‑78 °C) with n‑BuLi; temperature control was critical to avoid debromination and the process was operationally burdensome.
Solution_Description: Lithium trialkylmagnesiates (i‑PrMgCl + n‑BuLi) were employed at 0 °C (non‑cryogenic); CO₂ was added from the gas phase to control temperature, giving 80 % yield and a safer, faster process (730 g scale).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “strict low temperature control (−78 °C) was required … to limit the debromination side reaction (full debromination observed at −20 °C).”
• “We envisioned the use of lithium trialkylmagnesiates … A one‑pot reaction was evaluated at −5 °C … the reaction was highly exothermic … this undesired pathway was shut down when CO₂ was introduced above the surface … proved easy to perform on 730 g scale and provided acid 21 with 80 % yield.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The three‑step sequence to convert 17 to 28 required Boc protection, methyl ester formation, and a separate carboxylation, leading to a low overall yield (≈25 %).

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: The final N‑alkylation using alkyl chloride 26 generated a mutagenic intermediate and required handling of a hazardous solid.
Solution_Description: A borrowing‑hydrogen approach employing a Ru‑(p‑cymene)Cl₂ catalyst (2.5 mol %) and dppf enabled direct coupling of alcohol 25 with amine 17, producing 36 in 85 % isolated yield without generating the mutagenic chloride.

• “The borrowing hydrogen approach … they investigated the condensation of alcohol 25 with tricyclic amine 17 mediated with iridium‑ and ruthenium‑based catalysts … Entry 6 … 85 % isolated yield.”
• “Thus, we considered the borrowing hydrogen approach as very appealing … the process generates only water as by‑product.”

Paper Title: Systematic Investigation into the Formation of Significant Amounts of Unknown Impurity during Scale-up of NaBH
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the NaBH₄–I₂ reduction of nitro‑amide 4 to nitro‑amine 5, an unexpected impurity (compound 8a) appeared at ~10 % relative area, dramatically lowering the yield of the desired intermediate.

Paper Title: Investigation of a Flow Step Clogging Incident: A Precautionary Note on the Use of THF in Commercial-Scale Continuous Process
Problem_Description: During scale‑up of the Mannich step the flow stream showed a solid deposit at the contact point between substrate 2 and n‑hexyllithium, causing a pressure drop across the first static‑mixing element and a dramatic reduction in flow rate (from 800 kg h⁻¹ to ~50 kg h⁻¹).
Solution_Description: The deprotonation step was moved from a continuous‑flow segment to a batch operation, while the subsequent ketimine‑addition remained in flow. This redesign eliminated the solid formation at the static mixer and restored robust operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “deposition of an unidentified material at the point of contact … leading to an increased pressure drop across the first static mixer.”; “a compromise was made to carry out the initial deprotonation in batch mode and the anion addition in flow … successfully demonstrated … without incident.”

Paper Title: Investigation of a Flow Step Clogging Incident: A Precautionary Note on the Use of THF in Commercial-Scale Continuous Process
Problem_Description: A specific lot of tetrahydrofuran (THF Lot 3) caused severe clogging when the solvent run was performed at ≤ –5 °C. The culprit was identified as trace poly‑(THF) (≈ 1 ppm) that precipitated under the high‑shear, low‑temperature conditions, forming off‑white fibrous solids that fouled filters and static‑mixers.
Solution_Description: Subsequent runs employed THF lots that showed nondetectable poly‑(THF) levels, and a lot‑screening protocol (concentrated GPC analysis, MALDI‑MS) was instituted to verify the absence of the polymer before use.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reduction of flow was observed when the solvent temperature dropped below –5 °C… the clogging issue was encountered … with a different lot of THF no clogging occurred.”; “poly‑(THF) impurity … estimated to be in the magnitude of around 1 ppm.”; “current strategy being to use THF lots that show nondetectable levels of poly‑(THF).”

Paper Title: Investigation of a Flow Step Clogging Incident: A Precautionary Note on the Use of THF in Commercial-Scale Continuous Process
Problem_Description: The low‑level poly‑(THF) impurity was initially below the detection limit of routine GPC, creating a hidden risk of sudden equipment blockage and possible process interruption at commercial scale.
Solution_Description: An enhanced analytical workflow was developed: large‑volume THF samples were concentrated, then analysed by high‑sensitivity GPC (CAD) and MALDI‑MS to reliably detect poly‑(THF) at the ≈ 1 ppm level, establishing a robust control strategy for future batches.
Supporting_Evidence: “a larger aliquot sample of THF Lot 3 (300 mL) was concentrated and analyzed directly by GPC. Indeed, the more concentrated sample showed a peak corresponding to the isolated poly‑(THF) solids.”; “MALDI‑MS data… showed a repeating mass unit of 72 amu … unequivocally provided evidence that the solid collected … was poly‑(THF).”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x
Problem_Description: Attempts to reproduce literature routes for the sulfonamide 3 (seven‑step synthesis from N‑protected d‑aspartic acid and six‑step synthesis from Fmoc‑Asp(Ot‑Bu)‑OH) failed on scale‑up and the required chiral‑pool amino acids were very expensive, leading to inconsistent conversions and modest overall yields.
Solution_Description: A completely new synthetic sequence was developed starting from acid chloride 12, proceeding through Weinreb amide 13, thiophenyl substitution, Grignard addition, and telescoped oxime formation/reduction to give the difumarate 19, which was then converted to the diamine 20. This eliminated the costly chiral‑pool reagents and provided a robust, scalable pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: “We faced some difficulty when attempting to reproduce the conditions described in those two papers, especially during the scale up. Besides, the price of the starting materials (unnatural amino acids) could be a burden when one thinks about developing a commercial route.”; “Although this sequence allowed us to manufacture several kilograms of 3, we identified a few issues that could hamper a future commercial route.”; “The synthesis of compound 3 starting from 12 is depicted in Scheme 3… Treatment of acid chloride 12 with MeONHMe… yielded … a 28% yield over three steps.”

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x

Paper Title: Multikilogram Synthesis of a Potent Dual Bcl-2/Bcl‑x

['The original synthesis was unable to meet bulk API demands due to high step count and extremely poor throughput (∼0.2 % overall yield).',

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Formation of the unsymmetrical urea (7) was slow; the carbamoylimidazole intermediate (10) reacted sluggishly with amine 2, leading to prolonged reaction times.
Solution_Description: Dimethylformamide (≈2 vol) was added and the temperature raised to 40 °C to accelerate the urea formation, and the organic layer was added slowly to n‑heptane (reverse addition) to precipitate the product.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Due to the slow reaction of 10 with amine 2, adding dimethylformamide (≈2 vol) and increasing the temperature to 40 °C were needed to accelerate the formation of urea 7.',
'The slow addition of the organic layer to n‑heptane precipitated 7, which was easy to filter.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Oxidative deprotection of the DMB group using ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN) gave only a 3:1 mixture of desired product (11) and side amide (12), and prolonged reaction times caused product degradation and pH drop.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A potassium persulfate/K₂HPO₄ system was adopted: 4 equiv persulfate, 4.5 equiv K₂HPO₄, pH held at 6–7, temperature 70 °C, and continuous nitrogen sweep to keep O₂ < 6 % for safety. Periodic addition of K₂HPO₄ maintained pH, suppressing degradation.
Supporting_Evidence:
['Oxidative DMB cleavage with potassium persulfate in the presence of K₂HPO₄ in aqueous acetonitrile was tried, and a complete reaction was achieved at 70 °C without forming 12.',
'Using 4 equiv of potassium persulfate and 4.5 equiv of K₂HPO₄ to set the initial pH in 6–7 range and keeping the temperature around 70 °C were essential for both reaction initiation and fast progress.',
'As oxygen gas was a by‑product of the reaction, high nitrogen sweep was applied over the course to keep the oxygen level < 6 % in the headspace to meet our safety requirements (< 12%).',
'Periodically adding K₂HPO₄ to maintain pH in 6–7 significantly slowed down the product degradation.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Removal of the N‑Boc group with neat TFA at low temperature gave high conversion to the deprotected salt (14) but the product degraded severely when TFA was removed by vacuum distillation.
Solution_Description: A precipitation protocol was introduced: the TFA solution was slowly added to a cold slurry of diatomaceous earth in MTBE, forming a mixed solid that could be filtered, washed and stored without heating, preserving product integrity.
Supporting_Evidence:
['This challenge was overcome by implementing a precipitation protocol without heat.',
'The reaction solution in TFA was slowly added to a cold (10 °C) mixture of diatomaceous earth (220 wt % to 11) in MTBE, resulting in a well‑behaved mixed solid.',
'Further trituration in MTBE purged more TFA and therefore improved the stability of the mixed solid, which could be stored at ambient temperature for a couple of weeks with little purity loss.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Method A for amide bond formation (succinimidyl ester 18) required silica‑gel chromatography for product isolation, which is labor‑intensive and low‑throughput on kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The crude amide 19 was isolated by solvent exchange and reverse precipitation (addition of the ethyl‑acetate solution to n‑heptane), giving an amorphous solid that could be filtered directly, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
['As crystallization attempts were fruitless, silica gel chromatography was used for the first delivery.',
'Workup through pH adjustment with aqueous citric acid, solvent exchange to ethyl acetate, filtration … slow addition to n‑heptane precipitated amorphous crude 19 (81 % pure) in an 83 % yield.',
'This process, which circumvented the chromatography, was successfully demonstrated on a 100 g scale.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Sulfonation of 19 with 10 equiv SO₃·DMF gave the desired N‑sulfonic acid (21) together with 2–15 % of bis‑sulfonated impurity (22); using fewer equivalents resulted in incomplete conversion.
Solution_Description: The reaction mixture was quenched with a small amount of water and MgSO₄; MgSO₄ both dried the organic layer and promoted conversion of impurity 22 back to 21, delivering the product in 87 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The reaction was fast at ambient temperature and the reaction was complete in less than 30 min with forming side bis‑sulfonated product 22 (2–15 %).',
'Fortunately, 22 could be cleanly converted to 21 in the work‑up by treating the mixture with MgSO₄ in the presence of a small amount of water.',
'Quenching the reaction to a biphasic mixture of ethyl acetate and aqueous NaCl, removing DMF by aqueous washes, and drying the wet organic layer with MgSO₄ under vigorous agitation for 1 h converted 22 to 21.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: Global deprotection with excess BCl₃ generated vigorous exotherms and a boron‑complex that required a TFE quench; handling large volumes of BCl₃ posed safety concerns.
Solution_Description: The substrate solution (21) was added slowly (reverse addition) to a precooled BCl₃ solution (−5 °C to 0 °C) in n‑heptane, eliminating the need for TFE quench and improving product purity and safety.
Supporting_Evidence:
['When the BCl₃ solution (1 M) in dichloromethane was added over 60 min while maintaining the temperature between −5 and 5 °C, the mixture was warmed to 15 °C and stirred.',
'The reverse addition of the 21 solution in dichloromethane to a precooled (0–10 °C) 1 M BCl₃ solution in n‑heptane provided a slightly cleaner reaction with improved product stability that eliminated the need of trifluoroethanol treatment.',
'Excess BCl₃ was quenched with trifluoroethanol (45 equiv) in MTBE in an attempt to break up 1‑BCl₃ complex before filtration.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: For the first 500 g API delivery, the crude product contained residual boron and required reverse‑phase chromatography; iron‑containing solvents caused pink discoloration, violating API quality specifications.
Solution_Description: A resin‑capture‑release step using Amberchrom CG161M was employed to remove bulk water and residual boron, followed by precipitation from ethyl acetate, yielding an 88 % pure amorphous API without chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence:
['The slow addition of crude 1 to a mixture of DMF and 1 M aqueous ammonium bicarbonate solution, followed by filtration, gave a feed mixture (pH ∼ 4) for RP‑C.',
'To avoid chelation with iron, iron‑free solvents, reagents, and equipment were used, otherwise the product turned red/pink.',
'To remove the bulk amount of water without heating, a “resin‑capture–release” technique using Amberchrom CG161M resin was applied.',
'The product fractions were combined, and after the resin step the slurry was added to ethyl acetate at 2–8 °C to precipitate 1, affording 551 g (88.2 % pure) in a 35 % isolated yield.']

Paper Title: Enabled Process To Synthesize Monobactam
Problem_Description: The final API (1) showed poor crystallinity and limited solubility in water (≈2 mg mL⁻¹ at pH 1–3), making it difficult to isolate as a stable solid for later studies.

Supporting_Evidence:
['The solubility of 1 quickly decreased from pH 4 to 3 and stayed flat at ≈ 2 mg mL⁻¹ in the range of pH 1–3, likely due to its zwitterionic nature.',
'Crystallization of 1 was screened in buffered aqueous solutions at pH 0.7–2.5; crystalline solids were observed at pH 1.1 and 1.3, giving the same polymorph (Form 1) with ∼ 98 % purity.',
'The Amberchrom CG161M resin was applied not only as a “resin‑capture–release” tool to remove the bulk amount of water but also as an effective method to purify 1.',
'Adding 1 N HCl to adjust the aqueous solution of 1 to pH 1.12, followed by stirring at 22 °C for 24 h, produced a white slurry which, after filtration and drying, gave crystalline 1·5H₂O (Form 1, ∼ 94 % pure).']

Paper Title: A Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) Cascade for Handling Solid-Containing Photochemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Many photoredox reactions use insoluble starting materials or generate insoluble products, making it difficult to run them in continuous‑flow reactors because the solid phases cause poor mixing and block flow.

Supporting_Evidence: "many photoredox reactions involve insoluble starting materials or products that complicate the use of continuous flow methods";

Paper Title: A Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) Cascade for Handling Solid-Containing Photochemical Reactions
Problem_Description: To avoid solids, a homogeneous organic base is often substituted for the inexpensive inorganic base, but the replacement is more costly, may be less effective, and requires extensive solubility re‑screening that can change reaction selectivity.
Solution_Description: The original inorganic base (Na₂CO₃) was retained and fed as a suspension; the solvent system was later changed to pure DME, which kept the solid reagents in suspension while preserving the inexpensive base and eliminating the need for a costly organic alternative.
Supporting_Evidence: "the heterogeneous inorganic base is often replaced by a less compatible and more expensive homogeneous organic base";

Paper Title: A Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) Cascade for Handling Solid-Containing Photochemical Reactions
Problem_Description: When the reaction was first run in the wide‑tube CSTR 1, conversion and yield fell sharply after a few residence times, likely because broad residence‑time distribution allowed accumulation of a self‑inhibiting side‑product.

Solution_Description: A second CSTR cascade (CSTR 2) with narrow 0.7 mm inter‑connecting tubes was employed, giving a near‑ideal series‑CSTR residence‑time distribution that limited back‑mixing and prevented buildup of the inhibiting species.

Paper Title: A Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) Cascade for Handling Solid-Containing Photochemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Using the narrow‑tube CSTR 2 introduced a higher risk of plugging because solid particles could obstruct the small‑diameter connecting channels.

Solution_Description: The slurry pump was equipped with a magnetic stir bar and an external vibration motor on the outlet to keep solids in suspension and promote their transport through the narrow tubing, eliminating clogging during prolonged operation.
Supporting_Evidence: "CSTR 2… increased risk of plugging";

Paper Title: A Continuous Stirred-Tank Reactor (CSTR) Cascade for Handling Solid-Containing Photochemical Reactions
Problem_Description: Potential side‑products (e.g., NaBr precipitate) were observed to accumulate and could interfere with reaction progress or cause blockages, raising concerns about reactor stability and safe long‑term operation.
Solution_Description: Switching the reaction solvent to pure DME reduced the formation of NaBr precipitate and kept the majority of the solid reagents dispersed, resulting in steady conversion and yield even with the broader RTD of CSTR 1.
Supporting_Evidence: "use of pure DME as the solvent not only minimized the self‑inhibiting effect but also led to high conversion and yield";

Paper Title: A Scalable Process for the Synthesis of 1,2-Dialkyldiselanes and 1‑Alkaneselenols
Problem_Description: The process faced several scale‑up challenges: (1) the strong, malodorous vapour of low‑molecular‑weight organoselenium compounds made handling hazardous and unpleasant; (2) the selenocyanate intermediate partially decomposes under the basic, protic conditions to give the undesired 1,2‑dialkyldiselane (3a), reducing the yield of the target selenocyanate; (3) potassium selenocyanate, a key reagent, is expensive on a multi‑kilogram scale; (4) formation of potassium selenocyanate from cyanide and selenium is mildly exothermic, generating heat that must be controlled; (5) on large‑scale the use of potassium carbonate gave poor stirring and slurry handling; (6) the final reduction of the diselane to the selenol required 17 h reflux, slowing production.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The authors implemented a series of fixes: (1) they generated potassium selenocyanate in‑situ from potassium cyanide and selenium in methanol, avoiding the purchase of the expensive reagent and taking advantage of its high solubility (NEW ROUTE, SOLVENT CHANGE, COST). (2) The same methanol medium was used for the subsequent nucleophilic substitution and Krief cyclisation, allowing the three steps to be telescoped without isolating intermediates (TELESCOPE DIRECTLY, NEW ROUTE). (3) For large‑scale runs the exothermic formation of KSeCN was moderated by cooling the suspension to 15 °C before cyanide addition (TEMPERATURE OPTIMIZATION). (4) Potassium carbonate was replaced by potassium hydroxide, which gave a less viscous slurry and easier stirring (MIXABILITY, OTHER CONDITION CHANGE). (5) After the Krief step the crude diselane was distilled under reduced pressure and the volatile malodorous by‑products were trapped in a liquid‑nitrogen‑cooled receiver, removing the odor and simplifying work‑up (NEW PURIFICATION PROCEDURE). (6) Hypophosphorous acid, a cheap and safe reductant, was chosen for the final reduction (COST, SAFETY, CATALYST OPTIMIZATION). (7) To accelerate this reduction the amount of hypophosphorous acid was increased to 3 equiv and the reaction time cut from 17 h to 9 h (STOICHIOMETRY CHANGE, REACTION TIME CHANGE). (9) The 25 L batch reactor was equipped with a bleach scrubber and appropriate venting to control the malodorous vapours (SAFETY, MASS TRANSFER, MIXING AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL).

Paper Title: Stereospecific Amination of Mesylated Cyclobutanol in Continuous Flow
Problem_Description: Initial batch azidation gave only 69 % conversion after heating at 70 °C for 150 min, indicating insufficient conversion and a long residence time for the desired transformation.
Solution_Description: Increasing the temperature to 150 °C in the flow reactor enabled complete conversion within a 5 min residence time, eliminating the low‑yield and long‑reaction issue.
Supporting_Evidence: • “An initial batch experiment showed a partial conversion of 69 % to the azide … when the mixture … was heated at 70 °C for 150 min” (Table 1, entry 1). • “Increasing the temperature to 150 °C resulted in complete conversion (entry 3)” (Table 1). • “The flow reactor temperature was set to 120 °C … conversion of 82 % … Increasing the temperature to 150 °C resulted in complete conversion” (text).

Problem_Description: Isolation and handling of the pure azide intermediate (5) is hazardous because it exhibits an exothermic decomposition with an onset at 135 °C (ΔH = 1400 J g⁻¹), posing a significant safety risk.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow multistep sequence was devised that performs azidation followed immediately by a Staudinger reduction, avoiding isolation of the azide. Supporting_Evidence: • “We observed an exothermic decomposition with an onset of 135 °C … the isolation of this intermediate and his handling in batch mode should be avoided” (text). • “We investigated a flow multistep azidation/Staudinger reduction sequence to directly convert azide 5.” (text). • “the system was pressurized at 10 bar using a back‑pressure regulator … to confine the nitrogen gas evolution” (Scheme 3).

Supporting_Evidence: “Portion‑wise addition of sodium perborate to acetic acid at 28–33 °C resulted in an endothermic event and minor quantities of the gas (oxygen)… a slow nitrogen purge was recommended to avoid oxygen building up to higher levels.”

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Process for the PPAR‑α Agonist GW641597X Incorporating Baeyer–Villiger Chemistry and Retrospective ICH M7 Assessment
