Problem_Description: The LiAlH₄ reduction generated large amounts of hydrogen gas and an exotherm, causing splattering of the slurry and poor mixing during aqueous quench; magnetic stirring stalled in the presence of fine precipitates.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mechanical stirring was employed to keep the mixture homogeneous. The amount of LiAlH₄ was reduced from 20 equiv to 4 equiv, still affording full conversion. The Fieser work‑up (water → NaOH → water) generated larger alumina particles that filtered easily, avoiding foaming and filtration problems.
Supporting_Evidence: “...the large amount of solid which forms a fine precipitate during the aqueous quenching… would prevent magnetic stirring… we instead turned to mechanical stirring… vigorous mechanical stirring allowed us to use 75 % less of the total solvent… the original workup only quenched with water, resulting in a very fine precipitate… To address this, the Fieser workup (water, NaOH, water) was used instead to form large particles of alumina…”

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Dibenzoazacyclooctyne (DBCO) without Chromatography
Problem_Description: Acylation of the amine with methyl 4‑chloro‑4‑oxybutyrate (compound 5) was costly and the product required chromatographic purification, which was a bottleneck for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The expensive reagent 5 was prepared in‑house from succinic anhydride via a DMAP‑catalyzed ring‑opening and subsequent SOCl₂ conversion, avoiding commercial purchase. The acylation was performed under Schotten–Baumann conditions using 2 M KOH instead of Et₃N, and the crude product was isolated by simple precipitation and recrystallization from hot ethanol, eliminating chromatography.
Supporting_Evidence: “The high cost of 5… we sought to prepare this on scale as well… prepared monomethyl hydrogen succinate by DMAP‑catalyzed ring opening… conversion to acid chloride was performed by heating… The acylation … using 2 M KOH … The crude … was recrystallized twice in a minimum of hot ethanol, giving the product… without chromatographic purification.”

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Dibenzoazacyclooctyne (DBCO) without Chromatography
Problem_Description: The saponification of ester 6 to acid 7 was performed at low concentration (≈30 mg mL⁻¹) because of poor solubility, resulting in a 16 h reaction time.
Solution_Description: The concentration was increased to 500 mg mL⁻¹, allowing the reaction to go to completion in 1 h at reflux despite the substrate remaining largely insoluble; the work‑up was simplified by exploiting the poor solubility of the product for precipitation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Our original saponification procedure… low concentration (ca. 30 mg/mL)… We therefore increased the concentration to 500 mg/mL. … after 1 h of stirring at reflux with 6 equiv of LiOH, the product had fully saponified… the poor solubility of 7 was exploited for the workup… the reaction time decreased from 16 to 1 h.”

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Dibenzoazacyclooctyne (DBCO) without Chromatography
Problem_Description: During the bromination‑elimination sequence, the use of excess Br₂ generated large amounts of Na₂SO₃‑quench solution that caused emulsion formation, and the final elimination with KOtBu produced material that decomposed during traditional aqueous work‑ups.
Solution_Description: A stoichiometric amount of Na₂SO₃ was used to quench Br₂, minimizing emulsion. The elimination was performed with excess KOtBu at –78 °C; the reaction was quenched with dilute acid in Et₂O and kept cold throughout work‑up, with product isolated by cold precipitation and filtration, avoiding decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: “The key distinction of using a stoichiometric amount of Na₂SO₃ to quench excess Br₂… considerably reduced the formation of an emulsion… KOtBu… was found to work best when used in excess (3.5–4 equiv), resulting in the full conversion… workup of the reaction mixture proved challenging… dilution… aqueous extraction with H₃PO₄… the flask was removed from the rotary evaporator and 200 mL of diethyl ether was added… the product was left to crystallize at –20 °C… giving 9 with excellent purity.”

Paper Title: Highly Efficient Multigram Synthesis of Dibenzoazacyclooctyne (DBCO) without Chromatography
Problem_Description: The final product 9 is unstable and prone to decomposition if not handled promptly, making isolation difficult.
Solution_Description: The reaction was kept at –78 °C, and after completion the mixture was kept cold during solvent removal; the product was precipitated at –20 °C and filtered quickly, minimizing exposure to conditions that cause degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Since compound 8 is unstable, it should be eliminated on the same day… the flask was charged with anhydrous THF… cooled to –78 °C… after full conversion to 9… the flask was removed from the rotary evaporator and 200 mL of diethyl ether was added… left to crystallize at –20 °C… giving 9 as white crystals.”

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: The model substrate hypoxanthine (1) exhibits extremely poor solubility in many common solvents, which hampers its conversion to 6‑chloropurine (2) using conventional chlorinating agents.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a phosphorus‑free chlorination system based on bis‑(trichloromethyl) carbonate (BTC) dissolved in SOCl₂ and catalyzed by 5 wt % DMAP. This combination provides a clear reaction mixture and delivers a 96 % isolated yield of the desired product, overcoming the solubility limitation of hypoxanthine.
Supporting_Evidence: “hypoxanthine (1) … is hard to carry out this conversion … due to its extremely poor solubility of 1 in many solvents” (Sec 2.1); “BTC/SOCl₂ (a solution of BTC in SOCl₂) is effective for this reaction, especially, in the presence of 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), which shows best catalytic activity … entry 4, 96 % (90) isolated yield” (Table 1, entry 4).

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: Traditional chlorination with POCl₃ uses large excess of the reagent, which serves both as chlorinating agent and solvent and generates phosphorus‑containing waste streams that are environmentally hazardous and costly to treat.
Solution_Description: Replacing POCl₃ with the BTC/SOCl₂/DMAP system eliminates phosphorus from the process; the only waste products are HCl and SO₂, and the SOCl₂ solvent can be recovered by evaporation, simplifying work‑up and reducing waste disposal costs.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conventional method … includes POCl₃ or PCl₅ … the waste containing phosphorus thus produced … causes eutrophication … the phosphorus‑containing waste limits its industrial application” (Intro); “BTC/SOCl₂ … is effective … the resulting mixture … a slightly yellow clear solution, which gives light‑yellow powder… most SOCl₂ can be recovered by evaporation … particularly conducive to its industrial application” (Sec 2.1).

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: Using SOCl₂ alone as solvent (with either POCl₃ or BTC) leads to heterogeneous, turbid reaction mixtures and markedly reduced chlorination yields (31–42 %).
Solution_Description: Addition of 5 wt % DMAP to the BTC/SOCl₂ system converts the reaction mixture into a clear solution and raises the isolated yield to 96 %, demonstrating that DMAP acts as an efficient nucleophilic catalyst.
Supporting_Evidence: “Replacing POCl₃ with SOCl₂ … causes a significant decrease in the product yield … entries 2 and 3 … BTC/SOCl₂ … is effective … especially, in the presence of 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP) … entry 4, 96 % (90) isolated yield” (Table 1); footnote d: “Reaction presents heterogeneous and turbid mixture during the entire process.” (Table 1 footnote d).

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: Electron‑deficient pyridine and diazine substrates require longer reaction times (up to 12 h) and give slightly lower isolated yields compared with electron‑rich analogues, slowing throughput for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The authors extended the reaction to 12 h at reflux (90 °C) and used a slight excess of BTC (2 equiv for dihydroxy substrates) to achieve acceptable yields across a broad substrate scope.
Supporting_Evidence: “Electron‑deficient pyridine derivatives proceed with longer reaction time (not strictly) and slightly lower yields … entries 5–8” (Sec 2.2); footnote a for Table 3: “Conditions … reflux (90 °C oil bath), and 12 h.” (Table 3 footnote a).

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: Conventional two‑step syntheses require isolation of the chlorinated intermediate (filtration, pH adjustment, water quench), making the process time‑consuming and operationally complex on scale.
Solution_Description: A one‑pot two‑step protocol was developed: after complete chlorination, SOCl₂ is removed by evaporation and the next amine coupling is performed directly without isolating the intermediate, followed by simple aqueous work‑up and recrystallization.
Supporting_Evidence: “The drawback is obvious; cumbersome processes … are needed for isolation of the intermediate 2 … However, with the BTC/SOCl₂/DMAP system, the protocol can be simplified as one‑pot two‑step synthesis … SOCl₂ is removed after the complete conversion … reactants 7 are added directly to the mixture without isolation … then, simple workup and recrystallization … give the final product in good yields” (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Efficient Phosphorus-Free Chlorination of Hydroxy Aza-Arenes and Their Application in One-Pot Pharmaceutical Synthesis
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the POCl₃‑based chlorination generates a black, viscous solution that is difficult to handle safely and produces large quantities of phosphorus‑laden waste.
Solution_Description: The BTC/SOCl₂/DMAP system produces a clear, yellow solution that can be executed in standard reflux vessels (e.g., 1 L round‑bottom flask) and allows recovery of the SOCl₂ solvent, facilitating safer and more practical large‑scale operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “The resulting mixture of the latter is a black and viscous solution with a vast amount of phosphorus‑containing wastewater after workup … However, the BTC/SOCl₂ reaction only results in a slightly yellow clear solution … most SOCl₂ can be recovered by evaporation … conducive to its industrial application.” (Sec 2.1); Scheme 3 description of 50 g scale reaction in 1 L flask (Sec 2.3).

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: The initially chosen non‑polar solvent from literature could not be used because the presence of diethylamine (DEA) and water changed the phase‑mediator behavior, leading to poor solubility/miscibility between the polar DMF phase and the non‑polar phase and preventing efficient phase separation.
Solution_Description: A systematic screening of non‑polar solvents was performed and n‑dodecane was selected as the non‑polar component (together with DMF as polar solvent), giving a monophasic reaction mixture at high temperature and fast, clean biphasic separation at low temperature.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "the nonpolar solvent cannot be taken from literature, since the substrate amine and the coproduct water ... can act as a phase mediator ... the nonpolar solvent needs to be adapted to the different solubility properties to ensure an efficient phase separation." 
- "The results of screening of nonpolar solvents together with DMF show that n‑octane and n‑dodecane, in particular, outperform other solvents ... n‑dodecane leads to the highest product yield and the lowest amount of remaining intermediate enamine" 
- "Having chosen DMF and dodecane as polar and nonpolar solvents, respectively, for the TMS, the liquid–liquid equilibrium of this system needs to be considered to ensure the monophasic behavior at reaction temperature ... and biphasic behavior at lower temperature"

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: Significant loss of the polar solvent DMF (and thus the Rh‑catalyst) into the non‑polar product phase was observed during long‑term continuous operation, especially at high DEA : decanal ratios, causing catalyst depletion and a drop in product yield.
Solution_Description: The DEA : decanal molar ratio was reduced from 4 : 1 to 1 : 1, which lowered the transfer of DMF into the non‑polar phase by a factor of 8, stabilising catalyst concentration and maintaining a steady‑state yield. Additionally, a make‑up stream of DMF was introduced to compensate for the minor solvent loss.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "little leaching (3.5 wt %) of the polar DMF phase out of the process was expected; therefore, a ligand replenishment with DMF was implemented ..." 
- "the loss of DMF was much higher than expected ... real loss ... was four times higher at 16 wt % ... The reason for this loss was found to be the excess of DEA in the process" 
- "the next long‑term experiment ... was conducted with a DEA‑to‑decanal ratio of 1:1 to see if the lower amount of diethylamine decreases the loss of polar compounds ... Constant yield of the product amine of about 70 % over 75 h was achieved without any ligand or catalyst replenishment" 
- "Only a solvent (DMF) replenishment was established after 65 h to compensate for the small losses of DMF via the product phase"

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: During continuous operation the hydrogenation of the enamine intermediate was limited, leading to accumulation of enamine and formation of aldol condensates, which reduced overall amine yield.
Solution_Description: Residence time was optimized (1–2 h) and reactor temperature set to 100 °C with decanter at 5 °C, providing sufficient conversion of the enamine to amine while minimizing side‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "the reduction of the aldehyde to the respective alcohol 4 competes with the hydrogenation of the enamine ... For increasing the productivity and suppressing the formation of the mentioned side reactions, a fast reaction of the enamine 2 to the corresponding amine 3, and therefore a catalyst that is highly selective for the enamine hydrogenation, is necessary." 
- "A reaction profile ... shows that at least 2 h of reaction time is necessary to reach full conversion and a yield of product amine of about 90 % ... a residence time of 2 h is desirable." 
- "The influence of the residence time was investigated again. By looking at the product 3 yield ... a residence time of 1 h shows the same yield of 68 % as that at a residence time of 2 h ... therefore, the residence time of 1 h was chosen ..." 
- "When the pressure was increased to 35–40 bar, the yield of the product amine increased up to 93 % simultaneously diminishing the amount of unconverted enamine and aldol products"

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: Yield and selectivity differed between batch experiments (where pressure changes had little effect) and the continuous process (where pressure strongly affected hydrogenation), indicating inconsistent performance across scales.
Solution_Description: A dedicated pressure optimization study was performed in the continuous reactor, revealing that higher hydrogen pressure (35–40 bar) markedly improved amine yield, addressing the variability between batch and flow.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "In batch experiments, the increase from 20 bar to 40 bar had no significant effect on the yield of the amine 3, which always stayed at 64 %. In the case of the continuous process, the same pressure change lead to an increase in the product yield 3 from 58 % to 93 %" 
- "By lowering the pressure to 25 and 20 bar, the yield of the product amine 3 decreases slightly ... stepwise increase of the pressure to 35 and 40 bar resulted in a significant increase in the yield of the product amine 3, leading to yields of up to 93 %"

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: Efficient phase separation required rapid coalescence; initial decanter temperatures gave variable separation times (8 s to 30 s) affecting throughput.
Solution_Description: The decanter temperature was set to 5 °C, where DMF content in the non‑polar phase stabilised (3–4 wt %) within minutes, providing consistent phase separation and allowing definition of residence time.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "Figure 6 shows coalescence and phase separation in a separation funnel after 8 s and after 30 s at 5 °C. Generally, the concept of TMS is based on the efficiency of the phase separation, as the low solubility of the formed amine in DMF leads to good product separation and low solubility of DMF and the Rh catalyst in the n‑dodecane phase leads to good catalyst recovery." 
- "Figure 7 shows that efficient phase separation is achieved within minutes as the DMF concentration does not vary considerably after 8 min at all temperatures investigated, which determines the necessary residence time in the decanter. As the mass fraction of DMF in the nonpolar solvent n‑dodecane varies from 3 to 4 wt % in all cases, 5 °C was chosen as the set temperature for the decanter."

Paper Title: Process Development for the Rhodium-Catalyzed Reductive Amination in a Thermomorphic Multiphase System
Problem_Description: The reductive amination is highly exothermic; uncontrolled heat release could compromise catalyst stability and safety at scale.
Solution_Description: Reaction temperature and addition order were carefully controlled (pre‑formation of catalyst, controlled hydrogen addition, and staged temperature ramps) to manage the exotherm and maintain catalyst activity.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The parameters influencing the stability of the process were identified and optimized to develop the continuous process. ... Parameters influencing the stability of the process were identified and optimized ..." 
- "The continuous process consists of a 1000 mL continuous stirred‑tank reactors (CSTRs) ... The reactor is designed with a blade stirrer and baffle ... The miniplant is fully automated and is equipped with an online GC connect to the decanter (B2)."

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: With the sulfonic‑resin catalysts (Dowex 50WX2 and Amberlyst 15) the epichlorohydrin conversion required 24 h and the yields of the 1‑chloro‑3‑alkoxypropan‑2‑ols were only moderate; the yield for the trifluoroethanol substrate was as low as 10 %. The low yields stemmed from poor swelling of the resin in the less‑polar alcohols (isopropanol, butanol) which limited accessibility of the acid sites, and from the low nucleophilicity of 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol.
Solution_Description: The authors switched to heterogeneous acid catalysts that swell better in the chosen alcohols (Nafion NR50 for methanol/ethanol and montmorillonite K10‑H⁺ for butanol/isopropanol) and reduced the alcohol‑to‑epichlorohydrin molar ratio from 15:1 to 7.5:1 for the scale‑up, thereby improving mass transfer and reaction rates.
Supporting_Evidence: "When using the sulfonic resins, Dowex 50WX2 and Amberlyst 15, long reaction times (24 h) were needed…moderate yields…Only a yield of 10 % was reached because of the lower nucleophilicity of this alcohol"; "A better swelling of the resin in methanol and ethanol favors the accessibility…"; "Scale‑up…the ratio of alcohol 2/epichlorohydrin 1 was reduced to 7.5:1…the same results of yields and selectivity at the same reaction times were observed"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: In the second (base‑catalysed) step, the SN2 substitution of the chloride was very slow for some alcohols, requiring up to 72 h for trifluoroethanol, which also gave lower overall yields and risked side‑reactions or decomposition of the intermediate glycidyl ether.
Solution_Description: The reaction time was adjusted according to the nucleophilicity of the alcohol (≤2 h for butanol, 6 h for isopropanol, 72 h for trifluoroethanol) and a stoichiometric excess of potassium hydroxide (120 % mol) was employed to drive complete chlorine substitution while avoiding over‑decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence: "the reaction proceeded in less than 2 h with butanol…6 h was needed when using isopropanol…and 72 h in the case of trifluoroethanol"; "a stoichiometric amount of base is necessary for chlorine substitution"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: The earlier literature routes to nonsymmetric glyceryl diethers required pre‑made alkyl glycidyl ethers, which are commercially scarce and expensive, limiting scalability.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a tandem acid/base process starting directly from inexpensive epichlorohydrin and readily available alcohols, eliminating the need for costly glycidyl ether intermediates.
Supporting_Evidence: "This synthesis is thus limited by the commercial availability of the starting glycidyl ether…"; "We present a tandem process…starting from epichlorohydrin and several alcohols as reagents using readily available and recoverable heterogeneous acid catalysts"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: Large‑scale acid‑catalysed epoxide opening can be highly exothermic, posing safety concerns and risking degradation of sensitive substrates.
Solution_Description: Epichlorohydrin was added dropwise to the pre‑heated mixture containing the acid catalyst and alcohol, and the reaction temperature was maintained at 65 °C to control the exotherm and ensure safe scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: "Epichlorohydrin (4.35 mmol, 0.35 mL) was added. The reaction was stirred and heated at 65 °C under argon…"; "Scale‑up…the same results of yields and selectivity at the same reaction times were observed"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: Many homogeneous acid catalysts used in literature are expensive and difficult to recover, increasing process cost and waste.
Solution_Description: The study employed cheap, heterogeneous, fully recoverable acid catalysts (montmorillonite K10‑H⁺ and Nafion NR50) that could be filtered and reused up to five cycles without loss of activity.
Supporting_Evidence: "The best results being obtained with readily available recoverable and inexpensive montmorillonite‑K10 and Nafion NR50…"; "The catalysts were fully recoverable up to five consecutive runs without any loss of activity"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: Initial screening with 10 % mol catalyst loading gave slower reaction rates, especially with Nafion NR50, which could limit throughput.
Solution_Description: Catalyst loading was reduced to 5 % mol without sacrificing total conversion, thereby shortening the overall process time and improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: "The synthesis of 3 was carried out using 5 % mol of the catalyst…the reaction rates slightly slowed down, although this effect was more pronounced in the reactions catalyzed by Nafion NR50. Nevertheless, total conversion of epichlorohydrin and good yields…were achieved…demonstrating that 5 % mol of the catalyst is enough"

Paper Title: Readily Scalable Methodology for the Synthesis of Nonsymmetric Glyceryl Diethers by a Tandem Acid-/Base-Catalyzed Process
Problem_Description: During the acid‑catalysed step, the heterogeneous catalyst particles could cause a heterogeneous slurry, complicating stirring and mass transfer at larger scale.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Mechanical stirring in a thermostated glass reactor (2 L) was employed, and the reaction mixture was kept under inert argon atmosphere to ensure uniform mixing and avoid gas‑phase limitations.
Supporting_Evidence: "Reactions were scaled up…using a 2 L thermostated glass reactor with mechanical stirring…under argon"

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of Racemic Guaifenesin via Batch-Preferential Crystallization Processes
Problem_Description: In the CPCD experiment performed in isopropanol the very fast crystallization kinetics of the seeded enantiomer caused an early spontaneous nucleation of the counter‑enantiomer in the crystallisation tank. This forced an early interruption of the run and reduced the overall yield and reproducibility of the process.
Solution_Description: The process was operated at a crystallisation temperature of 25.5 °C – the highest temperature at which the fast crystallisation could be tolerated without premature nucleation – thereby tempering the kinetics and improving the achievable yield.
Supporting_Evidence: – "The faster crystallization kinetics observed in isopropanol caused a fast depletion of the preferred enantiomer… leading to a non‑optimal separation" (sec 4).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of Racemic Guaifenesin via Batch-Preferential Crystallization Processes
Problem_Description: The liquid‑phase exchange rate (30 mL min⁻¹) between the crystallisation and dissolution tanks was insufficient to compensate for the rapid removal of the seeded enantiomer, producing an imbalance that reduced separation efficiency and caused inconsistent results.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A higher exchange flow or a redesign of the pump/impeller system is required to increase mass‑transfer capacity, ensuring that the supersaturation in both vessels remains balanced throughout the run.
Supporting_Evidence: – "The exchange rate plays a crucial role in counterbalancing the depletion of the preferred enantiomer… As a consequence, the exchange rate between the two tanks was not sufficient to counterbalance the preferential crystallization… leading to a non‑optimal separation" (sec 4).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of Racemic Guaifenesin via Batch-Preferential Crystallization Processes
Problem_Description: Batch preferential crystallisation of guaifenesin in water required a production time of ≈ 4 h 20 min, giving a low productivity (0.8 g h⁻¹ L⁻¹) and modest yield (13 %).
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to isopropanol (same supersaturation) reduced the run time to 1 h 30 min, increased productivity ten‑fold and more than doubled the yield, demonstrating the benefit of solvent selection.
Supporting_Evidence: – Table 4 shows production time 1:30 h (isopropanol) vs ~4:20 h (water) and productivity 8.6 vs 0.8 g (h L)⁻¹.

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of Racemic Guaifenesin via Batch-Preferential Crystallization Processes
Problem_Description: The exact moment of spontaneous nucleation of the counter‑enantiomer could not be reliably detected with polarimeter data alone, risking premature or delayed stopping of the batch.
Solution_Description: Implementation of combined online monitoring (densitometer, polarimeter, turbidity probe) provides complementary signals that improve the detection of nucleation events and allow more reproducible process interruption.
Supporting_Evidence: – "The online and inline analytic tools… allowed to follow the progress of the resolution with time… optical rotation… turbidity…" (sec 2.5).

Paper Title: Efficient Resolution of Racemic Guaifenesin via Batch-Preferential Crystallization Processes
Problem_Description: The CPCD run delivered products with purities of 95 % (R‑enantiomer) and 80 % (S‑enantiomer), which required an additional recrystallisation step to reach the >99 % purity needed for API release.
Solution_Description: A simple post‑run recrystallisation of the collected solid increased the purity of both enantiomers to >99 %, demonstrating that an extra purification stage can resolve the residual impurity issue.
Supporting_Evidence: – "Despite the nucleation of the counter‑enantiomer, a high yield is achieved… The purities of the products collected … were 95 % (R) and 80 % (S)… Nevertheless, a simple recrystallisation of the product led to an upgrade of the purity up to >99 %" (sec 3.3).

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl
Problem_Description: Conventional Lewis‑acid promoted N‑glycosylation methods (SnCl4, TiCl4, TMSI, silanes/I2, pyridinium triflate) employ reagents that are toxic, flammable, expensive and difficult to handle safely on a multi‑kilogram scale.
Solution_Description: The authors introduced a mild, inexpensive ZrCl4‑mediated N‑glycosylation as a new catalytic route. Zirconium(IV) chloride is a solid, low‑toxicity Lewis acid that can be handled safely and is inexpensive at large scale.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, some of these methods are still associated with shortcomings based on their toxicity, flammable nature, high cost, and uneasiness while handling reagents… Therefore, there is a need for the development of a safe, efficient, inexpensive, and industrially viable catalyst for the glycosylation method.”; “Zirconium (IV) chloride… is relatively less toxic, easily operated, cost effective, and can withstand a small amount of moisture.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl
Problem_Description: Isolation of the enantiopure oxathiolane acetate (2c) required chiral resolution/crystallisation steps that recovered only ~46 % of the material and left a mixture of diastereomers, leading to low overall yield and difficult purification.
Solution_Description: The process was redesigned to use the racemic/diastereomeric acetate (2b) directly in the glycosylation step without prior isolation of a pure oxathiolane acetate, thereby avoiding the low‑yield resolution step.
Supporting_Evidence: “The oxathiolane acetate taken in situ in the solution gives a stereoselective single nucleoside isomer… The oxathiolane acetate (2b) was taken in a solution form as such without isolation for the further glycosylation step at a large scale.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl
Problem_Description: Previous routes required low‑temperature (‑20 °C) crystallisation of oxathiolane acetate for 36 h to obtain the pure isomer, a time‑consuming and energy‑intensive operation that inflates cost at scale.
Solution_Description: The new ZrCl4 protocol proceeds at ambient temperature (room temperature) and completes the glycosylation within 12 h, eliminating the need for sub‑ambient crystallisation and dramatically shortening the overall reaction time.
Supporting_Evidence: “The reaction completes within a short time for a large‑scale production with a high yield at room temperature (rt).”; Table 1 entry 6 shows ZrCl4 at rt, 12 h giving 60 % yield with excellent β/α ratio.

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl
Problem_Description: Addition of ZrCl4 and the subsequent cytosine silylation step generated measurable exotherms (ΔT_ad up to 27 °C) that could pose safety risks during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors controlled the exotherm by adding ZrCl4 portion‑wise, pre‑activating the donor before adding the acceptor, and maintaining the addition temperature between 20–40 °C with active cooling, thereby limiting temperature spikes.
Supporting_Evidence: “ZrCl4 (70.3 kg) was added… stirred … for 15–30 min at 20–30 °C. … the silylated cytosine mass … was charged … at 20 to 40 °C by applying continuous cooling to avoid an exothermic reaction.”; Reaction‑calorimetry data shows ΔT_ad values of 11.05 °C (ZrCl4), 13.03 °C (cytosine addition) and 27.71 °C (methanol quench).

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl
Problem_Description: After reduction of the nucleoside intermediate, lamivudine is highly soluble in water, making it difficult to isolate because inorganic salts (NaCl, KCl, boric acid) remain dissolved with the product.
Solution_Description: The team employed a co‑crystallisation strategy using (S)-BINOL to form a water‑insoluble lamivudine·(S)-BINOL complex, enabling removal of inorganic salts by water washing and subsequent recovery of high‑purity lamivudine after releasing the API from the co‑crystal.
Supporting_Evidence: “We used our earlier reported (S)-BINOL Co‑crystal strategy… the lamivudine‑(S)-BINOL complex was water insoluble… inorganic salts were removed by simply adding water slurry… (S)-BINOL reagent was later completely recovered and recycled.”

Paper Title: Large-Scale Stereoselective Synthesis of 1,3-Oxathiolane Nucleoside, Lamivudine, via ZrCl

Solution_Description: A 0.1 g mL⁻¹ solution of (R)‑ketamine hydrochloride in ethyl benzoate was used, providing a homogeneous reaction mixture at 150 °C and allowing efficient heat transfer and catalyst contact.
Supporting_Evidence: Reaction conditions: 0.1 g/mL (R)‑1 hydrochloride (98.5 % ee) in ethyl benzoate. ["Reaction conditions: 0.1 g/mL (R)‑1 hydrochloride … in ethyl benzoate."]

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: The previously reported manual flow‑photoredox ^18F‑difluoromethylation was not compatible with high‑activity runs because handling large amounts of radioactivity manually poses radioprotection issues and the manual process gave variable results.
Solution_Description: The entire two‑step radiosynthesis was transferred to a Trasis All‑in‑One (AIO) synthesizer, which provides more valve positions (36 vs 25) and an integrated HPLC system, allowing fully automated operation and better reproducibility.
Supporting_Evidence: "Because of the limited number of free positions on the FL cassette (25 valves) … the AIO module from Trasis (36 valves with an integrated HPLC system) was selected for the automation of the multistep procedure."; "Automation of the flow photoredox process on the AIO was the most challenging part of this work… to avoid radioprotection issues… and ensure better reliability of the production."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Changing the reaction solvent from MeCN to either 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) caused a dramatic drop in radiochemical yield (to 3.6 % and <0.5 %, respectively), indicating poor solubility and possible decomposition of intermediates.
Solution_Description: The authors retained MeCN as the reaction solvent together with K2CO3 and K222, which gave the highest labeling RCY (13.9 %).
Supporting_Evidence: "Changing MeCN to another solvent, such as 1,2‑dichloroethane (DCE) (entry 6) or dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) (entry 7), led to a dramatic reduction in the overall RCY (to 3.6 and <0.5 %)."; "The highest RCY for the labeling step was obtained using K2CO3 at 85 °C in acetonitrile (entry 1)."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Using tetraethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) or sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) as bases instead of K2CO3 resulted in significantly lower RCY for the sulfone formation (5 % and <0.5 % respectively).
Solution_Description: The standard protocol keeps K2CO3 (20 µmol) as the base, which maintains high RCY (≈12 %).
Supporting_Evidence: "Substitution of K2CO3 by tetraethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB) or sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO3) provided sulfone [¹⁸F]1 in significantly lower RCY (entries 4 and 5)."; "Standard conditions: ... K2CO3 (20 µmol), K222 (20 µmol), MeCN (1 mL), 85 °C, 5 min."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Running the labeling step at 120 °C gave no product, indicating that excessive heat leads to decomposition of the fluorinated intermediate.
Solution_Description: The labeling temperature was kept at 85 °C (optimal) and the oxidation step performed at room temperature to avoid thermal degradation.
Supporting_Evidence: "120 °C ... –" (entry 2, no RCY reported); "The highest RCY for the labeling step was obtained using K2CO3 at 85 °C in acetonitrile (entry 1)."; "Afterward, the oxidative solution … should be performed in the presence of the base and solvent previously used in the labeling step."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: The original photocatalyst Ir(ppy)₃ gave lower radiochemical yield (50 %) and is expensive and toxic compared with an organic alternative.
Solution_Description: The photocatalyst was switched to the organic dye 4CzIPN, which improved RCY to 80 % and is cheaper, less toxic and easier to remove.
Supporting_Evidence: "The replacement of Ir‑(ppy)₃ by the organic photocatalyst 4CzIPN was beneficial since [¹⁸F]5 was obtained in 80 % RCY (entry 1)."; "Ir‑(ppy)₃ catalyst … has the advantages of being organic, less expensive, easier to remove, and less toxic than Ir‑(ppy)₃."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Although a 10 s residence time in the flow photoreactor gave high conversion, the authors kept a 1 min residence to compensate for decay and residual water, which could otherwise lower conversion.
Solution_Description: A standardized 1 min residence time was adopted to ensure full conversion of [¹⁸F]1 despite the short half‑life and trace water present.
Supporting_Evidence: "With this catalyst, the reaction time could even be lowered to 10 s without affecting the RCY (entry 4). However, because of the small amount of fluorine decay between 10 s and 1 min as well as the presence of residual water … a residence time of 1 min was maintained in order to ensure full conversion."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Direct HPLC purification of the final ^18F‑difluoromethylacyclovir injected ~1.2 mL of DMSO; the product showed poor solubility in the MeOH/H₂O eluents, resulting in only 25 % isolated RCY after purification.
Solution_Description: An alternative work‑up using a hydrophilic‑lipophilic balance (HLB) cartridge was implemented; solvents were removed, the product was eluted with a small volume of ethanol and formulated in saline, achieving the required molar activity.
Supporting_Evidence: "Unfortunately, the injection of approximatively 1.2 mL of DMSO, the low solubility of [¹⁸F]5 in the purification eluents (MeOH/H₂O), and its high polarity resulted in an RCY of only 25 % after online HPLC purification (entry 6)."; "The HPLC solvents were removed on a hydrophilic–lipophilic balance (HLB) cartridge, and [¹⁸F]5 was recovered with a small volume of ethanol and further diluted with saline prior to injection."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: Performing the multi‑step synthesis with gigabecquerel levels of ^18F‑fluoride requires strict radioprotection to avoid operator exposure.
Solution_Description: The All‑in‑One module provides shielding and a closed‑loop design that contains the radioactivity throughout the synthesis, meeting GMP and radioprotection requirements.
Supporting_Evidence: "Automation of the process is mandatory, mostly to avoid radioprotection issues due to the use of high amounts of radioactivity and to ensure better reliability of the production."; "The fully automated three‑step radiosynthesis was performed in 95 min… and should provide enough final radioactivity for preclinical examinations while complying with radioprotection rules and GMP requirements."

Paper Title: Development of a General Automated Flow Photoredox
Problem_Description: The oxidation solution (NaIO₄/RuCl₃) is detrimental to the subsequent photoredox step; any residual aqueous/oxidant mixture could quench the photocatalyst and impede the reaction.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The oxidation was performed in liquid phase within the same MeCN/K₂CO₃/K222 medium, and the system was thoroughly washed and dried with nitrogen flow before the photoredox step to eliminate water and oxidants.
Supporting_Evidence: "During the design of the automated procedure, particular attention was paid to minimizing the contamination between the two parts of the synthesis, as the oxidative solution is detrimental to the ^18F‑difluoromethylation. This prompted us to modify the oxidation step from a solid phase in the FASTlab to a liquid phase in the AIO."; "The manifold was entirely dried with a nitrogen flow, syringes S2 and S3 were each washed with 4 mL of DMSO, and the manifold was dried again."

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: The hydrogenation of the aliphatic nitro compound is a highly exothermic reaction that is prone to thermal runaway, creating a safety hazard and requiring very careful temperature control during scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A high‑definition fiber‑optic temperature probe (Luna ODiSl) and an FLIR thermal‑imaging camera were installed to monitor the temperature profile inside the packed‑bed reactor.  The inlet liquid temperature was raised when necessary to shift the hot spot toward the top of the bed, providing real‑time control of the exotherm and preventing hotspot formation.
Supporting_Evidence: It is a highly exothermic reaction that is susceptible to thermal runaway.; The reaction is triphasic (gas, solid, liquid) making heat and mass transport important.; A Luna ODiSl high‑definition fiber optic temperature probe was placed inside the catalyst bed.; Measuring the outside wall temperature of the reactors would give an indication of the temperature inside the column using an FLIR E5 thermal imaging camera.; Raising the inlet temperature to 36 °C moved the hottest point of the column toward the top of the catalyst bed.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: Sponge‑metal catalysts such as Raney nickel are pyrophoric, making their handling hazardous on larger scale and limiting the use of traditional characterization techniques.
Solution_Description: The catalysts were loaded into a packed‑bed (trickle‑bed) reactor and operated continuously, which confines the pyrophoric material, eliminates the need for filtration, and reduces operator exposure.
Supporting_Evidence: Sponge metals such as Raney nickel are commonly used in early‑phase API routes but are then worked out of later‑stage development because of the perceived handling difficulties of these catalysts.; Because of the pyrophoric nature of the catalysts, traditional techniques such as laser diffraction would be hazardous.; Placing the catalyst in a packed‑bed reactor and running the reaction continuously reduces potential exposure to the metal catalysts, avoids a hazardous filtration step.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: During batch hydrogenations a significant amount of the hydroxylamine intermediate (compound 3) formed; this impurity is potentially hazardous, genotoxic, and difficult to purge in downstream steps.
Solution_Description: Screening identified Raney nickel catalyst 3111A (and later 2400 Raney) that gave clean reductions without any detectable hydroxylamine, eliminating the hazardous impurity and simplifying purification.
Supporting_Evidence: During the reaction a significant amount of hydroxylamine intermediate 3 was also observed, and this intermediate was flagged as potentially hazardous and genotoxic.; Reactions using 2400 Raney nickel gave repeatable clean reductions to the amine without any buildup of hydroxylamine.; Pleasingly, hydroxylamine 3 was not detected during this long run.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: Irregularly shaped sponge‑metal particles and wide size distributions caused high pressure drops and the generation of fines, risking bed fouling, variable conversion, and reduced productivity.
Solution_Description: 3111A Raney nickel, which exhibited the lowest measured pressure drop (2.7 bar) and the highest mechanical strength, was selected for scale‑up; its larger average particle size reduced fines formation and maintained a stable pressure drop.
Supporting_Evidence: Five of the tested catalysts had pressure drops of <10 bar over the 7 cm bed, with 3111A and 3202 Raney nickel showing the lowest values of 2.7 and 5.8 bar, respectively.; Irregularly shaped sponge metals with wide particle size distributions make some of the terms difficult to define.; A physically robust catalyst is desirable to prevent the buildup of fines, which would increase the pressure drop over the bed and ultimately lead to operational failure.; 3111A Raney nickel showed no change over a period of 3 h and was selected along with 2400 and 2800 Raney nickel for further testing.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: Insertion of an internal temperature probe caused channeling in the packed‑bed, leading to poor temperature measurement, hot‑spot formation and a potential safety risk.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The internal probe was replaced by non‑invasive wall‑temperature monitoring with an FLIR thermal‑imaging camera, providing reliable temperature profiles without disturbing flow.
Supporting_Evidence: It quickly became apparent that inserting a probe through the bed led to channeling, and the reaction as indicated by the hottest point was seen at the bottom of the probe.; Bed channeling can have a negative effect on the performance of the catalytic reactor.; Measuring the outside wall temperature of the reactors would give an indication of the temperature inside the column using an FLIR E5 thermal imaging camera.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: During daily startup/shutdown and feed‑bottle swaps the pressure drop spiked, indicating bed compression and inconsistent flow, which could affect conversion and selectivity.
Solution_Description: Startup and shutdown procedures were refined (e.g., controlled pump stops, consistent flushing) to minimise bed compression; further optimisation is planned to stabilise pressure drop.
Supporting_Evidence: Sharp spikes in pressure drop were observed when the pumps were stopped to swap solution feed bottles.; The larger step changes were attributed to the unoptimized startup and shutdown procedures used at the beginning and end of each day.; It is thought that a further compression of the catalyst bed takes place during startup or shutdown as well as during the feed bottle changes.

Paper Title: Evaluation of Sponge Metal Catalysts in a Trickle Bed Reactor for the Continuous Hydrogenation of an Aliphatic Nitro Intermediate
Problem_Description: Potential leaching of nickel and other metals from the Raney catalyst could contaminate the product and raise safety/environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: The reactor was washed with MeOH and water and stored under water between runs; ICP‑OES analysis confirmed no detectable nickel leaching, only trace sodium/aluminum.
Supporting_Evidence: An ongoing concern during the development work was the amount of nickel and other metals that would be leached from the catalyst bed over time.; Nickel was not detected, but trace amounts of sodium (33 µg/g) and aluminum (21 µg/g) were present.; The column was washed with MeOH and then water, removed from the system, and stored under water overnight.

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: When the electrode surface was enlarged for the 4 cm × 12 cm flow cell the electric power fed into the system increased, generating a large amount of heat (resistive heating, gas evolution, voltage drop, over‑potentials).  The electrolyte temperature rose dramatically, which forced the authors to install an active cooling circuit and caused a drop in yield (30 % under the first conditions).
Solution_Description: A dedicated meander‑shaped cooling channel was machined into the Teflon back‑side of the electrode and connected to an external cooling circuit, allowing precise temperature control (e.g., 10 °C) and preventing overheating of the cell during high‑current operation.
Supporting_Evidence: “...a significant part of the electric power generates heat due to resistivity, gas evolution on the electrode surface, voltage drop by electrolytes, and overpotentials. This can lead to an enormous temperature rise, which makes an effective cooling system mandatory. To realize this, a cooling system is incorporated directly onto the back of the electrode... the cell was cooled to 10 °C … the yield increased to 48 %.”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: Running the reaction in the 2 cm × 6 cm flow cell without any supporting electrolyte gave only 5 % isolated product, indicating insufficient ionic conductivity and poor conversion.
Solution_Description: The addition of a small amount of methyl‑tributylammonium methylsulfate (MeBu₃NO₃SOMe) (0.005 M) restored conductivity and raised the yield to 44 % in the small flow cell and to 59 % after further optimisation.
Supporting_Evidence: “Using no supporting electrolyte at all was not successful, as it gave only a 5 % yield… only using methyl tributylammonium methylsulfate (MeBu₃NO₃SOMe) increased the yield to 44 %.”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: Thermal expansion and shrinkage of the Teflon half‑cells during electrolysis could shift the spacer, cause electrode‑electrolyte leakage and, for very low temperatures, cracking of the brittle electrodes (graphite, BDD).
Solution_Description: The cell was built from three separate Teflon pieces (central section and two caps) with internal stainless‑steel rods and metal pins; screws can be readjusted in‑situ to compensate for thermal deformation, keeping the spacer fixed and preventing leaks or electrode breakage.
Supporting_Evidence: “The half‑cell was designed with a three‑part structure in order to prevent the electrodes from experiencing mechanical stress… this setup enables readjustment of the screws in order to prevent possible leakage of the cell due to thermal deformation/expansion of the Teflon block during electrolysis and the use of active chilling.”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: During the dehydrogenative coupling of 4 and 7 the high rate of hydrogen evolution (≈0.3 mL min⁻¹) filled the cell volume, causing the reaction to stop when the power‑supply reached its terminal voltage.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The inter‑electrode distance was increased from 0.12 mm to 0.50 mm, enlarging the cell volume and allowing the gas to escape more readily; this restored the voltage window and gave an 86 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence: “The excessive hydrogen evolution… occupied the cell volume almost completely. A larger cell volume would help to remedy this issue. Therefore, the electrode distance was enlarged to 0.50 mm… a yield of 86 % could be obtained.”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: High current densities on the larger cell caused over‑oxidation of the biphenol product, reducing the isolated yield (30 % at 5 mA cm⁻²).
Solution_Description: Systematic variation of the current density showed that 30 mA cm⁻² with the thinnest spacer (0.25 mm) gave the optimum balance between conversion and selectivity, raising the yield to 52 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “The highest yield… was obtained with a current density of 30 mA cm⁻² using the thinnest spacer (0.25 mm).”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: A single pass through the flow cell gave high residence time and high temperature, limiting productivity and causing over‑oxidation of the product.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A cascade (multiple‑run) strategy was employed, pumping the electrolyte through the cell several times at increased flow rates. This reduced residence time, kept the temperature lower, and removed hydrogen faster, achieving 59 % yield and a 21‑fold increase in productivity (2.53 g h⁻¹).
Supporting_Evidence: “The electrolyte can be pumped through the cell multiple times (cascade reaction)… this results in two major advantages: ... the electrolyte does not heat up as strongly. … a yield of 59 % could be achieved. In conclusion, we were able to increase the productivity… from 0.12 g h⁻¹ to 2.53 g h⁻¹.”

Paper Title: Large, Highly Modular Narrow-Gap Electrolytic Flow Cell and Application in Dehydrogenative Cross-Coupling of Phenols
Problem_Description: The original micro‑flow cells required expensive electrode materials (e.g., Pt, BDD) and were limited in scale, making them impractical for larger‑scale production.
Solution_Description: A scalable parallel‑plate cell with a narrow 0.12–2.0 mm gap was developed, allowing the use of inexpensive stainless‑steel cathodes and BDD anodes while maintaining low electrolyte consumption and enabling straightforward scale‑up (4 cm × 12 cm, 400 % larger electrode area).
Supporting_Evidence: “The flow cell is assembled from two Teflon half‑cells… the electrode distance can be controlled… a small interelectrode distance contributes to a minimisation or total renunciation of supporting electrolyte… the new 4 cm × 12 cm flow cell… electrode surface is increased by 400 %.”

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: Literature syntheses of boscalid employ palladium loadings of 1 mol % or higher in the Suzuki–Miyaura step, which makes the process expensive, consumes a scarce/ endangered metal, and raises safety/environmental concerns.
Solution_Description: The authors developed a water‑based micellar protocol that uses only 700 ppm (0.07 mol %) Pd(OAc)₂ together with the SPhos ligand, giving quantitative conversion while drastically reducing the amount of palladium required.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Literature approaches use … unsustainable levels of palladium catalysis.", "The key Suzuki–Miyaura coupling requires only 700 ppm (0.07 mol %) Pd …", "Quantitative conversion … with 700 ppm Pd at 55 °C (entry 7, Table 1)"]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: Previous routes rely on large volumes of organic solvents (e.g., THF, dioxane) which generate hazardous waste, pose flammability risks, and increase process cost.
Solution_Description: All three steps were performed in aqueous 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M nanomicelles (with 10 % THF as a cosolvent), eliminating the need for bulk organic solvents.
Supporting_Evidence: ["none of these methods offer an environmentally sustainable, benign approach.", "Each of the three steps can be carried out in water containing nanomicelles as reaction medium.", "Screening of surfactants … each led to excellent conversion."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: Using Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃ at 5000 ppm gave only 54‑73 % conversion to the biaryl product even after raising the temperature.
Solution_Description: Switching the ligand to SPhos enabled 100 % conversion at the same Pd loading and allowed further reduction of Pd to 700 ppm while maintaining quantitative yield.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Stirring 2‑chloronitrobenzene … with Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃ … led to 54 % conversion (entry 1).", "Increasing the temperature … did not increase the extent of conversion (entry 2).", "In this case, reaction was complete using 5000 ppm Pd at 45 °C (entry 6) with SPhos.", "Further lowering the catalyst loading to 700 ppm … sufficed to arrive at quantitative conversion (entry 7)."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: A Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling performed in pure THF gave markedly lower conversion than the same reaction in the aqueous micellar system, indicating poor solubility/mixability of the reactants in the organic medium.
Solution_Description: The reaction was run in 2 wt % TPGS‑750‑M/H₂O (9:1) with 10 % THF as a cosolvent; the surfactant forms nanomicelles that keep the reagents in a single homogeneous phase and dramatically improve conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["By contrast, the same coupling run … using pure THF … gave an inferior result compared to the aqueous micellar system.", "Screening of surfactants … each led to excellent conversion."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: Typical nitro‑group reductions with 1 % Pd/C under a H₂ balloon gave only 44 % isolated yield and produced a major dechlorinated side‑product (51 % of material), while the use of H₂ introduces a safety hazard.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced Pd/C/H₂ with carbonyl iron powder (CIP) and NH₄Cl (3 equiv) at 45 °C, which delivered the aniline in 85 % isolated yield with minimal dechlorination.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Pd/C … led to full conversion but resulted in only a 44 % yield … dechlorination (51 %).", "Carbonyl iron powder (CIP) together with NH₄Cl at 45 °C afforded an 85 % yield of the desired aniline."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: When the final amide formation was performed with Et₃N or pyridine as base, conversion to the product was only 65‑68 %, and no base gave a sluggish 28 % conversion.
Solution_Description: Using Hunig’s base (i‑Pr₂NEt) (2 equiv) gave quantitative conversion (100 %) and a 97 % isolated yield of boscalid.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Et₃N … gave 65 % conversion (entry 1).", "pyridine … gave 68 % conversion (entry 3).", "i‑Pr₂NEt … gave 100 % conversion (entry 2)."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: Isolation of each intermediate between steps would increase handling and could introduce variability in yield and impurity profiles during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The three transformations were telescoped in a single reaction vessel without intermediate work‑up; after the Suzuki‑Miyaura step the crude mixture was directly subjected to the iron‑mediated reduction, followed by the amide‑formation step, delivering boscalid in 83 % overall isolated yield on a 5 mmol scale.
Supporting_Evidence: ["Without workup or isolation, reduction to amine 4 followed via addition of CIP, which was complete in 12 h.", "The newly formed amine was treated directly with 2‑chloronicotinyl chloride … to afford boscalid (83 % overall yield)."]

Paper Title: A Sustainable 1‑Pot, 3‑Step Synthesis of Boscalid Using Part per Million Level Pd Catalysis in Water
Problem_Description: On gram‑scale the individual steps required extended reaction times (15 h for the Suzuki coupling, 12 h for nitro reduction, and a total of 16 h for the final amide step), potentially limiting throughput.
Solution_Description: The authors increased the temperature for the Suzuki step to 55 °C and for the reduction to 45 °C, and used 2 wt % surfactant at the appropriate concentration (10 mL H₂O‑TPGS for 5 mmol substrate) to maintain high reaction rates while preserving quantitative conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: ["The reaction mixture was stirred vigorously at 55 °C for 15 h …", "CIP … heated at 45 °C for 12 h.", "Finally … heated at 45 °C for 2 h … total 16 h reaction time, giving 83 % overall yield."]

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Continuous Flow Azidophenylselenylation of Galactal to Prepare Galactosamine Building Blocks
Problem_Description: The azidophenyl‑selenylation (APS) of galactal performed in batch gave highly variable yields (10–65 %, average 35 %) and poor reproducibility.  The authors attribute this to deficiencies in mixing and temperature control of a highly exothermic reaction, which lead to local hot spots and concentration gradients.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction was transferred to a continuous‑flow platform using HPLC pumps, a T‑piece mixer, a thermostatted residence‑time unit and a downstream back‑pressure regulator (17 bar).  This geometry guarantees efficient mixing, rapid heat removal and avoids gas‑liquid biphasic flow, thereby delivering consistent conversions and yields.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The highly exothermic APS reaction is commonly carried out… the poor selectivity and irreproducibility are likely a consequence of deficiencies in mixing and temperature control during batch reactions.” (Introduction) 
• “Pressurizing the system was essential to avoid the formation of a biphasic gas/liquid flow pattern resulting from the formation of N₂ to guarantee reproducible flow processes.” (Results) 
• “The flow setup … mixed in a T‑piece before entering a residence time unit that was immersed in a thermostatic bath.” (Results) 
• “The flow setup allowed for a straightforward scale‑up, as the results observed in an analytical scale were steadily reproduced throughout the entire process of a gram‑scale synthesis.” (Conclusion)

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Continuous Flow Azidophenylselenylation of Galactal to Prepare Galactosamine Building Blocks
Problem_Description: Azide reagents (TMSN₃) are intrinsically hazardous; they can generate toxic hydrazoic acid and pose explosion risks, especially when large concentrations are present in batch reactors.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The flow process operates at room temperature under pressure and the reaction stream is quenched immediately in a vigorously stirred mixture of DCM, aqueous Na₂S₂O₃ and NaHCO₃, which reduces azide concentration, prevents HN₃ formation and safely consumes residual BAIB.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The potentially explosive and toxic nature of azido compounds… the possibility of formation of poisonous and explosive hydrazoic acid must be contemplated at all times.” (Abstract & General Methods) 
• “Pressurizing the system was essential to avoid… gas/liquid flow… to guarantee reproducible flow processes.” (Results) 
• “The reaction mixture was collected and quenched by dropping it into a mixture of DCM (50 mL) and aq. sat. Na₂S₂O₃ (25 mL), NaHCO₃ (25 mL) … to prevent the formation of hydrazoic acid.” (General Procedure) 
• “Performing the reaction in flow… the concentration of potentially hazardous side products generated at any time is minimal during the flow regime.” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Continuous Flow Azidophenylselenylation of Galactal to Prepare Galactosamine Building Blocks
Problem_Description: During work‑up, especially solvent evaporation, the desired selenoglycoside (2) undergoes radical‑mediated C–Se bond cleavage or β‑elimination, forming bis‑azido (6–7) and 1‑O‑acetyl (8) side products, which compromises isolated yield.
Solution_Description: A silica‑gel plug is inserted before solvent removal; the quenched mixture is filtered through silica, which removes selenide impurities and stops the post‑reaction degradation, allowing clean evaporation and crystallisation of product 2.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Comparison of ¹H NMR spectra … revealed that 6–8 were formed during solvent evaporation rather than during the continuous flow process.” (Results) 
• “Filtration through a bed of silica of the quenched reaction mixture prior to solvent evaporation avoids this reproducibility issue.” (Results) 
• “Removal of selenide impurities through silica filtration is required for an adequate crystallization of 2.” (Results) 
• “The use of silica filtration prior to evaporation therefore does not introduce an extra step … it simply exchanges the order between silica filtration and solvent evaporation.” (Results)

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Continuous Flow Azidophenylselenylation of Galactal to Prepare Galactosamine Building Blocks
Problem_Description: Conventional batch APS protocols require 4–16 h residence times, slowing throughput and diminishing overall productivity.
Solution_Description: Systematic temperature screening identified room temperature (27 °C) as optimal; with 25 min residence time (flow) full conversion to product 2 (79 % NMR yield) is obtained, a >7‑fold reduction in reaction time compared with batch.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Reaction times are variable and typically range from 4 to 16 h.” (Introduction) 
• “Best results were obtained … at room temperature … to afford target product 2 in 79 % yield within 25 min.” (Results) 
• “The flow setup is readily scalable … producing 1.2 mmol h⁻¹ of product.” (Abstract) 
• “Lowering the reaction temperature to 0 °C resulted in a significantly reduced conversion … At higher temperatures (40 °C), significantly lower selectivity was observed.” (Results)

Paper Title: Safe and Scalable Continuous Flow Azidophenylselenylation of Galactal to Prepare Galactosamine Building Blocks
Problem_Description: Inconsistent product distribution and incomplete consumption of the galactal substrate were observed when the stoichiometry of Ph₂Se₂, TMSN₃ and BAIB was not optimized.

Paper Title: Cerium(III) Chloride-Mediated Stereoselective Reduction of a 4‑Substituted Cyclohexanone Using NaBH
Problem_Description: Initial reduction with NaBH₄ gave only a 3:1 trans/cis diastereomeric ratio (poor stereoselectivity) and low overall conversion; LiAlH₄ improved conversion but the isolation was tedious and afforded only 40 % isolated yield after multiple purification steps.  The LiAlH₄ reduction also required cryogenic temperatures, making the process unsafe and impractical for scale‑up.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The team screened a series of metal‑salt additives with NaBH₄ and discovered that sub‑stoichiometric CeCl₃·7H₂O (0.2–0.3 equiv) combined with 1.7 equiv NaBH₄ gave >16:1 trans/cis selectivity and near‑quantitative conversion in 5 min.  To control the highly exothermic (ΔH = ‑311 kJ mol⁻¹) and gas‑evolving (H₂) addition of NaBH₄, the borohydride was divided into at least four equal portions with a nitrogen sweep, keeping the reaction temperature below 0 °C.  The work‑up was re‑engineered (solvent swaps, Nutsche filtration) and the reaction was transferred to a 600 L Hastelloy batch reactor with precise temperature control, enabling a reliable scale‑up to >100 kg.
Supporting_Evidence:
- "The initial conditions employed to reduce 4 (NaBH₄) provided a 3:1 mixture of diastereomers 3 and 5 (entry 1)."
- "LiAlH₄ gave higher conversion and selectivity ... however, isolation of the product ... furnished 3 in only 40% yield after multiple isolation and purification attempts."
- "These issues coupled with the need for cryogenic conditions during the LiAlH₄ reduction deterred us from pursuing this option further."
- "It was found that the addition of sub‑stoichiometric cerium‑(III) chloride in conjunction with sodium borohydride provided the desired trans‑cyclohexanol ... in >16:1 selectivity and excellent conversion."
- "The use of stoichiometric CeCl₃·7H₂O as an additive with NaBH₄ led to clean and rapid reduction of 4 to provide a 16:1 ratio of diastereomers 3 and 5 in near‑quantitative conversion within 5 min (entry 10)."
- "Attempts to lower the stoichiometry of CeCl₃·7H₂O were successful ... with as little as 0.2–0.3 equiv of the additive."
- "addition of sodium borohydride to a mixture of 4 and CeCl₃·7H₂O was exothermic (ΔH = ‑311 kJ/mol) with an adiabatic temperature rise of 32 °C, and a maximum gas release rate of 58 L/min·kg."
- "we rationalized that the expected release of flammable hydrogen gas could pose safety challenges upon scale‑up and sought to minimize the risk by adding the borohydride in multiple lots (at least four) with adequate nitrogen sweep."
- "Compound 4 (3.30 kg ...) was charged into a pre‑cleaned 600 L Hastelloy reactor ... NaBH₄ (780 g, 1.7 equiv) was added in four equal portions over 30 min ... maintaining the internal temperature below 0 °C."
- "The workup procedure was further optimized, and the process was successfully scaled up to >100 kg scale."

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for Glecaprevir via Ring-Closing Metathesis
Problem_Description: Fluorination of aldehyde 9 using diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST) gave a low isolated yield (≈40 % on scale), generated hazardous HF‑containing waste, and produced substantial amounts of side‑products 12 and 13 that required chromatographic removal.
Solution_Description: The fluorination was re‑optimised in CH₂Cl₂ with 2.5 equiv of DAST (reduced from 5 equiv) and a catalytic amount of 2,6‑lutidine to suppress HF‑induced side‑reactions. The reaction mixture was quenched into aqueous K₂HPO₄, extracted with heptane, and the aqueous layer was treated with bisulfite to convert side‑product 12 back to aldehyde 9, which was isolated as its bisulfite adduct and crystallised (35 % recovery). The crude fluorination product 11 was then carried forward without chromatography. This work‑up allowed recycling of aldehyde 9 and avoided the hazardous handling of excess DAST.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The first major challenge was the fluorination of aldehyde 9, which proceeded in less than 50 % yield, employed the hazardous reagent diethylaminosulfur trifluoride (DAST)…” (Introduction)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for Glecaprevir via Ring-Closing Metathesis
Problem_Description: The original route to carbamate 5 gave only 12 % overall yield and required chromatographic purification of the diol intermediate, making the sequence inefficient for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: A new sequence was developed that employed an enzymatic kinetic resolution of acetate 23 using Novozym 435 (immobilised Candida antarctica lipase B). This gave the desired (R,R)‑alcohol 14 in 47 % overall yield from the racemic acetate, eliminating chromatography. Subsequent conversion to the chloroformate 25 and coupling with tert‑leucine proceeded cleanly, with the final carbamate 5 isolated by simple crystallisation (80 % yield) and only one distillation and one crystallisation required.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The overall five‑step sequence produced carbamate 5 in a 26 % yield from cyclopentene oxide, without chromatography and with only one distillation and one crystallisation required for purification.” (Sec 2.3)

Solution_Description: The indium‑mediated coupling was performed in a reactor with an agitator that nearly touched the bottom, preventing indium settling and restoring the 84 % yield of the alkylation step. The reaction was performed under nitrogen with degassed solvents to eliminate oxygen sensitivity. Oxidation of alcohol 32 to ketone 28 was switched to T3P/DMSO at 0 °C, avoiding Dess‑Martin waste and improving safety. A slight under‑charge of ethyl glyoxylate (0.9 equiv) reduced by‑product formation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The formation of the allyl indium species was found to be sensitive to the mixing efficiency… the indium settled on the bottom… resulting in a 10 % lower yield… the reaction was run in a reactor with an agitator nearly touching the bottom of the reactor.” (Sec 2.4)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for Glecaprevir via Ring-Closing Metathesis
Problem_Description: The key ring‑closing metathesis (RCM) to form the 18‑membered macrocycle gave only 59 % isolated yield, required 9 mol % of the expensive Zhan 1B catalyst, and generated cis‑alkene and dimer impurities that were difficult to remove by chromatography.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A systematic optimisation was performed: (i) toluene was chosen as the optimal solvent; (ii) the reaction temperature was set to 40 °C to minimise the cis‑isomer 36 while maintaining reasonable rate; (iii) a very high dilution (80 mL toluene per gram of diene 4, ~0.02 M) was used to suppress dimer formation; (iv) substrate and catalyst were added slowly over 6 h (later extended to 18 h for larger scale) to keep the concentration low; (v) the reaction mixture was sparged with nitrogen (10–12 SCFM) to remove ethylene and drive conversion; (vi) after reaction, imidazole and Filtrol were added to quench and adsorb catalyst, followed by two sequential silica‑gel plugs (2 g g⁻¹ and 6–7 g g⁻¹ of 4) that removed the catalyst, the dimer impurity 37 and reduced Ru to ~10 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The RCM reaction proved to be a significantly challenging step… 59 % yield, employed 9 mol % of the Zhan 1B catalyst, and required chromatographic purification.” (Sec 2.5)

Paper Title: Development of the Enabling Route for Glecaprevir via Ring-Closing Metathesis
Problem_Description: The final amide coupling of amino sulfonamide 2 with macrocyclic acid 3 required a laborious aqueous work‑up and offered negligible impurity removal; the reaction was originally performed in dichloromethane, a toxic solvent.

The HOPO‑activated ester of 3 was prepared in a separate reactor and added slowly to the amine 2/triethylamine mixture, allowing near‑quantitative conversion with only 1.1 equiv of 2. The crystallisation of the crude API gave 93 % isolated yield and rejected the cis‑isomer impurity to 0.37 % (further reduced to 0.15 % after a second recrystallisation).

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Vortex Reactor for Gram to Kilo Scale for UV and Visible Photochemistry
Problem_Description: Scaling the continuous Taylor vortex reactor to a 20‑30‑fold larger volume while preserving vortex strength and efficient gas (O₂) entrainment. The larger rotor must rotate slower to maintain the same tangential velocity, which reduces the amount of air drawn in and limits reactor productivity when relying on atmospheric oxygen.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A new reactor was built using a standard jacketed filter‑tube (glass) with a sealed steel base and polymer cap, housing a hollow polymer rotor. The gap was kept at 2 mm and rotation speed was set to ~1300 rpm (determined by CFD) to retain vortex strength. A dedicated gas inlet was added to allow controlled O₂ flow, removing the reliance on atmospheric drawing and enabling higher productivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “...by increasing the size of the cylinders while maintaining the gap size to achieve a scaled up reactor.”
2. “...the larger cylinder has to be rotated at only a fraction of the speed… However, one drawback of the slower rotation speed is that there is less air entrained… we opted to have the option of adding a gas flow into the reactor.”
3. “...the final design of the reactor … consists of the jacketed filter‑tube … with a hollow polymer rotor inside. The rotation is driven from a motor … Inlet ports for gas and liquids are bored through the steel base…"
4. “CFD studies indicated that … a rotation speed of 1300 rpm would be required for the large reactor … to generate vortices of a similar strength.”

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Vortex Reactor for Gram to Kilo Scale for UV and Visible Photochemistry
Problem_Description: In the UV [2 + 2] cycloaddition, a single 1.4 kW Hg lamp gave only 63 % conversion at 10 mL min⁻¹, and yield fell below 60 % at higher flow rates because the light intensity was insufficient to fully convert the substrate.
Solution_Description: The lamp power was increased by adding a second 1.4 kW lamp (total 2.8 kW) and then a pair of 2 kW lamps (total 4 kW). This raised conversion to 85 % and finally to quantitative conversion (>99 %) at higher flow rates, restoring productivity.
Supporting_Evidence:
1. “Using this set‑up … a single 1.4 kW lamp … conversion and yield dropped to 63 % and 59 % at 10 mL min⁻¹.”
2. “When a second 1.4 kW lamp was added … the yield increased to 85 %.”
3. “When 4 kW (2 × 2 kW) of lamp power was used … quantitative conversion … observed.”
4. “Switching the jacketed glass vessel from borosilicate to quartz opened up the possibility of capturing more light … however, fouling was observed.”

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Vortex Reactor for Gram to Kilo Scale for UV and Visible Photochemistry

Supporting_Evidence:

2. “No fouling of the reactor was apparent for this reaction when the borosilicate reactor was used.”

Paper Title: Scalable Continuous Vortex Reactor for Gram to Kilo Scale for UV and Visible Photochemistry

Supporting_Evidence:

2. “CFD studies indicated that when Ta is fixed … a rotation speed of 1300 rpm would be required for the large reactor … to generate vortices of a similar strength.”
