Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: Lawesson’s reagent is malodorous, hazardous to handle on‑kilogram scale, generates lipophilic by‑products that are difficult to remove by crystallisation, and requires large volumes (15–20 vol) of CH₂Cl₂ in the first acylation step.
Solution_Description: Adopt a new synthetic route that starts from the commercially available amino‑thiadiazole (5) and avoids the use of Lawesson’s reagent entirely.
Supporting_Evidence: • "the use of malodorous Lawesson’s reagent was assessed to be very challenging to handle in our kilolab" (Introduction).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: The Sandmeyer bromination leaves high levels of residual copper (> 1000 ppm) in the crude bromo‑thiadiazole (6), which poisons the Pd catalyst in the subsequent Suzuki–Miyaura coupling.
Solution_Description: Introduce an inline charcoal treatment (and an extra brine wash) after the aqueous work‑up to scavenge copper from the organic phase before crystallisation.
Supporting_Evidence: • "ICP‑MS analysis showed that the crude product was contaminated with high levels of residual copper (> 1000 ppm)" (Process Development).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: On kilogram scale the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling is sluggish, requiring 24 h and giving only 61 % isolated yield because residual Cu interferes with the Pd‑catalyst system.
Solution_Description: Apply the improved charcoal‑treatment of the Sandmeyer product, which reduces Cu to < 20 ppm and restores rapid, high‑yielding coupling at 1 mol % Pd.
Supporting_Evidence: • "the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling was very slow on a 1.0 kg scale, and we added a total of 3.0 mol % of the catalyst to reach full conversion after 24 h" (Scale Up).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: The fluorinated boronic acid (7) undergoes protodeboronation when heated above ~55 °C, leading to loss of the aryl partner.
Solution_Description: Run the Suzuki–Miyaura coupling at room temperature using a mild organic base (N‑methylmorpholine) and the Pd(OAc)₂/Xantphos catalyst system, which tolerates the sensitive boronic acid.
Supporting_Evidence: • "protodeboronation ... started to be observed ... after gradually heating to 55 °C" (Initial Experiments).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: Strong inorganic bases in THF/H₂O cause hydrolysis of the ethyl ester of bromo‑thiadiazole (6) to the carboxylate salt, reducing product purity.
Solution_Description: Employ a biphasic toluene/H₂O system with the mild base N‑methylmorpholine, which suppresses ester saponification while maintaining good mixing.
Supporting_Evidence: • "hydrolysis of the ethyl ester in the starting material … led to a diminished overall purity" (Process Development).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: At kilogram scale the Suzuki coupling required 24 h, leading to lower isolated yield (61 %) and partial hydrolysis of the starting material.
Solution_Description: After the copper‑removal improvement, the reaction could be performed at 1 mol % Pd loading, reaching full conversion in 7 h with 85 % isolated yield, demonstrating that the bottleneck was the copper impurity rather than reactor design.
Supporting_Evidence: • "the reaction was very slow … 24 h … isolated yield dropped to 61 %" (Scale Up).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: Crude bromo‑thiadiazole (6) is highly soluble in many organic solvents and tends to oil‑out from non‑polar solvents, making crystallisation difficult.
Solution_Description: Introduce a solvent‑swap step (iPrOAc/MeCN → EtOH) followed by addition of water to induce crystallisation from a 2:1 H₂O/EtOH mixture, giving a solid that can be filtered.
Supporting_Evidence: • "the crude product was highly soluble in a wide range of organic solvents … the crude product could be successfully recrystallized from a 2:1‑mixture of H₂O and EtOH" (Process Development).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: tert‑Butyl nitrite decomposes explosively (2175 kJ kg⁻¹ at 180 °C) and the Sandmeyer reaction releases a significant exotherm (≈93 kJ kg⁻¹) when added.
Solution_Description: Control the addition of tert‑butyl nitrite over 30 min at 23 °C, monitor heat with calorimetry, and keep the reaction temperature below 65 °C, ensuring a safe, dose‑controlled process.
Supporting_Evidence: • "DSC analysis of tert‑butyl nitrite showed a highly energetic, autocatalytic decomposition (2175 kJ kg⁻¹) at 180 °C" (Process Development).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: The free carboxylic acid of the target thiadiazole (1) decarboxylates instantly at room temperature, precluding direct use in amide coupling.
Solution_Description: Generate a stable lithium carboxylate (9‑Li) by reacting the ethyl ester with LiOH·H₂O in THF/H₂O at 45 °C; the salt crystallises directly and can be used in the subsequent amide coupling.
Supporting_Evidence: • "the free acid of 1 was found to be completely unstable and decarboxylated in minutes at room temperature" (Formation of Carboxylate Salt).

Paper Title: Development of a Scalable Route for a Key Thiadiazole Building Block via Sequential Sandmeyer Bromination and Room-Temperature Suzuki–Miyaura Coupling
Problem_Description: Potassium salt 9‑K formed from KOTMS is poorly filterable and insoluble in both organic solvents and water, hindering isolation.
Solution_Description: Switch to lithium salt formation (9‑Li) which crystallises quantitatively, filters easily, and is soluble in DMF for the downstream amide step.
Supporting_Evidence: • "9‑K showed poor filterability and was also completely insoluble in any organic solvent and H₂O" (Formation of Carboxylate Salt).

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: The one‑pot protocol reported by Olofsson required a non‑commercial, moisture‑sensitive alkynyl‑boronic ester (4b). Its preparation and purification are difficult, making the overall route impractical for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the problematic boronic‑ester with commercially available tri‑isopropyl‑acetylene (4c) and p‑toluenesulfonic acid, creating a true one‑step synthesis that uses only readily available reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “However, the used alkynyl boronic ester 4b is difficult to synthesize and purify.”; “We therefore wondered if commercially available tri‑isopropyl‑acetylene could be used directly in the Olofsson protocol.”; “The reaction proceeds smoothly on multigram scale to give TIPS‑EBX (1) in >80 % yield… only commercially available starting materials can be used without further purification.”

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: When the commercial TIPS‑acetylene was employed under the original Olofsson conditions (room temperature, 30 min), only a very low isolated yield of TIPS‑EBX was obtained because the terminal alkyne is insufficiently nucleophilic.
Solution_Description: The authors switched the solvent from dichloromethane to 1,2‑dichloroethane, raised the reaction temperature to 55 °C and extended the coupling time to 24 h, which gave complete alkyne transfer and high isolated yields.
Supporting_Evidence: “Only a very low yield of TIPS‑EBX could be isolated using the reported reaction conditions (rt, 30 min for alkyne transfer).”; “Replacing dichloromethane by 1,2‑dichloroethane and performing the reaction at 55 °C for 24 h led to full alkyne transfer.”

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: Hypervalent iodine reagents are known to decompose exothermically; uncontrolled heat release could present a safety hazard during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: The process was designed with controlled addition of m‑CPBA, subsequent heating at a modest 55 °C, and keeping reagent concentrations low, resulting in adiabatic temperature rises below 15 °C for the oxidation and cyclization steps.
Supporting_Evidence: “Thermal analysis of the synthesis procedure showed only weak exotherms.”; Table 1 shows adiabatic temperature rises of 11 °C (oxidation) and 12 °C (cyclization).; “The oxidation step was also conveniently run at the same temperature, after addition of m‑CPBA and p‑TsOH at room temperature.”

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: Residual p‑toluenesulfonate (tosylate) impurities were found to lower the decomposition onset temperature of TIPS‑EBX, compromising its thermal stability and safety.
Solution_Description: A rigorous work‑up involving three successive water washes, followed by recrystallization/precipitation from acetonitrile, removed the tosylate salts, raising purity to >99 % and increasing the DSC decomposition onset to >140 °C.
Supporting_Evidence: “Care had to be taken to completely remove traces of tosylate salts, as these impurities diminish the thermal stability of TIPS‑EBX.”; “Purity improved to almost 98 %… and the onset of the decomposition temperature increased to 131 °C.”; “Precipitation through addition of acetonitrile… solids had a purity above 99 %… and the onset of decomposition occurred now at 144 °C.”

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: In the original Zhdankin protocol, removal of solvents before basification was considered potentially hazardous.
Solution_Description: The new protocol performs the cyclization directly in the crude mixture by adding a saturated NaHCO₃ solution, eliminating the need to evaporate solvents prior to basification and reducing exposure to hazardous conditions.
Supporting_Evidence: “The cyclization step can be easily performed by just stirring the crude reaction mixture with a bicarbonate solution, avoiding the potentially hazardous removal of solvents prior to basification.”

Paper Title: One-Pot Synthesis of 1‑[(Triisopropyl­silyl)­ethynyl]-1,2-benziodoxol-3(1
Problem_Description: Batch‑to‑batch differences in impurity levels caused variability in thermal stability, raising concerns about consistency and safety.
Solution_Description: Standardized the washing, recrystallization, and storage (−20 °C) procedures, and used consistent DSC scanning protocols to obtain reproducible purity and decomposition data.
Supporting_Evidence: “A batch‑to‑batch dependency was observed, with decomposition starting from 100 °C to 140 °C.”; “Purity improved… and the onset of decomposition increased…”; “DSC analysis performed on TIPS‑EBX after 4 months of storage at −20 °C showed no significant difference.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Low solubility of the base in acetone limited conversion of the substitution step; the reaction required a stronger, more polar solvent to dissolve the base and proceed efficiently.
Solution_Description: The solvent was switched from acetone to DMF, whose higher dielectric constant (36.7 vs 20.7) improved base solubility and accelerated the reaction.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The higher dielectric point of DMF compared to acetone (36.7 vs 20.7) allowed better solubility of the base and permitted a faster rate of reaction.”
• “The Step 2 substitution reaction solvent was modified from acetone to DMF.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: During batch scale‑up the benzodioxan product decomposed when exposed to the high‑temperature SNAr conditions for an extended period, resulting in markedly lower isolated yields.
Solution_Description: A continuous‑flow plug‑flow reactor (PFR) with rapid heat‑up / cool‑down and precise temperature control was employed, limiting the residence time at high temperature and preventing product decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “We speculated that the product might not be stable under the reaction conditions over an extended period… lower isolated product yields… due to the extended cool‑down time.”
• “The continuous flow reactor allowed for rapid thermal equilibration, which minimized problematic product decomposition by reducing the time that the product was exposed to high temperature.”
• “We initially became interested in continuous flow technology for its safety and control aspects… This small reactor size permits a wide temperature range with rapid heat‑up and cool‑down time.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Traditional SNAr conditions using an alkali base in polar aprotic solvents generated a regio‑isomeric impurity (1b), lowering the isolated yield of the desired product.
Solution_Description: The impurity formation was suppressed by employing a less‑polar solvent (diglyme), an organic base (DBU), and higher reaction temperatures, which favored the desired cyclization pathway.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the starting material 2 was treated with alkali base in polar aprotic solvents, an undesired product regioisomer was observed.”
• “The formation of this regioisomer impurity could be suppressed by using a less polar solvent, an organic base, and high temperature.”
• “DBU remained our preferred base… The undesired impurity 1b was not observed under these reaction conditions.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Use of sodium hydride (NaH) in the SNAr cyclization posed safety hazards and required careful handling, prompting a search for milder bases.
Solution_Description: NaH was replaced with the milder organic base DBU, which provided comparable conversion while reducing safety concerns.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When the reaction was performed at 140 °C with NaH (60 % in mineral oil)… we were able to obtain a 54 % isolated product yield.”
• “In order to avoid the use of NaH, we turned to milder bases. … DBU remained our preferred base for this reaction.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Using DBU at 140 °C required a 20‑hour reaction time for complete conversion; the prolonged exposure at high temperature led to product decomposition and poor mass balance.
Solution_Description: Increasing the reaction temperature to 240 °C and raising the DBU equivalents (to 2.6–7.8 equiv) dramatically shortened the reaction time and gave >99 % conversion with minimal decomposition.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When DBU was used as a base, the reaction required 20 h to achieve complete conversion… we suspected that this was due to product decomposition over an extended period at high temperature.”
• “Increasing the temperature to 240 °C significantly increased the conversion… further improved by increasing the equivalents of base to 2.6 equiv, giving 99 % conversion.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Potassium carbonate gave no conversion, while tert‑butoxide caused decomposition of starting material and generated many impurities.
Solution_Description: The base was switched to DBU, which provided high conversion without the decomposition observed for t‑BuOK.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “When K₂CO₃ was used… there was no conversion of starting material.”
• “Stronger bases such as t‑BuOK led to decomposition of starting material, resulting in a significant number of impurities.”
• “DBU remained our preferred base for this reaction.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: Batch runs at larger scale suffered lower isolated yields and product purity due to incomplete cooling and difficulty removing residual solvent.
Solution_Description: A 16.4 m Hastelloy tubular PFR was used with a back‑pressure regulator (750 psi) to keep the reaction mixture liquid above its boiling point, and the solvent volume was reduced from 15 mL g⁻¹ to 10 mL g⁻¹, improving product purity and overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The back‑pressure of the reactor was set to 750 psi, and the oven temperature was set to 225 °C… The reactor could be heated to the desired temperature (220 °C) within 1 min and cooled back to room temperature within 1 min.”
• “When 10 mL/g of solvent was used… the purity of the isolated product was superior….”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: The original bromination step used pyrrolidone hydrogen tribromide, an expensive and less‑available reagent.
Solution_Description: The bromination reagent was changed to inexpensive N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS), providing an efficient and cost‑effective monobromination.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The bromination reagent in Step 1 was changed from pyrrolidone hydrogen tribromide to readily available N‑bromosuccinimide.”

Paper Title: Continuous Flow Conditions for High Temperature Formation of a Benzodioxan Pharmaceutical Intermediate: Rapid Scaleup for Early Phase Material Delivery
Problem_Description: The CBS reduction of ketone 6 gave poor enantioselectivity (79.1 % ee) and implied possible side‑reaction/decomposition.
Solution_Description: The CBS reduction was replaced with a ruthenium‑catalyzed asymmetric transfer hydrogenation, delivering >95 % ee and high isolated yield on multi‑kilogram scale.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The enantioselectivity of the Step 3 CBS reduction… was poor (79.1 % ee).”
• “Ruthenium systems are well established… we investigated several ruthenium catalysts… RuCl[(R,R)-Tsdpen]‑(p‑cymene) was selected… resulted in high quality alcohol 2 with high ee on 963 g scale (95.8 % ee).”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: The original tricomponent cyclization (Method A) required hyper‑toxic KCN and gave a low isolated yield of only 29 %.  Method B avoided KCN but employed the hyper‑toxic, foul‑smelling and very expensive isonitrile 3, which could dominate the cost of the whole route.
Solution_Description: A catalyst‑free bicomponent alkylation/condensation cyclization was developed using inexpensive, readily available 5‑bromo‑3‑methylpyridin‑2‑amine (2) and ethyl 2‑bromo‑3‑oxopentanoate (15).  This new route eliminates the need for KCN or isonitrile 3, removes hazardous reagents and improves the overall yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“First, the involvement of the hypertoxic KCN was an inevitable challenge to industrial manufacturing; more importantly, the cyclization reaction suffered from low yield (29%).”
“the involvement of 1,1,3,3‑tetramethylbutyl isonitrile ( 3 ) was indeed troublesome…hypertoxic…prohibitively expensive (5 g: ≈ 170 $; 500 g: ≈ 4096 $).”
“a catalyst‑free bicomponent cyclization … efficiently resulted in the imidazo‑[1,2‑a]‑pyridine skeleton 16.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: The initial solvent system (EtOH) in the cyclization gave only 87 % conversion and 69.1 % isolated yield; addition of bases (TEA, NaHCO₃) further reduced conversion, indicating sub‑optimal reaction media and possible phase/viscosity issues.
Solution_Description: Switching the solvent to n‑butanol (n‑BuOH) without any added base increased the conversion to >99 % and the isolated yield to 78.5 %, providing a more homogeneous, higher‑performing reaction medium.
Supporting_Evidence:
“EtOH was chosen as the solvent…87 % conversion…69.1 % yield…Although the unreacted 2 could be easily recovered…the relatively low conversion ratio was quite unsatisfying.”
“n‑BuOH resulted to be the preferred one, which could realize >99 % conversion ratio and 78.5 % yield.”
“Taking n‑BuOH as the optimal solvent (without bases), 16 could be obtained in the kilogram scale (yield 77.6 %).”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: Attempted Hofmann rearrangement of carboxylic acid 17 (using NaOH/Br₂ or NaClO) failed to produce the desired amine, providing no product and raising safety concerns with handling bromine reagents.
Solution_Description: A Curtius rearrangement was adopted, employing diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA) as the azide source to generate the acyl‑azide intermediate, which smoothly yielded the carbamate 19f in 79.3 % yield.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the following Hofmann rearrangement strategy (NaOH/Br₂ or NaClO) failed to produce 4.”
“the Curtius rearrangement reaction was thereby taken into consideration…DPPA was selected for the generation of acyl azide intermediate.”
“Screening…3,5‑dichlorobenzyl alcohol 18f (entry 6) turned out to be the best choice with a relatively high yield (79.3 %) and purity (95.4 %).”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: DPPA is an organophosphate ester that is toxic and can release large amounts of N₂ gas rapidly, posing a safety hazard during scale‑up.
Solution_Description: DPPA was added slowly (≤ 500 mL h⁻¹) to control the release of nitrogen gas and mitigate the toxic exposure, ensuring a safe exotherm‑controlled process.
Supporting_Evidence:
“It should be noted that the potential risk of DPPA may be reduced by slow addition (<500 mL/h), which could allow the slow release of N₂.”
“Caution! DPPA should be added slowly (<500 mL/h) under stirring.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: Multiple deprotection conditions for the carbamate 19f (Pd/C + H₂, NiCl₂ + NaBH₄, HCl (g), TMSI, Bu₄NF, 20 % NaOH, HBr in H₂O) gave either no conversion or undesired side‑products, showing poor reproducibility and low yields.
Solution_Description: Optimized deprotection using HBr (4–6 equiv) in acetic acid (33 % HBr/HOAc) gave >97 % conversion and 86–89 % isolated yields, providing a robust, high‑yielding protocol.
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 3 shows entries 1–7 with 0–53 % conversion or no product.
“Finally, 40 % HBr aqueous solution was tested with only a 10 % conversion ratio… HBr (4 equiv) in HOAc was first applied and a surprisingly 97 % conversion ratio was achieved, resulting in 8 in a high yield.”
“when the HBr amount was increased to 6 equiv, the raw material was completely consumed and an 89.1 % yield was achieved.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: The N‑alkylation of amine 8 with bromide 9 under NaH base caused hydrolysis of 9 (conversion to 9′) and low product yield, indicating base‑induced decomposition and safety concerns with strong base.
Solution_Description: The base was changed from NaH to K₂CO₃ in MeCN, which suppressed hydrolysis and afforded an 83.1 % yield of the N‑alkylated product 10 on scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence:
“the N‑alkylation reaction between 8 and 9 in the catalysis of NaH was proved to be unstable…hydrolysis product of 9 turned out to be the main product.”
“we alternatively utilized the K₂CO₃/MeCN system, which finally achieved a robust synthetic process…83.1 % yield in a scale‑up batch.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: In the Buchwald C–N coupling, the choice of phosphine ligand dramatically affected the yield of product 13 (e.g., JohnPhos gave 83.0 % while XantPhos gave 31.7 %).
Solution_Description: Systematic screening identified JohnPhos as the optimal ligand with t‑BuONa base in toluene, delivering >83 % isolated yield on 300–400 g scale; other ligands and bases were discarded.
Supporting_Evidence:
Table 4 shows ligand‑dependent yields: “JohnPhos…83.0 % yield”, “XantPhos…31.7 % yield”, “BINAP…22.3 % yield”.
“Screening verified that the original condition turned out to be optimal and an 82.7 % yield could be achieved in a 300–400 g scale.”

Paper Title: Catalyst-Free Cyclization- and Curtius Rearrangement-Induced Functional Group Transformation: An Improved Synthetic Strategy of First-in-Class ATX Inhibitor Ziritaxestat (GLPG-1690)
Problem_Description: The previously reported synthetic routes required three separate protecting‑group introductions and removals, leading to a very low overall efficiency and high material cost.
Solution_Description: The new eight‑step route integrates a catalyst‑free cyclization, Curtius rearrangement, and a single N‑alkylation, eliminating unnecessary protecting‑group steps and achieving a 20.4 % overall yield with cost‑effective reagents.
Supporting_Evidence:
“Generally, both the synthetic strategies mentioned above involved three independent introduction and removal of protecting groups, which accounted for their very poor efficiency.”
“The new route…avoided the hypertoxic KCN and the hypertoxic and costly isonitrile 3…a novel, scalable, and cost‑effective route was favorably developed to afford Ziritaxestat in a 20.4 % overall yield.”

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: Filter‑plate blockage caused liquid to remain trapped on the cake, leading to inconsistent solvent removal, lower filtration flow rates and variable product moisture.
Solution_Description: A “back‑pulse” of compressed air was added to the first filter plate and the wash‑in‑place (WIP) sequence was improved (longer contact time, larger solvent volume) to clear fines and prevent media blinding.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “blockage of filter plate, resulting in liquid volume not being fully drawn through the cake.” (Table 5) 
• “A “back pulse” feature will be added to port 1 where a back pulse of compressed air will be applied … helping to clear fines from the filter plate therefore improving filtration performance.” (Table 5) 
• “Improvement to WIP sequence. For example, WIP sequence will now include a “contact time” to allow more time for WIP solvent to dissolve material within the filter plate before being drawn through the filter plate.” (Table 5)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: Slurry splashes on the tube walls were interpreted by the vision system as liquid‑level changes, preventing the filtration step from halting at dry‑land and causing non‑consistent deliquoring.
Solution_Description: The vision‑software was modified to ignore transient jumps in the detected liquid level and a ‘drip‑check’ routine was added to filter out false signals caused by splashes.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “filtration (port 1, 2, and 3) did not halt at dry land due to slurry splashes on the walls of the tube.” (Table 5) 
• “splashes on the tube walls may cause the camera to briefly detect the splashes as a light‑to‑dark transition, therefore incorrectly measuring this splash as the liquid level.” (Table 5) 
• “to prevent this, if the liquid level detected by the camera momentarily jumps to another position, the software will ignore this and continue to measure the true liquid level.” (Table 5) 
• “a ‘drip‑check’ feature will be added to the software to ignore any disruption to the meniscus.” (Table 5)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: Drops of wash solvent falling from the atomizer disrupted the meniscus, leading to loss of liquid‑level detection and inconsistent washing.
Solution_Description: The pump was reversed after dispensing to reduce solvent dripping and a software ‘drip‑check’ was implemented to ignore meniscus disturbances.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “drops of solvent falling into the tube, resulting in disturbance of meniscus, leading to loss of liquid level detection.” (Table 5) 
• “reduction of solvent dropping from the atomizer by reversing the pump after dispensing.” (Table 5) 
• “a ‘drip‑check’ feature will be added to the software to ignore any disruption to the meniscus.” (Table 5)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: Low drying‑gas flow in production mode resulted in higher residual solvent (LOD ≈ 12 %) and solvent composition different from batch predictions.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Future units will use a larger‑ID heated transfer line, pressure regulators to increase inlet gas flow, and a floating base to improve the seal between carousel and filter base, thereby increasing drying‑gas throughput.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The discrepancy in LOD and solvent composition … due to … low drying gas flow through each cake.” (Section 3.2) 
• “The gas flowrate will be improved on future units by providing a larger ID heated transfer line. Pressure regulators on the inlet of the drying gas will be included to allow the use of compressed air with an inlet pressure of +250 mbar.” (Section 3.2) 
• “a floating base has been designed for the filter base, allowing for an improved seal between the base of the carousel and the filter base on future units.” (Section 3.2)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: During the first wash step the pure wash solvent caused API dissolution and subsequent precipitation (antisolvent effect), risking impurity incorporation and loss of product.
Solution_Description: An antisolvent‑screening study identified optimal mixed wash solvents; a 50 % ethanol / 50 % n‑heptane mixture was used for wash 1 to suppress API dissolution while still removing impurities.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “To avoid ‘antisolvent effect’ … the first stage wash was prepared using a mixture of pure crystallization and wash solvents. The composition was selected based on the wash solvent screening methodology.” (Section 3.1.2) 
• Table 2 shows the selected solvent mixtures, e.g., “ethanol – heptane = 50‑50 % (v/v)” for wash 1. 
• “The wash solvent used was a mixture of ethanol–heptane (50–50 % v/v), used to prevent antisolvent effect during washing.” (Section 3.1.3)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: High viscosity of the isoamyl‑alcohol crystallization solvent slowed filtrate flow and reduced filtration efficiency.
Solution_Description: Ethanol or isopropanol, which have lower viscosities, were selected as alternative crystallization solvents to improve filtration rates.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “The filtrate flow rate … faster flow rates were observed for less viscous solvents (ethanol 1.61 cP, isopropanol 2.88 cP, isoamyl alcohol 4.81 cP).” (Figure 6) 
• “The crystallization solvent also affects cake volume … isoamyl alcohol … higher density … reduces cake packing.” (Section 3.1.2) 
• “Ethanol, the least viscous and most volatile crystallization solvent, is retained least, causing a reduction of the LOD.” (Section 3.1.4)

Paper Title: Developing a Batch Isolation Procedure and Running It in an Automated Semicontinuous Unit: AWL CFD25 Case Study
Problem_Description: Isoamyl alcohol had a very low API solubility, which limited API loss but also reduced impurity removal efficiency.
Solution_Description: Isoamyl alcohol was identified as a promising crystallization solvent for low API dissolution while isopropanol was preferred for better impurity removal balance.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “Isoamyl alcohol … lower API solubility … 0.047 g/g at 20 °C.” (Section 3.1.2) 
• “The second most promising crystallization solvent is 2‑propanol for its low API solubility and high impurity solubility.” (Section 3.1.2)

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Stoichiometric use of DDQ generates equimolar DDHQ, leading to difficult purification on large scale, and DDQ is expensive and releases toxic HCN on work‑up.
Solution_Description: Replace stoichiometric DDQ with catalytic DDQ (10–20 mol %) together with catalytic HNO₃ as a co‑oxidant that regenerates DDQ from DDHQ, eliminating the need for stoichiometric DDQ and reducing HCN formation.
Supporting_Evidence:
• “the stoichiometric use of DDQ often causes purification difficulties … due to the concomitant formation of the corresponding hydroquinone (DDHQ) in equimolar quantities.”
• “DDQ is relatively expensive and poses some toxicity concerns due to the release of stoichiometric amounts of HCN upon workup.”
• “We became interested in developing a practical, cost‑effective, and scalable oxidation process using HNO₃ as a source of NO to regenerate DDQ from DDHQ.”
• “We initiated this study … using 10 mol % DDQ and 20 mol % HNO₃ … Increasing the catalyst loadings from 10 to 20 mol % DDQ and from 20 to 40 mol % HNO₃ led to the best results, with up to 85 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Several common solvents (THF, Me‑THF, DME, MTBE) gave poor conversion, indicating inadequate mixing/solubility of the catalytic system.
Solution_Description: Switch to chlorinated solvents (DCE, then DCM) which provided substantially higher yields (64–77 %).
Supporting_Evidence:
• “THF, Me‑THF, DME, or even MTBE … led to poor yields … while the chlorinated solvents DCE and DCM afforded the desired ketone … in 64 and 77 % yield, respectively.”
• “The higher yield and, more importantly, the lower flammability of DCM compared with DCE made DCM particularly suitable for the development of a potential aerobic oxidation process.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Initial conditions (10 mol % DDQ, 20 mol % HNO₃, 18 h) gave low conversions (<5 % in many solvents) and modest yield (28 % in DCM after 4 h).
Solution_Description: Increase catalyst/oxidant loadings to 20 mol % DDQ and 40 mol % HNO₃ and keep the 18 h reaction time, boosting isolated yields to up to 85 %.
Supporting_Evidence:
• Table 1 entries 1‑4 show <5 % yield; entry 6 (DCM, 18 h) gives 77 % yield.
• “Increasing the catalyst loadings from 10 to 20 mol % DDQ and from 20 to 40 mol % HNO₃ led to the best results, with up to 85 % isolated yield.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Potential exothermic behavior and unknown thermal stability of the DDQ/HNO₃/O₂ mixture raise safety concerns for scale‑up.
Solution_Description: Differential scanning calorimetry was performed; the reaction showed only a weak exotherm (ΔH = −34 J g⁻¹) with no rapid heat or decomposition, demonstrating that the process is safe for scale‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: • “Safety hazards were also evaluated by differential scanning calorimetry … The plot showed a weak exothermic phenomenon (ΔH = −34 J·g⁻¹) initiated at 184 °C … Evaluation of the thermal behavior of the reaction showed no rapid heat generation or rapid decomposition, and no risk of explosive hazards could be detected.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Bubbling air through the reaction releases hazardous nitrous gases, posing health and reactivity hazards.
Solution_Description: A second charging of 0.1 equiv DDQ and 0.2 equiv HNO₃ was added to complete conversion while minimizing gas release; future work will explore pressure vessels and flow chemistry to control the issue.
Supporting_Evidence: • “The introduction of air by bubbling did need to be assessed, however, as it caused the release of hazardous nitrous gas … To circumvent the latter issue, a second recharge of DDQ (0.1 equiv)/HNO₃ (0.2 equiv) was operated, which enabled quasi‑complete conversion … This gas release issue will be further examined … implementation of pressure vessels and flow chemistry.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: Running the reaction in an open flask or under O₂ bubbling gave inferior results compared with a sealed tube with an O₂ balloon, indicating poor gas–liquid mass transfer.
Solution_Description: Perform the oxidation in a sealed tube fitted with an O₂ balloon, which improves the gas‑liquid interface and overall conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: • “A rapid evaluation of the setup showed that running the reaction in a sealed tube fitted with an oxygen balloon led to better results than running the reaction in an open flask or under molecular oxygen bubbling.”

Paper Title: Scalable Aerobic Oxidation of Alcohols Using Catalytic DDQ/HNO
Problem_Description: After scale‑up, isolation of the ketone product could be simplified to avoid an additional purification step.
Solution_Description: After the reaction, a simple aqueous work‑up and concentration to dryness provided the product directly, allowing a solvent swap later if needed without intermediate isolation.
Supporting_Evidence: • “It is worth pointing out that a solvent swap from DCM (reaction and extractive solvent) to any other solvent can easily be performed after the workup, thus avoiding any isolation step.”

Paper Title: Investigation into an Unexpected Impurity: A Practical Approach to Process Development for the Addition of Grignard Reagents to Aldehydes Using Continuous Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: During the batch addition of MeMgBr to methyl 4‑formyl benzoate (1a) a significant amount of a trimerized by‑product (3a) is formed, reducing the isolated yield of the desired alcohol (2a). The impurity originates from an Oppenauer oxidation of the Mg‑salt of 2a by the remaining aldehyde, followed by two aldol condensations, i.e. a decomposition pathway that diverts material from the target product.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The reaction is transferred to a continuous‑flow platform equipped with a micromixer. Fast mixing dramatically shortens the time that 1a and the Mg‑salt of 2a coexist, suppressing the Oppenauer oxidation/aldol sequence and limiting formation of 3a to ≤0.5 % while maintaining near‑quantitative conversion to 2a.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “This led us to try applying continuous flow synthesis to the process to shorten the time during which the starting material coexists with the Mg salt of the target product…drastic suppression of the byproduct under very mild conditions.” (Abstract) 2. “The fast mixing by the application of continuous flow synthesis led to a short coexistence time of 1a and the Mg salt of 2a, which was effective for suppressing the byproduct 3a as expected.” (Results) 3. Table 4 shows that at total flow rates ≥4.98 mL min⁻¹ the byproduct 3a is ≤0.1 % whereas it is 10.2 % under standard batch conditions (Table 4).

Paper Title: Investigation into an Unexpected Impurity: A Practical Approach to Process Development for the Addition of Grignard Reagents to Aldehydes Using Continuous Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Scale‑up of the batch addition requires a much longer addition time for MeMgBr (up to 90 min for a 300 kg charge) to keep the internal temperature within 25 ± 5 °C. The large exotherm (184 kJ mol⁻¹) makes a slow addition necessary, but the prolonged residence of reactants leads to increased impurity formation and limits throughput.
Solution_Description: In batch, the addition time of MeMgBr is reduced to 10 s (ultrafast addition) which minimizes the coexistence window and limits heat release, thereby decreasing the impurity level from >20 % to 4.4 % at ambient temperature.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “When the addition time of MeMgBr was extended to 60 min, 3a increased to 21.5 %, whereas ultrafast addition of 10 s minimized 3a to 4.4 % at room temperature (entries 3–5, Table 1).” 2. “Calorimetry analysis…total heat of reaction was 184 kJ mol⁻¹…addition time of MeMgBr was estimated by simulations for a variety of manufacturing scales…30 min for 10 kg…90 min for 300 kg.” (Results) 3. Table 3 lists required addition times for different charge amounts, illustrating the impracticality of long additions.

Paper Title: Investigation into an Unexpected Impurity: A Practical Approach to Process Development for the Addition of Grignard Reagents to Aldehydes Using Continuous Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: Suppressing the impurity by operating under cryogenic temperatures (< ‑60 °C) is effective but impractical because cryogenic cooling equipment is scarce on production lines and the associated energy consumption is high.
Solution_Description: Instead of cryogenic operation, the process is run at ambient temperature using continuous flow, which provides precise temperature control through efficient heat exchange. This eliminates the need for expensive cooling infrastructure while still achieving < 0.5 % impurity.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Although the byproduct could be reduced under cryogenic conditions…the equipment for cooling to cryogenic conditions is very limited…avoiding such conditions would help conserve energy costs.” (Results) 2. “The trimerized byproduct 3a was drastically suppressed to 0.1 % at room temperature by the introduction of continuous flow synthesis compared with 10.2 % under the standard conditions in batch reactors.” (Results) 3. “The fast mixing…short coexistence time…effective for suppressing the byproduct 3a as expected.” (Results)

Paper Title: Investigation into an Unexpected Impurity: A Practical Approach to Process Development for the Addition of Grignard Reagents to Aldehydes Using Continuous Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: In batch reactors the addition of MeMgBr to 1a proceeds slowly, leading to a viscous mixture where the aldehyde and the Mg‑alkoxide of the product remain together for an extended period, favoring side‑reactions that generate the trimeric impurity.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: High total flow rates (≥4.98 mL min⁻¹) in the continuous‑flow micromixer ensure rapid homogenization and a short residence time (≤2 s), which prevents the formation of the Mg‑salt of the product and eliminates the side‑reaction pathway.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “The flow rate has an impact on mixing efficiency, and a low flow rate leads to low conversion in spite of a long residence time.” (Results) 2. Table 4 shows that at 4.98 mL min⁻¹ the conversion to 2a is >90 % and 3a is 0.1 % whereas at 1.66 mL min⁻¹ conversion drops to 20.7 % (entry 1). 3. “When the total flow rate was higher than 4.98 mL min⁻¹, conversion to the target product 2a could be almost completed within a few seconds.” (Results)

Paper Title: Investigation into an Unexpected Impurity: A Practical Approach to Process Development for the Addition of Grignard Reagents to Aldehydes Using Continuous Flow Synthesis
Problem_Description: For substrates bearing strong electron‑withdrawing groups (4‑cyanobenzaldehyde, 4‑nitrobenzaldehyde) precipitation occurs in batch reactions, hindering progress and making isolation of the product difficult.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: The continuous‑flow setup, with its high surface‑to‑volume ratio and rapid mixing, mitigates precipitation by maintaining a homogeneous phase, allowing the reaction to proceed without solid formation and simplifying downstream work‑up.
Supporting_Evidence: 1. “Precipitation was observed in batch procedures (entries 3 and 4, Table 7) … for which the flow procedure could not be evaluated.” (Results) 2. “The fast mixing by the application of continuous flow synthesis…effective for suppressing the byproduct 3a as expected.” (Results) 3. “The inner diameter and internal volume of the tube reactor were fixed, and various flow rates were examined…conversion to the target product 2a could be almost completed within a few seconds when the total flow rate was higher than 4.98 mL min⁻¹.” (Results)

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: Transfer‑hydrogenation with a series of Ru‑Noyori type catalysts gave only partial conversion even at a low substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio (S/C = 15); full conversion was never observed, making a low‑cost process infeasible.
Solution_Description: Switched from transfer‑hydrogenation to direct catalytic asymmetric hydrogenation under H₂ pressure using Ir‑based catalysts, which allowed higher conversion and scalability.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although in all cases the reactions were performed at a low substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio (S/C = 15), we never observed full conversion indicating that it would be difficult to develop a low‑cost process based on this technology.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: The first Ir‑catalyst screen (96 experiments) delivered a maximum enantiomeric excess of only 75 % and the effect of the iodine additive was highly unpredictable, giving mixed activity and ee across ligands and solvents.
Solution_Description: Performed a focused, 96‑well ligand‑only screening in a single solvent (DCM) testing each catalyst both with and without iodine, which enabled identification of the most promising ligand classes (WalPhos, UBAPhox, POX).
Supporting_Evidence: “the highest ee (75%) was obtained with a POX ligand… At this stage, we were mostly concerned by the rather modest enantiomeric excesses obtained thus far.”; “Only one solvent (DCM) was used… we tested again all catalysts with and without this additive.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: When the substrate‑to‑catalyst ratio was increased to 1000, conversion remained acceptable but the enantiomeric excess collapsed to near‑racemic values (3 % ee), indicating product inhibition/deactivation of the Ir‑ligand complex by the basic amine product.
Solution_Description: Added stoichiometric amounts of acetic anhydride (or later Boc₂O) to acylate the amine in‑situ, preventing catalyst deactivation and restoring high ee (≈94 %); Boc₂O also appears to interact with the Ir centre to generate a more robust catalytic species.
Supporting_Evidence: “with acetic anhydride, the acetylated product 2‑PG was obtained quantitatively at room temperature and with 94 % ee.”; “Boc anhydride probably reacts with the Ir centre to generate a more robust and/or active catalyst.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: Even after optimisation, achieving high turnover required relatively high Ir‑catalyst loadings (≥ 0.5 mol %); lowering the loading without additive led to loss of activity.
Solution_Description: Reduced Ir loading to 0.1 mol % while keeping 1.5 equiv. of Boc₂O; the additive maintained conversion and ee, thereby cutting catalyst cost dramatically.
Supporting_Evidence: “lowering of the catalyst loading to 0.1 mol % gave rewarding results… only about 50 % of the product was bocylated in all cases.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: Isolation of the hydrogenated product from the THF reaction mixture required a work‑up that preserved ee; simple concentration gave only moderate purity.
Solution_Description: Concentrated the crude mixture three‑fold and performed a slow addition of i‑PrOH at 23–27 °C, causing the product to crystallize directly; the crystals afforded >99 % ee after filtration and drying.
Supporting_Evidence: “After concentrating the reaction mixture (3‑fold), slow addition of i‑PrOH allowed the crystallization of the desired product 2 with a significant upgrade in enantiomeric excess.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: The presence of iodine dramatically altered activity and selectivity for many ligands (e.g., WalPhos‑003 gave high ee without iodine but near‑racemic product with iodine), making reproducibility difficult.
Solution_Description: Selected WalPhos‑003 as the lead ligand and omitted iodine from the optimized protocol, eliminating the source of variability.
Supporting_Evidence: “WalPhos‑003 gave full conversion and the highest ee… in the absence of iodine. In the presence of iodine… this same ligand gave a nearly racemic product.”

Paper Title: Enantioselective Synthesis of a 2,3-Benzodiazepine Intermediate of BET Inhibitor BAY 1238097 via Catalytic Asymmetric Hydrogenation
Problem_Description: For the pilot‑scale batch, the required catalyst loading (1.5 mol %) was higher than ideal, but rapid delivery of material was prioritized over cost.
Solution_Description: Accepted the higher Ir loading to meet the required production timeline, deferring cost optimisation to later stages.
Supporting_Evidence: “At this stage of clinical product development, speed of delivery … was more important than catalyst cost. Therefore, it was decided to accept a catalyst loading of 1.5 mol % while omitting addition of (Boc)₂O.”

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: The final chiral resolution of the racemic mixture by preparative HPLC was inherently inefficient, leading to low overall yield and high cost for the drug substance.
Solution_Description: An enantio‑selective reduction of the trifluoromethyl aryl ketone was introduced using Noyori asymmetric hydrogenation (Ru‑Xyl‑Phos/(R)‑DAIPEN catalyst), providing the chiral alcohol in high ee and eliminating the need for resolution.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "First, chiral resolution at the final stage by preparative HPLC or other means was inherently inefficient" (Introduction).
- "chiral resolution … was inefficient" (Introduction).
Solution:
- "Noyori asymmetric hydrogenation … is one of the most frequently used methods" (Introduction).
- "Noyori asymmetric hydrogenation in IPA using the (R)-Xyl‑P‑Phos RuCl₂/(R)-DAIPEN catalyst … afforded chiral alcohol 2 in 86% ee" (Section 2.1.3).
- "The reaction conditions were further optimized and implemented on a hundred‑kilogram scale, delivering chiral alcohol 2 in ∼56% yield with >99% ee" (Section 2.1.3).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: Sodium hydride (NaH), used for the S<sub>N</sub>Ar substitution, is hazardous and not suitable for large‑scale manufacturing.
Solution_Description: NaH was replaced with safer organic bases (triethylamine or N‑methylmorpholine) for the triflate formation step, and later with carbonate bases for the S<sub>N</sub>Ar reaction, eliminating the safety risk.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "NaH must be replaced with a process‑friendly base for the S_NAr substitution" (Introduction).
- "NaH is a hazardous reagent … not suitable for scale‑up" (implicit from safety concerns).
Solution:
- "Attempts to replace pyridine … with K₂CO₃ were unsuccessful … the reaction proceeded cleanly and rapidly with either triethylamine or N‑methylmorpholine (NMM) as the base" (Section 2.1.1).
- "NMM was selected for easier removal of colored materials by aqueous citric acid washes" (Section 2.1.1).
- "Strong bases such as sodium t‑butoxide … gave complex reaction mixtures … Thus, Cs₂CO₃ was used as the preferred base for the S_NAr step" (Section 2.1.4).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: The commercially sourced L‑BPA (compound 6) was extremely expensive (~$10 000 / 100 g) and not available in kilogram quantities needed for process development.
Solution_Description: A scalable synthesis of an L‑BPA surrogate (compound 9) was developed via palladium‑catalyzed borylation of a Boc‑protected L‑tyrosine triflate, eliminating the cost and supply limitation.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "<l>-BPA (6) was costly at the time ($10,000/100 g) and not readily available in kilogram quantities" (Introduction).
Solution:
- "An <l>-BPA surrogate, compound 9 was synthesized via borylation of the aryl triflate prepared from commercially available N‑Boc‑tyrosine methyl ester" (Introduction, Section 2.1.1).
- Detailed synthetic steps for compound 9 are given in the Experimental Section (Sec 4.2.4).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: Microwave heating (150 °C) required for the Suzuki‑coupling of pyrimidine chloride 5 and L‑BPA 6 was not amenable to scale‑up, leading to impractically long batch times.
Solution_Description: A right‑to‑left synthetic approach was adopted, coupling a more reactive aryl chloride (DCAP) with the boronate 9, which proceeds under conventional heating without microwave assistance.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "the microwave heating (150 °C) used for the Suzuki‑coupling … was not amenable to scale‑up" (Introduction).
Solution:
- "an alternative synthetic approach (right‑to‑left) involving Suzuki‑coupling with a more active substrate, DCAP (4), was explored" (Introduction, Scheme 2).
- The successful scale‑up of the right‑to‑left route is described in Sections 2.1.2 and 2.2.2.

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: Isolation of pyrimidine chloride 10 after the Suzuki‑coupling gave a sticky, gel‑like mass at pH 5.5–6.0, blocking stirring and resulting in low purity (≈76 %) and high residual palladium (>1000 ppm).
Solution_Description: The crude aqueous solution was slowly added into a citrate buffer held at pH 4, generating a free‑flowing suspension. Addition of (n‑Bu)₃P during the EtOAc wash improved palladium removal.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "… sticky mass at pH 5.5–6.0 which blocked the stirring… purity of the isolated 10 was only 76 % and the residual palladium level was >1000 ppm" (Section 2.1.2).
Solution:
- "… remedied by slowly adding the crude aqueous solution into a citrate buffer maintained at pH 4 … free‑flowing suspension" (Section 2.1.2).
- "… improved residual palladium control was achieved by adding (n‑Bu)₃P in the EtOAc wash" (Section 2.1.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: The Suzuki‑coupling of boronate 9 with DCAP produced significant amounts of bis‑coupling (14), amination (15), and solvolysis (16) impurities; impurity levels varied with DCAP stoichiometry, reaction time, and catalyst choice, reducing overall yield and consistency.
Solution_Description: DCAP equiv was increased from 1.2 to 1.8 to suppress bis‑coupling (14) to ~6 %. Catalyst screening (POPd6, Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃) was performed to minimize amination impurity (15) to <1 % while maintaining acceptable diacid levels.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "with 1.2 equiv of DCAP, bis‑coupling product 14 was about 20 %… The formation of this impurity was suppressed to ∼6 % by increasing DCAP to 1.8 equiv… amination impurity 15 increased to 4 %…" (Section 2.1.2, Fig 2, Table 1).
- "Impurities … generated at significant levels" (Section 2.1.2).
Solution:
- "Suppressed to ∼6 % by increasing DCAP to 1.8 equiv" (Section 2.1.2).
- "POPd6 … controlling 15 to 0.5–1 %" (Section 2.1.2).
- "Pd(OAc)₂/PPh₃ gave the most promising results… selected for further optimization" (Table 2).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: The S_NAr coupling of biaryl alcohol 3 with pyrimidine chloride 10 required strong bases; organic bases were ineffective, strong bases caused Boc deprotection, and the reaction was sluggish (15–24 h) with severe gelling of cesium salts below 70 °C, damaging agitators.
Solution_Description: Cesium carbonate (Cs₂CO₃) in dioxane at 90–100 °C was identified as the optimal base/solvent system. Addition of 18‑crown‑6 or Bu₄NHSO₄ (10 mol %) accelerated the reaction. Milled Cs₂CO₃ performed better than granular material, and the mixture was promptly cooled/quenced at the end of the reaction to avoid impurity buildup.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "Organic bases such as DBU and TMG were ineffective… Strong bases such as sodium t‑butoxide … gave complex reaction mixtures… The reaction was rather slow (15 h) even with 5 equiv of Cs₂CO₃… severe gelling of the cesium salts … could immobilize the reaction mixture" (Section 2.1.4, Table 5).
Solution:
- "The most promising result was obtained with Cs₂CO₃ in dioxane at 90–100 °C" (Section 2.1.4).
- "Adding 20 mol % 18‑crown‑6 seemed to accelerate the reaction… Inexpensive phase‑transfer agent Bu₄NHSO₄ (10 mol %) also seemed to accelerate the reaction…" (Section 2.1.4).
- "Milled Cs₂CO₃ performed substantially better than granular material" (Section 2.1.4).
- "Impurities continued to increase with age time mandating prompt quenching of the reaction" (Section 2.1.4).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: LX1031, a zwitterionic molecule with surfactant‑like behavior, formed gels when neutralized at its isoelectric point (pH 6.5); filtration, washing, and drying were extremely slow, leading to low overall yields (≈27 %).
Solution_Description: A controlled precipitation into a sodium phosphate buffer (pH 6.5) produced a manageable suspension. Crystallization of LX1031 as its dihydrochloride or tosylate salt (including dihydrate forms) allowed robust purity upgrades. Use of diatomaceous earth and EDTA improved filtration and removed trace metal contaminants.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "Isolation of LX1031 … behaved like a surfactant. Attempted isolation by neutralization to its isoelectric point (pH 6.5) gave a gel that was difficult to filter and dry" (Section 2.1.5).
- "Filtration/wash … was slow (23 h); drying … 4.5 days… overall yield 27.3 %" (Section 2.1.5).
Solution:
- "A manageable suspension … was obtained by slowly adding the solution of LX1031 in aqueous HCl into a sodium phosphate buffer maintained at pH 6.5" (Section 2.1.5).
- "Initial salt screening suggested that crystallization of LX1031 dihydrochloride could provide significant purity upgrade" (Section 2.1.5).
- "Salt screening showed that the tosylate salt was promising … dihydrate selected for development… 99.5 % purity, 82.3 % yield" (Section 2.1.6).
- "Switching to a pad of diatomaceous earth led to significant breakthrough of activated carbon… adding chelating agent EDTA … kept nickel in the mother liquor (3 ppm)" (Section 2.1.5).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: Residual palladium levels in the final product varied between batches (100–1000 ppm), and higher palladium correlated with slower reaction rates and darker reaction mixtures, affecting consistency.
Solution_Description: Extending the post‑reaction aging time by 3–5 h allowed palladium to precipitate as palladium black, consistently reducing residual palladium to <100 ppm.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "Residual Pd levels in most batches were higher (>100 ppm)…" (Section 2.2.2).
- "Retrospective data analysis revealed an inverse correlation between residual palladium and reaction rates…" (Section 2.2.2).
Solution:
- "By extending the aging time by additional 3–5 h after reaction completion, residual palladium levels were consistently below 100 ppm" (Section 2.2.2).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: High‑boiling solvents such as DME and dioxane were initially used for the Suzuki‑coupling but posed safety and environmental concerns for large‑scale production.
Solution_Description: The solvent system was switched to THF/EtOH (7:3) mixtures, which controlled diacid and amination impurities while offering safer handling and lower toxicity.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
- "DME and dioxane are not desirable solvents because of safety and environmental concerns" (Section 2.1.2).
Solution:
- "The reaction performed better in THF/EtOH mixtures than EtOH alone, controlling the diacid 14 and amination impurity 15 to <4 and <2.5 % respectively (entry 9, 10)" (Section 2.1.2, Table 3).

Paper Title: Process Development of Tryptophan Hydroxylase Inhibitor LX1031, a Drug Candidate for the Treatment of Irritable Bowel Syndrome
Problem_Description: Cesium salts of the starting material 10 and product 17 gelled below 70 °C, immobilizing the reaction mixture and risking damage to the agitator.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Starting material 10 was charged into a hot suspension of Cs₂CO₃ and the alcohol 3, allowing the reaction to proceed at 80–90 °C before cooling; this prevented gel formation and ensured smooth stirring.
Supporting_Evidence:
Problem:
