Problem_Description: Moisture in the generated SO₂ gas would react with organometallic reagents, leading to decomposition of the reagents and loss of yield.
Solution_Description: The SO₂ stream was passed through a concentrated H₂SO₄ trap followed by an anhydrous CaCl₂ cartridge to remove water before it entered the organometallic reaction.
Supporting_Evidence: “To ensure that SO₂ gas did not contain water that would consume the organometallic reagent, the gas produced was passed through a concentrated sulfuric acid trap and further through an anhydrous CaCl₂ cartridge (Figure 2).”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Sulfonamides Utilizing SO
Problem_Description: Aniline substrates gave only moderate sulfonamide yields and side‑product chloro‑anilines formed because anilines are poorly soluble and nucleophilic under the basic bleach conditions.
Solution_Description: Added CH₃CN as a co‑solvent to improve aniline solubility and pre‑formed N‑chloroaniline (via N‑chlorosuccinimide or succinimide) to suppress undesired chlorination; using 10 mol % succinimide further increased the yield to >80 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “It was postulated that the main cause of lower yields with anilines could be their reduced nucleophilicity and poor solubility in the aqueous media … the addition of a cosolvent (CH₃CN) would improve the solubility of anilines.”; “Indeed, the reaction carried out with preformed N‑chloroaniline … increased the yield to 74 % (entry 2). … the amount of succinimide could be reduced to as low as 10 mol % yet increased the yield to >80 % (entry 5).”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Sulfonamides Utilizing SO
Problem_Description: The original one‑pot sulfonamide protocol required 16 h reaction time, which limited throughput.
Solution_Description: Optimized conditions (10 equiv AcOH, 1.3–1.5 equiv amine) gave 83 % yield in only 3 h, greatly reducing the reaction time while maintaining conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “Although the reported result (entry 1) was well reproduced … efforts to either reduce the amine equivalents or shorten the reaction time resulted in drastically decreased yields … When acetic acid (10 equiv) was added … the yield of sulfonamide dramatically increased to 83 % in only 3 h (entry 4).”

Paper Title: Efficient and Practical Synthesis of Sulfonamides Utilizing SO
Problem_Description: Scaling the on‑demand SO₂ generation required a reactor capable of handling higher flow rates without excessive pressure buildup.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: Implemented a temperature‑controlled inline mixer (e.g., jacketed static mixer) with a continuous liquid‑gas separator, allowing continuous gas release and waste discharge for larger‑scale operations.
Supporting_Evidence: “Larger‑scale SO₂ gas generation could be realized using a temperature‑controlled inline mixer (e.g., jacketed static mixer) with a continuous liquid–gas separator … The system can be configured … to allow continuous gas release and waste aqueous stream discharge.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: The original Grignard synthesis of intermediate 4 gave a low isolated yield (68 %), required expensive bromocyclopentane (> US$14 000 ton⁻¹) in excess (> 1.5 equiv), and demanded strictly anhydrous/anaerobic conditions that impose intensive safety and equipment controls.
Solution_Description: The authors replaced the Grignard step with a Nenitzescu reductive acylation using cheap o‑chlorobenzoyl chloride and cyclopentene in the presence of AlCl₃, providing a milder, higher‑yielding process.
Supporting_Evidence: “the yield of the Grignard reaction was not high (68%).”; “the relatively high price of bromocyclopentane (14,300 U.S. dollars per ton in China) and large dosage (> 1.5 equiv) … increase the cost.”; “anhydrous and anaerobic conditions are always required for the Grignard reaction, which necessitate rigorous equipment and operation controls.”; “the cheaper o‑chlorobenzoyl chloride and cyclopentene were used to replace the Grignard reagent as raw materials to prepare 4 via the Nenitzescu reductive acylation reaction.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: The bromination of intermediate 4 traditionally used N‑bromobutanimide, Br₂ or CuBr₂, which have poor atom‑economy, generate hazardous waste streams and are expensive.
Solution_Description: A bromination system based on 48 % HBr combined with 30 % H₂O₂ was chosen; it gives 100 % Br utilization, low cost, produces only water as waste and avoids the hazards of the former reagents.
Supporting_Evidence: “The bromination step was typically poor atom economy with the use of N‑bromobutanimide (NBS), bromine (Br₂), or copper bromide (CuBr₂).”; “After comprehensive comparison, we finally chose hydrogen bromide (HBr) in combination with hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) as the bromination reagent with high atom economy, less environmental pollution, and low cost for the bromination reaction.”; Table 2 showing low cost, low hazard factor and 95 %–99 % conversion for HBr/H₂O₂.

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: Impurity 19 (≈ 21 %) formed from a side reaction between cyclopentene and cyclohexene generated during the reductive acylation, reducing the desired product yield.
Solution_Description: Cyclohexane was replaced by cyclopentane to suppress the competing pathway, and dichloromethane was employed as solvent to improve AlCl₃ solubility and reduce impurity formation.
Supporting_Evidence: “a larger impurity 19 was detected at approximately 21.2 % … generated as a result of the competitive reaction between cyclopentene and the byproduct cyclohexene produced from the dehydrogenation of cyclohexane.”; “Therefore, the cyclopentane was a good substitute for cyclohexane to avoid the generation of impurity 19. Moreover, dichloromethane was used to replace cyclopentane as the solvent to improve the reaction and reduce the amount of AlCl₃ due to the better solubility for AlCl₃.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: During the Nenitzescu reductive acylation, impurities 20 and 22 increased sharply when the reaction was prolonged beyond 3 h, leading to lower purity.
Solution_Description: The reaction time was strictly limited to 3 h, and the equivalence ratio of cyclopentene was optimized (1 : 1.1) to keep the formation of these impurities below the required limits.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction time was strictly controlled to 3 h because of the tendency of impurities 20 and 22 to increase gradually with the reaction time prolonging (Table 1, entry 4).”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: The original methylamination using liquid methylamine at –40 °C gave a high level (≈ 30 %) of impurity 27 and required handling of hazardous, cryogenic liquid methylamine.
Solution_Description: A 15 % aqueous methylamine solution (commercially available, safer) was used; the reaction was performed at 15–20 °C (room temperature) without added organic solvent, and the concentration of methylamine was adjusted to minimise side‑reactions, resulting in impurity 27 < 3 % and > 90 % conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “More abundant impurities … were detected at a level of approximately 30 % on LC/MS.”; “Considering that 40 % methylamine is more convenient to store and commercially available, liquid methylamine was replaced, and the experimental results are listed in Table 4.”; “Initially, the α‑bromo ketone 5 reacted with 15 % methylamine aqueous solution in THF at –20 °C for 24 h … conversion was less than 40 %.”; “the optimum reaction conditions for the preparation of α‑hydroxyimine 6 were determined as follows: 15 % methylamine aqueous solution reacted with 5 at 15–20 °C for 48 h without a solvent.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: Using dichloromethane as solvent for the methylamination created an oil–water two‑phase system, leading to high concentration of methylamine in the organic phase and a large amount of impurity 27.
Solution_Description: The reaction was performed under solvent‑free conditions (or in THF), and the methylamine aqueous concentration was reduced (15 % → 5 % → 15 % minimal) while keeping the temperature at 15 °C, which suppressed impurity formation to < 3 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “the reaction mixture becomes oil–water two‑phase, and methylamine will react with 5 in the same phase… the impurity 27 was mainly affected by the concentration of methylamine interacting with 5.”; “Therefore, we reduced the concentration of methylamine aqueous solution, and the results showed that the amounts of 27 decreased with the decrease in the concentration of methylamine (Table 5, entries 1–3).”; “When the temperature reduced to 15 °C, 27 dropped to approximately 3.8 % on HPLC (Table 5, entry 4).”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: Thermal rearrangement of α‑hydroxyimine 6 at 170–180 °C caused carbonization (black‑gray precipitate) and generated a large amount (≈ 25 %) of hydrolytic impurity 25 due to trace moisture, lowering yield to 70 %.
Solution_Description: The temperature was lowered to 140 °C (and later to 125 °C) and AlCl₃ (0.1–1.5 equiv) was added to catalyse the rearrangement while simultaneously absorbing moisture, reducing impurity 25 to ≤ 2 % and achieving > 95 % conversion in 5–6 h.
Supporting_Evidence: “the thermal rearrangement … at 170–180 °C … resulted in a black‑gray precipitate … hydrolytic impurity 25 … approximately 25 % on HPLC, resulting in a low yield of rearrangement (70 %).”; “When the temperature reduced to 140 °C, the rearrangement was conducted smoothly … the hydrolytic impurity 25 did not decrease.”; “AlCl₃ was selected … to catalyze the thermal rearrangement and absorb the trace moisture … the content of 25 was reduced to 2.1 % … the reaction time was shortened to 2 h.”; “the thermal rearrangement still could be successfully completed in 5 h at 125 °C.”

Paper Title: Process Research and Impurity Control Strategy of Esketamine
Problem_Description: Racemization of the undesired (R)-ketamine initially required 20 mol % AlCl₃, which is costly, and the reaction needed 24 h at 150 °C to achieve full racemisation.
Solution_Description: AlCl₃ loading was reduced to 10 mol % while extending the reaction time to 24 h at 150 °C, delivering quantitative racemisation with a much lower catalyst consumption; temperature was shown to affect rate, allowing further tuning.
Supporting_Evidence: “AlCl₃ (20 mol %) was required for the racemization …”; “when the time was extended to 24 h, a racemic mixture … was obtained.”; “To our delight, when the time was extended to 24 h, a racemic mixture … was obtained. However, when the reaction temperature was dropped to 130 °C … the racemization rate was much slower.”; Table 7 showing entry 2 (10 mol % AlCl₃, 150 °C, 24 h, 49.5/50.5 %).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Earlier literature routes to 6‑chloro‑5‑methylpyridin‑2‑amine relied on peroxide for oxidation and phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) for chlorination, which pose serious safety and environmental hazards on a manufacturing scale.
Solution_Description: A completely new four‑step synthetic route was devised that starts from commercially available 2‑amino‑6‑chloropyridine, eliminating the need for peroxide and POCl₃. This route therefore avoids the hazardous reagents and improves overall process safety.
Supporting_Evidence: “the use of peroxide and phosphorus oxychloride was averted” (Conclusion); “excessively used peroxide and phosphorus oxychloride may not be suitable for industrial production” (Introduction).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Initial bromination of N‑acetyl‑2‑amino‑6‑chloropyridine (compound 14) gave low conversion of the brominated product and required a large excess of N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS, 2.0 equiv) to obtain only 68 % overall yield for the two‑step sequence to compound 16.
Solution_Description: The order of operations was swapped: direct bromination of the free amine (13) was performed first with 1.0 equiv NBS at 0–5 °C, followed by acetylation. This change raised the bromination yield to 89 % and improved the overall two‑step yield to 82.8 %.
Supporting_Evidence: “low conversion of 14 and excessive consumption of NBS… providing 16 in a two‑step yield of 68.1 %” (Results); “Compound 13 was amenable to be directly brominated with equimolar NBS… affording 15 in 89 % yield… produced 16 in an improved two‑step yield of 82.8 %” (Results).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Three methyl‑boron reagents were screened; the more expensive potassium methyltrifluoroborate and the pinacol ester gave similar conversions but higher impurity levels, while the cheaper methylboronic acid gave slightly better performance.
Solution_Description: Methylboronic acid was selected as the methylating agent because of its lower cost, ready commercial availability, and marginally higher product purity (90.2 % 17, 8.5 % 2). This choice reduced material costs without compromising conversion.
Supporting_Evidence: “All of them achieved complete conversion… nearly 10 % of deacylated product 2 was detected… When the methylboronic acid was utilized… a slight increase of 17 along with a tiny decrease of 2 were detected. Moreover, in terms of cost and commercial availability, methylboronic acid displayed obvious merits” (Optimization of Methylation Reagents).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Using homogeneous solvents (toluene, 1,4‑dioxane, DME, EtOH) gave very low conversion (<14 %) and poor impurity profiles in the Suzuki‑Miyaura methylation step.
Solutions: [MASS TRANSFER, MIXING, AND GAS ENVIRONMENT CONTROL]
Solution_Description: A biphasic 1,2‑dimethoxyethane/H₂O (1:1) solvent system was adopted, which dramatically increased conversion to >99 % and yielded a product purity of 94.3 % 17 with minimal impurities, attributed to improved dissolution and phase contact of reagents and base.
Supporting_Evidence: “The conversion rates in biphasic systems… were generally much higher than that in homogeneous ones… an obvious improvement was observed using the 1,2‑dimethoxyethane/H₂O system… entry 8… conversion 99.9 % and 94.3 % 17” (Optimization of Solvents).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Strong bases (Cs₂CO₃, K₃PO₄, Na₂CO₃) generated higher levels of deacylated product 2 and other impurities, indicating base‑promoted decomposition of the acylated intermediate 16 or the product 17.
Solution_Description: Sodium bicarbonate, a weak base, was selected for the methylation step. It gave >99 % conversion while suppressing formation of impurity 2 to 1.1 % and maintaining low levels of other side‑products, providing a cleaner reaction profile.
Supporting_Evidence: “A high conversion rate of 16 was obtained in the presence of all four different bases… When sodium bicarbonate was used… the levels of the target product 17, impurity 2, and impurity 14 were acceptable” (Optimization of Bases).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: Various palladium catalysts and ligands gave incomplete conversion or higher impurity levels, limiting the efficiency of the key methylation step.
Solution_Description: Pd(OAc)₂ combined with the bidentate ligand DPEphos was identified as the optimal catalytic system, delivering 100 % conversion and 98.8 % 17 purity with all impurities below 0.6 %, thereby maximizing yield and minimizing side‑products.
Supporting_Evidence: “Pd(OAc)₂ displayed slight advantages… The level of 17 was able to achieve 98.8 % by utilizing the combination of Pd(OAc)₂ and DPEphos (entry 7)…” (Optimization of Catalysts and Ligands).

Paper Title: Improved Synthesis of 6‑Chloro-5-methylpyridin-2-amine: A Key Intermediate for Making Lumacaftor
Problem_Description: The original literature route required a linear four‑step sequence with low overall yield (1.3 %) and prolonged reaction times for each step, reducing throughput.
Solution_Description: By redesigning the sequence to start from a pre‑functionalized substrate and employing a Suzuki‑Miyaura methylation, the overall process was shortened to four steps with a 62.4 % overall yield, greatly improving productivity.
Supporting_Evidence: “Hadida Ruah et al. reported a four‑step linear synthesis… overall yield of 1.3 %” (Introduction); “Improved four‑step synthetic route… overall yield 62.4 %” (Conclusion).
